## Volume front matter

### Series title page

# Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library

of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have existed during the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, collated with one another and with a number of manuscript codices, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously illuminated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the extensive editions issued during the last three centuries had been completed; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; enlarged by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and by works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever any one of the Fathers has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it is immediately apparent to the reader which Fathers, and in which places in their works, commented on the individual texts of the individual books of Scripture.

An exceptionally accurate edition, easily to be preferred to all others if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, and the low price—and above all this collection, single, methodical, and chronological, of six hundred fragments and minor works hitherto scattered here and there, but gathered for the first time in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

## FIRST SERIES

In which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Complete Course in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning.

# In the year of the Lord 410. Rufinus, priest of Aquileia.

[Col. 0009C]

# Notice from Schoenemann

[Note: [Col. 0009] We have found it necessary to correct, and in some cases even to cut, several things in this Notice which Schoenemann seems to have expressed out of his hatred for the Catholic faith. EDITOR.]

(*Historical-literary Library of the Latin Fathers*)

## § 1. Life

[Col. 0009A]

His surname is usually written in very different ways: Toranus, Turranius, or Tyrannius. Blondellus gives his year of birth as 345. Fontaninus, whom we shall chiefly follow in sketching this doctor’s life, [Note: [Col. 0009B] Justus Fontaninus, archbishop of Ancyra, in his *Literary History of Aquileia*, which consists of five books and was published after the author’s death at Rome in 1742–1744, discussed Rufinus’s life, writings, and manuscript and printed codices with exceptional excellence and fullness. Nevertheless, many matters were examined more carefully and reported as established by Giovanni Francesco Bernardo Maria de Rubeis, distinguished for the reputation of his more exact scholarship, in the work entitled *Two Dissertations*, the first on Turranius or Tyrannius Rufinus, monk and priest, the second on ancient liturgical and other sacred rites; Venice, 1754. We compared the two works with one another, not without difficulty, and whatever Rubeis had explained more certainly or more plausibly, we either adopted immediately or did not fail to note.] dares to determine no year, although he assigns Concordia as his homeland; de Rubeis judges the arguments for this no more conclusive than those concerning the year of birth.

As a grown man he went to Aquileia, intending to enroll in the monastic way of life in a monastery whose beginnings owed their origin to the institutions of Athanasius. After spending some time there devoted to learning literature and the formulas of the Christian faith, he was baptized by the priest Chromatius, who perhaps then held the more distinguished position among the priests of the Church of Aquileia. The archdeacon Jovinus assisted, and the deacon Eusebius, who had previously instructed him in catechesis, acted as sponsor. [Col. 0009B] [Note: [Col. 0010B] Thus Rubeis, chapter 2, p. 8 ff., aptly interpreted Rufinus’s words in *Against Jerome* 1.4, in accordance with the rites of the Churches. He adds that it is uncertain why Bishop Valerianus was absent, but that there can be no doubt that after his baptism Rufinus was brought to him to be anointed with the sacred chrism. Fontaninus, by contrast, writes that he was baptized by Bishop Valerianus, with Chromatius, Jovinus, and Eusebius as his baptismal sponsors.]

During this period he formed a close friendship with Saint Jerome, who seems to have spent some time in the same monastery before his journey to Gaul and to have remained there after his return. Their friendship was nourished by contemplation of their mutual virtue, bound together by the most devoted affection. But before Rufinus received baptism, Jerome departed for the East, whose lands Rufinus also burned with desire to see. It therefore happened opportunely that Saint Melania, a noble Roman woman, had decided to travel to Jerusalem; Rufinus joined her as her companion in the very year in which he was baptized.

They left Rome in 371 and arrived at Alexandria in 372, while Athanasius was still alive. Rufinus then visited the monks of Egypt. Jerome, who was staying in Egypt, indicates that news of Rufinus reached him once and again in the desert. [Note: [Col. 0010B] Letter 1, alternatively 41; 2, alternatively 5.] When, after Athanasius’s death, the Arians, under Lucius, the usurper of the Alexandrian see, were raging against the orthodox in Alexandria and throughout the desert with unspeakable savagery and every kind of crime, the calamity of that raging storm struck Rufinus himself as well. [Note: [Col. 0010C] Rufinus, *Apology*, book II, chapter 3, where he describes that horrifying slaughter of the orthodox in bloody colors and says that he too shared in the sufferings of those who were oppressed.]

Finally, after spending six months in Egypt with Melania, he accompanied with her to Palestine the monk-confessors who had been condemned to exile. They settled near Diocaesarea.

Shortly afterward, in the year 373, after the fifth day before the Kalends of April, as Fontaninus prefers, [Col. 0011A] Melania set out for Jerusalem, while Rufinus returned to Alexandria. [Note: [Col. 0011D] De Rubeis assigns this either to the end, the beginning, or even the course of the year 373 or to the year 374. These matters evidently depend on the differing dates assigned for the year of Athanasius’s death. Fontaninus, in the passage cited and also in a separate dissertation appended to his *History of Aquileia*, dates Athanasius’s death to 11 May 372, defending Baronius’s view; Rubeis, on the other hand, after a new examination in chapters 4, 5, and 6 of the dissertation cited, argues that it should be assigned to the year 373.]

There he spent six years in the company and under the instruction of Didymus and the other teachers then flourishing at Alexandria, and he began to love Origen’s intellect, although he must not be thought to have embraced all of Origen’s teaching.

He returned to Jerusalem—if one follows Fontaninus’s calculation—in 377, for this was the sixth year running from his first arrival in Egypt. [Note: [Col. 0011D] Rubeis argues from the Guarnerian Codex that Rufinus lived in Egypt for eight years, with an interval in between. He calculates the matter in such a way as to conclude that Rufinus returned to Alexandria the first time in 375 and remained there until 380 or the beginning or middle of the following year. From there, he places a journey to Palestine either for business or to visit Melania, followed by a second return to Egypt, and finally a return to Jerusalem before the year 385, after spending several further years there.] He returned with the intention of thereafter devoting himself entirely to the monastic life, and he inhabited cells on the Mount of Olives, which were frequented by many other monks as well.

From Jerusalem he made excursions into various neighboring regions to visit distinguished men; perhaps he also traveled once more to Alexandria with Melania, who is known to have gone to Egypt at about the same time. Thereafter he spent several years with Melania in generously receiving people of every kind who came there for reasons of piety.

Meanwhile, although Jerome himself and his friends were joined by an old and lasting relationship and were held in suspense by their mutual desire to see one another as they drew closer together, a remarkable chain of circumstances and events repeatedly separated them—as though some hidden power, foreseeing that their meetings would break their union of minds, had promoted that union by the very division.

For when Rufinus first arrived in Palestine, Jerome was still living in the desert; but there Rufinus received letters written by Jerome in the middle of the summer of 373, witnesses to the old friendship they had once contracted at Aquileia. [Col. 0011C] While Rufinus was devoting himself to letters in Egypt, Jerome had remained for some time at Antioch, from which he had gone to Constantinople at precisely the time when Rufinus may perhaps, if one agrees with Rubeis, have returned to Palestine for a short period.

When Jerome finally returned in 385, after spending three full years at Rome, there is no doubt that he and Rufinus met at Jerusalem and renewed the memory of their former affection and services to one another—though this was destined now to last only a short time.

The first seeds of their disagreement were scattered by a certain Aterbius. When he arrived at Jerusalem, he attacked Rufinus as a follower of Origen’s opinions and, on the same charge, denounced Jerome as Rufinus’s friend and a praiser of Origen. Then for the first time Jerome became estranged from Rufinus. [Col. 0011D]

Soon afterward, in 394, both became involved in the dispute between Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis, and John of Jerusalem. For [Col. 0012A] Jerome not only joined Saint Epiphanius, the opponent of Origen and John, in order to make it evident to everyone that he rejected Origen’s heresies; through the monks of Bethlehem, too, he was drawn to Epiphanius’s side, since Epiphanius had founded one of the monasteries.

Rufinus, however, who had enjoyed an intimate association with John for nearly seven years and had undoubtedly been ordained priest by him, could not lightly be torn away from John. The two sides argued with hostile minds, each having a different reason for anger. Epiphanius pursued John as an Origenist; John insisted that Epiphanius had unjustly infringed his rights by ordaining Paulinianus, Jerome’s brother, as priest in his parish; and Jerome was irritated that the suspicion of Origen’s heresy, which had once arisen against him because of his intimacy with Rufinus, had not been entirely groundless. He was especially grieved that he had treated as a friend a man who had secretly devoted his mind to heresies.

Fuel was added to this indignation by a letter that Epiphanius wrote to John of Jerusalem concerning an ordination performed by him outside the proper place. For Jerome had translated it from Greek into Latin for the benefit of Eusebius of Cremona, who did not understand Greek, and for private use, since Eusebius was living in his monastery. But the letter, stolen and carried to Rufinus, gave him occasion, if not to accuse the translator of malice, at least to complain of his lack of truthfulness. [Col. 0012B]

Jerome endured this still more bitterly because, when Rufinus had been accused of heresy and doctrinal corruption, he had dared to answer nothing: he attacked the translator, quibbled over syllables, and thought that he had fully defended himself if he disparaged one who remained silent.

The way to reconciliation was blocked, since each demanded punishment from the other and feared deceit on the part of those who might reconcile them. Thus Theophilus of Alexandria and Archelaus, governor of Palestine, attempted peace between them in vain, and this resentment settled in their hearts for a period of three years. [Note: [Col. 0012D] De Rubeis, chapter 9, no. 6, p. 65.]

By whose agency that long-standing quarrel was finally extinguished is not clear. It is certain that Jerome and Rufinus were reconciled in the customary manner in the church of Jerusalem called Anastasis, after the celebration of Mass, and that Jerome acknowledged Rufinus as having been found guilty of no error.

Once peace had been restored, Rufinus became concerned with returning to the West. He departed in 397, in August or September. Jerome accompanied his departure after peace had been mutually given and received. [Note: [Col. 0012D] Many hold not only that Rufinus returned to Italy with Melania in this year, but also that Fontaninus does so, agreeing with Baronius and Pagius. Yet on the authority of more writers, among them Lebrunus in his *Life of Paulinus*, they assign Melania’s return to 402. De Rubeis clearly supports this view with new arguments, chapter 40, p. 70.]

Rufinus did not reach Rome immediately, but stopped at the monastery of the abbot Urseius, at a place called Pineta in the Roman territory. There many people curious about Eastern affairs and eager for books gathered around him. They questioned him, listened to his accounts, and finally begged him to translate Greek works into Latin for them.

Among them was the abbot Urseius himself. When Urseius asked him what the monks’ practice was in the East and what rules they observed, Rufinus replied that they followed Basil’s rules. Urseius then earnestly begged him to render the work into Latin, promising that this would win him great favor among Westerners, and Rufinus agreed.

Similarly, Macarius, a monk of that monastery, as Fontaninus thinks—or living at Rome, as Rubeis argues [Note: [Col. 0013D] Chapter 12, p. 84]—obtained from him Pamphilus’s *Apology for Origen*. Rufinus translated it at Rome, where he had gone toward the end of 397 or the beginning of 398, adding a short work of his own, *On the Corruption of Origen’s Books*, in defense of his faith.

When Macarius noticed that Origen’s books *On First Principles* (*Περὶ Ἀρχῶν*) were repeatedly praised in Pamphilus’s *Apology*, he again asked Rufinus to make them accessible to Roman ears. Even though Rufinus foresaw how much envy this compliance would bring upon him, he did not refuse to oblige him. He first published the two earlier books and, in the preface—whether in good faith or to avoid envy I shall not say—he appealed to Jerome’s authority because, in the preface to his two homilies of Origen on the *Song of Songs*, Jerome had spoken so magnificently of the author that he would have awakened in anyone a desire to read him, and because he had promised that he himself would later translate many of Origen’s works.

Meanwhile what Rufinus had feared came to pass. Enormous rumors arose throughout the city, and the agitation plainly turned into a whirlwind when the two later books were published. But something much worse happened to Rufinus: Pammachius and Oceanus had sent Jerome, without naming the author—as Jerome later claimed—Rufinus’s rough, unfinished notes, exactly as they had happened to fall from his hand. At the same time they asked him for a new translation of the books *On First Principles*.

At this same time Rufinus, having received news of his mother’s death, decided to travel to Aquileia. He reported this to Jerome and, having received letters from Pope Siricius, set out by the inland route through Milan. [Note: [Col. 0013D] According to Rubeis’s calculation, he arrived at Rome shortly before the death of Siricius, which, according to Baronius, occurred on 22 February 398, and according to Pagius on 26 November. He remained there for nearly a full year and reached Aquileia in August or September.]

At Aquileia he was especially refreshed by the companionship and goodwill of Bishop Chromatius. Whether Chromatius enrolled him in the Church of Aquileia, when Rufinus had been ordained priest by John of Jerusalem as a member of the monastic order, no one has established with certainty.

Meanwhile Jerome’s letters replying to the Rufinians had been intercepted by Pammachius and Oceanus. Other letters that Jerome had given them—in which he refuted Rufinus’s preface and declared himself alien to Origen’s doctrine—were circulating at Rome together with the new translation of the books *On First Principles*. They had been sent from Apronianus to Aquileia and moved Rufinus to prepare a reply, on which he labored from 399 to 401.

The passages Rufinus had written were sent to Jerome piecemeal by friends acting as informers; and, scarcely having completed the work and dedicated it to Apronianus, Rufinus shared it with friends who had been especially offended by Jerome’s words. Two books of Rufinus’s *Apology* against three volumes by Jerome—volumes not yet complete, but received only in summary—then appeared.

A copy of these works, carried to Aquileia by a traveling merchant and granted to Rufinus for only two days, forced him to produce a brief reply. [Note: [Col. 0014D] This letter is now lost. Jerome objected that it could not have been written in only two days.]

At the same time Rufinus sent Jerome the complete books of his *Apology* for him to read. They seem to have been returned in 402. Certainly in that same year, in March or April, Jerome published the third book of his *Apology*, although Chromatius had long before urged him to end in silence a controversy offensive to Christian minds.

Indeed, he sent this final *Apology* to Augustine as though to a witness of his moderation, believing that what he called Rufinus’s “slanders”—the name he gave to Rufinus’s *Apology*—had already reached Africa through Augustine’s efforts. Augustine replied:

> “I do not know what malicious writings concerning my name have reached Africa; but I have wasted away with grief and stiffened with fear when I read what that writing answered to those slanders. I should die of terror if what I have been told Rufinus cast at me with such unbridled passion should ever come into my hands.”

When, in 400, Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, summoned the bishops to eradicate the heresy, Anastasius also, and at his urging the bishops of Milan and Aquileia, condemned Origen’s doctrines. But Anastasius, to whom Rufinus had sent a brief *Apology for His Faith* because Rufinus himself could not travel to Rome, [Col. 0014C] found that Rufinus’s case was entirely different from Origen’s. He testified to this in a letter sent to John of Jerusalem. In it, after openly condemning Origen, he wrote that he would condemn Rufinus only if Rufinus had assented to what he had translated, a matter that Anastasius thought should be left to God’s judgment rather than human judgment.

Nevertheless, in the final letter he indicated that Rufinus was far removed from his communion. Jerome had interpreted this letter, together with another that has perished, in his own interest; consequently Rufinus refused to recognize either as genuine.

At last, when the sky had cleared again, Rufinus devoted himself entirely to writing books or translating them from Greek, and during the seven years that he still spent at Aquileia he completed a very large part of his writings.

He left Aquileia in 408 and withdrew once more to the monastery of Pineta. There he completed the second book *On the Blessings of the Patriarchs*, which he had promised Paulinus after sending him the first book from Aquileia, and then proceeded toward Rome.

When the barbarians were attacking Rome, he crossed over to Sicily in the same year with the fugitive group of Pinianus. There, in sight of Calabria, which Alaric had ravaged along with the other regions, he expended his remaining strength on several books of Origen—namely, the homilies on Numbers, which he dedicated to a certain Donatus, and those on the *Song of Songs*—for Pinianus’s benefit. Finally, he gave up his spirit in the embraces of his friends in the year 410.

## § 2. Writings

By far the largest part of Rufinus’s works consists of Latin translations of Greek books. The works he wrote himself are few. We shall provide a list of both kinds, arranged as Fontaninus, who treated them more accurately, compiled it.

## I. Genuine works

### 1. Original writings

Dissertation *On the Corruption of Origen’s Books*.

An exposition of the twelve blessings of the patriarchs.

An *Apology*, or two books of *Invectives against Jerome*.

An *Apology for His Faith to Pope Anastasius*.

Two books of *Ecclesiastical History*, namely books X and XI following Eusebius’s *History*.

*History of the Hermits*, or the *Lives of the Fathers*, commonly published under Jerome’s name.

An explanation of the Creed.

The translation of Origen’s homilies on Luke is not by Rufinus, to whom it is attributed, but by Jerome. [Col. 0016A]

The translation of Josephus’s works is not by Rufinus but by Ambrose.

Commentaries on the first seventy-five psalms of David.

Commentaries on Hosea, Joel, and Amos.

The *Life of Saint Eugenia*.

A fuller booklet *On Faith*.

One homily on John.

A work by the same author on Mary Magdalene.

## IV. Lost

A translation of several books from Latin into Greek.

## § 3. Editions

The fate of this excellent author and of his writings has been thoroughly unjust, especially since the art of printing became customary for multiplying and embellishing books. In that general competition to print books, chiefly those dealing with ecclesiastical subjects, which prevailed toward the end of the fifteenth century—and in which scarcely any distinguished author failed to receive his due honor—Rufinus alone remained excluded and without a gift.

To say nothing of collections, only one of which is known to have been produced at the end of the sixteenth century, and that one incomplete and interpolated with spurious books, no effort was devoted to even the individual booklets in that century or the following ones.

After Laurentius de la Barre published some of Rufinus’s minor works in 1580, publication ceased for more than a century and a half, until the celebrated editor of Jerome, Dominicus Vallarsius, undertook a new and complete edition. Its first volume appeared at Verona in 1745; the second is still lacking, so far as we know. [Note: [Col. 0015] Even today the Vallarsian edition lacks its second volume. EDITOR.]

His Latin translations of Greek writers met with less hostility. From almost the beginning they were highly valued among Westerners who did not know Greek, and in more recent times they have encountered greater goodwill among students of Christian wisdom.

Indeed, Fortune treated him with such insolence that his *History of the Hermits*, under Jerome’s own name, was printed more than twenty times within a century and translated into the idioms of several other languages.

Since matters stand thus, in listing the editions of Rufinus’s works we shall proceed first with those included in collections, whether they are his own writings or works wrongly attributed to him, whether printed separately or mixed with the works of other authors; then we shall report the editions of the *Ecclesiastical History*, the *History of the Hermits*, and the works he translated from Greek.

# Fifteenth century

[Col. 0017A]

## 1468. Oxford, quarto or octavo

B. Jerome’s *Exposition of the Apostles’ Creed to Pope Laurence*. Printed at Oxford and completed in the year of the Lord 1468, on 17 December.

A celebrated book because of its importance for the origins of printing in England; Maittaire discusses it at greater length in *Annals of Typography*, volume I, p. 279. Ames gives a specimen of its letters in *Typographical Antiquities*, p. 437.

Middleton, however, thought that there was a typographical error and that, with one X omitted, 1468 had been printed instead of 1478; he judged that nothing should thereby be taken away from the glory of Caxton, who is said to have been the first to practice the art of printing in England. See *The Substance of his Dissertation on the Origin of Printing in England*, in *Two Essays on the Origin of Printing*, second edition, London, 1776, octavo.

Although he found not a few supporters, [Col. 0017B] he also found opponents, among them the highly authoritative Meermann, in a letter to André Coltée Ducarel inserted in *Origins of Typography*, and subsequently in *Supplement to the Origin of Printing*, 1781, octavo, p. 236 ff.

## 1470. Rome, at the press of Sweynheym and Pannartz, folio

*Exposition of the Creed*, together with the first volume of Jerome’s letters.

Some writers, such as Cave, Ittigius, and others, also assign to this year an edition of Rufinus’s works said to have been produced at Rome. But this sort of edition is a mere fiction, and readers should beware of it.

Labbe was responsible for the claim, praising this edition as existing in the Royal Library of Paris in his *Supplement to the New Manuscript Library*, p. 340. Hence Maittaire, *Annals*, volume I, p. 298, and many others afterward copied the claim in good faith.

Yet in the catalogue of that library one finds no trace of it, [Col. 0017C] nor does it appear that it was ever seen by any other expert and inquisitive investigator of such matters.

One may easily conjecture that Labbe, misled by the preceding edition of the *Creed* together with Rufinus’s letters, assumed that there was an edition of Rufinus’s works because part of those works, however small, appeared at its beginning. Fontaninus is an adherent of this view. Perhaps an incompetently prepared catalogue deceived him.

## 1498. Oxford, octavo

B. Jerome’s *Exposition of the Apostles’ Creed*.

# Sixteenth century

## 1516. Venice, at the press of Lazarus Soardus, folio

Rufinus, *On the Blessings of the Patriarchs*, under the false title *Seventeen Homilies on Genesis*, together with Origen’s works on the New [Col. 0017D] Testament, folio 104.

The editor Constantius Hierotheus first published this work of Rufinus, but treated it as an offspring of Origen and handled it very badly.

## 1519. Basel, at the press of Froben, folio

The *Creed of Faith*, together with the works of Cyprian edited by Erasmus, who writes of it in a letter to Cardinal Laurentius Puccius:

> “The *Creed of Faith*, which in both printed and manuscript volumes bears the title of Cyprian, is attributed under Rufinus’s name among the works of Saint Jerome.”

In the notes following the letter he writes:

> “The style sufficiently proves that this work is not Cyprian’s, and among Jerome’s works it is inscribed to Rufinus. Its phrasing is not unlike Rufinus’s phrasing; and among his works Gennadius speaks magnificently of the *Creed*, saying that it was so excellently expounded that the others seem to have spoken only in reference to it.”

It was subsequently reprinted not only with all the Erasmian editions but also with nearly all the other editions of Cyprian, such as the Roman edition issued by Paulus Manutius in 1563, p. 381. Fontaninus praises that edition because it most admirably arranged the individual articles separately before the exposition and printed them in a different type. It was also reprinted in the editions of Pamelius, Oxford, and finally Baluze.

## 1555. Basel, at the press of Heinrich Petri, folio

Rufinus of Aquileia, *On the Blessings of Judah and the Remaining Patriarchs*, in Johann Herold’s *Orthodoxographs*, volume II, p. 1423.

Herold, unaware of Hierotheus’s edition, restored the book to its true author from a manuscript codex, which he describes in the following words, including several details that will seem worth reading and that Fontaninus also reports:

> “Georg Pistorius, a most distinguished man, an excellent physician at Ensisheim, and one who has rendered outstanding service to universal literature, had evidently acquired this little book for his library as a treasure, at the cost either of the utmost exertions of his intellect or of a mad expenditure of money. With the generosity toward good letters and toward his friends that was characteristic of him, he freely offered this little book also to Heinrich Petri, who was then publishing a library of sacred authors.
>
> “The book had been written in Roman capitals—indeed in letters such as those in which we have seen the Florentine Pandects written—without any divisions, more than a thousand years ago: truly a precious gem of venerable antiquity.
>
> “Time and the negligence of barbarians had grievously torn it apart. Since it treats, in a mystical interpretation, the blessing of Judah, three torn and lost leaves are missing; although a fourth survives, even an expert can scarcely guess where it should be restored.
>
> “The parchment was therefore so delicate that I would not dare affirm that I have ever seen more delicate parchment; and this brought all the more damage to the writing. The ink itself, through its corrosive quality, had caused several lines to be eaten away and rendered translucent, so that they could be read only from the traces, unless a line on the facing page corresponded to line on line; then the labor required on both sides was greater.
>
> “There was also this further problem: whether because the library in which the book was once kept had been moistened by rain, or because the book had been carried here and there for display as an ancient monument, it had become thoroughly wet at the margins, and the most delicate parchment, as though glued together, could be separated or opened only by tearing nearly every leaf.
>
> “Nevertheless, I wished to endure this burden so that the book, however it might be, could be transcribed by me as it had been offered. It does not reach its conclusion, although I suspect that only a little is missing.
>
> “I therefore urge all students to seek out in libraries, whenever an opportunity arises, whatever is lacking from this work, so that at last it may be offered complete and less defective to theologians.”

## 1569. Basel, at the press of Heinrich Petri, folio

Rufinus’s *Explanation of the Blessing of Judah and the Remaining Patriarchs*, in Johann Jacob Grynaeus’s *Monumenta Orthodoxa*, volume II, p. 1065; taken from Herold’s work, though Herold himself is not named.

## 1570. Lyons, at the press of Guillaume Rouillé, under the Venetian shield, folio

*Commentary of Rufinus, priest of Aquileia, on the Seventy-Five Psalms of David, now for the first time published from a very ancient copy of the library of the monastery on the island of Barbe near Lyons; with a most extensive index.*
The editor is Antonius Alboneus (de Albone), archbishop of Lyon and primate of Gaul. In the lengthy letter by which he dedicated the book to Pope Pius V (dated Lyon, 15 March 1570), he explains in the following manner how he came to obtain these commentaries:

“There is in the territory of Lyon an island which the inhabitants call Barbe, but learned men call Barbata, dividing the central channel of the Araris [Saône]. On it a very ancient and holy monastery had been built and was celebrated with great reverence throughout the whole province. Yet in the preceding war it was so disturbed and destroyed by the heretics that scarcely anything seems to remain there except the traces of a certain more sacred place.

“When, many years ago, I had undertaken to govern it, as is customary, by authority of the Apostolic See, I encountered there many memorials of ancient piety, but above all a rich library. When I had carefully examined it, I came upon the Commentaries of Rufinus, presbyter of Aquileia, on the seventy-five Psalms of David, written in letters and characters that displayed the highest antiquity, and preserved on parchments almost entirely eaten away and worn down by age and neglect. After I had eagerly read them through and had given them to other learned men to read, I judged that this treasure should not be buried again but exposed to the light and air.

“Nor, he continues, was he deterred from publishing this work by the fact that certain friends had observed that in very many, indeed almost innumerable, places it agrees with Augustine in his treatises on the Psalms, so that the interpretations are often the same, the words the same, and even the periods similar to one another. He considers that this happened in this work as it happened to Saint Ambrose in his books *Hexameron* and *On the Holy Spirit*: just as Ambrose transferred entire periods into his own work from Saint Basil, so Augustine, from Rufinus—or, elsewhere, from Jerome and Cyprian—derived very much for his own Commentaries. Moreover, from the very ease of the style and the even character of the expression, he thinks that Rufinus can be seen to be the author; and at the same time he finds a reason why these Commentaries were preserved so carefully by the monks of the Barbata islands from the beginning: namely, that Rufinus wrote almost exclusively on those Psalms which nearly all learned men had confidently asserted, without controversy, to be David’s.

“Finally, he brings forward the testimony of Gelasius, who reports that Rufinus expounded certain Scriptures; these, he thinks, refer to the explanation of these seventy-five Psalms. For some time, indeed, these Commentaries were regarded as the genuine offspring of Rufinus, but they could not deceive everyone. The first person to strip away their disguise, Fontaninus notes, was Jean Lorin; he quotes the relevant passage from the Commentaries on the Psalms published at Lyon by Jean Cardon in 1623 [Note: *Hist. litt. Aquil.*, p. 404]. He also observes that several exceptionally learned men have occasionally cited Rufinus on the Psalms as genuine, for example Jacques Usserius in his *History of the Scriptures and of Sacred Vernacular Languages*, p. 67, and Baluze in his edition of Cyprian.

“Nevertheless, Alboneus seems to have been convinced that this author had written Commentaries on more Psalms than these, since at the end of the book he appended a note urging readers to search out and publish any others that might exist.”

Labbe, in *New Bibliography of Manuscripts*, part I, p. 23, cites from the catalogue of the Library of Saint-Germain in Paris Rufinus of Aquileia’s Commentaries on the 76 Psalms, somewhat different from those published.

1576. Rome, at the Roman Printing House, folio. Rufinus’s *Exposition of the Creed*, together with the works of Saint Jerome, edited by Mariano Vittorio, volume IX, part 108.

1580. Paris, at the house of Michel Sonnius, folio. *Certain Short Works of Rufinus of Aquileia, presbyter, some never before published, others recently corrected and revised with the assistance of very learned men; with extensive indexes both of the passages of Sacred Scripture explained and of subjects and words.*

They contain:

1. Book I, *On the Blessings of Judah*, addressed to Paulinus, bishop of Nola;
2. Paulinus’s letter to Rufinus;
3. Rufinus’s letter to Paulinus, his brother;
4. Book II, Rufinus’s work on the blessings of the remaining eleven patriarchs, or Commentaries on Genesis, chapter 49;
5. Three books of Commentaries on the prophet Hosea;
6. Rufinus’s Commentary on the prophet Joel;
7. Rufinus’s Commentary on Amos;
8. Commentary on the Creed;
9. Two books of his *Ecclesiastical History*.

Of these, numbers 2, 3, 5, 6, and 7 are now published for the first time from a manuscript of the monastery of Mont-Dieu.

The editor, René Laurent de La Barre—already known to us from his editions of Tertullian and Arnobius, published at approximately the same time—discusses several matters concerning Rufinus and his extant and lost writings in his dedicatory letter to Jean de Saint-André, canon of the Church of Paris (dated 12 June 1580). In passing, he criticizes the studies of contemporary scholars who, having for the most part neglected the examination of manuscripts, referred everything to conjecture.

Fontaninus wrote that the Commentaries on the seventy-five Psalms, published by Alboneus ten years earlier, were reprinted in this year by the same Michel Sonnius under a changed title and constituted volume II of Rufinus’s works; we are not certain about this. Certainly, the earlier volume contains no indication of any added commentaries. The copy we have in our hands, however, was bound together with Alboneus’s 1570 edition of the Commentaries.

1745. Verona, [place of publication and printer omitted], folio. *The Surviving Works of Rufinus Toranius, presbyter of Aquileia*. Once again corrected against manuscript codices by Dominicus Vallarsius, presbyter of Verona, volume I.

The volume contains:

1. The *Book on the Blessings of the Patriarchs*, reviewed with the editor’s notes against a manuscript in the Library of Bologna;
2. The *Commentary on the Apostles’ Creed*, prepared according to Baluze’s edition;
3. The *History of the Monks* and the journeys through Egypt, reproduced from Rosweyde’s edition;
4. The two books of the *Ecclesiastical History*, compared with manuscript codices;
5. Two apologetic books against Jerome, followed by the *Apology to Anastasius*.

These are followed by an appendix containing doubtful and spurious works:

1. A Commentary on the first seventy-five Psalms, whose author Vallarsius argues must have been a Gaul and scarcely anyone other than Vincent, a Gallic presbyter, mentioned by Gennadius in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 80;
2. A Commentary on the three Minor Prophets—Hosea, Joel, and Amos—by some Spanish writer, perhaps Paul Orosius, as Vallarsius conjectures;
3. The *Life of Saint Eugenia, Virgin and Martyr*, taken from Rosweyde and accompanied by his notes;
4. A little book *On Faith*, formerly published under Rufinus’s name by Cardinal Sirmond from a Vatican codex and by Garnerius from a codex at Beauvais;
5. Rufinus, presbyter of the province of Palestine, *Book on Faith*, formerly published by Sirmond and now reprinted, with variant readings added from manuscript codices.

The *Life of Rufinus* composed by Fontaninus, corrected and revised by Vallarsius in several places, is omitted from all these materials.

This concerns volume I, the sole volume of this edition. Jean-Dominique Mansi, in his note on Fabricius [Note: *Bibl. M. et Inf. Lat.*, vol. VI, pp. 132 ff.], says so. We searched in vain for any mention of it, or at least its title, in learned journals and catalogues of distinguished libraries.

In the same place Mansi calls attention to a very ancient manuscript codex containing the two books of Rufinus’s *Ecclesiastical History*, which no one has yet collated. It is preserved in the cathedral library of Lucca and is believed to have been written in the time of Charlemagne. Mansi wrote a separate discussion of it elsewhere [Note: *In Opusculis P. Calogiera*, vol. XV, § 15].

Rufinus’s apologetic books against Jerome were also reprinted in various editions of the latter’s works; we do not wish to waste time listing these individually. They exist in French translation in the *Collection of Pieces Concerning the Life of Rufinus* (Paris, 1727, 12mo), a book already cited above in connection with Jerome.

## I. Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History*, translated by Rufinus and expanded by two books

The usefulness of a catalogue of editions of this work will, we trust, be greater because those editions are now less familiar through use and frequent reading. Ever since the translations of Musculus and Christophorson came into circulation, interest in Rufinus’s translation seems to have declined, and afterward, owing to the fame of Valesius, its use almost entirely ceased. Although Rufinus’s version cannot everywhere be called sufficiently faithful or complete, it nevertheless contains distinctive additions by Rufinus and is of no small importance for the textual criticism of the Greek text of Eusebius.

## Fifteenth century

1474. Without indication of place or printer, folio. *Eusebius’s Ecclesiastical History, translated by Rufinus from Greek into Latin.* Maittaire, volume I, p. 332, and, following him, Hamberger, volume III, p. 43. It was unknown to Fontaninus, who regards the following edition as the first [Note: *Hist. Aqui.*, literary history, book V, chapter 11, pp. 356 ff.].

1476. Rome, at the house of Johannes Philippus de Lignamine, folio. *The Book of Eusebius of Caesarea’s Ecclesiastical History, which Blessed Rufinus, presbyter, translated from Greek into Latin.*

This title is found not on the first page but after Lignamine’s dedicatory letter to Pope Sixtus. At the end: “In the year 1476, on 15 May, in the fifth year of Sixtus IV’s pontificate, this work was completed.”

Johannes Philippus, papal chief physician, dedicated it to Sixtus IV, whose interest in and patronage of literature and learned men he greatly praises in the prefixed letter. After mentioning many works printed and dedicated to Sixtus at his command, he says that he then turned to history and began with this translation of Rufinus.

In some copies, another letter, addressed instead to Cardinal Guillaume d’Estouteville, appears in place of this one. From this, Fontaninus concluded that the edition was immediately reprinted after the copies had been distributed, and he accordingly proposed two editions by the same printer. Audiffredi, on the other hand, does not deny that Lignamine may have intended to reprint the edition, but argues that the printer did not proceed beyond the first gathering of the volume and that the project was then abandoned. In any event, the second edition—whether it was entirely printed or merely begun—is extremely rare and elegant, though its type is somewhat heavier and its syllables are often contracted according to the custom of the period. Fontaninus discusses it, as well as other books printed by Johannes Philippus, in the cited work; more recently, P. Francis Xavier Laire has treated it in *Specimen*, pp. 232–233, and Audiffredi, pp. 212 ff.

1479. Mantua, at the house of Johannes Schallus of Herosfeld, folio. *Eusebius’s Ecclesiastical History*, etc. Johannes Schallus, a German physician skilled in printing as well as Lignamine was, adapted both the care and the type to this new edition, apparently without knowing of the Roman edition. Fontaninus calls it equally elegant with the Roman edition. It is dedicated to Federico Gonzaga, marquis of Mantua. A five-couplet epigram added at the end of the work may be seen in Fontaninus.

1497. Paris, at the house of Petrus Lovet, quarto. *Eusebius’s Ecclesiastical History*, etc.

## Sixteenth century

1514. Strasbourg, [printer omitted], small folio. The same work together with Bede’s *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*. It is considered extremely rare, though not corrected; indeed, Jean Gravius, cited by Fontaninus, calls it exceedingly corrupt and full of errors [Note: book V, chapter 11, no. 9].

Between 1514 and the following edition: Paris, without indication of year or printer, octavo. *Eusebius’s Ecclesiastical History, with Rufinus as translator.* Prepared and once again reviewed against manuscript codices and various editions by Gaufridus Boussardus, theologian of Paris. Dedicated to Étienne Poucher, president of the Parliament of France and later bishop of Paris.

1523. Lyon, at the house of Benedictus Bonnyn, octavo. The same, from Boussardus’s edition.

Basel, at the house of Johannes Froben, folio. *Nine Books of Eusebius Pamphilus of Caesarea’s Ecclesiastical History, with Rufinus as translator.* Rufinus, presbyter of Aquileia, occupies the first place among the authors of ecclesiastical history, in two books revised against ancient Latin exemplars by Blessed Beatus Rhenanus.

1525. Paris, at the house of Franciscus Regnault, octavo. The same, from Boussardus’s edition.

1528. Basel, at the house of Johannes Froben, folio. *Nine Books of Eusebius’s Ecclesiastical History, with Rufinus as translator*, etc.; a reprint of Rhenanus’s edition, though its prefaces have been omitted.

1533. Lyon, at the house of Benedictus Bonnyn, octavo. The same, from Boussardus’s edition.

1539. Basel, at the house of Johannes Froben, folio. The same, together with the same historical writers and several additional short works by Rhenanus.

1541. Paris, through Galeotus a Prato, folio. The same, together with the same works printed from Rhenanus’s revision.

1542. Basel, at the house of Henricus Petri, folio. The same, in volume III of Eusebius’s works published in Latin.

1544. Basel, at the house of Froben, folio. The same, from B. Rhenanus’s edition, among the authors of ecclesiastical history.

1548. Antwerp, at the house of Johannes Steelsius, octavo. The same, together with the same authors of ecclesiastical history, reprinted in two volumes.

1549. Basel, at the house of Froben, folio. Rufinus’s two books of *Ecclesiastical History*, together with the authors of ecclesiastical history, from the translation of Wolfgang Musculus. Likewise in the reprints of 1554 and 1557, and in the Henricpetrine edition, Basel, 1611.

1570. Basel, at the house of Henricus Petri, folio. The same, with brief scholia by Jean-Jacques Grynaeus, in volume II of the same works of Eusebius. There, however, book X is from the translation of Johannes Christophorson, while book XI is from Rufinus.

1571. Paris, at the house of Nicolas Chesneau, folio. Rufinus’s two books of *Ecclesiastical History*, by which he supplements Eusebius, together with Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History* from Christophorson’s translation and the scholia of Jean Courtier.

1580. Paris, at the house of Michel Sonnius, folio. Rufinus’s two books of *Ecclesiastical History*, together with his *Short Works*, edited by René Laurent de La Barre.

## Eighteenth century

1740–1741. Rome, printed by Antonio de Rossi, quarto. *The nine books of the Ecclesiastical History of Eusebius Pamphilus, with Rufinus of Aquileia as translator, and Rufinus’s own two books: a work divided into two parts, one containing Eusebius’s books and the other Rufinus’s books, prepared from Vatican manuscript codices and illustrated with notes through the labor and study of Father Pietro Tommaso Cacciari of Bologna, a Carmelite religious.*

The latter part also contains Cacciari’s historical dissertation on the life and faith of Rufinus and on Rufinus’s own translation of Eusebius, together with a very full index.

For 166 years Rufinus’s translation of Eusebius had not been committed to the press. Cacciari regarded the fate of this work, so highly commended by the ancients, as more unfortunate than a man devoted to the study of ecclesiastical history could any longer tolerate. He understood, however, that it was not enough simply to reproduce the Rhenanian text in print. He therefore undertook to purge and polish it of the countless blemishes that could easily be detected beneath its earlier appearance, and, after restoring it in this way, he dared to set it against Valesius’s translation, in case its younger and more polished form might lose something of the esteem enjoyed by the latter.

There is no need to explain at length how successfully he carried out this plan, since his learning and skill are abundantly evident from his edition of Leo’s works, which may be regarded, in a certain sense, as a preliminary exercise for this undertaking. He therefore presented a text collated with five distinguished Vatican manuscripts, imposing upon himself the rule that he would alter nothing in the reading of earlier editors unless at least two codices supported the alteration, even when he encountered passages whose corruption could scarcely be doubted.

He also added notes, though he wishes them to appear intended only for young students, not for learned men. In them he briefly marks historical matters and points concerning geography, as well as places associated with saints and Fathers.

Finally, in the third part of the aforementioned dissertation on Rufinus’s life and faith—which, together with the books written by Rufinus himself to supplement Eusebius, forms the second volume—he discusses Rufinus’s translation:

1. its authority, use, and value among earlier writers;
2. the translations of Eusebius by Musculus and Christophorson;
3. the translation of Valesius;
4. the merits of Rufinus’s translation, on the testimony of Valesius himself;
5. and, in comparison with the Greek text, the two translations of Rufinus and Valesius, which he examines against one another and judges Rufinus’s superior.

By this novel judgment he does not immediately despise or make light of Valesius. Rather, he attributes the latter’s inferior position chiefly to the Greek manuscripts of Eusebius, which he regards, without exception, as interpolated and corrupt. Rufinus, by contrast, was so close in time to Eusebius that Cacciari thinks it likely that he drew from clearer sources. He further adds that later translators followed Rufinus’s traces in the more important matters and sought assistance from him, and in the fifth paragraph supplies examples supporting both arguments.

### Cacciari’s codices

All are Vatican manuscripts.

The first, no. 1978, parchment, quarto, written around the thirteenth century, consisted of 174 leaves and contained only Rufinus’s translation, together with books X and XI written by Rufinus himself. The text was divided into columns. Various annotations had been scattered in the margins.

The second, no. 5989, in gatherings of four leaves, was written in 1448 and completed on 13 December at Verona. It contained only the books translated by Rufinus. Titles were prefixed to the individual chapters, and notes were written in the margins, not unlike those displayed by the Rhenanian edition. Cacciari testifies that he chiefly followed this manuscript because it had been written with the greatest accuracy.

The third, no. 564, large-format, parchment, and written in two columns, consisted of 77 leaves. It appeared to belong to the eleventh century and supplied excellent readings. It once belonged to the Queen of Sweden.

The fourth, no. 563, parchment, consisted of 72 leaves and belonged approximately to the twelfth century, according to Cacciari. Its initial letters were decorated in various ways. It also contains Rufinus’s translation of Clement’s *Recognitions*, under the heading: “Rufinus, bishop of Aquileia” [sic], “on the history of Clement called *Peter’s Itinerary*, or *Clement’s Recognitions*.”

The fifth, no. 385, written in a recent but exceedingly beautiful script and elaborately decorated with illuminated figures—leading the editor to suspect that it was copied from some very ancient and distinguished exemplar—consisted of 201 leaves. It is preserved in that part of the Vatican Library called the Urbinate collection.

## II. Rufinus’s *History of the Hermits*, or *Book on the Lives of the Fathers*

We learn that the Fathers, or saints whose lives are related by Rufinus in this little book, once flourished in the desert of Nitria. To establish more certainly which book we mean, it will be very useful to set down the names of the individuals and the order found in the most recent editions.

A prologue is prefixed, beginning with the words “Blessed be God” and ending: “And may they seek the palm of perfect wisdom or of patience.”

The book has thirty-three chapters:

1. On Saint John;
2. On Or;
3. On Ammon;
4. On Beno;
5. On the city of Oxyrhynchus;
6. On Theon;
7. On Apollonius;
8. On Ammon;
9. On Copres, presbyter, and Paternation;
10. On Abbot Syro, Isaiah, Paul, and Anuph;
11. On Helenus;
12. On Elijah;
13. On Pithyrion;
14. On Father Eulogius;
15. On Apelles, presbyter, and John;
16. On Paphnutius;
17. On the monastery of Abbot Isidore;
18. On Serapion, presbyter;
19. On Apollonius, monk and presbyter;
20. On Dioscorus, presbyter;
21. On the monks living in Nitria;
22. On the place called the Cells;
23. On Ammonius;
24. On Didymus;
25. On Cronius;
26. On Origen;
27. On Evagrius;
28–29. On the two Macariuses, the Egyptian and the Alexandrian;
30. On Ammon, the first monk of Nitria;
31. On Paul the Simple;
32. On Piammon, presbyter;
33. On John.

Finally comes the epilogue, *On the Dangers of the Journey to the Deserts*.

This little work, scarcely anything having been read and copied more frequently throughout the ages and having also been printed in recent memory, had readers uncertain about its author during the period closest to Rufinus. In time, such a harvest of opinions grew up concerning the matter that Rosweyde could enumerate ten or eleven names to which it had commonly been attributed; its true author was recognized only through the work of more recent scholars and restored to it after a long interval.

Rosweyde discovered that this was first done by Jacques Lefèvre d’Étaples [Note: In the preface to the *Paradise of Heraclides*]. The principal support for the attribution is Jerome’s testimony in Letter 43 to Ctesiphon, which for too long had been used to deprive Rufinus of what was owed to him by attributing the work to Evagrius. Support is also found in Rufinus himself, who, in *Ecclesiastical History*, book XI, chapter 4, indicates that after completing the sequence of his history he would devote himself to writing a work of this kind.

On this basis, and with many further and varied arguments drawn from the book itself, Rosweyde [Note: *Prolegomena* 4, § 10, p. 25] and Fontaninus [Note: chapter 12, pp. 360 ff.] established the attribution. They nevertheless differ among themselves in this respect: Rosweyde regards Rufinus merely as the translator of material that Heraclides or Palladius may have written in Greek, and considers this partly responsible for the ease with which Rufinus’s work could have been forgotten. He regards as another cause the fact that, because certain Origenists had been included in the work, Rufinus did not dare to bring forth and market his offspring under his own name.

Fontaninus, by contrast, defends through a straightforward argument the view that Rufinus himself was the writer, but that someone else who had lived in Egypt narrated to him the journeys and events he had seen, so that Rufinus might adorn them in Roman style. Fontaninus identifies this person as Petronius of Bologna, to whom Gennadius writes that the *Lives of the Fathers* were attributed in his own time [Note: *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 41].

So far is Fontaninus from thinking that Rufinus translated these lives from Greek that he considers it more plausible that Rufinus’s work was subsequently translated into Greek and incorporated into Palladius’s *History* because of the similarity of their subject matter, so that a single body would be formed from the two authors.

Fontaninus also gives a very plausible explanation for the custom of placing Jerome’s name at the head of the book. He says that certain *Lives of the Fathers* written by Jerome were joined to these Rufinian lives, which bore no name, because of the similarity of their subject matter, with the result that everything came to be attributed to Jerome as though he were the sole author.

At this point it will be appropriate to warn the reader that the *Lives of the Fathers* written by Rufinus were never circulated separately. In all manuscript codices, just as in printed books from the first edition down to the latest, they were joined to works by other authors—namely, those contained by Rosweyde in the first seven books. In earlier editions, however, they were variously dispersed or assembled according to the judgment of each compiler.

Rosweyde enumerates twenty editions of these Lives, which he thinks can conveniently be reduced to three families. He makes the first family the edition printed without place, year, or printer’s name, which he regards as older than all the others; we shall later give it in its proper place, following his arrangement, so that his method may be understood. He begins the second family with the Nuremberg edition of 1478 and establishes the third with the Cologne edition of 1548.

I would have considered this classification of the very diligent scholar valid if he intended it as a rule applying not to every edition existing anywhere but only to the twenty Latin editions he enumerated. We possess two editions, one entirely anonymous and the other lacking an indication of year, which differ both from one another and from the first edition identified by Rosweyde. I have no doubt that somewhat more numerous editions could be found which, when compared with one another, would demonstrate that no relationship at all exists among the oldest editions.

In the catalogue of individual editions, we have always maintained the practice of listing anonymous editions only after the remaining fifteenth-century editions. Here, however, we have decided once to abandon that practice and place them first, both because there can scarcely be any doubt that they are older than the edition of 1478 and so that we may not begin with Rosweyde’s second class of editions.

Furthermore, Rufinus alone is our concern. His book always stood out in the collection of lives and was understood exclusively as Rufinus’s work in ancient times, whenever people cited the *Lives of the Fathers*. For this reason, although Rosweyde explained many matters with admirable diligence by describing and comparing the editions generally—and especially the earliest editions, as he considers them—in order to make them known more accurately, you will find those matters omitted here which bibliographers should by no means regard as unimportant.

## Fifteenth century

### I. Without place or year, folio

The title is lacking. Rosweyde reports that it was printed in extremely crude type, clearly showing that it was produced at the very infancy of printing. The book begins as follows:

“Here begins the preface of Jerome, presbyter, to the first book on the Life of the Holy Fathers.”

Then: “Blessed be God,” etc.

The entire book ends with the monk Marinus. It consists altogether of five books. The first, after our Rufinus’s prologue, “Blessed be God,” etc., begins with the *Life of Saint John the Abbot*. It ends with the seven dangers of the journey.

In Rosweyde’s judgment this is the first of all the editions, and he thinks it was printed no later than 1471. He proves this first from Dionysius Carthusianus’s work *On the Four Last Things*. In article 52 Dionysius relates the story of Macarius’s discovery of the skull of a pagan priest and cites it from book IV of the *Lives of the Fathers*, where it is found as book IV in this first edition. According to Trithemius, Dionysius died in that very year.

He adduces a second argument from a manuscript of the monastery of Kortrijk. Since that manuscript agrees word for word with this edition, so that he thinks it was copied from it, its completion is recorded in a subscription dated November 1469.

This edition was therefore sent to press a third time in the same form and order, without any addition or alteration, as Rosweyde observes, except that the later two added and inserted chapter summaries, which are entirely absent from the first edition.

Fontaninus placed before this first edition of Rosweyde the Ulm edition printed by Johannes Zainer, about which we shall say more.

### II. Without place or year, folio

The title is lacking. It begins: “Here begins the prologue.”

We possess an edition of the kind Rosweyde indicates here, beginning: “Here begins the prologue to the *Lives of the Fathers*.” It appears to be of great antiquity, printed in very crude, spreading, and uneven Gothic type, on divided pages, without signatures or numbers for gatherings and leaves. Likewise, all large and small initial letters are absent.

The prologue is followed by a table of contents for book I, and a similar table precedes each of the remaining four books. At the end, which occupies the second half of the second column on the reverse of a page, stands:

“Here ends the fifth book on the Lives of the Holy Fathers. Thanks be to God.”

These final words are in large Gothic letters.

It nevertheless differs from the first edition as described by Rosweyde in that the *Life of Marinus*, which Rosweyde notes as following the completion of book V, appears in the present edition as part of that book itself, namely as chapter 94. In addition, chapter 95 is included, containing the *Life of Euphrosina*. It begins:

“There was a certain man named Paphnutius,” etc.

It ends with the words:

“Glorifying God the Father and his Son Jesus Christ, together with the Holy Spirit, for ever and ever. Amen.”

At the end of the volume an unknown hand added:

“I have found that this was printed by comparison with the most ancient edition of the year 1462, approximately at the same time.”

### III. Without year or place, folio

It begins without a title: “A prologue, unfruitful …”

### Without place or year, folio

The title is absent. First are presented the *Lives of the Fathers* attributed to Rufinus of Aquileia. Then, under the title *Exhortations of the Holy Fathers and Perfections of Monks*, which Jerome translated from Greek, come the *Lives of the Hermits*, written in Greek by an anonymous author and translated by Pelagius the deacon, John the subdeacon, and Paschasius the deacon, comprising books V, VI, and VII in Rosweyde.

In the final part, however, they differ considerably from Rosweyde’s text. The volume begins with Paschasius’s preface, above which is printed in large letters: “Preface of the Work.” Before the prologue appears the title:

“Here happily begins the little book of the divine Jerome on the Lives of the Fathers.”

The next chapter is entitled *On Saint John the Baptist*.

It was printed in small, elegant Gothic type of a kind we have seen nowhere else. At the end of our copy an unknown hand wrote:

“It seems highly probable that this work was printed at Naples by Master Matthias the Moravian around the year 1470.”

It is certainly Italian, for it did not derive from the family of German editions.

### Ulm, at the house of Johannes Zainer, without year, folio

The title is lacking. It was printed on broad pages in very clear Gothic type on exceptionally fine paper. It begins on the reverse of the first leaf with a register printed in two columns, which continues for nine complete leaves, except that the fourth column of the final leaf is blank. The text fills 375 leaves.

It consists of two parts or books. The first begins with the Rufinian *Lives*, presented in exactly the order listed above; it includes Jerome’s *Life of Saint Hilarion* and the lives of women that Jerome compiled, and finally appends many others from different authors.

Its title is:

“Here begins the prologue of Saint Jerome, cardinal and presbyter, to the books of the Lives of the Holy Fathers of Egypt, and also of those who dwelt in Scythia, Thebaid, and Mesopotamia—not only those whom he saw with his own eyes and examined with the greatest labor, but also the many whom he recorded as reported by trustworthy persons with notable diligence. Finally, he faithfully translated from Greek into Latin the little books of other authoritative writers and inserted into this work, for its completion, works translated by others.”

The subscription reads:

“Here ends the life of the blessed Father Ephrem and consequently the first book of the *Lives of the Fathers*.”

The second part begins on p. 215 with the book that is third in Rosweyde and is also attributed by him to Rufinus. Its prologue is:

“Who could doubt that the world stands through the merits of the saints?”

This is placed at the head of the entire second part.

The title of the text is:

“Here begin the exhortations of the Holy Fathers and the progress of the monks, together with the other little books which Saint Jerome, cardinal and presbyter, translated from Greek into Latin.”

It ends with Saint Macarius’s letter to the monks, in the words:

“May the Lord therefore grant us that he find in us such a dwelling, he who lives and reigns, God, for ever and ever. Amen.”

The final subscription reads:

“The book of the *Lives of the Fathers* of Saint Jerome, cardinal and presbyter, properly arranged according to the alphabetical order, printed by Johannes Zainer in the town of Ulm, happily comes to an end.”

De Bure, *Bibliothèque instructive*, volume I, p. …; Seemiller, *Bibliotheca Ingolstadiensis. Incunabula typographica*, fascicle 1, p. 128, no. 30. Add Helmschrot, volume II, p. 72. It is also held by the Royal Library of the Academy. From what has been cited it will be clear how great the difference is between this edition and the others.

1478. Nuremberg, by Anton Koberger, 5 May, folio. The title is lacking. Printed in large Gothic type on divided pages. It begins with a preface, which we shall note in the edition of 1483; this preface seems to concern the anonymous edition and the Ulm edition. See also Seemiller, *Incunabula Typographica of the Ingolstadt Library*, fascicle 2, p. 25, no. 9.

Rosweyde described it more accurately and, above all, clearly explained what the editor says about the arrangement of the entire volume according to the letters of the alphabet. From what he noted in *Prolegomena* 19 concerning the contents of this edition, we understand that it was compiled from the Ulm edition as well as from Rosweyde’s first edition. Rufinus’s book is presented from the beginning as in the editions above.

1483. Nuremberg, by Anton Koberger, folio. *The Lives of the Fathers of Saint Jerome, cardinal and presbyter.*

At the end:

“In the year of Christ’s Nativity 1483, on the Nones of April, for the advancement of the blessed Fathers who diligently pursue the eremitical life and whose deeds rightly deserve to be preserved in memory, this notable work, called the *Lives of the Fathers*, excerpted from very many codices by men highly skilled in the Sacred Scriptures, was most elegantly printed in the town of Nuremberg by Anton Koberger, an inhabitant of the said town, and happily brought to completion.”

The type is intermediate between Gothic and roman and approaches the latter. It was printed on divided pages.

After the subscription follows an index of subjects, preceded by the preface already mentioned above. It explains a new method of division, departing from the earlier editions, which the editor calls confused:

“‘I have divided and distinguished the work into four different parts,’ says the anonymous editor. ‘In the first part I collected historical material; in the second, little books and doctrinal works; in the third, material concerning regular observance; and in the final part, material concerning praise and the power of the virtues. Thus the first part is distinguished by histories, the second by little books and paragraphs, the third by rubrics, and the fourth by the chapters of the rubrics,’” etc.

See also the reprint of Koberger’s 1478 edition; Pray, *Index of Rare Books*, *Bibliotheca Budensis*, part I, p. 506.

Venice, by Octavianus Scotus of Modena, quarto. *The Lives of the Fathers of Blessed Jerome.* Rosweyde, in the *Catalogue of the Library of Saint Angelo at the Nidum in Naples* (1750, folio), p. 152, records it without an indication of the printer. The learned Helmschrot also mentions an almost identical edition of the *Lives*, truncated halfway through the final leaf, volume II, pp. 105 ff. I have no doubt that it is the same edition, but I refer the curious reader to that author.

### Without place or printer’s name, folio

*The Lives of the Fathers.* Rosweyde cites it and adds that he thinks it German.

1485. Nuremberg, at the house of Anton Koberger, folio. The same. Weislinger, *Catalogue of the Library of the Order of Saint John of Jerusalem*, Strasbourg, p. 110. Rosweyde, in eighth place, mentions another edition of the same year and format, but lacking the place and printer’s name. Whether one of them was mistaken, or whether both have reported the truth, others may judge.

## 1500

Venice, at the press of Bonetus Locatellus, quarto. *Lives of the Fathers*. The title is printed in capital letters intermediate in form between Gothic and roman type; the entire volume, however, is printed in smaller type. At the end:

> The books called *Lives of the Fathers*, by the most blessed Jerome, cardinal priest, chief doctor of the holy Roman Catholic Church, having been carefully examined, corrected with vigilant care, and divided by points and commas, were brought to completion at Venice by Bonetus Locatellus, priest, at the command and expense of the noble lord Nicholas, born at Frankfurt, in the year from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1500, on 6 April.

It begins with the words that follow the subscription of the 1483 edition and, like that edition, is printed in divided pages. Both editions are very clearly printed.

## Sixteenth century

### 1502

Lyons, by Nicolaus Wolff of Lutrea, and sold by Jacques Huguetan, quarto. *The Lives of the Holy Fathers* by St. Jerome. The title presents the bibliographer’s emblem, printed in wood but reflecting almost the precision (*ἀκρίβειαν*) and brilliance of copper engraving, with the inscription:

> “The mark of Jacques Huguetan, bookseller.”

Above it: *Lives of the Fathers*.

Around the sides of the same verse:

> If it is believed that virtue of mind surpasses perishable things,  
> I shall deem nothing worthy of cultivated books.  
> See, studious youth, you can henceforth acquire for yourself  
> With modest bronze what we have printed at great expense.

Below is read:

> It is sold at Lyons by Jacques Huguetan, bookseller and citizen of the same city, in the Mercurial quarter, at the alley leading to the Saône; and at Paris, in the Rue Saint-Jacques, beneath the Virgin, near Saint Benedict.

At the end is the following subscription, with additions to that given above:

> Printed at Lyons, that most delightful city, by Master Nicolaus Wolff of Lutrea, 1502, on 28 April.

It reproduces the Koburger edition, in small Gothic type and divided pages. Apart from Rosweyde, we have found it praised nowhere. It is preceded by a dedicatory letter from Hugo Dissutus, doctor of both laws, canon of Chalon, in which he explains to Jean de Ponpet, doctor of both laws, bishop of Chalon, and commendatory and perpetual administrator of the abbey of Saint Peter near the walls of Chalon, the value of his work. He attributes no soundness and no complete freedom from errors to the earlier editions, so that they may understand that they owe all correction to him alone.

### 1507

Lyons, by Jannot de Campis, quarto. The same work, with the same preface by Jean Dissutus. Rosweyde’s catalogue of the British Museum records an edition of the same year and format lacking a place of publication and printer’s name.

### 1508

Venice, by Bonnetus, quarto. The same work. The eleventh edition in Rosweyde.

### 1509

Lyons, by Stephanus Balann, quarto. The same work.

### 1512

Lyons, by Jacobus Sachon, quarto. *The celebrated work of St. Jerome on the Lives of the Fathers*. Rosweyde.

Venice, at the press of Nicolaus of Frankfurt, quarto. The same work. Rosweyde.

### 1515

Lyons, by Jacobus Myt, quarto. *The most celebrated work of St. Jerome on the Lives of the Fathers, opening heaven and the sky to mortal eyes.*

> Whoever wishes to climb the lofty stars of the highest heaven,  
> And finds my path made level by reading,  
> Will see here that the ancients reached heaven  
> With great labor; a lighter road is now given to the stars.

It is sold at Lyons by Jacques Huguetan, in the Mercurial quarter, at the alley leading to the Saône. At the end:

> The books called *Lives of the Fathers*, by the most blessed Jerome, cardinal priest and chief doctor of the holy Roman Catholic Church, having been carefully examined, corrected with vigilant care, and distributed by points and cola, have recently been brought to completion. Printed at Lyons by the worthy Jacobus Myt, 1515, on 17 August.

Pray, *Index of Rare Books*, Buda Library, vol. I, p. 507.

### 1520

Lyons, by Jacobus Mareschal, quarto. The same work. Rosweyde.

### 1536

Lyons . . . *St. Jerome on the Lives of the Fathers*. Catalogue of the Barberini Library.

### 1537

Lyons, by Antonius Vincentius, quarto. The same work. Rosweyde.

### 1547

Cologne, by Gaspar Gennepaeus, folio. *The Prototype of the Ancient Church*, containing the lives, deeds, and sayings of the holy friends of God of both sexes, partly by the author or compiler St. Jerome, and partly by various others.

This edition was prepared by Brother Theodoricus Loher of Stratum, prior of the Carthusian house of Maria in Brussels and provincial visitor. He dedicated it to Prince Otto, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and bishop of Augsburg. In his dedicatory letter, dated Regensburg in 1546, he explains that he had revised and restored the text by collating eight or ten ancient and trustworthy manuscript copies simultaneously; that he had then arranged it in a definite order, according to the sequence and chronology in which each Father had enlightened the world.

This edition consists of five books, like the first, but its order is greatly changed, and certain materials are added from the second edition and from elsewhere—including, for example, the Ulm edition, which Rosweyde did not know. Rufinus’s book is not presented as one continuous work but in fragments: of the three parts comprising its first book, the first, concerning holy men, and the second, concerning holy women, have been mixed and combined from Rufinus. For the rest, see Rosweyde.

### 1548

In the same place, from the same printer, folio. *The remarkable and admirable sayings and deeds of certain distinguished friends of God of both sexes, saints of the ancient Catholic and apostolic Church, containing lives, sayings, and deeds, partly by D. Jerome and partly by various others, whom you will be able to identify on turning the page. Received and approved by the Catholic Church more than 1,050 years ago.*

This edition also came from the same editor, who nevertheless prefixed a new dedicatory letter, dated Augsburg, 21 January 1548, to Henry, abbot of the Benedictine monastery at Wiblingen in the diocese of Constance. In it he asserts that he had cleansed the *Lives of the Fathers* of more than a thousand errors by reference to the oldest as well as differing copies. Rosweyde admits that he does not know whether this should be understood of the editor’s repeated work on this book or of his entire editorial labor, nor whether this is a new edition or merely a changed title for the earlier one. The order is the same as in the preceding edition, and the treatment of Rufinus’s work is exactly the same; Fontaninus writes that it differs in absolutely nothing.

### 1596

Alcalá, at the press of Juan Gracián, quarto. *Lives of the Holy Fathers*. Rosweyde.

## Seventeenth century

### 1615

Antwerp, from the Plantin press, folio. *Lives of the Fathers: On the Life and Sayings of the Elders, or the Eremitic Histories, in ten books, restored to their original authorship and pristine purity and illustrated with annotations, through the work and diligence of Heribert Rosweyde of Utrecht, theologian of the Society of Jesus.*

The overall structure of this work does not concern us here. It is enough to indicate which parts of it are Rufinus’s. The second book of this collection consists of the *Lives of the Hermit Fathers*. The editor, however, was not afraid to attribute the entire third book, entitled *Sayings of the Elders* and divided into 220 sections, to Rufinus as well. Its prologue begins: “Who would doubt that the world stands by the merits of the saints?” To justify his judgment, he appeals both to the general similarity of style and to the correspondence of individual passages in the prologues of the two books. The latter argument, however, can scarcely be admitted; it seems rather to reveal a different author who imitated Rufinus.

In the preliminary materials, as we have already indicated above, he discusses at greater length the fortunes of all these writers and of the books of the *Lives of the Fathers* and Rufinus. He added to each book notes of considerable learning and largely critical character.

### 1617

Lyons . . . folio. *Lives of the Fathers*, edited by Heribert Rosweyde. A reprint of the Antwerp edition.

### 1628

Antwerp, from the Plantin press, folio. *Lives of the Fathers*, edited by Heribert Rosweyde, second edition, variously enlarged and illustrated.

Rufinus’s first book extends from p. 445 to p. 491; the second, which is there numbered as the third, from p. 492 to p. 535.

## Translations

Fontaninus was not rash in asserting that the *Eremitic History* had been translated into Greek at an early date. Even now this translation exists in manuscripts, a thoroughly genuine version quite distinct from Palladius’s *Lausiac History*, though transmitted under Jerome’s name. Montefalconius noted that he had discovered such a text in the Coislin Library, under the title *History of the Monks of Egypt*. He did not know its true author; nor did Jean Meursius before him. In the preface to the *Lausiac History* of Palladius, which he published in Greek, Meursius says that he possessed a book on the *Lives of the Fathers of Egypt* that was undoubtedly no different from ours.

Moreover, Cotelerius published the preface and part of this translation in *Greek Monuments*, vol. III, p. 171, from the Colbertine and royal manuscripts, which he cites at p. 564. He notes there that in Colbert manuscript 1215 a Greek *History* of Rufinus, bearing the name of Jerome, priest of Dalmatia, follows Palladius’s *Lausiac History*. Rosweyde also writes that he obtained fragments of this translation from Venetian and Augsburg manuscripts, *Prolegomena* 4, § 8, p. 23.

It was translated not only into Greek but also transferred into Syriac and Arabic, as a certain Maronite told Fontaninus. Finally, it learned to speak in very many modern languages. The oldest of these translations are Italian; there are many French versions, and Belgian, German, and English versions are also found.

### Italian I

1476. Venice, at the press of Antonius Bartholomaei, folio, divided into six books. The first, bearing Jerome’s name, consists of materials from various authors but for the most part from Rufinus.

### Italian II

1589. Venice, at the press of the Gurri, “in the printing house of the Guerra,” quarto, with illustrations, from a new translation by Giovanni Marco Verdizotti.

Rosweyde mentions these two; but within a few years in fifteenth-century Italy there were far more. A booklet by Franciscus Carolus Alter, *Bibliographical Notices* (Vienna, 1779, octavo), lists eight of them:

1. 1475, Venice, printed by Master Gabriel di Pietro of Treviso, folio, in clear type and divided pages;
2. 1477, Vicenza, by Hermann Liechtenstein, folio;
3. 1479, Venice, by Master Nicolaus Girardengo, folio;
4. 1483, Venice, by Bernardino di Pino of Como, folio;
5. 1490, Milan, by the worthy associates Leonardo Pachel and Huldericus Scinzenzeller, folio, in small Gothic letters and without signatures;
6. 1493, Venice, by Giovanni, folio;
7. 1499, Milan, by Master Uld. Scinzenz., folio;
