8. 1499, Venice, by Christophorus di Pensa, folio.

### French I

1486, Lyons; it is praised in the English edition mentioned below.

### French II

1494. Paris, at the press of Jean Dupré, folio, with illustrations, translated by an anonymous author. Rosweyde notes that it was made from the second Latin edition.

### French III

Paris, without indication of year or printer, quarto, with illustrations. Rosweyde notes that it agrees entirely with the preceding version and perhaps is the earlier of the two.

### French IV

1605. Paris, at the press of Guillaume Chaudière, quarto, with illustrations, translated by an anonymous author. Rosweyde considers it to have been made from the third Latin edition. It contains only four books, omitting the entire fifth book and Paschasius.

### French V

1606. Paris, at the press of Guillaume de la Nove, octavo, translated by Jacques Gaultier. It contains the first and second books of Rosweyde’s collection, from the second Latin edition.

### French VI

1657. Paris, at the press of Pierre Petit, quarto, translated by Arnaud d’Andilly, vol. II of the fourth edition.

### French VII

Translated by Fossee; praised by Tillemont in the *Life of St. Apollonius*, vol. X, p. 36.

### Belgian I

1490, Zwolle, at the press of Peter van Os, folio. It consists of three parts, variously arranged and intermingled. It contains Rufinus’s entire book.

### Belgian II

1498. Delft, at the press of Hendrik Ekert van Homberch, folio, similar to the preceding edition.

### Belgian III

1511. Leiden, at the press of Jean Seversoen, folio, following the earlier editions.

### German

Without indication of year or place, folio, with illustrations. It generally agrees with the Belgian edition. Rufinus’s *Lives* extend approximately from folio 85 to folio 161.

### English

1495. Westminster, at the press of Wynkyn de Worde, folio, translated by William Caxton. It was made from the French edition printed at Lyons in 1486.

## Manuscripts

Among the many manuscripts of these *Lives* that were available to Rosweyde, the following contained Rufinus’s book:

- Manuscript of St. Florian, folio, written on parchment more than 800 years ago.
- Manuscript of the Ingolstadt College of the Society of Jesus, folio, written on very old parchment.
- Manuscript of Saint-Omer, from the collegiate church of Saint-Omer, old and especially complete. It presents Rufinus’s book under his own name.
- Manuscript of Affligem, from the abbey of Saint Peter near Aalst, folio, on good-quality parchment.
- Manuscript of Crespin, from the Benedictine monastery near Valenciennes, folio, written on parchment by an old hand.
- Manuscript of Anchin, from the Benedictine monastery near Douai, folio, on parchment.
- Major manuscript of Liessies, from the monastery of Saint Benedict under the patronage of Saint Lambert, folio, on parchment. Here the second book is attributed to Postumianus and said to have been sent to Fydosius.
- Minor manuscript of Liessies, formerly belonging to Saint Michael in Sars, quarto, on parchment.
- Manuscript of Bonne-Espérance, from the Premonstratensian abbey of that name near Binche in Hainaut, oblong quarto, on parchment, in good and old handwriting. It contains only fragments from various books and from Rufinus.
- Moret manuscript, folio, on parchment; not very old, but containing a great deal. It attributes Rufinus’s book to Postumianus, as does the major Liessies manuscript. Rosweyde received it from the sons of D. Moret.
- Manuscript of Saint James in Liège, where there is a Benedictine abbey, folio, written on parchment in 1312.

From the same abbey he possessed a paper booklet in octavo containing the *Life of St. Onuphrius*, written in a recent hand.

- Manuscript of Cambron, from the Cistercian abbey of Saint Mary of Cambron near Ath, folio, on parchment, written in a relatively recent hand. Rufinus’s book appears under this title: “Here begin the acts of the holy Fathers, edited by the monk Postumianus and sent to Fydosius.”
- Manuscript of Clairmarais, from the Cistercian abbey of Saint Mary of Clairmarais near Saint-Omer, folio, on parchment, in good but not very old handwriting. Rufinus’s book is assigned to no author.
- Manuscript of Saint Mary of Bibra in Germany, folio, on parchment, in somewhat old handwriting.
- Manuscript of Saint Peter at Münster, folio, on parchment, in more recent handwriting; it contains only certain passages from Rufinus’s book.
- Major manuscript of the Holy Sepulchre, from the Benedictine monastery of the Holy Sepulchre at Cambrai, folio, on paper, written in a recent hand. Rufinus’s book is attributed to Palladius and said to have been translated from Greek by Jerome.
- Another major manuscript of the Holy Sepulchre, quarto, on parchment, in a recent hand. It attributes Rufinus’s book to Jerome.
- Manuscript of the Carthusians of Maria de Gratia near Brussels, folio, written on parchment in 1460.
- Manuscript of Roermond, from the College of the Society of Jesus at Roermond, folio, on parchment; it appears to have been copied from the first edition.
- Manuscript of the Sion monastery of religious men of the Order of St. Augustine at Kortrijk, folio, on paper, written in 1469; undoubtedly based on the first edition.

## III. The Rule or Institutes of the Monks of Basil the Great

This translation by Rufinus, as it was formerly circulated by him in Italy, was commonly called the *Rule of St. Basil* in the age of St. Benedict. At that time and in the following centuries it was frequently read throughout the monasteries. In more recent times, however, after the invention of printing, it has not been particularly often printed.

The first person to publish it was Giovanni Francesco Brixianus, a monk of the congregation of Saint Justina, in the year

### 1500

Venice, at the press of Luca Antonio Giunta, quarto, in a book entitled *Four approved forms of life, first of all, for religious of every kind*. This edition was later renewed in the year

### 1519

Paris, at the press of Jean Petit, quarto. Here, however, as Fontaninus observes, Urseius—who is found in the manuscript copies—is mistakenly called Ursarius; perhaps Ursacius should be read.

The Brescian monk noted at the end that this rule was found in his Greek source in a fuller and more orderly form, and that he intended shortly to present it in Latin, together with various other treatises of the same Basil, translated by Rufinus. [Fontaninus, book V, chapter 1, p. 207.]

At our disposal is a Latin edition of the works of Basil the Great, prepared from the translations of John Argyropoulos, George of Trebizond, and Raphael of Volterra:

### 1523

Paris, at the press of Jodocus Badius Ascensius, folio. In it, the *Rule on the Institution of Monks*, translated by Rufinus, is read from folio 156 to the end. At the extreme end of folio 155 Rufinus’s preface to the work itself is found; the work consists of one hundred chapters.

At the end of the preceding treatise is printed:

> End of the works of D. Basil the Great translated by Raphael of Volterra.

The *Rule* and certain other works translated by Rufinus follow. Similar material is found more or less in the preceding treatises. I do not see what this should refer to, since the entire volume ends with this very treatise—unless perhaps one may infer something from the final subscription, which reads:

> The Institutes of the monks of St. Basil the Great, bishop of Caesarea, are completed. Under his rule all the monks of the East wage their campaign, both in Asia and throughout almost all Greece, and formerly the Carmelites as well, as they still do today, with not very many alterations.

The letter to Blessed Gregory of Nazianzus, previously among those translated by Raphael of Volterra, is placed first. Thus the editor—or at least the person responsible for publishing the works, Jacques Lefèvre d’Étaples—must have thought that this too was owed to Rufinus’s translation. Here also, however, *Ursarius* is copied for *Ursacius*.

This edition was, if I judge correctly, reprinted in the year

### 1531

Cologne, at the press of Eucharius, folio; Fontaninus praises it.

### 1575

Cologne, at the press of Gervinus Calenius, folio. The same *Rule*, with the *Rule of St. Benedict* added, illustrated by a commentary of Cardinal Juan de Torquemada, p. 537.

The version regarded as more genuinely and authentically Rufinian than the others is the one praised in the *Concordia* of Benedict of Aniane, where it is separately inserted into a manuscript of rules. From this source, Lucas Holstenius published a text reproduced exactly from the Cologne parchment manuscripts, formerly copied from the autograph of St. Marianas of Trier, in which the Rufinian *Rule* was read first:

### 1661

Rome, at the press of Vitalis Mascardus, quarto, in the edition of the *Codex of Rules* prescribed by the holy Fathers for monks and consecrated virgins. These rules had formerly been collected by St. Benedict of Aniane, abbot, part one.

Fabio Chigi, then bishop of Nardò and apostolic nuncio among the Ubii, later Pope Alexander VII, had copied the text from the Cologne parchments and sent it to Lucas Holstenius for publication in 1643. Soon afterward:

Paris, at the press of Louis Billaine, quarto. The same edition was reprinted, and very recently in the year

### 1759

Augsburg, at the expense of Ignatius Adam and Franz Anton Veith, folio, with the same manuscript enlarged and expanded by Marianus Brockie through many additions and divided into six volumes. In volume I, part one, pp. 67–108, this *Rule of Basil* was reprinted.

Furthermore, Fontaninus brings forward the following words from the preface to the Latin-Greek works of St. Basil, printed at Paris by Michel Sonnius in 1617, folio, concerning a plan—undertaken at the beginning of the seventeenth century, though by authors unknown to me—to publish this Rufinian *Rule* together with other works of Rufinus, a plan that never reached completion:

> There also exists an epitome of the ascetic books, or certainly of the rules set out at greater length, which Rufinus of Aquileia rendered into Latin and called the *Book on the Institutes of Monks*. It will be published separately at Cologne together with the other works of Rufinus, especially since it does not preserve the order of the Rules presented by the works of Basil.

The same author observes that Fronto Ducaeus, in the same work, volume II, p. 28, column 2, inserted in his notes on the *Rule* more fully expounded corrections to Rufinus’s Latin translation from two manuscripts of the Putean collection.

There is also another *Rule of Basil*, which Prosper Stellartius included in his book entitled *Foundations and Rules of All Orders*, published at Douai by Balthasar Bellerus in 1626, quarto, p. 138.

Finally, Fontaninus also, though only incidentally, praises the following manuscripts:

1. A very old parchment manuscript in the library of Santa Croce in Jerusalem;
2. Another extremely old manuscript in the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, in which the *Rule* is divided into two hundred questions and an equal number of answers placed beneath them.

## IV. Seven Homilies of Basil the Great Translated by Rufinus

These were published only by Julien Garnier in his edition of the works of St. Basil, Paris, 1722, volume II, p. 713, from the royal and Colbertine manuscripts. Fontaninus discovered the same homilies in a parchment manuscript of the Vatican Library, Urbinate 67, at the place cited, chapter 8, volume I, p. 299.

In the Benedictine edition of the works of St. Augustine, after the beginning of volume IV, there is a preface of St. Basil to his *Commentary on the Psalms*, formerly attributed to St. Augustine. The editors of that edition attribute it to Rufinus the translator; Fontaninus observes that the same attribution is made in volume II, p. 456, of a manuscript in the Thuane Library.

This is the preface to the first homily of St. Basil, translated into Latin by Rufinus. Thomasius likewise prefixed it to both editions of the Psalter, first and second, pp. 11 and 43. Fontaninus.

## V. The Apology of Pamphilus for Origen, Translated by Rufinus

Of the six books comprising this *Apology*, only the first was translated into Latin by Rufinus. He did not touch the remaining books: four had been composed through the combined efforts of Eusebius and Pamphilus, while the sixth had been composed by Eusebius alone.

This was one of the reasons—together with others of no greater weight—that Jerome devised for disparaging the true author; Fontaninus weighs the matter carefully in Book V, chapter 5, vol. III, pp. 254 ff.

This book was inserted, together with Rufinus’s *Apology*, in various editions of Origen and Jerome, for example in Martianay’s edition of Jerome, volume V, pp. 219–249, and in the edition of Origen by Ruæus, volume IV, among the works relating to Origen, where it stands first. It was collated against six manuscript copies:

1. The Corbie manuscript, formerly at Saint-Germain-des-Prés, from the ninth century;
2. The Royal manuscript, no. 1641, from the thirteenth century;
3. The Sorbonne manuscript;
4. The manuscript of Saint-Remigius at Reims;
5. The manuscript of Saint-Vaast;
6. The manuscript of “S. in periculo maris” (Saint [—] at Peril of the Sea);

as well as against those manuscripts according to which the books *On First Principles* had been corrected. It was published with a learned and extensive preliminary *Admonition*.

## VI. Origen’s Four Books On First Principles and His Homilies

These works are found, in Rufinus’s translation, in all editions of Origen’s works. The first edition of the books *On First Principles* seems to be the one published with various works of Origen by the efforts of Constantius Hierotheus, a canon regular of the monastery of San Salvatore:

### 1514

Venice, at the press of Lazarus de Soardis, folio.

From there it passed into the editions of Erasmus. In the latest edition of Ruæus it appears in volume IV.

As for the homilies, they likewise appear in all editions of the works, both Latin and those published in Greek and Latin. No one should be surprised if he learns that in the older editions their translation is attributed not to Rufinus but to Jerome; he should know that the same attribution is made in all the manuscript copies. In these manuscripts, moreover, the prologues of nearly all the books have usually been cut away to avoid hostility, lest fear of Origen’s errors—whose suspicion weighed upon Rufinus—deter readers from purchasing them, as Erasmus openly declared in the judgment appended to the homilies on Genesis.

Fontaninus mentions, if I remember correctly, one manuscript that explicitly names Rufinus as translator: a manuscript of the homilies on Leviticus in the library of St. Anthony at Venice, though it was subsequently destroyed by fire.

In Ruæus’s edition, the homilies on Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Joshua, and Judges appear in volume II (1733), pp. 52–489; those on the Psalms appear in the same volume, pp. 654–700. The ten books on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans are read in volume IV (1759), pp. 458–689.

There are also certain special editions, which we shall list according to Fontaninus.

Aldus Manutius was the first to publish together the homilies of Origen on Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Joshua, and the book of Judges, “with the divine Jerome as translator.” They were dedicated to Aegidius of Viterbo, an outstanding preacher of the divine word, of the Order of Hermits, later cardinal of the Holy Roman Church:

### 1503

Venice, folio.

A monk who concealed his name in the preface assisted with the edition. He professed to owe much to his fellow monk at the monastery of Santa Giustina in Padua, Jerome of Valentia, a Spaniard.

Although he makes Jerome the translator of the entire work—apparently because in the manuscript copies from which he extracted it the scribes had written Jerome instead of Rufinus, so that the volume might be more favorably received under Jerome’s name—he nevertheless omitted the prologue that he found in the manuscripts, as alien and unworthy of Jerome. He says that he has no doubt that both the author and the translator would have published the work without a preface, but that through the carelessness of copyists it had not reached them.

This edition was reprinted by Bernardino Benali:

### 1512

Venice, folio.

Jodocus Clichtoveus was the first to publish, under Rufinus’s name and from the Corbie manuscript, the sixteen books of the homilies on Leviticus:

### 1514

Paris, printed by Wolfgang Hopyl, folio.

In the Latin editions of the Fathers, these homilies are wrongly attributed to Cyril. Fontaninus especially cites two such editions: the Cologne edition printed by Melchior Novesianus in 1546, in two folio volumes, prepared by Peter Canisius, where they appear in volume I, p. 41; and the Paris edition printed by Michel Sonnius in 1573, folio, where they are found on p. 66.

The prologue to the homilies on Numbers, like the prefaces to the others, is absent from printed editions and from the manuscripts, but is found separately in certain manuscripts. Several of these are listed by Fontaninus, Book V, chapter 7, pp. 286 ff.

It was published from the Bigot manuscript by Henri Valois in his notes on Eusebius’s *History*, Book VI, chapter 38, and, with several manuscripts collated, by Pierre-François Chifflet in his edition of Paulinus, part II, chapter 25. Chifflet, however, attributed it not to Ursacius but to Donatus. Fontaninus discusses this error and its origin carefully.

Fontaninus records a manuscript of the homilies on the book of Joshua, published from the manuscript library of Antonio Agustín at Tarragona by Philip Mey:

### 1587

Quarto, manuscript 48, with the following heading:

> Sixteen homilies of Origen of Alexandria, also called Adamantius, on the book of Joshua, with Blessed Jerome—or Rufinus—as translator, addressed to Chromatius.

The book is on parchment, more than 300 years old, in a square format.

Constantius Hierotheus published the nine homilies on Judges translated by Rufinus, together with the prologue addressed to Apronianus, after Merlin’s first Latin edition of Origen’s works:

### 1516

Venice, at the press of Lazarus de Soardis, folio, together with other works of Adamantius on the New Testament, preceded by Jacques Merlin’s *Apology for Origen*. They appear there after the homilies on Luke, folio 87, and are also found in Vatican manuscript Urbinate 65, folio 34, part 2. Fontaninus.

Joannes Martianay inserted the homilies on the *Song of Songs*, attributed to an uncertain translator, in volume V of Jerome’s works, p. 603. In certain manuscripts they are attributed to Jerome and Ambrose. Erasmus also did not recognize the true author; but Cassiodorus makes Rufinus the translator in *Divine Readings*, chapter 5. This is confirmed by Peter Pithoeus’s manuscript, which bears the heading:

> Here begins Origen’s treatise on the *Song of Songs*, translated into Latin by Rufinus.

### Commentaries on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans

Theophilus Salodianus, of the Order of the Friars Observant, about whom Lucas Wadding is silent in his writings on the Friars Minor, found these commentaries in the library of the monastery at Fiesole under the name of Jerome the translator. He published them at Venice, at the press of Simon de Luere:

### 1506

Folio. He dedicated them to Alexander Portensis of Vicenza, a man of the equestrian order.

The same work was later reprinted by Bernardino Benalius:

### 1512

Folio.

Erasmus subsequently inserted it into his collection of Origen’s works.

Joannes Martianay, supposing Jerome to be the author, inserted Rufinus’s prologue to Heraclius in the letters he arranged in a new order, volume IV, no. 107, p. 808. Fontaninus briefly notes several manuscript copies, p. 297.

## VII. Ten Treatises of Gregory of Nazianzus Rendered into Latin by Rufinus

Rufinus himself noted in his *Ecclesiastical History* that he had translated ten short orations of Gregory. The first to publish them was Jean Adelphus Muling:

### 1508

Strasbourg, under the title:

> These are the ten books of Gregory of Nazianzus contained in this volume.

At the end:

> The book of Blessed Gregory of Nazianzus, translated by a certain Rufinus, is completed. Printed at Strasbourg by Johann Knoblouch in the year 1508, quarto.

The editor dedicated the book to Georg Bohem of Mainz and to Johann Fleming, priests of the churches of Boppard. He makes it clear to them that he was connected by personal friendship with Giovanni Francesco Pico, Count of Mirandola, and that he was bringing Rufinus’s writings into the light lest they finally perish.

They were later published with other works of Nazianzus, translated by Peter Mosellanus and Willibald Pirckheimer:

### 1522

Leipzig, octavo. Fontaninus.

The editors of the most recent edition of Nazianzus’s works, Benedictine monks (Paris, 1778, volume I), mention another edition omitted even by Fabricius. It bears the title:

> The thirty-eight orations, treatises, sermons, and certain books of Gregory of Nazianzus, surnamed the Theologian, in Latin, with Willibald Pirckheimer, the priest Rufinus, and Peter Mosellanus as translators, from the edition of Johann Straub and Desiderius Erasmus.

Finally, Fontaninus treated separately and briefly several manuscript copies of Rufinus’s Gregory; it is not unprofitable to repeat his information.

Vatican manuscripts nos. 4259 and 5259 contain the second treatise, *On the Nativity of the Lord*.

Urbinate 72 contains the *Apologeticus*, together with the prologue and the other treatises, but not the work on the Nicene Faith or on the Arians.

Palatine 66 likewise contains the *Apologeticus* with its prologue. This little book is also preserved in the library of Santa Croce in the Sessorian Field, after the pastoral rule of St. Gregory, manuscript 109; it is also found in the Bodleian Library among the manuscripts of John Selden, no. 3423.

Norwich manuscript no. 9333 contains the remaining treatises under the prologue addressed to Apronianus.

The Baluze manuscript, containing Rufinus’s works of Gregory of Nazianzus (Catalogue of the Baluze Library, vol. III, p. 24), passed into the Royal Library.

Labbe praises Royal manuscript no. 313, in which several of Gregory’s orations survive in Rufinus’s translation, in *Bibliotheca manuscripta*, supplement, p. 274.

## VIII. The Sentences of Sixtus

They are also entitled *Enchiridion* or *Ring*.

From the very age of Rufinus, conflicting opinions had been debated concerning the author of this collection of Sixtine *Sentences*: some judged him a pagan, others a Christian. Some attributed it to Sextius the Stoic philosopher praised by Seneca; others to some Pythagorean or other figure; still others made Sixtus II, Roman pontiff and martyr, its author.

A very large proportion of editors, not to mention countless other writers, occupied themselves with this question, yet, so far as I can see, made little progress. That century was indeed fertile in gnomographic works of this kind after the birth of Christ. The book could subsequently have been interpolated in various ways by pagans and Christians. And certainly it was very substantially interpolated and altered by Rufinus.

What, then, prevents us from accepting Jerome’s statement as true—though elsewhere, because of the hostility that he directed against Rufinus, I have attributed little weight to him—and from accepting his claim that the original author was a leading pagan?

Moreover, Galeus observed that the manuscripts of Rufinus’s *Sentences* differ from one another so greatly that it is almost certain that two editions of Sixtus were produced in antiquity. Some manuscripts contain more sentences, others fewer; in some places many are repeated, and occasionally their order is changed. Other copies proceed not in a single sequence but in two parts—a fact also noted later by Jerome, as Fontaninus observes.

Finally, Galeus asserts that he found no manuscript to which some addition could not be made after an accurate collation of the copies mentioned above.

The first edition was that of Symphorianus Champier, in 1507. Among the subsequent editions, whose catalogue we now establish, the outstanding ones are those of Hillesemius, Galeus, and Siberus, the last being the most recent.

### 1507

Lyons, at the press of Jannot de Campis, quarto. *The Ring of Sixtus*, with the prologue addressed to Apronianus, together with Symphorianus Champier’s book *On the Fourfold Life*.

In his preface to Philibert Naturel, the editor marvels that, as far as he knew, no Frenchman had previously printed this excellent book.

### 1514

Wittenberg, at the Grunenberg press, quarto. The same work, with the golden verses of Pythagoras.

### 1516

Basel, at the press of Johann Froben, quarto, with certain writings by other authors, under the following title:

> A dialogue of Aeneas the Platonic Christian on the immortality of the soul and the resurrection of bodies, entitled *Theophrastus*, translated by Ambrose of Camaldoli.
>
> *Athenagoras of Athens on the Resurrection*, translated by Marsilio Ficino.
>
> *The Sentences of Xystus the Pythagorean*, translated by Rufinus.

Rhenanus says, in a letter to Paul Volz, abbot of Hugshofen in the Vosges Valley, and in another letter serving as his preface to Xystus, that he had revised these sentences against an ancient copy that had been preserved at Saint Faith’s in Sélestat.

Fontaninus wishes the two editions to be compared with each other, p. 304. They differ especially with respect to the prologue.

### 1518

Louvain, quarto. The same work. Fontaninus.

### 1520

Basel, quarto. Undoubtedly a reprint of the Rhenanian edition.

### 1522

Cologne, quarto. The same work.

### 1541

Paris, quarto. The same work.

### 1552

Venice, at the sign of Hope, duodecimo. The same work. Without the prologue. On folio 122, after the index, appears a little book entitled:

> *Precious Sayings, or Commonplaces, Extracted by Defensor, a Very Ancient Theologian, from Nearly All the Doctors Who Wrote in Sacred Scripture.*
### 1574

Cologne, apud Maternus Cholinus, in octavo. *The Sentences of Sixtus or Xystus, filled with precepts of true wisdom and forming souls for heavenly discipline*, illustrated with learned explanations by Ludovicus Hillesemius of Andernach. Without the prologue. In addition to the commentary, the convenience of readers is served by distinctions among the sentences, indicated by numbers in the margin. Dedicated to Gregory XIII, supreme pontiff.

### 1575

Paris, apud Michael Sonnius. The same work, from Hillesemius’s edition, but with the notes omitted, in *Bibliotheca Patrum* of Bignon, vol. III, p. 962. It was also reproduced from the same edition in the remaining editions of *Bibliotheca Patrum*: 1589, 1609, 1624, 1634, 1644, (1654), vol. VI; in the Cologne edition of 1618, vol. III; and in *Bibliotheca Maxima Lugdunensis*, 1677, vol. III. In all these editions the prologue is absent.

### 1615

Helmstedt, apud Jacobus Lucius, in duodecimo. *The Gnomae, or Sentences on Morals, no less learned than pious, of Xystus the philosopher, Laurentius of Pisa, and Bishop Thalassius*, now published separately for the first time through the efforts of Johannes a Fuchte; here too without the prologue.

### 1670

Cambridge, apud John Hages, in octavo. *The Sentences of Sextus the Pythagorean, translated from Greek into Latin by Rufinus and falsely attributed to Xystus, bishop of the Roman Church, together with mythological opuscula by Thomas Gale*, 1671.

Gale took the text from *Bibliotheca Patrum*, acknowledging that he had not seen the Rhenanian edition. Hence the prologue is also absent.

### 1725

Leipzig, in the Weidmann printing house, quarto. *The Enchiridion of Saint Sixtus II, philosopher, Roman pontiff and martyr, published as a monument of the Christian third century according to the manuscript of Blessed Rhenanus, illustrated with observations, defended against the censures of Saint Jerome, Gelasius, J. M. Brasichellensis, and others, and offered to restore the book’s reputation at the Roman Council convened under the auspices of Benedict XIII, Roman pontiff, in the year of salvation 1725*, by Urbanus Godofredus Siberus, professor at Leipzig.

If the editor thought that the book’s reputation could be restored by demonstrating that its author, if not wholly, was nevertheless for the greater part a Christian, he will be judged to have left nothing undone that could serve to reclaim that glory for it. For he investigated the sources of most of the sentences in sacred writings or in the writings of the earliest Christians, with as much learning as acumen, and proved that they should be derived from those sources rather than from the teaching of the ancient Greeks. But if he thought the book’s esteem depended on regarding it as the work of Sixtus II, he will seem to have proved too much rather than what is true. In other respects, the arrangement and description are extremely convenient and altogether well suited to win the favor of readers.

## IX. The Opuscula of Evagrius

It is established by the testimony of Jerome (*To Ctesiphon*) that Rufinus translated some opuscula of Evagrius into Latin; and Gennadius, in chapter 17, expressly attributes to him a version of Evagrius’s *Sentences*. But since more than one book of Evagrius once existed under this title, it could not easily be determined on its own what book it was, unless another passage of the same Gennadius seemed in some way to assist this inquiry.

For, in chapter 11, when reviewing Evagrius’s writings, he mentions a book of Fifty Sentences: “I was the first,” he says, “to make it Latin. For when I saw that the earlier translation had been corrupted and confused by the passage of time, I restored it to the author’s truth, partly by translating it anew and partly by correcting it.” The earlier, or preceding, book is the book of One Hundred Sentences. Fontaninus therefore argues, in book V, chapter 9, § 4, that no one other than Rufinus could have been the author of this translation, formerly made and corrected by Gennadius. How rightly, let others judge.

To us, at least, these suspicions of Fontaninus do not appear strong enough for us to count this book of Evagrius, much less a second and a third together with it, among Rufinus’s works without hesitation. For when he says that Gennadius, in chapter 11, writes that some opuscula of Evagrius were translated by himself and some by another person whom he wishes to identify as Rufinus, and that he assigned those three little books to the latter class, this is false. Nor does Jerome write that these books, but rather that certain books of this Evagrius, translated by Rufinus, were read by Westerners.

Meanwhile, Fontaninus shows that the three books of Evagrius just mentioned, which had long been thought lost, have now been published in the appendix to a manuscript of the *Rules of Saint Benedict*, abbot of Aniane, which Holstenius made public from the Floriac manuscripts belonging to the Queen of Sweden and now in the Vatican. He notes, however, that the first two have been combined into one without distinction among the sentences, on account of their similarity, and that one epigraph has been imposed upon both. They must nevertheless be divided in this manner:

1. *Sentences of Evagrius the monk*.
2. *To those who live in monasteries and hospices*.

The first, consisting of one hundred Sentences, ends on p. 35 of the Paris edition with the words: “Honey is sweet, and the honeycomb is delightful; but the knowledge of God is sweeter than both.” The second begins with the words: “Hear, O monk, the words of your Father.” These are followed by a third opusculum, *Sentences to Virgins*.

He further adds that it is greatly to be wished that the individual works, separately arranged and with the sentences distinguished by numbers in the margin, might enter the printing houses together with the other works of Rufinus—both those belonging to him and those not belonging to him—having all been gathered into a single corpus.

## X. The Recognitions of Clement

This book bears various titles in different manuscript codices, and consequently sometimes different names in printed editions. It is therefore called now *The Recognitions*, or *Recognition of Clement*; now *The Itinerary of Clement of Rome to James, the brother of the Lord*; or *The Itinerary of Saint Clement concerning the deeds and sayings of Blessed Peter the Apostle*; likewise *The Acts of Peter the Apostle*, *The Circuits*, *The Periods of Peter*, *The Itinerary of Clement*; *History*, *Chronicle*, *Deeds*; and finally, simply, *The Book* or *Books of Clement*. Sometimes it is also entitled *On the True Disputation of Peter the Apostle against the Falsehood of Simon Magus*, or *On the Disputation of Peter with Simon Magus*.

The first person to have it printed was Jacobus Faber Stapulensis, in the year

### 1504

Paris, from the Bellovisian printing house, at the expense of Jean Petit, in small folio, in a book entitled *The Paradise of Heraclides, the Letter of Clement, the Recognitions of Peter the Apostle, the Completion of Clement’s Letter, and the Letter of Anacletus*. Twenty-two years later Sichardus’s edition followed:

### 1526

Basel, printed by Johannes Bebel, folio. *The ten books of the Recognitions of Saint Clement to James, the brother of the Lord, translated by Rufinus Toranus of Aquileia; to which has been added a noteworthy portion of the letters of the most ancient bishops, hitherto unseen, those who governed the Roman Church 1,200 years ago.*

Since Sichardus had not known Faber’s edition, he published this as a new work, recently recovered by himself from two codices, Basel and Schongau, and dedicated it to Bernard Cles, bishop of Trent and later cardinal.

Fontaninus criticizes two things in it: first, that Sichardus reported the *Recognitions* to have been excerpted by Eusebius; second—also criticized by Vossius and Barthius—that he did not hesitate to criticize the judgment of Gelasius and the seventy bishops concerning Clement. In fact, the received reading of the Gelasian Decree had misled him, and Sichardus had removed this stumbling block by publishing what he considered the genuine and very ancient Gelasius.

Fontaninus observes that the later editions derived from this one, for example:

### 1547

Cologne, from the printing office of Melchior Novesianus, in octavo, under the same title; and

### 1568

Paris, apud Audoenus Parvus, also apud Michael Sonnius and Sebastianus Nivellius, in octavo. This is the same edition, but with the title changed.

Fontaninus considers that no one devoted greater labor to Rufinus’s *Recognitions of Clement* than Lambert Gruterus, preacher to Maximilian II, emperor. He gathered into one volume everything circulated under the name of Clement of Rome and published it furnished with prefaces, summaries, notes, and admonitions. The work appeared in

### 1569

Cologne, apud Johannes Birckmann, folio, under this title:

*Clementina, that is, the works of Blessed Clement of Rome, which, having been collected, translated, and corrected in Latin by various authors up to the present day, are here all brought together, with a new preface concerning the genuine and spurious writings of Blessed Clement, and with a final faithful correction of them and a careful explanation of difficult arguments and passages, by Lambertus Gruterus Veriradius, to the Most Reverend Daniel, archbishop of Mainz, etc.*

The editors of *Bibliotheca Patrum* of Lyon later reproduced this edition, with some portions removed, in the edition printed by the Anissons in 1677, vol. II, p. 376.

Finally, the industry and care of all the editors praised thus far were surpassed by Jean-Baptiste Cotelier in his celebrated collection of the Apostolic Fathers. It first appeared in

### 1672

Paris, apud Jean Petit, folio; then, somewhat enlarged and in a more convenient format, in

### 1698

Amsterdam—under the name of Antwerp—at the expense of the Huguetans; and finally, for the third time, in

### 1724

Amsterdam, apud Johannes Wetstein.

The Amsterdam editions were prepared by Jean Le Clerc, who deliberately omitted Cotelier’s dedicatory letter and preface, in which the plan of the works is explained. Cotelier wrote the title as follows:

*The ten books of the Recognitions of Saint Clement to James, the brother of the Lord, translated from Greek into Latin by Rufinus Toranus, priest of Aquileia, together with the same translator’s preface to Bishop Gaudentius.*

Cotelier examined the entire work with the utmost care against six excellent codices, appended variant readings, and, wherever necessary, illustrated Clement throughout with brief but useful notes. Following Faber, he divided the books into chapters, though according to a different method.

The manuscript codices he used are enumerated in the preface to this edition:

1. The Sorbonnicus;
2. The Thuaneus;
3. The Regius;
4. That of Petrus Candelerius;
5. That of the Discalced Carmelites.

Nurris cites another, the Colbertinus, in his dissertation on these books, p. 224. The Vatican shelves also preserve a very ancient Palatinus manuscript. Fontaninus, p. 339.

Two further matters must be added, about which Fontaninus speaks more fully in its proper place.

First, no one should allow himself to be misled by a volume printed under this title: *An Epitome to James, bishop of Jerusalem, by Clement, bishop of Rome, concerning the deeds, journeys, and sermons of Saint Peter*. Paris, apud Hadrianus Turnebus, 1555, quarto.

For it does not contain the *Recognitions*, but a pure *Epitome*, composed not from the *Recognitions* alone as edited by Rufinus, but also from the *Homilies* and Clement’s *Letter to James*, as well as from his martyrdom and the narrative of Ephraem, bishop of Chersonesus. Cotelier demonstrated this long ago and published the work, collated with seven royal manuscript codices, on p. 749, after the *Recognitions* and *Homilies*.

The second matter concerns the *Letter* called the Clementine *Letter to James, the brother of the Lord*, appended to the books of the *Recognitions*, likewise with Rufinus as translator. Among Catholic scholars of the first rank there is an ongoing dispute concerning both its authenticity and its translator. Fontaninus nevertheless attempts to support both.

He also noted several collections of letters of Roman pontiffs and councils in which the letter found a place. Among these are the *Letters of the Supreme Pontiffs*, published at Rome in 1591 in the Roman People’s Palace, divided into three volumes. In the first volume, before all the others, this letter appears, with a spurious appendix on p. 7, whose marginal heading is: *A Brief Summary of the Christian Faith*.

Likewise Labbe’s *Councils*, where it is inserted in vol. I, p. 89, and concerning the addition the following is read: “Here the Letter ends in certain codices. The rest appears to have been added by way of an appendix around the year 800.”

The *Councils of Peter Crabbe*, Cologne edition, apud Petrus Quentel, 1538, vol. I, p. 14, where it is joined to the addition.

Theodorus Bibliander inserted the same letter, translated by Rufinus but with the appendix removed, in a book entitled *Christian and Catholic Doctrine*, Basel, apud Jacobus Parc, 1550, octavo, p. 221. Long before, it had been inserted without the translator’s name and without the appendix in another book entitled *Several Illustrious, Serious, and Learned Letters, Outside the Canon of the Bible but Nevertheless Apostolic and Pious*. Augsburg, printed by Alexander Weyssenhorn, 1529, octavo. Blondellus placed it first among the letters of Pseudo-Isidore.

The editors of the *Recognitions* sometimes joined this appendix to the *Letter*, and sometimes separated it from it. Faber did the latter. In his first edition, in 1526, Sichardus appended to the fourth of Clement’s letters an appendix entitled *A Summary of the Faith*. In another edition he joined it to the *Letter* itself. Gruterus followed him.

Cotelier, after publishing the same Letter in Greek and Latin after the *Recognitions*, without any addition, later presented Rufinus’s translation, collated with the older editions and manuscript codices and divided into twenty chapters.

### Versions

**German:** *The Recognitions, or History of the Journeys and Speeches of the Apostle Peter in Ten Books: Now Translated into German, with a Preliminary Account by Gottfried Arnold.* Berlin, by L. M. Rüdiger, 1702, octavo.

It was composed from Gruterus’s edition, a fact Arnold regretted, saying that he noticed it only when the work was nearly complete.

**English:** *The Recognitions of Clement, or the Travels of Peter, in Ten Books. Translated into English by William Whiston, with a Preface or Preliminary Discourse, together with two Appendices, in his* Primitive Christianity Revived. *Vol. V. London, 1712, octavo.*

## XI. The Paschal Canon of Anatolius of Alexandria, Bishop of Laodicea

It is thought that Rufinus interpolated the Eusebian *History* with a Latin version of this work. [Note: Eusebius mentions him in *History*, book VII, chapter 26.] It was first published from an old manuscript codex by Aegidius Bucherius in his *Commentary on the Doctrine of the Times*, p. 439. See also Fontaninus, book V, chapter 15, § 1.

# Preface to the Most Illustrious and Most Reverend Lord Daniel Delphinus, Patriarch of Aquileia

The immense merits that you possess, most illustrious and most reverend Patriarch Delphinus, in relation to this new edition of the works of Rufinus, are so continually before my eyes and mind that everything I might say in advance to commend either the author or even our own industry seems to be anticipated by them, and they appear rightly to claim precedence over every word of praise.

For although that distinguished honor of the Church of Aquileia may perhaps owe me something, since I have at last endeavored to restore it to its former dignity, it openly professes that it owes you much more: you ordered that everything conducive to shedding light upon its writings and restoring them to life should be investigated, so that I might have reliable and verified information from all the libraries of your most extensive dominion; and, to put it briefly, you have raised up with me, by your own hands, your son who was lying prostrate and had already been withdrawn from view for many centuries.

Moreover, you now bestow upon him the hope of undergoing the judgment of mankind with the greatest success, by continuing to pursue him with the most generous good will and zeal. Indeed, long ago, while he was still alive at Aquileia, he regarded you as the same support and ornament that he had in his bishop. For, relying upon the favor and protection of Chromatius, that most holy and most wise bishop, he could easily stand his ground against the great Jerome. With Chromatius also as an excellent mediator, he offered sacrifice to peace and transmitted to Christian posterity the distinguished opinion he had earned concerning himself and his faith.

Now, finally restored to life through your assistance, he looks upon you, his bishop, with the keenest eyes: another Chromatius, occupying the same ecclesiastical throne and following the same path of virtue, so that he lacks nothing in you that he once admired most greatly in him and experienced as favorable to himself.

Or should he lack something? On the contrary, he should now consider his situation much more illustrious, since in your Church he sees Piety and Learning, those two pursuits truly worthy of a prince of sacred affairs, increased through your outstanding efforts. Your Church shines and gleams so brightly through the many illustrious examples of these virtues that he now seems to encounter not merely one or two old friends, Jovinus and Eusebius, but almost countless ones. He may therefore congratulate you upon this happiness—produced by you, belonging to you, and achieved through the immortal work of your uncle—with the famous Jeromean encomium: “The clergy of Aquileia are regarded as a choir of the blessed” (*Chronicle*, under the year 378).

This is how I most rightly interpret the feeling and devotion that he must bear toward you. But what shall I say of myself? I should be the most ungrateful of men if I did not proclaim, in the first place and with the fullest possible declaration of my obligation, the extent to which I have profited from you, through whom I have made the greatest progress in preparing this edition.

I should also be failing myself, and would not seem sufficiently to understand how great an increase in esteem is thereby added to the writings and name of Rufinus. You not only embrace him with your protection and affection, but, since you have devoted all your efforts under God to increasing the dignity and glory of the Church of Aquileia, you rightly think that you have served him most excellently by judging him to share in that glory.

Behold, then, most illustrious and most reverend prelate, your Rufinus—not portraying his features and limbs as though he had emerged from the hands of painters, but speaking in his own words and language and treating most lucidly of divine matters.

His works possess such learning and doctrine that they yield very little to the works of the other Fathers whom that age produced as by far the noblest. Nearly all of them are closely connected and almost bound up with what the greatest Teacher of the Churches, Jerome, worked out, whether in respect of the subject matter underlying them or of the arguments advanced on both sides. They can scarcely, or perhaps not at all, be separated from one another.

Although some have little to do with Jerome, their purpose and character are nevertheless such that they continually invite and attract the lover of learning from Jerome to themselves. Yet here lies the first and principal source of the damage, from which, although it seemed that some additional value ought to accrue to them, the whole injury arose.

The author, because he was suspected of favoring Origen—a suspicion known to everyone—was sharply criticized by Jerome, with whom he had once been bound by the closest friendship, though Jerome acted from a sincere zeal for purer faith. Rufinus was therefore compelled to clear himself before those among whom he heard this accusation and to descend with Jerome into the arena.

I say nothing to conceal the truth: he was an unequal opponent of an Achilles. But, to state the matter as it truly is, another circumstance also caused our author to be regarded somewhat unfairly. Nature has arranged matters in human disputes, whatever their kind, so that when someone loses a case, both the products of his intellect and his praises seem to suffer some diminution.

The priest of Aquileia experienced this fate above all others. His intellectual monuments did not once find the devoted readers they deserved. In a later age, the glory of Jerome’s name, which increasingly and justly prevailed, cast a kind of darkness over them. The mere fact that they could appear to have been produced by a man hostile to the most holy Doctor was sufficient reason for them to be sought out with less eagerness.

Thus, little by little, the excellent writings of the priest of Aquileia became obsolete and were almost removed from the hands of readers. Yet, so that they might not perish, they were entrusted to those who practiced the book trade and furnished libraries. These men, however, compounded the problem through a new inconvenience, lest their profits suffer any loss.

For works that seemed liable to no criticism—namely, works that neither favored Origenian doctrines nor opposed Jerome’s principles and glory, and that were in other respects most worthy of being read eagerly and preserved forever—they inscribed under other names, in order to avoid among the learned public some stigma attached to the name of Rufinus.

They attributed them to authors of the first rank, Cyprian and Augustine, for example, and even, if heaven wills it, to Jerome himself. The result was that, while some works were nearly passed over, others were commonly believed to belong not to Rufinus but to the authors whose names they bore.

Moreover, from the invention of printing up to the present time, although nearly all these works had been published separately and in various books under different titles, they had never been brought together into a complete collection, as happened with the works of almost all other authors, and formed into a single corpus.

This was once attempted by René Laurent de La Barre, a man deserving well of literature and ecclesiastical learning, about 170 years ago. He gathered together, as the title of his book states, *The Works of Rufinus, some of which had never previously been published, others recently corrected and emended through the assistance of very learned men, in two volumes*.

He gathered them, however, into a single volume of no great size. One half, or “volume,” was manifestly filled by a spurious commentary on the first seventy-five Psalms, which, as he says, Antonius de Albone, archbishop of Lyon and primate of the Gauls, had recovered from a very ancient manuscript exemplar of the library of the Monastery of Île-Barbe near Lyon.

He also stuffed the first volume with commentaries on Hosea, Joel, and Amos belonging to other authors. If these are properly excluded, that collection contains only two books of the *Blessings of the Patriarchs*, two books of *Ecclesiastical History*, and an exposition of the *Creed* among the genuine works of Rufinus.

It contains nothing of the works he wrote against Jerome; nothing of the *History of the Monks*, which is the most distinguished part of his works; nothing of the *Apology to Anastasius* or of the other opuscula related to it.

And this is true of those works that we call original, or those which the priest of Aquileia composed on his own. For the works he translated from Greek into Latin—although they are considerably more numerous and demand a place among the Rufinian works—he did not touch at all, nor did he mention them even in passing.

It was therefore necessary for us to undertake a new and complete collection of his works, both in relation to the Jeromean works, as we have said—for we have already reviewed all of those, and this collection concludes them as with a crown—and in relation to Rufinus himself. His most distinguished intellectual monuments, to be valued as gold and gems, had been scattered here and there through various books, burdened with every kind of defect, given other titles and attributed to other authors, and finally deprived of their most important parts; they had almost disappeared from the minds of men.

What, then, is the precise aim we have set before ourselves in preparing this undertaking? That must now be explained more clearly.

We begin with the Life of Rufinus, which the distinguished Fontaninus worked on with incredible zeal for more than twenty years and read for the most part to me while we were in Rome. Indeed, he had already polished it to such perfection that nothing was lacking to make it public. But while he postponed publication, he died; and the work did not appear until several years after his death, together with other Lives of Illustrious Men written in a much shorter style, which together comprise the *Literary History of Aquileia*, for that is the title of the book.

Nothing could be more suited to our purpose. For what most properly belonged to an editor—to discuss in detail the writings of Rufinus, together with their causes, fortunes, and editions—the most learned man pursued there with extraordinary accuracy.

Nevertheless, he did leave some work for us. The things that seem to have escaped his diligence are minor, and we have noted them in their proper places or placed them before the eyes of the reader in brief marginal notes.

Still, it must by no means be denied that he is sometimes mistaken. We correct two such errors, especially concerning the proper chronology, in chapters 29 and 32 of the Jeromean Life that we recently prepared. It would be tedious to repeat them here.

Elsewhere he errs somewhat more seriously, when he insults Jerome, saying that Jerome spoke improperly of Saint John Chrysostom and even wrote something that might be called heretical. To establish this, he cites our Noris, who produces what he calls Jerome’s Letter to Theophilus—this is Letter 113 in our edition—in which Jerome rejoices that the bishop of Constantinople has been removed from his throne and mocks his misfortunes: “John, who formerly governed the Church of Constantinople,” and so forth.

Fontaninus reasons as follows: “Just as very few followed Jerome when, deceived by Theophilus of Alexandria, he attacked Chrysostom, a most holy man, as a heretic, so he was able to persuade very few that Rufinus should be branded with the mark of heresy.”

Yet that is by no means Jerome’s letter to Theophilus, but—what is even more surprising—the letter of Theophilus himself to Jerome, which Jerome translated into Latin and sent back to him together with the book of *Invectives*, in order to excuse the translation of the insulting work.

We established this with sound arguments in its proper place in volume I of the *Works of Jerome*. There we also separated the subsequent letter, which had previously been combined with it into one, and restored each letter to its true author.

Jerome therefore did not write against Saint Chrysostom on his own initiative, nor did he show himself unfair toward Chrysostom’s virtues. Thus the entire argument Fontaninus advances in that chapter is based on false reasoning and amounts to nothing.

Elsewhere, too, he allowed himself to be deceived by the commonly received reading in Rufinus, in the second *Apology*, no. 12. From this reading two full years of Rufinus’s life depend; when they are misunderstood, the sequence of his affairs is also disturbed to some extent.

Here is the situation. Rufinus, intending to mock Jerome’s boastfulness—Jerome had spent only thirty days in Alexandria but repeatedly gloried in having had Didymus as his teacher—says that he himself remained there for six full years, and then again, after some interval, for two other years.

This is how the Guarnerian manuscript codex reads; we shall discuss it later. We used it as the basis for our edition, and sound reasoning persuades us that this is what the author himself wrote and that it must certainly be read this way.

But the books printed up to the present day, to which Fontaninus himself gave credence, have the passage with an incongruous and false sense: “and again, after an interval, for some other days.” Thus the priest of Aquileia is made to say that, when he came to Alexandria a second time, he remained there not two years but only a few days.

Yet it is clear that the printed books are mistaken and that for far too long they misled learned men. What benefit would Rufinus claim from having spent a few days in Alexandria, when he boasts that six years had already been spent there by him, and when he wishes to set solid years, not days, against the few days that Jerome spent there?

To what else can “other” refer than to years? He had mentioned no earlier day, and everyone understands that the term refers back to what immediately precedes. He therefore wrote “another two,” namely, years, not days. For if he had wished to say “days,” he would not have added “other,” but only “some.”

From this it is also clear that he did not write *aliquot*—“some”—but *aliquod*—“a certain”—and that he intended it to refer to the interval, as both reason and the proper sequence and connection of the speech show.

For it is foolish to say that there was simply an interval, as the printed books give it, without any indication of its duration. No one can be induced to believe that Rufinus was so careless, especially when recounting his own affairs at this point, or that he would speak so foolishly about himself against his rival.

On the contrary, see how consistent everything is once the true reading has been restored from the codex: “I remained in Alexandria for six years, and again, after a certain interval, for another two.”

Nor should you doubt whether the passage could have been corrupted by the person who copied the codex. Rather, I want you to take from it an argument for the more ancient genuine reading.

The book reveals itself in countless places as having been copied by an incompetent antiquary. Although a critic of the highest genius would have been needed to restore its words, the copyist showed himself extremely deficient. Even in passages that are neither difficult to copy nor particularly difficult to understand, he frequently commits scribal errors and does nothing except rewrite exactly what he read in the exemplar before him.

We shall discuss the character and authority of the codex more fully below, in its proper place. For now, let it be absolutely certain that Rufinus wrote it in no other way and that, when he came there a second time, he truly spent two years in Alexandria.

No one doubts that his first stay must be reckoned from the year 372 to 377. This second stay, therefore, which lasted two years and occurred after an interval of some duration—say one year or two—seems to belong to the year 380 and the following year, or, if one prefers, to a somewhat later time, with the interval itself likewise understood as somewhat longer.

Certainly it occurred before 385, when Theophilus ascended the episcopal throne of Alexandria on July 20. For we learn from Jerome, in book III of the *Apology*, that Rufinus was not in Alexandria after Theophilus became bishop.

In this way, therefore, the lacuna in Fontaninus concerning Rufinus’s second stay, lasting two years, must be filled.

But those who have committed this same Life of the priest of Aquileia to writing, whether in whole or in part, have often been mistaken and have often misled others. I pass over the work that, about thirty years ago, the Abbot of Trappes comprised in two small volumes in the French language.

For although it was published while Fontaninus was still alive and had long been engaged in the same work, and although French books, learned and unlearned alike, enjoy among the Italian public the fortune they do, it found readers, yet Fontaninus never praises it even in a single word throughout his commentary. This indicates that the learned man did not esteem it highly enough to consider it worthy of remembrance.

In truth, it did not seem to us to deserve that anyone should spend good hours either reading or refuting it.

I also pass over the considerable discussion of Rufinus and his books by the distinguished Bernardus Maria de Rubeis, who recently gathered together the monuments of the Church of Aquileia in a *Historical, Chronological, and Critical Commentary*. Since he disagrees with Fontaninus at a few points, although he also seems to depart from the truth, it is sufficient to have indicated these matters in the notes; there is no need to reproduce here what cannot harm either piece of writing when the two are compared.

In other respects, the author knows ecclesiastical antiquities exceptionally well, and his book is filled with distinguished learning and scholarship.

But there is another author whom we cannot entirely pass over, lest he continue with impunity to mislead the general body of students. He belongs to the Carmelite order: Brother “Petrus Thomas Cacciari,” as he himself calls himself, Apostolic Examiner of the Roman Clergy and principal lecturer in theology at the Urban College of the Propagation of the Faith.

To the edition he prepared about three years ago, *Ecclesiastical History from Rufinus’s Translation of the Greek Works of Eusebius, with Two Books by Rufinus Himself Added*, he appended a historical dissertation in which he investigates the life and faith of Rufinus, as well as the translation itself.

He begins the matter from the beginning—from Jerome’s first friendship with Rufinus, that is—and then follows the whole sequence of Rufinus’s life, character, and studies.

But it is astonishing how often he is mistaken and how frequently he errs and blunders even in matters obstructed by no difficulty whatsoever.

We shall point out several errors that first strike the eye on reading, so that we may not appear to neglect our duty of examining matters more closely related to Rufinus. We shall willingly forgive the rest and shall not waste time dispelling the hallucinations of those who may perhaps be ashamed to be disabused.

> “He says [in] Chapter II that [Jerome] was then compelled to return to Dalmatia, his native land, when, writing to Rufinus, he says, ‘After a sudden storm tore me away from your side,’ etc. (Epistle III).” Indeed, a man is said to return to his homeland when he says that he was compelled to leave it, having bid farewell to his parents, sister, and relatives (Epistle XXII). Cantherius at the gate. See our discussion in Chapter 6 of the *Life of Jerome*. For even if several errors are heaped together in a single sentence, I do not intend to mark each one individually.

I pass over the absurdities with which nearly all of the following four chapters are filled. In Chapter VII he assigns the death of Athanasius—which is the principal chronological basis for the chief stages of Rufinus’s travels—to the year 372, on 2 May, and thereby turns that entire history upside down, although it is now absolutely certain that the holy bishop died a full year later, on 3 May. We have demonstrated this much more clearly than others from various records: the Paschal Letter of Proterius, the *History of the Coptic Patriarchs*, and especially the *Acephalous History of the Affairs of Saint Athanasius* himself, where his death is recorded under the consulship of Valentinian and Valens for the fourth time, in the eighth year of Pachomius. Let us pass over other matters that may seem less important.

In Chapter XI, which concludes the First Part, he commits two enormous errors in a few words. He says that the *History of the Hermits*, or *Lives of the Holy Fathers*, was written by Rufinus while he was residing in Alexandria—that is, as he supposes, somewhat later than 385. Yet it is easily evident, both from the author himself and from the work, at the end of chapter 28, and also from Book II of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 4, that Rufinus began writing it not in Alexandria but at Aquileia, and after the year 400—that is, at least fifteen years later than Cacciarius asserts.

He also recognizes not merely one but two books of that history as Rufinian, “the second of which,” he says, “although it may not appear to have been composed entirely by him, must certainly be regarded as having both been rendered into Latin and enlarged and illuminated for the most part by Rufinus.” Rosweyde might once have been forgiven an almost similar hallucination; but now, when one sees two Thebaids, and takes for Rufinus’s genuine offspring a work plainly alien and spurious, this seems hardly the judgment of a sane man.

To the accumulation of ignorance he adds the belief that Rufinus is speaking of himself and narrating his own journeys through Egypt [Col. 0053], although it is manifestly clear from the whole history of the events described—and Fontaninus has established it with compelling arguments—that the author speaks in the person of another, namely Petronius of Bologna, who asked him to commit to writing his own journeys through the retreats of Egypt.

The Second Part of the Dissertation is much longer and teems with many more errors. Above all, it is ridiculous that the lemma proposes to demonstrate that Rufinus and John of Jerusalem began to suffer a bad reputation because of Origenism. One would think that they began to renounce Origenism, whereas the truth was that they began to acquire a bad reputation among others because they favored Origen too enthusiastically.

Moreover, with what confidence—or, to say no more, with what audacity—he dares accuse of falsehood the genuinely authentic book of Jerome against John of Jerusalem, about which no one has ever doubted, except for one Wastelius, likewise a Carmelite, almost raving in favor of John, the presumed member of his own order; and he calls its author an obvious liar and a foolish enemy of John! Indeed, in Chapter VIII, where he undertakes to treat this matter in full, he continues to slander the work, to make its author guilty even of Pelagian doctrine, and finally to assail him with insults.

Formerly all learned men received this invention of Wastelius with derision. The most learned Tillemont also wrote:

> “This opinion is so strange and, as I believe, so little accepted among scholars, that we shall readily be excused from examining its reasons, which would take longer to refute than it would be difficult to do so” (*Notes on the Life of Jerome*, Note LII).

Let Cacciarius consider this said to him as well. Although to have deprived the great Jerome of his noblest part—namely, of an entire book—in defiance, so to speak, of almost the whole world, does not seem deserving of pardon.

For the rest, he should consider that we have dealt generously with him in passing over, in the six intervening chapters, all the countless trifles, absurdities, and idle inventions that he weaves together there, since they have no proper bearing on Rufinus. We likewise pass over those in the chapters that follow through Chapter XIV, in which he is wholly occupied with rescuing his John from the accusations of Jerome and of the bishops of Cyprus and Alexandria. There is one thing we deeply resent: his repeated and shameless insult to the gray hairs of the most holy man Epiphanius.

At length, after speaking ill of most good and learned men, he proceeded so far as suddenly to attack me as well. Observe with what learning and by what methods. In Chapter XV he says:

> “Jerome, having at some point realized that he had been deceived by the simplicity of the blessed old man Epiphanius, rejected the latter’s judgment and finally, in the year 396, restored peace and communion with his own bishop.”

He is guilty of at least a one-year prochronism, even according to the chronology of those who date that peace earlier than others. But what is more surprising is that, to establish this date, he uses evidence that indicates the year 401 or 402: namely, the well-known statement of Postumianus in the *Dialogue of Severus*, where Jerome the presbyter is said to have governed the church of that place—Bethlehem—which was a parish of the bishop of Jerusalem (*Dialogue* I.8).

Nor does he himself deny this chronological indication. He adds:

> “It may be inferred from that passage that the holy Doctor, who, according to Epiphanius’s testimony (Epistle 5.1), out of modesty and humility had refused to perform the duties due to his name [read: sacrifices], after the dispute had been settled, around the year 400, submitted his shoulders to the burden of the monastic”—so he calls it—“parish of Bethlehem, which had doubtless been entrusted to him by John’s authority.”

Here he errs again in supposing that Jerome only from that time onward performed the office of presbyter and ministered at sacred rites. Such is the harvest of his hallucinations that once having raved in a single sentence is not enough for him.

After he had babbled these and similar things—which it would weary me less to pursue individually than it would the reader—he suddenly tries to sneer at me and applaud himself, if he can. “These matters,” he says, “ought to have been noted by the Veronese Editor of the works of Saint Jerome”—thanks be to God that we have not been so foolish—“who, by assigning that Epistle [the Book against John of Jerusalem] to the year 399 or 400—that is, three or four years after the solemnly established agreement—makes the holy Doctor manifestly guilty of violating faith and friendship.”

May God grant me better things, and this error to my enemies. We shall not imitate the man at all, whether with our eyes or our heart; yet we shall nevertheless bear with equanimity the great frivolity of one who wishes to appear, in the eyes of the public, to have taught others.

The Veronese Editor—who is none other than myself—demonstrates in the preface to that book, with sound arguments, that it should be assigned to the year 399, though it may also belong to the beginning of 400. In the *Life of the Holy Doctor*, however, where these matters are discussed more fully and in continuous order, he assigns it specifically to 399, leaving no room for doubt once the calculations have been properly made. Let this man, eager for learning, read Chapter XXIX, especially from number seven through number twelve. If I wished to transfer that material here, I should make this too long, and it would no longer be a preface to the Rufinus edition but a transcription of the *Defence of Jerome*. I have no doubt that, even against his will, he will assent to the calculation.

But so that you may see the truth of the old proverb concerning Jerome—that Cacciarius had the will to harm but lacked the ability—suppose that we had supplied not the most evident but only weaker reasons for our chronology; or, if you prefer, suppose that we had postponed that composition not to 399 or 400 but much later, even as far as 406, as certain other learned men have thought. Would that mean that we had made the holy Doctor manifestly guilty of violating faith and friendship? Would he not see that we had established a different sequence of events and different arguments, and that the date of the peace should consequently be extended later—if, indeed, he is wholly made of lead and did not understand this?

He understood it perfectly well, but he wished to be held in high esteem among his own people, so that he might appear to have corrected us. We, while safeguarding the interests of Rufinus and Jerome, on whose behalf this case was argued, concede the insult.

The remaining seven chapters of this Part—which follow these matters—we shall traverse with some irritation, noting only the more serious points so as to spare both time and style. For the Third Part, in which he discusses Rufinus’s Latin version of the *Ecclesiastical History*, we reserve for the preface to the following volume.

Almost the whole of Chapter XVI is insulting to Jerome. He is said both to have employed the same frauds of which he accuses his adversaries and to have fostered the monks’ schism. Here too he commits a prochronism.

The same defect appears in the next two chapters, where the entire sequence of Rufinus’s writings is overturned, the order of his journey from Rome to Aquileia is confused, and the history itself is thrown into disorder. Most foolish of all is his belief that Rufinus remained in Rome for two whole years.

Nothing is more stupid than the words with which Chapter XIX begins: “For some time Pammachius had begun to think less favorably of Rufinus’s faith, on the basis of Jerome’s Epistle 61”—that is, the book against John of Jerusalem. Yet throughout the Dissertation, and in chapters specifically devoted to the matter, this Carmelite has argued that the work is not Jerome’s but that of a foolish man deeply hostile to Bishop John. We reject this audacious invention.

He ought to have remembered that he is a liar. For now he contradicts himself and has so quickly forgotten his own earlier position. Let him not say that he is speaking from the commonly accepted title of the work. Apart from the fact that elsewhere he never calls it Jerome’s but an epistle by an unknown author, unless he truly believed it to be Jerome’s and wished it to be regarded as such, he would be acting still more foolishly in his own interest and deceiving the reader. For he adds that it was read to Pammachius, that Pammachius gave it credence, and that prejudice against Rufinus’s reputation was thereby created.

Did another author occur to him—one whom the real Pammachius might have taken for the real Jerome, who might himself have called him Jerome by name, and yet who was not Jerome?

But the absurdities do not yet end. As for the matter itself, the Carmelite again disagrees both with every appearance of truth and with himself. For, following Tillemont and other learned men, he does not deny that the epistle was neither completed by its author nor sent to Pammachius, but was in fact suppressed (Chapter VIII).

What, then, are these impostures? It was Jerome’s epistle, and yet it was not his, but belonged to a foolish and malicious man. It was sent to Pammachius, who nevertheless was not the real Pammachius, since he had not received it from the real Jerome. It was read to him and circulated among the public, from which envy against Rufinus arose; and at the same time it was suppressed in a chest, never brought forth, and indeed never even completed by its author. Can such an abundance of absurd circumlocution be packed into two little paragraphs?

Moreover, because of his ignorance, which requires the whole Rufinian history to be reported as having slipped backward, I must add one or two examples from the final chapters, so that it may be plainly evident how unprepared he was in learning and in every branch of humane studies when he undertook to write about Rufinus’s affairs.

It is manifestly inferred that Rufinus was not condemned by Anastasius from the fact that he continued to enjoy communion and friendship with the holy bishops of Italy, especially. That good man corrupts this noble argument by exaggerating it as follows:

> “Pauline, Bishop of Nola, in letters sent to Rufinus full of affection and goodwill, asked for and obtained an explanation of the patriarchal blessings. He also asked him, when passing through Rome, to be willing to meet him at Nola. Certainly he would not have honored the presbyter of Aquileia with such expressions of devotion if his condemnation had ever been issued; and he could not have been unaware of it, since he had his see in the Suburban Province, subject to Roman jurisdiction.”

Good heavens! What is mental folly, if this is not? When Paulinus wrote those letters, he was not yet a bishop but was serving only in the rank of presbyter. Rufinus, moreover, was not under any suspicion of corrupt doctrine, so that anyone should have needed to avoid his company. Finally, Anastasius did not yet occupy the Roman See, so that he could strike Rufinus with an anathema.

Yet he continues to pile error upon error:

> “And when Chromatius had been taken from the living, Rufinus, leaving Aquileia, withdrew to the monastery of Pinetum near the city of Classis. Do you suppose that so many religious men would have tolerated the companionship—let alone the communion—of a convicted proscribed heretic?”

Absurdities of the utmost absurdity, mere dreams. When Rufinus withdrew to the monastery of Pinetum, he had not yet come to Aquileia; he had scarcely returned from the East. Chromatius was certainly still alive, for he did not die until nearly nine years later. Finally, the monastery of Pinetum stood not near the city of Classis—which never existed—but neither at Classis near Ravenna. It stood on the coast of the Roman territory, toward Terracina.

Could anyone, deliberately seeking to make the common people laugh, utter more delirious nonsense in fewer words? But it is both tedious and shameful for us to linger over these matters any longer. The reader will easily understand, if he merely wishes to glance through that historical Dissertation, that there are many other things which, since they have little bearing on us, we conceal rather than expose his monstrous errors.

Let us return to our edition of Rufinus’s works and continue to remind the reader of what we accomplished in preparing it.

We begin with the two books *On the Blessings of the Patriarchs*. Among all the treatises of the presbyter of Aquileia, these hold first place both with respect to the Scripture they explain and because of their chronological priority, by which they precede his other earliest writings, as I prefer to call them.

We received these books from the Barrean edition, which is far more accurate than all the others and is said in its preface to have been copied from the most ancient handwritten exemplars of the monastery of Monte dei. Nevertheless, we also consulted another and older edition contained in the *Monuments of the Holy Fathers, the Orthodoxographers*, which we often found to be of sound value.

We also used a manuscript codex which the distinguished Father Abbot Trombellius carefully copied from the Library of Saint Savior at Bologna and sent to us. It is not very old, nor does it reproduce Rufinus’s own explanation—which is the central point of the matter—but rather another work of the same title, compiled by some diligent scholar. We presented a specimen of it in the third volume of the works of Jerome, in the Appendix.

Yet since it follows almost the same traces, and since its author repeatedly derives certain material from Rufinus’s work for his own interpretation, it easily assisted our recension and certainly contributed greatly to its elucidation [Col. 0057]. The novelty of the document and the selective importance of the material it contains also add to its value. For it had not previously been published in its entirety, but only in its first and very small portion. Nor have we described the whole thing in the notes, but only those passages that seemed especially worthy of reading and properly useful to our purpose.

I think we and our edition would have fared better if we had succeeded, as we most diligently attempted, in obtaining the manuscript of Murbach in Alsace and the variant readings copied from it. But our hope was disappointed. In the meantime, the one thing that was possible was accomplished: we filled the enormous lacuna of nearly ten lines in the preface from that manuscript, as Fontaninus quotes it, and thus seem to have restored the life and meaning of this work.

For the rest, it will be worthwhile to consult in advance what the same most distinguished scholar discusses at greater length concerning these books. By contrast, nearly everything Cacciarius writes about them is either false or almost worthless—especially his postponement of their composition as late as the year 408.

Next follows the *Commentary on the Apostles’ Creed*, a work containing nothing more illustrious or learned in the entire record of ecclesiastical antiquity. There is scarcely any other work among the writings of the holy Fathers—of which there are and have been so many—that has been more frequently published, revised, reprinted, and read, or more thoroughly polished and illuminated by the observations and studies of learned men.

We did not so much propose to imitate the most recent Balusian edition—whether that means the edition by the Parisian Benedictines who undertook to complete and publish Baluze’s posthumous work on Saint Cyprian, to whom this composition was once attributed—as to adorn it, although it is both the most recent and the most careful of all.

We collated it with other older printed books, which the editor just mentioned knew nothing of, and especially with the Barrean codex. We have shown throughout how much it cost him either to have been unaware of it or not to have consulted it.
