With the assistance of this and the other books mentioned above, we restored many passages that the work of so many otherwise highly learned men had left incomplete and that still required a physician’s hand.

Furthermore, when we observed that Rufinus had borrowed much from Cyril of Jerusalem, whom he had used as his teacher while living there, and that he had transferred into his own work long sections from Cyril’s *Exposition of the Faith*, which Cyril expounded in various catecheses and which Rufinus translated into Latin almost word for word, we called those passages into the discussion and examined each one against the Greek exemplar, which we frequently cite there.

As a result, not only did a more accurate reading become known than those previously current, but the deeper sense and the precise force of the words also became clear. You will learn from the notes what else we contributed to the commendation and adornment of this most divine book, so to speak.

Next comes the *History of the Hermits*, or *Lives of the Fathers*, or finally, as Fontaninus preferred to entitle it, the *History of the Monks*, together with the journeys through Egypt written under the name of Saint Petronius of Bologna.

We took this work from Rosweyde’s most elegant edition, and we append to the text the annotations of a man who was certainly not without learning and was otherwise extremely diligent. In some places, however, we also correct it.

For it departs too far from the truth when it supposes that the second book of the *Lives of the Fathers* can at least be attributed to Rufinus as translator. More serious perhaps is the error of believing that, in this single book—which is Rufinus’s genuine offspring—Rufinus himself narrates his own, rather than another person’s, journey through Egypt.

For this reason Rosweyde composed in full, as a kind of prelude, the history of Rufinus’s and Melania’s journeys, and repeatedly imbued his notes with the same hallucinations by which he had allowed his mind to be preoccupied. It was therefore our task to warn the reader, in the appropriate places, not to allow himself to be deceived, and to add brief reasons for the matter in notes marked with an asterisk.

We guard against his other errors elsewhere—for example, his belief that Rufinus borrowed certain passages from Palladius, whereas it is now completely clear that Palladius transferred certain material from Rufinus into his own work. Finally, we removed several textual errors and, whenever the opportunity arose, made the author’s text somewhat better.

From here we proceed to the *Ecclesiastical History*—not that of Eusebius of Caesarea, which Our Author reworked from Greek into Latin, since translations have no place here, but the history that he himself composed in two books and appended to Eusebius’s.

Fontaninus reviews and discusses, in his customary sufficiently full and careful manner, nearly all of its editions printed in typographical form. In the fourth year after Rufinus’s death, F. Cacciarius, whom we mentioned shortly above, published his own edition at Rome. On the title page he declares that he had collated it with Vatican manuscript codices and illustrated it with notes.

The reader is rightly entitled to ask me what my judgment of it is. But before I do so, I shall briefly explain what I accomplished in preparing my own edition, so as to remain more closely with the task I began.

I proposed to polish and adorn the Barrean exemplar, printed about 170 years ago, which in many places is more accurately corrected than any other. I also collated it from time to time with other older printed books, especially the Paris edition of 1523, which Boussard published after a second revision and which I repeatedly found to be of sound value.

I then used two manuscript codices, collated from beginning to end with the printed edition. Since they came from different regions, it was of considerable assistance to test their reliability by comparing their variant readings with one another.

The first was supplied by the recently praised Abbot Trombellius from the Library of the Monastery of Saint Savior at Bologna. The second, which is of somewhat better quality, we received from the celebrated Guarneriana Library in the municipality of San Daniele. The distinguished Dominicus Ongarus collated it with the greatest diligence and examined it with the care and learning required in handling books of this kind [Col. 0059]. He was director of studies at the Seminary of Udine, and he will be praised more than once below for the benefits he conferred on our Rufinus through his collations of manuscripts.

We could also have called the Vatican codices that Cacciarius transcribed into the discussion, since we did not blindly follow the reading he preferred. After reexamining each passage in full, we rejected many readings that he had admitted into the text; conversely, we supplied readings that he had approved less.

Let us now examine that edition. In the preface the editor praises five manuscript codices against which he collated it: three Vatican codices and two others from the same library, one belonging to Christina, Queen of Sweden, and the other Urbinate. In the notes he falsely calls the latter the more recent Regius, or Queen’s, codex, and here he begs pardon for that error.

All of them are indeed of relatively recent date and scarcely precede the inventions of the typographical art. But another inconvenience must also be added: he admits that he used them in such a way that “he considered it a matter of conscience to alter anything in the reading of earlier editors only with the support of at least two exemplars.”

Thus he preferred such a trivial agreement to the manifest soundness of a reading, the continuity of the text, and the other abundant principles of the Critical Art. I mean the Critical Art, which he holds in contempt and teaches those who profess and cultivate it to avoid. For he says in the preface:

> “For those who have devised subtler arguments concerning the reckoning of times, or who dispute about other matters of this kind, since for the most part they serve no other purpose than to weaken things that otherwise seemed certain, are, in my judgment, less useful for the instruction of the young than for imbuing them with a certain freedom of opinion, by which they become accustomed to call even the most important matters into doubt.”

It is therefore sufficiently clear what sort of talent he brought to this undertaking, what selection of readings he made, and what he discussed in the notes. The readings that ought to have been examined, so that they might easily be admitted into the text, he generally rejected for this one reason: that they were solitary. Yet for that very reason they deserved greater consideration, as they truly do among those who understand manuscripts, because they reveal themselves to have been copied from an archetype belonging either to another place or to another hand. They are the readings that a bookseller dictated from one exemplar to various scribes.

As for the readings he admitted because they were commended by the testimony of several codices, if he had examined the matter properly, there would have been no reason to receive them merely because of the larger number of witnesses. Numerical support is not worth much when the codices agree with one another in everything and appear to have been copied one from another; in that case only the authority of a single codex should be recognized.

You will learn from a comparison with our edition how well he performed his work in other respects. If I tried to pursue the matter in detail, I should never reach the end of this preface.

Of his annotations—by which I mean those chiefly concerning this part of Rufinus’s history—he says in the preface to Volume I that “he used the particular method of defending his reading against excessively intemperate criticism, while also preparing for curious youth agreeable and sufficiently useful information concerning geography.”

Yet nearly all of them teach nothing other than what everyone knows, what may be sought from lexicographers, or what finally supplies new material for stale hallucinations.

One example should be presented so that what we have said may be established by an instance. Rufinus relates in Book II, Chapter XXIII, the destruction of Serapis: a soldier seized a double axe, struck the idol, and with repeated blows hacked at the smoky spirit of the rotten wood.

That good man annotates the passage as follows: “Theophilus also uses these words, ‘smoky spirit,’ when speaking of the Alexandrian temple of Serapis in his Synodical Epistle.” The latest editor of the works of Saint Jerome, however, thinks that the reading was **ὲνιον**, or **κὲνὶον** [sic], meaning a place where guests were received.

Consider, I beg you, reader, how many falsehoods, slanders, and absurdities he packs into so few words. Theophilus complains that the factional Origenists brought forward a woman and her adolescent son, on whose account Isidore was being badly spoken of, and placed them in a famous place in the city, “which,” he says, “I think they call *Genium*.” That is the whole of Theophilus’s meaning.

It is therefore false, first, that Cacciarius says Theophilus uses the words “smoky spirit.” It is false, next, that he says Theophilus is speaking of the Alexandrian temple of Serapis, a thought farther from his mind than anything could be. For apart from the fact that Theophilus expressly called it a famous place in the city—a street, perhaps, or a marketplace, or something similar—not a temple, the Serapeum no longer existed at that time. Theophilus himself had destroyed it and leveled it to the ground nearly ten years before writing these words.

It is false, third—and this is Cacciarius’s principal point—that the word *genius*, which alone Theophilus uses, even if the manuscript reading were correct, has anything in common in meaning with the smoky spirit of Serapis.

As for me, the editor of Jerome, I demonstrated with firm arguments that this epistle, which I also showed to be Theophilus’s Synodical Epistle translated into Latin by Jerome, was recovered by me for the first time from ancient parchment manuscripts, among which it had lain hidden almost until its death. I communicated it to the literary world as one of the most precious monuments of antiquity.

In the notes with which I undertook to illustrate it, I suspected that the passage just mentioned should be understood as **Ξένιον**, *Xenion*, rather than *Genium*, and that it denoted a place where strangers or guests gathered—namely, a square or street of foreigners.

Let us grant to the religious man’s ingenuity that he kept silent about the singular service I rendered to good letters, especially to sacred learning, by publishing this edition of the epistle, and preferred to send his reader to a work nowhere previously heard of or read rather than mention it with at least the praise of novelty that arose from noting the discovery.

But what is this, if not an attempt to impose upon the unlearned public with complete confidence and to fabricate the most obvious slander against me? It is false, fourth, that I said Theophilus pointed to a place where guests were received, as though I had written *xenodochium*. I said that it was a marketplace or street of foreigners, or a place where guests gathered.

For the proper name of the place—whether it was supplied by Jerome the translator, since the Alexandrian bishop could hardly have spoken hesitantly of the name of a famous Alexandrian street, or whether it was added by the author himself—must have been Greek, even if written in Latin letters. But *Genium* is not Greek and signifies nothing in Greek. I therefore rightly suspected that it had been corrupted by a Latin copyist, misled either by pronunciation or by the similarity of a more familiar word.

Accordingly, I proposed in the notes to the learned reader that a Greek word close to it and suitable to the proposed meaning of a famous place should be substituted. I suggested **Ξένιον**, believing that its etymology could suitably be derived from the gathering of guests.

Let others decide what mark should be branded upon the man who corrupts my words in order to appear to correct them.

Meanwhile, it is false, fifth, that he says I wrote **ὲνιον**, or **κὲνὶον** [sic]—monstrous verbal forms that he himself manufactured from his own brain—and that he adds, with a new and therefore particularly unjust reinforcement of the falsehood, that I thought these words signified the place designated by Theophilus.

I wrote one and only one Greek word: **Ξένιον**. He must have stripped himself of all shame who ascribes to me those two forms, more corrupt than which I do not know whether anything could be invented. For they signify nothing either in Greek or in Latin and are afflicted by several additional errors of writing, so that not even Oedipus could interpret them.

Nevertheless, you should not think that they were fabricated without malicious intent. They were devised precisely so that, among the unlearned and among those least eager to know the truth, they might bring disgrace upon the editor of Jerome, and so that the man who noted them might appear to be somebody.

I pass over the hallucinations and absurdities contained in these falsehoods; if I wished to place even one or two before the reader’s eyes, I should make this too long.

In truth, what is more careless than this man’s conduct? He insists that Rufinus’s “smoky spirit” corresponds to Theophilus’s *Genium*, yet praises us even though we have shown that the passage should be read differently and that it contains not *Genium* but **Ξένιον**.

If he thought *Genium* was the correct reading, why does he cite us when we reject it, and fail even verbally to refute us, appearing rather to agree? If he agrees with us and does not deny that the reading is corrupt, what does Theophilus’s **Ξένιον** have to do with the *Genium* of his own author?

Furthermore, what kind of mental frivolity is it to explain an unknown word by producing an even more obscure one, and to pronounce that as a pair with another which is not even similar and whose meaning he does not know? But let us at last withdraw our foot from this mire.

Rufinus’s reading was certainly not so insignificant that it should be compared with a copyist’s error in another author. We have once more examined it more carefully for the text, and now seem, after a second revision, to have approached the truth much more closely than we previously thought in our notes on that passage.

At first glance it seemed that *Genium* was written in Latin as a proper word, equivalent—though ironically—to Rufinus’s having said *deum*, “god”: “he hacks at the smoky *Genium* of the rotten wood”—that is, the god.

Now, however, it seems preferable to derive the name from Greek and to understand it properly as referring to the chin of the idol, which the soldier struck. I mean the Greek word **γένειον**, which means “chin” and is sometimes used for the face. For one also frequently encounters **γένεια** in the plural, meaning cheeks or jaws; lexicographers explain it as “beard,” “face,” and “jaw.”

Indeed, only three lines earlier the author said that the soldier first struck the old man’s jaw with a double axe, and then, repeating his blows, hacked at the smoky **γένειον** of the rotten wood.

And so that you may have no doubt that it signifies a part of the face, or the mouth of the idol, he constructs his account of the shattered image according to the order of its limbs. He immediately adds that the cast-down part, the **γένειον**, was set on fire and burned; then that the head was torn from the neck and, its modius having been knocked down, dragged apart with ropes; then that the remaining limbs were hacked to pieces with axes, and that, limb by limb, the image of the decrepit old man was burned throughout knife-bearing Alexandria.

He therefore wrote nothing there except **γένειον**, signifying the chin and beard—the projecting part that could be knocked off while the head was still almost intact.

He wrote it in Greek, not Latin, for two reasons: the Greek **γένειον** conveys somewhat more than the Latin *mentum*, “chin,” and he preferred to call it by its proper name, since it was almost peculiar and characteristic of the idol.

That part of the image was indeed more conspicuous than all the others: a goat-like beard, extending nearly to the middle of the chest, rounded and cylindrical in form, and so much more wedge-shaped toward the bottom that one can see it in the surviving images of that ridiculous god, one of which, made of bronze, we have before our eyes in our household museum.

Finally, that Rufinus wrote the word in Greek rather than Latin is proved by the hallucination of the Latin copyists themselves. They rendered the Greek word in Latin letters of the same number and, writing **γένειον**, produced *Genium*.

But enough of this.

Two books of the *Apology against Jerome* follow, together with an *Apology to Anastasius* appended in the same way. Although we included all of them in the Jerome collection of works as well, since they chiefly belonged there, I think the Reader will not find it unwelcome to have them presented here again in their proper place, adorned with a new appearance, so that they may seem almost to be different works. The amount of labor we have devoted to polishing them again and again will be demonstrated by the dense observations and notes that, when they were printed among the Jerome materials, we were formerly able to treat less diligently, since they stood in a foreign setting.

Nor at that time were we able to consult any books other than those previously published. Now we have enjoyed better fortune, and, with considerable assistance, have received very much from the Guarnerian manuscript. This manuscript is from the same library in the municipality of San Daniele which we praised earlier—the former Guarnerian Library—and it was likewise communicated to us by the distinguished man Domenico Ongaro, whom we mentioned there with praise and whom we again name here for the sake of honor.

It is not, indeed, a manuscript either of particularly ancient age, or one immediately suitable for establishing confidence; nor, what matters more, is it of sufficiently sound correction and quality. Nevertheless, it benefited us as much as manuscripts of the best quality and correction, and likewise of the greatest antiquity, ever could have done. For it was copied, as it reveals by many indications, from a very old manuscript, and specifically from one in the Aquileian archives, where the work was first written by the Author himself and was afterward preserved and more carefully maintained as part of the ancestral collection.

Finally, it was copied by a sufficiently unskilled antiquary—a man, however, who was by no means bad—who often makes scribal errors and departs from correct writing, but either does not dare, or does not know how, to add anything of his own. Certainly, in investigating the truth of the reading, he sometimes benefited us by his very errors, and at his prompting rather than at his command we restored passages that were neither insignificant nor few. Otherwise, whenever it differs from the printed texts in a consistent and correct reading—and it differs in many places—it rightly demands that confidence be placed in it; and it is almost certain that it often offers readings that are much closer to the truth.

Recall what we stated above, where, in discussing the *Life of Rufinus*, we printed an example from its distinctive reading (*Book II*, no. 12): by this reading Rufinus is proved to have stayed in Alexandria for a second period of two years, whereas until now he has been said to have remained there only a few days.

With these apologetic books, then—including the little work that he wrote to Anastasius, which we likewise edited according to the Guarnerian copy and improved in many places—the entire collection of Rufinian works that he himself published at his own expense, and which we call the original works, is brought to completion.

The genuine offspring of Rufinus is followed by spurious progeny. These are not, as is commonly the case with others, of servile and contemptible condition, such as would disgrace the Aquileian Presbyter; rather, they are of noble character and talent, and can stand alongside the genuine works without lacking dignity.

In order of arrangement, the first place is occupied by the *Commentary on the First Seventy-Five Psalms*. It would take too long either to report here all that Fontanini or all that we have observed in our annotations. It is preferable instead to investigate the Author of the work and to set forth the conjectures we have made.

For this purpose, what deserves notice above all is that the Author reveals himself, by no obscure indication, to have been a Gaul by nationality. In the brief preface to the title of Psalm XV, speaking of the arches that, as he says, people formerly had constructed for themselves whenever they celebrated a triumph over an enemy, he mentions no other than the arch at Arausio, which he perhaps had before his eyes, or certainly had not far away. “Hence,” he adds, “on the triumphal arch at Arausio, the Massilian war is represented in sculpture as a sign of Caesar’s victory.”

By Arausio I understand no other city than the one called Arausio, Arausiensis, and the city of the Arausians, which the Gauls now call Orange. Another observation will confirm the same point.

Although the Author frequently transcribes a large part of his Commentary from Augustine in exactly the same words, he does not use the version of Holy Scripture that Augustine used, but the Vulgate, which is specifically called the Gallican version and received its name from the use of that Church. The passages are too numerous, and occur in almost every treatise, to be produced here merely as evidence. At the beginning of the work, and wherever he transfers longer portions into his own text, we indicated them by noting Augustine’s name; later, by adding only quotation marks, we marked the passage as borrowed from him.

One may therefore look into the book and marvel at the skill of the excerptor, who is so scrupulous about departing from the Vulgate—that is, from the Gallican Scripture—that he is sometimes forced to speak ineptly and to depart from his subject in another direction. For when Augustine adheres closely in his explanation to the wording of the version he uses, our Author, in copying that explanation, fits it badly to the reading of his own version and misses the point.

You may therefore reasonably infer from this as well that he was a man from the Church of Gaul, who considered himself altogether unable to use any Psalter other than the Gallican Circle, as it is called—that is, the version of the Psalms received among his own people.

Moreover, he appears to have undertaken this work of explaining the Psalter for monks and to have delivered sermons in the assembly of the brethren. He sometimes addresses the brethren and speaks of the duties of monks. In Psalm XLI, verse 10:

> “We have great confidence, brethren, because God is our protector.”

And shortly before this, at verse 8, concerning their vices:

> “Hypocrites, wicked pretenders, joining themselves with feigned love . . . Many such are found within the society of the brethren,” and so forth.

A little later:

> “Do you wish to know what sort of heart a brother has? Observe what he prefers to talk about,” and so forth.

Then:

> “Let us guard, brethren, our entrance; let us remain inside,” and so forth.

Here wandering eyes and curiosity are noted, a vice that is accustomed to harm the Converts especially severely. Finally:

> “These are the three pursuits of idle men in the monastery: wandering eyes, an excess of words, and perversity of thoughts. These three vices drive a brother from the monastery.”

Indeed, the passage in Psalm XLV, no. 11, does not allow us to doubt that he himself lived with monks:

> “For this purpose we have now left behind the impediments of the world and the cares of the age, and have entered the seclusion of the MONASTERY, so that we may be more freely available to God.”

And near the end he indicates that he had also attended their choir, as it is called, or the stations of the singers:

> “In this Psalm, which we heard sung, to which we responded by singing, and about which we are going to say what you know.”

Was he therefore himself living as a monk, and was he one of their number, devoted to the institutions of monastic life? There seems to be no room for doubt, but only with the qualification that he was also distinguished by the dignity of the presbyterate. For we learn from the example of Saint Leo, who prohibited the practice in his Letter to Maximus of Antioch, that:

> “Apart from those who are the Lord’s priests, no one could claim for himself the right to teach and preach, whether he were a monk or a layman who prided himself on possessing some kind of knowledge.”

Accordingly, in ancient times monasteries contained one or more presbyters from among the monks themselves who performed the office of teacher (*Palladius, Lausiac History*, chapter 118; *Against John of Jerusalem*). Saint Jerome mentions five in his own monastery, which we understand to have consisted of four hundred brethren. That a presbyterate could be conferred without removing the monk from the monastic order, we learn from the example of the same holy Father.

The Author of this Commentary was therefore both a Gaul by nationality and a presbyter in a monastery; and, as is clear from this labor of his, he was neither uneducated nor merely superficially practiced in the use of the sacred writings.

Consider now whether he may appear to have been Vincent the Presbyter, whom Gennadius praises in chapter 80:

> “Vincent the Presbyter, himself also a Gaul by nationality and practiced in the divine Scriptures, possessing a tongue polished by the practice of speaking and by extensive reading, composed a commentary on the Psalms. He read some of this work to the man of God, Cannata, in my hearing, promising at the same time that, if the Lord granted him life and strength, he would labor with the same zeal over the whole Psalter.”

The fact that he calls him only a presbyter, and not also a monk, is certainly nothing more than an honorific designation according to the custom of those times, especially in relation to such men. Otherwise, the mention of Cannata and of Gennadius himself—who associated familiarly with him—shows that he belonged to the company of monks.

This also makes it possible to conjecture that he was not situated far away, since he had at some time lived among them and himself mentions the cities of Massilia and Arausio. He may readily seem, therefore, to have come from Provence or from Narbonese Gaul.

The remaining details fit even better, especially the fact that he is said to have been the Author of an incomplete Commentary, or one not yet completed on all the Psalms. For our Author’s work is half of the whole: it embraces in its explanation only the first seventy-five Psalms.

Finally, the chronology also agrees. We know that Gennadius’s Vincent became famous in the year 480—for he is a different person from the one whose Vincentian objections Saint Prosper refuted—and our Author appears to have turned his mind to writing at approximately that time, although it cannot be asserted with certainty. Many indications contained throughout the entire book point in that direction.

Our Author, then, appears to be no other than this Vincent. If you accept that conclusion, this Vincent is ultimately the true Author of the Commentary that the ancient manuscripts attributed to Rufinus, while more recent critics attributed it to an uncertain Author.

As for the work we devoted to polishing it, I would prefer that you learn about it from our annotations. I will state only one point in advance: while, with the help of Augustine’s Commentary and the Benedictine edition, I removed many corruptions from this Author’s text, I also corrected not a few passages in Augustine by means of this Author’s text—readings that had escaped the diligence of the very great editors [*τῶν πάνυ Ἐκδοτῶν*].

The second work is a Commentary on the three Minor Prophets Hosea, Joel, and Amos; but identifying its Author is much more difficult. The reasons why it is certainly not that Rufinus are already known to scholars, and Fontanini adduces sufficiently good arguments. If we linger over those arguments by expounding them more fully, though they would indeed be readily available, we would seem merely to be doing again what has already been done.

It will therefore be enough to investigate more carefully—something no one else has attempted—who the true Author of the Commentary was, and to try to discover his proper name and circumstances. Let us see by what indications this may be achieved.

First, the Author treats the great Jerome badly and shows himself unjust toward his labors. This was formerly the occasion for his being regarded as Rufinus. In the Preface he says that Jerome, in his Commentaries, when he insisted that the sequence of the text must be investigated, since the authority of the explanation ought to depend upon it, either did not wish or was unable to sustain the labor involved.

“Thus,” he adds, “his entire discourse flowed away either through Origen’s allegories or through the Jews’ fabulous traditions.”

In Hosea, chapter XI:

> “When Jerome wished to explain this verse, he proceeded to enumerate those who were said to have founded cities,” and so forth.

Who could consider such a color of explanation without ridicule?

At the beginning of Joel, he attacks him without naming him:

> “Certain commentators have pursued even the etymologies of names, gathering from them, so to speak, the seeds of praise—that is, Joel, *ἀρχόμενος* [‘beginning’] . . . . . These things, however childish and foolish they are, seem to involve more trouble than benefit.”

A little later:

> “Some have believed that there is a great difference among these terms, and on this account have expended a great deal of useless speech.”

Farther below, again, where he discusses the caterpillar, locust, and cankerworm, which Jerome interprets from Jewish traditions as enemies of the state:

> “Hence we refute the opinion of those who judge that all these things are spoken of enemies.”

He attacks him much more sharply in chapter II, concerning Peter, who had quoted part of the passage from Hosea:

> “For this reason we briefly call attention to it, so that the audacity of those who rashly and incompetently assert such things may be rejected,” and so forth.

He says similar things in chapter III.

In Amos, chapter II, near the end, concerning a certain Jewish tradition reported by the holy Doctor:

> “Since we do not regard this as of great weight, let us pass on to other matters.”

The same example appears at the end of the following chapter, chapter III:

> “For it is not my intention to pursue everything, including matters that may appear less important.”

Nor could he spare Jerome’s name for long. In chapter V he treats it with such abuse as this:

> “Jerome, in this passage, accepted an opinion so wretched that he said, ‘because for forty years,’” and so forth.

See our notes on that passage.

In the passages that follow, he is content, one might say, to brand Jerome’s doctrine with disgrace: in chapter VII he says that it contradicts history, and in chapter IX that it is refuted by the context of the passage.

Next we must investigate who the Author himself was, of what peoples, and of what institution. That he was a Latin must be beyond doubt. It must likewise be regarded as certain that he traveled at some time into the East and visited Syria, Palestine, and the Holy Places.

For in the Preface he boasts of knowing Greek interpreters and—something wholly unusual in a Latin writer—Syrians. In his Commentary on chapter I, verse 2, he presents the opinion held by Palestine and Egypt, that is, by the Churches of those regions and by those who everywhere knew the Scriptures there, concerning Hosea’s spiritual marriage, as something borrowed and heard from them by report; and he expounds all his arguments through that material.

On the other hand, he recounts in detail what position the Syrians took, and what arguments were used by those who believed that the marriage had been fulfilled carnally. He does so in a manner that sufficiently indicates that he received the account from their own mouths and made use of their customary way of thinking.

For if he had brought forward their written works, he would not have said simply “the Palestinians, Egyptians, Syrians,” and so forth. Rather, to establish credibility, he would have named some particular person who had committed their opinions to writing.

Add to this that it is scarcely plausible that he could have understood the language of the Syrians without having spent some time among them. If you object that he may nevertheless appear to have known it only imperfectly, I reply that he did not therefore read their writings but heard the matter from them as they related it.

For it is much easier to learn such opinions from the mouths of several people, in person from people present, than from books. Moreover, most of the Syrians knew Greek, and finally more than one Westerner—many of whom were living there in devotion to the Holy Places—could interpret into Latin.

As for his nationality, we think that he was a Spaniard. For, as we shall explain in its proper place below, he seems to lament the disasters of that region so grievously that it is unlikely he would lament those of any other land than his native country, which the Vandals in fact treated more harshly than the others.

This conjecture is made more plausible, and almost certain, by the distinctive Latin version of the Psalms that he uses. Since the old translation of this book, which everyone was accustomed to sing in sacred assemblies, necessarily remained in use, Jerome’s revision nevertheless prevailed in almost all of Gaul and in very many parts of Italy.

The version used by our Author differs almost continuously from that one, and frequently from the other ancient editions of the Psalter as well. Nor does it agree with Augustine’s correction or with the more ancient reading of the African Fathers.

Finally, no version seems able to come closer to the truth than the one that was once used in the Churches of Spain. Examples of this are found everywhere. One particularly striking example occurs in Psalm 138, at the beginning of Amos IX:

> “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you will be present. If I take my wings before the light and dwell at the farthest ends of the sea, there your hand will lead me, and your right hand will hold me. Even if I say, ‘The darkness will conceal me, and the night will be my consolation,’” and so forth.

I would particularly like the word *occultabunt* (“will conceal”) to be considered more carefully in place of the usual *conculcabunt* (“will trample”). See our discussion there.

Furthermore, his way of life reveals him to have been a churchman and therefore at least a presbyter. For, in preparing his explanations of Holy Scripture, he repeatedly indicates that he is speaking to the people.

At the end of his exposition of Joel, chapter I, he says:

> “In this passage, certainly, the diligent Auditor should inquire what beauty is praised in the deserts,” and so forth.

A little later:

> “If you consider it carefully, our Auditor, you will see that weight lies in the example.”

I will not deny that the term *Auditor* was used, as Varro reports, for a reader. But I will never be persuaded that our Author used it in that more obsolete sense. For he also addresses those simply standing before him in Amos, chapter I, verse 2, where, speaking of the causes of earthquakes, he says:

> “It is not necessary now to rehearse these matters to you.”

He therefore delivered these sermons, at least in part, in churches. Consequently, as was also noted above, if he was not a bishop, he was certainly a presbyter.

Let us now investigate the time at which he wrote this Commentary.

Fontanini reasons as follows: because the Author mentions the Commentaries of Saint John Chrysostom and Jerome on the Minor Prophets, but says nothing about Cyril of Alexandria and Theodoret, who dealt with the same subject, he thinks that the Author began the work no earlier than the middle of the fifth century.

Although this conjecture may perhaps come close to the truth, his reasoning is nevertheless weak and almost false. For although the Author does not praise Cyril and Theodoret by name, he could easily have included them in the statement that some such interpreters existed among the Greeks, from whom he had read a few things by Saint John Chrysostom.

We prefer to derive our argument from the fact that, as we have said, he presents himself as a rather unaccommodating reader of Jerome. From this we infer that he wrote shortly after the holy Doctor’s death.

After his death, I say. No one could persuade himself that a man of otherwise sound piety and faith would attack Jerome while he was alive, if he knew him and had no personal grievance against him. But a few years after Jerome’s death, before the reputation of the Jerome name had spread throughout almost the entire world—especially among those who spoke his language—to such an extent that it would have seemed sacrilegious even to write against him, a man who was not uneducated could freely state in writing opinions different from his.

I would therefore place the date of this Commentary roughly between the twentieth and thirtieth years after four hundred—that is, around A.D. 420–430. It could scarcely have been written much later, when no one remained who did not consider it a point of honor to praise Jerome more gloriously.

The same period is also indicated by the evils of the age that the Author laments. In Amos, chapter I, near the end, he says:

> “All these evils come through the victory of the enemy, as we demonstrate more by yearly disasters than by written annals.”

More vehemently still, in chapter VIII, at verse 10, where he speaks of sackcloth and baldness as signs of calamity:

> “Would that we knew this whole matter—which perhaps usually occurs during the time of captivity—only from the indication of the reading! But the condition of such things has become so common in our times that we must marvel at the audacity of those who hope for anything better.”

This was indeed the miserable condition of the Roman world, and especially of Spain, from approximately the year 410 for nearly thirty continuous years, during which those provinces were ravaged by sword and fire, both through the varying outcomes of wars and through the repeated incursions of barbarian enemies.

Read Prosper’s *Chronicle*, so that you may understand how well the account of those times—which we assign as the final period of this Commentary—accords with the adverse fortune with which Spain struggled longer and more severely than other lands.

I add that he also prepared a Commentary on the Books of Solomon, and prepared it before writing this one. He himself testifies to this in the Preface, where he says:

> “In explaining the volumes of Solomon, we have pursued the glory of his [God’s] arrangements, insofar as it was possible for us to do so.”

Now, when all these indications have been gathered together, either I am greatly mistaken, or this is none other than the celebrated Paulus Orosius, toward whom all the evidence points with perfect clarity.

Everyone knows that he was a presbyter. The anonymous writer of Melk, in chapter LXIX, reports that he was also regarded as a bishop:

> “The venerable Orosius, believed to have been a bishop.”

That he was a Spaniard by nationality is likewise generally known. Gennadius, chapter XXXIX:

> “Orosius, a presbyter, Spanish by birth,” and so forth.

It is also very well known that he once went to the East, and specifically that he was at Jerusalem in the year 415 and at the beginning of the following year. This is attested by Augustine’s and Jerome’s reciprocal letters concerning him, by his own *Apology*, and finally by the entire history of the Pelagian controversy [Col. 0069].

Gennadius again says:

> “This is Orosius, who was sent by Augustine to Jerome to learn about the nature of the soul,” and so forth.

From this it is also clear that he became famous in literature precisely in the period to which we have assigned the Commentary.

Nothing is more fitting or more plausible than that, after returning from Africa and from Augustine, to whom he had gone back, Orosius later composed this work in his homeland, a few years afterward.

Indeed, the anonymous writer of Melk, whom we have just cited, reports that Orosius published a Commentary under this title:

> “Among other works, he writes a Commentary on the Twelve Prophets.”

That is, on the book that, as we showed elsewhere in relation to Jerome, was entitled *The Twelve Prophets*. It makes no difference that this surviving work covers not all twelve but only the first three, since it is nevertheless correctly designated by that title.

Trithemius, in chapter XII, also bears witness that Orosius wrote on the books of Solomon; among these works he lists one on the *Song of Songs*.

One matter remains, and it may seem somewhat more difficult to believe: namely, that Orosius could repeatedly oppose and censure the great Jerome, at whose feet he had said in his *Apology* that he had sat, and whose eloquence against the Pelagians the entire West awaited like dew upon a fleece.

We have already indicated that this was the character of the man: perhaps excessively outspoken and ardent, he believed that he could state freely what he thought without diminishing the celebrity of Jerome’s name or the esteem in which he held him—which was certainly very high.

For in other places he praises Jerome; and even in this very work, in which he occasionally reproaches him, he grants him the greatest possible praise by making the very material of his own exposition Jerome’s translation from the Hebrew—a translation disliked by many and approved by almost no one, or by very few, before him—while the old version, which had long been in everyone’s hands, was set aside and marked as having corrupted expression and obscured meaning [in the Preface].

This great and distinguished achievement is so closely joined to the highest esteem for Jerome’s learning that the latter can scarcely, or perhaps not at all, be diminished by the passages and words in which some of Jerome’s opinions are refuted.

That Orosius was by nature the sort of man who felt whatever he believed very strongly, and who, according to the circumstances, took courage to himself, will be demonstrated by his often-mentioned *Apology*. In it he does not hesitate to accuse John of Jerusalem, a man of such rank, of favoring the Pelagian party, and he attacks him with almost abusive language.

Against Jerome, by contrast, he brings what I might call a literary charge, and he does so in a genre of writing in which it seems permissible for anyone to lay aside deference and refute whatever he judges incongruous or false among the opinions of different writers. Nor should he be regarded as having held Jerome in contempt merely because he sometimes differs from him.

In a word, this is not ultimately the reason why I reject the Commentary as Orosius’s. All the remaining indications identify him as its Author.

And these, Most Illustrious and Most Reverend Patriarch Delphinus, are the matters that, with my studies, I have contributed toward polishing Rufinus, chiefly from Your archetypal manuscripts. It is right that they be credited to You, and it is highly honorable to me to have presented them before Your judgment—for I would rather have my work criticized by Your judgment than praised by that of others.

[Col. 0069]

### Old Preface

To the most highly adorned and most learned man, Lord Giovanni of Saint Andrew, Canon of the Church of Paris:

Renatus Laurentius de la Barre, greeting.

How much is owed to you, D. de Saint-André, who strive with tireless zeal to give antiquity newness, authority to new things, polish to neglected things, light to obscure things, and—to use the whole of Pliny’s period—grace to things held in contempt, credibility to doubtful matters, and to everything its proper nature, together with all that belongs to its nature: this, I have always judged extremely difficult to express in words; indeed, I scarcely thought it possible to grasp it even in thought for one who fears the criticism of learned and prudent men.

Marcus Tullius, whom Latin eloquence proudly claims as its parent, in the fifth book of the *Tusculan Disputations* counted among the chief blessings of life—and considered that day more solemnly than any other—the day on which he discovered Archimedes’ tomb, long unknown to the Syracusans, who denied that it existed at all, enclosed on every side and covered with thorn bushes and tangled brush. For he retained certain little iambic verses which he had learned were inscribed on the monument: they declared that at the top of the tomb there was a sphere placed together with a cylinder. Thus that most noble city of Greece, once also the most learned, would have remained ignorant of the monument of one exceptionally brilliant citizen, had it not learned of it from a man of Arpinum.

[Col. 0071]

It would likewise have remained ignorant of the divine poems of its greatest poet, Homer, whose authority had elsewhere been entrusted with correcting the Greek language—the *Odyssey* and the *Iliad*—had Lycurgus of Sparta not brought them from Ionia into Greece, and had Pisistratus not later gathered their scattered portions and arranged them in the form in which they are read today, with Aristarchus employed as guide. No one has yet declared how much is owed to these men, nor perhaps will anyone ever declare it: so long as there are people who derive some benefit from their work. Indeed, no adequate commendation can ever be found for such watchfulness, toil, and sweat as their corrections required; far less can an equivalent reward be rendered for their merits.

The studies of other scholars have their own pleasures and varied retreats, by which the weariness of reading is relieved through new discoveries. But those who labor with Herculean effort to investigate and restore the monuments of antiquity—what, I ask, can they have to refresh their study? What can shake off their weariness, except another weariness? Thus, if some pleasure occasionally floods them from the discovery of the writings of an author, then, when they examine and repair those same writings because of lacunae, corrupt passages, halved pages, and characters eaten away, more sorrow arises than the delight previously gained from the discovery. I know some who, despairing of correcting treasures of this sort that they themselves had found, preferred to suppress them entirely rather than publish them in any condition—richer, certainly, in falsehoods than in syllables.

Therefore, if I may briefly wander from my subject, it would sometimes have been preferable for certain works now circulated never to have been printed than to have been printed in such a way that they are more truly seedbeds of errors and corruptions than of learning. And indeed, what limit can there be when we pursue almost everything by conjecture? What certainty can there be when one divines what may have occurred to someone else’s mind? Where, finally, is there any place of escape through the sandbanks and reefs of uncertainty, when we see eminent men becoming stranded, running aground, and quarrelling in shoal waters, raising great waves in a little dish, and sometimes making great tragedies out of trifles?

What makes all labor futile is that new editions follow every new correction. Moreover, we see other difficulties of this kind arising which, although they diminish confidence, do not lessen the difficulty of the task. Those who devote themselves to correcting and publishing authors must endure many things: they must doubt, consider, and examine both the greatest and the smallest matters, whenever anyone else has treated the same subject; and they must often change many things and restore some passages while conjecturing from the most insignificant details.

How much labor this involves is known to not a few men of our age—but to you above all, most accomplished sir. You, supremely experienced in these matters, never cease, with the greatest increase of learning and enrichment of the literary commonwealth, to bring excellent authors forth daily from your rich library. Out of your grateful devotion to the republic of letters, and at great expense, you search everywhere for manuscripts of the highest accuracy, against which printed books might be collated, and for works that might once again be printed with some real benefit.

Indeed, I have long heard learned men testify that no one among those then living—let envy be absent from the statement—had applied the *Chiromachian hand* to the book trade more successfully or beneficially than you; no one had more generously aided, enlarged, and promoted the printing of the finest authors, whose works scholars now enjoy reading. I am accustomed to say that you yourself were preserved by the best and greatest God for these calamitous times so that letters might not grow obsolete, and so that there might be someone to illuminate the honorable contests of printers concerning honorable subjects.

The many and substantial volumes that have appeared with some preface bearing your name have long testified to this. The work of Rufinus, now being published for the first time, will also testify to it. When you had indicated that a copy should be sought from my teacher, the theologian D. de la Bigne—most deserving in our age both for the purity of his character and for his extraordinary learning—from the remains of the venerable monastery of Mont-de-Dieu, it came about that amid the ruins of that devout house divine providence caused an ancient codex, though not intact after so many years, at least to be found in some sense almost whole, having escaped the ravages of our Gnostics.

Against such injuries and against the incursions of similar destroyers, if there is any means of defense, it must be summoned from the printing press. Printing alone, by the greatest gift of God, has refreshed the minds of men who in declining ages had already grown nauseated with study; by its pleasant facility it has restored writings to favor through their beauty and, at the same time, bestowed immortality upon them.

Would that this invention of God had been known in earlier ages! We would not have suffered so great a loss of the books and manuscripts that have been destroyed, especially through the warlike incursions of the Goths. The library of Pisistratus, Attalus, and Eumenes would not have perished; nor that of Ptolemy Philadelphus, which was consumed by fire during the reign of Augustus; nor that of Gordian, which contained more books than any other man possessed treasures of gold or silver, being rich in sixty-two thousand volumes of the greatest antiquity; nor that of the martyr Pamphilus, from which Eusebius drew his history; nor that library of one hundred and twenty thousand books which was destroyed at Byzantium by a most devastating fire under the Emperor Zeno; nor, again, that of King Matthias of Hungary, which in the memory of our fathers was scattered by the cruel invasion of the Turks.

Finally, the Vatican library of the Roman pontiffs, abundantly supplied under Clement VII with the most ancient Hebrew, Greek, and Latin books, as well as with the finest authors both ancient and recent, in manuscript and in print, would not have been burned by German and Spanish soldiers, carrying away so many books with them. Copies printed elsewhere in great abundance would still be extant—not, as happened, only a few copies, and those transcribed most corruptly by unskilled scribes.

Every nation would have possessed its own writers, and its own native works. The men most devoted to antiquity would have had no cause for complaint; nor would we have needed to search every region of the world to discover whether some bookworm was concealing something that ought to be brought into the light and displayed to the world.

There would have been no need for the Reverend Father in Christ, D. d’Albone, Prince of the Church of Lyon, to examine the cracks in the very ancient monastery of the island of Barbata in search of Rufinus of Aquileia’s commentaries on the seventy-five Psalms of David. Nor would we likewise have needed finally to commit the remains of Mont-de-Dieu to print for perpetual remembrance, since we would have possessed all the writings of all authors—and especially everything our Rufinus wrote: one book on the prophet Hosea, another on Amos, one on Joel, one book on his faith addressed to Laurence the bishop, one book on the sacraments, one book of exhortation to Proba, two books of letters to various persons, and one book according to the threefold sense of divine Scripture, which he wrote in Latin for Paulinus, bishop of Nola, at Paulinus’ request, concerning the blessing of the patriarch Judah.

Afterward, at the same Paulinus’ earnest insistence, we would have had a second book addressed to him, in which Rufinus treated the blessings of the other eleven patriarchs with a threefold exposition. Finally, from that same author we would have possessed, besides the works that survive, a very large part of the Greek library: the works of Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia; of Gregory of Nazianzus; and the books of Clement of Rome’s *Recognitions*; the ecclesiastical history of Eusebius of Caesarea in Palestine, to which Rufinus added the tenth and eleventh books; the *Sentences* of Xystus—if not the Roman pontiff, then at least some Pythagorean, as Jerome maintains; the *Sentences* of Evagrius; and the work of the martyr Pamphilus against the mathematicians.

He also translated Josephus’ history into Latin; a copy of it, written in Lombard letters, is preserved at Milan in the church of Saint Ambrose. He translated not all of Origen, since Jerome also translated certain works, which are distinguished by his preface. Rufinus likewise expounded the Creed, which is contained among Jerome’s works in volume IV of the Basel edition. Erasmus, in his preface to Cyprian, speaks of this work as follows: “He also answered the detractor of his little works in two volumes, charging and proving—as Gennadius reports—that, with God’s help, he had exercised his intellect for God’s sake and for the benefit of the Church, whereas the other, driven by the spur of rivalry, had turned his pen to slander.”

Rufinus’ treatise *On the Corruption of Books*, especially those of Origen, is read at the end of the first part of Origen’s works and again in volume II of the works of D. Jerome. On Origen’s behalf he also translated the *Apology of the Martyr Pamphilus*, which is found prefixed to Origen’s works. He published his own *Apology*, in which he showed that the opposing doctrines found in Origen’s books had arisen because those books had been corrupted.

His preface to Origen’s books *On First Principles* was commonly included by Desiderius Erasmus in volume III of Jerome’s works, so that Jerome’s *Apologies* might be more easily understood. Finally, Rufinus wrote very many works, but translated many more.

This Rufinus was Tharmus, or Thoranus, a monk by profession and an Aquileian presbyter by rank. He was greatly esteemed by the Emperor Theodosius, on whose behalf he interceded with Blessed Ambrose so that the emperor might be permitted to enter the church at Milan, from which he had previously been excluded because of the massacre of seven thousand people at Thessalonica, as Nicephorus reports in book XII, chapters 40 and 41, of his *Ecclesiastical History*.

Rufinus had also once been Jerome’s companion in study and was deeply beloved by him. This continued until a dispute arose between them concerning Origen’s writings. Rufinus then appeared to Jerome to be an excessive admirer and almost an advocate of Origen, and was consequently thought to share Origen’s opinions because he defended his own view of the books *On First Principles* (*περὶ ἀρχῶν*), which seemed to have been turned against the faith, somewhat too sharply against D. Jerome.

But if no one to this day has been found who said that Origen’s books of this kind ought therefore to be destroyed, neither, I think, will anyone be found who judges that Rufinus ought to be rejected because he thought they should be retained—unless he rashly prefers himself to Blessed Augustine, who valued our Rufinus so highly that he drew a very great deal from him into his own commentaries on the Psalms.

For Rufinus was older than Augustine in the year 400 of human redemption. Yet he possessed such authority with D. Augustine that Augustine wrote about him to D. Jerome with no small praise of piety and learning. He said that Rufinus had diligently tasted the “honey” of the Scriptures both with Jerome and against him, though he had once been Jerome’s dearest companion. Augustine attempted to restore both men to mutual goodwill, but concealed the cause of their enmity so carefully that he attributed blame for it to neither.

It should not seem strange that the works of so brilliant a writer remained hidden for so long to those who know from Trithemius that many books written by Rufinus—most of them now appearing for the first time—have still been lying buried beneath the dust of oblivion.

But lest anyone think our present undertaking less worthy because some of Rufinus’ little works are rejected by certain people as suspect in relation to apostolic authority, I shall say only this: absolutely nothing is established by that Canon against Rufinus that diminishes his authority or prevents the reading of these books. For Gelasius calls him a religious man (*Distinction* 15, canon “Sancta Romana”), and reports that certain Scriptures were explained by him—an observation that Primas of Lyon applied to the commentaries on the Psalms. Gelasius says that he regards certain works as suspect because Jerome wrote that Rufinus had argued less truthfully concerning human free will.

But, leaving aside the freedom that the same most holy and learned Jerome displayed in speaking and asserting the truth—and to whose judgment Gelasius refers us—nothing in these commentaries is more plainly taught than support for human free will, for good works, for the mystery of the Most Holy Trinity, for the most sacred Eucharist of the Church, for purgatory, for true human righteousness, and for many other matters of this kind, taught not once or in a single place.

Nor should that sudden estrangement of will between D. Jerome and Rufinus seem new to anyone, although it has always been serious and painful to all good people. Jerome, burning with zeal and relying on his learning, could tolerate nothing in another’s books that had not been purified and worked out with exact precision. Rufinus, however, fortified by his piety and by the example of many of the Church’s leading lights, proceeded boldly in reading Origen’s books and translating them into another language.

Above all, they fell into this dispute because of a certain diversity of opinions, as we learn from D. Augustine, and Rufinus may perhaps have entered it unwittingly. For Augustine, in the letter numbered XV among Jerome’s letters, while lamenting at length that so bitter a quarrel had arisen between Rufinus and Jerome—men who were such close friends, learned, famous, aged, and monastic, and that it had arisen to the grave scandal of the whole Church—says that he had previously thought such a thing could happen only to another person. From Jerome’s letters he perceived how much Jerome restrained himself and held back the goads of indignation; he says that he himself froze with fear and wasted away with grief, because he feared that Rufinus might do the same to Jerome.

Yet Augustine offers a defense of both men: Paul and Barnabas had contended with each other in no dissimilar kind of dispute, as had the Apostles Peter and Paul—whose opinion Augustine and Jerome themselves did not receive without disagreement. They had likewise previously disagreed over the little word *τῆς κολοκύντιδος* (“of the gourd”) in the prophecy of Jonah.

The controversy between Epiphanius and D. Chrysostom is well known from ancient history; so too are the disputes—more restrained because more ancient—between Victor and Irenaeus, and between Origen and Theophilus. Yet none of these matters branded such eminent men with disgrace in such a way that, if they had thought incorrectly about certain issues not yet treated and decreed by the universal Church in its sacred councils, they should therefore appear to have erred in everything else as well.

Let D. Gelasius retain his authority, and let D. Jerome’s innocence remain established. Yet neither should this diminish what Rufinus rightly said; indeed, if all his writings are found intact and examined in relation to the truth, they should instruct us no less in right belief and inflame us no less to right action than the works of those who perhaps habitually read and write with greater elegance and ambition than he did.

Meanwhile, my lord, de Saint-André, remember that these spoils of the civil wars have been consecrated to you; protect and preserve them to such an extent that, just as you are Catholic and have always lived and remained most Catholic, so whatever in them is to be approved or rejected may be left to the judgment of the Catholic—that is, the Roman—Church.

Farewell.

From my study at the Gervasians, on the Ides of June, 1580.

[Col. 0075]

# Tyrannius Rufinus, by Birth a Concordian, by Citizenship an Aquileian, by Priesthood a Hierosolymitan: Life

## Book One

### Chapter I

[Col. 0075A]

1. Rufinus’ birth and the spelling of his name.  
2. His homeland.  
3. Born at Concordia: his praenomen and family.  
4. He became a monk at Aquileia.  
5. There, together with Jerome, he was educated in the liberal arts; when grown, he was baptized. The minister and sponsors of his baptism.  
6. Jerome, separated from him, sailed to Syria.  
7. Shortly afterward Rufinus left Rome, intending to travel to Jerusalem with Melania.

Gelasius of Cyzicus, having read through the canons of the Council of Nicaea, considered it certain that Rufinus had attended that great assembly. In his preface to the acts of the Council of Nicaea, printed in Labbe, volume I, page 114, he says so in the clearest terms. Yet at that time—namely, in A.D. 325—Rufinus had not yet been born, as Natalis Alexander noted in *Century IV*, Dissertation XIII, conclusion II.

Blondel, thinking very differently, in *On the Primacy*, page 881, assigned Rufinus’ birth to A.D. 345, which was the twentieth year after the Council of Nicaea. I do not hastily embrace Blondel’s opinion, since it is supported by no earlier testimony. For nothing has been transmitted anywhere concerning the year or consul under whom Rufinus was born. The births of illustrious men, like those of rivers, are obscure, while their courses and endings are conspicuous.

Nevertheless, I think it can be shown from book II of Jerome’s *Apology*, written in A.D. 400, that Rufinus had been born not long after the Council of Nicaea. There Jerome calls him “old” and “gray-haired,” and mocks him for saying that he had once visited his parents: “You left them alive as a young man,” he says, “and now, an old man, you long for them dead.”

At the beginning of book III he calls Rufinus “the oldest of the monks.” Elsewhere he says: “You, an old man, fabricate so much against an old man.” A little later: “What edification is there in two old men fighting one another over heretics”—that is, over Origen? “We erred when young; let us amend our ways as old men.” Further below: “I shall forgive you for having written the *Apology* of his books—those of Origen—with a gray head.”

Could these words have been spoken of a sixty-year-old Rufinus? Perhaps he was then advanced in age, at least seventy, as Jerome was.

We must not omit what Caspar Barthius noted concerning the spelling of the name *Rufinus*, in his notes on Claudian, page 1073 of the second edition, and in his *Adversaria*, book LIII, chapter II: that it is found with a single letter *f* in all manuscripts. Barthius is speaking of the praetorian prefect Rufinus, whom Claudian attacks; but the spelling applies to all Rufinuses.

He therefore thinks those who double that letter are acting foolishly, since the pronunciation of the name itself permits nothing else. In any case, Latin speakers do not readily double *f* in such names, and it is known that they did not double it in the most ancient manuscripts of our Rufinus.

This is especially confirmed by the fact that the Greeks also write only one hard consonant in this name, and Latins reasonably follow their practice in similar cases. In Ezechiel Spanheim’s *Dissertation IX on the Excellence and Use of Coins*, volume I, pages 712–713 of the large edition, the name appears on Greek coins as ΡΟΥΦΙΝΟΥ. Peter Lambecius further confirms this same spelling from a very ancient manuscript of Rufinus’ work *On the Blessings of the Patriarchs*, in the *Caesarean Library*, volume II, page 800. Philippus Labbe likewise proves it from manuscript books in his notes on Bellarmine’s *Catalogue*, volume II, page 307.

These considerations overturn the opinion of Arnaldo Pontaco in his notes on Eusebius’ *Chronicle*, page 749, where he insists that the name should be written *Ruffinus* with a double *f*. Consult also the Gruterian Index, number XXIII, and Christoph Cellarius in his *Orthography*, where a single *f* is supported by inscriptions and coins.

## II. His homeland

Since more than one opinion is circulated concerning Rufinus’ homeland, I shall identify it through the certain testimony of ancient writers, by which the statements of those who affirm otherwise will be completely overturned.

Heraclides states in the *Paradise*—the old translation of Palladius’ *Lausiac History*, as the critics know—that Rufinus was born in a town of the Aquileian territory. For in chapter XXXIII the following is read concerning Melania: “There was with her a certain Rufinus by name, an Italian citizen from a town of the Aquileian territory.”

For this reason Jerome, in *Apology* II, mockingly calls it a “little town.” Cardinal Noris, in book I, chapter II of his *Pelagian History*, interpreted this as a village, countryside, or small fort. Learned men have long observed, however, that these terms signify different things.

Certainly, the ancient writers Livy, Pliny, and Mela used *town* for a city; and so did Sidonius and Eugippius in the fifth century, at the beginning of which Rufinus lived. Sidonius calls the city of the Arverni a “town” in book III, letter IV. Eugippius, his contemporary, applies the same designation in the *Life of Severinus, Apostle of Noricum*, to cities—and indeed distinguished ones—such as Lauriacum and Patavium.

Rufinus, therefore, was born in a town near Aquileia. Jerome confirms this in book II of *Apology* I: “Having left his homeland, he lives at Aquileia.” In *Apology* II, mocking him as though he had refused to go to Rome when summoned by Pope Anastasius, Jerome says: “When Rome asked you to illuminate her by your presence, you despised her out of love for your little town.”

Although Palladius, in chapter CXVIII of the *Lausiac History*, calls him “Rufinus from Italy, from the city of Aquileia,” and Gennadius, in chapter XVII of his *Catalogue*, calls him “an Aquileian presbyter,” this does not mean that he was born in the city of Aquileia itself. Rather, it indicates that he was raised in a monastery and baptized in the Church, though not ordained there, and that, because of the fame of the nearby city, he was called Aquileian. His true homeland, then, was in the Aquileian territory.

Nor would Jerome have called Aquileia a “little town,” since his contemporary Philostorgius called it a great city in book XII, chapter XI of his *Ecclesiastical History*.

Let us finally identify that little town with the help of the greatest Doctor, in letter IV—formerly VI, now V—to Florentius, an Aquileian monk then residing at Jerusalem. Speaking there of Rufinus, Jerome adds the following concerning the aged Paul of Concordia:

“A certain Paul, an old man from the homeland of the aforesaid brother Rufinus, also wrote to me, saying that his copy of Tertullian was with him, and he urgently demands its return.”

Paul and Rufinus therefore had the same homeland. Jerome identifies Paul’s homeland as Concordia in chapter LIII of his *Catalogue*:

“I saw at Concordia, which is a town of Italy, an old man named Paul who said that, when he was still quite young, he had seen at Rome the blessed Cyprian, already advanced in age, serving as his secretary; and he reported that Cyprian never allowed a day to pass without reading Tertullian.”

To this same Paul—who, at the age of one hundred, falsely claimed a youth belonging to another age—Jerome sent, in letter X, formerly XXI, the *Life of Saint Paul the Hermit*, asking him in return to send certain books, among them the commentaries on the Gospels by Fortunatianus, bishop of Aquileia.

Raphael Fabretti, in chapter X, number 636 of his *Inscriptions*, published the following inscription, borrowed from Cornelius Margarino and taken from the pavement of Saint Paul on the Ostian Way. It appears to belong to this same Paul:

**HERACLIAE. RELIGIOSAE. SORORI. PAVLVS. A. CONCORDIA. XVI. KAL. FEB.**

“To Heraclia, his religious sister. Paul, from Concordia. Sixteenth day before the Kalends of February.”

## III. Rufinus’ name and family

There is therefore no doubt that Rufinus was by origin from Concordia. This was not noticed by those who assigned him another birthplace.

Rigberius the Frank, or perhaps Gabriel Gerberonius, in his notes on Marius Mercator, page 112, confused our Rufinus with another man of the same name, a Syrian by nationality, and made him an Alexandrian by birth. He could have avoided this error by consulting Jerome’s single letter I, formerly XLI. Jerome says there that an Alexandrian monk hiding in the retreats of Syria had informed him that our Rufinus had penetrated the remote regions of Egypt, although that same Alexandrian monk did not know Rufinus’ homeland or name. He plainly would not have been ignorant of them if Rufinus had likewise been an Alexandrian.

The name by which he was distinguished from the other Rufinuses who would later be mentioned was Tyrannius, as I shall immediately show.

Gelasius of Cyzicus, in his preface to the acts of the Council of Nicaea, called this same Rufinus of ours Roman. By that term, as I have already noted, he intended “Latin.” Nevertheless, since the custom has prevailed for many centuries of calling him Rufinus of Aquileia, we too shall use that designation.

Rufinus may also have been a citizen of Aquileia. Johannes Jonsius proves this with many examples in chapter II and chapter XX of his book *On Writers of Philosophical History*: learned men were very often enrolled, for the sake of honor, as citizens of various cities. Consult also Gabriel Naudé, who discusses this matter carefully in his *Judgment on the Little Works of Augustine of Niphus*.

Cicero’s statement in book II of *On the Laws* is highly relevant:

“I, by Hercules, think that both he—Cato—and all municipal citizens have two homelands: one of nature, the other of citizenship. Thus, although Cato was born at Tusculum, he was admitted into the citizenship of the Roman people. Accordingly, although Tusculan by birth, he was Roman by citizenship: he had one homeland by place and another by law.”

For the same reason, Rufinus, born at Concordia but imbued at Aquileia with Christian morals and learning, and finally baptized there, was almost never called Concordian; everyone called him Aquileian. This is found not only in Gennadius but in nearly all the manuscripts of Rufinus’ works.

Then appeared the Portuguese hagiologist Georgius Cardosus. In volume III, under June 20, drawing from the muddy pools of the *Chronicle of Pseudo-Dexter*, he did not hesitate to make Rufinus Portuguese by birth, because the following words are found in that workshop of lies under A.D. 418, section 4: “Jerome writes to Paul of Concordia, the Lusitanian.”

Since Paul and Rufinus had one and the same homeland, Concordia, the credulous Cardosus extravagantly dragged both of them into his own Lusitania, where Pliny, in book IV, chapter XXII, had placed certain people called Concordians.

Franciscus Bivarius wonderfully encouraged this amusing error in his enormous commentary on the forged Dexter, page 432. There, generously disposed toward us, he imagined that Paul had crossed from Portuguese Concordia to our Italian Concordia.

There is no time to pursue such nonsense, nor is it worthwhile, since Nicolaus Antonius, the distinguished avenger of Spanish history defiled by the tricks of impostors, has thoroughly refuted these and similar errors in book III, chapter V, section 125 of his *Old Spanish Library*.

Nevertheless, Dupin, in volume III of his *Library*, called this same Paul a Spaniard from Concordia. Tillemont, volume XII, page 50, says that he does not know where Dupin got this. He got it from Pseudo-Dexter.

John Fell, in his notes on Rufinus’ exposition of the Creed, published with the works of Saint Cyprian in the Oxford edition, went elsewhere. From Tora, or Thora, a destroyed city of the Sabines, he derived Rufinus’ origin, having been deceived by corrupt inscriptions in which the name *Rufinus Toranus* was read.

Fell thought that this final form, distorted from Rufinus’ own praenomen, indicated a homeland rather than a person. From it, as commonly happens with corrupt readings, other monstrous forms of the name also arose: *Thoranus*, *Toranius*, and *Thermus*. In addition, there are *Turanius*, *Turranius*, and *Tauranius*; each of these forms has its own supporters—Barreus, Labbeus, Caveus, Dupinus, and Rosweidus.

Yet in the very same place where Fell read *Toranus*, he could immediately have read that Rufinus’ homeland was Aquileia. For the Clementine *Recognitions* contain the words: “Rufinus Toranus—*for Tyrannius*—interpreter, Aquileian.”

Therefore Aquileia, not Tora, was Rufinus’ homeland.

The proper and true name in a later age was the final form, says Sirmondus in his notes on Sidonius: “Everyone called Rufinus by his proper name.” Therefore it was not “Rufinus Tyrannius,” but “Tyrannius Rufinus,” as he is in fact called in the little book *On Twelve Ecclesiastical Writers*, attached to Isidore and Ildefonsus, chapter V.

The truth of this reading is confirmed by Jerome at the beginning of his earlier *Apology*, addressed to his friends Pammachius and Marcella, where he plays on Rufinus’ praenomen in the following way:

“From your letters and those of many others I have learned that I am accused in the tyrannical school”—*schola Tyrannica*—“by the tongue of my dogs, by that very enemy, of having translated the books *Periarchon* into Latin.”

The jest would have been pointless unless Rufinus had been called Tyrannius by another name.

Johannes Martianaeus, in volume IV, page 349, restored *Tyranni* at this passage from many manuscripts; perhaps *Tyrannii* would be more correct, although the received reading pleases us, since Tillemont too, in volume XII, page 32, detected a hidden barb in it.

Rufinus adopted Tyrannius as a praenomen in part according to the custom observed by Sirmondus. It was not a nomen but a praenomen, as Sidonius teaches us. Yet in his printed manuscripts *Turannius Rufinus* is wrongly read for *Tyrannius* in book II, letter IX.

I think the name of the family was once inscribed on a stone at Concordia, which, broken as it is, was published by the bishop of Adria in his *Dissertation on the Colony of Forum Julii*, page 343.

The other names by which Jerome mentions Rufinus once or twice—such as Grunnius, Calpurnius the Wool-worker, and Scorpius—came from elsewhere. The first perhaps arose from a defect of pronunciation and bodily heaviness. Referring to Rufinus at the end of his letter to Minervius, Jerome says:

“Why do my friends tear me apart, and why do fat sows grunt against one who is silent? Their entire concern—indeed, the height of their learning—is to gnaw at what belongs to others, and to defend the faithlessness of the ancients in such a way that they lose their own faith.”

In these words of *Apology* I, book I, Jerome, now an old man, mocks Rufinus’ defect of speech:

“You who mumble in Latin and move with a tortoise’s pace rather than walk.”

A little later, mocking him as wealthy and living sumptuously, Jerome says:

“Who breathes like a Croesus and a Darius? Letters do not follow the purse. They are companions of sweat and toil, partners of fasts, not of fullness; of restraint, not luxury. Demosthenes is said to have spent more oil than wine, and all craftsmen are said always to have preceded the night with their vigils.”

In *Apology* II he says:

“Who is so great and powerful that he would dare to fight Croesus in wealth? Who would not fear a sudden Demaratus and Crassus? You possess the means by which Danaë’s chastity was conquered, by which he preferred Gehazi’s master to holiness, and because of which Judas betrayed his Lord.”

In book III of the *Apology*, he also complains that a letter from the chamber of his brother Eusebius had been produced by Rufinus “with golden coins,” and that the truth had been attacked “with gold”—that is, with Rufinus’ own resources and those of his supporters.

It also seems possible to infer that Rufinus possessed a considerable household from the cells that he had built at his own expense on the Mount of Olives, not only for himself but also to accommodate others, as he himself testifies in book II of the *Apologies*.

Palladius likewise writes in chapter CXVIII of the *Lausiac History* that Rufinus supported at his own expense for twenty-seven years every kind of guest who came to Jerusalem and stayed there out of devotion.

Jerome, in letter XCV, formerly IV, now CXXV, to Rusticus, paints Rufinus—already dead—in the following colors:

“Grunnius moved with a tortoise’s pace when speaking and plucked out only a few words at intervals, so that you would think he was sobbing rather than speaking. And yet, when the table had been set and he had displayed a heap of books, he would raise his eyebrows, draw in his nostrils, and wrinkle his forehead, then snap his fingers together, summoning his students to listen by this signal. He would then pour forth sheer nonsense and declaim against each one individually.

“You would have thought Longinus had come from Crete, or that he was the censor of Roman eloquence: he would mark whomever he wished and exclude him from the senate of learned men. This man, well supplied with money, was more welcome at dinner parties.
