Nor is it surprising that one accustomed to baiting many people would go out in public with a cluster of noisy chatterers surrounding him: within, Nero; without, Cato.

“He was wholly ambiguous, so that you might have said that from contrary and differing natures one monster and a new beast had been fashioned, in accordance with the poetical saying:”

First a lion, last a dragon, middle a chimaera itself. Rufinus is called by Palladius εὐγενέστατος, “most noble,” in chapter CXVIII. Does this refer to his character, or rather to his lineage? Rufinus himself, in book II of the Apologies, p. 436, calls the holiness of his character—on account of which Jerome had praised him in the Chronicle together with Florentius and Bonosus—the “nobility of his life.”

Moreover, Rufinus’s native Concordia was not the town near Mirandola in Emilia, as Marianus Victorius judged from the similarity of the name in his Life of Jerome; rather, it was the city which Pliny assigns to the Venetians and Ptolemy to the Carnic region, a colony founded under the triumviral law and enrolled in the Claudia tribe, as the distinguished Philippus a Turre, bishop of Adria, recently demonstrated in his Dissertation on the Colony of Forum Julii, p. 346. The *Notitia Imperii* mentions a manufacture of arrows at Concordia; from this we learn that an armamentary decury, or corps assigned to the manufacture of arrows, existed there, as is shown by literate inscriptions on stone. Under the emperors Theodosius the Great and Valentinian II, [Col. 0080B] laws issued at this same colony in A.D. 391 are preserved in the Theodosian Code, book XI, title XXXIX, law XI, “On the Faith of Witnesses,” and book XVI, title VII, laws IV and V, “On Apostates.”

But alas! In A.D. 452, Attila, king of the Huns—the scourge and terror of the whole region—razed this Concordia, together with the neighboring cities Aquileia, Forum Julii, and Altinum, to the ground, as Paul the Deacon testifies in his *Miscellaneous History*, book XV, chapter III, in Gruter’s edition among the Latin writers of the *Historia Augusta*, volume II, p. 81, at the end of the work. I identify this edition because the passage is not found in the others. Later, however, they raised their heads from the ruins; for Cassiodorus, in book XII, letter XXVI of the *Variae*, lists the cities of Aquileia, Forum Julii, and Concordia as still standing. This third city, distinguished by its bishopric, was enriched with privileges by Charles and Otto the Great, and by other emperors. But since the celebrated colony was reduced to solitude by the harshness of the climate, the bishop now resides in the neighboring town which the ancients [Col. 0080C] called Portus Romatinus, according to Pliny.

### IV.

Since Concordia lay thirty-one miles from Aquileia, at that time the chief city of all Venetia, and the same distance from Altinum, Rufinus went to Aquileia to embrace the rule of monastic life. There, instructed in the teaching of the fathers and in devotion toward God in the monastery, he was washed in the saving bath of baptism by Saint Valerian, bishop of the city, in A.D. 371. He himself reports this in his first *Apology*, written in A.D. 400. Speaking as though of a matter universally known, he says:

> I, just as he himself [Jerome] and **everyone knows**, having already been placed in a monastery **nearly thirty years ago**, was regenerated through the grace of baptism and received the seal of the Faith through the holy men Chromatius, Jovinus, and Eusebius, bishops highly esteemed and approved in the Church: one of whom was then presbyter under Valerian of blessed memory, another archdeacon, and the other deacon; and together they were for me father and teacher of the creed and of the faith.

[Col. 0080D] This monastery, in which Rufinus is said already to have been residing when he received the grace of baptism in the church of Aquileia, owed its beginnings—being the oldest of all the monasteries of Italy and the West—to the institutions of the great Athanasius. Norisius observed in his *Pelagian History*, book II, chapter III, that Athanasius, expelled from Alexandria by the Arians, had remained for a long time at Aquileia; and Jerome testifies in his letter XCVI, formerly XVI (now CXXVII), to Principia that all Italy had received monastic discipline from Athanasius.

For when the youth of both sexes, inflamed to imitation by the monks whom he had as companions in exile and hardship, had been inspired, within a short time many monasteries were built at Rome and throughout Italy by bishops—for example at Milan, through the efforts of Ambrose, concerning whom Augustine writes in book VIII, chapter VI of the *Confessions*, and at Aquileia, through the zeal of Valerian. There, besides Tyrannius Rufinus, we learn from Jerome’s *Chronicle* and letters that the highly distinguished monks Heliodorus, Nepotianus, Florentius, Bonosus, Nicetas, and Chrysogonus also flourished.

[Col. 0081A] Here the ignorance of the Magdeburgians is refuted. Unaware of Rufinus’s institution, and perhaps also of the antiquity of monastic life, they rashly declared in *The Fourth Century*, chapter X, that Rufinus was the first to be called a monk by Trithemius. But is Jerome later than Trithemius? in the first year of the 281st Olympiad, 2393 from Abraham, and 378 after Christ according to the Eusebian era followed by Jerome—that is, A.D. 376 according to the Dionysian era—does he not write in the *Chronicle*: “Florentius, Bonosus, and Rufinus are regarded as distinguished **monks**”? In book I of the first *Apology* he likewise applies the name of monk to himself and Rufinus: “Whatever the title of **monk** demands, both of us have fulfilled.” And in the second *Apology*: “I believed a Christian; I believed a **monk**.”

### V.

Jerome, who was joined to the clergy of Aquileia by the closest relationship, also appears to have been educated from adolescence in this same monastery. For in letter XXXIX, formerly LXII (now LXXXII), he writes to Theophilus:

> Having been shut up from adolescence in the cells of a **monastery**, I preferred to be something rather than to appear to be something.

He had already long been bound to Rufinus by friendship. [Col. 0081B] At Trier, Jerome testifies in letter IV, formerly VI (now V), that he had copied with his own hand a very lengthy book of Saint Hilary’s *On the Synods* for Rufinus. After Rufinus had arrived in Egypt, Jerome writes to him in letter I, formerly XLI (now III):

> Oh, if the Lord Jesus Christ would now suddenly grant me either the translation of Philip to the eunuch or of Habakkuk to Daniel, how I would now clasp your neck tightly in my embrace! How I love that mouth which **once erred with me** or **once reasoned wisely with me**!

These words clearly indicate that both had devoted themselves to study together from adolescence. Bonosus may also be added to their number. Jerome writes to Rufinus in letter I, formerly XLI (now III): “Behold the boy, trained with us in the honorable arts of the world.” Rufinus himself confirms this more strongly in the second *Apology*: “Before he was converted, [Jerome] was completely ignorant, together with me, both of Greek literature and of the Greek language.”

Jerome testifies that his own conversion occurred on the half-barbarian banks of the Rhine, in letter I, formerly XLI (now III). Thus the monastery at Aquileia, according to Rufinus’s [Col. 0081C] words, already existed in A.D. 370. At that time, we read of no other monastery in Italy, except perhaps at Vercellae, where Saint Eusebius, having returned from the East, established the monastic life in A.D. 362.

Lucas Holstenius, in the preface to the *Code of Rules*, chapter II, says that the Italians were led to the monastic way of life by the *Life of Saint Antony*, which he thought Athanasius had disseminated when he first came to Rome. But Athanasius wrote it in Greek in A.D. 365, with Italian monks as his informants; at the beginning of the work the holy father intimates that this institution had long since begun to be practiced in the West, rejoicing that among them there were “very many monasteries” and that the name of “monks” was also renowned.

This life of Athanasius was brought to the West by couriers and translated into Latin in A.D. 370 by the presbyter Evagrius, who had come to Italy with Eusebius of Vercellae. Evagrius dedicated it to Innocentius, with whom he then returned to the East together with Jerome, Eusebius having already died. Our very dear friend Bernard de Montfaucon noted these facts in the *Life* prefixed to Athanasius’s works, p. 84, and in the preface to the *Life of Saint Antony*, p. 791.

[Col. 0081D] Furthermore, from the words quoted above it is clear that Rufinus, already an adult, was baptized at the sacred font at Aquileia, and indeed by Valerian, the metropolitan, with Chromatius the presbyter, Jovinus the archdeacon, and Eusebius the deacon administering the rite. In A.D. 400 Rufinus summoned these three, as survivors venerable in their episcopal character, as witnesses to his faith. Using the ancient and proper term, he called them “fathers”; elsewhere, as I shall say later, he called them “parents.” Our predecessors also called such persons sponsors, presenters, guarantors, and finally godfathers.

Rufinus referred to this in his *Apology for His Faith* addressed to Pope Anastasius:

> These things concerning the resurrection were handed down to us by those through whom we received holy baptism in the Church of Aquileia. I think that these are the very things which the Apostolic See has also been accustomed to hand down and teach.

These words expose Dupin’s error in volume III of the *Bibliotheca*, where he supposed that Rufinus had been baptized in the monastery. For the Sacrament of regeneration was then conferred not in any monastery, but only [Col. 0082A] in the episcopal church by its ordinary pastor. Nor does Rufinus say that he received baptism in the monastery, but in the Church of Aquileia. Although he writes in the first *Apology* that he was already residing in the monastery when he received baptism, he by no means asserts that he received it in the monastery. Indeed, in his exposition of the creed he expressly testifies:

> Nevertheless, we follow the order which we received through the grace of the washing in the **Church of Aquileia**.

In the same way Jerome reveals that, far from his native Stridon, he received baptism at Rome, in letters XIV and XVI, formerly LVII and LVIII (now XV and following).

Edmund Martene, in book I, chapter XVI, §12 of *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, and Gerard of Maastricht, in his *Essay on Sponsors*, p. 69, thought that formerly there had been only one sponsor. But Rufinus places three sponsors before our eyes, assigned to as many functions: catechesis, baptism, and confirmation, which was customarily conferred by the bishop immediately after baptism. Hence Gerard is refuted once more, [Col. 0082B] for on p. 24 he assigns a single sponsor to catechesis and baptism down to the sixth century.

By the “seal of faith” Rufinus means baptism; he uses the term in the same sense in book X, chapter III of the *History*: “Follow me to the Lord’s [house], and receive the **seal of this faith**.” Joannes Ernestus Grabius collects much material concerning this phrase in his notes to the *Spicilegium of the Holy Fathers*, volume I, p. 332.

### VI.

Jerome, already regenerated at Rome by Christ’s baptism before Rufinus, had returned to Aquileia to enjoy the companionship of Valerian and the others, to whom he later wrote letters as witnesses of his closest relationship. After remaining there for some time in the monastery with Rufinus, who was still a catechumen, he was compelled by an unforeseen turn of events to leave, as he testifies in these words when writing from the desert to Rufinus, letter I, formerly XLI (now III):

> A sudden **storm tore me from your side**, after an **impious separation violently ripped me away**, though I was clinging by the bond of charity.

At that time a violent persecution, of a kind unknown [Col. 0082C] to us, had been stirred up against him. Jerome left Aquileia and migrated to the East; traveling through Thrace, Pontus, Bithynia, Galatia, Cappadocia, and Cilicia, he finally descended into Syria, where he lived as a monk in the desert.

This period of his journey occurred together with Evagrius of Antioch, Innocentius, and Hylas, Melania’s servant. Basil of Cappadocia testifies in letter VIII to Eusebius of Samosata that Evagrius had then brought letters from Italy to him.

But it is better to hear Jerome himself announce his journey to Rufinus after he had left his side, in letter I, formerly XLI (now III):

> At last, wandering amid the uncertainties of my pilgrimage, when Thrace, Pontus, and Bithynia, the whole journey through Galatia and Cappadocia, and the land of Cilicia, exhausted by its burning heat, had broken me, Syria met me like a most faithful harbor for a shipwrecked man. There I experienced whatever illnesses there could be and lost one of my two eyes. For a sudden fever carried off Innocentius, part of my soul. Now I enjoy our Evagrius, alone and wholly mine, to whom, always weak and a burden added [Col. 0082D] to his labor, I came. Hylas was also with us, the servant of the holy Melania, who by the purity of his conduct had washed away the stain of slavery and here reopened a scar that had not yet healed. But since the Apostle’s words forbid us to grieve over those who are **sleeping**, etc.

Shortly afterward, still in the same year, A.D. 371, in which he had received baptism at Aquileia, Rufinus himself, moved by the reputation of the Eastern monks, planned to go to Jerusalem with Melania, the most noble of Roman women.

When Jerome received news of this from Paul of Concordia, who was demanding that Rufinus return a copy of Tertullian, he immediately sent a letter to Florentius of Aquileia, to be delivered to Rufinus; the letter is now lost. He recalls it in letter II, formerly V (now IV):

> Since brother Rufinus, who is **reported to have come from Egypt to Jerusalem with the holy Melania**, is joined to me by an inseparable love of brotherhood, I ask you not to hesitate to deliver to him [Col. 0083A] my letter, enclosed with this one of yours. Do not measure us by his virtues. In him you will see the clear marks of holiness. I am dust and the vilest part of clay; even as I am turned into ash, I am content if the weakness of my eyes can endure the splendor of his conduct. He **has just been washed**, and he is **clean**, and **whitened like snow**. I, defiled by every filth of sin, am covered day and night with trembling as I wait to repay the last penny.

Rufinus, praised so greatly by Jerome—who had “just been washed,” was clean, and was whitened like snow—had at that time only recently received the grace of baptism at Aquileia.

But when Florentius informed Jerome that Rufinus had not yet been seen at Jerusalem, Jerome wrote again in letter IV, formerly VI (now V):

> But Rufinus, brother, as you write, **has not yet come** [to Jerusalem]. And even if he comes, it will do little for my longing, since I shall no longer see him. For he too is separated from me by such a **long interval** that he cannot make his way here [to the desert of Chalcis]; and I am confined within the boundaries of the solitude I have undertaken, so that it has now begun to be impossible for me to do what I wished.

[Col. 0083B] When Rufinus arrived, Jerome asks that certain books be lent to him for copying. For this reason, he earnestly entreats Florentius to ask Rufinus to lend him the commentaries of the blessed Rheticius, bishop of Augustodunum, for copying; in them Rheticius had expounded the *Song of Songs* in lofty language.

Jerome adds:

> An old man named Paul, **from the homeland of the aforesaid brother Rufinus**, also wrote to me that a copy of Tertullian is with him, which he urgently demands back. For this reason I ask you to order the books which the attached brief will inform you I do not possess to be written out by a copyist’s hand on paper. I also ask you to have transferred to me the interpretation of David’s Psalms and the very lengthy book of Saint Hilary’s *On the Synods*, which I myself copied for him with my own hand at Trier. You know that this is food for the Christian soul, if he meditates on the law of the Lord day and night.

Thus Jerome wrote to Florentius concerning Rufinus and the books in his keeping. Jerome also explicitly left it on record that Rufinus was especially well supplied with books, not only before [Col. 0083C] but also after their quarrel. In book II of the first *Apology* he says:

> At great expense, as I know, you purchased the Jewish translators Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion, together with the fifth and sixth editions.

### VII.

Meanwhile Rufinus, intending to cross to Jerusalem with Melania, went to Rome and, as we think, departed from there at the end of A.D. 371. Melania’s departure is inferred from Jerome’s letter XXI, formerly XV (now CXXIV), to Marcella, in which he pours out praise upon Melania because, while her husband’s body was still warm and not yet buried, and after she had lost two sons together, leaving only one survivor, she sailed for Jerusalem at the onset of winter, intending to serve Christ.

Pliny, in book II, chapter XLVII, describes the beginning of winter in these words: “The setting of the Pleiades begins winter.” This time customarily falls on the third day before the Ides of November. Therefore Melania crossed into the East in November.

Jerome praises her for this deed also [Col. 0083D] in letter XXXVIII, formerly XCIX (now XLV), to Asella. Paulinus of Nola likewise sings her praises in letter XXIX, formerly X, §8, where he says:

> Besides the other bereavements which, while still sharing her husband’s life, she mourned after her fruitless labor in miscarried pregnancies, her troubles grew so great that within the space of a year she lost two sons and her husband, leaving herself only one little child, more as a memorial than as compensation for her affections.

And later:

> As the companion of three funerals in a mournful procession, widowed and bereaved alike, she **came to Rome with her only son**, who was rather the kindler than the consoler of her tears.

Palladius, in chapter CXVII of the *Historia Lausiaca*, says that she was Spanish by origin: Σπάνη ἦν τὸ γένος, “her race was Spanish.” The old translator concealed under the name of Heraclides renders this: “descending from a Spanish or urban family.” The particle *vel* (“or”) is used for the conjunction *et* (“and”) in medieval style. Cangius gives some examples in his *Glossary*; Blondellus gives many in *On the Primacy*, p. 986, to illuminate another passage of Rufinus. In explaining that passage, learned men stumbled because they imprudently understood the particle according to the sense of the ancient [Col. 0084A] Latins. Barthius notes that *vel* for *et* is a Greek usage in his *Adversaria*, book XXV, chapter III; he discusses the same particle again in his learned *Observations on Rutilius’s Hodoeporicon*, book I, verse 40. See also Reinesius’s letter XLII to Rupertus, p. 366. I have pointed this out so that no one may be perplexed by Palladius’s words.

In fact, Melania was Roman by birth but came from a Spanish family, as Tillemont correctly observes in volume X, p. 591. Perhaps she had lost her husband and sons in Spain; hence, according to Paulinus, she “came to Rome.”

Palladius, in chapter CXIX, testifies that the younger Melania, who was the daughter of Publicola and therefore the heiress and granddaughter of the elder Melania, sold all the possessions she had in Spain in order to renounce the world.

The bishop of Nola, in letter XXIX, formerly X, to Severus, §5, said that Melania was related to him by blood. Ambrose, in letter XXX, formerly XXXVI, to Sabinus, praises Paulinus for the splendor of his lineage, saying that in the regions of Aquitaine he was second to no one. For he was from Bordeaux, a city of Aquitaine; on both his father’s and mother’s [Col. 0084B] side he shone wonderfully in senatorial purple by his birth, as Uranius testifies in chapter IX of his *Life*.

Palladius, in chapter CXIX of the *Historia Lausiaca*, states that the younger Melania possessed exceedingly rich estates not only in Spain but also in Gaul; Heraclides says specifically that she had estates in Aquitaine, Gaul, Tarragona, and Spain, in chapter L of the *Paradise*. The paternal family of the elder Melania, therefore, came from the region of Aquitaine bordering on Tarraconian Spain. Hence the relationship between her and Paulinus.

The woman’s name itself was particularly common in Aquitaine. Ausonius, himself an Aquitanian of the same age, testifies in his *Parentalia*, poem XXIX, that he had a sister named Aemilia Melania.

Paulinus adds the following concerning the elder Melania:

> With everyone weeping, she joyfully cast off from shore; steadfastly she confronted the waves of the sea and sailed, determined to overcome not merely the waves but the world’s tumult. Changing both the world and the city, she chose the city of Jerusalem as a spiritual gift, in which she would live as a pilgrim away from the body.

[Col. 0084C] She did not, however, hasten directly to Jerusalem, but first crossed into Egypt, intending to proceed from there to the Holy City.

Baronius correctly places Rufinus and Melania’s voyage in the same year, A.D. 372, §33. Heribert Rosweyde, however, in his notes to the *Lives of the Fathers*, p. 439, thinks this impossible, because Rufinus’s stay in Egypt lasted six years, whereas Melania’s lasted six months—not eight, as has crept into Baronius, A.D. 372, §191, nor a year and a half, as Pagius wrote, A.D. 397, §5.

For Palladius, in chapter XXXIII of Heraclides’ *Paradise*, p. 973, affirms only six months. Gentianus Hervetus, Palladius’s translator, renders chapter CXVII as “about half a year,” not “a year and a half,” as Pagius supposed. Yet in A.D. 372, §18, Pagius himself, quoting Palladius, had observed that the Greek reads ὡς ἥμι ἔτους, that is, “about half a year.”

But if Rufinus accompanied Melania from Egypt to Jerusalem, why could he not afterward return alone to Alexandria, just as he also traveled alone through Mesopotamia [Col. 0084D], as we shall relate below? The arguments that we shall now adduce persuade us that their voyage was undertaken together.

1. Saint Paulinus, in letter XXVII, formerly IX, §5, calls the presbyter Rufinus “the companion of Saint Melania **on the spiritual way**.” This phrase appears to indicate both the journey to the holy places and the return from them. For in a later age the journey to Jerusalem was antonomastically called the “way of the saints,” the “way of God,” and the “holy journey,” as Cangius teaches in his *Glossary*. These are the same as the spiritual way, or *via spiritualis*.

2. Their stays in Egypt and Jerusalem are joined together.

3. Their return to the West is assigned to one and the same period, as we shall show later.

4. Jerome, alienated from Rufinus’s friendship, appears in the second *Apology* to reproach him for having traveled as a young man with Melania, herself also young, who had recently lost her husband at [Col. 0085A] the age of twenty-two, according to Palladius, chapter CXVII; Paulinus supports this in letter XXIX, formerly X, §8, where he says of Melania:

> Though still **in tender years**, she endured marriage and soon became a mother. But she did not long enjoy that happiness among mortals, lest she should love earthly things for long.

Let Jerome’s words be heard:

> Could I not also examine your **departure**? What was your age? Where were you from? At what time did you sail? Where did you live? What affairs did you take part in? But far be it from me to do what I criticize in you and to join the ravings of senile quarrels in an ecclesiastical dispute. Let it suffice to have said this to your prudence: take care not to say against another whatever can immediately be turned back against you.

5. After Rufinus returned to the West, he was again Melania’s companion on the spiritual way. While sailing to Jerusalem, she died in Sicily, as I shall demonstrate in its proper place. All these facts place before our eyes that Rufinus was devoted to Melania’s company from the beginning, that is, from A.D. 371.

Concerning Melania, Jerome writes in the *Chronicle* under the second year of the 288th Olympiad, 2390 from Abraham, and, according to the Eusebian era, the tenth year of the reign of Valentinian and Valens, corresponding to A.D. 373 in the Dionysian era:

[Col. 0085B]

> Melania, the most noble of Roman women and daughter of Marcellinus, once consul, leaving behind an only son, at that time urban praetor, sailed to Jerusalem. There she displayed such a miracle of virtues, especially humility, that she received the name of Thecla.

Learned men long ago noted that Melania was not the daughter but the granddaughter of Marcellinus, who entered the consulship in A.D. 241. In the first Mombritian edition one does not read *Marcelli*, as in the Scaligerian edition, but *Marcellini*, the form read by Freculph in the ninth century in his *Chronicles*, volume II, book IV, chapter XXI. The same reading is found in the editions of Sichard, Pontacus, and Miraeus, as well as in the Greek Palladius, chapter CXVII, and in the Latin translator Heraclides. It is more suitable than Gentianus Hervetus’s version of Palladius, in which he renders *Marcelli* rather than *Marcellini*.

Saint Paulinus, in letter XXIX, formerly X, §§6 and 8, calls her noble through consular grandparents and descended from Marcellinus [Col. 0085C] the consul. Rufinus agrees in book II of the *Apology*, p. 436. Quoting the words of Jerome already cited from his own copy of the Eusebian *Chronicle*, he calls her not the daughter of Marcellus or Marcellinus, but the granddaughter of the consul Marcellinus.

We think that Paulinus and Rufinus should be followed above the others. The former was a relative, and both were very close friends of Melania. Therefore either Jerome and Palladius used “daughter” for “granddaughter,” as Pontacus and Pagius maintain—I would not readily say that a corruption entered the words of both as they are now transmitted—or she was the daughter of Marcellinus, consul in A.D. 341, and the granddaughter of another Marcellinus, likewise consul, in A.D. 275, as Pontacus conjectured. The commonly transmitted Heraclides could perhaps support this view, since he calls her the daughter of Marcellinus, already an ex-consul, faithfully expressing the Greek of Palladius: τοῦ ἀπὸ ὑπάτων, “of one who had been consul.”

Jerome expresses the same point by calling her the daughter of Marcellinus, “once consul.” From this it is clear that Melania was born to Marcellinus after his consulship [Col. 0085D], not in A.D. 341, when he entered the consulship, as Tillemont seems to have thought without necessity.

In Jerome’s words quoted above, “leaving behind an only son, at that time urban praetor,” another difficulty remains. Gregory of Tours, in chapter XXXVI of his *History of the Franks*, thought that the son of Melania was called Urbanus; yet his surname was Publicola. This name belonged to the Valerian family, as is shown by Joannes Glandorpius’s *Onomasticon*, in the stemma of the Valerii, p. 969. Hence it is clear that Melania’s husband must be referred to the illustrious family of the Valerii.

Rufinus, faithfully expressing Jerome’s meaning in book II of the *Apology*, writes: “Leaving a little son at Rome.” Rosweyde, in the first edition of the *Eremitical History*, p. 443; Norisius, in the *Adventoria*, p. 14; Pagius, A.D. 372, §16; and Tillemont, volume X, p. 594, against the testimony of all editions and manuscripts, thought that, by changing a single letter, one should read not *praetore* (“praetor”) but *praetori* (“for the praetor”).

But Rosweyde himself, in the second edition, p. 444, judged that the reading should be retained, since the ancient [Col. 0086A] books agree among themselves in support of the common and original reading. This escaped Tillemont, who had used only the first edition. Accordingly, Rosweyde defends the view that the urban praetorship was conferred upon Melania’s son Publicola, while he was still a boy, on account of the splendor of his lineage, citing examples from periods in which both praetorian prefects and even consuls were boys.

On this matter consult Theodorus Sitzmannus, in his *Observations on Rutilius’s Hodoeporicon*, verse 173; Thomas Reinesius, *Various Readings*, book II, chapter XV; and Norisius, in his *Dissertation on the Pisan Cenotaphs*, II, chapter II, p. 103.

Tillemont was not far from the truth, volume X, p. 823, in thinking that this same Publicola later wrote letter XLVI, formerly CLIII, to Saint Augustine.

“Publicola,” or *Poplicola* and *Populicola*, meaning “cultivator of the people,” is a very ancient surname in that same Valerian family, as shown by the *Menagiana*, volume III, pp. 190–398.

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 0086B]

I. News of the arrival of Rufinus and Melania at Alexandria reaches Jerome in the Syrian desert.  
II. After the death of Athanasius, Rufinus flees to Nitria when persecution is stirred up against the Catholics.  
III. He suffers for the faith.  
IV. Melania follows Christ’s confessors.  
V. After they are recalled from exile, she proceeds from Diocaesarea to Jerusalem.  
VI. Rufinus spends six years at Alexandria, where he attends Didymus and Theophilus.  
VII. Rufinus goes to Jerusalem; from there Melania makes an excursion to Alexandria.  
VIII. Rufinus exercises himself in works of charity.  
IX. He hears of the conversion to the faith of Christ of Bacurius, king of the Iberians, and Aedesius, of the Ethiopians.  
X. Rufinus’s account is explained and defended.

### I.

When Melania, winter already approaching in A.D. 371, had set sail from the Roman port of Ostia, she arrived at Alexandria at the beginning of A.D. 372, while Saint Athanasius, bishop of the city, was still alive. The Latin translator of Palladius, who is concealed under the name Heraclides, says that this occurred “at the beginning of the reign of Valens,” in chapter XXXIII, p. 973, of Rosweyde’s edition. Hence learned men have assigned Melania’s journey approximately to the beginning of Valens’s reign. But Gentianus Hervetus, coming closer to the sense of the Greek expression, translated the Greek words, Οὐάλεντος τοῦ Βασιλέως ἀρχὴν ἔχοντος—“while Valens the emperor was holding imperial power”—in chapter CXVIII of the Greek-Latin edition of the Bibliotheca Patrum published by Morellus at Paris in A.D. 1634, vol. XIII, p. 1031.

There Palladius says, in chapter CXVII:

> When she had sold her possessions, Melania entered the mountain of Nitria, visiting the holy fathers: Pambo, Arsisius, the servant of Christ, the great Serapion, Paphnutius Scatirotes, Isidore the Confessor of Hermopolis, and Dioscorus. She remained among them for approximately half a year, traversing the desert and seeing all the saints.

At that time Rufinus also visited the monks of Egypt. Hieronymus reports that news of this was brought to him once, a second time, and a third time in Chalcis, in Letter I, otherwise XLI (now III), written to the same Rufinus while he was staying in Egypt.

First, the monk Heliodorus informed Hieronymus, who was living in the Syrian desert, that he had heard this from someone else. But, as the same Hieronymus says, since the novelty of the matter removed credibility from the report—“for I did not believe as certain what I wished to be certain”—once again, while his mind remained suspended in wavering hope, an Alexandrian monk, who long before had been sent, in service to the people, to the Egyptian confessors—men already martyrs in will—, drove him openly toward believing the report:

> I confess that here too my judgment faltered. For although he did not know your homeland or your name, he nevertheless seemed to bring greater confirmation because he asserted the same things that another had already reported.

But when at last a third messenger, whose report was confirmed by the testimony of many, declared with certainty that Rufinus was visiting the cells of Nitria, Hieronymus, overcome with excessive joy, immediately sent him a letter:

> At last the full weight of truth burst forth: the multitude of those who came and went repeatedly reported that Rufinus was in Nitria and had gone to the blessed Macarius. Here I completely released the restraints of belief, and then truly regretted being ill. Had the strength of my weakened body not held me back by a kind of fetter, neither the heat of midsummer nor the sea, always uncertain to sailors, could have prevented me, hastening in pious eagerness, from setting out.

These words show that Rufinus—who, having departed from the city with Melania when winter was already approaching in A.D. 371, was believed by Hieronymus, living in the farthest part of Syria, to be staying in Nitria in Egypt and to have gone to the blessed Macarius during the height of the following summer, A.D. 372—was known to have reached Egypt by then.

What more is needed? Rufinus himself fixes the same epoch for his baptism and for his journey from the West to Palestine. For in the *Apology* I, written in A.D. 400, he says that he was baptized at Aquileia “almost thirty years ago,” and that he had already been inactive in the Latin language for “nearly thirty years” through neglect. In the *Apology to Anastasius, the supreme pontiff*, he says:

> After almost thirty years I was restored to my parents.

Hieronymus, no longer his friend, mocks this in *Apology* I:

> This man, lying on his back and quite weary, cannot come in a carriage by the softest road through Flaminia after thirty years, and thus pretends the fatigue of a long journey, as though he had been running continuously for thirty years.

And in book II he again says:

> You remind us that, after devouring Greek volumes for thirty years, you do not know Latin.

When Rufinus distinguishes—or rather diminishes—the thirty-year span of his pilgrimage with the expressions “almost” and “nearly,” he indicates that the period consisted of thirty years not yet completed, or thirty years less one. The same number of years intervened between his departure in A.D. 371 and A.D. 400, when, having returned from the East, he complained of his nearly thirty-year neglect of the Latin language. For he who had left his homeland in A.D. 370 to sail to the East set out from the Roman port toward the end of A.D. 371, and in the following year, 372, entered the Alexandrian harbor together with Melania.

That Rufinus wrote these things in A.D. 400 we learn from book I of his *Apology*, where, criticizing Hieronymus’s teaching, he says:

> Why, then, did the teacher—for I shall address you in your own words—after almost four hundred years, when the Church, having learned that the truth of the Old Testament had not been handed down to it by the Apostles, send envoys to those whom they then called the circumcised, begging and imploring them to grant it something of the truth that exists among them? Let him confess that throughout those four hundred years he had wandered and remained ignorant of what is true.

And after other intervening remarks he writes again:

> Thus now, after four hundred years, the truth of the Law proceeds from the Synagogue, purchased at a price.

These passages show that learned men were mistaken in assigning the departure of Rufinus and Melania from the city, and their arrival in Egypt, earlier than A.D. 371 or later than A.D. 372.

Hieronymus was hiding in the interior Syrian desert, removed from human society, so that even letters from his friends did not fly to him unless, after reaching Antioch, they were gathered by Evagrius and sent on to him in the wilderness. He described the location more than once. In the *Life of Saint Paul* he says:

> I call Jesus and his holy angels to witness that, in that part of the desert which borders Syria and the Saracens, I saw, and continue to see, monks, one of whom lived for thirty years shut in with barley bread and muddy water.

In the *Life of Malchus*, chapter II:

> At last I reached the desert of Chalcis, which lies between Iramas and Beroea, somewhat farther toward the south.

In Letter IV, otherwise VI (now V), to Florentius:

> While I was staying in that part of the desert which borders Syria and the Saracens, a letter expressing your affection was brought to me.

In Letter VII, otherwise XLIII, to Chromatius, Jovinus, and Eusebius:

> A letter was brought to me through the agency of Saint Evagrius in that part of the desert which forms a vast boundary between the Syrians and the Saracens.

In the preface to *Obadiah*:

> When I and my dearest Heliodorus were striving together to inhabit the desert of Chalcis in Syria.

In Letter XIV, otherwise LVII (now XV), to Damasus:

> Because of my crimes I moved to that desert which separates Syria from the adjoining frontier of Barbaria.

In Letter XVI, otherwise LVIII (now XXII), to the same man:

> Now I am held by the barbarian frontier of Syria.

And in Letter XVIII, otherwise XXII, to Eustochium, concerning the preservation of virginity, he depicts his desert in these words:

> O how often, when I myself was established in the desert, in that vast solitude which, scorched by the sun’s heat, provides the monks with a dreadful dwelling, did I think that I was present amid the delights of Rome!

Chalcis was two days’ journey from Antioch, as Cardinal Norisius concludes in *Dissertation III on the Syro-Macedonian Eras*, chapter IX, § III.

From this it is clear that Evagrius, who later became bishop of Antioch, sometimes withdrew into the desert in order to remain with Hieronymus. Letter I, otherwise XLI (now III), to Rufinus says:

> Now I enjoy our Evagrius as my one and complete light; to my weakness he has always been an added burden for labor.

These final words demonstrate that Evagrius was connected with Hieronymus by an intimacy no less than that which bound him to Rufinus, dating from the time when he had been in Italy, and even at Aquileia. Hence Hieronymus writes of Evagrius in Letter VI, otherwise XXXVI, to Chromatius as of a man extremely well known to the latter; and in Letter II, otherwise V (now IV), he asks Florentius of Aquileia to give Evagrius his warmest greetings.

But let us now turn to Rufinus as he traveled about in Egypt.

### II.

From the Alexandrian port one could easily sail by trireme to Seleucia, and from there to Antioch and Chalcis. Thus, as soon as Hieronymus had been informed with certainty that Rufinus was staying in Nitria, he wrote the following to him, expressing his desire to embrace his dearest friend:

> Had the strength of my weakened body not held me back by a kind of fetter, neither the heat of midsummer nor the sea, always uncertain to sailors, could have prevented me, hastening in pious eagerness, from setting out to meet Rufinus.

He rightly mentions the heat of summer. Rufinus had fled to Nitria immediately after the death of Athanasius, which, according to the view set out separately in our account, occurred on May 2, A.D. 372.

It will appear below that the Egyptian confessors were then driven into Phoenicia, Pontus, Armenia, the Propontis, and Palestine. Those closest to Hieronymus were the bishops exiled in Palestine. Hence, during the schism that was tearing apart the Church of Antioch and the whole East, the holy doctor declared that he would remain in communion with them. He wrote this in A.D. 376 in Letter XIV, otherwise LVII (now XV), to Damasus:

> And because, on account of my crimes, I moved to that desert which separates Syria from the adjoining frontier of Barbaria, and because, with so many intervening distances, I cannot always seek from your holiness the Holy Lord—that is, the most holy sacrament of the Eucharist, customarily sent to those who are absent as a sign of Catholic communion—I therefore follow here your Egyptian colleagues, the confessors, and hide beneath merchant ships in a little boat.

The men whom the holy man, using the ancient language of the Church, calls Damasus’s “colleagues” were bishops forced by the command of the emperor Valens to remain in exile in Palestine. Rufinus says of them in *Ecclesiastical History* II, chapter II:

> Valens, favoring the heretics, followed the way of his fathers; for he drove bishops into exile, and subjected presbyters, deacons, and monks—while Tatian was prefect of Alexandria—to torture and handed them over to the flames.

These events belong to A.D. 372, while Tatian was still prefect of Egypt. For after the death of Athanasius, violence was exercised against the Orthodox under Lucius, the usurper of the Alexandrian see. The witnesses are Theodoret and Socrates, book IV, chapter XXI, and Sozomen, book VI, chapter XIX.

Rufinus, who was present during this persecution, divides this slaughter of Catholics into two parts: first, the Alexandrian citizens; second, the monks of Nitria. He places all these events after Athanasius’s death, partly under Tatian and partly under Palladius, who succeeded Tatian as prefect of Egypt in the same year, A.D. 372, according to Theodoret, book IV, chapter XXII.

Let us hear Rufinus’s account of both persecutions in book II, chapter III:

> At that time, when Athanasius, in the forty-sixth year of his priesthood, after many struggles and many crowns of endurance, had rested in peace, inquiry was made concerning his successor, and he chose Peter, a participant and companion in his tribulations. But Lucius, a bishop of the Arian party, immediately flew upon him like a wolf upon a sheep. Peter at once boarded a ship and fled to the city of Rome. Lucius, however, regarding this as an opportunity offered to his cruelty, became more savage toward the others, and proceeded to bloodshed in such a way that he seemed not even to preserve the appearance of religion. At his first entry, deeds so great and so shameful were perpetrated against virgins and women practicing continence in the Church that nothing similar is recorded even during the persecutions of the pagans. Then, after the flight and exile of the citizens, after killings, tortures, and flames by which he had destroyed countless people, he turned the weapons of his fury against the monasteries. He devastated the desert and declared war upon those who were at rest. He began at the same time to attack three thousand men, or even more, scattered throughout the desert in secluded and solitary dwellings. He sent a force of armed cavalry and infantry, choosing tribunes, commanders, and generals of war as though he were going to fight against barbarians. When they arrived, they saw a new kind of warfare: their enemies presented their necks to the swords and said nothing except, “Friend, why have you come?”

### III.

Regarding that savage persecution, Rufinus immediately adds:

> During that period Macarius, Isidore, another Macarius, Heraclides, and Pambus, disciples of Antony, were regarded throughout Egypt, and especially in the regions of the Nitrian desert, as fathers of the monks by merit of their life and age. They were men believed to share not their life and conduct with other mortals but with the angels above. I speak of what I myself saw while present, and I report the deeds of those whose sufferings I was privileged to share.

In the *Apology to Anastasius the Pontiff* he likewise boasts that he suffered at that time for the faith:

> Although our faith, during the persecution of the heretics, when we were staying in the holy Alexandrian Church, was proved in prisons and exiles inflicted on us for the faith, nevertheless, even now, if anyone wishes to test our faith, let him know, and so forth.

In the heat of the dispute Hieronymus replied to this in *Apology* II, near the beginning:

> I am surprised that he did not add: “A prisoner of Jesus Christ”; and “I was delivered from the mouth of the lion”; and “At Alexandria I fought with beasts”; and “I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; there remains for me the crown of righteousness.” What exiles? What prisons does this man name? I am ashamed of such an obvious lie—as though prisons and exiles were inflicted without judicial sentences. Nevertheless, I want him to identify the very prisons and to state in which provinces he says he endured exile. Surely he has the opportunity to name at least one of the many prisons and countless exiles. Let him produce the records of his confession, which until now we have not known, so that among the other martyrs of Alexandria we may also recount his deeds, and so that he may be able to say against his detractors: “From now on let no one trouble me, for I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus Christ.”

But from the same holy father’s *Apology* II we learn that Rufinus was called a martyr not only by himself but also by others:

> Take care that your teacher and fellow disciple do not hear this, and that you do not offend very many who call me a robber but you a martyr.

Again:

> After the Alexandrian exile and the gloomy prisons, may all the followers of Origen call you a martyr and an apostle.

Certainly Socrates, book IV, chapter XXIV, recording in writing the sufferings of the Alexandrians, does not deny that among the holy monks who were cruelly mistreated he included Rufinus, who narrated this about himself, in these words:

> Rufinus says that he both saw these things with his own eyes and suffered them together with those men.

Therefore Rosweyde, a pious and learned man, than whom no one has more accurately elucidated the history of the hermits, does not consider Hieronymus’s reproach so weighty that Rufinus should not be believed. Socrates believed him when Rufinus professed the same thing both in the dispute and elsewhere, although Hieronymus called it into question in the heat of a single argument.

Tillemontius holds the same view in volume VIII, p. 614, and volume XII, p. 40. He considers the arguments against Rufinus only weakly convincing, since we do not know what Rufinus himself could have replied to them, or what he did reply in his letter concerning the first two books of Saint Hieronymus’s *Apology*. Hieronymus mentions that letter, now lost, in book III of the *Apology*.

Tillemontius further observes that the Arians did not enter into the public records everything violent and inhuman that they inflicted upon Catholics; nor did they always wait for judicial sentences before thrusting those whom they hated into prison, punishing them with exile, and depriving them of life. For this reason he agrees that Rufinus may in this matter be granted the title of Confessor.

The father of the *Annals*, under A.D. 372, § 8, thinks that Rufinus ought to have recorded his own confession just as he recorded that of others, following the example of the Apostle Paul. But did he not record it when he said that he reported the deeds of those whose sufferings he had been privileged to share? And in his *Apology for his faith* to Pope Anastasius, does he not confess that his faith was proved, during the persecution of the heretics, in prisons and exiles inflicted for the faith?

Nor does Hieronymus himself entirely deny this, unless perhaps he did so ironically—a distinction that makes little difference. For in *Apology* II he says to Rufinus:

> You had already fought against the doctrine of Arius in Alexandria, in prisons and exiles, not with your voice but with your blood.

In the same book II, p. 399:

> Not even when you were staying in prisons and exiles were such mysteries revealed to you.

And on p. 407:

> In what dream, then, was it revealed to you in the Alexandrian prison that you should fabricate falsehoods about what Origen professes truly?

After Rufinus had narrated the admirable virtues and steadfastness of the monks of Nitria on behalf of the Catholic faith, he again speaks of those whom he had seen and admitted to familiar conversation in book XI, chapter VIII:

> Egypt was flourishing at that time not only with men learned in Christian philosophy, but also with those who, traveling through the vast desert, performed signs and wonders with apostolic simplicity of life and sincerity of heart. Among them, these are those whom we ourselves saw and by whose hands we were privileged to be blessed: Macarius of the upper desert; another Macarius of the lower desert; Isidore in Scetis; Pambus in the Cells; Moses and Benjamin in Nitria; Scyrion, Elias, and Paul in Apeliote; another Paul in Phocis; Poemen and Joseph in Pispiri, which was called the Mountain of Antony.

Rufinus also mentions these men as his teachers in *Apology* II, p. 424:

> To come to the teachers of the desert, to whom we devoted ourselves both more attentively and more frequently: Macarius, the disciple of Antony, and the other Macarius, Isidore, and Pambus, all friends of God—who taught us what they themselves had learned from God. If it were suitable or expedient, what material for boasting I could possess concerning all these men! But I am ashamed to unfold these things while wishing to show you that it was not, as you say, our teachers who failed our natural ability, but—what grieves me more—that our natural ability failed our teachers even more.

When Hieronymus wrote his *Chronicle* in A.D. 380, he adorned Rufinus with a truly magnificent eulogy under the first year of the 289th Olympiad, the Abrahamic year 2393, the year 378 of Christ according to Eusebius, that is, the Dionysian year 736:

> Florentinus, Bonosus, and Rufinus are considered distinguished monks. Florentinus was so merciful toward the needy that he was commonly called the father of the poor.

In all editions of the *Chronicle* this Florentinus is called Florentius by Hieronymus both once and again in the letters already cited, and also by Rufinus in *Apology* II. There Rufinus objects to Hieronymus, who had once written the same eulogy about him as a friend, after their friendship had been broken:

> You now tear apart the man whom you formerly praised in your letters and whom, in your *Chronicles*, you joined to Florentius and Bonosus on account of the nobility of life, as you call it.

A mutual bond connected these men, since they had all been educated together in the Church of Aquileia.

Concerning Bonosus Hieronymus writes to Rufinus in Letter I, otherwise XLI (now III):

> Your Bonosus—or rather mine, or, to speak more truthfully, ours—is already climbing the ladder foreseen in Jacob’s dream.

Bonosus had been Hieronymus’s foster-brother and fellow student. In order to devote himself more freely to God, he had settled alone upon a rock or island—perhaps in Dalmatia—having even abandoned the young Onesimus, whom Rufinus likewise knew:

> Not even the little Onesimus whom you know, with whom he enjoyed an embrace as with a brother, remains at his side as a companion in such vast desolation.

We gather from Letter VII, otherwise XLIII, that Chromatius, Jovinus, and Eusebius of Aquileia had informed Hieronymus of these matters. It is furthermore clear that Bonosus’s withdrawal occurred after A.D. 371, when Rufinus had gone to Egypt, since Hieronymus, writing about it as something new to Rufinus while he was staying in Egypt, informed him of it in Letter I, otherwise XLI (now III), where, as usual, he digresses into praise of Bonosus.

### IV.

We infer from Hieronymus that the twofold disaster inflicted upon the Catholics under the Egyptian prefects Tatian and Palladius lasted through A.D. 372 and 373. Speaking of the second persecution—carried out against the monks of Nitria after the first persecution of the Alexandrian citizens—he writes under the third year of the 288th Olympiad, the Abrahamic year 2391, the year 376 of Christ according to Eusebius, or the Dionysian year 374:

> Many monks of Nitria were killed by tribunes and soldiers.

That the persecution had not yet died down in this year is evident from this passage. Paulinus of Nola, Letter XXIX, otherwise X, § 2, reports that the holiest men were harassed to such an extent that Melania then fed five thousand monks who were in hiding for three days with food from her own supplies. Palladius likewise says in chapter VII that there were that many there. Hieronymus testifies in Letter XVIII, otherwise XXII, to Eustochium, concerning the preservation of virginity, that approximately five thousand lived there in separate cells; Rufinus says the same in *Lives of the Fathers* III, § 219, p. 533. In the prologue, p. 449, he also says that it is astonishing that they were both immense in number and incomparable in virtues.

After Melania had spent six months in Egypt, traversing the desert and seeing all the saints, she followed twelve bishops, together with presbyters, clerics, and anchorites—one hundred and twenty-six persons in all—who had been assigned to Palestine, near Diocaesarea, by the Alexandrian prefect. From her own resources she supplied them with the expenses required in their necessities and provided for them all, as Palladius reports in chapter CXVII.

I think it can be established that Rufinus accompanied her on this journey from the cited Letter II, otherwise V. Hieronymus, having learned that Rufinus had come to Jerusalem together with Saint Melania, sent a now-lost letter to Florentius to be delivered to Rufinus. From Hieronymus’s Letter IV, otherwise VI (now V), we infer that Florentius replied that Rufinus had not yet arrived there. Nevertheless, that Rufinus would come is demonstrated by the fact that Hieronymus asks Rufinus to lend him certain books there for copying.

Rufinus, as we have seen, teaches us in his *Apology to Anastasius* that he himself fought against the doctrine of Arius not only in prisons but also in exiles. Hieronymus repeats this, perhaps at the time when Rufinus was still staying with Melania and the Egyptian exiles near Diocaesarea. Norisius made this almost extinguished city of Palestine immortal in *Dissertation V on the Syro-Macedonian Eras*, chapter VI; more recently Hadrianus Relandus has discussed it in *Palaestina Illustrata*, book III, in a manner not accessible to everyone.

The Egyptian confessors, bishops, presbyters, and deacons who were then banished to Diocaesarea in Palestine—those to whom Peter of Alexandria wrote the letter whose fragments are preserved in Facundus of Hermiana, book XI, chapter II—were not sent there alone. They were also driven elsewhere. The same Peter of Alexandria, cited by Theodoret in book IV, chapter XIX, reports that some were condemned to Heliopolis in Phoenicia and to the mines of Proconnesus, an island of the Propontis, near Cyzicus.

Cassian, *Conferences* XVIII, chapter VII, mentions the mines of Pontus and Armenia. The mines are also mentioned by Rufinus in book XI, chapter VI.

Certainly, in Cassian, who was a monk in Syria and Egypt in A.D. 390, the Alexandrian monk Piammon testifies that, during the time of Lucius—who was a bishop of the Arian perfidy under the rule of Valens—he brought charitable assistance to brothers who had been banished from Egypt and the Thebaid to the mines of Pontus and Armenia because of their perseverance in the Catholic faith.

Rosweyde, p. 444, § 11, thinks that this same monk, passing through the desert of Chalcis at that time, informed Hieronymus of Rufinus’s arrival in Egypt. For in order for charitable assistance to be delivered to the exiles in Pontus, Armenia, and Phoenicia, it was necessary to pass through Syria and the desert of Chalcis. The monk, already passing through that region, had announced the matter to Hieronymus when he was heading toward the Egyptian exiles, not, as Tillemontius seems to have thought, when returning from them.

After that period had elapsed—perhaps one or two months—the full weight of truth finally burst forth: Rufinus was in Nitria. Therefore Hieronymus then wrote to him for the first time.

### V.

It is certain that the strong woman of great virtue traveled from Diocaesarea to Jerusalem. But Palladius, chapter CXVIII, and the commonly circulated *Heraclides*, chapter XXXIII—the *Paradise*, which, as I have already said, is an old translation of Palladius’s *History*—state that she did not establish a *parthenon* for herself and fifty virgins until after the holy men had been recalled from exile:

> After these men had been recalled, she built a monastery at Jerusalem, and so forth.

The date of the monastery must be connected not with Melania’s arrival in the holy city, as Pagius assigns it to A.D. 372, § 21, but with the monks’ recall from exile. This occurred around April of A.D. 377, as Baronius calculates under that year, § 2, and Hieronymus agrees in his *Chronicle*, year 2 of the 289th Olympiad, Abrahamic year 2394, year 379 of Christ according to Eusebius, that is, Dionysian year 377:

> Valens, compelled to leave Antioch, in late repentance recalls our people from exile.

Rufinus explains the matter even more clearly in *History* XI, chapter XIII, speaking of the time when the Gothic people spread throughout all Thrace:

> Then indeed the wars which Valens had been waging against the churches began to be turned against the enemy, and in late repentance he ordered bishops and presbyters to be released from exile and monks to be freed from the mines.

I know that Tillemontius, in *History of Arianism*, vol. VI, p. 800, sets against such clear testimonies the authority of Theodoret and Sozomen. In their accounts, book IV, chapter XXXI, and book VI, chapter XL, Saint Isaac rebuked Valens as he was departing from Constantinople against the Goths, one or two months before his death—which occurred on August 9, A.D. 378—and warned him to abolish the persecution of the Catholics and restore the best shepherds to their flocks. Theodoret and Socrates, book V, chapter II, and Sozomen, book VII, chapter I, affirm that this was later decreed by the emperor Gratian after Valens’s death, and that the shepherds were restored to their flocks.

But I am not easily persuaded that the eyes of Hieronymus and Rufinus—eyes not distant from the events but present at them, and of whom Rufinus especially, as we have seen, was a principal participant in so great a matter—could have been deceived. Rather, together with the great Baronius, whom that most distinguished man does not seem to have consulted on this matter, I do not doubt that later authors than Rufinus and Hieronymus, as well as Gratian’s edict, were referring to the restoration of the churches, which was to be carried out after the bishops had been recalled from exile.

The truth of this matter is established by Rufinus’s preface to the *Apologeticus* of Gregory of Nazianzus, which Petrus Franciscus Chiffletius edited according to the authority of a very ancient manuscript in his *Vindications of the Works of Vigilius of Tapsus*. There, on p. 59, Gregory is said to have gone to Constantinople when, because of the time of Valens the Arian, the Catholics had recovered the churches that the Arians had held for forty years.

Gregory entered Constantinople around the beginning of A.D. 379, according to Tillemontius, vol. IX, p. 707.

Then, in A.D. 377, when the exiles’ needs no longer demanded a large supply of resources from her, Melania devoted herself to building sacred dwellings. Hieronymus, in Abrahamic year 2396, the tenth year of Valens, Olympiad 285, places Melania’s arrival at Jerusalem. There, he says, she displayed such a miracle of virtues, and especially of humility, that she received the name of Thecla.

These words, which must be understood of her arrival at Jerusalem, not of her departure from Rome—as Pagius understood them in A.D. 372, § 14, wrongly accusing Hieronymus of chronological error—properly coincide with A.D. 373, after the fifth day before the Kalends of April. On that day Valens had entered the tenth year of his reign, and it was after the Kalends of October, when the Abrahamic year begins.

### VI.

There can be no doubt that Rufinus, whom Palladius joins to Melania as her companion, returned to Alexandria in order to study under great men. He himself relates that he spent six years there, not without leisure, and Hieronymus acknowledges that he stayed for a very long time.

Let us present Rufinus’s words from *Apology* II, p. 422, where he defends himself against Hieronymus’s reproach that he had used no teacher:

> I am surprised, he says, that he wanted to say this, when he had a greater and more genuine basis for criticizing me: namely, that although I had long remained among many distinguished teachers, I possess nothing worthy either of their teaching or of their instruction. Yet this man, who in his whole life did not spend even thirty full days in Alexandria, where Didymus was, boasts far and wide throughout almost all his little books that he is a disciple of Didymus the Seer and that he had Didymus as his instructor—κατηγητήν—in the sacred Scriptures. All this boasting was acquired in a single month. I, who stayed there for six years for God’s sake, and again, after an interval, for several other days—where Didymus was, whom you alone boast of knowing, and where there were others no less than he, whom you do not know even by sight: Serapion and Menites, men alike in nature, character, and learning; where there was the elderly Paul, a disciple of Peter the martyr; and, to come to the teachers of the desert, and so forth.

Peter was evidently the Alexandrian bishop of that name, the first, who suffered martyrdom in A.D. 311.

Hieronymus agrees with Rufinus’s account of himself. His testimony in *Apology* II reads:

> Pharus taught you for a long time what Rome did not know; Egypt instructed you in what Italy has so far lacked.

By “for a long time” he indicates the six years spent at Alexandria, which he designates by Pharus. He suggests that Rufinus was imbued there with the teaching of Origen. Rufinus passionately loved this teacher, in whom good and evil were mixed; but in his *Apology to Pope Anastasius* he does not wish to be regarded as either the defender or the advocate of Origen.

Rufinus certainly testifies that he heard Didymus, whom he praises in extraordinary and lofty terms as a man instructed in every branch of learning. He says the same in *Ecclesiastical History* XI, chapter VII:

> We, however, who were in part hearers of his living voice, and who read what some had written down while he was speaking, recognized in his discourses, especially in those that proceeded from his mouth, a much greater grace and I know not what divine quality, sounding above the human voice.

Didymus presided over the Alexandrian catechetical school after Macarius and before Rhodon. This is attested by Philip Sidetes, a disciple of Rhodon, in a fragment concerning the succession of the Alexandrian catechists, published by Henry Dodwell at the end of his *Dissertations on Irenaeus*, p. 469.

The same Didymus dedicated a book on the death of infants to Rufinus, according to Hieronymus in book III of the *Apology*, p. 464. From that same work, p. 455, we also learn that Rufinus boasted of having attended upon Theophilus of Alexandria from adolescence. Hieronymus, however, disputes this, since Rufinus was not in Egypt after Theophilus became bishop—that is, after A.D. 385—and Theophilus did not teach before becoming bishop:

> You boast, he says, that from adolescence you were a hearer and disciple of Theophilus, although he, before becoming bishop, never taught, because of the humility inherent in him, and you were not in Alexandria after he became bishop.

Nevertheless, this does not at all prove that Theophilus did not privately instruct those close to him. Nor is it plausible that, while Theophilus was still alive, Rufinus would have boasted of being his disciple if Theophilus could have convicted him of an obvious lie.

### VII.

After six years spent in the school of the Egyptians, Rufinus at last settled in Jerusalem, attaching himself to Melania, as Palladius testifies in chapter 118. The author who conceals himself under the name of Heraclides reproduces his words in Latin in chapter 23 as follows:

> There was also with her a certain Rufinus by name, an Italian from the town of Aquileia, a man of noble birth and of sufficiently steadfast character in his singular undertaking, who afterward deserved to attain the presbyterate. No one more gentle, more courageous, or more peaceful—being, as it were, all-knowing—could be found among men.

Calculating Rufinus’s six-year sojourn [Col. 0094A] in Egypt from his first arrival there in A.D. 372, we place his return to the Holy City in A.D. 377, when the Confessors of the Faith were recalled from exile. For then, peace having been restored to the Church, he went to Jerusalem in order to devote himself entirely to the monastic life. There, on the Mount of Olives, he writes in book II of the *Invective* that cells existed for his own use and that of others. Although he calls them his own, he affirms that they were not frequented by him alone but also by other monks, and by a very great number of them.

It is worthwhile to quote his words in full:

> I can also produce very many brothers as witnesses, who, while staying in my cells on the Mount of Olives, copied for him [Jerome] very many of Cicero’s dialogues. For I frequently held and reread the quires in my hands while they were writing them, and I recognized that he gave them much larger payments than are customarily given for other writings.

Rufinus adds concerning Jerome that, while living in the monastery at Bethlehem, he had until not long before been engaged in teaching grammar, and that he used to explain to the boys entrusted to him for learning the fear of God his Maro, as well as comic, lyric, and historical authors. It should therefore be thought that he arranged for Cicero’s dialogues to be copied for their use.

One of the brothers who lived in the cells on the Mount of Olives was at one time Saint Petronius of Bologna. Below it will become clear that Rufinus lent him his pen and talent for writing the *Lives of the Fathers*, for in the prologue to book II he says that he wrote that work at the request of those same brothers.

Rufinus nevertheless did not remain so fixed in Jerusalem that he never went out to visit distinguished men in other regions as well. For in book XI, chapter VIII of his *Ecclesiastical History*, he states in these words that he had visited the regions of Edessa and Carrhae, cities of the province of Osrhoene in Mesopotamia:

> At that same time Mesopotamia also possessed noble men distinguished by the same pursuits. We ourselves saw some of them at Edessa and in the regions of Carrhae; we learned of more by hearsay.

Jerome writes the following about the monks of Mesopotamia in his commentary on Isaiah, book V, chapter XIX, at the end:

> For these peoples above all flourish with swarms of monks: Egypt and Mesopotamia, and they vie with one another in equal piety.

Perhaps on this occasion Rufinus again turned aside to Alexandria in order to greet his old friends, especially Didymus. He had clearly hinted at this above, where he stated that he had stayed there not only for six years on God’s business but also again, after an interval, for some additional days.

Palladius also informs us that at about the same time Melania returned to Egypt, in chapter 10 of the *Lausiac History*. He does not, however, seem to have distinguished this second journey of the pious woman from her first arrival in Egypt. For he says that the monk Saint Pambo of Nitria died while she was present; after caring for his body, wrapping it in linen, and laying it down, the historian says, she withdrew from the desert. He testifies that he learned all this from her own mouth, in these words:

> Blessed Melania related it.

Below it will become clear that Palladius, like Rufinus, enjoyed Melania’s intimate acquaintance in Jerusalem.

Rufinus certainly states that on his first arrival in A.D. 372 he conversed with Pambo in the cells of Nitria. Yet this same Pambo by no means passed into the heavenly homeland before A.D. 385, since in the records of the Greek Church published by John Baptist Cotelier we read, vol. I, p. 462, that Pambo was visited by Theophilus when he was already bishop of Alexandria. Since Theophilus began to occupy the episcopal seat on 20 July A.D. 385, Pambo cannot have died before that year—unless we invent two Pambos out of our own imagination.

Therefore either Palladius did not distinguish accurately the conversation he had with Melania, or his words must not be taken strictly. Tillemont notes this in volume X, p. 823.

### VIII.

Now let us return to Jerusalem with Rufinus and Melania. Palladius, in chapter 118, assigns to both of them many years spent in generously receiving people of every kind who came there for the sake of devotion:

> With Melania there also lived the most noble and courageous Rufinus, from Italy, from the city of Aquileia, who was afterward considered worthy of the presbyterate; no one was found more learned or more gentle than he. For twenty-seven years they received those who came to Jerusalem because of a vow—bishops and monks and virgins, married persons, the distinguished and those of private condition—and they supported all who arrived at their own expense.

Palladius immediately adds that the monks who had been divided because of the schism of Paulinus, as well as the remnants of the Macedonian sect, returned to their former communion at the urging of Rufinus and Melania. He further affirms that the Jerusalem clergy were enriched by the beneficence of both with gifts and provisions.

After recounting these things, he concludes his account in these words:

> Thus they passed their lives, offending no one but helping almost the whole world.

Palladius quite clearly shows that Rufinus was not yet a presbyter in A.D. 387—the year in which, according to Tillemont’s calculations, Palladius knew him and Melania at Jerusalem—when he says of him:

> who was afterward considered worthy of the presbyterate.

Henceforth, therefore, we shall see him called by the name of presbyter [Col. 0095B], whereas formerly he was called only a monk and a brother.

When Jerome went to the holy places in A.D. 388, he renewed his former relationship with Rufinus. Rufinus himself later made this sufficiently clear in book II of his *Apology*:

> He cannot deny that on one occasion, when he had come from Bethlehem to Jerusalem and had brought with him a codex containing a dialogue of Cicero and that very Greek work of Plato, he gave the codex itself to me and was at one time staying with me.

### IX.

Among the eminent men whom Rufinus knew there, Bacurius, king of Iberia, stood out above all the others. He was a man of very famous reputation among historians, including Zosimus, book IV, near the end, and Socrates, book VII, chapter X.

Rufinus attributes to him the history of the Iberians’ marvelous conversion:

> These events, he says, were explained to us by Bacurius himself, a most trustworthy man, king of that people and, among us, a *comes domesticorum*, in whom the highest regard for both religion and truth was found. At that time he was living with us in Jerusalem in complete harmony, as commander of the Palestinian frontier.

The same author praises him as a man distinguished in faith, piety, and bodily and mental virtue also in book XI, chapter XXXIII, where he testifies that he fell while fighting bravely and energetically with auxiliary forces on behalf of the Emperor Theodosius the Great against the tyrant Eugenius.

This occurred while Rufinus was still living in Jerusalem, in A.D. 394, on 11 September, in the narrow Alpine entrance of our Aquileian region, beside the river called the Frigidus, now commonly the Vipava. There the battle was fought, and Theodosius triumphed over Eugenius with equal good fortune as six years earlier, at the third milestone from Aquileia, over another tyrant, Maximus. This is reported by Socrates, book V, chapter XXIV; Philostorgius, book XI, chapter II; Claudian in the panegyric on the third consulship of Honorius; Epiphanius Scholasticus in the *Tripartite History*, book X, chapter XLV; and others.

In the same way that Rufinus heard from Bacurius the account of the conversion of the Iberians, he also learned from the mouth of Aedesius, a presbyter of Tyre and companion of Saint Frumentius among the Indians, of the conversion accomplished by Saint Frumentius in farther India. He reports it in book X, chapter IX of his *History*, in these words:

> We learned that these things had happened not from popular rumor but from Aedesius himself, later made a presbyter of Tyre, who had formerly been Frumentius’s companion.

On this matter one should consult Pagi, A.D. 327, § 12, and our friend in the *Life of Saint Athanasius*, vol. I of the works, p. 16. He writes that the India mentioned by Rufinus, which received the Apostle Frumentius, was that part of Ethiopia called Abyssinia, whose royal city at that time was Axuma or Auxumis.

Moreover, all the more remote regions extending broadly toward the east and south were then called India. I see this usage observed in ancient authors by Frederick Brummer, a man of exceptionally elegant talent, in his exercise *On the Sabines*, p. 372 of his works.

Although Rufinus develops the story as though Frumentius had gone on to farther India, as Baronius supposed on 27 October, [Col. 0096A] where he posits two Frumentii, and as Charles of Saint Paul does in his *Sacred Geography*, p. 269, it is nevertheless established that this was a region bordering Egypt and a part of Ethiopia, separated by the entire breadth of the world from Asiatic or Gangetic India.

For the Ethiopians were anciently called by the name of Indians. Hence Virgil writes of the Nile, which rises in Ethiopia, in book IV of the *Georgics*:

> As far as the river flows down from the dark-skinned Indians.

It has been established that Frumentius first reached these colored Indians. From there he returned to Alexandria and was sent back again, ordained by Athanasius as bishop of Axuma or Auxuma, the metropolis of Ethiopia, where the royal residence was located.

See Stephen of Byzantium, *On Cities*; Arrian, *Periplus of the Erythraean Sea*; Nonnosus in Photius, *Codex* III; and Procopius, *Persian War*, book I, chapter XIX.

Frumentius was therefore sent by Saint Athanasius to this Axuma, and to this India—that is, the part of Ethiopia nearest Egypt—not to India within the Ganges, on the eastern side of the river Indus. [Col. 0096B]

Constantius wrote a letter to Aizanas and Sazanas, the tyrants of that region, ordering that Frumentius, bishop of Axuma, should be removed from there, as Athanasius says in his *Apology*. He calls those men brothers and grants them legal standing with the Romans. Yet none of the Roman emperors had allies beyond the Ganges.

The same Constantius enacted a law in these words:

> No one ordered to go to the people of the Axumites and Homerites is henceforth to remain at Alexandria beyond the space of one year.

Therefore, in the time of Constantius these Axumites, joined to the Homerites, were certainly contiguous and allied with the Roman Empire.

Legates frequently traveled to these peoples: first to Alexandria, then to Ethiopia, and from there back to Alexandria. The constitution cited above concerns them.

Rufinus, from whom Socrates, book I, chapter XV; Sozomen, book I, chapter XXIII; Theodoret, book I, chapter XXIII; Cassiodorus; Nicephorus; and other later writers received this history, does not mention the Ganges. His account can therefore be understood as referring either to Indians within or to Indians beyond the Ganges.

When Rufinus calls India “interior” with reference to the nearer India, *interior* here must not be understood as “exterior”—that is, as India beyond the Ganges, which is nearer to us. That would be absurd and contrary to the entire order of true geography.

Thus, when Rufinus says “nearer India” in book X, chapter IX, he also designates the region attached to Ethiopia, where Bartholomew preached the Gospel. No one should doubt that this was Ethiopia beneath Egypt, which reaches the Red Sea at Adulis and the entrance of the Arabian Gulf.

It follows that “interior India” here can mean nothing other than inner Ethiopia, not in Asia but at the extreme edge of Africa, above the source of the Nile. These Ethiopians are now called Abyssinians. Their metropolis was Axuma, into whose interior no herald of Christ had previously penetrated.

Axuma was eight days’ journey from the sea and the port of Adulis, according to Arrian, or according to another author, in the *Periplus of the Red Sea*.

In his letter XCV, formerly IV (now CXXV), [Col. 0096D] to Rusticus, Jerome describes the dangerous and lengthy voyage across the Red Sea to the city of Axuma. There, through a persistent but easily corrected error, *the very great city* has until now been printed instead of *the city of Axuma* [Note: [Col. 0095D] We have corrected it. Vallarsi]. His words are these:

> Those who sail across the Red Sea—which we should wish the true Pharaoh to be drowned in, together with his army—reach the city of Axuma only after many difficulties and dangers. On either shore dwell wandering and warlike peoples, exceedingly savage, always anxious, always armed; they carry provisions for the whole year. Everything is full of hidden rocks and extremely hard shoals, so that a lookout and pilot sits at the top of the ship’s mast and from there announces the directions by which the vessel must be steered and turned about. It is a fortunate voyage if, after six months, they reach the harbor of the aforesaid city of Axuma. From there the Ocean begins to open, across which one can scarcely reach India [Asian India] and the river Ganges in a full year.

Lucas Holstenius, a man of extraordinary learning and judgment, offered this excellent observation about Rufinus’s account in his notes to Charles of Saint Paul, p. 172:

> When ancient writers speak obscurely about more distant regions and events, they should be aided by a charitable interpretation.

He immediately notes that this passage from Jerome is uniquely useful for understanding Rufinus’s account correctly.

Holstenius should also be consulted on this matter in his notes to the *Roman Martyrology* on 27 October, and in the first part, chapter X, p. 184, second edition, p. 332, of the vigorous defender of the letters of Saint Ignatius.

One further point should be added. Dodwell, in *Irenaean Dissertation* I, § 40, p. 73, and in the *Addenda*, believes that the Ethiopians were the Indians whose embassy to Trajan Dio mentions in book LXVIII, p. 777. By the Indians called on coins “India reduced to a province,” he understands the Indians nearer to Arabia Felix—namely, the Homerites and Axumites bordering on the Roman Empire.

To these peoples Pantaenus was sent by the Alexandrian Christians, according to Eusebius, *History*, book V, chapter X; see that passage.

On coins mentioning the province of India, a rhinoceros is represented. The ancients report that rhinoceroses originated in Ethiopia; Pausanias calls them Ethiopian bulls in his accounts of Elis and Boeotia. By “Ethiopians” he means the eastern Ethiopians, about whom Strabo discusses so much from Homer.
