To avoid excessive length, consult Joseph Scaliger, book VII of *On the Correction of the Times*, p. 680; Ezekiel Spanheim, *Dissertation* IV, vol. I, p. 188; and Job Ludolf, *History of Ethiopia*, book II, chapter XI.

These remarks are offered to illuminate the account which the Church owes to Rufinus alone. On this subject Tillemont should also be consulted, vol. VII, pp. 284 and 709.

## CHAPTER III

I. The origin of the quarrels between Jerome and Rufinus.  
II. Jerome sides with Epiphanius against John of Jerusalem; Rufinus adheres to John.  
III. Rufinus admitted by Epiphanius at Jerusalem to communion and regarded as a Catholic.  
IV. The occasion of the disagreement between Jerome and Rufinus increased by Epiphanius’s letter to John, written in Greek and translated into Latin by Jerome.  
V. Melania defends the cause of Rufinus and John.  
VI. Theophilus of Alexandria likewise favors them.  
VII. He attempts unsuccessfully to reconcile the dissenting parties.  
VIII. Hence Jerome’s friendship with Theophilus cools.

The close relationship between Jerome and Rufinus, nourished by the great virtues of both men, grew to such a degree that all Christians admired those exceptionally dear and intimate persons, joined to one another by a bond of friendship known throughout nearly all the churches. Augustine wrote this from Africa to Jerome in Letter LXXIII, formerly XV, chapter III, where he says that he had first learned that so great an evil of discord had arisen between them.

This discord broke out openly in A.D. 394, when Saint Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis in Cyprus, also called Constantia, went to Jerusalem. Yet shortly before this, some cloud of disagreement had already arisen between them. A certain Aterbius, together with others, had begun to denounce Rufinus as a follower of Origen, while also involving Jerome in the same charge because he was Rufinus’s friend and had formerly proclaimed Adamantius [Origen].

Jerome cleared himself by condemning Origen’s teaching. Rufinus later insisted that he had not done the same, recounting the matter in book III of his *Apology* as follows:

> Who stirred up Aterbius against you, and the fury of the others? Was it not the man who also judged me a heretic because of my friendship with you? When I had satisfied him by condemning Origen’s doctrines, you, shut up at home, never dared to see him, lest you should either condemn what you were unwilling to condemn or, by openly resisting, incur the odium of heresy. Can he for that reason be a witness against you, because he is your accuser? Before Saint Epiphanius came to Jerusalem and gave you peace with both word and kiss, etc. Aterbius was barking against you at Jerusalem; and if he had not quickly departed, he would have felt a staff—not a literary one, but the staff of your right hand, with which you are accustomed to drive away dogs.

Although this first declaration by Jerome against Origen seemed to distance him somewhat from Rufinus’s friendship, it nevertheless did not develop into open hostility before the arrival of Saint Epiphanius. Around Easter of A.D. 394, Epiphanius was received by John, bishop of Jerusalem, at his lodging and table.

He was intensely hostile to Origen. Later, in the Anastasis, or Church of the Resurrection, he delivered a speech against him with great force of spirit, indirectly warning John, who was present and appeared to be a disciple of Origen’s teaching, that he ought not to praise the father of Arius—namely Origen—and the root and parent of other heresies. See his letter among Jerome’s letters, p. 824.

John despised Epiphanius. After ordering him to stop preaching through the archdeacon, John shortly afterward delivered a vehement sermon in the Church of the Holy Cross against the Anthropomorphites, who attributed human form to God and were completely opposed to Origen. He pointed to Epiphanius as though infected with this contagion.

Epiphanius then approved the sermon in every respect, himself condemning the heresy John had condemned, but in turn demanding that John also condemn Origen’s doctrines.

These and other seeds of discord [Col. 0098B] forced Epiphanius to withdraw to Bethlehem. There, with Jerome and the other solitaries separated from John’s communion, he elevated Paulinianus, Jerome’s brother, who was twenty-eight years old, first to the diaconate and then to the presbyterate, without consulting John, the bishop of the place. This took place in the monastery called the Old Monastery, between Jerusalem and nearby Eleutheropolis, which Epiphanius had formerly built.

For these reasons John was inflamed with excessive anger and threatened to write to Siricius, the pope. Epiphanius tried to calm him with a very long letter, excusing the ordination he had performed in another parish and answering the other charges brought against him. He again admonished John to abstain from Origen’s teaching.

We have extracted this account in summary from his Letter CX, formerly LX (now LI), which Jerome translated into Latin, and from two letters written by Jerome to Pammachius and to Theophilus of Alexandria against John—namely Letter XXXVIII, formerly LXI, [Col. 0098C] and Letter XLI, formerly LXV.

### II.

In this great dispute it is clear that Rufinus sided with John and Jerome with Epiphanius.

We observed above that Rufinus was not yet a presbyter in A.D. 387. In A.D. 394, however, we see him called a presbyter by Epiphanius in the celebrated letter written that year. John, therefore, the bishop of Jerusalem, had ordained Rufinus a presbyter of his church during that seven-year period.

In a subsequent letter to Pammachius, Jerome reproaches John in the following words. John had complained that Epiphanius had not privately confronted him before the public sermon concerning Origen’s doctrines, for which he later accused him openly:

> He says that he made the charge; you deny it. He produces witnesses; you refuse to hear those brought forward. He also mentions that there was another gathering; you pretend not to know about either matter.

It will immediately become clear that this “other” man was none other than Rufinus. For in book III of his *Apology*, p. 462, Jerome explains what he had previously concealed in silence:

> Therefore Epiphanius, who gave you peace while keeping deceit in his heart, will be polluted. Why should it not rather be true that he warned you first?

In his letter to Pammachius, shortly after the passage quoted above, Jerome reproaches John concerning Epiphanius’s sermon:

> When Pope Epiphanius was speaking against Origen in your church; when darts were hurled against you in his name, you and your chorus, scratching your heads with canine grin and contracted nostrils, were saying by your gestures, “The old man is delirious.” Did you not, before the Lord’s tomb, send the archdeacon and order him to be silent while discussing other matters?

But in book III of his *Apology*, p. 461, he reproaches Rufinus also with precisely what he had reproached John:

> At the same time I cannot restrain my laughter, because, having been warned by a certain prudent man, he turns to praise Epiphanius in these terms: “This is that delirious old man; this is the Anthropomorphite,” and so forth.

Thus Rufinus had been one of the members of the bishop John’s “chorus” in the Jerusalem church, mocking Epiphanius with gestures during the public sermon.

In Letter XXXIX, formerly LXII (now LXXXII), [Col. 0099A] to Theophilus against John, after saying that writings of Origen by himself and by Hilary of Poitiers had been translated into Latin, with harmful material removed, Jerome attacks Rufinus, with whom John was intimate, as follows:

> Let him read, if he knows how. For I suppose that through constant conversation and daily association with Latins he is not ignorant of the Roman language; or, if he has not thoroughly absorbed it, those who usually interpret for him will do so.

That Rufinus supported John’s party is also shown by what Epiphanius relates in his letter to John. He says that Rufinus was questioned by the presbyter Zeno, the companion of Gregory, likewise a presbyter and abbot of the monastery of Eleutheropolis, whether Epiphanius was going to ordain anyone in the diocese of Jerusalem.

Zeno said that when the presbyter Rufinus was speaking to him briefly about certain other matters, he had also said:

> Do you suppose that the holy bishop is going to ordain anyone?

At the end of the prologue to his *Apology for the Martyr Pamphilus*, Rufinus professes that he holds the faith of the Jerusalem church to which he was attached:

> These things are preached in Jerusalem in the Church of God by its holy priest John. We both say and hold them together with him.

At the end of his *Apology to Pope Anastasius*, he testifies that he professes the faith of four churches:

1. The Roman Church, the mother of all;
2. The Church of Aquileia, where he was baptized;
3. The Alexandrian Church, where he was taught for six years;
4. The Jerusalem Church, where he had been ordained a presbyter.

> Apart from this faith, which I have set forth above—that is, the faith held by the Roman Church, the Alexandrian Church, and our Aquileian Church, and which is preached at Jerusalem—I have never had, nor do I have, nor will I have, any other.

There is therefore no doubt that Rufinus received the presbyterate in the Jerusalem Church. From this alone it is evident that there is an error in the *Gennadian Catalogue*, chapter XVII, where Rufinus is called a presbyter of the Aquileian Church.

The error is rejected by a very ancient codex, highly praised by Holstenius and now preserved in the Vatican Library. There it reads:

> Rufinus, presbyter of Aquileia, by nationality—

with the expression referring to his homeland, not to his church.

John Candidus likewise has this wording when he quotes Gennadius’s words in book III from some manuscript codex.

It is therefore not surprising if Rufinus followed the cause of his bishop against Epiphanius, and if he worked with Melania to restore the Bethlehem monks to their former communion while they had broken with the bishop of Jerusalem in order to defend Paulinianus’s ordination.

On this subject Palladius writes in chapter 33 of the *Heraclides*:

> They also restored to the holy Church those four hundred monks who were separating themselves from the Church because of Paulinus—or Paulinianus.

But more on this below.

### III.

Jerome informs us in book III of his *Apology* that Rufinus was admitted by Epiphanius at Jerusalem to the kiss and to prayer. He also testifies that Rufinus was accustomed to boast of this token of peace and Catholic communion.

For Jerome, returning from the city, went to Cyprus, where, he says, he was received by the venerable bishop Epiphanius, whose testimony Rufinus boasted of.

Certainly, in his letter to John, Epiphanius calls eight heads of Origen’s doctrine of heresy [Col. 0099D] up for examination and urges John to condemn Origen. Yet he does not attribute those heresies, which he recites in order to arouse horror and hatred against their author, to John, and still less to Rufinus.

Indeed, he testifies that he had never withdrawn from communion with John, even though John was suspected of holding the same doctrine. He says that he was accustomed to pray for him during the sacrifice:

> Lord, grant that John may believe.

He also charges him with these words:

> You are breaking the charity which we had toward you, to such an extent that you have made us even repent that we communicated with you while defending the errors and doctrines of Origen.

Again, in the same letter, he speaks of John and his presbyter Rufinus as follows:

> But may God deliver you, brother, and the holy people of Christ entrusted to you, and all the brothers who are with you, and especially the presbyter Rufinus, from the heresy of Origen, from the other heresies, and from their destruction.

These words do not at all prove that John and Rufinus were believed by Saint Epiphanius to have fallen into the Origenist heresy. They express the wish that they not fall into it.

In book III of his *Apology*, Jerome uses this same testimony against Rufinus. Rufinus had denied that, after being received by Epiphanius with a kiss and prayer, he could have been represented as an Origenist. Jerome’s sole purpose is to cast suspicion upon Rufinus concerning Origen’s teaching. At that time this was especially easy, since even Chrysostom himself and other most holy men had been unable to avoid this stigma.

After Jerome has quoted the passage from Epiphanius that we have already cited, his words are:

> This is the testimony of the holy man concerning you. This is how he adorns you; this is how he praises you.

Yet Epiphanius does not here declare Rufinus a heretic any more than he declares John a heretic, or the holy people of Christ entrusted to John, or all the brothers who were with him. Epiphanius wishes all of them, just as much as John and Rufinus, to be free from the Origenist heresy; he does not say that they were heretics.

### IV.

Epiphanius’s letter to John was circulating from mouth to mouth, admired by both learned and unlearned for its doctrine and purity of language. Since Eusebius of Cremona did not understand Greek, Jerome, in order to oblige him while he was living in his monastery, hastily and rapidly rendered it into Latin at his request, after Eusebius had reciprocally undertaken to keep a copy at home and not readily make it public.

This same Eusebius had abandoned secular life and, turning from that evasion of public affairs to the monastery, had attached himself to Jerome, as Rufinus says in book I of his *Invective*.

Nevertheless, after a year and six months had elapsed, the letter traveled from Eusebius’s archives to Jerusalem through some new trick and reached the hands of Rufinus and Jerome’s other enemies.

> This is the letter which you produced from the bedroom of the brother Eusebius, together with gold coins, in order to slander the translator,

says Jerome in book III of his *Apology*, p. 461.

This would be closer to the truth if the thief had stolen only the letter and not also Eusebius’s money, as we shall see immediately.

Whatever the facts may have been, it is certain that from this arose new material for barking against Jerome, as though he had translated the letter less faithfully than he ought. I find the translation praised by Alvarus, a ninth-century writer, in his *Life of Saint Eulogius* apud Bollandus, vol. II of the March volume, 11 March, p. 92, no. 9.

To remove this insult from himself in Italy, Jerome wrote Letter XXXIII, formerly CI (now LVII), *On the Best Kind of Translation*, to Pammachius.

Since it nevertheless appears that the false monk laid his thieving hands not only upon papers but also upon expenses—that is, money—it is credible that he committed the crime not because he had been hired for payment, but rather in gratuitous malice, so that he might steal money rather than papers.

Rufinus certainly would not have ordered Eusebius’s money to be stolen. Nor could it have greatly mattered to him or to the others whether the letter, already published in Greek, was or was not published again in Latin.

Therefore the monk, Jerome maintained, had stolen the papers not for money received but out of gratuitous malice. The *corrupter*—namely Rufinus—tried to persuade people of this, according to Jerome, who adds the following about the same Rufinus:

> And one of them dares, with raised eyebrow and cracking fingers, to belch out and say: “What if he bought someone off? What if he suborned him? He did what benefited him.”

Jerome attacks the dead Rufinus in nearly the same words, under the name of Grunoius, in Letter XCV, formerly IV (now CXXV), to Rusticus:

> With raised eyebrow, contracted nostrils, and wrinkled forehead, he cracked two little fingers.

It is clear that Rufinus spoke in the manner reported by Jerome not as though he were admitting that the thief of the letter had in fact been redeemed or solicited by someone, but so as to show that, even if the matter were true, it should still be counted as a good deed because it was advantageous. In this way he was defending either himself or John, since both acted with one and the same spirit.

Jerome refutes this:

> What a marvelous defense of crime—as though robbers, thieves, and pirates did not also do what benefits them. Certainly Annas and Caiaphas, when they led the wretched Judas astray, did what they considered useful to themselves.

When reflecting on these quarrels and agitations of mind, one is reminded of what we find Epiphanius mentioning in the same letter to John: certain people were accustomed to carry rumors back and forth and always add to what they had heard, so as to stir up sadness and quarrels among brothers—namely, between John, Epiphanius, Rufinus, Jerome, and the others who favored one side or the other.

This seems relevant to Jerome’s charge against Rufinus in book III of his *Apology*, p. 439: through Rufinus’s work and effort, a certain codex had secretly been placed at Bethlehem, in the rooms of the elder Saint Fabiola and of Oceanus, without either of them knowing, although they had previously been unaware of it.

Rufinus, however, turned the same crime against others:

> Who stole from the bedroom of the brother Eusebius at Bethlehem the letter praising you? Through whose contrivance, and by whose agents, was the codex found in the lodging of Saint Fabiola and of Oceanus, a Christian and prudent man—although they had never seen it? Do you think yourself innocent for that reason, if you shift everything that belongs to you onto others?

Perhaps the codex had been written against Jerome.

Near the end of the frequently cited letter to Pammachius, Jerome writes the following about Rufinus, Melania, and another man:

> This is not the fault of the man whose person another has assumed in order to stage a tragedy, but of Rufinus and Melania, his teachers, who for a great fee taught him to know nothing.

The man whose name is withheld is Bishop John. Although Jerome does not name him, he immediately adds the following:

> Nor do I blame lack of eloquence in any Christian—and would that we possessed that Socratic saying, “I know that I know nothing,” and the other saying of a wise man, “Understand yourself.” I have always revered not wordy rusticity but holy simplicity. Whoever says that he imitates the Apostles in speech should first imitate their virtues in life, in which the greatness of their holiness excused their simplicity of speech; and the dead man rising again refuted Aristotle’s syllogisms and the twisted subtleties of Chrysippus. But it is ridiculous if one of us, living amid the riches of Croesus and the delights of Sardanapalus, boasts only of his rusticity.

These words, in which Jerome attacks John’s knowledge, morals, and material advantages, correspond entirely to what he writes openly against John in Letter XXXVIII, formerly LXI, p. 308:

> Certainly you are greater than he [Epiphanius] neither in age, nor in knowledge, nor in merit of life, nor in the testimony of the whole world. If age is at issue, you are a young man writing to an old man. If knowledge, you are not so learned writing to a learned man, although your supporters may claim that you are more eloquent than Demosthenes, sharper than Chrysippus, and wiser than Plato, and may perhaps have persuaded you of this yourself.

Finally, on p. 312 he mocks him as follows:

> A certain insignificant little man of our age has been found who, concerning all the questions of the Church, flashed brighter than the sun with a single turn of his tongue.

Such are Jerome’s remarks about John’s knowledge. His wealth is attacked in the passage that will soon be cited from p. 314:

> You who abound in wealth, and to whom the religion of the whole world is a source of profit.

But now let us return to Melania.

## V.

Hieronymus had once raised this most noble woman to the heavens with the highest praises, just as he had Rufinus. In Letter I, formerly XLI, and II, formerly X (now III and IV), he had called her holy. In Letter XXII, formerly XXV [Col. 0101D] (now XXXIX), which concerns the death of Blesilla, he had written:

“Holy Melania, the true nobility of our age among Christians (with whom may the Lord grant you and me a share on his day), while the body of her husband was still warm and not yet buried, lost two sons at once. I shall relate something incredible, but, with Christ as my witness, not false. Who would not then have thought that she would, in the manner of one frenzied, with her hair disheveled and her garment torn, assail her lacerated breast? Not a drop of tears flowed; she stood motionless and, having fallen at Christ’s feet as though she were holding him himself, smiled. ‘Now,’ she said, ‘I shall serve you more readily, Lord, because you have freed me from so great a burden.’”

But perhaps she was surpassed in other respects. Indeed, the contempt with which she regarded them she later demonstrated in the case of her only remaining son: after granting him all the property she possessed, when winter was already approaching she sailed to Jerusalem. In the Chronicle, under the name “the new Thecla,” and in Letter XXVII, formerly XCIX (now XLV), he had commended her to Asella for having abandoned her possessions and her children in order to follow the Lord’s cross.

But after he saw Melania defending the cause of John and Rufinus, he not only thereafter refrained from such a heap of praises, but even erased her name from his Chronicle, if we believe Rufinus, who reports this in *Invective* II, p. 436. Yet since he could not remove it from all copies of the *Chronicle*, Melania’s name is still read there.

In Letter XLIII (now CXXXIII), written to Ctesiphon after Melania’s death, he says that Evagrius wrote a book to her “whose name bears witness to the darkness of perfidy,” thus designating Melania through the meaning of her Greek name. Nevertheless, four years later, namely in A.D. 419, in Letter LXXXI, formerly LXXIX (now CXLIII), he sends greetings to Saint Augustine in the name of Albina, Melania the Younger, and Pinianus. Albina was the mother-in-law of Melania the Elder and the mother of the younger Melania, who had been given in marriage to Pinianus.

## VI.

The rumor of the controversy between the most celebrated men, which was daily intensifying in Palestine, reached even Egypt. Just as it is recorded in written monuments that very many there were passionately devoted to Origen, so it is especially clear that supporters of John and Rufinus were by no means lacking from the fact that a man of the highest rank and renown, Theophilus, Patriarch of Alexandria, undoubtedly supported John and Rufinus in this affair.

For, quite apart from the fact that at that time Theophilus favored Origen, he was also said to have acted against the Anthropomorphites, who opposed Origen’s doctrine; three years later he declared war on them, as Socrates reports in Book VI, chapters VI and X, and Sozomen in Book VIII, chapters XI and XI. Palladius, in his *Life of Chrysostom*, p. 151, mentions letters written by him to Siricius, Supreme Pontiff, against Epiphanius as a heretic and author of the schism—namely, on account of the ordination of Paulinianus. Socrates and Sozomen, in the places already indicated, also plainly testify that the most holy man was at least represented by Theophilus as an Anthropomorphite.

The friendship of Theophilus with John and Rufinus, formerly his own disciple, whose opinion had long since taken possession of him, added weight to all this. From Hieronymus’s lengthy letter to Pammachius, p. 330, we clearly gather that John had written on his own behalf to Theophilus. Accordingly, among other matters, the holy doctor gravely complains why he had arranged for his letters to be delivered to the Alexandrian Patriarch, to whom Palestine did not belong, rather than either to the metropolitan of Caesarea, under whose authority he stood and with whom the Bethlehemites, separated from John, were in communion, or to the Antiochene, Patriarch of the entire East. He later adds:

“You preferred to trouble occupied ears rather than render the honor due to your metropolitan. Nor do I say this because, apart from the friendships that give rise to suspicion, I find anything else blameworthy in your embassy.”

Rufinus, who boasted that he followed Theophilus’s opinion in all things, often incited him against Hieronymus, as though Hieronymus were employing some enemy of Theophilus as a familiar associate. Indeed, Hieronymus writes in Book III of his *Apology*, p. 455, that Theophilus’s letters were not delivered to him because Rufinus forbade it:

“But I shall call no other witness of my communion and of Pope Theophilus than the very man whom you pretend was injured by me. You know that his letters, always sent by me, were not unknown to you even at the time when you prevented them from being delivered to me; and that, by sending messengers daily, you kept asserting that his enemy was our friend and intimate. You were lying about those matters which you now write so shamelessly, in order to stir up his hatred against us and make the pain of an injury an oppression of the Faith.”

That enemy of Theophilus whom Rufinus wrote had attached himself to Hieronymus was a certain Paul, a bishop of uncertain see in Egypt, whom Theophilus had expelled and Hieronymus had received into his own monastery. For when Rufinus was pressed by Hieronymus as to when he had begun to follow the opinion of Theophilus—whom he constantly had on his lips—and to be joined to him in communion of faith, he replied:

“I suppose it was when you were defending with all your might and every effort Paul, whom he had condemned; when you were urging that, by an imperial rescript, he be restored to the priesthood which he had lost by episcopal judgment.”

Thus Rufinus speaks to Hieronymus shortly before the passage recently quoted.

## VII.

After these matters had been argued back and forth, the affair reached the point that Theophilus decided to send the presbyter Isidore to Palestine, at the urging of John and Rufinus, in order to restore peace to the Church of Jerusalem.

One or two months before Isidore’s arrival, and around Easter—which occurred in that same year, A.D. 396, on April 13—Archelaus, Count of Palestine, was acting in the matter. In the following year, 397, he governed Egypt. According to the Theodosian Code, vol. VI, p. 351, negotiations were undertaken to establish peace between John and Hieronymus.

The truth of the matter will be explained better in the words of the letter to Pammachius than in our own:

“When, through the most eloquent and Christian man Archelaus, Count, who was the mediator of peace, a meeting place for the treaty had been agreed upon, was this not demanded above all, so that it might lay the foundation for confidence in the future harmony? John promised that he would come. The day of Easter was imminent. A large crowd of monks had gathered. You were expected at the appointed place. You did not know what to do. Suddenly you sent word that some woman—I do not know whom—was ill, and that you could not come that day. When Archelaus postponed the meeting to the second and third day, John still did not appear, for, as Hieronymus wittily says, ‘the little woman did not stop vomiting.’”

Meanwhile, two months after this meeting, which had been arranged between the two parties but had not taken place, Isidore the presbyter and envoy of Theophilus of Alexandria arrived in Palestine around Pentecost to calm the minds so violently agitated.

Hieronymus says that he distrusted Isidore’s judgment because Isidore had long since joined John’s party. As evidence he cites letters written by Isidore to Rufinus against Epiphanius, which were never delivered to Rufinus but instead to Vincent, a presbyter and close associate of Hieronymus. Writing to Pammachius in Letter XXXVIII, formerly LXI, p. 330, he reveals the matter as follows:

“Letters written in his own hand by Isidore, which had been sent to us three months before the embassy and which brought ‘error’ (Petrus Wastelius prefers to read ‘terror’ in the *Vindiciae*, p. 533), were delivered to the presbyter Vincent. They remain in his possession to this day. In them he encourages the commander of his army to stand firm upon the rock of faith with steadfast step and not be terrified by our trifles. He promises that, before there was any suspicion of an embassy, he would come to Jerusalem, and that at his arrival the ranks of his adversaries would immediately be trampled down. Among other things he also uses these words: ‘As smoke is dissolved in the air and wax melts in the vicinity of fire, so those who have always resisted the ecclesiastical Faith and now attempt to disturb that same Faith through simple men will be scattered.’”

That the “commander of the army” was Rufinus is made clear from Book III of the *Apology*, p. 453, where, concerning these same letters of Isidore, he says against Rufinus:

“May he not be angry with you who, sending you letters against Pope Epiphanius, urged you to remain in the truth of the Faith and not change your opinion through any fear. This letter, written in his own hand, is held by those to whom it was delivered”—namely, by the presbyter Vincent.

Whether intercepted by chance or deliberately, these letters made Rufinus’s dealings with the Alexandrians against Epiphanius and Hieronymus publicly known on every side.

Suspicion of Isidore also increased greatly when, without John’s authorization, he refused to deliver the letters written by Theophilus to Hieronymus. Hieronymus tells us about this in his letter to Pammachius; in Letter LXXXIX, formerly LXII, to Theophilus, he again judges that it happened because the letters appeared less favorable to John than to Hieronymus:

“When you sent us letters of peace and reconciliation through the presbyter Isidore, we prove from this that those who falsely boast of peace were unwilling to deliver them.”

Yet in Book III of the *Apology*, p. 455, Hieronymus holds Rufinus responsible for the letters not delivered to him:

“You know that his letters, always sent to me, were not unknown to you even at the time when you prevented them from being delivered to me.”

Wastelius, however, in the *Vindiciae*, p. 535, judges that they were not delivered for this one reason: because they sharply censured Epiphanius and his supporters, and therefore there was good reason to fear that, once delivered, they would provoke Hieronymus and the other monks even more fiercely.

## VIII.

Since, then, Isidore was considered to share the same doctrine as John and Rufinus and was living with them at Jerusalem, he was regarded not as an envoy of peace but as John’s ally and Hieronymus’s adversary.

“This Isidore,” says Hieronymus in his letter to Pammachius, “whom you exalt to heaven with your praises, is accused at Alexandria of the very same thing as you are at Jerusalem. From this it would appear that he came not as an envoy but as an ally.”

A little later he asks whether Isidore is an adversary or an envoy.

For this reason Isidore went to Bethlehem three times in vain in order to reconcile Hieronymus with John. In the end, having accomplished nothing, he departed, carrying with him to Theophilus at Alexandria John’s letter, or *Apology*, dictated in Isidore’s presence and with his extensive assistance. Thus, says Hieronymus, Isidore was both its author and the bearer of the letter.

Hieronymus thoroughly refutes the same letter, which was especially biting toward him, in those that he wrote to Pammachius and Theophilus; Wastelius gathered fragments of them together on pp. 530–531. Gennadius, in chapter XXX of his *Catalogue*, also seems to refer to this *Apology* when he says that John wrote a book against those who disparaged his learning, in which he showed that he had followed Origen’s intellect, not his faith.

How deeply Theophilus resented Hieronymus’s rejection of the conditions of peace offered through his envoy he indicated clearly enough by refusing for some time to honor Hieronymus’s letters with any reply. But the frequent services by which Hieronymus assiduously appealed to the Patriarch, whether by word or in writing, eventually softened the man’s heart.

Thus Theophilus broke his prolonged silence, although he admonished Hieronymus concerning observance of the sacred canons—namely, because Hieronymus did not obey his bishop of Jerusalem at all and still defended the ordination of his brother Paulinianus.

The response of the holy doctor, in vol. IV, Letter LVIII, formerly LXVIII (now LXIII) of the new edition of his works, which we have followed thus far, displays more complaint than signs of union and friendship with Theophilus. He says:

“Let Your Blessedness remember that, during the time when you were silent toward us, my speech never ceased from acts of service; nor did I consider what you were then doing by way of administrative dispensation, but what it was fitting for me to do.”

A little farther on:

“As for your admonition concerning the ecclesiastical canons, we give thanks. For ‘the Lord chastises the one whom he loves, and scourges every son whom he receives.’ Yet know that nothing is more important to us than to preserve Christ’s rights, not to move the boundaries of the fathers, and always to remember the Roman faith praised by the apostolic mouth, of which the Alexandrian Church boasts that it is a participant.”

By these words he perhaps hinted that he had withdrawn from communion with John on account of the Faith, as though Theophilus himself followed it insufficiently.

Finally, he concludes that the impious heresy—Origenianism—which Theophilus tolerated with great patience, displeased many holy men. In the letter that immediately follows, he says that he had received writings from Theophilus correcting his “former silence.”

# CHAPTER IV

1. The end of the Jerusalem schism.  
2. It was brought to an end through the efforts of Rufinus and Melania.  
3. Palladius the historian and highly esteemed bishop wrongly confused with the heretical Palladius.  
4. The Anastasis, where Hieronymus and Rufinus returned to mutual peace.  
5. Rufinus found guilty of no error.  
6. The perfect relationship between John of Jerusalem, free from errors, and Hieronymus restored.  
7. Rufinus returns to Rome with Melania.  
8. The true reason for Melania’s return investigated.

## I.

The Jerusalem schism, which had grown strong over a period of three years, so that it seemed capable of being removed only by heaven, was finally brought to an end in A.D. 397. Its certain author, however, is unknown, although Baronius, A.D. 393, §32, reasonably believes that Theophilus finally achieved by his authority what he had long been unable to obtain.

But because the sequence of events in the laborious *Annals* is not rarely dislocated and weakened, the conclusion of that great controversy there suffers from an anachronism of four years. The truth of the matter is easily demonstrated. The Palestinian dispute was still raging at the time when Saint Hieronymus was commenting on Jonah. There, when speaking in chapter II about the corruption and incorruption of bodies, he wrote:

“They use this as an occasion for their heresy, so that under the guise of Christ they may fabricate Antichrist; they may HOLD THE CHURCHES, so that they may feed their exceedingly fat belly; and, living carnally, dispute against the flesh.”

These words, which most clearly strike at the defenders of Origen, agree with those already mentioned elsewhere as spoken by the holy man against John of Jerusalem. For the words “so that they may hold the churches,” which designate bishops, must be referred to John alone, against whom Hieronymus continued to contend until this year, A.D. 397. He would certainly not have written in this manner against him immediately after peace had been established.

Moreover, in the preface to the same prophet he plainly affirms that he had published two books to or on behalf of Nepotianus, which are called an *Epitaph*. We demonstrated above, in Chromatius, Book III, chapter III, §3, that the date of this epitaph must be assigned to A.D. 396. Therefore Hieronymus was commenting on Jonah only at this time, when he had not yet been reconciled with John of Jerusalem. Afterward, once restored to John’s communion, he never again attacked him in writing.

## II.

At this point we must not pass over what is read about Rufinus and Melania in Palladius’s *Lausiac History*, chapter CXVIII, since it can shed considerable light on our subject. These are his words from the ancient version of Heraclides:

“They also restored to the holy Church those four hundred monks who had separated themselves from the Church on account of Paulinus.”

Baronius, who cites this under A.D. 372, §99, thinks that Paulinus, Bishop of Antioch, is intended here. Lucifer of Cagliari, Bishop and legate of the Apostolic See, had placed him on the Antiochene see against Meletius, although Meletius was Catholic and had nevertheless been ordained by the Arians. From this arose the great schism there, which Chrysostom and others finally extinguished in A.D. 378—not Melania or Rufinus.

And indeed it is wholly incredible that four hundred monks should have existed at Jerusalem who were separated from the Church of Jerusalem on account of Paulinus of Antioch. If there had ever been such a person, it would have to be this one Hieronymus, whom Paulinus had ordained presbyter, according to Baronius under A.D. 378, §72. But it is not consistent with the truth that Hieronymus himself, still less four hundred monks, defected from the Jerusalem Church for this reason; after what has already been said, this cannot be maintained.

Accordingly, we embrace with open arms at this point the opinion of Petrus Wastelius, although we do not deny that we differ from him in other matters. He was the first of all to observe in the *Vindiciae of John of Jerusalem*, p. 534, that in Palladius, a Greek writer, one should read *Paulinianus*, not *Paulinus*. Thus the Bethlehemite monks, who under the leadership of Hieronymus had abandoned communion with the Church of Jerusalem because of the ordination of Paulinianus by Epiphanius and its disapproval by John, were finally restored to it through the strenuous efforts chiefly of Rufinus and Melania.

Hieronymus generally alludes to the number of monks living in schism in these words from his letter to Pammachius against John:

“SO GREAT a MULTITUDE of brothers and choirs of monks who do not communicate with you in Palestine.”

But the Antiochene schism did not consist of monks.

## III.

I am not unaware that highly learned men, led by Baronius under A.D. 388, §107, diminish the authority of Palladius as a friend of Rufinus, as though he himself, corrupted by the Origenian stain, had taken part in these disturbances. For this reason Epiphanius, at the end of his letter to John of Jerusalem, is supposed to have attacked him in these words:

“But beware of Palladius the Galatian, who was once dear to us and now needs God’s mercy, because he preaches and teaches the heresy of Origen, lest perhaps he lead some of the people entrusted to you into the perversity of his error.”

Palladius, whom Epiphanius says was then at Jerusalem, is also openly mocked by Hieronymus in the prologue to his *Dialogue against the Pelagians*:

“Palladius, a man of servile wickedness, attempted to restore the same heresy.”

But it will immediately become clear that this Palladius, the man of servile wickedness and a protégé of the Pelagian heresy, has been improperly confused with the Palladius of Helenopolis in Bithynia, bishop and author of the *Lausiac History*, who bore the same name.

The one Palladius was staying at Jerusalem in A.D. 394, when Epiphanius, in a letter written that same year, accused him as a heretic because he was present and attached to John’s side. But we see that Palladius the historian remained continuously in Egypt from A.D. 388 to A.D. 399—at Alexandria, in the deserts of Nitria, and in the Cells, a place in that same desert.

At the beginning of his *History* he says that he first reached the city of Alexandria in the second consulship of the elder Theodosius, which corresponds to A.D. 388. But once he had gone there, he never left before A.D. 399, when he testifies in chapter LXXXVI that he was present at the death of Evagrius. Evagrius died around the Feast of the Epiphany in A.D. 399, according to Tillemont, vol. X, p. 379.

Melania and Rufinus returned to Rome in A.D. 397, as we shall see below. Therefore Palladius could have associated familiarly with Melania and Rufinus at Jerusalem only before he migrated to Egypt, that is, before A.D. 388, when Rufinus was not yet a presbyter. He testifies to this about himself in chapters V and CXVIII.

He spent the whole of A.D. 388 at Bethlehem with the solitary Possidonius, who, as even holy men are sometimes not free from human feelings, we learn in chapter LXXVII to have spoken somewhat unfairly of Hieronymus.

But because this Palladius the historian, in addition to his friendship with Rufinus, attributes too much against Hieronymus to Possidonius—as he makes plain there and also in chapter CXXII—highly learned men easily believed that he was none other than Palladius the Galatian, who was scourged by Epiphanius and Hieronymus.

Palladius, moreover, assumed the see of Helenopolis around A.D. 400. In that year he participated in the Council of Constantinople against Antonius, Bishop of Ephesus, perhaps having been ordained by Saint John Chrysostom. Palladius’s alleged Origenism was brought against him in A.D. 403 at the false synod at the Oak, according to Photius, codex LIX.

The same Chrysostom, driven into exile in A.D. 404, wrote Letter CXIII to Palladius, commending himself and his cause to Palladius’s prayers. Palladius, wishing to aid him as far as he could, hastened to Rome, as the other Palladius testifies in his *Life of Chrysostom*, p. 36, and as Palladius himself records in the *Lausiac History*, chapter CXXI.

He too was deprived of his episcopate on account of Chrysostom and, afflicted by many hardships, eventually transferred to the Church of Aspuna, situated in First Galatia, as Socrates reports in Book VII, chapter XXXV.

After writing the *Lausiac History* around A.D. 420—a work named after Lausus, a chamberlain in the Imperial Court, to whom he dedicated it—he died before A.D. 431. In that year his successor, Eusebius of Aspuna, Bishop in Galatia, participated in the Council of Ephesus.

He is deservedly renowned under the title of Confessor for defending Chrysostom with unconquered courage. Contemporary writers attribute a prophetic spirit to him, and at Rome he was received by Innocent I, Supreme Pontiff, as a most Catholic prelate, such as he was regarded throughout the East, despite the accusation of Origenism and although three years earlier Rome had proclaimed against the Origenists.

On that occasion he testifies in chapter CXXI that he had been overwhelmed with every kind of service in Melania’s house and, when departing from there, had been assisted with the greatest generosity.

Tillemont treats these and other matters concerning this highly esteemed man fully and accurately in volume XI, p. 500. I therefore believe it sufficiently clear that his authority and reputation cannot be undermined by any charge of heresy, and that he was grievously wronged by being confused with the other Palladius the Galatian, a man of bad faith.

Just as, because many Palladiuses were living around the same time, it was easy for one to be confused with another—for Isidore of Pelusium wrote several letters to one Palladius, Saint Athanasius to another, while there was yet another Palladius whom Epiphanius mentions and another who was the author of the *Life of Saint John Chrysostom*—so our Rufinus of Concordia suffered the same fate. For since many Rufinuses flourished in the same age, we shall later show that he too was unjustly conflated with another.

Now that Palladius has been cleared of every suspicion, Hieronymus and Rufinus, embracing one another after so long a disagreement, call us to Jerusalem.

## IV.

That the minds of Hieronymus and Rufinus were solemnly prepared for peace in the Anastasis after the sacrifice of the Mass is made certain by Hieronymus, who reveals this in Book III of the *Apology*, p. 466, in these words:

“In the Anastasis, after the Lamb had been sacrificed, we joined right hands.”

In the new edition, *Anastasius* is wrongly printed for *Anastasi*, p. 462 [Note: [Col. 0107D] We have corrected it. Vallarsi.].

This Anastasis was a building constructed by Constantine the Great at the site of the Lord’s Resurrection, from which it took its name. For Constantine erected two basilicas at Jerusalem in two separate places: one at the site of the Passion, called the Cross and the Martyrium; the other at the site of the Resurrection, called by its proper name the Anastasis.

Hieronymus mentions both in Letter XXXVIII, formerly LXI (now among the *Opuscula*), to Pammachius against John of Jerusalem, p. 312:

“Was it not when you were going from the ANASTASIS to the CROSS, and a crowd of every age and sex gathered around him [Epiphanius], offering infants, kissing his feet, pulling at his fringes, and so forth?”

Thus one went from the Anastasis to the building of the Cross.

See more in Sirmond, vol. IV of his works, pp. 436 and 704, where he skillfully interprets an ancient coin inscribed in Greek, ΑΝΑCTACIC (*Anastasis*). Consult also Cangius, *Dissertation on Coins of the Lower Age*, §66, and Henri Valois, *Letter on the Anastasis and the Martyrium*, appended to Eusebius, p. 304 of the first edition, where he argues that there was a single building called the Anastasis, erected by Constantine.

Adamnanus, Book I of *On the Holy Places*, chapter IV, in Mabillon’s *Acts of the Saints*, third century, Part II, p. 506, testifies that between the Anastasis and the Martyrium, at the place of Calvary, there was a small street.

John Cantacuzenus also mentions this Holy Anastasis in Book IV of his *History*, chapter XIV, p. 757 of the royal edition, but in the Greek text.

This is what concerns the place where the divided minds of Hieronymus and Rufinus were united—surely a place more sacred could not have been found.

Before the words explained above, Hieronymus says, p. 462:

“We joined right hands and accompanied them as they departed.”

And Rufinus had said there:

“You gave us peace as we were departing.”

For shortly afterward Rufinus returned to the West, and Hieronymus, writing to him in Letter XLII, formerly LXVI (now LXXXI), affirmed under oath that, on his part, after their friendship had been restored, no resentment had intervened.

## V.

Baronius, under A.D. 393, §52, thinks that in this peace Origen’s errors were condemned in silence. But Hieronymus, in good faith, acknowledged that Rufinus had been found guilty of no error; Rufinus, for his part, professes in Book II of the *Invectives* that he had condemned no one:

“I have never followed one who was in error; nor shall I follow anyone other than the Catholic Church. Can you produce any writings of mine in which you can prove that I erred, even in my youth?” [Col. 0107D]

Once peace had been established, Paulinianus—whose ordination had been the principal source of the conflict—was permitted to live in the monastery at Bethlehem, which was subject to the Bishop of Jerusalem. Hieronymus later sent him to Stridon in the following year so that, after selling his patrimony, he could generously support the monastery that Hieronymus had built.

At the end of Letter LIV, formerly XXVI (now LXVI), to Pammachius, Hieronymus says:

“In this province, having built a monastery and a guesthouse beside it, lest perhaps Joseph too should now come with Mary to Bethlehem and find no lodging, we are overwhelmed by the crowds of monks flowing together from the whole world. We are unable to carry the work begun and to bear it beyond our strength. Therefore, since what happened in the Gospel concerning the future tower has almost happened to us—we failed to calculate the expenses beforehand—we have been compelled to send our brother Paulinianus to his HOMELAND, so that he might sell the half-ruined little estates that escaped the hands of the barbarians, along with the revenues of our common parents, lest, abandoning the ministry undertaken for the saints, we provide laughter for slanderers and rivals.”

In Letter XLII, formerly LXVI (now XC), Hieronymus thought that Paulinianus, returning to Palestine from his homeland, had been seen by Rufinus at Aquileia with Chromatius in A.D. 399.

## VI.

As for John the Bishop, the words of Severus Sulpicius in *Dialogue* I, chapter IV, also persuade us that a perfect concord had been established with him. There Postumianus testifies that Hieronymus exercised the office of parish priest at Bethlehem; he visited him once and afterward stayed with him for six months:

“Hieronymus the presbyter governs the church of that place; for it is a parish of the bishop who holds Jerusalem.” [Note: [Col. 0108D] Compare the *Life of Saint Hieronymus*, chapter XVIII.]

A bishop would certainly not have granted this to an adversary and someone not dear to him.

Rufinus, agreeing with Sulpicius in *Invective* II, p. 420, says that Hieronymus, having been entrusted with little children to teach them the fear of God—which is the office of a parish priest—also performed the grammatical duties and expounded pagan authors.

Afterward Hieronymus adhered to John to such an extent that in A.D. 397 he made John’s innocence clear to Theophilus of Alexandria, who had raised complaints against him, as may be gathered from the following words of Letter LIX, formerly LXX (now LXXXVI):

“Concerning the reception of a certain person, you ought not to be angry with the Bishop of THIS CITY [Jerusalem], since you gave no instruction in your letters. It was rash to pass judgment concerning something he did not know. Yet I think that he neither dares nor wishes to harm you in anything.”

Saint John also responded in a good spirit. For in A.D. 404 he attended at Bethlehem the very distinguished funeral of Paula of Rome, as Hieronymus himself left on record as a mark of honor in the epitaph of that pious woman, or Letter LXXXVI, formerly XXVII (now CVIII).

How well John was regarded by Saint Augustine the great doctor demonstrates most fully in Book II, chapter LI, against Petilianus, where he says:

“What has the chair of the Roman Church done to you, in which Peter sat and in which Anastasius sits today? Or what has the Church of Jerusalem done, in which James sat and in which JOHN sits TODAY? Through these churches we are joined in Catholic unity, while you separate yourselves from them in nefarious madness.”

Paulinus of Nola, in Letter XXXI, formerly XI, to Sulpicius Severus, and Pope Zosimus, in Letter IV to the Africans, in Labbe’s councils, vol. II, p. 1561, called him a saint both before and after his death. No one can rightly say that this title was given to a heretical man, according to Baronius in his commentary on the Roman Martyrology, chapter VII.

## VII.

With the minds of both parties now settled, after Rufinus had established his life for so many years far from his homeland, the desire to return to the West took hold of him. Accordingly, when Melania the Elder, to whom he had remained attached almost continuously from her first arrival in the East, was planning a journey to Rome, he joined her as a companion.

As Rufinus was departing from Jerusalem, Hieronymus gave him peace, joined right hands, and accompanied him as he left, as he confesses in Book III of the *Apology*, p. 462. Rufinus had reproached him for this:

“You gave us peace as we were departing.”

Hieronymus replied:

“We gave peace; we did not accept heresy. We joined right hands and accompanied them as they departed.”

In Letter XLII, formerly LXVI, Hieronymus calls the Lord to witness his state of mind: after their friendship had been restored, no resentment had intervened on his part that could injure Rufinus.

At the beginning of Book III of the *Apology*, he later does not deny that, before his final quarrel with Rufinus, which arose from the translation of the book *Periarchon*—about which we shall speak below—he had in turn been praised by Rufinus as a true colleague and brother.

Rufinus, therefore, restored to his former relationship with his old friend, after giving and receiving greetings, and serving as the spiritual companion of Saint Melania on her journey, crossed into Italy, as Paulinus testifies in Letter XXVIII, formerly IX, §5.

But I must examine Melania’s affairs somewhat more carefully, because the truth concerning Rufinus’s actions depends upon them.

## VIII.

Publicola, the son of Melania, who, as has been said, had been left behind as a boy in the urban praetorship, became distinguished in his mother’s absence by the glory of every virtue as well as of civil honors. He had married Albina, born from the most noble line of the Caejonii, whose genealogy, drawn by him from the innermost recesses of antiquity, was illuminated by Henri Noris in his *Adventoria*.

From the marriage of Publicola and Albina were born Melania the Younger and Publicola the Younger, as will be established later.

Melania the Younger married, against her will, Pinianus, a very distinguished young man whose father, Severus, had governed Africa and Italy in A.D. 382, according to the *Prosopography* of the Theodosian Code, vol. VI, p. 384, col. 2. She was being stirred by her grandmother Melania’s letters, reputation for virtue, and examples to undertake a more holy way of life.

After the deaths of the two sons born to her, while her parent Publicola was still alive, she obtained permission from her husband Pinianus, who was still a pagan, to preserve her chastity, and renounced every concern for earthly things.

Palladius, who had once been their host, relates this in the *Lausiac History*, chapter CXIX; the *Acts of Melania the Younger* in Surius, December 31, agree with him.

When Melania the Elder received news of this, she boarded a ship in order to turn her granddaughter, who had been confirmed in her purpose, away from corrupt opinions. Sailing from Caesarea, she reached Rome after a voyage of twenty days, says Palladius in chapter CXVIII.

Baronius, under A.D. 397, §3, assigns another reason for the journey: namely, a desire to introduce Origenism into Rome, for which the withdrawal of Melania the Younger had served as a pretext among the populace. But Baronius offered no authority for his opinion; he merely followed conjectures, says Huetius in *Origenianism*, Book II, chapter IV, section I, §16, p. 204.

The same Palladius, when he says that Melania the Elder was then sixty years old, reverses the chronology. She had reached that age only in A.D. 410, when she departed from the City to return to Palestine.

If Palladius assigns her twenty-two years of age in A.D. 371, when she first sailed there, in chapter CXVII—and Saint Paulinus, Bishop of Nola, agrees in Letter XXIX, formerly X, §8, declaring that she had bid farewell to the world while still young—then it follows that in A.D. 397, when she returned to the City, she was not sixty but only forty-seven years old.

Add the thirteen years that elapsed from A.D. 397 to A.D. 410, when she returned there, and the total is sixty. Palladius therefore appears to have committed a chronological anticipation of thirteen years on this point.

# CHAPTER V

1. The arrival of Rufinus and Melania at Nola.  
2. The time at which it occurred.  
3. The chronology of Paulinus of Nola’s letters restored, thereby confirming the dates of Rufinus’s and Melania’s departure and return.  
4. Palladius reconciled with Paulinus.  
5. The chronology of Paulinus’s *Natalia* restored, and the date of Rufinus’s and Melania’s return confirmed again.  
6. Baronius’s opinion concerning Rufinus as Melania’s inseparable companion defended.

[Col. 0109D] I. Although Palladius testifies that Melania came directly from the Caesarean harbor of Palestine to Rome, he had before his eyes the destination of the journey, not its route; for she first put in at Naples, whence, accompanied by a great throng of distinguished relatives who had come to meet her, she turned aside to Nola to visit Paulinus, as he himself records in Letter XXIX, otherwise X, §12, to Saint Sulpicius Severus. Paulinus, leaping for joy, describes to him, with marvelous eloquence, the praises of so great a woman.

But Paulinus’s words, which place Melania’s arrival before our eyes, must not be passed over here:

> I shall pass over the rest of her (Melania’s) affairs and the intervening time, and I shall cross over this very stretch by which she **sailed on her return**, so that, imitating her course, I may bring my speech to its conclusion more quickly by explaining her **arrival**. In this I was a spectator of God’s great grace. She was brought to Naples, a city separated (or distant) by a short interval from the Nolan city where we live; there, welcomed by the meeting of her sons and grandsons, she soon hastened to the lodging of our humility at Nola. She arrived among us surrounded by the ostentatious retinue of her wealthiest pledges.
>
> We saw the glory of the Lord in the journey of that mother and her sons, a single journey indeed, but in dress and manner utterly unlike. Seated on a lean little donkey, cheaper than an ass—*asellus buricus*, that is, a short horse—she was escorted amid the whole pomp of this world by Senators, as honored and wealthy men could be, sweeping along around her: with swaying carriages, caparisoned horses, gilded *pilenta* and many wagons, while the Appian Way groaned and glittered.

Thus Paulinus writes. In §5 of the letter he says that he wished to give Severus the woolen tunic which he had received from Melania; and in Letter XXXI, otherwise XI, §1, he mentions a portion of a particle of the wood of the divine Cross, brought to him at that time by her as a gift from John of Jerusalem. He sent its tiny fragment—or little splinter—enclosed in a small golden tube to Severus, while he deposited the remainder in the church of Saint Felix, which he had built, together with the epigram that is read in Letter XXXII, otherwise XII, §11.

According to Palladius, chapter CXX, Melania’s family lived in the countryside, at one time in Sicily and at another in Campania, where Nola was situated. We can therefore readily understand that relatives immediately came to meet Melania on her arrival. Norisius, in Book I, chapter II of the *Pelagian History*, is prevented from saying that she was magnificently welcomed by her family who had traveled from Rome as far as that point by the fact that her arrival at the Neapolitan harbor, after a short voyage of twenty days, was unexpected and had not been announced beforehand. Its exact date will become clear from a comparison of the passages in Paulinus.

II. In the aforementioned Letter XXIX, otherwise X, §6, Paulinus says that the monk Victor, the letter-carrier—or, as he calls him in the preceding letter, §4, the book-bearer—of Sulpicius Severus, arrived at Nola on the same days on which Melania had also arrived from Palestine. Yet in the same preceding letter he writes that he had received Victor at Nola when winter was already departing, that is, at the beginning of spring. Melania’s arrival is therefore certainly fixed to this season, which was suitable for navigation.

Paulinus’s words excusing Victor’s late return to Sulpicius are these, in Letter XXVIII, otherwise IX, §3:

> As for the fact that he (Victor) returned to you later than arranged, do not charge it to his feet, which remained longer with us not through the fault of sluggishness but from zeal for obedience. Consider, however, the time not when you indicated that he had been dismissed, but when you sent him, and you will see that I have a valid account of the agreement between us concerning Victor’s being retained. For he did not arrive at our place, as you had written, **to spend the winter** with us; rather, as he stated, after he had been sent back to you from Narbonne, where he had met our brother Postumianus, he set out from you again at the time when, having been directed to me, he could have arrived.
>
> Since, therefore, I received him **when winter was departing**, I necessarily detained him during the **spring months**. And because the interval seemed short, since the Paschal solemnity would immediately bring it to a close, and since I had also been extremely ill during that period, so that I was unable to undertake the business of replying, I added to his delay some days of summer, in order to make compensation with you, if I should take from your time as much through him as you had occupied of his winter days. Accordingly, I shall allow him, if he reaches your fellowship in autumn, to spend the winter with you once again.

From this it is clear that the published order of Paulinus’s letters is in some places reversed. Consequently, the letter in which Victor is said to have been sent back to Severus in Aquitania is placed first in the printed editions, although it must be placed after the letter immediately following it, in which Paulinus informs Severus about Victor, whom he had then recently received. Furthermore, in this latter letter Melania’s arrival at Nola from the East is described, after she had already set out from Nola for Rome. In the former, Rufinus’s departure is discussed, and Paulinus calls him Melania’s companion. Therefore this letter should be regarded not as earlier but as later, both in order and in time; and the other not as later but as earlier.

III. To the two letters addressed to Severus, Letter XLIII, otherwise XXXV, to the presbyter Desiderius must be attached. Paulinus writes to him that Victor, whom he had previously sent back to Gaul with Letter XXVIII, otherwise IX, at Severus’s instruction, so that he might arrive for the vintage season, had then returned to Nola because sudden obstacles had arisen, while winter closed navigation and roads through fear. Victor, hindered and **recalled**, submitted to necessity and caused a **long delay**, although, when asked, he had refused to deny his postponement to affection.

For five months, from June to November of A.D. 397, fear closed navigation and the roads because of the preparations for the Gildonian war, which was to be carried across to Africa, as Jacobus Gothofredus notes in the *Chronology of the Theodosian Code*, p. 137. To Victor’s autumn and winter detention was added a long illness and the need to regain his health; these kept him at Nola even during the following year, 398, until June. In that month Paulinus went to Rome with him, as was customary, to celebrate the feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul. After it had been celebrated, Victor departed, so that Severus might receive him—if not in the same year in which he had hoped for him, at least at the same vintage season at which he had ordered him to arrive. So Paulinus says.

During these delays of Victor, which clearly fell in the years A.D. 397 and 398, Paulinus wrote several letters to Severus at different times, according as the pressure of urgent business allowed, as their varying wording will show. Thus he writes to Desiderius:

> Of these letters, two already mentioned remain, carried to Gaul by Victor together with the others and with this third one.

But Joannes Baptista Brunus, who prepared a new edition of Paulinus’s works at Paris in A.D. 1685, distorted this third letter and dragged it unwillingly to A.D. 406, although it was issued in A.D. 398. Chiffletius, in arranging Melania’s chronology, committed an anachronism of one year and judged it to have been written in A.D. 399, in Part II of his *Illustrated Paulinus*, chapter XIX. For in chapter XI he joined the other two letters already mentioned to A.D. 398, to which he assigned Melania’s arrival at Nola, because he thought that she had been transported from Rome to Egypt not at the beginning of A.D. 372 but in the following year. Once this chronological error had been admitted, it was inevitable that he should repeatedly go astray thereafter.

Accordingly, in our judgment the order of these letters must be arranged as follows:

1. Letter XXIX, otherwise X, to Severus, was written in the spring of A.D. 397, after Victor had arrived at Nola and Melania had departed from there for Rome.

2. Letter XXVIII, otherwise IX, to Severus, was written at the end of the summer of that same year, 397, when Victor was ready to depart.

3. Letter XLIII, otherwise XXXV, to Desiderius, was written in A.D. 399, after the feast of the Apostles, when Victor was about to depart for Gaul.

Therefore Tillemontius, and Joannes Baptista Brunus, who followed him in the new edition of Paulinus, wrongly judged that the first two letters had been written in A.D. 402 and the third in A.D. 406.

As for the first two, if that were true, Melania would have sailed in the East in A.D. 377, after the persecution of the Arians had already ended. This is wholly impossible. For Paulinus, who affirms that Melania returned to him **after five lustrums**, testifies in the aforementioned Letter XXIX, §2, that she had been present at that time of Valens, when the fury of the Arians, with the emperor himself as the agent of impiety, was persecuting the Church of the living God and Catholics were being driven away and arrested. Palladius speaks in precisely the same way in chapter CXVII. There can be no controversy that this storm raged in A.D. 372 and 373, as we demonstrated long ago and at great length.

IV. In chapter CXVIII Palladius extends the five lustrums to twenty-seven years. But from the date of Melania’s departure and return, supported by the weightiest testimonies of Jerome and Paulinus, it is certain that only twenty-five years arise. [Note: See *Life of Saint Jerome*, chapter XXIX.] One or two months were spent on the first voyage, which began when winter was already approaching, toward the end of A.D. 371. Paulinus, using the rounded number of five lustrums, disregarded this same month or two; Palladius counted it as a whole year, and also added the whole of A.D. 398, in which he understood Melania, while he himself was living in Egypt, to have arrived in Rome.

Thus, once Palladius has been explained as necessity requires, he by no means disagrees with Paulinus and needs no correction from the critics, among whom are Pagius at A.D. 397, §5, and also Baronius in the same year, §2.

Moreover, Palladius, being less exact in arranging the sequence of years than the sequence of events, also mixes into the twenty-seven years which, as I have said, he counts as having been spent by Melania and Rufinus together at Jerusalem the entire six years which Rufinus, and the year and a half which Melania, spent in Egypt.

Nor does Palladius disagree with Palladius himself, when in one and the same chapter, CXVIII, after saying that Melania had received guests at Jerusalem for twenty-seven years, he then says that she performed this pious service there for thirty-seven years. In the first passage he was considering the time of the pilgrimage from A.D. 371 to A.D. 398; in the second he added the period and residence of the second pilgrimage, that is, from A.D. 410, when she returned from Italy to Jerusalem, to A.D. 420, when, as we see from this, she ceased to live there.

Tillemontius, otherwise exceptionally energetic in explaining the difficulties of ancient history, was unable to disentangle the knots concerning Melania’s departure, return, and residence that he found in Jerome, Paulinus, and Palladius. Since he agreed with no one and was least of all consistent with himself, he entangled himself in many digressions in his notes on her life, vol. X, p. 821. There is no opportunity, nor any advantage, in repeating them here, since from what has already been said his chronological guesses on this matter vanish, and the points that seemed troublesome become perfectly clear.

V. What has been said thus far had to be pursued at greater length in order to establish that the return of Rufinus and Melania could have occurred neither earlier nor later than A.D. 397, the year to which the great master of ecclesiastical history, Baronius, most correctly assigned it.

Yet the same matters, assigned by learned men to a wholly unsuitable time, were the reason why they made many other errors of the same kind. I shall briefly call these to examination here, lest they deceive anyone if, because they are not challenged at this point, they should pass unnoticed.

At the end of Letter XXXIX, otherwise X, Paulinus says that he recited the *Life of Saint Martin*, once written by Severus, to Melania, who was then his guest, just as he had previously recited it to the venerable and most learned bishop Nicetas, who had come from Dacia to the admiration of the Romans—plainly before Melania arrived. If she arrived in the spring of the year 397, Nicetas must therefore be said to have arrived in the preceding winter.

Pagius is consequently entirely mistaken when, at A.D. 397, §6, he contends that Nicetas arrived after Melania, that is, in the following year, A.D. 398. The published chronological order of the letters of Saint Paulinus led to the error. When Pagius saw no mention of Nicetas in Letter XXVIII, otherwise IX, he thought that this was sufficient reason to regard it as having been written before that bishop had come from Dacia to Nola—that is, before, rather than after, Letter XXIX, otherwise X.

Again, in the aforementioned Letter XXVIII, §6, Paulinus testifies that he was accustomed each year to sing a *Natalic poem* to Saint Felix, the Nolan presbyter, on his feast day, January 14. These poems began to be issued in A.D. 393, and a series of fifteen brought them to a close. Nicetas first attended the fifth of these *Natalia*, in A.D. 397, and afterward the ninth, which was issued in A.D. 401, according to Baronius at A.D. 397, §15.

For in this ninth *Natale*, which is Poem XXIV, Paulinus addresses Nicetas, then present at Nola, in verse 330:

> … Tell me, I ask, **have you returned?**
>
> And I hold you yourself, Nicetas, upon whom until now,
>
> Sick at heart, I have hung through nights and days?
>
> At last you have come, **returned to me in the fourth year**?

These words rightly persuaded the father of the *Annals* that Nicetas had been seen at Nola both at the fifth and at the ninth *Natale* of Saint Felix: first in A.D. 397 and afterward, four years later, in A.D. 401.

Indeed, since in the spring of A.D. 397 Paulinus recited the *Life of Saint Martin* to Melania, who was staying with him, and had previously recited it to Bishop Nicetas, it is clear that Nicetas had first been at Nola in the winter of that same year, 397, on January 14.

But Pagius, at A.D. 397, §7, following Chiffletius, Part II, chapter IX, disturbs these chronological dates of Paulinus’s *Natalia*. He removes *Natale I* from A.D. 393 and fixes it in the following year; he attempts to transfer *Natale XIII* from A.D. 405 to A.D. 406 because that *Natale* mentions the destruction of Radagaisus, king of the Goths. Since this occurred in A.D. 405, he therefore thinks that Paulinus composed the poem in the following year, A.D. 406. He consequently moves *Natale I* from A.D. 393 to A.D. 394, so that, on the authority of Chiffletius and Pagius, Nicetas first attended the fifth *Natale* at Nola not in A.D. 397 but in 398.

We cannot accept this opinion, even though it has been reproduced by another. For when the Goths were devastating Italy in A.D. 405 and pressing upon Rome itself, Paulinus, who was otherwise wholly devoted to the care of his flock, could hardly have had leisure to perform this work of peace and tranquillity on the customary day, January 14. He performed it afterward, once winter had passed and spring was approaching, in that same year, 405, and thus after Italy had already been freed from the Gothic invasion.

If I judge correctly, Paulinus sets this out explicitly at the beginning of *Natale XIII*, which appeared, together with XI and XII, from the Ambrosian manuscripts. For the holy poet begins *Natale XIII* in this manner, on p. 72:

> White peace, with the welcome return of springtime, leads the year
>
> **After winters have been endured**, in tranquil light,
>
> And, marked by the holy honor of Saint Felix,
>
> Opens it to secure peoples. Felix, rejoicing,
>
> Urges hearts to rejoice in serenity,
>
> With the dreadful darkness of **war wiped away**,
>
> Since he himself, as patron of peace,
>
> Together with the fathers, Paul and Peter, and the blessed brother martyrs,
>
> Has entreated the King of Kings, with friendly favor,
>
> To prolong the times of the Roman realm
>
> And **drive away the advancing Goths**
>
> Already at the very jaws of the City.

The reason is concealed why the person who brought this into the light thought himself permitted, contrary to the manuscript’s authority, to insert a third little word—*laetum* (“joyful”)—into the first verse from his own resources, after rejecting the original reading, which I know to have been *verni* (“of spring”), and which the words in the second verse, *Post hiemes actas* (“after winters have been endured”), elsewhere clearly confirm. That original word *verni*, upon which the whole issue turns, is represented clearly enough in the Ambrosian manuscript.

But this and many other matters of the same kind will easily become apparent to anyone who compares the ancient manuscript with the new edition. Moreover, *verni grata vice temporis, post hiemes actas* (“with the welcome return of springtime, after winters have been endured”) expresses what Horace says in Book I of the *Odes*, Ode IV: *solvitur acris hiems grata vice veris* (“the harsh winter is dissolved by the welcome return of spring”).

These points show that Paulinus sang this thirteenth *Natale* not in January, as he had customarily done on other occasions, but soon afterward in the spring, immediately after the Gothic army had been destroyed; its defeat is therefore connected with the winter of that same year, 405. Nor would Paulinus ever, in any year, have said on January 14, and therefore in midwinter, *post hiemes actas* (“after winters have been endured”).

There was also no reason why Paulinus should have transferred this thirteenth *Natale* to the following year, A.D. 406, and left the year 405 without its anniversary poem, even though he could not have sung it on the customary day, January 13.

Pauline certainly begins this *Natale* with a victory hymn on account of the Goths, who had been struck down before the beginning of spring in that same year, A.D. 405. Consequently, in Dungalus, who lists fifteen of Paulinus’s *Natalia* in his *Replies to Claudius of Turin*, in vol. XIV of the Lyons *Library of the Fathers*, p. 218, it is entitled in precisely these words: “On the destruction of the Gothic army together with its king.”

From this, I think, it is evident that the most devout poet, immediately after January 13 had passed and the Goths had been defeated, sang his thirteenth *Natale* in the spring itself of the year 405.

Since, therefore, the fifth *Natale* remains fixed in A.D. 397, the ninth in A.D. 401, and this thirteenth *Natale* in A.D. 405, it follows that the arrival of Nicetas, Rufinus, and Melania at Nola cannot by any effort be detached from A.D. 397.

It is otherwise to be hoped that all the works of Paulinus will once again be edited by a diligent and accurate scholar, carefully collated with the ancient manuscripts, especially the Ambrosian and the Freising manuscript, which belongs to the tenth century and contains twelve of Paulinus’s *Natalia*. R. P. D. Bernard Pezius mentions this manuscript in his *Introductory Dissertation to Volume I of the Treasury of Anecdotes*, p. 27.

VI. Let us return to Rufinus, whom Baronius calls Melania’s inseparable companion.

Rosweydus, in *Eremitic History*, p. 144, §27, derives his principal reason for opposing Baronius from Paulinus’s silence in Letter XXIX, otherwise X, to Severus, where, although he speaks at length about Melania, he says nothing at all about Rufinus.

But if this argument had any force, it would follow that the most celebrated woman had gone to Paulinus alone, although Paulinus received her accompanied by a very large retinue. He, absorbed in praising Melania alone, neglected to list the others individually. That Rufinus was among them cannot rightly be denied.

It is again best to listen to Paulinus, §13:

> Our little dwelling, however, which, raised above the ground by an upper room and extended farther by a single portico, with guest cells inserted between, seemed enlarged by the grace of the Lord. It provided sufficient space not only for the **saints who accompanied her (Melania) in great numbers**, but also for the throngs of those wealthy men.

Among these saints—that is, men of commendable life—one, and the chief one, was Rufinus. We see him mentioned in the preceding letter to this one, which, as we have shown, must be placed after it. There Paulinus replies to Sulpicius, who had requested from him the ancient annals that he might use in composing sacred history, in this fashion:

> Now, while attending to your work, in which you have judged that you are occupied for the benefit of our faith with the examination and comparison of the accounts of earlier times, I sought from the more abundant treasury of my unanimous brother what I did not possess myself. I have sent to Rufinus the presbyter the very note which you had sent in place of a memorandum, incorporated into my letter, so that he might examine it: Rufinus, **the companion of Saint Melania on her spiritual journey**, truly holy and piously learned, and for that reason joined to me by the deepest affection.
>
> If he does not provide the causes of those gaps in history that rightly trouble you, concerning the inconsistent reckoning of years or reigns—he who is rich in both scholastic and salutary literature, in Greek and Latin—I fear that we shall seek them in vain from anyone else in these regions. But if he satisfies my presumption concerning him, I shall, at the first opportunity, if the Lord favors me, send to your fellowship whatever he may write back to me concerning this matter.

Thus far Paulinus, who could not have disclosed such exceptional things about a foreigner whom he had not otherwise seen.

But because Rufinus, **the companion of Saint Melania on her spiritual journey**, had long before been at Nola with her on her return from the sacred journey to Jerusalem, Paulinus, having admired his piety and learning in person, now informs Severus for the first time of the praises of so great a man.

He does not do the same concerning Melania, because in the earlier letter—which through the ignorance of copyists is now the later one—he had already done so at length.

In Letter XL, otherwise XXVI, §6, Paulinus also indicates, not obscurely, that he had consulted Rufinus in person concerning Egyptian matters. He does so in these words, by which he explains verse 8 of Psalm CI:
