> I have learned from a certain holy man, a most learned person and very dear to me, who came to know many things not only by reading but also by traveling, that the pelican is a bird found in Egypt, or commonly seen in those neighboring regions, and that it wanders through the deserts near the Nile River, feeding on snakes, against which it has prevailed in combat. It therefore fights in order to conquer, and when conquered it dies. But when victorious, it both escapes death and gains nourishment.
>
> As for what is written *nycticorax*, he maintained more correctly that it should be *nycticora*; and he seemed to demonstrate this by a plausible argument, saying that the bird placed here is the one we call an owl, because it practices its singing and flying secretly at night and is illuminated by the darkness of night, in which nearly all animals are enveloped.

We shall say later that Rufinus also explained the Blessings of the Patriarchs at Paulinus’s request, and that, when he was about to return to Palestine, Paulinus invited him to Nola.

[Col. 0115]

## BOOK TWO. ON THE WRITINGS PUBLISHED BY RUFINUS AT ROME

### CHAPTER I

[Col. 0115A]

Macarius asks Rufinus to explain Origen’s teaching against fate. II. Macarius’s profession and studies. III. The location of the monastery of Pinētum, where Rufinus rendered the Rule of Basil the Great into Latin for the abbot Urseius. IV. Various statements are made concerning this Rule. V. Rufinus dedicates the first book of Saint Pamphilus’s *Apology for Origen* to Macarius. VI. Examination of that *Apology*. VII. Rufinus’s treatise in defense of Origen.

At last we approach the point from which the greatest odium against Rufinus arose—an odium that seemed greatly to damage his name among later generations, who were little concerned with the matter itself.

Rufinus had not yet arrived at Rome with Melania when a certain Macarius, a leading man and certainly a monk, as I shall prove later, was preparing to write against the mathematicians, or advocates of Fate. While hesitating over certain matters as though they were difficult, he saw in a dream a ship approaching from afar across the sea. When it occupied the harbor, it would undo the knots of his difficulties.

What more is needed? Scarcely had Rufinus appeared when Macarius asked him what Origen thought about the subject he had in hand, and begged him to explain Origen’s teaching to him.

Although Rufinus tried to withdraw from the task and mentioned that Saint Pamphilus the martyr had written something of this sort, at least in part, in his *Apology*, Macarius asked him once and again to translate that same work into Latin.

Although Rufinus denied that he had undertaken to do this, because he had already been almost thirty years languid in the Latin language through neglect, he nevertheless could not refuse to listen to Macarius. Accordingly, he considered translating Saint Pamphilus’s *Apology for Origen* and then the books of the *Periarchon* into Latin, inserting a short treatise of his own on the adulteration of Origen’s books, in order to remove the odium from the man whom he had learned was ill spoken of.

I have thought it useful to preface the individual matters with this brief account before treating them more distinctly and at greater length.

Rufinus tells the same story in *Invective* I, as it is commonly entitled, though it should more properly be entitled *Apology*, addressed to Apronianus against Letter XLI, otherwise LXV (now LXXXIV), of Saint Jerome to Pammachius and Oceanus.

II. Before proceeding farther, this passage reminds me that I should briefly discuss Macarius, since he gave rise to a controversy worthy of remembrance in every age.

Rosweydus correctly observed in his notes on Saint Paulinus that no other person seems to be meant than the Macarius to whom the Nolan bishop wrote Letter XLIX, otherwise XXVI. There he earnestly asks Macarius to aid Secundinianus, who was demanding back from the procurator of the senator Postumianus a shipwrecked vessel with its cargo, brought from Sardinia, which the procurator had seized on the coast of Bruttium. The man, wishing to evade the provincial judge, had fled to Rome.

It is clear that this is the same Macarius whom Palladius lists in the *Lausiac History*, chapter CXXIII, among those who visited Pinianus, the husband of the younger Melania, while he was living in the countryside of Campania and Sicily, for the sake of sacred discipline.

“Similarly,” says Palladius, “there was a certain Macarius from the Vicariate.”

In the Greek manuscript one reads ἀπὸ βικαρίας (*apo bikarias*), namely, “ex-vicar,” or a man who had held the office of vicar. Rosweydus illustrates this phrase with other examples in his *Onomasticon*, p. 1059. From this it is evident that Abraham Ortelius erred in his *Geographical Treasury*, where he thought Palladius’s “Vicaria” was some place, although it is the name of an office.

Bollandus corrected Ortelius’s error on p. 90 of vol. I of the January volume. Sidonius says *Vicarianus apex* in Book I, Letter III; others say *Vicarianus honor*, and *Vicariana dignitas* is common. It was also called simply *Vicaria*, as Sirmondus explains in his notes there.

There were three vicars of the prefect of the praetorium of Italy:

1. the vicar of Rome;
2. the vicar of Italy;
3. the vicar of Africa.

Picenum, Valeria, Campania, Bruttium, and the territory of the Avellinates were subject to the jurisdiction of the first, according to Book IX, Title XXX of the *Theodosian Code*. Concerning the use of horses, see Book V and Book LXVIII, Book XII, Title I, “On Decurions,” where Gothofredus should be consulted.

If desired, consult Blondellus, *On the Primacy*, p. 917, and Norisius, *Dissertation on the Fifth Synod*, chapter X.

Macarius had held this first Vicariate of Rome. Hence we understand why Paulinus asked him to intercede for Secundinianus’s ship.

Rufinus calls him a man distinguished by faith, learning, nobility, and life in Book I of the *Invectives*. As we have said, Macarius repeatedly requested that Rufinus translate the works of Saint Pamphilus and Origen into Latin. Rufinus dedicated them to Macarius in three prefaces, where he calls him “a man of desires” and a most faithful **brother**. By this term he indicates that Macarius then belonged to the same profession as himself, namely, that he was a monk.

Gennadius certainly reveals the same thing in his *Catalogue*, chapter XXVIII:

> Macarius the monk wrote at Rome a book against the mathematicians, in which work he sought the aid of Eastern writings—that is, of Origen and Pamphilus.

Saint Jerome had alluded to this in *Apology* II against Rufinus:

> Therefore, unless you had come from the East, that most learned man would still be lingering among the mathematicians, and Christian men would not know what to argue against Fate.

A little farther on, mocking the ship that had carried Rufinus, which Macarius had seen in a dream, Jerome says:

> Your ship, promised to the city of Rome by a revelation, promises one thing and accomplishes another. It had come to solve the questions of the mathematicians, and it solved the faith of Christians.

Again, in Letter XCVI, otherwise XVI (now CXXVII), to Principia, Jerome attacks Rufinus and Macarius, although he suppresses the names of both:

> Then came the infamous translation of the books *On First Principles* (*περὶ ἀρχῶν*); then the disciple *Olbios* (*ὄλβιος*), truly worthy of his name if he had not stumbled upon such a teacher; then the contradiction of our teachers (*διδακτικῶν*), and the school of the Pharisees was thrown into confusion.

Macarius is concealed under the name *Olbios* (*ὅλβιος*), which means “blessed.” The Greek word has the same meaning, and Macarius is counted among the saints by Bollandus in vol. I of the January volume, p. 90.

At that time, however, the term “mathematicians” did not mean astronomers, but haruspices, genethliacs, and those whom we now call judicial astrologers. They were widely held in the worst repute among Christians because, deriving everything from Fate and the stars, they completely undermined divine providence and human free will.

Saint Augustine rejects their deceptive divinations and impious ravings—in which he himself had once been involved—in the *Confessions*, Book VII, chapter VI; and he rejects them entirely in *The City of God*, Book V, chapters I and II.

Moreover, in chapter XLV of *On Various Questions*, he elegantly portrays them in these words:

> The ancients did not call those men mathematicians who are now so called, but those who investigated the divisions of time by the movement of the heavens and the stars. Against those who are now called mathematicians, who wish to subject our actions to heavenly bodies and sell us to the stars, and to take from us the very price for which we are sold, nothing shorter or truer can be said than that they give no answers except after receiving the constellations.

He has similar material in Book II, chapter XXI of *On Christian Doctrine*.

In Book IX of the *Theodosian Code* there is an entire Title XVI against sorcerers and mathematicians.

Thus, when Macarius was writing against such advocates of Fate, Rufinus came to his aid with the labor of Eastern writings, as Gennadius says: namely, by his Latin translation of Saint Pamphilus’s *Apology for Origen* and of Origen’s work *On First Principles*.

### III.

At that time the monastery of Pineta was famous in the Roman countryside [Col. 0117A]. Macarius and other professors of the monastic life, as well as Rufinus himself, had withdrawn there to devote themselves to God. We gather from his preface to the Rule of Saint Basil, which will be discussed later, that Rufinus entered that monastery immediately after returning from the East.

Learned men, however, dispute where in the world this place of Pineta stood. Norisius, at the end of book I, chapter II of his *Pelagian History*, calls it a suburban locality of Rome and supposes that it stood outside the Angelian Gate, one mile from the city. After Tillemont, vol. XII, p. 310, and vol. XIV, p. 127, Johannes Mabillon went in another direction in book I, § 15 of the *Annals of the Order of Saint Benedict*. While some placed Pineta in Sicily and others near Rhegium Julium, he located it in the town of Classis near Ravenna, believing it to be identical with the monastery of Saints John and Stephen, which Saint Gregory mentions in book VII, letter XVIII.

All these writers failed to seek the monastery of Pineta on the seacoast of the Roman countryside, where Rufinus explicitly places it when he says that, arriving from the regions of the East and already longing for the customary companionship of the brothers, he entered it [Col. 0117B]. Rufinus, therefore, returning from Jerusalem but not yet having entered Rome, was first cheered by the customary companionship of the brothers—that is, of the monks—in the monastery of Pineta.

He later described its location vividly in the already-mentioned letter to Ursejus, the abbot of the place, who is called Ursacius in a very ancient manuscript of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem:

> Set upon the narrow ridge of a sandy path, it is washed on either side by the wave of the surrounding sea. Only a few pine trees, visible from afar, reveal the hidden places; from one of them Pineta received its celebrated name in the world.

If the waves of the sea washed around Pineta, it therefore stood on the sea and far from the City. This agrees neither with Pineta outside the Angelian Gate nor with the town of Classis. If the few pine trees revealed the hidden places, it could not have been near Ravenna, where the pine is not rare but grows abundantly.

Finally, what need is there of many arguments? That Pineta stood between Campania and Rome may be gathered from letter XLVII, formerly XLVIII, of Pontius Paulinus. In A.D. 398, Paulinus commended to Rufinus, who was then staying at Pineta, Cerealis, returning from Nola to Rome and Saint Peter, although he was uncertain whether Cerealis would see Rufinus:

> Although Cerealis made me uncertain by saying that he would proceed TO YOU.

Rufinus, therefore, was then staying outside the City, between Nola and Rome, so that anyone wishing to visit him would have to turn somewhat aside from the Roman road. Paulinus adds that he had entrusted to Cerealis a letter to be delivered to Rufinus:

> Thus, preferring to incur the loss of the little letter IF HE SHOULD PERHAPS NOT SEE YOU rather than, as we believe, to discharge the obligation if he should visit you, we have entrusted this letter not to chance but to faith. For we believe that, with God’s help, the path of our message and of our son is directed toward you.

Paulinus was therefore hesitating over whether Cerealis, on coming to Rome, would turn aside on the very journey to Rufinus, or would instead send his letter to him outside the route. Cerealis, however, did not carry the letter to Rufinus but sent it ahead, as Rufinus himself testifies in the work by which he sent book II of *On the Blessings of the Patriarchs* to Paulinus. There he also names the place where he was then staying, namely Pineta [Col. 0117D]. I prefer to explain this in Rufinus’s own words:

> I had not yet seen our common son Cerealis. But he, knowing what pain he would cause me if he delayed delivering your letter, SENT IT ON AHEAD to me.

At the end he says:

> Since I wrote this reply to you during the days of Lent, while I was staying in the monastery of PINETA, I could not conceal my foolishness even from the brothers who were present.

Again, in the preface to book III of the *Periarchon*, he addresses Macarius as follows in vol. I of the Latin works of Origen, in Erasmus’s first edition at Frobenius, p. 818:

> The preceding two little books of the *Periarchon*, at your urging—indeed, at your compulsion—I translated DURING THE DAYS OF LENT. But since during those days you too, devout brother Macarius, were admonishing me MORE NEARLY and had more leisure, I also worked more. I explained the two later books more slowly, since a more infrequent visitor comes TO US from the farthest and most remote part of the City.

In the editions of Hierotheus, Erasmus, and Grynaeus, *orbis* is mistakenly printed instead of *urbis*.

I believe I have found Pineta in the *Acts of Saint Caesarius of Terracina*, in Boninus Mombritius’s *Sanctuarium*, vol. I, letter C. Near the end, the following is said about the holy martyrs Felix and Eusebius:

> Their bodies, when the day was already bright, the sea cast upon the shore near PINETA.

I therefore believe it sufficiently clear that the monastery of Pineta stood in the territory of Terracina, near the sea. To this place also referred the dream of the monk Macarius. While he was writing against fate, a certain ship appeared to him in sleep, approaching from afar across the open sea; when it had entered the harbor, it would loosen the knots of his hesitation, as Rufinus testifies in book I of the *Apology*, p. 360. For the ship seemed to be making for the coastal monastery of Pineta, where the monk Macarius was then staying.

While Rufinus was established in this monastery, as I have already said, he rendered the Rule of Basil the Great into Latin, in obedience to Abbot Ursejus, who had asked him what practice of the servants of God was followed in the East, what spiritual excellence was cultivated, and what institutions were observed in the monasteries.

Rufinus obeyed Ursejus all the more willingly because the abbot promised that, if the holy and spiritual institutions of this holy and spiritual man, Basil, became known throughout the monasteries of the western regions, and if all the progress of the servants of God that would arise from such institutions brought Rufinus some grace or reward through their merits or prayers, this would be a benefit to him also [Col. 0118B].

Thus Rufinus writes in his letter to Ursejus. At the end he asks him, together with the others who have read the Rule, to remember him and to provide copies to other monasteries, so that, following the example of Cappadocia, all monasteries might live according to the same institutions and observances rather than according to divergent ones.

### IV.

The promises of Ursacius, or Ursejus, and the hopes of Rufinus did not come to nothing. For Italians and other Westerners ordered their lives and customs according to this Rule of Basil, once it had been made available in Latin, as Mabillon notes in book I, § XIII of the *Annals*.

Three years later Rufinus commemorated this distinguished monument of his industry in book XI, chapter IX of his *History*:

> We also transferred Basil’s institutions for monks into Latin, hoping that, if we are able and God’s favor assists us, we may transfer more of the works of both Basils.

This Rule, the most celebrated of all those which Westerners endeavored to imitate, requires us to offer some less familiar information about it, information that greatly redounds to the praise of Rufinus the translator.

Basil the Great adorned the monastic institution in the East with various Rules published in Greek and refined it according to the standard of more perfect discipline. Benedict Haeftenus carefully lists these in book I, tract IV, inquiry XI of his *Monastic Investigations*. The following are beyond reasonable doubt:

1. The Rules discussed at greater length.  
2. The shorter Rules.  
3. The monastic Constitutions.  
4. The Rule translated into Latin.

Rufinus composed this last work, divided into two hundred and three questions, from Basil’s longer and shorter Rules. Hugo Menard sets this plainly before our eyes in his notes to the *Concordance of Rules*, compiled at the beginning of the ninth century by Saint Benedict of Aniane [Col. 0118D]. There, p. 56, he observed that both of Basil’s Rules—the one discussed at greater length and the shorter one—passed into Rufinus’s translation.

The oldest manuscript of the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés contains it divided into two hundred questions, with an equal number of answers placed beneath them. In the Holstenian edition, however, three additional questions are added.

The learned and pious Edmund Martene, in his commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict, p. 897, judged that Basil himself had combined from both of his Rules, the shorter and the longer, a third Rule which Rufinus translated into Latin. Yet no one other than Rufinus both combined it and rendered it into Latin.

His translation does not at all preserve the order of the Rules exhibited by the Basilian texts. Rufinus often acts less as a translator than as a paraphraser, inserting much of his own material as well, according to Haeftenus, book II, tract I, inquiry IX.

This explains why, whenever passages from the Basilian Rule are quoted in the Anianian *Concordance*, in which the Rule of Saint Benedict is compared with the Rules of twenty-five other Fathers, Menardus carefully compared those same passages with both of Basil’s Rules and with Rufinus’s translation. It is consequently clear beyond doubt that Anianus used Rufinus’s translation in his *Concordance*. Menardus shows this especially in chapter III, § 3, p. 115.

To make Rufinus’s translation of the Rule more readily available, Benedict of Aniane inserted it into his *Book of Rules*. Fabius Chisius, Apostolic nuncio among the people of Cologne and later Supreme Pontiff Alexander VII, sent this book to Lucas Holstenius in A.D. 1643. He had had it copied from Cologne manuscripts at the command of the most memorable man for later ages, the elder Cardinal Francesco Barberini. It was eventually published through Holstenius’s care at Rome by Vitalis Mascardus in A.D. 1661, in quarto, and soon afterward at Paris by Ludovicus Billaine in A.D. 1663, also in quarto.

Haeftenus notes that this same Rule, disseminated in Italy by Rufinus, was called by antonomasia in the age of Saint Benedict the Rule of Saint Basil: first, because, according to Rufinus, its substance was observed in the East; and second, because, through Rufinus the translator, it had first become known to the Western Church, not without the great applause of all, and was afterward adopted in practice by most monasteries. Ursejus had promised Rufinus that it would immediately be adopted under his care.

It is clear that very holy men kept this Rule before their eyes. The great Benedict not only knew it very well and commended it to his disciples in chapter LXXIII of his Rule—where the Anianian *Concordance* teaches us that he borrowed much from Rufinus’s version—but Gregory of Tours also testifies in book X, chapter XXIX of his *History of the Franks* that it was celebrated in the monasteries founded by Saint Aredius.

An anonymous author praises it in the life of Saint Eugendus, who flourished at the beginning of the sixth century, in the first century of the *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*, p. 576. On p. 253 another author writes that Saint Droctoveus was instructed in the Basilian Rule by Blessed Germanus.

In the seventh century, the author of Saint Filibert’s life testifies that the saint practiced this same Rule through assiduous reading; see the second century, p. 819. Smaragdus cites testimonies from it in his commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict, and Pope Innocent II also mentions it in Gratian, *Cause* XVIII, question II, chapter XXVI.

Moreover, the author of the preface to the works of Saint Basil the Great, printed at Paris by Michael Sonnius in A.D. 1617, in folio, speaks as follows of the Rule rendered by Rufinus:

> There also exists an epitome of the ascetic books, or certainly of the Rules set out at greater length, which Rufinus of Aquileia translated into Latin and called the book *On the Institutions of Monks*. It will be published separately at Cologne together with the other works of Rufinus, especially since it does not preserve the order of the Rules displayed by Basil’s works.

This Cologne edition has never been seen.

Fronto Ducaeus, in the same work, vol. II, p. 28, col. 2, inserted in his notes on the Rule discussed at greater length corrections to Rufinus’s Latin version from two manuscripts of the Putean collection [Col. 0119D].

The Rufinian Rule was first published in print by Johannes Franciscus Brixianus, a monk of the Congregation of Saint Justina, in a book entitled *Four First Approved Rules of Life for Religious of Every Kind*, published at Venice by Luca Antonio Giunta in A.D. 1500, in quarto. We later saw this edition renewed at Paris by Johannes Petit in A.D. 1519, in quarto. There, however, the name Ursejus, found in the manuscripts, is corruptly printed as Ursarius; perhaps it should be Ursacius.

The Brescian monk noted at the end that this Rule was regarded among the Greeks, in its original source, as fuller and more exact in arrangement, and that he would soon translate into Latin, through Rufinus the translator, this Rule together with other diverse treatises of the same Basil.

Let us add the testimony of Damianus de Sancta Maria in the preface to the Greek edition of Saint Basil’s works, published at Venice by Stephanus de Sabio in A.D. 1535, in folio. Addressing Cardinal Gaspare Contarini, he calls the Rule translated by Rufinus a fragment and an abridged little book.

It was published together with the letter to Ursejus among the Latin works of Saint Basil, p. 337, at Cologne by Eucharius Cervicornus in A.D. 1531, in folio, among translations by Johannes Argyropilus, Georgius Trapezuntius, and Raphael Volaterranus [Col. 0120A]. It was also published together with the Rule of Saint Benedict, illustrated by the commentary of Cardinal Johannes de Turrecremata, p. 537, in the Cologne edition issued by Gervinus Calenius in A.D. 1575, in folio.

Prosper Stellartius included another Rule of Basil in his book entitled *Foundations and Rules of All Orders*, published at Douai by Balthasar Bellerus in A.D. 1626, in quarto, p. 138.

But Lucas Holstenius, in a manuscript letter written to Fabius Chisius on June 6, A.D. 1643, testifies that he had found among others the genuine and authentic translation of Rufinus in the Rule praised in the *Concordance* of Benedict of Aniane, where it is separately inserted in the *Book of Rules*.

Accordingly, Holstenius published in exact conformity with the Cologne parchments—formerly copied from the autograph manuscript of Saint Maximinus of Trier, where the Rufinian Rule was read first—the text in volume I of the *Book of Rules*. In a very old parchment manuscript of the library of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, folio p. 177, it is entitled *Institutions of the Monks of Saint Basil, Bishop of Caesarea*, together with the preface of Saint Rufinus the presbyter to Ursacius.

Carolus Cointius, in volume VI of his *Ecclesiastical Annals of the Franks*, under A.D. 821, § 28, discussing Holstenius’s *Book of Rules*, makes a mistake by supposing that Chisius communicated his copy, formerly made at Cologne, to Holstenius only after he had ascended to the papacy. He had in fact communicated it much earlier, namely in A.D. 1643, as we have gathered from Holstenius’s own letters to Chisius on this matter.

Cointius observes in volume III, under A.D. 651, § 7, that the Basilian Rule explained by Rufinus and adopted in Gaul before A.D. 651—the year in which Saint Gislenus of Athens chose his seat in Belgium—may perhaps have been brought there by Saint Maurus, a disciple of Benedict the Great and a contemporary of Saint Aredius. Soon afterward Cointius also provides a precise and truly excellent analysis of the same Rule, thereby sparing us, through the work of so learned a man, the labor of proceeding through it point by point.

This is what we have discovered concerning the first work written by Rufinus after his return to Italy. But Macarius again calls us to other labors.

In Gratian, this Rule of Basil, called *the Institutions of Monks*, is cited from Rufinus’s translation in 26, question VII, chapter VIII, and also in Distinction II, chapter I, *On Penance*.

Let us now discuss Pamphilus’s *Apology for Origen*.

### V.

Rufinus wished this work to appear under Macarius’s name. Since he knew that Origen and those devoted to him were poorly regarded, he tried in the preface to Macarius, whom he calls—once and again—a “man of desires,” that is, another Daniel, to avert the odium from himself.

He does not deny that the work itself will cause the greatest offense to those who believe themselves injured by anyone who has not thought ill of Origen. Although he was explaining not his own judgment concerning Origen but the testimony of the holy martyr Pamphilus in response to Macarius’s inquiry, he nevertheless says that he does not doubt that some will consider themselves injured even if he says something on Origen’s behalf and in another’s words.

He nevertheless says that he is entreating them not to act with a presumptuous or prejudiced mind. Rather, since we shall come before God’s judgment, they should not refuse to learn what is true, lest they sin through ignorance. They should consider that to strike the consciences of weak brothers with false accusations is to sin against Christ.

Therefore, Rufinus adds, they should not lend their ears to accusers or learn another person’s faith from someone else, especially when they have the opportunity to test it in person and when each individual’s confession with his own mouth shows what and how he believes. For it is written:

> With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation; and by his words each person will be justified, and by his words each person will be condemned.

Having said this, and sending the reader, with respect to those things found in Pamphilus that contradict Origen, to the brief *Assertion*—as he calls it—*On the Adulteration of Origen’s Books*, which he immediately appended to the *Apology of Saint Pamphilus* [Col. 0121A], Rufinus presents a statement of his faith that is wholly opposed to the principal heresies attributed to Origen.

1. He professes that he believes the Holy Trinity to be coeternal and of one nature, one power, and one substance.

2. He professes that the Son of God became man in the final age and suffered for our sins; and that, in that very flesh in which he suffered, he rose from the dead. For this reason he also granted the human race the hope of resurrection.

3. He says:

> We do not speak of the resurrection of the flesh by means of any tricks, as some slanderously claim; rather, we believe that this very flesh in which we now live will rise again. We do not say that one flesh will be substituted for another, or that another body will rise instead of the body of this flesh. Whether, therefore, we say that the body will rise, we speak according to the Apostle—for he used this term—or whether we say “flesh,” we confess according to the tradition of the creed. For it is a foolish invention of slander to suppose that the human body is something other than flesh. Whether, then, “flesh” is said according to the common faith or “body” according to the Apostle, what will rise must be believed in the manner defined by the Apostle: what will rise in power will also rise in glory; it will rise incorruptible and as a spiritual body, because corruption will not possess incorruption. Therefore, while preserving these prerogatives of the future body or flesh, the resurrection of the flesh must be believed wholly and perfectly, so that the same nature of the flesh is preserved and the condition and glory of the spiritual body in incorruption are not diminished. For thus it is written.

Thus Rufinus spoke of his faith concerning the Trinity, the Incarnation, and the resurrection of bodies—matters concerning which Tillemont rightly agrees that no difficulty can be raised, vol. XII, p. 206.

Rufinus concludes all this in these words:

> These things are preached in the Church of God at Jerusalem by its holy priest John. We say and hold these things together with him.

After setting forth his rule of faith in this way, he condemns communion with those who believe otherwise and prays for peace upon those who agree with him:

> If anyone believes or teaches anything beyond these things, or thinks that we believe otherwise than we have explained, let him be anathema. If anyone wishes to possess a statement of our faith, let him take it from these things. For we either read or make this the rule of our faith, proving all things according to the Apostle, holding fast what is good, and abstaining from every appearance of evil. And if there are any who follow this rule, peace be upon them and upon the Israel of God. Amen.

### VI.

After these matters comes the *Apology of the martyr Pamphilus for Origen*, translated by Rufinus, as it is entitled in the commonly circulated editions. Yet those editions contain only the first book and certain passages excerpted separately from the six books of which Pamphilus’s *Apology* is said to have consisted.

The unconquered martyr wrote it at Caesarea in Palestine while imprisoned with other confessors of the faith, as Eusebius, Pamphilus’s companion in the same prison, testifies in chapter XI of his book *On the Martyrs of Palestine*. Photius also says this in codex CXVIII:

> The six books of the martyr Pamphilus and Eusebius for Origen have been read. FIVE of them were composed by Pamphilus in prison, with Eusebius also present. The SIXTH, after the martyr had already been deprived of life by the sword and had departed to the uniquely desired God, was completed by Eusebius.

Photius reviews the whole work as though it had both authors, and he uses plural verbs such as “they say,” “they add,” and “they mention.” At the end he writes again:

> The *Apology for Origen*, as we have said, was composed by Pamphilus and Eusebius, confined together in prison.

Both contributed their work to the composition of this *Apology*. We learn from Eusebius in book VI, chapter XXXV of his *Ecclesiastical History*, from Socrates in book III, chapter VII, and also from Photius himself—who read the entire work in the ninth century of Christ—that it was a substantial and lengthy composition.

The same authors teach us that the first five books were composed not by Eusebius alone but jointly by Pamphilus and Eusebius, while the sixth was composed by Eusebius alone after Pamphilus had been crowned with martyrdom. Hence the first five books were sometimes attributed indiscriminately to Pamphilus and sometimes to Eusebius, whereas the sixth always presented Eusebius alone as its author. At first, however, it had only Pamphilus, not Eusebius, as its named author, as will become clear later.

The subject of the entire work was the defense of Origen against the many accusations by which his teaching was attacked. Some people were incapable of understanding Origen’s writings; others were seized by a perversity of mind; and many were carried away by hostile feeling against Origen. They went so far as to denounce as heretics even students of sacred literature who read the works of Origen, although these people were otherwise distinguished by a reputation for innocence and piety.

Moreover, very many of Origen’s condemners had never read anything from his works and were entirely ignorant of the Greek language in which Origen had written. Nor were there lacking men who, although they had drawn from Origen’s writings all the learning of which they were capable, cursed both the teaching and its author in word and writing so that the others would not notice this dependence.

Thus Pamphilus wrote in his *Apology*, which, as Photius testifies, he addressed to the confessors condemned to the mines of Palestine because he saw that they were inclined to lend ready ears to the rumors and curses stirred up against Origen.

It is clear that the work consists almost entirely of complete passages and testimonies from Origen, apart from the opening, which is like a letter to the confessors just mentioned.

These matters have been stated in advance, for they will be discussed again below.

The *Apology of Pamphilus* mentions Origen’s book *On Prayer*, which was eventually published in Greek at Oxford from the Sheldonian Theatre in A.D. 1685, in duodecimo.

### VII.

Rufinus appended to his completed translation of the *Apology of Saint Pamphilus* a dissertation which he calls in the preface a “very brief little book.” It is part of the same *Apology*, although composed by Rufinus alone, and it too is addressed to Macarius.

In it Rufinus demonstrates by various arguments that the passages found in Origen’s books which contradict Pamphilus’s *Apology* were corrupted by heretics.

Rufinus divided this little work, *On the Adulteration of Origen’s Books*, into two parts. In the first he attempts to show that Origen’s books were corrupted by heretics. For this purpose he produces the examples of both Clements, Romanus and Alexandrian, and likewise of Dionysius of Alexandria, whose writings had suffered the same fate.

In the second part he insists that Origen himself, while still alive, complained in his letters about the corruption of his works. He also cites part of these letters, especially the one he wrote to the Alexandrians against those who adulterated his books while he was still living.

He further observes that certain Latin and Greek Fathers suffered the same misfortune. After explaining these matters, he adds:

> If, then, Origen himself complains in his letter, in his own voice, that he suffered such things at the hands of heretics and malicious men, and if the same things happened to many other catholic men, both living and dead, and similar frauds are shown to have been inflicted upon their writings, what obstinacy of mind is it to use unequal mercy in an equal case, but, from the same circumstances, to extend to some the reverence of an excuse and to others the disgrace of accusation?

Thus Rufinus. Nor does he conceal that the most bitter enemies of Origen were plagiarists of Origen and believed that, by this method, they had taken sufficient precautions to prevent their thefts from being discovered:

> Rather, the hidden truth must be disclosed here. It is impossible for any human being to judge so unjustly as to form unequal opinions about an equal case. But the authors of his defamation are those who are accustomed either to dispute at length in the Church or even to write books which speak or write entirely about Origen. They do this so that more people may not learn of their thefts; for if they were not ungrateful toward their teacher, they would certainly not appear criminal, nor would they deter the simpler people from reading him.

By these words he intended to touch Jerome, as Grynaeus correctly observed in volume I of the works of Origen, p. 781, of the edition which I shall mention later.

The words that follow attack Epiphanius, although Jerome, in book II of his *Apology*, p. 417, interprets both passages as having been produced by Rufinus against Epiphanius alone:

> Finally, one of those men, who thinks that he possesses, as though compelled to evangelize, the task of speaking evil of Origen among all nations and in every language, confessed, in the hearing of a very large crowd of brothers, that he had read six thousand of Origen’s books. If he was reading them, as he himself is accustomed to say, in order to learn Origen’s evils, ten books ought to have been sufficient for him, or certainly twenty, or at most thirty. To read six thousand books is no longer to wish to know him but to devote nearly one’s entire life to his teachings and studies. How, then, can such a man rightly be heard when he blames those who, for the sake of their instruction, have read very few of Origen’s works while preserving the rule of faith and maintaining unimpaired piety?

Here it is clear that Rufinus is attacking Epiphanius. Jerome says of him in book II of his *Apology against Rufinus*, p. 405:

> Do not send me to the six thousand books of his—Origen’s—which you accuse the blessed Pope Epiphanius of having read.

Again, in book III, p. 461:

> This is that delirious old man who, with you present, chanted the six thousand books of Origen; who thinks that preaching against Origen has been assigned to him in the languages of all nations; who therefore forbids him to be read, lest others discover his thefts.

In letter XXXIX, formerly LXII, p. 337, to Theophilus, Jerome reproves John of Jerusalem for having charged Epiphanius with reading all six thousand of Origen’s books:

> No one could read six thousand volumes of Origen, since he did not write them; and I more readily believe that the witness of this statement, rather than its author, was lying.

Yet Jerome says in letter XLI, formerly LXV, to Pammachius and Oceanus, p. 346, concerning Origen’s writings:

> More than a thousand treatises which he spoke and published in the Church. Besides these, innumerable commentaries which he himself calls volumes, and which I now pass over lest I seem to compile a catalogue of his works. Who among us can read as much as he wrote?

Petrus Halloix, in book IV of his *Defense of Origen*, p. 334, considers it by no means incredible that Origen wrote six thousand books, provided that individual homilies, short treatises, dialogues, letters, and *Apologies* are counted, rather than larger books in the sense in which we now commonly understand the term. For Theodore of Mopsuestia is reported to have written more than ten thousand books, according to Pope Pelagius II in his letter to Elias of Aquileia and also according to Facundus of Hermiane, book VIII, chapter I.

Moreover, Epiphanius himself, who states in heresy 64 that Origen’s writings were innumerable, later affirms in § LXIII that he wrote six thousand books.

An ancient author of Origen’s epitaph, which we shall present later, agrees with this. He says that Origen wrote as many books as a legion contains men. It is established that a legion consisted of six thousand infantrymen and six hundred cavalrymen.

Rufinus then concludes his dissertation with these words:

> I think that these things are sufficient to show how one ought to judge Origen’s books. Anyone who pursues not contention but the truth will readily assent to such evident assertions. But if anyone persists in his contentiousness, we have no such custom. For it has been determined among us that whenever we read him, we hold fast, according to the admonition of the holy Apostle, to what is good. But if anything is found in his writings that does not agree with the Catholic faith, we suspect that it was inserted by heretics, and we declare it alien both from his meaning and from our faith. Even if we are mistaken in this, we incur, as I think, no danger from such an error, for, with God’s help, we remain unharmed by avoiding what we suspect and reject. Nor shall we be found before God to be accusers of the brothers, since this work of accusing the brothers is said to belong properly to the Devil; hence the Devil received his name from accusing. At the same time, we avoid the judgment of slanderers, which separates those who are such from the kingdom of God.

Thus Rufinus.

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 0124A]

I. Rufinus translated the first two books of Origen *On First Principles* into Latin.  
II. Survey of the same translation.  
III. Outline of the entire work.  
IV. He explains the Blessings of the Patriarchs to Pontius Paulinus in two books.  
V. The exchange of letters between Rufinus and Paulinus on this subject.  
VI. Editions and manuscripts of the books *On the Blessings of the Patriarchs*.  
VII. Rufinus completed the translation of Origen’s third and fourth books *On First Principles*.

### I.

Macarius, especially eager for Eastern writings, had noticed that the books *On First Principles* were repeatedly mentioned in the *Apology of Saint Pamphilus*. He therefore urged Rufinus to adapt them for Roman ears.

Accordingly, to obey Macarius in this matter as well, Rufinus rendered Origen’s four books *On First Principles*, or *On Powers*, as he thought they might be called, into Latin in his preface.

He did not, however, complete this translation in one continuous effort. After translating the preface and the first two books into Latin, he devoted himself, at the urging of his friends, to composing other works, as we shall explain later.

This entire Rufinian translation appears among the various works of Origen, published in Latin at Venice by Lazarus Soardus in A.D. 1514, in folio, through the efforts of Constantius Hierotheus, a regular canon of Saint Salvador. Erasmus seems to have taken it from that edition, together with the other works, into the first volume of his *Works of Origen*. Having died while preparing the Latin edition, Erasmus left its completion to Beatus Rhenanus, who published it at Basel through Frobenius in A.D. 1536, in two folio volumes.

This edition appeared in an enlarged form at Basel, again through Frobenius, in A.D. 1551, and afterward in A.D. 1557, enriched with various works which Laurentius Humfredus and others had translated into Latin.

Joannes Jacobus Grynaeus then arranged for it to be printed again at Basel by Eusebius Episcopius in A.D. 1571, in folio, with the errors removed and notes added in various places. This edition is superior to the first four.

Hierotheus, in the preface to his *Corrections*, which he dedicated to Antonius Contarenus, Patriarch of Venice, and placed before the books of the *Periarchon*, pronounced the following judgment on the entire work [Col. 0124C]:

> In it, as in a handbook, he brought together the principles of the Christian religion. It discusses all the principal matters: God—namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—the divine minds, the world, the soul, and other subjects. In treating these matters, his statement became obscure either because the subject itself is such that, as Rufinus says, philosophers, after laboring throughout their entire lives, discovered nothing in it, or because the saying of Horace came to pass: “I strive to be brief, and I become obscure.”

## II

It is clear that, among all the works of Adamantius [Origen], this work *On First Principles* was the best known, as Petrus Daniel Huetius notes in *Origeniana*, book III, chapter III, section I, § 2, p. 266. For in it Origen attempts to establish the principles of what is to be believed in religion. Yet everyone agreed that these books suffered from extreme obscurity and difficulty. Rufinus himself, otherwise Origen’s herald, frankly admits this in the following words of his prologue to Macarius:

> “They are indeed also exceedingly obscure and difficult; [Col. 0124D] for there he discusses matters of such a kind that philosophers, after consuming their entire lives upon them, were able to discover nothing. But our author did what he could to turn toward piety the faith in the Creator and the account of created things which they had drawn toward impiety.”

What is still more troubling to hear is that all the heretics of later centuries took weapons against the truth from this same work, though it was written in Greek. Origen, in this work, followed human reasoning and Platonic philosophy more than the authority of the written and transmitted word of God. Perhaps he wished rather to test how far one could proceed by this method than to state what he himself truly believed.

For this reason Origen’s opponents devoted their greatest efforts to attacking the books *Periarchon* (*On First Principles*); the martyr Pamphilus likewise repeatedly calls them by that name in his *Apology*, because Origen’s adversaries concentrated especially on accusing these books alone. I shall speak later of Didymus’s commentaries on them. [Col. 0125A] Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, chapter XXIV, testifies that they were written at Alexandria, plainly before A.D. 231. Photius briefly notes their specific contents in *Bibliotheca*, codex 108.

Rufinus and Jerome translated them into Latin in competition with one another. Jerome’s translation, however, has long since perished, and the Greek text is no longer found, at least not in the libraries of Europe. We must therefore rely on the Latin version. Its author, Rufinus, confesses in his prologue to Macarius that he was especially careful not to reproduce those things found in Origen’s books that were inconsistent and contradictory, believing that these had not been written by Origen but added by heretics, just as he thinks he demonstrated sufficiently both in Pamphilus’s *Apology* and in his own little work *On the Adulteration of Origen’s Books*. Hence he says:

> “Therefore, whenever we found in his books anything contrary to what he had piously established elsewhere concerning the Trinity, we either omitted it as adulterated and foreign, or [Col. 0125B] presented it according to the rule which we frequently found him affirming.”

Huetius observed that passages of the Greek text quoted by ancient authors are missing from Rufinus’s version.

Tillemont considers it worthy of the greatest admiration, in volume III, p. 578 of the second edition, that Jerome, although he had by then openly become Origen’s most vehement opponent, nevertheless sent Paulinus of Nola to the books *Periarchon* in Letter 51, formerly 153, now 85, for the solution of a certain serious and important question. Jerome writes that he had recently translated them at the command of their friend Pammachius.

In his prologue Rufinus says that, in translating Origen’s books, he follows the example of Jerome, who, after introducing many works of Adamantius with an ornate and magnificent preface, translated them into Latin. Although certain stumbling blocks are found in the Greek, Jerome so polished and cleansed everything in translation that the Latin reader finds nothing in them contrary to our faith. But other statements made there must not be passed over. Rufinus says:

> “We therefore follow an undertaking begun and approved by him [Col. 0125C] [Jerome], but we cannot adorn the words of so great a man with equal powers of eloquence. Hence I fear that, through my inadequacy, it may happen that the man whom he rightly acknowledged as the second teacher of the Church after the Apostles, on account of his knowledge and wisdom, may appear far inferior because of the poverty of our language.”

After this, Rufinus closes the prologue to his translation by solemnly entreating the copyist and the reader, in the presence of God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; by faith in the future kingdom; by the mystery of the resurrection from the dead; and by the fire prepared for the Devil and his angels—so that the reader may not possess forever the place where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth, and where their fire will not be extinguished and their worm will not die—not to add, remove, or alter anything, but to compare the text with the exemplars from which it was copied, correct it literally, and supply punctuation and divisions. He must not keep an uncorrected or undivided manuscript, lest the difficulty of the meaning, if the text is not properly divided, produce still greater obscurity for readers.

Rufinus [Col. 0125D] clearly wished, by words of this sort—certainly not uttered casually—to weaken the chief and worst doctrines for which Origen was accused. Tillemont notes this very well in volume XII, p. 211.

Rufinus wrote these things during Lent at the monastery of Pinetum in A.D. 398. He testifies to this in the brief preface to book III of *Periarchon*, where he addresses Macarius as follows, on p. 711 of volume I of Origen’s works in Grynaeus’s edition:

> “You who read, remember me in your holy prayers, so that we too may be made imitators of the Spirit. The two earlier little books of *Periarchon*, at your insistence—not merely because you urged me, but because you compelled me—I translated during the days of Lent. But since during those days you too, religious brother Macarius, admonished me more closely and had more leisure, I too worked more extensively.”

He completed the two remaining books later and more slowly, because Macarius, who was pressing him, had withdrawn after Easter to Rome, and indeed to the farthest part of the city. In that year, A.D. 398, Easter fell on April 18, in solar cycle [Col. 0126A] 15, lunar cycle 19, with Sunday letter C.

Rufinus makes the same point in his letter to Paulinus of Nola, which in commonly circulated editions precedes book II *On the Blessings of the Patriarchs*. He writes:

> “Because during the days of Lent, while I was staying at the monastery of Pinetum, I wrote these things to you.”

In the preface to book I he clearly states that he was writing that work in the same monastery, at the time when he was engaged in translating Origen, in order to oblige Paulinus:

> “Therefore, insofar as the modest capacity of our understanding permits, or the time allows, or those who are urgently pressing written replies to Origen permit—however briefly so great a matter can endure—we express what we meanwhile think about this chapter, without prejudice to those who may be able to judge better, out of that love by which you command us to trust you concerning everything. This concerns chapter XLIX of Genesis, where Jacob, or the patriarch Israel, foretells what is to come concerning each of his sons, which Paulinus had asked Rufinus to explain to him.”

## III

In the preface to the books *Periarchon*, Origen outlined the arrangement of the entire work. He declared that he would discuss [Col. 0126B] God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; the soul; demons; the world; Holy Scripture; angels; and whether heavenly beings are animated.

In book I he treats the incorporeal God; Christ and his names; the Holy Spirit; rational souls; and angels.

In book II he pursues the subject of the world; corporeal nature; God; the incarnation; the Holy Spirit; the souls of human beings and animals; angels and the soul of Christ; the resurrection of bodies; and the punishments of this life and of the life to come.

In book III he discusses free will; demons and sins; the wisdom of God; temptations; the beginning and end of the world; and the supreme good.

In book IV he treats the sacred Scriptures, the method of understanding them, and the Trinity.

Erasmus corrected what seemed difficult, placing his observations in the margin. Hierotheus, however, prefixed his own *Corrections*. Before both of them, Didymus of Alexandria had found it necessary to write apologetic commentaries on these same books of Origen, as Socrates testifies in book IV, [Col. 0126C] chapter XXV. Jerome, book II *Against Rufinus*, p. 148, calls them brief commentaries.

Especially on account of these writings that blind Didymus incurred the hatred of many; consequently, in later centuries he was proscribed together with Origen at the Fifth Synod and elsewhere, as Norisius demonstrates in chapter VII of his *Dissertation*. The errors attributed to Origen were found chiefly in this work *On First Principles*, which served as a kind of introduction (*isagoge*) to theology.

As I have said, the work no longer survives in Greek. Photius nevertheless quotes its summary in codex 108 as a work that still existed in the ninth century, when he flourished. Fragments of it also occur in codex 235, in the *Philocalia*, and in the letter of the Emperor Justinian preserved by Labbeus, volume V of the *Councils*, p. 672. Nicolaus Fullerus also cites a passage from a manuscript codex in *Theological Miscellanies*, book IV, chapter XIII.

We possess the entire work in Latin, rendered by Rufinus. He corrected it as best he could, declaring in both prologues to books I and III that he had removed everything that seemed contrary [Col. 0126D] to the Church’s teaching. Nevertheless, we read in it bold and singular opinions which, since they were not derived from ecclesiastical tradition, are generally rejected by everyone, notwithstanding Origen’s great authority.

In this work Origen undertook thoroughly to overthrow the ravings of Valentinus, Marcion, and other heretics. To explain the origin of evil, they invented two principles, posited two souls, and imagined human beings of two different and opposed natures—some genuinely good and others genuinely evil.

In opposition to them, Origen states in book I, chapters V, VI, and VIII, that God alone is good and immutable by nature, while every creature is capable of good and evil and subject to change. He assigns the imperfection of rational creatures as the cause of evil. He shows that a rational creature, misusing its freedom, falls through its own fault from the perfection of its origin.

Thereafter, in book III, chapter I, he establishes free will as the foundation, proving it solidly by reason and Scripture and responding to all the passages which [Col. 0127A] heretics misuse in order to overthrow it. Yet he errs in this: in book II, chapters I and VIII, he treats the inequality of creatures as the effect of their merit.

For, according to his own account in book I, chapter VIII, and book II, chapters II and VIII, God created, before bodies existed, a certain number of equal souls. When most of them had sinned, they were enclosed, according to the measure and quality of their sins, in various bodies created for this purpose as punishments, like prisons. Thus from pure spirits arise the souls of angels, stars, and human beings. Origen believes that angels consist of soul and an exceedingly subtle body, and that each of them undertakes various ministries according to its merits.

He thinks that the stars are animated and are beautiful prisons assigned to spirits less guilty than those who inhabit the lower world. See book I, chapter VII, and book II, chapter VI.

The first of all the spirits, having adhered to God from the beginning with more perfect love, merited to be united with him in a more excellent manner and never afterward to be separated from him. This is the soul of Jesus Christ.

The remaining spirits can change from good [Col. 0127B] to evil and from evil to good, according to book II, chapter III. The happiness of the blessed does not make them incapable of sin, lest they attribute it to themselves rather than to God.

Moreover, he teaches in book I, chapter VI, that the Devil himself will at some point cast aside his hostility toward God and that his evil will will be destroyed, so that God may be all in all. This will not occur, however, until after a long succession of ages, because after this world there will be another, and several others, just as several existed before it. For there was no time without a world, nor will there ever be, lest God appear idle. This is found in book II, chapters I, III, V, and VI.

From book II, chapter XXI, we learn that Origen drew these opinions from the philosophy of Plato, which he knew extremely well. Certainly, from Plato’s *Gorgias*, among other things, Origen learned this attractive principle: that all punishments are medicinal and have as their purpose the correction of the person who undergoes them.

Origen considered this more suited to eternal punishments, [Col. 0127C] thinking that in this way the justice of God could easily be reconciled with his goodness. We infer this from book IV, chapter II.

He adduces nothing that he does not seem to confirm by some testimony of Holy Scripture, although he very often forces Scripture into a violent interpretation. He distinguishes three meanings of Scripture very well: the literal or grammatical, the figurative or allegorical, and the anagogical or mystical.

He points out the errors of Jews and heretics who took figurative expressions too literally, as well as those of people who imagined that they found mysteries everywhere. Yet in applying these rules he is often mistaken, assigning too much weight to the mystical sense and neglecting the literal sense too greatly.

These are Origen’s chief errors, so firmly established and fixed in the work *On First Principles* that they constitute its body and form. It is nevertheless true that Origen does not present these matters except tentatively and as opinions which he submits to the reader’s judgment.

First he sets out the faith of the Catholic Church and what it teaches in general. He treats the remaining matters as problematic opinions, presenting his thoughts about them with considerable modesty. This is the one excuse that can be offered for the opinions that [Col. 0127D] are truly his.

There were other views, however, which he himself wholly condemned, complaining that heretics had corrupted his writings, as we learn from the letter translated into Latin by Rufinus.

In the end, Origen’s works remained infected with many errors: both those which he himself had tentatively proposed and those which heretics afterward deceitfully inserted. Because of the author’s reputation, both groups acquired many followers and, in subsequent centuries, stirred up great commotion in the Church.

## IV

From what I said above, it is evident that Rufinus worked at Pinetum not only on the books *Periarchon* but also on other writings during the very period when, after returning from Jerusalem, he stayed in the regions around Rome—namely, from the spring of A.D. 397 until the autumn of the following year, 398. At the end of that year, on November 25, Pope Siricius died. Rufinus left Rome while Siricius was still alive, after receiving the customary formal letters from him, as we shall see below. [Col. 0128A]

Rufinus was famous for his religious learning, and pious and learned men flocked to him from everywhere to admire the treasures of Scripture and of Eastern authors which he shared with them. To the *Rule of Saint Basil*, Pamphilus’s *Apology*, his own *Dissertation on the Adulteration of Origen’s Books*, and the four books of *Periarchon*, he added two books *On the Blessings of the Patriarchs*. He composed these at the request of Pontius Paulinus, surnamed Nolanus, who was not yet a bishop but only a presbyter.

It has long been customary to call the words spoken by Jacob when he was near death, in Genesis chapter XLIX, to his twelve sons—the founders of the twelve tribes from which the entire Hebrew people was constituted—the Twelve Blessings of the Patriarchs. Yet, apart from Rufinus, Ambrose, in chapter II of his work on the same subject, and Theodoret, in his commentary on the final chapter of Genesis, observe that this title does not fit the speech itself, by which Jacob curses Reuben, Simeon, and Levi. Ambrose therefore maintains that it should be called a prophecy rather than a blessing.

Rufinus [Col. 0128B] had written a letter from Rome to Paulinus, now lost. In it, in response to the news brought to him concerning his mother’s death—as will be explained more clearly below—he had informed his friend Paulinus that he was in Rome amid the heat of anxiety and uncertain how long he would remain. He also urged him to devote himself to learning Greek literature thoroughly, since Rufinus did not greatly approve of Paulinus’s translation of Clement of Rome.

We learn this from Paulinus’s Letter 46, formerly 47. Paulinus replies that Rufinus’s letter, although brief, had brought him great relief and that he had been affected by Rufinus’s anxiety; nevertheless, he hoped to be refreshed again by Rufinus’s presence. He said that he could not learn Greek unless he enjoyed Rufinus’s companionship for a longer time and had fuller access to him, so that he might grow rich from Rufinus’s resources.

He then concludes the letter as follows:

> “At the very time when this letter was being written, while the proposed reading lay before my eyes, the passage from Genesis came before me in which Judah is blessed by Jacob (XLIX. 8). Since the Lord had provided so timely [Col. 0128C] an occasion, I decided, after some time, to knock at the door of your heart. Therefore, if you love me—or rather, because you love me greatly—I ask you to write to me, explaining as you understand it the blessing of the Patriarchs; and if you yourself know anything in them that is difficult in meaning and worthy of knowledge, please let me know it. In particular, concerning that passage of Genesis (XLIX. 11 according to the Septuagint), where it says, ‘binding his colt to the vine, and his donkey’s colt to the vine-shoot’—who is his colt, and who is the donkey’s colt? And why is his colt tied to the vine, but the donkey’s colt to the vine-shoot?”

Thus wrote Paulinus, who indicates in Letter 43, formerly 35, § 3, that the same question had previously been put to him by the presbyter Desiderius.

## V

Although Rufinus, as stated, was occupied with translating the books *Periarchon*, he nevertheless complied with the request of his dearest friend and sent Paulinus the first book of Jacob’s prophecy concerning Judah’s blessing. He prefixed to it a letter full of modesty and sound judgment, from which I shall transfer several passages:

> “The more I excuse myself to you and declare myself less capable of answering what you ask, the more insistently you question me and [Col. 0128D] investigate more difficult matters. It is as though, having detected the defect of a sluggish ox, you were to drive your more obstinate goads into its hesitant shoulders and retreating back.”

He also says of the matter itself:

> “It certainly requires no small amount of leisure and time—or, to speak more faithfully, it demands a mind illuminated by the Holy Spirit.”

It should further be noted that Rufinus consistently speaks of himself in his writings, in Christian fashion, with great modesty and humility. I see that Tillemont also observed this, volume XII, article 84, p. 210.

Hardly had Paulinus received Rufinus’s explanation when, through Cerealis, who was returning from the city of Nola to Rome, he sent Letter 47, formerly 48, to be delivered to Rufinus at Pinetum.

After asking Rufinus not to leave Italy and return to the East without visiting him, Paulinus also requested that Rufinus explain the blessing of the Twelve Patriarchs, whose beginning, he says, Rufinus had already presented to him in written pages, setting out the prophecy concerning Judah in a threefold interpretation, as requested. [Col. 0129A] Paulinus asks that Rufinus distribute the exposition among the remaining sons, so that through Rufinus he himself might become aware of the truth and might have you as the source of great gratitude and praise, if he could answer those—namely, Desiderius the presbyter—who, judging him above his true worth because of the difficulty of the work, had thought that he ought to be consulted, with answers divine and inspired by Rufinus’s spirit rather than inept ones from his own understanding. [Col. 0129B]

During Lent Rufinus sent Paulinus from Pinetum what he had requested: book II, concerning the blessings of the remaining eleven Patriarchs.

Gennadius mentions the entire work in his *Catalogue*, chapter XVII, in these words:

> “He [Rufinus] also discussed Jacob’s blessing upon the Patriarchs in a threefold sense, namely the historical, moral, and mystical.”

A serious error, however, slipped into Isidore’s *Catalogue*, chapter IV, where we read:

> “The presbyter Paulinus explained the blessings of the Patriarchs according to three kinds of understanding, composing a little book in sufficiently concise brevity.”

Honorius agrees with Isidore, copying him in his customary manner in book II, chapter CXVII.

Do you see? A work that Rufinus had written at the request of that distinguished Pontius Meropius Paulinus, later bishop of Nola, is attributed to a certain presbyter Paulinus. Isidore, and with him Aubert Miraeus in his notes, rashly confused this presbyter Paulinus with the deacon and notary of the same name belonging to Saint Ambrose of Milan.

The error concerning Rufinus’s work was noticed by Casimir Oudin in the *Bellarmine Supplement*, p. 61, and by Tillemont, volume XII, p. 126.

The author of *On Twelve Writers*, who is appended to Isidore and Hildefonsus, seems not to have known who Paulinus was to whom Rufinus sent the book. For he says in chapter V:

> “Tyrannius Rufinus wrote to a certain presbyter Paulinus a sufficiently concise book, composed with clear brevity, on the blessings of the Patriarchs according to a threefold understanding.”

He soon afterward criticizes Rufinus because he referred the sixth prophecy, concerning Dan, not to the Antichrist but to our Lord. He writes:

> “According to the mystical sense, he [Rufinus] incorrectly interprets of our Lord what is written concerning Dan, the son of Jacob, whereas the testimony [Col. 0129C] of the holy Fathers proves beyond doubt that these things refer to the Antichrist.”

Although some of the writers whom Benedictus Pererius lists in volume IV of his commentary on Genesis, chapter XLIX, understand this prophecy of the Antichrist, it is nevertheless certain that the Fathers apply it to other interpretations as well. Pererius cites eight of them: some interpret it of Samson, and others also of the Messiah.

## VI

Constantius Hierotheus first published this work of Rufinus, inverted and confused, though not in its entirety, under the false title *Homily XVII on Genesis*, presenting it as a work of Adamantius together with Origen’s works on the New Testament, after the homilies on the Psalms, folio CIV of the Venetian edition published by Lazarus Soardus in A.D. 1516.

Johannes Herold later restored the work to its true author, though without knowing the earlier edition, and inserted it into the second volume of the *Orthodoxographia of Sacred Theology*, p. 1423. From there I shall transfer what Herold says at the beginning about the manuscript from which he copied the work, for it is particularly worthy of reading:

> “Georgius Pictorius, a most distinguished man, an excellent physician at Ensisheim, and one who had rendered outstanding service to universal [Col. 0129D] learning, had acquired this little book of Rufinus for his library as a treasure, doubtless only through the greatest exertions of his intellect or an insane expenditure of money. In accordance with his generosity toward good literature and toward his friends, he freely offered this little book also to Master Heinrich Petri, who was then publishing a library of sacred authors.
>
> “The book had been written in Roman capital letters, indeed in letters like those in which we have seen the Florentine Pandects written, without any division whatsoever, more than a thousand years ago. It was a precious jewel of venerable antiquity. Yet the injury of time and the carelessness of barbarians had dreadfully torn it apart. Since it treats mystically of Judah’s blessing, three pages had been torn out and lost; although a fourth remained, it could scarcely be determined where it should be restored.
>
> “The parchment was consequently so delicate that I would not dare claim to have seen anything more fragile. This caused still greater damage [Col. 0130A] to the writing. The ink itself, through its corrosive quality, had eaten away and made transparent many lines, so that they could be read only from the traces, unless a line on the facing side of the other page corresponded to it; then the labor required on both sides was greater still.
>
> “There was also this difficulty: whether because the library in which the book had formerly been kept was moistened by rain, or because the volume had been carried here and there for the display of the ancient monument, the whole book had become wet at the margins. The extremely delicate parchment had become almost glued together, so that nearly every leaf could be separated or opened only by tearing it.
>
> “Nevertheless, I was willing to endure even this annoyance, so that I might transcribe the book, whatever its condition when it was offered to me. It does not reach its proper conclusion, although I suspect that only a little is missing.
>
> “I therefore urge all students to seek in libraries, whenever an opportunity arises, whatever is lacking from this writing, so that at last it may be presented complete and less mutilated to theologians.”

Johannes Jacobus Grynaeus likewise caused the work to appear in his *Monuments of the Holy Fathers*, in the *Orthodoxographia*, though copied from Herold and without naming [Col. 0130B] him, at Basel, with Heinrich Petri, A.D. 1569, volume II, p. 1065.

Laurentius de la Barre again published it, likewise without knowledge of the earlier editions, together with other works of Rufinus, at Paris, with Michael Sonnius, A.D. 1580, in folio. He supplemented his text from the editions of Herold and Grynaeus.

It is especially worth noting that Barreus not only published Rufinus’s letter, or preface, to Paulinus of Nola concerning book I as though it had never previously been published—although Herold and Grynaeus had published it long before—but also left the same lacuna in its final two lines that appears in the editions of Herold and Grynaeus. Immediately after the word *probabuntur* at the end of Rufinus’s letter, the mutilated word-fragment “. . . .mis caeteris” follows, with the lacuna indicated. In the margin is added:

> “Here some things are missing.”

Barreus says that he extracted Rufinus’s writings from the remains of the venerable monastery of Mont-Dieu.

This agrees with the very ancient imperial codex, written approximately twelve hundred years ago in capital [Col. 0130C] letters and without separation between individual words, described by Lambecius in his *Commentaries on the Imperial Library*, volume II, p. 800. This codex contains Rufinus’s two books *On the Blessings*, together with the two previously mentioned reciprocal letters of Paulinus and Rufinus. They are not separated but placed together at the beginning.

In the latter letter to Paulinus, as it appears in the imperial codex, an entire leaf is missing shortly after the end, following the word *probabuntur*. The leaf that follows immediately after the lacuna, at the end of the preceding leaf, begins with the final syllable of an incomplete word: [lacuna]mis *ceteris*, just as in the other three editions already cited. Thus the origin and antiquity of the lacuna, which was transmitted into all later copies, are evident.

Charles Caesar Baudelotius attempts in vain to diminish the great antiquity of the codex in volume II, p. 127 of the first edition of his *Usefulness of Travels*.

From this it follows that the judgment of Francesco Sacchini deserves to be rejected. Fronto Ducaeus calls him by the name “the Roman friend” in his notes to Paulinus’s Letter 47, p. 833 of the Plantinian edition of A.D. 1622, in octavo. Ducaeus says that Sacchini considered [Col. 0130D] Paulinus’s letters to Rufinus not to be by Paulinus, because the style seemed more affected, as though produced by someone imitating Paulinus, than genuinely Paulinus’s own.

Sacchini says the same in his *Life of Saint Paulinus*, p. 179. But the falsity and superficiality of this judgment are sufficiently refuted by the codices already mentioned, which come very close to the age of Paulinus. Nevertheless, Cotelerius, misled by Ducaeus’s deception in his judgment on the books of the *Recognitions*, p. 484 of the second edition, declared that Paulinus’s Letter 47 was not of undisputed authority.

But let us hear Brunus refuting him in *Dissertation I on the Letters of Saint Paulinus*, § 47, p. 113:

> “I do not possess such discernment that I can perceive what difference there is between his style—that is, Rufinus’s—and Paulinus’s. I could easily persuade myself that the only basis some people had for doubting these letters was a preconceived hatred of Rufinus. For some think that Rufinus could not have been loved without fault once the controversy arose [Col. 0131A] which alienated him from Jerome. Yet Augustine’s and Paulinus’s friendship toward both men suffered no damage on that account.”

But from the evidence cited above it is clearer than daylight that these letters were written by our Paulinus to Rufinus. Thus writes Brunus, whose statements we see strengthened by our observations.

Tillemont also specifically refutes Sacchini, volume XIV, p. 710.

After presenting a sample of the script, Lambecius concludes his description of the codex in these words:

> “Anyone who accurately compares this outstanding codex, admirable for its venerable age, from beginning to end with the printed editions, will certainly perform a worthwhile service.”

Edmundus Martenius, in *The First Literary Journey*, part II, p. 138, testifies that another Rufinus codex *On the Twelve Blessings of the Patriarchs*, written a thousand years ago, still existed in the Abbey of Murbach in Alsace. If only some learned man had compared it with the printed editions.

What Martenius did not do, the Most Eminent Cardinal Firaus arranged to have done at my request, when he was nuncio of the Roman See [Col. 0131B] among the Swiss. I shall insert here what the Murbach codex supplies to fill the ancient lacuna found in the manuscripts already mentioned:

> “[lacuna] They will be proved. [Col. 0131C] But when he says: ‘A prince shall not fail from Judah, nor a ruler from his thigh, until he comes to whom the kingdom has been reserved, and in him the nations will hope’—since the phrase ‘until he comes to whom it has been reserved, in whom the nations will hope’ is plainly spoken of Christ, we are compelled beyond doubt to understand that the one from whose seed a ruler will not fail until Christ comes is someone other than Christ himself.
>
> “For it is not fitting to understand as that Christ the one from whose seed a ruler will not fail until Christ comes, since that ruler certainly ceased to exist at Christ’s coming. This itself was evidence that the one to whom the kingdom had been reserved—that is, Christ—had come.
>
> “Certain things are referred to Judah, as in many other passages and also in this chapter.”

In the *Chronicle of Centula*, preserved by Dacherium in volume IV of the *Spicilegium*, p. 482 of the first edition, it is noted that in A.D. 831, at the Abbey of Saint Richarius, there was in one volume an *Exposition by Rufinus of the Twelve Blessings of the Patriarchs*.

These are the matters that arose for discussion concerning Rufinus’s two books *On the Blessings*, which he composed at the monastery of Pinetum during Lent itself, while he was engaged in translating Origen, as was amply demonstrated above.

It therefore becomes clear that this could by no means have occurred after A.D. 398. Rufinus departed for Aquileia before the end of that year and did not return from there to Rome before A.D. 408. Moreover, the rumor aroused by his translation of Origen’s books first spread not after A.D. 400 but before it.

Tillemont therefore errs in volume XII, p. 309, where he supposes that Rufinus, returning from his homeland to Rome in A.D. 410, undertook the work *On the Blessings*. Later, in volume XIV, p. 127, the learned man forgot his earlier opinion and assigned it to A.D. 408. Yet it should be assigned to neither of those years, but to A.D. 398, as we have said.

VII. Now we must return to the remaining books, namely the third and fourth of Origen’s *Periarchon*. From Rufinus’s second preface it may be gathered that the first two books, which he had translated in the monastery of Pinetum, [Col. 0131D] had circulated through other hands, while the remaining two had not yet been translated, and rumors had arisen against the interpreter on their account. The preface itself also informs us that those same two later books were translated after an interval, and later than the first two. During that interval Rufinus, at Paulinus’s urging, discussed the Blessings of the Patriarchs. Hence, to the same two later books of the *Periarchon*, as though to a new work, he prefixed a new prologue addressed to Macarius; he would not have prefixed it if he had published them together with the first two, to which he had already prefixed his prologue.

I shall append Rufinus’s actual words addressed to Macarius from his second preface to Book III of the *Periarchon*, for they wonderfully clarify the matter under discussion:

> May you who read remember me in your holy prayers, so that we too may be deemed worthy to become imitators of the Spirit. I translated the FIRST TWO little books of the *Periarchon* during the DAYS OF LENT, at your insistence and indeed under your compulsion. But since during those days you too, religious brother Macarius, both admonished me more closely and had more leisure (perhaps *called*, as it is read in Grynaeus’s edition, p. 711), I too worked more extensively. But we explained THESE TWO LATER BOOKS MORE SLOWLY, while you came to us less frequently as an inspector, in the farthest and most remote part of the city.

Thus far Rufinus concerning the two later books of the *Periarchon*. He soon afterward describes the rumors aroused in the City by his translation as follows:

> But if you remember what I warned you in the earlier little preface—namely, that certain people would be indignant if they heard us saying anything that was not evil—you have immediately shown that you approved what I predicted. If, in that work, those who incite human tongues to evil-speaking were so INFLAMED, namely the demons, in which he had not yet fully exposed their secrets, what do you think will happen in this work, in which he will reveal all their blind and hidden paths by which they creep into human hearts and deceive weak and fragile souls?
