You will see everything immediately thrown into confusion, seditions stirred up, shouts spread throughout the whole city, and the man summoned for condemnation who has attempted, by the light of the evangelical lamp, to drive away the darkness of diabolical ignorance. But let him who desires to exercise himself in divine learning, while preserving the rule of the Catholic Faith, pay little heed to this.
>
> I must, however, necessarily point out that, just as we did in the EARLIER BOOKS, so in these also we took care not to interpret those things which seemed contrary to his other statements and to our Faith. Rather, as though they had been inserted by others and adulterated, we passed them over. But if he seemed to have introduced something new concerning rational creatures, since this does not concern the essence of the Faith, I judged it useful, for the sake of knowledge and practice—especially since it may perhaps be necessary for us to respond in this manner against certain heresies—not to repeat in these little books what had been said in the earlier ones as well; and, for the sake of brevity, I thought it appropriate to cut some of these matters out.

Finally, attacking his opponents, he concludes the matter as follows:

> Nevertheless, if anyone reads these things with the desire to make progress rather than to criticize, he will act more wisely if he wishes them to be explained to him by more experienced men. For it is absurd that the fictitious poems of poets and the ridiculous tales of comedies should be explained by grammarians, while someone should imagine that he can learn without a teacher and explanation those things that are said about God, the heavenly powers, and the whole universe—things in which every perverse error of either pagan philosophers or heretics is refuted. And so it happens that people prefer, through rashness and ignorance, to condemn difficult and obscure matters rather than to learn them through diligence and study.

Thus far Rufinus.

This translation of the *Periarchon* is found in the Latin editions of Origen’s works mentioned above, Book V, chapter 2, section I. In the appendix to Volume VIII of the new edition of the works of Saint Augustine, two books *On the Incarnation of the Word*, addressed to Januarius, have been compiled from Rufinus’s work on Origen. Jean Mabillon, in the *Analecta*, Volume II, p. 665, states that the very ancient Corbie manuscript contains the books of the *Periarchon*—certainly in Rufinus’s translation—with prefixed to them Origen’s epitaph, which Mabillon quotes on p. 660 and which was composed by some admirer of Origen. Edmund Martene recently presented it as unpublished in his *Literary Journey*, Volume II, p. 185. [Col. 0132D] It is as follows:

> I am that Origen, once the truest teacher,
>
> Whom first the bright grace of Faith bestowed.
>
> If you wish to believe me, I wrote so many thousands of books
>
> As the legion sends men into battle.
>
> No blasphemy ever touched my thoughts;
>
> Upright and watchful, I was secure from the enemy.
>
> The title *Periarchon* alone brought me my downfall:
>
> Because of it, missiles assailing me from every side press me down.

Guido the Carmelite had previously produced this same verse in a badly corrupted form in his *Summary of Heresies*, chapter XLI, where he attributed it to Isidore. Someone else published certain verses from an Ambrosian manuscript, formerly written, as the title reports, in the library of Saint Isidore of Seville; but he did not know that in those same verses the epitaph of Origen just quoted, in a variant form somewhere, is also found.

## CHAPTER III

[Col. 0133A]

I. New rumors against Rufinus are aroused by Jerome’s friends because of his translation of the remainder of Origen’s work. II. Rufinus, after losing his mother, writes to Jerome and, having obtained letters of introduction from Pope Siricius, returns from the City to his homeland, Concordia. III. He passes through Milan for no reason other than the journey itself. IV. Jerome writes to him while he is staying in his homeland, but the letters are not delivered to him. In what year the journey of Paulinianus, Eusebius, and the other Rufinus from Palestine to Rome took place. V. Jerome writes another letter to Pammachius against Rufinus’s preface to the books of the *Periarchon*. From this the hostility between the two men increases. VI. Rufinus the Syrian brings both of Jerome’s letters to Rome, to be delivered to Pammachius and Rufinus. VII. The first of these letters is reviewed in summary.

I. The rumor concerning the first two books of the *Periarchon* translated by Rufinus had not yet properly subsided when, shortly afterward, the other two, presented in Latin, once again stirred up the smoldering fires. Rufinus had scarcely allowed the uncorrected sheets of his translation, which had not yet been made public, to slip from his hands when Pammachius and Oceanus—men of distinguished name among the Romans, but far more distinguished through their friendship with Jerome, Augustine, and Paulinus of Nola—immediately sent the same sheets, secretly placed in their hands and, as Rufinus indeed maintains, here and there secretly overlaid with corrupt opinions, to Saint Jerome in Palestine. This occurred in the same year A.D. 398, in which Rufinus had completed the translation after Easter.

Pammachius and Oceanus suppressed Rufinus’s name in the letter concerning this matter that they wrote to Jerome, either because it was absent from their copy or, more probably, because they thought Jerome would easily infer the interpreter’s identity without any further explanation. Certainly Jerome, in his response to the letter written to him at the same time by Rufinus, says that from the style he immediately recognized the author of the preface. Therefore his name [Col. 0133C] was absent from the written document.

Moreover, Roman dignitaries stirred up this eminent man, who was otherwise readily inflamed by zeal for the Catholic faith, against Rufinus—preferably, I would believe, with good intentions—by alleging that certain matters had been set forth less catholically in his translation, and that the interpreter had removed passages capable of displaying Origen’s impiety. For this reason, they said, he and all the Romans fervently desired a new version of the *Periarchon* by Jerome, so that it might expose interpolations and convict what had been badly explained. To inflame Jerome still further, they added fictitious praise of his genius and Faith in the preface to the work, as though Rufinus were thought to have wished to conceal his own heresy beneath the reputation of Jerome’s name.

It is better to bring forward the actual words of Pammachius’s otherwise brief letter, which is now Letter XL, formerly LXIV (now LXXXIII):

> A certain holy brother brought us some sheets belonging to SOMEONE, containing a volume of Origen translated into Latin, entitled *Periarchon*. And since in it there are many things that disturb the weakness of our understanding and that we judge to have been expressed less catholically, we also suspect that, by way of excusing the author, many passages have been removed from his books that could have displayed his manifest impiety. We ask your eminence to undertake this work—not so much for us as for all who live in the City—as a service of particular usefulness: namely, that you make known in your language, in accordance with the truth, the aforesaid book of Origen as it was published by the author himself; and that you expose what has been interpolated by his defender, so that you may refute and convict whatever in these sheets that we have sent to your holiness has been published either contrary to the Catholic rule or incompetently.
>
> Certainly, in the preface to his work he subtly mentioned your holiness without naming you, saying that he himself had completed the work promised by you, and insinuating indirectly that you held the same view. Therefore clear away people’s suspicions, lest, if you remain silent, you appear to consent.

Thus Pammachius and Oceanus wrote to Jerome, while the scars of the former hostility between him and Rufinus, arising from the Origenist affair, had scarcely healed.

II. At this same time Rufinus, about to depart for his homeland, wrote from the City to Jerome. He informed him both that he had remained in Rome longer than he had intended and that his mother had died in the city of Concordia. He said, however, that the longing of his spiritual parents, Chromatius and Eusebius, had recalled him to his homeland, although otherwise the grief caused by his mother’s death would have prevented him from going there, lest the sight of his mother’s house intensify the pain by bringing it closer—pain that, far from his homeland, he had been able only with difficulty to suppress in his heart.

He also complained indirectly about Jerome, as though he had suffered the attacks of the Romans without Jerome’s being unaware of them. This letter of Rufinus has been lost. Jerome’s replies to Pammachius and Oceanus, and to Rufinus himself, nevertheless survive, and below we shall attempt to review individually the contents of those letters, thereby illuminating the history of Rufinus.

In the meantime Rufinus, having spent a year and more in Rome and at Pinetum, gathered his baggage as he prepared to hasten to our Venetia, and customarily obtained from Pope Siricius letters of introduction—public tokens of faith, which bishops ordinarily gave only to Catholics departing for another parish. We infer that Rufinus later produced these letters from Jerome, in Book III of the *Apology*, where he says, on p. 459: “You produce a letter from Siricius, who rests in the Lord.” And below, on p. 462: “You argue something similar against Pope Anastasius, as though, because you possess a letter from Bishop Siricius, he could not write against you.”

He states the same matter more clearly in Letter XCVI, formerly XVI (now CXXVII), addressed to Principia, the *Epitaph of Marcella*: “They request and obtain ecclesiastical letters”—he means Rufinus—“so that they may appear to have departed in communion.”

Not much time intervened before the distinguished Anastasius succeeded to the pontificate. In its proper place it will become clear that Siricius, a most holy man, was unjustly accused, as though he had not hesitated to give letters of communion to a heretic.

[Col. 0134C] Rufinus therefore left Rome in A.D. 398, before November 26, the day on which Siricius died, according to Daniel Papebrochius in the *Propyleum*, Part I, p. 59, and according to Pagi on that year, section 2; otherwise he would have produced letters of communion not from Siricius but from Anastasius.

Baronius, under A.D. 398, section 1, where he says that Siricius died on February 22, took a translation occurring on that day and month, but in the following year, 399, as the date of his death. See the *Bollandists*, February, Volume III, p. 282.

The interval indicated by Jerome’s words “not much time intervened” perhaps comprised several months between the death of Siricius and the succession of Anastasius. For Anastasius was ordained soon afterward, on December 5, which fell on a Sunday, according to Pagi under A.D. 398, section 5, and A.D. 402, section 16.

Accordingly Rufinus, traveling by the gentlest route through Flaminia—as Jerome says at the beginning of Book II of the *Apology*—first made for Milan. There Simplicianus had succeeded Ambrose in the Milanese see after Ambrose had been committed to the earth on April 5 of the preceding year, 397, as Mabillon reports in the *Museo Italico*, Volume I, Part II, p. 115.

In Book I of his *Apology*, Rufinus complains that Eusebius of Cremona had recited to him at Milan an impious opinion inserted into his sheets, claiming that his translation of the *Periarchon* had been falsified by Eusebius:

> When Eusebius was reciting such an opinion at Milan, and I was saying that what he demanded from me was false, he was asked from whom he had received the copies. He replied that a certain matron had given them to him.

Eusebius, who in the earlier dispute between Jerome, who favored Epiphanius, and Rufinus, who supported John of Jerusalem, had openly adhered to Jerome, as has been stated, later arrived in Rome from the East before Rufinus departed from there.

His journey and arrival are accurately indicated by these words of Jerome in Book III of the *Apology*, p. 462: “Paulininus and Eusebius departed AFTER A YEAR from your voyage.”

We have established that Rufinus reached Nola at the beginning of spring A.D. 397. Therefore Eusebius, who seems to have crossed into Italy in the spring of A.D. 398, a season suitable for navigation, was already in Rome at the beginning of the summer of that same year, where he had Rufinus as a participant in his communion and companionship before the two of them set out—Rufinus for Concordia, Eusebius for Cremona—via Milan.

Rufinus himself testifies to this in Book I of his *Apology*:

> If Eusebius had found this in my letters, and had truly taken some offense from the reading itself, when he had me present in Rome, as you yourself know, he would certainly have investigated immediately and brought the very writings to me, since until that time he had been accustomed even to SEE ME, to GREET ME, and to SHARE COMMUNION with me in prayer.

That Rufinus is speaking here of Eusebius of Cremona is made certain by these words of Jerome against Rufinus in Book II of the *Apology*:

> Cry out and shout through the streets: “It is not my book”; and, if it is mine, “Eusebius stole the uncorrected sheets.”

The matron who gave Rufinus’s sheets to Eusebius, from whom Pammachius and Oceanus afterward received them to transmit to Jerome, was Marcella, as is clearly inferred from her epitaph, as I shall explain below. Jerome dedicated his commentaries on Jeremiah and Matthew to this same Eusebius.

III. Cardinal Norisius, attacking Rufinus everywhere, writes in Book I, chapter II, of his *Pelagian History* that Rufinus went to Milan in order to disseminate his heresies and draw Venerius, the bishop of that city, over to his side. He says that Rufinus then proceeded to Aquileia in order to enrich even his native soil with Origenist ravings, to instill the poison of new doctrines into Chromatius, the other metropolitan of Italy, and, in repayment for the Catholic instruction he had received from him thirty years earlier, when Chromatius was still a presbyter, to infect that most holy and learned old man with the most impious errors.

Nor was this eminent man content to assert such atrocious things about Rufinus without a witness; he immediately adds:

> Who would not abominate the attempt of a man who, at almost one and the same time, most insolently tried to add three chief Churches of Italy—the Roman, then the Milanese, and finally the Aquileian—to the Origenist sect?

But the most eloquent man seems to me to have adopted a false opinion. I would not, however, wish that, while rejecting his opinion, I should appear to insult a man who was once well disposed toward me. That would be sacrilegious.

Venerius did not occupy the Milanese see before A.D. 400, when he filled the place of Simplicianus. Simplicianus had succeeded Ambrose, as I have said; this is also established by the continuators of the Bollandist work in the *Exegesis* prefixed to Volume VII of May.

To say that Simplicianus, Gaudentius of Brescia, and Chromatius of Aquileia—men equally holy and learned, whom Rufinus certainly visited at that time—could have lent receptive ears to Origenist errors cannot be done without insulting such great bishops, especially since none of them ever avoided Rufinus’s society, but he himself lived in continual communion with each of them.

Rufinus had long known blessed Gaudentius, a disciple and successor in the see of Saint Philastrius, in the East. We shall later see that at Gaudentius’s request Rufinus translated Clement’s *Recognitions* from Greek into Latin.

This journey through Insubria was, so to speak, the proper and natural route for Rufinus on his return to his homeland, not an indirect route—less appropriate and undertaken for secret reasons—by a man traveling from Rome to lower Venetia. At that time, before Ferrara and Venice had yet been founded, Aquileia could be reached by three routes.

The first followed the coast. One traveled from Ariminum to Ravenna, from which one sailed across the seven seas as far as Altinum, as Antoninus says in the *Itinerary*. From Altinum the road continued to Concordia and Aquileia. In that age a marsh lay beyond Bologna; Vibius Sequester calls it the *Padusa of Gaul*, named from the Po.

The second route was inland and led from Ariminum to Caesena. From there it extended through Faventia, Forum Cornelii, Bologna, [Col. 0136A] Mutina, Regium, Parma, Fidentiola, Placentia, Laus, Milan, Bergomum, Brescia, Verona, Vicetia, Patavium, and Altinum.

The third, likewise inland, ran from Ariminum through Bologna, Mutina, Vicus Serninus and Varianum, Mons Anianus, Ateste, Patavium, and Altinum.

These routes are drawn from the highly reliable itineraries of Antoninus and the Peutinger Table. Of these three common routes Rufinus chose the second, as more convenient for him.

IV. In A.D. 399 Jerome’s Letter XLII, formerly LXVI (now LXXI), was written to Rufinus while he was staying in his homeland, but it was not delivered to him. In it the holy man responds to the letter Rufinus had written to him in the preceding year, when he was about to leave Rome.

Jerome says that it immediately became clear to him from the elegance of the Latin language in which our man had written the letter that Rufinus had remained in Rome for a long time, since he had become accustomed to the Latin language, which during his long wandering he had to some extent forgotten. This, naturally, could have happened only over a long period:

> Your own speech showed that you had remained in Rome for a long time.

He says that he has no doubt that the love of his spiritual parents had recalled Rufinus to his homeland, while grief over his mother’s death had turned him away from such a journey, lest he grieve more deeply in her presence over what he could scarcely endure while absent.

Then, after calling God to witness to his conscience and stating that, after their friendship had been restored, no resentment had intervened by which he might have harmed anyone, he immediately adds:

> True friendship ought not to conceal what it feels. The little preface to the books of the *Periarchon* was sent to me—namely, by Pammachius and Oceanus—and from the style I understood that it was yours, for Rufinus’s name was absent. In it I am attacked indirectly, indeed openly. You must judge with what intention it was written; what it means is clear even to fools.
>
> I too, who have very often declaimed figurative expressions, could have repeated something about you according to an old art and praised you in your own manner. But far be it from me to imitate in you what I criticize. Rather, I tempered my judgment in such a way that I might both avoid the accusation brought against me and, so far as lay in me, refrain from injuring my friend even though injured.
>
> But I beseech you, if henceforth you wish to follow anyone, be content with your own judgment alone. For either the things we pursue are good or they are evil. If they are good, they do not need another’s assistance; if they are evil, the multitude of sinners does not provide a defense for error.
>
> I preferred to complain of these matters to you privately as a friend rather than, when provoked, rage publicly, so that you may recognize that I cherish restored friendships sincerely and do not, in accordance with the saying of Plautus, hold a stone in one hand while offering bread with the other.

Thus Jerome addressed Rufinus, somewhat angered by the suspicions Pammachius and Oceanus had cast upon him, as though he were being drawn into the defense of heretics by Rufinus’s false and deceitful praises; although he says nothing at all about the errors of Rufinus’s translation.

Near the end of the letter he says that his brother Paulinianus, who in the preceding year, 398, had crossed into Italy with Eusebius of Cremona while intending to travel to his homeland, Stridon, had not yet returned to him in the year 399, when Jerome was writing. He nevertheless thinks that Paulinianus had seen Rufinus at Aquileia with Chromatius the metropolitan.

[Col. 0136D] He adds that he had sent another presbyter Rufinus through Rome to Milan and had asked him to visit our Rufinus, the man to whom he was writing, with goodwill and courtesy.

Who this other Rufinus was, and with what loss of truth the most celebrated writers have conflated him with our Rufinus, will be discussed later. Here it is enough to say that this man’s journey and arrival in Rome occurred in that same year, 399—namely, two years after our Rufinus had departed from there.

This is proved by Jerome’s words in Book III of the *Apology*, p. 462:

> Paulinianus and Eusebius departed AFTER A YEAR from your voyage. Rufinus was sent in the affair of Claudius AFTER TWO YEARS.

We do not know what this affair of Claudius was, on account of which the other Rufinus hastened from Syria to Milan, where the imperial court was then located. It must nevertheless have been a very serious matter, since Jerome testifies that the journey occurred because of danger to another man’s life.

After mentioning these matters as evidence of his sincere friendship with our Rufinus, [Col. 0137A] Jerome brings the letter to a close as follows:

> We have communicated the same information to the other friends—namely, so that they might greet Rufinus in my name—lest, by biting one another, we consume one another. Now it is for you and your friends to give no occasion to impatient men, lest you find that not everyone is like me, able to take pleasure in figurative praises.

V. Together with this reply to Rufinus, Jerome also sent another reply to Pammachius and Oceanus, in which he refuted Rufinus’s preface at greater length, showing that he was alien to Origenist doctrine. He also attached a new translation of the books of the *Periarchon* prepared by himself.

In this letter, however, the holy man everywhere spared the name of Rufinus the interpreter, thereby giving evidence of his very gentle disposition toward Rufinus—something the Romans by no means desired. As a result, they spread among the populace, as though by a commentary spoken aloud, those matters that were absent from Jerome’s letter according to their wishes, making Rufinus’s name still more hated in proportion as Jerome’s authority appeared to weigh more heavily against him.

See Book III of Jerome’s *Apology*, [Col. 0137B] p. 467.

Indeed, because Jerome’s letter to Rufinus, which we mentioned above, might have seemed somewhat more moderate, it was never delivered to him, so that the other letter, flying through the City to Pammachius, might wound Rufinus more severely.

Thus Rufinus, after the hostility had already broken out, learned only belatedly from his Roman friends of this same letter, which had indeed been written to him but not delivered. He thought that Jerome had composed it only recently, not long before, although under a false date referring it to an earlier period that had already elapsed. He judged that this had been done deliberately, so that he might be accused more severely—as though he had been unwilling to respond with equal moderation to Jerome’s moderation.

But Jerome shifts the blame for the undelivered letter onto his Roman friends in these words in Book I of the *Apology*, p. 363:

> I, that moderate man in the public letter—to Pammachius—who carefully took precautions lest you think anything had been said against you, wrote you a brief letter IMMEDIATELY, complaining about your praises. But because you were not in Rome, my friends DID NOT WISH TO SEND it to you, saying that you were making statements, together with your associates, unworthy of the Christian name about my manner of life. I have appended a copy of it to this volume, so that you may know how much sorrow I restrained through the moderation appropriate to our relationship.

Again, in Book III of the *Apology*, p. 468:

> You also suppose that I invented a new falsehood, composing a letter to you in my name, as though it had been written long ago, so that I might appear good and moderate—a letter which you never received at all. This matter can very easily be proved. Many people in Rome possess copies of it, dating from approximately THREE YEARS AGO, but they did not wish to send it to you, knowing what you were saying about my name and what unworthy and abominable things you were fabricating about a Christian man. I wrote it in ignorance, as though to a friend. They did not deliver it to one whom they knew to be an enemy, sparing both my error and your conscience.
>
> At the same time you argue that, if I had written such a letter to you, I ought not to have written many evil things against you in another little book—namely, in the letter to Pammachius and Oceanus. This is your entire error and your just complaint: you pretend that what we say against heretics was said against you. And unless we spared them, you think that you have been violated. For Rufinus was not named in the letter just mentioned to Pammachius and Oceanus.

VI. Since at the very time Jerome sent his letters to Pammachius and Rufinus he sent the other Rufinus to Milan in the affair of Claudius, and that man was supposed to greet our Rufinus in Jerome’s name, it is reasonable to suppose that this same Rufinus carried both of the letters mentioned above to Pammachius: from him the first, attacking Rufinus, was afterward spread among the people, while the other was by no means sent to Rufinus at Aquileia.

Jerome certainly alludes to Pammachius in these words, addressing Rufinus:

> They DID NOT WISH TO SEND it to you—

that is, to Aquileia or Concordia.

That other Rufinus, Jerome’s intimate and distinct from our Rufinus, was at that time staying in Rome with Pammachius, likewise Jerome’s intimate and our Rufinus’s enemy, is clearly taught by the acts of the Council of Carthage preserved by Saint Augustine in Book II, chapter III, *On Original Sin*, where the following is reported:

> Caelestius: “The holy presbyter Rufinus, who stayed in Rome with Saint Pammachius, said: ‘I heard him say that there is no transmission of sin.’”

That this occurred after the death of Siricius and the departure of our Rufinus for his homeland, under Pope Anastasius, is attested at the beginning of his *Commonitorium* by Marius Mercator:

> “This foolish question, no less hostile to the true Faith—whether there is no transmission of sin—was first introduced into Rome by Rufinus, formerly a Syrian by nationality, under Anastasius of holy memory, supreme pontiff of the Roman Church.”

Therefore this Rufinus, Syrian by nationality, previously sent from Syria to Rome and Milan, returned to his host Pammachius Jerome’s response against Tyrannius Rufinus, our Rufinus, who was Italian by nationality, together with the new translation of the books of the *Periarchon*, and also the letter to be transmitted to that same Rufinus at Aquileia. Pammachius, however, did not deliver it to him.

Huet, Book II, chapter IV, section I, paragraph 12, says that it was not transmitted because it arrived in Rome too late through delays in transport. Hear the true reason why the letter was not delivered: because the friendship between the two men had been severed, Jerome’s friends suppressed the letter after Jerome had prepared the new translation of the books of the *Periarchon*.

VII. Let us review the principal points of Jerome’s letter to Pammachius. Jerome attempts to dispel Rufinus’s preface to the books of the *Periarchon*, in which he is raised to the stars as the adorned and magnificent interpreter and herald of Origen’s works.

He admits that he regards this praise, previously spread by Rufinus at Alexandria and Rome, as an insult:

> The sheets you sent, he begins, have inflicted an honorable insult upon me, praising my talent in such a way as to remove the truth of my Faith.

He says that he praised Origen in two places: in the little prefaces to his homilies on the *Song of Songs* and to his book *On Hebrew Names*; but he says that in neither place did he speak about Origen’s doctrine:

> I praised the interpreter, not the dogmatist; the talent, not the Faith; the philosopher, not the Apostle.

And if they wish to know my judgment concerning Origen, let them read my commentary on Ecclesiastes; let them consult the three volumes on the Epistle to the Ephesians, and they will understand that I have always opposed his doctrines.

He repeats similar statements below and also in Letter XXXIX, formerly LXII (now LXXXII), addressed to Theophilus.

These excuses, however, do not greatly please the most learned Bishop of Avranches, by no means a partisan of Rufinus, in *On Origen*, Book II, chapter IV, section I, paragraph 17. For when the eloquent Doctor inserts the *Adamantian* sayings into his commentaries on Ecclesiastes and the Epistle to the Ephesians, he scarcely refutes them even once; indeed, he does not even identify Origen as their author. If he had then regarded them as false, he would certainly have marked them with a condemnation.

For Jerome says in the prologue to Book II of his Commentaries on Micah:

> They say that I have compiled the volumes of Origen and that it is improper for the writings of the ancients to be contaminated—which they regard as a very serious reproach. I consider it the greatest praise, since I wish to imitate one whom I do not doubt pleases all prudent men and you.

In the preface to his book *On Hebrew Names*, he says that only an ignorant person would deny that, after the Apostles, Origen is a teacher of the Churches.

Jerome then devotes the entire letter to showing, against Rufinus, that he did not praise Origen rashly but followed the examples of great men, from whom authors could nevertheless be praised for their talent, even though they otherwise abounded in errors.

Thus, he says, blessed Cyprian uses Tertullian as his teacher, as his writings prove; and although he delights in the talent of that learned and ardent man, he does not follow Montanus or Maximilla with him.

Apollinarius writes powerful books against Porphyry. Eusebius beautifully composed an Ecclesiastical History, although the one erred concerning the mystery of the Incarnation, imagining that the Word had assumed not a soul but only [Col. 0139A] flesh, while the other became a defender of Arius’s impiety.

He afterward adds:

> When I was young, I was carried along by an extraordinary eagerness to learn, and, contrary to the presumption of certain people, I did not teach myself.

Here he clearly attacks Rufinus, who, Jerome also records elsewhere, had boasted that he had learned Greek literature without a teacher.

Accordingly Jerome says that he heard Apollinarius of Laodicea, Didymus, and also Baranina the Jew; that he read all Origen’s writings thoroughly, while nevertheless carefully avoiding his errors.

He complains that letters he had once written to Didymus, as to a teacher, had been brought forward by someone—Rufinus—although they contained nothing beyond respect and greetings.

Finally he insists that he had never been an Origenist and that, if he had been one, he had now ceased to be so. He therefore urges the others—Rufinus—to imitate him; and after lavishly praising Adamantius and rejecting his errors, he dismisses everything Rufinus had written concerning the adulteration of Origen’s books. He also maintains that the *Apology* published by Rufinus under the name of the martyr Pamphilus was not Pamphilus’s work but the offspring of Didymus or someone else.

When Jerome wrote this letter, he said:

> It is almost one hundred and fifty years since Origen died at Tyre.

Tillemont shows that Origen died in A.D. 253, in Volume III, Article XXV, pp. 548 and 753. Add another 150 years to the year 253, according to Jerome, and you will have the year 403 of the Christian era—according to Jerome, that is, who follows the calculations of Eusebius as translated into Latin by himself.

Since this date is two years ahead of our Dionysian era, as I have noted elsewhere, subtract those two years and the year 401 remains. Therefore the word “almost,” within this period of 150 years, takes away another two years from itself, yielding the common year 399, in which Jerome wrote his letter.

He confirms the same date somewhat farther on:

> Why do you try to teach us, after four hundred years, what we did not previously know? Why do you bring forward what Peter and Paul did not choose to publish?

By these words he indicates that at the beginning of the Christian era 400 years had then already elapsed and the year 401 was in progress. Subtract the two years by which the Eusebian era exceeds our common era, and you will have the Dionysian year 399.

## CHAPTER IV

Apronianus sends Rufinus a copy of Jerome’s letter that had been circulated publicly. Various matters are presented concerning Apronianus and his family. II. Rufinus’s *Apology* against Jerome’s letter. III. Synopsis of Book I of the same *Apology*, containing doctrinal objections. IV. Rufinus demonstrates at length that he is entirely Catholic and free from the heresies attributed to Origen. V. Book II of the *Apology* examined in detail. VI. Various accusations gathered by Rufinus against Jerome. VII. Rufinus’s shorter *Apology* addressed to Anastasius.

[I.]

[I.]

Pammachius, Oceanus, and the other partisans of Jerome immediately arranged for copies of Jerome’s letter to be circulated from hand to hand, to Rufinus’s disgrace, while the Romans, as commonly happens, were meanwhile divided into opposing factions, some favoring Jerome and others Rufinus. Among Rufinus’s chief supporters, Apronianus stood out together with Macarius [Col. 0139D]. Apronianus sent a copy of the letter to a friend at Aquileia, whither he had withdrawn to Chromatius from his native city of Concordia.

Apronianus belonged to the Turcia Asteria Aproniana family, one of the most distinguished at Rome throughout the memory of past generations. The Quirinal and urban prefectures, together with military and palatine dignities, had adorned it through a long succession of years. Yet the most glorious purple of martyrdom had made it far more illustrious: the sisters Rufina and Secunda, from this same family, suffered death for the Christian religion in A.D. 257, on July 10.

This Apronianus Rufinus had converted from the worship of idols to faith in Christ. For that reason, in the individual prefaces to the works he dedicated to him, Rufinus calls him his son. By this expression—used shortly afterward by Saint Paulinus in the same sense—Rufinus showed that he had begotten Apronianus for the Christian faith, although Melania the Elder also instructed Apronianus in catechesis, as Palladius testifies in the *Lausiac History* [Col. 0140A], chapter CXIX. There he writes of a most noble woman who had returned to Rome:

> While she was there, she instructed in catechesis the blessed man Apronianus, a man of the highest reputation and distinction, who was still a pagan, and persuaded him to practice continence together with his wife, Avita, the daughter of his sister.

It is therefore evident that Avita was born of Melania’s sister, whose name is unknown to us. Palladius also mentions Eunomia, the daughter of Apronianus, in chapter CXXXIV:

> I also saw the blessed Avita with her husband Apronianus, and their daughter Eunomia.

The pious couple also had a son, Turcius Asterius, who received the grace of baptism together with his father, as Paulinus bears witness in *Natale* 13, verse 260, where he sings as follows of Pinianus, whom Paulinus himself had begotten for Christ, and of Asterius:

> Here the first son in my own flock stands out for me;  
> but in Asterius I have another light of equal brightness,  
> whom his parents, united in true devotion,  
> together established as sacred to Christ while still an infant.  
>   
> Thus, like Samuel, marked from his earliest years,  
> he might grow, devoted to the saints, with God sustaining him.  
>   
> As a child, under Christ’s name, he uttered his first murmurs,  
> and the Lord’s name was his first word.  
>   
> Now, born through God the Father into the heavenly kingdoms,  
> he shines equally in his starry name and in his speech.  
>   
> Pious grace made this child a brother to his father,  
> for they were both begotten in the holy stream;  
> those whom nature had separated by rank,  
> God, in his gracious gift, carries as brothers into his kingdoms.

At Apronianus’s request Rufinus translated many Greek writings into Latin: Origen’s *Homilies on Psalms* XXXVI, XXXVII, and XXXVIII; Gregory of Nazianzus’s *Apologeticus*; eight homilies of Basil the Great; and the sayings of Sixtus. He dedicated each of these labors, in a brief letter or preface—as he himself calls it—to Apronianus, his son.

We shall also see that Rufinus calls Avita, the wife of Apronianus, his daughter, because he had begotten both spouses for Jesus Christ.

Here I am detained, while hastening toward other matters, by Cardinal Norisius, a scholar of ancient history and its most diligent investigator. In Dissertation IV of the *Pisan Cenotaphs* [Col. 0140C], chapter II, §1, while restoring the Turcia Asteria Aproniana family to its ancient splendor, he lists our Apronianus together with other Aproniani and nearly allows him to pass without notice.

He appears to be the same person as Turcius Secundus Asterius Apronianus, who in A.D. 376 was a priest of the College of the Fifteen Men for Performing Sacred Rites, according to Onuphrius Panvinius in his commentary on book III of the *Fasti*, p. 302. Norisius seems to have regarded him as the son of another Apronianus, who was Urban Prefect under Julian in A.D. 363; for the chronology agrees, as does the title “most distinguished man,” with which Palladius honored him.

Paulinus sang of him in *Natale* XIII, verse 157:

> Apronianus, the glory of the Turcian race,  
> a boy in age, but an old man with gray wisdom,  
> noble through the ancient lineage of the toga,  
> but nobler still through the Christian name;  
>   
> whose glory is mingled with the birth of the OLD and the NEW,  
> old as a senator of the Curia, NEW as one belonging to Christ.

It is useful to set out here the genealogy of Apronianus’s ancestors:

[Col. 0140D]

**A.D. 311**

L. Turcius Secundus Apronianus, consul of uncertain year. From Panvinius’s commentary on book III of the *Fasti*, p. 296; Gruter, p. CDLXXVI, no. 7; and Norisius, Dissertation IV on the *Pisan Cenotaphs*, p. 433.

**A.D. 339**

L. Turcius Apronianus, Urban Prefect. From the same sources and the *List of Urban Prefects* in Aegidius Bucherius’s *Commentary on the Doctrine of Times*, p. 240.

**A.D. 363**

L. Turcius Apronianus Asterius [Col. 0141A], Corrector of Tuscia and Umbria and Urban Prefect. From the same sources.

**A.D. 376**

L. Turcius Secundus Asterius Apronianus, priest of the College of the Fifteen Men for Performing Sacred Rites. From Panvinius’s commentary on book III of the *Fasti*, p. 302, and Norisius, p. 435. Converted to the faith of Christ by Rufinus and Melania the Elder in A.D. 397.

**A.D. 397**

His wife, Avita, daughter of the sister of the same Melania. From Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter CXIX, and Paulinus, *Natale* XIII, verse 230.

**I**

**A.D. 398**

Eunomia. From the *Lausiac History*, chapter 134, and Paulinus, *Natale* XIII, verse 231.

Turcius Asterius Apronianus received the grace of baptism together with his father. From Paulinus, *Natale* XIII [Col. 0141B], verse 270.

I have explained these matters concerning Apronianus, Rufinus’s indispensable associate, because writers had almost entirely passed over in silence a man so distinguished by nobility, learning, and the glory of recognized truth.

**II.**

Rufinus, having received a copy of Jerome’s letter to Pammachius, thought that the accusations written against him were by no means matters he could neglect, and immediately applied himself to composing a reply. Huetius, in *Origeniana*, book II, chapter IV, §XVIII, and Cave in his *Literary History*, suppose that this reply has perished. Dupin also appears to be mistaken in the same way in volume III of the *Bibliotheca*, where he wrongly judged that the works commonly called Rufinus’s *Invectives*, which are in everyone’s hands, were written against the *Apology*, and not against Jerome’s letter.

But Rufinus set an *Apology* against the letter itself, and this work still survives under the false title *Invectives*. At the beginning of the letter Jerome had written:

> I shall omit personalities; I shall respond only to the matters and accusations. For it does not benefit a cause to answer abuse with abuse and to bite one’s opponents in retaliation.

Rufinus attacks both points at the very threshold of his *Apology*:

> Since, then, at the beginning of this *Invective* of his—for this is what he calls Jerome’s letter—he promises that he will omit personalities and respond only to matters and accusations, both statements are false. For how can he respond to an accusation which no one has made? And how does he omit personalities, when throughout the entire text of his *Invective* he continually attacks and tears apart the translator of the books?

Rufinus also says in book II that he is responding to Jerome’s letter:

> Among certain brothers, he has even tried to imprint this stain upon us, and now to repeat it in LETTERS.

These “letters” are the letter to Pammachius. I deliberately pass over many other passages, since these are sufficient to establish that Rufinus’s reply to Jerome’s letter has by no means perished, as learned men have believed [Col. 0141D].

Rufinus divided his *Apology* into two books. Later, the copyists gave it the offensive title *Invectives*. In book I Rufinus himself explicitly calls it an *Apology*:

> I think it appropriate to insert into this *Apology* of ours …

And shortly before the end of the same book I:

> I shall conclude the first volume of our *Apology*.

What is more, Jerome himself confirms the same thing in book III of his *Apology*, p. 353:

> From your *Apology* we have now learned what you think concerning the resurrection of the flesh.

Just as the copyists gave Rufinus’s *Apology* the name *Invectives*, so not only does Rufinus call Jerome’s letter, written against him, *Invectives* and an *Invective*, but Jerome himself calls Rufinus’s work *Invectives* in book III.

At the beginning Rufinus addresses Apronianus as follows:

> I have read through your writings, Apronianus, my dearest son, which you sent on to me after they had been sent from the East by a good friend and brother, Jerome, to the most distinguished man Pammachius. I recalled the prophetic saying: “The teeth of human beings are their weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword.”
>
> Yet for these wounds inflicted by the tongue there is almost no physician among human beings. Therefore I turned to Jesus, the heavenly physician, who gave me a most powerful antidote, brought forth from the vessel of his Gospel, to relieve the force of the pain through hope of the future just judgment that is with him.
>
> The potion Jesus prepared consisted of these words: “Blessed are you when they persecute you and speak every evil against you falsely. Rejoice and exult, because your reward is great in heaven. For so they persecuted the prophets who were before you.”

Having said that he was content with this medicine and had decided to remain silent about the rest, Rufinus adds that a just necessity of replying was imposed upon him in part, because, unless he repelled the charge of heresy brought against him by Jerome, his reputation among many people would appear to be in serious danger.

> Therefore, he says, I am compelled to reply against my will and contrary to my intention, lest by keeping silent I appear to acknowledge the charge, although, following the Lord’s example, it is glorious for a Christian to drive away other accusations by silence. Yet, if this charge is left unanswered, it generates the greatest scandal in the faith.

The first book of the *Apology* is occupied for the most part with refuting dogmatic accusations. Rufinus chose to begin it with the place in the letter where Jerome had written:

> I shall omit personalities; I shall respond only to matters and accusations. For it does not benefit a cause to answer abuse with abuse and to bite one’s opponents in retaliation.

Rufinus, after declaring in the words quoted above that both statements were false, says that, having set aside all irony and the evasive posturing of hypocrisy, which is detestable to God, he will reply, though in unpolished words and an uncomposed style. He trusts that his readers will grant him pardon for his lack of skill, because:

> We are not accusing others, but striving to clear ourselves of abuse; and therefore we take care that not so much eloquence as truth may shine forth in us.

Above all, he admits that Jerome had spoken truly when he said that he did not return abuse for abuse. Rufinus insists that this statement is sufficiently true, since he complains that insults and abuse, rather than being returned for abuse, are being returned to him for blessings and praise.

He presses this same argument repeatedly, maintaining that he had praised Jerome’s eloquence and his diligence in translating Greek, and asserting that he had never harmed Jerome’s faith. He asks Jerome’s pardon:

> If I say anything too harsh or too unpolished, it is because he provoked an inexperienced man to reply, although he knew that such a man could not, through a wealth of speech and eloquence, so conduct himself that the one whom he wished to injure and wound would appear neither wounded nor injured.

In short, Rufinus, wishing to remove the stains laid upon him and compelled by necessity to reply, urges Jerome to consider not how elegantly and ornamentally he responds, but how truthfully.

**III.**

Since Jerome had uttered these words at the beginning of his letter—“as though heretics could not exist without me”—Rufinus chose to repeat the same words as the principal subject of his argument. Accordingly [Col. 0142D], against all the heresies attributed especially to himself and to Origen, he immediately sets forth the most sacred rule of faith, which he had always preserved. To defend the catholic character of his doctrine concerning the Trinity and the resurrection of the flesh, he explains the custom of the Church of Aquileia, which he had received together with baptism.

In the eleventh article of the Apostles’ Creed, where we profess the resurrection of the flesh, he adds the pronoun “this” in order to refute the error of those who asserted that human beings would rise not in their own flesh but in another body.

Since the matter itself can scarcely be explained more suitably than in Rufinus’s own words, we shall quote part of them here:

> I, as he himself—Jerome—and everyone knows, nearly THIRTY YEARS AGO, having already entered the monastery and been regenerated at Aquileia through the grace of baptism, received the seal of faith through the holy men Chromatius, Jovinus, and Eusebius, bishops of the Church of God of the highest reputation and approval. One of them—Chromatius—was then the presbyter of blessed memory Valerian, the metropolitan of Aquileia; another was archdeacon; the other was deacon. At the same time, he was my father and teacher in the faith.
>
> They therefore handed this down to me, and this is what I hold: that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are of one divinity and one substance, an eternal, inseparable, incorporeal, invisible, incomprehensible Trinity, perfectly known only to itself as it is. For no one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son. And the Holy Spirit is the one who searches even the depths of God, and therefore lacks every kind of bodily visibility. Yet the Son and the Holy Spirit see the Father with that intellectual eye of divinity, just as the Father sees the Son and the Holy Spirit.
>
> There is absolutely no difference in the Trinity except that one is Father, another Son, and another Holy Spirit: a Trinity in the distinction of persons, unity in the unity of substance. The only-begotten Son of God, through whom from the beginning all things that exist, visible and invisible, were made, in the last days assumed flesh and a human soul, became human, and suffered for our salvation.
>
> On the third day, after that same flesh which had been placed in the tomb was raised, he rose from the dead. With that same glorified flesh he ascended into heaven, from which he is expected to come for the judgment of the living and the dead.
>
> In the same way he also gave us the hope of resurrection, so that we may believe that we too will rise in the same order, with the same sequence, and in the same and equal form in which the Lord himself rose from the dead—not clouds or thin airs, as they falsely accuse us, but receiving again these very bodies in which we now live or die.
>
> For how will it be true that we believe in the resurrection of the flesh unless the true and complete nature of the flesh is preserved in it? Without any trickery, therefore, we confess the resurrection of this true and complete flesh of ours, in which we now exist.

Thus Rufinus expounds the creed of the catholic faith, which he testifies that he had inwardly absorbed together with the sacrament of baptism.

Moreover, he presses the doctrines of the creed so strongly that he supports his faith more fully by the public and well-known evidence of the ancient discipline of the Church. The learned Geverhart Elmenhorst, in his notes on Gennadius’s *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, chapter LXXIV, p. 173, explains Gennadius’s statement—“the person to be baptized confesses his faith before the priest,” that is, before the bishop, the ordinary minister of that sacrament—by showing, through many testimonies of the ancients and also through Rufinus’s *Exposition of the Creed*, that the Aquileian forefathers required those about to receive the grace of baptism, adults in their own persons and infants through sponsors, to recite the creed openly and publicly before the assembled faithful [Col. 0143C].

Rufinus is not content merely to have said all this. He further explains the article of the resurrection, which he had set forth clearly and without any ambiguity, revealing, as he says, the singular and chief mystery of his Church of Aquileia. For while all the Churches, after the remission of sins, immediately say “the resurrection of the flesh,” the Aquileians, by adding a pronoun, said “the resurrection of this flesh.”

Here it is preferable to hear Rufinus’s own words:

> The holy Church of Aquileia, with the Spirit of God foreseeing future accusations against us, when it hands down the resurrection of the flesh adds a syllable consisting of one pronoun. In place of what the others say, “THE RESURRECTION OF THE FLESH,” we say, “THE RESURRECTION OF THIS FLESH.” Thus, touching the forehead at the end of the creed with the sign of the seal, as is customary, and confessing with our mouth the resurrection of “THIS flesh”—that is, the flesh which we touch—we block every avenue by which a poisonous tongue might accuse us.

We shall later hear Rufinus carefully recounting this same matter in his exposition of the creed, and also clearly condemning all the heresies attributed to Origen.

He immediately concludes everything quoted above with this emphatic exclamation:

> Is anything fuller than this confession? Is anything more perfect than this exposition? Yet, as I see, all this great caution of the Holy Spirit has benefited us nothing.

He pursues the article concerning the resurrection in one’s own true and tangible, though incorruptible, human flesh—which consists of its own bones and limbs—even more extensively, so as to remove from himself every shadow of ambiguity or suspicion [Col. 0144A], as though he had believed or were believing that the human race would rise in flesh and a body other than human.

After setting forth the matters concerning his faith in the Trinity, the Incarnation, the Resurrection, the second coming, and the future judgment of our Savior, he proceeds to his interpretation of the books of *Periarchon*.

Origen was accused of having taught that all sinners, and even the Devil himself, would be restored, and that souls had been created before bodies, brought down from heaven, and inserted into bodies. Rufinus replies that he is doing nothing on Origen’s behalf and is not writing an *Apology* for him:

> Whether he stands with God or has fallen, he must see to it himself.

Nevertheless, Rufinus is compelled to mention Origen, because while Origen is being accused, Rufinus himself is struck by Jerome—not obliquely now, but openly and with drawn sword.

He declares that he will explain in a few very truthful words why he undertook his translation. Although this may perhaps seem unnecessary to Apronianus, whom he is addressing and who knew the matter well, he continues:

> Nevertheless, it is appropriate for the ignorant to know this also, especially because not only he himself—Jerome—but also his entire school—Pammachius, Oceanus, Marcella, and Eusebius—proclaims against us that although we promised one thing in the prefaces to our translations, we did another in the work itself. Therefore we shall answer not only them but also others whose minds are disturbed either by personal envy or by another’s accusation.

These words show that Rufinus had been informed from Rome that many people had joined forces against him.

He therefore explains that the opportunity for his translation was owed to Macarius, a very well-known man at Rome, and not to himself—as though he had deliberately chosen to translate a work with malicious intent, one which neither Jerome nor any other ancient translator had chosen.

He defends himself against this charge with the following shield:

> Macarius, a man distinguished by faith, learning, nobility, and life, was holding in his hands little works against fate or astrology, and was composing them through useful and necessary labor. But in certain places, because the subject was extremely difficult, he hesitated while discussing the dispensations of divine providence. During sleep, he said that the Lord had shown him something like this: a ship appeared to be approaching from far away across the sea; when it had entered the harbor, it would untie the knots of his hesitation.
>
> When he arose and anxiously reflected on the vision, he said that we had arrived at the right time. He immediately explained to us both his little works and his difficulty, as well as the vision.
>
> Shortly afterward Macarius asked Rufinus what Origen thought about such matters, and requested that Rufinus briefly explain Origen’s views on each of the individual questions.
>
> Rufinus pleaded that the task was difficult to perform and added that the holy martyr Pamphilus had composed, in part, a work of this kind in his *Apology*. Macarius immediately asked that it be translated for him into Latin, without allowing Rufinus’s excuse to delay him. Rufinus had declined the burden because he had no experience with such a work and asserted that, after nearly thirty years of neglect, he had grown sluggish in the Latin language.
>
> Macarius nevertheless persisted, asking that, in whatever language Rufinus could manage, he alone be shown the substance of the matters he desired to know. At length Rufinus, compelled by Macarius’s entreaties and solemn appeals, completed both works and set forth his faith in the prefaces, declaring that he believed as the catholic faith teaches.
>
> After repeating each of the matters about which he wished the readers to be warned in those same prefaces, he maintains that they should be regarded as evidence of his faith. With that faith preserved intact, he says that he reads, discusses, and interprets according to the Apostle’s command: “testing everything, holding fast to what is good, and abstaining from every appearance of evil.”

Nor does he say that he was now making these statements because others had admonished or compelled him, although he had not previously held such views. Before anyone had attacked him, he had already prefaced the work with this profession concerning his faith, so that the first words of his confession might drive far away every suspicion of an opposing doctrine.

In interpreting the books of *Periarchon*, he says that he took care not to introduce statements contrary to Origen himself, rather than merely statements differing from other writers, just as he had promised in the preface. He declares that statements concerning God belong to faith, while statements concerning created things belong to reason.

He says that he introduced nothing of his own; that he did not praise Origen as though he were an apostle or prophet; and that he placed his own faith first, a faith agreeing in all respects with the Church’s confession.

In translating, he followed Jerome’s example and openly indicated his own purpose. While he removed what was bad from the translation, he restored what was good and added nothing of his own.

In one passage there was a dispute concerning the Valentinians and the Anthropomorphites, who said that God was corporeal and described him as possessing human limbs and appearance. There Rufinus affirmed that God’s nature is visible to no one:

> Seeing is one thing; knowing is another. Being seen and seeing belong to bodies; being known and knowing belong to intellectual nature.

After pursuing this point further, he complains about those who were sent from the East to lie in wait for him—here he means Eusebius of Cremona—who, he says, tried to defame him not only through a perverse interpretation but also through the adulteration of words.

Rufinus says that he had not spoken of a comparison between the Father and the Son, but of the very nature of divinity: whether the term “visible” seemed suitable to it. He says that he was responding to heretics who call God visible because they call him corporeal; for vision properly belongs to a body.

Therefore Origen, avoiding the term “vision” as suspicious, preferred to use, in speaking of the nature of divinity—that is, of the relation between the Father and the Son—the language defined by the Lord himself:

> No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son.

In this way he excluded an opportunity for heresies, speaking rather of knowledge within the nature of divinity than of vision, since vision appeared likely to give heretics some opportunity. Knowledge, however, preserves indissoluble truth between the Father and the Son, especially when supported by the authority of the Gospel.

Rufinus frankly admits that he altered words which had perhaps been set down too incautiously in the Greek, because the explanation he had given seemed useful against heresies. He leaves the matter to the judgment of readers whose minds are free from envy, favor, and hatred.

He says that this ought not to be turned into a charge against him, even if it may have been unnecessary, since the equality of invisibility between the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is thereby confirmed.

He goes on to complain that impious words, which he had mentioned above, had been inserted into his notes. To make this clearer, we shall present both readings together here.

### I. The genuine words of Rufinus’s version of Origen

> But if you ask me what I also think concerning the only-begotten himself—if I say that even he is not visible, since the nature of God is naturally invisible—let this not immediately seem either impious or absurd to you; for we shall give the explanation in due course.

### II. The adulterated words of Rufinus’s version of Origen

> But if you ask me what I also think concerning the only-begotten himself—if I say that even he is not visible, since the nature of God is naturally invisible—let this not immediately seem either impious or absurd to you, because, just as the Son does not see the Father, so neither does the Holy Spirit see the Son.

For this deed, which he calls unheard-of in the Church, Rufinus attacks Eusebius and Marcella with the greatest vehemence, although, out of modesty, he does not name either of them explicitly.

If an error of the writer or a slip of expression had been discovered, Rufinus says that he would have wanted the notes corrected and amended, not that false material be inserted so that his brother’s life might be defamed.

When Eusebius recited this false statement to him at Milan, and Rufinus told him that what he was reading was false, Eusebius was asked where he had obtained the copies. Rufinus indicates that Eusebius replied that a certain matron—Marcella—had given them to him.

Concerning her, whoever she may be, Rufinus writes that he says nothing, but leaves her to her own conscience and to the conscience of God. For himself, he says, the testimony of God, Macarius, and Apronianus is sufficient: they had read the autograph notes from the beginning, before they were complete, and even now that adulterated addition is preserved:

> Because just as the Son does not see the Father, so neither does the Holy Spirit see the Son.

After stating that he had not only never written this but that it had been falsified by someone else, Rufinus pronounces anathema on anyone who denies that the Son sees the Father in the same way that the Father sees the Son, or that the Holy Spirit sees the Father and the Son in the same way that the Father sees the Son and the Holy Spirit.

> For he does see, he says, and sees most truly—but as God sees God, and light sees light; not as flesh sees flesh, but as the Holy Spirit sees, not through bodily senses but through the powers of divinity. If anyone denies these things, let him be anathema forever.

From this it is clear that the addition inserted into Rufinus’s translation was added not to accuse the translator but to impose the charge of heresy upon Origen, as though the same statement had been found in the Greek and Rufinus had removed it from the Latin version.

This is indicated by Rufinus’s words:

> I certainly remember that when one of them was accused of having falsified these things, he replied to me that they were found thus in the Greek, but that I had wanted to alter them in Latin.

Rufinus denies that this statement exists in the Greek manuscript. Even if it did exist, he says, he would not be blameworthy for removing it from his translation, since he had explicitly promised in his prefaces that he would omit whatever offended catholic religion, whether it had been inserted into Origen’s writings by heretics or had been uttered by Origen himself through carelessness rather than deliberation.

He continues by showing that he had done nothing without a promise or a reason. In the four books he had translated into Latin, the Trinity is discussed at various points on nearly every page, yet no other passage resembling the one produced had been found. Therefore, if that distinction within the Trinity occurs nowhere throughout the entire body of the books, it cannot be said that Rufinus confirmed heresy in a single chapter when he had refuted it in a thousand passages.

He adds that, if the statement had truly been found in his notes, Rufinus himself—then present at Rome and sharing communion in prayer with Eusebius—ought to have been confronted and warned of the error, so that the unpublished writings might be corrected:

> If he had found this in my writings, and had truly taken some offense from the reading itself, then, since he had me present at Rome—as you yourself know—he would certainly have sought me out immediately and brought the writings themselves to me. For up to that very time he had been accustomed to see me, greet me, and share communion with me in prayer.
>
> Without doubt he would have discussed with me the matters that seemed offensive to him. He would have asked how I had expressed them and how they stood in the Greek. Certainly he would have thought it sufficient for his glory if he had appeared to have had something in my statements or writings corrected by his own efforts.
>
> Or, if the fury of his spirit had compelled him not so much to correct an error as to bring it into public view, he would certainly never have chosen to attack an absent man whom he could have refuted more effectively in person.
>
> But because consciousness of his falsehood frightened him, he did not bring to me the writings he wished to accuse, although they were mine. Instead, he carried them around from house to house, among matrons, through monasteries, and among individual brothers, so that he could disturb people by nothing more than what they heard.
>
> He did this precisely when he was about to depart from the city, so that he would not be caught and forced to give an account of his deed.

Rufinus attacks Eusebius for having, at the command of his master Jerome [Col. 0146D], stirred up disturbances against him throughout Italy, troubled the Churches, and polluted the ears of priests, or bishops, abusing Rufinus’s modesty as though it were a sign of guilt.

From the disciple he turns to the master, whom he accuses of preparing a new interpretation of the books of *Periarchon*, inserting into it everything that Rufinus himself had omitted as improbable:

> So that the Romans, he says, may learn through him Origen’s faults and remain ignorant of his virtues.

For Jerome had once written to Vigilantius:

> Through me all Latins know Origen’s faults and remain ignorant of his virtues.

Rufinus resents being brought under suspicion of heresy and complains that “dogs” are sent against him without ceasing, pursuing him through cities, villages, and even along the road as he travels, with the barking of their accusations.

At last he turns his speech directly to Jerome, who had long before praised Origen in ten places as a teacher of the Churches, when Origen was not yet a heretic.

He does not cease to harass Jerome more sharply on this point, always calling him “the master,” and exercising an unrestrained criticism of Jerome’s commentaries on the letters of Saint Paul, which had been published long before.

But since Sixtus of Siena, in the *Bibliotheca*, book VI, annotations 287 and following, has carefully set out each of Rufinus’s accusations together with Jerome’s responses, it will suffice to refer the reader to that work.

## IV.

After, as he says, replying in the first book of his Apology to the dogmatic objections unjustly brought against him, in the second he heaps various charges upon Jerome. First, he is distressed that it is being circulated that certain persons allied with Origen had conspired to commit perjury, and that this secret of mystical tradition was concealed in the sixth book of the *Stromata*. He denies, and emphatically denies, that he knows what the books of the *Stromata* written by Origen are, or that he has ever read them. He declares himself wholly free from every kind of perjury, and pronounces anathema upon those who think otherwise, in these words:

> Whoever teaches that one may swear falsely for any reason whatsoever, I say that he is alien to the faith of Christ and to the catholic unity of the Church.

From this he turns to accusing Jerome, extracting various statements from his writings which he does not hesitate to say were uttered wrongly or carelessly—namely, that in his books *On Virginity* Jerome had torn apart the ranks and orders of Christians; that he had devoted himself to Cicero, Porphyry, and the Jewish Barabbas, and had not abandoned their reading after being carried in a dream before the tribunal of the Judge and affirming under oath that he would henceforth abandon it. Nevertheless, he professes to suspend all judgment on these matters:

> Because the matter concerns the soul of a human being, the charge of perjury, and the sacrilege of denying Christ, condemnation cannot be reached hastily.

Hence he declares that absent persons, neither accused nor interrogated, ought not easily to be condemned. In this connection, arguing his own case, he concludes:

> Although all his little books testify to this, and my assertion on the subject may seem superfluous, nevertheless some special testimony must be used, lest what we say appear insufficient to those who perhaps have not read his writings.

He severely reproaches his adversary, as though he had preferred to use Porphyry as an introduction to logic rather than the one who introduces us to the Father. He charges him [Col. 0147C] with having arranged, through very many monks of Olivet, for a great sum to have numerous dialogues of Cicero copied in Rufinus’s own cells; with having come from Bethlehem to Jerusalem and given for copying a codex containing Plato’s dialogue translated into Latin by Marcus Tullius; and with having taught, while carrying out grammatical instruction in the Bethlehem monastery, Virgil and comic, lyric, and historical authors to the boys entrusted to him for the purpose of learning the fear of God.

The words by which he had been stung, as though Jerome had taught himself, Rufinus calls scarcely deserving a reply. He says that Jerome had purchased his teachers from the synagogue—and this he repeatedly reproaches him for—while Rufinus himself had deserved a greater and more genuine reproach, not because he had learned without a teacher, but because, after spending a long time among many distinguished teachers, his own abilities had proved unworthy either of their instruction or of their teaching.

Rufinus adds that Jerome himself had not remained in Alexandria, where Didymus was, for even thirty full days, and yet boasted that he had had Didymus as his teacher. Rufinus, however, had remained there for six years on God’s business, and again, after an interval, for several other days, hearing Didymus and others no less eminent than Didymus—men whom Jerome did not even know by sight, such as Serapion, Menites, Paul the disciple of the martyr Peter, and also Macarius, Isidore, and Pambus, all friends of God, who had taught him what they themselves had learned from God.

He says that he recounts these things not without shame—not because the teachers had lacked ability, but rather because his own ability had fallen short of his teachers’.

After again mocking Jerome for having devoted excessive attention to the Jewish Barabbas and to the writings of Porphyry, he displays not only Origen, whom Jerome had once lavishly praised, but also many of Origen’s Homilies translated into Latin. He says that he is not threatening to disclose what Jerome had done against him: Jerome had despised Ambrose as a plagiarist of Origen and Didymus, although without naming him, while exalting Origen to the skies with praises as an apostle, a dogmatist, and a teacher of the Churches. Rufinus says that he possesses a letter of Jerome in which Ambrose was attacked; nevertheless, he does not wish to publish it before the proper time, because it contains certain more confidential matters.

Since Ambrose had been praised for his learning and holiness, Rufinus calls himself, in comparison with him, a flea. Jerome therefore ought not to complain if Rufinus himself was attacked after so great a man—although Jerome had previously praised Rufinus in his letters and had associated him in his *Chronicle* with Florentius and Bonosus because of the nobility of his life.

Rufinus says that in the same *Chronicle* Jerome erased Melania’s name after seeing that her actions displeased a woman of stricter discipline. He declares that he had never followed either Jerome or any other person in error, but that he followed the Catholic Church in the virtue of Christ; nor, he says, could any of his writings be produced in which he could be proved to have erred even in his youth.

Jerome, he says, had removed much while interpreting Origen’s writings, and Rufinus had done the same:

> No writings of mine exist in which some error of mine needs correction;

whereas, he insists, Jerome has many such writings.

Jerome had previously condemned the method of translating word for word, but afterward, in translating Origen’s books *Periarchon*, had followed precisely this same rule, albeit in less useful language. Jerome, he says, had translated word for word in his new version, and accused those who designated Origen as a heretic, although he himself was acting against those who defended Origen as a Catholic; yet Jerome did not blame Rufinus for making Origen not a heretic but a Catholic.

It is not enough, he says, merely to assert that the *Apology for Origen* should be denied to the martyr Pamphilus:

> I do not believe it, because it belongs to a martyr.

He continues:

> If we wish to say this about all the little books of writers, what proof will there be in each case if I say, “It is not true,” because the books of the *Stromata* which you say are Origen’s are not his? On what basis are they proved to be his? Not from similarity of style, because anyone who wishes to fabricate a false work can imitate it.

To reject Pamphilus’s writings, he says, passages deserving condemnation ought to have been produced:

> Then each of the readers would have seen what there was in them that was absurd, what consistent, what unjust, and what certainly contrary to the Apostolic rules.

But even if it were granted—which he by no means grants—that the *Apology for Origen* was not written by the martyr Pamphilus but by some other member of the Church, the author had not used his own words in such a way that the force of the book depended upon the author’s merit. Rather, he had set forth examples from Origen’s writings and shown what he thought about each of them, not in his own defensive words, but in the words of the very man who was being accused. Thus Origen was defended not by the authority of an advocate but by his own statements; consequently, the question of the author was superfluous where the defense was such that it required no author.

### 5.

Jerome had said:

> Who among the prudent, or who among the saints, wished to undertake translating into Latin what you dared to translate? I myself, although often asked by many, did not do so.

To the first point Rufinus replies that it does not necessarily follow that one who is holy and prudent and Latin possesses sufficient knowledge of the Greek language, nor is the holiness of one who lacks knowledge of a foreign language thereby diminished. Nor, again, does it necessarily follow that someone who possesses knowledge of Greek also possesses the desire to translate; and even if he does possess that desire, one should not immediately ask why the person who translated a few works did not translate more, or why he translated these rather than those.

To the second point he replies that it was unnecessary for Jerome to translate books whose entire substance he had already set forth in other books, although Jerome was then criticizing Rufinus for having previously published the same material under Jerome’s name.

He attacks Jerome’s new Latin translation of the Bible, derived from the Hebrew source, since no one before him had undertaken such a work, out of reverence for the old Italian translation derived from the Seventy-two Interpreters, which the Apostles had handed down to the churches of Christ. He charges Jerome with cutting out the story of Susanna as though it were apocryphal, together with the hymn of the three youths, and with setting aside the single and harmonious voice of the Seventy-two men translating in their separate cells—a voice produced by the interpretation of the Holy Spirit—in favor of his own translation, made with the assistance of the Jewish Barabbas.

Regarding the Italian version, the following words of Rufinus seem worthy of notice:

> Peter presided over the Roman Church for twenty-four years. There can be no doubt that, just as he handed down everything else pertaining to instruction, he also handed down to the Church its books, which even then, while he was presiding and teaching, were being read aloud.

From this he takes occasion to inveigh at length and bitterly against Jerome for having himself produced another translation. He says that Jerome resorts in vain to the authority of Origen, whom Jerome himself condemns; besides, Origen had translated nothing, whereas Jerome had translated all the Scriptures from the Hebrew.

Rufinus speaks modestly about Pammachius, to whose letter written against Rufinus Jerome had replied. He says:

> I do not yet say what sort of letter it was, or what its character was. Nevertheless, since it bears the name of the noble man Pammachius, what would have been absurd if you had replied to him in such a manner? Brother, one must not rashly judge another person’s work. You yourself know what you did when I sent my little books against Jovinianus to Rome. When certain people understood them differently from the way I remembered dictating them, and when they were already being read by many and almost everyone was taking offense—including, as it seemed, you yourself—did you not remove the copies first from the marketplace and then from public circulation, and send them back not to someone else but to me, at the same time explaining the reason, since many appeared to be scandalized, and describing how I had written the *Apology* anew and brought what had been understood otherwise back, as far as I could, to a more correct understanding?
>
> It is therefore just that we do to others what we wish to have done to us. Just as you sent my books back to me to be corrected by me, so send his books back to him; and point out what appears blameworthy, so that he too, if he has erred in anything, may correct himself.
>
> Moreover, we have already exercised our talent in many matters, and many little works have already been produced through our labor. He—Rufinus—undertook this work almost for the first time, and perhaps under compulsion; it is therefore not surprising if he faltered at the beginning. One must not seize an occasion for disparaging Christians, but seek the benefit of correction.

Thus Rufinus would have wished Jerome to have written in reply to Pammachius’s letter.

In the summary of his entire Apology, which he immediately completes, Rufinus turns to Apronianus and again speaks of Pammachius:

> Let that holy man Pammachius also learn through you, dearest son Apronianus—the man whose letter my friend brought forward in this attack or accusation of his—that in the help of Christ one ought to favor not partisan zeal but innocence, and that in a matter of truth one ought to act more religiously than zealously. For the Lord has commanded us not to judge according to appearance, but to judge a just judgment. Just as Christ is present in each of the least of his people—in the one who hungers, thirsts, and is naked, and he himself is the one who is fed and clothed—so in those who are unjustly judged he himself is the one who is judged unjustly; and on behalf of those who are hated without cause he himself will say: “You hated me without cause.”
