He presses the point somewhat more sharply in these words:

> How does Pammachius think that this case and this action of his—inciting Jerome against Rufinus—will be judged at Christ’s tribunal, when his conscience reminds him that he removed from the hands of readers Jerome’s books written against Jovinianus, which were already being read publicly and criticized, prevented and censured those who blamed them, and sent the books back to the author himself, indicating what might be subject to criticism, so that Jerome might either correct it or take care of the matter in whatever way he could?
>
> My own writings, however, were not books but incomplete and uncorrected sheets, stolen and carried off through the fraud and deceit of some scoundrel. Although he had me present there, he did not offer them to me or complain to me; nor did he deign to rebuke or accuse me, whether through some friend or even through an enemy, but sent them to the East and incited the tongue of a man who could not restrain it.
>
> What would he have done against religion if he had approached me while I was present? Were we considered so unworthy of his conversation that we did not even deserve to be rebuked by him?

A little later he asks pardon if he had prosecuted his case more harshly than he ought:

> Although necessity compelled us to attempt a reply to the man who had attacked us most bitterly, nevertheless for this very reason we ask pardon if we have perhaps pursued the matter too harshly, because God is witness to our conscience that we withheld much more than we said. But we could not remain completely silent, since our conscience accused us, when some people were treating our silence as virtually a loss of their faith.

From these final words we infer that, just as the Romans had incited Jerome to reply to Rufinus, so the Romans also incited Rufinus to reply to Jerome, with partisans on both sides spreading the flames of discord in both directions—presumably with a good purpose, since both men were outstandingly Catholic, feared causes of scandal, and rejected errors.

But as long as we remain here, it is impossible for us to be entirely free from every human emotion on all sides. Nor is it surprising if men otherwise most holy and learned suffer something human, by God’s permission, whose judgments are inscrutable.

Rufinus had almost completed the whole Apology when a certain monk—Rufinus calls him “brother”—traveled from Rome to Aquileia and added a spur to the running horse by approving the Apology after Rufinus had reread it to him. The monk pointed out only one passage of defense that had been omitted, a passage which he had heard being criticized by Rufinus’s detractors at Rome.

In the first preface to the books of *Periarchon*, Rufinus had said of Jerome:

> In the works which he had translated from Origen, there were certain stumbling blocks in the Greek, but in translating them he cleansed them in such a way that the Latin reader finds nothing in them that differs from our faith.

The same monk—perhaps Chrysogonus of Aquileia, a follower of Rufinus, to whom Jerome wrote Letter IX, elsewhere numbered XLIV, and whom he attacks near the end of Book I—added that Rufinus’s rivals were spreading the claim that, if Rufinus had approved Jerome’s version as free from every stumbling block, then Rufinus’s own version must be condemned, since he had not rendered it free from every stumbling block.

Rufinus nevertheless replies that he had done what Jerome had previously done: he had judged Jerome’s writings without malice or slander, examining not what might be exposed to criticism but what the translator had intended. Jerome, he says, had criticized in Rufinus’s writings something that Jerome himself had previously written.

At the end Rufinus says that, if a synod of bishops should decree that Origen’s books must be condemned, they must first be condemned in Greek, so that they may then be condemned in Latin translation; finally, Rufinus would embrace the judgment of the Catholic Church against those same books of Origen.

It has seemed worthwhile to review these matters in summary from the two books of Rufinus’s *Apology*.

## VI.

At the same time that Rufinus sent the two preceding little books to his Roman friends, he directed another, shorter *Apology for His Faith* to Pope Anastasius, in order to dispel the ill will stirred up against him before Anastasius. Seven chapters may be distinguished in it. The first five concern doctrines attributed to Origen as author and to Rufinus as translator:

1. The Trinity.
2. The Resurrection.
3. The Last Judgment.
4. The eternal condemnation of the Devil.
5. The origin of souls.

In the remaining two chapters he discusses his Latin translation and his faith. It is preferable, however, to examine the chapters of the Apology individually.

### 1.

Rufinus says that he had learned how, in the controversies concerning the faith or certain other matters that had been raised before Anastasius, mention had also been made of him. Yet the Pope himself, as one instructed from infancy in the rules of ecclesiastical tradition, had not lent his ears to those making accusations against an absent man whom he knew well both in faith and in the love of God.

Nevertheless, Rufinus says that, after being restored to his spiritual parents and blood relatives after thirty years, he could not abandon them so quickly as to undertake anew the hardships of journeying to Rome. He consequently thought it proper to write these letters to Anastasius in defense of his reputation:

> Not, he says, to wipe away a stain of suspicion from your holy mind—which, like a sanctuary of God, admits nothing unjust—but to offer you, against those perhaps barking at me out of rivalry, a kind of staff of my confession with which they might be driven away.

Thus Rufinus indicates in the first chapter that he was well known to the Pope and that Anastasius had not summoned him to Rome to plead his case. Indeed, he clearly suggests that Anastasius had not lent easy ears to his enemies.

### 2.

Rufinus says that his faith had already been tested during the persecution of the heretics, when he was living in the Holy Alexandrian Church, in the prisons and exiles inflicted on account of the faith, and that he was prepared to prove it again to anyone.

Regarding the Trinity, he says that he believes it to be of one nature, one divinity, and one and the same power and substance; that there is absolutely no difference between the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, except that the one is the Father, the other the Son, and the other the Holy Spirit: a Trinity in subsistent persons, unity in nature and substance.

He also confesses that the Son of God was born in the last days from the Virgin and the Holy Spirit, and assumed flesh and a human soul, in which he suffered, was buried, and rose from the dead. He rose in that same flesh which had been laid in the tomb; with that flesh and soul together he ascended into heaven after the resurrection, from which he is expected to come as judge of the living and the dead.

Nothing more precise according to the rules of the Catholic faith could have been stated.

### 3.

He professes that he confesses the resurrection of our flesh, which will occur wholly and perfectly in this very flesh of ours in which we now live. He does not say, as some slanderously claim, that another flesh will rise in place of this one, but that this very flesh will rise, with none of its members amputated and no part of the body cut away; it will lack nothing whatsoever of its entire nature except corruption alone.

He says that the Apostle promises this and that this is what had been handed down to him concerning the resurrection by those from whom he had received holy baptism in the Church of Aquileia—namely, Saint Valerian the metropolitan, Chromatius, and Eusebius. He adds:

> I think that this is precisely what the Apostolic See also has been accustomed to hand down and teach.

### 4.

He professes that he believes there will be a judgment in which each person will receive what belongs to his body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil. He also believes that the Devil will be consigned to eternal fire; and if anyone denies this, may he receive a share with him in eternal fire, so that he may experience what he denied.

### 5.

From this he proceeds to the question of the soul. Since nothing had yet been definitively established concerning its origin, he says that he awaits the Pope’s judgment:

> I hear, he says, that questions have also been raised concerning the soul. You must determine whether a complaint concerning this matter should be accepted or rejected.

Among very many ecclesiastical writers, he says, he had read differing views on this question, which he reduces to three positions:

1. Some affirm that the soul is diffused through the transmission of human seed.
2. Others say that it is created by God each day and infused into bodies formed in the womb.
3. Others, finally, say that souls were made long ago, when God created all things from nothing, and are distributed daily into bodies.

He says that Origen and certain other Greeks held the last position. Concerning himself he adds:

> But although I have read each of these views, with God as my witness I say that up to the present I hold nothing certain or defined concerning this question. I leave it to God to know what is true, and whether he may deem it worthy to reveal it to anyone. I do not deny that I have read each of these views, and I confess that I remain ignorant of them, except for what the Church plainly teaches: that God is the creator of souls and bodies.

From this it is clear that Rufinus adhered to none of the three positions concerning the origin of the soul set out above, although he had reported the pre-existence of souls from Origen’s opinion, certainly not from his own. Cardinal Norisius shows, with a rich apparatus of learning, in the fourth chapter of his *Augustinian Vindications*, section 3, that not only Rufinus but also other men approved for learning and holiness remained in this uncertainty for many centuries.

Peter Halloix, in Book IV, Question IV of his *Defense of Origen*, p. 281, says that it is one thing to form an opinion about doubtful and uncertain matters; another to put them forward as true and certain; and still another to introduce various views for the purpose of discussing a question. It is also one thing to propose some position not approved or defined by the Church and to adhere to it.

Accordingly, this author maintains that Origen established no dogma concerning souls in the manner of one asserting a doctrine, but brought forward various conjectures in the manner of one conducting a discussion.

Saint Pamphilus the martyr, in his *Apology*, testifies that Origen held one doctrine with certainty:

> That all souls are of one substance, immortal, rational, and endowed with free choice and will; that they must also be judged according to what they have done in this life; and that they too were made by God, who founded and created all things.

The same martyr takes it as certain that Origen discussed souls existing before bodies not by asserting the doctrine but by investigating it, as a matter not contained in the Apostolic traditions and not yet defined by the Church.

It cannot be said that Rufinus believed, according to Origen, that souls were older than the structure of the body, since he professes that he holds neither this nor any other view concerning the origin of the soul, but only what the Church plainly teaches: that God is the creator of souls and bodies.

### 6.

Rufinus says that he had been informed that arguments were being brought against him because, when asked by the brethren, he had translated certain writings of Origen from Greek into Latin. Nevertheless, he thinks that everyone understands that he is being blamed solely out of envy. If something is displeasing in the author, it should not be twisted against the translator; he had merely given Latin words to Greek ideas.

Whether praise or blame belongs to those ideas, neither should be attributed to Rufinus. Indeed, he adds that he had also inserted in the preface the warning that, from time to time, passages might be found that appeared to have been inserted by others rather than spoken by Origen, because elsewhere Origen had expressed Catholic and contrary views on the same matters.

### 7.

He asks the Supreme Pontiff not to allow factions and calumnies to stir up ill will against him on this account:

> This, he says, is not permitted in the Church of God. For where will simplicity and innocence be safe, if they are not safe here?

He adds that he is neither Origen’s defender, nor his advocate, nor his first translator. Others had carried out the work before him; he had undertaken it last, after being asked by the brethren. If he is ordered not to do it, the order must be obeyed henceforth. If those who did it previously are blamed, the blame ought to begin with the first.

Finally, he concludes everything in these words:

> For, apart from this faith which I have set forth above—that is, the faith held by the Roman Church, the Alexandrian Church, and our own Aquileian Church, and preached at Jerusalem—I have never had, do not have, and will not have any other faith concerning this man, Origen. If anyone believes otherwise, whoever he may be, let him be anathema.
>
> Those who, solely out of envy and spite, generate stumbling blocks, dissensions, and scandals for their brothers will give an account on the day of judgment.

He mentions the faith of the Alexandrian Church after that of Rome because he had lived there for six years, and because throughout the ages the Alexandrian Church, after the Roman Church, had possessed such great authority that the Church of the West had made its communion especially important and had preserved its customs. Caspar Barthius demonstrates this from the acts of the Council of Aquileia, held in A.D. 381, in his notes on Zacharias of Mytilene, p. 294.

Jerome writes in Letter LVIII, elsewhere numbered LXVIII (now LXIII), to Theophilus:

> He praises with Apostolic lips the Roman faith, of which the Alexandrian Church boasts that it is a participant.

Pope Gelasius, in a decretal letter which we once published in an uncorrupted form, free from interpolations, states the following concerning the same Church:

> The second see is at Alexandria, consecrated in the name of blessed Peter by Mark, his disciple and Evangelist.

Aeneas of Paris plainly alluded to this at the beginning of his book *Against the Errors of the Greeks*, in D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, volume VII:

> This see is second after the first, the Roman see, as the provisions of the canons determine.

These canonical provisions are none other than those found in the letter of Pope Gelasius.

After the Alexandrian Church, Rufinus mentions the Aquileian Church, where he was then living and where he had formerly received the faith of Christ. Finally he mentions the Jerusalem Church, where he had spent a long time and had been raised to the rank of presbyter.

Rufinus wrote both Apologies in A.D. 400. For Jerome, in Book I of his own Apology, written in the same year, p. 377, says:

> I was compelled two years ago to reply in a brief book to your praises of me directed against myself.

He wrote this book to Pammachius in A.D. 398, as we have shown above. It will become clear that Jerome subsequently calls these two Apologies three books and three volumes.

# CHAPTER V

I. A synopsis of both of Rufinus’s Apologies is sent to Jerome.  
II. He immediately replies to both.  
III. The Origenian Apology, which Jerome denies to Pamphilus, is vindicated for that martyr.  
IV. What Pamphilus wrote.  
V. The conjectures advanced to deny the Apology to Pamphilus are examined.  
VI. Jerome’s reply to Rufinus’s accusations.  
VII. Jerome’s replies to Rufinus’s other accusations.  
VIII. Jerome’s refutation of Rufinus’s Apology to Pope Anastasius.

## [I.]

### I.

Rufinus shared both his Apologies with his Roman friends. In accordance with the author’s wish, they did not disseminate them publicly, but, as Jerome says, thrust them into the ears of their associates in corners for private hearing only.

At the beginning of Book I of his Apology, Jerome says that this was done both to strike the hearts of simple people and to deprive him of the opportunity to reply on his own behalf. Rufinus, on the contrary, says that he sent his books only to those who had been wounded by Jerome’s words, and not to a larger audience. This is gathered from Book III of the *Apology against Rufinus*.

The matter did not go unpunished. For when Pammachius and Marcella had been unable to obtain a complete copy of the Apologies, they at least arranged for their principal sections, carefully extracted here and there, to be brought hurriedly to Jerome—perhaps by his brother Paulinianus, returning from Dalmatia to Bethlehem.

To incite him more sharply to reply, there was also added a report of the sort of things that Rufinus’s friends were circulating about Jerome. Accordingly, as soon as the holy man learned from his friends’ letters and from Paulinianus’s own mouth that he had been maliciously misrepresented, he immediately composed an Apology for himself divided into two books and sent it to Pammachius and Marcella at Rome; Rufinus had attacked both of them, apart from Jerome himself.

In the title of the work as it has been published, the name has until now been read not as Marcella but as Marcellinus. Tillemont, in volume XII, p. 247, conjectured that this was the tribune who presided over the great Carthaginian Conference in A.D. 411, according to Baronius, A.D. 410, § 58.

But Martianaeus eventually restored *Marcella* in place of *Marcellinus* from manuscript codices, in which he found this title:

> Here begins the defense of Jerome, the distinguished teacher, against the three books of Rufinus, an envious slanderer, sent to Pammachius and Marcella.

The substance of Jerome’s Apology may be reduced to the following.

### II.

From the letters of Pammachius, Marcella, and many others, Jerome says that he learned that he was being accused in the school of Tyrannus—or by Rufinus’s friends, the followers of Tyrannus—because he had translated the books of *Periarchon*, although Jerome himself was accusing Rufinus because Rufinus had not hesitated to undertake the same translation.

Jerome calls those men shameless who accuse a physician for exposing poisons. Their purpose, he says, is to protect Rufinus—whom he openly portrays as an apothecary of the Origenists—not because of his innocence, but through participation in guilt, as though the number of sinners diminished the offense and the accusation concerned persons rather than facts.

Jerome is distressed that Rufinus’s Apologies, written against him, were being thrust upon everyone’s ears without being published:

> Thus, he says, they strike the hearts of simple people and deprive me of the opportunity to reply.

He calls it a new kind of malice to accuse what one fears to expose and to write what one conceals.

He says that he rejected Rufinus’s disguised praises because, under the name of a friend, he detected the ambush of an enemy. Rufinus was now turning into a charge against him what he had previously praised Jerome for once and again in the preface to the books of *Periarchon*, although, after their reconciliation, Rufinus ought also to have avoided even slight suspicions, lest something he had done accidentally should be thought to have been done deliberately.

If Rufinus was decorating his work with authority, Jerome says, he could have praised Hilary, Ambrose, and Victorinus—pillars of the Church and translators of Origen—whom he nevertheless passed over, praising only Jerome, who calls himself a flea.

Concerning his earlier letter written to Pammachius and Oceanus, Jerome says:

> I possess your letters, in which you write that I have been accused and urge me to reply to my accuser, lest, if I remain silent, I appear to acknowledge the charge.

From this we gather that not only Pammachius but also Marcella urged Jerome to write against Rufinus, in addition to Oceanus. Although Oceanus’s name is expressly mentioned in Pammachius’s letter to Jerome, Jerome never mentions him in his replies, nor does Rufinus touch him even lightly. The reason for this escapes us.

Jerome adds that he had already replied and that, although wounded, he had preserved the rights of friendship by defending himself without accusing the accuser. What one friend at Rome had alleged, he said, had been proclaimed by many enemies throughout the world, so that he might appear to be replying not to a man but to charges. He had never expressly named Rufinus, but had spoken as though he were referring to several persons.

He piles up further arguments to show that Rufinus’s praises had rightly aroused his suspicion and to restore himself, before the silent judgment of the reader, to a state of innocence, lest he appear to have been the first to cause injury.

He repeatedly rejects the Apologies that he had learned Rufinus had written against him. At one point, merely for purposes of mockery, he calls the three books “works composed with Attic elegance”; shortly afterward he threatens to reply to them in these words:

> But against those books which chatter in corners and bite me through secret accusation, when they have been published and have come forth from darkness into light, and when they have been able to reach us either through the zeal of the brethren or the rashness of rivals, I shall attempt to reply. For those books are not greatly to be feared whose author was afraid to publish them and decided that they should be read only by his confederates.

He immediately adds:

> Not content with having injured me, as though against one who is always without a tongue and always silent, he composed three books and fabricated Marcion’s antitheses from my little works.

These *antitheses* were a work in which Marcion dared, as Tertullian says, to set the Old Testament against the New, or to establish discord between the Gospel and the Law. Tertullian undertook the refutation of this work throughout Book IV *Against Marcion*.

The three books written by Rufinus, which Jerome refutes in the first two books of this Apology, are both of Rufinus’s Apologies. The first, divided into two books, attacks Jerome. The second, which is *For the Faith* and was addressed to Pope Anastasius, Jerome calls likewise a work written against him, although he had not yet seen it, because it contains taunts against him.

Rufinus’s followers were angry with Jerome because Jerome too had translated the books of *Periarchon*, although he condemned them as harmful and opposed to the faith of the Church. Addressing Pammachius, the old man of Bethlehem replies:

> Your letters, brother Pammachius, and those of your companions compelled me, when you said that the books had been fraudulently translated by another person—Rufinus—with certain passages interpolated and others either added or changed. And, lest I should place even little trust in your letters, you sent copies of that same translation together with a laudatory preface about me.

After reading these copies and comparing them with the Greek, Jerome says that he immediately noticed that Rufinus the translator had altered for the better what Origen had said impiously about the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The remaining doctrines, however—concerning the fall of the angels, the fall of souls, the illusions of the resurrection, Epicurus’s world or intermundia [read: *intermundia*], and the resurrection of all things to an equal state—had either been translated by Rufinus as fully as they stood in the Greek or had been strengthened by additions from Didymus’s commentaries. Thus someone who had read a Catholic doctrine concerning the Trinity would not have been on guard against heresy in the other matters.

After comparing Rufinus’s translation with his own, Jerome says that the first contains praise of the author, while the second contains blame. He explains in his letter to Pammachius why he had previously praised Origen in certain matters: he had then explained the reason for his own translation, namely, so that an impious man should not be handed over to the Churches as a pious one.

Jerome admits that he had translated seventy books of Origen into Latin, as Rufinus had said, but nevertheless says that Rome had not been disturbed by any of his works:

> I, he says, translated so many works over so many years and was never a cause of scandal; you, Rufinus, in undertaking your first and only work, previously unknown, became famous through rashness.

Before his return to Italy, Rufinus had never sent anything into circulation. After his return, however, he translated the Rule of Saint Basil into Latin before producing the books of *Periarchon*. But since that work had been written for the private use of the abbot of Pineto and had not yet become generally known, Jerome considered the translation of the books of *Periarchon* to be the first and only work produced by Rufinus.

### III.

Jerome repeatedly attacks the Apology of Pamphilus, translated into Latin by Rufinus, with all his strength, in order to strip Origen of the protection afforded by so great a name. I shall summarize the arguments greatly elaborated by Noris in his *Dissertation on the Fifth Synod*, chapter XIII, which deprive the martyr of authorship of the Apology, adding the responses on behalf of Pamphilus and Rufinus—especially those published by Count Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, or Phoenix, in *Questions* VII of his Apology, at page 132 of the Basel edition of his works printed by Henricpetrus in 1601. Because of this same Apology, Cardinal Robert Bellarmine also numbers Pico among ecclesiastical writers, as a man outstanding in intellect and learning for his age. [Col. 0155B]

These responses are certainly of the greatest importance to the Christian religion today, because they disarm the impious and abominable Arians of our time, and particularly Christoph Sand, the most shameless of mortals, by the protection of so great a martyr. They are incensed because the divinity of our Savior and his *homoousion*—his consubstantiality—are most explicitly asserted in the *Apology of the Ante-Nicene Father*. The vigorous defender of the Nicene faith, George Bull, likewise observed this most excellently; in section II, chapter IX, §20, page 207, and again in chapter XIII, §3, page 263, he devoted all his efforts to vindicating that work for Pamphilus.

Let us therefore hear Jerome, book I of the Apology, page 357:

> “Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, once the standard-bearer of the Arian faction—though Cellerius vindicates him from this charge—wrote six books on behalf of Origen, an extensive and elaborate work. By many testimonies he proved that Origen, according to himself, was Catholic, but according to us, Arian. You translate the first of these books under the name of the martyr. And we are surprised that you want me, a man of little worth, to be a praiser of Origen, when you have brought a slander against the martyr. After changing a few testimonies concerning the Son of God and the Holy Spirit, which you knew would displease the Romans, you left everything else intact to the end, doing in the Apology under the name of Pamphilus exactly what you did in translating Origen’s *On First Principles*. If this is Pamphilus’ book, which of the six books will be Eusebius’ first? In the very volume which you pretend is Pamphilus’, mention is made of the books that follow. In the second book and the remaining books as well, Eusebius says what he had already said in the first book and that he ought not to repeat the same things. If the whole work belongs to Pamphilus, why do you not translate the remaining books? If it belongs to someone else, why do you change the name?”

Jerome has similar statements in book II of the Apology, chapter IV, page 407:

> “The most learned Eusebius”—I said “most learned,” not “Catholic,” lest, as is your custom, you weave a slander against me on this point as well—“does nothing throughout six volumes except show that Origen belonged to his faith, that is, to Arian perfidy; and he supplies many examples and proves this consistently.”

Thus Jerome. Whether this work, consisting of six volumes or books, still exists anywhere, we have no knowledge at all. In the synopsis presented by Photius, codex CXVIII, and in the Latin translation of book I made by Rufinus, no trace whatsoever of Arian perfidy is detected. If Arian poison had truly been concealed in the same Apology, which Photius, the foremost of critics, carefully examined, there was certainly no reason why he—otherwise hardly indulgent toward Arius and Origen—should have passed over the matter in silence.

In fact, however, the Apology was written not by Eusebius alone, as Jerome believed, but by Eusebius and Pamphilus together, through their combined efforts, for the greater part of the work. This is expressly testified by the man who knew the matter best of all, Eusebius himself, in book VI of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter XXXIII:

> “Whatever must necessarily be known about him [Origen] may be learned from the Apology which I and Pamphilus, the holy martyr of our age, composed on his behalf. We worked upon it jointly with a common purpose and effort because of certain malicious accusers.” [Col. 0156A]

Rufinus, at the end of book VI, chapter XXIV, of Eusebius’ history, compressed this statement as follows:

> “These matters, however—Origen’s deeds—may be learned from the Apology written by the holy martyr Pamphilus for him together with me.”

Photius explains Eusebius’ passage. In the ninth century he read the entire Apology. In the codex already mentioned, CXVIII, he says:

> “The codex of Pamphilus the martyr and Eusebius on behalf of Origen was read. It consists of six volumes, five of which were composed by Pamphilus while he was living in prison, with Eusebius also present. The sixth, after he had been deprived of life by the sword and had gone to God, whom he desired, was finally completed by Eusebius.”

Earlier, in codex CXVII, Photius had reviewed an anonymous writer who composed another Apology on behalf of Origen, following Pamphilus the martyr and Eusebius especially closely:

> “Above all,” he says, “he relies upon the martyr Pamphilus and Eusebius.”

That writer was certainly not an Arian, since, according to Photius, he presents nothing erroneous concerning the Holy Trinity. Indeed, he asserts that Origen himself had made no error whatever concerning the doctrine of the Trinity. In this section he follows exactly the same reasoning and method as the Apology published in Latin by Rufinus under Pamphilus’ name. Therefore this very translation by Rufinus faithfully reproduces the codex of Pamphilus which the Anonymous writer, Catholic in his treatment of the Trinity, read in Greek.

Nor do I think that anyone could indulge in such conjectures as to say that Rufinus removed Arianism not merely from his own copy but from all the Greek copies that existed, so that he might more easily attribute Eusebius’ book to the martyr Pamphilus. Who could ever say or believe this?

These facts clearly show that the Apology of Origen was rightly attributed to Pamphilus, if Pamphilus worked on its composition just as Eusebius did. Add that Socrates, in book IV, chapter XXII, attributes the whole work to Pamphilus alone. His words are these:

> “Pamphilus the martyr also mentions him [Gregory Thaumaturgus] in the books which he composed on behalf of Origen.”

Yet in book III, chapter V, Socrates had stated that Pamphilus and Eusebius alike had written an Apology for Origen in distinguished books, each contributing jointly. The work was therefore attributed sometimes to both, sometimes to one or the other.

Certainly the *Synodicon* of the sixth century, published by Christian Lupus, whose author attacks Origen everywhere, cites Eusebius in an apologetic work on behalf of Origen. But a letter, number CXCVIII, in Baluze’s *New Collection*, volume I, page 895, testifies that it was headed with the names of the martyr and Eusebius himself of Caesarea.

We can now see where Jerome’s argument against the Apology translated by Rufinus leads. He says: “If the first book is not Eusebius’, but Pamphilus’, which of the six books will be Eusebius’ first?” It will be Pamphilus’ book. But another argument vindicates the first book for Pamphilus alone. Hear it; but first we must listen to Pico speaking on its behalf.

“Eusebius,” says Pico, “tries to prove that Origen was an Arian. Yet in Pamphilus’ Apology nothing else is done except to prove that Origen was not an Arian, and that whatever occurs in his books which confirms Arius’ heresy was not written by him but inserted by Arians. Therefore this book must be entirely different from the one that defends the opposite case. Moreover, this first book of the Apology, divided into six books, was written by Pamphilus alone, according to Jerome in the *Catalogue*, which he had published ten years earlier, and therefore at a time when he was still untroubled by any hostility toward Rufinus. For in chapter LXXV he says that Pamphilus wrote, ‘before Eusebius of Caesarea wrote,’ an Apology on behalf of Origen—that is, the book which is the first book of the Apology later divided into six books.”

By these words Jerome anticipated and explained what he later wrote in chapter LXXXV, where the following is read among the works of Eusebius:

> “Six books of an Apology for Origen.”

Of this Apology, Pamphilus and Eusebius later wrote the following four books together in prison, by their combined efforts. Finally, after Pamphilus had been crowned with the glory of martyrdom, Eusebius added the entire sixth book from his own work. Pope Gelasius I recognized only this one book as Eusebius’ in the *Decree* sincerely published by us. In chapter III he says of Eusebius:

> “He composed one book in praise and defense of Origen the Schismatic.”

Thus Eusebius did not produce six books from his own material, but only one—the sixth. In the Seventh Ecumenical Synod, session V, in Labbe, volume VII, page 367, Antipater, bishop of Bostra, is said to have refuted an Apology of Eusebius, not of Pamphilus, because, as I think, he refuted this one sixth book. For the passages quoted from the first *Discourse of Antipater’s Contradictions* refute the pre-existence of souls, about which Pamphilus is entirely silent.

Antipater flourished in A.D. 460, according to Noris in his *Dissertation on the Fifth Synod*, chapter XIII. He may have been the reason why Gelasius later, in A.D. 494, noted this single book in his *Decree*. It is now clear why the first book is attributed to Pamphilus alone and not also to Eusebius. Gennadius likewise attributes it to Pamphilus, as I shall show later.

In addition, the very ancient author of the *Predestinarian*, who clearly appeared before the birth of Eutyches’ heresy—that is, before A.D. 447—and whom some attribute to Primasius and others to Arnobius the Younger (on this matter see the preface to volume I of Sirmond’s works, §7), attributes the Apology itself to Pamphilus alone, in these words in chapter XXII:

> “Whoever has read Origen down to the present day, if he knows how to distinguish his writings by a prudent reading, discovers passages stained by heretics. Pamphilus declared in his Apology that this is so.”

Again, in chapter XLIII, he says:

> “This man [Pamphilus] published an Apology and excluded everything which ignorant Catholics falsely allege, showing that the things found to be reprehensible in Origen’s little works do not belong to Origen.”

This author wrote after the disputes on this subject between Jerome and Rufinus had been published, yet he preferred to adopt Rufinus’ judgment concerning Pamphilus. John Trithemius, in his *Catalogue*, chapter XLVII, and Baronius as well, under A.D. 256, §40, do not depart at all from this opinion.

Since the greater part of the entire Apology—that is, the four books lying between the first and sixth—had Eusebius and Pamphilus jointly and indiscriminately as authors, while the sixth was wholly Eusebius’, it is not surprising if Eusebius was sometimes called, or even believed to be, the author of the whole work by Jerome and others.

After the author of the *Synodicon* and Photius, Nicephorus Callistus, book X, chapter XIV, likewise attributed all six books jointly to Pamphilus and Eusebius, because they occurred together in one codex rather than separately. Nor should the first have been separated from the remaining five, if in all of them the two authors jointly treated one subject. Consequently, the whole work could rightly and properly be called, in general terms, the Apology of Pamphilus and Eusebius for Origen.

Lucas Holstenius entirely approved the weight of all these arguments in his manuscript notes on Bellarmine’s *Catalogue*, under the entry on Origen:

> “Indeed, the first book is unquestionably Pamphilus’ alone. The remaining books belong jointly to Pamphilus and Eusebius, except the last, which belongs to Eusebius alone.”

### IV.

Let us examine another conjecture of Jerome. The first book translated by Rufinus under Pamphilus’ name mentions the five books that follow. Therefore, all of them proceeded from the single mind of Eusebius; for Pamphilus, who alone authored the first, would not have mentioned the remaining books as though they were his own. Why this escaped so great a man is unknown.

For in the Apology of Pamphilus that still survives, no mention whatsoever is made of the subsequent books, nor was there any reason to make such a mention, since in his one book, complete however it may have been, the holy martyr Pamphilus fully answered the arguments raised in his own time against Origen. He was, as Jerome says in the *Catalogue*, chapter LXXV, so devoted to the man called Adamantius that he copied the greater part of Origen’s volumes with his own hand.

Noris, in his *Dissertation on the Fifth Synod*, chapter XIII, says that Jerome was speaking of book I not as it had been corrupted by Rufinus, but as it existed in the Caesarean autograph. I fear, however, that this is not true. Jerome’s words in book I of the Apology are these:

> “In the very volume which you pretend is Pamphilus’, mention is made of the books that follow.”

Yet the volume said to have been pretended by Rufinus as Pamphilus’ is the very one that Rufinus published. He was believed to have made this pretense through his Latin version, although he did not pretend to something which he actually asserted.

What Jerome of Stridon adds is this:

> “In the second book and the remaining books as well, Eusebius says what he had already said in the first book and that he ought not to repeat the same things.”

But this in no way overturns Pamphilus’ case. In the second and later books mention could certainly—and indeed had to—be made of the first, since the first had long before been written by Pamphilus alone, the next four subsequently by Eusebius and Pamphilus together, and the sixth finally by Eusebius alone.

The reason Jerome asked Rufinus why he had translated only the first book and not the remaining five was that Rufinus wished to produce, by itself, an intact and complete testimony on behalf of Origen from Pamphilus alone, not from Eusebius and Pamphilus jointly. Hence there was no need to translate the remaining books, which had been written by both, not by Pamphilus alone.

What is more, Rufinus himself testifies in his prologue to Macarius that he had undertaken to translate only one book of the Apology:

> “You requested that the book which is said to have been written by him [Pamphilus] in Greek on behalf of Origen be translated into Latin for you.”

He mentions not books but a book. The words “is said to have written” show us that the matter was universally reported and well known by common tradition, and therefore was certainly not fabricated for the first time then.

### V.

I have thought it useful to present these arguments so that it may be understood that the martyr Pamphilus has not yet been deprived of possession of the Apology. Let us now summon the remaining conjectures for examination.

Eusebius wrote three books on the life of Pamphilus. In the last of these he relates:

> “He himself wrote nothing at all that was his own work, except letters which he perhaps sent to his friends; so far had he humbled himself through humility.”

From the now-lost *Life of Pamphilus*, Jerome quotes these words in book I of the Apology, page 359, and adds the following from his own hand:

> “Eusebius, the defender of Origen and praiser of Pamphilus, says that Pamphilus wrote nothing at all and composed no work of his own discourse. He says this after Pamphilus had been crowned with martyrdom, so that you may have no refuge in claiming that Pamphilus wrote this after Eusebius’ books had been published.”

Whether the distinction between “his own work” (*proprii operis*) and “his own discourse” (*proprii sermonis*) reveals some difference in the Greek wording of Eusebius—for example, “his own doctrine”—we cannot determine, since Eusebius’ work itself is lacking.

Certainly, however, Eusebius does not say that Pamphilus composed no work, but that he composed no work of his own. And Pamphilus’ Apology contains nothing that is his own work or doctrine, since it opposes the true doctrine of Origen, expressed in Origen’s own words, to the false doctrine charged against him. The comparison of the two makes it plainly evident that Origen’s writings had been corrupted by heretics, since the work deals only with the question whether Origen’s books had been corrupted or not.

But this is not the composition of an original work. Moreover, anyone who testifies that Pamphilus wrote letters necessarily also testifies that he wrote something in his own discourse. For this reason Eusebius added “except letters,” because these were written in Pamphilus’ own discourse; perhaps he added this precisely in order to exempt this work as well.

For this reason Jerome counted the authors of letters among ecclesiastical writers, just as he did, apart from the Apostles, Ignatius, Polycarp, and others. Yet Pamphilus’ Apology consists, except for its beginning, of intact passages from Origen. The beginning is nothing other than a letter to the Confessors. Therefore, what belongs to Pamphilus in this work may more properly be called a letter than a book.

Another little work of the martyr Pamphilus, though not a work of his own discourse or doctrine, is an exposition of chapters of the Acts of the Apostles, most recently published by our friend, the distinguished Dom Bernard de Montfaucon, in the *Bibliotheca Coisliniana*, page 78. Earlier, another friend of ours, Laurentius Zacagnius, had published it under the counterfeit name of Euthalius, bishop of Sulca, in the *Monuments of the Greek Church*, page 428.

A comparison of this exposition with the Apology entirely confirms that Pamphilus was the author of both, although we possess only the Latin version of the Apology. In any event, Jerome did not declare that the style of the Apology conformed to that of Eusebius; indeed, the reader will not deny that there is some difference between them.

These same little works of Pamphilus may perhaps in some sense be included under the title “Indexes of Origen’s books,” which Eusebius, in book VI of his *History*, chapter XXXII, testifies were written by Pamphilus. For in fact they seem to contain indexes, or excerpts, of Origen’s doctrine and of his treatment of Sacred Scripture.

### VI.

Jerome himself had previously been cited on behalf of Pamphilus. Ten years earlier, in his *Catalogue*, he had mentioned the Apology as a genuine work of Pamphilus, written in Greek and not yet translated into Latin by Rufinus. At that time Jerome had detected in the short book no trace of fraud, no falsehood, and no heresy; otherwise he certainly would not have judged it worthy of a Catholic author and martyr.

Nor can it be doubted that he had read it, since in the prologue to his *Catalogue* he excuses himself if he has omitted authors whose writings he did not read.

Pressed by this argument, Jerome responds in book II of the Apology, page 419:

> “I also listed this book as published by Pamphilus, thinking it to be as it had been circulated by you and your disciples. Therefore you ought not to attribute your fraud to my error.”

Elsewhere, however, he says that the fraud was committed by Rufinus not in the Greek text but in the Latin text, and he makes this accusation in general terms. Rufinus nevertheless refuted all these charges in a letter, now lost, against which Jerome wrote book III of his Apology.

I think, however, that if there was any fraud, it lay in the title, not in the body of the work. But if Jerome later discovered a codex headed by the scribes only with the name of Eusebius, then Eusebius himself stands against him, since Eusebius attributed the work not only to himself but also to Pamphilus. Nor did Photius detect in the Greek codices of this Apology that survived in his day any of the errors which Jerome generally claims to have found and complains were removed by Rufinus in the Latin translation.

The same holy Father, before the end of letter XLI—also numbered LXV—to Pammachius and Oceanus, had tried to deprive Pamphilus of the book by many other conjectures, varying among themselves. It is not tedious to review them briefly.

1. He says that the work was compiled under Pamphilus’ name by Origen’s friends and followers, so that they might rescue Adamantius from disgrace by the testimony of a martyr. Jerome later thought little of this conjecture, since he devised others different from it.

2. He says that comparison of the style could not establish whether the work belonged to Pamphilus, because no other work of his could be found. I have already spoken above of other writings of Pamphilus. And if a genuine work cannot be recognized by comparison of style, that does not make it doubtful. Nor does Jerome say that the style of the Apology conforms to that of Eusebius.

3. He says that the beginning of Eusebius’ six-book Apology is contained in the Apology attributed to Pamphilus. We have shown, however, that this beginning belongs not to Eusebius but to Pamphilus.

4. Since Eusebius and Pamphilus were so closely united that one received his surname from the other, they could not have disagreed with each other in such a way that Eusebius approved Origen as an Arian while Pamphilus approved him as a Catholic. It is most certain that they were imprisoned together for the same cause, the Catholic faith. But even if Eusebius later departed in another direction, it does not follow that Pamphilus did not write what he wrote. Indeed, from this very fact it is evident that Pamphilus’ book is different from Eusebius’ books.

5. He argues from this that the Apology was not a work of Pamphilus but a little work of Didymus. Jerome later abandoned this opinion as well.

6. Or at least, he says, it was the work of someone else who assembled it from the beginning of Eusebius’ six books, the remaining books having subsequently been joined together. The truth of the matter remains firm even if the beginning of the six books belongs to Pamphilus and the rest to Eusebius.

7. He concedes that the work is Pamphilus’, but says that its author was not yet a martyr—though Pamphilus later erased by his martyrdom the error he had committed in defending Origen.

This argument, however, is all the weaker because, according to Photius’ codex CXVIII, Pamphilus wrote the work in the same prison in which he had been confined in A.D. 307 after undergoing the force of torture, as Eusebius testifies in *On the Martyrs of Palestine*, chapter VII. According to the custom of that age, therefore, he was then truly a martyr. Two years later he underwent his final martyrdom.

Let us present Jerome’s actual words, although they are more expansive, so that the weight of his conjectures may more easily become apparent from the words themselves:

> “As for those who produce Pamphilus as a praiser of Origen, I thank them in my own name for thinking me worthy to be slandered together with a martyr. For if you say that Origen’s books were corrupted by his enemies so that he might be disgraced, why may I not say that a volume was composed by his friends and followers under Pamphilus’ name, in order to rescue him from disgrace by the testimony of a martyr? You correct in Origen’s books what he did not write, and you are surprised if someone publishes a book which he did not publish? You can be convicted from a published work. But he [Pamphilus], who published nothing else, is more easily exposed to slander. Produce any work of Pamphilus: nowhere will you find one. How, then, am I to know that it belongs to Pamphilus? Surely style and saliva will be able to teach me. I shall never believe that a learned man devoted the first fruits of his intellect to questions and disgrace. The very name ‘Apology’ indicates an accusation; for one defends only what is under accusation.”

Thus far Jerome. At this point Tillemont forces me to interrupt his words. In the *Commentaries on Ecclesiastical History*, volume V, page 750, Tillemont says that he is surprised that Jerome, although in books I and II of his Apology he had called Pamphilus’ little work the first of Eusebius’ six books, later called it once and again the beginning of Eusebius’ sixth book. If it had been the first, why is it now called the beginning of the sixth?

Halloix, in book IV of *Origen Defended*, page 226, thinks that he detects Jerome contradicting himself here. Tillemont, however, says that this slipped out while Jerome was writing hurriedly. Noris, in his *Dissertation on the Fifth Synod*, chapter XII, discovered that the error was not Jerome’s but the copyist’s: the copyist had rendered the abbreviated words “VI books of Eusebius” in this way. Thus there is no contradiction in Jerome. His words, which immediately follow those quoted above, are these:

> “This book, which is called Pamphilus’, contains the beginning of Eusebius’ sixth book”—read “of the six books”—“on the defense of Origen, extending to nearly a thousand lines; and in the remaining portion the writer of the same work produces testimonies by which he endeavors to prove that Origen was Catholic. Eusebius and Pamphilus were so harmonious with each other that you would think them men of one soul, and one received his name from the other—for Eusebius wished to be called ‘Pamphilius.’ How, then, could they have disagreed with each other, so that Eusebius in his entire work proved Origen to hold Arian doctrine, while Pamphilus defended the Council of Nicaea, which came later? This shows that the little work belongs either to Didymus or to someone else who, after cutting off the beginning of the sixth book”—read “of the six books”—“joined together the remaining members.”

“But let us grant, for the sake of argument, that it belongs to Pamphilus, though not yet to the martyr. For he wrote it before he suffered martyrdom. But how, you will ask, was he worthy of martyrdom? He was worthy so that by martyrdom he might erase his error, so that he might purge one fault by the shedding of his blood. How many martyrs throughout the world were subject to various sins before they were slain?”

I have thought it useful to quote these words from Jerome at greater length because, when compared with his other testimonies, they clearly show that he himself placed little confidence in his conjectures concerning Pamphilus. He later tried to weaken the authority of the book by other arguments, as though its author were no longer Didymus but Eusebius.

In this matter Tillemont says that Rufinus and Jerome were both correct: Eusebius and Pamphilus jointly wrote the Apology for Origen through their combined efforts, as Eusebius, Socrates, and Photius testify. Nevertheless, the distinction expressed above by us must be maintained.

Jerome argues that the book is not Pamphilus’ because it would seem unjust for a martyr to defend a man whose writings were later condemned by Pope Anastasius and Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria. Jerome’s words are these in book I, page 359:

> “What will become of the letters of Bishop Theophilus? What of Pope Anastasius, who throughout the world persecuted the heretic, when your book, published under Pamphilus’ name, fights against their letters and the testimony of a martyr is set against an episcopal name?”

John Pico responds on Rufinus’ behalf that their purpose was to eradicate heresies and false doctrines, whoever might have held them, because they knew this belonged to the establishment of the faith and religion. Whether those doctrines were Origen’s, as many believed, or were not his, Pico thinks the pontiffs would have cared little. Indeed, they would have been pleased if it could truly have been proved that those heresies had not been taught by Origen. Such a defense would have been made for the faith, not against the faith; against heretics, not on behalf of the heretics who, relying upon the testimony of so great a man, defended their error under his name.

Therefore Pamphilus’ book did not fight against the letters of Anastasius and Theophilus. The heresies condemned by them were not excused in it; rather, their advocates were deprived of so great a patron—just as he is taken away from Sand and the other most wicked Arians of our time, Arians revived by Socinus.

Nor was the martyr Pamphilus the only person who tried to clear Origen from suspicion before Origen was condemned. Bernard de Montfaucon notes in the preface to his works, page 19, §6, that the great Athanasius also did this. Monsieur de la Motte, in his *History of Tertullian and Origen*, published at Lyons in A.D. 1691, book IV, chapter VI, page 416, likewise does not deny that some of Origen’s writings were corrupted by heretics.

Yet Athanasius should not for this reason be said to have fought against Anastasius and Theophilus. “If those letters [of Anastasius and Theophilus] persecute Origen,” says Pico, page 134, “it is certain that they persecute him only as the arch-heretic of the opinions believed to be his.”

Jerome promises in book II against Rufinus that he will answer Pamphilus’ Apology, but he did not fulfill this promise, although he lived another twenty years.

In any event, if Pamphilus always defended the Catholic faith of the Word, and if Rufinus, expressing Pamphilus’ Apology word for word, changed only certain passages concerning the Son of God and the Holy Spirit, as Jerome alleges—on the grounds that they had been written before such questions were defined in the Church in their proper formulas—it could have happened that Pamphilus was not everywhere sufficiently precise in investigating the clearest statements of Origen.

Those, however, who do not think that pious falsehoods can be counted as sins may also believe that Rufinus went so far as to substitute passages favoring consubstantiality for those which Pamphilus had actually written.

Blessed Beatus Rhenanus, in his preface to the *Sentences of Sixtus* published by Rufinus, expressed this very suspicion—or rather, this slander—in the following words:

> “In former times, when it seemed useful, the ancients were not altogether averse to pious falsehoods of this sort.”

I pass over another trivial statement of Rhenanus, where he says that it was not Rufinus but Eusebius who first dedicated the book on behalf of Origen to the martyr Pamphilus.

But since these matters cannot be known with certainty from any other source than the Greek codex of the Apology, which we do not possess, Rufinus ought not to be charged with bad faith merely on the basis of Jerome’s suspicions. Jerome himself left this written in book I of the Apology, chapter III:

> “Declared hostility gives rise to suspicion of falsehood.”

Moreover, Rufinus argues in the book of his Apology that absolutely no heresy occurs in the book of Saint Pamphilus as he rendered it into Latin, and that Jerome merely accuses him in general terms. If Jerome would make the charge specifically, Rufinus says, he will show everyone the injustice of the accusation.

Photius, certainly, who was especially hostile to anything that might smell of Arian contamination, found nothing deserving censure when he read this Apology in Greek. It may therefore rightly be affirmed that nothing favorable to the Arians occurs in it.

Bull makes the same assertion in his *Defense of the Nicene Faith*, section II, chapter II, §20. Nevertheless, he thinks that Rufinus removed certain passages which seemed to contain harsh and suspect statements, although he added no passage which Pamphilus had not written.

But if Photius, a man of the keenest judgment and Catholic in his treatment of the doctrine of the Trinity, did not see these things in the Greek codices he himself read, who could believe that Rufinus was able to see them and cut them out on his own authority?

### VI.

Let us now return to Jerome’s Apology. In book I he accuses Rufinus of complaining that Jerome considered statements in his letter against the Origenists to have been directed against him. After Rufinus had attacked him, alleging that he had employed a Jew named Barabbas as his teacher, Jerome cleverly shows that the man was called not Barabbas but Baraninas, and testifies that he had heard the Jew say that Rufinus had read Origen not for the truth of the faith but for the value of his learning.

When Theophilus of Alexandria’s Paschal Letter reached Rufinus at Aquileia—a letter in which Origen’s errors were extensively condemned—Rufinus was so horrified that he stopped his ears, while himself condemning errors previously unknown to him. Let us hear Jerome making this accusation:

> “It is said that, after recently reading the letters of Pope Theophilus, in which he sets forth Origen’s errors, he stopped his ears, openly condemned the author of so great an evil together with everyone else, and said that until that time he had not known that Origen had written such wicked things.”

Theophilus published the Paschal Letter in A.D. 400 for the year A.D. 401. It was the first in chronological time, although in Jerome’s works it is second in order; Jerome translated it into Latin together with the others. Noris later carefully restored each letter to its proper year in his *Pelagian History* and in his *Dissertation on Saint Siricius.

Jerome says that Rufinus could not have been ignorant of what he was translating. He is annoyed that Rufinus accused his commentaries on Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians. He admits, however, that he learned this from the report of friends, not from Rufinus’ writings:

> “The fame of his accusations, not his writings, came to me, and it is foolish, according to the Apostle, to strike the air with one’s fists.”

Yet he does not therefore silently pass over his own defense. He does not deny that in his commentaries on Ephesians he presented various opinions of Origen, Didymus, and Apollinarius—men whose doctrines contradict one another—for his readers to approve or reject according to their judgment, while nevertheless preserving the truth of his own faith.

He attacks Rufinus for boasting of his knowledge of Greek and forgetting his native language:

> “I pass over the Greeks, whose knowledge you boast, and while you pursue foreign things you have almost forgotten your own language, lest I should seem, according to the old proverb, to teach a pig to Minerva, or to carry wood into the forest.”

And below:

> “I am surprised that you, the Aristarchus of our time, did not know these childish matters, although, occupied with meanings and acting like a little deer in constructing a slander against me, you have despised the precepts of grammarians and orators, thinking little of restoring hyperbaton after its winding turns, avoiding harshness among consonants, and fleeing a gaping diction.”

And further on, unless he should perhaps swear that he had not learned letters—which, even without an oath, we readily believe of him.

Jerome does not want Rufinus to be regarded, like the Apostle Paul, as unskilled in speech but learned in knowledge. Instead, he presents him for ridicule as follows:

> “You who mutter in Latin and move with a tortoise’s gait rather than walk—either you ought to write in Greek, so that among men ignorant of the Greek language you may appear to know what is foreign; or, if you attempt Latin, you should first listen to a grammarian, withdraw your hand from the schoolmaster’s rod, and among the little boys learn the art of speaking from an *Athēnogérōn* (that is, an old schoolmaster).”

He then turns to the *Stromata* of Origen, intending to show that the Origenists are bound together among themselves by orgies of falsehood. From book VI of the *Stromata* he cites a passage in which Origen appears to teach that it is sometimes permissible to lie.

He defends at length his own interpretation of Psalm II and six passages in his Commentary on Ephesians which Paulinian had reported as having been criticized by Rufinus. Concerning this Commentary he says:

> “It is nearly eighteen years since I dictated these books.”

Jerome wrote these words in A.D. 401. Therefore he was commenting on Ephesians around A.D. 384, not in A.D. 387, as Tillemont thought in his *Life of Jerome*, article XLVIII, page 114.

In his response to the third passage of the Letter to the Ephesians criticized by Rufinus, we have another chronological indication in book I, page 377, where Jerome says:

> “On his behalf [Origen] I was compelled, two years ago, to answer your praises of him in a short book”—that is, in A.D. 399.

VII. Jerome, whom Rufinus had accused of being abusive and sacrilegious, first clears himself of the former charge by showing that he had spoken against no one except the envious. He calls such a person Luscius Lavinius, or Asinius Pollio of the Cornelian family. These names designate Rufinus and another monk, an admirer of Rufinus who traced his own lineage to the Cornelian family. To the latter charge, sacrilege and perjury concerning a dream, he replies as follows:

“I said that henceforth I would no longer read secular literature. This is a pledge concerning the future, not an erasure of the memory of the past.”

He pursues the matter further, complaining that his dream is being brought up against him, although it is written:

“Neither does adultery in a dream lead to Tartarus, nor does a martyr’s crown raise one to heaven.”

He also writes of Rufinus:

“Obviously this is the Sallustian Calpurnius who, through the great orator, had raised a not very great question for us, and to whom we gave satisfaction in a brief little book.”

Below, in Letter LXXXIII, otherwise LXXXIV, to Magnus, he says:

“But a question is being proposed to me through you by another person who, perhaps because of his love for the histories of Sallust, is Calpurnius by name, Lanarius by surname.”

Here he alluded to a scoundrel of the same name who appears as Livius Salinator in Plutarch’s *Sertorius*. Near the end of the work Jerome jabs at Rufinus as a severe and solemn man:

“For my part, so that I may make you, an exceedingly severe man, laugh, and so that you may sometimes imitate Crassus, whom Lucilius says laughed once in his life, I remember that as a boy I used to run about through the little cells of the servants, etc.”

He again taunts Rufinus as though he boasted that he had learned Greek letters by himself:

“You are amazed that I have not forgotten Latin letters, although you learned Greek without a teacher.”

[Col. 0163C] Soon afterward he mockingly ridicules Rufinus’s style and manner of writing:

“Come now, you who accuse me of possessing little learning and who think yourself something of a man of letters and a rabbi: answer why you dared to write certain things and to translate the most eloquent Gregory with an equal splendor of expression. Whence came to you such abundance of words, such brilliance of thought, such variety in translation, you who in adolescence scarcely tasted rhetoric with your first lips? Either I am mistaken, or you secretly read Cicero; and that is why you are so eloquent and bring against me the charge of reading him, so that you alone among ecclesiastical writers may boast in the flood of eloquence, although you seem rather to follow the philosophers—the thorns of Cleanthes and the convolutions of Chrysippus—not through an art which you do not know, but through the greatness of your native talent. And since the Stoics claim Logic for themselves, while you despise the ravings of that science, in this respect you are an Epicurean: you do not ask how you should speak, but what you should say. For what does it matter to you if someone else does not understand what you wish to say, since you speak not to everyone but to your own people?”

He concludes this criticism of Rufinus’s style as follows:

“Finally, when rereading your writings, although at times I do not understand what you are saying and think that I am reading Heraclitus, nevertheless I do not grieve or regret my slowness; for in reading I suffer what you suffer in writing.”

Finally, he brings Book I to a close by attacking Chrysogonus, a friend of Rufinus, who had criticized him for saying that baptism removes bigamy and for refusing to call a man a bigamist if he had married one wife before baptism and another after baptism. Jerome nevertheless replied to him in Letter LXXXII, otherwise LXXXIII, written to Oceanus, defending the ordination of Carterius, bishop in Spain, who had taken one wife before baptism and another afterward.

VIII. After Jerome had cleared himself in the preceding book of the charges Rufinus had brought against him, he soon undertakes to refute Rufinus’s *Apology to Pope Anastasius*, in which he seemed to himself to detect a calumny being contrived against him. He accomplishes this by repeatedly citing portions of the *Apology*. He finds Rufinus lacking in modesty where he praises his own faith and charity, and he cannot endure that Rufinus sent the supreme pontiff a staff of letters against his detractors.

He ridicules Rufinus’s excuse that, because of his age and because he had embraced his relatives after thirty years, he had not hastened to Rome in order to defend himself:

“That is ridiculous,” he says, “that a man who has neither father nor mother boasts that after thirty years he has returned to his parents, and that the old man longs for those whom, as a young man, he left alive—but who are now dead. Unless perhaps he calls his kinsmen and relations ‘parents,’ in ordinary military and popular speech; and because he does not wish to abandon them, lest he be thought inhuman or harsh, he therefore lives at Aquileia after abandoning his homeland, Concordia.

“His thoroughly tested faith is in danger at Rome. Yet here he is, lying on his back and exhausted, unable after thirty years to come by carriage along the very gentle road through the Flaminian region. Thus he pleads the weariness of a long journey, as though he had been running continuously for thirty years, or, sitting at Aquileia for two years, had been worn out by the exertion of his earlier journey.”

He does not believe that Rufinus endured imprisonment and exile at Alexandria for the Faith without judicial sentences, unless Rufinus produces the records of his confession. We shall answer this elsewhere.

He troubles Rufinus’s confession concerning the Trinity [Col. 0164B] and the resurrection with various questions. He also attacks his opinion concerning judgment and the Devil, as though Rufinus attributed human sins not to free choice but solely to the Devil. Yet he later seems to soften this criticism with these words:

“Still, these statements can be excused as those of a simple man; and although they do not escape the notice of the learned, among the uneducated they can preserve the appearance of innocence.”

Rufinus had written:

“We also say that there will be a judgment, IN WHICH judgment each person will receive what is proper to his body.”

Jerome attacks this as follows:

“He had said that there would be a judgment, but the cautious man feared to say merely IN WHICH and inserted IN WHICH JUDGMENT, lest, if he did not repeat JUDGMENT a second time, we should forget what came before and take an ass for the judgment.”

Rufinus had also said:

“Those who accuse their brothers will likewise share with them in the inheritance of eternal fire.”

Jerome likewise attacks this:

“Who,” he says, “has ever heard of sharing in fires, of enjoying punishments?”

He acknowledges that this is a translation from Greek, but says:

“I think the Greek has wished to interpret himself; and instead of what is said among them, κληρονομήσουσιν (*klēronomēsousin*, ‘they will inherit’), which can be expressed among us in one word as HEREDITABUNT, he has used the more ornate phrase HEREDITATE POTIENTUR, ‘they will possess as an inheritance.’”

His entire discourse bristles with such trivialities and improper expressions. There is certainly no doubt that Jerome, accustomed to handling Latin writers, surpassed Rufinus in abundance and elegance of language; Rufinus, after his own thirty-year sojourn among the Greeks, readily blamed that sojourn whenever he happened to offend by writing less correctly in Latin.

Yet Jerome repeatedly touches him on this point. He even calls him Theophrastus ironically and criticizes him for using “complaint” in place of “question.” Finally, he says:

“He speaks so offensively and confusedly that I labor more in criticizing him than he did in writing.”

Soon afterward he says that he takes Rufinus for Arcesilaus and Carneades, who declare everything uncertain, when Rufinus sets forth three opinions concerning the condition and origin of souls, none of which the Church had yet approved over the others. Below he again mocks his manner of expression:

“Wonderful eloquence, varied with Attic bloom! I am amazed that he dared to send these verbal monstrosities to Rome. You would think his tongue shackled and bound with inextricable knots, scarcely breaking out into human sound.”

Elsewhere he says that he flees from the disgust produced by Rufinus’s ragged and disjointed argument.

Nor is this the end. Jerome becomes angry with Rufinus because, in translating the books *Periarchon* (*On First Principles*), he added some things, removed others, and altered still others. Hence Jerome maintains that good and evil must be attributed not so much to the author as to the translator.

After enumerating at length the many evils—and especially the heresies—of Origen, Jerome observes that the following conclusion arises from the reckoning: the things Rufinus cut away from Origen do not belong to others; Rufinus interpreted Origen’s evil because he thought it good, and therefore both Origen’s good and his evil must be attributed to Rufinus, whose writings Rufinus had approved in his preface.

The charge against Rufinus is not that he translated Origen, but that, having translated his heretical material, he confirmed it by the praise of his preface and placed a book in its defense before the reader as though it were the work of a martyr. He then adds:

“Or certainly, if you translated him in order to convict him of heresy, change nothing from the Greek, and bear witness to this very fact in your preface. This is precisely what Pope Anastasius most prudently expressed in his letter against you to Bishop John: he acquitted me, who did this, and accused you, who refused to do it.”

And lest Rufinus perhaps deny this also, Jerome appended Anastasius’s example, so that, if Rufinus did not wish to hear a brother admonishing him, he might hear a bishop condemning him.

Although Rufinus had removed much from Pamphilus’s *Apology*, which he maintains was the work of Eusebius, and had attempted to alter it in a favorable sense concerning the Son and the Holy Spirit, Jerome nevertheless says that many stumbling-blocks remain in it.

He does not deny that Didymus, certainly Catholic in his teaching concerning the Trinity, composed commentaries on the books *Periarchon*; but he asserts that, apart from the Son and the Holy Spirit, Didymus descended into Origen’s doctrines.

Rufinus had said that the writings of other ancient authors had likewise been corrupted by heretics. Jerome does not accept this, thinking that those authors may either have erred simply, or written with another meaning, or that their writings may gradually have been corrupted by inexperienced scribes [Col. 0165B]. Alternatively, before Arius arose in Alexandria like a noonday demon, they may have spoken certain things innocently and with insufficient caution—things unable to escape the slander of perverse men.

Rufinus had cited a passage from the letter to the Alexandrians in which Origen asks whether his books had been corrupted by wicked men and denies that he had ever said that the Devil was to be saved. Jerome and Rufinus agree concerning the authenticity of the letter.

But in this passage the holy man criticizes two things in Rufinus’s translation: first, that he fraudulently omitted certain material; second, that he inverted the meaning. Halloix, however, in Book IV, p. 290, holds that Rufinus was guilty of neither fault and that what he omitted did not concern the corruption of the books. This can be seen at a glance in Jerome, where he cites the omitted material, and the comparison of both passages will make the matter clear.

As for the meaning, although Origen’s Greek is not available to us, the matter itself can easily be grasped from Jerome’s and Rufinus’s translations. Let us therefore compare them. Jerome wished this to be done in these words:

“Compare Origen’s words, which I translated above word for word, with those which were not translated by him [Rufinus], but mistranslated.”

### I. Fragment of Origen’s letter from Rufinus’s translation

*[lacuna]* [Col. 0165D–0166C]

“Some of those who gladly make a practice of accusing their neighbors impute to us and to our teaching the charge of blasphemy, although they have never heard it from us. Let them see to that themselves, since they are unwilling to observe the commandment which says, ‘For the abusive shall not possess the kingdom of God.’ They say that I assert that the father of the wickedness and destruction of those who are cast out of the kingdom of God—that is, the Devil—is to be saved. Yet no one who is even slightly deranged in mind and plainly insane could say such a thing.

“But it seems no wonder to me if my teaching is adulterated by my enemies and corrupted by such an adulteration as that by which the Epistle of the Apostle Paul was corrupted.”

### II. Fragment of Origen’s letter from Jerome’s translation

“What need is there to speak of the words of the prophets, by which they very often threaten and rebuke shepherds, elders, priests, and rulers of the people? Without our help, you can draw these things from the holy Scriptures and clearly perceive that perhaps this is the time of which it is said: ‘Do not believe friends, nor put your hope in rulers’; and that the prophecy is now being fulfilled: ‘The leaders of my people did not know me; they are foolish children and are not wise. They are wise in doing evil, but they do not know how to do good.’ We ought to pity such people rather than hate them and pray for them rather than curse them.

“For we have been raised up to bless, not to curse. Hence, when Michael disputed against the Devil concerning the body of Moses, he did not dare to pronounce even against so great an evil a judgment of blasphemy, but said: ‘The Lord rebuke you.’ We read something similar in Zechariah: ‘The Lord rebuke you, Devil; the Lord rebuke you, who has chosen Jerusalem.’

“Therefore we too wish those who do not humbly accept rebuke from their neighbors to be rebuked by the Lord. But when Michael says, ‘The Lord rebuke you, Devil,’ and Zechariah likewise, whether God rebukes the Devil or does not rebuke him, let God himself see to it; and if he rebukes him, let him himself know how he rebukes him …”

And after much more—these are Jerome’s words—which it would be lengthy to write out, he adds:

“We hold this opinion: that those who have committed great sins will be cast out of the kingdom of heaven—for example, fornicators, adulterers, and those who have intercourse with males, as well as thieves—but also those who have committed lesser offenses, according to what is written: ‘Neither drunkards nor abusers shall possess the kingdom of God’; and that there is a measure both in the goodness and in the severity of God.

“Therefore we strive to do everything with deliberation, even in the drinking of wine and in moderation of speech, so that we may dare to curse no one. Thus, because through fear of God we refrain from cursing anyone, remembering that saying concerning Michael and the Devil, ‘He did not dare to pronounce a judgment of blasphemy,’ and also the other passage: ‘They reject dominions, but blaspheme glories.’”

“Some of those who gladly seek out disputes impute to us and to our teaching blasphemy, concerning which let them see for themselves how they understand the statement, ‘Neither drunkards nor abusers shall possess the kingdom of God,’ although they say that the father of the wickedness and destruction of those who will be cast out of the kingdom of God can be saved. No one who is even mentally deranged could say such a thing.”

*[lacuna]* [Col. 0167A]

From these two translations we learn that Origen, together with his associates, once complained that his books had been corrupted by heretics and that things he had never said had been falsely attributed to him by his enemies.

Accordingly, after Rufinus had shown in his book *On the Adulteration of Origen’s Books* that heretics had also laid thieving claws upon the books of other Fathers—namely, both Clements, the Roman and the Alexandrian, and Dionysius of Alexandria as well—he then began, by Origen’s own words, to show that Origen’s books too had been corrupted by them. For this purpose he began to cite a passage in which Origen specifically demonstrates the point, beginning with the words, “Some of them.”

But what Rufinus omitted as superfluous does not concern the adulteration of the books, since it contains only Origen’s general complaints against certain bishops who opposed him and who had lent an easy ear to the heretics who corrupted his books. Jerome indeed says that Demetrius, bishop of Alexandria, is attacked throughout that entire letter. Yet before his own quarrels with Rufinus, he had written in his *Catalogue*, chapter LIV, that Demetrius had raged against Origen with such madness that he wrote throughout the whole world concerning Origen’s name.

It is therefore not surprising if Origen, protected by the communion of Saint Alexander of Jerusalem and of other bishops, complained in general about his enemies, who had been suborned by Demetrius—a man commended neither for doctrine nor for holiness. Rufinus nevertheless omitted these complaints, so that he could begin at the point where Origen complained about the corrupters of his books.
