As for the fidelity of Rufinus’s translation of Origen’s letter, although Origen’s Greek words are lacking to us, we can easily gather from the two translations taken together which interpreter expressed Origen’s meaning more faithfully.

Jerome testifies in his letter to Pammachius and Oceanus that from Origen’s teaching it follows that the Devil can be saved and Gabriel condemned. In the letter of Origen translated into Latin by Jerome, Origen objects this to his adversaries:

“Although they say that the father of the wickedness and destruction of those who will be cast out of the kingdom of God can be saved.”

Origen could not have said this of his Valentinian adversaries. Rather, they claimed that Origen had said it: namely, that the Devil, being of a ruined nature, could never in any way be saved and had never been able to be saved, while Gabriel could not be condemned because his nature was one destined for salvation.

But Origen declared both possibilities to be consistent with their respective natures, so that the Devil, if he used free will rightly, could be saved, while Gabriel, if he used it wickedly, could be condemned. Hence the Valentinians reproached Origen as though he had said that the Devil was to be saved.

Rufinus’s translation expresses this clearly:

“They say that I declare that the father of wickedness and destruction, and of those who are rejected from the kingdom of God—that is, the Devil—is to be saved. No one who is even mentally deranged and plainly insane could say such a thing.”

The following words of Jerome in Book II of the *Apology*, cited above, also confirm Rufinus’s translation, where Origen, the defender of the Catholic Faith, and Candidus, the champion of the Valentinian heresy, debate:

“Candidus asserts that the Devil is of the worst nature, one that can never be saved. Against this Origen rightly replied that the Devil was not a substance destined for destruction, but had fallen through his own will and could be saved. Candidus turned this into a calumny, as though Origen had said that the Devil’s nature was destined for salvation.”

Candidus had falsely made this accusation; Origen refutes it. From this it is clear that, when Origen says that the Devil could be saved, he understands this with respect to nature, not wickedness, just as the Valentinians unjustly reproached Adamantius [Origen].

Let us now pass through the remainder of Book II of Jerome’s *Apology*. What Rufinus had said about the falsification of the books of Hilary, Cyprian, and Tertullian, the holy Father casts into doubt. He cites the words in which Rufinus had attacked Epiphanius, although without naming him, and he defends Epiphanius against Rufinus’s criticisms.

Rufinus testified that Epiphanius had confessed, in the hearing of a very great multitude of brothers, that he had read six thousand books of Origen. Jerome replies:

“Among that multitude and throng of brothers you too were present, when in his letter he complained that, on account of Origen’s heresy, wicked doctrines had been uttered by you.”

He then rebukes Rufinus for having said that he was neither Origen’s defender nor his advocate. Jerome threatens that he will write against the books of Pamphilus and Eusebius if the Lord grants him time in this life. The Lord did grant it, as I have said, for nearly twenty years; nevertheless Jerome wrote nothing except what he recorded in these letters.

He wrote that he had first seen Pamphilus’s book in Rufinus’s codex and that he had not been concerned with what was said in defense of a heretic. He had always regarded the work of Pamphilus and that of Eusebius as though they were separate works.

Later, when the controversy arose, he wished to respond to their writings and for this reason read what each person thought in defense of Origen. He clearly discovered that the first book of Eusebius’s six-volume work was itself the book that had been published under Pamphilus’s name by Rufinus, both in Greek and in Latin, with only the passages concerning the Son and the Holy Spirit altered—passages that contained open blasphemy.

Hence Jerome says that, about ten years earlier, namely in A.D. 392, he had included Pamphilus in his *Catalogue*, chapter LXXV, as the author of that book.

He further complains that a fictitious letter had been circulated under his name in which he was said to repent that, as a young man deceived by Jews, he had translated into Latin Hebrew volumes in which there was no truth. Eusebius of Cremona had indicated that he had found this letter among African bishops who had come to the imperial court—namely, to the papal court—for ecclesiastical affairs.

The council held at Carthage in A.D. 401 had sent envoys to Pope Anastasius, to Venerius of Milan, [Col. 0168C] and to the Emperor Honorius, according to Tillemont, *Life of Saint Augustine*, §131. Those envoys must have brought the letter with them from Africa, as though it had been written by Jerome to the Africans.

This deeply disturbed Jerome after written communications from the city, not only from Eusebius but from many of the brothers there, informed him of the matter. They asked whether the letter was really as reported and by whom it had been disseminated among the people, and they indicated this tearfully.

Jerome shows from the letter’s style and form of expression that it should not be attributed to him, and on conjectural grounds attributes its fabrication to Rufinus. But when Rufinus protested under oath that he was not the author of the letter, Jerome replied in Book III of the *Apology* that Rufinus wrongly thought he had been named, since Jerome had assigned it to no one by name:

“To what point,” he says, “will unbridled audacity not burst forth? He has charged himself with another’s crime, so that we may appear to have fabricated it. What was said without a name he takes as said against himself; and while clearing himself of external sins, he is concerned only with his own innocence.

“For he swears that he did not write to the Africans under my name a letter in which I confessed that, having been led astray by Jews, I had translated lies. Yet he sends books containing all the same things, although he swears that he knew nothing of them.

“And I wonder how his prudence could agree with another man’s wickedness, so that what another had lied about in Africa he should harmoniously affirm as true, and so that some inexperienced person could imitate the elegance of his style.”

Nevertheless, Jerome seemed to judge that the letter was by no one other than Rufinus, on the basis of the similarity of style.

After Jerome had argued at length in favor of his new translation of the Scriptures and against the version of the Seventy translators, he brought the *Apology* to a close, indicating that he was eagerly awaiting the three books Rufinus had written against him:

“Awaiting the three volumes of my friend.”

These three volumes, as I have said, were Book II of Rufinus’s *Apology*—or, as they are commonly titled, the *Invectives against Jerome*—and Rufinus’s *Apology to Pope Anastasius in Defense of His Faith*.

# CHAPTER VI

[Col. 0169A]

I. Rufinus, after the two books of Jerome’s *Apology* had been brought to Aquileia, replies within two days in a letter now lost. II. He sends his books to Jerome, whom he attacks bitterly. III. Excerpts from the same lost letter. IV. He calls into question the letters of Pope Anastasius and Saint Epiphanius and, while clearing himself, strikes his adversary in various ways. V. Jerome, warned by Saint Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia, to refrain from writing against Rufinus, replies that he is compelled against his will to defend himself because Rufinus’s books had been scattered among the public. VI. The dates and numbers of Jerome’s *Apology* and of his translations of Theophilus’s paschal letters restored. VII. The judgments of M. Antonius Sabellicus concerning the disputes between Rufinus and Jerome.

## I.

Jerome had responded to the three volumes of Rufinus, which he had not yet received in full but only in summary, in scarcely two books of his *Apology*, cited above. Then a copy of these books was brought from the East to Aquileia, to Rufinus, by a merchant.

We do not know whether Jerome himself sent it to Rufinus or someone else did. That it was brought from the East by a merchant cannot be doubted. Since the merchant was about to return swiftly to the place from which he had come, Rufinus testifies that only two days were granted him for his reply:

“Two days before the bearer of these writings was to depart, what you had declaimed against me came into my hands.”

This response of Rufinus has nevertheless entirely perished, because he sent it only to Jerome in order to restrain him by terror and threats and did not wish it to be circulated throughout Italy. For this reason Gennadius does not mention it at all in his *Catalogue*.

Since, therefore, we lack this fourth work of Rufinus, to which Jerome immediately opposed his second *Apology*, or rather Book III of his *Apology*, we shall now attempt to extract a summary of it from that same Jerome’s Book III, in which Rufinus’s response is refuted.

Rufinus’s response was therefore a letter written to Jerome. The holy teacher reveals this repeatedly, and especially in these words:

“You testify that two days before you wrote us a letter, my little books came into your hands, and that for this reason you had no leisure in which to reply. Otherwise, if you had spoken against us after reflection and preparation, you would seem to be hurling thunderbolts rather than accusations.”

Rufinus said that he had written this letter to Jerome alone, in order to admonish him and to have him corrected, so that he might not cause a new scandal for others and so that, while they quarreled among themselves, others might not suffer spiritual death:

“You write me a letter,” he says, “to admonish me and to have me corrected, lest it cause scandal to others, and lest, while some rage, others be slaughtered.”

Jerome maintains that the letter was full of abuse, accusations, lies, and shameful injuries. In short, he calls it not merely a letter but volumes of accusation. On this occasion the holy man willingly grants Rufinus’s letters elegance of style, but he by no means concedes that they were written in two days.

## II.

From the passages cited by Jerome, who testifies that in replying he followed the order and traces of Rufinus’s letter, we see that Rufinus, at the very beginning of the letter, defends himself for having published an *Apology*.

Because the most learned old man had refuted Rufinus’s apologetic books before he had received them, using a summary sent to him by friends, Rufinus therefore arranged for his complete books, attached to the new letter, to be delivered to Jerome. He claimed that he had previously sent them only to those who had been injured by Jerome’s words, and not to a larger audience, because one ought to speak to Christians not for ostentation but for edification.

Jerome suggests the same in these words:

“You send me both the earlier books and the recent letter.”

Rufinus adds words which I shall here attach from Jerome:

“Do not redeem my secretary at a high price, as your friend Eusebius of Cremona did with my notes on *Periarchon*, not yet corrected and not yet properly arranged, so that he could more easily falsify what no one, or scarcely anyone, possessed. Accept from me without charge the codex of the *Apology*, which you would have wished to purchase at a great price.”

Jerome alludes to this confidence of Rufinus in Letter LXIX, otherwise XCI, to Augustine:

“Calpurnius, surnamed Lanarius, has sent me his abuse with his customary rashness. I have learned that through his efforts it has even reached Africa, and I have replied briefly and in part. I have sent you copies of his little book; when the opportunity arises, I shall send the larger work—the *Apology* divided into two books—at the first suitable occasion. In it I took care not to damage Christian reputation, but only to refute the delirium, ignorance, lies, and folly of a madman.”

Augustine replied in Letter LXXII, otherwise XCII—now CX among Jerome’s letters—that he did not know what writings against Jerome had reached Africa and that he by no means approved of hostility between such great men. But we shall discuss this elsewhere.

Rufinus continues against Jerome:

“I confess that I praised your eloquence in my preface. Even now I would praise it, unless you made it offensive by much boasting, contrary to the judgment of your own Tully.”

Rufinus was distressed that, after spending thirty years outside Latium, he was subjected to schoolmaster’s rods by Jerome. Jerome had ironically called him philosopher, rhetorician, grammarian, dialectician, Hebrew, Greek, Latin, and trilingual. Rufinus pours out the following against him:

“You who keep watch with the eyes of so many disciplines, how can you be forgiven if you err, rather than being covered by perpetual silence of shame?”

And below:

“I wished to imitate you, but since the man returning to you was hurrying, I preferred to write a few words to you rather than write more extensively to others in response to your abuse. It was superfluous for me to criticize you on a few points, when this is acknowledged of you in all things.”

Rufinus says that Jerome ought to have written only to Rufinus himself, and not to others, if he wished to correct him:

“Whom, excellent teacher, did you wish to correct in this matter, if those to whom you write had done nothing wrong? If you had not written to me, whom you accuse, but to others?”

## III.

As for his translations of Origen’s books, Rufinus says that he did nothing that Jerome himself had not previously done in his commentaries.

The statements Jerome had committed to writing in order to increase the authority of the book written by Pamphilus are ridiculed by Rufinus, because Jerome had judged only too late that the book should be removed from the martyr, although for many years he had thought it to be Pamphilus’s genuine offspring.

Rufinus later attacks Jerome as follows:

“Tell me, who permitted you, when translating, to remove some things, alter others, and add others? Look, I ask you: who permitted you, in your commentaries, to write some things from Origen, some from Apollinarius, and some from yourself, without stating whether they arose from Origen, from yourself, or from another?”

He says this in order to defend his own translation of the books *Periarchon*.

He confirms that his *Apology to Anastasius in Defense of His Faith* concerning the resurrection of the flesh had been accepted by all the bishops of Italy, with no member amputated and no part of the body removed.

The exposition of the Faith published by Theophilus of Alexandria, and mentioned in Jerome’s letters, had not yet reached him. Rufinus nevertheless promises that he will follow whatever Theophilus writes.

Jerome replies that he does not remember having written this. In Book I of his *Apology* he speaks of two letters of Theophilus, the synodical and the paschal letter against Origen, not of an exposition of the Faith. Perhaps Rufinus, then hurriedly reading Jerome’s books written against him and overcome by considerable indignation, understood one in place of the other.

He then adds:

“What do you think? Do you have anything else with which to stretch the sinews of your loquacity? And you are indignant when I accuse you of speaking offensively, although you take up the obscenities of comedies and the jests of prostitutes and lovers as an ecclesiastical writer?”

To return to Theophilus: Rufinus said that he followed Theophilus’s opinion in everything, although he had seen what Theophilus had written against Origen. Jerome therefore turns this argument against him:

“If you delight in the opinions of Pope Theophilus and think it sacrilegious that the decrees of bishops should be overturned, what do you say about the others—Origenists—whom he himself condemned?”

Jerome further taunts Rufinus by asking when he began to follow Theophilus’s opinion, and he answers:

“I suppose it was when you were defending Paul, whom Theophilus had condemned, with all your strength and every effort; when you were urging, by imperial rescript, that he be restored to the priesthood, which he had lost by episcopal judgment.”

Rufinus said that he had been Theophilus’s disciple and that he did not accuse those from whom he had learned, just as Jerome accused Origen and Didymus:

“I neither accuse nor alter my teachers.”

He then proceeds to Jerome’s letter against Vigilantius and attempts to defend the cause of Vigilantius as his friend.

## IV.

The same point he argues on his own behalf against the letter of Pope Anastasius to John of Jerusalem, which he seems to draw into suspicion of forgery, on the grounds that, although it was said to have been written from Rome to John, it nevertheless would not have been sent by John to Rufinus. Against this he sets the letter of communion delivered to him by Pope Siricius, Anastasius’s predecessor, when he was leaving Rome after his Latin translation of Origen’s *On First Principles*:

> “For what harm can it do me,” he says, “that he wrote—or, perhaps, did not write—without my knowledge? And if he did write, the testimony of the whole world is enough for me: for no one thinks it possible that the bishop of so great a city could either have wronged an innocent man or have done so in his absence.”

Jerome mentions not one but several letters of Anastasius against Rufinus, of which we possess only one. Nor is it difficult to believe that one of them, if not both, was fabricated by Rufinus’s enemies, just as I have related that Jerome’s adversaries sent letters to Africa fabricated under his name. Hear Jerome’s words:

> “Suppose that I forged the letter of the preceding year. Who sent the recent writings to the East, in which Pope Anastasius adorns you with such profuse flowers that, when you read them, you begin to wish more to defend yourself than to accuse us?”

Thus Rufinus later accuses Jerome:

> “Can I not also relate how you departed from the city? What judgment was presently pronounced about you? What was written afterward? Where you boarded the ship? How devoutly you avoided perjury? I could disclose it, but I have decided to preserve more than to report.”

Elsewhere he also says:

> “And in order that you may not approve our letter, you say that the letter of Pope Anastasius, too, is supported by a similar fraud; I have already answered you about it. If you suspect that it is not his, you have an opportunity to accuse us of falsehood before him. But if it is his—as the letter of this year against you also proves—then you strive vainly and falsely to accuse a false letter, since from his genuine letter we demonstrate that ours is genuine.”

Rufinus also mentions a letter of Saint Epiphanius, in which he himself was accused. He says that, after the kiss and the prayer, Epiphanius could not have written against him; and therefore he does not hesitate to cast that letter also under suspicion of forgery. Concerning both the letter of Anastasius and that of Epiphanius, he reports the following against Jerome:

> “May this be far from holy men. Such things usually proceed from your school. You gave us peace when we were departing, and from behind you hurled darts armed with poison.”

He again excuses his imperfect knowledge of Latin, for which Jerome had censured him, by referring to his thirty years’ association with the Greeks.

He moves on to the condition of souls, concerning whose origin—as also concerning other matters belonging to natural philosophy, which he enumerates individually—he declares that he knows nothing. He presses Jerome to answer concerning the nature of things. He again brings against him the charge of perjury: Jerome, having been warned in a dream, had promised that he would not read secular books, yet he continued to read them repeatedly.

After their friendship had been restored, he accuses him of disloyalty. He thinks that Letter 42, elsewhere numbered 66 (now 81), recently delivered to him as though it had been written long ago, falsely bears the mark of elapsed time and was in fact written recently.

He demands from Jerome the books of Pythagoras, which he asserts Jerome had boasted of reading, although no books of Pythagoras are to be found.

Finally, he exhorts Jerome to repentance and asks that he be admonished privately, not publicly. Unless Jerome keeps silent, he threatens him with destruction and declares that this stumbling-block, on account of the harm to the Church, will fall upon his head. He also seems to add that he would hand him over to the magistrates of the public tribunals.

Rufinus, however, says none of this anywhere; rather, throughout Book III of his response, Jerome repeatedly asserts that Rufinus threatened him with it. For at the beginning he says:

> “You terrify me with accusations . . . in the final part of your letter you threaten me with death, lest I dare to respond to your accusations—or rather, to your praises.”

And shortly afterward:

> “You threaten me with death . . . you threaten destruction unless I remain silent.”

And below:

> “You terrify me with your swords, and you threaten an accusation not now ecclesiastical, but judicial . . . If you believe otherwise, why do you wish to kill? Is anyone who disagrees with you to be killed? Who would fear a man who is ready to kill? If I say anything harsh against you, you immediately threaten me with proscription and swords . . . You reserve yourself for the tribunals of judges, so that, while sparing me, you may heap up accusations against me.”

Jerome adds that Rufinus wrote the following in his own hand at the end of the letter:

> “I wish you to love peace.”

At that time it was customary for a person who dictated a letter in another’s hand to add the greeting in his own handwriting.

This, then, is the substance of the whole Rufinian letter, which was never made public but was written to Jerome alone and therefore has been lost. We have attempted, as best we could, to glean its contents from Jerome’s response.

## V.

At the same time, apparently, as Rufinus wrote his letter, Saint Chromatius, Bishop of Aquileia, with whom Rufinus was staying, read Jerome’s *Apology* and, out of his charity, admonished its author to put an end to the dispute, which was offending the minds of Christians.

Jerome swore that he would obey the command of this most holy man; but he said that Rufinus’s threats had compelled him to respond, lest, if he remained silent, he should appear guilty of the crimes of which he was accused. His words at the beginning of Book III are these:

> “I call Jesus as witness of my conscience, who will judge both this letter and your letter, that, at the admonition of Saint Pope Chromatius, I wished to remain silent, to put an end to our quarrels, and to overcome evil with good. But because you threaten me with destruction unless I remain silent, I am compelled to respond, lest by keeping silent I seem to acknowledge the crime, and lest you interpret my mildness as evidence of a bad conscience.”

He nevertheless promises that he will respond in such a way as both to dissolve the charges brought against him and to refrain from insult, lest he rashly offend anyone, since he is not Rufinus’s accuser but his own defender.

He says that he refuted Rufinus’s accusation—for so he calls his *Apology*—because it had been disseminated at Rome, throughout Italy, and among the islands of Dalmatia. Rufinus’s *Cereales* and *Anabasii*, that is, his messengers, had traveled through the provinces, publicly reciting the invectives contained in Rufinus’s *Apologies*, which Jerome ironically calls his praises.

Crowds arriving from the West had reported Rufinus’s insults to him so accurately and consistently that he was compelled to respond not to writings which he had not yet read, but to the opinions formed about those writings, so that he might receive upon the shield of truth the darts of falsehood flying throughout the world.

He says that he, a poor man, had not bought Rufinus’s secretary with gold in order to obtain his translation and the notebooks of the books *On First Principles*, which had not yet been corrected or properly arranged. Eusebius of Cremona, he says, could all the more easily have falsified them because either no one possessed them or very few people did.

He says that he did not approve Eusebius’s accusation against Rufinus; indeed, he even reproved it as true. Yet he does not admit the alleged falsification of the notebooks on the authority of a man ignorant of Latin and Greek.

He says that he had not boasted of his own eloquence, but had not gladly accepted the praise Rufinus bestowed upon it in the preface to the book *On First Principles*.

If Rufinus had wished Jerome to be admonished and corrected so that he would not harm others, he ought not to have written books against him for other people and scattered them throughout the world to be read by his agents.

When Rufinus had handed his books over to everyone to read and recite, Jerome says that reports reached him one after another from Italy, Rome, and Dalmatia concerning the praises with which Rufinus was again adorning him. Therefore he immediately responded to the charges and sent the books of his *Apology* to those whom Rufinus had wounded, so that an antidote might follow the poisons.

Because of this fault, Rufinus sent him both the earlier books and a recent letter full of insults and accusations. Jerome says that, having been accused and challenged, he could not remain silent, although he reached these words unwillingly and reluctantly; if Rufinus had not challenged him, he would always have remained silent.

He says that he could not possibly believe that the books of his *Apology* had been brought into Rufinus’s hands at Aquileia only two days before Rufinus wrote his letter, and that Rufinus therefore had no time to respond at leisure. In fact, in two days Rufinus could neither have responded to nor even read Jerome’s writings.

For Jerome does not think that a merchant of Eastern goods—who had to sell what he had brought from the East and buy at Aquileia what he would transport back to the East—could have remained at Aquileia for only two days, so that Rufinus would have been forced to dictate a letter against Jerome hastily and on the spur of the moment.

Rather, when the merchant first arrived in the city, which, as the emperor Justinian said, was the greatest city in the West, he did not immediately deliver Jerome’s letter to Rufinus but delayed before handing it over. He could later have delivered it to Rufinus quite conveniently two days before his departure.

Concerning the books of Rufinus’s *Apology* sent to him, Jerome says:

> “Are your books, which you polished for three years, more eloquent?”

Rufinus had written them in A.D. 399, whereas Jerome was writing this in A.D. 402. Since he had previously noticed only summarily, and not in the complete copies sent to him, their obscurity and inelegance, after receiving the entire work three years later he says that Rufinus had polished it for three years, yet that the books had nevertheless reached his hands no more eloquent than before.

As often happens in prolonged disputes, even between highly learned men, many things are repeated here that had already been said elsewhere against Rufinus. Such matters include the following: that the *Apology for Origen* was not by the martyr Pamphilus; that Rufinus had acted in bad faith in translating the books *On First Principles*; that Eusebius of Cremona had neither stolen nor falsified the uncorrected notebooks; that Rufinus was ill regarded by Pope Anastasius and by Epiphanius; that he suffered from ignorance of Latin; and other points of this kind.

The Father of Stridon complains that Vigilantius had risen against him through Rufinus’s underground passages, and that Rufinus’s malice had raged against him through Vigilantius’s stupidity.

He maintains that what he himself had written about the doctrines of Pythagoras Rufinus had accepted as though it had been written about Pythagorean books. He says that he does not spare heretics, but does not wish to act madly against a madman or bite one who bites.

Finally, the blessed man closes his response as follows:

> “If you desire peace, lay down your arms. I can yield to one who speaks gently; I do not fear one who threatens. Let there be one faith between us, and peace will immediately follow.”

## VI.

This work was written by Jerome in March or April of A.D. 402, before news had been heard of the death of Pope Anastasius. For Jerome speaks of him in Book III of the *Apology*, page 468, as though he were still alive:

> “The letters of this year against you [that is, Anastasius’s] prove it.”

Anastasius died on 27 April of that year, 402, as most ecclesiastical tables report in Tillemont, note 69. This is also Baronius’s opinion for A.D. 402, section 42; Pagius unjustly accuses it of error in the same place, section 16.

The year of Jerome’s writing emerges from the following words in the same Book III, page 453:

> “I translated into Latin, over approximately these two years, two of his [Theophilus’s] letters, a synodical and a paschal letter, against Origen and his disciples, and others against Apollinarius and that same Origen; and I gave them to speakers of our language [Latin] to be read for the edification of the Church. I do not know that I translated any other of his works.”

According to Cardinal Noris, Book I of the *History of Pelagianism*, chapter II, and the *Dissertation on Saint Siricius, Pope*, page 5, Jerome translated only three paschal letters of Theophilus that still survive, not five, as Baronius thought for A.D. 399, section 51. For, according to the custom of his Church, Theophilus published a paschal letter every year.

The first, beginning *Christum Jesum Dominum* (“Christ Jesus the Lord”), assigned Easter for the year 401 to the nineteenth day of the month Pharmuthi, that is, 14 April, Solar Cycle 18, Lunar Cycle 3, Dominical Letter F. This letter, which discloses many of Origen’s errors, is improperly called the second in printed editions.

> **[Note: In our edition each is restored to its proper place.]**

The second, beginning *Primum solemnitatis augustae* (“The first of the august solemnity”), in which the errors of Apollinarius and Origen are refuted, assigned Easter for the year 402 to the eleventh day of Pharmuthi, that is, 6 April, Solar Cycle 19, Lunar Cycle 4, Dominical Letter E. This second letter is improperly called the first in printed editions.

The third, for the year 403, was not translated by Jerome, although Baronius thought that it was.

The fourth, beginning *Nunc quoque Deus* (“Now also God”), assigned Easter for the leap year 404 to the twenty-second day of Pharmuthi, 17 April, Solar Cycle 21, Lunar Cycle 6, Dominical Letters C and B.

From this everyone can see that the order of Theophilus’s paschal letters is reversed in all the editions: in volume IX of the works of Saint Jerome in the edition of Marianus Victorius; in volume IV of the new edition, page 689; in volume IV of the Cologne edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum* (1618), page 713; and in volume V of the Lyon edition, page 883. This is evident from the paschal chronological markers themselves. After Noris—although without giving him credit—Abbot Claudius Floriacus also observed it in his *Ecclesiastical History*, volume V, Book XXI, page 131.

In the words quoted above, Jerome says “over approximately these two years,” namely A.D. 401 and 402, because in the second of these years, 402, he wrote Book III of the *Apology*. He also sent to Rome, in the spring of that year, another paschal letter of Theophilus against Apollinarius and Origen, translated by him into Latin—or, as he puts it, “the Alexandrian riches”—to Pammachius and Marcella, together with Letter 187, elsewhere numbered 78 (now 97), while Anastasius was still alive.

For Jerome concludes his letter with these words:

> “To him [Anastasius] we pray for many years, so that, through his zeal, the revived plantings of heresy, long since dried up, may perish.”

The new edition of Jerome’s works, therefore, incorrectly assigns this letter to Anastasius to A.D. 405, volume IV, page 689, since Anastasius had died three years earlier, and Innocent I had been left in possession of the See of Peter, which he began to occupy in A.D. 402.

Again, the following words of Jerome provide another argument for establishing the year 402 as the date of Book III of his *Apology*:

> “The faction of the heretics, recently driven out of Egypt and Alexandria, came to Jerusalem and wished to join itself to this man [a certain Bishop Paul, deposed by Theophilus of Alexandria], so that those whose grief was one might also have one accusation; but he [Paul] rejected, despised, and cast them away.”

And shortly afterward:

> “What do you think of those who, having been condemned, besiege the palaces—that is, the nobles and ministers of the imperial court who are inciting them against Theophilus?”

Therefore the monks rejected, despised, and cast away by Theophilus went to Constantinople. Palladius relates the matter in his *Life of Chrysostom*, page 57; Socrates, Book VI, chapter IX; and Sozomen, Book VIII, chapter XIII.

In Theophilus’s second paschal letter, for A.D. 402—which is first in the proper order—he says of the Origenists:

> “They tear people apart in the great cities and besiege the doors of the rich . . . They commend themselves to effeminate ears and to the hatred of the Gentiles by slandering us,”

namely, to eunuchs and to men unacquainted with the Christian religion.

Thus the monks had already arrived at Constantinople when Jerome wrote these words. They arrived around the middle or end of the year 401, according to Tillemont, volume XI, pages 477 and 635.

Therefore Book III of the *Apology* was written in A.D. 402. Consequently, Jerome had published the biblical books from whose prefaces certain passages are cited in that work before this year; Humfredus Hodius is therefore mistaken in taking a different view in Book III, Part II, chapter II, page 357, of his work *On the Texts of the Bible*.

It is difficult, however, to believe that the first two books of Jerome’s *Apology*, which could not have been written before the end of 401, were brought to Aquileia to Rufinus before the year 402. Jerome composed Book III after receiving Rufinus’s response but before the end of the spring of that same year, 402. For he says that Anastasius was still alive, which he could not have said unless it was before news of his death—on 27 April—had reached the East.

Here the error of those who move the date of Anastasius’s death back to 14 December A.D. 401 becomes clear.

## VII.

As for these disputes between two highly distinguished men, M. Antonius Sabellicus, in Book VI of his *Examples*, chapter IX, under the heading “Rivalry,” attributes them in part to Rufinus:

> “What of the fact,” he says, “that even Jerome, in whom there was so great an infusion of light and so much eloquence, was not without a rival? Rufinus was able to contend with him in words, but not in holiness. Indeed, if that too is weighed in both men, the trumpet of Stridon surpassed that of Carnia by as much as the bellowing of an Indian elephant surpasses the buzzing of a gnat.”

Let us cite other words of Sabellicus from Book II of his *On the Antiquity of Aquileia*, where he judges Rufinus somewhat more mildly:

> “Among other things, there survive his [Rufinus’s] letters—or rather, invectives—to Jerome, and Jerome’s to him; they are not without evidence of mutual rivalry. Yet each differs considerably from the other in the same kind of writing. One is denser, the other more expansive; one fights more closely, the other more broadly; one relies on sharpness, the other on weight. The former is not altogether elegant, whereas the latter is not merely elegant but also polished; in short, he is such a man that one might believe him to have been rebuked as a Ciceronian before God’s tribunal—as he himself testifies. But I see how foolishly I am behaving, a man almost entirely unacquainted with letters, by weighing the talents of such men in a balance like another Aristarchus.”

Sigebert of Gembloux seems to have delivered a fair judgment on this quarrel in his *Chronicle* under the year 401, page 13 of Aubert Miraeus’s edition:

> “Jerome and Rufinus, a priest of Aquileia, having fallen into conflict with each other over questions of Scripture, wrote against one another in language sufficiently brilliant but excessively bitter.”

Saint Ado, in his *Martyrology* under 30 September, did list the works of Saint Jerome, but preferred to omit the writings against Rufinus.

Ado was Archbishop of Vienne, and it will be clear from what follows that the Gallic bishops favored Rufinus’s side. Ado had copied the *Martyrology*—a small work previously sent from Rome to Aquileia—in his own hand at Ravenna; for the greater part, it had been extracted from Rufinus’s history.

Meanwhile, a judge who is certainly most reliable, impartial, and free from every suspicion, being a friend to both men, must be brought forward here. This is Augustine, Bishop of Hippo. Jerome wrote to him after A.D. 402 in Letter 68, elsewhere numbered 13 among Augustine’s letters, saying that he had learned that the insults of Rufinus—or, as he calls him, Calpurnius by the surname Lanarius—had reached Africa also through Rufinus’s efforts. Jerome says that he had responded to them briefly and in part:

> “I have sent you copies of his little book, which consisted of the earlier *Apology*, divided into two books; the longer work [the second *Apology*, or Book III of the first *Apology*] I shall send at the first suitable opportunity.”

He also indicates that he took care not to injure anyone’s Christian reputation, but only to refute the falsehood and folly of a delirious and ignorant man.

After reading Jerome’s *Apology*, Augustine did not in any way join Jerome’s side, in keeping with his gentle character, although elsewhere he seeks to soothe Jerome’s irritation toward himself. He was satisfied to grieve deeply that the flame of discord had arisen between such great men.

Augustine replies that no writings of Rufinus against Jerome had reached Africa, and says that from Jerome’s apologetic letters he had learned how much Jerome had restrained himself in this matter. He says that the example of the dissension that had arisen between them frightened him, since in one of Jerome’s letters he had noticed certain indications of Jerome’s own anger.

It is better, however, to hear Augustine himself speaking in his own words, Letter 63, elsewhere numbered 15, chapter III:

> “I do not know what malicious writings concerning your name have reached Africa. Yet we received what you deigned to send, in response to those insults. After reading it, I confess, I grieved greatly that, among persons so dear and familiar, joined to almost all the Churches by the most renowned bond of friendship, so great an evil of discord had arisen. And how much you restrain yourself, and how you hold back the goads of your indignation lest you return insult for insult, is sufficiently evident in your letters.”

Thus Augustine immediately adds that, if the *Apology* in which Jerome indicated that he had restrained himself had frightened him so greatly, it was possible to infer what the writings of Rufinus would have done to him if he had ever read them, since, as Jerome had reported, they were full of insults.

Augustine says that Jerome himself had made these statements, although he did not dare openly to rebuke him. Nevertheless, he says:

> “If, when I read those very writings, I wasted away with grief and froze with fear, what would those writings have done to me which he wrote against you, if they had by chance fallen into my hands? Woe to the world because of scandals! Behold, it happens; behold, what the Truth says is fully accomplished: because iniquity will abound, the love of many will grow cold. To what faithful hearts, then, can one entrust oneself? Into whose bosom can faithful affection now wholly cast itself? Finally, what friend is not to be feared as a future enemy, if this thing which we lament could arise between Jerome and Rufinus? O miserable and pitiable condition! O unreliable knowledge of the present dispositions of friends, where there is no foreknowledge of the future! But why should I think that one man must lament this about another, when a human being does not even know himself in the future? For he knows, however imperfectly and scarcely perhaps even now, what sort of person he is; but what he will later become, he does not know.”

With these words Augustine seeks to soothe Jerome’s mind, which had been somewhat offended by his earlier letters; and the great teacher, speaking as though about himself, commends Christian charity in general.

At the end of the letter he returns again to Jerome’s hostility toward Rufinus and clearly suggests that he neither approves nor believes what Jerome had written about Rufinus:

> “Who among the prudent would not see how tolerably even you endure the hostility of one who was once your dearest and most intimate friend, with conscience offering you consolation? And how you count among left-handed weapons—by which one fights against the devil no less than with the right hand—the things that he boasts or that perhaps are believed by certain people [Pammachius, Oceanus, and Marcella]. Nevertheless, I would prefer him [Rufinus] to be in some way gentler rather than you, armed in this way [perhaps, more bitter]. It is a great and sad wonder that such friendships have reached such hostility. It will be a joyful and much greater wonder if such hostility returns to its former concord.”

Thus far Augustine. In Letter 166, formerly 28, which is inscribed to others as *On the Origin of the Human Soul*, he indicates in chapter V, section 15, that he had received Book III of Jerome’s *Apology*. From it he quotes these words:

> “But as for what you wrote in your book against Rufinus, that certain people slander this opinion because it seems unworthy that God should give souls to adulterous conceptions, and from this they try to establish that, on account of merits acquired in a life before the flesh, souls may justly be brought to such prisons, this does not trouble me, as I consider the many arguments by which that slander can be refuted.”

Almost all more recent writers openly disparage Rufinus as a heretic condemned by Pope Anastasius. But Augustine, the most ardent enemy of heretics, would not have lamented the disagreement of so great a man as Jerome with a heretic condemned by the Apostolic See, nor would he have wished Jerome to return from such hostility to his former concord with Rufinus. For there ought to be no fellowship between light and darkness.

Therefore, from Saint Augustine alone it is clear that Rufinus was never condemned or regarded as a heretic, as I shall demonstrate more fully later.

Meanwhile, let us continue to review the remaining writings of Origen translated into Latin by Rufinus.

# CHAPTER VII.

I. Seventeen homilies of Origen on Genesis were translated into Latin not by Jerome but by Rufinus. II. Thirteen on Exodus and sixteen on Leviticus. III. Twenty-eight on Numbers. IV. Twenty-six on Joshua. V. Nine on Judges, the same number on the Psalms, one on the First Book of Kings, and four on the Song of Songs. VI. Ten books on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans. VII. Doubtful homilies. [Col. 0177A] Those on Luke were translated not by Rufinus but by Jerome.

## I.

Since the connection of the subject requires us to set forth in order the remaining works of Origen which Rufinus, complying with his friends, gave to the Latin world—and which have been almost neglected by other writers of literary history—we shall begin with the seventeen Homilies on Genesis.

Aldus Manutius the Elder was the first of all to publish these in print, together with others, dedicating them to Aegidius of Viterbo, an outstanding preacher of the divine word, of the Order of Hermits and later Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, under the following title:

> *Origen’s Homilies on Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Joshua, and the Book of Judges, translated by Saint Jerome. Venice, A.D. 1503, folio.*

A monk, who concealed his name in the preface, prepared the edition, professing that he owed much to his fellow monk at the Paduan monastery of Saint Justina, Jerome of Valencia, a Spaniard. Bernardinus Benalius afterward reprinted this edition at Venice in 1512, in folio.

The same monk made Saint Jerome the translator of the entire work, doubtless because in the manuscripts from which he had drawn it he found Jerome written by copyists in place of Rufinus, so that the volume might become more acceptable under the authority of so great a man. Yet the monk seems doubtful whether that translation is rightly ascribed to Jerome:

> “We do not doubt that neither the author nor the translator published so excellent a work without a preface; but through the negligence of copyists it has by no means come down to us. Yet I do not deny that we found in certain copies something inscribed in the place of a preface, though worthy, as I judged, neither of our author nor of our translator. But I must restrain my pen; for the Latin translator could make bad Latin out of good Greek, as the comic poet says. It is, however, manifest that the translator of the prologue and of the work was not the same person. Therefore it did not seem proper to us to set upon a most beautiful body, so to speak, a foreign and ugly head, and rather to frighten than attract the reader at the very front of the little book.”

Thus, by rashly omitting the prologue which he had found in the manuscripts, the monk made Jerome the translator of all these homilies. Desiderius Erasmus, however, was not so credulous, and added this judgment concerning the Homilies on Genesis to his edition of Origen’s works:

> “Rufinus, not Jerome, translated the Homilies on Genesis. The preface has been cut off, since neither Rufinus nor Jerome was accustomed to publish anything without a prologue. Rufinus, moreover, lay under the gravest suspicion of being an Origenist; under this title the Arian heresy attempted to sprout anew. Thus, in place of Rufinus’s odious name, Jerome’s welcome name was substituted. Such are indeed the tricks of copyists: they remove what at first sight deters the buyer and attach what could attract him. The renown of an author is no small inducement. By similar deceit the crowd imposes on the unwary, pretending that cloth came from England when it has never seen England, and selling as Belgian wine wine grown near the walls of Louvain.”

So much, and very rightly, Erasmus on the true translator. On the work itself, however, he judges as follows:

> “The style has much clarity and flows quite agreeably, though it is not wholly pure. Would that he had added fidelity to that virtue, which we require of a translator. But this freedom—or rather licence—of adding, taking away, and changing proclaims Rufinus as the translator. He admits that he employed this licence in Leviticus, in the Epistle to the Romans, and in the Ecclesiastical History. What work, moreover, did he ever handle without corrupting it in this manner?”

George Bull, in his *Defence of the Nicene Faith*, section II, chapter IX, §20, p. 209, turns this very point, for which Rufinus is blamed, to the praise of a sincere and honest man, since Rufinus never did it without warning the reader. Bull’s words are:

> “It is certain that Rufinus added much of his own in translating most of Origen’s books; but whenever he used that freedom, he expressly warned his reader of it, as became an honest man and a lover of truth.”

Gennadius, in chapter XVII of his *Catalogue*, testifies that everything of Origen which was translated, apart from what Jerome translated, was translated by Rufinus. Jerome himself, moreover, in the *Catalogue* which he composed in old age, chapter CXXXV, when he lists by name what he had translated from Origen, says absolutely nothing of the Homilies on Genesis; and yet he testifies that he translated certain works of Origen while still a young man. Honorius, later than both, says the same in Book I, chapter CXXXVI, of his *Catalogue*.

“But what need is there,” Erasmus says, “of these arguments, when Rufinus himself, in the peroration which he added to the Commentaries on the Epistle to the Romans, professes that he translated Origen on Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, likewise on Joshua and on the Book of Judges, although I am not unaware that Jerome has been substituted there too, but most imprudently, as we shall shortly show?”

That peroration, appended to the commentaries on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, appears in volume II of Origen’s works, from Erasmus’s fourth edition prepared by Grynaeus, p. 634. Peter Daniel Huet, in the *Origeniana*, Book III, chapter II, section III, §1, rightly denies all credibility to an ancient manuscript of the royal library in which the very translation of the Homilies on Genesis now under discussion is attributed to Jerome. Following Erasmus and Gilbert Genebrard, he acknowledges that it belongs to Rufinus alone, since Rufinus expressly testifies in the prologue to the twenty-eight Homilies on Numbers that he had then translated all Origen’s homilies on the Pentateuch, or Law of Moses, except those written on Deuteronomy. But we possess Latin homilies on the first four books of the Pentateuch; who then would dare deny that Rufinus was their translator? Huet asks. Chiffletius also employs this argument in the passage to be cited later.

Accordingly, Genebrard rightly inserted, under Rufinus’s name, the Homilies on Genesis and those which Origen wrote on Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Joshua, and Judges, from p. 1 to p. 221 of his Latin edition of Origen’s works, which he published under this title:

> *The Works of Origen Adamantius, that great and ancient interpreter of Scripture and second teacher of the Church after the Apostles, all that could indeed be brought forth, long ago translated and revised through the diligence of most learned men. Paris: Guillaume Chaudière, A.D. 1574, folio.*

We have seen this edition afterward reprinted by other printers. In the Appendix to volume V of the new edition of the Works of Saint Augustine, Sermon IX, *On Rebecca*, is Origen’s Homily X on Genesis, translated into Latin by Rufinus.

## II.

By the same arguments it is established that Origen’s thirteen Homilies on Exodus and sixteen on Leviticus, which immediately follow those already mentioned in Grynaeus’s edition, volume I, pages 58 and 104, were rendered into Latin through Rufinus’s labor. For in the Prologue to the Homilies on Numbers he says that he translated into Latin everything written by Origen on the Law; and in the concluding section of the Homilies on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, volume II, page 634, he clearly asserts that he did the same for Exodus, and especially, he says, “in those works on the book of Leviticus which he [Origen] dictated in a declamatory style, but which we translated in the manner of an exposition.” Huetius likewise holds this view concerning Rufinus in the passage cited above, §2.

Sixtus of Siena is therefore mistaken in book IV of the *Bibliotheca* when he attributes these translations to Jerome. Erasmus offers the following criticism of the translation of the Homilies on Leviticus, somewhat too harshly:

> Rufinus admits that he translated these Homilies rather freely—that is, that he supplied from his own resources many things that he says were lacking. Such boldness is more tolerable when he explicitly indicates what he removed and what he added, as he did in the *Ecclesiastical History*, from which he removed book IX and inserted his own narratives in its place. Yet anyone who reads this work and the exposition of the Epistle to the Romans is uncertain whether he is reading Origen or Rufinus. By this artifice, a man desirous of glory thought that he had discovered a way by which, even against everyone’s will, he might be passed from hand to hand among men.

Matthaeus Petitdidier, in volume I of his *Animadversions on Dupin’s Bibliotheca*, page 15, rightly rejects Joannes Rodolphus Wetstenius, who incorrectly suspected that something had been altered by Rufinus in Origen’s first Homily on Leviticus, where the story of Susanna is discussed. Yet Origen’s commentary on Matthew, which still survives in Greek, presents almost exactly the same material as Rufinus’s Latin translation.

I do not understand why Labbe, in volume II of *On Writers*, page 141, made Jerome the translator of these Homilies. How unjust Erasmus is here toward Rufinus, as elsewhere most men are, is shown by the singular modesty with which Rufinus everywhere speaks of himself and his own works. Huetius, §3, page 245, although he too does not treat Rufinus fairly when he says that Rufinus liberally dispensed whatever he pleased from his own resources, nevertheless acknowledges that Rufinus deserves the credit that these Homilies on Leviticus, falsely circulated among Cyril’s works, have been restored to their legitimate author.

Jodocus Clichtoveus was the first of all to publish these Homilies on Leviticus, translated by Rufinus and arranged in sixteen books, at Paris, printed by Wolfgang Hopylius in 1514, in folio. He transcribed them from a Corbie manuscript, which had been given to him by Guillaume Parvus of the Order of Preachers, confessor to Louis XII, King of France.

From this it is evident how greatly Vossius is mistaken in book II, part I, thesis VI of his *Pelagian History*, where he thinks these commentaries on Leviticus belong to Cyril, or at least to an uncertain author. They are also wrongly attributed to Cyril in the Latin editions of that Father, and notably in the edition prepared by Petrus Canisius, published at Cologne by Melchior Novesianus in 1546, in two folio volumes. The cited Homilies appear in the first volume, page 41. They are likewise attributed to Cyril in the Latin edition of Cyril’s works published at Paris by Michel Sonnius in 1573, in folio, page 66.

A manuscript of these works, with Rufinus as translator, existed in Venice in the Library of Saint Anthony; a few years ago—alas!—it was consumed by flames. Consult Tomasinus, *Venetian Libraries*, page 10.

For this reason Robert Bellarmine, who in book IV, chapter XI of *On the Word of God* had not dared to decide whether the Homilies belonged to Origen, later acknowledged them without hesitation as Origenian in his *Catalogue*. Huetius therefore rightly censures a certain heterodox writer for rejecting them among Origen’s spurious works. He also concludes that there had been several collections of them, so that the Rufinian Homilies are distinct from the second Homily on Leviticus, a fragment of which is presented in chapter I of Origen’s *Philocalia*. The Prologues to the Homilies on Exodus and Leviticus, however, have been lost.

## III.

Erasmus expresses no judgment concerning the translation of the twenty-eight Homilies on Numbers; hence we do not know to which translator he attributed them. Cassiodorus, a reliable witness, attributes them to Rufinus in the *Institutions*, in the chapter mentioned elsewhere, chapter I, although he there testifies that there were thirty.

They survive without the translator’s name in volume I, page 182; Aldus, however, makes Jerome their translator, just as he does for the others. The Prologues, or prefaces, of Rufinus to Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers are entirely absent from the printed editions and also from the handwritten manuscripts, unless they are concealed somewhere. The disappearance of them must be blamed on the scribes, so that Jerome might more easily be passed off as translator of these Homilies in place of Rufinus.

Gennadius, in chapter XVII of his *Catalogue*, testifies that Rufinus prefixed a prologue to each of his translations. The fraud would have been unmasked by the Prologue, as indeed it was by that Prologue discovered in the libraries of France, in which Rufinus addresses a certain Donatus at the beginning of his translation of the twenty-eight Homilies on Numbers, which he completed in Sicily as he approached death. From there he himself, together with Melania and her company, watched Rhegium burning in Gothic flames.

Huetius refers more than once to this same Prologue, communicated to him from the Bigot manuscript: in book II, chapter IV, section I, §22; book III, chapter II, section I, §2; section II, §1; and section III, §§1 and 4. Yet Henry Valesius had published it from the same manuscript in his notes on Eusebius’s *History*, book VI, chapter XXXVIII; and Petrus Franciscus Chiffletius had published it in part II, chapter XXV of his *Pauline Illustrated*. Chiffletius nevertheless entitled it, on the basis of the Dijon, Rheims, Clairvaux, Graon, and Clermont manuscripts from which he published it, not “To Ursacius” but “To Donatus.” It is likewise so entitled in Vatican Urbinate manuscript 144.

This error, unnoticed by the learned men Valesius, Huetius, Labbe, Norisius, and Tillemont, occupied the title of an acephalous manuscript in the following manner. Ursacius, Rufinus’s secretary, is mentioned in the Prologue itself. The copyist, through gross ignorance, failed to distinguish him from the person whom Rufinus addresses there, and placed the name Ursacius at the beginning of the Prologue. The Prologue is likewise addressed to Ursacius in manuscript 1405 of Saint Benedict’s College, as recorded in part II, page 136 of the *Catalogue of Manuscripts of England*.

Pearson, in part I, chapter X, page 159 of his *Vindications of Ignatius*, cites a Cambridge manuscript in which the following was read:

> Here begins the Prologue … of Numbers to Ursacius,

with the remaining words plainly erased because of hostility toward Rufinus’s name.

In the manuscripts cited by Chiffletius—though not in the Vatican manuscript—the Rufinian Prologue is attributed to Jerome, but wrongly. Jerome was far away when Alaric was ravaging Italy, as is sufficiently demonstrated by Jerome’s prefaces to Ezekiel, books I and III, and especially by letter XCVI, formerly XVI, now CXXVII, to Principia, where in chapter V he says:

> While these things are taking place in Jebus, a terrifying report is brought from the West: Rome is under siege, and the safety of its citizens is being purchased with gold.

Therefore the Prologue is not Jerome’s, since he was far away, but Rufinus’s, who at that time, in A.D. 409, had fled to Sicily with Pinianus and his family, intending to return to the East. I shall discuss this elsewhere.

In manuscript volume II of the Jacobaean Library’s *Catalogue of the Manuscripts of England*, page 141, the translation of the Homilies on Numbers is likewise attributed to Rufinus.

This translation was Rufinus’s final labor, although, since we are following the order of the books themselves, we discuss it here in advance. Huetius writes aptly about it, §4, page 245:

> From the Prologue which Rufinus prefixed to his translation of Origen’s twenty-eight Homilies on Numbers, which survive to this day, and also from the style itself, it is understood that those who assign another translator rather than Rufinus are gravely mistaken.

In the same Prologue Rufinus says:

> Whatever we found written in the Book of Numbers, whether in homiletic style or among those works called *Extracts*, at your urgent request—he is addressing Donatus, not Ursacius—we collected from different sources and arranged into a single order in the Roman language, as best we could.

Huetius therefore observes that these Homilies were collected from various places and mixed together with scholia by Rufinus:

> This, he says, was worthy of Rufinus as translator.

He thus rightly censures Andreas Rivetus, who in his *Sacred Critic* contends that these Homilies are not the work of Origen but the offspring of a Latin author, because in the twelfth Homily a distinction is noted between *excudere* (“to hammer out”) and *excidere* (“to cut away”). Yet these expressions, Huetius says, must be attributed to the translator’s generosity.

## IV.

Now let us proceed to the twenty-six Homilies on the Book of Joshua, or Jesus Nave, which appear in Grynaeus, volume I, page 284. The heading of the Prologue to Chromatius attributes the translation to Jerome; but both the translation and the Prologue prefixed to it have Rufinus as their author, says Huetius.

Erasmus indeed assigns the translation of this work to Rufinus, but boldly declares that Jerome’s name and the Prologue were fabricated by the scribes. I have no doubt about the former, but I hold Erasmus certainly mistaken in the latter. Before demonstrating this, I shall quote his words:

> Here, says Erasmus, the booksellers’ audacity increased. On the title page of the entire work they were content to substitute Jerome for Rufinus after removing the preface; here they affixed a preface, but one so frigid and so inept that no more certain argument could persuade us that it was not translated by Jerome. Those agreeable fellows thought that no one would doubt this once the preface had been addressed to Chromatius, to whom Jerome sometimes wrote.

I shall omit the rest of his transcription, for I shall return to Erasmus later.

Rejecting Erasmus’s arguments, Huetius takes another course in *Origeniana*, book III, chapter II, section III, §5, page 246. He makes Rufinus the author both of the translation and of the Prologue, but nevertheless accuses the honest man of imposture, as though, realizing that he was generally suspected of Origenism and that his wares were consequently less marketable, he had wished by deceitful arts to mislead unwary readers and had placed the name of his adversary Jerome at the head of the work, thereby also bringing Jerome under suspicion of Origenism, a doctrine of which he had so often accused him.

Huetius adds that Rufinus used similar cunning in the preface to Origen’s commentaries on the Epistle to the Romans. We shall hear this calumny attributed elsewhere to Rufinus by another learned man. But this author, otherwise perceptive, who condemns hasty judgment in Erasmus, himself indulges excessively in empty conjectures.

For how could Rufinus, while Chromatius and Jerome were still alive, have devised so foul and ridiculous a fraud in broad daylight—offering to Chromatius, Bishop of Aquileia, under Jerome’s mask, a translation of Origen’s Homilies that he himself had published—and yet Chromatius, Jerome, and the rest of their associates, indeed Rufinus’s enemies, have been so dull and stupid that they did not smell out so great a fraud or compel Rufinus to pay publicly for his shamelessness?

The weakness of this conjecture is completely dispelled by Gennadius in chapter XVII of his *Catalogue*, where he attributes all the translations of Origen’s Homilies to Rufinus, except those translated by Jerome. These latter, which are known to everyone, are listed by Jerome himself in his *Catalogue*, and by Honorius in book I, chapter CXXXVI. “Those works that have Rufinus as translator,” says Gennadius, “are distinguished by their own Prologue,” thus clearly teaching that Rufinus was accustomed to prefix Prologues to each of his translations.

Accordingly, in Gennadius’s time the translation of the Homilies on Joshua was distinguished under Rufinus’s name. Rufinus therefore did not pass it off under the identity of his adversary Jerome. Rather, later scribes, wishing to deceive mortals by the shadow of so great a name, erased Rufinus, who was ill-regarded because of his conflict with Jerome, and substituted Jerome himself, both in the title and in the Prologue itself, after they had elsewhere torn away Rufinus’s name and entire Prologues from the earlier books.

I think no one is unaware that Chromatius was united in friendship with Jerome no less than with Rufinus. This is evident from the works of both, to such an extent that the great Bishop endeavored to restore the two men, whose spirits had been considerably embittered, to their former concord.

What, then, is surprising if Rufinus dedicated the Homilies on Joshua to the renowned metropolitan of his homeland and to his former teacher in the Christian faith, to whom he had also dedicated Eusebius’s *History*, translated by himself into Latin? For we shall say later that Rufinus undertook the translation of these Homilies after translating Eusebius’s *History*.

In the manuscript Library of Antonio Agustín, published at Tarragona by Philip Mey in 1587, in quarto, manuscript 48 is listed with the following heading:

> Twenty-six Homilies of Origen of Alexandria, also called Adamantius, on the Book of Joshua, with Blessed Jerome or Rufinus as translator, addressed to Chromatius. A parchment book three hundred years old or more, in a square format.

Yet, so that we may seem to omit nothing, let us review Erasmus’s arguments on this matter one by one.

### 1.

He says that the author of the Prologue addresses Chromatius in these words: “O my ever-venerable Chromatius.” Rather, the words are: “O my ever-venerable father Chromatius.” Rufinus addresses the same man in almost these words in the Prologue to Eusebius’s *History*. Nothing, therefore, could be more absurd than Erasmus’s criticism here.

### 2.

It is entirely false that the whole preface is of such a kind that it could be adapted to any work, or that the very argument was drawn from Jerome’s writings and expanded by an impostor with astonishing verbosity. The prefaces prefixed to Rufinus’s works are nothing other than personal letters in which he sends his translations to friends. Their character can therefore be abundantly inferred from the translations themselves, which accompany the individual letters, especially since the letters sent by Rufinus’s friends requesting those translations are no longer available.

What inept, commonplace, or foolish thing—if I may use Erasmus’s words—is contained in these words of the Rufinian Prologue?

> Since you, therefore, my ever-venerable father Chromatius, order and command me to contribute something from the riches and resources of the Greeks toward the edification and construction of the divine tabernacle, I have rendered from Greek into Latin for you, according to the smallness of my abilities, the twenty-six brief discourses on Jesus Nave, which the aged Adamantius delivered extemporaneously in the church.

What could have been expressed that was more serious, more religious, or more appropriate to the subject?

But Rufinus supplies no reason, Erasmus insists, why he undertook to translate this work of Origen. The reason is that he wished to comply with Chromatius, who had requested it from him.

### 3.

Erasmus denies that Origen delivered these brief discourses extemporaneously. Yet this is what Rufinus says, and Huetius establishes it by explicit arguments in book III, section II, chapter IV, §4. There he judges that Origen’s Homilies were partly written out after reflection and partly recited by him extemporaneously.

### 4.

The remaining part of Erasmus’s criticism, which he repeatedly directs against the style of the Prologue, proves not so much that it is not Jerome’s as that it is Rufinus’s. Rufinus always thought and spoke modestly of himself, repeatedly admitting that, because of his long residence among the Greeks, he had grown sluggish through thirty years of neglect in writing Latin.

We therefore see that he published his works in a popular rather than an elegant style. Let us hear the final words with which he concludes the Prologue itself:

> Let the whole of this, then, depend upon your judgment. If there is anything that can please, let it belong to the author; for we do not think it right to seize what others have acquired through labor and apply it to our own praise. But if the force of the meanings is made harsh by an uncultivated style, attribute this either to me or—to speak with your permission—to yourself, who seek from the unlearned a work that ought to be entrusted to the learned.

Thus not only does the translation of the Homilies on Joshua belong to Rufinus, on which Erasmus and Huetius equally agree, but so does the Prologue. The former denies this; the latter affirms it in such a way as to suggest that Rufinus fraudulently substituted it for Jerome’s, from the fifteenth Homily on Joshua, page 315, “with Rufinus as translator.”

Gratianus transferred a fragment of it into *Cause* XXXIII, Question I, chapter I. Moreover, the Magdeburg Centuriators, making Erasmus’s inept criticism even more inept, took what Erasmus wrote about Rufinus’s Prologue and published it as though it had been said about Origen’s Homilies, as if Erasmus had denied that the Homilies belonged to Origen. Nevertheless, other writers of the same stamp imprudently embraced the Centuriators’ opinion.

But Joannes Dallaeus ventured something even greater in book II, chapter XLI of *On the Writings of Dionysius*, where he attempts to tear apart Rufinus’s translations of Origen in every respect—certainly for no other reason than that he knew them often to contradict the novelty of his own doctrines. Yet a heterodox man usually does nothing other than boast that he is exposing the very license which he accuses Rufinus of having used in translating the writings of the Greeks.

## V.

The present occasion now requires me to show that the nine Homilies on Judges, in Grynaeus’s edition, volume I, page 377, about which Erasmus is completely silent, likewise had Rufinus as translator. Rufinus himself explicitly testifies to this in the concluding section of his exposition of the Epistle to the Romans, page 634; Huetius likewise notes it in book III, chapter II, section III, §5, page 246.

I am certain that the scribes, through their wickedness, removed the Prologue from these Homilies so that they might more easily be substituted for Jerome’s. For that reason, anyone who would search it out for us, together with all the others that suffered the same misfortune, in ancient manuscripts would earn great gratitude from us.

After the Homilies on Judges, there are found among Origen’s writings nine Homilies on the Psalter of David: five on Psalm XXXVI, two on Psalm XXXVII, and likewise two on Psalm XXXVIII. Constantius Hierotheus published these as translated by Rufinus and addressed, together with a Prologue, to Apronianus, along with other works of Adamantius on the New Testament, preceded by an Apology for Origen by Jacobus Merlinus, at Venice, by Lazarus de Soardis, in 1516, in folio.

They appear there after the Homilies on Luke, folio 87, and also survive in Vatican Urbinate manuscript 65, folio 34, part 2. Merlin had published Origen’s Latin works divided into four parts at Paris in 1512, in two folio volumes; that edition was later reprinted there in 1519, 1522, and 1530.

Erasmus, however, who inserted these same Homilies in volume I, page 440 of Grynaeus’s edition, hesitates in his frequently mentioned criticism over whether they reflect Origen’s character and phrasing. He thinks they come closer to Chrysostom and wonders whether they were the work of a Latin author, or whether Rufinus, in his customary manner, contaminated them as translator.

Huetius rightly disapproves of these and other things arrogantly and perversely said by Erasmus in book III, chapter II, section III, §6, page 247. He judges that Erasmus allowed his critical faculty too much freedom when he writes of the translator:

> Nor does the man who supplies the preface profess that he simply translated these Homilies as they existed among the Greeks, nor does he there state the author’s name.

Yet, Huetius says, Erasmus should have remembered that authors’ names are generally placed at the beginnings of works, and therefore Rufinus, who supplied the preface, had no need to profess that he had translated these Homilies from Origen, since the title itself proclaimed this.

This is what Huetius says. He considers even more futile the argument drawn from the concluding section, in which the author’s name was not expressed. Rufinus was discussing the works of Origen that he had rendered into Latin; he had named Origen himself and had mentioned his Homilies on Genesis, Exodus, and Leviticus. He later adds:

> Those works on the Book of Jesus Nave, the Book of Judges, and Psalms thirty-six, thirty-seven, and thirty-eight, which we have rendered plainly as we found them.

From this we can readily understand that these works, like those mentioned immediately before, belong to Origen. It would certainly have been superfluous and burdensome to append his name to each one.

If this omission of Origen’s name makes the author doubtful here, why did Erasmus, who doubted the author of the Homilies on the Psalms, have no doubt at all concerning the author of the Homilies on the Book of Judges? The grounds for doubt were equal in both cases, since Origen’s name is omitted in both.

Thus, in substance, Huetius; and before him Genebrardus in chapter V of his *Collections on the Life of Origen*, which he prefixed to his Latin edition of Origen’s works. Some material relevant to our subject must be transferred here from that work.

Genebrardus is speaking of Erasmus’s criticisms:

> In them, he says, he indulged his irritation in his customary manner, so that you may rightly demand from him sometimes greater attentiveness and sometimes firmer judgment. For example, he thinks that the Homilies on Psalm XXXVI are not Origen’s. Moreover, after noting that the style has the flavor of Chrysostom, he immediately adds that he suspects the writer was a Latin. Reconcile these statements, if you can, when Chrysostom’s expression is thoroughly Greek.

Furthermore, it is evident that they are Origen’s, because in the second Homily he attacks the Valentinians, as is his custom; and in the third Homily he cites the passage of Paul, 1 Corinthians IV, in the same words with which, in the sixth Homily on Exodus and the fourth on Numbers, he customarily rebukes those who clung to the letter while neglecting the spiritual sense, and proves from the verse, “I have not seen the righteous forsaken,” and so forth, that the spiritual sense must necessarily be maintained. Thus, in order to preserve the literal truth of the verse, it is clear that he is speaking of abandonment in spiritual matters, not bodily ones.

The third Homily names Valentinus, Marcion, and Basilides, against whom Origen struggles almost continually in his other books. Finally, the style, argument, and Origenian manner show that Erasmus’s judgments were rash. I mention this because of the itching ears of those men who immediately think that whatever they understand to have been scraped or bitten by someone must be destroyed.

This is what Genebrardus says. Nevertheless, the Magdeburg Centuriators, Robert Cook, and William Perkins do not hesitate, out of empty zeal, to expunge these Homilies from the catalogue of Origen’s genuine works.

Rufinus testifies in the Prologue that he undertook their translation as a favor to his beloved son Apronianus. Since it is brief, I shall transfer it here from volume II, page 439 of Grynaeus’s edition of Origen’s works:

> Since the entire exposition of Psalms thirty-six, thirty-seven, and thirty-eight is moral, setting forth certain principles of a more reformed life and teaching now the path of conversion and repentance, now the path of purification and progress, for that reason I have translated it into Latin for you, Apronianus, my dearest son, arranged as a single body in nine brief discourses, which the Greeks call Homilies, so that you might have collected within one book a discourse wholly directed toward the correction or advancement of conduct.
>
> This reading will provide the following benefit: without the reader’s labor, its meaning will lie open, so that the simplicity of life may be taught with clear understanding and in simple speech. Thus the prophecy may reach not only men but also devout women and cultivate simple minds, lest perhaps my devout daughter, your sister in Christ, be ungrateful toward our work if she always finds it burdensome to her understanding because of the difficulty of its questions. For even the human body could not have consisted solely of nerves and bones, unless divine providence had woven into them either the softness of flesh or the gentle comforts of fat.

Huetius, and after him Natalis Alexander, in century III, chapter IV, article II, make Rufinus the translator of a single Homily on the First Book of Kings, having rejected Rivetus. Cassiodorus likewise testifies that Rufinus translated the exposition of the *Song of Songs*. In chapter V of his *Divine Lessons* we read:

> In two Homilies on the *Song of Songs*, the same holy Jerome, that outstanding multiplier of the Latin language, provided us with Origen’s exposition in a sufficiently acceptable translation, as was his custom. Rufinus, likewise, the most eloquent translator, explained it in three Latin books, adding certain passages, up to that command which says: “Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards.”

In Grynaeus’s edition, volume I, the work begins on page 356 and ends on page 492. The customary Prologues, however, are lacking.

Rufinus divided the work, which is a continuous exposition, and its ten so-called books, into four Homilies. Pearson also discusses these in part I, chapter IX, page 111 of his *Vindications of Ignatius*.

Erasmus, however, having entirely failed to identify the author of this work, and still less its translator, conflates the two and thinks that it was written by a Latin—an elegantly learned and eloquent man, certainly not a Greek. Since this man, out of modesty, did not wish to attach his name, the scribes prefixed the name of Ambrose.

Thus Erasmus, immediately followed by the Magdeburg Centuriators in century III, chapter X, William Perkins in his *Problem*, and others whom we shall soon name. Such is the force of preconceived opinion against Rufinus that Erasmus, ignorant of the translator of these Homilies, praised the work itself to such an extent that he seemed to regard it as not translated into Latin by anyone, but as having been composed in its entirety by a Latin author.

Yet we have produced Cassiodorus’s most weighty testimony that it belongs to Origen and was rendered into Latin by Rufinus. Rufinus did add certain things from his own resources; hence Rivetus, Robert Cook, and that class of pseudo-critical heterodox writers seized the opportunity to deprive Origen of this exposition, wrongly attributing to the author what belongs to the translator.

Huetius collected from it the popular formulas and expressions especially characteristic of Rufinus, in book III, chapter II, section III, §7, page 249.

The Prologue of Rufinus was lost for the same reason as the others, like the one on Numbers, discovered long ago but never previously reproduced in the Latin editions. The matter is also confirmed by an old manuscript of Pierre Pithou, entitled:

> Here begins Origen’s Treatise on the *Song of Songs*, translated into Latin by Rufinus.
