For this reason Johannes Martianay, who had incorrectly attributed the book to an uncertain translator, placed it in volume V of Jerome’s works, page 603.

Since these things are so, it is of no consequence that in certain manuscripts this work is attributed to Jerome and Ambrose, as Huetius properly observes.

## VI.

Thus far we have discussed the Origenian writings on the Old Testament which Rufinus brought back from the East into Italy and, at the request of his friends, gave to the Latin world. It remains now to discuss the Origenian works concerned with explaining the New Testament, which Rufinus likewise rendered into Latin, although in the commonly circulated editions they are transmitted under other names.

First among these are the fifteen books of the *Commentaries on Saint Paul’s Epistle to the Romans*. This work, divided into ten books, Rufinus undertook to make available in Latin at Heraclius’s urging, at the very time when he was engaged in translating the Homilies, whose sequence he had to interrupt in order to oblige his friend. For in the Prologue he says:

> While I wished, carried in a small vessel, to hug the shore of a tranquil coast and gather little fish from the pools of the Greeks, you compel me, brother Heraclius, to spread my sails into the deep. You persuade me, having abandoned the work in ten books which I had undertaken in transferring the Homilies of the aged Adamantius, to explain in our language his fifteen volumes in which he expounded Paul’s Epistle to the Romans. In these, while pursuing the Apostle’s meaning, he is carried into so deep a sea that there is great danger in following him there, lest I be overwhelmed by the vastness of his thoughts, as though by the monstrous violence of the waves.
>
> Moreover, you do not consider that my breath is too weak to fill his magnificent trumpet of speech. But beyond all these difficulties is the fact that the books themselves have been interpolated. For in almost all libraries, through some circumstance that is certainly unknown, several volumes from the body of the work are missing. To supply these in the Latin work and provide a continuous whole is beyond my ability; but, as you believe—since you demand these things of me—it may perhaps be a divine commission.
>
> You add, lest anything be lacking from my labors, that I should abridge this entire body of fifteen volumes, which the Greek language extended to nearly forty thousand verses, or even more, and, if possible, compress it to half that length. Hard commands indeed, imposed as though by one unwilling to know the weight of this work. Nevertheless, I shall undertake it, if perhaps the Lord, through your prayers, makes possible what seems impossible to me as a human being.
>
> But now, if you please, let us hear Origen himself, and how he directs the preface to the work he has undertaken.

Thus far Rufinus. Tillemont praises his sincerity and good faith in this labor, vol. III, p. 558. The devout man frankly acknowledges that, in transferring these Homilies, he exercised freedom to add material and to supply lacunae from his own resources.

Theophilus Salodianus, of the order of the Observant Friars, as they are called—a man about whom Lucas Wadding is silent in his writings on the Minorites—found an Origenian work in the library of the monastery at Fiesole, under the name of Jerome the translator, struggling against bookworms and moths. He published it at Venice, by Simon de Luere, in 1506, in folio, and dedicated it to Alexander of Portus, a Vicentine of the equestrian order, as though leaping for joy over the discovery of a treasure. Bernardinus Benalius later reprinted the work there, in 1512, in folio. Erasmus inserted it into his collection of Origen’s works, vol. II, p. 455 of Grynaeus’s edition, leaving Jerome’s name on the title page, although in the censure prefixed to vol. I he denies that the work belongs to him and attacks Rufinus as its translator.

It is preferable, however, to hear Erasmus himself:

> Here the booksellers displayed magnificent impudence, both in the preface and in the conclusion, substituting Jerome for Rufinus—in other words, attempting to pass glass off to the reader instead of a gem—and in this way they have indeed deceived the unwary. For the preface could somehow appear to be Jerome’s; but in the conclusion they reveal themselves, like mice, by their own judgment.

From the same conclusion he then adduces words that reveal Rufinus as the author, although they carry Jerome’s name, stitched onto them by forgers. This is shown by the Thuani codex, whose words Cotelerius quotes in his judgment on the books of Clement’s *Recognitions*, among the works of the Holy Fathers who flourished in apostolic times, p. 484 of the second edition, 1698. I shall gladly reproduce those words here, since in more than one place they correct the common edition:

> After this, indeed, another work calls us—one formerly assigned to me, but now urged upon me with greater force by the blessed bishop Gaudentius: namely, the books of Clement, bishop of Rome, companion and successor of the Apostles, concerning the *Recognitions*, so that they may be translated into Latin. In this work I know well that I shall undertake labor upon labor, receiving a multiplied burden. Yet I shall satisfy my friends in this matter. I shall give it my name as a title, while the designation of the author nevertheless remains; for it will be entitled “Rufinus’s Clement.”

He immediately adds that he will proceed to translate the remaining works of Origen:

> And if the Lord permits me to complete this, we shall return to those works, and, in accordance with your wishes, say something, God permitting, on the books of Numbers and Deuteronomy. For these alone, from the Pentateuch and from the remaining Epistles of the Apostle Paul, are what, under the Lord’s protection, we owe you and are able to provide.

In the margin of this conclusion, p. 634 of Grynaeus’s edition, there is the following note:

> From this alone it may be gathered which books of Origen Rufinus brought into the Latin world.

Quite correctly so: he enumerates one by one everything he had translated and intended to translate. Elsewhere we shall hear that Rufinus actually translated Clement’s work into Latin.

Erasmus writes again:

> This passage should have been erased if they wished to persuade us that Jerome was the translator of this work. For it is clear both from Gennadius and from Rufinus’s own preface that Rufinus, not Jerome, translated Clement’s books of the *Recognitions*; and Rufinus also writes elsewhere to this Gaudentius. The booksellers therefore achieve nothing by repeatedly inserting Jerome’s name. Indeed, this diligence in repeating it increases suspicion of fraud.

He then cites a fragment from Rufinus’s conclusion which the booksellers corrupted, in which Rufinus speaks but under Jerome’s name, falsely attached by forgers.

Because he failed to notice this, Joannes Carolus Bovius, in the preface to his Latin edition of Clement’s *Apostolic Constitutions*, published at Venice by Jordanus Ziletus in 1563, in quarto, and Franciscus Turrianus, in the Greek prolegomena to the same *Constitutions*, published by the same printer in the same year and format, p. 7, believed that Jerome himself, and no other, was actually speaking. For this reason Jacobus Ussher corrects them in his *Dissertation on the Letters of Ignatius*, chap. VII.

The words of Pseudo-Jerome, or rather Rufinus, are these, p. 634:

> For they say to me concerning what you write: “Since many of your works are in circulation, give the title your own name and write, for example, ‘Jerome’s [read: Rufinus’s] Explanations of the Epistle to the Romans,’” …

And shortly afterward:

> I shall indeed satisfy my friends in this matter.

I have already quoted the rest.

Erasmus further says:

> There is also some argument in the fact that, to oblige Ursacius, at whose command he undertook this labor, he translated Basil’s *Rule*, and, to oblige Gaudentius, whom he mentions here, he translated Clement.

What Erasmus says about Ursacius is a lapse of memory in a man who was not always exact. Rufinus dedicates that work to Heraclius, not Ursacius; and he dedicated Basil’s *Rule* not to Ursacius but to Urseius. Ursacius, or Ursatius, was Rufinus’s secretary, as Rufinus himself testifies in the Prologue to the Homilies on Numbers, which, as I have already said, he headed with the name Donatus.

Both the prologue and the conclusion, in every edition, name Heraclius, including Erasmus’s edition. Manuscript codices support this: the Vatican Urbinas 62, fol. 96, and codex 1247 of Guillelmus Laudus, listed in the *Catalogue of the Manuscripts of England*, vol. I, p. 68. There an epistle of Rufinus to Heraclius is recorded, which we do not believe to be different from the prologue under discussion.

To reduce the matter to a few words: Erasmus’s observation is entirely correct in this respect, that no one ever charged Jerome with truncating, reversing, altering, or making his own what he had translated from another work. Yet Rufinus reveals that he himself was charged with this in the passage cited above, which through the booksellers’ fraud was wrongly attributed to Jerome.

Erasmus should also have observed that this deserves to be credited to Rufinus as no small praise, rather than as evidence of bad faith: he was not ashamed to confess openly that he had done these things whenever he had done them. For an honest man, he did not wish to deceive Roman readers by selling them what purported to be a faithful and simple translation of the Greeks. Rather, as befitted a truthful and conscientious man, he candidly warned them that from the Greek works—then circulating everywhere and passing through everyone’s hands—he had extracted, at the request of his friends, certain selections and abridgments.

Indeed, works hastily derived from Greek writings and communicated to the Latin peoples over a period of ten years, after his return to Italy, could hardly have been anything other than selections and abridgments, apart from other works which he composed himself during that same period. Therefore the very feature for which recent critics blame Rufinus ought to be counted to his credit.

Erasmus consequently should not have become so enraged when Rufinus frankly admits, in the conclusion to the *Commentaries on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans*, that he altered Origen’s Homilies on Genesis, Exodus, and especially Leviticus in such a way that what Origen had spoken popularly for the purpose of edification, Rufinus transferred under the appearance of exposition. Erasmus attacks this with an obelus:

> Cleverly indeed he distinguishes edification from exposition, as though exposition did not concern the edification of the hearers.

Rufinus’s words in the conclusion, p. 654, are these:

> Thus far, dictating on the Epistle to the Romans as best we could, we have labored with very great effort and expenditure of time. For I confess, dearest brother Heraclius, that while wishing to satisfy your desires, I almost forgot the commandment which says: “Do not lift a burden above your strength.”
>
> Yet even in the other works which, at your insistence—or rather because you demanded the daily measure of labor—we translated into Latin, we did not lack very great toil. We wished to supply what Origen had delivered extemporaneously in the church’s auditorium, not so much with the intention of exposition as of edification, as we did in the Homilies, or rather the brief discourses, on Genesis and Exodus, and especially in the book of Leviticus, which he dictated in a homiletic style, whereas we transferred them under the appearance of exposition.
>
> We undertook the labor of completing what was lacking so that questions which had been raised and then left unresolved—as often happens in his homiletic manner of speaking—would not produce weariness in the Latin reader. For what we wrote on the book of Joshua, on Judges, and on Psalms 36, 37, and 38, we rendered simply as we found it and translated without very great labor.
>
> Although, therefore, we also labored in the other works mentioned above to supply what he had omitted, in this work on the Epistle to the Romans an immense and immeasurable labor has fallen upon us, for the reasons which we set out in the preface. Yet we shall be glad to have submitted to these labors, provided that, unlike what we have experienced elsewhere, hostile minds do not repay our vigils with insults, our studies with detractions, and our labors with snares.
>
> For we are now subjected to a new kind of accusation. They say to me …

I have already quoted the rest.

Rufinus certainly did not deserve to be beaten by the harsh Erasmus for the meaning of these words. I am even more surprised that not only Erasmus but also Huetius, otherwise a man worthy of the highest praise, who supports Erasmus, should attack Rufinus in book III, chapter II, section III, § 15, p. 253, because he shortened this same work in some places and expanded it in others.

Yet Rufinus expressly states in his prologue to Heraclius that the books in the library codices which he consulted had been interpolated and mutilated. This is why he himself abridged and supplemented them. In addition, Heraclius had requested that he compress the fifteen volumes and reduce them to half their length. Yet Erasmus calls Rufinus’s having done precisely this an act of shamelessness.

I do not know how Johannes Martianaeus could have believed that this prologue of Rufinus to Heraclius was Jerome’s, and could have inserted it among Jerome’s letters, which he rearranged in a new order, vol. IV, no. 107, p. 808.

Tillemont, vol. XII, p. 308, thought that this Heraclius was none other than Heraclius the Deacon, whom Saint Jerome mentions in Letter 100, formerly 33, to Castrucius.

The very words of Rufinus, which I have already quoted above and which are full of candor, piety, and modesty, sufficiently and abundantly refute Erasmus’s judgment. I say nothing meanwhile about Huetius, who adds his own contribution to Erasmus’s criticism—not blaming the recent booksellers, but Rufinus himself—for having attributed this Origenian translation to Jerome. According to Huetius, Rufinus, through cunning and envy, as he puts it, omitted his own name in order to avoid the discredit attached to the deed—the name of Origen being then in bad repute—and to shift the blame onto Jerome, by whom he had often been attacked on account of Origenism, while pretending that what had been done by bad arts was the result of modesty.

I shall not spend more time dissipating these charges, since to recite such rashly written statements is already to refute them—especially when the ancient manuscripts cited above also give the name not of Jerome but of Rufinus the translator. Cassiodorus’s explicit authority in chapter VIII of *On the Institution of Divine Literature* supports us in these words:

> Origen explained Paul’s Epistle to the Romans in twenty books in the Greek language; but the aforementioned Rufinus, reducing them to ten books, translated them into Latin, still at considerable length.

What could be said more clearly against Huetius? Nothing at all.

## VII.

The foregoing shows that recent critics unfairly assail Rufinus, when gratitude ought to be returned to him for the outstanding service he rendered to ecclesiastical literature among the Latins. For after most of Origen’s Greek works had been lost, at least those which Rufinus rendered into Latin have reached us through his care and labor, like a few planks surviving from a great shipwreck.

Moreover, in vol. II of Origen’s works, p. 425, there are ten Homilies which the editor Erasmus states that he collected from various places into one volume. In his censure he says that some are not Origen’s but the work of a Latin author, while the rest were shamelessly corrupted by Rufinus. But he does not identify which they are.

Of these, I, III, IV, V, VI, VIII, and IX are on Matthew; II is on John; X is on Mary Magdalene; VIII is on the Epiphany of the Lord.

Lest I omit anything, Johannes Dallaeus and David Blondel also make Rufinus the translator of Origen’s Homilies on Luke. But both are refuted by Pearson in *Vindiciae Ignatianae*, part I, chap. IX, p. 118. Jerome translated those Homilies, although in Vatican Urbinas codex 65 they are attributed to Rufinus. There is no need to dwell at greater length on this matter, since Jerome acknowledges the translation as his own, while Rufinus criticizes it as Jerome’s; Pearson accurately observed this.

# CHAPTER VIII

I. Rufinus dedicates to Apronianus eight Homilies of Basil the Great and ten short works of Gregory of Nazianzus which he rendered into Latin.  
II. Some remarks are offered on these works of Gregory.  
III. Rufinus sends Apronianus the sayings of Sixtus the Pythagorean, translated into Latin, to be given to Apronianus’s sister Ayama.  
IV. Sixtus’s period, religion, and standing among the ancients.  
V. Rufinus was ill-treated on account of his translation of Sixtus, though he was no longer alive.  
VI. Why the Sixtine book was rejected by Gelasius I among the apocrypha. The opinions of various authors are presented.  
VII. Sayings of Sixtus frequently cited by the Greeks, and also by the Latins.  
VIII. His manuscripts and editions.

## I.

Rufinus, who while living in Rome had translated Origen’s Homilies on the Psalms into Latin at Apronianus’s request, later, when settled at Aquileia, also labored on the works of other authors, in order to win the favor of that same exceptionally dear friend.

First among these are the eight Homilies of Saint Basil, Bishop of Caesarea. Rufinus himself testifies in book XI, chapter IX of his *Ecclesiastical History* that he translated them into Latin:

> From the writings of Gregory and Basil we transferred into Latin nearly ten brief discourses by each of them, as well as Basil’s *Institutes for Monks*.

He says “nearly ten” because he transferred ten of Nazianzenus’s discourses into Latin, but only eight of Basil’s.

Labbe, in vol. II of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 310, and Cave, following him, speaking only in general terms, reported that certain works translated by Rufinus could be found in the ancient Latin editions of Basil’s and Nazianzenus’s works. Apart from the *Rule for Monks*, however, I was unable to find anything of Basil’s published from Rufinus’s translation.

The Vatican Library nevertheless supplied me with the parchment Urbinas codex 67, where on fol. 201 the eight Basilian Homilies translated by Rufinus are found together with a Prologue to Apronianus. Julian Garnerius later published these from the royal and Colbert codices at Paris in 1722, together with the works of Saint Basil, vol. II, p. 713.

Rufinus writes to Apronianus in the prologue:

> Long ago, dearest son Apronianus, you had asked me to translate certain works into Latin. I did part of this while I was in Rome; but now I have added something further. I have therefore translated these eight brief homiletic books of blessed Basil.

He wrote this away from Rome, namely in his homeland. Thus he translated eight, not ten, Homilies of Basil.

In later centuries, whenever these writings of Basil were praised among the Latins, I have no doubt that they were being praised from Rufinus’s translation. In this way it is clear that Origen, Eusebius, the Nicene canons, Nazianzenus, Sixtus, and likewise Basil’s Rules were frequently cited from Rufinus’s translations.

In the new edition of Saint Augustine’s works, after the beginning of vol. IV, there is a preface of Saint Basil to his *Commentary on the Psalms*, formerly attributed to Saint Augustine. The editors of the new edition assign it to Rufinus the translator. I see the same attribution in the codex of the Thuana Library, vol. II, p. 456.

This is the preface to the first Homily of Saint Basil, translated into Latin by Rufinus. Cardinal Thomasius of pious memory prefixed it to both the first and second editions of the Psalter, pp. 11 and 43.

Gregory of Nazianzus follows Basil immediately. Rufinus likewise dedicated to his Apronianus the short works of Gregory which he had rendered into Latin. Apronianus had requested their translation from his friend as Rufinus was departing for Aquileia, as Rufinus himself testifies in the epistle preceding the *Apologeticus*, where he addresses Apronianus as follows:

> When I was leaving Rome, dearest son, you strongly charged me to devote some work to you even while absent, and not to let the necessity of my departure restrain me from my customary studies. You asked me to translate Gregory of Nazianzus into Latin.

Thus Rufinus, who in his *History* mentioned that he had transferred approximately ten of Gregory’s discourses into Latin, as I have already said.

Johannes Adelphus Mulingus published them at Strasbourg in 1508, with the following title:

> These are the ten books of the divine Gregory of Nazianzus contained in this codex:
>
> 1. Book I, the *Apologeticus*.  
> 2. On the Epiphanies, or the Nativity of the Lord.  
> 3. On the Lights, which concerns the second Epiphany.  
> 4. Book I, On Faith.  
> 5. On the Nicene Faith, Pentecost, and the Holy Spirit.  
> 6. On Himself, after returning from the countryside.  
> 7. On the Words of Jeremiah, in the Presence of the Emperor.  
> 8. On the Reconciliation and Unity of Monks.  
> 9. On the Devastation by Hail.  
> 10. On the Arians: that it is not always permissible to dispute publicly about God.

In vol. I of the Paris edition of Nazianzenus’s works, published by Carolus Morellus in 1630, these short works—or rather discourses—are I, XII, XV, XVII, XXVIII, XXXIII, XXXVIII, XXXIX, XLIV, and L, at pp. 1, 190, 224, 265, 472, 529, 613, 624, 705, 727, and 736. The translator there, however, is not Rufinus but Jacobus Billus.

This shows that Julian Garnerius was mistaken in the preface to vol. II of Saint Basil’s works, p. 87, where he says:

> Today, neither in printed editions nor in ancient books, are more than seven or eight Orations of Nazianzenus translated by Rufinus extant.

At the end of the Strasbourg edition we read:

> Here ends the book of Blessed Gregory of Nazianzus, translated by a certain Rufinus, printed at Strasbourg by Johannes Knoblouch in the year of the Lord 1508, in quarto.

The editor Adelphus dedicates the book to Georgius Bohem, of Mainz, and Johannes Flamingus, priests of the churches of Roppard. He makes clear to them that he was connected by friendship with Giovanni Francesco Pico, Count of Mirandola, and that he was bringing Rufinus’s writings into the light lest they finally perish.

As we have seen, Labbe says nothing specifically about this edition of Rufinus, nor about the other edition which he published together with other works of Nazianzenus from the translations of Petrus Mosellanus and Willibald Pirckheimer, at Leipzig in 1522, in octavo.

Here Petrus Franciscus Chiffletius detains us. In his *Vindications of Vigilius of Thapsus*, p. 57, he denies that the fourth short work, *On Faith*, which alone survives in Latin, belongs to Nazianzenus. In this matter he calls Frederick Morellus as his supporter, vol. I of the Paris edition of Nazianzenus’s works, 1609, in the notes to Oration XLIX, p. 726. To Morellus, neither the discourse *On Faith* nor that *On the Nicene Faith* appears to be Gregory’s offspring; indeed, they do not seem to belong to any Greek author, but to a Latin one, although an ancient one, because the work cites the Old Latin version expressed from the Greek Septuagint.

Andreas Rivet, having stolen Morellus’s judgment, passed it off as his own in book III, chapter XXI of *Sacred Criticism*. These are roughly the arguments which easily persuaded Chiffletius—although he lacked the support of manuscript authority and ancient testimonies—that neither work, *On Faith* or *On the Nicene Faith*, belonged to Gregory.

He even thought this explained why, in the Dijon codex containing Gregory’s books translated by Rufinus, the prologue to Apronianus was prefixed only to the *Apologeticus*. Chiffletius published that prologue from the same codex.

This reasoning of the learned man is of little weight. Since all the Gregorian short works translated by Rufinus were bound together, one prologue, not several, ought properly to have been prefixed to them all. Theophilus Raynaudus rightly observed this in *On Bad and Good Books*, part I, Question X, vol. XI of his works, p. 269, col. 2. Yet there he falsely assigns this book *On Faith* to Gregory of Nyssa, supposedly on the authority of Cassiodorus.

Moreover, in the same prologue of Rufinus, prefixed to the *Apologeticus*, the first of the short works, not only the *Apologeticus* but Gregory’s writings in general are mentioned:

> You asked me to translate Gregory of Nazianzus into Latin,

Rufinus says at the beginning. At the end, however:

> Read this Gregory, then, without any scruple whatsoever.

Whoever professes to give us Gregory must be understood to give us not one *Apologeticus* alone, but also his other works under the same prologue.

Therefore, although Gennadius states only generally in chapter XVII of his *Catalogue* that Rufinus gave the writings of Gregory of Nazianzus, a man of the greatest eloquence, to the Latins, it is nevertheless easy to determine which works he gave: namely, all those which in the Strasbourg edition follow the same prologue.

For these correspond excellently to the number ten which Rufinus himself recorded in his *History*. Rufinus’s explicit testimony must be preferred above all the manuscripts, including those of Nicolaus Faber and Dijon, in which, according to Chiffletius, the fourth and fifth books of Gregory—*On Faith* and *On the Nicene Faith*—are absent, so that eight, not ten, short works bear there the name of Rufinus the translator.

In Morellus’s edition these are the eight Orations, in the following order: I, XXXVIII, XXXIX, XLIV, XVII, XII, XV, and XXVIII.

Jacobus Ussher, in his *Dissertation on the Symbol of the Roman Church*, p. 30, says that some attribute the short work *On the Nicene Faith* to Athanasius. Although it is listed in manuscript collections of Nazianzenus’s works with Rufinus as translator, Ussher says that Patrick Young showed him one copy in which the work was absent. Ussher therefore thought this was because it had neither been written by Gregory nor translated into Latin by Rufinus.

The Passionea Library contains the works of Saint Gregory of Nazianzus in Latin only, published at Basel by Johannes Herwagen in 1555, in folio, with manuscript notes by Latinius Latinius. On p. 392, in the margin of the treatise *On Faith*, Latinius wrote, with Rufinus as translator:

> We do not today find these works, which have been added before the letters from Rufinus, in the Greek codices—that is, in those printed before the year 1550.

The note seems also to include the treatise *On the Nicene Faith*, translated by Rufinus, which appears on p. 403 and is followed by Nazianzenus’s letters.

But it is not important that these short works cannot be found written in Greek, as though this were sufficient to deny them to Gregory. Many works rendered into Latin by Rufinus and others survive without their Greek codices. The argument carries equal weight when it is said that some codices contain more Rufinian works of Gregory and others fewer. It is enough that all ten occur in some copies, and that the codex from which Adelphus produced his edition contained the same number.

Rufinus used in his translations the passages of Holy Scripture from the edition of the Septuagint, then worn by everyone’s hands, rather than Jerome’s Vulgate, which he had criticized. The Greeks themselves used the Septuagint version of the Bible; he likewise taught the Latin translators to use the Septuagint version. Thus what Morellus brought forward against the Rufinian version actually supports it.

## II.

These translations of Rufinus were held in such high regard among Westerners that testimonies were frequently drawn from them. In the Church’s office of prayers, on the feast of the Most Holy Trinity, the second lesson of the third Nocturn is recited from the treatise *On Faith*, under this title:

> Homily of Saint Gregory of Nazianzus in the treatise *On Faith*.

This same treatise, which Augustine cites under the name of Gregory of the East in *Epistle* 111, formerly 111, chapter II, § 10, was concealed under Ambrose’s name in all editions of Saint Ambrose’s works and also in several manuscripts, bearing the title:

> On Orthodox Faith against the Arians; elsewhere, On the Divinity and Consubstantiality of the Son.

This moved the editors of the new edition to acknowledge in the Appendix to vol. II, p. 343, that the work should be assigned to Rufinus the translator. A fragment torn from it had entered the works of Saint Hilary, appended to the book *On the Divinity of the Father and the Son*, p. 1174 of the new edition, and also among the sermons attributed to Saint Augustine, specifically the sermon now numbered CXIII in the Appendix to the new edition of his works, vol. V, part II, p. 206.

Godefridus Hermannus, however, in his *Explanations to the Life of Saint Ambrose*, p. 30, and Quesnellus, in Dissertation XIV, § 7, on Leo the Great, assign the treatise *On Faith* to Gregory the Baetican. Caspar Barthius, by contrast, makes it another work of the Baetican, published long ago and interpolated by a certain Faustinus.

But enough of this. I shall now proceed to the remaining matters.

Leo the Great, in *Epistle* 134, formerly 97, to Leo Augustus, chapter IX, praised, from Rufinus’s translation, the second book of Gregory of Nazianzus—namely Oration XXXVIII, the Homily or discourse *On the Epiphany*, elsewhere *On the Nativity*. Vigilius of Thapsus, in book V against Eutyches, chapter XXIII, p. 79, quotes a fragment of it from the same translator.

I am therefore easily led to believe that Pope Gelasius, in the Roman Council of 494, referred to Gregory’s short works from Rufinus’s translation when, in his *Decree on the Books of the Holy Fathers to Be Received*, he designated them in these words:

> Likewise, the short works of blessed Gregory, Bishop of Nazianzus.

Nazianzus wrote very many works. Yet in Gelasius’s time ten short works translated by Rufinus were circulating among the Latins. Therefore, by the designation “short works,” Gelasius indicated these ten, which had shortly before been praised by Leo, his predecessor.

It is a great distinction for Rufinus that his Latin translation was approved by the Supreme Pontiff in the Roman Council.

Let us also offer some information about the manuscripts of Rufinus’s Gregorian volumes. Vatican codices 4259 and 5259 contain a Gregorian short work, or Book II, with Rufinus as translator. It is *On the Nativity of the Lord*.

Urbinas 72 contains the *Apologeticus*, together with the prologue and the other short works, but not *On the Nicene Faith* or *On the Arians*. Palatinus 566 likewise contains the *Apologeticus* with the prologue. This short work is also preserved in the Library of Santa Croce in the Sessorian Field, after the *Pastoral Rule* of Saint Gregory, codex 109. It is likewise found in the Bodleian Library among the manuscripts of John Selden, no. 3423.

In codex Norvicensis 9333 the remaining short works are found under the prologue to Apronianus. I learned this from the catalogue of the manuscripts of that library.

Philippus Labbeus says in the *Lesser Library*, Supplement VIII, p. 274, that several of Gregory’s Orations from Rufinus’s translation are found in royal codex 313.

Manuscript works of Nazianzus translated by Rufinus, in folio, were recently still found in the Baluzian Library, according to its catalogue, vol. III, p. 24. They later passed into the royal library.

## III.

Besides the books already discussed, Rufinus also dedicated to Apronianus the sayings of Sixtus the Pythagorean which he had rendered into Latin, to be given to Apronianus’s sister. He had converted her to the Christian religion just as he had converted Apronianus.

For Rufinus calls her his daughter in the prologue. Her name, which is absent from the common editions, is given by the author of the *Lives of the Philosophers*, chapter CX, who calls her Ayama. Therefore in the prologue of Rufinus the translator, instead of “my religious daughter,” we should read:

> Ayama, my religious daughter.

Let us now append the prologue itself from the edition of Beatus Rhenanus.

> **Rufinus sends greetings to his Apronianus.**
>
> I know that just as a flock gladly runs at the voice of its own shepherd, so a devout hearer rejoices in the admonitions of a teacher who speaks his native language. Therefore, dearest son Apronianus, because my religious daughter [read: Ayama], now your sister in Christ, had asked me to compose for her something suitable for reading, in which she would not labor to understand, I translated Sixtus into Latin in an open and sufficiently plain style.
>
> They say that this is the same Sixtus who among you, in the city of Rome, is called Sixtus and is honored with the glory of a bishop and martyr. When she reads him, she will find him so brief that she will see immense meanings unfolded in individual verses; so forceful that the thought of a single verse can suffice for the perfection of an entire life; so clear that not even the young girl attending the reader will complain that she lacks understanding.
>
> The whole work is so brief that it can never leave her hand, and the entire book may occupy the place of some former precious ring. Indeed, it seems fitting that for one to whom earthly ornaments had become worthless in exchange for the word of God, we should now provide adornment in the form of jewels of wisdom and the word.
>
> For the present, then, keep this in your hands in place of a ring. Soon afterward, as the book grows into a treasure, let it be preserved wholly in the heart, ready to draw forth from its innermost storehouse discourses of discipline and fellowship in good actions.
>
> I have also added certain selected sayings of a religious parent to his son, but the whole is brief, so that the little work may properly be called either *Enchiridion* in Greek or *Anulus*—“Ring”—in Latin. Farewell.

Thomas Gale inserted this Ring, or *Enchiridion*—for the work is found under both titles—into his *Mythological, Physical, and Ethical Opuscula*, published at Cambridge by John Hayes in 1671, in octavo, and later more elegantly at Amsterdam by Henry Wetstein in 1688, in octavo.

In these and other editions, however, an error was made through carelessness to the disadvantage of students: the sayings distinguished by numbers in the margin were not separated. Margarinus Bigneus had correctly divided them in the edition of Ludovicus Hillessemius, vol. III of the first Paris edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, 1575.

Rufinus’s prologue, omitted by Gale and elsewhere, suffered the same fate as many other prologues of Rufinus: because Jerome had brought Rufinus’s name into disrepute, it was removed. The entire prologue is found in the first edition of the *Ring*, which Symphorianus Champerius appended to his book *On the Fourfold Life*, published at Lyon by Jannot de Campis in 1507, in quarto.

Champerius dedicated his Sixtus to Philibert Naturel and said that he was surprised that, as far as he knew, this distinguished book had previously been printed by none of the French.

Beatus Rhenanus seems to have been unaware of this edition. Together with other ancient authors, he published the same work under the following title:

> Golden Dialogue of Aeneas the Platonic Christian on the Immortality of the Soul and the Resurrection of Bodies, entitled *Theophrastus*, translated by Ambrose the Camaldolese.
>
> Athenagoras of Athens, *On the Resurrection*, translated by Marsilio Ficino.
>
> Sayings of Xystus the Pythagorean, translated by Rufinus.

Basel, by Johannes Frobenius, 1516, in quarto.

In a letter to Paulus Volzius, and in another serving as his preface to Xystus, Rhenanus says that he revised the sayings from an ancient exemplar kept at Saint Faith’s in Selestat.

In any case, the editions of Champerius and Rhenanus deserve to be compared with one another, for they differ in certain places, especially in the prologue. Tillemont, vol. XII, chap. CXXIX, says that he had not seen it. Blondel, however, in *Pseudo-Isidore*, p. 58, denies that it can now be found.

For it is absent from all the *Bibliothecae Patrum* in which the book of Xystus is included: vol. III of the first edition mentioned shortly before; vol. V of the Paris editions of 1589, 1609, 1624, 1634, 1644, and 1654; vol. III of the Cologne edition of 1718; and finally vol. III of the last Lyon edition of 1677.

### IV.

Galeus discusses this Xystus, Sixtus, Sextus, or Sextius—for he is inscribed in all these ways—learnedly in the preface to his mythological works; but he seems to confuse him with other namesakes, or at least not to distinguish him adequately from them. For our man, already known by the reputation of his writings, could not have been praised by Cicero in Book II of *On Ends*; yet Eusebius records in his *Chronicle* that he flourished in the year 2016 of Abraham and the 194th Olympiad, in these words: “Xystus the Pythagorean philosopher is recognized, or is held in renown.” This is how the passage appears in the editions of Mombritius, Sichardus, Pontacus, and Scaliger, and it is the phrasing of Jerome’s translator.

“In the 61st Olympiad, Anacreon the lyric poet is recognized. In the 76th Olympiad, Aeschylus, writer of tragedies, is recognized. In the 74th Olympiad, Diagoras is recognized. In the 77th Olympiad, Herodotus, writer of histories, is recognized. In the 80th Olympiad, Ezra the priest, renowned among the Hebrews, is recognized. In the 81st Olympiad, Aristarchus, writer of tragedies, is recognized.” We encounter six hundred examples of this kind everywhere.

Marianus Scotus supports us in this matter. In his *Chronicle*, Age VI, chapter XXII, under the year 42 of Augustus and the second year of Christ, we read: “Sextius the Pythagorean philosopher flourished.” Nicholas Le Fèvre therefore argues in vain, in his notes on Seneca’s preface to Book II of the *Controversies*, that *nascitur* should be read for *agnoscitur* in Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, so that Eusebius may be understood to be speaking of the son rather than the father.

That year, expressed in the *Chronicle*, was the year 753 from the foundation of the City, the forty-third year of Augustus, and, according to Eusebius, the first year of our Lord Christ; Eusebius’s era, as I have said elsewhere, precedes the Dionysian era by two years. Following Eusebius, the author of *On the Lives of the Philosophers*, chapter CX, reports that Xystus flourished during the reign of the emperor Octavian.

But Cicero was killed during the consulship of Gaius Vibius Pansa and Aulus Hirtius, in the year 711 from the foundation of the City and the 184th Olympiad—forty-three years before Sextus was recognized and began to flourish.

Nicholas Le Fèvre, in the passage cited above, makes this Sextus, of whom Eusebius speaks, the son of another Sextus, often praised by Seneca, especially in Letter XCVIII, in these words:

> Sextius the father rejected honors. Born for the purpose of entering public life, he did not accept the broad stripe when the deified Julius offered it, since he wished to devote himself more freely to philosophy.

Julius Caesar was stabbed in the year 44 before the Christian era, 710 from the foundation of the City. Sextius the father therefore rejected senatorial rank by that time. Charles Sigonius assigns him the age of twenty years for this in Book II, chapter I of *On the Ancient Law of Roman Citizens*. Nothing, then, prevents Sextius the father from being the man who, according to Eusebius, forty years later flourished under Augustus and was distinguished by the glory of Pythagorean philosophy. We shall immediately see these praises applied to him.

In Letter LXIV, Seneca openly acknowledges that he derived his own gnomic manner of expression from our author. Scaliger, no. 2017, has no doubt about this either. I shall not hesitate to quote Seneca’s words, although they are somewhat lengthy:

> I have been reading the book of Quintus Sextius the Father, a great man, if you believe me; and this despite the Stoics’ denial. Good heavens, what vigor there is in him! What spirit! You will not find this in every philosopher. The writings of some possess only a celebrated name. Everything else is bloodless. They substitute, argue, quibble; they do not give courage, because they do not possess it. When you have read Sextius, you will say: “He lives, he is vigorous, he is free, he is above humanity; he sends me away filled with immense confidence.” For Sextius possesses this quality: he will show you the greatness of a blessed life, yet will not cause despair of it.

When Seneca distinguishes Sextius by calling him “the father,” so as not to mix up Sextius the son with him, why should he not show that both flourished in his own age? At any rate, he indicates that the book of Sextius which he had read was new and not especially ancient, but had then been recently published.

Again, in Letter LIX:

> See, I am reading Sextius at this very moment: an incisive man, philosophizing in Greek words and Roman customs.

These are the words of Seneca of Córdoba concerning Sextius. He may also be consulted in Book II, chapter XXXVI, and Book III, chapter XXXV, of *On Anger*, where he quotes the following maxim from the same Sextius: “It has benefited angry people to look at themselves in a mirror.”

Should our Sextus perhaps be identified with the man who first of all demonstrated the squaring of the circle, according to Simplicius in his commentary on Aristotle’s *Categories*, p. 94 of the Greek Basel edition of 1551, in folio? Yet Georgius Syncellus reports that another philosopher flourished under the emperor Hadrian, p. 349. Marcus Aurelius Augustus says that he heard yet another, namely Sextus of Chaeronea, the nephew of Plutarch, in Book I, section 9 of *Things Concerning Himself*. See Thomas Gataker’s notes on him.

The Sextus or Sextius so highly commended by Annaeus is certainly our Sixtus or Xystus, the Pythagorean philosopher whose exceedingly famous maxims throughout antiquity Rufinus rendered into Latin. He was a Roman who wrote in Greek, just as Scipio Carteromachus of Pistoia noted that many other Romans also wrote in Greek, in his oration *On the Praise of Greek Letters*, frequently published and especially printed in Basel by Johann Froben in 1517, in quarto.

Claudianus Mamertus likewise counts both Sextuses, father and son, among the Roman philosophers, in Book II, chapter VIII of *On the State of the Soul*. No one before Galeus had observed this: that Seneca’s maxims came from this Sextus, and that the vivid spirit with which the Latin philosopher traverses moral teaching was derived from Sextus’s Greek book. Rufinus therefore reasonably thought that he would oblige Roman ears if he adapted the Greek collection of maxims for them.

It is equally reasonable to believe that Rufinus knew well how highly Sextus was esteemed not only by Seneca and other pagan writers, but also by Christians, especially Greek Christians, and above all by one whose writings Rufinus himself delighted in. Everyone sees that I mean Origen.

Origen praised this same collection of Sextus’s maxims. There is a notable passage in Book VIII of *Against Celsus*, p. 397 of William Spencer’s Cambridge edition:

> It will not be out of place here to recall the beautiful maxim found in Sextus, which many Christians have celebrated.

This maxim is no. 101 among the Sixtine sayings:

> The eating of living creatures is indeed morally indifferent; nevertheless, abstaining from it is preferable and appears more consistent with reason.

The same Origen, in volume or Book XV of his *Commentary on Matthew*, shortly after the beginning, p. 369 of Huet’s edition, volume I, quotes another saying of Sextus from his book of *Maxims*, which he testifies to be of good quality and worn by the hands of many readers. I set down the saying:

> Whatever part of your body compels you to intemperance, cast it away from you; for it is better to live chastely with a mutilated limb than, possessing it, to live shamefully.

He immediately adds another maxim from the same book of Sextus:

> You may see people cutting off and casting away their limbs in order to preserve the health of the rest of their body. But how much more rightly should they do so to preserve chastity?

Both sayings, rendered somewhat differently, still survive in Rufinus’s *Ring*, nos. 10 and 291. But Adamantius approves neither, since they depart far from the proper sense of Holy Scripture concerning eunuchs. He therefore adds:

> But since they—Sextus and Philo—did not at all attain the teaching of the sacred writings concerning these matters, they are not to be trusted.

Did Origen therefore regard Sextus as a Christian, or at least as a Jew, as Philo had been? But who would believe him to have been a Jew, when he was known only to Gentiles and Christians? If we make him a Christian, as others have also done, we must say that he was converted to the Christian faith in extreme and advanced old age, perhaps under Claudius, through the work of the Apostles Peter and Paul.

Rufinus says that some believed him not merely a Christian but the bishop of the city of Rome, and Augustine himself sometimes held this view. Saint Maximus, in his scholia on Dionysius, volume II of the works, chapter V, p. 55, calls him “an ecclesiastical philosopher,” and quotes this maxim of his:

> Neither divinity, nor that which is unbegotten, nor fatherhood signifies the substance of God.

Thomas Reinesius, in Letter XC to Daumius, p. 225, correcting several of the *Maxims of Sixtus* in Rufinus’s version, makes him a Christian rather than a Pythagorean. Our distinguished friend Michael Le Quien likewise takes the same view, considering him a Christian but a philosopher, in his notes on Saint John of Damascus, who praises him under the name “Sixtus the Roman” in the *Sacred Parallels*, volume II of the works, p. 362.

The maxim quoted from him there is also cited in exactly the same words by Saint Maximus, volume II of Combefis’s edition of the works, Sermon LX, p. 670:

> Neither speech is to be sought among fish, nor virtue among fools.

The reasons that persuaded Le Quien to regard Sixtus as a Christian are three maxims, nos. 225, 383, and 399, of which the first suggests baptism:

1. Having professed that you are faithful, you likewise promised not to sin against God.
2. Those for whose sake the Word of God is reviled are without God.
3. Feed the soul with the word of God and the body with simple foods.

Let us quote here other passages from Saint John of Damascus. They occur in volume II, pp. 411, 420, 640, and 656:

1. The sins of women are contracted through the ignorance of men.
2. A wise and silent man honors God, since he knows the reason for his silence.
3. Good will is a sacrifice to God.
4. It is impossible for anyone to live according to God unless he does everything wisely and justly.

Let us append to these the remaining passages found in Saint Maximus’s *Sermons*, presented in excerpts, as Combefis calls them, volume II of the works, pp. 550, 564, 628, 631, and 685:

1. Do not take as your friend one to whom you do not entrust everything.
2. Let him who mocks his friend be worthy of no praise, even if he has spoken the truth.
3. While those necessary to you are still alive, take care of them. Once death has removed them, their corpses must be mixed with the earth; this too is pious and just, for the soul is not buried together with the body. Therefore the excessive labor expended on funerals is undertaken in vain.
4. A seal befits a bad woman.
5. There are two things that move a person to devote care to God: the punishment of impiety and the rewards of a religious mind.

If these well-expressed sayings are now absent from the *Ring of Sixtus*, the reason is what Vossius the elder notes in Book I, chapter XXXI of his *Pelagian History*:

> These sayings were not written in precisely this form by Xystus the philosopher himself, but were copied by another person from a work of Xystus.

Let us add the passages inserted among the moral sayings of Demophilus, Democritus, and Secundus, ancient philosophers, published at Rome by Lucas Holstenius through Mascardus in 1638, in duodecimo, p. 116. The learned man notes that the saying on p. 33 is Sixtine and that Rufinus divided it into two, nos. 79 and 80. Other sayings are mixed in among the Demophilean material on p. 117 and should be attributed to Sixtus; Rufinus interpolated them as nos. 401 and 402.

Thus far concerning the ancient and specifically Greek writers who mention Sixtus and his maxims.

### V.

What Rufinus says in the preface—that he added to the *Ring of Sextus* material “from a religious father to his son”—Galeus believes was taken, or rather restored, from the *Clementine Recognitions*. In Galeus’s judgment, the commonly circulated Clement scarcely contains anything in Book I of the *Recognitions* and in the *Homilies* that was not taken from this little book of Sextus.

Galeus adds, as though he had not said enough, that Rufinus deliberately concealed this, lest he diminish the authority of his own Xystus, or lest those beautiful books of Clement should be held in lower esteem if Sextius were discovered, with his persona removed, to be nothing but a pure Pythagorean. So he writes.

He soon goes further and believes that much was also fabricated from this Sextus in the book of the *Shepherd*, which he readily considers to be by Pseudo-Clement. But Galeus carried his criticism beyond what was proper, producing no reason and no testimony at all by which he might draw us to his opinion.

I therefore readily agree with Johann Albert Fabricius, who reasonably and deservedly doubts in the *Greek Library*, volume V, chapter I, p. 7, whether many people will agree with Galeus. I do not think any learned person will agree with him. Each of his individual claims requires stronger arguments.

As for Sixtus, Rufinus did not make him a pope or a martyr; he merely said that some people believed him to be one:

> I have translated into Latin the Sixtus whom they report to be Sixtus the bishop, who among you in the city of Rome is called Sixtus and is adorned with the glory of bishop and martyr.

The error was easy to make: Sixtus the Roman bishop might be believed to be the person in question, since he was commonly called “Sixtus the Roman,” just as Clement was called “the Roman.” Indeed, Le Quien says that when Damascenus, praising Sixtus, called him Roman, this shows that the Greeks regarded the *Maxims of Sixtus* as belonging to Sixtus the Roman pontiff.

Caesar Baronius, under the year 142, § 10, says that it is uncertain whether Rufinus published the book under the name of the earlier or the later Sixtus, likewise a martyr. Certainly, it was neither. Rufinus himself mentioned only Sixtus, not a pontiff or martyr. He affirmed that others called him a bishop.

There is therefore no reason why nearly all recent writers after Jerome should accuse Rufinus of the greatest fraud, as though he had attributed a book by a pagan to a Roman pontiff and martyr. Jerome, hearing this book circulating by the mouth of Pelagius and his followers as the work of Sixtus the pontiff, raged against Rufinus in Letter XLIII to Ctesiphon, as though Rufinus had truly attached the name of Sixtus the pontiff to the *Ring of the Pythagorean Sixtus*.

I nevertheless think that Jerome spoke in the East on the report of others, as commonly happens, without having seen either Sixtus’s book or its preface. I shall set out the substance of Jerome’s criticism in his own words:

> Who could explain in language worthy of it that audacity—or rather madness—of his, by which he placed at the head of the book of the Pythagorean Sixtus, a man without Christ and a pagan, the altered name of Sixtus the martyr and bishop of the Roman Church? In that book, following the doctrine of the Pythagoreans, who make man equal to God and say that he is of God’s substance, much is said about perfection, so that those who do not know the Philosopher’s volume may drink from the cup of Babylon under the name of a martyr.
>
> Finally, throughout the entire volume there is no mention of any prophet, patriarch, apostle, or Christ, so that he may maintain that a bishop and martyr existed without faith in Christ. Hence you also—the Pelagians—appropriate many testimonies against the Church.

The same holy man, near the end of Book I of *Against Jovinianus*, had praised a saying of Sixtus in these words:

> And Xystus says in his maxims: “The lover who is more ardent toward his own wife is an adulterer.”

Jerome, the father of Stridon, wrote this work before he broke into open conflict with Rufinus, and before the Latin translation of Sextus had been made. He therefore used a Greek manuscript. Rufinus’s edition, no. 222, renders the saying somewhat differently:

> Every shameless lover who is more ardent toward his own wife is an adulterer.

Jerome quoted the same saying again, bitterly mocking Rufinus, though he does not expressly name him, in Book VI of his *Commentary on Ezekiel*, chapter 18:

> Beautifully it is said in the little maxims of the Pythagorean Xystus: “The ardent lover of his own wife is an adulterer.” Someone translating this book into Latin wished to dignify it with the name of the martyr Xystus, without considering that throughout the entire volume—which he foolishly divided into two parts—the name of Christ and of all the Apostles is suppressed. Nor is it surprising that he transformed a pagan philosopher into a martyr and bishop of the city of Rome, since he also changed Eusebius of Caesarea’s first book in defense of Origen into a work bearing the name of Pamphilus the martyr, so that he might more easily reconcile the Romans to the exceedingly impious books of *Peri Archon* through such a praiser.

I have quoted this rather lengthy testimony so as not to distort, by my own words, the judgment of so great a man.

The same reason again leads me to transcribe from Jerome’s *Commentary on Jeremiah*, Book IV, chapter XXII, further words agreeing with those above:

> Wretched Grunnius—Rufinus—who opened his mouth to slander holy men and taught his tongue to speak lies! He translated into Latin one book of the Pythagorean Xystus, a most pagan man, divided it into two volumes, and dared to publish it under the name of the holy martyr Xystus, bishop of the city of Rome. In these books there is no mention of Christ, the Holy Spirit, God the Father, the patriarchs, the prophets, or the apostles. With his customary audacity and madness he called this book the *Ring*. It is read throughout many provinces, especially by those who preach *apatheia*—freedom from passions—and sinlessness. Just as the Lord threatens to cast Jeconiah from his hand and finger like a ring, so I beg the reader to cast away this wicked book and, if he wishes to read it, to read it like other books, not as an ecclesiastical volume.

Jerome rightly makes this final demand, and Rufinus the translator demanded no other treatment.

Here I am compelled to wonder at Gerard John Vossius, otherwise a man of extensive reading and sound judgment. In *On the Sects of the Philosophers*, chapter VI, § 43, after reporting that the *Enchiridion of Sixtus* had been printed several times in Germany with Rufinus’s preface to Apronianus, he could write the following words about the translator:

> In this preface he says that this Pythagorean Sextus is the same as Sixtus or Xystus, pope and martyr.

Rufinus nowhere said this. He says that this was reported by others. Yet prejudices fixed in the mind often prevent us from seeing things close at hand, even when they are clear and placed before our eyes.

Vossius had already stumbled over the same obstacle in Book I, chapter XXXI of his *Pelagian History*, where he says that Rufinus published, under the name of Xystus the martyr, the commentaries of Xystus the Pythagorean philosopher translated by himself.

It was therefore easy for other very learned men to strike the same anvil: Noris in Book I, chapter II of his *Pelagian History*; Bruno Neusser, or Honoratus Faber, in the *Prodromus velitarius*, p. 80, column 2; Aubertus Miraeus in his notes on Gennadius; and, to omit writers of lesser stature, others as well.

### VI.

The passage from Jerome just cited, directed against the book insofar as it had been rashly attributed to a martyr, may have been the reason why Pope Gelasius, at the Roman council of seventy bishops, rejected it among the apocrypha, as lacking public and canonical authority.

For in the *Decree*, which we have long attributed to Gelasius, we read:

> The book of proverbs written by heretics and marked with the name of Saint Xystus is apocryphal.

The words “marked with the name of Saint Xystus” deserve notice. The designation “Saint” was added by copyists, or perhaps by heretics, and certainly not by Rufinus. The matter itself makes this clear, and Rufinus acknowledges it.

Vossius says in his *Pelagian History* that it may seem strange that Gelasius says the maxims of Xystus were written not by pagans but by heretics. The pope says this because the Pelagian faction was abusing the authority of this Xystus as though he had been a bishop and martyr. Perhaps it was also because they had interpolated Xystus. It was certainly not because of the translator Rufinus, as Vossius suspects. For in this very *Decree* Gelasius names Rufinus honorably and counts the works of Gregory of Nazianzus, translated by the same man, among books to be received.

Add to this the fact that Galeus detected from manuscript codices that two editions of the *Ring of Sixtus*, differing from each other, had been produced in antiquity. Both could not have belonged to Rufinus. What, then, prevents us from supposing that one of them was fabricated by heretics, and that this was the edition Gelasius intended to condemn?

Baronius, under the year 410, § 64, thinks that the biblical passages inserted by Rufinus into Sixtus’s book gave occasion for the Gelasian censure. But Jerome does not charge Rufinus with this crime. Nor would he have kept silent if Rufinus had interpolated a pagan philosopher, believed to be a Gentile, with the written word of God.

As we have seen from Jerome, Rufinus divided that collection of Sixtus’s maxims into two parts. Champerius preserved the same arrangement, but Rhenanus, Bigneus, Galeus, and the others did not.

Let us quote a maxim from Champerius’s edition which, although Pelagius and Augustine recognize it as Sixtine, is sought in vain in all the other editions:

> God granted human beings freedom of their will, so that by living purely and without sin they might become like God.

This demonstrates that Champerius’s edition was based on the text of by far the oldest and most reliable manuscript.

When Pelagius cited this passage and two others as belonging to Xystus, bishop and martyr of the Roman Church, Augustine, sincerely believing them to be the words of the true author, the supreme pontiff and genuine martyr, tried to soften them into a Catholic meaning in chapter LXIV, § 77 of his book *On Nature and Grace against Pelagius*:

> What Christian, he says, is unaware that Pelagius is referring to the most blessed Xystus, bishop of the Roman Church and martyr of the Lord, when he says that God granted human beings freedom of their will so that, living purely and without sin, they might become like God?

Pelagius had cited this maxim under the name of Xystus the pontiff and martyr in support of his heresy. Augustine, in order to disarm the heresiarch by the authority of so great a name, attempts to make it Catholic in the words that follow:

> But it belongs to the very will to hear and believe the one who calls, and to ask from the one in whom one believes for help not to sin. For when he says, “They shall become like God,” they will become like God through the love of God, which has been poured into our hearts—not through the possibility of nature, nor through free will, which is in us, but through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us.

Augustine then brings forward two other maxims from Sixtus’s *Ring*, nos. 40 and 53:

> And when the same martyr says, “A pure mind is a holy temple for God, and a clean and sinless heart is an excellent altar for him,” who does not know that a pure heart is brought to this perfection as the inner person is renewed day by day, yet not without the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord?
>
> Likewise, when he himself says, “A chaste and sinless man has received from God the power to be a son of God,”—even if someone has become so chaste and sinless, though the question remains among whom and when this is accomplished, while it is nevertheless agreed that it can happen, and that it cannot happen without the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus—still, as I began to say, Sixtus wisely warned us that when someone has become such a person and is therefore rightly counted among the children of God, he should not think that this power was his own, since he received it by grace from God, when he did not possess it in his already corrupted and depraved nature, as we read in the Gospel.

Thus far Augustine, endeavoring to soften Sixtus’s maxims, which he had believed belonged to a pontiff and martyr.

Later, once their author had been discovered—not a Christian pontiff or martyr—Augustine candidly admitted that he had been deceived in Book II, chapter XLII of the *Retractions*. The Church of Lyons praises this excellent act, full of ingenuous modesty, in its book *On Three Letters*, volume II of the *Supplement to the Library of the Fathers*, p. 1194.

I shall quote Augustine’s words:

> In my book *On Nature and Grace against Pelagius*, I defended certain words which Pelagius had presented as belonging to Xystus, bishop and martyr of Rome, as though they truly belonged to that same Xystus. But later I read that they belonged to Xystus the philosopher, not to Xystus the Christian.

Augustine does not ask who that philosopher Xystus was. He merely says that he was neither a bishop nor a martyr. I think that, after reading Xystus’s own book and Rufinus’s preface, Augustine recognized the deception practiced upon him by the heresiarch. Certainly, a single examination of the preface would have been sufficient for him to recognize it, just as it was sufficient for Gennadius.

Gennadius, in the venerable ancient Vatican Alexandrian manuscript no. 8, after Jerome’s *Catalogue*, chapter CLII—or XVII—lists Rufinus’s Latin translations and says that Rufinus presented the maxims of Xystus the Roman. He certainly does not call him the bishop or martyr of the city of Rome.

In the commonly circulated editions of Gennadius, the word “Roman” is omitted, although Saint John of Damascus adds it when praising Xystus. Honorius, otherwise a faithful copyist of Gennadius, agrees with him in our matter, although he uses not the name “Roman” but “philosopher.” In chapter XVII he says that Rufinus translated the maxims of the philosopher Xystus.

He adds on his own: “Against the mathematicians.” For Gennadius distinguished the maxims *Against the Mathematicians* from the Sixtine maxims and said that they belonged to Pamphilus. We shall discuss them below.

But it is stranger than strange that, after every cloud of error concerning Xystus the philosopher rather than the pontiff had been dispelled, someone could still be found who made Xystus, originally a philosopher, into a pontiff. This was the author of the little book *On Twelve Ecclesiastical Writers*, appended to Isidore and Ildefonsus, who recorded the following in chapter I:

> Xystus, bishop and martyr of the city of Rome, composed, in imitation of Solomon, a book of *Proverbs* in so concise a style that individual maxims are explained in individual verses. Heretics inserted certain things contrary to the faith of the Church into this little work, so that the assertion of perverse doctrines might more easily be accepted under the name of so great a martyr. But let the person who remembers that he is Catholic read it with discernment and not accept what is contrary to the truth.
>
> Some people, however—Gelasius in the *Decree*—think that this book was dictated by heretics, not by Xystus. The most blessed Augustine refutes this opinion, for in one of his works (*On Nature and Grace*, chapter LXIV) he acknowledges that this work was composed by the same martyr.

But, my good man, you ought to have read Augustine’s *Retractions*, in which he does not deny that he had been deceived.

### VII.

With Fabricius, in Book IV, chapter III, p. 332 of the fourth edition of the *Latin Library*, we may reasonably wish that these maxims, most of them golden, could be found in Greek and compared with the ancient manuscripts of Rufinus’s version.

A few fragments of them occur here and there under the name of Pythagoras and others, and sometimes under no name at all, in John Stobaeus and in the *Maxims* of Saint Nilus, which Joseph Maria Suaresius, bishop of Vaison, inserted among Nilus’s works, p. 548.

Some, as I said, are found among the maxims of Demophilus and Democritus, published at Rome by Holstenius through Mascardus; he indicated this in his scholia. The same distinguished man, in his manuscript notes on the edition of Xystus by Ludovicus Hillessemio, preserved on the shelves of the Angelica Library, suggests that other maxims of Xystus survive in Hierocles and Iamblichus.

I collected above, in § 5, the passages found in Greek ecclesiastical writers—Origen, Maximus, and Damascenus.

As for Rufinus’s Sixtine version, it is given authority by Saint Benedict, patriarch of the Western monks, who used it in chapter VII of his *Rule*, near the end, where, as though quoting from a widely accepted book, he gives this maxim from no. 134:

> As it is written: “The wise man is known by a few words.”

The Master also quotes in chapter XI of his *Rule*, in Holstenius’s volume II of the *Code of Rules*, as though it were a maxim of Origen, a saying that nevertheless adorns the *Ring of Xystus*, no. 144:

> It is better to throw a stone in vain than a word.

In *The Cause of God against Pelagius*, pp. 101 and 104, Thomas Bradwardine, of the Order of Friars Minor Conventual, whom the scholastic order called “the profound doctor,” and who died as archbishop of Canterbury on August 18, 1349, according to Henry Wharton’s *Anglia Sacra*, volume I, p. 119, presents other passages.

The author of the *Lives of the Philosophers*, printed in the early days of typography, also inserted several in chapter CX.

Add to these the commonly circulated decretal letters of Isidore, several of which overflow with maxims of Xystus the Pythagorean in Rufinus’s translation: the third of Alexander I; the first of Sixtus I; likewise the first of Pius I; the later letter of Melchiades; the first of Zephyrinus; both of Callistus; the later letter of Pontianus; the single letter of Anterus; the later letter of Cornelius; and the single letter of Lucius.

What Blondellus says in his *Prolegomena*, pp. 64, 65, 66, and 71—that these maxims were translated into Latin by Rufinus in the year 390—cannot stand, since that would be seven years before he crossed from the East into Italy, where it is established that he prepared the translation.

After the censure in which Jerome generally attacked Xystus, John Maria Brasichellensis, in his *Index of Expurgated Books*, p. 189, warns that all the maxims listed below should individually be avoided:

> 7, 120, 124, 125, 184, 194, 200, 248, 252, 263, 265, 287, 299, 306, 336, 342, 343, 393, 396, 409.

“For,” he says, “they are either heretical, erroneous, or of bad tendency.”

He is referring to volume V, p. 769, of the second Paris edition of the *Library of the Fathers* of 1589, where the maxims of Xystus in Rufinus’s version are listed individually. There are 430 of them.

### VIII.

To bring this discussion of Xystus finally to a close, I shall briefly survey his manuscripts, both handwritten and printed.

From Galeus we learn that the Latin copies of these *Parables*, as Seneca calls them, differ so greatly among themselves that it is nearly certain that two editions of Xystus were produced in antiquity. Some manuscripts contain more maxims, others fewer. Elsewhere many passages are repeated and the order is changed.

Other copies likewise do not proceed in a single continuous sequence but form two parts. We have observed that this arrangement was later noted by Jerome and preserved in Champerius’s edition.

Finally, Galeus declares that he found no manuscript to which something could not be added after an exact collation with the copies mentioned above.

Paul Colomesius lists a Latin manuscript of Xystus among the manuscripts of the Vossian Library, now the Leiden Library, in his catalogue, p. 878 of Fabricius’s edition of the works.

So much for the manuscripts of Xystus written by hand. I shall now describe the printed editions.

1. Symphorianus Champerius. Lyons, Jannot de Campis, 1507, in quarto, with Rufinus’s preface to Apronianus.
2. Together with the golden verses of Pythagoras. Wittenberg, in the workshop of Grunenberg, 1514, in quarto.
3. Beatus Rhenanus. Basel, Johann Froben, 1516, in quarto, with the same preface, though somewhat different. I reviewed this edition and the first one above.
4. Leuven, 1518, in quarto.
5. Basel, 1520, in quarto.
6. Cologne, 1522, in quarto.
7. Paris, 1541, in quarto.
8. Venice, at the sign of Hope, 1552, in duodecimo, without the preface, folio 122, after the index of a little book entitled *Precious Sayings, or Commonplaces, Gathered from Nearly All the Doctors Who Wrote in Sacred Scripture, by Defensor, a Most Ancient Theologian*.
9. Cologne, Maternus Cholinus, 1574, in octavo, without the preface, with this title: *The Maxims of Sixtus or Xystus, Filled with the Precepts of True Wisdom and Forming the Mind for Heavenly Discipline, Illustrated by the Learned Explanation of Ludovicus Hillessemii of Andernach*. Hillessemius, who was the first to render an important service to Sixtus, dedicated the book to Gregory XIII, supreme pontiff, distinguishing the maxims by numbers in the margin and explaining them in a commentary. Margarinus Bigneus, omitting the notes, reproduced his edition in volume III of the *Library of the Fathers*, p. 962 of the first Paris edition, printed by Michel Sonnius in 1575; all the remaining editions descended from it.
10. Johann von Fuchte, Helmstedt, Jacobus Lucius, 1615, in duodecimo, without the preface. Its title is as follows: *Gnomes or Maxims on Morals, No Less Learned Than Pious, of Xystus the Philosopher, Laurentius of Pisa, and Thalassius the Bishop, Now Published Separately for the First Time through the Efforts of Johann von Fuchte*.
11. Thomas Galeus, Cambridge, John Hayes, 1671, in octavo; subsequently Amsterdam, Heinrich Wetstein, 1688, in octavo, without the preface.

## CHAPTER IX

I. The country and surname of Evagrius, whose little works Rufinus translated into Latin.  
II. The accusations heaped upon him.  
III. His praises.  
IV. Writings translated by Rufinus that still survive.  
V. The *Maxims of Pamphilus the Martyr against the Mathematicians*, translated by the same man, examined.

I. Besides the Xystine sentences, Rufinus also rendered the sentences of Evagrius into Latin. My authorities are Jerome and Gennadius. This same Evagrius, celebrated in both reputations, is called by Jerome in his letter to Ctesiphon [Col. 0200D] “the Pontic Hyperborite”; in the manuscripts of John Martianus, “Iberite” or “Hiberite”; more appropriately, “Iborite,” as I shall say later. The Father of Stridon immediately adds the following about him:

“He writes to virgins, he writes to monks, he writes to her” (Melania, whose name bears witness to the darkness of her infidelity). “He published a book and Sentences περὶ ἀπαθείας—concerning apatheia, which we may call impassibility or imperturbability, when the mind is never moved by any fault of disturbance; and, to put it simply, one is either a stone or God. His books are widely read in Greek throughout the East, and, through the translation of his disciple Rufinus, in Latin throughout the West.”

Thus far Jerome. In the preface to his *Dialogue against the Pelagians*, he again attacks Evagrius, attributing to him, together with other heretics, the opinion that human virtue and knowledge can reach perfection and—not merely likeness, but equality with God, so that, when they have ascended to the summit of completion, they claim that they can sin neither in thought nor through ignorance. In the preface to Book IV of his commentary on Jeremiah, written against Rufinus and Evagrius as followers of Origen and standard-bearers of his errors, he indignantly says:

“I was dictating my commentaries on Jeremiah at intervals, so that what leisure lacked might be supplied by industry, when suddenly the heresy of Pythagoras and Zeno—ἀπάθεια and ἀναμαρτησία, that is, impassibility and impeccancy—which was once slaughtered in Origen and recently in his disciples Grunnius (Rufinus), Evagrius, and Jovinianus, began to hiss not only in the West but also in the regions of the East.”

Evagrius wrote much. After Gennadius, chapter XI, his works are listed by Antonio Pagi under A.D. 388, §15; by Casimiro Oudino in the *Supplementum Bellarminianum*, p. 47; and also by Louis Dupin at the beginning of volume III of the *Bibliotheca*. Yet they all touch only briefly upon, or almost entirely pass over, the *Book of Sentences* which Rufinus translated from Greek into Latin—not even Tillemont excepted, although he treats Evagrius’s other matters at length in volume X [Col. 0201B] of his *Commentaries on Ecclesiastical History*.

According to Palladius, in the *Lausiac History*, chapter LXXXVI, Evagrius was by origin a Pontic of the city of the Iberians, or Hiberians; according to the *Paradise of Heraclides*, chapter XXV, and Sozomen, Book VI, chapter XXX. Yet Ibora—not Ibera—a city in Helenopontus in Asia Minor, is mentioned by Justinian in *Novella* XXVIII. Gregory of Nyssa, Evagrius’s friend, places this city near the monastery of Saints Basil and Macrina in volume II of his works, in the Paris edition of Aegidius Morellus, 1638, p. 212, in his *Oration on the Eleven Martyrs*. “Not far from it,” he says, “is a small city which they call Ibora.” Its bishop Uranius subscribed to Act VI of the Council of Chalcedon, in Labbe, volume IV, p. 589. Palladius’s manuscript in Rosweyde’s *History of the Hermits*, p. 789, no. 134, reads Ἰβόρων, *Iborōn*, “of the Iborians,” instead of Ἰβέρων, *Iberōn*, “of the Iberians.”

Therefore there can scarcely be any doubt that in Jerome one should read, with Rosweyde and Henri Valois in his notes on Sozomen, “Iborite,” or perhaps “Hyborite,” instead of “Hyperborite.” For Tillemont’s and Cotelerius’s violent and somewhat enigmatic explanations seem implausible. Tillemont conjectures that Jerome may have written “Hyperborite” by way of exaggeration, because Pontus, Evagrius’s homeland, was northern in relation to Palestine, where Jerome was writing. Cotelerius, however, in volume III of the *Monuments of the Greek Church*, p. 543, suspects that Jerome wrote “Hyperiboritе” or “Hyperiberite,” the name being twisted into an insult, as though to say: beyond the Iberians, his countrymen—an Iborite, and worse than an Iberite or Iberian. The Iberians, or Hiberians, and the other Pontic peoples, he argues, had a bad reputation, as is attested above all by Septimius near the beginning of his books against Marcion.

The same learned man—Cotelerius, I mean—says on p. 677 that he had seen many manuscripts in which “Hiborite” and “Hiberite” are read; also “Hyborite,” from which “Hyperborite” arose. But I consider it much more likely that the holy man, far from intending mockery, wished to identify Evagrius’s homeland, in order to distinguish him from the other Evagriuses who were then well known: for example, Evagrius, bishop of Antioch; Evagrius, the intimate associate of Saint John Chrysostom; and Evagrius the presbyter, who attended the Council of Aquileia in A.D. 381.

This Evagrius of ours, a monk by profession, whose small works Rufinus translated into Latin, served men distinguished above all in holiness and learning. He had Gregory Nazianzen as his teacher; was ordained Reader by Basil the Great and Deacon by Gregory of Nyssa; and served as archdeacon in the Church of Constantinople under Nectarius. From there he departed for Jerusalem, where Melania received him, and at her urging he assumed the monastic habit. Finally, wishing to devote himself to God under the two Macarii and other most holy men, he withdrew into the deserts of Nitria and the Cells, where he departed this life in A.D. 399, around the feast of the Epiphany, at the age of fifty-four, after he had withdrawn from Theophilus of Alexandria, who was trying to impose the burden of episcopacy upon him.

I have given this brief account of Evagrius the Iborite of Pontus, whose writings Rufinus, his intimate associate, made available to the Latins. Tillemont treats the rest with a more expansive pen.

II. Elsewhere I have discussed how fiercely Theophilus persecuted the Egyptian monks suspected of Origenism. Jerome, generally following Theophilus’s view, was the first to number Evagrius among the forerunners of Pelagius, as though he were filled with the errors of Adamantius. Indeed, it was enough to appear devoted to Origen for someone to fall under suspicion of Pelagianism.

The distinguished Peter Daniel Huet, in *Origenianorum*, Book II, chapter IV, section III, §14, and Henri Noris in his *Dissertation on the Fifth Council*, chapter VII, have shown that Evagrius, like Origen and Didymus, was condemned at that council, and consequently condemned in the Sixth and Seventh Councils as well. But Honoratus Faber, in the third part of his *Prodromus*, chapter II, §9, p. 77, against Noris—who had sharply attacked Peter Halloix as a patron of Origen—does not deny that the Fifth Synod condemned errors attributed to Origen and to others already dead, namely Evagrius and Didymus. Nevertheless, he does not for that reason admit that Origen was then condemned by the Church, nor certainly Evagrius or Didymus.

For it is established among Catholics that, before its confirmation by the Supreme Pontiff, the Fifth Synod was not ecumenical, as Baronius also testifies under A.D. 553, §124, since it was celebrated without the Western Church and without legates of the Apostolic See—indeed, not merely without its approval, but with Pope Vigilius explicitly opposing it. Vigilius subsequently approved it by a decretal letter, published by Peter de Marca, although Garnerius, in his notes on Liberatus the Deacon, doubts this. In any case, whatever the truth may be, he approved it only insofar as it had condemned the Three Chapters. This cannot be doubted, for Vigilius’s *Constitutum* on the matter is preserved in Baluzius’s *Councils*, p. 1552. There is profound silence there concerning Evagrius and the others.
