The pontiffs who followed—both Pelagiuses and Gregory the Great—closely following Vigilius’s footsteps, approved nothing from the Fifth Synod except the single condemnation of the Three Chapters. Therefore Vigilius and his successors approved the Fifth Synod only with respect to the condemnation of the Three Chapters, not with respect to the other acts conducted in that synod; many of these they could never have approved, as Faber demonstrates. One of them was the condemnation of Evagrius, whose errors had not come to the knowledge of the Apostolic See.

Other persons whom the same Fifth Synod condemned as heretics had already been condemned by the Apostolic See in other councils, and no new approval of their condemnation was then necessary. Theophilus, and Jerome with him, certainly desired—indeed demanded—that the Apostolic See confirm Theophilus’s condemnation of Origen; but he did not obtain it. Jerome says in Letter LXXVIII to Pammachius and Marcella: “May the Chair of Peter the Apostle confirm by its preaching the preaching of the Chair of Mark the Evangelist.” Yet it did not confirm it, although Jerome adds in the same place that it was commonly reported that “the blessed Pope Anastasius” had done so, and so forth. See Baronius, p. 99, volume V. The rest may be found in Faber.

I am not unaware that, after Jerome, John Climacus criticized Evagrius for his apatheia in Grade XIV of the *Ladder of Paradise*, p. 203 of the Paris edition of the works of Matthew Raderus. But Dionysius the Carthusian does not hesitate to prefer Evagrius’s meaning to that of Climacus in his *Expositions on the Ladder of Climacus*, Grade XXIX, fol. 127, of the Cologne edition published by Melchior Novesianus in A.D. 1540, in folio.

Several centuries after Evagrius, Antiochus the Abbot, a contemporary of the Emperor Heraclius, attributes to Evagrius, Origen, and Didymus the errors concerning the pre-existence of souls before the creation of the world and the restoration of all things that have existed. He does so in Homily CXXX, p. 234 of volume XII of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, Morellian edition, Greek and Latin, 1634. Cyril of Scythopolis in the *Life of Saint Sabbas*, and John Zonaras in his canon on the Mother of God, likewise attribute these doctrines to them; both passages are in Cotelerius’s *Monuments*, volume III, pp. 364 and 468.

To the same period John Moschus, or Sophronius, in the *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter CLXXVII, p. 916 of Rosweyde’s second edition, appends a narrative unfair to Evagrius’s reputation. Yet Suarez testifies, in his notes on Nilus, p. 610, that in the Barberini manuscript Evagrius is adorned with the title of sanctity. We shall see that this happened elsewhere as well.

As for the justice of all the accusations heaped upon Evagrius, God is the judge. For the present, however, the case in his favor is that the crime of Origenism was attributed even to men revered for their holiness, among whom no one denies that Chrysostom deserves the first place.

It is absolutely certain that Evagrius’s surviving writings are repeatedly praised by the Greek Fathers—Nilus, Maximus, and Damascene—including those for which Rufinus served as translator. We shall later show that Saint Benedict of Aniane valued these works highly. As for the word *apatheia*, no prudent person will readily condemn all authors who used it. The author of the *Life of Saint Pachomius*, entirely free from the errors of Origen, which he detests, uses the same word, just as Evagrius does, in Laurentius Surius under 14 May. Marcus, who wrote the *Life of Saint Porphyry of Gaza* preserved by Bollandus under 26 February, p. 660, §101, likewise used the word *apatheia*.

Here I also call as a witness Elias of Crete, metropolitan, in his scholia on Grade XXX of the *Ladder of Climacus*, p. 445, where he says:

“For I consider apatheia, or tranquility of soul, to be nothing other than the mind’s heaven in the heart, which thereafter regards all the wicked arts of the demons as a game and a mockery, and despises them.”

Compare Raderus’s learned observation on chapter IV, p. 471, attributing a good sense to *apatheia*, and adding the support of Bernardinus Rosignolius from Book II, chapter XXVII, p. 341, of *On the Discipline of Christian Perfection*. Basil the Great in the preface to his *Longer Rule*, and many others, are also relevant here. They were by no means averse to the word *apatheia*, since they knew very well that it could appropriately bear a correct meaning, although, strictly considered, it contained a bad one.

Hence, after the Pelagian heresy had emerged from the underworld, the word *apatheia* became generally suspect. Those were especially suspect who used the word in any manner whatsoever in their writings, such as Xystus, Evagrius Ponticus, and their translator Rufinus. For Pelagius also taught that a person could rise in this life to such a degree of perfection that, freed from the passions, he would no longer sin. So report the historians of the Pelagian controversy, Vossius in Book I, chapter III, and Noris in Book I, chapter I.

Yet Cotelerius, a man extraordinarily practiced in reading the ancient Fathers, makes an excellent observation in his notes on Clement’s *Recognitions*, Book I, chapter II, §13: *apatheia*, strictly understood, means imperturbability and impeccancy; but the ancient Fathers sometimes used it more loosely for the state in which a holy man, placed there by God’s grace, is exposed to fewer and lesser temptations and does not succumb to more serious sins.

Saint Maximus accepts *apatheia* in this explained sense. In volume I of his works, p. 399, *Century I on Charity*, chapter XXXVI, he calls it that peaceful condition of soul in which the soul is moved with difficulty toward vice. Consult this same most holy Father, thoroughly equipped with theological learning, again on pp. 441, 451, 521, 570, 571, and 654. By these passages, or by no explanation at all, one may understand what we repeatedly encounter concerning *apatheia* in many other pious writers, let alone in Evagrius.

III. I find no one who accused Evagrius while he was alive. After his death, no one accused him for a full span of one hundred and fifty years except Jerome—not even Theophilus of Alexandria, although shortly after Evagrius’s death Theophilus raged against many Egyptian monks as Origenists. For Jerome, in order not to approve Evagrius, it was enough that Evagrius had maintained friendship with Melania, Rufinus, Ammonius, and the other solitaries whom Theophilus had treated badly.

Otherwise, none of the ancient writers mentioned Evagrius without a preface of praise: neither Palladius, nor Rufinus, nor Socrates in Book IV, chapter XVIII, nor Sozomen in Book VI, chapter XXX; neither Saint Prosper in the *Chronicle* of Scaliger’s edition, nor finally Gennadius. Evagrius’s sentences were commonly received by the Greek Fathers—Nilus, Maximus, and Damascene. Moreover, his authority is cited more than once in the *History of the Hermits*, Book I, p. 568, §14, and p. 582, §5. He is also cited in the chains of the Greek Fathers, and Saint Dorotheus the monk praises him in Book XII of his *Doctrines*.

But one or another of these men has a bad reputation, since he was devoted to Origen. Most, however, are free from suspicion; nor did Novatianism, which is charged against Socrates, have anything in common with Origen or Pelagius. Finally, consult the *Rule of Saint Anthony the Abbot*, published by Abraham Ecchellensis, p. 75, where Evagrius is praised.

What shall I say now of the most holy men to whom he was attached by the closest bond of friendship? What of both Macarii? What of Arsenius? What finally of Isidore of Pelusium, whose Letter CCLI of Book I was written to Evagrius the Deacon?

What I said in Evagrius’s favor concerning the Fifth Council—namely, that it was approved by the Apostolic See only with respect to the condemnation of the Three Chapters, not of Evagrius—is confirmed by the authority of Saint Benedict of Aniane. The name *apatheia*, inserted in Evagrius’s writings, did not deter him from transcribing three of Evagrius’s small works into his own code of rules, since they were free from error and extremely useful for religious life.

Indeed, Evagrius’s writings were so highly esteemed among Westerners that at one time his book *On the Conflict of Virtues and Vices* was attributed to the principal doctors of the Latin Church, Augustine and Ambrose, and also to Pope Leo, Isidore, and Autpertus. Consult the Appendix to volume VI of Saint Augustine’s works, new edition, p. 219, where it is entitled *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*.

No one noticed that Evagrius’s *Antirrheticus* was translated by Gennadius except Lucas Holstenius, a man supremely skilled in such matters, in his manuscript notes on Robert Bellarmine’s *Catalogue*. From this it becomes clear why learned men have searched for Evagrius’s *Antirrheticus* in vain. Holstenius notes that what is read at the end of the book concerning the Rule of Saint Benedict is an addition not recognized by the ancient manuscripts.

The authors of the new edition I mentioned likewise testify that in certain manuscripts, and in the Erasmian edition, the book lacks the final two chapters, XXVII and XXVIII, and ends with these words:

“But you, man of God, attend with vigilant devotion to what I say, with the help of him who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.”

So much for Evagrius’s teaching. As for his conduct, nothing simpler or holier can be imagined than the history of his life, as Palladius relates it—Palladius, who knew him for nine full years.

IV. Having established these points in Evagrius’s favor, since his cause is shared by Rufinus, let us now turn to Evagrius’s works written in Greek and translated by our man. Gennadius lists them and divides them into two classes in chapter XI of his *Catalogue*. Some, he says, were translated into Latin by himself; others by another person—understand, Rufinus.

The works he assigns to this latter class are as follows:

1. A book of one hundred sentences for monks, or anchorites.

2. A book on the common life of coenobites, addressed to the *Synodites*—otherwise, *Sentences on Apatheia*.

3. A book addressed to virgins consecrated to God.

Concerning the first work Gennadius writes in the same chapter XI:

“He composed for the anchorites a book of one hundred sentences, arranged in chapters.”

Immediately afterward he lists another book:

“And for the learned and studious, a book of fifty sentences, which I translated into Latin. For the former book—the book of one hundred sentences—having been translated long ago, but finding it corrupted and confused by the passage of time, I restored it to the author’s true text, partly by retranslating and partly by emending it.”

In Gennadius’s oldest Vatican manuscript, some material is missing through the carelessness of the ancient copyist. It is clear from the commonly printed texts that the book of one hundred sentences had once been translated by another interpreter but had been corrupted through the negligence of scribes. Gennadius collated and corrected it against ancient manuscripts.

That first translator of the one hundred sentences was none other than Rufinus, if we explain Gennadius by Gennadius himself. For Gennadius, speaking generally in chapter XVII about Rufinus’s translations of Greek works, says that Rufinus presented the *Sentences of Evagrius*. Jerome clearly designated this same book together with the other two when he discussed Evagrius in his letter to Ctesiphon:

1. He writes to virgins.

2. He writes to monks.

3. He published a book and sentences περὶ ἀπαθείας—concerning apatheia, which we may call impassibility or imperturbability, when the mind is never moved by any fault of disturbance; and, to put it simply, one is either a stone or God. His books are widely read in Greek throughout the East and, through the translation of his disciple Rufinus, in Latin throughout the West.

Rufinus therefore translated not one book of Evagrius but several—namely, the three I have listed above. What could be clearer? Gennadius first calls the work a book of one hundred sentences in the same chapter XI. He describes the second as follows: “He also composed for coenobites and Synodites a doctrine suited to the common life.”

As for the Synodites, who are the same as coenobites, I shall not, as someone else did, plunder the repositories of Du Cange; consult both of his glossaries. Gennadius designates Evagrius’s third book in these words: “And for virgins consecrated to God, a little book appropriate to religion and sex.”

These three works of Evagrius still survive, although the name and preface of the translator Rufinus have been removed, just as elsewhere we have observed that these same elements were removed. For Gennadius made this particular observation about Rufinus’s translations:

“Whatever of all these works is read in Latin with the aforementioned prefaces was translated by Rufinus.”

The recent cataloguers of literature say nothing about these works. They did not point to the code of rules of Saint Benedict of Aniane, which Holstenius published for the public eight hundred years after it was written. Indeed, one of them, William Cave, counted among Evagrius’s lost works the small works translated by Rufinus, under A.D. 390.

But the appendix to that same code, preserved on the Floriacian parchment manuscripts of the Queen of Sweden, now in the Vatican, has transmitted to us the three aforementioned works of the Iborite monk, translated by Rufinus. The first two have merged into one through their similarity, without any distinction between the sentences. One heading has been placed over both, though they must be divided into two works, so that each book may have its own title, in the following manner:

1. *The Sentences of Evagrius the Monk.*

2. *For Those Who Live in Coenobia and Hostels.*

These are the Synodites. For among Du Cange’s entries in the *Glossary*, such coenobia were also called *synodochia* or *xenodochia*.

The first book of Evagrius, consisting of one hundred sentences, ends with these words on p. 35 of the Paris edition:

“Sweet is honey and sweet the honeycomb, but the knowledge of God is sweeter than both.”

Immediately afterward follows another little book: *For the brothers who live in coenobia and hostels*, that is, for coenobites and Synodites—not for solitaries, but for those living with others. It begins with these words:

“Hear, monk, the sayings of your father.”

After these two comes the third work, which, besides Jerome and Gennadius, Socrates mentions with the others in Book IV, chapter XXIII: *Sentences for Virgins*. In these books, especially in the first, one encounters *apatheia*, or impassibility, which had so offended Jerome in Evagrius’s Latin and Greek books. This will become clearer if I bring forward several examples, by which the matter may be plainly demonstrated.

Page 34: “He who subjects his flesh to slavery will be impassible.”

Page 35: “The seat of impassibility is a soul that acts well.”

Page 36: “Without impassibility the heart will not be exalted. Impassibility precedes charity; prudence generates impassibility.”

Page 37: “The long-suffering monk will rejoice in impassibility; the prudent monk will be impassible.”

Page 40: “She who pities her eyes when they are bruised and her flesh when it is wasting away will not rejoice in impassibility.”

We therefore possess three books of Evagrius translated by Rufinus and expressly indicated by Jerome, which had long been believed to have perished. It is now greatly to be desired that, arranged separately and marked at the margin with numbered sentences—as we noted was done with Xystus—and combined with Rufinus’s other works, both those of others and his own, they may enter the printing houses as a single corpus.

V. Since we have examined the sentences of Xystus and Evagrius translated by Rufinus, the occasion requires us also to examine the sentences of the martyr Pamphilus against the mathematicians, translated by the same Rufinus. We have mentioned these elsewhere, and Gennadius does so in chapter XVII.

Tillemont, however, in volume XII, article CXXIX, believed that there was a textual error in Gennadius’s wording, because Saint Pamphilus is said to have written not *Sentences against the Mathematicians* but an *Apology for Origen*, which Gennadius must have intended to indicate. Cave, under A.D. 390, following Labbe, volume II, p. 310, counted these same sentences among lost works, even suspecting that Gennadius had become confused over the name Pamphilus.

Noris, in his *Dissertation on the Fifth Synod*, chapter XIII, attacking our Rufinus, whom he confused with another Rufinus, a leader of the heretics, attaches to him the crime of fraud and imposture. He does so because, in the first *Apology*, Rufinus allegedly persuaded Macarius, who was writing against the mathematicians, that Saint Pamphilus the martyr had composed something of this sort in an *Apology*, promising to translate what Pamphilus had written, but afterward failing to translate it.

From this the learned Cardinal says that he recognized that Gennadius had been led into error by Rufinus. For, he says, in Pamphilus’s *Apology*, which Rufinus dedicated to Macarius, nothing is found that was brought forward against the mathematicians or advocates of Fate. The work discusses only the Father, the eternity and consubstantiality of the Son, the divinity of the Holy Spirit, the incarnation of the Word and Christ the Lord, the punishments of the damned, and the transmigration of souls.

Noris then asks: What work, therefore, did Pamphilus write against the mathematicians? How did Rufinus convey knowledge of the matters about which Macarius wished to learn? Finally, he thinks that the origin of the imposture lay in the remaining five books of *Apologies for Origen*, now lost, which the same great man attributed entirely to Eusebius, rather than, as he should have done, to Pamphilus.

He supposes that in one of these books Origen’s statements against the mathematicians were quoted, and that Rufinus intended to translate all these books. But, having scarcely translated the first, he withdrew his hand from the tablet. Noris says that he feared that, if he translated the remaining five books, they would be recognized as belonging not to Pamphilus but to Eusebius. Hence, according to Noris, Gennadius’s error: he treated as accomplished what had not been accomplished.

Noris adds this as well: Rufinus did not wish to give the title of “first book” to the *Apology* translated by him, lest it be thought to have been composed by someone other than Saint Pamphilus.

I have discussed the *Apology* itself at sufficient length, and whether Pamphilus alone was the author of the first book or not, in Book V, chapter V, §§3 and 4. I shall now show that Rufinus kept his promise to Macarius: he translated into Latin that one book of the one martyr Pamphilus—the first of the six books of the *Apology*—but did not translate the others, because Pamphilus had written against the mathematicians in that one book, which was his own and the first, and not in the remaining books.

Here is the explanation of a fact truer and clearer than midday light. In that very *Apology* of his which still survives through Rufinus’s translation in volume I of Origen’s works, p. 758, Grynaeus’s edition, Pamphilus defends the freedom of the human will against the mathematicians and advocates of Fate, who impiously attribute human actions to the course and movements of the stars.

These are Pamphilus’s words:

“It follows that we must understand that we are not subject to necessity, so that, whether we wish it or not, we are compelled in every way to do either good or evil. For if we are masters of our own will, certain powers may perhaps attack us toward sin, while others may assist us toward salvation. Yet we are not compelled by necessity either to act rightly or to act wrongly. This is what those whom they commonly call mathematicians and judicial astrologers believe: they say that the courses and movements of the stars are the cause of human actions—not of those things that occur outside the freedom of the will, but of those that lie within our power.”

Further, on p. 760, the holy man assigns to the list of heretics those who strive to take away from souls the power of free will. They must be judged, he says, to inflict a kind of stain upon common human life and upon the virtue of self-control by their pernicious doctrine, lest the human mind conclude that it is not to be credited with the ability to do, say, or think anything good. From this the human mind would be strengthened toward contempt for, or negligence of, the divine judgment.

And below:

“It must be held among ecclesiastical teachings that no human being has been handed over by God to destruction; rather, each of those who perish perishes through his own negligence and fault. For, possessing the power of free will, he both could and ought to choose what is good. The same must be believed concerning the devil himself.”

These testimonies against the astrologers, or mathematicians, excerpted from Saint Pamphilus’s own *Apology*, vindicate Rufinus’s integrity from the accusation of imposture and fraud. They rightly show that Rufinus, writing to Macarius against the mathematicians, said that Pamphilus had composed something of this kind in his *Apology*. That book was the first of six, and the only one composed by Pamphilus alone; the remaining four were composed not by him alone but by him together with Eusebius, while the last was composed by Eusebius alone.

What Pamphilus wrote still survives in the same *Apology*. Gennadius therefore was not led into error by Rufinus when he counted among Rufinus’s translated works *Pamphilus’s Sentences against the Mathematicians*, which did not exist. Rather, Gennadius expressed by the term *Sentences against the Mathematicians* what Pamphilus had truly written in his *Apology* and Rufinus had translated into Latin, although he should properly have called it an *Apology* rather than *Sentences*.

Gennadius did not attribute two books translated by Rufinus to Pamphilus—an *Apology* and *Sentences against the Mathematicians*. He attributed only one, using the title *Sentences against the Mathematicians* to make it clear that he was referring to a single *Apology* of the martyr. Since he could not leave the book without a title, he had to identify it by one name or the other. He identified it by the name *Sentences against the Mathematicians*.

Nevertheless, this point must not be concealed: in the oldest Vatican manuscript of Gennadius, the wording is not as in the commonly printed editions: “He also translated Pamphilus the martyr’s *Sentences against the Mathematicians*.” Instead, after the *Sentences of Evagrius* there immediately follows: “Of Pamphilus the martyr, against the mathematicians”—understand, perhaps, a book or an *Apology*.

Whatever Gennadius wrote, he certainly indicated the first book of the *Apology* and recognized it as the work of Saint Pamphilus. It is therefore now clear that in Saint Pamphilus’s *Apology* there truly still survive the *Sentences of this martyr against the mathematicians*, translated by Rufinus—sentences which learned men had judged either never to have existed or to have perished long ago.

Having made these observations in Rufinus’s defense, I do not wish to diminish anything of Noris’s praise. I have always held the man in the highest esteem, since he was born to adorn and enrich the inner disciplines of learning. But to make no mistake is granted to gods, not to men.

Let us now apply ourselves to examining Rufinus’s other translations as well.

## CHAPTER X

I. Rufinus translated the Greek *Recognitions of Clement* into Latin after their translation had once been unsuccessfully attempted by his friend Paulinus of Nola.

II. At the request of Saint Silvia, sister of Rufinus’s prefectural superior, he undertook the work and dedicated it to Gaudentius, Bishop of Brescia.

III. Rufinus was the true author of the preface and the translator of the *Recognitions*.

IV. Bellarmine’s passage concerning the *Recognitions of Clement* is examined.

V. The various titles of the *Recognitions of Clement* are recited.

VI. The author of the *Recognitions* is investigated.

VII. His date is established.

VIII. Dodwell’s opinion is refuted.

IX. Pope Gelasius’s judgment on the *Recognitions*.

X. The various editions of the *Recognitions* are enumerated.

I. Paulinus of Nola, Letter XLVI, formerly XLVII.

As I said elsewhere, Paulinus most graciously greeted Rufinus when Rufinus was traveling from the monastery of Pineto to Rome. He thanked his friend for having encouraged him to study Greek literature more attentively, after Paulinus had sent Rufinus the Latin edition of Saint Clement’s works which he himself had prepared.

The holy and very modest man attributes to his own incompetence the fact that in some places he translated the sense rather than the words, since he had not understood the words themselves. But let us hear Paulinus speaking in his own words:

“Certainly I gladly accept what you deign to urge upon me with that affection by which you love us as you love yourself: that I should devote myself more attentively to the study of Greek letters. But I cannot fulfill this unless perhaps the Lord helps my desires, so that I may enjoy your companionship for a longer time. For how shall I be able to make progress in an unfamiliar language if there is no one from whom I may learn what I do not know?

“I believe that, in the translation of Saint Clement, besides the other failures of my talent, you especially noticed this deficiency and poverty of my incompetence: that I translated certain passages whose words I could not understand by grasping the sense instead—or, to speak more truly, by conjecturing it. Therefore I need God’s mercy all the more, so that he may grant me fuller access to you; for it will be wealth to a poor man if he can gather with the eager mouth of a hungry heart the crumbs falling from a rich man’s table.”

No one has reason to doubt, with Heribert Rosweyde, that Paulinus is speaking here of Clement of Rome. For he distinguished himself by that name from the Alexandrian and other Clements in antiquity, by antonomasia. Rufinus, who had brought the *Clementine Recognitions*, divided into ten books, from the East to Italy together with many other Greek manuscripts, upon his return entrusted them to his host Paulinus for translation.

But Paulinus undertook the translation without ever putting the finishing hand to it, because Rufinus, from the specimen sent to him, recognized that it had been prepared less accurately. He therefore kindly urged the holy man to devote greater effort to Greek literature. Paulinus himself reveals all this to us.

Rosweyde notes that Rufinus or Paulinus either interpolated the translation or translated the Clementine work anew. In a clear matter the learned man should not have hesitated. The latter is certainly the case. Rufinus would not have claimed for himself someone else’s translation, one that he did not approve.

The following sufficiently overturns Rosweyde’s hesitation: Paulinus says that he translated certain passages whose words he could not understand by grasping the sense instead. Rufinus, however, declares that he departed not much from the sense, nor even from the wording and expressions. “This,” he says, “although it makes the language of the narrative less ornate, nevertheless makes it more faithful.”

## II

Rufinus had undertaken this labor of translating his Clementine work after being asked by Saint Silvia the Virgin, whom Paulinus praises in Letter XXXI, formerly XI, to Severus, bearing witness there that she had brought to Italy the relics of many martyrs from the East. Rufinus says of her in the prologue to the Clementine work addressed to Gaudentius, Bishop of Brescia:

> We, whom both the slightness of our talent renders less ready and old age now makes slow and sluggish, have at last restored—though after MANY DELAYS—the work which SILVIA, of venerable memory, had LONG AGO entrusted to us, namely, that we should render Clement into our language, and which you thereafter rightly demanded from us by hereditary claim [Col. 0208D]. Let us turn to the uses and advantages of our people a considerable spoil, snatched from the libraries of the Greeks, so that we may nourish those whom we cannot nourish with native provisions by means imported from abroad. For foreign things are often found more agreeable, and sometimes also more useful.

Rufinus says that Gaudentius had demanded this translation from him by hereditary right because Saint Silvia the Virgin, to whom Rufinus himself had promised it, had died at Brescia, in Gaudentius’s episcopal seat, where her body rests in the church of Saint John and her memory is commemorated on 15 December, according to the *Acta Sanctorum* of the Bollandists, 27 April, p. 495, § 3.

Palladius, who testifies in chapter CXLII of the *Historia Lausiaca* that he went to Egypt with Silvia when she was sixty years old, calls her Salvia, or alternatively Silvania, and the sister of the former prefect Rufinus. In the old version of the same history, however, entitled *The Paradise of Heraclides*, he calls her not Silvania or Salvia but Silvia, chapter XLII [Col. 0209A], p. 977 of Rosweyd’s second edition. Both Palladius and Heraclides, at the beginning of the following chapter, state that Saint Olympias, deaconess of the Church of Constantinople, set before herself the outstanding virtues of Silvia as an example to imitate. Such, surely, was Silvia’s distinction and renown for holiness that she was offered to others as an example!

There is no reason why Tillemont, vol. XI, p. 639, should say that the expression *expraefecti*, in Greek τοῦ ἀπὸ ἐπάρχων—that is, “of the former prefect”—must be referred to the time of Palladius’s journey with Silvia to Egypt, or to A.D. 388, when it ought properly to be referred to A.D. 420, the year in which Palladius was writing. For Rufinus, Silvia’s brother and Praetorian Prefect in the East under the emperor Arcadius, paid the penalty for attempted tyranny at Constantinople on 27 November [5 Kalends of December] A.D. 395, and therefore after A.D. 388, according to Gothofredus on Philostorgius, book XI, chapter III, and Socrates, book VI, chapter I.

After her brother Rufinus had been removed, Silvia crossed into Italy, where she was present in A.D. 398, according to Paulinus’s Letter XXXI, formerly XI. For in that year, after the feast of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul, as was stated in book IV, chapter V, § 3 [Col. 0209B], Paulinus sent Victor to Severus in Aquitaine with the same letter. Along with it, as a consecration-gift for the new basilica, he added a particle of the most holy Cross, obtained from Melania. He did not, however, add the sacred ashes requested by Severus, saying that he himself lacked them. Nevertheless, he says that Victor had abundant hope of receiving the same favor from Saint SILVIA, who had promised him relics of many martyrs from the East. Silvia, therefore, had returned from the East to Italy by that time.

She died at Brescia around the end of the fourth century, and Gaudentius, bishop of the city, demanded by hereditary right the *Clementine Recognitions* which our Rufinus had formerly promised to the living Silvia. The same Rufinus, near the end of his peroration to Origen’s commentaries on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, had pledged his faith to Gaudentius in these words:

> After this, indeed, the work calls us which was LONG AGO entrusted to us (by Silvia). But now (after Silvia’s death) it is pressed upon us more urgently by the blessed bishop Gaudentius: namely, the work of Clement, bishop of Rome and companion of the Apostles [Col. 0209C]. So that I may give knowledge of them to their successors, these books are being translated by us into Latin.

Rosweyd, in his notes on Paulinus’s Letter XLVII, which in the new edition is XLVI, and after him Cotelerius, are equally uncertain whether Rufinus dedicated this work to Gaudentius of Brescia or to Gaudentius of Novara. The first publisher of the book, Jacobus Faber Stapulensis, took a different path, having before his eyes Gaudentius, the glorious martyr of Christ and bishop of Ariminum. Yet that man had shed his blood for Christ under the emperor Constantius, long before this.

While various writers were thus pulling the saw in different directions, David Blondel understood the matter much better in his *Pseudo-Isidore*, p. 28, by taking it wholly to concern Gaudentius of Brescia. Let us hear Rufinus explicitly confirming this in his preface to Gaudentius:

> To you, Gaudentius, distinguished glory of our TEACHERS, there is such vigor of intellect, or rather such grace of the Spirit, that if anything is said by you even in the manner of DAILY SPEECH, and if anything is DECLARED IN THE CHURCH, it ought to be PRESERVED IN BOOKS and HANDED DOWN FOR INSTRUCTION [Col. 0209D] to posterity.

A little later he says:

> It is certainly right that I should disclose to you, who have also READ THESE THINGS IN GREEK, the purpose of our translation, lest you suppose that in some places we have preserved the order of the translation.

These praises, heaped by Rufinus upon Gaudentius the bishop, can be applied to Gaudentius of Brescia alone, and to no one else. For he was a distinguished Teacher, or Expositor. Thus ecclesiastical writers commonly called those who explained and taught the word of God and the sacred Scriptures either orally or in writing, as Franciscus Bernardinus Ferrarius noted in book I of *On the Rite of Sacred Sermons*, chapter II. He also adduces an example from Gaudentius of Brescia, who calls his sermons, delivered in the church—as Rufinus likes to say—“discourses” in the preface to Benivolus.

The distinguished scholar Paulus Galeardus, a Brescian canon, has recently prepared an excellent edition of these works. The same outstanding prelate says that he discovered from notaries, secretly stationed there, that his discourses had been collected from his spoken words [Col. 0210A]. Rufinus says the same in these words:

> If anything is said by you even in the manner of DAILY SPEECH, and if anything is DECLARED IN THE CHURCH, we see it PRESERVED IN BOOKS and HANDED DOWN FOR INSTRUCTION—

namely, by those who sent notaries to record all these things secretly.

According to Rufinus, Gaudentius knew Greek literature. Why should he not have, since he testifies that he undertook holy pilgrimages through the East, where the fame of his virtues had reached such a point that, at the urging of the Eastern bishops, the episcopal burden was announced to him through a delegation sent from his own people after the death of Philastrius, and he placed his shoulders beneath it?

There he also formed a close friendship with John Chrysostom, who was not yet a bishop; and later, when Chrysostom had been deprived of his episcopate, Gaudentius was sent to Constantinople as legate of the Roman Church. See also Gaudentius’s Sermon XVI, Epistle CLXXXIV; Palladius’s *Dialogue*, chapter IV; and Nicephorus Callistus, book XIII, chapter XXXIII.

Thus no doubt remains that the bishop Gaudentius to whom Rufinus dedicated his Clement was Gaudentius of Brescia, and no other [Col. 0210B].

## III

I have pursued this matter at greater length on account of the most learned men Sixtus of Siena and the venerable Cardinal Robert Bellarmine. The former, in book II of his *Bibliotheca*, and the latter, in his catalogue under A.D. 390, treated Rufinus’s preface to Gaudentius far too hastily as spurious.

I shall quote Bellarmine’s words because of a gloss which Labbe attaches to them in volume II, p. 309:

> Just as the *Recognitions* themselves are perhaps falsely attributed to Clement, so it is not incredible that Rufinus’s preface was also falsely attached to him, as though he were the translator.

Labbe writes in response:

> Yet Gennadius did not recognize the imposture, nor did his followers or Trithemius.

After Johann Rainolds, the faithless copyist of our writers, in his *Censure of Apocryphal Writings*, Gerardus Johannes Vossius took the same view as Sixtus and Bellarmine in book II, chapter IX of *On Greek Historians*, calling the preface that of Rufinus or of someone else under his name. Indeed, later he indicates that he would prefer to believe not only that the preface was entirely fabricated, but also that the books of the *Recognitions* themselves were translated by someone other than Rufinus [Col. 0210C].

Caspar Barthius had preceded Vossius in this error. I shall quote his words from *Adversaria*, book XLV, chapter V:

> It is not easy to decide whether the books inscribed with the title *Clement’s Recognitions* have Clement as their author and Rufinus as their translator.

I would that such words had not escaped men so highly cultivated in literature. Is it difficult to decide what the dense and abundant authority of ancient monuments confirms? What, then, of Rufinus himself in the *Peroration* to Origen’s commentaries on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, where he says that, under the pressure of the bishop Gaudentius, he is laboring to make Clement Latin? What of Gennadius, chapter XVII, when he relates that the books of Clement of Rome’s *Recognitions* were rendered into Latin by Rufinus?

It would take a long journey if I wished to review all the others who subsequently bear witness to the same matter. But I shall not allow one or two of them to go unmentioned.

Anastasius the Librarian, in a letter to John the Deacon, in volume III of the works of Jacobus Sirmondus, p. 472, says:

> Clement, whom Rufinus, writing to Gaudentius, indicates as having been rendered into our language [Col. 0210D], restored, and brought back.

Saint Aldhelm, or Althelmus, bishop of Sherborne, in chapter XXV of *On the Praise of Virginity*, p. 316 of the London edition corrected by Henry Wharton, praises the *Itinerary of Peter*—that is, the *Recognitions of Clement*—as having been translated into Latin by Rufinus from the libraries of the Greeks.

The manuscripts of the *Recognitions*—plainly all of them—agree with such explicit witnesses, bearing the name of Rufinus as translator. There can therefore be no doubt that these remarkably learned men, hurrying on to other matters, overlooked this evidence; otherwise they would not have treated a certain matter as fiction.

Among more recent scholars, Cotelerius, in his judgment on the books of the *Recognitions*, p. 484 of the new edition, says that Rufinus’s authorship of the preface to Gaudentius, as well as of the translation of the entire work, can be established even from the style; and he vindicates both for Rufinus on the authority of older manuscripts. One of the manuscripts he cites begins as follows:

> Preface of Rufinus the presbyter to Gaudentius the bishop, concerning the *Itinerary of Clement*, translated by him from Greek into Latin.

After the preface and Clement’s letter to James it reads:

> The first book of the *Itinerary of Clement*, successor of the Apostle Peter [Col. 0211A], translated by Rufinus, begins.

For the rest, Bellarmine acknowledged that the Clementine *Recognitions* had been translated into Latin by Rufinus and did not doubt this. For, according to Baronius, under A.D. 102, § 22:

> No one ought to doubt it, since Gennadius bears witness to this very thing concerning Rufinus.

And yet we find Dupin, in volume III of his *Bibliotheca*, attributing an entirely different opinion to Bellarmine—namely, the opinion we have refuted.

We also find Anastasius the Librarian entangled in this same dense error long before, in the letter already cited; and, along with him among more recent writers, Peter Daniel Huet, in his book *On Illustrious Translators*, p. 151. They understood the words with which Rufinus begins his preface to Gaudentius—“that we should render Clement into our language”—as though the *Recognitions* themselves had first been written in Latin, then lost, and finally restored by Rufinus from Greece to Latium, rather than translated from Greek [Col. 0211B].

But Rufinus plainly wrote something quite different. These learned men were led into error because, as often happens, they read only the first few words hastily.

## IV

Nor should another passage of Bellarmine be entirely passed over. In his catalogue under A.D. 92 he writes the following about the Clementine *Recognitions*:

> According to Epiphanius, heresy 30, Clement himself testifies that the *Circuits of Peter*, written by him, had been corrupted by heretics.

The purple-clad scholar drew this from the *Great Annals*, under A.D. 41, § 10, and A.D. 102, § 21. But Lucas Holstenius discovered that Epiphanius did not say this. Rather, Epiphanius says that these *Periods* are convicted of falsehood by the encyclical letters of blessed Clement, which are read in the churches. For they do not agree either with the style of Saint Clement or with his manner of teaching.

These are Holstenius’s words in his manuscript notes on Bellarmine’s catalogue, preserved in our museum. I have pointed out the error of so great a man so that no one may henceforth be scandalized by the authority of the person who made the statement, as recently happened to another learned man. Since I corrected him, I ought not to name him [Col. 0211C], lest I seem to injure the friendship that exists between us.

Epiphanius himself, in *Heresy* XXX, § 15, testifies that the Clementine books had been corrupted by the Ebionites. Photius likewise, codex CXIII, calls the work filled with absurdities and with very many blasphemies against the Son arising from Arius’s opinion.

These statements prompted the distinguished theologian Dionysius Petavius, in book I of *On the Trinity*, chapter III, at the end of § 3, to suggest that the books known to Photius had been more corrupted than Rufinus’s translation, because Rufinus had removed the material that, as he himself noted in his treatise *On the Adulteration of the Books of Origen*, had been inserted by heretics, especially the Eunomians—material which, according to Rufinus himself, the ecclesiastical rule entirely rejects.

But we must recall that Rufinus indicates in his preface to Gaudentius that there were two ancient editions of the *Recognitions*, just as we previously noted that there were likewise two ancient editions of Xystus’s *Sentences*. Let us hear Rufinus speaking about this:

> I think that you, Gaudentius, are not unaware that in Greek there are TWO EDITIONS of this Clement’s work, called ἀναγνώσεων—that is, of the *Recognitions* [Col. 0211D]—and that there are TWO CORPORA OF BOOKS, differing in some respects but containing the same narrative in many others. Finally, the last part of this work, in which the transformation of Simon is related, is found in ONE CORPUS. There are also certain matters discussed in BOTH CORPORA concerning the unbegotten God and the begotten God, and concerning several other things which, to say nothing more, have exceeded our understanding.

Now consider which edition of the Clementine work Epiphanius and Photius attacked with their censures. Certainly not the one Rufinus translated into Latin. For this edition is free from the corruptions of heretics; and the holy men Paulinus and Gaudentius, who labored to present it to Latium through a friend, compel us to believe that the Greek version too was free from them.

Fabricius, in *Bibliotheca Graeca*, volume V, chapter I, p. 35, thinks that ἀναγνώσεων should be read as ἀναγνωρισμοῦ in Rufinus’s words, on the basis of Rufinus himself in his little book *On the Adulteration of the Books of Origen* and of Photius [Col. 0212A], codex CXIII, although all the ancient manuscripts of the *Recognitions* exhibit ἀναγνώσεων. The difference is immaterial. The title of the work derives from this term because it relates how Clement, his parents, and his brothers recognize one another.

## V

After Cotelerius, p. 484, Jo. Ernestus Grabius treats the various titles of the Clementine *Recognitions* accurately in his *Spicilegium Patrum*, volume I, p. 275. There he also lists several excellent manuscripts of the work preserved in the Bodleian Library at Oxford.

1. *The Recognitions of Clement*  
2. *The Recognition of Clement*  
3. *The Itinerary of Clement of Rome to James, the Brother of the Lord*  
4. *The Itinerary of Saint Clement concerning the Deeds and Sayings of the Blessed Apostle Peter*  
5. *The Acts of the Apostle Peter*  
6. *The Circuits of Peter*  
7. *The Periods of Peter*  
8. *The Itinerary of Clement*  
9. *The History of Clement* [Col. 0212B]  
10. *The Chronicles of Clement*  
11. *The Deeds of Clement*  
12. *The Book of Clement*  
13. *The Books of Clement*  
14. *On the True Debate of the Apostle Peter against the Falsehood of Simon Magus*  
15. *On the Debate of Peter with Simon Magus*

Grabius removes the title *The Debate* or *Dialogue of Peter with Apion*, which Henricus Valesius and Cotelerius had assigned to this work.

The title *Itinerary*, or, which is the same thing, *Circuits* and *Periods*, adhered more frequently to the work because of the story of the journey which Peter was believed to have undertaken from Jerusalem to Antioch, passing through Caesarea, Dora, Ptolemais, Tyre, Sidon, Berytus, Tripoli, Orthosiades, Antaradus, and Laodicea.

Holstenius, however, in his manuscript notes on Bellarmine’s catalogue, thought [Col. 0212C] that the *Itinerary* differed from the *Recognitions* and was not an abridgment of them. He was referring to the volume published at Paris with the Latin translation of Joachim Perionius.

But Vossius, near the end of book II, chapter IX of *On Greek Historians*, observes that this work can be shown by many arguments—apart from its diction—not to be very ancient. This will become still clearer if one consults Barthius, who examines it in *Adversaria*, book XXXII, chapter XIV, and book XXXVII, chapter XXIII.

The book’s title reads:

> *An Epitome of Clement of Rome, Bishop, concerning the Deeds, Journeys, and Sermons of Saint Peter, to James, Bishop of Jerusalem.* Paris, apud Hadrianum Turnebum, 1555, quarto.

Cotelerius, who published this work after collating it with seven royal manuscripts, discovered on p. 749 that, after the *Recognitions* and the *Homilies*, it was nothing other than a pure epitome—not, however, compiled solely from the *Recognitions* published by Rufinus, but also from the *Homilies* and Clement’s letter to James. It also drew upon Clement’s martyrdom and the account of Ephraem, bishop of Chersonesus, which is appended there.

Cotelerius carefully supports this very point in the passages indicated in the margins, partly anticipated by Baronius under A.D. 102, § 22. He thought that the work had been composed by people who considered it part of their doctrine and piety either to remove, alter, or correct whatever seemed superfluous, false, or dangerous in the books already mentioned—though, as Baronius judged, in another edition remembered by the ancients.

Thus this book does not present itself as an epitome of a single volume of the *Recognitions*, as Perionius and Vossius believed when they looked only to Rufinus’s version. Rather, one may rightly call it a compilation of other collections of the same general character. Cotelerius learned from the manuscripts of the library of the kings of France that such a compilation had been made three times [Col. 0212D].

## VI

The books of the *Recognitions*, however, had an architect entirely different from Saint Clement, the third or fourth bishop of the Roman Church after Peter.

As for the author’s date, it is certain that he flourished before Origen. Origen, who began to flourish under Elagabalus, is the first of all to produce testimony from this author, as from a writer already known and specifically distinguished by the name Clement. He does so twice in volume III of his *Commentaries* [Col. 0213A] on Genesis, chapter I, verse 14.

Although nearly all of these writings have perished, Origen’s passage from book X, chapter X of the *Recognitions* still survives in the *Philocalia*, chapter XXII. Another passage is also read in the *Commentaries* on Matthew, chapter XXVI, verse 6, likewise drawn from book VII, chapter XXXVIII of the *Recognitions*.

Therefore the author of the Clementine work cannot be called younger than Origen, but somewhat older, since this concerns the time of its composition. Before Origen—or, if you prefer, before the third century of Christ—no one ever praised the *Recognitions*, and no one mentioned the Clementines.

Two facts reveal that the author of the book lived in the third century of Christ. First, he stole and appropriated for himself a fairly long fragment from Bardesanes’ Syriac *Dialogue on Fate against Abidas the Astrologer*, perhaps thinking that it would not easily be recognized because Bardesanes had written not in Greek but in Chaldaic. Second, he speaks not obscurely of the Roman citizenship granted to the whole world.

Bardesanes flourished under Marcus Aurelius around A.D. 171, to whom he dedicated his *Dialogue*. Caracalla, however, around A.D. 215, was the first to order by an issued constitution that peoples subject to the Roman Empire, who had previously lived under their own laws, should pass under the rights of the City, mistress of the world.

To prevent the matter from remaining doubtful, we shall proceed point by point. Eusebius, in *Preparation for the Gospel*, book VI, chapter X [Col. 0213B], preserved for us a portion of Bardesanes’ *Dialogue* translated into Greek. In the Clementine *Recognitions*, according to Cotelerius’s division, it appears in Latin from chapter XIX through chapter XXIX.

Johannes Ernestus Grabius, in *Spicilegium*, volume I, p. 290, set Rufinus’s Clementine translation and the Greek text of Bardesanes—whose author, Bardesanes, asserts that it was composed from his own ingenuity and not taken from elsewhere—side by side. He compared them so that anyone might immediately recognize the extent to which they agree or differ.

He also added various notes, whose principal purpose is to demonstrate that the author of the Clementines altered certain things, acted as a paraphrast in some places, misunderstood some passages, omitted others, and finally interpolated still others, so that what he had stolen from Bardesanes might be made to agree with his own narratives [Col. 0213C].

The decisive proof that the Clementine author borrowed from Bardesanes, as from an older writer, and that Bardesanes did not borrow from him, is found in book IX of the *Recognitions*, chapter XXVII. From this passage we clearly learn that the same work could not in any way have been composed before the constitution issued by the emperor Antoninus Caracalla, which Ulpian mentions in Digest 1.5.17, *On the Status of Persons*.

I shall quote the passage itself, joining to it Bardesanes’ words in parallel. By thus setting Bardesanes, in a sense, against the author of the *Recognitions*, I shall make clearer what the latter, presenting it as spoken by Clement of Rome, added on his own to Bardesanes’ words and what he altered.

### I. Clement, book IX of the *Recognitions*, chapter XXVII

> Surely it is readily understood how greatly the emperors altered the laws and institutions of the peoples whom they conquered. This is clearly shown to have been done by the Romans, who nevertheless transformed almost the ENTIRE WORLD, and all nations that at first lived according to their own and various laws and institutions, into ROMAN LAW and CIVIL DECREES.

### II. Bardesanes, in the *Dialogue on Fate*, quoted by Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book VI, chapter X [Col. 0213D]

> Πόσοι βασιλεῖς κρατήσαντες ἐθνῶν, παρήγαγον τοὺς πρὸ αὐτῶν νόμους, καὶ ἔθεντο τοὺς ἰδίους.

> How many kings, after gaining power over nations, altered the laws that preceded them and established their own.

> The printed Latin rendering: “Whatever kings or emperors, having gained control over nations, altered the laws that existed before them and established their own.”

The comparison of the two writers now makes the matter clear. Bardesanes spoke in general terms and had no particular law enacted before his time by the emperors in view, still less the constitution of Caracalla. Moreover, the words just quoted prove Bardesanes to have been entirely earlier than that constitution. This was precisely why those same words of Bardesanes were interpolated by the later writer Pseudo-Clement.

For Pseudo-Clement brings the Antonine Constitution directly before our eyes, without any circumlocution, and thus clearly shows that his *Recognitions* were produced not before but after the constitution promulgated by Caracalla. The evidence in the words just quoted is certain and manifest: the whole Roman world, as far as it extended, and the peoples subject to Roman rule, who had previously lived under various laws, finally passed into Roman law at Caracalla’s command [Col. 0214A].

Therefore Pseudo-Clement could not have written these things—which he expressed so clearly—before Caracalla.

Ezechiel Spanhemius splendidly illustrated this constitution of Caracalla in two dissertations published under the title *The Roman World*. He detected the date of Pseudo-Clement from the words I have extracted [Col. 0214B], on pp. 248 and 579.

From this we see how greatly those are mistaken who attempted to place the age of the Clementine writer in the second century. Blondel leads their company in the prolegomena to *Pseudo-Isidore*, p. 59, and in his critique of the First Epistle of Clement, p. 28. Cotelerius appears to have adopted Blondel’s opinion in his judgment on the books of the *Recognitions*, p. 484, and finally Grabius did so as well in volume I of the *Spicilegium*, pp. 277 and 279. Yet Sixtus of Siena had preceded all of them in this same opinion in book II of his *Bibliotheca*.

## VII

We must also contend with Henry Dodwell, who makes Bardesanes younger than Caracalla. In Dissertation IV on Irenaeus, § 35, p. 360, and Dissertation VI, § 11, p. 443, Dodwell disregards the ancient testimonies that say Bardesanes flourished under Marcus. Instead, he makes him a contemporary of Elagabalus, who, though descended from the Antonine family like Aurelius, likewise bore the praenomen Marcus.

Grabius, in volume I of the *Spicilegium*, p. 317 [Col. 0214C], promised that he would adopt this opinion and correct his earlier view. But I do not see that he kept his promise.

Baronius accurately assembled what the ancients transmitted about Bardesanes under A.D. 175, § 16. Almost all of them make him a contemporary of the elder Marcus Antoninus; indeed, they learned this with certainty from the earliest writers and especially from Bardesanes’ own works. These witnesses are Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book IV, chapter XXIX, and his *Chronicle*, under Olympiad 237, in the year of our Lord 173, corresponding to A.D. 171 of the common era.

Eusebius states that in that year the Valentinian heresy began to be openly disseminated by Bardesanes, although Bardesanes had previously written against the error of Marcion. This we learn, besides Epiphanius, *Heresy* LVI, and Theodoret, book I of *Heretical Fables*, chapter XXII, from Augustine, chapter XXXV of *On Heresies*. The Eusebian year 173 corresponds to the eleventh year of Marcus Aurelius Augustus.

Theodoret agrees completely, saying in volume IV of Sirmond’s edition of his works, p. 208, that Bardesanes flourished in the time of Marcus Verus Caesar. Epiphanius likewise confirms this in *Heresy* LVI, § 1 [Col. 0214D], testifying that Bardesanes, after the death of Abgar, dynast of Edessa, reached the age of Antoninus Verus.

Jerome, in his catalogue, chapter XXXIII, says that Bardesanes later refuted the Valentinian heresy, which he had initially followed, and established a new one; he also says that Bardesanes dedicated his book *On Fate* to Marcus Antoninus.

Tillemont, who discusses Bardesanes’s affairs at length in volume II, p. 454, following Henricus Valesius in his notes on Eusebius, inclines to think that this Antoninus was not the emperor but one of Bardesanes’ friends who converse in the *Dialogue*.

Yet he must certainly have been the emperor, who gained possession of Mesopotamia and Edessa, Bardesanes’ homeland. The name Antoninus did not belong to the Syrians, nor should the *Dialogue* have been dedicated to one of the friends conversing in it. Nor could there have been any reason preventing Bardesanes from dedicating a Syriac book to Antoninus, the most learned of the emperors, as Tillemont suggests. Aurelius merely lacked people who could translate it into Greek [Col. 0215A].

To this add the testimony of Epiphanius, according to whom Aurelius valued Bardesanes so highly that he attempted through Apollonius to draw him into his own superstition. Therefore the man whom others call Antoninus, and whom Jerome—who had read Bardesanes’ book in Greek translation—properly calls Marcus Antoninus, was the person to whom Bardesanes dedicated it.

Spanhemius shows in volume II, Dissertation X, p. 32, that among ancient writers the elder Aurelius is especially designated by the praenomen Marcus alone.

Let us add another argument for Bardesanes’ date, one of considerable force against Dodwell. Bardesanes says the following in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book IV, chapter X:

> Χθὲς οἱ Ῥωμαῖοι Ἀραβίας κρατήσαντες τοὺς τῶν Βαρβάρων νόμους ἤλλαξαν.

> THE DAY BEFORE YESTERDAY, after gaining possession of Arabia, the Romans changed the laws of the barbarians.

The emperor Trajan first subdued Arabia, according to Dio, book LXVIII, p. 777; hence antiquarians know that his coins bear the inscription ARAB. ADQUIS. See Spanhemius, volume I, Dissertation IX, p. 185.

It is also established that Arabia was again subdued by war under Marcus Aurelius, according to Dio, book LXXI, p. 812 [Col. 0215B]. Tillemont, in his *History of the Emperors*, volume II, p. 366, assigns this to A.D. 170.

Yet Bardesanes, if he lived under Elagabalus at the beginning of the third century, would have spoken foolishly in saying that Arabia had been subdued by the Romans “the day before yesterday,” if Trajan at the beginning of the second century, or Marcus Aurelius at that time, had only then subdued it. But Bardesanes himself, living under Marcus, could properly say this of either event.

I could produce other arguments of this kind. But these are more than sufficient to prove that Bardesanes flourished under the elder Marcus Aurelius Antoninus and therefore cannot in any way be called younger than the author of the Clementine *Recognitions*, much less their author—as Cave nevertheless conjectured.

Besides the Greek writers, Epiphanius and the other ancient Fathers, the author of the Edessene Chronicle, recently published by the distinguished Joseph Simon Assemani, also assigns Bardesanes to the time of Marcus Aurelius, in volume I of the *Bibliotheca Orientalis*, p. 389.

Photius, codex CCXXIII, while reviewing the eight books of Theodore, bishop of Tarsus, against Fate [Col. 0215C], says that in chapters I and L, while overthrowing the doctrine of Fate, Theodore also refutes the opinion of Bardesanes. For although he leaves the soul free from Fate and from the so-called birth-sign, preserving its freedom of choice, he nevertheless subjects the body and everything pertaining to the body to the governance of Fate.

These are the stains of the ancient errors which Bardesanes, according to Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book IV, chapter XXX, did not entirely discard when he abandoned the Valentinians. For this reason Jerome says of him that, although he refuted the Valentinians whom he had first followed, he nevertheless founded a new heresy.

Ernestus Salomon Cyprianus, in his notes on Jerome’s catalogue, writes the following about this:

> I wish he had said what the principles of that new heresy were.

A little later he does not hesitate to criticize Augustine for attributing to Bardesanes errors concerning Fate, although Bardesanes had written against Fate. This is certainly true insofar as the free choice of human beings is concerned. Nevertheless, he subjected the body and everything pertaining to the body to the governance of Fate, as Theodore of Tarsus testifies.

Augustine’s words about Bardesanes [Col. 0215D], in chapter XXXV of *On Heresies*, are these:

> He did not fall entirely into the heresy of Valentinus (after he had come to his senses), adding something of his own, namely, that he attributed human conduct to Fate.

But the editors of the new edition point out that the final words—“adding something,” and so forth—do not occur in the manuscript codices, although they explain what precedes.

This more extended discussion of Bardesanes was compelled by his plagiarist, Pseudo-Clement, the author of the *Recognitions*, since we are often dealing with plagiarists who think they can remain hidden.

Dodwell believes that the *Recognitions* were compiled between A.D. 218 and 231. He would have spoken more accurately had he placed them between A.D. 211 and 217. For in A.D. 211 Caracalla began to rule alone; he was the author of the new constitution mentioned in the books of the *Recognitions*. Then, in the same year A.D. 217, Caracalla was killed.

This refutes the great error of Peter Allix in his *Dissertation on the Year and Month of the Lord’s Birth*, p. 8, where he says that Pseudo-Clement lived not long before Sulpicius, although he lived two hundred years before him [Col. 0216A].

Origen, the first herald of the *Recognitions*, fleeing Caracalla’s anger, withdrew from Alexandria to Palestine. Huet observes in *Origeniana*, book I, chapter II, § 6, p. 10, that Origen made this journey to Palestine twice.

Huet assigns Origen’s first journey to Palestine, where he settled at Caesarea and became known to Saint Alexander, bishop of Jerusalem, to A.D. 215. There he was held in such honor that, although he had not yet entered the sacred ministry, he was entrusted with publicly explaining the word of God in the church before the bishops.

From this journey, after Caracalla was killed in A.D. 217, Origen must be regarded as having brought the *Recognitions* with him when he returned from Jerusalem to Alexandria. He then incorporated their opinions into his own commentaries. Eusebius shows in book VI, chapter XIX of his *Ecclesiastical History*, from the ninth volume of those commentaries, that the first eight volumes on Genesis were composed at Alexandria, and indeed after Origen’s first journey to Palestine.

We readily agree with Blondel that the *Recognitions* were composed in Palestine, since in them the throne of the Jerusalem Church is exalted above all others [Col. 0216B]. This is supported to some extent by the fact that Rufinus too was the first to bring the same work from Palestine into Italy.

The work acquired the name *Recognitions* from its subject. For recognition, or acknowledgment, according to Aristotle in the *Poetics*, occurs when people once most closely joined to one another finally, after many disasters in tragedies and comedies, recognize one another unexpectedly.

This is precisely what happens in the composition of Pseudo-Clement to Faustinian, Mattidia, and their sons Clement, Faustus, and Faustinus: they unexpectedly recognize one another. It is therefore highly plausible that the work acquired not only its title but also the form of a poetic composition, as Dodwell says on p. 444 of his *Dissertations on Irenaeus*.

We do not deny that the genuine and primary author of the *Recognitions* abounds in learning, variety, and richness of subject matter. Yet everyone can see that he reveals himself as a philosopher, though certainly a Catholic one—more a philologist than a theologian.

Because of the man’s reputation, I shall quote the judgment of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola [Col. 0216C], who says that the work contains apostolic doctrine. We owe this testimony to Jacobus Faber Stapulensis, in a letter to Jacobus Ramirus, bishop of Catana, placed before his first edition of the Clementine *Recognitions*.

Whoever this author was, however, since he preferred to remain hidden beneath a mask, he appears to have been poorly equipped with critical judgment. Above all, he reveals himself as very different from Clement, the apostolic man, from whose hand came that admirable letter in the name of the Roman Church to the Corinthians.

As I have said, Epiphanius had observed this many centuries ago. We shall refrain from continuing the analysis of the books, since Nolanus Nurrius has already carried it out in the *Apparatus to the Bibliotheca Patrum*, volume I, dissertation IX, p. 211.

### VIII

But Pope Gelasius, in the authentic Decree, from the very old Vatican manuscript that I formerly published, pronounced the following judgment concerning the *Recognitions* translated by Rufinus:

> *The Itinerary, under the name of the Apostle Peter, which is called that of Saint Clement, is apocryphal.*

Here, unlike the other editions, no number of books is specified, because that depended upon the discretion of the scribes. [Col. 0216D] Gelasius said that the work was indeed called that of Saint Clement, but that, by calling it apocryphal, he denied it public reading and canonical authority. There can be no doubt that Gelasius, defining this at the Roman Council of seventy bishops, referred to the *Recognitions of Clement* translated by Rufinus under the title *Itinerary*.

Nevertheless, this did not deprive them of private authority among many Latin ecclesiastical writers. I say nothing of the Greeks. Saint Isidore, Bishop of Seville, when discussing the Latin translation of Rufinus, cited testimony from it in chapters XVII and XXXI of *On the Nature of Things*, and in book III, chapter L of the *Etymologies*. I cited above a passage in Saint Aldhelm’s book *On the Praise of Virginity*. Bede uses the *Recognitions* in his *Hexaemeron*, on chapters I, VI, VII, and VIII of Genesis; in *On the Acts of the Apostles*, chapter V, §34; in his *Retractation* on the same passage; and in chapter III of *On the Reckoning of Time*, drawing from book I, chapter XXXI, §23. Agobard likewise uses them in chapter XVI of *On Jewish Superstitions*; Freculfus in the *Chronicles*, volume II, book II, chapter X; and, along with these, Hincmar in chapter IX of *On the Divorce of Lothair and Tetberga*. Honorius also uses them in chapter XV of *The Lamps of the Church*. In addition, the monk Caesarius transferred into his *Dialogues*, Response CXL, a passage supplied from book VIII, chapter XXIX, §70.

But Cardinal Humbert, Bishop of Silva Candida and papal legate at Constantinople, in his *Response to Nicetas Pectoratus*, after volume XI of Baronius’s *Annals*, p. 798 of the Cologne edition, rebuked his opponent for adducing, in support of the Sabbath fast, testimonies from the *Itinerary of Clement—that is, of Peter*, although apocryphal. He may nevertheless have used a Greek manuscript rather than Rufinus’s Latin version.

We agree with Nurris that these books, although apocryphal—that is, lacking public authority—can nevertheless yield considerable benefit because of their great antiquity. For they are an apology for the Christian religion, and in them the fables of the pagans, their cults, and the errors of those who defend Fate are refuted. Nor will they be useless to those who wish to know the opinions of philosophers, the customs and practices of nations, and the allegorical explanations of fables. Indeed, it would not be easy to understand many Latin passages if we lacked these *Recognitions*. The author of the preface to Cotelerius’s new edition also admits this, although, as is his habit, he says a number of other things incorrectly.

### IX

Grabius, in volume I of his *Spicilegium*, p. 290, extracted from a Bodleian manuscript a short fragment to be appended to book X of the *Recognitions*, which is absent from the other editions.

Let us now present the judgments of later writers, following those of the ancients, concerning these *Recognitions*, made public by Rufinus. Almost all writers of every rank deny that they belong to Clement of Rome.

First, from the College of Cardinals, comes Baronius, admirable for his prudence and gravity: *Annals*, A.D. 34, §§280 and 291; A.D. 41, §10; A.D. 44, §36; and A.D. 51, §53; A.D. 102, §22.

Baronius is followed by Bellarmine in his *Catalogue*, and in book II, chapter II of *On the Roman Pontiff*.

[Col. 0217C] From the order of bishops, Charles Bovius, Bishop of Ostuni, in his preface to the *Apostolic Constitutions*.

From the Order of Preachers, Francisco de Vitoria, volume II, *Relation* XII, *On Magic*, §35.

From the Jesuit priests, Benedictus Pererius, *Commentary on Genesis*, book II, question I, p. 40 of the first Roman edition; Joannes Lorinus, on Acts XIX, §9; Nicolaus Serarius, volume I of his *Opuscula on the Apostles*, §1, p. 27 of the Mainz edition of 1611; and Antonius Possevinus in the *Apparatus*.

From the University of Louvain, Joannes Driedo, volume I of *On the Dogmas of the Church*, part V, book IV, chapter V, fol. 235 of the second Louvain edition, 1572.

From the University of Paris, Natalis Beda, *Against Jacobus Faber*, proposition 103.

I shall not pass over Cotelerius’s words, which encompass the subject of the entire treatise in the preface to his edition, where he calls the work a compilation filled with theological, historical, philosophical, and astrological matters. Barthius should also be added. In *Adversaria*, book XLV, chapter V, he says that the books are ancient and full of good things. He often illustrates them, and also subjects them to sharp criticism, calling them an ancient fragment translated into Latin, written when the style of speech had not yet been greatly polluted by barbarisms and did not yet smell of the mixed filth of the Goths or their like, although it is not free from its own blemishes. He concludes by saying that, for the sake of their good admonitions, he willingly reads such works:

> “We are as secure regarding their truth as if we were turning over Apuleius, or some Apollonius, or Philostratus.”

Barthius is right to judge in this way concerning historical truth, if that is what one occasionally has in view. But he is not right concerning doctrine, about which Lambertus Gruterus, to be discussed later, judged otherwise:

> “Throughout this book human free will, the power, necessity, and dignity of baptism and the Eucharist are defended. Moreover, the Trinity of persons in one God and divine providence are affirmed. It is also taught that the miracles performed at the tombs of martyrs are not to be despised. Yet there are certain passages here, like blemishes, which the pious reader ought either to read cautiously or regard with suspicion. So that no one may be deceived, such passages are marked with their own numbers in their proper places, so that they may be observed.”

These blemishes, explained by Gruterus, number six; they may be consulted in his work.

Finally, let us add the judgment of Hugo Grotius concerning these books, from volume III of his works, p. 488:

> “The books called the *Recognitions* have value for me insofar as they agree with the statements of others. Otherwise, I approve Cardinal Baronius’s judgment concerning them: on the basis of Epiphanius, Rufinus, and others, he says that very many things were sewn into these books, including all those stories about what Peter is said to have done at Caesarea against Simon.”

### X

Let us now at last proceed to the various editions of the Clementine work. Jacobus Faber Stapulensis was the first of all to publish in print the books translated by Rufinus and divided into books and chapters, in a volume bearing the following title:

[Col. 0218B]

> *The Paradise of Heraclides. The Epistle of Clement. The Recognitions of the Apostle Peter. The Completion of Clement’s Epistle. The Epistle of Anacletus.*  
> Paris, from the Bellovisian press, at the expense of Joannes Parvus, 1504, small folio.

Sichardus, a hunter of the oldest books, as he boasts of himself in his letter to Bernard Clesius, Bishop of Trent and later Cardinal, was unaware of this exceedingly rare edition of Faber even twenty-two years later. For Sichardus dedicated to Clesius the same work, recovered by him from two manuscript codices, the Basel and Schönau manuscripts, together with certain other materials and occasional brief notes.

Vossius and Fabricius likewise failed to recognize Faber’s edition. The former, in book II, chapter IX of *On the Greek Historians*, and the latter, in volume V of the *Bibliotheca*, p. 36, called the Sichardine edition the first of all. I give its title below.

[Col. 0218C]

> *The ten books of the Recognitions of the divine Clement, addressed to James, the brother of the Lord, translated by Rufinus Toranus of Aquileia; to which has been added a not-unwelcome selection of letters of the most ancient bishops, hitherto unseen, namely, of those who have presided over the Roman Church for the past twelve hundred years.*  
> Basel, through Joannes Bebel, 1526, folio.

Ten years later this edition of Sichardus, augmented by the decrees of the first four councils of the Church, was issued again at Basel by Bebel, A.D. 1536, in folio. Barthius regarded this, which is the third edition, as the first, in book XLV, chapter V, at the end.

Vossius attributes a failure of judgment to Sichardus because he regarded it as the genuine Clement. This, however, should rather be attributed to the age, which was little accustomed to critical judgment. For Sichardus was not alone: before him Stapulensis, and afterward Perionius, Lambertus Gruterus, and many other otherwise learned men regarded it as the genuine work of Clement.

We consider two things in Sichardus intolerable. First, that he reported the *Recognitions* to have been supplied by Eusebius. The second, much more serious—not only in our view, but also in that of Barthius and Vossius—is that he dared to criticize the judgment of Gelasius and the seventy bishops concerning Clement. He was nevertheless misled by the common reading of the Gelasian Decree, where the Clementine *Itinerary* is divided into chapters and books, contrary to what the truth of the manuscript codices confirms.

Yet the division into chapters was not so unusual as Sichardus thought, as Faber’s first edition demonstrates. The genuine and most ancient Gelasius, published by me, has now removed this stumbling block: he gives an opinion only concerning the work written, not concerning the number of books, and still less concerning the number of chapters.

The remaining editions of the Clementine works derived from the Sichardine edition, such as the Cologne edition from the press of Melchior Novesianus, 1547, in octavo, and the Paris edition issued by Audoenus Parvus, and elsewhere by Michael Sonnius and Sebastian Nivellius, 1568, in octavo. The latter is the same edition, with only the title of the work changed.

But no one devoted greater labor to Rufinus’s *Recognitions of Clement* than Lambertus Gruterus, preacher to the Emperor Maximilian II. He collected into one volume everything circulated under the name of Clement, and published it adorned with prefaces, arguments, notes, and admonitions. Although the title of the work is excessively long, it is worth hearing, since it is not unworthy of literary history to pursue such details and to discuss even the titles of books.

[Col. 0219A]

> *The Clementina, that is, the works of Blessed Clement of Rome, disciple of the divine princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul, and successor of the Pontiff in the Roman See; a most wise philosopher and most steadfast martyr; works which, collected, translated, and emended into Latin by various authors, exist to this day in their entirety, together with a new preface concerning the true and false writings of Blessed Clement, and with a final faithful emendation of the same, as well as a careful explanation of difficult arguments and passages, by the distinguished Lambertus Gruterus of Venray, addressed to the Reverend and Most Illustrious Prince, Lord Daniel, Archbishop of the Holy See of Mainz, Prince-Elector of the Holy Roman Empire and Archchancellor of Germany.*  
> Cologne, through Joannes Birckmann, 1569, folio.

This edition, with some material removed, later passed into the Lyon edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, volume II, p. 376.

But Joannes Baptista Cotelerius, who rendered distinguished service to ecclesiastical antiquity, surpassed the industry and diligence of them all. He again brought into the light all Clement’s pseudepigraphal works translated by Rufinus, together with several others, in a volume entitled:

> *The Works of the Holy Fathers who flourished in Apostolic Times, illustrated with translations, notes, and indices.*  
> Paris, through Pierre Le Petit, 1672, folio.

This outstanding collection, subsequently enlarged by new labors, appeared at Amsterdam under the name of Antwerp, at the expense of the Huguetans, A.D. 1698, in two folio volumes, with Cotelerius’s notes and those of others placed on each page beneath the text of the Fathers, so that they might be more easily and conveniently available to readers, since previously they had appeared separately.

But Joannes Clericus, who supervised the edition, deliberately omitted the dedicatory letter and the preface in which Cotelerius explains to his readers the rationale of his work. By doing so, he made both editions partly necessary for those who study writings of this kind.

In this second edition, volume I, p. 487, there appear the ten books of *The Recognitions of Saint Clement to James, the brother of the Lord*, translated by Rufinus Toranus, priest of Aquileia, from Greek into Latin, together with the translator’s preface to Bishop Gaudentius.

Cotelerius collated the entire work with the greatest care against six excellent codices, added variant readings, and everywhere illustrated Clement, where necessary, with brief but substantial notes. Following Faber, he divided the books into chapters, though by a different method. The manuscript codices he used are enumerated in the preface to the first edition.

1. The Sorbonicus.  
2. The Thuanus.  
3. The Regius. [Col. 0219D]  
4. The codex of Petrus Candelerius.  
5. That of the Discalced Carmelites.

Nurris, in his dissertation on these books, p. 224, cites another, the Colbertinus. The Vatican shelves also preserve a very ancient Palatinus, no. 147.

In the margin of Rufinus’s preface to Gaudentius, where the unbegotten and begotten God are discussed, Faber noted these words:

> “That passage concerning the unbegotten and begotten God is known to have been corrupted by Eunomius, or by others who followed Eunomius’s error, just as Paul’s Epistle to the Corinthians had been corrupted by Marcion. Therefore that passage concerning Eunomius ought not to have been interpreted, any more than Marcion in Paul.”

This scholion is absent from the other editions, and from Cotelerius’s edition itself, although in the Cologne edition of 1547, which faithfully reproduces the Sichardine edition, a very similar scholion was read in the margin:

> “I suspect that this was corrupted by Eunomius, just as Paul’s Epistle to the Corinthians was corrupted by Marcion.”
