Vossius also cites the same scholion from what he calls the first edition of Sichardus, although it certainly is not read there.

What Rufinus omitted from his Clement, as having been corrupted by heretics, Cotelerius found inserted into the remainder of Rufinus’s translation in three codices—the Candelerianus, Sorbonicus, and Thuanus. They consist of ten chapters enclosed between the first and the twelfth. Concerning these, he says:

> “I do not know who therefore took upon himself to interpret what had been omitted by Rufinus.”

This addition indicates, if I am not mistaken, that Rufinus’s translation was anciently revised and collated against Greek exemplars.

In all the manuscripts, however, one reads *Rufinus Toranus*, not *Tyrannius Rufinus*. For the scribes, reading *Tyrannius*, Rufinus’s given name, as *tyrannus*, and later fearing the harshness of the expression, preferred to transform *Tyrannus* into *Toranus* and place it after Rufinus as though it were a surname. This subsequently so perplexed the ingenuity of scholars that someone even thought the name was derived from *Tora*, a destroyed Sabine city, as I said in book IV, chapter 1, §2, although Rufinus’s paternal designation, *Aquileiensis*, follows *Toranus* in that passage and is entirely different from it.

Here I shall note a few other matters. Joannes Albertus Fabricius, in his *Codex Apocryphorum Novi Testamenti*, published at Hamburg A.D. 1703, pp. 413 and 439, observed that many passages had been transferred word for word from Rufinus’s text of the Clementine *Recognitions* into the spurious *History of Abdias*, otherwise attributed to Melito. Wolfgang Lazius was the first to arrange for this work to be published from a manuscript codex of the monastery of Ossiach in Carinthia, at Basel through Joannes Oporinus, A.D. 1551, in folio.

Geverhardus Elmenhorstius, in his notes on Arnobius, in the edition published at Leiden by Joannes Maire, A.D. 1651, quarto, adduces many passages from the same text of Rufinus, from pp. 15 to 152 of book IV, to illuminate Arnobius’s discourse for his own purposes.

Let us now turn to the epistle appended to the books of the *Recognitions*. At Rome, from the printing house of the Roman People, A.D. 1591, the letters of the Supreme Pontiffs were published in three volumes. In the first, before all the others, appears the epistle called Clement’s, addressed to James, the brother of the Lord, with Rufinus as translator.

On p. 7 there is appended to it a spurious supplement, bearing in the margin the heading:

> *A Brief Summary of the Christian Faith.*

Labbe, who inserted it in volume I of the *Councils*, p. 89, writes concerning the addition:

> “Here the epistle ends in certain manuscripts. The rest appears to have been added as an appendix around the year 800.”

Mabillon says nearly the same in volume I of the *Analecta*, p. 142.

Petrus Crabbe had inserted the epistle together with the addition in volume I of the *Councils*, p. 14, Cologne edition, through Petrus Quentel, A.D. 1538. But in his first edition of 1526 Sichardus had appended a fourth epistle of Clement, with an appendix entitled:

> *A Summary of the Faith.*

In his second edition of 1536 this was joined to the epistle itself. Gruterus, following Sichardus, likewise joined it after the *Apostolic Constitutions*, p. 345, although Faber had previously kept it separate.

Theodore Bibliander, in a book entitled *Christian and Catholic Doctrine*, Basel, through Jacobus Parcus, 1550, octavo, p. 221, inserted the same epistle, with Rufinus as translator, but removed the appendix.

Nevertheless, without the translator’s name and without the appendix, it had already been inserted on p. 7 of another book entitled:

> *Several Distinguished, Weighty, and Learned Epistles: Outside the Canon of the Bible, Yet Apostolic and Pious.*  
> Augsburg, through Alexander Weyssenhorn, 1529, octavo.

Blondel rashly placed it first among the epistles of Pseudo-Isidore, and, as is his custom, attacked it with venomous notes.

How highly Franciscus Turrianus regarded it is clear from the fact that, in book II, chapters III and XIII of *On the Apostolic Canons and Decretal Epistles against the Magdeburg Centuriators*, Cologne, through Gervinus Calenius, A.D. 1573, quarto, he both defends it as genuine and repeatedly invokes its Greek text from a Vatican codex to strengthen the Latin translation.

Yet in book IV, chapter XXIV, he does not accept Rufinus as the translator of the version, since it lacks a prologue. But who does not know that, according to Gennadius, Rufinus ought to have supplied prologues only for longer Greek works translated by him, not for a short and simple epistle? [Col. 0221A]

The antiquity of the epistle is supported by Rufinus’s testimony, when he asserts in his preface to Gaudentius that he had formerly translated and published it. It was not placed before the *Recognitions* because it is later in time—namely, later than the *Recognitions*, which were thought to have been written earlier by Clement.

Cotelerius followed Rufinus’s decision and himself placed it after the Clementine work, although he had found it inserted in the Carmelite codex between the preface and the *Recognitions*. The codices used by Stapulensis likewise had it inserted there, and Photius also clearly says, in codex CXIII, that in Greek copies it was customarily placed before the books of the *Recognitions*. It is nevertheless placed after them in the Palatine codex, without the spurious appendix.

The epistle itself is added to the Vatican collections of Isidore, codex DCXXIX, fol. 127, and codex DCXXX, fol. 6.

There can therefore be no legitimate doubt that Clement’s epistle to James, which Rufinus rendered into Latin, is the unadulterated text commonly handled by everyone. Nor does Bellarmine doubt this, in book II, chapter XIV of *On the Roman Pontiff*, near the beginning. Blondel himself sufficiently establishes the same point, although he mixes the venom of his sect into his judgment.

After Cotelerius had published the same epistle in Greek and Latin after the *Recognitions*, without any addition, he immediately appended Rufinus’s translation, collated, as usual, with the ancient editions and manuscript codices and divided into twenty chapters. He observed that the eighteenth chapter is cited in the First Council of Vaison, held in A.D. 442, canon VI, in Labbe, volume III, p. 1458; in the *Capitularies of the Franks*, volume II, p. 1127; and in the Council of Metz, canon XII, in Labbe, volume IX, p. 416.

It is also cited by Pope Nicholas I in epistle XLIX, by John VIII in epistle CCXLIV, and by Gregory VII in book VIII, epistle XXI.

Sidonius alluded to its title long before this, in book VI, epistle I. The Bibliothecarius likewise praised it under Clement, saying:

> “It is believed to be exceedingly ancient, just as the books of the *Recognitions* are.”

Yet before Blondel, five distinguished cardinals of the Holy Roman Church had denied it to Clement: Turrecremata, *Summa of the Church*, book II, chapter CI; Cusanus, *Catholic Concordance*, book III, chapter II; Baronius, A.D. 69, §43; Bellarmine in the *Catalogue*; and Peronius in his renewed *Response to the King of Britain*, chapter XXXI, p. 159.

Among earlier writers, Peter Comestor had made the same determination in chapter CI of his *History of the Acts of the Apostles*, and later Marsilius of Padua in *Defender of the Peace*, part II, chapter XXVII, and Gobelinus Persona in *Cosmodromium*, age VI, chapter VIII.

I shall say nothing about Clement’s third epistle, whose translation is also attributed to Rufinus, since it plainly belongs wholly among the wares of Isidore.

I shall not yet take leave of Clement without exposing the errors of Patrick Junius and Dodwell. At the end of his preface to Clement’s golden epistle to the Corinthians, p. 131 of the Cotelerian edition, Junius flattered himself with the claim, drawn from a certain Lobbes catalogue, that a Latin translation of the same epistle by Jerome was hidden somewhere.

But Cotelerius later recognized that Junius’s hope was exceedingly slight or nonexistent. He suspected that scribes had erased the unwelcome name of Rufinus from the translation of Clement’s epistle to James in order to lend it the dignity of Jerome. We have reported that the same thing happened elsewhere.

I also observe that Dodwell says of Rufinus, in the additions to Pearson’s *Opuscula*, part I, chapter VI, §21, p. 214, that Clement was first adorned by him with the title of martyr. Hence Dodwell attempts to deprive Clement of the laurel of martyrdom. But you attempt in vain, Dodwell, and you certainly will not take it away.

For in the most ancient *Sacramentary Codex*, which the venerable Cardinal Joseph Maria Thomasius, a man of supreme learning and piety, made publicly available, the birthday of Blessed Clement the Priest and MARTYR is celebrated, book II, §65, p. 176.

Thomasius, who was by far the foremost authority in understanding and judging such matters, held with Joannes Morinus that the prayers and formulas of prayer in this codex were older than Constantine the Great.

During Rufinus’s lifetime, Pope Zosimus, in his third epistle to the Africans, speaking as though of a matter otherwise well known, says that Clement consecrated by his martyrdom the faith in Christ which he had learned from Peter and had taught.

Other examples of this kind may be found in Tillemont, volume II, p. 563. There he observes that Rufinus followed the primitive tradition of the Roman Church, truly derived from Clement’s age and martyrdom, when he honored him with the title of martyr in his treatise *On the Adulteration of the Books of Origen*.

## CHAPTER XI

1. Rufinus, obeying Chromatius, Bishop of Aquileia, renders Eusebius’s *History* into Latin and enlarges it by two books.  
2. What he accomplished in translating Eusebius, and what he accomplished in his own books, wrongly criticized by Dupin.  
3. Rufinus’s *History* highly esteemed by the Gauls, and likewise by English and African Fathers.  
4. Likewise by the Greeks.  
5. Two Greeks translate his two books into Greek and make them their own.  
6. The Second Council of Nicaea uses their testimony.  
7. The excellence of Rufinus’s Latin translation of Eusebius’s *History* is demonstrated.  
8. Gelasius’s judgment is explained.  
11. The various editions are reviewed.

### I

Let us proceed to the most celebrated work among everything Rufinus published. I speak of the *Ecclesiastical History*, written in Greek by Eusebius, which Rufinus translated and, sixty years after Eusebius’s death, delivered to Latin readers enlarged by two books, at the command of Chromatius, our bishop of Aquileia. He dedicated his translation to him, prefacing it with a prologue on death.

Learned men place Rufinus’s literary labor in A.D. 400, when Alaric, king of the Goths, crossed the Julian Alps and first invaded Italy. They suppose that Rufinus himself bears witness to this in addressing Chromatius, where he says that this work was imposed upon him by the most holy man at the time when, after the barriers of Italy had been broken open, a pestilential disease, under Alaric as leader of the Goths, spread through the land and ravaged fields, herds, and people far and wide.

Alaric, however, entered Italy not only once, but a second and a third time as a plunderer—in A.D. 400, 402, and 408. But there can be no doubt that Rufinus is speaking of his first incursion, which Prosper and Cassiodorus assign to Stilicho’s first consulship and therefore to A.D. 400. If he had wished to speak of another incursion by Alaric, he would certainly have indicated it more explicitly, so that it would not be confused with the first.

Rufinus’s words confirm this very point:

> “At the time when, after the barriers of Italy had been broken open…”

These words clearly place before our eyes a single invasion made by Alaric, as Rufinus writes.

The argument is all the stronger because of the evidence used by Tillemont, volume XII, note LXXIX. Rufinus, neither in the prologue nor in the *History*, says anything about Theodosius the Great that distinguishes him from the younger Theodosius, who was born at the beginning of April A.D. 401, proclaimed Augustus on 11 January A.D. 402, and succeeded his father Arcadius on 1 May A.D. 408. Thus, in Tillemont’s judgment, Rufinus published his *History* within two years.

Certainly he published it before A.D. 402, when Alaric came into Italy for the second time. But could there have been any fear that the splendid deeds of an emperor long since dead would then be attributed to an infant of the same name, unless the historian, explicitly distinguishing one from the other, removed the opportunity for error?

We shall reason somewhat more accurately as follows. Chromatius, to whom Rufinus dedicates his *History*, died in A.D. 506, as has been stated elsewhere. Therefore Rufinus, who after A.D. 400 applied himself to condensing his work, certainly completed it before A.D. 407—indeed before A.D. 402, when Alaric’s second invasion occurred.

Rufinus did not immediately after the first invasion turn his mind to writing, but only some time later, *after* the barriers of Italy had been broken, as Pearson also observes in part I, chapter VI of the *Vindiciae Ignatianae*, p. 88. The pestilential disease brought by the Gothic army into our Venetian region had first ravaged that flourishing land, which had borne the initial assault of the barbarians. This could not have happened in the blink of an eye, but required an interval of time.

Therefore Chromatius, fulfilling the duty of an excellent shepherd, arranged for Eusebius’s *History* to be translated by Rufinus from Greek into Latin. He wished, as though with the soothing medicine of a new reading, to relieve the memory of the past calamity in his own people and in our fellow countrymen who had survived such great evils. This could not quickly have been done by a priest already occupied with other matters.

I do not believe I could express the matter in more suitable words than those Rufinus himself used in explaining it:

> “Experienced physicians, they say, when they see general diseases threatening cities or regions, take care to provide some kind of medicine or drink by which people, being fortified, may be defended from the impending destruction. You, venerable father Chromatius, carrying out this kind of medical treatment, at the time when, after the barriers of Italy had been broken by Alaric, leader of the Goths, a pestilential disease poured itself forth and ravaged fields, herds, and people far and wide, seek some remedy for deadly destruction for the peoples entrusted to you by God. Through it, their sick minds, withdrawn from thoughts of the invading evil, might be kept occupied with better studies. You command me to translate into Latin the *Ecclesiastical History* which the most learned Eusebius of Caesarea composed in the Greek language. By its reading, the minds of the hearers, held captive while eagerly seeking knowledge of things done, might in some way receive forgetfulness of the evils that have arisen. When I wished to excuse myself from this work, as being inferior and unequal to it, and as one who, after so many years, had lost the practice of the Latin language, I considered that you did not give us this command without some conformity to apostolic instruction.”

Rufinus continues, as modestly as devoutly, to excuse his inadequacy for translating the work by the authority of the one giving the command.

He candidly admits that he joined book X to book IX, omitting what seemed superfluous, because book X contained very little concerning historical events and, in all its remaining material, treated of panegyrics on bishops—discourses contributing nothing to knowledge of events.

He says that he composed books X and XI in their entirety, partly from the traditions of earlier generations and partly from what had come within the range of his own memory.

He adds that the whole work of Eusebius contains the events that took place in the Church from the Savior’s ascension onward. He affirms that his own two books extend from Constantine and the beginnings of the Arian heresy to A.D. 395, when Theodosius the Great died, and that he added them briefly, partly from the writings of earlier generations and partly from his own memory, in order also to obey the commands of Chromatius, his devout father.

Radulphus de Diceto is therefore wrong when he says that Rufinus ended his *History* in A.D. 399. See him among the ancient writers of English history, published by Robert Twysden, volume I, p. 431.

### II

Critics loudly complain that Rufinus used excessive freedom in translating Eusebius. Certainly he removed much, added more, and altered some things.

Eusebius reports the revelations made to Alexander, Bishop of Jerusalem, insufficiently clearly in book VI, chapter XI; Rufinus explains them very well in the same book, chapter VIII. In book VII he inserted on his own account a narrative about the miracles of Saint George, which Eusebius lacks. In book IX he added, from his own material, a sermon of Saint Lucian the martyr.

I mention only a few of the many passages by which Eusebius was enriched through Rufinus’s agency. In addition, in books VI and VII he somewhat altered the order of the chapters.

Hence Vossius, in book II, chapter XI of *On Latin Historians*, thinks that Rufinus’s version of Eusebius cannot even be called a paraphrase, but is a work of its own, in which he nevertheless copied a great deal from Eusebius, while adding, omitting, and changing so much.

Later writers criticize Rufinus for having been credulous when composing the remaining two books of his *History* and arranging the years chronologically, and for following popular rumors more than was proper.

The chief example of this kind that they produce occurs in book X, chapter XIV, where he adds a narrative about boys baptized on the seashore by Athanasius when he was a boy. Socrates learned this from Rufinus, book I, chapter XV, and Sozomen from book II, chapter XVII. But learned men dispute the truth of the event.

For the Bollandist writers express partial doubt about it in their entry for 2 May, chapter I, §20, p. 188, whereas Antonius Pagius defends it as wholly true, A.D. 311, §27.

Our distinguished friend Bernard de Montfaucon takes the opposite position in the life of Saint Athanasius, which precedes his elegant edition of Athanasius’s works, and Tillemont embraces this judgment in volume VIII, note I.

The Bollandist scholars, however, have again attempted to defend their position in volume V of the June *History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria*. Montfaucon opposed them with a letter published at Paris in A.D. 1710, in which he carefully investigates whether Rufinus’s account of the boys baptized by the boy Athanasius is true.

In Rufinus’s favor it is enough to recall that he reports these matters not on his own authority, but on the testimony of others. His words are found in book X, chapter XIV:

> “We received this from those who lived with him [Athanasius].”

He could certainly not have heard more authoritative witnesses than those who had lived with Athanasius himself.

M. Antonius Muretus illustrates this game of the boys with other examples in book XIII, chapter X of his *Various Readings*.

These considerations prevent me from approving Dupin, who, in volume III of his *Bibliotheca*, accuses Rufinus of matters that are easily dispelled.

1. He says that Rufinus reports that Athanasius hid for six years in a cistern after the Council of Tyre. Rufinus does indeed say this, in book X, chapter XVIII, but he says it on the report of others. This is clearly established by the word *it is said*.

2. He complains that Rufinus reverses the order of events in the history of Athanasius. Dupin thought this because Rufinus did not provide a complete history of Athanasius, but culled a few items from many, as he makes clear in the following words at the end of book I, chapter XIV:

> “His deeds are so many and so great that the magnitude of the events does not allow me to pass anything over, while the multitude of his deeds compels me to omit very many. My mind hesitates uncertainly, unable to decide what it should retain and what it should omit. And therefore we shall record only a few matters pertinent to the subject. The rest his fame will relate, without doubt reporting things lesser than the truth. For it will find nothing that it could add.”

3. Our author is badly regarded by Dupin, as though he showed too little favor toward the great men Gregory of Nazianzus and Basil. But the very honorable eulogy that Rufinus attached to both of them in book I, chapter IX, clears him of this unjust charge. I say nothing for the moment about the zeal Rufinus devoted to giving both their works to the Latin-speaking world. That is the clearest sign of how highly he esteemed them.

Saint Aldhelm, in his book *On the Praise of Virginity*, p. 320, demonstrates how far Dupin’s judgment is from the truth in these words:

> “Rufinus, endowed with remarkable elegance of expression, set forth more fully in the prologue to his *Apologeticus* the praises of Gregory of Nazianzus.”

4. He says that Rufinus falsely stated that Hilary was devoted to curses and was sent into exile after the Council of Milan. But it would take too long to refute—or should I say, to recount—all Dupin’s hallucinations. He says that Rufinus falsely stated something which Rufinus never said anywhere in his History. In his little work *On the Adulteration of Origen’s Books*, Rufinus does indeed say that a book containing very full instruction, written by Hilary of Poitiers for the correction of those who had subscribed to the perfidy of Rimini, had been so corrupted by Hilary’s enemies that, when they later began calling him a heretic at the Council of Bishops on the basis of what they knew they had corrupted in his little book, and the book was produced and found to be such that Hilary did not recognize it, they caused him, after being excommunicated, to leave the council’s assembly. [Col. 0224D]

This is what Rufinus truly wrote. Jerome objects to it in Book II of his *Apology*: “The synod by which he was excommunicated—where was it held?” Dupin says, on the basis of Rufinus’s History, that it was held at Milan. “Name the bishops. Produce the judgments of those who subscribed, whether they differed or agreed. Show who the consuls were that year. Which emperor ordered this synod to be convened? Were the bishops only from Gaul, or also from Italy and Spain? At least, what was the reason for convening the synod?” You mention none of these things. What Rufinus would have replied to this, we do not know, since his letter has been lost.

But the distinguished Pierre Coustant, in the life of Saint Hilary which he prefixed to the works of Hilary as he edited them, p. 119, §107, believes that the book mentioned by Rufinus should be understood as the work in which Hilary had encompassed the history of the Synods of Rimini and Seleucia; fragments of it survive on p. 1279. Since Rufinus had learned merely by hearsay that Hilary had been called a heretic by the heretic Auxentius and, after an assembly had been held, had been ordered to leave the city of Milan, he easily imagined that, because of the corruption—carried out by heretics—of that book which he had heard had been falsified by fraud, Hilary, the author of the book, had been expelled not only from the city but also from the assembly. Thus Rufinus wrote this in his little work *On the Adulteration of Origen’s Books*, not in the *History*, which he had not yet composed. In the latter, however, Book XI, chapters XXX and XXXI, he recounts things about Hilary which no one condemns. Certainly not the things that the bankrupt Dupin invents; I cannot sufficiently marvel at his enormous negligence.

### III

Rufinus therefore opened up to the entire West, amid the greatest applause of all, the earliest sources of ecclesiastical history, previously unknown or scarcely known. Through him our Latin forebears were able to learn thoroughly the deeds of Christians, and especially the Gallic bishops were able to borrow the Nicene definitions, which Rufinus had abbreviated and divided into twenty-two canons in Book X, chapter VI.

Jacques Sirmond, exceptionally shrewd in probing the innermost recesses of ecclesiastical history, was the first to detect this, in his notes on the Second Council of Arles in Labbe, vol. IV of the *Councils*, p. 1813. Hence the Nicene canons, taken from Rufinus, passed into the Code of the ancient Gallican Church. Quesnell discusses this in *Leonine Dissertation* XVI, chapter XV. But the envious man deprives Sirmond of the credit for this first observation, which belongs to him alone.

The matter is clearly revealed by the Second Council of Arles, convened forty-two years after the publication of Rufinus’s *History*, in A.D. 444, in Labbe, vol. IV, p. 1012. It is also revealed by the excerpts from the canons attached to the letter of Pope John II to Caesarius of Arles concerning the examination of the case of Contumeliosus, Bishop of Riez, where they are printed under A.D. 535. There, in Labbe, p. 1756, a canon of the Council of Nicaea is placed first, copied word for word from Rufinus, and numbered the eleventh by him.

Canon I of the Second Council of Arles expresses Canon II of Nicaea as it appears in Rufinus. Canon VII of Arles is taken from Rufinus’s first Nicene canon. Canon X refers to Rufinus’s Canons XII and XIII. Canon XV derives from Rufinus’s second canon. Canon XVI faithfully reproduces Canon XXI of Nicaea according to Rufinus’s version.

It is therefore evident that, when the fathers of Arles were formulating their decrees, they had the Nicene canons written in their own code in Rufinus’s very words. Just as knowledge of those canons had been obscure in the Gallican churches before Rufinus, so afterward their version, supplied by our author in his supplement to Eusebius’s *History*, was eagerly absorbed.

Rufinus was held in great esteem by the most learned and holy men throughout the West—if we except Jerome, and him only for a certain period—and especially among the Gauls. Sirmond also noted this elsewhere. In particular, he observed it concerning Sidonius, who, fifty years after Rufinus’s death, commended his Latin translations very highly in Book II, Letter IX.

After Sidonius came Gregory, Bishop of Tours. In Book IX, chapter XV of his *History of the Franks*, praising Rufinus’s *History* together with his translation of Eusebius under Eusebius’s name, he says: “Arius, who, as the historian Eusebius narrates—or rather Rufinus, Book X, chapter XIV—cast out his entrails into a place of retreat…”

Finally, let the testimony of Hincmar, Archbishop of Reims, be added: it is truly most honorable to Rufinus. In vol. II of his works, p. 463, he says: “The tenth book of Rufinus’s *Ecclesiastical History*, which is listed in the catalogue of the Apostolic See among the books to be received.”

Because the sequence of events and the proximity of regions make it appropriate, I shall summon here from the English nation Saint Aldhelm and the Venerable Bede. In his book *On the Praise of Virginity*, p. 328, Aldhelm appeals to the authority of Rufinus’s tenth book. Bede, in *On the Reckoning of Time*, chapter XXVIII, transcribes the entire Eusebian passage from Rufinus, Book VII, chapter XXVIII.

If we cross from England to Africa, we shall hear Augustine of Hippo, Rufinus’s friend, praising his *History*. In *On the Care to Be Given to the Dead*, chapter VI, he says: “We read in the *Ecclesiastical History* which Eusebius wrote in Greek and Rufinus translated into Latin that the bodies of the martyrs were exposed to dogs in Gaul.”

In *On Heresies*, chapter LXXXIII, he praises it again: “When I had searched through the *History of Eusebius*, to which Rufinus added two books concerning subsequent times after translating it into Latin, I did not find any heresy which I had not read about among those Jovinianists.”

After the Bishop of Hippo came Victor of Vita. In his *History of the Vandal Persecution*, written in A.D. 487, Book V, chapter XVIII, he speaks magnificently of Rufinus’s *History*. Indeed, he confesses himself so unequal to the subject he was treating that Cicero, Sallust, Eusebius, or his translator Rufinus—adorned with Greek eloquence and Latin flowers—would scarcely have been sufficient to explain it.

Vigilius of Tapsus, too, who flourished around A.D. 560, had Rufinus at hand and used him, although he did not specifically name him. For he derived the entire first chapter of Book VI *Against the Arians* from Rufinus’s *History*, both in the understanding of the events and in almost the very words.

Concerning the death of Constantine the Great, Vigilius speaks as follows: “Finally, while his case—that of Arius—was being debated for a long time by the bishops, the emperor Constantine, after a final judgment had been issued in a certain suburban place named Nicomedia, ended his life in the thirty-first year of his reign.”

Rufinus, Book IX, chapter XI, had narrated the matter in these words: “Meanwhile, while these things were being fruitlessly debated at Alexandria, the venerable Augustus Constantine died in a suburban villa at Nicomedia in the thirty-first year of his reign.””

Vigilius supposed that the suburban villa, whose name Rufinus omitted, was Nicomedia. Yet Jerome reports in his *Chronicle* that in the second year of Olympiad 279, corresponding to A.D. 338 according to Eusebian reckoning, it was called Ancyron or Achyron—the manuscripts vary.

### IV

Nor did the Latins alone value Rufinus’s two books added to Eusebius; the Greeks themselves also esteemed them highly. This is made evident by the fact that they translated them for themselves. Thus Cyril of Alexandria, Gelasius of Cyzicus, and, more importantly, the Second Council of Nicaea approved their own proceedings with those same books of Rufinus translated into Greek.

To establish the truth of the matter, it is necessary to pause over each case. I shall speak of Cyril of Alexandria later.

Gelasius of Cyzicus, who flourished in A.D. 476, often confirms his narratives by Rufinus’s authority and takes him as his guide at the beginning of his work. Pierre-Daniel Huet, in his *Dialogue on Famous Interpreters*, p. 135 of the first edition, observed that this Gelasius transferred quite a few passages from Rufinus’s two books into his own work on the Nicene Synod, and that he did not so much interpret as borrow those matters which suited his purpose.

Photius, however, after stating that Gelasius of Caesarea in Palestine—different from Gelasius of Cyzicus—had pursued the history of Eusebius at the urging of his maternal uncle Cyril, Bishop of Jerusalem, seems shortly afterward to make Cyril himself the Greek translator of Rufinus’s *History*. I quote Photius’s words from codex LXXXIX:

“Elsewhere, while reading, I discovered this: that Cyril himself, together with this Gelasius, translated the *History of Rufinus the Roman* into Greek, and did not compose some separate history of his own.”

Photius adds that, if what he had discovered is true, this Gelasius of Caesarea was older than Gelasius of Cyzicus, whose history of the Council of Nicaea, likewise derived from Rufinus, he had discussed above in codex LXXXVIII. Nor does Photius pass over in silence the fact that Gelasius of Cyzicus praises the statements of the earlier Gelasius and of Rufinus.

Thus Photius enumerates not one but three Gelasiuses who were bishops of Caesarea in Palestine, and says that one could not distinguish them. The first Gelasius was the son of Cyril’s sister; his uncle appointed him bishop of Caesarea in Palestine in succession to Euzoïus, the successor of Acacius. See Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* LXXIII, §37, and Jerome, *Catalogue*, chapter CXXX. The second Gelasius wrote against the Anomoeans, in Photius, codex CII. The third Gelasius is Gelasius of Cyzicus.

But to make Gelasius, the son of Cyril’s sister, and Cyril himself translators of Rufinus’s *History* is nonsense. Cyril died on March 18, A.D. 384, according to Antonio Agustín Touttée, in his edition of Cyril, p. 85. Gelasius died in A.D. 394, and John succeeded him in the See of Caesarea in A.D. 395. At that time Rufinus had certainly not yet crossed from Palestine to Italy, where he later composed his *History*.

Tillemont, vol. VIII, Note VIII on Cyril of Jerusalem, relying on Photius, makes this Gelasius’s history different from Rufinus’s *History*, although he professes to augment the *History of Eusebius*. Yet this otherwise careful scholar is caught in a serious error. Photius is speaking there of the history of Gelasius of Cyzicus, which he had reviewed in the preceding codex, not of another history by the Gelasius who, as Photius himself believes, rendered Rufinus’s Eusebian supplement into Greek.

Photius’s words in codex LXXXVIII are these: “This Gelasius too—the Greek translator of Rufinus—differs from that one [Gelasius of Cyzicus] in his manner of expression, although both are far inferior to the Gelasius who wrote against the Anomoeans.”

Of Gelasius of Cyzicus he had written: “His diction, moreover, will be observed to incline more than is proper toward a humble and low style.” See Fabricius, *Greek Library*, vol. VIII, p. 370.

Photius wrote similarly in codex XV, so that there can be no doubt that he was comparing Gelasius of Cyzicus, insofar as he was the author of the history of the Nicene Synod, with that earlier Gelasius whom he believed to be Rufinus’s translator—not two Gelasiuses engaged in the same subject, one who augmented Eusebius’s *History* and the other its translator.

In Book I, chapter VII, Gelasius of Cyzicus cites Gelasius and Rufinus concerning the acts of the Council of Nicaea, presenting Rufinus as the principal author and Gelasius as the translator. This too caught Photius’s attention.

### V

Huet, in his *Dialogue*, p. 131, attributes to the dignity of the Roman language the fact that Gelasius’s Greek translation, being held inferior to the Latin exemplar, either could not preserve the sequence of events or was struggling with moths in the dust of libraries.

I do not deny this among the Latins; among the Greeks, however, the situation is different. In the catalogue of Greek manuscripts of the Constantinopolitan Library in Lambecius, vol. I, p. 149, a *Church History of Rufinus the Presbyter of the Great Church* is said to exist.

Moreover, in Christopher Justellus’s *Library of Ancient Canon Law*, vol. I, p. 405, there is a letter of Cyril of Alexandria to the African Synod, written in A.D. 419, in which Cyril sends a copy of the Nicene Synod: “This also,” he says, “you will find when you search in the *Ecclesiastical History*.” Justellus, in his notes, p. 443, informs us that Cyril here means Rufinus’s *History*, since at that time it was extremely widespread among Greeks as well as Latins, namely within a decade of Rufinus’s death.

But, reader, pause here briefly. For I believe that Cyril of Alexandria—the nephew and successor of Theophilus, and the first among the Greeks to praise Rufinus’s *History* as known to everyone—was not another Cyril who served as its translator. Photius, deceived by the identity of the name and failing to observe the order of events, seems to have confused him with Cyril of Jerusalem.

Touttée too recently recognized Photius’s error, *Dissertation* II on Cyril, chapter I, §5, p. 95. Cyril’s words, indicating a church history especially known not only to Greeks but also to Latins—that is, to the Africans, to whom he was then writing—refer to it by antonomasia. This was Rufinus’s history, composed in Greek and Latin; apart from it, there was no other.

Henry Dodwell observed that Socrates used the Greek translation of Rufinus in his *On the Law of the Laity*, chapter IV, p. 278. Petavius made the same observation concerning Theodoret in his *Dissertation on the Power of Consecrating*, chapter III, p. 83.

Indeed, neither of them could have drawn the history of Frumentius from anywhere but Rufinus, since Rufinus alone and first of all committed it to writing in Book X, chapter IX, reporting it to himself from Aedesius, a presbyter of Tyre. From him the other writers learned it, and Dodwell ably defends this point.

Socrates, in Book I, chapter XII, at the end, while discussing Saint Spyridon, Bishop of Cyprus, praises Rufinus’s history. Yet he seems to imply in Latin that he had read it in that language, unless he had read the Greek version, which I consider more likely, and was referring to the work Rufinus wrote in Latin.

Here are Socrates’ words: “I received these things partly by hearsay from many Cypriots and partly found them written in the collection of a certain presbyter Rufinus, composed in the Roman language. From that book I gathered both these matters and others which will be related shortly afterward.”

He praises Rufinus again at the end of chapter XV: “These things Rufinus recorded concerning Athanasius in his books.”

At the end of chapter XIX: “Rufinus narrates that he learned these things from Aedesius, who himself later became a presbyter of Tyre.”

Sozomen also took this history of Frumentius from Rufinus, although he does not name him, in Book II, chapter XXIV; and so did Theodoret in Book I, chapter XXIII. From Rufinus, as with many other matters, it passed into the Greek *Menologion*, into the *Martyrology* of Usuard, Greven, and Molanus, and later into the very calendars of the Roman Church, on October 27.

Socrates again praises Rufinus near the end of the same book, chapter XXI: “Rufinus writes that he learned these things from Bacurius.”

Socrates and Sozomen brought their histories down to A.D. 439, when they flourished. Theodoret wrote his in A.D. 450. Socrates likewise cites Rufinus at the beginning of Book II, who composed an ecclesiastical history in the language of the Romans. Yet he says that Rufinus was mistaken in certain chronological matters concerning Athanasius and omitted very many things. As we have said, Rufinus himself had warned the reader about these matters; critics exaggerate them beyond measure, among them Valesius in his *Life of Socrates* and Fabricius, vol. VI, p. 119.

Later, after acquiring better evidence, Socrates completely rewrote Books I and II in a subsequent revision, while nevertheless retaining those passages in which Rufinus had not deviated at all from the truth.

After these writers, Theophanes praised Rufinus’s history, written in Greek, in his *Chronography*, p. 19.

### VI

Rufinus receives his greatest honor, however, from the fact that the Second Council of Nicaea, in Session I, in Labbe, vol. VII, p. 79, when discussing bishops returning from heresy to the Catholic faith and to be immediately received, produced testimony from the ecclesiastical history of Rufinus, presbyter of Rome [Col. 0228C]. This passage occurs in Book X, chapter XXVIII.

To remain with the Latin Church, it always held Rufinus and his *History* in the highest esteem and came very close to declaring it worthy of public reading. Its martyrologies grew through Rufinus’s books, especially that venerable and very ancient one, distinct from the Hieronymian Martyrology, formerly called the proper and small martyrology of the Roman Church, which Heribert Rosweyd brought into public view together with the Adonian Martyrology.

Henry Valesius had already shown that this same martyrology was compiled in many places from Rufinus, in the dissertation which he appended to his excellent edition of Eusebius. Nor does the distinguished Joannes Baptista Sollerius, a vigorous defender of that small Roman Martyrology, deny it in his preface to Usuard, p. 34, §86. There he splendidly demonstrates, against Valesius, that it was compiled at Rome around A.D. 770 and sent by the Roman Pontiff to Aquileia so that our people might conform themselves to the Roman rite, and that it was copied at Ravenna by Saint Ado of Vienne before A.D. 860.

What the author of this martyrology specifically, what Ado, and what Usuard—from whose *Martyrology* the Roman Church later adopted its own—derived from Rufinus has been amply indicated by Sollerius and other hagiologists. There is therefore no need to go over the same ground again.

In Rufinus’s favor I add only this: most of the blemishes attributed to his *History* arose from the multitude of copies, and thus from the esteem in which the same history was held.

Therefore, when our forebears give thanks to Rufinus because he was the first of all to open up the sources of Christian history to the Latin Church, they should not be repaid with insults, as I see William Cave doing together with other recent writers. In his *Literary History*, under A.D. 390, while discussing Rufinus, Cave is mistaken on many points, especially when he calls Eusebius’s version prepared by Rufinus “of doubtful fidelity,” because Rufinus shortened many things, added many things, and omitted many things.

But since Rufinus openly admits in his prologue to Chromatius that he did not adhere to every letter like a grammarian, but followed the meaning rather than the words, adding and abridging not a few passages, and informing the reader of this, why does an English writer turn these same features into an accusation of doubtful fidelity?

Huet’s judgment of Rufinus in his *Dialogue on Famous Interpreters*, p. 151, is equally unjust. After listing the many works that Rufinus translated into Latin, and finally the *History of Eusebius*, Huet attacked our author—who had rendered such distinguished service to the Latin Church and especially to his own Gauls—in the harshest words, wholly unworthy of the gravity of so great a man:

“He raved to the point of madness and proceeded with excessively lavish verbosity beyond all measure. Moreover, he used the most corrupt manuscripts and lacked the critical judgment by which false things could be distinguished from true.”

Huet attributes excessively lavish verbosity to Rufinus. But the most learned of the Gauls did not judge him so. Mamertus Claudianus, himself a Gaul, calls Sidonius the most learned of the Gauls and says in Book IV, Letter III: “Orosius flows copiously; Rufinus is concise; Eusebius narrates.”

Joannes Savaro notes that this was said of Rufinus because he abridged the ecclesiastical history. [Col. 0229B] But Gaufridus, a regular canon, applies it differently in Letter XLVIII, in Martène’s *Thesaurus*, vol. I, p. 549, where he writes to John the Abbot: “You are concise like Rufinus.”

It is certainly unjust to charge with excessively lavish verbosity a man so devoted to brevity that he condensed ten books into nine.

Against Huet, whose words escaped him when he was still quite young, we shall set Henry Valesius, Rufinus’s rival in the same field. Although, in his excellent edition of Eusebius, Valesius does not always embrace the version of our presbyter, following the custom of newer translators who disparage earlier ones in order to exalt their own translations, he nevertheless frequently confirms his own version through Rufinus’s. He often says that Rufinus’s version serves as a commentary on the Eusebian text.

In sum, Valesius thinks very differently of Rufinus from Huet. In his preface he writes:

“Although Rufinus follows Eusebius’s meaning rather than his words, he is nevertheless polished and not unpleasant to readers. He deserves the highest praise for this reason above all: he was the first to give an ecclesiastical history to speakers of the Latin language, and the Western Church has used his translation down to our own age.”

Indeed, Hadrian Valesius teaches us that, after publishing the historians of the Greek Church, his distinguished brother Henry had also planned to publish and illustrate the historians of the Latin Church, and Rufinus above all. Hadrian states this in the separately published life of his brother Henry, issued at Leipzig in A.D. 1680, and later printed together with Eusebius at Frankfurt in A.D. 1695, under the second revision of Valesius, by Balthasar Christoph Wust for Henry Wetstein, bookseller of Amsterdam.

Here are Hadrian’s words concerning his brother Henry:

“He had decided, if he had been granted a longer life, to add to the Greek authors of sacred history the Latins—Sulpicius Severus, Tyrannius Rufinus [read: Turanius], the tripartite history of Cassiodorus Senator, Liberatus the Deacon, and several others—collated with ancient manuscripts, corrected by his own labor, and explained with commentaries.

Would that he had been granted it! For then the Latin Church would possess from her own writers something over which she would not be inferior to the Greek Church in any respect, especially with the commentaries of so great a man added to them. It is to be hoped that someone else will accomplish for the public good what Valesius could not.”

### VII

What learned men have discussed back and forth on the occasion of Canon VI of Nicaea, which Rufinus reported in Book X, chapter VI, I shall address elsewhere, lest I depart from my subject.

As for what Valesius observed concerning the excellence of Rufinus’s translation, which is especially suited to explaining the character of the Greek author, others have made the same observation. Through it, light has very often been shed upon obscure words in the original text, and the native integrity of the true reading restored.

Experts, those hunters of such elegances, have also observed in it expressions of the Roman language not yet touched by the invading barbarism. Hence Janus Gebhardus, whom I shall praise below, declared that Rufinus carried on Eusebius’s *History* in a polished style and with lucid eloquence in his narratives.

Let us not review Valesius’s examples, since their abundance makes it impossible to count them all. Scaliger, although elsewhere himself not very fair to Rufinus, will supply one or two.

Thus Scaliger, in his *Annotations on the Chronicle of Eusebius*, no. 2084, restored the Greek words in the conclusion of Book II of the *Ecclesiastical History* from no other source than Rufinus’s translation, and refuted Christophorson’s version. He does the same in no. 2086, when examining a passage from Book III, chapter VII.

Later, however, in no. 2203, concerning another passage from Book V, chapter XXI of Rufinus’s edition, he attacks Rufinus just as he does Jerome, as though both had misunderstood the Greek sense concerning Apollonius. Then he adds:

“Nor do I doubt that, when Jerome wrote that passage—in the *Catalogue*, chapter XLII—he had in his hands not the Greek exemplar of Eusebius but Rufinus’s Latin interpretation.”

What is this, great man? Jerome, who composed his *Catalogue* in A.D. 392, had in his hands Rufinus’s Latin interpretation, written after A.D. 400? Pearson, in the second edition of his *Vindications of Ignatius*, Part I, chapter VI, p. 293, corrected this lapse in Scaliger and likewise in Valesius’s notes on Eusebius, Book V, chapter XX, before me.

I pass over the ignorance of Rhenanus, who, in his letter prefixed to Eusebius, stated that Rufinus’s two books were taken from the *Tripartite History* and were a kind of epitome of it, although the authors of that work wrote long after Rufinus’s death and derived their material from him.

For Scaliger speaking elegantly of Rufinus, and using *thorax* instead of *shield* for the image or bust portrayed upon it, see again no. 2286. Yet he mocks Rufinus in nos. 2065 and 2285.

Holstenius, who was fairer and gentler toward Rufinus than Scaliger, frequently uses the words of Rufinus’s version, and not without praise, in his notes on the *Acts of Saints Perpetua and Felicity*, pp. 123, 144, 155, 167, 180, and 181, and in his annotations on the *Martyrology*, p. 257 of the Paris edition.

Distinguished critics agree with Holstenius, considering it a special honor to devote serious labor to illuminating the text of Rufinus’s *History*. Among them Janus Gebhardus stands out, in his *Crepundia*, or “juvenile studies,” as he calls them, published at Hanau by the Wechel press in A.D. 1615, quarto, and recently reissued by Joannes Hermannus Schminckius in Marburg in his *Critical Collection of Various Authors*.

In these *Crepundia*, Gebhardus repeatedly emends Rufinus’s *History* against the most carefully corrected Palatine and Gruterian manuscripts: Book I, chapters II, V, VI, VIII, XI, and XVI; Book II, chapters VI and VIII; and Book III, chapters VI and XXI.

He does the same in his *Ancient Readings*, first printed at Herborn in A.D. 1618, octavo, and reprinted by Schminckius, namely in Book [chapter] IV and chapter XXV.

Barthius likewise did this auspiciously in his *Adversaria*: Book I, chapter IV; Book IV, chapter XV; Book XXV, chapter II; and more extensively, Book XXIX, chapter XI.

Thomas Reinesius did so as well in his *Various Readings*, Book I, chapter IV.

Nor should Geverhart Elemenhorstius and Joannes Savaro be omitted. They illuminate the manners of expression of Arnobius and Sidonius by comparing them with Rufinus’s *History*: the former in his notes on Book I, p. 20, and the latter in his notes on Book I, Letter V.

### VIII

Exhausted almost to the point of weariness by gathering praises of Rufinus, Saint Gelasius the Pope brings me to a halt here. In the decree which he composed at the Roman Council of seventy bishops, chapter IV, he counted the *History of Eusebius* translated by Rufinus among the apocrypha:

“The *History of Eusebius Pamphilus*, apocryphal.”

I am surprised that Henry Valesius, a man distinguished in talent and learning, did not grasp the genuine meaning of the word *apocryphal* in his notes on Eusebius, Book VI, chapter XIV. Like Valesius, Pearson, Cave, and others also failed to grasp it. I examined them long ago in *Hortan Antiquities*, Book III, chapter III, §3, from which I shall transfer some material here.

Among the ancient Fathers, those writings are truly called apocryphal which are opposed to the canonical books. Hence Baronius, the father of the Annals, under A.D. 31, §60, says that apocrypha are “as it were non-hagiographical,” although this does not mean that Gelasius entirely banishes them from the Church.

Augustine states in *The City of God*, Book XV, chapter XXIII, that the name *apocrypha* designates writings removed from canonical authority after careful examination. There were two kinds of Scripture: canonical, whose author is the Holy Spirit, and apocryphal, whose sole author is a human being. The former could be read publicly in the Church; the latter could not be read in that manner.

Therefore, to call a book apocryphal is understood to mean that it lacks the authority by which canonical books may be read publicly in the Church.

Gelasius likewise enumerates two kinds of apocrypha: those of the orthodox and those of the heretics. The latter are entirely rejected; the former are opposed to the canonical books and are deprived only of public reading in the Church because of certain blemishes.

For there is a canon in Ferrandus’s *Breviary*, no. 238: “Let nothing be read in the Church apart from the canonical Scriptures.” Peter de Marca holds the same view in *On Concord*, Book III, chapter II, §7, as does Pierre-François Chifflet in his notes on Vigilius of Tapsus, p. 147.

These things show that Gelasius deprived Eusebius’s *History* only of public reading in the Church when he declared it apocryphal. In the same category come Lactantius, Sulpicius Severus, Commodianus, Arnobius, Clement of Alexandria, and many other outstanding authors.

Indeed, in chapter III of his decree, which concerns works to be received, Gelasius expressly testifies that he is not saying that Eusebius’s *History*, or even the *Chronicle* translated and augmented by Jerome, should be rejected altogether, on account of the knowledge of individual matters which, as he says, contributes to instruction.

This refutes the impudence of Beatus Rhenanus in the letter prefixed to Rufinus’s Eusebius, where he says that Gelasius intended to prohibit us from reading Eusebius; or that some donkey had added to Gelasius’s decree the statement that Eusebius’s *History* was apocryphal; or finally that Gelasius, contradicting himself, condemned a book which elsewhere he had approved.

Rhenanus wrote these things incorrectly because he did not understand the true meaning of *apocryphal*.

That the two books with which Rufinus continued Eusebius were entered by the Roman Church in the catalogue of books to be received is attested by Hincmar of Reims, whom I cited above. This refutes Algerus in *On Mercy and Justice*, chapter III, no. LII, in Martène’s *Thesaurus*, vol. V, p. 1045. Algerus condemns what Rufinus reports concerning children baptized by Athanasius when he was a child, on the ground that Rufinus’s *Ecclesiastical History* is considered less authentic. [Col. 0231C]

But Saint Gregory the Great did not hold this view. In his *Register*, Book IV, Letter XXXI, to the Emperor Maurice Augustus, he praised Rufinus’s *History* as authentic and generally accepted in these words:

“The ecclesiastical history also bears witness that, when written accusations against the bishops had been presented to the prince Constantine of pious memory, he indeed accepted the documents of accusation; but, summoning the bishops who had been accused, he burned the documents he had received in their presence, and so forth.”

The passage is found in Rufinus, Book X, chapter II. John the Deacon also alludes to it in chapter III of his *Life of the Great Pontiff*.

How highly this Rufinian *History* was esteemed by everyone is made still clearer by the many copies once dispersed throughout Europe, a considerable number of which still survive in various libraries.

To begin with our own region, the library of the principal church in the town of San Daniele preserves an elegant manuscript of Rufinus’s *History*. In the archive of the Canons of Cividale there is another excellent parchment codex in folio, containing Rufinus’s *History* and also Victor, Bishop of Vita’s account of the Vandal persecution; these are accompanied by Jerome’s and Gennadius’s catalogues and the Rule of Saint Pachomius.

Jacopo Filippo Tomasini lists four other copies preserved in the libraries of Padua, pp. 7, 17, 45, and 76. They are in the episcopal church, among the canons regular of Saint John in the Viridarium, in the monastery of Saint Justina, and among the Augustinian Hermits.

Bernard de Montfaucon mentions two in his *Italian Journal*, pp. 377 and 392: the first in the Florentine Abbey, the second at Fiesole.

Two are likewise preserved in Rome in the Vatican shelves, nos. 1978 and 5089. There is another in the Capranica Library.

Valesius, in the testimonies prefixed to his edition of Eusebius, praises a manuscript of the Church of Paris written more than eight hundred years ago. He brings it forward as assistance in his notes on Book IV, chapter XXII, and on Book VIII, chapters I and XVI, and calls it exceedingly ancient.

In the *Catalogue of Manuscripts of England*, vol. II, pp. 21 and 25, the Worcester manuscript no. 872 and the Salisbury manuscript no. 1001 are listed.

Another may be added, belonging to the monastery of Einsiedeln; I owe knowledge of it to the most illustrious Archbishop of Ephesus, Domenico Passionei, Apostolic representative of the Holy See to the Swiss Confederation.

Georgius Colvenerius, in his notes on Book II, chapter XXII, §2 of *On Bees*, p. 33, cites his own old manuscript of Rufinus’s *History*, where Book III, chapter I, reads that the Apostle Bartholomew went to Inner India rather than Hither India, as Cantipratanus has it there, p. 244.

Edmund Martène, in *Itinerary*, Part I, section II, p. 208, says that other manuscripts of Rufinus survive in the Cambron Abbey of Cistercian monks, in the diocese of Cambrai.

## IX.

Let us now review the editions of Rufinus’s *History* that were produced in printed form.

The first is owed to Giovanni Filippo de Lignamine of Messina, Count of the archiaters of Pope Sixtus IV, endowed with knightly rank by Ferdinand, king of Sicily and of the territory on this side of the Faro—that is, the other kingdom of Apulia, commonly called the Neapolitan kingdom, as the Roman Church is accustomed to call it—whom Lignamine himself, as papal commissioner, had received at Velletri and Valle dei Monti.

Giovanni Filippo also arranged for the *Eusebian History*, translated by Rufinus and enlarged by him, to be published from the printing shop that he had established in his own house at Rome, in the year of our Lord 1476. The title, which appears not—as elsewhere—on the first page, but after Lignamine’s dedicatory letter to Pope Sixtus, is as follows:

> The Book of the Ecclesiastical History of Eusebius of Caesarea, which the BLESSED Rufinus the presbyter translated from Greek into Latin.

At the end of the work, in folio form, these words are added:

> In the year 1476, on 15 May, in the fifth year of Sixtus IV, this work was completed.

In his letter dedicating the *History* to Sixtus IV, he praises him because, among the very few princes of Italy, he favors talent and raises up and supports learned and educated men with appropriate honors and rewards—“toward whom the whole company of learned men sighs and cries out.” He says that, after many works had been printed at his command and dedicated to the same Sixtus, he turned his attention to history and began with this work of Rufinus.

This edition, encountered by few, is rightly praised by Janus Gethardus as the most ancient. It is elegant, though its letters are somewhat heavier, and its syllables are often contracted in keeping with the spirit of the age. The conjunction *et* nearly corresponds to the ordinary numeral seven, as it sometimes appears in manuscripts from the eleventh century onward. See Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, pp. 423 and 429, second edition; and Johann Michael Heineccius, *Syntagma de sigillis*, p. 219. To these may be added the authors of the *Annotations on Giovanni Boccaccio’s Decameron*, p. 94, and Leonardo Salviati in his *Observations on the Italian Language*, vol. I, book III, chapters VIII–X. A stone in the Basilica of Saint Paul on the Ostian Way, cited by Margarino, p. 19, no. 252, supports the same point.

The paper is clean, firm, and large; its entire composition is enclosed on every side by a broad and spacious margin. Later printers, although in many other respects superior to those earlier printers, have certainly unlearned—or do not wish to attain—this splendid and magnificent form of printing.

At the beginning of each chapter of this edition are headings, which others call titles, by which readers can recognize almost at a glance what is treated in the books. Valesius observes in his notes on chapter I that this was done by Eusebius himself, not by anyone else, and that Rufinus found the same headings in his own copy. This is apparent from Rufinus’s manuscript copies, one of which, as I have already said, he possessed that had been written more than seven hundred years earlier. These facts show that Lignamine too printed his edition from an ancient manuscript. I discussed such headings in book III, § 5.

Everyone valued this first edition of Rufinus’s Eusebius, prepared by Lignamine, so highly that scarcely had it been published when it was immediately sold out. This is made clear by the fact that it had to be issued again in the same year, with the same letters and signs with which the earlier edition had appeared—except for one dedicatory letter and the first book, which underwent entirely new types, as will be evident to anyone comparing it with the earlier edition.

Lignamine wished this second edition, only slightly different from the first, to appear in the name of Guglielmo d’Estouteville, bishop of Ostia and cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, known as the cardinal of Rouen. He praises it as a work worthy of that prelate because of the knowledge of events it provides, the excellence of its author, and the fact that it conveys ecclesiastical discipline.

He praises the cardinal for restoring the churches of Saint Augustine and Saint Mary Major, and states that, up to that day—15 May 1476—five thousand volumes by various authors had been printed at his command. Among these he specifically names Sixtus IV’s little works *On the Blood of Christ*, *On the Power of God*, and *On Future Contingents*. For the benefit of bibliophiles, I shall incidentally record here the other authors printed by him whom I have observed.

1. Books III, IV, V, XIII, XVIII, and XIX of Homer’s *Iliad*, rendered in Latin verse by Niccolò della Valle and published by his father Laelius. Rome, in the house of Giovanni Filippo de Lignamine, 1474, quarto.

2. Terence’s comedies, in the manner of prose, quarto.

3. Giovanni Filippo de Lignamine’s *Chronicle of the Supreme Pontiffs and Emperors*, 1474, quarto.

4. *Il Pungilingua* by Domenico Cavalca of Vico Pisano, 1472, folio.

In the preface to Matteo Marci, abbot of Saint Placidus, he says that during the two years he had been living at Rome he had published the following books:

Quintilian; Suetonius; Leo; Lactantius; Ambrose, *On Duties*; Lorenzo Valla’s *Elegance*; and the minor works of Horace.

5. Proba’s *Cento*, together with little works by the Dominican Philip. Rome, at the press of Philip de Lignamine, 1481, quarto.

6. *On the Immortality of the Soul*, a dialogue by the Dominican Friar Jacopo Canfaro. Rome, etc., 1473, folio.

7. Flavius Blondus, *Italy and Rome Restored*. Rome, etc., 1474, folio.

8. *Letters of the Great Turk*, published by Laudivius, a knight of Jerusalem. Rome, etc., 1473, quarto.

The third edition of Eusebius, likewise elegant, followed the twofold edition which may nevertheless be counted as one. It had another physician as its patron, Johann Schall of Hersfeld, under whose care and through whose types it appeared at Mantua in the year of our Lord 1479, in folio, in ignorance of the Roman edition. Schall dedicated it to Federico Gonzaga, marquis of Mantua, appending this epigram at the end of the work:

> Rufinus translated this famous work  
> Of Eusebius of Caesarea  
> For Ausonian ears.  
>   
> John Schall, a German skilled in renowned art,  
> Imprints it in bronze, under Frederick, prince of Mantua.  
>   
> When the work was completed, Julius was recording  
> The year one thousand four hundred seventy-nine.  
>   
> Buy this book, if you seek the name of learning,  
> If you seek the threshold of Olympus.  
> This present gift possesses both.  
>   
> From it you will learn heavenly goodness  
> And the conduct of the saints;  
> No reading can be more beneficial.

The fourth edition appeared at Paris, printed by Pierre Levet in the year of our Lord 1497, quarto.

The fifth edition, in smaller folio format, in the types called Gothic, and without the printer’s name, was produced at Strasbourg in the year of our Lord 1514, together with Bede’s *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*. Peter Francis Chifflet, in his notes on the concordance of Bede and Fredegar, p. 319, mentioned it as extremely rare and as one he had not seen. According to him, Johannes Gravius calls this edition of Bede extremely corrupt and full of errors.

The sixth edition is owed to Geoffroy Boussard, a Parisian theologian. When he discovered that the Strasbourg edition of Eusebius, appended to Bede, was teeming with immense errors, he arranged for it to be published again at Paris in an edition revised by himself, in octavo, but without the printer’s name or date. He dedicated it to Étienne Poncher, president of the parliament of France and later bishop of Paris.

Soon afterward it appeared at Lyon, in the same kind of type as the preceding edition, at the press of Benedict Bonnyn, in the years 1523 and 1533, octavo.

In his preface to Poncher, Boussard says that, when he saw that this *History*, although already among booksellers, could nowhere be found—as if it did not exist—he had arranged for it to be printed with the greatest care and correction. For although, he says, it had been printed in previous years—at Strasbourg in 1514—the errors with which the manuscript was abundantly infected, both in its notes, signs, and punctuation and in its very words and entire sentences, could justly deter most lovers of letters from reading it and seriously offend those who did read it.

Accordingly, Boussard corrected and emended it with many copies and archetypes that he had gathered from various libraries, as accurately as he could—not only the sentences but nearly every syllable.

In Rufinus’s translation he praises the cultivation of the language, which is so great that, although the *History* is Greek, it is astonishing that Rufinus preserved such elegance in translating it. “Rufinus also, the presbyter of Aquileia, most skilled in both languages, made the Greek Eusebius Latin and presented him, lying silent, to the ears of our people. Nor did he do only this: he also added two later books to the nine books of Eusebius, composing them with equal cultivation, partly from the traditions of his elders and partly from what he had learned through experience of events.”

Publius Faustus Andrelinus of Forlì, poet laureate, praised the many labors Boussard had undertaken in a poem that is not inelegant. I transcribe it:

> If you seek the illustrious deeds of holy men,  
> This volume contains all their writings, refined in style.  
>   
> What had been buried and crushed beneath a great old age,  
> The eloquent file of my Boussard has polished.  
>   
> May Boussard be worthy to live through eternal years,  
> So that he may rescue the remaining deeds from their foul neglect.  
>   
> He has set everything down in a sure and orderly arrangement,  
> Opening an easier and shorter path.  
>   
> What does long time not obliterate through many years?  
> Yet there is nothing that diligent care cannot renew.

This edition of Boussard was printed again at Paris by François Regnault in the year of our Lord 1525, octavo. It may be counted as the seventh edition.

The eighth edition was prepared by Beatus—so called by name, not by merit—Rhenanus, at Basel, by Johann Froben, in the year of our Lord 1523, folio. I shall give the entire title:

> The authors of the Ecclesiastical History: nine books of Eusebius Pamphilus of Caesarea, translated by Rufinus; two books of the presbyter Rufinus of Aquileia, revised according to ancient Latin manuscripts by Beatus Rhenanus. Also twelve books from Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, Sozomen, and Socrates of Constantinople, translated by Epiphanius Scholasticus and abridged by Cassiodorus the Senator—whence they have received the name *Tripartite History*. These too have been corrected in many places, with numerous Greek letters of synods and emperors added here and there from the works of Theodoret, both to assist the Latin translation from these materials and to preserve them as memorials of Christian antiquity, so that the reader may possess something *philhellene* (*φιλέλλην*) to compare, not without benefit.

Rhenanus added his own brief notes in the margins throughout.

Froben repeated this eighth edition at Basel in the year of our Lord 1528, folio, removing Rhenanus’s prefaces. This was not done, however, in the third edition revised by Rhenanus, likewise at Basel by Froben, in the year of our Lord 1539, folio.

This edition, which is the tenth, was augmented by Victor of Vita’s *On the Vandal Persecution* and by book V of Theodoret, translated by Joachim Camerarius. Galeotus a Prato reproduced the same edition at Paris in the year of our Lord 1541, folio. It was then inserted into volume III of the works of Eusebius published in Latin at Basel by Henricpetrus in the year of our Lord 1542, folio.

The eleventh edition was made from Rhenanus’s tenth edition at Antwerp, at the press of Johann Steelsius, in the year of our Lord 1548, in two volumes, octavo. It added the *Life of Constantine*, translated by John Porte­sius, and Theodoret’s *History*.

To this let us append the thirteenth edition, with brief scholia by Johann Jakob Grynaeus, in volume II of the same works of Eusebius, likewise published at Basel by Henricpetrus in the year of our Lord 1570, folio. There, however, book X is from the translation of John Christopherson, while book XI is from Rufinus.

Eusebius’s *History*, translated into Latin by Christopherson, appeared together with the other authors of ecclesiastical history at Louvain, at the press of Servatius Sassenus, in the year of our Lord 1569, in two octavo volumes; at Cologne, at the press of Arnold Birckmann, in the year of our Lord 1570, folio, with the scholia of Johann Curterius; and at Paris, with Rufinus’s two books, at the press of Nicolaus Chesnau, in the year of our Lord 1571, folio.

After these fifteen editions of the *Ecclesiastical History*, the Greek writers, translated by Wolfgang Musculus, appeared more than once at Basel from the press of Froben, in the years 1549, 1554, and 1557, folio. There, after Eusebius’s *Life of Constantine*, are found two books of Rufinus’s *History*.

Johannes Dadraeus, however, excluded these from the works of Eusebius, which he published in Latin at Paris, at the press of Michael Sonnius, in the year of our Lord 1581, folio, using Christopherson’s translation and Curterius’s scholia.

An edition of Musculus, variously enlarged and adorned with the *Chronography* of Abraham Bucholzer, appeared at Basel, at the press of Sebastian Henricpetrus, in the year of our Lord 1611, folio.

Later, René Barre inserted Rufinus’s book X and book XI, separated from the rest, into his minor works, at Paris, at the press of Sonnius, in the year of our Lord 1580, folio.

Benedictus Aegius of Spoleto translated Rufinus’s *History of Eusebius* into Italian. Caspar Hedio translated it into German; it was printed at Strasbourg by Johann Herwagen in the year of our Lord 1545, folio.

# CHAPTER XII

I. Rufinus’s *History of the Hermits*. II. At one time attributed to Jerome. III. Rufinus relates another person’s, not his own, account of journeys through the deserts and monasteries of Egypt. IV. This person is Petronius of Bologna, and no other. V. The same is demonstrated by many arguments. VI. Difficulties concerning this are removed. VII. Why the work was attributed to Jerome.

## I.

We have now moved from Rufinus’s ecclesiastical *History* to a consideration of his *History of the Hermits*. I find that both ancient and modern writers who have composed commentaries on literary matters have scarcely touched upon it, passing it over without even lightly examining it because of the difficulties in which it is entangled.

When Rufinus was writing his own *History*, he indicates in book XI, chapter IV, that he had a work of this kind under way. For, after mentioning the deeds of the holy fathers whom he had known to flourish in the desert of Nitria, he says in passing that he would recount their deeds more fully in a work of his own:

> But if we wish to pursue the deeds of each of their miracles, we are excluded from the brevity we have proposed, especially since THESE THINGS DESERVE THE NARRATION OF A WORK OF THEIR OWN.

From Jerome we clearly understand that this subsequent narration, composed as a separate work by Rufinus, was the book of which Jerome speaks in letter XLIII to Ctesiphon, ridiculing the lives of the monks described by Rufinus in these words:

> The books of Evagrius—his *Sentences*—are read throughout the East in Greek and, with his disciple Rufinus as translator, in Latin throughout the West. HE [Rufinus] ALSO WROTE A BOOK, AS IT WERE ABOUT MONKS, and enumerates in it many who never existed.

I shall explain this rather obscure passage below. Critics have stumbled over it as though Jerome were saying that Rufinus enumerated people who had never existed, although it is absolutely certain that every one of them did exist.

Jerome continues:

> And those whom he writes did exist—Origenists condemned by the bishops—are undoubtedly Ammonius, Eusebius, and Evagrius himself, as well as Hor and Isidore and many others whom it is tedious to enumerate. And just as Lucretius says in book IV, verses 19 and following:
>
> And as when physicians, trying to give bitter wormwood  
> To children, first touch the rims of the cups  
> With the sweet yellow liquid of honey,
>
> so he [Rufinus] placed one John at the very beginning of his book—one whom there is no doubt was Catholic and holy—in order through him to introduce into the Church the others whom he had presented as heretics.

Jerome then attacks other works of Rufinus, adapted by him for Latin ears from Evagrius, Sixtus, Pamphilus, and Origen. It therefore cannot in any way be doubted that Rufinus wrote *About the Monks*, or the *Lives of the Fathers*, not indeed as a translator but, in a certain sense, as its principal author—contrary to what Erasmus believed in his notes on Jerome’s letter to Ctesiphon, where, on his own authority, he made Evagrius Ponticus the author of the entire work and Rufinus its translator.

Other learned men likewise attributed these *Lives of the Fathers*, which belong to Rufinus, to Evagrius. Heribert Rosweyde reviews their opinions in the fourth prolegomenon, p. 17, of the second Plantin edition of the *History of the Hermits*, published in the year of our Lord 1628. In its second book he established Rufinus’s work *About the Monks*, or the *Lives of the Fathers*, supported also by several ancient manuscripts, such as the excellent Audomar manuscript cited by Rosweyde in prolegomenon XXIV, p. 77.

Other manuscripts are cited by Heinrich Gravius in his notes on Jerome’s letter to Ctesiphon. I add one from the Bigot Library, p. 20, which is now in the royal library at Paris.

Rufinus himself also clearly reveals that he is the author of the same second book of the *Lives of the Fathers* in chapter XXIX, p. 482. Speaking of Macarius of Alexandria, he directs the reader to the place where he had written about him earlier—namely, to his own *Ecclesiastical History*. His words are:

> But many other marvelous things, as we have said, occurred in the works of Saint Macarius of Alexandria. Some of them were inserted in the eleventh book of the *Ecclesiastical History*; whoever seeks them will find them there.

They are found in book XI, chapter IV, and are absent from this second book of the *Lives of the Fathers*, namely:

1. The story of a blind man who received his sight after he wiped dust from Macarius’s cell, moistened it with water from the well from which Macarius customarily drank, and anointed his eyes with it.

2. The story of the cubs of a lioness being granted sight.

Finally, in confirmation that Rufinus is the author of this book, there is the fact that immediately after the preface the work begins with what Jerome had noted in his letter to Ctesiphon as occurring in the book whose author he makes Rufinus: namely, the life of Saint John the Hermit.

> He placed one John, he says, at the beginning of that very book, one whom there is no doubt was Catholic and holy.

From this it is evident how badly Johannes Martianeus went astray in his notes on the same passage of Jerome’s letter, volume IV of the works, p. 476, where he believed that the words just cited referred to John Chrysostom.

He certainly reached this conclusion without consulting Rufinus, who begins his book with John of Lycopolis, not with Chrysostom, the bishop of Constantinople. Why would he have placed a bishop at the head of a company of monks?

Rufinus subsequently also treats the others about whom Jerome had written that Rufinus discussed them in his book. According to Jerome’s order, they are:

1. Ammonius, Eusebius, and Euthymius, chapter XXIII, p. 478.

2. Evagrius Ponticus, chapter XXVII, p. 479.

3. Hor, or Or, chapter II, p. 457.

4. Isidore, chapter XVII, p. 475.

All these and so many other considerations make it absolutely certain that the *History of the Monks* attributed by Jerome to Rufinus is precisely the same work that now constitutes book II of Rosweyde’s *History of the Hermits*, *On the Lives of the Fathers*. It would scarcely be possible to devise anything clearer, stronger, or more eloquent for establishing Rufinus as the certain and legitimate author of the book.

Nor was a lesser store and weight of arguments needed to demonstrate this, because Rufinus’s own book contains doubts that seem to contradict the conclusion. Nearly everyone believed that these could be avoided only by denying that Rufinus was the author of the book or by asserting that Rufinus was merely its translator rather than its author.

Thus some attributed it to Palladius; others to Evagrius, bishop of Antioch, as Martin Delrio does in his notes on the tragedy *Octavia*, attributed to Seneca, p. 552; and still others, following Erasmus, to Evagrius Ponticus. Among the latter are Conrad Gesner in the *Bibliotheca*, Georg Wicelius in his letter preceding the *History of the Saints*, Johannes Molanus in chapter XIII *On Martyrologies*, Goldastus in his notes on Valerian of Cimiez’s *On the Good of Discipline*, p. 89, and Baronius in his notes on 15 and 17 January and 27 March. Baronius also does so in the *Annals* under the years 393, §§ 29 and 35, and 394, § 20, as well as very frequently elsewhere.

Nor are there lacking manuscripts that make the monk Postumian the author of the book. Rosweyde carefully examines each of these opinions in his fourth prolegomenon.

## II.

Yet none of the twenty editions of the work itself enumerated by that learned man presents any author other than Jerome. In this way Jerome became the author of the *History* that he had attacked in his letter to Ctesiphon, with the support of Johannes Trithemius in chapter C of his *Catalogue*, where he attributed to Jerome the book *On the Life of the Fathers*, beginning with the words “Blessed be God.”

Accordingly, Rosweyde, considerably troubled by so many opinions unfavorable to Rufinus, finally inclined in the fourth prolegomenon, § 10, p. 28, to believe that Rufinus was not the book’s principal author but its translator.

He imagines that Rufinus omitted his own name for two reasons:

1. He would not have dared to publish under his own name a book containing certain Origenists.

2. He was not so much the author of the book as merely its translator, since nearly everything narrated in it could be read in Palladius and Heraclides.

For this reason Rosweyde supposes that either one of them, or someone else, published the work in Greek without a name, and that Rufinus later translated it into Latin. This, more or less, is Rosweyde’s position.

The answer is easy. Neither the *History* of Palladius nor that of Heraclides—for they are one and the same work—was published before Rufinus’s death; both appeared only afterward. This is plainly demonstrated by the fact that Rufinus is mentioned in both as a man who had flourished long before.

Rufinus therefore could not possibly have translated this same *History* after it had been published and compiled.

Palladius himself explicitly tells us that his work was published in the year 420, in the preface to Lausus, where he says that in the twentieth year of his episcopate and the fifty-third year of his life he turned his mind to writing his *Lausiac History*.
