Palladius had been raised to the episcopate of Helenopolis in the year 400, and in May of that same year attended the Council of Constantinople, at which Antoninus, bishop of Ephesus, was accused of simony. See Tillemont, volume XI, article on Palladius, no. 6, p. 514.

Rufinus, however, had departed this life a decade before Palladius’s *History* was published, as we shall later see.

Moreover, in Jerome’s letter to Ctesiphon, Rufinus is attacked not as a translator but as the principal author of the *History of the Monks*. It is therefore clear how greatly Rosweyde is mistaken in making someone other than Rufinus the author of the book.

We must therefore take another route if we are to remove all the difficulties, which are neither few nor slight. This cannot be done accurately unless we bring back for examination the difficulties drawn from Rufinus’s own book—something Rosweyde failed to do.

## III.

The writer of the book *On the Lives of the Fathers*, whom we insist, with Jerome, is Rufinus himself, testifies in the prologue and throughout the work that he is describing an account of journeys which the person speaking in the book had previously undertaken at various times through the deserts and monasteries of Egypt, and the sequence of events that he had seen with his own eyes and heard with his own ears.

Now, the first chapter of the book makes it clear that what is narrated there about Saint John of Lycopolis cannot apply to Rufinus. For Rufinus, as I said in book IV, chapter II, was never in Egypt after the year 385, when Theophilus ascended the Alexandrian see.

By contrast, the person who speaks in book II, chapter I of the *History*, p. 457, was staying with Saint John of Lycopolis in the Thebaid toward the end of the year 394. He states that he had come from Jerusalem to visit him for the benefit and advancement of his soul, when the news reached Alexandria of the victory of Theodosius the Great over the tyrant Eugenius.

At that time Rufinus was not in Egypt or the Thebaid but in Jerusalem. During the quarrel among John, bishop of the city, Epiphanius, and Jerome, he supported John’s party, as I said in book IV, chapter III.

Nor does this exhaust the difficulties. Those who had visited the same holy man, John of Lycopolis, numbered seven. One of them, younger than the others, held the rank of deacon; the rest were laymen. This deacon and young man, whom Saint John exposed when he wished to remain hidden out of modesty, seems to me to be the same person as the speaker in the *History*.

But Rufinus in the year 394 could not be called either a young man or a deacon. In a letter to John of Jerusalem written in that same year, 394, not long after Easter, Epiphanius calls him by the name “presbyter” once and again.

As for the other holy men mentioned in the *History*, the author of the journeys says that he saw the blessed Apollonius, accompanied by two companions, when Apollonius was about eighty years old, chapter VII, p. 460. He says that this same man was fifty-five years old when Julian Augustus, who began to reign in the year 361 and died in 363, died.

Accordingly, the author of the journeys spoke with Apollonius around the year 388, while Rufinus was far away in Palestine.

The same author of the journeys, in chapter XXIII, p. 478, calls Dioscorus, the brother of Ammonius, Eusebius, and Euthymius, bishop of Hermopolis, at the time when he visited those men. Yet in the year 390 Dioscorus was not yet a bishop, according to Tillemont in his article on Theophilus of Alexandria, volume XI, no. 3, p. 447.

Thus the author of the journeys must not be said to have visited Ammonius before the year 390. That same Dioscorus was a bishop in the year 394, for on 29 September of that year he signed the Council of Constantinople, in Labbe, volume II, p. 1151.

Again, in chapter XXVIII, p. 479, the author of the journeys speaks of Evagrius as a monk who at that time was very famous. Evagrius, however, did not enter the Egyptian desert before the year 382, and he died in the year 399.

The author also says that Evagrius completely abstained from bread. Yet, according to his disciple Palladius, chapter LXXXVI, p. 764, he did not eat it except after the year 397.

Finally, in chapter XXVIII, p. 479, the author speaks of the two Macarii, but as monks whom he had not seen, since they had died before he came to Nitria. The first had died around the year 390, the other around the year 395.

Rufinus, on the other hand, testifies that he knew both Macarii once, twice, and a third time. See him in book II, *Against Jerome*, and in the *History*, book XI, chapters IV and VIII.

## IV.

It was necessary to pursue these matters at length in order to lay the foundations of our position. Thus, just as Jerome alone, serving as a witness sufficient for all, establishes that Rufinus was the writer of the book, so it is equally established that the author of the journeys and events related in the book—the person speaking there—is not Rufinus but someone entirely different, who was then in Egypt while Rufinus was living in Palestine.

Thus the writer of the book will be one person, and the author of the events recorded another. Rufinus lent his hand and pen to describe the journeys of the other. It also happened that, speaking in his book with another person’s voice, he praised his own *History* not as his own work but plainly as someone else’s.

The book therefore belongs to two persons: to the writer of the book and to the author of the events narrated in it. For this reason neither of them attached his own name to it, lest either should claim alone a work that belonged to both.

This was likewise the reason why Gennadius, when writing about Rufinus in chapter XI, did not list this book together with Rufinus’s other writings, although he knew it very well: it was partly another person’s work, not wholly Rufinus’s. Jerome, however, had listed it as Rufinus’s own.

But when Gennadius speaks of Saint Petronius of Bologna, he carefully records the matter in chapter XLI, and from this light shines upon us that dispels every obscurity.

The curtain is therefore drawn aside, so that we may see the entire matter clearly. Gennadius accordingly committed these words to writing:

> Petronius, bishop of the church of Bologna, a man of holy life, and TRAINED FROM HIS YOUTH IN THE STUDIES OF MONKS, IS THOUGHT TO HAVE WRITTEN THE LIVES OF THE MONKS OF EGYPT, which the monks embrace as a mirror and standard of their profession.

Gennadius refers to a book received and widely approved in the Church. His copyist Honorius says similar things in the *Catalogue*, book II, chapter XLI; Vincent of Beauvais in the *Historical Mirror*, book XX, chapter XXV; and Boninus Mombritius in the *Sanctuarium*, volume II, under the letter P.

Rosweyde, in the fourth prolegomenon, § 7, p. 21, supposes that Gennadius is referring to book II of the *Lives of the Fathers*, which Jerome had attributed to Rufinus.

Gennadius says of Petronius that he is “thought to have written” it because Petronius himself did not write the book, but Rufinus actually composed it under Petronius’s name.

It is therefore now certain that the *Lives of the Fathers*, divided into thirty-three chapters, with the perils of the journeys set forth therein, was related by Rufinus—not, however, under his own name but under that of Petronius. Throughout the book Petronius is the one who speaks, and as an eyewitness and truthful witness accurately describes, through Rufinus’s hand, the events that he himself had seen in the monasteries of Egypt.

Saint Petronius, according to Gennadius, was the son of another Petronius, the praetorian prefect, whom Baronius identified with Anicius Probus on 4 October. This father, however, was not distinct from Petronius, prefect of the Gauls, who is mentioned in the constitution issued in the year 418 by the emperors Honorius and Theodosius Augustus. Sirmond published it in his notes on Sidonius, second edition, p. 148.

Our Petronius is called by Eucherius of Lyon, in his letter *On Contempt of the World*, which he testifies on p. 29 of Rosweyde’s edition to have written in the year 1185 *ab urbe condita*—corresponding to the common year 433—“now in Italy a bishop from that fullest seat of worldly power.”

By these words the Gaul Eucherius indicates the prefecture of the Gauls held by Petronius’s father, which his son Petronius, the holy man, despised for Christ.

This man was much more devoted to Christian simplicity than to eloquence. He himself, adorned with the greatest modesty, admits as much in the prologue to this *History* that we are discussing:

> We are less suited to narrate such great events, nor does it seem fitting that small and insignificant authors should become the narrators of mighty deeds and that lofty virtues should be related in humble speech.

Soon afterward he says that he was induced to publish the work because the love of the brothers who live on the holy Mount of Olives had repeatedly requested this of him:

> To explain the LIFE of the MONKS OF EGYPT, their virtues of spirit, their practice of devotion, and the strength of their abstinence, which we SAW WITH OUR OWN EYES among them.

These statements clearly show that, after Petronius had returned to Italy, he maintained a relationship and correspondence concerning books with the monks of the Mount of Olives, from whom he had earlier journeyed to Egypt.

### V.

As I said in Book IV, chapter II, Rufinus had lived for a long time with the monks of Olivet. From there, Jerome, who lived at Bethlehem, near Olivet, learned that Rufinus was the author of the books sent by Petronius (or Rufinus) to the monks of Olivet, although the author’s name was by no means attached to them. Thus the old man of Bethlehem, when an opportunity arose, inserted this information into his letter to Ctesiphon; from there it passed into the memory of posterity.

That the events described by Rufinus in this History should be attributed to Petronius, not to Rufinus, is also supported by Gennadius. He says that Petronius was trained from adolescence in the disciplines of the monks [Col. 0239D], and that he died during the reigns of Theodosius (the second), son of Arcadius, and Valentinian (the third)—that is, sometime between the years 425 and 450. Although this chronological indication is not precise, it nevertheless sufficiently shows that Petronius was still an adolescent when he devoted himself in Egypt to the disciplines of the monks.

What is read in his own work, chapter I, concerning Saint John of Lycopolis, who questioned Petronius and his companions, entirely agrees with this:

> “If there were a cleric among us,” he said.

When all denied it, although John himself, warned by the Spirit of God, knew that there was a deacon among them who wished to remain hidden out of modesty, Saint John, as soon as he saw him—and since he was indeed younger than the others—pointed to him with his finger and said: “This man is the deacon.”

Petronius, therefore, who in A.D. 388 and 394 mingled with the Egyptian solitaries, was an adolescent and a deacon; later he became bishop of Bologna. Thus, from Gennadius, we recognize that Petronius spoke there about himself as though about another person.

But why say more? Gennadius testifies that Petronius did not at all excel in eloquence. For he rejects as Petronius’s the book circulated under his name, *On the Ordination of a Bishop*, for this principal reason: it had been elegantly written. “Its more elegant language,” he says, “shows that it is not his, but, as some say, his father’s.” These facts, taken together, indicate with a kind of unmistakable signature that Petronius, having returned to Italy from the East shortly after Rufinus and being less skilled in the art of writing, used his friend’s pen in describing the history of his travels—travels which, according to the custom of the age, he had undertaken through the retreats of Egypt.

The remaining words about this work, reported by Gennadius, place the matter still more clearly beyond controversy:

> “He is thought to have written the *Lives of the Egyptian Monks.”

For since Petronius knew how to express the customs of the Egyptian Fathers more through his life than through his pen, he did this by the hand of Rufinus. Hence some attributed the book to Rufinus, others to Petronius, and others to no one. This is the origin of Gennadius’s uncertain and doubtful expression, “he is thought to have written.”

The same Gennadius, in the Vatican manuscript, is altogether uncertain about the book’s true author. In chapter XI he mentions the work without any author’s name:

> “Evagrius the Monk, a familiar disciple of the aforementioned Macarius, distinguished in divine and secular learning (whose book entitled *The Life of the Fathers*, as of a most continent man, makes mention), wrote many works.”

This praise of Evagrius appears in Rufinus, *Lives of the Fathers*, Book II, chapter XXVII, p. 479. The following parenthesis misled Baronius, A.D. 388, §105, and Bellarmine in his *Catalogue*, and, before them all, Honorius in Book II, chapter XI. Misunderstanding Gennadius’s words, they believed Evagrius to be the author of the book.

Are we really to say that Evagrius was so lacking in modesty that he was not ashamed to heap upon himself in his own work as many praises as those attributed to him in that same chapter XXVII? Aubertus Miraeus, in his notes on Gennadius, and Rosweydus, in Prolegomenon IV, §5 [Col. 0240C], p. 18, rightly deny this. Lucas Holstenius, in his manuscript notes on Bellarmine’s *Catalogue*, under the entry on Jerome, observes that Gennadius’s passage concerning Evagrius has not been properly understood.

Gerardus Johannes Vossius, however, took a different view in Book II, chapter XIX, of *On Greek Historians*. He thought that most of the lives in Rufinus’s History had been taken from Timothy of Alexandria, whom Sozomen says wrote works of this kind in Book VI, chapter XXIX. Rosweydus had anticipated Vossius in this opinion, Prolegomenon IV, §1, p. 12. Nor does Tillemont contradict it, vol. XII, p. 658; he certainly allows that Rufinus was enriched, at least in part, by the writings of those who had previously become famous for such compositions.

One of these was certainly Timothy. Yet Petronius, speaking throughout the work, nowhere indicates that he had ever seen him. Moreover, Timothy, who in A.D. 385 had Theophilus as his successor in the Alexandrian See, could not have written about events that later occurred to Petronius among the Egyptian monks. Nor could Rufinus have copied Timothy while describing the journeys of his friend Petronius, which the brothers living on Olivet had asked to have recounted to them by Petronius himself, even though they could have read Timothy, who was widely available among Eastern Christians [Col. 0240D].

### VI.

From these considerations, I believe it is clear how groundlessly, after Rosweydus, Cotelerius in his notes on the *Greek Monuments*, vol. III, p. 566, made Rufinus the translator of the book rather than its author. For Jerome attacks him as its principal author, not as a mere translator, and attributes the entire work—and the complete lives of which it is composed—to him alone.

Rosweydus likewise says in Prolegomenon IV, §10, p. 28, that almost everything narrated in the book is found in Palladius and Heraclides, and therefore that one or the other of them must previously have written in Greek the material translated by Rufinus. But the opposite is more likely to follow from this: namely, that Rufinus’s Latin book was later translated into Greek and incorporated into Palladius’s History because of the similarity of their contents, so that one body might be formed from the two authors.

Indeed, in Palladius’s History, from chapter XLIII [Col. 0241A], p. 738, through chapter LXXVI, p. 760, of Rosweydus’s second edition, there appears everything that Rufinus related about the Egyptian solitaries, as comparison will show. Rosweydus carefully noted this in the margins of the individual chapters.

Cotelerius, however, in the volume cited above, pp. 564–565, lists four manuscript codices containing Rufinus’s History in Greek translation—not, as he himself supposes without having examined Rufinus, the work of Heraclides.

Palladius, who everywhere breathes extraordinary simplicity and fidelity, made it his particular concern to confess with ingenuous modesty through whom he had profited. He should therefore not be accused of committing so shameful a plagiarism as to appropriate Rufinus’s entire History without ever mentioning his name even once, especially since it contains many things that Palladius would have wrongly claimed for himself.

A single example will suffice. In Palladius, chapter XLIII, p. 738, and near the end of chapter XLVI, p. 745, there are passages concerning events that, as we have noted from chapter I of Rufinus’s History, happened to Petronius while he was with John of Lycopolis. This alone—and especially the messenger’s report of Theodosius’s victory over the tyrant Eugenius—is enough to show that someone other than Palladius once combined Rufinus’s History with the *Lausiac History*, after which others perhaps mixed in additional material, as often happens.

Anyone investigating the other indications of this mixture will readily find them. One such indication is the discussion of Saint John in two places, and likewise of the Nitrian and Tabennesian monks in two places: chapter XXXVIII, p. 736, and chapter XLVIII, p. 746. This confusion of materials greatly troubled learned minds attempting to distinguish the two Histories. Consequently, even Cotelerius, otherwise a perceptive man, believed that Rufinus had derived his work from this Greek source.

On the contrary, Rufinus’s composition passed into a Greek work. Rufinus’s History was indeed translated into Greek at an early date, and Cotelerius published its preface and part of the text in vol. III, p. 171, from Colbertine and royal codices, which he praises on p. 564. There he notes that in Colbertine codex 1213 Rufinus’s History appears in Greek, naming Jerome, presbyter of Dalmatia, and following Palladius’s *Lausiac History* [Col. 0241C].

Rosweydus had also noticed this from Venetian and Augustinian manuscripts, in Prolegomenon IV, §8, p. 23. What wonder, then, if twenty Latin editions attribute it to Jerome?

This same Rufinus’s History—pure and unaltered, translated into Greek and attributed to Jerome under the title *History of the Monks of Egypt*—is found in the Coislinian Library, according to our Montefalconius, p. 198, although he failed to recognize its legitimate author.

John Meursius also failed to recognize this. In the preface to the *Lausiac History* of Palladius, which he published in Greek, he says that he possessed a book of the *Lives of the Egyptian Fathers*, plainly none other than our work.

### VII.

Nor should one suppose that the practice of attributing this work of Rufinus to Jerome, and circulating it under his name, began only recently. By the age of Gelasius I, toward the end of the fifth century, it had already become established.

The cause of the error is as follows. Jerome had narrated certain lives of the Fathers. Rufinus’s lives, because of the similarity of their subject matter, were joined to these; and because of the reasons given above, they were attributed to no one. They were therefore immediately believed to belong to Jerome along with the others.

In Gelasius’s *Decree*, chapter III, concerning writings to be received, these words are read:

> “We receive with every honor the *Lives of the Fathers, Paul, Antony, Hilarion, and all the hermits*, which, nevertheless, the most blessed Jerome wrote.”

But Jerome had written only the lives of Paul, Hilarion, and Malchus; no others. For the *Life of Antony*, published in Greek by Athanasius, was translated into Latin by Evagrius, bishop of Antioch. Rufinus described the remaining lives, which Gelasius designated by the phrase “all the hermits.”

Thus these *Lives of the Fathers* were commonly regarded in the age of Gelasius as Jerome’s works. Palladius’s *Lausiac History*, in which the deeds of others are explained, was at that time scarcely or only slightly known to Westerners. Certainly it was never attributed to Jerome, but always to Palladius or Heraclides.

When Gelasius expressly accepted these Lives as written by Jerome, he did not thereby reject the others. Thus Rosweydus agrees with me in Prolegomenon XV, p. 48.

But I shall add something else of the greatest importance concerning Palladius, which will confirm what has been said. There still survives a very ancient Latin translation of his Greek History, one that exposes all the interpolations of the Greek manuscripts. It is entirely free of the additions that later entered those Greek codices from Rufinus, and it contains certain passages absent from the Greek, as Rosweydus notes in the margin.

This Latin translation, divided into fifty-eight chapters and entitled *Lausus*, was first published by Jacobus Faber Stapulensis from the Bellovisian press at Paris in A.D. 1503, on February 23, under the name *The Paradise of Heraclides*, together with Clement’s *Recognitions*, as I have said elsewhere. This date is read at the end of Heraclides. The printing of the entire volume, however, was completed in A.D. 1504, on the Ides of July, during the pontificate of Julius II.

In his letter to Jacobus Ramirius, bishop of Catania, Faber says that he found the books of Heraclides and Clement, decaying from age and neglect, in ancient libraries [Col. 0242B].

After Faber, Aloysius Lippomanus, bishop of Verona, distinguished for his literary reputation and his piety, inserted the *Paradise*, restored to Palladius by Franciscus Turrianus through comparison with a manuscript copy of Palladius in the Venetian Library, in volume III of *The Lives of the Saints*, published at Venice under the sign of Hope in A.D. 1554, p. 144.

Rosweydus later wished to append it to his *History of the Hermits*, p. 939. In its Prolegomenon IV, §103, he does not distinguish the *Paradise of Heraclides* from Palladius’s genuine History.

There are also other features in this *Paradise* that differ considerably in sense and order from the Greek text we possess, so that it is evident that this Latin translation was carefully made from manuscript codices more accurate than ours, and in some places different from them. Wherever it follows copies agreeing with ours, it expresses the character of the Greek author with unsurpassable fidelity.

Tillemont, whose industry has given us much, says in vol. XI, p. 642, that he does not know how the name *Paradise* became attached to the work. It came from the work itself, where the blessed are discussed and their dwelling is said to be Paradise.

I believe that the name Heraclides passed into the Greek codices and then into the Latin translation from Rufinus, who in Book XI, chapter IV, of his *Ecclesiastical History* adds a certain Heraclides to the Nitrian monks whom he mentions.

Cotelerius, vol. III, p. 563, lists Colbertine codex no. 4303, in which this History is attributed to Heraclides, bishop of Cappadocia. But another Heraclides, bishop of Ephesus and a Greek, must by no means be said to have composed this *Paradise* in Latin. For the author says in the Greek codex, just as in the Latin, p. 966, that he was bishop of Bithynia—namely, of Helenopolis, which was Palladius’s see, not Heraclides’.

After such clear evidence, it can rightly not be doubted that this masked Heraclides, inserted into Palladius’s preface to Lausus after it had been somewhat altered, invaded another’s possession. This has greatly exercised the ingenuity of critics.

Thus Bellarmine, in his *Catalogue*, makes Palladius the author of two works: Heraclides’ *Paradise* and the *Lausiac History*. Vossius, Book II, chapter XIX, of *On Greek Historians*, thought that the *Lausiac History* had been composed from two books, one by Palladius and the other by Heraclides; Cave adopted this opinion.

But once we have shown that Heraclides’ *Paradise* is Palladius’s genuine *Lausiac History*, no one will any longer struggle with phantoms—especially with the support of the manuscript codex of Cardinal Bessarion, which Lippomanus calls exceptionally well corrected.

For the three other Latin codices of this History, Rosweydus should be consulted in Prolegomenon XXV, p. 84.

These matters seemed necessary to say concerning the *Lives of the Fathers*, prepared by Rufinus under the name of Saint Petronius. They were translated not only into Greek but also into Syriac and Arabic, for the consolation of those who profess the monastic life, as I learned from the pious man Gabriel Eva, a Maronite monk from Lebanon and Archbishop of Nicosia in Cyprus.

In the many translations and editions to be mentioned in the following chapter, I find the truth of what Gennadius writes about these *Lives of the Fathers* in chapter XLI: monks embrace them as a mirror and standard of their profession.

For the avoidance of ambiguity, the work itself ought to have been headed with the following title:

> **The History of the Monks,**  
> **or the Lives of the Fathers**  
> **and Journeys through Egypt,**  
> **written under the name of Saint Petronius**  
> **of Bologna**  
> **by Rufinus, presbyter of Aquileia.**

Finally, it is to be hoped that Palladius’s genuine and original *Lausiac History* will be brought to light, carefully compared with and revised against the ancient manuscript codices available in Paris and elsewhere, together with the commonly circulated Latin version of Heraclides.

## CHAPTER XIII

[Col. 0243B]

1. Jerome’s testimony concerning this work of Rufinus explained.  
2. What should be said about the holiness of those whom Jerome attacks.  
3. The reasons are given why Jerome may perhaps have been less than fair to Rufinus and Petronius.  
4. The various editions of the work on the *Lives of the Fathers* are presented.

### I.

In the preceding chapter I examined the commentary on the *Life of the Fathers*, written by Rufinus under the name of Saint Petronius. Now it is necessary to investigate what has been said and done about it at different times.

The censure that Jerome, inflamed against his adversary, stamped upon the book in his letter to Ctesiphon has generally been treated as a private judgment concerning a historical matter; it has never received the unanimous assent of the Church. Hence it could not prevent the *History of the Monks* from circulating in the West as well as in the East through the hands and mouths of holy men—or even from assuming Jerome’s own name.

Yet I do not hesitate to repeat here Jerome’s very words, which I have quoted elsewhere, since learned men, having read them less carefully than they should, have so far seemed to conceal an ulcer requiring medical treatment. Here are the words of the holy Doctor:

> “He [Rufinus] also wrote a book *as though* about monks, and in it enumerates many who *never existed*. Those whom he writes *did exist* were Origenists and, there can be no doubt, were condemned by the bishops.”

Once, critics of great distinction clung to these words as to a source of water; I too, I confess, once clung to them, assigning Jerome a meaning entirely different from the one contained in his words.

The eminent Rosweydus does not blush to admit this of himself in his *Eremitical History*, p. 447, no. 4. He writes:

> “I cannot discover in this book people who never existed, since scarcely anyone appears concerning whom other authors do not also give testimony. Certainly Petronius, through the pen of Rufinus, testifies in the prologue that he is recounting things which, as he says, ‘we saw with our own eyes.’ But he could not have seen monks who never existed.”

Cotelerius says more correctly in *Monuments*, vol. III, p. 566, that the sense would be: “we know them to have existed,” instead of “he writes that they existed.” From this, he says, it may also be understood that the great Doctor either did not know, or at least concealed, that Rufinus was not the author of the book but merely its translator.

Indeed, he was not a translator but the principal author, as we have demonstrated at length. Then, on p. 678, Cotelerius thinks that the true reading from the Colbertine codex is:

> “And those whom he describes as having existed were Origenists.”

Tillemont, vol. XII, article 125, p. 306, considers it exceedingly difficult to believe that Jerome wrote that Rufinus dealt with monks who had never existed; and the construction of the passage seems obscure to him, vol. XII, p. 657, note LXXX.

What, then, shall we pronounce concerning the meaning of words that have proved a stumbling block to such great men? If they are examined carefully, they will appear clear and entirely free of obscurity.

Jerome, in Letter XVIII, formerly XXII, to Eustochium, on the guardianship of virginity, and after him John Cassian in *Conference* XVIII, chapter IV, distinguish three kinds of monks: two excellent kinds and a third lukewarm kind.

They are:

1. Cenobites, living in community.
2. Anchorites, living alone in the deserts.
3. Sarabaites, who separated themselves from the gatherings of the monasteries and individually cared for their own necessities, as Cassian says in chapter VII.

The two Benedicts—Benedict of Cassino in the *Rule*, chapter I, and Benedict of Aniane in the *Concordia of Rules*, chapter III—add a fourth kind, the gyrovagi, who are sufficiently well known in themselves.

Edmundus Martenius and Hugo Menardus, interpreters of both Benedicts, discuss each kind learnedly. To these add the third Benedict, namely Haeftenus, in *Monastic Investigations*, Treatise II, Investigation I.

Monks of the first kind, which is the monastic kind, serving under a rule and an abbot, were properly called monks, as the great Benedict says after Jerome and Cassian. According to Cassian, the greatest number of monks throughout Egypt belonged to this kind, living in separate and divided cells, as Jerome says, or “separated in cells,” according to Rufinus in the prologue to the book under discussion.

Petronius wonderfully confirms Cassian’s words in the same prologue:

> “They are immense in number” [Col. 0244B].

Furthermore, in chapter XVIII he testifies that he himself saw innumerable multitudes of monks. These were strictly and properly called monks.

This, therefore, was the only most ancient kind of monks, according to Cassian, chapter V. But Rufinus, or Petronius, besides the cenobitic monks, also enumerates certain anchorites who hid themselves in precipitous mountains and almost inaccessible places, in order to enjoy more intimate communion with God.

“These men,” says Cassian, “had first been trained in monasteries and, having already become perfect in active practice, chose the solitude of secluded places.” See Haeftenus, Treatise II, Investigation IV.

Because some anchorites are mixed with the monks in Rufinus’s History, Jerome said that Rufinus had published a book “as though” about monks—namely, about men who were not all cenobitic monks but also included anchorites. Such men are Elias in chapter XII, Pythirion in chapter XIII, Apelles in chapter XV, Paphnutius in chapter XVI, and perhaps others.

For this reason Prosper, speaking of John in his *Chronicle* under A.D. 395, called him not only a monk but also [Col. 0244C] an anchorite, in order to distinguish his manner of life properly.

These are the men enumerated by Rufinus who, according to Jerome, had never been cenobitic monks but had always been anchorites. Since they had lived so long in solitude, no one knew whether they had ever been in monasteries.

The holy man does not attack these men at all. Rather, he attacks the remaining anchorites whom Rufinus says had been cenobitic monks, declaring that they were Origenists and had been condemned by the bishops.

Who, then, can deny that Jerome’s words are perfectly clear?

### II.

As for the Origenists, no error is detected in these *Lives* by which they could be disapproved even in the slightest. On the contrary, everything narrated about them breathes extraordinary and profound holiness.

Nor is there any discussion here of ecclesiastical doctrines; only the conduct, manner of life, and examples of righteous men are recounted. Saint Petronius, who reports these matters and who never incurred even the suspicion of Origenism, would not have praised Origenists condemned by the bishops.

Georgius Colvenerius, in the preface to Thomas of Cantimpré’s *Universal Good on Bees*, which he entitled *Memorable Miracles and Examples* and which was published at Douai by Balthasar Bellerus in 1605, praises Rufinus of Aquileia, who wrote the *Lives of the Fathers*, p. 464.

Ludovicus Thomassinus praises Rufinus in the *Lives of the Fathers* in vol. I of his *Theological Dogmas concerning God*, when discussing sin arising from negligence, Book X, chapter L, p. 705, and likewise chapter LIII, p. 709, as well as p. 597. When treating grace and predestination in Book IX, chapter XV, he similarly praises him.

Moreover, in the ancient Greek *Menaea* and the Latin martyrologies, certain of these Fathers are regarded as holy men and are praised by holy men.

The tables of the Roman Church mention John from Rufinus on March 27; the *Menaea* on September 20. Not even Jerome himself doubted his great holiness.

He was well known among ancient ecclesiastical writers: Cassian, *Institutes*, Book IV, chapter XXIII, and *Conferences*, XXIV, chapter XXV; Augustine, *City of God*, Book V, chapter XXVI [Col. 0245A]; and Eucherius, *On the Praise of the Desert*, p. 29 of Rosweydus’s edition. In Usuard’s *Martyrology*, in Greven’s, and in the Maurolycan, he appears on November 12. In the *Menaea*, however, he appears on August 7.

After Rufinus, Sidonius mentions him among the Latins, *Carmen* XVI.5.101; among the Greeks, Sozomen, Book VI, chapter XXVIII, and Nicephorus Callistus, Book IX, chapter XXXIV.

The *Menaea* commemorate Ammonius on January 26, and Georgius of Alexandria discusses his holiness in his *Life of Chrysostom*. Sozomen, Book VI, chapter XXVIII, and Nicephorus, Book IX, chapter XXXIV, mention his disciples Beni and Theon. I have spoken elsewhere about Evagrius.

I would be excessive, however, if I wished to gather together everything said about each of these men in various places.

In the Ethiopian Calendar published by Job Ludolf at Frankfurt in A.D. 1691, Saint Philemon is commemorated on February 14. Knowledge of him came from Book II, chapter XIX, of Rufinus’s *Lives of the Fathers*. Rosweydus’s notes appended to the History should be consulted.

Theophilus of Alexandria, writing to Epiphanius in Letter CXI, formerly LXVII, among the Hieronymian letters, says concerning the monks whom the Stridonian Father censures in his letter to Ctesiphon:

> “I have learned that Ammonius, Eusebius, and Euthymius, slanderers of the true Faith, raving with a new frenzy on behalf of heresy, sailed to Constantinople.”

Theophilus learned this, of course, from men like himself.

Epiphanius informed Jerome more fully about the matter in Letter LXIII, formerly LXXIII, now XCI; and Theophilus did so in two other letters, LXIX and LXXIII, formerly LXXII, now LXXXVII. Jerome later congratulated Theophilus in Letters LIX, formerly LXX, and LXI, formerly LXXI, now LXXXVI and LXXXVIII, on the expulsion and condemnation of these same monks.

In Letter XXXVIII, formerly LXI, to Pammachius against John of Jerusalem, he writes:

> “This Isidore, who is lifted into heaven by your praises, is accused in Alexandria of the very thing for which you accuse him in Jerusalem—namely, Origenism.”

These four monks—Ammonius, Eusebius, Euthymius, and Isidore—are found in Rufinus’s composition.

These solitaries, whom Theophilus of Alexandria had driven from their cells in Nitria on the charge of Origenism, first fled to Jerusalem and then to Constantinople. John Chrysostom received them into his protection and communion as upright and Catholic men.

For this reason Theophilus, inflated by his learning, his cunning, and the authority of his see, became so enraged against that most holy man that he loaded him with vile accusations, deprived him of his episcopate by wicked devices, and condemned him to exile, ultimately compelling him to die. He did not hesitate to provoke a schism throughout the Church for this reason.

Baronius, whose hatred of heresy and regard for Theophilus clouded his judgment, prejudged the case of the Nitrians in A.D. 400, §52, believing that the agreement of East and West had been mobilized against the Origenists on Theophilus’s side.

He nevertheless excuses Chrysostom on the ground that, when the Nitrians denied that they were heretics and attributed Theophilus’s rage to private motives, Chrysostom believed them—supposedly because, as a man devoted above all to Christian charity and an arbiter of peace, he wished in this way to restore them to Theophilus’s favor and authority.

Rosweydus, however, a man distinguished for learning and religion, observing in Prolegomenon XV, p. 48, to the *Eremitical History*, that Jerome regarded these solitaries as Origenists, and seeing that some of them were enrolled among the saints of the Greek Church and praised by holy men, supposed that they had at some time been caught by the errors of Origen but later repented.

Menardus, however—or Godefridus Hermannus—in Book V, chapter III, of his *Life of Chrysostom*, excellently defended their case, which they shared with other most holy men.

In Photius, codex CLIX, in the pamphlet of Acacius presented against Chrysostom at the Synod of the Oak, the following is read:

> “Because the blessed Epiphanius would not communicate with Chrysostom on account of the Origenists Ammonius, Euthymius, Eusebius, Heraclides, and Palladius.”

As we have seen, Jerome likewise counted these men among the Origenists. But the suspicion was neither legitimate nor well established, if Chrysostom—a man supremely holy and supremely orthodox—continued to communicate with these same solitaries, although they had fallen under suspicion and had even been condemned.

### III.

So that we may omit nothing in a matter that concerns not so much the Nitrian monks and Rufinus, the author of the book, as the most blessed men Chrysostom and Petronius, eyewitnesses and eloquent heralds of the monks’ holiness, I shall add several further considerations. Christophorus a Castro, in Rosweydus’s Prolegomenon XV, p. 50, advanced these arguments on their behalf in order to answer Jerome and the others.

Most holy men stood on both sides, and bishops stood on both sides. These matters must be heard with great preparedness of heart. They should not offend us, but rather remind us of human weakness.

No one is unaware that truth is the soul of history, but the history of the Church is to be directed toward the edification and example of Christians.

Epiphanius and Jerome opposed Origen, and even Chrysostom himself, from zeal rather than malice; such great men were very far from malice. Nevertheless, Theophilus’s malice deceived them. It advanced so far that he published a savage book against Chrysostom, which Jerome translated from Greek into Latin.

Facundus of Hermiane quotes a fragment of Jerome’s translation in Book VI, chapter V, calling it an enormous and horrible book.

Chrysostom, Petronius, and Olympias, deaconess of the Church of Constantinople, were all moved by good zeal and supported the Nitrians. Yet the entire Church, together with its head, Innocent I, stood with Chrysostom against Theophilus.

Let us hear Castrius, a learned and deeply religious man. I shall reduce the matter to a brief account.

In the age of Theophilus and Epiphanius, toward the end of the fourth century, a controversy became widespread in the East concerning the nature of God: namely, whether He possessed human form or not.

The simpler people, especially among the monks, imagined Him as corporeal; hence they were called Anthropomorphites. They opposed Origen because he had taught that God is spirit.

Those who defended this teaching of Origen—all the wiser and Catholic men—were regarded by the simpler people as Origenists. Conversely, those who attacked Origen in any way were denounced as Anthropomorphites, as though they were hostile to Origen because he had taught that God is spirit.

For this reason Theophilus of Alexandria sometimes counted Saint Epiphanius, although Catholic in every respect, among the Anthropomorphites, according to Socrates, Book VI, chapter 9, Sozomen, Book VIII, chapter XIV, and Nicephorus, Book XIII, chapter XII.

Indeed, Rufinus, in his books of *Apology*, denounced Jerome himself under the same odious name when Jerome, previously devoted to Origen, began to oppose him. John of Jerusalem likewise treated Epiphanius in this way, according to Jerome in Letter XXXVIII, formerly LXI, to Pammachius.

Rufinus also reproached Jerome with the same heresy in Book I of his *Invectives*.

Others, on the contrary, rushed to the opposite extreme against the enemies of Origen. They attributed Origenist heresies to those devoted to his works, even when they were Catholic.

Thus Epiphanius, Jerome, and Theophilus attributed Origenist heresies to Chrysostom and the monks. Under this pretext Theophilus declared the most savage war on the Nitrian monks, who had withdrawn from him because they did not approve his conduct. He even assembled against them an army of Anthropomorphite monks.

When they fled to Constantinople, Chrysostom, moved by Christian charity but preserving the order of the sacred canons, received them in order to act as their intercessor before Theophilus on account of their danger. He also informed Innocent I, the head of the universal Church, about the matter.

Tillemont notes this in volume XI, articles 66 and 67.

But Theophilus, who ought to have been moved by the pious and holy duty of such an upright bishop, was so far from yielding that, driven by fury, he turned against the intercessor himself.

Thus arose the great hatred against Chrysostom, continuing until his deposition from the throne of Constantinople, his dreadful exile, and his final death.

As for the monks themselves, Georgius of Alexandria and Palladius in the *Life of Chrysostom*, as well as Socrates, Sozomen, Sulpicius, and Isidore of Pelusium, commend them with one voice, although Jerome, deceived by Theophilus, denounces them.

Nor was Epiphanius alone in doing this. After Chrysostom’s deposition, Theophilus himself restored the monks living in Constantinople to the same communion and favor.

This is nearly Rosweydus’s account based on Castrius.

To Castrius must be added Godefridus Hermannus, who treats the matter more fully and clearly in the *Life of Chrysostom*, published under Menardus’s name, Book V, chapters II and III; after him, Tillemont, vol. XI, pp. 183, 185, 477, and 485.

We are compelled to yield to their opinion rather than to Baronius, whose authority prejudiced the case in A.D. 400, §1, and to Aloysius Lippomanus, vol. III of *The Lives of the Saints*, p. 144, where he says that he could scarcely be persuaded that the six anchorites attacked by Jerome were the very men mentioned in Rufinus’s book. Some of these, he says, had been disciples of Antony, others pupils of Basil and Nazianzen; all were distinguished by the uprightness of their lives, endowed with divine gifts, renowned even for miracles, and brought their lives to an excellent end [Col. 0247B].

Yet Lippomanus bestowed all these praises upon the monks of Rufinus, who are not different from those of Jerome.

### IV.

Let us now review the various editions of Rufinus’s work, which number twenty.

The very first edition appears to be one printed in extremely primitive type, without a title, divided into three parts and issued with an index at the beginning. It was printed at Ulm by Johann Zainer in folio, without a date.

The second edition, without the printer’s name, place, or year, contained five books in folio format and began with these words:

> “Here begins the preface of the blessed Jerome, presbyter, to the first book on the Life of the Holy Fathers.”

Then:

> “Blessed be God.”

Here, as in the preceding edition, Rufinus’s book is placed first.

Rosweydus thinks that this edition was produced before A.D. 1471, because Dionysius Carthusianus, who died in that year, recounts in article 51 of *The Four Last Things* the story of Macarius’s discovery of a skull belonging to a pagan priest, taking it from Book IV of the *Lives of the Fathers*, where it appears as Book IV in this first edition [Col. 0247C].

The third edition, identical to this one in every respect, begins:

> “Here begins the prologue.”

The fourth, similar to both, begins:

> “Prologue to the fruitful work.”

The fifth edition, without a title and divided into four parts, was printed at Nuremberg by Anton Koberger in A.D. 1478, in large folio. Its preface begins:

> “So that the occasion of the style observed in this work may not…”

As in the earlier editions, the *Lives of the Fathers* described by Rufinus appear first under Jerome’s name.

The following twelve editions faithfully reproduce the arrangement of this edition, namely:

**Sixth edition.** Likewise printed at Nuremberg by Anton Koberger in A.D. 1480, in smaller folio.

**Seventh edition.** Apparently German, without place or printer, A.D. 1483, in folio.

**Eighth edition.** Venice, printed by Octavianus Scotus of Modena, A.D. 1483, in quarto.

**Ninth edition.** Apparently German, with place and printer uncertain, A.D. 1485, in folio.

**Tenth edition.** Lyons, printed by Nicolaus Wolff of Lutrera for Jacobus Huguetanus, A.D. 1502, in quarto.

**Eleventh edition.** Lyons, printed by Jannot de Campis, 1507, in quarto.

**Twelfth edition.** Venice, printed by Bonetus Locatellus, 1508, in quarto.

**Thirteenth edition.** Lyons, printed by Stephanus Balam, 1509, in quarto.

**Fourteenth edition.** Lyons, printed by Jacobus Sachon, 1512, in quarto.

**Fifteenth edition.** Venice, printed by Nicolaus of Frankfurt, 1512, in quarto.

**Sixteenth edition.** Lyons, printed by Jacobus Miit, 1515, in quarto.

**Seventeenth edition.** Lyons, printed by Jacobus Marescal, 1526, in quarto.

Source/review notes: “Historia Eremitica” was mistranslated as “Ecclesiastical History” twice.; The Creed’s exclusion of the preposition “in” before “the holy Church” was reversed.; Du Pin’s bibliographical reference was misconstrued as a claim limited to the fifth century.

Edition XVIII is headed as follows: “The pious and most useful work for the Christian reader, by the most celebrated and most learned D. Jerome, interpreter of sacred letters, on the Lives of the Fathers, whose frequent reading softens even the sinner’s heart of stone and strongly incites him to zeal for our Religion.” Lyons, by Antoine Vincent, 1536, in quarto. Rosweyde wrote that this edition was produced one year later. Celsus Hugo Dissutus, in the dedicatory letter to Jean de Poupeto, Bishop of Chalon, which accompanies all the Lyons editions, says that, having used an older copy, he cleansed the work of so many blemishes that scarcely anyone could detect the traces of the ancient book.

Edition XIX, divided into five books, appeared under this title: “The Prototype of the Ancient Church, containing the Lives, deeds, and sayings of the holy friends of God of both sexes, partly by the author or compiler St. Jerome, and partly by various others.” Cologne, by Caspar Gennepaeus, 1547, in folio. The editor of this edition, Theodoric Loher, a Carthusian, testifies in his dedicatory letter to Cardinal Otto Truchsess, Bishop of Augsburg, that he had revised these Lives of the Fathers by collating eight or ten ancient and trustworthy manuscript copies and restoring them to their former integrity. He arranged the Lives in a new order, and counted Petronius among their authors.

Edition XX, which differs from the preceding one only in its title-page and dedicatory letter, is entitled as follows: “The Lives of the Holy Fathers of the ancient Catholic and Apostolic Church, containing the notable and admirable sayings and deeds of several distinguished friends of God of both sexes, partly by D. Jerome and partly by others, whom you may learn from the reverse page; received and approved by the Catholic Church more than 1,050 years ago.” Cologne, by Caspar Gennepaeus, 1548, in folio. Loher gives the following account of his work to Henry, Abbot of Wiblingen of the Order of St. Benedict:

“We have now cleansed the Lives of the Fathers of more than a thousand errors that were scattered throughout them, consulting at the same time the oldest and the most diverse copies: for many things have been restored, very many added, some removed, and finally everything examined so exactly that this great treasure, not merely renewed but wholly reborn, may deservedly be welcomed by all devout persons, though not without great labor.”

Edition XXI was produced at Alcalá by Juan Gracián, 1596, in quarto.

But enough now of the Latin editions of Rufinus’s History of the Lives of the Fathers, which, under another man’s name, were printed before Heribert Rosweyde. To make the value of a work recognized by nearly all nations shine forth more clearly, let us also list its translations into foreign languages.

After the Greek, Syriac, and Arabic translations, we encounter:

Italian I, divided into six books. Venice, by Antonio Bartholomaei, 1476, in folio.

Italian II, with illustrations, translated anew by Giovanni Mario Verdizzotti. Venice, by the Guerra press, 1589, in quarto.

French I, Lyons, 1486, cited in the English edition mentioned below.

French II, with illustrations, translated by an anonymous translator. Paris, by Jean Dupré, 1494, in folio.

French III, Paris, without indication of year or printer, in quarto.

French IV, with illustrations, translated by an anonymous translator. Paris, by Guillaume Chaudière, 1605, in quarto.

French V, translated by Jacques Gualtier. Paris, by Guillaume de La Noue, 1606, in octavo.

French VI, by Arnaud d’Andilly. Paris, by Pierre Petit, 1657, volume II, in quarto, fourth edition.

French VII, translated by Fossee, cited by Tillemont in the Life of St. Apollonius, volume X, page 36.

Flemish I. Ypres, by Peter Van Os, 1490, in small folio.

Flemish II. Delft, by Henry Eckert, 1498, in small folio.

Flemish III. Leiden, by Jan Seversoen, 1511, in small folio.

German, with illustrations, in folio.

English, with illustrations, translated by William Caxton. Westminster, by Wynkyn de Worde, 1495, from the edition printed at Lyons in 1486.

Such a great and varied number of editions and translations did not at all deter Rosweyde from preparing a new edition of Rufinus and of other works on the same subject, calling ancient manuscripts to his aid. These manuscripts, most of them Flemish, against whose authority he testifies in Prolegomenon XXIV, page 76, that he had measured Rufinus’s book, are the following:

1. Affligem.  
2. Aulne.  
3. Saint-Omer, inscribed under Rufinus’s name.  
4. Biburg.  
5. Bona Spes.  
6. Cambron.  
7. Greater Cambrai.  
8. Lesser Cambrai.  
9. The Carthusian manuscript near Brussels.  
10. Clairmarais.  
11. Saint Crispin.  
12. Florennes.  
13. Ingolstadt.  
14. Saint James of Lille.  
15. Greater Liessies.  
16. Lesser Liessies.  
17. Moret.  
18. Rebdorf.

Collated and revised with these outstanding aids, Rufinus’s work became part of the great corpus of the Lives of the Fathers, or Eremitic History, prepared through the care and labor of Rosweyde, under the auspices of Antoine de Vinghe, Abbot of Liessies of the Order of St. Benedict. It was published at Antwerp by the Plantin press in 1615, in folio, and soon afterward at Lyons in 1617. Moreover, those acquainted with the studies of the great Baronius informed the other great man, Cardinal Jacques de Péron, that Baronius had once considered undertaking this work. Indeed, Baronius himself explicitly hints that he would do so in his notes on 18 January.

But the finest and most complete of all the editions is the one that Rosweyde revised anew eight years later, after the first copies had already been dispersed. Here I shall reproduce its complete title:

*The Lives of the Fathers, concerning the life and sayings of the Elders, or Eremitic History, in ten books, restored to their original authors and former purity, and illustrated with notes, through the work and study of Heribert Rosweyde of Utrecht, theologian of the Society of Jesus. To this is added an Onomasticon of more difficult things and words, together with a variety of indexes, including a preaching index.*

Second edition, variously enlarged and illustrated.

Antwerp, from the Plantinian press, 1628, in folio.

What appears first in the ancient editions as Rufinus’s History constitutes Book II here. Book I is devoted entirely to the Lives written by Jerome and others. This same Book II, illustrated with learned prefaces and notes, begins on page 424 and ends on page 491. It consists of thirty-three chapters, besides a prologue and also an epilogue, in which the eight dangers that St. Petronius underwent are finally enumerated as he traveled barefoot through the Thebaid, Tabenna, Nitria, and the other deserts of Egypt. Their locations are shown in the map of the stations of the hermits, which Rosweyde admirably designed and engraved and placed before his work.

Something must now be said about the title of our work. Rufinus says in the prologue that it is the Life of the Egyptian monks. We read in Rosweyde’s Prolegomenon I, page 3, that most of the ancients called it *Lives of the Fathers*—and quite properly, certainly according to Vossius, *On the Vices of Speech*, Book VII, after the letter Z. Although this name also embraces the other works attached to our book, it indicated by antonomasia, and especially, the one Rufinian work that was first of all, then commonly attributed to Jerome and translated into Greek under his name, as we have seen from the words of Gelasius and Gennadius.

This is also clear from St. Benedict, who, recommending the reading of these works to his monks in chapter XLII of his Rule, orders that one person should read the *Lives of the Fathers*, evidently in accordance with Gennadius’s statement in chapter XLI of his Catalogue, where, speaking of these very Lives of Rufinus, he says: “The monks embrace them as a mirror and NORM of their profession.”

The same work also seems to be indicated by Cassiodorus’s words in *On Divine Literature*, chapter XXXII: “Read the LIVES OF THE FATHERS, the confessions of the faithful, and the sufferings of the martyrs.” Gregory of Tours, Book I of *The Life of the Fathers of His Age*, chapter XII, praises the *LIVES OF THE FATHERS* and the instruction of monks. Fulbert of Chartres, Letter LXXIX, writes: “I am sending you Cyprian, together with Porphyry, and the LIVES OF THE FATHERS together with the Psalter.”

Since these and other writers had commended the *Lives of the Fathers* with the words *Vitas Patrum* in the accusative case, it came about that these same Lives of Rufinus were inscribed not only in most of the books printed in antiquity but also in one of the ancient manuscript codices almost as though in the nominative case—or *ἀπτώτως* (“indeclinably”)—and in a single indeclinable expression, *Vitas Patrum*. Rosweyde discusses this matter in Prolegomenon I, page 8.

From what has been said we readily understand how great the authority of this book once was everywhere among the holiest men. Pope Gelasius even called it a work to be read publicly and free from error. St. Eucherius, Bishop of Lyons, referred to it in his letter *On the Praise of the Desert*, where he says:

“What need is there now to mention John and Macarius, and many others, whose manner of life, though in the deserts, has become a life in heaven?”

For, as Rosweyde observes in his notes on Eucherius, page 45, this book was then almost constantly in people’s hands. John appears in chapter I. Nor does Sidonius speak of anyone else in *Carmen* XVI, verses 99ff.:

“Now Elias, now John commands you to go,

now the two Macarii, and now Paphnutius their heir,

now Or, now Ammon.”

All of these are mentioned in Rufinus’s book. Moreover, what is read in the Roman Martyrology on 28 March concerning St. John the Hermit derives from Rufinus.

In Prolegomenon V, page 29, Rosweyde also ascribes to Rufinus Book III of the *Lives of the Fathers*, appended to the preceding book and attributed by the printed editions to Jerome. Yet the good and learned man admits that he has no assistance from the manuscripts in discovering its author, apart from similarity of style and a certain allusion between these words of the prologue to Book II—“so that there should be no doubt that the world still stands by their merits”—and the beginning of the prologue to Book III—“Who could doubt that the world truly stands by the merits of the saints?”

Following Rosweyde, Vossius, *On Latin Historians*, Book II, chapter XI, likewise attributes this later book to Rufinus, declaring that this can be recognized from its diction. But others can easily judge otherwise. It is unnecessary to pursue the matter, since the very allusion discovered by Rosweyde shows that this later book was composed at a later date.

Book II, wholly one, complete, and finished, embraces the entire journey of St. Petronius through the deserts of Egypt. Jerome’s words in his letter to Ctesiphon indicate this one book: he wrote a BOOK—not books—as though about monks. All those whom he names there are in this Book II; none is in the third.

Rosweyde observes in his notes, page 534, that the prologue of Book III derives from the prefaces of Palladius. From this very fact it becomes clear that it appeared after the history of Palladius—that is, after A.D. 420—and therefore after Rufinus, who had already long been dead.

Tillemont, in the *Life of St. Jerome*, article 125, volume XII, page 306, says that the one sufficient proof that Book III was composed long after Rufinus is that chapter CLXIII, page 524, records the death of St. Arsenius, which, as he demonstrates in his *Life*, volume XIV, article 10, page 697, cannot be placed before A.D. 443. Therefore this book has no connection with Rufinus.

## CHAPTER XIV

I. Rufinus writes a commentary on the Apostles’ Creed. Its contents are briefly reviewed. II. Testimonies of both ancient and modern writers are adduced. III. Various editions of this Commentary.

### I

Gennadius, in chapter XVII of his *Catalogue*, counts among Rufinus’s other labors, completed through his own work—or rather through the grace and gift of God—an explanation of the Creed. He testifies that so magnificent a testimony concerning it was in circulation that, by comparison with it, others were scarcely believed to have written an exposition at all.

The reason is that our predecessors at one time considered it a work of the martyr Cyprian and at another of Jerome—both judgments plainly mistaken, as is sufficiently shown by the single testimony of Gennadius.

A certain Laurentius, a bishop of uncertain see, whom Rufinus immediately at the threshold calls “the most faithful Pope,” and whose love and devotion toward the divine Scriptures he praises elsewhere, had bound Rufinus by letter, invoking the mysteries of Christ’s sacraments, to compose something concerning the faith according to the tradition and meaning of the Creed.

I suspect that this Laurentius was one of the bishops assigned to the metropolitan church of Aquileia, perhaps the bishop of Concordia, Rufinus’s native city, whose see is vacant in Ughelli before the sixth century. Certainly, whenever Rufinus introduces the discipline of the Aquileian Church, he seems, by using the plural number, to make it Laurentius’s as well as his own.

I demonstrate this from Rufinus’s words:

“These two expressions are found in the Creed of the Roman Church. It is agreed that among US they were added on account of the heresy of Sabellius, namely that which among OUR PEOPLE is called Patripassianism.”

And shortly afterward:

“Therefore, so that such impiety concerning the Father might be excluded, OUR ELDERS seem to have added these words”—that is, the elders of Rufinus and Laurentius, if my conjecture is sound.

Elsewhere he says:

“And therefore OUR CHURCH teaches the faith of the Creed with sufficient caution.”

I scarcely think that these statements can always be referred to Rufinus alone, but rather also to Laurentius, the bishop whom he addresses.

Let us now return to the matter at hand. Rufinus, after first offering an apology that reveals his exceptional modesty, begins the work itself. Yet he does not wish to be regarded as qualified to write, nor does he fail to recognize how dangerous it is to commit a weak and limited intellect to the judgments of many. In these words he may perhaps allude to the hostility recently stirred up against him by Jerome’s associates.

Nevertheless, relying on the prayers of Bishop Laurentius—which, he asks, may obtain from God assistance in meeting the necessity imposed by the request—he declares that he will attempt to speak out of reverence for obedience rather than presumption concerning his own abilities. The things he is about to say seem suitable not so much for the exercises of the perfect as for the hearing of little children in Christ and beginners.

He testifies that some ecclesiastical writers had produced brief and devout works on the Creed, including Photinus, Bishop of Sirmium. But Photinus had done so not to explain to his hearers the account of the true faith, but simply to twist the words into support for a heretical doctrine.

Rufinus, for his part, says that he will expound the simplicity of the Creed in the words of the Apostle, or complete what appears to have been omitted by earlier writers.

He says that the Creed of the Faith was composed by the Apostles, who were united as one and filled with the Holy Spirit, as a norm for future preaching and a rule to be given to believers. In this matter he appeals to the universal tradition of all the Churches:

“This tradition was given to the Churches.”

“Our elders transmit it.”

Du Pin, in the fifth-century volume of his *Bibliotheca*, asserted that Rufinus was the first and only one to make the Apostles authors of the Creed. For this he is rightly charged with gross error by Matthieu Petitdidier, *Animadversions*, volume I, page 96.

For Rufinus, *symbolum* means in Greek “a contribution,” and in Latin “a sign” or “token,” because the Apostles contributed into one body what each had understood, and because they handed over this token—not to be written on little sheets or parchments, but to be sought in the hearts of believers—by which the one who truly preached Christ according to the Apostles’ rules could be recognized.

This was especially necessary at a time when many wandering Jews pretended to be Apostles of Christ and went out to preach for the sake of some profit or to fill their bellies. They named Christ, indeed, but did not proclaim him according to the complete line of the traditions.

Rufinus illustrates this by an example drawn from military service, where a comrade is distinguished from an enemy by a password or military token.

This Apostolic Creed, which he calls a “shortened word” and a “brief discourse,” I shall set out together with the Aquileian Creed, since Rufinus explains both in parallel.

### I. The Ancient Apostolic Creed

I believe in God the Father almighty, and in Christ Jesus, his only Son, our Lord, who was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary, was crucified under Pontius Pilate, and was buried; he descended to the underworld. On the third day he rose from the dead. He ascended into heaven. He sits at the right hand of the Father. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead. And in the Holy Spirit. The holy Church; the remission of sins; the resurrection of the flesh.

### II. The Aquileian Creed

I believe in God the almighty Father, invisible and impassible, and in Christ Jesus, his only Son, our Lord, who was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary, was crucified under Pontius Pilate, and was buried; he descended to the underworld. On the third day he rose from the dead. He ascended into heaven. He sits at the right hand of the Father. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead. And in the Holy Spirit. The holy Church. The remission of sins. The resurrection of THIS flesh.

Thus far I have set out both Creeds somewhat more accurately than they appear in the table of the four ancient Creeds before the first volume of the Dapintian *Bibliotheca*. In the Lyons edition, the word “Catholic” has crept in after “Church.” It is absent from the other editions, nor does Rufinus explain it.

The same interpreter, Rufinus, explains each article against heretics and pagans with such abundance and excellence of profound and genuine doctrine that nothing more worthy of a Christian teacher and theologian could be conceived.

He observes that in various Churches certain words are found added to the opening phrase, “I believe in God the almighty Father.” Yet, he says, this was not found in the Church of the city of Rome, which he thinks happened for the following reason: no heresy had originated there, and an ancient custom was preserved there, namely that those who were about to receive the grace of baptism should publicly recite the Creed—that is, with the people of the faithful listening.

For this reason, public recitation did not allow any addition. In other places, however, certain words appear to have been added on account of various heretics, so that the sense of novel doctrine might be excluded.

He immediately adds:

“Nevertheless, we follow the order that we received in the Aquileian Church through the grace of the washing.”

This alone ought to have warned the first editors of this little work not to attribute it either to Cyprian or to Jerome, neither of whom received the grace of baptism in the Aquileian Church.

He explains the order of the Aquileian Church as follows:

“To these words—‘the almighty Father’—are added ‘invisible and impassible.’ It must be understood that these two expressions are not found in the Creed of the Roman Church. It is agreed, however, that among us they were added on account of the heresy of Sabellius, namely that which our people call Patripassianism: the heresy that says either that the Father himself was born from the Virgin and became visible, or that he suffered in the flesh.

“Therefore, so that such impiety might be excluded, our elders seem to have added these words concerning the Father and to have called the Father invisible and impassible. For it is agreed that the Son, not the Father, was incarnate and born from flesh, and that through the birth of flesh the Son became visible and passible.”

He observes that almost all the Eastern Churches transmit the opening articles in the following form:

“I believe in one God, the almighty Father, and in Christ Jesus, his only Son, our Lord.”

The word “one” refers not to number but to universality: he is called one because there is no other.

He briefly explains what the terms “God” and “Father” indicate. He unfolds the ineffable mystery of the Son’s divine generation from the Father, but declares that God is to be believed as the Father of the one Son of God, our Lord, not subjected to investigation.

After saying much about the only Son of God, the Trinity, and the Virgin Mother, he rises against the taunts of the pagans, who mock us when they hear the Virgin’s childbirth proclaimed. After answering them according to their own way of thinking, he adds:

“Consider nothing impossible where the power of the Most High was present. Think nothing of human frailty where the fullness of divinity was present.”

He notes that neither the Roman nor the Eastern Creed contains the article “he descended to the underworld,” although the force of the expression is contained in the statement that he was buried. He explains this article, and the one that follows—“on the third day he rose from the dead”—at length and with great learning from the divine Scriptures.

He says that “to judge the living and the dead” does not mean that some living and others dead will come to judgment, but that he will judge souls and bodies together. By “the living” he means souls, and by “the dead” bodies.

In the commemoration of the Holy Spirit, he teaches that the mystery of the Trinity is completed. He summarizes the distinction of persons briefly, and points out that, where the Faith is ordered concerning divinity, it says “in God the Father,” “in Christ his Son,” and “in the Holy Spirit.”

In the other clauses, where the subject is not divinity but creatures and mysteries, the preposition “in” is not added. Thus one does not say “in the holy Church”; rather, the holy Church is to be believed not as God, but as the Church gathered by God. Likewise, one says “the remission,” not “in the remission,” and “the resurrection,” not “in the resurrection of the flesh.”

Thus, by the preposition “in,” the Creator is distinguished from creatures and divine things are separated from human things.

At this point, on the occasion of discussing the Scriptures, he lists the books that, according to the tradition of the elders, are believed to have been inspired by the Holy Spirit and handed down to the Churches of Christ. He says that he is setting them out in an evident number, as we have received them from the records of the Fathers.

He divides these books into two classes, Canonical and Ecclesiastical, arranged here by me.

## CLASS I. Canonical Books

### I. Old Testament

1. Genesis.  
2. Exodus.  
3. Leviticus.  
4. Numbers.  
5. Deuteronomy.  
6. Joshua.  
7. Judges, together with Ruth.  
8. Four Books of Kingdoms, which the Hebrews count as two.  
9. Chronicles, otherwise called the Book of Days.  
10. Two Books of Ezra.  
11. Esther.  
12. Isaiah.  
13. Jeremiah.  
14. Ezekiel.  
15. Daniel.  
16. One Book of the Twelve Prophets.  
17. Job.  
18. The Psalms of David.  
19. Proverbs.  
20. Ecclesiastes of Solomon.  
21. The Song of Songs.

### II. New Testament

1. Matthew.  
2. Mark.  
3. Luke. The four Gospels.  
4. John.  
5. The Acts of the Apostles by Luke.  
6. Fourteen Epistles of Paul.  
7. Two Epistles of Peter.  
8. One of James.  
9. One of Jude.  
10. Three of John.  
11. The Apocalypse of John.

Rufinus concludes this catalogue of the Scriptures as follows:

“These are the books that the Fathers enclosed within the canon, and from which they wished the assertions of our faith to be established. Yet it must be understood that there are other books that are canonical, but which our elders called Ecclesiastical. These are the following.”

## CLASS II. Ecclesiastical Books

### I. Old Testament

1. The Wisdom of Solomon.  
2. The Wisdom of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus.  
3. Tobit.  
4. Judith.  
5. The Books of the Maccabees.

### II. New Testament

1. The little book called *The Shepherd*, or of Hermas.  
2. The other, called *The Two Ways*, or *The Judgment of Peter*.

Thus, together with the most learned Cotelerius, in his *Judgment concerning the Shepherd of Hermas*, page 73, we think that these last two books should be distinguished. In Barrei’s edition, “Hermes” is incorrectly read for “Hermas.”

Rufinus writes that our elders wished these books to be read in the Churches, but did not wish them to be brought forward as authorities for confirming the Faith.

In compiling this catalogue, he followed the canon of the Hebrews, as it is known that other Fathers before him had also done. Nevertheless, in Rufinus’s own age the divine authority of these books of the second class of the Old Testament was acknowledged and accepted by the universal Church.

For the Third Council of Carthage, canon 47; the African Church’s code, chapter XXIV; Innocent I, Letter II to Exsuperius of Toulouse; and Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, Book II, chapter VIII, §13—excepting *The Shepherd* and *The Judgment of Peter*—all counted these books among the canonical books.

This refutes Andreas Rivet, who, after calling Rufinus’s work learned by universal agreement and most worthy of reading, immediately added in his *Pseudocriticus*, Book II, chapter XV:

“Unless what displeases the Papists is that, together with Jerome, he carefully distinguishes the canonical books from the noncanonical.”

Yet in that same age the authority of the Church distinguished them more correctly—something that heretics and Rivet by no means like.

It should nevertheless be noted that Rufinus assigns the Epistle to the Hebrews to Paul among the fourteen canonical epistles; otherwise there would be only thirteen.

Rufinus says that the remaining Scriptures, omitted from these two classes, are counted among the apocrypha, which they did not wish to be read in the Churches.

He says that the holy Church is the Church that preserves Christ’s faith intact and has neither spot nor wrinkle, in order to distinguish it from the Churches of the heretics, which are not free from the spot and wrinkle of unbelief.

He then appends the following list of heretics—not all of them, but those who gathered Churches of this kind and did not make them holy:

1. Marcion.  
2. Valentinus.  
3. Ebion.  
4. Mani.  
5. Paul of Samosata.  
6. Photinus.  
7. Arius.  
8. Eunomius.  
9. Donatus.  
10. Novatus.

In expounding the article concerning the resurrection of the flesh, Rufinus has much to say against the Valentinians, Manichaeans, and unbelievers, and perhaps also against objections made to him by Jerome—whom, however, he does not name—concerning this same article.

For what he had already said on his own behalf in Book II of his *Apology* about the distinctive discipline of the Aquileian Church, he repeats here: in the article on the resurrection of the flesh, that Church adds the pronoun “this” in order to show that true, natural, human, and proper flesh will be assumed.

“Therefore,” he says, “our Church”—that is, the Aquileian Church—“teaches the faith of the Creed with sufficient caution. For where the other Churches transmit ‘the resurrection of the flesh,’ it has transmitted, by adding one pronoun, ‘the resurrection of THIS flesh.’

“Without doubt, this means the flesh possessed by the person who makes the profession, with the sign of the cross placed upon his forehead, so that each of the faithful may know that his flesh, if he keeps it pure from sin, will become a vessel of honor, useful to the Lord and prepared for every good work.”

After a few remarks that he says he offers merely as a warning, he admits that he has explained this article in order to make his faith manifest:

“These things have been said as proof of our profession, and we confess in the Creed the resurrection of THIS flesh.”

Soon afterward, he brings the entire exposition to a close with a brief and genuinely pious summary, speaking without ambiguity according to the proper rule of faith concerning the article of eternal life.

Together with the additions by which Rufinus above condemns the doctrines of the heretics, these statements show that his faith is wholly Catholic. Nothing more modest, nothing more sincere, could reasonably have been expected from so great a man.

### II

Let us now hear Cassian’s distinguished testimony concerning this work of Rufinus, from Book VII of *On the Incarnation*, chapter XXVII:

“Rufinus also, a man of Christian philosophy and no negligible member of the body of ecclesiastical teachers, testifies in this way concerning the Lord’s birth in his exposition of the Creed: ‘For the Son of God,’ he says, ‘is born from a Virgin, not joined principally to flesh alone, but generated with a soul mediating between flesh and God.’”

Did he not clearly testify that God was born from a human being?

What Cassian cites from Rufinus appears on page 177 of Barrei’s edition. The same Cassian had stated in chapter XXIV that he would append the sayings of a few holy men and distinguished priests so that, as he says, “what we have already approved by the authority of sacred testimonies may also be strengthened by the faith of the present age.”

These are the Latin Fathers:

1. Hilary.  
2. Ambrose.  
3. Jerome.  
4. Rufinus.  
5. Augustine.

Afterward he adduces the Greeks.

Among more recent writers, Jacques Pamelius gives this work, which he published among the works of Cyprian, first place in the very beautiful confirmation of the articles of the faith from the prophets and Scriptures of both Testaments.

Andreas Saussay, in *The Glory of St. Andrew the Apostle*, Book II, chapter V, page 130, says:

“Rufinus, a priest of Aquileia, a man highly distinguished in learning and eloquence, interpreted this Creed so successfully that he himself was thought to be Cyprian. Hence his lucid exposition is still reckoned among Cyprian’s works.”

Next comes Jean-Baptiste Cotelier, *Monuments of the Greek Church*, volume III, page 677. He notes that he thinks Justin Martyr, in his *Dialogue with Trypho*, and Cyril of Jerusalem, in Catechesis XIII, just as Rufinus in his exposition of the Creed, page 181 of Barrei’s edition, interpreted the passage of Hosea, chapter X, verse 6, as applicable to Herod.

Indeed, Augustin Touttée, who prepared a new edition of the works of St. Cyril, declares in his notes on that Catechesis, pages 186, 193, and 200, that Rufinus derived his material from there.

Why should he not have done so, since he had spent so long among the writings of the Greeks, especially those of Cyril, whom he knew and whose Church’s priest he was?

He also refers to him generally when he says that ecclesiastical writers had produced certain brief and devout works on the Creed. Cyril had indeed written something brief about the Creed in the Catechesis mentioned above.

James Ussher, in his *Dissertation on the Creed of the Roman Church*, page 7, observes that Venantius Fortunatus followed Rufinus in his own exposition of the Creed. This happened because Fortunatus, like Rufinus, had received the grace of baptism in the Aquileian Church, as I shall show in its proper place.

Gerardus Johannes Vossius, Book VII of *On the Vices of Speech*, volume V of his works, page 380, column 2, noted that the word *nubor* occurs in this work of Rufinus, evidently taken from popular speech. Francis Sanctius, in *Minerva*, Book III, chapter III, §258, page 393 of Perizonius’s third edition, notes that Plautus used the same word.

The same Vossius, Book VIII, page 389, also observes that Rufinus says *Actus Apostolicos* and *Actibus Apostolicis*, whereas they are otherwise called *Acta* and *Actis*.

Gebhard Elmenhorst, in his notes on Arnobius, cites several passages from Rufinus’s work that correspond to Arnobius, in Book II, page 64 of the Leiden edition of 1651.

### III.

I think the first edition of this *Exposition* was the one cited by John Fell in his notes to the appendix of the works of Saint Cyprian, first printed at Oxford from the Sheldonian Theatre in 1682, in folio, and subsequently printed at Amsterdam and Bremen. Fell appended Rufinus’s exposition to that appendix because others had appended it as well.

The edition I mentioned appeared separately at the very beginnings of the printing art, bearing this title: *Exposition of Saint Jerome on the Apostles’ Creed, addressed to Pope Laurence*.
