Oxford, 1468, in quarto, without the printer’s name. Michael Maittaire saw this edition and reviewed it in his *Annals of Typography*, vol. I, p. 63, where he says that Thomas Barlow had added the following note in his own hand to his copy: “This Exposition is Rufinus’s, not Jerome’s.”

In Vatican manuscript 343, fol. 1, the same work likewise bears Jerome’s name. This false inscription misled M. Antonio Sabellico into thinking that Jerome had been baptized at Aquileia, whereas the author of the *Exposition*, Rufinus, says that he himself was baptized there. I quote Sabellico’s words from book III of *On the Antiquity of Aquileia*:

> Jerome himself testifies in the *Exposition of the Creed* that he was marked by the laver of baptism at Aquileia. From this it follows that we must either confess that he was born in that city, or at any rate not far from it—for it is plainly evident, even from this very fact, that he belonged to the parish of Aquileia.

Our countrymen willingly adopted this error of Sabellico, so highly flattering to their native Church, and above all Candidus, in book II of his *Commentaries*, near the end. Henry Palladius adds, rather weakly, in book IX: “Many have perhaps persuaded themselves of this, not without some plausible argument.”

But come now, gentlemen: Jerome plainly declares once and again that he put on at Rome, not at Aquileia, the white garment customarily given at baptism. His Letters XIV, otherwise LVII, and XVI, otherwise LVIII, addressed to Damasus, should be consulted.

This error, however, whose source was the corrupt inscription of the *Exposition on the Creed* just mentioned, was soon removed by the first edition of the first volume of Saint Jerome’s Letters. That edition was printed at Rome two years after the Oxford edition, in the house of Peter de Maximis near the Field of Flora, under the supervision of the masters Conrad Sweynheim and Arnold Pannartz, in 1470, in folio. In that volume the *Exposition on the Creed* appears attributed not to Jerome but to Rufinus, its legitimate author.

Labbe, in the *Lesser Library*, Supplement IX, p. 340, mistakenly believed that this volume contained all of Rufinus’s works, and Cave was likewise drawn into the error, although the volume contains nothing from Rufinus’s writings except the exposition of the Creed placed at its beginning.

The German manuscript, at the end of the works of Saint Cyprian, p. 198 of Baluze’s royal edition of 1726, in folio, likewise attributes it to Rufinus in these words: “The Exposition of the Creed of Saint Rufinus.”

Erasmus, who first inserted this offspring of Rufinus among the works of Saint Cyprian, printed at Basel by Froben in 1519, 1525, and 1530, and in the Hervagian press in 1540, all in folio, writes of it in a letter to Cardinal Laurence Pucci:

> The Creed of the Faith, which in both printed and manuscript volumes bears the title of Cyprian, is circulated among the works of Saint Jerome under the name of Rufinus.

In his notes after the letter he adds:

> The style sufficiently proves that this work is not Cyprian’s; and among the works of Jerome it is circulated under the name of Rufinus. Its phrasing is not unlike Rufinus’s phrasing, and among his works Gennadius speaks magnificently of the Creed, saying that it was so excellently expounded that the others seem to have spoken only in reference to him.

The index likewise contains the following entry:

> The exposition of the Creed is not Cyprian’s, since it lists later heretics.

In the *Censure of the Works of Origen* concerning the Basel editions, where Erasmus complains about scribes, he attributes this crime to them:

> They transferred the Creed explained by Rufinus under Cyprian’s name; but they changed so many things that the work itself cries out that this was done not by accident but deliberately.

In this way Erasmus erased what he had earlier written in his *Declarations on the Censures of the Faculty of Paris*, believing the work to be Cyprian’s offspring, vol. IX of the first edition of his works, p. 701:

> It is to be hoped that in a new edition of this most excellent Explanation, all the copies previously printed under the names of Cyprian, Jerome, and Rufinus will be carefully collated with the manuscripts and corrected, and that the text will be divided into chapters, so that the articles of the Creed—or “discourses,” as Rufinus calls them—may not indiscriminately and confusedly merge with the exposition itself, as they did in the earliest editions.

Paolo Manuzio made the best distinction of all in his Roman edition of the works of Saint Cyprian, published in 1563, in folio, p. 381. The individual articles should be set out separately and displayed before each portion of the exposition in a different type, in the middle of the page, before the eyes of readers.

The following editions should be added to those already cited: the Lyons edition, printed by Sebastian Gryphius with the works of Saint Cyprian in 1537, in octavo, vol. II, p. 154; Jacobus Pamelius’s edition with the same works, Antwerp, printed by John Steelsius, 1568, in folio; Mariano Victorio’s edition with the works of Saint Jerome, Rome, at the press of the Roman People, 1576, vol. IX, p. 108; and finally René Laurent de La Barre’s edition, which published the same *Explanation of the Creed* together with other works of Rufinus, Paris, by Michel Sonnius, 1580, p. 169.

## CHAPTER XV

I. The Paschal Canon of Anatolius of Alexandria, translated into Latin by Rufinus.  
II. All his letters lost.  
III. He translated some works from Latin into Greek.

### I.

Aegidius Bucherius was the first to publish, from an old manuscript, the *Paschal Canon* of Anatolius of Alexandria, bishop of Laodicea, in his *Commentary on the Doctrine of Time*, p. 439. He says on p. 450 that everyone likewise attributes its Latin translation to Rufinus, that is, as something to be appended to his Latin version of Eusebius’s *History*. Rufinus translated Eusebius’s *History* into Latin and also interpolated it. See James Ussher’s *Syntagma on the Seventy Interpreters*, chapter V, p. 50, where he cites a passage interpolated in book VI, chapter XIII.

Eusebius praises this nineteen-year canon in book VII, chapter XXVI of his *History*. Bede also praises it at the beginning of his *Letter on the Equinox*, which Peter Francis Chifflet published in a more correct form in his *Dissertation on Bede*, chapter III. Bede also praises it in chapters IV and XXXIII of *On the Reckoning of Time*. Then Colman, bishop of the Scots, does so in Bede’s *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, book III, chapter XXV.

John George Herwart, in chapter CCXXXVI of his *New Chronology*, derives the beginning of this Anatolian Canon from the common year 277 of Christ, the second year of the Emperor Probus. Bucherius, however, argues that it should be dated from the preceding year, 276.

### II.

Let this suffice concerning the sincere and genuine works of Rufinus that survive for us. For as to the many letters exhorting to the fear of God, mentioned in chapter VII of Gennadius’s *Catalogue*, we scarcely dare hope that, after the general silence of so many centuries, they may still be lurking somewhere among bookworms and moths.

“Among these,” says Gennadius, “those he addressed to Proba are preeminent.”

This was Anicia Falconia Proba, wife of Sextus Petronius Probus, outstanding above all the women of the Roman Empire alike in birth and virtue. John Chrysostom writes to her in Letter 168. Jerome also praises her with extraordinary and extensive commendation in Letter XCVII, otherwise VIII, *On the Preservation of Virginity*, addressed to the virgin Demetrias, daughter of Juliana and granddaughter of Proba. I shall attach a fragment of his praise here:

> That Proba, more illustrious in name than all dignities and the whole nobility of the Roman world—whose holiness and goodness poured out upon all peoples was revered even among the barbarians—was not exhausted by the ordinary consulships of her three sons, Probinus, Olybrius, and Probus. And now, when everything has been burned and plundered and the city is held captive, she is said to be selling her possessions and making friends for herself from the Mammon of iniquity, so that they may receive her into eternal dwellings; thus every rank of ecclesiastical ministry, and the empty names of monks, may blush to purchase estates while such nobility is selling them.

Jerome wrote this in A.D. 414, after Rome had long before been plundered by Alaric, and therefore after Rufinus’s death, as we shall say below.

Rufinus, therefore, was connected with so great a heroine, just as were John Chrysostom and Jerome, men of the greatest holiness. I have also said something about Proba in book II, chapter IV, § 3, of my *Antiquities of Horta*.

### III.

Jerome addresses Rufinus in these words in book III of his *Apology*, p. 468:

> You also translate Latin books into Greek. Will you forbid us to give foreign works to our own people?

We do not know which books Rufinus translated from Latin into Greek. This statement, however, sufficiently refutes Humphrey Hody, who says in book I, chapter IX, § 3, p. 51 of *On the Original Texts of the Bible*, that it is clear that Rufinus was not very skilled in Greek literature and did not understand what τοῦ πάνυ meant—Rufinus, that is, who lived for about thirty years among the most learned Greeks and thereafter presented the Latins with the greater part of the Greek library, as Gennadius says in chapter XVII of his *Catalogue*.

## CHAPTER XVI

I. Whether Rufinus was the Latin translator of the works of Flavius Josephus.  
II. Various matters concerning the ancient Milanese manuscript of Josephus.  
III. Whether Jerome and Ambrose translated Josephus into Latin. *Hegesippus* is Josephus’s *Jewish War* abridged into Latin by Ambrose.  
IV. The comparison by Frederick Gronovius of the phrases of Ambrose and Hegesippus approved and defended.  
V. Josephus’s translation is denied to Rufinus.

### I.

I now come to works by other authors attributed to Rufinus. The foremost place is occupied by the complete works of Flavius Josephus, whose ancient translation from Greek into Latin commonly bears Rufinus’s name as author.

Philippus Labbe has no doubt about this, in his notes to Bellarmine’s *Catalogue*, vol. II, p. 308, and after him Louis Dupin, vol. III of the *Library*. Hence Rufinus, as though he were Josephus’s certain and undisputed translator, is often savagely beaten by imperious critics such as Erasmus, Scaliger, Casaubon, and others.

Caspar Barthius is milder and more cautious in his *Adversaria*, book XLIV, chapter XXIII, at the end, where he remains uncertain whether Rufinus should be recognized in Josephus. In his commentary on Claudian, p. 1105, he writes:

> The translator of Josephus, who does not always bear the name of Rufinus, yet in many respects is not unworthy of him.

Vossius, speaking of Rufinus in book II, chapter XI of *On Latin Historians*, committed the following to memory:

> Among other works that Gennadius—and Honor­ius after him—mention, he translated the *Recognitions of Clement of Rome* and Flavius Josephus into Latin.

After Gennadius’s testimony, there is no reason for us to doubt the matter of Clement’s *Recognitions*. Yet Gennadius and Honorius are entirely silent about Josephus, at least specifically, unless we say that Gennadius speaks generally when he states that Rufinus presented the Latins with the greater part of the Greek libraries.

But he immediately explains this general statement by a particular enumeration: Basil’s works and what follows—among which Josephus would not have been omitted if he had belonged to them.

Among the ancients, the only writer who speaks of this is Cassiodorus, a writer of the beginning of the sixth century. He is indeed a sufficiently substantial witness, provided only that he made Rufinus Josephus’s translator in clear and explicit words.

Yet Cassiodorus is altogether ambiguous. He speaks only of the seven books of the captivity, or Jewish War, and not of the other books of the *Jewish Antiquities*, which he says he arranged to have translated into Latin by his friends at great labor, since they had not yet been translated into Latin by anyone.

His words concerning the seven books just mentioned are found in chapter XVII of *On the Institution of Divine Literature*:

> Josephus also composed seven other books of the captivity of the Jews with marvelous brilliance. Some attribute their translation to Jerome, some to Ambrose, and some to Rufinus. When it is attributed to such men, the extraordinary merits of its diction are fully revealed.

These words show the reputation Rufinus enjoyed. Let us investigate the reasons why the translation was attributed to each of them.

First, as far as Rufinus is concerned, he was widely celebrated for all his other translations. Thus the translation of Josephus could easily have been attributed to him as well.

### II.

For a long time a rumor has circulated that in the Ambrosian Library the autograph of Rufinus himself—or at least a very ancient copy—written on Egyptian papyrus, is preserved.

The first person I have found who mentioned it, at the beginning of the sixteenth century, is Ponticus Virunius, in his *Life of Manuel Chrysoloras*, before his *Hasty Declarations*—as he calls them—on the *Erotemata* abridged by Guarino, published at Ferrara by John Mazochus in 1509, in octavo.

It is worth hearing Ponticus’s astonishing judgment concerning this translation of Josephus’s work. He asserts that it was written around A.D. 350 and transcribed by Jerome. His words are these:

> There exists at Saint Ambrose’s in Milan an original book of Rufinus, said to be in Saint Jerome’s own hand, in a leaden chest, in poor condition—namely, badly preserved, if I may judge correctly—written on papyrus or in ancient Lombard characters [the wording is corrupt]. It is about 1,150 years old, or thereabouts; I, who am not ignorant of those forms of writing, turned over many pages before I could recognize anything.

Thus Ponticus Virunius. Concerning this man and his many writings, I have published several observations in the *Journal of Italian Scholars*, vol. XXIV, p. 245.

According to Virunius’s judgment, Jerome in the middle of the fourth century used characters that were not seen among us until the sixth century. For it was then that the Lombards entered Italy.

But let us leave these assertions to Ponticus, who also says that he saw in Ravenna papyrus tablets made under the Emperor Hadrian. Nor was he content to make these claims: he testifies that the Corcyraeans—or Phaeacians—had recently brought forth at Venice a privilege of two thousand years, written in golden letters and in Alexander the Great’s own hand. The senators, he says, bared their heads before it and granted still greater privileges.

Ponticus was certainly a remarkable man, but he indulged his divinations extraordinarily and was easily carried away by the ravings of his own ingenuity. Such men are never lacking.

Peter Paul Bosca, in book I of *On the Origin and State of the Ambrosian Library*, p. 10, relates that the Milanese manuscript was written not by Jerome but by Rufinus, 1,300 years ago. In assigning its date, he therefore comes close to Virunius.

Moreover, from John Peter Puricellus, in his *Nazarene Dissertation*, chapter LXIV, § 35, p. 372, we learn that he conjectures—by no foolish argument—that the autograph was brought to the people of Insubria by Attila after the destruction of Aquileia.

Good luck to those who divine so confidently and so successfully!

Jean Mabillon, who handled the manuscript and was exceptionally perceptive and experienced in judging such antiquities, testifies in the *Museum Italicum*, vol. I, p. 12, that it was written 1,100 years earlier, not long after Rufinus’s age. He too assigns the book to Rufinus and says that it contains several books of Flavius Josephus’s *Jewish Antiquities*, translated by Rufinus.

Of the form of the letters he judges as follows:

> The writing of the manuscript is not square but smaller, such as prevailed in the age of Justinian, and almost resembles the form that we reproduced from the Ravenna document in book V of *On Diplomatic Affairs*.

Thus Mabillon.

The manuscript consists of fragments of books VI, VII, VIII, IX, and X of the *Jewish Antiquities*, badly arranged by an incompetent binder. The distinguished scholar could not compare the manuscript with the published version of Josephus, because that edition was not available to him.

Cave regrets that this was not done in his discussion of Rufinus under A.D. 390. But I have been informed that the manuscript does not differ from the printed editions. Moreover, Rufinus’s name appears nowhere in it.

Why should it appear, if the work is not Rufinus’s?

Cassiodorus says that Rufinus was considered by some to be the translator of the books of the *Jewish War*, but he does not say this of these books of the *Jewish Antiquities*. For the latter, the Senator testifies that he arranged for his friends to translate them because they were read only in Greek.

I bring here Cassiodorus’s words from the same chapter XVII of *On the Institution of Divine Literature* cited above:

> This Josephus, however, concerning the *Jewish Antiquities*, because it is exceedingly subtle and complex, we caused to be translated into Latin by our friends, at great labor, in twenty-two books.

Let us see who these friends were, whose assistance Cassiodorus employed in giving Greek writings to the Latin world. In the *Institution* already cited, I find only three named by him. They are:

#### 1. Epiphanius Scholasticus

At the request of Cassiodorus, Epiphanius translated into Latin the *Encyclical* written in defense of the Council of Chalcedon. Cassiodorus says in chapter XVII of the work cited:

> We caused this document to be translated from Greek into Latin by the very eloquent man Epiphanius.

It appears in Labbe’s *Councils*, vol. IV, p. 891; Baluze published its corrections in his *New Collection of Councils*, p. 1400.

Cassiodorus also states, in chapters V and VIII, that Epiphanius translated for him Didymus’s *Expositions of Solomon’s Proverbs* and the *Seven Catholic Epistles*.

In addition, Epiphanius translated the histories of Sozomen, Socrates, and Theodoret and distributed them into twelve books. After these had been abridged, the Senator composed his *Tripartite History*. Consult its preface.

#### 2. Bellator the Presbyter

Bellator rendered Origen’s *Homilies on Ezra* into Latin, likewise at Cassiodorus’s request, as the same witness reports in chapter VII.

#### 3. Mutianus

Mutianus translated into Latin thirty-four homilies of John Chrysostom on the Epistle to the Hebrews, again to oblige Cassiodorus. See Cassiodorus’s testimony in chapter VIII.

These, then, were the three friends—and no others—whom Cassiodorus employed in translating the *Jewish Antiquities*. Perhaps, as I think, he employed above all the foremost of them, Epiphanius, to whom this translation is sometimes attributed, although Cassiodorus does not expressly attribute it to him.

Therefore there can be no doubt that the Ambrosian manuscript, written in Latin in Cassiodorus’s own age, under Justinian, was produced by Cassiodorus’s friends.

It is astonishing that learned men have thus far marched in a single company toward the opposite conclusion. Besides those already cited, René Laurent de La Barre writes of it in the preface to Rufinus’s minor works:

> He also translated Josephus’s history into Latin; a copy of it is preserved in Milan, in the church of Saint Ambrose, written in Lombard letters.

John Henry Hottinger has similar statements in *The Librarian*, chapter II, § 3, p. 33, as does Jerome Welschius in his letter to Bosius, following the *Reinesian Letters*, p. 470. They make Rufinus the author of the Ambrosian manuscript, although it is plainly evident that he translated nothing of Josephus’s works into Latin.

### III.

“But why,” you will ask, “was the Latin translation of the seven books of the *Jewish War* at some time believed to belong to Jerome as translator, according to what the Senator says?”

Here is the reason.

Jerome writes the following in Letter LII, otherwise XXVIII, now LXI, addressed to Lucinius Baeticus:

> Moreover, a false rumor has brought you Josephus’s books and the volumes of the saints Papias and Polycarp as though they had been translated by me, since neither my leisure nor my strength is sufficient to express such great works with equal elegance in another language.

These are Jerome’s words.

Later, it was thought that this great man had acquired enough leisure and strength to translate Josephus. Yet he never acquired them.

Ambrose must be discussed differently.

There exist five Latin books on the *Jewish War*, or *On the Deeds of the Jews*. They are also entitled *On the Destruction of the City of Jerusalem*, because they proceed from the time of the Maccabees down to the ruin of the city and temple of Jerusalem under the Emperor Titus Vespasian.

These books have long borne the name of their author as Egesippus, Aegesippus, or Hegesippus. This has caused modern critics considerable difficulty.

Some thought this was the Hegesippus who wrote five books of *Ecclesiastical History* under Pope Anicetus, around A.D. 170, as Eusebius testifies in many places and Jerome in chapter XXII of his *Catalogue*. The first author of this opinion whom I have seen was William Pastrengicus, a close associate of Petrarch, in his *Origins of Things*, fol. 27.

Others invented a certain genuine Hegesippus, though a later one. But afterward, when they tried to assign him a date, they were forced to gnaw their nails and scratch their heads. For the Greek manuscript of this Hegesippus, from which the Latin translation supposedly flowed, has nowhere been found.

The Latin author, just like this Greek Hegesippus, is generally unmentioned before the twelfth century, when John of Salisbury mentions him in books VI and VIII of the *Policraticus*.

Moreover, this later Hegesippus relates certain matters that were first heard of not merely in the fourth century but even in the tenth, if we follow Vossius near the end of book II, chapter XIV of *On Greek Historians*.

Philip Cluverius, in his *Commentary on the Three Channels of the Rhine*, p. 71, observed that Hegesippus calls the Rhine “two-horned,” after Virgil, and that he cannot be older than the Emperor Theodosius.

On the authority of Cluverius, we shall indicate the age of this author, about which no one has yet been able to assert anything certain.

This Hegesippus, who is a substitute or counterfeit author, encrusted somewhere and hiding beneath the mask of a corrupted name, very easily concealed himself and his age from the notice of critics.

But let us finally disclose the matter.

He is none other than Josephus himself, simply and plainly, his *Jewish War* abridged into Latin—the very work that Cassiodorus, somewhat obscurely, says was translated by Saint Ambrose of Milan.

This is amply confirmed by more than one parchment manuscript, and by many of the most ancient ones; by the language and style; by the structure of the work; and by the authority of certain eminent men in literary matters.

Andreas Masius, distinguished for his knowledge of sacred antiquity, also detected this, as far as we can gather from the reply sent to him by Latinius Latinius in 1566, vol. II of the *Letters*, p. 119.

Latinius expresses his surprise that Masius had read Hegesippus, since he did not think highly of the work. He is even more surprised that Masius had brought himself to believe it was translated into Latin by Ambrose, unless, he says, one wishes to suppose that Masius, as a young man not yet capable of judgment, had let slip something he had attempted merely as an exercise.

That is indeed the case. Ambrose, while still a young man and not yet a bishop, should be considered to have composed this work.

Latinius, and William Sirletus, whom he consulted, did not know that Josephus lay hidden within Hegesippus; nor had others before them known it.

Angelo Decembrio, a native of Vigevano in Insubria, writes the following in book I, part V, fol. 9, p. 2, of his *Literary Polity*, dedicated to Pope Pius II and printed at Augsburg by Henry Steyner in 1540, in folio:

> The venerable writer Hegesippus should be included among the authors of that same history—the history of the Jews written by Josephus.

Decembrio believed that the original author of the book was Hegesippus, though translated into Latin by Ambrose. He says in book VII, part LXXVI, fol. 138:

> Hegesippus is the name of a Greek historian, formed from *goat* and *horse*, who wrote about the war of Titus with the Jews and was translated into Latin by the learned Ambrose.

Let us add to Decembrio the Cardinal Georgius Cortesius. In his *Letters*, p. 354, he has no doubt whatever that Ambrose was the translator of Hegesippus. But later he too makes Ambrose’s *Hegesippus* identical with the man mentioned by Eusebius and Jerome.

Isaac Vossius, in the appendix to his book *On the Seventy Interpreters*, p. 127, observes that the name Hegesippus did not arise from “goat” and “horse,” as Decembrio declared, but from *Josippus*. For scribes changed the name *Josippus*, that is, Josephus, into *Igisippus*. Vossius says that the evidence for this is supplied by his very old parchments, in which, after the name *Josippus* had been erased, another name appears substituted in its place.

Paulus Colomesius reports the same thing on p. 685 of Fabricius’s edition of his works.

Other manuscripts, much more ancient and entirely sound, restoring the genuine reading of Vossius’s parchments, wrongly erased, will be numbered below.

For the moment, I scarcely think that this erasure is older than the twelfth century. For Orderic Vitalis, in his *History*, which he continued down to A.D. 1141, is the first person whom I encounter who praised this Hegesippus.

He praised him in book II, p. 408:

> Hegesippus, a holy and learned man, close in time to the Apostles, mentions James the Just in the fifth book of his *Commentaries*.

These words are found in book V of Barre’s edition.

In the same age as Orderic, John of Salisbury, together with other historians, praised Hegesippus in the *Policraticus*, book VI, chapter XVIII, p. 318, and book VIII, chapters XVIII and XIX, pp. 552 and 555.

An anonymous writer of *On the Manner of Reading Sacred Scripture*, recently published by Edmond Martène in the *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. I, p. 488, advised that Josephus and Hegesippus should be read side by side.

Henry Valesius, in his notes on Eusebius, book I, chapter X, observes that in a very ancient manuscript of Eusebius belonging to the Church of Paris, derived from Rufinus’s translation, *Joseppus* is always read where the Greek has Ἰώσηπος.

Peter Apollonius Collatinus de Cattaneis of Novara, a contemporary of Decembrio, composed, using material drawn from Hegesippus, a heroic poem describing the destruction of Jerusalem. He divided it into four books, in the second of which *Josippus* is used for Josephus and fitted into a dactylic verse.

Everything said thus far is confirmed from every side by the outstanding Mabillon, in vol. I, p. 14 of the *Museum Italicum*. He cites a very ancient manuscript of the Ambrosian Library, in whose upper margins on several pages one reads “Book V of Joseppus,” not “of Hegesippus.”

For just as Josephus is called Ἰώσηπος in Greek, so he was called *Joseppus* in Latin by the translator, rather than *Josep*. Hence *Josepoh*, then *Igisippus*, and finally the spurious *Egesippus* emerged in the likeness of that older form.

At the beginning of book II of the same Milanese manuscript, the following words are written:

> Bishop Ambrose translated this from Greek into Latin.

Mabillon also describes there another manuscript from Turin, corresponding to the Milanese one.

A manuscript of the monastery of Kremsmünster in Austria, cited by Fabricius in vol. III of the *Latin Library*, bears this title:

> Treatise of Bishop Ambrose on the History of Josephus the Captive, translated by him from Greek into Latin.

Another manuscript, bearing the names of Hegesippus and Saint Ambrose, is preserved in Florence in the Gaddian Library. I handled it in May 1717.

Cave, in his *Literary History* under A.D. 374, says that this same history, published under the name of Hegesippus, is a freer Latin rendering of Josephus, in which there are only a few things that are not found in Flavius Josephus’s *Jewish Antiquities* and *Jewish War*.

Paulus Colomesius calls it “a freer interpretation of Josephus’s *Jewish War*,” p. 695 of his works.

Francesco Petrarch, in his *Syrian Itinerary*, p. 562 of the Basel edition of his works, praises Hegesippus, who in book III of his *Histories* followed Josephus.

Hortensius Landus of Milan, a physician and ingenious and witty author of numerous Italian and Latin volumes, says in his work entitled in Italian *The Ferule of Ancient and Modern Writers*, p. 17, that Hegesippus corrected Josephus’s errors.

Neither of these men saw that Josephus was concealed within Hegesippus.

It should nevertheless be noted that Ambrose was not so much Josephus’s translator as the author of a new work. He condensed seven books into five and added certain material of his own, from which the date of the work can be determined.

Isaac Vossius therefore rightly refutes, in the appendix just cited, Christian Schoranus, who attributed the Latin translation of Josephus’s *Antiquities* to Rufinus.

He also rightly affirms that the translation of Hegesippus, or Josippus, belongs to Ambrose, and that this is as certain as anything can be.

But the distinguished scholar is mistaken when he thinks that the translation of the *Jewish War* can be shown by its style to be Rufinus’s.

### IV

Johannes Fridericus Gronovius published *Monobiblon of Observations on Ecclesiastical Writers* at Deventer, by Johannes Columbus, in the year of our Lord 1651, in duodecimo format. In this work the learned man compares the Ambrosian style with that of Josippus and observes, in six hundred places brought forward, emended, and elucidated on both sides, the same phrases frequently used by each, the same expressions, and the same verbal subtleties everywhere cherished by both writers, in chapters I, VI, XI, XVI, XXI, XXII, XXIII, and XXIV. He omitted those features which, although very familiar to Ambrose, were also common among his contemporaries and therefore seemed more indicative of the age than of the author.

These features, so numerous, so distinctive, so mutually alike, and found nowhere else, must be attributed not to two authors but to one alone. Anyone who has examined them with even moderate care could never easily persuade himself that they could belong to two men. Yet this is what Sebastian Le Nain de Tillemont allowed himself to be persuaded of in his *Ecclesiastical History*, vol. I, p. 541—not by his own judgment, but under the influence of others, namely the authors of the latest edition of the works of Saint Ambrose, printed at Paris by Jean-Baptiste Coignard in 1690, in folio.

For these learned men, and my very dear friends, say in the preface to the first volume, p. 5, that the comparison instituted by Gronovius is deceptive, since it is easy for anyone to cut out and juxtapose, here and there, expressions of speech that resemble one another from authors otherwise entirely different; and that this work contains nothing characteristic of Ambrosian style or judgment. Tillemont added his own vote, judging the manner of expression too calm and too smoothly flowing to be attributed to Ambrose, and maintaining that the same expressions readily occur in many writings of the same period.

But these statements are far too general. Ambrose’s style is neither devoid of calmness nor lacking in smooth flow. The expressions collected by Gronovius occur nowhere more densely than in Ambrose. Nor are the expressions themselves so few in number or so common in every writer that they can be attributed to many authors; they are distinctive, very numerous, and familiar to Ambrose alone—belonging to no one else.

In view of this, Philippe Labbe, himself an exceptionally competent judge of such matters, judged Gronovius’s conjecture not improbable in vol. I of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 420; or rather, he thought it should be said that Pseudo-Hegesippus was Ambrose’s contemporary and had stolen Ambrose’s words and thoughts through the most zealous imitation. “For,” he says, “an egg is not more like an egg than the speech of Ambrose and Pseudo-Hegesippus is like itself.”

We, however, in no way concede that the work belongs to two men; rather, along with these distinguished scholars, we maintain that both works proceeded from one and the same intellect and hand.

The authors of the great Bollandist work, *Writers*, vol. V, June, pp. 390, 391, and 400, speaking of our Hegesippus, plainly embrace Gronovius’s view after Labbeus. Long before them, Ludovicus Vives, in his commentary on book XXI, chapter X, of Saint Augustine’s *City of God*, had assigned Ambrose as the father of the work.

The first Brixian edition likewise assigns it to him, bearing this title:

> *The History of Hegesippus, a most faithful historian and among Christians the most eloquent, concerning the Jewish War, the removal of the sceptre, the dispersion of the Jews, and the destruction of Jerusalem, rendered from Greek into Latin by the holy Ambrose, bishop of the Milanese, together with his summary of the work and tables of correspondences, also including Josephus’s books on the deeds of the Maccabees.*  
> Brescia, by Antonio Moreto, 1500, in folio.

This was followed by the Paris edition, which bears the following words:

> *The History of Aegesippus concerning the destruction of Jerusalem, rendered from Greek into Latin by the holy Ambrose, bishop of Milan.*  
> Paris, at the house of Ascension, 1510, in folio.

The Cologne edition, printed at the expense of Godefridus Hittorpius by Johannes Soter in 1530, in folio, was likewise prefaced as follows:

> *The five books of Hegesippus the historian, among the most ancient of ecclesiastical writers, concerning the brave deeds performed by the leaders of the Jews during the siege, and concerning the destruction of Jerusalem and the neighboring cities, with the holy Ambrose, bishop of Milan, as translator.*

Gronovius himself, after carefully examining the matter in chapter I, judged that Ambrose, an eloquent man, composed this work in his younger years or at the beginning of his episcopate.

The editors of the Ambrosian edition, and among them Tillemont, say that Ambrose never had leisure to compose such a work. But they say this without any justification. Could he not have had leisure when he was governor of Liguria and Emilia? As though other men occupied with public office had not also found time to compose dense and even greater works.

But let us hear Gronovius:

> “So many corresponding and genuine features are found in both authors that, once they have been properly examined, you can scarcely refrain from proclaiming that there is one author, and that one of them has concealed the name of the author of the work while the other has allowed it to be known.”

The very learned Lucas Holstenius, unquestionably an exceptionally penetrating judge of such matters, settles the matter completely at the end of the first edition of *Monobiblon*, which Gronovius had sent him as a gift. There he wrote the following in his own hand:

> “What the learned man argues with erudition in the first chapter of these observations concerning the spurious name of Hegesippus and Ambrose as the true author of his *History* is confirmed by the authority of a most ancient manuscript of the Palatine collection in the Vatican Library, where the following title of the work is found: ‘Here begins the treatise of Saint Ambrose, bishop, concerning the history of Josippus the captive, translated from Greek into Latin.’ Therefore, once the false name of Hegesippus has been removed, the genuine title of the work seems to be established as follows: ‘The continuation by Saint Ambrose, bishop, of the history of the Jewish people from Josippus.’”

Thus Holstenius wrote in his copy, now in the Angelica Library.

Henri Valois, in his notes on Ammianus, book XVI, chapter VII, says that “Josippus was translated into Latin by Saint Ambrose.”

Johannes Price, himself also distinguished for his outstanding learning, agrees with this. At the beginning of the Hegesippus edition which Cornelius Gualther published with his own annotations at Cologne, by Maternus Cholinus, in 1559, in octavo, Price wrote the following note in his own hand:

> “Petrus Scriverius, in his notes on Martial, book I, epigram 76:
>
> ‘Pseudo-Hegesippus—who is cited in an old manuscript glossary under the entry *defoenero* as “Ambrose in Hegesippus”—says in book I, chapter XXXII, of *On the Jewish War and the Destruction of Jerusalem*: “Antony, having surrendered himself to Cleopatra’s love, served her and, enslaved to her lust, ministered to her.”’
>
> This Hegesippus is spurious, and a writer of wholly inferior antiquity. Not content with Josephus’s words, he often encrusts for us a sound vessel, so that he may appear to introduce something new. Such is the judgment of the great Scaliger in his *Notes on Eusebius*.”

From Scriverius, Price entered this note in his copy in the Angelica Library, adding another annotation in the margin:

> “The number of the old manuscript codices bearing the name of Ambrose, which I have mentioned, is increased by the Cambridge manuscript cited by Charles Daubuz in book I of *On the Testimony of Josephus*, §11, p. 16. In this codex, as in the Milanese manuscript, the following words are read at the end of book I: ‘The translation of the most blessed Ambrose from Josephus. The first book ends.’”

The editors of the Ambrosian edition added one Claromontane manuscript, which I mentioned above, in which book IV bears this title:

> “The fourth chapter of Saint Ambrose, bishop, concerning the dispersion of the Jews, from Flavius Josephus the historian.”

Barthius mentions two others in his *Adversaria*, book XXXIV, chapter XI, p. 1564. Yet there he himself, with considerable impudence, supposes that Ambrose was attached to the work as translator by the monks’ own invention. This is rashly and absurdly said. Why, and for what purpose, would monks have wished to attach Ambrose’s name—not some other name—to so many codices scattered everywhere?

“Because of the common reputation,” one might answer, of which Cassiodorus speaks, if we follow the editors of the Ambrosian edition. But if anything is rightly inferred from that reputation, the names of Jerome and Rufinus, as well as that of Ambrose, ought equally to have been attached to the codices of Pseudo-Hegesippus. For both of them, in addition to Ambrose, were commonly believed by the Senator to be translators of Josephus.

Barthius said this because he thought that this was a genuine Hegesippus, not a spurious one, although it had been interpolated with enormous additions taken from Rufinus’s Josephus. He expressed this view in book XLVI, chapter IV, p. 2128. But the arguments already presented make this disappear.

The correct conclusion, therefore, is as follows: on the basis of a reputation that was indeed genuine and certain—namely, that Ambrose had published in Latin some books of Josephus in abridged form and with additions of his own in certain places—the Latin translation of the seven books *On the Jewish War* was attributed to him, though with some hesitation, since the translator’s certain name was unknown.

From these observations I detect the error of Jacobus Durantius Casellius in book II, chapter XIII, of his *Various Readings*. After citing a passage from Josephus’s book V *On the Jewish War*, he immediately produces another similar passage from the commonly circulated Hegesippus, introducing it as follows:

> “Hegesippus, who followed Josephus *κατὰ πόδα* (*katà póda*, literally, ‘step by step’), and performed rather the office of translator than of author.”

On the contrary, he performed both offices—that of author and that of translator—contrary to Vossius’s view in book II, chapter XIV, of *On Greek Historians*.

Therefore the name Hegesippus is spurious and recent, while the work itself is genuine and ancient. Most people assign it to the Theodosian age, including those who do not acknowledge Ambrose as its author. Tillemont places it neither before nor after the fifth century, in vol. I, p. 54, and on p. 541 he offers no substantial objection to Gronovius’s observations concerning its conformity with the Ambrosian style.

Isaac Casaubon, in *Exercitation* III, p. 205 of the first edition, calls the writer ancient. This single distinction breaks through the confusions that entangled Vossius in the second part of book III of *On Latin Historians*, p. 706, where he placed Hegesippus among writers of uncertain date.

Accordingly, it was not Pseudo-Rufinus’s Josephus that some interpolator inserted into this Pseudo-Hegesippus, as Barthius believed and as Fridericus Gronovius rightly refuted in chapter XXIV, p. 265. Rather, into Josephus, abridged and expanded in places by Ambrose, certain additions were inserted—apart from the corruption of the name—which so altered the original appearance of the true author that he was taken for someone else.

Gronovius recorded the following concerning the work itself in chapter XVI, p. 165:

> “The author of the Jewish *Iliad*, who preferred to be known by the name of Hegesippus rather than by his own.”

He attributes to the author of the work what ought to be attributed to the copyists. For, as is manifest from what has already been said, they fashioned Hegesippus or Egesippus out of the name Josippus.

Erasmus writes as follows in letter 1303 to the bishop of Riva, p. 1420 of vol. III, part II, of his works in the new edition:

> “Rufinus certainly never translated anything faithfully, but in this author, Josephus, many people seem to have played according to their own inclination.”

Pearson places the writer in the fourth century in his *Pauline Annals*, p. 50, when there were still, in Tillemont’s judgment, people who cultivated the study of the Latin language; Ambrose, a noble Roman, must be considered one of them.

Cornelius Gualther, whose edition of Hegesippus appeared more than once, distinguished certain additions of his by comparing manuscripts. Barthius also corrected the work in many places.

The same work is included in the *Christian History* of Laurentius Barrei, printed at Paris by Michel Sonnius in 1563, p. 123, and in the Lyon *Library of the Fathers*, vol. V, p. 1123.

### V

I have written these matters at greater length so that we may not attribute any translation of Josephus to Rufinus and may remove his name from the manuscript codices just as from the printed books of Josephus—especially from the first edition among all those bearing Rufinus’s name, which is prefaced by this title:

> *The twenty books of Josephus’s Antiquities translated from Greek into Latin by the venerable Rufinus of Aquileia, a most learned man. The seven books On the Jewish War translated by the same.*  
> Venice, by Raynaldus de Novimagio, 1481, in folio.

This was followed by another Venetian edition, printed by Johannes Vercellensis in 1486, in folio; then another there, by Bernardinus Vercellensis, in 1502, in folio; and a Milanese edition by Alexander Minutianus in 1513, in folio.

These were followed by the Erasmian edition, distinguished by this title:

> *Certain works of Flavius Josephus, a native of Jerusalem, a Jew by religion, and among Greek historians especially eloquent, with Rufinus the presbyter as translator. After the first edition of the others, not a few passages, and passages by no means insignificant, restored from a comparison of the most ancient manuscripts.*  
> Basel, by Johann Froben, 1524, in folio.

A more elegant edition was prepared ten years later by Sigismund Gelenius, bearing the following title:

> *The twenty books of Flavius Josephus’s Jewish Antiquities, carefully revised against ancient copies.*
>
> *The seven books On the Jewish War, rendered more accurately than ever before through comparison with Greek manuscripts.*
>
> *The two books Against Apion, not only corrected from the Greek in place of the previously corrupt text, but also supplemented.*
>
> *One book On the Supremacy of Reason, or On the Maccabees, revised by Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam.*
>
> Basel, from the Frobenian press, 1543, in folio.

In his preface Gelenius testifies that he revised the books of the *Antiquities* against ancient Latin copies, and the *Jewish War* against two Greek manuscripts. But because of the inelegance of the *Antiquities*, he does not think that both works were translated into Latin by one person. He bases this on the following conjecture: since Josephus is everywhere consistent with himself in his speeches, when speeches of this kind occur in the work of the *Antiquities* they display astonishing stammering.

By contrast, in the speeches of the following work Rufinus comes closer to Josephus and expresses his declamatory ability much more fully than does that other translator, whoever he was. This is especially clear in two speeches: one in book III, where the speaker dissuades someone from taking his own life, and the other in book VII, where he urges the same course, the first spoken in the person of a certain Eleazar and the second in his own.

Thus Gelenius, like others, was mistaken about Rufinus.

A different edition, likewise in Latin, was produced at Basel by Froben in 1567, in folio. There, in the interpretation of the book *On the Maccabees* alone—which begins, “being about to argue”—Emericus Bigotius says that he recognizes Rufinus’s character, in the *Reinesian Letters* to Antonius Bosius, p. 382.

But from what has been said thus far this view too, unsupported by any ancient authority, is sufficiently and completely refuted.

Johannes Schusler published the twenty books of Josephus *On the Jewish War* and the seven books of the *Jewish Antiquities* without the translator’s name at Augsburg in 1470, in a large folio.

Five years later Bartholomaeus Platyna, librarian of the Apostolic See, showed himself exceptionally discerning in this matter. He published the seven books of Josephus *On the Jewish War*, revised by himself and accompanied by no translator’s name, under the following title:

> *The seven books of Josephus’s Histories.*

At the end one reads:

> “The distinguished and most diligent craftsman Arnold Pannartz, a German by nation, printed this in the house of the nobleman Peter de Max, a Roman citizen, in the year of the incarnate Word 1475, on the twenty-fifth day of November. Platyna corrected it, in the fifth year of Sixtus IV, supreme pontiff.”

It should be noted here that books III, IV, V, VI, and VII are titled by Platyna not “of Josephus” but “of Josippus,” so that no one will find it strange that in the Ambrosian version Josippus is called Josephus.

In the earliest editions he is likewise called Platyna, not Platina; the same form appears in the epitaph at the right-hand lesser door of the Liberian Basilica, which Mabillon copied in vol. I of the *Italian Museum*, p. 66. For the reason, see Lambecius’s notes on Platyna’s *History of Mantua*, p. 445.

I called him Bartholomaeus Platyna, not Baptista, because he called himself so, and others likewise called him so while he was still alive, in the *Journal of the Learned Men of Italy*, vol. XIII, p. 416.

I add Hieronymus Aleander the Elder, one of Platyna’s successors in the office of Apostolic Librarian, who calls him “Barptolemaeus” in a manuscript catalogue of his predecessors.

With the same intention, five years later Ludovicus Cendrata of Verona used no translator’s name when he arranged for the seven books of Josephus *On the Jewish War*, together with the two books *Against Apion* and the book *To Epaphroditus*, to be printed at Verona by the French master Peter Maufer in 1480, in folio.

Cendrata dedicated the work to Antonio Donato, then praetor of Verona, formerly ambassador of the Venetian Republic to the king of France and to the supreme pontiff Sixtus IV. The latter had bestowed on him not only equestrian rank but also, in a rare—indeed, perhaps unique—instance, a Golden Rose. Charles Cartharius did not know this in his *Historical Account of the Pontifical Golden Rose*.

We also possess an elegant Italian translation of the same seven books *On the Jewish War*, printed at Florence by Bartholomaeus P. in 1493, in folio, without the translator’s name. Its translator reproduced Platyna’s edition and therefore rightly omitted Rufinus’s name.

Vossius likewise omitted it, although in his *Etymological Dictionary*, under the entry *proeli*, he praises a learned translator of Josephus.

Therefore the insults hurled against Rufinus as Josephus’s translator by Erasmus in letter III of book XXIV to the bishop of Riva, by Scaliger in his notes on the fragments of Berossus, pp. 10, 35, and 45, and by Casaubon in *Exercitation* I, pp. 30, 59, 135, and 155, are owed not to Rufinus but to someone else.

Whether Rufinus should be called Josephus’s translator was a question on which Ezechiel Spanheim hesitated, attributing the translation to Rufinus, or to Epiphanius Scholasticus, in his notes on Callimachus, vol. II, pp. 57 and 695.

Let it belong to Epiphanius, if one wishes, provided that it does not belong to Rufinus. Gennadius writes in his *Catalogue*, chapter XVII, that Rufinus added prefaces to his translations from Greek so that they might be distinguished. Since all the ancient manuscripts of Josephus lack a preface, this alone is sufficient for us to deny Rufinus’s authorship of all such Latin translations.

Hence Holstenius spoke from common opinion in his *Catalogue of Manuscripts of the Medici*, where he recorded the following:

> “Shelf 66, codex 1. Josephus in Rufinus’s translation, written in Lombard script, on large leaves, remarkable in format and antiquity.”

For the name of Rufinus does not occur in the codex itself, which contains only seventeen books of the *Jewish Antiquities*, together with part of book XVIII. A preface does precede it, but it is not the translator’s preface; it belongs to Josephus the author, who can be seen painted in the initial letter, taking up his pen to write.

Other very old Latin manuscripts of Josephus are preserved in the same Medicean Library. In them Rufinus’s name is nowhere found, although one or two more recent manuscripts do bear it, having been written around the end of the fourteenth century.

## Chapter XVII

I. Commentaries on the seventy-five Psalms of David wrongly attributed to Rufinus.  
II. Likewise, commentaries on Hosea, Joel, and Amos.  
III. The *Life of Saint Eugenia* is by an uncertain author, not by Rufinus.

### I

Other offspring falsely attributed to Rufinus offend the ear.

Antonius de Albone, archbishop of Lyon and primate of Gaul, published a book in 1570 bearing the following title:

> *Commentary of Rufinus of Aquileia, presbyter, on the seventy-five Psalms of David, from a most ancient copy of the library of the monastery of Île-Barbe near Lyon, now published for the first time.*  
> Lyon, by Guillaume Rouillé, 1570, in folio.

The same book, ten years later, with only its first page altered—as booksellers customarily do—was printed at Paris by Michel Sonnius and formed volume II of the works of Rufinus, edited by René Laurent de La Barre.

In a very serious and elegant letter dedicating the book to Pope Saint Pius V, Albone says that he had encountered commentaries of Rufinus, presbyter of Aquileia, on the seventy-five Psalms of David, written in notes and characters that displayed extreme antiquity, preserved on almost worn-out parchment and commended by age and decay themselves. Having read them eagerly and given them to other learned men to read, he judged that this treasure ought not to be buried again but exposed to light and air.

He adds that he was not deterred from undertaking this edition by the fact that certain friends had observed that the author of the work agreed with Augustine in his treatises on the Psalms in many, almost countless, places, so that the thoughts were often the same, the words the same, and even the periods resembled one another.

For he thought that what happened to Saint Ambrose in his books *Hexaemeron* and *On the Holy Spirit* had happened here: just as Ambrose transferred entire periods into his own work from Saint Basil, so Augustine had drawn very many passages into his commentaries from Rufinus, just as elsewhere from Jerome and Cyprian.

Furthermore, he thinks that the work must be Rufinus’s on the basis of the eloquence of its style and the evenness of its expression, with—if God so wills—even Gelasius lending support, since Gelasius states in the *Decree* that Rufinus interpreted certain Scriptures, namely these Psalms, if we are to believe him.

Yet Gelasius is speaking not of the divine Scriptures but of writings of the Greek Fathers translated by Rufinus.

Apart from the style, which is very far removed from Rufinus’s, the single silence of Gennadius deprives Rufinus of the whole work. In the commentaries on Psalms I, III, and IV, verse 1, entire periods copied from Augustine are found.

In the commentary on Psalm IX, folio 242, there is a passage beginning “The first persecution,” translated word for word from Augustine’s commentary on Psalm III.

Cotelerius observed in his notes on Clement’s genuine first letter to the Corinthians, p. 166, §23, that Augustine’s exposition of Psalm XLIX, verse 21, had been inserted into these commentaries.

Johannes Lorinus, in the preface to his commentaries on the Psalms, chapter XVI, p. 13, was the first to strip the mask more closely from the spurious offspring:

> “That this is not, as the title nevertheless states, that presbyter of Aquileia, the opponent of Jerome, is demonstrated by more than one consideration. Anyone who reads the work will observe that it uses Augustine’s very thoughts, even his very words, although reduced to a summary. It is unlikely that a man somewhat younger than Augustine, and one who had dared to contend with Jerome, would have used Augustine’s teaching and words almost continually.
>
> “Indeed, he sometimes transcribes the thoughts of Gregory, a much later writer, as in the commentary on Psalm LXVIII, from Gregory’s twelfth homily on Ezekiel.
>
> “Nor have I found anyone who reckons this commentary on the Psalms among Rufinus’s works—not Gennadius, not Honorius.”

Thus Lorinus, who published the first volume of the same work at Lyon, by Jacob Cardon, in 1623.

These considerations led Labbeus, in vol. II of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 306, to make the author of the book later than the sixth century, or at least to regard it as concealed beneath alien patchwork by someone living after Augustine and Gregory.

I am surprised that Baluzius, in his notes on Cyprian, repeatedly praises this Rufinus *On the Psalms* as though it were genuine. But since all cataloguers without exception passed over this work in silence before 1570, we by no means believe it to be Rufinus’s, although Jacobus Usserius, in his *History of the Scriptures and Sacred Vernaculars*, p. 67, cites testimony from it as from Rufinus’s legitimate commentary.

At the end of the work something seems to be missing, which the Lyonese prelate wishes to have recovered and published from other sources. Labbeus notes that in the *Lesser Library*, part I, p. 23, there is preserved in Paris, in the Library of Saint-Germain, codex 73, containing various commentaries on the seventy-six Psalms by Rufinus of Aquileia, presbyter, different from those published.

### II

The other works, not previously published, which Barreus issued as Rufinian from the manuscript remains of the monastery of Mont-Dieu, vol. I, p. 25, are these:

1. Three books of commentaries on the prophet Hosea.  
2. One book on Joel.  
3. Two books on Amos.

The earliest person I have found to have attributed these books to our author is Johannes Columna of the Order of Preachers, in a manuscript *On Illustrious Men*, later preserved at Venice in the Library of the Monastery of Saints John and Paul. He flourished in the year 1255; Jacobus Echardus notes in his *Vindicated Summary of Saint Thomas*, p. 405, that Alexander IV raised him to the church of Messina.

After Columna, Andreas Dandulus, doge of Venice, attributed the same books to Rufinus in his manuscript *Chronicle*, book IV, chapter XIV, part XXVII. In the same period, Guillelmus Pastrengicus did so in his *Origins of Things*, folio 63 verso.

Then Johannes Trithemius did so in his *Catalogue*, chapter CII, where he divides all these books, which number six, into three. He also adds a book, unmentioned by others, *On the Sacraments*.

The author of our work testifies in the preface that he had also discussed the books of Solomon and had undertaken explanations of the twelve prophets who are called “Minor” not according to their merits but according to the number of their verses.

Dupin, in vol. III of his *Library*, says that he is surprised that Gennadius, while enumerating the author’s other works, did not mention this one. Dupin himself boldly declares it recognizable as a Rufinian work from its style and from other considerations, which, however, he does not state.

Tillemont nevertheless judged otherwise, and more correctly. In vol. XII, pp. 315 and 659, he finds it difficult to believe that so extensive a work could have been composed by Rufinus and then subsequently remained unknown to Gennadius, who was not ignorant of his smaller writings.

It appears to have been completed at least in the middle of the fifth century. For in the preface to book I on Hosea the author praises what Saint John Chrysostom and Jerome had published in their commentaries on the Minor Prophets, saying nothing about Cyril of Alexandria and Theodoret, who had worked on the same subject.

He designates Chrysostom by the title “Saint John of Constantinople.” He does not call Jerome “Saint.” These details reveal that the author of the book lived before general veneration and cult had developed around Jerome.

Nevertheless, he speaks of both as though they had long been dead. But Rufinus died ten years before Jerome and three years after Chrysostom.

He makes very little—indeed, makes nothing—of Origen’s explanations. No one fails to see how unfitting this is for Rufinus’s character. For Rufinus, who was devoted to Origen in every respect, could scarcely be credited with anything less characteristic than these words of the preface.

Origen, proceeding according to his own method, composes allegorical interpretations that are more pleasing than the solid and reliable explanations of the historical sense.

Soon afterward the author attacks Jerome, because his entire exposition flows either through allegories or through the fabulous traditions of the Jews.

These features do not point to Rufinus, an admirer of Origen. Nor do the attacks directed here and elsewhere against Jerome, on pages 86 and 147, belong to him. Rufinus never shows himself an adversary of the holy man except in the books deliberately composed against him in his own defense. Elsewhere, never.

But what is more troublesome is that the author professes to follow not the Itala, the edition of Sacred Scripture derived from the Septuagint translators, but the Vulgate, rendered by Jerome from the Hebrew sources and considered superior to the others.

What could be more absurd, or more alien to Rufinus’s character and writings? Let us hear the words of Pseudo-Rufinus:

> “Next, so that the reader of our work may know both which edition I have followed and what I chiefly had in mind when I undertook this task of extremely difficult interpretation—and, if he too is among their number, may recognize that I have not labored in vain in choosing **that later edition**, which is called ‘according to the Hebrew.’
>
> “For in the earlier editions, corrupt expressions frequently break the sense either of the teaching or of the narrative, so that the task seems to require divination rather than interpretation.
>
> “But **that later translation**, although it has not added much splendor to the context itself, nevertheless, through the integrity of its expressions, frequently avoids those losses caused by the interruptions that we have mentioned.”

Humphrey Hody cited this passage as Rufinian in the additions to his work *On the Original Texts of the Bible*, at the end of the *Syllabus of Chapters*. John Mill also cited it in the prolegomena to the Greek New Testament published at Oxford in 1707, in folio, p. 83, column 1. Yet he added in parentheses: “unless the title of the commentary happens to deceive us.”

There can be no doubt that it does deceive us.

Everyone knows that the genuine Rufinus stood against Jerome in favor of the old Septuagint edition, as one revised by his own Origen. For this reason he sharply rebuked the Stridonian doctor in book II of his *Apology*:

> “Are you now changing, with a new interpretation altered by the Jews, the books of the divine Scriptures which the Apostles handed down to the Churches of Christ as the fullest instrument of faith?”

And shortly afterward:

> “But how shall we receive these things which you are now interpreting and sending throughout churches and monasteries, towns and villages? As divine or as human? And what are we to do when you claim that those books which bear the names of the Prophets or the Lawgivers are more correct than those which the Apostles approved? Tell me how this offense can be corrected. Rather, how can such sacrilege be expiated?
>
> “If it is considered condemnable in your judgment to have understood something differently in explaining the Law, how often must it be judged condemnable to pervert the Law itself into something other than what the Apostles handed down?
>
> “Why should I not speak more boldly against this rashness: which of all the prudent and holy men who came before us dared to lay hands upon such a work? Who presumed to violate the sacred words of the Holy Spirit and the divine books?”

These are Rufinus’s words in defense of the Septuagint version against Jerome. The remaining passages are too long to reproduce in full here.

Augustine agreed with him in letter LXXXII, formerly XIX, §35. But what has already been cited is enough to establish how strongly Rufinus recoiled from a new interpretation of the Bible that followed not the Septuagint translators, praised by the Apostolic voice, but the Hebrew text.

Elsewhere he confirms this view once and again. Besides following the Itala version in his explanation of the Creed, he says the following in his *Ecclesiastical History* based on Eusebius, book VI, chapter XXIII:

> “Only that should be held as true in the divine Scriptures which the Seventy Translators rendered, because that alone has been confirmed by Apostolic authority.”

I know that the new translators of Eusebius—Musculus, Christopherson, and Valois—do not contain these words, perhaps because they happened upon corrupt and defective manuscripts, as Alphonsus Salmeron says of the first two in his fifth biblical prolegomenon, p. 54.

But Rufinus inserted these words of his own into Eusebius’s translation. For that reason they confirm our position all the more.

Could we really claim that Rufinus wished once again to insinuate himself into Jerome’s friendship by approving his new edition? But who does not see that this would itself be an insult to Jerome, who, after the translation of the book *On First Principles*, never again cultivated Rufinus’s friendship?

He ought, however, to have cultivated it after Rufinus rejected Origen and accepted Jerome’s biblical translation.

Now the enormous delusion of Sebastian Münster reveals itself. In the preface to the Old Testament, published by him in Hebrew and Latin at Basel from the Bebelian press in 1534, p. 11, in folio, he suspected that Rufinus had been the author of the Latin Vulgate translation: “whether it was Rufinus or someone else.”

Perhaps Münster was misled by a poorly understood passage of Gelasius, who says of Rufinus in the *Decree*:

> “He interpreted certain Scriptures.”

Before Münster, Paulus of Middelburg had drawn a similar error from Gennadius’s words in part II, book I, of *On Easter*:

> “Whatever is read by Latins with prefaces placed before it has been translated by Rufinus.”

But both Gelasius and Gennadius are speaking of certain short works of the Greek Fathers, not of any books of Sacred Scripture translated by Rufinus.

Although this is sufficient, other considerations drawn from the same source also exclude the Commentary from our author. For the author says that no one among the Latins had explained the prophets. He therefore seems to have been unaware of Jerome’s studies, whom he subsequently places immediately among the Syrians and Greeks. Of those who endeavored to expound the writings of the Prophets, he names Chrysostom and Jerome: the former accomplished this in Greek, the latter in Latin. Finally, the preface lacks the modesty characteristic of Rufinus.

Nor should we omit what he writes in Book I on Amos, p. 123: “Tekoa is said to be a village in which a multitude of shepherds dwells, seven miles from the city of Bethlehem.” These words strongly resemble Jerome writing in his prologue to Amos: “Tekoa is six thousand paces distant southward from holy Bethlehem.” And in chapter VI of his commentary on Jeremiah: “We daily see with our own eyes that Tekoa too is a village situated on a mountain and twelve thousand paces distant from Jerusalem.” Hadrianus Relandus discusses this village learnedly in *Palaestina illustrata*, vol. II, p. 1028.

But Rufinus, who lived for twenty years in Jerusalem, surely ought himself to have visited Tekoa, rather than writing about it on the report of others: “it is said to be a village”? It is likewise ill suited to Rufinus, who had spent so long among the Eastern peoples, that on p. 147 he says, again on the report of others, concerning the star of Venus, or Lucifer, worshiped by the Saracens: “whom the Saracens are said to worship to this day.” Jerome said this in Book II, chapter V, of his commentary on Amos: “The star of your god, called in Hebrew *Chochab*, that is, of Lucifer, whom the Saracens venerate to this day.” Consult John Selden, *Syntagma II de Diis Syris*, chapter IV.

Therefore this Pseudo-Rufinus lived before the rise of Muhammad’s sect. Yet Senator too, besides Gennadius, was unaware of the work, in chapter III of *De institutione divinarum litterarum*, where he records that among the Latins only Jerome and Ambrose wrote on the Prophets.

As for the character of the style, it is in no way close to Rufinian style, which is more elegant and lucid, and therefore less affected and inflated. Yet Theophilus Raynaudus departs from this view in *Erotema X de malis et bonis libris*, vol. XI of his works, p. 294, where, on the basis of the elegance and harmony that flourish in these Commentaries, he excludes them from Rufinus, whom he calls “an uncultivated and barbarous writer.” He holds a similar opinion concerning the *Explanation of the Creed*.

We, however, who are not permitted to be so eloquent, think that the style of both works must be judged quite differently from these learned men. The first of all to suspect that this work was falsely attributed to Rufinus, long before Raynaudus, his associate, was Franciscus Ribera, in his *Commentaries on the Twelve Prophets*, first published at Rome by Jacobus Tornerius in 1590, in quarto. There, on p. 91, § 78, commenting on the words of Hosea, chapter II, “Behold, I will allure her,” which Pseudo-Rufinus explains on p. 42 as follows—“The alluring seems also to indicate the food of manna”—Ribera writes:

“‘To allure’ in this passage means ‘to deceive’; and this verb, according to its meaning, deceived many, among them Rupert and Rufinus. I am indeed surprised at this, since Rufinus was sufficiently skilled in the Greek language and could have understood from the Greek verb what the Latin one meant. For some time I had begun to persuade myself that these Commentaries on the three Prophets were not by that Rufinus who wrote against Jerome (*an unequal contest with Achilles*), because the style of the two works is dissimilar; and now, from this interpretation of his, I understand it even more clearly.”

### III

The *Life of Saint Eugenia, Virgin and Martyr*, which Rosweydus published in *Historia eremitica*, p. 340, belongs to the same category. Its author is uncertain, although in the notes on p. 349 he seems to agree with Goldastus, who attributes it to Rufinus: “If,” he says, “he himself derived it from manuscripts, I readily agree. Certainly the style does not differ from Rufinus’s style.”

Vossius agrees in Book II, chapter XI, of *De historicis Latinis*. Yet this single and overly general argument from style is not always safe. Vossius’s words concerning Goldastus are these: “which I think was done on the authority of the manuscripts.” Indeed, Goldastus says that he is doing this on the basis of a simple conjecture, in his notes on chapter XVII of volume I, part I, of *Rerum Alamannicarum*: “The most ancient history of Saint Eugenia, translated by the same person, if I am not mistaken, Rufinus.”

In my manuscript codex there is a *History of Saint Eugenia*, considerably different from this one and bearing no author’s name.

# CHAPTER XVIII

I. Two *Books of Faith* were published under Rufinus’s name in the previous century. II. The first, containing twelve Anathemas, must by no means be attributed to our Rufinus, but to another. III. Still less may the later one be attributed to him, since it is infected with Pelagian error: seven Rufinuses are identified. IV. The later *Book* belongs to Rufinus of Palestine or to another author.

## I

I now undertake a very serious question, debated among critics and theologians of great reputation: whether the two *Books of Faith*, brought to light in the previous century from ancient manuscript codices, are rightly attributed to Rufinus of Aquileia.

In one of them, the shorter, various anathemas are pronounced against various heresies. In the other, the more extensive, Pelagian poison is disseminated. Hence all the heresies contained in these books have been charged, with every kind of insult, to Rufinus of Aquileia, believed to be the author of both.

Far be it from us to believe that our Rufinus—who to the very end remained attached by the bond of catholic communion to the holiest bishops of his age and to other men of thoroughly approved character, and whom, after his death, holy Mother Church recognized as a pious and religious writer—ever defected to the impious party of the heretics. With God’s help, I shall demonstrate this, and I begin by discussing the shorter book.

## II

In A.D. 1673 this same book was printed both in Italy and in France. Henricus Noris, in Book I, chapter III, of his *Historia Pelagiana*, published at Padua, and Joannes Garnerius, among the works of Marius Mercator published at Paris, volume I, p. 114, brought it into the public light from the Vatican and Beauvais codices, in which it is attributed to a certain Rufinus.

It consists of twelve Anathemas against not one but many and various heresies, most of them referring especially to Origen. These considerations easily led Noris to believe that the book was by our Rufinus, who, after returning to Rome, supposedly cast off by means of this profession of faith, before Pope Anastasius, the suspicion of error under which he had labored.

Hence Noris congratulates both his own province and ours—for they are one and the same—that the distinguished writer Rufinus had at last cleansed himself of every stain of Origenian heresy. Joseph Cardinal Aguirre embraced Noris’s opinion in his *Commentaries on the Theology of Saint Anselm*, volume III, tract VI, chapter LXVIII, disputation 111, section 5, § 39, p. 204 of the Roman edition.

Six eminent men were deceived by the spurious name of Rufinus. This is clearly revealed by the opening words of the book:

“Because of our reverence for the holy places, we came to Jerusalem and Bethlehem, and we learned that many of the brethren were scandalized in us, because they had heard that we professed many things that are heretical and contrary to the faith of the Church. Therefore, in the presence of God, we testify, etc.”

These words make clear that this profession of faith arose not in Rome but in the holy places, Jerusalem and Bethlehem. But once Rufinus had returned from there to Italy, he never again returned to those holy places; he died in Sicily, at Messina.

Noris, shortly before publishing this same formula, noted that “for this one reason alone it cannot be by Rufinus.” Garnerius—a man exceptionally perceptive and deeply versed in ecclesiastical affairs, who explained with outstanding skill how many secrets of both historical and dogmatic learning this very brief book contains—says that the first words I quoted establish where the *Book of Faith* was produced, namely, at Jerusalem or Bethlehem, where an immeasurable multitude of presbyters or monks used to gather.

Garnerius does not reject assigning it to the pontificate of Siricius, that is, to A.D. 398, when questions concerning Origen were raging in Palestine with great intensity of feeling, while Epiphanius and Jerome were opposed on one side, and John of Jerusalem and Rufinus on the other.

But the old man of Bethlehem—who did not remain silent even about lesser matters—would have reproached Rufinus, the author, with this recantation after their friendship had been dissolved, if he had sung it at Bethlehem, where Jerome was, or in the nearby holy city. Indeed, even if it had been published at Rome, it would have reached Jerome’s hands, since his friends were taking care to send him Rufinus’s books in their entirety on other occasions.

Nor would Jerome, who survived Rufinus by ten years, afterward have insulted him as a pious and corrected presbyter, as Noris does not deny that he did. Therefore these Anathemas cannot be ascribed to Rufinus without inflicting the greatest injury on Jerome.

Rather, as Garnerius judges on p. 122, column 2, they were marked with Rufinus’s name by incompetent copyists and attached to the letter of Pope Anastasius to John of Jerusalem, which follows them and in which Rufinus is mentioned. They then slipped into the *Acts of Marius Mercator*, where some Rufinus is mentioned.

More cautiously and perceptively, however, Rigberius the Franco-German, or Gabriel Gerberon, and later Stephanus Baluzius proceeded: in their editions of the works of Marius they wished the letter of Anastasius and the Anathemas of Pseudo-Rufinus alike to be absent, as writings wholly unrelated to those works.

Garnerius, on pp. 115–116, suspects that these Anathemas should be attributed to some Rufinus, a disciple of Jerome, not to Rufinus of Aquileia—specifically, perhaps, to the one whom the holy man says he sent from Syria to Rome and Milan on Jerome’s own behalf in the case of Claudius, in Letter XLI, formerly LXVI, to Rufinus of Aquileia, and in Book III of the *Apology*, p. 462.

Indeed, they were written by Jerome himself. The matter was discovered by Mabillonius, a man who rendered outstanding service to ecclesiastical literature, in *Museum Italicum*, volume I, p. 218. He testifies that he found a very ancient book in Lombard script in the Bobbio Library, bearing this title:

“Abbreviation of the Catholic Faith, expounded by Saint Jerome, so that certain men who had fallen into heresy might be corrected.”

Mabillonius adds that this Bobbio exposition consists of twelve articles, or Anathemas, published by Garnerius under Rufinus’s name among the works of Mercator, namely, in Appendix I to the first part, p. 114—not, as he says through a lapse of memory, in Dissertation X, which does not exist anywhere in the entire volume.

Therefore, if this book—which is rather a general formula of faith written by Jerome for the readmission into communion of those accused of Origenism than the recantation of a single individual repudiating his own errors—ever belonged to any Rufinus, he was certainly not Rufinus of Aquileia, but another; perhaps that Syrian by nationality who first introduced the heresy concerning original sin into Rome, as Mercator relates in his *Commonitorium*. Yet this confession contains nothing that appears favorable to the Pelagian heresy.

Garnerius, who analyzed each of its articles with exceptional skill, found Jerome’s doctrine throughout, even in some points where the Church does not follow him—for example, in that portion of the first article which teaches that Christians who hold the right faith, though sinners, are to be condemned not to eternal but to temporary punishment.

Thus all the Anathemas are directed against doctrines contrary to Jerome’s teaching, though not equally proscribed by the other Fathers. For even the twelfth Anathema, against those who say that souls existed before they were born and are not created daily by God together with the body, would not have been admitted by Augustine, who did not dare to define this question as though it were certain.

Hence Garnerius rightly says on p. 116 that this Confession was not public in any Church, but rather private and proper to some gathering either of clerics or of a monastery—perhaps the monastery at Bethlehem where Jerome lived.

Moreover, the word “anathema” is not taken in this formula in the sense in which it is commonly understood, namely, as a canonical sentence of execution, but in another general sense, meaning the condemnation of some statement, just as it was understood at the Council of Diospolis, where foolish speech was struck with anathema. See Baluzius’s *Councils*, p. 363.

In all the Anathemas of the book, Origen is struck down, together with the heresies of Paul of Samosata, Arius, Apollinarius, and Photinus that arose from him. No doctrine is condemned which Jerome had not at some time objected to Origen.

The authority of the Bobbio codex, already sufficiently strong in itself, is confirmed on every side by these considerations. At the time when the confession was made—according to Garnerius, around A.D. 394, when the controversy between Jerome and John of Jerusalem had not yet cooled—many other formulas of faith by various individuals came forth, as the questions arising here and there seemed to require.

Thus our Rufinus composed his *Apology* to Anastasius and his *Explanation of the Creed* to Laurentius. Thus Gregory of Nazianzus produced Anathemas against the Apollinarians. So did Theodore of Mopsuestia, Caelestius and Pelagius, and Julianus.

In any event, all the Anathemas of the Bobbio formula strike chiefly at the Origenian doctrines that Jerome detested, including those on which the Church had as yet made no definition, such as the origin of souls, which article 12 decrees are created daily.
