Our Rufinus says in his *Apology to Anastasius*: “With God as my witness, I say that up to the present I hold nothing certain or defined concerning that question.” Again: “I confess that I am still ignorant of anything beyond what the Church plainly teaches: that God is the creator both of souls and of bodies.”

Noris observes in his *Vindications of Augustine*, chapter IV, § 3, where he treats the matter at greatest length, that the opinion defended by Jerome was finally received in the twelfth century in the form it now has. Natalis Alexander follows him in century V, chapter IV, article III, § 10.

Aguirre, in *The Theology of Saint Anselm*, volume III, chapter LXVIII, disputation 111, § 41, p. 205, observes that no renunciation of the error that there is no transmission of sin appears in this book—the error on account of which a certain Rufinus had been regarded very unfavorably by Saint Augustine and other orthodox writers.

But even this should have warned the excellent man not to merge two Rufinuses into one and assign the book to the Rufinus of Aquileia, who was Augustine’s close friend and never denied the transmission of sin.

## III

From the shorter Pseudo-Rufinian *Book of Faith* our discussion now turns to the longer one. Jacobus Sirmondus was the first to publish it, a man equally renowned for bringing both his own writings and those of others from antiquity into the public light.

The book bears the title: *Book of Faith by Rufinus, presbyter of the province of Palestine, with notes by Jacobus Sirmondus*. Paris, Sebastian Cramoisy, 1650, in octavo.

Garnerius later published it again among the works of Mercator, Dissertation V, p. 285, omitting Sirmondus’s notes. Finally, Jacobus de la Baune included it, together with the notes, on p. 274 of volume I of Sirmondus’s works, published at Paris by the Royal Press in A.D. 1696.

Sirmondus divides the short work into sixty-one chapters and thought that it had first been written in Greek. Garnerius believes that it was translated into Latin by Julianus of Eclanum, the patron of Pelagius, the arch-heresiarch.

Garnerius thinks that Eclanum stood in Hirpinia and that it is now called Fricento, or Frequentum, joined to the bishopric of Avellino, p. 146, column 2. Holstenius is more accurate, however, in his notes on Cluverius, p. 273. Retaining the distance of fifteen miles given in the *Itinerarium Antonini*, he places Eclanum near Mirabella, between Fricento and Benevento, where very substantial remains of the city are visible.

Dupin, whose carelessness we encounter in many conspicuous examples, says in volume IV, part II, of the *Bibliotheca* that John the Deacon attributes this book to Rufinus the presbyter of Aquileia. This is false. For John the Deacon, in his manuscript exposition of the Heptateuch preserved at Paris in the monastery of Saint-Germain, uses the testimony of this book twice, once in Genesis and again in Exodus; in both places he uses this title: “From the *Book of Faith of Rufinus*.”

But whenever we hear the name Rufinus, we must not immediately think of Rufinus of Aquileia. For it is established by clear literary evidence that several Rufinuses, ecclesiastical men—perhaps even known to one another—flourished at one and the same time.

### 1

Saint John Chrysostom writes to Rufinus the presbyter in Letter CXXVI. He asks him to travel to Phoenicia to assist the monks whom, after they had survived the slaughter, the Gentiles had wounded.

### 2

Saint Nilus wrote various letters to Rufinus, whom he adorns with great praise, especially Letters XVII and LIV of Book IV. Nilus calls him a *ἡσυχαστής* (*hesychast*), that is, a solitary person and lover of quiet. Peter Possinus explains the term, while Joseph Maria Suaresius identifies this Rufinus with our own in the index of Nilus’s works, p. 612, column 2.

Tillemont, however, volume XII, § 45, p. 108, thinks that he was an anchorite or recluse, living in a desert and solitary place rather than a monk, and therefore different from our Rufinus. We entirely adhere to this opinion.

### 3

A Rufinus who was a deacon by office appears in Saint Augustine’s Letter CXLIX, formerly LIX—now XXCI—to Paulinus of Nola, a friend of our presbyter.

### 4

Saint Jerome suggests to us—both as I said elsewhere and as I say again—that there was a presbyter Rufinus different from these men and by no means to be confused with Rufinus of Aquileia. Jerome wrote Letter XLII, formerly LXVI, to our Rufinus after his return from the East; at its end we read:

“We also sent the holy presbyter Rufinus through Rome to Milan for a certain matter, and asked him to visit you”—that is, Rufinus of Aquileia—“in accordance with our wishes.”

Jerome mentions this Rufinus again in Book III of the *Apology*, p. 462, once and again:

“Yet I want you to know what those poisoned darts are which you complain that we threw behind your back. The presbyters Vincentius, Paulinianus, Eusebius, and Rufinus: Vincentius came to Rome long before you. Paulinianus and Eusebius departed after the year of your voyage, A.D. 398. Rufinus was sent two years later, A.D. 399, in the case of Claudius. All of them went either on family business or because of danger threatening another’s life.”

Vincentius, Eusebius, and Paulinianus crossed over to Italy on family business. Therefore Rufinus hurried to Milan because of danger threatening another’s life.

Rufinus of Aquileia suspected that Jerome had sent these men to create envy against him among the Romans by his own machinations. We do not at all think that this fourth Rufinus was the same as the Syrian.

### 5

Jerome’s letter on Solomon’s Judgment and the Division of the Infant, now in volume II of his works—now Letter LXXIV—p. 616, is consistently addressed in all manuscript codices to “Rufinus the presbyter at Doma [place-name uncertain].” We think that this Rufinus was different from those mentioned above.

### 6

The writers of Pelagian history mention a sixth Rufinus, a very close friend of Saint Prosper, who wrote him a highly learned letter on the grace of God and the free choice of the human will. It survives in the third Appendix to volume X of Saint Augustine’s works.

Gabriel Vasquez, in his commentary on the first part of Saint Thomas, disputation XCI, chapter V, no. 74, made the very gross error of taking him to be Rufinus of Aquileia, who had died in Sicily twenty years earlier.

### 7

Finally, in seventh place, we place our Rufinus of Aquileia.

To resume what I was saying about Rufinus’s book, Sirmondus says in his preface that he found it noted in two Corbie manuscripts as having been published not by Rufinus but by Pelagius under Rufinus’s name.

Yet he himself thinks that both attributions are easily refuted, because the book agrees neither with Rufinus of Aquileia, who repeatedly attacks Origen as impious and detestable, nor with Pelagius, whose principal decree it overturns—namely, that Adam would die whether he sinned or did not sin.

Baunius notes in the preface to volume I of Sirmondus’s works, § 3, that this book, at least in the portion touching on original sin, appears to have been copied almost word for word from Julianus’s *Book of Faith*, which Garnerius published from a manuscript codex of the Church of Verona.

Finally, concerning the book’s date, Garnerius thinks that it was written not only before the time of Nestorius and Eutyches but also, in Sirmondus’s opinion, before Pelagius’s condemnation, because no mention of the controversies concerning Christ’s grace is inserted in it. Baunius testifies that Garnerius’s dissertation on this matter exists, enlarged in a second edition and prepared for the press.

The editors of the latest edition of Saint Augustine’s works made several observations worthy of the greatest attention concerning the author of this book, which is wrongly attributed to Rufinus, in the additions to volume VIII, found after the indices at the end of volume XI. I shall therefore transfer a summary of their remarks here.

Augustine writes in Book XXXVIII of *On the Trinity*:

“A certain man gave a very clever answer to a heretic who asked with extreme cunning whether God begot the Son willingly or unwillingly. If he said ‘unwillingly,’ the most absurd misery would follow for God; but if he said ‘willingly,’ the heretic would immediately conclude, as though by an invincible argument, that the Son was not of nature but of will. But that man, in turn, most vigilantly asked him whether God is God willingly or unwillingly.”

These words of Augustine agree perfectly with what the Sirmondian *Book of Faith* attributed to Rufinus says in chapter LIII, p. 315:

“When, therefore, they ask us whether God begot the Son or not, and receive from us the answer, ‘He begot him,’ they immediately add a question of the following kind, which the Greeks call a *dilemma*: unwillingly or willingly? They do this so that, if we say ‘unwillingly,’ they may immediately add: ‘If he begot the Son unwillingly, how is it not impious to say this of God, that he was subjected to the necessity of generation?’ But if we say ‘willingly,’ they again add what suits their purpose: ‘Therefore, if he begot him willingly, since he was begotten by will, no distinction whatsoever can be maintained between him and all the other things that were likewise created by God’s will.’

“And below:

“We, for our part, shall ask them in return, using a similar form of questioning: Is God good willingly or unwillingly?”

Nothing could be more suitable or clearer for proving that, in the passage from Augustine quoted above, this Sirmondian book is intended.

Its author cannot be stated immediately. At the end of the oldest Corbie codex, written in uncial letters, the following is added:

“Here ends Rufinus, presbyter of the province of Palestine, *Book of Faith*, translated from Greek into Latin speech. Amen.”

John the Deacon attributes it to Rufinus the presbyter. Sirmondus, however, admits that the title is false, if only because throughout the book its author attacks Origen as impious and detestable.

Moreover, what sort of book appears to have been translated from Greek into Latin when in chapter LIII one reads: “a question of this kind, which the Greeks call a *dilemma*”? Again, in chapter LV: “his invention, which the Greeks call a *sophism*”? Finally, in chapter LX, concerning the Sabellians:

“They are accustomed to pronounce the one and only God as both Son and Father through a single part of speech, as though in Greek one said *υἱοπάτωρ*, ‘Son-Father.’”

These expressions sound rather like those of a Latin author attempting to explain his own ideas through Greek terms.

Indeed, in the Corbie manuscript the inscription just mentioned is completely cut through by transverse lines. In its place another note has been added by a second hand, almost equal in age:

“Thus far the blasphemies of Pelagius the heretic against the Catholic faith, which he inserted under the name of a Catholic with a false title.”

Moreover, at the beginning of the entire work there is the following warning, written in Merovingian letters, nearly faded away:

“This book, which is entitled Rufinus’s, must not deceive you, pious reader, because it is Pelagian and full of the blasphemies of the Pelagians. For while pretending to argue against the Arians, he inserted the poisons of his own heresy. Therefore I urge your charity to cut this blasphemer out of your codex, and in its place copy Saint Augustine’s book *On True Religion*, so that you may restore the quantity—that is, so that nothing may be lost from the size of the volume.”

The following is also written in the margin of the book itself:

“This book is not by Rufinus but by Pelagius the heretic; it contains many blasphemies against the Catholic faith.”

Against this very ancient and repeatedly renewed observation of the learned men, Sirmondus objects that the book does not suit Pelagius, since it approves that Adam would not have died had he kept God’s commandment, and thus overturns Pelagius’s principal decree, by which he maintained that Adam would have died whether he sinned or did not sin.

Yet Gennadius supports the notes mentioned above in his *Catalogue*, where he says in chapter XLII:

“Before he was exposed as a heretic, Pelagius wrote three books on the faith of the Trinity.”

John the Deacon adds weight to Gennadius, citing not only the already published *Book of Faith* but also a second book, which does not survive, under Rufinus’s name.

But an answer to Sirmondus’s objection is also readily available from Gennadius. There is nothing surprising in the fact that a heresiarch wrote something from the Catholic faith in which he had been born and raised before devising his own heresy.

As for Augustine, it was not wholly foreign to his character to mention with praise something that a heretic had judged rightly. If Pelagius himself had not previously wished his name to remain hidden, perhaps Augustine would not have kept silent about it.

From what has been said it follows that the false title attributing the *Book of Faith* to Rufinus, and the notes vindicating it for Pelagius, are neither rash nor to be rejected; nor should the opinion be disapproved according to which this same author is thought to be praised in Augustine’s *On the Trinity*, chapter XV.

From this we likewise learn how deeply the ancients cared that a heretical work should not be read incautiously—indeed, that it should be cut out and entirely suppressed—even though Augustine made useful use of it for the purposes of the Church, just as other Fathers used the arguments of Arius against Sabellius and those of Sabellius against Arius.

## IV

Thus Rufinus of Aquileia has been wrongly merged by some more recent writers with Rufinus the presbyter of Palestine, or with whatever other author the book just discussed may belong to. He has also been wrongly merged with Rufinus, the teacher of the heretic Caelestius, whether that man was distinct from the Palestinian or not.

For Marius Mercator, a Latin, calls him a Syrian in his *Commonitorium*. Yet he would not have called a man Syrian whom the entire West, and indeed the East as well, recognized as an Aquileian—and especially Augustine, who was as close a friend of Rufinus as of Marius.

For who among the Westerners was ignorant of Rufinus of Aquileia, so famous for so many writings, so many friendships, and even for the single controversy between him and Jerome, which Augustine himself condemned?

No one was unaware that our Rufinus of Aquileia—not a Palestinian or Syrian—had long before been praised by Jerome in the *Chronicle* and in his letters, and likewise by Paulinus of Nola in his letters.

Whether Mercator was a Campanian by nationality, as Garnerius thinks, or an African, as others conjecture, he alone could not have been ignorant of one whom no one was ignorant of.

Rufinus of Aquileia was commonly on the lips of fame not only in Campania, where Nola is located, but also in Africa, where Augustine lived. Augustine had cited testimonies from Rufinus’s published books, the *Ecclesiastical History* and the *Pythagorean Sextus*, in his own works, just as in the same century in which Marius flourished other Africans—Victor of Vita and Vigilius of Thapsus—also cited him in their writings.

Moreover, John Cassian, Rufinus’s and Marius’s contemporary, well known first in Syria, then at Rome, and soon afterward in Gaul, had praised Rufinus’s *Explanation of the Creed* in his own books. In that work Rufinus himself had declared that he was baptized at Aquileia.

How, then, could Marius, or any Latin, have regarded him as a Palestinian or Syrian? They say so, of course, because he lived for many years in Syria.

But Jerome also lived there and died there, and no one therefore called him Syrian or Palestinian. Palladius, himself a Syrian and likewise Rufinus’s and Marius’s contemporary, called him an Aquileian, not a Syrian. Gennadius, Marius’s near-contemporary, did the same.

All these considerations converging persuade me—and, unless I am mistaken, will persuade anyone—that Rufinus, who was an Aquileian, neither should nor could have been called Syrian or Palestinian.

Indeed, I think it can be clearly inferred from this that he was called Syrian or Palestinian precisely so that he would not be confused with Rufinus of Aquileia.

I would not have Joseph Cardinal Aguirre, in *The Theology of Saint Anselm*, volume III, tract VI, chapter LXVIII, disputation 111, section 4, § 30, and disputation 112, section 6, § 62, merge that Syrian Rufinus with Rufinus of Aquileia. The excellent man did this in defiance of all antiquity and was led to it by wholly frivolous arguments.

I revered Aguirre, a man deserving of the highest praise for piety and learning in the Senate of the Holy Roman Church. Had he lived, he would gladly have tolerated my disagreement, given the candor of his character. For it is otherwise established that this deeply religious Cardinal never hesitated, with honest modesty, to cast off his earlier opinions when they were not well supported.

Nor, as Quintilian says in Book X, chapter I, of *The Oratorical Institution*, should a reader immediately be persuaded that everything great authors have said is necessarily perfect. “For they sometimes fall short and yield under the burden.”

These remarks have been offered in advance concerning the Syrian Rufinus, distinct from the Aquileian, on the occasion of the *Book of Faith* published by Sirmondus and attributed by some to our Rufinus.

I shall return to the Syrian after the death of the Aquileian, whose acts I now continue to recount, since I have thus far reviewed all the genuine and spurious works of Rufinus, both extant and lost.

# CHAPTER XIX

I. The letter of Theophilus of Alexandria to Pope Anastasius concerning the celebration of Easter causes disturbances in the Church. II. Rufinus was by no means condemned by Anastasius. III. Among other things, this is shown by his communion with the principal bishops of Italy. IV. Only his translation of the books of the *Periarchon* was not approved. V. Rufinus’s replies to Jerome concerning the letter of Pope Anastasius to John of Jerusalem. VI. The hostility between Jerome and Rufinus condemned by Augustine.

### I.

To encompass Rufinus’s books in a single continuous and orderly sequence, it was necessary to set aside the remainder of his activities for a little while. Now at last I have completed my survey of all Rufinus’s works; therefore I return to the point from which I digressed.

While the dispute between Jerome and Rufinus was raging over the books of Origen’s *Periarchon* translated into Latin, Theophilus of Alexandria, in the year A.D. 401, had written his first Paschal Letter, which in the published editions of Jerome’s works is the second (now restored), as I have said elsewhere. This letter contained a catalogue of several of Origen’s errors, inserted into the letter on the pretext of announcing the date of Easter. Translated into Latin by Jerome and, as usual, sent to Rome so that it might announce the precise day of Easter in that same year, 401, it greatly disturbed Pope Anastasius.

For, as Norisius observes, the Latins had not yet discerned the errors of the Greek writer. According to Norisius, as soon as Anastasius received Theophilus’s letter, he judged that there was no reason for further delay and condemned Origen by a formal sentence. He says that Venerius and Chromatius, the two Italian metropolitans of Milan and Aquileia, did the same in their churches in that same year, 401.

This, however, is asserted without justification by a most learned man. The discipline of the Roman Church did not permit the Supreme Pontiff, stirred by a single letter of Theophilus that dealt only incidentally and covertly with Origen, immediately to condemn Origen without consulting the Western bishops, or at least a council or the Roman presbytery. That certainly could not have been done at once.

The purple-clad writer called the publication of Theophilus’s letter—which, besides announcing the date of Easter, contained a catalogue of Origen’s errors—a condemnation of Origen, although the publication of that letter announced only one Easter. The Roman Church did not announce condemnations issued by other bishops; rather, as mother and chief of all the churches, she had always been accustomed to issue her own condemnations for announcement to others.

The Alexandrian bishop was responsible for determining the day on which Easter was to be celebrated each year. He reported the fixed date to the Apostolic See long beforehand, so that the indication contained in this writing might generally reach the more distant churches, as Leo the Great says in Letter 94, formerly 64, to the Emperor Marcian. For the Pontiff, having received the Alexandrian bishop’s advice in advance concerning the coming date of Easter, announced it to all the priests of the western regions, as the same Leo the Great says in Letter 112 to the Emperor Marcian.

These priests were all the metropolitans of the Roman patriarchate established throughout Cisalpine Gaul, Venetia and Istria, Illyricum, Britain, Gaul, Spain, and Africa—in other words, throughout the whole of Europe as far as Thrace. It is clear that all these ecclesiastical provinces were included within the Roman patriarchate; Norisius demonstrated this long ago in his *Responses to the German Gerras of Franciscus Macedo*, p. 41.

That announcement of Easter was issued in accordance with Canon 1 of the First Council of Arles, in Labbe’s edition, vol. I, p. 1427. See Franciscus Bernardinus Ferrarius, *On the Rite of Sacred Sermons*, book I, chapter XXV. Among the Alexandrians it was customarily made at the preceding feast of Epiphany through the proclamation of the deacons; this is especially clear from Cassian, *Collation* X, chapter I, p. 364, Ciaconius’s edition.

Baronius correctly noted that the Paschal Letter, customarily sent in the preceding year by the Alexandrian bishop to the Roman bishop, from whom the remaining western churches were to receive it, was published at Epiphany; this was under A.D. 399, § 52. Norisius, in *Pelagian History*, book I, chapter II, and Pagius, under A.D. 401, § 8, unjustly refuted him.

I discuss these matters more fully elsewhere, while disputing the year of the death of St. Athanasius. Jerome, at the beginning of book III of his *Apology*, p. 453—a book he wrote at the beginning of A.D. 402—says that during approximately the preceding two years he had translated two of Theophilus’s Paschal Letters into Latin, and no others. Therefore Jerome translated the first of them, that for A.D. 401, at the beginning of A.D. 400, so that it could be sent to Rome and subsequently published throughout the West by the Roman patriarchal pontiff.

It was first published at Rome by Anastasius, who, as Primate and Exarch of all Italy, immediately sent it for publication also to the metropolitans of the two principal sees of his exarchate—the only ones then regarded as such in the whole of continental Italy: namely, Venerius of Cisalpine Gaul and Chromatius of Venetia and Istria. It was their responsibility to publish these solemn letters, as Cassian calls them, in the assemblies of their churches and to announce them to the remaining provincial bishops subject to them.

All this tends to make clear to everyone that when Anastasius, the Roman Pontiff, Venerius of Milan, and Chromatius of Aquileia published in their churches Theophilus’s Paschal Letter for A.D. 401, their sole intention was to announce to their peoples the fixed date of Easter for that year, even though the same letter incidentally listed certain errors of Origen previously unknown to the Latins. The condemnation of those errors had no connection whatever with the announcement of the date of Easter.

Theophilus had deliberately added to the Paschal Letter the errors of the Origenists, which he had carefully collected, so that Easter could not be announced without those same errors also being read aloud. Jerome expressed the matter in these words, *Apology* I, book II, p. 417:

> “The bishops Anastasius, Theophilus, Venerius, and Chromatius, and the entire Catholic SYNOD of both East and West, who with one judgment, because with one spirit, ANNOUNCE him [Origen] to the peoples as a heretic, etc.”

He calls the assembly of the Church, gathered on the feast of Epiphany to hear the announcement of the coming Paschal feast and the Alexandrian judgment against Origen, a synod.

Theophilus says the same in his letter to Emperor Justinian, or in his treatise against the errors of Origen, in Labbe’s *Councils*, vol. V, p. 685B. For he says in a sermon to monks accused of the taint of Origenism:

> “Anathematizing Origen and the other heretics, following our example and that of Anastasius, bishop of the Holy Roman Church, who, renowned from ancient struggles, was appointed leader of the most noble people; and whom the entire SYNOD of the blessed bishops of the West, which received and approved the judgment pronounced by the Church of Alexandria against the impious man, etc.”

Theophilus wrote this on the basis of the letter of Pope Anastasius, in which Anastasius replied that he had arranged for Theophilus’s Paschal Letter for A.D. 401—containing also the errors of Origen—to be published through the two Italian metropolitans, Venerius and Chromatius, and through the other bishops of the principal sees throughout the West. Jerome subsequently learned the facts from Theophilus.

The word “synod” misled the most learned Norisius, and Garnerius as well, in his notes to Liberatus, p. 227. They supposed that Origen had truly been condemned in Italian synods at Rome, Milan, and Aquileia, although those synods—or, rather, provincial assemblies—had not met to condemn Origen. They met to hear the letters of Theophilus from the metropolitans, letters that customarily announced the fixed date of the coming Easter each year.

Hear Jerome in his letter to Theophilus:

> “The presbyter Vincent came from Rome two days before I gave this letter, and greets you submissively; he repeatedly celebrates you in speech, saying that Rome and Italy have been freed by your LETTERS—not synods.”

They had been freed from Origenism because Theophilus’s Paschal Letters, read aloud at Epiphany by each metropolitan and by the bishops of Italy before their provincial communities and peoples, also contained the catalogues of Origen’s errors composed by Theophilus.

### II.

Rufinus was living at Aquileia when, at Epiphany in the year 401, these Paschal Letters of Theophilus were customarily read aloud by a deacon in the church. On hearing the catalogue of Origen’s errors, he was horrified and declared that he had previously been unaware of them. This was reported to Jerome in writing by Aquileian friends.

Jerome himself relates the matter in these words, *Apology*, book I, p. 363:

> “Recently, when the LETTERS of Pope Theophilus were read, in which he sets forth the errors of Origen, [Rufinus] is said to have stopped up his ears, condemned the author of so great an evil with a loud voice in the presence of everyone, and said that until that time he had not known that [Origen] had written such abominable things.”

These words of Jerome teach us that the “condemnation of Origen,” as he calls it, which Chromatius published at Aquileia in the presence of Rufinus, was nothing other than Theophilus’s Paschal Letter. The same must be said entirely of Anastasius and Venerius.

Jerome calls the publication of the Paschal Letter—which, besides announcing Easter, also explained the errors of Origen—a condemnation of Origen. Norisius, in *Pelagian History*, book I, chapter II, having understood Jerome’s words less accurately, says that in that condemnation of Origen Rufinus was not mentioned at all.

This is entirely true. Why should Rufinus have been named in Theophilus’s Paschal Letter, which was to be read throughout the world? Great names possess such authority that they can sometimes lead even the most famous men into error.

When Baronius, on the basis of a passage in Jerome that he had not properly understood, had stated that Origen was publicly condemned by Pope Anastasius and then, at his direction, by Venerius of Milan and Chromatius of Aquileia, under A.D. 400, § 63, other men distinguished for learning later followed in Baronius’s footsteps and repeated the same claim. They were, after Norisius, Johannes Garnerius and Pagius: Garnerius in his notes to Marius Mercator and in his dissertation on Liberatus the Deacon, chapter V, § 1, p. 227; Pagius under A.D. 401, § 9.

Indeed, the latter did not hesitate to assert that Rufinus too had been included in that same condemnation of Origen—something Norisius had rightly denied. Garnerius unwittingly misled him, for Garnerius interpolated Pope Anastasius’s letter to John of Jerusalem, newly edited by him from the Beauvais manuscript, by almost an entire chapter VIII, which involved the condemnation of Origen and Rufinus. Yet Garnerius candidly admits in his notes, p. 112, col. 1, that the interpolation was his own and that he had printed it in a different typeface, so as not to deceive anyone.

Baronius, among others, had published the letter free from interpolations under A.D. 402, § 26. In it we find no condemnation of Origen and no condemnation of Rufinus; nor is there any mention of Venerius or Chromatius condemning Origen and Rufinus in synods of their provincial bishops.

Anastasius says only one thing there about Rufinus: that judgment concerning him belongs to God alone. Therefore he himself passed no judgment upon him and did not condemn him. He adds that previously he had known nothing about Origen.

He then explains his view of Rufinus’s translation of the books of *Periarchon* to John: namely, that it had raised a kind of cloud before pure minds—those of Pammachius, Oceanus, and Marcella—as though Rufinus the translator had wished to injure the Catholic faith by it. Nevertheless, he declares that his judgment concerning the book depends upon the intention of Rufinus the translator.

If Rufinus condemns the errors, he says that he approves this. If he assents to the errors, he says that he neither accepts this nor fails to condemn it rightly and deservedly. He trusts that this will be pleasing to God’s providence.

He testifies that he had written the same things to the holy Venerius of Milan. Venerius, for his part, had written to Anastasius on behalf of Rufinus, urging him not to trouble himself with unnecessary fear or be disturbed by empty anxiety on account of Rufinus’s translation. Anastasius says that he would take care that the people entrusted to him should avoid Rufinus’s translation, lest it attempt to weaken devout minds by casting its darkness over them.

He also mentions letters of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius that had been brought to him, forbidding Catholics to read Origen. He concludes as follows:

> “Thus far the form of my judgment has proceeded.”

Yet in that same letter no form of a condemnatory judgment against Rufinus had proceeded, nor is such a judgment found in any other ancient document.

Complaints against Rufinus, the friend and presbyter of his own church, had been circulated. They had moved John to pour out his suspicions concerning their authors before Anastasius. In his reply to John on this matter, the Pontiff asks him to lay aside his suspicions and remember that it belongs to God to look into the hearts of human beings. He adds this about Rufinus:

> “He translated Origen’s words into Latin with his own mind and approved them; nor is he unlike one who gives assent to the faults of others. Yet I want you to know that he is considered so alien to our party that we wish not to know what he is doing or where he is. Let him himself see where he can be absolved.”

This is the substance of Anastasius’s letter to John, which Baronius assigned to A.D. 402, §§ 26 and 30, although the twenty-eighth of April had not yet passed, on which day the Pontiff ceased to live. Below we shall show that it was written earlier.

Anastasius did not, however, publish it at Rome or in Italy, since he gave it privately in writing to one John—if indeed he wrote it. Rufinus and various learned men of an earlier age had doubted this. But, for my part, even if it was written, I accept it as genuinely written.

Nevertheless, I think it follows from this that Anastasius’s private and familiar letter to the bishop of Jerusalem must by no means be regarded as a synodal decree publicly issued against Origen and Rufinus. For judicial decrees of the Roman Church were customarily published at Rome before anywhere else.

Rufinus was living in Venetia and therefore within the boundaries of the Roman Pontiff’s primacy and exarchate, to whom he had sent his *Apology*. Consequently, if he had deserved a public penalty of condemnation, he ought to have been condemned by the decisive judgment of the Supreme Pontiff, publicly issued at Rome in accordance with the discipline of the Roman Church and of the age.

This never happened.

I am utterly astonished that two most learned and religious cardinals, Baronius and, following him, Jacobus Peronius in his second *Response to the King of Britain*, chapter XXXIII; and also Pagius under A.D. 401, § 16, Tillemont, vol. XII, article 100, p. 242, and Natalis Alexander, fourth century, chapter VI, article 32, should have thought that a decisive sentence of anathema was pronounced against Rufinus at Rome by Pope Anastasius, yet did not notice that their credulity inflicted a very great injury upon the Apostolic See.

For if Rufinus had ever been struck by a sentence of anathema, it would have been lawful for the Apostolic See alone, and not for others, to remove it. The Apostolic Canon 25, elsewhere 33, and the fifth canon of the Council of Nicaea provide that one separated from communion with the Church by a sentence of condemnation may not be received by anyone else unless he has first been received by the one who separated him.

The sixth canon of the First Council of Antioch establishes the same. See Labbe, vol. II, pp. 46 and 563.

### III.

What could be imagined more absurd, or more injurious to the Roman See and to the whole discipline of the Church, than to say that Rufinus had been bound by the chain of anathema by the First See and had not been absolved, yet had nevertheless been kindly received into communion by the principal bishops of Italy?

For he was received by Venerius of Milan, Chromatius of Aquileia, Laurentius of Concordia, Petronius of Bologna, and Gaudentius of Brescia—bishops of Cisalpine Gaul and Venetia, all worthy of veneration for their great holiness.

Indeed, Chromatius advised the old man of Bethlehem to put an end to the hostilities, as Jerome himself testifies in book III of the *Apology*, p. 437. Would Chromatius have given such advice on behalf of a condemned man? Would he himself, and the others, have dared—despising the judicial sentence of Anastasius, the Supreme Pontiff and Primate of all Italy—to receive Rufinus into Catholic communion against the chair of Peter?

All these men held Rufinus, whom they dearly loved and who shared their communion, in their fellowship without anyone objecting, until the end of his life. In the meantime, I say nothing of the two Melanias and the other Romans, nor of Paulinus of Nola, Augustine of Hippo, and John of Jerusalem—men likewise highly distinguished and bishops celebrated throughout the Church—whose constant cultivation of Rufinus’s friendship is evident from the documentary evidence I have cited and may yet cite.

Would such eminent bishops have cherished the friendship of a man cut off from the communion of the faithful by the Roman Church’s senate? My spirit cannot bear to say this of such men.

Honoratus Faber thought it impious even to make such a claim, in his *Prodromus*, part II, chapter II, p. 84, col. 1. Indeed, since Rufinus had recoiled when he heard the Origenist errors and had issued a confession of his faith, Faber says that it appears certain that Rufinus was not condemned by Anastasius at all, but was left to his own conscience and to divine judgment.

One further point should be added. If Anastasius had wished to exclude Rufinus from the communion of the faithful, he would not have sent a judicial sentence of condemnation to John of Jerusalem or to Venerius of Milan, but—as bishop of the universal Church and also Exarch and Primate of all Italy—to Chromatius of Aquileia, in whose presbytery Rufinus was then present.

For Chromatius, as Primate of Venetia and Istria, had nothing to do with the bishop of Milan and nothing to do with the bishop of Jerusalem. Anastasius had made this perfectly clear when he sent Theophilus’s Paschal Letter for A.D. 401, translated into Latin by Jerome, not merely to Venerius, the Primate of Cisalpine Gaul, but also to Chromatius, the metropolitan of Venetia and Istria, for publication, together with the other bishops of his church, whether contributors or suffragans.

The same discipline would have been observed by the Supreme Pontiff in publishing an anathema against Rufinus. Rufinus was living in Chromatius’s parish—if he was at Aquileia—or in his province, if he was at Concordia. That he was living at Aquileia while this controversy was raging has been sufficiently demonstrated.

### IV.

From these considerations one may, indeed must, rightly conclude that Rufinus of Aquileia was not condemned by Pope Anastasius. Rather, only his Latin translation of Origen’s books *Periarchon* was disapproved—or, if one prefers, rejected—and this not by any edict or synodal decree, but by a private letter to John of Jerusalem.

Rufinus in Italy never received any knowledge of this letter from the Romans, nor from the very man to whom it had been written, although he was Rufinus’s close friend. He learned of it from Jerome alone, who was the first to reproach him with it and send it to him.

For Jerome says in book II of his *Apology*, p. 405:

> “Certainly, if you translate in order to prove him [Origen] a heretic, change nothing in the Greek, and attest to this very thing in your preface—the point which Pope Anastasius most prudently expressed in his letter, written against you to Bishop John.”

Jerome then appended the letter of Anastasius itself to his *Apology* and added:

> “And lest you perhaps deny this also, I have appended a copy of it, so that if you do not wish to hear your brother [Jerome] admonishing you, you may hear the bishop [Anastasius] condemning you.”

From this we learn that, for Anastasius’s letter to John to become known to Rufinus, it had to be sent to him from Rome, not from Bethlehem, and indeed by an adversary. If Jerome had known that the letter had been publicly circulated at Rome, he would have emphasized this repeatedly in his *Apology* and would have rightly reproached Rufinus with the fact that a copy of Anastasius’s letter had been sent to Rufinus from Palestine, without being compelled by any necessity to do so.

He sent it because he knew that it was unknown in Italy.

Jerome composed this *Apology* in A.D. 401. For in book I, p. 377, he says that two years earlier he had written against the praise that Rufinus had given him in the preface to his translation of the books *Periarchon*. He wrote this in A.D. 399, as I have noted elsewhere.

Therefore Jerome composed his first *Apology*, divided into two books, in A.D. 401. Pagius, against Baronius, Huet, and Norisius, presses the same point by other arguments under A.D. 401, § 10.

Venerius, mentioned in the letter of Anastasius, formerly a deacon of Ambrose, had succeeded Simplicianus in the see of Milan in A.D. 400.

### V.

Let us now see what Rufinus replied in his letter against the two books of Jerome’s *Apology* concerning the letter of Anastasius that Jerome had sent to him.

I have already noted that Rufinus’s letter, written to Jerome alone, has since perished. Its substance, however, can be gathered from Jerome’s reply, which is book III, formerly *Apology* II. I shall extract its passages from the same book III of Jerome, pp. 455, 457, 459, 462, and 468 of the new edition.

1. Rufinus says that no one could rightly believe that the priest of so great a city could have inflicted an injury, even upon an innocent man such as Rufinus, or even upon one who was absent.

2. He says that the letter of the holy Pope Anastasius was fabricated.

3. He says that it ought to have been transmitted to Rufinus by the very man to whom it had been sent, John of Jerusalem.

4. He says that he possessed the testimony—or *formata* letters—of Anastasius’s predecessor, Siricius, by which, as a pledge of his certain faith, he had been furnished when he departed from Rome for his homeland.

Concerning such *formatae* letters, Philippus Priorius should be consulted. Since Rufinus had openly obtained them after the Latin translation of the books *Periarchon* had been circulated at Rome, private letters fabricated under Anastasius’s name could no longer injure him. The testimony of the whole world was sufficient for him.

5. Jerome calls Anastasius’s letter, which he had sent from the East to Rufinus, the letter of the previous year. He also mentions other recent writings sent to the East in which Pope Anastasius adorns Rufinus with such flowers of praise.

What these writings were, we do not know. Were they of the same tenor as the letter under discussion? Certainly it is remarkable that none of the ancients mentions them, and that Jerome neither sent these writings to Rufinus nor wished to explain more clearly what they were, although they adorned Rufinus with such flowers.

Could they have been some reply to the Paschal Letters of Theophilus of Alexandria, in which the errors of Origen were set forth? That must be considered likely.

6. Rufinus again brings forward the *formata* letter of Siricius, given to him when he was travelling from Rome to Aquileia. He does not believe that this letter could have been invalidated by Anastasius, Siricius’s successor. He says that no errors had been discovered as having been spread by him after the death of Siricius. On the contrary, all the bishops of Italy had accepted his pure and open confession of faith and approved his exposition.

Jerome does not deny that the Italian bishops approved Rufinus’s confession of faith. He merely says that he is astonished:

> “I marvel how Italy approved what Rome despised; how the bishops received what the Apostolic See condemned.”

Anastasius made no reply to Rufinus’s *Apology for His Faith*. Jerome calls this contempt. He calls Anastasius’s letter to John of Jerusalem, which was unfair to Rufinus, a condemnation of Rufinus’s *Apology*.

7. Rufinus adds that the Apostolic See was not accustomed to revoke letters of peace once issued unless a new crime of heresy had arisen. Finally, he calls the letter of Anastasius FALSE and supported by fraud.

It should further be noted that Jerome certainly does not forcefully impose it as genuine. Jerome says only—and says this truthfully—that he did not fabricate it himself.

When Rufinus, in his homeland, suspected the authenticity of the letter, Jerome sent him to Rome; he sent him to the archives of the Roman Church. This itself proves that the letter had not been publicly circulated at Rome. Otherwise, why would a very recent letter, issued concerning so important a question and which ought to have been known and accessible to everyone, have to be sought in the secret archives of the supreme pontiffs as though it were an obscure and ancient document?

Would Rufinus’s enemies and Jerome’s supporters have tolerated such a letter being secretly hidden and not publicly available?

The great doctor counters that Anastasius could have written against Rufinus, even though Rufinus had previously been furnished with Siricius’s letters of communion; yet he does not say that Anastasius actually wrote it.

Nor does the great doctor ever reveal where he himself obtained the copy of the letter of Anastasius that was being circulated—whether from John of Jerusalem or from someone else. He ought certainly to have disclosed this publicly, so that the mouth of one denying its authenticity might more easily be stopped.

It is hardly credible that John, who had written to Anastasius on behalf of his friend Rufinus, would have wished to scatter among the public Anastasius’s reply, written solely to him about his friend and pleasing to neither of them, so that a copy of it would be sent not from Rome or from John’s side, but by Jerome himself to Rufinus as an object of ridicule.

Jerome, an inhabitant of the Bethlehem cave, raised in the camps of orators, and because of the distance of the regions not sincerely or adequately informed about Italian affairs by Rufinus’s enemies, conducts the case by the art of eloquence.

Rufinus had ended his letter with these words:

> “I hope that you love peace.”

Thus Rufinus himself, obeying the admonitions of the blessed Chromatius—which Jerome had excused himself from obeying against his will—made no reply to book III of Jerome’s work. The man who loved peace showed this by not scattering among the public his letter written to Jerome on his own behalf.

Nor did Jerome thereafter attack Rufinus by name. If he sometimes did so under other names and in riddles, he should not be said to have done so openly: what he did under a mask, he perhaps did because he did not wish it to be understood of whom he was speaking and was attempting in this way to avoid giving offense.

As for the letter of Anastasius, while such a violent conflict of minds was burning on both sides, it was by no means difficult for letters of this kind to be fabricated. Other letters had likewise been falsely attributed to Jerome, as though he were singing a recantation, and had flown into Africa, as he himself testifies in book II of his *Apology*, p. 419.

Nevertheless, we do not doubt that Jerome initially regarded this letter of Anastasius as genuine. But once Rufinus accused it of falsity, Jerome does not appear to have fought stubbornly for its authenticity. Anyone who carefully considers his third book will easily see this.

After Rufinus, Petrus Halloix, in *Origen Defended*, book IV, question 8, p. 333, and Honoratus Faber, in his *Prodromus*, part II, chapter II, p. 84, col. 1, certainly did not hesitate to call the letter of Anastasius into question.

### VI.

St. Augustine, who was a close friend of both men, could not approve these bitter quarrels between such eminent persons, given his gentle disposition.

In A.D. 402, Jerome entrusted to Asterius the subdeacon, who was returning from the holy places to Africa, a letter of his to be carried to Augustine. It is Letter 68 among Augustine’s letters, formerly 13.

In it Jerome mentions a reply that he had recently given to Rufinus’s letter. He says that reports of Rufinus’s writings had reached Africa and that he had previously sent Augustine a refutation of them. He promises to send at a more convenient time the more extensive work of his *Apology*, divided into two books.

Here are Jerome’s words:

> “With his customary recklessness, Calpurnius, surnamed the Wool-worker (*Lanarius*), sent me his curses”—that is, his letter against the two books of Jerome’s *Apology*.

He calls Rufinus by this name, alluding to the traitor of the same name who, according to Plutarch’s account of Sertorius, brutally cut down Livius Salinator, under whose standards he was serving.

Jerome continues:

> “I have learned that these things”—the curses, or Rufinus’s letter against the two books of Jerome’s *Apology*—“have reached Africa as well through his efforts. To these I replied briefly”—in *Apology* II, or book III of the *Apology*—“and I sent you copies of his little book. When the more extensive work”—his first *Apology*, divided into two books—“has become appropriate, I shall send it at the first opportunity. In it I took care not to injure Christian reputation in any respect, but only to refute the falsehood and madness of an ignorant and delirious man.”

Augustine was crushed in spirit when he read Jerome’s letter. For, in these significant indications of the old man’s goodwill toward him, he recognized that Jerome was somewhat irritated with him.

The most peaceful of men, struck by Jerome’s book in the case against Rufinus, almost trembled and wept when he saw such distinguished friends, previously celebrated by the praises of everyone, plunged into such a frenzy of anger.

Seizing this most timely opportunity, he wrote back to Jerome in Letter 15, now 73—a truly golden work, full of charity and moderation.

I shall quote here, as a lesson in human fickleness, the words that refer to the emotions of Jerome and Rufinus, from chapter III of that letter. The editors of the recent edition of Augustine’s works assign it to A.D. 404, that is, after both men had brought their writings to an end, at least publicly and principally on Rufinus’s side.

The words are these:

> “I do not know what abusive writings concerning your name may have reached Africa. Yet we received what you deigned to send in reply to those abuses. When I had read it, I confess that I was deeply grieved that, between persons so dear and intimate, joined by a bond of friendship known to almost all the churches, such a great evil of discord had arisen.
>
> “As for you, how much you restrain yourself and how much you hold back the goads of your indignation, so as not to return abuse for abuse, is sufficiently evident in your letters. Nevertheless, when I had read them, I wasted away with grief and grew stiff with fear. What would those things that he wrote against you have done to me if they had happened to fall into my hands?
>
> “Woe to the world because of scandals! Behold, it has happened; behold, it has been completely fulfilled which the Truth says: ‘Because iniquity will abound, the charity of many will grow cold.’ Upon what faithful hearts can persons now safely pour themselves out? Into whose bosom may trusting affection throw itself completely? What friend, finally, will not be feared as though he were going to become an enemy, if this thing that we lament could arise between Jerome and Rufinus?
>
> “O wretched and pitiable condition! O unreliable knowledge of what is present in the wills of friends, where there is no foreknowledge of what is to come! But why should I lament what happened to one concerning the other, when a human being is not even known to himself with respect to the future? He knows, scarcely and perhaps barely, what sort of person he is now; but what he will later become, he does not know.”

Thus Augustine.

The editors of the new edition of Augustine’s works, in their preface to volume II, chapter 68, remain uncertain which *Apology* Jerome sent to Augustine—whether the first or the second.

Certainly he did not send the first, divided into two books. Jerome calls that the more extensive work and promises to send it later. Therefore he indicates that he sent the second, in which he had already replied, partially or, as he says, in summary fashion, to Rufinus’s now-lost letter.

The bishop of Hippo, in Letter 166 to Jerome, chapter V, § 15, cites testimony concerning the origin of the soul from this same *Apology* II, p. 464.

From the words quoted earlier we infer that Augustine, although he had read Jerome’s *Apology* II and did not know Rufinus’s writings, sided with neither of the two in the disagreement that divided them. He did only this: he lamented such great enmity and earnestly desired that it be removed.

The man whom Jerome had called Calpurnius the Wool-worker (*Lanarius*), Augustine himself calls by his proper and true name, Rufinus.

Thus in A.D. 404, two years after the death of Anastasius, no condemnation of Rufinus had been heard. Otherwise the most holy bishop would have sided with Jerome, a thoroughly Catholic man, against a heretic struck down by the First See.

In religious affairs, middle courses are always the worst and never safe. Since Augustine sided with neither, he recognized both equally as friends and as genuinely Catholic men.

Honoratus Faber recognized the same point in his *Prodromus*, part II, chapter II, § 16, p. 82, col. 2.

## CHAPTER XX

I. Rufinus leaves the City with Melania in order to cross again into Palestine. The year of the death of Publicola the Elder, Melania’s son, is determined. II. Rome is besieged and sacked by Alaric, King of the Goths. III. The death of Rufinus, the place of his death, and the time are assigned. IV. Rufinus’s praises are reviewed.

## I

In what year of Christ Rufinus, after the *Apologies* and other writings which he had completed at Aquileia, took leave of his people in order to cross once more to Palestine with Melania is not yet well established by anyone. [Col. 0285C] I am certain that this happened after the death of Pope Anastasius, and indeed after the death of Chromatius, which I have shown must be assigned to A.D. 407 in Book III, chapter III, §9. Rufinus, then deprived of his most holy father, returned to Rome after having spent ten years with his household, when Anastasius’s successor, Pope Innocent, had already occupied the see for seven years.

In the following year, 408, while Alaric, king of the Goths, was pressing upon the city of Rome, the families of both Melanias resolved to provide for their safety and sail to Sicily, from where the elder Melania had intended to proceed to Jerusalem with Rufinus. With the elder Melania there were, besides Rufinus, Albina, Melania’s daughter-in-law, with her children; the younger Publicola; the younger Melania; and Pinianus, her husband. I have said something about them in Book V, chapter IV, §7.

Palladius, their friend and formerly their guest while he was prosecuting Chrysostom’s cause at Rome, reports these events in chapter 99, but omits the elder Publicola, the son of the elder Melania, the father of the younger Melania, and the father-in-law of Pinianus—a man who, in Christian virtues, deserved to be honored far more than his senatorial dignity. [Col. 0285D] He omitted him rightly, since he knew that he had already died.

The elder Melania possessed very extensive estates not only in Campania and Sicily, but also in Gaul, Spain, and Africa. When both Publicolas had died, these estates passed to the younger Melania, as the daughter of the elder Publicola and the sister of the younger. For Palladius attributes them to her.

For a long time, among the most distinguished scholars, a celebrated chronological question—upon which others depend—has been debated in various ways: in what year of Christ the elder Publicola ceased to live. The father of the *Annals* places it in A.D. 409, §27. The scholiast of the *Annals*, Pagi, likewise assigns it to that year, §9. Peter Francis Chifflet departed enormously from both of them in *Pauline Illustrated*, part II, chapter XXXIV, assigning it to A.D. 416. Norisius went in another direction in *Adventoria*, p. 20, where he argued at length for A.D. 399. But the editors of the new edition of Saint Augustine, and after them Tillemont in the places to be cited below, thought that A.D. 408 alone should be accepted.

[Col. 0286A] I believe that many chronological errors arising from this disagreement among distinguished men can easily be removed if I assign the death of the elder Publicola—marked by a definite chronological indication—to A.D. 400.

There exists Letter 46, formerly Letter 153 among Augustine’s letters, in which that same elder Publicola consults the bishop of Hippo about certain matters disturbing his tender conscience, namely, disputes between the African tenants of his estates in the province of Arzugitana and the pagans. The editors just mentioned dated this letter to A.D. 398. It is surprising that these excellent men, in *The Life of Augustine*, Book IV, chapter XV, §4, considered it uncertain which Publicola this was. Tillemont, volume X, p. 823, and volume XIII, p. 323, suspected that he should be understood as the son of the elder Melania. The cited passages do not permit us to doubt that he was.

When the mother Melania crossed to Africa to visit these estates of hers and enjoy Augustine’s sacred conversation, her son Publicola was still alive. [Col. 0286B] Saint Paulinus of Nola, in Letter 94, formerly Letter 249 among Augustine’s letters, after thanking Augustine for a letter—now lost—sent to him together with a certain book, which Paulinus and Melania had received at Rome for the feast day of the Apostles Peter and Paul from the deacon Quinctus, who had stayed there for some time, continues by praising the elder Melania and her only son Publicola. In earlier correspondence he had informed Augustine of Publicola’s recent death and asked him to console his kinswoman Melania in so great a loss.

It is therefore clear that the elder Publicola died at Rome, where he belonged to the senatorial order, and not elsewhere, after his mother Melania had crossed to Africa.

This is further confirmed by the following. After Augustine, writing to Paulinus, had praised Melania for her courage and steadfastness of spirit in the loss of her son, Paulinus, repeating these things in his subsequent reply to Augustine from the letter written to him, says once and again that he had previously written to Augustine about Publicola’s character and holiness. Therefore the elder Publicola died not in Africa but in Italy.

[Col. 0286C] It will be evident below, when I discuss the younger Publicola, that I do not say these things without reason. From Paulinus’s letter, in which he summarizes the Augustinian letter written to him, I shall bring forward several passages:

> You taught me, in the spirit of truth, the salutary moderation of mind to be maintained when mortals die; by this you saw that that blessed mother and grandmother, Melania—mother of the only son Publicola I, and grandmother of Publicola II and Melania II—had mourned the bodily death of her only son with a silent grief indeed, but with sorrow not dry of tears. Her restrained and grave tears you understood more deeply, as one whose spirit was nearer and more equal to her soul; and, preserving the strength of a manly spirit, you contemplated the maternal heart more fairly through the likeness of your own heart. Thus you perceived that she had wept, first moved by natural affection and then pierced by a weightier cause: she mourned not so much the human fact that she had lost, in this present world, her only son, dead by mortal condition, as that she considered him, almost forestalled by worldly vanity—for the ambition of senatorial rank had not yet left him—not received according to the holy yearning of her vows, so that from the glory of conversion he might have passed to the glory of resurrection, to receive with his mother their common rest and crown, if, following his mother’s example, he had preferred sackcloth and the monastery to the senate.[Col. 0286D]

Paulinus soon adds that he had previously written to Augustine about the virtues of this Publicola I:

> Nevertheless, that same man, Publicola, enriched by these works, departed—as I think I previously reported to your holiness—so that, although he did not wear the nobility of his mother’s humility in his clothing, he nevertheless preferred it in his mind.

And below:

> But I shall cease recounting more about the memory of a man so dear to me and so devoted to Christ, since I consider that in my earlier letters I narrated no little concerning him, and I can say nothing about the blessed mother of this son, Melania, sprung from the same holy root as the branches, either better or more sacred than what your holiness has deigned to utter and discuss concerning her.

[Col. 0287A] From these passages we learn that Paulinus first announced the death of the elder Publicola to Augustine by letter, perhaps even to Melania in Africa, before June 29, the day on which the feast of Saints Peter and Paul falls.

To establish the year with certainty, we must disentangle another matter connected with the year of the elder Publicola’s death. Augustine subsequently sent Paulinus Letter 95, formerly Letter 250, which Possidius, bishop of Calama, delivered to him while sailing to Italy, to the imperial court, in order to prosecute the case of his church, which the pagan inhabitants of Calama had overthrown:

> With regard to that joy—which the brother Possidius is sharing with you, and when you have heard from him what a grievous cause compelled him—you will recognize that I speak with complete truth.

Saint Augustine treats this matter specifically in Letter 91, formerly Letter 202, to Nectarius of Calama, a pagan, §8:

> Against the most recent laws, on the Kalends of June, during a pagan festival, a sacrilegious celebration was conducted without anyone preventing it, with such insolent audacity that—something not done even in the time of Julian—[Col. 0287B] a most shameless crowd of dancers passed directly through the same village before the doors of the church. When the clergy attempted to prohibit this most unlawful and disgraceful act, the church was stoned. Then, about eight days later, when the bishop Possidius had repeated the well-known laws to the magistrates, and while they were preparing to carry out what had been ordered by Augustus Honorius, the church was again stoned.

Augustine continues by narrating other deeds perpetrated by the pagans, horrible to hear.

The “most recent and well-known laws” which the great bishop mentions once and again had been issued by the emperor Honorius against the pagans of Africa in A.D. 399, during the consulship of Manlius Theodorus, vir clarissimus. For at that time, as Augustine himself testifies in Book XVIII, chapter XVIII of *The City of God*, in Carthage, the celebrated and most eminent city of Africa, the imperial officials Gaudentius and Jovius, on March 19, destroyed the temples of false gods and broke their images.

[Col. 0287C] This overthrow of pagan temples and destruction of images must also have been supported by imperial laws. Augustine indicates that the laws against which the pagans of Calama had offended—while celebrating their recently prohibited rites—were not one law but several, and calls them “most recent.” Let us investigate more precisely what they were.

In the Theodosian Code, Book XVI, title 10, *On Pagans, Sacrifices, and Temples*, laws XVII and XVIII, addressed to Apollodorus, proconsul of Africa, are extant. Both were issued at Patavium on August 20, A.D. 399, during the consulship of Theodorus, vir clarissimus. In the first, Honorius mentions another law which he had recently issued against pagan sacrifices:

> We have already removed profane rites by a salutary law.

That law is not presently extant. In the same law XVII, Honorius permits the festivals and games of the pagans, but without any sacrifice or damnable superstition. Law XVIII must also be referred to this matter, in which Honorius decrees:

> If anyone is discovered sacrificing, let the laws be enforced against him.

The people of Calama had offended against these laws when, as Augustine testifies, a sacrilegious celebration was conducted by them during a pagan festival. Augustine calls this pagan celebration sacrilegious, most unlawful, and most disgraceful because it represented the profane rites and sacrifices of the pagans forbidden by Honorius’s most recent laws.

[Col. 0287D] We therefore now possess the certain year and month in which Honorius undertook, by his enactments, to eradicate the superstitious celebrations of the Africans—celebrations which Augustine rightly called “most recent” and “well known” to the Africans, since the laws had been written to the proconsul of Africa.

The year of Publicola’s death now readily reveals itself. The pagans of Calama offended against these most recent and well-known laws, since they had only recently been published. Therefore the event occurred after August 20 of A.D. 399, on which date the laws were issued. The bishop of Hippo says that the crime was committed on the Kalends of June. It therefore occurred in the following year, A.D. 400, when Possidius, bishop of Calama, sailed to the imperial court on account of this same crime and carried Augustine’s letters to Paulinus at Nola, after the elder Melania’s departure for Africa and Publicola’s death.

[Col. 0288A] To summarize the matter briefly, the following must be established:

1. The Augustan laws against the pagans were issued on August 20, A.D. 399.
2. The elder Melania departed for Africa, and her only son Publicola died at Rome, before June of A.D. 400.
3. The disturbance at Calama broke out on June 1, A.D. 400.
4. Possidius undertook his journey to Italy to see the emperor in August of the same year.

On March 28, A.D. 401, almost eight months after Possidius’s voyage to Italy, Augustine received his letters. Nectarius had previously delivered Augustine’s letters to Possidius while Possidius was still staying at Calama. This is clear from Augustine’s Letter 104, formerly Letter 254, to Nectarius:

> I have read the letter of your kindness, in which you replied to me long afterward, after I had given my letters to be delivered to you. For I had written my reply while the holy brother Possidius was still with us and had not yet sailed. [Col. 0288B] But the letter which you deigned to give him on my account I received on March 29, almost eight months after I had written.

Counting back these eight months from March 27, A.D. 401, brings us to August of A.D. 400. In that month Possidius was still staying at Calama and had not yet departed for Italy; he received from Nectarius the letters Augustine had sent him.

[Col. 0288C] This explains why the editors of the Augustinian edition, in *The Life of the Holy Bishop*, Book VI, chapter V, following Tillemont, volume X, p. 608, and volume XIII, p. 460, assigned the death of the elder Publicola to A.D. 407 on the basis of erroneous calculations. They placed the return of the mother Melania from Palestine to Rome too late, in A.D. 402, although we have shown, together with the leading scholars of the chronological school, that it cannot by any means be removed from A.D. 397.

Once they had wrongly displaced Melania’s arrival in Rome, they likewise dragged her departure for Africa into a later, inappropriate place. For once one chronological error has been admitted, others necessarily arise in succession. The error was increased by conflating the two Publicolas into one and by accepting a single law of Honorius, issued in A.D. 408, instead of two others—or rather three—which had been issued by the same emperor in A.D. 399 for this very purpose.

Distinguished scholars, at the beginning of volume II of Saint Augustine’s works, nos. 99, 91, 94, and 95, and in the note to the same Letter 91, formerly 102, together with Tillemont, volume XIII, p. 997, thought that the bishop of Hippo was speaking of another law, which Sirmond published in the *Appendix to the Theodosian Code*, no. 12, and which Gothofred later transferred into the same code, Book XVI, title 10, Law XIX.

Yet when the holy bishop repeatedly calls the laws “most recent” and “well known,” he refers to several laws, and specifically to laws promulgated during the consulship of Manlius Theodorus, as I have said. These are the very laws which I have identified as issued in A.D. 399. They could not have been called “most recent” by Augustine after nine years, in A.D. 408, when only one of them—and that one the most recent—had been issued.

[Col. 0288D] The other law, issued nine years later, which these distinguished men believed Augustine meant without consulting the books of *The City of God*, was not sent to the proconsul of Africa, although it ought to have been sent to him if it concerned Africa, nor was it enacted during the consulship of Theodorus. As for the scholion appended to this law in Sirmond, in which it is said to have been promulgated at Carthage, Gothofred openly expresses doubt and considers the reading corrupt.

Moreover, this very law is said to have been issued at Rome, although Honorius was not at Rome on October 16, the date on which the law was promulgated, during the consulship of Bassus and Philippus in A.D. 408, but at Ravenna.

Nor are the difficulties yet exhausted. This law commands many things which had either long before been ordered and carried out in Africa or were wholly inapplicable to the crime of the pagans of Calama. These are:

1. The transfer of the grain allowances of the temples to the military grain supply.
2. The destruction of images.
3. The removal and destruction of altars.
4. [Col. 0289A] The confiscation of temples for public use.
5. The prohibition of banquets and celebrations.

Now that I have disarmed the advocates of the contrary opinion by means of this law itself, let us apply the other laws mentioned above to our case.

The pagans of Calama offended chiefly against law XVII and against another law, now lost, which had recently abolished profane rites. They offended against profane sacrifice and damnable superstition, as Augustine states in his letter to Nectarius, one of their fellow citizens, when he says that through them a sacrilegious celebration was conducted during a pagan festival.

This festival and this celebration require closer attention. The Floralia present themselves most opportunely, and Augustine certainly alludes to them. He had shortly before mentioned Flora:

> Her theatrical games are celebrated with such unrestrained and licentious obscenity that anyone can understand what sort of demon it is which cannot be appeased otherwise than by causing not birds, not four-footed animals, and finally not human blood, but something far more criminal—human modesty itself—to perish there as though sacrificed.

[Col. 0289B] Nothing, then, was equally foul and sacrilegious as the Floralia. These games, the same author testifies in Book II, chapter XXVII of *The City of God*, were accustomed to be celebrated with devotion proportionate to their obscenity.

Arnobius the African has very similar material in Book VII *Against the Pagans*. In the ancient calendars we indeed read that the Floralia were customarily celebrated at the beginning of May. But once the imperial calendars had abolished them, the pagan Carthaginians suddenly resolved to celebrate them on the Kalends of June. I recall having noted that the calendars sometimes varied even in celebrations of this kind, in Simeon Bosio’s letter II of Book XVI of Cicero’s *Letters to Atticus*.

Augustine’s words, “a celebration was conducted,” almost occur in the law which learned men attempt to turn to their own purpose, where pagans are forbidden to conduct any sort of celebration. The expression is common in designating the profane games and processions of the pagans and is frequently used; it means the same as “presented” or “exhibited.” See Gothofred’s *Legal Glossary*, under *agitare*.

[Col. 0289C] I have examined these matters at greater length in order to explain the question of the year of the elder Publicola’s death, which cannot be separated from the disturbance at Calama, and to demonstrate by firm arguments that the elder Melania, already long bereaved of her son, migrated with Rufinus and her relatives to Sicily before the destruction of Rome.

The conclusions I have set out agree in every respect with Palladius, a suitable witness, since he was an eyewitness. They also agree with the author of the *Life of the Younger Melania* in Laurentius Surius’s *Lives of the Saints*, under December 31.

For Palladius states in chapter 118 that the elder Melania returned from Palestine to Rome as soon as she heard about the condition of her granddaughter Melania: namely, that she had married and wished to renounce the world. This was in A.D. 397, the final year of Pope Siricius, as I have shown elsewhere.

In chapter 119, Palladius reports that the younger Melania married Pinianus at the age of fourteen. Together with the author of the *Life*, he testifies that in the twentieth year of her age, after she had lived seven years with Pinianus, she renounced the world, bereft of her two children and of her father Publicola.

[Col. 0289D] After these several chronological indicators, each supported by its own arguments and converging into a single account, I present them together, so that everything may be viewed at one glance according to chronological order:

**A.D. 397.** The elder Melania returns from Jerusalem to Rome, with her granddaughter Melania married to Pinianus in the fourteenth year of her age.

**399.** The emperor Honorius publishes three laws against the pagan Carthaginians, addressed to Apollodorus, proconsul of Africa.

**400.** After the elder Melania departs for Africa, Publicola, her only son, dies at Rome. Paulinus of Nola informs Augustine of this; he receives Augustine’s reply, written some time earlier at Rome, from the deacon Quinctus on June 29. The disturbance of the pagans breaks out at Calama. After the month of July, Possidius, bishop of Calama, sails to Italy.

**403.** The younger Melania, at her grandmother’s urging, in the twentieth year of her age and after spending seven years with Pinianus, bids farewell to the world together with her husband.

**408.** Both Melanias, with their households and Rufinus, cross from Rome to Sicily in order to preserve their chastity.

## II

[Col. 0290A] In that same year, A.D. 408, in which the most noble company of pious women and men arrived in Sicily, Rome was besieged by Alaric, king of the Goths, and redeemed with a great quantity of gold. Soon afterward, in the following year, A.D. 409, the faithless barbarian plundered and ravaged the mistress of the world in a pitiable manner.

That black day—fit to be numbered among the disasters of Egypt and Cannae—was August 24, together with the two following days. The elder Melania, foreseeing the future and having prophesied so great a calamity, rapidly sold her possessions and shortly beforehand provided for the safety and honor of her relatives by a swift flight.

According to Pagi’s calculations—which I find here carefully exact and preferable to the others—these events successively ennobled the years 408 and 409. See that eminent chronologer under A.D. 408, §§2 and 16, and under A.D. 410, §7 and the following sections.

Tillemont, who did not know Pagi’s work because it had not yet been published, assigned the destruction of Rome to A.D. 410 in *History of the Emperors*, volume V, p. 411.

Palladius narrates the matter thus in the *Lausiac History*, chapter 118:

> After all these people—the two Melanias, Albina, Pinianus, and, apart from Rufinus, the younger Publicola—had departed from Rome, [Col. 0290B] a certain barbarian storm, that of the Goths, which had long before been foretold even in the Prophets, burst upon Rome and did not leave behind even the bronze statues in the forum. Inflated by so great a destruction, Alaric ran furiously through Latium, Campania, Bruttium, and Calabria, filling everything with mourning and funerals.

We have a witness to the event in Olympiodorus, whose lucid fragments of history Photius preserved in codex 80. But Rufinus wonderfully illuminates the testimony of Olympiodorus.

Rufinus, having escaped with a distinguished company of Roman nobles to Messana, saw Rhegium Julii, situated at the tip of Italy and overlooking the Sicilian strait, burning in the fires of the Goths. At that time the devout man was placing the final hand on his Latin translation of Origen’s *Homilies on Numbers*.

Two celebrated scholars of these matters, Henry Valesius and Peter Francis Chifflet, have finally taught us this. They published Rufinus’s prologue, [Col. 0290C] customarily placed before that translation, at different times and in different places, each from different manuscripts. Valesius published it in his notes to chapter XXXVIII of Book VI of Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History*, printed at Paris by Antoine Vitré in A.D. 1659. Chifflet, unaware of Valesius’s edition, published it in part II, chapter XXV of *Pauline Illustrated*, from the Dijon edition of Philibert Chavance, A.D. 1662.

Because he had not seen Chifflet’s edition, Tillemont erred more than once in volume XII, article 128, p. 311. He believed that the prologue was addressed to Ursacius and distinguished Ursacius from the boy who served as Rufinus’s notary. I discussed the work at length in Book II, chapter VII, §3. Valesius’s edition is the more accurate, although in certain places it must be corrected with the help of Chifflet’s.

Rufinus addresses a certain Donatus with words taken from the martyr Cyprian’s address to another Donatus. He says that he had promised him a Latin translation of all Origen’s writings on the Pentateuch.

Was this Donatus a Sicilian? Certainly he was staying in Sicily with Rufinus in A.D. 409, while Rhegium Julii was being consumed by flames, which the army of King Alaric had brought upon it. Perhaps Donatus himself had taken refuge with Rufinus in Sicily after fleeing from Rome.

[Col. 0290D] Let us hear Rufinus speaking:

> The time for fulfilling my promise, as he says, was not seasonable but tempestuous and troubled. For what room is there for writing where hostile weapons are feared, where the devastation of cities and fields is before one’s eyes, where one flees amid the dangers of the sea, and where exile itself cannot be endured without fear? For, as you yourself also saw, a barbarian was before our eyes, while he was throwing the city of Rhegium into confusion by fire, held back only by the very narrow strait between us, where the Italian land is separated from Sicily.

> In such circumstances, what security could there be for writing, and especially for translating, when one is expected not to express one’s own meanings but to grasp those of another?

He soon adds that he had spent the nights, which were safer from fear of the enemy, as a consolation amid his misfortunes and to lighten his exile, rendering into Latin Origen’s *Homilies*—or perhaps excerpts or scholia—on Numbers.

[Col. 0291A] For, as Valesius observes from Sedulius and Jerome, Origen produced three kinds of work on Sacred Scripture:

1. Commentaries.
2. Scholia.
3. Homilies or treatises.

Rufinus also discusses this threefold work in his prologue, calling them:

1. Homilies.
2. Excerpts.
3. Explanations.

> Since you were pressing me, we arranged as best we could in Roman speech the materials gathered from different sources into a single order. You yourself also greatly assisted the labor of our Ursacius in many places, while, being over-eager, you thought the service of the boy-notary too slow.

Thus Donatus and Ursacius assisted Rufinus in preparing his Latin translation of Origen.

Ursacius, the brother of Exsuperantius, bishop of Lucania, is mentioned by Uranius in chapter III of the *Life of Saint Paulinus of Nola*.

Finally Rufinus says that, of everything Origen had written on the Mosaic Law, only the brief discourses on Deuteronomy remained for him to translate:

> If the Lord helps and grants health to my eyes, we desire to join these to the rest of the work, although my most loving son Pinianus, whose devout company, fleeing for the sake of chastity, we accompany, [Col. 0291B] imposes other tasks upon us. But pray together that the Lord may be present, grant peace to these times, give grace to those who labor, and bring the fruit of our work to the advancement of its readers.
