Donatus and Ursacius, therefore, also belonged to that most holy choir of Roman exiles, while Rufinus was then afflicted by an eye disease. But Rufinus was unable to bring to completion what he had promised his friend.

## III

For shortly afterward, weighed down by the illness he had mentioned and by old age, he brought his life to an end—at Messana, indeed, in sight of Rhegium Julii, the last city of Italy, to which he had fled after following that devout company.

Nor could this supremely devout man have breathed out his soul more happily than in the embrace of so pious a fellowship.

Norisius, who in Book I, chapter III of his *History of the Pelagian Controversy*, following Baronius, assigned the destruction of Rhegium to A.D. 410, thought that Rufinus’s death should be placed at the end of that same year or the beginning of the next.

[Col. 0291C] On August 27, three days after the capture of Rome, Alaric led his victorious troops into Latium and Magna Graecia, ravaging the country. Rufinus himself, addressing Donatus, refers to the fire of Rhegium as recent but already past, while he speaks of the illness from which he was suffering as present. Therefore Rufinus ended his days in A.D. 410, after Rhegium had been burned.

The month and day are not clear from the earlier authorities. The martyrology, however, which the Antwerp hagiologists frequently mention under the name *Florarius Sanctorum*, records Rufinus on June 14; see volume II, p. 782, column 2.

Jerome expressed the place and time of his death in magnificent words in the prologue to Book I of his *Commentaries on Ezekiel*. He began work on its interpretation at Bethlehem at the beginning of A.D. 411, taking up again the pen which, in the preceding year, A.D. 410, he had laid aside in grief after receiving the news of the capture of Rome. See Pagi, who explains the matter accurately under A.D. 410, §§17 and 27.

Later, when Rufinus’s death had become widely known in Palestine, where he had been famous, Jerome could not restrain himself from obscurely insulting the hands of his deceased adversary. Thus he addresses the virgin Eustochium:

> [Col. 0291D] You continually demand this, and the scar is gradually forming over the great wound—the scorpion is being crushed beneath the soil of Trinacria between Enceladus and Porphyrion, and the many-headed hydra has at last ceased to hiss against us.

[Col. 0292A] Rufinus had died earlier on the island which the ancients called Trinacria, among the Sicani, between the mountains which the poets’ fables say were laid upon the giants Enceladus and Porphyrion.

The Stridonian Father called Rufinus, by circumlocution, a scorpion with many limbs and a many-headed hydra, because of the great number of those who supported him.

In the printed editions of Jerome, *Porphyrius* has crept in in place of *Porphyrion*. This is the excellent emendation of the purple-robed scholar Jacob Peronius in his *Second Reply to the King of England*, section I, §9.

Apollodorus discusses both giants in Book I of the *Library*. Martial alludes to Porphyrion, the great giant, in Book XIII, epigram 75.

I have confirmed this point with particular care because Henry Valesius, a man who rendered distinguished service to ecclesiastical history, imagined in his notes to Book VI, chapter XIX of Eusebius’s *History* that Jerome was indicating the philosopher Porphyry.

But there is no evidence that Porphyry died in Sicily, although he acquired a great reputation for writing among the Sicilians. Jerome alludes to the dead and buried in Sicily—and specifically to giants who, by strength of arm and their enormous size, attempted to wage war against the gods. Such things cannot truly be said of Porphyry.

[Col. 0292B] See Lucas Holstenius, *Dissertation on the Life of Porphyry*, chapters II and III.

No critic had noticed the textual corruption in Jerome’s words which Peronius detected.

[Note: [Col. 0291D] We had corrected this long ago.]

But another error of Valesius must also be removed: he believes that Rufinus withdrew to Sicily after the capture of Rome, whereas Rufinus had withdrawn there before the city was besieged, as has been sufficiently demonstrated.

## IV.

This was the end of Rufinus the presbyter, a man who was a parent of Sacred History in the Latin Church. The Easterners as well as our own people always held him in the highest esteem for his learning and piety, as has been made clear throughout this entire history. Almost all who were especially distinguished in Catholic communion for their reputation for learning and holiness—and above all those who shone in the Church with episcopal dignity—appear to have cherished and honored him while he lived, and to have defended his cause at the very time when, because he disagreed with Jerome, he was counted among the heretics—by Jerome alone, evidently, and certainly not by the others.

That holy Father, although outstanding in every respect, was nevertheless quite unable in this controversy to induce those men, who knew Rufinus well and held him dear to the end of his life, to pass over to Jerome’s side. They were otherwise the fiercest enemies of heretics and, had Rufinus been one of them, would in no way have adhered to him. Indeed, we have shown that he was called blessed and holy as a term of honor.

Apart from Jerome and one or two men who followed him, no one of that age ever accused Rufinus of suspected heresy; none of the bishops excluded him from his communion. Certainly not Siricius, Anastasius, or Innocent, the pontiffs who successively occupied the chair of Peter, while Rufinus lived for twelve years within the bounds of the Roman primacy, at Rome, Aquileia, and Messana. Nor did Paulinus of Nola, Venerius of Milan, Gaudentius of Brescia, Petronius of Bologna, Chromatius of Aquileia, perhaps Laurentius of Concordia, Augustine of Hippo, or John of Jerusalem—men all of them most celebrated and accomplished bishops, who associated with Rufinus in the closest friendship.

Therefore, just as very few followed Jerome’s side when, deceived by Theophilus of Alexandria, he attacked Chrysostom, a most holy man, as a heretic, so he was able to persuade very few that Rufinus should be branded with the mark of heresy. Cardinal Noris, in *Pelagian History*, book I, chapter II, says that the Origenists brought it about that these most holy men were embroiled in mutual disagreements. Hence, from Jerome’s letter to Theophilus, he adduces the following words against Chrysostom, who had been deposed from the throne of Constantinople and was dead:

> “We have always desired that John, who formerly governed the Church of Constantinople, should please God, and we were wholly unwilling to believe the causes of his ruin, toward which he was being carried (though, as the context supplies, imprudently). But he, to say nothing of his other crimes, by receiving the Origenists into his intimacy and advancing many of them to the priesthood, and by causing great grief through this crime to Epiphanius, a man of blessed memory, a man of God who shone among the bishops as a brilliant star in the world, deserved to hear: ‘Fallen, fallen is Babylon.’”

[Col. 0291D] This letter is by no means Jerome’s to Theophilus; on the contrary, it is Theophilus himself writing to Jerome. Jerome translated it into Latin for that very reason and placed it at the head of the volume containing Theophilus’s invectives against Chrysostom, which he had likewise been compelled by Theophilus to translate into Latin, so as to avoid the odium attaching not only to the deed but also to the translation. We have explained the whole matter in our notes on that letter, restored it to its proper author, and separated it from another genuinely Jeromean letter with which it had previously been conflated. See volume I of our edition, pp. 750 ff. Moreover, Jerome never raged against Chrysostom, as Fontaninus falsely continues to claim. (BENEDICTUS.)

Facundus of Hermiane, in *Defense of the Three Chapters*, book VI, chapter V, testifies that words equal to these, and much harsher ones, against Chrysostom were read in the book of Theophilus of Alexandria that Jerome translated into Latin. Facundus rightly writes there, also in support of our case, the following words—certainly worthy of being fixed in everyone’s mind:

> “In that book we learn not what John was like—for he deserved none of these things—nor what Theophilus was like, whose virtue was proved in many respects, but rather what miserable human life is like, concerning which it is written: ‘For it is a testing upon the earth.’ For if such things happened to such men, what is there that we, and those like us, ought not to fear?”

No one, however, is unaware of the bitterness with which not only Jerome but also Cyril of Alexandria, in his letter to Atticus, raged against Chrysostom. Nicephorus Callistus offers this apology for them in *Ecclesiastical History*, book XIV, chapter XXVIII; Baronius also cites it under A.D. 412, §61: “For they were human beings and subject to human passions.” See other similar material in Noris, *Dissertation III on the One of the Trinity Who Suffered in the Flesh*, p. 169.

Jerome was truly a man of the greatest learning, penitence, and holiness, and supremely orthodox; he could tolerate no suspicion, however slight or insignificant, in matters of religion. It is therefore not surprising that, driven by zeal, and while absent, he sometimes attacked even men of sound faith after hearing such suspicions from others and having them magnified. Yet in matters of this kind, the testimony of one man, however great his authority, must not be preferred to the consensus of the whole remaining Church.

These considerations moved Noris, a man of great reputation and learning, to commit the following words about Rufinus to writing in book I, chapter IV of *Pelagian History*:

> “For the rest, Rufinus was not a heretic, although Jerome numbers him among heretics. For Saint Paulinus would not have maintained such a religious friendship with him; nor would Pinianus and Melania have brought him with them to Sicily; nor could he have lived in the suburban monastery of Pinetum if he had openly been infected with heresy.”

Add to this the other material that I have gathered in defense of his piety. Noris thinks that Rufinus himself shook off before Pope Innocent the suspicions of error under which he had labored before Anastasius, in the little book published by that same purple-robed scholar. But it has been shown by necessary arguments that this work does not belong to our subject. Rufinus, however, sufficiently and more than sufficiently drove all suspicions far from himself in his *Apology to Anastasius* and in his *Commentary on the Creed*. Jerome never opposed that Commentary in any way.

Before Noris, John Bollandus, volume I of the January series, January 2, p. 90, col. 2, §5, writing about Saint Macarius, the friend of Rufinus, had likewise stated that our presbyter had later renounced the errors of Origen, with which he had been imbued no less than Macarius, and that he would say so in its proper place when writing about Rufinus. Bollandus therefore had proposed to write somewhere about Rufinus as a saint. But certainly neither Rufinus nor Macarius could have renounced errors that they had never embraced.

[Col. 0293]

# Works of Tyrannius Rufinus, discussed above

## I. Genuine Works

### 1. Original writings

[Col. 0293C]

Treatise on the Adulteration of Origen’s Books. Explanation of the Twelve Blessings of the Patriarchs. *Apology*, or two books of invective, against Jerome. *Apology for His Faith* to Pope Anastasius. Two books of *Ecclesiastical History*, namely books X and XI, following the history of Eusebius. *History of the Hermits*, or *Lives of the Fathers*. *Explanation of the Creed*.

### 2. Translated from Greek into Latin

The Rule of Basil the Great. Eight Homilies of Basil the Great. Book I of Pamphilus’s *Apology for Origen*, containing the *Sentences against the Mathematicians*. Four books of Origen, *Περὶ ἀρχῶν* (*On First Principles*). Seventeen of his Homilies on Genesis. Thirteen on Exodus. Sixteen on Leviticus. Twenty-eight on Numbers. [Col. 0293D] Twenty-six on Joshua. Nine on Judges. Nine on the Psalms. One on the First Book of Kings. Four on the Song of Songs. Fifteen volumes, divided into ten books, on the Epistle of Saint Paul to the Romans.

Ten short works of Gregory of Nazianzus, namely: one book of the *Apologeticus*; *On the Epiphanies*; *On the Lights*; one book *On Faith*; *On the Nicene Faith, Pentecost, and the Holy Spirit*; *On Himself after Returning from the Countryside*; *On the Sayings of Jeremiah*; [Col. 0294C] *On the Reconciliation and Unity of the Monks*; *On the Destruction Caused by Hail*; *Against the Arians*.

The *Sentences of Sextus the Pythagorean*. The *Sentences of Evagrius C.* to the Monks. *Sentences on Apatheia* (*Freedom from Passion*). *The Book to Virgins*. The *Recognitions of Clement of Rome*. Nine books of the *Ecclesiastical History of Eusebius*. The Paschal Canon of Anatolius of Alexandria.

## II. Spurious and Other Men’s Works

A translation of Origen’s Homilies on Luke, not by Rufinus, to whom it is attributed, but by Jerome. A translation of the works of Josephus, not by Rufinus but by Ambrose. Commentaries on the first seventy-five Psalms of David. On Hosea. On Joel. On Amos. *Life of Saint Eugenia*. A shorter book *On Faith*. A fuller book *On Faith*.

## III. Doubtful Works

[Col. 0294D]

Seven Homilies of Origen on Matthew. One on John. *On Mary Magdalene*. *On the Epiphany of the Lord*—translated into Latin.

## IV. Lost Works

A letter to Jerome in which his first *Apology* is refuted. Letters to Anicia Faltonia Proba. A translation of several books from Latin into Greek.

[Col. 0295]

# Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 17

Rufinus, presbyter of the Church of Aquileia, was no small part of the Church’s learned men, and in translating from Greek into Latin he possessed an elegant talent. In the end, he made the greater part of the Greek library available to Latin readers: namely, the works of Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia; of Gregory of Nazianzus, a man of extraordinary eloquence; the books of Clement of Rome’s *Recognitions*; the *Ecclesiastical History* of Eusebius of Caesarea in Palestine; the *Sentences of Sextus*; and the *Sentences of Evagrius*. He also translated the *Sentences of Pamphilus the Martyr against the Mathematicians*.

Whatever of all these works is read by Latin readers with the prefatory prologues was translated by Rufinus; whatever is without a prologue was translated by another, who did not wish to compose a prologue. As for Origen, Rufinus did not translate everything, since Jerome too translated a number of works, which can be distinguished by their prologues.

By his own labor—or rather by the gift of God’s grace—Rufinus also expounded the Creed, so that in comparison with him others may scarcely be thought to have expounded it at all. He also discussed Jacob’s blessing of the Patriarchs in three senses: historical, moral, and mystical. He wrote many letters exhorting people to the fear of God, among which those he sent to Proba are especially notable.

He also added books X and XI to the *Ecclesiastical History* that, as we have said, was written by Eusebius and translated by Rufinus himself. He also answered a detractor of his little works in two volumes, arguing and proving that, with the Lord’s help, he had exercised his talent out of regard for God and for the benefit of the Church, whereas the detractor, driven by the spur of rivalry, had turned his pen to denunciation.

[Col. 0295]

# Two Books of Tyrannius Rufinus, Presbyter of Aquileia, on the Blessings of the Patriarchs

“I have addressed this note to Rufinus the presbyter, the spiritual companion of Saint Melania, truly holy and devoutly learned, and for that reason joined to me by the deepest affection.”

Saint Paulinus, *Letter XXVIII to Sulpicius Severus*. (C)

# Paulinus to Rufinus the Brother, Greetings

[Col. 0295] In Barraeus’s edition, “Bishop of Nola” was incorrectly added. At that time Paulinus had not yet obtained episcopal dignity; he was serving only in the rank of presbyter—namely, in the year 398, when he wrote this letter to Rufinus. Brunius, otherwise a learned editor of Paulinus himself, is therefore also mistaken in dating it nearly a full decade later, around the year 408, apparently following Tillemont’s arguments. After the arguments of the distinguished Fontanini, which may be read in the preceding *Life of Rufinus*, book and chapter II, there is no need for us to demonstrate this dating at greater length. There is even less reason for us to defend the genuineness of the letter against the suspicions of learned men who have accused it of forgery. The letter itself makes clear that the only motive was hostility toward the name of Rufinus to whom it is addressed, so that Saint Paulinus might not appear to have been joined to him in friendship.

(C)

### 1–2. I.

Even brief letters from your like-mindedness are a great refreshment to us, just as a thirsty field is revived by dew when rivers are scarce. Thus, although a short letter—yet yours—has refreshed us, we acknowledge this through the boy of our common children [Col. 0296: Rufinus’s letter is not extant]; but at the same time we are again distressed [Col. 0296: the recent edition incorrectly reads *affectus*], because you have now decided to seek Rome amid the heat of anxiety and the uncertainty of delays.

May the Lord grant that we may very soon rejoice in the outcome of our undertaking, so that, just as we sympathize with those who are anxious, we may likewise share in their happiness, and may nevertheless begin to hope for the benefit of your presence if you begin to be certain of your own judgment—or of the Lord’s will concerning you.

### II.

Certainly, I gladly accept your gracious admonition, by which, loving us as you love yourself, you urge me to devote myself more attentively to Greek literature; but I cannot fulfill it—unless perhaps the Lord assists my desires so that I may enjoy your companionship for a longer time. For how can I make progress in an unknown language if there is no one from whom I may learn what I do not know?

I believe that in the translation of Saint Clement [Col. 0297A: Roman Clement, whose Greek copy of the *Recognitions* Rufinus, as reported in his *Life*, brought back from the East to Italy and lent to his host Paulinus for Latin translation; when he sent a specimen of that translation to our author, it was found not to correspond sufficiently accurately to the Greek, and therefore he did not put the finishing hand to it]—besides my other failures of talent, you especially noticed this poverty caused by my ignorance: that wherever I could not understand or express the words, I translated by grasping the sense—or, more accurately, by guessing at it.

That is why our author kindly urged him to devote himself more attentively to Greek literature, so that when he was unable to grasp the words sufficiently or render them back into Latin, he would not be forced to sketch the sense according to his own opinion rather than report it. The man, humbler than any other, admits this about himself. It is clear from this, however, that Rufinus did not interpolate Paulinus’s translation but composed an entirely new one, since in his dedicatory letter to Gaudentius he professes that he departed neither from the ideas nor even sufficiently from the words and expressions. “This,” he adds, “although it makes the language less ornate, renders the account more faithful.”

I therefore need God’s mercy all the more, so that he may grant me a fuller abundance of you, because for a poor man it will be like riches—or even like gathering with the eager mouth of a hungry heart the crumbs falling from a rich man’s table.

[Col. 0298A] In the recent edition of Saint Paulinus, *ut micas* (“as crumbs”) was printed incorrectly instead of *vel micas* (“or even crumbs”).

### III.

At the time when these writings were being composed, the chapter from Genesis in which Judah is blessed by Jacob happened to fall beneath my eyes as the appointed reading. And because the Lord had provided this most opportune occasion, I thought it right, after a lapse of time, to knock at the doors of your heart [Col. 0298A: Desire had requested precisely this shortly before, in Letter XLIII: “But if you, blessed and pure vessel fit for God, have received an understanding of that blessing by which the Patriarch, enlightened by the prophetic Spirit amid bodily blindness, addresses his sons, set forth for me in your reply the mysteries of the kingdom and the sacraments laid up for ages and revealed for the ages,” etc.].

Therefore, if you love me—or rather, because you love me greatly—I ask you to write to me as you understand the blessing of the Patriarchs itself. And if you know anything difficult or worthy of knowledge in them, let me know it. Above all, however, write about that chapter in which he says:

> “Binding his colt to the vine, and the foal of his she-ass to the *cilicium*” (Gen. 49:11).

[Col. 0298A] Rufinus notes with great learning in the subsequent *Response* that *cilicium* in the Latin manuscripts arose from the Greek word ἕλικι through the addition of one or another small letter: “I think that this very Greek word was anciently placed in the Latin copies,” and so forth. Ambrose and Augustine, however, read it in this way. Rufinus translates it as *palmes* (“vine-shoot”). Other Latin writers, such as Cyprian in book I *Against the Jews*, prefer *ad helicem* (“to the helix”).

Who is his colt, or whose foal is it? And why is his own colt tied to the vine, while the foal of the she-ass is tied to the *cilicium*?

[Col. 0297B]

# On the Book of Rufinus, Presbyter of Aquileia, on Judah’s Blessing, to Paulinus the Presbyter

[Col. 0297] The original title may once have been “Tyrannius Rufinus to Paulinus the Presbyter,” as may also be gathered from the ancient author soon to be cited, the author of the book *On Twelve Writers*, which is appended to Isidore and Ildefonsus. Certainly it is hardly credible that Rufinus, at that time, when he had not yet returned to Aquileia after a long absence resembling a restoration from exile, should have called himself a presbyter of Aquileia. Moreover, he had not yet been ordained when he first left Aquileia, and therefore had not yet been enrolled in the presbyterate of that Church.

[Col. 0297B] To that holy and great man, Pontius Meropius Paulinus, who was later made bishop of Nola, and to whom belongs the letter to Rufinus that immediately precedes this one.

The most learned men have missed the point: they imagine some other Paulinus and have allowed themselves to be deceived, especially by the author just cited, of the book *On Twelve Writers*, who did not know him when he says that our author wrote to a certain Paulinus the presbyter about the Blessings of the Patriarchs, and so forth.

## Preface

### 3–4. I.

The more I excuse myself to you and declare myself less capable of answering what you ask, the more insistently you question me and seek out more difficult matters. It is as though, after discovering a fault in a slow ox, you were to pierce its reluctant shoulders and retreating back with more obstinate goads.

Consequently, you must immediately learn this as well: even if we can move the burden you place upon us, at least with bowed neck, we nowhere possess the ability, with a more abundant power of speech, to reach the open and spacious fields and traverse their extended distances in swift courses.

[Col. 0298B] The sense seems impeded and not entirely sound. Apply a corrective hand to it if you read *effundere* (“to pour forth”) for *effundenti* (“pouring forth”).

Therefore allow us, if we should happen to wish to proceed more slowly, to reach by the steps we can take the place to which you call us.

[Col. 0299]

### II.

You ask us how we are to understand what is written in Genesis about the Patriarch Judah. Israel, his father, while predicting to each of his sons what he foresaw would happen, says of him, among other things:

> “Binding his colt to the vine, and the foal of his she-ass to the vine-shoot” (Gen. 49:11).

You have written, “and to the *cilicium*, the foal of his she-ass,” whereas in Greek it reads:

> καὶ τῇ ἕλικι τὸν πῶλον τῆς ὄνου αὐτοῦ  
> “and to the *helix*, the foal of his she-ass.”

[Col. 0299A] We have restored the Greek in more than one place. The sense had also been obscured by faulty punctuation.

The Greeks call a *helix* (ἕλιξ) a vine, not so much a vine-shoot—as our copies have it—as those little tendrils, or branches of a tree, or stakes, or whatever supports they may be, which, as I suppose, farmers call *capreoli* (“tendrils”):

[Col. 0299A] I would rather read *ruscinulis* or *runcinulis*. One of these words may have been derived, in some fashion, from the pruning hooks called *ruscariae*, mentioned by Cato; the other from the *runces* mentioned by Columella. Certainly I have no idea what *rucinnulus* means, and I do not think it was ever known to writers on agriculture. What follows is illuminated by these words of Varro, book I, chapter XXXI, on vines:

> “On the other side it is called a *caprea* because it produces a *capreolus*, that is, a twisted vine-shoot like a curl; for, so that it may hold itself, the vine creeps toward a place where it can take hold. From this act of taking hold it is called a *capreolus*.”

Through these interlacings the vine-shoot is secure and in no danger of falling; either it is weighed down by fruit or it is stretched out in wandering height.

### 5–6.

I therefore think that this same Greek word was anciently placed in the Latin copies, as were several other words, and that in the course of time copyists who did not understand it supposed *cilicium* to be written instead of ἕλικι.

[Col. 0299A] Understand this as though it were treated like a proper name, *Elici*. This is a striking specimen of Rufinus’s critical art.

### III.

In this matter, indeed, the translator’s error is easily corrected. But it is not so easy to discover the meaning intended by the interpreter himself, unless the entire chapter is brought into consideration. The treatment of the whole chapter would be fuller and clearer if it had begun from the opening of the Blessings themselves.

That, of course, requires no small amount of leisure and time—or, to speak more accurately, it demands a mind illuminated by the Holy Spirit. Therefore, insofar as the modest measure of our understanding permits, and the time allows, and those who are urgently pressing us for responses to Origen [Col. 0299A] permit so great a matter to be treated with such brevity [perhaps: “carried out”], we shall state, without prejudice to those who may think more correctly, what we meanwhile understand about this chapter, in accordance with the trust with which you command us to confide everything to you.

[Col. 0299A] At that time Rufinus, living in the monastery of Pinetum, was translating into Latin Origen’s celebrated books *Περὶ ἀρχῶν* (*On First Principles*), in order to oblige the monk Macarius, a man exceedingly eager for the writings of Eastern authors and especially of the Origenists. Indeed, during those same days of Lent he had scarcely finished the first two books when he composed this Commentary for Paulinus. He himself clearly testifies to both matters. He mentions the first in the Preface to book III of *On First Principles*, addressing Macarius: “I have translated the preceding two little books of *On First Principles* during the days of Lent, not only at your insistence but even under your compulsion. But since …” He mentions the second in the following letter to Paulinus, which serves as the Preface to the second book of this very Commentary: “Because during the days of Lent, while I was staying at the monastery of Pinetum, I wrote these things to you, I could not conceal my foolishness even from the brothers who were present.” At that time, therefore, Macarius was pressing and urging him to finish the translation he had begun.

### IV.

I know that very many interpret this passage about the Lord in such a way that they assert that nothing said here applies to the Patriarch Judah. [Lacuna of approximately ten lines.] They argue that Judah is nowhere shown to have slept like a lion, nor to have been raised like a lion’s cub, nor can it in any way be proved that the nations hoped in him.

[Col. 0300A] One among many is Saint Ambrose, who in chapter IV, no. 17, of the treatise bearing his name—composed approximately ten years before Rufinus—says: “The address appears to be directed to the Patriarch Judah, but that later Judah, namely Christ, the true confessor, is expressed. He was born from that tribe and alone is praised by his brothers, of whom he says, ‘I shall declare your name to my brothers’: Lord by nature, brother by grace, whose hands, which he extended toward the unbelieving people, are upon the backs of his enemies,” and so forth, which he applies to each part of the passage.

[Col. 0300A] From the word *pro­babuntur* (“will be proved”) there is a great lacuna of approximately ten lines, extending to the mutilated word *mis*, where it says *plurimis caeteris*. The oldest manuscript of Murbach in Alsace, cited by Fontanini, supplies the missing text. See the lengthy discussion of this matter in *Life of Rufinus*, book and chapter II, no. 6.

I add one point concerning the cause and origin of the lacuna. The most ancient manuscript of Georgius Pictorius—which, as he himself says, was written in Roman capitals like those of the Florentine Pandects, without any punctuation, more than a thousand years ago—seems to be none other than the manuscript from which Herold’s first edition was taken and which was then copied by Grynaeus and Barraeus. Nor, I think, is it other than the imperial manuscript, which Lambecius reports to have been mutilated by that same passage of lines down to the final syllable of the incomplete word *mis*, although otherwise more than twelve hundred years old and written without division between words. I believe it passed from Ensisheim to Vienna and was brought into that library.

It should also be noted in this connection that when Barraeus says he extracted Rufinus’s writings from the remains of the venerable monastery of Mont-Dieu, he is not speaking specifically of these *Blessings of the Patriarchs*, but of other books of Rufinus, especially the Commentaries on Hosea and so forth. Fontanini seems not to have understood these two points sufficiently.

But when he says:

> “A prince shall not fail from Judah, nor a ruler from his thigh, until he comes to whom it has been entrusted—that is, the kingdom—and in him the nations shall hope,”

because the words “until he comes to whom it has been entrusted, in whom the nations shall hope” are plainly spoken of Christ, we are undoubtedly compelled to understand someone other than Christ as the one from whose seed the ruler shall not fail until Christ comes.

For it is not fitting to understand as that Christ the one from whose seed the ruler shall not fail until Christ comes, since that ruler certainly failed at Christ’s coming. This itself was an indication that the one to whom it had been entrusted—that is, Christ—had come.

Some things are referred to Judah. As in very many other passages, this chapter too must be understood in such a way that the exposition proceeds by alternating senses, and that the interruption of the historical meaning reveals the hidden mystery of the mystical sense.

# Book I: The Blessing of Judah

[Col. 0301A] 7

### 1.

He says, therefore:

> “Judah, your brothers shall praise you. Your hands shall be upon the backs of your enemies” (Gen. 49:8).

This may be referred either to Judah himself or to the kings who appear to have descended from him. Governing the kingdom of that people, they subdued the backs of their enemies.

But it is also suitably understood of Christ, who is rightly praised by his brothers—that is, by the Apostles whom he himself called brothers in the Gospels (Matt. 28). His enemies, upon whose backs his hands rest, are understood to be those whom the Father promises to place beneath his feet, saying:

> “Until I place your enemies beneath your feet” (Ps. 109).

They are enemies so long as they are unbelieving and faithless; therefore they are struck on the back. After they have been converted, they become brothers and praise him who, having called them into adoption by the Father, made them both his co-heirs and his brothers.

He rightly said that Christ strikes the backs of his enemies. For all who worshipped idols turned their backs to God, just as the Lord reproaches them through the prophet, saying:

> “For they turned their backs to me and not their face” (Jer. 2:27).

He therefore strikes these backs so that, once converted, they may at last turn their backs upon idols and raise their faces toward God, and do what is written in what follows:

> “And let the sons of your father worship you.”

For when they worshipped him—or perhaps, according to the conjecture, “when they shall have worshipped him”—they were made sons of the Father and received the spirit of adoption, in which they cry, “Abba, Father” (Gal. 4). For no one says “Lord Jesus Christ” except in the Holy Spirit (1 Cor. 12).

This statement is related somewhat harshly to Judah, unless we say, by an extended use of the expression, that the sons of Judah were worshipped as kings by their brothers—that is, by the other members of their tribe.

[Col. 0301D] The old author of the little book *On the Blessings of Jacob the Patriarch*, whose work we have presented in specimen form in volume III of the Jeromean works, Appendix, p. 739, should often be cited and compared with our author, both because of his own merit and because of his novelty. So far as I know, the work has not yet entirely appeared in print, but we possess a complete copy taken from a Bologna manuscript, as we explain in the Preface. Here he has no hesitation in referring the prophecy properly to Judah. “Clearly,” he says, “he established—or gave—the kingdom that Reuben had taken away to Judah, saying that he was to be worshipped by his remaining brothers, which plainly corresponds to royal dignity,” and so forth.

### 2.

> “Judah is a lion’s cub; from the shoot, my son, you have ascended. You lay down and slept like a lion and like a lion’s cub; who shall rouse him?” (Gen. 49:9).

In these little verses we are not merely confined but almost shut out. For if we explain “lion’s cub” as referring to Judah on account of his courage in warfare, how shall we explain the statement that a son is said to have ascended from a shoot?

The word “shoot” is called *βλαστόν* (*blaston*) in Greek. It is more properly interpreted as a shrub or branch, which is accustomed to sprout again from a root or from the very strength of a tree. From what shrub, then, or from what branch will Judah be said to have ascended? Or how did he lie down and sleep like a lion and like a lion’s cub, so that it is asked who will rouse him?

Unless perhaps someone, forcing the meaning, wishes to assert it in this way: Judah proceeded from a shoot—that is, as we said above, from a shrub or branch—which signifies something arising from the very strength and power of his father. In confidence of his strength he lies down and rests like a lion and like a lion’s cub; and no one dares to rouse him because, on account of the greatness of his strength and the power of his—

[Col. 0302D] I would prefer *bellorum* (“wars”) to be restored here, since the reading *beatorum* (“blessed ones”) is entirely irrelevant.

—because of the greatness of his strength and his power in war, no one dares to rouse him to battle.

But a mystical exposition will fit this passage much more suitably, in which the lion’s cub, Christ, is indicated not only *physically* (*φυσικῶς*, *physikōs*) but also figuratively (*τροπικῶς*, *tropikōs*).

For the *Physiologus* writes the following about a lion’s cub: when it has been born, it sleeps for three days and three nights. Then, at its father’s roar or bellow, as though the place of its lying were shaken, the sleeping cub is roused.

[Col. 0302D] The ancient author just cited says in his unpublished work: “He calls the Savior the lion’s cub … It is rightly called a lion’s cub, whose nature is said to be that, when born, it sleeps for three days and then rises, awakened by its father’s roar. This figure most beautifully suits the Lord’s sleep: he slept for three days and cried to the Father, ‘But you, Lord, have mercy on me and raise me up.’ Once raised, he ascended to seize the prey, because, having stripped Hell, he carried the righteous with him to the heights as an excellent spoil, triumphantly as a conqueror,” and so forth.

This cub therefore ascends from a shoot. For he was born from a Virgin—not from seed, but from a virgin without intercourse with a man and without natural seed: Christ. Like a shrub or branch, he is the one in whom the truth of the flesh assumed from the Virgin is most clearly declared in the sacred shoot, and he is shown to be free from the contamination of fleshly and human seed.

> “Lying down, you slept like a lion and like a lion’s cub.”

That he plainly lay down and slept is shown to have been spoken of the passion of death. But let us see why he sleeps like a lion and like a lion’s cub.

Regarding the cub’s sleep, it has already been said that it is most suitably applied to Christ, who, buried for three days and three nights in the heart of the earth, fulfilled the sleep of death.

As for “like a lion,” I think it should be understood in this way: Christ’s death was the crushing and triumph of the demons. For whatever prey that opposing lion had seized, after man had been struck down and cast away, our lion tore away from him. Finally, returning from the underworld and ascending on high, he led captivity captive (Eph. 4:8).

In this way, even in his sleep he was a lion, conquering and defeating all things, and he destroyed the one who held the power of death (cf. Acts 3). And like a lion’s cub, he is raised on the third day.

> “Who shall rouse him?”

The statement rightly signifies, as though in the person of a prophet asking who will raise Christ, because the Apostle says:

> “God raised him from the dead.”

And again:

> “He who raised Christ from the dead will also raise your mortal bodies, because of his Spirit dwelling in you” (Rom. 8).

Christ himself likewise says in the Gospels:

> “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.”

But he was speaking about the temple of his body (John 2).

Since he himself is said to have raised his temple, while God is said to have raised him, the Prophet, struck with amazement at so great a unity and undividedness of the Father and the Son, rightly says:

> “Who shall rouse him?”

[Col. 0303D] Saint Ambrose likewise notes that the present verse teaches that the Son of God is of one nature with the Father. The unpublished author says: “When he adds, ‘Who shall rouse him?’ the implied answer is, ‘Who but the Father?’ For no one—not merely any mortal human being, but not even any angel—could do so, except the one of whom the Apostle Peter said to the Jews, ‘Whom God raised from the dead, of which we are witnesses,’” and so forth.

### 3. “The Prince shall not fail from Judah, nor the ruler from his thigh, until those things come which are laid up” (and, as it is found in other copies, “Until he comes for whom it is laid up”), “and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. 49:10).

This passage plainly refers to Judah. For it is established that, until the birth of Christ, princes from the race of Judah did not fail, nor rulers from his thighs, up to King Herod, who, according to the historical account written by Josephus, was a foreigner and is said to have insinuated himself into the kingdom of the Jews through ambition.

[Note: In several places, but especially in Book XIV of the *Antiquities*. Yet this interpretation of the passage is commonly found among the ancient writers. Saint Ambrose says: “As we have taught in the Treatise on the Gospel, through Herod the adulterated succession lost the prerogative of dignity.” And the frequently cited unpublished author says: “Until Herod, a foreign king, was appointed over them.” A little later: “When Hyrcanus, the last king of the Jews, had been delivered over to the extremity of evils, Herod, a foreigner, received the Jewish kingdom from Caesar Augustus. In his time, in accordance with this prophecy and the testimony of the Gospel, he who was to be sent, our Lord and Savior, arrived.” I omit the others.]

As soon, therefore, as this happened, and the ruler from the thighs of Judah failed, he came for whom the kingdom had been laid up; in him the faith of the Gospel and the spread of the Churches teaches how the nations should hope. Those things are said to be “laid up” which are to be brought forth at the appropriate time, just as Christ is also said to have come at the end of the ages, when the Apostle says, “Behold, now is the acceptable time” (2 Cor. 6), namely, for salvation to be bestowed upon the nations.

[Note: The Greek copies, certainly; for although Rufinus praises the Latin text, the entire diversity of the Greek books—and especially of the distinguished ones—is involved here. If the reading praised first was common to the Latin edition, which is commonly called the Italic, we conjecture that it was derived from an Alexandrian manuscript, somewhere less carefully corrected, which preferred τὰ ἀποκείμενα αὐτῷ, “the things laid up for him.” It was most correctly restored from the Vatican manuscript, ᾧ ἀπόκειται, “for whom it is laid up.”]

If, however, someone wishes to accommodate the course of both interpretations in every respect, he may perhaps force the passage into being understood of Christ also in this way: “The Prince shall not fail from Judah”—that is, those who are appointed princes of the Churches after his resurrection; “nor the ruler from his thighs”—the rulers, too, of the Christian people, from the thighs of Christ.

In this manner he will explain that the members of Christ are undoubtedly to be understood spiritually, those whom the Apostle calls the people of the faithful (1 Cor. 6). His thighs, therefore, understood spiritually, can indicate those who, through the firmness and constancy of their strength, seem to support and bear the whole body of the Church. Or, because the generation of human seed is customarily expressed figuratively by the term “thighs,” while among us “the one who sows sows the word” (Luke 8), those who offer the ministry of the word to the Church may therefore be understood as rulers from the thighs of Christ.

“Until those things come which are laid up for him”: this may be understood to mean that, until the consummation of the age, these rulers will not be lacking, until those things come which are laid up—those things which God has prepared for those who love him.

“And he himself shall be the expectation of the nations”: namely, on the day of judgment, when all nations and peoples will await Christ the judge in fear of heart and trembling of conscience.

### 4. “Binding his foal to the vine, and the foal of his she-ass to the vine-shoot” (Gen. 49:11).

This is said of Christ, and of him uniquely. For he himself bound his foal to the vine, who said, “I am the true vine” (John 15). To this vine, therefore, he binds both his foal and the foal of his she-ass (Mark 11).

[Note: The still unpublished author agrees almost word for word: “In these words let nothing historical be sought, but let the whole be understood typologically. For our Lord and Savior bound his foal to the vine when he subjected the untamed people of the nations to the commands of the Apostles, and so forth. He also bound his she-ass to the vine—that is, the Synagogue—which at the end of the age he will recall from unbelief and, though oppressed by the yoke of the Law, subject to the discipleship of the Church; and thus there will be one flock and one shepherd,” and so forth.]

His foal is the people from the nations, upon whom the burden of the Law had never yet been imposed, and upon whom no one had sat except himself, the first (Luke 19). The foal of his she-ass, however, is that which had been chosen for salvation from the former people, who are now named figuratively under the image of a she-ass; concerning them the Prophet says, “If the children of Israel should be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved” (Hos. 1).

The she-ass, therefore, being rejected because she preferred to bear the burden of the Law in unbelief, the foal born from her is chosen—that is, a new people from the old is admitted through faith and joined to the people from the nations.

Christ is therefore called the vine in that aspect in which he assumed human nature. To this nature the Word of God binds his foal—that is, joins and unites his people to the manner of life which he himself lived in the flesh—so that, through imitation of him, the foal bound to him may become with him both a son of God and a co-heir of Christ (Rom. 8).

As for the vine-shoot, concerning which we explained at the beginning what it signifies, we can understand it in this way: it is the faith that is in Christ, which holds fast to the rule of the present life and supplies confidence in the hope of the future.

[Note: I restore the manuscript reading *tenet*, “holds,” which Barraeus rejected without cause in favor of *ministrat*, “supplies,” which he substituted on his own. For Rufinus, *regulam tenere* means the same as “to guide the reins” or “to hold the bridle.”]

The vine, then, seems to signify that the deeds of Christ living in the flesh are imitated by those who believe in him and cling to him. But the vine-shoot—that is, ἕλιξ (*helix*), which is understood not so much as a branch as the thing by which a branch is connected to a tree and secured against falling, an aid by which it is protected and withstands and rejects winds and storms—indicates the hope of future blessings.

[Note: This was no reason for Barraeus to reject the word *respuere*, “to repel,” and replace it with *donorum*, “of gifts,” on his own authority.]

For every believer awaits the completion of salvation not only in the things he has done, but also in those things which he hopes for and believes are to come; in this way, bound and strengthened by hope to a certain tree of patience, he endures the storms and tempests of temptations.

No consideration seems to permit me to interpret this historically of Judah, unless, attending to Jewish fables, we suppose that it may be understood according to what they say: that the portion of the tribe of Judah which he received as an inheritance in the land was so filled with vineyards that, as though no shoot of any other kind existed, such an abundance of vines appeared that not even an animal could be tied to another kind of tree.

[Note: Consult the *Sacred Critics*, whose unanimous judgment and interpretation of the passage refers also to the sense of the ancient writers concerning the immense abundance of vines in Judah’s inheritance. I do not sufficiently see why our author should be so fond of Jewish inventions.]

But these, as we have said, will appear to be more Jewish fables. For our part, the mystical exposition pleases us more, even if it stands alone.

### 5. “He shall wash his robe in wine, and his garment in the blood of the grape” (Gen. 49:11).

These words may seem to belong only to the historical exposition, signifying a fertile vineyard and, hyperbolically, an abundance of wine. But the mystical exposition produces a nobler meaning.

For the robe of Christ, which is washed in wine, is rightly understood as the Church, which he cleansed for himself with his blood, “not having spot or wrinkle” (Eph. 5). “You were not redeemed,” says the Apostle, “with silver or gold, but with the precious blood of the Only-Begotten of God” (1 Pet. 1).

In the wine of this blood—that is, in the washing of regeneration—the Church is washed by Christ. For “we are buried with him through baptism into death and his blood”; that is, we are baptized into his death.

But how does he wash his garment in the blood of the grape? The garment appears to be a somewhat closer, or more private, article of clothing than the robe. Those, therefore, who were first washed through the laver and had become his robe are said, after they have come to the sacrament of the blood of the grape, to become participants in his inner and more hidden mystery, as though in his inner garment.

The soul also is washed in the blood of the grape when it begins to grasp the meaning of this sacrament. For once the power of the blood has been recognized and understood through the power of the word of God, the more capable the soul becomes, the purer it grows, and it is washed daily as it advances in knowledge. Joining itself to the Lord, it will become not only his garment but already one spirit with him.

Opposed to this was that garment of the people of Israel which, to signify the indecency of the nation, he called not so much a garment as a loincloth; Jeremiah is commanded to gird it around his loins, then remove it and hide it again in the Euphrates (Jer. 13).

### 5. “His eyes are graceful from wine, and his teeth are whiter than milk” (Gen. 49:12).

Do you see how, especially toward the end, he cuts off and severs the historical understanding? For if, arguing still more stubbornly, we wished to say that Judah’s eyes are graceful from wine because of the abundance of wine, and the abundance of drinking, as we said above, what shall we answer concerning the white teeth, and their being superior in whiteness to the quality of milk?

[Note: Obviously, the answer is what the matter itself requires: teeth become white when milk is drunk. The following text, however, seems corrupt in *cubaro*, and the passage would indeed be more coherent if we read *ex*, “from,” instead of *pro*: “What shall we answer concerning the white teeth from the quality of milk?” After bringing out this reading, one may, if desired, delete the following word. Or else *praelatis*, “being superior,” must be read while retaining the conjunction, so that the meaning is that the teeth are superior to the whiteness, or quality, of milk—that is, whiter—which is the wording of the sacred text.]

In this matter we must not act shamelessly against the truth. But, having been driven away from the historical interpretation by the interruption of the sense, let us return to the order of the spiritual exposition.

“His eyes,” he says, “are graceful from wine.” We showed above, on apostolic authority, that worthy members of the faithful are called members of Christ, and that the individual members are named differently because each performs a service for the whole body of the Church.

There will be feet of Christ—those who run to make peace and go to assist those who are placed in need. There will be hands of Christ—those which are extended in mercy, bring help to the needy, and are stretched out as support for the weak.

So there will be eyes of Christ—those which provide the light of knowledge to the whole body, as it is written in the Gospel: “The lamp of your body is your eye” (Matt. 6:22).

These eyes, then, are graceful. For the word of wisdom is seasoned with salt, so that it may give grace to those who hear. They are called graceful not merely because they supply a discourse of knowledge, but because what they possess within themselves bestows grace.

“For when these things have been heard,” he says, “the wise man will become wiser” (Prov. 5).

His eyes, therefore, are graceful from wine, because there is nothing watery in the word of wisdom, nothing fluid, nothing cold. Rather, it is wine that gladdens the human heart and is poured into the wounds of the one who fell among robbers. Through it, the wounds of the hearers caused by sins are not only soothed by the gentleness of oil, but also cleansed by the austerity of wine.

“And who is it,” says the Apostle, “who makes me glad, except the one who is made sorrowful by me?”

“His teeth are white above milk.” We have already spoken frequently about the order and function of the members of Christ, and it seems absurd to repeat the same things more often in these passages.

[Note: Here *reperire*, “to find,” appeared corruptly in the text; we restore *repetere*, “to repeat.”]

His teeth, therefore, will be white above milk: these are those who can chew and reduce to the finest substance the strong and solid food of the word of God. Concerning them the Apostle says in the Letter to the Hebrews: “Solid food belongs to the perfect, who, by reason of their capacity for receiving it, have their senses trained for the discernment of good and evil” (Heb. 5:14).

Concerning the imperfect Corinthians he says: “I gave you milk to drink, not food; for you were not yet able” (1 Cor. 3:2). These statements concern those who are nourished on milk. Their teeth are white: that is, they are those who can receive and eat perfect food, above those who, like little children, still need milk.

Finally, in the Law, those animals which chew the cud (Lev. 11), bringing the food they have eaten back again to their teeth and, after minutely breaking it down, delivering it for the nourishment of the body, are designated as clean animals.

He most appropriately also says that his teeth are white. For all who are perfect and explain the nourishment of the Scriptures through worthy and suitable interpretations, supplying the Church’s body with a subtle and finely divided understanding—which is called spiritual—ought to be white and pure, free from every stain, lest it should perhaps be said to them: “You who teach another, do you not teach yourself?” (Rom. 2:21).

[Note: The unpublished author says: “By the teeth, the preachers of the New Testament are to be understood. By breaking up spiritual foods—that is, by explaining them—they transmit many things to us little ones into the stomach of memory. Milk may suitably be understood as the teaching of the Old Testament, which was prepared for the ignorant people, still incapable of solid food. Jesus therefore has teeth whiter than milk, because he appointed over his Church preachers conspicuous for the purity of their holiness,” and so forth.]

### 6.

Since divine Scripture ought to contain not only knowledge of the sacraments but also to shape the morals and conduct of those who learn—for Wisdom likewise says through Solomon, “Describe these things for yourself twice and three times in your heart” (Prov. 22), and the ark built by Noah is commanded to be made with two and three chambers (Gen. 6)—let us also, after having described these matters twice, insofar as we were able to understand them, namely according to the historical and the mystical understanding, now attempt to examine the moral meaning in this discourse, insofar as the passage permits.

Thus those devoted to the Scriptures may be taught not only what was done in others or by others, but also what they themselves ought to do within themselves.

“Judah” is interpreted as “confession.” Whoever, therefore, either confesses his sins and performs penance, or confesses Christ before human beings during persecution, will be praised by his brothers. For “there is joy and gladness among the angels in heaven over one sinner who repents” (Luke 15).

He is praised by them as by brothers—for human beings and angels are sons of the one Creator and Father. But the one who confesses the Lord Jesus, because he confesses in the Holy Spirit, has his hands placed upon the backs of his enemies.

For the one who had previously presented his members to serve iniquity unto iniquity now presents them to serve righteousness in sanctification (Rom. 6), and already attacks and strikes the backs of his fleeing enemies—that is, the demons.

Thus he fights, not as one striking the air (1 Cor. 9), but as one driving away demons. And whoever, on account of great progress, already possesses within himself something of God’s participation is also said to be worshiped by the sons of his father.

As a moral interpretation, we may understand “the sons of his father” as the sons of light, who rightly worship and venerate those who have advanced into the likeness of God through knowledge and the merit of their works.

[Note: The ideas of his teacher Origen are discernible here. Origen taught that the human being was created in the image of God but that he acquired the likeness of God for himself through the merit of good works and progress. In Book III of *On First Principles*, chapter 6, according to the interpretation of this same author, he says: “What he said, ‘He made him in the image of God,’ while he was silent about the likeness, indicates nothing else than that he received the dignity of the image in the first creation, while the perfection of likeness was reserved for the consummation: namely, that he should acquire it for himself through the efforts of his own industry, by imitation of God, and, having received from God the possibility of perfection through the dignity of the image, should finally complete a perfect likeness for himself through the fulfillment of his works,” and so forth. He has similar material in Homily I on Genesis, in Book IV on the Epistle to the Romans, and elsewhere.]

For just as Christ is the light of the world (John 8), so his disciples are the light of the world (Matt. 5): he by nature, they by grace. And Moses is said to be the god of Pharaoh (Exod. 7).

“Judah, a lion’s cub; from the germ, my son, you have ascended.”

He is rightly called a lion’s cub who has been crucified with Christ and has risen with him, as Paul also said (Rom. 6). Paul himself is rightly understood as Judah, for he confessed his sin, saying: “I am not worthy to be called an Apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (1 Cor. 15).

Again, he says that he himself is what Christ is when he says: “I have been crucified with Christ; nevertheless I live, yet not I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2).

He is therefore a lion’s cub who sleeps with Christ when he is dead to sin, and rises with Christ when he lives to God (Rom. 11).

The son who ascends from the germ is undoubtedly the one who, while he was a wild olive tree, was grafted into an [perhaps: good] olive tree, cast off the savage and wild habits of his carnal nature, and became an heir through the spirit of adoption (Phil. 4), remaining upon the true root of life and producing abundant fruit from his grafting.

“You reclined and slept like a lion.”

He sleeps like a lion, for the wise man is confident like a lion (Prov. 28), especially when he can say confidently: “I can do all things through him who strengthens me” (Phil. 4).

He is not roused by terrors, threats, or any enticements; rather, his purpose remains immovable and his mind fixed.

Nor can the Prince ever fail from Judah, nor the ruler from his thighs. For he will truly be able to rule himself, and will be a credible ruler, who first, through confession and penance, has cut off and subjected all the carnal vices by which he was previously driven, and does not permit anger, ambition, avarice, or lust to rule within him.

But he will have a ruler from the thighs of Judah—that is, from the one who has been corrected and reformed by confession—lest, if the blind gives guidance to the blind (Matt. 15), the mind still blinded by vices should govern the naturally blind body, and both fall into the pit.

“Until those things come which are laid up for him,” just as he also said: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us” (Rom. 8).

Or certainly, each of the saints rules himself and is the ruler of his own life for as long as it takes until that comes when God will be all in all; for this has been laid up for the end.

“And he himself shall be the expectation of the nations.” Since we have undertaken to pursue the moral interpretation, we must also seek within ourselves those nations which have an expectation.

[Note: Barraeus thinks that *justa emendati confessione*, “rightly by a corrected confession,” should be read. In my view, with a much lighter alteration of the words—or rather of a single little letter—where the text has *eo* instead of *ea*, the sequence of the discourse can be continued in a clearer and more suitable sense as follows: “They have the expectation of this person, corrected and perfected by that confession.” Then a complete stop is placed after τελείᾳ στιγμῇ. “We can understand the nations within ourselves,” and so forth. Certainly, according to Rufinus’s moral sense, the same person who has been corrected by confession, has cut off his carnal vices, and rules himself is the ruler from the thighs of Judah and the expectation of the nations. In the following book also he pursues this allegory according to the meanings of the patriarchs’ names and continuously refers it to the one human being.]

Of one so corrected and perfected by that confession, we can understand these nations within ourselves as all the movements of our soul which are stirred up more fiercely in us in our earliest age and act, as it were, in a Gentile manner. All these have hope and expectation of correction if the sense which is the prince and ruler of the human being, having confessed Christ and been illuminated by him, governs the reins of its actions.

“Binding his foal to the vine.” Here let us understand the foal itself as the sense directed toward renewal of life. Elsewhere the Lord calls it an infant, when he says: “Unless you turn and become like an infant, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 19).

When someone therefore joins himself to the Lord and becomes one spirit with him, he binds his foal to the vine, saying: “But it is good for me to cling to God” (Ps. 72).

“And the foal of his she-ass to the vine-shoot.” This vine-shoot—that is, the ἕλιξ (*helix*) which we explained above—we may understand as the subtle and winding understanding of knowledge, whose foal, that is, the sense and affection of the soul, preserves the soul from falling.

“He shall wash his robe in wine.” Just as the flesh of the Word of God is the food of the perfect, so his blood is the drink of the perfect.

Those, therefore, who are cleansed and renewed day by day through the Word of God are said to wash their robe in wine—that is, their visible actions—and their garment in the blood of the grape—that is, their inner thoughts—as the Apostle also said: “Purifying thoughts, and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of Christ” (1 Cor. 10).

Yet this may also be understood simply as the glory and suffering of martyrdom, which the righteous person hopes to suffer daily in the flesh, and as the garment alone in blood. Nevertheless, he also receives the martyrdom of conscience, which he continually endures within himself.

Finally, in what follows, he says that his eyes are graceful from wine and his teeth white above milk. There is no doubt that praise of the eyes is derived from the power of looking forward and seeing far ahead, which comes through either the grace or the study of knowledge.

For this reason, too, the teeth are white: they eat pure, spotless, solid foods of the word of God and do not allow the soul to be nourished on the milk of little children. Rather, they nourish it with solid and strengthening foods, transferring it from moral matters to mystical and doctrinal ones, by which, once illuminated, it may behold the glory of the Lord with unveiled face.

---

## PAULINUS TO HIS BROTHER RUFINUS: GREETINGS

### 19–20

Although the son of Cerealis made me uncertain whether he would proceed to you at the time when he was returning to Rome, to Saint Peter, we nevertheless judged that, through one who is equally yours and ours, not to write to you would be as culpable for us as it would be distressing for you.

[Note: Rufinus was still living at the monastery of Pinētum, situated in the territory of Tarracina near the sea. Fontaninus maintains this with good arguments, by which we have also tried to persuade others. For Cerealis, returning from Nola to Rome and Saint Peter, had to turn aside somewhat from the Roman road; hence the question whether on that occasion he turned aside to Rufinus.]

Therefore, preferring to undertake the loss of a sheet of paper if he perhaps did not see you rather than the loss of our duty, if—as we believe—he did see you, we have entrusted this letter not to chance but to faith.

For we believe that, in the Lord, the course of our words and of our son’s journey is to be directed toward you, since for those who desire what is good all things proceed toward good. He desires you as much as one ought to desire you who understands his own advantage in sharing your company.

And so I presume that, according to his faith and piety, his good desire will be preserved, that he will reach you and remain with you, and that saving assistance will be doubled for us before the Lord in both of you: when such a good son, companion, disciple, and helper comes to you, and you, granted by the Lord to him as father and teacher of every good thing, add to the effective power of his prayers the strength of spiritual grace.

For us, although our confidence is based on your affection, there is nevertheless fear that, if you are going to return to the East, you may not endure departing from us without visiting us.

[Note: Rufinus had this intention, and perhaps had even indicated to his friend Paulinus that, as soon as he had returned from the city, he would sail back to the East. He had decided to go to Rome, as he says in the preceding letter, while he was “in the heat of anxiety and uncertainty about delays.” Paulinus says that he fears Babylon’s daughter might detain him if he goes there. Matters turned out quite differently: coming from Pinētum to Rome, Rufinus soon afterward—in this very year, 398, around November—set out for his homeland, Concordia, and then remained at Aquileia for nearly ten years. These points had to be noted because Fontaninus does not seem to have properly grasped the meaning of this passage or of the preceding one: he explains both not of Rome, where Rufinus was preparing to travel, but the first of Concordia and this one of Italy, from which Paulinus asks him to return to the East without leaving without visiting him.]

Nevertheless, we fear for our sins lest Babylon’s daughter, though so near to us, should turn you aside from us.

[Earlier reading: *filiae*, “daughters.”]

[Note: There is no doubt that Rome is meant. For in the preceding letter he says expressly: “You judged that she should seek Rome.” In Letter XXIX also, to Severus, speaking of Melania’s arrival at Nola and then of Rome, he says: “Until now this daughter of Zion possessed and desired her; now the daughter of Babylon possesses and admires her, because now that city itself is in many respects more the daughter of Zion than the daughter of Babylon … although she is now seething amid the Roman crowds, far from her rest and hiding place in Jerusalem,” and so forth.]

Therefore we entrust our desires and prayers to the Lord, asking that he act for us not according to our merit but according to our desire, and direct your way to us in his way of peace. For those who do not walk in it are condemned to a reprobate mind, nor do they deserve to have you desire them.

### II

Indeed, through the importunity with which I have been accustomed to knock at your door, even in the middle of the night, I have now been compelled by fear of refusal to adopt greater modesty and restraint in making requests. I therefore entrust this task to you concerning me: you have published the Twelve Blessings of the Patriarchs, whose beginning—the prophecy concerning the person of Judah—you had already explained to me in written pages according to the threefold interpretation, as you were instructed. May you deign to explain it as distributed among the remaining sons, so that through you I may myself become acquainted with the truth and may have you as the author of great gratitude and praise, if I am to answer those who thought that I should be consulted about a work beyond my powers.

[Note: Especially Desiderius the Presbyter, who had proposed this explanation of the Blessings of the Patriarchs to him, as we observe in the preceding letter of Paulinus to Rufinus. Saint Paulinus himself explains the matter more fully in Letter XLIII, addressed to Desiderius, in which, with admirable humility, he withdraws from the burden and places it upon the author. “Concerning what you had written to me,” he says, “seeking sweet and abundant water in a bitter and dry stream, I leave it rather to your grace to explain. But you, blessed one, a vessel clean and suitable for God, if you have received an understanding of that blessing with which the Patriarch, enlightened in bodily blindness by the prophetic spirit, addressed his sons, explain to me in your reply the mysteries of the kingdom and the sacraments laid up from the ages,” and so forth.]

I may respond with something divine and from your spirit rather than with foolishness drawn from my own understanding.

[Note: Bruni correctly noted that perhaps something should be added here. Certainly either this word or something similar is required both by the sense of the passage and is suggested by the letter of Paulinus to Desiderius cited above. The following context also clearly demands the insertion of *operis*, “of the work,” or something similar, to complete the meaning.]

---

## BOOK II: ON THE BLESSINGS OF THE REMAINING ELEVEN PATRIARCHS

### Preface to Book II of Rufinus of Aquileia, Presbyter, to Paulinus, Presbyter

## RUFINUS TO HIS BROTHER PAULINUS, MAN OF GOD: GREETINGS

### 21–22

I had not yet seen our common son Cerealis, but he, aware of how much pain he would cause me if he delayed in delivering your letter, sent it ahead to me.

[Note: Refer here to what we said in the note at the end of the preceding page concerning Paulinus’s immediately preceding letter about Cerealis’s journey and the place of Pinētum where Rufinus was living. This will make it possible to correct certain recent writers who, in treating Rufinus and the history of Aquileia, repeatedly and seriously err through ignorance of the matter.]

As I read it, my longing for you—as is my habit—grew more and more, and at the end I found that you were commanding me to do the very thing for which I had frequently excused myself to you: namely, to respond by letter to some request concerning the interpretation of the Scriptures.

And so, the more you persisted in asking, the more I gave you a sign of my ignorance and unlearned discourse, once and again.

[Note: We do not know whether Rufinus gave Paulinus any other specimen of his learning—not, certainly, of his ignorance, as he calls it here out of humility—in explaining the Scriptures, apart from what is contained in the preceding Treatise, which is the First Book of this Commentary. It is easy to see what he means by “once and again”: he is referring to that earlier letter in which he excused himself concerning the question proposed to him, and which, as we have said, has perished.]

### II

But since you still did not cease to command me—

[Note: Someone had wanted a reply to be written, or something similar. I have no doubt that Rufinus received this instruction from him, although it may not have been written in Latin. The reader understands what it means more readily than it can be explained.]

—I have now added, as I was able, my discussion of the remaining eleven Patriarchs to what I had previously answered you concerning the blessing of Judah.

I judged that I had done the will of that father who, when he ordered me to go into the vineyard, said, “I will not go” (Matt. 21), but afterward went.

If there is any rashness in the undertaking—that, although we are less than suitable, we have touched upon so great a subject—then, with your pardon, it must most justly be charged to you, who, out of excessive love, do not see that the measures of our knowledge, as of our other virtues, are sufficiently small.

Since I wrote this reply to you during the days of Lent, while staying at the monastery of Pinētum, I could not conceal my foolishness from the brothers who were present. But they too, thinking that it was something substantial which might please you, nevertheless compelled me to copy it out for them.

Thus, even when you ask for food for yourself, you serve it also to others.

[Note: We have emended *escas*, “food,” in place of *nescis*, a word that was wholly corrupt. Barraeus had formerly conjectured the same correction, although he deleted *tuas*, “your,” which follows.]

Farewell in peace, most loving brother, truest worshiper of God, and Israelite in whom there is no deceit. Remember me, man of God, full of grace.

[Col. 0313B] 23 First, it should be known that, in the several passages where Scripture mentions the twelve Patriarchs, there is considerable variation in the very listing of their order. One order is recorded according to their actual births (Gen. 35); another when they are reported to have entered the land of Egypt together with their father Israel and the descendants of their posterity (Gen. 46); another here, when they receive the blessings of their father as he is about to die (Gen. 49); another when the tribes that had come out of Egypt, or are mentioned in the wilderness, are engaged in some activity (Exod. 14 and following), or, after entering the Promised Land, are stationed on Mount Garizim and Mount Gebal for the blessings and curses (Deut. 27). There is yet another when they receive by lot the division of the land of their inheritance (Josh. 15). This order varies so greatly that sometimes certain of them are found not even included in the list [Col. 0313C]—which certainly does not happen without some reason—but there are probable causes why one is placed before another in one passage, and another before him elsewhere. But you [Father Paulinus] have not now proposed these matters to us, except insofar as, as God grants, we may explain only what is contained in the blessings that they receive from their father at the time of his death. These may perhaps be called “blessings” solely because at the end it is said: “And their father spoke these things to them, and blessed them; he blessed each one according to his own blessing” (Gen. 49:28). At the beginning, however, when their father summons them, he does not call them as though to a blessing, but the text reads: “Jacob called his sons and said: Gather together, that I may tell you what shall befall you in the last days” (ibid. 2). This more properly signifies a prophecy, through which what is going to happen to them is foretold.

[Note: [Col. 0313D] That Jacob blessed most of his sons—indeed, nine out of the twelve—although he invoked anything but favorable things upon the first three, Reuben, Simeon, and Levi, has long been accepted among the Fathers of the Church as the reason why those prophecies are called the Twelve Blessings of the Patriarchs. Rufinus adds another reason from the sacred text itself, where it says, “And Jacob blessed each of them with their own blessings.” From their meaning he properly observes that they should be called prophecies. Saint Ambrose also, to say nothing now of others, would have preferred this designation. “Rightly,” he says, “he says that he is conveying rather a proclamation of what was to come in later times than a blessing.” A little later he adds: “And therefore it is a prophecy rather than a blessing. For prophecy is a proclamation of things to come, whereas blessing is a votive bestowal of sanctification and graces.”]

In the actual bodily sequence of the words, however, there are neither blessings alone nor merely a prediction of future events, by which either their death, or their purpose, or even certain deeds performed by them are distinctly reproved. This circumstance supplies us—as we have done elsewhere—with a threefold subject for explanation, so that the blessings occupy the place of History; prophecy, that of the Mystical and Dogmatic sense; and the correction and rebuke of conduct direct the Moral interpretation.

# THE BLESSING OF REUBEN

[Col. 0313]

[Col. 0313C] 1. “Reuben,” he says, “my firstborn: you are my strength and the beginning of my children, harsh in conduct, and harsh, reckless. You have inflicted insults; you do not boil over like water. For you went up upon your father’s bed; then you polluted the couch where you went up” (Gen. 49:3–4).

The history of the incest is known to everyone: how Reuben burned with the flame of lust for his father’s concubine and stained his father’s couch (Gen. 34).

[Note: [Col. 0314D] Saint Ambrose again says: “The Jews think that the old man says these things to his son Reuben because he lay with his father’s concubine Bala and polluted his father’s couch.” Others have similar statements, as does an unpublished author preserved by us: “By those words the crime of incest, which he committed with Bala, his father’s concubine, is plainly aggravated.”]

But since at the beginning he seems to ascribe something praiseworthy to him, saying, “You are my strength,” this is so that the one who was regarded as his father’s strength and the beginning of his children may be more severely marked in his crime because he did not know how to preserve reverence toward his father. The same applies to what is said through the Prophet: “I planted you as a fruitful vine, wholly fertile; how have you been turned into the bitterness of a foreign vine?” (Jer. 2).

2. According to the Mystical interpretation, Reuben seems to me capable of representing the former Jewish people, who are both the firstborn and the beginning of the children, just as the Prophet says: “Israel is my firstborn” (Exod. 4). For to those first people the oracles of God were given. That this people was harsh and reckless Scripture declares. The Prophet says of them: “Everything that this people speaks is harsh” (Isa. 8). And elsewhere he says of them: “You are always stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart” (Acts 7).

They inflicted insults upon God the Father when they turned their back toward him and not [Note: [Col. 0315D] Barraeus seems altogether erroneously to have read, “not doing good,” instead of “and not their face.” He knew that the latter reading was preferred by others and relegated it to the margin of the book. We have restored it, observing that Jeremiah 2:27 is being cited: “Saying to a piece of wood, ‘You are my father,’ and to a stone, ‘You begot me’; they have turned their back to me and not their face,” etc. In Greek: καὶ οὐ πρόσωπα αὐτῶν, “and not their faces.”] their face (Jer. 2).

But he polluted the couch of the concubine upon which he went up—that is, the law of the Old Testament, which he often stained by transgression. That the law of the Old Testament is represented in the person of the concubine Paul teaches when he says: “Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman; these things are the two covenants” (Gal. 4). In this allegory Hagar, who was a concubine, represents the Old Testament.
