For there was one perfect dove—or mother—who, as a chaste virgin and queen joined to the bridegroom king, is united to Christ through the Gospel.

3. The Moral sense of this passage may be treated as follows. Reuben, according to the interpretation handed down by the elders [Note: [Col. 0315D] Origen interprets it in Homily XVII on Genesis as “the son who is seen,” that is, visible, as has been noted by us in the Hieronymian Lexicon, although that work prefers the active sense, “seeing son.” Our author cites the book that was commonly available as coming from the elders. See our discussion there.], is interpreted as “the son who is seen,” that is, visible and carnal [Col. 0316A]. I believe this is the one of whom the Apostle says: “The first man was from the earth, earthly” (1 Cor. 15). Elsewhere also: “Although our visible man is being corrupted, yet the inner man is being renewed” (ibid. 4). He calls this same visible man the outer man. Again he says: “For it is not the spiritual that is first, but the animal” (ibid.).

Therefore, whenever a human being lives carnally in this world and is moved according to the flesh—and the first carnal movement is in the desire of lust, to which the time of early youth has already submitted—he becomes at once harsh, reckless, and wanton: he climbs upon his father’s bed and pollutes his father’s couch, that is, he transgresses even the precepts and admonitions of the natural law that is within us, which is now called the paternal couch.

[Col. 0316B] For within us there is a certain natural law that reproves each sinner and tells him that what he is doing wrong is evil. He therefore violates the bed of this law and pollutes the seat of its secret counsel when he rushes headlong and without restraint into vices.

# THE BLESSING OF SIMEON AND LEVI

[Col. 0315]

[Col. 0315B] 1. “Simeon and Levi are brothers; they completed the iniquity of their will. Let my soul not enter into their counsel, and let my inward parts not be invited to their assembly” (Gen. 49:5–6).

[Note: [Col. 0315D] To me, the negative particle seems first of all to require restoration, and “let them be angered” should be written instead of “let them be invited.” The Greek has μὴ ἐρίσαι, “not to be angry”; Saint Ambrose likewise has “let them not contend,” etc. [Col. 0316D]]

As far as the historical sense is concerned, he seems to condemn the deed they committed: they deceitfully and treacherously slaughtered Shechem, the son of Hamor, who, after having intercourse with their sister, wished to join himself to the family of Israel, and they killed all his people. Their father Israel therefore said to them: “You have made me hateful in this land” (Gen. 34).

[Note: [Col. 0316D] Saint Ambrose does not at all approve this interpretation; he says that it was devised by the Jews. “The Jews derive,” he says, “a very attractive interpretation, believing that the reason Jacob rebukes his sons is that, wishing above all their brothers to avenge the violation of their sister, these two deceived the Shechemites by pretending that they wished to make peace with them, and therefore,” etc. “But in this too the Jews are mistaken. For these men had causes of grief,” etc. Most other interpreters approve this view, as does an unpublished author preserved by us: “The literal sense is evident: these two brothers, in order to avenge the violation of their sister, deceived Shechem and his father Hamor by a feigned peace and pretended friendship,” etc.]

Thus he invokes a curse upon their reckless anger and declares that they are to be divided among the peoples of Israel, since from them would come the Levites and priests, who did not receive a share of the Promised Land.

2. A Spiritual explanation of these matters may, it seems to me, be applied in the following way: Simeon and Levi may represent the scribes and Pharisees of the Jewish people, of whom it is written: “The scribes and Pharisees took counsel together to seize Jesus by deceit” (Matt. 26). Of this counsel the holy man who saw God with his mind now says: “Let my soul not enter into their counsel”; and concerning their assembly, in which they condemned Jesus after producing false witnesses, he says: “Let my inward parts not be invited.”

[Note: [Col. 0316D] We said that “let them be angered” seemed to require restoration. Meanwhile, you see that the negative particle we mentioned as needing to be supplied has not been supplied. Recall the immediately preceding Note.]

Does this not seem to you to say: “I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man” (Matt. 27)—innocent of the sentence that you pronounce against the innocent? “In their anger,” he says, “they killed men.” I ask which men they killed, since it is certain that before the Lord’s Passion no one of the believers was punished—unless someone should also attribute to them the blood of the Prophets. For the Lord too says that “from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah” (ibid. 23), all the blood of the righteous that has been shed is to be required of that generation.

But let us see whether perhaps they also killed those men whom they persuaded to cry out: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (ibid. 27).

“And in their desire they hamstrung the bull.” In the figures of Scripture we read that the Son of God is called a bull, namely in the Gospel, where it is written twice under the person of the elder son speaking to his father: “I have always been with you, and I have never transgressed your commandment; yet you have never given me a young goat, that I might feast with my friends. But when this son of yours came, who has squandered all his substance, you killed for him this fattened calf” (Luke 15).

Therefore, the scribes and Pharisees are said to have hamstrung the bull—or the calf—by their counsel.

[Note: [Col. 0317C] Here Ambrose agrees in almost the same words: “Because the scribes are from the tribe of Simeon and the chief priests from the tribe of Levi, they completed their wickedness in the Passion of the Lord,” etc. Likewise the unpublished author: “Simeon and Levi designate the scribes and Pharisees. It is evident that the chief priests came from Levi,” etc. [Col. 0317D]]

Their anger is accursed because it is reckless, and their wrath because it is hardened. “I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel.”

We must consider whether this division mentioned here may be like that of which it is said in the Gospel: “When the lord of that servant comes, he will divide him and appoint his portion with the unbelievers” (ibid. 12).

[Col. 0317D] 28 Or certainly, as I heard one of the holy Fathers explaining:

[Note: [Col. 0317D] Earlier he had said “different.” It is not my wish to guess who this interpreter was, whom our author, while living in the regions of the East, certainly heard. The often-cited unpublished author says the same: “The same people, disinherited from their ancestral land, suffer the penalties of their unbelief among all the nations as a testimony to our faith,” etc.]

Because “division” and “scattering” are mentioned together, this may mean that some of them believed in the Lord while others remained in unbelief. Those are called “divided” who separate themselves from them and come to faith; those “scattered” are the people whose homeland and Temple have been overthrown and whose unbelieving race is dispersed throughout the world.

3. The Moral interpretation may perhaps be preserved in this form. It has seemed to many wise men that the soul’s power is threefold, that is, that there are three kinds of its movement: through anger, through desire, and through reason; nor, I think, can any other movement of the soul be found apart from these.

[Note: [Col. 0317D] Jerome, Commentary on Matthew, Book II, chapter XIII: “We read in Plato,” he says, “and it is a commonly held doctrine among philosophers, that there are three passions in the human soul: τὸ λογικόν, which we may translate as ‘the rational’; τὸ θυμικόν, which we may call ‘the spirited’ or ‘full of anger’; and τὸ ἐπιθυμητικόν, which we call ‘the appetitive’ or ‘concupiscible,’” etc.]

For everything upon which it relies or by which it is moved proceeds either from anger, desire, or reason. Therefore, the whole condition of human life seems to me to be foreshadowed in these three sons of Jacob, and through them this threefold movement of the soul is represented. In them Reuben preserves the first kind, that of desire, in which he is marked by the stain of his outburst. Simeon possesses the second kind, that of anger or fury, which is itself demonstrated by the reproach of his fury. Levi possesses the third form, that of rational movement, since he was also entrusted with the observance of the law.

Thus almost every soul that comes into this world seems to act culpably through these first movements until, weighed down by the vices of sins and wearied by the satiety of evils, it can reach the place of repentance. For Judas follows after this: he cleanses sins through confession, because Judas in the Hebrew language is interpreted as “confession,” which is said to free from death.

[Note: [Col. 0317D] From the Origenian Lexicon and from the same Adamantius’ Homily XVII on Genesis: “Judas is interpreted in the Hebrew language as ‘confession.’”]

Concerning Judas, I believe that what we have already said earlier, as best we could, is sufficient; if it pleases you, those remarks may either be joined to what follows or placed before it.

# THE BLESSING OF ZEBULUN

[Col. 0317]

[Col. 0317B] 29 1. “Zebulun shall dwell beside the sea, and he himself shall be the landing-place of ships, and he shall extend as far as Sidon” (Gen. 49:13).

Historically, this indicates the portion of the future inheritance and the allotment. As regards the Mystery, we read in the Gospel that some of the Apostles were taken from these regions, and that the Lord often taught in those places, as it is written: “Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles. The people sitting in darkness have seen a great light” (Isa. 9; Matt. 4).

But when he said, “And he shall extend as far as Sidon,” Sidon is interpreted as “hunter” or “huntress.”

[Note: [Col. 0317D] From Origen, in various places, especially Homilies XIV and XVI on Joshua: “Sidon signifies ‘huntress’ or ‘hunters,’ and the Sidonians are called hunters.” Finally, Homily XIII on Ezekiel: “There is a threat against Sidon, which is interpreted as ‘hunters.’” [Col. 0318C]]

Whom else, then, should we understand as laudably indicated here by “hunters” except the Lord’s Apostles, concerning whom the Prophet foretold: “Behold, I will send many hunters, and they shall hunt them on every mountain” (Jer. 16)?

[Note: [Col. 0318C] Jerome argues the opposite, that “hunter” is never taken in a good sense in Scripture. Commentary II on Micah, chapter V: “As far as I can recall from memory, I have never read ‘hunter’ in a favorable sense. Ishmael and Esau were hunters,” etc. Saint Ambrose likewise says in Psalm 118: “We find no righteous hunter anywhere in the sequence of the divine writings.” And Pseudo-Jerome in the Breviary on Psalm 90: “We find no holy hunter at all in the Holy Scriptures,” etc. [Col. 0318D]]

2. If a Moral interpretation is also required here, Zebulun is interpreted as “nocturnal flow.”

[Note: [Col. 0318D] The Origenian Lexicon, which we printed in Volume III of the Hieronymian works, prefers ῥύσις αὐτῶν, that is, “their flow.” I would rather correct it to νυκτός, “of night,” instead of αὐτῶν, “of them,” since that name is customarily explained as “the flow of night,” not “their flow,” as both our author here and six hundred other testimonies from the ancients demonstrate. Moreover, the great Jerome himself contends that this was incorrectly interpreted in the Book of Names, and rightly so, in his Questions on Genesis: “He incorrectly and arbitrarily interprets Zebulun in the Book of Names as ‘the flow of night.’”]

It may consequently be understood that, after the soul that was sitting in darkness has seen the Lord’s light and has turned to repentance through confession, all the things that it had done in the death of ignorance are taken away from it and flow away. After confession has preceded in Judas, conversion will also follow in this one, when everything that belonged to night and darkness has already flowed away—those things in which it tries, as it were, to strip off the old man and lay aside the things of night, so that it may walk honorably in the day (Rom. 13:13).

But the fact that it shakes itself out as far as Sidon—that is, as far as the hunters—may perhaps declare that it is also striving to become one of those to whom it is said: “Catch for me the little foxes that destroy my vines” (Song 2).

Therefore, it extends itself as far as the hunters so that it may itself learn to hunt, whenever wild beasts or deceitful foxes—that is, either savage demons or harmful thoughts—creep into its heart and wish to destroy the vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth. Thus it may seize them, having become a praiseworthy hunter of evil thoughts.

# THE BLESSING OF ISSACHAR

[Col. 0319]

[Col. 0319A] 1. “Issachar desired the good; he shall rest in the midst of the allotments,” [Note: [Col. 0319D] “Resting” seems to require correction, since both other Latin Fathers of ancient times and the Greek text itself have ἀναπαυόμενος, “resting.”] “and seeing that rest was good, and that the land was fertile.”

Here too the historical order is appropriately preserved: he dwelt in the midst of the allotments, that is, in the divisions of the land that were distributed to them by Joshua the son of Nun (Josh. 19). For the fourth allotment among the seven later tribes is reported in the Book of Joshua to have gone out to him, since two half-tribes—Judah and Ephraim—and half the tribe of Manasseh had received their allotments first. Reuben and Gad, together with half the tribe of Manasseh, possessed land beyond the Jordan.

Issachar is therefore in the middle, since he is fourth among the seven: an agriculturist of rich and fertile soil, willingly devoting labor to productive ground. Let this suffice as regards the Historical sense.

2. Since Issachar is interpreted as “reward,” he may preserve the figure of those who say: “For if I preach willingly, I have a reward” (1 Cor. 9). And of those concerning whom it is said: “Behold, the children of the Lord are a reward, the fruit of the womb” (Ps. 126).

The Apostles are rightly to be regarded as the reward of the Son of God, because he deigned to enter the Virgin’s womb. They are the ones who desired the good, and of whose souls it is said in the Song of Songs: “The maidens loved you” (Song 1); and they say to Jesus: “We shall run after you in the fragrance of your ointments” (ibid.).

Resting in the midst of the allotments—that is, in the midst of the good land, the land flowing with milk and honey—they rest in its midst. That land was Jesus, flowing with milk and honey; upon his breast not only John (John 13), but in John all the disciples, reclined. And they became agriculturists.

They were agriculturists and cultivated our land, which they had seen to be fertile and good, and which the Son of Man had come to sow. Its seed fell upon good soil (Matt. 13), which bore fruit—some thirtyfold, some sixtyfold, and some a hundredfold (Luke 8). All Scripture bears witness to this, and especially the Apostle Paul, who says: “You are God’s husbandry; you are God’s cultivation” (1 Cor. 3). Again he says: “The laboring farmer ought first to partake of the fruits” (2 Tim. 2). And again, speaking of himself: “Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit?” (1 Cor. 9).

But perhaps you will say: How is it true that the Apostles saw rest, as it is said here, “and seeing that rest was good,” when it is evident that the Apostles never had rest, but spent the whole of their lives in labors and persecutions, as the Apostle Paul indicates (2 Cor. 11)?

Let us see, then, whether the meaning of this statement may be that, contemplating the future rest, the blessedness of the kingdom of heaven, and the glory of all that had been promised, they willingly submitted their shoulders to labor. Looking toward those future good things, they patiently endured present evils, just as the Apostle Paul says of Moses: because he rejected the treasures of the Egyptians, he chose rather to bear the reproach of Christ; “for he was looking,” he says, “toward the reward” (Heb. 11:23).

3. But since we have undertaken to construct the ark of divine Scripture—not merely two-chambered, but three-chambered, as the Lord commanded Noah (Gen. 6)—let us now see how Issachar also builds a third nest for us.

In the foregoing we assumed him to be the man who, through the threefold movement of the soul—as is the whole [Note: [Col. 0319D] That is, “entire.” Similar expressions occur in other authors as well. The words that follow, “wandering in anger and fury,” are corrupt in the manuscript. Either “in anger and fury” must be deleted, or “in reason and desire” must be supplied. Then “wandering” should be rewritten as “wandering” or “having wandered,” according to the intended construction. For this purpose the passage to which Rufinus refers, near the end of the preceding Blessing, should also be attached: “Everything upon which the soul relies or by which it is moved proceeds either from anger, desire, or reason; and therefore the whole condition of human life seems to me to be foreshadowed in these three sons of Jacob, and through them this threefold movement of the soul is represented: in them Reuben preserves the first kind, that of desire . . .; Simeon possesses the second kind, that of anger or fury . . .; Levi possesses the third form, that of rational movement,” etc. From these words it is possible to restore the corrupt passage.] sickness of the soul—was wandering through anger and fury [Col. 0320B], signifying, as we distinguished, through Reuben desire, through Simeon anger, and through Levi prudence not rightly directed.

But we have now shown him repentant in Judas and converted to a considerable degree in Zebulun. In Issachar, whose name means “reward,” we now see him also awaiting the reward of good work: for he has not merely cast away evil, but has desired the good, and even rests in the midst of the allotments.

He is in the middle who, according to the admonition of Wisdom, turns neither to the right nor to the left. This is to hold the straight line and proceed along the path of virtue. In this sense the allotments may also be understood.

A lot is that by which a portion of the inheritance is assigned to each person—not as though it were determined by some chance event, as the nations suppose, but because it is decreed by God’s judgment and dispensation. In this Moral exposition, therefore, the allotments are to be understood as the commandments of God, through which the heavenly inheritance will be obtained.

Thus the one who has now been converted and also hopes for the reward of his works always rests in the midst of the allotments—that is, in the midst of God’s commandments—seeing that rest is good and that the land is fertile. After he had driven away and excluded the battle of thoughts that existed within him, while the flesh desired against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh, his spirit rested in God. Then he saw that rest was good, when Jesus could already say to him: “Come away for a little while and rest.”

He also saw that the land was good. When did he see the land to be good? When he had cleansed his flesh from vices and desires; then, without doubt, he saw it to be good and fertile land, producing the fruits of righteousness in good works.

Seeing this, he submitted his shoulder to labor [Col. 0322A] and became a husbandman. He is to be regarded as the farmer of his own land who continually breaks up and furrows the fields of his soul and the fallow ground of his heart with the plow of God’s word and the coulter of Scripture; who waters the plantations of faith, charity, hope, and righteousness from the springs of Israel; and who discovers the whole discipline of agriculture in the soil of his own soul.

# THE BLESSING OF DAN

[Col. 0321]

[Col. 0321A] 33 1. “Dan shall judge his people as though he were one tribe in Israel. And let Dan become a serpent on the road, sitting beside the path, biting the horse’s heel, and the rider shall fall backward. He shall await salvation from the Lord.”

As far as the Historical sense of this passage is concerned, it is not easy to find it clearly expressed in the Holy Scriptures—at least insofar as my limited understanding reaches—either how Dan judged his people as one tribe or how he sat beside the road. Lest we bring forward something that seems to have little support from Scripture, the matters written here appear to me better suited to a Spiritual interpretation. Unless perhaps these words can be applied to particular events in the wars recorded either by Joshua the son of Nun or in the Book of Judges.

Although we have investigated more carefully, we have not yet discovered anything that satisfies our purpose. Nevertheless, we present the interpretations held by some.

2. Some say [Note: [Col. 0321C] Rather, many say so; among them, to mention one, Saint Ambrose: “The prophecy signifies the Antichrist, who is to come from the tribe of Dan, a savage judge and monstrous tyrant; he will judge his people. Like a serpent on the road, sitting beside the path, he will try to cast down those who walk along the way of truth, wishing to trip up the truth.” It is especially worth adding to this the still unpublished author mentioned above: “This Dan prefigures the Antichrist, who will be like a serpent on the road and a horned serpent beside the path, because to those walking on the road and path of God’s commandments he presents himself, so far as he can, as an obstacle, armed against them with a twofold device. His cunning is prefigured in the serpent, because he subtly seeks to deceive those who tread the Lord’s way by the steps of their works. His fury is shown in the horns, which he will use against those whom he cannot deceive by crafty contrivance . . . When, therefore, the Antichrist comes and, before the eyes of those watching, performs great signs and brings down fire from heaven, he is the serpent on the road. But when he turns to inflict punishments and torments upon those who do not believe in him, he is the horned serpent beside the path,” etc. Saint Gregory has almost the same interpretation in Book XXXI of the Moralia, etc. [Col. 0322C]] that the Antichrist is foretold by these words and that he will come from this tribe. Others suspect that these words were written about Judas the betrayer and wish the rider and the horse to signify the Lord together with the flesh he assumed.

[Note: [Col. 0322C] Saint Ambrose himself adds this interpretation: “Judas the betrayer, tempted by the devil, lifted up his heel against the Lord Jesus in order to cast down the rider, who cast himself down in order to raise everyone up,” etc. A little later: “Judas was sleeping; indeed, he did not hear Christ’s words. Judas was sleeping, and he was sleeping the sleep of riches, since he was seeking a reward from his betrayal. The devil saw him sleeping and weighed down by the heavy sleep of avarice; he entered his heart, wounded the horse, and cast down the rider whom he separated from Christ.”]

But such an interpretation scarcely seems to me capable of being explained. For if they wish to place the Deity in the horse, it could not in any event be bitten by a serpent; if in the rider, it would be unfitting to say that the Deity of the Word fell backward and awaited salvation from the Lord.

Therefore I think that Dan may more properly be referred to him who is awaited as judge of the living and the dead, since Dan is interpreted as “judgment” or “judge.”

[Note: [Col. 0322D] This Mystical interpretation is by no means approved by others. Indeed, an uncertain author of the little book On the Twelve Ecclesiastical Writers, appended to Isidore and Ildefonsus, openly attacks Rufinus on this account in chapter V: “This Rufinus, applying a Mystical sense improperly, interprets what is written about Dan the son of Jacob as referring to our Lord, whereas the assertion of the Holy Fathers proves beyond doubt that these things pertain to the Antichrist.” He should have said “the greater part of them,” as we observed in the preceding Note. For others depart into different and still other interpretations, and there are those who interpret the passage as referring to the Messiah himself. That interpretation differs little or not at all from our author’s exposition, at least in the respect for which he is criticized. Add also the defense, worthy of consideration, which he himself supplies from the sequence and context of the prophecy. These matters influenced me in this passage, though I do not exclude the opinion of those who have been able to support their interpretation by the authority of Scripture.]

Thus the Lord Jesus Christ, who says, “For judgment I have come into this world” (John 9), and again, “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (ibid. 5), will himself judge his people as one tribe. For there will no longer be a division of tribes or any diversity, but, as he himself says: “There will be one flock and one shepherd” (ibid. 10).

3. What seems to deter some people in this passage is the statement that follows: “Let Dan become a serpent on the road.” Since the serpent is frequently used in Scripture as the personification of the devil, they think that this cannot apply to the Lord.

But if we return to Scripture, we find that the devil is called a lion, “who goes about seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. 5); and that hostile powers are called bulls, as in the words: “Fat bulls have surrounded me” (Ps. 21). On the other hand, the Lord is also called a lion, as Judas, whom we expounded shortly before, has taught us. We also find that the Lord himself is called a bull, the one who was killed for the salvation and return of the repentant son (Luke 15).

There are many other similar examples in Scripture, in which the same image is applied now in a good, now in an evil, sense. Thus the serpent too is sometimes written as representing the Lord himself, as he says of himself in the Gospels: “Just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up” (John 3).

And when the Apostle commands us to become wise as serpents, did he not apply the designation “serpent” in a favorable sense?

Therefore, this passage too may be understood of the Lord himself: “Let Dan become a serpent on the road, sitting beside the path”—that is, let him be the one who judges hearts and knows what is hidden within, seeing on the road, that is, in the course of this life, riders traveling along an unrighteous route.

The riders may be understood as souls placed in bodies, as it says there: “All who mounted horses slumbered” (Ps. 75)—that is, all who are in bodies have sinned, as the Apostle also declared.

This serpent, therefore, sitting beside the road, bites the heel of these horses or riders. It bites the heel when it torments the body with illnesses or with various other afflictions, so as to restrain the swift course of sinners.

For when the body is afflicted and the flesh is consumed, then the rider falls backward—that is, the soul that was running badly and hastening toward destruction falls backward and is recalled to patience [perhaps “repentance”]. Prevented from its evil course, it is turned backward and made to follow the one who says: “Come after me” (Mark 1).

I think something of this sort also happened with the Apostle Peter. When the Lord said, “The Son of Man must be crucified and die” (Matt. 16), Peter replied: “Be merciful, Lord; this shall not happen to you” (Luke 18). Because, through excessive love and ignorance, he was not riding correctly, he was finally bitten, as it were, by the Lord in the form of the serpent, when it was said to him: “Get behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling block to me, for you do not understand the things of God, but the things of men” (Mark 8).

Thus Peter, recalled backward, awaits salvation from the Lord through the Cross and Resurrection, which, when he was then riding and running more fervently, he did not know would come.

These things have moved me in this passage, though I do not exclude the opinion of those who have been able to support their interpretation by the authority of Scripture.

3. So that not even that third passage may pass us by, it may be understood as referring to the man whom we said long ago had made progress in Issachar, rested in the commandments, and become the cultivator of his own soul, and who may now also make progress in Dan, in that he has acquired the understanding necessary to discern and judge his own people—that is, the thoughts of his heart—as though they were one tribe in Israel; in other words, to bring all things into unity and harmony, so that there may be no disagreement among his thoughts or counsels. He also becomes a serpent, in accordance with the Lord’s command that we mentioned shortly before: “Be wise as serpents” (Matt. 10). Yet he sits by the road and never departs from the path. For the path is understood as narrower than the road, showing that he does not walk along the broad and spacious way that leads to death, but along the narrow and constricted way that leads to life (Matt. 7).

He bites the horse’s heel, doing what the Apostle Paul says: “I chastise my body and bring it into subjection, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should be rejected” (1 Cor. 9). This he does so that the horse may fall backward. Such a man always fears arrogance and exaltation, and wishes his soul to fall from a wicked height into a good humility, so that he may learn from Jesus, because he is “humble and gentle in heart” (Matt. 11). Indeed, it is characteristic of those who are making progress to fear arrogance. Finally, even that great and distinguished Apostle Paul said: “Lest I should be exalted, there was given to my flesh a thorn, an angel of Satan, to buffet me” (1 Cor. 12). Thus he recalls the soul from its height; and, brought back from its height to the humility of Christ, it awaits salvation from the Lord.

# THE BLESSING OF GAD

[Col. 0323]

1. “GAD [Note: From the Greek πειρατήριον (*peiratērion*), which is Latin *tentatio*, ‘temptation’; some other Latin Fathers likewise prefer this form. At the beginning, the name Gad seems to have to be placed before it.] will tempt him, but he himself will tempt them at their heels.” In the historical sense, we do not easily find anything of this kind referred to in Scripture, unless someone wishes, as it were, to force the text and say that this tribe obtained an inheritance beyond the Jordan, in the regions of Arabia, and that, since wars with brigands frequently arise there and they engage in continual clashes with one another, these contests among them are designated in these words as being conducted in the manner of pirates.

[Note: Not quite so Saint Jerome, who, translating from the Hebrew “girded” in place of *piraterium*, expressly declares that the battles fought by Gad, together with Reuben and half the tribe of Manasseh, against the neighboring peoples are clearly indicated; and that, after defeating the enemy, he fought bravely. An unpublished author among our materials likewise says: “The literal sense is evident to readers of the book of Joshua. Gad, who sought and received his inheritance from Moses beyond the Jordan, earned possession of it on the condition that, armed and going before Israel, together with Reuben and half the tribe of Manasseh, he should advance against his adversaries in battle; and this he also did under Joshua. Yet, after the enemies had been subdued, when he returned to his possession, he necessarily had to resist the incursions of neighboring peoples,” and so forth.]

2. But the spiritual understanding is more convincing, and can indicate the contest which our Lord and Savior, while placed in the flesh, waged against the devil. The dwelling-place of this tribe is therefore near the wilderness; and Gad is now interpreted as “temptations.”

[Note: He takes this from Origen, *Homily XXVII on Numbers*. “Galgad” [read: “Gadgad”] is interpreted as “temptation” or “confinement.” He consistently suppresses the name of his teacher in order to avoid envy. Yet it is remarkable that he now says that the word is interpreted in this way, as though the other various explanations, which are made according to individual preference, no longer prevailed. Saint Jerome, however, in Letter 78, *On the Stations*, to Fabiola, station 29, approves this interpretation so little that he does not even mention it among the others. See the passage.]

It may therefore be understood that the Lord Jesus Christ was led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil (Matt. 4). But observe how many mysteries are contained in the Patriarch’s words. “Gad,” he says, “will tempt him.” Let us suppose, as we said, that Gad represents the person of the Lord: a *piraterium* will tempt him. A *piraterium* is a certain troop and conspiracy of pirates. For it is certain that when the devil came to tempt the Lord, he did not come without his ministers and attendants. Just as angels were present with the Lord, watching his contest—those of whom the Gospel says after the temptation, “And angels came and ministered to him” (ibid.)—so the devil’s angels were also present with him, those for whom hell was prepared, as the Lord says: “Go into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (ibid. 25).

The saints, too, when they contend in the arena, are said to have become a spectacle to this world, to angels, and to human beings (1 Cor. 4). Thus the conspiracy of tempters was tempting the Lord when it said to him: “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves” (Matt. 4). In this way, then, the devil was tempting the Lord.

But let us see what is meant by the words: “He himself will tempt them at their heels.” How was the Lord tempting those who were tempting him? If, in the first temptation, the Savior had declared to the devil that he was the Son of God, it is certain that the devil would not have dared approach him a second time to tempt him. But observe how the one who tempts is himself tempted. The Lord remains in the wilderness for forty days and forty nights; afterward he became hungry. If he had not become hungry, the tempter would have recognized the Son of God. But now he is hungry, so that, by displaying in himself the weakness of the flesh, the one who tempts may himself be tempted and may approach again as though he were tempting a human being. Thus the tempters come to the Lord. “But he himself will tempt them at their heels”—that is, he tempts them with the same footprints by which the devil had approached to tempt him.

[Note: We have restored *tentat* (“he tempts”) in place of the earlier corrupt reading *tentatur* (“he is tempted”). We silently correct other minor matters above.]

3. The moral sense of the passage is therefore explained in a similar fashion. That inner man of ours, having confessed his error and repented, makes himself converted through understanding and has made some progress, so that after his progress he comes to be tempted by the enemy, and the strength of his soul and the constancy of his purpose are tested. For Scripture says: “He who has not been tempted is not approved” (Ecclus. 34).

[Note: Barraeus had likewise erroneously read *quia* (“because”) instead of *qui* (“he who”). Nor had he noticed that the words are those of Scripture.]

No one will ever reach perfection unless he has first given proof in his temptations [possibly: “his temptation”].

# THE BLESSING OF ASER

[Col. 0325]

1. “ASER: his bread is rich, and he will give food to rulers.” I believe that the advocates of the literal interpretation understand these words to mean that his region and inheritance were rich and fertile, so that they even supplied the needs of kings.

[Note: The frequently praised unpublished author says: “According to the literal sense, the fertility of the land is promised to this tribe. For in the portion of its inheritance it possessed Mount Carmel, distinguished for its fertility, and it also bordered the sea; consequently, there is no doubt that it offered even to its kings the luxuries with which it itself abounded, from both sea and land,” and so forth.]

Some among us, however, think that this was said also on account of Anna the prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel, from the tribe of Aser, who is reported in the Gospels to have been the first, together with Simeon, to prophesy about the Lord (Luke 2); and that, by the faithfulness of her prophecy, she gave food, as it were, to rulers—that is, to the Apostles and the other believers—the things that had been prophesied concerning him.

2. But since Aser is interpreted as “blessed,” we are gradually leading that man whom we have recalled from error through repentance, step by step, to the increasing blessings of blessedness. After conversion, spiritual understanding, and victory over temptations, he is now said to have rich bread. For he eats the bread that descended from heaven (John 1), which gives life to this world; and that bread is rich.

3. We can understand “rich bread” in this way. Those who understand nothing more in Christ than Christ Jesus crucified do indeed eat bread from heaven, but it is dry and scant. Those, however, who are worthy for the treasures of Christ’s wisdom and knowledge to be revealed to them (Col. 2) are those for whom the bread is rich, as it was for Paul, who said: “I know both how to abound and how to suffer need; in everything and in all things I have been instructed” (Phil. 4).

For if our Lord and Savior, when he deigned to assume the figure of a bull, is said to have been a fattened and well-fed bull slaughtered for the repentant son (Luke 15), why should those who attain blessedness not likewise be called rich bread? Such a man, for whom the bread has now become rich, will also give food to rulers. What kind of food? Without doubt, the word of God. He will give food not to just any poor people or recipients, but to rulers; for he too will speak wisdom among the perfect (1 Cor. 2).

# THE BLESSING OF NAPHTHALI

[Col. 0325]

1. “NAPHTHALI: a spreading tree [Note: Alternatively, “a loosened tree”; in Greek, στέλεχος ἀνειμένον, “a loosened or extended trunk.” Saint Ambrose also approves the reading of the exemplars cited here. Here too, however, the name Naphtali itself seems to have to be placed first. Compare Jerome, *Questions on Genesis*.], or, as our copies have it, “a spreading vine, producing beauty in its fruits.” The historical account indicates that Gad first began to possess an inheritance in fertile plains; and that after him Naphtali possessed fertile countryside, thick with shrubs and trees.

2. In the mystical exposition, when we discussed Zebulun above, we also spoke of the name Naphtali, as though it were associated with Zebulun in the Gospels, saying what seemed appropriate to us: namely, that from these places and this region came forth, as it were, the root and origin of the blessed Apostles, and that their people, who were sitting in darkness, saw a great light. The “princes of Zebulun and the princes of Naphtali” (Ps. 67), who are proclaimed through David, likewise refer to the persons of the Apostles.

3. As for the third explanation, the interpretation of the name Naphtali is precisely what his father expresses here while blessing him: either “a spreading tree” or “a vine.” That inner man of ours, therefore, who shortly before was feeding on rich bread and giving food from it to rulers—the bread that strengthens the human heart (Ps. 103)—has now, consequently, received from the true vine, Christ, a beautiful fruit, by which he may gladden with wine the heart that he had strengthened with bread. In both respects he seems to me already to have made such progress that he may even receive the mysteries of the priesthood.

But if we prefer to understand a spreading tree rather than a spreading vine, one that produces beauty in its fruits, what other tree could produce beauty in its fruits than the wisdom of God, of which Solomon says: “She is a tree of life to those who embrace her” (Prov. 3)?

# THE BLESSING OF JOSEPH

[Col. 0327]

1. “A SON INCREASED IS JOSEPH; an increased son.” In the blessing of Joseph, even the first appearance of the literal text blossoms. For rightly is he called an increased son whom the Lord, for the preservation of his family, had exalted to the second rank of the kingdom. Understand him, therefore, as increased in wisdom, counsel, steadfastness, chastity, honor, kingship, virtue, and—in which lies the summit of all virtues—piety. In all these respects Joseph is rightly said to have been enlarged and increased.

When he said, “My zealous son,” he seems to have expressed not one who is envious, but one who has suffered envy: that is, one whose glory is so great that it deserves envy. This, then, is what he says: “My zealous son, younger one, return to me”—my son not so much by birth as by merits.

It does not seem to me without significance that, when the Patriarch repeats the words a third time, he names Joseph as son, saying: “An increased son is Joseph, an increased son; zealous, and my younger son.” What does it mean that Joseph alone among all his brothers is called “son” three times? As far as I can understand in accordance with the weakness of my judgment, he was born once as a son when Joseph was born to him (Gen. 30), when, after despairing of offspring, he was reborn through receiving a child from Rachel. A son is born to him a second time, as it were, when he is informed that Joseph lives after he had believed him dead (ibid. 45). A son is made to him a third time when, by teaching, instruction, and all those virtues through which he himself saw God, he educated and instructed Joseph and thereby begot him as a son in the spirit.

Otherwise, the designation “younger son” would not suit him, since Benjamin was younger than he, unless he is called younger in relation to the father’s instruction. “Return to me,” he says. That is: turn your thoughts toward me, so that you may carefully observe and inscribe in your heart the things that are said.

You, son Joseph, against whom those who took counsel cursed and the “masters of the bows” laid ambushes (ibid. 42)—for Scripture also reports that his brothers at that time plotted to kill him, but Judah intervened and restrained the murderous plan. What he called “cursed” is what they said: “Behold, this dreamer comes” (ibid.).

The “masters of the bows” designate warrior men. The loosening of the arms and breaking of the bows signifies that their undertaking was frustrated by the hand of mighty Jacob—that is, the God of Jacob. Hence comes the one who strengthened Israel from the God of your father and helped you, “my God.” From the same source your help came from which your father Israel was strengthened, certainly when he wrestled on the way (ibid. 32), and God helped him and gave him the name Israel (ibid. 35).

That same God of mine has also blessed you: “with the blessing of heaven [Note: The word “with” is superfluous; neither the Greek text nor the other Latin authors recognize it.], from above, and with the blessing of the earth.” The blessing of heaven signifies wisdom; that of earth signifies kingship and power. “Because of the blessing of breasts and womb,” the blessing of your father and your mother. He explained what the blessing of breasts and womb is by naming the mother, since Joseph had received not only paternal but also maternal blessings.

“This blessing of your father and mother,” he says, “has prevailed over the blessings of everlasting mountains and the blessings of eternal hills.” Perhaps “everlasting mountains” and “eternal hills” are said in reference to the immobility of grace that remains in him, compared with things that are themselves immovable and enduring.

“These eternal blessings,” he says, “will be upon the head of Joseph and upon the crown of those over whom he was ruler among his brothers.” At the end of the statement, he seems to have extended the blessings to the whole number of the brothers, so that the blessings are principally upon Joseph’s head, but through Joseph they also come upon those over whom he was leader and teacher.

2. This is what we have understood according to the literal sense. But if we wish to investigate something deeper here, Joseph can perhaps be referred to the person of the Lord. Just as Joseph, after being thought dead, is found not only alive but also established in the kingdom, and is therefore said to have been increased, so also our Lord and Savior, who was thought dead among the Jews, is found alive and reigning in the hearts of the faithful.

Our Savior, therefore, was also increased after death. Before he died, Judea alone was the place where God was known (Ps. 75), and his name was great in Israel alone. But after he died through weakness and rose from the dead through power (1 Cor. 13), an offering is presented to his name throughout the whole earth.

He is also called the zealous Son of God. And who endured such jealousy? Of him it is written: “For Pilate knew that they had handed him over out of envy” (Matt. 27; Mark 15).

The younger son according to the flesh is the last Adam. What we marked in the historical exposition as the third designation of “son,” repeated here, we discover much more clearly in this exposition. He is a son before the ages, of whom the Father said: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. 106). Again, he is a son when he was born from Mary, and it is said through the angel: “The holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1). He becomes a son a third time when the Firstborn rises from the dead; and the paternal voice beautifully applies to him: “My younger son, return to me.” After he has risen from the dead, ascend victoriously into heaven, even to me, from whom you proceeded.

“Those who took counsel against him,” he says, “cursed” (Matt. 26). For the scribes and Pharisees had begun to devise a plan to seize Jesus by treachery. They cursed him, without doubt, when they said: “You are a Samaritan and have a demon” (John 8).

The “masters of the bows” laid ambushes for him, but their bows were broken by power, and the sinews of their arms and hands were loosened. Those lying in wait as “masters of the bows” are understood to be those who approached him with deceitful questions in order to catch him in his words, saying: “Tell us, is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar or not?” (Matt. 22).

They stretched these words toward Jesus like arrows drawn from the bow of their mouth, so that if he said it was not lawful to pay tribute, he would become liable to Caesar, while if he said it was lawful, he would appear to dissolve the Law. But when he, as the very wisdom of God, examined the inscription on the denarius and replied, “Give to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s,” the sinews of their arms were loosened by the hand of mighty Jacob.

His contest in the wilderness may also be understood, when he was tempted by the devil, who aimed at him arrows of evil suggestions. Driving them away by his replies, he loosened the arms and sinews of those who had aimed them.

“From there comes the one who strengthened Israel from the God of your father and helped you.” The Savior is also said to have been helped by God according to his humanity.

[Note: The frequently praised unpublished author says: “Because he was truly human and made a little lower than the angels, he required not only the Father’s help but also angelic assistance, evidently in order to manifest the twofold substance in him. Hence he cries: ‘My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?’ And in the Gospel: ‘An angel from heaven appeared to him and strengthened him,’ and so forth.”]

Finally, it is written in the Gospel: “As he labored in prayer, an angel approached and strengthened him” (Luke 22).

The exposition we have just given may perhaps seem too difficult at this point, since we indicated that the preceding words were spoken as though by the Father concerning the Son. Here, however, it is written: “My God helped you and blessed you.” How can this apply to the person of the Father? But let us see whether the following consideration removes the difficulty. Just as nothing prevents the Father from saying of the Son, because the Son is wisdom, “He is my wisdom,” and because the Son is power, it is not absurd for the Father to say of him, “He is my power,” and because the Son is truth, it is not incongruous for the Father to say, “He is my truth,” so, because the Son is God, it is not absurd for him to say, “He is my God.” Nor is it absurd for the Son to say of the Father: “I am going to my God and your God.”

“And he blessed you,” he says, “with the blessing of heaven from above, and with the blessing of earth possessing all things” (Job 14).

It will not seem inappropriate for Christ to possess the blessing of heaven, in accordance with the statement: “The second man is from heaven, heavenly” (1 Cor. 15). But when he said “the blessing of earth possessing all things,” on account of the blessing of breasts and womb, it seems to me a very remarkable and great matter how that earth which has been blessed in the Son of God can possess all things.

I think it should be understood in this way: each person receives the grace of the Spirit according to the measure of his faith. For to one, according to the measure of faith, is given the word of understanding; to another, the word of wisdom; to another, prophecy; to another, discernment of spirits; to another, kinds of tongues (ibid. 12). You will find these gifts distributed individually, one to each person, or sometimes two or three together. But in that earth—that is, in that flesh which was blessed in Jesus—not only were all these things present; they dwelt there fully and substantially, as the Apostle also says: “In him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily” (Col. 2).

“Because of the blessing of breasts and womb” (Col. 2).

[Note: Saint Ambrose also relates this passage. I cite him here in order to clear him of an error that remains even in the recent Benedictine edition. The passage reads: “He speaks of Mary’s breasts, which were truly blessed, with which the holy Virgin gave the people the drink of milk from the Lord’s cup” [correct *poculo*, “cup,” for *populo*, “people”]. Hence the woman in the Gospel says: “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that you sucked.” But when he says, “the blessing of the womb of your father and mother,” if we wish to understand Mary’s womb, the reason why he joined both blessings will remain obscure. Yet I think it more beautiful to understand, according to the spiritual mystery, the two births of the Lord Jesus: according to divinity, and according to the flesh, he who was begotten from the Father before the ages,” and so forth.]

A woman in the Gospel, undoubtedly mindful of these matters, is reported to have cried out: “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that you sucked” (Luke 11).

“Because of the blessing,” he says, “of your father and your mother”—of the heavenly Father, who gave the blessing, and of the virgin mother, who received it.

“It prevailed over the blessings of everlasting mountains.” This blessing given to you from the highest heaven and from earth, he says, prevailed over the blessings of everlasting mountains and the blessings of eternal hills.

What are the everlasting mountains, unless they are those to whom Jesus says: “You are those who have remained with me in my temptations” (ibid. 22)? The Apostles are rightly called everlasting mountains, because they remained to the end, and they themselves will be saved.

But whom else should we understand as the eternal hills except those who, in the second rank, are compared with the merits of the Apostles and attain eternal life?

For these will be believed much more truly to be eternal than the mountains and hills that perish together with the world.

All these blessings, then, “will be upon the head of Joseph and upon the crown of those over whom he was ruler among his brothers.” All these blessings are fittingly said to have been placed upon Christ’s head, from whose head they also come to the crown of those over whom he presides.

There is no other reason why he received all these blessings in the flesh in which he was born than that, having diffused them from the Father into himself as through a kind of transmission, he might in turn pour them forth upon believers. Having become the mediator between God and human beings, he received—through his mediation and first reception of them—the blessings that human nature, because of its weakness, could now receive, just as he himself said: “For their sake I sanctify myself” (John 17).

3. Now, as for the man who, restored to us through spiritual stages and increased as far as Joseph, ascends through these stages: who has shone forth so greatly through progress in faith and through the gifts of the Holy Spirit that he has grown even to the point of provoking envy—with what flowers of the things we have said will he be crowned, when, after fighting the good fight, finishing his course, and keeping the faith, God, the righteous Judge, prepares for him the crown of righteousness laid up for him (2 Tim. 4)?

Of him, then, the father says: “An increased son is Joseph, an increased son.” And who has been so increased as this man, who, after errors and falls, was restored and renewed through each stage of virtue until he reached the highest palm?

But because he ascends gradually, he is said to have been increased at each stage. He first began to be increased in Judah through confession; then, when he cast off the nocturnal works of darkness, he was increased in Zebulun; again, he was increased in Issachar when the reward of his labor grew. He was increased in Dan when he preferred right judgment to his own crooked thoughts. He was increased in Gad when, after being tempted, he prevailed. He was increased in Aser when he came to blessedness.

He is therefore rightly now also called an increased son, Joseph, since he is already attaining the good things of the future age.

When he is called a “zealous son,” this means one who is to be imitated by the good but persecuted by the wicked through envy and slander. The Apostle also describes this good and evil zeal when he says concerning the evil zeal of the Jews: “They are zealous for you, but not well” (Gal. 4). Concerning good zeal he says of himself: “I am jealous over you with the jealousy of God” (1 Cor. 11).

He is called a younger son. Why should he not be called younger, since he has put off the old man with his deeds, has risen with Christ, and walks in newness of life?

He too must be called a son three times. His first birth was according to the flesh; the second was through conversion, or through baptism; the third is that which is also called regeneration, namely, resurrection from the dead. He now seems to me to have become the kind of son that the blessed will be in the future.

Therefore the father next says to him: “Return to me.” All who have proceeded from God return after the resurrection. But the judgment of Holy Scripture is: “Do not praise anyone before death” (Ecclus. 11). For this reason, it seems to me more likely that such great blessedness belongs only to one who has risen from death after dying.

When he says, “Those who took counsel against him cursed,” he does not say “curse,” but “cursed”—at the time when, placed in the flesh in this world, you were being tempted. “And they laid ambushes for him, the masters of the bows” (Ps. 10)—those who sit in ambush to shoot the upright of heart in darkness.

“But they were broken with the power of their bows,” with the power of Jacob. He breaks the bows of the enemies who not only receives no arrow of the devil into himself, but also defends others from his darts and wounds.

“And the sinews of their arms and hands were loosened by the hand of mighty Jacob,” when the one who was mighty in Jacob and helped him in the contest—who strengthened Israel so that he might make him see God in his mind—

[Note: Thus Origen interprets “Israel” as νοῦς ὁρῶν θεοῦ, or elsewhere νοῦς ὁρῶν θεόν, “a mind seeing God,” or “a mind that sees God.” The great Jerome, however, by no means approves this etymology, especially in his *Questions on Genesis*, chapter 32, where he says: “But that interpretation in the *Book of Names*, ‘Israel, seeing God,’ worn away by the speech of almost everyone, seems to me to have been interpreted not so much truly as forcefully. For Israel is written with these letters,” and after several intervening remarks: “Although, therefore, they [Origen and others] possess great authority, and the shadow of their eloquence overwhelms us, since they translated Israel as ‘a man seeing God,’ we are guided rather by the authority of Scripture and of the angel or God who himself called him Israel.” See our discussion there.]

—also helped this man and blessed him with the blessing of heaven from above and with the blessing of earth possessing all things (Ps. 141).

For he received not only, as one meek, the inheritance of the earth, but, as one poor in spirit, he also obtained the kingdom of heaven.

That earth which possesses all things is Christ, whom the righteous receives as an inheritance and says to the Lord: “You are my portion in the land of the living.”

What is the reason for which he deserved to attain these things? “Because of the blessing,” he says, “of breasts and womb.” Whose womb, or whose breasts? Perhaps that womb which Paul indicates when he says: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor” (Gal. 4).

[Note: Barraeus praises a manuscript in which *gerebat* (“he bore”) was read instead of *indicat* (“he indicates”). The unpublished author among our materials seems to have taken his wording from this passage: “Those who have not yet advanced into the strength of faith, but are drawn toward it through teachers, hear from the Apostle: ‘My little children, for whom I am again in labor,’” and so forth; he relates this extensively and in detail to the blessing of breasts and womb.]

Hence it is clear that there is an apostolic womb which not only gives birth to children but, if they should deviate from the truth, receives them again and gives birth to them a second time.

From this womb, therefore, every righteous person is either born, or, if already perfect, himself gives birth to children; nevertheless he also sucks the apostolic breasts, or offers them to those who suck. Of these the Apostle said: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Cor. 3); and elsewhere, to express the apostolic breasts more clearly, he adds: “I was among you as a nurse cherishes her own children” (1 Thess. 2).

The fullness of blessing therefore comes to every righteous person because of the apostolic womb and breasts.

“And because of the blessing,” he says, “of your father and your mother.” Christ is the Father of the perfected, as he himself said: “Little children, I am with you only a little longer” (John 13); and the mother is the Church.

This blessing prevailed over the blessings of everlasting mountains and eternal hills—that is, of those who pursue knowledge and exalted, lofty works.

“These blessings,” he says, “will be upon the head of Joseph and upon the crown of those over whom he was ruler among his brothers.” Not only is the head of the righteous, which is Christ, blessed, but also the crown of those over whom he presided; for those who rightly cultivate and fruitfully establish themselves also benefit the faithful, as the Apostle said: “By doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you” (1 Tim. 4).

# THE BLESSING OF BENJAMIN

[Col. 0333]

1. “BENJAMIN, a ravenous wolf: in the morning he will eat, and in the evening he will divide the food.”

[Note: This is the reading of the manuscript, which Barraeus had rejected in the margin of the book. It is considerably more elegant and complete than the printed text, which read approximately: “I would like to introduce the history of this account, what Benjamin contains within himself,” and so forth. For the rest, the history does not seem to me especially difficult; it denotes the fierce and violent character of Benjamin and his tribe.]

Those who advocate the historical interpretation of this account should tell me what Benjamin had in common with a ravenous wolf, or how he divides food in the morning and evening.

But even among these matters the dull-hearted Jews themselves avoid the injury to the literal sense, and some refer what is written to the voracity of the altar, which was constructed in the territory of Benjamin, as though what is offered in the morning were divided by the priests in the evening.

[Note: Saint Jerome left testimony to this opinion of the Hebrews, and Rufinus perhaps intended to note it. “Thus,” he says, “the Hebrews explain it. The altar upon which sacrifices were offered was in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin. This, they say, signifies that the priests offer sacrifices in the morning and divide in the evening what has been assigned to them by the people according to the Law,” and so forth. They therefore place the voracious wolf over the interpretation of the altar, and the division of the spoils over the priests, who, serving the altar, live from the altar. The unpublished author among our materials likewise says: “It is the tradition of the Hebrews, and the agreement of Blessed Jerome, that these words signify the Jerusalem altar, which is known to have been constructed in the tribe of Benjamin. In the manner of a ravenous wolf, it devoured the morning sacrifice by the consuming fire. In the evening of the day, after the sacrifices and rites of the victims had been completed, they were accustomed to divide among the priests and Levites what remained from the fire and, by the command of the Law, was owed as food to the priests,” and so forth.]

Others, with various different—even fabulous—accounts, nevertheless admit that the sequence of the literal sense cannot stand on the basis of these words.

## 2.

In the Church, however, among very many people this opinion is held: that what is written appears capable of being referred to the Apostle Paul. [Note: The principal authorities that may be cited are Origen, *Homilies on Ezekiel* IV; Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, book V, chapter 1; St Ambrose on this passage; St Jerome, who says: “That this is a most evident prophecy concerning the Apostle Paul is clear to everyone”; St Gregory, *Morals*, book XVIII, chapter 16; and finally an unpublished author among us, who says: “The blessed Paul is signified, destined to come from the same tribe. In the manner of a rapacious wolf, in the morning—that is, in his youth—he devoured, since, while consenting to the killing of blessed Stephen and receiving letters from the chief priests and elders of the Jewish people to Damascus and the other cities, the more saints he tore to pieces by diverse slaughter, the more prey he devoured like a rapacious wolf. Yet in the evening he divided the spoils, when, struck down by the Lord’s voice and vision, he distributed suitable nourishment of divine teaching to the faithful established within the holy Church,” and so forth.]

We neither reject nor disapprove this interpretation, but endeavor to do what is written: “The wise man, hearing a word, will praise it and add to it.” Accordingly, to what our predecessors have rightly said about Paul—and we do not deny it—we add the following.

“Benjamin,” he says, “is interpreted as ‘son of sorrow.’ By lot of inheritance he received the place in which the earthly Jerusalem is situated, bearing the type and form of that heavenly Jerusalem. When, therefore, the time arrives for the heavenly Jerusalem, and for the Church of the firstborn enrolled in heaven, to be revealed [earlier reading: *manifestanda*, “to be made manifest”], this Jerusalem, which has now been cast away and rejected because of unbelief, after suffering, together with her children, prolonged famine of the word of God and spiritual thirst, [Note: It seems that *salva erit* (“will be saved”), or something similar, must be supplied.] will be saved when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, according to the Apostle’s promise. Then all Israel will be saved—the Israel that is now represented under the person of Benjamin.

“Thus Benjamin, the last son, receives the final blessing, because he too is to be saved last. He is called a rapacious wolf. He is called a wolf because of his greed: for he comes from great hunger and famine of the word of God. He is rapacious because he too violently seizes the kingdom of God.

“‘In the morning he will eat.’ I think that ‘morning’ still refers to the time when he received the Law; for then a certain illumination of knowledge was first given to the world, from which time the day of knowledge may be thought to have received its beginning. Thus he still eats in the morning the food that he had received in the morning: he still eats and meditates, following the law of righteousness, but has not attained to the law. [Note: Either some word is missing here, or *pervenerit* should be read in place of *pervenit*. We silently correct lighter matters below.]

“In the evening he divides the food. This evening [variant: *et*, “also”] is that final time in which he is converted, just as for us also ‘evening’ denotes this time of our conversion, in which we now are. Then he divides the food; for then he understands that in the Law the letter must be divided and separated from the spirit, and then he recognizes that ‘the letter kills, but the spirit gives life.’ Since, therefore, already enlightened by the grace of the Lord, he begins in the Law to divide and separate spiritual things from bodily things, he is said to divide the food in the evening: although he had meditated on the Law throughout the whole day, he had not previously done so.”

## 3.

A third sense, moreover, is almost still open to us in this passage, because what remains in Benjamin for that man of ours who was created according to God—who first went astray in the threefold movements of the soul, in Reuben, Simeon, and Levi; who, in Judah, recognizes his error, confesses it, and repents; who, in Zebulun, strips off the old man with his deeds; who, in Issachar, also awaits the reward of good works; who, in Dan, receives the grace of judging and separating good from evil and of discerning thoughts and spirits; who, in Gad, is also found approved in temptations; who, in Asher, also divides food for princes, that is, presents banquets to the various governors of wisdom; who, in Naphtali, has already received the mysteries of the vine or of the tree; who, in Joseph, reaching perfection and the highest point, already possesses the glory of the future age and of the resurrection—what, I say, remains in Benjamin for him?

After he has, like a hungry and rapacious wolf, seized the kingdom of heaven and invaded those things that he had read in the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospels—of whose knowledge he had here obtained a part, for the Apostle Paul too says that he possesses it in part—and, placed in the world as in the morning, had eaten these things [variant: *illa*, “those things”], since he did not live by bread alone but by every word of God: when he is placed there in the kingdom, he now sees everything not through a mirror and in an enigma but face to face; and there he divides and distinguishes everything. There at last he understands what things in the holy Scriptures were written for the present condition of life; what things indicated the glory of the future kingdom; what things were spoken concerning the inner man and what concerning the outer man. There he learns more fully and skillfully [variant: *cognoscent*, “they will learn”] which passages preserve the truth of history in those very matters that we now laboriously examine; which contain mysteries alone; and which ought to be expounded according to the pagan and moral interpretation of Scripture.

If, poor as we are in knowledge and still placed in the flesh, we have been able to explain these matters less worthily, you will grant pardon, because your excessive love causes us to dare to bring this very ignorance of ours into public view. If I did not obey you in this, I should incur a very great fault.

[Col. 0335B]

## COMMENTARY ON THE APOSTLES’ CREED, BY TYRANNIUS [Note: The two more recent Oxford editions and the edition of Baluze read “Rufino Torano,” evidently through a faulty transposition, placing the forename after the name. For it is clearly established by compelling evidence, cited by Fontanini in chapter 1 of his *Life*, that Tyrannius was the forename of the Aquileian presbyter. Fell, or the Oxford editor, thought that this name designated Rufinus’s homeland, namely Tora or Thora, a now-destroyed Italian city on the border of the Sabines—a highly inappropriate view and wholly contrary to the historical evidence.] RUFINUS, PRESBYTER OF AQUILEIA.

[Note: Barraeus likewise gives this as the title; in other copies it is called *Exposition*. The remarkable heading of the old Sangerman manuscript is distinguished above the others, in which Rufinus is also given the title “Saint”: “The Exposition of the Creed begins, by Saint Rufinus.” Baluze—or whoever published his edition of Cyprian—praises this work in the notes to this same book, which he reprinted in the appendix to the works of St Cyprian, to whom it was formerly attributed. In the past it was also attributed to St Jerome; indeed, a book published separately at Oxford under that title, at the very beginnings of printing, is cited under his name. I will not dwell on the false title; yet I know that such a work would have suited the great Jerome.]

(C)

[Col. 0335B] 51

### 1.

For my part, most faithful Pope Laurentius, [Note: It is uncertain to which Church this bishop belonged. That he had earned this rank is made clear by the name “Pope” with which our author addresses him, leaving no room for doubt. Fontanini suspects that he was one of the bishops attached to the metropolitan see of Aquileia, perhaps Concordia, Rufinus’s homeland; Ughellus records that see as vacant before the sixth century. He would have been in its vicinity and, so to speak, of the same rite; but I would not say that he belonged to the metropolitan jurisdiction. We once wondered whether *Gaudenti* should be restored, and whether the bishop of Brescia was meant—the man to whom Rufinus also dedicated his books of the *Recognitions*.]

I have so little eagerness for writing, and am so little suited to it, knowing that it is not without danger to entrust a slight and feeble talent to the judgments of many. But since—as I may say it with your indulgence—you rashly bind me in your letter by the sacraments of Christ, which we receive with the greatest reverence, requiring me to compose for you something concerning the faith according to the tradition and reasoning of the Creed, although the weight of your command is beyond our strength—for I am not unaware of that saying of the wise, which very rightly declares that it is dangerous even to speak truly about God—nevertheless, if you support the necessity of your request with prayers, we shall attempt to say something, more out of reverence for obedience than from confidence in our talent: something that may seem suited not so much to the exercises of the perfect as to the hearing of the little ones in Christ and of beginners (Rom. 6).

[Note: Barraeus and Frobenius read *petitioni* (“request”): less well. A little later, where the text says *quam quae*, nearly all others more elegantly reject the latter word. They also have *et quidem* instead of *equidem*, and finally *conscripsisse* instead of *scripsisse*.]

[Note: Some printed and manuscript copies omit the little word *ut*; others read *tua* instead of *tui*. Formerly Manutius read *ut conveniatis* (“so that you may agree with what I have said”), but this is faulty; shortly afterward we have removed the pronoun that had been rashly placed before the Greek article τῷ (*tō*).]

I have indeed discovered that some distinguished interpreters have written piously and briefly on these subjects. But I know that the heretic Photinus wrote about them not in order to explain the meaning of the statements to his hearers, but in order to draw the simple and faithful words into support of his own doctrine, although in these words the Holy Spirit took care that nothing ambiguous, nothing obscure, and nothing discordant with the rest should be placed. For in them the prophecy is truly fulfilled that says: “For he will complete and abbreviate the word in righteousness; for the Lord will make a brief word upon the earth” (Acts 2).

[Note: Previously the text had *comperitur* (“is found”), contrary to nearly all the other copies.]

We shall therefore attempt either to render and mark its simplicity in apostolic words, or to complete what seems to have been omitted by earlier writers. But so that the force of this “abbreviated word,” as we have called it, may become clearer, we shall trace from the beginning the reason why this tradition was delivered to the Churches.

[Col. 0336B] 52

### 2.

Our elders hand down that after the Lord’s Ascension, when, through the coming of the Holy Spirit, tongues of fire had rested upon each of the Apostles so that they might speak in different and varied languages—and thus no foreign nation and no barbarian language seemed inaccessible or impassable to them—the Lord gave them this command: that each should go to the several nations to preach the word of God.

[Note: All the other copies read *extera* (“foreign”), while some of the older printed copies, together with two manuscripts of Baluze, read: “No barbarian language seemed inaccessible or impassable.” Shortly afterward, where the text says “each should go to the several,” three manuscripts and other printed copies have *quosque* (“each”), a reading praised and followed by the recent editor of St Cyprian.]

As they were therefore about to depart from one another, they first established together a rule for their future preaching, lest, being drawn each in a different direction, they should explain something different to those whom they were inviting to the faith of Christ.

[Note: *Adducti* was faulty; the rest is correct, although many others prefer *alius ab alio abducti* (“being drawn away from one another”).]

All, therefore, gathered in one place and filled with the Holy Spirit, composed this brief token of their future preaching, as we have said, by each one contributing to the whole what he understood; and they determined that it should be given as a rule to believers.

[Note: They did not merely contribute their statements, but also orally formed among themselves a certain “pattern of sound words,” as Paul puts it in the Second Letter to Timothy—not one consisting exactly of the same words and meanings as those now used, but one containing the summary of apostolic teaching and constituting the form and essence of what rightly bears the name “Apostles’ Creed.” The more recent ὑπερκριτικοί (“hypercritical critics”) who attack this tradition as almost the most ancient of all may perhaps be sufficiently corrected if they observe that from the age of the Apostles this very Creed appears, in a form differing little from the present one, among writers who trace its origin back to the Apostles. Irenaeus, a disciple of Polycarp—who had heard John the Evangelist—praises it and affirms that the Church dispersed throughout the whole world received it from the Apostles and their disciples. Tertullian likewise says in *Against Praxeas*: “This rule has proceeded from the beginning of the Gospel.” Let them add that, although the Churches of those times did not use precisely the same Creed κατὰ λέξιν (*kata lexin*, “word for word”—since, as will soon be said, they did not write it on paper and ink but on tablets of fleshly hearts), they nevertheless agree in the greatest part, often even in the very words, and not merely in the articles, their arrangement, and their order. Unless this is traced back to the tradition of the Apostles, it cannot otherwise be accounted for. This is the one point Rufinus intends when he makes the Apostles the authors of the Creed. He explains his meaning below, about the middle of this treatise, where he does not even name the Apostles, but says with great caution: “Those who handed down the Creed, and also the time,” and so forth. Later writers exaggerated the matter, especially the author of Sermon 115 *On Time* among the works of Augustine, who assigned each article to a particular Apostle as its author.]

They wished this, for many and most legitimate reasons, to be called a *symbol*. For *symbol* in Greek may mean both “token” and “collation,” that is, something that many people bring together into one.

That is what the Apostles did in these statements, each contributing to the whole what he understood. It is called a token or sign because at that time, as Paul says in the First Letter to the Corinthians (1 Cor. 11), and as is related in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 15), many Jews went about pretending to be Apostles of Christ and set out to preach for the sake of some profit or of their belly. They did indeed name Christ, but they did not proclaim him with the complete lines of the traditions.

[Col. 0338A] 54

[Note: The editions published up to now, as well as all the manuscripts known to me, incorrectly read “from the circumcised” or “from circumcision,” as though Jews too were uncircumcised and were being identified. Maximus of Turin, *Homily on the Apostles’ Creed*, says: “The Apostles handed down the mystery of the Creed so that the seal of the Creed might distinguish the faithful from the faithless, and that the one who was alien to the faith and hostile to the Church might be exposed, whether, as a baptized person, he had failed to know it, or, as a heretic, had corrupted it.”]

For this reason they established that token by which the person who truly preached Christ according to the apostolic rules might be recognized.

Finally, they say that this is also observed in civil wars. Since the appearance of the weapons is alike, the sound of the voice the same, the custom one, and the methods of fighting identical, each commander gives his soldiers distinct passwords so that no deception may slip in. In Latin these are called *signs* or *tokens*. Thus, if someone should happen to appear whose identity was uncertain, he would reveal, when questioned about the password, whether he was an enemy or an ally.

[Note: Other copies read *dolo* (“by deception”), as well as *discreta* (“distinguished”) instead of *distincta*, and shortly afterward *nominantur* (“are named”) instead of *nuncupantur* (“are called”); finally, they read *hostis an socius* (“whether an enemy or an ally”) instead of *vel socius*.]
