For this reason, finally, they did not have these things written on little sheets or parchments, but handed them down to be retained in the hearts of believers, so that it might be certain that no one had learned them from reading—which sometimes reaches even unbelievers—but from the tradition of the Apostles.

[Note: The old Oxford edition likewise reads this way. Most others have *atque*, from which we restored *ex quibus* (“from which”), in place of *requiri*, which formerly stood here. All the other copies known to me omit the following word *credentium* (“of believers”). Conversely, the same copies add at the end of the sentence the word *didicisse* (“to have learned”), which our exemplar lacks and which is in fact unnecessary. We have already alluded to this discipline of secrecy concerning the Creed, and St Jerome praises it in nearly the same words in book I of *Against John of Jerusalem*: “The Creed of our faith and hope, handed down by the Apostles, is not written on paper and ink but on tablets of fleshly hearts.” St Peter Chrysologus likewise says: “Let the mind retain this Creed of life … lest perishable paper cheapen the precious gift of divinity, lest black ink darken the mystery of light,” and so forth.]

As they were therefore about to depart, as we have said, to preach, the Apostles established this token of their unanimity and faith—not like the sons of Noah, who, when they were about to disperse from one another, built a tower of baked brick and bitumen whose summit would reach to heaven (Gen. 11), but by building monuments of faith from living stones and the Lord’s pearls, monuments that would stand against the face of the enemy, which neither winds could drive against nor lightning overthrow nor the whirlwinds of storms and tempests move.

[Note: Previously the text read *monumenta*, and shortly afterward *quam neque*, and so forth. In place of the following *neque fulmina subruerent* (“nor could lightning overthrow”), Fell and Baluze, not to mention older editors, read *flumina subverterent* (“nor could rivers overturn”).]

Rightly, therefore, those who were building a tower of pride were separated from one another and condemned by the confusion of languages, so that each could not understand the speech of his neighbor.

But those who were building a tower of faith were endowed with knowledge and understanding of all languages, so that the former might be proved a sign of sin and the latter a sign of faith.

[Note: The cited editors read *uti ne*; and a little later, *contrectandum* instead of *tractandum*.]

But now we must also discuss something about the pearls themselves, among which the fountain and source of everything is placed first, when it is said:

### 3.

[Note: Baluze, Rembold, Erasmus, and two manuscript copies, rejecting the intervening words, read “I believe in God the Father,” or “I believe God the Father,” in the form “I believe in the Almighty,” which others prefer; we shall discuss this afterward. Fell, and formerly Barraeus, Pamelius, Morellius, Frobenius, and others with us retain the fuller reading. To Pamelius, that earlier reading seemed wholly mutilated. He also prefers that everything be read in the accusative, “God the Father,” especially since this is the reading not only of Frobenius and the old printed manuscript of Jerome but also of an even older copy from the first edition, produced when the art of printing first became known, which he saw in the Library of Toulouse. He adds that three other Creeds in Jerome have this form, and that Jerome himself, in the *Dialogue Against the Luciferians*, except in one place, as well as St Augustine everywhere, reads everything in the accusative. We, on the contrary, judged the ablative reading more correct and restored it; we shall add Baluze’s reasons for it shortly.]

### I BELIEVE IN GOD THE FATHER ALMIGHTY.

But before I begin to discuss the force of the individual statements, I think it should not inappropriately be noted that in different Churches certain additions are found in these words.

[Col. 0339B] In the Church of the city of Rome, however, this is not found to have been done. I think the reason is that no heresy has there taken its beginning, and that an ancient custom is maintained there: those who are about to receive the grace of Baptism give back the Creed publicly, that is, while the people of the faithful are listening. The hearing does not permit even the addition of a single statement by those who preceded them in the faith.

[Note: The old Oxford edition, Rembold, Erasmus, and the three manuscripts followed by Baluze read *esse* (“to be”) here. Shortly afterward, for *eos qui gratiam* (“those who receive grace”), two of the cited manuscripts, Rembold, Erasmus, and Morellius read *apud eos* (“among them”). Finally, three lines below this, we restored *unius* (“of one”) instead of *hujus* (“of this”), which Barraeus had read.]

In other places, however, so far as can be understood, certain additions seem to have been made because of some heretics, so that the meaning of novel doctrine might be excluded.

Nevertheless, we follow the order that we received through the grace of the washing in the Church of Aquileia.

[Note: The old Oxford edition cited above agrees. Other copies read “through the grace of the bath.” Shortly afterward, where the Apostle’s text says *primo omnium* (“first of all”), Baluze rejects *omnium*; Barraeus, Pamelius, Morellius, and both the old and new Oxford editions retain it. We have restored what follows, together with that and all the other copies: “he becomes a rewarder of those who believe in him.” Greek: μισθαποδότης γίνεται (*misthapodotēs ginetai*, “he becomes a rewarder”). Previously the text read *sit* (“may he be”); the words *in se* (“in him”) were missing.]

Thus “I believe” is placed first of all, just as the Apostle Paul says when writing to the Hebrews: “For whoever approaches God must first of all believe that he exists and that he becomes a rewarder of those who believe in him” (Heb. 11:6). The Prophet also says: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isa. 7:9).

Therefore, so that the entrance to understanding may be opened to you, you rightly profess first of all that you believe, because no one enters the sea and entrusts himself to the clear and deep element unless he first believes that he can be saved.

[Note: All the editions published up to now seem to have less correctly read *navem* (“a ship”) instead of *mare* (“the sea”), and shortly afterward *vitam* (“life”) instead of *sese* (“himself”). The printed readings were not even known to the learned editors Fell and Baluze, to omit the others, since they wholly ignored the Barraeus exemplar, which we use because it is more carefully corrected than the rest.]

Nor does a farmer bury seeds in the furrows and scatter crops upon the earth unless he has believed that rains will come and that the warmth of the sun will be present, by which the earth, warmed, may produce crops in multiplied harvest and nourish them as the winds blow.

[Note: Baluze preferred *segete multiplicata fruge* (“with the crop multiplied in fruit”), together with three manuscripts and three printed copies of Rembold, Erasmus, and Morellius.]

Finally, nothing can be done in life if belief has not preceded it.

What wonder, then, if, when we approach God, we profess that we must first of all believe, since without this even ordinary life itself cannot be carried on?

We have prefaced this at the beginning because the pagans are accustomed to object to us that, since our religion lacks rational arguments, it consists solely in the persuasion of belief. We have therefore shown that nothing can either be done or stand unless the force of belief has preceded it.

[Note: We inserted *quasi* (“as if” or “so to speak”), which was missing, from nearly all the other copies, as well as *ideo* (“therefore”) at the beginning of the following sentence.]

Finally, marriages too are contracted because it is believed that offspring will follow; children are handed over to the study of the arts because it is believed that the discipline of teachers will be transmitted to their pupils; and one person assumes the insignia of rule while believing that peoples and cities, and even an armed army, will obey him.

[Note: Some copies read *imperii quoque* (“also of rule”); then they read “he believes that cities and peoples, and even an armed army, will be prepared to obey him.” Shortly afterward, other copies read *breviatus* instead of *brevialis*.]

If no one undertakes any of these things without first believing that they will occur, how much more must one come to the knowledge of God by believing?

But let us see what this brief statement of the Creed now sets forth.

[Col. 0340C] 57

## 4.

“I BELIEVE,” he says, “IN GOD THE FATHER ALMIGHTY.”

[Note: As we stated above, we have continuously restored the ablatives in place of the accusatives here and in what follows, both on the authority of the better manuscripts and because of the evidence of the arguments supplied by Baluze. He says: “Three manuscripts, together with Rembold, Erasmus, and Morellius, read this way,” and likewise in the following articles, “and in Jesus Christ,” and so forth. Pamelius used the accusative in these places, both because he found it in the Frobenian edition and in two other old editions, and because three Creeds in Jerome have it, as does Jerome himself in the *Dialogue Against the Luciferians*, except in one place; Augustine also uses it everywhere. But Pamelius’s reasons prove only that “I believe in God” is commonly said in most Creeds; they do not at all prove that it existed in this form in the Creed of the Church of Aquileia. Indeed, the more usual the accusative was in Creeds, the less likely it is that scribes, either through carelessness or deliberately, would have placed the ablative in this Creed. It is not at all surprising, however, if, when they encountered the ablative, they inserted the accusative, offended by its unfamiliarity. Therefore the manuscripts in which “I believe in God,” “and in Christ,” and “and in the Holy Spirit” are read seem to me to preserve the custom of the Church of Aquileia more accurately than those that use the accusative. This manner of reciting the Creed does not seem to have been adopted by that Church without deliberation, but so that the distinction of the three divine persons from the subsequent articles might be clearer.]

Nearly all the Churches of the East transmit it in this way: “I believe in one God, the almighty Father.”

[Note: Others read *Orientis* (“of the East”); three lines below they have “thus they transmit it.” Rufinus seems by this observation to have intended to designate the professions of faith in the Churches of the East, namely the Nicene and Constantinopolitan Creeds.]

And again, in the following statement, where we say, “and in Christ Jesus, his only Son, our Lord,” they transmit: “And in one Lord of ours, Jesus Christ, his only Son,” thereby professing one God and one Lord, according to the authority of the Apostle Paul (1 Cor. 8).

But we shall return to this in the appropriate places below. For the moment, let us examine what he says: “in God the almighty Father.”

God, insofar as the human mind is able to conceive it, is the name of the very nature or substance that is above all things.

[Note: Others add [a word]; and shortly afterward they read “who is the author of all things” instead of “who is wholly the author of all things.”]

“Father” is the name of a secret and ineffable mystery. When you hear “God,” understand a substance without beginning and without end, simple, without any mixture, invisible, incorporeal, ineffable, and beyond estimation; in which nothing has been added and nothing created. For he is without an author, since he is wholly the author of all things.

When you hear “Father,” understand the Father of the Son, who is the image of the substance mentioned above.

[Note: Formerly the text read *supradictus* (“mentioned above”); the Sangerman manuscript reads *est* (“is”) instead of *sit* (“may be”). In my judgment the author of Sermon 181 *On Time* among the works of St Augustine appears to have taken his words from this passage of Rufinus. He says: “Observe that when he joins the name of God the Father in the confession, he shows that God did not first begin to exist and afterward become Father, but that he has always been both God and Father, without any beginning. When you hear ‘Father,’ recognize that he has a Son truly begotten, just as one who possesses something is called an owner, and one who rules someone is called a lord. God the Father, therefore, is the name of a secret mystery, whose true Son is the Word.”]

For just as no one is called a lord unless he has either property or a servant over whom he rules, and as no one is called a teacher unless he has a pupil, so no one can in any way be called a father unless he has a son.

By this very name, therefore, by which God is called Father, it is also shown that the Son subsists together with the Father.

[Col. 0341C] 58

But how God the Father begot the Son, do not investigate, nor pry too inquisitively into the depth of the mystery, lest, while you persist too obstinately in examining the radiance of inaccessible light, you lose even that small degree of vision granted to mortals by divine generosity.

[Note: We supplied *te* (“you”), which was missing, from other copies; these likewise have *inseras* (“you may insert”) instead of *ingeras* (“you may pry”), and read *in profundi hujus arcani* (“into the depth of this mystery”). Pamelius preferred *in profundum hujus arcani* (“into the depth of this mystery”).]

Or, if you think that every kind of investigation should be employed here, first set before yourself the things that belong to us. If you can explain these consistently, then hasten from earthly things to heavenly, and from visible things to invisible.

First explain, if you can, how the mind that is within you generates a word, and what the spirit of memory is in it; how these, though different in their things and activities, are nevertheless one in substance or nature, and, although they proceed from the mind, are never separated from it.

[Note: The old Oxford edition alone has *sint substantia* (“are substance”), omitting the preceding *vel*, which the other copies also lack. These copies in turn have *sed* instead of *et si*, then *in animae nostrae* (“in our soul”), and later *quanto et aspectui*; finally, they read *rapidum fertur fluentum* (“the stream is carried rapidly”), which seems less satisfactory and, I think, would not have been approved by the learned editors had they consulted the Barraeus copy.]

And if these things, although they are found in us and are the substance of our soul, nevertheless seem so hidden from us because they are invisible to bodily sight, let us inquire about clearer matters.

How does a fountain generate a river from itself, and by what impulse does it flow rapidly into the stream?

What is it that, although river and fountain are one and inseparable, nevertheless means and is called neither “river” for “fountain” nor “fountain” for “river,” and yet whoever sees the river also sees the fountain?

[Note: Other copies, even Fell’s, incorrectly have *quod quidem*, referring it to the stream immediately preceding. Baluze says that he restored the reading from the Sangerman manuscript, another manuscript from the Royal Library, and Morellius; but he did not know that the same reading had long before been restored by Barraeus, except that Barraeus had *dum* instead of *cum*.]

Exercise yourself first in explaining these things, and examine, if you can, what lies before you; then you will advance to the higher matters.

[Note: Some copies have *veniemus* (“we shall come”) and *veniamus* (“let us come”). They also read *quod* instead of *quia*, and shortly afterward *patet* instead of *videtur*, a reading also preferred by the old Oxford edition.]

Do not think that I immediately urge you to ascend from earth above the heavens. Rather, if you please, I shall first lead you to that firmament which is visible to the eyes; and there, if you can, examine the nature of this visible light: how this heavenly fire generates from itself the splendor of light, and how it also produces vapor; and how, although there are three things in reality, they are nevertheless one in substance.

Even if you have been able to investigate each of these things, know that the mystery of divine generation is still so much more different and more exalted as the Creator is more powerful than creatures, the craftsman more excellent than his work, and the One who always is more noble than the one who began to be from nothing.

[Note: The final clause is omitted by some copies.]

God, therefore, must be believed to be the Father of his only Son, our Lord; he must not be scrutinized. For it is not lawful for a servant to dispute about the birth of his lord.

The Father testified from heaven, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him” (Matt. 17).

The Father says that he is his Son and commands that he be heard. The Son says: “Whoever sees me sees the Father.” And: “I and the Father are one.” And: “I came forth from God and came into this world” (John 14:9).

Who is there who would insert himself as a mediator and examiner between these words of the Father and the Son, divide the Godhead, separate the affection, break the substance, sever the spirit, and deny what the Truth says?

[Note: Other copies read *medium se discussorem* (“an examiner interposing himself”) and the old Oxford edition retains *discussor*. A few lines later Baluze rejects, together with the Sangerman manuscript, Rembold, Erasmus, and others, the adverb *tanquam* (“as”) in the phrase “as a wise man.” We have restored from the same source *quasi* (“as if” or “like”), which is repeated seven times below, instead of *quia* (“because”) in all seven places. The old edition cited above reads *qua*, which is perhaps more pleasing. Baluze explains the reasons for the reading he restored as follows: “*Quasi sapiens sapientiam* means ‘as a wise man, wisdom’; the same is meant by *quasi* and the Greek ὡς (*hōs*). Morellius and Pamelius have *quia sapiens*, *quia justus* (‘because he is wise,’ ‘because he is just’). The reading we have restored rests both on the authority of three manuscripts and of Rembold and Erasmus and on more exact theological reasoning. For no one is unaware how customary it is among the holy Fathers to say that the Son is begotten from the Father as splendor from light. Rufinus himself says so not long afterward.”]

God the Father is therefore true, as Father of truth—not creating from outside himself, but begetting the Son from what he himself is: like a wise person wisdom, like a just person justice, like the everlasting one an everlasting one, like the immortal one an immortal one, like the invisible one an invisible one; as light [begets] splendor, as mind [begets] word.

### 5. But when we said that the Churches of the East transmit “one God the Father almighty, and one Lord,” this must not be understood as saying “one” numerically, but universally.

[Note: We removed *true*, which Barraeus, together with several other books, had inserted. Pamelius formerly advised deleting it; the better manuscripts, and their greater number, support this.]

For example, if someone says “one man” or “one horse,” he has used *one* numerically [Al. “has placed this one numerically”]: for another and a third man, or horse, can exist. But where another or a third cannot be joined to it, if “one” is said, it is not the name of a number but of universality.

[Note: Other copies have *second*, with which shortly afterward we too restored *of number* in place of *of unity*. The old Oxford edition is recognized to have read not “of number” but “of universality.”]

Thus, for example, if we say “one sun,” *one* is said in such a way that neither another nor a third can be added: for there is one sun. Much more, therefore, when God is called “one,” *one* is used not as a numerical term but as a universal designation—that is, he is called [Al. “be called”] one because there is no other.

The same must be understood concerning the Lord: there is one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom God the Father holds dominion over all.

[Note: We believe this to be the same old Oxford edition, together with the newly joined one. The latter adds, after the word *Christ*, “the almighty Son of God”; but Baluzius found this addition in no manuscript or edition whatsoever.]

Hence the following statement also declares God to be almighty.

[Note: The same long-praised old edition has this reading; others have *Lord*, and shortly afterward say, “he is said to be from him because he holds,” and so forth. Then the same old Oxford edition: “The Apostolic statement affirms this, where it says, ‘because through him.’” Properly, if anywhere, Rufinus explains the force of the word *almighty*. The principal meaning of the Greek word παντοκράτωρ is the same. It seems indeed that he received this from Saint Cyril of Jerusalem; compare Catechesis VIII. For we shall show below that he borrowed certain other things from him as well.]

He is called almighty because he holds dominion over all. The Father holds all things through the Son, as the Apostle also says: “For through him all things were created, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers” (Col. 1:16). And again, writing to the Hebrews, he says: “For through him he established the ages, and appointed him heir of all things” (Heb. 12).

[Note: The passage containing the words “but what he appointed” is understood to mean “what he begot.” In the copy of Barraeus supplied to us, and likewise in two editions corrected by Pamelius, namely the Hieronymian editions, this passage was lacking; we restored it on the authority of other books. The old Oxford edition has: “The Father appointed him heir, and through him all things were created,” omitting everything in between. The repetition of the words evidently deceived the antiquarians.]

When he says “appointed,” “begot” is understood. If, then, the Father established the ages through him, and through him all things were created, and he himself is heir of all things, then through him also he holds dominion over all.

For just as light is from light and truth from truth, so almighty was born from Almighty. Thus it is written in the Apocalypse of John concerning the Seraphim:

[Note: Here we supplied the words *concerning the Seraphim*, which were lacking. Shortly afterward Baluzius omits *Sabaoth* on the authority of two manuscripts, one of which also omits the preceding name *God*. Pamelius formerly restored it because it is found in the Apocalypse. On the other hand, Remboldus and Erasmus also omit the following two words, *who was*.]

“And they had no rest day or night, saying, ‘Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Sabaoth, who was, and who is, and who is to come, the Almighty’” (Rev. 4:8).

Therefore he is called almighty who is to come. And who is the one who is to come, if not Christ, the Son of God?

[Note: Some add *Jesus*. Shortly afterward others customarily place *invisible* and *impassible* before it. Recall that Rufinus himself states above that certain additions appear to have been made on account of some heretics, so that the meaning of the novel doctrine might be excluded.]

To these are added “invisible” and “impassible.” It must be understood that these two expressions are not found in the Creed of the Roman Church.

It is nevertheless established among us that they were added because of the heresy of Sabellius—specifically, that heresy which our people call Patripassianism: the doctrine which says both that the Father himself was born from the Virgin and that he became visible or suffered in the flesh.

Thus, so that such impiety concerning the Father might be excluded, our predecessors appear to have added these expressions and called the Father invisible and impassible. For it is established that the Son, not the Father, was incarnate,

[Note: Two manuscripts, which Baluzius follows—the Sangermanensis and the Regius—and likewise the editions of Remboldus and Erasmus, omit *incarnate* and have only “born in the flesh.” Pamelius has “born in the flesh and from the flesh,” to which the newer Oxford edition nearly agrees. Morelius agrees with us.]

and was born from the flesh; and through his birth in the flesh the Son became visible and passible. But as regards that immortal substance of the Godhead, which he possesses as one and the same with the Father, neither the Father, nor the Son, nor the Holy Spirit is believed to be visible or passible.

According to the condescension of the flesh assumed, however, the Son was both seen and suffered in the flesh. The prophet had also foretold this when he said:

“This is our God; no other shall be reckoned beside him. He discovered the whole way of discipline and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. After this he appeared on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch 3:36).

[Note: We removed the pronoun *who* here, on the authority of the sacred text and other books. In the following verse, instead of *among human beings*, some manuscripts, from the Greek ἐν τοῖς ἀνθρώποις, have *with human beings*.]

After this comes:

### 6. AND IN CHRIST JESUS, HIS ONLY SON, OUR LORD

[Note: We follow the other editors in placing the name *Christ* before the name *Jesus*, because Rufinus also explains the former first. Previously the text had *in Jesus Christ*, and likewise was in the accusative case, as we noted elsewhere.]

Jesus is a name of Hebrew origin, which among us is rendered “Savior.” Christ is called from *chrism*, that is, from anointing.

For we read in the books of Moses that Auses, son of Nave, when he had been chosen as leader of the people, was given the changed name Jesus instead of Ause, so that it might be shown that this was a name appropriate to rulers and leaders—namely, to those who would give salvation to the peoples following them.

Accordingly, the man who led the people brought out from the land of Egypt and freed from the errors of the wilderness into the Promised Land was also called Jesus.

And this Jesus, who brought the people out from the darkness of ignorance and recalled them from the errors of the world, led them into the kingdoms of heaven.

[Note: Others add *is called*, and shortly afterward have *called forth* instead of *called back*. Jerome wisely says in his Commentary on Matthew, chapter 16: “Christ is a common name of dignity; Jesus is the proper name of the Savior.” Add also Chrysologus, who follows Rufinus’s footsteps, Sermon 59. “Christ,” he says, “is from anointing, because the anointing which formerly passed through kings, prophets, and priests as a figure poured itself out in its entire fullness of the Spirit of divinity upon this King of kings, Priest of priests, and Prophet of prophets.”]

Christ, moreover, is either a priestly or a royal name. Formerly both priests and kings were consecrated with the oil of chrism. But they, as mortal and corruptible beings, were anointed with oil made from corruptible matter; whereas he, anointed by the Holy Spirit, is made Christ, as Scripture says of him: “The Father anointed him with the Holy Spirit sent from heaven” (Acts 10).

And Isaiah had prefigured this when he said in the person of the Son: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; therefore he has anointed me and sent me to evangelize the poor” (Isa. 61).

Since, therefore, we have shown what Jesus means—he who saves the people—and what Christ means—he who has become priest forever—let us now consider, in what follows, of whom these things are said.

[Note: Baluzius has “and in the only one,” and so forth. For us it was sufficient to restore the ablative in place of the accusative. Then we corrected *through this* in place of the former *after this*.]

“His only Son,” he says, “our Lord.” By this he teaches us that this Jesus of whom we have spoken, and this Christ whom we have explained, is the only Son of God and our Lord.

So that you do not suppose that these human terms teach you something earthly, he adds that this only one is the Son of God, our Lord. For one is born from one: there is one splendor of light, and one word of the heart. Incorporeal generation does not descend into plurality, nor does it fall into division, since the one who is born is in no way separated from the one who begets.

He is the only one: as sensation is to the mind, as a word is to the heart, as power is to strength, as wisdom is to the wise.

[Note: Formerly the text had *of one*, which Pamelius had long ago corrected from other books. Those books also place below the words “as wisdom is to the wise” before “as word is to the heart.”]

For just as the Apostle calls the Father alone wise, so the Son alone is called Wisdom. He is therefore the only Son. Although he possesses glory, eternity, power, kingdom, and authority in the same way as the Father, all these things are nevertheless not without an originator,

[Note: From most of the other books we restored *as the Father* in place of the former *are with the Father*. We also supplied shortly afterward the missing words *without beginning and equal*. The remainder of the section has been greatly disturbed by the editors. Since our reading seems sufficiently satisfactory, and since it was also taken up by Barraeus from a most ancient and excellent manuscript, we decided to change nothing, leaving any necessary correction to the judgment of the learned reader.

Baluzius therefore reads: “Although he himself is the head of all, nevertheless the Father is his author, begetting without beginning; for the Father does not precede the Son, nor does the Son follow the Father in being made, as though adopted, as we are. When you hear ‘Son,’ certainly …” He cites manuscripts and printed books as guarantors, preferring to follow them rather than Pamelius, who supplied a defective and incomplete sentence.

He gives the passage as follows: “Although he himself is the head of all, nevertheless the Father is his head. For it is written, ‘God is the head of Christ’; nevertheless the Father is his author, begetting without beginning. For the Father does not …” and so on, word for word as in those just mentioned.

He testifies that he added the material beyond the printed reading from two ancient Hieronymian editions, undoubtedly genuine. “It nevertheless seems,” he says, “that this or something similar should also be added: although the Son is the author of all; and then should follow, ‘nevertheless the Father is his author,’” continuing to the words “When you hear ‘Son.’”

To us, the additions beyond the printed reading appear to be glosses of some diligent scholar written in the margin of the book and subsequently inserted into the text.]

but from the Father as Son, without beginning and equal. Although he himself is the head of all, the Father is nevertheless his head. For it is written: “God is the head of Christ.”

### 7. When you hear “Son,” do not assume the idea of a carnal birth,

[Note: Formerly the text had *generation* instead of *thought*, which the other books unanimously prefer. Shortly afterward they also have *these things* instead of *this*, and *of simple nature* instead of *of a simple nature*.]

but remember that this is said of an incorporeal substance and of a simple nature.

For, as we have already said above, whether in the case of the heart generating a word, the mind producing a thought, or light bringing forth splendor from itself, none of these processes requires any such thing, nor is any frailty conceived in such generation. How much more purely and reverently, then, must we judge concerning the Creator of all these things?

But perhaps you will say: “The generation you mention is insubstantial; for light does not make splendor substantial, nor does the heart generate a substantial word. The Son of God, however, is asserted to have been generated substantially.”

[Note: We corrected *insubstantiality*, apparently a printer’s error, to *insubstantial*, since Rufinus says below both *an insubstantial spark* and *an insubstantial nothing*. Shortly afterward other books have *produces* in place of *makes*.]

To this [Al. “to these things”] we say first of all that, although examples are also brought forward from other things, they cannot preserve in every respect the likeness of that thing for which they are thought to provide an example; they retain the likeness only of the particular aspect for which they appear to have been adopted.

For example, when the Gospel says: “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven, which a woman hid in three measures of flour” (Matt. 13),

[Note: It was incorrectly printed as two words, *Now what*. The alternative is *Can it be that?* We also supplied the missing particle shortly afterward. The Oxford editor omits the adverb *thus*. Finally, we read *corrupted* in place of the corrupt form *corruptated*. Baluzius presents what follows as a question—“Is this example adopted only for this purpose?”—together with Morelius, Remboldus, and Erasmus.]

shall we suppose that the kingdom of heaven is in every respect like leaven, so that its substance is equally palpable and fragile, and so that it can both become sour and be corrupted? Rather, this example appears to have been adopted only to show that human minds can be brought together by the leaven of faith through a small amount of preaching of the word of God.

Likewise, when it is said: “The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea, which draws out every kind of fish” [Al. *attracts*] (ibid. 13), should we suppose that the substance of the kingdom of heaven is in every respect comparable to the nature of the linen from which we make the net, and to the knots by which the meshes are joined?

[Note: The reading *which is fitted* is less pleasing; all the others have it in place of *which we work*. It is entirely wrong, however, for *little net* to appear shortly afterward in place of *meshes*. Those are the meshes of the net which we call *maglie* in Italian. Cicero also spoke of a small net with tiny meshes. In what follows, Baluzius again uses a question: “Is the comparison adopted only for this purpose?” Shortly afterward he reads, with the Sangermanensis manuscript, *draws out* in place of *brings to*. We pass over some lesser matters.]

Rather, the comparison seems to have been adopted only to show that, just as a net brings fish from the depths of the sea to the shore, so human souls are freed from the depths of this world’s error through the preaching of the kingdom of heaven.

From these examples it is clear that examples are not similar in every respect to the things of which they are examples. Otherwise, if everything were identical, they would no longer be called examples; they would instead appear to be the very things under discussion.

Next, this too must be said: no creature can be such as its creator is. Therefore, just as the divine substance is without an example, so also its divinity is without an example.

[Note: In the Vallarsian edition which we are reprinting, a serious typographical error occurred in the folio numbers: folios 65, 66, 67, 68, 69, and 70 were omitted, although the reader is frequently referred to these numbers in the index appended to Rufinus’s works. So that the order of the pages would not be disrupted, we deliberately retained the same gap and substituted, wherever the above numbers are cited in the index, the numbers which occupy their place in the text. EDIT.]

[Note: The older Hieronymian editions have this reading. Pamelius, together with others, has *divine majesty*; Baluzius, with the Sangermanensis manuscript and the old Oxford edition, corrected it to *divine birth*, and has *then* instead of *afterward*, which follows.]

We add also this: every creature is from nothing. If, then, an insubstantial spark, which is fire, brings forth from itself a creature that was made from nothing, while preserving in this the condition of its origin, why could the substance of that eternal light, which always existed, because it had nothing insubstantial within itself, not bring forth from itself substantial splendor?

[Note: Baluzius—or the Benedictine monk who published his Cyprianic edition—removed the particle *why*, without the support of any manuscript or printed book, and likewise removed the question mark. He says that the question mark is present in the Sangermanensis manuscript but not in the editions of Remboldus and Erasmus.

The reason was evidently that the following context says, “An insubstantial thing could not bring forth substantial splendor from itself,” which appeared contrary to faith and to Rufinus’s meaning. For, he says, in this passage Rufinus refutes insubstantial generation and argues nothing other than that the Son is substantial splendor, substantial Word, substantially generated, quite unlike the examples drawn from created things.

Having removed the particle *why* and the question mark, Baluzius thought that he had sufficiently served both the author’s meaning and the faith. But neither is the corruption located there, nor is that the author’s meaning. It would have been preferable, as the editor mentioned below suspects, to read *substantial* in place of *insubstantial*: “to bring forth substantial splendor from itself,” with only the particle *why* deleted. It is clear that copyists added it because they were misled by the recurrence of the same word in the preceding clause. We have restored the passage in this form.]

And therefore the Son is rightly called the only one. For he [Note: The Oxford editor has only *for that reason alone*; Baluzius also has *because he was born*. Understand, as the Author explains below, this of birth from the Father. From the same books, three lines below, we supplied the name *son*, which was lacking.] alone and only is the one who was born in this way; and what is unique cannot have any comparison. Nor can one who is the maker of all things have a likeness in substance to his works [Al. “things made”].

This, then, is Christ Jesus, the only Son of God, who is also our Lord. *Only* may refer both to *Son* and to *Lord*. He is the only one,

[Note: The same copies have: “One is the Son, truly the Son”; with them we also supplied the second occurrence of *truly* below. Conversely, they omit the first occurrence of *son* and change the first occurrence of *yet* while omitting the second.

Rufinus also appears to have received these expressions from his Cyril of Jerusalem. “When you hear ‘Son,’” he says in Catechesis XI, “do not suppose that he is adopted, but a natural son, an only-begotten son who has no other brother. For this reason he is called only-begotten, because, whether you consider the dignity of the Godhead or his birth from the Father, he has no brother,” and so forth.

Again, in number IV: “When you hear that he is called Son, do not suppose that he is so called improperly or by a figure of speech, but understand that he is truly a son, a natural son,” and so forth.]

and truly a Son, and one Lord Jesus Christ. The other sons, although they are called sons, are called so by the grace of adoption, not by the truth of nature. And if others are called lords, they are called so by a power granted to them, not by an innate power.

But this one alone is the only Son, and alone is the only Lord, as the Apostle also says: “And one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things” (Eph. 4:6).

[Note: The same copies place first the words from the Apostle, “One Father God,” and so forth. Shortly afterward, by their unanimous agreement, we restored *of the Father’s birth* in place of *of the birth of the Father*.]

Therefore, after the proposed order of faith has expounded the ineffable mystery of the Son’s birth from the Father, it now descends to the condescension and dispensation of human salvation. The one whom it previously called the only Son of God and our Lord it now calls:

### 9. WHO WAS BORN OF THE HOLY SPIRIT FROM THE VIRGIN MARY

[Note: Formerly the text had *this one*, and shortly afterward *for this one*, in place of *now*. Thus Baluzius, following Pamelius, restored the reading. I would rather have attempted only the former word and written *now* there in place of *this one*.]

This is now the birth of his dispensation among human beings; the other is the birth of the divine substance. This belongs to condescension; the other to nature.

He is born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin; and at this point a purer hearing and a more refined understanding are required. Understand that for this one whom you have just learned to have been ineffably born from the Father, a temple was now fashioned by the Holy Spirit within the hidden recesses of the virgin womb. And just as no frailty is to be perceived in the sanctification of the Holy Spirit, so no corruption is to be understood in the Virgin’s childbirth.

A new birth has been given to this world, and not without reason. For he who in heaven is the only Son is consequently also the only one on earth, and is born uniquely.

[Note: The same editor omits the particle *here*. Joined by the Oxford editor and others, he has the fuller reading: “on earth there is one only Son, because he is also born uniquely,” and so forth.]

The prophetic writings concerning him, familiar to everyone and sung throughout the Gospels, say that “the Virgin will conceive and bear a son” (Isa. 7:14).

But Ezekiel the prophet had also previously prefigured the wondrous manner of his birth, calling Mary figuratively the Lord’s gate, through which the Lord entered the world. He says as follows:

“The gate that faces toward the East shall be closed, and it shall not be opened, and no one shall pass through it, because the Lord God of Israel shall pass through it, and it shall be closed” (Ezek. 44).

What could be said more clearly about the preservation of virginity? That gate of virginity was closed. Through it the Lord God of Israel entered [Al. *went in*]; through it he came forth from the Virgin’s womb into this world. The Virgin’s gate remained closed forever, her virginity having been preserved.

[Note: Some, with Baluzius, add *he himself* and shortly afterward prefer *by consecration* to *by preservation*, on the authority of the Sangermanensis manuscript and other printed books. Barraeus, Frobenius, Pamelius, and others agree with us.]

Thus the Holy Spirit is related to the Lord’s flesh as its creator, and to his temple. Begin from this point to understand also the majesty of the Holy Spirit.

For the Gospel narrative also bears witness concerning him: when the angel was speaking to the Virgin and saying, “You will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins” (Matt. 1),

she replied, “How will this happen, since I do not know a man?” (Luke 1:3). And the angel of God said to her, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God.”

[Note: The reading *that she replied to him* was incorrect. Shortly afterward some read *the angel of God said* instead of *he said to her*.]

Observe, then, the Trinity cooperating with itself. The Holy Spirit is said to come upon the Virgin, and the power of the Most High to overshadow her. What is the power of the Most High except Christ himself, who is the power of God [Al. “of the Lord”] and the wisdom of God?

And whose power is this? “Of the Most High,” he says.

[Al. *the word “is” is omitted*.]

The Most High, therefore, is present; the power of the Most High is present; and the Holy Spirit is present. This is the Trinity, everywhere hidden and everywhere revealed, distinguished by names and persons but inseparable in the substance of the Godhead.

Although the Son alone is born from the Virgin, the Most High is nevertheless present, and the Holy Spirit is present,

[Al. *the word “nevertheless” is omitted*]

so that both the Virgin’s conception and the birth may be sanctified.

### 11. But since these things are asserted from the prophetic Scriptures, they may perhaps refute the Jews, although they are unbelieving and obstinate.

But pagans customarily mock us when they hear us preaching the Virgin’s childbirth. For this reason we must answer their objections briefly.

Every birth, as I think, consists of three conditions: that the woman be of mature age, that she approach a man, and that her womb not be closed through the defect of sterility.

[Note: Baluzius reports that the two words *that woman’s womb* are lacking in the Sangermanensis manuscript and in Remboldus and Erasmus.]

Of these three, one was absent from the birth we proclaim—namely, the man. Since the one who was being born was not an earthly but a heavenly human being, we say that this part was completed through the heavenly Spirit, while the Virgin’s incorruptibility remained intact.

And yet why does it seem surprising that a virgin conceived, when it is established that the bird of the East, which they call the Phoenix, is born or reborn without a mate to such an extent that it is always one and always succeeds itself by being born or reborn?

Everyone knows that bees do not know marriage and do not produce offspring through the pains of childbirth. Several other examples are also found among forms of birth of this kind.

[Note: Other books have *in such a condition* instead of *under such a condition*.]

Will this, then, seem incredible when it was accomplished by divine power for the restoration of the whole world, although examples of it can also be seen in the birth of animals?

And yet it is surprising [Al. *the word “is” is omitted*] that this should seem impossible to the Gentiles, who believe that their Minerva was born from Jupiter’s brain. What is more difficult to believe, or more contrary to nature, than this?

Here there is a female; here the order of nature is preserved; here there is conception; here childbirth occurs at its proper time. There, there is no female sex at all, but only a male and a birth. If one believes that, why does one marvel at this? [Al. *why should one marvel?*]

They also say that Father Liber was born from Jupiter’s thigh. Here is another kind of prodigy, and yet it is believed.

They also believe that Venus, whom they call Aphrodite, was generated from the foam of the sea, as her entire composition itself shows. They affirm that Castor and Pollux were born from an egg, and the Myrmidons from an ant [Al. *ants*]. There are a thousand other examples which, although contrary to the nature of things, nevertheless appeared credible to them: for example, the stones thrown by Deucalion and Pyrrha, and the crop of human beings said to have sprung from them.

[Note: The same copies omit *although* here. Three lines later they have the fuller reading, “one thing alone seemed impossible to them.” Shortly afterward, with Pamelius, they have *inspiring* instead of *breathing*.]

Although they have believed these and so many other fictions, one thing alone seems impossible to them: that a young woman should have conceived a divine offspring, not through a man’s fault but through God’s breathing upon her.

If they are difficult to persuade, they certainly should not have commended belief in so many shameful and monstrous things. But if they are easy to persuade, they ought much more readily to have accepted this teaching of ours, so honorable and holy, than to believe those things, so unworthy and foul.

### 12. But perhaps they say that, if it was possible for God for a virgin to conceive, it was also possible for her to give birth.

[Note: Some read *they will say*; and then, “and it would indeed have been possible for God that she should give birth,” a reading which Pamelius formerly introduced. Frobenius, Morelius, and several older copies agree with us—or with Barraeus.]

They regard it as unworthy, however, that so great a majesty should have passed through the woman’s genital passage.

[Note: Here we retain *having emerged*, which seems more elegant, in place of *having gone out*, the reading preferred by Baluzius from the Sangermanensis manuscript, Remboldus, and Erasmus. Baluzius himself and all the others have quite wrongly placed here *mixture from male admixture*. It was a great loss to them to have been unaware of the Barraean copy.]

Although there was no contamination from intercourse with a man, there was nevertheless, they say, the offense of the obscene handling involved in childbirth. Let us answer them briefly according to their own way of thinking.

If someone sees a little child dying in a deep pool of mud, and although he himself is a great and powerful man, enters the mud on tiptoe, so to speak, in order to rescue the dying child, will you accuse this man of pollution because he stepped briefly into the mire, or will you praise him as merciful because he gave life to one who was dying?

[Note: Other copies have *with his extreme toes*, so to speak, “he enters.”]

But let this also have been said about an ordinary human being. Let us now return to the nature of the one who was born. How much, do you think, is the nature of the sun inferior to his? How much, without doubt, is a creature inferior to its creator?

Consider now: if a ray of the sun is lowered into some chasm of mud, does it acquire any pollution from it? Or is the illumination of foul things counted as an injury to the sun?

[Note: The same copies have: “Consider now the rays of the sun, if they are lowered into some mud,” and afterward add *they are sent down*; Pamelius had formerly introduced *they acquire* by conjecture from Cauchius through Frobenius, although the latter read all these words in the singular, with the old edition. For the following *does anything at all*, the Sangermanensis manuscript, Remboldus, and Morelius have *does anything already*. Instead of *is drawn into an injury*, they prefer *will be led into injuries*.]

Fire also—how much lower in nature is it than the things of which we are speaking? Yet no one believes that fire is polluted by any material, whether foul or shameful, applied to it.

Since, therefore [Al. *therefore* omitted], these things are evidently so in material realities, do you suppose that in that exalted and incorporeal nature, which is above every fire and every light, any pollution and [Al. *or*] obscenity can occur?

Then turn your attention to [Al. *to* omitted] this as well. We say that human beings were created by God from the mud of the earth. If it is counted as obscenity for God to seek out his own work, it will be counted as much more of an obscenity for him to fashion this work from the beginning.

It is superfluous to ask why he passed through foul things, when you cannot say why he created foul things. Therefore, it was custom, not nature, that taught people to call these things foul. For all the things that exist in the body are formed from one and the same mud and are distinguished only by their natural uses and functions.

[Note: The old Oxford edition has *to bring to a solution*; others have *to be free from absolution*; *from solution* is more correct. They also omit *in smaller number* and have *in every respect* in place of *wholly*.]

But let us not omit even this point, which is not without relevance to the resolution of the question: the substance of God, which is wholly incorporeal, cannot in principle be inserted into bodies or received by them unless there is some intermediate spiritual substance capable of receiving the divine Spirit.

For example, light can illuminate all the members of the body, yet it can be received by none of them except the eye alone. The eye alone is capable [Al. “may be capable”] of light.

[Note: Cassianus quotes this passage in Book VII of *On the Incarnation*, chapter 27, prefacing it with an extraordinary expression of honor and with the name and praises of its author, Rufinus:

“Rufinus,” he says, “a man of Christian philosophy and no negligible part of the company of ecclesiastical teachers, bears witness in his *Exposition of the Creed* concerning the Lord’s birth as follows: ‘For the Son of God is born from the Virgin, not joined principally to the flesh alone, but generated with the soul intervening between the flesh and God.’”

On the basis of this testimony of Cassianus, and also on the authority of other books, we restored several things here which were incorrectly printed in the Barraean copy—namely, “but with the soul intervening between the flesh … is generated.”

The sentence needs no greater guarantor. Nevertheless, Baluzius—or the Benedictine editor of the Cyprianic works—thought it necessary to warn the reader, lest the mention of Christ’s intermediate soul trouble anyone.

“So,” he says, “many other writers have spoken, whom Petavius lists in Book IV, chapter 13, of *On the Incarnation*. The principal caution which led them to speak in this way seems to have been that the pains which Christ felt, and the other movements in his soul aroused on account of bodily movements, should not be referred to the Godhead itself. That would be utterly impious and appropriate only to the Arian heresy.

In this passage Rufinus has no other purpose than to demonstrate that the divine majesty was neither contaminated in Christ’s birth nor grieved in his death.”]

Therefore the Son of God is born from the Virgin, not joined principally to the flesh alone, but generated with the soul intervening between the flesh and God.

Thus, with the soul as intermediary, and with the Word of God received in the secret citadel of the rational spirit, God was born from the Virgin without any of the injury you imagine.

Therefore nothing shameful is to be thought present there, where the sanctification of the Spirit was present and the soul, which was capable of God, became a participant also in the flesh.

Do not consider anything impossible where the power of the Most High was present.

[Note: The Sangermanensis manuscript, Remboldus, and Erasmus have this reading, although Baluzius, Fellus, and others prefer *you should say*.]

Do not imagine anything arising from human frailty where the fullness of divinity was present.

## 14. CRUCIFIED UNDER PONTIUS PILATE, AND BURIED, HE DESCENDED TO THE UNDERWORLD

[Note: The same editors prefer *into the underworld* (*in inferna*) instead of *to the underworld* (*ad inferna*), though they are not consistent with themselves in what follows. We have removed immediately afterward the word *divinity*, to which the word *height* had been appended, since very few books apart from Barraeus have it, the Apostle does not have it, and Pamelius had formerly deleted it. It is also more likely that it was introduced into the text from the margin, for it does not suit this passage.]

The Apostle Paul teaches that the eyes of our heart ought to be enlightened (Ephesians 1), so that we may understand what are the height, breadth, and depth (ibid. 3). The height, breadth, and depth, then, are a description of the cross. He called the part of it fixed in the earth its depth; the height, the part which rises aloft above the earth;

[Note: Other copies have *into the air*. On their authority, shortly afterward we too removed the word *hands*, which had been added needlessly “to the right and to the left.” The same copies omit below the little word *what*, and consequently also the question mark.]

the breadth, the part which, stretched out, extends its hands to the right and left. Since there are so many forms of death by which human beings customarily depart this life, what does the Apostle wish us, with enlightened hearts, to know: why was the form of the cross chosen for the Savior’s death rather than any of all these others?

We must therefore understand that this cross was a triumph.

[Note: Other copies give the fuller reading: “For the trophy is the distinguished emblem of triumph; a trophy is an indication of an enemy conquered,” and so forth.]

For a trophy is the distinguished emblem of triumph, and triumph is an indication that an enemy has been conquered. Since, then, when Christ came, as the Apostle says, he subjected three kingdoms to himself at once—for this is indicated when he says, “At the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Philippians 2:10)—and since he was conquering all these by his death, a death appropriate to the mystery was chosen: so that, raised aloft in the air and subjecting the powers of the air, he might display his victory over those who are above and heavenly.

The holy prophet says that he holds out his hands all day toward the people who are on the earth (Isaiah 65), both to bear witness against unbelievers and to invite believers.

[Note: Many others, including the more recent Oxford editor, have *expended* (*expensas*) rather than *outstretched* (*expansas*); Baluzius himself also has this reading: “his hands extended all day, as the holy Prophet says, toward an unbelieving people.” The word *unbelieving* may easily seem to others to require supplementation, but not to me. Pamelius is said to have restored the passage in this way from Cauchius, who evidently did not know Barraeus’s copy. Formerly the text was read much more corruptly: “he stretches out his hands,” and shortly afterward, “that part which is submerged beneath the earth, because it subjected the kingdoms of the underworld to itself,” and so on. Morellius reads: “The holy Prophet says that he extended his hands all day toward an unbelieving people who are on the earth,” and so forth. We pass over other minor matters.]

By that part which is submerged beneath the earth, he subjected to himself the kingdoms of the underworld.

## 15.

For—to touch briefly upon a few matters that are also more hidden—in the beginning, when God had made the world, he appointed over it and placed in charge of it certain powers of the heavenly virtues, by whom the human race was to be governed and administered. Moses indicates that this was done in the song of Deuteronomy, where he says: “When the Most High divided the nations, he established the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the angels of God” (Deuteronomy 32:8).

But some of these powers, like the one who himself is called the prince of the world, did not regulate the authority given to them by God according to the laws they had received. Instead, they taught the human race not to obey the divine commands but to submit to their own transgressions. Hence documents recording our sins were written against us, because, as the prophet says, “We were sold because of our sins” (Isaiah 50).

For each person receives the price of his own soul when he has satisfied his desire.

[Note: Omitting the preposition *by*, some others read: “Therefore each person’s document was held by those rulers,” and so forth.]

By this document, therefore, each person was held by those most evil rulers. Christ, when he came, removed it and stripped them of this power. Paul indicates this with profound mystery when he says of Christ: “Erasing the document that stood against us, and fastening it to his cross, he led principalities and powers in triumph, triumphing over them in himself” (Colossians 2).

Those rulers whom God had placed over the human race, having turned to the insolence of tyranny, began to attack the people entrusted to them and to subdue them in the battles of sin. The prophet Ezekiel designates this mystically in his utterances when he says: “On that day angels will go forth in haste to destroy Ethiopia, and there will be confusion among them on the day of Egypt, for behold, he has come” (Ezekiel 30).

[Note: The text had previously been read incorrectly as “for righteousness has come.” Most other books correct it, although two manuscripts in Baluzius and two printed editions, those of Remboldus and Erasmus, omit this clause. The rest read as follows: “Rightly, then, Christ, having stripped them of their omnipotence,” and so forth. The final words agree with us in the old Oxford edition.]

Therefore Christ is said to have triumphed after their omnipotence had been stripped from them, and to have transferred the power from them to human beings. Thus he himself says to his disciples in the Gospel: “Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy” (Luke 10).

The cross of Christ therefore subjected to their former subjects those who had abused the power they had received.

[Al.: *subjects them*.]

But us—that is, the human race—it teaches first of all to resist sin even unto death and willingly to accept destruction for the sake of piety. Then, on this same cross, it sets before us an example of obedience, just as it imposed upon those who had once been our rulers the penalties of their defiance.

[Note: Previously, as in other copies, the text read *as in*; the two manuscripts mentioned above, Remboldus, and Erasmus have *of insult* instead of *of defiance*.]

Hear, then, how the Apostle wishes to teach us obedience through the cross of Christ.

[Al.: *Hear how*.]

“Let this mind be in you,” he says, “which was also in Christ Jesus: who, though he was in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings, and found in appearance as a human being, he became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross” (Philippians 2:5–8).

Since, then, the great teacher is the one who both does and teaches, he himself taught that obedience must be preserved even when death has been accepted, by dying first for this very obedience.

[Note: Others have “even after accepting death, and himself first preserving it by dying for this,” and so forth. Frobenius and the old edition printed by Pamelius read: “Therefore he taught that what must be preserved, even after death had been accepted, was first preserved by him through his own death.”]

## 16.

But perhaps someone is alarmed by this kind of teaching: that the one whom shortly before we said was eternal with God the Father and begotten from his substance, and whom we taught to be one with God the Father in kingdom, majesty, and eternity, is now discussed in connection with his death.

[Al.: *is now to be discussed*.]

But do not be alarmed, faithful hearer: shortly afterward you will see immortal again the one whom you hear called dead. For he accepts death in order to strip death of its power.

The mystery of the flesh assumed by him, which we explained above, has this purpose: that the divine power of the Son of God, like a hook concealed beneath the appearance of human flesh, and—as the Apostle Paul said before—“found in appearance as a human being” (Philippians 2),

[Note: Some others omit the name Paul and read *found* rather than *discovered* shortly afterward. Baluzius says that Pamelius aptly restored the passage, except that he used *could* (*possit*) less accurately instead of *could* (*posset*), which is found in the Sangermanensis manuscript and the old editions. In fact, neither of them knew Barraeus at all.]

might invite the prince of the world to combat. Offering him his flesh as if it were food, the divinity held him fast from within, impaled upon the hook, through the outpouring of immaculate blood.

[Note: By restoring only one small letter—*inserted* instead of *inserted* in the appropriate grammatical form—the rest of Barraeus’s reading seemed sufficiently sound; the old Oxford edition also agrees for the most part. Others read: “He offered him food so that the hook of divinity might hold him fast within, inserted in him, and by the outpouring of immaculate blood, which alone knows no stain of sin, might erase the sins of all”—omitting “For he alone,” which begins another sense and is necessary—and so forth.]

For he alone, who knows no stain of sin, erased the sins of all—namely, of those who had marked the doorposts of their faith with his blood.

Just as a fish, if it seizes bait covered with a hook, not only does not remove the bait from the hook but is itself brought up from the deep to become food for others, so the one who possessed the power of death did indeed seize the body of Jesus in death, not perceiving that the hook of divinity was enclosed within it. But when he had swallowed it, he himself immediately became caught; and when the gates of the underworld had been burst open, he was dragged out as though from the deep, so that he might become food for the rest.

[Note: Others have *contained* instead of *covered*, and shortly afterward *with the hook* instead of *by the hook*, and *into death* instead of *by death*, and later *is offered* instead of *is handed over*.]

The prophet Ezekiel had long before signified that this would happen under the same figure, saying: “And I will draw you out with my hook, and I will stretch you out upon the earth. The fields shall be filled with you, and I will set all the birds of the sky upon you, and with you I will satisfy all the beasts of the earth” (Ezekiel 32).

But the prophet David also says: “You crushed the heads of the great dragon; you gave him as food to the peoples of Ethiopia” (Psalm 73).

Job likewise bears witness to the same mystery. For he says, speaking as though the Lord were addressing him:

[Note: Others have “You will bring the dragon up with a hook and place a bridle,” and so forth, instead of “You bring up” and “or place.” Shortly afterward, some read *he endured* instead of *he suffers*. They also add *salvation* in the middle of the earth, and before *he descended* the two words *through the flesh*, which seemed to us worthy of restoration. Finally, in the following verse they have *in death* instead of *from death*, and *about to rise by himself*, and so forth.]

“Will you draw out the dragon with a hook, and put a bridle around his nostrils?” (Job 40).

## 17.

Christ therefore suffers in the flesh without any loss or injury to his divinity. Rather, so that he might accomplish salvation through the weakness of the flesh, the divine nature descended into death through the flesh—not to be held by death under the law governing mortals, but in order to open the gates of death by rising again through his own power.

It is as though a king were going to a prison and, entering it, were to open the doors, release the chains, bonds, bars, and bolts, shatter the barriers, lead the prisoners out into freedom, and restore to light and life those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death.

Other words are inserted by some copies: “to a people among whom he had his own people bound by the bond of captivity; and after conquering it, he entered the prison in which the bound were confined, and having entered,” and so forth. We neither reject this passage entirely as having come from another hand, nor dare to receive it into the text, since the passage seems sufficiently complete without it and fully expresses the author’s meaning; nor does anything in the context indicate that it fell out through the error of copyists.

The king is therefore said to have been in prison, but not in the same condition as the others who were held there: they were there to pay penalties, whereas he was there to abolish penalties.

[Note: Others omit *had been*, and immediately afterward have *confined* instead of *in prison*. The reading of Barraeus, and consequently ours, is also supported by the old Oxford edition.]

## 18.

Those who transmitted the Creed very cautiously also specified the time at which these things took place, under Pontius Pilate, so that the transmission of the events might not waver in any respect as vague and uncertain.

It should certainly be known that the words “he descended to the underworld” are not added in the Creed of the Roman Church. Nor is this phrase found in the Churches of the East. Nevertheless, the force of the expression seems to be the same in the statement that he was buried.

But since you possess love and zeal for the divine Scriptures, you undoubtedly say to me that these matters ought rather to be confirmed by clearer testimonies of divine Scripture. For the greater the things that must be believed,

[Note: The Sangermanensis manuscript, Remboldus, Erasmus, and the old Oxford edition read *the greater*; shortly afterward they omit *the more suitable and indisputable* and also omit *more*. Those who read as we do—Frobenius, Morellius, Pamelius, Baluzius, and others—read the rest as follows: “they require”; this is the true and consequent proposition.]

the more they require suitable and indisputable witnesses. This proposition is true and follows logically.

But, speaking as to those who know the law, we leave aside the forest of testimonies for the sake of brevity.

[Al.: *we have left aside*.]

Nevertheless, if this too is required, let us bring forward a few from among the many,

[Al.: *even if this is required*; *let us bring forward*.]

knowing that for all who are devoted to the Scriptures, a vast sea of testimonies lies open in the divine writings.

## 19.

First of all, then, it must be understood that the meaning of the cross itself is not one and the same for everyone. It has one significance for the Gentiles, another for the Jews, and another for believers, just as the Apostle says: “We preach Christ crucified: to the Jews a stumbling block, to the Gentiles foolishness, but to those who are called, Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.” And in the same place: “For the word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to those who are being saved—that is, to us—it is the power of God” (1 Corinthians 1).

[Note: Others add *indeed* after *called*, and in the same place read *and elsewhere* instead of *and*. They also omit the words *that is, to us*, and instead of *but* in the following clause have *therefore*.]

The Jews, to whom it had been handed down from the Law that Christ would remain forever, were scandalized by his cross because they refused to accept his resurrection. To the Gentiles it seemed foolishness that God had undergone death, because they did not know the mystery of the assumed flesh. But the faithful, who had accepted that he was born and suffered in the flesh

[Al.: *accepted*],

and that he had risen from the dead, rightly believed this to be the power of God, which had conquered death.

First, then, consider this very fact: the Jews, to whom the prophets had foretold these things, would not believe, whereas those who had never heard such things from the prophets would believe. Hear how this is marked out in prophetic speech through Isaiah.

“To those to whom it was not announced concerning him,” he says, “they will see; and those who have not heard will understand” (Isaiah 52).

[Note: The words *through Isaiah*, which the old Oxford edition also retains, are omitted by nearly all the others. Consequently, later below, where Isaiah is again mentioned, they omit the same words so as not to appear to have anticipated them.]

But Isaiah likewise foretells in the following manner that the whole mystery would be transferred to the Gentiles rather than to those who had studied the Law from childhood to old age without believing:

“And the Lord God of hosts,” he says, “will make for all the nations on this mountain: they will drink joy, they will drink wine; they will be anointed with ointment on this mountain. Hand all these things over to the nations” (Isaiah 25).

[Note: In reciting this testimony, all the remaining editions err repeatedly. They read: “On this mountain there will be found joy; they will drink wine; they will be anointed with ointment. Hand these things over,” and so forth. For *there will be found* instead of *they will drink* is faulty and foreign to the sacred text, while omitting the repetition of *on this mountain* leaves the passage incomplete. Barraeus follows the Greek exemplar most accurately: “Upon this mountain they will drink joy, they will drink wine; they will be anointed with ointment on this mountain; hand these things over,” and so forth. The old Oxford edition repeats *on this mountain* once. Previously the text had *you will hand over* instead of *hand over*.]

For this is the purpose of the Almighty concerning all the nations.

[Note: Others add *of God* at the beginning and have more shortly afterward, reading “those who say thus.”]

But perhaps those who boast of their knowledge of the Law will say to us: “You blaspheme when you say that the Lord was subjected to the corruption of death and to the suffering of the cross.”

Read, then, what you have written in the Lamentations of Jeremiah, where he says: “The breath of our face, Christ the Lord, was seized in our corruptions; of him we said, ‘Under his shadow we shall live among the nations’” (Lamentations 4).

Do you hear how the prophet says that Christ the Lord was seized and, for us—that is, for our sins—handed over to corruption? Since that Jewish people remained unbelieving, he says that the Gentile has been subjected, because we live not in Israel but among the nations.

[Note: All the other books seem to have the passage incompletely: “That people, which remained unbelieving, was cast away,” and so forth, saying that we shall live not in Israel, and so on.]

## 20.

If it does not seem burdensome, let us briefly indicate, as far as we can, how the individual events reported in the Gospels were foretold in the prophets, so that those who are receiving the first elements of the faith may have these testimonies inscribed in their hearts, lest any doubt concerning what they believe ever steal in upon them as an enemy.

The Gospel teaches us that Judas, one of Christ’s friends and table companions, betrayed him. Hear how this is foretold in the Psalms:

“He who ate my bread,” it says, “has magnified treachery against me” (Psalm 40:10).

[Note: The old Oxford edition reads *was eating*; all the others read *eats*. The same edition, Remboldus, and the Sangermanensis manuscript support *has magnified*; others prefer *will magnify*.]

And elsewhere: “My friends and my neighbors approached against me and stood” (Psalm 37:12).

And again: “His words were softened above oil, yet they will be darts” (Psalm 54).

[Note: The same old edition reads *they were*; two others among Pamelius’s copies have *they stand*, while all the rest have *they are*. Fellus, Baluzius, and some older editions read *to see* instead of *to hear*.]

Do you wish to hear how they were softened? “Judas came to Jesus and said to him, ‘Hail, Rabbi,’ and kissed him” (Matthew 26).

Through the flattering softness of the kiss, therefore, he drove in the accursed dart of betrayal.

Then the Lord said to him: “Judas, do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?” (Luke 22).

[Note: Although Rufinus elsewhere, as we have noted in its proper place, transferred certain passages from Saint Cyril of Jerusalem—himself Archbishop of that Church, whose clergy Rufinus too had joined—and adapted them quite learnedly to his own purpose, he borrowed this section and the immediately preceding one from him so closely that he seems almost to have copied them. Father Touttée, who recently edited Cyril, observes this in his notes to Catechesis XIII, “On Christ Crucified and Buried,” from paragraph 7, where objections of the Jews are answered, almost to the end of the catechesis. He says in his notes: “These passages are so similar to those found in Rufinus’s exposition of the same article of the Creed, which Cyril here treats, that I have no doubt that Rufinus watered his little gardens from Cyril’s springs. The opinions are the same, the scriptural passages are cited in the same sense and in the same order, and the objections and answers to the objections are the same,” and so forth. Indeed, in the passage concerning Judas’s betrayal, Rufinus reproduces almost the very words, not merely the ideas, so that this part of his exposition may seem to be a somewhat freer translation from the Greek of Cyril. To cite the Greek passages would take too long. We shall note below only the principal passages of which our author presents himself as the translator.]

You hear that he was valued at thirty pieces of silver, through the greed of the betrayer. Hear the prophetic voice concerning this also:

“And I said to them,” he says, “If it is good in your sight, give me my wages, or refuse them” (Zechariah 11).

[Note: This reading is also preferred by the two manuscripts cited by Baluzius. Remboldus and Erasmus have *go away*, while Morellius has *or go away*. Shortly afterward, the Sangermanensis manuscript, Remboldus, and Erasmus read *he received, he sent*. Compare Cyril, Catechesis mentioned above, paragraph 10 and following.]

After this he says: “I received thirty pieces of silver and sent them into the house of the Lord, into the smelting furnace.”

Is this not what is written in the Gospels: Judas, moved by repentance, returned the money, threw it into the temple, and departed (Matthew 27)?

He rightly called them his wages, as though speaking with the feeling of one who imputes and reproaches. For he had performed many good works among them: he had given sight to the blind, feet to the lame, the power of walking to the paralytic, and life even to the dead.

[Note: Most other books add *their*—“he had given sight to their blind.” The same words are found in Greek in Cyril, paragraph 15.]

In return for all these good deeds, therefore, they repaid him with death, assessed at the price of thirty pieces of silver.

The Gospels also report that he was bound. The prophetic word foretold this through Isaiah, saying: “Woe to their soul, for they have devised an evil plan against themselves, saying, ‘Let us bind the righteous, because he is useless to us’” (Isaiah 3, according to the Septuagint).

## 21.

But someone may say: “Are these things to be understood of the Lord? Could the Lord be seized by human beings and dragged before a tribunal?”

[Note: The same copies also have *and dragged to judgment*. We have placed the pronoun *he himself* before the following testimony from Isaiah, with the Greek text also supporting it: *he himself, the Lord*, and so forth.]

The same prophet will refute you on this matter. For he says in these words: “The Lord himself will come into judgment with the elders and rulers of the people” (Isaiah 3).

According to the prophet’s testimony, then, the Lord is judged. Not only is he judged, but he is also struck with blows, beaten on the face with open hands, spat upon, and endures every disgraceful insult on our behalf.

[Note: Many other copies have *the insult of indignity*, and shortly afterward *astonishing* instead of *causing astonishment*. The old Oxford edition agrees with us in this last word. The same sentences are found in Cyril, paragraphs 12 and 13.]

Since these things were astonishing to everyone when they were proclaimed by the Apostles, the prophet therefore cries out even in their person and says: “Lord, who has believed our report?” (Isaiah 53).

For it is incredible that the God who is the Son of God should be said and proclaimed to have suffered. Therefore these things were also foretold through the prophets, so that no doubt might arise among those who were to believe.
