Christ the Lord himself says in his own person: “I gave my back to blows, and my cheeks to slaps; I did not turn my face away from the shame of spitting” (Isaiah 50).

It is also written among the rest of his sufferings that those who bound him led him to Pilate. The prophet likewise foretold this when he says: “And binding him, they brought him as a gift to King Jarim” (Hosea 10:6).

[Note: Pamelius admits that he was unable to discover the source of this reading; Baluzius says nothing about it. It is taken from Hosea 10:6, which the Septuagint renders as follows: “And binding him, they carried him away as gifts to King Jarim of the Assyrians.” The old printed editions have only “the king’s gift,” silently omitting Jarim. We supply what follows from most other books. Here too our author is acting as Cyril’s translator. Cyril says in paragraph 14: “Bound, he came from Caiaphas to Pilate. Is this also written? ‘And binding him, they brought him as gifts to King Jarim.’ But someone among the sharp listeners objects: ‘Pilate was not a king,’ and so forth. Then read the Gospel: ‘When Pilate heard that he was from Galilee, he sent him to Herod.’ Herod at that time was king and was present in Jerusalem,” and so forth. Nor should we omit here what Father Touttée noted concerning Cyril, which can shed light on Rufinus’s text. He says: “Cyril, following Justin in the Dialogue, page 331A, and Rufinus, following Cyril, apply this passage of Hosea to Christ being sent to Pilate and from there to Herod, although the prophetic text has an entirely different meaning. Omitting the various interpretations, the only true one is that which understands the prophet’s passage of the silver and gifts sent by Menahem, king of the Israelites, to Pul, king of the Assyrians, to purchase assistance. They say that among these gifts was a golden calf, one of those that Jeroboam had set up at Bethel; and the Greek text of the prophet strongly supports this account. The Assyrian king is called Jarim, which means ‘of the forests,’ whether the Septuagint translators wrote it that way or whether the final letter β was changed into μ through the carelessness of copyists, something that often happens in similar words. In Hebrew it is Jarib, as also in the Greek Complutensian edition, which Jerome translates as ‘avenger’ or ‘defender.’”]

But someone may object and say: “Pilate was not a king.” Hear, then, what the Gospel reports in what follows: “When Pilate heard that he was from Galilee, he sent him to Herod, who was then king in Israel.”

He also rightly adds the name Jarim, which means “of the forest.”

[Note: Saint Jerome, in the book of Names in Joshua, gives Jarim as “of the groves or forests”; but in Hosea, reading the Hebrew *Jarib*, he translates it as “judging” or “avenging.”]

For Herod was not from the house of Israel, nor from that Israelite vineyard which the Lord brought out of Egypt and planted on a fruitful hill. Rather, he was “of the forest,” that is, from the forest of foreigners; and therefore he was rightly called “of the forest,” because he had not sprung at all from the branches of the Israelite vine.

But he also suitably applied to this the prophet’s statement about a gift. At that time Herod and Pilate, as the Gospel testifies, were reconciled from enmity; and as a gift of their reconciliation, they sent Jesus, bound, to one another.

[Note: Others insert *also* throughout, and omit the words *and* and *also*.]

What does it matter, provided that Jesus, as Savior, reconciles those who disagree, restores peace, and brings back concord? Hence this too is written in Job: “The Lord reconciles the hearts of the rulers of the earth” (Job 12, according to the Septuagint).

[Note: Others read: “But also what the prophet says,” and so forth. Three verses after this, where it says “they sent him bound to one another,” the word *righteous* had previously been read before *bound*; Pamelius had formerly corrected this as well. Consult Cyril’s Greek here: “See the prophet’s precision. For he says that he was sent as a gift,” and so forth. The Greek passage is the same as Rufinus’s Latin: “Pilate and Herod became friends with one another on that day; previously they had been enemies. For it was fitting that the one who was about to reconcile earth and heaven should first reconcile those by whom he was condemned. For the Lord himself was present, who reconciles the hearts of the rulers of the earth,” and so forth.]

## 22.

It is also reported that when Pilate wished to release him, the whole people cried out: “Crucify him, crucify him!”

[Al.: *shouted*.]

The prophet Jeremiah also foretells this, speaking in the person of the Lord himself: “My inheritance has become to me like a lion in the forest; it raised its voice against me; therefore I hated it; and therefore,” he says, “I abandoned my house” (Jeremiah 12).

And again elsewhere he says: “Against whom have you opened your mouth, and against whom have you loosened your tongues?” (Isaiah 57).

When he was being judged, he is written to have remained silent. Many passages of Scripture bear witness to this. In the Psalms it is said: “I became like a man who does not hear and who has no reproofs in his mouth” (Psalm 37).

And again: “I was like a deaf man and did not hear, and like a mute man who does not open his mouth” (Psalm 37).

[Note: Others have *opening*; “I, however, was like a deaf man.” The manuscripts of Baluzius mentioned above and the old editions have *does not open* instead of *did not open*. Shortly afterward the Sangermanensis manuscript omits *he says* and adds *like a sheep led to slaughter, and like a lamb*, and so forth.]

Another prophet says: “As a lamb before the one who shears it, so he did not open his mouth; in his humiliation his judgment was taken away” (Isaiah 53).

It is also written that a crown of thorns was placed upon him. Hear about this in the Song of Songs, where the voice of God the Father, astonished at the injury done to the Son and at Jerusalem’s iniquity,

[Al.: *iniquities*; in some copies *God* is omitted.]

says: “Go out and see, daughters of Jerusalem, the crown with which his mother crowned him” (Song of Songs 2).

Another prophet likewise mentions the thorns: “I expected it to produce grapes, but it produced thorns; not righteousness, but a cry” (Isaiah 5).

Nevertheless, so that you may understand the hidden matters of the mystery, it was necessary that the one who came to take away the sins of the world should also cleanse the earth’s curses, which it had received when the first human being sinned and was condemned, as the Lord said: “Cursed is the earth in your works; it shall produce thorns and thistles for you” (Genesis 3).

[Note: Others insert *I say*, and with them we read, three verses later, *in your works* instead of *in his works*, in accordance with the Greek: *ἐν τοῖς ἔργοις σου* (“in your works”).]

Therefore Jesus is crowned with thorns so that that first sentence of condemnation might be annulled.

He is led to the cross, and the life of the whole world is hung upon the wood.

Do you wish to have this too confirmed by prophetic testimonies? Hear Jeremiah saying:

[Note: The words *about this* are omitted by the same copies, and almost more correctly. Shortly afterward they add *Moses, as though mourning*; the old Oxford edition has *as though mourning*. In the following scriptural testimony we also supplied the pronoun *your*, which was absent, in accordance with the Greek: “And your life shall be,” and so forth.]

“Come, and let us throw wood into his bread, and let us cut him off from the land of the living” (Jeremiah 11).

And again Moses, mourning, says of them: “And your life shall hang before your eyes, and you shall fear by day and by night, and you shall not trust in your life” (Deuteronomy 28:66).

But we must hurry on: we have already exceeded the limits of the brevity we proposed, and have stretched a brief discourse into a lengthy exposition. Nevertheless, we shall add a few things, lest we seem to have entirely passed over what we began.

## 23.

It is written that Jesus, when struck in the side, poured forth water and blood together. This is indeed mystical, for he himself had said that rivers of living water would flow from his belly (John 7:38).

[Note: Al.: *This indeed*; shortly afterward, *which the Jews had requested*.]

But he also brought forth blood, which the Jews had asked to come upon themselves and upon their children. He therefore brought forth water to cleanse believers, and blood to condemn unbelievers.

It may also be understood that this signified the twofold grace of baptism.

[Note: The old Oxford edition also has this; others omit it. Rufinus transferred this passage from Cyril as far as the end of paragraph 21.]

One grace is given through baptism with water, and the other is sought through the shedding of blood in martyrdom. For both are called baptism.

[Note: We have restored from most other books the reading “through baptism with water and through the shedding of blood in martyrdom,” instead of the earlier and less correct “through the water of baptism and through the mystery of the shedding of blood.”]

But if you also ask why water and blood are said to have been brought forth not from another limb but rather from the side, it seems to me that the woman is indicated in the side, through the rib.

[Note: We supplied the words *in the side* from the same books, which also have more below: “and therefore the fountain of redemption,” and so forth.]

Since, then, the fountain of sin and death proceeded from the first woman, who was the rib of the first Adam, the fountain of redemption and life is produced from the rib of the second Adam.

### 24.

It is written that during his Passion, from the sixth hour until the ninth hour, darkness fell. Receive also the testimony of the prophet concerning this, who says: “The sun shall set for you at midday” (Amos 8:9).

And again the prophet Zechariah says: “On that day there shall be no light; cold [Note: [Col. 0361D] In others: “but there shall be cold (Greek: καὶ ψῦχος) and frost [Col. 0362C] on one day, and that day shall be known to the Lord,” etc.] and frost shall occur on one day, and that day shall be known to the Lord, neither day nor night; and toward evening there shall be light” (Zech. 15:6). What could a prophet have said so evident that these things already seem less to be foretold as future than narrated as past? He foretold both cold and frost. For this reason Peter was warming himself at a fire, because it was cold; and he suffered not only from the cold of the weather, but also from that of faith.

He adds: “And that day shall be known to the Lord, neither day nor night” (Zech. 14:7). What does “neither day nor night” mean? Did he not plainly speak of the darkness inserted into the day and of the light restored again? It was not day, for it did not begin with sunrise. Nor was it a complete night, for it neither received the periods due to it at the beginning after the course of the day had ended, nor brought them to their appointed conclusion. Rather, the light, driven away by the crime of the impious, was restored toward evening. For after the ninth hour, when the darkness had been dispelled, the sun was returned to the world.

And again another gives testimony concerning this very matter: “The light shall be darkened over the earth in the daytime” (Matt. 24:29).

### 25.

The preaching of the Gospel teaches that the soldiers also divided Jesus’ garments among themselves and cast lots for his tunic. [Note: [Col. 0362D] Some have *supra* here and below. They shortly afterward omit even the name of David, which it seemed more correct to cite as in the Barraean edition. Moreover, Pamelius and Fellus, who copied him, omit the whole passage from “This also was a concern,” etc., together with the following testimony of Scripture—apparently through the carelessness of scribes. Baluzius says that he restored the passage from the Sangermanensis manuscript, also changing the punctuation, although Barraeus had restored it long before; the credit for this restoration therefore belongs to him. The following material too Rufinus received from Cyril, nos. 26 and 27.]

The Holy Spirit also took care to proclaim this through the voices of the prophets, when David says: “They divided my garments among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots” (Ps. 21:19).

Nor were the prophets silent even about that garment with which the soldiers are said to have clothed him in mockery, namely, the scarlet garment. Hear what Isaiah says: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with the redness of his garments from Bozrah? Why are your garments red, and your clothing like that of one who has trodden the winepress?” (Isa. 63:1). [Note: [Col. 0362D] Most others read *Bosor* instead of *Bosra*. The former is indeed found in the Hebrew, but not in the Greek. Saint Cyril also, from whom our author derives this passage, reads *Bosor*. This is evident both from the ancient manuscript reading and from the etymology of the name appended there.]

Therefore he himself answered: “I have trodden the winepress alone, daughter of Zion” (ibid.). He is the only one who committed no sin and took away the sins [Al. “sin”] of the world. For if death could enter through one human being, how much more could life be restored through one human being who was also God?

### 26.

It is also reported that he was given vinegar to drink, or myrrh-flavored wine, which is more bitter than gall. Hear what the prophet foretold concerning this: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. 68).

Moses, in answer to this, was already then speaking about that people: “Their vine is from the vines of Sodom, and their branch from Gomorrah [Al. Gomorra]; their grape is a grape of gall, and their cluster is bitterness to them” (Deut. 32:32). And again, reproaching them, he says: “You have repaid this to the Lord, foolish and senseless people” (ibid. 6).

The same things are also foretold in the Song of Songs, where the garden in which he was crucified is likewise indicated. It says: “I entered my garden, my sister, my bride, and I gathered my myrrh” (Song 5). [Note: [Col. 0363C] Some, with Pamelius, add *Canticorum* (“of Songs”), which most others omit, nor does the Cyril whom our author is copying add it. Conversely, we have deleted *mea* (“my”), which Barraeus had in addition before the word *sponsa* (“bride”), on the authority of nearly all the books. See Cyril, nos. 29, 32, and following.]

Here he clearly declared the myrrh-flavored wine which he was given to drink.

### 27.

It is also written that after this he gave up his spirit. This too had been foretold through the prophet, who speaks in the person of the Son to the Father: “Into your hands I commend my spirit” (Ps. 30:6). [Note: [Col. 0363D] The Sangermanensis manuscript reads *Commendabo* (“I shall commend”). Then some printed editions have: “He is also said to have been buried, and a great stone was placed,” etc. Here compare Cyril, no. 35.]

He is said to have been buried, and a great stone was placed before the entrance of the tomb. Receive also what the prophetic word foretold through Jeremiah concerning this: “They killed my life in the pit, and placed a stone over me” (Lam. 3:53). These are the clearest indications of his burial, designated in the words of the prophets.

Yet receive also other testimonies. “The righteous man was taken away from the sight of iniquity, and his resting place is in peace” (Isa. 57:1). [Note: [Col. 0363D] In others: “and his place shall be in peace, and the wicked in burial.” Shortly afterward Fellus has *Recumbens* (“lying down”) instead of *Recubans* (“reclining”). Rufinus copied all this concerning Christ’s burial from another catechesis of Cyril, namely XIV, no. 3.]

And elsewhere: “I will give the wicked for his burial” (Isa. 53:9). And again another says: “He reclined and slept like a lion, and like a lion’s cub; who shall rouse him?” (Gen. 49:9).

### 28.

But that he descended into the underworld is also plainly proclaimed in the Psalms, where it says: “You brought me down to the dust of death” (Ps. 21:16). And again: “What profit is there in my blood, when I descend into corruption?” (Ps. 29:10). And again: “I descended into the mire of the deep, and there is no substance” (Ps. 68:3). [Note: [Col. 0363D] With us, or with Barraeus, Morellius and Baluzius read *Descendi* (“I descended”) from the Sangermanensis manuscript; others read *descendisti* (“you descended”). The words *in infernum* (“into the underworld”) are certainly absent from Remboldus, Erasmus, and Pamelius. Morellius has *in inferno* (“in the underworld”).]

John also says: “Are you the one who is to come (without doubt, into the underworld), or shall we expect another?” (Matt. 11:3).

Hence Peter also says: “Because Christ was put to death in the flesh but made alive by the Spirit who dwells in him, he went down to preach to the spirits who were confined in prison, who had been unbelieving in the days of Noah” (1 Pet. 3:18). [Note: [Col. 0363D] All the others read: “but made alive in spirit. In this, he says, he also went to those imprisoned in the prison,” etc. Our Barraean reading seems closer both to the truth and to the Greek: ζωοποιηθεὶς δὲ τῷ πνεύματι, “but made alive in spirit,” ἐν ᾧ καὶ τοῖς κ.τ.λ.]

In this, too, what work he accomplished in the underworld is declared.

The Lord himself also says through the prophet, as though concerning the future: “For you will not abandon my soul in the underworld, nor will you allow your holy one to see corruption” (Ps. 35:10). This again shows prophetically that the saying was fulfilled when he says: “Lord, you brought my soul out of the underworld; you saved me from those descending into the pit” (Ps. 29).

After this follows:

### 29. ON THE THIRD DAY HE ROSE FROM THE DEAD

For the glory of the Resurrection glorified in Christ everything that had previously seemed weak and fragile. [Note: [Col. 0364C] Omitting the adverb, which Morellius and Pamelius retain, the others, together with them, have: “The glory in Christ freed everything that previously seemed weak and fragile,” which is less satisfactory. They also read *videbatur* (“seemed”) instead of *putabatur* (“was thought”).]

If shortly before you did not think it possible that the immortal one had come even to death, look now: since he is said to have risen after conquering death, he cannot be mortal.

But understand here the goodness of the Creator: for he descended in pursuit of you all the way to the place to which you had been cast down by sin. [Note: [Col. 0364D] The same witnesses have: “because he descended so far in compassion.” A little later they have *id reparaturus* (“to restore it”) instead of *salutem operaturus* (“to accomplish salvation”). Finally, three lines after this they have *intra praescriptae nobis legis terminos* (“within the bounds of the law prescribed for us”) instead of *intra regionis*, etc. The first two readings are certainly less good, while the third is wholly corrupt. The cause of the error is that Barraeus was not consulted. Rufinus compiled this and what follows rather freely from Cyril’s Catechesis XIV, nos. 4 and following.]

Do not accuse the God who created all things of impossibility, imagining that his work could have been confined by a perishable fall from which he could not reach the point where he would accomplish salvation.

The lower and the upper regions are spoken of with reference to us, who are confined within the definite limits of the body and enclosed within the boundaries of the region prescribed for us. But for God, who is everywhere and absent nowhere, what is below, or what is above? [Note: [Col. 0364D] Others have: “What is below, or what is above, is manifest,” without an interrogative mark. Then: “the flesh which had been laid down,” and shortly afterward: “that what had been said might be fulfilled,” omitting the pronoun. Finally, instead of *Rediit* (“he returned”), Baluzius, with the Sangermanensis manuscript, Remboldus, Morellius, and Erasmus, has *Redit* (“he returns”).]

Nevertheless, in the assumption of the body these things too are fulfilled. The flesh that had been placed in the tomb is raised, so that what was said through the prophet might be fulfilled: “For you will not allow your holy one to see corruption” (Ps. 15:10).

He therefore returned victorious from the dead, dragging with him the spoils of the underworld. For he led out those who were held by death, just as he himself had foretold when he said: “When I have been lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself” (John 12:32). [Note: [Col. 0364D] Others omit the pronoun *ipsum* (“himself”), but shortly afterward they have the additional words “because the tombs,” etc. A little later they again lack the preposition *in* where it says “into the holy city.” Finally, they omit entirely the following clause, “they entered the city,” which Morellius and the Sangermanensis manuscript have—except that the latter reads *sanctam* (“holy”) for *sunt* (“they are”). The others entirely lack it, apparently through the fault of ancient scribes who, when the same word recurred, omitted the intervening words in their customary manner.]

The Gospel bears witness to this when it says: “The tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep rose and appeared to many, and they entered into the holy city” (Matt. 27:52). Without doubt they entered that city of which the Apostle says: “But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is the mother of us all” (Gal. 4:26).

As he says again in the Letter to the Hebrews: “For it was fitting that he, for whom are all things and through whom are all things, who had brought many sons to glory, should perfect the author of their salvation through suffering” (Heb. 2:10). [Note: [Col. 0365C] Here again the others, except Baluzius from the Sangermanensis manuscript, Remboldus, and Morellius, omit the passage. They also omit the following pronoun, reading only “and through whom are all things,” and “bringing many sons to glory.” A little later, instead of *passionem* (“suffering”), the manuscripts, Remboldus, and Erasmus prefer *passiones* (“sufferings”). Then, with the manuscripts and the old Oxford edition, they have: “Therefore, having perfected the flesh through sufferings, and having restored through the power of the Resurrection the fall of the first-formed man in it.”]

Therefore, having perfected through sufferings the human flesh that had fallen into death through the fall of the first-formed man, and having restored it through the power of the Resurrection, he placed it, seated at the right hand of God, in the highest places. [Note: [Col. 0365D] Most others have: “he placed it at the right hand of the seat of the Most High God; whence the Apostle also,” etc., which is less correct. Baluzius too preferred the Sangermanensis manuscript’s reading *in altissimis* (“in the highest places”). Shortly afterward the same witnesses have *consuscitavit* (“raised together”) instead of *excitavit* (“raised up”).]

As the Apostle also says: “He raised us up together and made us sit together in the heavenly places” (Eph. 2).

For this was the potter who, as the prophet Jeremiah teaches, lifted up again with his hands the vessel that had fallen and been broken from his hand, and reshaped it as it seemed good in his sight (Jer. 18).

It pleased him to do so in such a way that the body which he had assumed as mortal and corruptible, raised from the stone of the tomb and made immortal and incorruptible, should now be placed not in earthly places but in the heavenly places and at the right hand of the Father. [Note: [Col. 0365D] The same witnesses have *collocaret* (“should place”) instead of *collocarit* (“placed it”). “The Scriptures of the Old Testament are full of these mysteries.” A little later: “And above these the prophet,” etc. Finally, shortly afterward: “Nevertheless, we shall set down a few, indeed very few, examples,” etc.]

The Scriptures of the Old Testament are full of these mysteries. No prophet, no lawgiver, and no psalmist was silent about them; almost every sacred page speaks of them. It therefore seems superfluous to linger over the gathering of testimonies. Nevertheless, we shall set down a very few, sending those who desire to drink more abundantly back to the very sources of the divine books. [Note: [Col. 0365D] The Sangermanensis manuscript, Remboldus, Erasmus, and Morellius, aiming at brevity, have: “we have set down more, leaving the rest.” The Sangermanensis manuscript also omits *et* (“and”).]

### 30.

Thus he says immediately in the Psalms: “I slept, and was overcome with sleep, and rose, because the Lord received me” (Ps. 3). [Note: [Col. 0365D] Instead of “I was overcome with sleep, and rose,” others have “I began to sleep, and rose”; the Sangermanensis manuscript has “I slept, and rose.” Shortly afterward it has *suscipiet* (“will receive”) instead of *suscepit* (“received”). Then all have “Again, in another place,” etc.]

Again: “Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, now I will arise, says the Lord” (Ps. 11).

And elsewhere, as we already said above: “Lord, you brought my soul out of the underworld; you saved me from those descending into the pit” (Ps. 29).

And in another place: “For when you had turned, you gave me life, and again brought me back from the depths of the earth” (Ps. 70). [Note: [Col. 0365D] We have removed *loco* (“place”), which had been added and which the other books more correctly lack. Conversely, shortly afterward we added *autem* (“but”), which was missing; and on the authority of the same witnesses we read *factus sum* (“I became”) instead of *est* (“he is”).]

Most plainly, the eighty-seventh Psalm says of him: “He became like a man without help, free among the dead.” It did not say “a man,” but “like a man.” For he was like a man who had descended into the underworld; but he was free among the dead, because he could not be held by death.

And therefore, in one place the nature of human weakness is shown, [Note: [Col. 0365D] The words “in another, the power of divine majesty,” which were missing, we supplied from other books. Most of those books, however, except Pamelius, Frobenius, and the old edition, omit the word *potestas* (“power”) that follows. Shortly afterward we have also restored *praenuntiat* (“foretells”) instead of *pronuntiat* (“declares”). Rufinus compiled this from Cyril, especially the testimony from Hosea and the interpretation he assigns to it.]

while in another the power of divine majesty is displayed.

The prophet Hosea also most plainly declares the third day in this manner: “He will heal us after two days; on the third day we shall rise and live in his sight” (Hos. 6). He says this in the person of those who, rising with him on the third day, are recalled from death to life. They are the ones who say: “On the third day we shall rise and live in his sight” (Hebr. 13).

Isaiah, however, plainly says: “He who brought up from the earth the great shepherd of sheep” (Isa. 63:11). [Note: [Col. 0366C] Others have *educit* (“brings out”), which is closer to the Greek ἀναγαγών. Saint Paul’s Letter to the Hebrews 13:21 has this reading. Conversely, *eduxit* (“brought out”) is closer to Isaiah’s ἀναβιβάσας. As has been carefully noted in the edition of Cyril’s works, Saint Cyril—whether through a lapse of memory or deliberately—composed this reading from both passages; Rufinus faithfully copied it from him. Isaiah has: ὁ ἀναβιβάσας ἐκ τῆς θαλάσσης τὸν ποιμένα τῶν προβάτων, “who brought up from the sea the shepherd of the sheep.” Some manuscripts and many Fathers, however, prefer ἐκ τῆς γῆς, “from the earth.” The Apostle has: ὁ ἀναγαγὼν ἐκ νεκρῶν τὸν ποιμένα τῶν προβάτων τὸν μέγαν, “who brings up from the dead the great shepherd of the sheep.” Here too ἐκ τῆς γῆς, “from the earth,” instead of ἐκ νεκρῶν, “from the dead,” is reported in some manuscripts and Fathers. At least, therefore, Cyril, and from him our author, added the word “great” from the Apostle.]

But Isaiah also foretold that women would see his Resurrection, even though the scribes, Pharisees, and unbelieving people did not believe. He predicted this too in these words: “Women, who come from the spectacle, come; for there is no people possessing understanding” (Isa. 27:11).

He also foretold the women who are said to have gone to the tomb after the Resurrection, sought him, and did not find him. Thus, concerning Mary Magdalene, who is reported to have come to the tomb before dawn and, not finding him, to have said in tears to the angels who were present: “They have taken away the Lord, and I do not know where they have placed him” (John 20), it is likewise foretold in the Song of Songs: “In my bed I sought him whom my soul loved; in the nights I sought him, and I did not find him” (Song 3). [Note: [Col. 0366D] Others omit *mulieribus* (“women”). Then they have in the nominative: “As Mary Magdalene,” although that surname is unknown to the Sangermanensis manuscript, Remboldus, Erasmus, and Morellius, “is reported to have come.” Shortly afterward we supplied two words, *qui aderant* (“who were present”), on the authority of the others. The following testimony of Scripture also contains: “whom my soul loved, I sought him in the nights,” etc. Cyril cites Isaiah’s passage with the same meaning, and our author drew from him. See no. 14.]

Concerning those who found him and held his feet, it is also foretold in the Song of Songs: “I will hold him and will not let him go, whom my soul loved [Al. “will have loved”]” (ibid.).

These are a few examples from many. Since we are aiming at brevity, we cannot heap up more. [Note: [Col. 0367C] The Sangermanensis manuscript, Remboldus, Erasmus, and Morellius, striving for brevity, have: “we have set down more and left the rest.” The Sangermanensis manuscript also omits *et* (“and”).]

### 31. HE ASCENDED INTO HEAVEN, HE SITS AT THE RIGHT HAND OF THE FATHER; FROM THERE HE WILL COME TO JUDGE THE LIVING AND THE DEAD

[Note: [Col. 0367C] Others have “into the heavens.” Shortly afterward the manuscripts, Remboldus, Erasmus, and Morellius have the consequent material. In keeping with their brevity, the Sangermanensis manuscript, together with Remboldus and Erasmus, contains this passage; Morellius also contains it.]

At the conclusion of the discourse these things are set forth in the consequent brevity. What is said is indeed plain, but the sense in which it should be understood must be sought. For unless you understand his ascending, sitting, and coming according to the dignity of his divinity, these expressions will seem to indicate something belonging to human weakness.

When the things that were being accomplished on earth had been completed, and souls had been recalled from captivity in the underworld, he is said to have ascended into heaven, as the prophet had foretold: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to human beings” (Ps. 63; Eph. 4). [Note: [Col. 0367D] Here it seemed that the singular *minori* and *anima ... revocata* (“the soul ... recalled”) had been read incorrectly, contrary to what nearly all the others have. Compare Cyril, nos. 31 and following.]

These are, of course, the gifts of which Peter spoke in the Acts of the Apostles concerning the Holy Spirit: “Therefore, exalted at the right hand of God, he poured out this gift which you see and hear” (Acts 2). [Note: [Col. 0367D] Others have *Actis* (“Acts”). We have discussed this reading elsewhere.]

He therefore gave the gift of the Holy Spirit to human beings, because Christ, through the Resurrection of his death, recalled to heaven the captivity which the devil had previously led into the underworld through sin.

He ascended into heaven—not to a place where the Word, God, had not previously been, since he had always been in heaven and remained in the Father, but to a place where the Word made flesh had not previously sat.

Finally, because this new entry through the gates of heaven seemed strange to the gatekeepers and rulers, when they saw the nature of flesh penetrating the secrets of heaven, they said to one another, as David, filled with the Holy Spirit, proclaims: “Lift up your gates, O rulers, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter. Who is this King of glory? The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (Ps. 23). [Note: [Col. 0367D] Pamelius likewise has “filled with the Spirit”; others have “filled with the Spirit, he proclaims,” and omit *Tollite* (“Lift up”), together with the following words. All the testimonies of Scripture that follow were borrowed by Rufinus from Cyril in precisely this order and sequence. See no. 24.]

This voice was uttered not on account of the power of the divinity, but on account of the newness of the flesh ascending to the right hand of God.

The same David also says elsewhere: “God ascended amid jubilation, and the Lord amid the sound of the trumpet” (Ps. 46). For it is customary for a victor to return from battle to the sound of a trumpet.

Of him it is also said: “He who builds his ascent in heaven” (Amos 9). And again elsewhere: “He who ascended upon the cherubim, he flew upon the wings of the winds” (Ps. 17). [Note: [Col. 0367D] Others have: “Of him also it is said elsewhere: He who builds his ascent,” etc. Also elsewhere: “He who ascended,” etc.]

### 32.

To sit at the right hand of the Father is likewise a mystery of the flesh assumed. These expressions cannot appropriately be applied to that incorporeal nature without the assumption of flesh. [Note: [Col. 0368C] The Royal manuscript, Remboldus, Erasmus, and Morellius add *assumtae* (“assumed”); the Sangermanensis manuscript has *addantur* (“should be added”). Then most others have: “Nor does the divine nature seek the advantage of a heavenly seat, but the human nature does.” Saint Cyril here, no. 27, refutes the Paulianists, who perversely asserted that the Son began to sit at the right hand of the Father only after the Cross, Resurrection, and return into heaven: Οὐ γὰρ ἐκ προκοπῆς ἔσχε τὸν θρόνον· ἀλλ’ ἀφ’ οὗπέρ ἐστιν (ἐστὶ δὲ ἀεὶ γεννηθείς), καὶ συγκαθίζεται τῷ πατρί. “For he did not obtain this throne through advancement; but from the time that he exists—and he exists as eternally begotten—he also sits together with the Father.” Compare carefully Cyril’s statement with Rufinus’s, and the readings of the others with our printed text.]

Nor is the perfection of the heavenly seat sought by the divine nature, but by the human.

Hence it is said of him: “Your throne has been prepared, O God; from eternity you are” (Ps. 92). [Note: [Col. 0368D] Others omit *est* (“is”), and shortly afterward read “the Lord Jesus was to sit” instead of “the Lord Jesus will sit,” in whose name, etc. Then they have “every knee shall bend and every tongue shall confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is,” etc. The Sangermanensis manuscript has *genuflectetur* (“the knee shall be bent”). See Cyril, no. 28.]

Therefore, the throne has been prepared from eternity, on which the Lord Jesus was to sit; at his name every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue should confess to him that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father (Phil. 2).

David also speaks of him: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet” (Ps. 109).

Yet when the Lord explained these words in the Gospel, he said to the Pharisees: “If David therefore calls him Lord in the Spirit, how is he his son?” (Matt. 22). By this he showed that according to the spirit he is Lord, while according to the flesh he is the son of David.

Hence the Lord himself again says: “Nevertheless I tell you: from now on you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of the power of God” (ibid. 26). And the Apostle Peter says of Christ: “Who is sitting at the right hand of God in the heavens” (1 Pet. 3). Paul also writes to the Ephesians: “According to the working of the power of his might, which he worked in Christ, raising him from the dead and making him sit at his right hand” (Eph. 2).

### 33.

That he will come to judge the living and the dead is taught by many testimonies of the divine Scriptures. [Note: [Col. 0368D] Others have *edocetur* (“is taught”); shortly afterward they have *velut reddituri* (“as though we were going to render an account”) instead of *tanquam*, etc. Here Rufinus begins to compile the following Catechesis XV of Cyril, which is entitled “On the Second Coming of Christ,” etc. Compare no. 2.]

But before we demonstrate that these things were foretold in prophetic utterances, I think it necessary to admonish you of this: this tradition of the faith wishes us daily to remain anxious concerning the coming of the Judge, so that we may prepare our actions as though we were about to render an account to the Judge who is near.

This is what the prophet also said concerning the blessed man: “For he orders his words in judgment” (Ps. 111).

When it is said that he will judge the living and the dead, this does not mean that some living and others dead will come to judgment. [Note: [Col. 0369B] Baluzius omitted the words *ideo dicitur* (“for this reason it is said”), producing an incomplete and disjointed sense, although he says that they occur in the Sangermanensis manuscript, Frobenius, and the oldest edition. No less corruptly, Remboldus, Erasmus, Morellius, Pamelius, and the recent Oxford editor who copied him have: “But what does it mean that he is said to judge the living and the dead, except that some living and others dead come to judgment?”—and then: “but souls together,” etc. The aforementioned Baluzius maintains that Rufinus believed everyone would die, and therefore wished to interpret the words of the Creed more subtly, lest anyone conclude from them that some living and others dead would come to judgment. He says this is clear from what follows. We were not able to be so confident in this conclusion. Rather, we understand from this that Rufinus borrowed this interpretation from Isidore of Pelusium, Book I, Letter 222. For Isidore says in nearly the same words: τὸ κρίνεσθαι ζῶντας καὶ νεκρούς, τοῦτό ἐστι τὸ καὶ ψυχὴν καὶ σῶμα εἰς κρίσιν ἐλεύσεσθαι, καὶ οὔτε ἓν θατέρου κεχωρισμένον, ἀλλ’ ὥσπερ κοινὴν τὴν ἐνταῦθα συνάφειαν ἐποιήσαντο, οὕτω καὶ τὴν ἐκεῖθεν δίκην ἡνωμένως ὑφέξουσιν. “To judge the living and the dead means that both soul and body will come to judgment, neither being separated from the other; but just as they conducted themselves here in union, so there they will jointly undergo the recompense.” Other interpretations may also be found, for example in Augustine’s *Enchiridion to Laurence* and in Gennadius of Massilia.]

Rather, it means that he will judge souls and bodies together, calling souls “the living” and bodies “the dead.”

Thus the Lord himself speaks in the Gospel: “Do not fear those who can kill the body but cannot do anything to the soul; rather, fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Matt. 10). [Note: [Col. 0369D] Others have: “souls will be judged together with bodies.” Shortly afterward: “the Lord himself says in the Gospel: Do not,” etc.]

### 34

Now, if it seems appropriate, let us also show briefly that these things were foretold through the prophets. When you wish for more testimonies, you yourself will gather them from the breadth of the Scriptures.

The prophet Malachi says:

> “Behold, the Almighty Lord will come, and who will endure the day of his coming, or who will endure his appearance? For he himself enters like a refiner’s fire and like fuller’s herb; and he will sit refining and purifying like silver and like gold” (Malachi 3).

[Note: The same manuscripts read *veniet* (“will come”), as Saint Cyril also cites it. The Sangermanensis manuscript and Remboldus have *ingredietur* (“will enter”) instead of *ingreditur* (“enters”); afterward those same witnesses and the Regius manuscript have *conflatores* (“refiners”) instead of *conflans* (“refining”).]

[Note: Others—so far as I know, all of them—read “like foam” (*spuma*) instead of “like herb.” The Greek has, as Saint Cyril also cites it, ὡς πόα (*hōs poa*, “like *poa*”), which is the fuller’s herb. Jeremiah 2:22 likewise mentions πόα πλυνόντων (“the herb of those who wash”), called *borith* in Hebrew in both passages. Jerome writes there: “For *borith* herb, which we have translated as it stands in Hebrew, the Septuagint translated as πόαν, so as to indicate the fuller’s herb, which, according to the custom of the province of Palestine, grows in green and moist places and has the same power for washing away stains as nitre.” See also our discussion there. He makes a similar statement concerning this passage in Malachi: “The Lord is called not only fire, but also the fuller’s herb, which in Hebrew is called *borith*, and which the Septuagint translates as πόαν, that is, fuller’s herb.” Nowhere is it called “foam,” nor is it possible to guess why others read it that way. In the Greek copy of the Septuagint—the Alexandrian copy recently reprinted at Zurich in Switzerland—ὡς ποιά is read instead of πόα; but ποιά also means “herb” in Callimachus. Immediately afterward the same editors add *eos* (“them”) to *conflans* (“refining”), although it is not a pronoun in the sacred text. We have restored the words “like silver,” which had dropped out of the Barraean copy through scribal error, on the authority of all the other witnesses.]

But so that you may recognize more clearly who this Lord is of whom these things are said, hear what the prophet Daniel also foretells:

> “I saw in a vision of the night—and behold, one coming with the clouds of heaven, like a son of man—and he came up to the Ancient of Days, and was presented before him. And to him was given dominion and honor and a kingdom; and all peoples, tribes, and languages shall serve him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed” (Daniel 7).

[Note: “Of the night” is absent from the manuscripts cited by Baluzius, from Remboldus, and from Erasmus. Immediately afterward, the same witnesses and others read “in the clouds” instead of “with the clouds,” and *perveniet* (“will come”) instead of *pervenit* (“came”); neither reading agrees well, at least with the Greek. In the words that follow, the Barraean copy added *liber* (“book”) after “was presented,” but we removed it as an intrusion from a note that some diligent reader may have written in the margin from the Apocalypse.]

Thus we learn from these passages not only about his coming and judgment, but also about his dominion and kingdom, because his dominion is eternal and his kingdom is without end of corruption. As it is also said in the Creed:

> “And of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1:33).

Therefore, he is very far from the faith who says that Christ’s kingdom will at some time come to an end.

[Note: We supplied the pronoun *eius* (“his”) from most other books, which immediately afterward also unanimously have *in Evangelio* (“in the Gospel”) instead of *in Symbolo* (“in the Creed”). We once doubted whether this title had been substituted for the other by a later hand when the so-called Constantinopolitan Creed began to prevail in the Churches. But since Saint Cyril also proposes this addition, as from the Creed, for explanation, and Rufinus’s following in his footsteps has been noted in so many places, we decided to change nothing. Indeed, it seemed more likely that he was citing Cyril’s own passage from the Creed than, as they wish, Luke’s Gospel, chapter 1, verse 33. For even if it may not have belonged to the Creed of the Church of Aquileia, it nevertheless certainly formed part of the more common Creed, which prevailed more widely, especially in the Churches of the East, and was commonly called Apostolic. See Cyril, no. 1, and the final three sections at the end of the Catechesis.]

We must nevertheless know that the enemy tries, by cunning deception, to imitate this saving coming of Christ in order to deceive the faithful, and, in place of the Son of Man who is expected to come in the majesty of his Father, to prepare the son of perdition with lying wonders and signs, so that, in place of Christ, he may introduce Antichrist into this world.

[Note: Others prefix *ipse* (“himself”); with them we also changed *Quia ego* (“Because I”) to *ergo* (“therefore”), and in the following passage from Matthew *Cum* (“when”) to *Tunc* (“then”), as well as other slighter matters below. I suspect that the following *erroris* (“of error”) should be corrected to *erronis*, namely, of Antichrist. Rufinus borrows these passages from Cyril, no. 11 and following.]

Concerning him the Lord also foretold to the Jews in the Gospels:

> “Because I came in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me; another will come in his own name, and him you will receive” (John 5).

And again he says:

> “When you see the abomination of desolation standing in the holy place, as the prophet Daniel says—let the reader understand” (Matthew 24).

Daniel, therefore, teaches more fully and at greater length in his visions about the coming of this error. It would now be very laborious to offer examples from them, since the subject is extended through sufficiently extensive narratives; and therefore anyone who wishes to know more fully about these matters we refer rather to the visions themselves.

The Apostle also speaks of him:

> “Let no one deceive you in any way; for unless the apostasy comes first and the man of sin, the son of perdition, is revealed, who opposes and exalts himself above everything that is called God or worshiped, so that he sits in the temple of God, displaying himself as though he were God” (2 Thessalonians 2:3–4).

And shortly afterward:

> “Then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth and destroy by the manifestation of his coming. His coming is according to the working of Satan, with every power, signs, and lying wonders” (ibid. 8–9).

And again, shortly afterward:

> “Therefore God will send them an operation of error, so that they may believe the lie, in order that all may be judged who did not believe the truth” (ibid. 10–11).

[Note: All the others read *revelabitur inimicus* (“the enemy will be revealed”) incorrectly instead of *revelabitur iniquus* (“the lawless one will be revealed”); for the Greek has ἄνομος (*anomos*, “lawless”), not ἐχθρός (*echthros*, “enemy”). Compare Cyril, no. 15, from whom our author took this passage.]

Therefore this error is foretold to us by prophetic, Gospel, and apostolic voices, so that no one may believe that the coming of Antichrist is the coming of Christ.

[Note: Others have *ne quis* (“lest anyone”), and shortly afterward *credat* (“may believe”); then *sed et ipse* (“but he himself”); and a little later *demonstrabitur* (“will be shown”) instead of *demonstraverit* (“will have shown”).]

Rather, as the Lord himself says:

> “When they say to you, ‘Behold, Christ is here,’ or, ‘He is there,’ do not believe it. For many false Christs and false prophets will arise, and they will deceive many” (Matthew 24).

But let us see how he demonstrates the judgment of the true Christ.

> “As lightning shines from the East all the way to the West, so will be the coming of the Son of Man” (ibid.).

When, therefore, the true Lord Jesus Christ has come, he will sit and establish judgment, as he also says in the Gospels:

[Note: The same witnesses have “as the Gospel says”; and then Baluzius’s Sangermanensis manuscript has *justos separabit* (“he will separate the righteous”) instead of *segregabit* (“he will set apart”). The other printed editions have neither expression, but Morellius has “the righteous from the unrighteous,” that is, “the righteous from the unrighteous.”]

> “And he will separate the sheep from the goats” (Matthew 25),

that is, he will separate the righteous from the unrighteous.

As the Apostle writes:

> “For we must all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what belongs to his own body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil” (2 Corinthians 5:10).

[Note: Others, except the old Oxford edition, falsely read *propria operis sui* (“what belongs to his own work”) instead of *propria corporis* (“what belongs to his own body”). The sacred text also has in Greek τὰ διὰ τοῦ σώματος (“the things done through the body”), whatever Pamelius may propose instead.]

A person will be judged not only for deeds, but also for thoughts, according to what the Apostle himself says:

> “Their thoughts accusing or even defending one another on the day when God will judge the hidden things of human beings” (Romans 2).

But let this suffice concerning these matters. After this, the following article is placed in the order of the faith.

### 35. AND IN THE HOLY SPIRIT

The things that were set forth somewhat more extensively above concerning Christ pertain to the mystery of his incarnation and passion. Since these matters intervene as part of his person, they have caused the commemoration of the Holy Spirit to be placed somewhat farther away.

[Note: Thus also Baluzius, from the Sangermanensis manuscript, Remboldus, and Erasmus; others have *coaptata* (“joined together”).]

However, if only the consideration of divinity is taken into account, then in the same manner in which at the beginning it is said, “I believe in God the almighty Father,” and afterward, “in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord,” it is joined as follows:

> “And in the Holy Spirit.”

All those things, however, which are mentioned concerning Christ refer, as we have said, to the dispensation of the flesh.

Thus, in the commemoration of the Holy Spirit, the mystery of the Trinity is completed. For just as one is called Father, and there is no other Father; and one is called the only-begotten Son, and there is no other only-begotten son; so also the Holy Spirit is one, and there cannot be another Holy Spirit.

[Note: Others omit “son”; and lower down, beginning three lines after this, they give the passage in this form: “and that he himself has no father, while the Son is as one who was born from the Father, and the Holy Spirit as proceeding from the mouth of God,” and so forth. Although the remainder is otherwise equally sound, this final phrase—“from the mouth of God”—instead of “from both” appears to have been fabricated by a later hand. On the other hand, the truth of this reading, which Barraeus alone has, is demonstrated by the very sequence of Rufinus’s discourse, as well as by the discussion undertaken concerning the relations of the Father to the Son, and conversely, and concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit from both. These words are taken by our author from Cyril almost verbatim—something astonishingly overlooked by Touttee. Cyril says in Catechesis XVI, no. 3: Ὅσπερ εἷς ἐστιν ὁ Θεὸς ὁ πατὴρ, καὶ οὐκ ἔστι δεύτερος πατήρ; καὶ ὥσπερ εἷς ἐστιν ὁ μονογενὴς υἱὸς καὶ Λόγος Τοῦ Θεοῦ, καὶ ἀδελφὸν οὐκ ἔχει; οὕτως ἓν ἐστι τὸ ἅγιον Πνεῦμα μόνον, καὶ δεύτερον οὐκ ἔστι πνεῦμα ἰσότιμον αὐτῷ κ.τ.λ. This means: “Just as God the Father is one, and there is no second Father; and just as the only-begotten Son, the Word of God, is one, and has no brother; so also the Holy Spirit is one, and there is no other Spirit equal to him in honor,” and so forth. These are almost Rufinus’s very words.]

Therefore, in order that the distinction of persons may be made, the terms expressing relationship are distinguished: by these the Father is understood as the one from whom all things are, and as having no father himself; the Son as one who is born from the Father; and the Holy Spirit as proceeding from both and sanctifying all things.

[Note: The word order was formerly less correct: “in one and the same Trinity,” contrary to all the other books. Compare Cyril, no. 4. Saint Epiphanius strongly presses this small distinction in the Creed to establish the divinity of the Holy Spirit, *Against the Heresies*, heresy 74, which is that of the Pneumatomachi: “For immediately the exposition confesses,” and so forth. It would take too long to quote it here.]

But so that the one and the same divinity in the Trinity may be taught: just as it was said that one should believe in God the Father, with the preposition *in* added, so also it is said concerning Christ his Son, and likewise concerning the Holy Spirit.

But so that what we have said may become clearer, it will be confirmed by what follows. For after this statement comes:

### 36. THE HOLY CHURCH. THE FORGIVENESS OF SINS. THE RESURRECTION OF THIS FLESH.

[Note: Pamelius, Frobenius, and the old Hieronymian edition add “Catholic” here and shortly afterward with Barraeus. Against this, the other printed editions as well as the manuscripts are silent, nor does Rufinus himself explain it. Conversely, we added the pronoun “this” to “resurrection of the flesh,” which Barraeus and certain others did not know, with Pamelius himself supporting us.]

He did not say, “in the holy Church,” nor “in the forgiveness of sins,” nor “in the resurrection of the flesh.” For if he had added the preposition *in*, it would have produced one and the same force with the preceding expressions.

[Note: Others have “there would have been one and the same force” along with the preceding expressions. We also supply the name Jesus shortly afterward. They then read: “concerning creatures and mysteries, let it be said, ‘in the holy Church,’ and not as in God,” and so forth. The Sangermanensis manuscript has “gathered by God.”]

Now, in those expressions in which faith is ordered concerning divinity, it is said, “in God the Father,” and “in Jesus Christ his Son,” and “in the Holy Spirit.” In the remaining expressions, where the subject is not divinity but creatures and mysteries, the preposition *in* is not added: one is not to say “in the holy Church,” but rather that the holy Church is to be believed—not as God, but as the Church gathered by God.

And they are to believe that there is forgiveness of sins, not “in the forgiveness of sins”; and they are to believe in the resurrection of the flesh, not “in the resurrection of the flesh.”

[Note: The same witnesses read “to be believed”; afterward they omit “the other.” A little later they read, “Therefore this Spirit,” and lower down, “of the instrument” instead of “of the Testament.”]

By this syllable of the preposition, therefore, the Creator is distinguished from creatures, and divine things are separated from human things.

This, then, is the Holy Spirit who inspired the Law and the Prophets in the Old Testament, and the Gospels and the Apostles in the New. Therefore the Apostle also says:

> “Every Scripture inspired by God is useful for teaching” (2 Timothy 3).

For this reason, since the books of the New and Old Testaments are believed to have been inspired by the Holy Spirit himself according to the tradition of our forefathers and handed down to the Churches of Christ, it seems appropriate to designate them explicitly in this place, as we have received them from the records of the Fathers.

### 37

Thus, first of all, five books of Moses were handed down in the Old Testament: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy.

[Note: Previously the text had *Numerus* instead of *Numeri*. Others have *Post hos* (“after these”); the Sangermanensis manuscript, Remboldus, Erasmus, and Morellius have *Post hoc*. Baluzius notes that shortly afterward the distinction occurs. *Judicium* was a corrupt reading for *Judicum*; for *Regnorum*, some have *Regum*.]

After these come Joshua son of Nun, Judges together with Ruth. After these, four books of Kingdoms, which the Hebrews count as two; Chronicles, which is called the Book of Days; and two books of Ezra, which they count individually, and Esther.

Among the Prophets are Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel; in addition, the one book of the Twelve Prophets. Job also is one book, and the Psalms of David are one book.

Solomon, however, handed down three books to the Churches: Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs.

[Note: Most others read: “Three books of Solomon, however, were handed down to the Churches.” Fellus and others have *tradidit* (“he handed down”).]

In these they included the number of the books of the Old Testament.

In the New Testament there are four Gospels, of Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John; the Acts of the Apostles, which Luke wrote; fourteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul; two Epistles of the Apostle Peter; one of James, the brother and Apostle of the Lord; one of Jude; three of John; and the Apocalypse of John.

[Note: The same witnesses read *descripsit* (“wrote”). Baluzius, on the authority of manuscripts and ancient editions, has “fourteen Epistles, two of the Apostle Peter,” and everything that follows in the accusative case rather than the nominative, which Pamelius formerly also retained.]

These are the books that the Fathers included within the canon and from which they wished the affirmations of our faith to be constituted.

### 38

It must nevertheless be understood that there are other books which are not canonical, but which our forefathers called ecclesiastical—that is, the Wisdom which is called Solomon’s, and another Wisdom which is called that of the son of Sirach. Among the Latins this book is called *Ecclesiasticus* by this same general designation; by that name it is not the author of the little book who is identified, but the quality of the Scripture.

[Note: Others omit *vero* (“however”), and shortly afterward read *Hermatis*. Baluzius, with two manuscripts, has *Hermetis*; Morellius, like us, has *Hermes*; others have *Hermae*. For *Judicium Petri* (“Judgment of Peter”), the Regius manuscript has *Judicium secundum Petri* (“Judgment according to Peter”), while the Sangermanensis and ancient editions have *Judicium secundum Petrum* (“Judgment according to Peter”).]

Of the same order are the little book of Tobit, Judith, and the books of the Maccabees.

In the New Testament there is the little book called *The Shepherd*, or *Hermas*; the work called *The Two Ways*; or *The Judgment of Peter*.

They wished all these to be read in the Churches, but not to be brought forward as authority for confirming the faith. All the remaining Scriptures they called apocryphal, and they did not wish them to be read in the Churches.

These things have been handed down to us by the Fathers, and, as I said, it seemed useful to designate them in this place, for the instruction of those who are receiving for themselves the first elements of the Church and of the faith, so that they may know from which fountains of the word of God they should draw their cups.

[Note: Some omit the words “which are,” and immediately afterward, where the text says “the first elements of the Church and of the faith,” Baluzius, together with two editions of Jerome and Fellus with the oldest Oxford edition, retains the phrase. Baluzius altered the text to “the first elements of the faith,” deleting “of the Church and of,” which seemed to him to have been mistakenly inserted, on the authority of manuscripts and ancient editions of Cyprian. For us, the greater authority belongs to the Barraean copy, and it appears to be supported by more witnesses.]

### 39

The order of the faith next contains:

> “THE HOLY CHURCH.”

We have already explained above the reason why they did not say here also, “in the holy Church.”

[Note: Others, using the singular, have *dixerit* (“he may have said”); afterward they add, “but the holy Church,” words which can also be absent without affecting the complete sense. The same witnesses then read: “they were taught to believe in one God,” and so forth.]

Those who above were taught, under the mystery of the Trinity, to believe in one God must also believe this: that there is one holy Church, in which there is one faith and one baptism; in which the one God is believed to be the Father, and the one Lord Jesus Christ his Son, and the one Holy Spirit.

This, then, is the holy Church, without spot or wrinkle.

For many others also gathered Churches: Marcion, Valentinus, Ebion, Manichaeus, Arius, and all the other heretics.

[Note: For the third occurrence of *et* (“and”), others have *ut* (“as”); after Manichaeus they add “Arius,” which we have also added on their authority. Finally, below they have *Odivi* instead of *Odi*.]

But those Churches are not without the spot or wrinkle of unbelief. Therefore the Prophet said of them:

> “I hate the assembly of the wicked, and I will not sit with the impious.”

But concerning this Church, which preserves the faith of Christ whole and entire, hear what the Holy Spirit says in the Song of Songs:

> “My dove is one, my perfect one is one with her mother” (Song of Songs 6:8).

[Note: Thus also the Sangermanensis manuscript. Along with the Greek Τῇ μητρὶ (“with her mother”), others prefer *genetricis* (“of her parent”); shortly afterward they have *susceperit* (“has received”) instead of *suscipit* (“receives”).]

Whoever, therefore, receives this faith in the Church should not turn aside into the council of vanity, nor enter with those who practice iniquity.

For the council of vanity is what Marcion teaches: he denies that the God who is the Father of Christ is the Creator, who made the world through his Son.

The council of vanity is what Ebion teaches: that Christ must be believed in such a way that circumcision of the flesh, observance of the Sabbath, the solemnity of sacrifices, and all the other observances according to the letter of the Law are retained.

[Note: The same witnesses have “and circumcision”; shortly afterward, “all the observances”; and two lines after this, “first, because he called himself the Paraclete.”]

The council of vanity is what Manichaeus teaches: first, because he called himself the Paraclete; then, because he says that the world was made by evil, denies God the Creator, rejects the Old Testament, and asserts that one good nature and another evil nature oppose one another; he maintains, according to the Pythagoreans, that human souls, coeternal with God, return through various cycles of birth into cattle, animals, and beasts; he denies the resurrection of our flesh; and he affirms that the Lord’s passion and birth occurred not in true flesh but in appearances.

[Note: We added “opposing one another,” which was missing, from other books; likewise shortly afterward “to God,” namely, “souls coeternal with God,” and so forth.]

The council of vanity is what Paul of Samosata asserted, and Photinus, his successor after him: he thinks that Christ was not born before the ages from the Father, but began from Mary; and that he was not born God as man, but was made God from a human being.

[Note: Others have a somewhat more correct reading: “and after him his successor.”]

The council of vanity is what Arius and Eunomius taught: they say that the Son was not born from the very substance of the Father, but was created from nothing; that the Son of God has a beginning and is lesser than the Father; and that the Holy Spirit is not only lesser than the Son but also a servant sent by him.

[Note: We are compelled to follow the authority and reliability of all the other books. Otherwise, the Barraean copy has *praefert* (“prefers”), a somewhat smoother reading in relation to the preceding *docuit* (“taught”). It does not recognize the passage extending for nearly four lines, beginning “and they assert that the Son of God has a beginning and is lesser,” and ending with “a servant sent by him.” This omission may indeed be more consistent with the sequence and context of Rufinus’s purpose; for there is no indication at all that the passage dropped out of this copy through scribal error. On the contrary, many things suggest that it was afterward inserted by an interpolator. Nevertheless, as we have said, we yield to the authority of all the others and prefer to err on the side of preserving anything that had long before been received as Rufinian. Baluzius added the word “Son” from the Sangermanensis manuscript.]

The council of vanity is also what those people assert who confess that the Son is indeed from the substance of the Father, but separate and distinguish the Holy Spirit, although the Savior plainly displays the one and the same power and divinity of the Trinity in the Gospel when he says:

> “Baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28).

It is manifestly impious to separate from a human being what has been joined together by God.

The council of vanity is also what stubborn and perverse controversy once assembled, asserting that Christ assumed human flesh but not a rational soul, although the same salvation was certainly bestowed by Christ upon both flesh and soul, and upon human sense and mind.

[Note: Other witnesses also omit *humano* (“human”); with them, three lines later, we read “the Church of tradition” instead of “the tradition of the Church.”]

The council of vanity is also what Donatus contracted throughout Africa by accusing the Church of betrayal; and what Novatus stirred up by denying repentance to those who had fallen; and by condemning second marriages whenever necessity might have required that they be entered into.

[Note: In the Sangermanensis manuscript, Remboldus, Erasmus, and Morellius: “and condemning second marriages from being entered into, even when necessity requires them.” The Regius manuscript reads likewise, except that it omits “them.”]

Therefore flee all these assemblies as assemblies of the wicked.

But also flee those, if there are any, who are said to assert that the Son of God does not see or know the Father in the same way in which he himself is known and seen by the Father; or that Christ’s kingdom will come to an end; or that the resurrection of the flesh will not restore it in the complete integrity of its nature; or who deny that God’s judgment will be just toward all; or who say that the devil will be released from the punishment of condemnation that is owed to him.

[Note: The same witnesses have “not in the complete integrity of its nature”; shortly afterward they have the somewhat more correct *absolvere* (“to release”) instead of *absolvi* (“to be released”). No one can fail to see that the impious doctrines of Origen—or those especially charged against him at that time—are being condemned here. This is a very certain proof of the thoroughly orthodox faith of Rufinus: by it alone he demonstrates that he recoiled from the errors of the author whose genius he chiefly admired and clears himself of every suspicion. Indeed, I think that those who fabricated Rufinus’s recantations, which we reprinted at the end of this volume, took their opportunity from these passages. See them, as well as what we have noted in Volume I of Jerome’s Works concerning Theophilus’s Synodical Letter and his Paschal Letters.]

From all these things, I say, let the hearing of the faithful turn away.

But let him hold to the holy Church,

[Note: The same witnesses again have *teneat* (“let him hold”), and shortly afterward “his only-begotten Son,” and then “having risen from the dead in the same flesh in which he was born, believes him to be coming as judge,” and so forth.]

which professes the almighty God the Father, and his only Son Jesus Christ our Lord, and the Holy Spirit, with a harmonious and concordant understanding of substance; and which believes that the Son of God was born from a Virgin, suffered for the salvation of humanity, and rose from the dead in the flesh in which he died.

Finally, it hopes for that same one as the judge of all, in whom the forgiveness of sins and the resurrection of the flesh are proclaimed.

### 40

Concerning the forgiveness of sins, mere belief ought to suffice. For who would seek causes or an explanation where the sovereign’s mercy is concerned? When the generosity of an earthly king is not subjected to investigation, divine generosity is examined by human presumption.

For pagans habitually say derisively against us that we deceive ourselves when we think that crimes committed in deed can be cleansed by words.

[Note: Others again have *qui putamus* (“because we think”) and “who committed murder.” Then they read “and not appear to be an adulterer,” and shortly afterward “how, then, can one guilty of such crimes,” without the intervening *ergo* (“therefore”). Finally, they have “suddenly appears and is pure” more fully.]

They say: “Can one who has committed murder not be a murderer? And can one who has committed adultery not appear to be an adulterer? How, then, will someone guilty of crimes of this kind suddenly seem holy to you?”

But, as I said, I answer these objections better by faith than by argument. For he who made this promise is King of all; he who makes these promises is Lord of earth and heaven.

“Do you not want me to believe that he who made me a human being from earth can make me innocent from a criminal? He who, when I was blind, made me see—or, when I was deaf, made me hear; he who restored a cripple’s step to me—will he not be able to recover my lost innocence?”

[Note: Some omit the word *vel* (“or”), and have: “when I was deaf, he made me hear”; then they add another passage of this kind: “he who made me healthy when I was sick.” Finally, they have *reparare* (“restore”) instead of *recuperare* (“recover”), and *et ut* (“and so that”) instead of *et tamen* (“and yet”).]

And let us come to the testimony of nature itself. To kill a human being is not always criminal; it is criminal to kill through wickedness, not according to the laws. Therefore, in such matters, it is not the deed—which is sometimes rightly performed—that condemns me, but the mind that counsels evil.

If, then, the mind in me, which has become criminal and in which the origin of vice existed, is corrected, why should I seem unable to become innocent, although I was previously criminal?

[Note: The same witnesses have *non videar posse* (“may I not seem able”), and then *ostendimus* (“we have shown”) instead of *ostendi* (“I have shown”). A little later the manuscripts and old edition have *bona voluntas* (“a good will”) instead of *in bonum voluntas* (“a will toward the good”).]

For, as I have shown above, if it is established that the crime lies not in the deed but in the will, then, just as an evil will, through the agency of the evil demon, made me subject to sin and death, so a will changed toward the good, through the agency of the good God, restored me to innocence and life.

The same reasoning applies to the remaining crimes.

[Note: Others omit *est* (“is”); then they have “and in this way,” and so forth.]

In this way our faith is not found to oppose natural reasoning, since forgiveness of sins is attributed not to deeds, which cannot be changed, but to the mind, which, as is certain, can be converted from evil to good.

### 41

This final statement, which proclaims the resurrection of the flesh, concludes the whole perfection of the faith in a concise summary, although the faith of the Church concerning this matter is attacked not only by Gentiles but also by heretics.

[Note: Pamelius, whom Fellus follows together with the old edition, has “and further,” falsely thinking that another article of the Creed is indicated: “And everlasting life.” At that time it did not yet have its own place, but was thought to be contained in the Resurrection. Saint Jerome says plainly in *Against John of Jerusalem*: “In the Creed, the whole sacrament of Christian doctrine is concluded by the resurrection of the flesh.” Our author likewise says: “The statement that proclaims the resurrection of the flesh concludes the sum of all perfection with concise brevity.”]

For Valentinus wholly denies the resurrection of the flesh, as do the Manichaeans, as we showed above.

[Note: Most others have, “and Manes,” as we showed above. They continue: “But these people, who refused to hear the prophet Isaiah when he said, ‘The dead will rise and those who are in the tombs will be raised,’ also refused to hear Daniel, wisest of all the prophets, when he proclaimed…” The old Oxford edition likewise prefers *protestantem* (“proclaiming”) for the final word.]

But these people refused to hear the prophet Isaiah, who says:

> “The dead will rise, and those who are in the tombs will be raised” (Isaiah 26:19),

nor Daniel, the wisest of the prophets, who declares:

> “For then those who are in the dust of the earth will rise: some to eternal life, but others to eternal disgrace and eternal confusion” (Daniel 12).

Nevertheless, they ought to have learned, even from the Gospels—which they appear to accept—from our Lord and Savior, who was teaching the Sadducees, when it was said:

> “But that the dead rise, have you not read how he says to Moses at the bush, ‘God of Abraham, God of Isaac, and God of Jacob’? God is not the God of the dead, but of the living” (Mark 12:26, 31).

[Note: The same witnesses have *inde* (“from there”) or “in the Gospels,” and afterward “by the Lord our Savior,” and *Moyses* (“Moses”) instead of *Moysi* (“to Moses”). The Sangermanensis manuscript has “but of the living”; those words are absent from the Regius manuscript and several printed books.]

In this passage he also previously indicated what and how great the glory of the resurrection is when he said:

> “In the resurrection of the dead they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but they will be like the angels of God” (Matthew 22:30).

The power of the resurrection, therefore, grants human beings an angelic condition, so that those who have risen from the earth may not again live on earth with the animals, but in heaven with the angels.

Yet the discipline of a purer life will have admitted them to this condition: namely, those who even now preserve their flesh for their souls in chaste acts of purity and have subjected it to the obedience of the Holy Spirit; and who, having attenuated it by every stain of vice and transformed it into the spiritual glory of sanctification by its power, have deserved also to bring it into the fellowship of the angels.

[Note: This reading is also preferred by Baluzius from the Sangermanensis manuscript and by the old Oxford edition; others have *prioris* (“of the former”). Then all have: “who no longer serve the flesh, but have subjected the flesh of their soul, with the chaste reins of purity, to the obedience of the Holy Spirit.” But the Barraean reading, which we endeavor to retain as far as possible, is not itself incongruous.

Others have “and into spiritual glory.” Instead of *consortiis inferre* (“to bring into fellowship”), two manuscripts cited by Baluzius have *consortiis inserere* (“to insert into fellowship”); Remboldus, Erasmus, and Morellius have *misceri* (“to be mingled with”).]

### 42.

But unbelievers [Note: [Col. 0379C] So too the old Oxford edition. In other copies, *reclaimant* (“they object”), and in the third line after this, *redintegrari* (“to be restored”) is supplied.] cry out and say: “How can flesh which decays and dissolves, or is even sometimes swallowed up in the depths of the sea and scattered by the waves, be gathered together again and restored into one, so that a human body may be reconstituted from it?”

To them let us first reply with the words of Paul, who says: “Foolish man, what you sow is not made alive unless it first dies. And what you sow is not the body that is to be, but a bare grain of wheat or of one of the other seeds. But God gives it a body as he wills” (1 Cor. 15). What you see happening year by year in the seeds that you cast into the earth—do you not believe that the same will happen in your flesh, which by God’s ordinance is sown in the earth? Why, I ask, are you so narrow and feeble in your estimation of divine power that you do not believe that the dust of each person’s flesh, though scattered, can be gathered and restored according to its own nature? [Note: [Col. 0379C] Others add *te* (“you”). Shortly afterward, the Sangerman manuscript, Rembold, and Erasmus read *existimator* (“judge, estimator”) instead of *aestimator*.]

[Note: [Col. 0379C] Previously *iterum* (“again”) had mistakenly stood for *interim* (“in the meantime”). For *dicentis* (“saying”), which follows, the old Oxford edition also has *dicentis*; others prefer *dicentes* (“those saying”). Likewise, for *vivificatur* (“is made alive”), which both the manuscripts, the same old edition, and Morellus retain, others prefer *vivificabitur* (“will be made alive”).]

Do you not judge this possible when you see that even mortal ingenuity searches out veins of metals buried deep in the earth? The craftsman’s eye sees gold where the unskilled man thinks there is only earth. Why should we not grant this to the one who made man, when the one who was made by him can attain so much? And when mortal ingenuity discovers that gold has one distinct vein, silver another, bronze a very different one, and that iron and lead lie hidden within another species of earth, will divine power not be thought capable of finding and distinguishing the proper substance of each person’s flesh, even if it appears to have been scattered? [Note: [Col. 0379D] Others read: “and the distinct kinds of iron and lead within the earth,” etc.; in this reading, *in terra* (“in the earth”) seems certainly less correct than *intra* (“within”), as the old Oxford edition likewise prefers with us and Barraeus.]

[Note: [Col. 0379D] We have restored here and below, with Baluzius, *censum* (“substance, account”) from the Sangerman manuscript, where *sensum* stood, both in the Barraean text and in the other printed copies. Immediately afterward the same copies add *esse* (“to be”) after *videatur* (“appears”), and, except for the old Oxford edition and Morellus, read *dispersum* (“scattered”) instead of *dispersus* (“scattered,” masculine). This too Rufinus derived from Cyril, *Catechesis* XVIII, no. 3.]

### 43.

But let us also try to assist souls that are failing in faith by natural reasoning. If someone mixes different seeds together and sows them indiscriminately, or scatters them randomly over the earth, will not each individual grain, wherever it has been cast, produce a sprout at the proper time according to the character of its nature, and restore the form and body proper to it? [Note: [Col. 0380C] We retain the Barraean reading, which, if it is the more correct, is certainly satisfactory. Others, omitting here *granum* (“grain”) and shortly afterward *jactum* (“cast”), express the passage thus: “will not each individual seed, wherever it may be, according to the nature appropriate to its place,” although, for *ratio* (“nature, character”), which Baluzius restored from the manuscripts, other printed editions read *satio* (“sowing”), as they had also read *fuerat* (“had been”) instead of *fuerit* (“may be”). Saint Cyril uses this same example of seeds in the sense which our author explains a little earlier concerning the distinction of metal veins. I shall give the passage only in Latin, both to be brief and so that you may recognize our author’s practice of transferring another writer’s ideas into his own words. “Suppose,” he says, no. 3, “that different grains of seed have been mixed together … and are held in your one handful.
