Is it difficult—or rather, is it easy—for you, a human being, to distinguish what is contained in your handful, and to gather each seed according to its proper nature and return it to its own kind? Can you distinguish things contained in your hand, while God cannot distinguish and restore things contained in his own hand?” You may compare the rest yourself, for he transfers the remaining material in much the same way.]

Thus the substance of each person’s flesh, although it may have been scattered in many different ways, nevertheless has within each body its own principle, which is immortal, because the flesh of the immortal soul is immortal. [Note: [Col. 0380D] Others omit these words; indeed, placing a full stop after *immortalis*, they begin a new sense from *Tempore* (“from the time”) in this manner: “From the time when, after bodies have been sown in the earth, the first word of God’s will has smiled upon what was gathered and drawn from the earth.” Baluzius likewise considered this passage corrupt; he says that he would readily emend it partly from Pamelius and certain others, in whom *immortalis* occurs only once, and partly from Morellus and the old edition cited by Pamelius, as follows: “The principle itself, which exists in each flesh, because the flesh of the immortal soul is immortal, from the time when, after bodies have been sown in the earth, it has responded to the will of the true God, gives back and restores what has been gathered and drawn from the earth,” and so on. This is almost the same as our Barraean text, which he did not know, except that he omits the two words *est immortalis*, occurring here first, and shortly afterward prefers *de terra* (“from the earth”) to *terrae* (“of the earth”). This seemed sufficient reason for us to prefer the Barraean reading, although there is no shortage of arguments by which it might be approved; only shortly afterward we have restored *censum* in place of *sensum*. Examine the entire sequence of the discourse and compare Saint Cyril, nos. 16 and following.]

From the time when, after bodies have been sown in the earth, it first responded to the will of the true God, it gives back and restores to its own substance what has been gathered and drawn from the earth, restoring it to the form that death had once dissolved. Thus it comes about that each soul receives back, not a confused or foreign body, but its own body, the body it had possessed, so that accordingly, in proportion to the struggles of the present life, its flesh may be crowned with its soul if it was chaste, or punished if it was unchaste.

And therefore our Church teaches the faith of the Creed with sufficient precision: whereas the rest transmit the words “the resurrection of the flesh,” she has transmitted them with one pronoun added: “the resurrection of this flesh.” [Note: [Col. 0381C] Others have more: “With a sufficiently careful and prudent addition our Church teaches the faith, by which it has transmitted …” A little later, for *tradidit* (“has transmitted”), they prefer *tradit* (“transmits”); and at the end of the parallel clause, where the text has *ignorant* (“they are unaware”), Erasmus reads *contingit* (“it happens”), while the Sangerman manuscript, Rembold, and Morellus read *contegit* (“it covers”). Rufinus discusses this addition at length, because he was said to have inherited from Origen the error of teaching that the body would indeed rise, but not the flesh. Saint Jerome attacks Origen especially on this point in his *Epistle*, in our recension no. 84, to Pammachius and Oceanus: “We believe that the resurrection of bodies will occur. If this is said properly, it is a pure confession; but because there are heavenly and earthly bodies, and air and thin vapor are called bodies according to their nature, they put ‘body,’ not ‘flesh,’ so that when the Orthodox hear ‘body’ they may think ‘flesh,’ while the heretic recognizes ‘spirit.’ Our author has removed suspicion of such deceit from himself in *Invective* I, asserting that he has frequently mentioned not only the body concerning which Jerome calumniates him, but also the flesh. See what more we shall say on this matter in his *Apology to Pope Anastasius*.]

Undoubtedly “this” means the flesh possessed by the one who professes it, after the sign of the cross has been placed upon his forehead. Thus each believer may know that his own flesh, if he preserves it clean from sin, will be a vessel of honor, useful to the Lord and prepared for every good work; but if he has contaminated it with sins, it will be a vessel of wrath destined for destruction. [Note: [Col. 0381D] Others read: “if it has been contaminated with sins, it will be destined …” Shortly afterward they omit *de* in *de magnitudine promissionum* (“concerning the greatness of the promises”), and, with the same witnesses, we have restored *indicari* (“to be indicated”) below in place of *judicari* (“to be judged”), which appears to have been written through a typographical error. Moreover, the author’s mention of the greatness of the promises indicates that the article concerning eternal life, although not expressed, is implicitly included in the immediately preceding statement concerning the resurrection of the flesh. Saint Irenaeus likewise explains this in his Creed, book I, chapter 2, where he says that after the resurrection of the flesh Christ will render judgment to each person and “send the impious, unjust, lawless, and blasphemous among humanity into eternal fire; but to the righteous and those who have kept his commandments he will grant incorruption and bestow eternal glory.” The same is found in another of his Creeds, book III, chapter 4. Tertullian likewise has it in his Creed, as do Cyprian and others.]

Now, if anyone desires to know more fully about the glory of the resurrection itself and the greatness of the promise, he will find it indicated in almost all the divine books. From these, recalling a few passages here merely as a reminder, we shall bring to an end the little work entrusted to us.

The Apostle Paul asserts by such arguments that mortal flesh will rise, saying: “If there is no resurrection of the dead, then Christ has not risen” (1 Cor. 15). “But if Christ has not risen, our preaching is empty, and our faith also is empty” (ibid.). [Note: [Col. 0382C] Others read: “that the dead rise,” followed by “he proves by such arguments.” Saint Cyril also presses the Apostle’s testimonies that follow, *Catechesis* XVIII, nos. 17 and following.]

And shortly afterward: “But now Christ has risen from the dead, the firstfruits of those who sleep; for since death came through a man, resurrection of the dead also comes through a man. For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive, but each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, then those who belong to Christ at his coming; then the end.” [Note: [Col. 0382C] The same witnesses read *primitiae* (“firstfruits”) instead of *initium* (“beginning”); the Greek has ἀπαρχή (*aparchē*, “firstfruits”). Shortly afterward, for *vivificabuntur* (“will be made alive”), which Pamelius also read from a manuscript and which the Greek *ζωοποιηθήσονται* signifies, some printed books and Baluzius with his manuscripts read *vivificantur* (“are made alive”).]

And in what follows he adds this also: “Behold, I tell you a mystery: We shall all indeed rise, but we shall not all be changed”—or, as we find it in other copies, “We shall all indeed sleep, but we shall not all be changed”—“in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed.”

Writing likewise to the Thessalonians, he says: “But I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve like the rest who have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus. For this we say to you by the word of the Lord: we who are alive, who remain until the coming of the Lord, shall not precede those who have fallen asleep, because the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God; and the dead who are in Christ will rise first. Then we who are alive, who remain, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord” (1 Thess. 4). [Note: [Col. 0382D] Others read *quoniam* (“because”), and “with the command, with the voice of an archangel, with the trumpet of God,” and so forth.]

### 44.

But lest you think that these things are marked out as Paul’s preaching alone, as though it were something novel, hear also what the prophet Ezekiel foretold long ago through the Holy Spirit. “Behold,” he says, “I will open your graves and bring you out of your graves” (Ezek. 42). [Note: [Col. 0382D] Baluzius, with others, reads *praedicatione quasi novella* (“as though it were a novel preaching”); the Sangerman manuscript and several printed editions read *praedicatione novella* (“a novel preaching”). Shortly afterward they all omit *sanctum* (“Holy”) where the Spirit is mentioned.]

Job also, overflowing with mystical utterances, proclaims the resurrection of the dead with remarkable clarity. Hear him: “There is hope for a tree: for if it has been cut down, it will sprout again, and its shoot will never fail. If its root has grown old in the earth and its trunk has died in the dust, at the smell of water it will blossom again and produce a shoot like a young plant. But if a man dies, he is gone; and if a mortal falls, will he exist no longer?” (Job 14:7). [Note: [Col. 0382D] Others add *totus* (“entirely”); shortly afterward, instead of *deficit* (“fails”), they read *deficiet* (“will fail”), and *erit radix ejus* (“its root will be”)—others among the printed editions and the manuscripts commended by Baluzius have *est radix ejus* (“its root is”), followed by *ad odorem aquae* (“at the smell of water”), and so forth. The Barraean reading, which we retain, has *in pulvere* (“in the dust”); it agrees with the Hebrew, and Jerome himself uses that word in his Latin version from the Hebrew. It is therefore all the more surprising if Rufinus could have preferred the version of Jerome to the reading received by everyone; but I think that this word was later substituted by copyists.]

Does it not seem that in these words he reproves human beings with a kind of reproach and says: “Is the human race so foolish that, when people see the trunk of a cut-down tree sprouting again from the earth and dead wood recovering life, they do not think that human beings themselves can have something similar—not even something comparable to wood or trees?” [Note: [Col. 0383C] Others have *jam* (“already”); shortly afterward they have only *e contrario* (“on the contrary”) in this passage, without the intervening words. Hear Cyril, whose interpreter Rufinus claims to be, in the *Catechesis* cited above, no. 16: μόνον γὰρ οὐχὶ δυσωπῶν, καὶ ἐπιτιμῶν· (οὕτω γὰρ ἀναγνωστέον ἐρωτηματικῶς τὸ, Οὐκέτι ἐστιν;) ἆρα γὰρ, φησὶ, ξύλου πίπτοντος, καὶ ἐγειρομένου, ἄνθρωπος αὐτὸς δι’ ὃν τὰ ξύλα γέγονεν, οὐκ ἐγείρεται; καὶ ἵνα μὴ νομίσῃς με βιάζεσθαι, ἀνάγνωθι τὸ ἀκόλουθον· μετὰ γὰρ τὸ εἰπεῖν ἐρωτηματικῶς, Πεσὼν δὲ βροτὸς οὐκέτι ἐστίν; λέγει· Ἐὰν γὰρ ἀποθάνῃ ἄνθρωπος, ζήσεται· καὶ εὐθὺς λέγει, Ὑπομένω ἕως ἂν πάλιν γένωμαι, κ.τ.λ.

“Indeed, he does almost nothing but shame and rebuke them—for the words ‘Will he no longer exist?’ must be read as a question. For he says: ‘When a tree falls and rises again, will man himself, for whose sake the trees were made, not rise?’ And, lest you think that I am forcing the passage, read what follows. After asking, ‘But when a mortal falls, will he no longer exist?’ he says, ‘For if a man dies, he will live’; and immediately he adds, ‘I shall wait until I exist again,’ and elsewhere again, ‘He who will raise up my skin upon the earth, the skin that now endures these things.’ The prophet Ezekiel says most explicitly: ‘Behold, I will open your graves and bring you out of your graves,’ and so forth. Compare the following note.”]

But so that you may know that what he said—“But when a mortal falls, will he not rise again?”—must be read as a question, receive the proof from what follows. [Note: [Col. 0383D] Formerly *ipsis* stood here, less correctly; then others read *nec lignis simile aliquid* (“nor anything like wood”), omitting *quidem* (“indeed”). Next, instead of *quod dixit* (“what he said”), both Oxford editions read *quod ut dixit patientissimus Job* (“as most patient Job said”). We have just said and shown that Rufinus copied these matters from Cyril, especially the principal point here noted: that Job’s statement must be read as a question. Père Touttée observes on this passage that no trace of a question to support Cyril’s—and thus Rufinus’—sense occurs either in the Hebrew text or in the translation of the Seventy. On the contrary, the Hebrew and Vulgate read, “Where, pray, is he?” as though the author meant the complete and irreparable destruction of a human being once dead. Yet this passage should receive the same interpretation that Cyril gives to another passage of Job: “If a man descends into Hades, he will not ascend again, nor return to his own house”—namely, that a dead person is no longer among the number of people who can return to the ordinary course of life. The two passages, “For if a man dies, he will live,” and “I shall wait until I exist again,” when read according to the Seventy, appear to have no meaning other than the general resurrection; but in the Hebrew and the Vulgate they have another force, namely, that no person once dead returns to the common life of humankind.] For he immediately adds: “For if a man dies, he will live.” And shortly afterward he says: “I shall wait until I exist again.” Again he says: “He who will raise up my skin upon the earth, the skin that now endures these things.” [Note: [Col. 0384D] The Sangerman manuscript has *de terra* (“from the earth”).]

### 45.

These things have been said as proof of our confession, by which we profess in the Creed the resurrection of this flesh. As for the word “this” that has been added, see how consonant it is with all that we have recalled from the divine books. [Note: [Col. 0384D] Others have *de exemplis divinorum voluminum memorabamus* (“we were recalling from examples in the divine books”). The Sangerman manuscript and the old Oxford edition agree with us in having the one word *memoravimus* (“we have recalled”). Add also these words from Rufinus’ own *Apology to Anastasius*, which we present below in their proper place: “We also confess that the resurrection of our flesh will occur wholly and perfectly, of this very flesh of ours in which we now live. We do not say, as some slander us, that another flesh will rise in place of this one; rather, this very flesh will rise, with no member of it cut off and no bodily part severed, lacking nothing at all from its entire nature except corruption.”]

For what else is indicated in the words of Job that we explained above, when he says: “He will raise up my skin, which now endures these things”—that is, which now suffers these torments? Does he not plainly say that the resurrection of this flesh will occur—of this very flesh, I say, which now bears the anguish of tribulations and temptations?

And when the Apostle says: “For this corruptible body must put on incorruption, and this mortal body must put on immortality” (1 Cor. 15:53), is it not the voice, so to speak, of one touching his own body and feeling it with his finger? Therefore, what is now a corruptible body will, through the grace of the resurrection, be incorruptible; and what is now mortal will be clothed with the powers of immortality.

Thus, just as Christ, rising from the dead, no longer dies, and death will no longer rule over him (Rom. 6:9), so those who rise in Christ will no longer experience corruption or death—not because the nature of the flesh has been cast aside, but because its condition and quality have been changed. The body, therefore, that will rise from the dead will be incorruptible and immortal, not only in the case of the righteous but also in that of sinners. In the case of the righteous, so that they may remain forever with Christ; in the case of sinners, so that without perishing they may pay the penalties they deserve. [Note: [Col. 0384D] The same witnesses have *absque internecione sui* (“without their own destruction”).]

### 46.

That the righteous will remain forever with the Lord our Christ we have already taught above, where we showed that the Apostle says: “Then we who are alive, who remain, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord” (1 Thess. 4:16). [Note: [Col. 0384D] The same witnesses again omit *nostro* (“our”); shortly afterward they have, as usual, *relicti* (“those who remain”) instead of *reliqui* (“the remainder”).]

Nor should you be surprised if the flesh of the saints will be changed through the resurrection into such great glory that, lifted upon clouds and carried through the air, it will be snatched up to meet God. [Note: [Col. 0385C] So also the old Oxford edition; most others read: “Nor should you be surprised if the most holy bodies of the saints will be changed into such great glory,” etc. Still others, with the Regius manuscript, read more poorly, “There is no delay: the most holy …”; shortly afterward nearly all read “to meet the Lord … and, borne through the air, be caught up.”] For the Apostle himself, explaining what God grants to those who love him, says: “He will transform the body of our lowliness so that it may be made like the body of his glory” (Phil. 3:21). [Note: [Col. 0385D] Two manuscripts cited by Baluzius read *qui transformavit* (“who transformed”); with Rembold and Erasmus, Morellus has *conforme fieri corpori Filii* (“to be made like the body of the Son”). A little later we have supplied the name *Dei* (“of God”) from other copies, in which *esse* (“to be”) is also added before *dicantur* (“are said to be”). Compare Cyril, nos. 18 and following.]

There is therefore nothing absurd in saying that the bodies of the saints will be lifted by clouds into the air, since they are said to be remade according to the form of Christ’s body, which sits at the right hand of God.

The holy Apostle also adds this, whether concerning himself or concerning others of his station or merit, and says: “He raised us together with Christ and made us sit together in the heavenly places” (Eph. 2:6). [Note: [Col. 0385D] Others read *coexcitavit* (“raised up together”) and shortly afterward *fecit* (“made”) instead of *faciet* (“will make”). They omit the words *Sancti Dei* (“of the holy God”) and read *habeant in resurrectione* (“may have in the resurrection”) instead of *habeat resurrectio justorum* (“the resurrection of the righteous may have”); finally, they read *praedixerunt* (“they foretold”) followed by “that the righteous will shine,” without *scilicet* (“namely”).]

Since the holy servants of God have many such promises concerning the resurrection of the righteous, it will no longer be difficult to believe what the prophets had foretold: namely, that the righteous will shine like the sun and like the brightness of the firmament in the kingdom of God (Wis. 3:7). Who will find it difficult to believe that those will possess the radiance of the sun and be adorned with the splendor of the stars and of this firmament, for whom either the life and conduct of God’s angels are prepared in heaven, or who are said to be conformed to the glory of Christ’s body?

Regarding that glory promised by the Savior’s own mouth, the holy Apostle says: “What is sown is an animal body; what will rise is a spiritual body.” If it is true—as it certainly is—that divine favor will join every righteous and holy person to the company of angels, it is certain that it will also transform their bodies into the glory of a spiritual body. [Note: [Col. 0385D] We have supplied the words “of Christ’s body, to which glory” from almost all the other books; through the customary scribal omission caused by the recurrence of the same word, they had fallen out of the Barraean copy. Below also, from the same witnesses, we read *quosque* (“and whom”) for *quoque* (“each”).]

### 47.

Nor should this promise seem to you contrary to the natural constitution of the body. For if, according to what has been written, we believe that God took dust from the earth and fashioned man, and that this was the nature of our body: that by God’s will earth should be changed into flesh, why does it seem absurd or contradictory to believe that, by the same processes by which earth is said to have advanced into an animal body, the animal body may again advance into a spiritual body? [Note: [Col. 0386D] Others have *quid* (“what”) and shortly afterward *quibus lutum profecisse dicitur* (“by which clay is said to have advanced”), followed by *proficere* (“to advance”). In the Barraean copy, *proficisci* occurs in both places, less correctly. The words *rursum corpus animale* (“again an animal body”) are absent from the manuscripts of Rembold, Erasmus, and Morellus.]

You will find many things of this kind in the divine Scriptures concerning the resurrection of the righteous. The condition of incorruption and immortality will also be granted to sinners in the resurrection, as we said above, so that just as God supplies the righteous with what is needed for the perpetuity of glory, so he may supply sinners with what is needed for the prolongation of shame and punishment. [Note: [Col. 0386D] Barraeus, together with Morellus and Pamelius, insert here the name *Deus* (“God”), which Baluzius removed on the authority of the Sangerman manuscript and likewise of Rembold and Erasmus; we have removed it with him. Shortly afterward others read *definit* (“defines”) instead of *definivit* (“defined”).]

For thus the prophetic utterance defined the matter, as we mentioned shortly before, when it says: “And many will rise from the dust of the earth, some to everlasting life, and others to everlasting shame and disgrace” (Dan. 12:2).

### 48.

If, then, we have understood with what reverence God the almighty Father is named, by what mystery our Lord Jesus Christ is held to be his only Son, with what perfection his Holy Spirit is named, and how the Holy Trinity is one in substance but distinct in affection and persons; and also what the Virgin’s childbirth is, what the Word’s birth in the flesh is, what the mystery of the cross is, what benefit is derived from the divine descent into the underworld, what the glory of the resurrection is, and what the captivity of souls brought back from the underworld is; what his ascension into heaven is and what expectation should be maintained of the coming Judge; likewise, [Note: [Col. 0386D] Others read *quae* (“what”) and omit the pronoun *ejus* (“his”) that follows.] what recognition the holy Church should have in opposition to assemblies of vanity, what the number of the sacred books is, and what gatherings of heretics must be avoided; and that, in the remission of sins, natural reasoning in no way opposes divine freedom; and that the resurrection of our flesh is demonstrated not only by divine utterances but also by the example of our Lord and Savior himself and by the consequence of natural reasoning—

if, I say, we have understood these things in due sequence according to the rule of the tradition set out above, we beseech the Lord to grant to us and to all who hear them, with the faith we have received preserved and our course completed, that we may await the crown of righteousness laid up for us and be found among those who rise to eternal life; but that we may be delivered from eternal shame and disgrace, through Christ our Lord, through whom glory and dominion belong to God the almighty Father, with the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0387]

[Note: [Col. 0387A] Rosweydus says: “The Prologue is wholly elegant and not unworthy of Rufinus, although the style does not correspond as well in the course of the whole book. But the narratives, I think, are translated from Greek [Col. 0388B].” Rosweydus is mistaken: Rufinus is not a translator from Greek but the primary author of this book, which he wrote under the name of Saint Petronius of Bologna. See the extensive discussion of this matter in the *Life*, book II, all of chapter 12. Rosweydus continues: “Having found them written among the Greeks in a humble and familiar style, he gave them to Latin readers in the same manner. In his preface to Clement’s *Recognitions*—which Gennadius testifies, in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 17, that Rufinus bestowed upon the Latin language—Rufinus explains to Bishop Gaudentius why his translation is less ornate: ‘In the other works, as far as we could, we took care to depart not only as little as possible from the meanings, but even from the words and modes of expression. Although this makes the language of the account less ornate, it makes it more faithful.’ Therefore, just as the translation of Clement’s *Recognitions* is less ornate because it is confined to the narrow path of the original wording, unlike the histories of Eusebius, where the translator walks and ranges with freer steps, it should not seem surprising that Rufinus’ diction is less florid here as well, since he seems to have adopted here the same method of translation that he adopted in the books of the *Recognitions*. Indeed, one may infer from the translation of Palladius how little Rufinus departs from the Greek text, since matters there rendered by Hervetus from the Greek are presented here by Rufinus in almost the same tenor.”]

# HISTORY OF THE MONKS, OR THE BOOK ON THE LIVES OF THE FATHERS, BY RUFINUS, PRESBYTER OF AQUILEIA (C, S)

## Prologue

### 115–116

“Blessed is God, who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Tim. 2), who also directed our journey to Egypt and showed us great wonders that would be useful for the memory of posterity. [Note: [Col. 0387B] From these words the following sentence in Palladius’ work has been sketched, where he says in his Proem: “So that they may emulate and imitate those who wish to lead a heavenly life and enter upon the life that leads to the kingdom of heaven,” and so forth, “so that an example may be set forth and love stirred in them.” The sense of the following sentence also, beginning *Quamvis* (“Although”), is found in Palladius. ROSWEYDUS.]

From these things there arose not only for us a cause of salvation, but also from the history an example of salvation and a most suitable instruction in piety, which opens, for those who wish to travel the path of virtue, a broad road through the faithful record of the deeds of those who went before.

Although we are not well suited to narrate such great matters, and although it may seem unworthy that small and insignificant authors should become the narrators of mighty deeds and that lofty virtues should be recounted in humble speech, nevertheless, since the love of the brothers who dwell on the holy Mount of Olives frequently requests this of us, namely, that we explain the life of the Egyptian monks, their virtues of spirit, their cultivation of piety, and the strength of their abstinence, which we saw with our own eyes among them, I shall undertake the task.

Believing that I ought to assist the prayers of those who impose this duty, I shall begin, seeking praise less from style than hoping that the narration of these events will edify the readers, while each person, inflamed by the examples of these deeds, is invited to shudder at the allurements of the world, to pursue quiet, and to devote himself to exercises of piety.

[Note: [Col. 0388A] “Those who dwell on the holy Mount of Olives.” Rufinus’ Prologue differs somewhat here from Palladius’ Proem. Rufinus says that he is writing the *Lives of the Fathers* for the benefit of the brothers dwelling on the Mount of Olives, whereas Palladius says that he is writing at the request of Lausus, the prefect. Palladius also differs from Rufinus in several other matters: in his Proem Palladius says that he partly saw and partly heard the things he reports; Rufinus says only that he saw them. Palladius adds that he will also speak about women, whereas Rufinus says nothing about that matter. Rufinus had a cell and monastery on the Mount of Olives. He himself bears witness to this in *Invective* 2: “Otherwise, if he denies it, I can produce very many brothers as witnesses who, while living in my cells, copied very many of Cicero’s *Dialogues* for him on the Mount of Olives; I frequently held and reread their quires in my hands while they were writing, and I learned that he paid them much more generous wages than are customary for other writings. He cannot possibly deny that once, when he had come from Bethlehem to Jerusalem and had brought with him a codex containing a dialogue of Cicero and also the Greek Plato, he gave that very codex to me and that it remained with me for some time.” ROSWEYDUS.]

I saw—and truly I saw—a treasure of Christ hidden in human vessels. When I had found this treasure, I did not wish to conceal it like an envious person, but, as though it had been discovered for the benefit of many, I wished to bring it into the open and make it common property, certain that the more people were enriched by it, the more it would increase my own gain. For I shall become richer when the salvation of others has been sought through the commerce of my ministry.

At the beginning of our account, therefore, we pray that the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ may be present with us; by whose power all these exercises of piety are practiced among the Egyptian monks. For we saw among them many fathers living a heavenly life while placed on earth, and certain new prophets raised up, alike in virtues of spirit and in the office of prophecy; and, as testimony to their merits, they did not lack even the efficacy of signs and wonders—and rightly so.

For why should those who desire nothing earthly, nothing carnal, not receive power over heavenly things? We saw some of them so cleansed of every thought and suspicion of evil that, even if something evil were still being done in the world, they would not remember it. So great was the tranquility of mind within them, and so deeply had an inclination toward goodness taken root in them, that it was rightly said of them: “Great peace belongs to those who love your name, O Lord” (Ps. 118).

[Note: [Col. 0389A] “They dwell throughout the desert, scattered and separated in cells.” He significantly said “scattered and separated,” to indicate not a coenobium but cells or a laura. Thus also in Book III (whose author [ [Col. 0390A] “Not at all.” Rosweyd could himself have been dissuaded by the very imitation of the Jerome passage which he cites. Nor is Rufinus the translator or, certainly, the preface-writer of this book, as that very Preface quite clearly indicates. See our General Preface.], or at least its translator or preface-writer, is considered to be Rufinus), no. 219: “For in the same place about five thousand lived in separate cells.” This was taken from St. Jerome, Letter 22 to Eustochium, On the Preservation of Virginity. See “Cellia” and “Laura” in the Onomasticon. ROSWEYD.]

They dwell throughout the desert, scattered and separated in cells, but joined by charity. They are separated in their dwellings for this reason: that, pursuing God in the quiet of silence and with concentrated minds, they may be disturbed neither by any voice, nor by any encounter, nor by any idle conversation. Each of them, intent in his own place, awaits the coming of Christ like a good father’s children; or, like a soldier prepared in the emperor’s camp, awaits the emperor’s presence; or, like faithful servants, awaits their approaching lord, who will grant them both liberty and gifts. None of them, therefore, is anxious about food, clothing, or any of the other concerns of this kind. For they know that, as it is written, “the Gentiles think about all these things” (Matt. 6). But they seek the righteousness and kingdom of God, and all these things are added to them according to the Savior’s promise.

Indeed, if many of them should happen to lack something necessary for the body’s needs, they turn not to human means of escape but to God, asking him, as a father, for what they need—and immediately receive what they have requested. For such faith is in them that it is able even to command mountains to be moved. Hence some of them have checked by their prayers the flooding of rivers that had been stirred up to the ruin of neighboring regions (see below, chap. 9, concerning Patermutius; chap. 2, concerning Ammon; chap. 11, concerning Helenus). They have also crossed the depths of their channels on foot, killed their enormous beasts, and accomplished many and countless signs such as had formerly been performed by the Apostles and Prophets, so that there should be no doubt [Note: [Col. 0389A] “That the world still stands because of their merits.” Rufinus, referring to this, begins his Prologue to Book III from this point [Note: [Col. 0390A] Not at all, for Rufinus is not the author of this book. See our preceding note.].] that the world still stands because of their merits.

[Note: [Col. 0390A] “Rufinus begins his Prologue to Book III here with reference to this.”] But this is very remarkable: although [Note: [Col. 0390A] “The best things are rare and difficult.”] the best things are generally rare and difficult—an old saying: Χαλεπὰ τὰ καλά, “beautiful things are difficult”—in these men both qualities have nevertheless come together equally: they are immense in number and incomparable in virtue. Some live in suburban places, others throughout the countryside, but more numerous and outstanding men are scattered throughout the desert. Like a heavenly army drawn up for battle and living in tents, they are always intent on obeying the King’s commands; fighting with the weapons of prayer and protected from the enemy’s ambush by the shield of faith, they win for themselves the heavenly kingdom.

They are adorned with good character, quiet, gentle, tranquil, and bound together by the bond of charity as though by kinship. Yet they engage in great rivalry and contests in their pursuit of virtue. Each strives to be found more merciful, kinder, humbler, and more patient than the others. If someone is wiser than the rest, he is nevertheless so common and unassuming toward everyone that, in accordance with the Lord’s command, he seems to be the least of all and the servant of all.

Since, therefore, by God’s gift it has been granted me to see them and to share in their manner of life, I shall now attempt to recount, concerning each of them, whatever the Lord recalls to my memory. Thus those who have not seen them bodily may learn their works, gather their perfected life from the evidence of reading, and be invited to imitate their holy practice and seek the palm of perfect wisdom or endurance.

# HISTORY OF THE MONKS

[Col. 0391]

## CHAPTER ONE. CONCERNING THE HOLY JOHN

[Note: [Col. 0391C] The Roman Martyrology, March 27: “In Egypt, Saint John the Hermit, a man of great holiness, who, among his other distinctions in virtue, being also filled with the prophetic spirit, foretold to the Emperor Theodosius his victories over the tyrants Maximus and Eugenius.” Concerning him, as I suppose, the Menaea, September 20: Μνήμη τοῦ ἐν ὁμολογηταῖς μεγίστου Ἰωάννου τοῦ Αἰγυπτίου, “Commemoration of John the Egyptian, the greatest among the Confessors.” He is very well known among ecclesiastical writers. Augustine discusses him in The City of God, Book V, chapter 26; Cassian in Book IV, chapter 23, of the Institutes, and in Conference II, chapter 9, and Conference XXIV, chapter 26; Eucherius in On the Praise of the Desert; Sidonius in Poem 16; and various others. Brother Theodoric Loher, a Carthusian, in his Cologne edition of the Lives of the Fathers, assigns this John, as I suppose from the Martyrology, to April 28; but that entry concerns another John, an abbot who contended under Leo the Isaurian for the veneration of images. This John, however, lived in the time of Theodosius, as is clear from the beginning and end of this chapter. ROSWEYDUS.]

[Col. 0391A]

As the true foundation of our work, then, let us first take John as an example of all good men. He alone is truly sufficient, and more than sufficient, to raise religious and God-devoted minds to the summit of virtue and urge them toward the heights of perfection.

We saw him (Palladius, chap. 43.) in the regions of the Thebaid, in the desert adjoining the city of Lycus, dwelling on a certain cliff of a lofty mountain. The ascent to him was difficult, and the entrance to his monastery was obstructed and closed, so that from the fortieth year of his life until the ninetieth, which he was then living when we saw him, no one had entered his monastery. To those who came, however, he presented himself to be seen through a window, and from there gave them either a word of God for their edification or, if there was some consolation to offer, a response. No woman ever approached that place—not even to see him—and men came only rarely and at designated times.

He permitted a guest-cell to be built outside, where those arriving from distant regions might rest for a little while. He himself, within, was alone and devoted to God alone [variant: “calling upon God”], never ceasing by day or night from converse with God and prayer, pursuing with complete purity of mind that divine reality which is beyond every mind. For the more he withdrew from human cares and conversations, the nearer and more closely God was to him.

Finally, he had advanced so far in such great purity of mind that he obtained from the Lord knowledge not only of things that were present [Col. 0391C] but also the privilege of foreknowing things that were to come. The Lord plainly bestowed on him the grace of prophecy, so that he foretold the future not only to his fellow citizens and provincials when they happened to inquire, but also to the Emperor Theodosius: he often foretold what the outcomes of his wars would be, by what means he would gain victory over the tyrants, and how many incursions of barbarian peoples he would have to endure.

[Col. 0392A] Once (Palladius, chap. 43.), when the Ethiopian people were attacking the Roman soldiers near Syene [“Cyrene,” Palladius]—the first city of the Thebaid on the borders of Ethiopia—and had inflicted many massacres on our people and carried off booty, a Roman commander came to John, fearing to engage them because his own number of soldiers was small while the enemy’s multitude was beyond counting. John indicated a fixed day and said: “Go without fear. On the day I have named, you will overthrow the enemy, seize their spoils, and recover the booty.” When this had been fulfilled, he also foretold that the commander would be dear and acceptable to the Augustus.

Yet the grace of prophecy was regarded by him in such a way that he attributed the matter more to the merits of those who questioned him than to his own. For he said that these things were foretold by the Lord not on his own account but on behalf of those who heard them.

The Lord also displayed through him another very remarkable thing (Palladius, chap. 43.).

[Note: [Col. 0391D] “A certain tribune.” Augustine, in Book On the Care to Be Shown for the Dead, chapter 16, discusses the manner in which saints, whether living or after they have departed this life, sometimes appear to the living. After many ambiguously expressed observations, he introduces this little story about John: “That John the monk must be believed to have been such a man—the John whom the elder Theodosius, the Emperor, consulted about the outcome of the civil war—for he also possessed prophecy. For I do not doubt that one person may possess not only one of these gifts but several.” A certain deeply religious woman ardently desired to see John and, in order to obtain this, pressed her husband insistently. John refused, since he had never permitted women to see him. He said: “Go and tell your wife that she will see me next night—but in a dream.” And so it happened. He instructed her in whatever a faithful wife ought to be instructed. When she awoke, she told her husband that she had seen such a man of God as he knew John to be and reported what she had heard from him. A serious and noble man, highly worthy of belief, learned this from them and reported it to me. See our Thyraeus, On Various Kinds of Apparitions. ROSWEYDUS.]

A certain tribune, setting out to lead the troops, came to John and began to beg him to permit his wife to come to him. He said that she had endured many dangers solely so that she might see John’s face. The old man replied that it had never been his custom to see women, especially since he had enclosed himself in the monastery on that cliff.

The tribune persisted in his entreaties and began to insist that, unless she saw him, she would certainly die of profound grief. When he repeated his request again and again, declaring that John would be the cause of his wife’s death, and that she would receive death from the very place from which she had hoped for healing, the elder, observing both his faith and his persistence, said: “Go. Your wife will see me tonight—not here, however, but she will remain in her own house and in her own bed.”

After these words the man went away, turning the ambiguity of the answer over in his mind. When he had reported it to his wife, the woman too was troubled by the same uncertain statement. But when the hour of sleep arrived, the man of God appeared to her in a vision. Standing before her, he said:

“Your faith is great, woman, and for that reason I have come to satisfy your desire. Yet I warn you not to desire the bodily face of God’s servants, but to contemplate their deeds and actions through the spirit. ‘It is the spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing’ (John 6).

“I, however, am not—as you suppose—a righteous man or prophet. It was for the sake of your faith that I interceded for you with the Lord, and he has granted you healing from all the illnesses that afflict your body. From now on, therefore, you and your husband will be healthy, and your entire household will be blessed.

“Remember the benefit God has bestowed on you, fear the Lord always, and do not ask for anything beyond what is due to your pay. Let it be enough for you that you have seen me in a dream, and seek nothing further.”

When the woman awoke, she told her husband what she had seen and heard; she also described the man’s clothing, face, and every distinguishing feature. Her husband was amazed. He returned to the man of God, gave thanks to God, received his blessing, and departed in peace.

At another time (Palladius, chap. 43.), a military commander came to John. The commander had left his pregnant wife at home. On the very day that he came to the blessed John, his wife went into labor and was in danger. Then the holy man of God said to him:

“If you knew the gift of God, because a son has been born to you today, you would give thanks to the Lord. But know that the child’s mother has been in danger. The Lord will nevertheless be present, and you will find her safe. Hurry back, then, and you will find the child seven days old. You shall call his name John. Let him be raised in your house without any Gentile contamination for seven years. When these years have been completed, hand him over to the monks to be instructed in holy and heavenly disciplines.”

Moreover, when many came to him (Palladius, chap. 43.), whether provincials or foreigners, he disclosed the secrets of their hearts whenever circumstances required. If any sin had perhaps been committed secretly by them, he rebuked them privately, exposed it, and urged them toward correction and repentance. He also foretold whether the Nile would have an abundance or a scarcity of water. If some plague or punishment from God threatened because of human offense, he likewise gave warning and identified the cause for which the chastisement would be introduced.

He also bestowed cures and healing of the body on those who requested them, but did so in such a way as to avoid every form of boasting. For he did not allow the sick to be brought to him; instead, he blessed oil and gave it to them, and those who were anointed with it were healed of whatever illness afflicted them.

Once, the wife of a certain senator became blind (Palladius, chap. 43.). She begged her husband [Col. 0394A] to take her to the man of God. When her husband replied that John was not accustomed to see women, she asked him merely to tell John the cause of her weakness and to beg him to pray for her. Her husband carried this message to John. John prayed, blessed oil, and sent it to her. After she had touched her eyes with it for three days, she recovered her sight and gave thanks to God.

There are many other things he did, but it would take too long to recount them. Therefore, leaving aside for the moment what we have learned by hearsay, let us come to what we ourselves saw with our own eyes.

[Note: [Col. 0394D] Palladius inserts some material about himself in the Lausiac History that is missing here.]

There were seven of us traveling together (Palladius, chap. 43.) who came to him. When we had greeted him and he had received us with every expression of joy, he addressed each of us graciously. We asked him to give us a prayer and blessing together—for this is the custom in Egypt: whenever brothers arrive, they immediately join one another in fellowship through prayer.

He therefore asked whether any of us was a cleric. When we all denied it, he looked at each of us and realized that one among us belonged to this order [Note: [Col. 0393D] He seems to be speaking of himself, in whose name this was written: Saint Petronius of Bologna. Gennadius says of him: “Trained in the studies of the monks from adolescence, he is thought to have written the Lives of the Egyptian Monks.], but wished to remain hidden. He was a deacon; apart from one person who was loyal to him, even his traveling companions did not know this. Wishing, out of humility, to conceal the honor of his rank from such and so great men, he wanted to be regarded as lower in rank than those whom he judged himself to be inferior to in merit.

When Saint John saw him—and he was younger than the others—he pointed to him with his finger and said: “This man is a deacon.” When the man still attempted to deny it, John took him by the hand, kissed him, and said:

“Do not deny, my son, the grace of God, lest you incur evil for the sake of good, and a lie for the sake of humility. One must avoid lying in every way, whether it appears to be spoken for an evil purpose or even for a good one; for every lie is not from God, but, as the Savior says, is from the evil one (Matt. 5; John 8).”

After hearing this, the man submitted and bore John’s gentle correction with equanimity. When we had offered a prayer to the Lord, one of our brothers, after the conclusion, was suffering severely from tertian fever [Note: [Col. 0393D] The heretic Goldastus foolishly thought that *tertiano pyrepo* should be read here. The word and meaning are rarer, but Galen knew it, having written a book *On Fevers*, and says that it means “a pattern of intensification and remission in fevers.” There is a prayer in the Sacramentary of Saint Gregory against tertian or quotidian fever. Isidore, *Orig.* IV.7: “Typhus fevers are cold fevers, which are improperly called *typhi* from the plant that grows in water. But in this minor matter Galen is more trustworthy.” ROSWEYDUS.] and asked the man of God to cure him.

John said to him: “You wish to cast away something necessary for you. Just as bodies are cleansed of dirt with soda or other such remedies, so the soul is purified by illnesses and other chastisements of this kind.”

After he had explained many things to us about this through mystical teaching, he nevertheless blessed oil and gave it to the sick man. When the man was anointed with it, he immediately vomited up an abundance of bile and, restored to perfect health, returned on foot to the lodging.

Afterward John ordered the duties of kindness and hospitality toward us to be fulfilled and care to be taken for our bodies. Though careless of himself, he was solicitous for us. By continual practice and long habit, he could no longer take food except in the evening, and then only a little. He was emaciated and dry of body from abstinence. His hair and beard were sparse and thin, as though from extreme wasting, since no sufficient food nourished them and no richer moisture refreshed them.

Even then, although—as we said above—he was already living into his ninetieth year, he observed the rule that he would eat no food prepared by fire. After the duties of hospitality, he returned and ordered us to sit down. Only then did he ask where and why we had come, even though he had already received us joyfully and with every delight, as though we were his own children.

When we replied that we had come to him from Jerusalem for the sake of our usefulness and spiritual progress, so that we might now see with our own eyes what rumor had long ago reported to our ears—for things seen by the eye usually remain more firmly in the memory than things heard by the ear—the blessed John, with a most serene expression and almost smiling from the abundance of his joy, answered us in this way:

“I am greatly astonished, dearest sons, that you have undertaken the labor of so long a journey, since you can see nothing worthy of it in us. We are humble and insignificant human beings, possessing nothing in ourselves that ought either to be sought or admired.

“Even if there were something in us corresponding to your opinion, would it be such as you read about in the Prophets of God and the Apostles? They are recited in all the Churches of God for this very reason: so that people may seek examples of life not in distant and foreign places, but so that each person may have at home and within himself what he ought to imitate.

“Therefore I am greatly astonished at the purpose of your labor and zeal: that for the sake of your spiritual progress you wished to cross such vast regions and undertake such great hardships, when we are bound by such laziness and sloth that we do not even dare to leave our own cells.

“Nevertheless, since you think that there is something in us from which you ought to profit, this must first be pointed out to you: that your coming to us and undertaking so great a labor to see us should not appear to arise from any desire for boasting. Each of you should not wish so much to advance in spiritual virtue as to display and boast that he has seen men whom others seem to know only by hearsay.”

[Col. 0395D]

[Note: [Col. 0396D] From here to the immediately following passage marked as coming from Palladius, almost all the material is lacking in Palladius.]

“Boasting is a grave and exceedingly dangerous vice, one that can cast souls down even from the summit of perfection. For that reason I want you first of all to beware of it.

“This evil has two forms. Some fall into it immediately at the beginning of their conversion, when they have devoted a little effort to abstinence or piously distributed some money to the poor. Although they ought to regard this as though they had cast away something that was an impediment, they behave and think as though they were superior to those to whom they have given something.

“Another form of boasting arises when someone reaches the highest virtue but attributes it not wholly to God, rather to his own labors and efforts. While seeking glory from human beings, he loses the glory that comes from God. Therefore, my little children, let us flee boasting in every form, lest we fall into the downfall into which the devil fell.

“Above all, we must exercise great diligence over our heart and thoughts. We must see to it that no desire, no perverse will, and no vain longing that is not according to God takes root in our heart. From such roots, vain and useless thoughts continually sprout. They are so troublesome that they do not cease even when we are praying; nor, when we stand in God’s presence and offer prayers for our salvation, are they ashamed. Rather, they carry our mind away captive. Although we seem to stand bodily in prayer, in feeling and thought we wander and are carried off in different directions.

“If someone thinks that he has renounced the world and the works of the devil, it is not enough to renounce them with his lips—to have abandoned possessions, estates, and the other affairs of the age—unless he has also renounced his own vices and cast away useless and vain pleasures. These are the things of which the Apostle says: ‘Vain and harmful desires, which plunge a person into destruction’ (1 Tim. 6).

“This, then, is to renounce the devil and his works. For the devil slips into our heart through the occasion of some vice and through an opening made by a perverse will [Note: [Col. 0395D] “Because vices are partly from him.” This exhortation of John is absent from Palladius. Melchior Goldast, in his *Collectanea* on Valerian’s *On the Good of Discipline*, thought that it should be read: “because vices are from that father,” and believed that no one would doubt this reading, since what follows concerns the devil as prince and author. But the reading from Wisdom, chapter 4, from which he himself quotes, would have been a firmer support: “Those who belong to him imitate the devil.” Therefore the Vulgate reading should be retained, with all the manuscripts agreeing. ROSWEYDUS.], because vices are partly from him, just as virtues are from God.

“If, then, there are vices in our heart, when their prince, the devil, comes, they give him room as to their own author and introduce him as though into his own possession. Hence such hearts can never have peace or quiet; they are always disturbed and always held captive. Now they are depressed by empty joy, now by useless sadness. For they have within themselves a most evil inhabitant, to whom they have made a place of entry through their passions and vices.

“By contrast, the mind that has truly renounced the world—that is, that has cut away and amputated every vice from itself and left the devil no opening through which to enter; that restrains anger, suppresses rage, drives away lying, detests envy; that not only does not slander but does not even permit itself to think or suspect evil of its neighbor; that regards its brother’s joys as its own and counts his sorrow as its own sorrow—such a mind opens a place within itself for the Holy Spirit.

“When he has entered and enlightened it, joys, gladness, charity, patience, long-suffering, goodness (Gal. 5), and all the fruits of the Spirit continually arise there. This is what the Lord was saying in the Gospel: ‘A good tree cannot bear evil fruit, nor can a bad tree bear good fruit’ (Matt. 7 and 12). For the tree is known by its fruits.

“There are some who appear to have renounced the world but take no care to cleanse their heart, cut away vices and passions from their soul, or order their conduct. They strive only to see some holy Father and hear from him certain words, so that they may boast when telling others that they learned this or that from him. If, perhaps, by hearing or learning they acquire a little knowledge, they immediately want to become teachers—not teaching what they have done, but what they have heard and seen—and they despise others.

“They aspire to the priesthood and attempt to thrust themselves into the clergy, not knowing that there is less condemnation if a person himself excels in virtues but does not dare to teach others than if he himself is weighed down by passions and vices and teaches others about virtue.

“Therefore, my little children, we do not say that the clerical or priestly office must be avoided in every way, nor again that it must be sought in every way. Rather, we must work so that vices are driven from us and the virtues of the soul are acquired. The decision whom God wishes, and whether he wishes to take someone for himself into ministry or the priesthood, must be left to God’s judgment. For it is not the one who thrusts himself forward but the one whom the Lord takes up who is approved (2 Cor. 10).

“The monk’s principal task is to offer pure prayer to God, possessing nothing blameworthy in his conscience, just as the Lord also says in the Gospel: ‘When you stand at prayer, forgive your brothers, if you have anything against them, from your hearts; for unless you forgive your brothers, your Father who is in heaven will not forgive you either’ (Matt. 6; Mark 11).

“If, therefore, as we said above, we stand before God with a pure heart, free from all the vices and passions we have mentioned, we shall be able, insofar as this is possible, even to see God: when we pray, directing our heart’s eye toward him, and seeing the invisible with the mind, not with the body; by the understanding of knowledge, not by the sight of the flesh.

“Let no one think that he can contemplate the divine substance as it is by imagining in his heart some form or image resembling a bodily image. No form is to be conceived in God, no limitation [Note: [Col. 0397D] He carefully guards against the error of the Anthropomorphites—that is, those who attributed human form to God—which had spread through the monasteries of Egypt at that time. It is well known what disturbances the question whether God was corporeal or incorporeal caused in the Alexandrian Church, when Theophilus, who rightly held him to be incorporeal, was brought into mortal danger by Egyptian monks who banded together against him and attacked him violently. See our observations on his Synodical Letter and elsewhere in Volume I of the Hieronymian Works.], but rather a sense and mind that can indeed be perceived and touch the mind’s feeling, yet cannot be comprehended, circumscribed, or described.

“Therefore (Palladius, chap. 43.) one must approach the Lord with all reverence and fear, and so balance the mind’s gaze upon him that, whatever splendor, brightness, radiance, or majesty the human mind can conceive, it should always perceive him to be above all these things. This is what we have said, provided that the mind is pure and not occupied by the filth of any perverse will.

“For this reason those who appear to renounce the world and follow God must work especially at this, as it is written: ‘Be still, and know that I am the Lord’ (Ps. 45). If one knows God insofar as this is possible for a human being, then at last one will also acquire knowledge of the remaining things that exist and recognize the mysteries of God. The purer the mind within a person, the more God reveals to him and the more of his secrets he shows him.

“He then becomes God’s friend, like those of whom the Savior said: ‘I no longer call you servants, but friends’ (John 15). Whatever he asks of God as a dear friend, God grants him. The angelic powers themselves and all the divine mysteries love him as God’s friend and attend to his requests.

“This is the one whom neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities nor powers nor any other creature separates from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus (Rom. 8).

“Therefore, beloved, since you have chosen to please God and attain his love, take care to become strangers to every form of boasting, every vice of the soul, and all bodily pleasures. By bodily pleasures, do not understand only those enjoyed by worldly people. For the abstinent must regard as a pleasure anything he consumes with desire, even if it is something cheap and ordinarily used by those who practice abstinence.

“Even water or bread, if consumed with desire—that is, not to satisfy the body’s necessity but the soul’s craving—is counted for the abstinent as the vice of pleasure. For one must become accustomed in all things to keep the soul free from vice.

“Therefore, wishing to teach the soul to resist its desires and pleasures, the Lord said: ‘Enter through the narrow gate, because broad and spacious is the way that leads to death’ (Matt. 7); but narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life. The way of the soul is broad when it has satisfied any desire whatsoever; it is narrow when it resists its pleasures.

“Private habitation and solitary life are greatly beneficial for attaining these things. For sometimes, through the occasion of visiting brothers and the traffic of those coming and going, the restraints of abstinence and frugality are loosened; through such occasions one gradually comes into the habit and practice of pleasures, and thus even men who have already attained perfection are sometimes captured.

“Therefore David also said: ‘Behold, I have fled far away and remained in solitude. I awaited him who would save me from a faint spirit [Note: [Col. 0398D] So too the old Augustinian manuscripts, and now also the Roman Psalter, read *e pusillo animo* (“from a faint spirit”); others read *a pusillanimitate* (“from faintheartedness”).] and tempest’ (Ps. 54).”

After the holy John had spoken to us at length (Palladius, chap. 44.) about the vice of boasting and many other matters useful for us, he finally added:

“I shall also recount to you what recently happened to one of our brothers, so that the examples already given may make you more cautious.

“There was a monk among us living in this neighboring desert. His dwelling was a cave. He was a man of the greatest abstinence, obtaining his daily food by the labor of his hands, persisting in prayer day and night, and flourishing in every virtue of the soul.

“But, lifted up by his successful progress, he began to trust in his attainments and to attribute what he had achieved not wholly to God but to himself. When the tempter saw this presumption of mind, he immediately approached and prepared his snares.

“One evening, he took on the appearance of a beautiful woman wandering through the desert. As though exhausted after excessive labor, she approached the entrance of the monk’s cave, pretending to be weary and fatigued, threw herself inside, and, falling at the man’s knees, begged him to have pity on her.

“‘Night has overtaken me, unhappy woman that I am, hiding in the desert,’ she said. ‘Command me to rest in a corner of your cell, lest I become prey to the beasts of the night.’

“At first, under the pretext of compassion, he received her into the cave, asking what had caused her to wander through the desert. She invented the story with considerable skill, and meanwhile interwove throughout her account the poisons of flattery and the venom of seduction, now presenting herself as deserving pity, now as deserving protection. By the elegance and sweetness of her speech she bent the man’s mind and turned it toward affection for herself through seductive love.

“Then, amid increasingly flattering conversation, jokes and laughter were mixed in. Her forward hand was extended toward his chin and beard, as though in a gesture of reverence; then she began to caress his neck more gently and smooth his throat.

“What more need be said? At last she led the soldier of Christ captive. Immediately he began to be disturbed within himself and to burn with waves of lust, remembering neither his past labors nor his profession and purpose. He made a bargain with the desire of his heart and, in the secret chambers of his thoughts, formed a pact with false pleasure.

“The fool bent his sides and became like a horse and a mule, which have no understanding (Ps. 31). And when he was already attempting to enter into obscene embraces, she emitted a most dreadful howl in a terrible voice and, thin as a shadow, slipped from the hands of the man who was embracing her. She abandoned him with the foulest mockery as he himself, moving disgracefully, pursued empty air.

“Then a multitude of demons gathered in the air for this very spectacle. With a great shout and a loud burst of derisive laughter, they cried:

“‘You who were lifting yourself up to heaven—how have you been plunged down to hell? Learn, then, that whoever exalts himself will be humbled’ (Luke 14 and 18).

“Then, as though driven mad and unable to bear the shame of his deception, he deceived himself more grievously than he had been deceived by the demons. He ought to have restored himself, renewed the struggle, and by self-discipline, tears, and the fruits of humility erased the guilt of his former pride. But he did not do this. Despairing of himself, he ‘gave himself over to every kind of impurity and wickedness,’ as the Apostle says (Eph. 4).

“For he returned to secular life, having become the demons’ prey. He avoided the sight of all holy men, lest someone should recall him from his downfall by salutary admonitions. If he had wished to return to his former life of abstinence, he would undoubtedly have recovered both his place and his grace.”

Finally, hear what happened to another man (Palladius, chapter 45), who was similarly tempted, but did not meet a similar end in the temptation.

There was a certain man in this neighboring city who led an utterly disgraceful life, committing every kind of crime, so that he was regarded as notorious for his vices. At one point, touched by God’s mercy, he was moved to repentance. He shut himself inside a certain tomb [Col. 0400B] and washed away the pollution of his former crimes in fountains of tears, prostrate on his face day and night. He did not even dare to lift his eyes toward heaven, nor to utter his voice or pronounce the name of God; rather, he persisted only in groans and weeping. As though buried alive, he was already uttering from hell, so to speak, the moaning and groaning of his heart.

When he had remained in this state for a week, demons came to him at night in the tomb, shouting and saying: “What are you doing, you most impure and most depraved man? After you have been sated with every filth and impurity, do you now wish to come forward as chaste and religious? And after you have grown old in crimes, when you no longer have sufficient strength to erase your misdeeds [Note: [Col. 0399] Perhaps more correctly *to complete them*, or else, with the clause placed first, it should be read: ‘when you no longer have sufficient strength for crimes to be erased’; now a Christian.], do you wish to appear a Christian, a modest man, and a penitent? As though any other place could now be given to you, once you have been sated with evils, except that place which is owed to you with us. You are one of us; you can no longer become someone else.

“Return, then—return to us instead. Do not waste whatever time remains to you in enjoying pleasure. We are preparing abundant delights; we are preparing the noblest courtesans and everything of that kind capable of restoring to you the bloom of your most delightful youth. Why do you wear yourself out with vain and empty torments? Why do you hand yourself over to punishments before the time? For what else will you suffer in hell except what you are now procuring for yourself? If punishment delights you, wait a little and you will find it ready. For now, enjoy our gifts, which you always considered sweet and pleasing.”

While they reproached him with these and many similar words, he lay motionless. He did not even turn his hearing toward them, nor did he answer them in any way. When they repeatedly said the same things, and then others still harsher, and he remained entirely unmoved, the demons fell into a fury. When they saw that their words were being despised, they began to beat him, and after torturing him with many punishments, left him half-dead. Yet even amid so many and such great torments he could not be moved from the place where he had lain for the sake of prayer.

The next day some of his people, looking for him merely out of human kindness, found him afflicted with incredible sufferings. When they asked the reason and learned what had happened, they begged him to allow himself to be carried home so that he might be cared for. He refused and remained in the same place. Then, on the following night as well, the demons returned and tortured him with heavier blows. But even then he refused to move from the place, saying that it was better to undergo death than to obey the demons any longer.

Nevertheless, on the third night a multitude of demons gathered. They rushed upon him without any pity and exhausted him with every kind of punishment and torture. Although his body had by then failed amid the torments, his final breath still resisted the demons’ command. When the impious spirits perceived this, they cried out in a loud voice: “You have conquered, you have conquered!” Then, as though driven away by some heavenly power, they immediately fled headlong and never again attempted any of their arts or crimes against him.

He himself meanwhile advanced so far in spiritual virtues, became so adorned with moral excellence, and was so filled with the power of divine grace, that the whole region seemed to see him as one fallen from heaven and believed him to be one of the company of the angels. Almost all said together, with one voice: “This is the transformation of the right hand of the Most High” (Psalm 76).

How many, by his example, had already despaired of themselves, yet returned again to the hope of salvation and undertook the amendment of their lives, which they had previously despaired of? How many, moved by admiration for him, were drawn back from the very hell of sins and restored to the natural disposition toward virtue? Once he had been changed by so great a transformation, everything seemed possible to everyone. For not only did the amendment of his conduct and the assumption of virtues flourish in him, but abundant grace from God was also bestowed upon him. The signs and wonders performed by him testified how great was his merit before the Lord. [Col. 0401C]

Thus humility and conversion provided the material for every good; pride and despair are the cause of ruin and death.

To avoid the dangers of falling, to seek the grace of God, and to gain a clearer knowledge of divinity itself, a more secluded manner of life and habitation in the deeper desert are exceedingly beneficial. I think I can teach you this better not by words than by the facts themselves and by examples.

There was a certain monk who lived in this desert, which lies farther inland than the others. After he had persevered for many years in abstinence, and, advancing with age, had nearly reached old age, he was adorned with every flower of virtue and exalted by the greatness of complete self-restraint. He served God diligently with prayers and hymns [Col. 0401D]. As though preparing rewards for his veteran soldier, the Lord judged him worthy—while he was still in the body—to perform the duties of an incorporeal life like the angels, and deemed it fitting to provide him in the desert with heavenly food, since he awaited the heavenly King with ever-watchful vigils.

Wishing, therefore, to reward even in this world his faithful purpose (Palladius, chapter 46), God entrusted the daily provision of his food to the care of his providence. Whenever the necessity of nature demanded food, he would enter his cave and find bread placed upon the table, of extraordinary sweetness and extraordinary whiteness. Refreshed by it and giving thanks for the divine generosity, he would return again to hymns and prayers [Col. 0402A]. Many divine revelations and warnings from God concerning future events were also given to him.

While he was thus established in such great advances, he began to glory as though these were merits of his own and declared that the gift of heavenly favor was owed to his life. Immediately a small degree of spiritual negligence entered him—so small that he could not perceive it. After this, his negligence grew greater, so that he became slower to sing hymns and rose more sluggishly for prayer. He no longer sang the Psalms with the vigilance he had formerly shown; once he had performed a small part of his accustomed service, his soul, as though fatigued by excessive labor, hastened to rest. His judgment had become corrupt and had fallen from higher things to lower ones, while his thoughts dragged him through various precipices. [Col. 0402B]

For there was already in his heart a certain clandestine, shameful, and wicked thought, although it was still opposed by his former habit—just as the current of water may continue to carry a ship forward by its former momentum even when the oars have ceased. In the same way, his old discipline drew him toward his customary duties, and for this reason he still seemed to remain in his former state.

When he had asked for food as usual after prayer, toward evening he entered the place where he was accustomed to refresh himself and found bread placed upon the table as usual. Refreshed by it, he did nothing to amend what was taking place in his heart, nor did he perceive the damage caused by his change. He did not understand that one who despises small things will gradually fall.

Meanwhile, when he was already being goaded by a fierce fire of lust and was being swept away by shameful desire [Col. 0402C] back toward the world, he restrained himself that day and performed the customary services of hymns and prayers in the usual manner. When he entered to take food, he found bread placed upon the table, but it was somewhat dirtier than usual. He was astonished and became sad, for he understood that this kind of sign concerned him. Nevertheless, after eating, he was refreshed.

On the third day, the goads began to press him threefold more severely. The image of a woman had taken possession of his thoughts as though she were already present with him and reclining beside him. He seemed to embrace her and to have her beneath him for shameful purposes.

Nevertheless, on the following day he proceeded to his customary duties of singing Psalms and praying, but his eyes wandered and his mind was captive. When, as usual, he entered at evening and sought food, he found bread upon the table, but it was extremely filthy and dry, as though gnawed all around by mice or dogs. When he saw this, he groaned and shed tears, but they did not come from the heart, nor were they abundant enough to extinguish the flame of so great a fire. Nevertheless, he took the food, though neither as much as he wished nor of the quality to which he was accustomed.

Meanwhile his thoughts surrounded him on every side like a barbarian army, hurled weapons against him from all directions, and dragged him, bound and captive, back toward the world. Rising, he began to travel through the desert by night, making his way toward the city. But when day came, the city was still far away.

As he was being scorched by the most intense heat and exhausted in the desert, he began to look around in every direction and search with his eyes for some monastery nearby. When he saw the cell of certain brothers, he made his way there so that he might rest with them. As soon as the servants of God realized that he was there, they immediately ran out to meet him. Receiving him and bowing before him as though before an angel of God, they washed his feet, invited him to prayer, set out a table, and fulfilled all the duties of charity according to the divine command [Col. 0403A].

When he had been refreshed and had rested for a short while, they began, as was customary with a most learned and renowned father, to ask him for a word of edification and to seek salutary admonitions. They also asked him how one might escape the snares of the devil, or how, whenever demons cast shameful thoughts into the mind, those thoughts could be driven away and rejected.

Then, compelled to give the brothers admonitions, teach them the way of salvation, and speak about the ambushes of the demons—which they set for the servants of God—he instructed them fully and adequately. But in himself he kindled goads of remorse. Returning to himself, he said: “How do I admonish others while I myself am being deceived? Or how do I correct others when I do not correct myself? Come, then, wretched man: be the first to do yourself what you teach others to do.”

When he had used such reproaches against himself and understood that he had been miserably overthrown, he bade farewell to the brothers and immediately hurried back into the desert. He returned to the cave from which he had departed, prostrated himself before the Lord in prayer, and said: “If the Lord had not helped me, my soul would almost have dwelt in hell” [Col. 0403C] (Psalm 93). And again: “I was almost in every evil, and they almost consumed me on the earth” (Psalm 118).

In this was fulfilled what Scripture says: “A brother helping a brother will be exalted like a fortified and strong city.” [Note: [Col. 0403D] The same verse seems to be quoted twice according to two different interpretations. Certainly in the Hebrew and Greek archetypes it is given only once. The Vulgate likewise has only: “A brother who is helped by his brother is like a strong city, and judgments are like the bars of cities.” [Col. 0404D] Earlier, the reading here was *vestes* (“garments”).] “A brother who helps a brother is like a strong city, and judgments are like the bars of cities” (Proverbs 18).

After this, he remained throughout his entire life in mourning and tears, seeing that he had lost the benefit of the heavenly table divinely granted to him. He began once again to eat his bread in labor and by the sweat of his face. He shut himself inside the cave and, lying in sackcloth and ashes, continued for a long time in prayer, mourning and weeping, until an angel of the Lord stood beside him and said: “The Lord has accepted your repentance and has been reconciled to you; but beware lest, once more exalted, you be deceived. Brothers whom you yourself instructed will come to you, bringing blessings. Do not refuse to receive them, and, taking food with them, give thanks to your God.” [Col. 0403D]

I have spoken these things to you, my little sons [136], so that you might know both how great is the strength found in humility and how great is the ruin found in pride. For this reason our Savior taught us humility as the first beatitude, saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 3).

He also gave examples of this kind so that you might be more cautious and not be deceived by demons through the subtlety of thoughts. For this reason such a practice is observed among monks: if anyone comes to them, whether man or woman, old or young, unknown or known, first of all prayer is to be made and the name of the Lord invoked. For if there is any transformation of a demon, it will immediately flee once prayer has been made.

But if the demons suggest anything in your thoughts by which you ought to be praised and exalted, do not yield to them. Rather, humble yourselves even more in the sight of the Lord and regard as nothing whatever they suggest to you concerning the pursuit of praise.

Finally, demons have often deceived me also at night. They would neither allow me to pray nor to rest, suggesting throughout the entire night various fantasies [Col. 0404B] to my senses and thoughts.
