In the morning, as though with some kind of mockery, they would prostrate themselves before me, saying: “Forgive us, Abba, because we caused you trouble throughout the night.”

I answered them: “Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity” (Psalm 6), and do not tempt the servant of the Lord.

You too, therefore, my little sons, love quiet and silence, devote yourselves to knowledge, and exercise yourselves so that by frequent instruction you may present your minds pure to God, lest your prayers be hindered before God.

Although those who live among secular people and devote themselves to good works, occupying themselves with religious and holy actions—whether by practicing hospitality, serving in works of charity, performing acts of mercy and visitation, or completing other deeds of this kind—also perform a good work, and although their conscience is commendable when they persevere in such works, and although they preserve themselves chaste, they are indeed commendable, and very commendable. They please God through their good actions and are workers of God’s commandments who will not be put to shame (2 Timothy 2).

Nevertheless, all these are earthly actions, and they are concerned with corruptible things. But the one who labors in the discipline of the mind and cultivates within himself spiritual senses must be judged far superior to them. He prepares within himself a place where the Holy Spirit may dwell. In a certain sense forgetting earthly things, he is concerned with heavenly and eternal matters. He continually sets himself before the sight of God, casts all the cares of present things behind him, and is bound only by the heat of divine desire. Established in the praises of God, in hymns and Psalms, day and night he cannot be satisfied.

With these and many other similar words, blessed John (Palladius, chapter 46), speaking to us continuously for three days, refreshed and renewed our souls.

When we began to wish to depart from him, he gave us his blessing and said: “Go in peace, my little sons. But I want you to know that today [Note: [Col. 0404D] The victory of the religious emperor Theodosius. Concerning this John and his prophecy, Prosper, in his *Chronicle* under A.D. 395 [Col. 0405D]. [Rather, A.D. 397, according to the calculations he adopted, though properly A.D. 394 is indicated. See our work and Reland’s *Fasti*.] In the sixteenth year of Theodosius, with Arcadius consul for the third time and Honorius for the second, John the anchorite monk was renowned; endowed with the grace of prophecy, he foretold to Theodosius, when he consulted him about the outcome of the war he was waging against the usurper Eugenius, that he would be victorious. ROSWEYDUS.] the victory [Col. 0405A] of the religious Prince Theodosius over the tyrant Eugenius has been announced at Alexandria. It is necessary, therefore, that Theodosius himself also should soon end his life by a natural death.”

When we had departed from him, we learned that these things had indeed taken place, in accordance with what he had predicted. A few days later some brothers caught up with us and announced that the holy John had fallen asleep in peace.

His death, they said, had occurred in this way: for three days he allowed no one to enter to him. Then, kneeling in prayer, he surrendered his spirit and went to the Lord, to whom be glory throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

## CHAPTER II. OR

[Note: [Col. 0405D] Hor. There is no record of him in the ecclesiastical calendars except in the Menaea on 7 August: “The venerable Or is brought to completion in peace.” He is also mentioned in Palladius’s *Lausiac History*, chapter 9. But Saint Jerome says that he was an Origenist in his letter to Ctesiphon. It is not established, however, that he died in that heresy, especially since his commemoration appears in the Menaea. See Response 2 to the argument of Prolegomenon 15, where the authority of these books is discussed. Sozomen also mentions him, book VI, chapter 28; Nicephorus, book IX, chapter 34; and certain more recent writers inserted him into their own Martyrologies on 12 November, such as the Carthusian of Cologne in his additions to Usuard, and Maurolycus. See Molanus, chapter 13, *On Martyrologies*. ROSWEYDUS.]

We also saw in the Thebaid another venerable man named Or (Palladius, chapter 9; he is called Orus). He was the father of many monasteries and, by his very habit, seemed to possess angelic dignity [Note: [Col. 0406D] No one will easily understand this unless he has before his eyes the dress of the Greek monks. The Greeks had two kinds of habit: that of novices, called *mikrou schēmatōs* (μικροῦ σχήματος, “of the lesser habit”), and that of the most approved men, called *megalou* and *angelikou schēmatōs* (μεγάλου and ἀγγελικοῦ σχήματος, “of the greater” and “angelic habit”). See the Greek *Euchologium*, chapter 79. ROSWEYDUS.]. He was already ninety years old, with a long beard and brilliant white hair. His face and appearance were so cheerful that the vision itself seemed to indicate that he possessed something beyond what is found in human nature. Earlier he had been trained in the deepest desert through many labors of abstinence; finally, near the city, he founded a monastery.

In the places adjoining his dwelling he himself planted and cultivated groves of various kinds of trees, establishing plantations where, as many holy fathers assured us, not a single shrub had existed before his arrival. He planted this grove so that the brothers whom he wished to gather there would not need to wander farther for firewood, since he cared for everything necessary for the service of the body, but especially for their salvation and faith.

While he was still in the desert, he fed on herbs and certain roots, and these seemed sweet to him. Whenever he found water, he drank it, occupying the whole of day and night with prayers and hymns.

When he had reached mature age, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a vision in the desert and said: “You will become a great nation, and a numerous people will be entrusted to you. Through you many thousands of people will be among those who are to be saved. For as many as you convert to salvation while you are in this life, over so many will you receive authority in the future. And do not be afraid: none of the provisions required for the use of the body will ever be lacking to you whenever you ask God for them.”

When he had heard this, he moved to the nearer regions and began to live alone under a small hut that he had built for himself, eating only vegetables that he had prepared, sometimes even after prolonged fasts.

At first he was ignorant of letters. But when he had come from the desert to the inhabited regions mentioned above, a gift was divinely granted to him. When a book was brought to him by the brothers, he began to read it as though he had long been acquainted with letters.

He was also granted power against demons, so that many of those whom demons tormented were dragged to him even against their will, protesting with loud cries about his merits. He also performed very many other healings.

Meanwhile great crowds of monks gathered around him. When we too arrived among them, he became exceedingly joyful at seeing us. After greeting us and praying according to his customary practice, he washed the feet of his guests with his own hands and began to teach us from Scripture matters pertaining to the edification of life and faith. God had indeed bestowed upon him the gift of teaching.

After he had wisely explained many passages of Scripture to us, he returned again to prayer. It was his custom never to take bodily food before receiving the spiritual Communion of Christ. After receiving it and giving thanks, he began to encourage us also to refresh ourselves. Yet while sitting with us, he never ceased to offer some reminder concerning spiritual studies.

He told us the following story: “I know,” he said, “a certain man in the desert who for three continuous years took no earthly food. For an angel of God brought him heavenly food every third day, and this was his food and drink.

“I also know a man of this kind: demons came to him in the appearance of a heavenly army and in the dress of angels, driving fiery chariots with great pomp, as though escorting some great king. The one who seemed to be regarded by the others as king said to him: ‘You have fulfilled everything, man. What remains is that you worship me, and I shall transport you as I transported Elijah.’

“But when the monk heard this, he said in his heart: ‘What is this? Every day I worship the Savior, who is my King. If this were he, how could he demand from me what he knows I do without ceasing?’ Then he answered him: ‘I have my own King, whom I worship every day without interruption. You are not my king.’

“Immediately the enemy disappeared at these words.”

Yet he told us these things as though they concerned another person, recalling his own deeds under the guise of someone else. The fathers who were present, however, assured us that he himself was the one who had seen and heard these things.

This was therefore a magnificent father. Among his other good deeds, he also did this for brothers who came to him and wished to live with him: he would summon the brothers who were with him, and in a single day they would build a cell for the visiting brother. There was great enthusiasm among the brothers in this work, each hastening to bring bricks, offer mud, pour water, or carry wood. When it had been completed, he handed the cell over to the brother furnished with every utensil and necessity.

On one occasion, when a certain false brother came to him and had hidden his clothes so that he might appear naked, he exposed him before everyone and brought out into the midst the things he had concealed. Everyone was so terrified that thereafter no one dared to deceive him in his presence.

Such was the strength of his spirit and the greatness of divine grace that he had sought through the labor of abstinence and purity of faith. The multitudes of brothers who lived with him were filled with such grace that when they gathered in the church, they seemed, shining in angelic garments and minds, to keep vigil in hymns and praises of God in imitation of the heavenly Powers.

## CHAPTER III. AMMON

[Note: [Col. 0407C] Ammon. Palladius calls him Ammonas in chapter 48. As I think, he is commemorated in the Greek Menaea on 26 January: “The venerable Ammonas is brought to completion in peace.” Also concerning him, Sozomen, book VI, chapter 28; Nicephorus, book IX, chapter 34. ROSWEYDUS.]

We also saw in the Thebaid (Palladius, chapter 48) another man named Ammon, the father of approximately three thousand monks called Tabennesiots. They were men of great abstinence, who customarily clothed themselves in *colobia* [Note: [Col. 0407D] The Greek word *kolobion* (κολόβιον), adopted into Latin, as in Cassian, *Institutes*, book I, chapter 5. Servius, commenting on *Aeneid* IX, on “and the sleeves of the tunic,” says: “Your tunics have sleeves,” which Varro also criticizes, saying: “Tunics with sleeves and reaching to the ankles.” For the ancients used *colobia*, which Saint Jerome reports in nearly the same words in his *Hebrew Questions*. Code of Theodosius, book 14, title 10: “Let no senator claim for himself a military dress, but, laying aside the terror of the military cloak, let him wear the quiet garments of *colobia* and *paenulae*. See in Cassian the mystical significance. ROSWEYDUS.]—as though in linen sacks—with leather extending from the neck down the back and sides. They also covered their heads with cowls, especially when they came to eat, and with these they veiled their faces, lest one should notice another taking less food.

They maintained such complete silence while eating that one might think no human being was present in the place where they sat at table. Their entire common life was conducted amid a multitude as though in solitude, for each person’s abstinence was so concealed that it could not be detected by another. They sat at table more to touch the food than to consume it, so that they seemed neither to have abstained from the table nor to have satisfied their stomachs. For the virtue of self-restraint is greater when one abstains from things that are before one’s eyes and in one’s hands.

## CHAPTER IV. BENO

[Note: [Col. 0407D] Beno. Palladius calls him Be in chapter 44. I find no record of him in the ecclesiastical calendars. Sozomen, book VI, chapter 28, says a few things related to the foregoing [Col. 0408D]—it is established that Sozomen received this material from Rufinus. The Greek reads: “Benos was never seen by anyone either burning with anger, swearing, lying, speaking rashly, lightly, boldly, or uttering a contemptible word.” He begins his account of him and Theonas with: “Benos and Theonas governed assemblies of monastic orders, men filled with divine foreknowledge and prophecy.” Also concerning him, Nicephorus, book XI, chapter 34. ROSWEYDUS.]

We also saw another old man, Beno (Palladius, chapter 49), surpassing all men in gentleness. The brothers who were with him asserted that neither an oath nor a lie had ever proceeded from his mouth, that no one had ever seen him angry or uttering a superfluous and idle word, but that his life was marked by the utmost silence, his character tranquil, and the whole man like one of the angelic order. His humility was immense, and in everything he regarded himself as nothing.

Finally, when we repeatedly begged him to let us hear some word of edification from him, we could scarcely persuade him to say a few things to us about gentleness.

On one occasion, when a certain beast called a hippopotamus was devastating the region near him, he came to the place at the request of the farmers. When he saw the enormous beast, he said to it: “I command you in the name of Jesus Christ not to devastate this land any further.” Then, as though driven away by an angel, it fled and disappeared completely. They also said that at another time a crocodile had been driven away by him in a similar manner.

## CHAPTER V. THE CITY OF OXYRYNCHUS

[Note: [Col. 0408D] The city of Oxyrhynchus. Stephen of Byzantium, indicating both the origin of the name and the word’s etymology, says: “Oxyrhynchus, a city of Egypt, which honors the fish of the same name.” Thus most Egyptian cities received their names from the superstitious worship of animals. ROSWEYDUS.]

This chapter is absent from Palladius.

[Col. 0408C]

We also came to a certain city of the Thebaid named Oxyrhynchus. There we discovered such great religious devotion that no one could adequately recount it. We saw the city filled within by monks and surrounded on every side outside by them. The public buildings—if there were any—and the temples of ancient superstition were now dwellings of monks. Throughout the city there seemed to be far more monasteries than houses.

Because the city is very large and populous, it has twelve churches in which the public assembly of the people takes place, apart from the monasteries, each of which has its own house of prayer. Nor are the gates themselves, the towers of the city, or any corner of it at all free of monastic dwellings. Everywhere throughout the city, day and night, monks offer hymns and praises to God, making the whole city, as it were, one church of God.

No heretic or pagan is found there. All the citizens are Christians, all Catholics, so that it makes no difference whether the bishop offers prayer in the street or in the church. The magistrates, leading citizens, and the other inhabitants carefully appoint men at each gate to watch whether a stranger or poor person appears anywhere, so that whoever notices one first may eagerly bring him in and ensure that he receives what is necessary.

But how can I recount what the people themselves did for us when they saw us passing through their city, meeting us as though they were welcoming angels and paying us honor? Or what can I say about the monks and virgins, whose innumerable multitudes, as we said above, are found in that city?

When we asked the holy bishop of the place, we learned that twenty thousand virgins and ten thousand monks lived there. To describe to you the affection and honor they all showed us, neither speech is sufficient nor modesty permits it—especially when they tore our little cloaks, each one pulling us toward himself and wishing to lead us away with him.

We also saw there many holy fathers possessing various gifts of God: some ministering in the word of God, others in abstinence, and others in signs and virtues.

## CHAPTER VI. THEON

[Note: [Col. 0409D] Theon. Concerning him, Sozomen, book VI, chapter 28; Cassiodorus, book VIII, chapter 1; Nicephorus, book XI, chapter 34.]

We also saw another man (Palladius, chapter 50), not far from the city, on the side leading toward the desert. His name was Theon. He was a holy man, shut up alone within his cell. It was said that he had maintained thirty years of silence and that he performed so many miracles that he was regarded among them as a prophet.

Every day a great multitude of sick people came to him. Extending his hand through a window, placing it upon each person’s head, and blessing them, he sent them away healed of every illness. Even by his appearance he was exceedingly venerable, and he bore such reverence in his face that he seemed an angel among men. He appeared so cheerful in his eyes and so full of every kind of grace.

As we learned, not long before this, robbers came to him at night, believing they would find gold in his possession. By prayer alone he bound them so completely that, fixed to his doors, they could not move at all. In the morning, when crowds had gathered before him as usual and saw the robbers at his doors, they wanted to hand them over to the fire. But he, compelled by the necessity of the situation, spoke only one word to them: “Allow them to depart unharmed,” he said, “otherwise the gift of healing will depart from me.”

When the people heard this, they did not dare to object and released the robbers. The robbers, seeing what had happened to them, abandoned their desire for crime, felt repentance for their many past offenses, fled to nearby monasteries, and there adopted the form and discipline of a more reformed life.

The man mentioned above was learned not only in the languages of the Egyptians and Greeks but also in Latin, as we learned both from him himself and from those who were with him. Wishing to reveal this and to console us in the labor of our journey, he wrote to us on a tablet [Col. 0410B] and displayed the grace and learning of his speech.

His food was prepared without the use of fire. They also said that when he went out into the desert at night, he was accompanied by a great multitude of the desert animals. He himself drew water from his well and offered them cups, repaying their labor of service. Clear evidence of this was given by the many tracks of buffaloes, goats, and wild asses found around his cell.

## CHAPTER VII. APOLLONIUS

[Note: [Col. 0409D] Apollonius. Timothy, bishop of Alexandria, wrote his life carefully, as Sozomen testifies, book VI, chapter 29; Nicephorus, book VI, chapter 34. Perhaps it is the same person as this one. See Prolegomenon 4, section 1. In Sozomen the Greek name is Ἀπολλώς (*Apollōs*), which some would render in Latin as *Apollos*. For another man called Apollonius follows in the same passage. ROSWEYDUS.]

We also saw another holy man named Apollonius in the Thebaid, in the territory of Hermopolis (Palladius, chapter 52, calls him Apollo). To this city, they say, the Savior came from the regions of Judea with Mary and Joseph, in accordance with the prophecy of Isaiah, who says: “Behold, the Lord sits upon a light cloud and will come into Egypt, and the works made by the hands of the Egyptians will be shaken before him, and they will fall to the ground” (Isaiah 19).

We therefore saw there also the very temple into which the Savior entered, and where, as they related, all the idols fell to the ground and were shattered.

We therefore saw the aforesaid man, who had monasteries in the neighboring desert beneath a certain mountain. He was the father of about five hundred monks and was regarded as most famous throughout all the regions of the Thebaid. For he performed great works, and through him God worked many virtues, signs, and wonders. From childhood he had been trained in abstinence; and when he reached mature age, the grace of God continually increased in him. He was about eighty years old when we saw him flourishing in the assembly of the monasteries. His disciples also, or at least those who appeared to be his disciples, were so perfect and distinguished that nearly all of them could perform signs.

They said that he had withdrawn to the desert at the age of fifteen and, after spending forty years there in spiritual exercises, had heard the voice of God come to him and say:

“Apollonius, through you I shall destroy the wisdom of the wise in Egypt, and reject the understanding of the prudent. You shall also destroy for me those among them who are the wise men of Babylon, and you shall overthrow the entire worship of demons. Go now to inhabited places, for you shall produce for me a substantial people, perfect imitators of good works.”

But he answered: “Take away from me, Lord, the desire for boasting, lest, if I become elated above my brothers, I fall away from all your good gifts.”

The divine voice answered him again: “Put your hand to the back of your neck, seize whatever you grasp, bind it, and bury it beneath the sand.”

Without delay he put his hand to the back of his neck and seized what looked like a little Ethiopian. He immediately buried him beneath the sand, while the creature cried out and said: “I am the demon of pride.”

After this God’s voice came to him, saying: “Go now, for whatever you ask from God, you shall obtain.”

After these events he went to the places where people lived. This happened during the reign of the tyrant Julian.

There was a cave in those regions, near the desert, in which he began to dwell, devoting himself without interruption, day and night, to prayer. They said that he bent his knees in prayer one hundred times during the day and an equal number of times during the night, sealing these prayers before God. He used food that was more heavenly than human. His garment was a *colobium* of tow (coarse flax), which among them is called *lebetes*.

[Note: [Col. 0411D] *Lebetes.* The author explains this term here and says that *cotobium* is the garment of which we spoke in chapter 3. Jerome, Preface to the Rule of Saint Pachomius: “They have nothing in their cells except a mat and two *lebitonaria*”—a kind of garment among the Egyptian monks, without sleeves, one of which was already worn out for sleeping or working. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XIX, chapter 22: “A *lebitonarium* is a sleeveless *colobium*, such as the Egyptian monks use.” It is also called in Greek λεβητών or λεβετών. So Palladius in the *Life of Abbot Pachomius*: λεβητωνάριον. So too Sozomen, book III, chapter 13, explains χειτῶνας ἀχειροδότους, “tunics without sleeves.” Below, in chapter 9, *Lebeta*. ROSWEYDUS.]

He also wore a linen cloth that wrapped around his neck and head. Yet these garments, they said, remained with him in the desert and never became worn out.

He lived in a place near the desert, dwelling in the power of the Spirit and producing marvelous signs and healings—so many that, because of their immensity, no voice could recount them, as we learned from the elders who were with him.

A splendid reputation about him spread everywhere. When he began to be regarded by everyone as some kind of prophet or apostle, monks from neighboring regions came to him from various places. Like pious sons approaching a father, each one offered him the great gift of his own soul. He received each of them with complete religious devotion, urging some toward good works and others toward right understanding. Yet he first displayed by his own example what he wished to teach by his words.

On other days he allowed each one to practice as much abstinence by himself as he was able. On the Lord’s Day, however, out of the grace of charity, he encouraged them all to eat with him, although he himself continued to observe his customary abstinence, using only herbs or vegetables and admitting neither the use nor the service of fire.

When he heard that, during the times of Julian, as we said above, a certain brother had been seized while serving in the army and was being held in prison, he went to him with some brothers to console him and to urge him to maintain steadfastness in his necessity and to despise and laugh at the dangers threatening him.

“For,” he said, “the time of combat has arrived, in which the minds of the faithful must be tested by trials and made known.”

While he strengthened the young man’s courage with these and other words, a centurion arrived and was indignant that he had dared to enter. He locked the prison from the outside and shut him in together with all who had come, intending, of course, that they too should be detained for military service. After appointing a great many guards, he departed.

In the middle of the night an angel appeared standing there, shining with immense light. The guards were stunned and terrified, and the prison’s bolts opened. Then the guards themselves fell at the feet of the holy men and begged them to leave, saying that it was better for them to die on their behalf than to resist the divine power that was caring for them.

In the morning the centurion himself came hurriedly to the prison with the leading men, asking that all those who appeared to be detained should leave. He said that his house had collapsed in a great earthquake and that it had killed the chosen among his servants.

When the saints heard this, they sang a hymn and praises to God. Then they returned to the desert and lived together, having, according to the example of the apostles, “one soul and one heart” (Acts 4).

The elder father taught them to advance daily in virtue and immediately to blunt the devil’s snares, which he brought against human beings through thoughts.

“For thus,” he said, “let the head of the serpent be broken”—[Alternative reading: “let it be weakened”]—“and its entire body will be rendered lifeless.” [147]

For this reason God commands us to watch the serpent’s head: so that from the very beginning we may not at all receive evil and filthy thoughts in our hearts. How much less, then, should we permit fantasies of thoughts to spread through our senses, when he forbids us even to receive them at the outset?

He also urged them that each should surpass the others in virtue and that no one should allow himself to become inferior to his neighbor.

“By this,” he said, “you will know that you are advancing in virtue: if you have no passion for worldly desires. This is the beginning of God’s gifts. But if one of you should reach the point of performing signs and wonders, let him not become elated on that account or exalt himself in his thoughts as though he were superior to the others. Nor should he display to people even this—that he has received this gift of grace. Otherwise he will mislead himself, be deceived himself, and lose the grace.”

Thus he possessed this magnificent teaching of the word of God, of which we ourselves also enjoyed something; but he possessed still greater grace in his works. Whatever he asked of God, he obtained without delay, and many revelations were shown to him.

Finally, he saw in a dream his elder brother, who had also died in the desert and with whom he had lived a perfect life for a very long time, seated in the apostolic seat and made one of the apostles, and leaving him an inheritance of virtues and grace.

When he also prayed for himself that the Lord might take him more quickly and grant him rest with him in heaven, he received this answer from the Lord and Savior: he must remain in this life a little longer, until many people became imitators of his life and conduct. For many peoples of monks and a kind of army of the devout were to be entrusted to him, so that through these he might find with God a reward worthy of such merits.

When he saw these things, they happened just as he had seen them. Monks came together from every place, attracted by his reputation and teaching. Especially through his example, very many renounced the world and formed a magnificent community with him in the aforementioned place on the mountain, preserving a common life and sharing one table in unanimity. We saw this as a truly heavenly and angelic army, adorned with every virtue.

None of them wore filthy garments. Rather, they shone equally in the brightness of their clothing and of their souls, so that even, according to Scripture, “the thirsty desert rejoiced,” and many children of the desert seemed to be present (Isa. 35). Although these words were spoken about the Church, they were also fulfilled historically in the deserts of Egypt. For just as such great crowds come through the cities to salvation, so the deserts of Egypt produced immense multitudes. As many people are found in the cities, almost so many multitudes of monks are found in the deserts.

Therefore it seems to me that the apostle’s saying was also fulfilled in them: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded still more” (Rom. 5). For at one time the unclean worship of idols abounded in Egypt as in no other nation.

[Note: [Col. 0413D] Porphyry rightly and truly observed in *On Abstinence*, book IV, chapter 9, that the Egyptians “worshiped the power of God over all things through the animals of their nomes, which each of the gods represented”: through the animals of their nomes they venerated the power of God over all things, which each of the gods signified. ROSWEYDUS.]

They worshiped dogs and monkeys and other monstrous creatures. They also believed garlic, onions, and certain vegetables to be gods, as we learned from the father Apollonius himself when he explained to us the reason for their ancient superstition in this way:

“At one time the Egyptians believed the ox to be a god because, by its labor, they cultivated the fields and obtained food and nourishment. They also worshiped the water of the Nile because it irrigated all the regions of Egypt. They worshiped the earth as well, because it was more fertile than other lands. As we said above, they worshiped dogs and monkeys, and various kinds of herbs and vegetables, because they believed that the opportunity for their salvation had come to them through these things in the time of Pharaoh.

“For each of these things seemed to have been the object of their activity when Pharaoh, while persecuting our fathers, was drowned. Each person considered as his god the thing by which he seemed to have been occupied, so that he would not follow Pharaoh, saying: ‘This is what God did for me today, so that I would not follow Pharaoh and be drowned together with him.’”

[Col. 0414A]

These, then, were the words of Saint Apollonius. But we ought much more to record the things he accomplished in works and virtues.

At one time about ten villages of Gentiles were situated around him. There demonic superstition was worshiped with the greatest zeal. There was an immense temple, and in it an image which the priests were accustomed to carry about in the manner of Bacchants, while the rest of the crowd went around with them and proceeded through profane rites as though seeking rainwater.

It happened that, at the time when they were celebrating such orgies, the blessed Apollonius was traveling through those regions with several brothers. When he saw the crowds of the wretched people, as though driven by some demon and reveling through the fields, he pitied their error. Kneeling, he invoked the Lord and our Savior, and caused all those who were being driven by demonic rites, together with their image, to stand motionless, unable to proceed anywhere at all.

Thus they remained throughout the entire day, scorched by the fiercest heat, not knowing why they had become fixed immovably in one place. Then their priests said that there was a Christian living in the regions near the desert, named Apollonius, and that this was his doing; unless he were appeased, danger would remain for them.

When people who had heard of this great miracle gathered from everywhere and asked what had caused such a prodigy, they confessed that they knew nothing at all. Nevertheless, they said that they suspected the aforesaid man and begged that he be asked to intercede for them.

Then one of them said that they truly believed this to be the case. They confirmed that they had seen him passing by on that journey, and they did not delay in employing whatever aids they thought might be useful. They brought oxen, believing that the image might be moved by their strength. But when they had made no progress even in this way and had been frustrated in every attempt, they sent envoys to the man of God, promising that if he released them from these bonds, he would also dissolve the bonds of their error.

When this was reported to him, he immediately went down to them. Having poured out a prayer to God alone, he released them all. At once they all fled to him with one accord, believing in our saving God and giving thanks. They immediately consigned the wooden image to the fire. Then, following the man of God and instructed by him in faith in the Lord, they were joined to the Church of God.

Many of them remained with him and even now live in the monasteries. The fame of this miraculous deed spread everywhere, and many people were converted to faith in the Lord because of it, so that scarcely any Gentiles remained in all those regions.

After some time a dispute arose over boundaries between two villages. When this was reported to the man of God, he hurried down to them for the sake of peace. But they were inflamed by the fury of their quarrel and could not be turned by any means toward counsel of peace. This was especially because the people of one side placed great confidence in the strength of a certain robber, who appeared to be the standard-bearer of the conflict.

When Apollonius saw that this man was resisting peace, he said to him: “If you are willing, my friend, to heed me and make peace, I shall ask my God, and he will forgive your sins.”

When the man heard this, he did not delay at all but fell at Apollonius’s knees and begged him. Then Apollonius turned to the crowds that had followed him and sent them all away in peace.

After they had withdrawn, the robber remained with the man of God, seeking the fulfillment of the promise. Apollonius then took him with him and traveled with him to the monasteries. He taught him that he must change his way of life, patiently seek mercy from God, and await the promise in faith, for, he said, “all things are possible for the one who believes” (Mark 9).

When they had rested together in the monastery during the night, both saw in a vision that they were in heaven and standing before Christ’s tribunal. They also saw God’s angels and all the saints worshiping the Lord. After seeing these things, they too worshiped God. Then God’s voice came to them, saying:

“Although there is no fellowship between light and darkness, nor any share between the faithful and the unfaithful (2 Cor. 6), nevertheless the salvation of this man, for whom you have pleaded, Apollonius, is granted to you.”

When they had heard many other things while placed in the heavenly vision—things which neither speech can recount nor the ear hear—they awoke from sleep and told the brothers what they had seen. Great astonishment arose when each of them recounted the very same dream.

The robber remained with the brothers, now a holy man, changing his life and conduct to complete innocence and devotion. He became like a lamb transformed from a wolf, so that the prophecy of Isaiah seemed to be completely fulfilled in him:

“Wolves shall feed with lambs, and the lion and the ox shall feed together on straw” (Isa. 11). [151]

We also saw there certain men of the Ethiopian race living with the monks. Many of them surpassed the other monks in religious observance and strength of character, so that the Scripture also seemed to be fulfilled in them which says: “Ethiopia shall stretch out her hands to God” (Ps. 67).

It was also reported among the deeds of Saint Apollonius that, at a certain time, a dispute arose between two villages, one of which was Christian and the other Gentile. Great armed crowds came forward from both sides.

It happened that Saint Apollonius arrived. While he urged them to peace, one of the Gentiles, who was regarded as their leader and the cause of that war—a savage and ferocious man—strongly resisted him, saying that he would not allow peace to be made as long as he lived.

Then Apollonius said: “Let it happen as you wish. No one else but you shall be killed. Yet a tomb suited to your honor shall be made for you—not the earth, but the bellies of beasts and vultures.”

Immediately his word became true: no one from either side fell except that man alone. After they had buried him beneath the sand, they returned in the morning and found that beasts had dug him up and torn him apart, and that vultures had devoured him.

When everyone marveled that the word of the man of God had been fulfilled in this way, they all turned to faith in the Savior and Lord, and they proclaimed Apollonius a prophet of God.

Nor should we pass over what we learned had been done by him in his earliest days, when he had begun to live in the cave with a few brothers.

The holy day of Easter had arrived. After the solemnity of the vigils and the Sacraments had been completed inside the cave, and a meal had been prepared from what they had among them—for they had only a few dry loaves and vegetables, of the kind they usually stored sprinkled with salt—Apollonius began to address the brothers who were with him:

“If there is faith in us, and if we are truly faithful servants of Christ, let each one of us ask God for whatever he would gladly like to eat as a festival meal.”

But the brothers themselves allowed the one who surpassed them in age and merit to ask these things from God, thereby declaring themselves inferior to this grace.

Then Apollonius poured out a prayer to God with complete eagerness. When it was finished and everyone had answered, “Amen,” suddenly they saw before the entrance of the cave certain men whom they did not know at all. These men had brought such abundant supplies of every kind of food that no one could easily have seen so much or so great a variety.

Among the provisions were certain kinds of fruit never seen at all in the regions of Egypt, grapes of incredible size, nuts, figs, pomegranates—and all of them out of season—as well as honeycombs, an abundance of honey and milk, immense *Nicolai*, and hot, perfectly clean loaves, which nevertheless appeared to have come from a foreign province.

[Note: [Col. 0415D] “Immense *Nicolai*.” This is absent from the printed books. I do not investigate why it was omitted. I know that the word is rare and not found everywhere. Athenaeus, book XIV, and Plutarch, *Table Talk*, book VII, chapter 4, write that a certain Nicolaus of Damascus sent Augustus dates, which Augustus called *Nicolaoi* after him. Likewise Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XVII, chapter 7: “The *palmulae* are Thebaic dates, also called *Nicolai*.” Photius, *Bibliotheca*, codex 189, has cakes instead of dates. So too Suidas under “Nicolaus,” and Hesychius of Alexandria. Palladius’s translator joins the word with “loaves.” I fear that he used a corrupt manuscript. For here you have, expressed in Greek word for word, what our text has: “immense *Nicolai*, and hot and very clean loaves.” [Col. 0416D] Rather, Palladius reworked this Greek material from Rufinus. Consult the *Life*, book II, chapter 12, no. 6.] Hervetus, Palladius’s translator, has: “*Nicolai*, very large loaves, and pure lupins,” because θερμός means “hot,” whereas θέρμος means “lupin.” Hervetus was thereby misled. ROSWEYDUS.] 

The men who had brought these things immediately departed, as though in haste and wishing to return to the one who had sent them. The monks then gave thanks to the Lord and began to eat from what had been brought to them. The supply was so abundant that what was distributed each day lasted until Pentecost. They were certain that these provisions had been sent to them by God for the sake of the festival.

We also learned this: one of the brothers, who lacked the grace of humility and gentleness, asked Apollonius to request from the Lord that this gift also be granted to him. While Apollonius prayed, such a great grace of gentleness and humility came upon the man that all the brothers marveled at his tranquility of mind and modesty, qualities in which they had previously seen nothing.

At one time famine arose in the Thebaid. The inhabitants of that land knew that the monks who served the Lord with Apollonius were often fed by the Lord’s grace even without food. Therefore they all went together to him, with their wives and children, asking for food and blessing.

Without hesitation he began to bring out what had been stored for the use of the brothers and to give it generously to each person. When only three baskets of bread remained, while the famine was pressing heavily upon the people, he ordered the baskets—the only provisions left, which were supposed to provide the monks with one day’s food—to be brought into the midst.

With the entire crowd that had gathered because of the famine listening, he raised his hands to God and said:

“Is the hand of the Lord not able to multiply these things? Thus says the Holy Spirit: ‘Bread shall not fail in these baskets until we are all satisfied with the new harvest.’”

As very many of those who were present at the time confirmed, for four continuous months bread continued to be distributed from the baskets, and it never became exhausted.

They likewise reported that at another time he had done the same with grain and oil. Moved by these virtues, the devil is said to have spoken to him:

“Are you Elijah, or some other prophet or apostle, that you have dared to do these things?”

He answered him:

“What of it? Were not the prophets and apostles human beings, who handed down to us both their faith and their grace? Or was God present then but is he absent now? Far from it. God is almighty, and whatever he can do, he can always do. If God is good, why are you, devil, so evil?”

As we have already said above, we learned through reliable testimony from elders—devout and holy men—that these things had been accomplished through him. Although their account ought to be regarded as trustworthy, the Lord gave even greater confirmation of the truth of these events through what we ourselves observed with our own eyes.

For we saw baskets full of bread being carried to empty tables. When the tables had been filled with bread and the bread had been consumed to complete satisfaction, the baskets were nevertheless gathered up full again.

I shall not keep silent about another remarkable thing we saw in his presence.

There were three of us brothers when we came to him. While we were still far from his monastery, brothers met us who had heard from him three days earlier about our arrival. They came to meet us with psalms, for it was their custom to do this at the arrival of all monks.

They prostrated themselves face-down to the ground, kissed us, and, pointing us out to one another, said:

“These are the brothers whose arrival Father Apollonius foretold to us three days ago, saying that after three days three brothers would arrive from Jerusalem.”

Some of the brothers went ahead of us and others followed us, but both groups sang psalms. When we had begun to draw near, Saint Apollonius himself also came out to meet us, having heard the sound of the psalmody.

When he saw us, he immediately prostrated himself to the ground. Rising, he welcomed us with a kiss. When we entered the monastery, after first offering the customary prayer, he washed our feet with his own hands and fulfilled the other services necessary for bodily rest. It was his custom to do this for everyone who arrived.

His practice was that the brothers who were with him did not eat before receiving the Lord’s Communion around the ninth hour of the day. After this, they sometimes continued until evening, listening to the word of God and being instructed without interruption in the fulfillment of the Lord’s commandments.

Afterward, once they had eaten, some of them withdrew into the desert and spent the entire night recalling the divine Scriptures from memory. Others remained in the same place to which they had come and kept vigil until dawn in hymns and praises of God, as I myself saw when present.

Some of them, having come down from the mountain around the ninth hour and received the Lord’s grace, immediately departed, content with this spiritual food alone. They did this for many days.

Joy and gladness beyond measure were present among them, and they possessed such exultation as no human being on earth could have. No one among them was found to be sad at all. If someone appeared even slightly sorrowful, Father Apollonius immediately asked the cause of his sadness.

Frequently, even if someone wished to conceal it, he revealed what was hidden in the man’s heart, so that the sufferer himself recognized it.

He therefore admonished them, saying that there ought absolutely to be no sadness in those whose salvation is in God and whose hope is in the kingdom of heaven.

“Let the Gentiles be sad,” he said, “and let the Jews mourn; let sinners lament without ceasing. But let the righteous rejoice. For if those who love earthly things rejoice over fragile and perishable matters, why should we, who possess hope of such great glory and expectation of eternity, not rejoice with every exultation?

“Or does the apostle not also admonish us in this way: ‘Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all things’ (1 Thess. 5)?”

But who could adequately explain his teaching and the grace of his words? Therefore I think it better to remain silent about these matters than to speak of them inadequately.

The blessed Apollonius also spoke to us, often in private, about the discipline of abstinence, the integrity of one’s way of life, and the practice of hospitality. He especially commanded us to receive visiting brothers as though the Lord himself were arriving.

“For this reason,” he said, “there is a tradition that visiting brothers are worshiped: so that it may be certain that, at their arrival, the arrival of the Lord Jesus is understood—he who says, ‘I was a stranger, and you welcomed me’ (Matt. 25). Thus Abraham also received those who appeared to be human beings, although the Lord was understood to be present in them (Gen. 18).

“Sometimes, even against their will, one should compel brothers to bodily rest. For this he proposed the example of holy Lot, who forcibly brought the angels into his house as guests (ibid. 19).”

He also urged that, if it could be done, monks should receive the Mysteries of Christ daily.

[Note: [Col. 0419D] Compare Saint Jerome’s Letter in our recension, LXXI, to Lucinius, no. 6, where he discusses whether the Eucharist ought to be received daily, as the Roman Church and the churches of Spain are said to observe.]

“Perhaps,” he said, “the one who keeps far from these things may be made far from God; but the one who receives them more frequently may appear to receive the Savior himself more frequently, because the Savior himself says: ‘He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him’ (John 6).

“Moreover, the very commemoration of the Lord’s Passion, when it is performed constantly by monks, gives them great benefit as an example of patience. It also admonishes each one to strive always to be found ready, lest he be considered unworthy of the Lord’s Mysteries. Add to this that through these things the forgiveness of sins is also granted to believers.”

[The following passage is enclosed in brackets in the source and is found in the *Decretum*, Part III, distinction 3, concerning consecration, chapter 16.]

“Certainly, he warned that the appointed fasts—that is, Wednesday and Friday—should not be broken unless some great necessity arose, because on Wednesday Judas had conceived the betrayal of the Lord, and on Friday the Savior was crucified. Therefore one who breaks the appointed fasts on these days without some necessity may seem either to betray the Savior together with the betrayer, or to crucify him together with those who crucified him.” [156]

He therefore said that if a brother happened to arrive on the aforesaid days and wished to eat before the ninth hour because of his journey, a table should be set for him alone. But if he did not wish to eat, he was not to be compelled. For this was the common tradition of the observance.

He severely censured those who either grew their hair long or wore iron around their necks, or who carried anything of that kind that appeared to be done to gain the support of human beings.

“For it is certain,” he said, “that such people seek praise from human beings and do these things for the sake of display, although it has been commanded that even the fasts themselves should be practiced in secret, so that they may be known to God alone, who sees what is done in secret and repays it openly.

“But, as it appears, these people are not satisfied with the testimony and reward of the one who sees in secret; they wish to be made known among human beings (Matt. 6). Every practice of abstinence must be carried out in secret, so that the body is wearied by fasts while one seeks not human boasting but the Lord’s recompense.”

He discussed these and many other matters concerning the conduct of monks throughout the entire week, confirming the truth of his teaching by the authority of his deeds.

When we began to depart from him, he accompanied us for a while and admonished us, saying:

“Above all, beloved, maintain peace among yourselves. Do not separate from one another.”

Then, turning to the brothers who were present and were accompanying us together with him, he said:

“Which of you, brothers, is ready to escort them as far as the monasteries of the fathers nearby?”

Almost all of them immediately offered themselves and wished to proceed with us. But the holy father Apollonius chose three from among them who knew Greek and Egyptian well—[Palladius adds: “and Latin”]—so that, whenever necessary, they could interpret for us and could also edify us in their conversations.

He sent them with us and commanded them not to leave us until we had seen all the fathers and all the monasteries we wished to see, although no one would be capable of visiting them all.

He blessed us and dismissed us, giving us this blessing:

“May the Lord bless you from Zion, and may you see the good things of Jerusalem all the days of your life” (Ps. 127).

## Chapter VIII. Concerning Ammon

[Note: [Col. 0419D] This Ammon is distinct from the Egyptian or Nitrian Ammon, who is mentioned below in chapter 30, and from the Tabennesiote who governed about three thousand monks at Tabenna and is discussed above in chapter 3. ROSWEYDUS.]

I have not thought it right to omit what we heard about a certain holy man named Ammon—[Palladius, near the end of chapter 52, calls him Amun]—whose dwelling place in the desert we also saw.

After departing from the blessed Apollonius, we proceeded toward the southern part of the desert. There we saw in the sand the trail of an enormous dragon.

[Note: [Col. 0419D] “Dragon.” Perhaps this is the same Ammon mentioned in book III of Rufinus, no. 214, concerning a basilisk that was destroyed. [Col. 0420D] It should again be noted, as we have said so often, that this is not Rufinus’s book, but that this and other material was assembled in various places from Rufinus. ROSWEYDUS.]

Its size was so great that it appeared as though some beam had been dragged through the sand. When we saw it, we were struck with immense terror. But the brothers who were escorting us urged us not to fear anything at all, but rather to take courage and follow the dragon’s trail.

“You will see,” they said, “how powerful faith is when you see us destroy it. For we have killed many dragons, snakes, and horned creatures with our own hands. Thus we read in Scripture that the Savior grants those who believe in him the power to tread upon serpents and scorpions and over all the strength of the enemy (Luke 10).”

While they were saying these things, however, we, because of the weakness of our unbelief, became more and more afraid. We begged them not to follow the dragon’s trail but to proceed by the direct route.

One of them, nevertheless, unable to restrain his eagerness, followed the dragon. When he found its cave not far away, he called to us to come and see how the matter turned out.

But a certain brother who lived in the neighboring desert came to meet us and forbade us to follow the dragon. He said that we could not even endure the sight of it, especially since we had never had such an experience of seeing anything like this. He himself, he said, had frequently seen the beast, which was of incredible size, and that it was fifteen cubits in length.

When he had dissuaded us from approaching the place, he hurried on and pulled away the brother who was waiting there for us, prepared to kill the beast. He brought him back with him and, by much pleading, persuaded him to leave, although the man was unwilling to do so before destroying it.

When he came to us, he rebuked our cowardice and unbelief.

When we reached his cell, he received us with great affection, and we rested with him. He then told us that in the place where he lived there had once been a holy man named Ammon, of whom he himself had been a disciple, through whom the Lord had performed very many miracles.

Among other things, he also told us the following about him.

He said: “Often robbers came to him, taking away the bread on which alone he lived, and anything else that seemed to have been set aside for his extremely frugal sustenance. Since he was frequently troubled by them, one day he went out into the desert. Returning from there, he ordered two enormous dragons to accompany him and commanded them to remain at the entrance of his monastery and guard the doorway.

“The robbers came as usual, not knowing [Col. 0421B] who the guards at the threshold were; but when they saw the dragons, they became lifeless with terror and bereft of reason, lost the power of speech, and immediately collapsed. When the old man learned of this, he went out and found them half-dead. Approaching and raising them up, he rebuked them, saying: ‘You see how much harder than beasts you are. They obey us because of God, whereas you neither fear God nor blush to disturb the life of God’s servants.’

“Nevertheless, he brought them into his cell, set a table before them, and ordered them to take food. Their hearts were then pierced with remorse, and they turned away from all the savagery of their minds. In a short time they became better than many who had previously begun to serve the Lord. Indeed, they advanced so far through repentance that, after not much time, they themselves performed the same signs and the same [Col. 0421C] miracles.”

On another occasion, when a most savage dragon was devastating the neighboring regions and killing very many people, the inhabitants of that place came to the aforesaid father, begging him to destroy the beast from their territory. At the same time, in order to move the old man to compassion, they brought with them a certain boy, the son of a shepherd, who, terrified by the mere sight of the dragon, had lost his reason and, rendered lifeless by the beast’s breath, was carried along swollen with it.

Then the old man anointed the boy with oil and restored him to health. But, while urging himself to kill the dragon, he would promise the people nothing, as though he could not help them at all. Rising early, he went to the place where the beast had withdrawn and fixed his knees upon the ground, beseeching the Lord. [Col. 0421D] Then the beast began to come upon him with tremendous force, first sending forth dreadful blasts, hisses, and screeching noises. But he feared none of this. Turning toward the dragon, he said: “May Christ, the Son of God, destroy you—the one who is to destroy the great sea-monster.”

When the old man had said this, the most savage dragon immediately vomited out all its venom together with its breath, burst apart, and split open in the middle. When the neighboring inhabitants had gathered and were struck with amazement at the miracle, they could not endure the intensity of the stench. They therefore heaped enormous masses of sand over it, although Father Ammon was standing there; for even after the beast was dead, they still did not dare approach it without him.

## CHAPTER IX. ON COPRES

[Note: I find no mention of him anywhere except in Sozomen, book VI, chapter 28; Nicephorus, book XI, chapter 34. “Copres,” says Nicephorus, “had received the grace of driving out demons and curing various diseases. Take care not to confuse this Copres and Patermutius with two others of the same names who were martyrs in the time of Julian the Apostate, concerning whom see the Menaea and the Menologion, 9 July. There was also another Coprius in the time of Theodosius the Coenobiarch, concerning whom the Greeks write on 24 September; for this one was the younger.” ROSWEYDUS.]

### COPRES THE PRESBYTER AND PATERMUTIUS

There was a certain presbyter named Copres (Palladius, chapter 54), who had a monastery in the desert itself. He was a holy man of about eighty years of age, who performed many miracles, cured illnesses and brought about healings, drove out demons, and did many wonderful things. He performed some of these even in our presence.

When he saw us, he greeted us with a kiss and, according to custom, washed our feet after prayer. He then asked us what was happening in the world. We, however, asked him to tell us something about his own deeds and to explain by what actions and merits the Lord had bestowed such grace upon him.

He did not disdain this request. He began to tell us the story of his own life and of his predecessors, whom he declared to have been far more illustrious, while he himself scarcely followed even a small part of their examples. He said:

“Nothing great, my little sons, is what you see in us, compared with the holy fathers.

“There was before us a most noble man named Patermutius [Note: The account of Patermutius is absent from the Latin Palladius. It is found in the Greek excerpts of the Augsburg Library.] . He was the first monk in this place, and the first here in all this desert to show us the way of salvation.

“At first he was a pagan, a great leader of robbers, a violator of tombs, and notorious for every kind of wickedness. Yet the opportunity for his salvation came to him in the following way.

“One night he went to the house of a certain virgin consecrated to God in order to rob it. Having climbed onto the roof of her house by means of certain devices well known to practitioners of that craft, he sought by what skill or through what entrance he might get inside. Entangled in the difficulty of carrying out his undertaking, he spent much of the night on the roof without accomplishing anything.

“After making many futile efforts, he was overcome by sleep as though exhausted. In a dream he saw someone standing before him in royal attire, saying: ‘Cease now from these crimes; stop shedding human blood; turn your vigils away from accursed thefts toward religious labor; take up the heavenly and angelic warfare; and from now on live by the virtues of the soul. I will make you commander and leader of this warfare.’

“When he gladly heard what was being offered to him, an army of monks was shown to him, and he was ordered to exercise authority over them. Awakening from this vision, he saw the virgin standing beside him and asking who he was, where he came from, and why he had come there.

“As though bereft of his senses, he answered her nothing, but merely asked her to show him the church. When she understood that there was in the man some work of God, she led him to the church and presented him to the presbyters. Falling at their feet, he begged to become a Christian and to be given penance immediately.

“The presbyters knew that this man was the chief of all wickedness, and they were astonished, wondering whether he was speaking truthfully. When he proved the truth of his request by his perseverance, they warned him that, if he wanted this, he must completely abandon his former life.

“After he had undertaken the beginnings of religious life, he asked that instructions be given him by which he might walk in the way of salvation. They gave him the first three verses of a psalm. After carefully considering them, he said that they were sufficient for him as a way to salvation and a knowledge of piety.

“After remaining with them for three days, he departed for the desert, where he stayed a long time, persevering day and night in prayer with tears and taking food from the roots of plants.

“When he returned to the church, he rendered back the three verses of the psalm that he had received from the presbyters, not only in words but also in deeds and actions. The presbyters were amazed that, having been suddenly converted, he immediately imposed upon himself the most severe abstinence. They instructed him more fully in the divine Scriptures and urged him to remain with them.

“But, so as not to seem disobedient, he spent one week with them and then went back to the desert. There he lived for seven continuous years in complete abstinence and received from the Lord such an abundance of grace that he knew almost all the Scriptures by heart.

“He took bread only on the Lord’s Day, and even this was brought to him by divine agency. For when he prayed, he would rise from prayer and find bread set down, although no human being had brought it. When he had eaten it with thanksgiving, it sustained him until the following Lord’s Day.

“After a long time he returned from the desert and, by the example of his abstinence, invited very many people to imitate him. Among them came a certain young man who desired to become his disciple.

“He clothed him in the monastic habit—that is, a *lebeta* [Note: That is, a *colobium*; see above, chapter 7.] , a hood, and a *melote*, which is a goatskin—and began to teach him the other practices of the monks.

“He took great care, whenever a Christian had died, to bury him. When his young disciple saw him dressing the dead with the greatest diligence, he said to him: ‘Master, I wish that, when I am dead, you would clothe and bury me in the same way.’

“He replied: ‘I will do so, my son, and I will clothe you so abundantly that you will say, “It is enough.”’

“Not long afterward the young man died, and the words spoken earlier were fulfilled. When he had wrapped him in many garments, he said to him in the presence of everyone: ‘Are these garments enough for your burial, little son, or do you still wish us to add something?’

“Then the dead man uttered a voice heard by all. His face was already covered and his features were set, yet he said: ‘It is enough, father. You have fulfilled what you promised.’

“Those present were astonished and marveled greatly at so extraordinary a deed of his. After burying the young man, he immediately returned to the desert, carefully avoiding ostentation.

“On another occasion he came again from the desert to visit the brothers whom he had instructed. When one of them was at the point of death, it was revealed to him by the Lord that the man would die. It was already toward evening, and so he hurried in order to see him.

“The village where the sick man lay was still a long distance away. [Note: Previously, *decumbat*; we silently correct certain other such readings that appear to be printers’ errors.] Since he was unwilling to enter the village at night, and was also meditating within himself on the Savior’s words—‘Walk while you have the light, lest the darkness overtake you’ (John 12), and ‘Whoever walks in the light does not stumble’ (John 11)—when he saw that the sun was already sinking, he said to it:

“‘In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, stand for a little while on your course and wait for me until I reach the village.’

“Although part of it had already begun to descend, the sun stopped and did not set before the man of God reached the village. This became evident to all who were standing there. For as they stood watching the sun’s delay in setting, they all wondered why it did not descend toward its setting for so many hours.

“When they saw Father Patermutius coming from the desert, they asked him what sign the sun had shown. He answered them: ‘Do you not remember the voice of our Lord and Savior, who said: “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will perform greater signs than these” (Matthew 17)?’

“When they understood that the sun had stood still because of his faith, they were seized with great fear, and many of them joined themselves to him as disciples and began to follow him.

“When he entered the house of the brother for whom he had hurried, he found him already dead. After praying, he approached the bed, kissed him, and said: ‘What do you desire more, brother—to depart and be with Christ, or to remain in the flesh?’

“Then the man recovered his breath, sat up for a little while, and said to him: ‘Why do you call me back, father? It is better for me to return and be with Christ. Remaining in the flesh is not necessary for me.’

“He said to him: ‘Sleep in peace, then, my son, and pray for me.’

“The man immediately reclined again on the bed and fell asleep. Those who were present were astonished and said: ‘Truly, this is a man of God.’

“Then Patermutius dressed the young man, as was his custom, with great propriety. He spent the entire night awake in psalms and hymns and committed the young man honorably to burial.

“On another occasion, when he visited a different brother who was lying ill, he saw that the man was having difficulty accepting the rest of death and was being severely reproved by fear of his conscience. He said to him:

“‘Why are you unprepared, my son, for your departure? As I see it, your conscience, accusing you of sloth, is traveling with you.’

“The man then begged him, saying: ‘I beseech you, father, intercede for me with God, that he may grant me a short period in which I can amend my life.’

“The old man said to him: ‘Now you ask for time for repentance, when you have completed the time of your life? What were you doing throughout all this time of your life? Could you not heal your wounds? Indeed, you were always adding newer ones.’

“When the man continued to plead, the old man said to him: ‘If you do not add evil to your evils any longer, we will pray to God for you. He is good and patient, and he will grant you a little more time of life so that you may pay all your debts.’

“After praying to God, he rose from prayer and said to him: ‘Behold, the Lord has granted you three years in this life, provided that you turn wholeheartedly to repentance.’

“He took the man by the hand and raised him from his bed. The man rose and, without any delay, followed him into the desert.

“When the three years had been completed, he brought him back to the place from which he had taken him, now commending him to God not as a human being but as an angel made from a human being, so that everyone marveled at his manner of life.

“When very many brothers had gathered around him, he placed the man in their midst and, taking him as his subject, continued throughout the entire night to teach the brothers about the fruits of his repentance and conversion.

“While he was speaking, that brother began to doze slightly, as though falling asleep, and immediately rested forever. After praying over him and completing all the customary rites of burial, Patermutius hurried away to the desert.

“He also frequently crossed the great Nile River on foot, with the water reaching to his knees.

“On another occasion, when the doors were closed and the brothers were sitting in the upper rooms, he entered to them. Frequently, he was transported in an instant to whatever place he wished, however far away it might be.

[Note: In the Greek text of Palladius, some material is inserted here.]

“For, early in the period of his conversion, when he was in the desert and had fasted for a week, they say that a man appeared to him in the wilderness, carrying bread and water. He encouraged him to accept food that had been appointed for him from heaven.

“On another occasion a demon appeared and showed him many treasures of gold buried beneath the earth, claiming that they had belonged to Pharaoh. Patermutius is said to have answered him: ‘May your money go with you to destruction and perdition’ (Acts 8).

“Thus the Lord performed through him these things and many others like them.

“There were also many other fathers before us, whose presence the world was not worthy to possess, who performed heavenly signs and wonders. Why, then, do you marvel if we insignificant men perform insignificant deeds, healing the lame and the blind—something that physicians can also do by their art?”

While the old man Copres was telling us these things (Palladius, chapter 54), one of our brothers, as though wearied by disbelief in what was being said, began to grow tired [Note: *Taediare* is peculiar to Rufinus, although it is a less Latin expression, meaning ‘to be wearied,’ ‘to be exhausted,’ and similar things. Thus, in the Preface to Book II of *On the Blessings of the Patriarchs*, addressed to Paulinus: “Since you do not even grow tired of commanding in this way,” and so forth. See us there.] and to doze from weariness.

When he had been overcome by sleep, he saw in a vision a book written in golden letters in the hands of the old man Copres, from which his account seemed to be unfolding. A man of exceedingly noble appearance, venerable with gray hair, stood beside him and said to him with a stern warning:

“Why do you not listen attentively to what is being recited, but sleep in disbelief?”

The brother awoke in confusion and immediately recounted to us privately, in the Latin language, what he had seen.

Meanwhile, we saw a peasant approach the old man’s door carrying a vessel full of sand and waiting until the old man had finished his account. Seeing him, we asked the presbyter what the peasant meant by standing there and holding sand in a vessel.

The old man answered us:

“It was not necessary, my little sons, for me to reveal this to you, lest we seem to glory in the work of God and the reward of our labor be lost. Nevertheless, for your edification and benefit—you who have come to us by so long a journey—I will not conceal even this from you, but will recount the works of the Lord, which he has deigned to accomplish through us.

“The soil of this region, which is cultivated near us, was extremely sterile and unproductive. Whenever it received seed from the cultivators out of necessity, it scarcely returned double the amount. For certain worms were born in the very stalks of the shoots and cut down the growing crops.

“The farmers of that place were pagans. After we taught them to believe in God and to accept the faith of Christ, they became Christians and came to us, asking us to pray to the Lord for their crops.

“We told them that we would indeed pray, but that their faith was required before God, since they had to be worthy to receive this favor. They filled their laps with this sand, which is trampled by our feet, and offered it to us, asking us to bless it in the name of the Lord.

“I said to them: ‘Let it be done for you according to your faith.’

“Then they took the sand away with them, mixed it with the seed they were about to sow, and scattered it through their fields. They gathered as much produce as no land anywhere in Egypt had ever been able to produce.

“From that time it has become their custom to come to us twice each year and expect the same thing from us.”

“I will not conceal from you another matter that the Lord granted me for the glory of his name.

“Once I went down to the city and found there a teacher of the Manichaeans deceiving the people. I engaged him in disputation. But because he was extremely crafty and I could not refute him by argument, I feared that the crowd of listeners might be harmed if he withdrew appearing verbally victorious. So, in the hearing of the crowds, I said:

[Note: You have an example—indeed, not merely a similar one—of this challenge to fire in the *Life of Saint Eugenia*, chapter 5. That work was likewise once attributed, although falsely, to Rufinus; we have reprinted it in the Appendix to this volume. There Bishop Helenus and the magician Zareas contend. The words are almost identical to those here. Helenus says: “Let a fire be kindled in the middle of the city, and let us enter the flames together; and whoever is not burned, let us believe that Christ has sent him.” Then everyone approved the proposal. A great fire was immediately kindled. Blessed Helenus ordered Zareas to enter the flames. Zareas said to him: “You enter first, since you proposed this.” The most blessed father Helenus then made the sign of the cross and, with hands extended, entered the enormous flames. Standing there for nearly half an hour, with neither his hair nor his clothing damaged in any part, he likewise ordered Zareas to enter. But Zareas began to resist and flee. When the crowd handed him over unwillingly to the fire, the flames immediately surrounded him and began to burn him. Saint Helenus rushed in and rescued him alive, though half-burned; the crowd then expelled him dishonorably from the territory of that region. Wherever he goes each day, the people accompany him in praise of God. The facts make clear that Rufinus borrowed this account almost word for word from the pseudonymous author.]

“‘Kindle a very great fire in the middle of the square, and let us both enter the flames. If one of us is not burned by it, let his faith be judged true.’

“When I had said this, it greatly pleased the people, and immediately a very large fire was kindled. Then I seized him and began to drag him with me toward the fire.

“But he said: ‘No, not in this way. Let each of us enter separately. You, however, must enter first, since you proposed this.’

“I made the sign of the cross over myself in the name of Christ and entered the middle of the flames. But the flame began to scatter in every direction and to flee entirely from me. I stood in the middle of the fire for nearly half an hour and, in the name of the Lord, was not harmed in the least.

“When the people saw this, they shouted with immense wonder and blessed God, saying: ‘God is wonderful in his saints’ (Psalm 67).

“They also began to press the Manichaean to enter the fire. But he began to resist and withdraw. Then the crowd seized him and threw him into the middle of the fire. The flame immediately surrounded him, burned him, and left him half-scorched.

“The people expelled him from the city in disgrace, shouting: ‘Let the deceiver burn alive.’

“But they took me with them, blessing the Lord, and led me to the church.

“On another occasion, while I was passing beside a certain temple, I saw pagans sacrificing there. I said to them:

“‘Why, since you are rational human beings, do you sacrifice to mute and senseless images? Are you not yourselves much more senseless than those to whom you sacrifice?’

“At these words the Lord opened their understanding. They abandoned the error in which they had been living, followed me, and believed in our Savior God.

“Once I had a small garden adjoining the monastery, in which we used to grow vegetables for the brothers who came to us. A certain pagan entered at night and stole the vegetables. When he had carried them to his house, he placed them on the fire to cook them.

“Although he kept a great fire under them continuously for three hours, they could neither boil, soften, nor become warm in any way. They remained as green as when they had been placed there, and not even the water itself could be heated, however slightly.

“The thief came to his senses, removed the vegetables from the hearth, brought them back to us, and threw himself at our feet. He began to beg that he might obtain forgiveness for his sin and become a Christian. He obtained both.

“That same day many of the brothers arrived as guests. The vegetables were conveniently ready for them. Giving thanks to the Lord for his wonders, we experienced a double joy: for the man’s salvation and for the divine benefits.”

## CHAPTER X. ON THE ABBOT SYRUS, ISAIAH, PAUL, AND ANUPH

[Note: Apart from what Palladius records in the margin, I have found nothing concerning these men. ROSWEYDUS.]

He added still more, saying (Palladius, chapters 55–58):

“Abbot Syrus, Isaiah, and Paul once met one another on the bank of a river. These men were righteous, of the highest abstinence and complete religious devotion. They were going to visit a man named Anuph.

“The monastery to which they were traveling was three stages away. When they wished to cross the river but had no means of crossing, they said among themselves:

“‘Let us ask the Lord for the grace that the journey of this good work may not be hindered.’

“Turning to Abbot Syrus, they said: ‘You, above all, ask the Lord. For we know that you are heard, because he will grant you whatever you ask.’

“He encouraged them also to kneel with him, and prostrated himself face down before the Lord in prayer. When they had completed their prayer and risen, they saw a boat drawn up and ready at the bank of the river, prepared for the journey they were about to undertake.

“They boarded it, and it began to carry them so swiftly against the current that within one hour they completed the distance of the entire journey, which otherwise would have taken them three days.

“When they had reached land, Isaiah said: ‘The Lord has shown me the man to whom we are hastening. He is coming to meet us and revealing the secrets of each one of our hearts.’

“But Paul said: ‘The Lord has also shown me that after three days he will lead him out of this world.’

“When they had begun to follow the road leading from the river to the monastery, and had advanced a little, the man whom they were going to visit met them. Greeting them, he said:

“‘Blessed is the Lord, who has shown you to me both now in the body and previously in the spirit.’

“He then began to recount the merits that each of them possessed before God and their deeds.

“Paul said: ‘Since the Lord has also shown us that after three days he will take you from this world, we ask you to tell us about your own virtues and deeds by which you pleased the Lord. Do not fear the charge of boasting. For as you are about to depart from this world, leave to those who come after a memory of your deeds, for them to imitate.’

“He replied:

“‘I do not remember having done anything great. Yet I have guarded this: from the time when I confessed the name of our Savior during the persecution, no lie has proceeded from my mouth after my confession of the truth.
