After loving heavenly things, I have loved nothing earthly. Nor was the Lord’s grace lacking to me in these matters.

“He never allowed me to lack anything earthly. He brought me, through the ministry of angels, every kind of food that I desired. The Lord concealed from me nothing of what takes place on earth. His light was never absent from my heart; awakened by it, I did not seek the sleep of the body, always desiring to see him.

“He also caused his angel always to stand beside me, teaching me about each of the virtues of the world. The light of my mind was never extinguished. Everything I asked of the Lord I obtained without delay.

“He frequently showed me multitudes of angels standing before him. I also saw assemblies of the righteous, gatherings of martyrs, communities of monks, and all the saints—those, at least, whose sole work is always to praise and bless the Lord in simplicity of heart and faith.

“On the other hand, I saw Satan and his angels being handed over to eternal fires, and again I saw the righteous enjoying eternal joy.’

“After he had recounted these and many other things like them to them throughout the three days, he gave up his spirit. Immediately they saw angels receive his soul and carry it to heaven. They themselves heard the sound of hymns, as his soul departed with the angels and praised the Lord together with them.

## CHAPTER XI. ON HELENUS

[Note: Sozomen, book VI, chapter 28; Nicephorus, book XI, chapter 34; Cassiodorus, *Tripartite History*, book VIII, chapter 1. In these sources he is called Helles, while Palladius calls him Hellen. ROSWEYDUS.]

There was also another holy man named Helenus (Palladius calls him Hellen, chapter 59). From childhood he had been raised in the service of the Lord with complete self-restraint and the most chaste discipline, and he attained the highest merits.

While he was still a boy in the monastery, whenever fire was needed and had to be fetched from a nearby place, he carried burning coals in his garment without damaging it. All the brothers who were present marveled at this and desired to imitate the zeal of his spirit, his way of life, and his merit.

Once, when he was alone in the desert, he conceived a desire to eat honey. Turning around, he saw a honeycomb attached to a rock. Understanding that this was a deception of the enemy, he immediately rebuked himself and said:

“Depart from me, deceitful and seductive desire. For it is written: ‘Walk by the Spirit, and you will not fulfill the desires of the flesh’ (Galatians 5).”

He immediately abandoned even that place and went away into the desert. There, as though punishing himself for the desire of the flesh, he began to afflict himself with fasts.

In the third week of his fast, he saw various fruits scattered in the desert. Understanding the enemy’s trickery, he said:

“I will neither eat nor touch them, lest I cause my brother—that is, my soul—to stumble. For it is written: ‘A human being does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God’ (Matthew 4).”

When he continued fasting during the following week, he was overcome by sleep for a little while. Then, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a vision and said:

“Rise now, and eat without hesitation whatever you find set before you.”

When he rose, he saw a spring filled with gentle-running waters, its banks all around covered with delicate and fragrant herbs. He approached and began to pluck and eat them, and likewise to drink from the spring.

He affirmed that throughout his entire life he had never tasted anything of such sweetness and pleasantness. In that very place he also found a cave, in which he rested for some time. Whenever the time and need to refresh his little body arose, by God’s grace nothing that he asked of the Lord was lacking.

On one occasion he was going to visit brothers who were ill, and he was carrying them whatever they needed to restore their bodies. When he was weighed down on the journey by the load he was carrying, he saw wild asses passing through the desert in the distance and cried out:

“In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, let one of you come here and take up my burden.”

And behold, one of the whole herd came to him with complete gentleness. The saint placed his burden upon the animal, mounted it, and was carried with great speed to the brothers’ cells, where he was going.

On another occasion, on the Lord’s Day, he came to a certain monastery of brothers. When he saw that they were not celebrating the solemnity of the day, he asked the reason.

They said that the presbyter was absent and lived across the river. No one dared cross because of fear of the crocodile.

Then he said: “If you wish, I will go and bring him to you.”

He immediately went to the riverbank. When he invoked the Lord’s name, the beast appeared. The creature that normally came to bring death to human beings now came as a vehicle for the righteous man. It took him upon its back and, completely subdued by fear, carried him to the farther bank.

Helenus immediately went to the presbyter and began to beg him to come to the brothers. He was wearing an extremely poor and wretched garment. The presbyter, astonished, asked who he was, where he came from, and what he wanted.

When he learned that he was a man of God, he began to follow him to the river. When he complained that no boat could be found by which they might cross, Abbot Helenus said to him:

“Do not fear, father. I will now prepare a vehicle.”

He cried out in a loud voice and ordered the beast to appear. It immediately came at his voice and calmly prepared its back to carry them. Helenus mounted first and invited the presbyter, saying:

“Climb on, and fear nothing.”

But when the presbyter saw the beast, he was terrified and began to retreat and shrink back. All who were present were seized with immense astonishment and fear when they saw the man of God carried across the riverbed by a crocodile.

When he had dismounted, he led the beast out onto the bank with him and said to it:

“Death is better for you than to be entangled in the guilt of so many crimes and so many murders.”

At once the crocodile collapsed and died.

Saint Helenus remained in the monastery for three days, teaching the brothers spiritual doctrine. He even brought into the open the thoughts of some of their hearts and their secret counsels. He exposed one as being driven by a spirit of fornication, another by a spirit of anger, another by greed for money, and some others as being deceived by vainglory and a spirit of pride [Note: We corrected the reading to “some others,” as required by the meaning and the sequence of the sentence. Previously, “none” (*nullos*) was read simply (*ἁπλῶς*). We silently correct other minor matters below.] .

Of another he gave testimony to gentleness, of another to justice, and of another to patience. Thus, magnifying on both sides the vices of some and the virtues of others, he wonderfully cultivated the progress of them all.

Each of them recognized that matters stood among themselves as he had announced. Struck in heart, they amended their lives.

When he was about to depart, he said to them:

“Prepare vegetables for the arrival of the brothers.”

While they were preparing them, the brothers immediately arrived. After receiving them honorably, Helenus hastened to the desert.

One of the brothers begged him to allow him to live with him in the desert. When Helenus replied that the undertaking was difficult and involved much labor in resisting the temptations of demons, the young man persisted all the more insistently. He promised that he would endure everything patiently, if only Helenus would grant him the opportunity to share his life.

When Helenus consented, the young man followed him into the desert. Helenus ordered him to live in a cave nearby.

Then the demons came upon him at night. First they tormented him with filthy and shameful thoughts; afterward they also attacked him violently and attempted to kill him.

The young man fled to the cell of Saint Helenus and explained the evils by which he was being oppressed. The old man consoled him with a few words and reminded him of the power of faith and patience. He immediately sent him back to the cave from which he had fled.

Then, like a furrow in the sand outside the cell, he drew a line with his finger and commanded, in the name of the Lord, that the demons dare not cross the boundary that had been established. By the power of his word, the young man thereafter remained safe.

It was reported of the young man that, while he was living in the desert, he too often received heavenly food. When brothers came to him and he had nothing to set before them, a certain young man appeared, bringing him bread and whatever was necessary. After setting these things down before his cave, he was nowhere to be seen again.

The young man said to the brothers: “Let us bless the Lord, who has prepared a table for us in the desert.”

While Father Copres was recounting these and many other things about the life and conduct of the holy Fathers to us, and instructing us with every affection, after the edification afforded by his discourse he led us into his little garden. He showed us palm trees and other fruit trees, which he himself had planted, and said:

“These things were planted by me in the desert because the faith of peasants admonished me to do so. For when I saw them possess such great faith that they gathered up the sand beneath our footsteps, scattered it over their fields, and transformed barren soil into an abundance of every kind of fertility, I say that it is shameful if we are found inferior to them in faith, whose faith has been sealed for God through us.”

## CHAPTER XII. ON ELIJAH

[Note: [Col. 0431D] On him, Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 28; Nicephorus, Book II, chapter 34; Cassiodorus, *Tripartite History*, Book VIII, chapter 1.]

We also saw another venerable old man, named Elijah (Palladius, chapter 51; and concerning another Elijah, chapter 3), in the territory of the city of Antinoe, which is the metropolis of the Thebaid. He was, as was said, already about one hundred and ten years old. They said of him that the spirit of Elijah had truly come to rest upon him, for many remarkable and magnificent things were reported about him.

They said that he had spent seventy years in a vast wilderness, whose desolation and terror no discourse could adequately describe. There the old man had sat throughout all those years, knowing nothing of the places inhabited by human beings. The path leading to him was narrow and rocky, and travelers could scarcely find it. The place itself where he sat was a certain dreadful cave, inspiring great horror in those who looked upon it. His limbs, already trembling, were shaken by the extreme weight of age. Nevertheless, every single day he continually performed signs, and completely released from whatever affliction they were bound by those who came to him.

All the Fathers confirmed that no one at all remembered when he had withdrawn into the desert. His food, until the very end of his old age, was a little bread and very few olives. In his youth, he was said often to have fasted for entire weeks.

## CHAPTER XIII. ON PITHYRION

[Note: [Col. 0431D] On him, Nicephorus, Book IX, chapter 14. Moreover, that Pithyrion elsewhere had an asceterium—that is, a dwelling for the practice of piety—at Athens. ROSWEYDUS.]

[Col. 0432C]

Meanwhile, on our return from the Thebaid, we saw a certain precipitous mountain rising above a river, with the threatening elevation of its crag and a terrifying appearance. In its very precipices were caves that were difficult to approach. Many monks lived there, whose father was a man named Pithyrion.

He had been one of the disciples of blessed Antony, and after Antony’s death he had lived with Saint Ammon. After Ammon’s departure, he had established himself on this mountain. He possessed such an abundance of virtues, such grace for healings, and such power against demons that he seemed, by the merit of two great men, to have inherited a double legacy by himself alone.

He instructed many by his admonitions and taught them much doctrine. Above all, however, he taught us about the discernment of spirits, saying that there are certain demons who attach themselves to particular vices. When they see the affections of the soul moved passively and viciously, they turn those affections toward every evil deed.

“Therefore, if anyone wishes to rule over demons, let him first rule over his own vices and passions. Whatever vice of your own passion you cast away, you will also be able to drive the demon of that vice out of possessed bodies. For this reason, one must strive gradually to overcome one’s own vices, so that [Note: [Col. 0434D] The small word required by the integrity of the passage and its meaning was missing.] we may also overcome the demons who attach themselves to such vices.”

He was refreshed twice during the week, receiving little porridge made from flour; neither his age nor his custom permitted him to take any other food.

## CHAPTER XIV. ON FATHER EULOGIUS

[Note: [Col. 0433D] On him, Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 28; Nicephorus, Book II, chapter 34; Cassiodorus, Book VIII of the *Tripartite History*, chapter 1.]

We also saw another holy Father, named Eulogius (Palladius, chapter 75; and concerning another Eulogius, chapter 26), who had received such great grace from the Lord in offering the Sacraments that he recognized the merits and sins of each person approaching the altar of God.

Indeed, he held back certain monks who wished to approach Communion, saying:

“How have you dared to approach the divine Sacraments when your mind and your purpose are set upon evil [Note: [Col. 0434D] A similar passage occurs in Pelagius, *Booklet* 18, section 20, concerning Paul the Simple.]?”

To one he would say:

“You had thoughts of fornication this night.”

To another:

“You said in your heart: ‘It makes no difference whether a righteous person or a sinner approaches the Sacraments.’”

Another had harbored doubt in his heart, saying:

“What can Communion do to sanctify me?”

He therefore removed each of them from sacramental Communion and said to them:

“Withdraw for a little while and do penance, so that, purified through satisfaction and tears, you may be considered worthy of the Communion of Christ.”

## CHAPTER XV. ON APELLAS THE PRESBYTER AND JOHN

[Note: [Col. 0433D] On him, Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 28; Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 33.]

[Col. 0433C]

We also saw another presbyter in a neighboring region, named Apellas (Palladius, chapters 60 and 61), a just man. He was an ironworker and made whatever things were necessary for the brothers.

One night, while he was keeping vigil over his forge-work in the silence of the night, the devil came to him transformed into the likeness of a beautiful woman, as though bringing him some piece of work. Then Apellas seized with his bare hand a glowing iron from the furnace and threw it into her face. She fled, crying out and howling, so that all the brothers living in the surrounding area heard the howling of the fleeing creature. From that time onward, the man acquired the practice of holding glowing iron in his bare hand without being harmed.

When we came to him and he had received us with the greatest kindness, we asked him to tell us either about his own deeds or about the virtues of those whom he knew to be distinguished in holy conduct. Then he said:

“There is a certain brother in this neighboring desert named John, advanced in age and surpassing everyone in life, character, and abstinence. When he first came to the desert, he stood beneath the overhang of a certain rock for three continuous years, always praying, so that he never sat down or lay down at all. He took only as much sleep as he could obtain while standing. He never took food except on Sunday. For the presbyter used to come to him then and offer the sacrifice on his behalf; that Sacrament alone was both his nourishment and his food.

“One day Satan, wishing to deceive him, transformed himself into the presbyter who used to come to him. He arrived before the customary hour and pretended that he had come on account of the Sacraments. But John, discerning the devil’s fraud with vigilance, said to him with a certain indignation:

“‘O father of every deceit and every fraud, enemy of all righteousness, you do not cease to seduce Christian souls; yet you have even dared to thrust yourself into those very terrifying and most holy mysteries.’

“The devil replied:

“‘I thought that I might win you over. In this way I also deceived another of your number, so that he lost his mind and understanding. After I had made him believe me and driven him mad, so many righteous men prayed for him that they could scarcely restore him both to his place and to soundness of mind.’

“After saying this, the demon fled from him.

“The man mentioned above continued steadfastly in the work he had begun and persevered in prayer. His feet, because they had remained immobile for so long, split open, so that pus flowed from them.

“When three years had been completed, an angel of the Lord appeared and said to him:

“‘The Lord Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit have received your prayers. They heal the scars of your body and grant you an abundance of heavenly food—that is, of his word and knowledge.’

“The angel touched his mouth and his feet, healed him of his ulcers, and filled him with the grace of knowledge and instruction, so that he no longer felt hunger for food. He commanded him to go on to other places, to visit other brothers as he traveled around the desert, and to edify them in the word and teaching of the Lord.

“On Sunday he always returned to the same place for the sake of the Sacraments. On the remaining days he also performed manual labor, weaving straps for pack animals from palm leaves, as is customary in those regions.

“Once, a certain lame man wished to go to him to be healed. It happened that the animal he was about to ride had a strap made by the hands of the man of God. When he was placed upon the animal, as soon as his feet touched that strap, he became well.

“He also sent blessed bread to whatever sick people he could, and as soon as they had received some of it, they were healed. The Lord accomplished many other miracles and healings through him.

“He possessed this grace above all the Fathers and other people: the conduct of each brother from the neighboring monasteries was revealed to him. He would write to their Fathers and warn them that this or that brother was acting sluggishly and did not maintain a proper purpose in the fear of God, while this or that other was progressing in faith and strength of spirit.

“He also wrote to the brothers themselves. To some he wrote that they were very wearisome toward their brothers and faint-hearted in patience; to others, that they were acting well, steadfastly, and attentively, and that they were sufficiently consoling their brothers. He proclaimed what reward from the Lord would come to one for his virtues, and what correction would threaten another for his laziness. Thus he described the deeds, motives, merits, or negligence of those who were absent so clearly that the people about whom he spoke, hearing it, could not deny it, convicted by their own consciences.

“He taught everyone to transfer their minds from visible and corporeal things to invisible and incorporeal ones. ‘For,’ he said, ‘it is time for us to pass on to such pursuits. We must not always remain boys, always infants, but at some point ascend to spiritual and higher things, acquire the understanding of men, and enter upon a more perfect comprehension, so that we may shine through the virtues of the soul.’

“The holy man of God Apellas also entrusted us with many other things about this man in an entirely trustworthy account. To write them all down seems both lengthy and, because of their greatness, scarcely credible to some hearers.”

## CHAPTER XVI. ON PAPHNUTIUS

[Note: [Col. 0435C] On him, Maurolycus, in his *Martyrology*, under the name Pannucius, November 29: “Saint Pannucius, abbot, who inhabited the desert of the region of Heraclea, and through whose work Thais, a prostitute of striking beauty, is said to have obtained forgiveness through repentance after throwing her ornaments into the fire.” *Florarium Sanctorum*, manuscript, March 8: “Paphnutius the confessor, who converted Thais the prostitute and won three men, rescued from the world, for God. He flourished in the year of salvation 321.” You have the latter account of the three men expressed in this chapter of Rufinus. Since there were various Paphnutiuses, I do not think that anyone should identify this man with any of them. For the one commemorated on April 28 by Metaphrastes, and from him by Surius, was a martyr in the time of Diocletian; the Roman Martyrology places him on September 24. There is no mention of him in the Menologion, although Baronius asserts that there is; he thought that what Galesinius said he had received from Greek records came from the Menologion. I think, however, that Galesinius meant Metaphrastes. In the Menaea, on September 25, only two verses concern him. The Greek Menologion on April 19 has Paphnutius of Jerusalem, and calls him a martyr; concerning him the Menaea on April 20 have only two verses and do not mention his martyrdom. The Greek Menologion on September 25 has Paphnutius the Egyptian, father of Saint Euphrosyne; concerning him the Menaea on the same day also have only two verses. The Roman Martyrology on September 11 has Paphnutius the Thebaid—otherwise called bishop and confessor of the Upper Thebaid by Nicephorus, Book VIII, chapter 19—who is very famous and known through the testimony of all historians. Concerning him, see the *Life of Saint Antony*, chapter 30. There was also another Paphnutius the Meletian, mentioned by Epiphanius in *Panarion*, heresy 68; another Paphnutius Cephalas, mentioned by Palladius, chapter 91; and another Paphnutius the Scetiote presbyter, surnamed Bubalus, in Cassian, *Conferences* III.1 and XVIII.15. ROSWEYDUS.]

### ON PAPHNUTIUS

We also saw the monastery of the holy Paphnutius, the man of God (Palladius, chapter 62), who was very famous in those regions as an anchorite and had been the last inhabitant of the desert in the territory of Heraclea, a splendid city in the Thebaid.

[Col. 0435C]

Concerning him we learned from the most trustworthy account of the Fathers (Palladius, chapter 63) that, having attained an angelic life, he once prayed to God to show him to which of the saints he might be considered similar.

An angel appeared and answered that he was like a certain musician who earned his livelihood by his skill in singing in that village. Astonished at the novelty of the answer, Paphnutius hurried to the village and searched for the man. When he had found him, he questioned him most carefully about what holy and religious work he had performed and investigated all his deeds with great attention.

The man replied that, as was the case, he was a sinner of the most disgraceful life. Not long before, he had fallen from being a robber into the shameful craft he now practiced.

Paphnutius pressed him further, asking whether perhaps, even during his time among robbers, he had performed some pious deed.

“Nothing good,” he said, “am I conscious of having done. This one thing, however, I know: when I was among robbers, a virgin consecrated to God was once captured by us. When the rest of my fellow robbers wished to violate her chastity, I threw myself into their midst and rescued her from their contamination. I led her during the night as far as the village and restored her unharmed to her own house.”

At another time, he said (Palladius, chapter 63):

“I found a woman of respectable appearance wandering in the desert. When I asked her why or how she had come to those places, she replied:

“‘Ask me nothing, most wretched woman that I am, and do not inquire into my circumstances. If you are willing to have a servant, take me wherever you wish. For I have an unfortunate husband who, because of a fiscal debt, is often hanged and scourged and subjected to every punishment, and is kept in prison; he is brought out for no other reason than to suffer tortures. We had three sons, but they too have already been sold because of the same debt. I also, miserable woman that I am, am being sought for similar punishments. Fleeing from place to place, exhausted by hunger and misery, I now wander in hiding through these regions, having gone three days without food.’

“When I heard this, I took pity on her and brought her to my cave. After restoring her spirit, which had collapsed from hunger, I also gave her three hundred solidi. With this money, she said, she and her husband and sons were bound not merely to slavery but even to punishments. After returning her to the city, the money freed them all.

“Then Father Paphnutius said:

“‘I have done nothing of this kind. Yet I believe that the famous name of Paphnutius is also known to you among the monks. For I have devoted no ordinary effort to cultivating my life in such disciplines. God has therefore revealed to me concerning you that, in his sight, you possess no less merit than I do. Since, then, brother, you see that you are held in no small esteem by God, do not neglect your soul.’

“Immediately the musician threw away the pipes he carried in his hand and followed him into the desert. Changing his musical art into the spiritual harmony of life and mind, he devoted himself for three full years to the strictest abstinence, exercising himself day and night in psalms and prayers. Traveling the heavenly road through the virtues of his soul, he gave up his spirit amid the angelic choirs of the saints.”

After Paphnutius had sent the aforesaid musician, perfected in every exercise of virtue, ahead to the Lord, he himself practiced more rigorous disciplines than before. Again he besought the Lord to show him who on earth was like him.

Once more the Lord’s voice came to him, saying:

“Know that you are like the principal man of the neighboring village.”

When he heard this, Paphnutius hurried there without delay and knocked at the door of his house. The man, who was accustomed to receive guests, came out to meet him, brought him into his house, washed his feet, set a table before him, and prepared a banquet.

During the meal, Paphnutius began asking his host what conduct he practiced, what pursuits he cultivated, and what work occupied him. Although the man answered humbly about himself and preferred to keep his good deeds hidden rather than make them public, Paphnutius pressed him hard, saying that the Lord had revealed to him that he was worthy of sharing in the company of monks.

The man, thinking even more humbly of himself, replied:

“I am conscious of no good in myself. Yet since the word of God has come to you, I cannot conceal them from him from whom nothing is hidden. I will therefore tell you what I practice while living among the multitude.

“It is now thirty years since anyone has known that my wife and I have agreed to continence. I have had three sons by her; for the sake of these alone I have known my wife, and no other woman, nor she again thereafter.

“I have never ceased receiving guests, and I have done so in such a way that I would allow no one to meet a stranger arriving before I did. I have never allowed a guest to leave my house without provisions for the journey. I have despised no poor person, but have supplied whatever was necessary.

“When I have sat in judgment, I have not accepted even my own son’s person against justice. The fruit of another’s labor has never entered my house.

“When I have seen a lawsuit, I have never passed it by until I had reconciled the disputants to peace. No one has ever caught my servants in wrongdoing. My flocks have never damaged another person’s crops.

“I have never prevented anyone who wished to sow in my field, nor have I chosen the more fertile new fields for myself and left the poorer ones to them. As far as it lay within my power, I have never allowed the stronger to oppress the weaker.

“I have always taken care in my life never to cause anyone grief. When I have been head of a court, I have condemned no one, but have tried to restore disputants to harmony. This, by God’s gift, has thus far been the rule of my life.”

When blessed Paphnutius heard these things, he kissed the man’s head and blessed him, saying:

“May the Lord bless you from Zion, and may you see the good things that are in Jerusalem” (Psalm 127).

“Since you have fulfilled these things well and appropriately, one thing is still lacking—the highest of all good things: that, leaving everything behind, you should now follow the true wisdom of God itself and seek its more hidden treasures. You will not be able to reach them in any other way than by denying yourself, taking up your cross, and following Christ.”

When the man heard this, he did not delay at all or make any arrangements in his house, but followed the man of God and went with him into the desert.

When they came to a river and found no boat anywhere with which to cross, Paphnutius ordered him to enter the river on foot with him, although the water was deep in those regions. They crossed the river together, and the water scarcely reached their sides.

When they came to the desert, Paphnutius placed the man in a small cell not far from his own monastery, gave him the rule of spiritual conduct, taught him the exercises of perfect disciplines, and entrusted him with the deeper secrets of knowledge.

After instructing him in everything, Paphnutius again devoted himself to greater exercises, regarding his former labors as slight compared with those to which the man who had been occupied with worldly affairs could now be subjected. For he said to himself:

“If those who live in the world perform so much good work, how much more—or how much beyond them—ought we to surpass them in the labor of abstinence?”

After some time had passed in these practices, and after the man had been brought to perfection in knowledge—he whom Paphnutius had already accepted as perfect in works—Paphnutius was one day sitting in his cell when he saw the man’s soul being taken up among the choirs of angels. They were saying:

“Blessed is he whom you chose and took up; he shall dwell in your tents” (Psalm 64).

When he heard this, he understood that the man had been taken from this world. Paphnutius then continued in fasts and prayers, extending himself toward greater and more perfect things.

Again he prayed to the Lord (Palladius, chapter 65) to show him to whom he was considered similar among human beings.

Again the divine voice answered him:

“You are like the merchant whom you will see coming to you. Rise quickly and go to meet him, for the man whom I have declared to be like you is here.”

Paphnutius immediately went down and met a certain Alexandrian merchant who was transporting merchandise worth twenty thousand solidi on three ships from the Thebaid. Since the merchant was religious and devoted to good works, he was sending ten sacks of vegetables, loaded onto his servants, to the monastery of the man of God. This was the reason he was going to Paphnutius.

As soon as Paphnutius saw him, he said:

“What are you doing, O most precious soul, worthy of God? Why do you labor over earthly things, you to whom a portion and fellowship with heavenly beings have been given? Leave these things to those who are of the earth and think about the earth. But you, become a merchant of the kingdom of God, to which you have been called, and follow the Savior, by whom you will shortly be taken up.”

The merchant did not delay at all. He ordered his servants to distribute everything that remained—he himself had already distributed much—to the poor. Then he followed Saint Paphnutius into the desert and was settled by him in the same place from which the earlier men had been taken to the Lord.

In the same way, instructed by him in everything, he persevered in spiritual exercises and in the pursuit of divine wisdom. After a short time had been completed, he too was transferred to the congregation of the righteous.

Not long afterward, while Paphnutius himself was spending his life in the exercises and labors of the strictest abstinence, an angel of the Lord stood beside him and said:

“Come now, blessed one, and enter the eternal tents that are owed to you. For the Prophets are here, ready to receive you into their choir. I did not reveal this to you earlier lest, perhaps becoming exalted, you should suffer some loss of your labor.”

After this, while he was still in the body, he lived one more day. When certain presbyters came to visit him, he made known to them everything the Lord had revealed to him, saying that no one in this world ought to be despised—even if he is a robber, or employed on the stage, even if he works the soil and seems bound by marriage, even if he is called a merchant and serves commerce. In every condition of human life there are souls pleasing to God, possessing certain hidden deeds in which God delights.

Thus it is clear that God is pleased not so much by a profession of life or an outward appearance as by sincerity, the disposition of the mind, and the integrity of one’s works.

After he had discussed similar matters concerning each person, he gave up his spirit. The presbyters who were present clearly saw him received by angels, who sang hymns and praised God together.

## CHAPTER XVII. ON THE MONASTERY OF ABBOT ISIDORE

[Note: [Col. 0439D] On him, Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 28, and Book VIII, chapters 12 and 13; Socrates, Book VI, chapter 9; Nicephorus, Book VIII, chapter 34; Cassiodorus, Book VIII of the *Tripartite History*, chapter 1. Saint Jerome numbers him among the Origenists in his letter to Ctesiphon. It should be considered whether he was also among the monks who later repented, concerning whom I dealt in Prolegomenon 15, in the response to the second argument that was brought against the authority of these books. ROSWEYDUS.]

[Col. 0439C]

We also saw in the Thebaid the very famous monastery of Isidore (Palladius, chapter 71), surrounded by spacious grounds and enclosed by a wall. The men living there were provided with ample dwellings. Inside were several wells, irrigated gardens, orchards of every kind of fruit tree, and everything necessary for their needs, supplied sufficiently—indeed abundantly—so that none of the monks living inside would have any need to go outside to seek anything.

A certain grave old man, chosen from among the foremost, sat at the gate. His duty was to receive those who arrived under the rule that, once they had entered, they would not go out again. If someone once wished to enter, the rule stood immovable. What was more marvelous, however, was that those who had entered were held there no longer by the necessity of the rule but by the blessedness and perfection of the life itself.

This old man at the gate, where he himself lived, had beside him a guest cell, in which he received those who arrived as guests and refreshed them with every kindness. When we too had been received by him, we were not granted permission to enter, but from him we learned what blessedness of discipline was practiced within.

He said that only two elderly men were permitted the freedom to go out and come in. They were responsible for administering the brothers’ labors and bringing in whatever was necessary. All the others lived in such silence and tranquility, devoting themselves to prayers and religious pursuits and growing strong in the virtues of the soul, that they all performed signs.

The truly marvelous sign among all these things was that none of them ever suffered any illness. When the end of life came to each one, he knew it beforehand in every respect and announced his departure to his fellow brothers. Then, bidding farewell to everyone, he would lie down for that very purpose and joyfully give up his spirit.

## CHAPTER XVIII. ON SERAPION THE PRESBYTER

[Note: [Col. 0439D] Concerning this Serapion, see Palladius, chapter 76. There was also another man surnamed Sindonites, because a sindon was his only garment; he was uneducated in letters. See Palladius, chapter 83. Baronius, in his notes on the Roman Martyrology, March 21, improperly calls him Syndonius. The sayings of Serapion the abbot are found in Pelagius, booklet VI, no. 12; booklet VIII, no. 9; booklet XI, no. 13; and booklet XV, no. 16. Concerning him, Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 28, from whom Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 34, derived his account, as did Cassiodorus, *Tripartite History*, Book VIII, chapter 1. ROSWEYDUS.]

### ON SERAPION THE PRESBYTER

*(This passage is absent in Palladius.)*

We also saw in the region of Arsinoe a certain presbyter named Serapion, father of many monasteries. Under his care there were many different monasteries, containing, as it were, ten thousand monks. All of them lived from their own labors, which they especially obtained by the work of their hands during harvest time. They contributed the greater part of their earnings to the father mentioned above, and he assigned it to the uses of the poor.

It was customary not only among them but among nearly all the monks of Egypt to hire out their labor for reaping during harvest time. From this wage each man obtained, more or less, eighty *modii* of grain, and they offered the greater part of it for the needs of the poor. Thus not only were the needy of that region fed, but ships loaded with grain were also sent to Alexandria, to be distributed to those shut up in prison, as well as to other travelers and the needy.

For within Egypt itself there are not enough poor people to consume the fruits and gifts of their mercy.

We also saw in the regions of Memphis and Babylon innumerable multitudes of monks, among whom we observed various graces of virtue and adornments of character.

They say that there are places there where Joseph is reported to have stored grain; these they call the Treasuries of Joseph. Others identify them as the Pyramids, which they say are the very structures in which, as they believe, the grain was then gathered.

## CHAPTER XIX. ON APOLLONIUS THE MONK AND MARTYR

[Note: [Col. 0441D] Baronius, in his notes on the Roman Martyrology, March 8, thinks that this Apollonius and Philemon are the men commemorated there in the Martyrology. But if the Acts written by Metaphrastes are compared with this account, they do not correspond. In the Menaea I find the commemoration of the martyrs Apollonius and Philemon twice, with different companions: first on November 14, concerning whom the Roman Martyrology treats on March 8; second on July 6. Yet in neither place are their Acts given, so that no indication can be drawn from them. See Nicephorus, Book IX, chapter 1. ROSWEYDUS.]

[Col. 0441A]

The elders used to relate that during a time of persecution there was among them a certain monk named Apollonius (Palladius, chapter 66). He had led a distinguished life among the brothers and had also been ordained a deacon.

During the persecution, he made it his concern to visit each of the brothers and exhort them to martyrdom. When he too had been arrested and thrown into prison, many Gentiles came to him as though to mock him, reviling him with blasphemous and impious words.

Among them was a certain man named Philemon, a very famous flute-player and beloved by the whole people. He wearied Apollonius with many insults, calling him impious, wicked, and a deceiver, a seducer of many mortals, and one worthy to be hated by everyone.

When he had spoken these and many other, even harsher, things against him, Apollonius replied:

“May the Lord have mercy on you, my son, and may he not count any of the things you have said against you as sin.”

When Philemon heard this, his heart was pierced. He perceived in his mind the power of Apollonius’s words, which exceeded ordinary human experience, so strongly that he suddenly confessed himself to be a Christian.

Immediately he hurried to the judge’s tribunal and, proclaiming in the sight of the whole people, said:

“You are acting unjustly, O judge of iniquity, by punishing men who are religious and beloved by God. Christians neither do nor teach anything evil.”

When the judge heard this, he initially thought that, as a man of that locality, Philemon was merely making some kind of joke. But when he saw him persist in this with determination and assert it with complete steadfastness, he said:

“You are insane, Philemon, and have suddenly lost your mind.”

Philemon replied:

“I am not insane. You are the most unjust and insane judge, for you unjustly destroy so many righteous men. I am a Christian, and Christians are the best kind of human beings.”

Then, in the presence of the people, the judge first began trying to bring Philemon back to what he knew him to be through many blandishments. But when he saw that Philemon was unshakable, he directed every kind of torture against him.

When he learned that this change had come about through the words of Apollonius, he also seized Apollonius and subjected him to harsher tortures, intensifying the charge that he had deceived Philemon.

Apollonius said to him:

“Would that you, O judge, and all who stand by and hear me, might follow this error and deception of mine, as you call it!”

When the judge heard this, he ordered both Apollonius and Philemon to be handed over to the flames in the sight of the people.

After they had entered the fire, blessed Apollonius cried out to the Lord in the hearing of everyone:

“Do not hand over, O Lord, the souls of those who confess you to beasts” (Psalm 73), “but show us your salvation clearly” (Psalm 84).

When Apollonius had spoken these words to the Lord in the hearing of the people and the judge, a cloud suddenly filled with dew surrounded the men, and it extinguished the flames of the blazing fire.

The judge and the people were astonished, and all began crying out with one voice:

“Great and one is the God of the Christians; he alone is immortal.”

When this was reported to the Prefect of Alexandria, he became more savage than before. He selected certain men from his staff, the most cruel and savage—not so much men as beasts—and sent them to bind and bring to Alexandria both the judge who had believed in the divine miracles and those through whom God’s power had appeared.

As they were all being led away together in chains, the grace of God was present in the word. Apollonius began teaching the faith of God to those who were leading him away bound.

When they had believed in God’s mercy and received the faith of God with complete firmness of heart, they presented themselves to the judge in chains together with those whom they had come to bring. They likewise declared themselves to be Christians.

When the Prefect saw that they all remained steadfast and immovable in the faith of the Lord, he ordered them all to be plunged together into the depths of the sea, the impious man not knowing what he was doing. For to the saints this was not death but Baptism.

God’s providence undoubtedly brought their bodies whole and undefiled through the waters of the sea to the shore. Those who had come at the same time to perform the service received them, took them back, and placed them together in a single tomb.

From that place, many virtues and wondrous signs have been accomplished for everyone down to the present time. They also receive the vows and prayers of all, and these are fulfilled with the fruit of their petitions. The Lord also deigned to lead us there and fulfill our vows and prayers.

## CHAPTER XX. ON DIOSCORUS THE PRESBYTER

[Note: [Col. 0442D] Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 28; Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 34; Cassiodorus, Book VIII of the *Tripartite History*, chapter 1. ROSWEYDUS.]

We also saw another venerable father in the Thebaid (Palladius, chapter 68), named Dioscorus, a presbyter, who had nearly a hundred monks in his monastery. At the time when they approached the Sacraments, we observed him exercising the greatest care and diligence, lest any of those who approached should bear any stain upon his conscience. He even warned them about things that commonly happen to people through dreams, through phantasies of women appearing to them, or through an excess of natural bodily fluid.

He therefore said: “If such a thing occurs without phantasies of women, it is not sin. For the bodily fluid that is innate in the body, when it has filled its proper receptacles, must necessarily be discharged through its natural channels; and therefore it is not drawn into sin. But when visions of women and the allurements of the flesh occur, he affirmed that this already provided indications that the soul’s desires had become occupied with such matters, as well as with thoughts and enticements of this kind. Monks must therefore, he said, repel such images from their thoughts by every means, and must not at all indulge their senses in these blandishments of the devil; otherwise there will seem to be no difference between them and those who live in the world. Monks must also labor to subdue and overcome the natural fluid through much abstinence from food and frequent prayers, and must restrain its flowing pollution by continuing in prayer and fasting. Finally, he said, those who live in luxury, if an illness of the body should demand it, will abstain from everything that the physician has judged harmful. Why should a monk not do this all the more, since he ought to seek the health of soul and spirit?”

## CHAPTER XXI. ON THE MONKS DWELLING IN NITRIA

[Note: On the monks in Nitria. Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 36. “They call this place Nitria because there is a neighboring village where nitre is collected. It was not an insignificant multitude that practiced the monastic discipline there. For there were about fifty monasteries adjoining one another, some consisting of communities, others of men living separately.” Rosweyd.]

We shall now come to the famous place of Nitria, celebrated throughout all the monasteries of Egypt (Palladius, chapter 69). It lies about forty miles from Alexandria and takes its name from the neighboring village where nitre is collected. Divine providence, I believe, already foresaw that in those regions the sins of human beings would be washed away and abolished like filth.

In this place nearly fifty, or not many fewer, shelters may be seen, close to one another and placed under a single father. In some, several dwell together; in others, only a few; and in some, individuals live alone. Although separated in dwelling, they remain united and inseparable in mind, faith, and charity.

When we were approaching this place and they perceived that traveling brothers were arriving, each of them immediately rushed out of his cell like a swarm of bees and hastened toward us with joyful and eager speed. Many of them carried pitchers of water and loaves of bread, in accordance with what the Prophet says when reproving certain people: “Because you did not go out to meet the children of Israel with bread and water” (2 Esdras 13).

After receiving us, they first led us with psalms to the church, washed our feet, and each of them dried them with the linens he used, as though relieving the weariness of the road, but in truth washing away the troubles of human life through mystical traditions.

What shall I say now about their kindness, their services, and their charity, when each of them eagerly wished to bring us into his own cell—not merely to perform the duties owed to hospitality, but also to teach us about the humility in which they excelled, or about gentleness and other virtues of this kind, which they learned there, as men set apart from the world for this very purpose, through diverse grace yet one and the same teaching?

Nowhere did we see charity flourish so fully; nowhere did we see the work of mercy burn so intensely or the practice of hospitality so completely fulfilled. Nowhere did we see such devotion to the study and understanding of the divine Scriptures, or to divine knowledge, so that one might almost think each of them an orator accomplished in divine wisdom.

## CHAPTER XXII. ON THE PLACE CALLED CELLIA

[Note: Cellia. The same account is found in Palladius, chapter 69. From him, I believe, Sozomen derived it in Book VI, chapter 31, where he reports almost word for word the same things as Palladius and Rufinus. Here is the Greek that you have already read in Latin:

“But when they have reached the inner desert, there is another place, about seventy stadia distant, called Cellia. In it there are many monastic dwellings scattered about, and from this it received its name. They are so far separated from one another that those who live there can neither see nor hear one another. Yet they all come together and assemble for church on the first and last day of the week. If someone does not appear, it is evident that he has been unwillingly prevented, either confined by some affliction or illness. They do not all immediately go to see and care for him, but at different times each brings whatever he possesses that is suitable for the illness. Except for such a reason, they do not converse with one another unless for words directed toward knowledge of God or the benefit of the soul, or unless someone comes to learn from one who is able to teach. Those who have reached the summit of the philosophical life dwell in Cellia, and are able to govern themselves and to live alone, having separated themselves from the others for the sake of quiet.”]

The blessed Bernard, in his letter to the Carthusian brothers concerning the mountain of God, speaks elegantly of the cell and heaven:

“According to the form of your vocation, dwelling in heaven rather than in cells, you have excluded the whole world from yourselves and enclosed yourselves wholly with God. For the habitation of cells and of heaven are related: just as heaven and cell seem to have some kinship in their names, so also in piety. The names heaven and cell appear to derive from *caelare*, ‘to conceal’; and what is hidden in heaven is also hidden in cells. What is done in heaven is done in cells. What is this? To be free for God, to enjoy God. When this is piously and faithfully practiced in cells according to due order, I dare to say that the holy angels of God regard cells as heavens and take equal delight in cells and in heaven. For when heavenly things are continually performed in a cell, the heaven of the cell becomes near to heaven itself through the likeness of the sacrament, the affection of piety, and the effect of similar works. Nor is a long or difficult road now found by the praying spirit, or even by one leaving the body, from the cell to heaven. From the cell one often ascends to heaven; yet scarcely ever does one descend from the cell into hell.” Rosweyd.]

### Cellia

After this place there is another, deeper in the desert (Palladius, chapter 69), lying about ten miles from it. Because of the multitude of cells scattered throughout the wilderness, they called it Cellia. Those who had first been trained there and now wished, having laid aside their former garments, to lead a more secluded life withdrew to this place. The desert is vast, and the cells are so far separated from one another that they are neither within one another’s sight nor within hearing of one another’s voice.

They live individually in their cells. Great silence and profound quiet prevail among them. Only on Saturday and Sunday do they come together at the church, where they see one another as though restored to heaven.

If anyone should happen to be absent from that assembly, they immediately understand that he is being detained by some bodily ailment. All go to visit him—not all at once, but at different times—each carrying whatever he has that might be pleasing to the sick man. For no other reason does anyone dare to disturb his neighbor’s silence, unless perhaps he can instruct him by a word and, like an athlete placed in the contest, refresh him with the consolation of speech.

Many of them travel three or four miles to the church. Thus far apart are their cells. Yet such is the charity among them, and so strongly are they bound to one another and to all the brothers by affection, that they are an object of admiration and an example to everyone. Consequently, if anyone wishes to live with them, as soon as they understand this, each offers him his own cell.

## CHAPTER XXIII. ON AMMONIUS

[Note: On Ammonius. Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 30; Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 37; Cassiodorus, Book X of the Tripartite History, chapter 7. St Jerome notes that these men were struck by Origen’s thunderbolt in his letter to Ctesiphon. Nevertheless, they were extremely close to Chrysostom, and some are said to have been honorably buried and even to have become renowned for miracles.

George of Alexandria, in the Life of Saint Chrysostom, says the following about Ammonius and Dioscorus, speaking of those monks whom Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, expelled from the desert:

“Ammonius, together with two ascetic brothers and one bishop, who had also borne the collar and were exiled under Valens, as all Alexandria knows. They were so learned that nothing escaped them of the many things that perplex people in the divine Scriptures. Two of them died in Constantinople; Ammonius also prophesied concerning the time of his death. His tomb is said to cure those suffering from chills. He was buried in the shrine of the apostles beyond the sea. The bishop Dioscorus, having died, was himself buried in the shrine at the Oak by the gate, as has been said. Most of the women had great faith in him, and, abandoning the oaths of the martyr, swore by the prayers of Dioscorus.”

“Ammonius, together with two religious brothers and one bishop, who had endured fetters and savage tortures under Valens, were expelled from those territories, as all Alexandria acknowledges. He was sixty years old, and they were so learned that nothing in the divine Scriptures was hidden from them, although many others become stuck and hesitate over them. Two of them fell asleep in Constantinople, departing this life; Ammonius, however, before he left life, uttered oracles concerning future events. His monument is said to cure those suffering from feverish chills. He was buried across the sea, in a church dedicated to the apostles. Dioscorus the bishop, after he had died, was buried in the martyr-shrine situated at the Oak before the gate or column mentioned above. Many women relied upon him with steadfast faith, so that if any woman had bound herself by an oath through the prayers of Dioscorus, she would by no means have allowed herself to become a faithless deserter of her oath.

See also certain things said above, and said on behalf of these men, in Prolegomenon 15, where the authority of these books is discussed, in the response to the second argument. At least we may be secure through the warning of Saint Jerome.” Rosweyd.]

We saw among them a venerable father named Ammonius [Note: Palladius, chapter 12, relates certain things about him. Jerome testifies that he was an Origenist, along with Eusebius and Euthymius.], a man upon whom God had bestowed the fullness of every spiritual grace. When you saw the grace of charity in him, you would say that you had never seen anything like it anywhere. If you considered his humility, you would judge him far superior to the others in this gift. Again, if you considered his patience, gentleness, and kindness, you would judge him so outstanding in each virtue that you would not know which quality to prefer to another.

The Lord had also granted him such an abundance of the gift of wisdom and knowledge that you would think scarcely any of all the fathers had penetrated so deeply into the halls of every kind of knowledge. All who had seen him acknowledged that no one had been so admitted into the inner chamber of God’s wisdom.

[Note: He had two brothers, and so forth. These four were called the Long Ones because of their bodily stature. George of Alexandria, Life of Chrysostom: “For the men who presided over the monasteries in Egypt—pious Dioscorus, Ammonius, Eusebius, and Euthymius—were brothers and received the name Long Ones from their height. Their fame had spread remarkably throughout Alexandria, because they had become illustrious both in speech and in the adornments of their lives.” He continues at greater length about them. The same historians cited earlier speak of the same designation, the Long Ones. Rosweyd.]

He had two brothers, Eusebius and Euthymius. Dioscorus, who was the elder of them, [Note: To the office of bishop. Dioscorus was bishop of Hermopolis, as George of Alexandria says in the Life of Chrysostom, where, concerning his death, he adds: “Shortly after the flight of Theophilus he died, and was considered worthy of burial in a very splendid tomb in the church of the martyr at the Oak, where the synod of calumny against John was held. This place was across the sea, in the suburb of Rufinus, as Palladius says in the Dialogue on the Affairs of Saint Chrysostom, who had observed everything. Nicephorus, Book XIII, chapter 15, calls it the suburban harbor of Chalcedon, where there was an *Apostoleion*, that is, a church built by Rufinus in honor of the apostles Peter and Paul, together with various dwellings of monks.”]

Dioscorus was elevated to the office of bishop. These brothers were related to him not only by flesh, but also by life, training, and every virtue of the soul. Together they instructed and consoled all the brothers who lived in those regions, as a nurse nurtures her children, and they strove to bring each one up to the highest perfection.

[Note: George of Alexandria differs from the foregoing concerning the burial of Dioscorus, saying: “Dioscorus had first died in Constantinople and was buried in the church of the martyr Mocius. Ammonius, shortly afterward, when the synod was being prepared, came to the Oak while ill; but there his illness grew worse because of the crossing, and soon he too died and was honorably buried there by his monks.” The church of the martyr Mocius is placed by the *Menaea* on 11 May, within the city of Constantinople itself. The days 10 and 11 May have improperly been joined together in the *Menologion*. On this church, see Baronius, notes to the Roman Martyrology, 13 May. Rosweyd.]

We saw, then, the aforementioned man of God, Ammonius, who had a monastery among them enclosed by a wall. In those regions, such a structure can easily be made large from fired bricks [Note: Earlier editions appeared to read *crucis* (“of the cross”), a wholly corrupt reading, in place of *coctis* (“fired”), which we have restored.], and it was supplied with everything necessary. He had also dug a well there himself.

A certain brother came, wishing to be saved under his guidance, and approached Ammonius, asking whether there might be an empty cell in which he could live. Ammonius replied: “I shall look into it; but until I find one, remain here in this monastery. I shall go out now to search.”

He left everything to him, together with the monastery, and himself found a very small cell far from that place, where he settled. He ceded the monastery in its entirety, with everything in it, to the brother who had recently arrived, although the man did not understand what had happened.

If there had been several others who wished to come and seek salvation, the aforementioned man, with all the brothers assembled and eagerly assisting, would build a monastery in a single day. When he had completed the appropriate number of monasteries, those who were to remain were invited to the church as though for refreshment. While they were occupied there, each of the brothers brought out from his cell whatever was necessary and furnished the new cells of the individuals, so that through the contribution of charity absolutely nothing was lacking—not utensils, nor anything needed for food—yet no one’s individual offering became known.

When they returned in the evening to the cells that had been prepared for them, they found everything necessary for use already placed there, and their dwellings furnished in such a way that they perceived that absolutely nothing was lacking.

## CHAPTER XXIV. ON DIDYMUS

[Note: Nothing is found concerning this Didymus in Palladius, but he speaks of another blind Alexandrian, whose blindness is discussed in Book III of Rufinus, no. 218. I have found his memory in no sacred calendars except the manuscript *Florarium Sanctorum* under 11 April: “Saint Didymus the Hermit.” Socrates, Book IV, chapter 18, says of this same man: “Another Didymus, also a monk, lived for ninety years and associated with no human being until his death.” Suidas copied this word for word under “Amous.” Sozomen, Book IV, chapter 30, says that he flourished in Scete. Rosweyd.]

### DIDYMUS

(Palladius has no account here of the blind Didymus.)

We saw among them one of the elders, a good man named Didymus, in whom there was much of the Lord’s grace, which his very countenance also revealed. He trampled underfoot like mere worms of the earth and crushed scorpions, horned snakes—that is, the beasts they call horned—and serpents, which in those regions are regarded as especially fierce because of the intense heat of the sun. He suffered no harm from them at all.

## CHAPTER XXV. ON CRONIUS

[Note: On Cronius. Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 30: “Cronion, who had reached the age of one hundred and ten years.” Palladius, chapter 25, mentions Chronius the presbyter of Nitria, and in chapter 89 also mentions Chronius the presbyter, abbot of three hundred fathers in the desert near the village of Phoenica, from which he came. Palladius says that both were known to Antony. I doubt whether either of them is the same as this man. According to Sozomen, our Cronius flourished in Scete. Rosweyd.]

### CRONIUS

(Palladius, chapters 25 and 89, speaks of Croniuses who were known to Antony.)

We saw among them another father of extreme antiquity, named Cronius, continuing in a good old age and in the fullness of life. He was one hundred and ten years old. He was still one of the disciples of the blessed Antony, and among his other virtues of soul we observed in him an immense grace of humility.

## CHAPTER XXVI. ON ORIGEN

[Note: On Origen. Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 30: “The aged Origen, one of the remaining disciples of the great Antony.” He adds that Origen lived in Scete. Rosweyd.]

### ORIGEN

There was also another of Antony’s disciples, named Origen, a man magnificent in every respect and of the highest prudence. His speech and account of the virtues of his excellent teacher, the man of God, edified all who heard him and inflamed them intensely, so that you might think that the things he related could be seen with the eyes.

## CHAPTER XXVII. ON EVAGRIUS

[Note: Those who have had little knowledge of Evagrius’ affairs sometimes praise him, such as Socrates the Novatian, Book IV of the Ecclesiastical History, chapter 18, and likewise Sozomen the Novatian, Book VI, chapter 30. Gennadius does the same in his catalogue and even attributes miracles to Evagrius. But since Gennadius was excessively favorable to the Pelagians, it is not surprising that he should exalt Evagrius, the parent of the Pelagians, with praise and falsely attribute miracles to him. For the present we say nothing of Palladius the Galatian, who celebrated the same Evagrius magnificently, since, being his equal in impiety and heresy and his disciple, “a mule scratches a mule in return.” We shall speak of him in his proper place, Book VIII.

But if we assess Evagrius according to his true worth—that he was a heretical Origenist and offered the Pelagians the broadest material for error—it will seem astonishing if this is not already perfectly clear to everyone. Let us hear what the Fathers say about him.

Saint Jerome writes the following about Evagrius in his letter to Ctesiphon:

“Evagrius of Pontus, the Hyperborean, who writes to virgins, writes to monks, and writes to her whose name testifies to the darkness of unbelief”—he means Melania—“published a book and maxims *περὶ ἀπαθείας*, concerning *apatheia*, which we may call freedom from suffering or imperturbability: the condition in which the mind is never moved by any fault of disturbance. To put it plainly, such a person is either a stone or God. Throughout the East many read his books in Greek, and in the West many read them in Latin through the translation of his disciple Rufinus,” and so forth.

This is what Saint Jerome says. In the preface to Book IV on Jeremiah he also writes:

“I was dictating my commentaries on Jeremiah at intervals, so that what leisure lacked might be supplied by diligence, when suddenly the heresy of Pythagoras and Zeno—*ἀπαθεία καὶ ἀναμαρτησία*, that is, freedom from suffering and freedom from sin—which was once cut down in Origen and recently in his disciples Grunnius, Evagrius of Pontus, and Jovinian, began to revive and to hiss, not only in the regions of the West but also in those of the East, staining many in certain islands, especially Sicily and Rhodes, and increasing day by day, while they teach secretly and deny publicly.” He adds other statements in the same sense.

But how highly the Roman Church has always valued the judgment of Saint Jerome concerning those whom he censured—Rufinus, Evagrius, Palladius, and many others, whom he knew thoroughly from within and without—and concerning their writings, hear Saint Gelasius I, who at the Roman Council of seventy bishops delivered this memorable judgment:

“Likewise, Rufinus, a religious man, published many books of ecclesiastical works and also translated certain Scriptures. But because the blessed Jerome censured him in certain matters concerning free choice, we hold the opinions that we know the aforementioned blessed Jerome held.”

And this was said not only of Rufinus, but also of various others whom that often-mentioned man censured out of zeal for God and reverence for the faith.

This is what Saint Gelasius says. His testimony seems all the more firmly to be received and retained in the mind because divine providence arranged that Saint Jerome himself should expose publicly the frauds, devices, deceptions, and errors he had detected in many who, in his own time, spread the poisons of heresy under the appearance of religion and piety. The Roman Church approved his judgment in this matter so that thereafter so many wolves in sheep’s clothing would not be imposed upon the Lord’s flock and slaughter it, although otherwise they might have deceived even the most cautious and perceptive. Such were Rufinus, Evagrius, Palladius, and the other Origenist monks whom Saint Jerome, as we have just seen, identified.

But let us return to Evagrius, concerning whom Saint John Climacus also says:

“Evagrius thought that he was made the wisest of all through the quickness of his intellect; but, having suffered deception, the wretched man deceived himself. By this very fact he was shown to be the most foolish of fools.”

Climacus says this because Evagrius introduced *apatheia*.

Furthermore, Saint Tharasius, bishop of Constantinople, in the profession of faith found in the Second Council of Nicaea, session 3; Nicephorus, Book XVII of the Ecclesiastical History, chapter 27; and Cedrenus in his *Annals* under Justinian, state that Evagrius, together with Origen and Didymus of Alexandria, was condemned as a heretic and that his errors were proscribed in the Fifth General Council.

Saint Martin, pope and martyr, also condemned Evagrius together with the same Didymus and Origen at the Lateran Council, Secretariat 5, Canon 18. Antiochus the monk, who lived under Heraclius, likewise condemned them in his homily on the kingdom, numbered 130. After enumerating many heresiarchs, he adds:

“After these, the monsters of heresy were Evagrius and Didymus, who held, according to Origen’s doctrine, the pre-existence of things and their restoration.”

This is what he says.

From all this, and from other evidence that we omit, anyone may easily discern the status and worth that should be assigned to Evagrius of Pontus, the Hyperborean.

Thus far Brother John Maria, master of the Sacred Palace. Rosweyd.]

### EVAGRIUS

We saw there (Palladius, chapter 86) a most wise and altogether remarkable man named Evagrius. Among his other virtues of soul, he had been granted such grace for discerning spirits and purifying—as the Apostle says—thoughts, that no other brother was thought to have attained such subtle knowledge of spiritual matters. Although he had received great understanding through actual circumstances, experience, and—above all—through the grace of God, he had also been instructed for a long time by the blessed Macarius, whom everyone knew to be most renowned in the grace of God and distinguished by signs and virtues.

Evagrius was extraordinarily abstemious. Above all, however, he warned the brothers, if any of them wished either to humble the body or to drive away from it the phantasies of demons, not to drink water in excessive measure. For he said: “If much water is poured into the body, it generates greater phantasies and provides more ample receptacles for demons.” He also taught many other things about abstinence, with the greatest deliberation.

He himself not only used very little water, but abstained entirely from bread. The other brothers who lived in those regions were content with bread and salt alone, so that among that entire multitude one could scarcely find anyone who even used oil. Many of them did not sleep lying down, but sitting, and, so to speak, positioned in meditation upon the divine words.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. ON THE TWO MACARIUSES, AND FIRST ON MACARIUS THE EGYPTIAN

[Note: On the two Macariuses. There are two celebrated Macariuses in the Roman Martyrology, both Egyptians. The one discussed here is called simply and significantly “the Egyptian,” whereas the other is called “the Alexandrian” because he had served as a presbyter in the Alexandrian Church, as Palladius says in chapter 20.

Sozomen, Book III, chapter 13, distinguishes them as follows:

“One was called the Egyptian, the other the civic one, as a townsman, for he was Alexandrian by descent.”

One of them was born in the countryside of Egypt, the other in the city—for he was Alexandrian by origin—and was educated in civic institutions, so that he was called *ἀστός*, that is, “urban” or “a townsman.”

Socrates, Book IV, chapter 18, distinguishes them still more precisely:

“One was from Upper Egypt, the other from the city of the Alexandrians.”

Rosweyd.]

The Egyptian Macarius appears in the Roman Martyrology on 15 January: “In Egypt, Saint Macarius, abbot, disciple of the blessed Antony, most renowned for life and miracles.” See the *Menologion* under 19 January. He was the teacher of Evagrius, as Socrates writes in Book IV, chapter 18, and Gennadius in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 11. Rosweyd.]

### MACARIUS THE EGYPTIAN, OR THE ELDER

[Col. 0449C]

Certain fathers who were there told us (Palladius, chapters 19 and 20) that in those regions the two Macariuses shone like two lights of heaven. One was Egyptian by birth and a disciple of the blessed Antony; the other was Alexandrian. Their names corresponded, as did the magnificence of their virtues and heavenly graces.

Both were Macariuses; both excelled equally in exercises of abstinence and virtues of soul. One surpassed the other only in possessing, as it were, the inheritance of the graces and virtues of the blessed Antony.

They relate that on one occasion a murder had been committed in the neighboring region, and the crime was charged to an innocent man. The man who was suffering the accusation fled to Macarius’ cell. Those who were pressing the charge also came, alleging that they themselves would be in danger unless they handed the apprehended murderer over to the authorities.

The man against whom the crime was charged solemnly affirmed that he had no knowledge of the bloodshed. After the dispute had continued for a long time on both sides, Saint Macarius asked where the man said to have been killed had been buried. When they had indicated the place, he went to the tomb with all those who had come to press the charge. There, kneeling and invoking the name of Christ, he said to those standing by: “Now the Lord will show whether this man whom you are accusing is truly guilty.”

Then, raising his voice, he called the dead man by name. When the man, summoned from the tomb, answered him, Macarius said: “I adjure you by the faith of Christ: tell me whether you were killed by this man who is suffering the accusation.”

The man then answered from the tomb in a clear voice that he had not been killed by him. When everyone, struck with astonishment, fell to the ground and began to roll at Macarius’ feet, they asked him to inquire who had killed the man. He replied: “I shall not ask that. It is enough for me that the innocent be set free; it is not my concern to expose the guilty.”

Another kind of miracle was also related of him (Palladius, chapter 19). In a neighboring town, the virgin daughter of a certain head of a household appeared to people, through magical phantasies, to have been changed into a horse-like animal, so that she was thought to be a mare rather than a girl. They brought her to Macarius.

He asked what they wanted. Her parents replied: “This mare that your eyes see was once a virgin girl, our daughter. But wicked men have changed her through magical arts into the animal you see. We ask you to pray to the Lord to change her back into what she was.”

He replied: “I see this person whom you present to me as a girl; she has nothing of a beast in her. What you describe is not in her body but in the eyes of those who look upon her. These things are phantasies of demons, not the truth of reality.”

He brought her, together with her parents, into his cell, knelt down, and began to pray to the Lord. He also asked the parents to implore the Lord with him. After this, he anointed her with oil in the name of the Lord, and, once every deception of sight had been expelled, he caused her to appear to everyone—including herself—as a virgin girl.

Another, younger girl was also brought to him (this is absent from Palladius). The obscene disease of her body had so utterly putrefied every part of her that, once the flesh had been consumed, even her inner organs and private parts were exposed, and an innumerable multitude of worms boiled forth from her. No one could even approach her because of the horror of the stench.

When her parents had brought her and laid her before his door, he pitied the girl’s suffering and said: “Be of good courage, daughter. The Lord has given this to you for salvation, not for destruction. Therefore it must be seen to more carefully, lest your health bring you any danger.”

After persevering in prayer for seven continuous days and anointing her limbs with oil blessed in the Lord’s name, he restored her to such health that no form or appearance of female nature could be seen in her. She lived among men without any impediment arising from suspicion of her sex.

They also said (this is absent from Palladius) that a certain heretic named Hieracitas once came to him. This type of heresy is found in Egypt. By an elaborate art of speaking he had disturbed many of the brothers who lived in the desert, and he even dared to assert the perversity of his faith before Macarius himself.

When the elder resisted him and Hieracitas contradicted him, he evaded his simple words with cunning arguments. But when the saint saw that the faith of the brothers was in danger, he said: “Why should we contend with words to the overthrow of those who are listening? Let us go out to the graves of the brothers who have gone before us in the Lord. Let everyone know that the faith of whichever of us the Lord grants power to raise a dead man from the tomb is approved by God.”

All the brothers who were present approved this proposal. They went to the graves, and Macarius urged Hieracitas to call the dead man in the name of the Lord. Hieracitas replied: “You, sir, who proposed this, call him first.”

Macarius prostrated himself in prayer before the Lord. When he had prayed sufficiently, he raised his eyes toward heaven and said to the Lord: “Show, Lord, which of the two of us holds the true faith, by raising this dead man.” Then he called by name a brother who had recently been buried.

When the man answered him from the tomb, the brothers immediately approached, removed what had been placed over it, and brought him out of the grave alive, [Note: After the strips with which he had been bound had been undone. Thus John 11:44: “Bound hand and foot.” I remember reading a few other examples of this custom. Rosweyd.]

When Hieracitas saw this, he was dumbfounded and took flight. All the brothers pursued him and drove him beyond the boundaries of that land.

Many other things were also related about him, but they are too lengthy to write down. From these few examples, however, the rest of his works may also be recognized.

## CHAPTER XXIX. ON MACARIUS THE ALEXANDRIAN, OR THE YOUNGER

[Note: On Macarius the Alexandrian, or the Younger. The Roman Martyrology, 2 January: “In the Thebaid, Saint Macarius, abbot.” The *Menologion*, under both Macariuses, 19 January: “The memory of the holy fathers Macarius the Egyptian and Macarius the Alexandrian, who were renowned for monastic discipline, life, conduct, admirable abstinence, and miracles.”

Palladius, chapter 19, says that this one was somewhat younger than the Egyptian. Concerning both, see Socrates, Book IV, chapter 18; Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 29; Rufinus, Book II of the Ecclesiastical History, chapter 4; Jerome, Letter 27; Cassian, Conference V, chapter 12, and Conference XXIV, chapter 13; Palladius, chapters 19 and 20; Nicephorus, Book IX, chapter 14; Suidas, and others.

The question of the two Macariuses is plainly intricate, especially when one must determine which was Saint Antony’s disciple and thus establish anything certain about their birth. The old martyrologies acknowledge two Macariuses and distinguish one from the other only by calling one of them Antony’s disciple.

The old Roman Martyrology, 2 January: “The blessed Macarius.” 15 January: “Macarius, abbot, disciple of Antony.”

Bellini’s Roman Martyrology, 2 January: “In the Thebaid, Saint Macarius, abbot.” 15 January: “In Egypt, the blessed Macarius, abbot, disciple of the blessed Antony, most renowned for life and miracles.”

Galesinius’ Roman Martyrology, 2 January: “In the Thebaid, Saint Macarius the Alexandrian, abbot.” 15 January: “In the Thebaid, Saint Macarius, abbot, this man being the disciple of the blessed Antony.”

Baronius’ Roman Martyrology, 1 January: “In the Thebaid, Saint Macarius the Alexandrian, abbot.” 15 January: “In Egypt, Saint Macarius, abbot, disciple of the blessed Antony, most renowned for life and miracles.”

In Bede, Usuard, Ado, and Notker there is no distinction of place. Galesinius and Baronius established the distinction between the Alexandrian and the Egyptian.

If Rufinus is to be trusted—he states at the beginning of the preceding chapter that the Egyptian Macarius was Antony’s disciple and heir to his virtue—then the Martyrology correctly designates the Egyptian as Antony’s disciple on 15 January.
