Peter of Equilinum likewise makes Macarius the Egyptian Antony’s disciple in his *Catalogue of Saints*, Book II, chapters 35 and 81.

But it must be considered whether Rufinus misunderstood Palladius, or whether he misunderstood someone else whom he rendered in Latin. Certainly, neither Heraclides nor the old and new Palladius says of Macarius the Egyptian that he was Antony’s disciple and heir to his virtues. Indeed, the new Palladius of Hervetus, chapter 20, attributes both facts to Macarius the Alexandrian. Rosweyd.]

### MACARIUS THE ALEXANDRIAN, OR THE YOUNGER
Another Macarius (Palladius, chapters 19 and 20) was Saint Macarius [Col. 0453A], who also accomplished magnificent deeds of virtue, some of which others have recorded—enough, perhaps, to allow his greatness in virtue to be seen. We therefore pass over them briefly.

They nevertheless reported that he was more devoted to the desert than anyone else, so much so that he explored even the most remote and inaccessible regions of the wilderness, until he found a certain place situated at its farthest limits, planted with various fruit-bearing trees and filled with every good thing. There, it was said, he found two brothers. He asked them to allow monks to be brought there to live, since the place was pleasant and supplied with everything necessary. They replied that more people could not be brought there, lest those coming through the desert be deceived by demons. For they said that many demons and monsters inhabited the wilderness, whose annoyances and tricks an unaccustomed multitude could not endure. Nevertheless, when he returned to the brothers and told them about the suitability of the place, many were inflamed with enthusiasm to go there with him. But when the other fathers perceived that the young men’s spirits had been stirred, they restrained them with wiser counsel, saying:

“If this place truly was planted, as is claimed, by Jamnes and Mambres, nothing else should be believed about it except that it was prepared by the devil’s work for our deception. For if it is truly, as they report, delightful and abundant, what shall we hope for in the age to come if we enjoy delights here?”

Saying this and other things of the same kind, they restrained the young men’s ardent spirits.

[Col. 0453C] The place where Saint Macarius himself lived (John, little work III, no. 15) is called Scetis. It lies in a vast desert, a day and a night’s journey from the monasteries of Nitria. There is no path there, nor is it marked or indicated by any earthly signs; one travels by the signs and courses of the stars. Water is rarely found, and wherever it is found it has a very foul smell, almost like bitumen, though its taste is harmless. There are therefore men there who are exceedingly perfect—for so terrible a place permits only inhabitants of perfect purpose and supreme constancy—yet they show the greatest zeal in charity toward one another and toward all who may happen to come to them.

Finally, it is reported (Palladius, chapter 20) that once someone brought Saint Macarius a bunch of grapes. He, who according to charity considered not his own interests but those of another (1 Cor. 10), carried it to another brother, who seemed somewhat weaker. That brother then gave thanks to God for the other’s kindness, but he too, thinking more of his neighbor than of himself, carried it to another; and that man likewise carried it to another. Thus the grapes were passed through all the cells, which were scattered far apart from one another throughout the desert, without anyone knowing who had first sent them, until at last they were brought back to the one who had sent them. Saint Macarius rejoiced that he had seen such restraint and such charity among the brothers, and he extended himself to still harsher exercises of the spiritual life.

We have also received a trustworthy account about him from those who had heard it from his own mouth: at a certain time during the night, a demon knocked at the door of his cell, saying, “Rise, Abba Macarius, and let us go to the assembly, where the brothers are gathered for the vigils.” But Macarius, who was filled with God’s grace and could not be deceived, understood that this was a trick of the devil and said: “O liar and enemy of truth! What fellowship or association have you with the assembly and gathering of the saints?” The demon replied: “Do you not know, Macarius, that no assembly and no gathering of monks takes place without us? Come, then, and you will see our works.”

Then Macarius said: “May the Lord rebuke you, unclean demon” (Jude 9). Turning to prayer, he asked the Lord to show him whether what the demon had boasted was true. He therefore went to the assembly where the brothers celebrated the vigil, and again prayed to the Lord to show him the truth of this statement.

And behold, he saw throughout the entire church certain ugly little Ethiopian children running here and there, as though carried about in flight. It was their custom there that, while everyone sat, one person recited a psalm and the others either listened or responded. These little Ethiopians ran among the seated worshipers, playing with each of them. If they pressed someone’s eyes with two little fingers, he immediately fell asleep; but if they thrust a finger into someone’s mouth, they made him yawn.

When, after the psalm, the brothers threw themselves down to pray, the demons nevertheless ran among them all. Before one lying in prayer they appeared in the form of women; before another they appeared as builders carrying something [Col. 0454C]; and they seemed to be doing various other things. Whatever the demons had fashioned as a kind of game, the praying men were turning over in the thoughts of their hearts. Yet whenever they began to do some of these things to certain men, they were hurled headlong away as though repelled by a force, so that they did not dare stand near them or even pass beside them. With other, weaker brothers, however, they played upon their necks and backs, because those men were not attentive in their prayer.

When Saint Macarius saw this, he groaned deeply and, pouring out tears before the Lord, said: “Look, Lord, and do not be silent, nor be quiet, O God” (Ps. 82). “Arise, so that your enemies may be scattered and flee from your presence, for our soul is filled with illusions” (Ps. 67).

After the prayer, however, in order to examine the truth, he summoned separately each of the brothers before whose faces he had seen demons playing in different dress and with various appearances. He asked whether, during prayer, they had entertained thoughts of building, traveling, or anything else that he had seen represented by the demons before each of them. Each confessed that these thoughts had indeed been present in his heart, just as Macarius had said. It was then understood that all the vain and superfluous thoughts which each person conceived during the psalms or prayers arose from the demons’ deception. But the ugly Ethiopians are driven away from those who guard their hearts with every vigilance. For a mind joined to God and intent upon him, especially at the time of prayer, receives nothing alien and nothing superfluous.

[Col. 0455A] He also added something much more terrifying, which he had seen at the time when the brothers approached the sacraments. When they stretched out their hands to receive them, he saw Ethiopians hastening ahead and placing coals in the hands of some, while the Body that appeared to be handed over by the priest’s hands returned to the altar. But when others, aided by the merits of better conduct, extended their hands toward the altar, he saw the demons withdraw far away and flee in great fear. For he saw an angel of the Lord standing beside the altar; when the priest distributed the sacraments, the angel placed his own hand over the priest’s hand.

From that time onward, God granted him this grace: during the brothers’ vigils, at the time of the psalms and prayer, he recognized whenever anyone entertained some other thought in his heart according to the demons’ deception; and among those approaching the altar, neither their unworthiness nor their merits remained hidden from him.

At another time (Palladius, chapters 19 and 20; John, little work III, no. 15), the two men of God named Macarius were traveling to visit a certain brother. They boarded a vessel of the kind used to cross the river. On the vessel were certain tribunes—wealthy and powerful men—with many horses and servants and much equipment. One of them, seeing the monks lying at the rear of the vessel in cheap clothing and unencumbered by anything, said to them: “You are blessed, you who mock this world and ask nothing from it except the cheapest clothing and the scantiest food.”

Then one of the Macariuses replied: “Indeed, as you say, those who follow God mock the world; but we pity you, because, on the contrary, the world mocks you.”

Struck by these words, the man, as soon as he reached his home, abandoned or sold everything he possessed and gave it to the poor. He himself began to follow God and hastened to the exercises of the monks.

Many other wonders, as we have said, are also reported concerning the works of Saint Macarius of Alexandria. Some of them have been inserted in Book XI [Note: [Col. 0456D] Since he writes under another’s name and not his own, as was shown above, Rufinus also avoids claiming that book of Ecclesiastical History as his own, lest he thereby reveal himself as its author. What is reported concerning Macarius may be found in chapters 4 and 8.] of the Ecclesiastical History; whoever seeks them will find them.

## CHAPTER XXX. ON AMMON

[Note: [Col. 0455D] Concerning Ammon. The Greek Menologion, 4 October: “Commemoration of Saint Ammon, the Egyptian Father.” Since he was Egyptian by birth and had been deprived of his parents, he was compelled by his uncle to marry under the Emperor Maximian. He lived with his wife for eighteen years, treating her not as a wife but as a sister; indeed, he persuaded her to preserve her virginity. Accordingly, leaving both her and all his possessions behind, he withdrew to Mount Nitria near the Egyptian desert, covering his body night and day with only one garment. He continued his way until the time of the great Antony under the great Constantine, the renowned and first Christian emperor. Antony admired this man’s holiness, especially because God’s goodness performed many miracles through him, a large part of which may be found on the same day in the Greek Menaea. They add: Αὐτὸς ἦν σχολάζων ἐν τῷ βαλσαμῶνι, πολὺν αὐτῷ πόνον καὶ κόπον παρέχοντι, “He was occupied with the balsam plant, which caused him much labor and toil”; in Palladius this is rendered: “He worked with balsam,” in cultivating and pruning which much labor is required. In Suidas he is called Αἰμοῦς, Αἰγύπτιος, “Aemus, Egyptian,” and Suidas contains a brief summary of his Life. ROSWEYDUS.] AMMON, THE FIRST MONK OF NITRIA

The beginning of the monastic settlements in Nitria was said to have originated with a certain Ammon, whose soul Saint Antony saw being carried up to heaven when it departed from the body, as the writing that describes the Life of blessed Antony relates. This Ammon, then, was born to wealthy and noble parents, who unwillingly compelled him to marry. Since he could not escape his parents’ force, he took a young woman as his wife. When they had entered the bridal chamber and the private silence of the room had been granted to them, he spoke to the girl about chastity and began to exhort her to preserve her virginity, saying:

“Since corruption undoubtedly finds corruption, while incorruption hopes for incorruption, it is much better if both of us persevere in virginity than that one of us be corrupted by the other.”

The virgin consented, and the treasure of incorruption was hidden in silence. For a long time they were content with God alone as their witness and were joined more in spirit than in flesh and blood. After both their parents had died, he withdrew to a place near the desert, while the virgin remained within the house. In a short time, she gathered a multitude of virgins, and he gathered a multitude of monks.

When he was already living in seclusion in the desert, a young man who had been driven mad by the bite of a rabid dog was brought to him, bound with many chains. His parents accompanied him and pleaded on his behalf. But Ammon said to them: “Why do you trouble me, men? What you ask is beyond my merits. Nevertheless, I can tell you that his healing is in your hands. Return to the widow her ox, which you stole, and your son will be restored to health.”

They were greatly terrified that things done secretly had not been hidden from the man of God. Yet they rejoiced that he had shown them this path to salvation. Without delay, when they had returned what they had taken, and the man of God had prayed, the young man was restored to health.

At another time, some men came to him. Wishing to test their dispositions, he said that he needed a jar in which to collect water for visitors. When they promised to carry one to him, one of them considered it a heavy burden, saying that his camel might be endangered if he placed such a weight upon it. He said to the other: “If you wish or are able, carry it. I shall spare my camel so that it does not die.”

The other replied: “As you know, I do not have a camel, but a donkey. Can a donkey carry what a camel cannot bear?”

The first answered: “Do as you wish; you will see. I shall not kill my camel.”

Then the other said: “I shall place upon my donkey a burden which you say is too heavy for your camel, and the merits of the man of God will make the impossible possible.”

He placed the jar upon his donkey and proceeded to the monastery of the man of God, with the result that the donkey did not even feel that it was carrying any burden. When Ammon saw him, he said: “You have done well to carry the jar on a donkey, for your companion’s camel has died.” When the man returned, he found that events had occurred just as the servant of God had foretold.

The Lord also displayed many other signs through him. When Ammon wished to cross the Nile and was ashamed to undress, he is said by God’s power to have been suddenly transported to the opposite bank. Blessed Antony is reported to have held his righteousness of life and the virtues of his soul in the highest admiration.

## CHAPTER XXXI. ON PAUL THE SIMPLE

[Note: [Col. 0457D] His commemoration is on 7 March in the Roman Martyrology: “In the Thebaid, Saint Paul, surnamed the Simple.” The Greek Menologion: “Of the holy father Paul, surnamed the Simple, because of his upright and simple integrity, proved by blessed and great Antony in many ways; God himself also confirmed it by miracles, as written records testify.” The Menaea on the same day recount his Life at considerable length. In the Triodion, p. 32a, he is called Παῦλος ὁ Ἁπλούστατος, “Paul the Most Simple.” Here [Col. 0458D] in Rufinus, Book III, no. 167, and in Pelagius, Book XVIII, no. 20, and in Paschasius, chapter 23, no. 2, you find his singular privilege of perceiving the thoughts of individuals. The last of these has almost the same wording as Rufinus here. [Note: [Col. 0458D] We have said a hundred times that the book falsely bears Rufinus’s name.] Some books do not contain this Paul in this book and place, but either in Book I after the Life of Malchus or in Book III among the Sayings of the Elders. ROSWEYDUS.] PAUL THE SIMPLE

There was among the disciples of Saint Antony a certain man named Paul, surnamed the Simple (Palladius, chapter 28). The beginning of his conversion was as follows.

When he saw his wife lying with an adulterer, he said nothing to anyone, left the house, and, stricken with grief of soul, devoted himself to the desert. As he wandered there in anguish, he came to Antony’s monastery and, prompted by the suitability and convenience of the place, conceived the idea of seeking counsel. When he approached Antony to inquire from him about the way of salvation, Antony, perceiving that he was a man of simple nature, replied that he could be saved only if he obeyed whatever Antony said to him.

Paul answered that he would do everything Antony commanded. To test his promise, Antony said to him as he stood before the door of the cell: “Wait here praying until I come out.” Antony then went inside and remained there for the entire day and the entire night. Through a window, however, he frequently looked out secretly and saw Paul praying without interruption, not moving at all, but standing in the heat of day and the dew of night, and remembering the command so faithfully that he did not shift his position even slightly.

The next day Antony came out and began to instruct and teach him how he should relieve the solitude through the work of his hands: working with the fingers of his body at physical labor, but with the understanding of his mind and the attention of his soul at the things of God. He also ordered him to take food in the evening, but to take care never to reach satiety, especially in drinking. He affirmed that mental fantasies were produced no less by an abundance of water than bodily heat was increased by wine. When he had fully instructed him how he ought to conduct himself in every matter, he established a cell for him nearby, three miles from his own, and ordered him to practice there what he had learned. He himself nevertheless visited him frequently and rejoiced when he found him persevering with complete attention and diligence in what had been handed down to him.

One day, brothers came to Saint Antony—men of great stature and perfection—and Paul happened to be present with them. As they discussed profound and mystical matters and treated extensively of the Prophets and the Savior, Paul, in the simplicity of his mind, asked whether Christ had existed first or the Prophets.

Blessed Antony, almost ashamed that he had asked such an absurd question, gave him the gentle nod that he used with simpler people and ordered him to be silent and leave. Since Paul had undertaken to observe everything Antony said as though it were a command from God, he withdrew to his cell and, taking this as a command, began to keep silence and did not speak at all.

When Antony discovered this, he began to wonder why Paul had adopted this observance, knowing that he had not commanded it. When he ordered him to speak and to say why he was silent, Paul replied: “Father, you told me to go away and be silent.”

Antony was astonished that Paul had observed so carefully a statement which he had uttered carelessly. “This man condemns us all,” he said. “Although we do not hear anyone speaking to us from heaven, this man observes whatever kind of word falls from our mouths.”

Saint Antony also wished to teach him much about obedience. He was therefore accustomed to command him to do things which reason and necessity did not require, in order to test his disposition toward obedience. At times he ordered him to draw water from a well and pour it out on the ground all day; to undo woven baskets and weave them again; to tear apart a garment, sew it again, and then undo it once more. He is said to have been trained in many exercises of this kind, so that he learned not to contradict at all even commands issued against reason. Thus formed through all these things, he soon reached perfection.

From his example blessed Antony taught that if anyone wished to reach perfection quickly, he should not make himself his own teacher or obey his own desires, even if what he wished appeared right. Rather, according to the Savior’s command, each person must observe above all that he deny himself and renounce his own desires. For the Savior himself said: “I have come not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (Matt. 16).

The will of Christ, of course, was not contrary to the will of the Father. But since he had come to teach obedience, he would not have been found obedient if he had done his own will (John 6). How much more, then, shall we be judged disobedient if we do our own wills?

Finally, the Paul mentioned above is an example for us. Through the merit of his obedience and simplicity, he rose to such a height of spiritual graces that through him the Lord performed many more and greater miracles than through the second Antony.

Because many people from every part of the world flocked to him on account of the abundance of his graces, so that he might cure them, blessed Antony feared that the burden of the crowds would drive him away. He therefore made him live in the inner desert, where no one could easily approach, so that Antony himself might receive those who came. If Antony could not cure some of them, he sent them to Paul, who possessed a more extensive grace of healing, and they were cured by him.

They report that his simplicity had such confidence before the Lord that once, when a man suffering from rabies was tearing to pieces anyone who dared approach him, and the man had been brought to Paul, Paul persisted in prayer so that he might drive away the demon tormenting him. When there was delay and no immediate result followed, he is said, in the manner of a child, to have indignantly said to the Lord: “Truly, I shall not eat today if you do not cure him.”

Immediately, as though God were complying with a pampered master, the rabid man was cured.

## CHAPTER XXXII. ON PIAMMON

[Note: [Col. 0459D] Piammon. Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 28:

“Piammon and John at that time presided over the most distinguished monasteries around Diolcos in Egypt. Being presbyters, they exercised the priesthood with the greatest care and with great reverence. It is said that once, when Piammon was celebrating the sacred rites, he saw a divine angel standing beside the holy table and recording in a certain book those of the monks who were present, while erasing those who were absent.”

In addition, Piammon and John at that time presided over the most distinguished monasteries around Diolcos in Egypt. They exercised the priesthood with the greatest care and with the utmost reverence, for they were presbyters. It is reported that once, when Piammon was celebrating the sacred rite, he saw an angel of God standing beside the altar, writing the monks who were present in a book and erasing those who were absent. Nicephorus also speaks of him in Book XI, chapter 35. ROSWEYDUS.] PIAMMON THE PRESBYTER

(Palladius, chapter 72, concerning Ammon the presbyter, who is Piammon here.)

I do not think that the inhabitants of the desert bordering the Porthenian Sea and lying near the town called Diolcos should be passed over in silence. There we saw a certain presbyter, an admirable man named Piammon, endowed with every humility and kindness and also possessing the grace of revelations.

Once, while he was offering sacrifice to the Lord, he saw an angel of the Lord standing beside the altar and writing the names of each of the monks who approached the altar in a book that he held in his hands, while not writing the names of some. The elder carefully observed who those were whose names he had not written. After the sacred mysteries had been completed, he summoned each of them separately and asked what hidden sin they had committed. From their confessions he discovered that each was guilty of mortal sin.

He then urged them to do penance. Prostrating himself with them before the Lord, he wept day and night as though he himself were guilty of their sins. He remained with them in penitence and tears until he again saw the same angel standing and writing the names of those who approached. After he had written everyone’s name, he also saw him calling those men by name and inviting them to reconciliation at the altar.

When the elder saw this, he understood that their repentance had been accepted, and he restored them to the altar with complete rejoicing.

It was also reported that at one time he was beaten so severely by demons that he could neither stand nor move from his place. When Sunday came and circumstances required the sacrifice to be offered, he ordered the brothers to carry him in their hands to the altar. As he lay there in prayer, he immediately saw the angel of the Lord who was accustomed to stand beside the altar. The angel extended his hand to him and raised him from the ground. At once all pain departed from him, and he was restored even healthier than before.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. ON JOHN

[Note: [Col. 0460D] John. We have already given something concerning him from Sozomen in the preceding chapter. Sozomen adds:

“God granted John such power against afflictions and diseases that he healed many suffering from gout and many whose bodily joints had been dislocated.”

ROSWEYDUS.] JOHN

In those regions there was a holy man named John, filled with every gift of grace (Palladius, chapter 73). He possessed such an abundance of the grace of consolation that whatever sadness or weariness oppressed a soul, it was filled with cheerfulness and joy after only a few words from him. The Lord also granted him a very great gift of healing.

## EPILOGUE: THE DANGERS OF THE JOURNEY TO THE DESERTS

In many other places of Egypt as well, we saw scattered holy men of God, performing many acts of virtue and miracles and filled with every grace of God; but of the many we remembered only a few. To describe them all is beyond our strength.

1. Concerning those said to inhabit Upper Thebaid—that is, around Syene itself—we learned by hearsay alone that they were considered almost all greater and more magnificent than those we had seen. We could not approach them because of the danger of the journey. Although all the regions of those parts are subject to the incursions of robbers, those beyond the city of Lycus also suffer attacks from barbarians. Thus we had no access to them, since in truth we had not seen even those mentioned above without danger.

We were in danger seven times on this journey; but on the eighth, as it is written, “evil did not prevail against us” (Job 1), because God protected us in all things.

Once, finally, we traveled through the desert for five days and nights and were endangered by thirst and exhaustion.

2. At another time we came upon a place where there was a certain valley that generated salty moisture from within itself. The sun’s heat immediately congealed it into salt, as winter frost is congealed into ice, and formed sharp spikes from that salt. All those regions were so rough that they drilled through and cut not only bare feet, as ours were, but even feet protected by shoes. When we found ourselves among these obstacles, we escaped only with great difficulty and danger.

3. A third time, while we were continuing through the desert, we came upon a valley that likewise produced moisture from within itself but retained it inside. Wishing to cross its floor, which was filled with rocks and foul mud, we descended into it up to our sides. When we were almost submerged there, we cried out to the Lord and uttered the words of a psalm:

“Save me, O God, for the waters have entered even to my soul. I am stuck in the deep mire, and there is no firm ground” (Ps. 16).

4. We endured a fourth danger in certain waters that remained after the flooding of the Nile. Afflicted there for three consecutive days, we scarcely managed to escape.

5. A fifth danger came from robbers when we were traveling beside the sea. They pursued us for ten thousand paces and, although they could not kill us with the sword, almost reduced us to lifelessness through the flight.

6. Our sixth danger occurred in the Nile itself, where, while traveling by boat, we were almost drowned.

7. In the seventh, during a violent wind on the lake called Maria, we were driven onto a certain island. A severe winter lay upon us, and a storm raged violently. It was the season when the days of Epiphany are celebrated.

8. The eighth occurred when we were coming to the monasteries of Nitria. We came upon a place where the receding waters of the Nile had collected and formed something like a lake, in which there were many beasts, especially numerous crocodiles. When they had come out in the heat of the sun, they lay scattered around the edge of the lake, relaxed and motionless, so that to us, who did not know otherwise, they appeared dead. As we approached to see and marvel at the size of the beasts, which we thought lifeless, as soon as they sensed the sound of our footsteps, they awoke and began to rush upon and pursue us violently.

We, with a great cry and groaning, invoked the name of Christ the Lord. His mercy came to our aid, and the beasts that had risen against us were immediately thrown back into the lake, as though repelled by an angel. We hastened toward the monasteries at full speed, giving thanks to our God, who delivered us from such great dangers and showed us such great wonders.

To him be glory and honor forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0461]

## PREFACE OF RUFINUS, PRESBYTER OF AQUILEIA, TO CHROMATIUS, BISHOP OF AQUILEIA, CONCERNING HIS OWN LATIN HISTORY AND THE LATIN HISTORY OF EUSEBIUS OF CAESAREA, WHICH HE TRANSLATED

(C, S)

[Note: [Col. 0461C] Barraeus writes “Supreme Pontiff,” certainly incorrectly; yet I have no doubt that he followed his manuscript exemplar. Since in ancient books, as also in Sichard’s first edition, Chromatius is written “Roman Bishop”—a matter that has been debated so extensively among the learned—the copyist of the Barraeus manuscript thought himself entitled to call him “Supreme Pontiff,” since he supposed that the man who was called the bishop of the City must be the bishop of Rome. I shall discuss below another interpolation of the Vatican codices arising from this same cause. Albinus is thought to have provided an occasion for the error in his Book Against the Heresy of Felix, in an old manuscript among the Palatine manuscripts of the Vatican Library—cited by Fontaninus, who considers it to have been written seven hundred years ago—which, among other testimonies of Latin Fathers following the Greek ones, has on folio 12: “Chromatius also, holy bishop of the Roman Church, in the little book which he wrote on the Eight Beatitudes,” and so forth. The aforementioned Fontaninus orders that “Roman” be understood as “Latin,” as though it said “from the Western, or Latin, Church.” In any case, this Chromatius is far too well known to require a verbal introduction. Jerome dedicated some of his works to him and in their prefaces calls him “the holiest and most learned of bishops.”]

### Preface

209–210 Learned men say that it is the duty of physicians, when they see general diseases threatening cities or regions, to provide some kind of medicine or drink by which people, having been fortified, may be protected from the impending destruction.

You too, Venerable Father Chromatius, carrying out this kind of medical treatment, at the time when, after the gates of Italy had been burst open by Alaric, leader of the Goths, a pestilential disease spread through the land and devastated fields, cattle, and men far and wide, sought some remedy for the deadly destruction threatening the peoples entrusted to you by God.

[Note: [Col. 0462C] This indicates the first invasion of Italy by Alaric, leader of the Goths, after he had crossed the Julian Alps, in A.D. 400; for two further invasions occurred later, in the years 402 and 408. Yet, just as it is certain that he is not speaking of the third, since Chromatius, to whom the work is dedicated, was no longer alive at that time, so neither is it reasonable to believe that he is speaking of the second: as Fontaninus observes, he would have indicated it more explicitly, lest it be confused with the first; and this first invasion is indicated both here and throughout the whole subsequent context. One may nevertheless infer from this that Rufinus did not set his hand to the work immediately after that invasion, but after some interval of time, in order to provide some remedy for the disastrous outcome and, as it were, to induce forgetfulness of the evils then occurring. Thus Rufinus wrote this in the following year, 401. The recent editor of this History, Father Cacciarius, a Carmelite, although he does not deny that this very invasion is meant, errs in his chronological calculations: he thinks that Alaric began to ravage Italy in 401 and assigns this work of Rufinus to the following year, 402. He also misleads the reader by directing him to consult the second part of his Dissertation, where he does not speak of this matter even in a word. We shall not omit to praise what is good in that edition—its reporting of variant readings from the Vatican manuscripts and its addition of them to ours; as far as possible, we shall pass over the blemishes with which it abounds.] You sought a remedy by which sick minds, withdrawn from the contagion of the approaching evil, might be occupied with better pursuits and therefore ordered me to translate into Latin the Ecclesiastical History which the most learned Eusebius of Caesarea composed in Greek.

[Note: [Col. 0463A] According to two Vatican manuscripts, as Cacciarius testifies, the words “he composed” are present: “which the most learned Eusebius of Caesarea composed in Greek.”]

Through reading it, the minds of those listening would be held captive while they eagerly sought knowledge of past events and would in some way gain forgetfulness of the evils then taking place.

When I tried to excuse myself from this work, as one inferior and unequal to it, and as someone who, after so many years, had lost the practice of the Latin language, I considered that you were imposing this upon me not without some order of apostolic institution.

[Note: [Col. 0464A] The same Vatican manuscripts insert “of the Apostolic See.” This is what we meant when we said that ancient copyists, failing to understand in what manner or sense Chromatius was called “Roman Bishop” and “bishop of the Roman Church,” supposed that he was being designated as the actual bishop of the City and holder of the Roman see. They did not hesitate to interpolate their exemplars, writing “Supreme Pontiff” in the heading and here “by the institutional order of the Apostolic See.” Recall what we have just observed above (in this edition, Col. 0461, note a). Saint Jerome also calls Chromatius “holy and venerable Pope” in the preface to his Commentary on Habakkuk; but no one could have been misled by that old and commonly used form of honorific address.]

For when the Lord once said to the hungry crowds of his hearers in the desert, “Give them something to eat yourselves,” Philip, one of the Apostles, understanding that the signs of divine power shine forth all the more when they are accomplished through the services of lesser persons, did not produce loaves hidden in the Apostolic purse. Instead, he said that a boy was present who had five loaves and two fish.

He then added, excusing himself modestly: “But what are these among so many?” (Matt. 14; Mark 6; Luke 9), so that divine power might shine more clearly amid narrow resources and desperate circumstances.

Knowing, therefore, that you too had learned from such examples, and recalling that perhaps, following Philip’s example, when you saw that the time had come to feed the crowds, you had assigned a little boy who would present the five loaves, doubled from what he had received, and, to complete the Gospel mystery, would add two little fish caught by his own labor, I undertook to carry out as best I could what you had commanded. I was confident that the authority of the one giving the command would excuse the faults of my inexperience.

It must be understood that, since the tenth book of this work in the Greek version had very little concerning historical events and was otherwise occupied with panegyrical treatises on bishops, which contribute nothing to knowledge of events, we omitted what seemed superfluous and joined whatever history it contained to the ninth book, bringing Eusebius’s narrative [Alternative: “of the narrative”] to an end there. But we ourselves composed the tenth and eleventh books partly from the traditions of our predecessors and partly from what our own memory had embraced; and we added them, as it were, as two little fish to the loaves written above. If you [Note: Cacciarius, together with five Vatican manuscripts, places “or with” before this, and shortly afterward also incorrectly has “and,” followed by “thereafter.”] approve or bless them, I shall confidently believe that they will suffice for the crowds. The whole work, moreover, contains the events accomplished in the Church from the Savior’s Ascension onward. Our two little books, however, cover the period from the time of Constantine after the persecution up to the death of the Emperor Theodosius.

## Preface to the Two Following Books of His History

### Rufinus to the Reader

[Note: We have collated these Rufinian books against two old manuscript copies: one, also the better of the two, from the Guarnerian Library in the town of San Daniele; the other from Saint Savior’s in Bologna. More about these will be said in the Preface. The Guarnerian manuscript places before the work the heading “Rufinus to the Reader,” although it also has this same brief preface at the end of Book IX of Eusebius’s History.]

[Col. 0463]

**213–214** Up to this point Eusebius [Note: The Guarnerian manuscript adds “of Caesarea.”] has handed down to us the memory of events accomplished in the Church. The remaining events, however, which have followed in sequence down to the present time—whether we have found them in the writings of our predecessors or whether our own memory has reached them—we shall add briefly, as far as we can, obeying the religious commands of the Father [Chromatius] and following them in this matter also. [Note: Here the same manuscript adds: “or whatever our memory has reached,” and so on. The Bologna manuscript adds “we shall add.”]

# Book One

[Col. 0467]

## Chapter I. On the Heresy of Arius

[Col. 0467A]

**217–218** When Alexander had assumed the priesthood at Alexandria after Achillas, who had succeeded Peter the Martyr, because peace and rest from persecutions had come to us and the glory of the Churches rejoiced in the merits of the Confessors, the prosperity of our affairs was disturbed by domestic contention. For a certain presbyter at Alexandria, named Arius [Note: Cacciarius needlessly repeats about Arius what has been published in six hundred books; yet he does not know what would shed light on the author’s text. What our author says—“Arius, a man religious more in appearance and outward form than in virtue”—is closely parallel to Epiphanius: “He was tall, with downcast countenance, and the whole configuration of his body was composed like that of a deceitful serpent for fraud and trickery, so that by that crafty external appearance he could easily insinuate himself into simpler minds. For, wearing a shoulder-cloth and a short tunic, he was especially charming in conversations and greetings and held everyone’s minds bound by the allurements of flattery.” An extremely ancient fragment of a History of the Meletian Schism, published about seven years ago from a manuscript of the Church of Verona, likewise says: “A certain Arius, wearing the appearance of piety and possessing a desire to be a teacher.” This is what our author says, adding that he was shamefully desirous of glory, praise, and novelty. In place of “novelty,” the Guarnerian manuscript reads “nobility,” which I would almost prefer, although the copyist has marked beneath it letters to be deleted—namely the intervening “li”—so that “nobity,” that is, “novelty,” should be restored.]—a man religious more in appearance and outward form than in virtue, but shamefully desirous of glory, praise, and novelty—began to advance perverse opinions about the faith of Christ, opinions that had never before [Note: The Guarnerian manuscript reads “arisen.” On the basis of it, the Bologna manuscript, one Vatican manuscript, and several printed editions, we have restored “cut off” in place of “cut,” found in Barraeus and others, including manuscripts.] arisen. He tried to cut off and separate the Son from the eternal and ineffable substance or nature of God the Father. This matter disturbed very many people in the Church.

But when Bishop Alexander, naturally gentle and peaceful, sought through continual admonitions to recall Arius from his wicked undertaking and impious assertions, and the matter nevertheless did not proceed as he wished [Note: The same Guarnerian manuscript reads “did not proceed, and because …,” followed by “had been spread about.”], since the contagion of the deadly assertion had already infected many—not only at Alexandria but also, having spread through other cities and provinces—he believed it would be disastrous to disregard such things and reported the matter to many of his fellow priests. The question became more widely known. The report reached the ears of the devout ruler, who with every care and diligence attended to our affairs. Then, following the judgment of the priests, he summoned an episcopal council at the city of Nicaea (in the year 325), and ordered Arius to appear there before three hundred and eighteen bishops [Note: The Bologna manuscript reads “with every zeal”; shortly afterward the Guarnerian reads “in accordance with the judgment of the priests.” The sense of the passage is too clear to require extensive explanation: it must not appear that the Synod was convened by the Emperor’s authority, but rather with his favor, assistance, and consent. Also noteworthy is the Guarnerian manuscript’s reading “with the bishops presiding” instead of “in attendance.”] [Col. 0468A] who were in attendance, so that judgment might be passed on his propositions and questions.

## Chapter II. On the Council Assembled at Nicaea

I do not think that the Emperor’s remarkable action at that Council should be passed over in silence. For when bishops had gathered from almost every place and, as usually happens, had brought before one another various quarrels arising from different causes, he was frequently approached by individuals: written complaints were presented, accusations were put forward, and they devoted their attention more to these matters than to the matter for which they had come.

But when he saw that through such quarrels the cause of the great business was being frustrated [Alternative: “of this kind of quarrels”], he fixed a definite day [Alternative: “a definite date”] on which each bishop who appeared to have some complaint should bring it forward. When he had taken his seat, he received written complaints from each of them. Holding them all together in the fold of his robe and not revealing what they contained, he said to the bishops:

“God has appointed you priests and has given you power to judge even us [Alternative: “you as well”]; therefore we are rightly judged by you. But you cannot be judged by human beings. For this reason, await among yourselves the judgment of God alone, and let whatever quarrels you have be reserved for that divine examination. For you have been given to us by God as gods, and it is not fitting that a human being should judge gods; but let Him alone do so, of whom it is written: ‘God stands in the assembly of the gods; in the midst He distinguishes among the gods’ (Psalm 81:1). Therefore, leaving these matters aside, distinguish without any contention of minds [Note: Cacciarius reads “dissension,” although all printed books and all our manuscripts, as well as the two Vatican manuscripts he used, oppose him. Barraeus and others, following the printed edition, have “unbind”; two Vatican manuscripts have “discern.”] those things that concern the faith of God.”

When he had said this, he ordered all the written complaints to be burned at once, so that no human being might learn of the priests’ pretense.

But when for many days the question of faith was debated in the Council of Bishops, and some held different opinions and strongly supported Arius’s undertakings, there were nevertheless more who detested his impious project [Manuscript reading: “imperial project”]. Since there was also a great number of priests who were Confessors at that Council, all opposed the novelties of Arius. Men skilled in disputation supported him and, for that reason, hostile to the simplicity of the faith.

## Chapter III. On the Conversion of the Dialectical Philosopher

How great a power the simplicity of faith possesses, we recognize also from what is reported to have happened there. For, because of the zeal of the devout Emperor, priests of God had gathered from the whole earth, and philosophers and dialecticians, men very distinguished and highly renowned, also assembled, moved by the report. Among them was a certain outstanding expert in dialectical art, who every day [Note: Both our manuscripts read “a conflict”; shortly afterward the Guarnerian has “equally,” instead of “quite as well.” Here the second chapter begins with this sentence: “Among them was a certain outstanding man,” and so forth. Socrates also mentions, in Chapter 8, “many laymen skilled in dialectic” (λαϊκοὶ πολλοὶ διαλεκτικῆς ἔμπειροι), who took the side of Arius and whom a certain layman from the number of the Confessors, endowed with sound and simple understanding, refuted. Gelasius of Cyzicus, who transferred much from these books of Rufinus into his own account of the acts of the Nicene Synod, also narrates and amplifies this same story of the philosopher’s encounter with the Christian Confessor in Book II, Chapter 13.]

engaged in a contest of the highest intensity with our bishops, men also not inadequately trained in dialectic. A great spectacle resulted, as learned and literate men gathered to listen. Yet no one could confute or constrain the philosopher by any method. For he met the questions put to him with such skill in speaking that, precisely when he seemed most tightly trapped, he slipped away like a slippery snake. [Note: Cacciarius is less correct when he says “would slip,” against the testimony of both printed and manuscript books. Our manuscripts restore “would slip away,” whereas most others, together with the printed editions, have “would fall away.”]

But to show that the kingdom of God consists not in speech but in power, a man of utterly simple nature from among the Confessors was present among the other bishops listening [Manuscript reading: “a bishop.”] He knew nothing except Jesus Christ, and Him crucified. When he saw the philosopher insulting our men and vaunting himself through the subtle art of disputation, he asked everyone for an opportunity, saying that he wished to converse briefly with the philosopher.

Then our men, who knew only the man’s simplicity and lack of skill in speech [Alternative: “in the matter of speech”], began to fear and to feel a kind of shame, lest holy simplicity should become a laughingstock among clever men.

Nevertheless the old man persisted and began his speech as follows:

“In the name of Jesus Christ, philosopher, hear what is true. There is one God who made heaven and earth and who gave the human being, whom He had formed from the clay of the earth (Genesis 1), the spirit. By the power of His Word He created all things that are seen and unseen, and by the sanctification of His Spirit He established them. This Word and Wisdom, whom we call the Son, took pity on human errors, was born of a Virgin, and through the suffering of death freed us from everlasting death; by His resurrection He bestowed eternal life upon us. We also await Him as the Judge who will come to judge all that we do. Do you believe, philosopher, that this is so?” [Alternative: “these things”]

But the philosopher, as though he had never learned any speech of contradiction, was so astounded by the power of the words that, struck dumb before everything else, he could answer only that it seemed so to him, and that nothing else was true except what [Note: Previously the text had a different and less suitable sense: “than what he had said,” referring to the old man. On the authority of all our manuscripts, we have removed the relative pronoun and restored the more probable sense from the philosopher’s point of view. Shortly afterward, instead of “do you believe,” both the Bologna and Guarnerian manuscripts, as well as two Vatican manuscripts, read “have you believed.”] he had said.

Then the old man said: “If you believe that these things are so, rise and follow me to the Lord’s house [Note: The Guarnerian manuscript adds, in the hand of an ignorant annotator, “sheepfold.” No one is unaware that the Lord’s house means a church. Shortly afterward the Bologna manuscript incorrectly has “Come” instead of “Hear,” and two Vatican manuscripts have “all learned men” instead of “O learned men.”], and receive the seal of this faith.”

The philosopher then turned to his disciples, or to those who had gathered for the sake of hearing, and said:

“Hear, learned men: as long as the matter was conducted with me by words, I opposed words to words and overturned what was said by the art of speaking. But when power proceeded from the speaker’s mouth in place of words, words could not resist power, nor could a human being oppose God. Therefore, if any one of you has been able to perceive in these things that were said what I have perceived, let him believe in Christ and follow this old man, in whom God has spoken.”

Thus the philosopher became a Christian and at last rejoiced that he had been defeated.

## Chapter IV. On Paphnutius the Confessor

There was also at that Council Paphnutius, a man of God [Note: Socrates says that he served as bishop in the Upper Thebaid; nevertheless he does not mention him among those who attended the Council of Nicaea. Both our manuscripts, the Guarnerian and the Bologna, read “Maximinus.” Socrates does not name the emperor; yet he openly declares that he received these accounts—as also the following account of Spyridon and many subsequent matters—from a work by a certain Rufinus, a presbyter, written in the Latin language (συντάγματι Ῥουφίνου τινὸς πρεσβυτέρου, Ῥωμαϊκῇ λέξει συγγεγραμμένῳ).], a bishop from the regions of Egypt and a Confessor from among those whose right eyes Maximianus had gouged out and whose left knees he had severed, condemning them to the mines. Yet such grace of virtues was present in him that signs were performed through him no less than they had formerly been through the Apostles. For he drove out demons merely by a word and healed the sick by prayer alone; it is also said that he restored sight to the blind and brought the paralytic back to bodily strength [Alternative: “the bodies’ strength”].

Constantine held him in such reverence and affection that he often summoned him into the palace and embraced him, and with eager kisses caressed the eye that had been torn out in his confession of the faith.

## Chapter V. On Bishop Spyridon and His Miracles

**222** It is said that Spyridon the Cypriot, a bishop and one of the order of prophets, was also from their number—and perhaps something even more eminent—as we have learned from the account of those who saw him [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts used by Cacciarius read “from the account of our people” instead of “from their account.”] He remained a shepherd of sheep even after being placed in the episcopate.

One night, when thieves had come to the sheepfolds and had stretched out their criminal hands to make an entrance through which they could lead away the sheep, they were restrained by certain invisible bonds and remained until dawn as though handed over to torturers.

When the old man went out early to lead the sheep to pasture, he saw the young men hanging in the folds, bound without human bonds [Note: The Guarnerian manuscript omits the little word “in.”] When he had learned the cause of their offense, he released by a word those whom their deeds had bound. And so that their nighttime occupation might not prove fruitless, he said:

“Take one ram for yourselves, young men, lest you appear to have come without cause; it would have been more fitting to seek it by prayer than by theft.”

They also relate this remarkable event about him. He had a daughter named Irene, who, after serving him well, died while still a virgin. After her death, a certain man came saying that he had entrusted a deposit to her. Her father did not know what had happened. The entire house was searched, but what was demanded was found nowhere.

Nevertheless the man who had entrusted it persisted, pressing the matter with weeping and tears. He declared that he would also bring about his own death unless he recovered what had been entrusted.

Moved by his tears, the old man hurried to his daughter’s tomb and called to her by name. Then she spoke from the tomb:

“What do you want, father?”

“Where did you put the deposit that he entrusted to you?” he asked.

Pointing out the place, she replied: “You will find it buried there.”

He returned home and, finding the object just as his daughter had answered from the tomb, handed it over to the man who demanded it.

Many other remarkable deeds of his are also reported [Col. 0472A], and they are still celebrated on everyone’s lips.

Thus, even in those times, very many such men shone in the Churches of the Lord, and many of them were present at that Council.

Athanasius also, at that same time, was present as a deacon of the Alexandrian bishop [Note: Not only printed books but also some manuscripts, including the Bologna manuscript, have “of Alexandria” instead of “of Alexander,” just as Cacciarius restored it from the Vatican manuscripts. The Guarnerian manuscript, however, reads “A deacon of the Alexandrians, of Bishop Alexander.” In place of “of the Alexandrians,” I would prefer to restore the common reading “of Alexandria.” In any case, what follows, “very greatly,” is more correct than “very many.” I disregard Cacciarius’s faulty punctuation. Shortly afterward, two Vatican manuscripts read “was being conducted” instead of “was being debated.”], assisting the old man with his counsel in very many matters.

Meanwhile the assembly met day after day, and they did not easily or rashly dare to decide on so great a matter. Arius was frequently summoned before the Council, and his assertions were examined through continual discussion [Note: The Bologna manuscript has “his assertion was examined” in the singular; then it reads “by deliberation,” as Barraeus also preferred, instead of “by weighing.” “By deliberation” is not objectionable and is the reading of several manuscripts, but the printed reading is especially supported by the Guarnerian manuscript.]; what ought to be held or decreed against them was sought with the utmost deliberation.

After a long and extensive discussion, however, all agreed, and as though with one voice and one heart it was decreed that ὁμοούσιον—*homoousion*, “of the same substance”—should be written: that is, that the Son should be confessed to be of the same substance as the Father. This was proclaimed with the firmest judgment of all.

At that time only seventeen are said to have remained who preferred Arius’s faith: they affirmed that the Son of God had been created externally, from nothing, and not begotten from the very deity of the Father. The judgment of the priestly Council was reported to Constantine. He revered it as though it had been uttered by God. If anyone attempted to oppose it, he declared that he would send him into exile as one acting against divine decrees.

Six alone, together with Arius, allowed themselves to be expelled. The remaining eleven, after conferring among themselves, agreed to subscribe with the hand alone, but not with the mind. The chief author of this pretense was Eusebius, Bishop of Nicomedia [Note: The Bologna manuscript omits Eusebius’s name. Shortly afterward, the Guarnerian manuscript, together with others, reads “fixing decrees” instead of “inventing decrees”; that manuscript also has “events” instead of “certainly.”]

Meanwhile, while some subscribed in whatever manner—some sincerely, others deceitfully, as their subsequent end demonstrated—and while they established definite decrees concerning each of the ecclesiastical observances, the Council was dissolved.

The form of the confession of faith of those who had assembled is written below.

## Chapter VI. The Form of the Nicene Faith (A.D. 324)

[Note: The Guarnerian manuscript supplies the heading; Cacciarius omits the chapter designation.]

**224** We believe in one God, the almighty Father, maker of all things visible and invisible.

And in one Lord, our Jesus [Note: Here the same manuscript omits “Christ.” I will spare Cacciarius his miserable fuss over a matter of no importance, when he appeals to all the Vatican manuscripts for the following reading, “that is,” instead of “this is.”] Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, born from the Father—that is, from the substance of the Father—God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, ὁμοούσιον τῷ Πατρί, *homoousion to Patri*, “of the same substance as the Father”; through whom all things were made, both in heaven and [Col. 0473A] on earth. Who for us and for our salvation came down, was made incarnate and became human, suffered, rose again on the third day, and ascended into the heavens; from there He will come to judge the living and the dead.

And in the Holy Spirit.

But those who say that there was a time when He was not, and that before He was born He did not exist, and that He was made from nothing [Note: Barraeus noted in the margin “from existing things” as an alternative; the Vatican manuscripts are said to prefer “from subsisting things.”], or from another subsistence or substance; those who say that the Son of God is subject to change—τρεπτόν, or convertible or mutable—the Catholic [Note: The Guarnerian manuscript adds, not inappropriately: “The Catholic Church and the Apostolic faith anathematize.”] and Apostolic Church anathematizes.

## Canons of Nicaea

**1.** They further decree that the following be observed in the Churches: no one who has castrated himself through impatience of lust may enter the clergy.

[Col. 0473B] **II.** No one recently taken from a pagan way of life or manner of conduct may, after receiving baptism, become a cleric before he has been more carefully examined.

**III.** No bishop or other cleric may live with women unrelated to him, except with his mother, sister, θεία (*theia*, “aunt”), or any other persons connected by relationships of this kind.

**IV.** A bishop should, if possible, be ordained by all the bishops of the entire province. If this is difficult, then certainly by no fewer than three, provided that the metropolitan bishops’ presence or authority is especially secured [Note: The same manuscript reads “and so that no bishop,” together with an older Vatican Royal manuscript. In place of the Greek word θεία, the Guarnerian and two more recent Vatican manuscripts have the Latin *amita*, “paternal aunt.”]—whether by their presence or by their authority. Without this, they wished the ordination to be invalid.

**V.** No one may receive a person whom another bishop has expelled from his Church [Col. 0473C], whether cleric or layman. But, so that this remedy might not be frustrated by the fact that such an expulsion could have been imposed unjustly through anger or contention, as often happens, they decree that in each province councils be held twice every year by all the provincial bishops and that matters of this kind be judged [Note: The Guarnerian manuscript reads “to judge”; shortly afterward the Bologna manuscript reads “by the others” instead of “by the other.”], so that if something has perhaps been done unjustly by one, it may be corrected by the others; if rightly, it may be confirmed by all.

**VI.** The ancient custom is to be maintained at Alexandria and in the city of Rome, so that the one may have charge of Egypt and the other of the suburban Churches [Note: The same manuscript reads: “or in the city … the custom be maintained, by which either he …”; together with the Bologna manuscript it has “suburban” in place of “suburban Churches.” The meaning of the Canon and of these words is not to be debated here; the question has been treated in substantial books well known to learned men.]

**VII.** If, in the ordination of a bishop, two or three should disagree because of some dispute, the authority of the others—and especially that of the metropolitan, together with the others—shall be regarded as the stronger.

**VIII.** The prerogative of honor anciently granted to the Bishop of Jerusalem is to be preserved, while the dignity of the metropolitan of that province nevertheless remains.

**IX.** If the Cathari—who among us are the Novatians—should happen to repent and return to the Church, they are to be received as clerics in their own order after confessing the doctrines of the Church; but [Note: We have supplied the little word “but” from the Bologna manuscript. Shortly afterward the same manuscript reads “in the place of the presbyterate” instead of “in the place of the presbyters.”] in the ordination given. If one of their bishops comes to our bishop, he is to sit in the place of the presbyters. The title of bishop, however, is to remain only with the one who has always held the Catholic faith, unless he himself should wish to honor the other with that title, or unless it should please him to seek for him an available episcopal place; this shall be in his power [Note: Some manuscripts have “for the bishop”; the Guarnerian has “in his own will” instead of “in his power.”]

[Col. 0474B] **X.** There must not be two bishops in one city.

**XI.** If any persons who have been indiscreetly advanced to the priesthood later confess something criminal about themselves, or are convicted by others [Note: Thus all our manuscripts and all printed books read. Cacciarius preferred, from the Vatican manuscripts, “examined,” but the context does not support it. In place of the later occurrence of “examined,” the Guarnerian and Bologna manuscripts most correctly have the two words “the matter having been investigated,” omitting the word “have been” that follows here, in this form: “the matter having been investigated, so that they may be expelled.” It is credible that this is also found in some Vatican manuscript, but Cacciarius says nothing.], so that they must be expelled; and if any of those who have fallen and have perhaps been ordained through ignorance are subsequently recognized, they too must be expelled.

**XII.** If anyone has fallen in the persecutions without being subjected to torture and repents from the heart, let him spend five years among the Catechumens and afterward join the faithful in prayer alone for two years; then let him be received.

**XIII.** Those who had abandoned military service because of their confession and afterward returned to it are to do penance for thirteen [Col. 0474C] years and then be received, provided that they truly repent from the heart. The bishop, however, has authority to moderate this provision if he sees that their repentance is fruitful and earnest [Note: Barraeus noted in the margin that “thirty” might be read instead of “thirteen.” Some Vatican manuscripts have “to perform” instead of “to undertake.”]

**XIV.** Concerning those who die while doing penance, they decree that no one should be deprived of the final provision. If someone survives after receiving communion, he must complete the prescribed periods, or at least proceed according to whatever moderation the bishop wishes to exercise.

**XV.** Concerning Catechumens who have fallen, they decreed that they be separated from the prayer of the Catechumens for three years and afterward be received.

XVI. [Note: [Col. 0474D] This entire Canon XVI is missing from the Bologna manuscript.] And so no one—whether bishop or any other cleric—should seek to transfer from a lower-ranking city to a greater Church.

[Col. 0475A] XVII. And no cleric who, having abandoned his own Church without any probable cause, wanders and roams through other Churches is to be received into communion.

XVIII. And no one, by taking away a person who belongs to another, is to ordain him a cleric in his own Church without the consent of the one to whom he belongs.

XIX. And no cleric is to accept interest, or an increase in grain or wine—which is what is usually given on a new loan—whether sixfold or even double 227; and if he does so, he is to be expelled as guilty of disgraceful profit. [Note: [Col. 0475C] The reading of the Guarnerian manuscript, *in novo dato*, is preferable. For *sexcuplum*, which follows, the Bologna manuscript has *sesquilium*, two Vatican manuscripts have *seplum*, and some printed editions have *sesquiplum*.]

XX. And deacons are not to be preferred to presbyters, nor are they to sit in the assembly of presbyters or, when presbyters are present, distribute the Eucharist; they are to minister only when the presbyters are officiating. If no presbyter is present, then—and only then—it is also permissible for them to distribute it. Those who act otherwise are ordered to be expelled.

XXI. And the Paulianists, who are Photinians, are to be rebaptized. [Note: [Col. 0475C] The Guarnerian manuscript has: “the Paulianists, who are Photinians.” Barraeus notes in the margin another reading, “Photiniacs.” It is nevertheless more surprising that the same Guarnerian manuscript has, in the opposite sense, “are not to be rebaptized.” No one, surely, will doubt that the negative particle was added by the hand of an interpolator. [Col. 0475D]]

XXII. But deaconesses also, since they do not receive the imposition of hands, are themselves to be counted among the laity. [Note: [Col. 0475D] Cacciarius repeats the old story concerning the Nicene Canons. Apart from the received twenty, Rufinus distributed them into twenty-two, and there were, as he says, many more, as is established by the testimonies of the holy Fathers, who mention others contained in neither the commonly circulated twenty nor the twenty-two. Just as it was not Cacciarius’s task, when reprinting Rufinus’s History, to undertake this discussion, so it is not ours to point out the errors scattered throughout it. But since he also calls Jerome to support his error in the Preface to Judith, we advise readers to consult what we noted concerning that passage in volume X, page 22. Moreover, since he appeals to Pope Julius for his case, saying that this first Nicene Canon occurs in Julius’s letter—“Councils ought not to be held without the judgment of the Roman bishop”—it is shameful for him to enlist as patrons of a good cause those who falsify it, namely, to take refuge in the long since exposed workshop of Isidore Mercator, who forged that writing and attributed it to the Easterners [Col. 0476C]. He should have cited Julius himself, Letter I to the Eusebians, §22, and still more Socrates, Book II, chapter 17, and Sozomen, Book III, chapter 10, or similar passages from genuine authors, even though they contribute little or nothing to Rufinus’s purpose.]

Therefore, when they had decreed these matters as the reverence due to the divine laws required, and had also handed down to the Churches the ancient canon concerning the observance of Easter, so that no further variation might arise, everything having been properly arranged, the peace and faith of the Churches in the regions of East and West were preserved as one and the same.

## CHAPTER VII. On Helena, the mother of Constantine

[Col. 0475C]

At that same time Helena, the mother of Constantine, a woman incomparable in faith and religious devotion and distinguished by singular magnificence, whose [Note: [Col. 0476C] Cacciarius restored from the Vatican manuscripts *vere* (“truly”) in place of *jure* (“legitimately”), which was the reading of the other books and seems to have been written deliberately by Rufinus. For there were those who said that Helena, the mother of Constantine, had not been legitimately married to Constantius. Eutropius, Book X, chapter 2, says: “After Constantius died, Constantine, his son by a less distinguished marriage,” and so forth. This is easily explained: she was not the daughter of an Augustus, and she was repudiated on account of a more noble marriage.] Constantine was both legally her son and believed to be so, prompted by divine visions, set out for Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0476D] The same reading, *petiit* (“set out”), and shortly afterward *propenderat* rather than *pependerat*, is found in our manuscript copies, contrary to all the others and to all printed editions. Concerning the statue of Venus mentioned below, see Jerome, Letter LVIII to Paulinus, §3, and our notes there.], and there asked the inhabitants about the place where the most holy body of Christ had hung upon the cross [Col. 0476A]. It was difficult to find this place because the ancient persecutors had fixed a statue of Venus there [alternative: *adfixum*, “attached”], so that if any Christian wished to worship Christ in that place, he would seem to be worshiping Venus. For this reason the place had become neglected and almost forgotten.

But when, as we said above, the devout woman had hastened to the place indicated to her by a heavenly sign, removing from it everything profane and polluted and clearing away the rubble, she found three crosses in confused order [alternative: *comperit*, “discovered”]. Yet the joy of the discovery was disturbed by the indistinguishable character of each cross. The inscription written by Pilate in Greek, Latin, and Hebrew letters was indeed present, but it too did not clearly reveal which cross was the Lord’s instrument of execution [Col. 0476B]. [Note: [Col. 0476D] From the Bologna manuscript and another older Vatican manuscript, formerly belonging to Queen Christina of Sweden, we have restored *hinc* (“hence”) in place of *hic* (“here”). Compare Sulpicius Severus, who relates the matter somewhat differently; those who report it in precisely the same way undoubtedly took it from Rufinus. In the final verse, *ad eum* (“to him”) should be read rather than *ad Deum* (“to God”).]

Hence, uncertain amid human ambiguity, she sought divine testimony. It happened that in the same city a prominent woman of the place, worn out by a serious illness, lay half-dead. Macarius was bishop of that Church at the time. When he saw the queen hesitating, together with all those who were present, he said: “Bring here all the crosses that have been found, and God will now disclose to us which one it is that carried the Lord [alternative: *Deum*, “God].”

He entered with the queen and the people to the woman who lay there, and, kneeling, offered the following prayer to God.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Cross of the Savior found by Helena in Jerusalem

You, Lord, who through the passion of the cross of your only-begotten Son deigned to grant salvation to the human race [Col. 0476C], and in these last times inspired the heart of your handmaid to seek the blessed wood upon which our salvation hung, clearly show, among these three, which cross belonged to the Lord’s glory and which served for the punishment of a slave, so that this woman, who lies half-alive, may immediately, when touched by the saving wood, be recalled from the gates of death to life.

When he had said this, he first brought one of the three crosses to her, but it accomplished nothing. He brought the second, and even then nothing happened. But when he brought the third, the woman suddenly opened her eyes [Note: [Col. 0477C] The Guarnerian manuscript has a fuller and, in general, more elegant reading: “the woman immediately rose”] and rose. Her strength restored and her vigor greater than when she had been healthy, she began to run throughout the house and glorify the power of God [alternative: “the Lord”].

Thus, by this clear sign, the Queen’s desire was fulfilled, and she built, with royal magnificence, a splendid church on the place where she had found the cross. She also carried to her son the nails with which the Lord’s body had been fastened. From some of them he made bridle-bits for use in war; and from others he is likewise said to have fashioned a helmet suitable for military use. A portion of the saving wood itself she brought to her son, while another portion, enclosed in silver caskets, she left at the place [Col. 0477B]; it is still preserved there as a memorial and guarded with attentive veneration.

The Queen also left this evidence of her devout spirit [Note: [Col. 0477C] The Bologna manuscript, with a full stop inserted here—*τελείᾳ στιγμῇ*, “a complete punctuation mark”—more elegantly reads: “the venerable virgins whom,” and so forth. Shortly afterward the Guarnerian manuscript has *famularum* (“female servants”) instead of *famulum* (“servants”); then two Vatican manuscripts have *ministraret* (“she might minister”) instead of *infunderet* (“she might pour”). Below, where she is called “mother of the empire,” I would restore “mother of the Emperor.”]: she is said to have invited to dinner the virgins whom she found there consecrated to God, and to have cared for them with such devotion that she considered it unworthy for them to use the services of servants. Instead, girded in the dress of a maidservant, she herself placed the food before them, brought the cup, poured water over their hands, and, though queen of the world and mother of the empire, counted herself a handmaid of Christ’s handmaids.

These things took place in Jerusalem. [Note: [Col. 0477C] From the words “Meanwhile, Constantine,” the Guarnerian manuscript begins another chapter, or Chapter VI; we very much approve this division. It also prefixes a new heading of the following form: “On the Emperor Constantine and Antony the Hermit.”]

Meanwhile, relying on his piety, Constantine subdued by arms on their own territory the Sarmatians, Goths, and other barbarian nations, except those that had forestalled peace either through friendship or by surrendering themselves. [Note: [Col. 0477D] This is found both in our manuscripts and in all the printed books. Cacciarius preferred the reading *nam* from the Vatican manuscripts.] And the more religiously and humbly he subjected himself to God, the more fully God subjected all things to him.

He also sent a humble letter to Antony, the first inhabitant of the desert, as though to one of the prophets, asking him [Note: [Col. 0477D] The Guarnerian manuscript has *uti* (“that he might”); five lines below, the Bologna manuscript omits the name Antony and somewhat farther on reads *gerens* (“conducting”) instead of *degens* (“leading”). The Life of Saint Antony, which our author praises, is found among the works of Saint Athanasius and has recently been revised by Montfaucon. Incidentally, note that the testimony concerning Constantine’s letters to him is found not in chapter 1 of his Life, as Cacciarius says, but in chapter 50.] to intercede with the Lord for himself and his children. Thus he desired to make himself acceptable to God not only by his own merits and by the religious devotion of his mother, but also through the intercession of the saints.

Since we have mentioned so great a man as Antony, and since he pleased God above all mortals by his virtues, discipline, sobriety of mind, and life in solitude—where he associated only with wild beasts and frequently triumphed over demons—and since he left monks to this day splendid examples of his way of life, I had wished to set out some account of these matters, but that little book written by Athanasius, which has also been published in Latin [Note: [Col. 0477D] Namely, in the translation of the presbyter Evagrius, which our Jerome also once read.] has forestalled me. Therefore, leaving aside what has already been reported by others, we shall relate those things which, although the reliability of the events preserves them, have nevertheless been obscured by the less certain report of those who lived far away.

## CHAPTER IX. On the captivity of Frumentius and Edesius, and the conversion of the Indians accomplished through them

[Col. 0478B]

In that division of the world which the Apostles, by lot, assigned for preaching the word of God, different provinces having fallen to different men, Parthia was assigned to Thomas, Ethiopia to Matthew, and the nearer India adjoining it is said to have fallen by lot to Bartholomew. Between this region and Parthia, but farther inland and at a considerable distance, lies Further India, inhabited by many different languages and peoples. [Note: [Col. 0477D] Pagius seems to charge Rufinus with an error against geography. Since Rufinus wrote his History in Italy after A.D. 400, when Parthia was a frontier of the Roman Empire, the region between the two Indias was Media, which Rufinus calls “Nearer India,” while India farther away was “Further India.” The region he calls Further India should therefore have been called Nearer India. He is also mistaken in saying that Metrodorus penetrated the India he calls Further India, or modern Ethiopia. Metrodorus did not travel through Ethiopia, or the India nearer to us, but through the true India, or Further India, as a man writing within the Roman Empire ought to have called it. See Fontanini, Life, Book I, chapter 4, §9, continuously.]

No plowshare of apostolic preaching had yet been driven into it, since it was so remote; nevertheless, in the time of Constantine it first received the seeds of the faith for the following reason. A certain philosopher named Metrodorus is said to have penetrated Further India in order to inspect its places and explore the world. [Note: [Col. 0478D] Two Vatican manuscripts are said to prefer *exemplum imitatus etiam* (“also following the example”). Valesius, however, maintains that this conversion of the Indians occurred through the work of Frumentius, not under Constantine, as Rufinus relates, but somewhat later, during the reign of Constantius. Pagius, on the contrary, demonstrates that Valesius is mistaken and that Rufinus accurately records the time of the event; see Pagius under the year 327, §§15 and following. See also Socrates, Book I, chapter 19—not chapter 13, as Cacciarius incorrectly notes—and Sozomen, Book II, chapter 7, not chapter 6. Cacciarius also errs elsewhere in these notes. Shortly afterward the Guarnerian manuscript reads *pueros* (“boys”) instead of *puerulos* (“little boys”).]

Following his example, a certain philosopher from Tyre named Meropius wished, for a similar reason, to visit India. He took with him two young boys, relatives whom he was educating in the liberal arts. One of them, the younger, was called Edesius; the other was called Frumentius.

After he had inspected and become acquainted with the places that interested him, the philosopher began his return journey. Because of the need for water or other supplies, he brought the ship in which he was traveling into a certain harbor [Col. 0479A] [alternative: *applicavit*, “brought it in”]. It is the custom among those barbarians that whenever neighboring peoples announce that their treaty with the Romans has been broken, all Romans found among them are slaughtered.

The philosopher’s ship was attacked, and everyone, including the philosopher himself, was killed. The boys were found under a tree, studying and preparing their lessons; out of pity the barbarians spared them and brought them to the king. He made one of them, Edesius, his cupbearer.
