Frumentius, whom he had recognized as perceptive and intelligent, he entrusted with his accounts and treasuries.

As a result [Note: [Col. 0479D] The Guarnerian manuscript has *cum honore*, “with honor”; together with the Bologna manuscript and others, it reads: “they were held in great honor and affection.” Finally, it reads: “he left him heir to the kingdom through his little son” [alternative: *relinquit*, “left”]. Shortly afterward the Bologna manuscript simply has *exorat* (“begged”), while the Guarnerian has *suppliciter exorabat* (“earnestly begged”); and then, especially, Frumentius, whose …]: they were held in great honor and affection by the king.

When the king was dying, he left his wife and his young son as heirs to the kingdom, while he gave the young men freedom to do whatever they wished. Nevertheless, the queen earnestly begged them, as one who had no one in the whole kingdom more trustworthy, to share with her the responsibility of governing the kingdom until her son came of age—and especially Frumentius, whose wisdom was sufficient to administer the realm. The other displayed pure loyalty and a sober mind in a straightforward manner.

While they were carrying out these duties and Frumentius held the reins of the kingdom in his hands, God stirring his mind and spirit, he began more diligently to inquire whether any of the Roman merchants were Christians. He gave them the greatest freedom and urged them to establish meeting places in each locality, where they could gather according to Roman custom for prayer. He himself did the same even more zealously, encouraging the others likewise, attracting them through favor and benefits, providing whatever was needed, supplying buildings and other necessities, and striving by every means to cause the seed of the Christians to spring up there.

But when the royal boy had come of age, and they had administered the kingdom for him, after everything had been completed and faithfully handed over, they returned to our part of the world, despite the queen and the son’s repeated attempts to detain them and their requests that they remain. Edesius hurried to Tyre to visit his parents and relatives, while Frumentius went to Alexandria, saying that it was not right to conceal the Lord’s work.

He therefore explained the whole matter to the bishop as it had happened and urged him to provide some worthy man whom he might send as bishop, since many Christians had now been gathered and Churches built on barbarian soil. Then Athanasius—for he had recently assumed the episcopate [Note: [Col. 0479D] The words enclosed in parentheses are treated more carefully, and the Bologna manuscript omits them.]—considered Frumentius’s words and deeds with even greater attention and enthusiasm. At a council of priests he said:

“And whom else shall we find such a man as this, in whom the Spirit of God is as he is in you, and who can accomplish these things in such a manner?”

After conferring the episcopal office upon him, he ordered him, with the Lord’s grace, to return to the place from which he had come. When he had gone to India as bishop, God is said to have granted him such an abundance of miraculous power that apostolic signs were performed through him and an immeasurable number of barbarians were converted to the faith. Thus, in the regions of India, Christian communities and Churches came into being, and the priesthood began.

We learned that these things happened not from popular rumor but from Edesius himself, who later became a presbyter at Tyre and had previously been Frumentius’s companion.

## CHAPTER X. On the conversion of the Iberian people accomplished through a captive woman

[Col. 0480B]

233 At the same time the people of the Iberians, who live beneath the Pontic sky, also received the covenant of the word of God and the faith of the future kingdom. [Note: [Col. 0479D] This is now Georgia, the more familiar name. See Cellarius. The Guarnerian manuscript has the aspirated form *Hyberorum*; together with the Vatican manuscript of Queen Christina it reads *suscepit* (“received”) instead of *susceperat* (“had received”), while the Bologna manuscript has *suscipit* (“receives”). Compare Socrates, Book I, chapter 20, not chapter 26 as Cacciarius notes, and Sozomen, Book II, chapter 7, not chapter 6.]

The cause of so great a blessing was a certain captive woman who had been found among them. Since she led a sufficiently faithful, sober, and chaste life and offered wakeful supplications to God throughout all her days and nights, the novelty of the matter itself began to make her an object of wonder to the barbarians, and they inquired more curiously what it meant. She simply confessed that by this practice she worshiped Christ as God.

The barbarians wondered at nothing beyond the novelty of the name. But, as often happens, her persistence aroused a certain curiosity among the women: they wondered whether some benefit could be obtained from such devotion.

It is said to be their custom that, if a young child falls ill, his mother carries him around to each house, so that, if anyone knows an experienced remedy, he may apply it to the sufferer. When a certain woman had carried her little boy around to all the houses as usual, but had found no remedy by visiting them all, she came also to the captive woman, to see whether she knew anything that might help.

The captive declared that she knew nothing of any human remedy, but affirmed that her God, Christ, whom she worshiped, could grant him a salvation of which human beings despaired. Having placed the child upon her hair shirt [Note: [Col. 0480D] The same manuscript has “having placed him underneath,” which is less accurate.] and poured out a prayer to the Lord over him, she returned him healthy to his mother.

The report spread to many people, and the fame of the remarkable deed reached the ears of the queen. She was afflicted by a very serious bodily illness [Col. 0480D] and was in the greatest despair. She asked that the captive be brought to her.

The captive refused to go, lest she seem to presume beyond what her sex permitted [Note: [Col. 0480D] Cacciarius inserted *foeminae* (“of a woman”) from one Royal Vatican manuscript, but the others he himself used, as well as ours and all the printed books, reject it; they do not add that word. Shortly afterward the Bologna manuscript reads *simpliciter* (“simply”) instead of *similiter* (“similarly”).] The queen ordered that she herself be carried to the captive woman’s cell.

Placed similarly upon her hair shirt and having invoked the name of Christ, the queen was immediately after the prayer made to rise healthy and vigorous. The captive taught her that Christ was God, the Son of the Most High God, who had bestowed this salvation, and urged her to invoke him, knowing him to be the author of her own health and life. For he was the one who both distributes kingdoms to kings [Note: [Col. 0481D] The Guarnerian manuscript, like the Bologna manuscript, has *distribuat* (“distributes”), and shortly afterward omits two words, *cum laetitia* (“with joy”).] and life to mortals.

The queen returned home with joy and disclosed the cause of her sudden recovery to her husband, who, delighted at his wife’s restoration, ordered gifts to be brought to the woman. But she said: “O king, the captive considers none of these things worthy. She despises gold and rejects silver; she feeds upon fasting as though it were food. We shall give her this one gift: if we worship as God Christ, the one who healed me when I invoked him.” [Note: [Col. 0481D] The Guarnerian manuscript again has “if we worship Christ the Lord.”]

At that time the king was slow to accept this, and he postponed the matter, although his wife frequently reminded him, until one day he was hunting in the forests with his companions. The daylight suddenly became obscured by the densest darkness, and when light had been withdrawn in the horror of a dreadful night, they could no longer find their way by sight.

The members of his company wandered off in different directions; he alone, surrounded by the thickest darkness, did not know what to do or where to turn. Suddenly this thought arose in his anxious mind, desperate for deliverance: “If that Christ whom the captive woman foretold to my wife really is God, let him now free me from these darknesses, so that from this moment I may worship him, abandoning everything else.”

As soon as he had made this vow—not yet in words but only in his mind—daylight was restored to the world and led the king safely back to the city [Col. 0481C]. He immediately disclosed the event to the queen. He demanded that the captive be summoned at once and teach him the manner of worship, and he declared that he would no longer venerate any god other than Christ.

The captive came and taught him that Christ was God, and explained, insofar as it was permissible for a woman to disclose such matters, the manner of supplication [alternative: *ritus*, “rite”] and worship. She nevertheless advised him to build a Church and described its design.

The king therefore summoned the people of the entire nation, explained from the beginning what had happened to him and the queen, and instructed them in the faith. Though he had not yet been initiated into the sacred rites, he became the apostle of his own people. The men believed through the king, the women through the queen, and a Church was immediately built for all who desired the same thing.

When the circuit of the walls had already been rapidly raised [Note: [Col. 0481D] The Guarnerian manuscript has *pertinaciter* (“obstinately”), incorrectly, and shortly afterward *erepta* (“snatched away”) instead of *erecta* (“erected”). We usually pass over such errors without comment.], the time came when the columns were to be placed.

After the first and second had been erected, they came to the third. All the machinery and the strength of oxen and men had been exhausted. The column had already been raised halfway at an angle, but the remaining portion could not be lifted by any machinery. They tried again, a second and a third time, and repeatedly applied their strength, but, with everything exhausted, they could not move it even from its place.

The whole people were astonished, and the king’s courage was failing; no one knew what should be done. But when night came and everyone had withdrawn, and all human beings and the work itself had ceased, the captive woman alone remained inside, spending the night in prayer.

Then, behold, the king entered at dawn, anxious and accompanied by all his people, and saw the column—which so many machines and so many people had been unable to move—standing upright and suspended above its base, balanced in the air, yet not resting upon it [Note: [Col. 0481D] The same manuscript has “placed beneath it, at a distance of one foot”; then “then indeed” instead of “then,” and so forth.].

At this, all the people gazed upon it and glorified God, bearing witness, through the testimony of the present miracle, that the king’s faith and the captive woman’s devotion were true. And behold, while everyone was still amazed and astonished, before their eyes the column was gradually set down upon its base without anyone touching it and settled there in perfect balance.

After this, the remaining number of columns were suspended with such ease that all those still outstanding were put in place that very day.

When the Church had been magnificently constructed and the people thirsted for the faith of God with even greater fervor, a delegation of the entire nation was sent, at the captive woman’s urging, to the Emperor Constantine. The event was explained, and they begged him to send priests [Note: [Col. 0482D] Cacciarius inserts “of God,” which is unnecessary here and is absent from our manuscripts and all the printed books. Shortly afterward the Bologna manuscript, together with the printed editions, has *oratur* (“is entreated”) instead of *exoratur* (“is earnestly entreated”).] who might complete the gift of God that had begun among them.

When he had sent them with every joy and honor, he rejoiced far more over this than if he had added unknown peoples and unfamiliar kingdoms to the Roman Empire.

The most faithful man Bacurius, the king of that nation and among us Count of the Household [Note: [Col. 0482D] Rufinus praises him highly in the following book, chapter 33, as a man distinguished in faith, piety, and virtue of both mind and body; he also records that he fell while bravely fighting for the Emperor Theodosius against the tyrant Eugenius in A.D. 394. Zosimus, Book IV, near the end, says that he was from Armenia, which borders Iberia, and describes him as entirely free from every vice and outstanding in military glory. In the Bologna manuscript his name is corruptly written *Bacurilis*. See Socrates, Book I, chapter 20.], who was deeply devoted to both religion and truth, related these events to us when, as commander of the Palestinian frontier, he was living with us in Jerusalem in close fellowship.

But let us return to the matter begun.

## CHAPTER XI. On Constantia, the sister of Constantine, and the presbyter introduced by her to her brother

After Helena, the mother of the devout Emperor, had been honored with the highest distinctions of the Roman realm and had departed this life, Constantia, left behind by Licinius [Note: [Col. 0482D] In our manuscripts she is described as having been left behind after her husband Licinius was killed and having been taken in by her brother Constantine. The presbyter who possessed such influence and authority with her is believed to be the man called Eustathius in the Acts of the Arian Council of Constantinople. The fact that his name is suppressed here was not sufficient reason for Valesius to regard the account and Rufinus’s reliability as suspect.], lived under the protection of her brother Augustus [Col. 0483A].

It happened that a certain presbyter came to her notice who secretly favored the party of Arius. At first he disclosed nothing at all about these matters to the Emperor’s sister. But when their close familiarity gave him the opportunity, he gradually began to introduce the subject [alternative: *aperire*, “to disclose”], saying that Arius had been subjected to fabricated hostility, and that his own bishop had attacked the matter contentiously because he was driven by the spur of rivalry, since Arius was sufficiently popular with the people.

By frequently suggesting these and similar things, he won over Constantia’s mind [Note: [Col. 0483C] The same manuscript has *efficit* (“he accomplishes this”). Shortly afterward one Royal Vatican manuscript adds “from her brother Constantine.”]. When she was on the point of death and her brother came to visit her and addressed her with gentle and religious affection, she is said to have asked him for one final favor: to receive the presbyter into his confidence and listen to whatever he might suggest concerning her hope and salvation. She herself, as she was already departing this life, cared nothing for these matters; but she was concerned for her brother’s position, lest he perhaps suffer the destruction of his kingdom in punishment for the innocent [Note: [Col. 0483C] The same manuscripts again have *ex luce* (“from the light”), with the pronoun silently omitted.]

Having accepted these admonitions from his sister and believing her concern for him to be sincere, he lent an ear to the presbyter. Meanwhile, he ordered Arius to be summoned from exile so that he might explain what he believed.

Arius then wrote out a statement of faith which seemed to contain not indeed our meaning, but our words and profession. The Emperor was astonished and thought that the same judgment was expressed in Arius’s exposition as in that of the Council previously held. Nevertheless, he relaxed none of the severity of his mind [Note: [Col. 0483C] The Guarnerian manuscript has *rigorem*. Compare again Socrates, chapters 25 and following, and the notes of Valesius at chapter 37.], but sent him back for examination by the Council, since priests from the whole world were being invited to assemble for the dedication of Jerusalem.

He wrote to them concerning Arius, asking that, if they approved his exposition of the faith and recognized either that he had then been surrounded by hostility, as he claimed, or that he had now corrected his error, they should treat him with a merciful judgment—especially since the Council had shown such moderation that its sentence had been directed not against his person but against the perversity of his doctrines—provided that the bishops also gave their assent [Note: [Col. 0483D] The Bologna manuscript omits the pronoun “his.” What follows it represents as though it read “the consent of Alexandria,” and thus the passage refers more clearly to the Church of Alexandria being accommodated. The Guarnerian manuscript itself prefers *commodaretur* (“might be accommodated”) to *accommodaretur*. If one reads *Alexandriae* (“of Alexandria”) instead of *Alexandri* (“of Alexander”), Rufinus could readily be freed from an apparent anachronism. For although we do not, as most scholars commonly do, think that Athanasius succeeded Alexander in the Alexandrian see in A.D. 326, but only two years later, in A.D. 328—a conclusion we infer from the recently published fragment of an ancient, headless History in volume III of the *Observationes Literariae*, where it says that “from the consulship of Gratian and Dagalaifus up to the following consulship of Lupicinus and Jovinus and the second consulship of Valens, on Payni 14 [June 8], the forty years of Athanasius’s episcopate were completed,” which coincides with A.D. 368, the fortieth year of Athanasius’s episcopate—nevertheless, when Arius returned from exile to Alexandria, it was no longer Alexander but Athanasius who governed the Church. The difficulty will therefore disappear if, suppressing the word “bishop,” one restores *Alexandriae*, as the manuscripts apparently permit. We shall discuss this matter again below in note h.]

He was readily received even by those who, initially favoring his undertakings, had signed with dissimulation. But when he went to Alexandria, all his undertaking there came to nothing. For deceit has scope among the ignorant, but to direct deceit against those who know is nothing other than to provoke laughter. [Note: [Col. 0484C] The Guarnerian manuscript has: “nothing other than to stir up laughter again,” and so forth.]

While these things were being attempted unsuccessfully at Alexandria, the venerable Augustus Constantine died in a suburban villa of Nicomedia in the thirty-first year of his reign [Note: [Col. 0484C] The same manuscript, together with the Bologna manuscript, has “thirty-first”; then, “he died.” Eusebius, *Life*, Book IV, chapter 53, says: “He completed the course of his reign in thirty-two years, excepting a few months and days,” and so forth. See our notes in the *Hieronymian Chronicle.]. He had named his sons heirs to the succession of the Roman world in his will.

At that time, since Constantius, to whom he had assigned the Eastern Empire, was not present, he is said to have secretly summoned the presbyter whom we mentioned above as having been recommended by his sister and thereafter treated familiarly. He handed him the will he had written and adjured him under oath to place it in no one’s hands except Constantius’s when he arrived.

Since the eunuchs who were in the palace favored the presbyter, they skillfully concealed the indication of the Emperor’s death until Constantius’s arrival. Although many attempted new measures, everything remained safe and intact [Note: [Col. 0484D] Earlier printed editions, as well as the Guarnerian manuscript, have *restitutae* in one word instead of *res tutae* (“things safe”). Other manuscripts correct it. Our manuscripts have *mansere* rather than *remansere*. Shortly afterward the Bologna manuscript, somewhat more correctly, reads “to rule over all” rather than “to rule,” and then has *semper* (“always”) instead of *sibi*, which occurs first. In what follows, the Guarnerian manuscript has “the Emperor bound to himself,” which is nearly more correct than “the Emperor.”]. When Constantius arrived, the presbyter returned the deposit.

Out of gratitude for this service, the Emperor, eager for the kingdom, became so attached to him that although he had desired to rule over everyone, he willingly allowed himself to be ruled by that man. Once he had bound the Emperor to himself, the presbyter began to suggest the restoration of Arius and to persuade him to compel the priests who were unwilling to consent.

## CHAPTER XII. On the conflict between Alexander, Eusebius, and Arius
At that time, in Alexandria Alexander, [Note: [Col. 0484D] One Regius manuscript has “at Jerusalem.” In any case, however broadly one understands this passage, as Cacciarius observes, since events belonging to Alexander’s time are here attached to years well after his death and to the period of Athanasius, it must be admitted that Rufinus suffers from a serious anachronism. This is all the more remarkable because he lived so close to those times that he could have known Athanasius himself, as well as many who took part in these affairs, and perhaps even known them by sight. But in former times there was evidently a certain contempt for, or ignorance of, chronology. In the Alexandrian Church, moreover, Arians, Meletians, [Col. 0485A] and others were confusing everything, so that it was difficult to describe accurately each event according to the exact order of time.] in Jerusalem Maximus the Confessor, and likewise in Constantinople Alexander, were serving as bishops, as we learn from the writings of Athanasius. But Eusebius, who was at Nicomedia—the Eusebius whose dissimulation when signing we discussed above—having gained a favorable opportunity and having become intimate with the Emperor through the presbyter, attempted to overturn everything and annul the acts of the Council. He caused Arius, who was lingering to no purpose at Alexandria, to come and soon afterward to be recalled [Note: [Col. 0485C] The Bolognese manuscript has “he caused him to come and then soon to be recalled.” Pagius teaches that this synod of Constantinople was convened around February 336, and that Athanasius was exiled to Gaul by order not of Constantius but of Constantine the Great.] and, by imperial edicts, summoned another council at Constantinople.

Those who came there were chiefly the followers of Arius and Eusebius, men who had often confronted Alexander and urged him to receive Arius, though they had not yet succeeded in anything [Note: [Col. 0485C] Cacciarius corrupts the text which he boasts of having emended. He changes the uniquely correct reading profligantes—preferred by our manuscripts, by most of those he himself used, and finally by all printed editions—to proficientes, on the basis of two Vatican manuscripts, which plainly had also suffered the hand of an ignorant interpolator. For profligare means what Rufinus intends, as the grammarians know: to bring to completion a matter that one has undertaken. Consequently the same editor also changes the sense, reading, with the addition of a negative particle, “not even from injuries,” etc. Against this reading we set the testimony and unanimous agreement of all the books we have mentioned.] while refraining from personal violence against him. At last they fixed and announced a definite day for him, declaring that either he himself must receive Arius or, if he resisted, must know that he would be expelled from the Church and driven into exile, and that another person would receive Arius.

Then, on the night before the appointed day, he lay beneath the altar, spending the entire night awake in prayer and tears, commending the cause of the Church to the Lord. When daylight had come and Alexander still did not cease praying, Eusebius and all his followers, like the standard-bearer of a heretical war, went early to Arius’s house and ordered him to follow them quickly [Note: [Col. 0485D] The Guarnerian manuscript inserts the word se: “that is, to follow him quickly.”] to the Church, declaring that, unless Alexander agreed while present, he would be expelled and forced to surrender his position.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the shameful death of Arius

Thus everyone waited anxiously to see which way matters would turn, whether toward Alexander’s perseverance or toward the pressure of Eusebius and Arius. While all minds were suspended in expectation, as is natural in such a matter [Note: [Col. 0485D] The same manuscript adds: “as is usual in such a matter, in expectation,” etc.], Arius, proceeding to the Church and surrounded by a crowd of bishops and people, turned aside to a public place because of a bodily necessity. There, as he sat, his intestines and all his entrails flowed out into the privy [Col. 0486A]; and in such a place he paid the death deserved by a blasphemous and foul mind [Note: [Col. 0485D] The same manuscript, together with the Bolognese, has blasphemiae; the old printed editions have blasphema, “blasphemous,” and foetida mente, “with a foul mind,” which is equally sound. Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book IX, chapter 15, citing this passage under the name of Eusebius, says: “Arius, whose entrails, as the historian Eusebius related, he cast out in the privy.”]

When this was later announced in the Church to Eusebius and to those who, together with him, had been harassing the holy and innocent man Alexander over receiving Arius, they were overcome by shame and, covered with confusion, withdrew. Then the saying was fulfilled to the glory of the Lord which Alexander had proclaimed in his prayer to God, saying: “Judge, Lord, between me and the threats of Eusebius and the violence of Arius” [Note: [Col. 0486C] The Bolognese has “and Arius” instead of “of Arius,” which is a corruption. Shortly afterward the Guarnerian has “if the event happened,” etc.].

For the moment, however, these events caused them some shame. But the heretics, meeting together and fearing that, if the matter reached the Emperor Constantius exactly as it had happened, he might not only withdraw from their false belief, in which they were being cunningly entangled [Note: [Col. 0486C] Barraeus likewise has this reading; Cacciarius is therefore mistaken when he says that the printed books have *delere* in opposition to the testimony of the manuscripts.], but might also, with royal authority, impose a severe punishment on the authors of his deception [Col. 0486B], arranged through the eunuchs—whom they already held deceived by their false belief—that the Emperor should learn of Arius’s death as calmly and ordinarily as possible, and should hear nothing that might appear to indicate divine vengeance [Note: [Col. 0486D] Both manuscripts add the little word *in*: “already in false belief.” Shortly afterward the Bolognese has *cum fieri* instead of *quam*, etc. Finally, the two Vatican manuscripts wrongly have “already something” instead of “not anything.”]. After these things, they continued the matter of the faith as they had begun it.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the beginnings of Athanasius the Bishop

Therefore, when Alexander had died, Athanasius had taken over the episcopal seat at Alexandria [Note: [Col. 0486D] We have said that Athanasius appears to have succeeded Alexander in governing the Alexandrian Church in the year 328, contrary to the opinion of others, who assign this to 326. Recall the passage cited above from the *Acephalous History* (in this edition, col. 483, note d). Add to it the much clearer statements at the end of the same paragraph: “Thus the episcopate of Athanasius lasted, as I have said, until the consulship of Valentinian and Valens (A.D. 368), on Payni 4 (June 8), for forty years.” Rufinus therefore returns to earlier events and interrupts—or rather confuses—the chronological sequence.]. Since this man was of vigorous intelligence and exceptionally watchful in ecclesiastical affairs, the fact had already become sufficiently known to the heretics when he had come to the Council of Nicaea with his aged bishop Alexander [Note: [Col. 0486D] Most of the printed books omit this passage.], whose suggestions enabled the frauds and deceptions of the heretics to be exposed watchfully. As soon as they learned that he had become bishop [variant: had become bishop already], judging—as events showed—that their affairs would not easily advance through his vigilance, they prepared every kind of machinery of deception against him.

Yet it does not seem inappropriate to repeat briefly above what concerns this man’s origin [Col. 0487A] and to recount, as we learned from those who lived with him, what sort of upbringing he had received from childhood. At the time when Bishop Alexander was celebrating the day of Peter the Martyr at Alexandria, and, after the sacred rites had been completed, was awaiting the clergy who were to come to his banquet [Note: [Col. 0487D] The Guarnerian manuscript has *conventuros*, that is, “the clergy who were to assemble.”], he saw from a distance, near the seashore, some boys playing at imitating a bishop and the customary actions performed in churches. But when he had watched the boys attentively for a long time [Note: [Col. 0487D] The same manuscript has *intentus diutino*; the two Vatican manuscripts have *intentu*; the Bolognese also has *diutine* instead of *diu*.], he saw them performing certain things that were even more secret and mystical.

Immediately disturbed, he ordered the clergy to be summoned to him and showed them what he had seen in the distance. Then he commanded them to go away, seize all the boys, and bring them to him. When they were present, he asked what their game was, what they had done, and how they had done it. They, frightened—as is natural at that age, first denied everything, then disclosed the event in order, and confessed that some catechumens had been baptized by them [Note: [Col. 0487D] The Guarnerian manuscript omits *esse*. Whether this is a true account of boys baptized by Athanasius when he was a boy is an ancient and traditional question. Among more recent writers, compare Pagius at the year 311; the Bollandist associates at May 2, chapter 1; and again in the *History of the Alexandrian Patriarchs*, volume V of June. Compare also Montfaucon in the *Life of St. Athanasius* and in the special dissertation published at Paris in 1710. Add what Fontaninus notes in *Life of Rufinus*, book II, chapter 5, no. 2.].

Athanasius had played the part of bishop in that childish game. He then carefully asked those said to have been baptized what they had been asked and what they had answered, and likewise questioned the one who had administered the baptism. When he saw that everything accorded with the rite of our religion, he is said, after consulting the council of clergy, to have decided that those upon whom water had been poured with the proper questions and answers should not be baptized again, but should receive what customarily remains to be supplied by priests.

But Athanasius and those who in that game had appeared either as presbyters or as ministers, after summoning their parents, he handed over under solemn adjuration to his Church to be raised [Note: [Col. 0487D] The same manuscript, together with the Bolognese, has *suae*; the old printed editions omit it in the phrase that follows. Our manuscripts have *Notario*, as do the printed editions; Cacciarius rewrote it as *Notariis*. Finally, the Bolognese shortly afterward reads *fide Domini* instead of *fidele*, etc.]. After a short time, when Athanasius had been adequately instructed by a Notary and sufficiently trained by a grammarian, he was restored by his parents to the priest, entrusted to the Lord like another Samuel, and was reared in the Lord’s temple. When the priest proceeded to his fathers in a good old age, Athanasius was chosen to carry the priestly ephod after him.

But such were the great struggles that this man endured in the Church for the integrity of the faith that what is written appears to have been said also of him: “For I will show him how much he must suffer for my name” (Acts 9:16). For the whole world conspired against his persecutions, and the rulers of the earth were stirred up: peoples, kingdoms, and armies joined together against him [Col. 0488D, variant: had joined together]. Yet he preserved that divine saying, declaring: “Though armies encamp against me, my heart will not fear; though battle rise against me, in this I will hope” (Psalm 26:3).

But since his deeds were so numerous and so great that the magnitude of the subject does not allow me to omit anything, while the multitude of his achievements forces me to leave out very many, my uncertain mind struggles, unable to decide what to retain and what to omit [Note: [Col. 0488D] The Bolognese omits “so great,” and shortly afterward has *enim* instead of *vero*.]. Therefore we shall mention a few matters relevant to the subject; the rest, without doubt, will be recounted by his reputation, though it will report lesser things. For it will find nothing that it could add.

## CHAPTER XV. On the error of the Emperor Constantius

When Constantius alone obtained the kingdom of the East, after his brother Constantine had been killed by soldiers near Aquileia at the river Alsas [Note: [Col. 0488D] The Bolognese has “Alsan.” Compare Pagius at the year 337, no. 7.], Constans, the brother of both, was governing the West with considerable ability. Constantius, however, possessing by nature and disposition a kingly character, while showing excessive indulgence to the first supporters of his reign, was cunningly deceived into false belief by the eunuchs and wicked priests; and with considerable zeal he complied with their depraved arguments [Note: [Col. 0488D] The two more recent Vatican manuscripts have “their intentions.”].

But they feared that Athanasius might at some point gain access to the Emperor and, through him, teach from the Scriptures the truth of the faith which they were corrupting. Accordingly, they began in every way to accuse him before the ruler and to present him as though he were guilty of every crime and outrage, until they displayed to the Emperor a human arm carried in a small chest [Col. 0488C], asserting that it had been cut off by Athanasius from the body of a certain Arsenius for the purposes of magical art. They also fabricated many other accusations, both criminal and disgraceful.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the council of the heretics convened at Tyre against Athanasius

For these reasons the Emperor ordered that Athanasius be condemned by a council. He ordered it to be convened at Tyre, sending one of his Counts from his own entourage, with the support also of Archelaus, then Count of the East, and of the governor of the province of Phoenicia [Note: [Col. 0488D] We have often warned about the inverted chronological order used by Rufinus. The same error recurs here: the Synod of Tyre took place in 335, whereas the Constantinopolitan synod mentioned above in chapter 12 took place the following year. See Pagius, who brings these events into accordance with the laws of history and chronology, at the year 332, no. 11.].

Athanasius was brought there. The little chest containing the human arm was carried around. Envy and horror seized not only religious souls but also the base [Note: [Col. 0488D] Perhaps *invidiae horror*, “the horror of envy,” is more correct in the Guarnerian manuscript; the two Vatican manuscripts have *invidiae error*, “the error of envy.”] and vulgar.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the severed arm of Arsenius and the other deceptions of the heretics exposed at the council

This Arsenius, whose arm was said to have been cut off, had once been a lector of Athanasius. Fearing correction because of a fault [Note: [Col. 0489D] The same Guarnerian manuscript has *correptionis*; the Regius-Vatican manuscript has *praesentia* instead of *frequentiae*.], he had withdrawn from public attendance. The men who regarded his hiding place as suitable for such a disgraceful fabrication had concealed and kept him there from the beginning of the contrived charge, in the custody of someone they believed utterly faithful to their crimes [variant: they believed].

Nevertheless, while still hidden, he learned what accusation was being brought against Athanasius in his name. Whether moved by ordinary human compassion or by divine providence, he secretly escaped during the silence of the night, sailed away from his confinement, and reached Tyre. On the day before the final day on which the case was to be heard, Arsenius presented himself to Athanasius [Note: [Col. 0489D] The two Vatican manuscripts have “and which,” instead of “and so”; likewise shortly afterward *agitur* instead of *cogitur*.], explained the course of events, and told him everything. Athanasius ordered him to remain at home and forbade anyone to learn of his presence.

Meanwhile the council was convened. Nearly all who were conscious of the fabricated calumny came together against Athanasius with hostile and prejudiced minds. At that time Paphnutius the Confessor, whom we mentioned above, was present, aware of Athanasius’s innocence. When he saw Maximus, Bishop of Jerusalem, who had been a fellow confessor with him after having one eye gouged out and one knee severed, sitting with the others whom the stain of faction had joined, although in his excessive simplicity he suspected nothing of the priests’ crime [Note: [Col. 0489D] The Bolognese and the two Vatican manuscripts have this reading. The Guarnerian, like the old printed editions, has *verum* and shortly afterward *suspicatum* instead of *suspicans*.], he did not hesitate to approach the assembly. He said:

“You, Maximus, with whom I share one and the same distinction of confession, with whom the loss of our mortal light alike won for us a clearer sight of divine light—you, I say, I will not allow to sit in the assembly of the wicked or to enter with those who commit iniquity.”

Then he laid hands on him, raised him from among them, instructed him about each of them, and thereafter united him with Athanasius in perpetual communion.

Meanwhile the case was heard. The first accusation introduced was that of a certain woman who claimed that she had once received Athanasius as a guest and that, while she suspected nothing, he had violated her during the night. Athanasius was ordered to be brought in. He entered with his presbyter Timothy and instructed him that, after the woman had finished speaking, Timothy himself should answer what she had said while Athanasius remained silent [Note: [Col. 0489D] Our manuscripts and Cacciarius, on the basis of two Vatican manuscripts, add the pronoun *ipse*. Shortly afterward the Guarnerian has *et vim tibi* instead of *aut vim*, etc.].

When the woman had completed the speech she had been taught, Timothy turned to her and said: “Tell me, woman, did I ever stay with you, or did I do you violence, as you claim?”

Then she, in the manner of the boldness characteristic of such women, rebuked Timothy: “You—you,” she said, “did me violence; you violated my chastity in that place.” Turning also to the judges, she began to call upon God as witness that she was speaking the truth.

Then all began to be seized by an absurd shame, because the faction’s fabricated charge had been exposed so easily while Athanasius remained silent [variant: while he taught]. Yet the judges were not allowed to question the woman about where, through whom, or how the accusation had been prepared, since the accusers held the freedom to judge.

The proceedings then turned to another charge. A crime unheard of through the ages was produced. “Here,” they said, “is a matter in which no one can be deceived by verbal tricks [Note: [Col. 0489D] The two Vatican manuscripts have *decipere*, “to deceive,” and shortly afterward *a te* instead of *hoc te*, as Cacciarius notes; he also wrongly has *Athanasi* instead of *Athanasius*. [Col. 0490D].]. The matter is being presented to the eyes, with words set aside. This arm accuses you, Athanasius, an arm that has been cut off. This is the right hand of Arsenius. Explain how and for what purpose you cut it off.”

He replied: “Which of you knew Arsenius well enough to recognize this as his right hand?” [Note: [Col. 0490D] The printed editions omit *esse*, “to be his”; this is equally acceptable. We are sometimes compelled to take account of such readings when Cacciarius places the entire substance of the matter in them.]

Several men stood up who claimed to have known Arsenius very well; some of them, however, were not aware of the faction’s plot. Athanasius then asked the judges to order that his man, whom he had requested [Note: [Col. 0490D] The printed editions add the preposition *in*, which the manuscripts do not have. The Guarnerian has *deposcerat* instead of *deposceret*.], be brought in.

When Arsenius had been brought in, Athanasius raised his face and said to the council and judges: “This is Arsenius.” Then, raising his right hand as well, he said: “This is also his right hand; this is also his left. As for the hand these men have presented, you must investigate whose it is.”

Then, as though a kind of night and darkness had been poured into the eyes of the accusers, they did not know what to do or where to turn. The witnesses who shortly before had declared that they knew Arsenius confirmed that this was indeed Arsenius [Note: [Col. 0490D] The Guarnerian has “they had said that they knew him.” With the Bolognese also, *acclamatur* appears instead of *conclamatur*.].

But because the council had been assembled not to judge the man but to crush him, a sudden uproar arose. They shouted that Athanasius was a magician, that he was deceiving the eyes of those who looked, and that such a man must not be allowed to live any longer. They rushed at him and prepared to tear him apart with their own hands.

Archelaus, however, who presided over the council with the others by order of the Emperor, snatched him from the hands of those who were tearing at him and led him out through hidden exits [Note: [Col. 0490D] The manuscripts and printed books have this reading. Cacciarius appears to have derived *deduxit* from his own conjecture. The Guarnerian begins a separate chapter with the words *Concilium tamen*. It also retains *omnino* with the printed editions in the phrase *nihil omnino*, whereas Cacciarius rejects it without informing the reader.], advising him to entrust his safety to flight, since that was the only means available.

Nevertheless, the council assembled again and condemned Athanasius as though nothing at all had been discovered, as though he had confessed the charges brought against him. They sent fabricated proceedings of this sort throughout the world and, by coercion from the Emperor, compelled the other bishops to consent to their crime.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the flight and hiding places of Athanasius

From that point Athanasius was driven as a fugitive throughout the whole world, and no safe place remained for him in which to hide. Tribunes, prefects, Counts, and even armies were set in motion by imperial edicts to search for him [variant: were stirred up]. Rewards were offered to informers if anyone delivered him alive, especially; if that was impossible, at least if someone brought Athanasius’s head [Note: [Col. 0491C] In the Guarnerian manuscript: “if not, at least.” Cacciarius notes that Rufinus is here writing a history of the persecution of St. Athanasius, after the Eusebians drove him from the Alexandrian see at the false synod of Antioch, which was assembled on the occasion of the dedication of the Golden Church. Gregory was installed in his place; surrounded by a guard of five thousand armed men, he occupied the Church by force and fire. The year then was 341. See Pagius.].

Thus all the strength of the kingdom was uselessly employed against him, while God was with him. Meanwhile, it is said that he hid for six continuous years in a cistern that had no water, so that he never saw the sun. But when he had been betrayed by a maidservant who alone knew the secret from the household of the masters who had provided his hiding place [Note: [Col. 0491D] The Bolognese omits *videbatur*, “it seemed.” Shortly afterward the Guarnerian has “when he came with the judges,” and, together with the Bolognese, *emigravit*, “he departed.” The Bolognese is wrong in what follows, reading “Thus those who had come were frustrated, and the false informer.” The Guarnerian correctly has “with the masters also turned to flight,” as do the printed editions.], as though warned by the Spirit of God, he moved to another place on that very night when the judges came to arrest him, after six years had passed. Thus those who had come were frustrated; and, when the masters had fled, they punished the maidservant as a false informer.

## CHAPTER XIX. How the Emperor Constans wrote to his brother Constantius on behalf of Athanasius and ordered him to be restored to his Church

But, lest his hiding place become burdensome to anyone and an opportunity for false accusation be sought against innocent people, he no longer considered anything safe for himself in Constantius’s kingdom and fled away to the side of Constans [variant: departed]. Constans received him with considerable honor and religious respect. After carefully learning from report the cause of his exile, he wrote to his brother, declaring that he had ascertained with certainty that Athanasius, priest of the Most High God, was suffering unjust flight and exile.

Constantius would therefore do well to restore him to his own position without causing any trouble [Note: [Col. 0491D] The Guarnerian has *tenebrae*, “darkness,” rather than *minus vere*, “less truly.” The same manuscript has *facere*; shortly afterward it reads “it would be his concern that he himself should fulfill it,” without the word *ipse*, which the old printed editions omit.], but if he refused, Constans would take care to accomplish this himself, penetrating the innermost parts of his kingdom and imposing the punishments most deserved by the authors of the crime.

Terrified by this letter—for he knew that his brother could do what he threatened—Constantius, pretending kindness, ordered Athanasius to come to him voluntarily. After reproving him lightly, he allowed him to return safely [variant: “into safety”] to his own Church.

The Emperor was nevertheless advised by wicked counselors. “It is not a great matter, Athanasius,” he said, “that the bishops ask of you: that you grant one of the many churches at Alexandria to the people who refuse to communicate with you.”

Then, with God suggesting the answer, Athanasius found a timely plan. “And what,” he said, “is there, Emperor, that may be denied to one who asks you, when you possess the power to command everything? But I have one request: grant my little petition willingly.”

When the Emperor promised that he would grant whatever Athanasius wished, however difficult it might be, provided he yielded on this one matter [Note: [Col. 0492C] The Bolognese has “if he granted this. Athanasius willingly,” etc.], Athanasius said:

“This is what I ask: since here also—for the matter was being conducted near Antioch—there are some of our people who refuse to communicate with these men, let them be granted one church to hold.”

The Emperor gladly promised that this seemed entirely just and ought certainly to be done. But when he brought the matter before the men whose advice he used, they replied that they did not wish to receive a church there, nor to give one here [Note: [Col. 0492C] The Guarnerian has *responderunt*, “they replied”; shortly afterward the Bolognese omits the pronoun *suam* in “his own Church.” Let us compare here the recently published *Acephalous History*, which we have cited above in one or two places, in volume III of the *Literary Observations* [Col. 0492D]. Constantius also wrote concerning Athanasius’s return, and the following letter is included among the Emperor’s letters: “And after Gregory’s death Athanasius returned from the city of Rome and the regions of Italy, and entered Alexandria on Phaophi 24, under the third consulship of Constantius and Constans” [the year is marked as 346, October 21], “that is, after six years” [supply: from his condemnation at the Antiochene synod, which we said was held in 341], “and he remained peacefully at Alexandria for sixteen years and six months.” Here there is an error in the numerical designation of the years, and XIII seems to need to be written instead of XVI, as the subsequent course of the history shows. From this it is possible to draw considerable light upon Rufinus’s narrative and, most importantly, to restore the sequence of events, in which Rufinus sometimes errs through displacement or transposition.].

They said this because each of them consulted his own interests more than those of an absent person. The Emperor therefore, amazed at Athanasius’s prudence, ordered him to hurry quickly to take possession of his own Church.

But when the Emperor Constans had been removed from the kingdom and from life at once through the crime of Magnentius [Note: [Col. 0492D] In the Guarnerian manuscript there is a blank space in place of the name Magnentius. The entire matter, which Rufinus touches upon briefly in this remaining chapter, is explained fully, and also in chronological order, in the recently cited *Acephalous History*, no. 3. It is worthwhile to transcribe it, although it is somewhat longer:

“After this time, Athanasius, hearing that a crowd would gather against him, while the Emperor Constans was established at Milan, sent a vessel to the court with five bishops: Serapion of Thmuis, Triadelphus of Niciota, Apollo of Cynopolis in the Upper region, Ammonius of Pachommon; and three presbyters of Alexandria: Peter the Physician, Astericus, and Phileas. After they had sailed from Alexandria, under the sixth consulship of Constantius Augustus and the second of Constans Caesar, on Pachon 24 [A.D. 353, May 17], four days later Montanus Palatinus entered Alexandria on Pachon 28 and delivered to Bishop Athanasius a letter of Constans Augustus forbidding them to come to the court. As a result the bishop was greatly troubled [perhaps *vexatus*, ‘distressed’], and all the people were very weary. Thus Montanus, having accomplished nothing, departed, leaving the Bishop of Alexandria.

“Later Diogenes, the imperial Notary, came to Alexandria in the month of Mesore [A.D. 355; read ‘Mesori’], in the consulship of Arbition and Lollianus—that is, two years and five months after Montanus’s departure from Alexandria—and pressed everyone, forcing the Bishop to leave the city and causing great distress. On the sixth day of the month Thoth (September 3), pressing hard, he attacked the Church and continued for four months: that is, from the month of Mesore, or from the intercalary day, until Choiac 26 (December 22). But the people resisted Diogenes and the judges vigorously, and Diogenes returned without accomplishing his purpose on Choiac 26 of the aforesaid month, in the consulship of Arbition and Lollianus, after four months, as stated.

“Accordingly Duke Syrianus and the Notary Hilary came from Egypt to Alexandria on Tybi 10, after the consulship of Arbition and Lollianus (A.D. 356, January 5). Having sent legions of soldiers throughout Egypt and Libya ahead of them, the Duke and the Notary entered by night with the entire military force into the Church of Theonas, on Mechir 13, during the night leading into the 14th (February 8–9), breaking open the doors of the Church of Theonas and entering with an enormous military force. Bishop Athanasius escaped their hands and was saved on the aforesaid day, Mechir 14 (February 9). This, however, occurred nine years, three months, and nineteen days after the Bishop had returned from Italy.

“After the Bishop had been rescued, his presbyters and the people remained in possession of the churches and held their assemblies for four months, until Cataphronius the Prefect and Heraclius the Count entered Alexandria in the month of Payni, on day 16, in the eighth consulship of Constans and the first of Julian Caesar (A.D. 356, June 10). Four days after they entered, the Athanasians were expelled from the churches, which were handed over to those belonging to Gregory [Note: [Col. 0493] Is “Gregory” here and below perhaps meant to be “George”? The *Acephalous History* itself has just taught us (col. 492, note i) that Gregory died before October 21, 346.]. They awaited the bishop and received the churches on Payni 21.

“Gregory also arrived at Alexandria in the ninth consulship of Constans and the second of Julian Caesar, on Mechir 30 (A.D. 357, February 24), that is, eight months and eleven days after they had received the churches belonging to him. Gregory therefore entered Alexandria and held the churches for eighteen full months. Then the people attacked him in the Church of Dionysius, and he was rescued only with danger and after a great struggle, on Thoth 1, in the consulship of Tatian and Cerealis (A.D. 358, August 29). Gregory was expelled from Alexandria on the tenth day after the riot, that is, on Phaophi 5 (October 2).

“The churches belonging to Bishop Athanasius, nine days after George’s departure—that is, on Pachon 14—were recovered by the people, who expelled Gregory’s men, and they held them for two months and fourteen days, until Duke Sebastian came from Egypt, expelled them, and once again entrusted the churches to those belonging to George, on Choiac 28 (December 24).

“After nine full months from George’s departure from Alexandria, the Notary Paul arrived on Payni 29, in the consulship of Eusebius and Hypatius (A.D. 359, June 23), produced an imperial order on behalf of George, and subdued many in order to avenge him. After five months George came to Alexandria, on Athyr 30 (A.D. 361, November 26), in the consulship of Taurus and Florentius, from the court—that is, three years and two months after he had fled.

“At Antioch, having expelled the Paulinians from the Church because of the Arian heresy, they appointed Meletius. When he refused to consent to their evil intention, they ordained Euzoïus, the presbyter of George of Alexandria, in his place. As was stated, George entered Alexandria on Athyr 30 and remained safely in the city for three days, until Choiac 3,” etc.],

the old instigators of the ruler began again to revive hatred against Athanasius. They drove him from the Church and sent in his place a certain George, a partner in their false belief and savagery. For earlier they had sent a certain Gregory. Once again there was flight, once again hiding places, and once again the ruler’s edicts against Athanasius were posted everywhere, promising rewards and honors to informers.

When Constantius himself came to the West to avenge his brother’s death and recover the kingdom, and, after the tyrant had been killed, alone possessed the throne, he began to harass the Western bishops and, through deception, to force them to consent to the Arian heresy, having first secured Athanasius’s condemnation and removed him as a most formidable obstacle.

## CHAPTER XX. On the council held at Milan and the exiles of Eusebius, Lucifer, and the other Catholic bishops

For this reason a council of bishops was summoned at Milan. Many were deceived. But Dionysius, Eusebius, Paulinus, Rhodanius, and Lucifer, proclaiming that there was a deception in the matter and asserting that the proposed signature against Athanasius was being contrived for no other reason than the destruction of the faith, were driven into exile [Note: [Col. 0494D] The same manuscript has “For this reason this chapter, Milan,” etc.; shortly afterward it has *Rodamus* instead of *Rhodanius*, and the Guarnerian has *Rodanus*. Compare Socrates, book II, chapter 36; among more recent writers, Pagius at the year 355, when this synod was convened at Milan; Montfaucon’s *Life of St. Athanasius*; and others.].

Hilary was also joined to them, while the others either did not know of the fraud or refused to believe it.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the Council of Ariminum
250 But that the matter had been conducted by such a plan was shown by the outcome. For when those men had been removed from the scene, a synod was immediately convened at Ariminum. [Note: The same edition omits *ibi* (“there”), for which the Guarnerian manuscript has the still worse reading *sibi* (“for itself”), as well as *quam* for *quae*. No one is unaware that the synod of the Westerners was convened at Ariminum in the year 359, and at the same time that of the Easterners at Seleucia. See Socrates, Book II, chapter 38, and the learned notes on him.] There, following what the Easterners had arranged at Seleucia, cunning and crafty men easily ensnared the simple and inexperienced Western bishops, putting the matter before them in this way: “Which would you rather honor and adore, *homoousion* (ὁμοούσιον), or Christ?” Since they did not understand the force of the word or what *homoousion* meant, the discussion was brought, as it were, into a kind of disgust and abhorrence, and they affirmed that they believed in Christ, not in the *homoousion*. [Note: The Guarnerian manuscript again has *quam magis* (“which more”) and so forth. For *quid ὁμοούσιον*, Cacciarius has *quod ὁμοούσιον*. Yet every time the Greek word is repeated, he corrupts it contrary to the rules of orthography. Our manuscript codices represent it in Latin letters as *homousion*.]

Thus the minds of many—apart from the few who knowingly fell—were deceived, and, acting against what the fathers had written at Nicaea, they decreed that *homoousion*, as a word unknown and alien to the Scriptures, should be removed from the exposition of the faith, and they polluted their communion by association with heretics. [Col. 0494B] So [Alternative: “And so”] the face of the Church at that time was foul and exceedingly shameful. For it was not previously being ravaged by outsiders, but by its own people. One man expelled, another was expelled, and both belonged to the Church. There was nowhere an altar, no offering, no libation; nevertheless there was transgression, apostasy, and the ruin of many. The punishment was similar, but the victory unequal. They were tortured alike, 251 but they were not glorified alike, because the Church grieved even over the fall of the man who drove others into apostasy.

## CHAPTER XXII. On Liberius, Bishop of the City of Rome

Accordingly Liberius, who, after Julius, the successor of Mark—whom Silvester had preceded—had held the priestly office in the city of Rome during the same period, was driven into exile; and Felix, his own deacon, was installed in his place by the heretics. He was stained not so much by difference of sect as by the connivance of communion and ordination. [Note: He had occupied the Roman see from the year 352; he was driven into exile at the end of 355 and, after two years and what remained beyond them, or at the beginning of 358, returned to Rome. The Guarnerian manuscript has *in quo ejus loco* (“in which, in his place”) for *inque ejus locum* (“and into his place”).] [Note: The Bononian manuscript has *cohibentia* (“restraint”), which differs little from *conniventia* (“connivance”) in the other manuscripts. The printed books, however, have *convenientia* (“agreement”), which is not itself an unsuitable reading, since Rufinus evidently also wished to indicate that he had been ordained by the Arians. Saint Jerome, in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, says that he was appointed Bishop of Rome by Acacius of Caesarea. See Athanasius, *Letter to the Monks*; also Socrates, Book II, chapter 37, near the end, and Sozomen, Book IV, chapters 11 and 15.]

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the Bishops of Jerusalem and Alexandria

At Jerusalem, Cyril, after Maximus, having received the priesthood through an already confused ordination, sometimes varied in faith, but more often in communion. At Alexandria, George, having seized the episcopate by force, exercised it with sufficient impudence, judging the fasces entrusted to him for the administration of justice more appropriate to himself than the priesthood to be exercised in religious duties. [Note: Recall what was said above about him from the acephalous History [in the preceding column, at the end of the note beginning in column 492]. We shall soon speak of his infamous end.]

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the Confusion of Bishops at Antioch

[Note: We read *De permixtione* (“On the confusion”), both on the authority of the manuscript codices listed in the Table of Chapters and because Rufinus’s purpose and the whole following context require it, which concern events at Antioch conducted in a highly confused fashion. The earlier reading was *ambitione* (“ambition”).]

At Antioch, certainly, many things were done at different times and in a very confused manner. For when Eudoxius had died, and many bishops from various cities were striving for that see with the greatest ambition, they eventually transferred Meletius from Sebastia, a city of Armenia, to it, contrary to the decrees of the council. Yet he was again driven into exile by those very men because, contrary to their expectation, he began to preach in the Church not the faith of Arius, but our own. A large crowd, following him when he had been expelled from the see [Alternative: “from the church”], was separated from association with the heretics.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the Schism of the Arians, Which Was Divided into Three Parties: Some Becoming Eunomians, Others Macedonians, and Others Remaining Arians

Meanwhile, so that malice, exceedingly rich, might at last rage even against itself, the priests and peoples who, under the leadership of Arius, had originally been separated from the Church were again split into three sects and parties. For those whom we said a little earlier had endured exile with Arius because they did not acquiesce in the pretenses of Eusebius and the others later refused even to communicate with Arius when he returned from exile, because he had communicated by a simulated confession with those who professed the Son to be of the very substance of God the Father. They themselves affirmed, with unrestrained—or rather shameless—blasphemy, that the Son was created and made, not begotten, from things that did not exist, as Arius had first taught. [Note: According to Cacciarius, two manuscripts have *substantibus* (“substances”), and he then reads *sed potius* (“but rather”) less well and against all our books, which have *seu potius* (“or rather”). The same editor notes that Aetius was ordained deacon of the Alexandrian Church by George, the Arian bishop. This is sufficiently learned. Socrates, however, in Book II, chapter 35—the chapter entitled “Concerning Aetius the Syrian, the teacher of Eunomius”—reports that he was ordained deacon by Leontius (ὑπὸ Λεοντίου), Bishop of Antioch. See which authority you prefer to follow.]

After the death of those men, a certain Aetius asserted the same doctrine, and Eunomius asserted it more forcefully and extensively after Aetius. Eunomius was a man leprous in body and soul, inwardly and outwardly corrupted by jaundice, yet exceedingly powerful in dialectical skill. He wrote many things against our faith and gave his followers rules for disputation. From him the Eunomian heresy is still named. Another man, named Macedonius, whom they had appointed Bishop of Constantinople after expelling—or rather killing—our bishops, confessed that the Son was like the Father. Although he blasphemed the Holy Spirit just as they did, he was expelled by them because he preached of the Son what they preached of the Father. Nor was he joined to our people, since he held opinions about the Holy Spirit different from theirs. [Note: The Guarnerian manuscript omits *sancto* (“Holy”); the Junctine and Bononian manuscripts have *infernis* (“from the lower regions”) instead of *inferis* (“from hell”). The printed editions read *vel potius* (“or rather”). It is worthwhile also to transcribe this account from the acephalous History, that frequently cited monument of exceptional reliability: “When Theodore with the others wished to place Eudoxius, a companion and participant in the Arian heresy, upon the throne of the city, after he had been ordained bishop of Germanicia, the people rose in sedition and allowed no one to sit upon the throne of the blessed Paul. They therefore took Macedonius, a presbyter of Paul, and ordained him bishop of the city of Constantinople. The whole assembly of bishops condemned him because he had impiously received the laying on of hands from heretics against his own father. Yet after Macedonius had communicated with them and subscribed, they introduced pretexts of no importance, removed him from the Church, and installed the aforesaid Eudoxius of Antioch. Hence, in this separation, they are called Macedonians, having suffered shipwreck with respect to the Holy Spirit.”]

Thus that destructive beast, which under Arius had first raised its head as though from the lower regions, suddenly appeared threefold:

- The Eunomians, who say that the Son is wholly unlike the Father, because a product cannot in any way be like its maker.
- The Arians, who say that the Son may indeed be called like the Father, but by the generosity of grace, not by the propriety of nature—so far as a creature can be compared with the Creator.
- The Macedonians, who say that the Son is wholly like the Father, but that the Holy Spirit has nothing in common with the Father and the Son.

Such things were done among them. But, as it is written concerning such people, “They were split apart, and they were not pierced with remorse” (Psalm 34:15): many of those who seemed to lead a more attentive life, as well as the monasteries at Constantinople and in the neighboring provinces, and distinguished Macedonian bishops, followed the error all the more.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the End of the Emperor Constantius and the Rise of Julian

But the Emperor Constantius, while preparing to march against Julian—whom he had left as Caesar in Gaul—because Julian had voluntarily presumed upon the dignity of Augustus, died in the twenty-fourth year of his imperial reign after his father’s death, in the town of Mopsucrenae in Cilicia. [Note: Earlier editions have *vita* (“life”) instead of *diem* (“day”); the Bononian manuscript has *functus* (“having fulfilled”) instead of *defunctus* (“having died”). Compare Jerome’s *Chronicle* under the year of Christ 364 and our notes on that passage.]

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the Bishops Released from Exile

After him Julian, who had first been presumptive and afterward [Note: The Guarnerian manuscript alone reads *demum ut legitimum solus obtinet principatum* (“finally alone holds the principate as its legitimate holder”). It has *vel ut* (“or as”) in two words, while Cacciarius has *velut* (“as if”), in the phrase “first, as though censuring…” Hear again the writer of the acephalous History: “On the fourth day of the month Choiac” (this is either the last day of November or the first of December in the year 361), “the prefect Gerontius announced the death of the Emperor Constantius and that Julian alone held the whole Empire. When the Alexandrians and everyone else heard this, they cried out against George; at that very moment they placed him under guard, and he was bound with iron in prison from the aforesaid fourth day of Choiac until the twenty-seventh day of the same month, twenty-four days. For on the morning of the twenty-eighth day of that month almost the entire population of that city brought George out of prison, together with the Count who was with him, and who was overseeing the construction of the Lord’s building called the Caesareum. They killed them both and dragged their bodies through the middle of the city: George’s on a camel, while men dragged Dracontius with ropes. Thus, after subjecting them to insults, they burned both bodies at about the seventh hour of the day. On the following day, Mechir 10, after the consulship of Taurus and Florentius, the command of the Emperor Julian was posted [February 4, 362], ordering that what had been taken from the idols, the neocori, and the public treasury in earlier times should be restored to them. Three days later, on Mechir 14, an order was issued to Gerontius, prefect under the same Emperor Julian, and also to the vicar Modestus, commanding all bishops who had previously been ensnared by factions and exiled to return to their cities and provinces. These letters were posted on the following day, Mechir 15. Subsequently, the edict of the prefect Gerontius was also posted, by which Athanasius the bishop was summoned to return to his church. Twelve days after the posting of this edict, Athanasius was seen at Alexandria, and entered the church on the twenty-seventh day of the same month, Mechir. From the time of his flight, which occurred during the episcopates of Syrianus and Hilary, until his return under Julian … Mechir 27, he remained in the Church until Phaophi 26, in the consulship of Mamertinus and Nevitta, for eight full months [October 23, 362].”] obtained the principate alone as its legitimate holder. He first, as though censuring the wrongful acts of Constantius, ordered the bishops to be released from exile. But afterward he rose against our people with every art of harming them.

Meanwhile the bishops who had survived were released from exile. Liberius, Bishop of the city of Rome, returned while Constantius was still alive. But whether he did so because he had yielded to Constantius’s will by signing, or whether Constantius granted it for the favor of the Roman people, who had pleaded with him as Liberius departed, I do not know with certainty. [Note: This is an old question, debated in hundreds of books on both sides. If you wish, consult Montfaucon among more recent authors in his *Life of Saint Athanasius*.]

But when Lucifer was asked by Eusebius—since both had been exiled in neighboring regions of Egypt—to go to Alexandria to see Athanasius and, in common deliberation with the priests who had survived, decide the condition of the Church, he refused to appear in person and sent his own deacon as his representative, while he himself hastened to Antioch. There, although the parties were still divided, they hoped that they could nevertheless be recalled to unity if a bishop were chosen for them whom both peoples, rather than only one, would welcome. In his haste he installed as bishop Paulinus, a Catholic and holy man, wholly worthy of the priesthood, but one whom neither people could accept. [Note: The Bononian manuscript has *pro sede Diaconum* (“a deacon in his place”), and shortly afterward *si ibi talis* (“if there such a one”) instead of *si sibi talis* (“if such a one for himself”). The Guarnerian manuscript below has *per omnia dignissimum* (“wholly worthy”) instead of *dignum* (“worthy”).]

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the Council of the Holy Bishops at Alexandria and Lucifer’s Separation from Them

255 Meanwhile Eusebius proceeded to Alexandria. There, after a council of the Confessors had been convened—few in number but rich in integrity of faith and merits—they carefully and fully debated how tranquility might be restored to the Church after the storms of the heretics and the whirlwinds of treachery. [Note: In other books Barraeus noted the reading *fidei integritate* (“in integrity of faith”), which I myself would prefer. See, for all others, Jerome’s *Dialogue Against the Luciferians*.] Some, burning with zeal for the faith, thought that no one who had in any way stained himself by the contagion of heretical communion should ever again be admitted to the priesthood. But those who, imitating the Apostle, sought not what was useful to themselves but what was useful to many, [Note: We have retained the common reading, which seems more polished and is also supported by the authority of the manuscripts, especially the Bononian. Cacciarius preferred, with the Vatican manuscripts, *quod multis expediret* (“what would benefit many”).] or who imitated Christ, who, although he was the life of all, humbled himself for the salvation of everyone and descended into death, so that life might be found even among the dead, said that it was better to humble oneself somewhat for the sake of the fallen and to bend down for the sake of those who had been crushed, so as to raise them up again. They should not claim the kingdom of heaven for themselves alone on account of their merit in purity; rather, it would be more glorious if they deserved to enter there with many others.

Therefore they thought it right that, once only the authors of the treachery had been cut off, the remaining priests should be given the choice—if they wished—to renounce the error of their treachery and return to the faith and ordinances of the fathers. The door should not be denied to those returning; instead, people should rejoice over their conversion. For that younger son in the Gospel, the squanderer of his father’s property, when he came to himself, not only deserved to be received but was also judged worthy of his father’s embrace [Alternative: “embrace”], received the ring of faith, and was clothed in a robe. What else do these signify except the insignia of the priesthood? Nor did the elder son appear acceptable to his father because he begrudged the one who had been received. [Note: The Bononian manuscript has *qui invidit* (“who begrudged him”); at the end it agrees with the printed editions in reading *notae* (“of recognition”) rather than *noxae* (“of guilt”).] His merit in not committing an offense was not as great as the guilt he incurred by refusing to forgive his brother.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the Matters Established in the Same Council

256 When that priestly and apostolic body had approved such judgments, brought forward on evangelical authority, the council decreed that the administration of the East should be entrusted to Asterius and the others who were with him, while the administration of the West was assigned to Eusebius. [Note: The same edition has *caeterisque qui cum Episcopis erant* (“and the others who were with the bishops”); the Guarnerian manuscript has *qui cum ipsis erant* (“who were with them”). Shortly afterward it reads *in loco Concilii* (“in the place of the council”) instead of *in illo* (“in that”).]

That decree of the council also included a fuller discussion of the Holy Spirit, so that the Holy Spirit might be believed to be of the same substance and divinity as the Father and the Son, and so that nothing at all in the Trinity might be said to be created, inferior, or later. A discussion was also raised by the scriptural text concerning the difference between substances and subsistences. The Greeks call these *ousiai* (οὐσίαι) and *hypostaseis* (ὑποστάσεις). [Note: The Guarnerian manuscript again has *motus est* (“has been raised”)—the terms which the Greeks call *ousiai* and *hypostaseis*. Some also add further material, including “because we do not call three substances in God.”]

Some said that substance and subsistence appeared to be one and the same; and since we do not speak of three subsistences in God, neither should we speak of three substances. Others, for whom substance seemed to signify something quite different from subsistence, said that substance designates the nature and account of some thing, by which it exists, whereas the subsistence of each person displays that very thing which exists and subsists. [Note: Two of our manuscripts, and two manuscripts cited by Cacciarius, have *substantia* here; the printed editions have *ipsa*. Shortly afterward the Bononian manuscript has *idcirco* (“therefore”) instead of *ideoque* (“and therefore”).]

Therefore, because of the heresy of Sabellius, three subsistences had to be confessed, since this seemed to signify three subsisting persons. Otherwise we might appear to be followers of the belief that confesses the Trinity in names alone, and not in realities and subsistences.

It was also established concerning the Lord’s incarnation that the body which the Lord assumed was assumed neither without sensation nor without a soul. When all these matters had been carefully and moderately arranged, each man departed in peace by his own route.

## CHAPTER XXX. On Eusebius and Hilary and the Restoration of the Churches through Them

257 But when Eusebius had returned to Antioch and discovered that a bishop had been ordained there by Lucifer contrary to his promise, he departed, compelled by shame and indignation alike, granting his communion to neither party. For when he had left, he had promised that he would act in the council so that a bishop would be ordained for them from whom neither party would separate.

That people, which had formerly followed Meletius, expelled from the Church as though for the sake of the true faith, had not joined itself to the earlier Catholics—that is, those who had been with Bishop Eustathius and Eusebius [Note: The printed books do not add *et Eusebio* (“and Eusebius”), nor does the Guarnerian manuscript, which is of the highest quality; others do add it, especially the Vatican manuscripts. To this passage should be referred the fragment of the History concerning the Meletian schism, recently published from the most ancient documents of the Church of Verona in volume III of the *Literary Observations*.]—among whom Paulinus also belonged. Instead, it maintained its own primacy and its own assembly. When Eusebius therefore wished to recall these people to unity, but could not do so because Lucifer had acted first, [Note: Here too we have supplied the name Eusebius in accordance with the manuscripts; the printed editions omit it, though without loss of meaning.] he departed.

Then Meletius returned from exile. Since he had the larger following, he took possession of the churches, and from that time held his own synod with the other Eastern bishops; yet he was not joined to Athanasius.

Meanwhile Lucifer, grieving over the injury that Eusebius had not accepted the bishop whom he had ordained at Antioch, did not himself intend to accept the decrees of the Alexandrian council. Yet he was bound by the act of his representative, who had subscribed in the council on his authority. For he could not reject the man who held his authority. [Note: The Guarnerian manuscript has “because he held his authority,” and shortly afterward reads “after deliberating long and earnestly about this.”] But if he accepted him, he saw that all his own undertaking would be rendered futile.

After deliberating over this for a long time and being hemmed in on both sides, he chose to accept his representative while maintaining toward the others a judgment different from, but pleasing to, himself. [Note: The same manuscript has “a judgment different from and pleasing to himself,” and adds “because he was overtaken by a speedy death.” The Bononian manuscript, with the printed editions, has *quia cita morte* (“because of a swift death”).]

Thus he returned to the region of Sardinia. Whether he was overtaken by sudden death and therefore had no time to change his judgment—for rash beginnings are usually corrected with time—or whether he had settled firmly in this state of mind, I cannot confidently determine. In any case, the schism of the Luciferians, which still continues among a few, took its beginning from him.
