Eusebius, meanwhile, traveled throughout the East and Italy and performed the office both of physician and of priest. He recalled each individual church from unbelief, once it had been renounced, to the health of the true faith. In particular, he found that Hilary, whom we earlier mentioned as having been driven into exile with the other bishops, had now returned and was in Italy, undertaking the same work of restoring the churches and repairing the faith of the fathers.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the Writings of Hilary

Except that Hilary, a man naturally gentle and peaceful, as well as learned and especially suited to persuasion, carried out this work more diligently and appropriately. He also published books nobly written on the faith, in which he so carefully exposed both the craftiness of the heretics, the deceptions of our own people, and their ill-advised credulity, that he corrected with the most complete instruction both those who were present and those far away, to whom he could not personally explain these matters by word of mouth. [Note: The Bononian manuscript omits the words *per se* (“personally”). Shortly afterward the Guarnerian manuscript has *mundi luminaria* (“lights of the world”) instead of *lumina* (“lights”); finally, the printed editions prefer *absconditis angulis* (“hidden corners”) to the earlier *abditis*.]

Thus these two men shone like two magnificent lights of the world over Illyricum, Italy, and Gaul, so that all the darkness of the heretics, even in hidden and obscure corners, was driven away by their radiance.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On Julian’s Gentle and Cunning Persecutions

After Julian had come to the East to wage war against the Persians, and the madness of publicly practicing the worship of idols—which he had previously concealed—had begun, he proved a more cunning persecutor than the others. Not by force or tortures, but by rewards, honors, flatteries, and persuasion, he overthrew almost the greater part of the people—more than he would have done by attacking them with cruelty. [Note: Recall what we mentioned above from the acephalous History: Julian’s decree of February 4, 362, ordering the restoration to the idols, the neocori, and the public treasury of what had been taken from them in earlier times.]

He forbade Christians to attend the schools of pagan authors and decreed that literary instruction should be open only to those who revered the gods and goddesses. He ordered that the military belt should be given to no one unless he sacrificed. He decreed that the administration of the provinces and the exercise of judicial authority should not be entrusted to Christians, since their own law had even forbidden them to use the sword. Each day he advanced in devising such laws—laws which, even if they contained something crafty or cunning, nevertheless decreed what seemed less cruel.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On His Cruelty toward Athanasius

But even toward Athanasius he could not maintain the appearance of a fictitious philosophy. [Note: The acephalous History says: “On the aforesaid day, Phaophi 27” (October 23, 362), “Julian’s imperial edict was posted, ordering Athanasius the bishop to depart from Alexandria. At the very moment when the edict was posted, the bishop left the city and stayed near Thereon. As soon as he had departed, the prefect Olympus, obeying Pythiodorus and those who were with him, men of the worst character, sent Paul and Astericius, priests of Alexandria, into exile and directed them to live in the city of Andropolis. Compare also Socrates, Book III, chapters 13 and 14. Cacciarius is mistaken when he directs the reader to Book IV, chapter 26, where Athanasius is not mentioned even in a word. He is also mistaken in adding that Socrates suppresses in silence a persecution stirred up by magicians and philosophers as instigators. For Socrates expressly states at the end of chapter 13 that there was an attack upon the Christians by those who claimed to be philosophers, τῶν φιλοσοφεῖν λεγόντων (“those who said that they were philosophers”).”]

For when a profane band of magicians, philosophers, diviners, and augurs advanced against him, as though foul serpents were boiling up from caves in the earth, they all alike declared that none of their arts would succeed unless Athanasius, as the obstacle to all of them, were first removed. [Col. 0502B] [Note: Barraeus formerly, as well as the Guarnerian manuscript, prefers this reading. Cacciarius and others have *actibus* (“acts”) instead of *artibus* (“arts”).]

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On Athanasius’s Flight Again and His Hiding Places

An army is sent again, commanders again, and the Church is attacked again. [Note: The Guarnerian manuscript has *et fluentes populi* (“and streaming crowds”). The acephalous History likewise says of Athanasius’s flight and hiding places: “But Bishop Athanasius, having stayed, as stated above, near Thereon, went up into the upper regions of Egypt, as far as Upper Hermopolis of the Thebaid and as far as Antinous. While he was living in these places, it became known that the Emperor Julian had died and that Jovian was emperor of the Christians.” Add Socrates, Book III, chapter 14.] When the sorrowful and weeping people surrounded him, he is said to have addressed them in prophetic language: “Do not be troubled, my children, for it is a little cloud, and it soon passes.”

When he had departed and was traveling by boat along the Nile, the Count who had been sent for this very purpose, having learned his route, began to pursue him energetically. When Athanasius’s little boat happened by chance to put in at a certain place, he learned from passersby that his pursuer was behind him and that, unless he took precautions, danger was already imminent. All his companions who were there with him were terrified and advised him to seek the desert as a refuge for flight.

Then he said: “Do not be frightened, little sons. Let us rather go to meet our pursuer, so that he may know that the one who defends us is far greater than the one who pursues us.” Turning the boat around, he set out to meet the man who was pursuing him. [Note: Two of our manuscripts and two Vatican manuscripts cited by Cacciarius read *obvius* (“to meet”) instead of *obviam* (“toward”). Shortly afterward Cacciarius has *possit* (“can”) instead of *posset* (“could”).]

The pursuer, unable in any way to suspect that the man he was seeking was coming to meet him, ordered some passersby to be questioned about where they had heard that Athanasius was. When they replied that they had seen him going not far away, he passed by at full speed and hurried on in vain, hastening to seize the man whom he could not see even though he was before his eyes.

But Athanasius, warned by God’s power, returned to Alexandria and remained there safely in hiding until the persecution ceased. [Note: The Guarnerian manuscript reads *rediit* (“he returned”). Socrates likewise relates that Athanasius escaped the hands of his pursuers, secretly came to Alexandria, and hid there until the persecution had subsided. Theodoret likewise tells the story. But the author of the acephalous History, in the passage cited earlier, indicates that he traveled meanwhile through the upper regions of Egypt as far as Upper Hermopolis and through the upper Thebaid as far as Antinous. “While he was living in these places,” he says, “it became known that the Emperor Julian had died and that Jovian, a Christian, was emperor.” He then adds: “Accordingly the bishop entered Alexandria secretly, his arrival being known to few, and went by boat to the Emperor Jovian. After ecclesiastical affairs had been settled, he received letters, came to Alexandria, and entered the church on the nineteenth day of Athyr [November 16, 364], in the consulship of Jovian and Varronianus. From the day he left Alexandria in accordance with Julian’s command until he returned on the aforesaid nineteenth day of Athyr, one year, three months, and twenty-two days had passed.” Ammonius too, a contemporary of Athanasius, testifies in a letter preserved in the *Acts of the Saints* under May 14 that Athanasius hid in the desert until Julian’s death and, continually fearing the plots of his persecutors, wandered among the monks from place to place. These accounts therefore wholly contradict and outweigh Rufinus’s narrative. Cacciarius’s note that the Regio-Vatican manuscript soon reads *tota* (“throughout”) instead of *tuto* (“safely”) is worthless. Even if one could somehow understand this to mean that Athanasius repeatedly changed his hiding places throughout Alexandria, the error lies in saying that he then came to Alexandria.”]

## CHAPTER XXXV. On the Tomb of the Martyr Babylas

Julian also gave another indication of his madness and fickleness. For when he was sacrificing to Apollo at Daphne, in the suburb of Antioch, near the Castalian spring, and received none of the answers he sought, he asked the priests of the demon the reasons for the silence. They said that the tomb of the martyr Babylas stood nearby, and that for this reason no answers were being given.

Then he ordered the “Galileans”—for this was the name he habitually used for our people—to come and remove the martyr’s tomb. Accordingly the whole Church assembled: mothers and men, virgins and young men, girded with immense rejoicing, drew the martyr’s coffin in a long procession, singing at the top of their voices and saying with exultation: “Let all who worship carved images be put to shame, and those who trust in their idols” (Psalm 96:7). [Note: The Guarnerian manuscript has *qui gloriantur* (“who glory”) as do several psalters, so far as I know, in all languages. Nevertheless, from the agreement of all the other manuscripts I have no doubt that Rufinus read *qui confidunt* (“who trust”) in his copy; this is the more noteworthy reading of the old version he used.]

The whole Church sang this in the ears of the profane ruler with such exultation for six thousand paces that the heavens echoed with their cries. [Note: The Bononian manuscript has *exultaret* (“would exult”). Hence he was driven into such shame and rage that on the following day he ordered Christians to be seized indiscriminately, thrown into prison, and afflicted with punishments and tortures. Although the rest of the passage seems less satisfactory, the reading *verecundiam et rabiem* (“shame and rage”) is certainly more appealing than *verecundiam et rabiem iracundiae* (“shame and the rage of anger”). Concerning the translation of Babylas’s relics, see Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book III, chapter 10. Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XXII, chapter 13, gives another cause of Julian’s anger against the Christians: the temple of Apollo at Daphne, which had been burned at that time, an act he attributed to the Christians.]

Therefore he was driven into such a frenzy of anger that on the following day he ordered Christians to be seized everywhere, thrown into prison, and afflicted with punishments and tortures.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On Theodore the Confessor at Antioch
What Sallustius the Prefect [Note: [Col. 0504C] The Guarnerian manuscript has, in a single word, “disapproving.” Socrates and Sozomen call this Sallustius the Praetorian Prefect, or ἔπαρχος (eparch), in the Greek version they made of this Rufinian History.] did not approve, nevertheless, although he was a pagan, carried out the order. He seized a certain young man who first came upon him, named Theodore, and from first light until [or “in”] the tenth hour tortured him with such cruelty and through so many successive executioners that no age remembers a similar deed. Yet while he was suspended high upon the rack [Note: [Col. 0504C] The same manuscript has “suspended” instead of “raised aloft.” Then, together with the Junctine and Bononian manuscripts, it omits, from the line following this one, the little word “which.” In place of *securo*, which follows, and which the Guarnerian manuscript, of excellent quality, also supports together with all the printed copies—and which is in fact more harmonious—Cacciarius, from the Vatican manuscripts, wrote *sereno*, “serene.”], with an executioner pressing upon him from either side, he did nothing but repeat, with a composed and joyful countenance, the psalm that the whole Church had sung the previous day. And when Sallustius perceived that, after expending every form of cruelty, he had accomplished nothing, he is said to have returned the young man to prison, gone to the Emperor, and reported what he had done, warning him not to attempt anything of the kind thereafter; otherwise he would procure glory for them and disgrace for himself. We ourselves later saw this Theodore near Antioch. When we asked him whether he had felt the pain in its entirety, he said that he had felt little pain, but that a certain young man had stood beside him, wiping his sweats [or “sweat”] from him with a very white linen cloth and frequently pouring cold water over him; and that he had been so delighted that he became sad only when he was ordered to be taken down from the rack.

The Emperor therefore threatened that, after his Persian victory, he would wage war against the Christians more effectively; he set out, indeed, but none returned [Note: [Col. 0504D] The Guarnerian manuscript has “returned.” Immediately afterward, where the text says “it is uncertain, whether by his own men or,” Cacciarius inserts from two Vatican manuscripts the little word *ne*: “whether by his own men, or whether,” etc. Nothing of the kind occurs in our manuscripts or in many others, as in all the printed editions. Moreover, to indulge him in matters concerning the narrative of events, we advise him to consult Libanius rather than the *Tripartite History*: Libanius makes Julian’s killer a Christian; Sozomen also adduces that passage at the beginning of Book VI, chapter 2. Let him then compare Eutropius, who took part in this very Persian war, Rufus Festus, and the author of the Victorine *Epitome*, who report that Julian was pierced by the enemy. Eutychianus the chronicler, cited by John Malalas, also took part in this expedition; he reports that Julian was divinely transfixed by Saint Mercury the Martyr. The author of the Alexandrian Chronicle agrees, and Theodoret in part, reporting that Christ directed the weapon by which he was killed. But it would take too long to dwell on these matters.]. There indeed, it being uncertain [Col. 0504C] whether he was pierced by his own men or by the enemy, after one year [Col. 0505A] and eight months of his assumed imperial rule, he ended his life [Note: [Col. 0505C] In the Guarnerian manuscript: “he ended,” without the intervening words “his life.”].

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On the efforts of the Jews, who, deceived by Julian, rebuilt the temple in Jerusalem

His subtlety and cunning in deceiving people were so great that he also mocked the wretched Jews, enticing them with empty hopes, just as he himself was being driven onward. He first summoned them all before him and asked why they did not offer sacrifices, since their Law commanded them to do so. But they, thinking that they had found an opportunity in the circumstances, 263 replied: “We cannot do so except in the temple of Jerusalem alone. For so the Law commands.”

Having received from him permission to restore the temple, they reached such a degree of insolence that one might have thought that one of the prophets had been restored to them. Accordingly, Jews gathered from every place and province [Note: [Col. 0505C] The Guarnerian manuscript has “to gather”; then the Bononian has “consumed,” instead of “having been consumed.”] and began to undertake the site of the temple, formerly consumed by fire, with a Count appointed by the Emperor to expedite the work. At public and private expense the undertaking was pursued with every effort.

Meanwhile they insulted our people, as though the times of their kingdom had been restored to them [Note: [Col. 0505C] Again the Bononian manuscript has *ibi*, “there,” instead of *sibi*, “for themselves”; it also omits the name of the kingdom that follows. Shortly afterward, in place of *in magno tumore*, “in great swelling,” which our manuscripts and all the Vatican manuscripts likewise have, the printed copies preferred, with somewhat greater correctness, *immani tumore*, “in monstrous swelling.”], threatened them more fiercely, displayed their savagery, and acted altogether in great swelling and pride.

Cyril was then regarded as bishop of Jerusalem, after Maximus the Confessor [Note: [Col. 0505D] The Guarnerian manuscript has: “Cyril, then, after Maximus,” etc.]. When the foundations had been opened and lime and cement had been applied [Note: [Col. 0506C] Here the consistent reading of the manuscripts should have been preferred to the printed text, which nevertheless seemed somewhat more elegant: “with lime and mortar having been applied.” Shortly afterward the Bononian manuscript has “on the following day,” etc.], nothing at all was lacking to enable them, on the next day, after the old foundations had been torn out, to lay new ones. Yet the bishop, having carefully considered the matter—whether from what [or “these things”] he had read in the prophecy of Daniel concerning the times [Col. 0505C], or from what the Lord had foretold in the Gospels [Note: [Col. 0506C] Cacciarius, incorrectly and contrary to the manuscripts’ authority, has “or because in the Gospels,” etc.]—persisted in declaring that it could not possibly happen in any way that the Jews should place stone upon stone there. The matter remained in suspense.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. How, by an earthquake there and by fire divinely kindled, the Jews were hindered from their unlawful undertaking

[Col. 0506A]

And behold, on the night that alone remained before the work was to begin, a great earthquake arose. Not only were the stones of the foundations hurled far and wide, but nearly all the buildings of the entire place were leveled. 264 The public colonnades also, in which the multitude of Jews who appeared to be engaged in the work had been staying, were razed to the ground and crushed all the Jews who were found there. When daylight came, and they thought that they had escaped their misfortunes, the remaining multitude hurried together to look for those who had been crushed.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On the terrifying signs and miracles that were turned to the destruction of the Jews

[Col. 0506B]

There was a certain building sunk into the lower parts of the temple [Note: [Col. 0506C] The Guarnerian manuscript has: “there was also a certain building.”], with an entrance [or “entrances”] between two colonnades that had been leveled. In it were kept tools and other things necessary for the work [or “works”]. Suddenly a kind of globe of fire burst out from it and, running through the middle of the street, moved back and forth, scorching and killing the Jews who were present.

Repeating this again and again, very frequently throughout that whole day, it restrained the obstinacy of the stubborn people with avenging flames. Meanwhile, all who were present, terrified by great fear and trembling, were compelled against their will to confess Jesus Christ as the only true God [Note: [Col. 0506C] The same manuscript has “the true God Christ Jesus”; the Bononian has “the true Lord Christ.”].

And, lest these things be thought to have happened by chance, on the following night a sign of the Cross appeared so clearly on everyone’s clothing [Col. 0506C] that even anyone who wished to wash it away because of his unbelief could not erase it by any means. Thus terrified, the Jews and Gentiles alike abandoned both the place and the work they had begun in vain [Note: [Col. 0506C] Again the Guarnerian manuscript has: “and abandoned the work of the empty structure that had been begun”; it also adds this conclusion: “This is contained in the tenth book of Ecclesiastical History.”].

[Col. 0505]

[Col. 0505D] I. On the origin and religious mind of the Emperor Jovinian [Note: [Col. 0505D] The Guarnerian manuscript has “Jovian,” which I would certainly prefer if it were clear that this reading agreed with the other passages. As for the beginnings of the chapters, where a manuscript occasionally differs from the printed division, we shall note the matter in its proper place.], and on his death.

II. On the origin of Valentinian and Valens.

III. On the repose of Athanasius and the persecutions of Lucius the heretic.

IV. On the virtues and miracles of the saints who were in Egypt.

[Col. 0506D] V. On the persecution that took place at Edessa.

VI. On Moses, whom the queen of the Saracens requested as bishop of her people.

VII. On Didymus of Alexandria, the Seer [Note: [Col. 0505D] The same manuscript adds a mark of negation: “not seeing,” evidently from the hand of some learned glossator. For since Didymus suffered blindness of the bodily eyes but, as Jerome says in the preface to his book *On the Holy Spirit*, looked far more deeply with the eyes of the mind, an ancient custom has been restored to us by which he is called “the Seer.” By that name the prophets were once called. Thus also in the table of contents of the book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*: Didymus ὁ βλέπων, “Didymus the Seer.”].

VIII. How many of the disciples of Antony, still dwelling in the desert, performed virtues and signs [Note: [Col. 0506D] In the same manuscript: “How many saints, among Antony’s disciples, lived in the desert, performing virtues and signs.”].

[Col. 0507A] IX. On Gregory and Basil, bishops of Cappadocia.

X. On Bishop Damasus and the usurpation of Ursinus.

XI. On Bishop Ambrose.

XII. On the death of Valentinian [Note: [Col. 0507C] The same manuscript has “of Valens” instead of “of Valentinian”; then the following chapter contains more, including “and the death of the Emperor Valens.” In the next chapter it again has “he assumed” instead of “he took as associate.”].

XIII. On the incursion of the Goths through Thrace and the death of Valens.

XIV. How the Emperor Gratian took Theodosius as partner in the kingdom and, after accomplishing many religious and courageous deeds, succumbed to the plots of the tyrant Maximus.

XVI. On the faithful steadfastness of Benivolus [or Benevolus], Master of the Memory.

XVII. How Theodosius avenged the death of Gratian and triumphed over Maximus.

XVIII. On Theodosius’ offense against the Thessalonians and his public repentance before the priests.

XIX. On the restoration of the churches that, after becoming Catholic, he restored in the East [Note: [Col. 0507C] Again the same manuscript has: “On the restorations of the churches that were restored by him to the Catholics in the East” [Col. 0507D].].

XX. On Apollinaris and his heresy.

XXI. On episcopal successions throughout the East.

[Col. 0508A] XXII. On the revolt of the pagans against the faithful [Note: [Col. 0507D] The same manuscript has: “On the pagan disturbances at Alexandria.”].

XXIII. On the location of the temple of Serapis and its overthrow.

XXIV. On the frauds discovered in the temples of the pagans.

XXV. On Saturn’s priest Tyrannus, the adulterer of almost the whole of Alexandria.

XXVI. On the origin and destruction of Canopus [Note: [Col. 0507D] We restore this from the Guarnerian manuscript; previously it had been read with a faulty transposition as “destruction and origin.” See the text of the chapter itself.].

XXVII. On the churches and martyr-shrines constructed in the places of idols.

XXVIII. On the violated tomb of John and the relics preserved at Alexandria.

XXIX. On the breastplates of Serapis at Alexandria being scraped away, and the sign of Christ being restored in their place.

XXX. How the measure of the water of the Nile River, called a *ποῦχυν* (*pouchyn*), was brought to the Church [Note: [Col. 0507D] The same manuscript has *petin* in Latin letters; then it has “is carried” instead of “is brought.” Moreover, it joins the following two chapters into one.].

XXXI. On the death of the younger Valentinian and the rise of Eugenius.

XXXII. On the answers of the monk John.

XXXIII. On Theodosius’ preparation for war against Eugenius and his victory, achieved more by prayers than by valor [Note: [Col. 0507D] The manuscript has *patrata*, “accomplished”; *parta*, “won,” would also be acceptable. At the end it adds: “The chapters are finished. The eleventh book begins.”].

[Col. 0508B] XXXIV. On the end of Theodosius after the victory, and on his sons and heirs to the kingdom, Arcadius and Honorius.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0507]

## CHAPTER I. On the origin and religious mind of the Emperor Jovinian, and on his death

[Col. 0507B]

267 After the death of Julian, the civil Empire was at last restored to us through Jovinian [Note: [Col. 0507D] Previously: “through Jovian,” perhaps more correctly, but the manuscripts disagree. Other authors call this man Jovian.]. For at one and the same time he was Emperor, Confessor, and the one who drove away the error unjustly inflicted upon us.

When the army was in battle array and the barbarian was pressing hard [Note: [Col. 0507D] The Bononian has “the barbarians.” Two Vatican manuscripts in Cacciarius’ possession have “and the army was being pressed by the barbarians.” Shortly afterward the Guarnerian has “they gave” instead of “they had given.”], our commanders, deliberating about matters of the highest importance, gave their vote to Jovinian. When he had been seized and was being dragged to receive the insignia of imperial power, he is said to have proclaimed to the army of the sacrilegious Julian that he could not rule them because he was a Christian. Then all are reported to have answered with one and the same voice: “We too are Christians.” They say that he was unwilling to consent to the imperial office until he had heard this declaration [Note: [Col. 0507D] Barraeus and Rhenanus note in the margin: “or, who were not Christians.” Then the Bononian manuscript has: “Nevertheless, all,” etc.].

Finally, divine mercy immediately came to his aid. Contrary to all hope, while they were shut in on every side by the enemy and had no possibility of escape, they suddenly saw envoys sent by the barbarians arrive and ask for peace. They also promised the army, which was being consumed by hunger, food and other necessities in exchange for payment, and sought to repair the rashness of our people by every act of humanity. [The concessions made to the enemy—or to Sapor, king of the Persians—included Nisibis and the regions beyond the Tigris. See Socrates, Book III, chapter 22.]

But when peace had been arranged for twenty-nine years, he returned to Roman territory. 268 A brighter light had arisen for our world and spread from the regions of the East [or “had risen”]. He undertook to restore the state, as though after excessive storms, with every moderation [or “with every possible method”], while not placing the care of the churches among secondary matters.

Yet he did not proceed recklessly, as Constantius had done. Warned by the lapse of his predecessor [Note: [Col. 0508C] Cacciarius incorrectly has “having fallen.” Then the Bononian manuscript has “of his predecessor” [Col. 0508D], and shortly afterward “most abundant” instead of “most dutiful.” Recall the passage noted in the preceding book from the *Acephalous History*: “Athanasius came by ship to the Emperor Jovian, and afterward, when ecclesiastical affairs had been settled, receiving letters, he came to Alexandria and entered the Church, on the nineteenth day of Athyr, in the consulship of Jovian and Varronianus,” etc. It is also worth noting what Rufinus adds below: that Jovian asked Athanasius for a statement of faith, which can only mean a formula of faith, or Creed.], he summoned Athanasius by honorable and most dutiful letter and received from him the form of faith and the method of arranging the churches [Note: [Col. 0508D] The Regional-Vatican manuscript has “he received.” On Jovian’s death, see Socrates at the end of Book III. Saint Chrysostom, in Homily XV on Philippians, says that he died from poison. Valesius proves in his notes on Ammianus Marcellinus that exactly ten days elapsed between his death and Valentinian’s accession, counting both endpoints and counting twice the sixth day before the Kalends—for that year, 364, was a leap year—from 17 February to 26 February.].

But death cut short beginnings so pious and so joyful. For after eight months of his accession, he died near Cilicia.

## CHAPTER II. On the origin of Valentinian and Valens

After him Valentinian assumed the Empire. Julian had expelled him from military service because of our faith. But the Lord fulfilled in him what He had promised, restoring to him in the present age more than a hundredfold. Because he had abandoned military service for Christ, he received the Empire [or “he receives the Empire”].

He took his brother Valens as partner in the kingdom. He chose the western regions for himself and left the eastern regions to Valens. But Valens, favoring the heretics, went the way of his fathers. He drove bishops into exile, as well as presbyters, deacons, and monks, and—while Tatianus was prefect of Alexandria—he subjected them even to torture and handed them over to the flames. He plotted many abominable and cruel deeds against the Church of God.

269 [Note: [Col. 0509A] It is worthwhile to insert here, beginning at number 10 and following, the *Acephalous History*, which in a sense breathes life into Rufinus’ narrative.

“After Jovian, Valentinian and Valens were called to the imperial office more quickly. Their command was issued everywhere, and it was also delivered at Alexandria on the tenth day of Pachon—5 May, in the year 365, in the consulship of Valentinian and Valens. It ordered that the bishops who had been deposed under Constantius and expelled from their churches, but who during Julian’s reign had reclaimed their bishoprics and recovered them, should now again be expelled from the churches. A penalty was imposed upon the municipal councils of three hundred pounds of gold unless they removed [perhaps ‘eliminated’] the bishops from the churches and cities.

“From this there arose great confusion and disturbance at Alexandria, so that the whole Church was wearied. The leading officials were few in number, together with the prefect Flavianus and his staff; and, because of the imperial command and the fine of gold, they threatened that the bishops should leave the city, while the Christian multitude resisted and contradicted the leading officials and the judge, affirming that Bishop Athanasius was not subject to this decree and imperial command. Constantius had not persecuted him but had even restored him; Julian likewise persecuted him, recalled everyone, and then expelled him again because of idolatry; Jovian restored him.

“This disagreement and disturbance continued until the following month, on the fourteenth day of Payni—8 June. On that day the prefect Flavianus, after making his report, declared that he had consulted the Emperors about the disturbance that had arisen at Alexandria. Thus everyone became quiet for a short time.

“After four months and twenty-four days—that is, on the eighth day of Phaophi, 5 October—Bishop Athanasius secretly left the Church by night and withdrew to a village beside the New River. The prefect Flavianus and the general Victorinus, unaware that he had withdrawn, reached the Church of Dionysius that same night with a military force. Having broken the small doors, they entered the courtyard and the upper parts of the house, seeking the bishop’s lodging, but did not find him. He had withdrawn shortly before and remained in the aforementioned estate from the seventh day of Phaophi until the sixth day of Mechir—that is, for four full months, from 5 October to 31 January.

“After this the imperial notary Bresida came to Alexandria in the same month of Mechir with imperial letters ordering Bishop Athanasius to return to the city and resume his customary administration of the churches. On the seventh day of Mechir—in the year 366, after the consulship of Valentinian and Valens, that is, in the consulship of Gratian and Degalaifus—the same notary Bresidas, meeting with the general Victorinus and the prefect Flavianus in the palace, announced in the presence of the municipal councilors and the people what the Emperors had ordered: that the bishop should return to the city.

“At that very moment the notary Bresida went out with the municipal councilors and a multitude of Christian people to the aforesaid village. Taking Bishop Athanasius with the imperial command, he led him into the Church called that of Dionysius, on the seventh day of Mechir—1 February.

“You understand in what sense Rufinus says that, while Athanasius was alive, Valens undertook nothing against the churches and did not dare to commit anything grievous against him.

“Now receive the remaining material concerning the action of Tatianus, the prefect whom our author deliberately names, and the rash efforts of Lucius, the pseudo-bishop. These events too occurred while Athanasius was alive, namely in the year 367. For the holy bishop died, as we shall soon say, in the year 373.

“In the consulship of Lupicinus and Jovinus, Lucius, specifically wishing to claim the bishopric for himself on behalf of the Arians, came after a long interval following his departure from Alexandria, in the aforementioned consulship—that is, in the year 367. He entered the city secretly by night, on the twenty-sixth day of the month Thoth—24 September—and, as has been said, remained hidden that day in a certain small house.

“On the following day he entered the house where his mother was staying. As soon as his arrival became known throughout the city, the whole people gathered and censured his entrance. The general Trajanus and the prefect Tatianus were greatly displeased by his unreasonable and audacious arrival, and sent the leading officials to expel him from the city.

“When the leading officials came to Lucius and saw that the whole people were angry and greatly inflamed against him, they feared to lead him out of the house themselves lest he be killed by the crowd. They reported this to the judges. Shortly afterward the judges themselves—the general Trajanus and the prefect Tatianus—entered the place with many soldiers, went into the house, and brought Lucius out themselves at the seventh hour of the day, on the twenty-seventh day of Thoth.

“As Lucius followed the judges, the entire Christian and pagan population of the city, together with people of various religions, followed after him. All alike, with one spirit, one judgment, and one decree, did not cease shouting from the house from which he had been led, through the middle of the city and as far as the general’s house, hurling vile and criminal abuse at him and crying: ‘Let him be taken outside the city.’

“Nevertheless, the general brought him into his own house. Lucius remained with him under guard for the rest of the day and throughout the night. On the following day, the twenty-eighth of the aforesaid month, the general, staying there with him, took him as far as Nicopolis and handed him over to soldiers to be escorted to Egypt.”]

But all these things occurred after Athanasius’ death. While Athanasius was alive, Valens, as though restrained by some divine power, raged against the others but dared to commit nothing grievous against him [Note: [Col. 0510C] The Bononian manuscript has: “while he raged for a long time,” etc.].

## CHAPTER III. On the repose of Athanasius and the persecutions of Lucius the heretic

At that time, when Athanasius, in the forty-sixth year [Note: [Col. 0510C] This is based on the calculations discussed above in connection with the *Acephalous History*, where we began to speak of Athanasius and considered his ordination to be recorded in the year 328. There is no doubt that the year of his death was 373. The same *Acephalous History* says that he fell asleep on the eighth day of Pachon, in the fourth consulship of Valentinian and Valens—3 May 373. I omit Proterius’ Paschal Letter, the *History of the Coptic Patriarchs* translated into Latin and published by Eckellensis, and other documents of that kind relevant here. Cacciarius, ignorant of the arguments by which learned men established this year, 373, clings to the old false opinion and compounds it with new errors.] of his priesthood, had rested in peace after many struggles and many crowns of patience, having inquired concerning his successor, he chose Peter, who had shared and accompanied him in his tribulations [Note: [Col. 0510D] Here ends the frequently cited *Acephalous History*: “After Athanasius had died on the eighth day of Pachon, five days before his repose he appointed Peter bishop from among the ancient presbyters. Peter, who followed him in all things, exercised the episcopate.” See his Encyclical Letter in Theodoret, Book IV, chapter 22, where he laments the violence inflicted upon him when newly elevated to the episcopate and curses Lucius’ savage attempts against the Alexandrian see.].

But Lucius, bishop of the Arian party [Note: [Col. 0511C] That is, first thrust into the chair of Samosata by the Arians after Eusebius had been expelled by force of arms.], immediately flew upon the sheep like a wolf. 270 Peter at once boarded a ship and fled to the city of Rome.

Lucius, however, as though material for his cruelty had been offered him [Note: [Col. 0511D] Perhaps the manuscripts’ *ablata* is more correct, meaning “the opportunity for raging against Peter having been removed.”], became more savage toward the others. And he proceeded so far in bloodshed that he seemed not even to preserve the appearance of religion. At his first entry, he committed such great and shameful acts against virgins and women living continently as are not recorded even during the persecutions of the pagans.

Then, after the flights of citizens and exiles, after killings and tortures and flames by which he destroyed countless people [or “condemned them”], he turned the weapons of his fury against the monasteries. He ravaged the desert and declared war upon those who were at peace. He undertook at the same time to attack three thousand men, or even more, scattered throughout the entire desert in secluded and solitary habitations 271 [Note: [Col. 0511D] The Bononian has “throughout the whole desert”; the Guarnerian has “scattered throughout the entire desert in secluded and solitary [habitations],” etc.].

He sent an armed force of cavalry and infantry. He selected tribunes, commanders, and leaders of wars as though he were about to fight against barbarians [Note: [Col. 0511D] The Bononian manuscript has *eligit*, “chooses,” which fits the preceding tenses better. Shortly afterward the Regional-Vatican manuscript adds: “to expose them to barbarian swords,” etc. These seem to be the men whom Saint Jerome, in Letter III to Rufinus, calls the Egyptian Confessors and, already in will, martyrs.]. When they arrived, they saw a new kind of war: the enemies thrusting their necks toward the swords and saying nothing except, “Friend, why have you come?”

## CHAPTER IV. On the virtues and miracles of the saints who were in Egypt

At that time, the fathers of the monastic life, renowned for the merit of their life and antiquity—Macarius and Isidore, another Macarius, Heraclides, and Pambus, disciples of Antony—were living throughout Egypt, especially in the regions of the desert of Nitria. They were men believed to share in life and action not with other mortals but with the angels above.

I speak of what I myself saw; I report the deeds of those whose sufferings I was privileged to share [Note: [Col. 0511D] This is what Rufinus says of himself again in the *Apology to Anastasius*, to be cited below: “Although our faith was tested during the persecution of the heretics, when we were living in the holy Alexandrian Church, in prisons and exiles inflicted for the faith, nevertheless,” etc. Jerome nevertheless seems to deny him this distinction in Book II of his *Apology*, right at the beginning; see our notes on that passage. Those illustrious coenobites are celebrated everywhere by the writers of Ecclesiastical and Monastic History, so that our work now has no need to add anything to their fame.].

They led the army of the Lord, armed not with mortal weapons but with the faith of religion—an army that conquered by dying and that, victorious through the shedding of its blood, followed Christ to heaven.

While they were staying in their dwellings and awaiting their killers in prayer, a man who had formerly been dry in all his limbs, especially in his feet, was brought before them [Note: [Col. 0512D] The Guarnerian has “dry,” and shortly afterward adds “in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ”; together with the Bononian and two Vatican manuscripts it also has “return to your house,” etc.]. When they had anointed him with oil in the name of the Lord, the soles of his feet were immediately strengthened. They said to him, in the name of Jesus Christ, whom Lucius persecutes: “Rise, stand on your feet, and return to your house.” He immediately rose and leapt about, blessing God and showing that God was truly in them.

A short time earlier, a certain blind man had asked to be led to Macarius’ cell, which was in the desert, a three-day journey away [Note: [Col. 0512D] The same manuscript has “asked” instead of “was asking”; and in place of “to be led,” which our manuscripts also have, Cacciarius preferred “to be brought.”]. When the blind man finally arrived after the great labor of those who led him, he did not find Macarius at home. He was deeply saddened and could not in any way lessen his grief, deprived as he was of the comfort of healing [Note: [Col. 0512D] The same manuscript has “comforts”; shortly afterward, “those who had led him”; two Vatican manuscripts have “those who had led him.”].

Then, growing warm with the fervor of faith, he said to those who had led him: “I beg you, bring me to that part of the wall where the old man usually sleeps.” When he had been brought there, he took a little dry mud with which the wall appeared to have been plastered and placed it upon his palm [or “under his palm”]. He also asked them to draw water from the well from which Macarius used to drink. Dissolving the little clod with that water [Note: [Col. 0512D] Previously: “which dissolves”; equally good. The Bononian has “dissolving”; finally, the Guarnerian has “applying it over,” that is, “anointing over.”], he spread the same mud over his eyes and washed them with the water that had been drawn. Suddenly he regained his sight, so that he returned to his own people without needing any assistance.

But, lest he behave like those lepers whom the Lord, in the Gospels, reproves as ungrateful after being healed by Him, he returned with his entire household [or “he returned”] and gave thanks to God, reporting the matter as it had happened.

That same Macarius [Note: [Col. 0512D] The Bononian adds “the elder.”] had a lioness’s cave near his cell. One day the beast brought her blind cubs to him and placed them before his feet. When he understood that the animal was pleading for sight for her cubs, he asked the Lord to restore their sight. After they received it, they followed their mother and returned to the cave.

Shortly afterward she returned with her cubs and brought the old man many fleecy sheep-skins as a gift in return for the favor received. She carried them in her mouth [Note: [Col. 0512D] Previously, incorrectly: “having killed them.” What follows is perhaps more correct and agrees with our manuscripts. Cacciarius, from the Vatican manuscripts, omits the conjunction and the pronoun “her,” and finally reads “she deposits” instead of “having deposited them,” then departs. Shortly afterward the Guarnerian has “we shall be shut out” instead of “we are shut out.”], deposited them before his door, and departed.

But if we wished to recount the deeds of each individual miracle, we would be excluded from the brevity we have proposed, especially since these events deserve to belong to the narrative of a work of their own [Note: [Col. 0512D] The printed copies previously lacked “to possess,” which our manuscripts also supply. Rufinus is alluding to the book *On the Monks*, written by him under the name of Petronius.].

273 Yet in all these matters Lucius did not blush, nor did he show any reverence toward the miraculous virtues. On the contrary, he ordered the fathers themselves to be taken away from their flock—or rather, secretly snatched away—and transported to a certain island among the marshes of Egypt [Col. 0513A], where he had discovered that there was absolutely no Christian, so that they might live there deprived either of consolation or of their customary activities.

The old men were therefore taken by night to the island with only two attendants. There was a certain temple on it, held in the highest reverence by the inhabitants of the place. When the boat carrying the old men first touched the shore of that island [Note: [Col. 0513D] The Guarnerian has: “When the boat of the old men,” and omits “first.”], behold, the virgin daughter of the temple’s priest was suddenly seized by a spirit. With tremendous cries and shouting sent up to heaven, she began to be driven through the midst of the people, repeatedly whirling about, hissing, and darting her frenzied face from side to side.

When the people had gathered to watch so great a portent—especially because she was the daughter of the priest, who held the highest honor among them—they followed her as she was carried through the air and came as far as the old men’s boat. There she threw herself at their feet and, prostrate, began to cry out:

“Why have you come here, O servants of the Most High God, to drive us from our ancient and age-old dwelling places? We were driven here from every side and were hiding; how then could we possibly remain hidden from you? We yield our ancient seats. Take back your peoples and your lands.”

As she said this, the spirit of error was rebuked by them and driven out. The girl, now healed, together with her parents, lay at the feet of the apostles of our own age. By preaching to them in this way the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, they suddenly brought them to such a conversion that on that very day [Note: [Col. 0513D] Our manuscripts and the Regional-Vatican supply the words “on that very day.”] they themselves immediately destroyed the ancient temple, which had been held in the highest reverence, and built a church without delay.

They had no need of time for deliberation, because it was not words but power that had convinced them of the truth of the matter.

274 When this was reported at Alexandria, Lucius feared that a just hatred against him might perhaps also arise among his own people, since he was now plainly declaring war not against men but against God. He therefore ordered them to be secretly recalled and sent back into the desert [Note: [Col. 0513D] The Guarnerian has the somewhat more correct “because he was openly” and concludes the chapter with this period. It begins a new, or fifth, chapter with the words: “While these things were happening in Egypt,” etc.].

While these things were happening in Egypt, the flame of persecution did not cease in other places either.

## CHAPTER V. On the persecution that took place at Edessa
Edessa, then, is a city of Mesopotamia of faithful peoples, adorned with the relics of the Apostle Thomas. [Note: Cacciarius is wrong when he says that Socrates, Book IV, chapter 14 (he had said 18), and Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 18, testify that the relics of the Apostle Thomas were transferred from India to Edessa. Although these authors describe Rufinus and reproduce nearly the same words in Greek, they mention a basilica—or *martyrion* (μαρτύριον)—and a place of prayer—*euktērion* (εὐκτήριον)—of Thomas, but not relics. Nor is it our task to discuss this matter at greater length. The words that follow are absent from our manuscripts.]

When the Emperor himself saw the faithful people, expelled from the churches, holding their assembly in the field, he is said to have been so inflamed with anger that he struck his prefect with his fist, asking why they had not also been driven away from there, as he had ordered. [Note: The Guarnerian manuscript has *undique* (“from everywhere”) instead of *inde quoque* (“from there also”).]

Although the prefect was a pagan and had been subjected to insults by the Emperor, nevertheless, out of consideration for humanity, on the following day, as he was about to proceed to devastate the people, he caused this very intention to be made known to the citizens by secret signals, so that they might take precautions and avoid being found at the place. [Note: The same manuscript has *mane vero processurus* (“but when he was about to set out in the morning”). The office held by Flavian the Prefect is also mentioned, in the same sense, by the anonymous History cited above (column 509, note a). Cacciarius describes the marginal note of Rhenanus, which is also found at the edge of Barraeus’s edition; he calls the *officium* “officials,” that is, attendants and guards.]

On the morning when he was about to set out, he caused an even greater terror than usual through his staff, and arranged everything so that as few people as possible—or, if it could be managed, no one—would be endangered. Yet he saw the people gathering at the place in greater numbers than usual, running headlong and hurrying as though they feared that someone might be absent from the appointed death.

Meanwhile he saw a certain little woman bursting forth from her house with such haste and urgency that she could neither shut the door nor cover herself as carefully as women’s dress requires; she was also dragging along with her a small infant and hurrying at a rapid pace, even breaking through the ranks of the prefect’s staff. Then, unable to endure this any longer, he said: “Seize the woman and bring her here.” When she had been brought forward, he said: “Where are you hurrying, unhappy woman, in such haste?”

“To the field,” she replied, “where the Catholic people are assembling.”

“And have you not heard,” he said, “that the prefect is going there to kill everyone he finds?”

“I have heard,” she replied, “and that is why I am hurrying, so that I may be found there.”

“And where are you dragging this little child?”

“So that he too,” she said, “may be found worthy to attain martyrdom.”

When the most temperate man heard this, he ordered his staff to turn back and the carriage to be redirected to the palace. Entering, he said: “Emperor, if you order me to undergo death, I am prepared. But we cannot carry out the task you command.” When he had explained everything about the woman, he restrained the Emperor’s madness.

## CHAPTER VI. On Moses, whom the Queen of the Saracen people requested as their bishop

At that time, while the Church seemed to be fanned by the fire of persecution, it shone forth more purely, like gold refined. For faith was tested not in everyone’s words, but in exiles and prisons, since being Catholic was not a matter of honor but of punishment—especially at Alexandria, where the faithful were not even granted freedom to bury the bodies of the dead. [Note: From these words the Guarnerian manuscript begins a new chapter, or Chapter VI, joining the preceding words closely to the previous chapter. Some manuscripts instead read “While Lucius was doing these things” for “While these things were being done by Lucius.”]

While Lucius was carrying on these things with every arrogance and cruelty, Mauvia, Queen of the Saracen people, began to shake the towns and cities of the Palestinian and Arabian frontier in a violent war and at the same time to lay waste the neighboring provinces. [Note: Socrates, Nicephorus, and Epiphanius Scholasticus call her Mavia, or Μαυία (*Mauia*). Sozomen, however, consistently has Μανία (*Mania*), Mani[a]. The Guarnerian manuscript writes *Mavia*. Pagius assigns the war with the Saracens to the year 372, and the peace made after Athanasius’s death, with Queen Mauvia converted to the Christian faith. I would prefer to place this later, as late as the year 374.]

After wearing down the Roman army through repeated wars, killing many and putting the rest to flight, she requested peace and declared that she would accept it only on the condition that a certain monk named Moses be ordained bishop for her people. He was living a solitary life in the desert near his own people and had become highly renowned for his merits, virtues, and the signs God performed through him. [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts have “well known.” Shortly afterward the Guarnerian manuscript reads *infideliter pugnaverant* (“they had fought faithlessly”) instead of *infeliciter* (“they had fought unsuccessfully”).]

Her request was reported to the Roman emperor, and our commanders—who had fought there unsuccessfully—were ordered to fulfill it without delay. Moses was seized to receive the priesthood and, according to custom, brought to Alexandria. Lucius was present, to whom the duty of ordaining him had been assigned. When he saw him, Moses said in the presence of the commanders who were pressing the matter and of the people:

“I judge myself unworthy of so great a priesthood. Nevertheless, if it is thought that some divine dispensation is to be fulfilled through me, unworthy though I am, I call our God, Lord of heaven and earth, to witness that Lucius will not lay upon me hands stained and bloodied with the blood of the saints.”

When Lucius saw that so grave a charge had marked him in the eyes of many, he said: “Why, Moses, do you condemn so readily one whose faith you do not know? Or, if someone has reported something else to you about me, hear my profession of faith, and trust yourself more than others.” [Note: The Guarnerian manuscript reads, “But if you have been told something about me,” and shortly afterward, with some Vatican manuscripts, “trust yourself more,” and finally “Then he,” instead of “At that point.”]

Then Moses said: “Cease, Lucius, from attacking me also with your deceitful images. Your faith is well known to me; it is proclaimed by God’s servants condemned to the mines, by bishops driven into exile, by priests and deacons banished beyond the dwelling places of the Christian name, and by those handed over—some to wild beasts, others even to the flames. Can a faith received through the ears be truer than one clearly seen with the eyes? For me it is certain that those who rightly believe in Christ do not do such things.”

And so, disfigured by even greater disgrace—for the necessity of caring for the state was pressing—Lucius was compelled to agree that Moses should receive the priesthood from the bishops whom he had driven into exile. [Note: The Regio-Vatican manuscript adds: “so that, after being led away from Alexandria, he might be ordained by the bishops,” and indeed Socrates, Book IV, chapter 37—not 29, as Cacciarius incorrectly notes—reports that Moses was ordained outside Alexandria, on the mountain to which he had been taken, by those who were exiled there. Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 38, likewise says that, after rejecting Lucius, Moses was brought to the bishops living in exile. These writers, as I have observed elsewhere, present Rufinus in Greek. At the end of the Guarnerian manuscript we read: “he obtained peace, and kept their fellowship undefiled.”]

After receiving this office, Moses both maintained peace with that most savage people and preserved their fellowship with the Catholic faith undefiled.

## CHAPTER VII. On Didymus of Alexandria, the seer

But when a dark gloom of foul treachery from an obscure teacher was spreading over the people and city of Alexandria, the Lord kindled Didymus there like a lamp shining with divine light. Since his life and discipline are believed to have been granted, by God’s gift, for the glory of the Church, a few things must necessarily be mentioned, although only in passing. [Note: The Guarnerian manuscript has “kindled”; then the Bononian manuscript, “although pressing forward in his course.” Concerning Didymus, others and I have said much elsewhere, especially in the notes to Jerome—who gloried in having him as his teacher, as Rufinus did also—so that it would be superfluous to repeat the same material here.]

While still very young, when he did not yet know even the first elements of letters, he was deprived of his sight and inflamed with a greater desire for knowledge of the true light. [Note: The Bononian manuscript has “was inflamed.” Shortly afterward, from the Guarnerian manuscript, we read “what he desired” instead of “what was desired,” as the other printed books and manuscripts likewise prefer.] Nor did he submit to despair of attaining what he desired when he heard what is written in the Gospel: “What is impossible with human beings is possible with God” (Matthew 19; Mark 10; Luke 18).

Trusting, therefore, in this divine promise, he prayed to the Lord without ceasing, not that he might receive the sight of bodily eyes, but that he might receive illumination of heart. Yet he mingled study and labor with his prayers, and devoted constant and unbroken vigils not to reading but to hearing, so that what sight gave to others, hearing might give to him.

When, after the labor of late-night study, sleep came to readers—as it ordinarily does—Didymus, regarding that silence not as something given for rest or idleness, recalled from the beginning, like a clean animal ruminating the food it had begun, the things he had learned earlier from the reading of books while others ran their eyes over them. He reconstructed them in memory and mind, so that he seemed not so much to have heard what had been read as to have written it out on the pages of his mind.

Thus, in a short time, with God as his teacher, he attained such learning and knowledge of divine and human matters that he became a teacher of the ecclesiastical school, greatly approved by Bishop Athanasius and by the other wise men of God in the Church. He was also so well prepared in the other disciplines—whether dialectic, geometry, astronomy, or arithmetic—that no philosopher who proposed a question in any of these arts could ever prevail over him or refute him. As soon as he received his answers, the philosopher would regard him as master even of the discipline he had proposed.

Some of his sayings and commonly discussed arguments, as well as his answers to those who posed questions, were written down by secretaries. They are still held in great admiration. We, however, who were to some extent hearers of his living voice, and who have read what some people wrote down while he was speaking, recognized far greater grace and a certain divine quality—something sounding beyond the human voice—in those discourses that came from his own mouth. [Note: The Guarnerian manuscript reads “we were”; shortly afterward, it has “have been written down.”]

When blessed Antony came down from the Thebaid to Alexandria to bear witness to Athanasius’s faith against the Arians, he also consoled Didymus with magnificent words:

“Let nothing offend you, Didymus, because you appear to be deprived of bodily eyes. For you lack those eyes that mice, flies, and lizards possess. But rejoice, because you have the eyes that the angels have, and by which God is seen; through them a great light of knowledge is kindled for you.” [Note: The Bononian manuscript has “from the Thebaid.” Compare this little story about Antony with Jerome’s Letter 68 in our recension, to Castrucius, section 2. At the end we read, with the Guarnerian manuscript, “and those to whom God,” instead of “by whom.” The Bononian manuscript has “by whom” instead of “through whom.”]

## CHAPTER VIII. How many of Antony’s disciples, who were still living in the desert, performed works of power and signs

At that time Egypt flourished not only with men learned in Christian philosophy, but also with those who, dwelling throughout the vast desert, performed signs and wonders through the apostolic simplicity of their lives and the sincerity of their hearts. [Note: The same manuscript reads: “and wonders, through the apostolic simplicity of their lives and the sincerity of their hearts, they performed.”]

Among those whom we ourselves saw and whose hands we were deemed worthy to bless are these: Macarius of the Upper Desert; another Macarius of the Lower Desert; Isidore in Scetis; Pambus in the Cells; Moses and Benjamin in Nitria; Scyrion [Note: I strongly fear that this name has been corrupted through scribal ignorance. This suspicion is increased by the reading *Quirtori* in the Bononian manuscript, which differs enormously from the printed *Scyrion*. Certainly neither Socrates, who follows Rufinus’s footsteps also in listing these Fathers of the Monks, nor Sozomen, who from Book VI, chapters 23 to 35, praises six hundred of them by name and recounts their more notable deeds, nor finally Rosweydus in his entire book *Lives of the Fathers*, ever mentions this Scyrion. The Poemen who follows is called *Pymen* in the Bononian manuscript, incorrectly. The same manuscript shortly afterward omits “men.”] and Elias and Paul in Apeliote; another Paul in Phocis; Poemen and Joseph [279] in Pispiri, which was called Antony’s Mountain.

We also learned by reliable report that many other men of this kind lived in the regions of Egypt, so that the saying of the Apostle might truly be fulfilled: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded still more” (Romans 5). [Note: The same thought occurs in the middle of Chapter 7 of our *History of the Monks*, together with the same scriptural passage cited here. It seems to me that the Apostle’s saying was also fulfilled in them: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more.” The Guarnerian manuscript concludes Chapter 8 with this testimony and begins Chapter 9 with the following words, “At that time Mesopotamia also had,” and so forth.]

At that time Mesopotamia also had noble men endowed with the same pursuits. Some of them we ourselves saw at Edessa [alternative reading: Edissa] and in the region of Carrhae; we learned of more through report.

## CHAPTER IX. On Gregory and Basil, bishops of Cappadocia

But Cappadocia was no less fruitful than either of these regions; indeed, it produced for us something even more delightful in Gregory and Basil. It too brought forth a sufficiently rich harvest of many saints, produced an abundant vineyard of devout people, and caused a young olive shoot of the Lord to spring forth. But these two in particular, like two sons of richness, standing on the right and left of the lampstand, shone like the two lights of heaven. Therefore I think it worthwhile to recall a few things about them.

Both were noble, both educated at Athens, both fellow students, and both, after leaving the lecture hall, were asked to teach rhetoric. Basil carried out this task magnificently, while Gregory rejected it even more magnificently. When Gregory had devoted himself entirely to God’s service, he presumed so much upon his love for his fellow student that he removed Basil from the teacher’s chair while he was seated there and, laying hands upon him, led him with himself to the monastery. There, for thirteen years, as they say, they devoted themselves, after removing all the secular books of the Greeks, solely to the volumes of sacred Scripture. They followed their understanding of Scripture not on the basis of their own presumption, but according to the writings and authority of their predecessors, who themselves were clearly understood to have received the rule of interpretation through apostolic succession. [Note: The Guarnerian manuscript has “of the students,” which is not itself an insignificant reading. Shortly afterward the Bononian manuscript has “their diligence” instead of “their understanding.” Cacciarius omitted the following proper name, contrary to the manuscripts we use and to other printed codices.]

Examining especially their commentaries on the Prophets [alternative reading: prophecies], they sought the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden in earthen vessels.

But when, having been sufficiently instructed, they were summoned by divine dispensation to teach the people, and each was drawn by a different road toward the same task, Basil traveled through the cities and countryside of Pontus, goading with words and kindling by his preaching the sluggish minds of that people, who were scarcely concerned with future hope. He began to remove the callus of their long negligence and compelled them, abandoning their concern for empty and secular matters, to regain knowledge of themselves, come together, build monasteries, and devote themselves to psalms, hymns, and prayers. He taught them to care publicly for the poor and to provide them with decent dwellings and what was necessary for food; he instructed virgins and made a chaste and modest life desirable to nearly everyone. Thus, in a short time, the appearance of the entire province was transformed: in a dry and barren field, a fertile harvest seemed to have arisen, and a flourishing vineyard.

Gregory, however, did not allow the good seed to lie either among thorns or scattered among rocks; rather, through constant cultivation and unceasing exercises, he worked the good soil of his own heart. [Note: Barraeus had omitted this passage, from “And much more,” through “was advancing”; we have supplied it from other books.]

And he himself advanced much further in himself than Basil did in others. Basil took care to receive what those renouncing the world brought to his feet and to distribute it as each person needed. Gregory, content with the vow of possessing nothing and possessing everything, clung greedily and eagerly only to the riches of wisdom. Basil taught many to come together as one and to care for one another in necessities. Gregory, by his own example—being detached and free [Note: The Bononian manuscript has “free from all things”; two Vatican manuscripts have “free from all things,” and so forth]—preached to all in the apostolic words: “I want you to be free from anxiety” (1 Corinthians 7:32), and “The Lord is near: do not be anxious about anything, but, as servants of Christ, be concerned only with when the Lord will return from the wedding feast.”

Basil taught compassion toward those who sinned and their recall from sin. Gregory, through the grace of the divine word, anticipated the incentives to sin and would not allow one who would be difficult to raise after falling to slip. Basil was pure in faith; Gregory was freer in preaching. Basil was humble before God; Gregory was humble even before human beings. Basil overcame the arrogant by contempt; Gregory overcame them by reason. Thus, in both of them, a different grace accomplished one work of perfection.

Not long afterward Basil became bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia. When Valens sought to force him into exile on account of the faith, he was brought before the prefect’s tribunal and, as is customary for that authority, was assailed with threats and the greatest menaces, so that unless he obeyed the Emperor’s commands he might expect his death to be imminent. [Note: The learned Benedictine editors of Saint Basil’s works refer this to the year 372 in the Life of Basil, chapter 20, from section 6 to the end. Shortly afterward, “that” is the reading of our manuscripts, which omit the verb.]

Then, fearless and without any disturbance of mind, he is reported to have answered the prefect, who was threatening him:

“If only I had some worthy gift that I could offer to this man who might release Basil more quickly from the knot of this bag.”

When he was given the night, which was already at hand, for deliberation, he is again said to have replied:

“Tomorrow I myself shall be the man I am now; I only hope that you will not change.”

During that very night the Emperor’s wife was tortured as though handed over to executioners, while the son who was their only child is believed to have paid the penalties for his father’s impiety by dying. [Note: The Regio-Vatican manuscript has “during that night”; the Guarnerian manuscript has “was being tortured” instead of “is tortured,” and “messengers were sent to ask.”]

Thus, before dawn, messengers were sent to ask Basil to intercede for them by his prayers, so that they too might not perish in the same way—and with much greater justice. It happened, then, that although Valens expelled all the Catholics, Basil remained in the Church until the end of his life with the sacrament of communion undefiled.

Gregory, meanwhile, was appointed bishop in place of his father at the town of Nazianzus and faithfully endured the storm of the heretics. [Note: The Bononian manuscript has the more nearly correct “Nazianzus”; afterward the Guarnerian manuscript has “in his father’s place,” and “he bore it successfully” instead of “faithfully.”] When peace had been restored, he did not refuse when he was persuaded to come to Constantinople to teach the Church. There, in a short time, he advanced so far in reforming the people, who had been infected with the ancient poisons of the heretics, that they seemed then for the first time to become Christians and to see the new light of truth. The teacher of religion taught much by words, but more by examples; his disciples did not see anything commanded by him that he had not first done himself. [Note: Our manuscripts have “he advanced”; one has “they might see” instead of “to see.” The same manuscripts unanimously, and one Vatican manuscript, have the nominative “disciples.”]

But when envy followed upon his glory, certain people began to resist and to employ unsound legal proceedings, so that, when he returned to his own country, another might be appointed bishop. When he sensed that this was being whispered and muttered under people’s breath, he himself brought forward what no one dared to say to him:

“Far be it from me that any quarrel should arise among God’s priests on my account. If this storm is because of me, take me and throw me into the sea, and the turmoil will cease for you.”

Then he returned and spent the rest of his life in his own church. Since he was already weakened by age and infirm in body, he himself chose a successor so that, while that man governed the Church, Gregory might enjoy the leisure of weakness and old age.

There remain magnificent monuments of the genius of both men: treatises that they delivered extemporaneously in the churches. From these we have translated into Latin approximately ten little speeches by each of them. In addition, we translated Basil’s *Institutes of the Monks*, hoping that, if we are able and God grants his favor, we may translate more of their works. [Note: Ten short works of Gregory, but eight homilies by Basil, together with the *Rule*, which he calls the *Institutes of the Monks*. We shall present all of these in the second volume. The sense had previously suffered from faulty punctuation, which we have corrected. Shortly afterward the Bononian manuscript has “we may be able” instead of “we shall be able,” and “they had been” instead of “they were.”]

Basil also had two brothers, Gregory and Peter. One equaled his brother in the word of teaching, the other in works of faith, so that either of them might have made Basil or Gregory present again. Some polished works of the younger Gregory also remain. But enough has been said about them. [Note: The Guarnerian manuscript begins a new chapter here, Chapter X.]

In the western regions, meanwhile, Valentinian, unshaken in the faith of his religion, governed the state with the ancient discipline of the Roman Empire.

## CHAPTER X. On Bishop Damasus and the usurpation of Ursinus

After Liberius, Damasus had received the priesthood in the city of Rome by succession. [Note: The more learned chronologists assign Damasus’s ordination to the year 367. The history of the schism of Ursinus, or Ursicinus, may be learned from the *Book of Petitions* of Marcellinus and Faustinus addressed to the younger Valentinian. I omit the many more recent authorities.]

Unable to tolerate Damasus’s elevation over himself, a certain Ursinus, a deacon of the same Church, broke out into such madness that, after persuading a rather inexperienced and rustic bishop—said to have been Paul of Tibur—he gathered a band of turbulent and seditious men and forcibly had himself made bishop in the basilica called Sicininus, in violation of law, order, and tradition. [Note: The Guarnerian manuscript has *Sycina*; Cacciarius has *Siciniana*. Others, however, call it the Basilica of Liberius, and some say that it was the Basilica of Julius. Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XXVII, chapter 3, near the end, says: “In the contest, Damasus prevailed, with the party supporting him pressing forward. It is established that in the Basilica of Sicininus, where the Christian rite has its assembly, one hundred and thirty-seven corpses of the slain were found in a single day, and that the savage populace was with difficulty calmed afterward.”]

As a result of this event, such a sedition—or rather, such wars—arose among the populations defending one side or the other, that the places of prayer were filled with human blood. This affair, through the faction of Maximinus, a savage prefect, was turned against the good and innocent priest, so that the case was brought even to the torture of the clergy. [Note: Thus all our manuscripts and all printed books read. Cacciarius emends it to “of Maximus,” but his note does not explain what he means. Shortly afterward the Guarnerian manuscript has “so that the case of the clergy was brought as far as torture”; the Bononian manuscript, together with most of the older printed editions, has “was brought.”]

But God, the defender of innocence, was present, and punishment was turned upon the heads of those who had devised the plot.

## CHAPTER XI. On Bishop Ambrose

Meanwhile, after Auxentius, the heretical bishop at Milan, had died, the people of both parties were carried along by differing passions. A serious disagreement and dangerous sedition were preparing a timely destruction for the city itself, if, while each side desired something different, neither could obtain what it had proposed.

At that time Ambrose held the office of governor of that province. [Note: The Guarnerian manuscript begins Chapter XI here: “But Ambrose then,” and so forth; it assigns what precedes to the preceding chapter as well. Cacciarius falsely says that the printed books read *regebat* (“governed”) for the verb that follows; the printed edition of Barraeus, to mention the one before my eyes, clearly prefers *gerebat* (“held”). Conversely, the Bononian manuscript has *regebat*.]

When he saw that destruction threatened the city, he entered the Church at once, in accordance with his position and office, in order to calm the people’s sedition. After he had delivered a long speech there, in accordance with the laws and public discipline, for the sake of peace and tranquility, a sudden shout and a single cry arose from the people who were fighting and disagreeing among themselves. They demanded Ambrose as bishop; they immediately shouted that he should be baptized—for he was a catechumen—and that he should be given to them as bishop. They declared that the people could not become one people and one faith in any other way than by being given Ambrose as their priest. [Note: The Bononian manuscript again has “the disagreeing people”; shortly afterward, it has “and any faith” instead of “and one faith.”]

Although Ambrose struggled against this and resisted strongly, the people’s desire was reported to the Emperor, and he ordered that it be fulfilled with all dispatch. “It is God’s doing,” he said, “that the faith of a divided people and their discordant minds have been recalled by a sudden conversion to one agreement and one judgment.” Soon, having received God’s grace, been initiated into the sacred rites, and become a priest, Ambrose was established.

## CHAPTER XII. On the end of Valentinian

Meanwhile, when Valentinian had come from the regions of Gaul to Illyricum for the Sarmatian war, he had scarcely begun the war when he was overcome by a sudden illness and died. [Note: Some printed editions have “to Illyricum,” although our manuscripts disagree. Compare Ammianus, Book XXX, chapter 6; Zosimus, Book IV; Idatius in the *Fasti*; and our Jerome, Letter 60 to Heliodorus, as well as the author who falsely bears the name of the Letter to Praesidius on the Paschal Candle. It is accepted that Valentinian died in the year 375, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December.]

He left his sons as heirs to the Empire: Gratian Augustus and Valentinian, still very young and not yet invested with the imperial insignia. Nevertheless, the necessity of those who were attempting to invade the Empire as though it were vacant compelled him, even in his brother’s absence, to be clothed in the purple, while Probus was then faithfully administering the office of prefect.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the incursion of the Goths through Thrace and the death of Valens

At that time, the Gothic people, driven from their settlements in the eastern Empire, poured throughout all Thrace and began savagely to lay waste cities and fields with arms. [Note: Two more recent Vatican manuscripts have “ferociously.” Shortly afterward the Guarnerian manuscript has “Then indeed,” and “he began to turn” instead of “he turned.”]

Then the wars that Valens had been waging against the Churches began to turn against the enemy, and, repenting too late, he ordered bishops and priests to be released from exile and monks to be freed from the mines. Yet, surrounded by the enemy in the estate to which he had fled in terror from the battle, he paid the penalty for his impiety by being burned to death in the fire. [Note: The reading of the Guarnerian manuscript, “in the stronghold,” instead of “in the estate,” is not without merit. Socrates, at the end of Book IV, says that Valens perished after fleeing into a village—εἰς κώμην (*eis kōmēn*)—which the barbarians who came upon it burned. Ammianus Marcellinus, reporting the opinion of others, says that Valens, carried near a rustic hut with a few guards and eunuchs, was surrounded by enemies who did not know who he was, and that the hut was set alight and burned. The Regio-Vatican manuscript has “to which he had fled” instead of “to which he had fled in terror”; the Bononian manuscript has “in the flames” instead of “in the fire.” The year was 378, on the fifth day before the Ides of August, as Idatius records, and Pagius explains from this. Compare also Libanius’s *Oration to Theodosius on Avenging the Murder of Julian.]

He had spent fourteen years in the Empire, first with his brother and afterward with his brother’s sons. This battle was the beginning of disaster for the Roman Empire, both then and thereafter. [Note: From this point the Guarnerian codex begins Chapter XIV, which it also, with some justification, joins to what follows. Saint Ambrose greatly praises Gratian in his *On the Death of Valens* and in his commentary on Psalm 61; so do Zosimus, Ausonius in the *Gratianic Act for the Consulship*, and Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XXXI.]

Thus Gratian, together with his still very young brother, also assumed the rule of the East after the death of his uncle. In piety and religion he surpassed nearly all the princes who had preceded him.
