He was energetic in the use of arms, swift in body, and good in character; but, through youthful exuberance, he was happier than was generally appropriate, and more modest than the interests of the state allowed.

## CHAPTER XIV. How the Emperor Gratian admitted Theodosius as a partner in the Empire and, after many religious and courageous deeds, fell victim to the plots of the tyrant Maximus

Seeing that it was useful to have a mature man share in such great cares of government, and because, as the divine word teaches, “Two are better than one” (Ecclesiastes 4:9), Gratian appointed Theodosius as his partner. [Note: This took place in the year 379, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February—not the seventeenth, as some incorrectly write—as Idatius, the Alexandrian Chronicle, the Alexandrian Compilation, and Marcellinus in his *Chronicle* show. From this arose a new division of the Empire. Theodosius received the East together with Thrace, while the Western Empire was divided between the brothers Gratian and Valentinian.]

He entrusted the administration of the East to Theodosius and reserved the western regions for himself and his brother. But after Gratian had accomplished many things with piety and courage, the tyrant Maximus, who had arisen in Britain, had him killed at Lyons through the general Andragathius, more by the treachery of his own people than by the force of the enemy. [Note: The Guarnerian manuscript has “But he himself,” and shortly afterward “through Andragathius.” Pagius demonstrates from the testimony of Victor in the *Epitome* that Gratian died on the eighth day before the Kalends of September in the year 383.]

## CHAPTER XV. On the child Valentinian, and how his mother Justina, defending the Arian heresy, attempted to disturb the Churches
286 But Valentinian, residing in Italy and terrified by his brother’s death and fear of the enemy, pretended that he willingly welcomed the peace offered by Maximus, while in fact merely feigning this acceptance. Meanwhile his mother Justina, a fosterer of the Arian heresy, confidently disclosed to her easily deceived son the poisons of her impiety which she had suppressed while her husband was alive. Accordingly, established at Milan, she began to disturb the condition of the Churches and to threaten the priests with expulsion and exile unless they revoked the decrees of the Council of Ariminum, by which the faith of the fathers had been violated.

[Note: The Guarnerian manuscript reads: “began to threaten the priests with expulsions, exiles, and so forth.” It seemed appropriate to restore *depulsiones* (“expulsions”) in place of the reading *depulsionis* (“of expulsion”) found hitherto. For *temerata* (“violated”), Barraeus and several other printed books preferred *intemerata* (“unviolated”). Cacciarius conjectures that *revocarent* (“they should revoke”) ought to be corrected to *renovarent* (“they should renew”).]

In this conflict she was assailing Ambrose, the wall and strongest tower of the Church. Harassing him with threats, terrors, and every form of attack, she was seeking an initial opening through which to overthrow the Church. Yet although that Jezebel fought armed with the spirit, Ambrose nonetheless resisted, filled with Elijah’s courage and grace. She herself began to chatter and make a din in the Churches, to rouse and inflame the peoples toward discord; but because matters were turning out less according to her wishes, she considered this an injury and complained of it to her son.

[Note: The Bononian manuscript omits the two words *garrire* and *strepere* (“to chatter” and “to make a din”).]

Thus the young man, inflamed by resentment over the insult which his mother had falsely fabricated, sent a band of armed men to the Church and immediately ordered the doors to be broken down, the holy places attacked, the priest dragged away, and driven into exile.

[Note: In two Vatican manuscripts the reading is *Sancta Sanctorum* (“the Holy of Holies”). In the editions previously circulated, *mitti* (“to be sent”) stood where *agi* (“to be driven”) is read here.]

But such was the perseverance of the faithful peoples that they preferred to lose their lives before surrendering their bishop.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the faithful steadfastness of Benevolus, Master of the Records

[Col. 0524B]

287 Meanwhile imperial decrees against the faith of the fathers were sent to Benevolus, who at that time presided over the imperial records office.

[Note: The Guarnerian manuscript reads *mittuntur* (“are sent”). Other manuscripts likewise have *Benivolo* instead of *Benevolo*. Sozomen, Book VII, chapter 13, calls him Μενίβολος (*Menibolos*), an easy interchange of the letters β and μ in Greek. Shortly afterward the Regius-Vatican manuscripts read *cara fides* (“dear faith”) instead of *sacra fides* (“sacred faith”). The Guarnerian manuscript also omits the conjunction that follows, and reads *deinde tunc vero* (“then thereafter”) instead of *tum* (“then”), and so forth.]

But he, for whom the sacred faith had been venerable from his cradle, denied that he could utter impious words or speak against God. Then, lest the queen should seem to have undertaken her project in vain, a higher honor was promised him if he fulfilled the order. But he, desiring to be nobler in faith than in honors, said:

“Why do you promise me a higher rank as the reward for impiety? Take away even this rank that I possess; only let the conscience of my faith remain unharmed.”

Saying this, he cast the belt of office at the feet of those who were issuing the impious command.

Ambrose, however, defended himself against the queen’s fury not with his hand or a weapon, but by placing himself beneath the altar in prolonged fasts and vigils; through supplications he secured God as defender of himself and of the Church. While the wicked Justina was devising these things at length through various devices and attacks, Maximus—who wished to strip himself of the disgrace of being a tyrant and to show himself a legitimate ruler—sent letters declaring that an impious undertaking had begun, that God’s faith was being attacked, and that the decrees of the Catholic Church were being overthrown. Meanwhile he began to approach Italy.

[Note: Our Italian manuscripts read *Italiam* (“Italy”) instead of *Italiae* (“of Italy”). At the end, the Guarnerian manuscript reads *parabat* (“was preparing”) instead of *praeparabat* (“was making preparations”).]

When Justina learned this, pressed by the enemy as well as by the consciousness of her impiety, she fled with her son and was the first to suffer the exiles which she had been preparing for God’s priests.

## CHAPTER XVII. How Theodosius avenged Gratian’s death and triumphed over Maximus

288 Nevertheless Theodosius stood forth, mindful of his loyalty to the empire and of Gratian’s goodness and benefits; rising with all the forces of the East to avenge him, he avenged righteous blood.

Meanwhile Valentinian’s impious mother died, and he restored the Catholic faith—which she herself had violated—and the kingdom, after tyranny had been driven away.

[Note: This means that Maximus was removed. As Pacatus relates in chapter 24, Theodosius defeated him in the fifth year of his tyranny and, according to Philostorgius, Book X, chapter 8, at the third milestone from Aquileia. Zosimus, Book IV, relates that Maximus was stripped of his imperial clothing and led before Theodosius, who briefly recounted, as if by way of reproach, the offenses he had committed against the state and then handed him over to the executioner.]

Afterward, when he had entered Rome in a splendid triumph, he returned once more to his own kingdoms.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On Theodosius’ offense against the Thessalonians and his public penance before the priests

[Col. 0525B]

At about the same time, through a certain deception of the devil, a shameful stain was laid upon the religious ruler.

For when a riot had arisen at Thessalonica and one of the military men had been killed in the attack of the raging crowd, Theodosius, inflamed by the horror of the sudden report, ordered the people to be invited to the Circus games and soldiers to be unexpectedly sent among them and to cut down indiscriminately whoever they encountered, and ordered vengeance to be inflicted—not as a crime, but in fury.

[Note: The Bononian manuscript reads *obtruncare* (“to cut down”). The Guarnerian reads *ut passim quisque* (“so that everyone indiscriminately”) and also *vindictam etiam dare* (“to exact vengeance as well”). Sozomen, Book VII, chapter 25, calls the military man who was killed Buthericus and says that he was *magister militum per Illyricum*, commander of the army in Illyricum; there he also reports the causes of the Thessalonian revolt. Theodoret, Book V, chapter 18, in turn states that seven thousand people perished in the massacre at Thessalonica.]

For this reason, when he was reproved by the priests of Italy—first and foremost by Saint Ambrose—he acknowledged his offense and confessed his guilt with tears, and underwent public penance in the presence of the entire Church. He patiently fulfilled the period assigned to him for this purpose without the imperial dignity.

[Note: Saint Ambrose reproved him in Letter 51. The emperor, as Theodoret relates in the passage cited, had abstained from the ecclesiastical assembly for a full eight months. He then wished to attend the feast of the Lord’s Nativity, but Saint Ambrose prevented him and, according to the bishop’s instruction, required him to submit to the beginning of public penance. See Ambrose’s *On the Death of Theodosius*.]

[Note: Cacciarius corruptly reads *ibi* (“there”) instead of *in hoc* (“for this purpose”). The Guarnerian manuscript has *fastu* (“with arrogance”) instead of *fastigio* (“imperial dignity”). Saint Ambrose, in the passage cited, writes: “He laid aside every mark of royal distinction on which he relied; he mourned in the Church for his sin, which had stolen upon him through the deceit of others; with groaning and tears he asked pardon. What private persons are ashamed of, the emperor was not ashamed to do publicly: to undergo penance,” and so forth.]

To all these things he added the following remarkable measure: by law he decreed for the future that sentences issued by rulers concerning punishment should be delayed by the executors for thirty days, so that an opportunity for mercy—or, if circumstances required it, for repentance—would not perish.

[Note: The Guarnerian manuscript reads *Legem* (“the law”). This law no longer exists today.]

## CHAPTER XIX. On the restoration of the Churches which, after he had become Catholic, he restored in the East

[Col. 0526A]

Accordingly, after returning to the East, and there, as from the beginning of his reign, expelling the heretics with the greatest care and zeal and beginning to hand the Churches over to the Catholics, he conducted this work with such moderation that, rejecting vengeance, he concerned himself only with the restoration of the Churches to the Catholics, so that the true faith might advance without hindrance to its preaching. He showed himself accessible to the priests of God; in faith, religion, and generosity he displayed a royal spirit to all; approachable and without imperial arrogance, he made himself available for conversation even to the humble. At his encouragement and through his gifts, many Churches were adorned and built with sufficient magnificence; he gave much to those who asked, but more often offered gifts unasked.

[Note: The Bononian manuscript omits the word *ut* (“so that”). Shortly afterward Cacciarius, on the authority of two Vatican manuscripts, reads *tradidit* (“he handed over”) instead of *tradere* (“to hand over”), and *coepit agere* (“he began to act”) instead of the simple *agere* (“to act”). These readings are certainly less satisfactory, since they conflict with the greater number of his manuscripts as well as with all our manuscripts and printed books.]

The worship of idols, which had begun to be neglected and destroyed under Constantine’s institutions and thereafter, collapsed under this emperor. For these deeds he was so dear to God that divine providence bestowed a special gift upon him. In fact, in the regions of the Thebaid it filled a certain monk named John with a prophetic spirit; Theodosius consulted his counsels and responses concerning whether it would be better to preserve peace or wage war.

[Note: The Guarnerian manuscript and several others among Cacciarius’ manuscripts read *repletum* (“filled”) instead of *replevit* (“filled him”). Recall what was said above about this Saint John in chapter 1 of the *History of the Monks*. Saint Jerome too, although otherwise particularly hostile to Rufinus’ history, does not doubt that John was “a Catholic and a holy man” (*Letter* 133 to Ctesiphon). See also our remarks there.]

## CHAPTER XX. On Apollinaris and his heresy

290 Meanwhile, before this same period, at Laodicea in Syria, Bishop Apollinaris, a man indeed well equipped in other respects, allowed himself to be driven to excess by the fault of contentiousness. Because he delighted in opposing everything that anyone said, he generated a heresy out of the vainglory of his ill-starred talent, asserting that in the Dispensation the Lord had assumed only a body and not also a soul.

[Note: The ancients used this name, “Dispensation,” for the mystery of the Incarnation. Theophilus, in his Second Paschal Letter, included among Jerome’s letters as Letter 98, writes: “Let the disciples of Apollinaris cease, and let them know that, in the Dispensation of the man whom the Only-Begotten Son of God deigned to assume for our salvation, he is not free from guilt who both understood and wrote perversely concerning his soul.” The Greek term is οἰκονομία (*oikonomia*). Jerome likewise writes in Letter 84: “Apollinaris introduced a divided economy of Christ.” We discuss more there. The Guarnerian manuscript reads *susceptam* (“assumed”) instead of *susceptum* (“assumed”).]

When he was pressed by the clear testimonies of the Gospel—which show that the Lord and Savior himself professes that he has a soul, that he lays it down when he wishes and takes it up again, and that he says it is troubled and sorrowful even unto death—he shifted his position so that he would not appear entirely defeated or overcome. He then said that Christ had indeed possessed a soul, but not the rational part of the soul; rather, he had possessed only that part by which the body is given life. In place of the rational part, he maintained that the Word of God himself had been present.

This assertion was first rejected at Rome by Damasus, in a council assembled together with Peter, Bishop of Alexandria, in the following judgment: If anyone should say that the Son of God, who was truly God and likewise truly man, possessed anything less of humanity or anything less of divinity, he was to be judged alien from the Church.

[Note: The *Synodical Book* in Labbe, volume III, states: “Peter, Bishop of Alexandria, expelled from Alexandria, proceeded to Rome. After receiving him, Pope Damasus convened at Rome a divine and holy synod, which condemned that madman Apollinaris, Stephen—and, easily, this should be corrected to Timothy—and the robber Lucius, who had seized the see of Alexandria, with an anathema.” Therefore there can be no doubt that the decrees appended below belong to this synod, in which Peter of Alexandria took part, and that it was held before Peter returned to Alexandria. According to Socrates, Book IV, chapter 37, Peter returned before Valens left the imperial city for the war against the Goths, in which he died on 9 August 378. Accordingly, the synod was held around the beginning of that year; Rufinus says that it was the first to pronounce an anathema against Apollinaris, and Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 25, bears witness to the same event in nearly the same words.]

This judgment was also confirmed at Alexandria and at Constantinople by a decree of the council. From that time the Apollinarists, withdrawing from the Church, defend their own bishops, belonging to their own party, as well as their own doctrines and Churches.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the succession of bishops throughout the East

291 Accordingly, in the city of Rome, after Damasus, Siricius assumed the priesthood of the Church.

[Note: Siricius succeeded Damasus toward the end of the year 384. For the bishops of the other principal Churches, consult Socrates, Book V, chapter 3, and among more recent writers, Pagius and others.]

At Alexandria, after Peter’s death, Timothy, and after him Theophilus, and at Jerusalem, after Cyril, John, restored the apostolic sees. At Antioch, after Meletius’ death, Flavian was substituted. But Paulinus still remained, having always persisted in the communion of the Catholics. Many quarrels and many controversies were repeatedly stirred up there; although some pressed forward with great force and others resisted—and although the elements of earth and sea themselves were wearied by this struggle—no settlement of peace could ever be obtained, even though there seemed by then to be no disagreement concerning the faith.

[Note: The Guarnerian manuscript reads *pacis illius* (“of that peace”). Shortly afterward it agrees with the Bononian manuscript in reading “with the testimony of Athanasius and by the Confessors.”]

The same thing occurred at Tyre. There, when Diodorus—a truly ancient Catholic, a man proven by the evidence of his trials—had been made bishop by the testimony of Athanasius and by the Confessors, another was ordained from the party of Meletius, his modesty being disregarded. In many other cities of the East likewise, contention among the priests produced confusions of this kind. At Constantinople, Nectarius, a former urban praetor, a catechumen who had only recently received baptism, assumed the priesthood.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the revolt of the pagans against the faithful

Meanwhile new disturbances arose at Alexandria against the Church and contrary to the faith of the times, originating from the following circumstance.

There was a certain basilica, a public building, ancient and greatly neglected, which was said to have been donated by the Emperor Constantius to bishops who proclaimed his perfidy. Through long neglect it possessed nothing sound except its walls. The bishop who governed the Church at that time decided to request it from the emperor, so that, as the faithful peoples increased, the houses of prayer might also increase.

[Note: One manuscript reads “the Emperor Constantine.”]

[Note: Earlier printed editions read *loca* (“places”). Cacciarius reads *domos* (“houses”) in the accusative, and then *quamquam* (“although”) in place of *quamque* (“and which”). We prefer our manuscripts.]

When he wished to restore the place after receiving it, certain hidden chambers and underground excavations were discovered there, more suitable for robberies and crimes than for ceremonies. Thus the pagans, seeing the hiding places of their crimes and the caverns of their wickedness exposed, could not endure that evils concealed for so many centuries and covered in darkness should be brought to light. As though they had drunk from a dragon’s cup, they all began to rage and openly run wild.

They now attempted to fight not merely with words and riots, as they had been accustomed to do, but with hands and weapons. They engaged in frequent clashes in the streets, and in open warfare the two peoples came together against one another. Our people were much more numerous and powerful, but because of the moderation imposed by religion they were less ferocious. As a result, when many of our people were frequently wounded and some even killed, they fled for refuge to the temple as though to a fortress.

There they captured some Christians and dragged them away with them; they compelled them to sacrifice at the burning altars. Those who resisted they killed after torturing them with new and elaborate punishments: some they fastened to gibbets, others they hurled into caves with their legs broken. Antiquity had carefully constructed these caves to receive the blood of sacrifices and the other impurities of the shrine.

[Note: Cacciarius altered the reading to *crucibus* (“crosses”), without even a word of notice to the reader. Socrates himself relates that some were fastened to a cross, since the pagans deliberately inflicted this punishment upon them as an insult to the holy Cross. Here, however, apart from the fact that “with broken crosses” would be quite unsuitable in meaning, the agreement and testimony of the manuscripts we consulted and of all the printed books do not permit the excellent reading *cruribus* (“legs”) to be changed to *crucibus*.]

But they carried on these acts day by day, at first with fear, then with confidence and desperation, and, shut inside the temple, lived by plunder and booty. Finally, as they continued their murderous assault upon their fellow citizens, they chose as the leader of their crime and audacity a certain philosopher named Olympius, who, by his name and dress, presented himself as a philosopher. Under his command they defended the fortress and maintained their tyranny.

[Note: Cacciarius, on the authority of two Vatican manuscripts, adds *solo* (“alone”), a word unknown to all the other books.]

Those to whom the guardianship of Roman laws and the administration of justice had been entrusted, having learned what had happened, were disturbed and terrified and hurried to the temple. They demanded the reasons for the perpetrators’ audacity and asked what that gathering meant, in which the blood of citizens was being shed before the altars with such great crime.

But those inside, having barricaded the entrance, gave no explanation of their action; they returned only confused and discordant shouting. Nevertheless, messengers were sent to them to remind them of the authority of the Roman Empire, the vengeance of the laws, and the consequences that ordinarily followed such acts.

[Note: Some printed editions read *solent* (“usually do”) instead of *subsequi* (“follow”). The Bononian manuscript reads *obsequi* (“obey”) instead of *subsequi*. The Guarnerian reads *vesaniam* (“madness”) instead of *vesano* (“mad”). A little farther on it reads *sanguis fusus* (“blood poured out”) instead of *sanguis effusus* (“blood shed”). The memory of these martyrs is said to be kept in the Roman Martyrology on 17 March.]

Since the fortification of the place permitted nothing to be done against those attempting such madness except by greater force, the affair was reported to the emperor. He, whose innate clemency of mind preferred to correct the erring rather than destroy them, replied that vengeance should not be sought against those whom the blood shed before the altars had made martyrs, since the glory of their merits had surpassed the grief of their death.

As for the rest, however, the cause of the evils and the roots of the discord—which had arisen in defense of the images—had to be cut away completely. Once these had been exterminated, the cause of the wars would likewise come to rest.

When this written reply arrived, and after a brief truce both peoples had gathered at the temple to hear it, as soon as the first page of the letter was opened, at the beginning of which the empty superstition of the pagans was condemned, an immense shout arose from our people. Amazement and terror seized the pagan population. Each person sought hiding places, searched out narrow paths of escape, or secretly mingled among our people, so that all who were present might recognize that the presence of God had given courage to his people and that the fury of the demon which had previously raged among them had been driven away.

[Note: Cacciarius, on the authority of two more recent Vatican manuscripts, reads *recitata* (“recited”)—a less satisfactory reading. Shortly afterward the Guarnerian manuscript, together with the printed books, reads *nosceretur* (“might be recognized”) instead of *dignosceretur* (“might be distinguished”).]

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the location of the temple of Serapis and its destruction

I suppose that everyone has heard of the temple of Serapis at Alexandria, and that most people have also seen it. It was a place elevated not by nature but by human labor and construction, rising for a hundred or more steps, and spread out on every side in square and enormous spaces. Everything was constructed with vaulted workmanship so that one could ascend to the highest floors. These structures, with immense upper windows and hidden chambers separated from one another, provided facilities for various services and secret functions.

At the upper levels, the outermost spaces of the entire circuit were occupied by exedras and pastophoria—that is, chambers or tabernacles—and by houses extending upward. In these the temple attendants lived, as did those whom they called ἀγνεύοντας (*agneuontas*), that is, “those who purify themselves.”

[Note: The Bononian manuscript reads “in Latin letters, *agnevotes*.” The Guarnerian reads *castigant* (“correct”) instead of *castificant* (“purify”). I pass over other lesser errors, as well as Cacciarius’ constant mistakes whenever a Greek word occurs.]

Porticoes, too, divided into square sections, ran around the entire inner circuit. In the middle of the whole space stood a building, raised on precious columns and constructed magnificently and broadly on all sides in marble stone.

Inside it stood a statue of Serapis so enormous that it touched one wall with its right hand and brushed another with its left.

[Note: The Guarnerian reads *pertingeret* (“reached”) and shortly afterward *interioris* (“of the interior”), together with the previously printed books, instead of *interiores* (“interior”).]

The monster was said to have been composed of every kind of metal and wood. The interior walls of the shrine were first covered with gold plates, above these with silver, and finally with bronze; these served as protection for the more precious metals. There were also various things constructed with ingenious trickery for the astonishment and admiration of those who saw them.

A very small window on the eastern side was arranged in such a way that, on the day appointed for bringing in the image of the Sun to greet Serapis, when the times had been carefully observed, a ray of sunlight entering through that same window illuminated the mouth and lips of Serapis. Thus, before the watching people, Serapis appeared to be greeted with a kiss by the Sun.

[Note: The same manuscript reads *direptus* (“snatched away”) and “the mouth and lips of Serapis,” and so forth.]

There was another deception of this kind. The nature of the magnetic stone is said to be such that it seizes and attracts iron. A statue of the Sun had been fashioned by an artisan from extremely fine iron for this very purpose. The stone, whose nature we have said is to draw iron toward itself, had been fixed above in the ceiling. When the statue was placed directly beneath the ray, in a balanced position, the stone’s natural force drew the iron toward itself, so that the statue appeared to the people to have risen and to hang in the air.

To prevent this from being exposed by a sudden fall, the ministers of the deception would say: “The Sun has risen; he is departing to his own place after bidding farewell to Serapis.”

But many other things had also been constructed by the ancients at the site for the purpose of deceiving people, which it would now take too long to enumerate individually.

But, as we had begun to say, after the imperial reply had been read, our people were indeed prepared to overthrow the author of the error. Nevertheless, the pagans had spread a certain belief: if a human hand touched that image, the earth would immediately gape open and dissolve into chaos, and heaven would suddenly collapse headlong. This caused the people some momentary astonishment.

Then one of the soldiers appeared, a man more strongly protected by faith than by weapons. Seizing a double axe, he rose up and struck the old deceiver’s jaw with all his strength. A shout rose from both peoples; yet neither did the sky fall nor did the earth descend.

[Note: We did not hesitate to restore *desedit* (“settled down” or “subsided”) on the basis of the author’s sense, in place of the previously read *descendit* (“descended”), which produces an incongruous meaning. It is surprising that none of the many manuscripts which Cacciarius calls archetypes varies here enough to warn anyone of the corrupt reading, at least through its own error. I could scarcely be brought to believe this, for in the two manuscripts I use—the Bononian and the Guarnerian—the latter, which is of better quality, differs by a single letter and thereby aroused suspicion that the printed reading was defective and alerted me to apply a remedy. The preceding context also, where *terra dehiscens* (“the earth gaping open”) is written, and the correct sense according to Rufinus’ intention, required *desedit* instead of *descendit*. Cicero used the word in this sense as well.]

Then, striking again and again, he struck the smoky spirit of the rotten wood.

[Note: Here Rufinus writes *genium* (“spirit” or “genius”) in its proper sense, but also ironically, as everyone can see. It is as though he had said: “He cut down the smoky god of rotten wood.” Cacciarius, however, neither understood his author’s meaning nor feared for himself—whether from a reader whom he might deceive or from me, whom he may perhaps have intended to mock—and in a three-line note makes four or five errors, embellishing them with an equal number of falsehoods. He says: “Theophilus also uses these words, ‘smoky spirit,’ when speaking of the temple of Serapis at Alexandria in his Synodical Letter.” It is scarcely possible to commit and invent more in a shorter style. First, it is false that Theophilus uses the words “smoky spirit.” It is also false that the word *genius*, which he alone mentions as the name of a place—even if the spelling is correct, about which we shall speak shortly—has anything in common with this “smoky spirit” in our author. Finally, it is false that Theophilus speaks of the temple of Serapis or of the spirit of its idol. He speaks of a district, marketplace, or something similar, in which his opponents had taken refuge in order to stir up riots against him and arouse greater hatred against him among the pagans. “In the most famous place of the city,” he says, “which, unless I am mistaken, they call *Genius*, they are stationed.” But consider what else that good Carmelite says in his remaining little note. “The latest editor of Saint Jerome’s works,” he says, “thinks that ἕνιον or κένιον—so he spells it—was a place where guests were received.” May God grant better judgment. When I first made known to the scholarly world that letter, to be valued more highly than gold and gems, together with several other works of great worth, close to perishing and rescued from bookworms and moths—I say this because the religious man suppresses it in silence, although it is necessary to mention it so that the reader may understand how much he praised Theophilus’ Synodical Letter—I suspected that *Xenion* might be read in place of *Genius*, since it was the name of a very famous place in the city, perhaps a street. I expressed this in only a few words: “But it seems to be *Xenion*, from ξένιον, a place where guests gathered.” It is therefore false, above all, that I said or thought that ἕνιον or κένιον—so he spells it—was a place where guests were received. It is much more false that I wrote the monstrous phrases which Cacciarius fabricated from his own brain and then compounded with several errors of defective spelling, so that they mean nothing either in Greek or in relation to the matter. He was apparently seeking a pretext for slander. This is a particularly disgraceful form of false accusation: to attribute his own hallucinations, misstatements, and errors to me, while imposing them on the general body of readers, who are by no means eager to know what the truth is. It is also false, and reeks of slander, that he says I considered that place one where guests were received—thus making it appear that I had called it a *xenodochium*, a hospice—when I understood it to be a marketplace or street where strangers gathered. I omit many other matters, for I am genuinely reluctant to answer a man who is called a religious, a theologian, an Apostolic Examiner of the Roman clergy, and a lecturer in Dogmatic Sacred Theology at the Urban College of the Propagation of the Faith.]

After the statue had been thrown down, fire was applied to it, and it burned as easily as dry wood. After this, its head was torn from its neck and dragged along with the modius pressed down upon it. Then its feet and other limbs, cut with axes and torn away with ropes, were dragged through the several places; limb by limb, before the eyes of slaughtering Alexandria, the aged and decayed idol was burned.

[Note: We have restored this from the excellent Guarnerian manuscript, in place of the less satisfactory reading previously adopted, *detrahuntur* (“are dragged away”). Shortly afterward the same manuscript reads: “the remaining trunk is burned with fire in the amphitheater.”]

Finally, the remaining trunk was burned in the amphitheater. This was the end of Serapis, of empty superstition, and of ancient error.

Different opinions about Serapis’ origin are reported among the pagans. Some think that he was Jupiter; the modius placed upon his head either signified that he governs all things with measure and moderation or that mortal life is supplied by the abundance of crops. Others think him the power of the Nile, by whose wealth and fertility Egypt is nourished. Some maintain that the image was fashioned in honor of our Joseph, because of the measure of grain by which he rescued the Egyptians in a time of famine.

Others say that the ancient histories of the Greeks tell of a certain Apis, a father of a household or king, who was established at Memphis in Egypt. When grain had failed at Alexandria during a famine, he supplied the citizens abundantly from his own stores. After his death, they established a temple in his honor at Memphis, in which an ox was nourished as an emblem of the excellent farmer. It bore certain distinctive marks of color and was called Apis after his name. They brought his body to Alexandria in a *soros*, that is, a “tomb,” and afterward, by composition, first called it *Sorapis* and later, through corruption, *Serapis*.

[Note: The Bononian manuscript reads *quae* (“which”). The Guarnerian reads *appellatur* (“is called”) and, in Latin letters, *Soron vero* (“but *Soron*,” and so forth).]

[Note: It is remarkable that Cacciarius adopted in his text the reading *deduxerint* (“they brought”), while at the same time rejecting it in his notes as contrary to the testimony of all the Vatican manuscripts. What, then, do the Vatican manuscripts actually report? He is silent. The Guarnerian manuscript in our possession certainly reads *deduxerunt* (“they brought”). Nevertheless, I prefer to retain the received reading, since it agrees better with the context, with the preceding *instituerint* (“they established”), and with the following *nominarint* (“they called”), and is also supported by the Bononian manuscript.]

[Note: Barraeus marked this at the margin of the book as another correction. The Guarnerian reads *correptionem* (“contraction”) instead of *corruptionem* (“corruption”), and shortly afterward *nominarunt* (“they called”). The Bononian reads *nominaverunt* (“they named”). He continues: “What the truth is, or whether there is nothing at all in these matters, God will see.”]

But whether this account is true, or whether it is entirely without substance, God will judge concerning these matters. Let us return to the subject we began.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the deceptions discovered in the temples of the pagans
After this, once the very head of idolatry had been cast down, through the efforts of the most vigilant priest [alternative reading: “also”] whatever monstrous objects rather than images had existed throughout Alexandria were exposed with an equal outcome and similar disgrace. [Note: From this point Guarnerianus begins Chapter 24; it also reads *praeparati sunt* shortly afterward, and, in Latin letters, *adyta*. It has *invecta sunt* for *inventa sunt*, while Bononiensis has *sunt* for *sint* and *truciabiles* for *cruciabiles*.]

The mind shudders to say what snares had been prepared by demons for wretched mortals, what deaths, what crimes were concealed in those places which were called [printed *dibebant*; alternative *dicebantur*] *adyta* (ἄδυτα, “inaccessible sanctuaries”): how many infant heads had been found there, their lips gilded; how many agonizing deaths of wretched people had been depicted. When these things were brought to light and exposed to the open air, although the Gentiles, overwhelmed by confusion and shame, fled, nevertheless anyone who was able to be present marveled that for so many centuries he had been ensnared by such abominable and shameful frauds. Hence very many of them, having condemned their error and recognized the crime, embraced the faith of Christ and the worship of true religion. For, to omit the other atrocities that were committed elsewhere—little children being killed by violence, and virgins being violated for the inspection of their entrails—I shall mention only one deed perpetrated in the temple of Saturn that came to everyone’s knowledge, so that from it the other matters we have omitted may also be assessed.

## CHAPTER XXV. On Tyrannus, the priest of Saturn and the adulterer of almost the whole of Alexandria

They had among them a priest of Saturn named Tyrannus. This man [alternative reading: *is*, “he”], as though in response to the deity, would say—when various noblemen and leading men were worshiping in the temple and their wives had pleased him for his lust—that Saturn had commanded him that the man’s wife should spend the night in the temple. [Note: The pronoun *sibi*, “to him,” is supplied by Guarnerianus and two other Vatican manuscripts.] Then the man who had heard this, rejoicing that his wife had been summoned by the deity’s favor, would send his wife to the temple, more elaborately adorned and additionally loaded with gifts, lest she should of course be rejected for coming empty-handed. With the matron shut inside in full view of everyone, Tyrannus would lock the doors and, [Note: These two words, “and having handed over the keys,” are certainly present in the two manuscripts; the Barraeus edition and the Basel edition of Rhenanus likewise have them. Our manuscripts, Bononiensis and Guarnerianus, also have them with complete agreement. What, then, is Cacciarius dreaming about, or what is he imposing upon his credulous reader, when he says that he added these words from an old Royal manuscript because they seemed to be missing—although they were wholly necessary for completing the fraud—in the printed editions? He himself knowingly commits a fraud, so that by whatever means he may place his own editorial work ahead of earlier editions and appear to have restored the passage by filling its gap. I would even dare to assert under pledge that these words were also found in the other Vatican manuscripts he used.] having handed over the keys, depart.

Then, after silence had been established, he would creep through hidden and subterranean passages into the very image of Saturn, through broad-open caves. [Note: Guarnerianus reads *infra*, “below”; Bononiensis has *patulis se repedabat cavernis*, “he made his way back through open caverns”; two Vatican manuscripts have *repebat*, “he crept.”] But that image was hollowed out at the back and carefully attached to the wall. [Note: Barraeus noted in the margin that elsewhere he read *excisum*, “cut out.”] With lamps burning inside the shrine, while the woman stood intent upon prayer, he would suddenly produce a voice through the image’s hollow bronze, so that the unhappy woman trembled with fear and joy because she considered herself worthy of being addressed by so great a deity.

After the impure deity had said whatever it wished, either to increase her terror or to inflame her lust, by some contrivance involving linen coverings all the lights were suddenly extinguished. Then Tyrannus, descending, would introduce the adulterer’s deception to the bewildered and terrified little woman through profane contrivances. [Note: The Guarnerian manuscript reads *numini impuro*, “to the impure deity.” Shortly afterward Cacciarius has *lineolis* for *linteolis*, which I would rather attribute to the carelessness of the printers.]

When these things had already been carried on for a long time among all the wretched matrons, it happened that a woman of chaste mind shuddered at the crime. By paying closer attention as it was being carried out, she recognized Tyrannus’s voice; and, returning home, she informed her husband of the criminal fraud. He, inflamed more passionately by the injury done to his wife—or rather to himself—had Tyrannus arrested and taken to torture. When the man had been convicted and confessed, and the dark frauds had been exposed, shame and disgrace had invaded all the houses of the Pagans: adulterous mothers, incestuous fathers, and illegitimate children had been discovered. When these things had been publicized and exposed, both the crimes and the images and buildings were swiftly cut down. [Note: Thus read both the printed books and our manuscripts. Cacciarius has *de fraudis scelere*, “of the crime of the fraud.” Bononiensis has *ad tormentum* for *ad tormenta*, and afterward *pudor omnes* for *pudor omnis*, perhaps more correctly. At the end Barraeus incorrectly cites *excitabantur* for *excidebantur*.]

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the origin and destruction of Canopus

Who could enumerate the superstitious crimes of Canopus? There, under the pretext of priestly writings—for that is what they call the ancient writings of the Egyptians—there was almost a public school of magical art. The Pagans venerated that place as a kind of fountain and origin of demons, so greatly that it enjoyed much greater fame there than at Alexandria. But concerning the error of this monster too, and the sort of origin they report for it, it will not be absurd to explain briefly.

[Note: This is the passage which Jerome, in the Prologue to the Rule of Saint Pachomius, in volume II of our edition of his works, recalls as once infamous for the disgraceful worship and luxury associated with an idol’s name, but sanctified after a monastery had been built there. “In the monastery,” he says, “of Metanoea, which was changed from Canopus into penitence by a fortunate transformation of its name.” Athanasius the presbyter, in the little book which he presented to the Council of Chalcedon against Dioscorus, calls it a suburb (*προάστειον*) of Alexandria. “Metanoea,” he says, “is a suburb of the great city of Alexandria, which was formerly called Canopus.” This suburb, from ancient times and by old custom, was a harbor and refuge for the wretched. For it appears to be entirely under the protection of the most holy monastery of the Tabennesiots, or rather even within the precinct of the most sacred Church of God, and so forth.]

They say that at some time the Chaldaeans, carrying Fire, their god, around with them, entered into conflict with the gods of all the provinces, so that whichever one prevailed might be believed by everyone to be God. The gods [alternative reading: “God”] of the other provinces consisted of bronze or gold, [Note: Thus from Guarnerianus; others have “and silver.”] silver, or wood, stone, or whatever material they were made of, all of which would unquestionably be destroyed by fire. As a result, Fire prevailed everywhere.

When the priest of Canopus heard this, he devised something cunning. In the regions of Egypt they make clay jars that are open all around with numerous very small holes, through which muddy water, seeping out, becomes clearer and purer [alternative reading: “would become clearer and purer”]. He stopped up the holes of one of these with wax, painted it on the outside in various colors, filled it with water, and set it up as a god. He carefully fitted on top the severed head of an old image which was said to have been that of Canopus, Menelaus’s helmsman [Note: Eustathius gives a long account of the story of Canopus, Menelaus’s helmsman, in his commentary on Dionysius Periegetes, line 13; see that passage. Add also Scylax, *Periplus*, p. 43, and others. Shortly afterward the Guarnerian manuscript again reads *minus bene*—“less well”—for *itur*, “they proceed.”] head.

After this the Chaldaeans arrived. They entered the contest. Fire was kindled around the jar. The wax with which the holes had been stopped melted. As the jar seeped, the fire was extinguished. Through the priest’s fraud, Canopus was shown to be the victor over the Chaldaeans. Hence the image of Canopus was fashioned with very small feet, a drawn-in neck, and a bruised, swollen belly in the form of a jar, with its back equally smooth. [Note: The Bononiensis manuscript indicates that *subligato*, “bound up,” should be read by means of an abbreviation of letters. Shortly afterward Guarnerianus has “from this persuasion” and then *Sed fecerit* in the singular; Bononiensis has *fecerunt*, “they did,” and *Chaldaei* in the nominative. The printed editions have *profecerint*, with a different sense. Theophilus himself, moreover, in the Synodical Letter previously praised, in the Latin translation from Jerome which we were the first to publish, also mentions the destruction of Serapis and the other idols (for thus we correct *Idolorum* to *Idoliorum*).]

Because of this belief it was worshiped as the god who had conquered all. But perhaps such things once benefited the Chaldaeans. Now, however, when the priest of God Theophilus approached, no sweat was of any benefit, nor did the fraud concealed by wax provide any assistance. Everything was destroyed and brought down to the ground.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the churches and martyr-shrines built on the sites of idols

But nothing was done that did not transform the place into desolation. [Note: Cacciarius overlooked Barraeus’s very learned marginal observation that the better reading may perhaps be: “And nothing was left undone.”] The caves of crimes and the mouldering tombs were cast down, and lofty churches of the true God were built. [Note: All the other books are silent about *celsae*, “lofty.” Shortly afterward Guarnerianus has *ex alio* for *altero*, “from one side.” See Socrates, book V, chapters 16 and 17, and the notes of Valesius and other learned men on that passage, as well as Pagius under the year 389.]

For in the tomb of Serapis, after the profane buildings had been leveled, a martyr-shrine rises on one side and a church on the other. I think it worthy to recall how the opportunity to build the martyr-shrine arose.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the violated tomb of John and the relics preserved at Alexandria

In the time of Julian, as though the reins had been loosened, the savagery of the Pagans boiled over into every kind of violence. It happened then that, at Sebaste, a city of Palestine, they attacked the tomb of John the Baptist with frenzied minds and murderous hands, scattered his bones, then gathered them up again and burned them in the fire, and scattered the holy ashes, mixed with dust, through the fields and countryside. [Note: Guarnerianus places *beati*, “blessed,” before the name. Shortly afterward Bononiensis has “they scattered the bones.” Concerning the relics of Saint John the Baptist, see—among others, which I mention first—Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book III, chapter 7.]

But by God’s providence it happened that at that same time certain men from Jerusalem, from the monastery of the holy man Philip, had come there for the sake of prayer. When they saw that so great a sacrilege was being perpetrated not merely by human hands but with a beastly mind, they preferred to die rather than be polluted by such a crime. Mingling with those who were collecting the bones for burning, they gathered them as carefully and reverently as the circumstances permitted; then, secretly withdrawing from those who were either stupefied or raging, they carried the venerable relics to the holy father Philip.

Considering himself unworthy to preserve so great a treasure by his own vigilance, he sent the relics of the immaculate victim to the supreme bishop Athanasius through his deacon Julian, who later became bishop of the city of Palestine. Athanasius received them and, with only a few witnesses, enclosed them beneath a hollowed-out wall of the sanctuary; [Note: The same manuscript has *sacrificii*, “of the sacrifice.” Shortly afterward, where the text says *Parum dixerim*, Barraeus notes in the margin: “Perhaps, *Parum si dixerim*,” ‘If I say too little.’] in a prophetic spirit he preserved them for the benefit of a future generation. Now that the traces of idolatry have been cast down and overthrown, golden roofs would rise in buildings that were once profane.

But after Serapis had fallen—although he had never lived—which shrine of another demon could remain standing? I should say too little if I said that all the little shrines of virtually every demon that had been attached to individual columns throughout Alexandria fell. Rather, throughout all the cities of Egypt, through the forts, villages, and every countryside, along the riverbanks and even through the desert, wherever temples or [alternative reading: “or else”], rather, tombs could be found, they were undermined and brought down to the ground by the energetic action of each bishop, so that the countryside that had unjustly been assigned to demons might once again be returned to cultivation. [Note: 302]

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the busts (*thoraces*) of Serapis erased at Alexandria and the sign of Christ restored in their place

A further event also occurred at Alexandria: the busts (*thoraces*) of Serapis, which were set into the walls of virtually every house, at entrances, on doorposts, and even [alternative reading: “on”] in windows, were all cut away and scraped off so completely that no trace remained anywhere—not even the name of any deity, whether his own or that of any other demon. Instead, everyone painted the sign of the Lord’s Cross on doorposts, entrances, windows, walls, and columns. [Note: Guarnerianus omits *omnes*, “all.” Shortly afterward Cacciarius and certain other manuscripts read *nominis*, “of the name,” for *numinis*, “of the deity.” Bononiensis likewise has *domini*, “of the Lord,” for *daemonis*, “of the demon.”]

When those Pagans who had survived saw this being done [Guarnerianus omits *esse*, “to be,” more smoothly], they are said to have recalled, in memory of the great event, something handed down to them from ancient tradition [alternative reading: *commendatae*, “commended,” for *commendata*, “handed down”]: Egyptians are said to have included this sign of our Lord’s Cross among what they call the *hieratic* (ἱερατικὰς), that is, priestly letters, as one of the other elements of writing that they possess. They assert that the interpretation of this letter or symbol is: “The life to come.” Therefore those who were then converted to the faith in amazement at the events said that the ancients had handed down to them the teaching that the things now worshiped would stand only as long as they saw this sign arrive, the sign in which there was life. Hence it happened that those who were priests or ministers of the temples were converted to the faith in greater numbers than those who took pleasure in the tricks of error and the machinery of deception. [Note: Guarnerianus is more nearly correct with *jeroclipas* in Latin letters, corresponding to the truth, *jeroglyphicas*, “hieroglyphic,” instead of the Greek word ἱερατικὰς, which in Cacciarius is itself not free from error. Bononiensis, with others, has *jeraticas*. Some prefer *jerogelistas* and *jerofanitas*. Barraeus and other printed editions have ἱερατικὰ. Socrates, book V, chapter 17, tells the story somewhat differently and does not seem fully to have understood Rufinus’s meaning. Learned men who traveled through Egypt, among them John Gravius of Oxford in his *Pyramidographia*, testify that they repeatedly encountered the form of a Cross among the hieroglyphs, and that it was sometimes placed, according to Egyptian custom, even upon coffins made of stone or baked clay.]

## CHAPTER XXX. That the measure of the water of the Nile, which they call a *pēchyn* (πῆχυν), should be brought to the church

It was customary in Egypt for the measure of the rising Nile to be carried to the temple of Serapis, as though to the author of the increase and flooding of the waters. Once his image had been overthrown and consumed by fire, everyone declared that Serapis, remembering the insult, would no longer grant the waters beyond their usual abundance [alternative reading: “and their usual abundance”]. [Note: The Guarnerian manuscript has *et affluentiam solitam*, “and the usual abundance,” perhaps more correctly.]

But to show that it was not Serapis—who came into existence long after the Nile—but God himself who ordered the river’s waters to rise at their appointed seasons, the flood from that time onward was so great that no age could remember one like it before. Therefore the very ulna, that is, the measure of water which they call a *pēchyn* (πῆχυν), began to be brought to the church, to the Lord of the waters. [Note: Cacciarius also corrupts this word, writing *ποῦχυ*—which means nothing—instead of *πῆχυν*, correctly found in the printed editions and meaning an ulna or cubit. And so that you may not attribute the error to the carelessness of the printers (we have pointed out scarcely any of the innumerable errors with which that edition teems), he repeats *ποῦχυν* in the table of chapters and in the heading of this very chapter. Guarnerianus writes *pechur* in Latin letters; Bononiensis writes *peochin*. Shortly afterward Cacciarius again has *caepit deferri*, “began to be carried,” from one manuscript instead of *coepta*, the reading of all the other books.]

When these events were reported to the religious Emperor, he is said to have raised his hands to heaven and exclaimed with great joy: “I give you thanks, Christ, that this ancient error has been extinguished without the destruction of that great city.” [Note: Bononiensis has *vociferatione*, “with loud shouting”; two Vatican manuscripts cited by Cacciarius have: “I give you thanks, Christ,” and so forth.]

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the death of the younger Valentinian and the rise of Eugenius

Meanwhile Valentinian, governing the state in the western regions with a spirit as ardent as his age permitted, ended his life by hanging, although the reasons still remain hidden. But some maintained that this had been done through the treachery of his commander Arbogast; this was the prevailing public opinion. Others said that the commander was innocent of the crime committed, but that he had supplied the causes by which the young man, in indignation, was driven to this act: namely, that he did not grant him free authority over everything, since he regarded him as not yet strong enough by reason of his age. [Note: Barraeus and Rhenanus note in the margin that another reading is: “since he was even less capable than his age allowed,” and so forth.]

Nevertheless, there were some priests who, having received a peace embassy from the man who was later appointed, testified before Theodosius that the commander was free from the crime of the death. [Note: In Guarnerianus: “only as much as his age allowed”; then *Arbogastis*. Shortly afterward: “Others said that he was alien from the crime committed,” and so forth. Saint Epiphanius, in his book *On Weights and Measures*, no. 20, records the death of the younger Valentinian with precise chronological markers, namely, during the consulship of Arcadius II and Rufinus. “He,” he says, “as they report, was found suffocated in the palace on the Ides of May, the day before Pentecost, on a Saturday; but on the day of Pentecost he was carried out for burial.” He was therefore killed on May 15 in the year 392. See Sozomen, book VII, chapter 22.]

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the responses of the monk John

But he, nevertheless inflamed toward vengeance, took up arms against Eugenius, who had been substituted in the place of the dead man, after first inquiring through the monk John—whom we mentioned above [at the end of Chapter 19]—what the will of God was. The same man who had previously foretold to him a bloodless victory over Maximus now promised him this victory as well, although not without a very great flood of blood on both sides.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On Theodosius’s preparation for war against Eugenius and his victory achieved more by prayers than by valor

Accordingly, he prepared for war not so much with the aid of weapons and missiles as with fasts and prayers; and he moved about fortified [Guarnerianus: *munitur*, “is fortified”] not so much by the vigils of sentries as by spending the night in supplication. With priests and the people he visited all the places of prayer, lay prostrate in sackcloth before the shrines of the martyrs and apostles, and sought reliable assistance through the intercession of the saints.

But the Pagans, who always animate their errors with new errors, renewed their sacrifices and stained Rome with murderous victims. They inspected the entrails of animals and, from their supposed foreknowledge derived from the fibers, announced a secure victory to Eugenius. [Note: Barraeus and Rhenanus note in the margin another reading: “they accumulate.”]

Flavianus was then prefect, and he pursued these superstitious practices with complete zeal. Relying on his assertions—for he had great precedence in wisdom—he had confidently assumed that Eugenius would be victorious. [Note: Guarnerianus has, in one word, *insipientiae*, “of folly,” and in this line it omits the word *verbum*; it also omits the word three lines later.]

But when Theodosius, relying on the aid of true religion, began to press toward the Alpine passes, the demons—for whom so many victims had vainly been sacrificed—were the first, trembling with awareness of their deception, to turn to flight. Afterwards their master and teacher in error, especially Flavianus, more guilty of shame than of crime, though a most learned man and able to escape, judged that he deserved death more justly for his error than for a crime.

The others, however, drew up their battle line. Having placed ambushes on the higher ridge, they awaited the battle themselves on the mountain’s descent. [Note: Bononiensis has “having placed ambushes in a higher place, they engaged in Christ’s battle,” and so forth. Shortly afterward Guarnerianus reads “and they surrendered themselves to the legitimate Emperor” for “immediately,” and so forth.]

But when the first troops were reached, they immediately surrendered themselves to the legitimate Emperor. A fierce battle was fought with the others, who had been caught in the lower valleys. Victory remained uncertain for some time. The barbarian auxiliaries were being slaughtered and were already turning their backs to the enemy. But this happened not so that Theodosius might be defeated, but so that he might not appear to have won through barbarians.

Then, when he saw his forces turning, he stood on a high rock from which he could both see and be seen by either army. Casting aside his weapons, he turned to solid assistance and prostrated himself before God in the sight of all:

“Almighty God,” he said, “you know that I have undertaken this battle in the name of Christ your Son, as I believe, for a just vengeance. If this is not so, take vengeance upon me. But if I have come here with a reasonable cause and trusting in you, extend your right hand to your people, lest the Gentiles say, ‘Where is their God?’” (Psalm 113:30). [Note: Guarnerianus, with two Vatican manuscripts, has *Dei omnipotentis*, “of Almighty God”; then: “You, God, know,” and so forth. Shortly afterward two Vatican manuscripts have: “If it is otherwise, take vengeance upon me, your servant.”]

Once the pious Emperor’s supplication had been accepted by God—as those who were present were certain it had been—the commanders were inspired to slaughter, especially Bacurius, a man distinguished by faith, piety, and bodily and spiritual virtue, and one worthy to be Theodosius’s companion and associate. With spear, javelins, and sword he struck down everyone near him, broke through the enemy ranks, densely packed and tightly massed, and forced a path through thousands who were falling. Having broken the ranks and poured out heaps of corpses, he made his way to the Tyrant himself. [Note: 306]

What happened may scarcely be believed by the impious. For it is known that after the Emperor had poured out that prayer to God, a wind arose with such violence that it hurled the enemy’s missiles back against those who had thrown them. While the wind persisted with great force, every weapon cast by the enemy was rendered useless. The enemy’s courage was broken—or rather, driven back by divine power—and Eugenius was brought before Theodosius’s feet, with his hands bound behind his back, while his commander Arbogast strove in vain against God, who acted mightily. [Note: The words *Deo adverso*, “with God opposed,” which Cacciarius introduced from two Vatican manuscripts, are also approved by our manuscripts.] There the end of his life and struggle occurred.

Then the religious Emperor’s victory over the frustrated expectations of the Pagans was more glorious than his victory over the Tyrant’s death. Their vain and false divination had contributed less punishment to the Tyrant’s death than it had preserved shame for their life. [Note: Guarnerianus has: “whose vain hope and vehement but false divination”; several Vatican manuscripts cited by Cacciarius have: “no less in the death,” and so forth.]

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On Theodosius’s end after the victory and on his sons and heirs of the kingdom, Arcadius and Honorius

After these events, when the Emperor, as one who foresaw the future, was burdened by concern for arranging the state, he immediately sent word to the East, where he had entrusted his children to secure protection while he was to come to the war. There he ordered Arcadius Augustus to preserve the kingdom previously handed over to him. He likewise ordered Honorius, endowed with equal dignity, to come swiftly to the rule of the West. Having received him and embraced him with paternal kisses and arms, he handed over to him the reins of the western kingdom. Then, after governing the Roman Empire successfully for seventeen years, he departed to a better life, destined to receive the rewards of his merits with the most devout Emperors. [Note: Bononiensis omits *feliciter*, “successfully.” Compare Socrates, book V, final chapter, and Pagius under the year 395, whom you should consult concerning Theodosius’s death.]

[Note: See at the end of the volume the index of variant readings collected by the distinguished Dominicus Ongarus and sent to Valesius after the edition had already been completed.]

# TWO BOOKS OF THE APOLOGY OF RUFINUS, PRESBYTER OF AQUILEIA, AGAINST SAINT JEROME (C)

## BOOK ONE

[Note: Previously the hostile title *Invectives* was in use, a title by which Saint Jerome himself designated these writings in the work addressed to him; Rufinus, in turn, consistently calls what Jerome composed against him an *Invective*. The true title of both writings, however, is *Apology*, which Our Author testifies that he gave his own work once, and again in this very book, no. 16. Antiquarians, somewhat unfairly toward him, called them *Invectives* and *Controversies*. Among them, the person who copied the Guarnerian manuscript prefixed the following title, not without insult: “Book I of the Controversies of the detractor Rufinus against the outstanding and most holy man Jerome the Presbyter begins.”]

[Col. 0541A] 307

### 1

I have read through what you wrote, my dearest son Apronianus, which you sent to me from the East by a good friend and brother—Jerome—and I remembered the prophetic saying:

“The teeth of human beings are their weapons and arrows,  
and their tongue is a sharp sword” (Psalm 56).

[Note: The Guarnerian manuscript has *relegi*, “I have read again,” as does Martianaeus; it also omits the pronoun *tua*, “your.” Concerning Apronianus and his most noble family, Turcia Asteria Aproniana, we have said something in our edition of this very *Apology* among Jerome’s works, volume II; these matters were later discussed very fully by Fontanino in his *Life*, book II, chapter 4, to which I refer the reader so that we may not appear to be repeating what has already been done.]

There is scarcely any physician for these wounds that are inflicted by the tongue among human beings. Therefore I turned to Jesus, the heavenly physician, who gave me a most powerful antidote, drawn from the box of his Gospel, which could soothe the force of pain by the hope of the future judgment that awaits the just. The potion that Jesus prepared consisted of these words:

“Blessed are you,” he said, “when they persecute you and speak every kind of evil against you falsely. Rejoice and be glad, because your reward is great in heaven. For so they persecuted the prophets who were before you” (Matthew 5:11 and following).

And I, for my part, as far as lies within me, content with this medicine, had decided thereafter to remain silent, saying to myself: “If they called the master of the household Beelzebub, how much more will they call his household servants”—though we are unworthy ones—“the same” (Matthew 10:25). [Note: The Guarnerian manuscript omits *et*, “and”; it reads *indignor*, “I am indignant,” for *indigner*, “I should be indignant.”]

And if it was said of him, “He is a deceiver, and he deceives the crowds” (John 7:12), why should I be indignant if I hear myself called a heretic, or, because of dullness—or rather blindness—of understanding, called a mole? And when my Lord, indeed the God of all, Christ, was called a gluttonous man and a drinker of wine, a friend of tax collectors and sinners (Matthew 11:19), why should I be indignant if I hear myself called a carnal man, living in pleasures?

### 2

But since there seems to be some just necessity imposed upon me to reply—because it is said that many were offended by what he wrote, unless the nature of the matter is disclosed—I am compelled to respond against my wish and intention, lest by keeping silent I seem to acknowledge the crime. Although, for a Christian, it is glorious to repel other crimes by silence, following the Lord’s example, nevertheless, if this is done in matters of faith, it generates the greatest scandal. [Note: Again the Guarnerian manuscript omits the little word *ex*, “from.”]

Therefore, since at the beginning of this *Invective* of his (Letter 84 to Pammachius and Oceanus) he promises that he will omit persons and respond only to matters and crimes, both claims are false. For what accusation does he answer when no one brings it? And how does he omit persons, when throughout the entire text of his *Invective* he continually accuses and tears apart the translator of the books?

We, setting aside all irony and evasive pretense (*ὑπόκρισις*, hypocrisy), which is abhorrent to God, shall reply, even if in unadorned words and an unpolished style. We reasonably presume that readers will grant pardon to our inexperience, because we are not accusing others but striving to clear ourselves of insults. Therefore we take care that truth, rather than mere speech, should shine forth in us. [Note: 309]

### 3

But before I begin to clear up the remaining matters, I confess that he was entirely right in saying, above all, that he does not return insult for insult. This is sufficiently true: for he does not return insults for insults, but abuse and curses for blessings and praises. Nor, as he says, does he offer the other cheek to one who strikes his right cheek; rather, to one who strokes and smooths his cheek, he thrusts in the bite of an unexpected tooth.

For when we praised both his eloquence and his diligence in our work—merely in translating from the Greek—and never detracted from his faith, he condemns both qualities in us. [Note: The Guarnerian manuscript omits *utrumque*, “both.”] Therefore let him also grant us pardon if we say anything too harsh or too unpolished. He provoked an inexperienced man to reply, although he knew that, through extensive rhetorical skill and abundant eloquence, that man could not manage matters in such a way that the person whom he wished to harm and wound would appear neither wounded nor harmed.

Let this kind of eloquence, then, be demanded from him who, stirred by the slightest rumor to censure or denounce, rushes up like some censor. But the man who wishes to remove stains cast upon him must, once the necessity of replying has been imposed, consider not how elegantly and ornamentally he should answer, but how truthfully. [Note: Here too the same manuscript is silent about *vero*, “but.”]

## 4

And since at the very beginning he says, “As though heretics could not exist without me” [Al. *cannot exist*], this must first be demonstrated to us: that we are heretics neither with him nor without him. Once it has been established what we are, no disgrace arising from the statements of others can then be turned back against us.

I, as he himself and everyone knows, having already been settled in a monastery nearly thirty years ago [Note: [Col. 0543D] Probably in the year 371. See *Life*, chapter 1], [Col. 0543C] 310 was regenerated by the grace of Baptism and received the seal of faith through the holy men Chromatius, Jovinus, and Eusebius, highly esteemed and thoroughly approved bishops in the Church [Al. *Churches*] of God. One of them was then a presbyter of the blessed memory of Valerian, another an archdeacon, [Note: [Col. 0543D] In the Guarnerian manuscript, “another a deacon”; and shortly afterward it has, “of one deity, and of one substance, co-eternal and inseparable,” etc.] and the other a deacon, who was at once my father and teacher in the Creed and in the faith.

They therefore handed the faith down to me in this form, and this is how I hold it: that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are of one deity and of one substance; an eternal, inseparable, incorporeal, invisible, incomprehensible Trinity, known perfectly only to itself, as it is. For “no one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son” (Matt. 11:27). And “the Holy Spirit searches even the depths of God” (1 Cor. 2:10). Therefore the Trinity is devoid of every bodily visibility, but with that intellectual eye of divinity [Note: [Col. 0543D] We have supplied from the Guarnerian manuscript the little word *thus*. Rufinus very properly clears himself here at the outset of the suspicion of error, and of the blasphemy usually attributed to the Origenists—or to those regarded as belonging to the Origenist sect—that neither the Son and the Holy Spirit see the Father, nor the Father the Son and the Holy Spirit. Compare what he himself brings forward below, no. 17, from Origen on this very matter. Consult also Jerome’s *Letter 124 to Avitus*, no. 13, and what we have written there.] the Son and the Holy Spirit see the Father, just as the Father sees the Son and the Holy Spirit. There is absolutely no difference within the Trinity, except that the one is Father, the other Son, and the other Holy Spirit.

There is a Trinity in the distinction of persons, and unity in the truth of the substance. The only-begotten Son of God, through whom from the beginning all things that exist, whether visible or invisible, were made, in the last days assumed flesh and a human soul, became man, [Al. *the word “became” is omitted*] and suffered for our salvation. On the third day, after that very flesh which had been placed in the tomb was raised up, he rose from the dead. And with that same glorified flesh [Col. 0544B] he ascended into heaven, from which he is expected to come for the judgment of the living and the dead [Note: [Col. 0543D] The Guarnerian manuscript omits *flesh*; it reads *from where* for *from which*, and shortly afterward has the additional words “as judge of the living,” etc. The same reading occurs in the following *Apology to Anastasius*, where the printed books also insert the name “Judea.”]

In a similar way he also gave us the hope of resurrection, so that we may believe that we too shall rise in the same order, with the same sequence, and in the same and equal form in which the Lord himself rose from the dead—not, as they slanderously claim, in clouds or thin breezes [Note: [Col. 0544C] The same manuscript has “and thin breezes,” as certain people falsely allege, etc.]—but that we shall receive these very bodies in which we now either live or die. For how will it be true that we believe in the resurrection of the flesh, unless the nature of the flesh is truly and completely preserved in it?

Therefore, without any trickery, we confess the resurrection of this true and whole flesh of ours, in which we now exist [Note: [Col. 0544D] The Guarnerian manuscript reads, “the true and complete nature of this flesh of ours.”]

## 5

But, to provide greater certainty concerning the matter, I shall add something further. Compelled by the necessity imposed by my slanderers, I shall disclose the singular and distinctive mystery of our Church [Col. 0544C]. For while all the Churches [Note: [Col. 0544D] The Guarnerian manuscript also has the adverb *thus*, which we previously supplied from an ancient edition. It is worth observing here the ancient discipline of the Church, which took the greatest care that the mystery of the Creed should not reach the ears of the profane. Saint Ambrose says: “Beware of carelessly divulging the mysteries of the Creed or of the Lord’s Prayer.” Thus it was handed down from the very order of the catechumens only to the Competentes. Our author excuses himself for making it public by the necessity of replying. For the rest, recall his earlier *Apology to Anastasius* and his *Exposition of the Creed*, where he presses this addition to the profession of his faith twice and even three times.]

hand on the sacrament of the Creed in such a way that, after saying “the forgiveness of sins,” they add “the resurrection of the flesh,” the holy Church of Aquileia, foreseeing by the Spirit of God the future slanders directed against us, adds a syllable belonging to a single pronoun when it hands on the resurrection of the flesh. Whereas the others say “the resurrection of the flesh,” we say “the resurrection of this flesh.”

Accordingly, when, as is customary, we touch our forehead at the end of the Creed with the sign, and confess with the mouth the resurrection of this flesh—namely, the flesh that we have touched—we close every avenue by which a venomous tongue might slander us [Note: [Col. 0544D] The manuscript reads *which*, and at the end, and below, “so that we may block every avenue of the poisoned...”].

Is anything fuller than this confession? [Note: [Col. 0545D] The same manuscript repeats, “Is anything...”] Is anything more perfect than this exposition? Yet, as I see, all this great precaution of the Holy Spirit has done us no good. Malicious tongues still find an opportunity for slander.

“Unless,” he says, “you name each individual member—unless you mention the head with its hair, the hands, the feet, the belly, and the parts below the belly—and specify them more explicitly, you have denied the resurrection of the flesh” [Note: [Col. 0545D] Here, by contrast, another manuscript omits the second *unless*.]

## 6

These are the inventions of a new wisdom, which escaped the blessed Apostles when they handed down the faith to the Church and were revealed through the spirit of the flesh to no saint except this one man. And now, although he puts the matter forward indecently, let him hear a more honorable and more truthful account than the one he puts forward [Note: [Col. 0545D] The same manuscript reads *in me* instead of *now*; perhaps this is more correct].

Christ is “the first fruits of those who sleep”; he is also called “the firstborn from the dead.” Thus the Apostle says concerning those who rise: “Christ the firstfruits, afterward those who belong to Christ” (1 Cor. 15:20). Since, then, we possess in Christ the indisputable firstfruits of our resurrection, why do we doubt concerning the rest, when it is certain that, with the members, the hair, the flesh, and the bones with which Christ rose, we too shall all rise? [Note: [Col. 0545D] The same manuscript has *all* here, and below, five lines after this verse, omits the little word.]

For this reason, after his resurrection, he offered himself to be touched by his disciples, so that no hesitation concerning his resurrection might remain. Since Christ has given us so evident—and, so to speak, palpable and tangible—an example of his resurrection, is anyone so insane as to think that he will rise in a different manner from the one who first opened the way to resurrection? [Note: [Col. 0545D] Here the manuscript adds, “why should anyone thus...”]

This also confirms the truth of our confession: the nature of this flesh is indeed the same flesh, and no other flesh will rise; yet it will rise cleansed of vices and having laid aside corruption. Thus that saying of the Apostle will be true: “What is sown in corruption will rise in incorruption; what is sown in dishonor will rise in glory; what is sown an animal body will rise a spiritual body” (1 Cor. 15:42 and following) [Al. “will rise” for “rose”].

Therefore, as a spiritual, glorious, and incorruptible body, it will be adorned and illumined with its own members, not with members assumed from elsewhere, in accordance with the glory whose pattern is preserved for us in Christ, just as the Apostle also says: “He will transform the body of our humiliation, conforming it to the body of the glory of his Son” (Phil. 3:21) [Note: [Col. 0545D] The Guarnerian manuscript reads *configured*, which more closely reflects the Greek *σύμμορφον* (*symmorphon*, “conformed”).]

## 7

Since, therefore, Christ is presented throughout as the pattern held out in the hope of resurrection, and since he himself is the firstborn of those who rise, and the head of all creation, as it is written, “He is the head of all things, the firstborn from the dead, so that he might hold first place in everything” (Col. 1:18) [Note: [Col. 0545D] The Guarnerian codex, less correctly, has *holding the firstborn place*], why do you vainly fight over words, and why do we stir up conflicts of evil suspicions, when the Church’s faith stands firm in the confession I explained above, and it is clear that no diversity of faith moves anyone to accusation, but only perversity of mind?

But since, in this passage, while arguing about the resurrection of the flesh, he has, as is his custom, mixed ridiculous and playful things with serious matters, saying:
