“Some women among our people, holding their breasts or stroking their smooth [Al. *gentle*] cheeks, and clapping their thighs and belly, are accustomed to say: ‘What benefit is there for us in the resurrection, if the body will rise fragile again? We shall be like the angels and will have the nature of angels.’” [Note: [Col. 0545D] The second occurrence of the word *angels* is found neither in the Guarnerian manuscript nor in the older edition.]

Let him himself see whom he accuses among these little women, and whether they deserve to be torn to pieces [Col. 0546B]. Or, if he thinks himself the man who preaches that one ought not to bite one’s own in retaliation, he is now biting even without retaliation; or, at any rate, if he calmly tolerates his own little women being bitten back with true rather than fabricated and fictitious words, let him himself, I say, see to this [Note: [Col. 0546D] The Guarnerian manuscript has a somewhat more correct reading: “if he thinks that he is...” Shortly afterward it reads *with fabricated inventions*, without an intervening *and*; and below, *he promised* instead of *he will have promised*, etc.].

Meanwhile, we shall fulfill what he promised: we do not return the bite. But, as I see, this man who is displeased by a woman who denies that she will have a fragile body after the resurrection undoubtedly approves of bodily fragility remaining. And where is the Apostle’s statement: “It is sown in weakness, it will rise in power; it is sown an animal body, it will rise a spiritual body” (1 Cor. 15:43)? What fragility do you want to exist in a spiritual body? And since it will rise in power, how will it again be fragile? How can what is fragile exist in power? [Note: [Col. 0546D] In the Guarnerian manuscript: “How can anything fragile...?”]

Do the little women not speak better than you, since they deny that fragility will continue to rule the body? Why do you ridicule those who follow the Apostle, who says: “For this corruptible thing will put on incorruption” [Note: [Col. 0546D] The same manuscript omits the remainder of this passage, “and this mortal thing will put on immortality” (1 Cor. 15:53), and shortly afterward also omits the word *Church*]? The Apostles did not teach that the body which will rise from the dead would be fragile; on the contrary, they say that it will rise in power and glory. Where do you now get this from? Unless perhaps some Jews are now promulgating a new law for the Church, so that we may learn these things as well.

For the Jews truly have such an opinion concerning the resurrection: they will indeed rise, but in order to enjoy carnal delights and luxuries and the other pleasures of the body [Note: [Col. 0546D] See, if you wish, Abarbanel’s commentary on the sayings of the Fathers, *Pirkei Avot*, and Pocock’s explanation of the *Gate of Moses*, chapter 6. Shortly afterward the Guarnerian manuscript adds, “for carnal riches, delights,” etc. A little later it reads *the corruption of diseases* instead of *of the members*]. What other bodily fragility is there, then, except the corruption of the members, the irritation of the appetite, and the provocations of lust?

## 8

But please permit, if indeed you love Christ, that the body which will rise from the dead exist in incorruption without these things; let it at last be permitted that these matters cease [Col. 0547A] [Al. *may this be permitted*]. Let us believe that lawful sexual intercourse also ceases in the resurrection, lest unlawful intercourse creep in there as well, so long as the memory of these things remains [Al. *of them*].

Why is the belly, and the region beneath the belly, examined and discussed so anxiously and carefully? And yet you call us carnal and pleasure-loving, although, as I see, you do not believe that these things must cease, or that they will cease in the resurrection.

For we do not deny that the nature of this flesh, in which we now live, will rise [Note: [Col. 0547D] The Guarnerian manuscript reads, “we do not deny it, lest the vices of the flesh...”]; nor do we again involve the vices of the flesh along with it. The flesh will indeed rise—not one flesh in place of another, but this very flesh. It will not lose its nature, but it will lay aside its fragility and its vices. Otherwise, what remained fragile would not be immortal.

Therefore we are heretics neither with you nor without you. For the faith of the Church, whose pupils we are, proceeding midway [Al. *falling midway*] between the two dangers, neither denies the truth of the nature of the flesh or body—which will rise from the dead—nor, contrary to the Apostle’s judgment, says that the incorruption of the future kingdom is to be possessed by corruption.

We therefore do not say, as you claim, that the flesh or body will rise after its members have been lost or amputated. We say that the whole and complete body will rise, with corruption, dishonor, and fragility laid aside, and with all the defects of mortality removed at the same time, so that absolutely nothing of its nature will be lacking in that spiritual body which will rise from the dead—except corruption.

## 9

I have answered this one heading concerning the resurrection at greater length than I had intended, fearing that through brevity we might again suffer slander from certain people. Therefore I have frequently mentioned not only the body, concerning which they slander us, but also the flesh [Col. 0547C] [Note: [Col. 0547D] This was the familiar error of the Origenists, who said that the body after the resurrection would be an airy body, not composed of flesh, and therefore cunningly avoided any mention of flesh. How strongly our author rejected this is shown most clearly here and elsewhere, especially in his *Exposition of the Creed* on this article; I recommend that you compare it.]. And not only the flesh, but I added “this flesh”; and not only “this flesh,” but I also mentioned the nature of this flesh. Nor was I content with that: I even said that the integrity of the members would not be lacking in those who rise [Col. 0547D].

All this, however, is to be understood according to the Apostle’s definition: the body that rises will be incorruptible instead of corruptible, glorious instead of dishonorable, immortal instead of fragile, spiritual instead of animal. Thus we may finally understand that the members of the spiritual body are free from every suspicion of corruption or fragility.

I have set forth my faith concerning the Trinity; I have set it forth concerning the Incarnation, the Passion, and the Resurrection; concerning the Lord our Savior’s second coming in glory and the future judgment. I have also set forth the resurrection of our flesh, and, as I think, I have left nothing ambiguous. What remains now? I think, as far as the faith is concerned, nothing.

## 10

“But I accuse you,” he says, “because you interpreted Origen, who says that there will be a restoration of all things, in which not only all sinners will be absolved, but even the devil himself and his angels will eventually be released from their punishments, so that the restoration of all things may consequently be understood. He also says that souls were created before bodies, that they were brought down from heaven, and inserted into bodies.”

I am doing nothing now on Origen’s behalf, nor am I writing an apology for him. Whether he stands with God or has fallen, let him see to it himself; he stands or falls to his own Lord (Rom. 14:4). But I am compelled to mention him in certain matters, because when our rhetorician accuses him, he no longer attacks me indirectly but openly assails me with drawn sword and directs his whole assault against me.

And why do I say that he assails me? Rather, in order to rage against me, he does not spare even his own teacher, since he thinks that from the books of Origen that I have interpreted he can turn some slander against me. Among the other things he censures in us, he spitefully added this: that I chose this work for interpretation although neither he nor any other ancient translator had chosen it.

I shall therefore briefly and truthfully explain the reason why I undertook this work, since this is the point at which I am chiefly bitten. Although the matter may seem superfluous to you, my dearest son Apronianus, who know well how it happened, it is nevertheless fitting that those who do not know should learn it. It is also fitting because he himself, and his entire school, boast concerning us that although we promised in our Prefaces to translate one way, we acted differently in the work. Therefore we shall answer not only them, but also those whose minds are disturbed either by personal envy or by another person’s accusation [Al. *may be disturbed*].

### 11

Macarius, a man distinguished by faith, learning, nobility, and way of life, had in his hands certain little works against Fate, or Astrology, and was composing them with useful and absolutely necessary labor [Al. *toil*]. But in some places, because the subject was extremely difficult, he hesitated while discussing the dispensations of divine providence [Note: [Col. 0548D] The same manuscript reads *which was*; shortly afterward it omits the verb *to discuss*, and a little later the adverb *from afar*. Recall what is recorded in the *Life*, book II, chapter 1.].

During sleep, he said that the Lord had shown him something like this: a certain ship appeared to be approaching him from a distance across the sea. When it had entered the harbor, it would untie the knots of his hesitation. When he arose and anxiously reflected on the vision, he said that we had arrived at the right moment. He immediately disclosed to us both his little works, with their difficulties, and his vision.

He then asked what Origen, whom he had heard was held in the highest esteem among the Greeks, thought about such matters, and briefly requested that his views on each point be explained to him [Col. 0548D] [Al. *was asking*].

I first said that the matter was difficult to accomplish, but I told him that the holy martyr Pamphilus had written something of this kind in part in his *Apology*. Immediately he asked that it be translated into Latin. I said that I had no experience in such a work and that I had already lain dormant for nearly thirty years in the use of the Latin language.

Nevertheless, he persisted in begging that, in whatever kind of language I could, I should at least make known to him those matters that he desired to see [Note: [Col. 0549D] The Guarnerian manuscript has a less satisfactory reading: “For he persisted, entreating...”]. When I had done this as well as I could, he was inflamed with an even greater desire to know more fully the very matters from which those few things I had translated appeared to have been taken.

He began to press me more vehemently, and, calling God to witness, urged me not to deny him the assistance that could help him in a good work. When he persisted forcefully, and I perceived that his desire was according to God, I finally consented and did indeed undertake the translation.

### 12

In the brief Prefaces to both works, and especially to Pamphilus’s little book [Note: [Col. 0549D] The earlier printed editions have *in the little book*. Continue here what is explained more fully in the *Life* at the place cited.], which I had translated first, I set forth my faith before everything else and declared that I believed precisely as the Catholic faith teaches. If anything was read or translated by me, I said that I was doing so without compromising the integrity of my faith.

In these little books *Περὶ Ἀρχῶν* (*Peri Archon*, “On First Principles”) [Al. *books*], I also gave this warning: since certain statements concerning the faith were found in the books, written in a way that agreed with the Church’s proclamation, while others contradicted them, although both kinds of statements concerned one and the same matter, it seemed to me that the former should always be presented according to the rule that Origen himself had set forth in his exposition of the Catholic position. Anything found in his writings that contradicted that rule, or that had been inserted by others—for his letter complains of precisely this [Note: [Col. 0549D] The Guarnerian codex reads *testifies*. This is Origen’s letter that was formerly found in the fourth book of his letters, addressed to certain Alexandrian friends against those who had corrupted his books while he was still alive. Jerome translated its first part into Latin in *Against Rufinus*, book II, no. 18; Rufinus himself presents the second part in his *Apology for Origen*]—I would reject; or at least omit anything that contained no edification in the faith.

I do not think it superfluous to insert the actual passages from my brief Prefaces, so that nothing may be without the testimony supporting what we say. To prevent an error in reading arising from the passages we now insert here from elsewhere, those that are mine have simple marks in the margin beside the headings; those of my accuser have double marks [Note: [Col. 0549D] We have followed Rufinus’s intention in this as well: we mark his fragments with a single marginal stroke, and Jerome’s with a double stroke.]

### 13

From the brief Preface to Pamphilus’s *Apology*, after a number of preliminary remarks, we said as follows:

“Let the tenor of this little book teach what Origen thinks. ‘As for those matters that are found in him to contradict one another’ [Note: [Col. 0550D] The Guarnerian manuscript reads, “that come before him in contradiction to one another.”], ‘we shall explain at the end, in a brief appended statement, what the reason for them is.

“‘But we hold, as it has been handed down to us by the holy Prophets, that the holy Trinity is co-eternal and of one power and substance; and that the Son of God became man in the last age [Col. 0549D] and suffered for our sins [Note: [Col. 0550D] The scribe of the same codex, deceived by the repetition of the same words, omitted this passage, including “in that very flesh in which he suffered.”]. In that very flesh in which he suffered, he rose from the dead [Col. 0550A], and for this reason bestowed on the human race the hope of resurrection.

“‘We do not speak of the resurrection of the flesh through any trickery, as certain people slanderously claim. Rather, we believe that this very flesh in which we now live will rise [Al. *will rise indeed*], and that there will not be one body in place of another, nor do we say that there will be a body other than this flesh.

“‘Therefore, whether we say that the body will rise [Note: [Col. 0550D] The same manuscript reads, “we believe”], we speak according to the Apostle, for he used this term; or whether we say “flesh,” we confess according to the tradition of the Creed. For it is a foolish invention of slander to suppose that the human body is something other than flesh.

“‘Whether, then, we speak of flesh according to the common faith or of body according to the Apostle, we must believe that what will rise will rise as the Apostle defined it: it will rise in power [Note: [Col. 0550D] The same manuscript reads, “it will rise in power, it will rise in glory,” etc.] and in glory, an incorruptible and spiritual body.

“‘While preserving, therefore, the prerogatives of the future body or flesh, the resurrection of the flesh must be believed to be complete and perfect, so that both the same nature of the flesh may be preserved and the condition and glory of the incorruptible and spiritual body may not be diminished. For it is written: “Corruption will not possess incorruption” (1 Cor. 15:50) [Al. *“just as”* for *“for”*].

“‘These are the things that are proclaimed in Jerusalem, in the Church of God, by its holy priest John; these are the things that we both say and hold together with him. If anyone believes or teaches anything beyond these things, or thinks that we believe otherwise from the way we have explained, let him be anathema.’

“If anyone wishes to possess a document of our faith, let him take it from these statements [Al. *from those statements*.] If we read, assert, or interpret anything, we do so without compromising the integrity of this faith of ours, according to the Apostle: ‘Testing everything, holding fast to what is good, and abstaining from every form of evil’ (1 Thess. 5:21–22). And if any follow this rule, peace be upon them and upon the Israel of God (Gal. 6:16).”

### 14

Since I had set forth these statements concerning my faith before any accuser arose [Note: [Col. 0550D] The manuscript again reads, “before any accuser”; shortly afterward, “compelled to say this way what I had said before”; and then *the necessity of interpreting* instead of *that necessity of interpreting*], so that no one might say that, having been warned or compelled by them, I was now saying what I had not previously believed; and since I had promised that, if the necessity of interpretation required anything of me, I would do it while preserving the integrity of my faith, how can the slanderers still be given an opportunity, when the first word of my confession plainly makes me safe and secure from every suspicion of contrary doctrine?

Moreover, as I said above, I learned from the Lord’s word that each person will be justified or condemned by his own words, not by the words of another [Col. 0550D].

The same may also be demonstrated from the Preface that we placed before the books *Περὶ Ἀρχῶν*, where we explained how the fidelity of our interpretation was to be observed [Note: [Col. 0550D] The old edition reads, “nevertheless in my...” and shortly afterward, “the things that now pertain to the matter.” The Guarnerian manuscript reads, “but so that in it...” and below, “from the statements themselves,” “and speeches”; finally, shortly afterward, “the things that do not pertain to the matter.”].

It is fair to insert from that Preface those matters that pertain to the question. For after we had mentioned, as a mark of respect, this man who now turns these words into an accusation—because before us he had already translated a great many of Origen’s works—and after we had praised either his eloquence in explaining or his diligence in translating, and had said that we ought to follow him in a similar work, we added this after a number of remarks [Al. *these*]:

“Therefore we too follow this man, although not in the strength of eloquence, nevertheless, insofar as we can, according to the rules of discipline, taking care not to bring forward those things found in Origen’s books that disagree with and contradict himself” [Note: [Col. 0551D] The Guarnerian manuscript inserts *in spirit*. Other editions have, “so that those things found in Origen’s books that disagree with himself may be brought forward.”].

Remember, reader, so that this brief statement does not escape you: I said that I would not bring forward those things found in Origen’s books that disagree with and contradict himself. I did not generally promise that I would not bring forward things contrary to the faith, but only things that contradicted one another [Note: [Col. 0551D] The old edition reads, “things that the books themselves said against one another.” The Guarnerian codex reads, “things that contradicted themselves and differed from himself,” while the remaining words have been omitted through the copyist’s negligence because of the repetition of the same expression], or that differed from himself—not things that differed from me or from anyone else.

Therefore let hostile people not seize upon this statement and generate slanders by saying that I promised to bring forward anything that was contrary to or differed from our faith. Even if I were able to do that, I would not dare to promise it.

If you find that I have done this in my work, you may approve it. But if some part seems to you to have been carried out inadequately [Al. *seems likely to be carried out inadequately*], you cannot accuse me, since you do not hold me bound by any such undertaking [Col. 0551C].

### 15

“But let us join the remaining passages as well:

“‘We have published the causes of this difference more fully for you in the *Apology* that Pamphilus wrote on behalf of Origen’s books, in a very brief appended treatise. In it, by proofs that are, as I think, evident, we showed that his books had been corrupted in very many places by heretics and malicious people, especially those books that you now demand that I interpret [Note: [Col. 0551D] Martianaeus, together with the Guarnerian manuscript, has the plural, “which you demand that we interpret”; the manuscript also omits *that is*, and in the earlier place omits *or*.]: namely, *Περὶ Ἀρχῶν*, which may be translated either *On First Principles* or *On Principalities*. These books are truly both exceedingly obscure and exceedingly difficult [Note: [Col. 0552D] In the Preface itself: “They are truly obscure in many ways and exceedingly difficult,” etc. An adverb is missing here.]. For he debates there about matters concerning which philosophers, after spending their entire lives on them, were unable to discover anything. But our author did what he could to convert to piety the faith of the Creator and the account of created things [Al. *created matters*], which they had drawn toward impiety.’”

Here too examine the wording carefully, so that you do not miss the fact that we spoke of “the faith of the Creator,” but of “the account of created things.” We know that the things said about God belong to faith, while the things concerning created beings that we discuss belong to reason.

But let us add what follows:

“‘Therefore, if anywhere in his books we found something contrary to what he had piously defined elsewhere concerning the Trinity, we treated it as adulterated and foreign [Al. *it is foreign*], either passing it over or presenting it according to the rule that we frequently found affirmed by him himself. Have we said anything carelessly here?’”

[Note: [Col. 0552D] The Guarnerian manuscript reads “things said about heaven,” and shortly afterward *they debate* instead of *we debate*. A little later the older editions have *we find something contrary*, while the manuscript has *we find something contrary to...*].

Did I say that, according to the rule of our faith, I presented something that had already gone entirely beyond the proper limits of a translator who renders from Greek into Latin? I said that I had presented it according to the rule that we frequently found affirmed by Origen himself.

We added the following as well [Al. *let us add that*]:

“‘If, while speaking briefly to people already experienced and knowledgeable, he expressed something obscurely because he wished to pass over it quickly, we have added material to make the passage clearer, drawing upon what we had read more plainly about the same matter in other books, and devoting ourselves to explanation. Yet we have said nothing of our own; although the words were spoken in other places, we have restored his own words to him’” [Note: [Col. 0552D] Other editions have *only*. The Guarnerian manuscript reads, “we have nevertheless restored his own words to him.”]

### 16

I think that this single confession ought to have been enough for even the most unjust judges: I said that we had said nothing of our own, but that, although the words had been spoken in other places, we had restored his own words to him. Have I made myself liable in any respect? Did I promise to say anything of my own?

Where is the accusation? Where is the slander? Where is the fiction that I said I had translated bad things, called them good, and translated whatever things were good? Let them at last be ashamed, and stop bringing forward falsehoods and undertaking within themselves the work of the devil by accusing their brothers.

Let them hear that we have said nothing of our own, and let them hear again and again that we have said nothing of our own, but that, although the words were spoken in other places, we have restored his own words to him.

And lest they think that we laid hands on this work without the mercy of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0552D] The same manuscript reads incorrectly, “lest they think that we contributed too little to this work without mercy”], let them see that we had already foretold these very things that they are now doing. For after this we added the following:

“‘I have given this warning in the Preface for the very reason that slanderers might not again think that they had found material for accusation’” [Note: [Col. 0552D] Recall also the *Book against John of Jerusalem*, especially nos. 25 and following.].

The reason I said “again” [Al. *another*] is that they had already slandered the letter of the holy bishop John concerning the faith, written to the holy Theophilus, when they were pretending that the human body was something—I do not know what—other than flesh. For this reason I used the word “again.”

But let them see, I say, what perverse and contentious people do:

“‘Meanwhile, this great labor has been undertaken by us—if indeed God, when you pray, will help us—not in order to close the mouth of slanderers, which cannot be done, although perhaps God might do even this [Al. *will do this*], but in order to provide material for those who wish to advance in knowledge of these matters.’”

But so that you may know that we both foresaw and foretold that they would falsify these things, see what we added afterward:

“‘I solemnly charge and adjure everyone who will either copy or read these books, before God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, by the faith of the future kingdom, by the sacrament of the resurrection from the dead, and by the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels [Note: [Col. 0553C] The words “by that eternal fire which is prepared for the devil and his angels” were absent here both from the earlier printed books and from the Guarnerian manuscript [Col. 0553D]. We have supplied them from Rufinus’s own Preface, according to the authority of the manuscripts. It is remarkable that the distinguished scholar P. Coustant, in his notes to Rufinus’s following *Apology to Anastasius*, so distorts this passage that he wants *thus not* to be read as *if not*, and supplies the words in a sense appropriate to someone uttering a dreadful imprecation. On the contrary, the particle *thus* expresses good wishes and a vow. Horace, to omit six hundred other examples, has in book I of the *Odes*, ode 3:

“Thus may the powerful goddess of Cyprus,

Thus the brothers of Helen, the shining stars...”]—’”

And may the Father rule the winds; in this sense it is also clear that Rufinus adjures those who will copy his book. Yet it cannot be denied that in the Guarnerian manuscript itself *si* is read in place of *sic*. (Matthew 7): “May he not possess that place in eternal inheritance where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth, and where their fire is not quenched and their worm does not die.” [Note: Col. 0553D. Guarnerian manuscript: “nor let anyone add to this Scripture or take away from it,” etc.] “Let him not add anything to this Scripture, nor take away, nor insert, nor alter anything.”

And yet, after all these adjurations, so horrifying and so terrible—[Note: Col. 0553D. Formerly the printed editions corruptly read *honorifica* (“honorable”) for *horrifica* (“horrifying”), which we now restore. The following *terribilia* (“terrible”) has likewise been taken from the Guarnerian manuscript, in place of the formerly read *horribilia* (“horrible”).]—those who say that they believe in the future resurrection of the flesh did not fear to falsify and corrupt these things. If they believed even this, that God exists, they would never commit deeds so criminal and wicked.

But where in the matters we have set forth above has Origen been extolled with praises to heaven, as he alleges? Where has either Apostle, Prophet, or anything such as he himself wrote concerning Origen been mentioned by us? [Col. 0553C] Or where at all do they find a basis for accusation? We set out beforehand our faith, which, I think, agrees in all things with the Church’s confession. We distinguished the rule of translation, in which indeed he himself, who now appears as accuser, had furnished us an example in very many instances. I indicated what purpose I pursued [Alt.: *silently omitted in some witnesses*] in translating. Now, whether I have been able to fulfill it fully or less fully, [p. 323] let this be approved by readers—[Note: Cols. 0554C–D. The Guarnerian manuscript omits the words “by readers” and “or the first thing that occurs.” We repeatedly omit what is plainly faulty.]—by whom one is accustomed either to be praised or laughed at, but not accused of a crime when another’s words are rendered into another language, either properly [Col. 0554A] or less properly.

### 17

But since we have mentioned those who, whatever these matters may be, could not possibly have accused them unless they were false, I think it fitting to insert into this Apology the very passage into which they have put their falsifying hands, lest they think that I deliberately withheld what they put forward as false charges by adding their own material. [Note: Col. 0554D. The manuscript reads: “because we have mentioned those who, whatever these things may be, nevertheless could in no way have accused them unless they were false, it is fitting to insert into this very passage, into which they cast their falsifying hands,” etc.; then, “lest they think that I withdraw it deliberately, while they, by adding [their own], put forward false [charges],” etc., without the pronouns “my” and “their.”]

For when in a certain passage of the aforesaid work which we translated there was a question against those who call God corporeal and describe Him with human limbs and bodily form—and this is especially what the heresy of the Valentinians and Anthropomorphites is accustomed to assert [Note: Col. 0554D. The same manuscript omits *praecipue* (“especially”), and then reads the plural, “heresies are accustomed.”] (to which these accusers of ours have, as I see, given far too much support)—and when Origen, defending the Church’s faith against them, affirmed in every respect that God is incorporeal and for that reason invisible [Col. 0554B], the course of the question prompting him, he answered the heretics in that place with certain words which we translated into Latin as follows.

From Book I of *περὶ Ἀρχῶν* (*On First Principles*), a little further on (chapter 1, no. 8):

> “Yet these assertions may perhaps seem to carry less authority with those who desire to be instructed concerning divine matters from the holy Scriptures and seek confirmation from them of how [Alt.: *also*] the nature of God [Alt.: *how greatly*] surpasses the nature of bodies. [Note: Col. 0554D. The same manuscript reads, “what the nature of God is, which surpasses the nature of bodies,” etc.; it then omits the word “speaks.”] See, then, whether the Apostle too says the same thing when he speaks of Christ: ‘Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature’ (Colossians 1:15).
>
> “For the nature of God is not, as some think, visible to one person and invisible to another, [Note: Col. 0554D. Elsewhere: “is invisible to some and visible to others.” The Guarnerian manuscript: “is visible to some,” etc.; and shortly afterward, “the Apostle did not say, the image of the visible God,” etc.] because [Alt.: *for*] the Apostle did not say, ‘the image of the invisible God to human beings,’ or ‘invisible to sinners’; but he pronounces with great firmness concerning the very nature of God, ‘the image of the invisible God’ [Col. 0554C]. [Note: Col. 0554D. The Guarnerian manuscript adds: “the firstborn of every creature.”]
>
> “John too, saying in the Gospel, ‘No one has ever seen God’ (John 1:18), plainly declares to all who can understand that there is no nature to which God is visible—not as though He were visible by nature and eluded or exceeded the sight of a weaker nature [Note: Col. 0554D. The same manuscript, together with other editions, has *creaturae* (“creature”) in place of *naturae* (“nature”).], but because it is naturally impossible for Him to be seen. [Note: Cols. 0554D–0555D. This is one of the passages in which Rufinus himself admits that some words may perhaps have been incautiously placed in Greek and that in translating he brought them into a Catholic sense. [p. 324] Compare Jerome’s book to Pammachius against John of Jerusalem. Moreover, Martianay corruptly read *si ne ipse quidem* for *ipsi*—that is, “to the Only-Begotten, to whom the divine nature might be visible”; it is not Origen, who is discussing this question.]
>
> “But if you ask me what I think also concerning the Only-Begotten Himself: if I say that even to Him the nature of God, which is naturally invisible [Alt.: *who*], [Col. 0555A] is not visible, do not immediately consider it impious or absurd. [Note: Col. 0555D. Again the Guarnerian manuscript either omits this, or, shortly afterward, reads *quidem* for *quippe* and again omits the following *quidem*; it proceeds: “One thing is to know.” To be seen and to see belong to bodies.] For we shall give the reason in due course.
>
> “To see is one thing, to know another. To be seen and to see belong to bodies; to be known and to know belong to an intellectual nature. Whatever, then, is peculiar to bodies must not be thought of either the Father or the Son. But what pertains to the nature of Deity is held in common between Father and Son.
>
> “Finally, He Himself did not say in the Gospel, ‘No one sees [Alt.: *has seen*] the Father except the Son, nor the Son except the Father’; but He said, ‘No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son’ (Matthew 11:27). From this it is plainly shown that whatever among corporeal [Alt.: *bodily*] natures is called seeing or [Alt.: *and*] being seen [Col. 0555B], between Father and Son is called knowing and being known, through the power of knowledge, not through the frailty of visibility. [Note: Col. 0555D. The Guarnerian manuscript inserts *constat* (“it is established”), a word that appears to have intruded here from the margin of the book.]
>
> “Since, therefore, with reference to an incorporeal and invisible nature, neither seeing nor being seen is properly said, neither is the Father said in the Gospel to be seen by the Son, nor the Son by the Father, but to be known.
>
> “But if someone puts to us the question why it is said, ‘Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God’ (Matthew 5:8), our assertion will, I think, be strengthened all the more by this. For what else is it to see God with the heart than, as we explained above, to understand and know Him with the mind? [p. 325]”

### 18

This is the passage—[Note: Col. 0555D. Guarnerian manuscript: “This is the passage.” Those whom the author says were sent from the East to ensnare him are to be understood as Paulinianus, Jerome’s brother, and the presbyters Vincentius and Eusebius.]—which those sent from the East to lay snares for me attempted [Col. 0555C] to defame not only by a perverse interpretation but by adulterating its words. For this reason I could not treat it with suspicion, as I did several other matters in the author I was translating, nor judge it fit to omit it: because it said nothing comparing Father and Son, but investigated the nature of Deity itself, whether the term “visible” appeared applicable to it in any manner.

As we have said above, I replied to those heretics who maintain that God is visible because they also call Him corporeal [Note: Col. 0556D. Again the manuscript reads *credunt* (“they believe”); from this line onward we read *quos* (“whom”) for *quod* (“because”).], since vision is properly a property of a body. Thus too the Valentinian heretics mentioned above say that the Father generated corporeally and visibly, and that the Son was so generated.

Origen, then, fleeing, as I think, the designation “vision” as suspect, says that it is better in the nature of Deity—that is [Alt.: *silently omitted: that is*], between Father and Son—to use [Col. 0555D] the expression defined by the Lord Himself: [Col. 0556A] “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son” (Matthew 11:27). He considered that every opening ought to be shut off from the aforesaid heresies if he spoke of knowledge in the nature of Deity rather than vision, since vision might seem to give heretics some opening. Knowledge, however, preserves the inseparable truth of the one nature between Father and Son, especially since such is the authority of the Gospel. [Note: Col. 0556D. In the same manuscript: “the indissoluble truth.”] At the same time, he thought this would provide very great caution lest the Anthropomorphites in any way hear God called visible.

Since this reasoning made no distinction in the Trinity, it seemed to me that it ought not wholly to be rejected, even if we avoided some words perhaps incautiously placed in Greek. Let it still lie open to the judgment of readers whether this too appears useful or less useful against the aforesaid heresies [Col. 0556B]. [p. 326] But let us suppose [Note: Col. 0556D. The same manuscript: “that even these men,” and then “in matters of this sort,” etc.] that even those who know letters and can judge matters and meanings of this sort, whose skill is accompanied by fear of God, who do nothing through contention or vain glory, and whose minds are free from envy, favor, and hatred, say that this passage has little value for instruction or for overthrowing [Note: Col. 0556D. The same manuscript omits “aforesaid.”] the aforesaid heresies. Is it therefore not permissible to pass it by and pass over it as less powerful for repelling adversaries? Suppose it is idle: is it also criminal? How can it be treated as criminal where equality of invisibility between Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is affirmed? I do not think this can seem so to anyone.

And why do I say “to anyone”? Not even these very accusers of mine found anything in my writings [Note: Col. 0556D. Manuscript: “my accusers found something in my writings which could offend,” etc.] that could offend [Col. 0556C]. For if they had thought this, they would have put forward my own words as I translated them.

### 19

But now listen to what they do, and ask whether any precedent for their crime has gone before. In the place where it was written: “But if you ask me what I think concerning the Only-Begotten Himself: if I say that even to Him the nature of God, which is naturally invisible, is not visible, do not immediately consider it impious or absurd; for we shall give the reason in due course”—[Note: Col. 0556D. Martianay corruptly reads, though here agreeing with the Guarnerian manuscript, *si ne ipse quidem* for *ipsi*. Recall the preceding note at column 0554. Below, as usual, the manuscript omits the first word that occurs.]—in place of what we wrote, “For we shall give the reason in due course,” they wrote: “Do not immediately consider it impious or absurd, because, just as the Son does not see the Father, so neither does the Holy Spirit see the Son.” [Note: Col. 0556D. Yet neither in the previously printed books nor in any manuscripts, according to those who consulted several, is there the palm’s breadth or trace of such an adulteration.]

If this man—Eusebius of Cremona—had committed such a deed in public court or secular affairs [Col. 0556D], he who was sent from the monastery to Rome [Col. 0557A] as though most skilled in calumny, everyone knows what would follow under public law for one guilty of such a crime.

But now, because he abandoned secular life [Note: Col. 0557D. The same manuscript adds “now,” and shortly afterward, more correctly, “that he may be taught by him again to rage under a show of modesty.” It then omits the second occurrence of “stir up.”], turned from those evasions of public proceedings to the monastery, and attached himself to a distinguished teacher, he is again taught [p. 327] by him to rage and go mad under the guise of modesty; to stir seditions instead of keeping quiet; war instead of peace; dissensions instead of concord; treachery instead of faith; and forgery instead of truth. Believe me, the wickedness of this crime would have had even a true model, had that Jezebel not occurred to you. [Note: Col. 0557D. Guarnerian manuscript: “had not come before you. For she …”] For she is the one who devised this accusation against Naboth the Jezreelite over the vineyard [Col. 0557B], and commanded the presbyters of iniquity to press him with false documents, as though he had blessed—that is, blasphemed—God and the king.

But who is happier [Note: Col. 0557D. The same manuscript: “happier in brief.” Five lines below, it reads *auditur* (“is heard”) for *additur* (“is added”).] in this matter: she who commands, or those who obey the command of iniquity? These things are grave, and, I think, a crime of this sort is almost unheard of in the Church. But something further is added. Do you ask what? That the accused become judges and those who laid the snares give sentence.

For a writer to err or slip in [Alt.: *silently omitted: in*] speech is nothing new and, I think, is worthy of pardon, since Scripture says, “For we all stumble in many things; but he who does not stumble in word is a perfect man” [Note: Col. 0557D. The same manuscript omits *vir* (“man”), which all the other books have.] (James 3:2). Is the error thought to be in a word? Let it be corrected, amended if usefulness requires it, and removed. But to insert in another’s writings things not written, and to insert falsehoods solely in order to defame a brother’s life; to violate another’s writings so as to impose a mark upon the writer [Col. 0557C]; to steal into the ears of the people [Note: Cols. 0557D–0558D. The same manuscript: “that you may remove the writer’s mark, that you may steal into ears,” etc. Though these readings appear plainly faulty, we thought it better to note them, as also the reading three lines below, *conficias* (“you accomplish”) for *conferas* (“you bring”).]; to disturb the hearts of the simple; and to bring about nothing else except a stain upon a person’s reputation among men—see whether this is anyone’s work except his who was a liar from the beginning and, by accusing the brethren, received the name devil, that is, accuser.

For when Eusebius recited such a false statement at Milan, and I said that what he was reading was false, he was asked from whom he had received the copies. He answered that a certain matron, Marcella, had given them to him. As for her, whoever she may be, I say nothing, but leave her to her own conscience and to God.

For me, the testimony of God and of you is sufficient in this matter: that is, yours and that of the holy man himself, Macarius, for whom I was doing this work. You read my very sheets from the beginning, or, though they were not yet complete and corrected in every respect, you retain the copies [Col. 0557D]: namely, the claim [p. 328] that “just as the Son does not see the Father, so neither does the Holy Spirit see the Son,” [Note: Col. 0558D. The manuscript omits the words “that is”; more correctly it soon reads, “what he falsified, I say,” for “because he falsified it, I point out.”] which I not only never wrote, but, on the contrary, expose as his falsification.

If anyone denies that the Son does not see the Father in the same way as the Father sees the Son, and that the Holy Spirit does not see the Father and Son in the same way as the Father sees the Son and the Holy Spirit, let him be anathema. For He sees, and sees most truly, but as God sees God and light sees light; not as flesh sees flesh, but as the Holy Spirit sees—not with bodily senses, but with the powers of Deity. If anyone denies these things, let him be anathema forever. “But whoever troubles you,” as the Apostle says, “will bear the judgment, whoever he may be” (Galatians 5).

### 20

I remember, indeed, that when one of them was charged with falsifying this, he answered that it stood so in Greek, but that I had wished to alter [Alt.: *change*] it in Latin. I pass over the fact that they are not even telling the truth; but let us suppose that it is so in Greek, and that I had not written it in Latin [Col. 0558B]. For I had promised in my prefaces that I would do something of this kind. If I had done it [Note: Col. 0558D. The manuscript reads *facerem* (“I might do”) here and at the end of the period; it then omits “this.”]—that I might write more suitably in Latin what was offensive there—what had I done without promise or without reason?

You certainly, who had not found this in my Latin copies, from where did you read it written in your little papers [Alt.: *one*]? I, who translated it, did not write it. You, who accuse me and do not possess writings of mine of this sort [Note: Col. 0558D. The same manuscript is briefer: “you who accuse, [but] do not possess my writings of that sort,” etc.], from where do you fashion a charge against me? Or ought I to be accused because you called me false? [Note: Col. 0558D. The old edition, under the sign of assertion: “I ought not to be accused for that for which you made me false.” The Guarnerian manuscript: “you made [me] false.”]

I state a very plain matter. These are four books which I translated, in which the Trinity is discussed throughout almost every page. Let the whole be reread: if anywhere in our translation a sense concerning the Trinity is found like that which they slander in this passage [Col. 0558C] [p. 329], then at last let it be believed that this too was uttered in the sense [Alt.: *in that sense*] they fabricate. But if throughout the whole body of the books there is nowhere that distinction in the Trinity, is it not an equally mad and foolish invention to say that heresy was confirmed in one passage by one who had overthrown it in a thousand passages?

The coherence of the matter itself also sufficiently instructs every prudent person. If he had found this in my writings and had truly taken some scruple from the reading itself, since he had me present at Rome, as you yourself know, he would immediately have investigated it and brought the writings themselves to me. For until that [Alt.: *that very*] time he was accustomed to see me [Col. 0558D], greet me, and share in prayer with me; beyond doubt he would have conferred with me about the matters that seemed offensive, and asked how I had rendered them and how they stood in Greek.

### 21

He would certainly have thought it glory enough if he had appeared to have corrected something in my words or writings by his own means. Or, if the fury of his mind had compelled him not so much to correct an error as to publish [Alt.: *be published*] it, he would surely never have chosen to tear apart in my absence one whom he could [Alt.: *was able to*] refute more severely in person.

But because awareness of his falsehood deterred him, he did not bring it to me [Alt.: *silently omitted: indeed*], whose writings he wished to accuse; rather, he carries it through houses, among matrons, through monasteries, and among every brother, so that by hearing alone he may [Alt.: *you may*] stir up disturbance. And he did [Alt.: *does*] this at the very time when he was about to depart [Alt.: *when you were about to leave*] immediately from the City, lest, if seized, he should have to give an account of his deed.

From this too, as may be understood, according to the master’s command, he goes through all Italy accusing me, stirring crowds, disturbing churches [Col. 0559B], polluting even the ears of priests, and in all these matters abusing our modesty as though it were evidence of guilt. Such are the disciples.

But the Eastern master himself, who wrote to Vigilantius, “Through me all Latins know Origen’s good things and are ignorant of his bad” (Letter 61, no. 22), has retranslated these very passages which I translated [Note: Col. 0559D. Guarnerian manuscript: he translated *ἁπλῶς* (*haplōs*, “simply”); then “all these things” for “and all,” and “were” for “had been.”], and inserted everything that I had omitted as objectionable, [p. 330] so that now, contrary to his own statement, the Romans may through him know Origen’s evils and ignore his good things.

From this point he tries to bring not merely Origen but me myself under suspicion of heresy. From this point he continually sends out [Alt.: *also*] his dogs, which pursue me through cities, villages [Note: Col. 0559D. The same Guarnerian manuscript: “through villages likewise while passing”; then “they utter all things speakable and unspeakable against me,” for which I would prefer in the last word *blaterant* (“they babble”) or something similar. Other printed editions: “they pursue.”], and even along the road as I pass, with the barking of calumny [Col. 0559C], and attempt [Alt.: *attempt*] every speakable and unspeakable thing against me. What crime, I ask, have we committed if we did what you did? But if it is wicked to use your examples, what judgment do you pass upon yourself?

### 22

Nevertheless, tell me, master—for now the reply must be directed at you—if there is any fault in a writer, is it rightly imputed to a reader or translator? “Far from it,” he says, “by no means. Why do you subtly entrap me?” [Note: Col. 0559D. This whole passage, “Why do you subtly entrap me,” is lacking in the Guarnerian manuscript.] “Did I not read too? Did I not translate too? But read what I translated and see whether you find anything dogmatic in it—certainly, whether you find any of the things I now summon for condemnation.”

Finally he says: “If you wish more fully to know how the suspicion of doctrines of this sort has always been abominable to me, read my Commentaries on Paul’s Epistle to the Ephesians, and from what I have written you will learn what I thought of him, whether reading or translating it.” [Note: Col. 0559D. The same manuscript omits “Paul”; it has, “and from those things which I wrote, you will learn what,” etc., “reading it and translating it,” etc. Tillemont finds it very strange that Jerome appeals to that Commentary, in which none of Origen’s opinions constituting specifically Origenist heresy is ever attacked; on the contrary, many opinions highly favorable to Origenist doctrine are set out. See vol. XII, p. 115.]

And this is the seriousness of so great a master: that you condemn in some places one whom in others you praise, and call heretic one whom in your prefaces you called the second teacher of the Churches after the Apostles. [Note: Col. 0560D. Guarnerian manuscript: “despise.”] What heretic could ever be called a teacher of the Churches?

“I erred in this,” he says. But for how long do you attach your little preface? Read the Commentaries—but those I specified. And who thinks it just that one who wrote so many books, in almost all of which he carries Origen’s praises to heaven, books read by all and still read for so many years, from which very many have departed this world [Col. 0560B] and gone to the Lord holding the opinion about Origen which they learned from that author’s assertions [Note: Col. 0560D. The same manuscript: “departed this world and went to God holding this opinion of Origen, which they learned from the assertions of the books.” The old edition likewise reads, “this opinion of Origen.”], and departed hoping on this testimony to find him the second teacher of the Churches after the Apostles—[p. 331] should now, as he writes again, find him condemned among impious heretics and pagans? [Note: Col. 0560D. By adding “him,” on the authority of the Guarnerian manuscript, we restore a passage whose sense in earlier printed books was broken and incomplete. We had previously suspected that it had dropped out. The manuscript also reads “will find” for “found,” and, more correctly for the following period, “only if he changes from preaching” for “How he changes from contention,” etc.]

How can he change through contentiousness and say, “The man whom for almost thirty unbroken years I read and wrote about, whom I equated with the Apostles, I now pronounce a heretic”? Has he now read any new books of his that he had not read before? But from these same writings he called him an Apostle then and a heretic now; and this cannot have occurred in any way. Either he spoke rightly then, and now is perverted by envy and contentiousness [Col. 0560C], and ought not to be heard; or, if he condemned him then and now condemns himself [Note: Col. 0560D. The same manuscript: “he himself condemns himself.”], what judgment from others does he expect concerning himself, one who, according to the Apostle’s sentence, is condemned by himself?

### 22

“And what?” he says. “Is repentance cut off?” No: one errs, especially in speech, and it is indeed permissible to repent of error. But does one repent, accuse, judge, and condemn all at once? As if a prostitute, if she abstained from prostitution for one night or two, ought immediately to write laws about chastity, and not merely enact laws, but overthrow [Note: Col. 0560D. The Guarnerian manuscript seems more correct here in reading *subruere* (“overthrow”) for *obruere* (“bury, cover over”).] the tombs of all women already dead because she suspects they lived a life like her own [Col. 0561A]?

You do well to repent because you were a heretic. What is that to me, who was never a heretic? You repent of error: you do right, provided you conduct repentance lawfully [Alt.: *that is*], not by accusing but by pleading, not by condemning but by weeping. For what truth of repentance is there where the penitent himself dictates to himself the decree of pardon? One who repents of things wrongly said does not heal his wound by speaking wrongly again, but by silence. For it is written: “You have sinned; be still.” [Note: Cols. 0561C–D. Where this is written one can scarcely discover—or perhaps not even scarcely. Roughly similar sayings occur in Ecclesiasticus 21:1, Isaiah 30:7, and elsewhere, but not in these exact two words, such that the passage could be identified. That the source must be sought nowhere but in the Pentateuch is taught by Theophilus in Paschal Letter III, among the letters of Jerome in our recension, Letter C, no. 3: “Hear Moses saying to one of this kind: ‘You have sinned; cease; by ending sin, overthrow the former things,’” etc. Indeed Jerome himself cites from Genesis in Letter 147 to Sabinianus, no. 9: “Think that what was said to Cain was said to you: ‘You have sinned; be still.’” What more? Thus it may once have stood in chapter 4 of the Greek exemplar and in the Old Latin, from which it was reproduced; now not even in Greek itself can any trace of that addition be found.]

But now you make yourself guilty, then yourself absolve yourself from guilt, and from being guilty make yourself judge. This is now not your misery, you who mock us, but ours, who endure being mocked in this way.

[p. 332]

### 23

But let us come to those two Commentaries [Col. 0561B], which, after condemning and renouncing all his other works, he alone excepted, and see how chastely and consistently he conducted himself in them. [Note: Col. 0561D. I would prefer, on the authority of the Guarnerian manuscript, that *caute* (“cautiously”) be restored. The same manuscript then omits the adverb.] For from these alone he wishes both that his faith be proved and [Alt.: *the word “and” is omitted*] that he opposes Origen in all things. Let those writings be produced [Alt.: *and let those*] which alone among all his works please him: the three books on Paul’s Epistle to the Ephesians, and, I think [Note: Col. 0561D. Guarnerian manuscript: “and, I think, one book.”], one book on Ecclesiastes.

But meanwhile let the first that occurs, the Commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians, be reread. There too I approve him as an associate, an ally, and a *symmystēs* (“fellow initiate”), as he himself says, in the matters which he attacks. First of all, concerning the little women whom he ridicules because they say that after the resurrection they will not possess a frail body, since they will be like angels, let us see what he himself thinks [Col. 0561C].

In the third book of the Commentaries on Paul’s Epistle to the Ephesians, under the passage, “He who loves his wife loves himself; for no one ever hated his own flesh” (Ephesians 5:28), he says a little later: “Let us therefore cherish both husbands their wives and [Alt.: *that*] our souls their bodies, so that wives may be reduced into husbands and bodies [Note: Cols. 0562C–D. The same manuscript reads *reducantur* (“may be brought back”), and at the end of the passage omits the pronoun “us.”] into souls, and there may be no difference of sexes; but just as among angels there is no male and female, so we too, who are to be like angels, may already begin to be what has been promised to us in heaven.”

### 24

Knowing that you wrote these things in your Commentaries, how do you offer them as an example of your faith and as material for more vigorous refutation [Col. 0562A]? How do you accuse women from your own words? [Note: Col. 0562D. The manuscript has more, though less well: “you in your ecclesiastical Commentaries,” etc.; and three lines later, “and how concerning your own,” etc.]

Further, what woman ever said that wives are turned into husbands and bodies reduced into souls, as you write? If bodies are reduced into souls, then, according to you, there will be not only no resurrection of flesh [p. 333] [Note: Col. 0562D. The same manuscript omits “of flesh”; two lines later it has more: “I confess even these,” and then “For where thereafter,” etc.; lower down it has “there will therefore be” for “there will be,” etc.], but not even of bodies, which you say those whom you made heretics confess. Where thereafter do we seek body, if it is reduced into soul? For all will then be soul and body nowhere.

And again, if wives are changed into husbands, because you added, “so that there may be no difference of sexes,” as if thereby you meant to show that the female sex will perish by being reduced into male, while only the male remains, I do not know whether the female sex itself [Alt.: *the sex itself*] will permit you to say this concerning it [Col. 0562B]. Yet even if they grant it, by what reasoning can you show that the male sex is necessary there where the female is not proved necessary? For by a natural bond each sex needs the other so much that, if one does not exist, the other has no use.

For if at the resurrection a human being is thought to receive only the clay form which he had in Paradise [Note: Col. 0562D. The manuscript is much briefer here: “a human being is thought to possess the form which he had in Paradise: ‘Male and female,’” etc.], where is what is written, “He made them male and female, and blessed them” (Genesis 1:27)? But if, as you and the little women you accuse say, there is neither male nor female, how will bodies be reduced into souls or women changed into men, when either Paradise does not admit both sexes [Note: Col. 0562D. The same manuscript, without the negative: “admits both sexes.”], or the likeness of angels, as you too confess, admits no sex at all [Col. 0562C]?

And I wonder how you demand from others an opinion on the distinction of sexes [Alt.: *demand*], when you, wishing to discuss it, entangle yourself in knots so great that you can in no way untie them. How much more rightly you would act if, in such matters, you imitated us whom you blame, and permitted God alone to know these things as truth itself has them; and if you confessed that you did not know them rather than wrote things which you yourself would soon condemn [Alt.: *this*]. [Note: Col. 0562D. The Guarnerian manuscript omits “rather,” and then the following pronoun “these.” Below we pass over a good many of its obvious errors, which the reader has no interest in knowing.]

I wish he would now tell me, with his conscience bearing witness, whether, if he had found it written—not in one of my little works, but even in a letter negligently written to some friend—that bodies are reduced [Alt.: *will be reduced*] into souls and wives into husbands, he would not have ordered these things [Alt.: *silently omitted: these things*] to be written in bronze letters over the gates of cities [Col. 0563A], and recited in forum, senate-house, and even from the rostra. How many headings for accusations would he have made from this, what volumes would he have written, how he would have pressed me with every weapon and missile of his most fertile breast, saying: “If you do not believe me when I say that he deceives when he declares body to rise and denies flesh, or when he confesses flesh but denies limbs and sex, look: see how he himself wrote in his letter [p. 334] that bodies are changed into souls and wives into husbands.”

But we, seeing you write these things, not only do not accuse you of heresy, but make excuse for you as for a master. Yet those women whom you tore apart with such unworthy and disgraceful insults will bring before Christ’s tribunal both what you teach in these Commentaries and what, forgetting yourself, you again write with insults [Col. 0563B]. There both will be recited, where human favor will already cease and applause bought by praise will fall silent [Note: Col. 0563D. The same manuscript: “applause will already fall silent; with you for these things,” etc.]; and with you they will be judged before Christ, the just Judge, for these words and deeds of yours.

### 25

But let us proceed to examine what he also writes concerning the questions—for this bears upon the faith—in which, regarding the resurrection of the flesh, he treats the remaining matters variously, as in the *Questions*.

Again, from the first book of the *Commentaries on Paul’s Epistle to the Ephesians*, concerning the passage in which the Apostle says, “Just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, so that we might be holy and blameless before him” (Eph. 1:4), he says:

> “In place of ‘the foundation of the world,’ the Greek has καταβολὴς κόσμου (*katabolēs kosmou*). But καταβολή does not mean the same thing as *constitutio* [foundation or establishment]. [Col. 0563C] Therefore, because of the poverty of our language and the novelty of the subject, and as someone has said, because Greek speech is broader and its language more fortunate, we shall try not so much to translate word for word—for that is impossible—as to explain the force of the word by a kind of circumlocution.
>
> “Καταβολή properly denotes when something is thrown downward and sent from a higher place to a lower one, or when something takes its beginning. Hence those who first lay the foundations of buildings yet to be constructed are said to have καταβεβληκέναι (*katabeblēkenai*), that is, to have thrown down the beginnings of the foundations. [Col. 0563D]
>
> “Accordingly, wishing to show that God contrived the universe out of nothing, Paul did not refer it to a creature, a condition, or a making, but to καταβολή, that is, to the beginning of a foundation, so that, contrary to Mani and the other heresies that posit both a maker and matter, there might not have existed beforehand something else from which creatures were made, but that all things might have come into being from nothing.
>
> “But when he testified that he chose us to be holy and blameless before him—that is, before God—before the construction of the world, this pertains to the foreknowledge of God, for whom all future things are already accomplished, and to whom all things are known before they come to pass: [Col. 0564A] just as Paul himself was predestined in his mother’s womb, and Jeremiah was sanctified and chosen in the womb, strengthened, and sent as a prophet to the nations in a type of Christ.”

[Note: The text has been restored from the Hieronymian version: previously it read less correctly, καταβολὴν τοῦ κόσμου (*katabolēn tou kosmou*). Compare the holy Doctor himself, vol. VII, col. 547 and following.]

[Note: Previously there was an addition which neither the manuscript nor Jerome’s own text knows. Other minor matters below have been silently corrected.]

[Note: In the old edition: “that is, the beginning of the foundation thrown down,” and so forth.]

[Note: The Guarnerian manuscript reads: “So also Paul,” and so forth.]

### 26

Thus far he has offered one interpretation; but he did not make clear under whose persona this sort of understanding should be received. He did only this: by what follows, he rejects what came before. For he says in the continuation:

> “There is another who attempts to demonstrate that God is just.”

[Note: The same manuscript, in the hand of an unlearned glossator, reads: “Another, however, who tries to show that God is just,” etc.]

Here he plainly shows that God’s justice is not demonstrated by the preceding interpretation—which is impious—but by this person whom he calls “another.” Without doubt, wishing to establish this person’s assertion as unquestionable and catholic in everyone’s judgment, he supplied as evidence that, by this assertion of his, that person attempts to demonstrate that God is just.

But let us see what this other person says, who proclaims that God is just:

> “There is another,” he says, “who attempts to demonstrate that God is just. He says that God does not choose each person on the basis of a prejudgment arising from his knowledge, but on the basis of the merits of the elect. He says that, before the visible creatures—heaven, earth, the seas, and all that is within them—there were other invisible creatures, among which were souls. For reasons known to God alone, these had been cast down downward into this valley of tears, into this place of affliction and our pilgrimage, in which the saint prayed to be restored to his former dwelling, saying: ‘Alas for me, that my sojourning has been prolonged; I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar. My soul has been a long-time stranger’ (Ps. 119:5). [Col. 0564C]
>
> “And elsewhere: ‘Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?’ (Rom. 7:24). And elsewhere: ‘It is better to depart and be with Christ’ (Phil. 1:23). And elsewhere: ‘Before I was humbled, I sinned’ (Ps. 119:67), and other things of the same kind.”

[Note: We have added the adverb *deorsum* (“downward”) from the Guarnerian manuscript, the old edition, and the text of the *Commentary* itself.]

[Note: Previously *incola* was read here. The Guarnerian manuscript has *peregrina est*, “my soul is a stranger,” which is closer to the printed reading of the *Commentary*. The same manuscript then has additional words: “and in another place, ‘Wretched man,’” and so forth.]

Therefore, they say, before souls were hurled into the world—

> “Master,” they say, “you say this, but you do not say who these people are who say that souls existed before they were hurled into the world.”

[Note: The Guarnerian manuscript omits *haec* (“these things”), and then the adverb *ergo* (“therefore”) in the following period.]

“Did I not therefore rightly say,” he replies, “that you are a mole and cannot see? I have already said above that it is those who assert that God is just who say these things. If you had any intelligence, you would understand that I myself am that person.”

[Col. 0564D] For I am not so impious as to claim that I am someone else and different from those who defend God’s justice—something done by everyone who possesses sound understanding.

[Note: The same manuscript reads: “which we do, who think soundly”; shortly afterward it omits “they say.”]

> “Tell us, then,”},{ tell us, master: who are these people who are you?” they say.
>
> “Therefore,” they say, “before souls were hurled into the world, and before the world was made from souls, when he himself had been cast down to the lowest place together with its inhabitants, God chose Paul and those like him before him, who were holy and blameless. No one, however, is chosen except from among many; and where there are some who are inferior, there the choice is made.
>
> “Just as, during the Babylonian captivity, when the people had been led by Nebuchadnezzar into Chaldea, the prophets Ezekiel, Daniel, the Three Children, Haggai, and Zechariah were sent—not because they had deserved captivity, but to be a consolation to the captives—so also, in that casting-down of the world, those who had been chosen by God before the world existed were sent for the instruction and teaching of sinful souls, so that by their preaching they might return to the place from which they had fallen.
>
> “This is what Moses says in the eighty-ninth Psalm: ‘Lord, you have become our refuge from generation to generation, before the mountains were established and the earth and the world were made’ (Ps. 89:1). That is, before the world was made and the whole generation took its beginning, God was a refuge for his saints.”

[Note: The manuscript reads, “in the captivity of Babylon,” when the people were led by Nebuchadnezzar into Chaldea. We have restored *abductus* for *pro ductus* from the *Commentary*. Elsewhere the manuscript reads *non quo et ipsi*, and *directione* for *dejectione*, and finally “so that, for their preaching,” and so forth.]

### 27

These are the things that you write in those works of yours which alone you choose from all your writings and order to be reread for the condemnation of the others.

[Note: The manuscript reads, “which you choose in all your works.”]

You say that the world was invisible before this visible world came into being; and that in that world, together with its other inhabitants—namely, the angels—there were souls. You say that, for reasons known to God alone, these souls are born in bodies in this visible world, and that those who had previously inhabited heaven in the former age now inhabit this place, namely the earth, not without certain causes that they themselves committed while living there.

And you say that all the saints, such as Paul and the others like him, have been sent by God—[Col. 0565C] or, according to another reading, predestined—through each generation for the instruction of these souls, so that by their preaching they might recall them to their own dwelling, from which they had fallen. You establish this with the most abundant testimonies of Scripture.

And what other statements, I ask, are there for which you summon Origen to judgment? What other things are there in which you order him to be condemned? Do you condemn someone else in your own writings?

[Note: The Guarnerian manuscript reads, “Do you condemn another in his [writings]?”—whence perhaps one should restore: “Do you condemn one man in his writings, another in your own?” It shortly afterward reads *tu primus* (“you first”) for *tu prius* (“you before [him]”).]

And if, as you advise, statements of this kind ought to be condemned, you will first pronounce judgment and condemn yourself before anyone else for such statements.

For you no longer have any avenue of escape. The tricks for which you accuse others will have no place here. In these very books, written after your conversion, when you had already been corrected and disciplined through repentance, you granted these statements authority—so that from them your judgment concerning the doctrines you say ought to be condemned might be established. Therefore what is written here must be heard as though you were now proclaiming and defining it. And here you define things of the very kind that you say ought to be condemned.

“But it is not I who define these things,” he says. “I say that someone else says them—that is, the very person whom I now say ought to be condemned.”

Let us therefore repeat, if you please, that very passage in which you change the persona of the interpreter, so that we may see who it is whom you say asserts such things.

You therefore say:

> “There is another who attempts to demonstrate that God is just, and he says the things we have already mentioned.”

If this person whom you call “another” demonstrates by this assertion of his, as you say, that God is just, and if he is someone else and different from you, what do you think about yourself? Do you deny that God is just?

Master, while you see so much and sufficiently accuse those whose eyes are captured of being moles, I think you have fallen into an ἀδυνώτατον (*adynōtaton*), an utterly impossible predicament, and are trapped on both sides.

Either you will deny that God is just, so that you may be someone else and opposed to the person who says these things; or, if you too confess—as the entire Church confesses—that God is just, then you are the one who says these things. You are the one who first receives the sentence that you pronounce against another, and you are the one who wounds yourself with your own sword.

I think this will suffice for judges of the greatest justice who await God’s future judgment—not because they ought to condemn the one who sees the speck in his brother’s eye but does not see the beam in his own, but because they ought to correct him and recall him to true repentance.

### 28

But lest perhaps this single passage should have escaped him in the books which he thought he had thoroughly revised, and whose text, after condemning all the others, he had presented as a confession of the faith, let us inquire how he also thinks in the remaining books.

Again, in the same book, concerning the passage where it is written, “According to the good pleasure of his will, to the praise of his glory” (Eph. 1:5–6), he says shortly afterward:

[Note: The earlier text mistakenly read *barbatos* (“bearded men”) for *barbaros* (“barbarians”), whom the author contrasts with Romans. The following text, too, was faulty: it read *sanos, ignobiles in diversas oras, vel partes generari*, and added *nobiles ad Romanos*. We have restored the passage from the text of the *Commentary*: *ignobiles vel nobiles in diversis oris et diversa parte generari*. The cited text has *in diversa orbis parte* for *in diversis oris et diversa parte*.]

> “Thus they seize upon an opportunity in this passage who think that, before the foundation of the world, souls existed with the angels and the other names of the heavenly powers in the heavenly Jerusalem. But this cannot be understood either according to God’s good pleasure or to the praise of his glory and grace: namely, that some should be born naked, barbarian, enslaved, weak; others rich, Roman, free, healthy; some ignoble and others noble, in different regions and different parts of the world, unless causes preceded by which each soul received these conditions according to its merits.
>
> “And what is written to the Romans, some think they understand, but they do not understand it: ‘Does not the potter have power over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?’ (Rom. 9:21). They refer this to the same meaning, so that, just as a bad or good life, difficult or easy, is lived in vain in this world unless we believe that God’s judgment will come, so also the diversity among those born in this world demonstrates God’s justice unless the merits of souls preceded it.
>
> “For, they say, if we do not understand these things in this way, it will neither be according to the good pleasure of God’s will nor to the praise of his glory and grace that he chose some before the foundation of the world to be holy and blameless and to have adoption through Jesus Christ, while he destined others for the final condition and everlasting punishments; that he loved Jacob before he was born from the womb and hated Esau before he had committed anything deserving hatred, unless causes preceded which establish God’s justice.”

[Note: We have supplied *futurum esse* from the *Commentary*. Other printed books and the Guarnerian manuscript omit it.]

[Note: We restored the passage from the *Commentary* and, in part, from the Guarnerian manuscript. Previously it read *non secundum beneplacitum*, and shortly afterward *et gratiae ejus referetur*. The cited manuscript also rejects the two words *secundum* and *referetur*. From the same sources we read below *conditioni* for *conditionis*, and *amare Jacob antequam oriatur* for the earlier printed *amasse et oriretur*.]

### 29

What could be more explicit than this assertion? What could be clearer—whether from Origen or from any of those whom you say you accuse—than that these doctrines could either be conceived or expressed: namely, that the diversity and inequality among those born in this world should be referred to God’s justice?

[Note: The manuscript reads, “or the inequality which is in this …”; shortly afterward it omits the words “of salvation or condemnation.”]

You say that each soul itself supplied the cause of its salvation or condemnation, on the basis, that is, of those movements of the soul which it previously enacted while living in the heavenly Jerusalem, which is the mother of all.

[Al. *inquis*, “you ask.”]

And you say that this was not spoken in your own persona, but that you recorded another person as saying it. Finally, you said: “For some seize upon an opportunity.”

I do not deny that you appear to be speaking about another person. [Note: Here the Guarnerian manuscript omits *alius* (“other”), and then the words *an vero* (“or indeed”). Shortly afterward it reads *quidem dicta* for *quaedam* (“some”) statements.] But you have not denied whether this other person whom you say makes these statements agrees and harmonizes with you, or whether he is opposed and hostile to you.

When you call someone else your opponent, you usually present some of his statements and immediately destroy and attack them—as in the case of Marcion, Valentinus, Arius, and the others. But when you call someone else “another” and write down his statements, supporting them with the strongest assertions and the most abundant testimonies of Scripture, do not even we, however slow-witted we may be—and whom you call moles—see that this person whose statements you present without destroying them is no one other than yourself, and that this is a rhetorical device by which speakers put forward their own opinion under another person’s persona?

Orators do this when they fear offending certain people or wish to avoid unpopularity. For if you think you have defended yourself by calling someone else “another” in these statements, the person whom you accuse will have a much more excusable position. For he not only has the practice of saying that others speak in this way, or that certain people hold such opinions; he is much more cautious and says that he does not define such matters, but rather forms an opinion about them. And if another view should seem better, he says that this is so, so that, once these matters have been set aside, those other things may be retained.

See with what caution he has acted—and yet you summon him to condemnation. [Note: The Guarnerian codex reads *usus sit* (“he has used”) and then *ad damnationem notatur* (“he is marked for condemnation”) for *vocatur* (“he is summoned”); it subsequently has *illum nominas* (“you name him”) for *alium* (“another”), and *putas, et ex his eum condemnas* (“you think so, and condemn him from these things”).] Because you merely call someone else “another,” you think you have escaped. For you condemn him on the basis of those things in which you follow and imitate him.

### 30
