But let us proceed by reading the *Commentaries*, lest, by lingering over individual passages, we be shut out from recognizing the greater number of them.

[Note: The same manuscript introduces this passage: “Again, concerning the passage where he says, ‘That we may be …’” Erasmus and Martianus print the following Greek word as προηλπικότας.]

> “Again,”},{ in the same book, concerning the same passage in which it is written, ‘So that we might be to the praise of his glory, we who previously hoped in Christ’ (Eph. 1:12): if he had said only ‘we hoped in Christ,’ and had not prefixed ‘previously hoped,’ which in Greek is προηλπικότες (*proēlpikotes*), the meaning would be clearer: namely, that those who hoped in Christ had perhaps been called and predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will.
>
> “But now the addition of ‘previously’ draws us toward that understanding which we discussed above when explaining what is written: ‘He blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ, just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, so that we might be holy and blameless before him.’ That is, just as he had already blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places and had chosen us before the foundation of the world, so also now we are said to have previously hoped in Christ, from the time when we were chosen, predestined, and blessed in the heavenly places.”

[Note: In the *Commentary* it reads that they were “called by lot” and predestined; in the manuscript, “that they were called by lot, predestined.”]

[Note: On the authority of the Guarnerian manuscript and the reading of the *Commentary* itself, we have removed the words *idest ante* (“that is, previously”), which had been inserted here and below, where the same passage is repeated. They evidently arose from a note written in the margin by some diligent reader and later introduced into the printed books.]

[Note: Here we have supplied the pronoun *nos* (“us”), which is found neither in the manuscript nor in the *Commentary*. It seems necessary after *elegerat* (“had chosen”), so that the syntax and meaning are complete. The manuscript, wrongly, reads *sperasse nunc autem dicamur in Christo ex tempore*.]

### 31

Thus far for the moment; for what follows is more important.

Now I give thanks to God, who has relieved me of the burden of the gravest suspicion. Perhaps some people thought that I was dealing too contentiously or maliciously with this “other,” when, according to the rhetorical device, I maintained that the person whom he calls “another” was himself.

But so that no doubt at all should now remain for any of the hearers concerning who this “other” was, he himself has revealed it. Like a truly good teacher, who does not wish any ambiguity to remain for his students in what he has said, he has taken the trouble in this passage to show more clearly who the person was whom he had previously called “another.”

He says:

> “But now the addition of the preposition draws us toward that understanding which we discussed above.”

You see, he says, that it is “we,” and not some unknown other person whom you supposed, who discussed above, explaining what is written: “He blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ.”

And what those of lesser understanding thought had been said there in the persona of another, so that no error might remain for those whom he had ordered to learn from these books what opinion he held concerning Origen, he now refers back to his own persona, naming no other person, and says what we read above:

> “Namely, just as he had already blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ and had chosen us before the foundation of the world, so also we are said to have hoped in Christ from the time when we were chosen, predestined, and blessed in the heavenly places.”

He has therefore, as I think, freed me by his own testimony from every suspicion of malicious accusation, since this “other” is no one other than that very person himself.

[Note: The Guarnerian manuscript reads: “that this other person is no one other than himself.”]

### 30

But let us demonstrate still greater matters from what follows, as we promised.

[Note: Other witnesses add “and.” The Guarnerian manuscript reads, “After these things which he had said,” etc. I pass over his manifest faults occurring everywhere. Of this kind is the instance below, where it omits the negative particle in the words, “But another, not accepting this doctrine.”]

After saying that we had previously hoped in Christ and that from that time—namely, before the foundation of the world and before we were born in bodies—we had been blessed and chosen in heaven, he again introduces that other person of his and says:

> “But another, who does not accept this doctrine—that we existed and hoped in Christ before we dwelt in this body—transfers the interpretation to that point.”

Here, whoever he may be, this “other” of his has exhaled all his stench. Let the person whom he wishes to be someone else tell us who does not accept this doctrine: that before we dwelt in this body, we existed, had being, and hoped in Christ. For this is precisely the doctrine for which he orders Origen to be condemned.

Whom does he wish to have understood this way? Some person opposed to himself?

What do you say, master? You are pressed by that two-horned dilemma which you customarily explain to your disciples. For if you say that this “other,” who does not accept that souls existed before they dwelt in bodies, is yourself, then what was concealed in the preceding passages has been exposed. By your own confession you are found to be that “other”—you who define all the doctrines that you order to be condemned.

[Note: The Guarnerian manuscript adds *omnia illa dogmata* (“all those doctrines”). Shortly afterward it reads *vis intelligi* (“you wish to be understood”) for *intelligamus*.]

But if you are not the “other” in the preceding passages, lest what you reject be attributed to you, then here too you will not be the “other” who refuses to accept that souls existed before we dwelt in bodies.

Choose whichever part of the defense you prefer. Do you wish us to understand that the “other” whom you frequently introduce is yourself, or someone else? Do you wish him to appear catholic or heretical? Condemnable or acquittable?

If this “other” of yours is catholic—the one who said above that, before this visible world, souls existed with the angels and the other powers in the heavenly Jerusalem, in the heavens, and that while living there they incurred the causes of their diversity, whether of being born into this world or of enduring any other conditions—then these will be catholic doctrines, and it will meanwhile be impious to condemn what is catholic.

But if you say that this “other” is heretical, you will designate as heretical the person who refuses to accept that souls existed and hoped in Christ before they were born in bodies.

Where can one go from here, master? Where can one break out? Where can one escape again? Wherever you turn, you will be stuck. I do not say that no means of withdrawing is available to you; there is not even room to breathe for a little while.

Did the *Commentaries* of your Aristotle of Alexandria help you so much? Did Porphyry’s Εἰσαγωγή (*Eisagōgē*, *Introduction*) help you so much? Did the discipline of so many and such great philosophers—Greek and Latin, and even Jewish learning—cultivate you so thoroughly that you came into such utterly inextricable straits and were hemmed in so miserably that you could not even find protection in the Alps?

### 31

But let us now spare him. We must leave the matter to his writings; and, as he himself says, sleep must not be assigned to a great work, although he spares no one and beats whomever he pleases not so much with reasoned arguments as with the whip of his tongue.

And if anyone flatters him insufficiently, he is immediately designated as a heretic, both in writings and in a hundred letters sent in different directions.

[Note: The same manuscript reads erroneously, “Let us spare him; now he must be abandoned to letters,” etc.; it also omits the pronoun *ipse* (“he himself”) and the following negative particle.]

Nevertheless, let us imitate not him but David the patriarch, who, when his enemy Saul had been caught in a cave and he could have killed him, did not wish to do so but spared him. He did this because the same mercy has been shown to him by us several times—not only in word but in fact and deed—even if he does not wish to confess it, but retains it in his heart and conscience.

[Note: This may refer to the time when disputes and hostilities were taking place between Jerome and the bishop of Jerusalem. The latter obtained an imperial rescript for Jerome’s deportation into exile. Rufinus then acted to prevent the holy Doctor’s deportation, and at other times as well worked to prevent him from being harmed by powerful rivals.]

Let us therefore grant pardon to one who does not know how to grant pardon, who judges another’s statements without any regard for humaneness. Meanwhile, let us lead him out of this cave, until he falls into that one from which, even if we all try and wish to do so, he will be unable to emerge.

[Note: Here too we have added *hac* (“this”) from the Guarnerian manuscript, as the context requires it.]

[Note: The manuscript reads, “because it can happen that in the preceding passages,” etc., and shortly afterward, “unless the ‘other’ whom he called [there] was truly the persona of someone else.” The word *alterum* seems certainly superfluous, and is the principal cause of the interrupted and gaping sense. I would prefer to restore the context approximately thus: “How can it be that, in those earlier passages (where this doctrine was confirmed by the person attempting to show that God is just), the ‘other’ whom he called was truly the persona of someone else—such a person as he now wishes to condemn—whereas here, when he is opposed and does not receive [the doctrine], he has called himself ‘another’?”]

Let him therefore say:

> “How can it be that, in those earlier passages, where this doctrine was confirmed by the person who attempted to demonstrate that God is just, the person whom he called ‘another’ was truly speaking in the persona of someone else, and was such a person as the one whom he now wishes to condemn? But here, where he is opposed and does not accept what was said earlier, he called himself ‘another’?”

For it may be that he was conscious of having held this opinion when he wrote, although he could not explain it adequately in writing. Let him therefore be forgiven, and let us suppose in this passage that this “other” is the very person who does not accept the doctrine that souls existed before we dwelt in bodies and hoped in Christ.

Let us repeat the passage itself and follow more carefully where it is again tending. He says:

> “But another, who does not accept this doctrine—that we existed and hoped in Christ before we dwelt in this body—transfers the interpretation to the coming of the Lord and Savior. At that time, when every knee shall bow in his name, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue shall confess”—or, according to another reading, “shall confess”—“that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2:10–11), when all things have been subjected to him, some willingly and others by necessity, those who previously hoped in him before the presence of his majesty will be for the praise of his glory and will be called προηλπικότες (*proēlpikotes*).
>
> “But those who are found believing by necessity, at the time when neither the devil nor his angels will be able to deny the one who reigns, will be hoping, but not for the praise of his glory.
>
> “We see this partly fulfilled even now, since the reward of one who follows God willingly is different from that of one who follows by necessity. Nevertheless, whether through pretext or in truth, so long as Christ is proclaimed, let him know that both the one who hopes and the one who hopes previously will receive different rewards according to the diversity of their hope.”

[Note: The Guarnerian manuscript reads *subjiciendo* (“by subjecting”) for *subjiciendos*. The Greek word that follows is written in the *Commentary* as ἀπελπικῶτας (*apelpikōtas*), while one Cistercian manuscript has προηλπικῶτας (*proēlpikōtas*).]

[Note: The Guarnerian manuscript reads *regnare* for *negare regnantem*, “to deny the one who reigns”; *et in me* for *et nunc*; *fit* for *sit*; and similar variants, whose details are not important here.]

### 32

Every opportunity for evasion is removed in this passage.

Above you said that those who previously hoped in Christ are those who, before they were born in bodies in this visible world, had hope in Christ while situated in the heavens.

But lest this doctrine of yours should appear to be your own, you introduced another interpretation, in which you say that, at the time when every knee shall bow to the Lord Jesus, the whole creation—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—will be subject to him in two ways: some willingly and others by necessity.

You say that all the saints are subject willingly, those who now believe in him through the words of preaching, and that these are called προηλπικότες (*proēlpikotes*), that is, those who previously hoped in Christ.

Those who are subject by necessity, however, are those who have not now believed through the preaching of the word but then will no longer be able to deny him, like the devil and his angels. Those who believe by necessity along with them—and all of them, including the devil and his angels, will believe later—will not be called “those who previously hoped,” because the former believed in Christ and hoped in him willingly, whereas the latter will do so afterward and by necessity.

Therefore, you say that they will receive different rewards.

Yet you assign rewards to all those who do not now believe—that is, to the devil and his angels—even if inferior ones; and the man whose mere opinion, rather than doctrinal assertion, concerning a future remission of punishments you criticize, you lead to second rewards in Christ’s kingdom.

And you want this to be understood in such a way that, just as it makes no difference whether Christ is proclaimed in truth or by necessity, so it makes no difference whether he is believed in by necessity or willingly.

### 33

These are the things that you order us to learn from your *Commentaries*. You teach us these rules of confusion concerning the faith,

[Note: Perhaps *εἰρωνικῶς* (“ironically”) is the truer reading; the Guarnerian manuscript reads *fidei confessionis* (“of the confession of faith”) for *confusionis*.] so that in others the very thing may be condemned which is learned at home.

For certainly, if you are now the “other” who does not accept that first doctrine, which says that souls existed in the heavens before they were born in bodies, then without doubt you are the one who not only grants forgiveness to the devil, his angels, and all unbelievers, but even promises that they will be rewarded with second rewards.

But if you reject this second doctrine, then you will be the father of the first doctrine.

And I wonder how those prudent and learned men who read these writings of his—writings in which he now teaches these things—can laugh at me because he calls me a mole, while failing to perceive that they themselves are judged by him to be even greater moles, since he thinks that they do not see these things buried in his books.

For if he thought that they could understand what they read, he would never have ordered copies of these books to be kept for the condemnation of what the master himself teaches. In these books the very doctrines that he urges us to condemn are contained more fully and more clearly.

For the moment, we have shown that in these selected *Commentaries* of his he himself asserts what he orders to be condemned in another’s books: namely, that souls existed in the heavens before they were born—or, according to another reading, before they were sent—into bodies in this world; and that all, whether sinners or unbelievers, together with the devil and his angels, at the time when every knee shall bow to Jesus—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—not only will receive forgiveness, but will also be summoned to second rewards.

[Note: Perhaps the reading is more accurately *εἰρωνικῶς* (*eirōnikōs*, “ironically”). The Guarnerian manuscript reads *fidei confessionis* (“of the confession of faith”) instead of *confusionis*.]

### 34

But since the novelty of this matter, I do not doubt, [Col. 0572D] will scarcely win credence—that anyone should be believed to condemn what he himself asserts—I know what you desire: that, if we can, we should produce from those same books examples of such things, and examples so evident that absolutely no room for doubt about them remains for anyone; that is, [Col. 0573A] passages where not even that other person of his is named. And so I shall do this.

340. Again, from the same book: that at the end of the age Christ and all his saints will have their seat above the demons, so that the demons themselves also may act according to the will of Christ seated above them and of his saints. [Note: [Col. 0573D] We read this from the Guarnerian manuscript; for the previously printed text had an obscure and impeded sense: “and so that the demons themselves,” etc.]

This is from the chapter where the Apostle says, “That he might show in the ages to come the exceeding riches of his grace, in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus” (Eph. 2:7). Shortly afterward:

> “We,” he says, “who were once held under the law of hell and, on account of vices and sins, were destined both to works of the flesh and to punishments [Al. punishment], now reign in Christ and sit with him. But we sit not in any lowly place, but above every Principality, Power, [Note: [Col. 0573D] The Commentary adds “and Virtue,” a word which Rufinus himself also inserts below. Next, the Guarnerian manuscript has *is named* for *is named* [a different Latin form]; and, in agreement with the Commentary’s reading, “having been raised from the dead, sits,” etc. Finally, after “Dominion” it adds “and Virtue,” omitting the following two clauses, “and above every name” through “in the age to come”; in their place the Commentary also reads “and so forth.”] and Dominion, and every name which is [Col. 0573B] named, not only in this age but also in that to come. For if Christ was raised from the dead and sits at the right hand of God in the heavenly places above every Principality, Power, and Dominion, and above every name which has been named, not only in this age but also in that to come, then we too shall sit and reign with Christ; it necessarily follows that we shall sit above those things above which he sits. But the diligent reader will immediately say and ask: ‘What then? Is man [Al. Is man] greater than the angels and all the powers in heaven?’ Since it is dangerous to answer this by referring Principalities, Powers, Virtues, Dominions, and every name which is named, not only in this age but also in that to come—especially since all things have been subjected beneath Christ’s feet—not to the good side [Col. 0573C] but to the opposite [Al. *refert*, “refers”], he says that they are the fallen angels, the prince of this world, and Lucifer who rose in the morning, above [Note: [Col. 0574D] The Guarnerian manuscript reads “above whom”; shortly afterward it omits “of the age” in the Commentary. Again, the manuscript, with the Commentary, reads “bestowing,” less well than “bestowed,” that is, by Christ. For the following *of hell*, which the manuscripts also prefer, I should certainly prefer to restore *unbridled*, as in the Commentary—or rather *unrestrained*. Finally, shortly afterward the Guarnerian manuscript omits the pronoun “their.”] whom the saints will sit with Christ at the end of the age, he also bestowing a benefit upon those who now are of hell and, wickedly abusing their freedom, wander [Al. wander] everywhere and fall headlong [Al. fall] into the precipices of sins.”

341. “But when they have such occupants, they will begin to be governed according to the will [Al. wills] of those who sit.”

Is any ambiguity left here, so that this passage needs an advocate [Al. assessor]? Here, with the utmost plainness, without any interposed person other than himself, he says that the fallen angels, the prince of this world, and Lucifer who rose in the morning will, at the end, when Christ sits above them and reigns with his saints, be partners and companions not only of his kingdom but [Col. 0573D] [Col. 0574A] also of his will. [Note: [Col. 0574D] The Guarnerian manuscript reads, almost more correctly, “for himself” instead of “for him”; it also adds a little later, “with him sitting above them,” etc. I pass over certain faults below.]

For to act according to the will of Christ and all his saints [Al. omits “his”] is to have attained the highest blessedness. Nor is there any other perfection of the prayer by which he taught us to supplicate the Father, except that his will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth.

### 35

But please listen patiently—not, indeed, while I run through everything contained in his books concerning these doctrines (for they are so numerous that, if I wished to pursue them, I should have to compose several volumes), but enough to satisfy readers: that this man did not happen upon these things by chance, which he now proposes for his disciples to imitate, but confirms them by the broadest and most frequent assertion. [Note: [Col. 0574D] The same manuscript adds “these things,” and again shortly afterward has more: “but let us still see what,” etc.]

But let us see what he teaches us from these most authoritative Commentaries.

Again, [Col. 0574B] from the same book: that there is ascent and descent for human beings not only in the present age, but also in the age to come. This is from the chapter in which he says: “Above every Principality, [Note: [Col. 0574D] The manuscript reads “where he says.” Shortly afterward it omits “and Dominion.” In the Hieronymian text, *sed quae* (“but which/things”) is wrongly printed for *si autem* (“but if”).] Power, Virtue, and Dominion, and every name which is named, not only in this age but also in that to come” (Eph. 1:21). Shortly afterward:

> “But if there are,” he says, “Powers, Virtues, Principalities, and Dominions, they must also have subjects, persons who fear them, serve them, and are strengthened by their power. These distributions of offices will exist not only in the present [Al. present time], but also in the future age, so that through successive advances and honors there may be ascents and descents as well: one person may increase [Al. someone may increase], [Col. 0574C] or 342 decrease, and come to be under one Power, Virtue, Principality, and Dominion after another.”

### 36

Why, master—to address you in your own words—do you teach these things to the quiet and simple minds of the Latins after nearly four hundred years? Why do you force upon unfamiliar ears new expressions which no one received from the Apostles? I beg you: spare Roman ears; spare the faith praised by the Apostle’s voice. Why do you bring into public what Peter and Paul were unwilling to publish? Until you wrote these things—not until I interpreted them [Al. shall interpret them], as you teach, but until you wrote them nearly fifteen years ago—was the Christian world without them?

For what are you now teaching: that in the future age there will still be ascents and descents, [Note: [Col. 0574D] In the Guarnerian manuscript: “so that some may advance and some decline”; then, “in this age it is acquired in life,” which is not true, omitting the two occurrences of “either” and the word “lost.” But see what Jerome replies to this in *Apology* I: “But if,” he says, “he thinks that I follow Origen because in my exposition I set down advances and honors, ascents and descents, increases and diminutions, let him know that it is very different to say that angels and Seraphim and Cherubim become demons and human beings—which Origen affirms—and to say that angels themselves have received among themselves differing kinds of offices, which does not conflict with the Church.”] so that some may advance and some [Col. 0574D] decline? Therefore what you say—that in this life [Col. 0575A] it is either acquired or lost—is not true. Or does it have some hidden interpretation? For you do not repent of what is contained in these Commentaries.

Again, that the Church is to be understood as one body composed not only of human beings, but also of angels and all heavenly Virtues. From the same book, from the chapter in which it is written, “And he gave him as head over the whole Church” (Eph. 1:22), shortly afterward:

> “The Church,” he says, “can be understood as consisting not only of human beings, but also of angels, all Virtues, and rational creatures.” [Note: [Col. 0575D] The Guarnerian manuscript omits “Church.”]

Again, that souls, because they knew God in that former life, now know him not as one unknown, but recognize him again after forgetfulness. In the same book he says:

> “As for what he says, ‘in the recognition of him’ (Eph. 1: [Col. 0575B] 17), that is, *ἐπιγνώσει* (*epignōsei*), some understand it in this way: that between *γνῶσις* and *ἐπίγνωσις*, that is, between knowledge and recognition, there is this difference: knowledge [Al. that] concerns those things which we did not know before and afterward began to know; recognition, however, concerns those things which, having known them before, we afterward ceased to know and later remember.” [Note: [Col. 0575D] The same manuscript omits “those things.” Conversely, the text of the Commentary is much fuller and seems to require supplementation here: “Recognition, however, concerns those things which, having known them before, we subsequently ceased to know and afterward remember.”] “They suppose that there was some former life in the heavenly places, 343 [Note: [Col. 0575D] Erasmus and the Maurists incorrectly read “we suppose”; for Jerome was not making the supposition, but Origen, whose exposition he recounts while concealing the name. Indeed, the Commentaries themselves read “they suppose.”] after we were cast down into these bodies and forgot God the Father, and that now we know him by revelation, according to what is written: ‘All [Al. all the] ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord’ (Ps. 21:28), and many similar passages.”

### 38

But as for his saying, “Because some say these things,” I think I have sufficiently shown above that whenever he writes, “Because some say these things,” or “Another says,” and nevertheless does not refute the things said, [Note: [Col. 0576D] The manuscript adds again: “Thirdly, from this verse onward, whenever he puts these expressions—‘because some say,’ or ‘another says’—and nevertheless does not refute … he himself is that person.” Below it again omits “of this sort,” and then has the very corrupt “they show fraudulently enough” for “I have shown frequently enough.” We pass over errors of that kind elsewhere.] that [Col. 0575C] “somebody” or “another” is he himself—especially since I have often shown that he speaks opinions agreeing with these, without any such interposition of another person.

But what else is it that displeases him in another? “He says,” he says [Al. indeed], “that the stars and the other things in heaven are rational and capable of sin.” Let us therefore see what he himself thinks concerning such things.

From the same book and same chapter, where it is written, “For he must reign until he has put his enemies under his feet” (1 Cor. 15:25), shortly afterward: [Note: [Col. 0576D] We read this with the Guarnerian manuscript, also placing a full stop before “From the same book”; previously it ran continuously: “from the same book, in the chapter,” etc.]

> “It can,” he says, “be answered in this way: that no one is without sin; that the stars themselves are not clean before God (Job 15); and that every creature fears the coming of the Creator [Al. Savior]. Hence the cross of the Savior is said to have purified not only the things [Col. 0576A] on earth, but also those which were in heaven.”

Again, that human beings are called children of wrath because of the body of humiliation [Al. humanity] and the body of death. From the same book, in the chapter where it is written, “We were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2:5), shortly afterward:

> “But let us say,” he says, “that first all human beings are by nature children of wrath because of the body of humiliation and the body of death; and because from adolescence the mind of human beings is inclined toward wickedness” (Gen. 8).

Again, that the soul is made first and the body then fashioned. From the same book, under the same chapter, after much discussion:

> “Observe carefully,” he says, “that he did not say [Al. should have said], ‘We are his shaping and fashioning,’ but ‘his workmanship’ (Eph. 2:9). For fashioning [Col. 0576B] derives its origin from earth and clay [Note: [Col. 0576D] The earlier printed texts read “from earth, from clay”; the Guarnerian manuscript reads “from earth and clay.” There are quite a few other readings which we correct above and below.]; workmanship, however, took its beginning according to the likeness and image 344 of God. In Psalm 118 these are placed together, though they signify different things: ‘Your hands, Lord, made me and fashioned me.’ Workmanship has the first place; fashioning follows.”

What else is there which he wishes condemned? Let him speak, [Note: [Col. 0576D] The word “that” is lacking in the Guarnerian manuscript.] so that we may produce it from his books—or rather, from his heart.

“For,” he says, “the assertion of one nature for souls and angels is troublesome.” But let us see what he himself thinks about this in the books which he sets before us as a model of confession and a rule of belief.

Again, from [Al. in] the same book, from the chapter where it is written, “Coming, he preached peace to those who were far off and to those who were near” (Eph. 2:17); after he had first [Al. at first] explained this as said concerning Jews and Gentiles, [Col. 0576C] he afterward added:

> “These things indeed,” [Note: [Col. 0576D] The manuscript inserts “he says.”] he says, “have been said [Al. are said] according to the common interpretation. But whoever reads the Apostle’s statement concerning Christ: ‘Making peace through the blood of his cross for the things which were on earth and the things which were in heaven’ (Eph. 2), and the other things said in the same passage, will not think that we who are called Israel according to the spirit were far off, while the Jews, who are called Israel only in the flesh, were near. Rather, he will adapt this whole interpretation to angels and heavenly Virtues, and to human souls, because Christ through his own blood joined earthly and heavenly things, which had been at variance with one another. [Note: [Col. 0576D] The manuscript reads “will adapt,” and shortly afterward “joined together”; then the Commentary’s text has more: “which had previously been at variance with one another.”] And the good shepherd, carrying the sick sheep back to the mountains [Col. 0577A] (Luke 15), made it one with the others; and he joined the drachma which had perished to the drachmas which had been safe [Al. were safe].”

### 39

Do you see what great difference of nature he establishes between souls and angels? “How great,” he says, “is the difference between one sheep and sheep, and between one drachma and drachmas.”

And shortly afterward he added:

> “But as for what he says, ‘that he might create the two [Al. two] in himself into one new man’—which seems to accord better with the preceding interpretation concerning Jews and Gentiles [Al. Gentiles]—he will adapt [Al. adapted] it to his own understanding in this way: he will say that the human being 345, made according to the image and likeness of God, will receive after reconciliation the same form which angels now possess and which he himself lost. But he calls the new man the one who is renewed daily [Col. 0577B] and who will dwell in the new world.”

Just as sheep differ from a sheep, and a drachma from drachmas, so he says that souls differ from angels; and he says that the human being formerly possessed and lost the same form which angels now possess, and that the human being will possess it in the future. [Note: [Col. 0577D] The Guarnerian manuscript reads, “as sheep differ from sheep, and drachma from drachma, in nature”; then, “angels and the first man possessed and lost man,” from which perhaps something sound can be extracted.]

If they differ neither in nature, nor species, nor form, how can an educated man feel no shame in condemning his own opinions under another’s name—especially when you decide that this is to be said not according to the common exposition but according to the Apostle’s meaning? But let us see what is added in the same place. Shortly afterward he says:

> “The restoration of the new man will then be fully and perfectly completed, when heavenly and earthly things [Al. earthly things] have been joined together, and in one spirit, understanding, and identical judgment we have approached [Col. 0577C] the Father. Paul hints at something of this kind in another Epistle also—if anyone accepts [Al. accepts] it—when he says: ‘All these, receiving testimony through faith, did not receive the promise, God having provided something better for us, that they might not be perfected without us’ (Heb. 9 [the printed citation; the quotation is Heb. 11:39–40]). [Note: [Col. 0577D] In the same manuscript, “began”; in the Commentary, “received.” Then the Maurists, following Erasmus, read “God for us,” etc.; and a little lower, “awaits” for “we await.” We pass over many similar errors.] Therefore the whole creation groans together [Al. will groan together] with us, who groan in this tent; and suffers together, which conceived in the womb through the fear of God; and we grieve and await the revelation of the sons of God, that it may be freed from the slavery of vanity to which it is now subjected, and that there may be one shepherd and one flock, and the Lord’s Prayer be fulfilled: ‘Your will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth’ (Matt. 6:10).”

He says that heavenly and earthly things—that is, angels and human beings—just as they formerly bore one form and possessed one fold, are to be restored likewise in the future. Because Christ came to make both one flock, you say that future [Col. 0577D] human beings will be either what angels now 346 are, or what human beings themselves formerly were—that is, [Col. 0578A] souls. [Note: [Col. 0577D] The manuscript inserts “to be.” In what follows it plainly makes repeated errors.]

And how, I ask you, my friend—indeed, no longer as a friend, but mockingly—did you ridicule the little women who, with clapping of belly and thigh, denied that after the resurrection they would again exist in a frail body, but said that they would be like angels, or would be precisely what angels are? You accuse women of saying these things with such ridicule, though they are produced from writings in those select Commentaries of yours.

Does this not seem to you like the case of someone accusing another of theft while concealing in his own bosom the very theft of which he accuses the other? After he has argued at length, magnificently inveighed against the thief, produced witnesses, and given the oaths required by law, after all this the theft itself—for [Note: [Col. 0577D] The manuscript reads “the theft itself from his bosom, for which … he had thought”; [Col. 0578D] shortly afterward it omits two words, “about such matters.”] which he thought he had already convicted another—is drawn from his own bosom.

Then [Col. 0578B] you accuse others because, when questioned about such matters, they do not answer promptly or immediately, but hesitate and act more by nodding than by words. Yet [Note: [Col. 0578D] The same manuscript reads “and he himself”; then it has more: “Paul hints at something of this kind to prudent readers.” Conversely, in the following period it omits the two words “but hints”; finally, it orders the text differently: “the Apostle did not state it openly.” I pass over its many errors below.] you yourself say of the Apostle that he hints at something of this kind in his Epistle to prudent readers.

If Paul does not indicate but hints, and not to all persons but to prudent ones, why do you mock us, unhappy people—O our penitent friend—when we say that if the Apostle did not openly state something, we either do not know it or doubt it, and understand it not so much explicitly as implicitly, and therefore do not so much indicate it as hint at it? Now, if those things have been revealed to you which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor entered the heart of man; if that which is perfect has come to you and those things which are partial have been destroyed for you, [Note: [Col. 0578D] The manuscript reads, “if it has now come to him,” etc.] cry out and preach them. What you say the Apostle only hinted at, you yourself declare—you who now condemn not only things which he hinted at, but also things which you write that he confirmed. For, while expounding the Apostle’s words, you had asserted all the things which you now command to be anathematized and taught that they were included in his meaning.

### 40

347. What else is there that he commands others to condemn? “They say,” he says, “that this body is the prison and chains of the soul, and they maintain that the soul does not go, but returns, as it were, to the places where [Note: [Col. 0578D] The Guarnerian manuscript reads, “where it had previously already been”; shortly afterward, “From those Commentaries there.”] it had previously been.”

Let us therefore produce testimonies concerning how he himself understood this matter. From these very Commentaries, book two, from the chapter where he says, “For this reason I, Paul, am the prisoner of Jesus Christ” (Eph. 3), shortly afterward:

> “Because in many places this body is said to be the chain of the soul, in which [Al. by which] it is held as though shut up in prison, we say that Paul is restrained by bodily [Al. of the body] bonds and cannot return to be with Christ, so that the preaching among the Gentiles through him may be completed.” [Col. 0578D]

Again, on the same matter, from the same Commentaries, book three, in the chapter where [Col. 0579A] he says, “For which I discharge an embassy in chains” (Eph. 6), shortly afterward, again through that person of his—or through another who is himself—he says:

> “Another person, however, will contend [Al. contends] that he said this because of the body of humiliation, and these chains with which we are surrounded, and because we do not yet know as we ought to know, and see through a mirror in an enigma; and that then he can truly disclose the mysteries with confidence in the Gospel, when he has laid down the chain and come free out of prison. [Note: [Col. 0579D] The same manuscript adds “this,” then wrongly reads “is surrounded,” “we do not yet know,” etc. See the Commentary itself.] Unless perhaps even one in chains is to be counted as being without chains, because he has his citizenship in heaven; and of him it may be said: ‘But you are not in [Note: [Col. 0579D] Neither the Guarnerian manuscript, nor Jerome’s Commentary, nor the Apostle’s sacred text itself has the words “in prison”; but all agree in preferring: “But you are not in the flesh”: *Ὑμεῖς δὲ οὐκ ἐστὲ ἐν σαρκί*. Yet, when we considered deleting those words, that did not seem reason enough, since other Rufinian manuscripts, as well as the course and context of the sentence itself, oppose it. Shortly afterward the Guarnerian manuscript has “from the Epistle” for “of the Epistle.”] prison, nor in the flesh, but in the spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you’ (Rom. 8:9).”

Again, on the same matter, from the Commentary on Paul’s Epistle to Philemon, in the chapter where he says, “Epaphras, [Col. 0579B] my fellow captive, greets you” (Philem. 23), shortly afterward:

> “Unless perhaps he reveals [Al. is revealed] something hidden and sacred, as some think, in the word ‘captivity’: that those captured together and bound together were led down into this valley of tears.”

### 41

You see how he says that these matters are reckoned mystical and sacred among certain persons, though we have often shown that he himself is one of them—348 yet he uses the figure in order to seem to avoid the odium of mystical knowledge.

“These things,” he says, “you will see [Al. you will see, plural] how they stand.”

Can you say that I declared that all things are to be restored into one condition and one body, not only human beings but demons and fallen angels also? [Note: [Col. 0579D] The Guarnerian manuscript reads “produce,” and through a copyist’s carelessness wrongly omits the following three lines. It also makes certain errors above, which make no difference to your understanding.]

“Let no wrong be done me,” he says, “if what I said in another person’s role [Col. 0579C] belongs to another; but if you read something said from that point onward and written without any intervening person, that must rightly be ascribed to me.”

Why then do we pour out all these efforts over which we labored above? Such is the force of shamelessness. But come: let us concede even this, not in order that the matter itself may be established, but that he may be convicted as he demands.

From these Commentaries, book two, concerning the matter which I proposed [Al. proposed], under the chapter where it is written, “Eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace: one body and one Spirit, just as you were called in the one hope of your calling” (Eph. 4:3–4), shortly afterward:

> “The question arises,” he says, “how there can be one hope of calling when there are diverse dwellings with the Father. To this we reply that the one hope of calling is the kingdom of heaven, as though it were [Note: [Col. 0580D] This is also the reading of the cited manuscript and the commonly printed Rufinian books. In Jerome’s Commentary, even in the manuscript, the less satisfactory reading is “as though one good thing.” Below likewise the less satisfactory readings there are “we are made in the present,” “we are re-formed,” and “is fulfilled”; the Guarnerian manuscript also prefers these, as it also reads “are” for “may be.”] one house of God the Father, [Col. 0579D] and in one house there are many dwellings. ‘One is the glory of the sun, another the glory of the moon, another the glory of the stars’ (1 Cor. 15:41). Or certainly this more subtle point is indicated: [Col. 0580A] that at the end and consummation of things all things are to be restored to their former condition, when we all become one body, are re-formed into one perfect man, and the Savior’s prayer is fulfilled in us: ‘Father, grant that, as you and I are one, so they also may be one in [Al. omits “in”] us’ (John 7:21 [the printed citation; the quotation is John 17:21]).”

### 42

You have received this further unambiguous statement of his view concerning the resurrection of all; receive another, and then I shall conclude the first volume of our *Apology*. For his statements about such matters are innumerable.

Again, from the same book, under the chapter where it is written, “From whom the whole body, joined and knit together through every joint 349 of supply, according to the working in the measure of each member, makes [Col. 0580B] the body grow for the edification of itself in love” (Eph. 4:16), he begins:

> “At the end of things, when we have begun to see God face to face and have attained the measure [Note: [Col. 0580D] The Guarnerian manuscript omits “of stature”; then, for “we all” the Commentary now reads “all.” The Guarnerian text further reads: “that he may not be in us in part, but wholly; and, leaving behind the vices of childhood, we may grow into that man of whom,” etc. In what follows, however, it makes a more serious error.] of the stature of the fullness of Christ, from whose fullness we have all received (John 1), so that Christ is not in us in part but wholly, and, leaving behind the rudiments of childhood, we have grown into that man of whom the Prophet says, ‘Behold the man; Dawn is his name’ (Zech. 6:12), and John the Baptist recalls, ‘After me comes [Al. will come] a man who has been made before me’ (John 1:30), because he was before me: then, in the meeting of one faith and one recognition of the Son of God—whom, because of the diversity of minds, we do not now know by one and the same faith and recognition [Al. by faith and recognition]—the whole body, which had formerly been scattered [Al. will have been scattered] and [Col. 0580C] torn in different directions, will be brought back into its own framework and articulation. Thus one supply, one and the same operation, and the completed perfection of one stature [Note: [Col. 0580D] Again the Guarnerian manuscript omits “stature.” Shortly afterward, from the same source and from the Commentary, we read “grows” for “will grow.”] will make the entire body grow equally, and all members will receive the increase of stature according to their own measure. This whole building, by which the body of the Church increases part by part, will be completed through mutual love.

> “Let us understand all rational creatures by the example of one rational living being; and whatever we say of this being’s members and parts, let us know [Al. omits “let us know”] that it is to be referred to every rational creature. Let us suppose this animal to be so [Al. omits “so”] torn apart in limbs, veins, and flesh that bone does not adhere to bone, nor nerve join nerve; that eyes lie separately, nostrils apart, hands occupy another place, feet are thrown into another [Al. another] place, [Col. 0580D] 350 and the remaining members are in this manner scattered and divided among themselves.

> “Let us imagine [Col. 0581A] [Al. Imagine] someone coming, a physician of such knowledge that, according to the tales of the pagans, he can imitate Asclepius and raise up a new form and a new man, Virbius. [Note: [Col. 0581C] Perhaps the truer reading of the Commentaries is: ‘and raise him into a new form and a new name, Virbius’; that is, Hippolytus, whom Asclepius restored to the upper world after he had been torn apart by frightened horses. Ovid reports that his name was changed by him, in *Metamorphoses* XV:

> “And he commands him to lay aside the name  
> which could recall the horses; and says:  
> ‘You who were Hippolytus, now be Virbius.’”

> [Col. 0581D] Yet the printed reading “a new man” is not itself unsuitable.] He will necessarily have to restore each member to its own place, join framework to framework, and by some adhesive, after restoring the parts, make one body.

> “So far one comparison has carried us. Now, in the same comparison [Al. the same comparison], let another example be drawn toward what we wish to understand. A little child grows [Al. may grow] and, in an unseen course of time, comes to perfect maturity [Al. may come to maturity]. The hands have [Al. will have and feel] their own growth; the feet feel their own increase; the belly is filled while we do not know it; the shoulders expand while the eyes are deceived; [Col. 0581B] and all members grow separately according to their own measure, yet in such a way that they seem to grow not for themselves but for the body. [Note: [Col. 0581D] The Guarnerian manuscript reads “so that now they seem not to grow for themselves.” Compare Jerome’s *Apology* I, 26, where he shows that these words are spoken from Origen’s meaning, not his own, and excuses himself thus: “We compressed into brief speech Origen’s very extensive exposition, which turns over the same meanings in different words, omitting none of his examples and assertions. And when we reached the end, we added this: ‘Therefore also in the restoration of all things,’ etc. See also the Commentary itself.]

> “Therefore also in the restoration of all things, when the true physician Jesus Christ comes to heal the body of the whole Church, now scattered and torn apart, each person, according to the measure of faith and recognition of the Son of God—who is said to recognize him for this reason, [Note: [Col. 0581D] The earlier text wrongly read “who had known before.” Shortly afterward the Guarnerian manuscript has “ceases” for “ceased.”] because he had known him before and afterward ceased to know him—will receive his own place and begin to be what he had been. Yet this will occur not according to another [Note: [Col. 0581D] By this qualification the holy Doctor had barred the way to calumny and had displayed his thoroughly Catholic meaning. “When,” he says in the cited book, “I say, ‘yet not according to another HERESY, in which all are placed at one age,’ I show that the things I am discussing are heretical and differ from another heresy.” What are the two heresies? One says that all rational creatures are re-formed into angels; the other asserts that, in the restoration of the world, each thing will be what it was created.] heresy, in which all are set at one age—that is, all are re-formed into angels—but so that each member may be perfect according to its own measure and office. [Note: [Col. 0582C] The pronoun “its own” was absent; we supplied it from the manuscript and the Commentary [Col. 0582D].] For example, so that the fallen angel may begin to be what it was created to be, and the human being expelled from paradise may be restored again to the cultivation of paradise. [Col. 0581C]

> “But all these things 351 will take place [Note: [Col. 0582D] The Guarnerian manuscript reads “may take place,” which accords better with the following reading of the Commentary, “and mutually.” Shortly afterward the same manuscript reads “Paul” for “in another place.”] in such a way that they are united with one another in love; and while member rejoices with member and delights in another’s advancement, the body of Christ, the Church of the firstborn, will dwell in the heavenly Jerusalem, which the Apostle elsewhere calls the mother of the saints.”

### 43.

All Latins read these statements of yours [Note: The Guarnerian manuscript’s scribe generally adds this.]—statements which you now also command them to read, where you say that all rational creatures, understood under the example of one rational animal, are to be restored into one body, just as if the severed limbs of one man were repaired by the art of Asclepius into the solidity of that same body. In this body, indeed, you define different future functions, as is proper to limbs, but you call it one body, that is, of one nature [Note: Conversely, the same manuscript here omits the words “that is, of one nature”; shortly afterward it reads “his own member” for “one member.”]; and this one body of all you call the primitive Church and name the body of Christ. You say that one member of this body, to be restored to its own function, is the apostate angel, who is certainly the devil, and is to be repaired into what he was created at the beginning. Likewise, you say that man, another member, is to be recalled as an original inhabitant to the cultivation of paradise [Note: Elsewhere, and also in Martian’s text, *Origenian*, which is not approved. “Original inhabitant” means that Origen says man was first placed in paradise to cultivate it. Likewise, shortly below: “let him be restored as he was at the beginning,” so that man is recalled to paradise and the apostate angel is exalted—in heaven, of course.].

And you pursue these claims without, as is customary when such matters are discussed cautiously and gradually, inserting the persona of another so that someone might suppose you to have been uncertain about matters so secret and hidden, as this Origen is always found to do [Note: Significantly, the Guarnerian manuscript adds even the particle *vel* (“perhaps”): “and perhaps you doubted,” etc.; it then reads *existimaret* (“might suppose”) for *existimet* (“may suppose”).]—although you do not deny that you are his disciple and confess that you are his betrayer. Rather, with an abrupt and definitive assertion, as though an angel were speaking in Daniel or Christ in Paul, you proclaim to mortal ears the secrets of future ages.

And you say:

“Believe none of the ancients, the faithful people chosen by Christ. If this Origen suspected anything concerning the more hidden matters of God’s dispensation, let no one accept it.” [Note: The same Guarnerian manuscript also omits “Clement,” although Clement is mentioned immediately afterward; it likewise improperly omits the word “teacher.”]

And if Clement—whether that disciple of the Apostles or that man of the Alexandrian Church, and Origen’s own teacher—said something of this kind; even if that Gregory of Pontus, a man of apostolic virtues, said it; even if this other Gregory of Nazianzus and Didymus the seer-prophet said it—both my teachers, than whom the world possessed no one wiser in the faith of Christ—all these erred as Origen did. But let them receive pardon for their error, since I too once erred and now do penance, and therefore ought to receive pardon. Origen, however, although he said the same things as I did, even if he has done penance [Alternative: “even if he should do penance”], will not receive pardon; indeed, for the things we all said, let him alone be condemned.

He is the one who did all the harm. For he disclosed to us the source of everything we say, everything we write, and everything for which we are thought learned [Note: The same manuscript reads “whatever we are thought learned to have said”; it then has *fecimus* (“we made”) for *facimus* (“we make”)]; and he is the reason that we turn Greek good things into bad Latin ones. Therefore let no one listen to any of these men, but accept only what you find in my Commentaries, especially in my Epistle to the Ephesians, where I refuted Origen’s statements with the utmost vigor.

I, however, have investigated the matter so that you ought to believe and hold that the resurrection of the flesh will occur in such a way that bodies will be changed into souls and wives will be transformed into men; that souls existed in the heavens before the foundation of the world and were brought down from there, for causes known only to God, into this valley of tears; and that they were inserted into the body of death [Note: The same manuscript has a fuller and more correct reading: “that they were inserted into this body of humiliation and into the body of death.” Shortly afterward it reads “he will be restored” rather than “he will be restored”; the rest is less correctly transmitted there.].

And that at the end of the ages every rational nature will be restored into one body as it was at the beginning, so that man too will be recalled to paradise and the apostate angel exalted above Peter and Paul. They, being human, are to be placed below him; but he is to be restored to what he was created at the beginning, so that all together may become the primitive Church in the heavens and, while each retains his own particular functions, may be members of Christ. The totality of all, however, will be Christ’s perfect body.

Holding these things, therefore, O faithful and prudent disciples, and guarding these my indisputable definitions [Note: The same manuscript prefixes the emphatic Greek adverb *ἐμφατικώτερον* (“more emphatically”): “and yet Origen …”], while nevertheless condemning Origen for these very statements, you will act well. Farewell.

### 44.

You see that you conduct the entire matter in mockery and say that you repent in order to deceive those to whom you write. For even if you truly repent, as you ought [Alternative: “as you ought to have done”], what will you do on account of all those souls whom this doctrine of yours—so poisonous, as you yourself say—has deceived for so many years?

Finally, who will ever be corrected through your repentance, when this very little book, in which you are at once penitent, accuser, and judge, sends your hearers back again to read and hold these same doctrines? And even if these things were not so, you yourself have nevertheless closed every avenue of pardon to yourself even after your repentance.

For you say that Origen himself repented of these statements in the Little Book of Repentance addressed to Fabian, then bishop of Rome; yet after his repentance, a hundred and fifty years after his death, you hale him into court and summon him to condemnation. How, then, will pardon be granted to you as a penitent, if the man who repented before you of these things does not deserve pardon?

As you wrote, so he wrote; as you repented, so he repented. Either you must be absolved alike on account of repentance, or, if you deny pardon to a penitent—which I do not desire [Alternative: “which I do not ask”], though you insist upon it—we must likewise be condemned according to a certain Gospel parable:

“An adulterous woman was brought before the Lord by the Jews, so that they might see what judgment he would pronounce concerning her according to the Law. The merciful and compassionate Lord said, ‘Let whoever among you is without sin cast a stone at her’ (John 8:3). And then, it says, they all departed.” [Note: The Guarnerian manuscript reads: “The merciful and compassionate Lord …”]

The Jews, although impious and unbelieving, nevertheless blushed at their consciences, lest, being sinners themselves, they should appear to take vengeance upon sinners.

And that thief on the cross said to the other thief who was hanging beside him and blaspheming: “Do you not even fear God, since we are under the same punishment?” (Luke 23:40).

When we condemn in others the very things that exist in us, we neither blush with the Jews nor show mercy with the thief. [Note: Improperly omitting the scriptural wording, the Guarnerian manuscript reads: “When we too condemn in others the same things …”]

## BOOK TWO [Note: The Guarnerian manuscript reads: “Here begins happily the second book of Rufinus’s Controversies.” See what we said at the beginning of the preceding book.]

### 1.

In the preceding little book, with him himself as witness, we turned back upon him the dogmatic objections that he unjustly brings against others [Note: The same manuscript reads: “as a witness against yourself”; some other books formerly had “against himself.”]. Now, with these excuses—which are close to matters of faith—brought to an end and cast behind us [Note: Both the Guarnerian manuscript and the old edition read “excuses,” which gives the more coherent sense; other printed editions had “precautions.” Shortly afterward, for “accusations,” the same manuscript reads “charges,” while the old edition reads “conclusions.”], we shall answer him more confidently concerning the remaining accusations.

For there is also this especially serious point in his accusation, which, like his other lies, must be cut away with the sickle of truth. He says that certain people are bound by an oath with Origen, and that the secret of this mystical tradition of his is hidden in the sixth book of the *Stromata*, and that throughout all the centuries it was detected by no one except himself [Note: Formerly, as also in the Guarnerian manuscript, “through so many centuries”; then the manuscript reads “unless it was reproved by him.”].

But, so that I may not provoke his laughter if I affirm that I am a stranger to the oath, I shall proceed by a clearer path from the alleged conspiracy of perjury to the manifestation of the truth, on the basis of what I can most easily prove: that I never possessed those books, nor read them when lent by anyone else. [Note: The manuscript omits *vel* (“or”); conversely, it adds: “or handed down by someone other than him,” namely the man whom Rufinus attacks so often in the preceding book and whom he maintains was no one other than Jerome himself. Three lines later it also adds: “unless he is the nearest,” perhaps more correctly.] And just as I cannot excuse myself concerning something whose nature I do not know, so neither can I be accused concerning something of which, even if it exists, I am completely ignorant.

Yet this man, who alleges either that the statement was handed down by Origen or that it was spoken by his disciples—that “the one who speaks the truth with his neighbor” (Psalm 14:2) is not a neighbor unless he is perfect and an initiate—also adduces what the Apostle says: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (1 Corinthians 2:6); and what is written: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast your pearls before swine” (Matthew 7:6) [Note: The manuscript again omits “cast.”], claiming through this that truth is not to be disclosed to everyone.

### 2.

Let us see what he himself writes in these very select commentaries of his [Note: Here the manuscript omits “his.”], in the second book, under the chapter where it is written: “Therefore, putting away falsehood, speak the truth, each one with his neighbor, because we are members of one another” (Ephesians 4:25).

A little later he says:

“Therefore Paul himself, being perfect, spoke in another Epistle: ‘We speak wisdom among the perfect’ (1 Corinthians 2:6). This, then, is what he commands: that each person speak with his neighbor whatever is mystical and secret, whatever is full of God’s truth, so that ‘day may pour forth the word to day, and night may declare knowledge to night’ (Psalm 18) [Note: This commentary reads “commands”; then the manuscript, three lines later, has “and day to day, and night to night,” omitting “may pour forth the word.”], that is, so that everything bright and shining may be disclosed to those who deserve to hear: ‘You are the light of the world’ (Matthew 5:14).

“But let him report things dark, obscure, and veiled by every night of sacred mysteries to others—or to these [Alternative: “to them”]—who themselves are night, darkness, or gloom [Note: The manuscript reads *fuerat* (“had been”) and, in the Psalm text that follows, “Cloud and darkness …”]. Of them it is said: ‘And gloom was beneath his feet’ (Psalm 17:10), undoubtedly referring to God. For on Mount Sinai Moses also enters into the whirlwind and gloom where God was (Exodus 19). And concerning God himself it is written: ‘He made darkness his hiding place’ (Psalm 17:12). [Note: Earlier printed editions inserted the name “God,” which neither the manuscript nor any other books contain.]

“Let each person therefore speak truth and mysteries with his neighbor, and let him not give what is holy to dogs or cast pearls before swine; but whoever possesses the oil of truth, let him bring them [Alternative: “it”] into the bridegroom’s chamber and the king’s storehouse.”

See, I ask you, and examine more carefully whether in all that he writes he condemns anyone other than himself and his own statements. If his enemies wished to tear him apart and charge him on the basis of his writings, what other procedure, what other arguments against him would they use except those with which he himself argues against himself as though against others?

If a condemnation is to be pronounced against this man, his own Epistle is sufficient: if only you change the name, the text of the accusations applies to no one else at all as it applies to him alone. The things he orders to be condemned, he orders to be observed again [Note: The manuscript has the words “these he again orders to be observed,” then omits “does”; the sense is not unsuitable or gaping, but is not complete.]; the things he does, he reproves; the things he detests, he practices. Blessed are his disciples, who either listen to him or imitate him.

### 3.

Nevertheless, since his doctrine of perjury is being brought forward [Alternative: “put first”], it makes no difference to me whether this man acts or writes, because he has also tried to brand us with this stain among certain brothers and now repeats it in letters, according to the rule he himself gave [Note: Omitting “also,” the manuscript reads *injicere* (“to cast upon”) for *inurere* (“to brand”); it then incorrectly has “now again to repeat,” followed by “given by himself,” and finally “of himself again” for “of himself to himself.”]. I shall state what I myself think about perjury, so that I may once again leave judgment concerning himself to himself.

For since our Lord and Savior says in the Gospels: “It was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not swear falsely, for you shall repay your oaths to the Lord’; but I say to you, do not swear at all” (Matthew 5:34), I say that anyone who teaches that one must swear falsely for any reason whatsoever is alien to the faith of Christ and to the unity of the Catholic Church [Alternative: “is alien,” rather than “is.”].

### 4.

But now, after I have satisfied, as I determined, the charge of anathema against me [Note: The old edition reads: “after I have satisfied the anathema against me, as he himself determined.” The Guarnerian manuscript has the worse reading: “after I have satisfied the middle,” followed by several minor corruptions that need not be pursued.], I should like, if you receive it patiently, to labor a little and disclose what adherents and fellow-initiates this man has for the perjury which he says is observed through certain orgies and mystical confederacies [Alternative: “of the confederacy”].

For that saying of God is certain and entirely true: “You will know them by their fruits” (Matthew 7:16); and again: “A tree is known by its fruits” (Luke 6:44). Accordingly, as this man says, we have accepted the doctrine of perjury [Note: The manuscript reads: “we have begun that man’s doctrine of perjury …”]. If we have been instructed for this purpose, and if such a tree has been planted in us, it cannot be that some such fruits have not often sprouted from us, indeed that they have not grown together by the authority of the mystical doctrine [Alternative: “would not have grown together”].

As far as my own person is concerned—the only one whom he thinks he is attacking in all that he writes—I shall not testify on my own behalf, nor shall I say that one must also swear when necessity demands it. Even if I am not cautious, I certainly desire to be fearful. Finally, even if I cannot observe the rule, let me know that I have erred [Alternative: “let them know that I have erred.”] [Note: I pass over the more evident corruptions.]

I shall not say these things. Nevertheless, whether I err in them or take precautions, this man has no case for which to accuse me in such matters [Alternative: “will have no case.”] I shall prove again from his writings, however, how sacred to him is the observance not of this doctrine but of the foulest and most genuine vice.

I shall produce nothing against him fabricated out of spite and envy, as he does against us. I shall produce himself as witness against himself, together with his writings, so that he may know that he is charged not by enemies but refuted by himself.

### 5.

While he was living at Rome, he wrote a little book on preserving virginity. All the Pagans and enemies of God, apostates and persecutors, and all who hate the Christian name, copied this book eagerly for themselves [Note: The same manuscript omits “apostates,” and, three lines later, “all.”], because in it he branded the entire order of Christians, every rank and profession, and the Church as a whole with the foulest reproaches. Things which the Gentiles were falsely thought to charge against us, he asserted to be true—indeed, to be practiced by our people in much worse forms than those of which the Gentiles accused us.

First he defames the very virgins about whose virtue he appears to be writing, and speaks of them in these words:

“Some, changing their clothing to a man’s dress, are ashamed to be women, though that is what they were born to be; they cut off their hair and shamelessly lift up eunuch-like faces. There are women who clothe themselves in hair shirts and, wearing skillfully made hoods so as to return to infancy, imitate owls and horned owls.”

He says a thousand other, still graver insults about them. Nor does he spare widows. For he says of them:

“They have no concern except for the belly and the things nearest the belly.”

He adds many other obscene remarks. It would take too long to prove from his own words and writings how foully and shamefully he tears apart every kind of monk.

As for deacons and presbyters, I am ashamed to rehearse the disgraces he has described concerning them. I shall nevertheless give the beginning of his attack, from which it may more easily be inferred [Alternative: “you may more easily infer”] how greatly his invective increases in what follows:

“There are others,” he says—I am speaking of men of my own order [Alternative: “of my own names”—probably a textual corruption]—“who seek the presbyterate and diaconate for the purpose of looking at women more freely [Alternative: “approaching women more freely”]. Their only concern is their clothing: whether they smell good, whether their foot protrudes from a loose shoe. Their hair curls in the traces of the curling iron; their fingers shine with rings; and, lest a damp road soil the soles of their feet, they scarcely set down the tips of their feet. When you see such men, you would think them bridegrooms rather than clerics.”

And after he had specifically reproached priests and ministers not merely for vices but for crimes, and had made even their entering and greeting matrons not only disgraceful but execrable, how can he spare himself after tearing apart and disgracing the entire Christian order? Listen.

### 6.

I return, after a certain digression, to the matter I had proposed, for which the circumstances of this little book required me to mention it. I shall show that this man regards perjuries as so permissible that he is not ashamed to be caught practicing them in his own writings.

In this very little book, therefore, when he warned that secular books ought not to be read and said:

“What will Horace do with the Psalter, Maro with the Gospels, Cicero with the Apostle [Alternative: “the Apostles”]? Will a brother not be scandalized if he sees you reclining in an idol’s shrine?”

—and after saying other things of this sort by which he asserted that the reading of secular books is foreign to a Christian—he also inserts a certain divine revelation granted to him, full of sufficiently terrifying commands [Note: Up to this point the printed text had “honorable commands.” On the basis of the Guarnerian manuscript, “terrifying commands” has been restored, which is more accurate and more appropriate. The same correction occurs at the beginning of the following passage.].

For he reports that, after he had renounced the world and turned to God, he nevertheless remained very strongly attached to secular books and could not easily be free of that desire:

“And because of this,” he says, “I was suddenly carried away in spirit and dragged before the tribunal of the Judge. There was so much light there, and such brilliance from the splendor of those standing around, that, thrown upon the ground, I did not dare to look upward. Asked about my condition [Alternative: “about my status”], I replied that I was a Christian. But he who presided said: ‘You are lying. You are a Ciceronian, not a Christian; where your treasure is, there your heart is also.’

“Immediately I became speechless, and amid the blows—for he had already ordered me to be beaten [Alternative: ‘whether he had ordered me to be beaten’]—I was tortured more by the fire of conscience. Nevertheless I began to cry out and, lamenting, say: ‘Have mercy on me, Lord, have mercy on me.’ This cry resounded amid the scourging.

“At last those who stood nearby fell at the knees of the presiding judge [Alternative: ‘those who had stood nearby’] and begged him to grant pardon to my youth and allow room for repentance concerning my error, intending thereafter to exact punishment if I should ever again read books of Gentile literature [Note: The Guarnerian manuscript omits “of literature.”].

“I, being so tightly pressed by the crisis and willing even to promise greater things, began to swear solemnly and, invoking his name, say: ‘Lord, if I ever possess secular books, or if I read them, I have denied you.’ Having spoken these words, I was released, he says, and returned to the upper world.” [Note: The manuscript here omits the small word “or.” For comparison, see Saint Jerome, *Apology III*, section 32, where he rejects this charge of perjury and professes that he swore only in a dream.]

### 7.

You have heard how novel and how terrifying a kind of oath he describes [Note: Here too “terrifying” has been restored on the authority of the Guarnerian manuscript in place of “honorable,” which earlier printed books appear to have transmitted incorrectly and with an inadequate sense. See also the preceding note.].

With the Lord Jesus Christ seated in judgment [Note: The manuscript omits the words “the Lord Jesus Christ”; conversely, it adds, “placed amid words and torments, he swears …”], with angels standing by and interceding for him, amid blows and torments he swears that he will never possess or read secular books. Let us now reread, I ask, what he writes. Is there a single page of his work that does not once again pronounce him a Ciceronian, or where he does not say: “our Tullius,” “our Flaccus,” “our Maro”?

Indeed, he scatters before his readers the names of Chrysippus, Aristides, Empedocles, and many other Greek authors, as though to appear learned and widely read, like smoke and mist. Finally, among other things, he even boasts that he has read the books of Pythagoras, which learned men assert do not even exist.

But, so that he might not omit any part of his oath concerning the authors of the Gentiles, he also writes that he has read works which were never written. In nearly all his little works he places far more and longer testimonies from these authors of his than from our Prophets or Apostles [Note: On the basis of the Guarnerian manuscript, “in nearly all his little works” has been restored; earlier this had been postponed and read “far more and longer testimonies in nearly all his little works.” The same manuscript also omits the second pronoun “his.”].

Writing even to girls and women—who certainly both wish and ought to be built up only by our Scriptures—he inserts examples from his own Flaccus, Tullius, and Maro.

### 8.

But in that little book which he entitled *On the Best Kind of Interpretation*, where, apart from the title’s notation, nothing is good but everything is worst—for there he asserts that those with whom he now communicates are heretics [Note: This evidently refers to John, bishop of Jerusalem, and his presbyters, with whom he had made peace.] and thereby incurs the saying of our Apostle, not his—for he calls his own Apostle either “his Flaccus” or “his Tullius,” who says: “But whoever doubts is condemned if he eats” (Romans 14:23)—in that little book, then, where reason allows no method of translating word for word, a method which has now again seemed reasonable to him [Note: The Guarnerian manuscript inserts “as he asserts”; later it reads “how once again to him,” apparently alluding to Jerome’s recent Latin translation of the book *On First Principles*, which Jerome had prepared and opposed to him.], he inserted entire chapters dictated from a manuscript of Cicero.

Did he not himself say:

“What will Horace do with the Psalter, Maro with the Gospels, Cicero with the Apostle [Alternative: “the Apostles”]? Will a brother not be scandalized if he sees you reclining in an idol’s shrine?”

In this he plainly makes himself guilty of idolatry. For if someone who sees a person reading such material is scandalized, much more will someone be scandalized who sees him writing it.

But since the man who falls into idolatry does not become wholly and completely profane unless he has first denied Christ, he himself says to Christ, visibly seated before him in judgment, with the illustrious ministries of angels also standing by:

“If I read or possess books of the Gentiles, I have denied you.”

And now he not only reads and possesses them, not only copies and acquires them, but also inserts them into divine words and discourses intended for the Church’s edification. The matter of which I speak is sufficiently known to everyone who reads his little books and requires no witness.

Yet, wishing to rescue himself from so sacrilegious an abyss of perjury, the man supplies himself with some excuse and says:

“I do not now read them; rather, because I have a tenacious memory, I bring forward what I learned in my youth, so that I can reproduce entire passages from different authors at once.”

If someone demanded that I prove that today, before the sun rose, there had been night upon the earth, or that daylight had illumined the world until sunset, what else would I say except that the person who doubted what everyone knew should be asked to explain the grounds of his doubt rather than demand proof from me?

But in this matter, although everyone knows that what we say is true [Note: The manuscript lacks the words “what we say.”] and everyone understands it, because the matter concerns the human soul, the crime of perjury, and the sacrilege of denying Christ, condemnation cannot be treated as easy.

Shall we imitate the man who condemns the accused without questioning them or hearing their response—not only those who do not respond, but those who are not even present; not only those who are absent, but also the dead; not only the dead, but those whom he had always previously praised; and not only those whom he had praised, but those whom he had followed and regarded as teachers? [Note: The negating particle formerly lacking has been restored from the manuscript: “not only the dead, but also those whom he had always previously praised”; the manuscript continues: “and not only those whom he had praised, but those whom he had followed,” etc.]

Let the Lord’s judgment be feared, first the one that says: “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged” (Matthew 7:1) [Note: The manuscript adds: “and you will not be judged”; shortly afterward it reads: “the same measure will be measured back to you,” etc.]; and again: “With the measure with which you have measured, it will be measured back to you” (Luke 6:38).

What, then? Although it is superfluous, I shall nevertheless produce one especially powerful witness against him, one against whom he cannot prescribe or impose any objection [Alternative: “cannot prescribe against”]. I shall again produce himself and his own writings.

Although all his little books bear witness to this, and my assertion about it may seem superfluous, some particular testimony must nevertheless be used, lest what we say appear insufficiently complete to those who perhaps have not read his writings.

### 9.
