When someone had reproved the little books he wrote against Jovinianus [Note: Not only the older printed books but also the Guarnerian manuscript read “had reproved,” as though Rufinus himself said that he had reproved those books. Shortly afterward the manuscript reads: “he who had possessed knowledge of everything.” Obvious errors are passed over.], namely Domnio, an old man of blessed memory who had reported this very matter to him, he replied in his defense and said that it was in no way possible for him to have erred, being a man who possessed knowledge of everything.

After he had listed either the forms of syllogisms or the arts of learning and writing—things which, evidently, the man who reproved him did not know—he immediately added:

“Fool that I was, thinking that I could not know this without the philosophers, when I had chosen the better part of style, the part that erases rather than the part that writes. In vain, then, did I translate the Commentaries of Alexander; in vain did my learned teacher introduce me to Logic through Porphyry’s *Introduction* (*εἰσαγωγή*, *isagōgē*). And, to leave human matters aside, without cause did I have Gregory of Nazianzus and Didymus as my instructors in the Scriptures (*κατηχησταί*, *katēchēstai* [Alternative: *εἰσαγηταί*, *eisagētai*, “introducers”]).”

This is the man who said to Christ: “I have denied you if I have ever possessed or read books of the Gentiles.” If nothing else, he ought to have kept silent about Porphyry, who is a particular enemy of Christ and who, insofar as he could, attempted completely to overturn the Christian religion by his writings—yet this man now boasts that Porphyry was his introducer and instructor in Logic.

Nor can he argue that he learned these things before that time. Before he was converted, he was as ignorant as I was of both Greek letters and the Greek language. All this occurred after the oath, after the pledge of the sworn sacrament.

We argue in vain. Immediately he will say to us: “You are mistaken, man. God is not mocked” (Galatians 6:7). Nor are syllogisms from Alexander’s Commentaries being inserted into his work [Note: The manuscript omits “among him”; it reads “are inserted” rather than “are being inserted.” Shortly afterward it has “Porphyry introduced you,” rather than “the faithless man”; then: “if you are at that place where he himself is, there also are weeping,” etc. “There” should certainly be read for the formerly printed “to you.”].

As I see it, brother, you have made a bad beginning by choosing Porphyry as your introducer. Where did that faithless man introduce you? To the place where he himself is? There are weeping and gnashing of teeth there. For there, perhaps, apostates, enemies of God, and perjurers also dwell.

### 10.

You did not choose a good introducer. Rather, if you accept my advice, let us turn together to that introducer who introduces us to the Father, who said: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 1) [Note: The manuscript reads: “No one goes to the Father”; shortly afterward it has “old parchments.” With it we then read “inexpiable sacrilege,” rather than the previously printed and less appropriate “inexplicable”; several other corruptions occurring below are passed over.].

I grieve, brother, if you believe; and if you do not believe, I grieve that you investigate suspicions of another’s perjury in ancient and very old parchments, while an unending and inexpiable sacrilege of perjury persists continually and without end in your own mouth.

Would it not rightly be said to you what the Apostle says?

“But if you are called a Jew, and rest upon the Law, and boast in God, instructed through the Law, confident that you are a guide of the blind, a light to those who are in darkness, an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of infants, possessing the form of knowledge and truth in the Law” (Romans 2:17) [Note: The Guarnerian manuscript reads “you boast in the Law of the Lord.” It then adds the continuation of the Apostle’s text, which is absent here in both the printed and manuscript books: “and you know his will and approve what is more excellent.” Shortly afterward the manuscript again reads “confiding” rather than “you confide.” The Pauline text adds: “and you know his will and approve what is more excellent,” which may have dropped out of this passage.].

“You who teach another, do you not teach yourself? You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who proclaim [Alternative: “say”] that one must not steal, do you steal? You who abhor idols, do you commit the sacrilege of perjury? And, what is last and most serious, God’s divine majesty is blasphemed among the Gentiles through you and your contentiousness (*φιληνεικία*, *philēneikia*) [Alternative: “your lust for disputation”].”

### 8.

But let us now pass from here to the cleansing of the other charge, if indeed, with his conscience also pressing him, he admits that he has been convicted of both perjury and betrayal of trust. Otherwise, if he denies it, I can produce very many brothers as witnesses who, while staying in my cells on the Mount of Olives, copied for him very many of Cicero’s *Dialogues*. I frequently held their quires in my hands while they were writing them, and I learned that he paid them much more generous wages than he usually paid for other writings.

Nor can he in any way deny that, when he once came from Bethlehem to Jerusalem, bringing with him a codex containing one of Cicero’s Dialogues [Note: The word “one” was missing. It was probably the *Protagoras*, a dialogue of Plato translated into Latin by Cicero. If only it had survived, together with Rufinus’s entire accusation!], and the same work in Greek by Plato, he gave that codex to me and that it remained with me for some time.

But why do I linger so long over a matter clearer than daylight? To all the things we have said above must also be added the fact that, while living in the monastery at Bethlehem, not long before then [Note: The Guarnerian manuscript reads “for a considerable time afterward”; shortly below, “in order to learn,” and “namely, so that he might teach,” etc. We do not pause over the many obvious errors.], he practiced the work of a grammarian and explained to the boys entrusted to him for learning the fear of God his own Maro, as well as Comic, Lyric, and Historical authors—so that he might become a teacher of the Gentile authors, even though he had sworn that if he merely read them he would deny Christ.

### 9

But let us see what else he still finds fault with. He says that these doctrines belong to the pagans: see by what judgment he condemns himself. He says that doctrines are pagan which he himself [Col. 0592B] sets down in writing. He is mistaken; but a hand must be extended to him, and he must not be pressed too harshly. For while he is wholly carried away in eloquence and swept along by reproaches and attacks, he forgets himself and slips away from reason. Do not, brother, rashly condemn yourself even in matters that are unnecessary. You must not immediately be reckoned among the pagans, either you or Origen, if—as you yourself said—wishing to defend God’s justice and to answer those who say that everything is moved either by fate or by chance, and wishing to show that God’s providence, which governs all things, is just, you said that the causes of inequality had been acquired by each soul for itself from the movements and perceptions it had possessed in an earlier life in the heavenly realm; or even if you said that it accords with the good, unchangeable, and simple nature of the Trinity that, at the end of all things, it restore all its creation to what it was created as in the beginning, and that, after punishments prolonged and equalized through the intervals of ages—punishments which God inflicts upon each person not so much in anger as with a healing purpose [Col. 0592D]—since he is free from the fault of failing to admonish, he should at some point establish an end to punishments in the capacity of one who heals and cares for the sick. How true these things are, God will see; nevertheless, they do not seem to me to contain much impiety toward God, nor anything pagan—especially if you say them with this intention, wishing by whatever means to defend God’s justice.

[Note: The same manuscript, though corruptly, reads: “but alas, the hand must be corrected; I am not to be pressed.” The reading should be: “a hand must be extended; he is not to be pressed too harshly.” The brother is silent shortly afterward.]

[Note: The Guarnerian manuscript is again defective, though it is transcribed in such a way that it yields “he inflicts upon each person commotion,” since it lacks this fault, rather than “admonition.” I would prefer *commotionis* to be corrected to *commonitionis* (“admonition”).]

### 10

Therefore do not distress yourself excessively over these matters, nor needlessly subject yourself either to penitence or to condemnation. But there is one matter for which we truly cannot defend or excuse you: it is demonstrated that you said something not merely in a pagan manner, but beyond all paganism—even impiously—in that very little work, the Letter to Eustochium (Letter 22), which we mentioned above: you said that God had a mother-in-law.

And what could any pagan poet have said that was so impious or profane? It would be foolish for me to ask where you read this in the holy Scriptures. I ask whether your Flaccus, or Maro, whether Plautus, or Terence, or certainly whether any satirist, amid all his obscenity and shamelessness, ever uttered this outrage against God from his own mouth. I believe that you were deceived and misled by this circumstance: the girl to whom the word of God was being spoken was called Christ’s bride, and so you thought that her carnal mother ought also to be called God’s mother-in-law.

[Note: The old edition, together with the Guarnerian manuscript, reads “so impure or profane.” Shortly afterward the same manuscript has “by any pagan poet.”]

[Note: In the published texts, the word “Comic” was unnecessarily added here; on the authority of the Guarnerian manuscript we have removed it.]

[Note: Here the Guarnerian manuscript more correctly omits the name “God”; I would prefer that it be deleted.]

You did not know that these expressions are not used according to the order of the flesh, but according to the grace of the spirit. She is called a bride because the word of God is joined to the human soul in a kind of sacred marriage. But if, through such a union, the girl’s mother also is joined to Christ by faith [variant: consecrated], you could more properly have called her Christ’s bride than God’s mother-in-law.

Now it remains for you also to call the girl’s father God’s father-in-law, her sisters his female relatives, and even to declare the girl God’s daughter-in-law. Thus, while you are wholly eager to appear a follower of Plautine and Ciceronian eloquence, you have forgotten how the Apostle calls the entire Church—that is, parents together with children, mother with daughters, brothers together with sisters—all at once a single virgin or bride, saying:

> “But I have betrothed you all to one man, to present a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:2).

But while you boast that you have Porphyry, not Paul, as your introducer, by following Porphyry—who wrote impious and sacrilegious books against Christ and against God—and by being introduced by him, as you say, you have fallen into this abyss of blasphemy.

[Col. 0593A] 365

### 11

[Col. 0594A] 366

But if you truly wish to do penance for your curses; if you are not mocking by saying these things; if you are not so contentious and quarrelsome in spirit—*philóneikos* (φιλόνεικος)—that, for this sole reason, you do not shrink from bringing infamy upon yourself, provided only that you disgrace another; if you have repented of your statements not through cleverness but in sincerity, then do penance for this so grave and shameful blasphemy. [Note: The Guarnerian manuscript has a lacuna here, extending for more than a verse, in place of the two words. The sequence of the argument indicates that somewhat more has fallen out.]

For here you blasphemed against God. For to say something about created things and to err—especially if it is done not from a desire to insult, but, as you say, while wishing to assert God’s justice—is not a very abominable offense, whoever might let it slip. But to direct one’s mouth toward heaven is serious. To speak injustice or insult against the Most High is ruinous. This is what must be mourned, because it is difficult to cure. For who, when suffering from jaundice and endangered in head, face, and life, would cry out loudly that it was not a minor *paronychion* (παρωνύχιον), an inflammation of the toe, or a very slight injury to his fingernail, that needed treatment?

[Note: The manuscript has more: “it is insulting and pernicious.”]

[Note: In the manuscript the word is written in Latin letters as *paranithitum*, incorrectly.]

### 12

But the following matter is of little importance indeed and scarcely worthy of a reply. In listing his teachers, whom he says he had acquired from the synagogue, and in goading us, he adds: “For I did not teach myself,” he says, evidently looking at us, against whom he directed the entire force of his assault from the beginning.

[Note: Thus the manuscript; previously the reading *mercatos* (“acquired”) was less satisfactorily printed.]

[Note: The manuscript reads: “he did not wish to say this.”]

And I am surprised that he wished to say this, since he had a greater and more genuine basis for slandering me: namely, that although I spent a long time among many distinguished teachers, I possess nothing worthy either of them or of their instruction. Yet this man, who in the whole course of his life did not remain in Alexandria, where Didymus was, for a full thirty days, boasts far and wide throughout almost all his little books that he was the disciple of Didymus the Blind, and that he had Didymus as his *kathēgētēs* (καθηγητής), that is, as his teacher, in the holy Scriptures.

[Note: The words “that is, as his teacher,” which were added in the printed texts, are absent from the manuscript; on both its authority and because they appeared wholly to proceed from a hand other than Rufinus’s, we have removed them.]

All this boasting was acquired in a single month.

I, who spent six years there for the sake of God, and again, after some interval, two further years—where Didymus was, of whom you alone boast,

[Note: This is especially a reading deserving fuller explanation: the Guarnerian manuscript, which we have restored, reads “again, after some interval, two further years,” whereas the printed books had “after some interval, on other days.” The account therefore differs considerably from the commonly received opinion, and it matters whether Rufinus remained at Alexandria for two years or merely a few days when he returned. In brief, the manuscript reading alone appears true. Why would the author have mentioned a few days on his second arrival and wished them counted when he had already said that he spent a full six years there on the first occasion, to which such a slight and scarcely noticeable addition of days would contribute nothing? Moreover, he says “other,” a pronoun plainly referring to what precedes; above he named years, not days. Had he intended days rather than years, he would not have added “other,” but would simply have written “a few days.” This is manifest evidence that he wrote not “a few,” but “some”—namely, an interval—to which the pronoun itself must refer. For it is inappropriate to speak simply of an interval without any indication of its duration, especially here, which is alien to Rufinus’s manner when narrating his own affairs. As to the history: although later writers on Rufinus, including Fontanini in his Life, deceived by the received reading, reckon only those few days, nothing conflicts with earlier accounts or is difficult to reconcile with their testimony. It is agreed that the author was twice at Alexandria, and scarcely anyone doubts his first residence there from 372 to 377. The second may be inferred from Jerome’s *Apology*, book III: he says that Rufinus was no longer at Alexandria after Theophilus became bishop. Theophilus began his episcopate on 20 July 385. Thus, after an interval of perhaps one or two years—about 379—and before the limit of 385 just mentioned, he came there again and remained two years. The two years might be demonstrated more precisely from Palladius’s testimony in the *Lausiac History*, chapter 10, where he speaks of Melania, Rufinus’s companion, and of Pambo’s death; but the limits of these notes do not permit us to answer the objections of learned critics. It is enough for the present that the sequence of events accords excellently. One further point may be added from the character, so to speak, of the Guarnerian manuscript: since it is mistaken in almost every place where it differs from the received reading, it reveals itself as copied by an unskilled antiquary, who could never have substituted this much more coherent reading on his own unless he had found it in the ancient exemplar he was copying.]

where Didymus was, of whom you alone boast, and where there were others no less distinguished than he, whom you do not even know by sight: Serapion and Menites, men kindred in nature, character, and learning; where there was Paul the old man, a disciple of Peter the Martyr; and, to come to the teachers of the desert, to whom we devoted ourselves both more attentively and more frequently: where there was Macarius, a disciple of Antony, and the other Macarius, and Isidore, and Pambas [variant: Pambos]—all friends of God, who taught us what they themselves had learned from God—what a fund of material for boasting I could possess concerning all these, if it were appropriate or useful to do so!

[Note: The manuscript has “Parrabas,” incorrectly; in the following passages it likewise continually calls Barabbas “Parraban.” Others read “Pambo.”]

But I am ashamed even to recount these things while wishing to show you that, contrary to what you say, it was not our natural ability that made our teachers—but, what grieves me more, that our natural ability was lacking in comparison with our teachers.

But why, foolish man that I am, do I enumerate holy Christian men? He does not say this on account of them, as though we taught ourselves, but because we did not accept his Barabbas as a teacher from the synagogue and were not introduced to Logic through Porphyry’s *eisagōgē* (εἰσαγωγή, “Introduction”).

[Note: Jerome calls him Baranina in Letter 84 and sharply rebukes Rufinus in his *Apology*, as though Rufinus had maliciously corrupted the name in order to arouse odium.]

Forgive me for having preferred to appear unskilled and ignorant rather than to be called a disciple of Barabbas.

[Note: The manuscript reads more correctly, “to be heard as ignorant and unlearned.” The context concerns Christ and Barabbas.]

With Christ and Barabbas set before me together, I, as an unlearned man, chose Christ. You, as I see, join those who say: “Not this man, but Barabbas” (John 18:40).

Now tell me, I ask, what did your Porphyry teach you? He wrote volumes of blasphemy against Christians and against our religion. What good did those men teach you in whom you boast so greatly—one from the idols of demons and the other, as you say, from the synagogue, a teacher of Satan?

[Note: Martianay incorrectly reads: “from the teachers of Satan,” and so forth.]

I see nothing except what they themselves knew. Porphyry taught you to speak evil of Christians, to attack virgins, the celibate, deacons, presbyters, and every rank and order of Christians, and to disgrace them utterly in published writings.

But your Barabbas from the synagogue, chosen instead of Christ, taught you to hope for the resurrection of the flesh not in strength but in weakness; to become a friend of the letter that kills and an enemy of the Spirit that gives life.

There are also other, more secret matters, which, if circumstances require, will later be brought forth at the proper time.

### 13

But why extend the speech at such length? Let us not answer his insults and injuries; let us not confront his attacks, for which Porphyry daily sharpens his pen. For our Jesus, not Barabbas the teacher, taught us to remain silent about this.

Let us come to the point, so that it may be shown how true are the things he wrote either in his own defense or in accusation of us.

He says that there are only two brief prefaces of his in which he appears to have praised Origen; nevertheless, he praised him in that work of interpretation

[Note: The manuscript has *enim* (“for”) in place of *duas* (“two”). It is scarcely credible, both from Jerome’s own meaning and from Rufinus’s charge, that only two of Jerome’s prefaces are said to lie under suspicion of favor toward Origen. Rufinus may not even have written this: either *enim*, as the manuscript has it, must be restored, or the word *duas* must be removed altogether.] in which nothing at all dogmatic was said, nothing concerning the faith, and in which nothing of the kind that he now criticizes, for the favor of the synagogue rather than for the edification of Christians, is introduced into the passages he himself interpreted.

And although it ought to be enough to make him keep silent that he condemns in another’s writings what is brought forth from his own, let us nevertheless see how truthful he was in this matter as well.

From the preface to the interpretations of Origen’s fourteen Homilies, or little Discourses, on Ezekiel, written to a certain Vincentius, he says:

> “It is a great thing, my friend, that you ask me to make Origen Latin and to present to Roman ears a man who, in the judgment of Didymus the Blind, is the second teacher of the Churches after the Apostles.”

And a little later:

> “And, briefly warning you of this also, so that you may know it: Origen’s works on the whole of Scripture are of three kinds. His first works are *excerpta*, which in Greek are called *scholia* (σχόλια). In them he briefly and summarily touched upon those things that seemed obscure to him or that appeared to contain some difficulty. The second is the homiletic (*homilētikón*, ὁμηλιτικόν) genre, of which the present translation also forms part. The third consists of what he himself wrote as *tomoi* (τόμοι), which we may call volumes. In this work he spread all the sails of his intellect to the winds and, leaving the shore, fled into the open sea.

> “I know that you wish me to translate every kind of his expression. I have explained in advance why I could not do so. Nevertheless, I promise this: if, at your prayer, Jesus restores my health, I shall translate not everything—for to say that would be rash—but very much, on the condition that I have often laid down for you: I shall provide the voice, and you the scribe.”

[Note: The Hieronymian text itself has *mi* (“my”) here.]

[Note: The manuscript has one word, *atque*, here. Shortly afterward it prefers “concerning which the present translation is being made”; Jerome’s text reads “and this present translation.”]

[Note: The manuscript presents the Greek words in Latin letters.]

### 14

Likewise, from the preface to the *Song of Songs*:

> “To the most blessed Pope Damasus. Although Origen surpassed everyone in his other books, in the *Song of Songs* he surpassed himself. For after completing eleven volumes, which nearly reach twenty thousand lines of verse, he discussed first the Seventy translators, then Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion, and finally the Fifth Edition, which he writes that he discovered on the shore of Actium, with such magnificence and clarity that it seems to me that in this work was fulfilled the saying: ‘The king brought me into his chamber.’

> “Therefore, setting aside that work—for it requires immense leisure, labor, and expense to transfer such great matters, such a worthy work, into Latin—I have faithfully rather than elegantly translated these two Treatises, which he composed in the manner of daily speech for little children still at the breast. I offer you a taste of his meaning, not the food, so that you may observe how highly those things must be valued which are great, since even small things can please in this way.”

[Col. 0597A] 370

[Note: Elsewhere the reading is “after having explained.” Then, from the manuscripts and from the preface itself, we read *pene perveniunt* (“they nearly reach”), whereas the published texts and the Guarnerian manuscript had only *pervenerunt* (“they reached”).]

[Note: Formerly it was read *Actaeo* (“Actaean”); the Guarnerian manuscript has *Actio*. Shortly afterward we have supplied *vel inde* (“even from this”) from the same preface and manuscripts, and have corrected other minor matters.]

[Note: Jerome’s text has “so worthy a work” (*tamque dignum opus*); a manuscript of the Queen of Sweden has “so worthy things, into Latin.” Here the Guarnerian manuscript may perhaps be more accurate: “so worthily into Latin.”]

### 15

Likewise, from the preface to the Commentary on Micah, written to Paula and Eustochium, after some preliminary remarks:

> “For when they say that I ought not to compile Origen’s volumes and contaminate the writings of the ancients—and they consider this a grave reproach—I regard it as the highest praise, since I wish to imitate those who please all prudent men and us [variant: you].”

### 16

Likewise, from the preface to the interpretation of the Hebrew Names, after some preliminary remarks, he says:

> “But lest, when the building had been completed, it should seem that the finishing touch was lacking, I also interpreted the words and names of the New Testament, wishing in part to imitate Origen, whom no one but an ignorant man denies to have been, after the Apostles [variant: the Apostle], a teacher of the Churches. For among the other splendid monuments of his intellect, he also labored at this: that what Philo had omitted as a Jew, he, as a Christian, might complete.”

[Note: The Guarnerian manuscript has “unless he is ignorant.”]

### 17

Likewise, from the Letter to Marcella:

> “Ambrose, by whose provision of paper, expenses, and scribes our Adamantius and Chalcenterus brought out truly innumerable books, reports in a certain letter In the letter, which he had written to the same man from Athens, he says that he never took food in Origen’s presence without reading, and never went to sleep unless one of the brothers was reciting the holy Scriptures. He did this by day or by night, so that reading might give rise to prayer and prayer to reading.”

[Col. 0598A] 371

[Note: The old edition incorrectly reads “unless Origen was present at the reading.” The Guarnerian manuscript likewise has *in lectione* (“at the reading”) instead of *sine lectione* (“without reading”). It also has shortly afterward “sleep never came,” where one word is missing; finally, it has “so that reading might undertake prayer.”]

### 18

Likewise, from another Letter to Marcella:

> “The blessed martyr Pamphilus, whose life Eusebius, Bishop of Caesarea, set forth in almost three volumes, wishing to rival Demetrius of Phalerum and Pisistratus in the cultivation of the sacred Library, and seeking throughout the whole world the images of intellects, which are true and everlasting monuments, then pursued Origen’s books above all others with the greatest zeal and dedicated them to the Church of Caesarea.

> “Acacius, and afterward Euzoius, who were priests of that same Church, attempted to restore this Library, partly corrupted, on parchment. Although he found many things and left us a catalogue of his discoveries, he confessed that he had not found the Commentary on Psalm 126 and the Treatise on the letter Phi, because he did not enter it [variant: entered it] in his catalogue, confessed that it had not been found. Not because such a great man as Adamantius had passed over anything, but because, through the negligence of later generations, it did not survive down to our memory.”

[Note: From the manuscript and from the text of Jerome’s Letter itself, we have added the word “Bishop,” which was lacking in earlier printed editions.]

[Note: The same manuscript has “then all the more”; the text of the letter has “then especially.” Shortly afterward both books omit “Library.”]

[Note: In the manuscript: “such a great man, Adamantius, surpassed all others”; at the end it has *duravit* (“endured”) rather than *durarit*.]

### 19

But perhaps you will say to me: “Why do you fill the pages with superfluous matter? Does he say that it is a crime to name Origen or to praise his intellect?”

[Note: The manuscript incorrectly inserts *reum* (“guilty”), and shortly afterward has *ejus* (“his”) for *ei* (“to him”). The old edition reads: “but if such a man is said to be praised,” while the manuscript reads: “if he is said to be praised, and a man; all the more if there are passages in which.” It also has “teacher of the Church of God,” as he himself adduces above, or “if,” and so forth.]

If such a great man is praised, all the more so if there are passages in which he is called an apostolic man or a teacher of the Church, as he himself cites above; or if there is anything of the kind that seems to commend not merely his intellect but his faith—then I shall indeed do this.

I have brought these things forward for this reason: when he calls him such a great man, in the little preface in which he says that he is defended as an Apostle or Prophet, or borne up even to heaven, I consider that discourse to be inscribed in praise of him.

And wherever we have perhaps praised his knowledge, all my praises of him are of this kind—praises for which such a fire is kindled against you, although he does not consider it worthy that they be charged to him on the basis of his own writings.

But because he does not deign to treat us as an equal party in judgment, condemning us even on the basis of suspicions, while he himself neither wishes to be bound by his own written documents nor thinks that the judgment of holy Scripture—which commands that judgment be rendered without regard to persons—ought to be observed in his case, let us satisfy him according to his own wishes, not according to equity.

For he says:

> “If you interpreted Origen, you are blameworthy; but if I said the same things for which he is blamed, I acted well, and they ought to be read and retained. If you praised his intellect or knowledge, you are guilty; but if I praised his intellect, there is nothing wrong.”

[Note: The manuscript unnecessarily repeated the pronoun *ejus* (“his”); we have removed it. Conversely, with the support of the same manuscript and the old edition, we have added the adverb *ita* (“thus”), which was missing. Below, the manuscript has *traxeris* (“you may have dragged”) instead of *duxeris* (“you may have led”).]

[Note: The old edition adds *solis* (“alone”), and the manuscript likewise has “from suspicion alone,” in the singular. Shortly afterward both agree on “the observance of Scripture in his case.”]

### 20

“But produce the passage,” he says, “where I praised him in such a way as to excuse his faith.”

Not equally so—but wherever you lead, I shall follow.

In writing a certain little book, he wished, as though in a brief catalogue, to indicate how much Varro had written among the Latins and how much Origen had written in Greek. He says:

> “Antiquity admires Marcus Terentius Varro because he wrote so innumerable a number of books among the Latins. The Greeks exalt Chalcenterus with wondrous praises because he composed so many books that none of us could copy them all by hand, even if they belonged to others.

> “And because it is now tedious to compile among the Latins a catalogue of Greek volumes, I shall recall some things about one who wrote in Latin, so that we may understand that we sleep the sleep of Epimenides, and that the zeal which they devoted to secular learning [Note: The manuscript appears more correctly to read “letters” rather than “writings”] we devote to gathering wealth.

> “Varro therefore wrote forty-five books of *Antiquities* and four on the Life of the Roman People.”

And when he had enumerated individually everything that Varro wrote, he added afterward:

> “You ask why Varro and Chalcenterus have been mentioned—obviously so that we may come to our Adamantius and our Chalcenterus, who labored with such zeal in the study of the holy Scriptures that he rightly received the name Adamantius.

> “Do you wish to know how many monuments of his intellect he left? The following title shows it. He wrote thirteen books on Genesis; two books of Mystical Homilies; Excerpts on Exodus; Excerpts on Leviticus.”

And after much else:

> “Likewise,” he says, “the *Monobiblia*; four books *Peri Archōn* (Περὶ Ἀρχῶν, *On First Principles*); two books on the Resurrection; and two other Dialogues on the Resurrection.”

And when he had enumerated all his little works according to the catalogue, he added and said:

> “Do you see that Greeks and Latins alike have been surpassed by the labor of one man [variant: this man]? For who has ever been able to read as much as he himself wrote? What reward did he receive for this toil?

> “He was condemned by Bishop Demetrius, except for the priests of Palestine, Arabia, Phoenicia, and Achaia; the city of Rome agreed in his condemnation. It itself summoned a Senate against him—not because of novelty of doctrine, not because of heresy, as rabid dogs now pretend against me, but because they could not endure the glory of his eloquence and knowledge, and when he spoke, everyone else seemed mute.

> “You can understand why I have written these things and dictated them in haste, in a brief discourse, by the little flame of a poor man’s lamp, but without caution [Note: The words ‘but not cautiously,’ which occur again below, are absent from the manuscript], if you imagine Epicurus and Aristippus.”

[Col. 0599A] 373

[Note: The manuscript has “our Adamantius and our Chalcenterus, who labored with such zeal in the study of the holy Scriptures.” We have supplied *studio* (“zeal”) from the edition of the Letter itself, since without it the sentence is senseless. It would perhaps be preferable to read: “who labored with such zeal in the study of the holy Scriptures.” Other matters below have also been corrected.]

[Note: The manuscript has *Monobibla*. The titles of the remaining books that follow are omitted, as are the two following verses up to the words “he added.”]

[Note: Previously the Letter’s text also had *pretii* (“price” or “reward”).]

### 21

[Note: The manuscript has “also” for “then”; the old printed editions have “now.”]

If, I ask you, while you were dictating these things by the little flame of a poor man’s lamp, as you say, in hurried but incautious speech, a prophet had stood beside you and cried out:

> “Writer, restrain this voice; check your pen. For a time will come, and not long afterward, when you will create a schism from the Church. And, in order to find some color of excuse for that schism, you will begin to disgrace those books which you now make objects of universal wonder.

> “And this man whom you now call your Chalcenterus and whom you say was named Adamantius on account of the merit of his praiseworthy labor—you will say that he composed not books for the benefit of the soul but poisonous doctrines.

> “This man whom you deny was justly condemned by Demetrius in a matter of faith, and whom you deny was accused on account of novelty of doctrine, you will call accursed because of the novelty of his doctrines. And the things which you now say rabid dogs pretend against him, you yourself will pretend.

> “You will also compel the Roman Senate against him, as you now write, by your admonitory letters, oaths, and bands of followers flying about; and you will repay your Chalcenterus such a return for all his labors.”

Therefore take care not to write these things now, lest, when you have written them and done those things, you be condemned far more truly by your own judgments than he was by the judgments of others.

Do you think you would have believed that prophet saying these things to you? Would you not rather have thought him insane then, just as you would have thought insane anyone who predicted that you would come to these actions?

But this is the quarrel that spares not even friends, provided that it injures enemies. You, however, have gone beyond this: you spare not even yourself, provided that you destroy not enemies but friends.

[Note: The manuscript again omits the word “this.” Shortly afterward it reads, “But you, having gone even beyond this.”]

### 22

Likewise, from the preface to the Hebrew Questions, after much preliminary material:

> “But concerning Origen,” he says, “I am silent. His name, if it is permissible to compare small things with great, is an object of envy because of my own name [variant: more enviously than my own]. Although in his Homilies, which he delivers to the common people, he follows the common edition, in his *Tomoi* he is overcome by the Hebrew Truth [Note: The edition of the preface adds ‘that is, in the fuller discussion’; these words may appear to have been inserted by others], and, surrounded by the ranks of his own forces, sometimes seeks the aid of a foreign language.

> “I say only this: I wish that, together with the envy directed at his name, I also possessed his knowledge of the Scriptures, making light of the images, shadows, and phantoms whose nature, it is said, is to frighten little children and chatter in dark corners.”

But I should no longer be surprised or complain about what he does against me, since he spared neither such men nor men of such stature. For I shall likewise show from his own prefaces how he mangles Ambrose, Bishop of blessed memory, with what figures of speech he tears him apart, and with what accusations he cuts him to pieces—even in those writings in which he nevertheless praises Origen.

[Note: The manuscript reads “in these very writings,” in which he nevertheless praises Origen; it then omits the heading, “Preface to the Homilies on Luke, to Paula and Eustochium.”]

The preface to the Homilies on Luke, addressed to Paula and Eustochium, says:

> “A few days ago you said that you had read certain Commentaries on Matthew and Luke, of which one was dull both in meaning and in words, while the other played with words and dozed in its opinions. Therefore you ask me, after rejecting such trifles, at least to translate the thirty-nine Homilies of our Adamantius on Luke, as they are found in Greek.

> “It is an irksome task, like a torture, to write for another’s stomach, as Tullius says, and not for one’s own. Nevertheless, I shall now do this because you do not ask for more exalted matters.

> “For that which holy Blaesilla once earnestly requested at Rome—that I should render into our language twenty-six volumes of his on Matthew, five others on Luke, and thirty-two on John—you can see is beyond my strength, leisure, and labor. But since your authority and desire have such weight with me, I have set aside for a little while the books of Hebrew Questions, so that, at your command, I might dictate these works, whatever they are—not my own but another’s—during hours gained from other labors.

> “Especially since I hear a raven croaking from the left, and, though he is himself wholly dark, laughing strangely at the colors of all birds. I confess, therefore, before he objects, that in these Treatises Origen plays like a child [variant: on tablets; the editions of the preface mostly read ‘I would play’ rather than ‘to play’]. His other works are manly and serious, worthy of old age. If you wish, and if I am able, if the Lord grants me passage to translate them into Latin, and if I complete the work previously set aside, then you will be able to see—or rather, through you the Roman language will know—how much good it previously did not know and has now begun to learn.”

[Col. 0602A] 376

[Note: The number thirty-nine is absent from the editions of this preface, and they therefore imply that Jerome translated all of Origen’s Homilies on Luke in that work. It is highly probable, however, that many more were written by Origen. The final six, which Jerome translated, do not refer back to the preceding homilies and appear to have been excerpted from a larger number. Origen himself, in volume 3 of his Commentary on Matthew, mentions certain matters written in these Homilies on Luke, none of which is mentioned in those translated by the holy Father.]

[Note: The Guarnerian manuscript likewise has twenty-six. The older editions prefer thirty-six, as do the editions of the preface itself. But both readings are false: there were neither thirty-six nor twenty-six, but only twenty-five volumes on Matthew composed by Origen. Jerome himself is the guarantor of this in the preface to his Commentary on Matthew: “I confess that many years ago I read Origen’s twenty-five volumes on Matthew, and the same number of his Homilies.” Compare what we note in the following section, where the same calculation of the books on Matthew recurs.]

[Note: It was formerly thirty-nine, but incorrectly; some have also read thirty-four.]

[Note: In the Guarnerian manuscript the reading is “unless he is ignorant.”]

[Note: The variant *tabulis* (“on tablets”) also occurs in the manuscript. The editions of the preface almost universally prefer *luderem* (“I would play”) to *ludere* (“to play”).]

23. See what he thinks about Origen and Ambrose [Note: The manuscript of Guarnerius omits the word *sentiat* (“thinks”).]. If he wishes to deny what everyone knows—that he was speaking about Saint Ambrose—he will first be refuted by the fact that among the Latins a Commentary on Luke is attributed exclusively to Ambrose and to no one else. Next, he knows that I possess one of his letters in which, while excusing himself precisely concerning these matters, he turns the suspicion against that man. But because that letter also contains certain more private matters, which for the present I do not wish to make public before the proper time, we shall establish the point further from other matters of the same kind.

Meanwhile, as we said above, he extols Origen’s books to the point of universal admiration [Col. 0602B] and says that “if he translates them, the Roman language will learn how much good it had previously not known and has now begun to know—that is,” he says, “twenty-six books on Matthew, five on Luke, and thirty-two on John” [Note: Here the manuscript of Guarnerius very correctly has XXV, in Roman numerals; the frequently cited old edition likewise gives this only at this point. Indeed, on the authority of these manuscripts it would have been possible to restore the true reading, had they not contradicted themselves at the earlier passage. In any case, it is better to alert the reader than to alter the text.].

These are the works he praises, in which precisely the same things are contained—only at greater length and more fully—as are found in those books *περὶ Ἀρχῶν* (*On First Principles*), for which he censures me. If he promises to translate these works, why does he censure me for similar things? But since we promised to prove how he tears apart Ambrose, a man worthy of every admiration [Al. *of all admiration*], Bishop Ambrose, who was not only a pillar and an impregnable tower of the Church of Milan but of all the Churches, we shall set down one more preface of his own [Note: Here again the same manuscript omits the pronoun *ipsius*, which could improperly be referred to Ambrose. It also omits the name Rome in what follows. I pass over the reading that is manifestly corrupt.], from which you may see either how foully and unworthily he tears apart so great a man, or again how he raises Didymus to heaven with his praises, whom he once more plunges down to the depths of hell [Al. *plunges down*]; or how, concerning the city of Rome, with God’s favor the head of the Christians, he says the things that were said at the time when pagan peoples and persecuting emperors dwelt there.

24. Preface to Paulinianus, *On the Holy Spirit* [Col. 0603A]:

“While I was living in Babylon, and was a tenant of the purple-clad prostitute, and lived under the law of the Quirites, I wanted to chatter a little about the Holy Spirit and to dedicate the little work I had begun to the bishop of that same city [Note: The manuscript has “to dedicate.” Another manuscript of Guarnerius, which appends this Preface of Jerome to the books *On First Principles*, adds: “with the battle of doctrines having been declared against me,” and so forth.]. And behold, that pot which is seen in Jeremiah after the rod began to burn from the face of the North, and the senate of the Pharisees raised its cry, and not a single scribe or Pharisee, but the entire faction of ignorance conspired against me, as though war had been declared against them.

At once, as though by the right of return, I came back to Jerusalem, and after Romulus’ hut and the naked Lupercal [Note: In this Preface, on the agreement of the manuscripts and printed editions, we read *ludorum* (“of the games”). Yet it would not be inappropriate to retain the received reading *nudorum* (“of the naked”). No one is unaware that the Luperci ran naked and that this was the rite of that purification. Of the manuscripts of Guarnerius, one has *ludorum lupercalium*, the other *ludorum lupercalia*.], I looked upon Mary’s lodging and the cave of the Savior.

Therefore, my brother Paulinianus, since the aforementioned bishop Damasus, who had first urged me to undertake this work, has now fallen asleep in the Lord [Note: One manuscript of Guarnerius omits the name Damasus; the other has *jam dormit* (“now sleeps”) instead of *dormivit* (“has fallen asleep”), and *hortatu* (“at the urging”) instead of *oratu* (“by the prayer”).], aided now by your prayers as well as by those of Paula and Eustochium, the venerable handmaids of Christ [Col. 0603B], I murmur here in Judea the song which I could not sing in a foreign land, summoned by you [Note: Martianay, following Erasmus, mistakenly retained *angustiorem* here, contrary to the holy Doctor’s meaning. Both manuscripts of Guarnerius are also corrupt.]. I consider that place much more august which gave birth to the Savior of the world than that which gave birth to a brother’s murderer.

And, to acknowledge the author in the title, I preferred to become the translator of another’s work rather than, as certain people do, adorn myself with borrowed colors like a misshapen little crow [Note: The two manuscripts of Guarnerius omit *quasi* (“as though”).]. I once read someone’s little books on the Holy Spirit, and, in accordance with the comedian Terence’s saying, I saw that from good Greek there had been made not-good Latin. There was nothing dialectical there, nothing manly or forceful that could draw the reader, even against his will, to assent; everything was flaccid, soft, polished, and beautiful, painted here and there with carefully selected colors [Note: The other manuscript of Guarnerius has: “nothing useful, and nothing that draws the reader toward understanding.” Below, both have: “colored with perfumes selected here and there.”].

But my Didymus, having the eye of the bride from the Song of Songs, and possessing those lights which Jesus commands to be raised high over the already whitening harvest [Note: The same manuscript has *in cadentes jam segetes* (“over the grain already falling”).], looks far more deeply from afar and restores to us the ancient custom, so that he is called a Seer—*Prophet*.

Certainly, whoever reads him will recognize and despise the thefts of the Latins, once he begins to draw from the springs rather than the streams. He is unskilled in speech, but not in knowledge, expressing an apostolic man through his very style, as much in the profundity of his thoughts [Note: The other manuscript of Guarnerius has *tam suo nomine* (“in his own designation”). We formerly printed *lumine* (“in the light”) in our edition of this very Preface of Jerome, on the basis of ancient books. Recall, however, what we said there about that reading. Saint Ambrose is not the person whom Jerome mocks under the name “little crow,” as Rufinus maintains; this is easily proved by the fact that the holy Doctor consistently held that most holy Bishop in the highest esteem, repeatedly names him honorably, and praises him. See our notes on that passage.] as in the simplicity of his words.”

25. You have heard how he previously called the man a crow, entirely dark, and now again calls him a little crow, painting himself with borrowed feathers or colors; and how shamefully he tears him apart, saying that the man has nothing manly in him—though he was chosen by God for the glory of Christ’s Churches [Col. 0604A], spoke in the testimonies of the Lord before persecuting kings, and was not put to shame.

Saint Ambrose wrote about the Holy Spirit not only with words but also with his own blood. For he offered his blood to the persecutors, his blood, which he shed in his own person; but God was reserving him for further labors.

Even if he followed the Catholic Greek writers among our own authors and drew something from their writings, it should not immediately have become your chief concern, your labor and study, to translate Didymus’s book on the Holy Spirit for this reason, so that the thefts of a man might be recognized who perhaps was even compelled to write in order to answer the heretics who were then raging.

Is this Christian modesty? Is this how we observe the Apostle’s admonition, which says, “Do nothing through contention or empty glory” (Phil. 2:3)? Then how is it that [Al. *I ask how*], to repeat the same point once more, you who proclaim that one must not steal, yourself steal?

A little earlier, you said that you had been charged with stealing Origen’s statements in your translation of Micah. You did not deny the theft, but you say: “What they consider a grave curse against me, I count the greatest praise, since I wish to imitate him who pleases all prudent people and us [Al. *you*].”

Your thefts provide you with the greatest praise; the thefts of others make them crows and little crows in your eyes. If you rightly imitate Origen, whom you call second after the Apostles, why do you cut down the man who followed Didymus, whom you nevertheless call both a Prophet and an apostolic man?

If, then, you spared neither so great and eminent a man as Ambrose, nor the one whom you write is second after the Apostles and pleasing to all prudent people, and whom in a thousand other writings—not two, as you say—you have raised to heaven with praise, while again you make a heretic of the one whom previously you place before the Apostles; and if you likewise accuse Didymus himself—whom now you designate as the Seer and eye of the bride from the Song of Songs, and as an apostolic man in his thoughts—as a perverse teacher, and with your censor’s mark, as you call it, separate him from the company of heretics: I do not know from whom you received that mark. We know that Peter received the keys once from Christ; who now distributes these censorial marks—or what spirit does so—you may see.

If, I say, you condemn with your own mouth all those whom you praised with your own mouth, why should I, a mere flea, complain about myself if you now tear me apart—me whom you had previously praised in your letters and whom, in your Chronicles, you had joined with Florentius and Bonosus on account of, as you say, nobility of life [Note: For *Florentio*, the manuscript of Guarnerius has *Florentino*. At the year 381, Florentinus, Bonosus, and Rufinus are called distinguished monks.].

26. Nor must that remarkable deed of his be passed over, lest we cause shame to those who hear it [Note: The Hieronymian manuscripts say “daughter,” not “granddaughter.” Yet she could have been called both granddaughter and daughter, since one consul named Marcellinus may have been her grandfather and another her father, as Pontacus notes. In any case, although I am not inclined easily to believe Rufinus, who leaves no accusation against Jerome unused, that notable testimony concerning Melania remains and is found in the manuscript and printed copies of the Chronicle: “Melania, the most noble of Roman women and daughter of the former consul Marcellinus, leaving behind at Rome her only son, then Urban Praetor, sailed to Jerusalem, where by the extraordinary glory of her virtues, especially her humility, she received the name of Thecla.” See, concerning the correct reading of this passage, in addition to our notes on the Chronicle, Rufinus’s *Life*, book and chapter I, no. 5.], namely that he had written in his own Chronicles that the granddaughter of the consul Marcellinus, whom he had described as the foremost woman of Roman nobility, had gone to Jerusalem after leaving her little son at Rome, and that there, on account of the distinction of her virtue, she was called Thecla; afterward he erased this from his copies when he saw that her conduct displeased a woman of stricter discipline.

We are indeed compelled to gather still more from his writings, so that the truth of what he writes here too may be recognized: that in only two brief prefaces of his he mentions Origen, praising in them not his faith but his talent, not the dogmatist but the interpreter.

For the present I have brought forward ten [Note: The old edition has “I have brought forward ten again,” as does the manuscript of Guarnerius.].

27. But lest the discussion become too long and burdensome, let these matters suffice for now—matters in which he praises him as almost an Apostle and almost a teacher of the Churches; and because the Roman order is not moved against him on account of faith or novelty of doctrine, as the rabid dogs now pretend; and because he follows the man who pleases all prudent people and even pleases him, as all those statements inserted in the Preface mentioned above bear witness.

But whatever the truth may be concerning all that you have with these ancient or recent writers—whether you call them Apostles, or call them *venerarii*—men of corrupt faith and conscience [Note: The same reading occurs here: *sive iterum venenarios* (“or again poisoners”); so also in Tertullian, *On Modesty*, chapter V. For *venerarios*, some read *venenarios*; either term denotes men of corrupted faith and conscience. One manuscript of Guarnerius adds the second *iterum* but reads *venerarios*.], whether you call them Prophets or perverse teachers—what does any of this concern me?

For these changes of yours, for your insults and your mutilations of good men, you will rightly do penance, if indeed you do so [Note: The manuscript reads *geris* (“you practice/do”) here and in the following passage; it has *dicas* (“you say”) instead of *dicis*, and *sequantur* (“let them follow”) is corrected; finally it reads “whether you or another is in error,” and so forth.].

Why do you say to me, “If they followed one who was in error, let them follow one who has been corrected”? Away with it; let it be far from me. I have never followed either you or anyone else who was in error, but in the virtue of Christ I will follow neither you nor anyone else except the Catholic Church.

You who wrote such things and followed those whom you believed to have erred, you who have been convicted of writing so unworthily about God—do penance, if indeed you think that the crime of blasphemy can be forgiven you.

27. Can you produce any writings of mine similar to yours, in which you can prove that I erred in my youth? You do not so much confess this as are convicted of it.

I said that I had merely imitated or followed you in the discipline of translation [Note: The manuscript of Guarnerius omits *tamen* (“nevertheless”) and soon after *esse* (“to be”); it reads *videam* (“I may see”) instead of *videram* (“I had seen”).]. Yet I followed you in no other respect, although you claim that you have been wronged in this very matter because I followed what I had seen you do in your Homilies on the Gospel according to Luke: namely, where you had not correctly found in the Greek something concerning the Son of God, you passed it over [Note: The word *ut* (“that/as”) is supplied by the old edition and the manuscript of Guarnerius.], as in the passage: “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior.”

You know that, wherever those things customarily said concerning the soul occurred, you did not pass them over [Al. *would not pass them over*], but wrote them still more clearly, adding certain assertions of your own—as in the passage, “Behold, when the voice of your greeting came to my ears, the infant leapt in my womb,” where you say that “this was not the beginning of his substance,” to which you added from yourself, “nor of his nature” [Note: When we formerly included and revised those Homilies in volume VII of the Hieronymian works, we found not even a trace of this addition. It therefore seemed likely to us that such words had subsequently been removed from the Hieronymian copies in order to avoid hostility. For no one should persuade himself that Rufinus could so confidently have brought this charge against his rival and constructed so shameless a calumny.].

You removed a thousand other similar things in your translations—whether in these very Homilies, or in Jeremiah or Isaiah, and especially in Ezekiel. Concerning the faith, that is, the Trinity, whenever you found in certain passages something different from what you believed, you omitted what seemed objectionable to you.

Both of us followed this method of translation. If someone else were to criticize it, you ought certainly to answer him, since you were the first to do it. Now you yourself criticize the very thing for which you are undoubtedly open to criticism [Note: In the manuscript: “You criticize the same thing … from which you yourself began”; below: “but because they contributed less to the faith,” and so forth.].

You previously declared that translating word for word was both foolish and malicious. In this I followed you. Do you wish me to repent of this because you have now changed your opinion and say that you translated word for word?

If some things contributed less to the faith, you removed them—but you removed them in such a way that you did not cut them all out, nor remove everything in every case. Finally, in the Homilies on Isaiah [Note: In the recension of the Hieronymian works contained in volume IV, we denied that this Latin translation of the Homilies on Isaiah belonged to Jerome, and argued the matter at length in the Preface. At that time, however, Rufinus’s lucid testimony escaped us, for he quotes this very passage and these words from that version and offers it as an example. Yet since the words cannot be found where they ought to occur—namely, in the context of the Homily entitled “On the Vision of God and the Seraphim”—it may perhaps have seemed to us that Rufinus was quoting them from memory and in that sense, not *κατὰ λέξιν* (*kata lexin*, “word for word”), from a Hieronymian manuscript. Now, however, since we have noticed that the very same words are read in an unfamiliar place, namely Homily I in our edition, column 1105 (Patrologia, volume XXIV, column 905), shortly after the middle, we seem to have lost the case and can no longer leave room for doubt that Jerome prepared that translation. Yet the holy Father himself is silent about it in the *Catalogue*, where he nevertheless lists individually the other Homilies—on Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Luke—which he translated from Origen’s Greek. Either, then, Rufinus allowed himself to be deceived and is mistaken in having taken another’s offspring for a Hieronymian work; or, what seems much closer to the truth, the holy Doctor himself rejected it because it had perhaps not yet been sufficiently worked over and was not worthy of being called his offspring. At any rate, he did not wish it to be counted among his works. See our Preface to volume IV.], you referred the Vision of God to the Son and the Holy Spirit [Col. 0607A].

Thus you translated it, adding from yourself what would draw the author’s meaning toward a gentler interpretation. For you say:

“Which are these two Seraphim? My Lord Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit” [Note: Elsewhere, *Qui sunt* (“Who are they”); the manuscript has “Because these two themselves …,” and so forth. The old edition has: “Because these two Seraphim are the Lord Jesus Christ,” and so forth. In the edition of the Homily by Genebrard and in our own edition, the name Christ is omitted. In the line following, *deserere* (“to abandon”) is read instead of *dissidere* (“to differ”). Recall the immediately preceding note and the genuine explanation of this passage by the holy Father in Letter XVIII to Damasus, and so forth.].

And you added from yourself: “Nor should you think that the nature of the Trinity differs because the functions of the names are preserved.”

I too did many things of this kind [Note: The manuscript reads: “But I cut out such things, or …”], either cutting them away or directing them toward a sounder understanding. For these things you order me to do penance. I do not think that you really mean this. But if neither you nor I need repent of these things, for what other matters do you invite me to penance?

28. None of my writings survive in which some error of mine needs correction. Many of yours survive which, as I see, must now all be condemned according to your own judgment [Note: The same manuscript omits *nunc* (“now”) and reads *damnata sunt* (“have been condemned”) instead of *damnanda* (“must be condemned”), and so forth.].

You had reserved for yourself your Commentaries on the Epistle to the Ephesians, in which you thought you had produced something more carefully corrected. You yourself [perhaps: there] saw how similar in every respect they were found to be to Origen’s ideas—or rather, how they contained even something more than what you demand should be condemned.

And unless you had already shut off from yourself the possibility of doing penance for these works by saying, “Read through my Commentaries on the Epistle to the Ephesians, and from them you will recognize how I opposed Origen’s doctrines,” perhaps you would wish to repent of these also and condemn yourself in them, just as in the others.

Nevertheless, as far as I am concerned, I grant you permission to repent even of these. Indeed, if you do penance, you do well to repent not only of everything you have said but also of everything you are going to say. For it is certain that everything you have written is subject to repentance.

But if someone thinks that I should be blamed here for having translated anything from Origen, if this is blameworthy, I am the last person implicated in this work, and the blame must begin with those who came first [Note: He said in his *Apology to Anastasius*, no. 7: “If those who acted before the command are blamed, let the blame begin with the first.” And immediately beforehand: “If it is commanded that something not be done, the command is ordinarily observed thereafter.”].

Yet no one punishes a deed which, before it was committed [Al. *before it was undertaken*], he had not previously forbidden. It was permitted, and we did it. If the law forbids something, it is ordinarily observed thereafter.

But someone says that the books should be condemned along with their author [Note: Earlier: *damnare* (“to condemn”). A little farther on the manuscript reads: “It will receive a similar and identical judgment.” I neither wish nor press this point.]. What, then, shall we do about this author, who writes the same things, as I have shown at greatest length above?

Let him receive a similar and identical judgment. I neither ask this nor press it, although he acts hostilely toward me. But, as I see, by rashly condemning others he brings this upon himself.

29. But, to speak with you once more from your own words, you yourself write in these Invectives of yours (Epistle 84) that by my translation I have shown that I am a Catholic, whereas Origen, whom I translated, is a heretic. For you say: “This is what it means to say: I am indeed a Catholic, but the man whom I translate is a heretic.”

You say, then, that I have read this [Note: The manuscript of Guarnerius adds: “and otherwise: ‘I have read this, as you say. If in my entire work I have shown this …’”]. If, as you say, I have shown throughout my entire work that I am a Catholic and Origen is a heretic, what more is sought? Are you not doing everything necessary to have him called a heretic and me a Catholic?

If you testify that I said this and that I dealt with it sufficiently throughout my work, what ground for accusation remains to you? What did this Invective of yours against us accomplish [Note: The same, together with the old edition, has “this whole Invective of yours.”]?

If I showed that Origen is a heretic and that I am a Catholic, did I act rightly or not? If rightly, why do you summon me to blame and accusation for what was rightly done? If it is not right to call Origen a heretic, why do you prosecute me under that name?

What need was there for you to interpret more maliciously what had been translated according to your own method of translating, even if in a less polished style? What need was there, certainly, to mock your hearers—to make them think you were doing one thing while you were doing another?

They think you are acting against those who defend Origen as a Catholic; yet you are accusing and indicting those who have designated him a heretic. Is this why you were inviting me to penance? I had not understood.

Nevertheless, know that I do not repent even of this: that I say not everything found in his books should be accepted as Catholic. Whether those things are his, as you say, or were inserted by others, as we think, God will judge. For our part, whenever the summit of faith and truth is reached, we reject them.

You, however, say what you demand from us. Do you want us to call Origen a heretic? You blame us for having done this [Note: We have removed the negative particle here for a more coherent sense; neither the old edition nor the manuscript of Guarnerius recognizes it.]. But do you want us to call him Catholic? You accuse us on that account. State more clearly what you want—if indeed you can find some middle position between these alternatives that you want.

These are all your clever sallies, gathered from the acumen of Alexander, Porphyry, and Aristotle himself. This is all that boasting by which you proclaim that from youth to old age you have been occupied in the schools and disciplines of grammarians, rhetoricians, and philosophers: so that you might go on to pronounce Origen a heretic and, in that very speech in which you passed sentence against him, accuse the man whom you asserted had designated him a heretic.

See that nowhere is there concern for truth or faith, nowhere contemplation of religion or judgment; there is only a lust for speaking evil and tearing brothers apart, only human contention on the tongue, only envy and spite in the mind. Indeed, when you had no cause for hatred [Al. *when no hatred was present], you received with indignation the fact that I called you brother and colleague, even though I did so with praise.

Forgive me: I did not know that you were called ἀκατονόμαστος (*akatonomastos*, “unnameable”) and were named “unaddressable.” Yet I am amazed that you ask me to condemn those things which you complain were pointed out by me.

30. As for that part of his accusation, it seems superfluous even to answer it, where he wishes the pious and religious statements of the martyr Pamphilus either to be called false or, even if true, decrees that they should be disregarded [Note: The manuscript has “it may seem,” and shortly afterward: “where you decide that statements of piety and religion, even if true, are to be despised.” Whom does this man now honor, and whom does he spare?]. Whom, then, will he honor? Whom will he spare?

All the ancient Greek ecclesiastical writers have erred in his view. How he disparages the Latins, how he attacks each one, whether ancient or recent, is evident to anyone who reads and examines his little works.

But now not even martyrs can possess any reverence in his eyes. “I do not believe,” he says, “that it is the martyr’s work” [Al. *that it belongs to the martyr*].

If we wished to say this about all the little books of writers, what proof would remain for any of them? If I say, “It is not true, because the books of the *Stromata* which you claim are Origen’s are his,” how are they proved to be his? “By their similarity to the others,” he says.

But just as someone who wishes to forge something in another’s writing imitates his hand, so whoever wishes to insert his own statements under another’s name will undoubtedly imitate the style of the person whose name he has assumed.

Then, to pass over for the sake of brevity all the things that could most justly be said: if you were so bold as to attack a martyr, you ought to have brought forward the very statements that seemed objectionable to you. Then each reader would have seen what in them was absurd, what consistent, what unjust, and what certainly contrary to the Apostolic rules [Note: In the same manuscript: “but nevertheless,” though not yet satisfactorily. The following context would almost be more correct if *vel* (“or”) were read instead of *sed* (“but”). A little later, the old edition has *interpretatis* (“translated”) instead of *impietatis* (“impiety”).]—but merely some unspecified impiety for expiating which, as you say, the martyr shed his blood.

If he himself read those words, he would then say—not according to your judgment but according to his own—either that the martyr had erred or that an absurd and impious composition had been produced by someone else under the martyr’s name.

But now, knowing that if the passages you criticize are read, the accusation will rebound upon the one who unjustly censures them, you do not produce the things you criticize. Instead, with your censorial mark and arrogant authority, you decree: “Let this man be barred from the libraries; let that man be admitted.” And again, this very man who is admitted today, if someone other than me praises him tomorrow, is to be expelled, together with the person who praised him [Note: The manuscript has “he will be expelled; then the one who praises him.” A little later it reads “even if he seems to have erred in some respects” instead of “even if he has sometimes erred,” and so forth.].

This man is to be regarded as Catholic, even if he sometimes appears to have erred; that man is to receive no pardon for error, even if he says what I have said. No one is to translate him or read him, lest anyone recognize my thefts.

“This man is a heretic, but he is my teacher. And this man, even if he is a Jew and hired from the synagogue of Satan to sell words for a price, is nevertheless my teacher and is to be preferred to everyone, because among them alone the truth of the Scriptures remains.”

If the entire Church had imposed such authority upon you collectively and required you to judge each person or everyone, ought you not to have excused yourself from the burden lest it be placed upon you, since it was so serious and dangerous?

But now, through our daily practice of disparaging others, we have advanced so far that we spare not even martyrs.

Let us suppose that this little book does not belong to a martyr but to some other member of the Church. Did that writer use his own words in such a way that one must yield to the author’s merits [Note: Again the manuscript has “one must believe the merits” instead of “one must yield,” which is almost certainly the better reading. A little later it has “even with defensive words” instead of “with the defender’s words,” and so forth.]?

He gives examples from Origen’s own volumes and shows what he thinks about each passage—not in the words of his defender but in the words of the man who was being accused. And just as the writings against you are now much more vehement in my words than yours, so that man is defended not by the authority of an apologist but by his own statements.

Therefore, where the defense is such that it needs no advocate, the question of the author is superfluous.

31. But now we must come to that most wicked and most invidious head of his accusation—or rather, not invidious but itself envious [Note: This passage of words—“or rather, not spiteful but envious”—is absent from the manuscript. It seems to have entered the text from a note written in the margin of the book.].

For he says: “Who among the prudent, or who among the saints, wished to undertake translating into Latin what you dared to do? I myself,” he says, “though often asked by many, did not do it” [Note: The manuscript omits the adverb *saepe* (“often”). We regularly pass over such minor matters.].

There is an easy excuse for why the saints did not do this. For not everyone who is a Latin saint and prudent person necessarily possesses sufficient knowledge of the Greek language. Nor is the holiness of someone who lacks knowledge of a foreign language thereby diminished.

Again, if someone possesses knowledge of Greek, it does not necessarily follow that he also has the desire to translate. Or even if he has that desire, one who has translated little should not immediately be interrogated as to why he did not translate more, or why this rather than that.

There is freedom in work of this kind, both in the writer’s discretion and in the desire of the person making the request. Yet he speaks of Saint Hilary and Saint Victorinus: of the former, I believe that he translated absolutely nothing from the Greek under the title of translator; of the latter, he himself says that Victorinus used the knowledge of a certain presbyter Heliodorus, so that what Heliodorus drew for himself from the Greek sources, Victorinus rendered in Latin because he himself knew little or no Greek [Note: Here the manuscript also omits *aut* (“or”); it has *cur hoc* (“why this”) instead of *cur haec* (“why these things”); and in the following line it adds: “you are certainly very much to be wondered at.”].

There is therefore an easy and evident excuse for why those men did not do this. It is you, rather, whose conduct is astonishing. What could be more audacious, or what more reckless, than translating these books of Origen, when you had already written almost their entire contents in other books—when you had already set forth all the statements you now call objectionable in a work bearing your own name?

32. Or was it so that you might now alter the books of the divine Scriptures, which the Apostles handed down to the Churches of Christ as the fullest instrument of the faith [Col. 0611B], by means of a new interpretation changed by the Jews?

Which of these two matters seems more unlawful to you? For Origen’s statements—whether they please you as human statements may please one, or displease you as the false statements of a human being may easily be disregarded [Note: The manuscript is shorter: “For Origen’s statements, whether they please or displease, as human statements they are easily disregarded.” A little later it has: “You send them through towns and villages; how shall we receive them as divine? What shall we do with writings bearing the names of prophets … as though they were truer than what the Apostles approved?”]—are one thing.

But these works which you now translate and send through Churches and monasteries, through towns and villages: how are we to receive them—as divine or as human? And what are we to do when you assert that the writings bearing the names of Prophets or Lawgivers are more true than those which the Apostles approved?

Tell me, how will this offense be corrected—or rather, how will this sacrilege [Al. addition: *this*] be expiated? If, when explaining the Law, to have understood something differently is judged blameworthy by you, how many times must it be judged blameworthy to pervert the Law itself into something other than what the Apostles handed down?

Why should we not say, in view of the rashness of this undertaking: “Who among all those prudent and holy men who lived before you dared to lay a hand upon this work? Who presumed to violate the sacred utterances of the Holy Spirit and the divine Volumes? Who besides you has laid hands upon the divine gift and the inheritance of the Apostles?”

### 33

And indeed, since it is reported that from the beginning there was a very large number in the Churches of God, and especially at Jerusalem, of those who had believed from the circumcision—among whom, as is certainly probable, the perfect knowledge of both languages and a competent familiarity with the Law are attested by the office of the episcopate exercised by them—who among this multitude of learned men dared to compile the divine Instrument which the Apostles delivered to the Churches and entrusted as the deposit of the Holy Spirit? Or is it not compilation when certain things are changed and error is said to be corrected? For the whole story of Susanna, which offered the Churches of God an example of chastity, has been cut away by this man, cast aside, and rejected. The hymn of the Three Children, which is sung above all on solemn days in the Church [or Churches] of God, has by him been completely erased [or rubbed away] from its place. And why should I recall one by one the things whose number I cannot encompass?

[Note: The manuscript inserts “so great.”]

To say nothing of the fact that the one and harmonious utterance of the seventy-two men translating separately in their cells—an utterance which there is no doubt was produced by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit—ought to possess greater authority than what was translated by one man, with his own Barabbas inspiring him.

[Note: The older edition reads “approved” instead of “produced.” Concerning the rejected story of Susanna, the hymn of the Three Children, and the other matters, Saint Jerome professes in *Apology*, Book II, no. 33, that he was not stating his own view but explaining what the Jews are accustomed to say against us. He very justly refutes the fable of the cells in six hundred places, which there is no room to indicate here. Nevertheless, he never detracts from the authenticity or authority of the Septuagint; rather, he denies that it was divinely inspired and certainly shows it to have been corrupted by numerous errors.]

[Note: The Guarnerian manuscript omits the word “that”; the other discrepancies below, where the text often differs, are scribal errors.]

But, to leave this aside, consider what we are saying, for example. Peter presided over the Roman Church for twenty-four years. There can be no doubt that, just as he transmitted the other things pertaining to instruction, so too he himself handed over to the Church the books of the Instrument, which were certainly read already then, while he was seated there and teaching. What, then? Did Peter, the Apostle of Christ, deceive the Church and hand it books that were false and contained no truth, while knowing that what was true was held among the Jews and wanting Christians to hold what was false?
