Perhaps he says that Peter was unlettered and indeed knew that the books of the Jews were more genuine than those which were in the Church, but could not interpret them because of his lack of skill in language. And what then? Was that fiery tongue, given from heaven through the Holy Spirit, accomplishing nothing in him? Were the Apostles therefore not speaking in every language?

### 34

But let us grant that the Apostle Peter could not do what this man has now done.

[Note: The Guarnerian manuscript reads “we grant”; then, concerning what he did here, it adds “without measure.” A little later it reads: “If you think anything was lacking to Peter, could he not have supplied it?”]

What shall we say about Paul? Was Paul also unlettered? A Hebrew of Hebrews, a Pharisee according to the Law, educated at the feet of Gamaliel—do you think that even when he himself was at Rome he could not have supplied whatever was lacking to Peter? How, then, did these men, who commanded their disciples to attend to reading, fail to give them corrected and genuine readings? And how did those who command us not to attend to Jewish myths and genealogies, which produce questions rather than edification, and again order us to beware of and keep special watch over those who are of the circumcision, fail to foresee through the Spirit—

[Note: The manuscript adds “through the Holy Spirit,” and shortly afterward “when it had been learned what had been handed down by the Apostles.” Origen, *Letter to Africanus*, no. 4: “It is time, therefore, if these things are not hidden from us, to abolish the copies that circulate in the Church and command the brethren by law that, having rejected the sacred Books they possess, they should persuade the Jews, by flattering them, to furnish us with pure copies containing no fiction,” and so forth. But Saint Jerome very prudently guarded against this objection in *Letter* 106 to Sunnia and Fretela: “We must know what the Hebrew truth contains. For what the Seventy translators translated must be sung because of its antiquity, while the learned must know the other form for the knowledge of the Scriptures.”]

—that after nearly four hundred years there would come a time when the Church, having learned that the truth of the Old Instrument had not been handed down to her by the Apostles, would send envoys to those whom they then called the Circumcision, beseeching and entreating them to give her something of the truth which existed among them?

[Note: The manuscript reads “which is usually there,” and gives “might give” in the singular.]

Would she confess that throughout all those four hundred years she had been in error and ignorant of what was true? That, indeed, she had been taken from the Gentiles as a bride for Christ through the Apostles, but had not been adorned by them with genuine necklaces? That she had thought the stones to be precious, but had now discovered that the gems which the Apostles of Christ had placed upon her were not genuine? That she was ashamed to go out in public adorned with false and counterfeit stones, and therefore begged them to send her even that Barabbas whom she had once rejected in order to marry Christ, so that he might come, together with one chosen man from among them, and restore for her the genuine ornaments which the Apostles had not supplied?

### 35

What wonder, then, if he tears apart me, a very small man of no account; if he cuts up Ambrose, Hilary, Lactantius, and Didymus, and reproves them? I ought not to grieve greatly over the insult to me, since in undertaking once again to interpret my work he has equated me in this insult with the Seventy translators.

But how is the following also to be understood? How much do you think the Gentiles have advanced toward unbelief as a result of this action?

[Note: The manuscript omits the words “as a result of this action.” A little later it reads, “Knowing that our Law has now been corrected,” or “Knowing that our Law has now been corrected.” The older edition likewise reads “now corrected.” After Erasmus, Martianay had incorrectly read “not corrected”; we have restored “now,” as formerly.]

For they are not unaware of what is happening among us. Knowing, then, that our Law has now been corrected or changed, do they not say among themselves: “These people are in error; there is nothing true among them”? “Look: whenever they wish, they correct and amend their laws.” But it is certain that error preceded wherever correction followed, and what is changed by a human being cannot appear divine. This is what your excessive wisdom has achieved for us: that even among the Gentiles we should all be judged fools.

I do not want a wisdom which Peter and Paul did not teach; I do not want a truth which the Apostles did not approve. These are your words: “After four hundred years the simple ears of the Latins ought not to be assailed by the voice of a new doctrine.”

Now you say: “Anyone who thought that Susanna provided married and unmarried women with an example of chastity was in error.”

[Note: The manuscript reads: “Anyone who thought that Susanna provided married and unmarried women with an example, apart from modesty …”]

“It is not true. And everyone who thought that the boy Daniel had been filled with the Holy Spirit and had convicted the adulterous elders was in error; it was not true. And the whole Church throughout the world—whether those who are in the body or those who have gone to the Lord, whether they were holy Confessors or even holy Martyrs—whoever sang the hymn of the Three Children in the Church of the Lord: they all erred and sang falsehoods.”

Now, then, after four hundred years, the truth of the Law comes forth from the Synagogue, purchased at a price. After the world has grown old and all things are being driven toward their end, let us also write upon the tombs of the ancients, so that those who had read otherwise here may know that Jonah had not the shade of a gourd but of ivy; and again, when the legislator wishes it, not of ivy but of another shrub.

[Note: It is commonly found on the tombs of ancient Christians that Jonah sleeping beneath a gourd is represented in relief. This, I think, is what Rufinus means when he says that it should be carved and written otherwise: so that the dead too might be instructed that Jonah rested not under the shade of a gourd but of ivy, as the holy Doctor restored the text. The Guarnerian manuscript incorrectly reads “let us write in the Scriptures.”]

### 36

“But Origen,” he says, “made asterisks, taking material from Theodotion’s translation in order to compose the volumes called the *Hexapla*.”

And why do you parade this Origen, whom you produce for condemnation whenever it pleases you and for imitation whenever it pleases you? It is plausible that you should employ the same man both as defender and as defendant. You may have as the author of your action someone whom you yourself first condemn and whose condemnation you compel the Roman senate to pronounce through your letters. You ought to have foreseen this beforehand.

No one cuts down the tree against which he is preparing to lean; no one appeals in his own case to the credibility of one whose credibility he himself rejects. Whether Origen did this or did not do it, what has that to do with you? If you wish to be judged by his example, reread your own judgments and see what you said. “This,” you say, “is not defending himself but seeking accomplices in crime.” Do not, then, seek accomplices in crime yourself, but demand a defense of the action.

[Note: The older edition reads “defend himself”; shortly afterward it also reads “let him seek” instead of “demand.”]

Nevertheless, let us see what this Origen, defendant and plaintiff at the same time, actually did.

[Note: After Erasmus, Martianay and the author incorrectly printed “defendant” instead of “plaintiff”; the manuscripts and the older edition have “plaintiff,” which we restore, although the manuscript also adds “his,” which is not quite satisfactory.]

I find not even one passage of divine Scripture translated by him from the Hebrews. How, then, can your action and his appear similar?

Apostates and Jews did indeed interpret those passages whose reading the Jews chiefly use. And because, whenever a dispute arose, they frequently falsely claimed either that some things had been altered, or that something was lacking, or that something had been added in our Scriptures, Origen wished to show our people what sort of reading of the Scriptures was maintained among the Jews. In their own pages, or in separate columns, he set out each of their editions individually; and what had been added or removed among them he marked at the beginnings of the verses with certain signs. In another man’s work, not his own, he fixed only his own signs, so that we might know not what was lacking or abundant in our copies, but what appeared to be lacking or abundant to the Jews contending against us.

This was like someone who, having received a small register containing the names of soldiers, sought to discover how many of the soldiers remained and how many had fallen in battle. The man sent to inspect it, finding the name of each dead soldier, would add his own mark—say, the letter Θ, as people commonly say—and would mark the survivor again with another proper sign. Would it appear that the man who placed a mark beside the name of the dead and another mark beside the survivor had done anything to assign the dead man’s case to this one or the living man’s case to that one? No; he merely designated by the marks of his annotation those who had been killed by others.

[Note: The customary letter used in condemnations is the first letter of the name θάνατος, “death,” or of the verb θάνε, used for ἀπέθανεν, “he died.” The Guarnerian manuscript renders theta in Latin letters.]

Thus he too marked with certain signs—namely, the little signs of asterisks and obelisks—those passages which had either been removed by other interpreters or had been given more abundantly by them. Otherwise, he did not insert even one word of his own, nor did he cause the reliability of our copies to waver in anything; rather, he showed that what seemed less clear according to the course of the letter was full of mysteries of spiritual understanding.

[Note: The manuscript, together with the older edition, reads “nor did he make the reliability of our copies …”; shortly afterward it has “plain or lucid,” and so forth.]

What comfort, then, can Origen’s action in this matter provide for you, when you can show no similar work of his, and when you labor so greatly in your own work that “the letter kills” what follows, while he, on the contrary, endeavors to be an advocate of the life-giving Spirit?

[Note: The manuscript omits the words “in this matter.” Rufinus’s statement that Jerome produced no such work is not entirely true: a Psalter with obelisks and asterisks, as well as the Book of Job and certain other works of this kind, still survive, not to mention others that have perished. Shortly afterward the manuscript reads *consequentiam* instead of *consequentem*, perhaps more correctly, though with a different meaning.]

### 37

Your action, then, brother, is your own, and it is certain that you had no one in the Church as companion or associate in this matter—unless it was that one whom you frequently mention, Barabbas.

[Note: The older edition reads, “You, therefore, are the craftsman.” It prefers “you indeed” to “your” at the first occurrence, as does the manuscript. On the authority of the manuscript, in the following verse we have removed the adverb *nunc*, which had been attached to the pronoun and interfered with the proper sense. Shortly afterward the manuscript also seems more correct in reading “of the Church” rather than “in the Church.”]

For who else would dare to violate the Instruments delivered by the Apostles to the Church, except a Jewish spirit? They, my dear brother—those Jews by whom you were captured—hurl you into these evils. They make you inflict marks upon Christians in published books; they make you spare not even the Martyrs and write shameful and abominable things about every rank of Christians, disturb our peace, and generate scandals in the Church. They even compel you to pass judgment against yourself and your own writings, as though you had at some time spoken as a Christian.

[Note: Previously the text incorrectly read “which, as though”; the manuscript restores the correct wording.]

And therefore we all seem filthy to you, while he pleases you excessively by his wicked arts.

[Note: The manuscript omits the second occurrence of “to you.”]

For if you had accepted Paul’s letters, when he says, “If a brother is overtaken in any offense, you who are spiritual should instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness” (Galatians 6:1), how could you have become so inflamed that you observed absolutely none of the order of spiritual instruction?

Suppose that I wrote something insulting; suppose that I injured you, a man of the highest eloquence, my brother and colleague, whom I said should be imitated in the discipline of interpretation. Even so, after that peace which had scarcely been restored through the greatest labor, this was still the first complaint about my injuries to reach you.

[Note: See *Life*, Book I, chapter 4.]

But let us also suppose that injury of yours: that, in imitating you when interpreting Origen, I passed over certain things which seemed to me to contain less edification in the faith. Was I perhaps to be blamed and corrected for this? Writings, as you say, were sent to you by the brethren,

[Note: Formerly the text read “which had been sent to you by the brethren.”]

who demanded that the interpreter’s faults be exposed. What do you, a spiritual man, do? What sort of pattern and example do you offer in such matters and in others like them? You do not merely report your brother’s shame, once exposed, to those outside; you uncover what had been covered.

Suppose that I did this not in imitation of you, but that some drunkenness, creeping in—as it did to the Patriarch—had exposed our shame. Would you have incurred a curse if, walking backward, you had covered our disgrace with the light cloak of your reply, and if the letter of one who was awake had covered what the pen of one who was asleep had laid bare?

[Note: In the manuscript: “having stolen away”; shortly afterward, with the older edition, “you had obtained” instead of “you would have been”; finally, “and if he had covered it” instead of “and if it had covered it.”]

### 38

But I could not reply otherwise to those who had sent me such a letter. Had I not replied as I did, or had I not reinterpreted word for word what you interpreted according to the sense, I too would have seemed to be following Origen.

I will not yet say what that letter was or what sort of letter it was. Nevertheless, since it contains the name of the noble Pammachius, what would have been absurd if you had replied to him with something of this kind? “Brother, one must not rashly judge another man’s work.”

For you yourself know what you did when I sent my little books against Jovinianus to Rome: certain people understood them otherwise than I remembered having dictated them. When they had already been read by many, and almost everyone was offended—including, as you yourself thought, you—did you not withdraw the copies from the marketplace and from public circulation, and send them back, not to someone else but to me, explaining that many seemed to be taking offense? How, then, did I write the *Apology* again, and, as far as I could, bring back to a sounder understanding those passages which had been understood otherwise?

[Note: The older edition reads, “with whom you yourself thought that you were included.” The manuscript reads, “with whom you yourself also thought you were included,” and so forth. Shortly afterward the manuscript reads “they likewise suffered scandal,” explaining how: “Therefore I wrote the *Apology* again.”]

It is therefore fair that we do to others what we want done to us. Just as you sent my books back to me so that I might correct them, so send his back to him, and point out what seems blameworthy, so that he may correct himself if he has erred in anything.

[Note: The manuscript reads, “You moreover”; this may be more correct. It also reads “the first work properly” instead of “the first work nearly”; finally, it has “of derogation” with the older edition instead of “of derogating,” and “to be investigated” instead of “to be demanded.”]

Besides, we have already exercised our talents in many things, and many little works have already been produced through our labor. He has undertaken this work almost as his first, and perhaps under compulsion; it is no wonder if he faltered at the beginning. One must not seek an opportunity to disparage Christians, but the usefulness of correction.

### 39

If you had written these things to him, would you not have offered greater favor and edification—both to him, who at least had begun in the fear of God, and to the other readers—than these Invectives of yours now offer to all who fear God? They see in you the most disgraceful desire to disparage, and in me the pitiable [or remarkable] necessity of replying.

For if, as I said, in the books you wrote against Jovinianus you now find yourself asserting the very things with which you were charging him; if you now fall so far as to affirm that the stains of marriage cannot be washed away even by the blood of martyrdom; and if you readily regard as a correction of yourself the doctrine of the Manichaeans in these books which you had already published and provided to many for copying—what difficulty was there in correcting me, not in my own work but in an interpretation of another man’s work, if something in it had perhaps been suggested not by reason but by spite? Especially since it was still in notebooks which I had not yet reread or fully worked through, and which its discoverers found unpublished?

[Note: The manuscript reads “you will prevent”; then, together with the older edition, “and that thing which,” and so forth.]

Could not what had not yet been corrected easily have been corrected? But he does not attack this part, where he had nothing to blame; instead, the whole work is bitten from the other side, because he feared being exposed through that from which everything he says derives—through which he appears learned and an interpreter of the Scriptures.

### 40

For this reason I explained the cause that led me to interpret, so that he may know that I produced these things not out of contention—as he himself usually acts—or from any rivalry, but out of the necessity which I explained above: that he who was himself fashioning a rough little work from ancient material might receive from it something useful for the construction of a good and beneficial work, whether of arrangement or of color.

[Note: The older edition perhaps more correctly reads “whether of fragrance or of color.” Shortly afterward the Guarnerian manuscript reads “he was nevertheless constructing a work” instead of “a little work,” and so forth.]

Do we not see ancient buildings contributing to new structures? Sometimes a stone is taken from the hidden and concealed parts of an old house to adorn the façade of a new house and decorate its entrance. Sometimes the entire structure of a new building is strengthened by the stability of a single ancient beam.

Let us therefore now act against those who make proper use of old things in new works. “You are not permitted,” they say, “to transfer material from an old house to a new one unless you join beam to beam and stone to stone; unless you transfer portico from portico, limb from limb; and this cannot be done unless you transfer recess from recess and sewer from sewer. A large house must necessarily contain these things too.”

For this is what “transferring word for word” means—something which you formerly judged blameworthy but now judge acceptable.

[Note: The manuscript again reads “praiseworthy,” and also “you defend even things which are not permitted,” while charging us with crimes for things which are permitted.]

But you defend for yourself the permissibility and expediency even of what is not permitted, while charging us with wrongdoing for what is permitted. For when you alter the sacred Letters and divine Volumes, you wish to be praised; but even if, imitating you, we omit something from human speech which we believe contributes less to edification, you grant us no pardon in matters for which you have provided the example.

### 41

Let him conduct himself in these matters as he thinks permitted or expedient. Meanwhile, to review at the end the things which we answered sporadically in our defense, when he said of me that I could not be a heretic without him: I displayed my faith and proved that, concerning the resurrection of the flesh, he himself errs more, since he wrote that the body which is to rise again is fragile.

[Note: The alternative reading is “had written.”]

I also showed how he erased the distinction of sex, saying that bodies would be reduced to souls and women changed into men. I set forth, as I think, entirely just reasons for my interpretation: that I did not transport the riches of ancient material to benefit the buildings of a new construction, moved either by contention [or intention] or by desire for glory, but prompted by the fear of God; and that I wiped clean old weapons already covered with rust, not to start a civil war but to repel an enemy.

I even inserted the very chapter upon which forgers had laid their hands, and showed that the adulteration of blasphemy against the Son of God and the Holy Spirit was foreign to my name but had been committed by their own crime.

### 42

In each of the matters for which he said that he was accusing Origen so that he might appear to be attacking us and defaming our work of translation, I showed from his own Commentaries—of which he had said that his faith ought to be expected and proved—that he himself had written the very things which he blames in Origen: concerning the condition of the soul, the restoration of all things, the devil, and the fallen angels.

I also reproached him for having himself said that souls were bound in this body and held as though in a prison.

[Note: The manuscript reads “are held,” and also: “that there is one body of the whole rational nature,” and so forth.]

I proved that he had written in those same Commentaries that there is one body of the whole rational creation, that is, of angels and souls. I showed that nowhere does the confederacy of perjury appear in such a sacred form as in his writings.

[Note: There is a lacuna in the manuscript. The word *conversari* (“to associate”) is transferred to the following period, where it is read as *conservari* (“to be preserved”): “the truth is equally to be preserved,” and so forth.]

I reproached him for teaching in those same Commentaries that the truth, and likewise more perfect doctrine, ought not to be published to everyone.

Then I demonstrated that, concerning the secular books for which he had said before the tribunal of Christ, while seated and beating himself, “If I ever read or possess the books of the Gentiles, I have denied you,” he now not only read and possessed them, but even displayed in them all the ostentation of his learning—to such an extent that he boasts that he was introduced to Logic through the *Isagoge* of the most impious Porphyry.

And although he said that the doctrines of the Gentiles were impious, however they might think about the soul or other creatures, I showed that he himself had spoken much more shamefully than the Gentiles by saying that God had a mother-in-law.

I also showed that although he had said that he mentioned Origen only in two little Prefaces, as a man ingenious rather than apostolic, I brought forward, for the sake of brevity, only ten Prefaces in which I asserted that he had treated Origen not merely as an apostolic man but as a second teacher of the Churches after the Apostles, and that he followed him together with all prudent men.

### 43

Moreover, we clearly showed that it is his custom to disparage all good men, and that he thinks himself to be something when he criticizes whatever men are held in esteem and whoever has acquired some reputation in literature.

[Note: The manuscript adds “of God.”]

I also showed how disgracefully he has torn apart the ministers and priests of Christ. Nor did he spare even the monks and virgins whom he had praised, or those who practice continence, and he disgraced every rank and degree of Christians in shameful little books.

[Note: The manuscript reads “or assemblies”; shortly afterward it reads “in published books” instead of “in shameful books.”]

I also reproached him for how unworthily and shamefully he had torn apart the holy man Ambrose, whose memory of a distinguished life still lives vividly in the minds of all. I showed that he had now placed Didymus—whom shortly before he had ranked among the seeing Prophets and Apostles—among those who teach things different from the Churches.

[Note: The alternative reading is “also among those.”]

I showed that he marks all writers, ancient and modern alike, now with ignorance, now with ineptitude.

[Note: The manuscript restores “whom,” which had previously been read.]

Finally, I showed that he spares not even the Martyrs. And all this, as I said above, I reproached him for—not on the basis of writings belonging to strangers, but by his own letters and with himself as witness—bringing forward, point by point, testimonies from those very books which he himself regarded as most authoritative.

Although he says that he regrets all his other statements and writings, not because he truly repents but because, driven into this position, he has reached the point where he must either pretend to repent or be unable to bite or injure whom he wishes, nevertheless he excepted those books alone, as I said, as though they were least deserving of repentance.

[Note: The manuscript reads “he takes care that he be exposed,” instead of “he feared being exposed.”]

I did not wish now to touch upon his other writings, so that he might be convicted almost solely from these, concerning which he had himself already closed off the opportunity for repentance.

After all this I showed that he had altered the sacred Books which the Apostles had commended to the Churches as the faithful deposit of the Holy Spirit; and that he who calls daring upon the alteration of human little works had himself, with a greater offense, overturned the divine utterances.

[Note: The manuscript reads “the sacred codices.” Shortly afterward it reads “marks daring” instead of “calls daring”; the older editions likewise have “which he altered” at the end of the section, where they read “which he overturned.”]

### 44

It remains, then, that everyone who knows these things should grant his favor to one of us according to the judgment by which he himself desires to be judged by God, and should not injure his own soul by granting unjust favor to another.

Let that holy man also learn through you, my dearest son Apronianus—namely, Pammachius, whose Letter my friend [Jerome] brought forward in this Invective or accusation—that, with Christ’s help, favor ought to be shown not to partisanship but to innocence, and that in a matter of truth one must act religiously rather than zealously.

[Note: In the Guarnerian manuscript: “Let that holy man also learn through you, my dearest son Apronianus, whose Letter …”; the name Pammachius, suppressed in the older edition, seems to have slipped from the margin into the text. I fear that “holy man” may be used ironically by Rufinus.]

For the Lord commanded that we judge not according to appearance but with right judgment. Just as Christ is present in each of his least ones—in the one who hungers, thirsts, and is naked, and in the one who feeds and clothes him—so in those who are judged unjustly, he himself is the one who is judged unjustly. And concerning those who are hated without cause, he himself will say, “You have hated me without cause.”

Let his conscience consider how he thinks this case and this action of his will be judged in the tribunals of Christ: he withdrew from the hands of readers the books he had written against Jovinianus, books which were already being read publicly and criticized, and prohibited and blamed those who found fault with them; yet he sent his books back to the author himself, explaining what invited criticism, so that he might correct it or deal with the matter in whatever way he could.

But my books—not books, but unfinished and uncorrected notebooks, stolen by the fraud and trickery of some scoundrel and brought to him—although he had me present there, he did not offer them to me,

[Note: The alternative reading is “did not produce them.”]

nor did he complain to me or even deign to rebuke or accuse me, either through some friend or even through an enemy. Instead, he sent them to the East and incited the tongue of a man who did not know how to restrain it.

[Note: The manuscript reads “to send and incite.” Shortly afterward it omits the word “not,” where the text says, “so unworthy were we of his conversation.”]

What would he have done contrary to religion if he had approached me in person instead? Did we seem so unworthy of his conversation that we did not even deserve to be rebuked by him?

Christ died for us, and for our redemption he shed his own blood. We are sinners indeed, but we belong to his flock and are numbered among his little sheep.

But because, for God’s sake, he despised his nobility and made himself entirely equal to the humble, we confess that his work in the faith of Christ is certainly excellent and ought to serve as an example to others.

[Note: The manuscript reads “we wish,” incorrectly, and shortly afterward “may he perceive a lesson” instead of “may he suffer harm.”]

For this reason we did not wish him to be dragged into human partisanships and disputes, lest he suffer harm in any respect to his faith.

Certainly, when he reads that the very things about which that teacher [Jerome] rebukes others were taught by him even in his selected Commentaries after his repentance—things which are not his own—then we shall see how true a judgment he preserves.

[Note: As with Pammachius above, the manuscript and the older edition omit the name Jerome, which seems more correct.]

For the earlier error will be thought to have arisen from ignorance, if recognition corrected it.

[Note: The alternative reading is “if argument corrected it.”]

Although compelled by necessity, we have therefore had to reply to the man who had attacked us most bitterly; nevertheless, for this very reason we ask pardon if we have pursued anything too harshly. God is witness to our conscience that we have withheld far more than we have brought forward.

[Note: In the manuscript: “we seemed”; shortly afterward: “and nevertheless for this very reason,” and so forth.]

But we could not remain entirely silent against our conscience when some people would have regarded our silence as almost a loss to his own faith.

[Note: Elsewhere: “some would regard our silence as a loss”; the manuscript reads more poorly, “some would say that silence should be regarded as a loss,” and so forth.]

### 45

After I had dictated these things, a certain brother who had come from Rome to us—

[Note: The manuscript, with the opposite meaning, incorrectly reads “had come from us to you”; it also omits “that one matter had still been left aside.”]

—while he was present as I reread them, said that one further place of defense had been omitted, which he had heard criticized there by the detractors.

He said that it concerned what was written in my little Preface: that I had said of this man, who now persecutes and accuses me, that in the things he had interpreted from Origen there appeared to be certain stumbling-blocks in the Greek, but that by interpreting them in such a way he had purged them, so that the Latin reader would find in them nothing that differed from our faith.

[Note: The manuscript adds “since he had removed certain stumbling-blocks,” and shortly afterward, with the pronoun omitted, reads: “yet in interpreting them in this way.” From the same source we have restored *Latin reader*, where the Latin wording had previously been less satisfactory. Finally, from the same source we have restored the plural “they say” instead of “he says,” which was incongruous.]

“They say,” he says, “concerning this passage: You see how he both praised his interpretation and himself gave him testimony that the things he interpreted were without offense, and promised that he would follow him. Why, then, are not the things which he himself translated also without offense, just as he himself testified that the other man’s writings were?”

### 46.

It is no wonder that I always deserve to be blamed there where I have praised him. And rightly so, indeed. Nevertheless, let us come to the matter. I said that he had cleansed in the Latin translation whatever stumbling-blocks to the faith seemed to be present in the Greek, and not without reason—yet in such a way that I too approve the same actions. For just as he interpreted the two Seraphim in the Homilies on Isaiah as the Son and the Holy Spirit, and added on his own account: “Let no one suppose that there is a difference of nature in the Trinity when the functions of the names are distinguished,” believing that by this he could remedy the stumbling-blocks, so we too, whether removing, altering, or adding certain things, have tried to bring the author’s meaning onto a straighter path of understanding. What different thing did we do here, or what contrary thing, or what thing that was not the same?

But since I was judging his writings without malice or slander, I considered not what might be exposed to detraction, but what the translator had intended. He, however, who seeks occasions for slander, criticizes in my writings what he himself had previously written before me. And truly I ought to be blamed if, according to my own judgment, what he wrote is correct, but according to his own judgment it is condemnable. This [or: “These things”] concerns the faith of the Trinity, where certainly it is regarded as a crime of blasphemy that he said the two Seraphim were the Son and the Holy Spirit, if he himself is judged according to the opinion with which he acts against me. But according to my judgment—by which I judged his writings without any intention of slander—he is acquitted on account of what he added from himself to explain the author’s meaning.

[Note: Above, in no. 27, Jerome’s words are quoted somewhat differently, though they are almost the same as those found in the cited edition of the Homilies: “Nor should you think that the nature of the Trinity is at variance if the functions of the names are preserved.” Recall what we noted about this passage; to that may now be added this new argument relevant to our case, arising from such a variety of readings. In the manuscript there is more: “Let no one, he says, suppose,” and so forth.]

### 47.

As for the resurrection of the flesh, I think that our translation contains the same things that are preached in the Churches. We have already said above that the remaining statements concerning the principles of created beings have no bearing on the faith in the Deity. But if he now calls these things into question for the sake of slander, although previously they offered no stumbling-block, I do not prevent him, if it pleases him, from withdrawing that judgment of mine by which he could have been acquitted, and putting forward his own, by which he ought to have been bound. Therefore it is not my judgment concerning him that ought to be considered blameworthy, but his own, since he censures in others what he approves in himself.

This is a new kind of judgment, in which I myself defend my accuser, and in which he thinks me finally defeated only if he proves himself guilty. Nevertheless, let us suppose that a Synod of Bishops follows your judgments and orders that all books containing such things, together with their authors, as they say, must be condemned. These books will first be condemned in Greek; and what is condemned in Greek is undoubtedly condemned in Latin.

[Note: In the manuscript: “We come to your books. They are found to contain the same things,” and so forth.]

Let us come to your books: they will be found, according to your judgment, to contain the same things; they must therefore be condemned together with their author. And just as it did Origen no good that you praised him, so it will do you no good that I excused him. For I must follow the judgment of the Catholic Church, whether it was issued against the books of Origen or against yours.

[Note: The older edition reads: “whether issued against you or against yours.” Through the carelessness of a manuscript copyist, the first half of the corresponding parallel phrase—“whether against Origen’s books”—has been omitted.]

## CONTROVERSIES OF RUFINUS AGAINST JEROME, BOOK II, ENDS

[Note: From the manuscript we have supplied this conclusion to the work, written below by the copyist, restoring in only one place the Roman numeral II, which had been missing.]

## APOLOGY TO ANASTASIUS

[Col. 0623]

[Note: Thus it is entitled in two manuscripts, the Coislinian and the Navarre manuscript, according to P. Coustant. In one Corbie manuscript it is shorter: “Rufinus’s Apology to Pope Anastasius.” In the Guarnerian manuscript: “The Apology of the same Rufinus, which he sent on his own behalf to Athanasius”—to be corrected to “Anastasius”—“Bishop of Rome.” This is the work which Jerome, throughout Book II against Rufinus, proposed to refute.]

## THE APOLOGY WHICH RUFINUS THE PRESBYTER SENT ON HIS OWN BEHALF TO ANASTASIUS, BISHOP OF THE CITY OF ROME

(C)

Rufinus, accused because of his translation of Origen’s books *On First Principles* (*περὶ Ἀρχῶν*), attempts to clear himself by publishing a statement of his faith: concerning the Trinity, the incarnation of the Word, the Resurrection, eternal Judgment, the condemnation of the Devil, and the origin of souls. Finally, he declares himself Origen’s translator, not his defender.

[Col. 0623B] 403

### I.

I have heard that certain people, when they were raising controversies before Your Beatitude, whether about the faith or about various other questions of which I know nothing, also made mention of my name. Your Holiness, indeed, having been instructed from your very beginnings according to the rules of ecclesiastical tradition, did not lend an ear to those who slandered an absent man whom you knew to be well disposed toward you and well established in the faith and love of God.

Nevertheless, since the report of the attack upon my reputation has reached me, I thought it right to satisfy Your Beatitude by letter—since I have been restored to my parents after almost thirty years [Note: Compare Jerome, in the cited book, no. 2. The Guarnerian manuscript omits “thirty”] and it would have been harsh and quite inhuman if I had so quickly abandoned those whom I had revisited only after so long a delay; and also because the hardship of so long a journey has made me less able to undertake further labors [Note: The Guarnerian manuscript reads “and likewise”; then, together with the Coislinian manuscript: “of such a long journey,” or, in another reading, “already long”]—that I should satisfy Your Beatitude by my letter, not to remove a stain of suspicion from your holy mind, which, like a kind of sanctuary of God, admits nothing unjust [Alternative: “admitted nothing unjust”], but to offer you, against those who perhaps bark at me out of rivalry, a sort of staff of my confession with which they might be driven away.

### II.

Although, therefore, our faith was approved during the persecution of the heretics, when we were living in the holy Alexandrian Church, in the prisons and exiles which were endured for the sake of the faith [Note: Jerome diminishes, and almost entirely begrudges, this praise of Rufinus in the cited book. Nevertheless, in this matter it is preferable to trust Our Author, who bears the same testimony about himself also in Book II, chapter 4, of his *Ecclesiastical History*: “I relate the deeds of those whose companion in their sufferings I was deemed worthy to be.” Recall what we wrote there, and in Book I, chapter 2 of the *Life*], nevertheless, if anyone now wishes either to test, hear, or learn our faith, let him know that we believe the following concerning the Trinity:

It is of one nature, one Deity, one and the same power and substance. There is absolutely no difference between the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, except that the one is the Father, the other the Son, and the other the Holy Spirit. The Trinity is in the subsistent persons; unity is in nature and substance.

[Note: The statements that follow here concerning the faith of the Trinity and the resurrection of the flesh, through the end of no. 4, were copied in almost the same words by Bachiarius in his *Booklet on the Faith*, published by the distinguished Muratorius in volume II of the *Anecdota*. This shows how highly Rufinus’s writing was already valued at that time.]

### III.

We also confess that the Son of God was born in the last days from the Virgin and the Holy Spirit; that he assumed human nature’s flesh and a soul, in which he also suffered, was buried, and rose from the dead; that, rising again in that same flesh, which had been laid in the tomb—

[Note: The Guarnerian manuscript omits this phrase, “which had been laid in the tomb.” From this passage, and from the following one where the resurrection of “this flesh” is mentioned, the recent commentator on Bachiarius argues that Rufinus should also be credited with that little work, or booklet, recorded in chapter 39 of the *Canons of the Roman Church*, volume II of the Quesnellian edition of the works of St. Leo, p. 74. It should be attributed to him, not as the translator of Gregory of Nazianzus, but as its original author; or at least to some Latin who extracted Rufinus’s writings on the resurrection of bodies—namely, this *Apology* and the first *Invective*, as he calls it, chapters 3 and 4. Quesnellius, in Dissertation XIV, chapter 7, attributes that little work to Gregory of Baetica, Bishop of Eliberis; the Benedictine monks in the *Literary History of Gaul*, volume I, part II, suspect that it belongs to Phoebadius of Agen. In every respect its style and character resemble those of another person—whoever he may have been—more than those of Rufinus.]

—with that flesh together with his soul he ascended into heaven after the resurrection. From there he is also expected to come as judge of the living and the dead.

[Note: The older published books and the Guarnerian manuscript add “judge” here, as well as in Book I, no. 4 of the *Apology against Jerome*, where these same words recur. The more accurate manuscripts omit it.]

### IV.

We also confess that the resurrection of our flesh will occur wholly and perfectly: of this very flesh of ours in which we now live.

[Note: The Guarnerian manuscript omits the pronoun “our,” not only here but also three lines later where it occurs again; at that later point the other manuscripts and most printed books likewise omit it. We once thought Rufinus had added it emphatically (ἐμφατικῶς), in order to remove from himself as far as possible every suspicion of the Origenist view.] We do not say, as certain people slanderously claim, that another flesh will rise in place of this one, but this very flesh, with none of its members amputated or any part of the body cut away, and with nothing at all lacking from its entire nature except corruption alone.

For this is what the holy Apostle promises: that the body is sown in corruption and rises in incorruption; it is sown in weakness and rises in power; it is sown in dishonor and rises in glory; and because the natural body is sown, the spiritual body rises (1 Cor. 15).

These are the teachings concerning the resurrection that we received from those by whom we obtained holy baptism in the Church of Aquileia. I think that these are the very teachings which the Apostolic See also customarily transmits and teaches.

[Note: In the Guarnerian manuscript: “which the Church, the seat of the Apostolic Lord”—apparently to be corrected to “of the Apostolic Lord”—“transmits.” The Navarre manuscript reads “faith” instead of “seat.” Our manuscript continues: “they customarily transmit and teach,” without the addition “as is customary”; the two manuscripts cited by P. Coustant likewise have this reading.]

[Col. 0625C]

### V.

We also say that there will be a judgment in which each person will receive what belongs to his body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil. But if human beings are to receive according to their works, how much more the Devil, who is the cause of sin for everyone? Concerning him we hold what is written in the Gospel: that the Devil himself and all his angels, together with those who do his works—that is, those who accuse their brothers—will receive with him the inheritance of eternal fire (Matt. 25).

Therefore, if anyone denies that the Devil is to be consigned to eternal fires, let him receive a portion of eternal fire with him, so that he may experience what he denied.

[Note: The same manuscript reads “fathers”; then, instead of “will receive the inheritance of eternal fire,” it has “will possess the inheritance of eternal fire.” A glossator wrote “receive” in the margin for the final word “possess,” and a later copyist inadvertently introduced it into the text. It is well known how vigorously Jerome attacked and mocked this expression, “to possess the inheritance of eternal fire.” “Who,” he asks, “has ever heard of possessing fires and enjoying punishments?” See him in Book II, chapter 6 and following. From these facts it is clear that the reading once found in Our Author—“they will suffer an inheritance”—was corrupt. Later, the Guarnerian manuscript lacks the adverb “therefore.”]

### VI.

I hear that questions have also been raised about the soul [Alternative: “that many questions have been raised”]. Whether the complaint about this matter ought to be received or rejected, you must determine. But if it is also asked what I think, I confess that I have read different opinions on this question among very many interpreters.

I have read some who say that the soul too is propagated together with the body through the transmission of human seed, and they confirmed this with whatever arguments they could. I think that among the Latins Tertullian held this view, or Lactantius, and perhaps several others.

[Note: Again the Guarnerian manuscript reads “is infused.” Earlier printed editions read “and they confirmed this with whatever assertions they could.” Consult St. Jerome in the book cited above, no. 8 and following.]

Others assert that, once bodies have been formed in the womb, God daily creates souls and infuses them. Others say that souls were made long ago—that is, when God created all things from nothing—and that he now assigns them to bodies according to his judgment.

[Note: The same manuscript omits the word “that.”]

Origen and some other Greeks hold this view. But I, having read each of these opinions, declare before God that up to the present I hold nothing certain or definite concerning this question. I leave it to God to know what is true, and to reveal it to whomever he himself deems worthy.

Nevertheless, I do not deny that I have read all these views, and I confess that I still do not know the answer, except for what the Church plainly teaches: that God is the creator of souls and bodies.

[Note: Again the same manuscript prefers “creator”; in the following sentence it omits the word “is.”]

### VII.

Since I hear that it has also been debated that, when asked by the brothers, I translated certain works of Origen from Greek into Latin, I think everyone understands that I am being blamed for this solely out of envy. For if there is something displeasing in the author, why is it turned against the translator?

As the Greek text contains them, I was asked to make them available to Latin readers. I gave Latin words to Greek meanings only. Therefore, if there is any praise in those meanings, it is not mine; if there is blame, it is likewise not mine.

Indeed, as I indicated in my Preface, I also added that, as far as I could, I should cut away certain things—those, however, which appeared suspicious to me because they seemed not to have been said by Origen himself but to have been inserted by others, since I had read the same author expressing orthodox views on the same subjects elsewhere.

[Note: The older reading was “which came under suspicion.” Jerome reproaches the Aquileian presbyter for the barbarism of the language being exposed to suspicion; and for what precedes, “indeed I also,” see Jerome’s criticism.]

Therefore, I beg you, holy, venerable, and blessed Father, let no one kindle hatred against me on this account; let no one use factions and slanders, which are not permitted in the Church of God. For where will simplicity and innocence be safe if they are not safe here?

[Note: Coustant preferred this reading and supplies “which I did.” The grammatical faults and incoherencies in question are neither Rufinus’s fault nor an actual fault. Here the adverb “where” answers to the preceding “where,” and the meaning is clear: slander is not permitted in the Church; for where will innocence be safe if it is not safe here, that is, in the Church? The Guarnerian manuscript soon reads “for I” instead of “for where.”]

I am neither Origen’s defender, nor his advocate, nor his first translator. Others had undertaken this same work before me; I did it last, when asked by the brothers. If it is ordered that it not be done, the order ought to be observed thereafter. If those who did it before the order are blamed, let the blame begin with the first.

### VIII.

Apart from the faith that I have explained above—that is, the faith held by the Roman, Alexandrian, and our own Aquileian Church, and preached at Jerusalem—I have never had, and do not have, and shall not have in the name of Christ, any other faith.

[Note: The Guarnerian manuscript reads: “I have never had any other faith in me, nor do I have any other faith in Christ,” instead of “in this man,” which the older editions, although corruptly, presented in a more coherent form. P. Coustant restored the printed reading from the manuscripts.]

And if anyone believes otherwise, whoever he may be, let him be anathema. On the day of judgment those who, solely out of envy and spite, generate stumbling-blocks, dissensions, and scandals among their brothers will give an account.

[Col. 0627]

## LETTER OF ANASTASIUS, BISHOP OF THE CITY OF ROME, TO JOHN, BISHOP OF JERUSALEM, CONCERNING THE NAME OF RUFINUS

[Note: Thus it is entitled in the very ancient Palatine-Vatican manuscript 234. In earlier editions either the words “concerning Rufinus’s name” are missing, or the title reads “An Opinion concerning Rufinus.” Jerome himself appended this letter, copied by him, to the second book against Rufinus. “If,” he says, “you translate him [Origen] in order to accuse him as a heretic, change nothing from the Greek, and attest this very thing in your Preface”—which Pope Anastasius most prudently expressed in his letter against you to Bishop John, freeing me, who did this, and accusing you, who refused to do it. And lest you perhaps deny this too, I have added an example of his letter, so that, if you are unwilling to hear a brother admonishing you, you may hear a bishop condemning you. For the rest of what he discusses concerning its authenticity and his judgment, consult the same book and the following, third book, near the end.]

(C, S)

Consulted by John on whether Rufinus should be condemned because he had translated Origen’s books *On First Principles* (*περὶ Ἀρχῶν*) from Greek into Latin, Anastasius replies that, with every suspicion set aside, one must consider with what intention Rufinus undertook the task. He must indeed be condemned if he translated them according to his own convictions, praising and approving them; but not if he translated them while accusing the author himself. Anastasius says that he is not troubled by an empty fear, but will take care that the Churches throughout the world are not corrupted by this.

### 1.

It is a sign of approved affection that one priest speaks laudably about another priest. Therefore, for the very great praise that you have lavishly bestowed upon my merits—

[Note: Earlier the reading was “most profusely.” Guarnerius, who published this letter at the end of Marius Mercator, reads “undeservedly toward me,” contrary to the testimony of the manuscripts.]

—I thank your love, just as your holiness’s splendor, and those virtues which you possess in the Lord, are in turn accompanied in some fashion by a favorable word from our littleness.

[Note: The Palatine manuscript and two others used by Coustant read “and those virtues.”]

For you shine with such a conspicuous brilliance of praise, most excellent man among all, that no language can be equal to your merits.

[Note: Thus the Palatine manuscript and the other manuscripts, together with Guarnerius. Earlier it read “so eminently.” Coustant, from a certain Cluniac manuscript reading “however eminent,” conjectures that “so very eminently” should be restored.]

Nevertheless, I am so carried away by the impulse of your titles that I shall not cease to venture even what I cannot fulfill.

[Note: Up to this point the reading was “to obtain.” I substitute “to fulfill,” from the most accurate Palatine manuscript.]

This too belongs to your praises: that you praised me so highly for the serenity of this heavenly spirit. For the order of your episcopate, resplendent throughout the world like a radiating light, has brought even to us the brightness of its splendor.

[Note: Coustant reads “because you praised me only concerning the heavenly…” Shortly afterward Guarnerius reads “throughout the whole world” and “of your splendor,” contrary to the manuscripts and printed books.]

You attribute everything in me to friendship itself, leaving nothing to examination. Or, if you praise me justly, ought you not likewise to be praised in return?

[Note: The word “himself,” which was lacking, has been supplied from the Palatine manuscript. That manuscript, together with the Bellovacian manuscript used by Coustant and with Guarnerius, then reads: “you too ought to be praised in the same manner,” without an interrogation mark. From the same manuscript we soon supplied the words “before me,” which were lacking in the printed editions.]

I beg you, therefore, for both our sakes, to stop praising me to myself. For a double reason constrains me, lest false praise bring grief to the feelings of your fellow priest, or true praise kindle embarrassment.

[Note: We read this with the Palatine manuscript and the more accurate printed editions. Previously it read: “For a double cause compels me to ask this,” although the phrase “to ask this” is not foreign to Anastasius’s meaning.]

### 2.

But, to return to the matter: Rufinus, concerning whom you have deigned to consult me, has the divine Majesty as arbiter of his conscience; before that Majesty let him himself see, with the whole duty of his devotion intact, how he ought to approve himself.

[Note: The word “that,” previously lacking, is supplied. Soon afterward the reading was: “Your conscience has the divine Majesty as its judge”; this has been corrected from the manuscripts.]

### 3.

As for Origen, whose compositions he transferred into our language, it is not our purpose to inquire either who he was before or to what utterances he proceeded.

[Note: Thus the Palatine and other more accurate manuscripts. Guarnerius altered the passage by conjecture: “Our study did not know; but what the purpose of my mind is, when I confer with your holiness…” The meaning is clear: in the present question it is altogether irrelevant to investigate Origen’s person and mind. Soon afterward I restore the adverb “above” from the same manuscript.]

But what the purpose of my mind is, when I confer briefly on this matter with Your Holiness, is the following. I have conceived this in my mind:

[Note: Again we read according to the testimony of the Palatine manuscript, although the following passage itself is not free from several scribal errors. Coustant reads likewise, and rightly criticizes Guarnerius, who altered the passage on his own authority: “I have conceived this in my mind: that he who, by the reading of Origen’s translated works, revealed it to the people of our city, had cast upon pure minds a kind of cloud of blindness and wished to dissolve, through crooked winding paths, the faith confirmed by the tradition of the Apostles and our forefathers.” The earlier editions read: “that he who revealed to the people of our city Origen’s translated reading, raising and injecting a kind of cloud upon pure minds, wished…” Neither edition therefore represents Anastasius’s mind and meaning, since he is not saying that Rufinus himself wished to undermine the apostolic faith, but that Origen had this intention, and that Anastasius understood it from Rufinus’s recent translation, whereas previously he did not know who Origen was or into what statements he had proceeded.]

—that the reading of Origen’s translated works disclosed to the people of our city that he wished, after casting a kind of cloud of blindness over pure minds, to dissolve through crooked winding paths the faith which alone, which is first, and which among Catholic Christians as the true faith has been held from the Apostles down to the present by the tradition of the forefathers.

[Col. 0630A]

### 4.

[Note: The editions, together with Guarnerius, generally read “to say.” Shortly afterward, together with the Palatine manuscript, they read “what will he do” instead of “what does he do,” and “a detestable deed, hateful to the people,” instead of the printed reading.]

At this point I should like to learn what this translation does to the Roman language. I approve it if it accuses the author and exposes his detestable deed to the people, so that the man whom reputation had long since constrained may at last be held in just hatred.

But if the translator gives his assent to such great evils and exposes them for the people to read, he has constructed by his labor nothing other than a means by which, according to his own arbitrary judgment, he might overthrow, under the title of an unexpected assertion, those doctrines which alone, which first, and which as the true faith among Catholic Christians have been held from the Apostles down to the present.

[Note: The Palatine reads “in himself” instead of “the translator.” Most printed editions have: “But if the translator gives his assent to such great evils by his errors and exposes impious doctrines for the people to read…” Jerome corrects this from the manuscripts in Book II against Rufinus, as noted above: “If you translate him in order to accuse him as a heretic, change nothing from the Greek and attest this very thing in the Preface”—which Pope Anastasius most prudently expressed in his letter against you to Bishop John, freeing me, who did this, and accusing you, who refused to do it.]

### 5.

Far be this from the Catholic discipline of the Roman Church. It will certainly never happen that we accept by any means what we rightly and deservedly condemn.

[Note: The older editions read: “Far be this entirely from the Catholic discipline of the Roman Church,” and shortly afterward: “so that we may accept by some means what…”—against the manuscripts and Guarnerius.]

Therefore that providence of Christ our God, spread throughout the entire world, will deign to approve that we are altogether unable to accept things that stain the Church, overturn approved morals, wound the ears of those nearby, and bring about quarrels, anger, and dissensions.

[Note: In most editions this passage was corruptly presented: “Therefore know what sort of letter our littleness sent to our brother and fellow bishop Venerius, written with more careful attention, and that I made this conscience for myself: that I do not labor with a superfluous fear, nor am I troubled by an empty dread,” and so forth. Guarnerius, suspecting that some words had fallen out of the text, thought the gap could be filled with the following words, which, merely by changing the typeface, he inserted into the text: “Moved by this, we condemned Origen’s writings and errors; but because the translator had not sufficiently cleansed himself either in his Preface to Origen’s books or in the Apology sent to us—or perhaps in reality agreed with the same errors—we summoned him to Rome for judgment before the Apostolic See, and when he refused to come, we involved him in the same sentence. We wrote the sentence of condemnation to our brothers Venerius and Chromatius.” Now, from the Palatine copy, the passage is restored to its integrity without foreign additions; Coustant likewise had restored it in this manner from other manuscripts of good quality. He would, however, have preferred “since the matter was moved” to “moved by this.” The Palatine has “examined” instead of “written with care.”]

Moved by this, you will be able to confirm from what follows what sort of letter our littleness sent to our brother and fellow bishop Venerius, written with more careful attention:

[Note: Venerius was Bishop of Milan, who succeeded Simplicianus. The earlier letter of Anastasius concerning Origen’s condemnation was addressed to him; we previously published it, when it was still unedited, in the first volume of Jerome’s works, no. 95. Anastasius testifies that he sent this letter to Venerius after composing it with particular care. The following appears to be a fragment of that letter, since the whole letter has not come down to us.]

From what, then, let the man who translated it derive his assurance, and let him keep this conviction for himself: I am not troubled by unnecessary fear, nor am I distressed by empty apprehension.

[Note: Anyone who thinks that these words contain two separate and mutually incomplete, highly complicated meanings is mistaken. Anastasius says that he is not concerned to investigate Rufinus’s conscience; above he had also said that the divine Majesty is its judge.]

For my part, I shall certainly not fail to take care that the faith of the Gospel is preserved among the peoples entrusted to me, and that I admonish by letters, as far as I can, those parts of my body dispersed through the various regions of the earth, lest any origin of profane interpretation creep in and attempt to weaken devout minds by the darkness it introduces.

[Note: Two manuscripts used by Coustant read “my concern will not be lacking.” Although this is less Latin, it may perhaps be the truer reading.]

[Note: The older printed editions read: “and the parts of my people dispersed through the various expanses of the earth, insofar as I can, by letters.” Coustant corrected the passage with the help of the manuscripts, supported by the Palatine, which is our principal authority. Guarnerius had omitted “my.” It is well known that Anastasius calls the Churches over which he presides parts of his own body. He also uses “to admonish someone by letters” in the previously mentioned letter to Simplicianus: “I admonish Your Holiness in the letter of Theophilus which has been mentioned,” and so forth.]

I could not remain silent about this either, something whose occurrence I rejoice in: responses from our most blessed Emperors have been issued, by which every person serving God is recalled from reading Origen; and he whom profane reading has exposed as guilty is condemned by the sentence of the Emperors.

[Note: The Palatine manuscript reads “may be recalled.” Most editions then read “and he must be condemned,” and shortly afterward “of affairs” instead of “guilty,” incorrectly. The responses of the Emperors, which Jerome also praises in Book I against Rufinus, must be understood as those of Arcadius and Honorius, although they do not survive today. Coustantius rightly judges that the Fathers of the Alexandrian Synod, especially Theophilus, when they saw that their condemnation of Origen had not achieved enough, requested imperial rescripts forbidding the reading of Origen’s works, in accordance with the provisions of the Theodosian Code, book 16, title 5, law 34, from the year 398, which prohibited the reading of Montanist and Eunomian books and ordered them burned.]

Thus far the form of my judgment has proceeded.

[Note: Guarnerius read “may have proceeded,” from a preconceived opinion by which he had filled the earlier gap with his own material concerning the condemnation of Origen and Rufinus.]

6. But as the complaint of the common people concerning Rufinus troubles you, so that you pursue certain persons with vague suspicions, I shall restrain this opinion of yours by an example from divine Scripture, as it is written:

> “Not as man does God; for God sees into the heart, whereas man sees the face.”

Therefore, dearest brother, setting aside every suspicion, weigh Rufinus according to his own mind: whether he translated Origen’s statements into Latin and approved them. He is no different from the guilty man who gives assent to the faults of others.

[Note: [Col. 0632B] Formerly it read: “so that you pursue certain persons with evil suspicions—this opinion also.” Garnerius and Coustantius emend it from the manuscripts, and our Palatine manuscript supports them. It is easy to believe that Jerome and his friends are meant—those whom John was pursuing with vague suspicions as Rufinus’s rivals.]

[Note: [Col. 0632B] Thus read the more corrected editions and the Palatine manuscript, which does not acknowledge the alternative reading found in Garnerius. Other printed editions have: “Not as man sees, so also does God, for God…”]

[Note: [Col. 0632C] Earlier editions, before Coustantius, read in the contrary sense: “Know Rufinus, that the statements of Origen were made according to his own mind,” etc. Above, Anastasius entrusts Rufinus to his own conscience, being uncertain with what intention he interpreted Origen’s writings. The manuscripts praised by Coustantius and the Palatine manuscript provide the emendation.]

Nevertheless, I want you to understand that he is regarded by our side as so much an outsider that we neither wish to know what he is doing nor where he is. Let him finally see for himself where he can be acquitted.

[Note: [Col. 0632C] Other editions read: “I want you to know.” Immediately afterward, “from our side” is explained by Coustantius as meaning “from our region,” specifically from the city of Rome.]

[Note: [Col. 0632C] Another reading is: “not know.” Coustantius interprets what follows—“where he may be acquitted”—as referring to acquittal from the suspicions cast upon him, not from a sentence of condemnation. Indeed, the entire context of this Letter proves that Rufinus was not condemned by Anastasius. Many arguments from ecclesiastical history prove the same: for it is not reasonable to believe that, if he had been struck with an anathema, he could thereafter, until the end of his life, have enjoyed the intimacy of holy men such as Paulinus of Nola, Chromatius, Bishop of Aquileia, Gaudentius of Brescia, and also Pinianus, Albina, and Melania, with whom he lived in the closest association. Nor is it reasonable that ecclesiastical writers should have praised him after his death—Palladius, Cassian, Sidonius Apollinaris, and even Pope Gelasius himself in the Decree, where he calls him a religious man, and so forth.]

[Col. 0633]

# APPENDIX TO THE WORKS OF RUFINUS

[Col. 0633]

## NOTICE TO THE READER

The writings that follow constitute, as it were, a second part of Rufinus’s works. Although they have been discussed at greater length in the Preface, the Reader must nevertheless be reminded here as well not to value them less because he sees them relegated to an Appendix.

Rufinus did not meet the same fate as others, especially Jerome, whom writers of later times tried in one way or another to imitate and whose great name they attached, with almost foolish ambition, to what they smeared across their pages. Nor did the reputation of the Aquileian presbyter provide scribes with an opportunity for fraud, enabling them to sell more dearly what they had labeled with that author’s name. Rather, the opposite occurred: to avert the odium that his enmity with Jerome had brought upon him, they sometimes attributed his own writings—works worthy of lasting forever and of being handled by learned men—not to him but to others, and not to writers of lesser standing, either, but some to Cyprian and others to Augustine, and others, if it please Heaven, even to Jerome himself.

Since, then, these works are in fact not his, yet are attributed to him because copyists generally err in this direction, seeking an author’s patronage for books, they must almost necessarily have reproduced Rufinus’s intellect and style so well that they might rightly seem attributable to him, and displayed such abundant learning that they would have nothing to fear from the slander attached to his name.

Such, in truth, are the works contained in this second part. The first to appear is a Commentary on the first seventy-five Psalms of David. Nearly two hundred years ago it was discovered by Antonio de Albone, Archbishop of the Church of Lyon and Primate of Gaul, among the ruins of an ancient monastery. He considered it entirely worthy—as he himself testifies—of being brought into the arena and sunlight against impious interpreters of the divine Scriptures. Nor was this merely his own judgment after he had read it eagerly. On the testimony of other learned men to whom he had given it to read, he says that this treasure ought to be brought into the light and open air. He recounts the matter clearly enough and argues at length for the excellence of the work in a Letter to Pius V, to whom he dedicated his edition. We have considered that Letter especially worthy of being read and have therefore reprinted it here.

Next comes a Commentary on the three Minor Prophets—Hosea, Joel, and Amos. It was included in this part chiefly on the authority of more recent learned men, who deny that it belongs to Rufinus, rather than on the strength of argument. Nevertheless, I do not wish its value to be diminished on that account. In the Preface I carefully press as many arguments as could be advanced in favor of the work’s authenticity, and I urge you to recall them. In the Notes, too, one is often moved to wonder whether there ever existed another person besides Rufinus who both displayed such intense hostility toward Jerome and wrote with nearly the same meaning, intellect, disposition, and finally style as Rufinus. Certainly no composition could stand among the Rufinian works with greater dignity. But more on this in its proper place.

Three other little books follow—or two, rather, since the first, entitled *On the Faith* and consisting of twelve anathemas against various heresies, is only a brief piece of a few lines. The other book *On the Faith* encompasses many parts of Christian doctrine and discusses them at length. Although it is clear that it was not written by the Aquileian presbyter—and some even attribute it to Pelagius—its learning is nevertheless not unworthy of him, and it contributes greatly to the history of controversies concerning the faith. There will, however, be another occasion to discuss these works.

[Col. 0633]

## DEDICATION AND PREFACE OF THE FORMER EDITOR, ANTONIO DE ALBONE, ARCHBISHOP OF LYON, ETC., ON THE COMMENTARY ON THE SEVENTY-FIVE PSALMS, WHICH HE DISCOVERED AND FIRST PUBLISHED

To the Most Blessed Father and Our Lord, Lord Pius V, Pope, Antonio de Albone, Archbishop of the Church of Lyon and Primate of Gaul, wishes long life and eternal salvation in Christ.

[Col. 0633]

Although it is a distinguished work—and, as he judged, a good one—to occupy the place of a bishop in the Catholic Church, Most Blessed Father, and although I am not so estranged from right and balanced reflection that I would not place the office and dignity itself, which I admire as the highest thing on earth, among the outstanding benefits of the all-good and all-powerful God, rather than attribute it to my own merits, nevertheless both the incredible magnitude of the duties by which this condition is burdened and my own evident humility so terrify and disturb me—from the day on which I was appointed president of this Church of Lyon—that, unless two things had refreshed and almost restored me, I do not know whether, amid the hostility and disorder of these times and of human dispositions, I should have proved equal to bearing the burden thus far.

One of these things is that I never ascended to this exceptionally eminent rank either of my own accord or through my own zeal and ambition. Rather, the wishes of others—those of my fellow citizens and even of my superiors—drove me here. In order that I might comply with them, the authority of the Apostolic See intervened. It unexpectedly pursued me here with its benevolence and generosity, as the late Pius IV testified in letters written to me. He wrote that nothing lay closer to his heart than that, after the most illustrious Cardinal of Ferrara, I above all should preside over the Church of Lyon, which had been shaken by so many wars and seditions and scattered by such pernicious opinions. He most generously sent the pallium and documents from Rome all the way to us.

Since this matter has always been for me nothing other than a certain oracle and an unqualified testimony concerning my calling and vocation, it has strengthened me amid so many labors and such great calamity among good men, so that I have always confidently hoped that the mission entrusted to us, which we perform on Christ’s behalf, would not be fruitless but salutary and productive for many.

For just as those who thrust themselves into this way of life without being called, and who without any author or guide put their hands to the mast and oars of so splendid a little vessel, always receive as the penalty of their rashness and audacity the futility of their zeal and industry, so those who are appointed to these duties and offices by public decree, as by a kind of heavenly suffrage, provided they do not dissolve into idleness and inertia, see every hope and support placed in the happy success of their affairs.

For while they carefully meditate on these things and remain occupied with them, “their progress,” says the Apostle (1 Tim. 4), “becomes evident to all.” Of those who stand in the council of the Lord it was rightly said that they made his words known to his people and turned them away from the evil way and their worst thoughts (Jer. 23).

The second thing that greatly consoles me in this office of mine and strengthens, with immense hope, the efforts of all my people and certainly of my fellow bishops as well is this very period into which our episcopates have fallen. In it Jesus Christ has placed over his Catholic and Roman Church such outstanding and truly supreme pontiffs that they have fixed all their concerns and efforts upon its restoration and proper ordering alone. It has now been a long time since they have contemplated anything other than the reform of morals and life among Christians and the correction of doctrine and dogmas among heretics.

Since the holy Council of Trent has recently arranged these two matters so wisely and magnificently, and with supreme agreement has both chastised the corrupted manner of life among our people and removed the destruction caused by every error and heresy through excellent decrees, you alone, Most Blessed Father, have been given to us by the all-good and all-powerful God as a prince who might confirm and stabilize these most holy decrees of the senate wherever the Roman pontifical name and authority extend. You omit nothing that might seem to belong to the recovery of that former splendor and the ancient dignity of the Christian commonwealth.

And lest anyone desire that an example of such disciplined living be set before him by another, you have imposed so exact a rule of life upon yourself, and have so subjected all the insignia of liberty—and, I might almost say, of majesty—that, if you have prescribed any good form of conduct to those over whom you preside, they immediately show themselves compliant and obedient to your edicts, provided only that they look upon your actions, your self-restraint, your frugality, and finally your piety and diligence.

For who would not rightly marvel at this: that neither your age, already worn out by illnesses and labor, recalls you from the austerity of life; nor the lofty eminence of your see inflames you with ambition; nor does the great abundance of worldly goods make you lavish toward your relatives and nephews, whom you have as excellent and deeply religious men. Rather, virtues crowd around you from every side, so that no vice can break in upon you. Not even the majesty of the highest princes, should it attempt such a thing, can move you from the right disposition of mind. You keep your gaze so firm and constant upon Christ and the Apostles that you consider nothing right, nothing magnificent, nothing finally deserving of great praise unless it is fashioned according to his law and will.

Hence those letters to us and to all the other pastors of Europe, so full of concern and affection; hence the frequent missions to the most powerful monarchs of the Church concerning the restoration of morals and the destruction of the most wicked opinions; hence, finally, so many excellent documents against every kind of error and ambition, that I dare to assert that I and all my colleagues serve beneath an angelic banner, both in reality and in name.

Indeed, since such outstanding principles of Christian and ecclesiastical renewal proceed from you as from our head—from whom, as from the head of the body, the truest perceptions and most reliable movements ordinarily flow into all of us as into the other parts of the body—we hope that the rest of the members will follow this conspicuous holiness, and that, in the eager and orderly succession of their duties, they will walk in your footsteps. Thus, as much evil reputation as the excessive license of heretics and the slander of men wise according to the flesh formerly brought into Gaul, so much praise and glory, according to God, may the integrity of the supreme senate and the Cardinal Fathers now bring to this same Gaul of ours under your leadership.

We plainly perceive this, and daily hear with our own ears the speeches of the most depraved men, who cannot speak of the integrity of your life and morals except with the highest praise, and who even cast back upon earlier times whatever error in faith and disgrace in morals has for many years sprouted in the Christian commonwealth—something which they ought rather to have attributed to their own people.

Thus I judge that I am living in almost the same period that those bishops of old lived through when the supreme pontiff Stephen was raised up at Rome to extinguish the teaching of Novatian.
