And—not to compare that small crowd of the most ancient times with this universal disturbance of affairs, but to offer something equal to our present evil—I seem to be living in the same days in which that Julius so fiercely fought against the Arians and stirred all the bishops of his time to spiritual warfare; in which Innocent I showed such ardent zeal against the Pelagians; and in which that great Leo so powerfully conquered the errors of Eutycheans and the other deserters.

I do not count here the other pontiffs whom the Christian Church has always used as sure leaders to break the madness of the most wicked heretics of their age and to preserve the faith and piety of Catholics with the utmost diligence and supreme determination. For if any victory or triumph over heretics has ever come to us and to our ancestors—and very many have indeed come—we attribute it to your Roman Church, the best mother of all the others.

Since that Church, built by Christ upon a firm rock, has so often fought against the gates of hell, it has always remained what it first began to be: the pillar and foundation of truth. It was not constructed merely at certain intervals of time, but was supported by an uninterrupted succession of the greatest men and holiest pontiffs. Those who entrusted themselves to this heavenly providence and divine order were never, shaken by human error and wickedness, tossed about by every wind of doctrine. Rather, “doing the truth in Christ” (to use the Apostle’s words [Eph. 4]), from whom the whole body is joined and knit together through every supporting joint, according to the working proportionate to each member, the whole body has received an extraordinary increase for the building up of love.

The other Churches and their pastors have often fought almost everywhere against very many enemies of the apostolic faith and religion—especially in Asia and Libya—and have defeated them, not without the highest praise. But when they refused to conform themselves and their successors to the standard and judgment of the Roman See, which those ancient men venerated so greatly, and voluntarily and imprudently withdrew themselves from its laws, it is incredible to say how great a disaster they suffered in a few years, and how unhappily and miserably they collapsed.

And indeed, although many things in this Gallican Church of ours are corrupted and disgraced by heretics, I nevertheless consider this one thing to have been like a most faithful anchor for her amid the supreme conflict of faith: that the good pastors and their flocks—once forced together in astonishing numbers, but later scattered in various places, as usually happens in a public calamity—have seen you and those like you alone in the Roman See, and have wished to depend upon the majesty of Apostolic authority.

Since this has to a great extent rescued these peoples from the wicked doctrines and most disgraceful opinions of the impious, and has preserved them in the state of the ancient faith, it is right that, in resisting what remains, we should rest upon the judgment and will of this Church of yours and our mother, and contend only with those weapons which she prescribes to us through you and by your counsel.

For my part, Most Blessed Father, I hold this opinion concerning the condition and whole order of matters belonging to religion: we bishops must strive above all to ensure that the minds of our people do not lack instruction, but are imbued with arguments and learning suited to preserving their goodwill toward the Church and nourishing their devotion to Christ. Otherwise, having accumulated teachers according to their own desires, with itching ears they will turn to novel things, and will despise the guides and parents of truth.

This reflection of mine plainly led me to ensure, through my diligence and authority, that those who labor in this matter—both in this city, which is now tossed by great waves of desire, and in other cities and towns—should not lack support as they perform this work among our people and common folk in my name and according to my will. And if any industry is needed for the instruction of this people and of the young, the College of the Fathers of the Society of Jesus that we have here most happily supplies it, having begun the work with the greatest care. Moreover, if anything can proceed from me for the broader benefit of neighboring and foreign nations, I make it my chief concern to bring it forward and share it with those who gladly make common use of such benefits with us.

Although I have done this more than once on other occasions, certainly in this edition of my Rufinus I have tried above all to leave you, Most Blessed Father, a testimony of the fact, lest this Church of ours should appear so languishing that it cannot bring not only more recent but even the most ancient Doctors into the arena and sunlight against impious interpreters of the divine writings.

Since I have called Rufinus mine, although he is now being brought before the public so unexpectedly and so late, and although some men criticize him in other works as one of an earlier and therefore more serious age, I thought it worthwhile to explain the matter to you, the supreme judge of affairs pertaining to the faith.

In the territory of Lyon there is an island which the inhabitants call Barbae, but learned men call Barbata. It divides the middle channel of the Saône, and on it a very ancient and holy monastery was built, celebrated with great reverence throughout the entire province. In the recent war, however, it was so disturbed and destroyed by the heretics that nothing seemed to remain there except the traces of some more sacred place.

When, many years ago, I undertook its administration by the authority of the Apostolic See, as is customary, I encountered many monuments of ancient piety there, but above all a rich library. As I carefully examined it, I came upon Rufinus the Aquileian presbyter’s Commentaries on the seventy-five Psalms of David, written in notes and characters that displayed the greatest antiquity, and preserved on parchments almost worn away, consumed by age and neglect.

After I had read them eagerly and had given them to other learned men to read, I judged that this treasure ought not to be buried again, but brought into the light and open air.

Nor did what certain of my closest friends noted in this work deter me from publishing it: that in many, almost innumerable places, it agrees so closely with Augustine in his Treatises on the Psalms that the opinions are often the same, the words the same, and even the periods similar to one another.

For I think that what happened to St. Augustine in this work is what happened to St. Ambrose in his books *Hexaemeron* and *On the Holy Spirit*: just as Ambrose transferred entire periods from St. Basil into his own work, so Augustine drew very many passages from Rufinus into his Commentaries, just as elsewhere from Jerome and Cyprian.

Rufinus was earlier than Augustine and enjoyed great authority with him. Thus Augustine writes to St. Jerome about him, not without praising his piety and learning, saying that Rufinus had diligently tasted the honey of the Scriptures both with Augustine himself and with his former adversary, once his dearest friend. Augustine tried to recall them both to mutual goodwill, while disguising the cause of their enmity so carefully that he assigns blame for it to neither.

Those so splendid Commentaries having remained hidden for so long should not seem surprising to those who know from Trithemius that several more books were written by our author but have nevertheless remained buried until now in silence and oblivion.

Moreover, the ease of the style and the even character of the discourse itself show that this is the same author. The monks of Barbata Island preserved it all the more diligently because he wrote almost exclusively on those Psalms which nearly all learned men affirm, without controversy, to be David’s.

And lest anyone value this work less because certain little works of his are considered suspect by Apostolic authority, I shall say only this: nothing at all is said in that Canon against Rufinus that would prevent the reading of this book.

For Gelasius calls him a religious man and reports that certain Scriptures were explained by him—I understand these seventy-five Psalms—and says that he regards certain things of his as suspect because Jerome wrote that he argued less correctly concerning human free will.

But, to set aside the freedom that the most holy and learned Jerome displayed in speaking and asserting the truth, to whose judgment Gelasius refers us, it is as clear to me in these Commentaries as anything can be that Rufinus teaches repeatedly and in more than one place in favor of human free will, good works, the mystery of the Most Holy Trinity and the sacred Eucharist, purgatory, true human righteousness, and many other matters of this kind.

Nor should anyone be surprised by that sudden alienation of will between St. Jerome and Rufinus, though it has always been serious and painful to all good men. Jerome, burning with zeal and relying upon his learning, could tolerate nothing in another’s books that had not been purified and measured with exact precision. Rufinus, however, fortified by holiness and by the example of many of the Church’s chief lights, dealt boldly with Origen’s books, whether in reading them or transferring them into another language.

The matter arose especially because, as we learn from St. Augustine, they had fallen into this dispute through a certain diversity of opinions. Rufinus himself perhaps, though unintentionally, fell into it with Jerome; yet, through the modesty of character and conduct that belonged to him, he yielded every claim to victory in debate to Jerome, thereby avoiding a dissension of mind and will, and scandal in the Church.

And, to pass over the fact that Paul and Barnabas, and also the Apostles Peter and Paul, contended with one another in a not dissimilar kind of dispute—certainly not without disagreement over doctrine, as Augustine and Jerome vigorously discussed it—the controversy between Epiphanius and St. Chrysostom is well known from ancient history. Still more modest, because more ancient, was the dispute between Victor and Irenaeus.

Yet none of these matters branded those great men with such a mark that, if they had thought something less correctly concerning certain matters that had not been examined and decreed by the universal Church in its sacred councils, they would therefore appear to have erred in everything else.

Let St. Gelasius therefore retain his sacred authority, and let St. Jerome’s innocence remain his own. Yet neither should these diminish what Rufinus rightly said. Rather, if everything here has been accurately preserved, they should instruct us no less in right belief and inflame us no less to right action than the works completed by those who perhaps are accustomed to be read and handled with greater outward display and ambition than he.

I hope, Most Blessed Father, that you will receive this little gift of ours as you usually receive works which, although more splendid, are perhaps not equally worthy of admiration because they have not come from this sole, barren and difficult soil of ours—a soil whose cultivation you labor greatly to promote by your preaching and by the Catechism and Breviary recently published. It is presented to you in this kingdom as spoils—or rather as the remnants—of the most cruel devastation inflicted upon all the Doctors of the ancient Church not yet brought into print.

If I possessed anything more excellent with which I could in some way oblige you, I would send it from this See of mine at Lyon with as willing a zeal and as noble a disposition as this little work itself. If, in reading it, the Catholic Church should encounter anything offensive that cannot be approved without qualification—although we have encountered nothing of that sort here—let her take care that it be corrected like the rest. But if she finds very many things pertaining to the instruction and piety of herself and her people, let her give immortal thanks to him who is the most abundant source of every good, God, from whom in my daily prayers I ask that happiness joined with the longest life be granted to you, Most Blessed Father.

Lyon, on the Ides of March, 1570.

[Col. 0641]

## ALSO, CONCERNING THE COMMENTARIES ON THE PROPHETS HOSEA, JOEL, AND AMOS, FROM THE DEDICATORY LETTER OF RENATUS LAURENTIUS DE LA BARRE TO THE LORD JOHN OF SAINT-ANDRÉ

[Col. 0641A]

You, most distinguished man, above all never cease to bring forth good authors daily from your rich library, with the greatest advancement of learning and enrichment of literary culture. In your grateful concern for the commonwealth, you search everywhere, at great expense, for manuscripts that may be as carefully corrected as possible, so that printed copies might be collated with them, and for works that might once again remain to be printed with some benefit.

And indeed, I have long heard learned men testify about you that no one living at that time—without prejudice to anyone—had applied himself more successfully and beneficially to the book trade [reading uncertain: *Chiromam manum admoverit rei librariae*], and that no one had more generously aided, increased, and advanced the printing of the best-quality authors, whose reading they now diligently enjoy.

I often say that you yourself were preserved by the all-good and all-powerful God for these calamitous times, so that letters might not grow obsolete and so that there might be someone to illuminate the honorable contests of printers concerning honorable subjects.

This has long been attested by so many and such great volumes bearing your name in some form of preface. It will also be attested at present by this work of Rufinus, never before committed to the press. When you indicated that a copy should be requested from my teacher in theology, Lord de la Bigne—most deserving of this age both for the brightness of his character and for his singular learning—it happened that, amid the ruins of the venerable Monastery of Mont-Dieu, divine providence caused an ancient manuscript, if not wholly intact after so many years, at least to be found in a condition that had in some manner escaped destruction by the violence of our Gnostics.

Against their attacks, and against the incursions of similar ravagers, if there is any means of defense, it must be summoned from the printing press. That art alone, as the ages decline, has by God’s greatest favor refreshed the minds of men already weary of study through its pleasant facility, conferred grace upon writings through its beauty, and at the same time granted them immortality.

[Col. 0642]

# COMMENTARY ON THE SEVENTY-FIVE PSALMS OF DAVID, ONCE ATTRIBUTED TO RUFINUS OF AQUILEIA

[Col. 0642]

## ARGUMENT OF ALL THE TITLES PREFIXED TO THE PSALMS

[Col. 0641C]

1. The titles of all the superscriptions are varied. For, besides those prefixed with the names of their authors, or with indications of causes or times, there are some whose title is “For the End”; others that have only “A Psalm of a Song” or “A Song of a Psalm.”

There must have been different reasons for the different superscriptions. For this order of titles is not varied amid such a great diversity of matters without reason, so that now “For the End,” now “Psalm,” now “Song,” now “Song of a Psalm,” and now “A Psalm of a Song” is set before the distinction of the psalm that follows.

Although in each individual psalm we shall strive to provide the reason for each individual inscription, nevertheless, for the sake of a concise and diligent understanding, we shall compress the force of all the superscriptions into this brief discussion.

The end is that for the sake of which other things exist, while it itself provides its own cause to nothing else. Everything is for the sake of the end; after the end I desire nothing else. For one strives toward the end, but in the end one comes to rest.

Thus the end is both the perfection of what precedes and, since it does not extend itself toward anything else, the possession of itself in itself. Therefore the psalms entitled “For the End” are to be understood as arising from the perfect and complete teachings and forms of eternal things, because the course of our faith extends toward the realities spoken of in them and, directing its advance no farther beyond them, rests in the very end of the blessedness it has desired and attained.

In the musical arts, however, these are the kinds and varieties of functions. A psalm occurs when, the voice having ceased, only the striking of the sounding instrument is heard. A song occurs when the chorus of singers, using its freedom and not bound to the accompanying service of the instrument, exults in a hymn through the melodious voice alone.

A psalm of a song occurs when, with the instrument leading, the following and rival voice of the singing chorus is heard, imitating through the modulations of the voice the manner of the psalter. A song of a psalm occurs when, with the chorus singing first, the art of the accompanying instrument is adapted to the hymn of human singing and modulates with an equal sweetness on the psalter, following the melodic patterns of the leading voice.

The superscriptions have therefore been fitted to the individual psalms according to these four kinds of musical art.

The reason for each superscription is shown by the virtues of the psalms and by the varieties belonging to musical doctrine itself. For in the psalm that bears only the title “Psalm,” there is either instruction or confession concerning faithful works and religious deeds. The Prophet, by recalling what he does, trains us in the doctrine of similar deeds, regulating the movement of our bodily instrument for the pious performance of duties.

2. But when only “Song” is placed before the psalm in its title, spiritual knowledge and heavenly understanding are signified. These are attained through the knowledge of wisdom, when, without recalling works of faith, the psalm displays only the teaching of perfect knowledge of God.

For not every kind of knowledge immediately consists in a good work, nor, conversely, does every good work attain true knowledge. Hence there is the third kind among the superscriptions. It is called “A Song of a Psalm” when the effectiveness of good works is joined to the teaching of knowledge.

One must first live in good works, so that the knowledge of the divine mystery that follows may be perfect, according to what was said: “You desired wisdom? Keep the commandments, and the Lord will grant it to you” (Matt. 19).

He will therefore grant wisdom to those who obtain the grace of understanding through the merits of good works. The reason for that psalm which is superscribed “A Song of a Psalm” must be understood from these pursuits of works and doctrine.

But where there is “A Psalm of a Song,” the practice of good work is treated through the knowledge of understanding, since the knowledge of God acquired beforehand provides us with the desirable performance of faithful deeds.

This fourfold diversity of musical art has therefore been fitted to the diversity of the psalms, as follows: “Psalm” occurs through the movement of the bodily instrument in the commemoration of deeds. “Song” contains the knowledge of doctrine through the understanding of wisdom. “A Psalm of a Song” occurs when the knowledge of understanding is granted in advance through the merit of deeds. Finally, “A Song of a Psalm” occurs when, through the knowledge that has been acquired, the work of faithful deeds is begun and performed.

We ought therefore to seek the meaning of the psalms through these properties of their superscriptions, because for each kind of prophecy, within the particular properties of the titles, a corresponding kind of musical comparison is appropriate.

Other superscriptions, however, which either signify historical events, times, days, or include something else, show what constitutes the psalm either through the interpretation of names, through comparison with deeds, or through the form of similar things.

Thus, wherever there is “For the Sabbath Day,” or “For the Hidden Things of the Son,” or “For the Eighth Day,” the composition of the particular psalm is to be understood through the bodily superscription and its signification. Likewise, where there is “Of David,” or “To David,” or mention of Absalom, Saul, or Doeg, we are to grasp the prophecy contained in the psalm.

As for the *diapsalma*, which is inserted in many psalms, it must be understood as marking the beginning of a change either of person or of meaning, together with a change in the musical meter. Thus, wherever a *diapsalma* occurs, we should understand that either something else is being said, or that it is being said by another person, or that it is being sung in another musical mode.

Wherever we find a *diapsalma* occurring in relation to persons or meanings, we shall attempt to explain the reason for it.

For the rest, Greek and Latin translation could not preserve the discipline of the musical modes. These remarks, expressed in concise brevity, may suffice.

Now let us hasten to turn our style to the exposition of the psalms themselves. A careful and attentive judgment must be devoted to the exposition of each psalm, so that it may be understood by which key of understanding each one is to be opened. For every book is like a beautiful and great city, in which there are many different buildings whose doors are closed with their own, different keys. When these keys have been gathered and mixed together in one place, they present the person wishing to open one particular building with the greatest difficulty, if he is ignorant, in finding the keys belonging to each building. It is either the mark of a familiar knowledge to select quickly from that confused abundance of variety the known key, or the work of immense labor to discover the suitable and fitting key for opening the entrance of each building, because reason and the nature of things do not allow one to fit keys that do not belong to them into different locks.

Accordingly, trusting in the mercy of God that we shall find the key for opening each psalm, let us open the entrance of this first Psalm with its own proper and appropriate key. Among the Hebrews this book is given three different titles for different reasons: namely, either the Book of Hymns, or the Book of Soliloquies, or the Book of Psalms.

Its title is therefore *Book of Hymns*, because this whole work pertains to the praise of God. Hymns are songs that sing the praise of God. If there is praise but it is not of God, it is not a hymn; if there is praise of God but it is not sung, it is not a hymn. Therefore, if it is to be a hymn, it must possess these three things: praise, of God, and song. Some also say that a hymn is properly called praise of God composed in meter. Hence it is properly called in Hebrew the *Book of Hymns*, because there the entire Psalter is written in meter.

Among us, too, it is rightly called the *Book of Hymns*, because although, on account of the impediment of translation, it does not retain the meter, it nevertheless retains what is most important: namely, that throughout every part of it, among us as among the Hebrews, it signifies the praise of God—which is evident.

It is also not improperly called the *Book of Soliloquies*, because in it the Holy Spirit alone speaks, without any human ingenuity or assistance. Or it is called a soliloquy, not because the psalms alone speak about Christ, but because they speak of him more worthily and more clearly than the other prophets. On account of this very dignity, this prophecy is used more frequently in the Church.

Again, it has rightly been called the *Book of Psalms*, because holy David wished to declare the sweet mystery of this prophecy with a sweet sound and a sweet instrument, that is, the psaltery. For, wishing to magnify the worship of the temple in honor of God, when he brought back the Ark from Shiloh, he selected three thousand men praising God with musical instruments and placed one hundred and fifty over them. He also appointed four others over all of them: Ethan, Heman, Asaph, and Jeduthun (1 Chronicles 16). He himself, too, accompanying himself melodically with the psaltery in the tabernacle, invited the others to divine worship and performed this prophecy on the psaltery (1 Chronicles 24).

And not without reason did he use this instrument rather than another, because, just as this instrument has ten strings and is hollow above, from which it resounds, so this prophecy resounds from things above and instructs us concerning spiritual realities. Nor is this done for the sake of human praise, but solely from desire for the heavenly homeland. The ten strings of the psaltery signify the ten commandments of the Law; whoever carries out the things that are sung as written in the psaltery fulfills them all well.

It is called prophecy, not because it foretells the future, but because it discloses hidden things. Its times are three: past, present, and future. It itself is sometimes produced through figures, sometimes through a dream, sometimes through hidden revelation—as in this passage, where the Prophet himself bears witness, saying, “I will hear what the Lord God speaks within me” (Psalm 10). And, “You have revealed to me the hidden things of your wisdom” (Psalm 50).

The common subject of this entire work is Christ, understood in three ways: according to his divinity, according to his humanity, and according to his body, which is the Church. Whatever is inserted concerning adversaries—that is, demons and wicked men—is not included because they belong to the principal subject, but because they are introduced as serving the principal subject in certain useful ways. Thus, in the first psalm, he introduces the wicked so that through their punishments he may deter human beings from resembling them and lead them to conformity with Christ.

Some ask to which part of philosophy it should be assigned. The answer is that, insofar as it deals with morals, it may be assigned to Ethics; insofar as it treats of nature, it may be assigned to Physics.

It should also be known that the holy David composed these one hundred and fifty psalms through the revelation of the Spirit of God. Although certain psalms bear the names of others, such as Solomon, Haggai, the sons of Korah, and various others, this was not done because they themselves composed the psalms, but because of the mysteries of their names or the offices to which the following discourse seems to pertain.

Nor were they arranged in the order in which they were composed by holy David. For when he had sinned with Uriah’s wife, he produced “Have mercy on me, O God” (Psalm 50); afterward, during Absalom’s persecution, “Lord, how they have multiplied” (Psalm 3). Likewise, when he was first anointed king by Samuel, he composed “The Lord is my light” (Psalm 26); but after Saul’s death, “I will love you” (Psalm 17).

Ezra the scribe, who supplied the titles, arranged the psalms differently from the order in which they had been dictated. Perhaps the Holy Spirit so disposed this so that, when the order of events or times is not maintained according to the literal sense, another, subtler order according to spiritual understanding might be sought.

There are also some who wish there to be five books of psalms, because they find the expression “Let it be done” four times; but that there is one book is confirmed by the Book of the Acts of the Apostles, where it says, “As it is written in the Book of Psalms” (Acts 1).

When Ezra had placed titles over the other psalms, he did not assign one to this psalm because this psalm is the title of all the others. Just as a title illuminates and anticipates the whole subject that follows, so this psalm, which precedes, touches upon the entire subject of the work that follows.

He treats this subject in the following manner: by displaying the power of divinity, the perfection of Christ’s humanity, the universality of the well-being of his members, the conversion of sinners, and the patience and glory of all.

His purpose is to admonish us to strive to restore in ourselves, and through our example in others, the blessedness lost in our first parent. In order that we may do this, he urges us to be conformed to the image of the new man, Christ; concerning him he proceeds in this first psalm as follows. He removes from him every evil, both of thought and of action. He commends in him the whole perfection of virtue. He shows that he is useful to us.

It should also be known that the perfections concerning Christ which he sets forth together in the earlier psalm, he develops in detail in various ways in the other psalms that follow. Since all people strive toward blessedness, and cannot be blessed except through Christ—for being blessed is so great a good that everyone, both good and wicked, desires it—he sets Christ before us as an example. And he begins with blessedness in this way.

[Col. 0645]

## Commentary on the Seventy-Five Psalms (C, G)

## Psalm One

[Col. 0645B]

### 1. “Blessed is the man,” etc.

After it has been said, “He did not walk,” it seems superfluous that “he did not stand” and “he did not sit” should be added. For whoever does not consent to sin can no longer stand or persevere in it. But he does this because he wishes to follow the order in which the first man sinned, so that he may show that the second man is wholly unlike the first.

“Blessed is the man who did not walk.” **[Note: As we warned in the Preface, our author borrows much from St. Augustine’s Commentary; this passage, which is the first to occur, will serve as an example of this. For the sake of brevity, we shall generally be content hereafter to indicate many other such passages by enclosing the name of the holy Father in parentheses.] “Blessed is the man” is to be understood of our Lord Jesus Christ, that is, of the Lordly Man, “who did not walk in the counsel of the wicked,” like the earthly man who consented to his wife, deceived by the serpent, so that he might transgress God’s commandments. Our author here omitted the words “that is, of the Lordly Man,” because he knew that Augustine himself later rejected them in *Retractations* 1.19. The remainder, marked by brackets, he copied in almost the same words.**

It is to be understood of our Lord Jesus Christ, who did not walk in the counsel of the wicked, like the earthly man who consented to his wife, deceived by the serpent, so that he might despise the Lord’s commandments (Genesis 3:6).

“And did not stand in the way of sinners.” He did indeed come into the way of sinners by being born like sinners, but he did not stand there, because worldly enticement did not hold him.

“And did not sit in the seat of pestilence.” For he did not desire an earthly kingdom with pride (John 7). This seat of pestilence is rightly understood in this way because there are few who are free from the love of ruling and who do not desire human glory.

Pestilence, however, is a disease widely spread, involving all or nearly all. Or the seat of pestilence may be understood as harmful teaching.

Next, the order of the words must be considered: “He walked, he stood, he sat.” He walked when he departed from God. He stood when he took pleasure in sin. He sat when, established in his pride, he could not return—unless he was freed by him who neither walked in the counsel of the wicked, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence.

It may also be understood of any righteous person when it says, “Blessed is the man who did not walk,” etc. To walk in the counsel of the wicked is to assent to depraved counsels. He stands in the way of sinners who perseveres in evil works. He sits in the seat of pestilence who teaches others the evil that he himself does.

Therefore, whoever strives to live blessedly must avoid depraved counsels with the greatest care. For it is written: “Bad company corrupts good morals” (1 Corinthians 15). Depraved deeds and examples must likewise be avoided, because just as those who are less good always advance toward better things through the deeds and examples of the good, so the weak sometimes move toward worse things through the deeds and examples of the wicked.

Hence the Psalmist says elsewhere: “With the holy man you will be holy.” And shortly afterward it is added: “And with the perverse you will become perverse” (Psalm 17). The more diligently, therefore, such things must be fled, the more easily they can deceive unwary minds.

The way of blessedness, then, is this: whoever desires to pursue a good work so that he may live blessedly should first strive to avoid evil, lest it hinder the good he is doing. Hence it is written: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Psalm 33).

The discussion now proceeds concerning our Lord Jesus Christ.

### 2. “But his will is in the law of the Lord, and in his law he will meditate day and night.”

That Christ’s will was in the law of God the Father is sufficiently shown by the text of the holy Gospel, where Luke relates that the boy Jesus was found in the Lord’s temple, sitting in the midst of the teachers and questioning them, while all were astonished at his understanding and his answers (Luke 2).

When questioned by his parents, he said: “Why is it that you were looking for me? Did you not know that I must be in the things that belong to my Father?” (ibid.) Therefore, “his will is in the law of the Lord.” The boy Jesus would certainly not have remained in the Lord’s temple against his parents’ wishes if his will had not been in the law of the Lord.

“And in his law he will meditate day and night.” For Christ preached by day and by night. By day he taught the crowds; at night he revealed the mysteries of the word to his disciples (John 8).

Or his will was in the law of the Lord because the Son never departed from the Father’s commandments. Hence he himself says: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me, the Father” (John 6).

From these words, what else do we gather except that we must obey the Lord’s commandments, not through fear but through love; not out of necessity but willingly? For it is not fear or necessity, but love alone that fulfills the law. Hence the Apostle says: “Whoever loves has fulfilled the law” (Romans 13).

Nor is it surprising that the person who is filled with love meditates on the law of the Lord day and night—that is, continually—or day and night, that is, in prosperity and adversity. Wherever true love is, there is meditation on the divine law; and the mind kindled by the love of God is changed neither by prosperity nor by adversity.

### 3. “And he shall be like a tree planted beside running waters, which will give its fruit in its season.”

Concerning wisdom, Solomon says: “She is a tree of life to those who take hold of her, and blessed is the one who holds her fast” (Proverbs 3). What, then, is Christ except the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1)? Whoever takes hold of him by loving and desiring him undoubtedly lives forever.

We read that there was a tree of life in paradise, concerning which it was said: “See that he does not perhaps take from the tree of life and live forever” (Genesis 3). If, then, someone who took from this tree would live forever, Christ is rightly compared to a tree, for he is the food of life; whoever feeds upon him will live and will not die.

In sacred Scripture, the name “waters” often designates a people, as it is read in the Apocalypse, where the angel says: “The many waters are many peoples” (Revelation 17).

“Running waters” (according to Augustine) signifies the falling away that occurs through sin. The Lord is therefore rightly described as planted beside running waters, because he deigned to be born among human beings flowing along through mortality and sin.

Like a tree, he grew green through the newness of life. Through new words he put forth what were like new leaves. Through miracles he blossomed. By granting the remission of all sins and eternal life, he bore fruit.

It is rightly added that “he will give his fruit in his season” (1 John 2). Concerning this season and fruit Paul says: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son into the world, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law” (Galatians 4).

Hence it was said to Abraham: “In your seed all the nations will be blessed” (Genesis 32). He does not say “in seeds,” as though in many, but “in your seed,” which is Christ (Hebrews 11), who says of himself: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14).

Or a person is planted like a tree beside running waters when every righteous person is rooted and grounded in love through the infusion of the Holy Spirit (Ephesians 3).

The name “tree” often expresses a righteous or even an unrighteous person, as it is said through the prophet: “I am the Lord who humbles the lofty tree” (Ezekiel 22). For according to the voice of Truth, “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Matthew 23; Luke 18).

Solomon also says: “If a tree falls toward the south or toward the north, wherever it falls, there it will remain” (Ecclesiastes 11). On the day of his death, the righteous falls toward the south, the sinner toward the north: the righteous is led through the warmth of the Holy Spirit to joys, while the sinner, together with the apostate angel who said, “I will sit on the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north” (Isaiah 14), is rejected in the coldness of his heart.

“Waters” commonly signify the grace of the Holy Spirit. Hence Truth says: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7). And: “Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give will never thirst” (John 4).

Through the irrigation of this water, the faithful soul advances in the greenness of faith and hope in the Lord and remains firmly rooted in his love. And because love is never idle—for when it exists, it accomplishes great things—it is rightly said that “he will give his fruit in its season.”

In the present season the elect give their fruit, because they attribute the good they do to the one by whom they were made. Or to give one’s fruit in its season is to present one’s works to the eternal Judge through this life.

Hence someone is said by way of comparison with a householder: “Lord, you gave me five talents; behold, I have gained five more” (Matthew 25). From these words it is very important to observe that whatever the almighty God grants us in this life, he gives as a loan and demands back with profit.

It is not enough to preserve what has been given; each person must take the greatest care to multiply it, so that, avoiding the sentence pronounced against the lazy servant, he may deserve to hear what is said there: “Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matthew 25).

Therefore, if we act faithfully in small matters while we live here for a short time—for all temporal things are small when compared with eternity—we shall be set over much. The heavenly goods are indeed many, concerning which it is written: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him” (Isaiah 64; 1 Corinthians 2).

“And his leaf will not fall, and everything that he does will prosper.”

By “leaf” the word is understood. What leaves do for a tree, the words of the Redeemer do for us by comparison. We are spiritually nourished by his fruit; by his word we are sheltered from vices.

How the leaf—that is, the word—does not fall away, he himself demonstrates in the Gospel, where he says: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matthew 24; Luke 21).

Even if the sound of the words passes away, the meaning expressed by the words endures. And whatever is spoken by the voice of truth, whether in the Law, in the Prophets, in the Gospel, in the apostolic books, or even through any religious persons, will all be fulfilled through action.

Hence it is written: “Not one iota or one stroke will pass away from the Law until all things are accomplished” (Matthew 5; Luke 24).

And because Christ is said to be powerful in deed and word—for he himself is the power and wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 2)—it is rightly added concerning him: “And everything that he does will prosper.”

The only-begotten Son of God, coming in the flesh (John 1), because he was true God and true man, taught and acted in some ways as God and in other ways as man. What he did or taught as God benefited us for believing rightly; what he did as man benefited us for living rightly.

Thus what is said was fulfilled: “And everything that he does will prosper.”

Perhaps, however, it is not believed that he acted successfully when he was seized, bound, scourged, crucified, and killed by the Jews (John 18). On the contrary, he acted successfully then, because by his death he destroyed our death. It would not have benefited us for him to be born in the flesh if he had not also undergone death and risen again.

And by the wondrous ordering of the Lord it came about that the Jews fulfilled their own will against Christ, while they accomplished Christ’s purpose, which they thought they were destroying.

But these words, spoken concerning the Head, can also apply to his members. Whoever desires to serve God perfectly desires to be righteous not only in deed but also in word.

Therefore let it be said of any perfect man: “His leaf will not fall, and everything that he does will prosper.” His leaf does not fall when his speech remains in the truth. His leaf does not fall because he restrains his tongue from an excess of words.

Hence Solomon says: “The wise man will be silent until the proper time” (Proverbs 11). The Psalmist also says elsewhere: “I said, I will guard my ways, so that I may not sin with my tongue” (Psalm 38). And James bears witness, saying: “Whoever does not offend in word is a perfect man” (James 3).

Of this perfect man, therefore, it is rightly said: “Everything that he does will prosper.” The deeds of the upright will prosper when evil is not mixed with good; when things well begun are brought to completion; when for them no temporal profit, earthly glory, or human favor is sought, but only the reward of the heavenly homeland.

Sometimes, however, it happens that someone who lives perfectly sins in word or deed. Yet even then his word does not fall away, for the fault remains in his heart until it is healed through the satisfaction of repentance.

And when, after his fault, he returns more cautiously to righteousness, even the sin that seems to have opposed him prospers. In a wondrous manner, he becomes more righteous in the very matter through which he sinned.

Thus Paul rightly says: “All things work together for good for those who are called saints according to his purpose” (Romans 8). All things—not only prosperous things but also adverse ones; not only good things but also evil ones.

Therefore, because every perfect man is mature in speech and discerning in action, it is rightly said: “His leaf will not fall, and everything that he does will prosper.”

But let us now hear what he adds concerning the reprobate.

### 4. “Not so the wicked, not so.”

Where repetition occurs, it is a threat, as though he were saying: “You will not be blessed in this way, nor will you be able to prosper in this way.”

“But they will be like dust which the wind drives from the face of the earth.”

The wicked man is rightly compared to dust, because it is said to the sinful man: “You are dust, and to dust you will return” (Genesis 3). When he is shaken by temptations, he is moved like dust by the wind.

When anger disturbs him, pride inflates him, empty glory lifts him up, lust weakens him, greed subjugates him, envy divides him, and sadness casts him down, he is driven by as many movements of temptation as dust is scattered by blasts of wind.

If “the face of the earth” is understood as the appearance of the heavenly homeland—for concerning this earth the Prophet says, “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Psalm 26)—then the wicked man is rightly described as driven from the face of the earth, because he is removed from the vision of heavenly glory.

### 5. “Therefore the wicked will not rise in judgment.”

Therefore, that is (according to Augustine), because they are weighted by no weight of virtues and have been cast away from the face of the earth like dust. Hence it is written: “Let the wicked be taken away, so that he may not see the glory of God” (Isaiah 26).

“Nor sinners in the counsel of the righteous.”

The sentence seems to be repeated so that what is said above as “the wicked” may be understood as “sinners,” and what was previously stated as “in judgment” may here be expressed as “in the counsel of the righteous.”

Or, if the wicked are one thing and sinners another—for every wicked person is a sinner, but not every sinner is wicked (according to Augustine, in the same words)—the wicked do not rise in judgment, that is, so that they may be judged, because they have already been assigned to most certain punishments.

Sinners, however, do not rise in the counsel of the righteous, that is, so that they may judge, but so that they may be judged.

But when David says that the wicked do not rise in judgment, what are we to make of Paul’s statement: “We shall all rise” (1 Corinthians 15)? By “all” he intends both the good and the wicked, both the godly and the ungodly, both sinners and the righteous.

It should be understood, however, that all, good and evil, are to rise for life, but not all will rise to glory. The same Apostle makes this sufficiently clear when he adds there: “But we shall not all be changed.”

All will rise so that they may live, both good and evil; but not all will be changed from life to glory—only the good. Why is this?

### 6. “For the Lord knows the way of the righteous.”

“Knows,” that is, approves.

“But the way of the wicked will perish.”

It is as though he were saying: The Lord does not know the way of the wicked. Thus “not to be known by the Lord” means to perish, while “to be known by the Lord” means to remain.

The knowledge of God is understood in two ways (according to Augustine): either “to know” means “to recognize,” or “to know” means “to approve.”

According to the sense in which God’s knowledge means recognition, the Lord knows both the good and the wicked. As it is written: “He knows both the one who deceives and the one who is deceived” (Job 12). For he would not judge anyone wicked if he did not recognize him at all.

And yet he does not know the unrighteous, because he does not approve their deeds. Thus he knows him because he detects him, and he does not know him because he does not recognize him as belonging to the appearance of his wisdom.

Hence he will say to them in judgment: “Truly I tell you, I do not know you” (Matthew 25).

According to the sense in which “to know” means “to approve,” the Lord knows only the good. Hence it is written: “The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Timothy 2). He knows them because he foreknew and predestined them to be conformed to the image of his Son (Romans 8).

Because, then, the almighty God knows the work of the righteous in such a way as to approve it, but does not know the activity of the wicked in such a way as to reject it, it is rightly said: “For the Lord knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked will perish.”

## Title of Psalm Two

The second psalm is entitled in this way: “A Psalm of David.”

It should be noted that titles are placed before some psalms in order to designate their purpose, before others to designate their subject, and before others to designate both.

A psalm is properly called *melos*, something that proceeds from the movement and labor of the hands upon the psaltery; and therefore it is often used for a good work, which cannot be performed without labor.

Since this work contains an exhortation to good action, that work is fittingly given the name “psalm.” This psalm, therefore—that is, the following exhortation to good action—is attributed to David, that is, to Christ, who is the true David. David is interpreted as “desirable in appearance” or “strong of hand.”

For who is so desirable as the one of whom it is written: “The whole earth desires to see his face, and into whom the angels desire to look” (1 Peter 1; Luke 11)? And who is stronger than he, who did everything that he wished (Psalm 134), who expelled the prince of this world from his kingdom (John 12), and who by his death destroyed our death (Hosea 13)?

It should also be known that whenever psalms are entitled with “Psalm” placed before them and not “Song,” it is signified that morals are being discussed. But when “Song” appears and not “Psalm,” the subject is not morals but mystical understanding.

The purpose of Christ, to whom these words apply, is that all the faithful should place the hope and confidence of a good life not in themselves but in Christ, both in its beginning and in its end.

Sometimes the holy prophets foresee future things as though they knew things past. Holy David wished to narrate as past what he foresaw would happen concerning Christ’s passion and his persecutors, so that through his words he might show that, by the revelation of the Holy Spirit, he was equally certain about future and past things.

Thus he speaks concerning Christ’s persecutors.

## Psalm Two

### 1. “Why did the nations rage,” that is, the Gentiles, “and the peoples,” that is, the Jews, “devise vain things?”

And why did the kings of the earth, Herod and Pilate (John 11), stand together, and the rulers, Annas and Caiaphas (Luke 23), gather together in one place and one counsel against the Lord, the Father, and against Christ, his Son (Matthew 26)?

Such madness of fury seized them, such blindness of malice struck them, that they did not fear unanimously even to kill their creator, whom they ought to have believed in and worshiped.

The word “why” is used (according to Augustine) as though it said, “In vain.” For they did not accomplish what they wanted.

Those who killed Christ in order to erase his name from the earth and to prevent themselves from losing their place and nation (John 7)—by killing the innocent Lord, they increased his name and lost both their nation and their place (John 11).

And it happened in a wondrous manner that, while they believed they were fulfilling their own counsel, they fulfilled the Lord’s counsel unwillingly and unknowingly.

Therefore they devised vain things. “There is no wisdom, no prudence, and no counsel against the Lord” (Proverbs 21).

But what vain things did they devise?

### 2. “Let us break their bonds,” they said, “and cast their yoke from us,” that is, let us destroy the bonds of the Christian religion, so that they may not be able to subjugate us.

Thus, thus proud minds frequently rise up against their creator when they desire to fulfill their own will rather than his; and they fall all the more disastrously the higher they strive above him by whom they were made.

But what follows?

### 3. “He who dwells in the heavens will laugh at them, and the Lord will mock them.”

Because those dwelling on earth presumed to laugh at and mock the heavenly Lord, they will be shown worthy of laughter and mockery by the heavenly God himself.

For he who rose from the dead and now dwells in heaven by reigning will, when he comes to judgment, show them worthy of laughter and mockery, as we have already said.

Hence Wisdom says: “Because I called and you refused, I stretched out my hand and there was no one who looked; you despised all my counsel and neglected my reproofs, I also will laugh at your destruction and mock you when what you feared comes upon you” (Proverbs 1).

“When sudden calamity falls upon you and destruction rushes upon you like a storm, when tribulation and distress come upon you, then they will call upon me and I will not hear; they will rise early and will not find me.”

### 4. “Then he will speak to them in his anger,” he who earlier remained silent in his gentleness.

“And in his fury he will trouble them”—those whom earlier, in the long-suffering of his patience, he tolerated.

The anger and fury of the Lord (according to Augustine) must not be understood as a disturbance of mind, but as the force with which he judges most justly.

“In his anger he will speak to them,” when in his judgment he rebukes them with harsh denunciation; “in his fury he will trouble them,” when he strikes the wicked with strict punishment.

Behold, the merciful God appears to us sinners not angry but reconciled: he sees our evils and patiently endures them. He tolerates them for a long time in order to lead us to repentance.

But whoever now neglects him when he is reconciled will certainly feel him when he is angry. And the more hardened someone now becomes toward repentance, the more severe he will then be for punishment.

But let us hear how he who dwells in heaven also reigns on earth. For he says:

### 5. “But I have been appointed king by him”—understand, by my Father—“over Zion, his holy mountain, proclaiming his commandment.”

“I,” that is, the one whose bonds they plotted to tear apart and whose yoke they devised to cast off.

By Zion (according to Augustine), which is interpreted as “watchtower” or “vision,” the holy Church is understood; its purpose is raised daily toward contemplating the glory of God. As the Apostle says: “But we, with unveiled face, contemplating the glory of the Lord” (2 Corinthians 3).

He calls this Church a holy mountain (2 Peter 1) on account of its eminence and firmness.

Over this Church, therefore, the only-begotten Son of God the Father has been appointed king—not to reign with an earthly authority but with a heavenly one. For he says in one place: “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 6). Therefore it is above the world.

And when they wished to seize him and make him king so that he might reign over them temporally, he fled and rejected an earthly empire.

Christ, therefore, has been appointed spiritual king within us, so that, after the evil prince has been expelled from our hearts, he himself may reign in the inner man according to the spirit, according to the gifts of grace, the bestowal of virtues, and the building up of moral character, for the salvation of our souls (Ephesians 3).

Then sin will no longer reign in our mortal body, nor shall we serve impurity for iniquity; rather, we shall serve righteousness for sanctification (Romans 6).

Christ therefore desires to reign in us in such a way that he may defend us from unclean spirits and vices, and fortify us with virtues and holy works. He desires to reign in us in such a way that by his rule he may lead us to the heavenly kingdom.

But because we are still in the struggle, he does not cease to admonish us with his commandments. Hence it is rightly said, “Proclaiming his commandment,” because he says not “commandments” but “commandment,” perhaps indicating the love in which all commandments are brought to completion (1 Corinthians 13). Whoever fulfills this one commandment will fulfill the others as well (Matthew 22).

Christ proclaims this commandment to us daily. By this commandment he lifts us from earthly things to heavenly ones. Whatever he says through the other commandments, he always intends to send us toward this one commandment.

This commandment is indeed twofold, for the love of neighbor is contained in the love of God. And it is written: “On these two commandments depend the Law and the Prophets” (Matthew 22).

Whatever the Law, whatever prophecy, whatever the Gospel, whatever apostolic teaching proclaims—all of it is brought to completion by one commandment, that is, by one love.

But since we have heard about his power, let us hear about the dignity of this king of ours. For the text continues and says:

6. The Lord said to me, “You are my Son; today I have begotten you.” What we hear through the Prophet, we also read in the Gospel. For there it is said that, when the Lord Jesus was being baptized, the Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove, and the Father’s voice resounded: “This is my Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (John 1; Matthew 17). There the Trinity plainly manifested itself to human nature: the Son of God appeared in the form of a man, the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove, and the Father’s voice in the likeness of a human voice (Luke 2; Matthew 2).

Although (according to Augustine) that day spoken of in the prophecy may be understood as the day on which Jesus Christ was born according to his humanity, nevertheless “today,” because it signifies presence—and in eternity there is neither past nor future, but only the present—is understood divinely according to the statement, “Today I have begotten you,” by which the Catholic faith proclaims the eternal generation of the power and wisdom of God, who is the only-begotten Son.

We therefore believe that there are two generations in Christ: one divine, the other human; one by which he was born from the Father in heaven without a mother, the other by which he was born on earth from a mother without a father. According to the former, when we were nothing, he created us. According to the latter, when we had been lost, he restored us.

The only-begotten Son, therefore, born from the Father outside of time, because he did not wish to possess his heavenly inheritance alone, fashioned human nature for the contemplation of his glory. But because it perished through sin, he also sought it out by being born in the flesh; and he who had made man in the image and likeness of God (Genesis 1), through the wondrous affection of his love, himself was made [Col. 0652A] in the likeness of man (Philippians 2). And by that whereby he humbled himself to our humanity, by the same means he raised us to the glory of his inheritance (Ephesians 4). Thus, in this generation and humiliation of the flesh, the Father says to him:

7. “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession as the ends of the earth.”

The one who asks seems indeed to be inferior to the one who is asked. And when Christ assumed flesh, he made himself inferior to his Father according to his humanity. For in that which he is in the form of God, equal to the Father, he does not ask the Father for anything, but works all things together with the Father. But in that which he deigned to humble himself for our sake, made inferior to the Father, he does not cease to intercede for us.

“Ask,” he says, “of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance.” The holy Patriarchs and Prophets asked on behalf of the Jews. The only-begotten Son of God himself, made man among human beings, deigned to ask on behalf of the nations. They asked for the salvation of their own nation, and God sent them a Savior. But because they saw him humbled in the flesh, they contemptuously rejected him with proud and blind hearts. The Gentiles, humbled, received the one whom exalted Judea cast away. The former lost the inheritance through pride; the latter came to the inheritance through humility.

But because this did not happen through their own merits, but because the Son of God willed it and his Father consented, it is rightly said to him: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance.” For he does not say, “Let those nations ask,” but, “Ask yourself.” From these words it is sufficiently clear that the Gentiles are not saved by their own merits, but that he asked for this to happen who obeyed the Father for our sake even unto the suffering of death.

And because the Gentile people were gathered to the faith from the farthest parts of the world, it is rightly said, “And your possession as the ends of the earth”—understand, “I will give it to you.” While persecution was being carried on in Judea, the holy preaching of the Apostles was scattered throughout the whole world, as it is written: “The word of God had to be spoken to you; but since you judged yourselves unworthy, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13).

For the cruelty of the wickedness [Col. 0652C] that burned through the mind of Judea, Almighty God took the nations as his inheritance. For because she persecuted her Redeemer and his members, while the holy Apostles were scattered through various regions, we who dwell around Judea behold the splendor of the true light by the gift of heavenly grace.

But because he found us in the strength of life and brought us back to the rule of righteousness, it is well added:

8. “You shall rule them with an iron rod, and like a potter’s vessel you shall shatter them.”

The iron rod is understood as inflexible justice: a rod because it is straight, iron because it is hard. It is straight toward us, hard against the wicked; gentle toward the just, harsh toward the perverse. And because through it the Lord rules spiritual people and shatters carnal people, it is rightly said: “And like a potter’s vessel you shall shatter them.”

For what are earthly hearts except earthen vessels? An earthen vessel is earthly and fragile (1 Corinthians 4). Carnal hearts, which desire passing things, love what is corruptible and worthless, and devote all their desires to earthly matters—what else are they but earthly vessels? The Lord shatters these through the iron rod when, by the straightness of his justice, he destroys their carnality; when he crushes the mind’s pride; when he recalls their own weakness to their memory; when he carefully considers the misery of corruption; and when he diligently weighs the breaking of their vices.

Therefore, since supreme mercy strikes us in such a way as to govern us, and shatters us in such a way as to restore us for the better—changing vessels of wrath into vessels of mercy, and making vessels fit for destruction fit for glory (Romans 9)—it is rightly said: “You shall rule them with an iron rod, and like a potter’s vessel you shall shatter them.”

The divine word now addresses these people when it adds:

9. “And now, kings, understand; be instructed, you who judge the earth.”

“And now,” that is, already renewed (according to Augustine), already with the muddy carnal coverings—the vessels of error belonging to carnal life—crushed: now understand, you who are already kings, that is, those able to rule whatever in you is servile and bestial, chastising your bodies [Col. 0653A] and subjecting them to servitude.

Those who serve the heavenly King are undoubtedly kings, for truly to serve him is to reign. The more freely a person is restored from vices, and the more powerfully he rules himself spiritually, the more humbly he serves his Creator.

“Be instructed,” he says, “you who judge the earth.” Spiritual people are signified, those who judge the earth. Whatever we judge is beneath us. Whatever is beneath the spiritual person is rightly called earth, because it is wounded by earthly defilement.

A person who accuses himself as a sinner, condemns himself by his own judgment, and pursues himself with harsh reproaches is not improperly called an earthly judge (1 Corinthians 11). To such people it is said, “Understand and be instructed,” that is, understand for the purpose of being instructed. For understanding does not advance if it does not reach the instruction of life. The instructed interpreter, however, is the one who strives to draw into the building up of his life whatever he is able to understand.

14 10. “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling.”

It often happens that one who serves the heavenly Lord purely rises through that very virtue into pride, and thereby soon distances himself from the Lord’s service to the degree that he departs from the virtue of humility. Therefore love must serve in such a way that fear always restrains the mind in humility, lest the wind of pride carry away the fruit that a good life gathers.

Or, because in this world we are placed between the joy of hope and the fear of temptation, the Holy Spirit addresses us, saying: “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling,” so that joy may arise from hope and trembling from temptation. For even if the conduct of the just sometimes prospers, it is nevertheless set within the life of which blessed Job says, “Human life upon earth is a temptation” (Job 7).

Since, therefore, we live amid pleasant and harsh things, amid prosperity and adversity, amid sadness and joy, amid hope and fear, it is rightly said: “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling.”

But because it is not enough to do good unless each person is also able to endure evil with equanimity, it is added:

11. “Take hold of discipline, lest the Lord become angry and you perish from the right path.”

Discipline is corrective tribulation, according to the saying, “The Lord reproves the one whom he loves; he scourges every son whom he receives” (Proverbs 3).

And because righteousness is practiced sometimes in prosperity, sometimes in adversity, fear is prescribed in prosperity, but patient endurance of discipline in adversity. Otherwise, if a person exalts himself in the former, he may fall into the pit of pride; or if he casts himself down in the latter, he may collapse, overcome by the vice of faintheartedness.

Whoever neglects to take hold of this discipline perishes from the way of righteousness and proceeds miserably along the paths of iniquity. He provokes Almighty God to anger all the more because he refuses to endure adversity for God’s sake.

For since it is written, “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Romans 8), and, “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, these things the Lord has prepared for those who love him” [Col. 0653D] (Isaiah 64; 1 Corinthians 2)—since God promises incomparable goods, while the world inflicts only small evils—the just Lord ought rightly to become angry when he sees such great things despised for the sake of such small ones.

For if they loved the sweetness of the heavenly homeland, they would endure all tribulations out of immense joy, since it is certain that through endurance of this tribulation the immeasurable reward of its sweetness increases.

But the reason for taking hold of discipline is further supplied when it follows:

13. “When his anger is kindled in a little while: blessed are all who trust in him.”

While the anger of the strict Judge is postponed, and the sinner is praised according to the desires of his soul (Psalm 9), while the just person endures tribulations and distresses, it does not appear what is the punishment of the wicked and what is the glory of the just.

Hence the Apostle John says: “Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. But we know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3).

Then it will certainly appear how deceptive the confidence of this world was, how transitory life, how brief glory, how small pleasure, how false prosperity, and how quickly everything that was dear and precious here has passed away. Unhappy, therefore, are those who trusted in such things. But blessed are all who trust in the Lord.

15 TITLE OF PSALM III

1. The Third Psalm is to be understood as spoken from the person of Christ, treating of his passion and resurrection. It directs us to that historical account in which David is said to have fled from the presence of his son Absalom, who was waging war against him (2 Samuel 15).

The prophet Ezra, understanding that this history prefigured the events that took place in Christ’s passion, placed before it the following title: “A Psalm of David, when he fled from the presence of his son Absalom.”

It is explained in this way: this Psalm—that is, this exhortation to moral conduct, contained in what follows—is David’s, that is, Christ’s, who is strong of hand. It is a Psalm, I say, concerning the things that occurred when he fled—that is, when, by withdrawing his grace, he departed from the presence of Absalom, his son [Col. 0654B]—that is, from the mind of Judas, whom, together with the other Apostles, he chose by his grace to be his son (Luke 6).

Absalom properly means “the peace of the father,” but here the betrayer of Christ is understood: for although he himself did not have peace with Christ, Christ nevertheless gave him peace with his mouth and kept it in his heart.

Seeing, therefore, that his chosen ones would suffer for righteousness not only from others but also from friends and relatives, the Lord intended in this work to exhort them to steadfastness in suffering, setting himself before them as an example. Just as he remained steadfast in his own passion, called upon the Lord in his tribulation, and benefited from his tribulation unto glory and exaltation, so they, considering that they would be exalted through tribulations, should turn to prayer, thinking of him as their head and advocate, and should not fail.

The Psalm follows.

PSALM III

2. “Lord, why have those who trouble me become so numerous? Many rise up against me.”

This inquiry is not made out of ignorance, but for the instruction of the perfect, so that by considering the outcome of their tribulation they may remain steadfast.

So numerous, certainly (according to Augustine), were those who rose up and troubled him that even one of the disciples was not lacking who joined the number of the persecutors.

O wondrous patience of Almighty God! Those whom he could have destroyed with a single word he deigned, in his marvelous gentleness, to tolerate, so that through himself he might demonstrate what the virtue of patience ought to be in us.

The eternal Creator made himself an example for us, so that, because the heavenly God humbled himself in this way, earthly man might now cease to be proud.

But the body of this head, which is the Church, still retains these words of its head. When it is pressed by tribulations, when it sees the perverse rising up against it, it cries out and says: “Lord, why have those who trouble me become so numerous?”

3. “Many rise up against me.”

The holy martyrs cried this out when they saw the persecutors of the Church multiplying. The present Church does not cease to cry this out, since in a time of peace it struggles amid many adversities: when it is harassed by the temptations of the hidden enemy; when it is burdened by the conduct of those who live wickedly; when it gravely endures the open injuries of carnal people; and when it bears still more heavily the pretense of certain people who seem just under the appearance of holiness.

It cries this out as long as the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh (Galatians 5), and “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wisdom 9). As long as it remains in this dangerous and laborious life, so long the faithful soul has reason to say: “Lord, why have those who trouble me become so numerous? Many rise up against me.”

“Many say to my soul, ‘There is no salvation for it in its God.’” It is clear that those who did not believe Christ to be God said this (Matthew 27). The words “If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross” (Luke 23) have the same force. For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Corinthians 2).

And because despair of healing often steals in through an accumulation of vices—as though the vices themselves were taunting the soul, or even the devil and his angels through harmful suggestions, in order to make us despair—it is most truly said: “Many say to my soul, ‘There is no salvation for him in his God.’”

But whatever adversary attacks us, whatever tribulation burdens us, we must always say what follows:

4. “But you, Lord, are my protector, my glory, and the one who lifts up my head.”

In sacred language, the name “head” usually signifies the mind (John 6; Luke 15). For just as the members are governed by the head, so the senses are governed by the mind.

Heavenly goodness willingly receives those whom it sees humbly fleeing to its help, and by the gift of its grace raises the head—that is, the mind—of those who delight to glory not in this world or in themselves, but in the Lord their God.

Hence the Apostle admonishes us, saying: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 1; 2 Corinthians 10). For if you glory in the Lord, God glories in you. If you seek not your own glory but his, he himself seeks how to exalt and glorify you (Mark 23; Luke 18).

Hence the holy Patriarchs and Prophets, the Apostles, and the other righteous men were exalted and glorified by the Lord God, because, despising themselves in this world, they sought the Lord’s glory, not their own (John 1).

Or the words “But you, Lord, are my protector,” and what follows, are spoken according to humanity [Note: [Col. 0655D] It seems that the word Deo, “God,” should be supplied from Augustine; then one should read “so that he might become God together with him,” instead of “so that he might become like him,” and so forth.]: for the assumption of humanity is the Word made flesh.

He also calls the Lord his glory—the one whom the Word of God so received that he became God together with him. From this principle we are instructed that no one should glory in himself.

Christ had his head exalted in his passion, because amid such great humiliation in his suffering he did not lose the strength of his mind.

5. “With my voice,” he says, “I cried to the Lord, and he heard me from his holy mountain.”

To cry to the Lord with one’s voice is to beseech the Lord earnestly. A person cries with his voice when he prays so intently that the sound of his voice does not differ from the intention of his heart.

Hence the excellent teacher says: “When you pray to the Lord with psalms and hymns, let what is expressed by the mouth be present in the heart.” And the Apostle says: “I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing also with the mind” (1 Corinthians 14).

The Lord willingly hears those whom he sees crying out in this way. Hence the blessing: “And he heard me from his holy mountain,” that is, from the height of his righteousness. For we read: “Your righteousness is like the mountains of God” (Isaiah 34).

And it was just (according to Augustine) that he should raise from the dead the innocent man who had been killed, to whom evils had been repaid for our sake (Isaiah 34), and repay those who persecuted him with what they deserved (Titus 3).

He also hears us from his holy mountain when he receives our prayers not on the basis of our merits, but from his own holy mercy. For we are not worthy to be heard, but he is merciful, so that he may hear us (1 Timothy 2).

Hence it is said through the Apostle: “Not by works of righteousness that we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us” (Titus 3).

The one through whom we have been saved himself says: “I slept, and was overcome by sleep, and I rose again, because the Lord received me.”

“Sleeping” may be understood of one who is dying, and “sleep” of one who is dead: so that “sleeping” is the passage into sleep, just as awakening is the passage into wakefulness.

It is therefore rightly understood: “I slept, and was overcome by sleep.” I surrendered myself to the passion, and death followed. Or Christ slept when, having accepted death, he rested from temporal suffering. He was overcome by sleep when he remained in the tomb on the following day; but on the third day he rose from the dead (Luke 24).

Hence he says here: “And I rose again, because the Lord received me.” Rising from the dead, he was received into the glory of God the Father.

Or any believer may say this while recalling the death of his sins and the gift of regeneration: “I slept,” and so forth. We slept when we grew numb toward good works; when we lay pleasurably in our wickedness; when it was sweet for us to sin and to persist in those sins.

But life-giving grace awakened us from this sleep of death when it recalled our evils to our memory; when it changed the sweetness of sins into bitterness; when it shaped our minds for the lamentation of repentance; and when it roused us, who were sluggish in vices, to good works.

The Lord’s grace is commended when it is said: “I rose, because the Lord received me.” For unless his grace received us, our soul could not have risen from the death of sin.

But because whoever is raised up by the Lord is made strong against every adversary, it is rightly added:

7. “I will not fear thousands of people surrounding me. Rise up, Lord; save me, my God.”

“Rise up,” that is, “make me rise.” It is the custom of the divine Scriptures (according to Augustine) to attribute to God’s person what he works in us. Hence there is the statement: “Do you seek proof of the Christ who speaks in me?” (2 Corinthians 13). He does not say, “By whose command I speak,” but plainly attributes the speaking itself to the one by whose gift he spoke.

Because the number one thousand is a complete number, “thousands of people” signifies the whole multitude of the wicked. Therefore the one whom the Lord raises and saves does not fear thousands of people, because, to the extent that he has the one Almighty God as his protector, he does not fear the whole multitude of evildoers.

Or, if the statement “I will not fear thousands of people surrounding me” is understood as spoken from the person of the Lord, it is clear that he no longer fears his adversaries, because they can no longer trouble him bodily. For Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death will no longer rule over him (Romans 6). And he has his enemies beneath him (Psalm 109), insofar as, seated at the right hand of God the Father, authority in heaven and on earth has been given to him (Matthew 28).

He gives the reason why he does not fear when he adds:

8. “For you have struck all those who oppose me without cause; you have crushed the teeth of sinners.”

Who does not know that Christ’s enemies opposed him without cause [Col. 0656C] (Isaiah 53)? For he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth (1 Peter 2).

But because God is just and merciful (Psalm 10), he struck all his adversaries (Psalm 110): some through the vengeance of punishment, to condemnation; others through the pain of repentance, to salvation.

If by “those who oppose” are understood evil spirits, or any wicked people who now persecute Christ’s Church, they will certainly be struck by the Lord at the end of the world.

“You have crushed the teeth of sinners.” By “teeth” (according to Augustine) are signified [Note: [Col. 0656D] I would prefer that maledica, “cursing,” be restored. Augustine likewise says, “Let us understand teeth as cursing words,” and so forth. Certainly the following passage is borrowed from him.] cursing words, of which the Apostle Paul says: “But if you bite and devour one another, take care that you are not consumed by one another” (Galatians 5).
