“Teeth” may also be understood as the leaders of sinners, by whose authority a person is cut off from the fellowship of those who live rightly and, as it were, incorporated into those who live wickedly.

Therefore the Lord crushes the teeth of sinners when he reduces them and their words to nothing. Let wicked adversaries fear, then: for if they strike unjustly, they have above them the Lord, by whom they are justly struck. Let evil powers fear: for if they oppress others, they have above them a power by which they are oppressed.

And what is our hope (2 Corinthians 4)?

9. “Salvation,” he says, “belongs to the Lord, and your blessing is upon your people.”

We are indeed weak and feeble (1 Corinthians 11). Let no one presume upon himself, since salvation belongs to the Lord, who saves from the death of sin: “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans 7).

Therefore salvation belongs to the Lord. But what is the blessing of his people except that of which it is said: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom that has been prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 27)?

May such a blessing be upon us and upon our children. Amen.

TITLE OF PSALM IV

[Col. 0657A]

It should be known that in some cases a psalm is placed first in the title in such a way that no song follows. In other cases a song is placed first, so that no psalm follows. In still others, a psalm is placed first and a song follows. In others, a song is placed first and a psalm succeeds it. This variety must be observed.

Where only a psalm is placed, it signifies that in the following treatment the subject is simply moral conduct. Where only a song is placed, it shows that the subject is joy. Where a psalm precedes and a song follows, the treatment concerns moral conduct, but in such a way that mention is made of the reward toward which morality is directed.

Where a song precedes and a psalm succeeds, the subject is the joy of reward, but in such a way that some mention is made of the moral conduct by which that reward is obtained.

This Psalm is entitled: “To the end: a psalm of a song, of David.” It is explained as follows: this psalm of a song—that is, the present exhortation to good moral conduct, in which mention is made of a song, that is, of the joy of eternal reward—is David’s, that is, Christ’s, or of some faithful person who believes and hopes in Christ.

David, I say, directs those whom he exhorts “to the end,” that is, to the one who is the end and completion of the Law and the Prophets. Or “end” means the goal and consummation of the entire contest. Or “end” means the consummate rest of blessedness.

The intention of Christ, or of any believer in him, in this Psalm is to persuade those who delight in earthly things that, by departing from the tribulation of vices and neglecting earthly matters, they should desire the eternal goods that are found at the end—that is, in Christ—setting himself before them as an example and speaking in this way:

19 PSALM IV

2. “When I called, the God of my righteousness heard me. In tribulation you enlarged me.”

This means (according to Augustine): when I prayed inwardly in my heart, the one from whom my righteousness comes heard me. “In tribulation you enlarged me” means: you led me from the narrowness of sadness into the breadth of joys.

“There is tribulation and distress for every human soul that does evil” (Romans 2). But the person who says, “We rejoice in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces endurance,” and that “the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5), does not suffer the narrowness of heart, even though it is inflicted outwardly by persecutors.

The harshness of tribulation benefits the just in this way: while they are afflicted in body, they are enlarged in heart; and the more tightly temporal evils press them, the more expansively they desire heavenly goods.

Since, therefore, the enlargement of the mind grows out of the narrowness of tribulation, it is rightly said: “In tribulation you enlarged me.”

The change from the third person to the second may perhaps occur in order to show how he was heard, as he speaks to God in the very enlargement: so that the heart’s being enlarged means that God has already been infused into the heart, with whom it converses inwardly. To him he now prays and says:

2. “Have mercy on me, and hear my prayer.”

He asks again, although he has already indicated that he was heard and enlarged. Perhaps this is because he seeks still to be heard in that respect in which he has not yet been heard; or because he must be perfected in that in which he is not yet perfect; or for the sake of others who are beginning, so that in those who believe what they have begun may be brought to perfection.

For the just have this characteristic: in everything they say and do, they seek not only their own progress but also the building up of their neighbors. Hence it is appropriately added:

3. “Children of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?”

It is as though he were saying: You who inhabit the mind in a carnal generation, how long will you keep a hardened heart, refusing to believe God and failing to consider invisible goods? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood? With what fruit, with what advantage, do you seek by loving temporal things, and love by seeking, things that are vain because they cannot endure, and false because they deceive their lovers?

4. “And know that the Lord has made his holy one wondrous.”

That is, the one whom he raised from the underworld and placed at his right hand in heaven [Col. 0658A] (Acts 3).

The human race is therefore rebuked so that it may at last turn from the love of this world to him. But if anyone is troubled by the conjunction added in the words “And know,” let him recognize that this kind of expression is familiar to the language of prophecy.

For one often finds such a beginning as: “And the Lord said to him”; or, “And the word of the Lord came to him.” When the conjunction is joined to a statement without a preceding sentence to which the following clause could be attached, it perhaps remarkably suggests that the utterance of truth in the voice is joined to the vision that occurs in the heart.

“The Lord will hear me when I cry to him.” Here (according to the same author) I believe we are admonished to implore God’s help with great attention of heart, since just as we should rejoice over illumination in this life, so we should pray for rest after this life.

Therefore this should be understood either as spoken by a faithful person evangelizing, or from the person of the Lord himself, as though it had been said: “The Lord will hear you when you cry to him.”

5. “Be angry, and do not sin.”

For the question arose (according to Augustine): Who is worthy to be heard? Or how does the sinner not cry out to the Lord in vain?

Therefore he says, “Be angry”—understand, with yourselves—repenting deeply of past crimes and being indignant that you have fallen into such low and worthless things; and cease to sin any further.

“What you say in your hearts”—understand, “say it.” Do not be the people of whom it was said: “With their lips they honor me, but their heart is far from me” (Isaiah 26; Matthew 15).

“In your chambers, be pierced.” Chambers are the places concerning which the Lord instructs us to pray inwardly with the doors closed. “Be pierced” refers to the pain of repentance: the soul should pierce itself by punishing itself, lest it be condemned and tormented in God’s judgment.

Or it refers to awakening, so that we may awaken to see the light of Christ, as though goaded by spurs. [Note: [Col. 0657] Earlier “exercise” was read instead of “awakening”; we correct it from Augustine.]

6. “Offer the sacrifice of righteousness, and hope in the Lord.”

The sacrifice of righteousness consists in the works of the righteous after repentance. For what is more just (according to Augustine) than that each person should be angry with his own sins rather than with those of another, and, punishing himself, offer himself in sacrifice to God?

It also suggests the passage from the old life to the new: once the old person has been extinguished after repentance, the sacrifice of righteousness according to the regeneration of the new person is offered to God, when the soul now offers itself [supplied: washed] and places itself upon the altar of faith, to be seized by the divine fire, that is, by the Holy Spirit.

Thus the sense is: “Offer the sacrifice of righteousness, and hope in the Lord,” that is, live rightly and hope for the gift of the Holy Spirit.

But what is hoped for except good things? Since, however, he wishes to obtain from God the good that he loves, and since there are few who love inward goods, he remarkably adds, after saying “And hope in the Lord”: “Many say, ‘Who will show us good things?’”

This is the daily question of all foolish and wicked people who desire the peace and security of the present life and doubt the future life promised to us. They often say: “Who knows whether these things are true?” (Wisdom 2). Or: “Who has come up from the underworld to announce them?”

Therefore he splendidly and briefly shows what goods should be sought, answering their question:

7. “The light of your countenance, Lord, has been marked upon us.”

This light (according to Augustine) is the whole good of the human being, perceived not by the eyes but by the mind. He said that it had been marked upon us, just as a coin is marked with the image of the king (Matthew 22).

For man was made in the image and likeness of God (Genesis 1), which he corrupted by sinning. His good, therefore, is true and eternal if, by being reborn, he is marked again (John 3).

“You have given joy to my heart.” Joy, therefore, should not be sought outside by those who, still heavy of heart, love vanity and seek falsehood, but inwardly, where the light of God’s countenance has been marked.

For Christ dwells in the inner person (Ephesians 3). But people who pursue temporal things know nothing else to say except, “Who will show us good things?” since they cannot see the true goods within themselves.

Consequently, it is said of them:

8. “They have multiplied from the fruit of their grain, wine, and oil.”

It is not without significance (according to Augustine) that “their own” has been added. For there is God’s grain (John 12), namely, the living bread that came down from heaven (John 6). There is also God’s wine, for it is said, “They shall be intoxicated with the abundance of your house” (Psalm 35). And there is also oil, of which it is said: “You have anointed my head with oil” (Psalm 22).

But these many people who say, “Who will show us good things?” have multiplied from the fruit of their own grain, wine, and oil: their own, not God’s—that is, temporal, not spiritual.

Leaving these people, who have multiplied through desire for temporal things, the faithful man rejoices and says:

9. “In peace, in the same place, I shall sleep and rest.”

For by such people every complete alienation of mind from mortal things and forgetfulness of the miseries of this world is rightly overcome; this is fittingly and prophetically signified by the terms “sleeping” and “sleep.”

But this is not possessed in the present life; rather, it must be hoped for in the future. The words themselves also show this, since they are in the future tense.

10. “For you, Lord, have established me uniquely in hope.”

He rightly says “uniquely.” For the multiplicity spoken of above has perished (according to Augustine), and singularity remains among the saints. Of them it is said in the Acts of the Apostles: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4).

We must therefore be singular and simple—that is, set apart from the multitude and crowd of things that come into being—and lovers of eternity and unity, if we desire to cling to the one God and Lord.

TITLE OF PSALM V

1. The title of the Psalm is: “For the one who receives the inheritance.” The Church is understood, for she receives the inheritance, that is, eternal life through the Lord Jesus, so that she may possess him and be possessed by him.

The intention of this Church in the Psalm is, through prayer and good works, to invite all the faithful to the inheritance of eternal blessedness, setting herself before them as an example and praying as follows.

PSALM V

2. “Attend to my words with your ears, Lord; understand my cry.”

The Church, having been called (according to Augustine), calls upon God so that, with his help, she may pass through the wickedness of this world and reach him.

And what are the ears of divinity except his compassion and mercy, by which he deigns to hear us? It is also his work to understand our cry, to attend to and approve the desire of our heart.

The Lord attends to our words as though with ears when he receives our prayers with piety and mercy. And “cry” is rightly added after “words,” because the words of our supplication please God when they proceed from the desire of the heart.

Hence it is said through the Apostle: “I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing also with the mind” (1 Corinthians 14).

But because it is not enough for God to hear our words and understand our cry unless he also brings them to fulfillment, it is rightly added:

### [Column 0659D]

#### 3. Give heed to the voice of my prayer, my king and my God.

As though he were saying: “Hear the words in such a way, and understand the desires in such a way, that the effects of the matter may show that you are attentive to my prayers.” And because the prayer of the holy Church is sent through the Son to the Father (Matt. 6), he appropriately says, “My king and my God.” By “king” he designates the Son; by “God,” the Father. And the Son says, “Through me one goes to the Father” (John 11). Therefore, rightly (according to Augustine), first “my king,” then “my God.” Yet he did not say, “Give heed,” in the plural, but “Give heed,” in the singular, because the Father and the Son are not two Gods, but one God. He also adds the reason why it should be heard, when he continues:

#### 3. For to you I shall pray, O Lord.

And immediately he adds, “In the morning you will hear my voice,” and so forth. What is the meaning of what he said above, “Hear,” as though he desired to be heard in the present, whereas now he says, “In the morning you will hear,” not “Hear”; and, “To you I shall pray,” and, “I shall stand,” and, “I shall see”? Perhaps his earlier prayer indicates the calling itself.

[Note: In Augustine—against all the printed editions and several manuscripts—and likewise in our author, the reading “invocation” (*invocationem*) has been restored.]

But because he is dimmed amid the storms of this age, since he perceives that he does not see what he desires, he therefore says, “In the morning you will hear.” As though he were saying: “You are not one who can be seen by those from whose eyes the night of sins has not yet departed. But in the morning—that is, when the night of my error has been completed and the darkness of sins has departed—you will hear my voice,” that is, “you will show that my voice has been heard.”

#### 4. In the morning I shall stand before you and shall see.

“I shall stand,” he says; “I shall not lie down.” For to lie down (according to Augustine) is to rest in earthly things. Therefore, if we wish to see God, we must not cling to earthly things. He explains the reason why he will stand and see in the morning: “For you are not a God who wills iniquity.” Iniquity, malignity, falsehood, murder, deceit, and everything of this kind are night. When it has passed, morning comes, so that God may be seen. As long as we are in this age amid temptations, we lie in the darkness of sins; we do not immediately possess truth, nor do we see truly. For to stand truly is to remain in the blessedness of eternity; and to see truly is to contemplate God in his majesty.

But he who truly exists and remains unchangeable, with whom—as James says—“there is no alteration or shadow caused by turning” (James 1), is not a God who wills iniquity. Therefore, in this age, where iniquity abounds, he does not show himself. But because it will come to pass that the night of this iniquity will pass away, and that in the morning—that is, in the resurrection—he will restore his elect to the state of immortality and to the vision of his contemplation, it is rightly said in the voice of the Church: “In the morning I shall stand before you and shall see; for you are not a God who wills iniquity.” Since, moreover, at the gathering of the righteous there will be the rejection of the ungodly (Matt. 25), it is rightly added:

#### 5. The wicked shall not dwell near you, nor shall the unjust remain before your eyes.

A wicked person is so called as though full of evil fire. By the name “wicked,” therefore, the number of unbelievers may be designated: while they persist in the error of unbelief, by their wickedness they despise the good fire of spiritual grace. The unjust are those who grow sluggish in good works.

The wicked, therefore, shall not dwell near the Lord, because then the number of unbelievers will be removed from the author of justice to the same degree that now it is separated from the justice of faith. Nor will the unjust then be able to remain before his eyes, because now they do not fear to persist in works of darkness. Something further is said concerning the reprobate:

#### 6. You hate all who work iniquity; you will destroy all who speak falsehood.

You will destroy all who not only do what you hate, but also speak falsehood, putting forward a false righteousness and not confessing their sins in repentance. But you will not destroy them if, by repenting, they speak the truth, so that by doing this truth they may come to the light.

By those who work iniquity are designated those who not only fail to do good, but also live perversely. Almighty God hates them—that is, he shows them to be worthy of his hatred—and because he does not acknowledge them within the rule of his justice, he punishes eternally those who have been rejected from his love.

By those who speak falsehood, heretics may rightly be understood: by their falsity they strive to destroy the truth of the faith, and the strict Judge will destroy them with the reprobate. For just as the latter are condemned because of evil action, so the former must also be condemned because of evil speech.

Or it may be explained in this way: “You will destroy all who speak falsehood,” that is, what is contrary to the truth; for they turn away from what is and incline toward what is not.

[Note: The final reading in Augustine’s later edition, *declinantur* (“are turned aside”), is less correct, and also conflicts with the earlier printed books.]

Hence the Apostle says: “Whoever says that he abides in Christ and does not keep his commandments is a liar” (1 John 7).

There are two kinds of lies (according to the same author) in which there is no great fault, though they are not without fault: when we lie either in jest or in order to benefit someone. The first, when spoken in jest, is not harmful,

[Note: In Augustine, “it is not most harmful.” Compare the same Father’s *On Lying*, chapter 5.]

because the person to whom it is said knows that it was said as a joke. The second is milder because it retains some benevolence. But the lie that intends to deceive is one that kills the soul, as it is written: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. 1).

But now there is a change of person, when it is added: “The Lord will abhor the man of blood and deceit.” It is customary for the prophets frequently to change persons, so that at one time they speak to God, at another to human beings, at one time to the head, at another to the members. They speak to God as to the one from whom they receive what they prophesy; they speak to human beings as to those to whom they prophesy. And they change their voice sometimes from the head to the members, sometimes from the members to the head; in this they signify to us the unity of the head and the members.

By “the man of blood,” the persecutors of the holy martyrs are designated. The deceitful are those who wish to deceive faithful souls with seductive words. The Lord will abhor them—that is,

[Note: Augustine says that people are commonly said to be “abhorred” when they are disinherited.]

he will separate them from the inheritance of the elect. Since, therefore, those people must be condemned for their evil merits, whereas the Church is to be saved through the Lord’s mercy, it is fittingly added:

#### 8. But I, in the abundance of your mercy, shall enter your house; I shall worship toward your holy temple in your fear.

The house of God is the holy Church itself, which is to reign in heaven while it still labors on earth. It is built from the faithful as from living stones, to whom Peter says: “You yourselves, as living stones, are being built upon” (1 Pet. 2). And Paul says: “You are God’s field, God’s building” (1 Cor. 3).

Whoever in the holy Church imitates the conduct of the saints enters the structure of this heavenly house. To enter this spiritual building is to behold how the holy man makes progress by loving. But because no one can do this by his own strength, it is rightly said, “In the abundance of your mercy.”

Great indeed is God’s mercy, because, as Paul says, “where sin abounded, grace abounded still more” (Rom. 5). In his mercy the gracious Lord frees us from sins, but in the abundance of his mercy he also grants us the gifts of spiritual grace. In his mercy he rescues us from eternal punishments, but in the abundance of his mercy he also leads us back to the house of our heavenly homeland.

Who could weigh the depths of divine mercy, which, in order to restore life to us, wished to become human (John 1) and to accept death (Phil. 2)? Let it therefore be said: “But I, in the abundance of your mercy, shall enter your house.”

The holy Church is called a house (Matt. 7) because it is inhabited by the almighty Lord. It is called a temple (2 Chron. 18) because it is consecrated by the Lord himself. Or it is called a temple because continual praises are offered within it to the heavenly Lord (Ps. 67). He therefore says: “I shall worship toward your holy temple in fear.”

Because (according to Augustine) he does not say “in the temple,” but “toward the temple,” it is to be understood that this is spoken not of perfection, but of progress toward perfection.

[Note: Augustine has “dwelling” in the earlier text.]

Perhaps he therefore added, “in your fear,” because “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110). “He who fears the Lord will do good” (Sir. 15). And in another psalm it says: “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord; he greatly delights in his commandments” (Ps. 111). And again: “Serve the Lord in fear” (Ps. 2). And because he cannot do this by his own strength, he therefore adds:

#### 9. O Lord, lead me in your righteousness because of my enemies; direct my way in your sight.

My enemies wish to lead me astray and turn me aside toward injustice. You, Lord, who are my creator, be my guide (Deut. 32). For you made us, and not we ourselves (Ps. 94). Rule us, then, and let us not rule ourselves.

After saying, “Lead me in righteousness,” he not inappropriately added, “your.” As though he were openly saying: “Righteousness given through yourself.” For through the holy prophets and his servants, according to the distribution of times, he gave lesser commandments to the people who still had to be bound by fear; through his Son he gave greater commandments to the people whom it was now fitting to set free by love.

Nor is it surprising that greater commandments are given on account of the kingdom of heaven, while lesser ones were given on account of the earthly kingdom, by the same living God who made heaven and earth and who alone knows how to provide the human race with medicine suited to its times.

He reminds us of this righteousness of his in the Gospel, saying: “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees” (Matt. 5)—that is, unless you fulfill not only those lesser commandments of the Law by which people make a beginning, but also these commandments that are added by me, who did not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it—you will not enter the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 5).

Let us hear the lesser righteousness. “You have heard,” he says, “that it was said, An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth” (Deut. 19). Let us hear the greater: “But I say to you, do not resist evil” (Matt. 5).

The lesser righteousness is not to exceed the proper measure in vengeance, so that no one repays more than he has received; and this is a great step. For no one is found who, having received a blow with the fist, wishes to return only a blow with the fist, or, having heard one insulting word, is content to return one word, if he is capable of returning an equal measure.

Either a person, disturbed by anger, takes revenge immoderately, or, because he considers the one who first inflicted the injury to be justly deserving of a heavier injury than the one he suffered, though he had inflicted none. The Law greatly restrained such a disposition when it said, “An eye for an eye,” and so forth. By these expressions a measure is signified, so that vengeance does not exceed the injury; and this is the beginning of peace.

Perfect peace, however, is entirely to refuse vengeance. Between the first condition—that which is contrary to the Law, namely, returning a greater evil for a lesser evil—and what the Lord says to disciples being brought to perfection, that evil should not be resisted, there lies the middle position: that as much should be returned as was received. Through this, according to the distribution of times, a transition was made from complete discord to complete harmony.

Yet it still seems too little to the Lord if, for the evil you have received, you repay no evil, unless you are also prepared to receive more. This is what he subsequently explains: “If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also” (Matt. 5).

But why did the Lord himself, who first fulfilled the commandments he taught (Acts 1), not offer the other cheek to the servant of the high priest who struck him, but instead say: “If I have spoken wrongly, testify to the wrong; but if I have spoken rightly, why do you strike me?” (John 16)? The answer is that this commandment is to be understood as referring to the preparation of the heart, not to the outward display of an action. Hence the holy man says elsewhere: “My heart is ready, O God” (Ps. 36).

Let it therefore be said: “O Lord, lead me in your righteousness because of my enemies.” He asks for the way of this righteousness when he adds: “Direct my way in your sight.”

Righteousness is one thing, and a way is another. Righteousness is the teaching of Christ; the way is Christ himself (John 14). He displays righteousness by preaching, and the way by acting. Hence it is written: “The things that Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts 1).

A right action is not itself virtue, but the way to virtue. For through action one comes to virtue. Faith, which works through love, obtains grace (Gal. 5). And the grace of God, poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. 5), fulfills righteousness.

“I am,” says the Lord, “the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14). Understand the way as Christ acting, the truth as Christ teaching, and the life as Christ rewarding. The way leads to truth, because through the way one comes to teaching; and the teaching of truth leads to life, because when what is commanded is fulfilled, the life that is promised is obtained.

He rightly says, “because of my enemies.” For the holy Church suffers many adversaries on the holy way of God: they oppress it by persecuting, frightening, flattering, and seducing it. How far they disagree with the way of truth is shown by the words that follow:

#### 10. For there is no truth in their mouth.

And he confirms this when he adds: “Their heart is vain.” For how can there be truth in the mouth if there is vanity in the heart? “The good person brings good things out of the good treasure of the heart, and the evil person brings evil things out of the evil treasure” (Matt. 12). “For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.” Concerning these people it is rightly added:

#### 11. Their throat is an open tomb; with their tongues they acted deceitfully. Judge them, O God.

Flatterers and seducers (according to Augustine) are rightly called open tombs: since they do not possess the life of truth, they are in a certain sense lifeless, and they receive the dead into themselves; those whom they destroy by lying words and a vain heart they take into themselves.

What he says, “with their tongues,” signifies “with evil tongues.” For the wicked have evil tongues. To act deceitfully is to have one thing in the heart and another in the mouth. Hence it is said in another psalm: “They speak peace with their neighbor, but evil is in their hearts” (Ps. 27).

Almighty God judges them, because at the final examination he condemns all false and deceitful enemies. Concerning them he further adds:

“Let them fall from their own counsels; according to the abundance of their ungodliness drive them out.”

This is prophecy (according to Augustine), not a curse. He does not wish that it should happen, but foretells what he foresaw would happen. They fall from their own counsels because whatever they conceived in pride they lose without fruit when they perish. Pride has ruin, whereas humility, conversely, has exaltation.

It is said elsewhere: “On that day all their thoughts will perish” (Ps. 145). They would certainly not perish if they were thinking of heavenly things. The same Psalmist testifies: “For there are remains for the peaceful man; but the unjust will perish altogether, and the remnants of the ungodly will pass away” (Ps. 36).

The thoughts of the ungodly will therefore perish because they do not find the eternal evils they never considered, and they suddenly lose the temporal goods over which they long meditated. They will be driven out according to the abundance of their ungodliness because, on account of the many evils they committed, they will be driven from the eternal inheritance and cast into the outer darkness (Matt. 8).

It is rightly added: “For they have provoked you, O Lord.” For they would not perish merely because they sinned, unless by persevering in evil they provoked the Lord. For after we have sinned, heavenly mercy calls us back to repentance and waits a long time. He does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live (Luke 15).

But if a person neglects to turn and uses the time of grace to increase his guilt, then, by provoking further—that is, by stirring to anger—the one whom he ought to have appeased through repentance, he gravely offends him. Hence Paul says: “But because of your hardness and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s righteous judgment” (Rom. 2).

For the strict Judge will condemn him then more severely in proportion as he now waits more mercifully. But what will become of the righteous? It follows and says:

#### 12. And let all who hope in you rejoice.

At first, the joy of the righteous is in hope; hence it is said, “rejoicing in hope” (Rom. 12). “For in hope we were saved” (Rom. 7). Later, however, it will be in the reality itself. Hence he immediately adds: “They will exult forever, and you will dwell in them.”

That will be eternal exultation (according to Augustine), when the righteous become the temple of God and he himself becomes their inhabitant.

[Note: Augustine formerly had “dwelling” (*incolatus*).]

#### 13. And all who love your name will glory in you.

And rightly “in you” (according to the same author), as possessing you all as an inheritance.

“For you will bless the righteous.”

This is the blessing: to glory in God and to be inhabited by God. And because our calling is not the result of our merits but of God’s goodwill and mercy, he adds:

#### 14. O Lord, with the shield of your goodwill you have crowned us.

For God’s goodwill (according to the same author) precedes our goodwill, calling the sinner to repentance. That goodwill itself is an unconquerable shield, by which the enemy is repelled when, through the multitude of tribulations and temptations, he suggests despair of salvation.

For God is at work in us both to will and to accomplish, according to his good will (Phil. 2). “He saved us,” not because of works of righteousness that we ourselves had done, but according to his mercy (Titus 3).

## 27. TITLE OF PSALM VI

The sixth psalm is entitled: “A psalm of David, for the eighth.”

[Note: Augustine does not approve this exposition.]

By “the eighth day,” the day of judgment is understood, because all times revolve through the repetition of seven days, and what takes place on one day can be changed on another. The eighth, however, is to be considered that which will not have this variation. What happens in it will remain eternal and unchangeable.

In this psalm there is the voice of a faithful penitent exhorting others by his example to repent likewise, lest on the eighth day—that is, on the final day of judgment—they incur eternal condemnation.

## PSALM VI

### [Column 0664B]

#### 2. O Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your wrath.

God, who is unchangeable in nature (Mal. 3), with whom—as the Apostle says—“there is no alteration or shadow caused by turning” (James 1), and of whom it is said, “But you, Lord of hosts, judge with calmness” (Wis. 12), does not undergo any disturbance of fury or anger in himself. By the name “fury” is understood that immense and immoderate execution of vengeance by which sinners will be punished at the final examination.

“Anger,” however, may be understood as that examination by which imperfect souls are cleansed in purgatorial fire. It is rightly said, “Do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your wrath.” For “correct,” which seems the milder term, serves for amendment; but for one who is rebuked—that is, accused—it is to be feared that the result will be condemnation.

At the day of judgment all who do not have Christ as their foundation are rebuked (according to Augustine). Those, however, are amended—that is, purified—who build wood, hay, and straw upon this foundation, that is, things fruitless, vain, and useless (2 Cor. 3). They will indeed suffer loss, but they will nevertheless be saved, though as through fire (ibid.).

What, then, does this person pray for, who does not wish to be rebuked in the Lord’s fury or corrected in his anger? What else but to be healed? For where there is health, there is no need to fear death, nor the hand of the physician who treats or cuts. Therefore it follows and says:

#### 3. Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am weak.

There are many weaknesses of our body and soul. The body is corrupted by mortality; the soul is oppressed by temptations. Unhappy humanity is wearied by many temptations and miseries. Therefore, when someone feels misery, what should he ask for so much as mercy? When someone feels weakness, what should he desire so much as health?

It remains, therefore, that he should say: “Heal me, O Lord, for my bones are troubled.” What is signified by “bones” except the strong parts of the soul? For lest you understand this as referring to bodily bones, he explains it when he adds:

#### 4. And my soul is greatly troubled.

The inner senses are indeed troubled by consideration of one’s own guilt. The soul itself, weak and sinful, when it contemplates the subtlety of the final examination in thought, deprived of all inward strength, trembles within itself.

For there it sees condemned whatever is found to be an evil deed, an idle word, or silence, even down to the smallest thought, if it has not been directed toward God’s will. On one side there is the burning conscience; on another, sins accusing; elsewhere, justice terrifying; beneath, the dreadful abyss of hell lying open, with horrible torturers; above, the angry Judge; outside, the world on fire.

“The righteous scarcely will be saved; where will the sinner appear?” (1 Pet. 4). Let him weep and groan again, lest he incur such torments. Does he fear justice? Let him seek mercy. Does he lack strength? Let him at least acknowledge his own weakness and say: “Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am weak,” and so forth.

For a great approach to God is the knowledge of one’s own misery. He complains about the delay of healing when he adds: “And you, O Lord, how long?”

Behold, the great day of the Lord is near; near and exceedingly swift is the day of wrath, that day of calamity and misery, the day of darkness and gloom, the day of trumpet and battle cry (Zeph. 1). O bitter voice of the day of the Lord! Behold the sinful soul, a fruitless tree, worthy of the axe and the fire; dry and useless wood. Fear troubles the guilty person, conscience confounds him, thoughts reproach him, and escape is not permitted. He stands suspended before a most severe sentence.

Behold the wretched person in narrow peril, needing urgent help: “And you, Lord, how long will you delay? How long will you not hear?” Yet even in this God should not be regarded as cruel (according to Augustine), but as a good persuader of the soul, showing what evil it has brought upon itself.

The gracious Lord often delays hearing out of his great mercy, so that the difficulty of healing may make the guardianship of the health received more diligent. For what is healed easily is not guarded carefully.

Sometimes he delays so that the extent of the punishment prepared for the ungodly may be recognized: if those who turn to God suffer such difficulty, what will become of the ungodly who refuse to turn to him? As it is written elsewhere: “If the righteous scarcely will be saved, where will the sinner and the ungodly appear?” (1 Pet. 4).

And because he delays, he therefore adds:

#### 5. Turn, O Lord, and rescue my soul; save me for the sake of your mercy.

As he turns himself, he prays that God may turn toward him, just as God himself promises: “Turn back to me, and I will return to you” (Zech. 1). But perhaps it is better understood as: “Turn, O Lord,” that is, “make me turn.”

For he feels difficulty in his very conversion. Our complete conversion always finds God prepared, as the prophet Hosea says: “His going forth is prepared like the dawn” (Hos. 6).

[Note: Our author prefers the Vulgate to Augustine’s reading, which has *inveniemus eum*, “we shall find him,” corresponding to the Greek εὑρήσομεν αὐτόν, “we shall find him.” He does not sufficiently observe that the explanation which follows agrees less well with his own reading.]

For it was not the absence of him who is everywhere that caused us to lose him, but our own turning away. While we are turning, that is, while through the transformation of our former life

[Note: Augustine has the more harmonious and accurate reading: “we reshape our harsh spirit,” and immediately afterward, conversely, he reads *praebentem*, “granting,” rather than *praebet*, “grants.” Moreover, in the following verse our author transfers Augustine’s exposition piecemeal into his own work. From that point onward he reproduces the remainder almost word for word to the end of the psalm.]

we are being reshaped, we feel our spirit—hard and laborious—being turned from the darkness of earthly desires toward the serenity of divine light.

In such difficulty we say: “Turn, O Lord,” that is, “help us, so that the conversion in us may be completed”—the conversion that finds you prepared and makes you available to those who love you.

And therefore, after saying, “Turn, O Lord,” he added, “And rescue my soul,” as though it were clinging to the perplexities of this age and, in the very process of conversion, suffering the thorns of desires that tear it apart.

“Save me,” he says, “for the sake of your mercy.” He understands that he is healed not because of his own merits, since just condemnation was due to the sinner who had also been given a commandment and passed it by. “Heal me,” he says, therefore, “not because of my merit, but because of your mercy.”

#### 6. For in death there is no one who remembers you.

He also understands (according to Augustine) that now is the time of conversion, because when this life has passed, nothing remains except the recompense of merits.

“But in hell, who will confess you?” Yet that rich man confessed in hell, of whom the Lord says (Luke 16) that he saw Lazarus at rest while he himself was suffering in torment. He confessed to such an extent that he even wished his own people to be warned to restrain themselves from sins, on account of the punishments that they do not believe exist among the dead.

[Note: The reading may be *creditur*, “is believed,” in Augustine.]

What, then, is the meaning of “But in hell, who will confess you?” Does “hell” mean the place into which the ungodly are hurled after judgment, where, because of the deeper darkness, they will no longer see any light of God to whom they might confess anything?

It may also be understood in this way: “death” is called the sin committed when the divine Law is despised; “hell” is the blindness of the soul, which receives and envelops the sinner—that is, the dying person. “As they did not approve of retaining God in their knowledge,” he says, “God gave them over to a reprobate mind” (Rom. 1).

The soul prays to be kept safe from this death and from this hell while it strives for conversion to God and suffers difficulty.

#### 7. Therefore, he continues (according to Augustine), saying: I have labored in my groaning.

And as though this had produced too little effect, he adds and says: “Every night I shall wash my bed.” The bed is called here the place where the sick and weak mind rests, that is, in bodily pleasure and worldly delight. The person who tries to withdraw from that delight washes it with tears.

For he already sees that carnal desires condemn him, and yet weakness remains held by pleasure and willingly lies in it. The mind cannot rise from it unless it has been healed.

What he says, “every night,” perhaps he intended to be understood in this way: the person who, being prompt in spirit, perceives some light of truth, yet through the weakness of the flesh sometimes rests in the pleasure of this age, is compelled to suffer as though days and nights alternated according to opposing inclinations.

When he says, “With my mind I serve the law of God” (Rom. 7), he experiences something like day; but when he says again, “With my flesh I serve the law of sin,” he inclines toward night, until the whole night passes and the one day comes of which it is said: “In the morning I shall stand before you and shall see” (Ps. 5).

Then he will stand; now he lies, since he is on the bed. He will wash that bed every night, so that through such abundant tears he may obtain the most effective discipline of God’s mercy.

[Note: At this point he departs from Augustine, who has “the most effective medicine of God’s mercy.” That reading was easily taken from the Augustinian exemplar lying before our author; he did not venture to supply it from his own invention. What follows, *permanat*, was formerly also Augustine’s reading; now he has *permeat*. Finally, at the end of this section, even a small word is omitted.]

“I shall water my bed with my tears.” We understand this bed to be the same as the one mentioned above. But watering is more than washing, since something can be washed on the surface, whereas watering penetrates inward. This signifies weeping down to the inmost parts of the heart.

The variation of tenses is also significant. He used the past when he said, “I have labored in my groaning,” and the future when he said, “I shall water my bed with my tears.” The former shows what someone ought to say when he has labored in groaning without result, as though he were saying: “It did not help when I did this; therefore I shall do that.”

#### 8. Hence he continues: My eye is troubled by fury.

Whether by his own fury (according to Augustine) or by God’s, in which he asks not to be rebuked, is uncertain. But if that fury signifies the day of judgment, how can it be understood now? Or is its beginning present, in that people here suffer pains and torments, especially the loss of understanding the truth?

As I have already recalled, it is said: “God gave them over to a reprobate mind” (Rom. 1). For this is blindness of mind. Whoever is given over to it is excluded from the inner light of God, though not yet completely, while he is in this life.

There is an outer darkness (Matt. 8 and 22), which is understood to pertain more particularly to the day of judgment, so that whoever, while time remains, has refused correction may be wholly outside God. But to be wholly outside God—what is that except to be in complete blindness?

For God dwells in inaccessible light (1 Tim. 6), into which those enter to whom it is said: “Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25). The beginning of this anger, therefore, is the blindness of mind that every sinner suffers in this life.

[Note: These two words, “blindness of mind,” are not found in Augustine.]

Fearing the day of judgment, therefore, he labors and weeps, lest he be brought to that condition whose beginning he now experiences as so destructive. And therefore he does not say, “My eye has been extinguished,” but, “My eye is troubled by fury.”

The word “fury” can also be understood as the immense fervor of the soul by which the penitent is accustomed to be angry with himself. Hence it is written: “Be angry and do not sin” (Ps. 4).

It is rightly said not that the eye has been extinguished, but that it has been troubled. For the fury produced by hatred blinds the eye of the mind; but the fury produced by zeal does not blind it, but troubles it. From what it is troubled for a time by the grief of repentance, it is afterward more brightly illumined by the consolation of grace.

When he considers his remaining vices, he finds himself surrounded by all of them. Since these vices belong to the former life and to the old person, whom we must put off in order to put on the new (Eph. 4), it is rightly said:

“I have grown old among all my enemies.”

This may mean among the vices themselves or among the people who do not wish to turn to God. For even if they do not rage, even if they spare him, even if they live with him in the same banquets, houses, and cities—without any quarrel intervening, but in frequent conversations as though in harmony

[Note: Augustine has “they use” rather than “they live.”]

—they are nevertheless enemies of those who turn to God because their purpose is opposed.

For while some love and desire this world, and others wish to be freed from this world, who does not see that the former are enemies of the latter? If they can, they drag them with themselves to punishment.

It is a great gift to move daily among their words and yet not depart from the path of God’s commandments. For often the mind, striving to proceed toward God, is shaken and trembles on the very journey; and frequently it does not fulfill its good purpose lest it offend those with whom it lives, who love and pursue other good things that are destined to perish and pass away.

Every healthy person is separated from these people, not in place but in spirit. Bodies are contained by places; for the mind, however, its place is its own affection.

#### 9. Therefore (according to Augustine), after labor, groaning, and the most frequent showers of tears—since what is requested so earnestly by one who is the fountain of all mercies cannot be in vain, and since it is most truly said, “The Lord is near to the broken, or contrite, in heart” (Isa. 13 and 51)—after such great difficulties the soul signifies that it has been heard.

[Note: Augustine has the more correct reading, *pia*, “devout,” in place of *ipsa*, “itself.”]

The Church may also be understood here. See what he adds: “Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity, for the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping.”

Either this is spoken prophetically, because the ungodly will depart—that is, be separated from the righteous—when the day of judgment comes (Matt. 13); or it refers to the present, because even if they are contained together in the same places of assembly and among the same groups, the grains have already been separated from the chaff on the threshing floor (Matt. 3), though they remain hidden among the chaff. They can therefore be together, but they cannot be carried away together by the wind.

#### 10. For the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping.

The Lord has heard my supplication; the Lord has received my prayer.

The repeated expression of the same thought (according to Augustine) does not show the necessity of a narrator, but the feeling of one rejoicing. Those who are happy commonly speak in this way: it is not enough for them to state once what makes them glad.

This is the fruit of that groaning in which one labors (1 Cor. 9), and of those tears by which the bed is washed and the couch watered.

“For those who sow in tears will reap in joy” (Ps. 125). And “blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted” (Matt. 5).

[Note: From this point Augustine’s own reading appears to be restored: “and of those tears,” rather than “and of that joy,” and so forth.]

11. Let all my enemies be put to shame and greatly troubled. “Depart from me,” he said above (following Augustine), and this can also happen in the present life, as has been explained. But what he says—“Let them be put to shame and troubled”—I do not see how it could take place except on that day when the rewards of the righteous and the punishments of sinners have been made manifest. For now the ungodly are so far from being ashamed that they do not cease insulting us; and often their mockery is so powerful that they make weak people ashamed of Christ’s name. Hence it is said: “Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words before human beings, of him the Son of Man will be ashamed before the angels and the Father” (Luke 9).

But the time will come when they will be ashamed, saying: “These are the ones whom we once held up to ridicule and made the object of reproach. We foolishly regarded their life as madness and their end as dishonored. See how they are counted among the sons of God, and how their lot is among the saints! Therefore we have strayed from the way of truth, and the light of justice did not shine upon us,” and so forth (Wisdom 5). When he says, “Let them turn back and be put to shame,” who would not judge it to be the most just punishment that those who refused to turn toward salvation should turn toward disgrace? Then he added, “Very quickly.” For when the day of judgment has already begun to seem hopelessly delayed, and they say, “Peace and security” (1 Thessalonians 5), sudden destruction will come upon them. Whenever it comes, it will come very swiftly—what people have despaired of seeing arrive.

This may also be understood in another way: since God heard her as one groaning and weeping so often and for so long, she may be understood to have been freed from sins and to have subdued all the perverse movements of carnal affection, as she says: “Depart from me, all you who practice iniquity, for the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping.” When this has happened to her, it is not surprising if she has already become so perfect that she prays for her enemies. Thus what she said—“Let all my enemies be put to shame and greatly troubled”—may refer to their doing penance for their sins, something that cannot happen without shame and distress.

Nothing, therefore, prevents us from understanding the following words in the same way: “Let them turn back and be put to shame,” that is, let them turn toward God and be ashamed of having once gloried in the former darkness of their sins, as the Apostle says: “What glory did you then derive from those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Romans 6). As for what he added, “very quickly,” this must either be referred to the emotion of one who desires it, or to the power of Christ, by which he converted the nations that had persecuted the Church on behalf of their idols to faith in the Gospel with such remarkable speed.

[Note: In Augustine, “so that, as one groaning.” We pass over other, lighter matters.]

# TITLE OF PSALM VII

1. The Seventh Psalm (following Augustine) is entitled: “To the end: a psalm of David, which he sang to the Lord concerning the words of Chusi, son of Jemini.” Here we are directed to that history in the Second Book of Kings, where Chusi, David’s friend, went over to the side of his son Absalom in order to investigate and report the plans that Absalom was devising against his father at the instigation of Achitophel. Achitophel had abandoned his friendship with David and was instructing his son against his father with whatever counsel he could provide.

Spiritually, Chusi is interpreted for us as “silence”; Jemini as “right hand”; and Achitophel as “the ruin of a brother.” Through Chusi, whose name is interpreted as “silence,” it is rightly understood that our Lord fought against those deceits by silence. In that silence he concealed the mystery of his venerable Passion, and he transformed the voluntary ruin of his brother—that is, the wicked crime of his betrayer—into the order of his own mercy and wisdom. What the betrayer did with a perverse mind for the destruction of one man, Christ transferred, through provident governance, to the salvation of all.

The perfect soul, therefore, which is now worthy to know God’s secret, sings this psalm to the Lord “concerning the words of Chusi,” that is, concerning knowledge of that same secret. God, who is the right hand—that is, favorable and merciful—worked this secret for the soul. The purpose of this perfect Catholic is to exhort all the faithful to place their hope in the Lord and to live so perfectly that they may confidently await the day of judgment. He proposes himself as an example and speaks as follows:

# PSALM VII

2. “O Lord my God, in you I have hoped; save me from all those who pursue me, and deliver me.” From these words the faith and hope of this perfect soul are commended to us, as though she were saying: “I believe that you are the true God and Lord, namely, the creator and ruler of all things. Therefore I have made you specially mine—not by presuming on myself now, but by hoping in you. For ‘blessed is the person who hopes in you’ (Psalm 33). It is mine to hope in you; it is yours to save and deliver me.”

Thus, as though nothing now resisted the perfected soul except an unclean spirit, after every battle and adversity of the vices had been overcome, she says: “Save me from all those who pursue me, and deliver me.” Save me from those who pursue me from behind, and deliver me from those who confront me face to face. It is not enough for me to be safe while you defend me unless, when you deliver me, I am also secure.

[Note: Our author seems here also to have borrowed from Augustine, whose healing hand he applies to the text. The reading there is less correct: “for whom nothing remains,” and so forth.]

3. Then he returns from the plural to the singular when he adds: “Lest he seize my soul like a lion, while there is no one to redeem or save me.” The evil spirits are many in nature, but one in wickedness. They are many in number, but they all possess one will to do harm. He designates the ancient enemy by the name “lion” because of his cruelty, agreeing with the Apostle, who says: “Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls around, seeking someone to devour” (1 Peter 5).

But how can human weakness resist so strong and cruel an enemy if the one who created it does not redeem and save it? Therefore he says: “While there is no one to redeem or save me”—that is understood to mean, unless you redeem and save me. It is greatly useful for the servant of God to recognize his own weakness and to place no confidence in his own powers or merits. Divine strength begins to be present precisely when human presumption begins to fail. Hence God says through Paul: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12). Hence Truth says: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Luke 9). Such was the same Apostle when he said: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Corinthians 15).

Therefore, while he hopes in the Lord his God, presumes nothing upon his own strength, and consequently implores heavenly salvation, let us hear what kind of holy man this was. Again he invokes the Lord his God, as though giving him thanks and attributing to his name the good he received from him, and he adds:

4. “O Lord my God, if I have done this”—what?—“if there is iniquity in my hands.” That is: if I have presented my members as weapons of iniquity for sinning (Romans 6); if I have not been innocent in my hands; and, what is more perfect,

5. “if I have repaid those who repaid me with evil.” That is: if I have not been patient toward the wicked. “Let me deservedly fall empty from my enemies.” That is: by the merit of my negligence, let me fall before my pursuing enemies, empty of the fruit of righteousness. For it is just that anyone who does not strengthen himself against his enemies with the weapons of virtues and good works should fall defeated by them.

And rightly (following Augustine) he does not say, “If I have repaid those who do evil,” but “those who repay me with evil.” Whoever repays has already received something. It is a greater act of patience not to return evil to one who, having received benefits, repays good with evil than it would be not to wish to harm someone from whom one had previously received no benefit.

He boasts vainly who, although he himself is human, desires to avenge himself upon another human being; and while he openly seeks to overcome another person, he is secretly overcome by the devil. The result is emptiness: a vain and arrogant joy that he supposedly could not be defeated. He therefore understands where the greater victory lies and where the Father repays, who sees in secret (Matthew 6). In order not to repay those who repay evil, let him conquer anger rather than a human being. “Better is the one who conquers anger than the one who captures a city” (Proverbs 16:32, according to the Septuagint).

He seems to swear by an imprecation when he says, “Let me deservedly fall empty from my enemies.” This is the most serious kind of oath, when a person says: “If I have done that, let me suffer that.” But an oath in the mouth of one who swears is one thing, and an utterance in the signification of a prophet is another. Here he says what rightly happens to people who repay those who repay evil—not that he invokes such a thing upon himself or anyone else by way of an oath. Therefore he adds:

[Note: Correct the Augustinian manuscripts again: they have *vere* (“truly”) where *jure* (“rightly”) is intended.]

6. “Let the enemy pursue my soul and seize it.” Again naming the enemy in the singular (following Augustine), he makes ever clearer the one whom above he called a lion. He is the one who pursues the soul (Matthew 10). Human beings rage as far as the killing of the body, but they cannot possess the soul; the devil, however, seizes the souls he pursues in order to possess them, if he can. When he possesses them, he tramples them underfoot. Therefore he adds: “And let him trample my life into the earth.”

That is: by trampling it into the earth, let him make my life his food. For he has been called not only a lion but also a serpent, to whom it was said: “You shall eat earth” (Genesis 3). And it was said to sinful humanity: “You are earth, and to earth you shall return” (ibid.). It is rightly added, therefore: “And let him bring my glory down into the dust.”

This is the dust that the wind drives away from the face of the earth (Psalm 1): the empty and foolish boasting of the proud, inflated and without solidity, like a ball of dust raised by the wind. He rightly placed “glory” here, which he does not wish to be brought down into the dust. He wishes to possess it as something solid in his conscience, where there is no boasting before the Lord (Isaiah 35). “Let the one who boasts,” he says, “boast in the Lord” (2 Corinthians 10).

This solidity is brought down into the dust if someone, through pride and contempt for the secrets of conscience—where God alone tests a person—wishes to boast before human beings. Hence elsewhere it is said: “God will crush the bones of those who please human beings” (Psalm 52). Whoever has learned well, or has experienced, the stages by which the vices are overcome understands that the vice of empty glory must be avoided by the perfect either above all others or entirely. For the vice through which the soul first fell is the last one it conquers. “The beginning of every sin is pride” (Ecclesiasticus 10).

7. Then he prays against the devil and his angels, whose possession is sinful and ungodly people, saying: “Arise, O Lord, in your anger, and be exalted at the boundaries of my enemies.” “Arise” means “appear,” using human language, as though God were asleep when he lies unknown in his hidden places.

[Note: Here again the Augustinian reading seems to require correction: “namely, and using hidden words.”]

But when the ungodly person is justified, he becomes righteous from being ungodly and passes from the devil’s possession into the temple of God. Since it is a punishment for the possessor to lose the possession over which he desires to rule, he calls this punishment God’s anger against the devil: that he should cease to possess those whom he possesses.

[Note: Previously, *damnare* (“to condemn”) was printed incorrectly.]

He called that possession “the boundary” where he wishes God to be exalted—that is, honored and glorified—rather than the devil, while the ungodly are justified and praise God. The Lord seemed to arise in his anger when, rising from the dead, he entered the prison of hell, broke its gates, and despoiled him of the righteous whom he held captive. He was exalted at the boundaries of his enemies when he ascended into heaven and his glorious and praiseworthy name shone forth, proclaimed to the ends of the earth.

Hence it follows: “And arise, O Lord my God, in the commandment that you gave, and the assembly of the peoples will surround you.” You gave the commandment to your Apostles. You said: “Preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16). Arise, then, in those to whom your commandment has been preached. Make them rise through yourself, so that, rising from their own iniquities, they may fulfill your commandment.

Or, alternatively (following Augustine): “Arise, O Lord my God, in the commandment that you gave”—you commanded humility; appear humble. First fulfill what you commanded, so that, conquering pride by your example, they may not be possessed by the devil.

8. “And the assembly of the peoples will surround you.” There is a twofold interpretation (following Augustine). The assembly of the peoples may be understood either as that of believers or that of persecutors. Both occurred through the humility of our Lord: the multitude of persecutors, despising him, surrounded him. Of them it was said: “The kings of the earth stood forth, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ” (Psalm 2).

The multitude of believers, however, surrounded him through his humility, so that it could most truly be said: “A partial hardening has come upon Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles enters” (Romans 11); and also: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and the ends of the earth as your possession” (Psalm 2).

“And for their sake return on high.” That is: for the sake of this assembly, return on high—something he is understood to have done by rising again and ascending into the heights. For, having thus been glorified, he gave the Holy Spirit, who could not be given before his glorification, as it is written in the Gospel: “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (Acts 2).

Having therefore returned on high for the sake of the assembly of the peoples, he sent the Holy Spirit. Filled with him, the preachers of the Gospel filled the whole world with churches (Acts 1).

9. And because (following Augustine) he is to come from there to judge the living and the dead, it is rightly added: “The Lord judges the peoples.” Who is the Lord, except Jesus Christ (John 13)? For “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5).

See how this soul, which prays perfectly, does not fear the day of judgment, and with truly confident desire says in prayer: “Your kingdom come” (Matthew 6). “Judge me,” he says, “according to my righteousness.”

In the preceding psalm the weak person prayed, seeking God’s mercy rather than recalling any merit of his own. Since the Son of God came to call sinners to repentance (Luke 5), he said there: “Save me for the sake of your mercy”—that is, not for the sake of my merit. But now, because the one who was called has held fast and kept the commandments he received, he dares to say: “Judge me according to my righteousness, and according to my innocence that is upon me.”

That is true innocence which does harm even to no enemy. Thus he rightly asks to be judged according to his innocence who could truly say: “If I have repaid those who repaid me with evil.”

What he adds—“that is upon me”—may be understood not only with “innocence” but also with “righteousness,” so that the sense is: “Judge me, O Lord, according to my righteousness and according to my innocence, which righteousness and innocence are upon me.” By this addition he shows that the fact that the soul is righteous and innocent is not something it possesses by itself, but through the Lord who enlightens and illuminates it.

Hence James says: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James 1). For he is the true light that enlightens every human being coming into this world (John 1).

10. Then (following Augustine) he speaks concerning sinners: “Let the wickedness of sinners be brought to completion.” The wickedness of the people who crucified the Son of God appears to have been brought to completion (Hebrews 10); but greater is the wickedness of those who refuse to live rightly and hate the commandments of truth, for whose sake the Son of God was crucified.

“Let the wickedness of sinners therefore be brought to completion,” he says—that is, let it reach the summit of wickedness, so that judgment may now be able to come. But since it was said not only, “Let the filthy become still filthier,” but also, “Let the righteous become still more righteous” (Revelation 22), he joins this and says: “And you will direct the righteous, O God who searches hearts and kidneys.”

How can the righteous be directed except in secret? When, at the beginning of Christian times, the saints were oppressed by persecutors (Acts 15), they seemed wondrous to human beings, and the saints who could endure such things for the name of Jesus Christ seemed to be directed.

[Note: The received text of Augustine reads: “When through those things which, at the beginning of Christian times, …”]

Now, after the Christian name has begun to stand at such a height, hypocrisy—that is, pretense—has increased, especially among those who prefer to please human beings rather than God under the name of Christ. How, then, is the righteous person directed amid so much confusion of pretense, except when God searches hearts and kidneys: all thoughts, which are signified by the word “heart,” and all pleasures, which are understood by the word “kidneys”?

Pleasure in temporal and earthly things is rightly attributed to the kidneys, because they are a lower part of the human being and the region where the pleasure of carnal generation dwells. Through that pleasure human nature is transmitted into this wretched life of deceptive joy through the succession of offspring.

God therefore searches our heart and sees us to be where our treasure is (Matthew 6)—that is, in heaven. He searches the kidneys and sees that we do not acquiesce in flesh and blood, but take delight in the Lord. Thus he directs the righteous person in the very conscience before him, where no human being sees, but only the one who observes what each person thinks and what gives each person pleasure.

For the end of care is pleasure: each person directs his cares and thoughts toward reaching his pleasure. He therefore sees our cares who searches the heart; and he sees the end [alternative reading: the ends] of our cares—that is, our pleasures—who searches the kidneys. When he finds that our cares are directed not toward the desire of the flesh, nor the desire of the eyes, nor the ambition of the world—all of which pass away like a shadow—but are lifted toward the joys of eternal things, which do not change through any alteration, then God, searching hearts and kidneys, directs the righteous.

[Note: Again, the text in that same edition is corrupt. Our author transcribes the remainder word for word.]

Our works, which we perform in deeds and words, may be known to human beings; but with what intention they are performed, and toward what end we wish to arrive through them, is known only by him who searches hearts and kidneys.

[Note: In Augustine: “who perceives.”]

11. And because this righteous person possessed such direction of heart through the Lord, he rightly adds: “My just help is from the Lord, who saves the upright in heart.”

There are two functions of medicine (following Augustine): one by which sickness is healed, and another by which health is preserved. With reference to the first, the preceding psalm said: “Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am weak” (Psalm 6). With reference to the second, this psalm says: “If there is iniquity in my hands, if I have repaid those who repaid me with evil, then let me fall empty from my enemies.” There the weak person prays to be freed; here the one who is already healthy prays not to be corrupted.

With reference to the first it says there: “Save me, O Lord, according to your mercy.” With reference to the second it says here: “Judge me, O Lord, according to my righteousness.” There he seeks a remedy in order to escape sickness; here he seeks protection in order not to fall back into sickness.

With reference to the first it says: “Save me for the sake of your mercy.” With reference to the second it says: “My just help is from the Lord, who saves the upright in heart.” Both save; but the former transfers a person from sickness to salvation, whereas the latter preserves him in salvation itself.

There, therefore, the help is merciful, because the sinner who still desires to be justified has no merit, believing in the one who justifies the ungodly (Romans 4). Here the help is just, because it is granted to one who is already righteous.

Let the sinner who said, “I am weak,” say there: “Save me, O Lord, according to your mercy.” And let the righteous person who said, “If I have repaid those who repaid me with evil,” say here: “My just help is from the Lord, who saves the upright in heart.”

For if he provides the medicine by which we sick people may be healed, how much more will he now provide the medicine by which we who are healthy may be preserved? “If, while we were sinners, Christ died for us, how much more, now that we have been justified, shall we be saved from wrath through him?” (Romans 5). “My just help is from the Lord, who saves the upright in heart.”

[Note: The word “now” seems superfluous here and is certainly not found in Augustine.]

12. Then, so that we may strive to turn toward the Lord and to be upright in heart, he commends his patience to us and threatens judgment, adding: “God is a righteous judge, strong and patient; does he become angry every day?”

Who is this God the judge (following Augustine), except the Lord who judges the peoples? He is the righteous one who will repay each person according to his works (Matthew 16). He is strong, for although he is supremely powerful, he endured even ungodly persecutors for our salvation. He is patient, for he did not immediately drag even those who had persecuted him away to punishment after his resurrection, but bore with them so that they might at some time turn from their ungodliness to salvation. He still bears with them, reserving the final punishment for the last judgment and continually inviting sinners to repentance (Matthew 4 and 11). He does not become angry every day, nor does he gather his ministers for vengeance.

For now the patience of God invites people to repentance. But at the last time, when human beings, because of the hardness of their heart and mind, have stored up for themselves wrath on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s righteous judgment, he will display his wrath. Hence it follows:

13. “Unless you turn back, he will brandish his sword.”

The Lordly Man himself—that is, Christ—may be understood (following Augustine) as God’s two-edged sword, that is, the blade, which he did not brandish at his first coming but concealed, as it were, in the sheath of humility.

[Note: At the beginning of his exposition of Book I of the Psalms, our author declines, on Augustine’s authority, to call Christ “the Lordly Man,” since he knew that Augustine later rejected this expression in *Retractations* I.19. Yet it was relevant there to the purpose of his exposition; here it is of scarcely any relevance.] He will brandish it when he comes a second time to judge the living and the dead, displaying to his righteous ones the light of his manifest splendor and flashing terror upon the ungodly (Matthew 24 and Luke 21).

In other copies, instead of “he will brandish his sword,” we find “he will make his blade shine.” I believe that this expression most appropriately signifies the final coming of the Lord’s splendor.

And because he has already established this judgment in his Scriptures, it is rightly added: “He has bent his bow and prepared it.” The tenses of the verbs should not be passed over carelessly: he spoke of the sword in the future—“he will brandish it”—but of the bow in the past—“he has bent it.” Then verbs in the past tense follow:

[Note: We have corrected the reading according to Augustine, whom our author continually transcribes. Previously it read *charitatis* (“of charity”) rather than the correct *claritatis* (“of splendor”).]

14. “And in it he prepared the instruments of death; he made his arrows for those who burn.”

I would gladly understand this bow (following Augustine) as the holy Scriptures, in which, through the strength of the New Testament, the hardness of the Old was bent and subdued, as though by a bowstring. From this bow the Apostles are shot forth like arrows, or they hurl forth divine proclamations.

“He made his arrows for those who burn”—that is, for those who, having been struck, blaze with divine love. For by what other arrow was she struck who says in the Song of Songs: “I am wounded by love” (Song of Songs 4:5)? By what other arrows is the person set aflame who, desiring to return to God and to come back from this pilgrimage, asks for help against deceitful tongues, and is told: “What shall be given to you, or what shall be added to you, against a deceitful tongue?” (Psalm 119)?

They are “the sharp arrows of the mighty one, with coals of devastation”—that is, arrows by which you may be struck and inflamed with such love for the kingdom of heaven that you despise the tongues of all who resist and wish to turn you back from your purpose, and laugh at their persecutions, saying: “Who will separate me from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? For I am certain,” he says, “that neither death nor life, nor angels nor principalities, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8).

Thus he made his arrows for those who burn.

In the Greek copies it is found as follows: “He made his arrows for those who burn.” Most Latin copies, however, have “burning arrows.”

[Note: Such is said to be the Chartres Psalter, or ancient version, which is entitled “according to the Greek” and occupies the third column in the threefold Psalter of Saint Peter of Chartres; the first column contains the version from the Hebrew, and the middle column the Vulgate. Our author does not report this from his own knowledge, but from Augustine, as he does many other things.]

Whether the arrows themselves burn, or whether they cause others to burn—which they certainly cannot do unless they themselves also burn—the sense remains intact.

But since he says that the Lord prepared not only arrows but also instruments of death in the bow, it may be asked what the instruments of death are. Could they perhaps be heretics? For they too leap from the same bow—that is, from the same Scriptures—into souls, not to inflame them with charity but to destroy them with poison.

This does not happen except according to merits; therefore this arrangement also must be attributed to divine providence—not because providence makes sinners, but because it orders things after they have sinned. Those who read with an evil intention are compelled by their sinful desire to understand badly, so that this itself becomes the punishment of sin. Yet through their death the sons of the Catholic Church are awakened from sleep, as though by thorns, and advance toward understanding the divine Scriptures.

“For there must be heresies,” the Apostle says, “so that those who are approved may become manifest among you”—that is, among human beings, since they are manifest to God (1 Corinthians 11).

Or perhaps he appointed the same arrows and instruments of death for the destruction of unbelievers, while he made them burning—or for those who burn—for the exercise of believers? For it is not false that the Apostle said: “To some we are an odor of life unto life, and to others an odor of death unto death” (2 Corinthians 2).

It is therefore no wonder if the same Apostles are instruments of death to those from whom they suffered persecution and fiery arrows for inflaming the hearts of believers.

[Note: In Augustine, “in them.”]

15. After this dispensation (following Augustine), righteous judgment will come. He speaks of it in such a way that we understand every person’s punishment to arise from his own sin and his iniquity to be turned into punishment. We must not think that the tranquility and ineffable light of God itself produces something from which sins are punished; rather, the sins themselves are ordered so that the things that were delights to the sinful person become instruments for God in punishing him.

“Behold,” he says, “he is in labor with injustice.” What had he conceived, then, in order to give birth to injustice? “He conceived pain,” he says, “and gave birth to iniquity.” He did not give birth to what he conceived.
