For what is born is not what is conceived: the seed is conceived, but what is formed from the seed is born.

The seed that is conceived is an evil will; the fruit that is born is a perverse action. First the evil will arises in the heart like a seed; afterward, from this seed, an unjust action—or, more seriously, an iniquitous action—is generated like fruit.

“Injustice” is what deviates from the rule of justice. “Iniquity” is what attacks the very uprightness of justice. An unjust person is one who does not keep the precepts of justice; an iniquitous person is one who offends the Lord through iniquitous works.

It is rightly said not that he “committed” iniquity but that he “gave birth” to it. For just as there is anxious pain and labor in childbirth, so all the perverse labor and anxiously pant to bring the evil they have conceived in their heart to the outcome of action.

It is also rightly said not that he conceived an evil will but that he conceived pain, because the evil will torments itself and is itself its own punishment. Almighty God, by a just and wondrous judgment, causes the soul that has sinned to punish itself by the very sin it commits. Hence it is rightly added:

16. “He opened a pit and dug it out, and he fell into the pit that he made.”

To open a pit (following Augustine) is to prepare a deception in earthly things—that is, as though in the earth—in which the more unjust person wishes another, whom he intends to deceive, to fall. This pit is opened when one consents to the evil suggestion of earthly desires. It is dug out when, after consent has been given, one presses forward into the execution of fraud.

But how can iniquity injure the righteous person against whom it proceeds before it injures the unjust heart from which it proceeds? Thus, for example, while the fraudster desires to tear another apart through financial loss, he himself is wounded by avarice. What sane person does not see how different these two things are, when one suffers the loss of money and the other the loss of innocence?

Therefore he falls into the pit that he made. As it is said in another psalm: “The Lord is known by executing judgments; the sinner is caught in the works of his hands” (Psalm 9).

17. “His pain will turn upon his own head, and his iniquity will descend upon his own crown.”

He did not wish to escape his sin; rather, he became subject to sin like a slave, as the Lord says: “Everyone who commits sin is a slave” (John 8). His iniquity will therefore be upon him when he himself is subjected to his iniquity, because he could not say to the Lord what the innocent and righteous say: “My glory and the one who lifts up my head” (Psalm 3).

He will thus be so far beneath it that his iniquity will be above him and will descend upon him. It weighs him down and burdens him, and does not allow him to fly back to the rest of the saints. This happens when reason is enslaved in a perverse person and desire rules.

[Note: Augustine’s version has “the upright,” and shortly afterward “because it weighs him down,” rather than “which weighs him down.”]

18. And because this perfect person had already escaped these things (following Augustine), he praises God and says: “I will confess to the Lord according to his righteousness, and I will sing psalms to the name of the Lord Most High.”

The confession of God’s righteousness is expressed when we say: “Truly, God, you are righteous, since you protect the righteous in such a way that you yourself illuminate them, and you order sinners in such a way that they are punished not by your wickedness but by their own.”

Because he sees that the merits of souls are so ordered by God that, while each receives what is his, the beauty of the universe is violated in no respect, he praises God in all things. This is not the confession of sinners but of the righteous. And lest we understand it as the confession of sinners, he added at the end: “And I will sing psalms to the name of the Lord Most High.”

To sing psalms belongs to joy, whereas the repentance of sinners belongs to sadness. Let us too confess to the Lord according to his righteousness, praising and glorifying him because he is righteous; and let us sing psalms to the name of the Lord Most High by acting rightly, living well, and rejoicing spiritually, so that what is said in another psalm may be fulfilled in us: “Praise is fitting for our God” (Psalm 146).

# TITLE OF PSALM VIII

1. Titles are placed before books so that through them the author of the Scripture and its subject or purpose may be disclosed. The title of this psalm is: “To the end: a psalm of David, for the winepresses.”

“Christ is our end,” as the Apostle testifies when he says: “Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10). We strive toward him; beyond him there is nothing toward which we ought to strive. For he is the highest good, supreme blessedness, and true eternity.

This Christ, whom the prophet David wrote about in the person of the Church, sends us toward the righteous end. It should be noted that he does not say “toward the end” but “in the end.” We are not sent merely to Christ so that we may reach him; we are also sent so that we may remain in Christ and be one with him.

But what does “for the winepresses” mean? The winepresses are commonly understood (following Augustine) as martyrdoms. When those who confessed the name of Christ were crushed under the oppression of persecutions, their mortal bodies remained on the earth like grape pomace.

The winepresses may also be understood as all the faithful, insofar as they endure the adversities of this world for God’s sake. For it is written: “All who wish to live piously in Christ will suffer persecution” (2 Timothy 3).

This psalm is therefore sung (following Augustine) “for the winepresses,” for the establishment of the Church, when our Lord, after rising again, ascended into heaven. Then he sent the Holy Spirit. Filled with him, the disciples preached the word of God with confidence (Acts 2), so that churches might be gathered together.

The prophet’s purpose in this work is to invite all people to faith in Christ, whose praise is so great throughout the whole earth, and through whose grace and power the universal Church has been established and strengthened. For he says:

# PSALM VIII
2. O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name throughout all the earth! As though he were saying: “O Lord of all by your power, who are our Lord by grace, how greatly you are admired by all who inhabit the earth! You were known, Lord, only in Judea, and your name was great in Israel” (Psalm 75). You appeared among us, died for us, rose again, ascended into heaven, and poured out your Spirit upon the hearts of the disciples. When they preached, their sound went out into all the earth, and your glorious name—which had been known among one nation—became wonderful throughout all the earth (Psalm 18). Why wonderful? Because your majesty has been exalted above the heavens. Rising from the dead, you ascended into heaven, and you who seemed humble appeared glorious. From this it becomes evident who you are that descended, when it was seen by some, and believed by others, whither you ascended.

3. From the mouths of infants and nursing children you perfected praise because of your enemies. I cannot understand by “infants” and “nursing children” anyone other than those to whom the Apostle says: “I gave you milk to drink as little ones in Christ, not solid food” (1 Corinthians 3). They were signified by those who went before the Lord praising him (Matthew 21). To them the Lord himself appealed to this testimony when, in response to the Jews who asked that he rebuke them, he said: “Have you not read, ‘From the mouths of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise’?”

[Note: We have restored *in quos* (“in whom”) from the commonly transmitted text of Augustine, in place of *quo* (“where”); then, also following him, we supplied the little word *jam* (“now”); finally, we have written *consuleretur* (“provision would be made”) in place of *consulerent* (“they might be consulted”).]

He rightly did not say “you made praise,” but “you perfected praise.” For there are also people in the churches who are no longer nourished on milk but eat solid food; the same Apostle signifies them when he says: “We speak wisdom among the mature” (1 Corinthians 2). Yet churches are not perfected by these alone, because if they alone existed, provision would not be made for the human race. Provision is made when those who are not yet capable of understanding spiritual and eternal realities are also nourished by faith in the temporal history

[Note: Here we have corrected *aeternarum* (“eternal”) from Augustine, in place of *externarum* (“external”). For *commonitus* (“instructed”), which occurs a little later, Augustine reads *commotus* (“moved”).] which, for our salvation, was administered after the patriarchs and prophets by the Wisdom of God himself through the mystery of the humanity he assumed. In that history salvation is found for everyone who believes (Romans 1). Thus, instructed by authority, a person may obey the commandments; purified and rooted and grounded in love, he may run with all the saints—no longer a little child on milk, but a young man on solid food—and comprehend the breadth, length, height, and depth (Ephesians 3), and also know the knowledge of Christ’s love which surpasses understanding.

You did this, Lord God, because of your enemies: “to destroy the enemy and the avenger.” Who is understood by “the enemy” except the pagan and the heretic, and by “the avenger” the Jew, who, as though avenging and defending his law, persecuted the Christian name? You destroyed and confounded them, Lord, when, with your inspiration, infants came to your faith while the learned in the law and philosophers remained in their error. Great is the enemies’ confusion when infants praise, while the wise blaspheme; and in this, Lord, your holy name is made wonderful, since through your grace the little one grasps in you what the great cannot grasp through his own wisdom. Hence it is written: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matthew 11). Hence also what follows:

4. For I shall see your heavens, the work of your fingers; the moon and the stars, which you founded. As though he were saying: “For I shall behold and understand the Scriptures which, through the working of the Holy Spirit, you wrote by means of your ministers.” Thus the heavens appear to be the work of God’s fingers, that is, the books are understood even by those whose capacity is as slow as that of infants. Through the humility of historical faith—through what was accomplished in time—they lead those who have been well nourished and strengthened to the sublimity of understanding eternal realities and establish them in it.

[Note: More correctly, Augustine has *erigunt* (“they raise up”) in place of our reading; and in our text the very accurate reading is *in eaque confirmant* (“and establish them in it”), whereas Augustine’s common text has *in ea quae confirmant* (“in those things which they establish”).]

From these words it is plainly evident that the holy prophet is speaking mystically. If he were speaking according to the literal sense alone, he ought to have said “the lesser light” first and then “the greater light” (Genesis 1), so that he would assert that the moon and stars were founded before the sun. But because he was speaking according to the mystical meaning, so that we should understand the holy Church as the moon and all the saints as the stars, he did not wish to name the sun, because he was speaking to the eternal Sun himself. Of him it is written: “For you who fear God, the sun of righteousness shall rise” (Malachi 4). Of him the wicked will say at the end: “The sun of righteousness did not rise for us” (Wisdom 5).

By saying “the moon and the stars which you founded,” and merely remaining silent about the sun, which was made, he indicated that he was speaking to the one Sun who not only makes the sun, moon, and stars bodily, but also makes the moon—the Church—and all the stars—the saints—spiritually. Thus, whenever something is absent from the historical account, clear reasoning guides us toward the allegorical meaning.

Next he mentions the earthly human being and the heavenly one, whom the almighty Father visited: raising one wonderfully through mercy and exalting the other ineffably through the glory of divinity. In admiration of them he adds:

5. What is a human being, that you remember him? Or the son of man, that you visit him? There is a distinction between “a human being” and “the son of man.” Every son of man is a human being, but not every human being is the son of man. Adam was indeed a human being, but not the son of man. Therefore those who bear the image of the earthly human being (1 Corinthians 15), who is not the son of man, are designated by the term “human beings.” But those who bear the image of the heavenly human being are called “sons of men.”

Thus in this passage “human being” refers to the earthly one, while “son of man” refers to the heavenly one. The former is far separated from God, while the latter is present to God. For that reason God remembers the former, as one placed far away; but he truly visits the latter, whom he illuminates by his present countenance. “Salvation is far from sinners” (Psalm 118), while “the light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Psalm 4).

6. The son of man, therefore, was first visited in the man of the Lord, born from the Virgin Mary.

[Note: Recall what was observed on verse 31 of the immediately preceding psalm.]

Because of the weakness of the flesh which the Wisdom of God deigned to bear, and because of the humility of his passion, the text rightly continues: “You made him a little lower than the angels.” But the glorification by which he rose and ascended into heaven is added: “You crowned him with glory and honor, and established him over the works of your hands.”

By the works of God’s hands the angels are understood, because the Lord made them more subtle and more noble than the other creatures. And because he deigned not only to possess an angelic nature, but also to redeem humanity after its fall and subject it to himself, the text rightly continues:

7. You subjected all things beneath his feet. It explains what “all things” are: “all sheep and oxen.” By the sheep are understood all the simple people in the holy Church, who, like sheep, live simply and humbly under the governance of shepherds. By the oxen the rulers themselves are signified, who never cease to plow and cultivate human hearts with the word of teaching, so that they may return spiritual fruit to the Lord from earthly minds. Thus the Lord subjected all the sheep and oxen to himself, because he orders and governs all the elect in the holy Church, both those subject to authority and those who preside (1 Peter 3).

8. And because the wicked are mingled here with the good, he rightly adds concerning the reprobate: “Moreover, the beasts of the field, the birds of the sky, and the fish of the sea.” He uses “moreover” to distinguish the good from the wicked. This “moreover” is to be referred not only to the beasts of the field, but also to the birds of the sky and the fish of the sea.

The beasts of the field are understood as people rejoicing in the pleasure of the flesh, where nothing arduous and nothing laborious rises upward. For the field is the broad way that leads to destruction. In the field Abel is killed.

The birds of the sky are the proud, who, swollen with thought and speech, consider others beneath them and fly, as it were, in the heights of their minds. Of them it is said: “Our lips belong to us; who is our lord?” (Psalm 11).

The fish of the sea are the curious, “who travel along the paths of the sea”; that is, they inquire into temporal things in the depths of this age, things which, like paths in the sea, quickly vanish and perish. He does not say “they walk,” but “they travel along,” displaying the most obstinate zeal of those who seek empty and passing things.

These three kinds of vice—namely, pleasure of the flesh, pride, and curiosity—embrace all sins. They are enumerated by the Apostle John (1 John 2), when he says: “Do not love the world,” because “everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of the age” (Ephesians 6). Curiosity is commonly understood by “the eyes.”

The Lord was tested by these three temptations (Matthew 4). When the enemy could not prevail against him, this is said of him: “After the devil had completed every temptation” (Luke 4).

And because the Lord is so wonderful that he teaches infants, destroys the cunning, has mercy on sinners, visits the saints, possesses the angels, contains human beings, and subjects every creature to himself, let us praise him who is the beginning and the end, at the beginning and at the end, and let us never cease from his praise, saying: “O Lord, our Lord,” and so forth.

## Title of Psalm IX

1. This psalm is sung “for the hidden things of the Son.” Since it does not say whose hidden things, the only-begotten Son of God is to be understood. For the Lord himself, when he uses “Son” without addition, wishes himself, the only-begotten Son, to be understood, as when he says: “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free” (John 8). He did not say “the Son of God,” but merely by saying “the Son” he makes it understood whose Son he is.

Such an expression is appropriate only to the excellence of the one about whom we speak in such a way that, even if we do not name him, he can be understood. Thus we say “it is raining,” “the sky is clearing,” “it is thundering,” and similar expressions; we do not add who is doing it, because the excellence of the agent spontaneously presents itself to everyone’s mind.

We believe that the Lord has two comings: one past, which the Jews did not understand, and another future, which both groups await. Since the coming which the Jews did not understand benefited the Gentiles, it is not inappropriate to understand “for the hidden things of the Son” as referring to that coming, when blindness occurred in part in Israel so that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter (Romans 11).

Two judgments are also indicated in Scripture: one hidden and the other manifest. The hidden judgment is the punishment by which a person is either tested for purification, admonished toward conversion, or, if he despises the admonition, blinded toward condemnation. The manifest judgment is that by which the Lord will come to judge the living and the dead. Those who are not corrected by the hidden judgment will rightly be punished by the manifest one.

In this psalm, therefore, the hidden things of the Son are to be observed: that is, his humble coming, which benefited the Gentiles amid the blindness of the Jews, and the punishment now secretly at work—not yet the condemnation of sinners, but either the testing of those being converted, the admonition of those who should convert, or the blindness of those being prepared for condemnation.

Let it be spoken by the voice of the Son; let it be spoken by the voice of all the perfected, to the Father:

## Psalm IX

2. I will confess to you, O Lord, with my whole heart; I will recount all your wonders. As though he were openly saying: “I will praise you with my whole heart—with an undivided heart, a perfect heart.” Blessed is the person who keeps nothing of himself back for himself, but spends everything in the praise of God.

God should be praised as much as he should be loved. Therefore, just as he is to be loved with the whole heart, the whole soul, and all one’s strength (Deuteronomy 6; Matthew 22; Luke 10), so he is also to be praised. And just as no tribulation, no distress, and no creature should separate us from the love of God (Romans 8), so nothing should separate us from the praise of God.

Whoever is such a person is fit to say: “I will confess to you, O Lord, with my whole heart.” But if the Lord is to be praised, should he not also be proclaimed? Therefore it is added: “I will recount all your wonders.”

“All” means both visible and invisible things, both spiritual and bodily things; both what you visibly do concerning the body to nourish faith and what you invisibly accomplish concerning the soul to grant eternal salvation.

Why are God’s wonders recounted? So that from his works we may recognize their author (Romans 1), and from the wonders may admire the wondrous one; and thus be stirred to know and love the Lord. In this way, having despised temporal things, we may place our hope and our joy in him, like this holy man, who adds:

3. I will rejoice and exult in you; I will sing to your name, O Most High. “I will rejoice,” he says, “in you—not in the age, not in the desires of the flesh, not in the pleasures of the world, which is vanity, but in you, who are truth.”

The joy of this age leads to destruction (Ecclesiastes 1), as it is written: “Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn” (Luke 6). But the joy that is in God begins in this life and endures forever, as the Lord himself said to his disciples: “Again I shall see you, and your heart shall rejoice, and no one shall take your joy from you” (John 16).

It should be understood that gladness (*laetitia*) pertains to the mind, exultation (*exultatio*) to the body, and the psalm (*psalmus*) to good action. Therefore let spiritual gladness be in the mind, holy cheerfulness in the body, and let divine praise agree with good action. Thus what is said will be fulfilled: “I will rejoice and exult in you; I will sing to your name, O Most High.”

4. When my enemy is turned backward, they will grow weak and perish before your face. Here he begins to recount what he understands concerning the hidden things of the Son.

When the Lord was tempted, the enemy was turned backward. He was told: “Go behind me, Satan; for it is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve’” (Matthew 16). Then the one who, by tempting him, wanted to place himself before him was made to stand behind him—not by deceiving the one who was tempted, but by having no power over him.

The enemy was therefore turned backward after he was unable to deceive the heavenly human being when he was tempted, and he turned toward earthly people, over whom he can rule. Consequently, no human being puts him behind himself except one who, laying aside the image of the earthly human being, has borne the image of the heavenly one (1 Corinthians 15).

The devil was also turned backward in the persecution of the righteous. It is far more beneficial to have him as a persecutor than to have him go before us as leader and prince. We should prefer to flee from him when he persecutes us rather than follow him as our leader. We have somewhere to flee and hide in the hidden things of the Son, because the Lord has become our refuge (Psalm 89).

And because there are many servants and members of the devil, it is rightly said in the plural: “They will grow weak and perish before your face.” The devil and his servants were weakened when he lost the power he had possessed over the human race. He will perish when he is cast into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels (Matthew 25).

It is also rightly said: “They will perish before your face,” because it is written: “Let the impious be taken away, so that he may not see the glory of God” (Isaiah 26). Or, because the enemy was turned backward, the unjust and impious will therefore grow weak because of their evil works and perish because of their impieties—before your face, that is, away from your knowledge. And deservedly:

5. For you have carried out my judgment and my case; you have sat upon the throne, judging righteousness. “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Corinthians 5). In Christ, as upon his throne, he judged the Jews who were judging Christ. They judged openly; he judged secretly.

They were caught, according to what the Lord himself says: “I will catch the wise in their craftiness” (Job 5). For by their judgment and counsel they thought they had acted so that Christ’s name would be erased from the earth; yet by that very judgment they acted so that Christ’s name would become wonderful throughout all the earth.

That judgment, therefore, by which he was judged by the impious, and that case in which he was condemned though just and innocent, did not belong to them but to Christ: it harmed them and benefited Christ. In a wondrous manner Christ accomplished what he willed through their perverse desires.

The words “who judge righteousness” are spoken in distinction from those who judged iniquity. And because, once the devil and his members had been condemned, the nations were converted to Christ, the text openly continues:

6. You rebuked the nations, and the impious perished; you erased their name forever and for age upon age. Those who had long persisted in iniquity deserved severe rebuke. Those who, having despised the Creator, worshiped idols deserved to be struck with a harsh rebuke.

It is rightly said, “The impious perished,” because from being impious he became pious. He perished with respect to what he was, as he began to become what he had not been. Hence it is written: “Turn the impious, and they will be no more” (Proverbs 12).

Their name was erased forever because they are no longer called pagans but Christians. They were fornicators and became chaste; they were angry and became gentle; they were greedy and became generous; they were unjust and became just. Their name, therefore, was erased forever and for age upon age, so that neither in this age nor in the future would they be reckoned idolaters or unrighteous, if they had truly converted.

7. The enemy’s swords have failed utterly, and you have destroyed their cities. The enemy’s swords are understood as the various opinions of error, by which souls are slain as though by swords. These swords fail utterly—that is, completely—when those who had been led astray by some error return to the faith.

Of such people the Apostle says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light, for the fruit of light consists in all goodness and righteousness” (Ephesians 5).

And because, when error is removed, vices and sins are destroyed, it is rightly said: “And you have destroyed their cities.”

The cities in which the devil reigns are those people in whom deceitful and fraudulent counsels occupy the place of a senate-house. Serving that principality like attendants and ministers are the functions of the bodily members: the eyes for curiosity, the ears for lust, the hands for robbery, and the remaining members serving perverse counsels.

The populace of this city consists, as it were, of all the indulgent emotions and turbulent movements of the soul, which devise daily rebellions in a person.

[Note: It seems that *agitantes* (“stirring up”) should be restored here from Augustine.]

Therefore, wherever a king, a senate-house, ministers, and populace are found, there is a city. Such things would not exist in wicked cities unless they first existed in individual people, who are like the elements and seeds of cities.

He destroys these cities when, after their ruler has been expelled—for it is said, “The prince of this age has been cast out” (John 14)—these kingdoms are laid waste by the word of truth; wicked counsels are subdued; shameful emotions are tamed; and the services of the members and senses are taken captive in injustice and transferred to the service of good works.

[Note: In Augustine, the text reads: “are taken captive and transferred to righteousness and the service of good works,” and so forth.]

Then, as the Apostle says, “sin no longer reigns in our mortal body, so that we obey its desires; nor do we present our members to sin for its service” (Romans 6).

At that point the soul is pacified, and the human being is ordered toward attaining rest and blessedness. Hence the text immediately adds: “Their memory perished with a great noise, and the Lord remains forever.”

A great uproar occurs when impiety is overturned and destroyed. No one passes into the highest peace, where there is supreme silence, unless he has first waged war against his vices with a great uproar. Then the human being becomes a most peaceful kingdom for God, when the tumult of the vices is destroyed in him so completely that their memory is entirely erased.

8. And the Lord remains forever where iniquity finds no place, whether outwardly through action or inwardly through thought. Or, according to the historical sense, the memory of the impious perished with a great noise because the shouting and savagery of those who persecuted Christ finally subsided.

For where are those who shouted with such uproar: “Crucify him, crucify him!” (Matthew 27; Luke 23; Mark 15; John 19)? Where are the persecutors of the martyrs? Who even remembers any of them? They thought they would extinguish the Christian name. They themselves perished, but the Lord remains forever (Psalm 101).

9. He prepared his throne for judgment, and he himself will judge the world in righteousness; he will judge the peoples in justice. The throne of God is the Son of the Father. Hence it is written: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Corinthians 5).

God prepared him by sending him to be incarnate, so that in the form of a servant he might be judged, suffer, rise again, and reign; and so that the one who was judged secretly might judge openly—not unfairly or unjustly, as human beings often judge, since, while loving some more and others less, they sometimes depart from the equity of judgment, and while judging according to deeds rather than hearts, they generally fail to preserve the straightness of justice—but as an equitable and just judge he will judge the world in righteousness, sparing no one and repaying all equitably.

He will judge the peoples in justice, with conscience bearing witness (Romans 2) and thoughts accusing or defending them.

10. And the Lord became a refuge for the poor, a helper in times of opportunity, in tribulation. However fiercely that enemy who was turned backward may persecute, what harm will he do to one for whom the Lord has become a refuge?

But this will happen if he chooses to be poor for Christ’s sake, loving nothing that either abandons a person while he is living or loving it, or is abandoned by him when he dies. To such a poor person the Lord has become a refuge.

He does not immediately help his poor person as soon as tribulation begins, but only when he knows that the appropriate time has come. “The Lord disciplines the one he loves, and chastises every son whom he receives” (Proverbs 3; Hebrews 12; Revelation 3). He tests such people in tribulation and helps them at the opportune time. Therefore:

11. Let those who know your name hope in you, for you have not abandoned those who seek you, O Lord. When the soul seeking somewhere to fix its hope is being torn away from this world, the knowledge of God’s name receives it at the proper time.

God’s name itself has been proclaimed everywhere; but knowledge of the name occurs when the one whose name it is is known. Since we have already come to know God through faith (1 Corinthians 13), let us fix our hope in him and seek him through love, so that when we have found him, we may remain with him.

He does not abandon those who seek him. Rather, by possessing them he guards them; by guarding them he glorifies them; and with them he reigns forever.

Hence the holy prophet admonishes us to sing to our Lord and proclaim his grace to everyone. He says:

12. Sing to the Lord who dwells in Zion; proclaim his pursuits among the nations. A psalm is so called when there is harmony between the voice and the instrument. In the psalm we understand two things: the voice of praise and harmony of conduct.

The person truly sings a psalm who praises God in such a way that he lives rightly.

The Lord dwells in Zion, which is interpreted as “watchtower” or “contemplation,” and bears the image of the Church that exists now, just as Jerusalem bears the image of the Church that will exist in the future (Galatians 4), that is, the city of the saints already enjoying angelic life, since Jerusalem is interpreted as “vision of peace.”

Contemplation precedes vision, just as this Church precedes the eternal and immortal city that is promised.

[Note: Here, following Augustine, we correct *promittitur* (“is promised”) in place of *promittit* (“promises”).]

[Note: We have restored the punctuation of a passage corrupted by faulty pointing; shortly afterward, following Augustine, we have written *civitatis* (“of the city”) where our text had *civitas* (“the city”).]

Here we practice contemplation (1 Corinthians 13) so that we may arrive at vision. Therefore we are commanded to sing to the Lord who dwells in Zion: to praise together the Lord who inhabits the Church and to proclaim to others the pursuits of holy preaching.

We ought to praise our Lord by our deeds, contemplate him in our minds, and proclaim him with our voices, so that in his praise our tongue, conscience, and life may sound together.

Because of those who suffer persecution for the word of God that they proclaim, consolation follows:

13. For, seeking blood, he remembered them. That is, the final judgment will come, when both the glory of those who were killed and the punishment of those who killed them will be made manifest.

When he says “he remembered,” no one should suppose that the expression means that forgetfulness can befall God. Since the judgment will occur after a long time, the wording is adapted to the feelings of weak human beings, who think God has forgotten because he does not inflict vengeance as quickly as they wish.

[Note: On the contrary, this word *vindictam* (“vengeance”), which is lacking in the commonly transmitted text of Augustine, seems to have been supplied from our text.]

To such people he also says what follows: “He has not forgotten the cry of the poor.”

14. What is this cry of the poor which God does not forget? The text continues: “Have mercy on me, O Lord; see my humiliation because of my enemies.”

Why, then, did he not say, “Have mercy on us, O Lord, and see our humiliation because of our enemies”? It is not as though many poor people are crying, but as though one is crying. Or is it because one person now intercedes for the saints—the one who first became poor for us, although he was rich (2 Corinthians 8)? His members are afflicted by enemies on earth, and he himself cries out for them in heaven.

15. He himself also says: “You who raise me up from the gates of death, so that I may proclaim all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion.” A human being is exalted in him—not only the man whom he bears, who [alternatively, “which”] is the head of the Church, but also every one of us who is among the other members—and is raised above all the depraved desires that are the gates of death, because through them one goes to death.

The gates of the daughter of Zion are all the finest pursuits in the holy Church, through which one comes to the vision of peace. In these gates all the praises of God are rightly proclaimed.

16. Then it follows: “I will exult in your salvation.” God’s salvation is our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have been saved. He transferred our hearts from the empty joy of this age so that we might truly rejoice in him.

But our joy is still in hope, not in possession (1 Corinthians 13). For as long as we live here, we are afflicted by wicked people (1 John 3). Concerning them it is added: “The nations are fixed in the destruction they made.”

Consider how punishment is preserved for the sinner from his own works, and how those who wished to persecute the Church are fixed in the very destruction which they thought they were inflicting. For while they wished to kill bodies, they themselves were dying in soul.

Concerning them the text further adds: “In the snare which they hid, their foot was caught.” The hidden snare is a deceitful thought. The foot of the soul is understood as love, which, when it is perverse, is called desire; but when it is upright, it is called affection or charity.

Love moves the soul as though toward the place to which it is directed. The place of the soul, however, is not some spatial location occupied by bodily form, but delight: the soul rejoices through love that it has arrived there.

The foot of sinners, therefore—that is, love—is caught in the snare they conceal, because when delight follows a fraudulent action, since God has handed them over to the desires of their hearts, that delight binds them so that they cannot break off their love of it and transfer it to useful things.

The text therefore rightly continues:

17. The Lord will be known when he executes judgments; the sinner was caught in the works of his hands. These are the judgments by which the Lord will be known: his very works, which he performs perversely, accuse, judge, convict, and punish the sinner. He seeks no other witnesses than a person’s life and conscience.

This is the just judgment of almighty God: that each person should receive according to what he has done in the body, whether good or evil (2 Corinthians 5).

Here a song of the interlude (*canticum diapsalmatis*) is inserted, as though it were the hidden joy of separation, which now takes place not in locations but in the dispositions of souls, between sinners and the just, as grain is separated from chaff while still on the threshing floor (Matthew 3).

Then it follows: “Let sinners be turned into hell, all the nations that forget God.” For those who persist in their sins because they refuse to turn to God, it is necessary that they be turned into hell; and they will rightly feel punishment there because here they neglect to correct their guilt.

And because they did not approve of having God in their knowledge, he handed them over to a debased mind (Romans 1). Of such people it is said in one passage: “They provoked me with one who was not God and angered me with their vanities” (Psalm 105). “And I will provoke them with one who is not a people; with a foolish nation I will anger them.”

But when those people perish and are handed over by God to oblivion, will God also forget those who knew him through faith, despised the age for love of him, and endured affliction in the world? By no means. For it follows:

18. For the poor will not be forgotten forever; the patience of the poor will not perish forever. For now the poor seem to be forgotten, so long as the Lord does not defend them from the tribulation they endure; and their patience seems to perish when no glory is presently recompensed for it.

But forever the poor will not be forgotten, nor will their patience perish forever, because they receive its glory when all their labors come to an end together.

19. From the words that follow, he seems to mention the Antichrist when he adds: “Rise up, O Lord; let man not grow strong. Let the nations be judged in your presence.”

That man of sin will grow so strong that he will sit in the temple of God, even naming himself God and causing many to turn to him. Against him, therefore, the Prophet asks the Lord to rise and, by his judgment, condemn those who are going to believe in him.

Concerning him he further adds: “Appoint, O Lord, a lawgiver over them; let the nations know that they are human beings.” He rightly calls him a lawgiver, because he will bring his own law just as Christ brought his, and will preach in his own name just as Christ preached in his own name.

By saying, “Let the nations know that they are human beings,” he asks that those who are going to believe in him recognize that he walks not according to God but according to man (1 Timothy 4).

20. Because that man is believed to be destined to reach such a summit of empty glory, and will be permitted to do so much against all people and against the saints of God, that at that time some weak people will truly suppose that God neglects human affairs, the psalm inserts an interlude and then presents, as it were, the voice of those who groan and ask why judgment is delayed.

“Why,” he says, “O Lord, have you withdrawn far away?” Then, as though he had suddenly understood, or as though he had asked the question knowingly in order to teach, he adds: “You disregard in times of opportunity, in tribulation”—that is, you disregard opportunely and cause tribulations in order to inflame souls with longing for your coming.

For that fountain of life is more pleasing to those who have thirsted greatly. Thus he intimates the reason for the delay, saying: “While the impious man exalts himself, the poor person is inflamed.”

It is remarkable and true that, through the activity of those who persecute them, the little ones are trained by the exercise of a good hope toward right living.

[Note: Augustine wrote, “with what zeal little ones of good hope are kindled to right living by comparison with sinners”; I do not see why our author changes the sense, while reproducing the rest in exactly the same words.]

By this mystery it comes about that even heresies are permitted (1 Corinthians 11)—not because the heretics themselves intend this, but because divine providence brings this about through their sins. It makes and orders light, while it merely orders darkness, so that by comparison with them the light may become more pleasing, just as the discovery of truth is more delightful by comparison with heretics.

For by comparison with them, those who are approved and known to God become manifest among human beings (1 Corinthians 11).

21. They are caught in the counsels by which they scheme. That is, their evil thoughts become bonds for them. But why? “Because the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the wicked person is blessed.”

The tongues of flatterers bind souls in sins. It is pleasing to do things for which one not only fears no reprover but in which the doer is even praised and blessed.

[Note: The commonly transmitted text of Augustine reads: “and even a praiser is heard.”]

Thus they are caught in the counsels by which they scheme.

22. Let no one congratulate the person who prospers in his way, whose sins lack an avenger but have a flatterer. This is the greater wrath of the Lord. “The sinner has provoked the Lord.”

Alternatively: “He has embittered the Lord,” so that he suffers these things and the chastising blows of correction are not inflicted.

According to the multitude of his wrath, he will not seek. He is greatly angry when he does not investigate, when he seems to forget, and when he pays no attention to sins, while through frauds and crimes a person reaches wealth and honors.

This will occur above all in that Antichrist, who will appear so blessed to human beings that he will even be thought to be God. But how great this wrath of God is, the following words show.

23. “There is no God before his eyes; his ways are defiled at all times.” He who knows from Augustine where joy in the soul is to be found knows how great an evil it is to be abandoned by the light of truth. Since people consider the blindness of bodily eyes a great evil, when this light is withdrawn, how great a punishment, then, does he suffer who, being led by the prosperity of his sins to this point, has God no longer before his eyes, and whose ways are polluted at all times—that is, whose thoughts and counsels are impure? “Your judgments are removed from his sight.” For a mind conscious of its own evil, when it seems to itself to suffer no punishment, believes that God does not judge; thus God’s judgments are removed from its sight, when this very condition is a great condemnation. “He will dominate all his enemies.” For it is handed down that he will surpass all kings and alone obtain the kingdom (Ps. 2). Then, according to the Apostle, who prophesies about him, “he will sit in the temple of God, exalting himself above everything that is called God” (2 Thess. 2), and above everything that is worshiped.

24. And because, having been handed over to the desire of his heart and destined for final condemnation, he will come through wicked arts to that vain and empty height and condemnation, therefore it follows: “For he said in his heart, I shall not be moved from generation to generation without evil.” That is: “My fame and my name will not pass from this generation to the generations of my descendants unless, by evil arts, I attain such an exalted power that later generations cannot remain silent about it.” For a ruined mind, lacking good arts and alienated from the light of justice, contrives by evil arts to open a way for itself to fame, so lasting that it will even be celebrated by posterity. Those who cannot become well known desire at least that people speak ill of them, provided only that their name spread as widely as possible. I think this is what is meant here: “I shall not be moved from generation to generation without evil.” What wonder, then, if that man of sin also—who will complete all the wickedness and impiety that all the false prophets began, and will perform such great signs that, if possible, he will deceive even the elect—will say in his heart, “I shall not be moved from generation to generation without evil”?

25. “His mouth is full of cursing, bitterness, and deceit; under his tongue are toil and pain.” By “cursing” may be understood open abuse; by “bitterness,” threats and terrors; by “deceit,” flattering and seductive words, by which he will turn the multitude to his side. It is rightly described that “under his tongue are toil and pain,” because his inner being will be filled with anger, hatred, and every evil intention. [52] There is nothing more laborious than wickedness and impiety. Pain follows this labor, because the labor is undertaken not only without fruit but also to one’s destruction. This toil and pain refer to what he said in his heart: “I shall not be moved from generation to generation without evil.” And for this reason it says “under his tongue,” not “in his tongue”: for he will think these things silently, while speaking other things to people, so that he may appear good, just, and a son of God.

26. “He sits in ambush with the rich.” With what rich people (Ex Augustine) does he sit in ambush, if not with those whom he will heap with the gifts of this age? For this reason he is said to sit in ambush with them: he will display their false happiness in order to deceive people; and those who, through perverse desire, wish to be such as they are and do not seek eternal goods will fall into his snares. Therefore it follows: “In secret, so that he may kill the innocent.” “In secret” means where it is not easily understood what should be sought and what should be avoided. To kill the innocent, however, is to make the innocent guilty.

27. “His eyes look upon the poor.” [Note: [Col. 0685D] In Augustine, “the just” is more correctly read instead of “them.”] For he will chiefly persecute those of whom it is said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5). “He lies in wait in secret, like a lion in his den.” He calls him a lion in secret because both force and deceit will operate in him. The first persecution of the Church was violent: through proscriptions and torments Christians were compelled to sacrifice. The second persecution was fraudulent, carried out through heretics and false brothers. The third remains to come through the Antichrist, and nothing is more dangerous than it, because it will be both violent and fraudulent. He will have force in his imperial power and deceit in his miracles. The word “lion” refers to force; “in secret” refers to deceit. And again these same things are repeated in the same order: “He lies in wait,” it says, “to seize the poor.” This refers to cruelty. But what follows—“to seize the poor as he draws him to himself”—is attributed to deceitfulness. [Note: [Col. 0685D] Conversely, the preceding isocolon refers to deceit and the latter to cruelty.] He will seize by raging and draw by flattering.

28. “In his snare he will humble him; he will bend down and fall when he has gained power over the poor.” The snare signifies ambushes; and he rightly says, “In his snare he will humble him.” For when he begins to perform those signs, the more marvelous they appear to people, the more those holy persons who will then exist will be despised and regarded as virtually nothing. [Note: [Col. 0686D] The reading was incorrectly *qui* (“who”); we also restore *autem* (“however”) in place of *ait* (“he says”) at the beginning of the following section.] But he whom they resist through justice and innocence will seem to overcome them by wondrous deeds. But “he will bend down and fall when he has gained power over the poor”—that is, when he has inflicted whatever punishments upon the servants of God who resist him.

29. But how will he “bend down and fall”? For he said in his heart: “God has forgotten; he has turned away his face, so as not to see to the end.” This is the most wretched bending and fall: the human mind, while it seems to prosper in its iniquities and thinks itself spared, is being blinded and reserved for the final and appointed vengeance. He speaks of this when he adds: “Arise, Lord God, and let your hand be exalted.” That is, let your power be made manifest. Earlier he had said: “Arise, Lord, let not man grow strong; let the nations be judged in your sight”—that is, in secret, where God alone sees. This happened when the impious reached the great happiness that is visible to human beings, and over them was established a ruler of the kind they deserved. But now, after that hidden punishment and vengeance, it is said: “Arise, Lord God, and let your hand be exalted”—not in secret, but now in the clearest glory. “Do not forget the poor,” as the impious think when they say: “God has forgotten; he has turned away his face, so as not to see to the end.” The Church, therefore, laboring in those times like a ship amid great waves and storms, rouses the Lord as though he were sleeping, so that he may command the winds and tranquility may return (Matt. 8; Mark 4; Luke 8).

30. Once the judgment has been revealed, they understand and rejoice, saying: “Why has the impious provoked God?” That is, what benefit did it bring him to do so many evil things? For he said in his heart: “He will not inquire.” But it is not as he himself thought. For: “You see that you consider labor and pain”—of the just—“so that you may deliver them”—that is, the impious—“into your hands.” That is, into the power of your judgment. Their wickedness is not hidden from you, nor will your hand cease from vengeance.

31. “To you the poor man is abandoned.” For this reason he is poor—that is, he has despised everything belonging to this world—so that you alone may be his hope. This poor man has been handed over to them for a time, for punishment; at the end he is abandoned to you for glorification. “You will be the helper of the orphan,” while the impious was his persecutor.

32. “Break the arm of the sinner”—that is, his power—“and of the wicked; his sin will be sought, and it will not be found.” He himself will be judged by his sin, and he himself will perish because of his sin. Let sinners and the wicked therefore fear, because God will break them and reduce their wickedness to nothing. Let the poor and the orphans of Christ be comforted, because God will receive them and, after their labor, lead them to eternal rest.

“The Lord will reign forever and for ages of ages; you will perish, nations, from his land.” The Lord will not reign with an earthly empire but with a heavenly one (Luke 1). For an earthly kingdom is transitory and fragile. This kingdom will pass away; this age will pass away. Another kingdom and another age will follow, in which the Lord will reign forever (Dan. 7; Matt. 24; Luke 21). What is his land, however, except the holy Church? It will then be true, firm, and established, when this mortal nature has put on immortality and this corruptible nature has put on incorruption (1 Cor. 1). From this land the nations will perish, along with the impious—that is, sinners—of whom it is said in another psalm: “Not so the impious, not so, but like dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth” (Ps. 1). Since they will have no weight of virtue, they will not be able to reach that blessed stability, concerning which it is written: “Let the impious be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isa. 26).

33. And then what follows will be fulfilled: “The Lord has heard the desire of the poor.” Namely, that desire with which they burned when, amid the afflictions and tribulations of this age, they longed for the Lord’s day. And this desire was the preparation of their hearts. Therefore he immediately adds: “Your ear has heard the preparation of their heart.” This is the preparation of the heart of which another psalm sings: “My heart is ready, O God” (Ps. 107). Of this the Apostle says: “If we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Rom. 8). The Lord’s ear, however, should be understood not as a bodily member but as his mercy, by which he hears us.

34. And what is that desire of the poor which the Lord will hear, except that he may come “to judge the orphan and the humble”? That is, not the person who conforms himself to this age, but the one who despises everything for God’s sake and acknowledges himself to be dust and ashes. It is one thing to judge the orphan, and another to judge for the orphan. He judges the orphan even who condemns him; but he judges for the orphan who gives sentence on his behalf. The desire of the poor, therefore, is that the end of the age may come and God’s judgment take place, so that, once the just have been separated from the impious, the wicked may no longer prevail to harm the good. And this is what follows: “So that man may no longer continue to magnify himself upon the earth.”

## TITLE OF PSALM X

The title of the following psalm is: “For the end, a psalm of David.” The present exposition concerns David—that is, those who are perfectly grounded in faith. Because of their knowledge of the Scriptures, and because they courageously resist the heretics, they rightly deserve to be called David. David, I say, directs those less firmly grounded in faith and less learned in the Scriptures “for the end”—that is, toward this goal: that the institutions and commands of Christ may be their end and sufficient means for defending the faith against heretics.

Their purpose is to invite others to place all their confidence for defending themselves against heretics in God, who is the true end. Let us therefore examine the text of the psalm.

One must beware of heretics who, by recalling and exaggerating the lives of many sinners in the Church—as though they themselves were righteous—attempt to turn and tear us away from the womb and breasts of the one mother, the Church. They assert that Christ is with them and, as though piously and earnestly advising us, urge us to pass over to them and migrate to Christ, whom they falsely claim to possess. It is known that in prophecy Christ, when he was indicated by names, was also allegorically called a mountain. They must therefore be answered and told:

## PSALM X

1. “In the Lord I trust; how then do you say to my soul, ‘Migrate to the mountain like a sparrow’?” As though he were saying: “Since my soul has such a mountain in which to place its trust—namely, Christ—for what reason do you say that it should pass to another mountain like a sparrow (Ps. 67), that is, like a cautious and clever soul? I hold to one mountain in which I trust. Why do you say that I should pass over to you, as though there were many Christs?

“Or, if you say in your pride that you are mountains, then one ought indeed to be a sparrow by the powers of wings and the commandments of God. But those very things forbid one to fly to these mountains and place one’s hope in proud people. I have a house in which I may rest, because I trust in the Lord. For the sparrow also finds a house for itself (Ps. 83), and the Lord has become a refuge for the poor (Ps. 9).”

Let us therefore say with complete confidence, lest while seeking Christ among the heretics we lose him: “In the Lord I trust.” By these words we are taught to beware of the crafty doctrines of the heretics.

2. Therefore it follows: “For behold, sinners have bent the bow.” That is, they have applied Holy Scripture to their own errors and their own interpretations. Scripture is rightly called a bow, because just as an arrow that strikes emerges from a bow, so from Scripture proceeds a judgment that pierces the heart.

“They have prepared their arrows in the quiver.” That is, they have fitted their poisoned interpretations into Holy Scripture itself, which contains judgments within itself as a quiver contains arrows. They have prepared them for this purpose: “To shoot in darkness at the upright in heart.” That is, to strike those who are upright in faith with obscure interpretations. Or “in darkness”—that is, in the condition of those who are less capable of understanding Holy Scripture and less firmly grounded in faith. For the darkness of the heart is ignorance.

And because such danger hangs over us from these people, one must say: “In the Lord I trust.” Therefore it is necessary, O Lord, to trust in you and have recourse to your help.

3. “For they have destroyed what you established.” That is, faith, which, although one, is possessed in diverse aspects: concerning humanity and divinity, and concerning past, present, and future things. It is therefore expressed in the plural because it consists of many elements. This faith you established—that is, by your grace you inspired a perfect and complete faith in the hearts of the faithful and proclaimed it through your teaching. “They have destroyed it,” insofar as it lay within their power, and denied it.

This turn of expression has been made for the sake of confirmation. Such things sinners contrive to do. But “what did the just man do?” That is, what did the Lord do, who acts justly in both respects, leaving no evil unpunished and no good unrewarded? What did he do? This question is not asked from ignorance but in order to instruct the ignorance of the weak. The Lord did what belonged to him. Therefore, after the question, the answer is given:

[Col. 0688A]

4. “The Lord is in his holy temple; the Lord’s throne is in heaven.” Those in whom the Lord dwells through faith are the temple of God. Therefore the Apostle says: “The temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Cor. 3). Those who advance after faith to contemplation are not merely a temple but also heaven. The Apostle designates them when he says: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3). In them the Lord sits as in heaven. These words show that the Lord neither abandons the greater for the sake of the lesser nor despises the lesser for the sake of the greater.

5. Therefore it is rightly added: “His eyes look upon the poor.” That is, the regard of his mercy is not turned away from the poor person—namely, from the one of whom it is written: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5).

It is no wonder that the just Lord dwells in the poor who trust in him, illuminates by his indwelling the wise who proclaim his faith, and blinds those who are lifted up through error. “For his eyelids examine the children of men.” The sacred Scriptures, which are closed in some places and opened in others, are like God’s eyelids. They examine—that is, test—the children of men, whether they are wearied by the obscurity of things or exercised by it; whether they are puffed up by knowledge of things or strengthened by it.

6. He says this still more plainly when he adds: “The Lord examines the just and the impious.” That is, he tests the good and the evil. But whatever is just in a person, he has from God; whatever is impious, he has from himself. How so? By loving iniquity and thus hating himself. This is what he says: “But whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul.” In contrast, the person truly loves himself who hates sin.

7. “He will rain snares upon sinners.” The same outpouring of the Scriptures, according to each person’s merit, is for the sinner a rain of snares and for the just a rain of abundance. When Scripture is wrongly understood, the Lord rains snares upon sinners; when it is rightly understood, he makes the breasts of the devout and faithful fruitful. Thus the same things benefit the good and harm the evil. Therefore Paul says: “To some we are the fragrance of death unto death, but to others the fragrance of life unto life” (2 Cor. 2).

8. “Fire, sulfur, and the spirit of storms are the portion of their cup.” This is their punishment and their end (Ex Augustine): those through whom the Lord’s name is blasphemed are first ravaged by the fire of desire, then as though covered by sulfur through the stench of their deeds, and finally burned with the evil spirits in eternal fire. This is the portion of their cup—that is, of their tribulation—so that, just as the just receive eternal life as their portion, the impious may receive everlasting condemnation as theirs.

I think it is called a cup for this reason: so that we may not suppose that anything beyond measure or proportion occurs, even in the punishments of sinners, through divine providence. Therefore, as though giving the reason why this happens, he adds: “For the Lord is just, and he loved justices.” He did not place “justices” in the plural without reason. In the many just persons, many justices seem to exist, although God’s justice is one, and all participate in it. Therefore he returns again to the singular when he says: “His face has seen equity.”

The Lord is just in himself, so that he loves his justices in us. He desires us all to be such as he himself is. Hence he admonishes us, saying: “Be holy, because I am holy.” Keep justice, and you will be like the Lord, and the just Lord will love you as just. But if you neglect justice, you will nevertheless not go unpunished. For it follows: “His face has seen equity.” In the good as well as in the evil, the severity of God’s face sees equity. Equity consists in his repaying good things to the good and evil things to the evil. Equity consists in rendering what is deserved according to one’s deeds.

Thus what he says, “The Lord is just, and he loved justices,” concerns the order of living rightly; what he adds, “His face has seen equity,” concerns the reward assigned to each deed.

## TITLE OF PSALM XI

[Col. 0689A]

1. Titles are placed before the psalms because the titles show what is contained in the text of the psalms. The title of this psalm is: “For the end, for the octave, a psalm of David.” This is a psalm of David—that is, of the perfect soul striving toward the end, namely Christ, and in this psalm acting and praying “for the octave,” which is understood as the eternal age that will be given to the saints after this present time, which revolves through seven days.

This psalm concerns the failing of the saints, the diminution of truth, the coming of Christ and the splendor of divine eloquence, the salvation of the just, and the destruction of the reprobate. This holy man, therefore, seeing that the world lies in wickedness (1 John 5) and that we are placed amid many miseries, intends to set before us a form of prayer, so that by his example we may pass through temporal things in such a way as to reach eternal life. He says:

## PSALM XI

[Col. 0689B]

2. “Save me, O Lord, because the holy man has failed, because truths have been diminished among the children of men.” He seems to look ahead to that time when there was neither ruler nor prophet in Israel, and each person did what was right in his own eyes (Dan. 3). Hence it is said in Hosea: “For many days the children of Israel will sit without a king, without a prince, without sacrifice, without altar, without priesthood, without manifestations” (Hos. 3).

When he says, “Truths have been diminished,” he does not mean that truths are diverse (Ex Augustine), since there is one truth by which holy souls are illumined. But because there are many souls, many truths may be said to exist in them, just as from one face many images appear in mirrors.

3. Where truth fails, vanity must necessarily abound. Therefore it follows: “Each person has spoken vain things to his neighbor; they have spoken with deceitful lips and with a double heart.” “Neighbor” should be understood as every human being (Ex the same), because there is no one with whom evil ought to be practiced. “Love of neighbor does no evil” (Rom. 13). By saying twice, “with a double heart,” he signifies a divided heart.

These words therefore show that the children of men have been so diminished in truth that they strive to serve vanity and double falsehood. He announces in prayer and prophecy that the dispersion and destruction of this vanity will come through Christ’s arrival, when he adds:

4. “May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips and the tongue that speaks great things.” He says “all” (Ex the same), so that no one may think himself excepted, just as the Apostle says: “Upon every soul that works evil” (Rom. 2). A tongue that speaks great things is a tongue that speaks lofty and proud words. The following words apply to such proud people:

5. “They said, ‘We will magnify our tongue; our lips belong to us; who is our lord?’” It is characteristic of the proud that, insofar as they can, they desire to appear as lords; they despise authority over themselves; they speak grandly; and whatever they have drawn from their own judgment, they defend as though it were reason, out of the swelling of pride.

We must therefore beware of the vice of talkativeness and pride, and of wishing to persist obstinately in what we ourselves have said, lest—God forbid—we be among those whom the Lord destroyed because of such vices. For pride brings confusion, just as humility, by contrast, brings exaltation. It is written: “For God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. 4). Therefore what follows is now spoken in the person of God the Father:

6. “Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, now I will arise, says the Lord.” The merciful Father himself, because of the needy and poor—that is, those lacking spiritual riches and impoverished in spiritual goods—deigned to send his Son. His preaching begins in this way in Matthew, on the mountain, when he says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5).

Therefore he immediately adds: “I will place him in salvation; I will act confidently in him.” He does not say what he would place. But because he said “in salvation”—that is, in Christ, according to the words, “For my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2)—it is understood that he placed in him that which pertains to removing the misery of the needy and consoling the groaning of the poor.

In him also he acted confidently, in accordance with the Gospel: “For he was teaching them as one having authority” (Matt. 7), “not as their scribes” (Mark 1). Concerning his authority Daniel spoke as follows: “I saw in the vision of the night, and behold, the Son of Man was coming on the clouds of heaven. And to him were given principality, honor, and a kingdom, and all peoples, tribes, and tongues will serve him. His power is an eternal power that will not be taken away, and his kingdom will not be destroyed” (Dan. 7).

7. Concerning the splendor of his eloquence it is added: “The utterances of the Lord are pure utterances, silver tested by fire, approved by the earth, purified sevenfold.” He says “pure” as being without the corruption of pretense (Ex Augustine). For many proclaim the truth impurely, because they sell it for the price of this age’s advantages. Of such people the Apostle says that they proclaim Christ “not purely” (Phil. 1).

They are rightly compared to silver tested by fire, because just as silver is tested by fire so that it may be pure and bright, so divine utterances have been tested by the fire of the Holy Spirit. Hence the Lord himself says: “The words that I speak to you are spirit and life” (John 14). The same Psalmist says elsewhere: “Your utterance is intensely fired” (Ps. 118).

It is rightly called “approved by the earth,” because the divine utterance is proven by the faithful of the holy Church to be right and true. It has been “purified sevenfold” through fear of God, piety, knowledge, fortitude, counsel, understanding, and wisdom (Isa. 11).

There are also seven degrees of blessedness, which the Lord sets forth in the same discourse that he delivered on the mountain: “Blessed are the poor in spirit; blessed are the meek; blessed are those who mourn; blessed are those who hunger and thirst for justice; blessed are the merciful; blessed are the pure in heart; blessed are the peacemakers” (Matt. 5; Luke 6). It may be observed that the whole extended discourse was developed from these seven statements. For the eighth—where it says, “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for justice”—signifies the very fire by which the silver is tested sevenfold.

What Christ’s coming accomplished through the tested utterance is shown when he adds:

8. “You, O Lord, will preserve us and guard us from this generation forever.” You will guard us from this wicked and perverse generation, so that we may not be corrupted by their life and conduct; and you will preserve us forever, so that we may rejoice with you eternally. Here you will guard us as needy and poor; there you will preserve us as prosperous and rich. These words concern the elect alone. For concerning the reprobate it is added:

9. “The impious walk in a circle; according to your exaltation you have multiplied the children of men.” They are rightly said to walk in a circle, because they revolve in desire for temporal things, which turn like a wheel in the repeated circuit of seven days. Therefore they do not reach the eighth, that is, eternity, for which this psalm is entitled.

So also it is said in Solomon: “A wise king is a winnower of the impious, and he will bring the wheel of evils upon them.” There is also a multiplication in temporal things that turns one away from the goodness of God. [Note: [Col. 0689] I would prefer that, in accordance with Augustine’s common text, *ab unitate* (“from unity”) be written instead of *a bonitate* (“from goodness”).] Hence “the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly habitation depresses the mind that thinks of many things” (Wis. 9). The just, however, are multiplied according to the exaltation of God when they go from strength to strength (Ps. 83).

## TITLE OF PSALM XII

1. The title of this psalm is: “For the end, a psalm of David.” The Apostle says: “Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10). We believe in him when we begin to enter upon the way; we shall see him when we have arrived. Therefore the End himself has been appointed as a psalm for praising God.

And because God is sung to in these verses, it is not without reason called a psalm, the text of this work. A psalm was customarily made through the movement of the fingers and the harmony of the voice. He struck the strings, the instrument resounded, and together with the instrument he himself sang the words (1 Chron. 15). This signifies that good works and praise ought to harmonize in us.

This is what the psalm urges us toward. It is inscribed with the name David, who represents the Church or any perfect soul. Therefore the holy man intends in this psalm to remind us that, following his example, we should continually lament the evils of this exile and ardently long for the vision of heavenly glory; that we should pray not to fall into deadly sins and not give the devil an opportunity to insult us; and that for this steadfastness we should give thanks not to ourselves but to God.

At the end he also shows that his heart rejoices in the Lord and that he sings and makes melody to him by praising him and living well. He prays as follows:

## PSALM XII

[Col. 0691B]

2. “How long, O Lord, will you forget me to the end? How long will you turn your face from me?” As Augustine says, just as God does not forget, so he does not turn away his face. But Scripture speaks according to our manner. God seems to forget us when he permits us to labor for a long time in this pilgrimage. He seems to turn his face away when he hides from us the manifestation of his vision.

Two kinds of compunction are therefore suggested to us in these words. One is that by which we should lament the misery in which we are. The other is that by which, weeping, we should sigh for the glory of the heavenly homeland in which we are not.

3. Other kinds of compunction are also shown when it follows: “How long shall I place counsels in my soul, and pain in my heart throughout the day?” “Throughout the day” signifies continuation. Counsel is needed only in adversity. To place counsel in one’s soul throughout the day is carefully and continually to anticipate and avoid the suggestions and sins by which the soul is corrupted. He placed counsel in his soul who said: “I have hidden your utterances in my heart, so that I may not sin against you” (Ps. 118).

To have pain in one’s heart throughout the day is to afflict the heart continually with sorrow over sins committed. Therefore in this counsel and sorrow of ours we ought to lament the past and beware of the future.

But because this is our struggle against spiritual wickedness (Eph. 6), and because “the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul” and “the earthly habitation depresses the mind that thinks of many things” (Wis. 9), the soul, seeing these enemies and groaning, adds:

4. “How long will my enemy be exalted over me?” The enemy is exalted over us whenever we are convicted of sinning. The Apostle says: “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin, which is in my members” (Rom. 7). This pertains to the enemy’s exaltation. Therefore, still groaning, he adds: “Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death?” But what follows? “The grace of God through Jesus Christ” (ibid.).

[Col. 0691D]

5. He implores this grace when he says: “Look upon me and hear me, O Lord my God.” “Look upon me” refers to what was said: “How long will you turn your face from me?” “Hear me” refers to what was said: “How long will you forget me to the end?” He rightly says, “O Lord my God.” “Lord” means Savior; “God” means Creator of all things, God by power; “my,” however, means mine by grace.

6. Therefore it follows: “Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death, lest at some time my enemy say, ‘I have prevailed against him.’” God is the light of our heart; sin is the death of the soul. Hence it is written: “The soul that sins, it shall die.” The Apostle awakens us from this sleep of death when he says: “Awake, you just, and do not sin” (1 Cor. 15).

We must therefore pray that the eyes of our heart may be illumined by the one who is true light, so that through negligence we may never sleep in the death of sin; lest our ancient enemy insult us at some time and say that he has prevailed over us, if he is able to subject us to himself through sin. For the prince of darkness will rejoice if he can disturb in us the state of uprightness. Therefore he adds:

7. “Those who trouble me will rejoice if I am shaken; but I have hoped in your mercy.” For this they trouble us; for this they frequently disturb us with innumerable tribulations, so that by their disturbances they may remove us from the state of uprightness. Placed amid such dangers, we must neither despair nor, on the other hand, presume upon our own strength. Rather, all our hope must be fixed upon his mercy, for he can both illumine us so that we do not err and strengthen us so that we stand firmly.

8. And because hope in God produces joy of heart, it is rightly added: “My heart will rejoice in your salvation; I will sing to the Lord, who has granted me good things, and I will make melody to the name of the Most High Lord.”

Here he commends three things to us: the heart rejoices; the voice sings; the works make melody. From these words we are shown the perfection of divine praise. If we wish to praise the Lord our God purely and perfectly, we must refer everything that is in us to his praise, so that all our things may resound in his praise—namely, our life, tongue, and conscience. This is because he saves us through his salvation, that is, through Christ; because he continually grants us temporal and spiritual goods; and because his name is Most High.

Since we cannot find a Lord higher or better than he, it is just that we persevere in his praise, love, and service.

## TITLE OF PSALM XIII

1. The title of this psalm is the same as the one above. It concerns the error of the nations and the unbelief of the Jews, who denied that the Lord Christ was God (John 19). Therefore, corrupted and made useless through error and depravity of conduct, they also attempted to corrupt others with themselves and lead them into their own error.

With these people rejected by the Lord, he declares that he dwells among a just generation and sends his Salvation from Zion, so that he may convert his people from captivity, so that Jacob may rejoice in him and Israel be glad.

These things have been written for us so that, attending to their condemnation and the salvation of the faithful, we may remain in faith in the Lord Jesus, avoiding the former and imitating the latter. He is our end and reward; when we have come to him, having spiritually become Jacob and Israel, we shall rejoice perfectly in him.

This is the purpose and usefulness of this psalm. Its subject is the fool himself.

## PSALM XIII
### 2

The fool said in his heart, “There is no God.” The Gentile people may be understood here: they so lost their reason concerning the natural law they had received that they did not believe that the very one by whom they were created was the Lord. Hence the Apostle says: “They exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for an image of corruptible man, and of birds, quadrupeds, and serpents” (Rom. 1). For this reason, God also handed them over to passions of dishonor, so that they might dishonor their bodies among themselves.

The words that follow agree with this: “They are corrupt, and have become abominable in their pursuits; there is none who does good, not even one.” They were corrupt in vices and sins, and became abominable by changing the natural use into that use which is contrary to nature (ibid.). He rightly calls their vices and sins “pursuits,” because they committed them not merely through ignorance or weakness, but—which is more serious—deliberately and willingly. Among them there is not one who does good, since they refuse to believe in the one God (Rom. 1). “For without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11). Hence Truth itself says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15).
