Because they first sinned in their hearts, they afterward sinned in their actions, and by the just consequence of their error they were punished with the penalty of corruption. Therefore, our mind must be guarded with every vigilance, lest it be corrupted by any vice, since our thoughts do not fly empty past the eyes of God. Within, he sees what he punishes outwardly: hidden guilt is followed by open punishment, so that inward faults are punished by outward evils, and the heart publicly collapses because it was secretly sinning.

### 3

The words that follow seem to concern the Jews. For he says: “The Lord looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see whether there is anyone who understands or seeks God.”

With regard to the Jews (from Augustine), they may be called more honorably “children of men” because of their worship of God, in contrast to the Gentiles, who, because of their worship of stones, became corrupt and abominable. Thus the Lord looks down upon the children of men through his holy souls. This is signified by the words “from heaven,” so that he may see—that is, make it manifest—whether anyone understands God in his heart or seeks him in his conduct.

Alternatively, by “children of men” we may understand imitators of the carnal (Eph. 6), just as, conversely, imitators of God are called children of God. For God looks upon sinners through righteous men; through the good he reproves the wicked; and through the life and teaching of the saints he makes known the error and injustice of the perverse. Concerning these, the following is added:

### [Column 0693B] 4

“All have turned aside; together they have become useless; there is none who does good, not even one.”

This should not be understood to mean that all have turned aside in such a way that there was not even one person in the human race who did what was good, since shortly afterward he says, “The Lord is in the righteous generation.” Rather, among those who are imitators of the carnal—whose life and self-restraint are corrupt—there is no one who does good. For as long as a person is wicked, he cannot do good.

How far they had turned aside from the way of truth is shown by the words that follow: “Their throat is an open tomb; with their tongues they acted deceitfully; the poison of asps is under their lips.” They are aptly compared to an open tomb: just as a tomb lies open to receive dead corpses, so they gaped in order to draw simple souls to themselves and incorporate them into themselves after those souls had been destroyed through error.

After saying “with their tongues,” he rightly added “their own,” to signify wickedness. The wicked have wicked tongues. The Jews acted deceitfully with their tongues when they asked the Lord whether it was lawful to pay the tax to Caesar or not (Matt. 22). They had deceit in their mouths but concealed the poison of malice in their hearts. If he said, “It is lawful,” they would immediately have accused him on the basis of the Law, in which it is commanded that one serve the Lord alone (Deut. 6). But if he said, “It is not lawful,” they had brought the Herodians, who would at once seize him and condemn him for prohibiting the royal tribute (Matt. 22).

They are rightly compared to an asp, because just as an asp stops up its ear against the voice of the charmer (Ps. 57), so they stopped their ears against the voice of preaching (Acts 6). “Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness; their feet are swift to shed blood.”

Their mouth was full of cursing when they said, “Are we not right in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?” (John 8). They were also filled with bitterness when they said to Pilate, “Crucify him; he is guilty of death” (Matt. 27; Mark 15; Luke 23; John 19). Their feet were swift to shed blood when they led him outside the city and killed him. Hence they were crushed by their enemies and brought to the misery of captivity.

Therefore it is added: “Destruction and misery are in their ways, and they have not known the way of peace.” For if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Cor. 2). “There is no fear of God before their eyes.” This was the cause of the hardness of their hearts: because they did not fear the Lord, they hardened their hearts against believing. What was written therefore happened to them: “He whose mind is hard will fall into evil” (Prov. 28). The prophet rebukes their wickedness when he continues:

### 5

“Will not all those who work iniquity understand, who devour my people as though eating bread?”

They did not know what they were doing when they killed the Lord. Hence, while praying, he himself said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23). But they will understand at the judgment, when they see the one whom they pierced (Zech. 12), and when they behold the holy martyrs whom they killed (Rev. 1). They are described as devouring them like bread, in order to indicate their attitude. For just as bread is sweet to eat, so the persecution of the saints was sweet to them. They are therefore described not as eating but as devouring, so that not only their will but also their eagerness may be signified.

### 6

“They did not call upon the Lord; there they trembled with fear where there was no fear.”

What wonder if they trembled, since they did not call upon the Lord (Rom. 10)? Who is secure without the Lord? For they said: “If we leave him alone in this way, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation” (John 11). They feared losing an earthly kingdom where there was no cause for fear, and they lost the kingdom of heaven, which they ought to have feared losing.

This is also to be understood of all temporal advantages: while people fear their loss, they do not attain eternal things. This is what all those who work iniquity do not understand. The following is added:

### 7

“For the Lord is in the righteous generation.”

Certainly not in the perverse one. Why is the Lord not among them? He adds the reason: “You have confounded the counsel of the poor, because the Lord is his hope.” For you said: “He trusted in God; let him deliver him now, if he wants him.” You despised the humble coming of the Son of God because you did not see in it the pomp of the world. Because he hoped in God, he was despised by you, who prefer earthly things to heavenly ones.

### 8

“Who will give salvation to Israel from Zion?”

The implied answer is: who else but the one whose humility you despised? He will come in glory to judge the living and the dead and to establish the kingdom of the righteous. Because, through this humble coming, a partial blindness has come upon Israel so that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter, through that other coming what follows will take place, and thus all Israel will be saved (Rom. 11).

[Note: Previously there was, incorrectly, the single word *Providens*; we did not hesitate to emend it to *Pro Judaeis ex Augustino* (“Concerning the Jews, from Augustine”).]

For the Jews the Apostle also applied that testimony of Isaiah in which it is said: “He will come from Zion, the one who turns away ungodliness from Jacob” (Isa. 57). To this agrees what is said:

### 9

“Who will give salvation to Israel from Zion, when God turns back the captivity of his people? Jacob will rejoice, and Israel will be glad.”

By Jacob are designated those who fight and struggle against vices. For Jacob is interpreted as “supplanter.” By Israel, however, are understood those who, after the battle against vices, have progressed as far as contemplation of God, since Israel is said to mean “seeing God.”

As long as the body, which is subject to corruption, weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling burdens the mind occupied with many thoughts (Wis. 9), we are in captivity. But when God turns back our captivity—which will happen when this corruptible body puts on incorruption and this mortal body puts on immortality (1 Cor. 15)—then there will be rejoicing in body and soul for those who have spiritually been Jacob, that is, who have supplanted vices.

There will be gladness in the mind of those who have spiritually been Israel, who have burned with love and contemplation of divinity. There the labor of the righteous will end and love will be perfected. There the active and contemplative life will be rewarded with eternal joy. There the everlasting recompense of those progressing and those perfected will be paid.

## Title of Psalm XIV

The Fourteenth Psalm is headed, “A Psalm of David.” Our David is Christ, as we have often said. Then we read in Exodus that the lamb is sacrificed on the fourteenth day, when the moon is full, when none of its light is lacking (Exod. 12). This psalm therefore signifies for us a certain fullness of light and a blessed satisfaction. Its purpose is to show us the royal way by which, through Christian warfare, we may journey toward our homeland.

It speaks of the perfect commandments of righteousness, through which it teaches us that we can enter the heavenly realm (Matt. 19). It also joins lesser commandments to them, so that in these the weakness of beginners may exercise itself and be able to advance toward higher things. But let us now hear what the prophet says:

## Psalm XIV

### 1

“Lord, who will dwell in your tabernacle? Or who will rest upon your holy mountain?”

Not first on the mountain and afterward in the tabernacle, but first in the tabernacle and afterward on the mountain. A tabernacle is not a permanent house; it has no foundation. It is a thing of war, moved from one place to another, and it moves when its inhabitant migrates. It signifies the Church of the present age. For we do not remain here as inhabitants (Heb. 13), but are going to migrate elsewhere.

Mountains, however, have firm foundations. Thus, by the name “mountain,” the stability of the future homeland is signified. Since we are going to migrate from the tabernacles to the mountain, we must learn who those are who will migrate to God’s holy mountain. Let us therefore hear what the Holy Spirit answers the prophet as he asks:

### 2

“He who enters without blemish and practices righteousness.”

He who enters is on the way. He did not say, “He who reaches the end without blemish,” but “he who is still on the journey and has no blemish.”

Someone might say: “I have no blemish; I have done no evil.” It is not enough for us not to do evil unless we also do good. But who can be without blemish, when the Apostle says, “We all offend in many ways” (James 3), and, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1)?

Yet before the merciful Lord a person is regarded as without blemish when guilt no longer rules him through delight. Hence the same prophet, when he prayed to be cleansed from hidden and alien sins, added: “If they do not rule over me, then I shall be blameless” (Ps. 18).

[Note: The Author clearly indicates that he read *dominata*, that is, “sins that have gained dominion”; this is the older and more genuine reading.]

The first entrance into righteousness, therefore, is to keep oneself unstained by sin; advancement consists in becoming perfect in goodness. Let us therefore strive to enter without the blemish of sin and to practice works of righteousness. Righteousness does not know father or mother; it knows truth, does not accept persons, and imitates God.

### [Column 0695C] 3

Let us hear the works of righteousness that follow: “He who speaks truth in his heart.”

Many speak truth with their lips but not in their hearts. They appear to speak the truth, but their hearts do not agree with their lips. For example (from Augustine), someone might deceitfully point out a road while knowing that robbers are on it and say, “If you go by this road, you will be safe from robbers,” and it happens that the robbers are truly not found. He has spoken truth, but not in his heart. He thought one thing and, without knowing it, spoke the truth.

Therefore it is not enough to speak truth unless it is also true in the heart.

“He who has not acted deceitfully with his tongue.” Deceit is practiced with the tongue when one thing is uttered by the mouth and another is concealed in the heart. He does not act deceitfully with his tongue who expresses in speech what he has considered in his mind.

“Nor has done evil to his neighbor.” By “neighbor” we must understand every human being (Luke 10). Therefore it is written: “What you do not want done to you, do not do to others” (Matt. 22), so that we do no one the evil that we certainly do not want another to do to us (Luke 6).

“And has not accepted reproach against his neighbors.” This is a great matter. “Never,” he says, “has a neighbor murmured against him” (Tob. 4). He never found any occasion to slander him. This virtue surpasses human nature; it is the grace of God.

### 4

“The wicked person is reduced to nothing in his sight.”

Even if he is an emperor, even if he is a prefect, even if he is a bishop, even if he is a presbyter—for these are the dignities in the Church—whoever is wicked is counted as nothing in the sight of the holy man.

Immediately it follows: “But he glorifies those who fear the Lord.” This holy man, who enters without blemish and despises the powerful because they are wicked, if he sees someone who fears God, he glorifies him, even if he is poor.

Just as the preceding words pertain to the perfect (from Augustine), so the words he is now about to speak pertain to beginners.

### 5

“He who swears to his neighbor and does not deceive; who has not lent his money at interest and has not accepted gifts against the innocent.”

Not to swear at all belongs to the perfect (Matt. 5). To avoid deceit in an oath, although it is not perfect virtue, is nevertheless some progress belonging to beginners. Likewise, not lending one’s money at interest is not a great virtue, but it is still the beginning of virtue.

For if we wish to be perfect, we must give away all that is ours (Matt. 19). Again, it is not a great thing not to accept gifts against the innocent; for we ought, if we can, to liberate the innocent.

Why, then, does the Holy Spirit join perfect commandments even to the smallest ones? Is it not because he intends mercifully to support our weakness in this way? Thus, if we are not yet able to attain perfection, we should at least strive to practice small things as we are able.

For if, according to our ability, we advance from small things to greater ones, and if we cannot immediately reach what we desire, nevertheless the reward of those who labor cannot be lacking. Hence it also follows:

“He who does these things will not be moved forever.”

That is (from Augustine), he will reach those greater things in which there is great and unshakable stability.

## Title of Psalm XV

In ancient times it was customary that, whenever someone had triumphed over his enemy, he had an arch constructed for himself, called a triumphal arch, on which that victory was depicted (1 Kings 15). Hence, on the triumphal arch at Aurasica, the war against Massilia is said to have been carved as a sign of Caesar’s victory.

[Note: Recall the arguments that, in the Preface for determining the author of this Commentary, we also drew from this passage. For we do not doubt that this is the city of Arausio, which was also called Aurasiensis and Arausicorum; nowhere else, so far as I know, was it called Arausica. It is now called Orange, as everyone knows.]

Similarly, after the devil had already been conquered through the victory of the Passion, God the Father had a title placed upon the cross, as though upon a triumphal arch erected from the kingdom of the whole world acquired for him: “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews” (Matt. 27; Mark 15; Luke 23; John 19).

The inscription of this psalm’s title is: “A Psalm for David himself.” Therefore (from Augustine) he added “for himself,” because our King himself speaks in this psalm in the assumption of a human person; concerning him, a royal title shone forth when it was inscribed at the time of the Passion [variant: *eminuit*, “stood out”]. Its purpose is to invite us to his kingdom, which he acquired for us through his humanity, Passion, and resurrection. This is what is treated here. He therefore says:

### [Column 0696C] Psalm XV

### 1

“Preserve me, Lord, for I have hoped in you.”

It was not necessary for him to pray for himself, for, insofar as he was God, he was able to preserve himself. But just as he came to be incarnate for us, so the merciful Redeemer deigned to pray for us, transforming us into his own person, because he willed to become one body with his Church.

Therefore, on behalf of his weak members, whom he transforms into himself, he says: “Preserve me, Lord, for I have hoped in you.” For we, who are mere human beings and have been ruined through sin, need to be preserved by the Lord. He himself is our hope; he himself is our God. We need his help, not he ours. Therefore he went on to add:

### 2

“I said to the Lord, ‘You are my God,’ because you have no need of my goods.”

[Note: Perhaps *pius* (“merciful”) should be restored.]

The Father redeemed us through the Son solely out of love, not necessity. For his perfect glory can neither be increased nor diminished. We ought therefore all the more to confess the Lord our God with our mouths, believe in him with our hearts, hope in him, and seek salvation from him. He does not seek our goods; rather, he bestows his own upon us. Hence it is also added:

### 3

“To the saints who are in his land he has made all my purposes wonderful in them.”

To the saints (from Augustine) who have placed their hope in the land of the living, the citizens of the heavenly homeland, whose spiritual conduct is anchored by hope in that homeland—which is rightly called God’s land, although they live in the flesh in these earthly regions—to these saints he has made all my purposes wonderful, in the progress of those [Note: In Augustine, “who understood what benefit they received”].

They understood how the humanity of my divinity benefited them, so that I might die, and the divinity of my humanity, so that I might rise again. It should also be noted that, after saying “he has made my purposes wonderful,” he immediately adds “in them.” From these words we should understand that he showed his purposes to the saints as wonderful in such a way that he caused those same purposes to remain in them. For they could not have been saints if they had departed from his acknowledged purposes.

This is sufficiently clear from the words that follow:

### 4

“Their infirmities have been multiplied; afterward they hastened.”

The more plainly the divine will is revealed, the more abundantly human weakness appears. For by the rule of heavenly righteousness the strength of our wickedness is exposed. Hence holy men, the more subtly they perceive divine things, the more strictly they mourn their own sins. From the light they have received from above, they recognize what they ought to correct in themselves. Therefore it is said: “Afterward they hastened.” For from the knowledge of their own weakness they hasten more quickly toward salvation.

And because they humbly confess themselves to be weak and sinners, they merit healing from the heavenly physician. Therefore it is added: “I will not gather their assemblies from bloods, nor will I remember their names through my lips.”

What is signified by the name “bloods” except sins? Hence it is written: “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 15). He rightly says “assemblies.” For not all who are subject to vices have one and the same will in sins. Some gather for robbery, others for greed, others for lust, others for pride. As many as there are varieties of vices, so many are the different assemblies.

But the merciful Lord does not gather their assemblies from bloodshed, because he does not accuse at the judgment those who have turned to repentance. What are their names, which he will not remember, except the names they acquired for themselves by sinning? Whoever commits adultery is rightly called an adulterer; whoever commits robbery, a robber; whoever commits perjury, a perjurer; whoever practices pride, a proud person.

He does not remember these names if the faults for which they received those names are corrected. Hence it is written: “He overlooks the sins of human beings because of repentance” (Wis. 1). From this the Apostle says: “If we judged ourselves, we would not be judged” (1 Cor. 11).

Therefore, because these people are transferred into the inheritance of the Lord, so that the Lord himself may also be their inheritance, it is rightly added:

### 5

“The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and my cup; you are the one who will restore my inheritance to me.”

They will possess the Lord himself as an inheritance with me. Let others choose for themselves portions in which they may take delight, earthly and temporal things; the portion of the saints is the eternal Lord. Let others drink deadly pleasures; the portion of my cup is the Lord. “You will restore my inheritance to me,” so that the glory that was with you before the world was made may be known also to those whom I set free.

The inheritance of the Lord had been destroyed when human nature, corrupted by vices, was held in the possession of the devil. The Savior was sent; sins were erased; free will was restored; the ruler of this world was cast out; weakness was healed; the inheritance was restored. Hence it is also added:

### 6

“The measuring lines have fallen for me in excellent places; indeed, my inheritance is excellent for me.”

Just as we divide our inheritance with measuring lines, so God divided his inheritance by faith, hope, and love. Those upon whom these measuring lines fell have entered into the Lord’s inheritance. They fell only in excellent places, among those who preferred heavenly glory to earthly glory and spiritual virtues to temporal honors.

Many flourish in wealth in this world, excel in power, rejoice in honors, and shine with temporal glory. They possess splendor, but not a lasting one. Those, however, who despise earthly things, desire heavenly glory, and burn with longing for spiritual joys—these are undoubtedly excellent.

Therefore he now says: “Indeed, my inheritance is excellent for me.” He rightly says “for me.” This spiritual inheritance is not excellent for those who do not know it. If they knew this glory, which he loves, they would not love the false one.

Those who, by his gift, are able to understand invisible things ought therefore to give thanks to the Lord. Hence he appropriately adds:

### 7

“I will bless the Lord, who has given me understanding.”

By “me” we must understand his members, who are joined to him in the unity of the body. The fact that they knew the Lord, and that, after despising temporal things, they understood spiritual things, was not their own virtue but God’s gift.

Therefore, when Peter said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16), lest he attribute this understanding to himself, he immediately heard: “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (ibid.).

For this reason the prophet elsewhere asks, saying: “Give me understanding, and I will search out your law” (Ps. 118).

But now the Lord’s Passion is commended to us when he adds: “Moreover, even until night my kidneys reproved me.”

“Moreover, for this I will bless the Lord: my kidneys”—that is, the Jews, from whose loins my fathers came and from whose flesh I was born—by reproving and blaspheming drove me to death and compelled me to go into the underworld. He rightly says “moreover.” To bless the Lord in adversity is a greater virtue than to bless him in prosperity.

When God bestows his good gifts upon human beings, both the good and the wicked commonly bless him. When he inflicts scourges, the wicked murmur, but the good bless him. This verse therefore instructs us to praise God in his gifts, so that we may not be ungrateful, and also in his scourges, so that we may be perfect. Thus what we read in another psalm may be fulfilled in us: “I will bless the Lord at all times” (Ps. 33).

### 8

The words that follow agree with this meaning. He says: “I kept the Lord always before me; because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved.”

Blessed is the person who always keeps God before his eyes. Such a one is neither lifted up in prosperity nor broken by adversity. In everything we do, say, or think, if we always keep God before us, we do not offend. Hence it is written: “In all your ways, consider him” (Prov. 3).

The Father is rightly said to be at the Son’s right hand, because the Son is equal to the Father. From him he drew strength, so that, when placed in the Passion under human form, he could not be shaken in any way.

If, following the example of our Redeemer, we always keep the Lord before us, so that neither love nor fear of anything may make us depart from his will, then he will indeed be at our right hand, so that we may not be moved. For he himself says: “Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28).

### 9

“For this reason my heart rejoiced and my tongue exulted; moreover, my flesh will rest in hope.”

What is signified by the joy of the heart and the exultation of the tongue except inward and outward joy? Whoever has God at his right hand ought to rejoice inwardly in conscience and outwardly with the tongue. Hence it is said elsewhere: “Let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice” (Ps. 104).

When he says, “And my flesh will rest in hope,” he signifies the Lord’s body, dead and placed in the tomb, which would rise on the third day. If we rejoice spiritually and imitate our head through suffering, we have a certain hope that we shall rise together with him (1 Thess. 3).

### 10

“For you will not abandon my soul in the underworld, nor will you allow your holy one to see corruption.”

You will not allow my soul to remain among the dead, nor will you permit the sanctified body—through which others too are to be sanctified (from Augustine)—to be corrupted.

This was the plan and grace of almighty God: that Christ’s soul should not remain long in the underworld, nor should his body lie lifeless on earth so long that it would undergo corruption. If he had delayed, all our hope would have perished.

He therefore willed to rise without delay and to have human beings as witnesses of that same resurrection, as it is written: “And many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep rose with him” (Acts 1 and 10). Thus, confirmed by such testimonies, we might believe in the true resurrection of both body and soul, provided that, having become his members, we hold to the way that leads to the homeland.

Hence he adds:

### 11

“You have made known to me the ways of life; you will fill me with joy in your presence; pleasures are at your right hand forever.”

First, the head of life himself knew the ways of life, which he showed us by his deeds and proclaimed in words. What are his ways, by which we journey toward life, except humility, love, patience, obedience, and the other virtues? The prophet urges us toward these ways, saying: “Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight” (Isa. 4).

Hence Truth itself says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Luke 3). He therefore rightly says: “You will fill me with joy in your presence.” For joy is not complete in this world. Hence it is written: “Woe to you who laugh now” (Luke 6).

There is no complete joy here either for the good or for the wicked, since tribulation is common to both. Holy men, although they rejoice in hope, still groan amid tribulation. But they will then be filled with joy when they see God face to face (1 Cor. 13).

“And pleasures are at their right hand forever,” because those who will be at his right hand will rejoice without end. Their pleasures will come from the vision of the Lord, the fellowship of the angels, blessed immortality, and eternal happiness.

Let us therefore strive to observe the ways of life, so that we may be able to attain such great joy and such great pleasures.

## Title of Psalm XVI

### 1

The title of this psalm is: “A Prayer for David himself.” It is attributed to the David who is signified here, who truly came as “strong of hand” to conquer the powers of the air.

But since prayers are found in many other psalms, it may seem surprising why this title was placed on this psalm more than on the others. Yet although other psalms briefly contain prayers interwoven within them, this one is called principally a prayer, by a certain excellence, because, when the time of his Passion was at hand, Christ sang this prayer to his Lord.

Its purpose is to instruct us always to strive to pray in our necessities, following his example. It treats of Christ’s righteousness, the tribulation of his Passion, the resurrection, and the satisfaction and manifestation of heavenly glory. It is the voice of Christ speaking in his own person.

## Psalm XVI

### 1

“Hear, O Lord, my righteousness; attend to my supplication; give ear to my prayer, which does not come from deceitful lips.”

The sacred Scripture testifies how righteous and sinless was the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2). It says: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (Isa. 33; 1 Pet. 2).

Some say that supplication and prayer differ in this way: supplication concerns avoiding adversities, while prayer concerns obtaining useful things. Nevertheless, both terms are used interchangeably in many places.

When he says both “attend” and “give ear,” he seems to say: “Receive what you hear; retain what you understand.” He therefore presents the righteousness of his action and the purity of his heart, so that he may be worthily heard by the Father in his prayer and supplication.

### [Column 0699D] 70

He prays well who prepares himself for prayer in such a way that he can present his righteousness in prayer and presume to ask for nothing except what ought justly to be granted. He should strive to pray not only for his own benefit and that of his friends, but also for the benefit of his enemies.

Therefore he says that he prays not with deceitful lips. Lips would be deceitful if words were at variance with intention or justice.

“Let my judgment come forth from your presence; let your eyes see equity.”

The one who directs his judgment toward God knows that his heart is pure. We know that Christ the Lord was judged unjustly by the Jews. But in the very judgment by which they openly judged him, they themselves were secretly judged. From God’s presence came the judgment by which he justly condemned those who judged unjustly.

Let human judges therefore fear, because above them they have God as judge. His eyes see equity, so that nothing remains unpunished and he repays each person what is due. This was said both to frighten the wicked and to console the good, as it is said elsewhere: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay, says the Lord” (Deut. 32; Rom. 12).

Holy men ought therefore always to examine their hearts, so that they may have them approved before the eyes of God. Then, when they are placed in tribulation, they may be able to say with their head what follows:

### 3

“You have tested my heart and visited me by night; you have examined me with fire, and in me no iniquity was found.”

God the Father tested the Son when he permitted him to suffer. He visited him by night because he assisted him in tribulation. He examined him with the fire of Passion because through it he transferred him to incorruption. No iniquity was found in him because, as we have already said above, he committed no sin (Isa. 53; 1 Pet. 2).

We too are tested by God whenever we are afflicted by tribulations. Hence it is written: “The Lord tested the chosen as gold in a furnace” (Wis. 3). But in the night of tribulation the grace of visitation is not absent, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “God is faithful, and he will not permit you to be tested beyond what you can bear, but with the testing he will also provide a way out” (1 Cor. 10).

He examines us with this fire in order to make us clean from the stains of sins. Tribulation is therefore useful to the servants of God, both because they are tested in their hearts, because they are visited by God, and because they are cleansed from sin. “No iniquity,” he says, “was found in me.”

### 4

“So that my mouth may not speak of human works; because of the words of your lips I have kept to difficult ways.”

He was worthy to speak of human works who had no sin in himself (John 8; Heb. 7). And he ought all the more justly to be heard by everyone, since no one could justly rebuke him.

Those who hold Christ’s place in preaching ought likewise, insofar as they can, to live irreproachably, because the teacher’s speech is greatly discredited if it is corrupted by his conduct.

If, because of the words of God’s lips, we must keep to difficult ways, the Lord consoles us through apostolic authority, saying: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. 8).

He kept to difficult ways who was obedient unto death (Phil. 2). To leave the world, subdue the flesh, punish sins with tears, and endure adversities and hardships for God’s sake—these are difficult ways, which the Lord’s lips command us to follow.

But if what is commanded is difficult, what is promised is marvelous. For “eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man what God has prepared for those who love him” (Isa. 64; 1 Cor. 2).

Let us therefore hold firmly to the way, so that we may be able to reach the homeland. Hence it is added:

### 5.

Perfect my steps in your paths, so that my footprints may not be moved. What do we understand by “steps” except the actions of good works? What by “paths” except the narrow and constricted ways of God’s perfected commandments? He had perfected steps in the Lord’s paths who said, “I have not come to abolish the law, but to fulfill it” (Matt. 5). His footprints were not moved, because he did not depart from the way of truth; hence he himself says, “I must be in the things that belong to my Father” (Luke 2; John 8; Matt. 24). We too have perfected steps in the Lord’s paths if we fulfill what he commands in such perfection that we remain immovable in it. For it is not enough to do perfect things unless we also happen to remain firmly in them.

Paul had perfected steps when he said, “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith” (2 Tim. 4). He had firm footprints when he said, “Who will separate us from the love of God? Tribulation? Or distress? Or famine? Or nakedness? Or danger? Or the sword? We know that neither present things, nor future things, nor any creature will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus” (Rom. 8).

Whatever good we have in ourselves, however, we ought to ascribe to God, not to ourselves, for he willingly grants it to the one who asks him (1 Cor. 4), as the Truth himself says: “Ask, and you will receive” (John 16). Hence it is now added:

### 6.

“I cried out, because you heard me, O God; incline your ear to me and hear my words.” A cry to the Lord is our desire. The more someone desires, the more he cries out. But what is the ear that God inclines toward us sinners except his mercy? Unless he inclines himself toward mercy, we are not raised up to righteousness.

But what does it mean that he now says he has been heard, while he still asks that his words be heard? Perhaps he had been heard in one respect, but had yet to be heard in another: he had been heard in himself, but was still to be heard in his members.

### 7.

The words that follow pertain to this: “Make your mercies wondrous, you who save those hoping in you.” For God to make his mercies wondrous is to make the unjust just. Who would not marvel at the Lord’s mercies in the thief, in Paul, in the sinful woman, and in the tax collector? When, for love of God, the miser despises worldly things, the proud person is converted to humility, the angry person to gentleness, and the lustful person to chastity—has God not made his mercies wondrous? When he brings the despairing back to hope, when he grants eternal rewards to the sinner who deserved eternal punishments—does God not make his mercies wondrous? Hence he immediately adds:

### 8.

“Guard me from those who resist your right hand, as the apple of your eye.” Christ is called the apple of the eye because he is dearer than all things and is the light by which all are illuminated. He is also the right hand of God, because he is equal to the Father and all things were made through him (John 1, 8, 10).

The elect may also be understood by “right hand” and “apple of the eye,” because through them God performs mighty works, and they themselves are the light of the world (Matt. 5). Those who resist are unbelievers and persecutors. The Son therefore asks the Father to defend him from those who resist him, so that injustice may not crush righteousness and unbelief may not corrupt faith.

In this way we too, following the example of our Head, ought to pray to the Lord that he guard us, lest some attacking adversity break us, or some opposing temptation deceive us and withdraw us from the shelter of his protection. Therefore it is added:

“Protect me under the shadow of your wings, from the face of the ungodly who have afflicted me.” Love of God and of neighbor is the New and Old Testament. Righteousness, charity, and the other virtues are God’s wings, by which holy souls can fly toward God. These spiritual wings both cool them from the heat of vices and moderate the affliction caused by the ungodly.

The Lord Christ was protected by these wings when he was afflicted by the ungodly Jews. Concerning them he continues:

### 9.

“My enemies have surrounded my soul; they have shut themselves up in their own fat; their mouth has spoken arrogance.” These things took place in Christ’s Passion. The Jews surrounded Christ’s soul, for they wanted to destroy his life (John 10). “They have shut themselves up in their own fat” (from Augustine), that is, they held the abundance of their arrogance enclosed within themselves. “Their mouth has spoken arrogance” when they said, “Hail, King of the Jews” (Matt. 27), and other such things.

### 10.

“Having cast me out, they have now surrounded me.” At first they believed that he would come, as they had read in their Scriptures; but now, when he came to fulfill what he had promised, when they ought to have received and worshiped him, they cast him outside the camp and crucified him.

“They set their eyes on turning toward the earth,” because they considered him not God but a mere human being.

### 11.

“They received me like a lion ready for prey.” They were comparable to that lion of whom it is written: “Your adversary the devil, like a lion, prowls around, seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. 5). “And like a lion’s cub dwelling in hiding places.” The lion’s cub and son is that people to whom it was said, “Your father is the devil” (John 3, 8). He rightly says “dwelling in hiding places,” since whoever does evil hates the light.

After such great persecution, he continues:

### 12.

“Arise, O Lord; go before him and trip him up; deliver my soul from the ungodly, your sword from the enemies of your hand.”

“Arise”—he whom they suppose to be sleeping (from Augustine) and not to care about human iniquities. [Note: In Augustine [Col. 0701D], “let them be blinded.”] Let wickedness be exercised beforehand, so that punishment may precede the deed. Or, for the Lord to go before that people is for him to turn the punishment of evil back upon them before it falls upon another, according to what is written: “Everyone who sins sins first not against another but against himself” (Eccles. 6).

Or the Lord went before them because, before the final judgment, he also judged them temporally. For he expelled them from his land; hence it says, “And trip him up.” From that land flowing with milk and honey, in which God had planted them, they were uprooted.

He delivered Christ’s soul from the ungodly people when he raised him from the dead. His soul was the sword of God the Father, which his hand—that is, his eternal power—took up, so that through it he might wage war against the kingdoms of iniquity and divide the righteous from the ungodly.

“O Lord, divide them from the few upon the earth during their life.” Scatter them throughout the world in this life, which alone they think is their life because they despise the eternal one. He rightly says, “From the few,” since the Jewish people are fewer in number than the whole human race.

He further reveals their wickedness when he adds: “And their belly has been filled from your hidden things.” Not only will a visible punishment overtake them, but, from the sins that are hidden like darkness, their memory has been filled and cut off from the light of your truth, so that they forget God.

“They have been satisfied with sons; they have left their remnants to their little ones,” saying, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27).

### 14.

“But I shall appear in righteousness before your presence.” I who did not appear to them (from Augustine), because those with a filthy and darkened heart cannot see the light of your wisdom, shall appear in your righteousness—that is, I shall be revealed to your righteous ones.

“I shall be satisfied when your glory appears.” When they were satisfied with their own impurity, so that they could not understand me, I shall be satisfied when your glory appears in those who understand me.

Therefore let our prayer, the affection of our devotion, our works, and the exercises of our patience all strive toward this: that we may be able to be satisfied with the Lord’s glory. Let our Redeemer be our example in prayer, in work, and in suffering; and let him also be our companion in rejoicing.

## TITLE OF PSALM XVII

### 1.

The title of the following Psalm is as follows: “For the end, for the child of the Lord, for David, who spoke to the Lord the words of this song on the day when the Lord delivered him from the hand of Saul and from the hand of all his enemies.”

“The words of this song,” that is, words signifying such a subject matter as gives rise to a song—that is, spiritual delight, which is possessed in true contemplation—are to be attributed to David, that is, to the strong-handed one, Christ, the child of the Lord, on account of his simplicity and purity.

I say “David” because he directs his faithful ones toward the end, that is, toward the highest good. These are the words he spoke to the Lord the Father in his eternal utterance.

I call it a song possessed “on the day,” that is, in contemplation of the day of his resurrection, or in contemplation of the fullness of time, by which the human race, through Christ’s resurrection, was to pass from the night of unbelief, ignorance, and sins into the light of knowledge, faith, and virtues.

On that day of resurrection, or of the fullness of time, the Lord delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul—that is, from the power of the Jews and of their king, whom they themselves had asked for. For just as David is said to be interpreted as “strong-handed,” Saul is said to be interpreted as “request.”

Let Christ and the Church speak—that is, the whole Christ, Head and body (Rom. 12).

## PSALM XVII

### 2.

“I shall love you, O God, my strength. The Lord is my foundation, my refuge, and my deliverer.”

This is the great reason why God should be loved: because he himself is our strength. The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. 5); it makes us strong to endure the adversities of the world, to overcome the vices and temptations of the devil, to practice spiritual goods, and to despise earthly goods.

The Lord should also be loved because he is our foundation, in whom we have a firm basis, so that we are not shaken by the winds of temptations; and because he is our refuge, to whom we flee lest we perish in this misery; and our deliverer, so that, liberated through him from the slavery of the devil and of sin, we may come to true freedom.

### 3.

“My God is my helper, and I shall hope in him.” He is my God because he created me from nothing. He is my helper because he assists me in the good work; therefore I shall hope in him, through whom I shall be saved in the future.

There is this difference between “God” and “Lord”: “God” is the name of nature, while “Lord” is the name of office. The former pertains to the majesty and dignity that he himself is; the latter pertains to the power and dominion that he exercises over us. In the former we are shown what we should love; in the latter, what we should fear. In both, we are shown what we should believe, hope for, and love.

In the first verse, charity and faith are commended to us; in the second, hope. And charity is rightly placed first, because it is the queen of virtues, the beginning of good things, and the root of virtues.

But let us hear what follows, and what rouses us to love God:

“My protector, the horn of my salvation, and my receiver.” For he protects us from evils, and, just as a horn projects outward, so he, our eminent salvation, has received us like a physician receiving the sick in order to heal them. Hence the Son himself is compared to the good shepherd carrying back the sick sheep (Luke 15). And therefore:

### 4.

“Praising him, I shall call upon the Lord, and I shall be saved from my enemies.”

Behold how great is the benefit of praising God. If you praise God with your whole heart in both prosperity and adversity, no enemy will be able to harm you.

For the many and great blessings that the benevolent Lord bestows upon us daily, we have nothing with which to repay him except praise. The praise of God confers a twofold gift upon a person: first, because God is honored in human praise; second, because through the merit of that praise the person is delivered from evils.

Hence the Lord himself admonishes us in another psalm, saying: “Sacrifice a sacrifice of praise to God, and pay your vows to the Most High; call upon me in the day of tribulation, and I shall deliver you” (Ps. 49).

### 5.

“The pains of death surrounded me”—that is, the Jews brought the distress of the Passion upon me.

“And torrents of iniquity troubled me,” because, behold, the crowd, and the one called Judas, came (Matt. 26; Luke 22; Mark 12; John 18). A torrent and the assault of the wicked came to trouble the flock of the disciples, because, when the shepherd had been struck, the sheep of the flock would be scattered (Zech. 13).

### 6.

“The pains of hell surrounded me”—that is, those whom the pains of hell await.

“The snares of death overtook me,” because they came upon him from every side with swords and clubs (Matt. 26; Mark 14; Luke 22). They are called “snares of death” because demonic deceptions were present in them.

But when he was surrounded by so many persecutors and overwhelmed by so many pains and disturbances—he who could have condemned them all with a single word and freed himself from every distress—let us hear what he did.

### 7.

“In tribulation I called upon the Lord, and I cried out to my God.” He does not avenge himself, but prays. Your Emperor teaches you patience. If the pains of death and disturbances of iniquity surround you, consider how much your Redeemer endured, and patiently bear everything by his example.

Call upon the Lord inwardly in your heart, and cry out to your God with the whole affection of your heart. For in him are power and divinity (Col. 2). Hence he is rightly called both Lord and God: his dominion and divine command can rescue the oppressed from every tribulation.

Therefore it is written: “From whatever tribulation they cry out to me, I shall deliver them, says the Lord” (Jer. 29).

It is rightly added: “And he heard my voice from his holy temple, and my cry in his presence entered into his ears.”

Christ is the temple of God. The Church is the temple of God. Hence Paul says, “The temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Cor. 3 and 6). God dwells in this spiritual temple and there hears the voices of those who pray.

It should be noted that he says, “And my cry in his presence.” One must pray there, in fact, where God is seen. Therefore the Gospel says: “But when you pray, enter your room, and, after closing the door, pray to your Father in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you” (Matt. 6).

We must therefore cry out in such a way that the Lord sees our cry and that it enters his ears. This cry, certainly, belongs not so much to the voice as to the heart. Hence it is said to Moses, “Why do you cry out to me?” (Exod. 14). The desire of our mind is a cry in the presence of God.

But let us hear what follows.

### 8.

“The earth was shaken and trembled; the foundations of the mountains were troubled and shaken, because he was angry with them.”

If we take this literally, when the Lord suffered, a great earthquake occurred, and even the insensible elements themselves bore witness to their Creator (Matt. 27).

But if by “earth” we understand the earthly, carnal hearts, and by “the foundations of the mountains” the rulers of the peoples—for the others were established upon them as upon foundations—then, after the Apostles preached and they recognized that they had incurred the wrath of almighty God (Acts 3) because they had crucified his Son, they were troubled and terrified on account of their guilt and immediately moved to repentance.

When Peter rebuked them, they are reported to have said, as though shaken: “Brothers, what shall we do?” (Acts 2). They were given the counsel that they should receive forgiveness of sins through the bath of regeneration.

### 9.

Concerning them it is further added: “Smoke rose in his anger, and fire blazed from his face; coals were kindled by him.”

What is his “face” except knowledge? What does “smoke,” which provokes tears, signify except the tearful compunction of the penitent? Fearing his anger, they washed away their guilt with tears. From the point at which they came to know God through faith, they received the Spirit and burned sweetly in his love.

They were kindled by him so that they might become burning coals, though previously, as sinners in the flesh, they lay dead like coals in ashes.

From these words, then, we learn that through compunction the divine fire is kindled. It illuminates the inner parts of the mind and completely destroys the blackness of sins. The sequence in which the things foretold took place is shown by the words that follow.

### 10.

“He inclined the heavens and descended, and darkness was beneath his feet.”

First he sent holy and elect men to preach his humble coming; then, following them, he descended in person. For “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1).

By the very fact that he appeared humbly in the flesh, he overthrew the prince of darkness in complete submission and gave him to be overthrown by his Church. Hence the Apostle says, “The Lord will crush Satan under your feet speedily” (Rom. 16).

He who through his humanity was made a little lower than the angels (Ps. 8) was shown through his divinity to be much higher than the angels (Heb. 1 and 2; Col. 2). Hence it is added:

### 11.

“And he mounted upon the cherubim and flew.” For insofar as he is God, he surpassed those angelic dignities in the fullness of knowledge.

“He flew upon the wings of the winds,” because by the height of his divinity he transcends the powers of the heavenly spirits. For to which of the angels did God ever say, “Sit at my right hand,” or, “Today I have begotten you” (Heb. 1)? He therefore flew upon the wings of the winds because he alone merited to sit at the Father’s right hand.

### 12.

“And he made darkness his hiding place.” Namely (from Augustine), the obscurity of the sacraments and the hidden hope in the hearts of believers, where he might remain hidden yet not abandon his own.

He made darkness his hiding place because he established his heavenly sacrament for us in obscurity. Hence we handle the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood daily (1 Cor. 13), yet we are still unable to see with our eyes the light and glory of it, which we believe by faith.

We are in darkness so long as we walk by faith and not by sight (1 Cor. 10).

“His tabernacle is around him.” For he is surrounded by a multitude of believers. The Church, placed in this pilgrimage, is rightly called God’s tabernacle, because a tabernacle has no foundation and belongs to those who are engaged in warfare and to those passing through.

The Apostle also said, “We do not have here a lasting city, but we seek the one to come” (Heb. 13).

“Dark water in the clouds of the air.” For knowledge is obscure in the prophets, who are rightly called “clouds of the air,” because they are lifted up into heavenly things by their life and pour down the rain of teaching upon those below.

At first the divine word was obscure in the holy fathers. Everything was covered under figure and shadow (Heb. 10). The Spirit had not yet been given for manifestation, because Jesus had not yet been glorified (John 7).

But afterward came the heavenly radiance, the one who is the true light, who illuminates every person coming into this world (John 1). He removed the darkness, explained the Scriptures, sent preachers, and terrified and illuminated the hearts of those who heard. Hence it is added:

### 13.

“Before the brightness in his presence the clouds passed by, hail and coals of fire.”

Because of the greatness of the brightness that is present in his manifestation, the clouds—that is, the Apostles, enlightened by divine light—passed from the Jews to the Gentiles, as it is written: “It was necessary that the word of God be preached to you first; but since you rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13).

They themselves became hail and coals of fire, crying out, threatening, sending fire everywhere, proclaiming the future judgment, and kindling human hearts with the ardor of faith.

### 14.

“And the Lord thundered from heaven, and the Most High gave his voice: hail and coals of fire.”

After saying “Lord,” he adds “Most High,” so that you may understand that the God of gods and Lord of lords spoke through himself. First he spoke through the patriarchs and prophets, through the ancient fathers; afterward, through himself (Heb. 1).

Even the Apostles’ preaching was not so much apostolic as it was the Lord’s. As the Lord himself testifies, saying, “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10).

The Lord seems to thunder when he terrifies us with his judgment (Matt. 25). He seems to give his voice when he gently consoles us.

The words spoken through John appear to be a frightening thunderclap: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?” (Matt. 3). He seems to give his voice when it is added, “Bear fruits worthy of repentance” (Luke 3).

Accordingly, in keeping with the capacity of those who hear, the Lord sometimes thunders by threatening, sometimes strikes like hail, and sometimes kindles like fire.

### 15.

“And he sent his arrows”—namely (from Augustine), the evangelists, flying straight along on the wings of virtues, not by their own strength but by the strength of him by whom they were sent.

“And he scattered them,” among those to whom they were sent, so that for some they might be the fragrance of life leading to life, and for others the fragrance of death leading to death (2 Cor. 2).

“He multiplied his lightning flashes”—that is, flashing miracles.

“And he troubled them”—with a beneficial disturbance leading to repentance.

### 16.

“And the springs of waters appeared,” namely, the gifts of the Holy Spirit, from which all spiritual knowledge proceeds.

Or by “springs of waters” the Old and New Testaments may be understood. They appeared to those who heard through the revelation of the one who holds the key of knowledge. These spiritual springs in turn send forth from themselves the other streams of Scripture.

“And the foundations of the earth were revealed.” The Prophets were revealed, previously not understood, upon whom the inhabited world, believing in the Lord, was to be built.

The order in which these things took place is shown (from Augustine) when it is added: “At your rebuke, O Lord, at the breathing of the spirit of your anger,” namely, of the one who said, “Unless you repent, you will all likewise perish” (Luke 13).

After saying “rebuke,” he adds “breathing.” For we are rebuked outwardly to good purpose when we are inspired inwardly, so that we may fear.

### 17.

Here Christ says: “He sent from on high”—that is, from the bosom of the Father—“and he received me,” namely, the Head of the Church, into equality with himself, at his right hand.

“And he took me up,” that is, my Church, which is my body.

“From many waters,” because he established me from many peoples; or because he drew me out from many vices; or because he delivered me from many tribulations.

And this is what follows:

### 18.

“He delivered me from my strongest enemies.” Who are these strong enemies except the evil spirits? We would surely be unable to escape their strength unless God, more powerful than all, deigned to deliver us, weak as we are.

“And from those who hated me, because they were strengthened against me”—understand: he delivered me. Who are those who hate the Church except unbelievers and heretics? At times they became so strong that they even killed some of the elect in the flesh and at other times caused them to err in faith.

But the merciful Lord deigned to deliver them, crowning those who were killed and restoring those who had gone astray to the way of truth. Hence it is also added:

### 19.

“They overtook me on the day of my affliction”—that is, they prevailed against me in the time of tribulation and persecution.

“And the Lord became my protector,” protecting me from the attack of my persecutors.

### 20.

“And because I suffered bodily distress, he led me out into the spiritual breadth of faith.” He saved me because he willed me to be saved—not because of any merits preceding on my part, but solely by his goodwill. For he is the one who works in us both to will and to act according to his good pleasure (Phil. 2).

### 21.

“And the Lord will repay me according to my righteousness, and according to the purity of my hands he will repay me.”

There are two things in a person according to which the Lord repays: namely, according to the righteousness of good will and faith, and according to the purity of good works.

Good works cannot be pure unless they flow from a righteous intention. Hence it is written, “The Lord looked upon Abel and upon his gifts” (Gen. 4). First he approved the devotion of his faith; afterward he received the offering of his sacrifice (Heb. 11).

And rightly he will repay me:

### 22.

“Because I kept the ways of the Lord”—that is, by persevering I kept the breadth of good works.

### 23.

“And I have not acted impiously away from my God.” [Note: [Col. 0705] So far as I know, all Psalter manuscripts read “away from my God.”]

That is, after I approached him by doing good, I did not withdraw from him by living wickedly.

Hence the prophet says concerning the holy living creatures: “They did not turn back as they walked, but each one went straight forward before its face” (Ezek. 1). So our paths toward God ought to be directed, so that they are no longer twisted toward wicked action.

It is no wonder that he kept the ways of the Lord and did not act impiously toward his God, for it follows:

“Because all his judgments are before my eyes.” That is (from Augustine), I consider with persevering contemplation the rewards of the righteous, the punishments of the ungodly, the chastisements of those being corrected, and the temptations of those being tested.

For carefully considering the final things is exceedingly useful for keeping righteousness and avoiding impiety. Hence it is written, “In all your works remember your last things, and you will never sin” (Eccles. 7).

It is therefore rightly added:

“And I did not thrust his righteousnesses away from me,” as do those who believe for a time and withdraw in the time of temptation (Luke 8). Concerning them the Apostle Peter says, “It is better not to know the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn back” (2 Pet. 8).

### 24.

“And I shall be blameless with him, in accordance with the delight of evil thought. And I shall keep myself from my iniquity.”

That is, from iniquity in action. Our striving and desire ought to be such that inwardly we are blameless and outwardly innocent, so that we may attain the eternal reward concerning which he adds:

### 25.

“And the Lord will repay me according to my righteousness,” not only on account of the breadth of faith, but also on account of the length of perseverance.

“And according to the purity of my hands in the sight of his eyes,” not according to what human beings see, but according to what he himself sees. “For the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal” (2 Cor. 4). A human being sees the face, but God sees the heart (Luke 11).

The works of the good are always before God’s sight, whereas he does not regard the works of the wicked (Prov. 10). Hence it is said elsewhere, “The Lord knows the way of the righteous, but he does not know the path of the ungodly” (Ps. 1).

### 26.

The Church says the things that have been set forth above in order to rouse and advance us toward right faith, firm hope, good works, and eternal reward. Hence it now admonishes each of us, saying:

“With the holy person you will be holy, and with the innocent person you will be innocent. With the elect person you will be elect, and with the perverse person you will become perverse.”

Look to him who is the Holy of holies, who is holy in himself and able to sanctify others; who is truly innocent, the spotless Lamb (John 1); who, when he was reviled, did not revile in return (1 Pet. 2), and when he suffered, did not threaten.

He is the one chosen by God the Father (Heb. 5), as it is written: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3, 17; Luke 3).

Join yourself to him, imitate him. Let it be good for you to cling to God, and you will be holy with the holy, innocent with the innocent, and elect with the elect.

But if you love the company of the perverse, you too will likewise become perverse.

Behold, two ways have been shown to you: one of the righteous, the other of the reprobate; one of salvation, the other of condemnation; one held by the humble, who are exalted by God; the other held by the proud, who are humbled by God.

Hence it is added:

### 28.

“For you will save the humble people, and you will humble the eyes of the proud.”

Therefore preserve humility. Recognize that you are dust and ashes; confess your sins; be lowly in your own eyes, so that you may deserve to be saved with the humble people.

Beware of lifting up your eyes, lest you appear glorious, wise, and great to yourself; lest, wherever you see yourself exalted, there the one who humbles the eyes of the proud cast you down.

Hence it is written: “Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and prudent in your own sight” (Isa. 5).

Let your eye therefore be simple within you, so that your whole body may be luminous (Matt. 6), and say what follows:

### 29.

“For you illuminate my lamp, O Lord; my God, my God, illuminate my darkness.”

Because you have illuminated me in the things I know, illuminate me in the things I do not know.

Or, because you have illuminated my lamp by granting faith, illuminate the darkness of my works, so that what I hold by believing I may follow by acting.

What are our darknesses except iniquities and negligences? We have fallen into such blindness that we do not know ourselves and do not quickly recognize the evils we commit.

Therefore we ought to ask the Lord to illuminate our darkness, to make us see our transgressions and crimes, so that by weeping and repenting we may be able to amend our life.

### 30.

“For in you I shall be delivered from temptation, and in my God I shall cross over a wall.”

“In you,” he says, “I shall be delivered,” not in myself. For in myself I am weak (Ps. 6), but in you I am strong.

You alone deliver from temptation (Phil. 4), cast out the prince of this world (John 12), and do not permit your servants to be tempted beyond what they can bear; rather, you also bring benefit out of temptation (1 Cor. 10).

“In you I shall cross over a wall”: either the hardness of heart or the obstacle of sins that the devil placed before me so that I could not come to you.

We cross over the wall in our God whenever, through his grace inspired within us, we overcome the heap of vices.

### 31.

Here the Church begins to commend her God, saying:

“My God, his way is undefiled; the sayings of the Lord are tested by fire; he is the protector of all who hope in him.”

And let her say in this way: “This God of mine is not like the others. His way is undefiled, his words are tested in tribulation, and hope in him is certain and firm; he protects those who hope in him, so that they do not fail in temptation” (Heb. 7).

What is as undefiled and pure as the power of God and the wisdom of God, Christ (1 Cor. 1), who says, “I am the way” (John 14)?

Let us therefore hold to this way, and we shall be cleansed. Let us guard his sayings, and we shall not go astray. Let us fix our hope in him, and we shall walk securely under his protection.

And rightly hope should be placed in him:

### 32.

“For who is God besides the Lord? Or who is God besides our God?”

God is the one who created us; God is the one who governs us; God is the one whom we love; the Lord is the one whom we fear. If we found such a one—or a better one—perhaps our hope should be placed in him.

But because he is better and higher than all—as he himself says, “I am the Lord, and there is no other; besides me there is no God” (Isa. 43 and 45)—it remains that our hope should remain fixed in him.

### 33.

“He girded me with strength,” namely, with faith, hope, and charity.

“And he made my way blameless,” namely, so that I might live innocently.

It should be noted that he does not say, “He girded me,” but “He girded me beforehand.” It is a great gift of almighty God when a person is girded beforehand, before he is loosened toward vices.

It is no wonder that he made the way of those whom he girded in this manner blameless; for where the belt of virtues precedes, the stains and looseness of vices cannot hinder.

Hence the Lord commands us to gird our loins (Luke 12), so that each person should restrain himself against vices before he falls, loosened and impeded by them.

### 34.

“He perfected my feet like those of deer.” That is (from Augustine), the affections of the soul by which I am supported and advance like feet, so as to cross over the thorny and shadowy entanglements of this age.

“And he set me upon high places,” that is, in the heavenly kingdoms, where the dwelling of the saints is. Hence the Apostle says, “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3).

Without doubt, therefore, we ought to order our affections and the steps of our works on this earth in such a way that, after trampling down the thorny desires of this age, we strive to establish our mind in heavenly things.

### 35.

“He teaches my hands for battle.” He teaches me (from Augustine) to act so as to overcome the enemies who attempt to block the heavenly kingdoms from us.

“And you made my arms like a bronze bow,” that is, you made them possess an indefatigable intention toward good works.

It is customary among the prophets to change persons quickly. At one moment the prophet, or the Church, speaks to God; at another, to the neighbor. He speaks to God as the one from whom he received what he says; to the neighbor as the one to whom he distributes what he received.

It is not enough for us to have straight steps for pursuing righteousness unless we have hands trained for battle. For righteousness cannot be retained without a struggle.

There are many kinds of battles. We have a struggle against “principalities and powers, the rulers of the darkness” (Eph. 6). We have a battle against the world. Within us there is discord between flesh and spirit (Gal. 5).

Against these we must be trained for battle and fight with the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left (2 Cor. 6). We must have a strong and inflexible intention, like a bronze bow, for striking and driving away the enemy.

Intentions are rightly compared to arms, because just as strength resides in the arms and the hands are attached to the arms, so our intention ought to be strong, and robust action ought to proceed from it.

But because we are weak and our enemies are stronger than we are, what follows must be done for us:

36. And you gave me the protection of your salvation, and your right hand received me. The Lord gives his elect his salvation, by which he protects them as though they were naked. He gives them his right hand—that is, the favor of his grace—by which he receives them as a physician receives the sick. If you fear the heat of vices and the weapons of invisible enemies, or the adversities of persecuting men, ask for the protection of divine salvation. If you recognize that you are a sinner and weak, corrupted by many vices and negligences, ask for God’s mercy and his sustaining right hand, so that you may be received and healed by him. For he is the true salvation that protects his own from outward persecution. He is the sustaining mercy that receives and heals them from the bodily and spiritual weakness proper to them. And because he sometimes chastises beneficially those whom he protects and cares for, it is rightly added:

“And your discipline corrected me to the end, and your discipline itself will teach me.” It is evident in this that our heavenly Father loves us, because he has deigned to give us discipline. Hence Holy Scripture admonishes us, saying: “My son, do not neglect the discipline of your father, and do not grow weary when you are reproved by him. For the Lord reproves the one whom he loves; he scourges every son whom he receives” (Prov. 1 and 3). The Lord’s discipline is useful for two things: it corrects conduct and teaches knowledge. God’s discipline makes a person well-mannered and well-taught. It corrects and teaches in such a way that it sends him to the end—that is, to Christ, who is the end of labor and the reward of work. Without doubt, the one who said, “We glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces patience, patience produces testing, and testing produces hope; but hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5), was corrected and taught by this discipline. Hence it is appropriately added:

37. “You enlarged my steps beneath me.”

[Note: [Col. 0709D] Augustine has, “Nor will they impede.”]

So that bodily narrownesses may not impede me (from Augustine), because you have made my love broad, working cheerfully even amid those mortal things and members that are beneath me. “And my footsteps were not weakened.” That is, the marks that I impressed for imitation of you. Whoever glories in tribulations has enlarged steps beneath him. If there is outward narrowness of sorrow, inwardly there is breadth of love. In the hearts of God’s servants, the love of God grows as the world’s adversity attacks outwardly. His footsteps, however, are not weakened who strengthens his heart to endure evils for God’s sake, and who can say with the Apostle: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, distress, persecution, famine, nakedness, danger, or the sword? I am certain,” he says, “that neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities nor powers, nor any other creature, will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus” (Rom. 8).

Whoever, then, is such as was described above—girded with strength, perfected in action, taught for battle, instructed by discipline, perfected in love, unconquered in tribulation—who is now overcome by no one, is fit now to pursue his enemies. Hence, in the voice of the perfect, it is added:

38. “I will pursue my enemies and overtake them; and I will not turn back until they fail.”

Holy men pursue their enemies when they drive away and suppress evil spirits or carnal desires from themselves by praying, keeping watch, subduing their flesh, and devoting themselves to spiritual studies. To overtake enemies means to investigate carefully and recognize the cunning devices of unclean spirits, and, once recognized, to avoid them. Or whoever binds the carnal movements of the soul under the authority of reason overtakes his enemies. He must not turn back from this intention and this endeavor until they fail—that is, until those things that unlawfully resist the soul have been entirely consumed. Therefore it is rightly added:

39. “I will crush them, and they will not be able to stand; they will fall beneath my feet.”

You will be able to crush your enemies if you do not permit sin to reign in your mortal body (Rom. 6), if you take away their strength so that you do not offer your members as weapons of iniquity to sin (ibid.). They will likewise be unable to stand if, as soon as you sense temptation, you repel it from yourself, and if, as soon as you see sin, you correct it. The Apostle teaches us to crush our enemies when he says: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth: fornication, impurity, lust, and so forth” (Col. 3). They will also fall beneath your feet if you have abhorred and despised vices and desires in your heart, and if, in addition, you have set in their place good affections and spiritual actions. Hence the perfect man says elsewhere: “I hated iniquity and abhorred it; but I loved your law” (Ps. 118). These two things make one perfectly overcome the devil and sin: love of God and hatred of evil.

40. And so that this may not seem to be attributed to his own strength, it is rightly added: “And you girded me with strength for battle, and you cast down beneath me those who rose up against me.”

If you wish the pride rising up against you to be cast down beneath you, pray God to gird you with humility. If you wish lust to be cast down beneath you, ask the Lord to gird you with chastity (Wis. 8). Whatever vice you see rising up against you, ask the Lord for the virtue opposed to that vice, by which it may be defeated; and then what follows will be accomplished for you:

41. “And you gave me the backs of my enemies”—that is, you turned them backward—“and you destroyed those who hated me.”

The backs of enemies are given when unlawful desires and vices are consigned to complete oblivion; when one does not look backward with pleasure, but directs the eye of the mind toward the contemplation of heavenly things and toward those things that lie before us and are to be desired. The Lord destroys those who hate us when he drives evil spirits away from us, so that they may not notice us or harm us.

Or, in what was said above—“I will pursue my enemies”—we may fittingly understand the enemies of Holy Church, whom holy and perfect men never cease daily to pursue by reproving, rebuking, forbidding, and excommunicating. Some of these they overtake and draw to faith, repentance, and conversion; nor do they turn back from preaching until those people turn away from iniquity. They crush them from their state of pride and place them beneath themselves in complete humility. Girded with the armor of virtues, they thus cast them down from their vices, so that those who had risen up against them while being pursued become their followers through repentance. Those who went before by threatening and dragging others become backward by obeying; those who had been united in hatred are converted to charity and are dispersed and divided from one another in their malicious alliance. And because some of the enemies mentioned above are rejected by the Lord—since they do not turn with their whole heart, do not truly confess their sins, and do not purely implore the Lord’s mercy—it is added:

42. “They cried out, and there was no one to save them; they cried to the Lord, and he did not hear them.”

For not everyone who says to me, “Lord, Lord,” will enter the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 7). Hence the Apostle says to certain people who were not crying out rightly: “You ask, and do not receive, because you ask wrongly” (James 4). The reprobate will also cry out on the day of judgment, saying, “Lord God, open to us” (Matt. 25). And there will be no one to hear them; rather, it will be said to them: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (ibid.). Concerning them, in the voice of the Head, it is added:

43. “And I will crush them like dust before the face of the wind; like the mud of the streets I will wipe them away.”

Because they were dry and did not receive the rain of God’s mercy, and because they were light and unstable before the wind of temptation, they will rightly be removed from the land of the living and crushed like dust when it is said to them, “Depart, accursed ones, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25). They are rightly called the mud of the streets (Matt. 7), because they lived in the broad and spacious way, in filth and vices. They will indeed be wiped away by the Lord, as it is written: “Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and let them not be written with the righteous” (Ps. 68).

44. “You will rescue me from the contradictions of the people.”

They said, “If we leave him alive, everyone will follow him” (John 11; Matt. 21).

45. “You will appoint me as head of the nations.”

So that the nations may believe in me, so that I may be their God and they may be my people (Hos. 2). Blindness has come upon Israel in part so that the multitude of the nations might be saved (Rom. 9). For the Jews did not wish to receive the word of faith (1 Pet. 2). Hence it was said to them: “It was necessary that the word of God be preached to you first; but since you rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the nations” (Acts 13).

Concerning them it continues: “A people whom I knew served me.” I did not visit them with bodily presence, yet they served me. “They obeyed me by the hearing of the ear.” They did not see me with their eyes; merely hearing my name, they received my preachers. You too should be among this faithful people, so that, although you have not seen Christ in the flesh, you may nevertheless serve him in spirit and be obedient to him in your whole will, so that you may deserve to be blessed with those of whom it is written: “Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed” (John 20). But beware of the example of those concerning whom it follows:

46. “Foreign sons lied to me; foreign sons grew old, and they stumbled from their paths.”
