The Jews were sons of God, but by killing Christ they became sons of the devil (John 8). Since they did not remain in the truth, they became transgressors of the Law and lied (Rom. 2). They grew old in the sin of the first man because they refused to receive the new man. “And they limped from their paths”—that is, from the Law and the Prophets, or in their understandings, or by standing on one foot in faith: worshiping the Father but not the Son; or following the Old Testament and not the New; or holding to the letter and not the spirit. Hence the Apostle says: “He made us competent ministers of the New Testament, not of the letter but of the spirit. For the letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3).

With these feet Holy Church walks; with these feet she is advanced toward heavenly things. Let us next hear what he adds for our edification.

47. “The Lord lives, and blessed is my God, and exalted is the God of my salvation.”

The gods of the nations do not live, nor can they save anyone. Hence the Psalmist says elsewhere: “They have mouths, but they will not speak; they have eyes, but they will not see” (Ps. 113). Therefore they are neither to be blessed nor exalted. But we have such a Lord and such a God, who lives forever, who rules us as Lord, created us as God, gave himself to us, and became the author of our salvation. Therefore he is rightly to be blessed, exalted, loved, worshiped, and revered by us.

48 and 49. “God, who gives me vengeance and subdues peoples beneath me, my deliverer from my angry enemies. And from those who rise up against me you will exalt me; you will rescue me from the unjust man.”

God not only grants salvation to his elect; he also gives them vengeance upon their enemies. God the Father gave Christ his Son such great vengeance upon his angry enemies—namely, the Jews—who were inflamed with such zeal of anger and fury that they rose up against their own God and, as one unjust man, assembled together against the Lord and against his Christ (Ps. 2). He gave him such vengeance that those whom he had received to rule and nourish as sons, because of their faithlessness and madness, he rejected and cast down as strangers. Christ was delivered from them when he rose from the dead. He was exalted when he ascended to the right hand of the Father. He was rescued when he handed over to the nations the word of faith that had been taken away from the Jews.

Hence it is well said: “And you subdue peoples beneath me.” For when he abandoned in a severe judgment the one Jewish people that rejected the yoke of faith, he mercifully called many peoples of the nations and subjected them to that same yoke. Hence it follows:

50. “Therefore I will confess to you among the nations, O Lord, and I will sing a psalm to your name.”

That is, through my faithful people I will praise you throughout the world, and they will do good works in your name. In this passage, confession signifies praise, while the psalm signifies good action. He truly and fully praises God whose tongue and life agree in praising him. It is further shown why God is to be praised when it is added:

51. “Magnifying the salvation of his king, and showing mercy to his Christ, David, and to his seed forever.”

His salvations had not yet been magnified when God was known only in Judea. But the magnificence of his salvations grew when his wondrous name was preached throughout the whole earth, when it was said to the Apostles, “Go, preach the Gospel to every creature.” Then without doubt he showed mercy to his Christ, David, when he willed that the one equal to himself in divinity should be born from David’s seed according to the flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0711] The passage in the author had been reversed through the error of scribes; it has been restored and explained.]

“And to his seed forever”—that is, he similarly showed mercy eternally when he granted those who believed in him the remission of sins and eternal life. Hence it is written: “I will call those who were not my people, my people; and her who had not obtained mercy, one who has obtained mercy” (Rom. 9). And, “Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved” (Joel 2; Rom. 10; Acts 2).

## TITLE OF PSALM XVIII

1. The title (from Augustine) of this Psalm is known because these words are not spoken by the Lord Jesus Christ, but are spoken about him. “For the end, a psalm of David.” Its subject is to commend the state of the Catholic religion, the preachers of the Church, and the one from whom they received their preaching. He does this so that sins may be recognized and corrected, and thus the blameless person may please God. It is the voice of the Prophet speaking through the Holy Spirit, or of the Church.

## PSALM XVIII

2. “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament announces the work of his hands.”

That is, the Apostles and Evangelists, who are rightly called heavens because of the loftiness of their life, and firmament because of the solidity of their faith and charity, declare the glory of divinity and announce to us the work of humanity. John declares the glory of God when he says, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1). He announces the work of God when he adds, “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid.). He also speaks of his glory, saying, “And we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (ibid.). True and Catholic faith consists of these two things, namely divinity and humanity. And because these must be preached with discernment, according to the capacity of the hearers, it is rightly added:

3. “Day pours forth the word to day, and night indicates knowledge to night.”

“Day to day”—that is, spiritual people to spiritual people; “night to night”—that is, carnal people to carnal people. Both indeed hear, although they do not both understand in the same way. The former hear it as a word belched forth; the latter, as knowledge announced. What is uttered is uttered to those present; what is announced is announced to those who are far away.

Day pours forth the word to day when Paul says, “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (1 Cor. 2). Night indicates knowledge to night when he transforms himself for those who understand less, as though he himself understood less, saying, “I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (ibid.). And again: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal people; I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Cor. 3).

4. “There are no speeches or words whose voices are not heard.”

In the Acts of the Apostles we read how, when the Holy Spirit came upon them, they were all filled with him and spoke in the languages of all the nations, as the Spirit granted them to proclaim (Acts 2). But they did not sound only in the place where they were filled with him.

5. “Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.”

Therefore we too speak here. For that sound has reached even us.

6. “He placed his tabernacle in the sun.”

The Lord (from Augustine), intending to wage war against the kingdoms of temporal error and to send not peace but a sword into the earth (Matt. 10), placed his military dwelling in time—that is, the dispensation of the Incarnation.

Or, “in the sun,” that is, in manifestation, he placed his tabernacle, namely his Church, which in this world has no foundation. Hence she herself says, “But our citizenship is in heaven.” And he is like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber—that is, from the virginal womb, where God was joined to human nature as a bridegroom to a bride. For “the Word became flesh” (John 1), and in the virginal womb he found a bridal chamber. From there, as though coming forth from a most chaste bed, he appeared in humble mercy beneath all and in majesty strong above all (Phil. 1).

Hence it follows: “He rejoiced like a giant to run his course.” He rejoiced like the strongest of men, surpassing all others by incomparable strength, not to dwell in the way but to run the way (Ps. 1). For he did not stand in the way of sinners. He was born, grew, taught, suffered, rose again, and ascended. He ran the way; he did not remain attached to the way. Do you wish to hear how far he ran?

7. “His going forth is from the highest heaven, and his meeting-place is to its highest point.”

His going forth from the Father (from Augustine) is not temporal but eternal, by which he was born from the Father; and he meets him in the fullness of divinity, up to equality with him. “His going forth is from the highest heaven,” because he went out from the Father and came into the world (John 16). “And his meeting-place is to its highest point,” because he again left the world and went to the Father (John 10). His course is from summit to summit, because in deity and power he is equal to the Father.

After he had run forth from there and returned by coming back, he sent his Spirit. Tongues divided like fire appeared to those upon whom he came (Acts 2). Therefore it follows: “And there is no one who can hide himself from his heat.” The Spirit came as fire to consume the hay of the flesh, to cook and purify gold (Isa. 11).

Or it may be understood in this way: “There is no one who can hide himself from his heat,” that is, no one who does not possess some warmth or some grace of the Holy Spirit (1 Cor. 12), since all possess understanding and reason.

8. “The law of the Lord is spotless, converting souls.”

The law of the Lord (from Augustine) is he himself, who came to fulfill the law, not to abolish it (Matt. 5). The law is spotless because he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth (1 Pet. 2). It does not press souls beneath the yoke of slavery, but converts them to freedom so that they may imitate him.

[Note: [Col. 0713D] Augustine’s text has “in freedom.”]

Or “the spotless law of the Lord” may be understood as the divine commandments, concerning which the Apostle says, “The law indeed is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good” (Rom. 7). “But I am carnal, sold under sin.” This law, with divine grace breathing upon it, converts souls: it sends sinners to repentance, kindles the lukewarm, rouses the sluggish, cleanses the unclean, and justifies the unjust.

“The testimony of the Lord is faithful, giving wisdom to the little ones.” Divine utterances are rightly called both law and testimony. Law, because they teach and command; testimony, because in them God deigns to prove how much he loves us. And the testimony itself is faithful—that is, worthy of belief. For by this testimony, seeing fulfilled in him what the divine law teaches, we also await and hope that the future things promised to us eternally will be fulfilled.

This law and this testimony give wisdom to the little ones—that is, to the humble (Phil. 3). Hence it is written: “Upon whom does my spirit rest, if not upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66). And again: “I confess to you, Father, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. 11). Therefore it gives wisdom to the little ones because it instructs the humble in divine things.

9. “The justices of the Lord are right, making hearts rejoice; the commandment of the Lord is luminous, enlightening the eyes.”

The justices of the Lord are right (Deut. 26)—that is, inflexible. They do not turn to the right or to the left; they are not bent by prosperity or adversity. They make the hearts of those who observe them rejoice with spiritual joy. The commandment of the Lord also (from Augustine) is luminous, without the veil of carnal observances, enlightening the eyes—that is, the inner perception of the human being.

10. “The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring forever and ever.”

The fear of the Lord is not the fear under the law that is penal, recoiling from the loss of temporal goods, through love of which the soul commits fornication (from Augustine), but the chaste fear by which the Church, the more ardently she loves her Bridegroom, the more carefully avoids offending him. Therefore perfected love does not cast out this fear (John 4); rather, it endures forever and ever.

11. “The judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves.”

His judgments (from Augustine)—of him who judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son (John 5)—are truly and unchangeably justified. For God deceives no one, whether by threatening or promising; nor can anyone take away either his punishment from the wicked or his reward from the godly.

“The judgments of the Lord are justified in themselves,” that is, through unity, not for quarrels of division but for the gathering of unity. For this reason he caused those upon whom the Spirit first came to speak in the languages of all: he announced that he would gather the languages of all nations into unity. What one man did then, having received the Holy Spirit, by speaking in the languages of all nations, unity now does: it speaks in every language throughout all nations.

And these judgments of the Lord are “more desirable than gold and much precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.” By the two things, gold and precious stone, which are most desired in this world, he wishes to comprehend all riches. By the other two, honey and the honeycomb, than which nothing in this world is sweeter, he wishes to signify all sweetness. Thus you should understand that nothing is so sweet, so precious, so beloved, or so desirable as the divine judgments. And when you have understood that they are so dear, love and keep them, so that you may deserve both to receive a heavenly reward from them and to have said of you what follows:

12. “For your servant keeps them; in keeping them there is great reward.”

Your servant proves how sweet these things are by keeping them. To one who does not keep them they are bitter, and punishment follows. But “in keeping them” (from Augustine) there is a great reward—not in some external advantage, but in the very keeping of God’s judgments there is a great reward, and one rejoices in them.

Amid these divine judgments, which he desires, and the heavenly reward that he hopes for, the holy man seems to fear his own sins, concerning which he adds:

13. “Who understands transgressions?”

Therefore prayer follows: “Cleanse me from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from those of others.” It is not surprising if someone does not understand his own sins, because they themselves are darkness; they obstruct the eye of the heart and permit neither the light nor themselves to be seen. Therefore (from Augustine) let us say to God, who knows what he must cleanse and knows how to examine what he must heal:

14. Let us say to him: “Cleanse me from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from those of others.”

My own sins defile me; the sins of others afflict me. Cleanse me from the former; spare me from the latter. Take evil thought from my heart; drive away from me the evil counselor.

These two kinds of sin—one’s own and another’s—first became evident at the beginning. The devil fell through his own sin; Adam was cast down through another’s. If they do not dominate me, then I will be blameless, and I will be cleansed from the greatest sin.

He does not say, “If sins are not in me,” but, “If they do not dominate me.”

[Note: [Col. 0713D] Again our author indicates what we observed shortly above: that he read “dominated,” or at any rate understood the expression as referring to sins.]

For it is impossible for a human being to be without sin as long as he lives a mortal life, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1). Therefore, even if we have sin in the flesh, and even if carnal desire pricks us, if we resist as much as we can by our will, and if we do not consent in spirit, we are blameless before God; sin will not be counted against us as long as it does not dominate us.

But what is the greatest sin of which he says, “And I will be cleansed from the greatest sin”? Without doubt (from Augustine), it is pride, so great a vice that it cast down an angel and made a devil from an angel, shutting him out forever from the kingdom of heaven. This is a great sin, the head and cause of all sins. For it is written: “The beginning of every sin is pride” (Eccles. 10). And lest you regard it as something slight, he says: “The beginning of human pride is apostasy from God” (ibid.).

This vice is no small evil, my brothers. In the persons whom you see in positions of distinction, this vice despises Christian humility. Because of this vice they disdain to submit their necks to Christ’s yoke, being more tightly bound by the yoke of sin. From this vice, which is the head of all vices—for the others arose from it—came apostasy from God, as the soul entered darkness, misused free will, and was followed by the other sins.

Because of this vice, because of this great sin of pride, the humble God came. This cause, this great sin, this sickness of souls brought the almighty Physician down from heaven; it humbled him to the form of a servant, subjected him to insults, and suspended him on the wood,

[Note: [Col. 0716D] It is remarkable how corruptly our author read this passage in Augustine. Augustine correctly has: “so that this swelling might be healed by the salvation of so great a remedy.”]

so that this fear might run to the saving medicine. Let the human being at last blush to be proud, for whose sake God became humble. Thus, he says, “I will be cleansed from the greatest sin,” because God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble (James 4). Truly he is blameless who is free from this sin, because this is the final thing for those returning to God, which was the first thing for those departing from him.

15. “And let the words of my mouth be pleasing, and the meditation of my heart always in your sight.”

Our words and meditations will be pleasing in your sight always if sins have first been subdued and pride extinguished. From these words we are certainly instructed to strive to please the Lord our God by restraining unlawful sins in our speech and thoughts and cleansing ourselves from pride. Therefore let us say what follows:

“Lord, my helper and my redeemer.”

Be a helper (from Augustine) in good things and a redeemer from evil things: a helper, so that we may dwell in your love; a redeemer, so that you may free us from our iniquity.

## TITLE OF PSALM XIX

1. “For the end, a psalm of David.” This psalm is to be attributed to the Prophet David, directing his contemplation toward the end—that is, Christ, who is the end and completion of the Law, as he himself says: “I did not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it” (Rev. 1; Matt. 5).

Therefore, in this psalm the Prophet, not from the necessity of seeking favor but from great affection, expressed by the form of a wish the things he foresaw, filled with the Holy Spirit, would come to pass. He intended that, once Christ’s resurrection had been set before us—a resurrection which he greets with joy—we might be confirmed in believing that we too will rise and sit in the heavenly places (1 Thess. 4; John 12), so that where the shepherd’s exalted state has gone before, the flock’s humility may follow.

By doing this in the form of a wish, he shows the desire and joy that he possessed concerning it. Therefore he said to Christ:

## PSALM XIX

2. “May the Lord hear you in the day of tribulation; may the name of the God of Jacob protect you.”

Why does he not say, “in the day of peace,” or “of prosperity,” or “of joy,” but instead, “in the day of tribulation may he hear you”? Tribulation in this world is pleasing to God and useful to the righteous. It humbles the heart, arouses it to prayer, and makes it worthy to be heard. Hence the same holy man says elsewhere: “In tribulation I called upon the Lord, and he heard me” (Ps. 17).

Therefore the Prophet says in wishing and foretelling future things: “May the Lord the Father hear you, O Christ, in the day of tribulation”—that is, at the time of your Passion. May he hear you, I say, so as to cause you to rise again. May the name of the God of Jacob protect you with immortality—that is, the one who was called the God of Jacob.

For the people born later belong to you (from Augustine), because the elder will serve the younger.

3. “May he send you help from the sanctuary.”

That is, from himself. For he himself is the Holy of Holies, from whom all good things proceed, as the Apostle testifies: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James 1).

“And from Zion may he protect you.” Making the sanctified body, the Church, secure for you from the watchtower, which awaits your coming from the wedding feast (from Augustine). For Zion is interpreted as “watchtower.” Those belong to Zion and to the body of Christ who, having despised earthly things, direct the eye of the mind toward heavenly things.

4. “May he remember all your sacrifice.”

That is (from Augustine), may he make us mindful of all the injuries and insults that you endured for us.

“And may your holocaust be made rich.” May he turn the cross, on which you were wholly offered to God, into the joy of the resurrection. His holocaust appeared rich when, hanging on the cross and offering himself to God for us, full of the richness of charity, he prayed for his persecutors, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23).

O sweet Lord, how rich your heart was, how sweetly it burned, how wonderfully its fragrance inwardly delights us!

5. “May he grant you according to your heart.”

You knew what benefit your Passion would bring (from Augustine).

“And may he confirm all your counsel.” Not only the counsel by which you laid down your life for your friends (John 15), so that the grain that had died might rise more abundantly, but also the counsel by which blindness came upon Israel in part, so that the fullness of the nations might enter and thus all Israel might be saved (Rom. 11).

6. “We will rejoice in your salvation.”

Not in earthly riches, not in passing glory, not in the vanity of this world, but in him who can save us forever.

“And in the name of our God we will be magnified.” Not in our own name, not in merits or in our own strength, but in the name of our God we will be magnified. Therefore let us invoke the name of the Lord our God upon ourselves (from Augustine), and confession of his name will not only not destroy us but will also exalt us.

7. “May the Lord fulfill all your petitions.”

Not only those you had on earth, but also those by which you intercede for us in heaven (Rom. 8). “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ,” says the Apostle (1 John 2), “and he himself intercedes for us.” We have great confidence because the one who will be our Judge does not cease to pray for us (Heb. 7). Let us take care only not to be ungrateful, lest the hardness of our hearts repel from us what he mercifully asks.

“Now I know that the Lord has saved his Christ.”

As though the Prophet were saying: I did not offer the preceding prayer from distrust, because now, so long before the time, I am certain that the Lord has saved his Son—by strengthening him in his Passion, preserving him in obedience, raising him from the dead, lifting him to heaven, and seating him at his right hand. Therefore he puts the past for the future, because what he understood would happen concerning Christ was as certain to him as though it had already happened.

“He will hear him from his holy heaven.” Not only from earth, where he asks to be glorified, but also from heaven, where he now intercedes for us at the Father’s right hand and from there pours out the Holy Spirit upon those who believe in him (John 14).

“In the powers is the salvation of his right hand.” Our powers are the salvation of his favor, since he also gives help in tribulation, so that when we are weak, then we may be strong (2 Cor. 12). For vain is the salvation of human beings, which belongs not to his right hand but to his left. By this salvation all who have been made temporally safe while sinning are lifted into great pride.

8. “Some trust in chariots and some in horses.”

They are carried along by the rolling succession of temporal goods (from Augustine), and some are dragged by proud honors and exult in them.

“But we will call upon the name of the Lord our God.” We, fixing our hope on eternal things and not seeking our own glory, will exult in the name of the Lord our God.

### 9

They themselves were bound, and they fell. And therefore they were bound by desire for temporal things, fearing to spare the Lord lest they lose their place because of the Romans (John 11); and rushing against the stone of stumbling and the rock of offense (1 Peter 2), they fell from the heavenly hope. Their blindness has occurred in part in Israel (Romans 10), since they were ignorant of God’s righteousness and wished to establish their own. But we have risen and been raised up. We, however, so that the people of the Gentiles might enter, have been raised from stones as children of Abraham (Matthew 3); although we were not pursuing righteousness, we seized it, and we rose again—not by our own strength, but, justified by faith, we were raised up (Romans 5).

### 10

**O Lord, save the king.** So that he who by his passion showed us an example of fighting may also offer our sacrifices, a priest raised from the dead and established in heaven (Hebrews 7). **And hear us on the day when we call upon you.** Since you will offer yourself for us: “Hear us on the day when we call upon you.”

## 91. TITLE OF PSALM XX

### 1

**For the end; a psalm of David.** The prophet, rejoicing over the prayer that has been heard, says that the king rejoices in the Lord. He shows how many and how great are the blessings with which God the Father rewarded him for his steadfastness, and, conversely, how many evils he will inflict upon his adversaries. He does this so that all may hope in the Lord and in the mercy of the Most High, lest his right hand find them for destruction. Here too the intention is indicated, where he says, “Let your hand be found by all your enemies,” and so forth. The voice of the prophet singing of Christ to the Father:

## PSALM XX

### 2

**O Lord, in your strength the king shall rejoice, and in your salvation he shall exult exceedingly.** As though he were saying: “O Lord Father, in your strength”—that is, in the Word made flesh (John 1)—“Christ Jesus, who has already been appointed king over your Church to vanquish the devil and govern it spiritually according to good works and virtues, shall rejoice; and over the salvation which you have bestowed through him upon that same Church he shall exult exceedingly.”

Joy pertains to the soul; exultation to the body. Within, he rejoices over the divinity joined to humanity; outwardly, he shows himself exulting over his Church, redeemed through his divinity and humanity. Hence it is added:

### 3

**You granted him the desire of his heart, and you did not withhold from him the request of his lips.** For he desired to eat the Passover and, when he wished, to lay down his soul and take it up again; and you granted this to him. You did not withhold from him the request of his lips by taking away the desire he manifested through his lips when he said to God: “Father, I will that where I am, there my servant also may be” (John 17). And again he says: “My peace I leave you” (John 14). There is also another reason why the king will rejoice and exult exceedingly.

### 4

**For you anticipated him with blessings of sweetness; you placed upon his head a crown of precious stone.** Before he became human, he was blessed by all the patriarchs and prophets. He was also blessed by the angel himself, who said to Mary: “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb” (Luke 1). God the Father therefore anticipated his Son the king with blessings, because he was blessed by many before he became human.

And “of sweetness” has rightly been added, because this abundance of blessing proceeded from the sweetness of his love. He changed the bitterness of anger into the sweetness of mercy and turned the sinner’s curse into the remission of sins. This is blessing.

He also placed upon his head a crown of precious stone, because, as Augustine says, at the beginning of his preaching his precious stones—his disciples—came and surrounded him; from them the beginning of his proclamation proceeded. Or, by the crown placed upon his head, we may understand the whole Church, surrounding Christ on every side. It consists of living and precious stones, namely apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins.

Nor should it trouble us that he does not say “of precious stones,” but “of a precious stone.” For many are one in the unity of faith; many are one in the bond of charity, as it is written: “They had one soul and one heart in God” (Acts 4).

### 5

**He asked life of you.** He asked for the resurrection, saying: “Father, glorify your Son” (John 12 and 17). **And you granted him length of days forever and ever.** That is, the long periods of this age which the Church would possess, and thereafter eternity in the age of the age. “For the one who has died to sin has died once; but the one who lives, lives to God” (Romans 6).

### 6

**Great is his glory in your salvation.** That is, in the fact that you saved and raised him, and made him incorruptible from corruptible and immortal from mortal. **But you will still place glory and great beauty upon him, when you establish him at your right hand in heaven.**

For great glory belongs to Christ the king in rising from death to life; but greater glory belongs to him in sitting at the Father’s right hand. And it is great beauty for a human being to be Lord.

Or, “You will place glory and great beauty upon him” means: you will build glorious and beautiful things upon him who is the foundation of the Church (Matthew 18). Concerning him the Apostle says: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Corinthians 3).

We may refer “glory” to immortality, blessedness, or divinity; “beauty,” however, to works and virtues. There is also another reason why the king will rejoice.

### 7

**For you will make him a blessing forever and ever.** First you bless him; afterward you give him as a blessing to the peoples, so that the one who is blessed may bless, the one who is sanctified may sanctify, and the one who is glorified may glorify. Hence it was said to Abraham: “In your seed all the nations shall be blessed” (Genesis 22).

Or, “You will make him a blessing forever and ever,” so that he may be blessed and praised by us in this age and in the age to come (Psalms 83 and 113). **You will make him joyful with gladness in your presence.** For Christ will rejoice on the day of judgment when the face and glory of God, which he promised to believers (Matthew 25), will be revealed. Our salvation and the vision of God will be his joy.

Then the joy of the Head and the body will be complete, when what was said through the Apostle is fulfilled: “We shall be like him, when we see him as he is” (1 John 3). And in the Gospel: “But I shall see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you” (John 16). And rightly you should make him joyful, whether in himself according to his humanity or in his members.

### 8

**For the king hopes in the Lord.** He does not become proud because of his royal dignity, but, humble of heart, he places his hope in you, the Lord and his Father. **And in the mercy of the Most High he shall not be shaken.** His humility was not disturbed by obedience unto the death of the cross (Philippians 2).

What does the Lord our God commend to us in this example of his (John 13) except steadfast hope and humility? If the king hopes in the Lord, how much more ought we to hope in him, since we are powerless and fragile human beings? If he who is without the stain of sin (1 Peter 2) is not shaken in the mercy of the Most High (Isaiah 52), how much more ought we to persist in that same mercy, who have been corrupted by so many vices and sins? For we must beware lest what follows happen to us:

### 9

**Let your hand be found by all your enemies; let your right hand find all who hate you.** What is his hand except his Son? He is also his right hand, insofar as he is equal to him (John 10).

Who are his enemies, whom he himself hates, and those who hate him, except those whom he rejected, and those who did not believe in him, or who, having believed, did not obey? For all these, on the day of judgment, the hand will be found—that is, Christ will appear according to his humanity. His right hand will find them—that is, the same Lord Christ will find them, in order to destroy them through the power of his divinity. Hence it is added:

### 10

**You will place them as a furnace of fire.** That is, you will establish them burning inwardly with the consciousness of their ungodliness. **At the time of your presence.** That is, at the time of your manifestation on the day of judgment, when they will see face to face the one whom they pierced (Zechariah 12).

Hence it is written: “And all flesh shall see the salvation of God” (John 19; Isaiah 40; Luke 3). Then the Lord will trouble them in his anger, saying: “Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire” (Matthew 25).

What will happen then? **And fire will devour them.** Alas, what grief and sadness! Once the sentence has been given, punishment will immediately follow. How terrible will be that anger, which will then be without mercy! How savage that turmoil, where no consolation will be possible! How miserable those souls whom the fire that will not be extinguished will devour (Isaiah 26)! There will be the worm that does not die, and weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matthew 13).

### 11

**You will destroy their fruit from the earth, and their seed from among the children of men.** If by “fruit” we understand a deed, and by “seed” a thought, you will destroy both from the land of the living and from the fellowship of the saints. For they would not be your enemies, nor would they suffer such great punishments, unless they had useless deeds and thoughts. And deservedly did these things happen to them.

### 12

**For they turned evils against you.** Saying: “It is better for us that one man should die and that the whole nation should not perish” (John 11). The evils which they thought threatened them while you reigned, they turned against you in order to kill you. They devised plans which they could not establish. For they planned to erase your name from the earth. They planned to kill Christ so that they would not lose the nation and the place. But they lost them precisely because they killed him.

They therefore could not establish their plan, because “there is no wisdom, no prudence, and no counsel against the Lord” (Proverbs 21). And from this I know:

### 13

**For you will make them turn their backs.** So that they may look backward and not be fit for the kingdom of God; so that in mind and desire they may pursue earthly things and lose heavenly things. But will you destroy them all? Certainly not. For blindness has occurred in part in Israel, so that the multitude of the Gentiles might enter (Romans 9). The remnant, however, will be saved.

Hence it is added: **In your remnants you will prepare their face.** That is, your face and your presence, which would have been theirs if they had believed. “In your remnants” means those whom you have left for yourself to save. And therefore:

### 14

**Be exalted, O Lord, in your strength.** That is, rise again and remain equal to the Father, so that you may show your power and majesty—you who previously came in humility. **But we shall sing and chant your mighty deeds.** Song pertains to praise; the psalm pertains to good action. As though he were saying: “We shall celebrate and make known your wonders in heart and in deed.”

## TITLE OF PSALM XXI

### 1

**For the end; a psalm of David, for the morning reception.** This psalm is to be attributed to David—that is, to Christ, “strong of hand,” who vanquished the devil and conquered death (Romans 1). He was called David because he was made for us from the seed of David according to the flesh.

He himself directs us toward the end, that is, toward the glorification of his resurrection. And it is a psalm for the morning assumption, that is, for the resurrection which took place in the morning. His resurrection on the first day of the week was a morning resurrection, by which he was received into eternal life, over which death will no longer rule (Romans 6).

These words are spoken in the person of the crucified one. For the words at the beginning of this psalm are those which he himself cried out while hanging on the cross (Matthew 27; Mark 14; Luke 23; John 19), while also maintaining the person of the old man, whose mortality he bore. For our old man was crucified with him.

He intends to invite us by his example to passion and endurance. As the Apostle says: “Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example, so that we might follow his footsteps” (1 Peter 2). He prays for himself and for his members; he says how despised he was by the Jews; he recounts his passion and asks that his soul be delivered. He invites us to praise God, foretells the conversion of the Gentiles, and says that the heavens—that is, the apostles—will proclaim his righteousness to the people who will be born spiritually, whom the Lord made—that is, reformed.

## PSALM XXI

### 2

**God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me? The words of my offenses are far from my salvation.** We heard this word on the cross. There the Lord says: “Eli, Eli, lama sabacthani” (Matthew 27). The Evangelist interpreted it and said that he had spoken in Hebrew: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (John 10 and 14).

What did the Lord mean? God had not forsaken him, for the Son is always in the Father and the Father in the Son, as it is written: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1). That Word, which was God, became flesh. He accepted death for us and made us his body, for which he prays to the Father when he says: “God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?”

As though he were saying: “O God of all by your power, but especially my God by grace, look upon me”—that is, upon my people—“with the regard of your mercy. Why have you forsaken me”—that is, my people? “The words of my offenses are far from my salvation.”

How does he say “of my offenses,” when he committed no sin, unless it is because he prays for our offenses and made our offenses his own, so that he might make his righteousness ours?

### 3

**My God, I shall cry out by day, and you will not hear; and by night, and it shall not be folly for me.** He said this about me, about you, and about himself. For he bore his body—that is, the Church.

“I shall cry out by day,” in the prosperous circumstances of this life, asking that they not be changed; and you will not hear, because I shall cry out to you with the words of my offenses. “And by night”—that is, in the adversities of this life—I shall cry out, asking that they be made prosperous; and likewise you will not hear.

Nor do you do this for my folly, but rather so that I may understand what you wish me to cry out for: not with words of offenses, nor from desire for temporal life, but with words of conversion to you for eternal life.

Many cry out and are not heard, but for salvation, not for folly. Paul cried out that the thorn of the flesh might be taken from him, and he was not heard. It was said to him: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12). Therefore he was not heard, but not for folly—rather, for wisdom, so that a person may understand that the Lord is a physician and that tribulation is medicine for salvation, not punishment for condemnation.

Placed under medicine, you burn, you are cut, you cry out. The physician does not hear according to your wish, but hears according to your health.

### 4

**But you dwell in the holy place, the praise of Israel.** You dwell in those whom you have sanctified. For you do not dwell in a body subject to sins. As the Wise Man says: “Wisdom will not enter into a malevolent soul” (Wisdom 1).

Those who are righteous, chaste, pure, and holy are the dwelling place of God. Present yourself as such, therefore, that God may dwell in you. Cleanse your heart; sanctify yourself, so that you may deserve to belong to those of whom the Apostle says: “The holy temple of God is what you are” (1 Corinthians 3 and 6).

And he rightly says, “the praise of Israel.” For Israel is interpreted as “seeing God.” Those who do not see or understand God do not know how to praise him; nor is praise comely in the mouth of a sinner (Ecclesiasticus 15). But he is truly praised by those who see him spiritually—that is, who believe, understand, and love him. Be spiritually Israel yourself, so that your praise may be God.

### 5

**In you our fathers hoped.** Nor did hope deceive them. They did not place it in themselves, but in you. For it is good to hope in the Lord rather than to hope in princes (Psalm 117). And elsewhere: “Let Israel hope in the Lord” (Psalm 130). And again: “Make your mercy heard by me in the morning, because I have hoped in you” (Psalm 118).

They hoped, and you delivered them—from enemies, temptations, and tribulations.

### 6

**To you they cried out in the time of tribulation, and they were saved.** They hoped in you, and they were not put to shame. They hoped that you would give them the promised land, and they received it.

We know and read how many of our fathers the Lord rescued when they hoped in him. He rescued the people of Israel from the land of Egypt (Exodus 12); he rescued the three youths from the furnace (Daniel 3); he rescued Daniel from the lions’ den (Daniel 14); he rescued Susanna from a false accusation (Daniel 13). They hoped, cried out, and were saved. And they were both sinners and pure human beings.

### 7

**But I am a worm and not a man.** “But I,” no longer speaking in the person of Adam, but properly as Jesus Christ, incarnate without seed, “am a worm”: mortal, born from flesh, generated without intercourse and without seed. “Not a man”—understand: not merely a man, but God, so that I might be in man beyond men.

“I, such as I am, without seed and without sin, became the reproach of men and the outcast of the people.”

Behold, so many fathers hoped and cried out, and were immediately delivered and saved. Yet they were, as I have said, pure human beings and sinners. But the Lord was scourged, struck with blows, disfigured with spittle, crowned with thorns, lifted upon the wood, and cried out: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27). And no one came to his aid.

Why was this? Could he not, by the power by which he was God, deliver himself? Certainly he could, but he did not wish to. He wished to die; he wished to redeem us; he wished to form us by his example, so that even human pride might deign to imitate the humility of God.

For although he was in the form of God, he humbled himself, becoming obedient—not merely unto some ordinary and common death, but unto the most disgraceful and cruel death of the cross (Philippians 2).

For this reason God wished to become man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people. “The reproach of men” because of the cross; “the outcast of the people” because they rejected him and asked for Barabbas, who had been imprisoned because of a certain sedition in the city and murder (Matthew 25). They asked that a murderer be granted to them, while they rejected the author of life by crucifying him. Thus he became the outcast of the Jewish people.

But now let us hear in the psalm how much Christ suffered.

### 8

**All who saw me mocked me; they spoke with their lips and shook their heads.** All—understand, all who had come to see and to crucify—held me up to ridicule in their hearts and spoke mocking words with their lips, such as “Hail, rabbi.” **And they shook their heads**, saying: “Ah, you who destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days!” (Matthew 26 and 27).

The Evangelist agrees with this prophecy when he says: “And those who passed by mocked him” (ibid.). Shaking their heads, they spoke these words with their lips:

### 9

**He hoped in the Lord; let him deliver him.** Hence the Evangelist says: “He trusted in God; let him deliver him if he wishes” (Matthew 28). “Let him save him by delivering him, because he wants him.”

As he himself says, the Jews spoke these words ironically about Christ, and yet they spoke the truth.

### 10

**For you are the one who drew me from the womb.** Not only from that virginal womb—for the law of birth is the same for all human beings, that they be drawn from the womb—but also from the womb of the Jewish people. Whoever places salvation in the carnal observance of the Sabbath, circumcision, and other such practices is covered by the darkness of that womb and has not yet been born into the light of Christ.

**My hope from the breasts of my mother.** My hope is God—not from the time when I began to be nursed at the Virgin’s breasts, for I existed even before that [Note: [Col. 0721] In the Vulgate Augustine: “and indeed even before.”]—but from the breasts of the Synagogue. As I said concerning the womb, you drew me out so that I would not suck in carnal custom.

### 11

**Upon you I have been established from the womb.** That womb is the Synagogue, which did not carry me but cast me out. Yet I did not fall, because you established me. [Note: [Col. 0721] And this is more correct in Augustine: “because you sustained me.”]

**From the womb of my mother, you are my God.** The womb of my mother did not cause me, like a little child, to forget you. And therefore:

### 12

**Do not depart from me.** For you will always be with me. And it is necessary, **because tribulation is near.** Hence in the Gospel: “Rise, let us go. Behold, the one who will betray me is approaching” (Matthew 26). **And there is no one to help.** Neither angel nor human being—only you.

### 13

**Many calves surrounded me.** The fat Jews, luxuriant and stiff-necked. **Fat bulls besieged me.** Annas and Caiaphas and the other leaders. Bulls, indeed, because they were proud; fat, because they were full of wickedness.

### 14

**They opened their mouths against me.** Blaspheming openly and in a loud voice. **Like a lion seizing and roaring.** As a lion seizes its prey, so they, out of malice and cruelty, seized me for suffering, roaring and making an irrational din and outcry: “Take him away, take him away; crucify him. He is guilty of death” (John 19; Luke 22).

### 15

**I was poured out like water, and all my bones were scattered.** Water poured out causes people, whose feet slip, often to fall upon it. I was poured out like water—that is, for their falling and ruin.

The bones of Christ are the apostles, by whom his body, which is the Church, is supported and strengthened. They were scattered because, after leaving him, they all fled, as it is written: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered” (Matthew 26; Zechariah 13).

Alternatively, water that is poured out either washes or irrigates. Christ was poured out like water. Those who were filthy were washed; those who thirsted were irrigated. The scattered bones are the apostles, sent out for preaching.

**My heart became like melting wax in the midst of my belly.** This may be understood as referring to the pain of death, since he said: “My soul is sorrowful unto death.” In his anguish, his sweat became like drops of blood running down to the ground, so that it was necessary for him to be strengthened by an angel sent from heaven (Matthew 26). For, as the Evangelist says, “an angel from heaven came, strengthening him.”

Or “my heart”—that is, my wisdom, which was written about me in the holy books and, like something hard and closed, was not understood—after the fire of my passion came near, was manifested as though melted and was received into the memory of my Church. Hence the veil of the temple was also torn (Luke 23) after Christ expired, because what had been veiled was revealed (1 Peter 2).

**My strength dried up like a potsherd, and my tongue cleaved to my jaws; and you led me down into the dust of death.** His strength dried up because he showed himself dead and without vigor and did not defend himself, although he used to help others. His tongue also cleaved to his jaws because, like a sheep led to slaughter, he did not open his mouth (Isaiah 53; John 19). He was led into the dust of death, namely, into the place of burial.

Or his strength dried up like a potsherd because what was weak in him became weaker through tribulation. Just as a potsherd is soft before the fire and hard after the fire, so the Lord’s strength was despised before the passion and honored after the passion. He who was previously mortal and corruptible was afterward made immortal and incorruptible (2 Corinthians 15).

And just as the tongue in us is useful only for speaking, so he said that his preachers, his tongue, had cleaved to his jaws—that is, to the two Testaments—so that they might draw wisdom from their depths.

He also says that he was led into the dust of death (Psalm 1). That dust signifies the ungodly and wicked, whom the wind of temptation casts from the face of the earth—that is, from the faith of the Church.

Nor is it surprising that I suffered these things, which I foretold.

### 17

**For many dogs surrounded me.** That is, the Jews, barking against the truth. **The assembly of the wicked besieged me.** Namely, the leaders, scribes, and Pharisees, who conspired together to seize and kill Jesus by deceit (Matthew 26; John 19).

Hence it is added: **They dug through**—that is, they fastened my hands and feet with nails—**they counted all my bones.** By stretching me out on the cross, they showed them as though they could be counted.

### 18

**But they themselves gazed and looked upon me.** The same people, unchanged in their purpose of wickedness, watched and, as they watched, asked among themselves who I was. They saw nothing in me except a mere human being.

### 19

**They divided my garments among themselves, and over my robe they cast lots.** By dividing the garments (Matthew 21), they signified their discord, error, and the division of the kingdom. But by not dividing the seamless and better garment, they figured the concord of the Church, which is without stain or wrinkle (Ephesians 5).

Or the divided garments signify the Scriptures and the other sacraments, which could be divided through heresies. But there was there a tunic woven above, which no one divided. What is this tunic, as Augustine says, except charity, except unity, woven from heaven by the Father and by the Holy Spirit, which no one can divide?

Heretics could divide the sacraments among themselves, but they did not divide charity. And because they could not divide it, they departed; but it remains whole. It fell by lot to certain people. Whoever possesses it is secure. No one moves such a person out of the Catholic Church. And if someone begins to possess it outside, that person is admitted inside, like the olive branch brought by the dove. When Noah had sent the dove out, he joyfully received it back into the ark (Genesis 8).

### 20

**But you, O Lord, do not distance your help from me.** Not at the end of the age, like the others, when you will come to judge them upon the seat of your majesty, but raise me up immediately.

And this happened: on the third day, after the pains of hell had been loosed and the devil conquered, he rose again. For if he had postponed it until the general resurrection, all our hope would have fallen.

**Look upon my defense.** So that nothing may harm me.

Observe in these words the humility and patience of Christ. He both suffers and speaks all these things for your sake. See, therefore, how he places all his help and defense not in himself but in the Father, although he himself is the power and wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1).

He wishes to form you by his example, so that when you are placed amid tribulations or temptations, you may endure humbly and patiently and ask for divine help, saying: “But you, O Lord, do not distance your help from me; look upon my defense.” Hence it is added:

### 21

**Deliver my soul from the sword, O God, and my only one from the hand of the dog.** By “sword” he wishes death to be understood, because a sword is a weapon, and people are killed by a sword. And so that we would not understand the death of the flesh, he did not say, “Deliver my body,” but “Deliver my soul.”

For we ought to pray more for the life of the soul, which will live eternally, than for the life of the body, which rots on earth. By “his only one” he designates the Church. By “the dog,” the barking, quarrelsome, biting, and enraged Jewish people. He asks that she be delivered from its hand—that is, from its power.

Whoever quarrels, disagrees, bites, or becomes angry is a dog. Hence it is also said: “Many dogs surrounded me; the assembly of the wicked besieged me.” Do not seek the companionship of such people, lest you eventually be bitten and torn by them; but pray to God that he may deliver you from them.

### 22

**Save me from the lion’s mouth, and my humility from the horns of the unicorns.** The lion signifies the devil, concerning whom the Apostle says: “Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour. Resist him, strong in faith” (1 Peter 5).

When he secretly lies in wait, he is a dragon; when he rages openly, he is a lion. Because he had roared for the open savagery of killing Christ, it is rightly said: “Save me from the lion’s mouth.”

By unicorns he means the proud. Therefore he added, “my humility.” “Save my humility,” he says, “from the horns of the unicorns”—that is, from the exaltation of the proud, who raise themselves up in isolation and tolerate no companions.

In them the invisible lion was lurking. Through them he roared in one respect and raged in another. He seized the prey, tearing the Lord’s flesh.

We have heard what Christ suffered and what he prayed. Let us now consider why he suffered. Hear the fruit:

### 23

**I shall declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the Church I shall praise you.** Who are these brothers except the disciples who love one another? The Lord said to them: “This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you” (John 15).

The Lord himself identifies them in the Gospel when it was said to him: “Behold, your mother and your brothers are standing outside, seeking you.” But he answered the one who told him: “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?” And stretching out his hand toward the disciples, he said: “Behold my mother and my brothers. Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother, sister, and mother” (Matthew 12). “My mother and my brothers” are those who hear the word of God and do it (Luke 8).

He rightly says, “In the midst of the Church I shall praise you,” because Christ came to preach his Father not secretly but openly. For he says: “I have spoken openly to the world; I have always taught in the synagogue and in the temple, where all the Jews assemble, and I have spoken nothing in secret” (John 18).

Elsewhere the same Savior says: “What I tell you in darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear in the ear, preach upon the housetops. For what you have said in darkness will be said in the light, and what you have spoken in the ear in private rooms will be preached upon the housetops” (Matthew 10; Luke 12)—that is, openly and before everyone.

He declares the name so that it may be known; he proclaims praise so that he may be loved; so that through faith and love God may be worshiped by spiritual brothers within the Church.

### 24

Then he invites us to his own praise when he adds:

**You who fear the Lord, praise him; glorify him, all the seed of Jacob. Let all the seed of Israel fear him.**

Here he includes three orders: beginners, those making progress, and the perfect.

Some, terrified by the magnitude of their sins and shaken by divine judgment, correct the evils they have committed and return to the Lord more out of fear of punishment than love of righteousness. Such people are here admonished to strive to praise God with voice and conduct, whom they previously blasphemed by living wickedly.

There are others who have advanced to higher things and now strive to exercise themselves in spiritual pursuits, labor diligently in good works, restrain the desires of the flesh through the rigor of the spirit, and supplant vices with virtues. These are the seed of Jacob, who is called “the supplanter.” They are commanded to glorify the Lord for their progress, so that they may advance all the more because they glory not in themselves but in the Lord.

And there are many who already attain the summit of perfection. Completely forgetting what lies behind, they keep the eyes of their minds fixed upon the vision of the true light. They transcend all earthly things; in spirit they dwell only among heavenly things; they extinguish carnal desires within themselves (Galatians 2); dead to the world, they live to God (Colossians 3).

These are spiritually the seed of Israel, whose name is interpreted as “seeing God.” They flee the defilements of flesh and soul so that they may deserve to see God. They are admonished to fear unceasingly the one whom they love—not with the servile fear by which sinners fear God lest they be punished, but with the chaste fear by which the perfect fear God lest they abandon him.

### 25

Why the Lord should be feared and glorified is shown when it is added:

**For he did not despise or disdain the prayer of the poor.** He did not despise it so as to reject it, nor disdain it so as to treat it as worthless—the prayer of the poor, that is, of the humble.

**Nor did he turn his face from me; and when I cried out to him, he heard me.**

O wondrous mercy of almighty God! A poor person comes to a rich person, humbly entreats the powerful, cries out in need, asks for help, or seeks assistance. What does a proud rich man do? He despises the humble person, turns away his face, does not deign to pay attention, and is disgusted by listening.

What a proud human being despises, the humble God receives. For the Lord on high looks upon the lowly (Psalm 112); he regards the poor mercifully and hears them with compassion. Let it rightly be said, therefore, what follows:

### 26

**With you is my praise in the great Church; I shall fulfill my vows in the presence of those who fear him.** The Church was small when God was known only among one people, that is, in Judea (Psalm 75). Now it is great, because it is spread throughout the whole world. In it praises are daily offered to God, vows and sacrifices are performed—not in secret, because of fear of persecutors, but openly, in the presence of believers.

Hence it is added:

### 27

**The poor shall eat and be satisfied, and they shall praise the Lord who seek him; their hearts shall live forever and ever.** Those who were fasting from the food of truth, who hungered and thirsted for righteousness, are now nourished by the divine Scriptures and refreshed by the heavenly sacraments.

They praise those who seek him, for the praise of the Lord is the overflowing expression of that fullness. Hence their hearts live forever, because that food is food for the heart and soul, concerning which it is written: “Whoever eats of this bread will live forever” (John 6). And: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matthew 5).

“For man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matthew 4). That the Church is great is shown by the words that follow. For it is said:

28. “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship in his presence.” By saying “all the ends of the earth” and “all the families of the nations,” he intimates that the Lord is worshiped and adored in every part of the world and among every nation. The holy man foresaw what we now see fulfilled. They remember God, whom they had forgotten, and turn to him from whom they had turned away, when they sought earthly things, failed to understand eternal ones, and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever (Rom. 1). And they worship him who had been accustomed to worship idols.

29. “For the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he himself shall rule the nations.” The devil has been expelled (John 12); Christ has recovered his inheritance. He rules his people spiritually, possesses them as his kingdom, and will rule among the nations with [Col. 0725D] perpetual power. And because he had said that the families of the nations would worship the Lord, he added concerning the powerful, saying:

30. “All the fat ones of the earth have eaten and worshiped.” Who are the fat ones of the earth if not the rich and those abounding in this world? They have tasted and seen that the Lord is sweet (1 Pet. 2), and therefore they have worshiped him. But when he says that all the ends of the earth, all the families of the nations, and all the fat ones of the earth turn and worship the Lord, this is not to be understood as though no one should remain at the ends of the earth, among the families or the rulers, who does not worship God. Rather, it is to be understood that in every part of the earth, from every kind of family, and from every kind of power, God is believed in and worshiped.

For that many are to be rejected is shown when he adds: “In his presence all who go down into the earth shall fall.” To go down into the earth is to bend the condition of the mind toward desiring earthly things. But, as the Apostle says, “The work of each one will be tested by fire” (1 Cor. 3). [Col. 0726A] God will come openly to judge the living and the dead. There the reprobate will fall into hell; there the elect will rise to heaven. The former will hear, “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire”; the latter will hear, “Receive the kingdom prepared for you” (Matt. 25). Hence it is also added:

31. “And my soul shall live for him, and my offspring shall serve him.” They already begin to live for him who say with the Apostle, “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3). Hence he himself says, “I live, yet it is no longer I; rather, Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2). Therefore holy men deny themselves and, as it were, lose their souls in this world, so that they may preserve them in eternal life (John 12).

Their offspring are their good works, or those who through them are converted and serve God. Christ sent his seed into the earth when he commanded the Apostles to preach the Gospel to every creature (Mark 16). A few grains were sown, and a great harvest grew (Luke 10). For they announced, spoke, and multiplied beyond number. When the holy man had foreseen that this would happen, he added:

[Col. 0726B] 32. “A coming generation shall be announced to the Lord, and the heavens shall proclaim his righteousness to a people who will be born, whom the Lord has made.” The coming generation is the generation of the New Testament, which is us. It is announced to the Lord—that is, to the Lord’s honor—so that we may remain his inheritance. Hence the Apostle says, “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for possession” (1 Pet. 2).

By the name “heavens,” however, the Apostles are signified: they proclaimed the righteousness of God to a people born from faith and created by God for good works. Therefore, if we have been announced to the Lord, let us believe in him and, enlightened by righteousness (John 5), learn to turn away from evil and do good (Ps. 33). Born in him by grace, so that we may deserve to be his children, and made by him a new creation (2 Cor. 5), it is right that we remain in this newness of life (Rom. 6) and serve our God in holiness and righteousness before him all the days of our life (Luke 1).

## TITLE OF PSALM XXII

[Col. 0726C]

“A Psalm of David.” The Church speaks throughout this psalm, rejoicing and giving thanks for the benefits bestowed upon her from heaven. It may be referred to the person of each individual believer who, having received the grace of baptism and been cleansed in the sanctification of the Holy Spirit, gives thanks to God. The Church’s purpose here is to instruct her weaker members, so that if some good has been completed in them or is to be completed, whether in this life or in the future, they may strive to attribute it to divine grace and not to their own merits. Throughout this psalm, therefore, divine grace is commended. He says:

## PSALM XXII

1. “The Lord rules me, and I shall lack nothing; he has placed me in a pasture.” It is said in another psalm, “You shall rule them with an iron rod” (Ps. 2), that is, with inflexible justice. For a king is appointed for this purpose: to rule his Church spiritually according to good conduct and virtues, so that, governed by his rule, she may be led from the poverty of present misery to the pastures of eternal life. [Col. 0726D] There she will lack nothing, where God will be “all in all” (1 Cor. 13). There is the pasture whose beginning in this world is faith, and in which one advances through contemplation. Hence the Truth says, “If anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and he will go in and out and find pasture” (John 10). He will enter, namely, into faith; he will go out into contemplation. He will find pasture when what is said in another psalm is fulfilled: “We shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. 16).

But because our Redeemer says, “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3), it is rightly added:

2. “He led me beside the waters of refreshment; he restored my soul.” The water of refreshment is the water of baptism. This sacrament is the beginning of regeneration and salvation. There the soul is refreshed and led forth when it is washed from sins, imbued with faith, and renewed in conduct. There it is turned from the devil to God, from evil to good, [Col. 0727A] from death to life, and from iniquity to righteousness. Hence it is also added:

3. “He led me along the paths of righteousness for his name’s sake.” What is signified by “paths” if not the stricter precepts of righteousness, by which faithful souls are led to the heavenly kingdom? For the way that leads to heaven is narrow and confined (Matt. 7). Nor would it be sufficient to be nourished by the waters of refreshment unless one were brought to perfection through works of righteousness. For, as the Apostle testifies, “Faith without works is dead” (James 2).

And lest this seem to be attributed to his own righteousness, he therefore says, “For his name’s sake,” as though he were saying, “Not because of my merit.” For “he saved us, not because of works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy” (Titus 3). Then this faithful soul shows not only that it is perfected in righteousness but also that it is fearless amid adversities, when it adds:

4. “For even if I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I shall fear no evil, because you are with me.” The shadows of death [Col. 0727B] are all the reprobate, imitators of the devil. He himself was called by this name, as John says, “And his name was Death” (Rev. 6). They were in the midst of the shadow of death to whom Paul said, “In the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom you shine like lights, holding fast the word of life” (Phil. 2).

Why he did not fear while placed among the wicked he shows by saying, “Because you are with me.” Great is the security of having God with oneself. Hence the Apostle says, “If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Rom. 8). Where the divine presence is, it is impossible for vices to prevail. Where divine power is, it overcomes every adversity.

And because God sometimes beneficially exercises those whom he inhabits with scourges, and sometimes mercifully refreshes them with spiritual and temporal goods, it is rightly added: “Your rod and your staff have comforted me.” We are struck by the rod and supported by the staff. By the rod we understand discipline; by the staff, the support of consolation. In both ways the Lord consoles us: by scourges and by gifts. [Col. 0727C] He scourges us for this purpose, so that in the future he may find nothing in us that must be punished. We are corrected so that we may be tested, and cleansed so that negligence may be amended, endurance tested, and a crown bestowed. Hence it is written, “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life” (James 1).

The Lord’s rod consoled the Apostle when he said, “We glory in tribulations” (Rom. 5). And because holy men, while troubled outwardly, glory inwardly, filled with the grace of God, it is fittingly added:

5. “You have prepared a table before me.” “So that now” (from Augustine) “I may no longer be nourished with milk, like a little child, but, strengthened, may take solid food like one who is more mature.” “Against those who trouble me.”

Or by the table we may understand Sacred Scripture, which has been prepared and set before us, presenting us with dishes of various teachings so that we may be refreshed by them as by spiritual foods and not fail amid the adversities of this world. Hence Paul says, “Whatever was written was written for our instruction, so that through the patience and consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope” (Rom. 15).

[Col. 0727D] And because Scripture itself is of no benefit without grace, it is added: “You have anointed my head with oil.” That is, “You have made my mind joyful with spiritual gladness.” “Head” rightly signifies the mind: for just as the members are governed by the head, so thoughts are ordered by the mind. The head is therefore enriched with oil whenever our mind is anointed by the infusion of the Holy Spirit.

Or the Lord prepared a table when, in his sacrament, he gave us his flesh to eat and his blood to drink (Matt. 26; Mark 14). Hence, at the Paschal supper, when the Lord was handed over, while the disciples were dining, Jesus took bread, blessed and broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying, “Take and eat, for this is my body” (Luke 22; 1 Cor. 11). He also offered the cup of his blood for them to drink from, for the remission of sins.

Concerning this cup it is added: “And how splendid is my intoxicating cup!” [Col. 0728A] Truly splendid is the cup in which the undefiled blood is offered. By this drink the affection of the faithful is intoxicated, and it puts on joy at the remission of sins; this is signified by the head enriched with oil. By this bread the heart of the righteous is strengthened; by this oil it is gladdened; by this cup, once intoxicated, it is changed from sins, washed by mercy, and endowed with virtues.

Then, through the gift of that same mercy, the faithful soul is raised to the heavenly homeland. Hence it is added:

6. “And your mercy shall follow me all the days of my life.” The Lord’s mercy both goes before his elect and follows them. It goes before the unwilling, so that they may will what is good; it assists the willing, so that they may bring it to completion; it follows those who are working, so that they may deserve to persevere. For “not the one who begins, but the one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 24).

Hence it is also added: “And so that I may dwell in the house of the Lord for length of days.” In that blessed house, where the dwelling of the saints is, there is no [Col. 0728B] variation of days, but one day and one eternity. For there the sun of righteousness shines, with whom there is no change or shadow due to alteration (James 1). But because we ordinarily measure long periods by the extent of days, Sacred Scripture, speaking according to our usage, wished to designate eternal life by the length of days.

See how our God rules us, so that he can lead us to the pastures of life. He washes us in the waters of baptism, turns our souls from vices and from the devil to God, raises us upon the paths of righteousness, strengthens us amid adversities, chastises us with discipline, supports us with consolation, satisfies our minds with the nourishment of truth, fills us with spiritual joy, and intoxicates us with charity. Finally, he grants us perseverance to the end and, after the end, makes us dwell eternally and happily in the heavenly house.

## TITLE OF PSALM XXIII

1. With the Lord’s help, let us lift the veil of the present title, so that the inner meaning of the psalm may become clearer to us. Its title is “A Psalm of David, for the first day of the week.” It signifies the Lord’s Day, the first day after the Sabbath, on which the Lord rose from the dead (Mark 16). Because of the excellence of so great a miracle, it is properly called the Lord’s Day.

The psalm says that the earth belongs to the Lord and was founded by him. It intends to admonish all the faithful to ascend the mountain of the Lord (Ps. 20), the mountain of righteousness; to cleanse themselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit; to advance in good works; and to guard themselves from every deceit, so that they may deserve to receive blessing and mercy from the Lord (2 Cor. 7).

They are likewise admonished to raise the gates of the virtues in order to admit the Lord, who is strong and powerful in defeating enemies and vices, the Lord of hosts and the King of glory. In this psalm, the voice is that of those rejoicing with Christ as he rises, like a victor returning from battle. Let it therefore be said:

## PSALM XXIII

2. “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it.” If we take these words according to the historical sense, we should consider [Col. 0728D] from visible things how worthy of veneration is so great and such a Lord, who was able to subject the whole world to his dominion.

But if we understand this spiritually, by “earth” we can understand the Church, and by its “fullness,” its works and virtues. All these belong to the Lord—that is, they were made and ordered by the Lord. And lest anyone suppose that only one land or one nation, namely the Jewish nation, belongs to the Lord, he added: “The world and all who dwell in it.”

When the glorified Lord (John 12) is proclaimed for the faith of all nations, his grace is distributed abundantly, and sins are forgiven far and wide. Thousands upon thousands are reconciled to the Lord, and the entire world becomes his Church. And rightly so: “For he founded it upon the seas, and prepared it upon the rivers.”

The earth, or the world, is said to be founded upon the seas because it is surrounded on every side by the waters of the sea. Thus we say that a city is founded upon the sea, not because the sea lies beneath it, but because it rises above the sea at the edge of the land.

[Col. 0729A] If, however, these words signify something else more pertinent to us, we can understand by “the sea” the world, and by “the rivers” the desirous people who flow onward into the age. The Church also surpasses these (from Augustine), having conquered, by the Lord’s grace, worldly desires and being prepared through charity to receive immortality.

The Church is founded upon the seas because it is situated beside the bitter surges of this age. Or she is founded upon the seas, not beneath the sea, because she is not overcome by the torments of the wicked; or because vices do not rule her, but she herself rules over vices.

She is also prepared upon the rivers because teachers and prelates are appointed over peoples, princes, and powers, who are signified by the name “rivers.” Behold, the Church has been placed on high; the Lord has set his world in a lofty place, like an emperor’s palace. And what soldier will ascend there to the emperor?

3. “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place?” Many ascend, but only the few and perfect [Col. 0729B] stand. Judas ascended, but did not stand at all. Many others ascended, but turned back and went away (John 6 and 18; Luke 8). Who, then, will stand in such a way that he does not fall, and does not withdraw in the time of temptation? He continues and says:

4. “The innocent in hands and pure in heart, who has not received his soul in vain, nor sworn deceitfully to his neighbor.” He is innocent in hands and pure in heart who neither does nor thinks evil. By the hands we understand works; by the heart, thoughts.

Whoever lives fruitlessly receives his soul in vain. Those who had received their souls in vain were the ones to whom the householder said, “Why do you stand here idle all day?” So that they might not devote themselves to the idleness of vanity, they immediately heard, “Go, you also, into my vineyard, and whatever is just I will give you” (Matt. 20). Whoever prepares himself for good works is the one who has not received his soul in vain.

To swear deceitfully to one’s neighbor is to affirm what is true as false, or what is false as true. He swears deceitfully to his neighbor who, by affirming certain words, makes a declaration [Col. 0729C] intended to deceive him. Whoever therefore does good in such a way that he is innocent in work, thought, and speech—

5. “He shall receive blessing from the Lord, and mercy from God his Savior.” For he will be among those to whom the Lord will say on the day of judgment, “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matt. 25). This blessing will not come from their merits, but from the mercy of their Savior, who saved us not because of our works of righteousness, but because of his mercy (Titus 3).

6. “This is the generation of those who seek him, who seek the face of the God of Jacob.” “The Church,” he says, “is constituted from such people”; those who seek him are born in this way—those who seek the face, that is, the knowledge, of the God of Jacob, the younger brother, in whom God commended his grace.

For before they had done anything good or evil, it was said, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. 1; Rom. 9). Just as divine grace was then given to the younger brother and not given to the elder, so even now the Lord resists the proud, as though they were elders, but [Col. 0729D] gives his grace to the humble, as though they were younger (James 4).

*Diapsalma.*

7. “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, O eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter.” A human being has five gates, namely the five bodily senses: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. Unless these gates are guarded by their individual guardians, the devil frequently enters and departs through them.

It is therefore necessary that these gates be closed to the devil and opened to God. Hence they are rightly called “princes,” because they exercise spiritual rule over these bodily senses.
