Those who strive to chastise their body and bring it into subjection (1 Cor. 9), so that sin may not reign in their mortal body (Rom. 6), are commanded to lift up their gates—that is, their bodily senses—and to raise the eternal gates, which are faith, hope, charity, and the other virtues.

They are rightly called eternal gates because through them entry into the eternal homeland [Col. 0730A] is opened. Through these gates God also enters human hearts. Hence it is said, “And the King of glory shall enter.” For he is the King of heaven and earth, the giver of glory and destroyer of pride, so that “whoever boasts may boast in the Lord” (2 Cor. 10).

8. Mortal nature, trembling with wonder, asks: “Who is this King of glory?” “The Lord, strong and powerful, the Lord powerful in battle.” He who took the form of a servant (Phil. 2)—behold, he is the Lord. Formerly weak through corruption, now strong through immortality. Formerly seemingly powerless when he was killed, now powerful in battle (1 Pet. 2), when by his death he destroyed death and, rising from the dead, defeated the devil.

And because there were two peoples, namely the Jewish and the Gentile, who were to be saved by God’s grace, what is first said concerning the Jewish people is rightly repeated afterward concerning the Gentiles, when it is added:

9. “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, O eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter.” Human frailty again trembles and asks:

[Col. 0730B] 10. “Who is this King of glory?” “The Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory.” It should be noted that above the Lord is described as strong and powerful in battle; here, however, he is called the Lord of hosts and the King of glory. For among the Jews he endured the contest of his Passion; among the Gentiles he obtained the glory of power. Among the former he is afflicted on earth with punishments; among the latter, already seated in heaven, he is proclaimed through virtues and miracles.

Let us therefore honor our Lord and King, who powerfully defeated the aerial powers (Eph. 2), and let us give thanks to him who mercifully grants his servants power and glory.

## TITLE OF PSALM XXIV

1. The title of the following work is “A Psalm of David.” Since we have frequently explained what a psalm is and what is understood by David, there is no need to delay over these matters. In this psalm, the voice is that of a faithful soul converted from the death of unbelief to faith, persevering in prayer. It intends to instruct us by its example, so that after we have been converted to faith we may not return to our vomit, but persevere in our good purpose and devote ourselves to prayer. [Col. 0730C] It is the voice of the Church.

## PSALM XXIV

2. “To you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul; my God, in you I trust; I shall not be put to shame.” When my soul abandoned you, it was trampled upon the earth by carnal desires. For a person who departs from God is immediately handed over to the power of vices. And because I trusted in myself, I was led into the misery that I now suffer. Having abandoned God, I wished to be like God; expelled from the joys of paradise, I was shamefully mocked for my pride and put to shame.

And because I was miserable without you (from Augustine), I turned and lifted up my soul to you. Now I confess you as my God and place my trust in you. I shall no longer be put to shame, corrupted by sin.

3. “Nor let my enemies mock me.” That is (from the same author), let them not bring me down by lurking with serpentine and hidden suggestions. Those who, deceived by diabolical persuasion, withdraw from their good purpose are worthy of mockery; so are those who return to the world after conversion and fall into vices after attaining virtues.

[Col. 0730D] But the enemies could not mock the one whom divine goodness caused to remain in his good purpose. Hence it is added: “For all who wait for you shall not be confounded.” One waits for God who cannot be moved away from him by any temptations. Hence the Truth says to his disciples, “You are those who have remained with me in my temptations” (Luke 22). These will certainly not be confounded; rather, they will glory, because it is written, “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life” (James 1).

In contrast, it is said of the reprobate, “Woe to those who have lost endurance” (Eccles. 2). They lose endurance when, thinking that they will remain for a long time amid visible things, they abandon hope in invisible realities. Concerning them it is added:

4. “Let all who act unjustly in vain be confounded.” [Col. 0731A] The reprobate act in vain, I say, because they carry away with them none of the fruit of their labor. One sweats in the pursuit of honors, another burns with desire to increase his possessions, another pants to earn praise. But since each person leaves all these things behind when he dies, he has wasted his labor in vain if he brings nothing with him before the Judge.

Then each reprobate is confounded when the Judge is seen outwardly and every fault is brought back before his eyes; when he endures an accuser within, and his mind is tormented over the fires of Gehenna by a fire more grievous still. It also contributes to the confusion of the reprobate that they behold the glory of the elect, so that, driven back to greater punishments for their guilt, they see what they have lost. The final state of this confusion is eternal condemnation (Matt. 7).

Lest this convert encounter it by walking along the broad way, he humbly entreats his Lord, saying, “Show me your ways, O Lord, and teach me your paths.” By “ways” the broader and lesser precepts of righteousness can be understood; by “paths,” the higher and perfect commandments.

The broader way of righteousness includes being commanded to give a tenth from one’s possessions [Col. 0731B] (Luke 18), refresh the poor, clothe the naked (Matt. 25), redeem sins through almsgiving (Dan. 4), and perform the other works of mercy. The paths, however, seem to include being commanded to renounce everything we have, despise all that belongs to the world, deny ourselves, and love God with our whole heart.

The Lord both shows these spiritual ways and paths outwardly to his elect in the Scriptures and never ceases to teach them inwardly in the heart through the inspiration of grace, so that, instructed, they may know how to avoid error and be directed in truth. Therefore he adds:

5. “Guide me in your truth and teach me, for you are God my Savior, and I have waited for you all day long.” Since I have nothing in myself except the crookedness of sin and the falsehood of error, it is necessary that you direct what is crooked in truth and teach the ignorant. You ought to do this because you are my God, who created me, [Col. 0731C] and my Savior, who redeemed me—he whom I have awaited all day long, that is, whom I have continually expected.

Not a single day has passed in which I did not wait for you. Neither prosperity nor adversity could move me so far that I did not always place my hope in you.

Or, after learning the ways and paths—that is, after learning the broader commandments, such as “You shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal,” and the like (Matt. 19), and after learning the higher commandments, such as “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Luke 10), “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do also to them” (Matt. 7), and “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Matt. 5), and so forth—after you have shown and taught these ways and paths, “Guide me in your truth,” that is, make me upright in the practice of righteousness; “and teach me,” that is, make known to me that you are God my Savior, that is, my Creator and Redeemer.

It is as though he were saying: “Teach me the ways by which I may come to the truth; and when this has been accomplished, may I attain to knowing and enjoying you yourself, who are the truth and the life (John 14), and, having attained you, may I abide in you.”

[Col. 0731D] 6. “That this may happen, remember your mercies, O Lord, and your compassion, which are from eternity.” No forgetfulness falls upon God, so that he could need to remember; for everything is present to him who is true wisdom. But he speaks according to human usage when he entreats God to remember. It was as though God had forgotten his mercies when, as if angry, he allowed the human race to remain subject to sin.

He therefore prays that God remember his mercies and compassion, which he ordained from eternity (Prov. 8). For from eternity God had predetermined, through his mercy, to redeem the human race.

He rightly says “mercies” and “compassion.” Mercies pertain to their manifestation; compassion pertains to their predetermination, arising from his great mercy. “Great are his mercies” (Ps. 111). From the fact that he is merciful in himself, he is compassionate toward us. He therefore recognizes himself as miserable when he asks that the mercy by which he may be spared [Col. 0732A] be brought back to remembrance. Hence he adds:

7. “Do not remember the sins of my youth or my ignorances.” He says “of my youth” because that age is always more inclined to sin. At that age especially each person ought to correct himself, as it is written, “My son, receive instruction from your youth” (Eccles. 6).

And it should be understood that every sin occurs in three ways: either deliberately, through weakness, or through ignorance. Judas sinned deliberately, Peter through weakness, and Paul through ignorance. He includes sins of deliberation and weakness when he says, “The sins of my youth.” For youth, as we have said, is both perverse and weak in committing offenses.

He designates sins of ignorance when he adds, “And do not remember my ignorances.” It is as though he were saying: “Do not bring back to remembrance the sins I committed either deliberately, through weakness, or through ignorance; do not reserve them for punishment, but let them fall from your memory. And so that you may forget my sins, let your mercy remember me.”

[Col. 0732B] This is what he adds: “According to your mercy, remember me, you.” Not according to the anger I deserved, but “because of your goodness, O Lord.” Not because of my merit. I am miserable; you are merciful. I am evil; you are good. Do not therefore regard me according to what is in me, but regard me according to yourself. For from myself comes condemnation; from you, salvation. Hence it follows:

8. “The Lord is sweet and upright; therefore he will give a law to those who sin [Col. 0732C] on the way.” Sweetness signifies gentleness; uprightness signifies justice. Often, when we pursue uprightness, we abandon gentleness; and when we wish to preserve gentleness, we deviate from the uprightness of justice.

But the Lord and our Redeemer so harmonizes both in himself that neither sweetness diminishes uprightness nor uprightness diminishes sweetness in any respect. The Lord is so sweet that he forgives sins; he is so upright that after the grace of calling and forgiveness he seeks worthy merits at the final judgment.

Therefore the law is given to those who sin on the way, so that each person may recognize from the law shown to him in what he has sinned and how he may correct what he has done. Because the Lord is sweet, he does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live (Ezek. 33). Again, because he is upright, he does not leave that same sin unpunished.

For this reason, then, the law is given to sinners, so that according to the law they may either be corrected or judged. When you hear that your Lord is sweet, consider what you should love. When you hear that he is upright, consider what you should fear, so that, stirred up by love and fear of God, you may keep his law.

For charity fulfills the law (Rom. 13), and chaste fear preserves charity. These two virtues both extinguish vices and generate virtues. Hence it is added:

9. “He will guide the meek in judgment; he will teach the gentle his ways.” Those are called meek who are quiet within themselves, who do not become angry, contend, or quarrel. The gentle are those who patiently endure the insults, anger, and injuries of others.

The Truth himself says of such people, “[Col. 0732D] Upon whom does my spirit rest, if not upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66). The Lord guides such people in judgment because they possess the Spirit of God (2 Cor. 7), and “the spiritual person judges all things, while he himself is judged by no one” (1 Cor. 2).

Such people do not presume to rule themselves, and therefore they are guided by the Lord. They make him their ruler and do not resist when a gentle yoke and a light burden are placed upon them (Matt. 11). What ways he will teach them he shows when he adds:

10. “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth, for those who seek his covenant and his testimonies.” These ways (from Augustine) he will teach them—that is, mercy, by which he is appeasable, and truth, by which he is incorruptible. He offered the one by forgiving sins; the other by judging merits. Therefore all the ways of the Lord are these two.

There are two comings of the Son of God: one in mercy, the other in judgment. They understand the Lord as merciful in his first coming and as judge in the second. [Col. 0733A] The meek and gentle seek his covenant, by whose blood he redeemed us into new life; and in the Prophets and Evangelists they seek his testimonies, which bear witness to that same redemption. Therefore he adds:

11. “For your name’s sake, O Lord, you will be favorable to my sin, for it is great.” Since your way is mercy, you will be favorable to my sin, not because of my merit, but for your name’s sake.

It is necessary for us not only that you should not remember the sins of our youth and our past negligences, but also that you should be favorable toward our daily sin. For it is great, as the Apostle testifies when he says, “We all offend in many things” (James 3). As long as we live here in mortality, we cannot be without much sin. But we have Christ as our propitiator, who intercedes for us (Rom. 8).

We ought therefore not to presume upon ourselves, but to fear. By fearing God, we begin to avoid sin, abandon the path of error, and hold to the way of truth. And [Col. 0733B] because it is a great thing to fear God, while few are those who fear him, he asks who fears him and shows what fruit proceeds from that fear. He says:

12. “Who is the man who fears the Lord?” As though he were saying: Whoever he is, he is great and blessed. From this he begins to approach wisdom. “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110).

Hence it is added: “He will establish a law for him on the way he has chosen.” This is no longer addressed to one who is sinning, but to one who turns to God through fear and humility. God establishes him for perseverance—not with the law of the letter, which was given to those who sin on the way (for the law was given because of transgressors [James 2]), but with the law of grace, which is not merely given but established and fixed immovably for one who is progressing—not on just any way, but on the way he has chosen, which is Christ (John 14).

The one who fears God is placed on this way, and there the divine law is established for him, by which he may live spiritually for God. Hence it is added:

13. “His soul shall dwell among good things, and his offspring shall [Col. 0733C] inherit the earth.” For he delights in the law of God according to the inner person; he burns with heavenly desires, clings to spiritual pursuits, and exercises himself in good works.

His offspring are indeed good works. Hence the Apostle admonishes us, saying, “Let us not grow weary in doing good, for in due time we shall reap, if we do not grow faint” (Gal. 6). And again, “Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly” (2 Cor. 9).

He rightly said that his offspring would inherit the earth, because the good work that he sows, as it were, when he performs it will cause him to possess the heavenly inheritance and the land of the living. And lest he seem to presume upon his good works, as though he were strong through them, he therefore adds:

14. The Lord is a stronghold for those who fear him, and his covenant is that he may be manifested to them. In itself the Church is fragile and weak; but because it has been founded upon the firm rock (1 Cor. 3), therefore the gates of hell shall not prevail against it (Matt. 18). Yet because he strengthens it in this way by his grace, he promises in his covenant that he will also show himself to it. Hence, in the Gospel, Truth says of one who loves him, “I will love him, and I will manifest myself to him” (John 14). The reward of our labor is the vision of God; when we have seen him, there will be nothing further for us to seek. Hence Philip says, “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (ibid.). And because, so long as the Church of the elect lives bodily here, it continually makes its desires known there, he therefore adds:

15. My eyes are always toward the Lord, for he will draw my feet out of the snare. These should not here be understood as bodily eyes. For God is not seen by bodily sight (John 1; 1 John 4). By “eyes,” therefore, the perception of the inner person may be understood; by “the snare,” every temptation; by “feet,” the affections of the soul. No one is drawn out of this snare of various temptations unless his attention and desire are lifted to things above. Do not therefore look back if you wish to be fit for the kingdom of God (Luke 9). Let your eyes, your perception, your heart, and your desire be directed toward the Lord your God. And he himself will draw you out of every snare and impediment, from every temptation and deception. Therefore, praying, he adds:

16. Look upon me and have mercy on me, for I am solitary and poor. I attend to you; look upon me: I attend by desiring, you look upon me by showing mercy. For it is mine (according to Augustine) to love you; it is yours to save me. For I am your solitary one, preserving the unity of your one Church [Note: [Col. 0733D] The Vulgate has *humilitatem* (“humility”), according to Augustine.]—which no schisms or heresies possess (Eph. 4)—and persevering in one faith, hope, and charity. And I am your poor one, seeking neither gold nor silver, neither possessions nor riches above you; not presuming upon myself, nor puffed up in spirit, but humble in heart, seeking nothing else but you. Therefore, look upon the solitary one; have mercy on the poor one.

17. The tribulations of my heart have multiplied; rescue me from my distresses. The tribulations of the heart are understood as the inner passions of the soul, such as vices and perverse desires, mental pleasures and lusts, and other things of this kind by which the heart is afflicted (2 Cor. 6). Distresses pertain to the body, by which the outward person is troubled: hunger and thirst, cold and heat, illness and the corruption of the flesh, and similar things. They are called “distresses” because they are, as it were, natural and come upon us whether we wish it or not. The holy man asks to be rescued from these tribulations of the heart and distresses of the body, so that he may be clothed with blessed immortality. And because there are some who, when they experience such things, bear them impatiently, resist in their hearts, murmur with their tongues, and despise the scourges of almighty God—and thus, from the very things by which they ought to have been purified, proceed toward something worse by growing proud—he therefore adds:

18. See my humility and my labor, and forgive all my offenses. Affliction of heart and body is the punishment of sin. But if it is endured with a humble and patient heart, the wondrous mercy of almighty God is at work, so that forgiveness follows from the very thing by which guilt is punished. Therefore he asks that his humility be seen, by which he patiently bears his labor, so that through enduring his labors he may merit forgiveness for his offenses. “Forgive all,” he says—that is, past, present, and future offenses. Not only those of my youth and ignorance, before I believed, but also those which, now living by faith, I commit through weakness or through the darkness of this life. To the greater accumulation of the tribulation he suffers, he adds:

19. Look upon my enemies, for they have multiplied, and they hate me with an unjust hatred. For enemies are found not only outside, but also within the very communion of the Church. Outside (according to Augustine) are Jews and pagans; inside are heretics, who err in the faith, and false Christians, who attack the faith by their conduct. These are the ones who hate the Church with an unjust hatred. Hatred is just when guilt is hated and nature is loved. Hatred is unjust, however, when guilt is loved and nature is hated. Or hatred is unjust when someone hates a friend. “Look upon my enemies”—as though he were saying: By attending to them, protect me. Therefore he adds:

20. Guard my soul and rescue me; I shall not be put to shame, for I have hoped in you. Guard it, lest it perish; rescue it, so that it may escape; let me not be put to shame, lest I fall away from my purpose. And you ought to do these things because I have hoped in you. What the Church prays for, the Lord never ceases daily to accomplish in his elect, whom he both abandons, as it were, by guarding them, and guards by abandoning them. He permits their hearts to be shaken by temptations, their bodies to be afflicted by distresses, and to be exercised by the hatreds of the wicked; but while he gives these things over to the enemy, he always reserves the soul for himself. For the ancient enemy, both personally and through his members, maliciously seeks to tempt holy men. Almighty God permits this to happen only in his goodness, namely so that the good which lies hidden may appear, and virtue may increase through patience. But the elect, while they experience the temptations of the wicked enemy inwardly and outwardly, presuming on nothing in themselves, immediately turn to the help of God their protector. So that they may not commit anything shameful, they entreat him humbly; and so that they may merit being heard, they strengthen themselves with the firmness of hope. When the perfect do this, they draw the rest to themselves by their example. Hence it is also added:

21. The innocent and upright have clung to me, because I have waited for you. Innocent in conduct, upright in faith; innocent in the things they do below, upright in the highest things they perceive. Those who live innocently and desire the heavenly homeland long not only to be separated from the wicked but also to cling to the good. For just as evil conversations corrupt good morals (1 Cor. 15), so good conversations build up good morals. And it is written, “With the holy you will be holy, and with the innocent man you will be innocent” (2 Sam. 22). Thus the holy cling to the holy, and the innocent to the innocent, so that they may build one another up by words and conduct and communicate their own good things to one another through charity, so that one may grow in goodness through the other. Meanwhile, while they patiently endure so many evils, labor ardently in good works, and are made firm by the rectitude of hope, lest their endurance fail amid such great tribulations, they humbly implore God their deliverer so that they may escape, saying:

22. Deliver, O God, Israel from all his tribulations. “Israel” is interpreted as “a man seeing God.” It is as though he were saying (according to Augustine): “Deliver, O God, from all his tribulations the people whom you have prepared to contemplate you.” Not only from those things which they endure outwardly, but also from those which they suffer inwardly. Let us also strive to lift our souls to the Lord, to place our trust in him, and to learn his humble and exalted commandments, so that we may merit being guided in truth and contemplate wisdom itself—which is God—with the mind. Thus, by his mercy, may we be stripped of the sins of youth and ignorance; may we, made gentle and meek, pursue the ways of mercy and truth; and, cleansed by the Lord our propitiator from daily sin, may we fear him and, established in the way—which is Christ, may we possess his law of grace. Through him may we abide in good things and enjoy an eternal inheritance. Meanwhile, having God as our stronghold, let us direct toward him the eyes of our mind, until we are drawn out of the snare of this world and, by his mercy, delivered from all tribulations, having become spiritual Israel and contemplating the Lord our God in his majesty.

## Title of Psalm 25

1. The title of the following psalm is, “A Psalm of David.” This text is to be attributed to the more excellent member of the Church, who above prayed to God and here shows that he has been heard and has obtained innocence and perfection through divine mercy; thereafter he prays that he may not be moved from his purpose. He does this so that, from those from whom he is morally separated, he may also be eternally separated. His intention is to invite us by his example to innocence and perfection. Thus he says:

## Psalm 25

2. Judge me, Lord, for I have walked in my innocence; and, hoping in the Lord, I shall not be weakened. Whoever has guilt fears judgment. He, therefore, is perfect, because he saw that his cause was just and asked to be judged by the Lord. He rightly recalls that he walked in innocence, because spiritual innocence is the way by which one advances toward God, and living innocently pertains to the inner person (Eph. 3). When he declares himself innocent, this is not the pride of an arrogant man, but the confession of one who is not ungrateful. It is as though he were saying (according to Augustine): “After the mercy which you have bestowed upon me, I possess some merit of innocence, whose way I have guarded.” Yet even so, not trusting in myself but hoping in the Lord, I shall not be weakened in my work but shall remain, so that, as I began, so I may also be perfected. If he presumed upon himself or gloried in himself, he would undoubtedly be weakened. But because he places his hope in the Lord, he can no longer be weakened, because the Lord himself is his strength.

3. Test me, Lord, and try me; burn my kidneys and my heart. I said, “Judge me”; but if there is anything in me that must be purified, O Lord, try me here and correct me with the scourge of sons, and thus test me—that is, render me approved. Burn my kidneys—that is, destroy the pleasures of the flesh, since pleasures abound especially in the kidneys—and my heart, that is, my perverse thoughts. “Burn my kidneys and my heart”: as though he were saying, Apply spiritual medicine to my outward and inward vices. Even if holy men live perfectly, they still desire paternal scourges, so that they may advance toward their homeland all the more perfectly, insofar as the discipline that chastises them lovingly purifies them daily even from the smallest faults. Therefore they endure discipline in order to obtain mercy, concerning which it is added: “For your mercy is before my eyes, and I have been pleased with your truth.” A truthful teacher scourges a lying pupil; the scourged pupil pays attention and asks mercy from the teacher. Thus the heavenly teacher and loving Father acts toward us. We have sinned, and therefore we are scourged. He scourges; we wait for him to spare us. “Your mercy,” he says, “is before my eyes. I patiently endure your discipline, but I continually await your mercy.” And now I have pleased you in the truth of the punishment which I deserved, whereas previously I displeased you in the falsehood of the guilt by which I sinned. And because, having fallen, I deserved anger, once corrected by you I found mercy.

4. From this it is evident that I have walked in my innocence, because “I have not sat with the council of vanity, and I will not enter in with those who do iniquity.” Those sit with the council of vanity who linger in their assembly, who come together deliberately and devote themselves to speaking about vanity. To enter in with those who do iniquity is to thrust oneself into the company of those who act perversely and, by one’s own choice, to join oneself with the wicked in wicked deeds. Such is the zeal of the perverse and carnal. Either they sit and devote themselves to empty talk, or they labor at iniquitous action. In contrast, holy men, so that they may be innocent in word and deed, restrain their tongue from vanity and preserve their life from wicked action. And because first one must not love an evil thing, and afterward must also hate it, it is rightly added:

5. I have hated the assembly of the wicked, and I will not sit with the impious. I have hated not human beings but transgressors; not nature but guilt. The wicked are those who labor so that, by their malice, they may surpass those like themselves. The impious are unbelievers who do not worship the Lord. Piety properly pertains to the worship of God. Although the Church is not separated bodily from all these people, it is separated from them in life and conduct: from those sluggish in idleness and devoted to vanity; from those engaged in wicked deeds; from those who deliberately magnify their own malice; and from unbelievers. It should be noted that he first said, “I have not sat”; here he says, “I will not sit with the impious.” The former indicates a beginning; the latter, perseverance. For the good that is begun must be carried through to the end. But since he separates himself from the wicked, with whom he is joined, let us hear what follows:

6. I will wash my hands among the innocent and surround your altar, Lord. You do not wash your hands with visible water when you think devoutly about your deeds; and you are innocent before the eyes of God, who is also the altar before the eyes of God, into which the priest entered, who first offered himself for us. There is a heavenly altar, which only the one who washes his hands among the innocent embraces, having himself become innocent. For many touch this altar unworthily, and God tolerates the injury done to his sacraments for a time. But just as you are received with the wicked within the walls of the Church, so you will not be received with the wicked in the bosom of Abraham (Luke 16). Therefore do not be afraid: wash your hands and surround the altar of God, where you offer vows to the Lord, where you pour out prayers, where your conscience is pure, and where you tell God who you are. If there is something else that displeases God, he to whom you confess it will heal it. Why do you surround the altar of God, holy man? The text continues and says:

7. That I may hear the voice of praise and recount all your wonders. To hear the voice of praise is to understand inwardly, because whatever evil is in you comes from your sins, while whatever is good comes from God’s acts of justification. Thus you will hear the voice of praise without praising yourself. And when you are good, you also hear inwardly the divine praises which the Lord your God speaks within you; and by hearing them there, you say that you may recount all his wonders, bodily and spiritual, visible and invisible. It belongs to the wonders of the Lord when someone is raised up in the body. But it belongs to greater wonders when someone is raised up in soul. It is a great miracle when one who was dead rises alive. It is greater when one who was impious rises up pious; when one who was lustful rises up chaste; when one who was proud rises up humble. These outward wonders contribute to faith; the inward ones to the building up of conduct; the praises of the Lord to love. For this your Lord God is praised; for this he is proclaimed wonderful: so that you may love, believe, and hope. Love the One worthy of praise; believe and hope in the Wonderful One. To this belongs what follows:

8. Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where your glory dwells. The house of God is the Church; its beauty is righteousness; the place where he dwells is eternal rest. He rightly placed the beauty of the house first, and afterward the place of habitation, because by loving and pursuing righteousness one reaches the glory of eternal rest. And because each of the elect, however much he may advance, still fears being rejected, he humbly entreats the merciful God, saying:

9. Do not destroy my soul with the impious, O God, nor my life with men of blood. The impious are those who hate God; men of blood are those who hate their neighbor. For whoever hates his brother is a murderer (1 John 2 and 3). These are the assembly of the wicked, who hold the council of vanity, with whom the holy man declares that he has not sat. It should be noted that he does not say, “In the council,” but “With the council.” For someone may sit in the council of vanity for a useful purpose, when he sits there in order to free an innocent person or to rebuke the vanity itself. But to sit with the council of vanity is to consent to that council. Since he did not do this, he now prays that, because he was not a participant in the guilt, he may not be a participant in the punishment either. This is the judgment he asks from the Lord: that he be distinguished from the wicked among whom he lives.

10. In whose hands are iniquities, and their right hand is filled with gifts. Just as what we hold in our hands we have readily available, so those are said to have iniquities in their hands who always have wrongdoing readily available. Iniquities are in the hands of those who are prepared for murder, theft, robbery, and the commission of other evils. These are the people who devote themselves with ardent zeal to acquiring profits and search everywhere so that their right hand may be filled with gifts. But because he says not “hands” but “right hand,” something more subtle is signified by this expression. It is the practice of the wicked to turn the gift of grace into an increase of guilt. He therefore says well, “Their right hand is filled with gifts,” because (according to Augustine) what was given to them for obtaining eternal salvation they have converted into receiving the gifts of this age, supposing that piety is a means of gain (1 Tim. 6). These are the people who sell their wisdom, demand a price for righteousness, and sometimes labor even at spiritual pursuits so that they may acquire something earthly. But because the man of God shakes his hand free from every gift and does whatever he does purely and for God’s sake—not desiring to store up treasure here (Matt. 6), but so that he may escape from this captivity—he humbly implores his Redeemer, saying:

11. But I have walked in my innocence; redeem me and have mercy on me. May the price of my Lord’s blood be sufficient for me (according to the same author) for the perfection of my deliverance, so that in the dangers of this life your mercy may not abandon me.

[Note: [Col. 0737] The word *meum* (“my”) is superfluous and is not found in Augustine.]

12. My foot has stood on level ground. That is, my affection has not departed from righteousness. Why on level ground? Because above he had said, “And, hoping in the Lord, I shall not be weakened.” The one who does not hope in the Lord totters among the wicked. From this arose schisms. But what conclusion is reached? “In the churches I will bless you, Lord.” Whoever blesses the Lord with his tongue but curses him by his deeds does not bless the Lord in the churches. Rather, he is one of those about whom it is said, “Woe to those through whom the name of the Lord is blasphemed” (Isa. 52). To bless the Lord in the churches therefore means to live in such a way that the Lord is blessed through each person’s conduct.

## Title of Psalm 26

A Psalm of David, before he was anointed a second time. This psalm is to be attributed to David, that is, to the perfect Church. It is a psalm, I say, dealing with the matter that occurred before he was anointed with a second anointing. David is read to have been anointed twice. First by Samuel in his father’s house (1 Sam. 16), which prefigured the second anointing. Then, when he was received by the people and made king over Judah at Hebron (2 Sam. 2 and 5), he was anointed a second time. In the same way Christ was anointed twice, not with bodily but with spiritual anointing. First, when he was established as king over the Jewish people, free from sin; afterward, following the resurrection, he was anointed when he was made immortal and incapable of suffering. And he was given the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Phil. 2).

In the same way the faithful are anointed twice: first in baptism, when they receive the pledge of the Spirit (2 Cor. 1 and 5), an anointing that is a foreshadowing and, as it were, a pledge of the future anointing; and second after this life, when they attain immortality and freedom from suffering (Eph. 1). After his first anointing David was not confirmed in the kingdom until Saul had been defeated. He defeated many adversaries before he was anointed a second time. Likewise, in this life the faithful have many adversaries before they are anointed a second time. And they will never be confirmed in the kingdom until Saul has been defeated—that is, until the devil has been utterly overcome and death destroyed.

In this way the title may be explained of both the head and the members. In this psalm the perfect soul intends, by its example, to exhort each person who has received the pledge of the Holy Spirit, so that, if he desires to be blessed, he may act courageously in the temptations of the present life and, by conforming himself to the benefits which God has bestowed in this life—benefits enumerated at the beginning of the psalm, where it says, “The Lord is my light,” and so forth—endure the burden and heat of the day with devout perseverance. Thus he says:

## Psalm 26

1. The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The Lord is the protector of my life; from whom shall I tremble? He names three things: illumination, salvation, and protection. These three make a person fearless against every adversity. For if God illumines him so that he may see what is right; if he heals him so that he may accomplish in deed what he has seen to be right; and then if he protects him so that, when tempted, he may not fall—what remains that he ought to fear? The true light has come, which enlightens every person coming into this world (John 1). He redeemed my soul, illumined it, and protects it so that it may not be lost; from whom shall I tremble? I see enemies; I see tyrants rushing upon me. But, relying upon the Lord’s admonition, I fear no one, for it says, “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10). Hence it is added:

2. When the evildoers draw near against me to eat my flesh, those who trouble me, my enemies, have themselves been weakened and have fallen. Evildoers draw near; enemies attack me; foes besiege me, so that they may eat my flesh—that is, tear me apart and kill me, deceive the carnal and imperfect, and join them to their nefarious body. Or “to eat flesh” means to consume carnal affections in the fire of tribulation. Yet in this they are weakened in their own strength and fall defeated, because they cannot break into the inner parts of the soul. Therefore he adds further:

3. If armies should encamp against me, my heart will not fear. If the army of the impious, the assault of vices, and the gathering of demons should rise up with their forces assembled and their battle line arranged, my heart does not doubt, because almighty God confirms it by illuminating, healing, and protecting it. If battle should rise against me, so that the enemies mentioned above may wish to overcome me, in this I shall hope. In what? The text continues and says:

4. One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life. The temptations and tribulations of this age are useful to us for attaining the kingdom of God. Therefore, while the holy Church endures battles below, it lifts its hope to things above; and the more grievous the things it suffers here, the greater the reward it expects there. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel, “When people curse you and persecute you because of me, rejoice in that hour, for your reward is great in heaven” (Matt. 5; Luke 6). Let us therefore see what the one thing is that he asks, who, placed amid adversities, fears nothing. What is that one thing? “That I may dwell,” he says, “in the house of the Lord all the days of my life.”

That is called a house in which we shall always remain. In this pilgrimage it is properly called a tabernacle, which pertains to those who are soldiers and fight against the enemy. What shall we do in that house? In another psalm you have the answer: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; forever and ever they will praise you” (Ps. 83). Burning with this desire and fervent with this love, he longs to dwell in the house of the Lord throughout all the days of his life. Days, I say, that will not end, but will be eternal. They are called days in the same way as the years of which it is said, “Your years will not fail” (Ps. 101; Heb. 11). For the days of eternal life are one day without sunset.

This, therefore, is what he says: “From the Lord I have desired this; this one thing I have asked; this I shall seek.” And as though we were to say, “What will you do there? Why do you ask this?”—“That I may see,” he says, “the will of the Lord and visit his temple.” [Note: [Col. 0739D] This is an old variant reading, which Augustine prefers, or perhaps substitutes himself, in place of the words “that I may see the will”; other books, with the Vulgate translator, have “delight.”] Behold what I love; behold why I wished to dwell in the house of the Lord: so that I may contemplate his delight. For now we see through a mirror and in an enigma, but then face to face. Now I know in part, but then I shall know even as I am known (1 Cor. 13). He rightly says, “and visit his temple,” because that blessed vision will not be fulfilled except in the vision of the temple of God, which he properly calls both a house and a temple. It is called a house because it is inhabited by the saints; a temple because praises are offered there to the Lord. But in order that I may reach that place, from which I make my hope, the text continues and says:

5. For he hid me in his tabernacle on the day of evils; he protected me in the hidden place of his tabernacle. The day of evils is the present life, in which evil is done. Hence the Apostle says, “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil” (Eph. 5). The present Church is the tabernacle in which we serve as soldiers. The Son of God received flesh from this tabernacle and became for us the hidden place of the tabernacle. He hides us in the tabernacle through faith; he protects us in Christ for salvation. We are children of God, but what we shall be has not yet appeared (1 John 3). For we walk by faith and not by sight. “You have died,” says the Apostle, “and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. 3). And because God hides us from vices and protects us in Christ so that he may exalt us to virtues, he rightly adds:

6. He exalted me upon a rock, and now he has exalted my head above my enemies. The Lord Jesus Christ is both rock and head (1 Cor. 10; Eph. 1 and 2). Concerning this rock the Lord himself says, “Upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 18). Firmly founded upon this rock, the Church is exalted from the world to heaven and from the devil to the Lord. And now, while the body remains and labors on earth among enemies, it says that its head—that is, Christ—has already been exalted: “For he rose from the dead and sits at the right hand of the Father in heaven” (Eph. 1; Mark 16).

Let the members therefore be confident and not fear their enemies, since even now they see their head exalted above them. For where the head is, there the members will also follow. We too are above with him; he is also below with us. Behold what a pledge we possess. Therefore, by faith, hope, and charity, we are with our head in heaven forever, because he himself, by goodness, divinity, and unity, is with us on earth until the consummation of the age (Matt. 28). Hence the Church never ceases to offer him praises and sacrifices (Ps. 115). Therefore it adds: “I went around and offered in his tabernacle a sacrifice of jubilation; I will sing and utter a psalm to the Lord.”

I have considered the faith of the whole world, in which my head has been exalted above those who persecuted me. And in that tabernacle—that is, in the Church spread throughout the whole world—I praised the Lord with all my strength. To shout means to raise one’s voice with great power. We offer God a sacrifice of jubilation (Ps. 118) when we offer him praises with great devotion and contrition of heart. In saying, “I will sing and utter a psalm,” he indicates the frequency of divine service. Song pertains to the joyfulness of praise, while the psalm pertains to the exercise of good works. Our praise is acceptable to God when we praise him with voice, heart, and deed. Then he asks to be heard, adding:

7. Hear, Lord, my voice with which I cried to you; have mercy on me and hear me. Let us groan now; let us pray now. Groaning belongs only to the afflicted; prayer only to those in need. Prayer will pass away, and praise will follow. Weeping will pass away, and joy will follow. Meanwhile, while we are in the days of evils, let our prayer to God not cease; from him let us ask that one thing. Let us not desist from that petition until, by his giving and leading us there, we reach it, all desires come to an end, and there is one thing in the heart and in the petition. Hence it is also added:

8. My heart has said to you, “My face has sought you”; your face, O God, I shall seek. It is as though he were saying: My prayer is not only on my lips but has been uttered from the heart. “My face has sought you”—that is, my intention, my faith, my mind, in which you know me. “Your face, O God, I shall seek.” I do not seek honor, glory, or riches; your face, your beauty, your vision are what I desire.

9. Do not turn your face from me; do not turn away in anger from your servant. Perhaps he turns away from some, not in anger—as from those who say to him, “Turn your face from my sins” (Ps. 50). When he turns his face from your sins, he does not turn away from you in anger. Let him therefore turn his face from your sins, but let him not turn his face from you. His anger is nothing other than the turning away of his face.

Be my helper; do not abandon me or despise me, O God my Savior. Behold, I am on the way. I asked one thing of you—free will—and I have it. I know what I ought to do rightly, but without you I can do nothing (John 15). Be my helper, therefore, so that I may advance; do not abandon me, lest I fall; do not despise me, lest I perish. You ought to do this because you are my God, who created me, and my Savior, who redeemed me. I have no helper apart from you.

10. For my father and my mother have abandoned me, but the Lord has taken me up. Apart from those two parents from whose flesh we were born, we have here another father and another mother—or rather, we once had them. According to the world, the father is the devil (John 8), and he was our father when we were unbelievers. For the Lord says to unbelievers, “You are from your father the devil” (ibid.). He is the father of all the impious; he works in the children of unbelief (Eph. 5).

The mother is that Babylonian society of all the lost, from east to west. It possesses the earthly kingdom. This was our first mother; in her we were born. We came to know another Father, God (Matt. 6 and 23), and abandoned the devil. We came to know another mother, the heavenly Jerusalem, which is the holy Church (2 Cor. 5), whose portion is on pilgrimage upon earth; we abandoned Babylon. We have been separated from the world and from the devil.

The Lord took us up as a Father, because he created us, calls us, commands us, and rules us. He took us up as a mother, because he loves us, nourishes us, suckles us, and holds us. But let us hear what the one taken up by the Lord asks:

11. Establish your law for me, Lord, in your way, and guide me on a straight path because of my enemies. The way of the Lord may here be understood as faith; the straight path as charity, concerning which the Apostle says to his disciples, “I show you a still more excellent way” (1 Cor. 12), and then began to speak about charity. The enemies of the holy Church are those who live carnally and heretics, who oppress God’s servants by living badly and teaching perversely. The holy man therefore asks that the law be established for him in the way and that he be guided by God on the path, so that, instructed by the law, he may believe rightly and, directed by grace, may walk rightly in loving and acting. He does this because of his enemies, who, when they find people less instructed or imperfect, draw them, if they can, into error or iniquity. Concerning them he adds further:

12. Do not hand me over to the desires of those who trouble me, for unjust witnesses have risen up against me, and iniquity has lied to itself. If you hand my flesh over to their hands, do not hand me—that is, my soul—over to their desires, that is, their wills, so that they may fulfill their entire intention and desire against me; so that, even if they kill the body, they may not kill the soul (Matt. 10). For they rose up against me to turn me back from you, bearing witness to iniquity and falsehood.

False witnesses have often risen up against the saints (Matt. 26), affirming that they were transgressors of the law and deceivers. But iniquity lied to itself (Acts 6), not to the saints, because their lie turned into punishment and condemnation for themselves, but into glory for the saints. For it must be noted that good things are not only not weakened by the attacks of the wicked, but are recognized as being even more truly good because of them.

If the Church’s teaching were simple and no one from outside pressed it with assertions of heretical doctrines, our faith could not appear so clear and so thoroughly tested. For this reason the teaching of the Catholic faith is besieged by the attacks of those who contradict it, so that our faith may not grow sluggish through idleness but may be refined through exercise. Therefore the Apostle also said, “There must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest” (1 Cor. 11).

If you remove from among us the devil himself and the opposing powers that fight against us, the virtues of the soul cannot shine forth without an adversary. Likewise, the glory of the faithful cannot shine unless the rejection and punishment of unbelievers commend it. After that circuit and jubilation, after these dangers and labors, placed among the hands of those who trouble him, burning, panting, laboring, yet firm and confident, with the Lord receiving, leading, and guiding him, let us hear what he adds:

13. I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living. O sweet, immortal, everlasting good things of the Lord, when shall I see you? “I believe,” he says, “that I shall see.” For the righteous lives by faith (Rom. 1). What is faith? Believing what you do not see. For the things that are seen are temporal; they belong to the land of the dying. But the things that are not seen are eternal; they belong to the land of the living (2 Cor. 4). It is called “land” by analogy, because of its stability. No one perishes there, but always remains and lives in blessedness. But what does the Apostle say? “If we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Rom. 8). Therefore divine Scripture rightly admonishes us, saying:

14. Wait for the Lord; act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, and endure the Lord. Hence it is said through the Prophet: “If he delays, wait for him, for he will surely come” (Hab. 2). If it is delayed, it is not taken away. Many neglect to wait for the Lord because his reward is not given in the present but reserved for the future (Matt. 5). Therefore they grow weary and remain on the way. For this reason you are divinely admonished to act manfully, that is, courageously, and, strengthened in heart, to endure patiently. For it is not enough to do good courageously unless, through the strength of your spirit, you strive also to endure evils with equanimity. Do not collapse, lest you be among those of whom it is said: “Woe to those who have lost endurance” (Eccles. 2)! Whoever loses endurance has become effeminate and has lost vigor. Therefore act manfully in your work and endure patiently, so that by living well you may be just, and by suffering you may be perfect. Thus you will see the good things in which you believe. Thus you will bring righteous works to their perfect end.

## TITLE OF PSALM XXVII

A psalm of David himself, that is, of the more excellent member of the Church. [Col. 0742B] It is the concern of the Church crying out to the Lord, asking him to hear her prayer in such a way that he does not destroy her together with those who work iniquity, but grant her what she has deserved, while not leaving the wicked unpunished. By doing this, it intends to persuade each believer, following its example, to place his heart in the Lord, so that his flesh may blossom again in him. Or, because it is said “of David himself,” it is the voice of the mediator himself, strong-handed in the struggle of his Passion. What he appears to pray for against his enemies is not a wish born of ill will, but a proclamation of punishment. He does not wish for what he says; rather, he foretells what is about to befall them. Therefore he speaks for himself and his members as follows:

## PSALM XXVII

### 1

“To you, Lord, I will cry out; my God, do not be silent toward me, lest at some time you be silent toward me and I become like those who descend into the pit.”

He rightly calls him “Lord” to whom every creature is subject, as it is written: “All things serve you” (Ps. 118). Although he is the God of all by creation, he is properly the Son of God by nature, or specially the God of the Church by grace. To cry out to him is to pray with one’s whole desire and whole affection.

“Do not be silent toward me,” he says, with respect to outward instruction; “and do not at any time be silent toward me,” with respect to inward inspiration. For it is necessary that the merciful God, just as he once spoke for the salvation of the human race through the Prophets, and in these last times through his Son (Heb. 1), should likewise not now be silent, but continually speak to us through his representatives, instructed by word and grace; that he should teach us and inspire us.

“And if,” he says, “you are silent, I shall become like those who descend into the pit.” If Christ had been silent, he would have appeared like the other mortals. But because God spoke in him, Peter therefore said to him: “You have the words of eternal life” (John 6), and: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 18). “Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ” (Rom. 10).

Again, if he is silent through the teachers of the Church, his silence is our destruction. In another sense, by saying “I will cry out,” he indicates that he cries out incessantly to the Lord throughout the whole time of his obedience. By adding “Do not be silent,” he indicates the pious relationship between God and humanity, because from the moment a human being begins to cry out, God hears.

The Hebrew truth [Note: He learned this from Jerome’s own translation from the Hebrew; for, as far as I remember, the Holy Father does not note it elsewhere.] does not have “lest at some time you be silent toward me”; but the Seventy Interpreters added it, and not without reason. Through it they make us understand that he cried out concerning his first and second glorification.

The first glorification was before the resurrection, when he was free from every sin and through him God performed miracles that no one else could perform. The second glorification was in the resurrection, through which his humanity received impassibility and immortality.

“And if you are silent, removed from me, then I shall become like”—that is, I shall be like—“those who descend into the pit,” that is, into the misery of this world. For if the human nature of the Lord were deserted by the protection of the divine Word united to it, it would certainly be found like other human beings.

He rightly says “those who descend,” because the greatest descent is to turn away from God and incline oneself toward the miseries of this world. The ascent, by contrast, is to abandon these miseries and hasten toward everlasting goods. Therefore he adds:

### 2

“Hear, Lord, the voice of my supplication when I pray to you, when I lift up my hands toward your holy temple.”

He presents two reasons for which he ought rightly to be heard, saying: “when,” that is, because, “I pray to you.” And because I lift up my hands upon the cross toward the temple—that is, toward the Church that is to be built—so that it may be the holy temple of God.

The incarnation and Passion of the Redeemer were a great merit for being heard. He became, as the Apostle says, “the propitiation for our sins in his blood” (1 John 2), by which he would wash us from sins (Rev. 1) and prepare for himself “a Church without spot or wrinkle” (Eph. 5).

You too, consider your head: learn from his example to pray, to endure, and to love. Stretch out your hands toward the temple. Extend yourself toward good works for the sake of the kingdom of God. Hear and pray what follows:

[Col. 0743B] ### 3

“Do not hand me over together with sinners, and do not destroy me together with those who work iniquity.”

Christ was indeed with sinners, because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1), and he was “numbered among the wicked” (Isa. 53). Yet he was not handed over together with sinners so as himself to be a sinner, because “he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2).

He descended into hell, where the wicked descend. But he did not perish with those who work iniquity, because although he was killed by the wicked, he nevertheless rose from death and redeemed us by dying. Thus that death was not destruction but life.

Pray also that you may not be handed over together with sinners, lest you be corrupted by the wicked ways of those with whom you live; and that you may not be destroyed with those who work iniquity, lest you perish eternally with the wicked whose persecution you endure temporarily.

The wicked are so not only in deed but also in speech. For it follows: “Those who speak peace with their neighbor”—those who said, “We know that you have come from God as a teacher” (John 11)—“but evil is in their hearts.” For they were plotting to seize Jesus by deceit and kill him (Matt. 26).

Christ is called the neighbor of the Jews (Matt. 15), both according to the flesh, because he came from their lineage, and because he had come to show them mercy (Rom. 1). In accordance with this, the Gospel says of the Samaritan that he is called the neighbor of the man who fell among robbers because he showed him mercy (Luke 10).

How many such people are found in the Church of God, who still persecute the body of Christ (Rom. 12)! These are the ones who come “in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves” (Matt. 7). And because they themselves are such, he says:

### 4

“Give them according to their works, and according to the wickedness of their inventions let the recompense of punishment be made.”

Someone may say: Their works were good, even when they killed Christ, because through this the human race was redeemed. Therefore it follows: “And according to the wickedness of their inventions.” It is as though he were saying: I do not mean that they should be repaid according to the benefit that proceeded from their works, but according to the wickedness which they thought they had devised for their own benefit.

For they did not kill Christ in order that the human race might be redeemed, but so that they would not lose their place and nation. In this matter it must be noted that the same action is called both good and evil according to different intentions. For the Jews handed over the Son whom God the Father had handed over. The action on both sides was one; but the intention was different. The Father handed him over in order to save us by his resurrection. The Jews handed him over and arranged for him to be condemned to the most shameful death so that he might perish completely.

Therefore justice or injustice lies not in the action but in the will. Thus it follows: “According to the works of their hands, repay them; render their recompense upon them.”

What did he wish to designate by “the works of their hands” except the extraordinary iniquity that they committed in the Lord’s death? By adding “hands” after “works,” he shows that they applied great zeal and devotion to that deed. The expression “of their hands” is drawn from the artisan, because he wishes to call those works the works of their hands which they performed deliberately.

He rightly says “recompense,” because although Christ had done good to them, they repaid him with evil. It is as though he said plainly: Just as they repaid me with evil, repay them with evil in the same way. And rightly so:

### 5

“Because they did not understand the works of the Lord”—namely, those mystically written in the Law, or those which he later secretly accomplished through his Son, such as causing him to be incarnate from the Virgin and sending him for our redemption—“nor the works of his hands,” that is, they did not understand the manifest works.

The Hebrews have: “They did not look upon the works of his hands.” [Note: He seems to have taken this from Jerome’s translation from the Hebrew.]

What are those works? That he healed the sick, cleansed lepers, raised the dead, and performed many other great miracles which the Father accomplished through his Son. Hence the Truth said to the Jews: “If you do not believe me, believe the works. For the works that I do bear witness about me” (John 10).

They might have been found excusable concerning hidden matters, but not concerning those that were manifest. Since, therefore, they did not understand the manifest works so as to grasp divine things with their minds, it follows:

“You will destroy them,” spiritually and bodily, as happened in the destruction under Titus and Vespasian. And the Prophet, foreseeing that this destruction would be irreparable, added: “And you will not build them up again.”

In other destructions God had restored them, as in the destructions of Babylon and in the Egyptian captivity. Or even if they had been spiritually destroyed—for example, if they had become idolaters under one leader—God liberated them from idolatry through another leader.

But from this final spiritual blindness they will not be restored until the end, when their remnant will be saved; bodily, however, they will never be restored.

With this verse he begins to give thanks for having been heard. For he says:

### 6

“Blessed is the Lord, because he has heard the voice of my supplication.”

Whenever we are heard by the Lord, we ought to bless him. A human being has nothing to offer God in return for such great benefits except blessing and praise. No one becomes blessed by God’s gifts if he is ungrateful toward the giver. Thus we worship the Father of lights, from whom every good gift and every perfect gift descends: namely, through the sacrifice of praise and acts of thanksgiving.

### 7

“He not only heard me concerning the removal of evils, but the Lord is also my helper” for doing good, “and my protector,” lest I be wounded by the arrows of my persecutors.

“And in him my heart”—that is, my intention—“hoped”; it hoped concerning the resurrection. “And therefore I was helped.” The almighty God helps us in good and protects us in evil so that we may place our hope in him. The more confidently we hope in him, the more abundantly we are helped by him. Thus it comes about that through God’s help hope is generated in us, and then through the merit of hope God’s help is increased.

He shows in what respect he was helped by God: “And my flesh blossomed again.” [Col. 0744D] Christ’s flesh had blossomed before, when it was free from every sin; it blossomed again when, by rising, it received impassibility and immortality.

Therefore it follows: “And according to my will I will confess to him.” God loves willing confession; he does not accept forced service. Hence it is written: “The servant does not remain in the house forever; the son remains forever” (2 Cor. 9; John 8). A servant is one who serves from fear; a son is one who obeys from love. The former is excluded from the heavenly house because he is a servant; the latter is admitted because he is a son.

Let us therefore confess to the Lord with our whole will and whole affection, so that, as devoted sons, we may obtain God’s inheritance. For confession is rightly owed to him, of whom it follows:

### 8

“The Lord is the strength of his people,” that is, of those devoted to him. God’s strength consists in this: that he rescues human beings from the yoke of the devil and makes them his own.

“And he is the protector of the salvations of his Christ,” that is, of those who have been saved through Christ. Here he plainly indicates that the mysteries of Christ benefit human beings for salvation.

And because the Lord is the strength of his people, therefore, “Lord, do what belongs to you”:

### 9

“Save your people, Lord,” rescuing them from the power of their enemies and guiding them to faith.

“And bless your inheritance,” granting increase to the virtues already begun; “and rule them,” according to their morals and virtues; “and lift them up,” from virtue to virtue, forever—that is, until they reach eternity.

## TITLE OF PSALM XXVIII

### 1

“A psalm of David at the completion of the tabernacle.”

After the ark of the Lord had been returned by the Philistines and brought back to Jerusalem, the prophet Nathan forbade David to build a house for the Lord because he was a man of blood. Therefore he made a tabernacle of tents in which to place the ark of God (2 Kings 6 and 7). When it was completed, he invited many people to come to that temple (1 Chron. 17), not empty-handed, but to sacrifice there the offerings they had brought.

After this completion he wrote this psalm—not as though he were writing about the historical completion, but so that through the Holy Spirit he might prophesy to us the future completion of the Church, whose figure that tabernacle was.

Knowing that the prophet Ezra understood David in this way, he gave the psalm this title. The title is read as follows: This psalm belongs to the prophet David, who speaks here. I say, it is a psalm composed at the completion of the tabernacle, that is, in contemplation of the completion of the Church.

We rightly call the Church a tabernacle, because here we wage war as in a tabernacle. This is the subject of the psalm. The prophet’s concern, speaking in the person of the Church, is to show how God’s tabernacle is constructed—that is, with what virtue and magnificence—through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, which is conceived from the voice of the Lord repeated seven times.

In doing this, he intends that those who have been made sons of God by adoption offer God the sacrifice of a pure mind. Therefore he says:

## PSALM XXVIII

### 2

“Bring offerings to the Lord, sons of God; bring offerings to the Lord, sons of rams.”

Bring yourselves to the Lord—you whom the Apostles, leaders of the flocks, have begotten through the Gospel, possessing, as it were, two horns, the two Testaments. Hence Paul, a spiritual ram, says to his flock: “In Christ Jesus I begot you through the Gospel” (1 Cor. 4). And again: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor” (Gal. 4).

We offer ourselves to God if we devoutly do what we hear through wisdom. “My son,” he says, “give me your heart” (Prov. 27). But it is necessary that this offering of the heart also demonstrate itself in the completion of action. Hence it is added:

“Bring to the Lord glory and honor.” Show yourselves to be such that God is honored and glorified in you, in accordance with what is written: “Let your light shine before human beings, so that, seeing your good works, they may glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5).

“Bring to the Lord glory for his name.” Let him become gloriously known throughout the world.

“Adore the Lord in his holy court,” that is, in your enlarged and sanctified heart. We ought to give ourselves to the one by whom we were created. To him honor and glory are rightly offered by us for so many and such great benefits, which are applied to the building of the spiritual tabernacle, that is, the Church. For it is said:

[Col. 0745D] ### 3

“The voice of the Lord is over the waters.”

The voice of the Lord is over the peoples, who are rightly signified by waters, because, like waters, they continually flow onward in the course of mortality.

“The God of majesty thundered.” The God of majesty, from the cloud of flesh, preached repentance in a terrifying manner. He himself thundered, who is the God of majesty, power, and exalted strength. Hence the Church says in the Song of Songs: “My soul melted when my beloved spoke” (Song 6).

The voice of the Lord also thundered over the waters because in the Jordan the Father’s voice was heard over Christ: “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. 3). It now thunders over the waters of baptism as well, because believers are baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

And because it is he who baptizes, it rightly follows: “The Lord is over many waters.” For it is written: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Eph. 4).

Or, “The Lord is over many waters” means that the Lord Jesus himself, after uttering his voice over the peoples and terrifying them, converted them to himself and dwelt in them.

### 4

“The voice of the Lord is in power,” as in the saying: “Lazarus, come out” (John 11).

“The voice of the Lord is in magnificence.” For Jesus did not speak like the Pharisees, but as one having authority (John 11). Hence someone said: “Never has a human being spoken like this one” (ibid.).

Such was the power of this voice of the Lord that it raised the dead, gave sight to the blind, and cleansed lepers. Or the voice of the Lord was in power and magnificence when he first instructed the Apostles in the power of faith and afterward accomplished great things through them. Hence it continues:

### 5

“The voice of the Lord breaks the cedars, and the Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon.”

What are signified by cedars except those lofty in pride? And he rightly added “of Lebanon” after “cedars.” For Lebanon is interpreted as “whiteness” or “whitening.” The voice of the Lord breaks the cedars of Lebanon because through it even those are crushed who are exalted in honors, riches, and the splendor of earthly nobility.

Hence the Apostle says: “God chose the weak things of the world in order to confound the strong” (1 Cor. 1).

But it must be understood that the voice of the Lord breaks cedars in two ways: some by condemning them, others by drawing them to himself and thoroughly humbling them. Concerning these it is added:

### 6

“And he will shatter them like a calf of Lebanon.”

After cutting down their proud height, he will bring them low in imitation of his humility, he who, like a calf, was led to sacrifice through the very nobility of this world. For “the kings of the earth stood forth, and the princes gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ” (Ps. 2).

“And the beloved, like the son of unicorns.” For the beloved himself, the Father’s beloved and only-begotten Son, emptied himself of his nobility and became human, like the son of Jews who were ignorant of God’s righteousness and arrogantly boasted of their own righteousness as though it were unique.

[Col. 0746C] ### 7

“The voice of the Lord cuts through the flame of fire,” that is, divides the raging anger of his persecutors, so that some said, “Could this perhaps be the Christ?” while others said, “No, but he is leading the people astray” (John 7). Thus he cut through their previous insane tumult, drawing some across while leaving others in their wickedness.

### 8

“The voice of the Lord shakes the wilderness,” that is, moves to faith the gentile people, who once were without hope, without God, without a prophet, and without a preacher.

“And the Lord will shake the wilderness of Kadesh,” that is, the Lord will truly cause the holy word of his Scriptures to be celebrated, which was being abandoned by the Jews who did not understand it.

### 9

“The voice of the Lord prepares the deer, and he will reveal the thickets.”

The deer signify the Apostles, who, when the Holy Spirit prepared them to run and proclaim the Gospel, were swift and did not fear the deadly poisons of the devil and the heretics.

To them he revealed the thickets, because he opened the Scriptures and manifested the divine mysteries. Hence Paul says: “I heard secret words which it is not permitted for a human being to speak” (2 Cor. 12). And it is written: “He opened their understanding, so that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24).

Then he revealed to them the obscurities of the divine books and the shades of the mysteries, where they might pasture with freedom. And because through these gifts God perfects his Church, it rightly follows:

“And in his temple all will speak of glory.” That is, having been made temples of God in themselves, they will proclaim glory to the Lord, from whom they received the good things they possess.

### 10

“The Lord makes the flood to dwell.”

For he makes his elect, guarded in the Church as in an ark, overcome and despise this world. The world is rightly signified by the flood, because it extinguishes the carnal within itself and repels the spiritual above itself.

And because the Lord will reign in his Church forever after the flood, it is rightly added: “And the Lord will sit as king forever.” [Col. 0747A]

For the saints are the seats of God, and he is their king, defending them from the power of the devil and ruling them spiritually, so that sin may not reign in their mortal body (Rom. 6). Concerning them it continues:

### 11

“The Lord will give strength to his people,” so that they are not overcome by enemies and vices.

“The Lord will bless his people with peace,” so that after the storms and whirlwinds of this world they may rest happily in eternity.

## TITLE OF PSALM XXIX

### 1

“A psalm of a song at the dedication of the house of David.”

This psalm is a song—that is, an expression of joy—composed at the dedication, that is, in contemplation of the dedication, of the house of David (2 Kings 7).

The dedication of the house of David is understood as the resurrection of the Savior, in which all the bodies of our life are dedicated. The house of David is built when humanity is assumed. The house of David is built when he is raised from the dead.

The house of Christ is his humanity. Just as a house becomes celebrated at its dedication, so Christ became more celebrated at his resurrection, when he assumed impassibility and immortality.

The first part of the psalm is thanksgiving for deliverance; in it he also exhorts the saints to give thanks to God for this deliverance, which is their own, because through it they have been delivered.

In the second part, which begins, “But I said in my abundance,” the merit is shown for which it was fitting that he should be delivered.

In the third part, which begins, “The Lord heard,” he shows how the dedication itself takes place. Near the end he plainly sets forth the resurrection.

The subject is Christ. The intention is to exhort people to praise God for his deliverance, which is theirs as well. We note this where it says: “Sing to the Lord, his saints.” Therefore he says:

## PSALM XXIX

### 2

“I will exalt you, Lord, because you have received me.”

I will magnify your name among many nations because you have united my humanity to your Word.

“And you have not delighted”—that is, you have not caused—“my enemies to rejoice over me.” For although they thought that in the Passion they had prevailed over me, that joy was nevertheless turned into sorrow.

What is said here now from the person of the foundation will later be said from the person of the entire house. The dedication of the house has already taken place in its head, as the dedication of the foundation. The house—that is, the Church—is still being built; afterward it will be dedicated.

Then the glory of the Christian people, which is now hidden, will appear. Let the enemies rage for now. Let them rejoice in the building of the house; they will be confounded at its dedication.

Then the righteous will stand with great steadfastness against those who afflicted them. Repenting and groaning in anguish of spirit, they will say among themselves: “What did our pride profit us?” (Wis. 5), and what did the boasting of riches bring us? All those things passed away like a shadow.

And what will they say about the righteous? “How have they been counted among the sons of God, and their lot is among the saints?” Then what is now said will be fulfilled: “You have not delighted my enemies over me.”

### 3

“Lord my God, I cried out to you.”

He cried out when he said: “Father, glorify your Son” (John 12).

“And you healed me.” For he was weak according to the part of the flesh. The Father therefore healed him by making that very flesh immortal and incorruptible through the resurrection.

Hear the Apostle and see true healing: “Death,” he says, “has been swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your sting? Where is your contention?” (1 Cor. 15).

He adds another reason for which he ought to exalt the Lord:

### 4

“Lord,” he says, “you brought my soul out of hell.”

For he stripped hell and led the souls of the saints with him into heaven.

“You saved me from those who descend into the pit,” that is, you freed me from the hands of the Jews, who of their own accord descend into hell, death, and the jaws of the devil.

And because his deliverance pertains to universal salvation, he therefore admonishes us, saying:

### 5

“Sing to the Lord, his saints, and confess to the memory of his holiness.”

It is as though he said: You who, through my deliverance, have been made his saints, sing to the Lord. Bless him by your actions, and confess with mouth and heart to the memory of him whom you had forgotten, but who did not forget you (Isa. 49).

The fact that he remembered you proceeded not from your holiness but from his. Therefore sing and confess also for this reason.

### 6

“For there is anger in his indignation, and life in his will.”

He first avenged the original sin upon you, which you paid for with death; and he gave eternal life, to which you could not return by any of your own powers, because he willed it.
