When you hear, “There is anger in his indignation,” you have in God something to fear. For God is indignant with the human being and brings anger because of sin. Again, when you hear, “And life in his will,” you have in God something to hope for and love. In the former, justice is commended; in the latter, grace.

To anger and life belongs what follows: “In the evening weeping will linger, and in the morning joy.”

Evening occurs when the sun sets. Evening began when the light of wisdom withdrew from the sinful human being, when he was condemned to death. For the sun of righteousness had set for him, and he no longer rejoiced in the presence of God. From that evening this whole mortal life began.

From that very evening, weeping will linger as long as the people of God await the day of the Lord amid labors and temptations. Then morning will come, when the joy of the resurrection will take place. Then light will rise for the faithful, which had set for sinners.

Therefore the Lord Jesus also rose from the tomb in the morning, so that what he dedicated in the foundation he might promise to the house.

In our Lord [From the same source], evening occurred because he was buried, and morning because he rose on the third day. You too were buried in the evening in paradise and rose on the third day.

How on the third day? If you consider the world, the first day is before the Law, the second under the Law, and the third under Grace. What your head displayed during those three days is displayed in you during the three ages of the world.

We must hope and rejoice, but for now we must endure and groan. He shows himself to be the opposite of Adam when he adds:

### 7

“But I said in my abundance, ‘I shall not be moved forever.’”

Adam, placed in the paradise of delight (Gen. 2) and abounding in every good, was moved by the serpent’s persuasion (Gen. 3). But Christ, in the abundance of virtues, said—that is, resolved—not to be moved forever, but to be obedient to the Father unto death (Phil. 2).

Nor did he attribute this to his own powers, and therefore he adds:

### 8

“Lord, in your will you granted strength to my beauty.”

That I am beautiful in righteousness and strong in patience—I do not possess this from my own power, but from your will.

“You turned your face away from me, and I became troubled.”

For the Father appeared to have turned his face away from the Son when he abandoned him in the Passion. Hence the Jews said: “If he is the Son of God, let him deliver him, if he wills” (Matt. 27; Luke 23).

He became troubled when he said: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Luke 23; Matt. 26). Here the great merit of Christ is shown: even when tested in this way, he did not withdraw from obedience.

“You turn your face away from me, but I am not turned away from you.” For it follows:

### 9

“To you, Lord, I will cry out, and I will entreat my Lord.”

I will cry out concerning the obtaining of good things; I will entreat concerning the removal of evils. For you are my Lord, who rule me, and my God, who created me.

Here we are shown in our head what we ought to do. If the Lord turns his face away from us and is indignant because of our sins, we ought immediately to be troubled through repentance and cry out to his merciful ears until we obtain forgiveness.

What Christ cried out is shown when he adds:

### 10

“What benefit is there in my blood, when I descend into corruption?”

What benefit will my shed blood provide for me or for others if I descend into corruption? If my body decays in the tomb? If I do not rise on the third day?

“Will dust confess to you, or will it proclaim your truth?” Will flesh reduced to dust confess to you—that is, will it be the cause of your confession and praise? Or will it proclaim your truth—that is, will it be the reason your truth is proclaimed concerning the restoration of the human race which you are going to accomplish through me?

He indicates that he was heard in response to this cry when he immediately adds:

### 11

“The Lord heard, and had mercy on me; the Lord became my helper.”

He had mercy on me so that I would not be corrupted; he helped me so that I might also rise.

Mercy pertains to the remission of sins. Help pertains to progress in good works and virtues. First he has mercy on us without preceding merits, so that, freed from sin, we may will the good. Then he helps us so that we may fulfill the good we will.

That we correct our sins is God’s mercy. That we rise again to virtues is God’s help.

He shows in what respect he was helped, turning familiarly to the Father and saying:

### 12

“You turned my mourning into joy for me.”

You changed the mourning of the Passion into the joy of the resurrection; “for me,” that is, for my benefit and that of my members.

“You tore my sackcloth and surrounded me with joy.”

Sackcloth [From Augustine, Enarration 2] is made from goats and kids. Both goats and kids are placed among sinners. The Lord took sackcloth only from our condition; he did not assume the merit of sackcloth, which is sin.

Sackcloth is mortality. He tore the sackcloth because he destroyed mortality, and moreover he surrounded him with joy, because the Lord clothed him in the garment of immortality.

He was surrounded with joy in order to do what follows:

### 13

“So that my glory may sing to you,” that is, my resurrection and my blessedness; “and I may not be pierced,” that is, I may not die.

For Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death will no longer rule over him (Rom. 4). What has happened in the head will happen in the body. Our glory will sing to God when we are like him and see him as he is (1 John 3).

For what follows will occur: “Lord my God, I will confess to you forever.” This is my glory: to confess to you forever, because nothing comes from me but everything from you, who are God, all in all.

Therefore confess now [From the same source, Enarration 2] what you have done against the Lord—that is, your sins—and you will confess what God has done for you by forgiving your sins, so that, confessing to him forever, you may not be pierced by sin.

## TITLE OF PSALM XXX

[Col. 0749C]

### 1

The title of the following psalm is: “To the end; a psalm of David himself; ecstasy.”

The psalm is attributed to David himself, the mediator, strong-handed in persecutions, who speaks here not only for himself but also for his martyrs, directing toward the end.

“Ecstasy,” which has been added in the title, signifies an “excess of mind” [From Augustine], which occurs either through fear or through some revelation. But in this psalm fear appears chiefly: the fear of the people of God, troubled by the persecution of all nations and by the failure of faith throughout the world.

First the mediator himself speaks. Then the people redeemed by his blood give thanks. Finally, after being troubled for a long time, he speaks in a way that pertains to ecstasy.

The person of the prophet himself is inserted twice: near the end and at the end.

The subject contains two opposites: the help of divine mercy and the misery of human frailty. Its intention is to admonish people neither to despair when they consider their miseries nor to foolishly become proud by presuming upon God’s mercy. Thus it clearly directs us toward the end, that is, toward Christ. Therefore he says:

## PSALM XXX

[Col. 0749D] ### 2

“In you, Lord, I have hoped; I shall not be confounded forever.”

You see that he is afraid, but this fear is not without hope. If there is some disturbance in the human heart, divine consolation does not depart. He does not deny that he suffers the insult of enemies, but such confusion does not last forever.

That confusion is to be dreaded which is eternal. For there is a certain temporal confusion [From Augustine, Enarration 2] that is useful: the disturbance of the soul as it looks upon its sins, the horror arising from that contemplation, and the correction produced by shame at the horror.

Hence the Apostle also says: “What glory did you have in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. 6). The Christian does not fear this confusion; indeed, if he does not have it, he will have eternal confusion.

What is that? “Depart, you accursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25).

And therefore he immediately adds: “In your righteousness deliver me.” For if you attend to my righteousness, you condemn me. God’s righteousness and ours come to be when it is given to us. It is therefore called God’s righteousness so that a human being will not think he possesses righteousness from himself and thus vainly glory in himself.

And because my voice could not ascend to you,
### 3

Incline your ear toward me; hasten to rescue me. God did this when he sent Christ himself to us. The inclination of the ear is the assumption of humanity. God inclines his ear toward us, laying down mercy upon us. What greater mercy is there than that he should give us his only Son (1 John 4)—not to live with us, but to die for us? But he asks that the mercy, once inclined, should quickly rise again when he adds: “Hasten to rescue me.” As if he were saying: “Quickly, make me rise again.” For if he had postponed it until the general resurrection, the hope of all believers would have perished. Or “Hasten” is placed here so that we may understand that all this which seems long to us, for as long as this age revolves, is but a moment. It is not long when it has an end. Times fly past, and what seems slow to you is brief in the eyes of God.

[Note: [Col. 0749] It was formerly written incorrectly, *quandiu volvitur*; according to the punctuation, etc. The received Augustine corrects it.]

“Be for me a protecting God, lest I be wounded by the darts of enemies, and a house of refuge, so that you may save me”—that is, a house of security, in which I may rest when these labors have ended and remain saved forever. If you wish to escape the arrows of temptations, the heat of vices, and the fury of persecutors, invoke the Lord as protector. If he protects you, there is no one who can strike. If you wish to be safe and secure, make him your refuge. For no refuge can be so safe for you as your God, of whom it is next said:

### 4

“For you are my strength and my refuge.” Strength by which I may be able to resist those who attack me; refuge in which I may remain secure. Strength in battle, refuge after triumph; strength by which we conquer, refuge in which I shall rest.

“And for your name’s sake”—which is to be spread abroad and glorified—“you will lead me, lest I go astray, and nourish me, lest I fail along the way.” Or Christ is led when he is proclaimed everywhere through the Apostles. He is nourished when the little ones are refreshed with the milk of faith and the joy of miracles.

Lord our God, you are our guide, by whom we journey spiritually, and the true food by which we are nourished spiritually. He leads us by commandments and nourishes us by the sacraments. Concerning him it is further said:

### 5

“You will lead me out of this snare which they hid for me.” By the snare he wishes deception to be understood, the deception which the Jews concealed for Christ. Hence they said to him: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth. Tell us, therefore: Is it lawful to pay the census-tax to Caesar, or not?” (Matthew 22). Behold the snare which they concealed. If he had said, “It is lawful,” he would have fallen into the snare. For they would have opposed him: “You are acting against the Law, which says, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve’” (Deuteronomy 26). If he had said, “It is not lawful,” he would have fallen into another snare. For the Herodians would have said: “You are acting against the king; you are liable to death” (Matthew 26).

Or, “You will lead me out of the snare,” that is, out of death, which is therefore called a snare because they thought that through death they would hinder his name. “Which they hid”—that is, secretly prepared—“for me,” from whom no secret is hidden. In the same way God rescues his own from the snares of the devil (Hebrews 4), that is, from temptations. Therefore I know that you will lead me out, because you are my protector. One who has such a protector cannot be ensnared. And therefore it follows:

### 6

“Into your hands I commend my spirit.” This was fulfilled when, placed upon the cross, he said: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23). Behold how prophecy and the Gospel agree in the same utterance. Understand, therefore, that the same Christ who speaks in the Gospel also spoke in the psalm. Immediately he adds:

“You have redeemed me, Lord God of truth.” The soul of Christ and of others was redeemed through his perfect obedience (Philippians 2). And rightly he says, “Lord God of truth,” for he did not deceive in his promise but faithfully fulfilled what he had promised. And therefore, because you are the God of truth:

### 7

“You have hated those who observe vanities in vain.” They observe vanities in vain who cling so closely to earthly things that they forget heavenly ones. God hates such people, who hope in the false happiness of this age. But I have not hoped as they do—those who hope in what is vain and observe vanity—but in the Lord, who is not vanity.

Therefore I shall rejoice in body and be glad in spirit because of your mercy, which granted me the ability to hope in you. And rightly shall I rejoice:

### 8

“For you have regarded my lowliness”—that is, you have had mercy on my weakness and affliction, lest I be overcome by my persecutors.

“By regarding my lowliness, you saved my soul from distress”—that is, from the bodily miseries which the soul suffers in this life because of guilt. Unless you had first humbled yourself, he would not have heard you, the one who would free you from distress. He was humbled who said: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death?” But hear the continuation of salvation: “The grace of God,” he says, “through Jesus Christ” (Romans 7). Hence it follows:

### 9

“And you did not deliver me into the hands of the enemy.” For he was held neither by those who guarded the tomb (Matthew 28), nor by evil spirits in hell; rather, “you set my feet in a spacious place.” For the Apostles preached not only in Judaea but throughout all the kingdoms of the world (Romans 10), although they had first been commanded to preach only in Judaea (Matthew 10).

Or, “you set my feet,” that is, you firmly established my afflictions in the spacious place of charity. Here he begins to enumerate the miseries of human weakness, saying:

### 10

“Have mercy on me, O God, for I am afflicted.” He describes the affliction itself when he adds: “My eye, my soul, and my belly are troubled in anger”—that is, my understanding, my will, and my memory.

Although he was certain of God’s promise—he had said, “I will glorify” (John 12)—we do not mean that the understanding, will, or memory of Christ God was troubled in such a way that he failed in any respect. Rather, he wished to be disturbed voluntarily, so that he might leave an example for others (1 Peter 2), lest they despair merely because they were troubled.

### 11

“For my life has failed in sorrow.” After experiencing the anger of God, by which it was said to the first man, “You shall surely die” (Genesis 2), this mortal life has had many failures of sorrow. And because his life might have been spent in sorrow for one day or two, which would not seem significant, he therefore added: “And my years in groaning.” For the whole span of the present life is labor and groaning for the saints (Job 7).

Hence it is also said: “My strength has been weakened in poverty”—that is, in consideration of my poverty, because I possess nothing from myself. “And my bones”—that is, my firmness or bodily strength—“have been troubled.”

When Christ says that he is weak both in body and in soul (Matthew 25), he shows that all pride has been removed from him and that no one ought to presume upon himself. He sets forth other miseries as well, saying:

### 12

“Above all my enemies I have become a reproach to my neighbors, and a great fear to those who know me.” Whom does he mean by “those who know me” except the Apostles? And whom by “my very near neighbors” except those who were already drawing near to his faith? He becomes a reproach and a cause of fear to them when he is suspended on the cross by the Jews.

He rightly says that he became a reproach above all his enemies, because he himself, who was killed without guilt, appeared more despised than even those wicked men who were condemned for their crimes. Hence he adds:

“Those who saw me fled outside, away from me.” For the Apostles saw the Jews seize Christ and, abandoning him, all fled (Matthew 26).

### 13

“I have been forgotten as one dead from the heart.” They forgot me as though I were dead from their hearts.

“I have become like a ruined vessel, for I heard the reproach of many who dwell around me.” A ruined and broken vessel is fit for no useful purpose. The thieves were like ruined vessels when, as useless men, they were handed over to destruction. Thus Christ also became like a ruined vessel, because he was even counted among the wicked.

How many reproaches he heard from those standing around him is recognized by those who read the account of his passion. “While they gathered together against me, they plotted to take my life.” While the wicked Jews gathered together against me, he says, they plotted nothing else in that assembly except how to destroy my life.

What do these words teach us except contempt for the world and for death, humility and patience, and that we should place our hope in God? Hence it is also said:

### 15

“But I have hoped in you, O Lord; I said, ‘You are my God. In your hands are my lots.’”

The hope that is placed in God is sound. In whomever else a person hopes, his hope will be frustrated (Malachi 3). But whoever hopes in God: just as God is unchanging, so his hope cannot be changed.

“I said to the Lord”: I proposed, vowed, and fixed in my mind, “You are my God.” For you do not fail; you do not deceive. Therefore I hoped in you, whom I chose as my God.

“In your hands”—that is, in your power—“are my lots.” A lot is not something evil but something uncertain among human beings that reveals the divine will. The Apostles also cast lots (Acts 1). God was consulted about which of the two disciples he wished to be an Apostle, and the lot fell upon Matthias (ibid.).

By the name “lot” in this passage the grace of God is signified, because in a lot there is no election but the will of God. For where it is said, “This person does it; that person does not,” merits are being considered. And where merits are considered, there is election and not a lot. But when God finds no merits of ours, he saves us by the lot of his will, because he wills it, not because we were worthy. This is the lot.

“You have been saved by grace through faith,” the Apostle says, “and this is not from yourselves” (Ephesians 2). Hence Peter says to Simon (Acts 8): “Because you thought that the gift of God could be purchased with money, you have no part or lot in this faith”—that is, you do not belong to this grace, which we have all received freely.

He rightly says not “lot” but “lots,” because there are many divisions of grace (1 Corinthians 12), which the Lord distributes to believers. “In your hands are my lots.” As if he were plainly saying: “All my elect are in your power.” And therefore:

### 16

“Rescue me from the hand of my enemies and from those who persecute me”—that is, from the power of those who hate me and of those who inflict evil upon me.

Let each person say this concerning his enemies. For it is good, and we ought to pray, that God may rescue us from the hands of our visible and invisible enemies.

### 17

Among these, groaning, he says: “Make your face shine upon your servant.” For it is considered a kind of disgrace when all are called Christians, both those who live badly and those who live well. All are marked with one sign; all approach one altar (Ephesians 4); they are washed in the same baptism; they recite the same Lord’s Prayer; they participate in the celebration of the same mysteries. When will they be distinguished? When the Lord makes his face shine upon his servants: in the judgment. Then the good will be separated from the evil (Matthew 25). Hence it is written: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isaiah 26).

And therefore he adds: “Save me in your mercy, not in my righteousness.”

### 18

“O Lord, let me not be put to shame, for I have called upon you.” Whoever now calls upon the Lord—that is, calls him inwardly—with a pure heart, an undivided heart, praying devoutly, living rightly, and making voice, heart, and deeds agree, will not be put to shame in the judgment.

But those of whom he next speaks will be put to shame: “Let the wicked be ashamed, and let them be led down into hell”—namely, the Jews who crucified their Lord; or the Gentiles who worshiped idols; or false Christians who neglected to worship the Lord.

Then they will certainly be ashamed when they hear from the Lord: “Truly I say to you, I do not know you.” And again: “Go, you cursed, into the eternal fire” (Matthew 25). Then what follows will take place:

### 19

“Let deceitful lips be made mute, which speak iniquity against the righteous with pride and abuse.”

For the Jews spoke proudly and abusively—that is, against the proper use of servants—against the Lord when they shouted, “He is guilty of death!” and “Crucify him!” (Matthew 26; Luke 23; Isaiah 52).

Every day now the wicked cry out against the good, the proud against the humble. Every day they blaspheme, bark, slander, and chatter with wicked and deceitful tongues. But then their lips will be made mute, when the glory of the saints appears and they see torments threatening them. The clamor of their words will be turned into mourning. For there will be weeping and the gnashing of teeth (Matthew 8 and 13).

In contrast, contemplating the happiness of the saints, he praised and admired the sweetness of the heavenly kingdom, saying:

### 20

“How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you!” It is marvelous; it is delightful; it cannot be expressed in words. For “what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, you have prepared, O God, for those who love you” (Isaiah 64; 1 Corinthians 2).

But you have hidden it for those who fear you. What does “you have hidden it for them” mean? You have preserved it so that they alone may reach it. For as long as they still fear, they themselves have not yet arrived; but they believe that they will arrive, and they begin from fear. Nothing is sweeter than the immortality of wisdom; but “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Psalm 110; Proverbs 1), which you have hidden for those who fear you.

“But you have perfected it for those who hope in you, in the sight of the children of men”—that is, you have perfected your sweetness for those who hope in you in the sight of the children of men.

How does the Lord say: “Whoever denies me before human beings, I also will deny before my Father” (Matthew 10)? Therefore, if you hope in the Lord, hope in him before human beings, lest you hide that hope in your heart and fear to confess it when it is brought against you as a crime that you are a Christian.

If you wish to walk in the way of God, hope in the Lord even in the sight of human beings—that is, do not be ashamed of your hope. As it lives in your heart, so let it dwell upon your lips, because Christ did not wish his sign to be fixed upon our forehead without reason, as upon the seat of modesty, lest a Christian be ashamed of Christ’s reproach.

If, therefore, you do this in the sight of human beings; if you are not ashamed of it before them; if, in the sight of the children of men, you deny Christ neither by mouth nor by deeds, hope that the sweetness of God will be perfected for you.

God begins to give this sweetness to the faithful in the present life, but perfects it in the next. Concerning them it is further said:

“You will hide them in the secrecy of your face”—that is, in the hidden place of divine contemplation—“from the disturbance of human beings,” so that no one can now trouble them.

But again, while they journey as pilgrims in this age (2 Corinthians 5), because they suffer many tongues contradicting them, what do you do for them? He continues and says:

### 21

“You will protect them in your tabernacle”—namely, in the present Church, in which we serve as soldiers—“from the contradiction of tongues,” so that the tongues of heretics, contradicting the truth, cannot incorporate them into themselves.

Then, for such great benefits, he breaks forth into praising and blessing God, saying:

### 22

“Blessed is the Lord, for he has made his mercy wondrous to me in a fortified city.”

The Lord is to be blessed and glorified for this reason: he has shown his mercy to me in a wondrous way—that is, for my benefit and that of my own—in a fortified city, that is, in the saints, who are called a city because many are joined together under one divine Law, and fortified because they are strengthened by many virtues and the various gifts of the Holy Spirit.

The Lord has acted wondrously; but I have experienced miseries. Hence he adds:

### 23

“But I said in the excess of my mind, ‘I have been cast away from the sight of your eyes.’”

“Excess” is said either when a person is carried away into contemplation of divine things—as Paul says, “whether we are beside ourselves,” in mind, for God (2 Corinthians 5)—or when someone, because of grief, goes beside himself and no longer remains himself.

Thus this person saw himself trembling under some great tribulation, such as is not lacking. Observe his fearful and anxious heart, and he says: “I have been cast away from the sight of your eyes.” If I were in your sight, I would not be so afraid; if you regarded me, I would not tremble so.

And because I confessed, because I was humble, because I accused my heart, and because I cried out in fear, “you heard the voice of my prayer.” He presents a certain merit for being heard when he says: “When I cried out to you”—that is, because I cried out.

A cry to the Lord is not made with the voice but with the heart. Many who were silent with their lips cried out in their hearts. Many who made noise with their mouths, while their hearts were turned away, could obtain nothing.

Therefore, if you cry out, cry inwardly, where God hears. But now let us hear what he exhorts us to do:

### 24

“Love the Lord, all his saints.” As if he were saying: “Believe me.” I have experienced it myself: I had tribulations; I called upon him and was not deceived. I hoped in God and was not put to shame. He enlightened my thoughts and strengthened my trembling.

“Love the Lord”—you who do not love the world—“all his saints.” For “the Lord will seek out truth.” Although he permits it now to be trampled underfoot, he himself will seek it out at its appointed time.

From whom will he seek it? From those who held to it against falsehood. He will seek it from them in order to reward them. He will also seek it from those who proudly neglected it. Concerning them it is said:

“And he will repay abundantly those who act proudly”—not sparingly. Who are those who act proudly except those who despise the truth of God?

Therefore, lest we be condemned with them, let us hear and do what follows:

### 25

“Act manfully.” Do not let your wounded hands fall during tribulations. And if there is weakness or weariness in the body, let there be in the heart, for enduring the evils of the world, the strength of patience. This is what he adds:

“And let your heart be strengthened.”

But to whom does he say this? To lovers of the world? No. Hear to whom: “All you who hope in the Lord.”

Brothers, inscribe in your hearts the words you have heard in the psalm; transform yourselves in accordance with them; praise the Lord through them. If the psalm prays, pray; if it groans, groan; if it rejoices, rejoice; if it hopes, hope; if it fears, fear. Everything written here is our mirror.

# Title of Psalm XXXI

### 1

“An understanding of David.” This writing, issued by David, produces understanding in those who read it. It teaches specifically that no one can be saved except through the forgiveness of sins.

The first understanding is that you should know yourself to be a sinner. The consequent understanding is that, when you have begun to act well through faith working by love, you should attribute this not to your own strength but to the grace of God (Galatians 5).

The subject is the prophet David, or any other faithful person who repents with understanding: previously ignorant of his sins, he now recognizes them. The psalm also sets forth his confession, and then commends that confession. Afterwards it introduces Christ promising many good things to such a penitent.

The intention of this penitent is to exhort us to understand this kind of confession. In the first part he shows that he recognizes his sins when he says:

# Psalm XXXI

### 2

“Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven, and whose sins have been covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not reckoned sin, and in whose spirit there is no deceit.”

There are some penitents whose iniquities have been forgiven through the washing of regeneration, and they are blessed. Again, there are many who sinned after baptism but returned to confession; through repentance and amendment, their sins, which they had committed, have been covered. They too are nonetheless blessed.

There is another kind of vigorous man—“one” because he is rare—supported by strength of spirit, who guarded himself from every criminal sin; when guilt arose through carnal desire, he firmly restrained it by the rigor of the spirit. He was not delighted by it and did not consent. This is the blessed man to whom the Lord did not reckon sin.

Hence the same Psalmist says elsewhere: “If they do not rule over me, then I shall be blameless” (Psalm 18).

And the Apostle says: “There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8), who do not walk according to the flesh.

And while this holy man does not justify himself in this matter, but confesses himself a sinner and accuses himself, “there is no deceit in his spirit.”

[Note: [Col. 0753D] See Psalm XVIII, no. 14.]

Because this penitent did not do this, he indicates what harm he suffered when he adds:

### 3

“For when I was silent, my bones grew old, while I cried out all day long.”

What he says—“I was silent while I cried out”—seems contradictory. But he was silent about one thing and cried out about another. He was silent about confession and cried out in presumption.

As long as we conceal our sin, the sin itself cries out to the Lord. Hence the Lord says to Cain: “Behold, the voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me from the earth” (Genesis 4). Because he had denied it when questioned, the very shedding of the blood was a cry to the Lord.

“For when I was silent,” he says, “my bones grew old.” If he had cried out his sins, his bones would have been renewed—that is, his whole strength would have been made strong in the Lord, because he would have found himself weak in himself. But now, because he wished to be strong in himself, he became weak. His bones grew old; he remained in oldness because he refused, by confessing, to love newness.

What does “while I cried out all day long” mean? While I persisted in defending my sin. And because he was silent, he felt the hand of the Lord avenging him, saying:

### 4

“For day and night”—that is, continually—“your hand was heavy upon me.”

The Lord lays his hand heavily upon the one whom he humbles when he exalts himself (Luke 18). He who refused to be humbled by confessing his humility was humbled by the weight of God’s hand.

And therefore he adds: “I turned in my distress”—that is, in consideration of my misery—“while the thorn was fixed.” While his conscience was pierced, he felt the weight of the scourge through the striking hand of the Lord; he felt within himself the prick of sin.

He was given a perception of pain, and thus he discovered his weakness, having been silent about confession. Hence he immediately says:

### 5

“I made my sin known to you, and I did not hide my iniquity.”

By “sin” the sin of thought may be understood; by “iniquity,” the sin of deed. Or “sin” is when we abandon God’s commandment, while “iniquity” is when we perpetrate in deed the very things which God’s commandments prohibit.

The penitent had previously concealed both these sins. Hence he felt the hand of the Lord avenging him; and thus, scourged and instructed, he came humbly to confession and amendment.

By the gracious dispensation of the Lord it came about that what had been the punishment of sin became itself an opportunity for virtue. Hence he says:

“I said, ‘I will confess my iniquity against myself to the Lord’; and you forgave the impiety of my sin.”

See how swift God’s mercy is toward the sinner. He proposed that he would make a declaration, and God had already forgiven him. The word had not yet come to his mouth, but God’s ear was already in his heart.

After he said, “I will confess,” he immediately added, not without reason, “against myself.” For many declare their impiety, but against the Lord himself. When they are found in sins, they say: “God willed this.”

If someone says, “I did not do it,” or, “This deed you accuse me of is not a sin,” he declares it neither against himself nor against the Lord. But if he says, “I did it [Note: [Col. 0755] We restore the passage from Augustine by correctly reinstating the punctuation.]; it is certainly a sin, but God willed what I did,” he declares it against the Lord. Many say this. They also say: “Fate did it to me; chance did it to me.” And in this way, by a circuitous route, they wish to arrive at accusing God.

This penitent, therefore, removes such excuses in sins, lest he incline his heart toward words of wickedness, and he confesses his iniquity against himself to the Lord.

What does “against himself” mean? Accusing and reproving himself, and no one else.

Swift forgiveness follows such a confession. Therefore he says: “And you forgave the impiety of my sin.”

It should be noted that he does not say “sin” but “the impiety of sin.” When we do, say, or think something evil, it is indeed sin. But when we wish to hide that same thing from God, it is no longer merely sin but also the impiety of sin.

From these words, therefore, he shows that, because he resolved to confess his sin, God forgave him not only what he had done wrongly but also what he had impiously concealed.

Although God forgives sins as soon as a person repents in his will, nevertheless one must confess to the ministers of the Church, because unless they confess, they would be condemned for their disobedience. This was shown in Lazarus, who, after he had been brought back to life, still needed to be loosed.

### 6

“For this”—namely, for this impiety of sin—“every saint will pray to you.” He will pray to you because you have forgiven sins. For if you did not forgive sins, there would be no saint to pray to you.

“He will pray in an opportune time.” Now is the opportune time for praying, confessing one’s sins, and correcting one’s ways. Now is the time of grace and the time of mercy, of which the Apostle says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6).

Now those who wish may draw near to God, if they punish their former evils, correct their conduct, and live soberly and justly. Afterwards there will be a time of judgment and a time of vengeance, when those who now disdain to draw near will no longer draw near.

This is what he adds: “Nevertheless, in the flood of many waters they will not approach him.” The flood rightly signifies God’s judgment, because just as sinners were condemned previously in the flood, so they will be condemned in the final judgment.

No one should suppose that, when the end suddenly comes—as in the days of Noah—there will remain an opportunity for confession by which one may draw near to God. Now the Lord is not seen, and yet he is near. Then he will be seen, and he will no longer be near.

Many waves of floods will stir the hearts of the wicked. Those who now flee to the harbor of divine mercy will not experience them.

This is what the penitent did when he said:

### 7

“You are my refuge from the tribulation that surrounded me.”

Great is the tribulation that surrounds us on every side, as the Apostle testifies: “Without are conflicts, within are fears” (2 Corinthians 7). And in another psalm it is said: “Many are the tribulations of the righteous” (Psalm 33). Finally, this whole mortal life is tribulation for the servants of God (Job 7).

But from this tribulation by which a person is surrounded in the world, he finds no refuge so safe as God himself. Let others flee to their own strength, their own fortifications, and their defenses of sins. For me there is no refuge except you, who are also “my exultation,” because I rejoice in you.

And therefore: “Rescue me from those who surround me”—from enemies and vices.

I hear the voice of joy: “My exultation.” I hear a groan: “Redeem me.” Do you rejoice and groan? “Yes,” he says. “I rejoice in hope; I still groan in reality.” “For by hope we were saved” (Romans 8): behold the source of joy. “But hope that is seen is not hope. If we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (ibid.): behold the groaning. Therefore he says: “Rescue me.”

### 8

**Diapsalma. Response of God.**

“I will give you understanding.” So that you may always know yourself and always rejoice toward God in hope, until you reach that homeland where there will no longer be hope but reality.

“And I will instruct you”—with the weapons of righteousness (1 Corinthians 3), with knowledge, good conduct, and virtues—“and I will fix my eyes upon you in this way,” the way of virtues in which you will walk.

The Lord fixes his eyes upon us in our way when he mercifully attends to our progress along the way of virtues. He also guards us perseveringly on that same journey. For it would not be enough to give understanding and form us through good living unless he also caused us to remain in these things.

After this understanding and protection, he turns to the proud who defend their sins and shows us what understanding is:

### 9

“Do not become like a horse or a mule, in which there is no understanding.”

The horse signifies the proud and the pleasure-seeking; the mule signifies the lazy and unfruitful. Such are the people of this age: they raise themselves up in arrogance, serve carnal pleasures, and produce no fruit for the soul.

And while they cling only to earthly things, living like beasts like a horse and a mule, they have no understanding of heavenly things.

How such people are to be treated follows: “With bit and bridle bind their jaws, since they do not approach you.” They must be restrained by harsh bonds of discipline; their boastful mouths must be repressed by repeated blows, because they live perversely and untamed and speak without restraint. While they flee, they rush toward death.

It is therefore no wonder that scourges follow when a bridle is applied to such people. Hence it is added:

### 10

“Many are the scourges of the sinner.”

He wished to be an untamed animal; it is broken by bit and scourge. And would that it might be thoroughly broken! For it must be feared that, by resisting God the ruler [Note: [Col. 0757D] For the two words *Deo dominatori* (“God the ruler”), the received text of Augustine has the single word *indomitum* (“untamed”); it is noted there, however, that many manuscripts read *resistendo dominatori* (“by resisting the ruler”).] too stubbornly, it may deserve to be abandoned and go into its own wayward license, so that it may be said of it: “His iniquity will come forth as from fat” (Psalm 72)—as of those whose sins now go unpunished.

Therefore, when he is scourged, let him be corrected and tamed, because he himself said that he had been tamed in this way. He had called himself a horse and a mule because he was silent. But by what was he tamed? By scourges, having turned in his distress while the thorn was fixed.

Whether you call them scourges or goads, God tames the beast upon which he rides, because it is advantageous for the beast to be ridden and tamed by the scourge, so that it may obtain God’s mercy.

Hence it is added: “But mercy will surround the one who hopes in the Lord.” Tribulation first surrounds him; afterwards mercy surrounds him, because the one who wished us to be justly afflicted on account of our sins will grant mercy.

Therefore he adds by way of exhortation:

### 11

“Rejoice in the Lord and exult, you righteous.” Rejoice in your heart; exult in your body—not in yourselves, not in the world. Not lovers of the world, not sinners, but the righteous.

“And glory, all you who are upright in heart.” It is not a great thing to glory in joys. The upright in heart glories even in tribulation (Philippians 4).

Observe the upright heart. “Knowing,” he says, “that tribulation produces patience, patience produces testing, and testing produces hope. And hope does not put us to shame, because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Romans 5).

Therefore, if we are righteous, if we have an upright heart, let us rejoice in our hearts in the Lord; let us exult in body; let us glory in tribulation.

# Title of Psalm XXXII

“An ending psalm of David.”

This psalm is appropriate to David the prophet. Its subject is the praise of God, whether his benefits or his power. It exhorts us to praise God by presenting reasons why we ought to praise him. This is its intention.

In the second part it shows that those who have praised God are blessed. It begins in this way:

# Psalm XXXII

### 1

“Exult, you righteous, in the Lord.” The unrighteous exult in the age; when the age has ended, the exultation of the unrighteous will end. While the Lord remains, the exultation of the righteous will remain.

And I rightly say that the righteous should exult in the Lord, because “praise is fitting for the upright.” Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner.

Who are the upright? Those who direct their hearts according to the will of God; and if human weakness disturbs them, divine righteousness comforts them (Augustine, *Enarrationes*, 2).

The righteous are those who serve through faith and good works. The upright are those who are neither lifted up by prosperity nor broken by adversity, and who give thanks to the same Lord in both.

Thus righteousness lies in faith and action, while uprightness lies in the will. Those who are such are fit to praise God and exult in him. The psalm exhorts such people when it adds:

## 2. Give thanks to the Lord on the lyre; sing praise to him on the ten-stringed psaltery.

The lyre sounds from its lower part, the psaltery from its upper part. We possess life from this earth, as from a lower region: there is earthly prosperity and earthly adversity, and in both God is to be praised. What is earthly prosperity? When (as Augustine says in the same passage) we are healthy in the flesh; when the crops yield abundantly; when everything by which we live is plentiful—whoever does not praise God for this is ungrateful.

Adversities, however, consist in pains, illnesses, pressures, loss of possessions, and tribulations. Therefore give thanks to the Lord on the lyre, whether something earthly abounds for you or is lacking; give thanks to him who gave or took away (Job 1). For he who gave has not been taken away from you, although what he gave has been taken away from you.

Strike the strings, then, in your heart; and say, as though on the lower part of the lyre: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away. As it has pleased the Lord, so it has happened” (Job 1). “Blessed be the name of the Lord.”

But when you attend to the higher gifts of God—what he has bestowed upon you by way of commandments, with what heavenly teaching he has imbued you, and what he has given you above all else from the fountain of that truth—turn also to the psaltery and sing praise to God on the ten-stringed psaltery.

[Note: [Col. 0758D] This is the truer reading, retained also by the Augustinian codices Regius and Vaticanus, rather than the printed reading *praeceperit* (“what he has commanded”), differing by one word.]

For the commandments of the Law are ten. In the ten commandments of the Law you have the psaltery. It is a perfect instrument: in it you have love of God in three commandments and love of neighbor in seven. And surely you know that the Lord says that the whole Law and the Prophets depend upon these two commandments (Matt. 22).

God says to you from above: “The Lord your God is one God.” You have one string. “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain”: you have another string. “Observe the Sabbath day”—not carnally, nor with Jewish pleasures, as those do who abuse leisure for wickedness. It would be better for them to dig all day than to dance all day. Rather, contemplate the rest in your God, who accomplishes all things.

He abstains from servile work. For everyone who commits sin is a slave (John 8)—would that he were a slave of a human being and not of sin. These three commandments concern love of God: consider his unity, his truth, and his will. For there is a certain will in God in which the true Sabbath and true rest are found. Hence it is said: “Delight in the Lord, and he will grant you the desires of your heart” (Ps. 36). For who delights in him as does the one who does everything that gives delight?

In these three commandments is the love of God; in the other seven is the love of neighbor. “Do not do to another what you do not wish to suffer” (Tob. 4). “Honor your father and mother” (Luke 6), because you wish to be honored by your children. “You shall not commit adultery” (Exod. 20), because you do not wish your wife to commit adultery after you. “You shall not kill,” because you do not wish to be killed. “You shall not steal,” because you do not wish to suffer theft. “You shall not bear false witness,” because you hate one who bears false witness against you. “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife,” because you do not wish your own to be coveted by another. “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property,” because if someone coveted yours, it would displease you.

Turn the tongue also upon yourself when you are displeased by the person who harms you. All these are God’s commandments. They were given by Wisdom’s gift; they sound from above. Strike the psaltery; fulfill the Law, which your God came not to abolish but to fulfill (Matt. 5). You will fulfill by love what you could not fulfill through fear. For whoever refrains from doing evil through fear would prefer to do it if it were permitted. Thus, even if opportunity is not granted, the will remains guilty.

Meditating on these things, the upright in heart say: “Give thanks to the Lord on the lyre; sing praise to him on the ten-stringed psaltery.”

## 3. Sing to him a new song.

Put off the old condition. For the new song does not belong to old people (as Augustine says in the same passage). No one learns it except those renewed by grace from their former state and already belonging to the New Testament, which is the kingdom of heaven.

All our love sighs toward him (2 Cor. 5). The new person, new grace, and new life are commended to us. To act concerning these things, to praise the Lord in them, and to sing a new song in the newness of the spirit is to sing.

“Sing praise to him well with a shout.” One sings praise well who lives well. But this very good life of ours ought to have a kind of spiritual shout in God’s ears, so that whatever we do in living well, we may do—with all our affection, all our faith, and all our devotion—for the praise of God, insofar as we are able (Col. 3). For this reason he adds:

## 4. For the word of the Lord is upright, and all his works are in faithfulness.

The Lord’s word is upright because it teaches what is right, commands what is right, proclaims what is right, and promises what is right. It is twisted toward no falsehood or vanity; it turns neither to the right nor to the left. By a straight course, the royal road, it leads us to our heavenly homeland.

God is upright not only in his word, but also faithful in his works, giving human beings what he has promised. Let us hold fast to the most faithful debtor, because we hold fast to the most merciful promiser. All the gifts in which we rejoice come from him (2 Tim. 2). All his works are in faithfulness. All things instruct us; all things send us toward higher realities.

## 5. He loves mercy and judgment.

He does not say this because he does not love other things, but because he acts especially according to these. He acts according to mercy when he forgives sins; according to judgment when he repays both good and wicked people according to the quality of their merits.

The time of mercy is now; the time of judgment will come afterward. Now he calls those who have turned away and grants forgiveness to those who turn back. He is patient with sinners until they repent. Judgment will come. There will be repentance then also, but it will already be fruitless.

You too should love mercy and judgment. For it is written: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5). Whoever loves mercy shows mercy; whoever shows mercy will obtain mercy.

Again, concerning judgment it is written: “Can one who does not love judgment be healed?” (Job 34). Whoever carefully examines his ways loves judgment; entering into the secret chamber of his heart, he weighs what the Lord grants him and what he himself owes the Lord God.

Hence the same Psalmist says elsewhere: “The honor of the king loves judgment” (Ps. 98), so that one who already honors God through faith may diligently judge what he owes him in action.

Solomon also says: “The thoughts of the righteous are judgments” (Prov. 12). For every righteous person, thinking and fearing within himself, considers how strictly the Lord will one day strike and how long he patiently waits. He fears the things he remembers having done. By weeping, he punishes what he understands himself to have perpetrated. He hates himself as he recognizes what he was. The person he now is persecutes the person he once was; and a quarrel arises in his soul that gives birth to peace with God. He does this so that the judge whom he fears may prove merciful.

Of this it is also said:

“Full of the mercy of the Lord is the earth.”

What of heaven? (As Augustine says in *Expositions* 3.) It does not need mercy, where there is no misery. On earth human misery abounds, while God’s mercy overflows. Does heaven, then, because it does not need mercy, not need the Lord? Everything needs the Lord—both misery and happiness. Without him the miserable are not raised up; without him the happy are not lifted higher.

Therefore, lest you ask about heaven, he adds:

## 6. By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their power.

They were not their own foundation, nor did the heavens themselves provide their own firmness. Hear of one work of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. When the Lord the Father establishes the heavens through the Word, the Son, and strengthens them through the Spirit, it is clearly shown that the Father, Son, and Spirit perform one work (Heb. 1).

Here, however, we also understand other heavens established by divine power—namely, the Apostles, of whom it is written: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. 18). The almighty God made these heavens out of weak human beings; he instructed them through the Word, strengthened them through the Spirit, and sent them throughout the whole earth. He commanded his mercy—that is, the forgiveness of sins—to be preached.

They were so filled with the Spirit of God’s mouth (Acts 2) that it was said to them: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10).

At that time the sea—that is, the world—raged with the enormous waves of persecutors; now it remains enclosed within its own boundaries. Hence it is added:

## 7. Gathering the waters of the sea as in a wineskin.

For the salty water of the sea—that is, the unbelieving and bitter people who remained among the Christians—no longer dares to rage (as Augustine says in the same passage). [Note: [Col. 0759] More correctly in the common text of Augustine: *remansit, in Christianos saevire non audet, occultum autem murmur rodit in se, et intra*, etc.: “it remained; it does not dare to rage against Christians, but a hidden murmur gnaws within itself, and within,” etc.] Yet the hidden murmur gnaws within; the brine enclosed within mortal skin growls.

Hence it is said elsewhere: “The sinner shall see and be angry; he shall gnash his teeth and melt away” (Ps. 111). Mortal skin covers the bitter thought. Those who fear for their skin keep within themselves what they do not dare to utter. The bitterness is the same, but those who once raged openly now do so secretly.

Let us therefore recognize that God does not now lack material from which to bring forth what will correct us when we need it. Hence it follows:

“Putting the abysses into storehouses.”

By “storehouses” he wishes the secret purpose of God to be understood; by “abysses,” the reprobate. He knows the hearts of all. He knows what to bring forth at the proper time, from where to bring it, and how much power to grant the wicked against the good—power by which the wicked are judged and the good instructed.

Let what follows therefore be fulfilled:

## 8. Let all the earth fear the Lord.

You do not know from where your Father will bring forth what is needed to chastise you. He possesses the storehouses of the abyss for your discipline, through which he will educate you for the storehouses of heaven.

Return, then, to fear, you who were already moving toward security. And lest a person turn to fear anything other than God, he confirms us in the fear of God when he adds:

“Let all who inhabit the world be moved by him.”

Let everyone be moved by him. Let them fear no one other than him. It rages, it is violent, the serpent lies in wait, a human being hates, the devil attacks: fear God. For all creation is subject to the one whom you are commanded to fear.

Hence he adds:

## 9. For he spoke, and they came to be; he commanded, and they were created.

He made all things, and all things follow his command. He spoke—that is, he willed—and all things came to be from unformed matter. From unformed matter, at his command, every creature received its form.

He who made all things by his word and created them by his command: when he commands, they move; when he commands, they rest. Human wickedness may possess the desire to harm, but it has no power of its own unless he grants it. “There is no authority except from God” (Rom. 13).

Therefore he adds:

## 10. The Lord scatters the counsels of the nations.

Those nations thought they would destroy the Church and build idols and temples of the gods. But he rejects the thoughts of the peoples—that is, of the Jews, who, because of the Law in which they ought to have lived, were not improperly called a people. Their thoughts concerned preserving their nation and their place (John 11).

He also rejects the counsels of the rulers—that is, of demons, kings, leaders, and high priests. Their counsel was indeed that they should kill Jesus (the same passage). But it was scattered because they could not keep in death the one whom they had killed.

“For there is no wisdom, no prudence, and no counsel against the Lord” (Prov. 21).

## 11. But the counsel of the Lord remains forever.

Of whom could this be spoken except of us, whom he foreknew and predestined beforehand? Who can abolish the predestination of the Son of God before the foundation of the world (Rom. 8)? He saw us, made us, cleansed us, sent to us, and redeemed us. This counsel of his remains forever.

“The thoughts of his heart are from generation to generation”—that is, his arrangements, which are called those of the heart because they are ordered rationally, extend through every generation.

Hence it is added:

## 12. Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord.

Who, hearing this, would not lift himself up? Human beings love all forms of blessedness, and for this reason they are perverse: they wish to be wicked but do not wish to be miserable. Although misery is inseparably joined to wickedness, these people perversely wish not only to be wicked and not miserable—which cannot happen—but wish to be wicked precisely so that they will not be miserable.

Someone commits theft. You ask why: because of hunger, because of necessity. Thus, in order not to be miserable, he is wicked—and therefore more miserable, because he is wicked.

Everyone, then, wishes always to be blessed, whether living wickedly or living well. But only those who are righteous will be blessed. Ask, therefore, what you possess in order to be blessed. It is impossible for something inferior to you to make you better.

Receive, then, reliable counsel. Do you wish to be better than you are? Seek what is better than you, and by that you will become better than you are.

What you seek is within the soul. You wish to be blessed; seek within your soul what is better. [Note: [Col. 0761D] With the help of the Augustinian copy, we have removed faults of punctuation and other slight errors. Conversely, there are some matters here by which Augustine himself may be corrected.] For since there are two things, soul and body, and of these two the better is what is called the soul, your body can be made better through what is better, because the body is subject to the soul. When your soul is righteous, your body too will afterward become immortal (1 Cor. 15). Through the illumination of the soul the body merits incorruption, so that the lower may be restored through the better.

If, then, your soul is the good of your body because it is better than your body, when you seek your good, seek what is better than your soul.

What, then, is your soul? Consider: in your soul is the image of God. The human mind received it, but by turning toward sin it discolored it. The one who had originally formed it came to restore it. The Word came, as we have heard from the Apostle: “Be transformed in the renewal of your mind” (Rom. 12).

It remains, then, for you to seek what is better than your soul. What will it be, I ask, except your God? You will find nothing better than your soul, because when your nature is perfected, it will be equal to the angels (Matt. 22). Above it there is nothing except the Creator. Raise yourself toward him.

Do not say, “He is too much for me” (Matt. 6). Perhaps possessing gold is more difficult for you than possessing the Lord. If you want gold, perhaps you will not have it; when you want God, you will have him. For even before you wanted him, he came to you; when you were unwilling, he called you (Prov. 1); when you had turned back, he terrified you; and when, terrified, you confessed, he consoled you.

The one who provides you with everything, the one who made you exist, the one who gives the sun, rain, fruits, and health even to those who are with you—including the wicked—that one keeps something for you which he will give to no one but you. What does he keep for you except himself?

Desire cries out; iniquity says: “Blessed is the one who owns this estate, this house, this field.” Restrain desire; listen to truth:

“Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord.”

What does this mean? Is not the Lord God the master of all things, who made and governs everything? Indeed, he is master of all things, but especially ours, for we live from him as from God our Father.

Let him be our Lord and God; let him govern us, he who created us, so that we may be his blessed nation and his blessed possession. Thus what follows may belong to us:

“Blessed is the people whom he chose as his inheritance.”

He commends his mercy, by which he looked upon this blessed nation, when he adds:

## 13. From heaven the Lord looked down; he saw all the children of human beings.

First he said that the nation whose God is the Lord was blessed, his possession and inheritance. And to show that it was likewise the Lord’s possession and inheritance, he added: “The people whom he chose as his inheritance.” Thus, in a marvelous and delightful way, each possesses and is possessed by the other, as heir and inheritance, possessor and possession.

Now he says that the same Lord, from heaven—as from an exalted place, whether from the height of his divinity or from the loftiness of his mercy—saw all the children of human beings, who are placed below and are very far removed from him. He saw them, I say, and regarded them mercifully. He saw them because he pitied them.

Thus, when we ask someone for mercy, we often say, “Look upon me.” There is therefore a kind of seeing that belongs to a compassionate heart, not to one that punishes. In this way the Lord deigned to see all the children of human beings who belong to the Son of Man.

## 14. From his prepared dwelling place.

From the dwelling place that he prepared for himself—that is, from the Apostles, the preachers of truth, and the angels whom he sent to us—he looked upon all who inhabit the earth, as pilgrims in a foreign place.

Hence elsewhere the blessed inheritance groans and says: “Woe is me, for my sojourning has been prolonged; I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar; my soul has been a long-time sojourner” (Ps. 119).

## 15. He who fashioned their hearts individually.

For to one was given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, to another kinds of tongues, and to others various and different gifts of grace, which the one and same Spirit works in them (1 Cor. 12).

“He understands all their works”—that is, he sees them more secretly and inwardly. This is expressed more precisely than if he had said, “He sees all their works.” For God not only sees all the works we perform; he also understands and carefully considers with what will and intention we perform them.

Two people give to the poor (as Augustine says in *Expositions* 3). One seeks a heavenly reward for himself; the other seeks human praise. In the two people you see one outward act; God understands two inward intentions. And as he understands, so he judges and distinguishes. Hence it sometimes happens that in one and the same work he condemns one person and rewards another.

Since he had said above, “Blessed is the people whom he chose as his inheritance,” lest it appear that he chose the rich and powerful rather than the poor, he therefore adds:

## 16. A king is not saved by great power, nor will a giant be saved by the abundance of his strength.

The kings of the earth, proud giants, and powerful people who trust in themselves and in their own strength will not be saved. Who is more powerful than a king? Who is stronger than a giant? Since such people are not saved by their power and strength, let everyone seek for salvation through nothing except the mercy of God.

## 17. The horse is deceptive for salvation; in the abundance of its strength it will not be saved.

The horse—that is, human prosperity, which lifts a person as a horse lifts its rider—is deceptive for salvation. It appears to promise salvation but cannot give it.

When you walk proudly in any position of honor (as Augustine says in the same passage), the higher you go, the more you falsely believe yourself not only higher but also safer. For how it may cast you down, you do not know. The higher you are carried, the more heavily you will be dashed down.

And I do not say merely that the small prosperity of this world is deceptive; however great it may be, it remains deceptive. This is what he means by “in the abundance of its strength”—that is, in the abundance of possessions and riches—no human being will be saved.

From where, then, will I be safe? Do not search long. Do not search far.

## 18. Behold, the eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear him.

Behold—that is, salvation is plainly evident. He does not say, “The eyes of the Lord are upon kings, nobles, or the rich,” but “upon those who fear him.” For God does not show partiality to persons (Matt. 22; Acts 10); he does not consider riches or honors, but looks mercifully only upon those who fear him and hope in him.

Therefore he adds:

“And upon those who hope in his mercy.”

Understand: the eyes of the Lord are upon them. For what purpose?

## 19. To rescue their souls from eternal death.

God promises us eternal life, yet he does not abandon us in this pilgrimage. For it follows:

“And to feed them in famine.”

The time of hunger is now; the time of fullness will come afterward. “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled” (Matt. 4).

Meanwhile, the merciful Lord feeds us in this wilderness with his sacraments, his word, and his grace, so that we do not fail on the way. Then there will be complete refreshment, when what is said elsewhere is fulfilled: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. 16).

What must we meanwhile do and profess? He continues and says:

## 20. Our soul waits for the Lord.

As long as there is hunger, as long as there is pilgrimage, our soul will be patient in the Lord. To such people the Lord will say: “You are those who remained with me in my temptations” (Luke 22).

By contrast it is written: “Woe to those who have lost endurance” (Eccles. 2).

And how will you be able to wait for the Lord (Phil. 3), O holy soul? He continues and says:

“For he is our helper and protector.”

He helps in battle; he protects from the heat. He helps in good things; he protects in adversity.

For what reward do you endure?

## 21. For our heart will rejoice in him, and we have hoped in his holy name.

Our heart will not rejoice in ourselves, where there is great poverty without him, but in him. Therefore we shall hope that we will come to him because, while we are absent, he has sent us his name through faith.

Hope here, so that you may rejoice there. Hunger and thirst here, so that you may feast there. He has set before us what we should love and in whom, and in whom alone, we should place our confidence. He has filled us with the joy of hope (Rom. 15).

## 22. After this comes a brief and salutary prayer:

“Let your mercy, Lord, be upon us, just as we have hoped in you.”

For we have already placed our hope in you; we already venerate your holy name, in which we hope, and call upon it over us. Therefore, just as we have hoped in you, so may we feel your mercy above us.

# Title of Psalm 33

## 1. A psalm of David, when he changed his appearance before Achimelech, who dismissed him, and he departed.

This is how he changed it. For he beat the drum (1 Sam. 21), pretended madness, struck himself with his hands, and saliva ran down his beard. He did this at the gate of the city of David because the Philistines were seeking to destroy him.

When Achis, who was king of Gath, saw these things, he said: “Why have you brought this madman to me?”

David beat the drum—that is, Christ was dying on the cross. He pretended madness when he humbled himself with compassionate affection. He struck himself with his hands when he said: “This is my body” (1 Cor. 10). Saliva ran down his beard—that is, his words, when he said: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man,” and so forth (John 6).

These things seemed childish to those who are “Achis”—a name interpreted as “How is it?” or “What is this?”—but to the bearded, that is, to mature men, they were manly.

The true David, before Achimelech—that is, before the kingdom of his Father, namely, among the Jewish people—changed his appearance, that is, the form of the former sacrifice, which was according to Aaron. He dismissed him and departed to the nations, where he established the priesthood according to the order of Melchizedek.

The subject is the alteration of the priesthood according to the order of Melchizedek, which is indicated where it says: “Magnify the Lord with me.” Its commendation occurs when it says: “For the Lord is gracious.”

In this psalm the prophet urges everyone to fear God, because those who fear him suffer no want. He calls them to filial fear by affectionately inviting good people when he says: “Come, children, listen to me.” In doing this, he intends to generate love in them when he says: “The Lord guards all their bones; not one of them shall be broken.” He deters them from sin by saying that the death of sinners is most grievous.

# Psalm 33

## 2. I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth.

Christ said this; let the Christian say it too, because he is in the body of Christ. “At all times,” he says—that is, in prosperity and adversity—I will bless and praise the Lord.

When prosperity follows, both good and wicked people praise and bless God. If adversity comes, the wicked murmur, but the good bless him. Hence blessed Job, after losing his possessions and being deprived of his children, said: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1).

But because some people wish to be praised for their own good, he guards against this fault when he adds:

## 3. In the Lord my soul shall be praised.

It shall not be praised in itself, nor in the wisdom of the world, nor in loftiness of speech (1 Cor. 2), but in the Lord, from whom it received both virtue and power.

And because holy men desire to share their good things with others, he immediately adds:

“Let the meek hear and rejoice.”

He rightly does not say “the angry,” but “the meek.” For when the meek hear, they rejoice; the non-meek become angry. These are the people (as Augustine says in *Expositions* 2) who say that they did not make themselves donkeys. The Lord wishes to have tame animals.

The horse and the mule, of which we spoke shortly before, sometimes stiffen their necks and in their fierceness throw off their rider. They are tamed by reins, bit, and blows until they learn to carry their master.

Before your mouth is struck by the bit, however, be meek and carry the Lord. Do not seek to be praised; let him be praised who sits upon you.

But let us now hear what he admonishes us:

## 4. Magnify the Lord with me, and let us exalt his name together.

Whoever is in the body of Christ ought to strive for this: when magnifying the Lord, to draw others with him into magnifying God.

We magnify the Lord when we proclaim him great, wondrous, and ineffable. To exalt his name is to make it known throughout all nations, as widely and as highly as we can, as eternal.

What does “together” mean? In unity and concord (1 Cor. 1), as the first preachers did, whose heart and soul were one (Acts 4).

Then he states the source of his blessings when he adds:

## 5. I sought the Lord, and he answered me, and he delivered me from all my tribulations.

I sought God beyond all things, setting temporal matters aside, with my whole heart and all my strength; and he answered me so that I might find him.

But those who seek the Lord are afflicted in this world in many ways. For all who wish to live devoutly in Christ suffer persecution (2 Tim. 3). Their consolation is that afterward they will be delivered from all tribulations. When? When death is swallowed up in victory and this mortal nature has put on immortality (1 Cor. 15).

Then this lover, who does not wish to embrace alone what he loves, exhorts us and says:

## 6. Draw near to him, and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be put to shame.

We draw near to God through good pursuits and spiritual exercises: by reading, meditating, praying, and loving. We are enlightened through understanding, grace, teaching, and life.

Those who are enlightened are not put to shame: they do not blush because of their sins, nor do they blush because of the reproaches and insults inflicted upon them. Hence Paul is not ashamed of the Gospel (Rom. 1). Hence the Apostles are not put to shame; rather, they glory because they were considered worthy to suffer insult for the name of Jesus (Acts 1).

He sets before us a certain poor man as an example when he adds:

## 7. This poor man cried out, and the Lord heard him and saved him from all his tribulations.

Who is this man? Notable, lovable, worthy of imitation—and perhaps he is Christ himself, who, although he was rich over all things, became poor for our sake to such an extent (2 Cor. 8).

He cried out in the form of a servant (Phil. 2), and the Lord the Father heard him. This poor man became obedient unto death, even death on a cross (the same passage). Therefore God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name (the same passage).

Behold how the Lord heard him. He is delivered from all tribulations because Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more; death will no longer rule over him (Rom. 6).

Through this poor man the way by which you may return to your homeland is shown to you. He became poor so that you would not fear poverty, but rather love it. He suffered so that you too might suffer. He cried out so that you too might cry out. He was delivered so that you too might hope to be delivered.

He gives you great assurance when he adds:

“The angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear him, and he will deliver them.”

Only fear God, and be secure. For this poor man, who is called “the angel of great counsel” (Isa. 9), places himself around those who fear him, guarding and defending them on every side, so that the enemy may break through at no point.

## 9. But he wishes to speak openly about that sacrament in which he was carried in his own hands, when he adds:

“Taste and see that the Lord is gracious.”

He shows you (as Augustine says in *Expositions* 2) that healthy madness and sober drunkenness of that David who, in a figure, was displaying—I do not know what—when those miserable people said to him before King Achis: “How is it?” (Ps. 110).

Thus the Lord said: “Unless someone eats my flesh and drinks my blood, he shall not have life in himself” (John 6). And those in whom Achis reigned (1 Sam. 21)—that is, error and ignorance—said: “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” (John 6).

If you do not understand, taste, and see how gracious the Lord is. The one who loves tastes; the one who understands sees.

But if he does not understand, he is King Achis. David changed his face, withdrew from you, dismissed you, and departed.

Therefore:

“Blessed is the man who hopes in him.”

Not in a human being, not in the world, not in himself, but in God. By contrast, whoever does not hope in God is miserable.

[Note: [Col. 0763] The Benedictines reject the word *miseri* (“wretched men”) in their Augustine; ours formerly read it and maintains it.]

And lest, after tasting, they should become secure, he immediately adds:

## 10. Fear the Lord, all you his saints.

To fear God is to humble oneself before him and, through fear, take care not to offend him in what we do—whether in thought, word, or deed. Those who do this are holy.

And as though someone were to ask, “What benefit comes from fearing the Lord?” he continues:

“For those who fear him suffer no want.”

He proves this when he adds:

## 11. The rich have been in want and have hungered, but those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing.

It might seem to you that those who despise the world, become poor, and seek the Lord ought rather to hunger, while those who abound in earthly riches should lack no good things.

But do not consider people according to their material resources; consider them according to the virtues of their souls. These lovers of the world, who appear rich outwardly, suffer no small poverty of mind within. Those who seek God within themselves and desire nothing apart from God lack no good thing; rather, they are filled with the highest good, which is God.

They are filled with faith, hope, and love. They are filled with holy conduct and virtues, which are true riches and drive poverty from the soul.

Therefore he admonishes us, saying:

## 12. Come, children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord.

It greatly edifies us that he says, “Come,” as though he were saying: “You who are idle, or who are occupied with earthly vanities; you who labor and are burdened” (Matt. 11), leave behind what hinders you and come to me.

“Listen” with the ears of the heart. Obey as children; with a father’s affection I will teach you the fear of the Lord.

He appropriately says “fear.” It is the first step of spiritual teaching and heavenly wisdom, as it is written: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110; Prov. 1). Whoever approaches the service of God should make this his first concern: to learn how he ought to fear God.

But first we should observe how skillfully this holy man uses the art of teaching. He first seeks to win the goodwill of his hearers. He sets before them what they most enjoy hearing, saying:

## 13. Who is the person who desires life?

I am not speaking of a life situated in misery; rather, who is the one who loves to see good days? He puts before them what everyone desires, so that he may kindle them to do what he commands.

If you desire life, desire eternal life. If you love good days, love eternal days. This is true life: to live in God. There are always evil days in the world; there are always good days in God.

Therefore, if you desire life and good days, listen and act.

## 14. Keep your tongue from evil.

Do not speak evil openly. And let your lips not speak deceit. Do not utter good words with your mouth while hiding evil in your heart, as those do who speak peace with their neighbor while evil is in their hearts.

He commands the tongue to be restrained from sin before the other members, because it is the most unruly member in the whole body. Of it it is written: “In the power of the tongue are life and death” (Prov. 18). The Apostle also says of it: “The tongue is an unsettled evil, full of deadly poison” (James 3).

Because it kills the soul if it is not restrained, and because we most often stumble through the tongue, the holy man rightly commands that it be curbed first, since he saw that it prevailed more powerfully than the other bodily members toward sin.

Then he adds universally:

## 15. Turn away from evil.

And because this is not enough, he immediately adds:

“And do good.”

Again, because these two things could not suffice for perfect righteousness, he straightaway adds:

“Seek peace and pursue it.”

To abandon evil belongs to beginners. To do good belongs to those who are making progress. Righteousness consists in these two commandments.

The end of perfect righteousness is to be so peaceful within oneself that the flesh agrees with the soul, and the soul with God, so that no adversity can now move it from this tranquility.

Alternatively, by the name of peace we may understand the Lord Christ, who is true peace and who made both one (Eph. 2). We ought to seek him among ourselves with our whole heart and all our affection. We certainly pursue him if, by living perfectly, we imitate him.

He commends God’s mercy toward us when he adds:
