16. The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous; that is, the gaze of divine mercy is upon those who live righteously. And if they ask for something, his ears—that is, his clemency and power—are ready to hear their prayers. He sees those who work and labor; he hears those who groan and pray. Therefore live in such a way that you may be worthy to appear before the eyes of God. Pray in such a way that your prayers may reach his ears. But perhaps some wicked person will say, “I may sin without concern, because God does not see me.” Hear what follows.

17. But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth. By “face” understand the terror of God’s severity. To the good he is gracious and favorable; to the wicked, terrifying and strict. And just as the righteous will be in everlasting remembrance (Ps. 111), so the wicked will be removed from everlasting remembrance. Their memory will then be destroyed, when none of the saints will be moved toward them by any compassionate affection. Hence Abraham said, “Between us and you a great chasm has been fixed” (Luke 16). He proves that the Lord’s ears are ready for the prayers of the righteous when he adds:

18. The righteous cried out, and the Lord heard them, and delivered them from all their tribulations. The three youths cried out in the furnace (Dan. 3). Daniel cried out in the pit (Dan. 4). The children of Israel cried out in captivity (Exod. 3). Christ cried out on the cross (Heb. 5). The Apostles cried out in persecution; the martyrs in death; confessors and virgins in faith. However many cried out, they were heard by the Lord, either bodily or spiritually, and were delivered from all their tribulations. Strengthened, then, by so many examples of the saints, let us cry out to the Lord with complete humility and affliction of heart, so that we too may be heard and delivered from tribulation. For it follows:

19. The Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart, and he will save the humble in spirit. In this world the hearts of the saints are troubled in four ways: by the grief of repentance, by anxiety over the present life, by longing for the heavenly homeland, or by fear of future punishment. It is therefore our task to crush the heart. It is the Lord’s task, through his mercy and grace, to draw near to the contrite heart, so that he may enlighten, strengthen, and establish it. From the crushing of the heart humility is generated. For virtue proceeds from action. From contrition of heart we perceive the divine presence. From humility of spirit we already attain salvation itself. Where there is action, there is grace; where there is virtue, there is already healing.

A great mystery: God is above all things. You raise yourself up, and you do not touch him; you humble yourself, and he himself descends to you. It is characteristic of the righteous, however, that they are troubled in this world. Hence it is also added:

20. Many are the tribulations of the righteous. But consolation follows in what he immediately adds: And the Lord will deliver them from all these things. Christians do not become righteous, nor do they hear the word of God, so that they may suppose they will not be afflicted by tribulations. God does not promise this. Rather, if they are wicked, they have fewer tribulations; if they are righteous, they have many. But [from Augustine, *Enarrationes*, 2], after few or no tribulations, the former come to everlasting tribulation, from which they will never be rescued. [Note: In Augustine: “But the righteous …”] The latter, however, after many tribulations, will come to everlasting peace, where they will suffer no evil. Meanwhile:

21. The Lord guards all their bones; not one of them will be crushed. The bones are the supports of the faithful. And just as flesh is sustained by bones, so the soul is sustained by virtues. The Lord therefore guards all their bones, so that not one of them is broken, because he preserves the virtues of his saints in such a way that none of them fails in temptation. And he rightly does not say, “Not one of them will be broken,” but says, “will not be crushed”: for the virtue of the saints is sometimes broken in temptation, but is not crushed—that is, it does not perish completely—because it remains whole in its intention. And from the point at which those who are tempted fall for a moment, they rise again, once roused to virtue, with greater strength.

But let us hear what he adds concerning the reprobate:

22. The death of sinners is most evil. But because there are many kinds of sinners, and because it is difficult, or perhaps impossible, not to be a sinner in this life, he immediately specified what kind of sinners have the worst death: And those who hate the righteous will sin. Whom does he mean by “the righteous,” except him who justifies the ungodly? Whom does he mean by “the righteous” [from the same source, in the same place], except our Lord Jesus Christ, who is also the atoning sacrifice for our sins (Rom. 4)? Those who hate him therefore have the worst death, because they die in their sins (John 8), since they are not reconciled to God through him. Death is to be understood according to the soul as either worst or best, not according to the body, in the case of condemned sinners.

23. Again he says concerning the righteous: The Lord will redeem the souls of his servants. For all were servants of sin. The blood of Christ was poured out, and they were redeemed at so great a price. Consider, therefore, who redeemed you, and from whom and at what price he saved you by redeeming you. God himself, your Creator, redeemed you; he himself poured out his blood for you. He saved you from the devil and from sin. Having therefore become the servant of so great a Lord, strive to serve him in holiness and righteousness (Luke 1).

But a great question arises when he adds: And none of those who hope in him will transgress. For what does the Apostle say? “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (1 John 1). And again: “In many things we all offend” (James 3). But Paul resolves this question for us when he says: “If I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me” (Rom. 7). If, then, those who hope in God transgress through the desire of the flesh (Gal. 5), they themselves no longer do it, but the sin dwelling in them does. For insofar as they hope in God, they are no longer in the flesh but in the spirit (1 John 2). And if the flesh desires, those who are in the spirit do not consent; therefore they do not transgress.

# TITLE OF PSALM XXXIV

1. The title of the following psalm is, “A Psalm for David.” This psalm is attributed to David, that is, to Christ, who speaks here. The expression “for him” may be understood as indicating distinction or excellence: “for him,” that is, for the notable one—not a carnal king, but the King of kings, the Lord. David is interpreted as “strong of hand” or “desirable.” In the first sense [from Augustine, *Sermon* 1], he is strong of hand because he conquered our death. In the second, he is desirable because he promised eternal life. What is stronger than this hand, which touched the bier and raised the dead man? What is stronger than this hand, which conquered the world—not armed with iron, but pierced by wood? And what is more desirable than the one whom the martyrs, though they did not see him, wished to die for, so that they might merit to reach him?

Therefore let the psalm sing a worthy song to him, to him; let our heart belong to him, and our tongue to him. [Note: We have emended this from Augustine: previously *ste* stood in place of *illi* (“to him”).] It intends to admonish us to endure suffering, so that we may bear adversity if we wish to possess glorious rewards. Its subject is the passion and resurrection. It treats them in this way: in the first part it sets forth a prayer; in the second it enumerates the passion together with the joy of the resurrection; in the third, what that passion and resurrection accomplish—speaking as follows:

# PSALM XXXIV

1. Judge, O Lord, those who harm me; fight against those who fight against me. Those who harm and fight against us are our visible and invisible enemies (Col. 1). “Judge,” he says, “and fight against them,” as though he were openly saying, “Distinguish and destroy them.” How?

2. Take up arms and shield, and rise to my assistance. A great spectacle it is [from Augustine, in the same place] to see God armed on your behalf. His weapons, with which he strikes the enemies, will be us, if we have made good progress. For just as we have weapons with which he arms us, so he is armed with us. His shield is his good will, as it is said elsewhere: “O Lord, with the shield of your good will you have crowned us.” Or the shield is our faith, by which we are protected lest we be struck by the fiery arrows of the enemy.

But what are we now, as God’s weapons—however splendid, however sharp, however flashing with the light of wisdom? What can we do unless God takes us up and fights through us? The finest weapons lie useless if they have no warrior. Let God therefore take us up; and when we are in his hand, let him use us as he wishes. “Rise,” he says, “to my assistance”—that is, become known, appear, be perceived, and help me to fight.

3. Draw out the sword, and shut the way against those who persecute me. As though he were saying, “Multiply vengeance, and let the way be closed against those who wish to destroy my name.” Or by the sword he designates any faithful soul. Let the righteous abound, and the sword is drawn out. The way is shut against the one who has nothing wicked to say against the saints.

And because their cry is, “There is no salvation for him in his God” (Ps. 3): Say to my soul, “I am your salvation.” Say it, and it will come to pass. I will seek no other salvation besides my God. And if a human being helps me, or an angel, or any other creature, God helps me through that agent. For all things are subject to him; therefore it is not that agent but he who is my salvation.

Then he begins to pray for his enemies; but this is prophecy. What are expressed in the form of wishes are explained in the mind of prophecy. “Let this happen, and let that happen” means nothing other than “This also will happen.” Hear the prophecy, then:

4. Let those who seek my soul be confounded and put to shame. As though he were saying, “They will be confounded and put to shame”; for it has happened. Many [from Augustine, in the same place] were healthfully confounded; many, put to shame by the persecution of Christ, passed over with devoted piety into fellowship with his members. This would not have happened unless they had been confounded and put to shame.

Let those who devise evil against me be turned back and confounded. Let them not go before, but follow; let them not give counsel, but receive it. Peter wished to go before the Lord when he said, “Far be it from you, Lord; may God be gracious to you, this shall never happen.” But what did the Lord say? “Get behind me, Satan” (Matt. 16). By going before, you are Satan; by following, you will be a disciple.

So may it be with these people also. Let them be turned back and confounded because of their sins; let them blush with shame unto repentance. And when they begin to follow behind, they will no longer devise evil against me, but will desire good things. He rightly wished this for them.

But because there are two kinds of those who are confounded—for they are either confounded so that they may be converted to Christ, or confounded so that they may be condemned by Christ—after speaking of the converted, he adds concerning the reprobate:

5. Let them become like dust before the face of the wind, and let the angel of the Lord hem them in. The wind is temptation; the dust is the wicked person. When temptation comes, the dust is lifted up; it neither stands nor resists. The angel hems such people in when he brings them under the power of the invisible enemy. Concerning them he adds:

6. Let their way become darkness and slipperiness, and let the angel of the Lord pursue them. [Note: This reading is more appealing than the one printed in Augustine, “darkness alone.”] Who would not dread darkness alone? Who would not beware slipperiness alone? In darkness and slipperiness, where can you set your foot?

These are two great evils and punishments of the human race, which proceed from the temptation of the hemming-in angel. By “way” action is signified; by “darkness,” blindness of heart; by “slipperiness,” the precipitousness of conduct. When the reprobate, tempted and confounded by the evil angel, are hemmed in, the first result is that they are darkened by blindness of mind; then they slip into evil. They can no longer be converted, because the tempting angel pursues them, so that he may make them stumble [reading uncertain: Ant. has *impinguat* instead of *impingat*] from evil into worse, until they fall into the pit of iniquity and sink into the depths of despair and death.

But from where do such great evils arise? For what merit? He continues and says:

7. For without cause they secretly hid for me the destruction of their snare. That is, they prepared hidden plots for my destruction. And this was without cause, because I did no evil and harmed them in nothing.

They reproached my soul without reason. For they spoke many reproaches against the Lord. But they did so without reason, because they spoke falsely and proved nothing.

But how did they hide a snare for him who saw the hearts of those hiding it? He merely appeared among them to be ignorant, as though he were being deceived, while they were deceived in thinking that he could be deceived. This happened as an example of our patience, since it was necessary for us to live among the wicked and to endure the wicked, whether knowingly or unknowingly.

But what happened to this people of reprobates? He continues and says:

8. Let the snare that he does not know come upon him. A magnificent retribution [from Augustine, in the same place]. Nothing is more just. They hid a snare, and from the very point from which they wished to deceive, they are deceived unknowingly. They are harmed from the point at which they attempted to harm.

For it follows: And let the trap that he concealed seize him. It is as if someone prepared a cup of poison for another and, forgetting, drank it himself. Or as if someone dug a pit so that his enemy might fall into it, and then, forgetting that he had dug it, walked first along that road and fell into it.

Thus everyone who harms another harms himself before the other. Therefore it is rightly added: And let him fall into the snare itself—not into another snare, but into that very one. For from the point at which he seeks to deceive another, he first deceives himself. It can happen that his malice does not harm another; but it cannot happen that it does not harm him.

But what of me?

9. My soul will rejoice in the Lord. As though [from Augustine, in the same place] in him from whom it heard, “I am your salvation”; as though it were not seeking riches from elsewhere. As though it were not seeking to overflow with pleasures and earthly goods, but loving him freely [Note: In Augustine: “but loving the true one freely,” etc.]. It does not wish to receive from him something that may delight it, but sets him alone before itself as the one in whom it may delight. For what is better than God?

And it will delight in his salvation. That is, in his Son, through whom we have been saved (Luke 2), through whom we have access to God (Eph. 2), so that, rejoicing in him, we may believe with the heart unto righteousness and confess with the mouth unto salvation (Rom. 10). Hence it is also added:

10. All my bones will say, “Lord, who is like you?” The bones [from Augustine, in the same place] are all the righteous in the Lord’s body: firm, strong in heart, yielding to no persecution or temptation by consenting to evil. And how can they yield to no temptation unless they believe that God is almighty, beyond measure, and able to deliver them from every tribulation? Hence they say, “Lord, who is like you?”

Delivering the poor from the hand of one stronger than he; the needy and the poor from those who plunder him. For the devil was stronger in holding you, because he conquered and plundered you, to whom you consented. But what did the strong-handed one do? He bound the strong one, drawing out the sword and shutting him in; and from his hand—that is, from his power—he rescued the helpless, the one without strength, the poor in spirit, the needy who had no helper.

For who is your helper except the one to whom you say, “The Lord is my helper and my redeemer” (Ps. 18)? If you wish to presume upon your own strength, you will fall from the very point on which you presumed. If you presume upon another, that one wishes to rule, not to help. He, therefore, must be sought who both redeemed and makes free.

But let us hear what he adds in his own person:

11. Unjust witnesses rose up; they questioned me about things I did not know. Unjust witnesses rose up when, with wicked intent, they gave false testimony against him (Matt. 26).

But what did he not know [from Augustine, sermon 2], who saw the hearts and plots of the wicked? He did not know sin—not as though he failed to judge it, but because he did not commit it. Such expressions are also common in everyday speech. When you say of someone, “He does not know how to do evil,” you mean that he does no evil. What is alien to one’s actions is alien to one’s conscience; what is alien to one’s conscience is alien to one’s knowledge; and so it is said, “He did not know.”

Christ did not know how to blaspheme, and for this reason he was questioned by his persecutors (Matt. 22, 26, and 27). Concerning them it follows:

12. They repaid me evil for good: barrenness for my soul. I [from Augustine, in the same place] brought fertility; they repaid me with barrenness. I brought life; they, death. I brought honor; they, insults. I brought healing; they, wounds. And in all that they repaid, there was indeed barrenness.

13. But when they troubled me, I clothed myself in sackcloth. We do not find, according to the literal sense, that the Lord Jesus wore sackcloth. Therefore it is to be understood that the Lord called the mortality of his flesh “sackcloth” by way of likeness.

Why sackcloth? Because of its likeness to sinful flesh. For the Apostle says [from Augustine, in the same place], “God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and concerning sin he condemned sin in the flesh” (Rom. 8). That is, he clothed his Son in sackcloth, so that from the sackcloth he might condemn the goats—not because there was sin in the Lord, but because there was the likeness of sinful flesh. For death exists only because of sin, and that flesh was certainly mortal.

When, therefore, they troubled him, he clothed himself in sackcloth—that is, he hid himself in flesh. He did not avenge himself; he did not reveal himself. In this regard the Apostle admonishes us, saying, “Do not defend yourselves, beloved, but give place to wrath” (Rom. 12).

Therefore he adds: I humbled my soul with fasting. According to the literal sense, we do not read that the Lord fasted in his passion; but spiritually Christ hungers for our good works. And because he found no good in those who crucified him, he fasted. For what kind of fast was his, when he scarcely found one thief whom he might taste upon the cross? The Apostles also fled from him (Luke 23; Matt. 26).

There is no greater or better task in tribulation than to withdraw from the tumult that is outside, enter into the inner secrets of the mind, and there pray to the Lord that we may not be overcome in temptation. Then, too, we should pray that those who persecute us may be converted to the health of righteousness. Therefore it is added:

14. And my prayer will return into my bosom. By a sign we recognize secrecy. We must pray in the secret place of the heart, where God sees and where God hears. Hence it is said in the Gospel, “But when you pray, enter into your room,” and so forth (Matt. 6).

And we are rightly admonished in this way. But in Christ the Lord we must understand something more. I understand it thus: he had the Father in his bosom. For God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself (1 Cor. 5). He therefore had within himself the one whom he was to beseech, because he himself had said, “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 10 and 14).

How greatly he loved those for whom he prayed (John 17), he shows when he adds:

15. As for a neighbor, as for our brother, so I was pleasing; as one mourning and sorrowful, so I humbled myself. Some say that one case is used in place of another, as though he were saying, “as though concerning a neighbor and a brother.” Christ was therefore pleasing to God the Father because of his persecutors, as though they were his brothers and neighbors; for he loved them as his neighbors and brothers (John 15). “Greater love than this no one has, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (ibid.).

And because they were unwilling to heed him, he humbled himself as one mourning in body and sorrowful in soul. We are therefore admonished by the Lord’s example not only to love those whom we endure, but also, saddened by their wicked deeds, to mourn for them.

I humbled myself in this way on their behalf; but what did they do? He continues and says:

16. And they rejoiced against me. They rejoiced over the things that were adverse and contrary to me. They gathered together in one council and with one purpose, so that they might betray and seize me deceitfully (Matt. 26).

Scourges were gathered—that is, multiplied and joined together—against me, and I did not know. For I knew of no guilt in myself for which I ought to be scourged.

They were scattered and were not pierced with remorse. According to the inner person, they were destroyed and separated from the bond of charity. Or “they were scattered” when they saw the earthquake and the signs (Matt. 28). They were not pierced by these things unto repentance. This signifies the great hardness and wickedness of their hearts.

17. They tempted me. For they said, “If he is the Son of God, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him” (Matt. 28).

They mocked me with mockery. Since he first said, “They mocked,” and then added, “with mockery,” he clearly indicates that this mocking did not arise from a hasty utterance, but from deliberate intention and purpose of heart.

They gnashed at me with bestial ferocity in their teeth—that is, with their corrosive attacks.

From these words he shows us how great the humility, charity, and patience were that our pious Redeemer displayed toward people so wicked, perverse, and faithless. For we must understand that this was the reason our Head suffered: namely, that he might provide his body with an example of patience (1 Pet. 2).

The Lord suffered willingly, not by necessity. His voluntary passion is our necessary consolation, so that whenever we happen to suffer such things, we may look to our Head and, instructed by his example, learn to suffer with him. “If we suffer with him, we shall also be glorified with him” (Rom. 8).

They acted against me in this way; but you, O Lord—

18. When will you look upon me? When will you, attending in mercy, act so as to rescue me from their power? Restore my soul from their wickedness, my only one from the lions. As though he were saying, “My soul, which is unique and free from sin.” For no other soul is without sin.

Restore this soul, I say, rescued from the murderous people and from the lions—that is, from the rulers and priests—deliver it from the passion, so that you may restore it to the body and make it immortal and incorruptible together with the body.

What will you do, holy soul, after you have risen again?

19. I will confess to you in the great church; in a weighty people I will praise you. Confession does indeed take place [from Augustine, sermon 2] in every multitude, but God is praised among all. In this great Church, spread throughout the whole world, there are chaff and grain. The chaff flies away; the grain remains (Matt. 3). Therefore God is praised among the weighty people whom the wind of temptation does not carry away. For among the chaff he is always blasphemed.

And because I will praise you:

20. Let those who oppose me unjustly not rejoice over me, those who hate me without cause and wink with their eyes. They would indeed have rejoiced if Christ had not risen; but because he rose, their joy was turned into mourning.

He rightly says that they opposed him unjustly: not from love, but from hatred; not with the intention of correcting, but with the desire to harm. They hated him without cause—that is, without guilt or merit.

Those who wink with their eyes are hypocritical pretenders who proclaim by their countenance what they do not carry in their hearts. Concerning them it immediately follows:

21. For they spoke peacefully to me. They said, “Good Teacher, we know that you are truthful and do not regard a person’s status” (Matt. 19 and 22). These and similar peaceful words were spoken under the guise of flattery.

And while speaking in the anger of the earth, they devised plots. They spoke in anger, fearing that they would lose the land and the nation (John 11). They spoke in anger on behalf of their land for this reason: so that they might seize Jesus deceitfully and kill him. Such was their thought.

22. And they opened their mouth wide against me, blaspheming openly. And they cried, “Crucify, crucify!” They said, “Good! Good!”—that is, “Well done! Well done!” (Matt. 26 and 27). It is praise uttered in mockery.

“Our eyes have seen it.” We have seen what sort of man he was, and at last we have recognized him. Where are the wonders he used to perform? Why does he not save himself, who saved others? [From Augustine, in the same place.]

But the Lord was patient. On the cross he had not lost his power; he was displaying his patience. For what great thing would it have been for him to descend from the cross, when afterward he was able to rise from the tomb? But he would have seemed to yield to those who mocked him. And this had to happen, so that when he rose again he would show himself to his own, and not to them, because his resurrection signified a new life; and new life is known to friends, not to enemies.

23. You have seen, O Lord, their mockeries and insults. You have recognized their wickedness and my innocence. Therefore, Do not be silent. But issue your judgment. You who do not keep silent concerning the commandment, do not keep silent concerning the judgment.

Lord, do not depart from me. Although he is secure in the knowledge that God does not depart from him—for the Man and the Word are one person in two natures—nevertheless, because he knows that according to his humanity he possesses nothing of himself, he prays in order to give an example of prayer to others, who ought to place no confidence whatsoever in their humanity.

I say, “Do not depart,” but rather:

24. Rise up and help me, and attend to my judgment. That is, consider what sort of judgment has been made concerning me. And lest anyone suppose that the judgment should be considered according to the punishment, he therefore adds: My God and my Lord, attend to my cause. As though he were saying, “You who are my Creator and my Redeemer, attend not to the punishment but to my cause.”

Not [from Augustine, in the same place] to what I have in common with the thief, but to that which belongs to the blessed, who suffer persecution for righteousness. For the cause is distinct. The punishment is similar for the good and the wicked. Therefore it is not punishment that makes a martyr, but the cause. And so he adds:

25. Judge me according to my righteousness, O Lord my God. Because you are righteous, distinguish me, who have been judged unjustly; and do what is just. That is, judge according to righteousness: issue the sentence of judgment according to the cause, not according to the punishment.

26. And let them not rejoice over me. Let them not say in their hearts, “Good! Good! for our soul”; let them not say, “We have devoured him” (Lam. 2)—that is, “We have utterly destroyed him.” They were not able to do this when they heard that he had risen again.

He prays this without doubt concerning himself, but so that he may set before us an example of prayer. He also asks concerning such people that they may be converted, when he adds:

27. Let those who rejoice at my misfortunes be ashamed and show reverence together. As though he were saying, “Let those who rejoiced in my passion repent and honor me.”

Hence also the pious Lord admonishes us in his Gospel, saying, “If you love only those who love you, what reward will you have? Do not even the tax collectors do this? But love your enemies. Do good to those who hate you. And pray for those who persecute and slander you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5).

Therefore, speaking still through the voice of our Head, he adds: Let those who speak evil against me be clothed with shame and reverence. That is, let them likewise be converted, ashamed of their evils and showing reverence to me, against whom they have sinned, whether in deed or in word.

He said, “Let them be clothed,” so that their former evils might be covered through repentance.

In contrast:

28. Let those who desire my righteousness exult and rejoice. Exultation belongs to body and soul together; joy belongs only to the soul. To exult and rejoice, therefore, is to be filled with joy outwardly and inwardly.

Those who wish to turn away from evil and do good (Ps. 33) are the ones who desire the righteousness of God. And it should be noted that he does not say, “Those who do,” but, “Those who desire.” For many perform works of righteousness without willing them. No one does good unwillingly, even if what he does is good. For although the action appears good, the will is nevertheless held guilty. The virtue of righteousness lies not in action but in the will.

Those who desire righteousness are therefore rightly commanded to exult, because love of righteousness generates both a new life and spiritual joy. And lest they wish to glory in themselves because of this, it is immediately added: And let them always say, “The Lord is magnified.” For we must always magnify and praise the one who works in us both willing and working according to his good pleasure (Phil. 2).

He rightly adds: Those who desire the peace of his servant. It is not enough for God’s servants to desire righteousness unless they also strive to desire peace. Hence, after saying above, “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 33), he immediately added, “Seek peace and pursue it.”

Peace exists when flesh and spirit are in harmony in God. In this peace righteousness is completed. Nothing remains except perseverance. Hence he aptly adds:

29. And my tongue will meditate on your righteousness, all day long on your praise. Meditation seems to belong more to the heart than to the tongue. But because holy men meditate day and night on the law of the Lord (Ps. 1), and speak what they meditate upon, their tongue is therefore said to meditate on God’s righteousness.

Hence it is written, “The mouth of the wise is in their heart” (Prov. 16). But whose tongue endures in meditating on the praise of God all day long? Good works and a good life have their own tongue before the Lord. If you live well all day, you will praise God all day.

# TITLE OF PSALM XXXV

1. “For the end, to the child of the Lord, David.” Our end is Christ, to whom this psalm sends us. It is attributed to the same Lord Jesus Christ, who was called David because he was made from the seed of David according to the flesh. He is called “child” because of his purity, since he was without sin; this is clearly declared in this psalm.

In it it is shown that the sinner has all his sins from himself, not from God, whereas the righteous possesses no righteousness except from God’s generosity alone. The subject is first the righteous person, and secondarily the ungodly. In the first part of the psalm he describes the ungodly together with his accusation. In the second part he describes the righteous, not with his own praise, but with the praise of God.

He intends to admonish us to recognize that our vices come from ourselves, but our good comes from God, lest the foot of pride overtake us and we fall (Hos. 13). Thus he begins.

# PSALM XXXV

2. The unjust person said within himself that he should sin. Many say this: “We cannot be without sin” (1 John 1). “Such is our nature. God made us this way. If he did not wish it, we would not sin.”

Why does the unjust person say this? There is no fear of God before his eyes. If he feared God, he would not say this; rather, he would accuse himself, not God. Where there is no fear, there is dissolution of mind. But the fear of God is the bridle of sin.

Since he therefore wishes to hide from God what he is, it is rightly added concerning him:

3. For he acts deceitfully in his sight, so that his iniquity may be found worthy of hatred. Whoever wishes to hide his sin from God acts deceitfully in God’s sight. This is the iniquity that God hates and severely punishes.

When a person sins, then repents and acknowledges that he has acted wrongly, blaming or accusing no one but himself, and from that point turns with all his heart and with complete lamentation toward the mercy of God, such iniquity is not found in him as something hateful to God. Indeed, it is easily forgiven.

But because this person not only lives badly, but also proudly defends his evil life, he is the one whom God hates. According to the hardness of his heart, and his unrepentant heart, he stores up wrath for himself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s righteous judgment (Rom. 2). Concerning him it is also added:

4. The words of his mouth are iniquity and deceit. He unfolds iniquity part by part, showing it in knowledge, deed, and word.

Many act deceitfully so that their iniquity may be discovered—that is, they do not act sincerely so that they might discover and hate it. They would discover it if they wished; but they do not wish to, so that they may defend and excuse themselves in this way. And just as there is deceit in the investigation, so there is also deceit in the defense.

For if you say to one of them, “Why are you doing this evil?” he answers you, “How many people do this! Will God destroy everyone?” Thus, by speaking iniquity and concealing himself evilly, iniquity and deceit are found in his mouth.

He did not wish to understand, so that he might do good. There are people who wish to understand but cannot. But there are others who do not wish to understand, and therefore do not understand.

It is one thing when someone tries to understand something but cannot because of the weakness of the flesh, as it is written, “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling burdens the mind with many thoughts” (Wis. 9); and as the Apostle says, “The natural person does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2).

But it is another thing when the human heart acts more destructively against itself, so that it does not understand what it could understand if good will were added—not because the matter is difficult, but because the will is opposed. The former is weakness; the latter, utter iniquity. The former is incapacity; the latter, deliberate choice.

But let us hear what he adds concerning that unjust person.

5. He meditated iniquity in his bedchamber. That is, in the secret place of his heart. He stood by every path that was not good. That is [from Augustine, in the cited passage], he sinned perseveringly.

But he did not hate wickedness. There is the fruit; there is the end. Are you unable not to have wickedness? At least hate it. For when you hate it, it scarcely creeps upon you so that you do something evil.

Sin exists in the mortal body. But what does the Apostle say? “Let not sin reign in your mortal body, so as to obey its desires” (Rom. 6). And shortly afterward the same Paul says: “When you were servants of sin, you were free from righteousness” (ibid.).

It is one thing not to fight and to be in true and perpetual peace. It is another thing to fight and conquer. Another thing is to fight and be defeated. Another is neither to fight but to be dragged along.

For there are people who do not fight at all, such as the person about whom he is speaking. When he said, “He did not hate wickedness,” how can he fight against what he does not hate? This person is dragged along by wickedness and does not resist.

There are others who begin to fight but fall because they presume upon their own strength. And there are those who fight and are not overcome, because they do not presume upon themselves, but entrust themselves wholly to divine mercy. Concerning these he adds, turning to familiar speech with the Lord and saying:

[Col. 0774C] **6. Lord, your mercy is in heaven.** God’s mercy is understood in two ways. One is that which he commonly grants to good and evil alike, such as the ability to possess things, bodily health, knowledge, instruction, prophecy, and other things of this kind. But because these are transitory, this mercy is temporal. There is another mercy, which God grants only to the good and holy: the remission of sins, divine charity, and eternal life. This is not earthly but heavenly; not transitory but eternal. But how was this announced? The text continues: **And your truth reaches to the clouds.** That is, knowledge of your truth has come to the preachers. These preachers, through whom the Gospel of God is proclaimed, are God’s clouds. They thunder with warnings, rain down words, and flash with miracles. Let us therefore hope for mercy—but for that mercy which is in heaven.

**7. Your righteousness is like the mountains of God.** Just as God’s mercy makes people heavenly, when it raises them from earthly things to heavenly ones; and just as God’s truth makes people clouds, when it illumines them through his wisdom; so divine righteousness makes people like the mountains of God, when it exalts and strengthens them through virtues and good works. And just as, when the sun rises, it first clothes the mountains with light, and from there the light reaches the lowest places of the earth, so, when the Lord Jesus Christ came, he first shone upon the height of the Apostles, first illumined the mountains, and thus his light descended into the valley of the earth. And lest anyone ask why he chose these people rather than rejecting others, he immediately added: **Your judgments are a great abyss.** They are of such depth that no one can investigate them (Rom. 11; Prov. 18). Or by “abyss” may be understood the wickedness of the reprobate. Hence it is written: **When the sinner comes into the depths of evil, he despises** (Prov. 18). After speaking of the elect, therefore, he immediately added what concerns the reprobate, saying: **Your judgments are a great abyss.** It is as though he said: Just as mercy, truth, and righteousness save the righteous, so your judgments condemn the reprobate; they are called a great abyss because they are darkened by manifold iniquity. And because he had previously said that divine mercy was in heaven, he now shows that it has also come to earth. For he says:

**8. You will save human beings and beasts, Lord; how you have multiplied your mercy, O God.** The merciful Lord has multiplied his mercy to such an extent that he has saved not only rational human beings but also brutes and the unlearned. **Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more** (Rom. 5). **But the children of human beings**, that is, the whole Church continuing to the end of the age, **will hope under the shelter of your wings**—that is, under the protection of the two commandments, namely, love of God and of one’s neighbor (Matt. 22; Luke 10). Whoever is not protected beneath these wings will be scorched by the heat of vices.

Or, because he mentions human beings first and then the children of human beings, we may understand by “human beings” the ancient fathers, who did not have the Law but were a law to themselves; they rationally understood and obeyed the Lord’s commandments. **When the Gentiles, who do not have the Law, by nature do what belongs to the Law, these, not having the Law, are a law to themselves. They show the work of the Law written in their hearts, while their conscience bears witness to them** (Rom. 2). They were saved by God’s mercy, as are we, who are the children of human beings—that is, of the prophets and Apostles—belonging to the Son of Man, Christ the Savior. We have been nourished under the Law and regenerated through grace in the hope of eternal life. This grace is commended to us when the text continues:

**9. They will be intoxicated by the abundance of your house, and you will give them drink from the torrent of your delight.** The grace of God, poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. 5), is itself the abundance of God’s house. Those who have been so filled with love of almighty God that, their minds transformed, they seem like strangers even to themselves are intoxicated by this abundance. It is rightly called a torrent of delight, because it comes with great force, and because those who thirst for righteousness drink from it with great sweetness and pleasure. The martyrs were intoxicated by it when they went joyfully to their deaths, despised torments, and did not recognize their weeping parents. Let us therefore hope beneath the shelter of God’s wings, so that we may deserve to be intoxicated by his sweetness.

**10. For with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light.** Who is the fountain of life if not Christ? He came in the flesh, sprinkled the thirsty with dew, and satisfied those who hoped. Here the fountain is one thing and the light another; there it is not so. For what is the fountain is also the light. Call it whatever you wish, since it is not confined by whatever name you call it. Since (according to Augustine) you cannot find a suitable name, do not confine the reality to a single name. He is a fountain because he satisfies the thirsty; light because he illumines the blind. In this light we see light, because, illumined by Christ, we see wisdom, righteousness, and charity.

Or, in this light we see light, just as he himself says: **Whoever sees me sees the Father also** (John 14). And in order that this may happen, do what follows:

**11. Extend your mercy to those who know you, and your righteousness to those who are upright in heart.** First comes knowing God through faith, and then having an upright heart—that is, willing what God wills. God extends his mercy to those who know him when he first grants forgiveness of sins to those who believe in him. Then, when they have begun to have an upright heart, so that they too will what God wills, they obtain God’s righteousness and are made righteous from sinners. But now let them beware lest they become proud. Hence one must pray and say:

**12. Let not the foot of pride come against me, and let not the hand of the sinner move me.** He who said this feared the root and head of sin (according to Augustine). The first Adam was not without righteousness, but the foot of pride came against him. And the hand of the sinner moved him—that is, the devil’s temptation. Through pride, therefore, we fell and came to this mortality. Pride casts down; humility raises up. Preserve, then, what is within: your foot, that is, your affection; and you will not fear outwardly that the hand of the sinner may move you. Why is this said against pride? Because:

**13. There the workers of iniquity fell; they were driven out and could not stand.** Those who are now wicked first fell through pride. First came the one who did not stand in the truth (John 8); then, through him, those whom God expelled from paradise (Gen. 3). Therefore, when the Lord warned the Church, he said: **She will watch your head, and you will watch her heel** (ibid.). The serpent watches so that the foot of pride may come against you, so that your affection may be moved away from God, and thus he may cast you down. But you must watch his head: pride, the beginning of every sin (Ecclus. 19).

The first origin of sinning is a will turning away from the highest good, and this is the foot of pride. From it proceed two vices: ignorance of what ought to be done and desire for harmful things. From these two others are derived: fear and love. From them, in turn, every harvest of evils is generated. We must therefore take the greatest care that the foot—that is, our affection—not be moved away from the highest good, lest it slip through pride, and thus fall among the hands of the sinner and be excluded from blessedness. To the extent that anyone loves God less, to that extent his foot slips toward sinning. And the more he loves God, the more firmly he stands, and the less pleasure he takes in sinning.

## TITLE OF PSALM 36

**1. A psalm for David himself.** That is, for the more excellent members of the Church. The Prophet—or any righteous person speaking here—seeing the wicked prosper and the righteous trampled by the wicked, and seeing that certain simple righteous people envied their power and wished to avenge the injuries inflicted by them, or even wished to become like them, sets forth against these things a very salutary teaching.

The subject is the righteous person and, conversely, secondarily the wicked person. Yet he divides it in this way. First he speaks about the righteous person, admonishing him not to be moved toward the wicked by envy, imitation, or anger, while interspersing certain remarks about the wicked. In the second part he sets forth what the wicked do against the righteous, admonishing the righteous person to endure patiently. In the third part he sets forth the rewards of the righteous with admiration and the condemnation of the wicked; through this he deters the righteous from wishing to imitate evil. His purpose is by these means to console simple souls, so that they may in no way be disturbed by the wickedness or injury of the wicked.

## PSALM 36

**Do not emulate the wicked**, he says. The wicked are so called as though they were nourishing an evil fire, that is, desire. Hence it is written: **Whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul** (Ps. 10). And again: **Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world will be constituted an enemy of God** (James 4). These are the wicked, who work evil within themselves, hating God and their own souls and loving sin.

“Emulate” has several meanings. Sometimes it means “to love,” as the Apostle says: **I am jealous over you with a godly jealousy** (2 Cor. 10). Sometimes it means “to imitate,” as he says again: **Emulate the better gifts** (1 Cor. 12). Sometimes it means “to envy,” as here. Thus every faithful but imperfect soul is admonished not to wish to emulate—that is, envy—those who delight in evil, nor to be jealous—that is, persecute—those who commit iniquity. And this is what follows:

**Nor be jealous of those who do iniquity.** The weak spirit of the elect is disturbed against the reprobate in two ways: either when it envies their prosperity or when it becomes angry at their iniquity. Do not do this, but remain even-tempered. For both their prosperity and their iniquity are brief.

**2. For they will quickly wither like grass.** For a time they rejoice and flourish, but soon they dry up and are reduced to dust (Isa. 40). And as vegetables—that is, the greenness of plants—so they will quickly fall away. Hence Isaiah says: **All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass. The grass withered, and the flower fell** (ibid.). First he removes wickedness; then he commends good conduct when he adds:

**3. Hope in the Lord and do good.** For hope without a good work is not useful. Nor (according to Augustine) is any good work without charity. Hence it immediately adds: **And inhabit the land, and you will be fed on its riches.** The Lord’s land is the Church. The farmer, the father of many who practice good works, cultivates it and waters it; but those who do not inhabit the land do not belong to the farmer. To inhabit the land is to live spiritually and harmoniously within the holy Church. No one can do this unless he has charity. Charity itself is the riches of this land. **God is charity** (1 John 4). The Church seeks no other riches than her God; hence she also sang: **You are my portion**. Therefore delight, O soul, in your riches. For this is why people seek riches: that they may delight in them. Hence it follows:

**4. Delight in the Lord.** With what result? The text continues: **And he will give you the petitions of your heart.** Some petitions belong to the flesh, others to the heart. The former are bodily; the latter spiritual. Delight in God does not ask for what the flesh wants, but for what the spirit wants. What else does the heart of one delighting in God ask for except God himself, the light itself, wisdom itself, and eternity itself? This God promises to those who delight in him. Hence it is written: **What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, God has prepared for those who love him** (Isa. 64; 1 Cor. 2). This is the petition of our heart. This is the reward of one who delights in the Lord.

And because someone might say, “I cannot delight in or hope in the Lord, because I have many sins,” against this he gives a salutary counsel when he adds:

**5. Reveal your way to the Lord.** Confess your sins (Eccles. 17). Accuse yourself and correct yourself (James 5). **And hope in him, and he will act.** For he promises hope to sinners (1 John 1), and grants pardon to those who do penance (Matt. 4). O how salutary are these commands: not to envy the wicked, not to love iniquity, to hope in the Lord, to delight in the Lord, and to confess our ways and works to the Lord! If you do this, he himself will act. What will he do?

**6. And he will bring forth your righteousness like the light.** So that it may never be obscured by darkness and vices (according to Augustine). Your righteousness is your faith (Rom. 1). For **the righteous person lives by faith** (Heb. 10). This righteousness is now hidden. It exists in faith, not yet in appearance (1 Cor. 3). You believe one thing in order to act, but you do not yet see what you believe. When, however, you begin to see what you have believed, your righteousness will be brought forth into the light (Isa. 58).

**And your judgment like midday.** It was not enough to say “like the light.” Light exists when the sky grows white, when the sun rises; but the light is never brighter than at midday. At present you judge that you should follow Christ; this you have proposed and chosen. Your judgment is hidden (John 8), and is still criticized and mocked by unbelievers. When will he bring it forth like midday? **When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory** (Col. 3). Meanwhile, what?

**7. Be subject to the Lord and pray to him.** Let this be our life: to obey his commands and beseech him. Let good works and prayer persevere until he gives what he promised. If you see the wicked flourishing, do not let vanity move you. **Do not emulate the one who prospers in his way, the man who commits injustices.** He prospers (according to Augustine) in his own way? You labor in the way of God. For him there is prosperity on the road and unhappiness at the destination; for you there is labor on the road and happiness at the destination. His road is broad, and its end leads into the depths of hell; your road is narrow (Matt. 7), and its end is eternal life.

I say: do not emulate him. And if in any way you have been moved, whether in mind or in body, correct it. This is what follows:

**8. Cease from anger and abandon wrath; do not emulate, so as to act wickedly.** Anger belongs to the mind, wrath to the body. It is as though he said: Let neither the iniquity of the wicked move you to anger nor their prosperity to envy. **For those who are wicked will be exterminated**, that is, cast outside the boundaries of the heavenly Jerusalem. As it is written: **Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God** (Isa. 26).

**9. But those who wait for the Lord will themselves inherit the land.** Who are those who wait, except the patient? Hence the Lord says to his disciples: **You are those who have remained with me in my temptations** (Luke 22). In contrast, it is written: **Woe to those who have lost endurance** (Eccles. 2). The land is the heavenly homeland, of which it is said elsewhere: **I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living** (Ps. 26). Those who wait for the Lord will inherit this land, that is, possess it by hereditary right. And lest you think this waiting would be exceedingly long, he immediately adds:

**10. And yet a little while, and the sinner will not be.** That is, he will not appear. The life and prosperity of the wicked are brief. And even if the span seems long while they live, it seems brief when they die. Times pass quickly; what cannot endure is brief. Hence the Apostle says: **What is your life? A vapor of smoke appearing for a little while** (James 4).

But what follows must be carefully noted: **And you will seek his place, and you will not find it.** Now seek the sinner’s place, and you find it. His place is his usefulness. For the sinner has some use (according to Augustine). God uses him to test the righteous, just as he used the devil to test Job (Job 1), and as he used Judas to betray Christ (Matt. 26). Thus there is something to be done with the sinner in this life. This is his place. As straw is in a goldsmith’s furnace, and the straw burns so that the gold may be purified, so the wicked rage so that the righteous may be tested. But when the time of our testing has passed—when there are no longer any to be tested—there will be no one through whom they may be tested. Then, if you seek their place, you will not find it.

**11. But the meek will inherit the land.** The meek are those who do not resist the Lord, who humbly bear his yoke (Matt. 11), who endure the adversities of the world with equanimity (Rom. 12), not returning evil for evil or abuse for abuse, but, on the contrary, blessing (1 Thess. 5). They will be fit to inherit that holy land, Jerusalem, which will be liberated from this pilgrimage and will live forever with God and from God.

**And they will delight in the abundance of peace.** For they will enjoy the eternal God, who is the source and fullness of all good things. Hence that heavenly city is called Jerusalem, which is interpreted as “vision of peace.” So great is the good of peace that among earthly things nothing more pleasing is ordinarily heard, nothing more desirable sought, and nothing better can finally be found.

In all things, a certain peace and the order of nature are sought. The peace of all things is the tranquility of order. Order is the arrangement that assigns to equal and unequal things their proper places. The peace of an ordered household is the concord of those dwelling together in commanding and obeying. The peace of the rational soul is the ordered agreement of knowledge and action. The peace of soul and body is the ordered life and health of a living creature. The peace between mortal humanity and God is obedience ordered in faith under the eternal law. These are the things on which the meek person of God must nourish himself, so that he may be able to reach heavenly peace.

The peace of the heavenly city, however, is the most orderly and harmonious fellowship of enjoying God and one another in God. And because, as long as they live here, the righteous suffer the plots of the wicked, it is added:

**12. The sinner will watch the righteous.** For the wicked do not cease to investigate the life of the good, carefully observing whether they might in any way be able to harm them. Hence it is written of the Lord: **And they were watching him** (Luke 14). The wicked therefore watches the good in order to seize and destroy him. What he cannot accomplish in deed, he practices through the savage and bestial gnashing of his words. This is what follows:

**And he will gnash his teeth at him.** That is, with the teeth of wickedness and impiety, by which he attempts to devour him. Bodily movements often signify the affections of the mind.

**13. But the Lord will laugh at him, because he foresees that his day is coming.** The Lord possesses the eyes of knowledge. He foreknew that the day of judgment would come, when hidden things would be made manifest. On that day the sinner will be shown by the Lord to be worthy of mockery, when, having lost his power, he will be handed over to eternal punishments. Even here they are already beginning to be mocked, when they unknowingly turn against themselves the military sword with which they think they can harm others.

**14. Sinners have drawn their sword; they have bent their bow.** By the sword we understand open and manifest persecution. By the bow, however, we understand the hidden and deceitful deception with which they lie in wait for the saints. To draw the sword is to put into practice a wickedness previously concealed in the heart. He bends the bow who prepares a deception with which to strike the unwary. With a sword one strikes at close range; with a bow one shoots from a distance. The striking sword is therefore persistent persecution; the bow is an unexpected and apparently remote deception.

By these two kinds of persecution the wicked attack the good: **to deceive the poor and needy, to slaughter the upright in heart.** By the poor and needy are designated simple people who lack knowledge and virtue. By the upright in heart we understand the perfect. Thus they secretly strive to deceive the simple with the bow, while they endeavor to slaughter the perfect openly with the sword of persecution.

Let the enemies of the Church be blinded by whatever error or corrupted by whatever wickedness; if they receive the power to afflict her bodily, they exercise her patience. And because even enemies are loved, they exercise her benevolence. For **God works all things together for good for those who love him** (Rom. 8). Whatever the enemy does against the Church is turned to his own harm. Therefore it follows:

**15. Let their sword enter their own hearts, and let their bow be broken.** They wished to kill in the body; they die in the soul. Whoever attempts to harm another first strikes himself with his own dart. The bow is broken when deceit and evil will do not reach their intended result. It is clear that the wicked harm themselves more than they seem to harm others. For it is more serious for the soul to be killed by vice than for the body to be slaughtered by a sword.

He then commends the modest condition of the righteous, saying:

**16. Better is a little to the righteous person than the many riches of sinners.** The poverty of the righteous is better than the riches of sinners. The former abounds in little; the latter, though full, thirsts. The former saves the soul; the latter loses both body and soul (Matt. 16). **For what does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?** (Matt. 13). Faith, which is compared to a grain of mustard seed, is better for the one who possesses it than the faithlessness that wanders everywhere is for the other.

**17. For the arms of sinners will be broken.** That is, their virtue, power, and riches, in which they trust. But the Lord strengthens the righteous, so that they are not overcome by injustice. For, as the Apostle says: **Tribulation produces endurance, endurance proven character, and proven character hope; but hope does not disappoint, because God’s charity has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us** (Rom. 5).

Hear the voice of the strengthened righteous person: **Who will separate us from the charity of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or sword?** (Rom. 8). How does he strengthen them? The text continues:

**18. The Lord knows the days of the blameless.** For he knows how they lived and in what condition they ended their lives. Or, he knows them because he loved them. Hence, in contrast, he will say to the wicked: **Truly I say to you, I do not know you** (Matt. 25). For everyone who does not know will himself be unknown. Therefore **their inheritance will be forever**.

Be pure and clean throughout all the days of your life, so that you may please the Lord your God in all your conduct (1 Cor. 14). And when you have completed these days, you will inherit forever.

**19. They will not be confounded in the evil time, and in the days of famine they will be satisfied.** The present is an evil time, in which the righteous labor. Hence they say daily in prayer: **Deliver us from evil** (Matt. 6). In this time, the proud, while seeking their own glory, are ashamed if injuries or insults are inflicted upon them. In contrast, holy men who seek not their own glory but God’s, when they are mocked or dishonored by insults and punishments, not only are not ashamed but even glory in them. Hence the Apostle says: **We glory in tribulations** (Rom. 5).

They are satisfied in the days of famine with the food of truth and heavenly sacraments. In this famine, in which the saints of the Lord hunger, they meanwhile take his word as food, lest they fail on the way, until they are satisfied by the vision of him in the homeland. And because he had said above, **The arms of sinners will be broken**, he proves this when he adds:

**20. For sinners will perish.** How? The text continues: **But the enemies of the Lord**—that is, the sinners themselves—**as soon as they have been honored**, having been held in reverence, **and exalted**, through powers and dignities, **will fail, like smoke they will fail**.

Smoke rising from the place of fire is lifted on high and, by that very elevation, swells into a great mass. And the larger it becomes, the more insubstantial it is. So the wicked, the more they are raised up, extended, and spread in every direction into a greater expanse, become all the more slender, failing and disappearing. In many ways it has therefore been shown that the modest condition of the righteous is better than the riches of sinners. He then gives the reason why the sinner will fail, when he adds:

**21. The sinner will borrow and will not repay.** No one possesses anything that he has not received as a loan. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: **A certain man going abroad called his servants and handed over his goods to them. To one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one** (Matt. 25). Behold, the servants received the Lord’s money as a loan.

But whoever has faithfully dispensed it in this world and, with increase, is able to repay it when the Lord returns will hear this from the Lord: **Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your Lord** (ibid.).

The rich dispense faithfully when they give alms from their riches. Teachers dispense faithfully when they teach correctly and live well. But sinners, borrowing riches and wisdom, virtues and understanding from the Lord, neither give him thanks nor distribute to the poor what they possess, nor repay what they owe by living well. Therefore they will fail like smoke.

**But the righteous person has compassion**, that is, he is moved by a pious affection toward those afflicted, **and he will give.** He always has something to give whose breast is full of charity. This is the charity also called good will (1 Cor. 13; Matt. 5). If he has external means, charity gives them. If he does not, he gives benevolence, offers counsel, and gives assistance if he can. If he cannot, he helps at least by his wish or prays for the afflicted; and perhaps this is more valuable than if he were to extend bread. Good will cannot be idle.

The poor themselves provide one another with the benefit of good will. You see a blind man led by one who can see: because he has no money to give, he lends his eyes to one who lacks them. Why did this happen except because good will is a virtue, the treasure of the poor? Whoever has compassion and gives will receive a good reward. For it follows:

**22. For those who bless him will inherit the land.** Those who live well and, with thanksgiving, give to others whatever good they can give are the ones who bless the Lord. To such people he will say at the judgment: **Come, you blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world** (Matt. 25). Behold that land which the righteous will inherit. Why? **For I was hungry, and you gave me food** (ibid.). He will then begin to recount the works of mercy by which the righteous blessed the Lord, when they fulfilled those works for his honor.

**But those who curse him will perish.** For they will hear: **Go, you accursed, into the eternal fire** (ibid.). They refused to repay what they had received as a loan. And because by living badly and unjustly retaining what had been entrusted to them they cursed the Lord, they themselves are justly cursed.

And so that each person may know toward what he ought to strive, lest he likewise perish, it follows:

**23. The steps of a person will be directed by the Lord, and he will desire his way.** For within himself a person finds nothing but error and sin. Therefore the Lord himself has become our guide and our way (John 14). And if we do not wish to go astray, let us direct the steps of our good works toward him. Let our will be in him, who is the way, the truth, and the life (ibid.).

Do not wish to go by another way than the one by which he himself went. It may seem hard, but it is safe. Another way may perhaps have pleasures, but it is full of robbers. It is better now to wish to hold to the way of the Lord by fasting, praying, and suffering, so that afterward we may rejoice in the homeland, than to wish to hold to the way of the world by laughing, seeking pleasure, and following the flesh, so that afterward we may mourn in eternal punishment.

And because even on this way of the Lord there is no one who does not sin (3 Kings 8), consolation follows when it is added:

**24. When he falls, he will not be shattered, because the Lord supports him with his hand.** Peter fell (Luke 22), but he was not shattered. For the Lord placed his hand beneath him and raised him up by the help of his mercy. For it is written: **The Lord looked upon Peter, and he wept bitterly** (ibid.).

But why? The Lord permitted his chosen one to fall so that in temptation he might learn about himself, since before temptation he had presumed upon himself. The Lord does not cease to do this daily in his chosen ones. A person would think himself possessed of great strength if he always remained fixed in virtue. Therefore the Lord mercifully sometimes withdraws his grace and shows the presumptuous person how he may become weak. When he slips in temptation, he is wisely instructed through that same temptation. For when he falls while being tested, he rises afterward more truly because more humbly. And from the point where virtue seems to be lost, it is possessed more securely.

He proves that the righteous person will not be shattered when he adds:

**25. I was young, and indeed I have grown old; and I have not seen the righteous abandoned, nor his seed seeking bread.** Here the body of Christ speaks as one person: he was young in the first ages but old in the final times. Throughout so long a span he has not seen the righteous abandoned so that he would perish, nor his seed—that is, any believer summoned by him—seeking bread.

If we take this as referring to bodily bread, we find many righteous people who seek it. The statement would then not be true according to the literal sense. We must therefore understand spiritual bread, namely that of which the Lord says in the Gospel: **A person does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God** (Matt. 4).

The Lord has never ceased to distribute this bread to his faithful, both in the first ages and in the last: speaking to them through angels, patriarchs, and prophets; then through his Son (Heb. 1), through the Apostles, and through teachers, to refresh and strengthen their hearts so that they may not fail on the way. The righteous person is nourished by such bread, so that he may live in God and give to his neighbors whatever good he can. Hence it also follows:

**26. All day long he has compassion and lends.** This has already been explained. He rightly said “lends,” because he expects what he dispenses to be returned to him not by the poor but by God. Hence he immediately adds:

**And his seed will be in blessing.** The seed of the righteous is good works, concerning which the Apostle says: **In doing good, let us not grow weary, for in due time we shall reap** (Gal. 6). Therefore, while we have time, he says, **let us do good to all**. And again: **Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly; and whoever sows in blessings will also reap from blessings** (2 Cor. 9).

Hence it is said elsewhere: **Going forth, they went and wept, casting their seeds** (Ps. 125). We have heard of the seed; let us hear the future blessing of this seed: **But coming, they will come with exultation, carrying their sheaves** (ibid.). See therefore what follows, and do not be lazy.

**27. Turn away from evil and do good.** Turn away from sin, flee the devil, follow what is good, **and inhabit the age of ages.** Where? In the Church, in unity, in truth, in God, and in right judgment.

**28. For the Lord loves judgment**, that is, discernment, by which good is separated from evil, false from true, and temporal from eternal. **And he will not abandon his saints**, whom he chastises for a time. **They will be preserved forever.** “I,” says the Lord, “rebuke and chastise those whom I love” (Prov. 3).

Hence Paul says: **All discipline at the present time does not seem to be joy but sorrow; afterward, however, it will yield the most peaceful fruit of righteousness to those exercised by it** (Heb. 12). Therefore holy men are chastised for a time and, like grains on the threshing floor amid the chaff, are threshed (Matt. 5), so that afterward, once purified, they may be stored in the eternal granary.

**But the unjust will be punished**, that is, eternally condemned. **And the seed of the wicked will perish**, that is, their work will bear no fruit. Therefore at the judgment they will say: **What did pride profit us? Or what did the boasting of riches contribute to us?** All those things passed away like a shadow.

In every direction this prophetic Scripture surrounds our weakness. Now it instructs us with words; now it shapes us by examples. Here it sets before us the punishment of the reprobate, there the glory of the righteous, so that the former may terrify us and restrain us from love of this world, while the latter may stir us up and invite us to love the heavenly homeland. Hence it also follows:

**29. But the righteous will inherit the land of the living.** And not for a time, but forever. Therefore it adds: **And they will inhabit it for age upon age.** “Upon” is rightly said, because they will be its possessors and lords.

Do not therefore love this transitory inheritance, in which you cannot dwell for long. Everything that passes away is to be despised; only that which cannot pass away is to be loved. Its way is wisdom, concerning which it follows:

**30. The mouth of the righteous will meditate wisdom.** The mouth of the inner person is our heart. Just as we speak with our bodily mouth to human beings, so we speak with our heart to God. All spiritual progress proceeds from meditation; this is the bread of which we spoke above.

See therefore (according to Augustine, sermon 3) how willingly the righteous person eats, how he turns wisdom over and chews it again in his heart, so that afterward he may pour forth a good word (Ps. 44). Hence it adds: **And his tongue will speak judgment.** To speak judgment is to utter a discerning word. First the righteous person considers within his heart what he ought to say and what he ought to keep silent about; when he is silent about what should be silent and says what should be said, his tongue speaks judgment.

He shows that the wisdom which the righteous person meditates is not worldly but divine when he adds:

**31. The law of his God is in his heart.** The reprobate also sometimes possess the law of God, but only in their mouth, not in their heart. They utter God’s words but do not love them; by praising them they magnify them, but by living they trample them. In contrast, because the righteous person loves the word of God by meditating upon it and fulfills it by loving it, it is rightly said: **The law of his God is in his heart.**

And what benefit does it bring him? The text continues: **And his steps will not be supplanted.** The word of God in the heart frees one from every temptation. Hence it is said elsewhere: **I have hidden your words in my heart, so that I may not sin against you** (Ps. 118). God is with the one whose word does not depart from him. What harm, then, can be suffered by one whom God guards? For see what follows:

32. The sinner considers the righteous man, in order to trip him up (Ex. eod., ibid.) and distort his steps. He says what was foretold in the Book of Wisdom: “He is grievous for us even to look upon, because his life is unlike that of others” (Wis. 2). And therefore he seeks to put him to death. The wicked man seeks to kill the good man in two ways. [Col. 0782D] First, he seeks to make him consent, and thus kill him in soul. Then, if he does not consent, he seeks to kill him in body. But what follows?

33. “But the Lord will not abandon him into his hands.” The Lord would abandon his righteous man into the hands of the wicked if he caused him to consent to the wicked man. But he does not abandon his righteous man there; rather, he brings forth from captured flesh an unconquered soul. And although the man is scourged and killed outwardly, he is nevertheless always guarded inwardly. “Nor will he condemn him when judgment is passed upon him”—that is, when judgment is rendered concerning him. For “we shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that there each one may receive what he has done through the body, whether good or evil” (2 Cor. 5). When, therefore, that judgment has come, and the Lord has heard the case of his righteous man, he will no longer condemn him, even if he now appears to be condemned by human beings.

34. “Wait, therefore, for the Lord,” who will vindicate you, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay, says the Lord” (Rom. 12). “And keep his way”—that is, observe his commandments. “And he will exalt you”—from vices to virtues, from earthly things to heavenly things—“so that you may inherit the land,” namely, that which no one will be able to take away from you. “When sinners have perished, you will see.”

But what glory will there be for the righteous man because he will see the sinner perish? When he now sees someone erring and perishing, does he not usually grieve and groan out of compassion? But then, joined to the justice of his Creator, he will be constrained by such uprightness that no compassion for the reprobate will move him. The righteous, therefore, will see the punishments of sinners “and will rejoice” (Ps. 57), because they themselves will not be such.

Here it must be understood that almighty God would never have created those whom he foreknew would perish eternally, unless he had foreseen that he would derive some good use from them. Their iniquity now benefits the good by increasing their holiness; in the same way, the punishment of the wicked will benefit those same righteous people by increasing their blessedness. For from the condemnation of the reprobate, the elect will learn what they have merited through justice, because from their own salvation they will perceive what they have received through grace. And they will cling to divine goodness with a love all the more ardent, since by its gratuitous gift they will not undergo the punishment they have deserved and will receive unmerited glory.

Then he shows how entirely fleeting the prosperity of the wicked is when he adds:

35. “I saw the wicked man exalted above measure and raised up like the cedars of Lebanon.” [Verse 36.] Then I passed by, and behold, he was no more; I sought him, and his place was not found.”

The wicked man appears exalted above measure and raised up like the cedar of Lebanon when, swollen with pride in his heart and surpassing even the mighty of this world in power and glory, he is seen lifted up. But if you pass beyond this in your mind and carefully consider what is to come, you will see with the eyes of faith that the glory or power of the wicked man is nothing, even when it appears to be something. His place likewise is not found when the condition of his present life is reckoned as nothing.

This happens continually. For now we see some people flourishing in honors and riches, and behold, as if in passing and in a moment, we see those same people perish. Hence we say: “Where is that man? Where is such glory, such wealth, such power?” And we groan, saying: “Alas, man is nothing.”

But it belongs to the imperfect to despise the glory of one who is dying only at the moment of death. Even then, those who followed and loved that glory to the end disparage it. They would act more rightly if, when they saw a man in glory, they then considered his death and recognized that his passing power was nothing. Human exaltation must be considered as to how nothing it is when it raises itself above others through its successes.

37. “Therefore keep innocence and observe equity, because there is posterity for the peaceful man.”

True innocence is that which harms neither oneself nor another. This is the soul’s treasure, which the enemy is always striving to take away. Hence he persuades us to pursue earthly things, love present glory, and serve the pleasures of the flesh.

“Equity” means the divine utterances, according to what is written: “What you do not want done to you, do not do to another” (Tob. 4); and, “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do also to them” (Luke 6). They are called equity because they proclaim that good things are repaid to the good and evil things to the evil.

To keep innocence is to preserve oneself unstained by vices and sins. He observes equity who carefully weighs both what he has received from the Lord and what he ought to repay to him. Whoever does this is himself the peaceful man, whose posterity will be incorruption, immortality, and eternal life.

38. “But the unjust will perish,” because they will be destroyed in body and soul. “The posterity of the wicked will likewise perish.” As it is said elsewhere in the Psalm: “When a man becomes rich, and the glory of his house is multiplied, when he enters, he will not take it with him,” and so forth (Ps. 48). The posterity of the wicked will therefore perish, because the riches they loved will no longer exist.
