39. “But the salvation of the righteous is from the Lord.” The first salvation, which concerns the soul and which the righteous receive from the Lord, is the forgiveness of sins through the grace of faith. Hence they are also righteous, because “the righteous man lives by faith” (Rom. 1).

But because this salvation is not yet perfect, and the righteous man is still endangered in tribulations (Heb. 10), it is rightly added: “And he is their protector in the time of tribulation.” For if divine power did not protect its faithful, who could have endured so many darts of temptations or such great heats of vice?

40. “And the Lord will help them”—to fight and to do good works. “And he will deliver them”—from tribulations. “And he will rescue them from sinners,” when he leads them out of this life. “And he will save them,” with everlasting salvation. Why? “Because they have hoped in him.”

Consider, O soldier of Christ, how much your commander does for you. He is your salvation, your protection, your weapons, and your deliverance, so that here he may rule and guard you, and afterward lead you to eternal life.

## TITLE OF PSALM XXXVII

1. A Psalm of David, for the remembrance of the Sabbath.

This Psalm suits the prophet David, or another penitent, for the remembrance of eternal rest. For this is how “Sabbath” is interpreted: that is, “rest.” The subject of this Psalm is a penitent afflicted by many miseries and many pains on account of his sins.

At the beginning he seeks to win the judge’s goodwill. In the second part he recounts his misery and extreme abasement, where he says, “I have become wretched.” In the third part he shows that amid so many evils he never abandoned God, but always hoped in him and was prepared to endure still greater suffering. In the conclusion he introduces a certain exultation over the pardon he has obtained.

He intends to admonish us—not so that we may understand, as he did in another penitential Psalm, but so that we may now patiently endure whatever evils arise for the cleansing of sins—saying:

## PSALM XXXVII

2. “Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor correct me in your anger.”

“Fury” signifies the Lord’s vehement indignation, by which the reprobate will be accused in the judgment. Hence in his fury he will say to them—after they have first been terrifyingly rebuked concerning the good works they neglected to do—“Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire” (Matt. 25).

Those who are not now softened to repentance during the time of mercy will be accused in this fury. “Anger” may be understood as the examination by the fire of purgatory, in which those who now build fruitlessly upon Christ as their foundation will be corrected. They will suffer loss, but they will be saved—yet as through fire (1 Cor. 3). That fire, however, will be more severe than anything a human being can endure in this life.

This penitent therefore begs to be safe from that anger and fury, citing the many miseries by which he is already afflicted in this world, saying:

3. “For your arrows are fixed in me, and you have strengthened your hand over me.”

We are pierced as if by the Lord’s arrows when, because of sin, we are wounded by pains of body and soul inflicted by the Lord. The human soul is punished precisely where it found delight. The Lord strengthens his hand over us because the punishment for sin, with which he first struck the human being, still endures in the human race. He strengthened his hand over us to such an extent that he did not even spare his own Son (Rom. 8).

The first virtue is to avoid sins before they are committed. The second is at least to correct them once committed. But very often we not only fail to avoid impending faults; we do not even acknowledge those we have committed. The sinner’s mind grows darker in proportion as it fails to understand the harm caused by its blindness.

Hence, often through the generosity of divine grace, punishment follows fault, and scourges open the eyes of the delinquent, which security had blinded amid vices. The sluggish spirit is touched by a blow so that it may be awakened; thus the person who lost the state of his uprightness while secure may, once afflicted, consider where he lies. The very harshness of correction becomes the beginning of light. Hence it is added:

4. “There is no health in my flesh because of your anger.”

For, as Augustine says, we bear a mortal body full of temptations and anxieties, subject to bodily pains and necessities, changeable and weak, and in need of medicine. Food is the medicine of hunger; drink is the medicine of thirst; sleep is the medicine of fatigue. Take away these medicines, and those things that exist fail. But why do we suffer these things? We behold the face of God’s anger. “Face” is said on account of knowledge, because we usually recognize people by their faces. Through knowledge of God’s anger, knowledge of sin also comes.

Therefore he adds: “There is no peace in my bones because of my sins.” By “bones” the strong elements of the soul are understood. Behold: because of our sins, which are the cause of God’s anger, we suffer many things in the members of the body and many things in the powers of the soul. In the body, the human being lost health; in the soul, he lost peace. Because he did not wish to be in harmony with his Creator, he justly found discord within himself.

He had great peace with God when, in eternal light and without opposition from any affliction, he continually clung to him. But after sinning he merited God’s anger; immediately falling miserably from that blessed immutability and incurring the punishment of mortality and mutability, he lost peace, as we have said.

Behold: just as bones support flesh, so prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice support the mind. But now sluggishness creeps into that same mind, and prudence grows cold. For when it is weary and sluggish, it does not foresee what is to come. At another time pleasure creeps into the mind, and temperance grows cold: insofar as we are led toward delight in earthly things, we are less restrained from what is unlawful.

Sometimes fear insinuates itself into the heart and disturbs the strength of our fortitude. We are weaker against adversity insofar as we fear losing certain things that we have loved excessively. Sometimes, however, self-love intrudes upon the mind and, through hidden delay, turns it away from the uprightness of justice. The more it neglects to give itself wholly back to its Creator, the more it resists the law of justice within itself.

Folly also disturbs the soul’s wisdom, dullness its understanding, rashness its counsel, fear its fortitude, ignorance its knowledge, and pride its fear. Again, charity is disturbed in the heart by scourges, hope is shaken by fear, and faith is battered by questions. And because virtues are disturbed by vices and sins in countless ways, it is rightly said: “There is no peace in my bones because of my sins.”

Nor is this surprising:

5. “For my iniquities have risen above my head,” that is, they have prevailed over my mind, which is the head of the inner person. They are what take the mind captive under the law of sin and death (Rom. 7).

“And like a heavy burden, they have become heavy upon me.” No burden can be as heavy as iniquity; only those who desire to lay it down feel its weight. It does not seem heavy to the person who still delights in it. But the one who desires to lay it down and lift the mind toward heavenly things feels how heavy iniquity is.

It is raised with labor; it lies down willingly; by the weak it is scarcely raised, and yet, once raised, it immediately slips away. By laboriously conquering himself, he looks upon heavenly things; but weighed down by his own burden, he continually falls back into himself. Hence he adds:

6. “My scars have become fetid and corrupt because of my folly.”

This is said by way of comparison. For just as wounds first become putrid and afterward the flesh breaks open, so sins healed in baptism become putrid when they are renewed in the will. They become corrupt when we carry them out in action. This happens because of the face of our folly—that is, because of the folly that is present to us. For the more foolishly we act, the nearer we approach rottenness and corruption.

Therefore it is further added:

7. “I have become wretched and have been bowed down to the end.”

Previously I was blessed; now I have become wretched, bearing many miseries both in soul and in body. Previously I was upright as far as God; now I am bowed down to the end—that is, into sin—or “to the end,” that is, until death.

Hence the Apostle groans and says: “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7).

“All day long I went about sorrowful.” Having lost spiritual joy, this sorrow is generated by remembrance of the Sabbath. While the minds of the elect see that all transitory things are nothing, they seek to know for what they were created. And since nothing outside God is sufficient for them, they rest in him through hope and love. The more they contemplate heavenly things, the more they lament the misery they endure.

Hence this penitent further adds:

8. “For my loins are filled with illusions, and there is no health in my flesh.”

Let sorrow remain in us until our soul is stripped of illusions and our body is clothed with health. True health is immortality. He mentioned the loins because carnal pleasure is in the loins, from which illusions are generated.

But who can enumerate how many illusions fill the soul, and in how many ways? Because of those illusions, we can sometimes scarcely be permitted to pray. Thoughts often rush upon us that we do not seek. We want to go from one thought to another, and from that one to another; sometimes we want to return to what we were thinking and abandon what we are thinking, but cannot, and something else occurs to us. We want to remember what we had forgotten, but it does not come to mind; instead something else comes, which we did not want, and innumerable things that were not sought present themselves in its place.

I have said this so that you may understand what it means to lament the soul’s illusions. The soul received punishment in the form of illusion and lost truth. For just as illusion is the soul’s punishment, so truth is the soul’s reward.

9. “I am afflicted and humbled exceedingly; I roared because of the groaning of my heart.”

From affliction comes humiliation, and from humility proceeds groaning. The sinner is afflicted by punishments and scourges so that he may be humbled in every way because of his pride, so that the one who joyfully and arrogantly committed sin may return to lamentation, afflicted and humbled.

When he says, “I roared because of the groaning,” this is a sign of the most vehement pain: in the anxiety of his heart, the person emits from his groaning a kind of wild and intelligible roar. It should be noted that he does not say, “Because of the groaning of my flesh,” but, “Because of the groaning of my heart.”

Many people groan vehemently because of some temporal loss or inconvenience. But the servant of God roars from remembrance of the Sabbath, where the kingdom of God is, which “flesh and blood will not possess” (1 Cor. 15). Therefore he appropriately says, “I roared because of the groaning of my heart.”

This is clearly shown when he adds:

10. “Lord, all my desire is before you, and my groaning is not hidden from you.”

Let your desire be directed toward him, and “your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you” (Matt. 6). Observe what he says: “Before you,” as though he were saying, “I desire nothing except what pleases you.” For a perverse desire is not before God but against God.

If a good desire is present, groaning is also present. Even if it does not always reach human ears, it never departs from the ears of God. He commends this inward groaning when he adds:

11. “My heart is troubled.”

Why? “Because my strength has abandoned me”—namely, immortality, impassibility, innocence, and justice—“and the light of my eyes,” that is, the light of reason. “Even that which was natural to me is not with me.”

Or “the light of my eyes” is God himself. This light is not yet with me, but is present as though among those who see in hope. It is not yet that light of which it is said, “I will show him myself” (Ps. 90).

We possess some light because we are children of God (John 1), and certainly we hold this light by faith. But it is not yet the light that we shall see, for “it has not yet appeared what we shall be” (1 John 3). We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, when we see him as he is.

For now, it is the light of faith and the light of hope. As long as we are in the body, we are away from the Lord (2 Cor. 3). “For we walk by faith, not by sight.” And as long as we hope for what we do not see, “we wait for it with patience” (Rom. 8).

Amid these tribulations, let us now hear, for our consolation, the voices of our Head. Let our Head begin to shine in his Passion. He says:

12. “My friends and my neighbors approached and stood against me.”

As though he were saying: “Why do you complain? See me afflicted and crucified, bearing your sins, carrying the miseries of the world, and taking them away.”

This is what he says: “My friends”—that is, the Jews, who pretended to be my friends—and “my neighbors according to the flesh” (Matt. 1 and 15) “approached against me” with swords and clubs (Matt. 26 and 27) in order to hand me over, “and they stood,” persisting rigidly in their wickedness.

It is grievous to sin, but it is more grievous to persist stubbornly in sin. It should be noted that he does not say “enemies” or “strangers,” but “friends and neighbors.” The evils we suffer from friends are indeed more grievous than those we suffer from enemies. For it is not only the punishment inflicted by them that torments us; the loss of love also torments us.

“And those who were near me stood far away”—that is, the disciples, because after abandoning him they all fled (Matt. 26). “And they who sought my life used force.” They dragged him to judgment and death. “And those who sought evil for me spoke vanities.” For they bore false witness against him (Luke 22 and 23). “And all day long they meditated deceit”—what accusations they might bring against him before Pilate (Matt. 26).

But now let us hear the patience of our Redeemer:

[Col. 0787B] 13. “But I, like a deaf man, did not hear.” Hence one of them said: “Do you not hear how many things they testify against you?” (Luke 22). “And like a mute who does not open his mouth,” as it is written: “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and he did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53).

This was said according to his action. Although he possessed the capacity to hear and speak, he did not use it for vengeance. This pertains to his power, as follows:

14. “And I became like a man who does not hear”—that is, who is unable to hear—“and who has no rebukes in his mouth.”

That is, although I had the means by which I could rebuke them, I was nevertheless as one who had none. What else is condemned in this than our pride? If it is even slightly provoked, it returns sharper insults than it received. It does what evil it can and threatens what it cannot do.

Behold: God receives insult and does not become angry; he does not answer with insulting words. And as though someone were saying to him, “Why did you not open your mouth?” he continues:

15. “For in you, Lord, I have hoped; you will hear me, Lord my God.”

Hence they also said: “He trusted in God; let him deliver him now, if he wants him” (Matt. 26). You easily overcome adversity if your hope is fixed in God. And if you are troubled for a time, the Lord your God will hear you at the appropriate time.

But how will he hear him? It follows:

16. “Because I said, ‘May my enemies never rejoice over me.’”

We, who are mere human beings, when we wish to obtain something, humbly entreat the Lord. But the Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2), because he is God from God, says that something should happen, and it happens. He prays when he wishes, on account of the weakness of the flesh; he commands when he wishes, by the power of his divinity.

But what did he say? “May my enemies never rejoice over me”—that is, rejoice over me as one defeated. For they would have rejoiced if he had not risen again. “And when my feet are shaken and seem to slip, they spoke great things against me in my Passion.”

For, casting off his yoke and holding him in contempt, they arrogantly said: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19). And they said many other things against him. Why?

17. “Because I am ready for scourges.”

Sometimes, as Augustine says, sinners in this life are scourged either not at all or only lightly, because their intention has already become hopeless. But those for whom eternal life is prepared must necessarily be scourged here, because this saying is true: “My son, do not grow weary of the discipline of the Lord, nor be exhausted when you are rebuked by him” (Prov. 3). “For whom the Lord loves, he corrects; he scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12; Rev. 5).

Therefore let my enemies not insult me or speak great things. If my Father scourges me, I am ready for scourges, because an inheritance is being prepared for me. Do you not want the scourge? Then no inheritance is given to you. Every son must be scourged. Indeed, every son is scourged, so much so that he did not even spare the one who had no sin (1 Pet. 2). “And my pain is always before me.”

Was he in pain because of the scourge? Far from it. Why, then? It follows:

18. “For I will declare my iniquity, and I will think upon my sin.”

Behold, as Augustine says, the source of pain: not the scourge, not the wound, not the medicine, but sin. For the scourge is medicine against sin.

Do not be secure when you have confessed your sin. This is not enough unless afterward you think about your sin. By confessing, you uncovered the wound; the priest, who is the physician of your soul, gave you the prescription for the medicine. He told you what to abstain from and what to apply to your wound. You must therefore think about your sin, retain it continually in your memory, do what you have heard, take care, and apply yourself so that you may be healed.

He thought about his sin who said: “For I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always against me” (Ps. 50). He was not yet secure, although he had heard from the prophet, “The Lord has taken away your sin from you” (2 Sam. 12). These words are spoken in our person, since we are sinners.

19. “But my enemies live.”

They are well off; they rejoice in the prosperity of the world, while I labor and roar from the groaning of my heart. “And they were strengthened against me”—that is, as Augustine explains, they gathered together and grew strong in order to oppress me. “And those who hated me unjustly were multiplied.”

Many enemies appeared during the Passion who had previously seemed to be friends. Christ loved them, but they hated him unjustly. It is unjust hatred to hate a friend. It is unjust hatred to hate the human being rather than the sin. This is the whole and great guilt of those people. For what harm could they do by persecuting one who was dying voluntarily, not under compulsion? Yet the hatred itself is the persecutor’s greatest crime.

20. “Those who repaid evil for good slandered me.”

And for no other reason than that I pursued goodness. They ought to have repaid good for so many benefits; not only did they fail to do so, but they returned evil for good. They harmed him not only by deed but also slandered him by word.

For this reason he prays and says:

21. “Do not abandon me, Lord my God”—that is, do not permit me to fall into temptation. “Do not depart from me”—do not, by the absence of your grace, allow me to perish. This is said in our person.

22. “Attend to my help”—that is, turn your attention to me so that you may help me to do good—“Lord, God of my salvation,” my ruler, my Creator, and the author of my salvation.

## TITLE OF PSALM XXXVIII

1. For the end; a song for Jeduthun, of David.

As Augustine says, the words of a certain person called Jeduthun are to be awaited and heard. And if each one of us is able to become Jeduthun in what he sings, he discovers and hears himself. For “Jeduthun” is interpreted as “one who leaps over them.”

If someone who leaps over them has sung, let him rejoice that he is what he has sung. If someone still clinging to the earth has sung, let him desire and strive to become what he has sung.

It is called a song because it contains spiritual joyfulness. For it teaches us in mind to leap from earthly things to heavenly things. It sends us “to the end,” that is, to Christ.

Its subject is that one who leaps over and is perfect: having set aside every worldly pleasure, he longs only for heavenly things. Such a person has been perfected by God so that he completely restrains even his tongue from sin.

He arranges the Psalm in parts as follows. In the first part, the one who leaps over shows that he is silent toward the world—that is, toward wicked people who oppress him, try to criticize his words, and speak about him. In the second part, he compares these worldly things with heavenly ones, showing that the former are vain and the latter worthy of desire. In the third part, he offers a prayer that he may be freed from evils and able to obtain heavenly things.

His intention is to admonish the righteous, so that, setting aside worldly things, they may pass over to heavenly things.

## PSALM XXXVIII

2. “I said, ‘I will guard my ways, so that I may not sin with my tongue.’”

Our ways toward the Lord are our actions and our words. By speaking well and acting rightly, we advance toward eternal things. And because the holy man had already guarded the ways of wrongful action, he also decided to guard the ways of unlawful speech. For “the man who does not offend in word is a perfect man” (James 3).

Hence Solomon says: “He who guards his tongue guards his soul” (Prov. 21). “I said,” I mean, “and I did it.” For it follows: “I placed a guard over my mouth.”

When? When some pious, religious, and holy person was present? Certainly not. Such people, as Augustine says, hear in such a way that they praise what they approve; but, amid the many things they perhaps praise, they grant pardon to what they do not praise rather than prepare calumny.

When, then? When a sinner stood against me. A proud sinner stands out through a certain particular awareness of himself. An envious person hears the one who leaps over, catches at his words, and sets snares. It is difficult for him not to find something that was not said precisely as it ought to have been; and he does not forgive even while listening, but slanders out of envy.

With such people it is better to remain silent than to say anything. For what can one say to turbulent, slanderous, contentious people? Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast your pearls before swine” (Matt. 7).

How, then, he placed a guard over his mouth, he indicates when he adds:

3. “I was mute, and I was humbled, and I kept silent from good things.”

After saying “I was mute,” he rightly immediately adds, “and I was humbled,” so that we may understand that the righteous man became mute not out of anger or indignation, but solely out of humility. He kept silent from good things so that he would not sin in evil things.

“And from this,” he says, “my pain was renewed.” For, as Augustine explains, I had seemed to find rest in silence from a certain pain that slanderers and critics had inflicted on me, and that pain caused by their slanders had ceased. But my pain was renewed because I began to grieve more over having kept silent about what I ought to have said than I had grieved over having said what I ought not to have said.

And therefore:

4. “My heart grew hot within me.”

My heart began to be restless. I saw foolish people and wasted away. I did not rebuke them, and while I remained silent, zeal for your house consumed me (Ps. 68; John 2).

And lest we think this heat was slight, he immediately adds: “And in my meditation the fire will burn.”

By saying not “the fire burned” but “the fire will burn,” he shows that the fire grows more and more through silence. It is as though he were saying: “The longer I remain silent, the more fiercely the fire will burn.”

Placed in this uncertainty between speaking and remaining silent, among those ready to slander and those eager to be instructed, endangered lest he cast pearls before swine and endangered lest he fail to distribute food to his fellow servants, he sought another and better place. Sighing toward an end where he would no longer have to endure these things, he said:

5. “I spoke with my tongue.”

But why does he speak with his tongue to one who knows his thoughts? Perhaps he speaks with his tongue so that, through his speech, the lives of his hearers may be instructed.

He therefore says: “Make known to me, Lord, my end.”

Since he already knew the ways in which he walked and guarded them as best he could so that he would not stumble, he also wished to know the end toward which he ought to move, lest, running into uncertainty, he be able to go astray.

The Apostle shows us the end of our way when he says: “The end of the law is Christ, for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 16). Christ is the end of our work and the reward of our labor. We move toward him; beyond him there is nowhere further for us to go. For he is the highest good and supreme blessedness.

Whoever does not know this end does not move toward it. Even if he appears to live rightly, he runs in vain.

He asks to know not only the certain end but also the true life when he adds: “And make known to me what is the number of my days.”

Why? So that I may know what is lacking in me. These days do not truly exist. They depart almost before they arrive; and when they arrive, they cannot stand. They press upon one another, follow one another, and do not hold together. Nothing past is recalled; what is future is awaited only to pass away. It is not possessed while it has not come; it is not held once it has come.

The number of days, then, is the very infinity of eternity, which truly exists because it cannot pass away. It is not called “the number of days” because it is so in reality, but because we designate long stretches of time by a plurality of days according to our capacity. He improperly wished to call the infinite expanse of eternity “the number of days.”

He rightly desires to know these things first, so that afterward he may know what is lacking in him. For we cannot fully know what is lacking in us in temporal things unless, with the Lord revealing them, we first recognize the eternal goods that we have lost.

Therefore the reprobate cannot discover what is lacking in them, because they succumb through love to earthly things. Since they do not lift their hearts toward what endures, they think exile is their homeland, darkness is light, and motion is stability. Those who do not know greater things cannot judge lesser things.

By contrast, when the servant of God lifts his heart to heavenly things, he weighs the deficiency of temporality more accurately by considering eternity. Hence, as one who knows his end and “the number of days,” he attends to the things that pass away and says:

6. “Behold, you have made my days measurable”—that is, not eternal but subject to decline. Everyone lives within a certain measure.

“And my substance”—not the renewal that Christ accomplished, but the bodily essence that we drew from Adam—“as nothing before you.”

Some people appear great in their own eyes, concerning whom it is written: “Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes” (Isa. 3). But before God they are nothing, as the Apostle testifies: “If anyone thinks he is something when he is nothing, he deceives himself” (Gal. 5).

Nor is such a person great because of this. Inflation and swelling imitate greatness but do not possess health.

The first human being was handed over in such a condition that, through the increase of time, his life could only be extended, not unfolded into perfection. But because he voluntarily fell into guilt when he touched what was forbidden, he endured decline.

Therefore this holy man now sees his days as transitory and recognizes that he is nothing but dust. Hence he adds:

“Nevertheless, every living human being is complete vanity.”

I have now passed beyond all mortal things. I have ascended to delight in God’s law. I desired an end, as Augustine says, that has no end, and “the number of days,” and I long for what remains within it.

Nevertheless, as long as I live temporally, as long as human life upon earth is a time of temptation (Job 7), and as long as human nature, both in body and in soul, is subject to decline, “every living human being is complete vanity.”

For everything in the human being, both inwardly and outwardly, undergoes diminution or mutability. Everything, I say—the human being who remains, the one who leaps over, and even Jeduthun himself, as long as he lives here—is subject to universal vanity.

Hence Solomon says: “I saw all the things that are done under the sun, and behold, all is vanity” (Eccl. 1). Hence it is also added:

7. Nevertheless, man passes by in an image, and yet is troubled in vain. Although he bears the image of God, he not only passes, but passes away. To pass is, at every moment, to tend toward the end; to pass away is to bring life to its end by dying. Nor does he suffer only these things: he is also troubled in vain by earthly concerns. Hence it is added:

“He amasses treasure, and does not know for whom he will gather it” [Col. 0790D].

This is a vanity still more grievous to lament: when man fell away from love of his Creator, he immediately clung to worldly love and worldly striving, to such an extent that he willingly endures his exile; unwillingly departs; and, deprived by blind desire, gathers treasures, yet does not know for whom he gathers them. Hence it was said to a certain man: “Fool, this night they will demand your soul from you. Whose will those things be which you have prepared?” (Luke 12).

Do you wish to possess what God possesses and not lose it? I will show you a safe place. Hear the Lord in the Gospel: “Store up treasures for yourselves in heaven, where thieves do not break in and steal, nor rust or moth destroy” (Matthew 6). But then, you say, how do I place them in heaven? Place them in the hands of the poor (Luke 11); give to those in need. Hear and do what this man who passes away adds:

8. “And now, what is my expectation? Is it not the Lord?” Since everything here passes away and nothing is now held as certain or secure—that is, in this vanity, in this pilgrimage, while I am still unable to possess—what should I do except await God? And turning to the one whom he awaits and loves, he says to him in familiar and ancient speech: “And my substance is with you.”

Whoever distributes all that he has for God’s sake, or spends what he retains in God’s honor, and desires nothing whatsoever apart from God, has his substance with the Lord. After despising worldly things, he asks forgiveness of sins when he adds:

9. “Deliver me from all my iniquities.” From all, I say: from those of thought, speech, and deed; from hidden sins as well as from those of others; from venial as well as grave sins.

And because I despise earthly things, because I do not wish to rejoice in what passes away, because I seek humility and poverty, and desire only invisible things, “You have made me a reproach to the foolish.”

Hence the Apostle says: “We have become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to human beings” (1 Corinthians 4). “On the right and on the left we have weapons with which we fight: through glory and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute, as deceivers and yet truthful” (2 Corinthians 6). Elsewhere the Psalmist says: “We have been filled exceedingly with contempt” (Psalm 122). “Our soul has been exceedingly filled: reproach to the rich, and contempt to the proud.”

Placed amid these reproaches, the holy man reveals his patience to us when he adds:

10. “I was silent and did not open my mouth.” I did not answer them a word, nor did I murmur against you. Since he could have fallen silent first and spoken afterward, after saying “I was silent” he immediately added, “and I did not open my mouth,” to show the long-suffering of his silence.

Then he asks for mercy and healing, first giving the reason, when he adds:

11. “Because you made me: remove your scourges from me.”

What are these scourges with which almighty God has struck sinful humanity, except corruption, susceptibility to suffering, and mortality? He desires to be healed of these scourges and restored to true health—that is, to impassibility and immortality. “And you ought to do this,” he says, “because you made me; or because you made those scourges, you ought to remove them from me.” For just as it belongs to you to strike the sinner in justice, so it belongs to you to spare in mercy. You are not only just, but also merciful.

He shows how greatly afflicted he is when he adds:

12. “By the force of your hand I have failed under your rebukes.”

The force of God’s hand is the striking of the scourge. When he scourges us, we fall away from the rigidity of our pride. His blows are rebukes to us. For in striking us, he rebukes us because we have sinned.

Hence, commending the Lord’s justice and revealing our guilt, he adds [from Augustine]: “Because of iniquity you have corrected human beings.” [Note: The Augustinian reading is “Because of iniquity you corrected.”] Everything that I do, the fact that I am weak, the fact that I cry out from the depths—all of it is because of iniquity; and in this you have instructed humanity. Hear this more clearly from another psalm: “It is good for me, O God, that you have humbled me, so that I may learn your justifications” (Psalm 118). I have been humbled, and it is good for me: it is both punishment and grace.

Elsewhere it is said: “You fashion labor in the commandment”—that is, you shape labor so that the commandment may be labor for me. I say: remove it. And you must remove it, because I have failed—that is, I could not endure it—“by the force of your hand,” that is, by your powerful vengeance carried out in rebukes.

By saying “in rebukes,” he indicates that God exercises his vengeance for the purpose of drawing humanity back from sin. When I speak of your scourges or your strong hand, I do not accuse you; rather, I confess that I have iniquity, on account of which you have corrected me, a human being, through your disciplines.

Here God’s judgment and mercy are both indicated: judgment, in that he scourges because of iniquity; mercy, in that through correction he chastises like a father, so as to restore us to the way of truth. Hence he adds:

“And you have made his soul waste away like a spider.”

Consider that creature itself, how frail it is. Place it upon a finger: it is ruined. Nothing is more fragile than it. You have made the human soul like this, in order to instruct it because of its iniquity. The instruction of the just God has produced this weakness. There was a kind of strength in vice; by a certain strength humanity displeased God, so that it might be instructed through weakness. And because pride displeased him, humanity is instructed through humility, or weakness.

This verse can be applied both to the good and to the wicked. To the good, in this way: You corrected humanity so that it might mortify itself completely to the world, just as a spider mortifies itself in its work. The soul of the righteous wastes away like a spider when it is deprived of the fatness of carnal pleasure; when it disciplines the flesh through fasts and vigils and chastises the mind’s unlawful desires; when it strives to mortify itself against vices and desires, to make itself lean through virtues, and to weave, so that it may appear worthy of the heavenly bridegroom in a wedding garment.

Or, just as a spider draws out and consumes its inner parts in making a useless work, so the sinner foolishly expends the inner substance of his soul in the pursuit of earthly things. For the greedy person even holds his soul for sale.

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “What does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?” (Matthew 16). And therefore it is added:

“Nevertheless, every human being is troubled in vain.”

That is, every human being who lives according to the flesh is troubled uselessly while striving through desire to pursue earthly things.

Who, [asks Augustine,] is secure even concerning his own good? What is certain on this earth except death? Consider all the things of this life, whether good or evil, whether in justice itself or in iniquity itself: all are uncertain. You know what you are today; you do not know what you will be tomorrow. Are you poor? It is uncertain whether you will become rich. Are you uneducated? It is uncertain whether you will be instructed. Are you weak? It is uncertain whether you will recover. You were born? It is certain that you will die. Wherever you turn, everything is uncertain. Death alone is certain—and it alone is greatly feared, though it cannot in any way be avoided.

Therefore, whoever is troubled should cast his care upon the Lord and say what follows:

[Col. 0792C]

13. “Hear my prayer.” So that you may make my end known to me.

“And my supplication.” So that you may deliver me from all my iniquities.

And you ought to hear me, because I entreat you with devotion and tears. This is what he means when he says: “Listen attentively to my tears.”

The holier a person is, the more abundant are his tears in prayer. The merciful God listens to them when he receives them with mercy. If you wish to be heard by the Lord, pray with tears; crush your heart. No greater sacrifice can be offered to God than a contrite and humbled heart (Psalm 50). Where there are tears, there the divine fire is kindled.

It is often asked why God should be prayed to, and what need there is for prayer, since he knows what we need before we pray (Matthew 6). But we must pray for this reason: the concentration of prayer makes our heart tranquil and purifies it, making it more capable of receiving the divine gifts that are poured into us spiritually.

The merciful Lord offers us his grace and is always ready to give. We, however, are not always ready to receive, since we are inclined toward earthly things and held in darkness by desire for temporal possessions. Thus, in prayer, the heart is turned toward God, and through that turning we become purer and more worthy.

Hence it is further added: “Do not be silent, for I am a sojourner with you.”

For God speaks his hidden speech in the hearts of his faithful and pours into them the inspiration of his grace. Therefore elsewhere he asks, saying: “Say to my soul, ‘I am your salvation’” (Psalm 34). And again: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks within me,” and so forth (Psalm 84).

You ought not, therefore, to be silent toward me, “for I am a sojourner”: transferred from the city of Babylon, in which I was born through original sin (Psalm 50); remaining with you, serving you, and belonging to your household. Yet I am not still in your city. Therefore he adds:

“And a pilgrim, as all my fathers were pilgrims.”

That is, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and the others. For as long as we are in the body, we are pilgrims away from the Lord (Hebrews 13). We do not have a lasting city here, but we seek one that is to come in heaven.

What, then, remains? I must ask, since without doubt I am going to depart. He continues and says:

183 14. “Forgive me, so that I may be refreshed”—in my conscience, so that it may be relieved of the heat of anxiety over my sins—“before I depart” from this life; “and I shall be no more,” that is, it is not true that I will be, if I depart from here without my sins having first been forgiven.

## TITLE OF PSALM XXXIX

1. The title of the following psalm is, “A psalm of David, for the end.”

This psalm applies to David, that is, to Christ—namely, to the head and the members. Its subject is the transformation of the former sacrifice. In the first part he sets forth testimony concerning this renewal. In the second he introduces Christ himself abolishing the legal rites and confirming their renewal. In the final part he introduces Christ’s followers, that is, those who proclaim him.

He intends to persuade us that the legal institutions have already reached their end and that through Christ we must approach God: namely, that, leaving aside the superstitions of the Jews and the idolatry of the gentiles, we may approach the faith of Christ.

He therefore says:

## PSALM XXXIX

2. “With expectation I awaited the Lord, and he attended to me.”

As if he were saying: I awaited the Lord in such a way that every day I continued awaiting him; and because I persevered, the Lord attended to me—that is, for my benefit, by granting his grace. “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 24).

Hence the Prophet admonishes us, saying: “If he delays, await him, because when he comes, he will come” (Habakkuk 2).

But how the Lord attended to him, he explains when he adds:

3. “And he heard my prayers.”

In what way did he hear them? Hear what follows:

“And he brought me out of the pit of misery”—that is, from the certain depth of error which makes human beings miserable—

“and from the mire of filth”—that is, from the desires of the flesh, which make souls muddy before the Lord and lying at the bottom.

4. “And he set my feet upon a rock, and directed my steps.”

[Verse 5.] “And he put a new song into my mouth, a hymn to our God.”

The order of the words should be noted. First he is brought out of the mire of depravity, so that his feet may be made firm upon the rock through faith. But because right action must follow right faith, his steps are directed, so that after the direction of his steps—that is, the perfection of good works—he might also receive in his mouth the new song of proclamation.

While we are still lying in the confusion of weakness, the authority to proclaim should not yet be given to us. But when we rise through good works, when we have begun to stand upright, it is fitting that we should be sent to proclaim in order to win others.

It is also very important that after saying “song” he immediately added “hymn,” that is, praise to our God. There are some to whom the grace of teaching is given by the Lord, but who try to turn that same grace back toward their own glory. Such people indeed receive a song in their mouth, but they refuse to render a hymn—that is, praise—to the Lord our God for the grace they have received.

But because this holy man received the word of proclamation from the New Testament—namely, concerning the Lord’s incarnation, passion, resurrection, ascension, and the other matters pertaining to the new life and the new human being—and devoted all these things to the praise of almighty God, he rightly testified that not only was a new song put into his mouth, but also a hymn to our God.

Be a new human being; proclaim Christ—and thus you have sung a new song. Do not seek your own praise, but invoke the Lord while praising him—and thus you have uttered a hymn to our God. To proclaim faith in the Lord and, moreover, to praise him devoutly is to sing a song and hymn to our God.

And because the holy man saw that, after hearing this song and hymn, many would be converted to the faith, he immediately added:

“Many shall see, and fear, and hope in the Lord.”

Those who were blind and understood nothing about God were enlightened when they attended to and imitated the singers of the new song. Believers will therefore see; penitents will fear; those who desire heavenly things will hope.

After a person has been enlightened by faith, the first step toward God is fear, as it is written: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Psalm 110). And the more someone is humbled within himself through fear, the more he is raised up in God through hope. Raised by hope toward invisible goods, he begins to love heavenly things and despise earthly things (1 Corinthians 13).

Here are faith, hope, and charity, by which God is worshiped and the human person is made blessed. Hence it is added:

5. “Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord.”

The name of the Lord is Jesus, which is interpreted as “Savior” (Matthew 1; Luke 1). Blessed, therefore, is the one who hopes to be saved by Jesus.

“And he did not look toward vanities and false insanities,” so as to serve greed or worship idols. To desire earthly things is to look toward vanities. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “No one who looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9). Therefore in another psalm he prays, saying: “Turn my eyes away, lest they see vanity” (Psalm 118).

To worship idols, adore stones, and serve the creature rather than the Creator (Romans 1)—the one who made all things and orders all things by wise thought—is a great and false insanity.

Therefore, turning himself toward the Lord in faith and devotion, so that he might likewise turn the hearts of others toward him—those who look toward vanities and false insanities—he says:

6. “You have done many wonderful things, O Lord my God.”

For you made heaven and earth and all that is in them; and these things are yours—that is, subject to you and serving you.

“And in your thoughts”—by which you order all things—“there is none who is like you.” For “who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor?” (Romans 11).

These wonderful works of yours, both visible and invisible, and your incomprehensible wisdom, proclaim that you alone are to be worshiped, that you alone are to be loved and desired—not these vanities and false insanities.

“I proclaimed”—these things to those who did not know them.

“And I spoke”—to those who knew them. “I am a debtor both to the wise and to the foolish” (Romans 1).

Or: I proclaimed them earlier through the fathers, and in the last days I spoke through myself.

“They have multiplied beyond number.”

For many, having heard the proclamation, joined the fellowship of believers, though they are not among the number of the elect, as the Truth testifies when he says: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matthew 20). Believers therefore multiplied beyond the number of those predestined to life.

And because at the time when the faith was proclaimed the former sacrifice was also changed (Hebrews 7), this is shown when he adds:

7. “You did not desire sacrifice and offering, but you perfected ears for me.”

Behold how the holy man foresaw that the sacrifice would have to be changed and the law understood spiritually. This did not happen in his own times, but in ours. He foresaw it when the Holy Spirit revealed it.

We, however, as we heard, so we saw in the city of the Lord. Behold: the Lord did not desire sacrifice and offering as they had previously been customary. He himself became priest and sacrifice for us. He is the true Lamb of God who was sacrificed for us, who takes away the sins of the world.

The shadow has passed away; the Truth has appeared. The old things have passed away, and behold, all things have become new.

He perfected ears for us so that we might understand spiritually what we hear from the law. Christ was seeking these ears when he said: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke 8). He perfected ears for his disciples when he opened their understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures (Luke 24).

Or ears are perfected for us by God when we are made perfect in obeying him in all things. Hence it is written: “Obedience is better than sacrifices” (1 Samuel 15).

That people had perfected ears from the Lord concerning whom the Lord says elsewhere through the Psalmist: “The people whom I did not know served me” (Psalm 17); “at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me” (ibid.).

“You did not ask for burnt offering or sacrifice for sin” (Hebrews 10).

The difference between a burnt offering and a sacrifice is this: when some part of a victim was offered to God, it was called a sacrifice. A burnt offering, however, was entirely burned (Leviticus 1), namely, when the whole victim was consumed by fire in the sacrifice.

But the Lord requires neither the lesser nor the greater sacrifices of the old law, since what pleases him now is not the shadow but the truth; and indeed he did not ask for these things.

What, then, did he ask for? It follows, and he says:

8. “Then I said, ‘Behold, I come.’”

This is Christ’s voice in his own person: “Then”—that is, at the time when it seemed appropriate to me that the old things should be changed into the new—“I said, ‘Behold, I come’” (Hebrews 10), that is, I determined that my coming should take place in manifestation.

He draws testimony concerning this coming from Scripture when he turns to the Father and says:

“In the heading of the book it is written concerning me, ‘To do your will, my God, I desired it; and your law is in the midst of my heart.’”

In the first psalm of this book it is written: “That I may do your will,” that is, that I may fulfill the obedience imposed upon me by you. And thus it is written: “So I desired, O my God.” I have not come to do my own will, but the will of the one who sent me, the Father.

Observe what is written concerning Christ at the beginning of this book. There it says: “Blessed is the man who has not walked,” and so forth. Here, however, he says: “Behold, I come.” There it says: “But his will is in the law of the Lord”; here, however, he says: “To do your will.” There it says: “And he will meditate on the law of the Lord day and night”; here, however, he says: “And your law is in the midst of my heart.”

These statements are sufficiently equivalent. What is in the middle does not incline more toward one side than the other. Therefore, the one who has God’s law in the midst of his heart meditates on and keeps his commandments in such a way that he does not turn aside to the right or to the left (Deuteronomy 5).

The one who has God’s law in the midst of his heart is the one who loves the Lord God with all his heart, with all his soul, and with all his strength, and his neighbor as himself (Luke 10). Whoever is such a person is surely right not to cease proclaiming to others the justice that he himself possesses (Galatians 3).

Hence it is added:

10. “I proclaimed your justice in the great Church”—spread throughout the whole world.

I proclaimed that justice does not come from the legal institutions, but from you.

“Behold, I will not restrain my lips.” If some should wish to restrain me, I will not be silent.

Peter had lips so ready to proclaim justice when the rulers commanded him not to speak any further about Jesus. He himself answered courageously: “We must obey God rather than human beings” (Acts 4 and 5).

“And because my lips are ready to proclaim the truth, O Lord, you know.” For you are the knower of the heart and the witness of conscience. Whatever our lips may say, God always attends to our heart and judges us according to it.

We must therefore present ourselves in such a way that we may please the Lord our God both in heart and in lips. “With the heart,” says the Apostle, “one believes unto justice, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10).

Let your lips sound forth what is near to your heart, so that you may be able to invoke the Lord as the witness of your heart, saying: “Lord, you know.” For “our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Corinthians 1).

Hence it is added:

11. “I have not hidden your justice in my heart.”

As did that lazy servant who hid his talent in the earth (Matthew 25). Hence the Lord says to his disciples: “Whatever I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15).

Therefore he also commanded the Apostles not to carry a purse (Luke 9). For the one who hides divine words in his heart carries a purse.

In this passage, “justice” is understood as faith. “The just person lives by faith” (Romans 1). “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as justice” (Galatians 3).

Many have hidden this justice in their hearts through fear of death. Many still hide God’s justice, either because they fear punishment or because they fear loss. But those who fear neither punishment nor loss belong to those of whom it is said: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for justice, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5).

“Your truth and your salvation I have declared.” That is, I proclaimed Christ, who said of himself: “I am the Truth” (John 14), and concerning whom Simeon says: “My eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2). Elsewhere the Psalmist asks, saying: “Give us your salvation” (Psalm 84).

“I have not hidden your mercy and your truth from the great assembly.”

In assemblies and synagogues, before kings and governors, the holy Apostles and martyrs proclaimed the mercy and truth of Christ with great authority and boldness (Acts 5).

Do you wish to hear God’s mercy? Do penance, and your sins will be forgiven (Matthew 4). Do you wish to hear the truth? Hold fast to justice, and an eternal reward will be given to you (Ecclesiasticus 18).

Hear mercy and truth together: “Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matthew 4). Penance belongs to mercy; the kingdom of heaven belongs to truth. Mercy is proclaimed now; truth will be manifested afterward. Again, whoever now despises mercy will later experience truth strictly—not indeed unto glory, but unto punishment.

Then he turned his attention to the wounded members and prayed for them, saying:

12. “But you, O Lord, do not remove your mercies far from me”—that is, from those who are mine.

Consider sinners, and do not remove your mercies far from them. Whoever feels himself drawn away from the Lord by an evil life or evil will should say devoutly and tearfully: “But you, O Lord, do not remove your mercies far from me.”

I am wretched; you are merciful. My iniquities are many, but your mercies surpass them. “Your mercy and your truth have always received me.” I attend to you because you are merciful; I attend to you because you are truthful. I love the merciful one; I fear the truthful one. Thus love and fear lead me to you, because your mercy and truth have always received me. Therefore I pray: do not remove your mercies far from me.

13. “For evils without number have surrounded me.”

My sins are numberless; my negligences are infinite. They surround me on every side and obstruct me on every side. Let us say these things from the marrow of our hearts. Let us show our sufferings to our physician; let us humbly entreat him to receive us for healing.

Let no one consider himself just. For, as the Apostle testifies, “we all offend in many ways” (James 3). It belongs to us to cry out, groan, and confess—not to boast or glory in merits. And if there are any merits, “what do you have that you have not received?” (1 Corinthians 4).

It is rightly added:

“My iniquities have overtaken me, and I was unable to see.”

Our iniquities overtake us to such an extent that even if we wish to escape, we cannot do so without help. Hence elsewhere the Psalmist says: “The ropes of sinners have entangled me” (Psalm 118). Therefore he asks, saying: “Turn back our captivity, O Lord” (Psalm 125).

Having lost the light of truth, we have come into such great blindness that we do not know even ourselves. We commit evil and do not quickly recognize either what we are doing or what we have done. When the inner light has been excluded, the soul finds nothing in itself except darkness. It has lost the ability to see itself because it despised the vision of its Creator. From the loss of light grew the multiplication of iniquity.

Therefore he adds:

“They have multiplied beyond the hairs of my head.”

He refers to the hairs of the head as a measure of great number. Who counts the hairs? Much less does anyone count sins, which exceed the number of hairs.

You no longer kill, commit adultery, steal, or bear false witness, and so forth—such great sins. These are masses of sins. You have guarded against the great ones; what are you doing about the small ones? You have thrown off the mass; see that you are not buried beneath the sand.

But what follows is still much more grievous:

“And my heart has abandoned me.”

That is, the strength of my heart has failed, and it is not capable of knowing itself. Whenever we wander outward in our mind, delight in earthly things, abandon our proper pursuits, and either do, speak, or think what is empty—so often our heart abandons us.

Whenever we do not think about God or about the things that pertain to the salvation of souls, so often we lose our heart. Hence a certain wise man says: “Whenever you do not think about God, consider that time lost.”

The prayer that follows therefore comes appropriately:

14. “May it please you, O God, to deliver me, O Lord; look upon me to help me.”

He rightly says, “May it please you.” For God justifies a person not on the basis of merits, but solely by his good pleasure (Titus 3), solely by grace, solely by his goodness. The merciful Lord has mercy on us because it pleases him to do so, not because we have deserved it.

Therefore he says to his disciples: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15). And the Apostle says: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Corinthians 15).

Thus, commending grace, he humbly entreats the Lord to deliver him from the many and great evils he has described, and, by looking upon him mercifully, to help him in what is good.

Then he prays against persecutors, saying:

15. “Let those who seek my soul be confounded and put to shame together.”

What should they fear or reverence? The Lord, perhaps, or the punishment by which they are to be punished?

Many sought Christ’s soul, but he had power to lay down his soul and to take it up again. They rejoiced when he laid it down; they were confounded when he took it back.

Many still seek the body of Christ and seek to destroy souls (John 10). They will certainly either be confounded now, so that they blush at their evils, repent, and, fearing, show reverence; or afterward they will suffer eternal confusion, when it is said to them: “Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire” (Matthew 25).

Hence it is added:

“Let those who desire evil for me be turned backward and put to shame.”

Let those who were wrongly raised up through pride be turned backward through humility; let those who went ahead, dragging and killing, follow by obeying. Let them also be put to shame—that is, let them fear and honor God, though previously they blasphemed; and thus let them be converted from the evil will by which they persecuted me.

16. “Let them immediately bear their shame.”

That is, let them quickly return to repentance—

“those who say to me, ‘Good, good.’”

That is, “Well done, well done”: it is derisive praise.

In these three verses, note three kinds of persecutors. First he prays for those who seek his soul in order to take it away: these are to be understood as those who try to kill God’s servants through open persecution. Such were those who seized Jesus with swords and clubs and placed him on the cross (John 18).

Then he prays for those who desire evil for him (Matthew 26). These are to be understood as those who do not yet persecute openly, but carry hatred and hostility in their hearts. At times they use pretense and crafty arguments to deceive those whom they hate; at times they break loose into words of malice. Such were the Jews against the Lord (Matthew 12 and 22).

Afterward he prays for those who say to him, “Good, good.” These are those who customarily mock the religion and simplicity of the righteous. Such people were also present during Christ’s passion.

All of these persist in his body. But just as the Lord did not avenge himself upon them, but prayed for them (Luke 23; Hebrews 5), so we must not seek vengeance against our enemies, but offer a humble prayer, as he himself commanded, saying: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Matthew 5).

And as if someone were to ask, “With what benefit, with what reward?” he immediately adds: “So that you may be,” he says, “sons of your Father who is in heaven.”

And giving us an example from himself, he adds: “He makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust” (ibid.).

Consider how great an honor it is to be a son of God, if you patiently endure injuries from an enemy.

Then, turning to the Lord, he consoles and admonishes us, saying:

17. “Let all who seek you rejoice and be glad in you.”

Let all who seek you through faith and love rejoice in body and be glad in spirit—not in themselves, but in you, so that “whoever boasts may boast in the Lord.”

The Lord has promised us a twofold reward: the immortality of the body and the blessedness of the soul (2 Corinthians 10). Therefore we are commanded to rejoice with a twofold exultation, when it is said: “Let them rejoice and be glad.” Exultation pertains to the body; gladness to the soul.

The praise of the Lord is commended when it is added:

“And let those who love your salvation say always, ‘May the Lord be magnified.’”

For what should we praise, proclaim, and magnify so much as the God and Father of lights, from whom every good gift and every perfect gift comes (James 1)?

He brought our first fathers, who awaited him, out of the mire of filth and set them upon the firm rock, which is Christ (Ephesians 1). He gave them good works, taught them a new song, and through them enlightened others. He gave them fear and hope, drawing them away from false vanities. He increased them both in number and in virtue.

Then he sent the Son in the flesh, who would do his will and proclaim his justice in the great Church, along with his mercy, truth, and salvation, so that we might be freed from innumerable sins and enemies and rejoice and be glad in the Lord.

These are the reasons of the righteous, so that they may always say: “May the Lord be magnified.”

But who should say this? “Those who love,” he says, “your salvation”—that is, your Son, through whom eternal salvation has been given to us.

Whoever does not love our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 16) does not have beautiful praise in his mouth. Our praise before the Lord is commended only by affection and charity. What, indeed, should we love more than the one by whom we were created and saved?

Again he returns to consideration of the misery and poverty he suffers in this pilgrimage, and says:

18. “But I am a beggar and poor.”

But immediately consolation returns when he adds:

“The Lord is solicitous for me.”

Behold, we are the Lord’s beggars: we sit at the door of his mercy; we beg and cry out, “May your kingdom come,” “Give us our daily bread,” and “Deliver us from evil” (Matthew 6).

For we are poor; we have nothing from ourselves. Behold the great hope: “The Lord is solicitous for me.”

Someone established in the Lord’s service may say: “I am a beggar; I am poor; I have nothing from which to live.” Do not despair, poor ones of the Lord. Cast all your care upon him, because he cares for you.

And do not say: “What will we eat?” or “What will we wear?” for these are the things the gentiles think about. What, then, should be done? “Seek first the kingdom of God and his justice, and all these things will be added to you” (Matthew 6).

“The Lord,” says the poor man, “is solicitous for me.” Therefore, if the Lord is solicitous, let us also be secure.

But because he has awaited the Lord for a long time, he asks him when he adds:

“You are my helper and my protector, O my God; do not delay.”

I have awaited you, my Lord, with expectation. You have attended to me, granting many benefits; you are solicitous for me. In this life you have become my helper in good things and my protector in adversity. Your coming alone remains for me, my God; do not delay.

As long as I do not see you or possess you, I am a beggar and poor. Nothing apart from you is sufficient for me. You are my expectation; you are my salvation; do not delay. For one who desires and burns with longing, an hour’s delay is long. My God, do not delay.

## TITLE OF PSALM XL
1. The title of the following psalm is *For the end, a psalm of David*, since it has already been expounded often enough that it need not be repeated. Its subject is Christ, God and man: insulted according to his humanity, glorified according to his divinity. This psalm has three parts. In the first part, he admonishes us, with good promises, so that Christ may be understood to be God above man. In the second part, he sets forth the reasons why some regarded him simply as a man, because they saw him insulted in many ways. In the third part, he assures us that he was more than a man. His purpose is to admonish us that the mediator between God and human beings was simultaneously man and God (1 Tim. 2): for the glory of the passion of Christ, the emperor of martyrs, who did not spare himself, commanding his soldiers to battle, but fought first and conquered first, so that by his example he might encourage those who were fighting, aid them by his majesty, and crown them by his promise.

Let us hear (from Augustine) something in this psalm that pertains to his passion. We frequently emphasize what it is useful for us to retain: that the Lord Jesus Christ often speaks from himself—that is, from the person of himself, who is our head—and often from the person of his body, which is us and his Church. Yet he speaks as though the words sounded from the person of a single man [Note: Col. 0797. In Augustine, *ore* (“mouth”) is more correctly found in place of *persona*, and that word is said to be absent from the manuscripts, so that *persona* is understood], so that we may understand the head and the body to subsist in the unity of their integrity and not to be separated from one another, like that marriage of which it is said, “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2; Matt. 19). If, then, we recognize two in one flesh, let us recognize two in one voice. Let us hear, therefore, what is said.

## PSALM XL

2. **Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and the poor.**

That is, concerning Christ. To understand concerning the needy and the poor is to think something higher concerning Christ’s humanity and weakness. This, certainly, is what must be understood: that our Lord and Redeemer, although he was in the form of God, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings, and being found in appearance as a man (Phil. 2). Rich with the Father, he was poor among us. Yet his poverty is our riches; his weakness is our strength; his foolishness is our wisdom; his mortality is our immortality.

It must also be understood that the poverty and weakness of our Savior gave us an example of humility, patience, obedience, gentleness, and charity. To understand and ponder these things, to believe them and imitate them, is true blessedness. And as though someone were to ask, “What fruit will come from this understanding?” he continues and says:

**On the evil day the Lord will deliver him.**

That is, on the day of judgment, when the wicked are to be punished, the Lord will deliver him from every evil, from every punishment, from every tribulation and distress of this world, and from the power and torments of the devil and of hell; and he will transfer him into the freedom of the glory of the children of God (Rom. 8).

He recounts other benefits also, which the Lord bestows on the blessed man who understands, adding:

3. **May the Lord preserve him, give him life, make him blessed in the land, and not hand him over to the soul of his enemies.**

This prayer is a promise. The Lord preserves the one who understands this. Amid the dangers and temptations of this laborious life, he does not allow him to perish. He does not permit him to be tempted beyond what he can bear (1 Cor. 10). Whatever he does, wherever he turns, he is always in God’s keeping. The Lord gives him life by his Spirit, more and more according to the inner person (Eph. 3), so that each day he may live more justly and purely in God.

And he makes him blessed not only in heaven but also on earth, by bestowing spiritual virtues. As it is written: “Blessed are those who hope in you, Lord” (Ps. 38), and “blessed are those who love your name”; “blessed are the poor in spirit; blessed are the meek; blessed are the merciful; blessed are the peacemakers; blessed are the pure in heart,” and so forth (Matt. 5).

The Lord promises us blessedness in the life to come; but if we pay careful attention, even in this earthly life we already possess a portion of the reward. It is certainly a great part of happiness to have been able to despise the world and to have begun serving almighty God; to have escaped the most miserable domination of vices; to be free from the wretched slavery of the devil and sin (John 8); not to be tormented by desires for vain things; not to become entangled in crimes; to live innocently; to devote oneself to blessed chastity; to possess the sufficiency of glorious poverty; to seek nothing apart from God; and to rest sweetly in his love and contemplation.

Let us consider how much the Lord has bestowed upon us by his merciful calling, and from how many frauds, adulteries, robberies, perjuries, sacrileges, impurities, vices, and sins he has freed us. Then we shall recognize how true is what we hear in the psalm, where it says, “and make him blessed in the land.”

Although God sometimes hands this understanding person over to the hands of his enemies, so that they may have power to kill the body, he never hands him over to their souls (Matt. 10)—that is, to the wills of his enemies—so that they might make him obey their wicked wills. Hence the holy martyrs emerged victorious even in their sufferings: although they could be killed bodily, they could never be broken in spirit. Those who killed them, however, were defeated, because they were completely unable to accomplish what they wished.

For this reason, at the deaths of martyrs we do not weep but sing, because we rejoice in their triumph. We do not announce deaths but birthdays, because, happily reborn through martyrdom, they began to live blessedly in glory. Let it therefore rightly be said: “And do not hand him over to the soul of his enemies.”

Another great gift follows.

4. **May the Lord bring him help upon the bed of his pain.**

By the bed of pain is understood our flesh, which suffers in its weakness. Just as someone lies and rests on his bed, so a weak soul lies and rests in its flesh. For it delights in carnal pleasures. Human nature, simply because it was created in weakness, is always liable to fail and continually slides toward worse things, unless it is sustained by the help of divine grace.

The bed carried you; you did not carry the bed. You were an inward paralytic; there is one present who says to you, “Take up your bed and go to your house” (John 5).

And as though someone were to ask, “Why, then, when God brings us help, do we suffer so many evils in this life—so many labors and so much restlessness of flesh and of the world?” he turns to the Lord and, as though explaining to us the remedy’s prescription, adds:

**You have turned his entire bed in his weakness.**

By the bed he wishes the body together with the mind to be understood. He says “entire” according to all the senses, so that you may understand the weakened human being according to the flesh and according to the mind, both inwardly and outwardly.

The bed of the flesh is weakened by hunger, thirst, cold, heat, suffering, pain, corruption, mortality, and countless other means. The bed of the mind is weakened by ignorance, foolishness, dullness, fear, pride, vainglory, envy, anger, and many other things. This weakness is the punishment of sin. Because the human being did not wish to be strong in God, he is weak in himself. Because he delighted in flesh and spirit, he has been punished in flesh and spirit.

Let it therefore be said: “You have turned his entire bed in his weakness.” For this reason he is still left in this weakness even when the original sin, on account of which he was punished, has been forgiven: so that he may not again become proud and be able to forget the fault he committed. He is a wicked servant; he must always be held beneath the whip. But now, having been scourged, he asks for mercy and asks for healing; he returns from pride to humility. He confesses his sin, saying:

5. **I said, ‘God, have mercy on me; heal my soul, because I have sinned against you.’**

“I said,” he says. I did not hide my sins; I did not keep silent about confession, as someone kept silent and therefore his bones grew old (Ps. 34). For the one who does not disclose the evil he has done also loses the virtues he possesses. It is a mark of true humility to acknowledge one’s fault and to disclose it through the voice of confession.

Therefore our Lord commands us to confess our sins to priests (Luke 15), so that by confessing we may be humbled and, through the merit of humility, receive the remission of sins. For “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4).

Great is the fruit of confession. A certain penitent says in another psalm, “I said, ‘I will confess,’ and you forgave the wickedness of my sin” (Ps. 13). Consider how swift God’s mercy is toward the confessing person. He has not yet confessed, but has resolved in his heart to confess; therefore he is cleansed from sin. This is signified by what the Lord commands the lepers: “Go, show yourselves to the priests.” And as they went, they were healed (Luke 17).

What does the tax collector say? “God, be merciful to me, a sinner.” He went down justified (Luke 18). O blessed confession! How many are cleansed, healed, and justified through you!

Therefore let each one of us say humbly, say tearfully, say with affection, say from the heart:

“I said, ‘God, have mercy on me; heal my soul, because I have sinned against you.’”

What does “I have sinned against you” mean? I have sinned before you, or against you. What does “I have sinned against you” mean? I will have to render an account to you for my sin. Such things are said by friends when they confess. Let us hear what enemies said when they went astray.

6. **My enemies spoke evil to me.**

These words properly pertain to the head, as though he were saying: “I came as the mediator between God and human beings” (1 Tim. 2). But the enemies, paying no attention to this and believing me to be only a man and not God, spoke these evils to me—that is, about me: **“When will he die, and his name perish?”**

For they wished him to die and his name to be erased from the earth (Jer. 11). Christ died, and his name became wonderful. The grain of wheat, falling into the earth, died, and from it was multiplied still more (John 12). Thus Christ’s body, too, is accustomed to grow through tribulation.

The Jewish enemies were saying, “When will he die? When shall we be able to kill him? And thus his name will perish”—that is, his reputation.

He also makes mention of his betrayer Judas, who was the head of the enemies, when he adds:

7. **And if he entered to see, he spoke emptiness; his heart gathered iniquity for himself.**

He entered like a fraud, like an investigator, like an ambusher—not to imitate but to see what he could criticize, what he could accuse, what he could slander. His heart was devising Christ’s death, and thus he was gathering iniquity for himself. It would have been better for him if that man had not been born (Matt. 26).

What the head suffered, the members also suffer. “If they persecuted me,” he says, “they will also persecute you” (John 15). The Apostle says, “Because of the false brothers who slipped in, who entered secretly to spy on our freedom” (Gal. 2).

These are hypocrites, wicked pretenders, joining themselves with feigned charity, watching all the movements and all the words of the holy, seeking snares in everything. Many such people are found within the fellowship of the brethren. Abandoning spiritual pursuits and growing sluggish through idleness, they daily desire to hear, see, and speak vanity. They spend the entire day in gossip, curiosity, and foolishness. Subjugating their minds to depraved desires and unlawful thoughts, they gather iniquity for themselves—that is, to their own detriment.

They gathered it for themselves, not for me, just as Judas gathered it for himself, not for Christ. **He went out and spoke the same thing.** He went out to the Jews (Matt. 16) and spoke the same thing—that is, with one plan and one conspiracy. The Apostle says of such people: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2).

Whether they are inside or outside, they always speak what belongs to vanity, and they always gather iniquity and damnation for themselves. Many are inside in body but outside in heart, as it is said of certain Israelites, that “in their hearts they turned back to Egypt” (Exod. 16). And elsewhere someone says in a psalm, “And my heart abandoned me” (Ps. 39).

Whoever wanders in mind and thinks about empty things goes out. If our heart delightfully meditates on what is useless and vain, our tongue also gladly speaks the same thing. Do you wish to know what sort of heart your brother has? Pay attention to what he speaks about most willingly. “For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (Matt. 12). “The good man out of the good treasure of his heart brings forth good things, and the evil man out of the evil treasure brings forth evil things” (ibid.).

Let us guard our entrance, brothers; let us remain inside, and let us draw great edification for ourselves from these words. Earlier he said, “He entered,” but he did not say “in order to act”; he said “in order to see.” The wandering of the eyes and curiosity are already being marked—vices that are especially accustomed to harm those who have entered religious life.

Hear of another vice: **He spoke emptiness.**

Hear of a third: **His heart gathered iniquity for himself.**

“Perverse thoughts separate from God” (Wis. 1). These are the three pursuits of idle people in the cloister: wandering of the eyes, excess of words, and perversity of thought. These three vices drive a brother out of the cloister. For this reason he willingly goes outside, so that he may more freely see and speak the vanity he carries in his heart.

Judas went out and spoke to the Jews (Luke 22). But what did they say to him?

**All my enemies whispered against me; they thought evil against me.**

They sought what was adverse and harmful to me through secret counsels and thoughts. For they were afraid that perhaps a tumult might arise among the people (Matt. 26).

It must be understood, however, that whispering is a great sin. Hence it is said through a certain wise man: “The whisperer and the double-tongued person are accursed, for they have disturbed many who were at peace” (Sir. 28).

9. **They established an iniquitous word against me.**
