They established that false testimony should be spoken against Jesus (Luke 22). The word was also iniquitous when they said, “Let him be crucified,” and, “He is guilty of death” (Matt. 26 and 27). They did this against me.

But will not he who sleeps rise again? He who can rise from death as easily as a sleeping person can be awakened from sleep—will he not add resurrection to his death? Will he not rise who said, “I have power to lay down my life and power to take it up again” (John 10)?

Adam slept when Eve was formed from his side (Gen. 2). Adam was a figure of Christ, and Eve a figure of the Church. While Christ slept on the cross, the sacraments of the Church flowed from his side (John 19). And from what did he sleep? From him who entered in order to see.

10. **Indeed, the man of my peace, in whom I hoped, who ate my bread, magnified his supplanting against me.**

It was not surprising if my enemies thought evil against me, because the man of my peace—that is, Judas—with whom I was at peace and who pretended to be peaceable; in whom I hoped, as far as human estimation was concerned—for they thought that I trusted him greatly and relied greatly upon him—he who ate my bread—that is, to whom I offered the dipped morsel, or who ate my spiritual bread because he heard my preaching every day—magnified his supplanting against me more than the others, because he also betrayed me with a kiss.

Do not suppose, brothers, that all those who come to religious life and assume the habit of holy religion are saints or religious. Judas too was an apostle among the Apostles; he was expected to be holy, and yet he was a thief and a robber (John 12).

But just as Christ patiently endured him, so, if we have among us certain pretenders who sit at our table and are joined to us in the kiss of peace, they are to be tolerated with equanimity, following the example of our Lord. For whoever does not tolerate evil is himself, through his impatience, a witness against himself that he is not good.

If such a person is patiently tolerated by us, it is a great loss for him, but because of the virtue of patience a great reward will be returned to us by the Lord. We must understand that just as it is highly praiseworthy and belongs to great perfection to be good among the wicked, so conversely it is exceedingly detestable and belongs to great perversity to be wicked among the good.

O how glorious and acceptable to God it is if, among many proud people, one is humble; among many angry people, one is meek; among many lustful people, one is chaste; among many disorderly people, one is religious! Conversely, how shameful it is, and how greatly displeasing to God, when among many humble people one is proud; among many chaste people one is impure; among many gentle people one is angry; among many religious people one is perverse.

He must be tolerated, because the Lord commanded it; but he will not escape God’s anger. And just as the good person, because of his praiseworthy perfection, will receive a greater recompense from the Lord than other people, so the betrayer, like Judas, will receive a greater condemnation. For he magnified his supplanting against Christ because by his perverse example he strove to overthrow Christ’s members from their good purpose.

Christ, however, does not presently avenge himself; rather, he patiently tolerates and prays. In the future, unless they repent now, he will repay them for the evils they commit. Therefore he says:

11. **But you, Lord, have mercy on me, raise me up, and I will repay them.**

Let this be what it means for you to have mercy: that you raise me from death; and I will repay them in the future. We shall all stand before Christ’s tribunal, to render an account and to receive according to what each one has done in the body, whether good or evil (2 Cor. 5).

I know, however, that he will raise me up. He gives the reason why he knows this when he adds:

12. **By this I know that you have willed me, because my enemy will not rejoice over me.**

That is, as though I had been overcome. For the Jews rejoiced when they saw Christ crucified. They thought that they had fulfilled their will to do harm, having attained the fruit of their savagery. [Note: Col. 0803D. The printed Augustine reads: “they saw Christ, etc., the accomplished fruit of their cruelty.”]

They saw Christ hanging on the cross and shook their heads, saying, “If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross” (Matt. 27). He did not come down, although he could have. He was not demonstrating inability but teaching patience. For if he had come down from the cross while they were saying these things, it would have appeared that he had yielded to their insults and that, having been defeated, he had been unable to endure their reproaches.

Rather, he remained on the cross while they insulted him, fixed there while they were shaking their heads. They shook their heads because they did not cling to the head. He clearly taught us patience. For he did what was stronger: he refused to do what the Jews were provoking him to do. It is much more powerful to rise from the tomb than to come down from the cross.

**Because my enemy will not rejoice over me.**

They rejoiced, therefore [Note: Col. 0803D. There, “then” is read in place of “but,” with different punctuation], but Christ rose; Christ was glorified. Now they see the human race converted in his name. Let them insult now; let them shake their heads—indeed, let them now fix their heads.

13. **But you received me because of my innocence.**

You received me, scourged without deserving it, killed without owing it, because of my innocence, because of my integrity, without sin, for healing, as a physician receives a sick person.

**And you strengthened me.**

By giving me immortality and freedom from suffering.

**In your presence.**

In your majesty and divinity.

**Forever.**

Because Christ, rising from the dead, no longer dies; death will no longer rule over him (Rom. 6).

Behold: because of his innocence Christ is received, and, once received, is strengthened forever. Attend, brothers: innocence is the way to the Lord. This was asked in another psalm: “Who will ascend the mountain of the Lord?” And immediately it was added: “The innocent in hands and pure in heart” (Ps. 23).

That person is innocent who harms neither himself nor another. Let us therefore contemplate our head placed in our weakness. For “blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and the poor.” Let us learn from him the virtue of innocence: when he was reviled, he did not revile; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but handed himself over to the one who judged him unjustly (1 Pet. 2). “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer he did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53).

Rightly, therefore, he says, “But you received me because of my innocence,” and for this reason he was deservedly strengthened forever. He did this; he taught this. Let us imitate his innocence as far as we can, so that sin may not reign in us (Rom. 6), and so that with our head we may deserve to be received by God the Father and strengthened forever.

And so that we may not be ungrateful, let us give him thanks for such great benefits and say with all our heart and complete devotion what follows:

**Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel.**

He is blessed and praised as the ruler and creator of Israel—that is, of those who see him through faith and believe that they will see him by direct vision—those who understand that his Son is God and man.

May this blessing begin in the present age and continue into the age to come.

**Let it be, let it be.**

Here the Hebrew has *Amen, amen*. This repetition of the word signifies an indissoluble confirmation. The Lord himself used this repetition in the Gospel when he said, “Amen, amen, I say to you” (John 3), plainly to confirm his statement. In this he grants us understanding that what Truth thus repeats, he firmly affirms.

## TITLE OF PSALM XLI

1. This psalm is entitled in the following manner: *For the end; understanding for the sons of Korah.* The title is to the psalm as a key is to a house. For just as a house is unlocked by a key so that its interior may be seen, so the psalm is opened by its title so that the spiritual things within may be understood.

It is a matter of great mystery that Christians are called the sons of Korah. For Christians are called the sons of the Crucified One. By Korah, however, Christ is understood, because *Korah* is interpreted as “calvary”; and Christ was crucified at the place of Calvary (Matt. 27; Mark 15; Luke 23; John 19). That place, as some say, was called Calvary because criminals were accustomed to be scalped and beheaded there.

Therefore the understanding generated for us by the words of the following psalm is attributed to the sons of Korah—that is, to the sons of the cross—directed toward the end, that is, desiring to reach the highest blessedness.

The subject is the righteous person according to both powers of the soul. Or the subject may be called the desire for the highest good. In the first part, the righteous person is shown desiring God according to the soul’s higher power, seeking only heavenly things, and not fearing the adversities of this life. In the second part, through that higher power, he strengthens the animal faculty, which is quickly moved by tribulation.

This is the voice of the perfect, consoling themselves in this psalm with hope of future blessedness and patiently enduring the tribulation of this life. They consider that “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. 8).

Their purpose is to urge us, when placed amid tribulations, to console ourselves by their example and, under pressure, not to lose heart because of hope in the future reward. At the beginning of the psalm, those who desire to strive toward the end explain their desire in this way. It is the voice of the perfect:

## PSALM XLI

2. **As the deer longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God.**

The nature of the deer is said to be such that it draws out a serpent with its breath and swallows it for its own renewal. Once it has swallowed it, it burns with such thirst because of the venom that it is not enough for it to drink from one spring; rather, it runs to several.

In this manner this perfect soul declares that it has desired God, saying: “As”—that is, as ardently—the deer longs and hastens, after swallowing the serpent, not to one spring of water only but to several, so my soul, in the same manner and with the same ardor and fervor, after swallowing its vices, desires to reach you.

For just as several springs refresh the deer’s thirst, so you will be refreshment for me from many miseries, so that through you I may lay aside all the oldness of sin and be renewed in spiritual newness (Rom. 6 and 12). For with you is the fountain of life, to which you yourself have deigned to invite souls, saying, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7). And again, “Whoever drinks from the water that I will give him will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4).

Therefore:

3. **My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain.** [Note: Col. 0804D. The Ambrosian Psalter—the only one known to the editor—reads *fontem* (“fountain”) in place of *fortem* (“strong”); moreover, *fortem* too is absent from most ancient books.]

Here the person turns to the listeners, so that they may be admonished and edified. For this is characteristic of the righteous: in everything they say or do, they seek not only their own progress but also that of others.

God is the living fountain, the unfailing fountain. Or: the strong and living fountain—that is, incorruptible and immortal. Run to the fountain, or to the strong and living one. Let your course be your affection; let your course be your desire.

But do not run just anyhow, or as just any animal: run as a deer. The deer, after killing the serpents, burns with greater thirst and runs more eagerly to the springs. Your serpents are your vices. Consume the serpents of wickedness (Prov. 13); then you will desire the fountain of truth more intensely.

But let us hear what this blessed soul thirsted for:

**When shall I come and appear before the face of God?**

“When shall I come?” What is sooner is slow to desire. This is what I thirst for: to come and appear. The Apostle says, “We are children of God, but it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know, however, that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3).

This is what he thirsts for. “I thirst in my pilgrimage; I thirst in my course; I shall be satisfied at his coming.” Hence he says elsewhere: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. 16).

Meanwhile, while I meditate, while I run, while I am on the road, before I come, before I appear:

4. **My tears have been my bread day and night, while it is said to me every day, ‘Where is your God?’**

“My tears,” he says, “were not bitterness but bread.” Those tears themselves were sweet. Thirsting for that fountain, because I could not yet drink, I ate my tears more eagerly. For he did not say, “My tears became my drink,” lest he appear to have desired them in the same way as the springs of water. Rather, while that thirst was preserved by which I burn for the springs of water, my tears became bread for me while I was being delayed. And certainly, by eating my tears, I thirst for the springs more intensely.

For day and night my tears became bread. Human beings eat the food called bread during the day; at night they sleep. They eat the bread of tears day and night, whether you understand the whole day and night, or understand “day” as the prosperity of this world and “night” as the adversity of this world.

“Whether,” he says, “I am in the prosperous circumstances of the world or in its adverse circumstances, I pour out the tears of my desire. I do not abandon the hunger of my desire. Even when things go well for me in the world, it is bad for me before I appear before the face of God.”

Why, then, do you compel me to rejoice as though it were day? If some prosperity of this world smiles upon me, is it not deceptive? Is it not fleeting, perishable, mortal, transitory, and passing away? Does it not contain more deception than delight? Why, then, should my tears not become bread even because of these things? For even when the happiness of the world shines around us, as long as we are in this body we are away from the Lord (2 Cor. 5).

And every day it is said to me, “Where is your God?” If a pagan says this to me, can I not say to him, “Where is your god?” He points out his god with his finger. For he points to some stone and says, “Behold, this is my god.” “Where is your God?”

When I have mocked the stones and the person who pointed them out has been ashamed, he turns away from the stone, looks up to heaven, and perhaps, pointing his finger at the sun, says again, “Behold, my god.” “Where is your God?”

He has found something to show with his bodily eyes. I, however, do not lack someone whom I could show; rather, he lacks the eyes with which I could show him. He could point out his god, the sun, to the eyes of my body; but with what eyes could I show him the creator of the sun?

Nevertheless, by hearing every day, “Where is your God?” and by having my daily nourishment in tears day and night, I pondered what I had heard: “Where is your God?” I myself also sought my Lord, so that, if I could, I might not merely believe but also see something.

I see what my God has made, but I do not see my God himself, who made these things. Yet, since the deer longs for the springs of water, and with God is the fountain of life, and the psalm itself is written for the sons of Korah with understanding, and “the invisible things of God are perceived through the things that have been made” (Rom. 1), what shall I do to find my God?

Shall I consider the earth? The earth was made. There is great beauty in the lands, but they have an artisan. Great are the marvels of seeds and growing things, but all these have a Creator.

I attend to the vastness of the surrounding sea [Note: Col. 0805D. Augustine reads, “I show”]: I am astonished and amazed; I seek its artisan. I look up at the sky; I admire the beauty of the stars, the splendor of the sun, sufficient for the day it unfolds, and the moon, consoling the darkness of night.

These things are wonderful; these things are worthy of praise, or even worthy of amazement. For they are not earthly only but heavenly as well. Yet my thirst does not cease. I admire and praise these things, but I thirst for the one who made them.

I return to myself and search and examine who I myself am within such things. [Note: Col. 0805D. Augustine more correctly has *qui* (“who”) in place of *intra* (“within”); shortly afterward it has another reading, “by which I may be governed.”] I find that I have a body and a soul: one that rules and another that is ruled. The body serves; the soul commands. I discern that the soul is better than the body, and I see that it is the soul, not the body, that investigates such things.

Yet I recognize that I have examined all these things through the body. I praised the earth; I knew it through my eyes. I praised the sky, the stars, the sun, and the moon; I knew them through my eyes. The eyes are members of the flesh; they are windows of the mind. There is an inner being who sees through them; when that being is absent through thought, they stand open in vain.

My God, who made these things that I see with my eyes, is not to be sought with those eyes. Let the soul itself also perceive through itself whether there is something that it does not sense through the eyes, as it senses colors and light; not through the ears, as it senses songs and sound; not through the nostrils, as it senses the sweetness of odors; not through the palate and tongue, as it senses taste; not through the whole body, as it handles hardness and softness, rigidity and heat, roughness and smoothness—but whether there is something that it sees inwardly.

What does “sees inwardly” mean? Something that is neither color, nor sound, nor odor, nor taste, nor heat, nor cold, nor hardness, nor softness.

Let someone tell me what color wisdom possesses. We contemplate its justice, because inwardly, in the very act of contemplation, we enjoy its beauty.

What is like sound to the ears? What rises like vapor to the nostrils? What is brought to the mouth? What is handled by the hand? [Note: Col. 0805D. Augustine reads, “What sounds to the ears, what is, as it were, vaporous, etc.” Other variant readings of lesser importance are passed over.] Yet it delights, it is inward, it is beautiful, it is seen, and it is praised. And if these eyes are in darkness, the mind enjoys its light.

What was it that Tobias saw when, though blind, he gave the counsel of life to his seeing son (Tob. 4)? There is therefore something that the soul itself, the ruler, director, and inhabitant of the body, sees—something that it does not sense through the body’s eyes, ears, nostrils, palate, or bodily touch, but through itself.

And surely what is perceived through itself is better than what is perceived through its servant.

For it sees itself through itself, and the soul itself, in order to know itself, sees itself. [Note: Cols. 0805D–0806D. In the same place, with a *τελείᾳ στιγμῇ* (“full stop”) placed before it, another clause begins from these words: “It certainly is so, for it sees itself through itself, etc.” Shortly afterward, the words “it gathered itself together” are omitted.] To see itself, it certainly does not seek the assistance of bodily eyes. Rather, it withdrew from all the bodily senses, as from things that hindered and clamored, and drew itself back to itself, so that it might see itself in itself and know itself with itself; it gathered itself together.

But is God himself something of the same kind as the soul? God certainly cannot be seen except by the soul, yet he cannot be seen in the way the soul can be seen. For this soul is seeking something that is God, concerning whom those who say, “Where is your God?” should not insult it.

It is seeking an unchangeable truth, without any failing of substance. The soul itself is not such: it fails and progresses; it knows and is ignorant; it remembers and forgets; now it wills one thing, now it does not will it. Such mutability does not fall upon God.

If I say, “God is mutable,” those who say, “Where is your God?” will insult me. Seeking my God, therefore, in visible things and not finding him; seeking his substance in myself, as though it were something of the kind I am, and not finding it; I seek something above my soul, and behold, I perceive that my God is something above my soul. [Note: Col. 0806D. The printed Augustine seems capable of restoration from these witnesses; there it reads only: “and not finding [it], I perceive that my God is something above my soul. Therefore, etc.”]

Therefore, that I might touch him,
### 5

“I remembered these things, and poured out my soul within me.” When would my soul reach what is sought above it, unless my soul poured itself out beyond itself? For if it remained within itself, it would see nothing other than itself; and when it saw itself, certainly it would not see its Lord. Let my mockers now say, “Where is your God?” I shall say, for as long as I do not see him, for as long as I am delayed: “I shall eat my tears day and night.” Let them still say, “Where is your God?” I therefore seek my God throughout every body, whether earthly or heavenly, and I do not find him. Yet I meditated on the search for my God, desiring, through the things that have been made, to behold the invisible things of my God understood [Rom. 1]. [Note: At [Col. 0806D] the earlier reading was incorrectly *tempore*, which we correct from Augustine.] I poured out my soul over myself. And now nothing remains for me to touch except my God.

[Col. 0806D] For there is the dwelling of my God above my soul. There he dwells; from there he created me, from there he governs me, from there he counsels me, from there he awaits me, from there he calls me, from there he directs me, from there he leads me, and from there he brings me to the end. For he who has a most exalted dwelling in secret also has a tabernacle on earth. His tabernacle on earth is his Church [2 Cor. 5], still on pilgrimage. But the one who is found in the tabernacle must be sought: he is the way by which one reaches the dwelling.

Indeed, when I poured out my soul over myself in order to touch my God, why did I do this? “Because I shall enter into the place of the tabernacle.” For outside the place of the tabernacle I shall wander, seeking my God. “Because I shall enter into the place of the wondrous tabernacle, even to the house of God.”

See how many things I admire in the tabernacle. For the tabernacle of my God on earth is the faithful human being. I admire in them the obedience of their very members, because sin does not reign in them so as to make them obey its desires, nor do they offer their members as weapons of wickedness to sin [Rom. 6]; rather, they offer them to the living God in good works. I admire the bodily members serving the soul that serves the living God as soldiers.

I also regard the soul itself, obedient to God, assigning to God the works of its activity, restraining its desires, driving away ignorance, extending itself toward enduring every hardship and severity, and bestowing justice and charity upon others. I marvel at these virtues in the soul as well, but I am still walking in the place of the tabernacle. I pass beyond these things too; and although the tabernacle is wondrous, I am astonished when I reach the house of God.

While he marvels at the members of the tabernacle, he is led in this way to the house of God, following a certain inner sweetness, some hidden pleasure—as though an instrument were sounding sweetly from the house of God. And as he walked in the tabernacle, hearing a certain inner sound, led onward by the sweetness of God, following what was sounding, withdrawing himself from every tumult of flesh and blood, he reached the house of God. For he himself recalls his way and guidance as though we were saying to him: “You marvel at the tabernacle on this earth, but how did you reach the hidden dwelling of God?”

[Col. 0807C] “In the voice,” he says, “of exultation and confession, the sound of one feasting.” In the house of God there is an everlasting festival. Nothing is celebrated there and then passes away: it is an eternal feast, a choir of angels, the present countenance of God, joy without failing. The festival there is such that it is neither opened at a beginning nor closed at an end. From that eternal and perpetual festival some melodious and sweet sound reaches the ears of the heart. But if the world does not make a din around one who walks in this tabernacle and considers the miracles of God in the redemption of the faithful, the sound of that festival soothes his ear and carries the deer away to the springs of water.

But since, brothers, “as long as we are in the body, we are away from the Lord” [2 Cor. 5], and “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” [Wis. 9]; and even if, with the mists in some measure dispersed, we reach this sound by walking through desire, sometimes, striving, we seize something from that house, yet because of a certain burden of our weakness we fall back into our customary state and slip back into these familiar things. And just as there we found something over which we could rejoice, so here there will be no lack of something over which we may groan.

For this deer, eating his tears day and night, carried away by desire to the springs of water—that is, to the inner sweetness of God—pouring out his soul over himself, walking in the place of the wondrous tabernacle even to the house of God, and led by the delight of an inner and intelligible sound so as to despise all outward things and be carried away toward inward things—nevertheless is still a human being. He still groans here; he still carries fragile flesh; he is still endangered amid the scandals of this world.

He looked back upon himself as though returning from there, and, placed amid these sorrows, said to himself, comparing them with those things which he had entered to see and from which he had emerged after seeing them: “Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me?” Behold, we have already rejoiced through a certain inner sweetness. Behold, with the eye of the mind we have been able to perceive something unchangeable, though only briefly and in passing. Why, then, are you still sad, my soul? You do not doubt your God. Surely you have something to say against those who say, “Where is your God?” I have already sensed something unchangeable; why do you still trouble me? “Hope in God.”

And as though his soul answered him in silence: “Why should I trouble you, except because I am not yet there where that sweetness is, by which I was so carried away as though in passing? Do I already drink from that fountain without fear? I no longer dread any scandal; I am already secure concerning all desires, as though they had been subdued and conquered. Is the devil not watching against me? Does my enemy not daily spread the snares of deception for me? Do you not want me to trouble you, placed as you are in the world and still on pilgrimage from the house of my God?”

“Hope in God,” he replied to his soul as it troubled him and, as though giving an account of its disturbance because of the evils with which this world abounds. “Meanwhile,” he says, “dwell in hope. For hope that is seen is not hope. But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” [Rom. 8].

“Hope in God.” Why do you hope in God? [Verse 7.] “Because I shall still confess to him.” What will you confess to him? “The salvation of my countenance and my God.”

Salvation cannot come from me to myself. For this reason I shall say this; I shall confess: Your salvation, O God the Father, is my countenance—that is, he is a human being, as it is written: “Taking the form of a servant and being found in appearance as a human being” [Phil. 2]; and he is also God. Rightly, then, I call your Son your salvation, because through him, made human, you have accomplished eternal salvation for us.

And as though someone were saying: “Why do you reproach your soul in this way, and seem to grow angry with it when you say, ‘Why are you sad, my soul?’ and the rest?” He replied: “My soul—that is, my animal and sensory nature, namely that lower part of the soul which animates and gives life to the body—is troubled with respect to myself, because of the tribulations inflicted upon me. The author is not to be blamed for this; rather, it must be referred to myself, that is, to my own fault.”

Therefore, because my soul is troubled with respect to myself, and pride caused this disturbance, “I will remember you from the land of the Jordan and from Hermoniim, from the little mountain.” From where do I remember you? From the small mountain and from the land of the Jordan—that is, baptism, where there is remission of sins.

For no one hastens to the remission of sins except one who is displeased with himself. No one hastens to the remission of sins except one who confesses himself a sinner. No one confesses himself a sinner except one who has humbled himself before God. Therefore I will remember you from the land of the Jordan and from the little mountain, so that you may make the little great. For “whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” [Matt. 23; Luke 18].

But if you seek the interpretation of the names, Jordan means “their descent.” Descend, therefore, so that you may be lifted up. Do not exalt yourself [Rom. 9], lest you be dashed down. And “from Hermoniim, from the little mountain.” Hermon [Note: The Benedictines nevertheless prefer to read *anathematio*, and shortly afterward *anathema*.] is interpreted as “anathematization.” Anathematize yourself by being displeased with yourself. For you will displease God if you please yourself.

Therefore, because God grants us all good things—because he himself is good, not because we are worthy; because he is merciful, not because we have deserved anything—“I will remember you from the land of the Jordan.” For this reason also I will remember you, because—

### 8

“The abyss calls to the abyss in the voice of your cataracts.”

An abyss is a certain depth that cannot be penetrated or comprehended. Surely the human heart is an abyss? For what is deeper than this abyss? Human beings can speak; they can be seen through the activity of their members; they can be heard in speech. But whose thought can be penetrated? Whose heart can be seen? Who comprehends what someone carries within, what he can within, what he does within, what he arranges within, what he wills within, and what he does not will within?

“The abyss calls to the abyss”: human being gains human being. Yet this does not happen in his own voice, but “in the voice of your cataracts,” that is, of your preachers, who through their voice open to us the splendor of the heavenly kingdom.

For *cataracts* are said to mean windows. According to some, however, *cataracts* properly signify conduits through which water gushes forth. Such are the holy prophets and Apostles, from whom true doctrine flows down to us. Or, “in the voice of the cataracts,” that is, of those who preach, the abyss calls to the abyss, because the words they preach are confirmed from the New and Old Testaments.

The abyss calls to the abyss because the two Testaments mutually provide a certain assistance to one another: the Old is the prophecy of the New, and the New is the exposition of the Old Testament.

After the preaching has been heard, “all your heights”—that is, all your judgments, lofty and unsearchable—“and your waves,” that is, your threats, terrifying and striking, have passed over me. They overwhelmed me and plunged me into the depths, but nevertheless they passed over. Anger departed; mercy came. The waves passed over; calm came.

The little boat was tossed by the winds and covered by the waves. Those who were in danger cried out to God, “Save us!” And he commanded the waves and the sea, and there was a great calm [Matt. 8; Mark 6]. “Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” [Rom. 5], because in his anger God did not withhold his mercies. Hence it is also added:

### 9

“In the day the Lord commanded his mercy.”

What is “in the day” except in the time of grace? Hence it is written: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” [2 Cor. 6].

But because the day also has a night, and grace has tribulation—for “all who wish to live devoutly in Christ suffer persecution” [2 Tim. 3]—therefore, in the night of tribulation, he commanded a song of praise. And this is what follows: “And at night, his song.” A song at night is praise of God in tribulation.

By this the children of wrath are distinguished from the children of grace: when prosperous circumstances arrive, both good and wicked alike praise God; but when adversity comes, the wicked murmur, whereas the good praise him. Hence it is said elsewhere in the psalm: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth” [Ps. 33].

Alternatively, by “day” may be understood the Gentile people enlightened by faith, and by “night” Judaea blinded by unbelief. “In the day the Lord commanded his mercy,” because among the believing Gentiles he commanded the remission of sins and eternal life to be preached. “And at night, his song,” because to Judaea, deprived of this, he left only the Old Testament.

Hence it is said elsewhere: “Upon the willows we hung our instruments” [Ps. 136]. The instruments are hung among the Jews as among unfruitful willows, because the legal and prophetic words are with them. They hang there, but do not resound, because those among whom they are hung lack the art of spiritual understanding.

We have said that a song at night is praise of God in tribulation. But because, while we are afflicted, we are in danger, we must not only praise God but also pray. Therefore it is added:

### 10

“With me is my prayer to the God of my life; I shall say to God, ‘You are my protector.’”

Since our Redeemer commands us to pray and likewise says, “For your Father knows what you need before you ask him” [Matt. 6], it may seem necessary to ask why we are commanded to ask one who knows what we need. Certain heretics are accustomed to object that we speak to one who already knows in vain.

Apart from the example of the Lord, who prayed to the Father on the Mount of Olives, and apart from the authority of the command by which he is known to have instructed us to pray, a brief answer may be given: we do not devote ourselves to prayer in order to inform the one who knows all the things we need, but in order to obtain the things that are necessary for us.

For it is one thing, by narrating, to wish to inform someone of something; it is another thing, by praying, to wish to obtain something. In narration, diligence must be displayed; in prayer, however, the merit of being heard. And because in the one who knows all things there is mercy as well as justice, what he kindly wishes to bestow upon those in need through mercy, he also wishes those same needy persons to obtain from his justice through prayer.

In the sacred writings, prayer is more frequently understood as the useful and proper petition of honorable things from God or from his saints. There is nothing a servant of God can do that is more useful than pray and praise God.

But if we truly wish to pray, we must pay close attention to and commit to memory what is said: “With me is my prayer to the God of my life.” Often, when I pray, my mind wanders outward and I do not understand what I am saying. At that time my prayer is not with me, nor am I myself with me. Concerning such people the Lord says: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” [Isa. 26].

How, then, does God attend to my prayer when I do not attend to it? But if, in the innermost secret place of my heart, I pray to my God and ask for those things that pertain to the salvation of my soul, then I can truly say: “With me is my prayer to the God of my life”—that is, to the God who grants me both the present life and eternal life.

And in that prayer I shall say to God, “You are my protector”—that is, you have taken up me, who am weak, in order to heal me; or, “You are my protector,” lest I succumb in tribulation.

Great is our confidence, brothers, because God is our protector. Therefore, after so many iniquities and negligences, let us hasten to repentance; let us run in spiritual fervor to grace, which wishes no one to perish but wishes to save all [1 Tim. 2]. “Come,” he says, “to me, all you who labor, and I will refresh you” [Matt. 5].

Again, the weak soul, seeing itself on pilgrimage and afflicted amid troubles and temptations, complains in sorrow and groaning, saying: “Why have you forgotten me? And why do I go about sorrowful while the enemy afflicts me?”

The Lord seems to forget his servants when he permits them to be sorrowful, to be afflicted by persecutions, and to be shaken by temptations; when he does not quickly hear them, does not visibly help them, and does not rescue them bodily.

For this reason he says, “Why?” because no one knows whether he is suffering these things for testing or for condemnation. But what follows is greatly to be feared:

### 11

“While my bones are broken, my enemies who trouble me reproached me.”

For bones [according to Augustine] are the strong; and sometimes even the strong yield to temptations. When each person considers these things as a member of Christ, does he not cry out, in the voice of Christ’s body: “Why have you rejected me? Why do I go about sorrowful while the enemy afflicts me? While he breaks my bones?”

Not my flesh alone, but even my bones: so that, in those parts where some strength was thought to exist, you may see it yielding in temptations, and so that the rest who are weak may despair when they see the strong succumb.

How great are these dangers, my brothers! “They reproached me who trouble me.” Again comes that voice: “While they say to me each day, ‘Where is your God?’”

They say this especially in the temptations of the Church: “Where is your God?” How much the martyrs heard this, strong and patient for Christ’s name! How often it was said to them: “Where is your God? Let him deliver you, if he can.”

For they saw their torments outwardly, but did not see their crowns outwardly. And I, because my soul is troubled on account of these things, what else shall I say to it but: “Why are you sorrowful, my soul, and why do you trouble me?”

And as though it answered, “Do you not want me to be troubled, placed here amid such evils? Sighing for good things, knowing and suffering, do you not want me to trouble you?”—“Hope,” he says, “in God, because I shall still confess to him.”

He states the confession itself and repeats the confirmation of hope: “The salvation of my countenance and my God.”

## TITLE OF PSALM XLII

The title of the following psalm is: “A psalm of David.”

This psalm suits a certain just person afflicted by the fellowship of the wicked and by the miseries of this life, directing us toward the end, that is, toward Christ.

The subject of this psalm is the separation of the just: here, separation only in cause; in the future, separation in person and place as well. For one who is distinguished here in cause from the wicked can be secure, because at the final judgment both body and soul will be wholly separated.

In the first part, the just person asks to be separated from the impious. In the second part, he affirms that he will enter the secret place of God. In the third part, he exhorts his animal nature [Col. 0811A] to hope in the Lord. Here the intention is clear: by strengthening himself, he intends also to strengthen the weak through his example. The voice of the faithful:

## PSALM XLII

### 1

“Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation; rescue me from an unjust and deceitful man.”

Let the enemy not judge me; let it not be the false opinion of human beings, which makes good evil and, conversely, evil good. Rather, judge me, you who are just and merciful. And distinguish my cause; if you find it just, “rescue me from an unholy nation,” that is, from unbelievers; “and from an unjust man,” that is, from an open persecutor, “and deceitful,” who secretly seeks to deceive me.

I do not fear your judgment [according to Augustine], because I know your mercy. “Perfect love casts out fear” [1 John 4]. I do not fear you with penal fear, because I love you.

Meanwhile, during this pilgrimage, you do not distinguish my place, because I live together with the weeds until the time of the harvest [Matt. 13]; you do not yet distinguish my light.

Or, “distinguish my cause”: let there be a difference between one who believes in you and one who does not believe in you. Equal weakness, but unequal [Note: In the received text of Augustine, *conscientia* (“conscience”) is more correct than *continentia* (“continence”).] restraint. Equal labor, but unequal desire. And you ought to do this.

### 2

“For you are God, my strength.”

I do not presume upon my own powers, nor do I expect to have any strength from elsewhere except from you alone; and I place all my hope in you. “In God we shall act valiantly” [Ps. 59], and he will bring our enemies to nothing.

At times a person makes strength for himself. He desires to reign, to dominate, to appear superior to others. He does not endure injuries but avenges those inflicted upon him. What kind of strength is this? Human, not divine; carnal, not spiritual. He repays evil for evil and curse for curse. He is ashamed to appear defeated. But while he conquers another human being, he himself is more grievously overcome by vice. Such strength belongs to pride.

The strength that comes from God, however, is not of the flesh but of the soul; not against human beings but against vices and the devil. It is patience, humility, obedience, charity, and the other virtues of the soul that come from God. It is written: “Those who trust in the Lord will change their strength” [Isa. 40]. Hence the Apostle admonishes us: “Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” [Rom. 12].

Let God, then, be our strength. In him we shall be rescued from temptations; through him we shall overcome the world and the devil, vices and sins, the flesh itself and evil desires. By force we shall also seize the kingdom of heaven, according to what is written: “And the violent seize it” [Matt. 11].

But what follows seems contrary to these statements, when he says: “Why have you rejected me? And why do I go about sorrowful while the enemy afflicts me?” If God is his strength, how has he been rejected? How is he sorrowful and afflicted by the enemy? Is the Lord’s hand powerless?

We must understand that the merciful Lord, through a certain providential mercy, often both holds back his chosen ones by rejecting them and rejects them by holding them back. This is what happened when the devil asked to tempt blessed Job. “Behold,” says the Lord, “he is in your hand” [Job 1]. But because he held him back by rejecting him, this is shown by what he immediately adds: “Only preserve his life.”

How great this man was, who was abandoned by God and handed over to the devil, we learn from the Lord himself when he says to that same devil: “Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on earth? A simple and upright man, fearing God and turning away from evil” [ibid.].

Since he was such a man, he could rightly say to the Lord: “Why, then, have you rejected me? And why do I go about sorrowful while the enemy afflicts me?” The Lord could have answered him even more appropriately: “Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline”; for “the Lord chastens every son whom he receives” [Prov. 1]. And: “Blessed is the one who endures temptation, for when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life” [James 1].

Behold why the Lord usefully rejects his servants. But because holy men do not know God’s hidden judgments, and know that many are abandoned and tempted to their condemnation, they seek, if it can be done, to know God’s purpose: so that if they displease him in some respect and are therefore abandoned, they may correct themselves more quickly lest they be rejected. Hence he immediately adds:

### 3

“Send forth your light and your truth.”

For unless he enlightens us, we are in darkness. Unless he teaches us the truth, we shall go astray. What else is the light of God [according to Augustine] but the truth of God? Or what is the truth of God but the light of God? Or what are both together but the one Christ? “I am,” he says, “the light of the world. I am the way, the truth, and the life” [John 8 and 14].

Rightly, then, it follows: “They themselves have led me and brought me to your holy mountain and to your tabernacles.” As though he were saying: “Your light and truth have led me from error to faith in you, and have brought me to your holy mountain”—that is, to the perfection and eminence of the virtues—“and to your tabernacles”—that is, to the unity and fellowship of the saints.

For this reason the present Church is called a tabernacle: because the Lord is served in it. A tabernacle, however, is the dwelling of soldiers, and “the life of a human being upon earth is warfare” [Job 7].

It is good that he does not say *tabernacle* but *tabernacles*, because there are many congregations of saints, and in many places Christian service is rendered to the Lord. There are the tabernacles of married believers, of the continent, of beginners, of those making progress, of the perfect, of hearers and subjects, and of prelates and preachers. All serve one King. And although their pursuits are different, their intention is one.

When you hear “light,” cleanse the eye. That light of the heart requires a clean eye: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” [Matt. 5].

When you hear “tabernacle,” understand war and beware of the enemy. But now that we have been led into the tabernacle and placed upon his holy mountain, what hope do we have? It follows and says:

### 4

“I shall enter the altar of God.”

What altar is that? “To God, who makes my youth rejoice”—that is, who will make me young again, once all oldness has been laid aside, by giving me immortality and freedom from suffering.

The altar of God is the Son of God himself. We enter this altar now through faith; afterward we shall enter it through sight. On this altar we now offer vows and sacrifices to God the Father: a contrite and humbled heart [Ps. 50], prayers and petitions. Hereafter, when all sorrow has been driven away, on that same altar, in the divinity itself, we shall offer only the sacrifice of praise and no longer that of petition.

Our youth will rejoice in the resurrection, and after God has become all in all [Phil. 3], nothing necessary will remain for which we must ask; we shall devote ourselves only to divine praises.

But whoever desires to reach that praise must first begin it here. Therefore he adds: “I will confess to you on the lyre, O God, my God.” The repetition indicates affection and devotion.

In this the lyre differs from the psaltery: the psaltery produces its sound from the upper part, while the lyre produces its sound from the lower. In many passages of the psalms we are commanded to confess to the Lord on these two instruments. Both [according to Augustine] are pleasing to God and sweet to his ears.

When the Apostle said that he preached the gospel of God and had received it neither from human beings nor through a human being but through Jesus Christ [Gal. 1], the strings sounded from above. But when he said, “We glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces patience,” and so forth [Rom. 5], the lyre sounded from below, though sweetly nonetheless. For all patience is sweet to God.

He therefore says, “I will confess to you on the lyre,” because of what he had said: “Why do I go about sorrowful while the enemy afflicts me?” He suffered affliction from below, yet in that very suffering he wished to please God and eagerly desired to give thanks, strong amid tribulations. And because he could not be without these things, he owed patience to God, and said: [Note: With a different sense and punctuation in Augustine: “because he could not be without tribulation, he owed patience to God.” This variation is to be attributed to the ancient manuscripts.]

### 5

Amid these things he addresses his soul, consoling it, and says: “Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me?”

But who is it that speaks to the soul? We understand that we possess something in which the image of God is present: namely, the mind and reason. It is this that calls upon the light and truth of God. It is this by which we grasp what is unjust and what is just, by which we distinguish truth from falsehood. It is called the intellect, which beasts lack.

Our intellect, then, addresses our soul: the higher part of the soul addresses the lower. In tribulations the latter is withered; in sicknesses, weary; in temptations, contracted; in labors, sick. The mind lifts it up from above, grasping the truth. It hears that inner voice of God. It hears an inward rational song.

For something sounds from above in silence—not to the ears but to the minds—so that whoever hears that melody becomes wearied by bodily noise, and this whole human life becomes for him a kind of tumult, obstructing the hearing of a certain inward sound that is exceedingly delightful and ineffable.

And when this happens, and a person suffers violence from some disturbance, addressing his soul he says: “Why are you sad, my soul?” The present address makes something sound forth; faithful confession purifies what remains. Hence he adds: “Hope in God.”

Await the Lord, who rewards, because, having confessed already, I shall still confess to him. Now I confess while afflicted; it will come to pass that I shall still confess, renewed and made joyful.

And this is, and will be, my confession: “The salvation of my countenance and my God.” And this is also the great reason for hoping: because my Savior is he who has my countenance—that is, he has my countenance and my form, and for my sake became human [Phil. 2]; and he himself is my God.

## 208. TITLE OF PSALM XLIII

### 1

“For the end; for the sons of Korah; for understanding.”

This psalm is proposed for the sons of Korah—that is, for the sons of passion and the cross—in order that they may possess understanding, with the following understood: that they may understand that, through the temporal goods given to the ancient people, the spiritual goods now given to the Christian people, and to be given more fully in the future, were signified.

I speak of the sons of Korah, directed toward the end, through this understanding. The subject is the martyrs, who also speak.

In the first part he sets forth the distinction between the benefits of God: those which God grants to this people and those which he granted to the earlier people, showing that the former are eternal, whereas the latter were temporal.

In the second part he sets forth the evils they endure in this life, although they will possess many good things in the future. The fact that the just suffer temporal evils in this life is set against the fact that the earlier people were delivered from bodily punishments.

In the third part he prays to be delivered from the evils of this life at the time of the resurrection. The intention is to invite us to patience, so that we may not be saddened by temporal punishments.

The voice of the martyrs, showing what good things God did for the ancient fathers, says:

## PSALM XLIII

### 2

“O God, we have heard with our ears.”

We must note that he does not merely say “we have heard,” but adds “with our ears.” The words of the prophecy accord with the words that the Lord speaks in the Gospel: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” [Luke 8].

Many possess ears of flesh but not of the heart, because they hear outwardly but do not receive inwardly. For this reason he says “with our ears,” so that we may hear what is said with attention and understanding, which are the ears of the heart.

And to commend these things as worthy of hearing, he says: “Our fathers”—not just any human beings, but the patriarchs and prophets—“have declared to us through their Scriptures the work that you worked in their days.”

How you delivered them from Egypt, led them out through the Red Sea, guarded them in the desert [Exod. 13], and other such things. They also declared to us the work that you worked in ancient days: what you did at the beginning, in the creation of heaven and earth, and concerning the events that took place before the flood. This is the work that you did in their days, which our fathers declared to us.

### 3

“Your hand”—that is, your power and might—“destroyed the nations,” namely the Amorite, the Jebusite, and the Perizzite; “and you planted them,” namely our fathers.

This is spoken by comparison with a planted tree, which is planted for the purpose of taking root and bearing fruit. In this way your hand destroyed those nations: first you afflicted them through many wars, and so drove them from their land, in order to bring these people in and plant them, and to establish their kingdom by your mercy.

But perhaps they were able to accomplish these things because they were strong, because they were warriors, because they were unconquered, because they were experienced. Our fathers did not tell us this. Scripture does not say this. What does it say except what follows?

“For they did not possess the land by their own sword,” that is, by their own armor, “and their own arm,” that is, their own strength, “did not save them” from their enemies. For if they could not save themselves from those nations, it is much less credible that they could have possessed those nations’ land by their own power. [Note: This is the reading of the Vallarsian edition, which omits folio numbers 209 and 210 without any interruption of the text. Ed.]

Their arm, I say, did not save them. “But your right hand”—that is, the favor of your grace, because we often place those whom we favor at our right hand—“and your arm”—that is, your strength, because a human being has strength in his arms—“and the light of your countenance”—that is, wise counsel, or the miracles that were for them a manifestation of your countenance, that is, of your grace and goodwill.

What does it mean that you were present with them through such signs, so that you might be understood to be present? Surely, when God is present to us through some miracle, do we see his face with our eyes? Rather, through the effect of the miracle he makes his presence known to human beings. Hence those who marvel at such deeds say: “We have seen God present.”

You did these things for them “because you were pleased with them.” This means [according to Augustine]: you dealt with them in such a way as to be pleased in them, so that anyone who considered how they were treated would say: “Truly, God is with them, and God acts for them” [Note: In the received text of Augustine, *agit* (“acts/deals”) is read instead of *adjuvat* (“helps”).]

### 4

But because these things happened to them in figure—as the Apostle says—and were written for our instruction (1 Cor. 10), the title too was supplied for understanding. This work of the Lord, which we have heard took place temporally in our ancient fathers through the dispersion of the nations, we now also see being fulfilled spiritually in spiritual men.

Moses mentions these nations when he says:

“When the Lord your God has brought you into the land which you are entering to possess, and has destroyed before you many nations—the Hittite, the Girgashite, the Amorite, the Canaanite, the Perizzite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite—seven nations much greater in number than you and stronger than you; and when the Lord has delivered them to you, you shall strike them down to complete destruction” (Deut. 7).

These seven nations are the seven spiritual vices, which every spiritual soldier is admonished to overcome by the grace of God and utterly exterminate. As for the statement that they are greater in number, the reason is this: there are more vices than virtues. Thus, seven nations are counted in the catalogue, but in their conquest they are mentioned without an assigned number. For it says: “And has destroyed before you many nations” (ibid.).

For the people of carnal passions, which proceeds from this sevenfold fuel and root of vices, is more numerous than Israel. From gluttony arise feasting and drunkenness; from fornication, filthy speech, buffoonery, frivolity, and foolish talk. From avarice arise lying, fraud, theft, perjury, the pursuit of disgraceful gain, false testimony, violence, inhumanity, and rapacity. From anger arise murder, shouting, and indignation. From sadness arise rancor, faintheartedness, bitterness, and despair. From acedia arise idleness, drowsiness, importunity, restlessness, transgression, instability of mind and body, verbosity, and inquisitiveness. From vainglory (*kenodoxia*, κενοδοξία) arise quarrels, heresies, boasting, and presumptuous innovations.

[Note: I have no doubt that *kenodoxia* should be restored here, written in Greek letters κενοδοξίᾳ, which means “empty glory.” It is also plausible that this rather lengthy passage was borrowed by our author from Augustine; but since it does not occur in the *Expositions of the Psalms*, which he seems to have set before himself as the sole work to be excerpted, I have no leisure to investigate it more carefully elsewhere.]

[Col. 0815A] From pride arise contempt, envy, disobedience, blasphemy, murmuring, detraction, and many other similar things.

Although these are much more numerous than the virtues, nevertheless, once those seven principal vices from whose nature these others proceed have been conquered, all the rest immediately become quiet and likewise are destroyed in perpetual annihilation. That these plagues are also stronger, we plainly perceive from the very assault they make upon our nature. For the delight of carnal passions fights more powerfully in our members (Rom. 7) than the pursuits of virtue, which are acquired only through the utmost contrition of heart and body.

As for the command that we should healthfully possess the territories of these destructive nations, it is understood as follows. Each vice has its own station in our heart. But when the vices have been overcome by the people of Israel—that is, by the virtues fighting against them—the place which the spirit of lust or fornication had occupied in our heart will thereafter be held by chastity. Patience will reclaim the place which fury had taken. The place which sadness had occupied by producing death will be possessed by a salutary and joy-filled gladness. The place devastated by acedia humility begins to cultivate.

And so, once each vice has been expelled, the sons of Israel—that is, souls who see God—will possess their places, meaning the contrary affections. Since, therefore, almighty God does not cease even now to perform spiritually in us what he formerly performed bodily in our ancient fathers, the Church rightly says to him what follows:

### 5

“You are yourself my king and my God.”

You are yourself—that is, unchanged, as Augustine explains. Times have changed; the Creator of times does not change. You are accustomed to lead me as a king; you are accustomed to help me as God.

“You who command salvations for Jacob.”

What does “who command” mean? Although you are hidden in your very substance and nature, by which you are whatever you are, and although by virtue of what you are you were not present to the fathers so that they might see you face to face, nevertheless, through any creature whatsoever you command salvations for Jacob. You are not present only through yourself; rather, through whatever creature you are present, you command that what those to whom you give the command perform for the salvation of your servants should be done.

“You are yourself,” he says, through whom our fathers destroyed their enemies; you are my king, spiritually ruling me according to good conduct and virtues, so that the devil and the vices may no longer dominate me, and sin may no longer reign in my mortal body (Rom. 6). And you are my God, because I adore and worship you, who command salvations for Jacob—that is, who save through your saving commands those who struggle and overthrow the vices. For Jacob is interpreted as “supplanter.”

These things belong to the past. What will happen in the future?

### 6

“In you we shall scatter our enemies with the horn.”

In you, our horn—that is, our strength and defense—we shall scatter, that is, cast down and disperse, our enemies, both carnal and spiritual. This will happen at the judgment, where holy and perfected men, by judging, will separate the wicked from the good, just as one separates the chaff from the grain by winnowing (Matt. 13).

This is what the Lord promises his disciples when he says:

“In the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19).

Then what follows will be fulfilled:

“And in your name we shall trample on those who rise up against us.”

For now they trample on us, because we invoke your name, because we leave vengeance to you, because for your name’s sake we are humble and poor. But in the very name in which we have believed, those who now rise up against us to persecute us we shall in the future despise as vanquished, regarding them as vile and rejected. And rightly do I say, “in your name.”

### 7

“For I shall not hope in my bow.”

That is, in my cunning. A bow shoots from a distance; therefore the bow signifies human foresight or prudence. The person who trusts in his own understanding and relies upon his own prudence hopes, as it were, in his bow. Hence it is written:

“Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and prudent in your own sight” (Isa. 5).

By contrast, Solomon admonishes us, saying:

“Have confidence in the Lord with all your heart, and do not rely on your own prudence” (Prov. 3).

Therefore, the person who does not trust in his own understanding and prudence does not hope in his own bow.

“And my sword shall not save me.”

That is, my armor and my strength shall not save me, just as our fathers were not saved by the sword. These are the two things in which worldly people place great confidence: their own cunning and their own strength. But he establishes his entire salvation in God when he continues:

### 8

“For you have saved us from those who afflict us.”

He uses the past tense in place of the future. It is the practice of the prophets to foresee certain future things in this way and to regard them as so certain that they seem already to have happened. It is as though he were saying: “In the future you will save us from those who now afflict us for your sake.”

“And you have confounded those who hate us.”

That is, you will confound and put to shame those who persist in their hatred of us, showing them the evils they have committed, the losses of the good things they have forfeited, and the eternal punishments by which they are to be punished.

O how savage and harsh will be the confusion of those to whom it will be said:

“Amen, I say to you, I do not know you.”

And:

“Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire” (Matt. 25).

### 9

“After the enemies have been confounded, in God we shall glory all day long.”

Then there will be one day, one eternity. Then each person’s praise will come from God. We shall both praise and be praised: we in you, and you in us.

“And in your name”—that is, to the honor of your name—“we shall confess to you forever,” because it is written:

“Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O God; forever and ever they shall praise you” (Ps. 83).

These future things are as certain to us as those past things which we heard from our fathers. But what about the present?

### 10

“But now you have rejected us.”

That is, you appear to have rejected us because at present you permit us to be afflicted. You have put us to shame, not in our conscience but in the sight of men, and you do not go forth with our armies.

We advance against our enemies, and you do not advance with us. They prevail; we are weak. Where is that power of yours? Where are your right hand and your might? Where is the sea dried up? Where are the Egyptians who pursued us and were overwhelmed by the waves? Where is Amalek, resisting but overcome through the sign of the cross?

“And you will not go forth with our armies.”

### 11

“You have turned us back before our enemies.”

So that they seem to be in front and we behind; they are counted victorious and we defeated.

“And those who hate us plundered us for themselves.”

They plundered us as their booty, dragging some away, scourging others, casting others into prison, and killing others (Matt. 24).

### 12

“You have given us like sheep for food, and you have scattered us among the nations.”

Some of us, as Augustine explains, have been eaten by the nations. These signify those who suffered in such a way that they passed into the body of the Gentiles. The Church mourns them as members that have been devoured.

Or they have been scattered among the nations when Peter was crucified at Rome, Thomas died in India, and countless martyrs were killed in countless places. The Lord Jesus also foretold their dispersion when he said:

“If they persecute you in one city, flee into another” (Matt. 10).

### 13

“You have sold your people without a price.”

It was as though the people of the holy martyrs were sold without a price when such precious blood was poured out that no one was converted to redemption and salvation by their example. At times the holy martyrs were regarded as so worthless, and thought to have perished so completely, that those who killed them even believed they were thereby rendering a service to God (John 6).

Thus they were given away without a price when they were killed and won no one over. And if there were some who were converted, they were few in comparison with the martyrs. This is what follows:

“And there was no multitude in their exchanges.”

That is, in the exchanges of the martyrs who died for the expansion of your name. Or, “in their exchanges” means that when the martyrs were killed there was no great number of communities gathered together to serve God in churches, monasteries, and the various orders, as we now see in a time of peace. For they hid because of the persecutions and separated from one another, so that they might remain concealed more effectively and not be discovered and captured so quickly if many were together.

### 14

“You have made us a reproach to our neighbors.”

Our persecution was so great that we became a reproach to our neighbors—that is, to those who were approaching the faith and directing their hearts toward it. For when they saw our death to be so shameful, they withdrew from the faith.

“And you have made us a mockery and a derision to those who surround us.”

Those who surround us in order to capture and kill us. Mockery is made through the nose; derision through the mouth.

### 15

“You have made us a likeness among the nations.”

This is what it means to make someone a likeness, as Augustine explains: when cursing people give an example from the person whom they detest, saying, “May you die as he died; may you be punished as he was.”

Even today there are enemies of Christ, the Jews, who, when we defend Christ against them, say to us: “May you die as he did.” For they would not have inflicted that death if they had been able to understand the merit of martyrdom.

“You have also made us a shaking of the head among the peoples.”

Shaking the head is a sign of insult. Hence elsewhere it is said:

“They spoke with their lips and shook their head” (Ps. 21).

This they did to the Lord, and to his saints, whom they were able to persecute, seize, mock, hand over, afflict, and kill.

### 16

“All day long”—that is, continually—“my shame from so many reproaches is before me,” that is, before my eyes.

“And the confusion of my face has covered me.”

This is said by comparison, because when we are confused and blush with shame, our face is covered with the redness of blood.

This shame comes to me:

### 17

“From the voice of the one reproaching,” that is, from the one who resists and speaks against me—secretly detracting or speaking against the truth; “and from the face of the enemy,” that is, from the enemy’s presence or pressure, in his will to persecute and in his action.

What is the meaning here? As Augustine explains, the things that belong to the past are not happening to us; the things that belong to the future, which we hope for, are not yet visible.

The past: the people were led out of Egypt in great glory, freed from their persecutors, led through the nations, settled in the kingdom after the nations had been expelled.

What belongs to the future? The people will be led out of this Egypt of the world by Jesus Christ, who will appear in his glory. The saints will be placed on the right and the wicked on the left, to be condemned with the devil to eternal punishment (Matt. 21). We shall receive from Christ an everlasting kingdom with the saints.

These things are future and past; in between lies tribulation. Why? So that the spirit of the one who worships God may appear—how greatly he worships God—and so that it may be seen whether he worships God freely, from whom he freely received salvation.

Therefore, so that this faith of ours, by which we are purified, may be prepared for invisible things—that is, for understanding—all these things happened to the sons of Korah: so that what they possessed might be taken away from the saints, and temporal life itself might also be taken away; so that they might not worship the eternal One for the sake of these temporal things, but might endure through pure love of him everything they would suffer for a time.

Finally, because the sons of Korah understood this, what do they say?

### 18

“All these things have come upon us, yet we have not forgotten you, nor have we acted wickedly against your covenant.”

We have conducted ourselves according to your commandments. Amid so many adversities, we have not withdrawn from you either in faith or in action. Great constancy and perfection are commended here in the martyrs.

What shall we say about ourselves in comparison? If even a slight word of insult is spoken against us by anyone, we immediately burn with anger, lose our composure, and speak like madmen. We seek revenge if we can; if we cannot, we carry hatred in our hearts—the poison of the devil. We forget God; we forget charity and patience. We act wickedly against God’s covenant, having become transgressors of his commandments.

For this reason we read these things: so that we may attentively consider how much the holy martyrs endured for the love of God; that, considering our own frailty and impatience, we may lament and correct ourselves.

But let us continue to hear what they say.

### 19

“And our heart has not turned back.”

Rather, we have always stretched ourselves toward the things that lie ahead, hastening toward the promised prize. When the heart is lifted up in hope, it becomes patient in tribulation. By thinking about eternal rewards, transitory torments are easily despised; and when the way of life is loved, the way of the world is immediately avoided.

Hence it follows:

“And you have turned aside our paths.”

That is, you have caused them to turn aside: the paths of carnal thoughts, desires, and pleasures, away from your narrow and constricted way, which leads to life (Matt. 7).

This is a commendation of divine grace. Whoever enters the Lord’s way should not glory as though in his own righteousness. He ought to recall his former ways and consider from how many lusts and evil desires, from how many negligences and pleasures, the merciful Lord has freed him by his grace.

For this reason the Apostle Paul says:

“I was formerly a blasphemer and a persecutor, but now I have obtained mercy” (1 Tim. 1).

The Lord turns our paths aside from his way when, with his help, we do what is written:

“Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 33).

In this, then, you have turned aside our paths.

### 20

“For you humbled us in a place of affliction.”

That is, in this world, during the time of our pilgrimage. Because God humbled us by afflicting us, he turned us away from our pride, so that, once humbled, we might abandon our paths and follow the ways of the Lord.

“And from that humiliation the shadow of death covered us.”

Not true death, but a shadow; not the death of the soul, but the death of the flesh. The shadow of death is the mortality of the flesh; true death is condemnation with the devil.

Earlier it was said that we had not forgotten you. We would not have been restored to health unless you had sought us. This is what follows:

### 21

“If we have forgotten the name”—that is, the honor—“of our God, so that we withdrew from the faith;

and if we have spread out our hands to a foreign god,” to be revered and worshiped, who neither created us nor did us any good;

and if we have been idolaters,

### 22

“Will not God inquire into these things?”

But he will not inquire into them from us. For he himself knows the secrets of the heart. He knows that we have not forgotten him; this is evident from the fact that we are continually put to death for his sake.

This is what follows:

“For because of you we are put to death all day long.”

That is, continually. Many labor in this world, many are afflicted, and many die for some other reason, not for God. Therefore, when he is about to say “we are put to death,” he rightly first says “because of you,” since it is not punishment but the cause that makes a martyr.

Hence blessed Peter says:

“For what credit is there if, when you sin and are struck, you endure it?” (1 Pet. 2).

“But if, when you do good and suffer, you endure it, this is gracious in the sight of God. For to this you have been called, because Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example so that you might follow his footsteps.”

He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten (Isa. 33).

Therefore what follows is fitting:

“We have been counted as sheep for slaughter.”

That is, we are regarded as suitable for nothing except slaughter. Holy men are rightly compared with sheep because they are simple and innocent, possessing no bite of wickedness. Hence the Lord instructs his disciples when he says:

“My sheep hear my voice” (John 10).

And again:

“Behold, I send you as sheep among wolves” (Matt. 10).

Moses says to Pharaoh:

“We shall sacrifice to the Lord our God the abominations of the Egyptians” (Exod. 8).

The Egyptians disdain eating sheep. But what the Egyptians abominate, the Israelites offer to God. For the simplicity of continence, which every unjust person despises as lowly and worthless, the righteous transform into a sacrifice of virtue. Cultivating upright purity and gentleness, they sacrifice to God what the reprobate, in their folly, regard with abhorrence.

There are two kinds of martyrdom: one of the mind and one of the body; one manifest and one hidden. It is manifest when the body is killed for God; it is hidden when vices are cut away for the love of God.

Therefore the Apostle admonishes us, saying:

“Put to death your members that are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, and so forth” (Col. 3).

Since holy men desire to live for God and die to the world, they continually afflict themselves by mortifying the flesh with fasts, washing away sins with tears, and extinguishing vices, it is rightly said now in their voice:

“For because of you we are put to death all day long. We have been counted as sheep for slaughter.”

But since, placed amid these tribulations, they do not trust in their own strength, they ask for the Lord’s help, as follows:

“Awake! Why do you sleep, O God? Awake, and do not reject us forever.”

To sleep belongs to one who is at rest; to rise belongs to one who is fighting or helping. Christ was sleeping, and the little boat was being covered by the waves. He was awakened; the disciples entreated him, and he commanded the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm (Matt. 8).

So now the Church labors amid the dangers of this world as though amid the waves of the sea. The Lord seems to sleep when he does not rescue. He is awakened by prayers and helps those who labor.

For this reason it asks, “Why do you sleep?” For as long as someone is permitted to labor and the Lord does not wish to help, it is uncertain whether this proceeds from anger or mercy: whether he wishes to test and correct him for a time, or to abandon him entirely.

For this reason the prayer is made when it continues:

“Awake, and do not reject us forever.”

That is, completely. If you abandon us, do not reject us. If you wish us to suffer tribulation, do not wish us to be broken. If you permit us to be tested, do not allow us to perish.

### 23

“Why do you turn your face away?”

As though angry, as though you were not present, as though you had forgotten us.

“Do you forget our poverty?”

That is, that for your sake we abandoned earthly things and are now as though without help and without consolation.

“And do you forget our tribulation?”

That we suffer for love of you and are not rescued.

### 24

“For our soul has been humbled in the dust.”

It has been afflicted by those who are unstable and fruitless, like dust. Of them it is said elsewhere:

“Not so the wicked, not so” (Ps. 1),

but they are like dust which the wind drives from the face of the earth.

Our soul has been humbled in the dust to such an extent that our belly has also clung to the earth.

Augustine appears to have expressed the punishment of excessive humility: whoever is thrown down lies with his belly attached to the earth; he has nowhere further to be humbled. Humiliation has already reached its highest point. Let mercy also come.

The belly of the Church is glued to the earth when the softer and weaker members cling to earthly things out of desire. The Church mourns such people and prays for them when it continues:

### 25

“Rise up, O God; help us and deliver us for the sake of your name.”

Help those who labor; deliver the oppressed. Help us in our weakness; deliver us from evils. And do this not because of our merit, but for the sake of your name, so that it may be spread abroad and glorified, and so that you may be known and praised, who are blessed forever. Amen.

# TITLE OF PSALM 44

### 1

“For the end; for those who are troubled; for the sons of Korah; for understanding; a song concerning the Beloved.”

This epithalamium—that is, a nuptial song—is a song presented to its hearers for delight.
