It is given concerning the Beloved—that is, for the commendation of Christ, who is the Bridegroom of the Church and the Beloved of the Father, according to the saying: “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. 3 and 17; Luke 3).

The reason why the Bridegroom is commended is stated beforehand: it is “for those who will be changed at the end, for the sons of Korah.” That is, it is for those who will be transformed from the body of this humiliation into conformity with the body of Christ’s glory (Phil. 3), who first in this life were sons of Korah—that is, imitators of the sufferings of the Crucified.

This song is presented to the faithful for understanding—that is, so that they may understand the excellence of Christ’s divinity and humanity. Christ is commended in this psalm both according to his humanity and according to his divinity.

The subject of this psalm is the Bridegroom and the bride, that is, Christ and the Church. The psalm proceeds in the following way. In the first part it presents the commendation of the Bridegroom, that is, Christ; in the second, that of the Church. The prophet’s purpose in this psalm, where he introduces God the Father speaking, is to exhort the faithful to strive to live in such a way that they may present themselves to one man—understand, Christ—as a chaste virgin (1 Cor. 11), so that at the wedding they may sit at the right hand of their Bridegroom.

# PSALM 44

### 2

“My heart has uttered a good word; I speak my works to the king.”

The heart of God the Father uttered the Word, because his hidden things and divine essence generated the Son, who is truly and uniquely good, since, as he himself says, “No one is good except God alone” (Mark 10). Whatever other things are good are good from another source; nothing is good in itself except he alone, who is the highest good.

These words show that the Word is consubstantial with the Father. The Father also says that he speaks his works to the king, because he orders all things together with his Son; and through this the Son is understood to be almighty with the Father.

We understand the Father’s divinity by “heart,” because just as through a word we disclose the secrets of our heart to someone, so through the Son the Father’s divinity has been manifested. No one knows the Son except through the Father.

Lest you think that God required some marriage by which to generate the Son, he says: “My heart has uttered a good word,” that is, “From myself I have eternally generated the Son.” Today, human being, your heart generates a plan, and you do not seek a wife. Build something according to the plan born in your heart. Before that structure stands, the plan stands, and already present in the plan is what you are going to make, through which you are going to make it.

Praise the structure that does not yet exist—but praise it in the testing of the plan. Therefore, if all things are through the Word, and the Word is from God, look upon the structure made through the Word, and in this building admire the plan.

“I speak,” he says, “my works to the king.” Do you wonder that God speaks in this way? God’s speaking in this way is eternal. It is written in another psalm: “God has spoken once” (Ps. 61).

God has spoken so many times through the prophets, through the Apostles, and through teachers (Heb. 1); even today he speaks through the saints. How, then, has God spoken once, except because of the good Word?

And why does he say, “I speak my works to the king”? Because all God’s works are in him (Rom. 11). Whatever he was going to make in creation was already in the Word, as it is said in the Gospel: “What was made in him was life.”

I do not merely order all things with the king; I also make all things through him. This is what follows:

“My tongue is the pen of a swift-writing scribe.”

“My tongue”—that is, the Word itself, with the cause put for the effect—is the pen of my scribe. For just as a scribe impresses figures through a pen, so I produce creatures through my Word.

Creation itself is, in a certain sense, a Scripture for us, in which we read and recognize God, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “His invisible things are understood and perceived through the things that have been made, and his eternal power and divinity” (Rom. 1).

And he rightly says, “of one writing swiftly,” because “he spoke, and they were made” (Ps. 148).

“Swiftly”—as Augustine explains—God’s swiftness is such that nothing is swifter. In writings, one letter is written after another, one syllable after another, and one word after another; one does not proceed to the second until the first has been completed. But there nothing is swifter, where the words have not been changed; yet nothing has been set down beforehand, since everything is contained in one.

He has commended the Son according to his divinity, showing him to be consubstantial and co-powerful with the Father. Now he commends him according to his humanity, as follows:

### 3

“You are beautiful beyond the sons of men.”

Why not also beyond the angels? What did he wish to say by “beyond the sons of men,” except that he is human? He is beautiful beyond the sons of men because he alone was free from sin, whereas no other human being was.

When he says, “beautiful in form,” he speaks by way of intensification, just as it is said, “You shall live life” (John 8).

The prophet was representing the person of the Jews when he said: “We saw him, and he had neither form nor beauty” (Isa. 53). Why? Because they did not understand. For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Cor. 2).

But for those who understand, the Word made flesh possesses great beauty. “But far be it from me to glory,” said one of the Bridegroom’s friends, “except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6). It is not enough that you do not blush with shame because of it; you must also glory in it.

Why, then, did he have neither form nor beauty? Because “Christ crucified is a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles” (1 Cor. 1). Why, then, did he have beauty on the cross? Because “the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men” (ibid.).

For us, then, who now believe, let the Bridegroom appear beautiful everywhere. Beautiful was God the Word with God. Beautiful in the Virgin’s womb, where he did not lose his divinity but assumed humanity. Beautiful was the Word as a newborn infant: while he was an infant, while he suckled, while he was carried in hands, the heavens spoke, the angels sang praises, and the star guided the Magi.

He was worshiped in the manger, the food of the gentle. Beautiful in heaven, beautiful on earth, beautiful in the womb, beautiful in his parents’ hands, beautiful in miracles, beautiful under the blows, beautiful inviting to life, beautiful not fearing death, beautiful laying down his soul, beautiful receiving it again, beautiful on the wood, beautiful in the tomb, beautiful in heaven.

Hear the song with understanding, and do not let the weakness of the flesh turn your eyes away from the splendor of his beauty. The highest and true beauty is grace. The prophet’s voice turns toward Christ:

“Grace has been poured upon your lips.”

“The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1). He came among us, preaching repentance for the forgiveness of sins by the word of grace.

So much grace was poured upon Christ’s lips that at his voice the blind saw, lepers were healed, the lame walked, and the dead rose. Of the abundance of this grace Paul says: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Rom. 5). And John says: “From his fullness we have all received” (John 1), “grace upon grace.”

And because you are such, “therefore God has blessed you forever.”

The first covenant promised an earthly land. One thing was promised under the law and another under grace: the land of Canaan was given to the Jews placed under the law, while the kingdom of heaven was established for Christians placed under grace. Therefore, what belonged to those under the law has passed away; the kingdom of heaven, which belongs to those under grace, has not passed away.

Thus, “God has blessed you” not for a time but forever; both now and in the future Christ will always be blessed. And you, such a king,

### 4

“Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most powerful one.”

That is, use the word of your preaching powerfully, of which the Apostle says: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. 6).

By the thigh we understand the Lord’s body, because the place of generation is in the thighs. He girded the sword upon his thigh because he preached the Gospel in the flesh he had assumed.

Hence the Truth says: “I have not come to bring peace, but a sword” (Matt. 10). This sword separates a son from his father, a daughter from her mother, and a daughter-in-law from her mother-in-law.

The father contends with the son, as Augustine explains, because the son wishes to serve God. The father promises an earthly inheritance; the son desires a heavenly one. The father fights; the son resists. But the spiritual sword that separates is stronger than carnal nature that unites.

He rightly says, “upon your thigh, O most powerful one,” because “the weakness of God is stronger than men.” He used this sword most powerfully in the flesh, because he conquered not only human beings but also the powers of the air; he not only destroyed vices but also despoiled hell.

This sword subdues the flesh, cuts away vices, strengthens the spirit, nourishes virtues, and consumes evil desires.

Behold, our king is girded with his sword. Let us now hear how he fights, how he reigns, and with what weapons he advances:

### 5

“In your appearance and your beauty, direct yourself, proceed prosperously, and reign.”

“Appearance” may refer to innocence and holiness of conduct; “beauty” to the splendor of divinity. Through these Christ directs himself—that is, makes himself intent—not to act negligently, but to advance prosperously to battle and reign by conquering.

Or it may be said: “Proceed prosperously from one nation to another, and reign over those you have acquired according to good conduct and virtues.”

This may also be understood in the following way: “Direct yourself in your appearance and your beauty,” so that you may deign to renew and reform in your children the image and likeness which you first gave to our parent.

“Proceed prosperously”: proceed prosperously from the Virgin’s womb; rise prosperously from the tomb; return prosperously from the underworld to the Father. For all these things are prosperous and joyful for us.

“And reign” over the whole world by your authority, O Redeemer, through your precious blood, “because of truth, meekness, and righteousness.” For all these things befit a king. Reign, therefore, since you are true, meek, and righteous.

“And your right hand shall lead you wondrously”—that is, your strength, virtue, and power.

But where will it lead you? To the Father (John 12). Why wondrously? Because, though dead, you conquered the devil.

Or Christ is said to reign because of the truth of the Gospel, the meekness with which he suffered, and the righteousness by which he will judge the good and the wicked.

“And his right hand shall lead him wondrously,” as Augustine explains, doing divine things and enduring human things, laying low the malice of human beings by his goodness.

[Note: The sense seems to require supplementation from the Augustinian exemplar with the words “his right hand shall lead him.” A full stop should then be placed: “It has been said…”]

It has been said concerning the sword; let us now speak of the arrows. For our king has many kinds of armor.

### 6

“Your arrows are sharp.”

They are your words, piercing the heart and arousing love. Hence it is said in the Song of Songs: “I am wounded by love” (Song 2).

In this respect God’s words are called arrows because they secretly attract human beings to the fear and love of God. In the respect that they make human beings cling to God through manifest and compelling reasoning, they are called a sword.

And because you are so equipped for battle, “peoples shall fall beneath you.” They shall worship you and humble themselves before you.

And where will they fall? “In the heart of the king’s enemies”—that is, in the very heart in which they had previously been hostile to you, the king, and in which they had risen up against Christ.

Where will they fall? Before Christ.

They blasphemed Christ; now they plead with Christ. They call him king. They received your arrows; they fell before you. In the heart where you see, they have become friends from enemies. The enemies have been slain; the friends live. The proud have been prostrated; the humble rise.

### 7

Your seats have been made, O God, forever and ever. You dwell in them eternally, according to what is written: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom” (Prov. 14). The rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom. This rod is justice. By such a rod our King governs his kingdom, which is us. For he does not rule who does not correct (from the same author). Just as he is a priest for sanctifying us, so he is a king for governing us.

The people of his kingdom were crooked; they were distorted. They wished to rule themselves, loved themselves, and did not subject their will to God, but wished to bend his will toward their own desires. The King came with the rod of uprightness. He set us straight in justice and corrected our crookedness according to the straightness of his rule. Of this rod it is said elsewhere: “You will rule them with an iron rod” (Ps. 2). It is called iron because it is hard. Justice is inflexible. It rules some and crushes others: it rules the spiritual and crushes the carnal. I rightly say that your rod is one of uprightness, because you—

### 8

You have loved justice, both in yourself and in others, and to such a degree that you have also hated iniquity. And so that you might be such, therefore he anointed you spiritually: O God, your God—that is, he who is consubstantial with you—with the oil of gladness, that is, with the Holy Spirit, above your companions: above the other human beings whom you wished to be companions with you in your kingdom.

The Holy Spirit is rightly compared with the oil of gladness, because just as oil nourishes the flesh and drives away pain, so the anointing of the Holy Spirit both gently cherishes the mind that it fills and makes it joyful. Christ was anointed with this spiritual oil above his companions, because the Holy Spirit was given to the others in portions, whereas in him “all the fullness of divinity dwelt bodily” (Col. 2).

It should be noted that he does not say, “You performed justice,” but “You loved justice.” Nor does he say, “You abandoned iniquity,” but “You hated it.” For many do good more from fear of punishment than from love of justice. Although their action appears good, their will nevertheless remains guilty. Although they appear righteous in their deeds, they are unjust in that they would wish to sin if they could do so with impunity. They abandon wicked deeds but still retain evil desires.

There is some progress in performing works of justice, but this is still insufficient for attaining the kingdom of God, because they do not yet possess the virtue of justice in their hearts. Two things, then, truly make a person righteous: love of the good and hatred of evil. Whoever can possess these two is worthy of the anointing of the Holy Spirit, which grants health and gladness to the soul.

God is anointed by God. Do you hear “anointed”? Understand “Christ.” For Christ is so called from *chrism* (anointing). This name, “Christ,” is the name of anointing. Nor were kings and priests anointed anywhere else except in that kingdom where Christ was foretold.

God, then, was anointed by God. With what oil, if not spiritual oil? For visible oil is a sign in the sacrament, while spiritual oil is the power.

> [Note: [Col. 0823D] From this point, the Augustinian reading seems to require restoration; it is both more obscure and bears the mark of an interpolator’s hand, in both printed editions and manuscript codices: “For visible oil is in the sign; invisible oil is in the sacrament; spiritual oil is within.”]

God, therefore, is man; and therefore God is anointed, because God is man, and he became Christ. We have heard what he was in himself; let it now be told what he was in his own people.

### 9

Myrrh and liquid myrrh and cassia are from your garments, from ivory houses. You are anointed with oil above your companions, and from your garments also—that is, from your humanity, or from your Apostles, who adorn and embellish you, just as a garment adorns its lord—there proceed myrrh, liquid myrrh, and cassia, that is, good fragrances and a good reputation.

Myrrh is a very bitter substance, with which the body of a dead person is anointed so that it will not decay; it drives away worms. By it is signified the mortification of the flesh, which is very bitter and drives away worms—that is, the temptations of the devil—and preserves body and soul from the corruption of vices.

Liquid myrrh is likewise a substance that drives away swellings of the lungs. It is humility, which drives away inflation and every movement of pride.

Cassia is an herb that grows in a watery place, rises to great height, and gives off a strong fragrance. It is faith, which arises in the waters of baptism, grows greatly in the righteous, and gives a good reputation to others.

All these things have proceeded for us from Christ’s humanity; or they are present in the Apostles, who set all these things before us in themselves as an example. These same things have proceeded for us from the ivory houses—that is, from the holy Apostles themselves. They are called houses because the Lord dwells in them; they are ivory either because of their strength or because of the whiteness of their simplicity, or because they were cut, carved, scraped, and polished by various torments.

From them the daughters of kings delighted you in your honor. It is as though he said: because of these fragrances, the individual churches pleased you. Their fathers and rulers were the Apostles, who begot them through the font of baptism—not in their own honor, but in yours.

To this sacrament belongs what is written in the Law: “If a brother has died, his brother shall take his wife and raise up offspring for his brother” (Matt. 8; Deut. 25). Christ died; he withdrew bodily. His brothers took his wife, the Church, in order to generate children through the preaching of the Gospel—not through themselves, but through the Gospel, for the sake of their brother’s name. “In Christ Jesus,” Paul says, “through the Gospel I begot you” (1 Cor. 4). Thus, raising up offspring for their brother in their brother’s name, all those whom they begot named them not Paulines or Petrines, but Christians. This is “in your honor,” because they did not seek their own honor, but yours.

From all these there was formed one bride for the King, one queen, concerning whom it follows:

### 10

The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in a garment of gold and surrounded with variety. The Church is called queen because she rightly rules her children. She stood ready to serve at your right hand—that is, in your better gifts—in a garment of gold, in the adornment of virtues, where wisdom shines most brightly, since wisdom is signified by gold, as it is written: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise.”

The garment of this queen (from Augustine) is both precious and varied in different languages. One language is African, another Syrian, another Greek, another Hebrew, and another this or that. These five languages create the variety of this queen’s garment. Just as every variety of the garment agrees in unity, so all languages agree in one faith. Let there be variety in the garment, but no division.

We have understood the variety as referring to the diversity of languages, and the garment as referring to unity within that variety. What is the gold? Wisdom itself. Whatever the diversity of languages may be, one gold is proclaimed—not a different gold, but the truth represented by gold. For all languages proclaim the same wisdom, the same teaching, and the same discipline. Variety lies in languages; gold in meanings.

Let the prophet address this queen, for he gladly sings to her—and so does each one of us, provided that we know where we are, strive to belong to that body, and belong to it in faith and hope, united to the members of Christ. For he addresses us.

### 11

Hear, daughter, and see. He addresses her (from the same author) as one of the fathers, because the daughters are the kingdom; whether it is the prophet who addresses her or the Apostle, he addresses her as a daughter. Thus we say: “Our fathers the prophets,” and “our fathers the Apostles.” We regard them as fathers, and they regard us as children. One paternal voice addresses one daughter: “Hear, daughter, and see.”

First hear, afterward see. He came to us with the Gospel, and what we do not yet see was preached to us. By hearing, we believe; and by believing, we see.

> [Note: [Col. 0824D] More correctly, in Augustine: “we shall see.”]

Hear, so that you may believe; cleanse your heart by faith. And when I have cleansed my heart, what shall I see? “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5).

And incline your ear—that is, listen humbly. And forget your people: namely, the sects of the Jews or of the Gentiles; the legal rites of Judaism and the idolatry of paganism. And the house of your father—that is, the way of life of the devil. Or “the house of your father” means the vanities of this world, in which, as in his own house, the devil has ruled until now (John 14). You were his daughter through your imitation of evil works.

### 12

And the King will desire your beauty—that is, he will desire you as beautiful after you have forgotten the things that have been mentioned. Therefore you ought gladly to hear the commands given to you. For the one who desires you is not only your King and bridegroom; he himself is the Lord your God—that is, your creator and ruler.

You are married to God the King; from him you have received your dowry, from him your adornment, healing, and redemption. Whatever you possess that pleases him, you possess from him.

These things that have been said about the Church can each of us apply to ourselves. The soul that, abandoning error, believes rightly is adopted as a daughter by God, who was previously a stranger. Once adopted, let it incline its ear and surrender itself entirely to the teaching and understanding of what is said.

Let it first forget its former people; and, like Abraham departing from Chaldea, let it leave the land of its birth and its kindred (Gen. 12). No one doubts that, before we were adopted by God, our father was the one of whom the Savior says: “You are of your father the devil” (John 8).

Therefore, he says, when you have forgotten your ancient father and have been renewed through baptism or repentance, then the King will desire your beauty. Let the soul therefore present itself in such a way that it may be loved by the King. For he himself is its Lord God, to whom it ought to bend the knee and, laying aside pride, take up the yoke of humility (Phil. 2). And they will also worship him—

### 13

And the daughters of Tyre with gifts. The daughters of Tyre are the daughters of the Gentiles; a part signifies the whole. Tyre, being near the land where the prophecy was given, signified the Gentiles who would believe in Christ. They worshiped the Lord with gifts, according to what is written: “Lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven” (Matt. 6), and, “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke 11).

Tyre is interpreted as “distress,” and signifies sinners whom the devil was crushing. Thus the daughters of Tyre worship the Lord: sinners whom the devil afflicted with tight bonds. And they do so with gifts, because they offer themselves to the Lord.

They will entreat your face—that is, they will devoutly pray to God to grant them the ability to attain conformity to you.

All the rich of the people—that is, the rich of every kind, whether consuls, generals, kings, or emperors. Concerning such rich people Paul admonishes his disciple, saying (1 Tim. 6): “Command the rich of this age not to be proud in mind, nor to place their hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who abundantly provides us with everything for enjoyment. Let them be rich in good works, generous in giving, storing up for themselves a good foundation for the future.”

After showing the dignities of the Church, he commends her as praiseworthy according to her interior qualities, saying:

### 14

All the glory of the king’s daughter is within. Hence Paul says: “Our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1).

The foolish virgins did not take oil with them (Matt. 23), because they did not possess glory within their conscience, while they sought it from the mouths of their neighbors. It should be noted that all are said to have lamps, but not all are said to have oil. For the elect and the reprobate alike often display good works in themselves, but only those come to the bridegroom with oil who seek glory not outwardly but inwardly for the things they have done outwardly.

It is therefore necessary not only to do good, but also to guard those deeds with great care, so that “whoever boasts may boast in the Lord” (1 Cor. 10).

And that daughter of the King is clothed around in golden fringes, in varied adornments. She is indeed surrounded with variety, because faith, hope, love, prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance surround her on every side. These virtues are like golden fringes in the Church, since wisdom, knowledge, and the radiance of miracles hang from them. Fringes are placed on garments for adornment. Thus golden fringes proceed, as it were, from the variety of the garment when miracles shine forth from the virtues.

### 15

Virgins will be brought to the King after her. Many others follow the Apostolic and primitive Church that goes before them: virgins—that is, those whole in soul and body—will be brought to the King to serve him.

Here he also indicates that they cannot attain that dignity by themselves unless they are brought to it through preaching and with the help of grace. Hence the bridegroom himself says: “No one can come to me unless my Father draws him” (John 6).

Here there is a transition to the King himself when it follows: Her companions will be brought to you. For those who will be brought are not strangers (from Augustine), but her companions, belonging to her.

By the virgins we can understand those souls who, always preserving bodily integrity, served the heavenly bridegroom in virginity; they occupy the first rank. There are others who, although not virgins, are continent. Although they are not in the same rank, they are nevertheless companions, because after the fall of the flesh they strove to preserve continence of mind.

Among these companions is contained the order of married people who guarded themselves from an adulterous union. Thus these who follow the Church and are placed in the first rank—those who persevere in virginity of body and soul—and the companions, that is, widows and the continent within marriage—all—

### 16

Will be brought in joy and exultation, because even in the present Church the saints greatly rejoice in the purity of their conscience. And concerning this it follows: They will be brought into the temple of the King—that is, into the heavenly Jerusalem.

They will be brought into the temple as priests of God, and into the bridal chamber as the brides of the King and bridegroom. Or they will be brought into the temple so that they may be the temple of the King, so that the Lord may dwell in them as in a temple. As Paul says: “The temple of God is holy, and that is what you are” (1 Cor. 3; 6).

The temple of the King exists in unity. The faithful of God are living stones. This is not a ruined temple, nor one torn apart or divided. The bond joining the living stones is love.

Led, therefore, by grace, they will be brought into the temple of the King, into the unity of perfect love, where they may praise God forever. Then he addresses the Church, saying:

### 17

In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you. The Apostles begot you. They were sent; they preached; they are the fathers; they have been received into glory. In their place, sons have been born: bishops have been appointed.

Do not therefore think yourself abandoned because you do not see Paul, because you do not see those through whom you were born. From your offspring your fatherhood has increased. Sons have been born to you for your work. You will appoint them—that is, you will establish them—in faith and in works, as princes, teachers, and instructors, over all the earth—that is, over the Church spread throughout every part of the earth.

And because the Church has thus been ordered and confirmed, therefore:

### 18

I will remember your name, Lord. That is, I will proclaim the memory of your fame and glory in every generation spread throughout the whole earth, and afterward in the succeeding generation.

Therefore the peoples who are to come, seeing such great glory of your Church, will confess you—that is, they will praise you as its author and ruler—forever, throughout this present life. Not because this life is eternal, but according to their intention and devotion: for if they were always to live here, they would always praise you here.

And into the age that follows this age. O happy are those who will be worthy to praise the Lord forever and ever!

## TITLE OF PSALM XLV

### 1

A psalm of David, for the sons of Korah, for the hidden things, toward the end. This psalm is attributed to the sons of Korah—that is, to imitators of the Crucified, namely the Apostles, who invite future sons of Korah to press toward the end, that is, toward perfection: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 24).

They act to reveal hidden things. In this psalm the coming of Christ is revealed, which had been greatly hidden; also the conversion of the Apostles from the Jews to the Gentiles, the salvation of the Jews in the last times, and peace between God and humanity at the time of Christ’s birth.

The subject is the coming of Christ, from which all the hidden things that have been mentioned proceeded. In the first part he shows that all hope rests on the coming of Christ and on the Apostles’ passage to the Gentiles. In the second part he shows that the Church has been founded upon Christ, to whom the nations and kingdoms are subjected. In the third he admonishes us to attend to the works of this Lord.

The intention is that people should place the hope of their liberation in the coming of God, or that he should assure us of that coming and of the salvation of the Gentiles. In this psalm the primitive Church presents itself to posterity as an example of patience, namely, so that they may not fail under the weight of tribulations when they hear that those who sought the salvation of all endured so many and such great things patiently.

## PSALM XLV

### 2

Our God is refuge and strength. He who is God of all by power, but our God by will and grace, is our refuge—that is, our security. And because there are many refuges that are not safe, he adds: “and strength”—a strong, unconquerable refuge.

There are certain refuges (from Augustine) where there is no strength; when someone flees there, he becomes weaker rather than stronger. If, for example, you flee to some powerful person in the world in order to make him a powerful friend on your behalf, it seems to be a refuge. Yet the uncertainties of this world are so great, and the evils of the powerful increase daily to such an extent, that when you flee to such a refuge you begin to fear more there. Previously you feared only for your own affairs; when you flee to such a person, you will fear him as well.

For many who had fled to such refuges, when those to whom they had fled fell, were themselves sought out—people whom no one would have sought had they not fled to such places. Our refuge, however, is not like that: our refuge is strength. When we flee there, we shall be safe.

And he not only defends us from enemies, but is also our helper, so that we may not merely avoid being conquered, but may be able to conquer others, in the tribulations that have found us exceedingly.

For we would be troubled beyond what the frailty of the flesh could bear (1 Cor. 10) unless we were aided by divine assistance. It is one thing to encounter tribulations and another for tribulations to encounter us. We encounter tribulations when we endure those for which we have already prepared ourselves. They encounter us when they seize us unexpectedly. The weapons that have not been foreseen strike more heavily.

Since the holy martyrs therefore sometimes suffered tortures so great that they could not previously even have imagined them, they rightly declare that they have been found by tribulations exceedingly. “Exceedingly” means what cannot be imagined or endured.

But because they receive help and strength from almighty God, they remain unconquered and fearless amid those very excessive torments and say:

### 3

Therefore we will not fear while the earth is shaken and the mountains are moved into the heart of the sea. A little earlier they were anxious, but suddenly, because of their excessive tribulations, they are secure and placed in great tranquility. To fear nothing is great tranquility of mind.

Let the earth be shaken, let the sea be shaken, let all the elements be shaken: the servant of God remains fearless.

The sea (from Augustine) signifies this world, in comparison with which the Jewish people appeared like land. It was not covered with the bitterness of idolatry, but was like dry land, surrounded by the bitterness of the Gentiles as by the sea.

It was destined that the earth should be shaken—that is, that very Jewish people—and that the mountains should be moved into the heart of the sea (Isa. 2). First, the great mountain itself was prepared on the summit of the mountains. For it abandoned the Jewish people and came to exist among the Gentiles, transferred from land to sea by the Apostles, to whom he had said: “If you have faith in yourselves like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here and cast yourself into the sea,’ and it will happen” (Matt. 17).

That is, through your most faithful preaching it will happen that this mountain—that is, that I myself—will be glorified among the Gentiles, recognized among the Gentiles, and proclaimed among the Gentiles; and that what had been foretold about me will come to pass: “The people whom I did not know served me” (Ps. 17).

And when those mountains too had been moved, Scripture tells us this. When the Apostle was preaching, the Jews rejected the word, and the Apostle Paul said: “We had been sent to you, but because you rejected the word of God, we are going to the Gentiles” (Acts 13). Thus the mountains were moved into the heart of the sea.

In truth, the Gentiles believed in the mountains, so that those mountains might be in the heart of the sea—not like the Jews, of whom it was said: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 26).

For in the New Testament the Lord promises this through the Prophet, saying: “I will place my laws in their hearts” (Jer. 31). These laws and commandments, implanted through the Apostles in the faith and belief of all the Gentiles, are called mountains moved from the mountains into the heart of the sea.

Then we who have been pierced in heart will not fear, lest we become part of the rejected Jews, like branches that have been broken off. For they believed and came to the Apostles. Let those, then, fear from whom the mountains depart. We have not withdrawn from the mountains; and when they were moved into the heart of the sea, we followed them.

What follows (from the same author) from the fact that the mountains were moved into the heart of the sea? Attend and see the truth. When these things were being said, they were obscure because they had not yet come to pass; but now who does not recognize the events that have occurred?

Let the divine page be an open book to you, so that you may hear these things. Let the world be an open book to you, so that you may see them. In those books, only those who know letters can read them; throughout the whole world, even the unlearned can read.

What happened, then, when the mountains were moved into the heart of the sea?

### 4

Their waters roared and were troubled. When the Gospel was preached, they said [the implied words are]: “What is this? This preacher seems to be an announcer of foreign demons.” Thus said the Athenians (Acts 17).

And with what tumult did the Ephesians wish to kill the Apostles when, in the theater, they raised such an uproar for their Diana that they cried out: “Great is Diana of the Ephesians!” (Acts 19).

Amid these waves and sounds of the sea, those who had fled to that refuge did not fear. Finally, the Apostle Paul wanted to enter the theater, but the disciples restrained him, because it was still necessary for him to remain in the flesh for their sake (Phil. 1).

Nevertheless, their waters roared and were troubled. The mountains were shaken by his strength. Whose strength? Was it the sea’s—or rather God’s, of whom it was said: “Refuge and strength, helper in tribulations that have found us exceedingly”?

For the mountains were shaken—that is, the powerful of this age. There are mountains of God and mountains of the world. The devil is the head of the mountains of the world; Christ is the head of the mountains of God. But through these mountains, those mountains were shaken.

Then they issued laws against the Christians, when the mountains were shaken.

> [Note: [Col. 0827D] Thus too the seven Augustinian manuscripts read; the received reading, however, is “voices.”]

As the waves roared, the mountains too were shaken, and there was a great earthquake when the waters were disturbed (Matt. 28). But for whom were these things? For that city founded upon a rock (Matt. 7). Let the waters roar and the mountains be shaken when the Gospel is announced. What of you, city of God? Hear what follows:

### 5

The force of the river makes the city of God glad.

> [Note: [Col. 0828D] The reading was *Conturbantur* as one word; we correct other, slighter matters below.]

When the mountains are shaken and the sea rages, God (from Augustine) does not abandon his city through the force of the river.

What is this force of the river? It is that outpouring of the Holy Spirit of which the Lord said: “Let the one who thirsts come and drink. Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7).

Thus these rivers flowed from the belly of Peter, Paul, John, and the other Apostles, as well as from the other faithful Evangelists. As these rivers flowed from one river, many currents of the river made the city of God glad.

And so that you may know that this was said about the Holy Spirit, in the same Gospel the Evangelist immediately says: “Now he said this about the Holy Spirit” (John 7), whom those who were to believe in him would receive. “For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified.”

When Jesus was glorified after the resurrection (Mark 16), and glorified after the ascension, on the day of Pentecost the Holy Spirit came, filled the believers, and they spoke in tongues (Acts 2). They began to preach the Gospel to the Gentiles (Matt. 28).

From this the city of God was made glad, while the sea was troubled by the sound of its waters and the mountains were shaken, seeking what they should do, how they might drive away the new teaching, and how they might eradicate the Christian race from the earth. Against whom? Against the force of the river that makes the city of God glad.

And it follows: The Most High has sanctified his tabernacle. Since the name of sanctification follows, it is clear that the force of the river is to be understood as the Holy Spirit, by whom every devout soul believing in Christ is sanctified, so that it may become the city of God.

> [Note: [Col. 0828D] In Augustine: “so that it may become a citizen of the city of God.”]

There is one river, one Spirit, divided into seven horns, which are: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord (Isa. 11).

The Holy Spirit is therefore called a river because he extinguishes the desires and fires of the flesh. He is called forceful because no one resists him.

The Church is called a city either because of the concord of its inhabitants, or because of the fortification of its virtues, or because it has a law and a king. The Spirit makes it so glad that it even rejoices in tribulations (Eph. 4).

It is also called a tabernacle (Rom. 5), because the Lord is served as a soldier in it. This tabernacle is sanctified through the Spirit. For everyone who has the Holy Spirit is holy; and whoever does not have him cannot be holy.

God not only makes his Church glad and sanctifies it, but is also in its midst, so that it may not be moved from good to evil. This is what follows:

### 6

God is in its midst; it will not be shaken. Therefore (from Augustine), is God enclosed by a place? And are the things surrounding him broad, while he who is surrounded is confined? Far be it from you to think anything of the sort about God, who is contained by no place and whose seat is the conscience of the devout.

God’s seat is in human hearts in such a way that, if a human being falls away from God, God remains in himself—not as though he falls because he cannot find a place where he is. Rather, he lifts you up so that you may be in him when you lean upon him, so that, if he withdraws himself, you may fall. If you withdraw yourself, he will not fall.

> [Note: [Col. 0829D] I prefer the reading in the received text of Augustine: “rather than that you lean upon yourself.”]

What, then, does “God is in its midst” mean? It signifies that God is equal to all and shows no partiality. Just as what is in the middle has equal distances from all boundaries, so God is said to be in the midst because he cares equally for everyone. He is in the midst—that is, in what is common—because he is set before all equally.

Or he is there because he is the column that supports every part of the house. And he not only supports it so that it may not collapse, but will also help it to act well: in the morning—that is, at the beginning of conversion—in the dawn, that is, through the illumination of the Holy Spirit.

Morning properly means the time before the light. Dawn is when the day first rises. When, because of the sins we have committed, we hasten toward repentance or conversion, leaving the darkness and drawing near to the light, this is our morning.

But after morning comes dawn, because through the beginning of conversion one comes to the source and light of virtue. Since this does not happen through our own powers but through divine assistance, it is rightly said here: God will help it at morning, at dawn.

The Church is firm not only because God is in its midst; through its preaching others have also come to conversion. Hence it follows:

### 7

The nations were troubled—with a good trouble, leading to repentance—and the kingdoms bowed down. The rulers or regions were humbled, according to what is written: “All kings will worship him; all nations will serve him” (Ps. 71).

And how did this happen? It follows and says: He gave his voice—that is, his preaching—and the earth was moved—that is, earthly people were moved to conversion.

This is the voice of which the same Psalmist says elsewhere: “The voice of the Lord in power; the voice of the Lord in majesty” (Ps. 28). He gave this voice through the Apostles, and the earth was moved from unbelief to faith, from vices to virtues, from the devil to God.

Who is the one who gave his voice? Let the Apostles speak; let the Church speak; let the renewed people speak:

### 8

The Lord of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our protector. Who is not moved by this voice? Who does not tremble with joy? Who does not marvel at such great grace?

The Lord of hosts, the Lord of angels, is himself with us in the flesh. He was received by us, and he received us. He took our humanity and received us into his divinity (Phil. 2). He became a participant in our mortality so that he might make us participants in his immortality (Rom. 8).

Let Christians therefore say what neither Jews, nor pagans, nor heretics can say: “The Lord of hosts is with us.” He himself had also promised this through his Prophet, saying: “I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they will be my people” (Jer. 31).

Hence the Truth himself says to his disciples: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28).

The Lord of hosts and the God of Jacob himself gives strength to those who are spiritually Jacob—that is, to those who wrestle with the flesh and overcome vices. For Jacob means “one who supplants.”

And because this grace is wondrous and saving, he adds, inviting and admonishing everyone:

### 9

Come and see—that is, believe and understand—the works of the Lord, which he has done for us.

“Let us go,” says the Church; “let us forget the things that lie behind. Let us pass from earthly things to spiritual things, and with the eyes of the heart let us see the wonders that he has placed as a sign.”

For wonders are called those things in which something other than what appears is signified: upon the earth—that is, upon earthly people. What are those wonders?

### 10

He removes wars to the end of the earth. For he made peace between God and humanity, and removed idolatry and the worship of the old Law, through which Jews and Gentiles were at odds, and made both one (Col. 1).

That peace of God with humanity was not confined to one land, but extended to the ends of the earth. For “from the rising of the sun to its setting, the name of the Lord is praiseworthy” (Ps. 121).

The Lord also removes wars within us when he extinguishes the vices that fight against one another. Hence it follows: He will break the bow, shatter the weapons, and burn the shields with fire.

The bow (from Augustine) is ambush; the weapons are open assault; the shield is the empty protection of presumption. The fire by which these things are burned is the fire of which the Lord says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12), and of which he says in the Psalm: “There is no one who can hide from its heat” (Ps. 18).

When this fire burns intensely, no weapons of impiety will remain in us. Everything must be broken, crushed, and burned. Remain unarmed, possessing no aid of your own; and the weaker you are, having none of your own weapons, the more he receives you, of whom it was said: “The God of Jacob is our protector.”

You were strong, as though by yourself, but you are shaken in yourself. Lose the weapons in which you presumed. Approach the Lord, who says: “My grace is sufficient for you.” You too say: “When I am weak, then I am strong.” This is the Apostle’s voice (2 Cor. 12).

He had lost all his weapons, as though they were his own strength, when he said: “I will boast in nothing except my weaknesses” (ibid.).

But when the Lord receives us, does he send us away unarmed? He arms us, but with the weapons of evangelical truth, self-restraint and salvation, faith, hope, and love (2 Cor. 10).

We have these weapons, but not from ourselves. The weapons that we had from ourselves have burned; nevertheless, we have been kindled by that holy fire.

Earlier we were invited to see the works of the Lord. Now the Lord himself invites us to see him, saying:

11. Be still, and know that I am God. You have seen my works. Now prepare yourselves to see the craftsman himself. And, so that you may be fit for this: Cease from earthly things; empty yourselves of evils. Let there be no tumult in your mind. Let everything be peaceful, everything cleansed. For blessed are the pure in heart, because they shall see God (Matt. 5).

For this purpose we have now left behind the impediments of the world and the cares of the age, and have withdrawn to the solitude of the monastery [Note: [Col. 0830D] He plainly reveals himself to be a monk. Compare what we said about his profession of life in the Preface.] [Col. 0830D] so that we may devote ourselves more freely to God, and not to those things in which our adversary delights, 231. For it is certain that when we are idle and negligent, when we do not raise our minds toward heavenly desires, when we grow cold toward the love of God, when we spend the day in chatter and in evil thoughts, then we are more at leisure for the devil than for God.

This is signified by what is written: “The enemies saw her and mocked her Sabbaths” (Lam. 1). The Sabbath is called rest. And our Sabbaths are mocked by the enemies when the evil spirits see us devoting ourselves to idleness and vanity. Let us therefore strive to possess what the Lord chiefly desires in us: namely, a mind freed from every wickedness. Having avoided those things by which the Holy Spirit is offended, let us devote ourselves to humility, tranquility, and charity; so that what is said may be fulfilled by us: “Be still, and know that I am God.” For we shall be worthy to see God if we first strive to cease from unlawful things and to remain tranquil in mind.

A little earlier (from Augustine) I said that by the name “earth” the Jewish people are signified, and by the name “sea” the other nations: “The mountains were moved into the heart of the sea. The nations were troubled, the kingdoms were bowed down; the Most High gave his voice, and the earth was shaken. The Lord of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our protector.” Miracles were performed among the nations; faith among the nations is fulfilled; the weapons of human presumption burn; one rests in tranquility of heart, so that God, the author of all his gifts, may be known.

And after their glorification, does he then abandon the Jewish people? Concerning them the Apostle says: “For I say to you, do not be wise in your own eyes: blindness in part has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter”—that is, until the mountains should be moved here, so that the clouds might rain here, and here the Lord might bow down kingdoms by his thunder, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter. And what afterward? “And so all Israel shall be saved.” Therefore here too, preserving the same order, he says: “I will be exalted among the nations, and I will be exalted in the earth”—that is, in the sea and in the earth—so that all may now say what follows:

12. “The Lord of hosts is with us; our protector is the God of Jacob.”

The Lord our God has spread among us in many different ways, through his books and his Scriptures, the faith in which we live and from which we live. While varying the mysteries of his words, he commends one faith. For one and the same reality is expressed in many ways, not so that it may be varied through weariness of the manner of speaking, but so that the one reality may be held through their agreement.

And so, in this psalm, which we have heard sung and to which we have responded by singing, we shall say things that you know. Yet perhaps, with God’s help and gift, we shall bring you some sweetness when, having been reminded, you ruminate on things that you knew in one place and another. For even in that “rumination” by which God signifies clean animals, he wished to suggest that every person who hears ought to take what he hears into his heart and not be too sluggish to ponder it: so that, when he hears, he may be like one eating. But when he recalls what he has heard and remembers it through the sweetest reflection, let him become like one ruminating.

In another way the same things are said, and they cause us to think sweetly about what we know and willingly to hear those same things again: the manner of speaking is varied, and the ancient reality is renewed by that very manner of speaking.

## TITLE OF PSALM XLVI

1. The title of the psalm reads: “For the end; for the sons of Korah; a psalm for David himself.” This psalm suits the prophet David, who speaks here in the person of the Apostles. I say that it is a psalm proposed to the sons of Korah, directed through this toward the end. Its subject is Christ ascending. Or its subject is the converted Gentiles, namely the sons of Korah themselves, who are the sons of Christ.

In the first part he exhorts us all to the praise of God. In the second he describes the kingdom of Christ through his ascension [Col. 0831D]. His intention is to invite us to the praises of God. The psalm is sung for the sons of Korah. Therefore it was sung for Christians.

Let us listen as the sons of that bridegroom whom foolish boys crucified at the place of Calvary (John 19). They deserved to be devoured by beasts; we deserve to be crowned by angels. For we recognize the humility of our Lord and are not ashamed of it. We are not ashamed of him who was mystically called “bald,” because of the place of Calvary. For the very cross on which he was mocked did not allow our forehead to be bald, since he marked it with his sign. Finally, so that you may know that these words are spoken to us, see what is said:

## PSALM XLVI

2. “All nations, clap your hands.” Were the Jewish people all nations (from Augustine)? But blindness in part happened to Israel, so that foolish boys might cry, “Bald one, bald one” (2 Kings 2); and thus [Col. 0832A] the Lord might be crucified at the place of Calvary, pour out his blood, redeem us, and fulfill what the Apostle says: “Blindness in part has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter” (Rom. 11).

Let the vain, dull, and foolish mock, and let them say, “Bald one, bald one.” But you, redeemed by that blood (1 Pet. 1), which was poured out at the place of Calvary: “All nations, clap your hands”—for grace has come to you.

What does “clap” mean? Rejoice. But why “with your hands”? Because of good works. If there is only the voice, it is not good, because the hands are sluggish. If there are only the hands, that too is not good, because the tongue is mute. Let hands and tongue agree: let the tongue confess, and let the hands act.

“Shout joyfully to God”—that is, conceive in your mind such great praise of God that it cannot be expressed in words, so that the shout of joy may be in a voice of exultation. That is, praise God not only in your heart but also with an exultant voice. Proclaim him to others. And he adds the reason why he should be praised, saying:

3. “For the Lord”—because he rules every creature; “the Most High”—because he is powerful and effective in carrying out his will. And so that you may not trust in his goodness if you do evil, he is also “terrible,” because he will be the future judge: he will punish the ungodly. And he is “king,” because by his power he spiritually rules his own.

“Great over all the earth,” because there is no part of the earth where he does not rule. He who seemed small and despised has been made terrible and exalted; he who had been only in the kingdom of the Jews now reigns over the whole earth. It is not enough for him to have only one nation under him; therefore he gave so great a price from his side that he might purchase the whole world. Therefore, through the voice of the preachers, it is added:

4. “He subjected peoples to us”—that is, the Jews—and “nations under our feet.” He says “under our feet” so that we may understand the utter humility of those subjected, 233. For the Lord so ordered the Church that he willed some to be rulers and others subjects. Hence in another psalm those subjected say: “You have placed men over our heads” (Ps. 65).

The duty of rulers is to preach, exhort, correct, and hold the place of Christ in the churches (1 Tim. 3). The duty of subjects is to listen, obey, and show every submission to their rulers as to the Lord Christ himself (Heb. 13).

For when they say, “He subjected peoples to us,” they do not say this in their own person, but in the person of him whose ministry they perform. Hence Peter admonishes some, saying: “Be subject to every human creature for the Lord’s sake” (1 Pet. 2). That submission which is made for God is exhibited not so much to human beings as to God.

Therefore, when the holy preachers say, “He subjected peoples to us, and nations under our feet,” it must by no means be understood as though they wished to attribute this to themselves. The Apostle Paul rebukes those who wished to submit to him as a human being, saying: “Was Paul then crucified for you, or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” (1 Cor. 1). Thus, in this statement they do not seek to commend themselves, but rather him whose authority was in them, and to whom obedience was given through them more than to them.

By their voice he further adds:

[Col. 0832D] 5. “He chose for us his inheritance.” That is, he chose the nations to be joined to us as an inheritance. Or, “he chose for us” means that, standing in his place, we might cultivate the inheritance, removing the thorns of vices by plowing with the plowshare of discipline and sowing the seeds of virtues.

In the word “chose,” divine grace is commended, in accordance with what the author of grace himself says to his own: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15). This grace is declared even more clearly when it is added: “The beauty of Jacob whom he loved.”

There were two brothers, Jacob and Esau (Gen. 25); and before they had done anything good or evil, the Lord said: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. 1; Rom. 9). Through Jacob, therefore, those chosen by grace are understood.

The Lord therefore “chose the beauty of Jacob whom he loved”: not because he was beautiful when he was chosen, or because he was loved on account of a beauty he already possessed, but because he already loved in Jacob that beauty which he was afterward going to give through grace. Thus he chose for himself a Church “not having spot or wrinkle” (Eph. 5), not because it was without spot when it was chosen, but because he chose the foul in order to make it beautiful.

Then he shows in what order the nations were chosen, when he adds:

6. “God has ascended with jubilation.” For after the ascension the Holy Spirit was sent upon the Apostles (Acts 2), and the Gospel was preached to the Gentiles (Matt. 28), and thus they were chosen.

What is jubilation (from Augustine) except an amazement of joy that cannot be explained in words? How astonished with joy were those who saw going into heaven the one whom they had mourned as dead (Mark 16)! Truly, words would not have sufficed for that joy. It remained to exult with a shout over what no one could explain.

There too was the voice of the trumpet, that voice of the angels. For it was said: “Like a trumpet, lift up your voice” (Isa. 38). The angels proclaimed the Lord’s ascension. The disciples saw the ascending Lord [Note: [Col. 0833D] Augustine’s text should again be emended. He prefers, with a different meaning, “the disciples ascending with the Lord.” The Author and the nine manuscripts praised by the Benedictine editors agree with one another. Below we restore our Author’s reading, adding the mark of interrogation in place of the affirmative mark.]—clinging, wondering, astonished, saying nothing, but exulting in their hearts.

And now there was the trumpet’s voice in the clear voice of the angels: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus is he” (Acts 1). As though they did not know that he was Jesus! Had they not shortly before seen him before them? Had they not heard him speaking with them (John 20; Luke 24)? Indeed, they had not only seen the appearance of one present but had touched his limbs.

Did they themselves therefore not know that he was Jesus? But in their amazement at the joy of jubilation, as though beside themselves, the angels say: “He is Jesus.” He at whose crucifixion your feet faltered; when he was killed and buried, you thought that you had lost your hope (Matt. 26). Behold, he is Jesus. He has ascended before you; “he will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1). His body is taken from your eyes, but God is not separated from your hearts.

Therefore you, sons of Korah, if you have now understood yourselves and look upon yourselves here, and rejoice because you see yourselves here—

[Col. 0833C] 7. “Sing praise well,” by doing good, “to our God”—that is, for the honor of our God; sing praise in your mind. And he must be praised not only insofar as he is God, but also insofar as he is human. Yet not merely any human being, but a king. And therefore he adds: “Sing praise to our king; sing praise.”

God must be praised because he created us. He must be praised because he redeemed us. This king is God and human: God before the flesh, God in the flesh. He must therefore also be praised because:

8. “God is king of all the earth.” What then (from Augustine)? Was he not previously God of all the earth? Is he not God of heaven and earth as well? Since all things were made through him, what could anyone say was not his? But not all people had recognized their God; and where he was recognized, it was as though he were God only there: “God is known in Judea” (Ps. 75).

The sons of Korah did not yet say, “All nations, clap your hands.” Now he is recognized by all, because what Isaiah says has been fulfilled: “He himself, your God who rescues you, shall be called the God of the whole earth.” Therefore he adds:

“Sing praise wisely”—that is, act well, not for earthly things, lest you be comparable to the foolish virgins who, taking their lamps, did not take oil with them in their vessels (Matt. 25). They signify souls that live continently and perform good works, which are represented by the lamps. But while they seek to please human beings by these things, they neglect to have oil in their vessels—that is, the brightness of glory in their consciences.

Such people seem to sing praise to God insofar as they do good things; but they sing foolishly, because they lose those same good things through vain glory. To sing praise wisely, therefore, is to do what is right and, concerning those very right actions, to wish to please God alone.

It is not without purpose that “sing praise” is said so many times. He repeats it and presses it upon us in order to rouse the sluggish; and the frequent repetition of the same word expresses an excess of joy. Or, “sing praise” five times may be referred to the five bodily senses, so that we may turn sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch to good use.

Then he shows how he is king of all the earth, when he adds:

9. “God has reigned over the nations.” And so that no one might understand that he also reigns in evil things, he specifies: “God sits upon his holy throne.” That is, he reigns among the nations in such a way that he nevertheless remains among the holy. Hence it is written: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom” (Wis. 7).

Where the devil reigned, Christ now reigns. The devil reigned through pride, lust, anger, and vices. Christ reigns through humility, chastity, gentleness, and the other virtues, so that we may no longer be slaves of sin but free in righteousness (Rom. 6). If we do these things, we shall be the kingdom of God and the seat of God.

He explains how it happened that he reigns over the nations.

10. “The princes of the peoples have been gathered together with the God of Abraham.” It is as though he said: kings and other powers who formerly opposed God have been gathered together through faith with the God in whom Abraham believed (Heb. 11).

Among those princes was the centurion whose faith is commended in the Gospel (Matt. 8). See how what John says has been fulfilled: “God is able to raise up children to Abraham from these stones” (Matt. 3). Were not the nations stones when they worshiped stones, as it is said of them elsewhere in the psalm: “Let those who make them become like them” (Ps. 113)?

And so they approached the faith, because “the gods of the earth are greatly exalted”—that is, the Apostles and holy preachers: gods by grace, strong through faith, greatly elevated in signs and virtues. And thus it happened that many were born into the faith.

## TITLE OF PSALM XLVII

[Col. 0834C] 1. “A psalm of song for the sons of Korah, on the second day of the week.” This psalm is proposed to the sons of Korah—that is, to the sons of Christ, who was crucified at the place of Calvary. For Korah, as has often been said, is interpreted as “Calvary.”

It is called a psalm of song because it concerns something over which we ought especially to exult: for it sets forth the great dignity of the Church. It is a psalm, I say, assigned to the second day of the week—that is, concerning the foundation of the Church, which is signified by the foundation of the earth, which took place on the second day (Gen. 1).

For on the first day light was separated from darkness (ibid.), signifying the resurrection of Christ, by which the light of immortality was separated from mortality. On the second day the firmament was made, signifying the time after the resurrection in which the holy Church was founded.

In the first part he describes the Church and commends it in many ways: at one time through its founder, at another through the situation of its place, and at another through its extension. He also praises it for its gifts. He commends it as well because certain people who wished to destroy it, recognizing its dignity, were converted to it. Then he commends one particular and notable gift of the Church: that the mercy of God dwells in it.

In the second part he treats of the orders of that Church. His intention is to exhort all people to enlarge this city. This is the voice of the perfect.

## PSALM XLVII

[Col. 0834D]

2. “Great is the Lord and exceedingly worthy of praise.” That is, he is of great dominion and great power, and therefore exceedingly worthy of praise, beyond what the tongue can express.

And this greatness and praiseworthiness is especially perceived “in the city of our God”—that is, in the construction of the Church, which is fortified by virtues, enlarged by charity, and gathered together through faith for right living, 236. Such a city is not Babylon’s—that is, it is not a city of the confused or of heretics—but it is the city “of our God.”

Here he commends the Church through God the craftsman. It is a city, I say, “set upon his holy mountain”—that is, upon Christ, or upon the mountain of virtues or steadfastness. This city has been possessed by such a lord. It has been constructed from stones of this kind—that is, from Jews and Gentiles. And this is what he adds:

3. “It is founded in the exultation of the whole earth.” That is, it has been firmly built from inhabitants of the whole earth who exult in the remission of sins; or, “it is founded in the exultation of the whole earth” means that it is founded for the exultation of all believers.

He explains this in parts when he adds: “Mount Sion, the sides of the north, the city of the great king.”

Mount Sion, on which the head of the Jewish kingdom was situated, signifies the Jews themselves. By “the sides of the north” the Gentiles are designated, who, numbed by the cold of unbelief, were possessed by the devil. Since the north wind constricts with cold, it is not inappropriate that the name “north” should be taken for the torpor of the evil spirit.

Isaiah also bears witness to this, reporting that the devil said: “I will sit on the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north” (Isa. 14). The evil spirit held the mountain of the covenant because he subjected to unbelief the Jewish people, who had received the Law. He still presides over the mountain of the covenant when he holds the hearts of teachers. He also sat on the sides of the north because he possessed the cold minds of the Gentiles.

Hence, in the voice of the bridegroom, it is said in the Song of Songs: “Rise, north wind, and come, south wind; blow through my garden, and its spices will flow” (Song 4). For when the north wind—that is, the evil spirit—withdraws, the Holy Spirit fills minds like the south wind. When he blows upon them and warms them, the fragrances of virtues immediately flow from the hearts of the faithful.

Such people (from Augustine) become “the city of the great king”: people freed from unbelief and the superstition of demons, believing in Christ [Note: [Col. 0835D] Augustine has “were joined closely together” (colliniati).] and joined closely to that city. They came together at the corner of the wall from the circumcision (Rom. 15). And they became the city of the great king, those who had been the sides of the north.

All who cling to the devil are the sides of the north. Let them cling to Christ, and they will belong to the city of the great king. In these people there is great glory and honor for the Almighty. For a physician’s glory is great when a sick person recovers from a condition of despair.

Another commendation follows:

4. “God will be known in her houses when he receives her.” In the houses of this city—that is, in individual believers, who are called houses because the Lord dwells in them—God will be known, because they will have knowledge of God when he receives her to guard and protect her from enemies.

Or “in houses” is said because of the two walls, the Jews and the Gentiles (Eph. 2). Grace is commended when it says, “when he receives her.” For what would this city be if he had not received her? Would she not immediately fall if she did not have such a foundation? Let no one therefore glory in his own merits. But “whoever glories, let him glory in the Lord” (2 Cor. 10).

Now see how those sides of the north come:

5. “For behold, the kings of the earth have been gathered together.” Behold, the kings and powers of this age have been gathered from many places and many peoples. They have come together into one: to the cornerstone, which makes one from many [Col. 0835D] (Eph. 2).

237 6. “They themselves, seeing thus,” understanding the city of God thus founded, thus constructed, thus adorned, and thus firm, “were astonished.” After their astonishment at the miracles of the Church of Christ, “they were troubled” because of their sins; they were moved to repentance. “Trembling seized them,” because of fear of the future wrath.

The order of the words should be noted. First they see, and by seeing they are astonished; then, returning to themselves, they are troubled and tremble.

And you do likewise. Let the eyes of your heart be opened. See and admire the glory of this city of God. Consider how powerful it is in virtues, how it shines with miracles, how it despises earthly things, with what desires it longs for heavenly things, and how great its future reward and blessedness will be.

As you consider and admire such things, return to yourself and mourn your sins. Fear the strict judgment of God; tremble within yourself, so that you may be able to be joined to this blessed people, concerning whom it is added: “There were pains, as of a woman in labor.”

In that trouble and trembling there were fruitful pains, like those of a woman in labor. For the old human being gave birth to the new (Rom. 6). When a woman gives birth, she is sorrowful; but when she has borne the child, she no longer remembers her distress because of the joy that a human being has been born into the world (John 16).

So a sinful soul, when it repents, suffers great pain and feels great anguish within itself. But after it has received the fruit of repentance—that is, absolution and the remission of sins—it no longer remembers the distress of repentance because of the joy of salvation.

“Because of fear,” Isaiah says, “we conceived and were in labor and bore the spirit of salvation” (Isa. 26). Thus the kings conceived through fear of Christ, so that by laboring they might give birth to salvation.

And the fact that those pains were fruitful did not arise from their own merits but from the grace of God. Therefore it is added:

8. “With a vehement spirit you will crush the ships of Tarshish.” According to [Note: [Col. 0835D] Not, however, in his own interpretation, but in that of Eusebius of Caesarea, whose book On Places the holy Father was translating into Latin. “Tarshish, from which gold was brought to Solomon . . . is understood, according to the prophet Ezekiel, as Carthage. For in the place where we read ‘Carthage’ in the Septuagint interpreters, the Hebrew has ‘Tarshish.’ What he himself thought, he immediately explains, saying that he had expounded it in his book of Letters to Marcella [Col. 0836D] and in the books of Hebrew Questions. In fact, in these places—Letter 37 to Marcella and Questions on Genesis, chapter 10—he takes an entirely different view, which there is no time to recount. In his Commentaries on Isaiah, book and chapter II, and likewise book XVIII, chapter 66, he reports that, according to the opinion of the Hebrews, the name Tarshish simply (ἁπλῶς) signifies the sea, or, according to others, the region of India.] Jerome, Tarshish is the same as Carthage.

The beginnings of the kingdom in Carthage flourished through its ships, to such an extent that it excelled other nations in commerce and navigation. Hence that city became excessively proud, so that the pride of the nations, presuming upon uncertain things as upon blasts of wind, is rightly understood through its ships.

But “with a vehement spirit the ships of Tarshish will be crushed,” because through the power of the Holy Spirit all the exaltation of this world is destroyed. This vehement spirit drives away all the winds of temptation and divides all the clouds of thought. It makes everything serene in the mind; “it blows where it wills” (John 3), and changes whom it wills. It crushes vices and nourishes virtues.

The establishment of the Church, however, was not made without prior planning, but had long before been prophesied and was now fulfilled. Therefore it adds:

9. “As we have heard, so we have seen, in the city of the Lord of hosts.” The Lord is rightly called the Lord of hosts because he rules angels, archangels, thrones, dominions, and all the ranks of heaven. And such a Lord, who reigns among the angels, does not disdain to reign in us.

Therefore it immediately adds: “In the city of our God.” He who is the Lord of hosts is also our God—that is, the Lord and God of angels and human beings. There is one city for all, and one Lord and God of all (Eph. 4).

What does “we have heard, and we have seen” mean? It follows and says: “God founded her,” not for a time, as the Synagogue, but forever. To found something is for God to establish it unchangeably.

At a certain time he saw it. He heard it in the promise and saw it in its fulfillment. He heard it in prophecy and saw it in the Gospel. Everything that is now being fulfilled was previously prophesied.

He founded his city by sending his Son, so that everyone who believes in him might not perish but have eternal life. And the Savior himself became our mercy. Concerning him the Church says to that same Lord in his praise:

10. “We have received your mercy, O God, in the midst of your temple.” The Son is rightly called the mercy of God, because through him God had mercy on us. Concerning him it is also said in another psalm: “My God, my mercy” (Ps. 58).

If he had only forgiven sins, Christ could have been called merciful. But because he both forgave faults and, beyond that, gave eternal life to those who did not deserve it, he is rightly called not merely merciful but mercy itself.

He is rightly said to be placed “in the midst,” because he relates equally to all—to noble and ignoble, to uneducated and wise—just as it is written: “Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” (Joel 2). And again: “But to as many as received him, he gave power to become the sons of God” (John 1).

Therefore it is rightly added:

11. “According to your name, O God, so also is your praise to the ends of the earth.” Just as your name, O God, has been spread throughout the world, so your praise proceeds and grows to the ends of the whole earth. For there is no land in which the name of Christ has not been heard.

And truly there will be many righteous people who will praise you, because “your right hand is full of justice”: through your omnipotence you have already converted many to righteousness. They are many who will stand at your right hand (Matt. 25). There will not merely be many who stand at the left; rather, there will be a full mass appointed to the right. And therefore:

12. “Let Mount Sion rejoice, and let the daughters of Judah exult.” That is, both peoples: Judea and the Gentiles.

Why? “Because of your judgments, O Lord.” For you will judge the living and the dead and separate the chaff from the grain (Matt. 13; 25). And although your elect now suffer many troubles while still placed among the wicked, because your judgments are not yet discerned, then surely there will be complete joy and perfect exultation, when, after judgment has been rendered, they will hear: “Come, you blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25).

The Jews are understood by Mount Sion because, as was already said above, the head of the kingdom is there. The daughters of Judah are rightly understood as the Gentiles, but because of their confession of faith. For Judah means “confession,” and all the daughters of confession are daughters of Judah.

Hence (from Augustine) the Apostle says: “For he is not a Jew who is so outwardly, nor is that circumcision which is outward in the flesh; but he is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is of the heart, in the spirit, not in the letter, whose praise is not from human beings but from God” (Rom. 2).

Be such a Jew. Glory in the circumcision of the heart. Others are admonished to be converted when it is added:

13. “Surround Sion, and embrace her.” Surround her through faith, through action, and through good conduct; embrace her with the sweetest embraces of charity.

Do not (from the same author) surround her with scandals, but with charity, so that you may imitate those who live well among you; and through their imitation may you be incorporated into Christ, whose members they are (Rom. 12).

“Tell it in her towers.” That is, established in the height of her fortifications, proclaim her praises. Hence another prophet admonishes, saying: “Ascend upon a high mountain, you who evangelize Sion” (Isa. 40).

For one who still lies below through wicked living ought not to preach the word of God. Hence it is written in another psalm: “But to the sinner God says, Why do you declare my justices and take my covenant in your mouth? But you have hated discipline,” etc. (Ps. 49).

Therefore the divine word must be proclaimed in the towers and on the high mountain. It is right that one who preaches lofty things should live loftily, so that his life may agree with his teaching.
