Accordingly it is appropriately added:

14. “Set your hearts upon her strength.” The strength of this city is the power of charity itself. Nothing is stronger than this virtue, concerning which Solomon says: “Love is strong as death” (Song 8).

For just as, when death comes, it cannot be resisted by any arts or medicines, so against the force of charity the world can do nothing. Hence Paul says: “Who shall separate us from the charity of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? I am certain that neither death nor life, neither things present nor things to come, nor any creature will be able to separate us from the charity of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Rom. 8).

Where charity reigns, greed does not reign, nor pride, anger, envy, lust, or the other vices. Charity extinguishes vices (1 Cor. 13) and nourishes virtues. It is the virtue of virtues and, so to speak, the soul of virtues.

Just as flesh cannot live without a soul, so the other virtues may have an outward form without charity, but they cannot have reality. And just as the soul animates the body, so charity gives life to the other virtues.

For through charity humility flourishes, chastity shines; through charity obedience serves and patience conquers. Thus each virtue derives its whole appearance and all its strength from nowhere other than charity.

Set your hearts, therefore, upon her strength, and “distribute her houses, so that you may declare them to another generation.”

Two houses are to be understood: one from the uncircumcision, the other from the circumcision. It was established (from Augustine) that the Apostles should distribute—that is, distinguish—these houses.

When Saul was called and became Paul (Acts 9), after he had joined himself in unity with his fellow Apostles, he agreed with them that they should go to the circumcision, while he went to the uncircumcision (Acts 11). Through this arrangement of their apostolate they distributed the houses of the city of the great king; agreeing at the corner, they divided the Gospel according to their dispensation and bound it together through charity.

These houses of the city are also distributed among different regions, different congregations, different orders, and different merits. This distribution of houses has a corresponding distinction of rewards in heaven. Hence the Savior says: “In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places” (John 14).

Just as now there are different houses of grace in one city, so then there will be different dwellings of glory in the same eternity (1 Cor. 15).

But what does it mean that you are commanded, O holy Apostles, to “declare them to another generation”? It follows and says:

15. “For this is God, our God, forever and for ever and ever; he will rule us forever.”

We are the other generation. Truly it is another, because it is new. These things were prophesied in the carnal generation, preached and fulfilled in the spiritual generation. Therefore it is declared to us that this God, who is so great and so worthy of praise, is our God—not for a time, but forever.

O sweet joy! O ineffable gift! The Jews had the God of heaven, but not forever, because they rejected him. The Gentiles had many gods of bronze, wood, stone, and gold, but not forever, because they were made from corruptible matter. Concerning them it is written: “The gods who did not make heaven and earth shall perish from the earth and from under heaven” (Jer. 10). “For all the gods of the nations are demons, but the Lord made the heavens” (Ps. 95).

He is the Lord, our God, forever, destined to reign both in this age and in the age to come. He alone, and no other, will rule us forever. If he is our God, he is also our king. He protects us because he is God, so that we may not die. He rules us because he is king, so that we may not fall.

By ruling us he does not break us. For those whom he does not rule, he breaks. Concerning those whom he rules it is written: “You shall rule them with a rod of iron” (Ps. 2). Concerning those whom he does not rule, it is immediately added: “And like a potter’s vessel you shall break them.”

Let us therefore desire to be ruled and liberated by him here, forever and for ever and ever.

[Note: [Col. 0837D] This passage belongs to the immediately following psalm and could easily be attached to the Prologue, or, as Our Author calls it, the Title. Indeed, Augustine, from whom Our Author copied it, inserted it into the little preface to the following psalm [Col. 0838D]. We have thought it better to separate it from the preceding context by a short interval of verses and to inform the Reader of this fact.]

People commonly murmur (from Augustine) who wish to worship God for this reason: that things may go well for them here, when they see those who do not worship God thriving and flourishing in earthly happiness, while they themselves, worshiping God, labor amid hardships, [Col. 0839A] fasts, and the other difficulties of human mortality. [Note: [Col. 0839D] In Augustine: “in necessities.”] Against this disease the divine word speaks to us in this psalm.

# TITLE OF PSALM XLVIII

1. The title is as follows: “For the end, a psalm of David for the sons of Korah.” This psalm is appropriate to the prophet David, who speaks here, and is set forth for the sons of Korah to understand. Its subject is Christ, the Redeemer not of the wicked but of the righteous. Or its subject is contempt for the world. In the first part he sets forth a prologue, to commend the matter about which he is going to speak. In the second part he presents Christ as Redeemer, not of the wicked and lovers of this age, but of the righteous; and in the same part, while reproving their folly, he marks the vanities to which the lovers of this age are devoted. In the third part he admonishes the poor righteous not to concern themselves with these rich people, because their riches will quickly perish.

The Apostles or the Prophet intend in this psalm to dissuade all who exist in faith—Jews and Gentiles alike, free and enslaved, of whatever condition [Col. 0839B] they may be—from desire for earthly things and to turn them toward love of heavenly things. Thus there will be nothing to fear on the day of judgment. At the outset, however, they make their hearers attentive in several ways: because they speak to them prudently, that is, morally; because they speak parabolically; and also because they will learn what they are to proclaim aloud to others from the teacher who presides inwardly, and will fulfill in their works what they preach with their voice.

# PSALM XLVIII

2. “Hear these things, all nations; perceive them with your ears, all you who inhabit the world.” What I say—“perceive with your ears”—means: do not hear casually or in passing. Just as there is some distinction between “Hear” and “Perceive with your ears,” so there is some distinction between “all nations” and “inhabitants of the world.” For he wants us to understand more significantly what he says, “All you who inhabit the world,” so that by “nations” we understand all the wicked, and by “inhabitants of the world,” all the righteous. For he who inhabits is not held fast. But he who is held fast (from Augustine) does not inhabit; rather, he is inhabited.

These words were going to be heard not only by sinners and the impious, but also by the righteous. For now all hear them together, but when the time comes to render an account, those who heard without purpose will be separated from those who perceived with their ears. Let sinners therefore hear. This is what he says: “Hear these things, all nations.” Let the righteous also hear—those who did not hear without purpose, and who govern the earth rather than being governed by the earth. This is what he adds: “Perceive with your ears, all you who inhabit the world.” And again he says:

3. “Both earthborn and sons of men.” What he says (from the same source), “earthborn,” he refers to sinners; what he says, “and sons of men,” to the faithful and the righteous. You see, then, that this distinction is preserved. Who, then, are the earthborn, if not the sons of earth? Who are the sons of earth? Those who seek earthly inheritances. Who are the sons of men? Those who belong to the Son of Man.

We have already distinguished these matters for your holiness on some occasion. And we found that Adam was a man but was not the Son of Man. And Adam himself was not God; but Christ was both the Son of Man and God. Whoever belongs to Adam is earthborn; whoever belongs to Christ is a son of man. Yet let everyone hear. I withhold my word from no one. Is someone earthborn? Let him hear because of judgment. Is he a son of man? Let him hear because of the kingdom.

Together, rich and poor. The same things are repeated again. What he says, “rich,” belongs to the earthborn; what he says, “poor,” to the sons of men. Understand the rich to be the proud, and the poor to be the humble. Let someone possess many financial resources: if he is not puffed up by them, he is poor. Let him possess nothing, yet desire and inflate himself; God counts him among the reprobate rich.

The Lord questions both rich and poor in heart. The Prophet indicates that he is not going to say something insignificant, since he summons everyone so extensively. And he gives the reason why he ought to be heard when he adds:

[Col. 0840A] 4. “My mouth shall speak wisdom, and the meditation of my heart understanding.” Wisdom is knowledge of divine things. Understanding concerns instruction in conduct. Here the prophet or the Apostles announce wisdom when they proclaim Christ, the Son of God and Redeemer of all the righteous. They shape conduct when they teach that earthly things are not to be desired and that the riches of the rich are to be disregarded. They declare that they have spoken these things not merely with their lips, but thoughtfully, so as to make their hearers more attentive. They also assert that they hear and speak these things not from themselves but from the inner teacher, namely the Holy Spirit, when they add:

5. “I will incline my ear to a parable; I will open my proposition upon the psaltery.” To incline one’s ear to a parable is to hear that same parable humbly (Matthew 23). Those who do not do what they say do not hear it—such were the Pharisees, whom the Lord says sit upon Moses’ chair (Matthew 5). But one who is a teacher (from Augustine) and not a hearer benefits another but does not benefit himself. Those who do what they say, [Col. 0840B] and thus speak, hear what they say. Therefore they speak fruitfully what they hear.

Such was this holy man. First he humbly hears the parable, so that, instructed by the inner teacher, he may then open his proposition upon the psaltery. Parables are likenesses of things, compared with the matters under discussion. Propositions are questions containing something that must be resolved through discussion.

Why does he hear the parable? Because now we see through a mirror in an enigma, as the Apostle says. As long as we are pilgrims away from the Lord, that vision of ours is not yet face to face, where there are no longer parables, enigmas, or likenesses. An enigma is an obscure parable that is difficult to understand. If, then, we see in an enigma, let us incline our ear to the parable. And thus let us open our proposition upon the psaltery.

Let us hear what is said and do what is commanded. “I will open,” he says, “my proposition upon the psaltery,” because what I propose to make manifest in this psalm I will accomplish not only in word but also by example, so that what I teach with my mouth I may fulfill in my works. We have often said that the psaltery, on which the strings are struck with the hands so that the melody—that is, the psalm—may be heard, signifies good action. To open a proposition upon the psaltery, therefore, is to demonstrate through works the words that are set forth.

“I will incline my ear to a parable.” As if he said: I will hear the Holy Spirit speaking within me and announcing future things in parables and propositions. Therefore I will incline and humble my ear toward this parable, nor will I be one of those of whom it is said: “Woe to the prophet who prophesies from his own heart” (Ezekiel 13). Afterwards I will open my proposition upon the psaltery.

For the prophet heard, and reveals in this psaltery of the psalm what he had heard, saying:

6. “Why should I fear on the evil day?” That is, on the day of judgment. Someone says: “Because you committed theft, murder, or some other grave sin.” “I will not fear for that reason,” he says. “Why, then, shall I fear?” He continues and says: “The iniquity of my heel,” that is, final iniquity, “will surround me.” That is, it will show me damnable on every side. It is therefore not so much iniquity as the end of iniquity that must be feared. For it is not the one who has lived badly, but the one who has ended his life badly, who will perish.

If, then, he avoids the iniquity of his heel and walks in the ways of God, he will not fear when he comes to the evil day. Why, then, should we fear on the evil day? Or why should we not correct ourselves before the evil day comes? Eve was commanded to watch the head of the devil, because the devil watches her heel (Genesis 3). Eve is our flesh. Through the flesh a human being slips more easily. If, therefore, the iniquity of the heel will surround us, why should we fear on the evil day? For, with the Lord’s help, we have it in our power (from Augustine) not to commit iniquity—or, if we have committed it, to amend it. [Col. 0841A] Then there will be nothing to surround us. On the last day we shall not fear but rejoice.

7. Who, then, are those whom the iniquity of their heel will surround? Those who trust in their own strength and glory in the multitude of their riches. Woe to you, Jews, who trust not in Christ but in your own righteousness. Woe to you, rich people, who glory in your riches. You must fear what follows in the psalm:

8. “A brother does not redeem; will a man redeem?” Who is this brother if not Christ, who saved the other brothers? Joseph was a type of him, for he delivered his brothers from famine (Genesis 42–43). After his resurrection this brother said to someone: “Go, tell my brothers” (John 20). Our Lord wished to be our brother by taking our nature. For Christ, who is called—and is—the Son of God, is called our brother (Hebrews 2).

If Christ will not redeem, will a man redeem? If he will not redeem who is God and man, will someone else who is merely man redeem? Certainly not. Hence: “He will not give his propitiation to God.” A wicked person cannot placate God, neither by offering, nor by prayer, nor by sacrifice. Therefore Paul says: “For if we sin voluntarily, there is no sacrifice left for sin” (Hebrews 10). As long as a person remains willing to sin, he cannot placate God with any gifts, sacrifices, or good works. Therefore he adds:

9. “Nor will he be able to give the price of the redemption of his soul.” For an almsgiving is not pleasing to God when the person’s will still remains held by guilt. “And he will labor forever” [Verse 10], “and will still live to the end.” The one who delighted in riches for a time will labor in torments forever (Revelation 9). He will desire to die but will not be able to. He will live for this one purpose only: always to labor. Woe to you, evil desire, how wickedly you deceive your lovers.

11. “He will not see destruction when he sees the wise dying.” They see the wise die. They notice temporal death, but do not foresee the future destruction of condemnation. They commonly say things like: “Was that wise man not dead? If the one who possessed wisdom had been capable of anything, he would not have died. I shall therefore make things pleasant for myself while I live.”

These are the people who think pleasure the highest good and cling to every bodily delight. These are the people who say: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (Ecclesiastes 7). The Jews saw Christ hanging on the cross and despised him, saying: “If he were the Son of God, he would come down from the cross” (Matthew 27), not seeing what destruction is. [Note: [Col. 0841] The words inserted here in Augustine—“If they saw what destruction is, if they saw”—smell of a glossator’s hand.]

He was dying temporally so that he might live again eternally. They were living temporally, destined to die eternally. Concerning them it is immediately added: “The foolish and the senseless shall perish together.” The senseless person is one who does not believe in future punishment. The foolish person is one who, although he believes, nevertheless does not take precautions.

Therefore beware of senselessness; beware of foolishness; provide for future destruction. Make friends for yourself from the mammon of iniquity (Matthew 6). Go to the ant (Proverbs 6) and learn wisdom, which gathers in summer what it will live on in winter, and you will not perish forever.

But these will perish together, “and they will leave their riches to others.” All wicked people leave their riches to others, whether to children, parents, or neighbors to whom they leave them. Yet these people are outsiders in this respect: they cannot help those others from their riches.

12. “And their tombs”—that is, pyramids and mausoleums, which they build like great houses, as though those tombs were going to be their houses forever. They are received into costly tombs and wrapped in costly garments; they are buried with ointments and spices.

Then what kind of memorial do they have? “Their tabernacles are from generation to generation; they have called their names in their lands.” Their houses and families praise them and sacrifice to them through the third and fourth generation. He touches upon the custom of the Gentiles, who on appointed days used to hire certain people to invoke the names of the dead around their burials. In this the Prophet marks their great folly: although they thought by these means that they would possess an eternal memorial, they did this only in their own lands.

Or otherwise: “their tabernacles,” that is, the stone houses they built from their riches, in which they lived for a time, remain through the generation of their sons and the generation of their grandsons. “They have called their names,” that is, they were the reason their names were kept in memory—and not everywhere, but in their own lands, that is, in their neighborhood.

All this pertains to reproving the empty exaltation of the rich, so that they may not spend their labor on magnificent buildings, since in the end they possess nothing except the tomb. They do this because they have lost their understanding. This is what follows:

13. “Man, when he was in honor, did not understand.” What greater honor could have been given to a human being than reason and understanding, and likeness to God? Placed in such great honor, he did not understand—that is, he did not act intelligently—[Col. 0842B] “but was compared with senseless beasts.” He was compared with them only in senselessness, and “in his action he became like them.” For just as beasts are inclined toward the earth and obedient only to the belly, so lovers of the world are devoted only to earthly things.

14. “This way of theirs is a scandal to them.” This way of theirs, inasmuch as they were in honor and did not understand, desiring only earthly things, will be a scandal to them—that is, an offense that will lead them to destruction.

“Let it be a scandal to them” (from Augustine), not to you. When will it be a scandal to you? If you think that such people are blessed. But if you understand that they are not blessed, their way will be a scandal to them, not to Christ and not to his members.

“And afterwards they will be pleased in their own mouth.” When they have become such that they seek nothing except temporal goods, they will praise themselves, taking pleasure in themselves. Or, “afterwards they will be pleased in their own mouth,” when they say at the judgment: “Lord, God, open to us” (Matthew 25). But then what follows will happen: “Like sheep they have been placed in hell; death will feed upon them.” For, having become a flock shorn of riches and stripped by a great multitude of black spirits, they will be led into darkness. And rightly so: since they did not wish to have Christ as their shepherd, they will be grazed upon by death and devoured by the ravenous wolf.

15. “And the righteous will rule over them in the morning.” For they will be their judges at the judgment. “And their help, which they have in this age, will grow old”—that is, it will fail—“in hell, because of their glory,” that is, because they gloried in their riches. It is rightly said that their help grows old because of their glory, since their glory and riches will be able to provide them no help in hell.

16. “Nevertheless God will redeem my soul from the hand”—that is, from the power—“of hell, when he receives me.” That is, my humanity. For now there are labor, pressure, and tribulation for the righteous; true joy lies in future hope. Now those who open their eyes to worldly joy and close their hearts see their happiness pass away and punishment arrive. Conversely, the temporal punishment of the righteous passes away and eternal happiness arrives.

The Spirit of God therefore rouses us when it adds:

17. “Do not fear when a man has become rich.” And not only when he himself has become rich, but “when the glory of his house has been multiplied,” that is, the honor of his riches. Do not despair or think that God loves him because he abounds in riches, and has abandoned you because you are poor.

18. “For when he dies, he will not take everything.” You see him living? Think of him dying. You pay attention to what he possesses here? Pay attention to whether he takes it with him. He has much gold, much silver, many estates, slaves, and many other things. When he dies, he will not take everything. Nor will his glory descend with him. What will decaying flesh have in the tomb? What will a lost soul have [Col. 0843A] in hell? His glory will not descend with him because during his life he sought temporal glory. This is what follows:

19. “For his soul will be blessed in his life.” Those who consider these temporal things of great importance, when they see people flourishing in honors and riches in this world, usually praise and call them blessed, as it is said elsewhere in the psalm: “For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the wicked is blessed” (Psalm 9). And again: “They called the people blessed who have these things” (Psalm 143).

His soul, therefore, will be blessed during his life, but in death he will be tormented and will experience eternal punishment—the one who pursued passing glory. “He will confess to you when you have done good to him.” It belongs to the perfect to praise the Lord in adversity. The reprobate, however, praises him only in prosperity. Has profit come to him? He gives thanks. Has an inheritance come? He gives thanks. Has loss come? He blasphemes. Therefore it follows:

20. “He will enter into the generations of his fathers.” Who are their fathers if not the devil and his angels? Hence the Lord says to certain people: “You are from your father the devil” (John 8). The offspring of the devil are all the reprobate. Hence John says: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?” (Matthew 3).

Therefore he will enter into the generations of his fathers, because he will perish together with the reprobate in eternal fire. “And he will not see light forever.” For he will be sent into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matthew 8 and 13). Everyone who does evil hates the light (John 3). Since, therefore, while he lived he loved darkness, he will never see the light.

And that he has lost the light of his heart is shown when he adds:

21. “Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them.” The repetition of the sentence is a confirmation; or he repeats it because the chief point of the psalm’s purpose and usefulness depends especially upon this verse.

Defend your honor, O man. Do not abandon the understanding God gave you for this purpose: that you might perceive divine things, love eternal things, and despise earthly things. Use your understanding; use your reason; disdain temporal things, so that you may deserve to reach heavenly things.

# TITLE OF PSALM XLIX

The following psalm treats the calling of all nations, the manifest coming of Christ, the transformation of the old sacrifice into the new, the condemnation of the undisciplined sinner, and the fact that the way to the Lord is the sacrifice of praise.

Its title is: “A psalm of Asaph.” Asaph is interpreted as “assembly.” This psalm must therefore be attributed to Asaph, that is, to the assembly of the faithful who existed before Christ’s coming and believed that Christ would come in the flesh and for us—which we believe has been fulfilled.

The subject of this psalm is Christ himself, now calling us through preaching and then judging strictly. The aforementioned faithful, by introducing the person of the Lord Christ, intend to speak with greater authority and persuade their hearers to desist from carnal observances and pass from shadow to truth, and not to preach with their voice in such a way that they fail to fulfill their preaching in their works.

The reasons why the commands of Christ, who urges such things, must be obeyed are set forth at the beginning of the psalm, up to the place where it says: “Hear, O my people.” [Col. 0843D] At the beginning, however, this commendation of his preaching is made. It is the voice of the synagogue.

# PSALM XLIX

1. “The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken, and has called the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting.” It was not just any human being or any angel who spoke, but the very God of gods, namely our Lord Jesus Christ, who makes and deifies the saints, as he says elsewhere to certain saints who have been made gods by grace: “I said, You are gods and all of you sons of the Most High” (Psalm 81). Hence the Apostle says: “He gave them power to become sons of God” (John 1). And again: “We are sons of God, but it has not yet appeared what we shall be” (1 John 3).

This one, so great and such as he is, spoke through angels, through prophets, through himself (Hebrews 1), and through his faithful people; and he called the earth, that is, the people who dwell on earth. And not on one land only, but “from the rising of the sun to its setting.” [Col. 0844A] For the Holy Spirit was given to the Apostles, and it was said to them: “Go, preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16). And because the preaching began from Jerusalem, it is rightly added:

2. “From Sion is the beauty of his splendor.” Hence another prophet says: “From Sion the law will go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isaiah 2). From there the beauty of splendor began to be preached, that is, the beauty of Christ’s divinity. He is “beautiful above the sons of men in appearance” (Psalm 44), concerning whom it is also added:

3. “God will come manifestly: our God, and he will not keep silence.” He first came hidden and appeared weak in the flesh. The appearance of glory was in his divinity, but this was hidden in his humanity. For if they had known him, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Corinthians 2). He came hidden so that he might be judged. He will come manifestly so that he may judge (Matthew 16).

And this is what he says (from Augustine), “and he will not keep silence.” Now he is silent concerning judgment, hidden in heaven. He is patient toward sinners, not exercising wrath but awaiting repentance. “I was silent,” he says; “shall I always be silent?” It should also be noted that he says, “our God.” For he is not God who is not our God. “For all the gods of the nations are demons” (Psalm 95), but the God of Christians is the true God.

Because he will come for judgment, the following words teach this: “Fire will burn before him.” For he will come to judge the world by fire. Hence the Apostle says: “The fire will test what sort of work each one’s is” (1 Corinthians 3). Those who have not yet tasted the sweetness of God, if they do not yet desire to behold God’s face, should at least fear the fire. Let punishments terrify the one whom rewards do not invite (from the same source). Is what God promises worthless to you? Tremble at what he threatens. “Every tree that does not bear good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matthew 7).

Alternatively: Christ comes to judgment, and then the fire of evil desire will blaze and burn the reprobate who will be in his presence, because they will see him whom they pierced (Zechariah 12; John 19).

“And a mighty tempest around him.” That is, the angels; for just as a mighty tempest blows straw toward the fire, so they will blow the wicked into hell (Matthew 13). A mighty tempest will winnow so great a threshing floor. In this tempest (from the same source) will be that winnowing by which every unclean thing will be separated from the saints, every pretense from the faithful, and every despiser and proud person from the devout and God-fearing.

When the Lord therefore comes to judgment, what will he do?

4. “He will summon heaven from above.” By heaven (from the same source) he wishes all the saints and perfect people to be understood, whom he will summon to sit above and judge together with him. “And he will call the earth to distinguish his people.” He will call heaven to judge with him. He will call earth to distinguish his people from the wicked people.

Hear the calling of the earth and the separation of his people: “Come, you blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom that has been prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25). “Receive,” I say. Why? “For I was hungry, and you gave me food,” and so forth.

This is why they are called earth: namely, because of the fertility of good works. If they could not be heaven by despising everything, they were at least good earth by producing the fruit of mercy (Matthew 5 and 25).

Then the Prophet, seeing future things as though they were present, exhorts the angels who are gathering them. For the Lord will send his angels, and all nations will be gathered before him (Matthew 13 and 25).

5. “Gather his saints to him from the various parts of the world.” And not such saints as persist in carnal observances, but such as establish and place his new testament above the legal sacrifices. For those sacrifices of the Old Testament were a shadow and prophecy of the truth.

To establish the testament above the sacrifices, therefore, is to offer oneself as a sacrifice to the Lord and to fulfill spiritually what the letter commands. Or the testament is placed above the sacrifices when the new is preferred to the old, when, after the sacrifices of animals have been abolished, the order of Melchizedek is preached everywhere (Hebrews 5, 7, and 10). To this order of newness belongs what follows:

[Col. 0845A] 6. “And the heavens will announce his righteousness, because God is judge.” The heavens announce God’s righteousness when spiritual men preach faith in our Lord Jesus Christ and good works. Hence it is said elsewhere: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Psalm 18).

This righteousness is preached to us so that, carrying it out, we may deserve to avoid the judge’s wrath. “Because God is judge,” who will judge the living and the dead (Matthew 16), since he will repay each one according to his works and merits.

The holy men, continually attending to this with the eyes of their minds—because God is judge—never cease examining their lives, mourning their sins, and advancing themselves toward better things, so that afterwards they may be able to appear uncondemnable before the strict judge.

Up to this point the synagogue has commended Christ, either by explaining the order of his preaching or by commending his second coming. From now on it introduces him speaking in this way:

7. “Hear, O my people, and I will speak, O Israel.” Israel is the name of election. “You shall not be called Jacob, but you shall be called Israel” (Genesis 32). Therefore hear as Israel, as one who sees God—even if not yet by hope, nevertheless already by faith—for this is what Israel means: “seeing God.”

“Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke 8). He wins their goodwill when he says: “My people.” As if he said: an elect people, a special people (1 Peter 2).

“And I will testify to you.” That is, I will establish it by the testimonies of Scripture. What? “I am God, your God.” That is, I am God, your God. Whoever understands the Scriptures of the Apostles and Prophets recognizes that the Lord Jesus is our God.

“Your God” is also said properly of the one whom God holds more familiarly, as his slave, as part of his own possession. What more do you want? Are you seeking something first from God? Behold, God himself is your God. What do we say to God? You were seeking gifts from him; you have the one who will give them.

And what does the Lord our God demand from us? Let us hear what he adds:

8. “I will not reprove you because of your sacrifices.” I will not say to you (from Augustine): “Why did you not slaughter a fat bull for me? [Col. 0845C] Why did you not offer the best goat from your flock? Why does that ram walk among your sheep and not get placed upon my altar?”

“Your burnt offerings, however, are always before me.” *Holon* means “whole”; *caustum*, “burnt.” A whole burnt offering is one entirely consumed by fire.

There are certain burnt offerings that God does not accept, concerning which it is said in another psalm: “You will certainly not delight in burnt offerings” (Psalm 50). These are the burnt offerings of brute animals, in which God does not delight.

What, then, are those that are always before me? “Do good,” God says, “in your good pleasure to Sion. Then you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness, offerings, and burnt offerings.” There is the fire of most ardent love. Let the spirit be inflamed with love; let it seize its members for the service of that same love. Let it not permit them to serve desire, so that the whole person may blaze with the fire of divine love.

God calls such burnt offerings “always before me.” Yet Israel may still be thinking of oxen, sheep, and goats. Therefore it is added:

9. “I will not accept calves from your house, nor goats from your flocks.” [Note: [Col. 0845D] Previously it read *pronuntiat* (“he declares”), which we emend from the commonly transmitted Augustine, as also shortly afterward *praenuntiatum* (“foretold”) in place of *pronuntiatum* (“declared”).]

He foretells (from Augustine) the New Testament, in which all those old sacrifices have ceased. For at that time a future sacrifice was foretold, by whose blood we would be cleansed. Why will I not accept calves, goats, and such things from your house?

10. “For all the beasts of the forests are mine.” As if he said: Since I possess all the wild beasts, I have no need of the calf or goat that is in your house.

But perhaps Israel says (from the same source): Those are God’s beasts—the wild animals that I do not enclose in my fold, that I do not tie to my manger. But those that are with me belong not to God but to me.

Therefore the Lord adds: “The beasts on the mountains and the oxen are mine.” Both what you possess [Col. 0846A] and what you do not possess are all mine. For if you are my servant, your entire possession is mine.

11. “I have known all the birds of heaven.” That is, I have weighed and counted them all. God’s knowledge is one thing, human knowledge another. Just as (from the same source) possession by God is one thing and possession by a human being another.

For you do not have everything you possess under your control. As long as your ox lives, it is in your power. These birds of heaven were made from water by the word of the Lord who said: “Let the waters bring forth the birds of heaven” (Genesis 1). Where did he know what he had commanded the waters to bring forth? Certainly he already knew what he had created; indeed, he knew it before he created it.

Such, then, is God’s knowledge: in some ineffable manner those things were with him before they were created. And he expects you to give him what he possessed before it was created.

“And the beauty of the field is with me.” That is, the abundance of everything produced on earth is with me. The field is with him, the appearance of the earth is with him, the appearance of heaven is with him, all the birds of heaven and every creature [Col. 0846B] are with him (Jeremiah 23), because he is everywhere (John 1).

12. “If I were hungry, I would not tell you.” He will not hunger or thirst, he will not labor or sleep, who guards Israel (Psalm 120). But [Note: [Col. 0846D] The same source has *ecce* (“behold”); *haecce* (“this”) would be preferable.] these words are spoken according to your carnality, because you may perhaps think that, just as you suffer hunger before you eat, God too becomes hungry in order to eat.

Even if it were possible for him to hunger, he would not tell you. He takes from all that is before him whatever he wishes. Nothing is necessary to him. Therefore he adds: “For the world and its fullness are mine.” Do not, then, trouble yourself about what you should give me; without labor I have what I want.

13. “Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?” Since you do not seek these things, say then: “Lord our God, what do you wish your people Israel to offer you?” It follows and says:

14. “Sacrifice a sacrifice of praise to God.” God always loves inward sacrifices more. For he pays more attention to devotion than to wealth. Therefore he immediately adds: “And pay your vows to the Most High.”

Let your altar be your conscience. Let your fire be divine love. Let your sacrifice be the praises of God. Praise God in your heart in such a way that, kindled by spiritual fire in the very offering of praise, you may sacrifice, mortify, and offer yourself to God.

And rightly, together with sacrifice, we command that a vow be paid to the Most High. For God weighs sacrifices according to vows. Your sacrifice will be greater before God in proportion to the greater devotion you have in the sacrifice itself.

Hence it is written: “By faith Abel offered a greater sacrifice than Cain offered to God, through which he received testimony that he was righteous” (Hebrews 11). For God weighs the heart, not the substance. He does not consider how much is in the sacrifice, but from how much it is brought forth.

Hence it is said elsewhere in the psalm: “My vows are upon me, O God; I will repay them to you as praises” (Psalm 55). As if he plainly said: Even if I do not possess external gifts to offer, nevertheless within myself I find something to place upon the altar of your praise. For you, who are not nourished by our giving, are better pleased by the offering of the heart.

“Sacrifice,” I say, “a sacrifice of praise to God,” so that you may have him appeased and favorable. And what follows?

15. “And call upon me on the day of tribulation; I will deliver you, and you will glorify me.” When you are afflicted, do not despair or wish to trust in your own strength. Call upon me, and I will deliver you.

For this reason the day of tribulation has been permitted to occur: perhaps, if you were not afflicted, you would not call upon me. When you are afflicted, you call upon me; and because you call, I will deliver you. When you have been delivered, you will glorify me, so that you may no longer depart from me.

Tribulations are therefore beneficial to us, because they rouse us to honor God. In affliction we recognize our own weakness; in deliverance we experience divine grace. We honor him all the more when we know that our deliverance comes not from ourselves but from him.

And it should be understood that this entire mortal life is tribulation (Job 7) for holy men. Besides the countless anxieties of this world, they are sorely afflicted because they are separated from God, because they are still pilgrims in the world (2 Corinthians 5), and because the body, which is subject to corruption, weighs down the soul (Wisdom 9).

And the more frequent tribulations are among us, the more frequent our prayers ought to be before God. But we must beware lest we live badly while singing well. For it follows:

16. But to the sinner God said, “Why do you recite my justifications?” That is, “Why do you preach my commandments that justify?” Of such people the Apostle says (Rom. 2): “You who preach that one must not steal, steal; you who teach that one must not commit adultery, commit adultery; you who abhor idols, commit sacrilege.” “And you take up my covenant through your mouth”? That is, “Do you presume to proclaim the body of Christ and the cup of the New Testament, which was poured out for many for the remission of sins” (Matt. 26; Mark 15; Luke 22; 1 Cor. 11)? Or, “You take up my covenant through your mouth”—that is, “Do you dare to preach my Gospel with such polluted lips?”

[Col. 0847B] 17. “But you hated discipline.” That is, corruption. “And you cast my words behind you,” because, neglecting them, you did not keep them. In hating discipline, an evil will is reproved. In casting God’s words behind oneself, a negligent and perverse life is condemned. To cast God’s words behind oneself is, having despised them, to act perversely. 251 Behold how you cast my words behind you:

18. “If you saw a thief, you ran with him; and you placed your portion with adulterers.” Perhaps (from Augustine) you would say, “I did not commit theft. I did not commit adultery.” But what if you took pleasure in the person who did it? Did you not run with him by that very pleasure? Did you not place your portion with the one who did it by praising him? Even if you do not do evil, yet if you praise evil, if you consent to it in desire, you run with the evil person and receive a portion of his evil.

19. “Your mouth abounded in wickedness, and your tongue fashioned deceit.” He indicates the wickedness and deceit of certain people [Col. 0847C] who, although they know that the things they hear are evil, do not rebuke them at all. And it is not enough that they do not say, “You have done evil”; rather, by flattering they say, “You have done well.” They know that the things are evil, yet they abound in wickedness, and their tongue fashions—or adorns—deceits. Deceit is a kind of fraud in words, when one thing is promised and another is intended.

[Note: [Col. 0847D] I would certainly prefer *promitur* to be restored, for Augustine too has *promendi*.]

It is not enough that you do evil: you also praise it by flattery, and mock and deceive the sinner. Or, the sinner’s mouth abounds in wickedness when he provokes others by curses and insults. His lips fashion deceit when they utter words pleasing to the ear while concealing fraud. Hence he continues:

20. “You sat and spoke against your brother.” This occurs when someone who considers himself strong, or already a teacher of some importance, disparages his brother, who perhaps is acting well and living rightly. In the word “sat,” delay or deliberation is signified. There is another person who is weak and imperfect, against whom he places a stumbling-block by speaking similarly and perversely. For this reason that weak person is called the son of his mother, not yet of his father: he still requires milk and clings to the breast. He is still carried in the bosom of Mother Church, not yet able to approach the solid food of his Father’s table. He is scandalized because he is not yet perfect. For if he were perfect, he could in no way be scandalized. “Great peace have those who love your law, and for them there is no stumbling-block” (Ps. 118). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever causes one of my little ones to stumble” (Matt. 18). He does not say “one of the great,” but “one of the little ones,” because only the little ones are subject to being scandalized. It is characteristic of the wicked, however, to disparage the perfect, place stumbling-blocks before the imperfect, and continually sow discord.

21. “You have done this,” says the Lord, “and I was silent”—that is, I did not rebuke you or exact vengeance. For now is the time of mercy, when the gracious Lord patiently [Col. 0848A] awaits us, so that we may be converted. “He is not angry every day” (Ps. 7), but, as it is said in another psalm, “Unless you are converted, he will brandish his sword” (Ps. 17). Hence he adds: “You have wickedly supposed that I would be like you.” It is not enough (from Augustine) that your evil deeds please you; you suppose that they please me as well. Because you do not suffer me to be an avenger, you want to have me as your accomplice. “I will rebuke you and set you before your face.” The more patiently the merciful Lord now endures sinners, the more severely he will rebuke them in judgment. And because (from the same source) here they neglect to attend to themselves and correct themselves, there he will set them before his face, so that they may see their own foulness—not, however, so that they may amend, but so that they may be all the more ashamed.

Now, therefore, whoever you are who are such a person, do what God threatens to do to you. Take yourself from behind your back, where you pretend not to see yourself by disregarding your deeds, and set yourself before yourself. Ascend the tribunal of your mind. Be your own judge. Let fear torment you. Let confession burst forth. And say to your Lord: “For I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me” (Ps. 50). For if, as Paul says, “we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged” (1 Cor. 11). Therefore, by way of admonition, he adds:

22. “Understand these things, you who forget God.” You who have forgotten God while doing evil, weigh rationally what has been said, so that you may correct yourselves. Attend here to the depths of divine mercy. Even those who forget him he does not forget; he does not reject them, but rather recalls them to understanding, so that they may come to their senses and not perish. He does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live (Ezek. 18).

And why, merciful Lord, do you admonish those who forget you, so that they may understand? Hear the reason: “lest at any time that adversary—the devil, who prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (1 Pet. 5)—should seize them, and there be no one to rescue them. If you do not wish to understand, the Lord does not rescue those who forget him, those who disdain understanding the things that pertain to the salvation of their souls. Hence it is written: “Everyone who is ignorant will be ignored” (1 Cor. 14). In contrast, let us hear what he adds about those who understand and praise God:

23. “The sacrifice of praise will honor me; and there is the way by which I will show him the salvation of God.” What is called *salutare* in Latin is called *Jesus* in Hebrew. Thus, in the sacrifice of praise, a way is made for the showing of Jesus, because while compunction is poured forth through psalmody, a path is made for us in the heart by which we finally reach Jesus. As he himself speaks of his manifestation, saying: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him, and I will manifest myself to him” (John 14).

# TITLE OF PSALM L

1. “For the end, a psalm of David, when Nathan the prophet came to him, when he went in to Bathsheba” (2 Sam. 12). This psalm is attributed to the prophet David, who looks toward the end—that is, toward Christ, from whom he had withdrawn through sin, who is the end of the Law and the Prophets. Or “the end” means the perfection of all good works.

The psalm, I say, was composed concerning that affair on account of which the prophet Nathan came to rebuke him. And because Nathan had come to him many times, to make clear on which visit he was the cause of this psalm, it specifies the time: namely, when he went in to Bathsheba. King and prophet David was captivated by the beauty of this woman, another man’s wife. This is not read in the psalm itself, but appears in its title. In the Books of Kings it is read more fully (from Augustine). He arranged for her husband to be killed in battle. After this deed, Nathan the prophet was sent to him by the Lord to rebuke him for so great a crime (2 Sam. 11).

Many wish to fall with David but do not wish to rise with David. The example set before us is not an example of falling, but of rising if one has fallen. Take care not to fall. Let the fall of the great not be a source of pleasure to the lesser; rather, let the fall of the great be a trembling for the lesser. Let those who have not fallen hear, so that they may not fall. Let those who have fallen hear, so that they may rise.

Such an example also admonishes no one to exalt himself in prosperous circumstances. Many fear adversity but do not fear prosperity. Prosperity is more dangerous to the soul than adversity is to the body. David did not commit this sin when he endured Saul as his persecutor. One must always keep watch against happiness.

The subject of this psalm is David, or any other penitent person. In this psalm the prophet principally intends to pray concerning the threefold guilt of the crime mentioned above: adultery, murder, and deceit. Then he prays also concerning all other sins, that God may forgive him this offense and all others, and restore the grace of the Holy Spirit, so that he may never again lose it.

David is proposed in this psalm to all the righteous as an example—not of sinning, but of rising again if they should fall. They must not presume upon their own virtue, since it is written: “Let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Cor. 10). To the unrighteous he is proposed so that some may not despair because of the greatness of their offense, looking to David, who obtained forgiveness for so great a crime through fitting satisfaction. David therefore speaks as follows:

# PSALM L

3. “Have mercy on me, O God.” This is spoken by analogy with someone caught in a legal case, whose crime is already manifest to the judges and who no longer strives to defend it, but seeks only to obtain pardon by entreaty, displaying his repentance, pleading his former merits, and promising that he will do good in the future.

First he prays concerning his sin; then he voluntarily confesses his crime. It is as if he were saying: “O God”—that is, my Creator, from whom my great and manifold iniquity is not hidden—“have mercy on me, according to your great mercy.” That is, in accordance with the measure of your mercy, which is great, forgive my great sin.

“And according to the multitude of your compassions.” That is, in accordance with the measure of your compassions, which are many in their effects, blot out my iniquity, which is manifold. That is, blot out murder, deceit, and adultery. Here he shows both that his sin is great—for it was adultery (2 Sam. 11)—and that it is manifold. In it, murder and deceit, along with many other things, may be understood.

This is the difference between *misericordia* (“mercy”) and *miseratio* (“compassion”): God is always merciful in himself by nature, but he acts compassionately toward us in practice. The virtue of mercy exists inseparably in God. When certain benefits are bestowed upon us from this mercy, they are called compassions.

It should also be noted that the person who implores great mercy confesses great misery. Great mercy is therefore set against great sin; the multitude of compassions is set against the multiplicity of faults. Therefore he continues:

4. “Wash me more than I am able to ask you to wash me from my iniquity”—so that you may forgive what my conscience fears and add what prayer does not presume to request. “And cleanse me from my sin.”

Although the Apostle John declares that there is no difference between iniquity and sin when he says, “Iniquity is sin” (1 John 1), yet in ordinary usage *iniquity* conveys something more than *sin*. Everyone freely confesses that he is a sinner, but at times he is ashamed to call himself wicked.

When this penitent therefore prays to be washed from iniquity and cleansed from sin, he appears to request healing both from the more serious and from the lesser fault. He then supplies the reason why he asks that what he has done be forgiven, saying:

5. “For I acknowledge my iniquity”—in repentance and satisfaction, and not merely for an hour, but continually. Therefore he adds: “And my sin is always against me.” “Against me,” that is, before my eyes.

He did not forget his sin and iniquity, although he had already heard from the prophet: “The Lord has taken away your sin from you” (2 Sam. 12). In his conscience, as in an image, he held adultery and murder depicted; every day he saw their corruption. Therefore he said, “And my sin is always against me.” I see it; may you not take it into account.

Attend to what God does. If you remember your sin, he will not remember it. If you forget it, God will remember it. “I am he,” says the Lord, “who blots out your iniquities” (Isa. 43). But you should remember them.

Someone may perhaps say, “Why should I remember them?” “So that my mercy may be more gratefully received,” he replies, “and so that you may perceive what I have granted you.” For if you remember the mass of your sins, you will also remember the greatness of God’s kindness.

Such were the saints: they did not bring forward their virtues, but recalled the memory of their sins—not like people nowadays, who forget their sins and wish to conceal them, but, if they have done anything good, bring it out publicly and hasten to proclaim it to everyone.

Have you done something good? Conceal it, so that your Lord may see and praise it. Have you done evil? Acknowledge it and amend, and God forgives. Confess to God and say what follows:

6. “Against you alone have I sinned.” To him alone an account of sin must be rendered, since he alone is without sin (John 8). “And I have done evil before you.”

What does this mean (from Augustine)? Before human beings, was there not another man’s wife as an adulteress, and a husband who had been killed?

[Note: [Col. 0849D] Augustine’s reading, with the interrogative note, seems preferable: “Before human beings, was there not an adulterated wife belonging to another and a husband who had been killed?” [Col. 0850D]]

But in this respect every human being sins against God alone: God alone can heal a human being from sin. It is as though a sick person were to say to an excellent physician: “Against you alone have I sinned; no one can heal my illness except you alone.”

Hence, in another psalm, this heavenly physician is addressed concerning the sinful soul: “He who forgives all your iniquities” (Ps. 102), “who heals all your diseases.”

He rightly says that he has done evil before God, because God alone knows what and how great each person’s evil is. Human beings see the face, but God sees the heart (Job 35). Human beings see the sin of the deed; God also examines the root of the intention.

Or: “Against you alone, who are without sin, have I sinned, and I have done evil before you, from whom no secret is hidden.” He is the just punisher who has nothing in himself that deserves punishment. Therefore I pray: cleanse me. Why? “So that you may be justified in your words.”

Your word is: “Turn to me and you shall be saved” (Isa. 45). Your word is: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11). Your word is: “At whatever hour the sinner turns, he shall live and shall not die” (Ezek. 18).

And I have indeed turned and come to you, seeking mercy. Forgive, therefore, what I have committed, so that you may be found just and truthful in your words. “And prevail when you are judged.”

That is, when certain people who understand perversely judge that you do not show mercy to those who have fallen into grave crimes. Prevail over them and destroy their judgment by sparing me, who have fallen into a grave crime.

Alternatively: I confess my sins to you alone; therefore I uncover my evils before you, so that you may be justified in your words and I may be condemned in my deeds; and, as though judgment had been established, may you prevail and may I be defeated.

For often, when we carefully examine God’s case against us and our case against God, we judge God himself before the tribunal of our reason. A human being ascends the tribunal of his mind: thought becomes the accuser, conscience the witness, reason the judge, and fear the executioner. When he discovers himself unjust and convicted, he becomes more humble and renders himself more pleasing to the Lord.

Or, “Prevail when you are judged,” that is, in the judgment of your Son, who was condemned to death, may you appear victorious through the glory of the resurrection and ascension. For you surpass all judges, and whoever thinks himself just before you is unjust.

Nor (from Augustine) is it enough for David to confess only his own grave sins: he also brings to the physician the very origin of sin. He confesses everything and humbles himself in everything, so that he may deserve forgiveness for all sins. Hence he now adds, speaking both in his own voice and in that of the entire human race:

7. “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me.” My mother conceived me with the pleasure of sin. I, once conceived, contracted with me the iniquity of original sin.

Was David born of adultery? He was born of Jesse, a just man, and his wife. What, then (from the same source), does it mean that he says he was conceived in iniquities, unless it is because iniquity is drawn from Adam (Rom. 5 and 13)? No one is born without drawing along both guilt and the punishment of guilt.

The word “behold” signifies what is manifest. Everyone sees this; everyone experiences it. A human being living in corruptible flesh bears within himself the imprint of the uncleanness of temptations, because he plainly drew them from his very origin. Indeed, because of the pleasure of the flesh, his conception is uncleanness.

Hence he is often tempted unwillingly. Hence he suffers certain uncleannesses in his mind, although his judgment resists them, because, having been conceived from uncleanness while striving toward purity, he tries to overcome what he is.

Therefore, whoever has already reached the place of purity should look back upon the path of his conception by which he came there, and from this infer that he does not possess purity of life through his own virtue, since the beginning of his existence came from uncleanness.

8. “For behold, you have loved truth.” Therefore I acknowledge sin in repentance, because it is evident—“behold”—that you have loved truth, that is, true confession.

Or: you loved truth, and (from the same source) you did not leave the sins of those whom you forgive unpunished. You granted mercy in such a way as also to preserve truth. You forgive the person who confesses while punishing himself.

“You have made uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom manifest to me.” You loved and honored me so greatly that, through the prophetic spirit, you revealed to me the hidden mysteries of your wisdom—that is, of your Son—namely, the incarnation, passion, resurrection, ascension, and many other things.

He calls them “uncertain” on account of the Jews, who read them and doubted; “hidden” on account of the Gentiles, who knew nothing of them at all.

Tell us, holy David, about the coming of Christ, if anything has been revealed to you.

“He will descend,” he says, “like rain upon a fleece” (Ps. 71).

Tell of the assembly of the persecutors: “The kings of the earth stood forth, and the princes gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ” (Ps. 2).

Tell of the passion of the cross: “They pierced my hands and my feet” (Ps. 21).

Tell of food and drink: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. 68).

Tell of the burial: “They placed me in the lowest pit” (Ps. 87).

Tell of the resurrection: “You will not abandon my soul in the underworld” (Ps. 15).

Tell of the ascension: “God has ascended amid jubilation” (Ps. 46).

Tell of the glory of the Church: “The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold” (Ps. 44).

It would be lengthy to recount how many and how great secrets were revealed to him. If so great a man fell, who can be secure about himself? And yet, if it should happen that someone falls, let him observe that David repented and not only received forgiveness but was also restored to his former standing. Hence he adds:

9. “You will sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed.” We know hyssop (from Augustine) as a lowly but medicinal herb, which is said to cling to rock with its roots. You too should grasp your rock—that is, Christ (1 Cor. 10)—with the root of love. Be humble before your God, so that you may be exalted in your glorified God.

Do not despise the herb; consider the power of the medicine. Hyssop removes the swelling of the lungs. In the lungs pride is commonly signified: there are inflation and panting. Humility cures such an affliction.

In the Old Law, the blood of a heifer was sprinkled with hyssop for the cleansing of the children of Israel (Lev. 14). Let us too be sprinkled with hyssop; let us imitate the humility of Christ’s passion, and we shall be cleansed from sins.

But it is little to be cleansed from the filth of sins unless we also happen to be adorned with the brightness of virtues. Therefore he adds: “You will wash me with consecrated blood, and I shall be made whiter than snow,” in which no trace of blackness can be seen.

He rightly says that he will be made whiter than snow, because the brightness of a justified soul surpasses all the brightness of visible creation. Christ’s garment on the mountain shone, whitened like snow (Matt. 17); it signified the Church, which was to be cleansed from every stain of sin. Thus cleanse and whiten me:

10. “You will give joy and gladness to my hearing.” Truth heard inwardly gives great delight. The servant of God rejoices greatly and is glad when he is instructed inwardly concerning the remission of sins, the promise of eternal salvation, or certain divine ordinances.

Hence it is said of John: “But the friend of the bridegroom stands and listens, and rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice” (John 3).

Joy may be referred to present grace; gladness to future glory. “And because joy has been restored to me, the humbled bones will rejoice.” That is, the virtues that were depressed by sin will become a cause of rejoicing for me.

Or “the humbled bones” may signify perfect men, because, having been humbled, they will rejoice, in accordance with what is written: “Everyone who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 18; Matt. 23). And so that this may happen, he adds:

11. “Turn your face away from my sins.” God does this when, on account of human repentance, he overlooks human sins. He turns his face away from sins, as it were, and, as though he did not remember them, does not punish.

You rightly and properly ask God to turn his face away from your sins if you do not turn your own face away from them. Hence he said above: “And my sin is always against me.” 257

I pray not only concerning these sins but also concerning all the others. This is what he says: “And blot out all my iniquities.” When you have blotted them out,

12. “Create a clean heart in me, O God.” Create, as God, something new: cleanse my heart; remove evil thoughts. “And renew a right spirit within me.” He rightly says “renew,” for the house that sin had made old has been built again; I ask that grace renew it.

Through my deed the uprightness of my spirit had been bent; through your grace let it be directed, so that I may walk rightly and in truth before you, as I did before.

13. “Do not cast me away from your face.” That is, from your presence. Let my sins be cast away from you, not me. Until now, he says, I have stood before your face and understood your secrets. I beg you, Lord, do not repel me from such knowledge of you. “And do not take your Holy Spirit from me.”

14. “Restore to me the joy of your salvation.” Let the coming, incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension of your Son be manifest to me now as they once were. “And strengthen me with a principal spirit.”

In what does he strengthen me? (From Augustine.) Because you have forgiven me; because I am certain that what you have pardoned is not counted against me. Having thereby been made secure and thus strengthened by grace, I will not be ungrateful. What will you give in return for this gift?

15. “I will teach the unjust your ways.” This is characteristic of holy men: they strive to share with others, out of charity, the spiritual goods they receive from God, and they seek the salvation of others just as they seek their own.

Hence he adds: “And the ungodly will be converted to you.” They do not teach others in order to win approval for themselves or seek some temporal profit from their teaching, but with the sole intention of being able to draw the ungodly toward conversion.

Great is the commendation of divine mercy, and great the consolation of sinners, when it is said: “And the ungodly will be converted to you.” Thus (from the same source) God is so full of the richness of mercy that salvation is promised not only to the converted but even to the ungodly themselves. Hence Paul says: “So that the faith of those who believe in him who justifies the ungodly may be reckoned as righteousness” (Rom. 4).

Considering his many iniquities and attributing them to the corruption of flesh and blood, he adds:

16. “Deliver me from bloods, O God, God of my salvation.” You, God, who are God and the author of my salvation, deliver me from bloods—that is, from the corruptions of the flesh.

The Latin translator expressed the meaning of the Greek with a word that is less Latin. We all know that in Latin one does not normally say *sanguines* (“bloods”); nevertheless, because the Greek has the plural number, and because he found this usage in the original Hebrew language, the translator preferred to say something less Latin rather than fail to preserve the exact meaning.

[Note: [Col. 0851] Thus most Augustinian manuscripts also have *pius*; nevertheless, *pius* is printed there. From the following passage in our text [Col. 0853D], the received text of Augustine may again be restored.]

Why, then, did he say “from bloods” in the plural? By “many bloods,” as though in the origin of sinful flesh, he wished many sins to be understood, referring to the sins that arise from the corruption of flesh and blood. Hence the Apostle says: “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 15).

“Deliver me from bloods,” that is, from iniquities. “And my tongue will exult”—that is, by exulting it will proclaim—“your justice,” if I am able to proclaim your justice, provided that you first deliver me from iniquity.

And because he had said, “My lips will exult in your justice,” lest he seem to attribute this to his own strength, as though speech were in his own power, he commends the grace of God by adding:

17. “Lord, you will open my lips, and my mouth will proclaim your praise.” You will make my lips fit to preach, though previously they had been closed because of sin. “Praise is not seemly in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. 15). Hence God said to the sinner: “Why do you recite my justice?” (Ps. 49). In contrast, “praise becomes the upright” (Ps. 32).

It is therefore yours to open my lips; it is mine afterward to proclaim your praise, which is more acceptable to you than to offer legal sacrifices.

18. “For if you had desired sacrifice, I would certainly have given it”—a legal sacrifice rather than an offering of praise. But for this reason I decided to offer the sacrifice of praise instead, because you are certainly not pleased with the ancient holocausts.

What, then? Did holy David not offer God sacrifices and holocausts of calves and bulls, as the Law prescribed? He certainly did. But in the very offering he displayed the new sacrifice more than the old. When he slaughtered the animals, he sacrificed himself inwardly to God in the contrition of his heart, and there offered God vows and praises, which he knew were more acceptable to God than offering the flesh of animals.

This is the true meaning of the sacrifice he conveys to us when he adds:

19. “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit.” A merely bodily sacrifice does not please God; rather, a troubled spirit—that is, one greatly distressed on account of sins—is a sacrifice pleasing to God.

He proves this by the words that follow: “A contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise.” From this it is clear that a troubled spirit is a sacrifice pleasing to you: for you, O God, will not despise, but will graciously receive, a heart made contrite by compunction and humbled.

Having commended the new sacrifice, he prays that God establish a Church from both walls, one that will offer such a sacrifice. He says:

20. “Deal graciously, Lord, in your good will with Zion.” You, Lord, who are pleased with such a sacrifice, deal graciously with Zion—that is, bestow abundant blessing and mercy upon your future Church—not according to its merits, but “in your good will,” that is, with your gratuitous grace.

“And let the walls of Jerusalem be built from living stones,” namely faithful souls: let both walls of the Church, the Jewish and the Gentile, be constructed in faith, hope, and charity (Eph. 2).

Zion is interpreted as “watchtower,” and Jerusalem as “vision of peace.” Recognize yourselves, therefore, in Zion and Jerusalem if you await with firm hope the future and if you have peace with God.

21. “Then you will accept the sacrifice of justice.” Now, in place of iniquity, God will not despise the sacrifice that consists of a troubled spirit and a contrite and humbled heart. “Then,” that is, in the future age, you will graciously accept the sacrifice of justice alone, and of praise, as it is written: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O God; forever and ever they will praise you” (Ps. 85).

“You will also accept offerings and holocausts.” When the entire animal was placed upon the altar to be consumed by fire, this was called a holocaust. The divine fire will consume us wholly.

For not only will our soul be consumed there by the divine fire of wisdom, but our body too will there deserve immortality.

“Then they will place calves upon your altar,” that is, upon the memorial of your venerable passion and resurrection—calves signifying themselves: innocent, new, and free from the yoke of the Law.

[Note: [Col. 0853D] We have corrected *absumet*, “will consume,” so that it agrees with the following *absumetur*, with Augustine’s support, in place of *assumet* and *assumetur*.]

# TITLE OF PSALM LI

1. This psalm concerns two kinds of human beings: one earthly, the other heavenly; one persecutes, the other suffers; one glories in wickedness and will be uprooted; the other glories in God and will endure.

The perverse kind is treated in the first part of the psalm, and its wickedness is described in detail. The race of the elect is shown at the end.

The title is as follows: “For the end, an understanding of David, when Doeg the Edomite came and announced to Saul and said to him: David has come to the house of Ahimelech.”

The history records that, at the time when Saul was persecuting David, David himself, driven by hunger and by his enemies, having nowhere to flee, entered the house of Ahimelech the priest and ate there from the loaves of the Presence. When a certain Edomite servant of Saul, Doeg, saw this, he was moved by envy and reported to Saul, saying: “David has come to the house of Ahimelech” (1 Sam. 21 and 22).

This persecution and Doeg’s accusation were fulfilled, and they are fulfilled every day in the Church.

Doeg is interpreted as “moved.” Edomite is interpreted as “earthly.” Saul means “desire”; Ahimelech [Note: [Col. 0847D] It has been established that *Abimelech* should be read in place of *Achimelech*, so that the etymology may be sound. Saint Augustine himself testifies that in copies of the Psalms he found *Abimelech* more often than *Achimelech*, and he prefers that reading. See him on this point.] means “the kingdom of my father.”

The explanation of the title is this: the understanding produced by the words of this psalm is not to be completed in the present life, but “for the end,” that is, in the future; or “for the end,” namely Christ. Through this understanding, the wicked, because of the present license they possess to do evil, are believed to be destined for condemnation to eternal punishment. The good, however, because they suffer those evils at their hands, will be rewarded in the future.

This understanding is attributed to David—that is, to every believer. It is an understanding, I say, concerning the affair signified when Doeg the Edomite came—that is, some earthly person moved by wickedness—and announced it to Saul, who is interpreted as “desire” and through whom death is signified. He announced it to him, inciting him to persecution: “David”—that is, any believer—“has come into the house of Ahimelech”—that is, into fellowship with the Church, which is rightly signified by Ahimelech, interpreted as “the kingdom of my father,” because God the Father reigns in it.

Nor is it without reason that we understand death through Saul. Just as the sinful people asked God for this man as king, so through illicit desire we acquired death. Saul, as we have said, is interpreted as “desire.” Evil desire of the soul is death. This king rules over the children of distrust (Eph. 5). He persecutes us both directly and through his ministers.

But we will triumph over this king when this mortal nature has put on immortality, when the saying written in Scripture is fulfilled: “Where is your contention, O death? Where is your sting?” (1 Cor. 15; Hos. 13).

Meanwhile, so that we may be patient and not grow faint on the way, let us be refreshed with the bread of holiness in the house of Ahimelech—that is, with the word of God and the heavenly sacraments in the house of the Church.

The subject of this psalm is both kinds of human beings: persecutors and sufferers. The faithful soul, possessing this understanding—that those who now glory in wickedness will later be condemned, while those who now suffer for the sake of justice will afterward receive eternal glory (Matt. 5)—speaks here against the wicked themselves, intending to recall them from perversity and show them the way of truth. Thus it says:

# PSALM LI

3. “Why do you glory in wickedness, you who are powerful in iniquity?” You persecutor and lover of the world, to whom license and power to practice iniquity have been granted: for what fruit, for what advantage, do you glory in wickedness?

Or surely this ought to recall you: that no benefit can be found in this glory. To glory in iniquity is plainly worse than to practice iniquity. For there are some who indeed do unjust things, but whose conscience reproaches them for their sin, so that they tremble within themselves. It also commonly happens that, although they cannot yet restrain themselves from everything, they nevertheless strive to restrain themselves from some evil deeds.

There are others who rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things (Prov. 2). These are the ones who, with loose reins, plunge themselves into every kind of evil. Such people are rebuked in this psalm.

Because they glory in wickedness and are powerful in iniquity, both their perverse will and their depraved action are condemned. He develops the wickedness in detail when he adds:

4. All day long—that is, continually—your tongue devised injustice. Either you do evil, or, when you cannot do it, you speak evil; or, when you cannot even do that, you desire and devise evil. Here he commends the tongue of the heart, not of the mouth; for our heart has its own tongue. What the tongue outside does in speaking, the tongue of the heart does within in thinking. Hence it is that we often speak to ourselves in our hearts without any sound of words.

Nor did you merely devise injustice; you also practiced deceit. This is what follows: You practiced deceit like a sharp razor. Your deceit performs the work of a razor. Just as a sharp razor scrapes dirt and hair from skins, so your deceit, when you strip the faithful of their earthly possessions, or wound or kill their bodies, removes only what is superfluous and does no harm to the soul. Indeed, you make it brighter and more perfect. See what the wicked do to the saints: they shave off the hair. Let the wicked, then, sharpen his razor and sharpen his deceit as much as he can: he is going to remove temporal superfluities, not eternal necessities. He takes away temporal life and sends one toward eternal life. He removes temporal things and drives one toward eternal things.

It should also be noted that in this verse the thought and action of wickedness are contained; in the following verse, however, even the affection is indicated, when it says:

5. You loved wickedness more than goodness. You not only thought and did evil, but also loved evil. And you loved it not merely in order to do it, but also in order to speak it. Therefore he adds: Iniquity rather than to speak righteousness. You loved is understood. This certainly always applies to the reprobate: they prefer to think, do, and speak evil rather than good. And in this there is a double iniquity and condemnation, because they choose what ought to have been rejected and despise what ought to have been chosen. Woe to the wicked heart! It turns away so as not to see what it ought to have seen. Of such a person it is said in another psalm (from Augustine): “He refused to understand, so as to do good” (Ps. 35). Therefore it is rightly added:

6. You loved all words of destruction, deceitful tongue. He no longer cares what he says, what he lies about, or how he deceives. He abandons himself headlong to every falsehood, deceit, and vanity. The deceitful tongue is the servant of deception. A deceitful tongue [from the same source] belongs to those who carry one thing in their heart and bring forth another with their mouth. But in these there is headlong ruin and submersion.

7. Therefore God will destroy you forever. Even if you now seem to stand and flourish like grass in a field, God will uproot you at the end, when he says: “Go into the eternal fire” (Matt. 25). And although you may have fixed the root of your heart in the love of the world, he will uproot you and remove you—that is, he will make you depart—from your tabernacle, that is, from this world, or from the body, or from the Church, in which you ought to have stood. And your root from the land of the living.

Even the reprobate sometimes have a root of goodness. This is signified by the seed that fell upon the rock. For it sent out a root, but when it had sprung up it withered, because it had no moisture. “These,” the Lord says, “are those who believe for a time, but in a time of testing fall away” (Luke 8).
