By believing, therefore, they send down a root; but because they do not persevere, they are uprooted from the land of the living—that is, from the fellowship of the saints—because they did not possess the moisture of divine grace.

8. The righteous will see and fear, and they will laugh at him. Let us understand and distinguish these two times: the time for fearing and the time for laughing (Eccles. 3). We read what is reserved for the wicked at the end. And because we understand and believe, we see and fear. The Apostle says: “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling” (1 Cor. 2). And the Psalmist says: “Serve the Lord with fear” (Ps. 2).

The righteous, therefore, who exist now and live by faith, understand that the wicked are to be condemned. For this reason they fear, also, for themselves. What they are today, they know; what they will be tomorrow, they do not know. But when our day comes, when Christ, our life, appears, then we also will appear with him in glory (Col. 3). Then the righteous will laugh at him, because there will no longer be any occasion for sympathy or grief—not as now, when you see a person living unjustly and wish to labor alongside him and bring him back to the way of truth. Hence [from Augustine] you grieve over him and pray for him.

But when the time of judgment comes, there will no longer be an opportunity for correction, but only for condemnation. There will be repentance there, but fruitless because it will be late. Then the righteous will see the wicked and laugh at him (Wis. 5), that is, appearing superior, they will judge him worthy of mockery. And they will say, in the inward speech of their hearts:

9. Behold the man who did not make God his helper. We must carefully observe what Scripture condemns in this wicked man. It does not say, “Behold the man who was rich,” but, “Behold the man who did not make God his helper.” But he hoped in the abundance of his riches—that is, in his supply of gold or silver, power, glory, and other such things. He is not condemned because he possessed riches, but because he hoped in them. Therefore he is condemned, therefore he is removed from the tabernacle, and therefore his root is torn out from the land of the living.

And he prevailed in his vanity. For what is more vain than a person who thinks a coin worth more than God? Having condemned this man, what do you say about yourself, O David? What do you say about yourself, O body of Christ?

10. But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God. I remain in the Church, which is the house of God, like a fruitful olive tree in the richness of charity and the fruitfulness of good works. I hoped not in riches or honors, but in the mercy of God: I, he says, am to be brought into eternity. He explains this when he adds: And into the age that follows this age.

Just as the olive tree loses neither its greenness in winter nor in summer, so holy men lose neither the beauty of their virtues in prosperity nor in adversity.

11. I will give thanks to you forever, because you have done it. Since you have made me such, therefore I will praise you forever. It is a great confession and a great commendation of grace to say to God, “Because you have done it.” What have you done? Certainly this: that I, like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God, have hoped in the mercy of God. For what have I done except evil? But God is the one who works in us both to will and to act according to his good pleasure (Phil. 2).

And therefore with patience I will await your name—that is, the glory and deification of your name; or, your name, Jesus—that is, Savior—because it is good in the sight of your saints. He does not say that the Lord’s name is good in the sight of the wicked, but in the sight of the saints. For they do not have the eye or palate of the heart by which they can see or taste how good and how sweet the Lord is. A person who does not know what honey is does not know what he is talking about unless he has tasted it. Therefore the Psalm, inviting us more fully to experience it, says: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet.” As if it were saying: You will see then, if you have tasted.

If nothing sweet existed for martyrs, they would never endure such bitter tribulations with equanimity. Your name is good in the sight of your saints. It is good for me when I hear “God.” It is good for me when I hear “Jesus.” Both the good and the wicked can hear this name, but only the saints can taste it. And the holier each person is, the more sweetly and pleasantly the Lord’s name tastes in his heart. He also waits with greater patience and desire to be found worthy at last to see what he loves.

## Title of Psalm 52

1. For the end; concerning Mahalath; an understanding of David. This understanding is attributed to David, that is, to Christ, who invites us to conformity with himself, who is the end of the law. The same Christ is set before us in this psalm for our understanding, so that we may be transformed into him, who is the end of the law, and believe that he is the salvation of Israel.

Christ, I say, acts concerning Mahalath—that is, in the place of a woman giving birth or of one grieving. For Mahalath is interpreted as “grieving” or “giving birth”; but it conveys the effect of one who grieves or gives birth, namely, one who seeks by reproving and rebuking Jewish faithlessness to transform it from oldness into newness.

“My little children, whom I am again in labor with until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. 4)—this is “concerning Mahalath,” and “for the end.” The subject of this psalm is the foolish people who do not know God. Our head intends in this psalm to refute those who denied that Christ was Lord, showing that they are bringing themselves to completion and have become corrupt, and are therefore so detestable to God that none of them does good until they are converted to the one—that is, to God.

He also shows that, because of the wickedness of some, their plans and free choice are to be scattered by God, and that they themselves will be punished forever, while the righteous will obtain salvation. Thus he begins:

## Psalm 52

2. The fool said in his heart, “There is no God.” Since this psalm has already been expounded above (Ps. 13), it requires no explanation except for this one verse, which is not found in the earlier psalm:

[Verse 6.] For God has scattered the bones of those who please men. The Jews wished to please men rather than God when they said, “We have no king but Caesar.” And again: “If you release him, you are not Caesar’s friend” (John 19). The Apostle says: “If I were still pleasing men, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Gal. 1).

Because, desiring to please men, they refused to be servants of Christ, God therefore scattered their bones—that is, the virtues of their souls—and destroyed in them their inward senses, namely, reason and understanding, memory, and other things of this kind. They are called “bones” because, just as flesh is sustained by bones, so the soul is sustained by the virtues.

They were confounded after losing their place and nation and being scattered into captivity throughout all the lands. This happened to them because God despised them. They had first despised him, just as he said through his prophet: “I have nourished and brought up children, but they despised me” (Isa. 1). Because they despised God, therefore, by the just judgment of the almighty God, they were despised.

## Title of Psalm 53

1 and 2. For the end, in songs; an understanding of David, when the Ziphites came and said to Saul, “Is not David hidden among us?” (1 Kings 23).

The understanding of this psalm is to be attributed to David, that is, to Christ pressing toward the end—that is, toward the perfection of his obedience. And this is “in songs,” that is, in gladness, because the life of our Lord was a discipline of conduct: what he himself understood, he set before us to understand.

What did he understand? That one must persevere in praises to the end. When did he understand this? When the Jews, flourishing only in this world, betrayed him to death and refused to believe in God hidden in a man. This betrayal was prefigured when the Ziphites came and said to Saul, “Is not David hidden among us?” (1 Kings 23).

There was a certain village called Ziph, whose inhabitants were the Ziphites. David had hidden himself in its region when Saul wanted to find and kill him. When these Ziphites learned of this, they betrayed him to the persecuting king, saying: “Look, is not David hidden among us?” Their betrayal profited them nothing, nor did it harm David. For their evil disposition was revealed.

Ziph is interpreted as “flower.” Hence they are called Ziphites, that is, “those who are flourishing.” Through them the Jews are signified, for they flourished in temporal goods. Saul signifies death. The Ziphites, therefore, betrayed David to Saul because the Jews handed Christ over to death (Matt. 25). The Ziphites also signify the lovers of this world, who still persecute the body of Christ.

The subject of this psalm is the head and body, placed among and afflicted by the wicked. In the first part of the psalm he prays to be delivered from strangers by whom he is afflicted. In the final part he shows that they will be scattered, while he himself will be rescued from every tribulation and exalted above his enemies.

This, therefore, is set before us to understand in this psalm: just as the Son voluntarily offered himself to the Father (Heb. 9) and asked the Father not for present salvation but for future salvation (John 17), so, if those flourishing in the world rise up against us, we should pass through the troubles inflicted upon us with a joyful spirit and ask that they benefit us for the life to come.

Thus the head prays in this psalm and offers himself, as we have said, as an example of praying and persevering. He foresees that he will suffer for the redemption of the human race, so that he may be raised from death and, according to the power and omnipotence of God, be worthily exalted at last. Thus he said:

## Psalm 53

3. God, save me by your name. The voice of Christ to the Father, as though he were saying openly: Glorify me by your name. Save me by raising me from the dead. And in your power judge me—that is, let my judgment increase according to the excellence of your power, so that all may discern and know that you sent me (John 11).

And the Prophet says: “Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved” (Rom. 10; Joel 2). Let us therefore call upon the name of the Lord, so that we may be saved (Acts 2).

God, by your name—that is, through invocation of your holy name—save me from sins; and in your power—that is, in your might, by which you will judge the living and the dead—judge me, that is, distinguish me from the wicked.

It should be noted that he first asks to be saved by the name, and then to be judged by the power. For the one whom he has first saved through the preceding name, he will afterward judge beneficially through the power that follows. Be confident: that judgment will not be punishment for you, but discernment.

He asks that this prayer, which he sends to the Father, be heard when he adds:

4. God, hear my prayer. Namely, the prayer he has just offered concerning salvation and judgment. Give ear to the words of my mouth—that is, to the prayer held in the heart and uttered by the voice.

The Lord has no other ears than his grace and mercy. When it is said, “Give ear,” nothing else is meant than: Attend, and hear with remembrance and mercy. If he gives ear so as to hear mercifully, we are certain that the Lord will hear our prayer.

In the first verse, therefore, a prayer is made for salvation; in the second, a prayer is made to commend the prayer that has been offered and to gain God’s favor. Then he gives the reason why he must pray, saying:

5. For strangers have risen up against me. The Jews rose up to oppose Christ (John 10). They were strangers, not indeed by race and nature, but by conduct and life. And not only the lesser people, but also the powerful sought my soul. As it is written: “The kings of the earth and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ” (Ps. 2).

They were powerful according to the pride and power of the age. And they did not set God before their eyes. For if they had known him, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Cor. 2). The cause of so great a sin was therefore blindness of heart and unbelief. The cause of blindness was pride.

Woe to the person who does not set God before his eyes! For the Lord is our illumination. When a person understands, he is enlightened; when he neglects understanding, he is darkened. Thus he falls into every error and iniquity.

These are the strangers who persecute the body of Christ. They are not from God, but from their father the devil (John 8). They did not understand that I am God; but now it plainly appears that I truly am God.

6. For behold, God, the Father, insofar as I am man, helps me in my passion, so that I do not fail; and the Lord, his Son, is the receiver of my soul. He receives it to himself in the unity of person. Or, he is the receiver of my soul because, after the passion in which he heard me, he received my soul into glory.

He promises this help also to his members when he says: “Behold, I am with you always, to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28). And elsewhere in the psalm he says: “I am with him in tribulation; I will rescue him and glorify him” (Ps. 90).

Do not fear your persecutors, then, because God is with you in tribulation. Do not fear those who kill the body (Matt. 10), because the Lord is the receiver of your soul.

Perhaps for this reason he turns his voice toward us. Until this point he has spoken in prayer to the Father. Now, wishing to show us that he has been heard and helped by the Father, he no longer speaks to the Father but to us, saying: “For behold, God helps me,” and so forth.

It was not necessary for him to tell the Father what he knew and what he himself accomplished; but it was necessary for us to hear this, so that we might learn the example of Christ’s patience. From these words we are instructed that, when evils are inflicted upon us by our enemies, we ought not to become angry, curse, or seek revenge, but to pray and await God’s help.

“Vengeance is mine, and I will repay,” says the Lord (Deut. 32; Rom. 12; Heb. 18). Hence he continues not so much by praying as by prophesying:

7. Turn the evils against my enemies. Behold what sort of vengeance God carries out. The evils that the wicked inflict upon the good, God turns away from us and sends back upon the wicked. For what harm do persecution and tribulation do to martyrs? Rather, they benefit them for salvation. But they harm the wicked for condemnation.

Hence it is said elsewhere: “His sorrow will return upon his head, and his iniquity will descend upon his own crown” (Ps. 7). Therefore it is rightly added: In your power—that is, by your just judgment—destroy them.

He rightly did not say, “Destroy,” but “scatter,” because the Jews, ruined in different places, were scattered throughout the regions because of the evil they committed against Jesus. God will also scatter the wicked in his truth when, at the final judgment, he hands them over to be tormented by diverse punishments and tortures, saying:

8. I will sacrifice to you willingly. Every good work offered to God can be called a sacrifice. And he rightly prefaced this with “willingly.” For in every sacrifice God weighs the will and affection and considers the good intention of the one offering, not the greatness of the gift. The greater the devotion and willingness of the one who offers, the greater his sacrifice is before God.

Hence Moses says: “The Lord looked upon Abel and his offerings” (Gen. 4). The Lord is said to have looked first not upon the offerings, but first upon Abel, because he does not weigh the will by the gift, but the gift by the will. But he did not look upon Cain and his offerings (ibid.), because he did not see in him a good will.

The Son voluntarily offered himself to the Father as a sacrifice for us, willingly indeed, because not out of necessity but out of love. For God does not love compelled gifts or compelled service.

And I will give thanks to your name, O God, because it is good. Truly it is good and beneficial for our souls that we do everything we do for the praise and glory of your name; that we sacrifice to God with our whole will and give thanks to the Lord’s name with our whole heart. This is sweet, this is good, this is pleasant.

He gives the reason why this must be done when he adds:

[Col. 0859C] 9. For you have rescued me from every tribulation. Therefore, he says [from Augustine], I said that your name is good. For if I had been able to recognize this before the tribulations, perhaps they would not have been necessary for me. But tribulation was applied as an admonition, and the admonition was made for your praise. I would not have understood where I was unless I had been admonished of my weakness.

Therefore you have rescued me from every tribulation. And my eye has looked down upon my enemies.

[Note: Augustine, along with certain other ancient Psalter manuscripts, read “looked upon” (*respexit*). Our text, which preferred the reading of the Vulgate version known as the Gallican Psalter, changes Augustine’s reading to “looked down upon” (*despexit*) even in the exposition that follows, and adapts the subsequent statements to its own meaning.]

My eye has looked down upon those Ziphites. I passed beyond their flower, raised the height of my heart to you, and, having arrived there, looked down upon them. And I saw that all flesh is grass, and that the glory of man is like the flower of grass (Isa. 40).

Do this, therefore, brothers, with your souls. Lift up your hearts. Polish the edge of your mind. Learn to love God freely. Learn to despise the present age. Learn willingly to sacrifice an offering of praise. Learn also to praise and invoke the Lord’s name, admirable and great, so that, rising above the flower of grass, you may look down upon your enemies.

## Title of Psalm 54

[Col. 0859D]

1. For the end, in songs; an understanding of David. The understanding of this psalm is to be attributed to David, that is, to Christ persevering to the end—that is, toward the completion of his obedience. And this is “in songs,” that is, in gladness of mind.

The subject of this psalm is the whole Christ, namely, the head and body afflicted by the wicked—but delivered. In this psalm Christ sets before us, his members, something to understand—that is, something not to be negligently committed to memory: that, placed amid adversities according to his example, we should never fall away from hope, but confidently pass through torments, hope for eternal recompense from God, and believe in the irreversible condemnation of our persecutors.

This is briefly contained near the end of the psalm, where it says: “Cast your care upon the Lord.” And shortly afterward: “But I hoped in you, O God.” In the earlier parts of the psalm he plainly declares what adversities he endured amid his hope, and what he obtained by hoping for his own deliverance and the condemnation of his adversaries.

[Note: Perhaps *promit*, that is, “relates.”]

He prays for himself, lest he fail in his passion, and for his resurrection and glorification. He also treats of the Jews’ present rejection and eternal condemnation, the adoption of the Gentiles, and the eternal glorification of the faithful, saying:

## Psalm 54

267 2. Hear, O God, my prayer, and do not despise my supplication. [Verse 3.] Attend to me and hear me. As if he were saying:

O my faithful ones placed in tribulations, do not fail, but hope in the Lord and await your recompense from him; pray according to my example. For I, placed in my passion, prayed thus to the Lord:

O God the Father, hear my prayer because of the dignity of your Son, by raising me from death and glorifying me in my passion. As if he were saying: “Father, glorify your Son, so that your Son may glorify you” (John 17).

And do not despise my supplication—that is, because of the humanity I assumed, do not regard my supplication, which I make to avoid evils, as contemptible; rather, attend to me—that is, make that humanity intent, persevering in prayer, or in virtues and the increase of good works. And thus hear me.

When prayer and supplication are placed together in sacred Scripture, they differ from one another. Prayer is made when we ask for something honorable, namely, something we wish to obtain. Supplication, however, is made to avoid evils, namely, things we wish to be driven away from us.

It should also be known that the almighty God often both hears and disregards the supplication of certain people. Hence, when the Israelites wrongly asked for meat, he gave it to them in anger (Exod. 16), but he also showed, by punishing them, how displeasing their request was to him. Therefore it is written: “While the meat was still in their mouths, the anger of God rose against them” (Num. 11; Ps. 77).

Likewise, when they asked God for a king according to the custom of the nations that surrounded them, he did indeed permit them to have a king; but he signified to Samuel how displeasing their request was to him, saying: “Hear the voice of the people in all that they say to you. For they have not rejected you, but me, so that I should not reign over them” (1 Kings 8).

Samuel also testified to this, saying: “But you have cast away the Lord your God, who alone saved you from all your evils and tribulations” (1 Kings 10).

Thus he asks that his prayer be heard in such a way that God not despise his supplication, but that the hearing of it contain both grace and benefit. The words that follow seem to agree with this meaning:

3. Attend to me and hear me. The Lord attends to me, then, and hears not only my prayer but me, when he grants for the benefit of my soul what I ask. And as though someone might ask, “What necessity do you have for asking to be heard in this way?” he says: I am sorrowful in my trial, and I am troubled by the voice of the enemy and by the tribulation of the sinner.

Our Lord Jesus Christ was made sorrowful and troubled in the trial of his passion when the enemy Jews cursed and afflicted him. Hence he himself says: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 26).

Even now the enemies of the Church do not cease either to do evil to its members, if they can, or, if they cannot, at least to slander and disparage them. Hence it is said in another psalm: “Those who repay evil for good slandered me” (Ps. 37). And elsewhere: “All my enemies whispered together against me; they devised evil against me. They established an evil word against me,” and so forth (Ps. 40).

Concerning them it is further added: For they have turned their iniquities against me. By accusing and charging me with crimes, as it is written: “Do we not rightly say that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?” (John 8).

And in anger they were troublesome to me. By beating and striking me, and not justly, but in anger—that is, because of their anger. For it is written: “My son, when you approach the service of God, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for testing” (Eccles. 2). It does not say “for rest and security,” but “for fear and testing.”

For all who wish to live devoutly in Christ suffer persecution (2 Tim. 3). The Wise Man likewise speaks of the righteous: “Their affliction was regarded as an ending, and they went from the righteous way into destruction” (Wis. 3). Similarly the Apostle says: “They were stoned, they were cut in pieces, they were tested; they died by the slaughter of the sword; they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, needy, afflicted, oppressed” (Heb. 12).

Moreover, the Savior himself, speaking of himself, says: “Was it not necessary for Christ to suffer these things and so enter into his glory?” (Luke 24). To this belongs what follows:

5. My heart is troubled within me, and the fear of death has fallen upon me. Hence it is written in the Gospel: “Jesus began to be afraid, to be distressed, and to be sorrowful, and an angel of the Lord strengthened him” (Luke 22).

Yet we must not believe that our Redeemer, who had power to lay down his life and to take it up again (John 10), had any fear of death with respect to his own person. Rather, we understand this according to his members: although they are strong in spirit, nevertheless, because the flesh is weak (Matt. 26), they are sometimes troubled within themselves because of punishment and fear the bitterness of death.

Therefore he adds:

6. Fear and trembling came upon me. Fear may be referred to the soul, trembling to the body. Hence he himself says: “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26).

And to show that he had been seized by the greatest fear, he prayed not only once but three times, saying the same words (Matt. 26); and, being in agony, he prayed at greater length. “His sweat became like drops of blood running down upon the earth” (Luke 22).

These words also pertain more to the members than to the head. And darkness covered me—that is, the Jews, darkened and blind. For if they had not been blind and overshadowed by diabolical darkness, they could at least have recognized Christ from such great virtues and miracles (John 10).

Or, in what he says, “My heart is troubled within me,” anger can be understood, concerning which it is said elsewhere: “My eye was troubled because of anger” (Ps. 6). And if the eye was troubled, what follows? And the fear of death fell upon me.

Our life is love; death is hatred. When a person begins to fear that he will hate the one whom he loved, he fears death—a sharper and more inward death, by which the soul, not the body, is killed. Hence fear and trembling came upon me, and darkness covered me. For “whoever hates his brother is in darkness” (1 John 2).

And what does he say to himself, placed in that trial and weakness?

7. And I said, Who will give me wings like a dove’s, and I will fly and rest? In this tribulation I did not despair, but I said—that is, I prayed to my Father in this way: Raise me up, Father, to yourself.

For who else besides you will give me, who am like a dove—that is, innocent and without the bitterness of gall—wings, that is, agility and ability, so that I may fly—that is, pass from this world to the Father (John 13), from the Jewish people to the Gentiles—and rest there? And my prayer will not be frustrated.

8. For behold, I have gone far away by fleeing, and I remained in solitude. It is evident that I, fleeing—that is, rising quickly from death—have put the world or the Jewish people far away, and remained in solitude—that is, in heaven or among the Gentiles.

Holy men desire wings like a dove’s, that is, spiritual virtues, so that, leaving earthly things behind in their minds, they may fly through heavenly contemplation and rest in the love of God. And often the merciful Lord fulfills their desire, so that, fleeing far from the tumult of carnal thoughts, they may remain in solitude—that is, rest with delight in the quiet of their minds.

And so that this might happen to me, I did not trust in my own strength.

9. I awaited him who saved me from faintness of spirit and from the tempest. That is, I placed my hope in the Lord, who saved me from becoming fainthearted. And from the tempest—that is, from every disturbance.

Peter had faintness of spirit when he saw the strong wind and the storm of the sea and became afraid. And when he began to sink, he awaited the help of his Savior. Hence he cried out: “Lord, save me!” Jesus stretched out his hand, took hold of him, and saved him from faintness of spirit and from the tempest. Yet he rebuked him, saying: “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matt. 14).

Thus the elect often, when they see the powerful assaults of temptations, fear the storm and danger to their salvation because of the weakness of their spirit, and so begin to sink. Yet they do not perish, because, awaiting and asking for divine help, they are saved.

But just as they are saved, so, conversely, the reprobate are submerged. Concerning them he immediately continues by prophesying and praying:

10. Hurl them down, O Lord, and divide their tongues. They are the ones who have raised themselves up wickedly. It is beneficial for them [from Augustine] to be hurled down; those who have wickedly conspired should have their tongues divided.

Certain people built a high tower through pride, and the Lord divided their tongues (Gen. 11). Then they began not to understand one another. From this came the origin of the many languages. Previously there had been one language. But one language benefited humble hearts.

[Note: In Augustine: “One language benefited the concordant; one language benefited the humble.”]

When that assembly, however, had been hurled down amid a conspiracy of pride, God spared them by dividing their tongues, lest, by understanding one another, they should form a pernicious unity. Through proud people the tongues were divided; through humble Apostles the tongues were gathered together. The spirit of pride scattered language; the Holy Spirit gathered languages together (Acts 2).

Those who desire one language should come to the Church, because amid the diversity of the languages of the flesh there is one language in the faith of the heart.

Hurl them down and divide their tongues. Why? Because I saw iniquity and contradiction in the city: iniquity in action, contradiction in words; I saw them in the city—that is, in the society of the wicked.

There is a certain turbulent city. It was the city that had built the tower. It was confused and called Babylonia; it was scattered among innumerable nations (Gen. 11). From there the Church is gathered into the desert of a good conscience.

Christ came, and the wicked city contradicted him. He stretched out his hands toward an unbelieving and contradictory people.

What he calls “iniquity” here can be understood as their faithlessness. For if the one who lives by faith is righteous, the one who does not have faith is wicked. Thus unbelief is iniquity. Nor is only the one who does not believe wicked, but also the one who lives badly. Of such people the Apostle speaks: “They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Rom. 1).

Even now the remnants of that city rage and contradict. Concerning it he further adds:

11. Day and night—that is, continually—iniquity will surround it upon its walls, that is, upon its leaders.

People often say: “No one would remain a pagan if those people became Christians.” Those who therefore do not yet become Christians are like the walls of that city, which neither believes nor ceases to contradict. Whoever defends another in sin is a wall of the wicked city.

And labor is in its midst, and injustice. There is labor there because there is iniquity there, because there is injustice there. Wherever you see iniquity, understand that labor is present. Whoever is wicked will never have peace. For his conscience torments him, and he himself is his own enemy. There is always labor in pride, just as, conversely, there is rest in humility.

Hence the Savior admonishes us, saying: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11). Why do they labor, then, except because they are not meek and humble of heart?

12. And usury and deceit have not ceased from its streets. Consider the Jewish people, and see how these two vices—namely, deceit and usury—have always reigned among them. The streets of this city are pride, lust, covetousness, greed, and other such things. The way of this city is broad and spacious, and leads to death (Matt. 7).

Usury is when more is demanded than was lent. There is another, worse kind of usury: when you do not forgive what is owed to you, and the eye of your heart is troubled by the verse that says, “Forgive us our debts,” etc. (Matt. 6). Have you heard an insulting word? Do you wish to exact the punishment of damnation? You are a usurer of injuries. Have you been struck with a fist? Do you seek a killing? That is evil usury. Such usuries abound in that city.

Deceit is when one thing is concealed in the heart and another is pronounced by the mouth. [Col. 0863B] The wicked always wish to conceal what they are and to display what they are not. Then he shows that this people deserved punishment precisely because it had formerly been intimate with the Lord and afterward cursed its own Lord. The evils inflicted by friends are more grievous.

13. For if my enemy—that is, the Gentile people—had cursed me as the Jewish people cursed me, I would certainly have endured it and judged it more tolerably and mildly. And if the one who hated me, when he worshiped idols, had spoken great things against me—that is, had insulted me through pride—and had exalted himself over me and threatened me with whatever he could, I would perhaps have hidden myself, that is, withdrawn from him.

These words can be understood more particularly of Judas the betrayer, because Jesus hid himself from the Jews, but did not hide himself at all from Judas. But what does “perhaps” mean? Can anything be uncertain with God? This ambiguity of speech is used according to ordinary human expression. Thus we commonly say: “Perhaps I shall go there; perhaps I shall do this.” I say, then, that enemies would have been more tolerably dealt with.

14. But you, O Judas, a man according to the flesh, united with me through pretense, my leader through preaching, and known to me through faith—you who lived together with me and received sweet food, both bodily and spiritual—you, I say, O Judas, O perverse people, when you persist in so great an evil, are you to be tolerated?

Judas and his people signify false brothers within the holy Church. While they live hypocritically, they oppress the elect all the more grievously because they are inwardly among them. Yet by his example the Lord teaches us to endure them; they themselves, however, will not escape eternal punishment. Let those who are such hear the sentence of death that follows:

15. Let death come upon them, and let them descend alive into hell. Death will come upon them when eternal damnation covers them. The living descend into hell (from Augustine) who understand that what they are doing is evil and yet do not desist from it. What does “alive” mean? Knowing that they are perishing. A much heavier damnation rests upon such people than upon the rest, as it is written: “The servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it shall be beaten with many blows” (Luke 12).

Therefore let false brothers, hypocrites, slanderers, those who display religion by their clothing but do not live in accordance with religion, be afraid. This sentence applies to them: “Let death come upon them, and let them descend alive into hell.” Why?

16. Because wickedness is in their dwellings—and not only in their corners, but also in their midst. It is as though he said: They are full of wickedness everywhere. Or, “in their dwellings,” that is, in their bodies, in which they temporarily wander as strangers and serve as soldiers (2 Cor. 5), there are wickednesses. And “in their midst,” that is, in their heart: the wickednesses they commit, they commit with their whole heart. Those who are such perish.

But I cried out to the Lord, and the Lord saved me. If an enemy afflicts you, cry out to God, and he will save you. Hence in another psalm he says: “Call upon me in the day of tribulation, and I will deliver you” (Ps. 80).

18. In the evening, morning, and midday I will tell and proclaim, and he will hear my voice. “In the evening” (from Augustine), the Lord is in death; “in the morning,” in resurrection; “at midday,” in ascension. In the evening I will tell of the endurance of death. In the morning I will proclaim the life of the one who rises. At midday I will pray that he may hear, at the right hand of the Father. He will hear me, the one who intercedes for us.

Therefore, brothers, those whom you see within this very congregation of these walls—troubled, arrogant, perverse—are the chaff of the Lord’s threshing floor. When he winnows at the end, all the chaff will fly away (Matt. 3). But what are we to do except sing, pray, and mourn in the psalm with this one? And nevertheless, let us confidently say what follows: “Truly he will hear my voice,” because:

19. He will redeem my soul in peace. For he himself is true peace. The soul is redeemed in peace when, by the grace of almighty God, it is transferred from vices to virtues, or from this world to the Father.

From whom will he redeem it? “From those who draw near to me.” For as to those who are far from me, the matter is easy. The one who says, “Come, worship the idol,” does not deceive me so quickly. He is far from me, because he is a pagan. It is more dangerous for me when the threat comes from a Christian who lives with me in the same house and, under the appearance of religion, prepares for me a snare of deception.

I rightly say, “those who draw near to me,” because they were with me among many. There is much chaff and little grain. “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20). These were not among the few who would be saved; rather, they were with me among the many—that is, among those who belong to the chaff and to perdition. They were not with me in the wheat, but with me in the chaff, because the chaff is close to the wheat. They were with me in the sacraments, but not with me in charity.

20. God will hear, and he will humble them, he who is before the ages. For although Christ our God came in time from the Virgin Mary, nevertheless, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1). He will hear the humble in eternity; he will humble in condemnation those who have risen up in dissension. And rightly so: “For there is no change in them.” They do not change for the better, but descend into worse things.

“And they did not fear God.” Just as the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom (Ps. 110; Prov. 1 and 9), so not fearing God is the beginning of death. Blessed is the person who is always fearful. But the one who is hard of mind will fall into evil (Prov. 28). Hence it is also added:

21. He will stretch out his hand in repayment. This will take place in judgment, when God will enlarge his avenging hand for punishment. Hence elsewhere he threatens, saying: “I will lift up my hand to heaven. If I sharpen my sword like lightning, and my hand seizes judgment, I will repay vengeance to my enemies, and I will repay those who hate me” (Deut. 32).

And truly they deserve to be punished: “For they have defiled his covenant.” They despised the one who was declared for salvation by the covenant of the law. Therefore:

22. They were divided by the anger of his countenance. For the anger and severity of God, because of this sin, divided them throughout the various regions of the world.

These words also seem to apply to heretics. They do not cease to defile God’s covenant, since they perversely understand and explain the holy Scriptures. They defile God’s covenant because they do not cease to approve falsehood and error from it itself. Therefore they were divided by the anger of his countenance: they were divided from the anger of God’s severity. For what Donatus says, the Sabellian does not say; nor does the Arian say what the Sabellian says. Separated from the unity of the Catholic Church, they have been divided through many errors.

“And his heart drew near.” This means that we are to understand his will. The division of heretics is of great value to us for understanding God. For many things were hidden in the Scriptures, and when the heretics were cut off, they stirred up questions in the Church of God. What had been hidden was opened, and the will of God was understood.

For was a complete treatment of the Trinity given before the Arians resisted? Nor had those things concerning the very unity of Christ been explained with precision, except after that separation began to press upon the weaker brothers. Therefore those who knew how to handle and resolve these matters, lest the weak perish—troubled by the questions, speeches, and arguments of the impious—brought the obscure things of the law into public view.

Thus they were divided by the anger of his countenance, and his heart drew near to us for understanding. “There must be heresies,” says the Apostle, “so that those who are approved may become manifest among you” (1 Cor. 11).

“His words were softened above oil, and yet they are arrows.” For certain things in the Scriptures seemed hard; once explained, they were softened. And rightly “above oil,” because oil comforts the flesh, while the sweetness of God’s words comforts the soul. “And yet they are arrows.” For they armed preachers (from Augustine). These words themselves are directed into the breasts of hearers by those who persist in season and out of season.

That the words of God are arrows, the Apostle testifies when he says: “The word of God is living and effective, and sharper than every two-edged sword,” etc. (Heb. 4). But perhaps you are not yet fit to be armed with these arrows.

23. Cast your care upon the Lord. That is, expect everything from him and nothing from yourself. Solomon calls human care a worm, by which a person is gnawed like cloth by a moth (Prov. 26). Cast your care, therefore, upon the Lord. Think upon him so that you may remain tranquil within yourself. And he will nourish you in faith and conduct, in doctrine and virtues.

Although for now he has temptation here, he will not give the righteous eternal fluctuation—that is, agitation or disturbance—but will make him peaceful in eternal life. He will not give the righteous eternal fluctuation. For although we fluctuate, are tempted, and are afflicted for a time, we have our anchor fixed in heaven. Therefore he will not give the righteous eternal fluctuation, because after the turbulence of temptations he will prepare for him forever a harbor of rest.

What is that harbor? “Come, you blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25).

24. But you, O God, will lead them into the pit of destruction. From there he will say: “Go, you accursed, into the eternal fire” (ibid.). He calls hell a pit because of its depth and darkness. This place has been prepared for the wicked, so that they may fall and perish in it as in a deep pit.

God will lead them into the pit of destruction—not because he is the author of their guilt, but because he is the judge of their iniquity. He indicates what their iniquity is when he adds: “Men of blood,” that is, persecutors and shedders of blood; “and deceitful,” those who through pretense and fraud deceive unwary souls. “They will not halve their days”: they will not turn back to repentance, but will continue in wickedness to the end.

This is not to be understood of everyone. Many, after shedding blood and practicing deceit, have turned to repentance and salvation. It applies only to those who were divided by the anger of his countenance.

Holy men halve their days because whatever they do wrong on the other days, they repay through fasting and prayers during the forty and other penitential days. Or because some turn to God in childhood, others in adolescence, and still others in old age.

Rightly, therefore, it is added: “But I will hope in you, O God.” That is, I will place my hope not in the world, nor in a human being, but in you.

TITLE OF PSALM 55.

1. The title of the following psalm is this: “Unto the end, for the people who were made far from the saints, David, in the inscription of the title, when the Philistines held him in Gath” (2 Kings 1 and 21). This psalm is attributed to David, that is, to the Church, and is directed unto the end. I mean, it is composed for the people, namely, that it may itself be delivered from the people who were made far from the saints in the inscription of the title: because, while the saints confess Christ to be King of the Jews, as the title says (John 19), this people contradicts it—whether by words, as Jews and pagans do, or by deeds, as evil Christians do—when the Philistines held him in Gath.

Gath was a city of the Philistines, that is, of foreigners, indeed a people far from the saints. Gath is interpreted “winepress.” David fled to this city, but we do not read in the historical account that he was detained there. Therefore our David, Jesus Christ, was not only held but is still held by the Philistines—that is, foreigners—in Gath, that is, in the winepress, namely in the pressure of this life. The subject is Christ and the Church, and she herself speaks concerning herself.

In the first part she asks to be delivered from demons and from their members, placing her confidence for deliverance in God. In the second, beginning where he says, “All day long my words,” etc., she enumerates the evils which that people inflicts upon her. In the third, beginning where he says, “In me, O God, are thy vows,” she says that she will praise God eternally. The purpose is to admonish us patiently to endure the evils of this life, while also attending to those who inflict evils upon us being converted to us. And although the Church trusts in God for her deliverance, nevertheless, considering her own weakness, she begins to pray thus:

PSALM 55.

2. Have mercy on me, O God. Grant aid against the persecution of evils. And it is necessary: “For man hath trampled upon me.” The devil too is called “man” in the Gospel, where it is said concerning the tares: “An enemy, a man, hath done this” (Matt. 13). This enemy man, both in himself and through his members, does not cease to persecute and oppress the servants of God.

When you have begun to live devoutly in Christ, you have entered the winepress. Prepare yourself for pressures. Do not fear because man tramples you. You have become a grape, in order to be trodden. In the winepress pressure is fruitful. A grape on the vine does not feel pressure. It appears whole, but nothing flows from it. It is put into the winepress; it is trodden and pressed. An injury appears to be done to the grape; but this injury is not barren—indeed, if no injury were done, it would remain barren.

Let us therefore consider the two enemies, the one whom we see and the one whom we do not see: man and the devil. Let us love the former; let us beware of the latter. Let us pray for man; let us pray against the devil; and let us say to God: “Have mercy on me, O God, for man hath trampled upon me.” All day long—that is, continually—assailing me by words and suggestions, he has afflicted me by open attacks. This psalm strengthens us against such persons. For it is necessary that we endure such persons to the end; we would not endure them unless it were expedient for us. For every temptation is a testing, and every effect of testing has its own fruit. And he shows through whom the devil makes this sort of attack upon the Church when he adds:

3. My enemies have trampled upon me all day long. Like a grape pressed in the winepress, the members of the devil have oppressed me; and they were able to do this, “for many are they that fight against me.” What he first stated concerning one, he now says concerning many, because the devil is the head of all the reprobate, and now through himself, now through his members, tramples upon and attacks Christ’s body, as he formerly did the Head also. But let us hear what he adds, strong amid adversities.

4. Shall I fear “from the height of the day,” that is, from temporal pride? Far be it; or, shall I fear from height, that is, power? This indeed is not to be feared, because it is “of the day,” that is, granted for a time. I shall not fear this, but rather place my hope in thee. And this is what follows: “But I will hope in thee.” When the days have passed which are high—for they are high only for a time—at the end of the time of their height they will fear. But I will hope in thee. On the day of judgment the wicked will indeed fear (Wis. 5), but the righteous will be secure. For then that will come which they hoped for, desired, and prayed might come. He now shows himself strong and steadfast when he adds:

5. In God I will praise my words. He praises his words in God who, in what he says, commends not himself but God. Hence Truth itself says: “My doctrine is not mine, but his, the Father’s, who sent me” (John 7). A book is praised when it is said to have been composed by some renowned philosopher or accomplished grammarian. How much more ought those words to be praised which are from God.

But what in you is God’s is honored by you, and you, made in God, will be honored by God. But if you honor as your own, rather than God’s, what in you is God’s, then, just as that people was made far from the saints, so you are far from the Holy One. Therefore, “In God I will praise my words.” If in God, why “my”? But they are both in God and mine: in God, because they are from him; mine, because I have received them. “I have hoped in God.” A little before he had said, “I shall hope.” Now he has said, “I have hoped,” as one who does not fear, as one made steadfast. “I will not fear what flesh may do unto me,” that is, any fleshly person. Hope fixed in God expels every fear. It also despises passing torments. For it produces charity and produces patience, by which the world is trodden underfoot and the devil overcome. You say, “I will not fear what flesh may do unto me”; and what does it do to you?

6. All day long they cursed my words. That is, they judged my preaching abominable. All their thoughts against me are for evil. For the reprobate think nothing against the righteous but evil (Ps. 7): how they may destroy and annihilate them and their speech. Nor do strangers alone persecute, but also household members and intimates. Therefore he adds:

7. They will dwell and hide themselves; they will watch my heel. They dwell with me in one house, in one Church. They conceal themselves beneath sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves (Matt. 10). They hide themselves as plotters and spies; they prepare snares. If they cannot immediately do the evil they intend, they watch the heel, so that at least in the end they may be able to accomplish their designs. It is the devil’s custom, or the custom of those who are his ministers, to watch with crafty guile our heel—that is, our last end. Hence the Lord said to the serpent concerning the woman: “She shall watch thy head, and thou shalt lie in wait for her heel” (Gen. 3).

Therefore the servant of God must always be watchful and circumspect against the head of this cunning serpent, and, with the Lord’s help, so order his life and conduct that those who dwell with him and conceal themselves, who watch his heel, may find nothing to blame either in the beginning or in the end. Thus they watched my heel, “as they waited for my soul.” For evil men bear the life of the righteous as though it were a heavy burden; hence the Jews said of the Lord [printed: “Demonio”]: “He is burdensome to us even to behold, for he is unlike our works” (Wis. 2). Yet the psalm teaches us to pray even for such people. However great a sinner a person may be, the good God is able to save him. Therefore he adds:

8. “For nothing”—that is, for no preceding merits—thou wilt save them. Or thus: thou wilt save them so that there will be no labor for thee. Thou wilt not toil in healing, although we are astonished in beholding. “In anger thou wilt break the peoples.” The anger appears paternal. A father is angry with a son who despises his commands. In anger he strikes, beats, and sends him to school; he breaks him, humbling him from pride through discipline. How many have filled the house of God after being broken in his anger, that is, worn down by tribulations. Thou wilt break them, and I will contribute my part toward their conversion. I will declare to them that I committed many evils and that through confession they were forgiven me, so that, hearing this, they may not despair of their sins but may obtain through confession the medicine of salvation by my example. Therefore he says:

9. O God, I have declared my life to thee. Paul declared his life in this way, saying: “I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an injurious man; but I obtained mercy” (1 Tim. 1). He declared his life, not to himself but to God, because he declared it in such a way that credit was given to God, not merely to his own advantage but to God’s. If you declare your life for this reason, that by your example you may invite others to confession and to receive the life which you received, you declare your life to God, from whom you received grace; and you will have a greater reward, because you have not been ungrateful for what you received.

“Thou hast placed my tears in thy sight.” Those tears which I shed while declaring my sins thou hast placed in thy sight; that is, thou hast held them acceptable and hast heard me. “As also in thy promise.” For, as Augustine says, just as thou hadst promised, thou hast done this. Thou saidst that thou wouldst hear one weeping. I believed, I wept, I was heard. I found thee merciful in promising and true in giving.

10. Then—that is, through thy breaking them and through my declaration—my enemies will be converted from their evil life, so that they may be “backward,” that is, may follow thee. A person is not corrected by going ahead. It is good for him to turn backward and follow the one whom he wished to precede. A person goes ahead through pride; he turns backward through humility. The person who wishes to do his own will desires to go ahead. He becomes backward who is always ready to obey. Therefore let enemies turn backward, that those who had been proud may become humble. Thus those who had been enemies will be friends.

Then he shows how swift God’s mercy is when he adds: “In whatever day I call upon thee, behold, I have known that thou art my God,” that is, the one who hears me. It is like what is elsewhere said: “In whatever hour the sinner is converted” (Ezek. 18) and groans, all his sins will be forgiven him. For he does not delay through days and years; rather, “Turn to me,” he says, “and I will turn to you; follow backward, and I will lead you” (Zech. 1).

[Note: [Col. 0867] The negative particle seems to require deletion; or “I have known, but …,” or something similar, must be supplied.]

Therefore, considering so great a divine mercy, the Church does not say, “Behold, I have known,” that is, “I have understood manifestly, that thou art my God.” This is great knowledge. She does not say, “I have known that thou art God,” but “that thou art my God.” For he is yours when he helps you; he is yours when you are not estranged from him. Hence it is said: “Blessed is the people whose Lord is its God” (Ps. 143). Whose God is he not? He is indeed God of all, but properly of those who love, fear, possess, and worship him. Now, made one with them through conversion and participation in God’s grace, she repeats the verse which she has already said, so that they too may say with her and by her example:

11. “In God I will praise the word, and in the Lord I will praise the sayings,” etc. “Word” is preaching concerning faith: how we ought to believe in the threefold and one God, as the Apostle says: “The word is near thee, in thy mouth and in thy heart; this is the word of faith which we preach” (Rom. 10). “Saying” concerns morals, when it is preached to us how chastely, soberly, justly, and devoutly we ought to live. We ought to refer all these things to God, so that in our believing well, living justly, or speaking rightly (Titus 2), both we in God and God in us may be praised and honored.

And because strength of hope ought to follow the word of faith, it is rightly added: “In God I have hoped; I will not fear what man may do unto me.” Faith is so called because it is made in God. Hope is, as it were, a foot, because it rests upon him. Faith avails us for righteousness, because “the righteous lives by faith” (Rom. 1). By believing in God you turn from evil and do good (Ps. 33). This is righteousness. Hope avails us for patience and contempt of the world. In hoping for eternal things, we easily despise temporal things and bravely endure adversities (Heb. 6). Our hope in God is, as it were, an anchor. When a sailor fears a storm, he fixes his anchor. If we have the anchor of hope fixed in God, we shall fear no storm of this world. “I will not fear,” he says, “what man may do unto me,” because, even if he takes temporal things away, I nevertheless have spiritual things which I may offer thee.

12. “In me, O God, are thy vows, which I shall render to thee as praises.” These are the true gifts and grateful sacrifices which God requires of us: devout vows, holy desires, right faith, certain hope, perfect charity. Whoever pays such vows renders praises to the almighty Lord. These are true riches, which a person does not fear losing unless he himself wishes to take them away. Whoever wishes to vow and render a freely offered vow to the Lord God should vow and render himself. For this is required; this is owed. Let Caesar’s image be rendered to Caesar; let God’s image be rendered to God (Matt. 22). And this indeed is just. Why?

13. “For thou hast delivered my soul from death.” He puts the past for the future. For one who considers eternity in the mind reckons as already past whatever can pass away. It is as if he said: Since in the other life thou wilt deliver my soul from eternal death. “And my feet from falling,” because there my affection will in no way be moved toward evil. There will be no falling where there is no temptation; there will be no falling where the blessed Trinity is. Therefore it is rightly added: “That I may please before God in the light of the living.” We shall please before God in the light of the living when we appear before him immortal and without sin. For we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3). There is the true light and eternal life. There the righteous shall shine as the sun in the kingdom of their Father (Wis. 3).

Therefore may all these things avail us, that we may love God freely, hope in him, and fear neither man nor devil. Let us endure the evil and be good; let us despair of no one. Let us pray for all whom we endure (from Augustine), so that both here in the light of faith and there in the light of sight, as in the light of the living, we may please in God’s presence. Amen.

TITLE OF PSALM 56.

1. “Unto the end: Destroy not; David, in the inscription of the title, when he fled from the face of Saul into the cave” (1 Kings 22 and 24). This psalm tends unto the end, that is, unto Christ, warning you, whoever you are, “Destroy not David,” that is, do not dishonor Christ by an inscription of the title altered by you—that is, by withdrawing yourself from Christ’s kingdom, namely by denying that Christ is King of the Jews. The inscription of the title was altered by certain persons when David—that is, Christ—fled from the face, that is, from the knowledge, of Saul, that is, of the devil or the Jews, into the cave, that is, into his humanity or the tomb. For because they knew only Christ’s humanity and saw him dead in the tomb, not at all attending to his being God, some altered the inscription of the title, denying that Christ is King of the Jews (John 19).

The subject is Christ. In the first part, as in the other psalms where he treats of the Passion, he begins with prayer. In the second part, beginning, “He sent from heaven and delivered me,” he briefly touches upon his Passion and glorification. In the third, beginning, “My heart is ready, O God,” he shows that from his glorification he renders great praise to God. In this psalm Christ shows that, through the mystery of his incarnation, Passion, resurrection, and ascension, the whole world is to be subjected to the Christian faith. By this he intends, namely, to admonish all that none should wish to withdraw himself from his kingdom through unbelief. He does this by setting before us his incarnation, Passion, resurrection, and ascension. Thus, therefore, he begins:

PSALM 56.

2. Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy on me. You hear the master praying: learn to pray. For he prayed in order to teach prayer. He suffered in order to teach suffering. He rose again in order to teach hope in the resurrection. By repeating the prayer, he impresses upon us a great necessity. This repetition of the prayer can also be referred to different matters as follows: Have mercy on me, O God, by giving me constancy in the Passion; have mercy on me by causing me to rise again. And thou oughtest to have mercy, “for my soul trusteth in thee,” not in another. It is as if he said: I trust in thee not only in the present, but also in the future; not only according to the body, but also according to the soul. Therefore he further adds: “And in the shadow of thy wings I will hope.” This is spoken by analogy: as the Lord says to Jerusalem in the Gospel, “How often would I have gathered thy children, as a hen gathereth her chicks under her wings, and thou wouldst not?” (Matt. 23). Divine goodness, with an almost maternal affection, protects and defends from the heat of vices those who hope in it, under the wings of its mercy and power.

It is rightly added: “Until iniquity pass away.” Now, in this age, so long as iniquity endures, hope is necessary for every righteous person, so that, in hoping for eternal goods, they may patiently endure temporal evils. Hence Paul exhorts, saying: “Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation” (Rom. 12). And again: “If we hope for that which we see not, we wait for it with patience” (Rom. 8). Therefore iniquity now abounds and oppresses; patient righteousness and unfailing hope resist it. At the death of the righteous, or at the end of the age, iniquity will pass away, and hope will no longer exist, because one begins already to possess what one patiently awaited. Hence the Apostle says: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been proved, he shall receive the crown of life” (James 1). Meanwhile, established in tribulation, let us hear what he adds:

3. I will cry out to God Most High. He commends our God to us when he calls him “Most High,” so that by his example he may stir us to cry out, namely because he is Most High, most powerful, and above all. Crying out to God is our desire. The more a person desires, the more loudly he cries. He calls him Most High, and calls him gracious also when he adds: “God who hath done good to me.” Hear how great are the benefits, that you may love God more and cry out more devoutly.

4. He sent from heaven, that is, from his height or from his secret place, and delivered me; he gave those who trample upon me over to reproach. They were scattered among all nations (from Augustine), having stability nowhere and no fixed dwelling anywhere. The Jews still exist for this reason: that they may carry books to their own confusion. Consider what book they carry: the Jew carries the codex from which the Christian may believe. They have become our copyists. Then he clearly indicates what God sent from heaven, or from whom he delivered him, when he adds: “God sent his mercy and his truth.” Paul says of this sending: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son upon the earth,” etc. (Gal. 4). Therefore Christ is God’s mercy, because he forgives sins. Christ is truth (John 14), because he fulfills what he promised. Consider the mercy sent to you, and turn from sins. Consider truth, and be secure concerning the promises.

5. And he delivered my soul from the midst of the lion cubs. Who are the lion cubs? The people badly led astray by the chief priests: they are the lions; these, the lion cubs. All roared; all surrounded him, from whose midst the soul was delivered, though the body was killed. Therefore he adds: “I slept in distress.” “Do not fear,” says the Lord, “those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10). For what can they harm the good merely by killing the body? Rather, they help them by sending them sooner to the kingdom.

He plainly says, “I slept.” For death was sleep to him: as easily as anyone can be awakened from sleep, so easily could our Lord rise from death. Hence he himself says: “I have power to lay down my soul and power to take it again” (John 10). “I slept,” he says, first distressed in the Passion. They troubled him; he slept. Great was the humility of the troubled one; great the power of the sleeping one. Nor could they trouble him except as much as he willed. Who were those troublers? “The sons of men,” that is, the Jews, who ought to have been imitators of the patriarchs and prophets, living rationally. How did they kill, though they had no iron? “Their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword.” The teeth signify biting utterances, by which, as with weapons and arrows, they attempted to wound him now at close range, now from afar, now openly, now secretly. Do not attend to unarmed hands, but to the armed mouth. From there came forth the sword by which Christ was killed, just as from Christ’s mouth came forth the sword by which the Jews would be killed. For he has a two-edged sword, and, rising again, struck them in order to make them his faithful ones. They had an evil sword; he a good one. They had evil arrows; he good ones, namely good words, with which he wounds the faithful heart that it may love.

When, then, did they strike, except when they cried, “Crucify, crucify” (Matt. 27; John 19)? And what did they do to thee, O Lord? Here the Prophet exults: he saw in the Spirit the Lord humbled, scourged, crowned with thorns, and hung upon the wood; them raging, but him enduring; them exulting, but him as though conquered. And after so great a humiliation he knew that he would rise again, and that all those things which the raging Jews did had been done in vain. Exulting with joy, as though he saw it happen, he cries out and says:

6. Be exalted above the heavens, O God. Man upon the cross; God above the heavens. Let those who rage remain on earth; do thou be in heaven, judging. “And thy glory in all the earth.” For while the Lord sits in heaven at the right hand of the Father, the glory of his resurrection and divinity has been preached throughout all lands (Mark 16). We do not see the Lord exalted in heaven, but believe it. His glory in all the earth, however, we not only believe but also see. Then he returns to the words of the Passion, and in the person of the Lord says:

7. They set a snare for my feet, that is, they held out deception against my actions, after the likeness of a bird whose feet are caught in a snare. And they bent down [Col. 0871B] my soul—so far as their opinion was concerned. For they thought that they had bent it down so completely that it could no longer return to the body and rise again. But what is said concerning our Redeemer is enacted daily against us by the evil spirits. For they set snares for our feet because they hold out hidden temptations against our good actions, in order to hinder them. The soul is bent down when it is turned from good toward evil. The soul is bent down whenever it becomes entangled in earthly desires. Hence the Prophet says of the unclean spirits: “They said to your soul, ‘Bend down, so that we may pass over’” (Isa. 51). The soul stands upright when it desires heavenly things and is in no way bent toward what is below. But when the evil spirits see it standing in its uprightness, they cannot pass through it. Their “passing through” means scattering unclean desires within it. Therefore they say, “Bend down, so that we may pass over”: for if it does not cast itself down to desire what is below, their perversity cannot prevail against it in any way, nor can they pass through [Col. 0871C] it, since they dread it standing rigidly against them in its heavenly aspiration.

Let us therefore, dearest brothers, give the evil spirits a road within us when we desire earthly things, when we bend ourselves toward the pursuit of temporal things. Let us therefore be ashamed to desire earthly things and to offer the backs of our minds to adversaries climbing upon them.

“They dug a pit before my face, and they fell into it.” They prepared death for me, but inwardly killed themselves. No one sins against another before he has sinned against himself. The sinner’s pit is a bad conscience. There all the wicked must fall. Do you suppose that the one who has lost the light of Christ and been struck with blindness has not fallen into the pit? If he had not fallen into the pit, he would see what lay before him. He does not know where he is going. Just as one walking along a road, when he falls into a pit, loses the road.

Does an evil person afflict you? He is preparing a pit for you, so that you may perish. You are in distress; he rejoices. The joy of the one who commits injustice is [281] itself the pit. Whoever falls into it loses his eyes there; he also loses his life through an evil conscience. [Col. 0871D] And he rightly says, “before my face,” because it did not escape his notice. He was handed over knowingly and killed willingly. From these words our Lord’s true endurance is made known to us. Hence he adds:

8. “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready.” They prepared death, and my heart is ready to endure everything with a willing spirit. He repeats this in order to indicate perseverance in endurance. For he might have endured for a time and afterward failed. Thus the repetition of the word is a confirmation.

The endurance of the good receives God’s will by the preparation of the heart and glories in tribulations, saying: “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready.” They—[From Augustine]—prepared a pit in order to crush me, but I shall prepare my heart to endure. Therefore they fell into it, but “I shall sing and recite a psalm.”

“Song” refers to gladness of spirit; “psalm” to good action. Song must agree with psalm in praise of almighty God, so that what is uttered by the mouth may be [Col. 0872A] commended by one’s deeds. Then, after the Passion had been completed, he declares that his flesh will be raised, when he adds:

9. “Rise up, my glory; rise up, psaltery and lyre.” He speaks by command: “Rise up,” as one possessing the power to lay down his life and to take it up again (John 10). He calls his flesh “glory” because of its immortality and divinity. For it was a great glory for Christ to rise and sit at the right hand of the Father.

He also declares the hour of his resurrection when he adds: “I shall rise at dawn.” For the Lord Jesus rose in the morning, on the first day of the week (Mark 16). And from the one flesh that rose there arose two instruments: namely, the psaltery and the lyre. The psaltery sounds from its upper part, the lyre from its lower part.

Through his flesh the Lord accomplished two kinds of deeds, namely miracles and sufferings. The miracles were from above, the sufferings from below. The miracles he performed were divine, but he performed them through the flesh. Thus the flesh performing divine works is the psaltery. The human flesh [Col. 0872B] suffering is the lyre. The blind are illumined, the sick are healed, the dead rise: this is the sound of the psaltery. He hungers, thirsts, sleeps, is scourged, killed, and buried: this is the sound of the lyre. You therefore have both psaltery and lyre in one flesh.

These two kinds of deeds fulfilled the Gospel and are preached to the Gentiles. This is the fruit of the Passion and resurrection.

10. “I will confess you among the peoples,” that is, I will acquire confessors for you among the Jews, “and I will sing a psalm to you among the Gentiles,” that is, I will acquire among the Gentiles people who will sing a psalm, that is, who will perform good works.

Or, “to you,” that is, for your honor: I will confess and sing a psalm to you, that is, I will preach praise and good action, not only among the Jews but also among the Gentiles. Observe that the Son of God himself, in carrying out such a great work of righteousness, does not seek his own glory but the glory of the one who sent him, so that no flesh may glory in itself, but “whoever glories, let him glory in the Lord” (2 Cor. 10).

And rightly will I confess to you? And I will sing a psalm:

[Col. 0872C] 11. “For your mercy has been magnified even to the heavens, and your truth even to the clouds.”

By “the heavens” in this passage we understand angels, archangels, and the other heavenly powers. By “the clouds,” however, we understand preachers of the truth—human beings bearing [282] this darkened flesh—from whom God thunders through commandments and flashes through miracles.

In heaven the angels praise God, seeing the very form of truth without any cloudiness of vision. There is truth, and mercy is not needed above, where no one is wretched. Here, however, in our misery, mercy is certainly necessary. It might therefore seem more fitting to say: “For your truth has been magnified even to the heavens, and your mercy even to the clouds.”

But if the statement is examined carefully, what is said is far more excellent and wondrous: “Your mercy has been exalted even to the heavens, and your truth even to the clouds.” For almighty God, through his mercy, has raised sinful human beings even to the level of the angels. Hence it is now said: “For your mercy has been magnified [Col. 0872D] even to the heavens.” And because the truth that prevails among the angels has come to human beings, it is rightly added: “And your truth even to the clouds.”

Glory to our God, because he neither abandoned us in making us blessed through mercy nor deprived us of the truth; rather, he healed the eye of our heart, so that afterward we might be able to see him face to face (1 Cor. 13). For such great joy and benefit the Psalmist repeats the verse he has already spoken:

12. “Exult above the heavens, O God, and your glory above all the earth.” Perhaps it is repeated for this reason: because the principal purpose and benefit of the psalm centers especially on this verse.

## TITLE OF PSALM LVII

1. “To the end: Do not destroy. Of David, in the inscription of the title.”

This psalm looks toward the end, that is, toward Christ. It warns: “Do not destroy David,” that is, do not dishonor Christ, by altering the inscription of the title through certain people; that is, do not diminish Christ’s kingdom by withdrawing yourself from his kingdom, but confess Christ through the King of the Jews.

And this is its purpose, [Col. 0873A] as in another psalm: “Do not destroy Christ.” The subject, by contrast, is the Jews, because Christ ought to be the principal subject. In this psalm we are warned not to withdraw from Christ’s kingdom, that is, from the fellowship of the saints.

Christ accomplishes this by setting before us the blindness of the Jews, their dispersion in earthly places, and their future condemnation, so that, seeing the condemnation of the wicked, we may be frightened away from imitating them. He also sets before us the joy of the righteous, which they possess in hope of future glory, so that, seeing their joy, we may be drawn to imitate them.

The voice of the Prophet:

## PSALM LVII

2. “If indeed you speak justice, judge rightly, sons of men.”

It is as if he were saying: You Jews, who are sons of men and ought to be imitators of your fathers, the prophets who lived rationally: if you truly speak justice in the Law and the Prophets—as indeed you do—judge rightly, that is, discern and believe that Christ our Lord is himself God. For your justice, as taught by your Law, commends and prophesies him to you.

Or, “Judge rightly,” that is, live rightly, discerning [Col. 0873B] good from evil according to the justice that you speak. For to speak good things and do evil is a judgment of condemnation. Hence Truth itself says to the Pharisees: “Hypocrites, how can you speak good things when you are evil?” (Matt. 12).

3. “For in your heart you work iniquities, [283] on the earth.” To work iniquities in the heart is to harbor an evil will. For a perverse will is counted by God as a deed. And he rightly says, “on the earth,” that is, clinging to earthly things. For when the heart is fixed on earth, iniquity is generated there in the heart.

“Your hands construct injustices.” That is, your perverse actions agree with your perverse wills. Or, for the hands to construct injustices means to add unjust actions to unjust actions, in accordance with what the Psalmist says elsewhere: “Add iniquity upon their iniquity, and let them not enter into your justice” (Ps. 68). And in accordance with John: “Let the filthy still be filthy” (Rev. 22).

Then he turns to his hearers and displays their error and hardness of [Col. 0873C] heart, so that each hearer may take care not to err in the same way and perish in the same way. He says therefore:

4. “Sinners have been estranged from the womb,” that is, from the very moment of emergence; “they have gone astray from the uterus,” that is, from the very moment of conception. “They have spoken falsehoods,” having abandoned the truth.

This should not be understood as though we were to suppose that they went astray in their mother’s womb; for at that time a child cannot yet possess sensation or understanding. Rather, it should be understood in this way: from the womb itself, before they are born, almighty God foreknows which will sin and remain in error and falsehood.

Hence, while Rebecca was still pregnant and carrying twins in her womb, it was said: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Gen. 25; Rom. 9). There is a hidden judgment of God, and for that reason it is all the more to be feared.

In another sense, little ones are born within the entrails of the Church. It is good that they emerge fully formed, lest they slip from the moment of birth. Let your mother give birth to you; let her not miscarry. Be patient until you are formed. Let your mother’s entrails hold you until the doctrine of truth has become secure within you.

But if through impatience you shake your mother’s [Col. 0873D] entrails, she indeed thrusts you out with pain, but more to your harm than to hers. One who has been instructed in doctrine but does not believe or lives badly emerges from the womb as though fully formed, but is rejected as a stranger. One who begins to be instructed but, not yet fully taught, goes out from the fellowship of the saints: this person is cast out like a miscarriage from the womb of Mother Church.

Therefore, because the Jews, from the time they came to know the Law, withdrew from the faith and justice of that motherly Law, it is rightly said of them now: “Sinners have gone astray from the womb.” But because certain people from that same people refused to be instructed, being less capable of instruction, it was said of them: “They have gone astray from the uterus.” And because they were estranged and went astray, they therefore spoke falsehoods. For one who abandons the truth must necessarily speak falsehood.

See to what madness those who go astray have come.

5. “Their fury is according to the likeness of a serpent.” Their error has turned into fury—not human fury, but serpentine and venomous fury. For the venom of envy was in their fury.
