Hear whose serpent’s fury was in them: [Col. 0874A] “Like a deaf asp, and one that stops its ears.” It is deaf because it stops its ears.

6. “Which will not hear the voice of charmers, nor of the magician who charms wisely.”

Here a certain comparison is given from Marsus. The charmer who chants in order to draw an asp out of its dark cavern certainly wishes to bring it out into the light. But because it loves its caves, in which it hides itself wrapped up, it is said that, when it refuses to come out and rejects hearing the voices by which it feels itself compelled, it presses one [284] ear to the ground and blocks the other with its tail. Thus, avoiding those voices as much as it can, it does not come out toward the charmer.

The Spirit of God called certain people like these: people who do not hear the word of God (Matt. 23; Luke 11), and who not only do not do it but altogether refuse to hear it lest they do it.

Thus, when preachers wish to draw them out of the pit—that is, from the depths of their vices—and to slaughter them insofar as they are sinners (whence it was said to Peter, “Slaughter and [Col. 0874B] eat” [Acts 10]), and to draw out the venom, that is, their sins, they themselves, unwilling to obey the truth and remaining in their own pit, unwilling to aspire to the true light, apply one ear of their heart to the earth, that is, to present pleasure; but they block the other with their tail, that is, with the memory of past pleasures.

[From Augustine] He does not say “wisely” in order to praise the incantation, but the expression serves as a comparison.

This also happened in the earliest times of the faith. The martyr Stephen preached the truth (Acts 6), and, as though to darkened minds, he chanted in order to lead them out into the light. When he came to speak of Christ, whom they absolutely refused to hear, what does Scripture say about them? “They closed their ears,” it says. What did they do afterward? The account of Stephen’s Passion makes clear (Acts 7). They were not deaf, but made themselves deaf.

They, I say, spoke falsehood. But what will God do? Hear what follows.

7. “God will crush their teeth in their mouth.” That [Col. 0874C] is, he will destroy their biting questions in their own response, as is written concerning the tribute to Caesar (Matt. 22).

What does “in their mouth” mean? It means that they would pronounce judgment against themselves with their own mouths. For he compelled them to give the answer with their own mouths, by which their teeth would be crushed.

When they said that Caesar’s image was on the coin, and the Lord commanded that what belongs to Caesar be rendered to Caesar and what belongs to God to God, they had nothing to answer (ibid.)—nothing with which to bite, because their teeth had been crushed in their own mouth.

The same happened when they were questioned about John’s baptism: they did not know what to answer (Matt. 21).

The Jews were therefore asps when they lay in wait for Christ, attempting to hiss and inject venom; but their teeth were crushed in their own mouths. Afterward they cried, “Crucify, crucify!” (John 19). Now it is no longer the tongue of an asp but the roar of a lion. “But the Lord will break the molars of the lions.”

Just as by “teeth” we understand biting questions, so by “molars” we understand stronger and sharper arguments concerning Christ’s death. At first they tried secretly to deceive [Col. 0874D] like asps; afterward they began openly to roar like lions for Christ’s death.

He was crucified; he rose; he ascended into heaven; he was glorified and worshiped by human beings and by kings. The molars of the lions have therefore been broken, that is, the accusations and false testimonies that they can no longer bring forward against Christ. Concerning these he adds:

8. “They will come to nothing, like water running away.” All the proud and impious, roaring against the rocks of their pride, run away like water and come to nothing.

Consider the persecutors of the martyrs. For a time they roared like a torrent; they ran through the channels as far as they could; the channels dried up, and scarcely any memory of them is found. Not only they, but this entire age roars for a time and runs like water. It flows through vices and desires, seeking someone to carry away.

Therefore, let the wicked not be feared: they cannot [285] endure. They must run down to [Col. 0875A] their own place, to their own end. Yet God drinks from this torrent (Ps. 109). And because he drank, he exalted his head; because he suffered, he rose again. If he had not wished to drink from the torrent on the way, he would not have died, risen, or been glorified.

Therefore he drank from the torrent on the way; for that reason he exalted his head. Our head has already been exalted; let its members follow it by drinking from the torrent. Let them not fear the waters roaring, the threatening peoples, or the persecutors, because God “bends his bow until they are weakened.”

God’s bow is God’s threats, which do not cease. The bow is bent; it does not yet strike. Many have been weakened, terrified by the tension of that bow. For this reason the one who said, “What do you command me to do?” was weakened: “I am Jesus of Nazareth,” he said, “whom you are persecuting” (Acts 9). The one who cried from heaven was bending the bow.

Many, therefore, who were enemies have been weakened and converted. They were unwilling for long to raise their necks against the perseverance of the drawn bow. The one who said, “When I am weak, then I am strong” (1 Cor. 12) was also weakened. [Col. 0875B] And when he prayed that the thorn of the flesh might be taken from him, he received the answer: “Power is made perfect in weakness.”

Or, “to bend the bow” means to prepare vengeance; “until they are weakened” means until they are utterly deprived of their strength, so that afterward they are no longer able to harm the good. For God permits the wicked to rage against the good only as far as he knows this to benefit the good, either for the correction of their morals or for the increase of their virtues, as it is written: “God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but will also provide a way out along with the temptation” (1 Cor. 10).

Hence he adds further concerning the rejected:

9. “Like wax that melts, they will be taken away.” He does not say, “They will be converted,” but “They will be taken away.” For the heat of vices consumes them like fire consumes wax. They are dissolved from every firmness of virtue, going loose and fluid into their lusts.

The Apostle speaks of such people: “God handed them over to the desires of their hearts, to impurity, so that they might do what is unfitting” (Rom. 1). Then he lists many evils into which they flow in dissolution [Col. 0875C] like wax, and afterward adds: “Those who do such things are worthy of death” (ibid.).

Hence the text continues and says: “Fire has fallen upon them, and they have not seen the sun.”

[From Augustine] One fire is the fire of avarice, another of lust, another of pride, another of envy, another of anger. Such fire is smoky and dark; whoever falls beneath it will not see the sun.

I do not mean the sun that the Lord made to rise upon the good and the evil (Matt. 5), but the sun of which they will say in the judgment: “The sun did not rise for us” (Wis. 5). “All those things passed like a shadow; we went astray from the way of truth, and the light of justice did not shine upon us.”

Therefore, brothers, fear the fire of desire if you do not wish to be melted like wax before the face of God.

It should be noted that the punishment of the impious has two forms: one in the present, the other in the future. One is the fire of desire; the other is eternal fire. The Spirit of God commends this punishment of desire to us throughout the rest of the psalm. Let us avoid it, and we shall not fall into that dreadful punishment.

[From the same source] Carnal pleasure is born [Col. 0875D] with a human being. But one who is well instructed soon sees his enemy, attacks it, wrestles with it, and quickly conquers it. One who neglects to conquer that desire with which he was born through the propagation of sin, and who still arouses and brings forth many lusts, overcomes them with difficulty; [286] divided against himself, he is burned by his own fire.

And lest they understand that this takes place only in the future, he turns toward them and, making them more attentive, defines it thus: “Fire has fallen upon you, O Jews,”

10. “Before your thorns understood the buckthorn.” That is, before your sins made you understand that they resemble the buckthorn.

The buckthorn is a plant that is soft at first, but when it matures has extremely sharp spines. So are sins: at first they are soft and pleasurable, but afterward they prick most grievously. Temporal pleasure is followed by the pains and stings of torments.

Then there will also be the sting [Col. 0876A] of repentance, but it will be late and fruitless, like the sterility of thorns. Repentance in this age is a medicinal pain; repentance in that age is a penal pain.

Those who love this passing pleasure do not understand this, because “Fire has fallen upon them, and they have not seen the sun.” This fire, “like the living, like wrath, will swallow them up,” that is, it will devour and lay them waste.

Why does he not say “the living,” but “like the living,” except because the life of the impious is false? For one who is separated from the Lord does not truly live. And why does he not say “in wrath,” but “like in wrath,” except because God does this calmly? As it is written: “But you, Lord of hosts, judge with tranquility” (Wis. 5).

Or, “like in wrath,” and not truly to be called wrath when compared with the wrath that is to come in the judgment.

From the same source of punishment by which the wicked are punished, the good advance toward righteousness. For it follows:

11. “The righteous man will rejoice when he sees vengeance.” He will not rejoice because the vengeance of the wicked is a cause of joy for the righteous. Rather, he will rejoice because he will not share in their punishment.

Consider the punishment of the wicked even [Col. 0876B] in this age, even amid their pleasures. While some possess what they desire, they desire other things that they cannot attain. For what they do not have, they are tortured by desire; for what they do have, they are tortured either by boredom or by fear.

One man burns with avarice, another blazes with lust, another is kindled by anger, another is inflamed by the torches of envy. Thus almighty God avenges himself upon the wicked in the present, scourging them by their own desires and vices.

When the righteous sees this vengeance, he will rejoice, because, helped by the Lord’s merciful grace, he is not entangled in such things.

While living in this way also, “he will wash his hands in the blood of sinners,” that is, he will cleanse his actions through consideration of the vengeance inflicted on the rejected. When he sees the sinner’s punishment, he himself advances, and another’s death becomes the means of his own life.

Therefore observe the wicked person perishing and cleanse yourself from sins. In this way you will, so to speak, wash your hands in the sinner’s blood.

12. “And a man will say: ‘Indeed there is fruit for the righteous; indeed there is a God judging them on the earth.’”

The one who uses his reason is truly called a man. He will say, “Indeed there is fruit for the righteous,” even in this life, before eternal life comes. There is fruit in faith, fruit in temptation and tribulation, fruit in endurance, and fruit in charity for the righteous.

And if this is so, then indeed there is a God judging, that is, considering those evil people worthy of condemnation—not yet on the last day, not yet in eternal fire, not yet in hell, but here on [Col. 0876C] earth.

He proves this by contrast, as if briefly saying: If there is the fruit of salvation for the righteous on this earth, in that he is [287] righteous, then likewise there is a judgment of condemnation for the impious on this earth, in that he is impious. For opposites correspond to opposites.

Let the discerning person therefore attend and judge. For the psalm thus admonishes: “Judge rightly, sons of men.” Let him distinguish the good from the evil and, by their example, flee those who perish, lest he himself perish with them. Let him strive to imitate those who are being saved, so that he too, with the Lord’s help, may be able to attain the same salvation. [Col. 0876D]

## TITLE OF PSALM LVIII

1 and 2. [From Augustine] Scripture is accustomed to place the mysteries of the psalms in their titles and to adorn the front of the psalm with the sublimity of the sacrament, so that, when we read what is done inside as though written above a doorway, we may know whose house it is or who is the owner of that estate. So also in this psalm a title is written concerning a title.

For it has: “To the end: Do not destroy David in the inscription of the title, when Saul sent and guarded his house in order to kill him” (1 Sam. 18 and 19). This psalm reaches toward the end, that is, toward Christ. It warns you, whoever you are, not to destroy David, that is, Christ, by the inscription of the title. This is what I called “a title concerning a title.”

What the inscription of this title is—which it forbids to be corrupted—the Gospel indicates. For when the Lord was crucified, Pilate caused a title to be inscribed and placed there: “King of the Jews” (Matt. 27), in three languages, Hebrew, Greek, and Latin—the languages that are preeminent throughout the whole world.

Therefore, if the King of the Jews was crucified, and the Jews [Col. 0877A] crucified their own king, by crucifying him they made him king of the Gentiles even more than they killed him. Certainly, insofar as it lay within their power, they destroyed Christ—but for themselves, not for us. He died for us, redeemed us by his blood, and the title was not corrupted, because he is king not only of the Gentiles but also of the Jews themselves.

Therefore, “Do not destroy” is most fitting and prophetic. For the Jews themselves then urged Pilate and said: “Do not write ‘King of the Jews,’ but write that he said, ‘I am the King of the Jews.’” For, they said, “This title will confirm that he is our king.” And Pilate said: “What I have written, I have written” (John 19). Thus “Do not destroy” was fulfilled.

I speak of the title as confirmed then, when Saul, that is, the Jewish people, sent guards and guarded his house, that is, his tomb. But what does the addition “in order to kill him” mean? Was Jesus not already dead when he had been placed in the tomb? But there was something else they sought to kill in him: his name and reputation.

They therefore guarded the tomb lest the disciples steal his body and say, “He has risen from the dead” (Matt. 27). The Jewish people therefore guarded Christ’s tomb “in order to kill him,” that is, to extinguish his reputation. For this is truly to wish to kill Christ: to extinguish the name of his resurrection, so that a lie might be preferred to the [Col. 0877B] Gospel.

But just as Saul could not accomplish the killing of David, so neither could the Jewish kingdom bring it about that the testimony of sleeping guards would have greater force than that of the watchful Apostles.

The subject is Christ, concerning whom the psalm proceeds in this way. In the first part he asks for deliverance and exaltation. In the second he shows the conversion of the Gentiles, which proceeds from that exaltation and deliverance of Christ; it begins there: “They will be converted toward evening.” In the third he sets forth the conversion of the Jews, which begins there: “And from their cursing and falsehood.” In the fourth he presents the praise offered by the whole Christ for his deliverance and for the conversion of the Jews and Gentiles; it begins there: “But I will sing.”

The purpose is “Do not destroy David,” as in the other psalms. [288] In this psalm Christ shows that through his Passion the Gentiles will attain the grace of conversion, and that, following their example, the Jews will be converted at the end. Those who persist in unbelief, however, will be punished without mercy.

Through these examples he intends to admonish us to avoid their faithlessness, to conform within ourselves to the faith of those who have been converted, and not to withdraw ourselves from his kingdom, but to strive to submit ourselves to it.

The voice of Christ:

## PSALM LVIII

[Col. 0877C]

3. “Deliver me from my enemies, my God, and free me from those who rise up against me. Deliver me from those who work iniquity, and save me from men of blood” (v. 3).

In these two verses four classes of Christ’s persecutors are designated. Some were hostile to Christ in such a way that they concealed their hatred in their hearts (Matt. 25 and 27). Others were hostile in such a way that they rose up against him and resisted the truth with an open voice. Therefore, in the first verse, he asks to be delivered from his enemies and freed from those who rise up against him.

Moreover, some committed wicked deeds, going so far as to seize the Savior himself with their hands, drag him, and scourge him (John 18 and 19). Others raged to such an extent that they hung him on the cross, drove nails into his hands and feet, pierced his side with a lance, and, after his blood had been poured out, killed the author of life (Mark 15; Luke 23).

Therefore, in the second verse he prays to be rescued from those who work iniquity and saved from men of blood. And it is necessary that you deliver him:

[Col. 0877D] 4. “Because, behold, they have seized my soul”—that is, openly. He has put the part for the whole. For they could not have held Jesus’ soul without the body. “They have seized my soul,” he says, and they did this with a certain greedy, disordered, and ruinous violence. Hence he adds: “The mighty have rushed upon me.”

It must be carefully considered who these mighty ones are. First, the Lord called the devil himself mighty. “No one,” he says, “can enter the house of a strong man and plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man” (Matt. 12). For he bound the strong man with the bonds of condemnation and plundered his goods, that is, souls, and made them his own.

Among human beings there are also certain mighty ones, mighty in a blameworthy way, who presume upon temporal prosperity. The Spirit of God reproves such a one in another psalm, saying: “Why do you glory in wickedness, you who are powerful in iniquity?” (Ps. 51).

Again, there are other mighty ones who do not presume upon vices but upon their own righteousness. Such strength [From Augustine] hindered the Jews. [Col. 0878A] Since they regarded themselves as righteous and healthy, they refused medicine and killed the physician. That strength is not health but madness.

For this reason the teacher of humility came, becoming a sharer in our weakness, to teach us to become weak and confess our sins, so that we might be strong not in ourselves but in God.

Having shown the necessity of his deliverance, he shows that he is worthy to be delivered when he adds:

5. “Neither is there iniquity in me, nor sin, O God.” “Iniquity” with respect to one’s neighbor; “sin” with respect to oneself. Or, “iniquity” refers to graver offenses, “sin” to lesser ones.

The mighty, that is, the proud, may be understood to have rushed upon me, but they [289] did not find guilt. Rather: “Without iniquity I ran,” that is, I acted well; and “I directed others toward good action” through preaching and example.

To run and direct without iniquity means to live perfectly without any admixture of evil and to display a good example to others. For good things mixed with evil cannot please God.

It should also be noted that he does not say, “I walked,” but “I ran,” [Col. 0878B] because it is not enough merely to perform good works; one must also hasten in the very progress of good action. In accordance with what is written: “Whatever your hand can do, do it earnestly, because there is neither work nor reasoning among the dead, where you are hastening” (Eccles. 19). And the Apostle says: “Run so that you may obtain” (1 Cor. 9).

Or, the running of our Redeemer means freely and without any impediment carrying out obedience to the Father, as it is written elsewhere: “He rejoiced like a giant to run the course” (Ps. 18). And again: “All that he does will prosper” (Ps. 1).

And lest this seem to attribute the matter to his own powers, he adds a prayer:

6. “Rise up to meet me.” It is as if he were saying: Help me in the advancement of virtues by giving me resurrection. “And see,” that is, make me appear equal to you.

This is spoken according to that figure by which it is also said to Abraham: “Now I know that you fear God” (Gen. 22), that is, “Now I have made you known.” For everyone is unknown before the questioning of temptation.

“Rise up, therefore, and see,” that is, make others see and know my [Col. 0878C] exaltation, so that those who saw me humbled may see me exalted.

“And you, Lord God of hosts, God of Israel, attend to visit all the nations.” May you deign to visit those who are weak and weighed down by sins, giving them the grace of healing and sending your preachers, so that, just as you are the God of hosts, that is, of angels, and the God of Israel, that is, of the Israelite people, so you may also deign to be the God of the Gentiles, making them fellow members both of the angels and of the Israelite faithful.

But what follows is greatly to be feared: “Do not have mercy on all who work iniquity.” For who is without iniquity (Prov. 20)? But he wishes this to be understood of those who persist in iniquity.

Let us therefore punish our sins if we seek God’s mercy. For if we do not punish them, he does not show mercy but punishes. Every iniquity, whether great or small, must necessarily be punished, either by God himself as judge or by the repentant person himself.

And truly you will attend to visit all the nations, because, with you inspiring them, [Col. 0878D] they will be converted. This is what follows:

7. “They will be converted toward evening, and they will suffer hunger like dogs, and they will go around the city.”

This has already happened and continues to happen. Having abandoned idolatry, toward evening, in this final age, they are converted to the worship of God. Hungering and thirsting for righteousness, they suffer hunger like dogs, as sinners.

The Gentiles are rightly designated by the name “dogs” because of the uncleanness of sin. The Canaanite woman was one of these, to whom the Lord said: “It is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.” Recognizing this, she humbly replied: “Yes, Lord.” But because she was hungry like a dog, she immediately added: “Yet even the little dogs eat from the crumbs that fall from the table of their masters.”

The Lord therefore attended to visit her because of her faith and humility, and said to her: “O woman, great is your faith; let it be done for you as you wish” (Matt. 15).

Such dogs do not cease to go around the city of God, investigating with watchful [Col. 0879A] [290] minds the life and conduct of the holy fathers from whom the city of God was built.

Or, “dogs” may be understood as the holy preachers who, in defending the truth against thieves and robbers, gave out great barks, so to speak. They suffered hunger, desiring that all people should be incorporated into them and united with them through faith, and they went around the city, that is, the world, preaching everywhere.

Hence he adds:

### 8.

“Behold, they will speak,” that is, they will openly preach, “with their mouth,” that is, in a manner suited to them. For what they speak in word, they will confirm by deed and example. Or “with their mouth,” that is, freely, boldly, and with authority.

“And a sword is in their lips.” This is the two-edged sword of which the Apostle said: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. 6). Why two-edged? Because it strikes from both Testaments. With this sword those people were slain of whom it was said to Peter: “Kill and eat” (Acts 10).

“But they will be indignant,” because there will be many who will not listen with an obedient ear. And this is what follows: “For who has heard?” Hence the prophet says: “Who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. 53). “We preach,” says the Apostle, “wisdom hidden in a mystery” (1 Cor. 2), which the world did not know. Even in the time of the martyrs, those who would hear the word of God were rarely found.

“I said, Do not have mercy on all who work iniquity”—and so it will be. Hence he adds:

### 9.

“And you, Lord, will deride them,” that is, you will show them to be worthy of derision. This will occur in the judgment, when he says to them: “Go into the eternal fire” (Matt. 25).

From this also it becomes clear that the Gentiles will be converted: “For you will bring all the nations to nothing.” Everyone who is converted to God must first be brought to nothing. Hence the Truth says: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Luke 9). He denies himself who, changing himself for the better, ceases to be what he was and begins to be what he was not.

Paul had been brought to nothing when he said: “I live, yet it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2). Hence he also says: “If anyone thinks he is something when he is nothing, he deceives himself” (Gal. 6).

Abraham had been brought to nothing when he said: “I will speak to my Lord, although I am dust and ashes” (Gen. 18). Thus everyone, first failing in himself, begins to be strong in God. He recognizes himself as such when he immediately adds:

### 10.

“I will keep my strength from you.” Those who were strong and rushed upon me therefore fell, because they did not keep their strength from you, but presumed upon themselves. I, however, will keep my strength from you: for if I withdraw, I fall; if I draw near, I become stronger.

See what there is in the human soul. It does not possess light from itself; it does not possess strength from itself. Everything beautiful in the soul is virtue and wisdom. Yet the soul itself is neither its own light nor its own virtue. God is a certain source and origin of virtue and wisdom. When the soul withdraws from him, it is darkened; when it draws near, it is illumined.

Therefore, “I will keep my strength from you”: I will not withdraw from you; I will not presume upon myself. And rightly so, “because you are God, my protector.” You have taken up my humanity, joining it to your divinity; you have taken me up in order to heal me, as a physician takes up the sick—my God, who created me.

### 12.

“His mercy has gone before me.” Where was I lying? To what place have I been raised? Behold why I ought not to presume upon myself: my merits did not go before me, but divine mercy went before me, so that I might become righteous.

We should not be disturbed because he frequently changes persons. Such is the practice of prophecy. At one moment he turns to the Lord in familiar speech, receiving from him the revelation of prophecy; at another he turns to his hearers, in order to edify them by what he has learned through the Lord’s revelation; at another he speaks in his own person; at another in the person of his members; at another in the person of Christ.

Hence it now says: “God has shown me concerning my enemies.” How great a mercy he had toward me, he showed me in those toward whom he did not show it. For unless the debtor is condemned, the one whose debt is forgiven gives less thanks.

What does he say about those enemies? “Do not kill them, lest at some time they forget my people.” Do not kill those very enemies who killed me. It was not without reason that, when Cain had killed his brother, God placed a mark upon him so that no one would kill him (Gen. 4). This is the mark that the Jews bear. They retain the remnants of their Law: they are circumcised, observe the Sabbath, and eat unleavened bread. Thus the Jews exist; they have not been killed.

They are necessary for believers, so that God might demonstrate his mercy toward our enemies. In the branches of pride that were cut off, he showed his mercy by grafting in the wild olive. Behold where those who were proud lie; behold where you, who were lying low, have been grafted. And do not become proud, lest you deserve to be cut off.

Therefore, lest the faithful people forget the grace of God, the Jews live—blinded before their eyes—so that from their blindness they may continually recall how great are the thanks they ought to offer to almighty God for their own illumination.

“Scatter them by your strength.” This was fulfilled by Titus and Vespasian, who took the Jewish people captive. Yet this must not be attributed to their strength, but to God, who granted them the ability to do it. “For all authority is from God” (Rom. 13). Therefore it is not said, “Scatter them by the strength of the enemies,” but “by your strength,” because, as has been said, all strength is from God.

And not only “scatter them,” but also, O Lord, who protect and defend me, “bring them down from the fear of pride.” This is what follows: “And bring them down, my protector, Lord.” Then he shows what he wishes to be brought down in them.

### 13.

“The sin of their mouth, the word of their lips.” The word of their lips and the sin of their mouth occurred when they said concerning Christ: “He has a demon”; “He is guilty of death,” and other things of this sort (John 7 and 19). He calls this sin “the word of their lips” because they spoke such insults openly and proclaimed them publicly.

Bring down and destroy such a sin, such a word; take it away from their mouth and lips. In this I wish you to bring them down—not according to nature, but according to guilt. They attempted to kill me. But you, by raising Christ whom they wished to destroy, killed “the sin of their mouth, the word of their lips.” For the one whose destruction they loudly demanded, they feared when he lived; and the one whom they despised on earth, they were astonished to see worshiped by all the nations in heaven.

“Thus let their sins be blotted out: and let them be caught in their pride.” And indeed they were caught. For the one whom they killed in their pride rose again; their deed was nullified, but their sin remained. Since, therefore, the deed was annulled while the sin remained upon those who committed it, “they were caught in their pride”: they were convicted of having acted wickedly and proudly.

It remained, then, that they should confess their sin, and that he should forgive who had come to release sins (John 3). This has already happened in some; later it will happen in many. Therefore it is added: “And from the curse and the lie they will be proclaimed at the consummation.”

Because they cursed the Lord and lied that his body had been stolen (Matt. 28), after being brought out of this through repentance and confession, they will be proclaimed at the consummation—that is, they will be preached as having become perfect. They will be humbled all the more by the greatness of their sin, and will deserve to be raised up through greater humility. They will be more perfect because they will grieve that they committed so execrable a sin.

And this will happen:

### 14.

“In the wrath of consummation, and they will not exist.” Every vengeance of God is called wrath. Yet God often takes vengeance in order to perfect, as it is written: “He scourges every son whom he receives” (Prov. 3; Heb. 12). Often he takes vengeance in order to condemn, as he will say to the reprobate: “Go into the eternal fire” (Matt. 25).

The “wrath of consummation,” therefore, is the wrath of correction, when God’s paternal wrath punishes sins in this age in order to amend and perfect. Thus they will be proclaimed as consummated in the wrath of consummation—that is, in such wrath as will bring them to completion and perfection.

“And they will not exist”—the implied sense is: they will not be such as they previously were, namely, proud, blaspheming, and lying. In the same way it is said elsewhere: “Turn the wicked, and they will not exist” (Prov. 12).

“And they will know that the Lord will rule Jacob,” that is, the Jewish people, “and the ends of the earth,” that is, the Gentiles throughout all lands. Then they will acknowledge that the same God belongs both to the Jews and to the Gentiles.

Previously they seemed righteous to themselves because they had received the Law and observed God’s commandments. It was shown to them that they had not observed them, because they did not understand Christ within them. They will see that they ought not to despise the Gentiles. “For all have sinned and lack the grace of God” (Rom. 3). They will lay aside their pride and will not envy the salvation of the Gentiles, because they will recognize that their weakness is equal to that of the Gentiles; and, joined together in the cornerstone (Eph. 2), they will worship God together.

Thus what was said above concerning the Gentiles is also said concerning the Jews:

### 15.

“They will return in the evening,” that is, at the end of the age. “For the remnant will be saved.” And they will suffer hunger for the word of God like dogs, that is, like sinners. “And they will go around the city,” that is, the Church of the saints, investigating its life and conduct; or they will go around the city, that is, the world, preaching the Gospel. Hence it plainly follows:

### 16.

“They themselves will be scattered in order to eat,” that is, in order to incorporate others into themselves through faith in the Lord Jesus Christ. “But if they are not satisfied,” that is, if their preaching does not bear fruit according to their desire, they too, like the Gentiles, will murmur, just as was said above: “Lord, who has heard?”

But now let the psalm be brought to its conclusion. Behold, says Augustine, the rejoicing cornerstone, already taking joy in both walls. The Jews were proud and have been humbled. The Gentiles despaired and have been raised up. Let them come to the cornerstone. Let them meet there: the one group from circumcision, the other from uncircumcision. Let them hold fast to the cornerstone.

And now let us hear what the whole Church adds: “But I will sing of your strength, and I will exult in the morning in your mercy.”

The holy Church of the elect will sing of his strength, by which he conquered the devil, overcame death, and despoiled hell; and of his mercy, by which he redeemed the human race and forgave sins. The Church will sing and exult in all these things—and in the morning, that is, in the resurrection, when, after the darkness of this age has passed, the sun of righteousness will appear (Mal. 4), and the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father (Wis. 3; Matt. 13).

For now it cannot perfectly sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land (Ps. 136), so long as it sits and weeps beside the rivers of Babylon, amid the currents of the present life. But when it passes into the place of the wondrous tabernacle, to the house of God, then there will be singing with a voice of exultation and praise (Ps. 41). Hence it is said elsewhere: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O God; for ever and ever they will praise you” (Ps. 83).

And he gives the reason why it ought to sing and exult when he adds:

### 17.

“Because you have become my protector and my refuge on the day of my tribulation.” In the present life, in which everyone who lives justly is afflicted, you have become my protector amid the tribulation itself and a secure refuge from the dangers that press upon me. For unless you had taken me up and saved me, there would have been no one who could have endured amid so many and such great evils.

Therefore he adds further:

### 18.

“My helper, to you I will sing psalms.” The good works that I have performed through your inspiration and assistance I will attribute to you. And rightly so, “because you are God, my protector.” Not a human protector, but God my protector, who also deifies the one he has taken up.

“My God,” says Augustine, “who created me; my mercy, who saved me.” Considering all the good things we can possess—whether in nature or in conversion, in faith, hope, charity, good conduct, righteousness, or fear of the Lord—and recognizing that everything comes from his gifts [Note: In Augustine: “gifts”], he concluded: “My God, my mercy.” When filled with good things, he found nothing by which to call his God except “my mercy.”

O sweet name, under which no one should despair, a name that consoles everyone and invites everyone to conversion! If he had merely forgiven us our sins, he could rightly have been called merciful. But since he both forgave sins and added gifts—and, what seemed unbelievable, even granted heavenly glory to undeserving sinners—he is not merely called merciful; he is rightly called mercy itself.

Therefore let the Church say with voice and heart; let every faithful soul say: “My God, my mercy.”

# TITLE OF PSALM LIX

### 1–2. “God, you have rejected us.” [Verse 1.] “For the end; for those who will be changed; with the inscription of the title, to David himself, for instruction” [Verse 2], “when he set fire to Mesopotamia of Syria and Syria of Zobah, and turned Joab, and struck Edom in the Valley of Salt, twelve thousand” (2 Sam. 8 and 10; 1 Chron. 18).

After Saul’s death, when David had obtained the kingdom, he set fire to Mesopotamia—that is, a part of Syria—and to Syria of Zobah, another part of Syria. He turned Joab, his enemy, to himself, and struck Edom, that is, the Idumean people, because that people came from the land of Idumea (Gen. 25). It received this name from Esau, its inhabitant, who was called Edom because he loved earthly things.

By these victories David understood the victories of Christ, which he was to accomplish among the Jews and the Gentiles.

The title is thus understood: This psalm was made “for those,” that is, in honor of those “who will be changed in the end,” that is, in Christ, or in perseverance. It sets forth two changes of the righteous: one in this life, from sin to righteousness; the second in the other life, from mortality to immortality.

This change will take place through the inscription of the received title by faith, namely, because they believe Christ to be the King of the Jews. The inscription is said to be made “to David himself,” that is, to Christ, “going into instruction,” that is, into his commandments, submitting himself to the law of Christ, so that they may act according to that law. “For faith without works is dead” (James 2).

“They will be changed,” I say, “when he set fire to Mesopotamia of Syria,” that is, to the Jews, whom he raised to a lofty dignity by calling them. Previously they were lofty—that is, exceptionally proud of their knowledge of God—for Mesopotamia is interpreted as “high calling,” while Syria is interpreted as “lofty.”

The same Christ also set fire to Syria of Zobah, that is, to those very Jews who were lofty and proud because of their vain antiquity, that is, their carnal observances of the Law. For Zobah is interpreted as “vain antiquity.”

“And he turned Joab” from idolatry to his faith, that is, the Gentile people, who had no knowledge of God.

“And he struck Edom,” that is, he moved the Gentile people from unbelief to faith—those devoted to earthly things, or to the blood of sin. For Edom is interpreted as “earthly” or “bloody.” He struck the earthliness of the nations, so that they would no longer seek earthly things.

Through this he turned Joab, that is, the Gentile people, and struck them so that they would be in the Valley of Salt. They were in the valley, that is, in humility, which is the mother of the virtues and the seasoning of all things, just as salt is the seasoning of foods. For whoever gathers virtues without humility carries dust into the wind.

He struck, I say, “twelve thousand,” that is, everyone in the four regions of the world who confesses the faith of the Holy Trinity. By “a thousand,” perfection is understood.

The material consists of those who are to be changed: Jews and Gentiles converted to faith through Christ’s blows. The structure is as follows: In the first part he shows, by many arguments and by the authority of God himself, that they are to be changed from sin to righteousness. In the second, which begins, “Save with your right hand,” he shows that through the same change they arrive at another change, namely, from mortality to immortality.

The purpose is that no one despise these blows, but that they patiently endure the adversities of this world, because through them they will obtain both changes.

The voice belongs to those converted to faith through Christ’s victories. And because they were going to say that they would be changed, it is first shown from what they will be changed, when it says:

# PSALM LIX

### 3.

“God, you have rejected us”—from the joys of paradise, from the intimate contemplation of vision—“and you have destroyed us,” through the corruption of suffering and mortality. “You were angry,” because of our sins; “but through your goodness you had mercy on us.”

Hence it is said elsewhere: “When you are angry, you will remember mercy” (Ps. 39).

A great approach to God is the knowledge of one’s own unhappiness. It is very useful for the soul to consider from where it fell and to see where it lies; to mourn its destruction through the loss of righteousness; and in these things to fear the anger of the judge. Whoever does this will obtain the mercy of the Lord.

“You were angry,” he says, “and you had mercy on us.” As though he said: You are angry in order to have mercy; you are angry in the present so that you may have mercy in the future. Your very anger is mercy.

And he explains how he has shown mercy:

### 4.

“You have shaken the earth,” that is, earthly people, with the plow of preaching; “and you have troubled it,” toward repentance. “As you have begun, Lord, so complete it. Heal its breaches,” that is, remove from it the miseries it endures, or the sins for which it has a contrite heart.

And it is fitting that you heal it, because it has been shaken and has freely consented to your grace as it moved it.

Through such stages, with God’s inspiration, the sinful soul begins to approach healing. First it is shaken by the fear of the Lord. Then it is troubled by grief over sin. It fears that it may perish; it grieves because it has sinned. Thus established between fear and grief, while conscience accuses and guilt terrifies, it begins to repent, to crush and torment its heart with severe anguish, and through contrition it returns to health.

“It has been preached to us: Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 4). Behold from where the earth has been shaken and troubled.

The sinful soul heard this. Perhaps it is not moved and is therefore not worthy to be healed. It heard, says Augustine, another message: it is moved and prodded; it beats its breast and pours out tears. “Heal, Lord, its breaches, because it has been shaken.”

Thus, after the earthly person has been struck, the old self set aflame, and the human being changed for the better, hard and harsh things follow. Hence it is added:

### 5.

“You have shown your people hard things.” Not only through a vision but also through experience, as it is written: “All who wish to live devoutly in Christ will suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3). “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14). Hence the Lord says to his disciples: “In the world you will have distress” (John 16).

“You have given us to drink the wine of compunction.” You have made us delight in the cup of suffering. For just as wine gives pleasure when it is drunk, and the very thing that stings contributes to the drinker’s pleasure, so the sufferings and tribulations of this age are a delight to the servants of God.

Hence Paul glories in tribulations (Rom. 5). And the Apostles went rejoicing from the presence of the council because they had been deemed worthy [Supp. “to be deemed worthy”] to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus (Acts 5).

The Lord offered this drink to the sons of Zebedee when he said: “Can you drink the cup that I am about to drink?” (Matt. 20).

Or, “You have given us to drink the wine of compunction,” that is, the sweetness of tears, repentance, and confession.

The first labor, therefore, is for a person to become displeasing to himself, to conquer his sins, and to be changed for the better. The second labor is, because he has been changed, to endure the tribulations and temptations of this age and to persevere among them to the end.

It should be noted that he does not say “the wine of destruction,” but “of compunction.” This drink of suffering is not one that destroys, but a medicine that burns. Hence it further follows:

### 6.

“You have given a sign to those who fear you”—namely, these tribulations that indicate and signify—“so that they may flee from the face of the bow,” that is, from the presence of the future and threatening judgment.

Through temporal tribulations, he says, you have signified to your people that they should flee from the wrath of eternal fire. Here let each person consider what awaits sinners afterward, if such powerful scourges chastise even the righteous here.

Hence Peter says: “It is time for judgment to begin from the house of the Lord; and if the righteous will scarcely be saved, where will the impious and the sinner appear?” (1 Pet. 4). How will he strike those with whom he is angry, if he permits those in whom he delights to be afflicted in this way?

The bow rightly signifies judgment, because just as an arrow is shot from a bow, so from judgment the sentence will be brought forth. The bowstring is drawn backward when the arrow is about to be sent; and the farther back it is drawn, the greater the force with which the arrow flies forward. So, the more judgment is delayed, the greater the force with which it will come.

Therefore let us give thanks to the Lord for temporal things, because he has given his people a sign, so that they may flee from the face of the bow. Why is this?

### 7.

“So that your beloved may be delivered.” The signs of present evils are given for this purpose: that those who love the Lord may be delivered from eternal evils.

And in order that this may happen, he earnestly begs, saying: “Save with your right hand,” that is, in your better gifts, in everlasting blessedness. Save me in such a way that I may stand at your right hand.

I do not ask for temporal salvation; concerning that, let your will be done. I ask for eternal salvation, which you command us to seek. “And therefore hear me.”

Here he turns to his hearers in order to strengthen them, saying:

### 8.

“God has spoken in his Holy One.” From this I know that he will save with his right hand, because God the Father has spoken “in his Holy One,” that is, in his Son. Hence Paul says: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5). And again: “In these last days he has spoken to us in his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things” (Heb. 1), in whom he promised this salvation.

Concerning this speech, I, the faithful people, will rejoice: “I will divide Shechem, and I will measure out the Valley of Tabernacles.”

When Jacob was returning from Laban his father-in-law with all his people, Rachel concealed in Shechem the idols that her father had possessed in Syria. Jacob made tabernacles there for his sheep and cattle and called that place Tabernacles (Gen. 31). And the Church says, “I will measure these out” [Note: [Col. 0883] “Or ‘will I divide?’ Augustine has: ‘and these I will divide,’ says the Church.”].

What is signified by Shechem, where the idols are hidden, except the Gentiles, worshipers of idols? “I will divide Shechem,” that is, I will divide the nations. For not everyone has faith. Some believe; others do not. Among those who believe, some live well and others badly. Among those who live well, some will persevere, while others will fall and perish.

Therefore those who believe should not fear because they are among unbelievers, nor should those who live rightly fear because they are among those who resist with wicked conduct. They are now divided by faith and conduct; at the judgment they will be divided, with the sheep at the right and the goats at the left (Matt. 25).

Shechem is interpreted as “shoulder.” According to the interpretation of the name, the shoulders are divided, so that some are weighed down by their sins while others carry Christ’s burden, as he himself urges us, saying: “Take my yoke upon you. For my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matt. 11).

“I will measure out the Valley of Tabernacles.” Perhaps, on account of Jacob’s sheep, the Valley of Tabernacles signifies the Jewish people; and it too is divided. For those who believed passed over from there, while the remnant remained outside.

This division is now demonstrated when it immediately adds:

### 9.

“Gilead is mine, Manasseh is mine; Ephraim is the strength of my head.”

Gilead is interpreted as “heap of testimony.” This was the name given to the heap of stones that Jacob and Laban made as a sign of the covenant. Through the heap of testimony the multitude of martyrs is signified. For *martyrs* in Greek means “witnesses” in Latin.

“Gilead is mine,” my heap of testimony is mine, my number of martyrs is mine—that is, it belongs to my fellowship.

Manasseh is interpreted as “forgetfulness.” Whoever forgets his former condition is likewise mine. Hence it is said elsewhere: “Forget your people and your father’s house, and the king will desire your beauty” (Isa. 144).

Ephraim is called “fruitfulness.” Those who produce good fruits are the strength of the head, that is, of Christ. By these, above all, the teachers of the Church are understood, who produce fruit in themselves and in others. The Lord says to such people in the Gospel: “I chose you, that you should go and bear fruit” (John 15). They are the strength of the head, because they sustain Christ’s weaker members.

### 10.

“Judah is my king.” Those who confess their sins and spiritually rule themselves are mine. For Judah is interpreted as “confession.”

Or Christ, who is from the tribe of Judah (Matt. 1), will be born as “my king.”

“Moab is the pot of my hope.” Moab is interpreted as “from the father,” because he was born from a father and daughter. By Moab the people of the Gentiles are understood, born from sin—from the daughters of Lot, who lay with their drunken father, using their father wrongly (Gen. 19).

In this they signify those who use the Law wrongly. The Apostle, however, says: “The Law is good” (1 Tim. 1), if someone uses it lawfully. Those daughters of Lot did not use their father lawfully.

Just as good works are born when someone uses the Law well, so evil works are born when someone uses the Law badly. Therefore those women, using their father—that is, using the Law—badly, generated the Moabites, through whom evil works are signified.

From this, says Augustine, comes the Church’s tribulation; from this, the boiling pot. Concerning this pot the prophet says elsewhere: “A burning pot from the north” (Jer. 1). From where, except from the devil’s side, who said: “I will set my throne toward the north” (Isa. 14)?

Tribulations therefore arise against the Church especially from those who use the Law badly. And just as food is boiled in a pot, so the saints are refined in tribulation.

It is plainly called “the pot of my hope,” because the hope of the saints comes from tribulation, as the Apostle testifies: “Tribulation produces endurance, endurance produces tested character, and tested character produces hope” (Rom. 5).

The pot of iniquity burns, but the flame of charity is greater. Do not fear the Moabites, that is, the evil works of those who use the Law badly. Your king Judah went before you. Do you not know that the Jews, using the Law badly, killed your king? Therefore hope, and follow where your king went before you.

Established in this pot of tribulations, let us hear how great a hope the Church has. For it follows:

“I will stretch out my sandal over Idumea.”

Idumea is interpreted as “earthly” or “bloody.” By the sandal the Gospel is understood. Hence it is written: “How beautiful are the feet of those who announce peace, who announce good things!” (Isa. 52); and, “with your feet shod in the preparation of the Gospel of peace” (Eph. 6).

Let the pot boil as much as it can; let the world rage as much as it is able. “I will stretch my sandal over Idumea,” that is, as far as the earthly and bloody, my preaching will extend. Or the sandal is stretched as far as Idumea when the humanity of God is preached to the Gentiles. For divinity was, so to speak, shod with our mortal flesh.

“Foreigners are subject to me.” Even those who do not belong to my race or inheritance are subject to me. Many come to faith who do not attain to the inheritance, as it is written: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20). How many worship Christ who will not reign with Christ!

And lest he seem to attribute this to their own strength, he commends the grace of God that leads him when he adds:

### 11.

“Who will lead me into the fortified city,” fortified with saints, that is, the heavenly Jerusalem? “Who will lead me as far as Idumea,” that is, into the Gentile world, so that many from the Gentiles may be incorporated into me and the city may be enlarged through the fellowship of its members?

Or this city may be understood as Judea, which is rightly called fortified, namely, by patriarchs and prophets, by the Law and by various institutions. Christ was first sent to it. The Apostles were first led to it. The Gospel was first preached to it.

Let the primitive Church speak; let the apostolic voice speak: “Who will lead me into the fortified city,” that is, “into Idumea”? “Who will lead me as far as Idumea,” that is, into the whole Gentile world?

### 12.

“Will it not be you, God, who rejected us?” You yourself who rejected us will lead us. You yourself who were angry will have mercy. For you will not contain your mercies in your anger.

“And will you not go forth, God, in our strengths?” The world is to serve; it is to become a heap of testimony through the blood poured out by the martyrs. The pagans will say: “Where is their God?” (Ps. 41). Then you will not go forth, God, in our strengths; you will not appear against them.

You will not display your power as you displayed it in Moses, Joshua, David, and the others, when the nations yielded to their strength and, after the slaughter, you brought your people into the land you had promised.

Certainly, when the martyrs were led away in chains, killed by the sword, burned by fire, tortured by various torments, and despised as though abandoned and without a helper—was God therefore absent from them because he did not go forth in their strengths? Did he not rather, by not going forth, lead the Church in their strengths as far as Idumea?

For if the Church wished to fight and use the sword, it would seem to be fighting for the present life. Because it despised the present life, therefore a heap of testimony concerning the future life was made.

You, then, God, who do not go forth in our strengths because you do not grant temporal help, grant eternal help. This is what follows:

### 13.

“Give us eternal help from tribulation,” that is, on account of the tribulation that we endure here. Therefore we do not seek this human salvation, because it is vain and transitory. Hence he immediately adds:

“And the salvation of man is vain.” Hence Solomon says: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Eccles. 1). And again he said: “I saw all the things that are done under the sun, and behold, all is vanity and affliction of spirit” (ibid.).

Rightly, then, the Church adds:

### 14.

“In God we will do valiantly.” Not with the sword, not with horses, not with breastplates, not with the power of an army. “And he himself will bring to nothing those who afflict us.”

This has happened, says Augustine: the martyrs were trampled down through suffering, persevering, and in God they acted valiantly. And he himself did what follows: “He brought to nothing those who afflicted us.”

Where are the persecutors? Where are those who raged, dragged people away, and killed them? Who even remembers any of them? The savagery of the persecutors has been brought to nothing; the strength and glory of the saints flourish.

We too will act valiantly in the Lord, so that we may deserve to be free from every tribulation and temptation. For “if God is for us, who can be against us?” (Rom. 8). Let our strength therefore be in God, and no adversities will prevail to harm us.

# TITLE OF PSALM LX

### 1.

The following psalm is entitled in this manner: “For the end; in hymns; of David.” This psalm directs us toward the end, composed in hymns, that is, in praises of Christ.

In this psalm the whole people from every part of the world, throughout all generations, are shown crying out to Christ. It is also shown that through Christ this people will attain the same inheritance that Christ himself possesses.

The subject is the faithful people who speak here. In the first part of the psalm, it shows itself crying out to Christ, as has been said. In the second part, which begins, “For you, my God, have heard my prayer,” it is shown to possess Christ’s inheritance.

The purpose is to exhort us, so that, praying after its example and hoping for future goods through the attainment of present goods, we may persevere in praises to the end. This purpose is discerned at the end of the psalm, where it says: “Thus I will sing a psalm to your name,” and so forth.

It sets before us a form of prayer, saying:

# PSALM LX

### 2.

“Hear, O God, my supplication; attend to my prayer.”

God attends to our prayer when he graciously receives what we ask. At times he hears certain people in anger, not so much for their salvation as for their condemnation. Therefore, after saying “Hear,” he immediately adds “Attend,” so that he may graciously and beneficially deign to hear.

It can also be divided in this way: “Hear my supplication” concerning the avoidance of evils; “attend to my prayer” concerning the pursuit of good things.

Some distinguish supplication from prayer in this way: to supplicate God is to seek that he avert evils from us; to pray is to ask that he grant good things.

And because the Church is spread throughout the whole world, it indicates that it cries out from every direction when it adds:

### 3.

“From the ends of the earth I have cried to you.” Our cry to God is our desire. The more intensely someone desires, the more intensely he cries out.

And he gives the reason why: “When my heart was anxious.” He shows himself to be throughout all the nations in great glory, yet not without great temptation. For “all who wish to live devoutly in Christ suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3).

Our progress is accomplished through temptation, and no one comes to know himself unless he is tested. Nor can anyone be crowned unless he has conquered (2 Tim. 2); nor can he conquer unless he has fought; nor can he fight unless he has an enemy and temptation.

Let him, then, be anxious, crying out from the ends of the earth, but he is not abandoned, because it follows: “You have exalted me upon a rock.”

The rock was Christ (1 Cor. 10). Hence the Truth himself says: “Upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16). He is exalted upon the rock who is founded upon faith in our Lord Jesus Christ (Rom. 1).

And he rightly says “You have exalted,” because the righteous person who lives by faith (Phil. 3) rises above all temporal things, and his citizenship is in heaven.

And because the one who gives faith advances his own people toward action and hope, and confirms them in that very faith so that no one may fail when tested, it rightly follows:

“You have led me from strength to strength, from good to better.”

4. For you have become my hope, a tower of strength against the face—that is, the presence—of the enemy.

[From Augustine:] If he had not become our hope, he would not lead us onward. He leads as a guide, leads us into himself as the way, and brings us to himself as our homeland. Why is he our hope? Because he suffered, because he rose again. What do we say when we read these things? God does not abandon us, for whose sake he sent his Son to be tempted, crucified, to die, and to rise again. God does not despise us, for whose sake he did not spare even his own Son, but handed him over for us (Rom. 8). Thus he became our hope. [Col. 0887B]

In him you see your labor and your reward: labor in his passion, reward in his resurrection. We have two lives: one in which we are now, and another for which we hope. The life in which we are is known to us; the one for which we hope is unknown to us. Endure the life in which you are, and you will possess the one you do not yet have. How do you endure? Do not be conquered by the tempter through any labors. [Note: [Col. 0887] In Augustine: “that you may not be conquered by the tempter.” By his labors, temptations, passion, death, etc.] By his temptations and his death he showed you the life in which you are; by his resurrection he showed you the life in which you will be.

For this reason he became your guide. Your very Creator suffered, so that you would not fear suffering. He died, so that you would not fear death. He rose again in your flesh, so that you too might hope to rise. For by hope we have been saved (Rom. 8).

He who is our hope also became for us a tower of strength against the face—that is, the presence—of the enemy. Such is God’s fortification for us: in it we can be secure from the enemy and hurl weapons against him.

[From Augustine:] Christ is before you. Remember Christ and enter the tower. Whatever you suffer, consider that he suffered first [Col. 0887C]; and consider the end for which he suffered—namely, that he might die and rise again. Hope for an end like the one that preceded in him, and you have entered the tower by refusing to consent to the enemy.

For if you consent to the enemy, the missile of the attacker reaches you. Rather, hurl against him the weapons by which he may be struck and conquered. What are these weapons? The words of God, your faith, your hope, and good works.

I now put it this way: remain in that tower so that you may dwell there, and let it be enough for you, because the enemy’s weapons do not reach you. Do something there; let your hands not cease. Your good works are swords that kill the enemy.

Strengthened, therefore, by such a fortification, he promises that he will persevere when he adds:

5. I shall dwell in your tabernacle forever.

Because the Church will remain here until the end of the age, waging war for God, I shall remain in concord and fight in the unity of faith until the end. For it is not the one who has begun, but the one who has persevered to the end, who will be saved (Matt. 24).

But from where will you persevere? What are your strength and power amid so many scandals and such great struggles? The text continues:

I shall be protected under the shelter of your wings—that is, under the protection of virtues. [Col. 0887D]

Hence the angel says to the blessed Virgin: The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you (Luke 1).

Behold why we are secure amid so many temptations until the end of the age comes and the eternal ages receive us: because we are protected under the shelter of his wings.

[From the same source:] The heat of vices is great, but the shadow beneath God’s wings is great. Therefore I am confident of protection,

6. because you, God, have heard my prayer concerning the reception of good things.

You have given an inheritance to those who fear your name.

Benefits already bestowed are evidence of things to come. Here we are admonished not to cease praying as long as the time of temptations lasts. “Pray,” says the Lord, “that you may not enter into temptation.” Frequent prayer drives away the devil’s darts. This is the first virtue against the assaults of temptations.

A servant of God can do nothing more useful [Col. 0888A] in this world than pray to God. Prayer clears the heart, withdraws it from earthly things, cleanses it of vices, raises it to heavenly things, and makes it more capable and worthy of receiving spiritual blessings.

Let us therefore persevere in prayer and in fear of God’s name, so that we may be worthy to obtain the heavenly inheritance. Then he explains what inheritance God will give, saying:

7. You will add days to the days of the king; his years will extend to the day of generation and generation.

[From Augustine:] You will add eternal days to the temporal days of our king Christ, so that Christ may reign in his Church not only during these passing days, but that the saints may reign with him in those days that have no end.

God’s eternity is called “days” and “years” (Dan. 7), though improperly. Hence another psalm says: “And your years will not fail” (Ps. 101). If they are called years, they may likewise be called days, or a single day. Whatever you wish to call it, you speak of eternity in an inadequate way. Yet it is necessary to say something, so that there may be a basis for contemplating what cannot be said.

And because he could have added two or three days or years, he says, “You will add”—until the day of the present generation [Col. 0888B] and of the future generation, or of the fleshly generation and the spiritual one, the temporal and the eternal.

And the king himself, together with his generation, remains forever in the sight of God. This is the reward of the saints: the glory of seeing God. Hence the Apostle says: “We shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3).

And because God’s recompense is so great, and blessedness so great, “who will seek his mercy and truth?”

He is called merciful because God does not consider our merits, but his own goodness, by which he forgave us our sins and promised eternal life. He is called truthful because he does not fail to give what he promised.

Let us recognize this mercy and truth here, and let us act so that, just as he showed us mercy by forgiving our sins and truth by granting what he promised, so we too may show mercy here toward the needy, the sick, and even our enemies. Let us show truth by not sinning and by not adding sin upon sin.

He says, “Who will seek?” [Col. 0888C] in the form of a question, as though inviting us, because although this good is ineffable, there are nevertheless few who seek it or persevere in seeking it. Human misery is so great, and iniquity has so greatly abounded, that many seek vanity and falsehood, while few seek truth.

Let us strive, however, to be among those few, so that with the elect we may say what follows:

8. Thus I shall sing praise to your name forever and ever, so that I may fulfill my vows from day to day.

Placed under this hope—because I hope that you will give me an inheritance in the future and that I shall remain forever in your sight—I shall sing praise to your name. That is, I shall work well for the honor of your name, reaching toward the age that follows this age, so that I may fulfill my vows—that is, myself, whom I have vowed—from day to day, that is, continually; or from day to day, that is, from virtue to virtue.

Or, “Thus I shall sing praise,” so that I may fulfill my vows: that is, I shall sing with my voice in such a way that the voice of my mouth agrees with the devotion of my heart. For the voice of those who sing praise to God ought to agree with the heart, so that the Apostle’s saying may be fulfilled [Col. 0888D]: “I shall sing praise and also with the mind” (1 Cor. 14).

God is not pleased with the praise of those of whom it is said: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 26; Matt. 15). Our psalmody is acceptable to God when we sing with our mouths in such a way that our hearts are kindled; when tongue, life, and conscience come together in the praise of God.

Let us strive to offer such praise and such vows to the Lord God forever and ever, from day to day.

## TITLE OF PSALM LXI

1. To the end, for Jeduthun (1 Chron. 25), a psalm of David.

The psalm applies to David and to the other righteous, and is given for Jeduthun—that is, “for those who leap across”—directed “to the end,” that is, toward Christ.

Those who leap across are its subject: people who cannot be prevented by any tribulation or persuasion from leaving earthly things behind [Col. 0889A] and striving toward heavenly things alone.

In the first part he shows that he cannot be prevented from completing his leap, rebuking the wicked who wish to hinder him either by persuasion or by tribulation. In the second part, which begins, “Nevertheless, to God…,” he admonishes himself and others to be subject to God. In the third part, which begins, “Nevertheless, they are vain…,” he rebukes the wicked for their evil and says that one must not put confidence in earthly things.

Its purpose is to admonish us not to be hindered by any tribulation from passing over from earthly things to heavenly ones. Therefore it is now spoken in the voice of every perfect person against the envious.

## PSALM LXI

2. Shall not my soul be subject to God?

For he knew [from Augustine] that “the one who exalts himself will be humbled.” Fearing that he might become proud in leaping across, he was not lifted up by those things that were below, but was humble before God, who is above. As though responding to envious people threatening him with ruin because they were displeased that he had leapt across, he said:

“Shall not my soul be subject to God?” That is, obedient to him and observing his commandments.

“My soul,” I say, “my own”—that is, subject to my authority. For although the body may be subject to your authority, the soul will never belong to anyone but me. [Col. 0889B] However much I approach, ascend, or leap across, I shall be under God, not against God. I shall be secure in transcending all else when he holds me beneath himself, he who is above all.

And it is right that I should be subject to him. For from him—that is, from God the Father—is my salvation, that is, my deliverance. This is proved as follows:

3. For he himself is my God, who created me, and my Savior, who saved me.

He is my protector, who received me from death into life and from punishment into glory. Therefore, “I shall not be moved any further.”

Although I was once moved, now I have been received and healed by my Creator and Redeemer. I shall no longer be moved.

It should also be noted that there is a difference between “Savior” and “salvation.” By the name “Savior,” Christ is understood; “salvation” signifies the salvation accomplished through him.

And since I have such a Savior, from whom I shall no longer be moved, then, O fools—

303 4. How long will you rush upon the man—that is, the outward man?

303 That is, how long will you attack irrationally [Col. 0889C]? For although you may afflict the body, you cannot reach the soul (Matt. 10).

There is no loss for us. But consider your own destruction in what you are doing. For “you all kill yourselves.” Whoever tries to remove good people from their purpose, whether by dissuading them or by persecuting them, kills himself inwardly in doing so. You condemn your own souls.

But you rush upon him like a leaning wall—that is, just as a leaning wall is prone to collapse, so you think us easy to bring down, as though we were entirely without help.

“And like a tottering fence?” That is, just as a wall without mortar is fragile and, if pushed, easily collapses, so you think us to be without cohesion and prone to ruin. But it is not so.

5. Nevertheless, the wicked do not cease for that reason, but they have planned to drive away my price from me.

That is, to take from me my God, the glory for which I hope, and the reward of my labor.

Therefore “I ran in thirst”—not as one who is sluggish and disgusted, but as one who thirsts and desires to die for righteousness. I was eager for the passion. [Col. 0889D] For blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, because they will be satisfied (Matt. 5).

During this running and thirsting, “they blessed with their mouth,” so that they might deceive me with words of flattery; “but with their heart they cursed,” plotting iniquity and death.

The wicked and deceitful do this when they do not dare to persecute the good openly. They speak good things with a deceitful mouth, but poison lies hidden within the heart.

Yet although they do this and devise such things; although they push, lay ambushes, persecute, and slander, I shall nevertheless remain fixed in God. Therefore, exhorting his soul amid so many dangers, he adds:

6. Nevertheless, be subject to God, my soul.

As you began, recognize that you received from him the good things you possess. Humble yourself before him as much as you can.

And indeed you will do so, “because my patience comes from him.”

Or, because Christ himself became an example of patience, as the Apostle says: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, so that you might follow in his footsteps” [Col. 0890A] (1 Pet. 2).

Or because he himself makes a person strong and patient in tribulations. No one could endure such great open conflicts or hidden snares among open enemies and false brothers unless almighty God granted the strength to suffer.

Again he gives another reason why the soul ought to be subject to God, saying:

Because he is my God, who calls me; and my Savior, who redeemed me; my helper in doing good.

Therefore, “I shall not emigrate”—I shall not depart.

He already stated this verse above. But there he warned his hearers through it; now he repeated it to exhort himself. It is useful advice always to remember our God as Savior and helper, so that no temptations may cause us to depart from him.

Hence he continues:

8. In God is my salvation.

That is, through God I possess salvation. For the whole salvation of the righteous must be referred to him who justifies the ungodly.

And my glory—that is, so that, according to the Apostle, “the one who boasts may boast in the Lord” [Col. 0890B] (1 Cor. 10).

Or because through him the glory of eternal life is granted. Meanwhile, amid temptations and scandals, amid open attacks and crafty words, God is my helper. For he gives help to those who struggle.

And my hope is in God.

[From Augustine:] Hope exists as long as what was promised has not yet arrived and what is not seen is believed. When it comes, it will be salvation and glorification. Yet while these things are delayed, we are not abandoned. “God is my helper, and my hope is in God.”

Now he exhorts the others by his example, as one who runs in thirst and desires all to be saved. For it is right that those who run toward God by living well should hurry to draw along with themselves as many as they can. He says, therefore:

9. Hope in him, every congregation of the people.

All you who have been gathered into the unity of faith.

And so that you may be able to hope in him worthily, “pour out your hearts before him.” That is, empty them of every stain, so that they may be before him—that is, in his good pleasure. For whoever does not have a heart [Col. 0890C] empty of evil, if he hopes, possesses not hope but presumption.

[From the same source:] Do not keep your hearts shut up within your hearts; pour them out before him by mourning, confessing, and entreating.

Because God is our helper forever.

God is not such a helper as a human being is. Human beings help temporarily; God helps even by granting eternity. God, I say, is our helper forever.

10. Nevertheless, the children of men are vain.

They do not attend to these things, but are vain—that is, devoted to vanities. He calls them “children of men” because they imitate those who live according to the flesh.

The children of men are also liars “in the balances,” that is, in the scales of justice and in deliberating between good and evil, when they make evil outweigh good. This is said by comparison with those who deceive buyers using balances, in which justice appears to reside.

Hence he adds: “so that they may deceive each other through vanity.” The phrase “unto one and the same end” signifies that although there are different frauds, different errors, and different doctrines, all tend toward one vanity and one kingdom of destruction and perdition. [Col. 0890D]

He therefore endeavors to dissuade them from such vanity when he continues:

11. Do not hope in iniquity.

He explains this iniquity part by part when he adds:

And do not desire plunder.

This was said to the poor, who might perhaps seize something out of necessity. Let the rich also listen:

“If riches increase, if they overflow and run as though from a fountain, do not set your heart upon them.”

[From the same source:] Do not trust in riches; do not presume upon them; do not hope in them. Let it not be said: “Behold the man who did not make God his helper” (Ps. 51), “but trusted in the abundance of his riches and prevailed in his vanity.”

Blessed, however, is the one whose hope is the Lord God, who has not turned toward vanities and false insanities (Ps. 58).

Behold: one person does not possess, another possesses. Let the one who does not possess not seek to seize what he lacks. Let the one who possesses not set his heart upon what he has; let him not fix it there, but rather fear.

Paul commands: “Instruct the rich of this age not to be proud in mind [Col. 0891A] and not to hope in the uncertainty of riches” (1 Tim. 6).

Therefore, do not desire fraud or plunder. Do not place your hope in the things you possess.

And to dissuade them still more from vanity, he sets forth two things: one terrifies, the other soothes. He says:

12. God has spoken once; I have heard these two things: that power belongs to God, [verse 13] and that mercy belongs to you, Lord; for you will repay each person according to his works.

If you disregard a human voice, pay attention because God himself has spoken—and spoken once, that is, unchangeably; or once, that is, in his one Word.

For God the Father has one Word, the only-begotten God (Heb. 1). All things are in him, because all things were made through the Word (John 1). In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col. 2).

He has one Word: “God has spoken once.” I heard in it these two things that I am about to tell you. I do not speak from myself.

Perhaps he heard many other things, but it is not necessary for him to tell us. For the Lord himself says: “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” [Col. 0891B] (John 16).

Leaping across the whole of creation, he reached the only-begotten Word of God. When the Word revealed these things, he heard two matters that are extremely necessary for us: that power belongs to God—for all power is from God (Rom. 13)—and that mercy belongs to you, Lord.

Nearly all the Scriptures are contained in these two things. For their sake the Patriarchs, the Prophets, the Law, our Lord Jesus Christ, and the Apostles spoke. For their sake all proclamation and celebration of the word takes place in the Church.
