Fear his power; love his mercy. Do not presume upon his mercy in such a way that you despise his power. Nor fear his power in such a way that you despair of his mercy.

It belongs to his power to punish the wicked for their evil work. It belongs to his mercy to reward the righteous for their good work.

Therefore he says: “For you will repay each person according to his works”—good things to the good, and evil things to the evil.

Before this happens, then, let us strive to turn away from evil and do good. Let us strive to pass from this world to God [Col. 0891C], and from vice to virtue.

This is the fruit and purpose of this psalm, and of the one who leaps across.

## TITLE OF PSALM LXII

1. To the end, a psalm of David, when he was in the desert of Idumaea (2 Sam. 28).

Historically, David fled from Saul and came into the desert of Idumaea. He understood that, in this figure, the Church is placed in the desert of this life; and he sings in this psalm about the reality signified by it.

This psalm applies to the prophet David, to all the righteous, and to the Church itself when it is in the desert of Idumaea—that is, in this life, where there is nothing but earthliness.

The subject is the Church placed in the desert of this life. In the first part it shows that, having been admonished through the desert of this life, it hastens toward God with every desire. In the second part, which begins, “If I remembered you,” it shows that, through God himself, it possesses security in this desert.

Its purpose is to admonish them to choose God alone for themselves, or to teach them how to live in the midst of a corrupt generation. The voice is that of the whole Church.

## PSALM LXII

2. O God [Col. 0891D], my God, I keep vigil toward you from the dawn.

O God of all by creation, my God according to a special and singular love: I keep vigil—that is, I diligently strive and am attentive—to win your favor and carry out your will.

And this “from the dawn,” that is, through the purity of a good conscience. The Gospel speaks of this vigilance: “Blessed is that servant whom, when his Lord comes, he finds watching” (Matt. 24).

He calls a pure conscience “light.” Conversely, following the Apostle, we call a bad conscience darkness: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5).

Or, “I keep vigil toward you from the dawn,” that is, from the time when I came to know you, which is the cause of my vigilance. The sleep of the soul is forgetting God.

Paul awakens such a person when he says: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (ibid.). Christ enlightens souls and makes them keep vigil. Therefore our life and conduct ought, through Christ, to keep vigil toward God.

He shows the cause of this vigilance [Col. 0892A] when he adds:

My soul thirsted for you; how greatly my flesh also thirsted for you.

Whenever someone wishes something to be granted to him in the ardor of desire, that desire itself is the soul’s thirst. Human hearts have different desires. One thirsts for gold, another for silver, another for property, another for an inheritance, another for this, another for that. A person who thirsts for God is scarcely found.

But the holy soul rejects everything belonging to this world as bitter and burns with all its desires for that ineffable sweetness which is in God. It desires to be filled from the abundance of God’s house, where there is the fountain of life and the source of wisdom.

“And my flesh,” he says, “thirsted for you” (Ps. 35), so that in that resurrection and immortality it might appear before you, which you promised.

And this “how greatly,” that is, for far more reasons than the soul, because the flesh is subject to greater miseries. “The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. 26).

Although the soul experiences many temptations and disturbances, it does not fail in the same way as the flesh.

[From Augustine:] At present [Col. 0892B], because of the corruption of the flesh, if we do not eat, we fail and grow hungry. If we do not drink, we fail and grow thirsty. If we eat and drink for a long time, the very prolonged refreshment becomes exhaustion. If we sleep for a long time, we fail, and therefore we keep watch. If we keep watch for a long time, we fail, and therefore we sleep. If we stand for a long time, we grow tired, and therefore we sit. If we sit for a long time, we become tired even there, and therefore we rise.

There is therefore no stable condition for our flesh. At one moment our age passes from infancy to childhood, from childhood to adolescence, from adolescence to youth, from youth to old age, from old age to extreme old age, and from extreme old age to death. Our age does not stand still: everywhere there is weariness, everywhere corruption.

Therefore, just as the flesh is wearied in many ways, so in many ways it thirsts for the unfailing incorruption that comes from God.

Where does it thirst?

3. In a deserted, pathless, and waterless land.

That is, in this world, which is a deserted land, lacking, as far as it is concerned, every good thing, without the way of truth or the refreshment of true salvation.

Yet the Lord had mercy on us [Col. 0892C] in this desert. “Truth has sprung up from the earth, and our earth has yielded its fruit.” Our Lord Jesus Christ became the way. He gave us water in the desert, filling his preachers with the Holy Spirit so that a fountain of water springing up into eternal life might be formed in them.

We possess these things here, but they do not come from the desert. Therefore the psalm first commended the desert’s character, so that when you heard what evil condition you were in, if you possessed here any consolations, fruits, a way, or water, you would not attribute them to the desert but to the one who deigned to visit you in the desert.

Unless a person first thirsts amid the evil in which he is, he will never reach the good that God is.

“Thus I appeared to you in the holy place”—that is, I prepared myself in such a way that you ought to look upon me, specifically because I am in holy desire or purpose—“so that I might see your power and your glory.”

That is, so that I might understand your Son, in whom is the power of omnipotence, because all things were made through him (John 1), and the glory of divinity.

Those whose hearts have been sanctified [Col. 0892D] now see this power and glory through faith; afterward they will see them by direct vision.

Again he gives another reason why he kept vigil and thirsted, saying:

4. For your mercy is better than lives.

[From Augustine:] There are many human lives, but God promises us one life. He does not give it to us because of our merits, but because of his mercy.

One person chooses for himself the life of doing business, another of lending at interest, another of farming, another of military service, another this life, another that. There are many lives, but your mercy is better than our lives. What you give to those who have been corrected is better than what the perverse love. You give one life, which is to be preferred to all the lives we might choose in the world.

Or, alternatively: there are many lives of the saints in this world. One serves God in marriage, another through continence, another through the common life, another through solitude, another through active service, another through contemplation—each in a different way [Col. 0893A], according to the measure of grace given by God to each person (Rom. 12).

However perfectly one may live, however holily and purely one may serve God, no one is brought to the heavenly kingdom unless divine mercy is joined to good works.

Let it rightly be said, therefore: “For your mercy is better than lives.” Therefore “my lips will praise you”—that is, I shall proclaim you, worthy of praise, to others.

We must not be ungrateful for the great mercy of the pious Lord; we ought to offer him whatever praise and thanks we can. Hence he continues:

5. Thus I shall bless you in my life, and in your name I shall lift up my hands.

What does “thus” mean? That I attribute my life to your mercy, in which I praise you, not to my merits.

Or, “my lips will praise you” in such a way that I shall also bless you in my life—that is, throughout my whole life. A person praises God worthily when his life agrees with his lips.

To lift up one’s hands is to perform good works with regard to the heavenly homeland. “In your name,” he says—that is, for the honor and glory [Col. 0893B] of your name. As it is said elsewhere: “Not to us, Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory” (Ps. 113).

And so that he may be able both to praise God worthily with his lips and to bless him by right living and good works, he asks to be enriched by the gift of God’s grace when he adds:

6. Let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness, and my mouth shall praise you with lips of exultation.

“Marrow” properly denotes the fatness found inside, around the vital organs. It signifies the love of God poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us (Rom. 5).

The fatness found in the external limbs signifies the soul’s eagerness, which makes the body perform good works eagerly. For a lean soul does not please God, just as a lean victim was not said to please him in the old sacrifice.

This was therefore written so that we might understand it figuratively: he is not asking for bodily fatness but spiritual fatness—not that which is in the flesh, but that which is in the soul. [Col. 0893C]

The soul is filled with marrow and fatness when love is in the mind, affection is outwardly expressed, and spiritual joy appears in action. For God loves a cheerful giver (2 Cor. 9).

Hence he says that he will praise God with lips of exultation, because in the service of the Lord and in his praise there ought to be not sadness but joy. Therefore the Holy Spirit elsewhere admonishes us in the psalm: “Serve the Lord with gladness” (Ps. 99).

God’s praise ought not to be only in the mouth, but also in meditation and action. Hence he adds:

7. If I remembered you upon my bed, I shall meditate on you in the morning.

He calls his bed his rest. Often, when people are at rest, they become lax through their repose and forget God. This holy soul remembers God in its rest.

From this it is clear that it will also meditate on God in its actions. “If I remembered you upon my bed”—that is, when I was at rest—“I shall meditate on you”—that is, in works of light.

308 We ought to perform worthy deeds as people in the light [Col. 0893D], because we are not of night and darkness, but sons of God and of light (1 Thess. 5). Hence the Apostle admonishes us to walk honorably as in the day (Rom. 13).

And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5).

He commends God’s grace when he adds:

8. Because you have been my helper.

For unless the Lord helps our good works, we cannot complete them. Behold, the Church has now shown that it is secure in the desert through the help of God’s grace.

Therefore, exulting, it says:

And I shall exult under the shelter of your wings.

I rejoice in good works because the shelter of your wings is above me—that is, the refreshment and protection of virtues.

Nor shall I merely exult, but already with affection and desire:

9. My soul clung after you.

Not in such a way as to go before you, as Peter did when he said to the Lord, “Be favorable to yourself; this shall never happen.” For this reason he was rebuked and heard: “Get behind me, Satan. You do not understand the things of God, but those of men” [Col. 0894A] (Matt. 16).

Rather, it clung to you so as to be behind you—that is, so as to follow you continually and obey you.

And because it clung in this way, “your right hand received me”—that is, your power and grace lifted me into great dignity from the degradation in which I was because of sin; or your grace received me in order to place me at your right hand.

This may also be understood specifically of our head, who after his resurrection and ascension was placed at the right hand of the Father. In his person the text continues:

10. But they sought my soul in vain.

The Jews sought to destroy Christ’s soul (John 11), but in vain, because they could not accomplish what they wished. Hence the punishment that was to come upon them is foretold:

They shall enter into the lower parts of the earth; they shall be handed over to the sword; they shall become portions for foxes.

They were led into captivity as far as the lower parts of the earth, defeated by their enemies and handed over to the power of warriors. [Col. 0894B] They were divided into portions by the kings and princes of this world, who were called foxes because of their cunning and craftiness.

Hence the Lord himself calls King Herod a fox: “Go and tell that fox” (Matt. 13).

But with these people thus scattered, let us hear what he adds concerning our king:

12. But the king shall rejoice in God.

He who is rightly called king because of salvation, who is King of kings and Lord of lords, who rules us according to good morals and virtues, whose kingdom will have no end (Rev. 1 and 19)—such a king will rejoice in that unchangeableness which is in God, namely, in the Father’s divinity.

And all who swear by him—that is, all who promise and keep faith with God—will also be praised and shown worthy of praise through him, because they vow their souls to him and fulfill their vows.

Great indeed will be the praise of the saints when they hear from the Lord himself at the judgment: 309 “I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty [Col. 0894C], and you gave me drink,” and other such words. And again: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25).

When the king and his soldiers have thus been established in great joy, the opposing party will be confounded. Concerning them he adds:

For the mouth of those who speak iniquity has been stopped.

[From Augustine:] How many iniquities did the Jews speak! How many evils did the pagans utter, who persecuted Christians because of their idols! When they thought that the Christians could be brought to an end, the Christians increased, and the pagans themselves came to an end. Their mouths have been stopped. They no longer dare to speak against Christ.

This will nevertheless be fulfilled more perfectly at the judgment, when they see our king reigning. They will not be able to deny God when they see the saints standing in great steadfastness against those who afflicted them, and when they see those whom they once held in derision counted among the sons of God (Wis. 5).

Then the mouth of the wicked will indeed be stopped, when it will no longer have anything it can say.

Let us therefore strive to keep vigil toward God [Col. 0894D] from the dawn and, in this dry desert, thirst for the fountain of life. Let our heart be in holy desire. Let our lips, our life, and our works praise and bless God. Let there be the fatness of love in the heart and cheerfulness in action. Let us remember God evening and morning. Let our joy be in him. Let our soul cling to him with total desire.

Let us beware of the example of the wicked, who perish, so that we may be able to rejoice and reign with our king Jesus Christ in the heavenly kingdom.

This is the benefit of the psalm.

## TITLE OF PSALM LXIII

1. The title of the following psalm is: To the end, a psalm of David.

This psalm applies to David—that is, to Christ, who speaks here—directed toward the end. Christ is its subject, suffering and glorified. For it briefly touches upon his passion and glorification.

In the first part it describes the malice of the Jews and prays to be delivered from them, affirming that he will be delivered. In the second [Col. 0895A] part, which begins, “The arrows of the little ones,” it presents the mockery of their folly.

In this psalm he shows his steadfastness in the passion, intending by his example to instruct us in how we ought to conduct ourselves among enemies and how, when praying, we ought to persevere in tribulations. We should attend especially to this: the harsher and more unjust our tribulation has been, the greater our progress will be in the future, while theirs will be the greater failure.

Here Christ prays that he may not yield to his enemies in the passion, although he knew with complete certainty that he would never fail. He does this for the instruction of the faithful: if he, who knew the future beforehand, wished to pray, then those who are uncertain should devote themselves to prayer all the more diligently.

Thus he begins:

## PSALM LXIII
## 2

Hear my prayer, O God, when I entreat you. Now, Father, I entreat you; now hear my prayer. But when Christ asks to be heard, this must be understood not according to his divinity, but according to his humanity. For in that respect in which he was human, he was weak, mortal, and subject to suffering. Therefore, in this respect he sought mercy, since he needed mercy. What this prayer is, the following words make clear. For he says:

“Rescue my soul from fear of the enemy.” In the Psalm the servant prays for what the Lord commands in the Gospel: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10). Let him therefore pray that he may grant what he commands. He does not pray that he may not be killed, but that he may not fear the one who kills, lest perhaps he should succumb through fear. The Lord Christ does not ask this because he could be broken by any fear, but in order to give his members, in their weakness, a pattern of prayer and steadfastness in suffering. That he is confident of being heard, he shows by the words that follow. For he says:

## 3

“You have protected me from the assembly of the malicious”—that is, from the gathering of those who were plotting evil against me—“and also from the multitude of those who work iniquity,” that is, from the many who perpetrated that singular iniquity against me, namely, the crucifixion. For he was protected (as Augustine says), God protecting him, and the Son himself protecting his flesh. What could his enemies do? They killed the body, but they could not kill the soul. It would have been little for the Lord to encourage his martyrs by word, unless he strengthened them by example. “Hear me,” he says, “and it is necessary that you hear me.” Why?

## 4

“For they sharpened their tongues like a sword; they bent the bow toward a bitter thing, so that they might shoot the blameless in secret.” Just as a sword is sharpened so that it may cut more deeply, so they devised with the utmost sharpness what worse things they could say against him. This was the sharpness of the Jews. They sought this as their great objective: that, if they killed him, they would not appear to be murderers. Therefore they bent the bow, that is, they prepared ambushes. They fought at once with both sword and bow: with the sword of the tongue, and with the bow of deception. One fights with a sword at close quarters. He who shoots an arrow deceives in order to strike. And rightly does he call this bow, this fraud, a bitter thing. For what is as bitter as killing Christ?

They bent it, then, in order to shoot the blameless, that is, to kill the innocent. And they did this “in secret,” that is, covertly. For this purpose they sought ways by which he might be betrayed by a disciple (Matt. 26), condemned by a Roman judge, and crucified by the Romans themselves (Luke 22). This was the sharpness of the tongue, this the bow, this the arrows. Through others they shot Christ; by the sword of their own tongue they killed him. Hence it is further said:

## 5

“Suddenly they will shoot at him and will not fear; they have strengthened for themselves an evil word.” “Suddenly” means, as though unexpectedly. Three things arising from the perversity of the Jews are commended in this verse. First, the cruelty of their deed, where it says, “They will shoot at him.” Second, the perversity of their mind, where it says, “And they did not fear.” Third, the insane persistence of their speech, where it adds, “They strengthened for themselves an evil word.” These words indicate to us that they were corrupt in everything—in word, deed, and thought.

O hard and impenitent heart! He was handed over to the judge. The judge trembles, but those who handed him over to the judge do not tremble. Authority quakes, but savagery does not quake. He wishes to wash his hands, but they defile their tongues. But why? “They strengthened for themselves an evil word”: “Crucify him, crucify him” (Matt. 27; Luke 22). Truly an evil word—none could be more evil. Repetition is a confirmation of the malicious statement. They strengthened it, however, not for the Lord but for themselves, that is, for their own condemnation. For how could it not be for themselves, when they say, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27)?

And because one who sins in secret desires not to sin publicly, it is rightly added:

## 6

“They recounted how they might conceal snares”—that is, how they might secretly seize and kill Christ: betraying him through a disciple, judging him through the Roman governor, and killing him through the governor’s soldiers (Matt. 26). Such was the concealment of the snares, concerning which they also said, “Who will see them?” For they did not think that this could be detected by anyone. But it did them no good. For it follows:

## 7

“They searched out iniquities”: ways by which they could refute Christ in argument, or because they set up false witnesses against him (ibid.). “But those who searched out searches failed,” that is, in that subtle and repeated investigation they could accomplish nothing. This is plainly shown when it is added:

## 8

“A man will approach a deep heart, and God will be exalted.” “To a deep heart” means to a hidden heart, a divine heart—not revealing what he knew, nor revealing what he was. They, supposing him to be nothing more than what appeared, killed the man in the deep heart. “God will be exalted” in the divine heart. From the very place where he is humbled, he is exalted all the more. For Christ died, rose from the dead, ascended into heaven, and sent his preachers into the world. He was believed to be God. He was magnified and exalted—not in the sense that he could ever be exalted in himself, but in the sense that greater knowledge of God came to be held concerning him.

Hear how God was exalted, and how those who persecuted him were humbled.

## 9

“The arrows of children became their wounds; their tongues were weakened against them. All who saw them were troubled. And every person feared.”

Those who shot and did not fear are now struck by the arrows of children, and, troubled, they are afraid. Those who strengthened an evil word for themselves now find their tongues weakened against them. Threats and blasphemies ceased. They recognized that their investigations were useless, and fell silent after so great a tumult of words.

Such is “the change of the right hand of the Most High” (Ps. 76). For it was not by the powerful weapons of mighty warriors, but by the humble arrows of simple children, that almighty God cast down such great and savage enemies. “God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong” (1 Cor. 1). For who are these children except those to whom it is said in the Gospel: “Unless you turn and become like this child, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18; Mark 10)?

Therefore all were troubled toward repentance—that is, people from every class. “And every person feared,” that is, everyone endowed with reason, so as to understand what had happened. The fear of the Lord subjected itself: “They proclaimed the works of God,” namely, his birth, passion, resurrection, humanity, and divinity, together with his powers and miracles. “And they understood his deeds”: namely, that our redemption and salvation had been accomplished by God. And therefore it follows:

## 10

“The righteous person will rejoice”—not in himself, not in the world, but in the Lord—and will hope in him for eternal life. “And all the upright in heart will be praised,” that is, all who believe rightly and live well will appear worthy of praise. Those are upright in heart who, abandoning their own will, submit themselves entirely to the divine will.

Let us therefore pray to God to grant us steadfastness, so that we may not fear the assembly of the malicious, nor the swords of tongues, nor the bows of deceptions. Let us approach God with a humble—and therefore deep—heart, so that we may deserve to be exalted in him. Let us fear him with a chaste fear; let us proclaim his works, so that, justified through him, we may always be able to rejoice in him. This is the benefit of the Psalm.

# TITLE OF PSALM LXIV

## 1

The title of the following Psalm is this: “For the end, a Psalm of David, a Song of Jeremiah and Haggai concerning the word of pilgrimage, when they begin to set out” (Jer. 5, 50, 52; Hag. 1 and 2).

The people of Israel were taken captive (as Augustine says): they were led from the city of Jerusalem into servitude in Babylonia. The holy Jeremiah prophesied that after seventy years the people would return from captivity and restore that same city, Jerusalem, which he had mourned after it had been conquered by enemies. Haggai, however, did not prophesy the captivity, but succeeded Jeremiah, who died while the Jews were in captivity. Haggai himself prophesied the return and was present at the return, because, after Nebuchadnezzar died, another king succeeded him who, fearing God, released God’s people.

But since, as the Apostle says, “these things happened to them in figure, and they were written for us, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. 10), we too must first know our captivity and then our liberation. We must know the Babylonia in which we are captives and the Jerusalem for whose return we sigh. These two cities are made by two loves. Love of God makes Jerusalem; love of the world makes Babylonia. Let each person therefore ask what he loves, and he will discover of which city he is a citizen.

If he finds that he is a citizen of Babylonia, let him uproot desire and plant charity. If he finds that he is a citizen of Jerusalem, let him endure captivity and hope for freedom.

Some, instead of Haggai, give Ezekiel in the title, since he was in the Babylonian captivity. And where this text says “concerning the word of pilgrimage,” some say, “from the people of the transmigration.” Although the wording differs, the meaning does not disagree. But now let us examine the explanation of the title.

This Psalm applies to the prophet David and to the others who were returning. It is the song of Jeremiah and Haggai because it explains to us the subject over which Jeremiah and Haggai—or Zechariah or Ezekiel—rejoiced, all of whom belonged to the people of the transmigration. I call it a song composed “concerning the word of pilgrimage,” that is, concerning the revelation made to them by God for the sake of the captives’ pilgrimage, “when they began to set out,” that is, to return from Babylonia to Jerusalem.

Their rejoicing prefigured ours, which we possess when we begin spiritually to set out from this pilgrimage. By no longer directing our attention toward this Babylonia, we direct it toward loving God. For the conception of love is the beginning of setting out. He begins to go forth who begins to love. The feet of those who go forth are the affections of the heart. Although they are still bodily mingled with the children of Babylonia, they are distinguished from them by holy desire.

The subject is the returning people themselves, who speak here. In the first part they proclaim God worthy of praise. They pray that they may return from captivity, declare their misery, affirm that God is propitious, and tell of the blessed person whom he has chosen. They commend his house, dwelling, and blessings.

In the second part, where it says, “The hope of all the ends of the earth,” the subject is the power of the Savior, the strength and grace of preachers, the fear and transformation of converts, the gift of the Holy Spirit, the multiplication of the faithful, and their fruit.

In the third part, where it says, “You will bless the crown of the year,” the blessing and blessedness are commended which God, through his grace, will give in the future to his saints, to each according to his merits. For all these things, at the end—as at the beginning—it declares that a hymn must be sung to God.

The voice of the Church to Christ.

# PSALM LXIV

## 2

“To you, O God, praise is due in Zion.” O God, who are our Redeemer, praise is due to you—not in Babylonia, not in the confusion of sinners, but in Zion, that is, in the contemplation of virtues. “Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Eccles. 15), but “praise befits the upright” (Ps. 32).

When someone begins to be renewed and, in mind, to be raised toward heavenly things, then for the first time it is fitting for him to praise God. And because we must praise God in such a way that we dedicate ourselves to him—beginning this in the newness of life (Rom. 6), but completing it in eternal peace—it is rightly added:

“And to you the vow will be fulfilled in Jerusalem,” that is, in the vision of peace. Here, in this Zion, where “we see through a mirror and in a riddle, but not yet face to face” (1 Cor. 13), we begin to offer our vow to God; but we cannot fulfill it completely so long as within us remains what the Apostle says: “To will is present with me, but to accomplish the good I do not find” (Rom. 7).

For our good works will be perfected when the flesh has so consented to the spirit that it can no longer desire anything against it (Gal. 5). This is what we desire whenever we long for the perfection of righteousness. Therefore it is said, “To will is present with me.” But because this cannot at all be fulfilled in our present corruption, it is immediately added: “But to accomplish the good I do not find.” For the perfection of the good exists where there is no desire for evil.

Then, therefore, the vow will be fulfilled in that heavenly peace, when there will no longer be any evil, but the highest good. There we shall be complete—that is, whole—not only in soul, but also in the flesh itself, in the resurrection of the righteous. Peace will prevail and war will end; death will be destroyed and life will be everlasting. Then our desire will be fulfilled. Then what is now prophesied will come to pass: “And to you the vow will be fulfilled in Jerusalem.”

For this the Church sighs; hence she also humbly prays, saying:

## 3

“Hear my prayer, O God,” so that I may fulfill my vow in that heavenly Jerusalem. For I know that not only souls, but “all flesh,” will come to you. Here the prophet openly announces the resurrection. Hence the Apostle says: “All of us, whether good or evil, shall stand before the tribunal of Christ” (Rom. 14). And elsewhere: “‘As I live,’ says the Lord, ‘every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess’” (2 Cor. 5; Isa. 45).

He then adds the reason why it is necessary that he be heard, saying:

## 4

“The words of the wicked”—that is, of the devil and Eve, who persuaded Adam—“have prevailed over us,” because they plunged us into sin. “And yet you, O Lord, will be merciful toward our iniquities,” by forgiving them.

The first sin was committed through a word, and through words many evils are committed every day. Therefore the Apostle, describing the evil of the tongue, says: “The tongue is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison” (Jas. 3). And elsewhere it is said: “In the power of the tongue are life and death” (Prov. 29).

The evil of the tongue must therefore be guarded against, so that we do not say what causes harm, nor are corrupted by the words of the impious. And if we offend in this respect, let us correct ourselves. For we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; “and he is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 2). His propitiation, by which the chosen and saved human being is commended, is shown when it adds:

## 5

“Blessed is the one whom you have chosen,” that is, separated from the mass of the lost by converting him to faith, “and taken up into dignity.” He is blessed, therefore, because “he will dwell in your courts,” that is, in the heavenly Jerusalem, which he calls courts because of its spaciousness.

Christ assumed in himself one blessed person; and although he has assumed many, the statement is not made about many but about one. Thus he commends the unity that he assumed. For he rejected heresies and schisms. Those who remain joined to Christ and are his members form, in a certain way, one man, of whom the Apostle says: “Until we all come to the knowledge of the Son of God, to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Eph. 4).

And because this one consists of many, he again passes from the singular number to the plural and points out another cause of blessedness, saying: “We shall be filled with the good things of your house.”

What are the good things of God’s house? They are marvelous and ineffable. For “what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, God has prepared for those who love him” (Isa. 64; 1 Cor. 2). We must therefore hunger and thirst for them now, so that afterward we may deserve to be filled with such great blessings.

Behold, great are the good things of God’s house, and blessed is the one who is filled with them. Let us now hear what this house is.

## 6

“Your holy temple,” he says, “is marvelous in righteousness.” The holy Church of the elect is called a house because it is inhabited by God. It is called a temple because it is sanctified by God. Hence the Apostle says: “The temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Cor. 3 and 6).

This holy temple of God is called marvelous—not in columns, not in marble, not in gilded roofs, but in righteousness. What is righteousness? “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another.” And, “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do likewise to them” (Luke 6). In these two commandments are righteousness and justice.

When righteous men, who are the house and temple of God, observe these things, they appear marvelous in righteousness, in justice, in holiness, in conduct, in actions, and in virtues.

To obtain this righteousness, therefore, he humbly entreats, saying: “Hear us, O God our Savior.” When he said “God,” he immediately added “Savior,” so that he might more clearly indicate which God he meant. For Jesus Christ is properly called Savior, through whose incarnation we have been saved. He himself, as man, “the mediator of God and human beings,” intercedes for us (1 Tim. 2), and as God he hears us.

In God is our salvation and our hope—not merely of one corner, not only of Judea, nor of the East or West alone, but “the hope of all the ends of the earth.” For even those who dwell in the remotest parts of the earth hope in him. Nor do only those hope in him who live on solid land; so do those who dwell on the most distant islands. This is what follows:

“And in the distant sea.” How he has become hope even there is shown when it adds:

## 7

“Preparing the mountains by your strength.” The Apostle calls the preachers mountains because, by the height of their life, they transcend all earthly things. Almighty God prepared them and prepares them by calling, justifying, and forming them through grace, teaching, and conduct.

And rightly can you prepare them, because you are girded with power. Our Lord and Redeemer is called “girded with power” according to his humanity. Hence the Psalmist says to him elsewhere: “Gird yourself with your sword upon your thigh, most powerful one” (Ps. 44). And again: “The Lord is clothed with strength and has girded himself” (Ps. 92).

But insofar as he is the Word with the Father, he is neither clothed with strength nor girded with power. Rather, he himself is strength, power, and wisdom (1 Cor. 1). Since the incarnate Lord is surrounded and fortified on every side by his divinity, he is rightly said to be girded with power. He is girded as one prepared for battle against the devil and the world. Hence he immediately adds:

## 8

“You disturb the depths of the sea, the sound of its waves.” The bottom of the sea (as Augustine says) is the heart of the impious. For just as all things are moved more violently from the bottom, and the bottom contains everything, so whatever has proceeded through the tongue and hands for the persecution of the Church has proceeded from the depths. If the root of iniquity had not been in the heart, none of those things would have proceeded against Christ.

He disturbed the bottom, perhaps in order to drain the bottom; for in certain evil people he drained the sea from its depths and made the sea into a desert. Another Psalm says: “He turned the sea into dry land” (Ps. 65). All the impious, like the pagans who believed, were the sea; they became land: **[Note: Augustine has the erroneous reading *falsis* (“false”).]** at first barren with salty fruits, afterward fertile with the fruit of righteousness.

He disturbs the sound of the waves when he scatters the threats of the proud. Or he disturbs the sound of the waves when God stirs up the tumult of thoughts in the hearts of the impious. Thoughts rise in the heart when they recall their wickednesses to mind. The sea is disturbed because the bitterness of repentance trembles; and what is at the bottom is brought to the surface when the evil that lay in the heart is revealed by the mouth’s confession.

Who does this in the sinner’s heart except the loving power of the Redeemer? Concerning this it further says:

## 9

“The nations will be troubled, and those who dwell at the ends of the earth will fear because of your signs.” For this reason the Lord and his disciples performed so many signs and wonders (Mark 16): so that when the nations who did not possess faith saw them, they might be troubled on account of their sins, fear God, and be saved by believing.

And because the way of God begins with fear (Prov. 1 and 9) but is completed in charity, it is rightly added:

“You will delight the departures of morning and evening.”

Morning (as Augustine says) signifies prosperity, evening tribulation, because morning is joyful, as though the sadness of night had passed. Darkness is sorrowful when evening comes. God therefore delights—that is, causes his servants to delight—in the departures of morning and evening, so that they may go forth from the prosperity and adversity of this age.

They are not lifted up by prosperity, nor broken by adversity. They pass through all things with a strong mind, joyful and eager as they press toward the end. Such was Paul when he said: “I desire to depart and be with Christ” (Phil. 1).

The order of the words should be noted: first is placed the disturbance of fear, then the delight of love. Fear excludes vices; charity despises earthly things. He therefore says magnificently, “You will delight the departures.” For if departure does not delight you, you do not labor to go forth. “Delight in the Lord,” and the world will become distasteful to you.

The following verse appears to refer back to what was stated above, “Preparing the mountains by your strength”:

## 10

“You visited the earth and intoxicated it; you multiplied it to enrich it. You sent your clouds so that they might rain the preaching of truth.”

The earth was intoxicated, that is, earthly hearts were filled with the heavenly rain of wisdom, so that they might produce the fruit of life in abundance. Almighty God visits the earth whenever, through his grace, he breathes upon a sinner. He intoxicates it when it is so filled with his love that its life and conduct are changed for the better.

For the senses of drinkers are commonly changed through drunkenness. Hence it is said elsewhere of the elect: “They will be intoxicated with the abundance of your house” (Ps. 35), because they have been so filled with the love of almighty God that, with their minds changed, they seem to themselves to be strangers to themselves.

A kind of intoxication appears in this: to despise riches and love poverty, to hold oneself in contempt, to rejoice in tribulations, to love death more than life, and to yearn with all one’s desires for things that are not seen. In this way the intoxicated earth cannot be barren.

It is enriched by God in many ways through spiritual gifts. Hence Paul says: “To one is given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, to another kinds of tongues, to another the grace of healings.” After listing several others, he says: “All these things one and the same Spirit accomplishes, distributing to each as he wills” (1 Cor. 12).

And because God enriches his earth in this way, it is rightly said: “You multiplied it to enrich it.”

He explains this Spirit of manifold grace when he adds: “The river of God is filled with waters.” What should be understood by the river of God, the Lord himself indicates when he says: “Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7). The Evangelist says that “he spoke this of the Spirit whom those who believed in him were to receive” (ibid.).

And just as many waters converge in one river, so in one Spirit there exist many divisions of grace. The Holy Spirit is therefore called a river because he comes with force and cleanses from the filth of sins the mind into which he flows. He is called water because he gives the mind drink and cools it from the heat of carnal desires.

But since we have heard about drink, let us now hear what he adds concerning the soul’s food: “You prepared their food, for such is its preparation.” What food? Certainly that of which he himself says: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever” (John 6).

How did he prepare this food for us? Because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1). It is rightly said, “You prepared,” because he acted with great zeal and great labor, so that he might refresh the minds of the elect with himself.

Hence it appropriately says: “For such,” that is, through you, “is its preparation.” For neither an Apostle, nor a prophet, nor an angel could have prepared so great a food, but only “the mediator of God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. 2).

Holy Scripture is also food prepared for us by the Lord, by which we are refreshed daily so that we do not fail in the desert of this pilgrimage. Hence it is written: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. 4).

Behold, the food has been prepared; behold, the river has been prepared. But fragile human beings cannot receive these things unless heavenly goodness deigns to help them. Therefore he prays, saying:

## 11

“Make its streams drunk; multiply its offspring.” He calls the streams of the river the Apostles and teachers, through whom the Holy Spirit flows into the hearts of hearers. Hence it is written: “It is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit who speaks in you” (Matt. 10).

When the Apostles received this Spirit, sent from the Father out of heaven, they were so filled with him that, while speaking of God’s mighty works in various languages, some thought them drunk (Acts 2). And in truth they were drunk—but spiritually, not carnally.

But from that with which God intoxicates preachers, he multiplies the faithful. “Multiply,” he says, “its offspring.” Those who are regenerated from water and the Holy Spirit are called offspring. He does not say “their offspring,” but “its,” because, as a certain intoxicated stream says: “Neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the increase” (1 Cor. 3).

And because within the holy Church not only overflowing wisdom but also a limited and small teaching bears fruit for God, it is rightly added: “In its droplets the budding thing will rejoice.”

For the little ones and those who are still weak (as Augustine says), certain things concerning the sacraments are distilled drop by drop, because they cannot grasp the fullness of truth. Hear how Paul drips his teaching to those with less capacity: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal, as little ones in Christ” (ibid.).

The budding thing rejoices in droplets, therefore, when one who has recently been encouraged in the faith cannot yet grasp great things, but nevertheless gratefully receives the few things he hears and strives to produce, as far as he is able, the fruits of good works and virtues.

In the present life you will give these benefits that have been mentioned. What will you give in the future? He continues and says:

## 12

“You will bless the crown of the year of your goodness.” That is, you will reward your saints, who will stand around you like a crown of palm and victory and will be a sign of victory for you.

Or otherwise: when you hear “crown,” the glory of victory is signified. Conquer the devil, and you will have a crown. The year, because it is a complete period, signifies the span of eternal life. The crown of the year, therefore, is perfect glory pertaining to eternal life, which God will give to his saints after the struggles of this life—not on the basis of their merits, but from his blessing and grace.

Hence he will also say: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25). He therefore added “of your goodness,” so that God’s grace might be commended and no one might glory in his own merits.

He carries out in parts this blessing of the crown that he mentioned earlier, when he adds: “And your fields will be filled with abundance.”

## 13

“The beautiful places of the desert will grow fat, and the hills will gird themselves with rejoicing. The rams of the sheep are clothed, and the valleys will abound with grain” (v. 14).

What are the fields except the righteous who bear fruit? What did he wish to designate by the desert except barren sinners? Paul suggests that certain righteous people are like fields when he says: “You are God’s cultivated field” (1 Cor. 3).

Consider how great are the depths of divine mercy. For the sake of the fields he does not abandon the desert; for the sake of the righteous he does not reject sinners. He will fill the former with abundance, that is, with eternal refreshment, as has already been stated: “They will be intoxicated with the abundance of your house.” He will make the latter grow fat with the sweetness of his grace, so that “where sin abounded, grace might abound all the more” (Rom. 5).

It should be noted that he does not say, “The desert will grow fat,” but “the beautiful places of the desert,” because God will not save the entire mass of sinners, but only those who come out from the filth of vices and become beautiful through faith, moral uprightness, and the splendor of virtues.

Or by “the beautiful places of the desert” the Church of the Gentiles may be represented. She will then grow fat, when she possesses all things perfectly. For God will be “all in all” (Eph. 1), and the gifts of the Holy Spirit will not be divided.

The hills may be understood as the holy martyrs, who surpass the fields—that is, the righteous—in the virtue of suffering. These are those who came out of the great tribulation (Rev. 7). Therefore they will rightly be girded, that is, surrounded on every side, both in soul and in body, with rejoicing.

Everlasting joy will be for them like a kind of belt, surrounding them on every side, holding them together on every side, and clinging to them inseparably. Hence the Lord says to some: “Again I will see you, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you” (John 16).

They will also be girded with rejoicing when they have been surrounded and filled by divinity itself. Then the Lord will clothe the rams of the sheep—that is, the leaders of souls—with the robe of joy and the garment of immortality. Or they will be clothed with rejoicing because, together with their flock, they will rejoice in eternal peace.

Rejoicing will be like a garment for them when no part of distress remains, either in soul or in body. For the Lord will wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints; “and death will be no more, nor mourning, nor crying, nor pain, for the former things have passed away” (Rev. 21).

“And the valleys will abound with grain,” because obedient and humble souls will be refreshed with heavenly nourishment. The Lord himself will be their grain. For he is the true food of souls (John 12 and 6).

And there all will cry out—not so much with the voice as with the mind, not so much with the tumult of words as with the affection of the heart—in ineffable joy. Their cry will be nothing other than the praise of God. Therefore it adds: “For they will sing a hymn.”

Hence it is said elsewhere: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; forever and ever they will praise you” (Ps. 83). Let us therefore begin here to sing a hymn to our Lord, so that we may deserve to praise him perfectly in the future. For whoever does not begin now will not praise him afterward either.

# TITLE OF PSALM LXV

## 1

The following Psalm is entitled in this manner: “For the end, a Song of the Psalm of the Resurrection.”

In this Psalm a song is proposed to us, so that we may rejoice over our resurrection, which God will bring about for all who strive toward the end—that is, toward Christ (Rom. 8; Phil. 3). This resurrection is the subject of the Psalm.

In the first part he urges all nations to praise, proclaim, glorify, and worship the terrible God with heart, voice, and deed.

In the second part, which begins, “Come and see,” he commends the works of God as terrible; there he signifies the calling of the Gentiles and the rejection of the Jews.

In the third part, which begins, “Bless God, nations,” he urges the nations to bless their God for the many and great benefits bestowed upon them: both because he frees their souls from death and causes them to persevere in goodness, and because, after many temptations and trials, he leads them into eternal refreshment, where they may always rejoice, and where they may perfectly fulfill to their God the vows that they began here.

In the fourth part, where it says, “Come, hear,” he presents himself as an example, proclaiming the good things that the Lord did for his soul. And because he cried out to him with mouth and heart without iniquity, God therefore heard him. In this he exhorts us to do likewise, so that we may deserve to be heard by him and obtain his mercy.

This is the purpose and benefit of this Psalm. Therefore it is now spoken in the voice of the primitive Church, or of any perfected person:

# PSALM LXV

## 2

“Shout for joy to God, all the earth.” That is, nations converted from the whole earth, shout for joy to God with the mind’s exultation. See how the universality of the Church spread throughout the whole world is commended when it says, “all the earth.”

But what does “shout for joy” mean (as Augustine says)? Break forth in the voice of joy if you cannot do so in words. For it is not a word that is shouted for joy, but only the sound of rejoicing is produced, like the sound of a heart in labor and giving birth. “Shout for joy,” he says—that is, conceive in your voice a joy that cannot be expressed in words.

“Sing a psalm to his name; give glory to his praise.” To sing a psalm is also to take up an instrument, which is called the psaltery, and to make the voice correspond with the striking and work of the hands.

If, then, you shout for joy so that God may hear, sing a psalm also so that people may see and hear—but not to your own name. For beware of doing your righteousness before people in order to be seen by them (Matt. 6).

What does “sing a psalm” mean? The Gospel explains this to us when it says: “Let your light shine before people” (Matt. 5). What is added here, “Give glory to his praise,” is made clearer there when it continues: “So that, seeing your good works, they may glorify your Father who is in heaven” (ibid.).

He gives glory to God’s praise whose good life agrees with right proclamation. He sings to the Lord’s name when, in the good work that he performs, he seeks not his own praise but the Lord’s.

Sing, therefore, to his name, not to your own. You sing; let him be praised. You live well; let him be glorified. He directs our entire intention toward the praise of God. He left us nothing by which we might be praised. God does not want us to glory in ourselves, lest our glory be empty; rather, he wants us to glory in him, so that our glory may be sound. Hence it is also added:

### 3

Say to God: “How awesome are your works, O Lord!” Why “awesome”? Because a partial blindness has occurred in Israel, so that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter (Rom. 11). You should therefore be even more afraid, because you see the natural branches being cut off. For the Jews, who came through the Patriarchs, were born from Abraham’s flesh. And what does the Apostle say? “But you will say: ‘Branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in.’ Good. They were broken off because of unbelief; but you stand by faith. Do not be high-minded, but fear. For if God did not spare the natural branches, neither will he spare you” (ibid.).

Therefore, when you observe the broken branches and yourself grafted in, do not exalt yourself over the broken branches, but rather say: “Tell God: How awesome are your works, O Lord!” Fear him in his awesome works, and do not be arrogant because he has called you on high, lest he not spare you, he who cut off the natural branches. Their cutting off is shown when it is added:

“In the multitude of your power”—that is, in your many powers and miracles—“your enemies will lie to you,” that is, the Jews, who are especially to be called his enemies. And they were all the more deserving of rejection because, amid so many powers and miracles, when they ought to have believed, they remained unbelieving.

They lied by giving false testimony about Christ, asserting that his body had been stolen from the tomb (Matt. 28), and denying the resurrection. It is especially noteworthy that when he said, “They will lie,” he immediately added, “to you”—that is, for your benefit. For the Jews’ lie served to commend your great power. Why do our enemies usually lie? So that they may diminish the power of the one about whom they lie. “To you,” he says, “the opposite has happened.” For your power would have appeared less if they had not lied about you. They lied, and Christ was killed; he rose from the dead, and was proclaimed everywhere (Mark 15 and 16). His power grew on earth, and what follows was fulfilled:

### 4

“Let all the earth adore you, O God, and sing psalms to you; let it sing a psalm to your name.” That is: let every kind of person dwelling on earth worship you, who are the true God, by adoring you. Adoration properly belongs to divine worship; faith is also commended in it. But because that same faith is dead without works (Jas. 2), it is rightly added: “And let it sing psalms to you”—that is, let it do good works for your honor. “Let it sing a psalm”—that is, let it proclaim a good work; and let it do this not for itself but for your name, that is, for the praise and glory of your name.

We worship God usefully, then, when we add to the worship of faith a good work in which God is honored, and when by word and example we draw along with ourselves as many others as we can into the service of God. He appears to do this here when he immediately adds:

### 5

“Come and see the works of God.” O Gentiles (Augustine), O farthest nations, abandon the lying Jews. Come, confessing; draw near with the steps of the mind and with the affections of love. Come to the Lord, hasten to faith, run to the Church. “See”—that is, believe and understand—the works performed by the Lord, who is “awesome in his counsels over the children of men.”

The children of men plotted a plan to crucify Christ (John 11). The crucified one blinded those who crucified him. You plotted plans for destruction; he, for blinding and saving—for blinding the proud and saving the humble. He blinded the proud themselves for this purpose: so that, having been blinded, they might be humbled; having been humbled, they might confess; and having confessed, they might be enlightened.

He is therefore awesome in his counsels over the children of men. And truly awesome. For behold, a partial blindness has occurred in Israel. Behold, the Jews, from whom Christ was born, are outside. Behold, the Gentiles, who were opposed to the Jews, are inside, in Christ. Therefore, what did he do through the terror of his counsel? He continues and says:

### 6

“He changed the sea into dry land.” The sea was the world: bitter with salt, turbulent with storm, raging with the waves of persecutions. It was a sea; it has been changed into dry land. Now the world, which had been full of salt water, thirsts for fresh water. Hence he says elsewhere: “My soul is like land without water for you” (Ps. 142).

Those same people who were changed into dry land, although previously bitter, “will pass through the river on foot.” The river is (Augustine) the whole mortality of the age. For, like a river, one thing comes and passes away, and another, destined to pass away, succeeds it. What is born and flows on earth? [Note: Col. 0903D. We have restored “flows” (*manat*) from Augustine in place of “remains” (*manet*).] Everyone who has been born must yield to the one who is being born.

Thus the entire order of passing things is like a river. If a desirous soul throws itself into this river, it perishes. How, then, will it pass through the pleasures of things destined to perish? Let it believe in Christ, and under his guidance it will pass through the river on foot.

What does it mean to pass on foot? To pass easily. It does not seek a horse in order to cross. It is not lifted up by pride in order to cross the river. The humble person crosses, and crosses more quickly. [Note: Col. 0904D. Augustine has “more safely.”]

The Lord also did this literally among the ancient people; but, as the Apostle says, “all these things happened to them in figure” (1 Cor. 10). It should be noted that he does not say, “They will cross,” but “They will pass through.” To pass through the river on foot means, by living humbly and simply in this mortality, to hasten toward heavenly things. To pass through means to bring the course of right living to its end by dying well.

Paul was also passing through when he said: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith. From now on the crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will award me on that day” (2 Tim. 4).

Hence what follows is appropriately added: “There he will rejoice in him.” Here we sit and weep beside the rivers of Babylon (Ps. 136), and our tears are bread, while it is said to us every day: “Where is your God?” (Ps. 41). But there, once the river has been crossed, mortality ended, and incorruption received, “there he will rejoice in him”—that is, in our God (1 Cor. 15). Then our joy will be true and perfect, when we are like him and see him as he is (1 John 3).

### 7

“He rules over all”—and this in his own power, that is, by an inherent power, forever. This is truly omnipotence and belongs to God alone. For those who rule in this world rule neither by their own power but by God’s, nor forever but temporarily.

If our power were eternal, we would not have fallen into sin, nor would we have deserved punitive death. We were therefore weakened through ourselves, but made strong through him who rules in his own power forever. Through him we shall share in his power.

That this was accomplished not by our merits but by his mercy is shown when it is added: “His eyes look upon the nations.” The fact that the Gentiles believed was accomplished by the regard of divine mercy, which, when the Gentiles are chosen, rejects the Jews.

Hence he also adds: “Let those who provoke him not be exalted in themselves.” The Jews’ provocation was their unbelief; it was pride, anger, and envy as well; it was wicked behavior and words of reproach and blasphemy against Christ and the Church. Since they were lifted up in themselves, they deserved not to be exalted but to be led by the Lord.

He seems to have cursed them when he said, “Let them not be exalted.” Rather (Augustine), let them be exalted—but not in themselves. Let them be humbled in themselves and exalted in God. “For whoever humbles himself will be exalted, and whoever exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke 18).

Having recognized these works and received such great benefits, he urges us to bless God and says:

### 8

“Bless our God, O nations.” Now (the same source) the seed of Abraham has come, in whom all the nations will be blessed (Gen. 22). Bless him, therefore, in whom you will be blessed. For whoever blesses him will himself also be blessed.

We are not commanded to bless God because our blessing contributes anything to God, who has no need of our goods (Ps. 15); rather, we are commanded to bless him so that, through the affection of blessing, we may deserve the grace of the one whom we bless, and so that the blessing itself may be turned back upon us.

It also belongs to our religion and the practice of faith to bless, proclaim, and praise our God with all our heart and all our affection. Therefore he still adds: “And make the voice of his praise heard.” Do not praise him only among yourselves; also make the voice of his praise heard by others and proclaim it. Bless God within yourselves in such a way that you announce him to others by preaching.

### 9

“For he is the one who set my soul toward life.” God set our souls toward life because, having redeemed them from death through faith, he gave them life. Death is in us; life is in God. Thus the Apostle says to certain believers: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5).

But what remains to be done except that we persevere to the end (Matt. 24)? He himself also granted this, concerning which he says next: “Who did not let my feet be moved.” The one who set my soul toward life himself governs my feet, so that they may not totter and so that good affections may not be moved away from the good they have begun.

Why do you say, “He did not let your feet be moved”? For, he says, “we have suffered many things.”

### 10

“For you tested us, O God”—that is, you showed us to be tested and approved, both to ourselves and to others. “You tested us by fire, as silver is tested.” Either by material fire, as in the case of Lawrence; or by fire—that is, by whatever tribulation—you did not burn us like hay, but purified us like silver.

By applying fire to us (Augustine), you did not turn us into ashes, but removed our impurities. [Note: Col. 0905D. Augustine has “washed them away.”] The Lord tests his saints and examines them by the fire of tribulations, so that they may be cleansed of every earthly impurity and every pleasure of the flesh. The delights of the flesh, moreover, diminish greatly in adversity.

He explains these examinations in detail when he adds:

### 11

“You brought us into a snare; you placed tribulations on our back; you set men over our heads” (v. 12).

By “snare” he means bonds, prisons, or any temptations. It is not to be understood as though God himself brings anyone into a snare—for he is not a tempter of evil (Jas. 1)—but he is said to bring someone in when he permits that person to be brought in. Hence in the prayer we say: “Do not lead us into temptation” (Matt. 6)—that is, do not permit us to be led into it.

Whether tribulations are placed upon the backs of the saints, ask Paul. He will not conceal that he received from the Jews five times forty lashes less one (2 Cor. 11).

Men had been set over their heads who ruled them, to such an extent that they could issue capital sentences. All these things (Augustine) the Church suffered through various and differing persecutions. Even now it suffers the same things individually. No one in this life can say that he is free from these temptations.

Therefore men are also set over our heads. We tolerate those whom we do not want. At times we suffer those above us whom we know to be worse. For we had been wrongly erect in our pride. Wrongly erect, we were bent down, so that, once bent down, we might be rightly raised up.

It is good for us to consider that we are sinners and thus endure those set over our heads, so that we may confess to God that we suffer deservedly. For what do you suffer undeservedly that has been done by the one who is just?

“You placed tribulations on our back; you set men over our heads.”

God seems to rage when he does these things. Do not be afraid: he is a father. He never rages in such a way as to destroy. When you live badly and he spares you, he is more angry. These tribulations are altogether the scourges of one who corrects, lest they become the sentence of one who punishes. Hence it is also added:

### 12

“We passed through fire and water, and you led us out into refreshment.”

Fire and water are both dangerous in this life. Certainly water appears to extinguish fire, and fire appears to dry up water. So these very temptations abound in this life. [Note: Col. 0905. More correctly in Augustine: “So these very temptations,” etc.] Fire burns; water corrupts. Both are to be feared: the burning of tribulation and the water of corruption.

When circumstances are narrow and there is some misfortune—what is called unhappiness in this world—it is like fire. When circumstances are prosperous and worldly abundance flows around us, it is like water. Take care that the fire does not consume you and that the water does not corrupt you.

Stand firm against the fire; you must be cooked. Like a vessel made [or: fashioned] of clay, you are put into the furnace so that what has been formed may be strengthened. Once the vessel has been strengthened by fire, it does not fear water. If the vessel has not been solidified by fire, it will be dissolved by water like clay.

First, therefore, comes the fire. Then, once fear has been removed, we must fear lest prosperity corrupt us. When the fire has not made you crack and you are not submerged in the water but have swum through it by discipline, passing into rest, and when you have passed through fire and water, you will be led out into everlasting refreshment.

“You led us out,” he says—that is, “you will lead us out”: he has put the past for the future. For the spirit of prophecy knows future things as though they were past.

Then, once the tribulations have passed, what will happen? It follows:

### 13

“I will enter your house”—not one made by hand, that is, the heavenly house—“with burnt offerings,” that is, with every corruptible thing consumed.

Then the burnt offering will be made perfect, when this corruptible thing has put on incorruption and this mortal thing has put on immortality (1 Cor. 15). Then the saying written in Scripture will be fulfilled: “Death has been swallowed up in victory” (Hos. 13). Victory is like a divine fire when it swallows up our death.

May your fire consume all that is mine. Let nothing remain for me; let everything be yours. Such a burnt offering the body of Christ—that is (Augustine), the Church, which is speaking here—will offer.

A burnt offering is called wholly burned when it burns entirely and is wholly consumed by divine fire. Nothing mortal will remain in the flesh, nor anything blameworthy in the spirit. In that house:

### 14

“I will pay you my vows, which my lips have distinguished.” That is, they have chosen me above all others—myself, that is, the vow that is preferred to everything.

There is also distinction in vows: that you accuse yourself and praise him; that you understand yourself to be a creature and him the Creator; yourself darkness and him the one who gives light. Whatever we distinguish here with our lips—in promise, ordinance, or vow—we will pay in full to the Lord our God when we enter that house.

Alternatively, to distinguish vows with the lips means to discern by mind and reason those things that are offered to God. Hence it is written: “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned” (Gen. 4). Whoever offers a good work to God offers rightly but does not divide rightly if he seeks from it worldly glory or some profit apart from God.

The holy Church therefore distinguishes its vows with inward lips, because the vows it offers to God it separates from all human praise and earthly advantage.

Nor did I vow vows only in prosperity; I also maintained confession in adversity. Hence he adds: “And my mouth spoke in my tribulation.” For the holy martyrs confessed Christ in their torments: “We are servants of Christ; we hold the faith of Christ; we desire to die for Christ.”

Hence Paul says: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10). Faith must therefore be held in the heart; truth must be proclaimed with the mouth.

Then he shows how he enters the house of God with burnt offerings, and he explains the burnt offerings themselves, saying:

### 15

“I will offer you marrow-filled burnt offerings, with the incense of rams.”

What does “marrow-filled” mean? Fat, sweet, full of love and tenderness. I will offer myself to you as a fat sacrifice, with the incense of rams—that is, with every height and hardness of pride burned up and consumed. In my marrow there will be what I love you with. For nothing is more inward than our marrow. Bones are inward in relation to flesh; marrow is inward even in relation to the bones.

Whoever worships God only on the surface wishes rather to please human beings. But if he feels something different within, he does not offer marrow-filled burnt offerings. The one whose marrow he inspects receives the whole person.

The whole body of Christ speaks this. It has something to offer to God, namely, the incense of rams. The rams are the leaders of the Church. The incense is the prayer of the saints. Above all, the rams pray for the flocks. Incense is rightly understood as prayer, because in it the hearts of the elect are kindled by divine fire. And just as the smoke of incense gives off a pleasant fragrance to human beings, so the devotion of prayer burns sweetly before God.

“I will offer you oxen with goats.” We find oxen threshing, and they too are offered to God. The Apostle said that what is written must be understood of those who proclaim the Gospel: “You shall not muzzle the ox when it is treading out the grain” (1 Cor. 9; Deut. 23). Those, then, are great rams and great oxen.

What about those who are perhaps conscious of certain sins? Will they remain outside and have no part in the burnt offering? Therefore, so that they themselves would not be afraid, he added “goats.” Goats are not saved by themselves; they are accepted when joined to the oxen. They “made friends for themselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that they too might receive them into eternal dwellings” (Luke 16). Such goats, therefore, will not be on the left (Matt. 25), because they redeemed their sins by almsgiving (Dan. 4).

Oxen can therefore signify the virtues of the elect, by which the hardness of the mind is plowed so that it may be made fit to bear spiritual fruits. They offer oxen to God who humbly attribute the virtues they possess to his grace. To offer goats to God is to confess humbly to the Lord the impure and lustful movements of the soul. We offer goats to God when we sacrifice every form of lust and wantonness within ourselves.

Again he invites the Gentiles to understand other benefits, saying:

### 16

“Come, with the steps of the mind; hear, with the ears of the heart, and I will recount”—to all who fear God.

“If you do not fear God, I will not recount them.” There is no one to whom they can be recounted where the fear of God is absent. The fear of God will open the ears, so that there may be an entrance for what I am about to recount.

I will tell how many benefits he bestowed upon my soul—beyond those already mentioned—if you also wish them for your own. For he granted me to cry out to him and, by crying out, to rejoice in my heart, and so forth. This is what he says:

### 17

“To him I cried out with my mouth, and I exulted beneath my tongue.”

He says that this very thing was done to his soul: that it cried out to God with its mouth. Formerly the Church from among the Gentiles worshiped stones and cried out to mute images. Now the image of God has turned toward its Creator. The one who used to say to a stone, “You are my father,” now says to God: “Our Father, who are in heaven” (Matt. 6).

“With my mouth,” he says, “I cried out,” not with another’s mouth. When they cried out to stones, they cried out with another’s mouth. When I cried out to God, because he himself inspired it, I cried out to him with my own mouth.

To exult beneath the tongue means to conceive joy in the heart from the cry of the voice. This is the true cry to God: the affection of the heart. I proclaimed him publicly; I confessed him in secret. It is not enough to exalt God with the tongue, but also beneath the tongue, so that what you speak with certainty you may silently think.

The person who exults beneath the tongue cries out joyfully when his conscience does not reproach him. But the prayer of one whose conscience is sinful is also useless (John 9). This is clearly declared when he adds:

### 18

“If I have seen iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear.”

Iniquity is said to be seen in the heart when it pleases the eyes of the mind, when it delights, when reason itself approves and loves it. For we are accustomed to look willingly upon the things we love.

But because, as it is written, “to the impure and unbelieving nothing is pure” (Titus 1), whatever proceeds from an impure heart—whether prayer, preaching, or action—is regarded by God as wholly impure and fruitless.

God therefore will not hear the prayer of one whose mind he sees to be corrupted by iniquity. Do not, then (Augustine), look upon it in your heart—that is, do not love it within yourself. Whatever it promises cheerfully in order to entice you into sin, whatever it threatens sorrowfully in order to drive you into wrongdoing, deserves to be despised and trampled underfoot, not contemplated and accepted.

### 19

“Therefore God heard me and attended to the voice of my supplication.”

What does “therefore” mean? Because I did not look upon iniquity in my heart. Hence the Apostle says (1 John 3): “If our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence, because whatever we ask, we will receive.” This is not from our merits but from his grace. Therefore he adds:

### 20

“Blessed be God, who has not removed my prayer from me, nor his mercy from me.”

Thus the one who speaks has reached the resurrection, where we too now exist in hope, and this is our voice. Therefore, as long as we are here, we pray to God that he not remove our prayer from us or his mercy from us—that is, that we may pray perseveringly and that he may himself show mercy perseveringly.

Many, however, grow weak in prayer. Although they are fervent at the beginning of their conversion, afterward they become cold and negligently secure. The mind grows sluggish; prayer is interrupted. You sleep, while the enemy keeps watch; temptations increase.

Therefore the Lord commanded that we must always pray and never grow weary (Luke 18). Let us not fail in prayer, confident in the promise, because if he delays, he does not withdraw. With devout affection let us say: “Blessed be God, who has not removed my prayer from me, nor his mercy from me.”

When you see (Augustine) that your prayer has not been removed from you, be confident that his mercy has not been removed from you either.

## TITLE OF PSALM 66

### 1

The title of the following psalm is: “For the end; a psalm of a song of David.”

This psalm suits the prophet David, or any faithful person. It is called a psalm because it urges us to confession. It is called a song because it sets before us the greatest exultation over the illumination of both peoples, namely the Jews and the Gentiles, which was to come through Christ.

It is a psalm, I say, “set among hymns”—that is, among the praises of God—or “among hymns,” that is, among those compositions that are called hymns in an eminent sense. The prophet understood that God was to be praised for the illumination he was going to give the world, for which we must all praise him with the greatest zeal.

This is what the psalm intends to urge: it directs us toward the end, that is, toward Christ. Its subject is Christ the illuminator. In the first part he prays for illumination. In the second part, which begins, “Let the peoples confess to you, O God,” he urges the twofold confession, namely, of sin and of praise. He gives as its cause God the just judge: “You judge the peoples with equity.”

In the third part, where he repeats the same verse, he urges the same confession but for another reason: because the earth, previously barren, has now, at the coming of the Son, given its fruit. And because he saw that all good things come from the mercy of God, before speaking of illumination he prays for mercy, saying:

## PSALM 66

### 2

“May God have mercy on us”—by forgiving sins—“and bless us,” that is, multiply us both in number and in virtue. Let this happen in the following order: “May he make his face shine upon us.”

That is, let him cause his Son, his Wisdom, who is his face and image, to shine in the higher part of us, in our mind. For the Father is represented through the Son, as he himself says: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14).

Then he adds what he had placed first: “And may he have mercy on us.” Both things are necessary for us, and we read of both: “His mercy will go before me” (Ps. 58), and “His mercy will follow me” (Ps. 12).

The first mercy concerns the remission of sins, the abundance of virtues, and the illumination of wisdom. The second mercy concerns the good things God bestows, so that he may deign now to preserve us in them.

The psalms urge both things: that God bless us and that we bless God. When God blesses us, we grow; and when we bless God, we grow. Both benefit us. The Lord’s blessing comes first in us, and what follows is that we also bless the Lord.

The former is rain; the latter is fruit. “May he make his face shine upon us,” he says. His light, impressed upon us, has been darkened and almost extinguished in us by sin. Therefore let him himself remove sin and illuminate us. Let him send the ray of his wisdom. Let him drive away our darkness, so that his image may shine in us.

Why does he turn to familiar speech with God and say:

### 3

“So that we may know your way on earth.”

On what earth? Among all the nations. What way? “Your salvation”—that is, your Son, by whom we may be saved. For he himself says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14).

Therefore have mercy for this purpose; illuminate for this purpose, so that we may know the way by which we may be able to reach you.

Observe how Christ became the way for us. Let the Evangelist speak: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1).
