In the fact that God became man, confidence was given to us that man could become God. And because he made our flesh immortal, he gave us certainty that what is mortal can reach immortality.

This is the way God showed us on earth, by which we may walk toward heavenly things. And this is our faith.

### 4

“Let the peoples confess to you, O God; let all the peoples confess to you.”

Because they have known your way, let them confess their sins. Let them also confess your praise. And not one people only, but all peoples, because all are invited to grace.

First let them accuse themselves; first let them condemn themselves, so that afterward they may worthily praise you. Why are you afraid to confess, O human being, when by not confessing you cannot remain hidden? You will be condemned in silence, though by confessing you could be freed.

God requires confession for this purpose: to free the humble. And because this confession does not lead to punishment but to joy, it follows:

### 5

“Let the nations rejoice and exult.”

Joy refers to the soul; exultation to the body. Therefore, when they are saved in body and soul, let the nations rejoice and exult.

And he says why: “Because you judge the peoples with equity,” rendering to each according to his merits.

And because he would not be praised greatly for this—since unless he also visited human beings mercifully in this life, all would be condemned—he therefore added: “And you direct the nations on earth,” with the implied sense, “so that they may walk by living rightly.”

The nations were crooked. The hand of God came; it was extended mercifully. He directed through justice those whom he found crooked through guilt. The nations have been directed: they walk in faith, rejoicing in their God and doing pious works.

He therefore repeats the same verse in the exhortation he has already introduced, but adds another reason:

### 6

“Let the peoples confess to you, O God; let all the peoples confess to you.”

Hear the reason: “The earth has given its fruit.”

The earth, which had previously been cursed and produced thorns and thistles—in the curse God pronounced to Adam, “Cursed is the earth in your work” (Gen. 3)—has become (Augustine) fruitful by giving its fruit, that is, its fitting works.

The whole earth was full of thorns. The hand of the one who uproots them came; his majestic and merciful calling came. The earth began to confess. Now the earth gives its fruit. For God did what follows:

### 7

“May God bless us, our God; may God bless us, and may all the ends of the earth fear him.”

May he bless us again and repeatedly (the same source). For blessing is usually and properly understood above all in multiplication, as is clear in Genesis.

When God made the light and separated it from darkness, and made the firmament and distinguished the sea from the dry land, nowhere there is it said, “God blessed.” But when he came to those things that were going to possess the seed of fertility, he blessed them, saying: “Increase and multiply, and fill the waters of the sea; and let the birds multiply upon the earth.” Likewise, blessing the human being, he said: “Increase and multiply, and fill the face of the earth” (Gen. 1).

It is therefore clear that multiplication is understood in blessing.

It should also be noted that when God was mentioned for the third time, he did not say, “Let them fear them,” but “let them fear him.” In this the Trinity is clearly declared: three in persons and believed to be one in substance.

“And let them fear him,” he says, “all the ends of the earth.” May God bless us abundantly in the name of Christ, so that he may fill the whole face of the earth with his sons, adopted into his kingdom as co-heirs with his only-begotten Son (Gal. 4).

He rightly says, “And let them fear him,” because there is no true security in this world. “Blessed is the person who is always fearful” (Prov. 28). No one knows the day or the hour when he will pass away (Matt. 25). No one knows whether he is worthy of hatred or love (Eccles. 9). Let us therefore fear God. Let us fear his judgment, so that afterward we may be able to be secure.

## TITLE OF PSALM 67

### 1

The title of the following psalm is: “For the end; a psalm of a song of David.”

This psalm, designated as a song and as one of the greatest exultations, is attributed to the prophet David, who here speaks while looking toward the end—that is, toward Christ—or considering what was to come at the end of time.

This psalm is a song because it sets before us something over which we ought to exult: it represents the mystery of our restoration. For this psalm is filled with Gospel mysteries.

It speaks of the Passion, where it says: “The exits of death belong to the Lord God.” It speaks of the resurrection, where it says: “Let God arise.” Of the ascension, where it says: “You ascended on high.” Of the sending of the Holy Spirit, where it says: “Strengthen, O God, what you have wrought in us.” Of the incarnation, where it says: “Command, O God, your power.”

All these things ought to be songs and exultation for us. Its subject is Christ, exalted and exalting the Church. Its purpose is to urge us toward Christ’s exaltation, so that we may sing to Christ and exalt him.

This purpose is noted in several places in the psalm. The prophet invites all future children of the Church, so that, attending to the benefits assigned to them through Christ’s Passion and resurrection, they may not receive the grace of God in vain (2 Cor. 6), nor be ungrateful. Rather, they should celebrate with the utmost zeal, in word and deed, the grace given to them through these mysteries, and in that same grace—as is added near the end of the psalm, “Kingdoms of the earth, sing to God”—they should exult in the Lord with every kind of joy.

It should be noted that, as has often been said, in order to express his affection more fully in the prophetic manner, he speaks at the beginning of the psalm in the form of one wishing for something. Yet according to the meaning of a declarative statement, he begins as follows:

## PSALM 67

### 2

“Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered.”

It has already happened (Augustine). Christ has risen, and his enemies have been scattered throughout all the nations. The Jews were defeated in the very place where they had exercised their hostility, and from there they were dispersed throughout the whole world.

Even now they hate, but they fear; and by that very fear they do what follows: “Let those who hate him flee from his face.”

Flight is a movement of the mind, namely fear. For in bodily flight, where could they flee from his face, since he is present everywhere? “Where shall I go,” he says, “from your spirit? And where shall I flee from your face?” (Ps. 138).

They flee in mind, therefore, not in body—by fearing rather than by hiding. And they flee not from the face they do not see, but from the face that they are compelled to see. His face is called his presence through his Church. Let them therefore flee from his face. Let them fear the presence of his saints and faithful ones.

Or let them flee from his face as it is written: “Let the impious be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isa. 26). Concerning them he adds:

### 3

“As smoke disappears, so may they disappear.”

For they lifted themselves up (Augustine) from the fires of their hatred to a swelling of pride [Note: Col. 0909D. Augustine has *typhus*, “swelling”]; and, setting their mouth in heaven and crying out, “Crucify him, crucify him!” (John 19), they swelled up as though victorious. But soon, defeated, they vanished.

It is characteristic of the proud to disappear like smoke. Just as smoke proceeds from fire, so their exaltation proceeds from the burning of desire. And just as smoke vanishes more the higher it rises, so the proud person, the more he is exalted in arrogance, the more he falls away from truth.

He further intensifies their punishment when he adds:

“As wax melts before the fire, so may sinners perish before the face of the Lord.”

Perhaps here he signified those whose hardness is dissolved by tears of impenitence [Note: Col. 0911. In Augustine, in another and truer sense: “into tears of repentance”]. Yet another meaning is also possible: that he is threatening the future judgment.

For because in this age they disappeared by raising themselves up like smoke, at the end an ultimate condemnation will come upon them, so that they may perish eternally from the face of God—that is, from his presence—when he appears in his glory, like fire for the punishment of the wicked and light for the good.

Sinners will perish, not so that they utterly cease to exist, but just as wax melts before the face of fire, so they will dissolve in conscience before the terror of the strict judge.

After showing what follows for the wicked from Christ’s exaltation, he next indicates what comes from it for the good, saying:

### 4

“And let the righteous feast”—that is, let them be refreshed by him, namely, by God, who will be all in all (Eph. 1)—“and let them exult in the sight of God.”

Their exultation will not involve any empty boasting before human beings, but will be before him who sees without error what he has given. Or the righteous will exult in the sight of God because they will see him face to face (1 Cor. 15).

Hence he rightly adds: “And let them delight in gladness.” Then gladness will truly be delightful, when every fear and anxiety has been excluded, when eternal security and secure eternity endure.

Then (Augustine) he turns to those to whom he has given such great hope. He addresses and exhorts those who are living here as follows:

*[The supplied source ends here.]*
### 5. Sing to God; sing a psalm to his name.

He admonishes us to complete in deed the things that are said. Some have distinguished between a *canticum* and a psalm: since a *canticum* is uttered by the mouth, whereas a psalm is sung with the aid of a visible instrument, namely, the psalter, the *canticum* is understood to signify the mind’s understanding, while the psalm signifies bodily works. Thus some have distinguished the words in this way: “Sing to God” is said because what the mind does within itself is known to God but is not seen by human beings. Good works, however, ought to be seen by human beings so that they may glorify our Father who is in heaven (Matt. 6); therefore it is rightly said, “Sing a psalm to his name,” that is, to his reputation, so that he may be named with praise.

He sings to God who lives for God. He sings a psalm to his name who acts for his glory. Thus: “Sing to God”; thus “sing a psalm to God,” that is, live in this way and act in this way. “And also make a way for him,” that is, open the hearts of your hearers to him by preaching. He for whom you ought to prepare the way “ascended above the setting”—he conquered death, as he says through his prophet: “I shall be your death, O Death” (Hos. 13; 1 Cor. 15; Heb. 2).

“Make a way for Christ” (from Augustine), so that through the beautiful feet of those who evangelize, the hearts of believers may be opened to him. For he ascended above the setting when, by rising again, he conquered the fall of the body. Those also make a way for Christ who cleanse hearts from wicked thoughts and adorn them with faith, good morals, and virtues. When this has been done, the house of a chaste breast suddenly becomes the temple of God.

And you ought to make a way for him because “the Lord is his name.” The name “Lord” especially suits him because he rules by himself, and no one can rule except through him. And because good work and the preaching of God ought also to be carried out with alacrity, it is rightly added: “Rejoice in his sight.” While you are making a way for him, while you are preparing the road by which he may come and possess the nations, you will suffer much sadness in the sight of human beings. But you (from the same source) must not only refuse to lose heart; you must also rejoice—not in the sight of human beings, but in the sight of God: “rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation” (Rom. 12).

Those, however, who now trouble you will later be troubled by his presence. For at the judgment they will hear: “Go into the eternal fire” (Matt. 25). “They will be troubled by his presence.” Whose presence?

### 6. Of the father of orphans and judge of widows.

By the presence of the just and true God, who troubles the impious as a severe power, but gathers widows and orphans as a merciful father. Blessed are the orphans and widows who have such a Father and Judge. These are the orphans and widows whose father and husband, the devil, has died. They are the ones who say: “For my father and my mother have abandoned me, but the Lord has taken me up” (Ps. 26).

Of these orphans and widows (from Augustine), that is, those deprived of the fellowship of worldly hope, the Lord builds a temple for himself, concerning which he says next: “God in his holy place.” He makes this place more evident when he adds:

### 7. God makes many people dwell together in one manner in a house,

that is, with one will according to faith and charity in one Church. These are the people of whom it is written: “They had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4). Those are of one manner whose purpose is not changed into different directions. God is in such people as in his holy place. For just as, in a great human house, its master does not rest in just any place but in some more secluded and honored place, so God does not dwell in everyone, but only in those who are of one manner, who live unanimously and harmoniously.

Nor should they ascribe this to their own strength, since they themselves are not the ones who accomplish it. Rather, God does this through them, he who “makes those of one manner dwell together in a house.” His grace is commended still more when it is added: “Who brings out the prisoners in strength.”

The ancient enemy held the human race captive, and the Lord freed it by his own strength. The Patriarchs and Prophets were held captive in hell, and he led them out with great power. Peter was held captive, and he drew him out of Herod’s prisons (Acts 12). He also released the heavy bonds of sins by which people were prevented from walking on the way of the commandments.

Similarly, “those who provoke him,” that is, those whom he brings out with such strength and power—others who, by resisting righteousness, provoke God to anger. “Those who dwell in tombs,” that is, those who consent to the pleasures of the flesh; for the flesh is the tomb of the soul, because there the soul, consenting to the flesh, decays as flesh decays in a tomb.

Those (from Augustine), perhaps shackled, wish to walk but cannot; and they beseech God that they may be able to do so. They say to him: “Deliver me from my necessities” (Ps. 24). When they have been heard, they give thanks, saying: “You have broken my bonds” (Ps. 115).

But these provokers who dwell in tombs belong to the class signified by Scripture elsewhere when it says: “From a dead person, as from one who does not exist, confession perishes” (Sir. 17). Hence there is also the saying: “When the sinner has come into the depth of evils, he despises” (Prov. 18).

For it is one thing to desire, another to attack righteousness, another to wish to be freed from evil, and another to defend one’s evils rather than confess them. Yet the grace of Christ brings both groups out in strength. With what strength, if not so that they may fight against sin even to the shedding of blood? From both classes are made those who are fit to be assigned a place in his holy place. The former are released; the latter are raised again.

And what is now being fulfilled spiritually was previously displayed figuratively. How? He continues and says:

### 8. God, when you went out before your people,

by the pillar of cloud during the day and by the brightness of fire during the night (Exod. 13), “when you passed through the desert,” leading your people through the desert.

### 9. The earth was shaken.

For Mount Sinai seemed to be moved. “Indeed, the heavens dripped manna” (Exod. 16), “from the presence of God of Sinai,” that is, of God dwelling on that mountain; “from the presence of the God of Israel,” that is, of the God to whom the people of Israel belonged. You who then performed such great miracles will also do what follows:

### 10. You will set apart a willing rain, O God, for your inheritance, and it became weak. But you perfected it.

Now, however, let us see the hidden meanings of these mysteries, with the Lord revealing them. His going forth is understood when he appears in his works. He does not appear to everyone, but to those who know how to contemplate his works. I am not now speaking of those works that are visible to everyone—heaven, earth, sea, and all that is in them—but of the works by which he brings out the shackled in strength, likewise those who provoke him and dwell in tombs, and makes them of one manner in a house.

Thus he will go forth before his people, that is, before those who understand this grace of his. Finally, it follows: “While you were passing through the desert, the earth was shaken.” The Gentiles, who did not know God, were a desert. It was a desert where no law had been given by God himself and where no prophets had dwelt who foretold that the Lord would come.

Therefore, when you were passing through the desert, when you were preached among the Gentiles, “the earth was shaken”: earthly people were roused to faith. But from where was it shaken? “Indeed, the heavens dripped from the presence of God of Sinai.” For the earth to be moved to faith, when the Gospel passed through the desert of the Gentiles, the heavens dripped from the presence of God.

These are the heavens of which another psalm sings: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. 18). Of these, a little later in that psalm, it is said: “There are no speeches or words whose voices are not heard.” The heavens did not drip from themselves, but “from the presence of God of Sinai,” that is, of God who dwells in them, just as he dwells on Mount Sinai.

These are the mountains of which it is said: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains” (Ps. 120), and again: “You who wondrously illumine from the everlasting mountains” (Ps. 75). And he is the God of Israel, that is, of the people who see God.

And just as the heavens dripped manna (Exod. 16), so you, O God, will set apart “a willing rain,” that is, gratuitous grace, for your inheritance, that is, you will give it separately to your Church. A willing rain is rightly understood as the grace of God, because it is given freely, with no preceding merits. “But if it is by grace, it is no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace” (Rom. 11).

This willing rain begot us by the word of truth. God set this rain apart for his inheritance. “And it became weak.” For it recognized that it was nothing by itself, not by its own strength, and that what it was had to be attributed to the grace of God. It recognized what is said: “I will glory in my infirmities” (2 Cor. 12), and again: “Do not be high-minded, but fear” (Rom. 11).

It became weak in itself, but you perfected it, because “power is perfected in weakness” (2 Cor. 12). It became weak in itself so that it might be perfected in you.

### 11. Your animals will dwell in it.

In this inheritance animals dwell, because within the holy Church the gentle and meek—those for whom God’s yoke is easy and his burden light (Matt. 11)—persevere in humility of life.

Alternatively, the animals of God may be understood as the teachers and leaders of the Church, who dwell in this inheritance and compassionately bear the burdens of others upon themselves. There they are nourished by the sacred Scriptures as by a kind of spiritual hay, and they are imbued from a heavenly spring and by the Holy Spirit.

And appropriately, when he says “animals,” he adds “your,” that is, subject to you, not free for themselves.

“And you prepared this rain in your sweetness for the poor, O God.” You bestowed your grace upon the humble, not on the basis of their merits, but solely from the sweetness of your charity. Because you loved the poor, you enriched them with your grace.

He appropriately says, “in your sweetness.” For what is sweeter (from Augustine) than charity? The work of grace is not accomplished out of fear of punishment, but out of love of righteousness.

Then he shows what preparations God made for his poor. He says:

### 12. The Lord will give the word to those who evangelize with great power.

“I,” he says, “will give you a mouth and wisdom which all your adversaries will not be able to resist” (Luke 21). And again: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Ps. 80).

These are the provisions that God generously gives his animals in his inheritance. How great a sweetness they possess is suggested by one of these animals, who says: “How sweet are your utterances to my throat, sweeter than honey to my mouth” (Ps. 118).

“To those who evangelize,” he says, “with great power,” that is, with great steadfastness. They can be killed, but they cannot be bent.

Hear the power of those who evangelize: “Who,” they say, “will separate us from the charity of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? We know that neither death nor life nor any creature will be able to separate us from the charity of God, which is in Christ Jesus” (Rom. 8).

For “the Lord will give the word to those who evangelize.”

### 13. The King of the powers of the Beloved, of the Beloved,

that is, God the Father, who is the King of the powers of his Beloved. What powers belong to the Beloved, that is, to his Son?

When “Beloved” is used without specifying who is beloved, the only Son is understood by antonomasia. When he says “of the Beloved, of the Beloved,” he repeats the noun in place of a pronoun, as though he were saying, “of his Beloved.” Such a mode of expression is frequently found in divine Scripture, as in the statement: “Moses did as the Lord commanded Moses” (Exod. 25), that is, commanded him.

Or it may be read in this way: “You speak of the powers of the Beloved.” Whose Beloved? “Absolutely,” he says, “and always Beloved above all.” Concerning him the Father himself says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” All powers belong to this Beloved (Matt. 3 and 17; Luke 3). He himself is the power and wisdom of God (1 Cor. 1). And whoever is strong is strong through Christ.

But because the Son has nothing from himself except from the Father (John 8, 13, and 16), God the Father is rightly called the King of the powers of his beloved Son. To him the Beloved himself says: “All that is mine is yours” (Luke 15). And again: “I do nothing from myself. My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 6).

When he had therefore said, “The Lord will give the word to those who evangelize with great power,” because that very power is ruled by him and serves him from whom it is given, he says: “The Lord himself is the King of the powers of the Beloved.” Then it follows: “And the beauty of the house divides the spoils.”

As though it were said (from Augustine): “Christ the Beloved also makes the beauty of the house by dividing the spoils.” For Christ made a beautiful house, that is, the Church, by dividing spoils among its members, just as a body is beautiful through the distribution of its members.

Spoils are what are stripped from conquered enemies. What this means the Gospel teaches us, where we read: “When a strong armed man guards his courtyard, his possessions are in peace. But when one stronger than he comes upon him and conquers him, he will take away all his weapons in which he trusted and distribute his spoils” (Luke 11).

The strong armed man is the devil, who possessed this world. But Christ, coming upon him as the stronger, conquered him; he took away his weapons and distributed his spoils. The Lord cleansed these vessels by the remission of sins. He sanctified these spoils, taken from the enemy who had been struck down and bound, and divided them among the beauty of his house, appointing some as apostles, others as prophets, others as pastors and teachers, for the work of ministry and the building up of the body of Christ (Eph. 4).

For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so also is Christ (Rom. 12). Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all powers? Do all possess gifts of healing? Do all speak in tongues? Do all interpret? Yet one and the same Spirit accomplishes all these things, dividing to each person his own gifts as he wills (1 Cor. 12).

This is the beauty of the house to which the spoils are divided, so that its lover, inflamed by this beauty, may exclaim: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house” (Ps. 25).

Now, in what follows, he turns by addressing those very members from whom the beauty of the house is formed, saying:

### 14. If you sleep among the middle portions.

O you (from Augustine) who are divided like spoils of the beauty of the house: if you sleep, that is, if you rest, removed from worldly tumult, “among the two Testaments,” obeying both by holding them in common—“middle,” that is, common to both—so that you understand that what was said figuratively in the first has been fulfilled spiritually in the second, you will be “the feathers of a silvered dove,” that is, the adornment and exaltation of the Church.

For just as a dove is raised aloft by its feathers, so the Church will be exalted to heavenly things through your preaching. The holy Church is rightly called a dove because it has no gall of bitterness and because it possesses the virtue of simplicity, concerning which it is said elsewhere: “My dove is one” (Song 6).

It is silvered because it has been instructed in divine utterances. For in another place the utterances of the Lord are called silver tested by fire and purified sevenfold in the earth (Ps. 10).

If, then, these two portions signify the two Testaments, what else are we admonished to do except to recognize that the Testaments agree with one another rather than contradict one another, and to acquiesce through understanding? We ourselves should be the sign and evidence of their harmony, when we perceive that neither has said anything against the other and when, with peaceful wonder, we are shown as if in a sleep of ecstasy.

We understand the divine Scripture by “portions” because *cleros* in Greek is interpreted in Latin as “lot.” We possess divine Scripture not by any human decision, but solely by lot, that is, solely by God’s election.

Another sense presents itself here (from Augustine), perhaps preferable: we should understand “portions” much more plausibly as the inheritances themselves. Since the inheritance of the Old Testament is earthly happiness, whereas the inheritance of the New Testament is earthly immortality, to sleep among the middle portions means not to seek the former eagerly, but patiently to await the latter.

For those who serve God—or rather, those who refuse to serve him—while they seek happiness in this life have sleep taken away from them and do not sleep. Driven on by flaming [variant: inflamed] desires, they are propelled into crimes and wicked deeds; they do not rest at all, desiring to acquire and fearing to lose.

But “whoever listens to me,” says Wisdom (Prov. 1), “will dwell in hope and will rest without fear from every vanity.” This, as far as I understand, is to sleep among the middle portions, that is, among the middle inheritances: to dwell not yet in possession, but in hope of the heavenly inheritance, and already to cease from desire for earthly happiness.

When what we hope for has come, we will no longer rest between two inheritances; we will reign in the new and true inheritance, of which the old was a shadow.

And because the Apostles had slept so well, the Church now flies about like wings and is exalted by their praises. When the others also sleep in this way, following their example, wings are added, by which the Church may be preached in exalted fashion until the end of the world.

“And the hind parts of its back will be in the pallor of gold,” that is, in the brightness of wisdom. By this brightness we understand charity. For the warmth of divine wisdom is charity.

But why “from the back,” and not from the breast? Is it because the roots of the wings are there? Charity “bears all things” (1 Cor. 13). And it is written: “Bear one another’s burdens, and thus you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. 6).

Or otherwise: What are the wings themselves except the two commandments of charity, on which the whole law and the prophets depend (Matt. 22)? What is the light burden itself except charity, which is fulfilled in these two commandments? Whatever is difficult in a commandment is easy for one who loves.

Nor is there any other reason why the saying “My burden is light” (Matt. 11) is rightly understood except that he gives the Holy Spirit, through whom charity is given in our hearts (Rom. 5), so that by loving freely we may do what the person who acts out of fear does slavishly.

Therefore “the hind parts of its back are in the pallor of gold,” because whatever the Church bears, whatever it endures, it does entirely in love, entirely in wisdom, entirely in joy. In heart it is simple, in word radiant, in deed illustrious.

As long as it does this, he determines the time, saying:

### 15. While the heavenly one distinguishes kings over her.

That is, as long as the Son of God orders and appoints holy persons and leaders who reign well over both themselves and others, namely, over the dove.

Who is this heavenly one except the one who ascended above all the heavens in order to fill all things (Eph. 4)? And what else is it to distinguish kings over her except to prepare them for the work of ministry and the building up of the body of Christ (1 Cor. 12)?

They are also called kings (from Augustine), certainly from *ruling*—and what do they rule more than the desires of the flesh? Thus sin must not reign in their mortal body so that they obey its desires; they must not present their members as weapons of iniquity to sin, but present themselves to God as living from the dead, and their members as weapons of righteousness for God (Rom. 6).

Thus they will first be distinguished as kings from foreigners, because they do not bear the yoke with unbelievers. Then they will be distinguished among themselves harmoniously by their proper gifts.

And in order that they may be distinguished, “they will be whitened with snow in Selmon.” They will receive the remission of sins from him who says: “Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be made white as snow” (Isa. 1).

He therefore rightly says, “in Selmon,” which is interpreted as “shadow,” that is, in Christ. A shadow consists of light and body. That true light, which was the Word in the beginning with God (John 1), became, as it were, a shadow for us: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” To God, the human being was joined as a body to light, and those who believe in him were covered by the shadow of protection.

They are therefore whitened with snow in Selmon who, through the grace that is in Christ, are cleansed from the stains of sins. “Selmon,” I say, is:

### 16. The mountain of God, a rich mountain.

For Christ is called, by prerogative, the mountain of God the Father, through the eminence of his divinity. He is so rich that “the whole fullness of divinity dwelt bodily in him” (Col. 2).

Nor was he rich only in himself; from himself he also enriched others. Hence it is added: “A curdled mountain,” with respect to those whom he nourishes with milk. “A rich mountain,” with respect to the mature, whom he refreshes with the more abundant sweetness of his wisdom.

Even milk, from which cheese is made, signifies grace in a wondrous way. It flows from the abundance of a mother’s viscera and is poured freely, with delightful mercy, into little ones.

And because some doubted concerning Christ and believed certain saints to be equal to him in grace, he rebukes them for their error when he adds:

### 17. Why do you suspect curdled mountains?

For the other saints too are called mountains of God. Nor were there lacking those who said that he was John the Baptist, others Elijah, and still others Jeremiah or one of the prophets (Matt. 16).

To restrain their error, he further indicates another excellence by which he proves that this holy mountain differs from the other holy mountains. He therefore says: “The mountain in which it pleased God to dwell.”

It pleased God the Father to dwell in this mountain, which is prepared at the summit of the mountains, to whom he says: “You are my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3 and 17; Luke 3).

God does not dwell in him through a particular grace, as he does in the other saints, nor only for a time. He proves this when he adds: “Indeed, the Lord will dwell to the end,” that is, to the perfection of dwelling.

He dwells in him to such an extent that he cannot dwell more fully—in the unity of person and equality of power. Not that he does not dwell in others (from Augustine), but because in others he dwells through him. For in him dwells the whole fullness of divinity, not in shadow, as in the temple made by Solomon, but bodily (Col. 2), solidly and truly, because “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5).

Or he says, “The Lord will dwell to the end,” because this will be manifested more clearly at the end, when he appears in his majesty and equality (Matt. 25).

Or, the Lord Jesus Christ will dwell in his saints, bringing them to the end, that is, to himself. For “Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10).

After he has shown Christ’s height, he next indicates what proceeds from it for his Church. It is as though it were said: Behold, the great and incomparable mountain, the Lord Jesus. What will become of those who were thought to be curdled mountains?

### 18. They will be the chariots of God, he says.

And lest they be thought few, he adds: “Ten thousand times multiplied thousands of rejoicing ones.” For who is the charioteer? “The Lord is among them,” he says. Where? “In Sinai, in the holy place.”

By this name he signified the immense multitude of saints and believers who, by bearing God, become in some way the chariots of God, using a finite number for an infinite one. By dwelling in them and ruling them like a good charioteer, he brings them to the end as his chariot, as though to some appointed destination.

In the statement that the number is “multiplied in ten thousands,” the perfection of doctrine is commended. Ten signifies doctrine because of the Decalogue; a thousand, because it is a perfect number, signifies perfection.

Therefore the chariot of God exists multiplied in ten thousands, because the number of the saints lives according to the ten commandments of the law in manifold and perfect fashion.

Wondrously, after saying “thousands of rejoicing ones,” he immediately adds: “The Lord is among them.” Let us not be surprised that they rejoice: the Lord is among them. Thus, even if they are “as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing” (2 Cor. 6), they do not rejoice in the end itself, which they have not yet reached, but in hope: “rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation” (Rom. 12).

“For the Lord is among them, in Sinai, in the holy place,” that is, in the commandment. For Sinai is interpreted as “commandment.” The Apostle says: “The law indeed is holy, and the commandment holy and good” (Rom. 7).

But what benefit would the commandment provide unless the Lord were there? Concerning him it is said: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work according to his good pleasure” (Phil. 1).

Thus the Lord is in them, in the commandment, helping them to fulfill the commandment. How is he in them? “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5). This is what fulfills the commandment, and therefore the thousands rejoice.

How did this come about? He turns to the one who accomplished it and shows us how it happened, saying:

### 19. You ascended on high,

that is, into heaven, by rising again. “You took captivity,” that is, you redeemed the human race, which the devil had taken captive through sin.

“You received gifts among human beings,” as it is said elsewhere: “I will give you the Gentiles as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 2).

Our captivity was taken captive by the Lord our God so that it might become freedom. Hence it was said to Peter: “From now on you will be catching human beings” (Luke 5).

We were taken captive because we were subjected; placed under that gentle yoke, we were freed from sin, whose slaves we were, and made slaves of righteousness, from which we had been free (Rom. 6).

Thus he himself, who gave gifts to human beings and “received gifts among human beings,” is in them. Therefore in this captivity, in this journey, under this yoke, there are not thousands of weeping people, but thousands of rejoicing people. For the Lord is among them, in Sinai, in the holy place.

And truly those whom you received were captivity: “Indeed, even unbelievers, that the Lord God might dwell in them.” The unbelievers themselves are the captivity. By not believing, they were possessed by the devil, who works in the children of distrust (Eph. 4). “Among whom you also once lived,” he says, “when you lived in them” (Eph. 5).

Faith freed them from that state, so that now, as believers, they might be inhabited by God, having become the house of God and the chariot of God, thousands of rejoicing people.

Therefore the one who sang these things, foreseeing them in the spirit, filled with joy himself also poured forth a hymn, saying:

### 20. Blessed be the Lord day by day.

That is, continually, to the end. And because he saw that the chariot was being led eternally, he continues and says: “God of our salvations will make the journey prosperous for us.”

For “all things work together for good for those who are called saints according to his purpose” (Rom. 8), and he does not permit them to be tempted beyond what they can bear, but also makes a way out of the temptation (2 Cor. 10).

Therefore he is rightly called the God of salvations, because he directs our journey toward salvation and makes it so prosperous that he causes us to pass from this world to the Father, so that what the Lord himself said may come to pass: “I will that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17).

Who is this God? He continues and says:

### 21. Our God is the God of salvation.

Grace is greatly commended (from Augustine). For who would be saved unless he himself healed? But lest the thought arise, “Why then do we die, if we have been saved by his grace?” he immediately adds: “And the Lord’s, the Lord’s are the issues of death.”

It is as though he were saying: Why do you resent, human condition, having the issue of death? The issue of your Lord was also none other than death. Take comfort, then, rather than resenting it.

Let us therefore endure death itself patiently, following the example of the one who, though he owed nothing to death because of sin and was Lord—so that no one could take his life from him, but he himself laid it down of his own accord—nevertheless also had death as his issue.

But although he died in humility, he will nevertheless condemn the proud. This is what follows:

### 22. Yet God will crush the heads of his enemies.

To crush heads is to humble proud minds, according to what is written: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled” (Matt. 23; Luke 17).

He will also crush “the crown of the hair” of those who walk in their sins, that is, of those who persevere in sins. The heads of enemies—that is, the dominions and rule of unbelievers—have also been crushed, and are crushed daily, so that the whole world may be subjected to Christ, the one Head.

Alternatively, “heads” may be understood as capital, that is, criminal, sins. By “the crown of the hair,” however, minor and venial sins may be signified. Whoever walks in these with delight, and does not bring them to an end by correction while he lives, God himself, undiminished in divinity after death, will crush and destroy him by the punishment of his strict judgment.

We understand thoughts by “hairs” because, just as hairs cling to the head, so thoughts cling to the mind. Good thoughts adorn the mind; evil ones disfigure it.

He will crush some and convert others to himself, making some martyrs and others preachers. To confirm this he introduces the Lord speaking in this way:

### 23. The Lord said,

that is, he firmly ordained: “From Bashan I will turn into the depth of the sea.”

Bashan is interpreted as “confusion.” From the confusion of sin comes conversion to God (from Augustine). Hence the tax collector did not dare to raise his eyes to heaven. Considering himself in this way, he was ashamed, but he descended justified (Luke 18).

Again, Bashan is interpreted as “dryness.” Such was the soul that said: “My soul is like land without water for you” (Ps. 42). “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled” (Matt. 5).

Then what does “the depth of the sea” signify except the deep wickedness of the sinner? Hence it is written: “When the sinner has come into the depth of evils, he despises” (Prov. 18).

The sinner is turned into the depth of the sea when, with the Lord impelling him, he is driven back into his own conscience, so that he may reconsider the evils he has committed and mourn them in repentance.

Hence a certain penitent says to God: “I will recall my years to you in the bitterness of my soul” (Isa. 38). True conversion occurs when what was formerly sweet—sin—becomes bitter to the soul.

God therefore turns even the most desperate sinners into the depth, in order to free them. How perfect this conversion is, he indicates when he adds:

### 24. So that your foot may be dipped in blood.

Each preacher, as he walks about announcing the word of God, performs the function of a foot among the members of Christ. Hence it is written: “How beautiful are the feet of those who announce peace, who announce good things” (Isa. 52).

Paul was such a foot when he said: “I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die for the name of Jesus” (Acts 21).

The foot of God is dipped in blood when a preacher of Christ is dyed by martyrdom for the faith of the Gospel.

Then he adds: “The tongue of your dogs from the enemies, from him.”

He calls those very people (from Augustine) who were going to fight even to the shedding of blood “dogs”—not detestable dogs, but praiseworthy ones, keeping faith with their Lord and barking against his enemies on behalf of his house.

For he did not merely say “of dogs,” but “of your dogs”; nor did he praise their teeth, but their tongue. The prophet foretold that they would come from enemies, through that conversion of which he was speaking above.

Thus merciful God made his friends from enemies, so that those who had been blasphemers might later become preachers, and those who had persecuted Christ might afterward die for Christ (1 Tim. 1).

And as though it were asked where they received so great a good, the answer immediately follows: “From him,” that is, from God. For when could they have received it from themselves? “When we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son” (Rom. 5).

Hence it is also added:

### 25. They saw your entrances, O God.

How you entered this world, how you were incarnate, how you became human, how you were killed, how you were exalted and glorified. They saw and believed, and, insofar as they could, they followed those same entrances by imitating them.

Whose entrance? Not that of an angel, patriarch, prophet, or any just person, but “the entrances of my God.” For you, who are God, begotten of the Father, my King, will assume flesh for my benefit. You will be my king in your humanity.

This means that your entrances are not to be despised, because you will be God and human, restoring and ruling human beings.

Concerning him it is rightly added: “Who is in the holy place.” For God does not dwell in a body subject to sins (Wis. 1), but in one whose conscience is holy and pure.

### 26. To make these entrances known, the princes went before,

that is, the first preachers, the Apostles, to whom leadership over the Church was given. They went before the others as princes and teachers, and not alone, but joined by those who sang psalms. Through their good works, like visible instruments, God was glorified.

These princes, as ministers and overseers, will be “in the midst of young women,” that is, Churches that were still young, like the primitive Churches. I mean those “who beat the tambourines,” that is, who praise God with the flesh mortified.

For tambourines (from Augustine) are made from dried and stretched hide.

For all these good things, O faithful:

### 27. Bless God in the Churches.

There is the place for blessing, because those who are outside the Church cannot worthily praise God. I speak of God, the Lord, who created and rules us.

Bless him “from the springs,” that is, on account of the springs: on account of the holy Apostles, who refresh you with spiritual teaching. I speak of the springs, Israel—that is, those proceeding from Judea.

For from there (from Augustine) he first chose those whom he would make springs. For the Apostles were chosen from there, and they were the first to hear: “Whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst; but the water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water welling up into eternal life” (John 4).

[Col. 0919C] **28. There Benjamin is, the youth, in an ecstasy of mind.** There, as elsewhere [in the same source], is Paul, the last of the Apostles, who says: “For I too am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin” (Rom. 12). He was caught up in an ecstasy of mind when he was carried away to the third heaven and heard unspeakable words, which it is not permitted for a human being to utter. “Whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know; God knows” (1 Cor. 12).

And from where are the princes who went before? He continues and says: “The princes of Judah, their leaders; the princes of Zebulun, the princes of Naphtali.” According to the same source, these names are Hebrew: Judah is interpreted to mean “confession,” Zebulun “dwelling-place of strength,” and Naphtali “my enlargement.” All these disclose to us very truly the princes of the Churches, worthy of leadership, worthy of imitation, worthy of honors. For the martyrs hold their place in the Churches and excel at the summit of holy dignity.

Now, in martyrdom, confession comes first; and for its sake strength is assumed to endure whatever may occur. Then, after everything has been endured and the tribulations have come to an end, enlargement follows in the rewards.

[Note: The Vulgate and Augustine read “they hold the highest place.”]

It can also be understood in this way: since the Apostle especially commends these three things—faith, hope, and charity [1 Cor. 13]—confession is in faith, strength in hope, and enlargement in charity. For it belongs to faith that one “believes with the heart unto righteousness,” while “with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10). In the sufferings of tribulations, the person is sorrowful; but hope is strong. [Note: The same source reads more fully, “the matter is sorrowful”; shortly afterward, at [Col. 0920D], it incorrectly has “diffuso” for “diffusio.”] “If we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Rom. 8). Charity, however, provides enlargement through its diffusion in the heart. For perfected charity casts out fear (Rom. 5). That fear contains torment through the narrowness of the soul.

The princes, then, of Judah, their leaders, are those who bless the Lord in the Churches. The princes of Zebulun, the princes of Naphtali: the princes of confession, strength, and enlargement; the princes of faith, hope, and charity. With such great princes joined to you,

[Col. 0920A] **29. Command, O God; give orders to your strength, your Son, through whom you work mightily.** For he is the commander of the princes; he is your strength and wisdom (Heb. 1), through whom you do whatever you do. Your command is your will. Command your strength: let your will be fulfilled; let your power be declared. Strengthen, O God, what you have worked in us.

Command the Word, that it may come to be. Command through the Word. Strengthen through the Holy Spirit. Command,

[Note: The same source reads “by teaching.”]

by speaking; strengthen by helping. Command what you will; do what you command. And if you do this, what follows will come to pass:

**30. From your temple in Jerusalem, which is our free mother.** It too is your holy temple. From this temple of yours, the kings will offer gifts to you—namely, themselves, or sacrifices of praise.

Or, “Command,” as was said, “from your temple in Jerusalem.” For the preaching of the Apostles began there. When the Lord therefore commanded the Apostles to preach the Gospel to every creature (Matt. 28; Mark 16), he said: “Beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24). Another prophet had foreseen this long before when he said: “From Zion the law will go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. 2).

Foreseeing, however, that heretics would arise in the Church of God, he added:

[Col. 0920B] **31. Rebuke the beasts of the reeds.** Heretics are not improperly called beasts, because they tear apart simple souls as beasts tear sheep. And they are rightly called “of the reeds,” because their speech is shifting and unstable. The Apostle Peter says that they are unlearned and unstable and that they twist the Scriptures to their own destruction (2 Pet. 3).

Because they are of a hard and untamed neck, not subject to the peaceful and gentle yoke of discipline, impatient of the plow and of teaching, they are therefore also designated by the name of bulls, when it is added: “The gathering of bulls among the calves of the peoples.” For they do not lead astray all peoples, among whom there are grave and steadfast persons. Hence it is written: “Among a grave people I will praise you” (Ps. 34). Rather, they gather among those peoples whom they find to be like cows—namely, simple and frivolous souls, who readily follow by listening.

This gathering takes place for the purpose of excluding those who have been tested by silver. For this is the intention of heretical teachers: to separate from the ears of the souls whom they endeavor to mislead those who have been tested by silver—that is, those instructed in divine speech. Hence the Apostle says: “There must be heresies, so that those who have been tested may be made manifest” (1 Cor. 11).

Concerning these heretics, lest they prevail, he asks, saying: “Scatter the peoples who desire wars.” For, according to Augustine, they do not devote themselves to correction but to contention. By contradicting the truth, they seek to introduce discord into the Catholic faith. Let them, then, be scattered instead, if they refuse correction—those who desire to scatter Christ’s flock.

He called them “peoples,” not on account of the generations of families, but on account of the generations of sects, where a succession of descent confirms error. And truly you will scatter them. For:

**32. Envoys will come from Egypt; Ethiopia will stretch out her hands to God.** According to the same source, through these envoys you will scatter the heretics. By the name of Egypt, or Ethiopia, he signified the faith of all nations, using a part for the whole. He calls the preachers of reconciliation “envoys.” Hence Paul says: “I am an ambassador for Christ” (2 Cor. 5); “as though God were exhorting through us, we beseech you on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God.”

Thus, again according to the same source, it was mystically prophesied that preachers of Christian peace would arise not only from the Israelites, from whom the Apostles were chosen, but also from the other nations.

“Ethiopia” too, that is, the soul blackened by sins, “will stretch out her hands,” that is, will forestall his vengeance by believing in God, so that her sins may be forgiven and she may not remain sinful and be punished. Or, because faith precedes so that good works may follow—and there are no good works except those that follow preceding faith—nothing else seems to be meant by “Ethiopia will stretch out her hands to God” than “Ethiopia will believe in God.” For in this way she will precede her hands, that is, her works. Whose works, if not those of Ethiopia herself?

This is not ambiguous in Greek, because there “her” is most clearly placed in the feminine gender. Let it therefore be said: “Ethiopia will stretch out her hands to God,” that is, by believing in God she will precede her own works. “For I consider,” says the Apostle, “that a person is justified by faith without the works of the law” (Rom. 3).

Having now, as it were, run through all the events that we already see fulfilled, the prophet exhorts us to praise Christ and then announces his future coming, saying:

[Col. 0921A] **33. Kingdoms of the earth**—that is, people from every kind of earthly nation—**sing to God**, with voice and heart; **sing praises to the Lord**, by good works.

He does not invite one kingdom or only one nation to praise God. For merciful God does not wish anyone to perish, but everyone to come to the knowledge of his name (1 Tim. 2). Hence he adds: “Sing praises to God.” And as though someone might ask, “Who is this God?” he continues and says:

[Col. 0921B] **34. He who ascends above the heaven of heaven toward the East.** He repeats this in order to stir us to praise God and to commend the identity of the one who is praised. Hence the Apostle says: “He is the one who ascended above all the heavens” (Eph. 4).

By adding “toward the East,” he also indicated the very place, since it is in the eastern regions that he rose and from which he ascended. And because he will come from there to judge the living and the dead, he shows this in what follows: “Behold, he will give his voice, the voice of strength.”

He who was formerly without a voice, “like a lamb before its shearer” (Isa. 53), behold, will give his voice. Not the voice of weakness, as one to be judged, but the voice of strength, as one who will judge. For God will no longer come hidden as before, but God will come manifestly—our God—and he will not be silent. Therefore:

**35. Give glory to God over Israel.** That is, show by voice and heart that God is glorious over those who are spiritually Israel. Of them it can truly be said: “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit” (John 1).

Then “his magnificence and his strength will be in the clouds,” when you see “the Son of Man coming in the clouds with great power and majesty,” and “the powers of heaven will be shaken” (Matt. 24; Luke 12).

[Col. 0921C] **36. Wonderful is God in his saints**—understand: “he will be.” He will be wonderful when he judges the world through his Holy One; when the righteous shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father (Matt. 13); when God himself is all in all (Eph. 1).

It is rightly added: “God of Israel.” For then the name itself will be fulfilled most truly and completely: Israel, which is interpreted as “seeing God,” because “we will see him as he is” (1 John 3).

And it will not be someone else, but he himself will give strength—the strength that he first displayed in his flesh, namely immortality and freedom from suffering. And he will give fortitude, because the enemy, death, will be destroyed (Hos. 13). He will give it to his people, that is, to those who serve him to the end.

Or, he will give his people strength with respect to the soul, making it divine and blessed. And he will give fortitude with respect to the body, making it incorruptible (1 Cor. 15) and eternal.

For such great benefits of his, blessed be God, and so forth.

## TITLE OF PSALM LXVIII

**1.** The following Psalm is entitled in this manner: “For the end; for those who will be changed; a Psalm of David.”

This Psalm corresponds to David in its meaning, that is, to Christ, who speaks here. And it directs us toward the end, that is, toward himself. It is a Psalm, I say, composed for the exhortation of those who will be changed: from unbelief to faith, from oldness to newness, from corruption to incorruption.

The subject of the Psalm is Christ suffering according to the frailty of human nature. He carries out the account of his Passion through many parts of the Psalm, up to its completion. Hence he also says: “They gave gall for my food,” and so forth.

Christ’s purpose in this work is to invite us to his endurance. Concerning his Passion, as is the prophetic custom, he begins by speaking in prayer, and he shows that he asks the Father’s help in all things, so that he may teach by example those to whom he has shown the way how to pray in tribulations—and especially those for whom this is necessary. He therefore says:

## PSALM LXVIII

**2. Save me, O God.** And he gives the reason why: **For the waters have entered**, that is, just as water, with noise and force, the Jewish people rose up against him and, inflicting ever greater evils, advanced until they reached my soul, to take it away.

They entered as water reaches the soul when senseless crowds prevailed even to the point of killing Christ (John 10 and 19). But could they have done this unless they had been permitted by him? Why, then, does he cry out as though he were suffering something against his will? Because the head prefigures its members. He suffered because he willed to suffer. The martyrs suffered, even though they did not will it. Hence it was said to Peter: “Another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go” (John 21).

Although we pass from evil things to good things, the passage itself is nevertheless somewhat bitter and contains gall, which the Jews gave the Lord in his Passion. It also contains something that must be endured, by which those who gave him vinegar to drink are represented. Therefore, in order that we may be delivered, let us cry out, lest perhaps in afflictions we consent to iniquity and so be truly swallowed up irreparably.

Finally, he himself indicates how fiercely their malice raged against Christ when he adds:

**3. I am stuck in the mud of the deep, and there is no firm ground.** Earthly people, when they desire empty things and wish to draw others into agreement with themselves, are mud. Among them are some who are utterly wicked and despairing. Such people are not only mud but also “the deep.”

Those were the people in whom our Lord was stuck—that is, in whom he remained caught, so that he might be seized and killed by them. The Son of God therefore came to the mud of the deep, and there was no substance in which he was stuck, because he was stuck in their iniquity. We possess vices from ourselves and from our own will, and vices are not substance.

The Lord was stuck in these things when he suffered persecution—not in the substance of human beings, which was made through him, but in the vice of the Jews, which was produced by them. Nor am I stuck because I was unable to protect myself. For I offered myself voluntarily. And this is: **I came into the depth of the sea, and the storm overwhelmed me.**

He calls them “sea” because of the bitterness of life, and “depth” because of their pride. Christ therefore came, under no compulsion but by spontaneous will, among proud and bitter people; and their seditious upheaval, like a violent storm, overwhelmed and extinguished him. He shows that they are inexcusable in this when he adds:

[Col. 0922C] **4. I have labored, crying out; my throat has become hoarse.** What does Christ cry out? “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees” (Matt. 23); “Woe to the world because of scandals” (Matt. 18). Every day also he was teaching in the temple and in the synagogues (Luke 19); but because he produced little fruit among them, he therefore labored. Hence he says through the prophet: “I have labored in enduring” (Isa. 1).

Therefore his throat is said to have become hoarse, not with respect to himself, but with respect to those by whom he was neither understood nor believed. His persecution was so great that not only did these people fail to believe, but even those who had already believed began to doubt. This is what he adds:

**My eyes have failed while I hope in my God.** For while he perseveres in his Passion and, turning toward his Lord, hopes to rise from the dead, his eyes failed, because even the Apostles themselves—who stood out in the body like lamps—doubted.

And lest those who persecuted him seem to have been few, it is added:

**5. Those who hate me without cause have multiplied beyond the hairs of my head.** As though he were saying plainly: Those who hated me without cause have increased beyond number.

To hate one who causes harm is, in a certain sense, human. Hence the Lord, speaking in the Law as to carnal people and accommodating himself to their weakness, commanded them to love their friends and permitted them to hate their enemies (Lev. 19). But to hate one who causes no harm is not merely inhuman; it is also diabolical.

Hatred of an enemy appears almost natural, though it nevertheless arises from the corruption of nature. Hatred directed against an innocent person is contrary to nature. There is therefore a great difference between one hatred and another. One is produced by weakness; the other is stirred up by malice alone.

The Jews burned with the latter so fiercely that in their hatred of Christ they exceeded both number and nature and all measure. Their malice is further intensified when it is added:

**Those who persecute me, my enemies, have grown strong unjustly.** First those who hated him without cause—that is, without reason—multiplied. Then they grew strong and were emboldened to fulfill in deed, by persecution, the hatred that they had conceived in their hearts. They did this unjustly as well, because they found no cause for which they ought to persecute me or become my enemies.

But amid such great malice our Lord discloses his innocence when he adds:

**What I did not take, I then repaid.** For who took? Adam. And what did he take? The forbidden fruit. “Taste,” he says, “and you will be like gods” (Gen. 3). They wanted to seize divinity and lost happiness. They usurped for themselves what was not theirs, and this is theft.

Therefore they were handed over to the devil, the exactor, so that they might repay the penalty of death for sin. Christ, however, took nothing, because he did not sin; nevertheless, he paid the debt of sin, that is, death.

He came to death like any human being, but not by the way by which every human being comes to it [Ant. reads quia, “because,” for qua, “by which”]. For all others came to death through guilt; he alone came to death through righteousness. Both Adam and Christ therefore paid death, which is the debt of sin. But because Adam sinned, his death was the punishment for sin. Because Christ did not sin, his death became a sacrifice for sin.

Yet the world did not understand this fruit of Christ’s death, and therefore regarded it as folly (Heb. 9 and 10). “We preach,” says the Apostle, “Jesus Christ, and him crucified: to the Jews a stumbling block, but to the Gentiles folly” (1 Cor. 1).

[Col. 0923C] **6. O God, you know my folly.** The benefit of my Passion, which some regard as folly, has been provided, approved, and ordained by you, God the Creator. You know what they did not know. “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2).

And what is so like folly as this: although he had it in his power to strike down his persecutors with a single word, he allowed himself to be seized, scourged, spat upon, struck on the face, crowned with thorns, and fastened to the wood? Yet “what is foolish in God is wiser than human beings, and what is weak in God is stronger than human beings” (1 Cor. 1). For from the point at which God was humbled and suffered, humanity was raised up and healed.

Likewise, **my offenses**, that is, the deeds that were reckoned as offenses—such as this statement: “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the sabbath” (John 9), and other things of this kind—are not hidden from you.

What they considered folly, namely, that I should suffer; and offenses, namely, that I should heal their sicknesses—you knew to be wisdom and strength.

It should be noted that these words instruct us to attend always more to God’s will than to human beings in everything we do. Our action should be what God approves, even if a human being does not approve it. Hence Paul admonishes us to deserve to be wise before God, even if we are utter fools before human beings (1 Cor. 1).

Or, his offenses are not hidden because his members do not cease daily to confess their sins. And because it was to be reproached as folly against Christians that they believed in a human being who had died and been crucified, he asks on their behalf, saying:

**7. Let those who wait for you, Lord, not be put to shame because of me, Lord of hosts.** For many, hearing the disgrace of Christ’s cross, were ashamed and withdrew from the faith and hope that they had begun to have in God.

For this reason Paul, to strengthen the minds of the weak, declares that he is not ashamed of the Gospel of God. Indeed, he was so far from being ashamed that, when bound and chained, he rejoiced all the more (Rom. 1 and 5; Eph. 3 and 4).

Let them not, therefore, be ashamed because of a humble and crucified human being—those who await God, the Lord of hosts. For he who appeared despised in the flesh will appear powerful and glorious in divinity (Phil. 2).

Therefore it is further added:

**Let those who seek you, God of Israel, not be confounded because of me.** Let them not be confounded in mind or ashamed in face because I have been killed—those who await your coming and, moreover, do not cease to seek you by living well and loving.

This should protect them from confusion and shame: you, who sent me and willed that I be humbled, are the Lord of hosts and the God of Israel—that is, you are the same Lord and God of angels and human beings.

By the name “hosts” he designated the angels. By “Israel” he represented those who spiritually see God through faith and charity.

He shows another reason why they ought not to be ashamed when he adds:

**8. Because for your sake I endured reproach; confusion covered my face.** Reproach is what an enemy casts at someone. It would not be remarkable that he says, “I endured,” unless he added, “for your sake.” If you endure because you have sinned, you endure for your own sake, not for God’s sake. “For what glory is it,” says Peter, “if you are punished for sinning and endure it?” (1 Pet. 4).

But if you endure because you have kept God’s commandment, a reward remains for you forever, because you endured reproaches for God’s sake.

Since Christ therefore heard many reproaches in his Passion and endured them all in silence for God’s sake, he appeared, as it were, ashamed in his face. They regarded the virtue of his meekness as a sign of confusion.

He has said what he endured for God’s sake. Now he shows from whom he endured it:

[Col. 0924B] **9. I have become a stranger, he says, to my brothers, and a sojourner to the sons of my mother.** Although the same thing may seem to be repeated with similar words, “sojourner” nevertheless conveys something more than “stranger.”

We call someone who is not a member of the household or known by face a stranger, even if he is from the same land. But we customarily call someone from another homeland a sojourner.

Christ had been a stranger to his brothers because he appeared unlike his carnal parents in life and conduct. He was also a sojourner, according to what he says: “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18).

We may also understand “brothers” as the Apostles and “the sons of his mother” as the sons of the synagogue. He was therefore a stranger to his brothers when he was no longer believed even by the Apostles themselves. He was a stranger to Peter when Peter began to affirm and swear that he did not know the man (Matt. 26; Luke 22).

He was also a sojourner to the sons of the synagogue, who said: “But we do not know where he is from” (John 9).

Why did these things happen to him?

**10. Because zeal for your house consumed me.** He was consumed by zeal for God—that is, he was burning inwardly—when he drove the buyers and sellers from the temple and poured out the money-changers’ coins (Matt. 21) [Ant. reads mentes, “minds,” for ementes, “buyers”].

No sacrifice is such to almighty God as zeal for souls. There the fire of God is kindled. There the pure mind is burned by the heat of holy zeal.

Hence the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove and fire (Matt. 3; Acts 2), because he makes those whom he fills both simple and ardent.

**And the reproaches of those reproaching you fell upon me because of this zeal.** Because he corrected them, they were all the more indignant against him and plotted his death. They could not inflict greater reproaches upon God than by denying Christ, his Son. No one reproached Christ without reproaching God, and no one honors the Father except one who also honors the Son.

Those reproaches, according to Augustine, fell upon Christ when those who reproached him killed him. But amid these things the pious Lord commends his meekness when he adds:

**11. And I covered my soul in fasting.** Christ’s fast was commended spiritually in another Psalm [XXXIV]. His fast was when all those who believed in him failed, according to the same source. His thirst was when he said to the woman: “I thirst; give me something to drink” (John 4). For he thirsted for her faith; and from the cross, when he said, “I thirst” (John 19), he was seeking their faith.

Finally, he refused the gall that they offered him (ibid.). He chose to fast rather than to receive bitterness. For bitter things do not enter his body.

And in this fast I covered—that is, humbled—my soul. Humility was Christ’s covering. For because he was humbled, he was not recognized. This very thing became a reproach to him. The humbler he was, the more despised he was considered among the reprobate.

**12. And I made sackcloth my clothing.** I offered them something against which they might rage: my flesh.

[I concealed my divinity. Penitent sinners are clothed in sackcloth.]

And in a certain sense it became the garment of sin, because “from sin he condemned sin in the flesh” (Rom. 8). Not because Christ’s flesh was sinful, but because it bore the likeness of sinful flesh.

And because of this I also became a proverb to them. A proverb, according to Augustine, is a likeness given concerning someone when a curse is directed against him: for example, “May he perish as that man did.” This is a proverb—that is, a comparison and likeness of a curse:

[Col. 0925B] **13. Those who sat at the gate spoke against me.** That is, in public. Where there is idleness, there is loquacity. They spoke against me publicly. They publicly opposed me. They defamed me before everyone.

**And those who drank wine sang against me.** Even sinners themselves mocked me.

Consider, O human being, what God endured for you. Consider in your Head the rule of discipline and the pattern of virtue. “Learn from me,” he says, “because I am meek and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11).

Amid so many scandals and reproaches, amid such great persecutions and tribulations, what were you doing, most gentle Jesus?

**14. But I directed my prayer to you, O God.** They mocked; he prayed (Luke 23). They attacked; he loved. “Not repaying,” he says, “evil for evil or cursing for cursing, but, on the contrary, blessing” (Rom. 12; 1 Thess. 5).

For this is the perfection of charity: to love enemies and pray for them (Matt. 5). When you are cursed and have no means of action; when reproaches are hurled at you and you are unable to correct them; nothing remains for you except to pray.

These are the weapons of the righteous: by praying, they conquer.

And because now is the time for praying and appeasing God (Eccl. 3), he therefore adds:

**It is the time of good pleasure, O God.** Behold, says the prophet, now is the acceptable time; behold, now are the days of salvation (Isa. 49; 2 Cor. 6).

For the fullness of time had come, in which God sent his Son into the world, in which God’s good pleasure was accomplished (Gal. 4), and through whom he gave his grace to the human race.

Hence he says: **In the abundance of your mercy, hear me, in the truth of your salvation.** For if there were not an abundance of your mercy, what would we do with the abundance of our iniquity?

Since, therefore, I directed my prayer to you, O God; since the time has come to fulfill your good pleasure by redeeming the human being whom you formed—for this reason hear me, not according to human merits, but according to the abundance of your mercy, and also according to the truth of your salvation, so that by granting the salvation that you promised you may appear truthful.

Two things are placed here: truth and mercy. In accordance with these he asks to be heard; in them too are all the ways of the Lord (Ps. 24). Mercy consists in forgiving sins; truth in fulfilling promises.

But let us now hear in what he wishes to be heard:

[Col. 0925D] **15. Rescue me from the mud, that I may not become stuck.** Here he asks to be delivered where he previously said that he was stuck. He explains whom he understands by “mud” when he adds:

**Deliver me from those who hate me, and from the depths of the waters.** Reprobate people are mud because they love the earth, and they are the depth of the waters because they are dissolved in the abyss of carnal pleasures.

He had therefore been caught in the flesh, according to Augustine, but he had not been caught in spirit. He says this from the weakness of his members.

When perhaps you are seized by one who presses you toward iniquity, your body is indeed held; according to the body, you are stuck in the mud of the deep. But as long as you do not consent, you have not become stuck. If you consent, you have become stuck.

Let your prayer therefore be offered there: since your body is already held, let your soul not be held. Hence it is further added:

**16. Let not the storm of water drown me.** It drowned him according to the flesh, according to the same source; let it not drown him according to the soul. **Nor let the deep swallow me**, that is, let iniquity not envelop me. **Nor let the well close its mouth over me.**

The well closes its mouth over a human being—that is, the depth of iniquity—when a person not only lies submerged in sins but also loses access to confession. Hence it is written: “When the sinner has come into the depth of evils, he despises” (Prov. 18).

But when a person says, “I am a sinner,” the depth of the well is illuminated by some light.

Then he gives the reason why he ought to be heard when he adds:

**17. Hear me, O God, because your mercy is gracious.** The mercy that is naturally in you is full of goodwill and grace. Nor do I ask to be heard only according to it, but also according to the multitude of your mercies, which you displayed to the ancient fathers: to Noah in the Flood, to Daniel in the pit, and to many others.

For the sake of your mercy and your mercies, hear me; and look upon me. One of these is naturally in you, while the others are shown through the bestowal of benefits.

Look upon me, I say,

**18. And do not turn your face away from your child as though angry,** that is, from your little one. He says this to commend such a person, for God is the lover of such people. “Let the little children come to me,” he says, “for of such is the kingdom of heaven” (Mark 10).

Our Lord is called a child because of purity, simplicity, and innocence. He also wants us to be such. Hence he says: “Unless you turn and become like this little child, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18).

He gives another reason, saying: **For I am afflicted; hear me quickly.** Let your mercy move you; let my misery move you. Tribulation presses upon me. Therefore your consolation must come quickly. Hear me quickly.

When the Lord permits or causes us to be in some tribulation, even then he is merciful. For he does not remove nourishment; rather, he arouses desire.

There is no longer any reason for you to delay. My tribulation has reached the fixed measure of calamity. Let your mercy come to perform the work of goodness.

I said, “Do not turn your face away,” but rather:

[Col. 0926C] **19. Attend to my soul and deliver it,** that is, look carefully within to see what virtue of meekness and what purity of intention are in my soul, so that this may be the merit of my deliverance.

And deliver me not only for my sake, but also for the sake of my enemies. For it would be exceedingly unworthy if they were to rejoice in my Passion as though they had conquered.

Or, deliver me for the salvation of my enemies, so that when they see my deliverance and glorification, they may turn from error and be saved.

And you ought to deliver me, for you know how much I have endured for your love.

**20. You know my reproach,** that is, how shameful the words they brought against me were; **and my confusion**, which they attributed to me; **and my disgrace**, how dishonorably they treated me.

To be ashamed of the accusation of a false crime is not itself a crime. Or, even if it is a crime, it is not the crime of the person against whom it is brought. Nevertheless, the weakness of the human soul often feels shame even when something false is alleged—not because it has been alleged, but because it has been believed.

All these things are in the Lord’s body. You see me afflicted, and you also see those who afflict me.

**21. All those who afflict me are before your sight.** They afflict; I am afflicted. Between the two of us, you are the observer and judge (Matt. 16). Consider injustice in them and innocence in me, and repay each according to his merits.

And lest he seem to be afflicted as though he had not foreseen or known it, he immediately added:

**My heart expected reproach and misery.** My heart—that is, my will—foresaw reproach in words and misery in deeds. For unless he himself had foreseen and willed this, he would certainly not have been born, suffered, or died.

But whose misery did the Lord foresee? Surely the misery of those who afflicted and crucified him. In them was misery; in him was mercy. Hence, while hanging on the cross, he said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23).

Let all who afflict others therefore fear, because they are before God’s sight. They cannot escape his vengeance. And those who inflict evil remain themselves miserable. For those who suffer on account of righteousness are blessed (Matt. 5).

You have told us, merciful Lord, what you suffered outwardly. Make known also what anxiety you suffered inwardly. **And I endured one who would grieve with me, and there was none; and one who would console me, and I found none.**
