What does this mean? Were not the Apostles saddened by the Lord’s death? Does not Mary sit and weep at the tomb? Does not the Lord himself say to two disciples on the road: “What is this that you are discussing with one another as you walk, and why are you sad?” (Luke 24).

But they were saddened by the death of the flesh. The Lord alone was saddened by the death of the soul—that is, because all remained in unbelief. Therefore he did not say, “one who would grieve,” but “one who would grieve with me,” he says, “I endured,” that is, I awaited him, “and there was none.”

Many were carnally saddened, but no one was spiritually saddened except him alone. It would also have been a great consolation for him if he had found people believing in him. Because he did not find them, he groans as though complaining. Hence he further adds:

[Col. 0927B] **22. And they gave gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.** They gave me no other food or drink except vinegar mixed with gall. This was symbolic.

The Lord thirsted for their salvation, while they offered him bitterness and oldness. According to Augustine, those who live badly and bring scandal upon the Church still offer gall and vinegar to Christ.

For the Jews who crucified him while he walked on earth sinned less than those who despise him while he dwells in heaven. They offered him gall to drink; the Lord tasted it and did not wish to drink (Mark 15).

If we did not have to endure them, we would not even taste them. But because we must endure them, we must taste them. Yet because such people cannot be members of Christ, they can be tasted but cannot be received into the body.

And because they gave bad food, they were deservedly punished in the matter of food. Hence it is added:

### 23

“Let their table before them become a snare.” By “their table” he means Sacred Scripture, which God had prepared for them as nourishment for their souls. This table became a snare for them because they are caught and convicted of error by Christians from their own law. Why “before them”? For there are people of this kind who understand their iniquity and yet persist in it most obstinately: they know the snare, and offer their necks to be caught in it.

“And let it become a retribution for them,” so that they may receive evil in return for evil, and so that those who sinned through the law may be punished through the law. “Let it also become a stumbling-block.” For what greater stumbling-block could have befallen the Jews than that, later blinded by malice, they crucified God and their Savior, whom the law and the prophets had foretold? Hence Paul says: “We preach Christ crucified, a stumbling-block indeed to the Jews” (1 Cor. 1).

But when he says “Let it become,” he does not speak by way of wishing, but by way of prophecy—not that it should happen, but because it will happen. Nor can it be otherwise than that such things should befall people of this kind. When we hear through the Spirit of God that such things will happen to the wicked, let us understand these matters as applying to them so that we may avoid such things ourselves. Malice, I say, blinded them; and therefore he adds:

### 24

“Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see.” For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Cor. 2). The first sin is pride (Eccles. 10); the first punishment of sin is darkness of heart. Because they were proud, they were made blind. Hence it immediately follows: “And make their back continually bent.”

For this always follows: if the eye of the mind is deprived of the light above, the soul immediately inclines toward those things that lie behind and are to be desired. This is to have a bent back: to bend the posture of the mind toward lower things. Another punishment follows:

### 25

“Pour out your wrath upon them, and let the fury of your anger overtake them.” Wrath is poured out when the vengeance of almighty God is exercised against them in many ways. The fury of God’s anger is the future execution of vengeance. Thus “wrath” pertains to present punishment, while “fury” pertains to future condemnation. It is called “fury” because there will be no remedy there, no mercy there.

“Let it overtake them,” he says, as fugitives. For there will no longer be any place of escape when eternal torment has swallowed them up. Nevertheless, no agitation of wrath or fury is to be attributed to God; rather, according to human usage, he is called angry or furious when the guilt of sinners is struck by him so severely and strictly. Hence he continues:

### 26

“Let their habitation become desolate, and in their tents let there be no one who dwells.” By “habitation” he means the city of Jerusalem itself, in which they dwelt together. By “tents,” however, he designates each person’s individual houses, where they were able to cry out against the Lord.

There [according to Augustine] the Lord does not permit them to dwell. All those places are full of human beings, but empty of Jews. Why is this?

### 27

“Because they persecuted the one whom you struck, and they added to the pain of my wounds.”

We have been struck by God because we sinned, and our wounds are our sins. The pain of the wounds is affliction on account of sin. The stroke is mortality and corruption. The Son of God himself accepted this stroke, although he had not sinned. “Truly,” says the prophet, “he himself bore our infirmities, and he carried our pains” (Isa. 53).

But the Jews added to it, because the one whom God the Father had wounded with the blows of mortality and corruption, they killed in addition. Mortal human beings are born here with punishment, and this punishment is the Lord’s stroke. Whoever persecutes others adds to this punishment. And because they added pain to pain, observe the manifest justice that follows:

### 28

“Add iniquity upon their iniquity,” he says, “so that, as it is said elsewhere, ‘Let the one who does harm do harm still, and let the one who is filthy be filthy still’” (Rev. 22), “and so let them not enter into your righteousness.”

For guilt arouses guilt; and when one fault is not corrected, another is thereby generated. The more charity grows cold, the more iniquity abounds.

Or place the iniquity of the children upon the iniquity of the fathers, so that their iniquity may extend from generation to generation, just as they themselves said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27).

But what he says, “Add,” is not to be understood as though God places or adds iniquity in anyone, but as though he does this when he permits it to happen. For he does not destroy the human mind by conquering it, but by withdrawing from it; once abandoned, it is sufficient for its own destruction. Hence Solomon says: “Consider the works of God, that no one can correct the one whom he has despised” (Eccles. 7).

Therefore he continues:

### 29

“Let them be blotted out of the book of the living.” By the name “book” God’s predestination is understood, because just as what is written in a book remains fixed, so whatever is predestined by God is unchangeable.

How, then, does he say “Let them be blotted out,” if those who have been written cannot be erased? This was said according to the hope of those who thought that they had been written there.

What is “Let them be blotted out of the book of life”? [According to Augustine:] Let it become clear even to them that they are not there. Those who hoped that they had been written in God’s book as though by the merit of their own righteousness—those to whom it is said, “Search the Scriptures, in which you think that you have eternal life” (John 5)—when their condemnation has been brought to the knowledge of them also, will be blotted out of the book of life; that is, they will recognize that they are not there. I said “Let them be blotted out” according to their hope.

What, then, is meant by “according to your righteousness”? “And let them not be written with the righteous.” At the end of the verse he confirms what was stated at its beginning.

We have heard what we must beware of in the wicked; let us now hear what is to be imitated in Christ. They were such people, and so they perished. But you, gracious Lord, what do you say about yourself?

### 30

“But I am poor and afflicted; your salvation, O God, has received me.”

Let us learn from the example of our Lord to be poor and afflicted. “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. And blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5).

He first showed this very thing in himself for our sake; therefore he says, “I am.” His whole body says this. The body of Christ on this earth is poor and afflicted. Yet let Christians be rich: if they are truly Christians, they are poor. For in comparison with the heavenly riches that they hope for, whatever they possess here they regard as nothing.

Nor are such poor people forsaken, because God’s salvation has received them. So that they may no longer be poor and afflicted, but rather joyful and blessed, let them do what follows:

### 31

“I will praise the name of God with a song”—that is, with joy—“and, exulting within myself, I will magnify him with praise.”

These are my riches: namely, that with joy and gladness I should never cease praising and magnifying my God.

### 32

“And that praise will please God more than every legal sacrifice.”

He demonstrates this also by a part, when he adds: “More than a young bull producing horns and hooves.”

For such a bull was sought for sacrifice—one that would be young, yet so large that it would put forth horns and have strong hooves. This was done as a sign. Whoever is well instructed and rich in the praise of God ought to have horns with which to drive away the adversary, and hooves with which to stir up the earth; he is young because of the new life.

Perhaps some heretic contradicts him: let him be driven away by the horns of the New and Old Testaments. Another has an earthly understanding: let him be stirred up by the hooves of discernment and the strength of virtue.

Over this bull my praise will please you, in that eternity where the saints will praise you perfectly, without any contradiction.

### 33

“Let the poor see and rejoice.” Let them believe these things and rejoice in hope; and let them become poorer, so that they may deserve to be enriched.

And he turns to admonish them, saying: “Seek God, and your soul shall live.” God is the life of the soul. Are you seeking bread so that your flesh may live? Seek God, and your soul shall live.

How do you prove this?

### 34

“Because the Lord has heard the poor.” He heard none but the poor. If you wish to be heard, be poor.

Do not [according to Augustine] presume upon yourself, nor seek anything apart from your God. If you are a sinner, do not despair on that account.

“And he did not despise his prisoners”—those bound in sins by which they seemed to be rejected by God. God does not despise those prisoners who belong to him—that is, those who seek him through repentance and satisfaction.

### 35

“Therefore let the heavens and the earth praise him, the sea and all that creeps in them.”

Let man, the rational creature, praise God, and through man let every creature praise him, since the very forms and substances of things are given to man as a reason for praising his Creator and Savior.

Why should they praise him?

### 36

“Because God will save Zion”—that is, the Church that now beholds God through faith and will later contemplate him by sight (1 Cor. 13).

“And the cities of Judah will be built”—that is, souls confessing their sins. The beginning of good things is confession of sins, and the righteous person is first of all his own accuser (Prov. 18).

Therefore people must first confess their evils and be changed for the better in their conduct; and thus they will be built in the city of God. Hence the psalm is entitled for those who will be changed.

“And they will dwell there”—that is, in that blessed city, in that exalted Zion. They will not acquire it for an hour, but as an inheritance, so that they may possess it forever—not one single generation of the righteous, but through all successive generations.

### 37

“And the offspring of his servants”—that is, imitators of the faith—“will possess it.”

And because faith is of no value without love (Jas. 2), he immediately adds: “And those who love his name will dwell in it.” These are they who serve God not out of fear but out of love. They are the offspring, and they will dwell in it as in their inheritance. No one will inherit there except through love.

“God is love. And whoever remains in love remains in God, and God in him” (1 John 4). This is the end; this is the inheritance.

## Title of Psalm 69

### 1

The title of the following psalm reads: “For the end. A psalm of David, for remembrance, because the Lord saved me.”

“For the end”—that is, this psalm directs us toward Christ. It is attributed to David, that is, to Christ himself, or to any righteous person placed in tribulation. “For remembrance” means for consideration of remembrance, because, he says, “the Lord saved me.”

For one who remembers salvation and also the benefits that God bestowed upon the world—as was shown in another psalm—asks confidently to be delivered, although he is pressed by many evils.

Thus, in this psalm there is the voice of those in tribulation who are in danger amid sufferings, yet presume upon their head. They are the subject of the psalm. In the first part they ask God for their deliverance, and then for the conversion of their persecutors. In the second they exult in the Lord and magnify him. Finally they commend their poverty and need as an example to others; then they indicate that they have been helped and delivered by God.

They intend to exhort everyone to turn to God, and to make them secure concerning eternal good, even if they are pressed by evils; and, amid these things, not to lose confidence but to invoke the help of almighty God. Let us hear them, and let each one of us say from the affection of the heart what follows.

## Psalm 69

### 2

“O God, attend to my help. Lord, hasten to help me.”

You who are my God and my Lord, my Creator and Governor, attend mercifully to my help; help me swiftly. First observe the pressing need; then hasten the consolation of your aid.

When he says “to my help,” he shows that he performs something through free will and asks for divine assistance to cooperate with him. This little verse is to be said against all adversities and temptations. Both when we are afflicted and when we are active, we always need divine assistance.

Then he also prays for his persecutors, when he adds:

### 3

“Let those who seek my soul”—that is, in order to destroy it—“be put to shame because of their sins and stand in awe,” that is, fear you as judge.

This voice properly pertains to martyrs, who were sought for the purpose of being killed. And when they pray for their enemies, they indicate to us the perfection of charity. “Love your enemies,” the Lord says. “Do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Mark 5).

Therefore he continues:

### 4

“Let those who desire evil for me be turned backward and put to shame.”

At first [according to Augustine] there was the assault of the persecutors; now the malice of those who think evil remains. The Church has experienced distinct periods of persecution. An assault was made upon the Church when kings and rulers persecuted her. They came to believe; peace was granted to the Church, but the roar of the persecutors did not disappear. They turned their assaults, however, into thoughts.

It was said of these periods of the Church: “The sinner shall see and be angry; he shall gnash his teeth and waste away” (Ps. 111).

For these the martyr prays, as he also prayed for the former persecutors: that they may be turned backward—that is, that they may believe in Christ and follow him. Let them also be ashamed of the sins they have committed. For the more a sinner and penitent displays shame in recalling his offense, the more abundant grace he deserves from the Lord.

Did not the Publican prefer this, when he did not even dare to raise his eyes toward heaven? Therefore he is more justified by the Lord’s judgment than the Pharisee, whom presumption disfigured (Luke 18).

“Let those who say to me, ‘Good, good’”—that is, “Well, well”—“be turned backward, immediately putting on shame.” Likewise let those who flatter me be turned backward, ashamed of their evils. And let this happen immediately, so that their conversion may not be delayed. For a fault that is corrected quickly is easily amended.

In these three verses three classes of persecutors are identified: evildoers, malicious people, and flatterers. The first acts through deeds, the second through thought, and the third through speech.

The body of Christ is afflicted in these three ways. The wicked do not cease to inflict upon the good whatever evil they can. And when they cannot do the evil they wish, they do not cease to devise it in thought. And when they are unable—or unwilling—to harm openly, they do what they can by pretending, flattering, praising, and attracting others. These are the ones who say, “Good, good”; they deceive those whom they can with false praises.

Nevertheless, the Church prays for them, that they may be converted and that what follows may come to pass:

### 5

“Let all who seek you exult,” according to the body, “and rejoice,” according to the soul—not boasting in themselves, but in you, from whom they have the ability to rejoice and exult. For others do not possess in you the means of rejoicing or exulting.

“And let them always say, ‘Let the Lord be magnified.’”

Are you a sinner? “Let him be magnified,” so that he may call you. Do you confess? “Let him be magnified,” so that he may forgive. Do you now live righteously? “Let him be magnified,” so that he may govern you. Do you persevere to the end? “Let him be magnified,” so that he may glorify you.

Therefore let the Lord always be magnified. Let the righteous say this; let those who seek him say this. Whoever does not say this does not seek him.

Let those who love your salvation say this—that is, your Son. Salvation comes to them from him, not from themselves. Nor can those who do not love God the Son, through whom they were saved, worthily praise God the Father.

Let them say: “The Lord is great, who saved us so powerfully.”

But let each person say about himself what follows:

### 6

“But I am needy, begging for my salvation—or for that of others—and I am poor,” that is, insufficient in myself to seek it. Nevertheless I do not despair on that account, for God helps me, so that I may possess the salvation I desire.

Thus we ought to praise God: while we magnify him as best we can, we should judge ourselves weak and useless. He is abundant; we are needy. He is rich; we are poor. When we recognize these things, and, distrusting ourselves, place our trust in him alone, then God helps us as the poor and needy.

Therefore, turning familiarly in speech toward him whose help he possesses, he adds: “You are my helper”—in good things—“and my deliverer”—from evils—“you are, and there is no other.”

And this alone remains for me to ask: “Lord, do not delay,” but do what you are going to do, leading me into your glory.

Here he plainly indicates that he remembers God’s benefits, as the title announced. Let us also implore the help, deliverance, and glory of the Lord our God, and let us say to him with our whole heart: “Lord, do not delay.”

## Title of Psalm 70

### 1

The following psalm is entitled in this manner: “For the end. A psalm of David, of the sons of Jonadab and of the first captives.”

This title touches upon the history of how the sons of Jonadab were led away to Babylon in the first captivity (Jer. 35). Their father Jonadab commanded them not to drink wine and to dwell in tents.

Jonadab, whose name means “spontaneous” or “voluntary,” prefigured the Lord Christ, who commanded his sons and imitators not to drink wine (Luke 21)—that is, not to cling to earthly pleasure—and to become accustomed to dwelling in tents, that is, in the service of the Lord.

Christ freely submitted to the Lord, becoming obedient to God the Father even unto death (Phil. 2).

The title is explained as follows: This psalm is attributed to David himself, that is, to Christ, because Christ speaks in this psalm. It is a psalm, I say, of the sons of Jonadab—that is, of Christ’s imitators—because it works for their benefit; and of the first captives, because the sons of Christ, previously sons of Adam, were first led captive in captivity by the devil.

For, as the Apostle says, “the spiritual was not first, but the natural” (1 Cor. 15). In Adam we were natural, living in the flesh; in Christ, however, we are spiritual, that is, living by the Spirit.

The subject is every righteous person who hopes in the Lord. Many benefits of God toward one who hopes in him are described.

In the first part he asks to be delivered from evils so that he may praise God. In the second part, which begins, “Do not cast me away in the time of old age,” he asks that, just as God offered him his benefits in youth, so he may do so in old age, when the need is greatest. In the third part, which begins, “What great things you have done, O God; who is like you?”, he gives thanks for the benefits bestowed.

The true Jonadab invites us, his sons, to conformity with him, so that we may not drink wine and may dwell in tents, as explained above. And just as he was exalted through the humility of his obedience (Phil. 2), so may we deserve to be exalted by following the traces of his humility.

This is the intention. Throughout the psalm the grace of God is commended. He says, therefore:

## Psalm 70

### 2

“In you, Lord, I have hoped; and if now I am put to shame”—or, “I shall not be put to shame forever.”

By departing from God, man falls into sin and is put to shame. By approaching the Lord, he corrects himself and will not be put to shame forever. And so that he may not be put to shame, he asks, saying:

“In your righteousness deliver me and rescue me.”

There are two things that reduce us to slavery: sin, namely, and the punishment of sin. Therefore he now asks to be delivered from sin through righteousness, and to be rescued from the punishment of sin by passing from death to glory.

And rightly he says, “In your righteousness”—that is, righteousness given by you. For it is God who, through his grace, works righteousness in man without merits. He gives his faith, which is reckoned to us as righteousness (Rom. 4); and, through grace at work, this faith makes free the one who had been a slave through sin (John 8).

And because my merits would not be worthy to reach your height, therefore: “Incline your ear to me”—that is, condescend to me through your clemency—“and save me.”

This [according to Augustine] is a confession of humility. For whoever says “Incline to me” confesses that he lies prostrate, like a sick person fallen before a physician who is standing.

“Save me,” he says. How?

### 3

“Be to me a protecting God.” Let the arrows of the enemies not reach me, for I cannot protect myself.

And “a protector” is not enough; therefore he adds: “And a fortified place, so that you may save me.” This will be in the other life. For there we shall be secure, where no enemy will be able to attack us.

First, therefore, we must be protected here by God, where the battle is, so that afterward there may be a fortified place in which we are saved, where there is eternal rest. For what is more secure once you have fled to that place? What adversaries shall we fear there?

And therefore you must save me, because I have strength from no one except you. This is what follows: “For you are my strength and my refuge.”

From you and through you I am strong; and if anywhere I become weak in myself, I shall flee to you. The grace of Christ makes you firm and immovable against all the temptations of the enemy.

But human fragility is still present. The first captivity is still present; the law in the members, warring against the law of the mind, is still present (Rom. 7). And still “the corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wis. 9).

Therefore, however firm you may be through the grace of God, you must still fear the corruption of the flesh. “You are my strength,” then, so that I may be firm in this world against temptations. But if they are many and trouble me, “you are my refuge.”

And because above he said, “Rescue me,” he now specifies from whom, when he adds:

### 4

“My God, rescue me from the hand of the sinner”—that is, from the power of the devil, who is properly called “the sinner,” because he is the persuader of every sin.

You can rescue me because you are God; and you ought to, because through grace you have deigned to become mine.

And rescue me not only from the hand of the invisible enemy, but also from the hand of the one who acts against the law and of the wicked.

Here [according to Augustine] every kind of sinner is indicated: either a transgressor of the law, if he has received the law, or merely a wicked person without the law, if he has not received the law.

The Apostle speaks of both kinds, saying: “Those who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law, and those who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law” (Rom. 2).

Between both of them the body of Christ groans and is afflicted by both. It does not avenge itself, but patiently endures and prays. Hence he continues:

### 5

“For you are my patience, O God; O God, you are my hope from my youth.”

Therefore you ought to rescue me, because you are both the cause and the fruit of my patience. On your account I am gravely afflicted; on your account I endure patiently. You are not only my patience, but also my hope—that is, my certainty.

He rightly placed hope after patience, because certainty of hope is generated from the virtue of patience. Hence Paul says: “Tribulation produces patience, patience produces tested character, and tested character produces hope; but hope does not put to shame” (Rom. 5).

The more grievous things we endure here on God’s account, the greater rewards we hope for from the Lord in the future.

“My hope,” I say, “from my youth”—that is, from the time of my strength. For [according to Augustine] he does not speak of youth with reference to age, but with reference to strength of spirit.

“From my youth I began to hope in you,” from the time when you armed me against the devil, so that, fortified by faith, hope, love, and the other spiritual weapons, I might fight against adversaries both visible and invisible.

Not only from youth, but also:

### 6

“In you I have been strengthened from the womb; from my mother’s belly you are my protector.”

By the womb of the Church he means that preparation by which a person is instructed when he begins to believe. In that womb he is first spiritually formed, so that afterward he may be born into the light of true knowledge.

And you are also my protector from the womb of my mother, the Church—that is, from the time when I was reborn through baptism.

The whole passage commends divine grace, which works in us both to will and to work according to the good pleasure (Phil. 2). It is therefore just that he be praised for the benefits of his grace. Hence he rightly adds:

“In you is my song always”—that is, at all times, both in prosperity and in adversity, I shall praise you.

For this reason:

### 7

“I have become like a portent to many.”

Many lovers of the world think me mad and bizarre when they see me praising and desiring invisible things, which they despise, while avoiding through contempt the visible things that they themselves desire.

“And you have become my strong helper against all reproach.” For you supply spiritual strength to despise the insults of men.

### 8

Therefore: “Let my mouth be filled with praise.”

Before I existed, because you created me; when I existed, because you saved me; when I had sinned, because you forgave me; when I had turned back, because you helped me; when I had persevered, because you crowned me.

Thus, plainly, let my mouth be filled with praise, so that I may sing your glory and your greatness all day long. So that [according to Augustine], exulting, I may proclaim how glorious and how great you are.

And this “all day long”—that is, without interruption—both in prosperity, by which you console me, and in adversity, by which you correct me.

I say that you are my hope from my youth. And just as you do not abandon me in youth, so:

### 9

“Do not cast me away in the time of old age.”

And he determines what he means by old age, saying: “When my strength fails, do not forsake me.”

He calls the failure of strength “old age,” just as above he designated strength by the name “youth.” It is as though he says: Do not cast me away from you; do not permit me to sin through weakness. And if it should happen that I sin through frailty, do not abandon me completely, so that, failing in strength, I may persist in sin.

God cast Peter away when he permitted him to sin, but he did not abandon him, because he caused him to repent (Luke 22).

This verse cannot be read as spoken by Christ, asking the Father not to abandon him at the time of his passion, when his strength in miracles seemed to have failed. And it is necessary, he says, that you not abandon me,

### 10

“Because my enemies have spoken against me, and those who guarded my soul”—not in order to imitate it, but to destroy it—“have taken counsel together,” that is, in a single will to do harm.

They said: “God has abandoned him.” Hence the saying in the Gospel: “This man is not from God,” and “He has a demon” (John 9; 10).

### 11

Therefore: “Pursue and seize him. You can do this securely, because there is no one to rescue him.”

This was said concerning Christ. For he who, by the power of his divinity, had raised the dead suddenly became weak among the hands of his enemies and was seized as though he had no power at all.

But when would he have been seized, unless they had first said in their hearts, “God has abandoned him” (John 18)?

Against this he asks, saying:

### 12

“O God, do not be far from me; my God, look to my help.”

And so it is. God the Father has not been far from his Son; rather, he is always coeternal with him.

He is not far even from those who are brokenhearted; indeed, he is near to them (Ps. 33): near to hear, near to look upon them mercifully, near to help.

“The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous,” while “the face of the Lord is against those who do evil” (ibid.).

Nevertheless, he prays for such people when he adds:

### 13

“Let those who slander my soul be put to shame and fail.”

This benefits them, so that they may recognize their sins; therefore let those who presumed wickedly concerning themselves be put to shame and fail within themselves. Let those who seek evil for me be covered with great shame inwardly and with disgrace outwardly.

### 14

“But I will always hope.”

Whatever they do, however much they persecute me, I shall not be broken by any adversity, but shall always have firm hope in you.

“And I will add to all your praise.”

What does this mean? What can man add beyond all the praise of God?

But God had been praised in all his creation: in the governance of the ages, in the ordering of times, in the height of heaven, in the fruitfulness of the earth, in the surrounding sea, in the very children of men, in the giving of the law, and in all his other marvelous works.

He had not yet been praised in this: that he raised flesh to eternal life. Therefore praise of God is added beyond all previously existing praise when the incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven of his Only-begotten Son are proclaimed.

Hence he continues:

### 15

“My mouth will proclaim your righteousness.”

And he adds what he calls righteousness: “your salvation”—that is, your Son, who both saves those who hope in him and justifies them.

“And this all day long”—that is, throughout the whole time.

This is the praise that surpasses all praise: to proclaim the righteousness of God, by which the ungodly person is justified, and the salvation by which the condemned person is saved.

“And for this reason I proclaimed your righteousness: because I did not know learning [literaturam].” That is, I did not approve of the letter.

Concerning this Paul says: “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3).

For some people gloried not in grace but in the letter, because they had received the law (Matt. 5). The law without grace is merely the letter, and it remains to convict iniquity, not to give righteousness.

For if a law had been given that could give life, then righteousness would certainly have come through the law. But Scripture imprisoned everything under sin (Gal. 3), so that the promise might be given to believers through faith in Jesus Christ.

Glorying in this grace [according to Augustine], I did not know the letter—that is, I rejected with all my heart those who presumed upon the letter and recoiled from grace.

Therefore he rightly adds:

### 16

“I will enter into the powers of the Lord.”

For the spiritual person, when he does not cling to the letter, deserves through understanding to enter into the inner things of the Spirit, so that he may know the powers of the Lord—that is, the grace and virtues by which, no longer weakened by the flesh, he may powerfully fulfill the divine commandments.

Here also he commends the grace of God, not his own righteousness, when he immediately adds: “Lord, I will remember your righteousness alone.”

For some, ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish their own, have not submitted to God’s righteousness (Rom. 10). I acknowledge none of my own; I will remember your righteousness alone. Your righteousness alone delivers me; mine is nothing but sins.

I will not glory in my strength, lest I remain in letter-learning [literatura], but in your grace, through which, by working, I may fulfill the letter.

Nor does he attribute only the doing but also the very knowing to God, when he adds:

### 17

“O God, you have taught me from my youth, and until now.”

From the very beginning of faith, when you renewed me, until now [according to Augustine] you have taught me that I ought to remember your righteousness alone.

For when I consider my former life, I see what was owed to me and what I received in place of what was owed to me. Punishment was owed; grace was given. Gehenna was owed; eternal life was given.

From the time when I was converted, I learned that no merits of mine preceded, but that your grace came to me freely.

Having been taught in this way, “I will proclaim your wonders”—that is, I will preach to others what you have wondrously accomplished.

For what is more wondrous among God’s wonders than that the Creator himself became a creature? God assumed human nature. By his blood he redeemed the lost human being and led him from death to life, from the world to glory.

These are the wonders I will proclaim, which you taught me from my youth.

And just as you, merciful Lord, have begun to act up to this point, so do not cease to act until the end. This is what follows:

### 18

“And even unto old age and gray hairs, O God, do not forsake me.”

You helped the strong; do not abandon the weak.

In the time of the Apostles and martyrs, the Church was young: strong in virtue, patient in tribulation, and perfect in wisdom. But now, because charity grows cold, wisdom diminishes, and strength fails, she has begun, as it were, to enter old age.

In the time of Antichrist she will fall into extreme old age, when her strength will have been so diminished that, if possible, even the elect will be led astray (Matt. 24).

Therefore Christ’s Church asks that, just as from her youth she has been governed by the grace of almighty God, so she may be governed by the same grace until the end.

“Until my old age and my gray hairs”—that is, until my final day, until the end of the age—“may your grace persevere with me.”

“Until I proclaim your arm”—that is, your Son—“to every generation that is to come.”

Hence elsewhere it is said: “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. 33; John 12; Rom. 10).

Christ is called the arm of the Lord because he is the power and strength of God, through whom all things were made and by whom the power of the devil is overcome.

This arm is proclaimed to every generation, so that, by believing in the Lord Jesus Christ, they may remain strong and, trusting in such great power, may overcome the devil and vices with strength.

19. “I will proclaim,” he says, “not my own powers or righteousnesses, but your power and your righteousness, O God, which extend to the highest places, you who have done great things”—that is, to the very heavenly powers, which you created far more wondrously than your other works. God’s great works are the Angels, Thrones, Dominations, Principalities, and Powers. These very great works owe you the fact that they exist, that they live justly, and that they live blessedly. Not only human beings are governed by God’s grace, but also those highest and eternal powers. Hence he exclaims in wonder, saying: “O God, who is like you?”—understand: in doing great works?

The first angel wished to be like you, and he fell (Isa. 14). The first human being also wished to be like you, when the serpent said to him, “And you shall be like gods” (Gen. 3), and he lost his dignity. Yet humanity is read to have been made in the likeness of God (Gen. 2), and the Lord himself invites us to his likeness, saying in the Gospel: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you, so that you may be sons of your Father” (Matt. 5). And the Apostle says: “We shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3).

In what, then, did the human being sin, if he wished to be what God had made him to be? He wished this perversely: just as God has no one by whom he was formed and no one by whom he is governed, so he himself wished to be in his own power, without a lord and without a ruler, so that he might use his own will. Yet he could also have wished this without sin—namely, that he should be like God. For whoever wishes to be like God in such a way that he remains attached to him, guards his strength from him, and, clinging to him, is marked by him like wax by a seal-ring, possesses his image, doing what has been said: “But it is good for me to cling to God” (Ps. 72).

Such a person preserves the likeness and image in which he was made, and he does not sin. But because the human being first scorned doing this, he now cries out as a captive: “O God, who is like you?” I perversely wished to be like you, and I became like an animal. Under your dominion, under your command, I was truly like you. “But the human being, when placed in honor, did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48). And because he touched what was forbidden, he found punishment. Hence, groaning, he adds:

20. “How many evil and numerous tribulations you have shown me!” Evil was shown to the human being through experience. Hence it is written: “And their eyes were opened” (Gen. 3). For they came to know that they had sinned. The inner eyes, by which they saw spiritual good, were closed; and the outer eyes were opened to experience evil. Who, however, can say or imagine how many and how great are the tribulations and anxieties that wretched humanity sees and feels in this mortality and corruption? They are evil for this reason: they cannot exist without guilt. Yet they become discipline, and are admonition, not abandonment. For he immediately adds: “And turning, you gave me life.”

As though, after anger, turning toward mercy, you gave life to the human race, which had died in its first parent. For just as all die in Adam, so also all shall be made alive in Christ (1 Cor. 15). “And from the abysses of the earth”—that is, from the depth and engulfment of sin—“you brought me back again.”

What does “again” mean? God does not bring us back from sins only once, but now through baptism, now through penitence, now through conversion; and thus we are brought back to salvation in many different ways. We repeat our guilt; the merciful Lord repeats his mercy toward us.

Alternatively, by “the abysses of the earth,” that is, sins that plunge us into destruction, God brought back the human race: first through faith, and again through sight; now by living rightly, and again by enjoying eternal blessedness. We have risen in mind, faith, hope, and charity. It remains that we rise also in body. And because we already possess this in hope, it is rightly said: “And from the abysses of the earth you brought me back again.” But for me, thus brought back,

[Col. 0936B]

21. “You multiplied your magnificence”—that is, in many ways you bestowed great and manifold gifts of virtue. “And turning,” through the mediator Christ (1 Tim. 2), “from the anger” that you held against the human race on account of sin, “you consoled me,” making me secure concerning the eternal promise.

And because, according to Augustine, he had spoken of two restorations—one according to the spirit, already in reality, and the other according to the body, in hope—he commends these two when he adds:

22. “For I too will confess your truth to you in the vessels of the psalm, O God.” This concerns the spirit. For the psalterium sounds from above; it is, as it were, a certain spiritual vessel in which psalms are contained and in which the Lord’s truth is proclaimed to his honor. The vessels of the psalm are instruments on which psalmody is performed, and they signify the enlivening of the spirit.

What of the body? “I will sing to you on the lyre, O Holy One of Israel.” The lyre produces its sound from the lower part. “I will sing to you on the lyre”—that is, in the mortification of the flesh. To you, I say, who are the Holy One of Israel—that is, who sanctify those who are spiritually Israel, that is, who see God. And therefore:

23. “My lips shall rejoice when I sing to you, and my soul, which you have redeemed.” Saint David was so certain of the redemption of his soul that he already called accomplished what he foresaw in the spirit as future. He does not say, “And the soul which you will redeem,” but “my soul, which you have redeemed.”

Therefore, while he sings to the Lord, he rejoices not only with his outward lips but also inwardly in his soul. For one ought to praise God in such a way that the mind agrees with the voice, so that the Apostle’s saying may be fulfilled: “I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing also with the mind” (1 Cor. 14). Nor will my lips alone sing out:

24. “But my tongue shall meditate on your righteousness.” That is, it will meditate on how my soul was redeemed and justified by you, not by any merits preceding on my part, but solely by your gratuitous mercy.

When will it meditate on this? “In the end, when those who seek evil for me have been confounded and put to shame.” According to Augustine, they will be confounded and ashamed in two ways: either when they believe in Christ, or when Christ comes. For all the dead will rise (1 Cor. 15), each with his own cause; the good will be separated to the right, but the wicked to the left. Then those who previously rejoiced will be confounded, and those who chattered will be ashamed, when it is said to them: “Go into eternal fire” (Matt. 25).

It should also be noted that he does not say, “And my tongue shall speak,” but “shall meditate.” For then tongues will cease (1 Cor. 13), because in that blessed life the desires and thoughts of all will be visible to one another.

## TITLE OF PSALM LXXI

1. A Psalm of David, concerning Solomon.

This treatise tends toward Christ, who is the true Solomon—that is, the peaceful one—who established peace between God and the human race (Eph. 2). In this psalm Christ is its subject according to both natures, namely, the divine and the human.

In the first part, he asks that judgment be given to him and affirms that he will have it. In the second part, which begins, “Justice shall arise in his days,” he speaks about the kingdom, commending that kingdom in many ways. In the third, which begins, “Let his name be blessed,” there is a commendation of the king himself.

He intends to admonish us to submit to this Solomon. It is the voice of the Prophet foreseeing Christ as the future king, who prophesies in prayer that the kingdom be given to him, saying:

## PSALM LXXI

2. “O God, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king’s son.”

The Lord confirms this concerning himself when he says in the Gospel: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5). He is also the king’s son, because God the Father is certainly king; and he himself established his incarnate Son as king over his people, so that he might rule them spiritually according to righteousness and judgment, according to good morals and virtues, and place them eternally in his heavenly kingdom.

It is as though he were saying: O God the Father, give to Christ the King your judgment over human beings, so that, just as you have the power to judge, he may have it also. And to this king’s son—that is, to the son of you, who alone are king and who truly rule your own—give your righteousness, that is, righteous judgment, because that king will always judge just judgments.

[Note: [Col. 0937D] From the Greek, Ἓν διὰ δίς.]

It is an *hendiadys*, because he says the same thing through different expressions. In this passage, righteousness and judgment are the same; they signify nothing other than righteous judgment.

“Give him the power to judge your people in righteousness”—that is, so that he may judge everyone justly, both good and wicked. Nor should it trouble anyone that he says “your.” Even the perverse are his, and they can do nothing except by God’s permission.

Similarly, “your poor in judgment”—understand, give him the power to judge them. Christ judges the good and the wicked in this life. He will also judge them afterward, when he separates the wicked from the good (Matt. 25).

It should be noted that, when he said “the poor,” he immediately added “your,” thereby designating the true poor. For not all poor people are God’s poor, but their own poor, because they are not humble but proud. There are also some rich people who more readily give all they possess to the poor than the poor themselves do.

Therefore, to designate his poor, the Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5). He does not say “poor in possessions,” but “in spirit,” because this is the blessed poverty acceptable to God, in which there is no presumption of spirit. Christ will judge and save such poor people in the future judgment, because, as it is said elsewhere: “The patience of the poor shall not perish forever” (Ps. 9).

Nor merely give him judgment, but cause him to be proclaimed throughout the whole world by your preachers. This is what follows:

3. “Let the mountains receive peace for the people, and the hills righteousness.”

The mountains in the Church are those who are eminent in outstanding holiness and are capable of teaching others (2 Cor. 3). Let these mountains receive peace to be preached to the people, just as the Lord commanded them: “Into whatever house you enter, first say, ‘Peace to this house’” (Luke 10).

The hills are the lesser ones. Let them receive righteousness—that is, obedience, which is in human beings and in every rational creature the origin and perfection of all righteousness.

Alternatively, by the mountains and hills may be understood both kinds of preachers of evangelical peace, whether those who came before or those who followed. Let them receive peace and righteousness—that is, Christ, who makes us peaceful toward God and justifies us through faith (Col. 1)—and let them proclaim him to the people.

First he asks, and then affirms that Christ will truly have judgment. Hence he also says:

4. “He shall judge the poor of the people”—that is, the true and spiritual poor—“separating them from the people,” just as the Lord said to his disciples: “I chose you out of this world.”

“And he shall save the sons of the poor”—that is, imitators of the Apostles—“and he shall humble the slanderer”—that is, he shall crush the devil, who is the unjust accuser of our brethren.

He was humbled because the one whom he had killed rose again and took away the kingdom of death. The devil held its power in such a way that, through the one human being whom he had deceived, he dragged all people through death to condemnation. But he was humbled, because, if through one person’s offense death entered the world (Rom. 5), much more shall those who receive an abundance of grace reign in life through Christ, who humbled the slanderer.

5. “And he shall remain with the sun”—that is, with the divinity. It is called the sun because, through true knowledge of righteousness, it illumines the soul, once the slanderer has been humbled. He remains with the sun because, after conquering the devil through the resurrection, he sits at the right hand of the Father, where he no longer dies, and death shall no longer rule over him (Rom. 6).

“And this before the moon.” He is like the firstborn from the dead, going before the Church, which wanes and grows by turns.

“From generation to generation.” Or he refers to the generation by which we are born mortally. Then he announces the incarnation of the divinity when he adds:

6. “He shall descend like rain upon a fleece.”

For what is done as silently and without disturbance as when rain descends upon fleece (Judg. 6)? It strikes no one’s ears with sound. It sprinkles no one’s body with the moisture of beaten-down dew; rather, without disturbing anyone, it pours the whole rain through its many permeated parts. Through the entire body, knowing no division or fissure, its solid softness provides many passages; and what seems closed because of its density is open because of its fineness.

We therefore rightly compare Mary to fleece. She conceived the Lord in such a way that she drew him in with her entire body and suffered no rift in that body; she was soft in obedience and firm in holiness. Rightly, therefore, Mary is compared to fleece, from whose fruit garments of salvation are woven for the peoples. Mary is plainly fleece. For from her soft womb came forth the Lamb, who himself, bearing the wool of his mother—that is, the flesh—covers the wounds of all peoples with soft fleece.

Every wound of sin is drenched with Christ’s wool and warmed by Christ’s blood; and in order to recover health, it is clothed in Christ’s garment. And because “from his fullness we have all received” (John 1), it is fittingly added: “And like drops falling upon the earth.”

Since the whole divinity poured itself into Mary, he descended like rain upon fleece; since, through the divisions of graces, he poured himself over the Church, he descended like drops falling upon the earth.

Gideon, about to go into battle, asked the Lord for a sign of the outcome of the war (Judg. 6). He therefore placed fleece upon the earth; it appeared wet at first and afterward dry. The earth, however, was first dry and afterward wet.

Christ is understood as the rain, Judea as the fleece, and the multitude of the Gentiles as the earth. First the rain fell upon the fleece: Christ first descended into Judea. The earth was dry because the people of the Gentiles were still ignorant and unbaptized. But would it always remain dry? No. Once the fleece had been shaken out, Christ’s name was spread through all the lands. Thus from the fleece into the earth, from Judea into the Gentiles, Christ’s name and the teaching of heavenly dew flowed.

And what benefit will there be from Christ’s coming?

7. “In his days righteousness shall arise, and an abundance of peace.”

This was also fulfilled according to the letter. At the time when the Lord was born, the whole world rested under the rule of one region. Spiritually, however, peace and righteousness arose in his days: sinners were made righteous, and those who were at odds were made peaceful.

“In his days righteousness arose”—that is, the grace of faith by which the elect are justified. It is rightly said, “and an abundance of peace,” because throughout the whole world there will be abundant reconciliation, and people from every quarter will be reconciled to God.

This peace will persevere among the saints “until the moon is removed”—that is, until the present Church becomes immortal and incapable of suffering. For what is “until the moon is removed” except “until it comes about that it no longer exists”? Namely, the abundance of peace will be brought to such a point that opposition and rebellion will be utterly destroyed, and peace will increase to such an extent that, with death completely conquered, an unshaken concord and undivided unity will be possessed forever between flesh and spirit, and between human beings and God.

Then he shows the extent of the kingdom when he adds:

8. “And he shall rule from the eastern sea to the western sea, and from the river Jordan to the ends of the world, throughout the whole circuit of the earth.”

Through the river Jordan, in which Christ was baptized, we have received baptism, through which Christ is spread throughout the whole world.

9. “Before him the Ethiopians shall fall, and his enemies shall lick the earth.”

Through the Ethiopians, according to Augustine, he signified the whole by a part, choosing the nation situated at the ends of the earth as the one he would name most prominently.

“They shall fall,” he says, “before him”—that is, they shall adore him. “And the enemies of God shall lick the earth” when Jews, heretics, and pagans take delight in the teaching of the Apostles. For the Apostles are the salt of the earth (Matt. 5).

The enemies of God shall also lick the earth when they try to deceive the saints with the blandishments of falsehood and flattering words.

10. “The kings of Tharsis and the islands shall offer gifts; the kings of Arabia and Sheba shall bring presents.”

The Magi, led by the star (Matt. 2), fulfilled this bodily as well; and the kings and princes of the whole earth still do not cease spiritually to imitate them each day.

*Tharsis* is interpreted as “exploration of joy” or “contemplation.” For some who come from an exploration of joy, having tested and despised the empty happiness of this world, make themselves kings by ruling their carnality rationally, and offer themselves as gifts to the Lord the King.

By the islands—which are dry land surrounded by the sea—we understand those who are dry with respect to the waves of this world. They are not at all submerged by its storms, although they are battered on every side by its tempests. Such islands offer gifts because they attribute the good works they perform to the Lord.

*Arabia* is interpreted as “humility.” *Sheba* means “burning.” The humble, and those who set their vices aflame within themselves, likewise, having become kings, bring themselves as gratuitous gifts to the Lord.

For it is customary to bring those things that are able to walk. Is this said concerning victims to be sacrificed? Far be it that such righteousness should arise in his days! Rather, by these gifts that are proclaimed as being brought to the Lord, faithful people are signified—people whom the authority of kings brings into the fellowship of Christ’s Church.

11. “And all kings shall adore him”—those who previously used to be adored, that is, some from every class of kings—“and all nations,” which previously used to serve earthly kings, “shall serve him,” namely, our heavenly King. And rightly so,

12. “Because he shall free the poor from the powerful.”

According to Augustine, the one called “powerful” here is he who above was called the slanderer. What made him powerful for subjecting human beings to himself and keeping them in bondage was not his own virtue, but human sins.

But he who humbled the slanderer and entered the house of the strong man in order to bind him and plunder his goods (Luke 11) freed the poor from the powerful, and the poor man who was so desolate and miserable that he had no helper. Neither any righteous human being nor any angel could accomplish this. They could not be freed through free will either, except solely through Christ.

And how will he free them?

13. “He shall spare the poor and the needy.”

The poor person is one who has nothing. The needy person is one who requires another’s help. The pious King will not condemn this poor and needy person, empty and abandoned with respect to virtues and good works, according to his own merit; rather, he will spare him by releasing him from punishment and forgiving his guilt.

And thus: “He shall save the souls of the poor,” while the souls of the rich have been handed over to demons.

And how will he save the souls of the poor?

14. “He shall redeem their souls from usuries and iniquity.”

For they will no longer practice either usury or iniquity. Or, alternatively, “from the usuries and iniquity of the devil.” For he is the worst moneylender: to some he lends lust, to others greed, and to others pride. After sinners have been exercised in these things, they repay their soul to the devil as interest.

The devil’s money is iniquity, which we received from him. On this money he demands interest from us—that is, punishments that we did not receive but nevertheless pay.

The souls of the poor are redeemed from these usuries and from this iniquity by that blood which was poured out for the remission of sins.

“And thus their name became honorable before him.” For now, according to Augustine, he does not remember by his lips the names by which they were previously called—idolaters, adulterers, or murderers—because, abandoning the vices by which they were marked with such names and turning to Christ, they received a new name, so that they might be called Christians by Christ (Acts 11).

This name is certainly honorable before him, even if it is considered contemptible before his enemies. Hear also another honorable name, full of every delight, which the merciful Lord himself deigned to give his disciples, saying: “I shall no longer call you servants, but my friends” (John 15¹).

The commendation of this king follows, concerning whom he says:

15. “And he shall live.”

For he will not remain in death, as the Jews supposed, but will rise from the dead. “And he shall live forever,” as the Apostle clearly says: “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer rule over him” (Rom. 6).

“And gold from Arabia shall be given to him.” For many of the wise among the Gentiles will be converted to him. Alternatively, the gold of Arabia signifies wisdom in humility. We have said that Arabia is interpreted as “humility.” Nothing more precious or valuable than this treasure can either be possessed or offered to God.

“And they shall adore him continually”—that is, they shall honor him with the highest and singular veneration. And the fact that they adore him “shall proceed from him”—that is, from his gift. For “we do not know how to pray,” but the Holy Spirit intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings (Rom. 8). If anyone prays well, he has it from him. From him they draw whatever good they possess.

Rightly, therefore, “all day”—that is, continually—they shall bless him, giving thanks and attributing their good things not to themselves but to the Lord.

Another reason is also shown why he should be blessed, when it is added:

[Col. 0940C]

16. “There shall be a firmament upon the earth.”

For “all the promises of God have been confirmed in him” (Gal. 3). Whatever was prophesied for our salvation has been, or will be, completely fulfilled in him. Faithful souls also, placed upon this earth, have no other firmament except Christ. He is a firmament for those who fear him.

Behold, he is a firmament. Is he also high? Certainly. For “he shall be lifted above the summits of the mountains”—that is, among those mountains that are higher than others, when Christ comes, he alone will appear higher than all (Matt. 24).

Hence another Prophet says: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the summit of the mountains” (Isa. 2). For if other mountains are exalted in holiness, our Lord is exalted above them in divinity.

Behold, he is a firmament, and high. Is he also fruitful? Yes: “His fruit shall be above Lebanon.”

According to Augustine, we usually understand Lebanon as the dignity of this world, because Lebanon is a mountain containing lofty trees, and its very name is interpreted as “whiteness” or “splendor.” What wonder, then, if the fruit of Christ is lifted above every splendid height of this world, since the lovers of that fruit have despised all the summits of worldly things?

If, however, we understand Lebanon in a good sense, on account of the cedars of Lebanon that he planted, what other fruit is to be understood as rising above Lebanon except that of which the Apostle speaks when he is about to discuss charity: “I show you a still more excellent way”? For this is also placed first among the divine gifts, where he says: “The fruit of the Spirit is charity.” From there the remaining gifts are woven together in succession.

It is fittingly added: “And they shall flower from the city like the grass of the earth.”

The city in this passage designates the society of this world. Thus Christ’s fruit is exalted above Lebanon—that is, above enduring trees and imperishable wood, because that fruit is eternal. All human splendor according to the temporal loftiness of the world is compared with grass, because believers who already hope for eternal life despise temporal happiness, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “All flesh is grass” (Isa. 40), “and all its glory is like the flower of grass. The grass withers, and the flower falls; but the word of the Lord remains forever.”

And because of all these benefits:

17. “Let his name be blessed forever”—that is, as far as human beings are concerned, let the fame and glory of his name increase, and let it be proclaimed and magnified here and forever, ever more and more.

It is rightly to be blessed, because his name also endures “before the sun”—that is, before all times. He does not mean the name as a word that passes away, but the divine substance is understood here, which is signified by the name. And it follows that whoever blesses God is blessed by God.

Holy Isaac showed this when, in a figure of Christ, he blessed his son and said: “Whoever blesses you shall himself be blessed” (Gen. 27). Hence it is said to Abraham: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22).

Therefore it is rightly said now: “And all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed in him.”

Tribes are called, as it were, curiae, though improperly. The Lord God commanded his people to be divided among different tribes (Num. 34; Josh. 13 and 14), and holy Jacob blessed his sons according to their different tribes (Gen. 50).

The different tribes in God’s Church designate elect souls according to their different merits; hence there are also “many dwelling places in the Father’s house” (John 14).

It is as though he were saying: Not only will he himself be blessed, but all his people through him. Hence rightly, “all nations shall magnify him”—not by making him great, for he is great through himself, but by praising him and proclaiming his greatness.

Therefore, on his own behalf, he blessed God, saying:

18. “Blessed is the Lord God of Israel, who alone does wondrous things.”

For whoever performs anything does not do it by himself, but the Lord does it through him.

19. “And blessed is the name of his majesty forever.”

By the name of his majesty is understood the glory of his divinity.

Why, when he said “the God of Israel,” did he not rather say “the God of all human beings,” or “the God of the whole creation”? Because he intends to commend God according to grace. Later he commends him according to power, where he added the name of his majesty. For this reason he immediately adds: “And the whole earth shall be filled with his majesty.”

Here it should be noted that, although almighty God fills all things through the power of his divinity, he nevertheless fills certain things in a special way through the grace of his indwelling. Hence, as we have said above, he was called the God of Israel in order to commend his grace, because he specially chose this nation for himself. Concerning this, another Prophet says: “I shall dwell among them and walk among them, and I shall be their God, and they shall be my people” (Lev. 26).

Thus he placed four blessings in these four verses. The first concerns the eternity of God. The second concerns the blessing of the nations in him. The third concerns the spiritual grace bestowed upon Israel, in which he also proclaimed God alone to be wondrous, because in this work of grace he proved far more wondrous than in his other works. The fourth concerns the glory of his majesty, in which our blessedness and our end consist.

For the whole earth shall be filled with this majesty; the whole Church shall be filled with it. And from all these things, blessed be God. Let it be, let it be. Because he greatly desires it, he repeats the word.

## TITLE OF PSALM LXXII

Just as we enter a house by a key or a door, so through the meaning of titles we enter into the understanding of the psalms.

The title of this psalm is: “The hymns of David, son of Jesse, have failed; a Psalm of Asaph.”

[Note: [Col. 0941] In the Vulgate edition these words close Psalm LXXI and constitute verse 20; the title of Psalm LXXII then has only “A Psalm of Asaph.” EDIT.]

Hymns are songs containing the praise of God. If there is praise but it is not of God, it is not a hymn. If there is praise and it is of God but it is not sung, it is not a hymn. Therefore, if it is to be a hymn, it must have these three things: praise, praise of God, and song.

When he therefore said, “They have failed,” he appears to announce something distressing. For one who sings praise not only praises, but praises joyfully. One who sings praise not only praises, but also loves the one whom he sings about. In praise there is the proclamation of confession; in song, affection.

*Asaph* is interpreted as “synagogue” or “assembly.” The voice in this psalm is that of the synagogue, since the hymns of David have failed—not of David the Son of God, but of David the son of Jesse.

He added “son of Jesse” so that in this passage, as in the other psalms, Christ would not be understood through David; rather, through David would be understood the carnal Jewish people, over whom King and Prophet David presided.

The praises of this David—that is, of the carnal people—failed when the temporal goods by which the carnal people used to praise God failed. But why did those things fail, unless so that other and better things might be sought, things that cannot fail?

The subject is the faithful synagogue itself. In the first part, now as though confirmed, it praises God; previously it had almost gone astray in doubt. In the second part, which says, “This people of mine shall turn,” its conversion from what it had doubted is commended. In the third, which begins, “Nevertheless, because of their deceits,” it shows that this prosperity is deceptive and draws its lovers toward death. In the fourth, which begins, “For what is there for me in heaven?” it shows that it possesses true understanding and no longer seeks temporal things, but God alone.

The purpose is to restrain the simple, so that they do not murmur against God on account of the prosperity of the good or the adversity of the wicked, since it is certain that he is good and just in all things. Therefore he says:

## PSALM LXXII

1. “How good is the God of Israel.”

He is wonderfully and unspeakably good. Yet his supreme goodness is not known to everyone, but only to those who are upright of heart—that is, those who are neither puffed up by prosperity nor broken by adversity, and who understand God to be good and righteous in both circumstances.

Then he begins to disclose his former doubt for the confirmation of others, when he adds:

2. “But my feet were almost moved”—that is, the affections of my soul were almost moved away from God. “My steps were almost poured out”—that is, my works.

Our steps are poured out when we labor in pursuit of various earthly things. But when we labor only for eternal things, the steps of good action are no longer poured out; rather, they tend toward one thing, namely, God.

According to Augustine, “my feet were moved” toward error; “my steps were poured out” toward falling—not altogether, however, but almost. It is as though he were saying more plainly: I almost departed from God both in will and in action.

He says “almost” because he came to his senses. For if he had not come to his senses, he would have departed from God completely. But why did this happen?

3. “Because I was jealous of the wicked, seeing the peace of sinners.”

I saw that those who despised God possessed peace and flourished in riches. But I, who was a worshiper of God, lacked all these things. Therefore I was jealous of them. For this reason I was indignant; for this reason I envied them.

But now I see why they have this peace. Why?

4. “Because there is no regard for their death.”

There is no regard among them for divine mercy, by which they might be delivered from eternal death. Therefore they enjoy this temporal peace here, so that in the future they may be punished with everlasting condemnation.

“And there is no firmness in their affliction”—understand, there is none. He calls their affliction their guilt, in which there is no firmness—that is, no medicine of repentance or salvation.

5. “They are not in the labor of human beings, and they shall not be scourged with other people.”

That is, they do not labor as other human beings do, nor are they afflicted. For they are not among the sons of God, whom the merciful Father scourges so that he may receive them (Prov. 3).

Almighty God can never show greater anger toward a sinful human being here than when, in this life, he permits that person to prosper.

6. “Therefore pride took hold of them.”

Because they do not feel the scourges, they live arrogantly. For if they were scourged, perhaps they would be humbled. Pride therefore took hold of them, bound them, fettered them, and subjected them like captives and slaves.

Because of this continued captivity, they are “covered”—that is, completely filled—with iniquity as regards their neighbor, and with impiety as regards God.

O unhappy people, whom pride holds as though bound, and whom iniquity covers as though submerged! The source from which this proceeded is shown when he adds:

7. “Their iniquity came forth as though from fatness.”

That is, from abundance of riches, from the swelling of pride, from will and delight. From this it should be noted that iniquity does not always proceed from one and the same origin. Sometimes it comes from necessity; sometimes from abundance.

There are certain wicked people, according to Augustine, who are like those suffering from emaciation: thin, small, poor, and needy, afflicted by a kind of wasting caused by necessity. A poor person commits theft: iniquity has proceeded from emaciation. A rich person, abounding in wealth, seizes what belongs to others: iniquity has come forth as though from fatness.

When you say to the lean person, “Why did you do this?” he responds humbly, afflicted and abject: “Necessity compelled me.” If you say to the rich person, “Why are you doing this?” he scarcely deigns to listen and even despises you.

It is one thing to sin from necessity, and another to sin from abundance.

Behold, these people began from pride. Where did they arrive? “They passed over,” he says, “into the affection of the heart”—that is, as far as fulfilling their perverse desires.

8. What they did, they did not do without forethought, but as though through delay and filing, because they first thought about it among themselves for a long time; afterward they spoke to others, teaching their wickedness. And they did this not in secret, but openly.

Hence he adds: “They spoke iniquity in the high place.” Not with fear, but with boldness, clearly and openly, while everyone listened. Nor did they speak proudly and perversely of evil only against human beings; they also spoke against God.

9. “For they set their mouth against heaven,” blaspheming God and reviling the heavenly beings themselves. “And their tongue passed through the earth.”

First they transferred their tongue against heaven, and afterward against the earth, because first they spoke against Christ and afterward against the Church.

Alternatively, for their tongue to pass through the earth means that, having despised the heavenly Lord, they praise and magnify themselves in this life, as they said elsewhere: “We shall magnify our tongue; our lips are with us. Who is our lord?” (Ps. 11).

And truly their tongue passed through the earth in this respect: their loquacity exceeded the limits and measure of human nature, when they exalted themselves so far that they despised the idea that God was above them.

And because they went so far astray and reached such wickedness from their peace and prosperity, their condemnation became an occasion of conversion for others. Therefore he adds:

### 10

“Therefore this people of mine will turn back.” Here, he says, amid such blindness and such destruction as they incurred by loving riches, my people will turn back when they consider this rationally, through the zeal and envy they previously had on that account, lest they be punished with a similar condemnation together with the lovers of riches. “This people of mine will turn back,” he says—that is, when they have considered the destruction of the wicked. Or, “here,” that is, in this world, while the acceptable time for conversion and the day of salvation remain (2 Cor. 6). Concerning them he immediately adds: “And days full will be found in them,” namely, full of pardon, mercy, and grace. For “the fullness of time” came, in which God sent his Son onto the earth (Gal. 4). Or, in those who will turn here to God, days will afterward be found full of blessedness, full of eternity. Truly, days are full there where the Sun of righteousness shines, where divine and eternal splendor shines forth (Wis. 5; Mal. 4).

Next he explains how they first went astray and how afterward they were converted. For he says:

### 11

“And they said,” namely, thinking within themselves before their conversion: “How does God know?” That is: How can we know that he knows that the good are afflicted in this way and the wicked prosper? “And is there knowledge in the Most High?” If he knows this, how can he tolerate it? This is aposiopesis, that is, an incomplete statement, where something must be supplied for the sentence to be fully understood. Such was their error. For they thought that God either did not know human affairs or did not care about them, since the good were afflicted and the wicked flourished. Hence they subsequently say:

### 12

“Behold, these are sinners and prosperous in the world; they have obtained riches.” I, who serve God, am in need; they are sinners, and in the world they have obtained abundant riches.

### 13

“And therefore I too, joined to them before my conversion, said likewise: ‘So I have justified my heart without cause, that I might be pure in thought; and I have washed my hands among the innocent.’” That is, I purified my actions together with the innocent, and I did this without cause. Where is the reward of a pure conscience? Where is the prize of an innocent life? I live well and am in need; he sins and prospers.

### 14

“And I was scourged all day long.” The scourges of God do not depart from me. I serve well and am scourged; he does not serve and rests. These are dangerous, almost blasphemous words. He did not say, “God did not know,” but, as though asking, he hesitates and wavers. He did not say, as Augustine has it, “There is no knowledge in the Most High.” This is what he said shortly before: “But my feet were almost moved.” He does not affirm the proposition, but the doubt itself is dangerous.

Nevertheless, through danger he passes to healing; hence it is added: “And my chastisement is in the mornings,” that is, without delay. He is chastised when he is healed from error. The chastisement of the wicked is postponed; mine is not postponed. Theirs is late, or nonexistent; mine is “in the mornings.” Now hear the voice of the chastised. For he restrains himself from what he had said and, recognizing his error, says:

### 15

“If I said, ‘I will speak in this way,’ behold, I would reject the generation of your children.” For this to be understood more clearly, the punctuation should be arranged as follows: “I said, thinking within myself, ‘If I speak in this way,’”—namely, as I have spoken above, or as those who said, “How does God know?” and so forth—“behold, it is manifest and certain that I would reject the generation of your children,” that is, of your righteous ones.

“I am about to say something different from what Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the prophets said. For all of them said that God cares for human affairs; I am about to say that he does not care. Is there greater prudence or understanding in me than in them?” A most salutary authority recalled his thoughts from impiety. Therefore, lest he reject God’s righteous ones—or rather, so that he might come to share their sound judgment—he no longer stubbornly defended his error, but humbly confessed what he did not know. For it is no small advance in knowledge not to be unaware of one’s own ignorance. Hence someone says: “This one thing I know: that I know nothing.” And this is what follows:

### 16

“I considered this in order to understand it; it is labor before me.” I thought I knew the truth: why the wicked flourish and why the good suffer. But now, converted and chastised, I have recognized that this is labor before me.

What does “before me” mean? As long as I remain within myself, as long as I persist in carnal understanding, as long as I attend only to visible things, I cannot easily form a true judgment about earthly affairs. How long will this labor last?

### 17

“Until I enter the sanctuary of God, and understand their final destiny.” Until I pass in mind to spiritual understanding, and understand—that is, fix my understanding upon—their last things.

Therefore, to possess true knowledge of temporal affairs, two things are necessary for us. First, that we weigh eternal things with a good disposition. Then, that we carefully consider the end of those things that pass away. When both have been accomplished, it is easily understood that whatever is loved temporally is vanity (Eccl. 1).

Nothing other than the divine judgment can be understood as the sanctuary of God. Whoever enters it through reason considers with unwavering understanding that the omnipotent and just God permits the wicked to flourish in this world so that they may be punished more severely in the future. He wills the good to be afflicted temporarily so that, once purified, they may afterward rejoice eternally.
