Now, as though he had entered the sanctuary of God and had been spiritually instructed there, he recognizes not only what must be understood about their final destiny, but also indicates why good things are given to the wicked, when he adds:

### 18

“Nevertheless, because of their deceits you placed riches for them”—that is understood—“in which they trust and which they acquired through fraud and deceit.”

This must not be understood as though the omnipotent God, who is just and good, places these temporal goods before the wicked because of their deceits in order, by placing them there, to deceive them. Rather, in these goods—which the good God himself rightly bestows upon the wicked—their own ready will and perverse use corrupt them. For, having received earthly goods from the good God—goods by which they ought to have become better through prudent distribution and merciful generosity—they were instead corrupted by the fault of their own greed and pride and practiced fraud, deceit, envy, and other evils.

“Nevertheless,” he says, “because of their deceits you placed them for them.” Although I speak of their final destiny, you already punish them here in a certain way by a hidden judgment. Hence he adds: “You cast them down while they were being lifted up.” He does not say, “You cast them down because they were lifted up,” but that in the very thing by which they were lifted up, they were cast down. For to be exalted in this way is already to fall; and the more they are outwardly exalted and grow proud, the more they are inwardly blinded. The higher they climb, the more completely they vanish like smoke.

Therefore he adds in amazement:

### 19

“How they have become desolation!” For where there is pride, there is desolation. When the mind is lifted above every virtue, it is emptied of every fruit of good works. There is also great desolation where God is absent.

“For this reason they suddenly failed.” Honors are suddenly lost; power is quickly lost; loss suddenly arrives; whatever is possessed temporally is suddenly emptied. Hence we read in the Gospel concerning a certain man: “Fool, this night your soul will be taken from you” (Luke 21).

“And after they failed, they perished because of their iniquity.” This has often happened, and happens every day. Such is the fruit of riches. These are the final things understood by the one who has entered God’s sanctuary. They perish because of their iniquity—those who desired earthly things, who vanished in pride, who rooted themselves in their pleasures as though they would live forever. Where is their glory? Where is their power? Where is their peace, where is the abundance of their riches?

### 20

“Like the dream of those who awaken.” Thus everything failed. Imagine, as Augustine puts it, a man finding treasures in a dream. He had gone to sleep poor; in his dream he is rich—but only until he wakes. He awakens and finds again the misery he had left behind when he fell asleep.

So these people will find the misery they had acquired for themselves when they awaken. For now they sleep, as it were, in sin: they live peacefully and pay no attention to the misery that is to come. After death they will be compelled to awaken, when they begin to render an account of themselves.

Then they will truly fail and perish, when what follows is fulfilled: “Lord, in your city you will reduce their image to nothing.” Are they not worthy to suffer this—that God should reduce their image to nothing in his city—because they themselves reduced the image of God to nothing in their earthly city?

Alternatively, their image may be understood as transient goods and earthly glory, because, although they do not bestow blessedness, they promise it. These things are reduced to nothing in the city of God because, in the hearts of the saints, who are the city of God, all this earthly glory and wealth are reckoned as nothing.

And as though someone were to say, “O Asaph, where did you get the right to speak in this way? From where came such contempt for temporal things?” he says:

### 21

“Because my heart has been set aflame.” Since the hearts of the saints have been kindled by the fire of the Holy Spirit, they can desire nothing except spiritual things. Hence Paul exhorts us, saying: “Fervent in spirit, serving the Lord” (Rom. 12).

And since the love of God consumes carnal pleasure, he rightly adds: “And my kidneys have been changed,” that is, carnal pleasures have been changed and removed.

### 22

“And I have been reduced to nothing,” by denying myself. “And I did not know,” that is, I regarded myself as ignorant and foolish. Hence Paul says: “If anyone thinks he is something, when he is nothing, he deceives himself” (Gal. 6).

When divine love completely occupies the mind, it immediately destroys pleasurable desires; whatever carnal thing it finds, it reduces entirely to nothing and kills. “Love is strong as death” (Song 8).

Three highly useful things are shown to us in this verse: first, the fervor of charity; then, the mortification of the flesh; afterward, the perfection of humility. In the verse that follows, two things are commended: obedience and perseverance. For he says:

### 23

“I have become like a beast of burden before you, and I am always with you.” Happy is the soul that can be God’s beast of burden, so that, gentle and meek for love of him, it willingly bears all things and patiently endures all things (1 Cor. 13). Having begun well, may it always advance and remain always with God in its holy purpose, so that it may not be separated from him by any temptations or shaken by any adversities, and may truly say: “And I am always with you.”

Such was Paul when he declared that no tribulations, no distresses, and finally no creature could separate him from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus (Rom. 8).

And lest he appear to attribute this to his own strength, he commends God’s grace, saying:

### 24

“You have taken hold of my right hand; in your will you have led me, and with glory you have received me.” By his hand he means his works; by the right hand, works directed toward eternal life. For he did not work for earthly things but for eternal ones, according to what is written: “Let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing” (Matt. 6).

Nor did he do this by his own strength. Rather, he was held and governed by the one who said: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15).

He speaks here by a certain likeness. Just as a child or a sick person cannot walk by himself unless he is held by the hand, so great is our weakness that we cannot progress in goodness by ourselves at all unless divine power continually holds and draws us.

“You placed me,” he says, “in the fulfillment of your will, so that I might never do anything except what you will; you led me from strength to strength; and at last, with glory you received me,” that is, you will receive me.

Happy is the soul that is always subject to God’s will, so that it wills what God wills and rejects what God rejects, and commits itself wholly to the divine will without any resistance, so that he may do with it whatever he wishes, as with his beast of burden, and lead it wherever he wishes. For God will lead such a soul into his glory.

This glory is prepared for the saints in heaven, and it is truly wondrous and ineffable. Therefore, in amazement, he says:

### 25

“For what is there for me in heaven?” He began to consider that heavenly blessedness itself and to rebuke himself for having desired earthly things, saying: “And apart from you, what have I desired upon earth?”

As Augustine explains, he compared the earthly reward he desired with the heavenly reward he is to receive. He saw what was being reserved for him there and, reflecting and burning in the contemplation of an ineffable reality—“which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart” (1 Cor. 2)—he did not say, “This and that are mine in heaven,” but, “What is there for me in heaven?” What is it? How great is it? What is it like?

And since what I possess in heaven is so great, “apart from you, what did I desire upon earth?” Why did I ever desire earthly things? Why did I ever long for things that pass away?

“You,” he says, “reserve for me in heaven immortal riches: yourself. And I desired from you on earth what even the wicked possess, namely gold and silver.”

Thus, while this Asaph marvels at heavenly things and despises earthly ones, turning his mind between the two, he afflicts himself grievously in repentance and, having rejected inferior things, draws his whole self toward higher things. Hence he says:

### 26

“My flesh and my heart have failed.” He presents himself as wholly spiritual and aflame with the fire of the Holy Spirit when he declares that the desires of the flesh and his former thoughts have failed within him.

Our flesh fails when it is so restrained by the rigor of discipline that it can no longer resist the spirit. Our heart also suffers failure when every self-will and presumption is cut away inwardly. Thus, he says, “God has become the possessor of my heart while I live temporally.”

“God will afterward also be my portion forever.” In this world people choose portions for themselves: some riches, some honors, some military service, some commerce; different people choose different things for themselves. Among them the people of God cry out: “God is my portion,” not for a time but forever.

Such an inheritance is good and true, one that can remain forever. And why have you chosen this inheritance for yourself?

### 27

“Because, behold,” that is, it is manifest: “those who distance themselves from you will perish,” that is, they will be condemned and will lose the truth, and they will truly perish. “And you have destroyed”—that is, you will destroy, or, according to your predetermination, you have destroyed—“all who commit fornication away from you.”

Every illicit union may be called fornication. Hence it is written: “Israel fornicated with the gods of the nations” (Judg. 8). And he rightly says, “away from you,” because the one who sins is far from God (1 Chron. 5). When a person begins to fail in the love of God, he begins to distance himself from God. If he is joined to temporal things by illicit love, he is already committing fornication. For the soul has abandoned its proper husband—that is, its creator—and has joined itself in wanton love to one who was not its own. For this reason it rightly incurs the penalty of destruction, because it voluntarily abandoned its salvation.

They, therefore, because they abandoned God, perished. But what of you?

### 28

“But for me it is good to cling to God.” This is all my good: to cling to my God by will, faith, and love.

And while I am on pilgrimage, I wish to place my hope in the Lord God. Since I cannot yet cling to my God by sight, meanwhile I will at least cling to him by hope. And rightly so, because, as Augustine explains, he is my Lord, who governs me, and my God, who created me. This is good for me; this is sweet and pleasant for me.

And what are you doing here, placing your hope in God? What will your task be except to praise the one whom you love and to make others love him with you? This is what follows:

“So that I may proclaim all your praises,” that is, so that I may preach everything about you that ought to be preached, “in the gates of the daughter of Zion,” that is, in the hearing of the children of the Church.

For ears are gates through which proclamations enter the inner recesses of the hearts of the saints. Or the gates are the virtues of the soul, through which one travels to the heavenly Jerusalem. God’s praises are therefore preached in the gates when the voices of teachers are accompanied by the opening of virtues. He preaches in the gate whose life commends his speech.

## TITLE OF PSALM 73

The title of this psalm is: “The understanding of Asaph.” That is, the understanding produced for us by the words of this psalm is Asaph’s understanding—that is, the understanding of the Synagogue, not according to the branches that were cut off, but according to those that were confirmed.

In this psalm the converted Synagogue speaks to all Jews, whether those who are to be converted in the present or at the end of the world. It sets forth for their understanding what it understands, namely, that they should believe that Christ has come, just as it itself believes. It does this through the following subject matter: it presents the twofold dispersion of the Jews that the Prophets had foretold would occur after Christ’s coming. It therefore rightly exhorts them through this subject matter to believe that Christ has already come when they see these signs fulfilled.

First it explains the Jews’ local dispersion, and afterward their interior dispersion, namely, their present blindness.

The voice of the Synagogue.

## PSALM 73

### 1

“Why, O God, have you rejected us forever? Is your fury angry against the sheep of your pasture?”

He does not reproach God but asks. It is as though he were saying: O God, who, precisely because you are God, govern all things by eternal disposition; who exceed no measure in anything, but arrange everything with supreme discernment (Wis. 8, 9, and 12): why have you rejected your people forever, so that you will never again restore them to Jerusalem?

It is as though he were saying: You did not do this without cause, nor were you angry in any ordinary way, but to such an extent that your anger became fury, as far as human judgment can see. You were angry, I say, not with just anyone, but with the sheep of your pasture—that is, with the Jews, whom, like a good shepherd, you led through the desert, whom you fed with manna, and afterward settled in a land flowing with milk and honey (Exod. 13).

Why, as Augustine explains, did you do this, except because we clung to earthly things and did not know you? Do not be angry, I beg you, Lord, but do what follows.

### 2

“Remember your congregation, which you possessed from the beginning.” Recall that you gathered us from many nations and places into one and possessed us as your own inheritance from the beginning—that is, from the time of the Patriarchs whom you first chose.

They were possessed from the time of the Patriarchs, since they were in their loins. The Lord possessed the people of Israel from them, and from them it received both its name and its origin. He always guarded it until, provoked by them, he permitted them to be afflicted because of their sin.

Remember that you gathered and possessed us, and let this be the cause of your mercy. Therefore remember also that you redeemed the rod of your inheritance.

What are we to understand by “rod” except a scepter, rule, and dominion? And what by “inheritance” except the same people? The Lord therefore redeemed the rod of his inheritance because he liberated the kingdom of the Jews from Pharaoh’s slavery (Exod. 12).

Or, by an intransitive grammatical usage, the inheritance itself is called “rod,” since it was prefigured by Moses’ rod. When God first wished to possess that inheritance, freeing it from Egypt, he gave Moses a sign. Moses had said: “What sign shall I give them, so that they may believe me, that you have sent me?” And the Lord said to him: “What are you carrying in your hand?” “A rod,” he replied. “Throw it,” he said, “on the ground.” He threw down the rod, and it became a serpent; Moses was terrified and fled from it. The Lord then said to him: “Take hold of its tail.” He took hold of it, and it returned to its former state (Exod. 4).

What does this signify? First, death came from the serpent. Therefore, as Augustine explains, the rod in the serpent signifies Christ in death. For this reason, when people in the desert were bitten and killed by serpents, God commanded that a bronze serpent be raised up; those who looked at it were healed from the serpent bites (Num. 21).

What does it mean to be healed from a serpent by looking at a serpent? It means to be healed from death by believing in the one who died.

Nevertheless, Moses was terrified and fled. Christ died, and the disciples were terrified and withdrew from the hope in which they had stood. Yet they took hold of the tail, because afterward they believed. This is also signified by the words: “You shall see my back” (Exod. 33).

The serpent returned to a rod because Christ rose from death to life (Rom. 6). At the end of the world, as the tail, we shall return to God’s hand and become his established kingdom, so that the words may now be fulfilled in us: “You redeemed the rod of your inheritance.”

But because the Synagogue is speaking here, this is determined by the words that follow: “Mount Zion, in which you have dwelt.” I call this inheritance Mount Zion. Their city, Jerusalem, was there; there was the capital of their kingdom; there were the temple and the sacrifice, in which he says that God dwelt.

And to express his dwelling more emphatically, he immediately added, “in it.” For although he dwells in all things as God, he dwells in it in a more special way: in all things by power, in it by grace.

After asking God for mercy upon herself, she next asks vengeance upon the enemies by whom she is being devastated, adding:

### 3

“Lift up your hands against their pride forever,” that is, exercise your power and strength to destroy their pride completely. As you rejected us forever, so crush their pride forever.

And his hand was rightly lifted against their pride forever, because, through the operation of divine power, the nations that had previously devastated his people in their pride have now been humbled and have come to know Christ. He rightly says, “forever,” because “Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes,” which he rightly wishes for them.

He marvels at the wickedness of the Roman ruler in the devastation of Jerusalem, saying:

“How greatly the enemy has acted wickedly in the sanctuary!” That is, as Augustine explains, in the temple, in the priesthood, and in all those sacred rites. And truly he was an enemy. For that king and his army, who did these things, worshiped false gods, adored images, and served demons. They perpetrated many evils in God’s holy things.

This is what follows:

### 4

“And those who hate you gloried in the midst of your solemnity,” that is, amid the assembly of the Jews, who had gathered from every region for the feast (Exod. 23).

This must be carefully noted, as Augustine explains. For he says that Jerusalem was overthrown while the very solemnity was being celebrated—a solemnity during which they crucified the Lord (Matt. 26). They gathered and raged; they gathered and perished.

He then shows how they gloried:

### 5

“They set up signs”—not the Lord’s signs, as Augustine explains, but their own signs: their standards, their eagles, their dragons, and their statues; or perhaps signs that they had heard from the prophets of their demons.

“And they did not recognize, as in the going forth, [what was] above the Most High.” They did not recognize [what was] above the Most High—that is, with the Most High God—as something that occurred in the going forth, that is, as something proceeding from the divine disposition.

For unless power had proceeded from the Most High God, their wickedness could not have been carried out. Thus, just as it proceeded from the Most High God, so it was carried out by that army. “All authority is not from man but from God” (Rom. 13).

God is indeed the giver of all authorities, but he is not the giver of all wills. Therefore every authority is just, but one will is just and another unjust. If the authority was good, why was the action evil? Your disposition gives a name to your deed.

Accordingly, what the just God justly wished to be done was evil because they wished it unjustly; and what they did proceeded from the Most High, but they did not understand it.

He continues to describe their wickedness, saying:

### 6

“Like men cutting down trees in a forest with axes, they cut down its doors together.”

All this happened literally. Just as trees are cut down in a timber forest, so they cut down the doors with axes, treating them contemptuously and without any reverence, all pressing toward the same end, because they came together with one heart and one will for evil.

“With the axe and the hatchet they brought it down.” The axe is for cutting down; the hatchet is for breaking apart. For they did not merely cut it down but also brought it down.

### 7

“They set fire to your sanctuary; they profaned on the earth the dwelling-place of your name.” They even profaned the dwelling-place itself, which had been dedicated to your holy name. They threw down the altars, tables, books, vestments, and similar objects and trampled them underfoot.

### 8

“They said in their heart”—which is more significant than if they had said it with their mouth. For when they are said to have spoken in their heart, their will, disposition, and intention are indicated.

They did not say this as four or five individuals, but as their entire kindred—not divided into separate groups, but all together. What did they say?

“Let us cause all the feast-days of God to cease from the land.” Let us scatter everything in such a way that they will never again be able to assemble or celebrate a feast in the land.

Up to this point it has been shown how greatly the enemy acted wickedly in the sanctuary. It has been shown what evils were inflicted by the enemies. Next he indicates what benefits had been withdrawn from them by God himself, saying:

### 9

“We have not seen our signs.” We have seen, he says, the destruction of our city, but we have received no sign from God, as Gideon once did, along with our other fathers (Judg. 7). There is no longer a prophet who can announce good or evil. “And he will no longer know us,” that is, God has entirely forgotten us.

Afflicted by such evils, therefore, and groaning before the Lord, he says:

### 10

“How long, O God, will the enemy reproach you? Will the adversary provoke your name forever?”

How long—until what end—does the enemy, the adversary, reproach and provoke you? Does he provoke you for this purpose: that, in anger, you may chastise him and, by chastising him, bring him to know you? And does he do so until the end comes in you?

Let everyone who is afflicted because of his sin, everyone who has been abandoned by God as though by an angry God, attend to these words. Let him not despair; let him groan and show his misery to the physician. For God strikes in order to spare; he grows angry in order not to remain angry.

Hence this Asaph continues:

### 11

“Why do you turn away your hand,” that is, the Judea signified by the hand of Moses, “and your right hand,” namely, the Judea mentioned above, which you used to favor more than the nations, leading it first through the Red Sea (Exod. 12) and feeding it with manna (Exod. 16)? Why do you turn it away “from the midst of your bosom,” that is, from the common fellowship of the saints, who are called your bosom because they are filled with spiritual mysteries?

“Do you do this forever,” or, “toward what end are you proceeding through this?”

Here he touches upon the story of Moses’ hand, which, as long as it was in his bosom, was clean; when he drew it out, he found it leprous. Then he put it back into his bosom, and it recovered its former cleanliness (Exod. 4). This prefigured the Jewish people: as long as it remained in the Lord’s bosom and protection, it was clean; but when it went out, it became unclean and full of sins. Again, at the end of the world, it will return to the Lord’s bosom and remain in its former health.

“Why,” he says, “do you turn your right hand away from your bosom, so that it remains unclean outside?” As Augustine explains: Call it back, I beg you, to your bosom. Let it return to its proper color; let it recognize its Savior.

He was asking why, and now he has understood, as the title indicates: “The understanding of Asaph.” Therefore he adds:

### 12

“But God is our king from before the ages,” he who is “the Word in the beginning,” through whom all things were made (John 1). This same king, having become human, “worked salvation in the midst of the earth.”

For this reason he temporarily turned his hand away from his bosom—that is, the Jewish people from his protection. For this reason partial blindness came upon Israel, so that the fullness of the nations might enter (Rom. 11), and so God the King might work salvation in the midst of the earth—that is, in the midst of the nations.

Or “in the midst of the earth” means in the flesh he assumed; or in the city of Jerusalem, which is situated in the middle of the earth, where the Lord was crucified for the salvation of the whole world.

Next he shows how he worked salvation, turning to God himself, the worker, and saying:

### 13

“You established the sea by your strength.” By the sea he signifies the nations, because of the abundance of their vices and the bitterness of their morals. Christ, however, is the power of God and the wisdom of God. By this power the nations were established through faith, hope, and charity.

God so established this sea that he made it dry land, as it is said elsewhere: “He turned the sea into dry land” (Ps. 65).

He then adds in sequence how this happened: “You crushed the heads of dragons in the waters.” You crushed the vices and sins suggested by dragons—that is, by evil spirits who lie in wait for holy souls.

He also shows that almighty God destroyed the devil himself and all his exaltations and pomp when he adds:

### 14

“You crushed the heads of the dragon.” The heads of the dragon may be understood as the wicked suggestions that proceed from the devil. This enemy, the dragon, has many heads. His heads are the eight principal vices. The first of them, however, is the vice of pride, from which the others arise. For “the beginning of every sin is pride” (Eccl. 10).

Hence it was commanded that the seed of Eve should watch the serpent’s head (Gen. 3). The Church was warned to avoid the beginning of sin.

The heads of the dragon have therefore been crushed; the vices of the devil have been destroyed. For where God reigns, pride cannot reign, nor vainglory, envy, anger, sadness, acedia, gluttony, or lust. Such are the heads of this crafty dragon, which our king crushed by his power.

By crushing them he worked salvation in the midst of the earth, which had previously been corrupted and weakened by the invasion of such enemies.

And what did he do with the one whose heads he crushed?

“You gave him as food to the peoples of the Ethiopians.” Those who had been black are called to the faith. It is said to them: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5). From them the Church is formed, of which it is said: “Who is this woman ascending, made white?” (Song 6). “I am black but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem” (Song 1).

These are the peoples of the Ethiopians, to whom this dragon was given as food. This is signified by the calf that the unbelieving people worshiped, which Moses crushed and gave the people to drink after casting it into water (Exod. 23).

What does this mean except that the worshipers of the devil became the body of Christ? Hence Peter was told concerning the nations: “Kill and eat” (Acts 10), that is, kill what they are and make them what you are. It is as though it said: Crush and drink.

It was necessary that the body which belonged to the devil should, through faith, pass into the body of Christ, and thus the dragon should be crushed by the loss of its members.

This too was prefigured in Moses’ serpent. For the magicians did likewise: they threw down their rods and produced dragons. But Moses’ dragon swallowed all the rods of the magicians (Exod. 7). Let the body of the devil therefore be understood as swallowed up by believers.

Thus it is rightly said: “You gave him as food to the peoples of the Ethiopians.”

Or it may be understood in this way: “You gave him as food,” because now everyone bites him by reproving, accusing, and cursing him.

He next shows how this happened:

### 15

“You split open springs and torrents, so that waters might flow.” As Augustine explains, you caused streams of wisdom and faith to flow, so that they might irrigate the saltiness of the nations and, by their sweetness and watering, convert the others.

It should be noted that in some people the word of God becomes a spring, and in others a torrent. Torrents are properly rivers that flow down in summer but are swollen and run with the waters of winter.

[Note: I would prefer to emend this, following Augustine, to “they fail.”]

You see a faithful person who will persevere to the end, who will not abandon God in any temptation, and who endures every hardship. From where does this person derive strength except that the word of God has become in him “a spring of water welling up to eternal life” (John 4)?

Another person receives the word, preaches it, does not remain silent, and runs. Perhaps he is touched by some temptation; he cannot endure the heat, fails, and dries up. Heat therefore tests springs and torrents. Nevertheless, let the earth be watered by both, by the one who worked salvation in the midst of the earth.

“You dried up the rivers of Ethan.” In one place God breaks open springs so that they may flow; elsewhere he dries up rivers so that they do not flow. But he says, “the rivers of Ethan,” which means “the strong one.”

Those who presume upon their own strength are, as it were, strong. Let their rivers dry up; let the teachings of the nations make no progress; let every empty and swollen doctrine wither. Let them be flooded by the sweet and pleasant spring of the Gospel of truth.

### 16

“Yours is the day, and yours is the night.” Who does not know that he himself made all these things? Yet we must understand something that pertains to the salvation he worked in the midst of the earth.

Who are the day except spiritual people? Who are the night except carnal people? “I could not speak to you as spiritual,” he says, “but as carnal.” When spiritual people speak spiritual things, “day pours forth the word to day” (Ps. 18). But when carnal people themselves do not keep silent about the faith, “night declares knowledge to night.”

Therefore, yours is the day and yours is the night. The spiritual are yours, and the carnal are yours. You illuminate the former with the unchanging truth of wisdom; you console the latter by the manifestation of the flesh.

“You fashioned the dawn and the sun,” that is, you made grace and wisdom. For just as dawn follows night, so grace follows guilt. And just as the sun blazes after dawn, so, through the effect of God’s grace, wisdom grows hot in the hearts of the elect through love.

And just as there is no day except through the sun’s illumination, so there is no righteous person unless he has been illuminated by the light of divinity.

17. You made all the boundaries of the earth. For God apportions the grace that he gives to his Church according to measure (Rom. 12). Each person does not advance in virtue and grace as much as he wishes, but as much as it pleases him to distribute to his earth, who sets its boundaries. “I wish,” says the Apostle, “that all were as I myself am, but each has his own gift from God: one in this way, another in that” (1 Cor. 7). “Summer and spring, you fashioned them,” that is, those mature in character: for in summer fruits are mature, while in spring they blossom—namely, they send forth the beginnings of virtues, because flowers are born in spring. “You fashioned them” is said in the neuter, as though one were to say: “You made them all, both the mature and the newly budding.” You are the one who gives the earth, and you set its boundaries; as much as you wish and in whatever way you wish, you make it bear fruit. Therefore let them not boast as though they had not received; you fashioned them. Great is the commendation of God’s grace in the Church of Christ. Then he also prays for his own, saying:

[Col. 0952A] 18. Remember this, namely, your congregation, for which I prayed above. He also sets forth its blindness, as though understanding and lamenting it, when he adds: “The enemy will reproach the Lord.” For the Jewish people, full of iniquity and hostility, said to Christ, “You are a Samaritan and have a demon” (John 8), and brought many other insults against him. Hence it is further said: “And a foolish people provoked your name,” that is, provoked you. Truly foolish, truly senseless, truly stiff-necked (Exod. 23), who saw so many miracles and did not believe; moreover, they killed the one whom they ought to have worshiped. But since some of those who were going to kill Christ would later return to confession and repentance for so great a sin, he asks on their behalf and says:

19. Do not hand over to beasts the soul that confesses you. To what beasts [Ex eod.] except those whose heads have been crushed in the waters? For the devil himself is called a beast, a lion, a serpent, and a dragon. Do not give to evil spirits the soul that confesses you. For Peter spoke to the Israelites, since they themselves had killed Christ. Struck in the heart, they said, “What shall we do?” “Repent,” he said, “and let each one of you be baptized in the name of Christ; and your sins will be forgiven you” (Acts 2). Let it therefore be said: “Do not hand over to beasts the soul that confesses you.” For in paradise the sinful earth was granted to that serpent (Gen. 3), not a confessing soul. And do not forget forever the souls of your poor, that is, of those who despise the world. For now they seem almost forgotten by you, while they hunger, while they thirst, while they receive no earthly consolation from you, while they are afflicted and despised. But you will not forget them forever, when they are eternally rewarded.

20. Look upon your covenant. Give back what you promised. We hold the tablets; we await the inheritance. And it is necessary that you look upon it, because “those who have been darkened by the houses of iniquities of the earth are filled.” Our houses [Ex Aug.], our hearts. There the blessed willingly dwell who are pure in heart. Look, therefore, upon your covenant, so that the remnant may be saved, because many who attend to the earth have been darkened and filled with earth. Dust entered their eyes and blinded them. Thus has come to pass what is said elsewhere: “Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see” (Ps. 68). Why this? Because those who have been darkened by clinging to the earth are filled with houses of iniquities, that is, with evil hearts. And therefore I say, “Look upon it,”

21. “lest the humble man, having become confounded, be turned away.” He says this about the one of whom he shortly before said, “Do not hand over to beasts the soul that confesses you.” He asks that the one who, confessing his sins, has become humble, not be turned away from God’s mercy, from the regard of his clemency. For if he were turned away, he would be confounded and handed over to beasts. Then he also mentions that poor man of whom he spoke in the same passage, adding: “The poor and needy will praise your name.” God’s poor man is one who desires nothing in this world, who does not presume upon himself, who eagerly longs for heavenly goods. The needy man is one who, deprived of every human aid, seeks help nowhere else except from God alone, in whom he has placed all his hope. “Such,” he says, “poor and needy people will praise your name.” For such people are fit to praise God: desire does not constrict them, charity enlarges them, and their life commends them. And just as he asked pardon for those who confess, so now, on behalf of those who persist in sin, he stirs God to vengeance. Hence he continues not so much by praying as by prophesying:

22. Arise, O God; judge your cause. Make the cause that we have undertaken to defend appear just to them—namely, that Christ had to suffer in this way, rise from the dead, and thus enter into his glory (Luke 24). “Arise, so that you may judge.” For unless you first rise from the dead, you will not judge at all. For [Ex Aug.] he would not come to judgment unless he had risen from the dead. Christ was foretold as the one who would come; he came [Col. 0953A] as Scripture had foretold. He fulfilled righteousness and preached eternal life. Yet he was despised on earth and is still despised in heaven. This is why almighty God will come to judgment: there he will display and judge his cause, showing how just a cause he had and how unjust a punishment he endured; and he will judge strictly those in whom he finds guilt. Hence it is also added: “Remember your reproaches, those that come from the foolish all day long.” A certain person is foolish: he did not know, or, knowing, lived perversely. Such people reproach the Lord God and his members—now by blaspheming, now by mocking, now by threatening, now by flattering. God will remember such people at the judgment, in order to judge and condemn them—not all of them, however, but only those who remain in this sin all day long, that is, continually. For God does not remember those sins that are corrected through repentance before the end. What follows must be noted very carefully:

23. Do not forget the voices of your enemies. Their voices were those reproaches that they brought against God. Why, then, does he repeat this? Because a judge in a case must carefully consider both parties: the one against whom the reproach is brought, and likewise the one by whom it is brought. Since those foolish people brought their reproaches not against a human being but against God himself, their own Creator, they were unquestionably more deserving of condemnation. Again, their guilt was also more serious because the reproaches were brought not merely by fools but by enemies. For it is far more culpable to sin out of hostility than out of ignorance; nevertheless, both sins bound them. What follows is also entirely worthy of condemnation: “The pride of those who hate you has risen continually.” They do not turn their eyes back, but advance further and further into evil.

TITLE OF PSALM LXXIV

1. The psalm that follows is entitled in this way: “For the end, Do not destroy, a psalm of song of Asaph.” This psalm, which is for us the cause of song—that is, of great joy and delight, because it promises the humble the reward of eternal blessedness—is proposed to Asaph, that is, to the faithless Synagogue, so that it may press toward the end, that is, toward conformity to Christ. It is proposed, I say, to Asaph, with Christ exhorting that Synagogue: “Do not destroy yourself,” that is, do not become proud. For just as humility is the guardian of all virtues, so, conversely, pride is their corruption. The subject of this psalm is Christ himself and the Synagogue whom he exhorts here. They speak sometimes in their own person, sometimes in the person of their members, exhorting the proud to humility. He does this by setting before them the condemnation that the proud will have in the future and the exaltation that the humble will attain. Its purpose is to invite everyone to humility, so that they may thereby escape the strict judgment of almighty God. Hence he also sets himself forth as an example and says through the voice of his humble members:

PSALM LXXIV

2. We will confess to you, O God; we will confess and call upon your name. Confession of sins is the beginning of good things. For “the righteous man is first of all his own accuser” (Prov. 18). Therefore first confess your sins to God. This is the beginning of righteousness. And not once only, but again and again: as often as you sin, so often confess. The repetition of the word commends perseverance. You cannot return to baptism a second time. If you sin, return to confession. Why do we confess to God, when he knows our sins even if we do not confess them? Because confession produces compunction. It gives birth to humility, which is pleasing to God and through which the converted person is reconciled to him. Confess your sin in this way, and then call upon God. For if you call upon him first, you will not be heard. What is it to call upon him except to call him inwardly? First, therefore, cast out sin, and so invite God into your heart. [381] For then you will be worthy to call upon the Lord’s name and to proclaim his works to others. Hence it is also added: “We will recount your wonders.” What is so wondrous as that the Creator becomes a creature, that the immortal dies, that death is destroyed by death, and that the sinner condemned to punishment is recalled to grace and glory? These are God’s wonders, which the members of Christ never cease to recount. But since judgment will follow, the Lord himself now speaks through his own person.

3. When I receive the appointed time, I will judge righteous judgments. The time itself has not yet arrived. In the grace of his mercy, he first proclaims righteous judgments, and thus judges with righteousness. For if he wished to judge before proclaiming, he would find no one to set free. “When I receive,” he says, “the appointed time.” He could not receive the time in what he is as the Son of God, but in what he is as the Son of Man. Hence the Evangelist says: “He gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man” (John 5). Now, therefore, is the time of preaching. Hence he says: “I will recount your wonders.” Hear the one who recounts; hear the one who preaches. For if you despise him, he himself, as judge, threatens you with judgment, saying: “When I receive the appointed time, I will judge righteous judgments.” To judge righteous judgments is to repay each person according to his merits. “We will recount,” he says, “your wonders.” And how great a work this is is shown when he adds:

4. The earth melted. And what do you call “the earth”? “All,” he says, “who dwell in it,” that is, all who persist in earthly things by inclination and desire. For each person is what he loves. If you love the earth, you are earth; if you love God, you are among those of whom the Lord himself says: “I said, You are gods” (Ps. 81). The earth is melted when earthly hearts flow away into vices and desires. Hence one is said to “fall into sin,” as though flowing away from the stability of the firmament of virtue and righteousness. Everyone who sins through desire for inferior things; and just as he is strengthened by love of higher things, so he weakens and, as it were, melts through desire for lower things. Thus, with the earth melted, the Lord says: “I have established its pillars.” He calls the Apostles pillars. Hence Paul says about his fellow apostles: “Those who seemed to be pillars” (Gal. 2). And what would those pillars have been unless they had been strengthened by him? For they too wavered in a kind of earthquake when they saw the Lord being killed. But he rose again and demonstrated that death was not to be feared. Having sent the Spirit from on high, he inflamed the hearts of the disciples, and thus established the pillars of the earth. Let him therefore say: “I have established its pillars.” Having established them, because he sent them to preach, he rightly continues:

5. I said to the wicked, “Do not act wickedly.” They did not say it, but he did. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you (Matt. 28). Nor did he say it to the righteous, but to the wicked. For he did not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance (Mark 2). “Those who are well have no need of a physician,” he says, “but those who are sick” (ibid. and Matt. 9). The Law said, “Whoever does this or that shall die.” I said to the wicked, “Do not act wickedly.” Thus also he said to the adulterous woman: “Go, and from now on do not sin anymore” (John 8). Therefore grace preserves those whom justice killed; the only requirement is that they repent (2 Tim. 2) and prostrate themselves in humility. Hence he further adds: “And to sinners, ‘Do not exalt your horn.’” Do not be lifted up in pride. Do not defend your sins arrogantly. In this verse God warns the sinner about two things: first, that he should depart from evil; then, that he should not become proud in sin. First, he warns him to beware of the future; second, to repent of the past. Another prohibition follows:

6. Do not lift your horn on high, that is, do not raise yourselves up against God. Do not become so proud as to turn the blame for your sins back upon your Creator. For there have been those who said, “It is not our fault if we sin, since God created us such. If God wished it, no human being would sin.” Thus the wicked ordinarily exalt their horn in two ways: either by defending themselves or by accusing the Most High himself. Therefore he adds: “Do not speak iniquity against God.” Do not say, “God does not judge human affairs; he does not care what is done on earth.” In neither of these ways should you speak iniquity against God, O Jews.

[Col. 0955A] 7. For neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the desert mountains [understand: do they speak] iniquity against God. The nations who inhabit these three regions of the world have already begun to think well and reasonably about their Creator. You alone, to whom the southern region was granted for habitation, must not blaspheme. Or it can be understood in this way: “Jews, do not speak iniquity against God”—which indeed was done by those who cried, “He is guilty of death,” and “Crucify him!” (Matt. 26–27)—because from neither the east, nor the west, nor the desert mountains [the sense is] is anyone free from God’s judgment.

8. Because God is judge. He called them desert mountains because of the uninhabitable region that lies in the north. If a human being were judge, he might perhaps be feared less. But because God is judge, let no one now speak against him; rather, let everyone serve him. He commends God as judge when he adds: “He humbles this one,” that is, the Jewish people, “and he exalts that one,” that is, the Gentile:

[Col. 0955B] 9. For there is a cup in the Lord’s hand. For Holy Scripture is in the Lord’s power. For he alone holds the key of knowledge (Rev. 5). I say, a cup full of unmixed and mixed wine, with dregs. For in the Lord’s cup there is unmixed wine, mixed wine, and dregs. Those who receive divine understanding from sacred discourse drink the unmixed wine, as it were, from the cup. They drink the mixed wine who understand some things clearly but do not yet discern others. They drink the dregs who derive error from the same source. Jews, heretics, and pagans drink the dregs; their confused and foul doctrine is never separated from error. “And he inclined it”—from this one, the Jewish people, toward that one, the Gentile. Understanding was clarified from that side. Yet “its dregs were not emptied.” For neither the unbelief of the Jews, nor the error of the heretics, nor the foolishness of the pagans has been entirely diminished. “All the sinners of the earth will drink” first the dregs, then death. Or, “its dregs were not emptied,” because among the Jews the carnal sacraments remain. “All the sinners of the earth will drink,” because all delight in earthly promises. Wonderful is this cup, from which both the good and the evil drink, and in which the good receive what gives them life, while the evil receive what destroys them. Such also was the Word of the Father, our Lord Jesus Christ, of whom holy Simeon testifies, saying: “Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many, and as a sign that will be opposed” (Luke 2). Thus also in the preceding psalm, calling Scripture a bow, he says: “He prepared in it the vessels of death” (Ps. 7), that is, statements which, when wrongly understood, serve death to many. Thus from this cup some live and some perish. What does Christ say amid all this?

10. But I will proclaim forever. For as long as this age lasts, Christ and his own will preach the Gospel. I will sing with joy to the God of Jacob. I will praise the one who is specially the God of those who are spiritually Jacob. Then he foretells the judgment, where he predicts that the wicked will be humbled and the good exalted. Hence he adds:

[Col. 0955D] 11. And I will break all the horns of sinners, but the horns of the righteous will be exalted. Sinners have their horns in this age—namely, power, domination, honors, riches, and that pride which surpasses all the rest. With these horns, like untamed bulls, they attack some, assault and drive back others. But almighty God, in his judgment, will break all the horns of sinners and reduce all their power and pride to nothing. The righteous also have their two horns: the two Testaments, or faith and charity, together with the other virtues, by which they defend themselves against the enemies of the Church; with these they also courageously attack and overthrow those enemies. When this wondrous God comes in his glory to judgment, he will exalt them wondrously. Let each person gather from these words what kind of person he ought to show himself to be. And let him beware—as was stated at the beginning in the title—not to corrupt and destroy himself by imitating proud sinners and resisting the Lord. Rather, let him strive to imitate the humble and righteous, so that in the future kingdom he may deserve [Col. 0956A] to be exalted by the Lord. For this is the purpose and benefit of the psalm.

TITLE OF PSALM LXXV

1. The titles of the psalms reveal their meanings; therefore this psalm is entitled: “For the end, with praises, a psalm of Asaph, a song for the Assyrians.” This psalm is proposed to Asaph, that is, to the faithful Synagogue, so that it may persevere until the end of its life not out of sadness or necessity, but with praise and exultation. This psalm is a song of the Synagogue—that is, a cause of song and joy—because at the beginning it says that it is Judah and Israel from Zion. The psalm is proposed not only to Asaph but also to the Assyrians, that is, to all who live rightly. “Assyrian” is interpreted as “one who directs.” The subject of this psalm is the Synagogue. Its purpose is to exhort all the faithful who have vowed themselves to God, Jews as well as Gentiles, to persevere in their vow, so that in the future they may return to God those whom here they have vowed to him—themselves. In the first part it is said that God is known among the holy, that he dwells in them, and that there he breaks all the weapons of the devil. In the second part, which begins, “They have slept their sleep,” the hardness of the reprobate and the terrifying judgment of God are commended. Hence at the end everyone is exhorted to fulfill his vows, lest he be punished by the terrifying king. He says, therefore:

PSALM LXXV

2. God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel. At one time it was the case that this nation alone—Judah, namely—acknowledged and worshiped the true God, while the other nations honored idols and were entirely ignorant of the God of heaven. But through his grace he was proclaimed to the Gentiles (1 Tim. 3; Acts 13), and his name, which had been known only in Judah, has now become wondrous throughout the whole earth (Ps. 8). Let the Jews no longer boast: if the Lord’s name is called great among them, among us also it is proclaimed as wondrous. But since that nation fell away from the knowledge of God through error and blasphemed the Lord’s great name, the statement that he is known in Judah and great in Israel must now be understood only spiritually. For “Judah” is interpreted as “confession,” while “Israel” means “a man seeing God.” Rightly, therefore, God is said to be known in Judah, because knowledge of God is obtained through confession of sin. Judah is also rightly mentioned before Israel, because through confession one arrives at the vision of almighty God. Nor should the statement, “In Israel his name is great,” be understood as though God were greater in one place and smaller in another. Rather, God’s name is called great wherever he is named according to the greatness of his majesty. Thus also in prayer we ask, “Hallowed be your name” (Matt. 6). This is not requested as though God’s name were not holy, but so that it may be held holy by human beings—that is, so that God may become known to them in such a way that they consider nothing holier, nor fear offending anything more. He has told us where he is known and where he is great. Let him also tell us where God dwells.

3. “His place,” he says, “has been made in peace, and his dwelling in Zion.” As long as [Ex Augustine] you do not confess your sins, you are, in a certain sense, quarrelling with God. But by confessing, you begin to have peace with him, and thus a place is made for him in your heart. In peace there is perfection, where nothing resists. Those at peace are those who are at peace within themselves, who order and subject all the movements of their soul to reason and have subdued their carnal desires. In them everything is so ordered that what is preeminent in a human being—namely, reason—rules the other parts without opposition and is itself subject to what is superior, namely, God. This is the peace given on earth to people of good will (Luke 2). This is the consummated life of the perfect sage. From this most peaceful and well-ordered kingdom the prince of this age is cast out (John 12), the one who rules over the perverse and disordered. “Zion” is interpreted as “watchtower” or “contemplation.” It is the Church, which dwells in the height of divine contemplation and will later enjoy the blessedness of the unveiled vision itself. In this Zion is his dwelling, as he himself says: “I will inhabit them and walk among them” (Ezek. 43).

4. There he broke the powers—namely, the bow, the shield, the sword, and the battle. In Zion, or in peace, he broke whatever they considered great, by which they temporarily protected themselves, and the battle that they waged against God by defending their sins. There is also the bow of deception among heretics, the shield of hardness among unbelievers, the sword among tyrants, and battle among vices. These are the devil’s powers, which almighty God destroyed and broke in the peaceful heart. Then he turns to God himself, as though saying: You, Lord, who break such great powers, do this in the following way:

5. You, wondrously illuminating from the everlasting mountains. Truly, you and no other. The word “you” is spoken with great force, so that no other illuminator is understood except God alone. A human being preaches; God illuminates. Nor does the preacher’s external speech accomplish anything unless the grace of the illuminator works inwardly. And who are these everlasting mountains except the holy preachers? They are mountains because of the height of their righteousness; everlasting because they will always remain with the Lord. The everlasting sun first illuminated these mountains, so that through them it might afterward illuminate its earth, that is, the Church—and this wondrously, because spiritually. Or “wondrously” means with signs and wonders, as it is written: “But they went out and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed” (Mark 16). When they preached,

6. All the foolish in heart were troubled. The truth was preached. Eternal life was proclaimed, which is not of this earth. People despised the present life and loved the future one. [A corrupt phrase here appears to mean: “that eternal life was proclaimed through the illuminated mountains.”] But the foolish were troubled. Hence came the persecution of the martyrs, the uproar of the heretics, the dissension of the carnal, and the enemies of the Church. Even while the wise man preaches, the foolish man is troubled. One wishes to correct; the other grows indignant and angry. “Reprove a fool,” it says, “and he will hate you; reprove a wise man, and he will love you” (Prov. 9). What did those troubled people do? “They slept their sleep.” They loved present things and slept—that is, they delighted in the things present. Their sleep is the present life. There they slept; there, by delighting in it, they rested. And so these present things became delightful to them. It is like someone who dreams that he has found a treasure: the dream made him rich, but waking made him poor. This sleep passed away; this life passed away; and “all the men of wealth found nothing in their hands,” because they had placed nothing in the hands of Christ. Such are earthly riches. Such is the sleep of the present life. In the present they flourish and take delight; in the present they make some promise; but in the end they tend toward nothing. Then he commends the hardness of their hearts, because when earthly things are loved, the heart is hardened against what is above. Hence it is also added:

7. At your rebuke, O God of Jacob, all who mounted horses fell asleep. They are so sunk in earthly things that they do not hear the marvelous rebukes of almighty God. They have not kept watch in their hearts, because their hearts have been hardened by rebuke. For hardness of heart is a falling asleep. Behold, the God of Jacob himself—not a new god, but the one who performed so many wonders in the house of Jacob—now rebukes sinners, thunders his anger, sounds the evangelical trumpet, and threatens judgment and eternal punishments. Amid such thunderclaps the proud still sleep; they still refuse to condemn their old life or to awaken to a new one. Why is this, except because they mounted horses—that is, raised themselves up in pride, honors, powers, and the uncertainty of riches? Such are their horses, upon which, like untamed creatures, they are carried into eternal punishment. He rightly says, “They fell asleep,” because here they begin to sleep. Their perpetual sleep will be in eternal death. Or, at your rebuke, when you will say, “Go into the eternal fire” (Matt. 25), those who mounted horses—that is, those who were proud—will begin to sleep, that is, to enter into the eternal sleep of death. Those who now sleep here amid riches will afterward be buried there in torments.

8. You, O God who will do this, are terrifying—that is, you will appear terrifying—and who will resist you? Amid such terror of yours, what human being will be able to oppose you? [Col. 0958A] Nor will you first begin to grow angry there and then. From the time when they mounted horses, your anger was already upon them. You were angry then and threatened; you rebuked them because you desired their conversion. And because they despised you when angry, they will afterward find you terrifying. Hence it is also added:

9. You caused judgment to be heard from heaven. They have no excuse. For you caused your judgment to be heard beforehand; indeed, it was announced to them from heaven. “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. 18). The heavens proclaim the judgment of God. Or, you will descend from heaven in order to cause your judgment to be heard. For the Gospel testifies: “Then they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds with great power and majesty” (Matt. 24). For the powers of heaven will be shaken (Luke 21). Then what follows will take place:

10. The earth trembled and became still. The earthly conscience, which now troubles and labors, will then tremble and become still. It will no longer find anything to do that is evil, but it will feel many torments at which it will tremble. From one side will be accusing sins; from another, terrifying justice; beneath, the dreadful abyss of hell lying open; above, the angry judge; within, a burning conscience; outside, a world aflame. “The righteous scarcely will be saved; where will the sinner appear?” (1 Pet. 4). When God rose up for judgment, he did so “to save all the meek of the earth.” Not those who mounted horses, but all who on this earth were meek for God’s sake—simple, patient people—God will save in his judgment. The Truth itself testifies to this in the Gospel, saying: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth” (Matt. 5). The meek are those who yield to wrongdoing and do not resist evil, but overcome evil with good. They will inherit that earth of which it is said elsewhere: “God is my portion in the land of the living” (Ps. 141). This is certainly the rest and life of the saints, because they were meek and possessed a good and humble confession. Therefore they will rejoice in the Lord. This is what follows:

11. For the thought of a human being will confess to you, and the remnants of his thought will keep festival for you. At first, when a person turns to God and recalls all the evils he has done, said, and thought, and humbly discloses them through confession, he experiences shame, sadness, and compunction. But afterward, once he has done penance and obtained forgiveness and grace from God, when he begins to recall what he once thought and to consider from how many impurities, vices, and sins the merciful Lord has freed him, and how many spiritual goods he has bestowed upon him besides, he begins to rejoice within himself and give thanks to divine goodness. Thus, rejoicing within himself, he keeps a festival for God. The first thought, therefore [Ex August.], contains confession and departure from the former life. The remnants of the thoughts celebrate solemn festivals for God if the person, freed from sin, remembers what he once was and does not allow the memory of the one who healed him to fade. Then, after he has shown how the reprobate are condemned because of pride and delight in the world, and how the meek are saved through humility and a good confession, there follows a useful admonition for all, when it is said:

12. Vow and fulfill your vows to the Lord your God, all you who bring gifts around him. It is just and useful for us not to perish with the reprobate in the same way, but rather to be saved with the righteous, and therefore to strive to appease the terrifying God by whatever vows and gifts we can offer. To vow is within our choice; but to fulfill is not within our strength, but belongs to the grace of God. Nevertheless, we must not despair on that account, because if we begin what is ours to do, he who commanded us to vow will give us strength and will complete what is his. But since God is unbounded light, fills all things with his majesty, and contains everything, how can everyone be around him? Yet God is truth (John 14), and truth itself is common to all—neither mine, nor yours, nor this person’s or that person’s. “There is no distinction,” says Paul, “between Jew and Greek or barbarian; but whoever calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved” (Rom. 11; Joel 2). Therefore, because [Ex Aug.] truth is common to all, he says that all who love the truth are around it. Those who understand God in this way and subject themselves, as is fitting, to his service offer gifts around him. And it should be known that one vow is common and another individual. Believing in God, hoping in him for eternal life, loving him, and living according to God constitute a common manner of life. Not becoming proud, not killing a human being, not hating one’s brother, and not violating within oneself the temple of God are commanded to everyone. We must all commonly vow and fulfill this entire rule. There are also personal vows belonging to individuals: one person vows fasting to God, another chastity, another virginity, another to abandon everything and enter the common life. Let everyone therefore vow a vow to the Lord, this one or that one, according as divine grace has given to each person, and so let all offer gifts around him. To whom?

388 13. To the terrifying one, and to him who takes away the spirit of princes. [Col. 0959B] Since the psalm speaks to the Synagogue, that is, to the carnal people, God is rightly commended to them as terrifying, so that those who do not yet know how to love the Lord as kind and merciful may at least learn to fear him when they hear that he is terrifying. It should also be noted that he does not say, “Who takes away the spirit of human beings,” but even “of princes,” so that God may be understood as prince over princes and power over powers, as King of kings and Lord of lords (Rev. 1 and 19). Rightly, therefore, it is added: “Terrifying among the kings of the earth.” And he does not say that he takes away life—which even those who kill the body do—but that he is said to take away the spirit itself, so that the one who has power to destroy both body and soul in Gehenna may be feared all the more (Matt. 10). Or, because the spirit of princes is the spirit of pride, it can be read as: “Who takes away the spirit of princes,” that is, the boldness of the proud.

There is also another interpretation of why God is called terrifying in this passage. Holy and perfect men, so that they may find God placated in his judgment, always consider him terrifying here within themselves and judge their own sins strictly, so that in that strict judgment they may be found beyond judgment. Let it rightly be said, therefore: “Terrible among the kings of the earth are those who rule their flesh spiritually.” Paul was a king of the earth when he said: “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should be rejected.” Be a king of the earth, and God will be terrifying to you.

[Note: [Col. 0959] A corrupt phrase, which perhaps ought to be repaired in this way: “Let it be said . . . among the kings of the earth. The kings of the earth are,” etc. EDITOR.]

[Note: [Col. 0959B] We do not know whether the author continued to explain the remaining psalms. The first person who brought these works to light, D. d’Albone, head of the Church of Lyon, addresses the reader in these words at the end: “These, then, dear Reader, are what we now bring forth into the light from the Commentaries of Rufinus on the Psalms, having drawn them out of darkness. And if anyone should be able to discover the remainder of the work, let him publish it in the light under favorable auspices and with happy success. Let him be persuaded that this will be pleasing to us and useful to the commonwealth.” VALLARSI.]

[Col. 0959]

COMMENTARY ON THE THREE MINOR PROPHETS, HOSEA, JOEL, AND AMOS, ONCE ATTRIBUTED TO RUFINUS, PRESBYTER OF AQUILEIA.

[Col. 0959]

Preface. (C, S)*
[Col. 0959C] 389 That most sacred lyrist, and one as distinguished in the art of ruling as in singing—namely, the blessed David—when recounting the wonders of the Law, frequently inserts: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever” (Psalm 105 and following). Whether you consider spiritual or bodily gifts, we are rightly reminded at least to give thanks to our Creator, to whom we can never make an adequate return. Yet nothing is more pleasing than such diligence, and nothing more precious than such an offering. For this itself is his clemency, neither wearied by gifts nor by the ages; by it he makes the devout and often causes those who ask to seem worthy of obtaining what they seek.

And so, offering him this sacrifice of a grateful heart, let us trust that we shall obtain what we pray for, since we already seem to have received what we requested. For, in explaining the books of Solomon, [Note: [Col. 0959C] Antiquity records nothing similar, nor that a work of this kind was once prepared by Rufinus. Still less does it record this Commentary on the three Minor Prophets. Yet we have attempted to disclose the author of this work by arguments that are not improbable, in the Preface, which you may consult.] we have carried out, insofar as he granted us the ability, the glory of his arrangements, so that nowhere did the sequence—on which the authority of an explanation ought to depend—abandon us. Here, however, the fruit of our previous labor commends diligent work. Nothing more strongly urges the investigation of new matters than the welcome attainment of what was previously sought, especially under so pious a Lord, who is ready to grant those things after which he has commanded us to yearn.

Nor ought we to be frightened by the depth of the work, lest, after receiving pledges of confidence, hesitation continue to accuse us not only of cowardice but also of ingratitude. Therefore, as I undertake an explanation of the twelve Prophets, who are called “Minor” not on account of their merits but because of the number of their verses, I first admonish you who imposed this work upon me to assist me with pious and attentive prayers, so that I may attain an understanding of the truth.

Next, so that the Reader may recognize the character of our work, which edition I followed, and with what particular consideration [Note: [Col. 0961B] I would prefer *consideratu* to be restored here, that is, “with regard to,” “with understanding,” “with purpose,” and so forth.] I undertook this exceedingly difficult task of explanation, let him know—if he himself belongs to those whom devotion to reading exercises—that it was not without reason that I chose that final edition which is called “according to the Hebrew.” [Note: [Col. 0961B] It is immediately attached to the preceding passage and concerns the first part of the following Commentary on Joel, where he says: “when an inquirer approached … [lacuna] … which edition I should choose—for there are several—I marked the last, which is called ‘according to the Hebrew,’ because in it the integrity of the expressions was greater, whether they expressed the feeling of one teaching or of one threatening. From the judgment, therefore, of that Translation we learn …” That Rufinus could ever have thought or written this about Jerome’s version of the Scriptures, let the Jew Apella believe it.] For in the earlier editions, corrupted expressions frequently break the sense either of the teaching or of the narrative, so that the task seems to require divination rather than understanding.

391 This later Translation, although it added little brilliance to the text itself, nevertheless, through the integrity of its expressions, frequently avoids the losses of interrupted meanings that we have mentioned. Now, although among the Latins silence concerning the interpretation of the Prophets had been so unbroken that it seemed even to have been sworn to, among the Greeks and among the [Note: [Col. 0961B] Saint Ephraem the Syrian, great both in reality and in name, had composed a work of this sort; it may even at that time have been translated into Greek, for I am hardly persuaded that our author knew Syriac. But since he praises not one person from that language but several, perhaps someone will wish him to mean other, more recent writers—for example, Abraham of Beth-Rabban and Hanan of Adiabene, who flourished at the end of the sixth century. He himself, therefore, would seem to indicate an age much more recent than is commonly believed. Consult our Preface.] Syrians there were some who attempted to discuss their writings.

Among them I was able to read a few works of the holy Bishop of Constantinople, John; but, following his usual practice, he devoted nearly all his effort to exhortation rather than exposition. Origen, proceeding according to his own manner, composes allegories more graceful than the solid and reliable explanations of historical matters. [Note: [Col. 0962B] Jerome says in his Preface: “Origen wrote a small book on this Prophet, to which he gave the title *περὶ τοῦ πῶς ὠνομάσθη ἐν τῷ Ὠσηὲ Ἐφραΐμ*, that is, ‘Why Ephraim is called so in Hosea,’ wishing to show that whatever is said against him must be referred to the person of the heretics; and another book, *ἀκέφαλον καὶ ἀτέλεστον*, ‘without a head and unfinished,’ which lacks both a beginning and an end.”]

392 [Note: [Col. 0962B] Nor is it plausible that Rufinus wrote this about his own Origen—that he pursued things more graceful in allegory than solid in explanation—or that he wrote it about Jerome, with whom he was engaged in the bitterest hostility, saying that Jerome, a man of capacious intellect and persistent devotion, was such.] Jerome, moreover, a man of capacious intellect and persistent devotion, arranged commentaries on the books of the Prophets, but, as though content merely to proceed among genuine traditions, he was unwilling or unable to sustain any concern for investigating the sequence. Thus his entire discourse flowed either through Origen’s allegories or through the Jews’ fabulous traditions. Since, therefore, it seemed to me that he had passed over many useful matters, I judged it a pious service toward the Lord and a useful one toward human beings to undertake, in obedience to you, an explanation of the Prophets, insofar as my ability, assisted by divine grace, might carry it through. Let us therefore approach the knowledge of the work with attentive minds, so that we may see how much they have set forth at length, how much with acuteness, and how everything has been presented piously and coherently.

[Col. 0961]

# COMMENTARY ON HOSEA. (C,G)*

## BOOK ONE

### CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0961D]

## Verses 1 and 2

“The word of the Lord that came to Hosea son of Beeri in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash, king of Israel. The beginning of the Lord’s speaking in Hosea.”

According to the customary practice of those who narrate events occurring at different times, the mention of the kings also appears to have been made so that we might know the period in which the history was composed. Yet it was much more necessary for the Prophets to observe this practice, because although they do not simply pursue the task of history—namely, recounting events that have occurred, but also announce future things through the impulse of prophecy—nevertheless, since they present those future events as coming not by chance but by judgment, and discuss them according to the decision of that sovereign whose violated laws and frequently polluted rites they lament, they quite properly place the names and reigns of the kings at the beginning of the work. Thus, instructed by history, we may recognize what was committed during their reigns and admit that the Prophets had worthy and weighty reasons for their denunciations.

It is therefore contained in the annals of Kings and Chronicles that, while those whose names have been listed were reigning, the entire Jewish people was indeed polluted by the worship of idols. Yet the ten tribes which, after the division made under Jeroboam, were called Israel, were both defiled by the final forms of sacrilege and oppressed by the calamities impending over them. He therefore mentioned four kings of Judah, whose reigns coincided with the period of his prophecy, and one who had ruled over the Israelite side. But when he had begun his prophecy, those whom he named were governing those regions.

Not long afterward, however, domination at Samaria came to an end. For Zechariah son of Jeroboam, who had held the government by succession for six months already, was destroyed by a civil revolt—that is, by Shallum’s rebellion. Shallum, however, after reigning one month at Samaria, was succeeded by Menahem son of Gad, who, renewing the rebellion, destroyed the aforementioned tyrant. He himself, for ten years, served the king of the Assyrians, who was called Pul, under so great a burden of tribute that open poverty was evident, exercising not so much an orderly rule as a turbulent one.

Already, then, the storms of calamities aroused against that portion of the ten tribes were rushing upon it. Thus, while the kingdom remained among the people of Jerusalem, captivity was announced against the ten tribes. After the people of Samaria had migrated to the borders of Assyria, the holy Hosea, remaining in the region of Judah, witnessed the famous period of King Hezekiah’s miraculous deeds and, under him, also exercised the office of prophecy. Therefore, when he announced the disaster that was already threatening Israel, he named only the ruler of one part of it, under whom he had begun to prophesy.

As for what he wrote, “The beginning of the Lord’s speaking in Hosea,” this seems clearly to indicate that Hosea was the first to be summoned to this kind of speech, not that there had been no prophets before him [Note: [Col. 0963D] Saint Jerome says on this passage: “Others do not wish Hosea to have been the first of all the Prophets … [lacuna] … but they show that the Lord first spoke to Hosea the things that follow,” and so forth.], 393 since the same history of the kings records the deeds and sayings of the blessed Elijah, Elisha, and many others. Rather, it means that Hosea was the first of them to undertake the work of committing to writing for perpetual remembrance what each of them had foretold.

Nor do we deny that the blessed David and the most wise Solomon, with the Gospel and the Apostles as witnesses, were legitimate prophets and committed their sayings to writing. Yet the experienced Reader will notice that there is no small difference between them and the writings of those whom we are now attempting to explain. Although those earlier prophets said some things about the captivity of the people, they foretold what they had once foreseen as future with minds at rest—that is, without trembling at the proximity of disaster.

These later prophets, however, placed amid the very crashes of vengeance, with hearts wholly stunned, since they themselves were also made participants in the calamities, unfold everything as if in tearful laments. They portray the feeling of our Lord, who is compelled only with great reluctance to exact vengeance, while sometimes imploring the help of divine mercy; but for the rest, they pursue the sequence of calamities in something like a tragic style.

Let us therefore recognize that the beginning of these seers, who were marked especially by this title and called “prophets,” was undertaken by the blessed Hosea. Distinguished by the holiness of his character and lineage, he assumed the work of a preacher in such a way that he bore the person both of the Redeemer and of the Judge, as will become clearer throughout the work.

## Verses 2, 3, 4, and 5

“And the Lord said to Hosea: ‘Go, take for yourself a wife of fornications and children of fornications, because the land, committing fornication, will commit fornication away from the Lord.’ And he went and took Gomer daughter of Diblaim, and she conceived and bore a son. And the Lord said to him: ‘Call his name Jezreel, because in a little while I will visit the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu, and I will cause the kingdom of the house of Israel to cease; and on that day I will break the bow of Israel in the valley of Jezreel.’”

We must note the custom—or rather, the dignity—of holy men: after they have risen to such a height of distinction that our Lord uses their tongues as a scribe’s pen, not only their words but also their deeds are clothed with prophetic honor. In proclaiming mysteries, they serve either by teaching or by acting.

Thus, at the very beginning of the address, the sacred Author commanded the blessed Hosea, saying that he should disregard both the glory of his purpose and the splendor of his lineage and unite himself in marriage to a most vile and commonly prostituted woman.
