Nor should he tolerate merely the name of husband; he should also disturb his own reputation by enduring an equal share of disgrace [Note: [Col. 0963D] Perhaps *jura*, “rights,” should be read instead of *jure*, “by right.”], so that he might be believed to be the father of uncertain offspring, as though he had raised children born of another’s obscenity.

I am not unaware of the great dispute among learned men concerning the interpretation of this passage, so much so that entire regions disagree about its meaning. For Palestine and Egypt, together with all those who are deeply influenced by Origen’s authority [Note: [Col. 0963D] Saint Jerome also stands with these, maintaining that this was spoken figuratively, although, as we shall observe below, he wishes to defend the possibility that the blessed Hosea acted historically—not for the sake of lust, not from desire, and not by his own will, but in obedience to God’s command, so that what we read here carnally we might understand to have been accomplished spiritually by God. See his Preface.], deny that this marriage was physically contracted by the prophet Hosea.

Just as many things are narrated as having been done by the Prophets in the spirit, they say that this marriage with a prostitute was completed only in speech. For it was not appropriate to the circumstances of that time that Hosea, going forth to preach, should indulge in lust contrary to the ordinances of the sacred Law, which had declared association with a prostitute to be impious, and that, while he was about to pronounce judgment against sins, he should himself first commit what the entire people was subsequently to be accused of committing.

How inappropriate it would have been if, in defense of his disgraceful conduct, he had put forward the person of the one giving the command [Col. 0964B], asserting that, as far as his own morals were concerned, he had indeed detested the foulness of that association as foul, but had yielded to the authority of the Lord who had sent him to accuse the peoples. He would plainly seem to have supplied matter for ridicule rather than fear to the one who, speaking in God’s person, intended to accuse the obscenities of others, while Hosea himself proclaimed God to be the author of the disgrace he had committed.

It is also asked by what similar example throughout the Law this can be supported, namely, whether our Lord anywhere commanded something to be done contrary to the commandments whose transgressors he was going to avenge by announcing disasters through the Prophets. If, to teach this point, the parricide commanded to the blessed Abraham is brought forward, we shall be reminded, at the very conclusion of the work—although it was enacted before the time of the Law—not of the cruelty of the killing but of the piety and faith chosen in the father’s heart.

For he was offering his only son, the one who possessed the promises, to whom it had been said, “For in Isaac your offspring shall be called” (Genesis 21:12), showing that God could even raise him from the dead. Nevertheless, just as firm faith protected him against the fear that the promise might fail, so God did not permit the parent’s devotion to proceed all the way to the child’s destruction. He restrained the hand of the one about to sacrifice him, inserting praise of his tested virtue.

“It has become clear,” he said, “that I wished to make public only this: nothing is more powerful in you than either love for me or honor toward me. Now spare the blood, which neither another person was permitted nor you were worthy to shed. Yet do not appear to have been deprived of the priestly office. Behold, a ram stands there for you, its horns caught in the thorns. Just as its life has been able to provide immediate assistance by releasing the son, so it will also be worthy to signify a future mystery.”

In the affair of the blessed Hosea, however, not only the command but also its fulfillment—the association itself, repeated and continued over many years—seems defensible neither by the propriety of the deed nor by the authority of the command. To this is added the fact that even within the prophetic figures themselves the proper order has not been preserved. For a prostituted woman is taken as a symbol of the Tribes, which, living as though in God’s household and companionship, had burst into adulteries—that is, sacrileges. Yet this woman, although noble, is purified by the relationship; she receives children not from a dishonorable but from a respected husband, namely, the prophet; and, in honor of marriage, forgetful of her former vices, she enjoys fertility rather than lust.

How, then, can this woman, who is distinguished by matronly insignia, be shown to represent the person of that nation which, before marriage, did not shrink from the vices of obscenity, but is described as pursuing shamefulness after it had first been established in the sacred companionship of its Lord? By these and many other arguments they attempt to demonstrate that the prophet did not physically unite himself with a prostitute.

395 In opposition to this, the Syrians and those who think that the marriage was physically consummated rely especially upon the testimony of the names. For the woman, her parents, and her region are plainly identified, and the matter of the union is confirmed by the children that followed. Whatever the prophet undertook in obedience contrary to the customary standards of his conduct should be attributed rather to his devotion than to a violation of the Law. Moreover, that action could also be defended as a work of moral goodness [Note: [Col. 0965D] Read “the office of a wife” instead, if the phrase is derived from “the profession of a prostitute.” Jerome says: “Nor is the Prophet to be blamed if he converted a prostitute to chastity; rather, he is to be praised because he made a good woman out of a bad one,” and so forth. In his Preface, however, to prove that this occurred figuratively, he presses the same example as our author: Jeremiah hid his loincloth by the Euphrates, and so forth.], namely, if he had transferred the woman from the profession of prostitution to become thereafter a chaste wife and undertake a wife’s duties.

Since they therefore contend with one another in this dispute, they have rendered both opinions suspect. In reality, it seems both more concise and safer, and more suited to the meaning of the events, to believe that the matter was performed in the spirit. Thus, just as the blessed Jeremiah, without leaving the borders of Judea, is nevertheless described as burying a loincloth in the region of the Parthians; and just as the holy Ezekiel, while situated in the midst of the Babylonian captivity, is introduced as a spectator in the Jerusalem temple, viewing mere images of places and actions while being far away; so also the blessed Hosea, in order to signify the events of many periods, saw both the sequence of sins and the punishments through appropriate images.

Under whichever opinion one inclines, the dignity of the prophet is clearly displayed by the testimony of this office. The Creator of events seems to clothe himself in the prophet’s person, so that from the deeds of the man an account of the divine judgments may also be gathered. Such a close relationship exists between the eternal Lord and his faithful servant that the reputation of each seems to be intertwined; and if the prophet’s action requires cleansing, it may also appear to provide an excuse for divine mercy.

But if the majesty that surpasses all things overwhelms and rejects the service of our attestation, let it also ascribe to itself such authority as pleases it, so that it may be shown to have no need whatever of human judgment. The judgment of the Apostle Paul also declares this when he says: “For me it is a very small matter that I should be judged by you or by a human day; nor do I even judge myself. For I am conscious of nothing against myself. But the one who judges me is the Lord” (1 Corinthians 4:3–4). Thus, under one and the same reverence, both the command of the Creator and the action of the prophet stand.

The sequence and order of the words must also be carefully noted, since they rather suggest the interpretation according to which the union was not physically accomplished. “Go,” he says, “take for yourself a wife of fornications and children of fornications, because the land, committing fornication, will commit fornication away from the Lord.” Yet that period was touching not the beginnings of the sacrilege it accuses under the name of fornication [Perhaps something is missing here], but already its final stages.

From the time of Jeroboam, corruption of religion had especially begun, and the worship of the calves had been commended to the people; it continued for many generations without interruption. In the days, however, when the office of prophecy was imposed upon the blessed Hosea, it was not transgressions but rather vengeance that began to emerge. This plainly conflicts with the meaning that the prostitute taken in marriage seemed to display, indicating the insult that the Lord would have to endure for a long time. Let us therefore examine what the order of the announcement contains.

“Go, take for yourself a wife of fornications and children of fornications, because the land, committing fornication, will commit fornication away from the Lord.” And he went and took Gomer daughter of Diblaim, and she conceived and bore a son. And the Lord said to him: “Call his name Jezreel, because in a little while I will visit the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu, and I will cause the kingdom of the house of Israel to cease; and on that day I will break the bow of Israel in the valley of Jezreel.”

This expression is frequently found throughout the sacred books, that our God accuses sacrileges under the name of fornication. Because God, known in Judea, had chosen one nation to associate with himself and, as though in the place of a wife, had taken it to himself through the intervening tablets of the Law, so that he might raise children from it by instruction, he calls those chaste who preserve the rights of religion inviolate. Conversely, he calls those shameful and polluted who have violated the covenant of sacred worship through the infection of errors and the pursuit of heresy.

By this image he expressed both the greatness of his love toward the pious and the intensity of the severity with which he persecutes these impious people, because he rises to exact vengeance not merely as a censor or judge but as a husband raging in anger.

[Col. 0966B] But since the passage proceeds in its own sequence toward this understanding, we must ask what he accomplished by employing so elaborate a figure. Why was it necessary for all these matters to be contained not in a simple narrative, but for the prophet to be commanded—whether in the body or only in images—to enter into union with a prostitute?

To those who think about this matter piously and wisely, a profound insight into both divine goodness and prophetic dignity presents itself. Our God, who inserts his providence into human affairs, indeed takes thought for mortals generally; but, as though he considered only those to be truly human who had attained reverence through the virtues of their conduct, he shows himself moved by their judgments and hastens to instruct them especially both by commands and by images.

He therefore wished to show what I have already mentioned: that he has the most serious regard for holy men and does not treat their complaints as trivial; or perhaps that he is accustomed to be softened by the prayers of the saints when the time has come for him to begin bringing vengeance. Before them he first presents the matters by which he has been inflamed, so that, by explaining the merits, he may remove the obstacles to their intercession; and he first places on his own side those whom he could have found delaying the sentence, encouraging them to become angry with him.

Hence it is that, when the blessed Moses had sent spies from each of the twelve tribes to explore the Promised Land, and, with the exception of two, all the rest had terrified the cowardly people, the blessed Moses himself was also shaken by the rebellion that arose. But when he had fled to the tabernacle, “the glory of the Lord appeared,” he says; and showing how highly he regarded him and how much he preferred him to all those peoples, God said: “Let me alone, that I may destroy this people and make you into a nation much greater than this” (Exodus 32).

Understanding from these words what power the holy man possessed with God, he immediately softened the Judge’s indignation. So also, when the destruction of the Jerusalem temple was impending through the Babylonian captivity, God led the prophet Ezekiel, by the contemplation of the spirit alone, through the inner chambers that had once been objects of veneration. Seeing how the people were sinning, Ezekiel would cease to wonder if so great a change took place in the opposite direction, so that a nation recently exalted by singular reverence should perish in the utmost disgrace.

Thus a similar apparatus of events is also assigned to the blessed Hosea, through whom the destruction impending over the people was announced—a people whose ancestral merits and whose prophets’ intercessions would avail nothing. This was done so that, in his own example, he might sense and weigh whether God could or ought to endure that mound of insults.

“Assume,” he says, “the person of a kindly husband who has long endured the prostitute’s conduct in his wife; receive children who may be considered uncertain or, more appropriately, attributed to another’s obscenity; and test whether you can maintain continuous patience, and whether you think there can be a singular remedy for an old grief if you are separated (*dissidio*) from the woman whom, despite your many benefits, you have never corrected.”

Whether, then, the commanded union occurred only in the affections of the mind or also in the affairs of the shameful body, it appears to concern the prophet’s honor. In order faithfully to indicate the Judge’s severity, the prophet experiences a taste of the insult with which God was afflicted; and, as though an obligation to bring vengeance upon the impious might thereby arise, [lacuna]: that the prophet had endured an undeserved disgrace for the signification of the matter [Note: [Col. 0967D] At least two words are missing, perhaps “he assumes” and “signifies,” or something similar.].

Since, therefore, the explanation of the parable that we have offered seems to provide an adequate reason, let us now follow its sequence.

“Take,” he says, “for yourself a wife of fornications and children of fornications, because the land, committing fornication, will commit fornication away from the Lord.” This repetition belongs to the idiom of the Hebrew language: “doing, he will do”; “speaking, he will speak”; and other expressions of this kind. Thus here also: “committing fornication, he will commit fornication.” Some distinction could perhaps be applied to this expression [Note: [Col. 0967D] Some word also seems to be missing here.], but we must not neglect the concise usage that derives from the custom of the Scriptures.

Notice carefully that by the name “fornication” he designates not so much the time when transgression was to be committed as the captivity that was already about to be undergone. This is not without reason. Since obscenity had provided the material for the condemnation of profane minds, the punishment is marked by the name of its cause, so that we say that the people “commit fornication” when they are condemned for fornication.

The present passage also teaches that this had a major occasion. For although it is clear that punishment is not the same as guilt—since the one is opposed to honor and the other to wantonness—and although it has been sufficiently established that the definitions of things cannot be confused by a community of names, so that punishment is not guilt, he nevertheless did not pronounce the people “fornicators” without reason at the time when they were about to enter the evils of captivity.

He knew that correction itself would produce different results according to the diversity of minds: some would become better through affliction, while others would become more shameless. He therefore rightly says that, because of the impiety they had perpetrated in their own territories, they would bear punishments; and that, in the very time of captivity, some would acquire the marks of amendment, while others would acquire proofs of their crime, according to what he threatens elsewhere: “You served gods in your land, gods whom your fathers did not know; you shall serve foreign gods in a land that is not yours.”

Because the nation, while free, had celebrated the profanation it had committed, and, once enslaved, had continued to celebrate it, it is also foretold to be committing fornication in the midst of its punishments.

The first son, whom the prostitute is said to have borne, is introduced under the name of the region itself, upon which captivity was impending. For he says: “Call his name Jezreel.” This was the name by which the valley adjoining Samaria was designated. Through the name of this place, therefore, he announces what the region will suffer.

Finally, the text continues: “Because in a little while I will visit the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu, and I will cause the kingdom of the house of Israel to cease; and on that day I will break the bow of Israel in the valley of Jezreel.”

“The time for exercising vengeance,” he says, “is at hand. For this reason anger rises against the kingdom of Samaria, which is indicated by the name Jezreel, the neighboring valley, as I have said. Let a child therefore be born to your mind, destined for punishment, so that you may know that what you seem to have arranged against your own children is to be carried out against my children.”

“For I will visit the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu.” In explaining this, a twofold interpretation would arise according to the customary usage of the Law, unless what follows established one of them. The descendants of Jeroboam ruled down to the family of Ahab, who was Jezebel’s husband. But because Ahab had been defiled by his own crimes and by those of his wife, whose will he served, the prophet Elisha raised Jehu son of Nimshi, at God’s command, to assume the kingdom.

Moved by severity for similar reasons, Jehu destroyed by slaughter the entire family of Ahab and Jezebel, together with all the priests and ministers of the idol Baal. In return for this work of vengeance, it was promised to him that his descendants would rule the Israelite kingdom to the fourth generation.

But because Jehu himself, and his sons and grandsons, by failing to abandon the sacrileges of Jeroboam, lost the marks of their devotion by which they had persecuted the worshipers of Baal—clinging instead to the worship of the calves at Samaria and serving various crimes of conduct, as the worship of profanity requires—anger is therefore said to rise also against these descendants of Jehu, who had destroyed the family of Ahab, so that he might avenge the blood of those who had been killed by them.

This is not because the slaughter had been unjust, but because those who had carried it out lost the honor of judges through imitating crimes; by committing deeds like those of the people they had destroyed, they passed into the number and fellowship of the guilty. Thus those whom the sword of criminals had killed appeared worthy of vengeance. We could easily show that this manner of expression is also frequent in the Scriptures.

Therefore, I say, the prophetic verse could be explained in two ways: in the manner we have first set out, and in another that will follow, if the progress of the work did not more strongly support the former. For by the name Jezreel he wished to indicate the people themselves, and by the name Jehu the kingdom of the people.

That is: “Behold, the time has now come for the people of Israel, who are to be defeated either in the valley of Jezreel or in the city whose royal seat is situated in that same valley, and who have a king descended from the stock of Jehu, to begin to experience the force of the vengeance they deserve.”

Finally, to confirm this interpretation, he added: “And I will cause the kingdom of the house of Israel to cease, and on that day I will break the bow of Israel in the valley of Jezreel.” Accordingly, he called the visitation “punishment,” and the cessation “the end of the kingdom.” To make both points clearer, he said: “I will break the bow of Israel in the valley of Jezreel.”

## Verse 6

“And she conceived again and bore a daughter, and he said: ‘Call her name Without Mercy, because I will no longer continue to have mercy on the house [Jerome: household] of Israel, but I will utterly forget them.’”

Because he had determined to anticipate the outcome of events through images that would serve as judges of those same events, a daughter is described as having been born, receiving a name that signifies another’s calamity, namely, “Without Mercy.”

“For,” he says, “I will no longer continue to have mercy on the house of Israel, but I will utterly forget them.” This sentence contains a double weight of meaning. He does not merely say that he will deny mercy during the time of their miseries; he also says that he will not permit them to return to his memory.

It would be some consolation, even in the extremity of suffering, if at some time he took into his memory those whom he had cast away. But now, so that the preceding threat may grow harsher, he promises that both things will come upon them: the memory, so to speak, of those who are to be condemned, and the fullest forgetfulness of those who have been condemned.

Since this could arouse in the ears of a wise servant [Col. 0968D] the appearance of cruel envy—so that he might think or say something like this: “How did so much bitterness flow into that kindness which is the cause of all things? Do not forget the offenses if you forget the offenders; be attentive to the delinquent if you never remember the afflicted. I fear that the salvation of the penitent too must be despaired of, if forgetfulness of those who have fallen should creep upon so great a ruler”—he therefore immediately added that he had not abandoned the concern to show mercy, but had applied the balance of due judgment. That is, he would forget only those who, even after their blows, would not think about amendment.

### Verse 7

“For I will no longer continue to have mercy on the house of Israel, but I will utterly forget them. Yet I will have mercy on the house of Judah [Jerome: “to the house”] and save them by the Lord their God; I will not save them by bow, sword, battle, horses, or horsemen.”

When, he says, I have subjected the people of Samaria, defiled by transgression, to disasters and destruction, and have allowed them to become so worthless because of their guilt that I may seem entirely to have forgotten them, then I will not merely protect those settled in the territory of Judah, who place the hope and confidence of their salvation in religious worship; I will also rescue them by a wondrous novelty, so that it may plainly be evident that they were not defended by weapons but by merits, and that they achieved victory not by battle-line but by devotion.

He announces the time when, with Hezekiah ruling among the people of Jerusalem, Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, came against that city with a great army to besiege it. After uttering many things there in insult to God and to sacred religion, he provoked the divine sentence against himself, and in a single night all his forces fell, struck down by the Angel.

> **Note:** Jerome has the same account: “For he saved them when Israel had been handed over to the Assyrians, from the hand of Sennacherib—not by bow, sword, battle, or a multitude of horsemen, but by his own strength, when he sent an Angel and struck down, in one night, 185,000 from the army of the king of the Assyrians.” From this you may gather that Our author did not refuse to borrow certain things from him.

After the loss of 185,000 warriors, Sennacherib himself is described as having fled with a few men into his own country and perished there (4 Kings 19). But let us examine what follows as well.

### Verse 8

“He weaned,” he says, “her who was without mercy; and she conceived and bore a son and said: ‘Call his name Not-My-People, because you are not my people, and I will not be your God.’”

> **Note:** No copies of the Scriptures add the name “God” here.

The title indicates that the blessed Hosea remained alive and prophesied until the time of Hezekiah. Whatever, therefore, was accomplished throughout the whole period of his prophecy, he briefly marks out in this opening, so that through the entire book he may now disclose the series and order of events.

When, therefore, the profanity of the ungrateful nation had driven Our God to undertake the work of vengeance, he declared that he would punish the guilty and leave them in misery in such a way that he would seem wholly to have forgotten them. But lest this forgetfulness, once received into the sacred heart, should also arouse fear in the devout, he immediately indicated that he assumed forgetfulness not through fault but through judgment, since he was establishing a deserved distinction among related peoples: Israel would be handed over to destruction, while the people of Judah, who clung to the worship of his religion, would be protected more by miracles than by weapons.

Although this would be revealed at the proper time, nevertheless, because that portion of the Jewish nation itself was by no means pleasing through constant devotion, but—as the other prophets reproach it—burned with zeal for the worship of idols, it too suffered a similar sentence and was carried away from its borders when Babylon prevailed. Yet concerning that captivity, the return of nearly all the people was promised in the prophecies of the prophets and was fulfilled under Cyrus, king of the Persians.

The speech of the blessed Hosea therefore now proclaims both periods. To signify the captivity of Israel, a daughter is introduced who is to be called “Without Mercy.” As a figure of Judah, however, a boy is introduced whose name is “Not-My-People.”

Among the images of the children, only the girl is said to have been weaned, clearly to show that in the ten tribes the sentence of the captivity inflicted upon them had, as it were, grown strong. For the captivity of the ten tribes is in fact recorded as having lasted much longer; therefore the advancement of age is marked by the girl’s weaning.

The third child, who finally promises the captivity of Judah, received the name “Not-My-People.” For as long as Judah remained within its own borders, there was a multitude that could be called God’s people. But after the storm of captivity also tore Judah away, that people, formerly distinguished from the confusion of the Gentiles, seemed to have perished through dispersion.

Therefore he says: “You are not my people, and I will not be your God.” That is: the distinction by which you were formerly conspicuous will be taken away from you, so that you will no longer be called God’s people throughout the whole world, nor will I be called your ruler or your God. For it is just that those who corrupted, through their zeal for sin, the institutions of the sacred Law that separated you from the other nations should also be deprived of the adornment by which you were distinguished.

Yet after briefly announcing these matters from the side of severity, he turns to the blessings that the revered dispensation fulfilled in events just as it had woven them together in prophetic speech.

### Verses 10–11

“For the number of the children of Israel,” he says, “will be like the sand of the sea, which cannot be measured and cannot be numbered. And in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ they will be called children of the living God. And the children of Judah and the children of Israel will be gathered together, and they will appoint for themselves one head, and they will go up from the land, because great is the day of Jezreel.”

By these sacred words he promises the people’s return from the Babylonian captivity. A great display of that return is also described by the other prophets, but especially by the blessed Isaiah. This serves to commend God’s mercy and to console and strengthen the faithful, who, contrary to the dignity of their merits, endured the fellowship of that calamity because they belonged to the nation and were therefore offered the consolations of hope, resting upon the expectation of prosperity.

Those blessings are said to be so great that they even require a novelty of names. For when they fell from happiness into misery, they ceased to be called God’s people, as though they had been poured into the contempt of the remaining nations. But when the time of liberation arrived, the change from misery to happiness was restored with such abundance that the restoration of their former dignity was not enough: the distinctions of their names were increased.

The number of the faithful will exceed that of the sands. In them such splendor of reverence and grace will shine that they will no longer be called merely the people of God, who contains all things, but his children. Corrected by the anguish of their former servitude, they will be joined to one another by blood and by love. They will avoid especially that separation which had been for them the great cause both of crimes and of divisions; and, rejoicing under one ruler, they will ascend joyfully to the Temple of God. They will be placed in such a condition of happiness that they will acknowledge the day of Jezreel to have been great.

That is, either the time when adversity began, concerning which the Prophet said above, “I will break the bow of Israel in the valley of Jezreel.” The liberated people will recall this, so that their joys may grow greater by comparison; or certainly it will proclaim that the interpretation of Jezreel itself applies to it. In our language, Jezreel expresses “seed of God,” and the sense would be as follows: When the time of captivity has been released, such an abundance of exultation will exist that it will be said that a great day has dawned for the children of God.

The blessed David, like the other prophets, especially celebrates this festival in that song:

> “I rejoiced in the things that were said to me:  
> We shall go into the house of the Lord.  
> Our feet were standing in your courts, Jerusalem,  
> to praise your name, O Lord.  
> For there the seats sat in judgment,  
> seats over the house of David.  
> Pray for the things that are for the peace of Jerusalem”  
> (Psalm 121).

Accordingly, in accordance with the historical sequence contained in the prophetic announcement, he briefly indicated everything that he was going to do: namely, that the ten tribes, corrupted under Jeroboam and captured by the Assyrian, would be carried away; that Judah, which trusted in its God, would be miserably delivered under King Hezekiah; and that afterward, having followed the traces of its brother’s impiety, that tribe itself would be handed over to Babylonian domination.

Yet the promised freedom would once again release its bonds; and the brothers, no longer separated from one another but standing under one ruler, would celebrate the honor of God in the inner sanctuaries of his Temple. The happiness of that time would be so great that it would even be pleasant to remember adversity and to call it the great day of Jezreel—that is, the time of the captivity inflicted, whose occasion had created such abundant exultation.

“They will appoint for themselves one head, and they will go up from the land.” Concerning this time the blessed David also says:

> “From the ends of the earth I cried to you when my heart was in distress;  
> you lifted me up upon a rock.  
> You led me, because you became my hope”  
> (Psalm 60).

> **Note:** Earlier editions wrongly read *augeretur*; the Vulgate has *anxiaretur* (“was distressed”).

It must also be noted that the blessed Paul applied the promise of this passage concerning the multitude of the faithful who would come together at the preaching of the Gospel. He asserted that the proclamation of evangelical devotion had surpassed the narrow limits of a single nation.

Not only would companies of Jews, who had formerly been called God’s people, come together to attain the dignity marked out by God, but also companies of Gentiles, who had lived in manifold error. As he says in Hosea:

> “I will call those who were not my people, my people,  
> and her who was not beloved, beloved.  
> And it will be in the place where it was said to them,  
> ‘You are not my people,’  
> there they will be called children of the living God”  
> (Romans 9:25).

The teacher of the Gentiles therefore shows that the promise of this happiness would be fulfilled in the time of the Gospel. He did not deny what the entire text of the prophecy insists upon—namely, that the release from the Babylonian captivity had also been promised—but showed what rule of interpretation we ought to observe in the prophetic books: when, under the narration of Jewish affairs, something is promised that is greater than the limitations of a single nation could contain, we should recognize that it was partly fulfilled in that people and that, through its deeper meaning, it also applies to others, that is, to all nations.

> **Note:** René Laurentius de la Barre, who first published this commentary in print, thought that *promereretur* might more correctly be read here. He missed the rationale: the sense and construction are that something greater is promised than the capacity of a single nation could contain. It would indeed please one to divide the word *etiam* in the following verse into two, and now …

Now *theoria* is, as the learned have judged, an apprehension, usually in brief forms or causes, of those things that are more important.

Therefore it would not properly be said that the return of the Jews from Babylon is signified according to history, while the freedom bestowed through faith in Christ is signified according to allegory, since the prophetic speech solidly promised both, so that the smaller matters stated earlier might indicate the greater accumulations that followed. For what was first said by way of exaggeration was afterward scarcely equaled by the magnitude of events.

Thus the captivity then announced, which terrified the Jewish people, and the freedom later restored, which raised them up, bore indications also of other captivity and freedom—of things much graver than those. This is the captivity of which the Apostle says:

> “We were by nature children of wrath, even as the rest. But God, who is rich in mercy, because of his great love with which he loved us, when we were dead in sins, made us alive together in Christ”  
> (Ephesians 2:4).

The stronger one who came bound that enemy of the human race who had long oppressed the guilty under his domination, plundered all his vessels, and dissolved the captivity of the nations by restoring freedom. He ennobled the redeemed with gifts of grace, so that those who had once been strangers and foreigners might suddenly be called his people—having obtained mercy—or rather, an elect race, priestly and royal people (1 Peter 2).

Thus what Hosea had announced concerning the times of Babylon, Paul transferred to the work of the Savior. He did so not as though the prophet were refusing or reluctantly following where he was led, but because the prophetic text itself strongly favored the apostolic understanding. It taught that the gifts and joys begun in that former age had here been increased almost to their consummation.

Up to this point the prophet’s speech has proceeded in such a way as briefly to indicate whatever affairs and times he was going to discuss.

Now, however, he returns to the order of the censure or complaint he had begun. He did this deliberately and prudently, lest what contributed to the splendor of the prediction should begin to harm salutary instruction.

Since, in the force of his prophecy, he had touched upon matters that would follow only after long ages, and since the confidence with which he announced both adversities and prosperities supplied credibility to his declarations, this might otherwise extinguish at once both the merit of correction and the desire for improvement. Once the necessity of punishment had been announced by the prophet, the effort to correct oneself might appear useless; and the hope of prosperity might no longer seem necessary, since everything had to be fulfilled in accordance with the truth of the announcement.

Therefore the speech is directed to the people, who are summoned into fellowship with the judgment, so that they may examine their mother—the multitude of their ancestors, whose crimes had provoked God—with attentive eyes, and admonish her concerning the divine mercy, which is accustomed to remove even punishments already announced if the guilty person is seen to have fled to correction.

They therefore ought not to despair of salvation if they are made better by fear, since the master of merits presides over those who have been expunged, and he is pleased far more by smiling indulgence than by bitter severity.

## Chapter II

### Verse 2

“Judge your mother, judge her, because she is not my wife, and I am not her husband.”

A great memorial of my kindness, he says, is your liberation. Therefore the merits of your deformed parent are exposed: because of them she has been driven away from my companionship, and they are so shameful that she cannot be acquitted even when judged by you.

But because we are now passing judgment not upon one person but upon the whole nation, we hope that there will be some whom the announced severity may move toward better pursuits. Therefore wait to see what I am about to require.

“Let her remove her fornications from her face and her adulteries from between her breasts.”

### Verse 3

“Otherwise I may strip her naked and set her up as on the day of her birth.”

That is, she had driven modesty, which usually restrains obscenity, away from her face, and had hardened her countenance by openly professing shamefulness. Now, therefore, let her take up the opposite dispositions: let her clothe a brow stripped of shamelessness with modesty and know that she must not be content merely to have done this with her lips,

> **Note:** The word *sciat* (“let her know”) is superfluous and should be deleted.

 as though on the surface; rather, let her cast out the poison drawn from between her breasts, so that she may immediately be cleansed in her whole heart.

If she neglects to do this, I will gird myself for works of severity and will impose punishments such as I exercised at the time when this people was being born for me. He indicates the exodus of the Synagogue from the land of Egypt, when it had received none of the institutions of the Law, neither ornaments nor clothing, and did not possess any distinguished insignia of garments. As far as the value of its morals was concerned, it remained in the same degradation as the Egyptians, yet it was preserved by great miracles because of the sole honor of its ancestors.

Finally, because they resisted God’s commandments both through insolence and through sloth, all of them are read to have been consumed in the solitude of the wilderness. Apart from the two men Joshua and Caleb, no one among the 600,000 men of military age who had marched entered the Promised Land.

This, therefore, is what the Lord now threatens through the prophet: if that nation does not cleanse the secrets of its heart and advance through a change for the better, no support will be able to compare with that by which, over so many generations, it had been distinguished from other nations and had flourished in the institutions of the Law and in spiritual gifts.

> **Note:** Earlier editions read *discrea*. We often silently correct similar errors that appear to be printers’ blunders. Many scarcely curable errors remain, as the reader will see, although we too have corrected innumerable ones [EDITOR].

He presses this point through the sentence concerning its crimes. Just as in that former age, he says, when it came out of Egypt and rejoiced in its recent adoption, nothing profited those wretched people, so that they perished as though they were naked of every privilege.

The Apostle Paul carefully developed this same sense when writing to the Corinthians:

> “All were liberated by the same miracles; all partook of the same spiritual food and drank from the same springs bursting forth from the rock. Yet,” he says, “God was not pleased with all of them, nor with many of them. In that age of exile they were horrified by different sins and perished under different punishments.”

He shows why we should remember them:

> “These things were written for our instruction, so that we may not imitate the pursuits of those whose ruins we read about”  
> (1 Corinthians 10).

Through this prophet, therefore, Our Lord reveals the intention of his counsel. He warns that the people should hasten to help themselves through correction and drive out from between their breasts—that is, from their heart—the impiety called fornication, lest they experience the trials of that severity whose execution is delayed only by difficulty.

For whether he proceeds to consume the wicked through vengeance, the multitude of those perishing will not be able to resist; or whether he commands the children of the punished to be restored to salvation because of the honor of their innocence or the merits of their correction, not even the accumulation of the calamity already announced will be able to create any obstacle.

To indicate all this briefly, the prophet preserved in the example the same order as in the prophecy. Just as in the title he marked the entire period of his prophecy by mentioning the kings, so he also showed what matters his preaching contained: first the captivity of Israel, then that of Judah; afterward the concord of those same peoples once their captivity had been released; and, with freedom restored, their gathering for the worship and Temple of the true God.

Yet the splendor of this return was described in such a way as to signify a greater matter: namely, to proclaim both the freedom and the generosity of the Gospel. Transcending their hopes through its gifts, it would call not merely a people but also the children of God those whom it had freed from deadly servitude.

Having briefly passed through these matters, he returned to the exhortation appropriate to those times. As though addressing children, he assigns them the task of rebuking and instructing their mother, so that she who had taken no care to preserve holiness might at least take care to seize repentance. She must not suppose that, contrary to the value of her conduct, she could be defended merely by the nobility of her blood, since adoption would profit nothing those whom devotion did not also unite.

> **Note:** That is, *quando* (“when”) is used as a single word in place of *quoniam* (“because”).

To infer the future from the past, she should reflect upon the end of those companies that had been miraculously led out of Egypt. Their iniquity was not defended by the dignity of their ancestors, as we have said, and their slaughter created no obstacle to the children who were to be led into the promised joys.

The same order of judgments, he says, will now also be maintained in your expunging, so that those who are foul with sacrileges will be overwhelmed by destruction, while their descendants—who have differed from the purpose of their forefathers through better pursuits—will either, though abandoned, attain freedom, or be increased still more by the successes of prosperity.

These changes of the times, he says, since they assign the reason of divine providence and just administration both for sad things and for joyful things, now require us to pursue what the present circumstance demands.

He therefore announces that they should anticipate the burden of the condemnation hanging over them by the zeal of correction and the lamentation of repentance, lest, when he begins to rage of his own accord, the entire nation should perish in annihilation, just as though it had never been marked by any privileges:

“Otherwise I may strip her naked and set her up as on the day of her birth; I may make her like a wilderness and set her like an impassable land, and kill her with thirst” (verse 4), “and I will not have mercy on her children, because they are children of fornication, for their mother has fornicated; she has been put to shame who conceived them.”

Because he had once introduced the recollection and likeness of the exodus from Egypt, he proceeded through a description of the same places, naming the wilderness and an impassable land deprived of the comfort of springs. Then, again taking up words from the circumstances, he added the danger of thirst after recalling the desolation of the wilderness.

“I will kill them with thirst,” he says—not because the people led out of Egypt perished through deprivation, but because, as the Apostle says, “they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them” (1 Corinthians 10), that is, from the power of their leader, not from the condition of the region. The camp received drink from that source. If it had been absent, the people would have perished at the first danger of thirst.

He likewise announces that the wicked will be led into similar necessities and that his mercy will not come to meet them, since even the offspring of such people, by imitating their faults, acknowledge that their parents are shameful, and sons blush because of their parents just as parents blush because of their sons. He promises that they will perish from thirst.

### Verses 5–7

“For she said, ‘I will go after my lovers, who give me my bread and my water, my wool and my flax, my oil and my drink.’ Therefore, behold, I will hedge your way with thorns and wall it in with a wall, and she will not find her paths.

> **Note:** The Vulgate, and Jerome’s translation from the Hebrew, read, “who give **me** my bread and **my** water, my wool,” etc. Our author adheres more closely to the Hebrew in the first instance, but departs from it in the second. She will pursue her lovers, but she will not overtake them; she will seek them, but she will not find them.”

From the beginning of the book he assigned the character of a prostitute to the profaned nation.

> **Note:** Earlier editions wrongly read *quis ab initio librum* (“who, from the beginning, the book”). He continues the rest in an elevated description and introduces her speaking in the manner of a harlot, although she is convicted of having carried out this speech not with her lips but in her deeds.

Thus, according to the custom of the Scriptures, the wicked are accused because they have said in action what they might also have said in words as a consequence of their more sinister way of life.

So this woman too, he says, shamelessly presents the appearance of usefulness to her pursuit of wickedness, pretending that her lovers follow her on account of their generosity rather than her disgrace. She praises them for having supplied her with wool, flax, oil, and drink—that is, food and clothing overflowing even into luxury.

Although these words also add the crime of an ungrateful mind to the sins of sacrilege, they seem likewise to introduce something that even now circulates on the lips of the profane: among various opinions, no testimony to a certain religion is considered stronger than what the voice of prosperity supplies.

Therefore she too declares that she is going after her lovers, suppresses the crime in silence, and invents apparently more respectable reasons by which to attract them. She calls them “lovers” either the leaders of the Gentiles, by pursuing whom she was profaned, or the gods of the nations themselves, more worthy of laughter than of worship. The Synagogue, forgetful of the Law of her fathers and of the true and only God, succumbed to them.

“Let adversity,” he says, “follow her hopes, and let her be entangled in unforeseen anguish.” First, let her have no opportunity to make a covenant with the nations she most desires, and let her not use in adversity the help of those whose example she followed in prosperity.

Thus I will hedge her way with thorns, and not merely with briars but also with walls, so that she cannot afterward enter the paths she formerly trod.

He appended all these matters in sequence, looking to the character of the woman he had introduced, who frequented the author of her disgrace by secret paths, as it were. This does not mean that the people of Israel secretly mingled with profane nations, but that the likeness transferred from a woman, as we have often said, required this order of description.

When avenging severity begins to confront her, and all those whom she loved are unable to offer any help to her anguish, she will begin to remember her former happiness—not now moved by reason but by distress.

> **Note:** Earlier editions wrongly read *revivisci* here.

“And she will say, ‘I will go and return to my first husband, because it was better for me then than now.’” (Verse 8.)

“And she did not know that I gave her grain, wine, and oil, and multiplied these for her, and gold, which they made into Baals.”

> **Note:** “And silver” must plainly be supplied here; it occurs both in all the other books and in the Hebrew text. The following exposition shows that our author did not have those words in his copy.

If, at least when aroused by the dangers facing her, she decides to return to her former husband, how does the following statement fit: “And she did not know that I gave her grain, wine, and oil”?

The sense is therefore of this kind, so that harmony may be preserved among the prophetic statements. At the first appearance of correction, this woman suffers what all who pursue vanity suffer. Frightened by the frustration of her hopes, she attempts these things not through a change of judgment but through the fickleness of judgment—seeking what she would reject if she were corrected—and promises to submit herself to God only in order to escape the impending losses of prosperity.

This accords with what the blessed David reproaches:

> “When he slew them, then they sought him;  
> and they returned and came early to him,  
> but their heart was not right with him,  
> nor were they counted faithful in his covenant”  
> (Psalm 77:34–37).

Since, therefore, the guilt of the nation remains—the nation that, like cattle, was aroused not by the teaching of the word but only under the action of the whip—my anger will not be tested by her saying, “I will go and return to my first husband.”

Rather, I will lead her through a long experience of punishments, because she failed to know and acknowledge that all these things could be given by no one except me, by whom they had also been created.

Therefore, when he says, “And she did not know that I gave her grain, wine, and oil,” he points to the blameworthiness of deliberate slowness, in accordance with the saying of David:

> “He refused to understand, so that he might do good”  
> (Psalm 35).

Thus, amid the dangers of her tribulations, she will begin to confess what she had previously neglected to know: namely, that I alone am the one from whom sustenance is supplied, and that I also created the substance of human beings.

“For I gave her grain, wine, and oil, and gold, which they made into Baals.” Thus she was not only equipped but also wealthy, and she abused my gifts for crimes. To my insult, she fashioned idols from the riches she had received from me.

Therefore I, whose dispensation the prophet intelligently praised when he sang:

> “With the holy you will be holy;  
> with the innocent man you will be innocent;  
> with the perverse you will become perverse”  
> (Psalm 17),

will finally take up the office of judgment, so that I may withdraw from the ungrateful what had been bestowed upon them. The very riches will thus obtain a kind of liberation when they are withdrawn from profane uses.

### Verse 9

“For this reason I will take away my grain in its time and my wine in its time,” because there is not one single gathering of crops: each thing is harvested at different times of the year. Therefore summer will deny the harvest, autumn the vintage, and winter will take away the mobility of the seasons. Creation itself, he says, will experience a kind of liberation if the unworthy do not make use of it.

“And I will rescue my wool and my flax, which covered her disgrace.”

He elegantly alluded to a woman’s toilette: the whole body, including whatever parts are shameful, is covered in such a way that it is also beautified. Yet he seems to point out sharply that often the ugliness of the guilty lies hidden beneath the prosperity of life; when worthy poverty overtakes them again, their previously concealed merits are also exposed.

### Verse 10

“And now I will reveal her foolishness before the eyes of her lovers.”

That is, those very people who had been the authors or accomplices of the crime will be compelled by subsequent events to confess that nothing is more foolish than this nation. It neither directed its plans wisely nor corrected its dangers, but provoked the Lord of ungrateful mind with its crimes, even though it experienced his power, which contains all things, in its adversities as well as in its prosperity.

“Therefore I will reveal her foolishness before the eyes of her lovers, and no man will rescue her from my hand.”

That is, none of the princes whose profanity she followed will be able to defend her from my indignation. This does not mean that anyone would dare to do so; rather, because the speech is woven through the likeness of the woman and the men, he says that when divine indignation strikes her, her lovers will be unable to come to her aid or to bring any comfort to the miseries with which she is to be overwhelmed.

### Verse 11

“I will take away all her joy, her solemnity, her new moon, her Sabbath, and all her appointed festival times.”

Jerome’s version and the Vulgate read: “I will cause to cease,” which follows the Hebrew more closely.

He has named the holidays in which she took the greatest pleasure, when the whole region indulged in dances, songs, and feasts. Such luxury flourished only when the people enjoyed profound peace.

“All these things,” he says, “will be changed into their opposites.”

> **Note:** “Joy,” or something similar, must be supplied after *cessante* (“ceasing”).

With joy ceasing, mourning will be imposed; captivity will occupy the times of the festivals; the rest of the Sabbaths will be filled by the grievous labor of servitude. Not only will freedom be changed by such captivity, but the fruitfulness of the lands will also be changed into mournful sterility.

### Verse 12

“For I will corrupt her vine and her fig tree, concerning which she said, ‘These are my rewards, which my lovers gave me.’ And I will make her into a forest, and the beast of the field will devour her.”

He has explained what the loss of her resources would accomplish: when diligent cultivation is continually followed by frustration, the countryside, once pleasant, will display its former beauty replaced by desolation. The whole region will become more like a lair than like fields, that is, more suitable for wild beasts than for human beings.

Because the scarcity of cultivators would bring about this appearance, he expressed it elegantly by saying that the beasts of the field would feed on her produce.

> **Note:** For the deponent form. At the beginning of the following period the earlier editor notes that some copies read *et* (“and”) for *quod* (“because”); at the end, *vescendas* should be read for *vescituras*.

She voluntarily cast away the light of reason, he says, and after being filled and fattened, she kicked against her benefactor. This most shameless nation favored its own error so greatly that it dared to attribute to its corrupters the joys of peace and the abundance of resources whose continuance I had promised it if it had remained chaste and devoted.

Therefore this will be the first part of her vengeance: she will be stripped both of the joys and of the resources which she had not used well, and she will learn that the one who had previously bestowed these things in his favor was also able, when angered, to take them away.

“I will make her into a forest, and the beast of the field will devour her.” I will permit her, he says, to be consumed by hostile invasion, and I will not surround her with any defense of my arrangement, just as a farmer does not enclose forests or wild-animal lairs with cultivated hedges.

And because he seemed to have pronounced a true sentence, he again adds the reason for this admonition, to show that whatever he had thundered forth was supplied more by justice than by anger.

### Verse 13

“And I will visit upon her the days of the Baals,” he says, “on which she burned incense, adorned herself with her earring and her necklace, and went after her lovers, while she forgot me, says the Lord.”

She is not now, he says, at the beginning of sin, so that it might be thought that her wrongdoing should be covered over with the passage of time. Long ago our patience contended with her wickedness, yet we accomplished nothing toward her correction, when she grew old in her profanity.

Therefore, lest prolonged impunity stain even the reputation of the judge, and I seem to favor what I have allowed to continue for so long, I will undertake the work of vengeance, though late—indeed, at last—and I will erase even those days on which she, adorned with necklaces, served the Baals, the idols of disgrace.

The fact that he mentioned not only a necklace but also earrings may certainly be explained by saying that he named a few of the many things with which women adorn themselves. Yet the passage permits us to offer a more subtle interpretation: by the name of earrings, obedience may be indicated.

Since at that time the Jewish people alone had received the precepts of the Law, which they were to obey, it deservedly wore them as ornaments of earrings. But after it was deceived by a fatal error and subjected itself to the rites of idols, we should understand this very point as being especially reproached.

It is as though he said: The gold and silver that the earth had brought forth because I created it, and that the Synagogue had received because I bestowed it, together with the abundance of other things, she used in the worship and adornment of idols. And that distinctive mark of obedience, by which alone she excelled among the other peoples, she devoted to shameful rites.

Believing that she remained in the beauty she had once possessed, she followed her lovers with such confidence that she almost incurred forgetfulness of our name.

> **Notes:**  
> — In one place the earlier text read *discrea*; this should be *discreta*. Other such errors, which seem to be typographical blunders, we often correct silently. Many others remain scarcely curable, as will be evident to the reader, although we have corrected innumerable errors as well.  
> — The earlier editor preferred *erubescendis* (“to be ashamed of”) here rather than *erubescentibus* (“those who are ashamed”).  
> — Near the end of the paragraph, where the sequence of words and the sense give *eam plena ut nostri numinis*, read *eam pene ut*; perhaps *nominis* is also more correct than *numinis*.

## Verses 14–17

“Therefore, behold, I shall nourish her, and lead her into the wilderness, and speak to her heart, and give her vinedressers from that place, and the Valley of Achor as an opening of hope; and she shall sing there as in the days of her youth and as in the days of her ascent from the land of Egypt. And it shall be in that day, says the Lord, that she will call me ‘My husband,’ and will no longer call me ‘My Baals.’ And I shall remove the names of the Baals from her mouth, and she shall no longer remember their name.”

The order of the prophetic discourse must be carefully noted. [Col. 0977B] Whenever necessity requires that he announce torments and display the grounds of divine severity, he immediately appends the causes that deserved them. Nor is he content merely to enumerate the faults of mortals: he proceeds to describe the joys of the prosperity that will follow, showing that our God makes use of that brief concealment of pardon, as it were, in preparation for reconciliation. By this same argument, however, just as divine clemency is praised, human wickedness is cast down; for its magnitude causes the Lord of such great goodness sometimes to be stirred to anger.

After he had therefore declared that, amid the universal joys, a sorrowful cessation would have to be imposed, and that no one would come forward to bring either help or consolation to the wretched, he immediately set forth the crimes of the people—that is, the causes of his indignation—and, recalling their magnitude and their duration, showed that no one ought to suspect his judgment of excessive severity. For if it is compared with either the extent or the duration of their crimes, its restraint must be excused, and its delay must be excused. [Col. 0977C]

Yet, as I have said, he does not commend this sweet and familiar clemency in only one way. By adding the announcement of blessings to the wounds already inflicted, he confirms the same point and describes it with such greater elaboration, as though he wished not merely to compensate for what he had struck, but also to excuse it.

[Note: [Col. 0977D] Or it would be preferable to read: “color, this, I say,” or “sweet, I say,” etc.; but to pursue minute errors of this kind would be lengthy.]

Therefore, when he had said that he would place her in a forest, so that the beasts of the field might devour her—that is, after removing all the defenses of the kingdom and the cities, she would be handed over to the power of her enemies—[the judgment, as once in Egypt, being an insult or misery of clay-bound servitude], since by pursuing idols she had forgotten her God, nevertheless, because he himself would act as one compassionate and merciful, he announces joys of return after the end of the captivity.

[Note: [Col. 0977D] The words we enclosed in parentheses seem to have slipped into the text from one or two marginal notes in the book.]

And because above he had introduced a mention of the liberation from Egypt, asserting that this too would be granted to the Israelite peoples after the pattern of that earlier deliverance, he now pursues the same example at greater length.

“Behold,” he says, “I shall nourish her, and speak to her heart; and I shall give her vinedressers from that place, and the Valley of Achor as an opening of hope.” By calling the time of the liberation from Egypt the birth of the Synagogue, he also seems to indicate by the “nourishing” the food of manna. Speech directed to the heart indicates the promulgation of the Law, which formed the hearts of its hearers. [Col. 0978A]

But what does “I shall give her vineyards from that place, and the Valley of Achor as an opening of hope” signify? [Note: [Col. 0978D] We have rewritten *accipito* here, in place of the corrupt reading *acceptio*.]

Before the people entered the Promised Land, the scouts who had been sent brought back an excellent fruit of the vine, namely, a cluster of grapes of such size that one bearer could not carry it alone. But after they had captured the exceedingly wealthy city of Jericho by a remarkable victory, a man of the tribe of Judah, named Achar, son of Charim, stole something from the spoil that had been devoted to destruction. Since the happiness of the victors was suddenly obstructed by adversity, when strong measures had been taken, the thief who had violated the ban was tracked down.

[Note: [Col. 0978D] We emend *fur*, “thief,” for which the earlier text had *suo*, without sense. On his name, whom Jerome calls Achan, see our observations in volume III on the Book of Hebrew Places.]

After he had brought out everything he had hidden, he is said to have been killed and buried in the Valley of Achor, while the people stoned him (Joshua 7).

That expiation proved so effective in making God favorable that thereafter they obtained bloodless triumphs. Thus that valley appeared as hope of prosperity to those taking possession of new fields, whereas guilt had previously closed it.

[Note: [Col. 0978D] The old editor would prefer that *placandum Deum* (“God must be propitiated”) be restored. I would prefer, a little later, where it says “those taking possession of new fields,” that *arma* (“arms”) be restored instead. Compare Joshua chapter VIII.]

[Note: [Col. 0978D] The same old editor conjectures that *aperuit* should be restored; I would prefer *apparavit*.]

After recalling these events, which were known to have occurred at that time, [Col. 0978B] he also promises that the return of the Jews from the Babylonian captivity would be equally joyful. Finally, it follows:

“And she shall sing there as in the days of her youth and as in the days of her ascent from the land of Egypt.”

For just as then they passed through the divided waters, traveling by a dry route through the sea, while Miriam, the sister of Moses, taking up musical instruments, led the praises of God with the choirs following, so in this manner, when they came out of their Assyrian captivity, they sang—not, indeed, because they were going to destroy another Jericho or to find another cluster of grapes, but because such joyful times would follow that they seemed to have recovered the glory they had possessed under Moses and Joshua.

Consider, nevertheless, how joyful the memory of this history is, both as an example of sorrow and as an example of joy. For above he had said:

“Lest I strip her naked, and set her as on the day of her birth, and make her like a wilderness, and set her like a dry land, and kill her with thirst.”

He was referring to the likeness of those whose corpses, [Col. 0978C] as the Apostle Paul says, were struck down in the wilderness (Hebrews 3:17). 411 But now, when he promises that servitude will be released and that joys will come from freedom, he recalls the same number of periods of time during which the glorious deliverance had been celebrated in sacred songs.

The sweetness of this happiness—that is, the happiness to be experienced after the Babylonian captivity—consoled the Jews; its greatness, however, signified the peoples who were to be gathered for the preaching of the Gospel. Those who sing a new song to God—for “he has made known his salvation to the world and revealed his righteousness in the sight of the nations” (Psalm 97:2)—and who, by free forgiveness and sanctification, dissolved the servitude by which we were subjected to sins and unclean spirits, so that, freed from iniquities, we might serve righteousness and, having become a people of possession, shine with the insignia of divine descent: they have from our own body—indeed, from our own people—vine-dressers who either impart to us in the mysteries the grace of the enormous cluster of grapes, or indicate the very skill and diligence by which God’s vineyard is cultivated. [Col. 0978D]

Accordingly, when the things we have enumerated as objects of desire have occurred, the usefulness of the punishment inflicted beforehand will also be made known by the correction of morals. [Col. 0979A]

“With all her heart,” he says, “she will be joined to me,” so that she will no longer worship me intermittently, but will offer me continuous worship and constant devotion.

[Note: [Col. 0979D] Thus we emend *meque*, “and me,” for the earlier reading *neque*, “nor.”]

She will call me alone her husband and Lord; nor will she any longer attribute my name to the Baals—that is, to idols. Concerning the word *Baalim*, Jewish tradition has attempted to devise some interpretation.

[Note: [Col. 0979D] Unless I am mistaken, our author mocks the interpretation which Jerome here reports from the Hebrew language concerning *Baalim*.]

But the more substantial explanation is evident, and the whole sequence proceeds on this basis: he promises that the names of idols will be removed from the mouth of the corrected nation, and that she will call him alone God and Lord.

When he says, “She shall no longer remember their name,” he either indicates a correction that would be complete, or he looks back to what he had said above: “She went after her lovers and forgot me, says the Lord.” Thus, by closing off this vice through punishment, she will pass over into the opposite disposition, abandoning her zeal for profanation in complete forgetfulness.

## Verses 18–20

“I shall strike a covenant with her on that day, with the beast of the field, and with the bird of the sky, and with the creeping thing of the earth; I shall shatter bow and sword and war from the land, and I shall make them sleep securely. I shall betroth you to myself forever; I shall betroth you to myself in judgment and righteousness, and in mercy and compassion. I shall betroth you to myself in faithfulness, and you shall know that I am the Lord.”

[Note: [Col. 0979D] The Hieronymian edition more correctly has *eis*, “with them.” Moreover, a portion of the verse was certainly omitted shortly afterward: “And I shall betroth you to myself forever.” The copyist, deceived by the recurrence of the same words, had passed over it, as is clear from the context of the exposition that follows. [Col. 0980D]]

“It follows,” he says, “that she who lay disfigured by wounds should, once corrected, possess all good things. And therefore, just as our indignation had made all creatures not merely hostile but even harmful to her, so our reconciliation should again make those same creatures favorable and beneficial.

“I shall therefore strike a covenant with her and the beast of the field, so that neither the savagery of wild animals may ravage the crops of the fields, nor the multitude of birds seize their vineyards or olive groves, nor serpents spread their poisons through the limbs of the weary. When all these things are said to cease at the time of liberation, we are thereby taught that they had been inflicted during the days of punishment.

“With these calamities, wars too will cease, so that they may sleep in their ancestral territories—that is, rest securely—since they will fear neither invasions nor ambushes. [Col. 0979C]

“‘I shall betroth you to myself forever’ means: instructed by events themselves, you will recognize that the separation by which you were afflicted occurred not through my fault but through your own. Nevertheless, I am prepared for you to remain my bride forever; that is, if you are such as the corrective judgments have now made you, the former covenant with you will be preserved forever.

“Thus I make this pact: you shall remain in our fellowship, provided that the judgments inflicted upon you test your righteousness. Or, if creeping negligence should wound you, and yet you should ask me for healing with the full urgency of lamentation, I shall nevertheless betroth you to myself in mercy and compassion. When you have experienced these as faithful and constant—for this is what he means by ‘I shall betroth you in faithfulness’—you will proclaim with fitting eagerness that I am the Lord.”

[Note: [Col. 0980D] The text was corruptly read *persenseret*, “she might perceive.” Almost innumerable and very serious errors of punctuation are silently corrected.]

All this will appear more clearly fulfilled if we transfer it to the calling of the Gospel. For the one who is “beautiful beyond the sons of men” (Psalm 44:3), from whose lips grace poured forth and gave salvation to the world, took into his fellowship and betrothed to himself as queen the one whom he had chosen as his bride for the honor of virginity: in righteousness, which he gave by justifying her; in judgment, when he chose her who would labor lawfully; in mercy and compassion, when he forgave her former debts; and in faith, by which one believes with the heart unto righteousness, while confession is made with the mouth unto salvation (Romans 10:10)—or, as is beyond doubt, because for those who love the Lord all things work together for good (ibid. 8:28).

## Verses 21–24

“And it shall be on that day: I shall hear, says the Lord, the heavens, and they shall hear the earth, and the earth shall hear the grain, the wine, and the oil, and these shall hear Jezreel. And I shall sow her for myself in the land, and I shall have mercy on her who was ‘Without Mercy.’ And I shall say to ‘Not My People,’ ‘You are my people’; and he himself shall say, ‘You are my God.’”

[Note: [Col. 0980D] The Hieronymian and Vulgate editions, following the Hebrew more closely, repeat “I shall hear”; at the end they more correctly read, “and he himself shall say, You are my God.” Previously the text read “he says,” etc.]

He extends the sequence of the promised blessing and, through various images, constructs a figure familiar in the sacred books: the elements desire to perform their respective tasks for the support of human frailty, yet they cannot do so unless the Creator gives his assent. [Col. 0980A]

At the time when, in his peacefulness, he has driven away adversity, he promises that he will provide everything abundantly. Prosperity would begin to falter if the liberty desired for so many ages were not accompanied by abundance.

As we have said, this sweetness of joy was also shut off in that age when the Babylonian captivity was ended. It was restored in still greater fullness in the time of the Apostles, when the entire multitude of believers used the sober abundance of their possessions in such a way that they had “one soul and one heart” (Acts 2). [Col. 0980B]

Then, for the first time, the equality praised by all the wise shone forth: in so great a company of disciples no one was lifted up by riches, and no one was weighed down by poverty. Just as there was one common agreement among all in virtue, so there was common ownership. For none of them said that any of the things they possessed was his own; since everything was held in common, even the prices of fields were laid at the Apostles’ feet, so that distribution might be made according to the needs of each person. 413

And because the condition of the spiritual people was contained within the history of the Jewish people, he returns to the names from which the prophecy had begun and says:

“The earth shall hear the grain, the wine, and the oil, and these shall hear Jezreel”—that is, the people named after the valley in which he was defeated.

He has shown that the very nation whose sins he had previously set forth and whose punishment he had announced—remaining not in the same individuals but in the same tribes, and cleansed by the blows of punishment—will, once he has been reconciled, be received into his fellowship. As though into good soil, he will entrust various seeds of his commandments, so that through the breadth of the prosperity that follows, even that day of Jezreel on which calamity was imposed may be judged precious and desirable. [Col. 0980C]

“I shall have mercy,” he says—perhaps, “he says”—“on her whose name I had shortly before abhorred. I shall call my people those who had been deserters from me and had rightly defected from me to my enemies.” In turn, confidence will be given to them, so that they may call him their true and only Lord.

But after extending the announcement of prosperity this far, he brings the discourse back again to the condition of the present time. For it follows:

# Chapter III

## Verses 1–5

“And the Lord said to me: ‘Go again, love a woman loved by a friend and an adulteress, as the Lord loves the children of Israel, while they look toward foreign gods and love grape pomace. And I bought her for myself for fifteen silver pieces, a *cor* of barley, and half a *cor* of barley. And I said to her: You shall wait for me many days; you shall not commit fornication, and you shall not belong to a man; I too shall wait for you. For the children of Israel shall sit many days without a king, without a prince, without sacrifice, without an altar, without an ephod, and without teraphim. And after this the children of Israel shall return and seek the Lord their God and David their king; and they shall fear the Lord and his goodness in the latter days.’”

Since the Prophet had undertaken the beginning of his prophecy by promising, in various expressions, the return of that people from captivity, here, as he had taught at the beginning, he announced from the person of God things that were sorrowful but already impending. Under the same direction of the Holy Spirit, he wove the oracle as though from opposites.

For when he has thundered threats, he immediately adds joyful words with which to comfort the wounded, so that either the people may grow accustomed to hearing sorrowful things, or he may show that the Lord himself delays and, as we said above, postpones his action deliberately, even though he is going to exact vengeance. At the same time he teaches that they should never despair of salvation under such a judge, one so ready to pardon that, by narrating peaceful things amid adversity, he seems deliberately to excuse the fact that he was angry.

He therefore commands the Prophet not to abandon the love he had shown to the shameless woman because of her prior offense, but to oppose her shamelessness with a publicly professed kindness. Whether by the event itself, or by revelation of the spirit alone—for the latter appears more likely—he is to recognize that the prostitute could be hired for a small price, not only so that she might be content with the prophet’s company, but also so that she might abstain from intercourse with him and with others alike. This would show that she had prostituted herself more from the necessity of obtaining food than from pursuit of lust. Indeed, if even a modest livelihood were provided for her, she would easily give up the pleasure of her disgrace.

By this example the case of the Synagogue is made worse: it did not preserve the covenant that even a prostitute would fear to violate, whether invited by abundant resources or constrained by the greatest poverty.

“Therefore,” he says, “we grant time to those who are wandering, so that they may either burst forth in tears toward correction or finally succumb to severe vengeance.” Those who now prefer precious things to worthless ones, forget their own God, and follow foreign gods are like people who, rejecting grapes, gather grape-pomace, which is more suitable for pigs than for human beings.

The first measure named was the *cor*, containing thirty *modii*. Then he says “half a cor of barley,” thereby establishing by the agreement that the woman’s service of continence was to be purchased in the image of the condition that the Synagogue would endure in the Babylonian captivity, [Col. 0981C] where she would endure exile, indeed, but under hope of return; she would cleave properly neither to God nor to idols, but would live as though stripped of every consolation.
