For this reason he says: “You shall not commit fornication, and you shall not belong to a man; I too shall wait for you.”

[Note: [Col. 0981D] The text previously read *aut* corruptly; as very often elsewhere, the words of Scripture were not distinguished.]

The Jews, or those who follow them, insist that this passage concerns the judgment of the present time: expelled, they say, from Jerusalem, they possess none of the insignia of priestly service that the prophet enumerates. He promises that they will be without a king, without a prince, without sacrifice, without an altar, without an ephod, and without teraphim. Yet, they maintain, they retain tokens of their return—namely, the word of God, who promised that he too would wait for them.

But the evidence of all the nations admitted to the faith of Christ proves that they are mistaken in this opinion, or are deceiving others. After they refused to believe in the Gospel of Christ, the vineyard was taken away from them and entrusted to other cultivators who would render its fruit in due season (Psalm 1).

Therefore, in the age when they were serving the Babylonians, the nation and God are rightly said to have waited for one another—not because the whole people was free from the profanities that are also charged against them by other holy teachers, but because righteous men were mingled among them, and because a better offspring than their parents would enjoy the joys of liberation.

For the sake of these, God promises that he would wait for them: that is, he would not immediately admit another nation in place of the expelled one, until it returned, as we have also said above, improved by punishment and receiving again the ornaments of the ancient priesthood that it had lost.

[Note: Variant: *admiserat*, “had admitted,” for *amiserat*, “had lost.”]

In the gathering of the faithful, it would encircle the horns of the altar, offering to God the vows that its lips had distinguished; and they would fear his goodness in the latter day (Psalm 65). [Col. 0982A]

He has therefore explained the cause of its expulsion, so that through it the afflicted nation might become accustomed to abstinence from profanations, until, corrected by legitimate blows, it might once more deserve admission into his fellowship, from which a pious and joyful remnant would emerge.

# Chapter IV

## Verses 1–2

“Hear the word of the Lord, children of Israel, for the Lord has a judgment with the inhabitants of the land: there is no truth, no mercy, and no knowledge of God in the land. Cursing, lying, murder, theft, and adultery have overflowed, and blood has touched blood.”

I have already reminded you once and again why, in the very surge of his threats, he also spoke of those blessings that would come after a long period: so that either the exiled nation might have consolation, or the clemency of the author might be apparent, since he approached vengeance as though unwillingly.

With this purpose, therefore, after speaking also of future things, he returns to the age of the present, as he had done above, and examines the merits of the people destined for punishment, so that he may resolve the question raised by the appeal to divine pity.

Such a thought would arise appropriately if the fixed sentence remained that the captivity imposed should be ended and a glorious return should occur. Why was liberty not continued? Or what magnitude of guilt could there have been that would inflame the mind of our ruler to such great severity? [Col. 0982B]

[Note: [Col. 0981D] The text had *quum*, without sense; we have restored as much as we could.]

An enumeration of crimes must therefore be added, so that the gravity of the one who punishes may become apparent.

“Hear,” he says, “the word of the Lord, children of Israel, for he does not refuse to enter into conflict with you and to set forth the reason for his judgments and your merits. To him blessed David says: ‘That you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged’” (Psalm 50).

“Hear,” I say, “the word of the Lord, children of Israel—you yourselves, about whom the matter is being decided. Judge for yourselves concerning the practices of the people of which we complain. If any understanding remains in you, flee to confession and repentance.”

“There is no truth, no mercy, and no knowledge of God in the land.”

“They do not sin,” he says, “as though at intervals, so that some mixture of punishment and virtue might appear; rather, everything has yielded to the worst things, so that nowhere does even a trace of goodness appear. No faith, I say, remains in testimony, no justice in judgments, no piety in religious observances. [Col. 0982C]

“What do I mean by saying that their hearts are empty of fear of God, when forgetfulness even of his name has seized everyone, and cruelty and lust contend with one another? When crimes rush upon them and offenses overflow, they refrain neither from shame nor from bloodshed. Rather, they join curses to lies, murders to thefts, and adulteries to sacrileges.”

[Note: [Col. 0981D] On the earlier editor’s advice, we restore *jungunt*, “they join,” in place of *jungentes*.]

They filled all the places of the once-holy land with slaughter, so that through the multitude of the slain, blood was mixed with blood. History shows that this was said not by exaggeration but in truth. [Col. 0982D]

These were the very times when blessed Elijah, asked by God what he was doing in the wilderness, replied in grief: “Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have destroyed your altars, and I alone am left, and they seek my life” (3 Kings 19).

The people had therefore been so corrupted by extreme profanation that they strove to destroy all the godly—that is, the worshipers of God—by a final massacre. This abominable corruption of religion had nothing for which the price of pleasure might be sought, but it promised impunity for both shameful and savage deeds. Thus the worshipers of the Baals and of the calves served the fury of Jezebel by pouring out the blood of the righteous.

## Verse 3

“Therefore the land shall mourn, and every one who dwells in it shall grow weak; with the beast of the field and the bird of the sky, and even the fish of the sea, they shall be gathered together.”

[Note: [Col. 0981D] The Hieronymian edition has the singular “every one shall grow weak,” which our author himself confirms in his subsequent repetition of the passage.]

After setting forth the causes of his indignation, he appropriately exclaims that the land itself will be covered with mourning, just as it is covered with crimes. If such numerous and immense crimes had gone unpunished, even providence would be denied.

“Every inhabitant of the land will grow weak,” he says, “along with the beast of the field and the bird of the sky.” Scripture commonly calls herds and flocks “beasts of the field.” Therefore, when scarcity of grain and fruit comes upon the land, shortage and want of livestock will follow as well.

Nor is this the end of their anguish. Even the fish will be gathered up—that is, they will fail, so that no food may be found even in the waters. [Col. 0983A]

## Verses 4–5

“Nevertheless, let no one judge, and let no man be reproved; for your people are like those who contradict the priest. And you shall fall today, and the prophet shall fall with you.”

[Note: [Col. 0983D] The same edition reads “today” for “you,” with the Hebrew. Our author again retains that reading, but when he repeats the passage a third time in explaining the following verse, he finally reads correctly: “you shall fall today, and he shall fall,” etc.]

“If the state were still standing,” he says, “and some guilty persons perished by the sentence of judges, one would certainly be reproved and another would reprove, for the office of judgment would be carrying out its proper function. [Col. 0983B]

“At the same time this shows that the corruption of crimes had not possessed the entire people all at once, like a disease or plague; some followed shameful things, while many pursued honorable ones.”

[Note: [Col. 0983] We have removed the negative particle, which had here been wrongly repeated.]

“But when iniquity, as though by conspiracy, has possessed nearly every assembly, as the prophet Hosea laments that it had done in his own time, both teaching and judgment will rightly cease, so that punishment may rage unchecked against the wicked.

“Thus, under the appearance of a command, the force of judgment is expressed:

“‘Nevertheless, let no one judge, and let no man be reproved’—that is, no one will judge, and no one will be reproved. You are to be devastated by hostile fury, not subjected to the decisions of judges.

“‘For your people are like those who contradict the priest; you shall fall, and the prophet shall fall with you.’

“The prophet uses ‘like’ for judgment, not for comparison. Therefore you will see nothing new in the vengeance, but will recognize in your punishments what you practiced in your crimes.

“Your people resisted the priest—that is, by pursuing idols, you withdrew from the true priesthood. ‘You contradicted the priest,’ he says, when you rejected sacred ceremonies, salutary admonitions, and commandments that shape morals; and you handed yourself over to profane prophets just as you had to impious leaders.

“It is therefore deserved that the sentence now imposed should envelop both groups, so that you collapse together with your prophets—that is, with your diviners.” [Col. 0983C]

## Verse 6

“By night I made your mother keep silent. My people have become silent because they had no knowledge. Because you rejected knowledge, I too shall reject you, so that you may not serve as my priest; and because you forgot the law of your God, I too shall forget your children.”

It is a customary expression of Scripture, as I have often warned, that when the discourse is directed to a nation, it appears to address it both by its own name and by the name of the parent whose daughter it is.

Therefore, when he had said, “You shall fall today, and the prophet shall fall with you”—that is, the time of your devastation has come, and you who formerly ceased to learn and speak righteousness will now also cease from profane speech—he added:

“By night I made your mother keep silent.”

This should not be understood as though he permitted her to speak during the day and only made her silent at night. Rather, he wished to express the culmination of the silence imposed upon her. To show that she had been struck dumb by the onset of destruction, he introduced the mention of night, as though he were saying:

“I shall clothe her in overflowing grief, just as night customarily covers the earth, so that, just as the condition of the dark hours introduces a universal and common silence, so this crowd of elders, whom I called your mother—who shortly before resounded with the chatter of profanation—may become silent beneath the night of adversity.” 417

Afterward, following the established order, when he has resounded with terror, he adds the cause of the disturbance: [Col. 0984A]

“My people have become silent because they had no knowledge.”

“It was just,” he says, “that the lips of my people should be closed in mournful silence, since they did not wish to learn through speaking.”

Therefore, lest you refer the statement that knowledge was lacking among the people to some necessity, he immediately shows what he had accused:

“Because you rejected knowledge, I too shall reject you, so that you may not serve as my priest; and because you forgot the law of your God, I too shall forget your children.”

“You did not wish to understand in order to do good” (Psalm 35), he says. Instead, meditating on iniquity in your chamber, you dared, at your own discretion, to divide among yourselves the parts of my law, so that, while neglecting righteousness, you retained the regulations concerning sacrifices.

Therefore a fitting frustration will confront your perversity: there will be no permission to offer sacrifices for one who had no concern to pursue virtues. A harsh silence will threaten you, because you drove salutary admonitions away from your ears.

“You forgot me; I too shall forget your children,” so that you who willingly suffered blindness in your duties may experience the bitterest bereavement of your children. [Col. 0984B]

This should be understood in such a way that we do not suppose that the people, while enslaved to idols, served the true God by offering sacrifices. Indeed, this was especially the reason for consecrating calves in the land: to prevent them from having an opportunity to approach the Temple by offering sacrifices.

A twofold interpretation should therefore be adopted. Either the statement is placed under the condition of their situation, as though we were to say:

“Even if you were fulfilling the duties of the priesthood with complete seriousness, it would contribute nothing to your defense, since the depravity of your morals convicted you. In consequence, you would also lose these narrow and ridiculous consolations of your superstition, since you had lost the aids provided by merit.”

Or else, because among the tribes themselves there were prophets and legitimate priests living scattered about, and because some from the common people were accustomed to offer the same small gifts, they believed that through this they could obtain impunity for their crimes. To such men also he threatens, under the person of the people, that when open captivity arrives, they will be stripped even of those supports of their opinion by which they considered themselves, at least intermittently, generous toward the Lord. [Col. 0984C]

## Verse 7

“The more numerous they became, the more they sinned against me; I shall change their glory into disgrace.”

It was as though the people had deliberately and zealously resolved to contend against my benefits, so that the more abundantly I had given, the more insane they appeared in abusing what they had received.

Finally, when I had raised him up through the succession of his descendants, so that, advancing as a cultivator, he filled the broad spaces of extensive lands, he matched this action by crimes directed toward my insult. It was altogether as though he feared that the people might have more members than there were crimes. 418

Therefore, because they placed their glory in a multitude of crimes as much as in a multitude of soldiers, I shall change that glory into disgrace when disgrace takes its place, so that, as their troubles consume them, they may be reduced to the utmost fewness.

## Verse 8

“They eat the sins of my people, and they lift up their souls toward their iniquity.”

The whole passage should be read with reproach. It refers to the priests—or to those who were ministers of idols and who therefore claimed to offer themselves to God—or to the rulers together with the people, who had adopted a zeal for destructive error.

Among the other practices for which they deserved punishment, they also appropriated terms derived from the tradition of the Law. For just as the Samaritan tribes observed circumcision and Sabbaths, although they served idols, so the diviners themselves should be believed to have appropriated certain institutions of the Law.

Under the institution of blessed Moses there were various kinds of offerings, including the offering made for sin. After certain parts of its fat had been consumed by fire, the remainder became food for the priests.

And because God was propitiated by these rites, the priests were said to “eat,” or consume, the sins of the people for whom they prayed. In the same manner, the diviners, so that they might promise impunity for various offenses through the profits of their gain, claimed that they consumed the sins of the people.

Through the prophet God now attacks this practice in a voice and expression of indignation, as though he were saying:

“Behold the wonders of men who sought fame not for any beautiful deeds but solely for their crimes, and who dared to misuse the institutions of the revered Law under cover of its terminology. They promised the deceived people that, if they offered sacrifices through their hands, they would immediately become innocent and obtain forgiveness of sins.”

Thus they “lifted up”—that is, consoled and caused to grow proud—the souls of the guilty, allowing nothing of compunction to remain in them. [Col. 0985A]

Therefore, since neither teacher nor disciple had become accustomed to speaking or hearing what pertains to salvation, but guilt, which pollutes, had made them equal, the sentence rightly follows and joins them together, so that they may receive without fraud the fruit of their works and priest and people may suffer one and the same destruction.

We can make the interpretation of this passage easier if we introduce the person of Judah, whom he names shortly afterward. Although he chastises that tribe too with a serious admonition—it was less guilty at that point, but not entirely purified—he may also be understood to have introduced the fact that priests eat the sacrifices offered for sins. The sense would then be:

“But what is surprising about tribes that withdraw from the worship and fear of God and are enslaved to the worship of idols, and that are sullied by various crimes? Even that portion of the people which still appears to preserve the mystical ceremonies is being driven mad by a similar error, while corrupt priests flatter those who sin by telling them that impunity comes to them through the offering of sacrifices, which the priests themselves devour.”

They therefore lifted up by such consolations the spirits whom consciousness of their crimes depressed. What the priests promised with the greatest shamelessness the people gladly heard. Therefore, in the time of calamity, there will be no distinction between the people and the priests; those who lived promiscuously will also perish ignobly. [Col. 0985B]

[Note: Variant readings preserved in the apparatus include *itidem* for *totidem* (“likewise” for “the same number”); *diversis* for *reversis* (“various” for “returning”); *subripiens* for *subrepens* (“stealing” for “creeping”); *admiserat* for *amiserat* (“had admitted” for “had lost”); *comminatus* for *comminatur* (“he threatened” for “he threatens”); and *dicam* for *dico* (“I shall say” for “I say”).]

[Col. 0985C] **Verses 9–10.**—“I will visit their ways upon him, and repay his thoughts to him. They shall eat, and not be satisfied; they have committed fornication, and have not ceased.”

When, he says, the judgment of vengeance begins to act, those measures of suffering which they themselves had fashioned through their sins will be fulfilled, so that in punishments they may experience what they committed in their desires. For they committed fornication, whether by pursuing obscenities or profanities, nor were they ashamed of the foulness they had adopted, so that, having fallen from their first station, they might at least have considered secondary remedies and ceased to repeat what ought not to have happened. Thus a cessation brought to bear might have imitated abstinence from error. But although they had committed fornication, they did not cease.

Therefore, let them experience in punishments what they practiced in vices, so that they may eat and not be satisfied: that is, let them be filled with afflictions, yet not cease to drain them, so that they appear to endure a kind of hunger. For when you hear “fornication,” do not suppose that only a limited indulgence in bodily pleasure is meant. Rather, he says, by violating the terms of the sacred covenant, they abandoned the omnipotent Lord, into whose fellowship they had been admitted.

And therefore they were deprived of the light of understanding, not considering, after the religious distinctions they had possessed, into what kinds of ritual practices they had fallen. Such folly of opinions would never have entered their minds had drunkenness and gluttony not reconciled them to it. Thus, while claiming to be wise, they became fools, to such an extent that they sought the prophetic office from dry pieces of wood, and a staff indicated to each person what was going to happen. The Greeks call this form of profanity *rhabdomancy* (*rhabdomantias*).

The spirit of profanity—which they call fornication—deceived them, so that they departed from the true God and became entangled with many different demons, quite literally in the mouths and foreheads of adulterers.

**Verse 13.**—“They sacrificed upon the tops of the mountains, and burned incense upon the hills, beneath oak, poplar, and terebinth, because its shade was good.”

Not content, he says, with having erred in one way, those who despised divine ordinances followed old-wives’ inventions. They were moved not only by staffs smoothed for some deception, but also by somewhat more elevated hillocks and by the somewhat denser shade of trees; they believed that divinity was most present wherever they saw some pleasantness.

Thus they sacrificed on the summits of the mountains, a practice frequently condemned by the historical books, when they say of the kings: “He did this or that; nevertheless he did not remove the high places, but the people still sacrificed upon the high places.” Here he adds that they also burned incense beneath oak, poplar, and terebinth, and, explaining the reason for their admiration, he appended: “because its shade was good.”

Rejecting the creator of light and brightness, they—truly like children of darkness—were captivated by the little shaded retreats of the grove. Let us therefore hear what punishments such madness deserves.

**Verse 14.**—“Therefore your daughters shall commit fornication, and your brides shall be adulteresses. I will not visit your daughters when they have committed fornication, nor your brides when they have committed adultery.”

You have committed shameful acts, he says, and have not ceased from your conduct. Thus, if you did not feel the emotions of those who are innocent—or at least of those whom the guilty ordinarily experience; that is, if the violators of decency were not ashamed of what they had done—you confirmed your boldness in criminal deeds. You pursued disgraceful practices to such a degree that you preferred the shadows of sticks and stones to the creator of all the elements.

Let the outcome of the final calamity therefore reckon with this impiety, so that, in a marvelous form of vengeance, the punishment may be shaped according to the likeness of the offenses. It will be all the more bitter because they had not previously experienced judicial correction. Your brides and daughters will be subjected to the lust of their conquerors; and no judge, neither husbands nor parents, will accuse them of this disgrace.

The entire outrage will be consummated in dishonor, so that nothing remains of it to constitute a charge. Thus, as though with sharp reasoning, he concluded that nothing is more bitter than to have been placed under such a condition of servitude, in which one continues to witness the ultimate outrages of one’s relations but dares not accuse them.

Therefore, since he had foreseen that this would be the final limit of their misery—something that captivity alone could inflict—he immediately supplied the cause of so great an upheaval by repeating what had already been said: “For they themselves consorted with prostitutes and sacrificed with effeminate men, and the people, lacking understanding, shall be beaten.”

They do not know, he says, how much grief I experience over the perversity of the one who once lived in my fellowship. Therefore, in the disgrace inflicted upon their relations, they will recognize the magnitude of their former crimes. Those who followed effeminate men and brothels, from whom they had received the worship of demons, will be dragged away by obscene enemies who abuse them, and will experience, through the insults inflicted by victorious tyrants, the fruit of their voluntary folly.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0985]

## CHAPTER IV (continued)

[Col. 0985D]

**Verse 15.**—“If you commit fornication, Israel, let Judah at least not offend. Do not enter Gilgal, and do not go up to Beth-aven; [Note: The part of the verse ‘nor swear, “As the Lord lives,” which was missing, we have supplied, with the author himself guaranteeing it, since he explains it individually—and more than once—in the exposition that follows.] nor swear, ‘As the Lord lives.’ For Israel has turned aside like a wanton cow; now the Lord will feed them like a lamb in a broad place.”

Although the judgment of the prophecy itself demonstrates that all the tribes had been defiled by the worship of idols, nevertheless he declares Israel’s condition to be worse, as though it were more capable of condemnation than correction. For Israel not only confined the audacity of its profanity within its own boundaries and practices, but also sought the contamination of its brother as though it were some gain.

The prophet proves this by denouncing to Israel that Judah should at least not offend. He was not imposing upon Israel a concern for fraternal compassion, as though Israel were being admonished to become dutiful; rather, under the appearance of this commandment he also aggravates the crime of preferring to make Judah like itself rather than thinking about its own correction.

The sense is accordingly as follows:

“O Israel, who, following the leader of error, namely Jeroboam, withdrew from fellowship with your brother Judah for no other reason than that the honor of the Temple and the celebration of the sacred days might not provide you an opportunity to breathe again and return to better things: if you cannot preserve the covenant of your ancestry—or of your crime—and if, unwilling to maintain a praiseworthy harmony, you intend to persist in the separation you once undertook, then remain firm in your repudiation of brotherhood. Do not by the corrupter’s artifice insinuate yourself into a profession of rejected kinship. At least, content with your own pollution, allow your companion’s innocence to remain, and cease inviting him into the condition whose arrival you lament in yourself.

“For now folly is spreading most grievously, if, from fear of the remedy for which you chose separation, you enter into fellowship with the same people out of love for sacrilege. Preserve at least that feeling which customarily arises in those who sin, so that you may be ashamed of your disgraceful act.

“Why, then, do you exclude from yourself even this slight consolation, so that you may appear to have been deceived? For the ascent will not escape guilt. Yet there is some distinction between the unwary and the insolent: the audacity of some makes them hated, while fear makes others objects of pity. But when you allow no one to remain free from your foulness, what else do you confess but that you are most guilty, not through error but through a deliberate and detestable judgment?

“‘If you commit fornication, Israel, let Judah at least not offend.’ Why, I ask, do you join this error to your earlier ones, so that you imagine you will perish with less pain if you perish with many rather than with few? Why, prodigal of your own honors, do you also pollute your brother’s rights? Why do you wish to enclose the whole race in one tomb? Allow some portion of your bloodline to survive, that you may be helped by its support and reformed by its example.

“‘If you commit fornication, Israel, let Judah at least not offend. Do not enter Gilgal, and do not go up to Beth-aven, nor swear, “As the Lord lives.”’”

He made clear through what follows how he had commanded Israel not to cause Judah to offend: he forbade them to go up to Gilgal and Beth-aven, places adjoining the tribe of Judah, out of a desire to mingle their worship, and to swear, “As the Lord lives.” This is to be understood as follows: because they had consecrated calves in those places, as in Samaria, and had also attached to them the name of the true God, swearing by their name and divinity, he now commands that, since the people of Judah were flowing there because of their proximity—namely, to Beth-aven and Gilgal—these people should stop going there and swearing, “As the Lord lives.” In other words, in those places consecrated by the people’s agreement, Judah must not be deceived by this familiarity of language and begin first not to shudder at the calves, and then even to swear by them.

It also seems to indicate the following: the impiety of the people caused confusion, so that those who served the calves also swore by the true Lord whom Judah worshiped in whatever business they undertook, binding their appeals by invoking his name. They apparently judged it best to venerate both names with equal honor, so that by this practice they might persuade even those who had remained in the faith to worship the calves, while the reverence of their former religion remained intact. Thus the change in devotion might appear not so much an alteration as a certain addition.

But this practice, undertaken against the commandments of the Law, undoubtedly polluted the wretched people through accumulated profanity. Therefore, do not frequent those places—which you have made famous through sacrilegious rites—with such zeal that Judah’s hearts too may be poisoned by your crime. Let Judah look, if it has not yet completely withered, and observe what condition has overtaken Israel; then it will recognize what awaits it as well, unless it takes precautions.

**Verse 16.**—“For Israel has turned aside like a wanton cow; now the Lord will feed them like a lamb in a broad place.”

The comparison with a cow is entirely appropriate, so that it might signify the character of the sin itself, the swelling pride of the sinners, and the lowing of those who were perishing.

Israel, he says, with the yoke of my Law shaken off, sinned in the worship of the calves and turned aside from the paths of virtue, believing that it would enjoy its rich goods without interruption. But such frustration of their hopes followed the impious that they descended from something resembling the bulk of a bull to the smallness of a lamb.

Thus the whole nation, which trusted in its strength, saw its glory changed, with disgrace following, and found itself placed beneath the shepherd’s staff, restrained with the same ease with which a lamb is ordinarily restrained.

Nor was this all. Just as a lamb led into desolate places—weak, solitary, deprived of the comfort both of its mother and of the flock—fears whatever it sees and whatever it hears, so this people, subjected to savage enemies, will be forced to travel through a wilderness.

Even so, divine providence did not wholly abandon it, and for this reason he says, “Now God will feed them.” But so that the people may understand and confess, through the discipline of the calamity imposed upon them, that the precepts of the sacred Law were not contemptible, nor their own crimes unpunished, nor their desires fruitful, he adds what follows.

**Verses 17–19.**—“Ephraim is a companion of idols; let him alone. Their feast is separated; they have committed fornication upon fornication; they loved to bring shame upon their protectors. The spirit has bound him in its wings, and he will be confounded [another reading: ‘they will be confounded’] because of their sacrifices.”

After the prophetic word had addressed Israel concerning its desolation and announced its end because Israel had not listened to his words, he turned to Judah, intending next to admonish it. For lest the judgment directed against Israel appear to have exempted Judah from guilt—although Judah would certainly never be corrupted except by voluntary assent—he also addresses Judah with similar force.

“You have seen,” he says, “that Ephraim, withdrawing its ungrateful and unhappy neck from the yoke of my Law, has decided to become a companion of idols. Therefore do not join yourself to him by any covenant. Leave him, and separate yourself from him entirely, both in place and in purpose.

“But if any association binds you to him, calamity too—surely an equal calamity—will seize you. Do you wish to escape the contagion of profanity? Surround yourself with a wall of continual separation. Never enter into either public treaties or private banquets with sacrilegious people. For what fellowship has light with darkness (2 Cor. 6:14)? What agreement has the temple of God with idols?

“‘They have committed fornication upon fornication.’ And lest you think this happened because they were deceived by error, they loved to bring shame upon their protectors. With deliberate zeal and burning love they pursue profanities; and they do not sin only among the common people. From the leaders down to the lowest, they have been permeated by funeral-like profanity.

“Therefore, if you delight in the sacraments of pure faith, do not mingle anywhere with their understanding or their assembly [another reading: ‘to mingle’]. For the swift condemnation of such people has been provided for you, O tribe of Judah, as an aid to your judgment, so that, seeing the punishment of the guilty delayed, you might not also become uncertain about their merits. While you remain unharmed, sudden Samaria will seize them like a wind, and they will be confounded because of their sacrifices; that is, they will blush and confess the vanity of their hope—those who promised themselves liberty and security through the sacrifices they offered to idols.”

He described the wings of the spirit by which the people would be carried away according to the common opinion that customarily equips representations of the winds with wings. Thus he says:

“These people, who have followed sacrileges, will be ruined and carried into the various exiles of captivity upon the storm of captivity, so that they may appear to have been borne upon the wings of the winds.”

When we read these things, however, we must consider how lightly the mad people regarded the voices of the prophets. For when priests, kings, and even the mass of the people had openly conspired in error, the few spiritual and poor men were granted no opportunity either to rebuke or to preach. Rather, as another Scripture testifies, they were called madmen and publicly mocked as though they were monstrosities.

Yet these men, equally lacking in wealth and honors, deserved to enter into conversation with God and, as though from the throne of the upper air, to pronounce judgment upon souls stretched out and clinging to the earth.

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 0989D]

**Verses 1–2.**—“Hear this, priests, and attend, house of Israel, and listen, house of the king, because judgment is for you. [Note: Here the second part of the verse seems to require supplementation, namely, ‘because you have become a snare at Mizpah, and a net spread over Tabor, and you turned aside the sacrifices,’ or, as our author prefers, ‘you plunged the sacrifices into the deep.’ These words are explained individually below, since they had previously been set out together with the rest of the context.]”

You are all proceeding toward sacrileges, and in sinning you have shown no distinction such as you formerly possessed among your ranks. Now, therefore, since you are exalted by priestly or royal dignity, and since the whole multitude of Israel is already threatened with destruction, it is fitting that you understand that you are perishing not according to your strength but according to the equity of the judge.

You have perpetrated two things that might seem opposed to each other: you became both a snare and a net, but one stretched upon the summit of a mountain as though in a lofty lookout place. The sacrifices that ought to have been offered to the ruler of heaven and carried upward, as if borne by smoke, you, changing their proper order, plunged into the deep.

This is what I accuse in the priests and kings: when they had received a position among the people in which they ought to be revered no less for honesty and religion than for power and dignity, and when they ought to have encouraged their subjects toward what was right both by speech and example, they instead supplied either an occasion for crimes or a model of them. Retaining from their former height only this—that what they had done might be seen from afar—they spread snares and nets by which the unhappy multitude might be caught. With the same perversity, he says, “you turned the sacrifices into the deep,” that is, as though into the underworld.

And what else did you do when you slaughtered them either for demons or for the spirits of the dead?

Therefore, since through your love of sinning you have confused the proper order of action, so that a certain ambition appears among you, listen now, unable as you are to discern what follows.

“I will be the instructor of all of you, so that, taught by punishment, you may learn what you did not know because you rejected instruction.”

**Verse 3.**—“I know Ephraim, and Israel is not hidden from me, because now Ephraim has committed fornication, Israel has been defiled. They will not direct their thoughts to return to the Lord their God, because the spirit of fornication is among them, and they have not known the Lord.”  
[Note: Neither Jerome’s version nor the Hebrew text itself adds “the Lord” here; moreover, the same books shortly afterward have “fornications” in the plural.]

How obstinately Israel has sinned, he says, no one knows better than I, who see into the interior of sins. No part of its entrails can escape my gaze. Thus, examining it all carefully, I have learned that it has now committed fornication completely and has been completely polluted.

Lest you think this was said merely in explanation of former sins, he immediately made clear through the following words what he intended to indicate by such an assertion. He says:

**Verse 4.**—“They will not direct their thoughts to return to the Lord their God, because the spirit of fornication is among them, and they have not known God.”

Therefore, after the acceptance of sin, remorse was concealed, and the crime was received into the breast. Not only the practice of guilt but also forgetfulness of correction was preferred to their former errors, so that this alone was judged either the first or the greatest iniquity.

“They will not,” he says, “direct their thoughts to return to the Lord their God, because the spirit of fornication is among them.” He showed that the reason they thought nothing about correction was that the unclean spirit itself—the demon, or the love of sacrileges—was present among them.

If they sinned only intermittently, the unclean spirit might be thought to be near them. But since they devote the entire span of their lives to crimes, the author of sacrileges is rightly said not to be near them but in their midst. With him seated in their breasts, they think nothing about correction, and therefore they are handed over to destruction.

**Verse 5.**—“The arrogance of Israel will answer to his face, and Israel and Ephraim will fall in their iniquity; Judah too will fall with them.”

As with rural laborers, to whom the abundance of the harvest often responds, he says that these people will immediately receive the wages of their efforts.

“Worthily,” he says, “their industry will answer”—that is, they will blush beneath calamities, those who had taken such great pride in their crimes.

**Verses 6–7.**—“With their flocks and with their herds they will go to seek the Lord, and they will not find him; he has been taken away from them. They have transgressed against the Lord, because they have begotten foreign children; now the harvest will devour them with their offspring.”  
[Note: No one will fail to suppose that this arose from a copyist’s error, so that *messis* was read for *mensis*, and *partubus* for *partibus*. The Hebrew text itself in fact has it, to say nothing of Jerome’s version. But since the sense is not at all incongruous—one that could in some fashion have been derived from the Septuagint—and since the similarity of the words in Latin is so great, while our author repeats the same reading in the exposition below at the end of this paragraph, we have scrupled to alter anything. This is all the more so because his own interpretation indicates that he read this in his copy, where he says that both shoots and fruits are promised to be cut down by a single sword.]

After saying above that the justice of judgment required those who had given themselves to crimes to bear worthy wages—or perhaps, “had handed themselves over”—he joined Judah to Israel, since he knew that Judah too, though somewhat later, would come into a similar guilt.

After commending the justice of the examination, he returns to the distinction of times and pursues the actions of Israel, which he knew would soon perish. First, after saying that Judah too would be joined to Israel in calamity, he added something that applied more particularly to Judah, which possessed the Temple consecrated to God.

Although Judah was polluted by idols, it nevertheless also offered sacrifices to God. Since it gave little attention to correcting its morals, it imagined that it would obtain support from constant sacrifice.

“Therefore,” he says, “with their flocks and herds they will go to seek the Lord, and they will not find him; he has been taken away from them.”

He used “they will go” instead of “they were going,” for the entire denunciation is disclosed through a shift into past time. Proceeding, therefore, along the path of superstition rather than religion—for the offering of sacrifices is judged in this way if concern for virtues is absent—they could not find that God to whom no one is led except by the path of complete devotion.

“He has been taken away from them”: not that God could be taken away, but that his assistance would nowhere meet them, as though he appeared to have been utterly removed from them.

Afterward, turning his speech toward Ephraim—that is, the Samaritans—he attacks another form of transgression, which nevertheless reveals the antiquity of the impiety committed: they despised the statutes of the Law so completely that they mingled with profane nations even through marriages, striving and hastening to strip themselves of the name of their own people and to be called anything other than the people of God.

“They have transgressed against the Lord, because they have begotten foreign children.”

“They conceived,” he says, “such hatred for my name that they believed they could escape threats and be freed from troubles if their offspring migrated into the number of other nations.”

Therefore, “now the harvest will devour them with their offspring.” By the name “harvest” he indicated the approaching and imminent calamity: in it he promises that both shoots and fruits will be cut down by a single sword.  
[Note: Unless you take *in quo* as meaning “in which matter,” it must refer to *mensis*, “month,” not *messis*, “harvest.” In that case the reading of Jerome’s and the Vulgate’s versions, discussed in the immediately preceding note, must be restored. The only change we dare to make is *demetendos*, “to be cut down,” at the end of the sentence, in place of the reading *demittendos*, “to be sent down.”]

**Verses 8–9.**—“Blow the trumpet in Gibeah, and the horn in Ramah; howl in Beth-aven; behind you, Benjamin. Ephraim will be desolate, etc.”

Since he had declared that they would soon be consumed, and knew that the weight of the sentence was advancing toward fulfillment without any delay, he ordered it to be announced, as though the events had already been accomplished, throughout those cities that were most populous, with trumpets sounding and mournful wailing resounding: total devastation would seize Ephraim.

We gather that all the places he mentioned—that is, “behind Benjamin,” the tribe bordering the territory of Judah, and Gibeah, Ramah, and Beth-aven—were near Judah’s boundaries. Thus, although the calamity that had preceded ought to have made them anxious through the example of fear itself, it not only did nothing to advance their correction but also furnished an increase for sinning.

He therefore reproaches them sharply and says that they had thereby shown themselves worse through the very means by which they ought to have become better—or better by virtue of their humanity itself.

**Verse 10.**—“The princes of Judah have become like those who remove a boundary; upon them I will pour out my anger like water.”

That is, during the Assyrian captivity, when the ten tribes were driven from their territories, the princes of Judah ought to have been moved to tears by their brother’s calamity and diligently to have considered the beauty of their conduct, lest they too should slip into similar hardships.

Instead, they not only felt no fear or remorse, but also made their murderous disposition public, rejoicing that their territories had been enlarged through the expulsion of their brother.

On the day of desolation—that is, at the time when the Israelite tribe departed from its territories—he revealed Judah’s faithfulness, so to speak; the occasion exposed its hidden desire. Judah made so light of the differing fates of the brothers that it even said they had been advantages for itself. This was surely so great a guilt that it compelled the anger of the avenger to increase.

For what follows says: “Upon him I will pour out my anger like water.” After saying, “I will pour it out,” he openly added, “like water.”

“Judah,” he says, “appeared worse because of the crime of this exultation. Therefore it will be submerged in a flood of punishments, because, although among the other benefits our clemency had also granted it this—that Ephraim’s destruction should serve its fear and correction—it abused the event to increase its insolence and considered that its brother had been given not examples of warning but estates.”

**Verses 11–15.**—“Ephraim suffers oppression, crushed by judgment, because he began to go after filth. And I am like a moth to Ephraim and like rot to the house of Judah. Ephraim saw his sickness, and Judah his bond. Ephraim went to Assyria and sent to the avenging king; but he will not be able to heal you, nor will he be able to release the bond from you. For I am like a lioness to Ephraim and like a young lion to the house of Judah. I, I will go and seize and carry away, and there is no one who can rescue. Going away, I will return to my place until you fail and seek my face.”

God presents himself as gravely offended because Judah felt no remorse over its brother’s condemnation. Instead, Judah remained and insulted the exile, rejoicing whenever its own boundaries could be extended by any opportunity.

God therefore judged this sin so seriously that he promised not merely to apply anger but to pour it out entirely like water. Since the increase of punishments made Judah appear more culpable—because, as judgment overflowed, it was to be ravaged—he continued to develop the color he had assumed.

He said that Judah’s guilt was so much greater that, when compared with Judah, Israel appeared to have suffered oppression.

The sense is accordingly as follows:

“If the reckoning of merits demanded the evil of captivity, why did Judah—polluted by the customs of the nations and infected with hatred of its brother—delay the force of vengeance? But if, after so many crimes, Judah still did not deserve to be expelled, was not the one who was captured oppressed more by injustice than by the justice of the teacher?”

“Ephraim suffers oppression, crushed by judgment.”

He took care to explain what it meant to suffer oppression: namely, to be brought low not by the equity but by the power of the judge.

The same sense is intended by the words, “because he began to go after filth.” In the preceding passages he had reproached Israel for the multitude and antiquity of its sins. But when he attacked Judah’s crime—its pursuit of profit from and rejoicing in its brother’s captivity—and judged this crime to outweigh the others, he continued in the same manner by saying that Ephraim had also been ensnared in judgment and that Judah itself had possessed the beginnings of error.

It is as though he said:

“Judah, you have made such cruelty of your mind public that, in the crimes for which Israel was condemned, you appear more savage and more ancient in guilt.”

Therefore, according to the difference of merits, I will sharpen the measure of my judgment: I will consume Ephraim like a moth, but you like an abiding rot.

It is well known how much less destruction consumes the things a moth nibbles than those through which rot spreads.

“Ephraim saw his sickness, and Judah his bond.” That is, you will both see and endure the vengeance appointed for your pursuits. Nor will it benefit you to seek help from different kings; by what happens, you will confess that they have provided you only examples of corruption, not assistance for salvation.

“Ephraim went to Assyria and sent to the avenging king; but he will not be able to heal you, nor will he be able to release the bond from you.

“For I am like a lioness to Ephraim and like a young lion to the house of Judah.”

He promised to meet both peoples in the form of a lion, but he preserved the force that he had not expressed through outward appearance in the distinction of sex: he would appear to one as a lioness, and to the other as a lion.

He fulfilled the assumed comparison by saying:

“I, I will seize and go away; I will carry off, and there is no one who can rescue. Going away, I will return to my place until you fail and seek my face.”

“There is no shepherd,” he says, “who would dare to tear away prey that I have seized. Despising the tumult of rustics, I will exert my strength until the hunger of my indignation is satisfied.”

He used “I will return to my place” for “to my lair,” to which a lion customarily withdraws without fear.

This will continue until you, exhausted by hardships and pains, seek my face, he says. That statement, however, lies outside the rules of the lion comparison and is introduced from the reality of the matter. For, insofar as the comparison is concerned, who, wearied, would wish to see the face of one whom even when strong he could not resist?

Thus, after expressing the indignation he had assumed, through the lion’s hunger he added something concerning the majesty of his person: he would not come to liberate them until the people, made better by the very abrasion of suffering, desired his countenance and began to ask relief from the one from whom they had experienced punishment.

# CHAPTER VI

[Col. 0992D]

**Verses 1–3.**—“In their tribulation they will rise early to me [another reading: ‘they rise early’]. Come, and let us return to the Lord, for he has struck us, and he will heal us; he will wound us, and he will cure us. He will revive us after two days; on the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live in his sight. We shall know and follow, that we may know the Lord. His going forth is prepared like the dawn, and he will come to us like the seasonal rain and the late rain upon the earth.”

He had said that, having gone forth like a lion to hunt, he would rage against the profane people, exercising the office of vengeance. Once this vengeance had begun to be stirred up and to crush the impious, it would not cease inflicting punishments until they turned themselves entirely, through the full range of their prayers, to seek the Lord.

But since there is a great distinction within the very profession of supplication—some offer it when struck solely by terror, while others are corrected by reason together with fear—he took care to express what difference there was between the two. Although the same outward form appeared in both, we should understand that they rested upon different roots: one upon disturbance alone, the other also upon the virtue of correction.

Since he had said that he would not come forth to help them unless, humbled by chastisement, that people turned to seek his face, he necessarily proceeds to explain what kind of supplication he awaited. First, he runs through the words of the former in mockery, showing that he rejects it because of its shallowness: it flatters with words alone, while lacking the weight of deeds. Its character and kind are also condemned by the sacred song.

“When he was killing them,” he says, “they sought him, and they turned before dawn and came to him; but their heart was not right” (Ps. 34).

“In their tribulation they will rise early to me. Come, and let us return to the Lord, for he has struck us and he will heal us; he will wound us and he will cure us. He will revive us after two days; on the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live in his sight. We shall know and follow, that we may know the Lord. His going forth is prepared like the dawn, and he will come to us like the seasonal rain and the late rain upon the earth.”

“When you begin to seek me,” he says, “I will not be appeased by this prayer that you carry upon your lips. Nor will I be appeased if you praise my power and clemency together, saying that I am so ready to forgive that I anticipate your prayers with benefits, and that I will not allow the wound I inflicted to remain for the space of two days, but will come on the third day to revive you.

“And we shall live in his sight,” that is, we shall possess the happiness of the life he grants. Let us know and investigate him who drives away the nights of our anguish and pains like the morning light, and who pours upon us an abundance of resources like the timely and late rain.

“These things,” I say, “which you are accustomed formally to sing without correcting your morals, I will despise. But observe what I shall say.”

**Verse 4.**—“What shall I do with you, Ephraim? What shall I do with you, Judah? Your mercy”—the mercy which, in the songs mentioned above, you said would come from me toward you, using my own images—“is like a morning cloud; it has vanished, and like the dew of dawn it has dried up when the sun came.”

That is, what once moved me to spare you is consumed by the vapor of my indignation, so that nothing remains from which you may obtain relief from your evils.

This did not happen because my disposition changed, but because yours did not. For I, preserving equally the rights of justice and clemency, had been unwilling to punish those whom I had terrified. But you, unmoved even by the announcement of blows, forced the terrors to pass into fulfillment.

### Verse 5

[Col. 0993D] “Therefore I hewed them down through the prophets; I slew them by the words of my mouth, and your judgments shall go forth like the light”—that is, I applied the axes of prophetic threats and described the evils that were to be inflicted with such massive accumulation that the guilty would easily be terrified by the very hearing of them. But since this elaborate display of terror could not restrain your folly, it is necessary to attack you with what did not suffice merely to announce. Therefore “your judgments shall go forth like the light,” so that no one may now be unaware of what you deserve, and your deformity may not lie hidden beneath some appearance of religious observance, such as you maintained in offering sacrifices.

[Col. 0994A] Moreover, with the outcome of events pending, it will become clear [429] that I sought good dispositions more than rich sacrifices [Note: This explains the following sixth verse: “For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice, and knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.” He himself, as usual, placed it earlier, but the carelessness of copyists omitted it.]—and that the person was acceptable to me who showed diligence in helping his neighbor through mercy rather than in steeping the altar with sacrifice, and who preferred knowledge of God, his commandment, to all sacrifices. You, therefore, who, scorning to learn these things, thought nothing about conduct and nothing about virtues, but supposed that you could appease me—though you had offended me through long-continued actions—with gifts of praise and sacrifices: at least through the dangers confronting you, understand how stern I am. The mercy you praised, though undeserving, has passed away like a morning cloud; but the judgments by which you stand convicted will shine like full daylight.

### Verse 7

[Col. 0994B] “But they, like Adam, transgressed the covenant; they dealt faithlessly with me.”

Following the established order of discourse, he proceeds so that, after threatening punishments, he may add their cause—that is, the sins by which the offense was aroused. Thus here too, after promising that vengeance would be clear, he added the offense by which they were bound. To explain its weight, he recalled an example from ancient times. Here the prophet’s expression deserves notice, since in many such passages it brings the light of explanation. He says, “As Adam they transgressed the covenant; there they dealt faithlessly with me.” [Note: “Where” had previously been read incorrectly. A little later, “to be sinned against” had been printed instead of “in sinning.”]

This does not mean that these people appear to have committed transgression in Paradise; rather, because he had said that they had transgressed the commandment just as Adam had, he added that they had sinned there—that is, they had fallen into sin in the same likeness. Yet this requires a discerning understanding. Adam, although he was a violator of the commandment, is nevertheless not read to have worshiped any idols or committed any of those crimes with which Israel is charged.

[Col. 0994C] How, then, is a people immersed in the greatest crimes compared with that first man? Surely for no other reason than that, although they were not equally sacrilegious, they are nevertheless taught to have been equally ungrateful. For just as Adam, who had been brought into Paradise so that he might enjoy its unlabored abundance [Note: That is, “not acquired through labor.” Previously it had been read as two words, “in labors.”], when no cause of anguish or complaint had arisen, preferred to fulfill the command of the seducer rather than that of the Creator—and when the flattering promise of falsehood had greater influence over him than the Creator’s command, supported by so many gifts and miracles, which had granted the use of everything except one fruit—immediately, as a violator of the commandment, began to experience exile, and exchanged the highest happiness for almost the extremity of captivity, so that thereafter the fields punished his sin by denying their fertility:

In the same manner the people of Ephraim, who enjoyed the abundance of the land as though it were the beauty of Paradise, finding no cause for offense—that is, nothing for which they could complain about God’s indulgence and generosity—but appearing to suffer solely from hatred of virtue, preferred error to truth and, rejecting the religion that brought salvation, fell away into the worship of idols.

Thus they are said to have fallen into the same guilt as the one whose condition they appear to have imitated; and they are struck by the great odium attaching to ungrateful nations, who preferred the one who was the author of no gift, but was skilled only in overthrowing, to their own maker, who abundantly bestowed every good thing. [Col. 0994D]

### Verses 8–9

“Gilead is a city of those who work idols, marked by bloodshed; and like the throat of bandits, it is an accomplice of priests on the road who murder travelers from Shechem, because they have committed crime in the house of Israel.” [Note: The previous editor states: In the Vulgate edition these words, “in the house of Israel,” are not joined to what precedes, as here, but to what follows. Jerome preserves the same order in his explanation. Indeed, our author himself says in the following section: “so that you may readily think that these words were inserted here by nothing other than the carelessness of copyists.”]

Because, as we have often said, he indicts not just any single person but the people, he both reviews what has been done in general terms and enumerates the things in which individual cities committed greater offenses than the others. Although the entire region bristled with the worship of idols, there were undoubtedly particular places that had accumulated more sacrilege because they possessed greater prominence, whether from the advantages of commerce or from the number of their inhabitants.

[Col. 0995A] From among these he introduces the notable cities of Gilead and Shechem, distinguished by their profanities. “Gilead,” he says, “their leading city of idol-makers, is no less eager for cruelty than for profanation. For just as bandits’ throats, so its citizens pant for the blood of the innocent.” Serving the persuasions of their priests—that is, their diviners—if anyone wished to go up to the temple of God, they attacked him on the way, turning him aside from the temple of God and dragging him into partnership with their own error; and if persuasion achieved little, they carried out the matter even by slaughter.

Therefore he says, “an accomplice of priests on the road who murder travelers from Shechem, because they have committed crime.” First, they themselves fell into sacrilege; then, not content with their own fall [Note: We restored “were,” which had previously been read as “they give,” with almost no sense.], they either led others into a similar ruin by persuasion or compelled them to it.

[Col. 0995B] This is rightly called a crime: they possessed such zeal for impiety that they even attempted to pour it into those who were unwilling and resisting.

### Verse 10

“In the house of Israel I saw a horrible thing; there are the fornications of Ephraim; Israel has been defiled.”

To show that the whole region had been profaned, he also mentions different places. Just as above he said that the Gileadites, in the manner of bandits, leapt upon travelers in order to lead them away from the straight road, so now he declares that he saw a horrible thing in the house of Israel—or in Samaria, or throughout the entire region—that is, that the whole people of Ephraim, without exception, was stained with sacrileges.

Since he had often already said that punishments hung over these crimes, he now contents himself with enumerating their merits and passes on to Judah, warning him to understand that the severity of the judge cannot be corrupted, and that he too, unless he hastens to reform, will receive the wages of similar calamities.

### Verse 11

[Col. 0995C] “But you too, Judah, set a harvest for yourself, when I restore the captivity of my people.”

Do not suppose, O tribe of Judah, that you will be exempt from condemnation [431] because, while the people of Israel are going into captivity, it comes to a halt within your borders. Israel had preceded you in iniquities; it followed that it should precede you in miseries. But you, who accompany it in crimes, will also follow it in calamities—yet you are to be judged worse because it did you no good that Israel was condemned first.

“Therefore set a harvest for yourself, when I restore the captivity of my people.” See to it, he says, that you do not doubt: when the time of deserved vengeance arrives, the captivity that my people—that is, your brothers—have now endured, with justice pronouncing sentence, will be turned upon you, so that you too may reap in the same way. For just as those who sow in the tears of repentance bring back sheaves of joy [Note: The previous editor would have preferred “they reap”; the manuscript actually read “they return.”], so those who pursue polluted joys will gather a harvest of grief and lamentation [F. “of laments”].

## Chapter VII

### Verse 1

[Col. 0995D] “When I wanted to heal Israel, the iniquity of Ephraim and the wickednesses of Samaria were revealed, because they committed falsehood; the thief entered, plundering, and the bandit was outside.” [Note: The Vulgate and Jerome’s edition, less correctly, have “wickedness” in the singular, although the Hebrew has it in the plural. Here, however, “qua” had been read incorrectly for “quia.”]

[Col. 0996A] He takes great care to show how ready he is to forgive, and that, as though unwillingly, he assumes the role of avenger; if justice permitted it, he would use the part of mercy much more readily and joyfully. “When, therefore,” he says, “I had conceived something like an impulse of indulgence and was considering rising to assist the wretched, I turned my eyes aside for a moment so that I might see those whom I was about to free. And behold, a troop of iniquities committed by Ephraim rushed into my face, crying out in a way that no one could spare such people except at the cost of violating justice, since they were so steeped in hatred of truth that they were always constructing deadly falsehoods with intense zeal.”

“When I wanted to heal Israel,” he says, “the iniquity of Ephraim and the wickednesses of Samaria were revealed, because they committed falsehood.” Besides their various moral vices, he attacks sacrilege under the name of falsehood, just as above he attacked obscenity. For those who had ceased to worship the true God devised gods for themselves to venerate; and thus they are exposed as having committed falsehood, because they ascribed the divine name to images.

Hence the teacher of the nations also says: “God handed them over to the desires of their hearts, to impurity, so that they might dishonor their bodies among themselves—those who exchanged the truth of God for falsehood, and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever. Amen” (Romans 1:24).

The magnitude of the crime they had committed therefore ended my deliberation, in which I had considered sparing them; and because they had fabricated falsehoods in insult to sacred truth, it did not allow them to escape.

From there a skillful plunderer entered all their inner chambers, with the confidence of a victor and the diligence of one raging, entering so that, among the things that had to be seized, he would leave nothing behind through negligence or reject anything through abundance. He therefore assumed both the likeness and the name of a thief and a bandit who ravages within and without, so that you might understand the enemy compared with him to be not hesitant but swift.

### Verse 2

“And lest they should say in their hearts that I have remembered all their wickedness.” [Note: The previous editor marked this passage with a cross, indicating that he suspected a textual error. Yet the sense of the passage is almost the same as Jerome’s explanation, which arises from the reading of the Seventy (*τῶν LXX*). “What we read in the Septuagint,” he says, “so that they may sing together, as though singing in their hearts, must be referred to the fact that the thief entered, or the bandit plundered, so that, remaining in their former riches and garments, they would not reject the agreement of thief and robber,” and so forth.]

This verse has been inserted to commend modesty. In any case, the words belong with the following context—that is, “the thief entered, plundering; the bandit was outside.”

[Col. 0996C] “Now their inventions have surrounded them; they have been made before my face. And lest they should say in their hearts that I have remembered all their wickedness”—or I shall disclose some portion of their committed profanation, so that they may understand the punishments to be far less than their deserts.

Enemies surrounded them and, by right of victory, took possession of them, examining everything so carefully as though thieves had burst into the inner rooms of houses or bandits into the open fields. “Their inventions have surrounded them,” inventions that were made before my face, just as he had said above: “When I wanted to heal Ephraim, the wickedness of Samaria was revealed.”

In accordance with this, blessed David confesses in the person of the same people: “You have set our iniquities before you, our age in the illumination of your countenance; and all our days have failed, and in your wrath we have failed” (Psalm 89).

You are therefore bound by your crimes; you bear the weight of your own inventions. You fabricated false gods, but you endure the reality of sorrows. Let us now hear what he means by saying that these things were revealed.

### Verses 3–7

[Col. 0996D] “In their wickedness they made the king glad, and the princes in their falsehoods. All adulterers, like a furnace heated by the baker: the city rested for a little while from the mixing of the leaven, until the whole was fermented. The day of our king: the princes began to rage from wine; he stretched out his hand with mockers. For they applied their heart like a furnace while he lay in wait for them; all night the baker slept, baking them; in the morning he himself was burning, like a flame of fire [Al. ‘the flame’]. All of them grew hot like a furnace, and devoured their judges.”

[Col. 0997A] He recalls that festival and that period whose order is contained in the history of the Kings. For when, through the folly of Rehoboam, the people had been divided and Jeroboam had begun to rule the ten tribes, he said, as the text reports (3 Kings 12:26ff.):

“Jeroboam said in his heart: ‘Now the kingdom will return to the house of David, if this people goes up to offer sacrifices in the house of the Lord at Jerusalem.’ And having devised a plan, he made two golden calves and said to them: ‘These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up from the land of Egypt.’ He placed one in Bethel and the other in Dan, and this became an occasion of sin; for the people went to worship the calf as far as Dan. And he made shrines on the high places, and priests from the lowest of the people, who were not of the sons of Levi. He appointed a solemn day in the eighth month, on the fifteenth day of the month, after the likeness of the solemnity celebrated in Judah. And ascending, he likewise made an altar in Bethel, to sacrifice to the calves that he had made. He appointed priests of the high places that he had made in Bethel. And he ascended the altar that he had constructed in Bethel on the fifteenth day of the eighth month, which he had devised from his own heart, and he made a solemn feast for the children of Israel.”

[Col. 0997B] Because, therefore, he relates that King Jeroboam, concerned only for his own power, drove away the worship of the true God—which had been commended by so many miracles and so many ages—with a trivial invention, and that the whole nation so obeyed the profanities of the court that it demonstrated with insistence that it possessed no observance of truth, he describes a kind of contest between the impiety of flatterers and rulers, each striving to be first in crimes [Note: We restored “between” (*inter*) so that the sense might be clear; previously “within” (*intus*) had been read, which yielded no sense. A little later I prefer “whoever” (*quisnam*) instead of “each one” (*quisque*).]

The tribes therefore made the king glad, who was anxious about his own interests in case the people should go up to worship at the temple; by scorning religion they removed the scruple of fear from his mind. “The princes also in their falsehoods”—that is, either the royal attendants or his relatives—they made glad through their falsehoods, and they applied such ardor to their deadly inventions that they appeared to burn like a furnace to which flame has been applied.

[Col. 0997C] Or certainly, just as leaven is accustomed to be hidden in a mass that is being fermented and soon becomes wholly sour, so the iniquity of one man, calling all the tribes to depravity, penetrated and infected them all. Thus, degenerate from their profession of virtue and made dreadful by the opportunity for impiety, they began to call that time “the day of their king,” a time to be celebrated with games and banquets—namely, the time during which either the life of their king or their own security had been granted to them.

Such a festival was consequently seized by drunkenness, so that not only the common people but also the nobles, whom he calls the princes of the nation, began to rage from wine. The king himself, the defiler of that dignity and the maker of sacrilegious error, stretched out his hand with the mockers who openly flattered him.

[Col. 0997D] Because they had prepared their hearts to be like a furnace that would grow hot with the fires of impiety placed beneath it, he slept throughout the night while baking them—that is, he did not remove the burning that had been kindled, but, like a furnace packed with wood [Note: The previous editor would have preferred “heated.” I prefer “them” rather than “their” in the verse immediately following this one.], he calmly surrendered himself to sleep, knowing that throughout the night their drunkenness and profanation would be baked through.

Nor did the craftsman’s expectation deceive him. With every light of reason extinguished, they were found at dawn so inflamed by their crimes that they unambiguously surpassed their judges—the teachers of impiety whom they had had.

“All their kings have fallen, and there is no one among them who calls to me.”

Why, then, do you wonder if all are compelled to undergo torments, when they all committed crimes in such a way that not even one—not merely among the common people, but not even among the nobles—was found who escaped the fall of public impiety?

### Verse 8

[Col. 0998A] “Ephraim himself was mixed among the peoples.”

Above, having passed through the several divisions, he had condemned [perhaps, “indicated”] the transgressing nation, showing that the people had obeyed their kings and that thereafter the princes had fallen together with the common people, thereby showing that no one remained to undertake the office of intervention. In the following verse he indicated this same thing fully and briefly, saying: “Ephraim himself was mixed among the peoples.”

That is, it was not one or another, nor a few or many, who came from the stock of Israel and inserted themselves into the errors of the nations; rather, Ephraim, in his entirety, as far as he could be, mingled with profane peoples. He sought to erase the very name by which he had been distinguished and preferred to be known by the designation of the nations.

Although this desire always broke out in him amid adversity, he was by no means made better by affliction. Therefore, to mark him as senseless amid the extremity of his miseries, he brought forward an appropriate image:

“Ephraim has become like a cake baked under the ashes [Note: The Vulgate adds “bread,” a noun that we formerly printed in the edition of Jerome as well. But it is not present in the Hebrew, which signifies only a cake, or bread baked under the ashes; yet the term “bread” itself is not added there. Even the Seventy omit it. In the following context of the exposition we correct three or four copyists’ errors.]. It is not turned.”

[Col. 0998B] “Foreigners have consumed his strength, and he himself did not know.”

Just as a small piece of bread, not prepared by a baker’s skill but hastily made by a hungry person, may happen to be placed beneath the ashes and not turned, but roasted only on one side, while the other remains raw, so, although frequent affliction had struck his strength, he nevertheless remained, he says, in his zeal for impiety. Thus he is called both raw, because untamed, and burnt, because he groaned under the wasting disease that afflicted him.

He maintained the metaphor: since he had compared the foolish and battered people to a cake that is not turned, he also called their devastators its eaters. He says:

### Verse 9

“Foreigners have consumed his strength, and he himself did not know.”

That is, he had neither acquired discernment between good and evil through meditation on virtue nor received it through the blows inflicted upon him. He does not know at all who were consuming his strength, and with marvelous stupidity he loved his own destruction.

Nor did he, which is the final stage of education, become wise even after experience; rather, he remained in the foolishness that he embraced in early life [Note: The clause explained by the supplied portion of the verse should be added: “and gray hairs also are scattered over him, and he himself did not know.”], even to his gray hairs—that is, until the time of old age.

[Col. 0998C] He emphasizes not that gray hair merely appeared, but that it faded and was scattered—that is, he shows that it did not merely approach, but as though it filled out the years of old age—and yet that ignorance of what is wrong or right, scarcely excusable in little children, continued to the very end.

We have already noted above that he calls the people’s infancy and adolescence the period in which they came out of Egypt and occupied the Promised Land. Their middle youth he calls the period in which they reigned in that region; their old age, however, he calls the years of captivity, whose end the prophet names renewal. In that renewal, their youth may be seen to fly again like that of eagles.

### Verses 10–11

[Col. 0998D] “And the pride of Israel will be humbled before his face; they did not return to the Lord their God, and they did not seek him in all these things. And Ephraim became like a dove deceived, without understanding.”

The prophets freely alter the tenses of events, although consideration of what has been said can adapt the sequence. Thus here he used “will be humbled” instead of “the pride of Israel has been humbled before his face.” That is, it appeared even to Israel itself how deformed it was.

Having lost the beautiful appearance of its former security, Israel saw itself covered with the squalor of miserable servitude, and yet not even then did it seek the God whom it knew it had offended.

[Col. 0999A] “Ephraim became like a dove deceived, without understanding.” What he above called folly that had advanced even to old age, he now calls simplicity—open, that is, to the deceits of seducers.

We must remember that all the comparisons which divine discourse customarily takes from creatures can be established either for blame or for praise. Thus here the prophet applied blameworthy foolishness to doves, whereas in the Gospel the Lord named them as an image of praiseworthy innocence: “Be shrewd as serpents and innocent as doves” (Matthew 10).

“Ephraim became like a dove deceived, without understanding.”

### Verse 12

“They were calling upon Egypt; they went to Assyria. And when they have gone forth, I will spread my net over them; like a bird of the sky I will bring them down; I will strike them according to the report of their assembly.”

Having been deprived of the help of God, whom they had abandoned, and already being battered by frequent incursions, they sought assistance from the Egyptians, as the history of the Kings relates, asking them to protect them against the Assyrians.

But they experienced nothing more than the loss of their money, and they were captured by those to whom the divine sentence had subjected them. This, then, is what he says: because they were calling upon the Egyptians, they went to the Assyrians. Since the Egyptians were unable to help them, the Assyrians transferred them to the regions of Media.

And because he had called Ephraim a dove, which he also calls a bird of the sky, preserving the metaphor, he announces that he will bring it down and cover it with a net.
