That is: “You abandoned my rule by transgressing, but you will not undergo captivity outside my authority. Even when you migrate to other fields, the fixed dominion of my power will threaten you. Therefore, do not suppose that by this migration you have escaped all dangers. Behold, I foretell that there also you will suffer the net of my vengeance and will be unable to escape my indignation unless you correct the practices by which it was aroused.”

### Verses 13–16

[Col. 0999B] “Woe to them, for they have departed from me; they will be laid waste, because they have dealt faithlessly with me. I redeemed them, and they spoke falsehoods against me. They did not cry to me in their heart [Note: We supplied the words “to me” from Jerome’s edition and others, since the Hebrew text especially requires them. In the following verse, Jerome’s edition and the Vulgate, as well as our author below, read “I strengthened” instead of “I confirmed.”], but they howled on their beds; they ruminated over wheat and wine; they departed from me. And I instructed them, and I strengthened their arms, and they devised evil against me. They returned so as to be without a yoke; they became like a deceitful bow. Their princes will fall by the sword, because of the fury of their tongue. This is their derision in the land of Egypt.”

“It is necessary,” he says, “that those who have departed from me should be harassed by calamity pressing upon them [Note: The old editor advises that ‘pressing upon’ should be restored.], and should be tormented because they transgressed the statutes of my law. Nor were they content to commit this only once; they resisted all the remedies of my judgments that I applied to heal them. And as though gifts and benefits made them resentful, so they contended against my benevolence through the crime of an ungrateful mind.”

For, just as they had done from the time of Egypt, so also on many other occasions they protested loudly even in their circumstances; and when they had been freed from anxieties, they repaid true remedies with false services. This is what he says: “They spoke falsehoods against me.” That is, they did not submit to me from the heart, but only with their lips.

To make this clearer, he added: “They did not cry to me in their heart, but they howled on their beds.” Where the affection of a sincere mind is absent, a supplication poured out by the drunken is rightly called a howling.

[Col. 0999D] Finally he added: “They ruminated over wheat and wine; they departed from me.” Since I had bestowed an abundance of every kind of produce, so that they passed from banquet to banquet, and, like animals naturally given to rumination, they repeatedly reconsidered the foods they called theirs—either by praising them or by renewing them—as though they knew nothing better, while continually departing from me, who was the giver of that very abundance.

[Col. 1000A] “And I instructed them, and I strengthened their arms, and they devised evil against me.”

“But when,” he says, “the time had come for them to go forth to war, I fulfilled the role of a vigorous commander, so that their arms might be strengthened for battle and they might taste the sweetness of victory. But they, abusing my benefits against me, immediately employed the strength they had gathered in contempt of the law. And because they had shaken off the hostile yoke, they refused to submit to me as well, expressing this in their deeds by saying: ‘Our lips belong to us; who is our lord?’” (Psalm 11).

“They became like a deceitful bow.” That is, they possessed such perversity that they appeared to be a deceitful bow which, through monstrous fraud, directed its arrows against the very person whose hands drew it [Al. “itself”]. “So these people,” he says, “turned into contempt and insult of us the boldness that, by my favor, they had conceived against their enemies.”

“Their princes will fall by the sword, because of the fury of their tongue. This is their derision in the land of Egypt.”

This can be understood in two ways. First, after enumerating their various crimes according to their different ages, he may have declared it entirely just that the princes should perish together with the people, and that they should learn what derision in the land of Egypt meant—that is, what they had despised when they awaited assistance from the Egyptians, despite the threats of the prophets. Thus, after enumerating the blows, the words may appear to have been added almost mockingly by one who was convicting them: “This is their derision in the land of Egypt”—that is, the ruin of the princes and peoples.

Or, since he had said, “They returned so as to be without a yoke”—that is, they had withdrawn their necks from the law of God and desired to be freed from his dominion—he says: “They did not begin to want this only now. While they were situated in Egypt, before they had been freed from Pharaoh’s rule, they likewise resisted Moses and Aaron with a similar impiety.”

Their princes, therefore, will fall by the sword. They violated the law of God with such atrocious blasphemy that they appeared not so much to err as to rage. [Col. 1000B]

## Chapter VIII

### Verses 1–3

[Col. 1000C] “Let a trumpet be in your throat: like an eagle against the house of the Lord, because they transgressed my covenant and violated my law. They called upon me: ‘My God, we Israel have known you.’ Israel has cast away the good; the enemy will pursue him.”

Even in the preceding sections, I warned that one should observe the manner of prophetic speech: whenever it has sounded with a grave threat, it either immediately adds the causes of indignation or produces similar examples, and thereby asserts its judgments both from the reputation of iniquity and by proving that they conform in every respect to justice.

Thus now also, after explaining the sins and calamities of the Israelite people, and showing that they had been horrifying not only because of their severity but also because of their antiquity, lest they appear to have been convicted indeed of crimes but nevertheless judged less worthy than the tribe of Judah—which, although not defiled by such great errors, had nevertheless been stained by similar ones—he suddenly introduces a mention of its captivity as well, although it was known that this would be fulfilled many years later.

He says: “Let a trumpet be in your throat”—that is, let your throats cry out like a trumpet, because an eagle, a savage predator, is coming against the house of God, namely, the temple situated at Jerusalem.

[Col. 1000D] This does not mean that the sanctity of the place and the power of the divine presence accustomed to appear there could not defend it, but because the inhabitants themselves, by their actions, transgressed the covenant that had been struck between God and human beings—that is, they violated the obligations of religion by serving the idols of the nations.

The sense is therefore as follows: understand how great is the severity of the judge. I did not spare even that tribe which, while you were transgressing, preserved the ceremonies of the law for a time; which, in the days of Sennacherib, was defended by a very great miracle; which conducts the affairs of the altar and Temple with conspicuous and reverent support. Nor, I say, did I delay striking it once it had fallen into your ways [Ant. “surpassed”].

For mere boasting of names is cold and powerless to defend, and it proves the speaker’s shamelessness more than his religion. This is what those polluted by profane practices nevertheless dare to say: “Our God, deliver us, for we alone throughout the whole world have known you, and we glory in the name of Israel given by you.”

[Col. 1001A] For before a good judge the weight of deeds is greater than that of words. Therefore the people of Israel, who cast away their good—that is, the worship of sacred religion—will lie under the pursuit of enemies.

### Verse 4

“They reigned, but not from me; they appointed princes, and I did not know them. From their silver and gold they made idols for themselves, so that they might perish.”

“This is the ancient madness of the people’s defiance toward me,” he says. “Long ago it hastened to cast off my rule [Ant. ‘they cast off’]. For as though it were not enough that, like the surrounding nations, it had decided to obey kings rather than priests, in a short time it also abandoned the reverence with which it had asked me for a king. Desiring to stand wholly outside our dominion, it made princes for itself whom neither the election nor the blessing of priests or prophets ennobled or consecrated; rather, as though I did not know, they assumed the rights of the court, and obtained a position among crimes by bestowing their support and wealth upon the most undeserving and upon idols.”

[Col. 1001B] “From their silver and gold they made idols for themselves, so that they might perish.”

Above he had said: “I multiplied silver and gold for them, which they made into Baals.” Therefore, although they had been enriched by my generosity, they sacrilegiously abused what had been granted, fabricating from their ornaments mockeries for houses and shrines.

“From their silver and gold they made idols for themselves, so that they might perish.”

This expression deserves notice, since the authority of the sacred books uses it especially frequently, placing first what is actually consequent. That is, they made idols for themselves so that they might perish, although they did not make the images with the deliberate intention of perishing; but because they made them, they deserved to perish. [Col. 1001D] [Note: The previous editor likewise warned that “not with intention” should be restored; previously it read “with our intention.”]

## Verses 5–6

“Your calf has been rejected, Samaria; my anger has been kindled against them. How long will they be unable to be cleansed? For it too is from Israel: an artisan made it, and it is not God.”

[Note: [Col. 1001D] It was erroneously written *Pictus* (“painted”); read *Projectus* (“rejected”).]

[Note: [Col. 1001D] Here too *acrem* was wrongly read for *aciem* (“edge”), which we have restored. We have also restored the word *oblimaverit* (“has blunted/clouded”), which follows shortly and was previously wrongly read as *oblineaverit*. Claudian used it in exactly the same sense: “abundance blunts minds” (*oblimat copia mentes*). And our author says below: “you ought to have fostered the fire of reason, clouded over, by vigorous experiences.”]

The whole passage is a complaint filled with indignation. “That you have fallen through voluntary iniquity,” he says, “O people ungrateful for the benefits of your creator, is proved above all by the testimony of adversity. Suppose, then, that the abundance of possessions and security had clouded the edge of your discernment, and that you had thought divinity to reside in images of cattle—for you saw even neighboring nations holding this opinion. At least when you exchanged joyful circumstances for grievous ones, and the victorious enemy devastated the shrines in which you had placed your confidence, and, at his will—though he was serving the indignation of me whom you had abandoned—your calves, which you had consecrated, were either thrown down or melted, you ought to have shuddered at the crime of your opinion. You should have realized that no help could be brought to you by images of mute beasts, which had not been able to rescue themselves either from mockery or from destruction.

“And, to review what has happened: you, O people, knew that you yourself had supplied the material for those images, that you had contributed their form, and therefore understood that you were impiously calling gods those who existed through your benefaction—though you could not have given them life, but only shape. Yet, although you had occupied with these drunken rites all that time which had slipped away in luxurious idleness, at least after the misery that followed proved the emptiness of such worship, you ought immediately to have taken care about correction, and to have nourished the fire of reason, clouded though it was, by vigorous experience, and to have stripped off the filth with which you had clothed yourself.

“Because you did not do this, the prophet rightly cries out: ‘How long will they be unable to be cleansed?’ For it too is from Israel; an artisan made it, and it is not God. For the calf of Samaria will be like a spider’s web.”

[Note: *Al. telas*: “webs” in some manuscripts.]

## Verse 7

“For they sow the wind, and they will reap the whirlwind. A standing stalk is not in them; the sprout will produce no meal. And even if it does produce some, strangers will eat it.”

[Note: Jerome and the Vulgate have *in eo* (“in it”) in the singular. The Hebrew text likewise has the singular.]

“Unless imitation disturbed your plans,” he says, “you would judge that those things were not gods which you knew had been fashioned by an artisan’s hand. Then came the hostile invasion: your divinities perished together with their worshipers, and they could no more delay the devastators than spider threads could. Yet even amid these dangers you persisted through obstinacy and folly, and did not take care to cast off the filth of such profanations.

“Therefore your vows and all your labors will rightly be followed by such tearful frustration that you will appear to have sown not grain but wind, and to have reaped not ears of grain but a whirlwind. That is: nothing fertile or firm will remain with you, as happens with a stalk whose height, through some injury from the air, has not produced the fullness of an ear. So, too, I say, you will gain no benefit from your labors, nor will any effort of cultivation be repaid. And even if something begins to appear from the remnants of former fertility, all of it will come under the power of the enemy.”

## Verses 8–10

“Israel is swallowed up; now it has become among the nations like an unclean vessel. For they themselves went up to Assyria, a wild ass alone by itself; Ephraim gave gifts to his lovers. They also hired nations with payment. Now I shall gather them, and they will rest for a little while from the burden of king and princes.”

By repeated reiteration he aggravates what he threatens, so that the long description of adversity may sharpen the sense of fear, if perhaps the guilty may be corrected in terror before they are punished. Accordingly, he now introduces the actual condition of the captive people and consequently calls them “swallowed up,” since they have been placed under the will of those who consume them, and nothing remains of them for destruction except what the ferocity of their conquerors, satisfied by its successes, may have spared.

“Israel is swallowed up,” he says; “it has become among the nations like an unclean vessel.” The surfaces of the statements seem to conflict; but as regards their meaning, what was said earlier is explained by what follows. For he shows what he meant by “swallowed up”: namely, one whose entire strength has been drained, and who could easily be consumed in destruction if the anger of his rulers demanded this as well.

Moreover, by adding insults, they compensate for the fact that they have been less savage; and therefore they do not kill everyone, so that they may always have people to fear, and may seem to have begrudged them the consolations of death rather than granted them the benefits of life. They did not preserve these wretched people to enjoy the light, but to endure contempt. Therefore he says: “Israel has become among the nations like an unclean vessel.”

Some interpreters translated this as “chamber pot.”

[Note: By “interpreters” I think he means the Greeks—Symmachus, Aquila, Theodotion, and others. Yet none of their fragments survives here to establish the matter with certainty. Still, if it should seem worthwhile, this testimony of our author, together with several other readings that we have observed in Jerome, could be added to the recent collection of the *Hexapla*. This holy Father, however, makes the Hebrews, not others, the authors of this interpretation: “The Hebrews,” he says, “call an unclean or useless vessel a *matula* [chamber pot], with which…” He does not even mention the Greeks.]

“Israel was never assigned an honorable office, so that after the insignia of freedom and dominion it might at least be counted honorably among slaves. Rather, like a vessel made for natural functions, it was filled with the filth of disgrace.” And he rightly intensified the insult by recalling the condition of the nations, saying: “Israel has become among the nations like an unclean vessel.”

As though he were saying: “Alas, alas, how grievous and how great was the transformation—that the people who alone, through instruction in the sacred law, had learned to distinguish between clean and unclean, and who had therefore been separated from all nations so that no contagion might pollute them, are now judged unclean even by those nations whose way of life, from its earliest beginnings to its final end, has been sullied by the filth of every crime.” Therefore: “It has become among the nations like an unclean vessel.”

“For they themselves went up to Assyria, a wild ass alone by itself.” That is, they will suffer what we have described, with the Assyrian bringing it upon them. They will perceive that such eminence in power has been granted to him that the person who reaches him is said to have “gone up” to him.

“An ass, solitary by itself,” however, refers to Ephraim: “An ass, solitary by itself; Ephraim gave gifts to his lovers.” The Jewish people, he says, had endured no rule imposed from outside, but, like a wild ass ignorant of yoke and burdens—of whom blessed David had sung in praise of God, “He makes the one-minded dwell in a house” (Psalm 67)—had been made to dwell in the Promised Land, possessing a distinctive institution.

This people, then, I say, which had been free from human condemnation and subject only to divine commands, has now become so angry and sorrowful that it considers itself fortunate if even honorable servitude falls to its lot.

“They gave gifts to their lovers. They also hired nations with payment. Now I shall gather them.”

When the multitude of the ten tribes deserved to be punished for its profanations, and the prophets announced it, dominion by the Assyrians was promised to them. But the Jews, displaying toward the threats precisely the disposition that the tribes had displayed, remained obstinate in every respect. They preferred to hire even the Egyptians with money rather than be subjected to the Assyrians, to whom the divine sentence was subjecting them.

This, then, is what he says: because they had resolved to fornicate, they wished to try the Egyptians as lovers and voluntarily sent them gifts, promising to provide annual payments if, with their help, the Assyrians were driven back and the prophets’ threat defeated.

Therefore he says: “They also hired nations with payment”—that is, the Egyptians. “Now I shall gather them” into captivity; that is, I shall drag them away and assign them to the announced rule of the Assyrian nation. “I shall gather them,” he says, so that no one might appear to escape.

“And they will rest for a little while from the burden of king and princes.” This appears to have been introduced mockingly, as though he called the captivity that had been imposed a “rest.” That is, they will recognize how much they advanced their own plans and efforts when they have been gathered and have migrated as exiles into foreign fields. For, ceasing to provide either what the Assyrians commanded or the voluntary tribute promised to the Egyptians, they will execute the orders of their masters with all their strength, and confess that the cessation of their tribute has worked only to increase their miseries.

## Verses 11–14

“For Ephraim multiplied altars for sinning; altars became for him occasions of guilt. I shall write for him my many laws, which have been counted as foreign. ‘Bring sacrifices, bring sacrifices’; they will slaughter the flesh and eat it. The Lord will not accept them. Now he will remember their iniquities and visit their sins. They themselves will return to Egypt. Israel forgot his maker and built shrines. Judah multiplied fortified cities; I shall send fire upon his cities, and it will devour his houses.”

[Note: The sacred text has *ei* (“for him”) in the singular rather than *eis* (“for them”). Likewise, in the following verse, instead of the phrase repeated twice, “bring, bring,” some manuscripts read *afferent* (“they will bring”) only once. The Hebrew archetype agrees, having the expression only once. Nevertheless, that our author read it in this way—whether in the copy of Jerome that he used or in another Latin manuscript—is made certain by the beginning of the following paragraph, where, explaining this passage specifically, he says: “They place their hope of salvation solely in the offering of victims,” and introduces the voice of people exhorting one another, namely, “Bring, bring sacrifices,” and then responds, etc.]

He shows by what progression they had summoned the aid of the Egyptians in order to sin: namely, by resisting the holy admonishers in every respect, so that, just as they had despised the prophets when teaching, they might also despise them when threatening—not merely despise them, but even attack them, and, insofar as it lay within their power, prove them false by driving back the Assyrians after hiring the Egyptians.

Now blessed Hosea, rightly enumerating the evils that would come with the captivity, runs through both punishments and sins. He laments that Ephraim multiplied altars to idols and complains that the altars had been turned into a crime for him.

As though he were saying: “The administration of divine worship was instituted for this reason: that the altars might purify those whom crimes had polluted. But now these altars involve the wretched in such deadly entanglements that they are never more grievously defiled than at the altars.”

“I shall write for them my many laws, which have been counted as foreign.” By fleeing to the nations and eagerly seeking to mingle with their rites, he says, the ungrateful people thought that it would be freed from the burdens of our law. But because my judgment is ready to crush the profane mouths of the obstinate with bit and bridle, the outcome itself will reveal that contempt for the commandments will not go unpunished.

“For I shall write for them my many laws, which have been counted as foreign.” He expressed what he was about to do by an image taken from a judge’s procedure, who is accustomed to read aloud the sentence written in a document. I shall therefore write my laws—which were formerly promulgated and are contained especially in the book of Deuteronomy—in many ways against them; that is, I shall execute them and heap them up.

To mention a few things out of many, the speech concludes in this fashion:

“But if you will not hear the voice of the Lord your God, so as to keep and do all his commandments and ordinances that I command you today, all these curses will come upon you and overtake you. You will be cursed in the city, cursed in the field; cursed will be your granary, and cursed your storehouses; cursed the fruit of your womb and the fruit of your land; the herds of your oxen and the flocks of your sheep. You will be cursed when you enter, and cursed when you go out.”

These, then, are the laws that he threatens to multiply against the profaned peoples.

“They offer sacrifices, and they will slaughter the flesh and eat it. The Lord will not accept them. Now he will remember their iniquities.”

The people of Samaria—that is, the ten tribes—had despised no less the sacrifices that ought to have been offered to the true God than his judgments and commandments. The tribe of Judah, however, although not yet stained by a sisterly impiety, had nevertheless abandoned its care for sacrifices.

Therefore, in the quality of their morals, the prophecy continues to join them together, and under the accusation of Israel passes over to Judah, so that, as it has already done above, it may reproach them because, thinking nothing of moral justice, they place their hope of salvation solely in the offering of victims. It introduces, as it were, the voice of people exhorting one another: “Bring, bring sacrifices.” Immediately it responds: “The Lord will not accept them; now he will remember their iniquities.”

The gravity of the judgment must certainly be considered. For he says that he will be especially reminded of their iniquity at the time when, under the consciousness that justice has been despised and neglected, they think that they can protect themselves by offering victims. Gifts are pleasing, of course, when they are offered by the persons of friends rather than of enemies. But it is closer to insult if you offer trivial gifts to one whom you have aggravated with crimes, as though you were approaching him not as a suppliant but as a giver.

The sentence that Cain the parricide experienced therefore suits you: slaughter the flesh and consume it yourselves, since the Lord does not accept it. Why should he accept it, when he prefers obedience to sacrifice and care for justice to a burnt offering?

“Now,” he says, “he hastens his vengeance above all when you place your hope of liberation in the shedding of the blood of animals.”

Now he will visit the sins of all who turn toward Egypt, both in mind and at a price. For all Israel—that is, both Judah and Ephraim—had so completely forgotten their own Creator that, after making him their bitterest enemy, they took no care for correction. Some consumed their wealth and labor in restoring fortifications, others in hiring nations, as though they did not know that the sacred song had announced:

“Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain. Unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it keeps watch in vain.”

Their impiety therefore grew to such a degree that, after provoking the omnipotent Judge to anger, they nevertheless thought that they would be blessed through their own industry—if, that is, they built many fortifications against enemy attacks and remained secure in them, with God not merely failing to help but even fighting against them.

Therefore, he says, a fitting frustration will strike them, so that they will appear enclosed by their fortifications rather than defended by them, and raging flame will consume all such buildings.

Since these things are so—that is, since no difficulty impedes God’s justice and no deceit eludes it—

# Chapter IX

## Verse 1

“Do not rejoice, Israel; do not exult, because you have departed from the covenant of the law through sacrilegious pollution.”

That is: do not think that it will pass unpunished for you that you have mingled with the other nations. For the pursuit of such flight does not vindicate you for the empty freedom that you desired; it merely subjects you to severe vengeance.

## Verses 2–3

“You loved payment above all threshing floors of grain. The threshing floor and winepress will not feed them, and wine will deceive them. They will not dwell in the land of the Lord.”

Do not, I say, O our people, rejoice shamelessly; rather, know that you will change all your desired things into their opposites. For you have been worthless and undisciplined not only in the duties of religion but also in every action.

You loved payment, certainly, above all threshing floors of grain; that is, you judged nothing better or more desirable than the fertility of the land and the expenditures of the belly. All abundance of grain and fruit will therefore be taken away from you. And, to make your desires torment you more severely, the vintage, though it appears for a long time, will disappear in sudden storms, so that, to your grief, it will seem not only damaged but also deceptive.

[Note: Formerly [it read]: “so that they might examine their desires more closely. For a long time, etc.”]

But why should I mention lesser losses, when exile will follow upon your poverty, and no opportunity will be given you to cultivate your native soil? Yet you will not be able, as though lamenting, to marvel sufficiently at the magnitude of this calamity, since you are convicted of having been a voluntary deserter of this land as regards your inclinations. For you desired both the crimes and the assistance of the Assyrians and Egyptians.

[Note: Read “you will be convicted,” or “you have been convicted.” Then supply the part of the verse that is explained: “Ephraim has returned to Egypt, and in Assyria he has eaten what is unclean.”]

With what shamelessness, then, will you seek the fertility of this region whose distinguishing features you rejected both in rites and in morals? You will depart from it, driven away to the place to which you previously wished to go after being corrupted.

[Note: The earlier editor also noted that *ire* (“to go”) should here be read instead of *isti* (“this”).]

And just as you went to Egypt in desire, so you will go to the Assyrians in captivity. You will endure such poverty that, in grief, you will eat polluted and common foods.

## Verse 4

“They will not pour out wine to the Lord, and they will not please him. Their sacrifices will be like the bread of mourners: all who eat it will be defiled, because their bread, their very life, will not enter the house of the Lord.”

He now describes the evils of captivity and says that, when abundance of possessions has been changed into the utmost want, and no trace of happiness or consolation appears, they will spend all their time in mourning. For they will neither be permitted to offer sacrifice to God nor to hope for anything concerning the expiation of their sins—through the very services by which they imagine that they will please God.

Thus all their offering, more suitable for funerals than for festivals, will defile rather than cleanse those who approach it, because their bread, their very life, will not enter the house of the Lord.

The same pointed judgment appears here as above, when sacrifices rejected by God are said to belong to those who offered them. “Therefore now also,” he says, “I have rejected the offerings of those whom, because of the excess of their crimes, I drove out even from their native soil after being provoked.”

[Note: Correct the text to: “whom I drove out even from their native land.”]

That bread, which they do not deserve to bring into the house of God, will become the nourishment of their funeral rites.

## Verses 5–6

“What will you do on the solemn day, on the day of the Lord’s festival? For behold, they have departed from devastation; Egypt will gather them, Memphis will bury them. The desirable things of their silver will be inherited by nettles; thistles will be in their tents.”

[Note: Jerome’s edition and the Vulgate have *argentum* (“silver”). In the Hebrew, with the so-called construct article, the form is different. The text soon afterward had *vertice* (“summit”) written quite incorrectly instead of *urticae* (“of nettles”), which we have restored. The Vulgate and Jerome have the singular *urtica* (“a nettle”) as the subject of “will inherit.”]

Although blessed Hosea’s chief concern is to review the deeds of the ten tribes and to dwell upon either the heightening of their crimes or the explanation of their calamities, nevertheless, by the authority of prophecy, he touches upon what would also happen to the tribe of Judah. And because he knew that the people of Jerusalem, though somewhat later, would suffer things like those of the Samaritans in proportion to their merits, he also mentions the Temple and the sacrifices, assigning them, as belonging to the whole nation, to what particularly agrees with the two tribes.

Therefore, when he had said that they had lost the consolations of the offerings by which they thought they were purified, he developed the incidental image. And because the cessation of such polluted services becomes especially grievous on the days when a joyful solemnity was celebrated, he says:

“What will you do on the day of the Lord’s solemnity?”

What darkness, what bitterness, what anguish of spirit will fill you when you spend in exile, unwillingly, in chains and barbarous servitude, that day of the Lord’s festival which formerly the gathering of the people and their songs made illustrious and sweet for you?

And because, on the occasion of Ephraim, he also marked what, as we have said, would come upon Judah, he continues:

“For behold, they have departed from devastation; Egypt will gather them, Memphis will bury them.”

When their region has been devastated by hostile rule, he says, this will happen to all the tribes as punishment for what they previously committed through sinful desire: just as part of them was led away to the Assyrians, so Egypt will gather another part, and the land of Memphis will consume those received there.

This happened after the victory of Nebuchadnezzar, who overthrew Jerusalem, to those Jews whom the Babylonians had left as cultivators of the fields, as both blessed Jeremiah and the history of Kings relates.

As for what follows—“The desirable things of their silver will be inherited by nettles”—if only reading, and not experience as well, had taught us that this happens according to the practice of captivity. It is well known that either houses built at great expense, once their inhabitants had perished, became covered with woodland, or that buried treasures of gold and silver, after those who had hidden them were killed, were lost in perpetual oblivion.

## Verse 7

“The days of visitation will come; the days of retribution have come. Israel, know this: the prophet is a fool, the spiritual man is mad, because of the multitude of your iniquity and the multitude of your madness.”

[Note: Some manuscripts of Jerome also add *te* (“you”), as we have noted; other printed books omit it, as does the Hebrew text itself. Likewise, at the end of the verse, we have noted that some Hieronymian manuscripts contain *multitudo* (“multitude”) rather than *multitudinem* (“the multitude”).]

It would have been preferable for reason to teach you discernment rather than calamity. But because, as though entirely without reason, you demanded whips and goads, even now, when the time of your visitation—that is, of your condemnation—has arrived, wake up so that you may understand what you deserve.

Acknowledge that such harsh wages are owed to your pursuits, which you perceive yourself to have gathered through contempt for spiritual teachers. For you had burst forth into such madness that you said of the prophets, who spoke at the command of the Holy Spirit and announced what awaited you through the zeal of the fathers—perhaps so that fear, having been announced beforehand, might bring about repentance before vengeance found those whom it would punish—not only that they foresaw nothing beyond other people, but even that they were deprived of human reason and moved more by insanity than by revelation.

The history of Kings also shows that, through the abundance of their profanation, people at that time were accustomed to call prophets by this name. For when a certain prophet, sent by blessed Elisha to anoint Jehu king, had arrived at Ramoth-gilead, the nobles sitting around Jehu said: “What does this fanatic want?” (2 Kings 8).

Thus among them the authority of divine speech had fallen into such disuse that they judged the commands of virtue to be not merely beggarly but insane. The preacher, shuddering at the magnitude of this crime, therefore cries out with judicial force:

“Because of the multitude of your iniquity, and the multitude of your madness.”

As though he were saying: “This is not a simple error, but multiplied madness: to despise spiritual teachers, who shine with prophetic splendor, as fools and madmen precisely at the time when you yourselves suffer such a poverty of prudence that you think the gods you have cast are truly gods.”

## Verse 8

“The watchman of Ephraim is with my God; the prophet has become a snare of ruin upon all his ways; madness is in the house of his God.”

[Note: *Loquens* (“speaking”) was erroneously read instead of *laqueus* (“snare”).]

Some have thought that Jeroboam is signified here by the name Ephraim. He is known to have come from the tribe of Ephraim, to have been zealous for the worship of the Temple, and for this reason to have fallen into conflict with Solomon. But after he obtained rule over the tribes, he also became the author of profanation, leading the hearts of his subjects to the worship of calves.

Therefore they think that Jeroboam is called Ephraim, and that he is said to have been a watchman “with God” because at first he had both cared for religion and carefully observed what was right.

[Note: Jerome, whom our author clearly had before his eyes, is among those who give this interpretation. “Jeroboam,” he says, “was appointed as a watchman among the people, and as a prophet with my God—that is, with the God who speaks these things through Hosea.”]

But the one who once was a prophet, I say, so suddenly defected to evil that he became ruin and a snare to his followers. Why would he not, since he was engaged in the greatest possible madness in the house of his chosen god?

This passage, however, can be explained more briefly in the following way. Since he had begun a complaint about the insults directed against the prophets, he continued in the same vein, as though he were saying:

“O people, subjected to profane rites, you have added insults against spiritual teachers to the accumulation of your iniquity, so that you called God’s prophets mad and spiritual teachers foolish. Such madness burst forth from the magnitude of your iniquity.

“For at times you dared to enter into a kind of contest with their promises and to say: ‘Let us both undertake the task of watching and observe whether all those things which these men announce as future will come to pass.’ You added that the prophets should be regarded as nothing other than a hostile snare fashioned for the ruin of wretched citizens. And so, joining blasphemy to insults, you said that there was madness in the house of God, that is, among the prophets.”

The statement that follows proves that this opinion is a very grave sacrilege.

## Verse 9

“For they have sinned deeply, as in the days of Gibeah. He will remember their iniquity and visit their sins.”

“This crime,” he says, “is not such that the judge’s sentence can forget it. And because he had mentioned an ancient history, he says: ‘He will remember their iniquity.’ He will avenge,” he says, “the present insult against the prophets no later than if he were bringing to judgment that crime which they committed before the age of the kings, when the Judges ruled the Jewish nation.”

At that time a certain Levite, returning to his own dwelling, turned aside at evening into a city of the tribe of Benjamin called Gibeah. Since he found no host there in the public square, he sat down with his wife. But the degenerate youth of the city, not content with refusing hospitality, seized the Levite’s wife for sexual violation and perpetrated such outrageous wickedness that the woman, after her chastity had been violated, was also deprived of life.

The next day the Levite arose, placed the corpse of his dead wife upon his donkey, cut it into pieces, and sent it throughout all the tribes of that people, so that, once they had learned the cause of so terrible a spectacle, they might undertake a common vengeance.

Thus they declared war against the Gabaonites unless they surrendered the guilty, and after three battles, scarcely overcoming them, they destroyed them, so that it is reported that no more than five hundred men remained from the entire tribe of Benjamin (Judges 19).

The prophet compared the present sin with that crime: namely, their calling spiritual men foolish and mad. The equivalence of the offenses commends reverence for the prophets; it shows that the honor of the prophets, violated in bold speech, constitutes no lesser guilt than that which public, bloody, and incestuous obscenity once incurred.

## Verse 10

“Like grapes in the wilderness I found Israel; like the first fruit on a fig tree at its top I saw your fathers. But they themselves went to Baal-peor, and they alienated themselves in shame, and became abominable like the things they loved.”

He gathers into one account events that occurred at different times, so that, as we have said, he may make equal the guilt of violated religion and of insults against the prophets.

He makes an advance in praising the ancestors, so that, as their children degenerated, their envy may increase and it may become clear from what height of holiness they descended into what depths of crimes.

“When human nature was bristling and covered with the dense thorns of impiety,” he says, “Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob displayed the marks of noble birth. Producing, as it were, grapes and figs, they exhibited the sweetness of the confession owed to God. I did not despise their faith and virtue because of their small number; rather, I judged them worthy of all the greater honor and favor because they rejected the many examples of profane nations.

“Just as I gathered a vine sprouting in a vast wilderness, and just as I gathered early figs, whose ripeness and sweetness would stir desire, so I gathered them diligently into my embrace, lest any of their fruits or praises should perish.

“But when I had chosen to be called the God of those whose Lord I was, I continued also to multiply their offspring. Yet the degenerate people, forgetting alike their own evils and their Creator, entered into the worship of those idols which obscenity alone had consecrated—namely, to Baal-peor, an image which they said represented Priapus.”

The history in the book of Numbers commends this account: according to the counsel of Balaam, the women of Midian, dressed and gesturing like prostitutes, came out to meet the Israelite army, so that after arousing the men’s desire for lust, they would not grant them the opportunity for sexual violation until they had polluted them with sacrifice to their idol, Baal-peor.

Finally, such a plague arose against the people that twenty-three thousand perished together in one day.

Therefore shame seized the obscene, so that they might not become less abominable to God than the idols themselves, through pursuit of which they had sinned.

[Note: The earlier reading *consectationem* (“pursuit”) should be *consectatione* (“through pursuit”).]

The people of that age whom the prophet Hosea addresses are not said to have sinned against Baal-peor; rather, because the ancient event has been introduced and the noble character of the holy fathers praised, the deeds committed by their descendants in different ages are explained, so that it may appear to whom those now being accused are similar.

It is as though he were saying to them:

“Behold into what disgrace they flowed from an illustrious stock. Behold how great was their forgetfulness of their ancestral dignity: while their ancestors had deserved to be chosen for salvation as the world perished, these later descendants, with folly and obscenity vying within them, worshiped Priapi and calves.”

## Verses 11–12

“Ephraim flew away like a bird; their glory was from birth, from the womb, and from conception. And even if they raise their children, I shall make them childless among men. But woe to them when I withdraw from them.”

[Note: The singular *enutriverit* (“he has raised”) was consistently read, though less correctly; the plural *enutriverint* (“they have raised”) is preferable. In the following verse we have added the conjunction between “but” and “woe,” which is also present in the Hebrew. We silently correct less significant errors above.]

“Ephraim,” he says, “flew away like a bird.” He had already said above: “Ephraim became like a deceived dove without a heart.” They called upon Egypt; they went to the Assyrians.

Therefore this people, which refused to distinguish between the devout and the impious, but became abominable like the images themselves, will rightly be transferred into captivity with such speed that it will seem not so much to have walked as to have flown.

Yet it will suffer not only the scourges of exile. The preceding calamity of poverty and disease will consume its swarms of children, so that childlessness may punish the hearts that fertility had previously exalted.

“Their glory,” he says, “was from birth, from the womb, and from conception. And even if they raise their children, I shall make them childless among men.”

That is: although they had aggravated the eternal Judge by their crimes and took no care to appease him, they nevertheless rejoiced in multiplying their families, considering it their happiness and glory if they were permitted both to unite those who were marrying and to see pregnant women and hear those giving birth.

There, therefore, I shall strike them where they were rejoicing most, so that they may not be permitted to raise the children they have received—or, if they happen to raise them, so that the children may perish—until the lack of the offspring long desired brings them to the desolation of solitude.

[Note: I would prefer to read: “through the loss of the offspring long desired,” and so forth.]

Thus they will perceive that, since it cannot be well with those whom I abandon, it is much worse for those against whom I fight.

### Verses 13–14

“Ephraim, as I saw it [Ant.: ‘as he saw,’ *vidit*], was a Tyre founded in beauty, and Ephraim will bring forth [Ant.: ‘brings forth,’ *educit*] his children for the slayer. Give them, Lord—what will you give them, Lord? Give them a womb without children and dry breasts.”

[Note: I have preferred to read *vidi* (“I saw”) where previously *vidit* (“he saw”) was printed; then *educet* (“he will bring forth”) instead of *educit* (“he brings forth”); and finally, where it says “what will you give, Lord?”, the Hebrew and nearly all books omit the second *Domine* (“Lord”).]

We read elsewhere among the prophets of the beauty and populousness of the city of Tyre, so that blessed Ezekiel’s Canticle even called it a prostitute, evidently because of the multitude of songs with which the whole city resounded in luxury throughout the night. Since, therefore, he had here threatened the people with Samaria’s transformation, he magnifies its beauty when it was prosperous in order to heighten the sense of their grief, as though he were saying:

“The magnitude of this calamity, by which the Jews, their offspring destroyed, migrated from their own territory, is not properly understood except by one who considers what came before. Then he will perceive how great the change for the worse has been, when he reflects how they had previously flourished in such a bloom of joy.”

“Ephraim,” he says, “as I saw it, was Tyre”: a people teeming with population, overflowing with resources, resounding with amusements and songs, so that its location delighted those arriving both from the shore and from the mainland. Its very foundations could therefore be said to have been established in a kind of beauty.

“But for this city,” he says, “though surrounded by pleasures, yet acquiring no protection for itself through justice and religion, he commanded that it should bring forth its children for slaughter and suffer the will of savage enemies, because it had trampled upon the precepts of our law.”

When the times had turned toward decline—events that are still future under Nebuchadnezzar—he speaks as though they had already happened.

[Note: The earlier editor preferred *quasi jam facta* (“as though already accomplished”).]

Ephraim, therefore—that is, Samaria and the multitude of the remaining tribes—was so overwhelmed by the terror of the avenger that it almost prepared its own offspring to be offered to those who were killing them.

This is said to have fulfilled the matter not by doing it themselves, but by deserving it. In accordance with the customary manner of Scripture, the form is that of someone hesitating and announcing under the guise of a question what is about to happen:

“Give them, Lord. What will you give them? A womb,” he says, “without children, and dry breasts.”

“With that plague,” he says, “let them be condemned, and let them know that they are destined to be wiped out by destruction.” For above he had said that if they nourished children, they would immediately endure their bereavement; now he adds dry breasts and a monstrous barrenness to be inflicted upon the women, so that even the restoration of the peoples whom captivity had devoured might be despaired of.

### Verses 15–17

“All their wickedness is in Gilgal, for there I hated them. Because of the evil of their inventions, I will drive them from my house; I will not continue to love them. All their princes are departing. Ephraim is struck down; their root is dried up; they will bear no fruit. And even if they beget children, I will kill the beloved offspring of their womb. My God will reject them, because they have not listened to him; and they will be wanderers among the nations.”

[Note: Here we have supplied the pronoun *eum* (“him”), supported by all the books and by our author himself below.]

They are reported to have worshiped idols especially at Gilgal. He therefore declares that all their wickedness had been gathered there, on account of which he testifies that he hated them. Some, however, have thought that the prophet also recalled this place because of Saul. At Gilgal he had received the leadership of that nation; and because the nation had sinned under Jeroboam, who consecrated the calves, the prophet therefore uses the present guilt as an occasion to accuse that origin of error as well, when Israel, scorning priestly rule, desired to be under kings in imitation of the neighboring nations.

Thus he says: “All their wickedness is in Gilgal,” as though he were saying:

“The impiety that has now devoured them had its causes there; there it received its beginning, when they transferred the government from priestly to royal authority.”

This interpretation may seem subtler; but the other is clearer and stronger, in view of the tenor of the discourse that has been begun: in Gilgal and in other places he reproves the worship of idols, and because of this error the just judge threatens that he will cast them out of his house. He adds to this sentence something still more painful: “I will not continue to love them.” This had also been signified at the beginning, when that daughter was called “Without Mercy.”

He announces that the tribes are to be driven from his house—that is, from the Promised Land—because, as far as the Temple is concerned, they had long ago departed from him through the murderous schemes of King Jeroboam. He promises that the severity by which the impious are expelled from their own territory will remain fixed against them, apparently not to be softened by any subsequent exercise of mercy.

Since this showed the weight of a grave punishment, he immediately adds the reason, which was itself serious: “All their princes are departing.” He does not say this merely to indicate that the nobles alone had fallen into sin, but so that no doubt might remain concerning the wickedness of the common people, since not one of the princes had remained who did not depart from the worship of God.

The remaining verses simply repeat the sentence stated shortly before, by which both bereavement and barrenness had been threatened against them:

“Ephraim is struck down; their root is dried up; they will bear no fruit. And even if they beget children, I will kill the beloved offspring of their womb. My God will reject them, because they have not listened to him; they will be wanderers among the nations.”

“Captivity,” he says, “will swallow them up, while their offspring, than whom nothing is sweeter to parents, will be consumed by manifold and varied calamity.”

## CHAPTER 10

### Verses 1–3

“Israel was a luxuriant vine; its fruit was abundant. According to the abundance of its fruit, it multiplied altars. In proportion to the richness of its land, it luxuriated in images. Their heart was divided; now they will perish. He himself will break their images; he will devastate their altars, because now they will say, ‘We have no king, for we do not fear the Lord; and what can a king do for us?’”

[Note: I cannot be persuaded that the preposition *a* was inserted here through the rashness of copyists or scholars, although both the Hieronymian and Vulgate editions, as well as most other books, omit it. The Hebrew text has a word that, although its origin or root is somewhat obscure and difficult, can nevertheless easily be judged to have been formed from the preposition rendered in Latin by *a*. The Septuagint, who translated it as στῆλας (*stēlas*, “pillars” or “stelae”), appear to have gone astray, whether from the Hiphil form of a verb meaning “to make swollen” or “to raise up,” or from a verb meaning “to stand,” as we gather from other passages and from 2 Kings 1:19. Thus we do not deny that the formative element of the noun, as they call it, may seem to be *mem*. But the word means “statue.”]

The prophet’s discourse proceeds throughout on one and the same material: to magnify the crimes of that people, announce punishments, and therefore often repeat similar and identical images, while adding, as far as he can, something by which they may be startled. Thus, calling Israel a luxuriant vine, he declares that its fruit was abundant.

When this vineyard, transplanted from Egypt, had filled the Promised Land, it stood, he says, flourishing with spreading branches. It produced such an abundance of fruit—that is, of sons and grandsons—that the narrow spaces of the lands they had received were made insufficient.

But what benefit was there in having an increase of offspring, when they strove to burst forth so perversely that, in proportion to their numbers, they armed themselves against me, the author of so great a gift, and attempted to make their crimes equal to their forces, fashioning for themselves publicly and privately gods whom they might worship?

Thus that vine, which had been planted from the stock of the elect fathers, was turned into a cluster of bitterness and a vine-shoot of Sodom, so that both the common people and the rulers rejoiced not merely in neglecting justice but even in attacking it.

“Therefore their heart was divided; now they will perish.” That is: they were wholly separated from me, and their resolve departed from the worship of the Law once it had been confirmed.

What remains except that they should waste away through an irrevocable disaster and recognize the vanity of their opinion, by which they had accustomed themselves to console one another, saying that their condition should be considered better under captivity than when they were governed by holy men, priests, or kings?

Among themselves, therefore, he says, they will speak shamelessly, as though they then possessed a kind of freedom in which they were compelled neither to obey the Law nor to obey a king, since their ruler had been carried away by the enemy and they had cast off the yoke of religion through their ancient profanation.

Rejoicing in these crimes, they consider it happiness that they are not summoned to the continuing duties of their kings but, living far away, pay annual tribute to their conquerors.

For just as those of whom the Apostle says, “Having lost all sense, they gave themselves over to licentiousness for the practice of every impurity and greed” (Ephesians 4), or like those whom the prophet refers to when they said, “We will exalt our tongue; our lips are our own; who is our lord?” (Psalm 11), so blessed Hosea declares concerning these people that they had burst forth to such a degree of profanation that they seemed either to have said or to be able to say:

“We have no king, for we do not fear the Lord; and what can a king do for us?”

That is: “We have been freed from the annoyances of divine fear, nor do we have a king who can punish this license of speech.”

Because this moved a grave horror in anyone who considered it carefully, he rebukes and exclaims:

### Verse 4

“Speak the words of a useless vision, and you will strike a covenant; and judgment will spring up like bitterness upon the furrows of the field.”

That is: you whose hearts have been set on such madness will understand that you have entered into a covenant with the extremities of calamity, and all your regions will be filled with various disasters, so that in those very lands dangers will appear to sprout more abundantly than crops.

Appropriately, because he had indicated that they had sinned not through negligence but through deliberate purpose and devoted effort, he called them “furrows”—marks impressed upon fields in which the bitterness of judgment, that is, the severity of vengeance, would arise.

They should therefore know that they would reap what they had sown.

## BOOK THREE

### CHAPTER 10 (continued)

### Verses 5–6

“The inhabitants of Samaria worshiped the cows of Beth-aven, because its people mourned for it; and its keepers exulted over it, over its glory, because it had departed from it. Indeed, it too was carried away to Assyria as a gift for the avenging king. Ephraim will be seized by shame, and Israel will be ashamed of its counsel.”

[Note: From this point blessed Jerome also begins his third Commentary. This indicates that, in the older division of the sacred text, a new chapter began here, contrary to the arrangement now in use.]

Jewish tradition has customarily explained this passage by the following tale, told in an old Hebrew book entitled *Seder-Olam* and also recounted by St Jerome, from whom our author seems to have taken it. At the time in question, the Israelites had not yet been transferred to the territories of the Medes but were still settled in their own region and paying tribute to the Assyrians. Their treasury exhausted, they sent the calves they worshiped to the Assyrian kings—especially King Sennacherib—as gifts among the other tribute.

Jeroboam had made the calves of gold, but the keepers entrusted with their custody secretly replaced them with bronze ones covered with gold. When necessity arose for the calves also to be sent to supplement the tribute, the people mourned, thinking that they had lost their gods, while those who knew of the fraud rejoiced, because, once the images had been transferred elsewhere, they no longer feared that the theft would be investigated or detected.

[Note: The earlier editor preferred *exultavere* (“they rejoiced”) rather than *resultavere* (“they leapt back”).]

[Note: The earlier editor’s reading was *Salmanassarum* (“of Shalmaneser”) in the cited book *Seder-Olam*; Jerome, as noted above, says “Sennacherib.”]

Although the reading seems to have provided an occasion for this interpretation, the passage can also be understood according to the explanation begun at the outset. After the threatening authority had declared that bitter vengeance would sprout through the furrows of the field for the wretched people, he immediately adds, in his customary manner, the cause of his indignation:

“The inhabitants of Samaria,” he says, “worshiped the cows of Beth-aven”—that is, the people of the royal city, who ought to have recalled others from error, hurried to small towns to worship the images of calves.

After this, the order of the following verse is altered by hyperbaton, and the division becomes:

“Because the people of Samaria will be confounded when adversity reveals the worthlessness and uselessness of their gods.”

For under the pressure of poverty they themselves will be joined to the tribute, possessing no more value than the quantity of metal warrants. Therefore the unhappy people will follow with tears those whom shortly before they had consecrated with the greatest honor and with the rejoicing of diviners.

“Ephraim will be seized by shame, and Israel will be ashamed of its counsel,” when it recognizes its great deformity and its bitter tribute.

### Verses 7–8

“Samaria has caused its king to pass away like foam upon the face of the water. The high places of the idol, the sin of Israel, will be destroyed. Thorn and thistle will grow upon their altars, and they will say to the mountains, ‘Cover us,’ and to the hills, ‘Fall upon us.’”

As far as divine piety and clemency are concerned, he says, I had wished them to possess their land for a long and secure time; but their grave sacrileges resisted this, and they compelled [Ant.: *compulerant*, “had compelled”] the king—that is, their kingdom—to be destroyed with a swift end.

Thus, like foam floating upon the currents of water, both the profanation of the nation and its dignity slipped away.

When all the shrines whose frequentation had habitually provoked me have been consumed by hostile fire, thickets will cover their altars. Whoever remains will wish to hide, driven either by shame or fear, if nowhere else then beneath the ruins of some mountains.

It should be noted that the Lord also took up this verse in the Gospel (Luke 23:30), to express the prayers of those who were afraid. This accords with the practice of Scripture, by which statements first spoken in one context are appropriately applied to similar circumstances.

### Verse 9

“From the days of Gibeah Israel has sinned; there they stood. The battle against the sons of iniquity overtook them at Gibeah.”

[Note: On the contrary, according to the Hebrew exemplar, with which Jerome’s translation and all the other books agree, the battle will not overtake them.]

Above he had already mentioned that period when he said that those who mocked the words of the prophets had sinned in such a way as that youth of Gibeah—the youth that had violated the Levite’s wife to the point of death.

But, lest the repetition be empty, he now sets forth those whom he had compared there, saying:

“The crime of those who sinned through incestuous obscenity may indeed seem similar to that of these people, who considered spiritual men foolish and insane.”

Therefore captivity would rage against them in likeness to that calamity which had nearly destroyed the Benjamites.

Now, as though suspending for examination the circumstances of the guilt and the stages of punishment, he declares this later vengeance to be the more severe—not without reason, since there the eleven tribes had long waged war against one another, and the Gibeahites, although few in number, had nevertheless been overcome only with great difficulty.

Here, however, the wealth of all the Samaritans, together with the calamities and devastations preceding the final destruction, had been consumed to such an extent that no one remained who had confidence to resist.

He therefore declares that Israel had sinned from the days of Gibeah, but that at that time they had stood for some while and displayed proofs of their strength in the gravest conflicts. Only after the third battle did the Israelites, imploring God’s help with tears, achieve complete victory.

Now, however, since no one not only advanced into battle against the Assyrians but not even wished to defend his own walls, the prophet says that the magnitude of their iniquity must also be understood from the accumulation of their miseries.

“At that time,” he says, “the Benjamites resisted so bravely that for a while they did not even seem to have been overtaken in battle. But these people of the ten tribes, with their kings and princes, because they had offended me, did not stand.”

Since, therefore, I must pronounce sentence against the guilty without a genuine contest:

### Verse 10

“According to my desire I will chastise them.”

This appears to have been said entirely according to our ordinary manner of speaking. When we are moved by indignation, we say that we desire vengeance and take pleasure in the affliction of the guilty.

Now, therefore, he promises that they will be chastised according to his desire. For it follows:

“Nations will be gathered against them”—that is, a multitude of plunderers will assemble as though for prey already prepared, so that these people may receive the punishments of a twofold iniquity.

Thus he says: “They will be chastised for their two iniquities.”

Although he has indicated the number, he has not specified the kinds. We could therefore say that another prophet identified the iniquities that he does not distinguish here: namely, that they had abandoned God, the fountain of living water, and dug for themselves cisterns (Jeremiah 2:13)—that is, idols—from which they could experience no refreshment.

But since the best rule of interpretation is that which is drawn from the sequence of the passage, let us suppose that he called “two iniquities” the two that he reproves in the present passage: namely, that they not only overwhelmed the true prophets with insults and calamities but also honored false prophets, servants of demons, from their own territory with offices and gifts.

By this they were shown not to have fallen through error but by deliberate choice, since they pursued both things with equal zeal: honoring destructive teachers and detesting those who brought salvation.

By contrast, the holy person is described as walking in this way:

“Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle, or who shall rest upon your holy mountain? He who walks without blemish and practices righteousness; who speaks truth in his heart and has not dealt deceitfully with his tongue; who has not done evil to his neighbor and has not accepted reproach against his neighbor. The wicked man has been brought to nothing in his sight, but he glorifies those who fear the Lord” (Psalm 14).

“Because of these two iniquities, therefore, I will consume the wicked in an affliction that is not pleasing to me.”

### Verses 11–12

“Ephraim is a heifer trained to love threshing, and I passed over the beauty of her neck. I will mount Ephraim; Judah will plow [Ant.: *orabit*, “will pray”]; Jacob will break up his furrows.

“Sow for yourselves in righteousness, and reap according to the mouth of mercy. Renew [Ant.: *invocate*, “call upon”] the fallow ground for yourselves. It is time to seek the Lord, when he comes [Ant.: *quod*, “that which”] who will teach you righteousness.”

He displayed the feeling of his indignation in mocking words, calling the nation, which was liable to punishment, a heifer suitable and deserving for threshing its crops.

He marked its weakness both by sex and by age, placing it in every respect below the Gibeahites.

Thus, in mockery, he calls it both a heifer and beautiful, and diligent in those afflictions that it had earned through its evil pursuits—not because an afflicted creature could love its own troubles, but because by the sentence imposed upon it it would be bound to them, just as breasts inflamed with love are accustomed to cling to one another.

He promises that its neck, deserving to be subjected to torments, will be made to endure heat and breezes over a broad expanse. In mockery he threatens it, while declaring it eager for and experienced in the evils of which it is entirely worthy.

“Ephraim,” he says, “is a heifer trained to love threshing, and I passed over the beauty of her neck. I will mount Ephraim; Judah will plow; Jacob will break up his furrows.”

“I will so break the proud neck of Ephraim,” he says, “that he will finally experience as an avenger the one whom he had despised as a teacher and benefactor.”

Nor will the usefulness I seek fail to result from my judgment. Although I subject these people to destruction, I will heal others through their example.

Ephraim, who refused to be leaven and was not filled with the marrow of piety but dissolved wholly into straw through the frivolity of his mind, will endure the labor of the threshing floor that burns him.

Judah, however, will follow under the yoke of fear in a more fortunate condition. Fixing the plowshare of the commandments, he will distinguish between good and evil. Subduing the clod of his heart through religious discipline, he will sow the seed of knowledge together with the work of righteousness and mercy, and entrust it to renewed fallow fields from which he has removed the wild growth, so that a harvest worthy of such labor may properly answer to it.

This seems to have been fulfilled at the time when heavenly assistance delivered Hezekiah and the whole city from the hands of Sennacherib.

Finally, it follows:

“It is time to seek the Lord, when he comes who will teach you righteousness.”

The sacred histories testify that blessed Hezekiah devoted himself to promoting religion, so that he fulfilled the duty both of ruler and of teacher. For he was not content to recall the inhabitants of his own tribe to the worship of God; he also sent messengers and decrees throughout the neighboring regions in which some of the Israelites who had been captured and transferred still remained, so that, rejecting the errors of idols, they might return to the worship of the true God.

This, then, is what he says: the people of Jerusalem will reap mercy when devotion to the ruler who teaches [Ant.: *docentes*, “teaching,” plural] them righteousness also stirs them to seek God.

Although this work and office may seem to have been briefly accomplished under Hezekiah, it was more fully brought to completion by our Lord, who is King of kings and Lord of lords. Through him the light of piety was displayed and the discipline of virtue delivered not to one tribe or region but to all lands and nations.

For this reason the Apostle also says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (Romans 13:11), giving no offense to anyone, so that the ministry may not be defiled.

Then the opportune time for seeking the Lord appeared, when the Word became flesh to dwell among us, and we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth (John 1).

But let us also consider their impiety.

### Verses 13–15

“You plowed impiety; you reaped iniquity; you ate the fruit of falsehood, because you trusted in your ways and in the multitude of your mighty men.

“Tumult will arise among your people, and all your fortifications will be devastated, just as Salmana was devastated by the house of him who vindicated Baal on the day of battle, when the mother was dashed to pieces upon her children.

“Thus Bethel did to you, because of the face of the wickedness of your iniquities.”

[Note: In place of *Arastis*, a verb supported both by Jerome’s and the Vulgate’s version and by the Hebrew text, we have restored the reading *Arastis*, which had previously been corruptly printed as *Aras reliquistis* (“you left altars”). Perhaps, he says, our author originally wrote *Aras*; a copyist who did not understand the writing, or some critic who misunderstood it, changed it into *Aras reliquistis*. The phrase “their impiety” was also missing.]

[Note: The Hebrew has “the house of Arbel on the day of battle”; in place of the words “of him who vindicated Baal,” it has a single word. The Septuagint likewise render this by the single name Ἱεροβαὰλ (*Hierobaal*, “Jerobaal”), which Jerome especially approves in his exposition of this passage: “As it is contained in the Hebrew, from Arbel, signifying the same thing as Jerobaal.” Nevertheless, he himself translated it “he who vindicated Baal,” and confirms this in the following exposition, where he says: “There is no doubt that it signifies Gideon, who, because he destroyed the shrine of Baal and cut down the sacred grove, while Baal could not avenge himself, received the surname Jerobaal—that is, ‘Let Baal avenge himself.’” There is likewise no doubt that here in our author *vindicated* should be read instead of *indicated*, following Jerome’s version, which he praises. The Vulgate reading, which has *judged*, should likewise be restored; the contrary reading is plainly a scribal error.]

Through the occasion of Ephraim, whose sins he magnifies throughout almost the entire book, mention had been introduced of Judah, in whom it had become apparent what devotion and faith had earned in times of danger.

Having briefly noted this digression, he returns to the order of the action undertaken and continues to indict Israel’s crimes.

“But you,” he says, “people of Samaria, acted quite differently from Judah and Benjamin when you had come into the extremity of danger. You trusted not in God but in your counsels and in the strength of your armies.

“Therefore you will receive the fruit appropriate to you: hostile tumult will destroy and overthrow your people and your fortifications. You will be consumed in the likeness of that most impious leader named Salmana, whom, as we read in the Book of Judges, Gideon defeated and destroyed—either together with the relatives whom the name of the wretched mother reveals, or together with the very city in which he had reigned, which may be called his mother” (Judges 4 and 8).

“Just as Gideon,” he says, “destroyed Salmana, who had demolished the idol of Baal, so Bethel has acted toward you. In that city you established the idols that you, a deserter from your God, would worship.”

Following the manner of Scripture, to express the accumulation of their profanation, he repeats the same words:

“Thus Bethel did to you, because of the face of the wickedness of your iniquities.”

The “face of wickedness,” composed of manifold iniquity, wishes to show nothing other than that they received the fitting payment for their conduct—namely, captivity.

## CHAPTER 11

### Verse 1

“As morning passes, the king of Israel has passed away, because Israel was a child, and I loved him, and from Egypt I called my son.”

[Note: Others read *transiit* (“passed away”) rather than *transit* (“passes”).]

Above he had already said: “Samaria has caused its king to pass away like foam upon the face of the water.” Now, therefore, he repeats the same point by saying:

“As morning passes, the king of Israel has passed away”—that is, the kingdom of your nation. By sinning you desired it; by sinning you also destroyed it. The whole display of your arrogance withered, because the royal power that you desired in imitation of the neighboring nations provided you no defense without my help.

For this reason the prophet also warned you:

“Do not trust in princes, nor in the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation. His spirit will go forth, and he will return to his earth; on that day all his thoughts will perish” (Psalm 145).

Thus neither their insignia profited you nor your support profited them.

Everything they seemed able to do or to be was consumed so swiftly that it appeared no longer than the morning twilight, which is contracted by the departure of night and the rising of day [Ant.: *dies*, “day”], in accordance with what we read in a similar context from blessed David:

“When sinners have arisen like grass, and all who work iniquity have appeared, it is that they may perish forever and ever and beyond” (Psalm 91).

[Note: We have supplied the needed words “that they may perish.” The addition “and beyond,” so far as I know, occurs in no Hebrew, Greek, or Latin Psalter.]

Thus the rule of Israel collapsed, vengeance adhering to its crimes, so that it seemed not so much to have flourished as to have appeared briefly [Ant.: *raptum*, “snatched away”] and then vanished.

“Because Israel was a child, and I loved him, and from Egypt I called my son.”

Blessed Matthew, the evangelist, took the final part of this verse as referring to the person of our Lord Jesus Christ, commending that it was providentially fulfilled when Joseph and Mary went to Egypt to avoid the fury of Herod, who was persecuting the infancy of our Redeemer (Matthew 2:5).

For it was necessary that what the prophet had declared should be fulfilled: “From Egypt I called my son.”

The prophetic text shows that this had been spoken about the people. Apostolic authority, however, demonstrated that it could also be transferred to the person of the Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the marks of divine kindness given to the Jews were bestowed upon us more abundantly and more graciously.

The structure of the explanation reveals the force of a censor, who introduces a memory of former nobility in order to strike those whom he accuses of degeneration.

After enumerating the crimes and announcing the punishments, he suddenly introduces the memory of their former dignity, as though saying:

“Alas for the grief! Alas for the tears! What sort of people are these, who are now held in such contempt?”

Then, as though replying to an objection already raised, he exclaims:

“Because Israel was a child, and I loved him, and from Egypt I called my son.”

“This is the one,” he says, “whom I lamented because he had set the seed of impiety and reaped sorrows, and whom I declare destined to be devastated like Salmana destroyed by Gideon.”

[Note: The earlier reading *seviente impietatis* was nonsensical; we restore *sementi* (“seed”).]

“This is the one who caused his kingdom to be abolished, so that it passed as swiftly as the time of dawn.

“This is the one who, descending from the stock of the saints, had been consecrated to me from his very beginnings. Among all the nations scattered throughout the whole world, one people called Israel was chosen. Anticipating his merits with affection, I called him my child—my son, I say—and while he was still being led out of Egypt I bestowed such honor upon him that both words and events made it clear that, in my sight, the distinction between this people and the Egyptian multitude was as great as the distinction ordinarily existing between the best of sons and the worst of slaves.

“Since at that time, beyond all the miracles of deliverance and the sweetness of that freedom, he had received from me this distinction, that he should be called my son, he has now sunk so far into profanation that, having forgotten both me and himself, he obeys only the worshipers of demons.”

[Note: The verse of the sacred text should be placed before this, which he explains: “They called them; thus they departed from their presence. They sacrificed to the Baals,” and so forth.]

To prove how entirely devoid of religion and reason remained in the mind of this people, they did not devise elaborate schemes by which they might be led astray, but called them as though they were sheep prepared for destruction, and drew them wherever they wished with an obvious sign.

### Verse 2

“They sacrificed to the Baals and offered sacrifices to images.”

That is: they called themselves to the worship of various idols, to which they would serve under different rites, and they followed with such ease that they were shown to have desired an opportunity of this kind.

### Verse 3

“And I, like a nurse, carried Ephraim in my arms, but they did not know that I cared for them.”

The two intervening verses have interrupted the continuity of the simple narrative and thereby created difficulty for understanding. But when he says, “Like a nurse I carried Ephraim in my arms,” he responds to the sentence stated earlier:

“O child Israel, I loved him, and from Egypt I called my son.”

After this, inserting what crimes he had committed, he returns to the sequence in which his fickleness is recalled.
