This appears to serve the purpose of exposing the waves of indignation, so that the discourse does not proceed in a single uninterrupted flow, but even at the moment when events long past are recalled, the force of the present lament breaks forth, as though unable to endure even a brief concealment.

When he had begun to touch upon the ancient distinctions in order to burden the guilt of the degenerate people—both that he had loved them through spontaneous kindness and that he had honored them with the title of sons—he suddenly exclaimed that they had stopped up their ears against the frenzied servants of demons [the printed reading is corrupt], and that they had followed them so quickly that they created no difficulty in assenting.

If, as we have said, you set aside for a moment the impetuosity of the lament, what follows will clearly connect with what precedes:

“Because Israel was a child, I loved him, and from Egypt I called my son; and I, like a nurse, carried Ephraim in my arms, but they did not know that I cared for them.”

It is as though he were saying:

“The profanation of this people is not new, since it displayed the signs of an ungrateful mind from the very beginning. When I had called him my son, I also added tender consolations, and, like a most indulgent nurse, exercised care for my little one.

“Why should I not have done so, when I did not permit him to experience the discomforts of the vast wilderness, nor to be tormented by the labor of a strange and lengthy journey?”

[Note: Thus the printed text reads. The sense requires *obturassent* (“they had stopped up”) or something similar.]

[Note: To make the sense coherent, we have ventured to restore *delinimenta* (“tender consolations”) in place of the entirely corrupt reading *delineamenta* (“outlines” or “sketches”).]

### Verse 4

> [Note: [Col. 1017D] Here the subsequent fourth verse has been explained; it is useful to set it out here so that one may grasp the author’s meaning: “With the cords of Adam I shall draw them, with the bonds of love; and I shall be to them like one lifting the yoke upon their jaws, and I bent down to him so that he might eat.” No prior indication of this matter existed; indeed, the continuity of the sentence and period with what precedes was unbroken. [Col. 1018D]]

“Like his cord”—that is, his lot—for when Adam, the first man, had fallen from happiness, having been made a cultivator and inhabitant of paradise so that he might eat of hard-won provisions [Ant.: unworked provisions], so this man too received foods and drinks incomparable with those of human beings and comparable only with miracles. Thus I bound him with the bonds of love alone and with the reins of the commandments.

For this one purpose—that they might walk safely—I composed their mouths [Perhaps: restrained them], showing that I had bent down to their repose for this reason: that they might enjoy suitable rest and pleasure. For they did not experience a crushing power; rather, in that necessity, they had me walking with them through the desolate places, with the yoke raised—that is, removed—as we see happening with carts, in which, when the yokes are loosened, they rise up.

Yet that people, observing neither my providence nor my indulgence, by which it was both to be instructed and healed, continually displayed a spirit of resistance toward me, until by stubborn shamelessness it reached the condition in which it now stands.

### Verses 5–7

> “He shall not return to the land of Egypt, and Assyria itself shall be his king, because they refused to return. The sword began in his city, and it shall consume his chosen ones and devour their heads. And my people shall hang upon my return; but a yoke shall be imposed upon them together, which shall not be removed.”

> [Note: [Col. 1018D] Other books read “in the cities,” in agreement with the Hebrew. Shortly afterward *cupita* was read for *capita*, and in the third place after this verse *vocaverunt reos* (“they called the guilty”) was read, just as *abierunt* (“they went away”) was read for *vocaverunt eos* (“they called them”): “thus they went away,” and so forth.]

Above he had said, “They called them; thus they went away from their presence.” Now, however, he says, “They refused to return”—that is, those who had readily offered obedience to those who diverted them from piety, but who now refused to return from evil to better things and were not compelled by various afflictions to do so.

For when, having lost their possessions, they were disputing over a change of servitude, wishing to be subjected to the Egyptians rather than the Assyrians, they did not even deserve to obtain this, because the sentence that had proceeded from my mouth is immovable: namely, that for the time being they would serve no masters other than the Assyrians.

Thus vengeance will advance toward its work, so that the sword may break through the cities and steel and flame alike lay waste all the nobility, while the enemies plunder everything that is ordinarily dear to the wealthy.

Thus this people, once mine, deprived of all strength and even of every consolation, will await my return in prolonged expectation, entreating me with belated prayers and ungrateful groans to deign to become its helper.

“But a yoke shall be imposed upon them together, which shall not be removed.” Their tears will prove by events to have been ineffective, because I shall not withdraw this proclamation, which, compelled at last by their many crimes, I ordered to be put into effect. And because he had said that the decree would remain and that they would immediately undergo the yoke of Assyrian captivity, he also assumes the posture of one deliberating: he proposes what sort of vengeance will consume the guilty and sets forth examples of cities over which a fire sent down from heaven had spread destruction.

### Verses 8–9

> [Note: [Col. 1018D] The recurrence of the same words—“How shall I give you?”—deceived the copyist, whose eye, being misled, omitted the first part of the verse, “How shall I give you, Ephraim? I shall protect you, Israel.” In place of *apponam*, which follows immediately, the other books have only *ponam*.]

“How shall I give you over like Admah? Shall I make you like Zeboiim?” My heart has been changed within me; at once my compassion has been stirred. I shall not carry out the fury of my anger, and I shall not turn back to destroy Ephraim, because I am God and not man: the Holy One in your midst, and I shall not enter the city.

By recalling what once happened, he shows that the Israelites, no less than the Sodomites, could either be consumed or deserved to be consumed. Yet, mindful of the benefits that he had bestowed—even upon their unworthy descendants—for the honor of their holy ancestors, he did not wish to cut them off to such an extent that he would consume them in complete destruction.

Therefore he declares that he has been moved and shaken by something like paternal affection and has undertaken a kind of repentance, because he had threatened Israel with the destruction of the Sodomites, even under the appearance of deliberation. Immediately he adds: “I shall not carry out the fury of my anger, and I shall not turn back to destroy Ephraim.” That is, I shall not so far alter my clemency through indignation that I permit no Israelite to survive.

“For I am God and not man”—his benevolence, flowing forth in abundant streams, could not be drained dry by offense. [The intervening transmitted text is corrupt: roughly, “those about immediately to undergo, even the plan of one deliberating, offense.”]

> [Note: [Col. 1018D] We have enclosed in brackets words that disturb the sense of the sentence and seem partly to have been brought in from a marginal note, partly to result from the transposition of words that have dropped out.]

Nor could the fault of the ungrateful alter his disposition, which rejoices in the firmness once devoted to it. This too the Apostle to the Gentiles briefly indicated when he said: “For the gifts and calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29). “For I say,” he says, “has God rejected his people?”—namely, the people whom he foreknew (ibid., 1)? He will never permit it to be destroyed in the manner of the impious nations.

And now, therefore, after declaring the deserved blows against the polluted armies, he nevertheless shows that he takes account of those whom he will spare. “The Holy One in your midst,” he says, “and I shall not enter the city.”

> [Note: [Col. 1019C] The earlier editor says: “I marvel that it occurred to the holy man, who heard nothing less than a slanderer, to attribute this to Jerome, since Jerome speaks at considerable length otherwise in his interpretation of this passage than it is presented here—unless perhaps Rufinus had encountered it in another copy than those of this Commentary that have come down to us.”]

> We are more astonished at this same editor, otherwise not unlearned in his observations. First, we utterly fail to understand what he means by “the holy man”; then his assertion that Jerome transmitted something very different in his interpretation of this passage seems contrary to the truth.

> Hear briefly, then, what we think about this passage, for more will be said in the Preface. The holy Father certainly did not enumerate those who founded cities; but he does indeed mention Cain in explicit terms for this purpose, because he was the first to build a city. “We can also say otherwise,” he writes, “because Cain, the first fratricide, built a city in the name of his son Enoch. The Lord does not enter such a city, which has been constructed from crime, blood, and fratricide.”

> This clear passage escaped the editor just mentioned; it should immediately have come before his eyes had he consulted Jerome’s Commentary. Moreover, the holy Father discusses there at length the five cities—Sodom, Gomorrah, and the others—and quite neatly and learnedly adapts what Scripture records about them to his purpose.

> Such a discussion could have misled our author, who was running through the text with hurried eyes, into thinking that the subject was the founders of cities. Something similar may also have existed in Jerome’s Commentary, already at that time attached by some unknown interpolator—a license that often invaded the writings of the ancients, and especially those of Jerome.

> This is still more plausible because whoever that old patchwork compiler was could have borrowed scraps from another work of the holy Doctor, for example, the *Questions on Genesis*, chapter 10.

> But however the matter stood, what troubles me more is that our author adds that this coloring of the explanation should be received with ridicule. Whether that interpolation was genuinely part of a copy of Jerome or not, there is certainly contempt for that name and an injury that only an enemy seems capable of inflicting upon him.

> Could the author of this Commentary therefore have been Rufinus, as is commonly believed—the man who exercised the gravest hostility against him?]

When Jerome wished to explain this, he proceeded to enumerate those who were said to have founded cities. He said that Cain first acquired the stronghold of a city, and that afterward some persons notorious for their crimes were also founders of cities.

Therefore, since God was commending reverence for holiness in particular, he said that he avoided entering the city. In this manner he went on [Ant.: set forth] to assert that all holy men, and those who devoted their lives to philosophy, avoided the prominence of cities and loved the solitude of the mountains.

Yet who could consider such a coloring of the explanation without ridicule? For our God did not, by saying that he would not enter the city, pronounce that he generally detested cities. Of him we read: “The Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the dwellings of Jacob,” and, “God is in her midst; she shall not be shaken. God will help her with his countenance” (Psalm 86).

Rather, because he had introduced the memory of Sodom and the neighboring cities—which, as we read in Genesis 19, he entered in order to destroy them—and had said, “How shall I give you, Ephraim? How shall I defend you, Israel? How shall I give you over like Admah and make you like Zeboiim?” and had immediately added, “so that I shall not carry out the fury of my anger, and I shall not turn back to destroy Ephraim,” he consequently added:

“For I am God and not man: the Holy One in your midst, and I shall not enter the city.” That is: I chose you from all peoples, that I might preside over you by a special divine authority; and I decreed and promised this in honor of your ancestors, who had lived most acceptably to me. Even if you had deserved my anger by violating the sacred law, I would visit your iniquities, but I would not entirely remove my mercy, so as to allow you to be consumed in destruction and the memory of your name to be utterly erased.

And because I am God and not man, whose decree no alteration can overthrow, therefore I am indeed present in your midst, distinguished by eternal holiness. Through this I rise up as a chastiser against your sins, but I do not violate the covenants made with your fathers. Yet I shall by no means enter your cities in the manner in which I entered the gates of Sodom when it was to be destroyed.

And since he had introduced a discussion concerning prosperity, he was not content to say that the Israelites would by no means perish like the other nations. Mercifully, he also briefly recounts what else he had ordained concerning them and mentions the time when, after their captivity had been ended, they were to be brought back to their native soil.

### Verses 10–11

> “They shall follow after the Lord; he shall roar like a lion, for he himself shall roar, and the children of the sea shall be afraid. And they shall fly like a bird from Egypt and like a dove from the land of Assyria; and I shall settle them in their houses, says the Lord.”

“What wonder is it,” he says, “if our piety should then restrain the vengeance at its hottest, when even now I am shaping the joys of the liberation that is to be bestowed, and I do not wish it to remain hidden with what majesty I intend both to free them from barbarian servitude and to recall them to their native land?”

The time will come, I say, when, as I undertake the work of vengeance, the children of the sea—that is, the throng of hostile nations—will be terrified and scatter no less violently than the waters of the Red Sea were divided when Israel passed through.

> [Note: [Col. 1020C] We did not hesitate to write the same words again, in place of what had previously been read as “David.” We are not so certain of the restored true reading as we wonder that the reading we reject could have prevailed for so long.]

By the same power of command by which the waters had shortly before been suspended for the salvation of the faithful, they will flow back upon the ruler of the Egyptians.

Thus, returning like flocks of doves, the Israelites will fill their former nests—that is, their ancestral regions—with a settled habitation, both from Egypt, to which they had fled after the Babylonian triumph, and from the region of the Assyrians, to which Sennacherib had led them away.

### Verse 12

> [Col. 1020C] “Ephraim surrounded me with [Note: [Col. 1020C] There is no doubt that *negatione* (“denial”) should be read in place of *negotiatione* (“commerce”). All the books prefer this reading, and Jerome, whom our author professes to follow, clearly confirms it in these words of his Commentary: “He surrounded him with denial, or falsehood, while they deny the Lord and confess idols.” This reading is indeed as faithful as possible to the Hebrew.

> Nevertheless, we were not permitted to restore the true reading. The error does not belong to those who copied this Commentary, but to the author himself, who encountered a copy of Jerome’s version already corrupted at that time, in which *negotiatione* had been read for *negatione*.

> What we say is established most clearly both by his repetition of the word below and especially by the exposition that follows there. “That is,” he says, “just as a wicked merchant rejoiced in the fraud that the people had practiced against me”; and shortly afterward: “He wished it to be understood that Ephraim had traded to my dishonor, complaining.”

> We also learn something else from our author concerning the division of the sacred text that he proposes to explain. For, according to the Vulgate, he joins the final verse of this chapter to the first of the following one. This indicates that the edition of Jerome’s version before him once began a new chapter—namely, chapter XII—with the verse that is now last.

> This arrangement is in fact more correct, and is especially supported by the ancient division of the Hebrew archetype, where chapter XII begins with that same verse, “Ephraim surrounded me,” and what precedes consists of only eleven verses. It will therefore be preferable to refer our edition of Jerome likewise to this arrangement.]

“Ephraim surrounded me with commerce, and the house of Israel with deceit. But Judah goes down with God as a witness and is faithful with the holy ones.”

## Chapter XII

### Verse 1

“Ephraim feeds on wind and pursues the scorching heat. All day long he multiplies lies and desolation; he makes a covenant with the Assyrians, and he carries oil into Egypt.”

When, amid the thunderings of the threat required by the circumstances of that time, the joys of liberation had briefly appeared by way of digression, he returns to the action he had undertaken and pursues Ephraim’s practices, either as one grieving or as one indignant. As I have frequently noted, he carefully places beneath the punishments he has announced descriptions and measures of their crimes, so that no room for resentment against his indignation remains and it may be shown that those punishments were pronounced not through vice but through judgment.

Thus what has been inserted by way of digression will easily establish a connection between the present verse and what precedes: “A yoke shall be imposed upon them, which shall not be removed.”

Accordingly, when he says, “Ephraim surrounded me with commerce, and the house of Israel with deceit,” he means: like a wicked merchant, the people rejoiced in the fraud that it had practiced against me. It thought that, while it prayed, it was mocking me; and, because it knew that my clemency comes to the aid of the afflicted, it confessed its error only at the time of the blows. But because its heart was not upright with me and it did not faithfully promise amendment, it resembled Pharaoh, who, as soon as he had drawn breath after his calamities, returned to his crimes.

Or certainly, as the prophet reproached it earlier in the very volume of the book, because they devoted to the worship of idols the gold, silver, and other things pertaining either to sustenance or to worship that they had received from God, he now likewise wished it to be understood that Ephraim had traded to his dishonor, complaining that it had obtained from idols everything it had received from God.

But although the ten tribes had been defiled by the crimes we have described under the kings whose names appear in the title, Judah, still somewhat unlike its brother, went down with God as a witness and remained faithful with the holy ones.

That is, following the pious ruler Hezekiah, it strove to display the majesty of divine protection and the faithfulness of the promise, and placed its hope of salvation in his strength even amid the extremity of its miseries. Thus, having deserved to be liberated by a marvelous defense, it showed that its fathers had not been deceived when they worshiped this one God with their whole mind, nor could it be overwhelmed by the flood of captivity, since it enjoyed a true defense.

Thus each people reached its appropriate end: Judah, by following the true God, became a witness both of its holy fathers and of miracles; but the Samaritans, having abandoned the truth and worshiped false gods, are shown to be fed by winds and to pursue the scorching heat—that is, vanities and destruction.

Having abandoned the defense of God, which was to be obtained by merits and not purchased at a price, they bought assistance now from the Assyrians and now from the Egyptians, sending money to the Assyrians and oil—that is, gifts produced by the soil—to the Egyptians. Through one example he signified many things.

Let us hear, then, what follows.

### Verse 2

“Judgment with Judah [Al.: of the Lord], and visitation upon Jacob. According to his ways and according to his deeds he will repay him.”

> [Note: [Col. 1021D] The earlier editor would have preferred *visitationis* (“of visitation”).]

By the name Jacob he indicated the people of the ten tribes. “The diversity of their practices,” he says, “also required a diversity of punishment, so that the Lord’s judgment might stand for Judah’s salvation, while a severe visitation might strike the Samaritans.”

### Verses 3–6

“In the womb he supplanted his brother, and in his strength he was directed aright with the Angel. He prevailed [Al.: was victorious] over the Angel and was strengthened; he wept and entreated him. At Bethel he found him, and there he spoke with us.”

> [Note: [Col. 1021D] The recurrence of nearly identical words deceived the copyist, so that, through the customary lapse of scribes, he omitted the intervening verse, “And the Lord God of hosts, the Lord is his memorial.” The verse that follows in Jerome, the Vulgate translator, and the Hebrew text reads: “And you shall return to your God,” and so forth.

> Shortly afterward, in place of “guard and hope,” as we have restored it, “he will guard; hope,” and so forth, had previously been read incorrectly.]

“And you shall return to the Lord your God: keep mercy and judgment, and hope in your God always.”

He recalls, as he began above, the nobility of ancient times, so that whatever honor the chosen stock earned, and whatever virtue it displayed, might serve to expose the worthlessness of its descendants.

It is as though he were saying: See from what sort of parent they were born and to what disgrace they have come; see how far they have degenerated from the virtues of their ancestors.

Jacob was so desirous of glory that, before he came into the light from his mother’s womb, he entered into a prophetic contest with his brother (Genesis 35).

What nature itself scarcely permits us to believe, he did: he seized the heel of his brother, from whom he was to take away the birthright—not by fraud but by merit. He therefore assumed the omen of his birth together with a testimony to his dignity, showing that he possessed a God-pleasing nobility, since even before he had the power of perception he had been granted to promise the fruit of a virtue yet to come.

Then, when he had reached youthful age and had become distinguished by having received the blessing of the firstborn, he was attacked by his brother’s savage plots. Following the counsel of his holy mother, he undertook a long exile, trusting in no human resources but only in God, to whom, when he appeared to him at Bethel, he had vowed tithes.

> [Note: [Col. 1022D] We have removed the preposition *de*; then, in the following verse, in place of *decimus noverat*, which had persisted until now with serious damage to the sense, we have restored *decimas voverat* (“he had vowed tithes”). We judge that the true wording and the integrity of the passage have thereby been sufficiently secured. The earlier editor merely noted that other copies read, “trusting in no human resources but only in God,” and so forth; he did not understand that the gravest error lay precisely here.]

With God’s help he prospered and came to recognize the magnitude of his virtues and strength, which he had not previously known by experience.

For when, after a long period of time, he returned home enriched and was suddenly terrified by the approach of his brother, an Angel in human form met him. He deigned to wrestle with the fearful man, but in such a way that he did not crush him by manifest majesty; rather, as an equal with a rival—or as an inferior—he engaged him in combat.

When blessed Jacob, whose strength was fortunate and whose understanding was equally discerning, saw this, he understood that his Lord was submitting himself in great compassion for the purpose of revealing what he had ordained concerning the exaltation of his servant: namely, that he was to be exalted by the protection of the one over whom he had shown himself victorious in wrestling.

He was thereby enabled to understand that no mortal would violate him in such a way that even a superior nature could accomplish the same thing. Accordingly, when the patriarch perceived so profound a plan, he immediately assumed a spirit of humility rather than exultation and tearfully begged a blessing from the one over whom he seemed to have prevailed.

Nor was he deceived by the apparent weakness of his wrestling partner into thinking himself stronger. Just as he was courageous in enduring adversity, so he was attentive in discerning hidden things. He understood that this was the very one who deigned to clothe himself in perceptible forms, the one whom he had seen at Bethel leaning upon the horns of the ladder reaching from earth to heaven.

There, therefore, through a brief address, he deserved to learn both how great was the divinity of the one who had appeared and what duty belonged to a faithful servant, without which one cannot wholly please God: namely, that he should believe and confess the omnipotence of his Creator and trust in him with his whole mind throughout all his life.

“The Lord God of hosts, the Lord is his memorial.” That is, you must remember your God in such a way that you always confess him to be your defender and your Lord.

But this pertains to doctrine. As regards conduct, keep to the practice of justice and mercy.

> [Note: [Col. 1023D] Previously, *misericordiaeque custodis* (“and you keep mercy”) was read incorrectly. “Hope,” and so forth. The whole history of Jacob should also be compared with Jerome’s exposition.]

“Hope in your God always,” so that either you may remain continually with him in virtue, or, if your devotion should be interrupted, you may hasten back to him after undertaking amendment.

These rules of virtue, which lead by a sure course to the summit of blessedness, he both practiced successfully and left to his descendants to preserve. Hence from a humble beginning he rose to such dignity that the Promised Land was given to his descendants.

### Verses 7–8

“Canaan—there is a deceitful balance in his hand; he loved fraud. And Ephraim said, ‘Nevertheless I have become rich; I have found an idol for myself. None of my labors will find in me the iniquity that I have committed.’”

When he was recounting the noble deeds of blessed Jacob, from whom he complains that his descendants had degenerated, he suddenly introduced Canaan—not to transfer the speech to another nation, but, in the manner of the prophets, through excessive indignation to call the descendants of Israel themselves Canaan, since in their conduct they had become like him.

We find this kind of invective elsewhere as well, but especially in blessed Isaiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel, when he convicted the elders of adultery.

In keeping with this form of censure, the mention of Canaan is introduced here as well, that the sense might be as follows:

“But why do I unfold the various distinctions of their ancestral nobility, when this throng that I lament is shown to have fallen so far from it that it is not unjustly called the offspring of Canaan?”

In his hand, therefore, fraud rests upon a careful but exceedingly deceitful balance. This means that I am showing him to sin not through error but rather deliberately and by judgment.

For when the disposition of a soul is such that it commits wicked acts not impulsively or through negligence, but with deliberation, as though weights were suspended on both sides, it is said to have sinned beneath the balance.

In this sense we also read in blessed David: “Nevertheless the sons of men are liars upon the balances, so that they deceive themselves through vanity.”

Since it is the chief function of human understanding to weigh what it ought to obey and what it ought to avoid by the measure of reason and by the moments of comparison, the profaned people, suppressing the truth in falsehood, did indeed bring a balance to its affairs—but a deceitful one. It preferred worse things to better and yielded more readily to harmful than to useful things.

As for what he says, “He loved fraud,” this can also be referred to what he accused them of above: namely, that the ungrateful people had assumed such shamelessness, like an obscene woman, that it lied that everything which the one Creator of all things had bestowed upon it, whether for worship or for sustenance, had been obtained from its lovers.

For this reason the angry Lord promised that he would take away the wool and the flax that had covered its shame, so that the ugliness and nakedness following upon the crimes of the ungrateful would expose them.

This false accusation is also denounced by blessed Jeremiah. When Jerusalem had perished after calamities had been announced through many prophets, and when the whole Jewish people had been transferred to Babylon while a few were left to cultivate the fields, they publicly proclaimed such obstinacy of mind in wrongdoing that they were not afraid to say that, from the moment they had ceased to worship the queen of heaven and the other idols of the neighboring nations, all adversity had followed them.

Thus, by opinions of this sort, they brought an accusation against the true and most merciful God, falsely proclaiming that they had enjoyed happy days when they departed from him and miserable days when they returned to him.

Consequently, the deceitful balance of their minds caused them to be called descendants of Canaan more than descendants of Israel. They were not sinning, as we said, through a momentary impulse, but through tested impiety.

> [Note: [Col. 1023D] The earlier editor noted in the margin that *sed* should be read in place of *caeterum*, contrary to the author’s usual manner and style.]

And therefore, possessing no weights of true judgment, they placed their confidence in salvation and prosperity upon very brief things, which slip away like shadows.

“None of my labors,” he says, “will find in me the iniquity that I have committed.” That is, although they were oppressed by the crimes they had perpetrated, they nevertheless declared that they would be safe through their acquired wealth, saying that they had amassed so much riches that calamity could not reach them.

Thus they were mocked by the frauds of their balance: when the most high God came forth for the judgment of their deeds, they thought that their varied possessions or hoarded money would protect the guilty.

> [Note: [Col. 1023D] It was correctly observed that this is better read as “for the judgment of deeds,” in place of “for judging deeds.”]

### Verse 9

“And I, the Lord your God from the land of Egypt, shall still make you dwell in tents, as in the days of the feast.”

> [Note: [Col. 1023D] The edition of Jerome inserts here the words “who brought you out,” but since both the Vulgate translator and the Hebrew text lack them, they seem now, with the support of our author, to be properly removed.]

You will recognize the frauds of that balance—that is, of your deliberation—when the outcome of events bears witness, so that what you refused to acknowledge by reason you may confess in anguish: that I am your one and only God, who, from the time of your liberation from Egypt, deigned to take you up as a people specially belonging to me.

You will be unable to avert his punishment by any defenses or riches, so that you will not only be compelled to undergo the yoke of the servitude that has been announced, but also to remain under it for the appointed periods, after which you will finally taste the joys of liberty.

In this sense, amid the thunderings of the threat, something concerning prosperity appears to have been inserted, so that it might serve to confirm the captivity that was to precede, lest anyone doubt that the miseries would be imposed—miseries that, as he would learn, were destined to be ended when prosperity followed.

We could also offer the interpretation that accords with the customary usage of Scripture: announcements of sad or joyful things are interwoven, so that uninterrupted joys may not dissolve the mind, nor continuous grief weaken it.

But the context seems to support the former interpretation. Finally, he proceeds in a severe speech, as he had begun.

### Verse 10

“I have spoken through the prophets, and I have multiplied visions, and through the hands of the prophets I have been represented.”

> [Note: [Col. 1024D] We have restored *super* (“through” or “concerning”), in place of *per* (“through”), which alone had been present. The immediately preceding word *sum* probably misled the copyists.]

I never laid aside the concern of healing. Through my prophets, both by speaking and by acting, I persisted so that they might understand and acknowledge my providence. I cared for them with such indulgence that, when I came nearer to them, I took upon myself forms not sufficiently worthy of my majesty.

> [Note: [Col. 1024D] The earlier editor suspects that *institi* should be restored. Shortly afterward he more correctly orders *Ego idem* (“I likewise”) to be written in place of *Ergo idem* (“therefore likewise”); nevertheless, the integrity of the passage does not seem to have been sufficiently secured. The fault here belongs to the author.]

“I likewise, by works [sic], did not disdain, before the eyes of the prophets, to be made like these forms or persons”—forms or persons which befitted clemency. As I said shortly before, in order to drive fear from the heart of Israel I assumed the person of a weak wrestler; in the time of blessed Moses I chose to be transformed into the fire by which the bush was not consumed; and, as though by the blood of a lamb, I marked the doorposts of the Israelites. We read of many other things performed in this manner at different times.

Thus it was evident that our God appeared in those images which the dispensation he had undertaken required, not in those appropriate to his majesty.

But let us examine what follows.

### Verse 11

“If Gilgal is an idol, then they were uselessly sacrificing oxen at Gilgal. Their altars too are like heaps upon the furrows of a field.”

After recalling what he had mercifully done, he returns to the point from which the complaint had begun, with a sense such as this:

“See what crimes I experience from an ungrateful people after so many benefits, so many gifts, and so many miracles! It pursues open errors in contempt of me and is subjected to acknowledged madness, not deceived by any subtle argument.”

“If Gilgal is an idol, then they were uselessly sacrificing oxen at Gilgal.”

Concerning this place he also said above: “All their wickedness is at Gilgal.” He therefore introduced the statement of accusation by means of the causal conjunction “if.”

That is: since no one doubts that only images of irrational beasts had been set up in those places—and even if they had set up the animals themselves, they could not have helped those who prayed to them—now, when images more worthless than worthless things are seen there, incapable of perception and destined to provide no benefit either to themselves or to others, nevertheless they were [Al.: will be] uselessly sacrificing oxen at Gilgal.

It is as though he were saying: Could anyone have believed, before it happened, that a people once renowned for its virtues would follow such manifest folly and profanation, containing nothing more than ultimate guilt, and that after abandoning rites venerable even for their majesty it would descend to the worthless institutions of fanatics and gaze with useless reverence—that is, without any benefit, even a brief one—upon idols that would be objects of ridicule to anyone possessing moderate intelligence?

But although it would have been clearer than daylight if human beings thought that sacrifices should be offered to animals, there would nevertheless be crowds who believed that happiness could be conferred upon them by images of oxen.

> [Note: [Col. 1025D] The earlier editor orders *quis unquam existimaret* (“who would ever have thought?”) or something similar to be supplied after *frustra*. But the evident isocolon also shows that this depends upon the preceding “Could anyone have believed?”]

“For their altars too are like heaps upon the furrows of a field.”

Consequently, the very worthlessness of their observances also condemns their profane rites: without any selection of places, they build altars and worship disgraceful gods at makeshift shrines.

Thus the utterance was made, as we have explained, with something like a groan and amazement:

“If Gilgal is an idol, then they were uselessly sacrificing oxen at Gilgal; for their altars too are like heaps upon the furrows of a field.”

But let us hear what he adds.

### Verses 12–13

Jacob fled to the region of Syria, and Israel served for a wife, and for a wife he served.

[Note: [Col. 1025D] It should be read *servavit* (“he guarded”), as the other books prefer and as the Hebrew word plainly indicates. Yet *servivit* (“he served”) does not seem to have been written here in our author through a scribal error. For, having read it in this way himself, he suggests as much in his exposition of the passage below [Col. 1026D]: “There is a doubled condition of servitude and marriage.” For this is what he says: “For a wife he served,” that is, he performed pastoral service in order to obtain the marriage, as the narrative relates. But when he says, “And for a wife he served,” that is, with marriage proposed as his wage, he guarded the flock of his father-in-law. Only the final word, *custodivit* (“he guarded”), corresponds properly to the Hebrew [word] and therefore to the Latin *servavit* (“he guarded”); this leaves it uncertain to whom the blame for the corrupt reading should more truly be assigned.]

But in the prophet the Lord brought Israel out of Egypt, and in the prophet he was saved. Since he did not introduce this recollection of the ancestors in the steady sequence of historical narrative, but recalled their deeds amid an impulse of indignation and grief with which to reproach their degenerate descendants, his speech advances as though tossed about, so that reproach and praise succeed one another in turn, and the proclamation of ancient nobility adds weight to his rebuke. [Col. 1025D]

Accordingly, as he had begun, he enumerates the labors of blessed Jacob, who was also called Israel, and their results. By his name, of course, the whole nation is signified. For this reason he made particular mention of him, and—as we had begun to say—that Jacob, from whose stock they descend, obeying the counsels of his holy mother and placing all his hope and confidence for future prosperity in his God, left his native land and entered alone and as an exile into the territory of Mesopotamia, having no resource to commend him except his noble character. [Col. 1026A]

His uncle Laban immediately desired his association and, so that the labor of the noble young man might not be without payment, betrothed him to the marriage of the maiden he loved, in return for seven years of service that he would have to endure. During this period, when his faithfulness and industry had become fully evident, there arose a doubled condition of servitude and marriage. For this is what he says: “For a wife he served,” that is, he performed pastoral service in order to obtain the marriage, as the narrative relates. But when he says, “And for a wife he served,” that is, with marriage proposed as his wage, he guarded the flock of his father-in-law.

But in the prophet he was brought out, because the Lord brought Israel out of Egypt, and in the prophet he was saved. From small beginnings—so small that he supported himself by hired labor—he reached such greatness of people and wealth that all Egypt could scarcely contain him, so to speak. And just as Egypt had first envied his prosperity, so afterward it envied his deliverance [Sup. “would envy”]; Pharaoh and his forces perished, and Egypt recognized that the glory it had gained, now worn down, was not achieved by human strength, but through the merits of the fathers being made manifest and through the sacred rites being established. [Col. 1026B]

Yet he was saved not by some warlike commander, but by a prophet—namely, blessed Moses, who rescued him through those famous miracles that we read about. What complaint, then, could be sufficiently worthy of the fact that a nation distinguished by so illustrious a stock was now renowned for folly and acted solely as a byword for crimes?

### Verse 14

Ephraim provoked me to anger by his bitter deeds, and his blood will come upon him, and his Lord will repay his reproach.

The recollection of the fathers made the crime of the sons more horrifying, and this is indicated by the censor’s ensuing exclamation, in which he testifies that he had been driven to bitterness and indignation—an indignation that would proceed to a worse act of vengeance. Therefore, although he rises with the force of one pronouncing judgment, he nevertheless removes from himself the odium of the vengeance, and declares that Ephraim perished under carefully prepared punishments—Ephraim who, abandoning salutary discipline, made himself wholly the author of his own degeneration and fall. [Col. 1026C]

## Chapter 13

### Verses 1–2

When Ephraim spoke, terror seized Israel; he sinned in Baal, and he died. And now they added to sinning: they made for themselves a cast image from their silver, as though it were the likeness of idols. The whole thing is the work of craftsmen. To these they say, “Sacrifice, you who worship calves.”

He has introduced a mention of the things they had committed from the time of the division of the tribes, but in the order demanded more by indignation than by narrative. In the present passage he calls Ephraim Jeroboam, the leader of the division, who ordered the people to worship images of cows. Later, Ahab, together with Jezebel, adopted the worship of the idol Baal; that profanation, we read, Jehu punished with appropriate severity.

Thus this consecration of idols began among the people at the beginning and ceased at the end. But although this is the historical order that we have described, the invective has now altered part of it. For when Ephraim spoke—that is, when Jeroboam summoned the people to the worship of demons—terror seized Israel. [Col. 1026D] It immediately assumed, of course, the fear of superstition and dreaded him as a true deity; or certainly it accepted the effect of worshiping him, by which it would deserve to be dreaded by the eternal Judge.

Nor was it content to have committed this offense. It subjected its neck to other sacrileges as well, embraced the institutions of Baal, and also experienced the disasters that followed. Yet it took up no effort of correction, even from the ruins of those who had fallen through various incursions of the enemy, or when, under Jehu’s vengeance, the idol itself and its worshipers were destroyed. Nevertheless, he says, no impulse toward correction could be aroused in them. [Col. 1027A]

“But now,” he says, “they added to sinning; they made for themselves a cast image from their silver, as though it were the likeness of idols.” This does not mean that they began to worship images of calves after the time of Ahab, but that they are said to have added those practices which they had not abandoned even after their chastisement. For the profanation itself could not have continued unless it had been increased by rebellious zeal.

“The whole thing,” he says, “is the work of craftsmen. To these they say, ‘Sacrifice, you who worship calves.’” He has not repeated this without reason, although it has already been discussed throughout the book, but in order to produce a meaning such as this:

[Note: [Col. 1027D] The old editor advises that *levitati* (“to lightness”) should be read, which is somewhat better, and directs that it be joined to the following verb *conciliet* (“may reconcile”), with *gratiam*, *reverentiam* (“favor,” “reverence”), or something similar supplied.]

Although novelty, if it is heedless, may reconcile people to things that are trivial, with time examining them they certainly grow cheap; and continuous veneration is not offered except to things that possess recognized distinctions. [Col. 1027B]

Here, however, since the worthlessness and vanity of the work had been exposed both by reason and by long experience—that is, since the gods of the nations possess, I will not say no power, but no form at all, unless the hand skilled in fashioning had bestowed one upon them—

[Note: [Col. 1027D] The same editor likewise advises that *quam* (“which”) be written instead.]

nevertheless the profane people willingly listen to the voices of soothsayers, who plainly command human beings to bow down in supplication to calves devoid of reason and sensation, serving them with offerings of prayers and sacrifices.

### Verse 3

Therefore they will be like morning clouds, and like the morning dew that passes away, like dust swept away by a whirlwind, and like smoke from a chimney.

[Note: [Col. 1027D] Jerome’s version and the Vulgate have a different and fuller reading: “like dust swept away by a whirlwind from the threshing floor”; the Hebrew text itself agrees with them. [Col. 1028D]]

Above he had said that their blood would be upon their own head and that their reproach would be repaid to them. Now he repeated the same thing, or heaped it up by way of a curse: because they had subjected themselves to the utmost folly, transferring the honor of God to images of animals, they themselves would likewise perish in such a contemptible way that they would be consumed like smoke, like dust, like dew, like morning mist under the sun’s rays.

### Verse 4

But I am the Lord your God; I brought you out from the land of Egypt. You shall know no God besides me, and there is no savior apart from me.

[Note: [Col. 1028D] The words “I brought you out” are found neither in the Hebrew exemplar nor in the Vulgate translator, nor finally in several Hieronymian manuscript books.]

These verses are connected with what precedes, so that their meaning is as follows: When I was shaking the yoke of Egyptian domination from your necks, and, while you were enslaved, making my majesty known through those famous miracles, I also established this with an unambiguous declaration: that a nation always devoted to my worship should never submit to anyone else as to a god, since it would not find another who could grant it salvation, because at that time you seemed to have been bound to the elements that served you. [Col. 1027C]

### Verse 5

I knew you in the wilderness, in the land of desolation.

“But why now,” he says, “should I be stirred by your sacrileges as though they were something new, when even at that very time of your deliverance I always experienced you as you are now revealed—that is, ungrateful and insulting?”

By adding “in the land of desolation,” he clearly wished it to be understood that their example did not always corrupt them, since they sinned even in those places where they had no one whom they could imitate.

[Col. 1027D] ### Verse 6

According to their pastures they were filled; they were filled and became sated; they lifted up their hearts and forgot me.

“With my benefits,” he says, “the whole nation contended not through devotion but through wickedness.” To make this readily clear, he connects these events with those times as well and, in the course of his invective, returns to the present age from which he had begun. Yet in a brief passage he also introduces the statement that had been uttered in the Song of Deuteronomy by blessed Moses: “The beloved grew fat, became sleek, and kicked; he made for himself new gods, like barley bread, which their fathers did not know” (Deut. 22). [Col. 1028A]

“For according to their pastures they were filled,” he says, “and they were filled and became sated; they lifted up their hearts and forgot me.” He placed this sequence of sins first so that the vengeance he was about to inflict might be shown to be not aroused by passion, but fortified by justice and reason. For what follows is:

### Verses 7–8

And I will be to them like a lioness, like a leopard on the way to Assyria. I will meet them like a bear deprived of her cubs; I will tear open the inward parts of their liver, and I will consume them there like a lion. The beast of the field will tear them apart.

He teaches that the calamities the barbarity of the enemies was about to inflict were both commanded and brought about by him. Nor does he disdain to express his warning through images of wild beasts, which he knows to be fitting—though not according to their own nature or intention—for the misery of the condemned.

Elegantly, after placing the bear among the lions’ gaping jaws, he sharpens its ferocity with the goad of bereavement, lest the comparison introduced should lose force: “Like a bear,” he says, “deprived of her cubs.” “And I will tear open the inward parts of their liver”—of those, namely, who inflicted similar losses upon me. [Col. 1028B]

For while I was shaping this people for myself as sons with great diligence, and forming their hearts as though by licking them, they deprived me not only of the offspring I desired but also of offspring gained through labor, by committing crimes that would demand the destruction of the whole nation.

### Verses 9–11

Your destruction, Israel; only in me is your help. Where is your king? Let him save you now, in all your cities; and your judges, of whom you said, “Give me a king and princes.” I will give you a king in my anger, and I will take him away in my indignation.

This is a sentence well suited to the question, one that can be resolved only by the rule of piety. For it is spoken in the person of God: “Your destruction, Israel; only in me is your help.” Yet the sure defense of the faithful exists when confidence in deliverance is placed in God. This is what the blessed prophet accuses throughout the book in the people’s profaned ways: they trusted not in God but in the protection of their favorites.

How, then, now, as though the order had been reversed, does he announce to Israel that destruction plainly threatens it because its salvation rests in the power of God alone? [Col. 1028C]

That distinction must therefore be observed which clarifies what seemed ambiguous. He is not mocking the faith of the people, who were placing the hope of their joy in the power of God alone—which, since they had offended him, why would they not have done?—

[Note: [Col. 1028D] The old editor thinks that the reading should better be *cum non fecisset* (“since he had not done so”).]

but he merely declared that such a quantity of blows was about to fall upon them that no one could bring help except divine power alone.

“Therefore,” he says, “destruction is imminent for you, Israel; only in me is your help.” If you consider this carefully, you will see that it has been introduced not only without absurdity but also morally and in accordance with ordinary human speech. For this is why, whenever we see someone overcome by a serious illness or by a desperate calamity, we say that his hope is in God: we are not necessarily indicating the duty of his mind, but the weight of the disaster that is oppressing him.

“Undeniable destruction,” he says, “will therefore seize you—a destruction from which no one except the Almighty can rescue you. Since you have made him hostile to you by your crimes, it remains that you be snatched from the destruction that hangs over you.” [Col. 1028D]

To make this meaning clear, he added:

“Where is your king? Let him save you now in all your cities, and your judges, of whom you said, ‘Give me a king and princes.’” [Col. 1029A]

Following prophetic custom, he also reproaches the people for that error which they committed when, withdrawing from priestly government, they desired a king. Since they had acquired this desire through rivalry with neighboring nations, their earlier counsels are now condemned when matters have gone badly, as though he were saying:

“You have long been afflicted by this madness: you think that you can provide for yourself better than I can. From the beginning of this opinion you asked that princes be given to you in imitation of the other nations. Let the fruit of your self-government now appear, and let the ability of kings protect you against my indignation. These powers, sought out in your ambition, ought surely to teach you what benefit they provide.”

But let us proceed to what follows:

“I will give you a king in my anger, and I will take him away in my indignation.”

Some understood the king given in anger to be Jeroboam, who was responsible for dividing the tribes, and the one taken away in indignation to be Hosea, under whom Israel was captured.

[Note: [Col. 1029D] Jerome bears witness to the same interpretation: “Others,” he says, “think that the king given in anger was Jeroboam son of Nebat, and that the king taken away in indignation was Hosea, the last king of the ten tribes.” Then, concerning the interpretation preferred by our author, namely that the sentence should be understood as referring to the future—“I will give you a king and take away a king”—the same holy Father notes that it is derived from Jewish interpretations. “What we have explained,” he says, “as ‘I gave you a king and took away a king in my indignation,’ the Jews refer to the future tense,” and so forth.]

Although this interpretation can be accepted, since the sentence is pronounced in the future tense it indicates both things. That is, “I will give you a king, and I will take him away,” may be understood more suitably and concisely in this way: the Israelite ruler is announced as one who will be taken away, while the Assyrian is announced as one who will be given.

Finally, following prophetic custom, after the burden of condemnation he added its cause:

### Verse 12

The iniquity of Ephraim is bound up; his sin is stored away.

That is, the crimes he committed over many years, without being interrupted by any virtues but heaped up in a funeral-like accumulation, stood preserved in the Judge’s memory as though kept under a seal.

By their recompense—

[Note: [Col. 1029D] The old editor would prefer *cumulatione* (“by their accumulation”); I would write *rememoratione* (“by their recollection”), which adheres more closely to the printed reading.]

it was brought to completion that, deprived of the marks of freedom, they should be subjected to the most savage slavery and should feel those pains and anxieties that women ordinarily experience in childbirth.

[Note: This refers to the following part of the verse: “The pains of a woman in labor will come upon him.” [Col. 1030D]]

### Verse 13

He is an unwise son; for now he will not stand at the breaking forth of sons.

Above, too, he argued in the same colors that Israel’s revealed folly was indicated by the testimony of its adversities, and that the deformity of its merits, which had been hidden for some time under prosperity, was finally exposed when hardships bore witness against it.

Therefore, it is proved by grave testimony that you are a son and not wise, because at the time when the enemy invaded you did not deserve to stand.

[Note: [Col. 1030D] In place of *sapientia* (“wisdom”), which had previously been read, we have restored *sapientem* (“wise”), as the old editor also preferred. He likewise preferred *grandi* (“great”) to *gravi* (“grave”).]

And since by the name of folly he was designating profanation—which, as he charged from the beginning of the book, the ten tribes had devoted themselves to with all their zeal—and since the storm of captivity seized them on account of that folly, he appropriately turns to Judah. He reveals Judah not only by name but also by the judgment of its deeds, so that he might show at once what outcome awaited wise sons and expose the one who had remained foolish.

The prophetic speech therefore moves toward the more favorable events that were accomplished under King Hezekiah through great miracles, and says:

### Verses 14–15

I will deliver them from the hand of death; I will redeem them from death. I will be your death, O death; I will be your sting, O hell. Consolation is hidden from my eyes, because he himself divides among the brothers. The Lord will bring a burning wind from the desert, rising up; he will dry up its channels and desolate its spring, and he himself will plunder the treasure of every desirable vessel.

First, as usual, he announces the joys of deliverance by promising prosperity; afterward, through that same delight, he heaps up acts of vengeance.

“Therefore, I will deliver them from the hand of death”—that is, when they have come into such extreme difficulty that death seems to have laid its hand upon them, seized them, and held them, then I, the deliverer, will come.

This was expressed especially by the prayer of blessed Hezekiah, who said that the day of affliction and reproach had come, since the children had come as far as birth but there was no strength to give birth.

When, therefore, they were being pressed by Assyrian forces and the enemy had shut up the city under siege, destruction threatened so closely that it seemed ready at any moment to devour the wretched people. But because they obtained divine assistance through righteous prayers, God performed that great miracle: when one hundred and eighty-five thousand Assyrians had been destroyed by the stroke of an angel, deliverance shone forth as a desired gift to the devout, in accordance with what the sacred songs had proclaimed:

“This poor man cried, and the Lord heard him, and delivered him from all his tribulations. The Lord will send his angels around those who fear him, and he will deliver them” (Ps. 33).

Thus “death” and “hell” designate the Assyrian king and his entire army, which the divine sentence promises to destroy. After first announcing the crash of vengeance, he adds, in his customary manner, the cause that provoked that indignation:

“Consolation,” he says, “is hidden from my eyes, because he himself divides among the brothers.”

He assumed the attitude and words of one who mourns, in order to increase the Assyrians’ crime. Speaking as though in the person of Judah, concerned more for its brother—that is, the Israelites whom Sennacherib had led into captivity—than for its own calamity, he says that his eyes had become so wet with tears that they could not receive consolation, because the proud and savage king had brought about a grievous separation among the brothers by transferring the ten tribes into captivity to the region of Media. [Col. 1030B]

Here an attentive reader may properly ask why this feeling, which mourns the secession of its brother, is attributed to the tribe of Judah, when above the prophet, speaking of the same matter, reproached it for rejoicing. For after he had said, “Ephraim was in desolation,” he added:

“On the day of desolation I showed faithfulness among the tribes of Israel. The princes of Judah became like those who move a boundary; upon them I will pour out my anger like water.” [Col. 1030C]

Since there they are said to have rejoiced at the expulsion of their kinsmen because they thought that the boundaries of their own fields had been enlarged, how are they now represented as mourning the expulsion of their brother without any consolation?

This can be resolved by a twofold interpretation. Since, as I said, the speech is often not about individual persons but about entire groups, we understand that different dispositions existed within that multitude. Thus one statement is brought forward from the persons of the devout and another from those of the impious.

We therefore conclude that some were present there whose brothers’ expulsion caused them grief, while more were pleased by the extension of their boundaries.

But let us now examine the other manner of explanation, which will be so applicable to the judgment that it seems to fit causes more than persons. Let this be the voice of kinship, which the prophet placed near the end of the book: namely, that he grieves the calamity of his expelled brother and invokes upon the enemies the retaliation they deserve. But let what gave pleasure to some be directed toward the crime of parricides, so that the meaning may be as follows: there were some in whom profanation disturbed not only the laws but also the rights of nature, so that, when their brothers were taken captive, they preferred to glory rather than to show the compassion they owed.

[Note: [Col. 1030D] The old editor would prefer *parricidae* (“parricides”), and shortly afterward *aspicere* (“to regard”). But where *profanitas* is read a little later, he wrongly thinks that *profanas* (“you profane”) should be restored.]

“The Lord will bring a burning wind from the desert, rising up; he will dry up its channels and desolate its springs, and he himself will plunder the treasures of every desirable vessel.”

[Note: [Col. 1030D] Some copies have *thesaurum* (“the treasure”) rather than *thesauros* (“the treasures”).]

He calls the burning wind from the desert an angel, who destroyed the Assyrian army in a single night. This does not mean that angels are believed to live in the desert—for the Gospel’s authority commends that they daily see the face of the Father (Matt. 18)—but because of the speed of the vengeance, since one hundred and eighty-five thousand are reported to have been slain in a single night, he assumed the likeness of fire. He introduced the desert in order that the entire army might seem to have been consumed by a breath rather than by any physical operation. [Col. 1031A]

Thus blessed David had also said:

“He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a burning fire” (Ps. 103).

He therefore signified that this burning would be summoned from places made uninhabitable by the heat of the sun, and that it would destroy the Assyrians’ springs and channels—that is, the king together with his army and offspring.

“And he himself will plunder the treasure,” and so forth. If you consider the custom of the prophets, who do not observe changes of tense with excessive anxiety and precision, he seems to have indicated the wealth that King Sennacherib had amassed from his triumphs. He was consumed by the aforesaid burning because he had acted cruelly in many things, and because his greed had not been satisfied even by what he had seized. Now, therefore, he is compelled to vomit up whatever he had previously swallowed through iniquity.

## Chapter 14

[Col. 1031B]

### Verse 1

Let Samaria perish, because it stirred up its Lord [Al. “God”] to bitterness, and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 1031D] That is, “May they perish by the sword; may their little ones be dashed to pieces, and may their pregnant women be ripped open.”]

A little earlier he had said: “Consolation is hidden from my eyes, because he himself divides among the brothers,” and he had shown the attitude by which he took pity on Israel. Now, however, after describing the destruction of the Assyrians, he burns again against Samaria.

He did this not because of a change of mind but because of the gravity of his sentence. For after he had displayed both the mercy and the power of the true God, who had destroyed the proud king as though with no effort, and had shown that he was prepared to defend the devout in such a way that he would inflict vengeance upon mighty nations for their sake, he rightly wished Samaria to perish, as though inflamed against it. By its crimes it had brought about the situation in which this supremely good Lord became not its defender but its destroyer. It was as though he were saying:

“When I behold the benefits of our eternal ruler, I shudder more and more at Israel’s crime, since they have labored to be deprived of such a protector.” [Col. 1031C]

### Verse 2

Return, Israel, to the Lord your God, because you have fallen through your iniquity.

The speech advances with remarkable coherence. He had exclaimed something that could serve to aggravate Samaria’s sin, but because he had done this more out of compassion than execration, he now brings forward at least a second remedy to heal the wound. Since they had been unwilling to embrace the safeguards of continuous devotion, they should take up the aids of repentance and amendment.

“If dangers make you better, O Israel, return to the Lord your God, from whom you should never have turned away. Abhorring the very fact that you fell through your iniquity, accept the gifts of confession.” [Col. 1031D]

For this is what he says:

### Verse 3

Take words with you, return to the Lord, and say to him: Take away all iniquity and receive what is good.

For you alone can remove the guilt under which we are burdened.

What the good thing was that they begged him to receive, the following verse shows:

“And we will repay the calves of our lips.”

For the sacred songs have also taught us to offer God a sacrifice of praise (Ps. 50), since praise offered from a pure heart is pleasing to him, in place of a young bull producing hooves and horns.

Therefore, Israel, declare your injustices against yourself to the Lord, since you desire to merit their remission. But let us hear what he adds to these words.

### Verse 4

Assyria will not save us; we will not mount a horse; nor will we say any longer, “Our gods,” to the works of our hands, because you will have mercy on the people who remain in you [the printed reading is *populi*, “of the people,” though the note reports *pupilli*, “of the orphan,” in the other witnesses].

[Note: [Col. 1031D] *Pupilli* (“of the orphan”) should be read, as both all the other books and the Hebrew text itself indicate. Yet the fact that our author read *populi* (“of the people”) is demonstrated by his exposition of this passage near the end, where he says, “because you, as a good judge, do not cease to have mercy on the people who remain in your worship.” It was therefore not permissible for us to alter the word, since it had plainly been corrupted through its resemblance to another word.]

What he says—“Assyria will not save us”—seems to have been taken from Judah’s example. For the history of Kings relates (4 Kings 18) that when the Assyrian commander sent by King Sennacherib under the name of Rabshakeh arrived to address and terrify those who were shut up in Jerusalem, he declared among the other things he boastfully and arrogantly said about the Assyrians that Sennacherib was prepared to provide two thousand horses, for which the entire army of Judah could not furnish riders. He asked with what madness they were provoking against themselves the forces of so great a prince. If they wished to provide for their safety, they should surrender to his authority, since he showed himself no less generous to his subjects than severe toward the rebellious. [Col. 1032B]

But the inhabitants of Jerusalem, placing their confidence for deliverance in the power of God alone, silently rejected the enemy’s threats and boasts.

The present speech therefore instructs Israel to imitate Judah’s confidence, so that Israel, corrected by its long servitude, might now begin to imitate the devotion that its brother had shown during the Assyrian siege.

[Note: [Col. 1031D] It seemed better to read *monentis* (“of one admonishing”) rather than the previously printed *momentis*.]

“And we will not say any longer,” he says, “Our gods, the works of our hands.” That is, we will cease to worship images made by craftsmen’s hands, after learning, with our brother as witness, that you, as a good judge, do not cease to have mercy on the people who remain in your worship. [Col. 1032A]

But receive what our God gives in response to this offering of your confession.

### Verses 5–8

I will heal their wounds; I will love them freely, because my anger has turned away from them. I will be like dew to Israel; he will blossom like a lily, and his root will spring forth like Lebanon. Those sitting in his shade will return; they will live on grain, and they will blossom like a vine; his memory will be like the wine of Lebanon.

[Note: [Col. 1031D] Here *Israeli* (“to Israel”) is rightly read in the third case and joined to the preceding parallel clause: “I will be like dew to Israel; he will blossom,” contrary to the Vulgate and to our own Hieronymian edition, which read, “I will be like dew; Israel will blossom,” and so forth. [Col. 1032D] The sequence of the Hebrew text and the word’s prefixed article establish this as the truest reading, and I would wish the Hieronymian text itself to be corrected and restored accordingly.]

By various comparisons he describes the sweetness of deliverance, the marks of freedom, and the pleasantness of cultivated fields—fields that, just as they are covered in great squalor when the enemy rages, so, when the security of peace calls forth the industry of the cultivators, display abundance and beauty everywhere.

Thus, Israel, when the prosperity that has been promised drives away your captivity, the beauty of freedom and the sweetness of joy will so fill and clothe you that meadows dripping not with worthless shoots but with lilies and roses will be seen. My mercy and my grace will descend upon you like dew, so that, after every foulness has been cast aside,

[Note: [Col. 1032D] *Innovationis* (“of renewal”) would certainly be preferable. Perhaps a little later one should more correctly read *praecedit in fratre* (“it precedes in the brother”) rather than *procedit* (“it proceeds”), and so forth.]

you may receive the adornments of invocation.

Do not doubt that this can happen to you on account of its greatness: it already precedes in your brother—that is, in Judah, which is to be delivered from the hands of the Assyrians. [Col. 1032D]

What glory, then, will the longed-for though scarcely hoped-for freedom bestow upon him? Such glory will also remain for you, provided that you prove worthy of receiving it. [Col. 1033A]

[Note: [Col. 1032D] The old editor would have preferred *contulit* (“he bestowed”), and this is more accurate because, as we were just saying, *praecedit* (“it precedes”) was the proper reading. But it seemed sufficient to safeguard the correct meaning by rewriting it as *conferet* (“he will bestow”), where previously the corrupt reading was *conferret* (“he would bestow”). Moreover, another and much graver error has been removed in the following verse, where we have written *te manebit* (“it will remain for you”) instead of the previous single word *remanebit*, which made scarcely any sense.]

You will live on grain, and you will blossom like a vine that, transplanted from Egypt, had occupied Palestine over broad territories. Your memory will be like the wine of Lebanon—that is, your glory will possess as much brilliance as the wine of the highest quality produced on Mount Lebanon.

### Verse 9

Ephraim, what have I any longer to do with idols? I will hear him and guide him like a green fir tree; from me your fruit has been found.

“Since these things are so,” he says, “as our discussion has fully taught”—that is, since this is the one way of salvation that the worship and religion of our deity have revealed—“at least set a limit to your profanation, whose beginning you should never have experienced. Cling with complete faith and devotion to the one Lord who is true, and do not think that his truth can be held together with falsehood, by assigning the incommunicable name to idols.

“But know what you have learned not only from precepts but from the very voice of events: I alone am he whose worshipers enjoy eternal happiness, while those who abandon him are overwhelmed by eternal miseries.

“For I am the one who hears those who plead, who can and is accustomed to heal the broken, straighten the crooked, make the barren fruitful, find the lost, raise the dead, and raise those whom I have made vigorous to such an exalted height that they seem to have advanced from palms or thorn bushes into firs and cypresses.”

475 **Verse 10.**—Who is wise, and understands these things? Who is discerning and will know them? For the ways of the Lord are upright, and the just will walk in them; but transgressors will stumble in them.

[Note: [Col. 1033B] Earlier it read, “the wise understands,” although that reading is rejected by the other books and by our Author himself at the end, where he repeats this verse.]

He rightly concluded his book with an expression of wonder, whose usefulness he had demonstrated both through precepts and through examples. At the same time, to teach that the whole cause of sins and miseries arose from folly, he praised the wise person who, weighing everything that had been discussed, would recognize the benefit of the sacred ways and their end: namely, that through them the just would walk with steadfastness, while transgressors would fall, by committing sacrileges and enduring ruin.

It should certainly be noted that even these passages—which, according to the history previously set forth by the prophet, I have interpreted as our understanding permitted—can also serve to signify greater realities. For what was said concerning Sennacherib, “I shall be your death, O Death; I shall be your sting, O Hell,” can also be understood of a more extensive matter, in the sense indicated by the Teacher of the Gentiles. For when he was speaking to the Corinthians about the manifestation of the resurrection, he said: “Where, O Death, is your sting? Where, O Death, is your victory? But thanks be to God, who has given us the victory through Jesus Christ our Lord” (1 Cor. 15).

For he is said to have risen from the desert like a burning wind—since he came to cast fire upon the earth (Luke 12)—because he sprang from the Virgin’s womb, to whom, according to the laws of nature, a man, as a cultivator, had ceased to approach.

[Note: Either this word had been erased and should be understood in the sense of negation, so that the meaning is “had failed,” followed continuously by “failed”; or “no one had approached” should be read. The former sense is more natural and more consonant with the Author’s intention; the latter is expressed in somewhat clearer words. The context of the sentence and the sequence of the proposed mystical interpretation altogether require one or the other.]

He caused the veins and fountain of death to dry up, so that it would have no right to reclaim a second time those whom the Redeemer had once raised to eternal joys. Through the mystery of his Incarnation, the dew of grace descended upon the fields of the Churches,

[Col. 1034B]

so that vines fruitful in various virtues and lilies might spring up everywhere, and the happiness of the faithful’s multiplication might become as great as that of a field rejoicing in its abundance of crops, fruits, and flowers. Thus “those sitting in his shadow” would be converted: that is, various nations would desire to rest under the protection of the Church, so that they might obtain nourishment for bodily and spiritual strength in wine and wheat.

Therefore, the deliverance accomplished under Hezekiah should be explained more fully and more gratefully in relation to the liberty that Christ bestowed. “Who is wise, and will understand these things?”

[Note: Previously it read, “understands.”]

“Who is discerning, and will know them?” For the Lord has been appointed for the fall and resurrection of many; and no one may walk confidently along his paths—on which the followers of crimes collapse—unless he confesses with his whole heart that Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God, and strives through vows and efforts to become one spirit with him.

[Col. 1033B]

# COMMENTARY ON THE PROPHET JOEL

[Note: The old title was: “Of Rufinus, Presbyter of Aquileia, on Joel,” etc. The author is certainly the same one who composed the preceding Commentaries on Hosea, and he reveals this himself in the course of the present work.]

(C, G)*

[Col. 1033]

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 1033B] 477 When I approached these prophetic writings—whether obscure, or, if I may put it more appropriately, wooded thickets—venturing indeed boldly, but bound by the supports of religious devotion rather than of rashness, as an investigator: if I were permitted to enjoy meanings that were clear not by some common light, but by a secret and reverend splendor, I would have chosen which edition to take up (for there are several). I observed, naturally, the last one, which is called “according to the Hebrew,” because in it there was greater integrity of expression, whether expressing the feeling of the teacher or that of one issuing threats.

[Note: The text had previously been read in the opposite sense as “up to this point,” or as *aut*, in place of the negating particle *haud*, which we have substituted. Shortly afterward, *assumerem* had also been written corruptly in place of *assumere*. I pass over errors of punctuation, which nearly destroyed the meaning. In addition, this passage should be compared with the one the Author has at the beginning of his Commentaries on Hosea, concerning the same translation from the Hebrew, which he calls “Hieronymian” after its name.]

By the judgment—or perhaps, *indication*—of that Translation, therefore, we discovered that the order of the Twelve Prophets among the Hebrews is different from that contained in the more widespread edition.

[Note: From Jerome, who says in the Preface to his Commentary on this same prophet: “The order of the Twelve Prophets among the Seventy interpreters is not the same as that which is preserved in the Hebrew text. For they …”—and so forth, which should be referred here word for word. At the beginning of the Commentary he also says: “Just as in the prophet Hosea the prophecy under the name of Ephraim is applied to the Ten Tribes … so in Joel, who according to the Hebrews is second, everything that is said must be understood as pertaining to the tribe of Judah and to Jerusalem … We must also accept the same periods in which he prophesied as those which we read in Hosea,” etc.]

Although the titles indicating dates are not prefixed in all the prophets, it by no means becomes uncertain in what periods each of them prophesied. For tradition handed down maintains that those prophets read without titles flourished under the same kings under whom the prophets furnished with titles had prophesied before them.

Thus let it be considered whether blessed Joel is proved to have been contemporary with holy Hosea, whom we read before him: enduring the cruelty and insults of the same kings, accusing the same sacrileges of the frenzied people, and announcing the same punishments impending over the guilty.

## CHAPTER ONE

He begins with a mood more of wonder and, as it were, compassion:

**Verse 1.**—“The word of the Lord that came to Joel, son of Pethuel.”
