“The eternal Teacher,” he says, “assigned this charge of instruction—or rather of judgment—to his servant.” For by the name “word” he indicated at once the whole teaching that he was about to see.

Nor is the prophet’s father mentioned without reason. Whenever not only the virtues but also the ancestors of holy people are named, an equality of dignity is thereby established between them and their parents; and so their parents too are judged to have been righteous, prophets, or priests. Thus the praise of the root in the offspring is taught to be both honorable and weighty.

But as for the fact that certain commentators pursued even the etymologies of the names,

[Col. 1035C]

gathering from them, as it were, seeds of praise—namely, that Joel

[Note: There is something here that does not itself identify Jerome by name, although he certainly had him in mind, whether singling him out above all others or alone. Jerome’s are those etymologies of the names Pethuel and Joel, from which he derives highly learned and especially allegorical meanings for his own purpose. “Pethuel,” he says, “is translated in our language as ‘the breadth of God,’ or ‘God opening,’ as we read in Mark when the Savior says to the deaf and mute man, *Ephphatha*, etc.” He then skillfully applies this from three other testimonies of Scripture. Next: “From breadth and opening he is begotten and is called Joel, which in our language sounds as ‘beginning,’ or ‘God exists,’ as the Apostle says, ‘Brothers, I do not consider that I have apprehended,’” and so forth, gathering material from Exodus, Esther, John, and the Psalms and adapting it to his purpose. When our Author dares to call these things childish and foolish, and says that they involve more trouble than benefit, he shows himself to be a fastidious man and alien to the genius of the one whose name he falsely bears—namely, Rufinus, the rival of Jerome—who diligently pursues such etymologies in his Commentaries, as can be seen in the *Blessings of the Patriarchs*. He had long since become accustomed to them through the teaching of his master Origen.]

[Note: It had to be guessed what was meant by the monstrosity of a word formerly printed there. For in place of the Greek ἀρχόμενος, which we have restored, there had been written in these letters, “apoKe. Hoc.” The old scribe evidently intended to copy Greek characters, as the strokes themselves suggest; but in copying an unknown word it is usual to go astray, and a certain resemblance to Latin letters easily deceived him. The first editor, too, not understanding what it meant, seems to have corrupted the word still further by inserting a stop. In the exemplar he used, it had perhaps been written in larger letters, ME, which he took for Ke, and NOC, which he took for Hoc. Whatever the case, the old error itself points to the reading ἀρχόμενος that we have restored; the interpretation of the word, “beginning,” which is the etymology of Joel’s name, proves it, and Jerome confirms it in the Preface to Joel: “ἀρχόμενος, that is, beginning.” See also the Book of Names, translated into Latin from the Greek in volume III of the same holy Doctor’s works.]

which we can translate as *archomenos* (ἀρχόμενος), “beginning”; and Pethuel, “the breadth of God”; and the rest in this manner: although these interpretations are childish and foolish, they seem to involve more trouble than benefit.

**Verse 2.**—“Hear this, elders, and give ear, all inhabitants of the land. Has anything like this happened in your days, or in the days of your fathers?”

He enters in the manner of a preacher, about to narrate the magnitude of the calamity that had befallen the Israelites. “Behold,” he says, “I anticipate the sound of your weeping; and what would have stirred your resentment in complaint, I announce first. You have not merely been subjected to one or another succession of blows, driving away calamities raised like foaming waves, with new miseries always preceding them.”

“Therefore, all inhabitants, now assemble to hear: whether you are those who through the old age of life have accumulated the greatest dangers, or those who, although you have fewer years, can nevertheless retain in vigorous memory whether you have received from your fathers anything similar to what has converged upon the present age. Indeed, what am I saying? Let us consult only the annals, as though seeking consolations from examples, when I consider that the miseries of our nation have risen to such a heap that nothing similar could exist even among those who come after us.”

Thus the elders and the inhabitants of the land, who are commanded either to give ear or to hear, do not designate different classes or different dispositions; the command is simply that they should hear. It is like what we read in the Psalm: “Hear this, all nations; give ear, all who inhabit the world, both earthborn and children of men, together, rich and poor alike” (Ps. 48). By several expressions he plainly designated nothing other than human beings whom he summons to judgment.

I have briefly noted this because some have believed that there is a great difference among these words, and thereby have spent a great deal of useless verbiage.

[Note: Here again he attacks the great Jerome without naming him, and calls useless the words in which Jerome presents and most brilliantly explains mysteries worthy of the closest attention in this verse. In defense of the holy Doctor, it is enough to refer the reader to his highly learned exposition of the passage; after reading it, one may judge whether he will regard such matters as worthless and insignificant.]

But let us hear what the prophet conveys with so great a display of wonder.

**Verse 4.**—“What the caterpillar left, the locust ate; what the locust left, the bruchus ate; and what the bruchus left, the rust consumed.”

[Note: Previously it was read incorrectly as *Diversitas* (“difference”).]

He comprehends various kinds of calamities which he laments as having been inflicted upon the Jewish people. When each of them occurs, it consumes the year’s fruit and hope so completely that it breaks the hearts of farmers with anguish and fear alike.

We gather that these misfortunes had happened to them not once but repeatedly, either from the prophet whom we are discussing or from Deuteronomy, which announces them. Hence we reject the opinion of those who think that all these things were spoken about enemies.

[Note: Here for the third time our Author censures Jerome’s interpretation. But the holy Father is speaking there from the traditions of the Hebrews and from the testimony of those who knew the antiquity and affairs of their people best. “The Hebrews,” he says, “interpret the caterpillars as the Assyrians, Babylonians, and Chaldeans, who, proceeding from one region of the world, laid waste everything belonging both to the Ten Tribes and to the Two—that is, to the Israelite people. They interpret the locusts as the Medes and Persians, who, after overthrowing the empire of the Chaldeans, held the Jews captive. The bruchus they interpret as the Macedonians and all Alexander’s successors, especially King Antiochus, surnamed Epiphanes, who sat upon Judea like a bruchus and devoured all the remnants of the earlier kings. They refer the rust to the power of the Romans, who, as the fourth and final power, oppressed the Jews so greatly that they expelled them from their own borders,” etc.]

For they thought that the caterpillar, locust, bruchus, and rust could signify the Assyrian, Chaldean, Macedonian, and Roman peoples, respectively. By their power, of course, the commonwealth of the Jews was worn down, since they believed that the succession of enemies had been made known under the description of locusts.

They would seem to have conjectured this with some logical basis if the Jews had suffered no calamities except from enemies. But when they are shown to have endured both a very severe famine and a prodigious drought, such as occurred in the days of blessed Elijah, as well as sudden death and various forms of corruption, why was it necessary to apply that scarcity too—which, although caused by locusts and bruchuses, is mentioned—to invasions of foreign peoples?

Therefore, understanding the prophetic words simply rather than transferring them elsewhere according to our pleasure, let us understand the locusts and caterpillars not as armored horsemen or shield-bearing foot soldiers, but as small, thin-legged insects, winged and minute. At that time they succeeded one another in tormenting the profaned nation in such a way that they carefully maintained their turns of destruction, and whatever the preceding ones had left, those that followed consumed entirely.

Saint Joel observes this destruction in prophetic vision as impending rather than already inflicted. Therefore, while those of whom he speaks are numb in pitiable security, he himself, like a kindly man horrified by such a spectacle, cries out:

**Verse 5.**—“Awake, drunkards, and weep; howl, all who drink wine in sweetness, because it has perished from your mouth.”

The complaint begins in an entirely moral manner, addressing first, amid the common calamity, those who are taught to suffer it more severely than the rest. Scarcity bites more bitterly those accustomed to luxuries, and for the luxurious not only want but frugality itself is a torment.

Since he was about to narrate the miseries of poverty, he began with moderate matters and touched upon the losses of luxury alone—losses that are not to be feared by everyone indiscriminately, but only by those who gorge themselves. He estimates them so cheaply that he declares them to have wished to live for pleasure alone.

And in accordance with what the condition of such people deserves, he adds that they should “love” and “awake,” at least when the loss threatens of those things in whose company they had chosen to sleep.

[Note: It would certainly have been preferable to read “that they should keep watch.”]

“You have hitherto,” he says, “been held by no concern for serious pursuits, nor has the consciousness of so many crimes aroused the goad of remorse. You served every desire, as though you were free from righteousness. The patience of the eternal Judge has been overcome by the shamelessness and obstinacy of sinners. He has determined to subject you to the blows you deserve and to take away the first instruments of the pleasures you abuse.”

Although the advance of this scarcity will also reach ordinary and poor people, its very beginnings will torture you. Therefore, those whom the discipline of righteousness taught nothing should at least begin to experience the goad of fear.

[Note: Previously *stimulos* (“goads”) was read. I would not have changed it if *incipiant* (“they should begin”) had also been read in the plural.]

[Note: Either an error lies here, or at the end of this isocolon after the word *evigilat*, and “or let him awake” (*vel expergiscatur*) must be added; the latter seems nearer the truth.—Ed.]

“Give tears to vices for which you gave none to duties; and you who never grieved over wounded innocence, weep at last over drunkenness deprived of its means.”

“Awake, drunkards, and weep; howl, all who drink wine in sweetness, because it has perished from your mouth.”

“You supplied,” he says, “the causes of the gravest offense by pursuing luxury. You were not content with elegant and well-timed banquets or with simple drunkenness, but mixed wine with sweetened concoctions and devised stimulants for your feasts, so that the whole span of life might perish between wantonness and intoxication.

“Now the time of such vengeance has arrived—a vengeance that, in laying waste the fruits of the earth, takes away above all the instruments of luxury. This calamity, therefore, will trouble you first, because for those ignorant of frugality the experience of punishment consists in the reduction of resources.”

And because you have forgotten reason and made yourselves like beasts, howl, at least upon the very couches and beds to which you cling, all who drink wine in sweetness, because it has perished from your mouth.

When the censor’s reproach is mingled with the prophet’s denunciation, he shows that “humanity, placed in honor, did not understand” (Ps. 48), and therefore is compared with the irrational creatures to which it made itself similar. For, as we have said, it thinks the loss of its enjoyments to be loss of life; and because luxury awakens with difficulty even amid the very crash of punishment, and does not know how to weep, let it at least howl. The following saying might apply: “They will suffer hunger like dogs and go around the city” (Ps. 58).

It would therefore have been proper for reason to prod you toward remorse rather than for the pain of calamity to awaken you through its bites. But since through excessive feasting you have lost the power of foresight, so that you can no longer provide for anything but merely feel it, howl when struck, you who did not fear when warned.

And what is the cause of such tears?

**Verses 6–8.**—“For a nation has come up upon my land, strong and innumerable; its teeth are like the teeth of lions,

[Al. “of a lion”]

and its molars like those of lion cubs. It has made my vine a desert and stripped the bark from my fig tree; stripping it bare, it has robbed it and cast it away; its branches have become white. Lament like a virgin girded with sackcloth for the husband of her youth.”

In those times contained under the title of blessed Hosea, frequent incursions of the Assyrians are also reported. But because the Creator afflicted those who violated his law in more than one manner, we infer that, amid the devastations by enemies, these plagues too occurred which the prophet announces.

In describing them he expends great effort with the attentiveness and skill of a physician, so that he might stir in the hearts of his hearers that salutary fear which compels them to shudder at seductive things. He did not hurry past the goads of the announced terror through the brevity of judgment,

[Note: The old Editor advises that *judicii* (“of judgment”) should be read; shortly afterward, in place of *consideratione* (“by consideration”) his manuscript copy had *consideraturis* (“of those who are about to consider”).]

but taught the hearer to dwell upon the consideration of the events, for whose correction this entire elaboration of the plagues had been prepared.

Nor was he content merely to describe them; he proceeds also to magnify what had happened through the weight of his words. Finally, he assigned the name of a nation to the swarm of locusts, as though it were advancing in companies and battalions, and as though its novelty were no less alarming than its size.

For if you consider its effectiveness rather than its limbs, you will see that its teeth should be compared with those of lion cubs—or even with the lions themselves, skilled as they are in hunting. For the shoots are not destroyed by these with less difficulty than herds are destroyed by those.

And just as it is less costly for mortals to provide herds for food than crops, so much more damaging is the destroyer of crops than of herds, with the beasts’ throats gaping for blood.

But the raging locust consumes the very milk of crops and grasses, and therefore also kills even the cattle that do not eat them. [Perhaps: “which do not eat.”] For it strips all the woods of their greenness and imitates, through the violence of its destruction, as it were, the condition of nature itself.

Just as, when the sun is at its winter declension, the moisture of trees is driven inward, and, once the honor of their foliage has been laid aside, their trunks stand bare—so that if someone ignorant of farming sees them, he despairs that they can become green again—so this swarm, whose arrival I lament, will consume not only tender grasses but also ripe vineyards. It will not spare the harvest whitened with fruit; it will ravage sweet figs with its bitter tooth and pursue the entire bark with such deliberate thoroughness—the bark through which, of course, life-giving sap might flow—that a white woodland will be seen in place of a green one.

Therefore, when the earth does not restore the crop entrusted to it [Ant. “lest”], when the vine does not spontaneously bend its fruit-bearing shoot, and when the suffering year supplies no consolation of fruit to the distressed farmers, what remains, my people, except for you to pursue your calamity with tears? But let them be as abundant and flowing as those of women whom the grief of widowhood has overwhelmed and who have been deprived of the companionship of the husbands to whom they had been joined from the time of their virginity.

**Verse 9.**—“Lament like a virgin girded with sackcloth for the husband of her youth. Sacrifice and libation have perished from the house of God.”

[Al. “of the Lord.”]

The discourse has appropriately shifted to the land. For since he had said that the mourning of the whole nation should be equated with the grief of a widow, he completes the reason for offering this comparison by recalling the condition of the land.

For, as often elsewhere, so also in blessed Hosea, our God declares that he took the Synagogue to himself as a wife; but he says that she violated the terms of this union in the manner of an adulteress and subjected herself to the worship of various gods.

Therefore, since here too the narrative has advanced from the beginning of the impending calamity to an immense extent, and since, after the losses that he marked as the first consequences of drunkenness and that the luxurious should mourn, the misery of poverty has been inflicted in full measure—devastating alike cultivated fields and uncultivated regions, so that not only the common nourishment of all but also what was to be offered according to religion would remain—he compares the people to a widowed woman.

For she appears to be tortured by her husband’s departure because she has lost the means of offerings and ceremonies by which she believed that, through daily sacrifices, she both pleased God and clung to him.

**Verses 10–12.**—“The priests, the ministers of the Lord, mourn. The region has been devastated; the soil mourns, because the grain has been destroyed, the wine has been confounded, and the oil has languished. The farmers are confounded; the vinedressers have howled over the wheat and barley, because the harvest of the field has perished. The vine has been confounded, and the fig tree has languished; the pomegranates [Ant. “malogravata”; Al. “pomegranate tree”], the palm, the apple tree, and all the trees of the field have dried up, because joy has been confounded among the children of men.”

The public poverty had advanced so far, through the devastation caused by the locust, bruchus, and rust, that even the lack of sacrificial victims followed, and the Bread of the Presence could no longer be placed upon the altar. Consequently, the priests and Levites mourned first.

The rest of the people, as though rejected by an eternal husband, groan like widows, as we have said, because the earth itself, having lost every adornment of greenness and fertility, has been covered with the squalor of one who mourns.

The reaper did not snatch the grain from this sorrowful devastation; the vine did not bring its fertility—which had stood weighed down with fruit—to sweet new wine; rather, it disappointed the farmers so completely that it seems ashamed of its own false promise.

A similar blight struck the olive trees; the pomegranates languished along with the figs; and no kind of fruit could remain in better condition. Together with the joys and hopes of mortals, both shoots and grasses perished.

This is no time to conceal grief. Assume the appearance and mind of all who mourn, for the most dreadful kind of ruin is impending, in which both the hope of the year and its actual produce must be lamented.

**Verses 13–14.**—“Gird yourselves and mourn, priests; howl, ministers of the altar; enter, lie in sackcloth, ministers of my God, because sacrifice and libation have perished from the house of your God. Sanctify a fast,

[Ant. “Offer a sacrifice.”]

summon the assembly, gather the elders, all inhabitants of the land, into the house of your God, and cry out to the Lord.”

Having described the magnitude of the calamity, he had declared that weeping threatened all the people. But since to be moved merely by the spectacle of tears belongs more to the office of one who pities than of one who teaches, the prophet, assuming the mind of a father, arranges everything solely for their benefit.

Now too he properly directs them toward lamentation, so that they may not waste the time in empty tears by pursuing their miseries with mournful cries—something that would indeed befit religious and courageous minds—but may order the very offerings of their tears according to the rules of sacred law and prepare a harvest of joys. Let them indulge their minds in anguish only as much as is sufficient to provoke the indignation of the Judge,

[Note: Something should be supplied here, such as “of that Judge,” or a similar expression.]

grieving over the offense against the Judge rather than over the loss of possessions.

“Therefore,” he says, “you priests, exchanging soft garments for harsh ones, assume the clothing and disposition of fugitives, and also plead what specially pertains to your care: namely, that what is needed for the service of divine worship is lacking.”

As for the people: “Sanctify a fast”—that is, proclaim it with such a denunciation that anyone who might disregard it may be accused as though he had violated something holy. This is what he means by “Sanctify a fast.”

“At the same time,” he says, “summon everyone”—that is, not only those strong in age, but also those whom infancy or old age renders weak—to share in the duty in proportion to the magnitude of the danger. For it follows that the affliction of all should repel a calamity that was about to rage against all alike.

Nor should we allow the opportunity for a subtle interpretation to escape us. The fast is commanded to everyone in common: “Gather the elders, all the inhabitants of the land, into the house of your God.”

But if the poverty described above occupied the entire region, so that the customary sacrifice could not be offered, how is fasting again enjoined upon those same peoples with such solemn sanctification? Under such extreme want, would it not be more difficult to prepare food than to continue fasting?

Therefore, we must observe that hunger is one thing and fasting another. The latter belongs to the exercise of virtue; the former to the anguish of mortality. Hence it is not the affliction of the guilty but the correction of penitents that appeases the Lord; nor do those who are to be healed need food, but remorse.

For the filth of luxury is driven away not at all by a calamity common to good and evil alike, but by a discipline especially congenial to noble minds. Therefore, “I ask for the fast,” he says, “that proceeds from duty, not the hunger that usually arises from punishment. Rather, reconcile fasting even to those who are hungry, so that what poverty had made burdensome, devotion may render fruitful.”

But we have said these things for the edification of our hearers. Otherwise, the prophetic statements can claim a more concise interpretation. The prophet announces a calamity that is impending rather than already breaking upon them, and rightly admonishes the priests to summon the people to fasts and to meet through lawful supplications the calamities that they hear are approaching.

Finally, it follows:

**Verses 15–18.**—“Ah, ah, ah, for the day! For the day of the Lord is near, and like devastation from the Mighty One it will come. Has not food perished before your eyes, from the house of your God, joy and exultation? The animals have rotted in their dung; the granaries have been demolished, the storehouses have been scattered, because the grain has been confounded. Why has the animal groaned, and the herds of cattle bellowed? Because there are no pastures for them; even the flocks of sheep have perished.”

[Note: All the other books, and the Hebrew text itself, read “our” in place of “your”; shortly afterward they read “there is no pasture” in the singular rather than “there are no pastures,” etc.]

After the prophet had arranged that those who mourned should assemble covered with sackcloth—that is, clothed in haircloth—he now adds what form their prayer should take. Repeating the exclamation of the grieving person two or three times, he expressed, as it were, the force of the blows by which the plagues would be inflicted.

He did this for no other reason than to arouse in the hearts of his hearers fear and remorse through the magnitude of the announced calamity, as though he were saying:

“Believe my eyes; believe my senses, which through prophetic sight behold not only what has been inflicted but also what is to come. The weight of a calamity that cannot be endured is pressing upon you, and at each of its blows we collapse as though our entrails had been torn apart.

“For the caterpillar, locust, bruchus, and rust will succeed one another in such a way that the cessation of the preceding misfortune—which seemed to promise some breathing space—will bring more grievous torments to the wretched.

“And that day of the Lord, on which he has destined to punish the guilty, is not terrifying as though it would involve some slight affliction; it will bring a devastation such as any exceedingly powerful avenger would inflict. Against his strength, neither the boldness of those who resist could stand nor the cleverness of those who hide could conceal anything.”

[Al. “of those who see.”]

Accordingly, when he says, “Devastation will come from the Mighty One,” either understand that a comparison has been made, so that we know the chastisement will be no less powerful than if the victory of some exceedingly powerful king were raging.

The same figure appears in the Psalm: “The Lord awoke as one sleeping, like a mighty man overcome with wine”; and, “He struck his enemies in their hinder parts; he gave them everlasting disgrace” (Ps. 77).

Or else let us understand the mention of the Mighty One to have been made not by way of example but on account of his singularity: not meaning one or two who accomplish what they wish, but one who performs without difficulty everything he wishes. Thus “the Mighty One” would seem to express the Omnipotent.

“For the day of the Lord is near, and devastation will come from the Mighty One. Has not food perished before your eyes?”

“It is not,” he says, “time for you to fear some moderate impediment, as though calamity would affect only the gathering of fruits and not those already gathered. Rather, before your very eyes, while you still place confidence in stored provisions, I announce that poverty threatens not only private homes but also the treasury of the temple, so that all joy—or rather all consolation—may perish.

“Nor will the animals provide food after the crops have been taken away, because the mountains themselves, consumed by destruction, and the extinction of their greenness testify to the ruin.”

Through these evils drawing near, the prophet shows that he himself is being assailed. This may be understood either in relation to the judgment of spiritual meanings, which extend far beyond these bodily realities, or in relation to the pomp of description—as we have said—which arouses the feeling of fear in the hearts of the peoples.

Therefore, he assumed the appearance of one asking a question when he said: “Why has the animal groaned, and the herds of cattle bellowed?” Then, from the side of the one answering, he added: “Because there are no pastures for them.” “Even the flocks of sheep have perished.”

Therefore, since affliction intolerable surrounds me on every side, I raise my hands, my voice, and my prayers to you, the one Lord; and, lying prostrate in mind and body, I implore you to look with favor and gentleness upon the disasters of the earth. For behold:

**[Verse 19.]** “Flame has consumed the beautiful places of the wilderness.” In this passage, an attentive reader may reasonably ask what beauty of fields is being praised in the wilderness, which this unprecedented fire has consumed so destructively—especially since no complaint about a fire had previously been made. The subsequent course of the reading shows that “the beauty of the fields” here means leafy woods and flourishing pastures. He praised the pleasant places not of cultivated, but of wilderness land, because he had mentioned herds and flocks: since they rejoice among woods and pastures, when these have been damaged by some disaster, the animals too are subjected to destruction.

He used “fire” for the devastation brought by the locust and the young locust, just as we also read in the Psalm: “He made their rains hail, fire consuming their land; he struck their vines and crushed every tree within their borders” (Psalm 104). Since, therefore, the locust and young locust have consumed all the green growth of the woods and grasses so completely that they appear not merely gnawed but burned, consequently even the wild beasts have reached the dangers of famine and, taught by nature’s own instruction, look to you alone for relief from their danger.

For, as the sacred songs testify with truth and sweetness: “All things look to you, that you may give them food in due season. When you give it, they gather it; when you open your hand, all things are filled with goodness. When you turn away your face, they are troubled. For you take away their spirit, and they fail and return to their dust” (Psalm 103). Thus the herds of wild beasts also ask relief from you—though lacking articulate voices—by the various sounds of their throats, just as a field prepared to receive seed awaits either dew or rain by which its shoots may grow. If you consider this carefully, my reader, you will see that the example has weight: he has compared the thirst of souls with the natural appetite of the elements, which is certainly much more intense.

But let us examine what follows.

## CHAPTER II

**Verses 1–2.** “Blow the trumpet in Zion; wail upon my holy mountain. Let all the inhabitants of the earth be troubled, for the day of the Lord will come; for it is near. A day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and whirlwind, like morning spread over the mountains.”

He says that, when the time of great devastation approaches, the inhabitants of the city and of the fields should assemble and anticipate the announced time of calamity with prayers and tears. If I could explain in words, before the actual experience of events, how severe it would be, I think its darkness would be like the darkness produced if blackness were doubled, so that night might be made denser by gloom and darkness; indeed, if you joined dense clouds and whirlwinds to these, so that the consolation of the stars were entirely excluded and the terror of lightning flashed through the blind air.

These images, however, have attempted only to indicate the quality of the evil; its severity is increased still further by consideration of its magnitude. For the force of the evil of which we are speaking has filled the whole extent of our region, as though the boundaries had been unfolded and a bright morning—that is, a glowing dawn—had simultaneously flooded all the mountains and hills.

He therefore compared the same thing both with night and with light, not to introduce anything contradictory, but to express its breadth and severity through the diversity of the comparison.

“An immense and mighty people; there has been none like it from the beginning, and after it there will be none throughout the years of generation after generation.”

The continuation of the discourse shows that this account concerns locusts more than enemies. He has now likened the very swarm of locusts and young locusts—whose invasion is described as having produced manifold calamity—to an armed and roaring army. He could not have introduced this comparison if the description had concerned soldiers.

Thus he continues to explain the effect of the evil through various images, and says what appearance of the land it found when it came and what it left when it departed. “No age,” he says, “has seen anything like this among our ancestors, and no age among our descendants will see anything like it.”

**Verse 3.** “Before its face a consuming fire, and behind it a flame burning; the land before it is like a garden of delight, and behind it a desolate wilderness; there is no one who can escape it.”

By the words “before its face” he wished to indicate the actual advance of the locusts—not that some other fire should destroy what was before the locusts and that they should afterward devastate the burned fields, but that their invasion would lay waste entire regions as thoroughly as fire had consumed them.

Since fire is shown to be effective not by destroying everything equally, but because it usually consumes quickly and completely whatever is light—such as leaves, stalks, and straw—with crackling and leaping flames, while it overcomes materials of greater solidity only after a longer delay, he declares that the flame prevails both before and behind them.

Maintaining the order of amplification with artistic skill, after comparing the locust with fire he says that the region which has been devastated could previously have been compared with pleasant and well-watered lands: “The land before it is like a garden of delight, and behind it a desolate wilderness; there is no one who can escape it.” Thus the force of the advancing evil may become apparent, since it has consumed what was exceedingly pleasant.

**Verses 4–11.** “Their appearance is like the appearance of horses, and they run like horsemen. Like the sound of chariots, they leap over the mountaintops; like the sound of a flame of fire devouring stubble; like a mighty people prepared for battle. Before its face the peoples will be tormented; all faces will be changed into a pot. They will run like mighty men; like warriors they will climb the wall. The men will walk in their ways, and they will not turn aside from their paths. No one will jostle his brother; each will walk in his own track. They will also fall through the windows, and they will not be destroyed. They will enter the city; they will run upon the wall; they will climb into the houses; they will enter through the windows like a thief. Before its face the earth trembled; the heavens were shaken; the sun and moon were darkened, and the stars withdrew their brightness. And the Lord gave his voice before the face of his army, for his camps are exceedingly numerous, for they are mighty and perform his word. For great is the day of the Lord and exceedingly terrible; and who will endure it?”

A little earlier I pointed out that, as the discourse proceeded, it would become increasingly clear that the narrative had been composed simply not about armed battle lines, as some have thought, but about young locusts and locusts. To mark their force and effect, therefore, he gathered together the likenesses of armed men and horsemen.

Following not merely the ambition of narration but also the art of comparison, he explained with both grandeur and elegance what he had undertaken: he compared the very running of the invading locusts with the gait of four-footed creatures and their sound with the crackling that fire usually produces in straw.

Because he saw that these images had been appropriately adopted, he lingered over them with great care. He compared not only their hissing and their invasions with fire and cavalry, but also carefully marked the fact that they advanced not in a scattered but in a formed and compact line, at full pace—plainly like legions moving under standards and centurions, since the cause of terror demanded this image.

“Like a people,” he says, “prepared for battle, before its face all the peoples will be tormented; all faces will be reduced to a pot.” If, he says, even military discipline adds force to troops, so that they do not advance wandering about like brigands, but arranged in companies and battle lines, proceeding to war with steady courage and ordered ranks, the enemy are easily undone by fear itself even before the battle begins, so that their faces are often clothed in the pallor of impending death.

“So,” he says, “the ranks of our people will be unable even to endure the sight of the approaching calamity. Like a pot blackened by smoke, they will not merely grow pale but will be utterly drawn together,” since they will find no help in the strength of the open field or in the walls of their cities.

For the swarms of locusts whose coming I announce, carrying out the work of devastation, will rush wherever indignation or desire summons them, like the most warlike men. They will not merely lay waste the fields but will also penetrate within the roofs of the cities. No multitude of those who resist will impede them; no obstacle will delay their advance. The victorious crowd will proceed along unobstructed paths.

This is what he means: “No one will jostle his brother; each will walk in his own track; they will also fall through the windows, and they will not be destroyed.”

Nor, he says, will they be content, as though satisfied with a public terror, to invade only the buildings of the cities; they will enter the inner rooms of private houses like thieves.

Thus a deadly anxiety will seize all the inhabitants of that region, so that they will seem to see the heavens moved and the earth tremble, the stars withdraw their brightness, and the sun and moon clothed in tangible darkness.

I would certainly not doubt that all these things will come with so great a mass of evils, since the one who is Omnipotent himself directs these troops as their leader, employs such an army for the destruction of the guilty, raises the signal of the command by which they are stirred, and supplies them with the strength by which they execute his sentence.

“For great is the day of the Lord,” and it is to be feared in the very manner and pomp of its vengeance; its crushing ruin is shown to be unbearable by the first sight of it.

We can also transfer these complaints of blessed Joel, who is preaching, to figures of the soul through a more subtle interpretation, although they are useful for edification with all the force of his severity. Through his description of the calamities which he declares will hang over entire regions because of sinners’ punishment, he may be understood to have signified the squalor of criminal minds.

For the judgment of the wise does not consider those more wretched whom it sees subjected to hardships than those whom it sees subjected to vices. Following this principle, he both pities and rebukes the condition of the most profane nation, which abstained from absolutely no crimes. First he declares that deeds such as had occurred in his own time could neither be remembered as having happened nor believed as future possibilities: namely, that creatures of tiny size, scarcely deserving the name of living beings, had brought upon the land a force like successive waves, so that they erased the entire prepared face of the region.

**“What the young locust left, the locust consumed; what the locust left, the young locust consumed; what the young locust left, the rust consumed.”**

If, therefore, you inspect human souls with careful judgment [perhaps: “with discerning judgment”] and consider vices not yet punished, you will surely discover in them a condition such as that which the pitiable plague had brought upon the regions.

He introduced four kinds that bring the harms of corruption and are joined to one another by a certain affinity: the young locust, the locust, the bruchus, and the rust. These four can suitably be applied to the four passions of the soul: hope, joy, fear, and grief. From these four affections, which arise from one origin of movement—namely, from the fact that we are affected—every evil and every variety of harm is produced.

Let us distinguish them in this way. Since the young locust pursues only the green leaves of trees, while the locust advances by leaps more than by walking, let us refer them to hope and joy, since their sinful movement is expressed through a kind of leaping. By contrast, let us assign the bruchus and the rust to fear and grief, since they consume without any vigor of action, by sitting upon and clinging to what they attack.

When we see someone sinning through the things said to be joyful—being, for example, alien to modesty and shame—and, after corrupting the ornaments of integrity, also surrendering his patrimony and livelihood to his vices, we may cry out: “The locust consumed what the young locust left.”

But when, conversely, we see another so enslaved to sluggishness that he considers no honor of freedom worthwhile, and, while he himself displays no garment of serious dignity, the wickedness of some superior discovers him wishing to remain hidden and demands him either as an accomplice or as a servant in its crimes—or, if he attempts to refuse, threatens him immediately with some evil or disadvantage—and then we see him submit himself to crimes greater even than we had thought, we may say with the prophet: “The bruchus consumed what the locust left, and the rust consumed what the bruchus left.”

If we turn our gaze with discernment upon the whole life of mortals according to this principle, we find that, amid their various occupations but in nearly all their pursuits and circumstances, there are many situations in which these exclamations of the prophet may appropriately be used.

The multiplication of vices has reached such completeness that not only the grasses and shoots, as though nature’s fertility itself were dying, but also the products of vines, olive trees, and fig trees—which had been appointed, as it were, for the offerings of religion—were corrupted, together with their fruits and strength.

When, therefore, you see even those established under the Christian name and rejoicing in their adoption through the sacraments taking no care for virtue, and indeed the very ministers of the altar serving only ambition and luxury, cry out with pity and indignation:

“He made my vineyard a wilderness, he stripped the bark from my fig tree, he laid it bare and cast it away; its branches have become white, the wine has been confounded, the oil has languished, the farmers have been confounded, because the harvest of the field has perished.”

This condition of the churches, such as we observe especially in the present age, has kindled that indignation of God before which the prophet trembled: “Great is the day of the Lord and exceedingly terrible; and who will endure it?” Let us hear, then, by what purpose the one who cannot be endured has been revealed.

**Verses 12–14.** “Now therefore, says the Lord: Return to me with all your heart, in fasting, in weeping, and in mourning. And tear your hearts and not your garments, and return to the Lord your God, for he is gracious and merciful, patient and abundant in mercy, and relenting concerning calamity. Who knows whether he may turn and forgive, and leave behind him a blessing, sacrifice and libation for the Lord your God?”

[Note: “Your own” should be supplied; the other books and the Hebrew text itself contain it.]

As you contemplate the pomp of severity with which the eternal Lord, going forth to punish, is surrounded, know that he terrifies you not from a desire to rage but to restrain you from despair and to produce the effect of a better hope.

For he did not sound forth the noise of such a manifold and violent punishment because he had forgotten his own goodness, but in order to awaken within you the feeling of fear. Finally, by the very voice of events he calls you to bring your sick hearts to him at last and, committing yourselves to his remedy with your whole strength, to fulfill not merely the outward appearance of mourners but their entire inward feeling, tearing your hearts rather than your garments.

By intensifying the command, he also gave an elegant reminder: since it is the custom of mourners to pull apart their garments at the breast, he urged them as though hands had been placed upon their breasts to press more deeply, and, if it were possible, to tear not only their clothing but their very entrails.

He also found a word perfectly suited to the matter at hand: “Tear your hearts and not your garments.” This tearing seems to prescribe, beyond the ostentation of mourning, a discernment between good and evil, and separation from the crimes with whose mixture they had been defiled.

Change your purpose, then, for the better, or mourn the things previously done wickedly, since your cause is before a gracious and merciful Lord, one who relents concerning calamity—that is, one who willingly grants remission of the calamity which he calls “calamity” when he sees those whom he had alarmed by his threat become repentant.

Following the usage of Scripture, he assumed the appearance of one who is uncertain, saying: “Who knows whether he may turn and forgive, and leave behind him a blessing?” This is inserted out of reverence for the judge, whose terror he wishes to be so great that even what is safe is feared.

He says “leave behind him a blessing” because above he had said that such a force of want would be brought upon them by the devastation of the locusts that, after their passage, the land would remain like a desolate wilderness. Therefore he now says: “Offer tears; offer groans.” Perhaps the announced force of punishment will be satisfied by such sacrifices, so that, if it diminishes abundance, it may not also consume nourishment.

“And leave behind him a blessing, sacrifice, and libation for the Lord your God” [variant: “your”].

He responds in due order to what came before. Above he had said that the magnitude of the famine would advance so far that sacrifice and libation would perish from the house of the Lord. Here, therefore, when he claimed hope of consolation for the corrected and repentant, he added that the Lord would leave behind a blessing to supply the altar's sacrifices and libations.

**Verses 15–17.** “Blow the trumpet in Zion; sanctify a fast; call an assembly. Gather the people; sanctify the Church; assemble the elders; gather the little ones and those nursing at the breast. Let the bridegroom go forth from his chamber and the bride from her bridal room. Between the vestibule and the altar the priests, the ministers of the Lord, will weep and say: Spare, Lord; spare your people; and do not give your inheritance to reproach, so that nations may rule over it. Why should they say among the peoples, ‘Where is their God?’”

It is characteristic of the prophets not to preserve anxiously the times or the kinds of expressions in their changes; rather, content to convey the sense, they use readily available forms of speech. Thus, after saying, “Let the bridegroom go forth from his chamber and the bride from her bridal room,” he added, “Between the vestibule and the altar the priests will weep,” instead of saying, “Let the priests weep.”

Content with the office of a censor, he was not concerned with the niceties of grammatical moods. Or, certainly, to show that his exhortation had been effective, he said that they would take care to do what he had commanded them to do.

“Between the vestibule and the altar,” he says, “let the assembly of mourners resound.” And you, chief priests, to whom the guardianship of the sacred rites has been entrusted, cry out with faces wet with tears: “Spare, Lord; spare your people. Do not permit those whom you decreed to possess by hereditary right to become objects of execration and contempt to the profane nations by whom we are surrounded. If nothing else, let this at least plead for us before your clemency: we cannot perish without bringing dishonor upon you.”

You wished us to be believed and called your servants and sons—not merely by creating us, but also by adopting us. Do not allow the nations to say: “Where is their God?”—the God in whose protection they once used to rejoice.

After he had explained these matters in the capacity of a teacher, he immediately promises with the confidence of a prophet that the prayers of the people had been effective and that the Lord of events, as though stirred by zeal, had undertaken the defense of the faithful.

**Verse 18.** “The Lord was jealous,” he says, “for his land and spared his people.”

[Note: It seems that the following verse, or the first part of the verse—“And the Lord answered and said to his people”—has dropped out. Since it ended with the same words as the immediately preceding phrase, “to his people,” the eyes of an ancient copyist could easily have been deceived. Certainly, our author proceeds to explain the things that follow from that answer of the Lord.]

He says that, considering what was appropriate to his own dignity, lest the nation that was reckoned by his particular name should perish as though it lacked a defender, he prevented it from despairing and filled it with the hope of joy. From his answer the following is added:

**Verses 19–20.** “Behold, I will send you grain, wine, and oil, and you will be filled with them; and I will no longer make you a reproach among the nations. And I will drive far from you the one who is from the north, and I will expel him into a land impassable and desolate, with his face toward the eastern sea and his rear toward the western sea; and his stench will rise, and his decay will rise.”

Blessed Jeremiah and the other prophets say that the Assyrians and Chaldeans would come from the north. The Assyrian, therefore, could also be understood here, unless—as I noted above—it were established that other plagues too had been inflicted upon the profane people according to what had been decreed in Deuteronomy.

Accordingly, following the established order, let us understand the locusts and young locusts, whose removal the appeased Lord promises. He added this to the grace and sweetness of liberation: he ordered those swarms to perish in the wilderness, lest the magnitude of the stench arising from their corpses create disease for the inhabitants.

Thus their stench and decay will rise there, because they acted arrogantly. In declaring that it acted arrogantly, he did not indicate a defect of mind but expressed the magnitude of the calamity.

**Verses 21–23.** “Do not fear, land; exult and rejoice, for the Lord has done great things. Do not fear, animals of the region, for the beautiful places of the wilderness have sprouted; the tree has borne its fruit, the fig tree and the vine have given their strength. And you, children of Zion, exult and rejoice in the Lord your God, for he has given you a teacher of righteousness.”

The speech is appropriately directed to the whole region, so that renewed fertility may be promised to the land whose devastation had been announced. The speech proceeds through the same images by which it had passed during the adversity.

He says, then, that the mountains will be clothed with pastures, that the leafy appearance of the woods will return, and that fig trees and vines will offer the gifts of their fertility. Since all these things have been assigned to human use, he rightly added: “And you, children of Zion, exult and rejoice in the Lord your God, for he has given you a teacher of righteousness.”

He crowned the preceding admonitions with a sentence full of instruction. After the removal of hardships and the success of the most desirable prosperity, it marked the proper basis on which the people should claim joy—not that they had acquired objects for enjoyment, but that they had found a teacher of righteousness.

“And you,” he says, “children of Zion, exult and rejoice in the Lord your God, for he has given you a teacher of righteousness.” He is indeed merciful, and by one act of assistance he removes sadness and by a second grants benefits. But you, my people, ought especially to exult in this, by which you surpass the other nations: namely, that you have received teachers of righteous conduct, under whose guidance you might act both modestly and happily.

This resembles the saying of another prophet: “We are blessed, Israel, because what pleases God is known to us” (Baruch 4:4).

**Verses 24–25.** “And he will cause the early and late rain to descend for you at the beginning. And the granaries will be filled with grain, and the winepresses will overflow with wine and oil. And I will repay you for the years which the locust, the young locust, the rust, and the eruca consumed—my great army which I sent against you.”

He continues what he began and describes the future change from sorrowful things to joyful ones. Since he is about to promise fertility, he foretells that timely and late rain will descend: “He will cause the early and late rain to descend at the beginning.”

The Septuagint translated this not as “at the beginning” but as “as at the beginning,” in order to produce a coherent sense: once the disturbances by which the seasonal order had been thrown into confusion were removed, the year would return to its customary course, so that, according to the variety of seeds, the fields would be watered by either timely or late rains.

These rains will create such fertility that both your granaries and your wine-vats will overflow. The phrase “the early and late rain at the beginning” may therefore be understood as indicating the order of benefits, without any contradiction in the meaning—as though one asked how rain can be said to come “at the beginning” when it is also called “late.” Rather, fertility is said to be preceded by rain, so that the sense is: “I will first send rain, and afterward the joy of crops will follow.”

When this has filled the cultivators with joy and strength, it will pour forgetfulness of the former famine into them and continue to erase the traces of hardship, so that not only will the distress of want cease, but the losses that had preceded it will also be restored.

This is what he means by: “I will repay you for the years which the locust consumed.” He does not mean that moments of time themselves will be restored, but that the fertility of the years will be restored.

It should also be noted that God called both the eruca and the locust his strength and his great army. This does not mean that such worms can in any way be compared with the coeternal power of God, but that through their service and devastation they fulfilled the task of vengeance in the affliction of the guilty.

The very smallness of the erucas and locusts therefore indicates the power both of the Creator and of the avenger. When he has determined to crush peoples, he uses neither the teeth of some beast nor poisons, but through the young locust and the rust consumes kingdoms that had shortly before been wealthy. It is therefore called the strength of God, because it fulfilled his sentence like a vigorous executioner.

When, therefore, fertility, he says, has repaired the losses of those times as desired:

**[Verses 26–27.]** “You will eat and be satisfied, and you will praise the name of the Lord your God, who has done wonders for you; and my people will never be put to shame. And you will know that I am in the midst of Israel, and that I am the Lord your God, and there is no other; and my people will never be put to shame.”

It is customary in prophetic speech that whenever it has promised joyful things, it also declares that they will endure forever. We should understand this either under the condition celebrated in Scripture—namely, that if they devote themselves to upright conduct, prosperity too will remain—or, certainly, as a feature of the prophet’s office, in which something from the side of hope is always joined to the prediction.

The sense can also be introduced in a way to which the progression of the discourse itself points. For above he had already said: “Children of Zion, exult and rejoice in the Lord your God, for he has given you a teacher of righteousness.”

Although this can be understood in many ways, insofar as it concerns the sequence of times it seems specifically to point to the blessed Hezekiah, whom the testimony of the annals shows to have burned with great zeal for the worship of God. His royal person, as the prophet Isaiah especially demonstrates, seems to have been chosen to signify a greater matter.

Let us therefore transfer what was accomplished through Hezekiah to the work of our Redeemer, so that what was fulfilled to a moderate extent in that period may be seen to have acquired immense dimensions under the Gospel.

For the true teacher of righteousness is the one in whom “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden” (Colossians 2), who “was handed over because of our offenses and rose again because of our justification” (Romans 4), so that, “justified freely by his grace through the redemption which is in Christ Jesus” (Romans 2 [as printed]), we might be freed from ancient errors and subjected to righteousness alone.

Driving away all our former poverty in salutary things through a new fertility, we would be filled both with teaching and with abundance, as the Gospel promises: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matthew 6).

Thus the people who have acquired these things will never be put to shame, because they rest upon the Redeemer’s declaration: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28).

With that leader dwelling in their midst, the ranks of the faithful always remain secure and cheerful. Whatever adversities they endure in their struggles, they experience them as being so erased by the prosperity that follows that they seem to have occurred only to enhance the joyful things.

**Verses 28–29.** “And it will be afterward: I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters will prophesy; your old men will dream dreams, and your young men will see visions. Moreover, upon my male servants and female servants in those days I will pour out my spirit.”

Blessed Peter mentions this passage in the Acts of the Apostles, saying that this prophecy was fulfilled at the time when the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles (Acts 2).

It should therefore be observed that the Apostle took from the context of the prophetic speech only what suited his own time, namely: “I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters will prophesy.”

Because the apostles had miraculously acquired knowledge of languages, the teacher of the Church showed that this promised outpouring of the Spirit had occurred and called knowledge of languages prophecy. Although it did not speak of future events but of the recent mysteries of the Lord’s incarnation, it could nevertheless have occurred only through the power of the Holy Spirit.

He was not, however, content merely to mention the gifts; he also added those things that belonged to the pomp of terror.

Editorial notes and apparatus from the supplied text:

- [Col. 1041D] The author passes over the explanation of the following nineteenth verse: “To you, Lord, I shall cry, because fire has consumed the beautiful places of the wilderness and flame has set ablaze all the trees of the region.”
- [Col. 1041D–1042D] He now explains the other, or twentieth, verse, which it is also worthwhile to transcribe: “Even the beasts of the field have looked up to you like a threshing-floor thirsting for rain, because the springs of waters have dried up and fire has devoured the beautiful places of the wilderness.”
- [Col. 1042D] The other books read *expansum* (“spread out”) for *extensum* (“extended”).
- [Col. 1042D] Recall what was said above at col. 480.
- [Variant] “has filled” (*implevit*); alternatively, “will fill” (*implebit*).
- [Col. 1043D] *Exient* (“they will go out”) had previously been read corruptly.
- [Variant] “like” (*sicut*); alternatively, *velut* (“just as”).
- [Col. 1043D] The Jerome-based and Vulgate editions more correctly, and more closely to the Hebrew, read: “The peoples will be tormented; all faces will be reduced to a pot.” Moreover, our author himself, when repeating this passage below, establishes that *redigentur* means “will be changed.”
- [Variant] “like” (*sicut*); alternatively, *quasi* (“as if”).
- [Variant] “performing his word” (*facientia verbum eius*); alternatively, “performing his words” (*facientia verba eius*).
- [Earlier edition] It reads *gradus* (“steps”) here, and shortly afterward *signi* (“of the standard”).
- [Col. 1044D] The old editor thought that *laetalis* (“deadly”), rather than *laetabilis* (“joyful”), should be restored; that is certainly our author's meaning.
- [Col. 1044D] Perhaps *dubitet* (“should doubt”) ought to be restored in place of *dubitem* (“I should doubt”).
- [Col. 1045D] Consult our Preface, where we discuss the author of this Commentary.
- [Col. 1045D] “Your” (*vestro*) must be supplied; both the other books and the Hebrew text itself have it.
- [Col. 1045D–1046D] The cited Jerome-based Palatine manuscript reads “and abundant in mercy” in place of “and of much mercy.” Then the missing words “and relenting concerning calamity,” which all the other books together with the Hebrew exemplar add, had to be supplied. Our author himself acknowledges them in the explanation that follows.
- [Col. 1046D] The following verse, or the first part of it—“And the Lord answered and said to his people”—seems to have dropped out. Since it ended in the same words as the immediately preceding phrase, “to his people,” it could easily have escaped an ancient copyist's eye. Certainly, our author proceeds to explain what follows from that divine response.
- [Col. 1046D] Jerome omits the preposition *ex* (“from”); the Vulgate instead has the plural “them” (*eis*); the Hebrew indication is illegible in the supplied text.
- [Col. 1047D–1048D] The Vulgate edition adds the adverb “as” (*sicut*) here, but our author's testimony shows that it should be deleted: neither the Jerome-based codices nor the Hebrew text recognizes it. This is made clearer by the following exposition, which also explains its source: “The Septuagint,” he says, “translated not ‘at the beginning,’ but ‘as at the beginning.’” Conversely, the same author's later use of *sic* (“thus”), in “and thus the granaries will be filled,” seems, on the authority of those books, to require its removal there. Other minor matters are silently corrected.
- [Col. 1048D] *Plumis* (“feathers”) has hitherto been read corruptly; we restore *pluviis* (“rains”).
- [Col. 1048D] The other books add “eating” (*vescentes*), as the Hebrew verb also conveys. Shortly afterward, for “has done wonders for you,” the Vulgate reads “has done wonders with you”; the Jerome-based edition less correctly has “with us.” In the following verse, the two words “and I” (*et ego*), missing through the habitual error of copyists but present in all the other books, have been supplied on their authority.
- [Variant] In “for the Lord your God,” some witnesses read “our God”; another reading is “your God.”

Verses 30–31.—“I will give portents in heaven and on earth: blood, and fire, and vapor of smoke. The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes; and everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.” Thus, throughout that entire continuation, he hastens to persuade us that, since the day of the Lord—that is, the time of the final judgment—will come with such power and din that, while the stars tremble and are struck with terror, this structure of the universe, as though consumed by fire, will burst apart, and faith alone will protect the ranks of the godly while the world collapses, they must believe the Gospel if they desire to attain salvation.

Since blessed Peter had undertaken not to explain the prophet but to preach the Gospel, he seized from the prophet’s words as much as suited his purpose; yet by doing so he certainly did not abolish the explanation supplied by the context of the prophetic work. We mention this briefly so that the audacity of those who rashly and incompetently insist that the prophet indicated only that period about which the Apostle Peter was speaking may be rejected. For the entire structure of the work, I say, teaches that it embraces first the time of the Jewish people and thereafter our own as its culmination [Ant. *doceatur*, “may be taught”]. Just as it does not conflict with the prophetic meaning, when it is transferred to the concerns of the Gospel, that the whole volume recounts Jewish history, so also—and indeed much more readily—among an educated readership it must never be permitted that the continuity of the passage be denied credibility if some prophecy can also be applied to the affairs of believing Gentiles.

[Note: I do not know whether the great Jerome could have been treated more unjustly and reproved more sharply by Rufinus himself, when they were mutually engaged in the bitterest hostility. He is the very man whom our author, as he often does elsewhere, now attacks, accusing him of audacity, rashness, and ignorance. For he is the same man who both refers the whole prophetic statement to the time of the salvation restored through Christ and argues at length that it must be so referred. “Since Peter,” he says, “mentions that Joel’s prophecy was fulfilled at the time when the Lord suffered, we ask only how the earlier, middle, and following passages, all the way to the end of the book, can cohere with one another,” and so forth. Then, having related each passage in order, from the beginning to the point where it is written, “The great and terrible day of the Lord,” and from there onward to this passage, “I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh,” he says that the proposed text appears to have preserved the continuity of the discourse. Although what follows is somewhat more difficult—a point he himself by no means denies—he nevertheless fits it together and shows, from the very understanding of the Jews, that the promises are to be fulfilled in Christ: “We differ from them,” he says, “only in this, that they maintain these things are future, whereas we prove that they have already happened.”

To this extent he also refers those portents of heaven and earth to Christ. “In heaven,” he says, “because the sun was turned into darkness and the moon into blood; on earth, because the earth trembled with so violent and unusual a movement that tombs were opened and rocks split apart.” And a little later: “The sun also was turned into darkness when it did not dare to look upon its Lord hanging on the cross; and the moon into blood—either because we believe that this happened according to the historical account but was passed over in silence by the Evangelists, for not everything Jesus did is recorded in writing, and so forth; or certainly”—and so on. “The great and terrible day of the Lord, however, must either be understood as the day of the Resurrection or, at any rate, as the day of Judgment after a long period. But since it follows, ‘And everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved,’ it is more appropriate to understand it as the day of the Resurrection. Finally, the very word ‘pouring out’ also indicates the abundance of the gift: the gifts of the Holy Spirit did not descend upon only a few prophets, as formerly happened in the Old Testament, but upon all believers in the name of the Savior, and so forth. The old men also saw dreams when Paul, already an old man, heard the Macedonian man, and so forth.”

We place these few points before the reader’s eyes, so that he may judge with what injustice they are insultingly attacked by our author. On this man himself we speak at greater length in the Preface, taking occasion from this passage also.]

Let us therefore see how the thread of an almost historical explanation proceeds. We infer that the holy prophet Joel prophesied under the blessed Hezekiah. During that king’s reign there were both serious conflicts and great miracles. Among the other disasters by which the ten tribes are said to have been afflicted up to their deportation, some cities belonging also to the territories of Judah and Benjamin fell; and we find that the Jews suffered from disease and scarcity. Finally, when Rabshakeh addressed the besieged and announced destruction unless they immediately surrendered to the king of the Assyrians, he also promised them the evils of famine and thirst to endure. Therefore the merciful Lord promises them this as well: when sad things are changed into joyful ones, the losses caused by scarcity will also be repaired.

But let us hear what sequence of events and times he establishes: “I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy; your old men shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions. Moreover, upon my male servants and female servants in those days I will pour out my Spirit, and I will give portents in heaven above.” The promise is furnished, as it were, with a prophetic mouth. For after he has passed through the advantages of the present life, he joins spiritual distinctions, in which the people of God especially gloried. Accordingly, he promises that, besides the bodily goods mentioned, they will also acquire the adornments of revelations and attain an abundance of spiritual gifts.

Thus, when he says, “I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh,” he signifies both sexes and the diversity of ages. Finally, it follows: “Your sons and your daughters shall prophesy; and your old men shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions.” They will behold what is to come through different kinds of revelations. “Moreover, upon my male servants and female servants I will pour out my Spirit”—that is, just as no age will be excluded from these marks of holiness, so neither will any social condition regarded as lowly be excluded. Indeed, this sacred inundation will flow even among servants, if they are found capable of such gifts.

All these things are said to be fulfilled in the days of blessed Hezekiah, at least as a first stage. Since he had been hemmed in by the onset of dangers and confined within severe straits, and had been defended against the hope of the neighboring nations by religion alone, the prophet therefore describes that very time with great rhetorical grandeur and in a corresponding pattern, clearly to express the power of God, by whose aid the city could emerge from so great a flood.

According to this interpretation, the speech of our prophet proceeded in due order. For besides the consolation of restored resources, he promised the distinguished gifts of the Spirit—that is, of revelations—by which that people would be shown especially to belong to God. Therefore they ought to trust amid adversity, since one who was dear and even precious to God could not perish miserably. Through the testimony of the prophet whom we are discussing, we also gather that something was shown through dreams, as through lesser and more familiar oracles, which could serve for consolation.

On this occasion, it seems necessary to distinguish what we read in Deuteronomy (chapter 18), namely, that we should not believe dreams. For how are dreams now referred to the gifts of the Holy Spirit, if faith in them is there understood to be entirely abolished? Hence it is clear that, although both statements possess equal authority, a distinction of reasoning must be applied, and that the matter depends on whether the case of the dreamer is appropriate: just as one statement is judged according to the merits of the person, so the other is to be assessed according to its own weight. We should understand that some assistance may have been conveyed through dreams. But if there is no testimony that the time or the person warrants, the images of dreams must be rejected as having no legal authority.

[497] But let us hear what he has now added at length. “I will give portents in heaven and on earth: blood, and fire, and vapor of smoke. The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes; and everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.”

It is customary for prophets, whenever God is announced as rising in indignation either to defend or to avenge, to describe the appearance of the heavens as changed and the elements themselves as trembling. Such is the passage in blessed David, who, fleeing from the encounter and appearance of the heavenly champion, says: “Smoke rose up in his anger, and fire flared from his face; coals were kindled by him. He inclined the heavens and came down,” and the rest.

Accordingly, in the manner just mentioned, which derives from the usage of the Law, the prophet now too, as the time of a heavenly visitation approaches, announces beforehand that the elements will be traversed by fire and the stars covered either with smoke or with blood [Note: “Blood” would be preferable. The meaning is that the stars are to be changed into the nature of blood.]. This is not because these things happened exactly as they are stated, but either because such an arrangement of the heavens was appropriate to the heavenly ruler, or because his sentence would bring about an effect so easily—as though the terrified world and the elements rushing about carried it out—that such anxiety would finally seize the minds of the guilty as if the structure of the heavens were being dissolved, the moon were becoming bloody, the earth were turning to ash, and the stars were growing black.

What therefore occurred in the minds as something to be feared is narrated as though it happened to the elements themselves. For that final convulsion, and the only one of its kind, is believed to be inflicted upon the earth or the stars at the very end of the world. But in the time of the prophet whom we are discussing, it was not such a disturbance that fell upon heaven and earth, as I said above, but upon the minds of the guilty alone. Since we have discerned its character and manner, let us investigate the sequence of the narrative as well.

He therefore declares all those things that are recorded as having been fulfilled in the days of blessed Hezekiah. Since the ten tribes had already been transferred to the lands of the Medes and the Assyrian army had invaded the territory of Judah, and since Sennacherib was besieging other cities, he sent to Jerusalem a certain Rabshakeh with a large portion of his forces. As we began to say above, Rabshakeh tried to entice the people to surrender in the Hebrew language, which he knew. Those in command of the walls began insistently to request that he speak in the Syrian language and not in Hebrew.

Then Rabshakeh added the weight of the greatest terror, asserting that he had brought disaster and the greatest destruction not upon a few families but upon the entire nation, unless it accepted the king’s authority. By these threats blessed Hezekiah and the remnant of that people were so crushed that they turned to the prophet Isaiah with a great outpouring of tears, saying: “The children have come to the point of birth, but there is no strength to bring forth”—that is, they had reached the constriction of spirit that they would have felt at the time of childbirth if there were no strength in the woman giving birth [Note: This reading is not satisfactory here. Perhaps *usque* should be restored, or something similar.].

With Hezekiah and the Jews placed amid that heat of impending danger, the sun seemed to be turned into darkness and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of the Lord came—the day that would transfer that mass of atrocious destruction from the Jewish people and turn it against the Assyrians by a sudden exercise of power. He therefore called the day of the Lord terrible and great, not because it was grievous to the faithful, but because it was worthy of reverence on account of the majesty of its action.

Finally it follows:

**Verse 32.**—“And it shall be: everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved. For on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there shall be salvation.”

On that mountain, I say, where shortly before the exhaustion of their strength had promised scarcely any defense; in that city, I say, which had conceived its peoples for liberty as a feeble mother conceives children to be brought forth into this world—or rather, which, deprived of the strength to give birth, threatened certain destruction to the fetus—there suddenly appeared so glorious a defense that nowhere except there was salvation secure.

“And it shall be: everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved. For on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there shall be salvation, as the Lord has said, and among the remnant whom the Lord shall call.”

All these events, which were accomplished with the highest praise of our divine champion, are taught to have been fulfilled more abundantly in spiritual gifts at the time of the Lord’s Incarnation. Thus the miracles that preceded in the time of the fathers appear to have possessed not only historical but also prophetic force, since they were effective signs of things that would be brought about much later.

For in this way, at the time of the Lord’s Passion, when the author of life entered into the bitterest death, an unexpected night took away the daylight at midday. “From the sixth hour,” he says, “darkness came over the whole land until the ninth hour” (Matthew 24)—so that the luminary, having laid aside the beauty of its innate brightness beneath a darkened face, seemed either to perform the office of one mourning or of one afraid: they were unwilling to look upon the insult offered to the Creator or the crime of the Jews before the great and terrible day of the Lord should come, that is, before the glory of the Resurrection should shine forth.

Or certainly this was the day that our Lord arranged in the Gospel, as it were, under a twofold account. For when he presented the signs of the final age, he first described the destruction of Jerusalem and the calamities with which the region of the Jews would be filled. Just as there he joined the end of the world to the overthrow of Jerusalem, so also this entire disturbance of the elements and stars in the prophet will be fully accomplished at the end of the world, when, as blessed Peter says, “the heavens, burning with great force, shall pass away, and the elements shall be dissolved by the heat of fire” (2 Peter 3:10).

Then [Ant. “Now”] faith alone will protect its own, and whoever calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved. “For on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there shall be salvation, as the Lord has said, and among the remnant whom the Lord shall call.”

“Jerusalem,” he says, “the heavenly city, which is the mother of the godly: all who migrate to eternal joys shall be enrolled in its citizenship. Yet they are all called ‘the remnant,’ because many are called but few are chosen” (Matthew 13).

But let us also examine what follows.

# CHAPTER III
