**Verses 1–3.**—“For behold, in those days and at that time, when I restore the captivity of Judah and Jerusalem, I will gather all the nations and bring them down [Al. *lead them*] into the valley of Jehoshaphat; and there I will contend with them concerning my people and my inheritance Israel, whom they scattered among the nations and divided my land. They also cast lots over my people; they gave a boy to a prostitute and sold a girl for wine, so that they might drink.”

Having brought to an end the extended exposition of the meaning that had proceeded at length, he returns to the times with which the prophecy had begun, and dwells upon those events that he sees about to be fulfilled. He does this either to confirm, by the testimony of those events, the credibility of what he promised would come much later, or to show that he has not abandoned his concern to provide counsel, since he has assumed the impulse of one prophesying—as though he were saying: “If those things that are to come in the distant future are summoned according to the reckoning of their own time, let us now deal with what is present and imminent.”

By now the ten tribes have migrated under the Assyrian’s transfer; an army hostile to Judah is laying waste the land, and no hope remains of forces with which to resist. I therefore announce that the champion is now especially at hand: he will repel the captivity of his people, namely Judah, which already seemed to be impending, and after its hope of salvation had been abandoned, he will bestow the glory of vengeance, to be celebrated throughout the world.

When the Assyrian multitude has gathered for the siege of Jerusalem, he says, “I will make them subject to punishment in such a way that they will appear to have been brought not so much to war as to a tribunal. When I begin to conduct the case in the valley of Jehoshaphat, I will repay the Assyrians and their various enemies what they deserve, so that the destruction sent upon them may consume the nobles, while the people left behind are subjected to the evils of captivity. Those who sold the children of my people into slavery or disgrace will themselves also suffer the decisions of those who conduct the slave market; and they will experience the fruits of their former audacity, since, because they recently invaded my fields, they must endure the harshest ravagers of their own lands.”

**Verses 4–8.**—“But what have you to do with me, Tyre and Sidon, and all the territory of the Philistines? Will you repay me with vengeance? And if you take vengeance, will you take vengeance against me? Quickly and swiftly I will return your recompense upon your head. For you took my silver and gold, and you brought my desirable and most beautiful things into your temples. You sold the children of Judah and the children of Jerusalem to the children of the Greeks, in order to remove them far from their borders. Behold, I will raise them up from the place where you sold them, and I will return your recompense upon your head. I will sell your sons and your daughters into the hands of the children of Judah, and they shall sell them to the Sabeans, a distant nation, because the Lord has spoken.”

The wickedness and hatred of the neighboring peoples by whom the Jews were surrounded was often exposed even by a slight occasion. Since they could not attack the Jews with their own forces, they joined the armies of more powerful enemies. In condemning their crime, the psalm sings:

“The tent of the Edomites, the Ishmaelites, Moab and the Hagarenes, Gebal and Ammon, Amalek, and the foreign peoples with the inhabitants of Tyre. For Assur also came with them; they became an aid to the children of Lot” (Psalm 82).

Accordingly, when the neighboring nations had mixed their forces with the Assyrians to overthrow Zion, the divine judgment of the speech confronts them and, as it were, demands from them an account of such an injury.

Then he responds to those who have been convicted and remain silent, lest they perhaps recall the memory of an earlier grievance—namely, when the children of Israel, under the leadership of Joshua son of Nun, came out of Egypt, entered the Promised Land, and possessed what had been handed over to them according to fixed boundaries.

“Are you therefore,” he says, “preparing, in a rebellious spirit, to avenge that time? And, as though you had found an opportunity, are you attempting to recover the territories you occupied? But if such a meditation has stirred you, the vengeance rushing upon you will expose both your weakness and your profaneness. For you will not merely be unable to alter anything of the ancient decrees; you yourselves will stand under the authority of those whom you think you are going to oppress through your conspiracies.”

He enumerates the evils of captivity through various forms, which are inflicted according to the whims of the wrongdoers. Thus, after saying that they had carried off gold and silver with the greed of plunderers, he added, “and you brought my desirable and most beautiful things into your temples,” indicating either the remaining household furnishings or various ornaments.

Together with these ornaments of their homes, you also sold the children of the wretched. You will experience in return what sort of grief this creates for bereaved parents. For, when the one whose judgments you attempt to overturn exacts vengeance, the time will come when the Jews will not only obtain the joys of liberation but also feed upon the pleasure of revenge. They will sell your sons not to neighboring nations, from whom they might hope for their return, but to the Sabaeans, whom pagan writers called Meroe.

[Note: Ptolemy places the Sabeans in Arabia between the Macae and the Anchitae, above Mount Climax. Agatharchides likewise calls the people of the Sabeans the greatest of all, *kata tēn Arabian* (κατὰ τὴν Ἀραβίαν, “throughout Arabia”). Eustathius, in his commentary on Dionysius, considers them the same people whom he calls Sabas (Σάβας), and says that they inhabit Arabia Felix, Εὐδαίμονα. Later, however, drawing from the same Dionysius, he notes that they are also found in Persia: “they are also found among the Persians” (εὕρονται δὲ καὶ Περσικοί). Moreover, they are found in India: “the Sabaeans are also an Indian people” (καὶ Ἰνδικὸν ἔθνος οἱ Σάβαι εὑρίσκονται). Finally, in Thrace: “there was also a Thracian people called the Sabaeans” (ἦσαν δὲ καὶ ἔθνος Θρακικὸν Σάβαι).

To these I add Jerome on this same passage of Joel. “The Sabaeans,” he says, “are said to be a people beyond India; the Queen of Sheba, who came, belonged to them,” and so forth, although some suppose the Sabaeans to be Arabians.

Thus, amid the various opinions of the authors, you see no one who agrees with our author and interprets the Sabeans as Meroe, or summons them from that peninsula or island of Ethiopia beneath Egypt. For the region of Meroe, together with its city of the same name, lies between the rivers Nile and Astaboras, as ancient and modern geographers report.

Our author seems to have learned this not from pagan writers, as he wishes it to be believed, but from Josephus, who in Book VII, chapter 2, of the *Antiquities* thought that the Queen of Sheba who came to Solomon was the queen of Ethiopia; and earlier, in Book II, chapter 5, he calls the city of Saba the royal city of Ethiopia, which Cambyses later named Meroe after his sister.

I would not deny that there was also a Saba and Sabaeans in Ethiopia. But as far as the passage before us is concerned, I would dare to accuse our author of error, and likewise Josephus, from whom he allowed himself to be deceived. To omit the fact that Ethiopia’s Saba is by no means famous for an abundance of frankincense, as is the region in Arabia Felix near the Arabian Gulf, by which name it is praised in Scripture: the former, the Saba located in Ethiopia, is written with *samekh*, whereas the latter, that of Arabia, is written with *shin*. Psalm 72 carefully distinguishes the two: “kings shall offer gifts, Shaba and Saba,” of which the Greek translator renders the first as Ἀράβων (“of the Arabians”), and from him the Vulgate has *Arabum*, while he renders the second as Saba.

This Saba, then—the one for whose sake we have pursued this discussion of the passage in Joel—is written with *shin*, so that the reference should by no means be understood of the Ethiopians but certainly of the Arab Sabeans.]

This entire event seems to have been fulfilled either immediately after the departure of the Assyrians, or after the return from the Babylonian captivity, in the days of the Maccabees.

It must be noted, however, that not everything that happened in those times can reasonably be transferred to a spiritual understanding, that is, to the signification of the Gospel gift, just as other matters that we mentioned shortly before—concerning the disturbance of the stars, the magnitude of the portents, and the outpouring of gifts—both occurred in those times and are believed to have been and to be more abundantly fulfilled in the Lord’s Passion or at his final Judgment.

Therefore, I say, not everything that the prophet appended to these matters is joined to the spiritual interpretation in the same way. For whom shall we understand as the Tyrians, the Sidonians, or the remaining territories bordering the Philistines, beyond the simple meaning, so that we may imagine them to have sold the children of the faithful? If, nevertheless, we imagine that they seduced them into vices and also sold them [Ant. *fingantur*, “may be imagined”], how will he threaten them with the same recompense, so that we might in turn hand their children over to Sabean merchants?

We must therefore retain this rule of interpretation: while the discourse proceeds according to its straightforward sense, matters appropriate to future mysteries may sometimes be interwoven through prophetic excess. But once that task has again been completed, the narrative must be brought back to the circumstances of its own time and proceed accordingly, either by way of threat or exhortation.

Thus blessed Joel, after indicating briefly, in the prophetic impulse, what would come even in the final ages, returns to the circumstances of his own time. Having threatened the neighboring enemies with destruction, he proceeds to unfold the joys whose approach he already perceived, so that they might both give credibility to what would come much later [Note: Earlier the reading was *ventis*. Do not think this was a printer’s error: the older editor had distinguished it in the so-called Italic type and had taken it as the word of the sacred text.] and announce what was about to be displayed; and so that he might flood those for whom he was preparing consolation with the joy they were to receive.

He then introduces the spectacle, as he had begun, for the announcement of these events.

[Col. 1055B] **Verses 9–12.**—“Proclaim this among the nations; sanctify war; stir up the strong. [Note: Here we have restored the word *Accedant*, “Let them approach,” which had dropped out because of the similarity of what follows; likewise *vestra*, “your,” after *aratra*, “plowshares”; and finally *Dominus*, “the Lord,” after *faciet*, “will make.” All these words are found both in the Hebrew and in most copies.] Let all the men of war approach and ascend. Beat your plowshares into swords and your pruning hooks into spears. Let the weak man say, ‘I am strong.’ Break forth and come, all you nations from every side, and gather yourselves together. There the Lord shall cause your strong men to fall. Let the nations arise and ascend into the valley of Jehoshaphat.”

He expressed, through this image of exhortation—which contains the force of judgment—with how great a desire for war they would ascend to the destruction of Judah. “Every cultivator of the fields,” he says, “has seized weapons; they have changed their sickles into swords and their plowshares into javelins. Some, even though they declined military service either because of bodily weakness or because of the disadvantage of old age, nevertheless ran willingly to battle, trusting that they would surely achieve victory because of the multitude of forces that both the Assyrian prince of war and the other lesser neighboring enemies were bringing.”

You, however, know the profound plan of our champion [Note: It seems that *aut nescitis*, “or you do not know,” should be read, or something similar.]. For when all your multitude has gathered at the valley of Jehoshaphat—that is, at the siege of Jerusalem—with a proud and savage spirit, he says, then just destruction will take its turn against you.

And because you directed insults against me as you used to hurl weapons at those whom you encountered, you will tremble from the very place from which you could not at all have suspected danger. No battle lines will advance against you with standards, nor will any cry of combatants resound. Instead, all of you will fall in a single night, struck by the Angel; and, as though incapable of a great contest, you will be handed over, with a certain contempt and mockery, to eternal sleep by the night’s pleasant rest that had previously deceived you.

**Verses 13–16.**—“Multitudes, multitudes in the valley of destruction, for the day of the Lord is near in the valley of destruction. The sun and the moon have been darkened, and the stars have withdrawn their brightness. And the Lord shall roar from Zion and give his voice from Jerusalem. The heavens and the earth shall be shaken; but the Lord is the hope of his people and the strength of the children of Israel.”

“Properly,” he says, “the valley of Jehoshaphat is called the valley of destruction. For, as the enemies supposed, the destruction of the Jews was destined to occur there. But because their profane hope failed them and the sentence of vengeance was directed against them, this valley will be called the valley of destruction—but Assyrian destruction.

When the hostile forces first gathered there, such anxiety and fear seized those shut up in Jerusalem that even the great stars seemed to shine for them no longer. But when the Almighty champion undertook the work of vengeance, the darkness created by anguish of mind fell upon the minds and eyes of the barbarians. Our God sprang forth to avenge with such majesty that he seemed to emit not merely a cry like that of battling commanders but even certain roars and growls. The elements themselves could not have expressed the force and magnitude of these things, any more than human hearts could.

For he says: ‘The Lord shall roar from Zion and give his voice from Jerusalem; and the heavens and the earth shall be shaken. The Lord is the hope of his people and the strength of the children of Jerusalem.’”

Thus, as we have said, this reversal will take place: the darkness that the Jewish people had first experienced—not as resting upon the stars but as resting upon the breasts of the fearful—will thereafter be suffered by the hostile multitude, so that the stars themselves will seem to grow black and the elements to totter.

Strength, therefore, will come to the children of Israel [503] [Note: This alludes to the first part of the following verse: “And you shall know that I am the Lord your God, dwelling on Mount Zion, my holy mountain.” From this passage also one may learn how different the division of the verses once was from that which now prevails.], and, instructed by the dangers of events, they will know that their God is the Lord of the whole earth, who nevertheless, because of his great mercy, deigns to dwell on Mount Zion.

## Verses 17–18

“And Jerusalem shall be holy, and strangers shall no longer pass through it. And it shall come to pass on that day that the mountains shall drip sweetness, the hills shall flow with milk, and waters shall run through all the streams of Judah.”

“The appearance,” he says, “of the whole region shall be changed from sorrowful to joyful.” And since it is the distinctive mark of our nation to be called holy, not only the Temple but also the entire city’s walls shall be made so venerable by the wonder of its prosperity that no profane person will be thought able to approach it.

Such abundant prosperity shall accompany this sweet freedom that honey will seem to flow not only from beehives [Al. “baskets”] or trees, but from the mountains themselves; and that, as though in return for the grace of springs, all the torrents will be changed into streams, so that they may not cease to pour forth an uninterrupted abundance.

[Col. 1056C] “This new blessed abundance of streams,” he says, “they shall obtain from that fountain which bursts forth from the inner sanctuaries [*adytis*] of the house of God.”

[Note: We have corrected the text to read *qui de domus Dei erumpit adytis consequentur*—“which bursts forth from the inner sanctuaries of the house of God, they shall obtain [it]”; that is, the people, or my nation, which has just been praised, shall possess it. Formerly the reading was corrupt and meaningless: *de domo Dei erumpit, aditis consequentur*. The Author alludes to the second half of the proposed verse 18, which he omits: “And a fountain shall go forth from the house of the Lord and water the Torrent of Thorns.”]

All these things are certainly said either by way of exaggeration, or because peoples rejoicing in the recovery of their well-being experience such emotions: just as above, when they were sorrowful and placed in the utmost danger, the stars seemed to be darkened and the elements to tremble, so now, in an outpouring of joy, milk seems to flow from the rocks to those overcome with delight, honey from the mountains, torrents to be filled with springs, and not only meadows but even rocks to bloom with various flowers as though in springtime.

The fountain, too, shall go forth from the house of God and water the Torrent of Thorns—that is, it shall make places formerly occupied by brambles suitable for cultivation, by continually supplying the nourishment of irrigation.

This passage, in which Jerusalem’s prosperity is proclaimed, now also embraces the mysteries of the Church. The Church endured both the attacks of hostile power and those of the Jews and Gentiles alike; yet, when all these adversaries had melted away like water, it wonderfully grew strong and spread as a vineyard to the ends of the earth. Having crushed the profanation of idols, it flourished and, as though seated upon a throne of dominion received, took its place in august dignity. Insofar as its rules of instruction are concerned, it has been surrounded by the holiness of the commandments in such a way that no stranger—that is, no profane or criminal person—can pass through it.

Why should this be surprising, since Christ gave himself for it so that he might present to himself a Church “not having spot or wrinkle” (Eph. 5), but one that should remain holy and undefiled?

This virgin, therefore, dedicated to the fellowship of the eternal King, is separated in the present age from all the wicked by the discipline of virtue, and in the age to come by the happiness [504] of its rewards, so that no one may rest in those tabernacles except one who “walks without blemish” (Ps. 14) and practices righteousness.

Whoever, then, has received that eternal happiness in the blessed citizenship of that city will be so intoxicated with the abundance of God’s house (Ps. 35) that he will drink from a kind of torrent of holy pleasure and will perceive that pain and sorrow have likewise fled away.

This blessedness will indeed be bestowed in its fullness at the time of the resurrection; yet even in this life the Apostles and their disciples claimed for themselves the greater part of it. For when they were beaten by their persecutors, they rejoiced because they had been found worthy to suffer disgrace for the name of Christ (Acts 5).

From these lofty mountains of saving doctrines, then, we see honey flowing. For, as the prophet testifies, the sayings of God are sweet to the mouths of the devout, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb (Ps. 18).

From the hearts of the Apostles, I say, life-giving streams flowed forth into the world, and from the thickets into which they had fallen they restored fields, adorned with flowers and made heavy with crops. Why should this be surprising, since they received abundance from that fountain from which whoever drinks will thirst no more, but from whose own belly “rivers of living water” will flow (John 14).

Through these increases of gifts, therefore, which were conspicuous in the fullness of happiness, he promises the sweetness of vengeance.

## Verses 19–21

“Egypt,” he says, “shall be a desolation, and Edom a desert of destruction, because they acted wickedly against the sons of Judah and shed innocent blood in their land.”

The prophet has brought his discourse to a prophecy concerning his own time. Just as above he announced to the Tyrians and Sidonians a corresponding change of fortune, so now he threatens the Egyptians and Edomites on account of the same crimes.

We can transfer this to the affairs of the Church in the following way: if we call the Edomites and Egyptians cruel and darkened minds.

“And Judah shall be inhabited forever, and Jerusalem from generation to generation. And I will cleanse their blood, which I had not cleansed, and the Lord shall dwell in Zion.”

[Note: *Aedificabitur* (“shall be built”) appears to have been written through a copyist’s error; both the Hebrew and all the books of Jerome’s version read *habitabitur* (“shall be inhabited”).]

“When the Assyrians and the other peoples who had joined arms with them have been destroyed by a wondrous vengeance,” he says, “the inhabitants of Zion shall increase in all their hopes and actions, assume responsibility for religion, and become conspicuous with me as their protector.”

Just as we read that this was partly accomplished under Hezekiah, so we proclaim that it was fulfilled even more abundantly under the mediator of God and humanity. For he died on account of our sins and rose again for our justification (Rom. 4), so that, having been justified by faith, we might have peace with God—the one who promised that he would dwell in the midst of the city of Zion, saying: “Behold, I am with you all the days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28).

[Col. 1057]

# COMMENTARY ON THE PROPHET AMOS

## Book One

[Col. 1057C] With the explanation of the holy Joel completed, insofar as our ability, with God’s help, has brought it forth, the very order of our task calls us to the third prophet, who is called Amos—a man distinguished no less by the lowliness of his birth than by the eminence of his virtue.

Supported by no ancestral honors, he obtained a place among the prophets by his merits alone. I mean those prophets who provided not only instruction for the Synagogue but also the foundation of the Church, as the teacher of the Gentiles testifies when he commends the Church as being built upon the teaching of the apostles and prophets (Eph. 2).

Thus he advanced to that company shining with a star-like radiance, without the aid of illustrious birth but, as we have said, through the progress of his conduct and of his entire holy life. Even if he had taught nothing by speech, he would abundantly have proved by his example that devotion and dedication of mind are sufficient for attaining the true glory of happiness, since neither poverty nor obscurity can provide an obstacle to it.

And since we have learned how great were his merits, let us hear what he taught.

# CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 1057D]

## Verse 1

“The words of Amos, who was among the shepherds of Tekoa [Al. Thecue], which he saw concerning Israel in the days of Uzziah king of Judah and in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash king of Israel, two years before the earthquake, and he said.”

We must first observe that the period of this prophet is the same as that of the preceding prophets, namely Hosea and Joel. At that time impiety prevailed most strongly among the Ten Tribes, which are called Israel. It was as though the lights by which they might have been distinguished had been entirely gouged out, and the people loved the darkness with which they had clothed themselves, so that they paid no attention whatsoever either to salutary admonitions or to severe blows. Joining shamelessness to impiety, they seemed to embrace both their sins and their miseries.

Since, therefore, our Lord, girding himself for the task of vengeance, announced the same thing beforehand in various ways—especially since his intention was more to correct than to punish—he foretells what he knows he will bring upon them.

“Two years,” he says, “before the earth was shaken by a prodigious movement.” Although the history of the Kings does not record that this happened, we are satisfied with the prophet himself as our authority, and we do not doubt that the shaking of the earth preceded the coming calamity as its indication.

Thus, through intervals of time that delayed the vengeance, the people are admonished to consider correction, and a display of terror is made lest they begin to experience the full weight of terror itself.

[Note: Earlier editions read *serio*; we have restored *serius* (“more slowly” or “later”).]

When this arrangement accomplishes nothing among them, they are deprived not only of security but also of excuse.

The moderation of the preacher himself, who was exalted by the greatness of his revelations, should also be noted. He attained the dignity by which he became renowned through the support of his character alone, not of his birth, unlike others whose ancestors are enrolled in titles. Yet he did not conceal the humble occupation by which he had been trained; rather, he indicated that he had always persisted in tending flocks at Tekoa.

Tekoa is said to have been a village in which a large number of shepherds lived,

[Note: Its ancient inhabitant Jerome counts only six miles. “This prophet,” he says, “was from the town of Tekoa, which lies six miles south of holy Bethlehem,” and so forth. In his second commentary on Jeremiah, chapter 6, he says: “Tekoa, a village situated on a mountain and separated from Jerusalem by twelve miles.” We see it daily with our own eyes. By this he indicates that it lay on the road leading from Jerusalem to Hebron. As for what Our Author says—that from there the wilderness extends as far as the Ocean—Jerome states this more precisely, extending it to the Red Sea and to the boundaries of the Persians, Ethiopians, and Indians.]

and was separated from the city of Bethlehem by seven miles; beyond it a vast wilderness already stretches as far as the Ocean.

Thus, among shepherds who sought uncultivated places suitable for livestock, he commends the fact that he had been brought up, lest he appear elevated by the occasion of his new office and think too highly of himself.

He explained this purpose of serious modesty in the course of his work as well, saying: “I was not a prophet, nor the son of a prophet, but I was a shepherd, plucking fruit from brambles; and the Lord took me and sent me to prophesy.”

This is the virtue of modesty that the Doctor of the Gentiles also displayed when he said: “Lest I should be exalted by the greatness of the revelations, a thorn in my flesh was given to me, an angel of Satan, to buffet me. For this I besought the Lord three times, that he might depart from me, and he said to me: ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness’” (2 Cor. 12).

It was therefore evident to prophetic eyes that the earthquake signified the convulsion of an empire; and he calls it the roar of the angry Lord.

[Note: The word *esse*—“to be”—seems to have to be deleted. The following verse begins: “And he said: The Lord shall roar from Zion,” and so forth.]

## Verse 2

“And from Jerusalem,” he says, “he shall give his voice.”

This was plainly a voice appropriate to his anger, not to his nature, that roared.

[Note: It would certainly be preferable to supply an understood verb, and to arrange the text with a *τελεία στιγμή*—a full stop—placed here, in this manner: “Therefore the eternal Judge has roared; the trembling of the world …”]

Therefore the trembling of the world proclaims the eternal Judge. Its violence was so great that immediately the green growth of the grasses perished, and nourishment was withdrawn not only from human beings but also from flocks.

For he called the lovely places the cheerful pastures of the shepherds, and intended the dried-up summit of Carmel to bear the same significance.

[Note: The sacred text reads: “And the beautiful places of the shepherds mourned, and the summit of Carmel was dried up,” etc.] Shepherds are accustomed to seek pasture especially on the summits of hills during the summer. In announcing that all these places would be dried up by that convulsion of the earth, he seems also to have indicated that something had occurred in accordance with natural expectation.

Many who have been curious about such matters suppose that they can establish drought as a cause of earthquakes, and attempt to prove this by examples and persuade others through argument. It is not necessary to repeat those arguments to you now; I have mentioned them briefly because the movement, scarcely begun, inflicted a double blow.

Whether the great convulsion produced drought, as though the channels of the springs had been disturbed; or whether a prior lack of moisture first caused the earth to dry out and afterward to tremble, so that, as the pastures perished, the harms of drought became evident—in either case it displays the same power of the Judge. As he preserves what he has created through his goodness, so, when necessary, he disturbs those same things through his indignation.

By way of allegory, we might suppose that the name “shepherds” signifies the rulers and kings of different nations, and that the summit of Carmel signifies the power they possessed when they lived prosperously—especially since this prophet’s speech is also directed toward various nations. Yet the former explanation is simpler and more appropriate to the histories, if we understand the various kinds of affliction to have been imposed upon profane peoples.

But let us now see what the avenging one cries out as he roars.

[Col. 1060A]

## Verses 3–5

“Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Damascus, and for four, I will not turn him back, because they threshed Gilead with iron threshing-sledges. And I will send fire upon the house of Hazael, and it shall devour the houses of Ben-hadad. And I will break the bar of Damascus, and destroy the inhabitant from the plain of the idol, and the one who holds the scepter from the house of pleasure and luxury, and the people of Syria shall be carried away to Cyrene, says the Lord.”

[Note: “And luxury” is an ancient addition. Although other books, and especially the Hebrew text, do not contain it, older manuscript copies of Jerome’s version retain it; three of these were cited in our edition.]

“We know,” says the Apostle, “that whatever the law says, it says to those who are under the law” (Rom. 3:19).

Since, therefore, the prophets also had the task of reproving the crimes of the people living under the law, and blessed Amos was directing his attention especially to the Ten Tribes called Israel, our God nevertheless, for the sake of a providential and manifold purpose, introduced mention of other nations as well, whom he distinguishes according to the standard of just judgment. He did this just as he did with the Jewish people, who were excessively arrogant toward him because they lived separately from the others, despite their lives not deserving such a distinction.

When they hear that neighboring nations are summoned for examination no less than their own Tribes, they will surely understand that the Lord is the one creator of all nations.

In the very fact that Israel’s suffering is avenged upon neighboring peoples, their pride is also humbled, so that they may finally perceive that he is not only the God of the Jews but also of the Gentiles, since no nation’s actions are stripped of their due recompense, whether of consolation or of vengeance.

Finally, he shows how ready he is to spare, since he rises to anger with such difficulty that one fault or two never moves him unless three or four have come together. Yet this number is taught to have been assumed for an indefinite quantity—not to signify literally four crimes, but many.

He likewise indicates that he exercises the same desire to forgive even toward other nations when he excuses his own anger by the example of another’s iniquity.

“For three crimes of Damascus,” he says, “and for four, I will not turn him back, because they threshed Gilead with iron threshing-sledges.”

Justice, coeternal with my throne, acted, he says, so that at last I might assume the office of judge, and demonstrate to them, when the condition of the guilty had been turned to sorrow, a cruelty that was at once manifold and shameless.

[Note: *Horrorem* (“terror”) seems preferable to *horrore*, and likewise *impudentem* (“shameless”) to *impendentem* (“impending”).]

For the people of Damascus did not ravage Israel’s fields only once or twice, but very often. They crushed Gilead with iron threshing-sledges and threshing instruments so thoroughly that they considered it an agreeable spectacle if, like ears of grain and stalks, the limbs of the inhabitants were scattered across the fields and trampled.

[Note: Supply *si* (“if”), *cum* (“when”), or something similar here.]

Since I could not and ought not to endure this savagery unpunished for so long, I will send fire into the house of Hazael, king of Damascus, and it shall devour the houses of Ben-hadad, who succeeded his father Hazael in the kingdom.

I will break the bar of Damascus and destroy the inhabitant from the plains of the idol, and the one who holds the scepter from the house of pleasure—that is, I will involve in the evils of captivity the profane inhabitants of those places, as well as all the leading men and nobles who spent all their time in pleasures.

[Note: Here, although I make no change, I would nevertheless prefer *onus*—“burden”—to *ejus*, since the sense is disturbed.]

And so that they may neither be unaware of that captivity nor claim hope of return, when they see their houses collapse into ashes, they themselves shall be led to the fields of Cyrene.

In the book of Kings we read again how these kings whom the prophet mentions—namely Hazael and Ben-hadad—harassed the Ten Tribes with frequent incursions and brought them to the extremity of misery.

Therefore, lest that victory seem to have come happily to the Syrians, the cause of the calamity and punishments that are described is also set forth.

[Note: The earlier Editor testifies that *causa* was written for *causam* in an ancient manuscript, from which alone he published these Commentaries. I would therefore prefer, without changing that word, to try the following correction, replacing *illic* with *illis* and restoring the remainder with it, including *futurae* for *facere*, in this form: “The cause of the future calamity of those people is also described in the punishments.”]

But let us proceed to the remaining matters.

## Verses 6–8

“Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Gaza, and for four, I will not turn him back, because he carried away a complete captivity, to shut it up in Edom. And I will send fire upon the wall of Gaza, and it shall devour its houses; and I will destroy the inhabitant from Ashdod, and the one who holds the scepter from Ashkelon. And I will turn my hand against Ekron, and the remnants of the Philistines shall perish, says the Lord.”

Following the same order of narration that he had used above against Damascus, he enumerates the crimes and punishments of the city of Gaza as well. He assumes the character, so to speak, of one asking whether he ought to maintain such long patience toward people so attached to crimes that they thought they had perpetrated nothing cruel unless they had repeated it three or four times, and had displayed extraordinary eagerness in wrongdoing—people who fed not only upon their own crimes but also upon those of others.

For Gaza took pains to ensure that the Edomites, the descendants of Esau—whom history records as the brother of blessed Jacob (Gen. 25)—would inflict punishment upon the Jewish people.

“These men,” says the prophet, “who, though joined to us by blood, were separated from us by murderous hatred, made use of the aid of the Gazans. The savage nation did not devote my blood to alien hatreds for its own advantage, but raged against me as much as parricides would deem sufficient.”

He shows how he will destroy this profession of wickedness:

“And I will send fire upon the wall of Gaza, and it shall devour its houses; and I will destroy the inhabitant from Ashdod, and the one who holds the scepter from Ashkelon; and I will turn my hand against Ekron, and the remnants of the Philistines shall perish, says the Lord.”

Under cover of one city, he runs through the names of other towns as well, cities of which we frequently read in the history of the Kings that they were engaged in almost continual conflict with the Jewish people.

These are the people who, after defeating the Jewish army, carried the Ark of the Covenant away as though it had been captured and transferred it to the shrine of the idol called Dagon (1 Sam. 5 and following).

After the Ark had made its power known by the shattering of Dagon’s statue and the ensuing calamity among the people, they returned it with the proper ceremonies; yet they did not embrace the worship of God on account of such miracles, but persisted in their ingenuity [Note: that is, “resourcefulness,” “obstinacy,” and so forth], character, and rites.

These people, therefore, raging continually against God’s people with hatred, whenever they could not wage war in their own name, joined their forces and arms with those of greater enemies. This happened especially at the time when the Assyrians invaded the territories of the Jews. The prophet whom we have been discussing complains that Israel, exhausted by them, was afflicted, and he shows that all the nations surrounding the Jews labored with a kind of competitive zeal for their destruction.

Since, therefore, you too added heaps of evils during their adversity, and their misery aroused in you not a more neighborly feeling—that is, mercy—but rather greater savagery, you shall at least learn the magnitude of your crime when vengeance overtakes you, since you refused to understand it by reason.

The fire of invasion will be sent, and it will devour not only houses but also groves—that is, it will consume ornaments and memorials alike.

Thus it will destroy your inhabitants with slaughter, so that there will be no exception even among the nobles who hold scepters, whether they were truly supported by power or conspicuous for the pleasures and delights of this life, so that they could even be called kings. I shall stretch out the hand of my aversion over them all, so that even the remnants of the Philistines will be consumed and one devastation will rage from the highest to the lowest.

This is also what the preceding prophet indicated when he accused Tyre, Sidon, and all the territories of the Philistines because they had carried away silver and gold and everything precious from the borders of Israel, and had sold the sons of the people—born in freedom—to Greek and Barbarian merchants, so that, carried far from their ancestral regions, they might suffer exile and slavery together.

## Verses 9–10

“Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Tyre, and for four, I will not turn him back, because they shut up a complete captivity in Edom and did not remember the covenant of brothers. And I will send fire upon the wall of Tyre, and it shall devour its houses.”

He accuses Tyre of the crime that he had recently charged against Gaza: namely, that it hastened to shut up not some small portion but a complete captivity in Edom, so that it might fill the Edomites with the miseries of the Jews, out of hatred for their hostile brother.

Therefore vengeance will come, which will both imitate and surpass the form of your crime. You stirred up, through your assistance, the burning envy that sought the destruction of your brothers, and you did not remember—that is, you were entirely unwilling to consider—the covenant that nature itself established between brothers,

[Note: The words *germina nos*, which had previously been read as two words with no meaning, have been corrected without hesitation. We have restored the single word *germanos*—“brothers.”]

whose virtue would not consist so much in loving one another as their crime would consist in hating one another. You stirred them not merely into quarrels but even into battles, as though they were complete strangers to one another, neither known to one another by speech nor recognized by reputation.

Consequently, burning vengeance will seize you, and the great pleasures for which you had become famous will be changed into horrible squalor. Such devastation will be applied that both the foundations and the summits of the lofty tower and wall will lie in ashes.

## Verses 11–12

“Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Edom, and for four, I will not turn him back, because he pursued his brother with the sword, violated his mercy, continued his fury beyond measure, and kept his indignation to the end. I will send fire upon Teman, and it shall devour the houses of Bozrah.”

He continues the established order of his discourse and addresses various nations in reproach, nations that he knew to be connected with the Jews both by their crimes and by their borders.

He placed the Edomites after Tyre in an orderly fashion because they too burned with murderous impiety against the Jews. What he had announced would be punished in the case of the Tyrians—namely, that they had aided the raging Edomites by their counsels, so that they might feed more easily upon their brothers’ miseries—he now likewise charges against the descendants of Esau for the same crimes and assigns them to vengeance. He did this lest, after announcing that recompense was due to the allies of the Jews’ crimes, he should seem to have spared the actual authors of the crime.

He therefore says that this people sinned with a murderous spirit not once but repeatedly, and that, if a single offense might perhaps deserve pardon, its persistent and deadly repetition demanded vengeance.

He pursued his brother not with a quarrel but with the sword, and forgot the mercy—or [Note: This word had previously been corruptly read as *claritatis*. The preceding correction also sheds light on this passage.] the love—that kinship required.

Nor was he content to rage in a kind of outburst of indignation.

[Note: There can be no doubt that this derives from the verb *furo*, “to rage.” A little later we likewise read: “Thus he raged, as though …”; and again near the beginning of chapter 3, the prophet charges that they raged in this way.]

“He devoted a long period,” he says, “to his crime.”

He added considerable force to the accusation by saying: “He continued his fury beyond measure and kept his indignation to the end.”

For he not only departed from the conduct proper to brothers by pursuing his brother with battles, but also failed to preserve the very custom of those whom he inflames to bloody struggles with the torches of indignation.

For he raged as though he would soon cease; he persisted in hatred as though he had been moved by justice rather than by fury.

Therefore the fire shall rightly remain upon him until the consummation, so that cities and fortresses, just as they had been stained by the same crimes, may likewise be worn down by the same calamities.

By several names—namely Edom, Teman, and Bozrah—he indicates one people, the descendants of Esau, whose metropolitan city was called Bozrah.

He says that these people will be conquered in battle and siege, will suffer savagely at the discretion of their conquerors, and will perish through slaughter and burning. Some of these things are reported to have been inflicted by the Chaldaeans, others by the Maccabees.

## Verses 13–15

“Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of the sons of Ammon, and for four, I will not turn him back, because they ripped open the pregnant women of Gilead in order to enlarge their territory. And I will kindle a fire upon the wall of Rabbah, and it shall devour its houses amid a howl on the day of battle and amid a whirlwind on the day of commotion. And Milcom shall go into captivity, he and his princes together, says the Lord.”

Nor are these peoples—Ammon, namely, and Moab, descended from the stock of Lot—freed from murderous envy toward the Israelites. Thus those who are closest are exposed: although related to them, they could not endure Israel’s former glory and omitted no opportunity to harm Gilead.

Finally, when the Ammonites hastened to invade the region that, as Scripture relates, two Tribes and a half had received beyond the Jordan,

[Note: Perhaps *et dimidia* should more correctly be read instead of *in*, and so forth. The Transjordanian region was received from only half of one Tribe by Manasseh; the two complete Tribes were Reuben and Dan.]

they did not even refrain, he says, from slaughtering pregnant women. They desired to kill the very offspring of the Jews, so that, once the inhabitants had been destroyed, the entire territory of the Gileadites might be joined to their own borders.

“Therefore I will repay this people also according to what it deserves,” he says, “and I will cause the buildings of Rabbah, which was its capital, to grow old beneath the hostile fire.”

In the whirlwind of that war they will be so terrified that they will seem to die in advance. Not only their princes but also Milcom—that is, the idol whose divinity they believed would protect them—shall be carried away as a mockery into captivity.

# CHAPTER TWO

## Verses 1–3

“Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Moab, and for four, I will not turn him back, because he burned the bones of the king of Edom to ashes. And I will send fire upon Moab, and it shall devour the houses of Kerioth [Note: *Camoth* had previously been read here; shortly afterward we also removed the conjunction that disturbed the sense before the words ‘I will kill’]. And Moab shall die amid tumult and the sound of the trumpet. And I will destroy the judge from its midst, and I will kill all its princes with him, says the Lord.”

We must observe that, whereas he had charged all the nations he enumerated with the insults and dangers they had inflicted upon Israel, he now accuses the Moabites of having acted savagely against the king of Edom. He charges them with having raged so violently that, not content to wage war against a living man, they displayed their hatred even toward his corpse.

Through this the arrogance of the Jews, who believed that they alone belonged to the Lord, was also restrained; and a consolation of hope and a light of understanding were offered to the Gentiles, so that they might perceive that they existed under the providence and government of one Creator—one who would avenge not only injuries against the Jews but also those inflicted upon other nations.

## Verses 4–5

“Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Judah, and for four, I will not turn him back, because he rejected the law of the Lord and did not keep his commandments. For their idols deceived them, after which their fathers walked. And I will send fire upon Judah, and it shall devour the houses of Jerusalem.”

Having charged various nations with savage crimes, he comes to Judah and imputes to it the crime of neglected religion. He announces, in the same deliberative pattern with which he began, the necessity of conversion: those who stubbornly pursued every shameful and profane practice would suddenly pass from prosperity to sorrow.

We must not suppose that, because he judged the peoples whose crimes he had just reviewed to be acceptable in matters of religion, he found nothing to charge against them in that respect. Their profanation was manifest a thousand times over: they had always been devoted to the worship of idols and had no proper judgment concerning pious rites. He therefore does not charge them with neglecting a religion they had never possessed; rather, he charges them with those moral wounds that they could have recognized and avoided even while standing outside the true religion.

But he first charges Judah with that offense because it was more horrifying than all the others, and because the other crimes had rightly sprung from that stock.

“For they rejected,” he says, “the law of the Lord, by which alone they were conspicuous throughout the whole world. And, not content with rejecting it, they also passed over to the worship of idols.”

They shall therefore receive the payment they deserve, so that fire from the enemy may consume Judah and Jerusalem. This was fulfilled when Babylon conquered them.

### Verse 6

“Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Israel, and for four, I will not revoke it, because they sold the righteous for silver, and the poor for a pair of sandals.”

He accuses the Ten Tribes, which he calls Jerusalem, not—as he does Judah—of ritual offenses, but of crimes of conduct, so that he might show that they were so deeply stuck in profanation that they neither blushed nor feared to be reproved on this account. He therefore accuses the wounds of their conduct—not because they were more serious than those of their religious rites, but either because these fruits plainly appeared to arise from their corrupt religion, or because in this sphere of action too they proved themselves worse than the other nations. “My judgment,” he says, “will no longer tolerate their remaining in a condition in which shamelessness never breathes toward better things. A change from prosperity to adversity will overtake them, so that what they refused to learn when warned, they may begin to understand when condemned: namely, that I care for the poor, and that those who are destitute of this world’s resources are not deprived of the protection of my providence. Let concern for uprightness flourish among them alone, and their very modest circumstances—which made them lower than the rest—will render them acceptable and dear to me.”

I said this because the people of Israel neglected to regard the righteous and the poor, as though the latter relied upon a twofold advocacy before me. Yet, always hostile to my judgments, they trampled upon the poor and regarded the ornaments of the world as cheap as footwear—that is, they sinned in offices and business dealings with such success that they fed not only on the often enticing profits of short-lived gain, but frequently even on the unmerited sufferings of the righteous, considering it a kind of pleasure to trample into the dust the very heads of humble men—that is, men who avoided the evil of pride through the holy innocence of their lives.

[Note: We have substituted *si* (“if”) for the word formerly printed, *sui*. In the following verse the Author continues his exposition: “Those who trample upon the heads of the poor into the dust of the earth and turn aside the way of the humble; and a son and his father went in to the girl, to profane my holy name.”]

But when he says, “they turn aside the way of the humble,” this may be understood in two ways: either they turn away from it and follow a path of life altogether different, or else in their judgments they corrupt by fraud the just case of the poor. Such is the saying in the Psalm:

> “If you saw a thief, you ran with him,  
> and you placed your portion with adulterers.  
> Sitting, you spoke against your brother,  
> and against the son of your mother  
> you cunningly laid a snare” (Ps. 49:19).

[Note: I know of no original text or ancient Latin translation which agrees with the reading of this passage preferred by our Author (Col. 1064D).]

The guilt of the offenders is intensified in this interpretation, because they are shown not merely to neglect justice but deliberately to pursue what is ruinous, and even to hate it.

The prophet proceeds to recount different crimes. For after injustice and pride come the sins of lust.

[Note: Earlier editions read, “and the proud sins of lust,” etc. (Col. 1065D).]

“A son,” he says, “and his father went in to one girl, to profane my holy name.” He shows the heights to which the habit of sinning advances. “First,” he says, “you denied your fellow citizens justice in judgments and compassion in their distress. It immediately followed that even the laws of nature itself could no longer stand among you. Passing from other crimes to incest, sons rushed with their fathers upon prostitutes, so that they showed no reverence toward their parents any more than they had previously shown it toward their fellow citizens. By this crime of yours my holy name also was profaned, as the nations spoke among themselves: ‘What sort of God is that whose supposed special people appear so deformed?’”

[Note: The reading had hitherto been corrupt, with *secundum* (“second”) printed instead of *sanctum* (“holy”).]

### Verse 8

“And upon pledged garments they reclined beside every altar, and they drank the wine of those condemned in the house of their God.”

It was indeed to be expected that idolaters would exist amid manifold filthiness. Yet in everything this prophet reproves, he is concerned to express that they resisted the divine commandments deliberately, by which they violated every class of precept. Therefore, enumerating everything prohibited in the Law, he also declares that they reclined upon pledged garments.

He carefully added “beside every altar,” because their impiety had multiplied their altars. And therefore “they drank the wine of those condemned”—that is, they feasted in the temples on the money they had received from the prices paid for the innocent, plainly those of whom he had said shortly before that they had sold the righteous for silver and the poor for a pair of sandals.

### Verses 9–10

“Yet I destroyed the Amorite from before them, whose height was like the height of cedars and who was as strong as an oak; I destroyed his fruit above and his roots below. I am the one who brought you up from the land of Egypt and led you through the wilderness for forty years, so that you might possess the land of the Amorite.”

He maintains his customary practice: in order to aggravate the crime of the ungrateful, he recalls the benefits previously bestowed. Therefore, after reviewing their perverse and profane pursuits, to which they were devoted, he introduced a mention of the good things of which they had been seized by forgetfulness.

It is as though he said that he had been thoroughly deceived when he drove out ancient nations, superior in strength and power, in order to prepare a dwelling for these people, since they considered it a glorious contest if they could both imitate and surpass the crimes of those nations.

“Yet I destroyed the Amorite, whose height was like that of a cedar, and who was as strong as an oak; I destroyed his fruit above and his roots below” [Ancient edition: *above* instead of *below*].

“I cut down,” he says, like a diligent surveyor laying out a camp, the forest of the nations, already vigorous through long ages, threatening with lofty crowns and relying upon deep roots, so that they would not experience even slight hindrances to their habitation.

Whatever strength they possessed, therefore, I cut away by the roots, so that the forests of the natives—which my decision was removing—would not grow again, but so that the security added to the victory I had granted would complete its joy.

Why should I not have done so, since I had also bestowed benefits upon them in ancient times? When they were oppressed by Egyptian slavery, I raised them to the heights of freedom. Through pathless deserts I led them for forty years, supplying food and drink by miracles, so that possession of the fortunate lands that had been decreed for them might taste all the sweeter because it came later; and so that they might also learn that human life depends not on the fertility of trees but on God’s governing providence.

Nor was I content merely to provide the means of the present life. I also made you conspicuous through spiritual adornments:

[Note: These are the words of the sacred text, verses 11 and following: “And I raised up prophets from your sons, and Nazirites from your young men. Is this not so, sons of Israel?” says the Lord. “And you gave the Nazirites wine to drink, and commanded the prophets, saying, ‘Do not prophesy.’”]

“I raised up,” he says, “prophets from your sons, and Nazirites from your young men”—that is, men distinguished both by a special devotion and by sacred illumination, some possessing certain knowledge of future things, others a glorious struggle against sins.

Yet you not only regarded all these gifts as worthless; you also rejected them utterly, daring both to command the prophets not to prophesy and to give the Nazirites wine so that they might become drunk.

### Verses 13–16

“Behold, I will creak beneath you as a wagon creaks when loaded with hay. Flight shall perish from the swift; the strong shall not retain his strength, and the mighty shall not save his life. He who holds the bow shall not stand; the swift-footed shall not save himself; the rider of a horse shall not save his life. The strong-hearted among the mighty shall flee naked on that day,” says the Lord.

It is characteristic of the sacred Scriptures to employ images taken even from insignificant things for the purpose of conveying what they wish to illustrate, while ensuring that the kernel of mystical meaning remains within them. Thus here, because the just Judge had endured a people sinning for a long time, he declared himself weighed down like a wagon, though it was loaded with a worthless material.

When he says, “I will creak beneath you as a wagon creaks when loaded with hay,” he did not intend this to be understood as though a wagon filled with hay creaked in one way and one filled with silver in another. Rather, because he adapted for himself the likeness of a creaking wagon, he mingled the meanings artistically, as though he said: If a wagon loaded with cargo had any power of discernment, it would undoubtedly creak more indignantly if it carried worthless things than if it carried precious ones.

Thus, as the Apostle teaches, upon the foundation of religion some pile up gold, silver, and precious stones according to the diversity of their merits, while others pile up hay, wood, and straw (1 Cor. 3). Our God therefore rightly declares that he experiences a heavier burden when he tolerates the sins of those in whom he can find nothing of precious pursuits, but who have all approached the worthless hay that is easily consumed by fire.

When I have creaked—that is, when I have groaned—your arrogance or confidence will immediately perish. Swiftness will not rescue anyone from destruction; strength will not protect the fighter; finally, neither the ranks of foot soldiers nor the troops of cavalry will delay the divine sentence. Those who had been renowned for the art of war will desire, after losing their coverings, to hide wherever they can, even naked, in order to preserve their lives.

We confirm that all these evils occur through hostile victory more by the disasters we repeatedly suffer than by the testimony of historical records.

At this point the Jews follow a certain opinion, namely, that the persons of various commanders were represented by various forms of equipment:

[Note: Jerome, following Hebrew tradition, names each one individually, and I have no doubt that Our Author received this from him. I am more surprised that he does not, as is his custom, use stronger language in rejecting the opinion praised by the holy Doctor. Jerome says: “The Hebrews understand the swift man as Jeroboam, son of Nebat, who had previously fled into Egypt; the strong man they interpret as Bashan, who was very ready for war; the mighty man they take to mean Omri; and the one holding the bow, Jehu son of Nimshi, who struck King Joram with an arrow; the swift-footed man they understand as Menahem, who, hurrying in vain, is said to have offered gifts to the king of the Assyrians,” and so forth, as you may recall. “This,” he adds, “the Hebrews assert, and as it was handed down to us by them, we have faithfully explained it for our readers.” Our Author, however, considers it of little weight.]

We, considering this of no great importance, shall pass on to other matters.

## Chapter 3

### Verses 1–2

“Hear the word that the Lord has spoken concerning you, sons of Israel, concerning all your kindred, saying: ‘You alone have I known among all the families of the earth; therefore I will visit all your iniquities upon you.’”

Surely, he says, you especially glory in this distinction: that I, who am the creator of the world, became known to no nation throughout the whole earth except you alone. Although I formed all nations with the same care with which I formed you, I chose to be called and to be your God alone. I anticipated all the services of your devotion with gifts and miracles, destroying powerful kingdoms both of the Egyptians and of the Philistines, so that a glorious departure and a wealthy possession might be secured for you.

Nor was I content to confer joys merely by removing slavery; I also added the lights of spiritual teaching, showing through all these things that I had chosen you from among all nations, whom I would also instruct through sacred teaching, so that those who had received many things without merit might learn how they might also become worthy of them.

Yet this generosity did not make me a more negligent judge of your conduct. Rather, I punish your evil deeds all the more because I preferred you to all the nations. For it follows that what is valued more highly is examined more carefully.

Thus the honor bestowed upon your nation, whether acquired through my indulgence or through the virtues of your ancestors, permits no fault to remain unpunished, because an inherited nobility becomes worthless if it is not removed from the unworthy. Acquired nobility therefore commends not impunity from crimes but observance of the commandments.

But let us consider what follows.

### Verses 3–8

“Will two walk together unless they have agreed? Will the lion roar in the forest unless he has prey? Will the lion’s cub cry out from his den unless he has seized something? Will a bird fall into a snare on the ground without a bird-catcher? Will the snare be removed from the ground before it has caught something? If the trumpet sounds in a city, will the people not be afraid? If there is evil in a city, has the Lord not done it? For the Lord God will do nothing unless he has revealed his secret to his servants the prophets. The lion has roared; who will not fear? The Lord God has spoken; who will not prophesy?”

[Note: Read “to his servants the prophets,” as all the other books do; the Author himself, repeating this passage twice below, reads it in that form.]

There have been various opinions concerning this passage, but they do not correspond sufficiently to the meaning of the examples. We shall now present the passage with the distinctions it requires.

The discourse encompasses different meanings. The first verse teaches that the rejection of the ungrateful nation was necessary—that is, just—the nation whom he had declared to be chosen from among all the nations. Since it had changed its pursuits toward perversity and inflamed the anger of the Judge, it was rejected and delivered over to destruction. The text explains why such a separation had occurred.

“Will two walk together,” he says, “unless they have agreed?” That is: “Why are you surprised that you have been stripped of the protection of my companionship, when the just association of travelers cannot remain long except among those who agree? You therefore chose to have a will opposed to my laws. Acknowledge that it necessarily followed that you would be stripped of the help of my companionship, because you began to enter upon a path separate from my ways.”

I will not be content merely to have abandoned you, nor will my indignation end there. From being your protector I will turn against you as a raging lion, one whom, moving through vast wildernesses, not lightness but the sight of prey stirs to roaring. Once he has become victor over what he desired and has carried the intended prey back to his den, he will force the caves themselves to resound with his growling; and never empty of this kind of possession, he growls only after he has obtained his prey.

In these two verses he expressed the disposition of one taking vengeance.

Then follows:

“Will a bird fall into a snare on the ground without a bird-catcher? Will the snare be removed from the ground before it has caught something?”

Having completed the part concerning vengeance, he addresses those upon whom vengeance is inflicted—people whom he judges so easily crushed that they appear like a bird that has entered a snare.

“Will a bird fall,” he says, “into a snare on the ground without a bird-catcher?” As though he said: Even if all the prophets were silent together, the voice of events themselves could sufficiently instruct you. These calamities by which you are terrified could not have come together of their own accord or by some accident for your destruction, unless the hand of the bird-catcher—that is, of the Judge—had brought them upon you.

Through the prophetic warning, then, misery is shown to have been set out like a snare, so that those who abandon the path of justice may fall into it.

[Note: The text was extremely corrupt and nearly meaningless in this form: “so that they may fall into it, to know the path, and those who abandon justice, nothing …” We have restored *callem* (“path”) and the proper punctuation, and have silently corrected several other matters of this kind below.]

Therefore, let no intervening delay often provide you with comfort. Once the snare has been set—that is, once the sentence has been proclaimed by the mouths of the prophets—it will not be removed until it has completed the capture for which it was set.

“If the trumpet sounds in a city, will the people not be afraid? If there is evil in a city, has the Lord not done it? For the Lord God will do nothing unless he has revealed his secret to his servants the prophets.”

By what follows he has shown his exposition to be internally consistent, making public both the snare, the trumpet, and the evil—that is, the affliction by which the cities of the sacrilegious would perish—unless that affliction had been set in motion by divine indignation.

At the same time, however, he commends both the purpose of his compassion, by which he intended to spare them if they had permitted it, and the reverence due to the sacred judgment. This shows that it cannot be despised with impunity. He calls “evil,” as often elsewhere, not sins but torments, by which the guilty are afflicted, not the innocent defiled.

“For the Lord God will do nothing unless he has revealed his secret to his servants the prophets.”

Most appropriately, the dignity of the saints is commended after the contempt of the guilty has been made public. Otherwise, what appeared to be the lowliness of those who were to be overwhelmed by so many punishments might have been attributed more to the condition of their nature than to the envy aroused by their wicked conduct.

It has therefore been added providentially and usefully, for the honor of human beings—that is, of the prophets—who stand in the same nature as everyone else, yet differed from others in the value of their character to such an extent that God could say of the others, “I will not remember their names with my lips” (Ps. 15), but of these he could say that he would do nothing without first bringing it to their knowledge.

“Just as,” he says, “no calamity will arise in these cities except one which the divine judgment has stirred up, so no punishment will be brought against you except one which has first been announced to the conscience of the saints.”

He compressed what he had said into a still briefer form:

“The lion has roared; who will not fear? The Lord God has spoken; who will not prophesy?”

Since above he had expressed his indignation by the image of a lion, he now completes what he had signified, saying: “The lion has roared”—that is, when God threatens and makes public the punishment that hangs over them, what mortal is there whom fear will not dissolve?

But let us now examine the character and display of the threats.

### Verses 9–10

“Proclaim it in the houses of Ashdod and in the houses of the land of Egypt, and say: ‘Gather upon the mountains of Samaria and see the many insanities in its midst, and those who suffer oppression in its inner chambers.’ And they do not know how to do what is right,” says the Lord, “storing up iniquity and plunder in their houses.”

Divine speech maintains its customary practice: it indicates with what reluctance it is moved to punish. Therefore, after unfolding the form of terror, it repeats and renews its complaints and commands neighboring peoples to be summoned, so that they may see the filth with which that people, once belonging to God, is encrusted and the crimes with which it rages.

“Announce,” he says, “to the Philistines and the Egyptians that they should gather as though for a spectacle upon the mountains of Samaria”—that is, from the heights of the mountains they should look down upon its valleys and cities—

[Note: *Edicto* (“by decree”) had been printed incorrectly instead of *edito* (“height” or “elevated place”), referring to the mountains.]

—and should consider that there is no disgrace or crime which merely approaches their pursuits, but none which is not established in their midst as though on a fixed foundation.

If you turn your eyes to those who are oppressed by false accusation, you will find the gates of the cities in which they were accustomed to judge, as well as the inner chambers, crowded in such a way that no voice seems to be heard except that of the afflicted.

All who had undertaken the office of judging had fallen into such forgetfulness of what is right, whether through greed or pride, that they appeared not merely unwilling to love but even unable to know what is right.

Let no one therefore resent my severity, since I showed such long patience toward delinquent servants that my judgment even came to be forgotten by them.

“You nations,” I say, “whom I had destroyed for the liberation and glory of these people, come together again, so that with you yourselves as witnesses both the greatness of my indulgence and the impiety of Ephraim may be exposed.”

### Verse 11

“Therefore thus says the Lord God: The land shall be distressed and surrounded; your strength shall be taken away from you, and your houses shall be plundered.”

As we have said, he often complained of their crimes and offenses so that at last he might pronounce sentence. He therefore answered, in the exposition, the meaning he had established at the beginning: “For three crimes of Israel, and for four, I will not revoke it.”

Since, therefore, justice demanded that a change be decreed for Israel and Judah, so that they would fall from prosperity into sorrow but would not perish by complete destruction, hear in what manner the destroyer would rage.

### Verse 12

“As a shepherd rescues from the lion’s mouth two legs or the end of an ear, so shall the children of Israel be rescued who dwell in Samaria, on the side of a couch and on the bed of Damascus.”

Because our God chastised the Israelites with the intention of correcting them, he indicated this both through the prophets who commended the same purpose and through the language of his dispensations. Although their beloved profanation continually made them hateful, the Almighty nevertheless varied their condition: at one time afflicting them with adversity, at another comforting them with prosperity.

The Syrian, therefore, who was nearer—that is, the inhabitant of Damascus—harassed the Ten Tribes with frequent incursions, as the history of Kings records. At one time the Samaritans were driven by a long siege into such poverty that mothers ate the flesh of their children, and scarcely ten horses could be found in the whole army.

But when the blessed Elisha had announced to King Joram that on the following day an abundance of grain would be visible at the gates of Samaria, such a sudden change took place that, when the besieging Syrians fled, the Israelites not only escaped but also received the rich spoils of victory (2 Kings 6 and following). We read that salvation and joy often came to them in this manner.

Our God, therefore, sparing in punishment and rich in mercy, announces that although he has undertaken the office of Judge, he has not abandoned the office of Shepherd.

Moreover, from the bed of Damascus—by whose cords, so to speak, and by whose fevers they were held, and through whose very proximity they endured a prolonged illness—he would deign to rescue their remnants, just as one draws from the jaws of lions the limbs of a people that has been torn apart by kings.

### Verses 13–14

“Hear and testify against the house of Jacob,” says the Lord God of hosts. “For on the day when I begin to visit the transgressions of Israel upon him, I will also visit the altars of Bethel; and the horns of the altar shall be cut off and fall to the ground.”

As far as the context of the reading is concerned, he promises hostile devastation and says that the horns of the altar which Jeroboam had set up at Bethel would be shattered. For we read that he placed one of the two calves in Dan and the other in Bethel.

The sense of the present passage is therefore as follows: Although I will not allow you to be destroyed completely, but am prepared to draw the remnants of your nation out of captivity, and although the neighboring enemy—the ruler of Damascus—will not consume you, nevertheless I will not allow what you are doing to pass unpunished.

It could be said that under the name of Jacob he intended Judah to be understood, had the continuation of the discourse not more clearly marked and expressed Israel—that is, the Ten Tribes.

Concerning this destruction of the altar, we also read in the Books of Kings that a prophet came to Jeroboam, who had fashioned the calves, and promised under threat that this would happen to the altar while Jeroboam was sacrificing. When Jeroboam ordered that the prophet be seized with an outstretched hand, he immediately perceived the prophet’s power when his own right hand withered. He then, broken by fear, turned to prayer and recovered the use of his hand; but he also heard that Josiah would arise to avenge that sacrilege (1 Kings 13).

Thus the long periods embraced either by the chastisement of the people or by the final, prolonged captivity are simultaneously indicated by the present prophecy, although they were to occur at different times.

### Verse 15

“And I will strike the winter house together with the summer house,” he says, “and the ivory houses shall perish, and the many houses shall be destroyed,” says the Lord.

He does not attack only one particular vice of the profane nation but also touches upon the sins of greed and luxury. Therefore he complains that they built various dwellings suited to the pleasures of different seasons of the year, as instruments of luxury for themselves, although they were entangled in manifold sins and had thought nothing at all about remorse or correction. They were concerned only with pursuing pleasant surroundings: some houses they had prepared for the heat, others for the cold. All these, together with their various structures, were to be removed at the time of punishment and burned in the fire of the enemy.

## Chapter 4

### Verses 1–3

“Hear this word, fat cows, who are on the mountain of Samaria, who oppress the needy and crush the poor, who say to your lords, ‘Bring it, and we shall drink.’ The Lord God has sworn by his holiness: Behold, days are coming upon you when they will lift you up on poles, and your remnants in boiling pots. You will go out through breaches, each one straight ahead, and you will be cast into Harmon,” says the Lord.

Although the profanation of the whole nation had to be reproved, he directed his rebuke especially against the rich and wealthy, who used not a single dwelling but dining rooms varied according to the season, and adorned them with the gleam of ivory. He therefore rightly assigns them the name of fat cows, because their voice was destined for lowing, their belly was their god, and their glory was in their shame.

[Col. 1070D] It may also appropriately be added that they are called this not only because of the vices of their conduct but also because of the character of their impiety itself: those who had accepted calves as objects of worship are marked by the name of cows.

They are called “fat” according to what blessed David condemns:

> “Their iniquity came forth as from fatness;  
> they passed into the desires of their heart.  
> They thought and spoke wickedness;  
> they spoke iniquity on high” (Ps. 72).

Thus, standing on the mountain of Samaria—that is, in the royal city—and swollen with courtly familiarity, you wore down the poor, seeking from their spoils the instruments of your luxury.

When he says, “who say to your lords, ‘Bring it, and we shall drink,’” this may be understood either as referring to the idols themselves, whom they called their lords and from whom they earnestly begged an abundance of possessions, since they had placed all their happiness in untimely and lavish banquets; or certainly as referring to their various subordinates, who hired themselves out to the nobles for the work of their crimes and requested this payment from those for whose profit they often sinned, so that drink would not be lacking to them.

What do they receive for this insolence?

“The Lord has sworn by his holiness”—that is, he has decreed by the holiness that cannot permit his judgment to be violated—that the time will come, indeed is already approaching, when your flesh will be lifted upon poles and your remnants in boiling pots.

He has transferred the comparison from cows that are served at banquets to revelers or soldiers. And because he had marked their profane people by the word “cows,” he again announces that they are to be subjected to destruction.

He therefore uses “poles” for spits—that is, stakes on which the flesh of cows is commonly inserted and roasted by the heat of coals. By “remnants” understand either the intestines or those portions which, because they are smaller, are cooked more readily in pots than on spits.

And since he had said that, having forgotten all decency and fear, they even measured the price of crimes by the appetite of their stomachs, he rightly added that, once seized by the fire of captivity, they would be exposed to enemies who luxuriated in them and devoured them as though at a feast.

“And you will go out through breaches, each one straight ahead, and you will be cast into Harmon,” says the Lord.
