In the preceding verses he had completed the metaphor drawn from cows and a banquet. In the final statement, however, he returns to a straightforward judgment: he says that they will be dragged out through breached walls, which indicates the overthrow of the city.

“Each one straight ahead,” according to the Hebrew idiom, shows captives meeting one another, or following one another in succession, as they are transferred to the mountains of Armenia when the Assyrian is victorious.

But let us consider what follows.

### Verses 4–6

“Come to Bethel and act impiously; to Gilgal and multiply transgression. Bring your sacrifices every morning, your tithes every three days. Sacrifice praise from what is leavened, proclaim voluntary offerings, and announce them; for this is what you wished, sons of Israel,” says the Lord God.

“And I also gave you dullness of teeth in all your cities and lack of bread in all your places; yet you did not return to me,” says the Lord.

The entire text of the rebuke itself shows that this was the chief—or rather the sole—reason why the prophets announced what calamities threatened sinners: namely, that fear might produce correction in them.

Because they resisted this purpose of a Judge more inclined toward mercy through the shamelessness of their delinquency, a kind of contest seemed to exist between God and human beings. But since the struggle was unequal—for he was the one making the judgment while they endured what was bitter—he sometimes immediately addresses them with derision, reproaching them with the very contest they had chosen.

“Come,” he says, “to Bethel and act impiously.” In the imperative mood, but through irony and mockery, he declares the very actions by which they offend him, a figure that is also common in secular literature.

Thus he tauntingly charges profaned Israel to persist in the pursuits it has chosen and not to cease frequenting Bethel and Gilgal, cities that the preceding prophets also indicated were swarming with idols, but to bring an increase of transgressions. Let them offer morning sacrifices, devote themselves to the offering of sacrifices, and place upon the altar leavened loaves which, so to speak, were called offerings of praise or voluntary offerings.

The whole passage is to be understood in this way: They had transferred to idols the ceremonial ordinances and rites received from the sacred Law, since they had decreed that those idols should be venerated as God; and, just as they had impiously transferred those observances to idols, so they also frequently altered them at will.

He reproves both things equally: either that they had enslaved legal institutions to the idols to which they had defected, or that they had corrupted those institutions according to their own pleasure. Both actions amounted to the same impiety—either to transfer to profane shrines the observances God had commanded to be offered to him, or, as though out of arrogance and with the intention of correcting something, to alter what had been instituted.

Finally, intensifying this crime of a proud mind, he says:

“Thus you wished it, sons of Israel,” says the Lord God.

“Persist, then,” he says, “in the pursuits you have chosen, so that punishments worthy of you may accompany you, the taste of which you have already experienced to a great extent. For I gave you dullness of teeth in all your cities and lack of bread in all your places; yet you did not return to me,” says the Lord.

He placed lack of bread after dullness of teeth so that the meaning might be this: their teeth seemed to have been brought into forgetfulness of their function, and to have lost the habit of biting or grinding food, suffering a certain numbness after a long interval of time.

But although such a bitter chastisement had struck you, you did not return to me, says the Lord.

In this verse he indicated two things at once: their obstinacy in sinning and his own kindness in admonishing them. He had inflicted those blows not in order to punish them but to correct them.

Resisting this purpose disastrously, they entered, as we said above, into a kind of contest. Let us therefore hear what he adds.

[Editorial and textual notes: In Verse 8, the alternative reading is *vestimentis pigneratis* (“upon pledged garments”), rather than *super vestimenta pignerata* (Col. 1065B). In Verses 9–10, the alternative reads *in deserto*, “in the wilderness” (Col. 1065C), and the conjecture *quorum* (“of which”) is proposed for *quibus*. The phrase “as a diligent surveyor laying out a camp” corrects the corrupt earlier reading *meator* to *metator* (Col. 1065D). In Verses 13–16, *suis* (“his own”) was absent and has been supplied on the authority of other books (Col. 1065D); an earlier text read *nudis* (“naked [men]”) for *nudi* (“naked”) (Col. 1066D).

For Chapter 3: at 3:1–2, other Hebrew, Greek, and Latin witnesses read “which I brought up out of the land of Egypt” in place of “your” kindred; the Author’s subsequent exposition shows that he read the latter (Col. 1067D). At 3:3–8, *concinentes* (“agreeing, corresponding”) corrects the corrupt *continentes* (Col. 1068D). The alternative at “before it has caught something” is *quid*, “anything”; at “what the Lord has done” it is *fecerit*, “has done/will have done.” The corrupt text concerning those falling into the snare has been corrected to *in eas incidant callem quique iustitiae relinquentes*: “so that all who abandon the path of justice may fall into them” (Col. 1068D). At 3:9–10, *edito* (“elevated place”) corrects the erroneous *edicto* (“by decree”), referring to the mountains (Col. 1069D). At 3:11, the older reading is *et* (“and”) for *e* (“from”). At 3:12, *si eruantur* (“if they are rescued”) has been corrected to *si eruat* (“if a shepherd rescues”), in accordance with the Hebrew text and other manuscripts (Cols. 1069D–1070D).

For Chapter 4: the note at 4:1–3 observes that *ritus* (“rite”), or something similar, seems to be missing (Col. 1071D). The ancient alternative at “you will go out” is *exhibitis* (“you will present/show”) for *exibitis* (“you will go out”). At 4:4–6, the editor prefers *idcirco* (“therefore”), and shortly thereafter reads *ipsum* (“itself”) for *ipsam* (“it”) (Col. 1071D); the ancient reading *quippe* occurs for *quique* (“the lesser persons”).]

### Verses 7–8

I also withheld rain from you when three months still remained until the harvest; and I rained upon one city, but upon another city I did not rain: one part was watered, while the part upon which I did not rain dried up. And two or three cities came to another city to drink water, but were not satisfied; yet you did not return to me, says the Lord.

[Note: Some books read, “to one city.” The Hebrew likewise has this reading.]

Having shown above that a sudden blight had destroyed the abundance of the crops, and that no amendment had followed, he next makes clear that he had furnished even more evident testimonies of his indignation: at the very first sprouting of the grasses, by withholding the rains, he had suffocated the seeds. Consequently he adds that he did not withdraw the relief of rain from everyone alike, lest they should attribute what had happened to chance rather than to his indignation.

“But,” he says, “so that you might perceive that the dryness came by judgment, I rained upon one city and did not rain upon another, so that, while relief was denied to you, O people, you might at the same time be stung by the example of your neighbor.” So slight, moreover, was the rain that even the thirst of the very places which it seemed to have sprinkled was not quenched. Yet you, who ran like cattle at the report of rain, were unwilling to return to me by correcting your will. Thus it came about that the calamities fixed upon you, and my acts of providence, were alike rendered utterly fruitless.

### Verse 9

I struck you with scorching wind and mildew; the locust devoured the multitude of your gardens and your vineyards, your olive-groves and your fig trees; yet you did not return to me, says the Lord.

This accumulation of your sins will rightly be reckoned, because, although I have so often undertaken the work of severity, I have nevertheless accomplished nothing toward your correction. Therefore I enumerate whatever hardships you have endured in place of benefits, and confess that I seemed to have forgotten my own kindness while striving to overcome your ruinous persistence in sinning.

Therefore I did not hesitate to redouble—indeed, to multiply—the blows, and, after depriving people of the support of crops, I also withdrew the consolations of fruit and gardens: so that, just as prolonged drought consumed the hope of the harvest, either the pestilential air or the frequent locust might likewise consume the blessings of autumn and winter; yet you did not return to me, says the Lord.

[Col. 1072D]

### Verse 10

I sent death upon you in the manner of Egypt; I slew your young men with the sword, even to the captivity of your horses; and I caused the stench of your camps to rise into your nostrils; yet you did not return to me, says the Lord.

The mention of Egypt can be understood in two ways. For when we are taught that the people—said to have numbered six hundred thousand—who were twenty years old and above, with the exception of Joshua and Caleb, perished in the wilderness, God is rightly said here to have caused them to fall in the likeness of the Egyptian departure, declaring that they were to be destroyed by slaughter.

Or else, since, when the Assyrians were threatening, the Israelites sought help from the Egyptians, as the blessed Hosea teaches, and nevertheless obtained no remedy, the prophetic word consequently announces that death was sent against them by the road of Egypt, through which, plainly, not allied arms but a more enraged enemy burst upon them.

The following words fit this interpretation better: namely, that both the young men and the horses, corrupted in the camps by the siege or cut down by captivity, were judged to have been destroyed. “But when,” he says, “the stench of the camps, in which you were shut up, tormented you, and you saw that the evils of captivity were immediately to be inflicted upon you, even then you did not return to me, says the Lord.” How, then, do you suppose I can bear that the fruit of so many chastisements has perished through you?

### Verse 11

I overthrew you, as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and you became like a brand snatched from the fire; yet you did not return to me, says the Lord (Hos. 14).

Who is wise and understands these things? Then he will understand the mercies of the Lord, which he never ceases to commend in all his acts of providence. Accordingly, even in the present passage, although the discourse proceeds with a very great display of severity, he nevertheless shows that those mercies abound and overflow, so that [or: “and thus”] he teaches that the blows he has inflicted appear to him much heavier than they do to those who suffer them.

“I overthrew you,” he says, “as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah.” The fact that this did not happen to the Israelite peoples is also confirmed by the hope of the promised deliverance. The sense is therefore as follows: “Because the calamities I inflicted raged so violently against your blood that even the Sodomites themselves seem to me not to have suffered greater things, this accumulation of hardships must, according to the measure of the relationship, be compared to those fires, since I had taken you to myself; those fires in which the obscene multitude was burned together with its houses and lands.”

Although I have granted you hope of recovering your freedom, nevertheless you seem to me more like some half-burned brand dragged from the fires than like something standing firm in flourishing strength.

[Note: Up to this point it had been read corruptly as “to be carried out.”]

### Verses 12–13

Therefore this is what I will do to you, Israel; and after I have done this to you, prepare to meet your God, O Israel. For behold, he who forms the mountains and creates the wind, and declares his word to a human being, who makes the morning mist and walks upon the heights of the earth—the Lord God of hosts is his name.

“And because,” he says, “you have decided to contend with my benevolence through shameless obstinacy, and impose upon me the necessity of displaying severity, I will do to you what the order of chastisements demands. For it would not be fitting that your shamelessness should appear to have had greater strength than our judgment, and that these things should cease as though wearied before either your iniquity or your life came to an end.

“As far as I am concerned, therefore, I will continue my purpose of healing. It will depend upon you whether this manifold chastisement profits correction or rather vengeance. Since I recently enumerated those misfortunes—the scarcity of crops and rain, the abundance of locusts and caterpillars consuming whatever greenness remained, the blight ravaging the growth of the year and human bodies, and finally the evils of the hostile siege, which turned the entire camp into corruption, together with the sword raging at home and abroad—things which, through compassionate mercy, I compared to that destruction by which Sodom perished, so that captivity would seem likely to leave your remnants like the remains of burned brands—since, I say, all these things proved ineffective for correction, I will do this to you under the same settled purpose, so that, once your ruinous impiety has been driven away, you may take up the disposition to amend.

“Therefore, after what I announce has been inflicted upon you, gird yourself to meet your Lord, having acquired a better hope. Do not, struck by part of the sentence, either despair of salvation or fear to appear before the eyes of the Judge. For you have to do with one who by no means desires the death of the dying, but who even comes to the aid of those condemned, if he sees them repent of their offenses.”

[Note: Here “a certain person” is none other than Jerome, whose exposition our author habitually never misses an opportunity to criticize. Jerome interpreted the passage as follows: “When he has said, ‘I will do this to you,’ he keeps silent about what he is going to do, so that, while Israel remains uncertain about the several kinds of punishment—and these are all the more terrifying because they suspect everything—it may repent, lest God inflict the things he has threatened,” and so forth. Compare the many passages above, not without contempt for Jerome’s name. Our author dares to bring this charge against the holy Doctor.]

Some have thought that the passage, “Therefore this is what I will do to you,” should be understood as though the form of the threat had deliberately been concealed, so that whatever the hearer could imagine as most terrible, he would believe had also been promised. But it can be observed that the matter was not promised to those terrified by suspicions; rather, shortly afterward he disclosed what he would do. For, after inserting words concerning the Creator’s power, he adds, almost as a repetition:

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 1074B]

### Verses 1–2

Hear this word which I raise over you as a lamentation: The house of Israel has fallen and shall not rise again. The virgin of Israel has been cast upon her land, and there is no one to raise her up.

Thus the sequence of the ideas is woven together, so that, as usual, our God carefully explains the causes of the captivity he has inflicted, which he seems to have fulfilled almost unwillingly. But let us return to the order of the reading.

After he said, “This I will do to you, Israel. And after I have done this to you, prepare to meet your God, O Israel. For behold,” he says, “he who forms the mountains and creates the wind, and declares his word to a human being, who makes the morning mist and walks upon the heights of the earth—the Lord of hosts is his name.”

[Note: “Walking” was written in the text, and it might seem more acceptable to someone paying only slight attention to the flow of the discourse. But the Hebrew exemplar, and Jerome’s version based upon it, do not allow us to be deceived; on their authority we restored “walking.”]

To arouse reverence for the Judge in the breasts of the guilty, he inserts the works of the Creator, so that an attentive hearer may understand either the censor’s disposition toward them or may not doubt the effect of the vengeance, since he sees that the one threatening him is he by whose power the whole universe subsists.

That is: “O Israel, consider who is the one who examines your merits: he through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made (John 1); he who formed and arranged the elements by his command; he who gave light to the stars, caused the valleys to subside, the plains to lie flat, and the mountains to swell; [Note: Here *desiderent* had mistakenly been read, in place of which we restore *desinerent*. In our view, however, the former reading is excellent rather than mistaken: for “to lie low” (*desidere*) suits valleys perfectly, whereas “to cease” scarcely does.] he who commanded the air we breathe—which fills the empty space between heaven and earth—to be condensed into cloud and moved into winds; whose providence is revealed by new works through the various functions of the elements; who, although so great in the eminence of his power, nevertheless deigns to make his word, that is, his law, known to human beings.

“And amid the marvels of his governance—by which he causes mists to exhale from the earth after the morning sun has breathed upon them, until, through the lingering of that vapor, they are either compressed or completely dried, and, when necessary, are gathered into clouds and carried upward, made higher than all the mountains, so that they pour the water of their accumulated rains over the lands beneath and thereby impress and mark upon everything the traces of his governance—he himself, I say, the Maker of the elements, whose name is Lord of hosts, that is, whose power is such that the ranks of angels serve at his command and acknowledge him as their King and Creator, he himself, I say, contends with you in such benevolence that he announces the torments to be inflicted upon you, so that perhaps, by awakening in your minds a disposition to repent, even a late amendment may rescue the guilty from vengeance.

“But because you corrupt this remedy through obstinate perversity, hear the voice of our lamentation, whose admonitions you have always rejected: the voice, I say, with which we accompany your final condition. ‘She has fallen, she has fallen; she shall not rise again. The virgin of Israel has been cast upon her land; there is no one to raise her up.’”

That is: “That nation, descended from the illustrious stock of Israel, which either deserved or was accustomed to be called a virgin”—whether because no impurity had violated her chastity, by which she had been admitted into the fellowship of her own ruler, or because no captivity had seized her prosperity, which was strong through continuous integrity—“is now exposed to the trampling of the conqueror and endures insults and torments alike.

“She claims no consolation from the removal of her calamity. Rather, in her own land she has lain like a woman subjected to pollution, and, pressed down by misery, has reached the grave. There is no one able to bring aid or lift up the fallen woman whom the judgment of the Almighty has crushed.”

From the verse in which he says, “forming the mountains and creating the wind,” up to the present passage, the words may be understood as spoken in the person of the prophet, who is discussing the power of God.

But when he says that Israel has fallen upon her land in such a way that she will not rise again at all—although both the preceding and following statements promise consolation through the eventual removal of miseries, and although, even at the time of the punishment itself, they threaten rather the diminution than the destruction of the people—we should understand this either as an expression in which he, in the emotion of mourning, estimated the calamities inflicted as greater than they were, and thus called those utterly destroyed whom he saw crushed for the greater part; or else as signifying, in the case of those whom captivity was consuming, that Israel was being brought low and could not be raised up by anyone.

### Verse 3

For this is what the Lord God says: The city from which a thousand went out shall have a hundred left in it; and from which a hundred went out, ten shall be left in it, in the house of Israel.

That the miseries of captivity did not burst upon them suddenly, but that the people were chastised over many periods while amendment was awaited, is shown by the history of the Kings. For this reason our God addresses them through the prophets in various ways: at one time announcing destruction and declaring it fixed, at another promising prosperity if they should amend.

Therefore do not suppose that, by compressing everything into a single period, there is any discrepancy in the statements. Rather, when you distribute the utterances across long periods and their appropriate occasions, you will find that their sequence is consistent throughout. The evils gradually increased, and the kingdom of the profane people was diminished until it reached the final destruction of captivity.

Accordingly, in those cities and regions that were still being devastated while the capital—namely, Samaria—remained standing, we should understand that a tenth of the nation was made to survive, so that, when the nobler parts had perished, what remained would be the remnant.

Since this tenth was brought about for the purpose that, just as he rightly handed some over to destruction, so he might correct others by the example of those who were perishing, the exhortation of the Judge himself immediately rang out.

[Col. 1075D]

### Verses 4–6

For this is what the Lord says to the house of Israel: Seek me, and you shall live. Do not seek Bethel, and do not enter Galgala, and do not cross into Beersheba, because Galgala shall be led into captivity, and Bethel shall become nothing. Seek the Lord, and live, lest [variant: “nor lest”] the fire consume the house of Joseph; it shall devour it, and there will be no one to extinguish Bethel.

[Note: The other books, as well as the Hebrew text itself, read “as fire.”]

“For what you ought to have learned from the law and from piety,” he says, “namely, that you should cling in continual devotion to your one Creator, who, when gracious, would make you blessed and, when angry, most miserable, savage dangers have finally taught you. Even now, therefore, take up the zeal of repentance, and, if you wish to live, consider the correction of your conduct.

“Seek me, then, whom you abandoned while serving profanation. Seek me, I say, ready to be found, and, as soon as you begin to seek, finding me coming to meet you; for everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened (Matt. 13.).

“Do not add concealment of our inquiry to your sacrileges, lest, by neglecting the remedies offered, you be exposed as more hardened than you were by violating the commandments that had been proclaimed.

“Seek me, and you shall live. Do not seek Bethel, Galgala, and Beersheba.” As the history of the Kings reveals, these cities were devoted both to the calves made by Jeroboam and to the remaining idols (3 Kings 12). The Lord therefore warns them, in his concern for them, to cease frequenting places that profanation had made abominable, lest they perish along with them, since they too [perhaps *quique*, “and they”] had been destined for destruction.

Seek the Lord, then, because he does not desire the death of the dying; return to him as you seek him, and you shall live, lest you begin to be burned when the fire sent against the roofs of the profane takes hold of you. But let us examine what follows.

### Verses 7–8

You who turn judgment into wormwood and abandon righteousness upon the earth; who makes Arcturus and Orion, and turns darkness into morning, and changes day into night; who calls the waters of the sea and pours them over the face of the earth—the Lord is his name.

Following the same order as above, in order to explain the Judge’s power, he reminds them that this one is also the Creator. He thereby displays the purpose of the one who, insofar as it depends upon him, wished to provide for all things, since his goodness alone had supplied them with the cause of their existence. He says that they had made his judgment, which would have been sweet to the innocent, as bitter to themselves as wormwood.

Therefore, when he says, “You who turn judgment into wormwood,” we should understand this either as a complaint that they had turned into bitterness the divine judgment which, by their merits, they had compelled to become destructive for them; or else as saying that the examination of human reason itself had been corrupted into bitterness, namely, by preferring the worship of idols to the sacred rites they had received through Moses.

He then adds, “and you abandon righteousness upon the earth.” We might refer this to the guilt of their choice, as though they had abandoned the standard of judgment as something to be trampled underfoot, were it not that the following verses show what he called righteousness.

For he says, “who makes Arcturus and Orion, who turns darkness into morning.” He therefore called our God himself “righteousness,” who is rightly named both virtue and wisdom (1 Cor. 1:24). After complaining that the profane had abandoned him—that is, rejected him—he enumerates his works, by which the world is governed, in order to heap condemnation upon those who had not feared God of such majesty.

As for the names he introduces for the stars, which seem to have been imposed by the Gentiles—although other interpreters may have mentioned only “stars”—we may reasonably understand that the prophet used familiar names to distinguish the stars, not to confirm the myths associated with them, in accordance with the fact that the Apostle did not disdain to adopt statements of the poets (Acts 17).

It should also be noted that, when he wished to embrace a description of the structure of the heavenly sphere, he expressed the four regions—also called climates—through the names of stars. He assigned the north to Arcturus and the south, which lies opposite it, to Orion, while indicating the rising and setting of the sun through the alternation of day and night.

Here, admiring the power of the Maker, he beautifully says that he turns darkness itself into morning. For when the sphere of the sun has completed its revolutions, it pours sudden brightness over the earth, so that it seems not merely to have driven away the darkness it found but to have changed it into light.

“Who calls the waters of the sea and pours them over the face of the earth—the Lord is his name.”

With the greatest elegance and knowledge, while speaking of the functions of the elements, which belong to the Creator’s establishment and governance, he says that this one does everything—his power both formed those orders and preserves them. Yet he shows that the Creator especially uses the service of a particular heavenly body to produce crops: namely, the sun, whose departure prepares night for us and whose return prepares day.

Since the discourse had touched upon a description of natural things, he also adds that moisture exhaled from the earth, or streams drawn from the sea’s waters, are carried upward by the same vapor; and that, once suspended in clouds, when they can no longer rise to the highest regions of heaven by virtue of their own weight, they shed their bitter salt through the process of transmission and are finally returned to the thirsty earth.

Thus, through the mixture of opposites—moisture and vapor—an admirable abundance comes about for the nourishment of crops. Such a work of such magnitude could not be explained unless by him who alone is shown to be Lord of all by right of creation. But let us examine what follows.

[Note: He seems to have taken this from Jerome, where he says: “Symmachus rendered it simply ‘stars’; Theodotion interpreted it as ‘evening’; but the Hebrew, who instructed us in the holy Scriptures, thinks that *Chazil* should be interpreted as ‘splendor’ and signifies generally shining stars.” Shortly afterward he says: “The Hebrew names, which among them are called by other names, have been transferred into our language through the names of the Gentile myths, since we cannot understand what is said except through those names which we have learned by custom and absorbed along with error.”]

### Verse 9

He who smiles at devastation against the strong and brings desolation upon the mighty.

He subsequently made clear for what purpose the preceding description of power had been given: namely, to arouse fear in the breasts of the hearers, so that they might understand what a heap of calamities threatened those against whom the Judge of such great power was angry.

“He,” he says, “who is the Creator of all things continues to examine every merit. Although no one can resist his strength, he smiles at the torments of the guilty who seemed powerful to themselves; he will crush them with such ease that he indicates his indignation by a smile rather than by a shout.

“Why should he not, since all things serve his command, and according to the diversity of merits both adversity and prosperity follow at his word?”

He therefore smiles at devastation against those who seemed powerful to themselves and were accustomed to say: “We will magnify our tongue; our lips are our own; who is our God?” (Ps. 21.). Against such people, who most profanely arrogate prosperity and strength to themselves, the eternal Avenger, he says, smiles at the torments of affliction and declares his indignation by adopting a grin of the sort that is out of keeping with the occasion.

He calls the Israelites strong and powerful either because of the envy aroused by their pride or because of the memory of their former prosperity. Yet he has already announced that they have been largely consumed and are soon to be carried away into captivity.

[Note: “Perhaps ‘laughter’.”]

### Verses 10–11

They hated the one who rebuked in the gate, and they abhorred the one who spoke with integrity. Therefore, because you plundered the poor and took a choice possession from him, you will build houses of hewn stone, but you will not dwell in them; you will plant most desirable vineyards, but you will not drink their wine.

The established pattern of prophetic speech is maintained: after punishments have been announced, the cause of the severity is immediately supplied, so that it may not appear that the Lord of such great piety has acted from indignation rather than reason. At the same time, he shows how greatly he cares for the poor, since he joins their insults and plunder to the violation of religion.

From this he proves that profane minds contain no civic concern for justice and no feeling of humanity; instead, they rush upon their fellow citizens as though driven by a wind of fury and tear apart every poor person with declared savagery. Hence those who had sacrilegiously departed in mind for the worship of idols refrained from no crimes at all. They were as harmful to their associates and fellow citizens as they were ungrateful to the Lord whom they had rejected.

When he says that they pursued with hatred those who rebuked in the gates, he reveals the custom of the Jewish institution, which had been arranged so that arbiters of disputes would sit at the gates of every city. Thus anyone who needed their judgment would not have to struggle through some separate inquiry, but would encounter at the very entrance those before whom his case could be examined.

[Note: Jerome puts this most elegantly, and it is pleasing to praise him again: “In the gate, according to the ancient custom of the Jewish people, judgments were held; we often read this and have frequently interpreted it. Thus neither would a farmer coming to court be frightened by the crowds and unfamiliar sight of the city, nor would a city-dweller have to travel far from the city and seek transportation for his animals.”]

[Note: The word *apud*, or something similar, is missing. Moreover, I do not see why the author denies that this Israelite custom of administering justice at city gates remained in force at that period, since certain evidence establishes that it continued long afterward and among other nations as well. Perhaps more is missing, and the corruption of the passage prevents us from grasping his meaning. Certainly, below at verse 13 he says: “In the gate of the city, that is, in places of judgment, while the people look on,” etc.]

We should not, however, suppose that the Israelites—especially those already living under the power of profane kings—retained this custom, which had been established by the blessed Moses in the priestly commonwealth. Rather, the passage shows that they had violated civil law along with religious rites, and that they had conceived hatred for virtue together with hatred for those who preached it. If anyone wished to exhort them to correction and holiness, he was immediately destroyed by the united force of their hatred.

He explains why they opposed the admonitions of their censors: “You plundered the poor,” he says, “and took a choice possession from him.” Therefore, so that you might advance without any impediment of fear or shame through the losses and insults of the poor, you hated sober admonishers.

It should be noted, however, that he says they took a choice possession from the needy, although one of two alternatives would seem more consistent: either those whom he calls poor did not have great possessions to lose, or they should rightly be called wealthy if a robber took precious things from them.

We should therefore understand either that he called poor those whom the robbers had made needy from being wealthy, or else that, considering more the feelings of the owners than the magnitude of the losses, he said that things small in themselves, but precious to the poor precisely because of their scarcity, had been taken away through atrocious greed.

As testimony to this, let us recall at least one example: the vineyard of Naboth, a holy man. It was small in extent, but most dear to its owner and precious because of its very pleasantness. The utterly foolish King Ahab coveted it. When he sent word to its owner about a sale, Naboth replied that he could not disregard his ancestral inheritance and did not wish to be deprived of it, if it could be avoided.

Then the king, provoked by the urging of his most profane wife, added an act of cruelty to his greed. After Naboth had been killed, he seized the vineyard he had coveted (3 Kings 21).

Thus they seized choice possessions—things which, plainly, their owners regarded as more precious than anything else—with bloody violence. Let us hear what he announces to them because of these actions.

Because you stripped the poor, you will build houses of hewn stone, but you will not dwell in them. You will plant most desirable vineyards, but you will not drink their wine.

### Verse 12

For I know your many crimes and your mighty sins.

The audacity of your plundering consisted in this: that you had the means of luxury, and cultivated your dwellings at great expense, as though they were destined both for security and for pleasure. But two things will happen to you at once: you will indeed build, but you will not be able to dwell in what you have built. You will be tormented both by the effort of construction and by the loss of the work, and you will feel your pain multiplied by the fact that you are deprived not of makeshift but of elegant dwellings.

Nor will you be able to complain of your calamity or hope for divine help amid your groans, since the multitude of your faults resists your prayers. Why should you not suffer this, when it is evident that you have committed equally atrocious acts against citizens and neighbors?

According to the history, all these things were endured by the ten Samaritan tribes, often at the hands of neighboring enemies but especially from the Assyrians. Judah also shared the same disasters when Babylon laid it waste.

Therefore, when you have been deprived of extensive and splendid houses and of fertile vineyards, planted through your own labor—and when captivity has been added to this—attribute it to the sins you committed, which were exceedingly great.

### Verse 13

They are enemies of justice, accepting a bribe and oppressing the poor in the gate. Therefore the prudent person will keep silent at that time, because it is an evil time.

Through various features he magnifies the condition of the corrupted city. Just as he said above that those who urged justice had been despised, indeed even struck down, so now he consequently calls them enemies of justice.

This can be understood in two ways. The phrase “enemies of justice” may be taken as though *justi* were a genitive singular, so that they are called enemies of justice. In this sense I accuse you not merely of neglecting justice but of hating it. From this attitude proceeds the deadly perversity of your pursuits: joining shamelessness to iniquity, you do not even wish to conceal what you are doing. Rather, in the city gate—that is, in the places of judgment—while the people watch, you do not evaluate cases according to merit but according to payments, and you support the iniquity of the wealthy from the resources of the poor.

Or else the phrase may be understood as though “just enemies” were being called by the plural nominative, so that, after listing many great crimes, the prophet, as though moved by indignation, added that they were just enemies—that is, that they openly displayed themselves as legitimate adversaries of religion and of God.

This is a familiar expression among eloquent writers, who are accustomed to call armies and provinces “just,” meaning great. But let us examine what follows.

[Note: Here we changed *negligentes* to *negligenter*; shortly afterward we changed *impudentiam* to *impendentiam*. The author himself, however, should more properly be charged with ignorance: he claims that “enemies of justice” can be understood in two ways, whereas the first interpretation—that they are pronounced enemies of justice—is the only correct one. The second, that they are called “just enemies” in the plural nominative, cannot in any way stand with the sense of the Hebrew original or of the other copies.

Indeed, this passage permits us to infer that he was entirely ignorant not only of Hebrew but also of Greek. The Greek words do not admit the ambiguity available in Latin: *καταπατοῦντος δίκαιον* (“trampling down the just/righteous”). If he had known this—which is the actual situation—it is hardly credible that he would have wished to pursue an absurd interpretation based on a Latin ambiguity.

Nevertheless, as we have said in the Preface to the Commentary on Hosea, he appears to have been sufficiently skilled in those languages.]

### Verse 13

“Therefore,” he says, “the prudent person will keep silent at that time, because it is an evil time.”

He has altered the tense of “time.” Since he is recounting either the past or the present deeds of the people, it would be more consistent to say, “the prudent person kept silent at that time,” rather than “will keep silent.”

Since he had declared that they had undertaken a just—that is, legitimate—war against honesty and religion, he rightly says that the mouths of those who summoned them back to justice had been silenced. Every prudent person became silent with groaning and sorrow, considering that no place remained for saving instruction and that he therefore ought to take care of himself by remaining silent, since argument was no longer accomplishing anything.

These are the prudent people who were compelled into silence by public horror, the same of whom he had said above: “They hated the one who rebuked in the gate, and they abhorred the one who spoke with integrity.”

When the audacity of the profane masses has conspired to such a degree that it persecutes the truth and piety of teaching as though war had been formally declared, every prudent teacher will indeed weep, but will remain silent, seeing that, like deaf adders, they have stopped up their ears so that nothing of the saving songs can penetrate to them.

This very point seems to raise a question, which must be resolved by a brief explanation. The teacher’s prudence is praised when, if hostility blows from the side of the hearers, he withdraws into the safety of silence. Yet the Apostle to the Gentiles commands, reproves, and entreats “in season” (2 Tim. 4.), and almost all sacred Scripture commends such perseverance.

A distinction must therefore be supplied, one capable of reconciling the commands. As long as the people, although committing many offenses through negligence, nevertheless remain committed to learning, the legitimate teacher ought not to fear the concealed offenses of certain individuals, but should care for everyone who has gathered to listen through constant teaching. For he has heard that the money entrusted to him must be deposited with the money-changers, so that another may come and demand both the principal and the interest.

But if there has been such a great change for the worse that, through the impiety of the people, they withdraw their necks from discipleship itself, and, suffering from itching ears, listen only to foolish stories, then silence is plainly necessary for teachers, who can say with the prophet: “I was mute and humbled, and I was silent concerning good things, and my sorrow was renewed” (Ps. 38.).

[Note: “And so” had been read instead of *atqui* (“yet”); shortly afterward, the adverb *opportune* (“in season”) appears to require the corresponding *importune* (“out of season”).]

### Verses 14–15

Seek good and not evil, so that you may live; and the Lord God of hosts will be with you, as you have said. Hate evil and love good, and establish justice in the gate; perhaps the Lord God of hosts will have mercy upon the remnant of Joseph.

[Note: Here we supplied the name “God,” which was missing. Then, instead of *dixit* (“he said”), we read *dixistis* (“you have said”), as required in both places by all the other books and especially by the Hebrew exemplar. A little later, where the text says “keep in the gate,” those same authoritative books read “establish in the gates.”]

These verses seem to have been inserted in the person of the compassionate prophet, admonishing [variant: “stirring”] the Israelites—even though they were already placed under destruction—to unite in the resolve and efforts of correction, in the hope that perhaps the God of hosts, whose clemency is as great as his power, might be appeased by such amendment and refrain at least from destroying the remnants of the battered nation.

He then adds something that connects with what precedes.

Verses 16–17.—Therefore thus says the Lord God of hosts, the Sovereign: In all the squares there shall be mourning, and in all the places outside it shall be said, “Woe, woe!” And they shall summon the farmer to mourning, and those skilled in lamentation to the dirge. And in all the vineyards there shall be mourning, because I shall pass through your midst, says the Lord.

[Note: Here we supplied “God,” which was missing; and we restored “and to mourning those who know how to mourn,” in accordance with the Hebrew archetype and Jerome’s version, whereas previously the text read corruptly, “farmers to lamentation and mourning.” There is no doubt that these errors must be attributed to copyists.]

Having set aside those verses which, as we said, were inserted in the person of the compassionate prophet, the sequence of the denunciation proceeds. After what he had said about the enemies of the just, who accepted bribes and oppressed the poor in the gate, it now appears coherently connected that the prudent man would keep silent at that time because it was an evil time. Hence follow: “Therefore thus says the Lord God,” and the rest—that is, lamentations to be heard in all the squares.

“And in all the places outside,” he says, “it shall be said, ‘Woe, woe!’” Because he had said that there would be mourning in the squares, he added “and in the places outside,” which likewise were to be joined in the lamentation [perhaps: in collective mourning], so that he would not seem to threaten the cities alone. Thus “Woe, woe!” shall be said throughout the entire region, and vineyards, fields, and mountains alike shall resound with pitiable laments.

“Because I shall pass through your midst,” says the Lord. For a long time, he says, you treated me as though I were absent and wholly unaware of what you were doing; for throughout such long delays you gave no thought whatever to reform. But now I shall enter your land, polluted by sacrilege, as its avenger, and you will no longer be able to mock me.

He says that he will pass through in order to recall that time when, as we read, he brought about the destruction of either Egypt or Sodom, consuming the firstborn of Egypt or the houses of the Sodomites. Thus I shall pass through, he says, to inflict the vengeance that their deeds deserve.

Accordingly, blessed Hosea says, when discussing the mitigation of the sentence: “For I am God and not man, the Holy One in your midst, and I will not enter the city” (Hos. 11:9). What he had there promised in compassion that he would not do, he now, in anger, promises to do: namely, to pass through the midst of the people with the intention of taking vengeance.

When the accumulated mass of these calamities has burst upon them, the farmers will gather not for cultivation but for lamentation, summoning with them those who know how to mourn. This was introduced according to the custom of that region, a custom which also prevailed among other peoples. There were funeral songs which, with some leading the rhythm, the crowd echoed. Thus, as though to express the legitimate funeral of the people, he declares that those skilled in lamentation are to be summoned.

Verses 18–20.—Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord! Why do you want it? The day of the Lord is darkness and not light. It is as though a man were fleeing from the face of a lion and a bear met him; or as though he entered a house and rested his hand against the wall, and a snake bit him. Is not the day of the Lord darkness and not light, gloom and not brightness in it?

Showing the purpose and intention of divine mercy, the teacher of the nations says: “The goodness of God leads you to repentance, but according to your hardness and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath” (Rom. 2:5), so that by the very delay you may receive vengeance accumulated over time.

With this purpose of providing an opportunity for amendment, the prophetic threat resounded through the reigns of many kings. The elaborate description of calamities preceded it, arousing fear in the hearts of the hearers and an impulse toward correction. But those accustomed to abuse remedies turned the delay of punishments and deaths into an argument for falsehood, saying that the prophets, by speaking of the day of the Lord, were stirring up empty terrors.

Thus, among the other things which they said wantonly and wickedly, they also said mockingly that they desired the day of the Lord and wished at last that it might be revealed—not because they sought it with genuine desire, but because, if it never came, the falsehood of those who threatened it would be exposed.

Therefore the judgment that knows the truth concerning the sacrilegious declares that the profession of longing for that desired day will be followed by manifold affliction, and that the time will answer them not with favorable arguments but with harsh recompense. Storms of calamity will arise such that, wherever the wretched think they should flee, a more bitter danger will always confront them.

“That day,” he says, “will be so dark with the gloom of anguish that it will leave no light of safety. They will rush from destruction to destruction, driven onward by miserable fear: as when someone fleeing a pursuing lion encounters raging bears, suffers the added terror of sudden fear, and then bursts into some house to hide. When, after such panic, he places his hand against the wall to rest for a little while, he encounters the bite of a serpent lurking in a hole, and, as its poison spreads through his entrails, perishes.”

“Is not the day of the Lord darkness and not light, gloom and not brightness in it?” I declare that night to be not only dark but also shrouded in gloom: in it the light of security will be driven away, and no stars of consolation will shine forth.

[Col. 1081D] Verses 21–24.—I hate and reject your festivals, and I will not accept the fragrance of your assemblies. Even if you offer me burnt offerings and your gifts, I will not accept them, nor will I look upon the vows of your fattened animals. Take away from me the noise of your songs; I will not hear the music of your lyre. But judgment shall be revealed like water, and righteousness like a mighty torrent.

Although, in reproving Israel—that is, the ten tribes—he devoted the greater part of his discourse to them, his words also reach Judah. Indeed, at the beginning of the work, when he had mentioned various nations, he came to Judah and said: “For three crimes of Judah, and for four, I will not revoke it, because they rejected the law of the Lord and did not keep his commandments. Their idols deceived them, after which their fathers went; and I will send fire upon Judah, and it shall devour the houses of Jerusalem.”

Although, therefore, he had addressed Israel more forcefully, once the discourse reached the exposition of the day of the Lord—that is, the time of vengeance—and sought to explain its severity through various images, that terrifying display of retribution threatened the populations of Judah no less than those of Samaria. He therefore also showed the ceremonial consolations which Judah still appeared to be observing after Israel had been profaned to be weakened and rejected. Taking the opportunity to commend his judgment, he indicated that, amid the ruin of moral conduct, such appeasements had no value, and that he would be an impartial judge toward both tribes.

Thus, while delaying the sentence, he declares to Judah along with Israel that he despises their assemblies and offerings and scorns the vows in which they habitually sacrifice fattened victims. He is so offended by the songs with which they sing God’s praises that he declares himself to perceive noise rather than an assembly.

All these duties of religion are pleasing and acceptable to God only when they are performed together with good morals. But if sacrilegious people employ them while serving wickedness and injustice, they accomplish nothing toward obtaining salvation, so that their prayer becomes sin (Ps. 108).

When all these consolations have been convicted and removed, God’s judgment shall be revealed like water. To ensure that this was not obscure, he added: “and righteousness like a mighty torrent.” The flood of calamity sent upon them will sweep them away and extinguish them like a deluge. Through various images he desires to express the power and knowledge of the avenger: before it bursts upon them, it may be appeased by tears; once it has fallen, it cannot be evaded.

Verses 25–27.—Did you offer me sacrifices and offerings in the wilderness for forty years, house of Israel? And did you carry the shrines of your Moloch and the image of your idols, the star of your god, which you made for yourselves? And I will cause you to migrate beyond Damascus, says the Lord—God of hosts is his name.

[Note: We supplied “your,” which was missing, in accordance with the Hebrew text and the support of the other books.]

Blessed Stephen also remembered this passage at the time of his glorious passion. For when, surrounded by the ranks of raging Jews, he was arguing about the mystery of our Redeemer foretold by the holy prophets, he said: “God turned and handed them over to serve the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the prophets: ‘Did you offer me victims or sacrifices for forty years, house of Israel, and did you receive the shrines of Moloch and the star of your god Remphan—the figures which you made in order to worship them? And I will transfer you beyond Babylon’” (Acts 7:42–43).

[Note: Most books, together with the text of the prophet himself, add “in the wilderness”; conversely, they omit “for yourselves,” where it says “which you made for yourselves.”]

Although the passage itself seems to have an evident purpose—namely, a censure reproving wicked peoples—it has nevertheless mingled statements belonging to different periods in such a way that it has cast over them considerable obscurity.

[Note: Finally, he does not spare the name of the holy Doctor either. Having hitherto passed over it in silence, he was content to introduce a criticism of his teaching. We do not deny that this opinion of his concerning the almost continuous idolatry of the Israelites in the wilderness is less approved by other learned men, especially among more recent writers. But whoever dares to call it a wretched opinion thereby reveals himself as wretched and as displaying a Rufinian temperament. There is also evidence of an unfair and hostile disposition in the fact that he calls Jerome simply “Jerome” (ἁπλῶς), without adding any expression of honor—not even “Presbyter,” although he himself once complained that this form of address had been denied him by John, bishop of Jerusalem, and treated it as an insult from an enemy.

To understand how that teaching of the holy Father can nevertheless be defended without impropriety, one must observe his meaning. He declares that all the sacrifices offered at that time were offered to idols because those offered to the true God did not seem to be offered sincerely. “From the time,” he says, “when they transformed the gold into the head of a calf, saying, ‘These are your gods, Israel,’ and so forth, everything they did is shown to have been done not to God but to idols. And although afterward we read that they offered certain things to the Lord, they did so not willingly but out of fear of punishments, and because of the killing of those who fell on account of the idols. The Lord, however, considers not what is offered but the will of those who offer it. Finally, whenever the opportunity arose, they always returned in their hearts to Egypt, desiring garlic, onions, cucumbers, and Egyptian meat, and despising the manna given from heaven.”

So that we may understand this in that sense, Stephen, the first martyr of the Gospel, worthy of his name, relates in the history of the Apostles, and so forth. See our Preface.]

Finally, Jerome accepted so wretched an interpretation of this passage that he said that, during the forty years which they are reported to have spent in the wilderness, they seem to have served not God but idols. Yet the historical account records nothing of the sort. It records only that they fashioned the head of a calf while Moses delayed, and that they immediately afterward crushed it at his command.

They therefore did not offer the Legal ceremonies to stars or angels; our author himself composed their ritual and ordinances with his own mouth and commanded that everything be offered to him alone. In accordance with the customary manner of the Scriptures, the discourse of the reprover has therefore joined together different periods, though similar in character, to show that in their present sacrileges they were imitating their profane ancestors, who wickedly demanded that gods be made for them and then perished in the vast wilderness.

“What wonder, then,” he says, “if these too are driven from their own territories beyond Damascus, destined to perish in Babylon and beyond?”

Where he says “the star of your god,” the Hebrew text is said to have the name of a star, namely Lucifer, whom the Saracens are said to worship even to this day.

[Note: Jerome received this from the same source, whose name he does not mention. “What this image or idol is,” he says, “he shows in the following discourse. ‘The star of your god,’ which in Hebrew is called Chocab—that is, Lucifer—whom the Saracens venerate to this day.” He makes the same observation in the Life of Saint Hilarion, vol. II, col. 27, noting that the nation of the Saracens was devoted to the worship of Lucifer.]

Yet Scripture says nothing of this, namely, that at the time when the idol’s head was fashioned—obviously in the likeness of the Egyptian ox which they call Apis—they also decided to serve the stars. We infer, rather, that by imitating Egyptian superstition they were being assimilated to other nations as well, as though there were no form of profanation which they would not be judged to venerate and worship through the adoption of a single idol.

The sequence of thought becomes coherent if, setting aside what had been inserted, we connect this with what he had said—“Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord”—and understand the words “Did you offer me sacrifices and offerings in the wilderness?” in this sense: By abusing my patience and benevolence, through which I defer vengeance for long periods, your profanation argues that the destruction will never come simply because it has not yet come, even though it has often been promised. It is as though examples were not available by which you might recognize my custom: namely, that I grant a long period for repentance to those destined for destruction.

But, to pass over the rest, consider at least this: when the people led out of Egypt reached Mount Sinai and, standing amid miracles worthy of my power, nevertheless returned to the worship of the idols they had abandoned, they deserved to be assigned to destruction. Yet I was not appeased by their sacrifices or offerings; I granted them a period of forty years, and I did not [perhaps: permit] my anger to rage suddenly against the guilty. Rather, I gradually consumed the ranks already condemned by the sentence. Thus neither did the length of the time granted frustrate the judgment that had been announced, nor did the horror of their kindled crime hasten its vengeance.

Why, then, do you doubt that what you now see has happened will happen again? The coming calamities are announced to you and are not immediately inflicted in order to provide time for amendment, not in order that vengeance should vanish; no passage of time will be able to hinder it. But because you shamelessly abuse God’s goodness, the end of those ancestors whom you have imitated in sacrilege will overtake you: just as their corpses fell in the vast wilderness, so you too, driven from your ancestral territories, will die in a foreign land.

## BOOK TWO

[Note: The old Editor begins the second book at this point, adding a marginal note, “Book 2.” We likewise retain his division, although we have found no further indication of it.]

[Col. 1083]

## CHAPTER VI

[Col. 1083C]

Verse 1.—Woe to you who are wealthy in Zion and trust in Mount Samaria, nobles, chiefs of the peoples, entering the house of Israel in pomp.

That pride has always been hateful to God is frequently affirmed by Scripture, since such pride was the beginning of sin and changed angels into demons. Hence blessed David earnestly prays that he may not fall under the trampling of the proud: “There,” he says, “all who work iniquity have fallen” (Ps. 35).

Here, however, the prophet preserves the order of prophetic reproof, showing that pride is the fruit of impiety. The Apostle’s discourse also seems to have followed this pattern. After saying that they had served creatures while abandoning the Creator, he subsequently enumerated their crimes and shameful deeds, declaring that they overflowed with abominable acts because they had violated the obligations of devotion toward God.

“Woe,” he says, “to you who are wealthy in Zion and trust in Mount Samaria”—not that we judge the crimes of the poor more leniently, but that greater reproach presses upon you, whose greater wealth has made you conspicuous. The more prominent you are in honor and resources, the greater zeal for religion you ought to have shown. But now you strive to be rich no less in impiety than in money.

Therefore grievous lamentations will seize you, because, according to the divine judgment, some measure of mercy can be shown to the lowly, whereas “the powerful will suffer powerful torments.” Amid the many miseries of the regions, which it experiences either through the loss of its strength or through the calamities already breaking in, you trust in the defenses and fortifications of particular places, believing that you will be safe in Zion and Samaria against the anger of the judge.

“Woe to you who are wealthy in Zion and trust in Mount Samaria, nobles, chiefs of the peoples, entering the house of Israel in pomp.” You never revealed more clearly than in the time of adversity how much ambition had filled you with luxury. Although the power of the nation had already been largely exhausted, you still swelled with wealth and dissolved yourselves in luxury within besieged cities.

Verse 2.—Cross over to Calneh and see; go from there to great Hamath; descend to Gath of the Philistines, and to the best of these kingdoms—are their boundaries broader than your boundary?

He appropriately introduced the mention of foreign nations and, in the course of another statement, showed that the Creator of all things had assigned other regions for those peoples to inhabit and kingdoms in which they might flourish. Those peoples, he teaches, desired no more, whereas these people were ungrateful and profane. They had been so destructive to the cities that, after previously corrupting those whom they had influenced by their example, they later trampled them under the arrogance of plunder.

The form of divine judgment must be noted: it weighs not only the condition of the afflicted but also the merits of those who afflict them. Thus, even if those who are crushed were not guilty, the injury inflicted by their oppressors would not thereby appear excusable. Rather, the oppressors are accused as though they had violated holy people. They do not attack out of hatred for another’s wickedness but through the impulse of their own iniquity, bringing the spirit of plunderers rather than of judges. To expose their iniquity, the moderation and a certain integrity of the neighboring profane nations are set before them.

“Cross over,” he says, “to Calneh, to great Hamath, to Gath of the Philistines, and carefully observe whether they received lands broader than yours to inhabit—lands whose lot [earlier reading: “perhaps” (forte), for “lot” (sorte)] they are so content with that they seem to desire nothing else.”

This reproach, while accusing them of greed, requires further explanation. It seems inconsistent that, after charging them with wealth and luxury, he should bring forward as proof those who appeared to inhabit smaller territories. One might say that these people displayed greater arrogance because they had amassed greater wealth from the revenues of the territory allotted to them, and that the comparison would have no force as a reproach, since the consequence itself required this arrangement.

What, then, is the meaning here, when the words do not fully disclose it? It is surely the meaning that proves the sacrilegious peoples to have possessed murderous dispositions, as another prophet—blessed Hosea—clearly shows when he says: “In the days of desolation he revealed faithfulness; the leaders of Judah became like those who move a boundary,” that is, when the ten tribes had been transferred after the Assyrian victory.

The people of Judah, strangers to mercy and remorse, rejoiced that an enlargement of their boundaries had come to them. With this in view, the prophet now shows that wicked leaders exulted not only in Judah but also in Israel itself, which had earlier fallen under captivity: after the inhabitants and natives of the region had been consumed by various disasters, these men, as though they alone were being preserved within the walls of the cities, acquired a broader possession. This, however, lays the greater charge upon the tribe of Judah, whose name he mentions in what follows.

He therefore rightly condemned both their sacrifices and offerings after praising the restraint of the neighboring nations. But let us examine what follows.

Verses 3–6.—You who set yourselves apart for the evil day and draw near to the seat of iniquity; who lie on ivory beds and luxuriate upon your couches; who eat lambs from the flock and calves from the midst of the herd; who sing to the sound of the psaltery and, like David, think that they possess instruments of song; who drink wine from bowls and anoint yourselves with the finest oils, yet suffer nothing over the ruin of Joseph.

Having previously called them nobles entering the house in pomp, glorying in their wealth and banquets, crushing the heads of the lowly, and rejoicing even in the captivity of their brothers, he appropriately proceeds to their feasts and pleasures.

“Woe,” he says, “to you who set yourselves apart for the evil day”—that is, for the time of vengeance which hangs over you, to which you have been so devoted that you seem to have been chosen precisely for it.

When he says, “and you draw near the seat of iniquity,” we may understand the conjunction placed before it—“and you draw near”—as having the force of a rational connection, that is, “because.” The sense would then be: those set apart for the evil day are to be punished because they have drawn near to the seat of iniquity, having exercised unjust judgments against others.

Or certainly he calls “the seat of iniquity” that tribunal at which injustice will be examined and condemned. Thus we speak of the judgment of peculation or murder, not as the place where embezzlement or homicide is committed, but as the tribunal whose examination punishes such acts.

Living under such atrocious crimes, you think so little about the work of repentance that you pursue every instrument and variety of luxury. Not content to devote entire days to amusement, you recline upon ivory couches and soft beds, so that bodies warmed by silks may be fit for obscene acts. You season your banquets with the pleasure of your ears as well.

For while you consume selected lambs from the flocks and calves from the herds, and pour down wine until drunkenness, you make psalteries and lyres resound. To these crimes you add insults against antiquity, claiming that you possess the instruments which were available to the most blessed David.

Wretched people, you do not consider how great the difference is between your pursuits and your merits and his. David resounded with sacred song the praises of the Creator, the laws of virtue, and remedies for disturbance. You, by contrast, make the incentives to luxury resound together with an insult to the Creator, whose law is despised.

He delighted in and fortified himself with sober feasts and prophetic oils; you are drenched in drunkenness and gluttony, and in common oil that has been adulterated by artificial preparation. Finally, full of compassion, he lamented and entreated the calamities that would come upon his people many ages later. You behold those same calamities, already inflicted and already raging, with such dry eyes that you rejoice with murderous delight that they have come.

When he says, “they suffered nothing over the ruin of Joseph,” he refers to the compassion which, as he knew, ordinarily arises in the hearts of those who love or pity. That hardness is also reproved by the song spoken in the person of the just: “I looked for someone who would grieve together with me, and there was none; and for those who would comfort me, and I found none” (Ps. 68).

When captivity seized Joseph—that is, the ten tribes—Judah showed no feeling of mercy and no sentiment of compassion. Why would it, when it rather thought that an opportunity had been offered for increasing its wealth, if it could join the lands of its brother to its own borders? Let us hear what such a wish and intention receive in return.

Verse 7.—Therefore, he says, they shall now go into exile at the head of the exiles, and the company of the revelers shall be removed.

[Note: The text had been written incorrectly as “shall be offered.”]

That is, they will immediately acknowledge the emptiness of their hopes when the captivity, which had been delayed for a little while, overtakes them. They will be driven from their territories at the head of the exiles: those who had believed themselves safe will be the first to go into exile. Thus the ranks of the luxuriant will be scattered.

Verse 8–9.—The Lord God has sworn by his own life, says the Lord God of hosts: I detest the pride of Jacob and hate his houses, and I will hand over the city with its inhabitants. And if ten men remain in one house, even they shall die.

[Note: Here we supplied the name “God,” which was missing.]

To show how deeply he had abhorred their contempt for their brother’s captivity, he swore in announcing the vengeance. When the prophet says that God swore by his own life, understand this according to our manner of speaking and that of those to whom he spoke. Since we consider nothing more precious or dearer than our own life, he too—though not as an animal composed of soul and limbs, but as one who designated his majesty and life by the term “life”—swore that he detested the houses and pride of Jacob and would subject them to such calamities that the members of populous families would be consumed by repeated deaths, with no one remaining among them able to bury the dead.

By the name Jacob he indicated Judah and Israel alike, since just above he had already joined them together in calamity.

When many houses have been reduced to such desolation that no one can be found to perform the funeral rites, neighbors will come and attend to the burial of their relatives. They will not entomb them in honored graves according to custom but will consume them in an ordinary fire. The neighbors we have mentioned will enter, searching the inner rooms lest anyone remain hidden or be left behind, and they will speak to one another:

[Note: He passes over the following verse as already explained: “And the relative will take him up and burn him, in order to carry the bones out of the house; and he will say to the one who is in the inner rooms of the house, ‘Is anyone still with you?’ And he will answer, ‘It is finished.’”]

Verses 10–12.—And he will say to him—[Variant: “they will say to him”]—“Be silent, and do not mention the name of the Lord. For behold, the Lord will command, and he will strike the great house with ruins and the small house with fissures.”

What does he mean by saying, “Be silent, and do not mention the name of the Lord,” when the greatness of their misery could surely have bent even hardened hearts toward remembrance of their judge and Creator? It would seem more fitting to say, “Let us remember the name of the Lord, whose indignation has laid waste to us with such manifold calamity” [Variant: “will lay waste to us”].

Let us therefore gather the hidden meaning of this passage from what precedes: “Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord! Why do you want it? The day of the Lord is darkness for you, and not light.” This does not mean that they could genuinely seek the time of their condemnation, but rather that, as we explained, they abused the delay of vengeance and accused the prophets themselves of falsehood, as though they were threatening evils that would never come at any time.

Therefore he now says that, when the promised captivity of the guilty has overtaken them and that day—that is, that time—has arrived which they had boastfully claimed to desire in mockery, such terror of the divine name will fill them that they will say to one another that no one should dare to remember the name of the Lord. His severity, once offended, will have appeared so great that even the mention of him will seem likely to provoke further disturbance.

“For behold, the Lord will command, and he will strike the great house with ruins and the small house with fissures.” Just above, under the name Jacob, we said that Judah and Israel were both indicated—that is, all the tribes which had been divided from one another. The present verse completes this thought, announcing that both the great and the small house will be struck with fissures and ruins. Although different words are used, the same thing seems to be indicated: the overthrow of the houses. Since fissures in the walls ordinarily precede a collapse, he signified that both would fall through collapse and fissuring. He called Israel the greater house because of the number of tribes, and Judah the smaller; and he declares that, because both were polluted by similar iniquity, both would perish through similar calamity.

Verse 13.—Can horses run upon rocks, or can one plow with buffaloes? For you have turned judgment into bitterness and the fruit of righteousness into wormwood.

The meaning is most agreeable and is veiled by a particular form of expression. In allegorical words he reproaches the people for the vices with which they were covered. He is not simply referring here to four-footed animals, horses, or buffaloes; rather, he magnifies the pride of the profane nation.

They had already turned the sweetness of judgments into bitterness by crushing the innocent, and they presumed so much upon their own strength that they thought themselves incapable of being shaken by any misfortune. They had acquired such wealth that, like buffaloes—animals which never submit their necks to plows—they seemed to enjoy continuous freedom. Nor did they travel along roads difficult for horses, as a horse released from the reins might run across fields and meadows.

“Therefore,” he says, “it is certain that neither does the buffalo carry a yoke, nor does a horse willingly advance over rocks. But you, who rejoice as though you had shaken off yokes and broken reins, and who imagined yourselves to be horses in luxury and buffaloes in virtue and freedom, prove by your deeds what you have drawn from your hopes—that is, that you are subject to no commands.”

Since the opposite is plainly happening, and you are driven at the will of your enemies along the roughest roads and endure heavy labors with your necks broken, you must confess that you are neither horses nor buffaloes, and that you have acquired neither any protection or strength nor wealth for yourselves or firmness of mind.

Verses 14–15.—You who rejoice in nothing, who say, “Have we not taken horns for ourselves by our strength?” For behold, I will raise up against you, house of Israel, says the Lord God of hosts, a nation; and they will crush you from the entrance of Hamath to the brook of the wilderness.

The preceding interpretation is entirely supported: namely, that they had considered themselves free and strong like buffaloes and horses, not from any awareness of their actual strength but from their own opinion and the emptiness of their hopes.

“You have rejoiced,” he says, “in nothing, saying among yourselves, ‘Have we not taken horns for ourselves by our strength?’”—horns which seemed to display the form of buffaloes.

[Note: We restored this passage to the Hebrew text and Jerome’s version, where the carelessness of copyists had introduced errors. Instead of “Have we not,” the text had only “Have we”; instead of “we have taken,” it had “we take”; the name “God” was also missing before “of hosts”; and “I will crush” had been read as “they will crush.” Several other minor matters below are likewise corrected according to the same standard.]

[Note: Previously the reading was “which seemed offensive”; this was judged corrupt.]

You have arrogated so much to yourselves from your own strength that you thought you could safely despise the commandments. A powerful army will come against you and, through the power of those who conquer, will first lay waste to you, O Israel: from the entrance of Hamath—that is,

[Note: The writer appears to be mistaken in two or three ways in a single phrase. First, he either fails to recognize the distinction between the two places called Hamath—Great Hamath and Lesser Hamath—or assumes that the passage here concerns the former, Great Hamath, whereas it plainly concerns Lesser Hamath. For, as Saint Jerome correctly observes, the sacred text speaks of the boundaries of the land of Judah, extending toward the rising sun to the brook of the wilderness, or of the west. Moreover, no writer has ever identified this Lesser Hamath with Antioch. Rather, as far as I know, they all call it Epiphanea, as does Josephus, whom our author often uses as an authority in Book I of the Antiquities, and Jerome in several places, including here: we said that Hamath was Epiphanea, which received its name from Antiochus, whose epithet was Epiphanes (Ἐπιφανής).

But even if Great Hamath could be intended—which is the second error in which our author is mistaken—it should not be believed to be Antioch. That city, whose founders were the kings of Syria, is much more recent than the time of Amos. Indeed, Theodoret, an exceptionally skilled authority on such places, states in his Commentary on Jeremiah, chapter 39, that Great Hamath is none other than Emesa, the most distinguished city of Syria, which also preserves the similarity of the name.]

—from Antioch, to the brook of the wilderness, namely, the part that touches the desert. He will ravage all your boundaries with hostile cruelty. And you, O Judah, though remaining for a short while longer, will nevertheless be scorched and overthrown by the neighboring fire.

## CHAPTER VII
### Verses 1–3

The Lord God showed this to me, and behold, a maker of locusts at the beginning of the sprouting of the late growth; and behold, the late growth after the flock’s mower.

> **Note:** I have no doubt that *king* should be written instead of *flock*, chiefly on the basis of Jerome’s version and, above all, the Hebrew text. But since the old reading, however corrupted, might nevertheless have seemed more appropriate and might have deceived our own author, who consistently repeats it below, I have changed nothing and consider it sufficient to alert the reader. Jerome prefers: “after the late growth, the king’s mower” (or “the king’s mowing”); in manuscript copies: “the late growth after the king’s mower” (or “mowing”); the Vulgate edition: “after the tension,” and so forth.

And it happened, when they had finished eating the grass of the land, that I said: “Lord God, be gracious, I beg you; who will raise up Jacob, because he is small?” The Lord had pity concerning this. “It shall not be,” said the Lord.

He composed his prophetic speech in the customary manner.
