Indeed, he showed what sort of revelations they who were in the spirit of prophecy were accustomed to behold—for this reason they were also called “seers”: namely, that brief images of future events appeared to them under various forms, though they already grasped their meaning; and thus they were moved to different emotions, concerned either with judgment or with mercy.

Therefore, after he had announced that a nation would be raised up which would bring destruction upon them, lest the very brevity of the judgment fail to move the hearer sufficiently, he dwells upon explaining the images he had seen. Through them he shows how earnestly he prayed on their behalf, so that no one might suppose that he announced those calamities in a spirit of mockery or without feeling.

Hear, then, into the spectacle of what images our God led me. A certain figure stood there who fashioned locusts in the manner of a potter—that is, he formed swarms—and assigned them this task in numbers beyond counting: to feed, as though with tireless bites, upon all the fibers of the crops and every shoot.

When he says “at the beginning of the sprouting of the latter rain,” he indicates an increase of the disaster. It is as though a severe drought had occupied the season of the early rains, and the farmers, exhausted and harassed by the long expectation of rain, had begun to receive some relief from the latter rain, and thus had hastily sown crops whose prospects they had despaired of. But when even those seeds, scarcely and very slowly covered over, had begun to sprout, before they could rise into stalks and ears they would perish as the locusts fed upon them.

Yet, lest even a small hope temper their misfortune, another late growth would come after the locust. “Behold,” he says, “the late growth after the flock’s mower”: that is, the one who followed would consume down to the roots those shoots which the locusts had sheared.

Since he has suppressed the name of this creature, let us infer from the preceding prophecy what he meant. Blessed Joel says: “What the caterpillar left, the locust ate; what the locust left, the grub ate; and what the grub left, the rust consumed.” Therefore the prophet Amos also indicated the grub as the latter creature following the remnants of the shearing.

As for the fact that he sees a maker of locusts, although he could have shown him as the summoner of an already existing creature, this serves to proclaim the immeasurable multitude of those animals. It is not swarms gathered together in whatever number could be found in the world; rather, new swarms are fashioned by the power of the Judge, who is also the Creator of the universe.

When he had thus disclosed the reason for their formation—the devastation completed and the multitude of the dying creatures consuming their food—“I cried out,” he says: “Lord God, be gracious, I beg you; who will raise up Jacob, because he is small?” That is: “If, through your indignation, our nation is reduced to such insignificance as these figures promise, who will thereafter be able to raise it up, when you have exhausted it by such devastation?”

“The Lord had pity concerning this. ‘It shall not be,’ said the Lord.” That is, the change which followed the sentence showed that my prayer had been effective. God, ever ready to show mercy, removed that blow, whose magnitude he saw had terrified me; and he replied that what I had begged might not happen would not happen. But he introduced another punishment, which he judged to be milder.

### Verse 4

For this also the Lord God showed me: “Behold, the Lord God will summon judgment by fire, and it will consume the great abyss and devour the portion at the same time.”

> **Note:** Here the word “Lord,” followed shortly by “Lord God,” had fallen out through the carelessness of copyists; we have supplied it. Furthermore, the Jerome edition prefers *he will call* and *he will devour* rather than *he called* and *he devoured*; the Vulgate has *he was calling*, *he devoured*, and *he ate*.

Unless we understand carefully and intelligently what has been said, a considerable absurdity will appear in its meaning. After the destruction inflicted by the locust as it fed and by the grub that followed it, fire is introduced as though it were a milder blow, although it is entirely beyond doubt that a conflagration causes a far greater calamity than all the shearing of the shoots.

How, then, does the prophet say that God, having shown pity and having been moved, as it were, by the tears of the intercessor, summoned judgment to fire—that is, assigned the guilty to burning—when he had removed the danger of famine from them?

We must therefore observe that here, under the name of fire, he intended to indicate the passage of a flame. Although, by its own violence, it burns whatever it touches, nevertheless, so long as it does not linger upon the things it has struck, descend into their depths, or consume the timbers which it seemed to have seized, it does not destroy everything.

Thus, by the images of locusts and grubs—creatures intent upon the work they had undertaken—he wished to show the extermination of the condemned nation. When the prophet saw this in the spirit, he was shaken both by his affection for the people and by the reverence due to the Judge; he intervened and obtained that the severity of the sentence be changed.

But since the people’s long-standing profanation did not permit full pardon to be granted, a punishment follows which, although it consumes a large part when inflicted, nevertheless allows remnants to remain. Thus he says:

“Behold, the Lord God will summon judgment by fire, and it will consume the great abyss and devour the portion at the same time.”

But when the prophet had been encouraged by the effect of his first supplication, he dared to oppose this second denunciation also. He says that little Israel—meaning that its diminished forces would be destroyed by extermination—would perish if the one who judged, acting as chastiser, were himself to kindle the anger of the enemies.

Some have thought that the Assyrians are signified by the image of the locust and the Babylonians by the image of the fire.

> **Note:** He says “some” in the plural, but he specifically means Jerome, and perhaps intends to refer to one person while speaking improperly of him. For the holy Father understood the passage as follows: Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, with the immense multitude of his army, is said to come like a locust shearing everything at the beginning of the latter rain. Then, in the following section, he says: “After the shearing”—that is, after King Sennacherib had sheared and devastated all ten tribes—“the same Lord now shows Nebuchadnezzar; indeed, he calls him and commands him to come against Judah and Jerusalem, to set the Temple and Jerusalem on fire and to execute judgment by fire upon the people who had once been his own.” Yet this does not appear to conflict with the historical account, as our author foolishly claims, since these kings, having gained victories, devastated Jerusalem and Judah with great slaughter. Consult the whole context of Jerome’s exposition, so that you may take his side in its various parts.

They did not see that this conflicted with the historical account. For the prophet says that the plagues of the locust and the fire were removed through his prayers, and that the Lord answered the supplicant concerning both: “It shall not be”—that is, “This devastation will by no means come upon them.”

But the Assyrian and Babylonian enemies, having gained victories, ravaged both Israel and Judah with great slaughter. Here, then, our God showed through the prophet, who had become a spectator of the images, both that the Jewish people deserved a far heavier destruction than it endured and that the heavenly Judge could have destroyed it utterly if he had wished either to multiply the number of the enemies or to inflame their indignation; and also that he tolerated a certain necessity of afflicting that nation, since he did not wish it to perish completely.

### Verses 7–9

But after he had removed these two forms of impending danger, he said: “This the Lord showed me. And behold, the Lord stood upon a wall of plaster, and in his hand was a mason’s trowel. And the Lord said to me: ‘What do you see, Amos?’ And I said: ‘A mason’s trowel.’ And the Lord said to me: ‘Behold, I shall place a trowel in the midst of my people Israel; I shall no longer continue to pass over him. And the high places of the idol shall be demolished, and the sanctuaries of Israel shall be laid waste; and I shall rise up against the house of Jeroboam with the sword.’”

> **Note:** The Hebrew text and Jerome’s version do not contain the second occurrence of “the Lord.”

The prophet about whom we are speaking revealed a large part of the arrangements of God under which the life of mortals proceeds. The preceding sentences had shown either a threatening Judge or one raging and, like a lion, thirsting for the deaths of the guilty—movements and emotions which, according to the principles of doctrine, are taught to be foreign to the nature of God, who enjoys continual tranquility.

The present passage has disclosed the particular manner in which our God would rise up to punish: by abandoning them rather than by raging against them. For since a mass of calamities would immediately rush upon them if he withdrew his protection only reluctantly, he says that they collapsed beneath his blow. To arouse remorse in the hearts of the guilty, he assumes for himself the posture and movement which an enemy would have had when, by his permission, he raged against them.

Therefore, when an intervening prayer had removed the twofold sentence he had proposed according to the merits of the Jews, he introduced a third. Since the prophet, as though before the mildest possible sentence, did not dare to oppose it, he says:

“For the Lord of all things seemed to me to be standing upon a wall of plaster”—that is, one constructed by the art of masonry—with a mason’s trowel in his hand. Through this, he indicated the office he was accustomed to perform: namely, that he both defended them continually and applied frequent remedies by which they might be healed and rebuilt.

But if this providential care, which conferred such benefits upon the wretched, were withdrawn, none of them could remain joined together or continue standing. “Therefore,” he says, “I shall lay down this trowel”—that is, my care by which their cracks were plastered and strengthened—and I shall indicate a certain cessation of kindness, since Israel compels me to do so. I shall no longer endure the labor of contending, through ineffective mercy, with shameless profanation.

Then at last they will recognize what they have done, when I am not striking them but nevertheless not protecting them, and they perish—or perhaps, *will perish*.

“And the high places of the idol shall be demolished, and the sanctuaries of Israel shall be laid waste; and I shall rise up against the house of Jeroboam with the sword.”

For enemies will come, and, carrying out a complete triumph, they will rage with sword and fire, burning temples and profane places together with entire cities; and they will devastate the family of Jeroboam under the avenging sword.

But after the prophet’s speech had proceeded this far in his preaching,

> **Note:** He expounds the following verse, 10: “And Amaziah the priest of Bethel sent to Jeroboam king of Israel, saying: ‘Amos has rebelled against you in the midst of the house of Israel; the land cannot bear all his words.’”

a certain man named Amaziah, a priest of idols, sent to Jeroboam, who at that time ruled over the ten tribes. He reported to him that Amos, prompted more by the spirit of a rebel than of a prophet, was announcing destruction to him personally—that is, to the king—and was so terrifying the whole people with repeated threats that even the king was made uncertain whom he should follow.

Briefly embracing the purpose of the entire prophetic book, he said:

### Verse 11

“For Amos says this: ‘Jeroboam shall die by the sword, and Israel shall go into captivity away from his land.’”

From these words we consequently perceive what we also experience in the affairs of our own times: the lower part of the nation—that is, the common people—were more easily moved by the words of the prophets in proportion as they had less aristocratic pride.

But the priests and nobles, while striving to favor the king’s vices, rejected the prophets’ words, indeed accused them, and, if permitted, killed their beneficial teachers.

But let us continue in the order of the reading. After he had sent a message to King Jeroboam, by which he could be incited against the prophet of God, he was not content to await the outcome of the dispute he had stirred up. Wishing that the holy man be driven away by any means, the intermediary himself approached him.

### Verses 12–13

And Amaziah said to Amos: “You who see, go away; flee to the land of Judah. Eat bread there, and there you shall prophesy. But at Bethel you shall no longer continue to prophesy, because it is the king’s sanctuary and the royal house.”

Fearing, I suppose, that reverence for the prophet might restrain even the king’s anger, he tried personally to drive him out. Addressing him respectfully, he said: “You who see, go away, and flee to the neighboring region of Judah, where you may both live safely and teach.

“But in this place—namely, Bethel—in which you see the palace that has been built, and the king’s sanctuaries,” meaning the idol whose worship we, together with the prince himself, are devoted to, “do not continue any longer to resound with such words. You will perhaps understand that they will by no means go unpunished for you.”

### Verses 14–15

Amos answered and said to Amaziah: “I am not a prophet, nor am I a prophet’s son; I am a herdsman, one who nicks sycamores. And the Lord took me when I was following the flock, and the Lord said to me: ‘Go, prophesy to my people Israel.’”

From the circumstances of replies, even what is left unsaid usually comes to mind, as now in the case of the prophet. When the seer told him to flee, he replied that he did not descend from the stock of prophets, that he had not undertaken this office from the beginning, and that he nevertheless ought not, as though prophesying falsely, to be despised by his hearers.

Rather, what they were accustomed to say as an insult, he professed even with joy: that he was neither from the company nor from the lineage of prophets. He had devoted himself only to the work of a shepherd, leading herds through the pastures and gathering the cheapest possible food from trees. Yet he had been chosen by God, the examiner of hearts, and appointed to this prophetic office.

In accordance with this pattern, the Apostle also glories when he says that, when it pleased God to reveal his Son through me, he immediately did not consult flesh and blood, nor go to the apostles who were before him, but went away to Arabia and then returned to Damascus (Gal. 1:17). That is, he sought neither some teaching nor any privilege; rather, he promptly and eagerly obeyed our Redeemer, who called him, so that he might enter upon the work of preaching.

Therefore blessed Amos also professes himself a shepherd of animals. He had come to this work through no ambition, but solely through the election of the one who called him. “He said to me,” he says, “‘Go, prophesy to my people Israel.’”

Therefore, Amaziah, you and all who share your position ought to have received what I previously uttered in threatening language not as my words but as the words of God speaking through me. You ought not to doubt that I announced by God’s will what I had learned was to come.

To ensure that you do not remain ignorant of this, receive proof of the one who speaks in me—Christ:

“Your wife shall fornicate in the city; your sons and your daughters shall fall by the sword; your land shall be measured with a line. And you shall die in a polluted land, and Israel shall go into captivity away from his land.”

What benefit, then, is it to you to refuse to hear what you must endure, when it is not the words of the one announcing the event that torment you, but the wounds of the one who attacks?

Therefore, so that you may perceive that the impending sentence cannot be removed by any stratagem, I foretell that you will suffer the torments of every emotion: those endured by a husband, by a father, and by a distinguished citizen.

Your wife will not be polluted by some secret disgrace, but in the midst of the city she will be subjected to the lust of the conquerors. The sword will devastate your children before your eyes, though you will not be permitted to mourn. And you, struck at once by disgrace and bereavement, will die in a polluted land—that is, either in the very region of the Jews, which first the sacrileges of its citizens and afterward the crimes of its enemies polluted; or certainly in foreign lands, which you have always considered extremely polished.

> **Note:** I would most emphatically emend the reading to “most polluted,” as the entire context of the Prophet and the Interpreter requires.

And Israel will be driven into exile in the storm of captivity.

But let us examine what follows.

## Chapter VIII

### Verses 1–3

The Lord God showed this to me, and behold, a hook for fruit. And he said: “What do you see, Amos?” And I said: “A hook for fruit.” And the Lord said to me: “The end has come upon my people Israel; I shall no longer continue to pass over him.”

“And the hinges of the temple shall creak on that day,” says the Lord God. “Many shall die; silence shall be cast everywhere.”

Up to this point he had announced calamities that were owed to their crimes, and had shown that the sentence of the eternal Judge was fixed and that the profane would by no means escape punishment. But after the force of this declaration had continued for so long, he now shows that the time for enduring the punishments is near and, in accordance with the custom of the prophets, introduces an image expressing the same thing.

Just as above the mason’s trowel made known the care of providence, which the Judge, laying it down from his hand in indignation, showed that he had ceased to protect them, so now, by showing the nearness of their condemnation, he took up a hook for fruit. This is the tool customarily used by those who climb trees to gather fruit. Since they cannot advance to the outermost branches because of the branches’ delicacy, they stand upon a solid place and bend the ends of the branches toward themselves, gathering the fruit they see to be ripe.

Thus, since the eternal Judge already saw that vengeance was timely, he made the people understood as having ripened, as it were, to receive it. He declares that he has undertaken the task of vengeance and that Israel can no longer remain unpunished.

“I shall no longer continue to pass over him,” just as fruit-gatherers pass over what they see still unripe but pluck what is ready to be eaten. The form of the hook therefore showed that the time had come for the sentence to be fulfilled: it would drag to the deserved punishments those who seemed to flourish in wealth and abound in children.

“The hinges of the temple shall creak on that day,” says the Lord. “Many shall die; silence shall be cast everywhere.”

Do not suppose, O people, that it is unclear what this form of the hook announces. “The hinges of the temple shall creak”: that is, when all the shrines in which you trust are destroyed together with the cities, their doors will not gradually open for the services of worshipers. Rather, they will burst apart under the violence of the attackers, and the profane multitude will die in a confused slaughter. Thus the crossroads that had resounded with the crowds of citizens will be filled with mournful silence.

The name “temple,” whose hinges he says will creak, might seem to announce the calamity of Judah and the destruction of the Temple situated at Jerusalem, unless the entire context clearly applied to the ten great tribes. Therefore, he said that the hinges of that temple would be torn away, concerning which he had also said above (chap. 7:9): “The high places of the idol shall be demolished, and the sanctuaries of Israel shall be laid waste.” A little later he says more clearly:

> **Note:** This occurs at the end of this chapter, where the sacred text has the words somewhat differently; but since it is quoted here as though in a foreign setting, the wording is sufficiently appropriate to the purpose and does not differ materially in meaning.

“He who swore by the sin of Samaria and said, ‘Your God lives, Dan’—the ways of Beersheba shall fall and shall not rise again.”

### Verses 4–6

“Hear this, you who crush the poor and bring the needy of the land to an end, saying:

‘When will the month pass, so that we may sell our merchandise,
and the Sabbath, so that we may open the grain-market,
that we may reduce the measure,
increase the shekel,
and substitute deceitful balances?

That we may acquire the needy for silver,
and the poor for a pair of sandals,
and sell the refuse of the grain.’”

The prophetic speech is composed according to the same principles by which it was established. Although above all crimes it accuses them of the worship of idols, by which, in abandoning God, they became utterly profane, nevertheless it does not remain silent about other areas of life—namely, the remaining sins of conduct.

Thus it either shows that they despised the teaching of the sacred law because of their love of vices, or what sort of fruits of conduct impiety produces. Although impiety ranges through nearly every kind of wickedness, it is especially devoted to avarice, which the Apostle also calls the service of idols (Gal. 5:20).

Therefore, when this divine speech had accused the sacrilegious and was already threatening them with near destruction, it suddenly cried out, as though wishing to break through the deafness of the profane. If they neglected to judge by the merits of their pursuits, and preferred what was shameful to what was beautiful and what was useful—or what is perhaps to be emended as “what was worthless”—then at least, now that their circumstances had been brought into straits and the crash of the advancing vengeance was sounding close at hand, they might see for what purpose they were gathering money and with what wealth they were trying to fill their purses, since they were certain that these things would immediately pass into the power of their enemies.

“Hear this,” he says, “you who crush the poor and bring the needy of the land to an end” (Ps. 4). “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy-hearted? Why do you love vanity and shamelessly gape after deceptive riches?” You will feel no help from these things—indeed, no consolation—though they make you both guilty and punishable.

With what hope did you accept the bribes of judges and corrupt their decisions, so that you might receive bloody spoils from the poor whom you had oppressed and killed, and so that no form of your industry might remain innocent? For you sinned not only by corrupting judgments in the courts, but also when you continued to turn the produce of the fields into money. You polluted the very commercial activities that could have been conducted honorably, mixing crimes with the permitted pursuit of profit.

For you said: “When will the month pass, so that we may sell our merchandise, and the Sabbath, so that we may open the grain-market, that we may reduce the measure, increase the shekel, and substitute deceitful balances?”

Thus, sinning no less through avarice than through injustice, you awaited and desired public scarcity. Although exceedingly luxurious and therefore exceedingly idle, you were nevertheless annoyed by the Sabbath holidays, because the prescribed rest restrained you from frauds for at least one day.

Therefore, you complained, he says, about the delay caused by the passing rest, hastening toward active periods in which you might sell to the hungry people at high prices not only grain but even the refuse that you ordinarily threw away. Among yourselves you devised such schemes of mutual injustice “that we may acquire the needy for silver and the poor for a pair of sandals.”

Since you acted as enemies of humanity, so that the richer you were than others, the more cruel the mass of citizens found you to be; and since not even the abundance of your possessions summoned you to generosity, you ought surely to obtain no mercy from the eternal Judge, whom you denied to your neighbors with such obstinacy and shamelessness.

### Verse 7

“The Lord swore by the pride of Jacob: ‘If I forget all their works to the end.’”

> **Note:** The words that follow—“the greatness of your iniquity, O Israel”—had been joined to the preceding words as though they were part of the sacred text. We silently correct many similar errors, especially those of punctuation.

The Creator’s indignation revealed the greatness of your iniquity, O Israel. He bound himself even by an oath, declaring that he would not become forgetful of so many evils but would maintain the force of his severity until he brought them to their final destruction.

At the same time, he exposed the hidden dispositions of the guilty. Although they appeared to have sinned through fraud in measures and weights solely because of avarice, he threatens to rise up against their pride. He thereby clearly shows that they would never have committed so many crimes except through contempt for the law, and that they valued the commandments of God as cheaply as they valued money immoderately.

“It is not,” he says, “that their arrogance ends with insults against the poor. The audacity of the impious has advanced much farther: they have drunk in contempt for me. Therefore, rightly, I, who inspect their minds, detest their pride; and I have sworn in my anger: ‘They shall not enter my rest’” (Ps. 94).

For what pity can temper judgment when they rage with such cruelty that their entire region deserves to tremble, longing to be freed from the burden of those whom it has nourished in their degeneracy?

### Verse 8

“Will not the land be shaken because of this, and every inhabitant of it mourn? And it shall rise up altogether like a river; it shall be cast out and flow away like the river of Egypt?”

He explained what it meant for the land to be shaken—something he had declared figuratively as a warning of terror—in the following words: “And every inhabitant of it shall mourn.”

“Captivity,” he says, “which was once promised and until now postponed, will come. The hook of my sentence, which I mentioned above, has already drawn forward the business of vengeance. And the entire people of Israel will flow out and be compelled to pass over to the Assyrians with no greater difficulty than the river of Egypt, namely, the Nile.”

The appearance of that time will be so sad and bitter

> **Note:** He continues by expounding the following verse, 9: “And it shall come to pass on that day, says the Lord God, that the sun shall set at noon, and I shall darken the earth in the day of light.”

that at midday the sun will seem to have failed and night to have rushed in. For no distinction of ranks will remain, nor any light of counsel, as though tangible darkness had simultaneously taken earth and heaven away from the eyes of the wretched.

### Verse 10

“And I shall turn your feasts,” he says, “into mourning, and all your songs into lamentation. I shall bring sackcloth upon every back of yours and baldness upon every head. And I shall make it like the mourning for an only-begotten child, and its end like a bitter day.”

Since the speech being composed here designates not one person but the people as a whole, a change of number and gender occurs, so that they are addressed now in the plural and now in the singular.

“I shall turn your feasts into mourning and your songs into lamentation”: that is, everything corresponding to joyful things will follow them in rivalry, and the captivity inflicted upon them will subject to mourning the things you prepared for pleasure when you were free. The bodies of the nobles, shortly before clothed in precious ornaments, will be covered with sackcloth and rags.

Would that we knew that all this would occur in the time of captivity merely because the reading indicates it. But in our own times the condition has become so common that we marvel at the audacity of anyone who hopes for something better.

“I shall bring sackcloth upon every back of yours and baldness upon every head.” You will lose the adornments of your bodies and the supports of your strength, so that your hair will begin to fall away, whether consumed by ridicule or by disease.

“And I shall make it like the mourning for an only-begotten child, and its end like a bitter day”: that is, the condition of the Israelite nation will descend from the summit of its ancient happiness to the depths of wretched servitude, so that it will be worthy of mourning as bitter as that which ordinarily results from the death of an only child, when not only the lost offspring but also all future descendants are mourned as extinguished.

But let us examine what follows.

### Verse 11

“Behold, days are coming,” says the Lord, “and I will send famine upon the land—not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the word of the Lord. And they shall be shaken from sea to sea, and from the North to the East they shall wander about, seeking the word of the Lord, and they shall not find it.”

Among the extreme calamities of that people, which had flourished under the order of the Law, he has shown that the failure of sound teachers must be reckoned. Why should this not be so, since the condition is such that, if you do not hear what must be learned, ignorance overtakes you, and through it you are enveloped in the night of unknowing and run into manifold miseries, as though deprived of sight? For whoever, as another prophet declares, has not learned righteousness will not practice truth upon the earth; and thus those who speak lies will perish.

For this reason, the same crime is charged in the present passage under threat of punishment against the people who, through the prophet Hosea, had been reproached for rejecting knowledge [Col. 1095C]—and who thereby deserved to be rejected themselves by the omnipotent Lord—so that those who had hated the teachers of piety with profane zeal might recognize how industriously they had labored for their own destruction. By sinning in this way, they would incur what their Judge threatens among, indeed above, all other punishments: that amid the hardships of captivity they would be struck by a poverty of instruction, and would be deprived of that distinction by which they had been conspicuous among all nations. No prophet would instruct them in their ignorance or console them in their affliction.

That all this can occur under the judgment of an enemy, our repeated perils have taught us. Blessed Isaiah likewise affirmed this form of threat, predicting that the ruler and elder, the counselor and teacher, would be taken away from Judea, and that boys as kings and effeminate princes would be substituted in their place.

As for his saying that there would be imposed upon those peoples not a famine of bread or a thirst for water, but of hearing the word of the Lord, the wording of the passage appears to have been introduced with this meaning: it would not be merely a famine of bread or merely a thirst for water, but such a scarcity of hearing the word of the Lord that they would nowhere be able to find a teacher, even if they sought him with the greatest eagerness.

For he was not terrifying them merely by the removal of teachers, as though they were eager for spiritual instruction and deeply valued its loss. [Note: The earlier reading *per quae*, as two words, was incorrect. But neither is what is said immediately afterward, *edicenda*, entirely satisfactory.]

Accordingly, in keeping with expressions familiar in Scripture, he certainly did not deny that they would be afflicted by hunger and thirst; rather, he left it to be understood that they would not merely be subjected to those goods and evils which, according to the condition of mortal life, sometimes happen indiscriminately, [Col. 1096A] but would be punished by another and greater calamity—one that concerns everyone and cannot befall those who are not guilty. That is, divine teaching would not instruct them, but their ear, even if they protested that they wished to learn, would reject it.

It would be as though the following saying applied to them, which we read in another prophet: “But to the sinner God said, ‘Why do you recount my righteous acts and take up my covenant in your mouth?’” (Psalm 49:16).

A meaning is constructed from the whole passage: because of their crimes and their religious and moral conduct, the once-beloved Jewish people would be subjected to barbarian captivity. They would have fallen so far from the height of their former dignity that they would recognize the crimes of their will in their punishments, and, enduring the commands of harsh masters, would nowhere hear the teaching of the sacred Law resounding—the very precepts that, while they still dwelt within their ancestral borders, they had scorned, though those precepts had enlightened them.

But since the context of the passage itself demands this line of interpretation, we must also observe that these words apply to the meaning of things to come, namely, to those times in which the Jews, sinning with the utmost wickedness, suffered the most grievous fall.

After that vineyard which had been transplanted from Egypt (Isaiah 5) was planted in fertile regions, and, after the Temple had been built, received the winepress of the sacred altar; after it had been expected to produce grapes but produced thorns, and not justice but a cry; when its cultivators, enraged against the son of the master of the household (Mark 12; Luke 20), believed that they would retain without difficulty what they had seized after killing the rightful heir; the Lord God swore by the pride of Jacob: “If I forget to the end all their works.”

Their wickedness had risen to such a height that their very land was shaken and mournful darkness removed the middle of the day. For at the sixth hour darkness occurred until the ninth hour, and the earth was shaken and the rocks were split (Matthew 27). Thus their festivals came to mourning and their songs to lamentation; the backs of the impious were covered with sackcloth, and their heads experienced baldness.

When the nations came to avenge their offense, Jerusalem was surrounded by siege and so battered to the ground that it could never again rise. That people, which had violated the Only-Begotten of God with insults and blows, experienced something like the mourning for an only son and was brought to its bitter end.

Then truly came the time when it was consumed by famine of spiritual goods. We see those who had been defiant toward the word of the Lord suffering—not a lack of bread or a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of the Lord. Does not this calamity of theirs shine forth in the very testimony of events?

When the source of spiritual philosophy—namely, piety toward the Lord, kindness toward one’s neighbors, and uprightness in teaching—departed from them, they sank into such poverty of study and instruction that, from the rising of the sun to its setting, that is, scattered throughout the whole world, they nowhere hear the word of God by which they might be nourished, nor are they touched by the radiance of the shining Gospel. Instead, like children, in place of the virtues of conduct and life-giving sacraments, they swell with shameful and frivolous things: namely, circumcision of the flesh and glorying in Sabbaths [Note: *Sabbaticis* appears to require restoration; perhaps “festivals” or “Sabbath observances” should be read.]

Consequently, there exists among them no learned teacher, no ruler, and no priest by whom they may be reformed. For when Moses speaks, their eyes are covered by a veil, which is removed in no other way than when it is abolished in Christ, who redeemed us.

“They shall wander about,” he says, “seeking the word of the Lord, and they shall not find it” (John 1), because they denied him who is the Word made flesh. Thus “the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.”

### Verses 13–14

“In that day the beautiful virgins shall faint, and the young men shall thirst. Those who swear by the guilt of Samaria and say, ‘As your God lives, Dan, and as the way of Beersheba lives,’ shall fall and shall rise no more.” [Note: The Hieronymian version and the Vulgate more correctly read “those who swear,” corresponding to the Hebrew “swearing,” just as they consistently read “say” rather than “says” shortly afterward. More correctly, too, what follows is read as *Dominus nomen nesciunt* [reading uncertain], which our author consistently cites below.]

Although the prophetic utterance censures the customs of its own time, we nevertheless show, by the accumulation of its judgment, the signs of the future as well. Therefore, even if the advancing discourse looked toward events that seemed imminent, it can nevertheless apply to the condition that now holds the Jews.

It is not absurd if the Tribes themselves are called beautiful virgins on account of their former dignity. Just as they are read to have been condemned to destruction then by following idols, so now, when they denied their Redeemer, they are said to have committed the same offense as when they worshiped the calves placed in Dan and Beersheba.

The meaning is therefore this: the Jews, refusing to believe in Christ the Lord, should not vainly consider themselves free from impiety merely because they worship no idols. Nothing of the ancient piety of the patriarchs remains among them, because by violating the name of Christ through obstinate unbelief they are covered with the guilt of, and made equal to, idol-worshipers. [Note: Perhaps *conleguntur* should be restored; alternatively, *convincuntur*, “are convicted,” or something similar.]

For this reason the examiner of hearts also declares in the Gospel: “Whoever hates me hates my Father also” (Matthew 16). Condemnation therefore accumulates upon those who, by denying the Son, are pronounced enemies of the Father.

As for the words, “As your God lives, Dan, and as the way of Beersheba lives,” he indicated the custom of the common people, who, sliding into superstition, commonly swear by the roads along which they go to shrines.

“They shall fall,” he says, “and shall rise no more”—that is, they will no longer be allowed to rely upon the consolations of hope, imagining that such threats sound only to frighten them and that the joys of deliverance will immediately appear, as they are often read to have experienced. But because the time of vengeance has finally seized them with its hook, they will learn through suffering what they had previously learned by hearing, and they will fall in such a way that the realities themselves, bearing them down, will crush them.

## Chapter IX

### Verse 1

“I saw the Lord standing upon the altar, and he said: ‘Strike the hinge, and let the lintels be shaken. For avarice is at the head of them all, and I will kill the last of them with the sword.’”

Some believed that this altar, upon which the Avenger stood, was the legitimate altar situated in the Temple of Jerusalem. According to the saying of another prophet, “Begin from my sanctuaries,” it might seem that the destruction of the Temple itself was also being threatened. But the context of the passage refutes this interpretation. [Note: Jerome is one of these interpreters, against whom our author composed this anti-rhetorical commentary. Jerome, however, says little and almost in passing, though not without his characteristic appropriateness and learning: “This man,” he says, “will see the Lord standing upon the altar and commanding the prophet—or, as many think, the angel appointed to inflict the punishments for sins—to strike the hinges of the Temple [Col. 1098D], or the propitiatory, and to shake its lintels or vestibules. And when,” he says, “the Temple has been scattered and destroyed because of human wickedness, and my wrath has begun from my sanctuary, let each person recognize,” etc. Here, after *crediderunt*, add *ut*, or something similar.]

No mention of Judah had preceded it; rather, the threat specifically concerned the Ten Tribes. After saying, “They swear by the guilt of Samaria,” and, “Those who say, ‘As your God lives, Dan, and as the way of Beersheba lives,’ shall fall and shall rise no more,” he then added: “I saw the Lord standing upon the altar.”

Since he had most expressly struck at the Ten Tribes and at Samaria, we must understand the altar and shrine that he commands to be overthrown as the very one about which he had shortly before said: “The end has come upon my people Israel; I will not pass by them again,” and, “The hinges of the Temple shall creak on that day, says the Lord.”

A little earlier, Amos said to Amaziah: “Now hear the word of the Lord. You say, ‘You shall not prophesy against the house of Israel, and you shall not drip words against the house of the idol.’ Therefore thus says the Lord: ‘Your wife shall fornicate in the city, your sons and daughters shall fall by the sword, your land shall be measured by a measuring line, and you shall die in a polluted land; and Israel shall go into captivity, departing from its land.’”

Since he had said that those who swore by the guilt of Samaria would be subjected to the punishment they deserved, he follows through on the effect of this threat and says that he saw the Lord standing to destroy the altars of the profane.

Although he appears under different images, now as one who approaches and now as one who stands, everything is nevertheless accomplished at his command. He therefore says to his servants—or plainly to angels or nations coming at his will—that they should strike the doors, so that the lintels, shaken, might split apart and the ruin of the entire building follow.

Immediately he reveals the causes of the shaking: “For avarice is at the head of them all, and I will kill the last of them with the sword.”

There appears to be some deficiency in the expression, but if one looks carefully, it was adopted deliberately rather than by accident. Since throughout the whole book he had arranged their crimes and the punishments owed to them, he now rightly chose a concise form of speech, so that by indicating one vice he might mark the wounds of their conduct and, in a suitably compressed statement, touch upon the weight of their condemnation.

By the striking of the hinges and the movement of the lintels he signifies the ruin of the shrines. By the term “avarice,” which dwells at the head of them all, he declares that everyone, from the princes to the lowest, is foul with impurities and sacrileges. By saying that he will kill “the last of them,” he shows that even the least will not be spared, but that the nobles and the common people alike will perish in indiscriminate slaughter.

“There will be [Ant.: ‘was’] no flight for them,” he says. “They will flee, and none of those who flee will be saved.”

He had used “flight” to mean escape; to explain this, after saying, “There will be no flight among them,” he immediately added, “He will flee, and none of those who flee will be saved.” Thus, because fleeing offered no benefit to those destined to be captured, he declares that they will not succeed in escaping by flight.

So that this might not remain uncertain, he added an explanation: “He will flee, and none of those who flee will be saved.” The same sense appears in the Psalm: “Let their way be darkness and slippery ground, and let the angel of the Lord pursue them” (Psalm 34:6).

But so that even this briefly indicated meaning would not escape the attention of the hearers, he proceeds to enlarge the statement through a series of images, intensifying the feeling of fear through the length of the description. At the same time, he commends the fact that, when the one who surveys the whole world is angry, there is no religion and no creature able to provide any help or consolation to the condemned. [Note: *Regionem* should perhaps be restored; it certainly yields the more appropriate sense.]

After saying, “There will be no flight for them; he will flee, and none of those who flee will be saved,” he continues:

### Verses 2–4

“If they descend,” he says, “even to the underworld, from there my hand will bring them out; and if they ascend even to heaven, from there I will drag them down. And if they hide themselves on the summit of Carmel, searching from there I will take them away; and if they conceal themselves from my eyes in the depths [the Vulgate has *profundo*, ‘deep place’] of the sea, there I will command the serpent, and it will bite them. And if they go into captivity before their enemies, there I will command the sword, and it will kill them.”

This is not because captive Israel could or would wish to reach any of the places he has listed. Rather, in order to display the greatness of the eternal Judge, he gathered examples from impossibilities:

Even if, while I pursued them, they could fly up to the heights of heaven, or be swallowed by the clefts of the earth so as to remain hidden, or—as is often the folly of those who are afraid—seek the summit of Carmel as a safe hiding place, or sink into the depths of the sea’s whirlpools, nowhere would they be able to escape the force of my vengeance.

Yet lest the very condition by which they are punished flatter them, and they imagine that they will escape captivity with nothing further remaining under my authority once I have handed them over to barbarian domination, I declare that they will not be protected even by the lot of captives—those whom the cruelty of their masters often spares when it is weary or satisfied.

Even there, at my command, weapons will pierce their throats. No one will be permitted to pity those against whom I too have been compelled to rage.

The author of the sacred songs developed this same theme in praise of God:

“Where shall I go,” he says, “from your spirit, and where shall I flee from your face? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into the underworld, you are present. If I take my wings before dawn and dwell at the ends of the sea, there your hand will lead me, and your right hand will hold me. Even if I say, ‘Darkness will conceal me, and night will be my consolation,’ I consider and perceive again that darkness is no less visible to him than light”—that is, the darkness of the thickest night is as plainly before the eyes of God as the light of day. [Note: Both Roman Psalters, as also the Gallican and Hilarian Psalters—the one said to have been used by St Germanus and the one elucidated by St Hilary—prefer “before dawn” for “at dawn.” But I know no Psalter that, immediately afterward, reads “even if I say” in place of the Vulgate’s “and I said,” perhaps as our author does. This shows that he used a Psalter peculiar to his Church, different from those known hitherto. Above all, note *occultabunt* (“will conceal”), where the Vulgate has *conculcabunt* (“will trample”). A similarity in the two words may seem to have caused either a critic to substitute the former, which better suits the nature of darkness, or an unwary copyist to be deceived by the sound of the latter. But the Greek text, from which that Latin version derives, has καταπατήσει, and the Hebrew codex itself signifies properly ‘to crush’ or ‘break in pieces.’ Yet the great Jerome rendered *operiunt* (‘they cover’) in his translation from the Hebrew; from this *occultabunt* may perhaps have been introduced later by some enthusiast in place of the old *conculcabunt*.]

Therefore, just as blessed David enumerated these and other things under the wonder of divine power, so now, through Amos, our God has set them forth both as an indication of his power and as something destined to increase fear. He also showed that they could find no consolation by saying:

“I will set my eyes upon them for evil and not for good”—that is, I will look upon them in order to punish them, so that amid their sufferings they may feel what power belongs to the God whom, throughout their long and wretched existence, they had despised.

### Verse 5

“And the Lord God of hosts, who touches the earth and it melts [the Vulgate has ‘will melt’], and all who dwell in it mourn.”

He appears to have mentioned the whole earth and the entire world as an indication of his power: if God should command it, the earth would dissolve without any difficulty, in accordance with the words of the apostle Peter: “What sort of people ought we to be in holy conduct, awaiting the coming of the Lord, at which the heavens will pass away with great force and the elements will melt in the heat of fire” (2 Peter 3:11–12). [Note: This passage differs considerably in its wording from the Vulgate.]

The sense would therefore be as follows:

“O people of the Jews, devoted to profanations, do not take what I have said—that you cannot escape the force of my vengeance by any refuge—as though I had expended everything I possess upon the magnitude of your calamity. How small this effect of my power is, you can understand from this [Ant.: “here”; and shortly afterward, “the whole”]: if, in anger, I look upon the entire mass of the earth, it will dissolve no less easily than wax is melted by the heat of fire.

“For I am the Lord Sabaoth, that is, of hosts; innumerable companies of angels serve me. Although I delay for a time, I finally gird myself for vengeance.” [Note: For the sense, the word *mentem* should be deleted. It appears easily to have entered from a manuscript margin where some glossator had written *mentes* in connection with the angelic hosts.]

Consider, then, the magnitude of your calamity, since everything is possible to the one whose anger now pursues you.

But the continuity of the passage is better served if this too is understood as having been said about the region of Judea, against which threats had resounded from the beginning of the book. After saying, “I will set my eyes upon them for evil and not for good,” and that no element could either dare or be able to conceal them, he consequently added that the Lord was the King of hosts and Lord of lords, who would clothe the polluted region in desolation.

“And it shall rise like the whole river, and shall flow away like the river of Egypt”—that is, the entire nation will migrate into captivity.

As another prophet says, “They shall come to nothing like water running away” (Psalm 57:8). He calls the Nile the “river of Egypt.” When it has covered the Egyptian fields with its annual flood, it withdraws its waters again into its channel so completely that scarcely any trace of water remains in the plains.

Thus the people of Samaria, who once filled the land of Palestine as though they would enrich it, will, having been stripped of dignity and freedom, enter the confines of foreign domination and retain no sign of their former glory.

### Verse 6

“He builds his ascent in heaven, and has founded his bundle upon the earth.”

The discourse now continues with praises of God. This statement is connected with what he had said: “The Lord God of hosts, who touches the earth and it melts, and all who dwell in it mourn.”

“He builds his ascent in heaven, and has founded his bundle upon the earth”—that is, you could not escape his eyes either by ascending to heaven or by sinking into the depths of the sea. He is Lord of the angels, who created and sustains the world.

“He builds his ascent in heaven, and has founded his bundle upon the earth.”

The meaning is that, although he sits in the throne of heaven according to his majesty, he has nevertheless deigned to have upon earth a bundle as his own possession: namely, the descendants of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, whose God he chose specifically to be called, although he is Lord of the universe.

He therefore called them a “bundle,” as a possession, in accordance with the words of Deuteronomy: “When the Most High divided the nations, he established their boundaries [Note: According to the Greek, *κατὰ ἀριθμὸν ἀγγέλων θεοῦ*, ‘according to the number of the angels of God,’ which differs greatly from the Latin edition], according to the number of the angels of God; and the portion of the Lord became Jacob, and Israel his inheritance” (Deuteronomy 32:8–9).

By briefly introducing this point, he showed how great was the benevolence he had shown toward the Jews and how greatly their crimes had provoked him.

He is the one who builds—that is, who built and, from the beginning of creation, arranged matters by sacred laws—so that he himself might ascend into heaven, as into the heights of the world, as its ruler, and might dwell there in eternal dominion, while assigning the earth to the habitation of his servants. [Note: *Damnatione* (‘for condemnation’) was written here, an impious error as well as a corrupt one. Shortly afterward *fancolatui* was written for *incolatui* (‘for habitation’), which we attribute to a printer’s error; nevertheless, *famulatui* (‘for service’) would not be displeasing.] As blessed David declares: “The heaven of heavens belongs to the Lord, but the earth he gave to the children of men” (Psalm 113:24).

Although he is thus exalted upon his throne and holds the scepter, and although not only the stars but the heavens of heavens receive him with trembling, he nevertheless inclines the eyes of his mercy toward the lowest things and regards them so humbly that he abandons no creature to the neglect of his providential governance.

Although he deigned to possess a bundle, as we have said—namely, the nation to be instructed in sacred rites in honor of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—nevertheless, as the sacred song declares, “The Lord is good to all, and his mercies are over all his works” (Psalm 145:9), and, “He makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil and sends rain upon the just and the unjust” (Matthew 5:45).

He supplies nourishment not only to human beings but also to birds and beasts, in accordance with David’s words: “All look to you, that you may give them food in due season. When you give it to them, they gather it; when you open your hand, all things are filled with goodness. When you turn your face away, they are troubled” (Psalm 103:27–29).

And elsewhere: “He gives food to the beasts and grass to the service of men, to gladden the face with oil and strengthen the hearts of men with bread” (Psalm 103:14–15). [Note: This is a distinctive reading of the Psalter used by the author; similar readings are observed elsewhere and would be worth collecting.]

Thus, so that the earth may produce grains and fruits for human nourishment, it is made fertile by rain falling from the clouds. Its softness was created for this purpose: that, when rain is poured into it, it may be filled like a sponge with waves of water. [Note: This touches on the pericope of the same sixth verse, which also occurs above, in the same words, at Chapter V, verse 8: “He calls for the water of the sea and pours it out upon the face of the earth.”]

When those same waters are cleansed of their natural saltiness by this process and changed into drinkable sweetness, they pour over the thirsty fields and multiply the diversity of seeds with wondrous abundance. We confess that there is one Lord who has ordered these things.

But let us see what purpose is served by this preceding description of divine power.

### Verse 7

“Are you not like the children of the Ethiopians to me, you children of Israel?” says the Lord. “Am I only the God of the Jews? Is he not rather also the God of the nations? For there is one God who justifies circumcision by faith and uncircumcision through faith” (Romans 3:30).

Although, by the testimony of my providence—which cares for all mortals alike—you could and should have recognized that I specially chose your race for the honor of your holy ancestors, nevertheless I did not reject the other nations from my care.

At least learn from what has happened that I am Lord of all. Do not claim so much for yourselves, when you have fallen into crimes, that you imagine yourselves alone to be preferred above the others merely because you were miraculously brought out of Egyptian slavery and possess a fertile region after expelling its inhabitants—which is even more significant.

I did not exercise this kind of dispensation only toward you. Just as I brought the Israelites up from the land of Egypt, so I brought the Philistines from Cappadocia and the Syrians from Cyrene and led them into the places of those who deserved to be expelled. [Note: The remaining words of this verse are: “Did I not bring Israel up from the land of Egypt, and the Philistines from Cappadocia, and the Syrians from Cyrene?”]

Do not therefore imagine that your virtues earned what I have always bestowed through my justice. I have shown that it is the special concern of the rightful Lord to destroy kingdoms polluted by sacrilege and to leave no one unpunished whom he sees giving no thought to correction.

### Verse 8

“Behold, the eyes of the Lord God are upon the sinful kingdom, and I will destroy it from the face of the earth.”

Learn, therefore, at least from the dangers of events, that no mortal is safe through wealth or strength unless surrounded by innocence. [Note: This is plainly a scribal error. Since it may not be permissible to emend from conjecture, we have not altered it. We suspect that the author wrote *bravitate*, meaning energy, strength, or valor—an apparently barbarous term, but one that may nevertheless be his own, perhaps related to the Italian *bravura* or *valore*. Alternatively, *gravitate*, “gravity,” or something similar could readily be restored.]

My justice always requires that not merely one or two, but even an entire kingdom, if it is subject to sins, should perish.

Nevertheless, the holiness of your ancestors obtained from me that I should not allow you to be destroyed completely. Even if, weighing the merits of each side, I stir up vengeance against your crimes, the forgetfulness of mercy will never steal upon me. Even if I crush the guilty, I will not allow the name of the Israelites to perish.

There will therefore be a distinction between you and the rest: you will be chastised, while the others will be taught through extinction. Since, even in the very force of his indignation, God has revealed that he will spare the remnant, he continues with the things that bring joy.

### Verses 9–10

“For behold, I will command, and I will shake the house of Israel among all the nations, as grain is shaken [the Vulgate adds ‘wheat’] in a sieve, and not a pebble will fall upon the earth. All the sinners of my people will die by the sword, those who say, ‘Evil will not approach; it will not come upon us.’”

What has therefore roared throughout the whole book as my indignation will not spread in indiscriminate destruction. Rather, with a cautious hand and attentive scrutiny, I will shake you like a sieve in which grain is cleansed.

Its narrow openings do not allow either the grains or the pebbles to fall, but separate only the dust, the darnel, and whatever else is useless. As for his saying that pebbles remain among the grain, he appears to have referred to the custom of those who cleanse grain. They often put pebbles into the sieve for the purpose of adding force to the shaking, as the stones strike against its edges and prevent any of the refuse from remaining.

According to the more refined sense, however, and one more closely touching the matter for which the image was introduced, by the name “pebbles” he indicates the firmness of those who are not easily corrupted by evil examples. We read that in those times there were prophets and other righteous people who, while the rest of the populace perished like wood and straw, remained like solid and therefore precious stones.

Upon such people the Church was rightly founded, since no storm could overthrow it.

Therefore, although he says that the captivity sent upon them will carry all away alike, I will nevertheless not regard you as worthless, so that you should perish in indiscriminate slaughter. The balance of judgment will be exercised, so that no sword will touch the innocent and no guilty person will escape.

“All the sinners of my people will die by the sword, those who say, ‘It will not approach, and evil will not come upon us’”—that is, those who resisted the sacred prophets and, as though eager to refute them, asserted that none of the calamities they announced would come, and that they would experience none of the evils.

“Vengeance,” he says, “will pursue these people in its fury.”

As for all who are conspicuous either for innocence or for tested virtue, our hand will defend them in such a way that, though disciplined, they will not be destroyed. But let us see what follows.

## Verses 11–12

“On that day,” says the Lord, “I will raise up the fallen shelter of David; I will rebuild its breaches, and restore what had collapsed; I will rebuild it as in ancient days, so that they may possess the remnant of Edom and all the nations over whom my name has been invoked,” says the Lord who does these things.

[Note: Two words, “says the Lord,” are absent from the other books.]

Because He had promised that, even during the time of His kindled indignation, He would nevertheless show such consideration for the Jewish people that He would not allow them to be utterly destroyed—but that, amid the very tempest of captivity, when savage barbarism already possessed them, He would still defend those endowed with innocence or justice by a wondrous aid, so that destruction would have no power over them, something that certainly seemed difficult—He suitably and necessarily added what favorable events were to follow. In this way He accumulated clearer proofs of the clemency whose signs He had promised and showed that He cared for those whose merits He judged, so that they might understand that He would allow no one to perish without judgment, since He exercised this distinction not only among persons but also among nations.

[Note: We judged that “distinction” must be restored here; previously “crime” had apparently been read erroneously. We correct several other minor matters below.]

For, after the ten tribes had been taken under Assyrian rule, He defended Judah and Benjamin—who are indicated by the single designation “Judah”—from Sennacherib’s attack.

[Note: “Defend” was perhaps intended to be supplemented by “or something similar,” or else the text should more correctly be emended.]

Thus, in prophetic fashion, He names the time, saying: “On that day I will raise up the fallen shelter of David; I will rebuild its breaches, restore what had collapsed, and rebuild it as in ancient days.” By these words He plainly indicates that period when the tribe of Judah, together with the others, was freed from the Babylonian captivity. For this was confirmed by the outcome of events, just as almost all the prophets had harmoniously foretold.

Thus, after narrating all the grievous events under the person of the ten tribes, when he comes to the prediction of joyful things, he runs through their sequence by way of Judah. At the same time he indicates that the inhabitants of Jerusalem would come under adversity, from which he plainly promises that they would be brought out. Signs of this liberation appeared under Hezekiah, when God, by a wondrous protection, defended Jerusalem from the hands of its besiegers, even though it was suffering from severe scarcity.

[Note: Here “appeared” had to be restored, since the sense is correct and the whole sequence of the sentence requires it. Previously the text read “perished.”]

After all the adversities had therefore been driven away, He says: “I will take up again the mason’s trowel which, in My indignation, I had laid down, so that I may rebuild the breaks in the walls that had been shaken by the assaults of the enemies; and I will raise up all the houses that had grown old and restore them to the vigor of their ancient prosperity. Nor will I grant only the sweetness of liberty, but also vengeance: namely, that they may possess the remnant of the Idumean nation, descended from the stock of Esau, whose continually murderous hatred they had endured, and all the nations as well, placing them under their own dominion. Thus it will become evident how great a fruit of piety they have received, since, by invoking My name, they have gained rich and repeated victories.”

It should be noted, however, that blessed James, in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 13:15), recalled this passage in a subtler understanding, in order to proclaim the mystery of our Redeemer, calling David’s shelter the body of Christ. When that body, in accordance with the condition of nature, had fallen into death, it was raised by the power and mystery of the resurrection. Then indeed David’s faithful sanctification—that is, the eternal sanctification—shone forth, when God did not permit His holy one to see corruption (Psalm 15), but glorified him before the face of all peoples, for the glory of His people Israel.

[Note: Saint Jerome approves this single interpretation as far superior to all the others. “Wherever,” he says, “the authority of the Apostles precedes, especially that of Peter and James, whom he calls pillars of the Church and vessels of election, there every suspicion of varied interpretation must be removed; and what such men explain must be followed. In the Acts of the Apostles, when a question arose among the Apostles why Paul and Barnabas had received people from the Gentiles without circumcision and without observance of the Sabbath, Peter replied as he ought. James, approving his judgment, spoke as follows, and so forth. It was worthwhile to refer these words here.”]

Following the Apostles’ teaching, then, let us understand that the books of the prophets are to be read in this way: they embrace events through the sequence of their own time, yet by sudden digressions or accumulations of meaning they also signify future things and teach us to contemplate their greatness in the narration of what preceded them.

For this is how the present passage is structured. As far as its historical meaning is concerned, the punishment of the Babylonians was brought to an end, the captivity endured by the Jews was broken, and long-awaited liberty, as had often been promised, shone upon those in distress. Yet if you examine this liberation according to the rule of virtue, since it happened to mortal people who endured the bitterness of this life, you will admit that it was exceedingly limited.

[Note: Previously the text read “of you”; this was erroneous.]

But the liberation that the mysteries of Christ have bestowed upon the faithful, once it has come, is without end and incomparably more exalted. Its walls of strength and sweetness are so great that the treasures stored within them need fear neither assault nor fraud.

The remnant of Edom is believed to be possessed when this body—which appears to be represented by the red color of the Jews—just as it was sown in dishonor, will rise in glory (1 Corinthians 15:44), and will produce no distress arising from weakness either for the understanding or for the senses. Rather, God will be all in all.

Having briefly explained these matters, let us return to the sequence of the reading.

## Verse 13

“Behold, the days are coming,” says the Lord, “when the plowman will overtake the reaper, and the treader of grapes the sower of seed; the mountains will drip sweetness, and all the hills will be cultivated.”

“I will not be content,” He says, “merely to restore liberty to you; I will also make you rejoice in the abundance of crops, so that the harvest will provide enough to gather throughout the whole year, and the time of harvest will advance with such great richness that it will reach the vintage, and the vintage will be followed by the sowing.”

[Note: It seems that “vintage” should be read, giving a sounder and more coherent sense.]

This accords with what is sung by blessed David: “You will bless the crown of the year of Your goodness, and Your fields will be filled with abundance. The wilderness regions will grow fat, and the hills will be girded with rejoicing” (Psalm 64).

[Note: “Mountains” corresponds to the Greek ὄρη, which has been read and explained variously by interpreters: some, with the Vulgate, preferring “beautiful places”; others, “mountains”; and others, “regions.” In our text, however, most psalters of individual churches read this word.]

Thus here also, after the preceding promises, he adds: “The mountains will drip sweetness, and all the hills will be cultivated.” In the time of adversity there had been a great scarcity of cultivators; now, by contrast, restored tranquility will multiply the inhabitants, and the cultivation of the mountains will testify to the blessing of public peace, so that they seem to drip sweetness—that is, wine to flow from the rocks and honey from the mountains.

## Verse 14

“And I will restore the captivity of My people Israel, and they will rebuild the deserted cities and inhabit them; they will plant vineyards and drink [Ant.: ‘drinking’] their wine, and they will make gardens and eat their fruits.”

What he had expressed by exaggeration—namely, that nectar would seem to burst forth everywhere from the mountains—he explains in the following account, saying that, enjoying the blessings of liberty, they would build the walls of cities and repair their houses; they would plant vineyards and would not fear a plunderer, but would be filled with their desired fruits.

Nor would the rich alone cultivate gardens diligently; people of moderate means would do so as well and would gladly eat the produce they had obtained.

## Verse 15

“And I will plant them upon their own soil, and I will no longer uproot them from their land, which I have given them,” says the Lord your God.

That is: When I look upon—or perhaps, “restore”—the people whom the scourges of captivity have corrected, I will make them enjoy such continual security that they will no longer experience the commands of arrogant masters or taste exile again in its bitterness, but will remain in their own regions in everlasting possession.

In saying this He certainly did not promise that they would never be changed into an evil disposition, since it is clear that afterward they both denied the Redeemer of the human race and violated Him by persecuting Him, and were driven from the lands they had received to such an extent that they are continually prevented from inhabiting them.

Rather, the Lord made His purpose known: He would restore them to their ancestral boundaries in such a way that He would never wish them to be expelled, if their conduct allowed it. Thus it would be clear that all the adversities which later followed were to be attributed to their own ways.

In the body of Christ, however—that is, in the members of the Church—all these things appear faithfully and fully accomplished. To them has been granted such a happiness of hope that, when the time of resurrection arrives and they attain the blessedness that is true, they will confess that their goods are precious not only in sweetness but also in eternity.

# Miscellanea

## Notice to the Reader

The writings that follow are of a very different kind and character from those we have reviewed so far. So far are they from appearing to have Rufinus as their author that it is surprising that highly learned men could ever have attributed them to him.

The Life of Saint Eugenia, which comes first, Rosweydus himself had titled “of uncertain author,” because he found the name of no author either in the manuscript or in the printed books. Yet the style seemed to him not unlike Rufinus’ style, and he preferred to lend an ear to Goldastus, who praised the Acts of Eugenia as translated by Rufinus. Goldastus, however, spoke not on the authority of manuscripts but solely from conjecture, and moreover with hesitation, when he said in his notes to chapter 17, volume I, part I of *Rerum Alamannicarum*: “the most ancient history of Saint Eugenia, translated by the same person, if I am not mistaken, Rufinus.”

Vossius, in book II, chapter 11 of *De Historicis Latinis*, not only supports Rosweydus—as he commonly does in matters of this kind—but also exaggerates Goldastus’ conjecture and meaning, entirely supposing that Goldastus had spoken with the support of manuscript authority.

Yet Goldastus neither thought in this way, as we have shown, nor has any manuscript exemplar ever been found bearing Rufinus’ name. Finally, no argument could be produced for including this little work among Rufinian writings except a certain similarity of style. To me that similarity is slight, and even if it may appear substantial to others, it by no means establishes the matter.

The twofold *Book of Faith* that follows has enjoyed somewhat better fortune. The shorter work that comes first, consisting of twelve anathemas against various heresies, was published by my distinguished countryman Henricus Norisius in book I, chapter 3 of *Historia Pelagiana*, and by Jean Garnier among the works of Marius Mercator, from manuscripts in the Vatican and at Beauvais.

The fact that it bears Rufinus’ name was considered more than sufficient for it to be attributed to Rufinus of Aquileia, as though to its own indisputable parent, as a genuine offspring.

The second and more extensive work was published by Jacques Sirmond, who also believed that it had first been written in Greek. Garnier later included it among the works of Mercator in Dissertation V; finally, Jacques Baunius inserted it, with notes, in volume I of Sirmond’s works.

That neither work belongs to our Rufinus—that is, Rufinus of Aquileia—has been demonstrated clearly enough by the distinguished Fontaninus, who has given us leisure to mention more matters concerning this subject. See him in the *Life of Rufinus*, book II, chapters 17 and 18, lest we appear to be repeating what has already been done.

## Life of Saint Eugenia

[Note: The Roman Martyrology, 25 December: “At Rome, in the cemetery of Apronianus, Saint Eugenia, virgin. In the time of the Emperor Gallienus, after many outstanding marks of virtue and after the sacred choirs of virgins had been joined to Christ, she struggled for a long time under Nicetius, prefect of the city, and was finally beheaded with a sword.”

The Greek Menologion, 24 December, gives a brief account of her life: “The contest of Saint Eugenia the martyr and her companions.” She was the daughter of a tribune in the city of Rome under the Emperor Commodus. Her father was sent by the Emperor to the city of Alexandria to exercise the office of tribune, and he took his wife and children with him; among them was blessed Eugenia.

While she was learning literature and reading many books, she came upon the letters of the holy Apostle Paul, through which she learned the faith of Christ. Accordingly, abandoning the tumult of her family and the deceitfulness of the world, she went with two eunuchs to the monastery situated outside the city of Alexandria, dressed in male clothing.

Having been received as a guest by Bishop Helenus, and explaining why she had come there, she was deemed worthy of divine baptism together with those who had accompanied her. She was enrolled among the monks and, after some time, took charge of the monastery entrusted to her.

Because of the miracles God performed through her, she became familiar with a woman of senatorial rank named Melanthia. Later Melanthia accused her of having solicited her to intercourse, bringing against her a charge contrary to her nature. Believing Eugenia to be a man because of her appearance and wounded by her beauty, Melanthia had repeatedly attempted to seduce her; after being rejected by her, she reported her to the tribune Philip.

When her father ordered her to be summoned, the truth was revealed: not only was a woman concealed in male clothing, but she was also the tribune’s daughter. For this reason she brought her father, mother, and many members of the household to the Christian faith.

Her father, having resigned his rank as tribune, was baptized and afterward attained the perfection of martyrdom. Infidels attacked him in a temple of idols and killed him with swords.

Saint Eugenia was brought to Rome with her mother and brothers. Her eunuchs, Protus and Hyacinthus, were beheaded; she herself was tied to a heavy stone and thrown into the river Tiber. Having been preserved from there, she received her consummation by the sword.”

The *Menaea*, also on 24 December, touch upon her life in several iambic verses.

Her Acts, written by Metaphrastes, are found in Lipomanus, volume V, and Surius, volume VI, translated by Gentianus Hervetus. They agree entirely with the Acts transmitted by Metaphrastes and are arranged in the same order. Thus either this is an ancient translation closely rendered from Metaphrastes, or, more probably, this translator and Metaphrastes drew from the same source, since the later translation by Metaphrastes contains some matters stated at greater length, while this ancient translation contains others absent from the later one.

Unless one prefers to suppose that the Greek Metaphrastes translated this Latin text into Greek, since he follows the same order and at times seems not to have understood the Latin text correctly. Certainly, what is said here in chapter 1 about the seventh consulship of Commodus he understood as the seventh year of Commodus’ reign, plainly in error, as I shall soon explain.

Later authors who were older than Metaphrastes also remembered Eugenia, and it is likely that they derived their accounts from this Latin source.

Alcimus Avitus, bishop of Vienne, remembers Eugenia as a most celebrated martyr in book VI, chapter 20 of his poem to his sister Fuscina on the praise of chastity. Fortunatus does so in book VIII, poem 4, on virginity, and Aldhelm likewise in *On the Praise of Virginity*.

Rosweydus.]

## The Life of the Virgin and Martyr Eugenia, by an Unknown Author

[Note: “By an unknown author.” I gave it this title because I found the name of no author either in the manuscript or in the printed editions. Yet I see that Goldastus cites the Acts of Eugenia as translated by Rufinus. If he drew this from manuscripts, I readily agree. Certainly the style is not unlike Rufinus’ style.

Rosweydus.]

*(C, G)*

## Chapter I. Eugenia’s Parents. Philip Expels the Magicians from Egypt.

### 563

[Note: “In the seventh consulship of Commodus.” According to Baronius, volume 11, this is the year of Christ 194, which was the thirteenth year of Commodus’ reign. Yet the same Baronius places the prefecture of Egypt’s Augustal prefect Philip in the year of Christ 188, the seventh year of Commodus’ reign.
