“For,” he says, “although it is more properly said to have occurred after Commodus’ seventh year had ended, this happened because he did not receive the title and office immediately upon being chosen by the Emperor, but only when he entered Alexandria.” Ulpianus confirms that this was done according to the law of Augustus (*Digest*, single law, *On the Office of the Augustal Prefect*).

Here Baronius follows the Acts of Eugenia transmitted in Greek by Metaphrastes, which express “the seventh year of the reign” in place of “the seventh consulship.”

But this position of Metaphrastes and Baronius agrees in no way with the Acts themselves, whether Latin or Greek. For here, in chapter 17, it is said that when the persecution stirred up by Severus began, Philip had governed Egypt blamelessly for nine years and lost everything in the tenth, precisely because he favored the Catholics. The same account is found in Metaphrastes.

Now more than ten years lie between the seventh year of Commodus’ reign—which they say was when the prefecture of Egypt was conferred upon Philip—and the tenth year of Severus’ reign—which they say was when the same prefecture was taken away from him.

For since Baronius makes Commodus’ seventh regnal year correspond to the year of Christ 188, and Severus’ tenth year to the year of Christ 204, it is clear that between the two Christian years, even if the terminal years are excluded, fifteen years intervene; or seventeen years arise if both terminal years are counted. Yet Philip is said to have been removed from his administration in the tenth year of his prefecture.

Therefore the Latin text most correctly places the prefecture of Egypt’s being conferred upon Philip in the seventh consulship of Commodus, that is, in the thirteenth year of Commodus’ reign, corresponding to the year of Christ 194. Thus it is also entirely correct that Philip is said to have been deprived of it in the tenth year of his prefecture, that is, in the tenth year of Severus’ reign, the year of Christ 204. From the year of Christ 194 to the year 204 there are exactly ten years.

From this it is evident that the Latin Acts are more authentic than the Greek. I wish the great Baronius had insisted on this point, as he often does elsewhere, leaving aside the corrupted Greek texts.

Rosweydus.]

In his seventh consulship, the Emperor Commodus appointed the most illustrious man Philip to Egypt, so that he might exercise the prefecture at Alexandria and so that all the authorities administered throughout Egypt might be subject to his discretion.

Thus, when he had come from the city of Rome to the city of Alexandria with his wife Claudia, his two sons Avitus and Sergius, and his daughter Eugenia, and was exercising the prefecture with Roman dignity, ordering the whole province of Egypt according to Roman laws, he put an end to all who practiced magical curiosity. He did not even permit the Jews to retain the designation of their name, while he decreed that the Christians must remain far from Alexandria.

Although he was more a friend of philosophers than a supporter of idols, he nevertheless pressed upon the Roman superstitions as though he were a devout worshiper, agreeing not with reason but with tradition.

## Chapter II. Eugenia Is Taught Philosophy. She Rejects the Marriage Proposal of the Consul Aquilius’ Son. A Husband Must Be Chosen for His Character, Not His Ancestors.

Having thoroughly educated his daughter Eugenia in liberal studies and instructed her equally in Latin and Greek eloquence, he also allowed her to be taught philosophy. She had a keen intellect and such a capable memory that whatever she could grasp after hearing or reading it once, she retained permanently.

Eugenia was beautiful in face and elegant in body, but more beautiful in mind and more lovely in chastity.

When, therefore, at the age of fifteen, a marriage was sought for her by Aquilius, the son of the consul Aquilius, her father asked whether she consented to the young man, who was born of the most illustrious lineage.

[Note: “Aquilius, son of Aquilius.” The old edition reads *Aquilio Aquilini*. Baronius, in volume II under the year of Christ 188, reads *Acilio*, who held the consulship in that year together with Commodus—“unless,” he says, “we suppose this to be one of the suffect consuls.” Dio testifies that Commodus designated twenty-five consuls for a single year, something never done before; but since the name agrees with that of the ordinary consul, no other suffect consul need be sought.

What Baronius believes in the same place—that Eugenia was betrothed to the consul Aquilius—I think he took from Metaphrastes, where Aquilius is said to have betrothed Eugenia. But it must be understood that he betrothed her not to himself but to his son, as this Latin text has it. For parents used to promise and betroth brides to their sons.

Rosweydus.]

She replied: “A husband must be chosen for his character, not his birth; for it is he himself, not his parents, with whom one must live.”

Accordingly, when she resisted in spirit the requests of various suitors, the teaching of the blessed Apostle Paul came into her hands. Although she lived under thoroughly pagan parents, she began in spirit to be a Christian.

## Chapter III. Christians Are Ordered to Leave Alexandria. Eugenia Rejects the Philosophical Schools. The Monastery of Saint Helenus. Theodorus, Superior of Saint Helenus’ Monastery. Eugenia Arranges to Have Her Hair Cut in the Manner of a Man.

Since the Christians had been ordered to leave the city of Alexandria, she asked her parents to allow her, for the sake of sightseeing, to visit their estates situated in the suburbs of Alexandria.

As soon as she had obtained what she requested and was hurrying from the city toward the estate, she heard Christians singing psalms and saying: “All the gods of the nations are demons, but our God made the heavens” (Psalm 95).

Hearing this, she sighed and wept, and said to the eunuch youths named Protus and Hyacinthus:

“I know that you were educated with me in literature. Together we have read the worthy and unworthy deeds of human beings, and with the most painstaking diligence we have worked through the syllogisms of philosophers, constructed with vain labor: the arguments of Aristotle, the ideas of Plato, the schools of Epicurus, the teachings of Socrates, and those of the Stoics.

“To embrace everything briefly, whatever the poet sings, whatever the orator discovers, whatever the philosopher thinks, is excluded by this one sentence, which we hear the Christians singing with rejoicing: ‘All the gods of the nations are demons, but our God made the heavens.’ ‘Splendor and beauty are before Him; holiness and magnificence are in His majesty.’

“She therefore ordered that they discuss these matters. The Apostle was read and the Prophet praised. Agreement in faith was established, and with ardent counsel they determined by what means they might reach the inner chambers of divine wisdom without separating from one another.

“Power assumed over you,” she said, “has made you call me mistress, but wisdom has made you a sister. Let us therefore be brothers, as divine wisdom has ordained, not as human arrogance boasts itself to be.

“Let us go together to the Christians and hasten as I shall arrange. I hear that Helenus is a bishop, whose dwelling is that place where men are heard singing day and night to their God. Whenever we pass by, we too hear them singing psalms.

“But this bishop is said to be occupied with various duties of his church. For those who devote themselves to divine praises he has appointed a certain presbyter, Theodorus, whose miracles are said to be so great that he even gives sight to the blind by his prayers, drives out demons, and brings health to the sick.

“Indeed, he allows no women to come to the lodging of this congregation, where praise is sung to God. Considering this, I think I will have my hair cut, so that our planned journey by night tomorrow may give us passage through them.

“With you two walking beside the litter and the others going ahead, let me be set down by you at the place. When the empty litter has passed, we three, in our master’s clothing, shall hasten together to the men of God.”

[Note: “Litter.” Soon afterward he calls it a *basterna*, a traveling carriage. Ammianus, book 14: “In that procession many matrons, with covered heads and riding in litters, travel throughout every side of the city.” See the *Onomasticon*.

Rosweydus.]

[Note: “The litter for the three of us.” Thus the manuscript correctly reads. The printed editions incorrectly have “three litters.”

Rosweydus.]

Both approved the plan, and on the following night it was carried out as she had arranged.

## Chapter IV. Saint Helenus, Bishop of Heliopolis

### [Column 1109C]

Christ was pleased to display such great grace toward those who believed in Him that, at the very hour when they arrived at the monastery, Saint Helenus the bishop came there.

Since it is customary in Egypt that, when bishops visit the monasteries, a company of psalm-singers follows them, Helenus, bishop of Heliopolis, arrived with more than ten thousand men, singing psalms and saying: “The way of the righteous has been made straight, and the path of the saints prepared.”

Hearing this, Eugenia said to her companions: “Consider the power of these songs, and see that whatever they sing with melodious voices is directed toward us.”

Finally, while our discussion of the true God was taking place through an exchange of conversation, we heard them singing this: “For all the gods of the nations are demons, but our God made the heavens.”

“And now, as we take the road by which we wish to withdraw from the worship of idols and to arrive at Christian worship, seeking to obtain grace, behold, thousands of people meet us, crying out with one voice and saying: ‘The way of the righteous has been made straight, and the path of the saints prepared.’

“Let us therefore understand where this people is going. If they are going to this dwelling-place to which we have decided to go, let us join the singing crowds and, counted among those who are arriving, enter as companions until we can gather information.”

## Chapter V. Saint Helenus Carries Burning Coals with His Garments Unharmed. Saint Helenus’ Encounter with the Magician Zareas. Protected by the Sign of the Cross, Saint Helenus Remains Unharmed in the Fire.

When they had joined the psalm-singers, they asked who the elder was who alone rode in a small vehicle amid the people following and preceding him. They learned that he was Helenus, a Christian bishop from infancy.

While he had grown up as a little boy in the monastery, he had increased in such great virtues of holiness that whenever he had been sent to fetch fire from a nearby place, he carried burning coals in his garment without damaging it.

[Note: “Fire.” A similar account of Helenus the abbot is found in book II of the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 9, where he likewise carries burning coals in an unharmed garment, in almost the same words as here. I cannot easily say which account derived from the other. Rather, one might infer from this that Rufinus was also the author of this Life, as he was of book II of the *Lives of the Fathers*. Palladius gives the same little story about Helenus in chapter 58.

Rosweydus.]

“Indeed,” he said, “a few days ago a certain magician came, attempting by arguments of words to overthrow the people of God. He said that this bishop whom you see was false and that he had been sent by Christ to teach.

“He was extremely crafty and led the people astray by means of the divine Scriptures. Finally, the entire Christian crowd approached this father of ours whom you see and said to him:

“‘We have heard that Zareas claims to have been sent by Christ. Set a day on which you may either receive him as your companion or, if you can, convict him of speaking falsely.’

“A day and place were therefore appointed in the middle of the city of Heliopolis. The magician Zareas came with his arts, and Bishop Helenus came with his prayers.

“After greeting the people, Helenus said: ‘Now you will test which spirits are from God.’

“Turning to Zareas, he began a great struggle of words. But because Zareas was exceedingly crafty and Helenus could not refute him by rational argument, Helenus saw that the people were being seriously harmed because Zareas was prevailing in debate. He asked for a brief silence and said to the people:

“‘The advice of the Apostle Paul must be followed absolutely in this matter. For he says to his disciple Timothy: “Do not contend in words; it is useful for nothing except the subversion of those who hear”’ (1 Timothy 4).

“‘But let us not offer this testimony as cautious men rather than fearful ones. Let a fire be kindled in the middle of the city, and let us enter the flames together. Whoever is not burned, let us believe that Christ sent him.’”

Then everyone approved the proposal. A great fire was immediately kindled.

Blessed Helenus ordered Zareas to enter the flames. Zareas replied: “You enter first, since you proposed this.”

Blessed Father Helenus therefore made the sign of the cross over himself and, with his hands extended, entered the huge flames.

[Note: “He enters the flames.” Such challenges to fire frequently occur in sacred histories when other arguments for proving and spreading the faith are lacking. I have collected various examples in my dissertation *On Faith to Be Kept with Heretics*, chapter 42.

Rosweydus.]

Standing there for nearly half an hour, with neither his hair nor his garments harmed in any part, he likewise ordered Zareas to enter.

But Zareas began to resist and flee. When the people forced him into the fire against his will, the flame immediately surrounded him and began to burn him.

Saint Helenus threw himself in and rescued him alive, though half-burned. The people expelled him dishonorably from the borders of that region.

As you see him, the people accompany him daily wherever he goes in praise of God.

## Chapter VI. Eugenia’s Petition

When blessed Eugenia heard this, she groaned and fell at the feet of the man who had told her these things. She said:

“I beg you to introduce me to him together with these two brothers of mine, for we wish to turn from idols to Christ. Since we have decided this together and are brothers, we also wish to obtain from him that he never allow us to be separated from one another.”

He replied: “Now be silent until he has entered the monastery to which he is going and has rested for a little while. When the opportunity arises, I will tell him everything according to your request.”

Meanwhile, as he approached the monastery to which he was going, behold, its inhabitants came out to meet the father, singing a hymn to God:

“We have received Your mercy, O God, in the midst of Your temple” (Psalm 47).

As the bishop and the people entered, Eugenia also entered with her companions Hyacinthus and Protus, known only to the man with whom she had spoken.

## Chapter VII. Morning Praises. The Sixth Hour’s Mysteries Are Celebrated. The Ninth Hour’s Meal. Saint Helenus’ Vision. Eugenia Is Recognized by Saint Helenus through Divine Revelation Even after Changing Her Clothing.

### [Column 1111B]

Having therefore completed the morning praises, the bishop rested for a short while and ordered that everything be prepared for the sixth hour, so that he might celebrate the divine mysteries and, when the sixth hour had begun, the ninth hour might arrive suitably for the refreshment of those who were fasting.

While the bishop was resting, he saw a dream in which he was being led to a statue of a woman so that he might sacrifice to it. “Then,” he said, “in the dream I said to those who were holding me: ‘Permit me to speak with your goddess.’ When they had allowed me to speak, I said to her: ‘Recognize that you are a creature of God; come down, and do not allow yourself to be worshiped.’ At this she came down and followed me, saying: ‘I will not leave you until you restore me to my Creator and Maker.’”

While these things were turning over in the bishop’s mind, Eutropius, with whom Eugenia had spoken, approached him and said: “Three young brothers, unanimously abandoning the worship of images and desiring to join the company of those serving Christ in this monastery, entered here today, following in your footsteps. They asked me with tears to request that they might be admitted to the knowledge of your blessedness.”

Then the blessed Helenus said: “I give thanks to you, good Jesus, who have caused me to know of this matter beforehand.” He then ordered the young men to be summoned before him. Taking Eugenia by the hand, he poured forth a prayer. When he had completed it, he took them aside and, with the gravest expression, asked what they were called and inquired, as he thought necessary, of what nation they were.

To this Eugenia replied: “We are Roman citizens. One of these two brothers of mine is called Protus, the other Hyacinthus; I myself am called Eugenius.”

The blessed Helenus said to her: “You rightly call yourself Eugenius, for you act manfully, and may your heart be strengthened for the faith of Christ. Therefore you are rightly called Eugenius. For know also that, through the Holy Spirit, we foresaw both you and ourselves: that you were Eugenia in body, and how you came here. Nor did he allow me to pass over the fact that these are your brothers. But the Lord has deigned to reveal this to me: you have prepared for him, in your body, a most welcome dwelling place by preserving the reward of virginity and rejecting the deceitful enticements of the present age. Know, however, that you will suffer much for your chastity; but he will not abandon you to whom you have given yourself entirely.”

Then, turning to Protus and Hyacinthus, he said: “Placed in a body of servitude, you have bravely maintained—and continue to maintain—the freeborn dignity of your spirit. Therefore, while I am silent, Christ the Lord speaks to you, saying: ‘Amen, I say to you, I will no longer call you servants, but friends’ (John 15). Accordingly, I proclaim you blessed, because you have agreed with the Holy Spirit and have unanimously consented to the admonitions of the Savior. Together you will reach that glory and receive it.”

The blessed Helenus spoke these words with no other witness present but God, and ordered her to remain in this masculine clothing. They did not leave him until, instructed in the sanctification of Baptism, they joined the monastery to which they had hastened.

## CHAPTER VIII. The Alexandrians mourn Eugenia as lost. A statue of Eugenia is made as though she were a goddess.

Let us return to the time when Protus and Hyacinthus took Eugenia away and departed. The litter, therefore, with the beasts walking and the boys going ahead, arrived empty at her mother. When they saw the boys hurrying from a distance and the litter approaching, everyone ran out joyfully to meet them. But when they found the conveyance empty, they all together uttered a lowing cry, and suddenly the whole city resounded with uproar.

Who, indeed, could hear that the Prefect had lost his dearest daughter? There was immeasurable mourning and boundless weeping. Everyone lamented in confusion: the parents, their daughter; the brothers, their sister; the servants, their mistress. Sorrow and infinite anguish of spirit held them all.

An investigation was conducted throughout the entire province. The haruspices were questioned, the pythonesses consulted, and demons were interrogated through sacrifices and criminal superstitions, so that they might reveal where Eugenia had gone. They all said only this: that she had afterward been snatched up into heaven.

Her father believed that this had happened. Recalling his tears to consolation, he held celebrations in response to the oracles and consecrated her among the number of the gods. He had a statue of her made of pure gold, and it began to be honored in such a way that they paid it no less respect than to their own gods.

Her mother Claudia, however, and her brothers Avitus and Sergius could find no consolation by any means; they mourned her inconsolably.

## CHAPTER IX. Catalogue of the virtues of Saint Eugenia.

The blessed Eugenia, in masculine dress and spirit, remained in the aforementioned monastery of men. She progressed so far in divine instruction that within her second year she retained all the sacred Scriptures in memory.

Such tranquility of spirit was in her that everyone said she alone belonged to the company of the angels. For who could discover that she was a woman, whom the virtue of Christ and immaculate virginity protected, so that she was wondrous even to men?

Her speech was humble in charity, clear in moderation, free from vices, and avoided eloquence; she surpassed everyone in humility. No one was found to be more prompt than she in prayer. She became all things to everyone: she consoled the sorrowful, rejoiced with the joyful, and softened the angry with a single word. She so edified the proud by her example that he would rejoice to believe himself suddenly transformed from a wolf into a sheep.

She received such grace from God that whenever she visited someone in pain, all suffering immediately withdrew and complete health arrived.

[Note: It had previously been written, “she had avoided.”]

Her companions Hyacinthus and Protus accompanied her and obeyed her in everything.

## CHAPTER X. She is compelled to preside over the monastery. She performs the lowliest duties. Most devoted to the hourly prayers.

[Col. 1112D]

In the third year after her conversion, the abbot who presided over the brothers in the monastery departed to the Lord. After his departure, it seemed right to everyone to choose the blessed Eugenia as their abbot.

Then the blessed Eugenia, fearing that she would be placed over men as a woman contrary to the rule, and likewise fearing that she would reject all of them when they unanimously entreated her, said to them: “I beg you to bring the Gospel here before us.”

When it had been brought, she said: “Whenever Christians must choose something, Christ must be listened to before all else. Let us therefore see, in this choice of yours, what he himself commands, so that we may attend both to your orders and to his admonitions.”

She unrolled the book and came to the passage, beginning to read: “Jesus said to his disciples: ‘You know that the rulers of the nations are greater than those over whom they rule, and exercise authority over them. But it shall not be so among you. If anyone among you wishes to be first, let him be your last; and if anyone among you wishes to be master, let him be your servant’” (Matthew 20).

After saying this, she added: “Behold, in obedience also to your commands, I have resolved to accept leadership and to obey the Lord’s commands. I make myself last for your love.”

Everyone rejoiced because she consented. Yet before all others she undertook the work of the monastery that the lowest-ranking person customarily performed: carrying water in every circumstance, cutting wood, and attending to cleanliness.

Finally, she chose her dwelling in the place where the monastery’s doorkeeper lived, so that she would not appear superior even to him. She diligently cared for the brothers’ meals and faithfully maintained the order of psalmody to God. She attended so carefully to the third, sixth, and ninth hours, to evening, night, and morning prayers, that she seemed already to have perished to God if any hour or even the smallest portion of time passed without divine praises.

Thus she began to become so dear to God in this work that she drove demons from possessed bodies and opened the eyes of the blind. But since I intend to narrate many things one by one in order, let us proceed as brevity permits.

## CHAPTER XI. She cures Melanthia of quartan fever with sacred oil.

A certain Alexandrian matron, superior to the other matrons, named Melanthia, heard of Eugenia’s reputation and came to her, since she had been gravely afflicted by quartan fever for a year and more.

When the blessed Eugenia anointed her with oil, she immediately vomited up all the violence of the bile.

[Note: Perhaps “virulence” should be restored.]

Restored to complete health, she hurried on foot to her residence, which she possessed near the monastery. Meanwhile she arranged gifts, filled three silver cups with solid coins, and sent them to the blessed Eugenia as a token of gratitude for her healing.

Eugenia gratefully returned what she had sent and said: “We abound and overflow with every good thing. Therefore, dearest Melanthia, I exhort and urge you rather to distribute these things to the needy and to those suffering want.”

## CHAPTER XII. Melanthia burns with illicit love for Eugenia. Eugenia resists courageously.

When Melanthia heard this, she was distressed. She came and began to plead and promise even greater gifts. She became constant in her visits to the blessed Eugenia. Finding nothing that revealed her to be a woman, she was deceived by the elegance of youth.

Seeing her, she truly thought her a mortal young man. Believing that she had been saved not by Eugenia’s holiness but by some art, she fell into desire for her. Thinking Eugenia more desirous of greater wealth, she began to offer limitless gifts and promise still more.

When she repeatedly made the same requests and saw that the offerings she made were returned to her by Eugenia with gratitude, she turned toward even greater ruin, pretending to be ill. When the blessed Eugenia, having been asked, visited her, Melanthia began to address her while seated before her own bed:

“An unbearable love for you agitates my breast, and I have been unable to find any remedy for my distress except to make you master of all my possessions. Why do you torment yourself with empty and futile abstinences? Behold, the limitless abundance of estates; behold, an immense weight of gold; behold, an ample supply of silver; and an innumerable household. I possess the dignity of noble birth. This year I have been bereaved of children. Take their place in my wealth, and be not only master of my possessions, but from now on be my master as well.”

When she had said these and similar things, Eugenia said to her:

“Your name rightly bears witness to the treachery of blackness, for you have prepared a great dwelling place for the devil. Withdraw from the servants of God, deceiving and seductive Melanthia, for we serve in another manner. Let your riches have masters like yourself; we delight in begging with Christ. He is abundantly rich who is poor with Christ.

“Let images of desire flee from you; this madness that has seized you is not for your salvation. Having become a dwelling place of the dragon, you pour forth poison. But we, invoking the name of Christ, escape the venom of your poisons and find the mercy of the Lord.”

[Note: This appears to have been taken entirely from the reproach with which Saint Jerome attacked Melania in Letter 133 to Ctesiphon, where he said that her name, by testifying to blackness, indicated the darkness of faithlessness. For Greek μελανία (*melania*) means “blackness” in Latin. From this one may infer, by a new argument, that Rufinus was not the author of this writing, since he certainly would never have used these words, with which Saint Jerome attacked Melania, his companion, a most holy woman, with excessive sharpness.]

## CHAPTER XIII. She is falsely accused of attempted rape. The Alexandrian Prefect orders Eugenia to be arrested. Bound in chains, she is brought before the Prefect.

[Col. 1114B]

Then, unable to bear the shame of her deception and hoping that she would be exposed unless she exposed her first, Melanthia returned to Alexandria and decided to approach the Prefect, speaking as follows:

“I have encountered a wicked young man pretending to profess the Christian religion. When I allowed him to come to me for the sake of healing—for he is said to be able to help the sick—and when he thought me one of those against whose chastity he was accustomed to rage, he dared to address me shamelessly and, with insolent words, urge me toward crime. Unless I had cried out at once and been freed by the assistance of my maidservants, he would have taken me captive to his lust in barbarous fashion.”

When the Prefect heard this, he was inflamed with immense fury and ordered men to be sent to the monastery’s premises to bring him down in chains of iron together with everyone who lived there.

They were all therefore placed in bonds. Since one prison could not contain them, they were divided among different places of custody. After this, a day was appointed for their execution, on which some would be condemned to the beasts, others to the fires, and still others to various punishments.

An immense rumor arose, and shameless report traveled throughout the whole province of Egypt. Everyone believed and everyone condemned them; it seemed plausible to all that the illustrious woman Melanthia could not be lying.

What more need be said? The appointed day of execution came, and all the neighboring cities gathered to see the corrupters given over to the bites of wild beasts. They were brought in chains, with iron collars, together with the blessed Eugenia. Since no one recognized that she was a woman, the people’s clamor assailed them with various judgments.

Then the Prefect ordered her to be brought nearer, so that he might hear her not through intermediaries but learn the truth from her own mouth. The racks, whips, flames, torturers, and all the other instruments ordinarily used to draw out the secrets of the heart were prepared.

## CHAPTER XIV. The Alexandrian Prefect, Eugenia’s father, acts against his unknown daughter. Eugenia’s most prudent reply.

[Col. 1114D]

Then the Prefect Philippus said:

“Speak, most wicked of Christians. Did your Christ hand this down to you as a command: that you should devote yourselves to corruptions and ensnare the modesty and shame of matrons by deceitful cunning? Speak now, scoundrel. What rashness compelled you to desire the illustrious woman Melanthia and, entering under the guise of a physician, to provoke the noblest chastity to the shame of a brothel?”

When the blessed Eugenia heard this, she lowered her head so that she could not be recognized and gave the Prefect this reply:

“My Lord Jesus Christ, whom I serve, taught chastity and promises eternal life to those who preserve bodily integrity.

“We can now expose this Melanthia as a false witness, but it is better for us to suffer evil than for her, once convicted, to suffer something, lest the fruit of our patience also perish. Nevertheless, if your Highness will swear by the victory of the emperors that you will not turn the judgment against her herself and that this deceitful witness will suffer no harm, we shall now prove that the crime she brings against us rebounds upon her.”

## CHAPTER XV. The maidservant’s false testimony against Eugenia.

But when the Prefect had sworn by the safety of the emperors, promising to fulfill everything she requested, Eugenia said:

“O Melanthia, whose name is blackness, dark Melanthia! You have caused the spikes to be applied and ordered Christians to be suspended. Condemn, strike, burn: you treat us well. Yet Christ does not have servants such as you describe in your testimony.

“Nevertheless, order the maidservant whom you said was a witness to our crime to be brought forward, so that the lie may be stripped bare from her own mouth.”

When she had been brought before the judge, she began to say:

“This most shameless young man, frequently exposed in adulteries involving low-status persons, was driven by the very impunity he enjoyed to go further. He entered my mistress’s bedchamber shamelessly at the first hour of the day. At first, in his conversation, he declared that he had come for her health; secondly, he spoke on behalf of his own desire; and thirdly, he proceeded even to violence, if I had not quickly entered and summoned the household, which is a witness to this crime today.”

Then the Prefect ordered several members of the household to appear and confirm by their testimony that this had happened in that way. When they were brought forward one by one, they testified that it was as she had said.

Then the judge, greatly angered, said:

“What will you say to this, wretch, when so many witnesses refute you and so many indications make the truth evident?”

## CHAPTER XVI. Eugenia clears herself magnificently. She confounds all her accusers by revealing her sex.

To this the blessed Eugenia said:

“It is time to speak, because the time to be silent has passed” (Ecclesiastes 3). I had indeed wished for the alleged crime to be exposed at the future judgment and to show my chastity to him alone for whose love it must be preserved. Nevertheless, lest deceitful boldness boast against Christ’s servants, I shall establish the truth in a few words—not for the ostentation of human declamation, but for the glory of Christ’s name.

“For such is the power of his name that even women placed in his fear obtain manly dignity; nor can the difference of sex be found superior to faith in him, since the blessed Apostle Paul, teacher of all Christians, says that with the Lord there is no distinction between male and female: ‘For we are all one in Christ’ (Galatians 3).

“Accordingly, I took up this rule with fervent spirit. Because of the confidence I had in Christ, I did not wish to be a woman; rather, preserving immaculate virginity with the whole intention of my spirit, I steadfastly bore myself as a man in Christ.

“I did not assume a wanton pretense of morality in order to pretend, as a man, to be a woman. Rather, by acting manfully as a woman, I bore myself as a man, embracing courageously the virginity that is in Christ.”

Having said this, she tore the tunic with which she was clothed from her head, and she appeared as a woman.

Immediately she said to the Prefect:

“You are indeed my father according to the flesh; Claudia is my mother; and these two brothers sitting with you are Avitus and Sergius. I am Eugenia, your daughter, who for the love of Christ rejected the whole world with its pleasures as dung.

“Behold Protus and Hyacinthus, my eunuchs, with whom I entered the school of Christ. But Christ proved so effective there that, through his mercy, he made me victorious over lust and every pollution. In him I believe that I shall remain continually to the end.”

## CHAPTER XVI. She is recognized by her parents. The entire household is baptized. Peace is granted to the Christians.

When the father recognized his daughter, the brothers their sister, and the servants their mistress, they immediately ran to her. Pouring out tears before the people, they embraced her.

The event was reported to her mother Claudia, who at once hurried swiftly to the spectacle. Garments woven with gold were brought, and although she was unwilling, she was dressed in them. Placed upon a high tribunal, she was raised on high, and the whole people cried out:

“One Christ, one true God of the Christians!”

The priests and bishops who were with a large Christian crowd before the amphitheater—and who, after those who were accused had been killed, buried them themselves—entered, singing a hymn to God, and all cried out with one voice:

“The right hand of the Lord has been glorified in power; the right hand of the Lord has shattered the enemies” (Psalm 117).

Eugenia was therefore carried in triumph. And lest, amid the people’s great joy, proof of her chastity be lacking, a fire seemed to descend from heaven and surround Melanthia’s house, so that not even a trace of anything belonging to her remained.

The people rejoiced with fear of God. The church, which had been closed for eight years as though widowed, was reopened. The Christian people were recalled. The Prefect, still holding office, was baptized; his sons were baptized; and their mother Claudia was baptized.

He restored the Christians’ privileges and sent a report to the emperor Severus concerning the Christians, stating that they benefited the state sufficiently and therefore ought to live in the cities without any persecution.

The Emperor agreed to the reports, and the entire city of Alexandria became, as it were, one Church. There was joy in all the cities, and the dignity of the Christian name flourished.

## CHAPTER XVII. Persecution is stirred up. The emperors’ letter to Philippus.

But because the enemy’s rivalry always follows holiness and malice fights against goodness, certain distinguished Alexandrian worshipers of idols, acting on the devil’s counsel and taking offense that he had granted privileges to the Christians, went to the emperor and said that the condition of the state had been thrown into disorder by Philippus, who, although he had administered his office irreproachably for nine years, had now ruined everything in the tenth year.

[Note: “Now in the tenth year.” Baronius, volume II, in the year of Christ 204, the first year of Pope Zephyrinus and the tenth of the Emperor Severus: “It ought not to seem so very surprising,” he says, “that Philippus continued so long in the exercise of that office. For since that prefecture—called Augustal, that is, the prefecture of Egypt—was of the greatest importance of all, and Augustus had retained it for himself as a hostage of the Roman Empire, decreeing that no senator should be sent to it but rather some outstanding man from the equestrian order who could never stir up disturbances out of love of power, once the Emperor had found a supremely trustworthy man worthy of that prefecture, he did not readily remove him. He knew especially that this was advantageous to the peace and security of the Roman Empire, since the Egyptians were the most eager of all peoples for innovation and the most fickle in stirring up disturbances and rebellion. But Dio discusses these matters at greater length.” ROSWEYDUS.]

“In the end, he abandoned the rites of the immortal gods and converted the entire city to the worship of a certain man whom the Jews killed. There is no respect for your laws. Anyone may enter the revered temples wherever he wishes, not to profess goodwill toward the worship but not even to believe that those whom we worship are gods; rather, he speaks endless blasphemies and calls the images signs of stones or metals rather than of the divine power [formerly, “Name”].”

Many such things were said to Severus and Antoninus Augusti.

[Note: “Who, being provoked…” Baronius, volume II, in the year of Christ 204, the second year of Pope Zephyrinus and the tenth of the Emperor Severus, places the persecution stirred up by Severus. He also says that Severus seems to have been provoked to stir up persecution against the faithful because he understood that Philippus, administering the noblest prefecture in all Egypt—the Augustal prefecture—had already become a Christian. Thus far Baronius. Since this chapter says that it was the tenth year in which Philippus had held the prefecture, this calculation does not agree with the seventh year of Commodus, in which he is said to have assumed the prefecture. ROSWEYDUS.]

Severus and Antoninus, moved by these allegations, issued to him decrees of this kind:

“Divine Commodus, our father, formerly Augustus, appointed and established you in Alexandria not as prefect but [Note: “As king.” Baronius, above, in the year of Christ 204. As for the fact that Severus says in that letter—according to Metaphrastes in Hervetus’s translation—‘He chose you as ruler of Egypt more as a king than as a prefect’: this clearly confirms what Tacitus writes in these words: ‘Ever since the divine Augustus, Roman knights have held Egypt in place of kings. It seemed expedient to keep at home a province difficult of access, rich in grain, divided by superstition and licentiousness, fickle, ignorant of laws, and unacquainted with magistrates.’ ROSWEYDUS.]

“as king, so that, as long as you lived, you would accept no successor. Therefore, wishing to add to these benefits of his, we decree that you offer the customary worship to the omnipotent gods—or, having laid aside your dignity, that you also surrender your personal possessions.”

## CHAPTER XVIII. Philippus distributes his property to churches and the poor. He is considered worthy of episcopal honor.

Having received this imperial authority, he pretended to be ill until he had disposed of everything and donated it throughout the province to churches and the poor. The Prefect himself, in fear of God and in the worship of Christ, also strengthened others in Christ.

Meanwhile all Alexandria conspired in favor of his episcopate.

[Note: “For his episcopate.” Baronius, volume II, in the year of Christ 204, the second year of Pope Zephyrinus and the tenth of the Emperor Severus, says that the Acts of Philippus should be corrected where they say that he was made bishop of Alexandria. For, he says, “as I note under September 13, his prefecture was secular, not sacerdotal. For Eusebius, both in his Chronicle and in his History, when he sets out the succession of the Alexandrian bishops, as do Bishop Nicephorus, Nicephorus Callistus, and others who performed the same task, does not number Philippus among the Alexandrian bishops.” ROSWEYDUS.]

The state began to regard him as its Prefect, because no successor had yet arrived, and the Church began to regard him as its bishop, because on account of his faith it had rightly chosen him as priest. He remained in the episcopate for one year and three months.

## CHAPTER XIX. Perennius, Prefect of Alexandria. Philippus is struck down with a sword. Eugenia builds a monastery of virgins. Claudia establishes a hospice over Philippus’s tomb.

After this interval of time, Perennius the Prefect arrived.

[Note: “Perennius the Prefect.” Thus in the manuscript. In the printed editions, “Herennius.” In Metaphrastes, “Terentius.” Baronius, in the year cited immediately above, says: “The man whom Eusebius calls Laetus may perhaps be the same as the one called Terentius Laetus.” Perennius is found in the *Menaea*, in manuscripts, in Ado, and in Usuard’s *Martyrology*. Herennius Celsus also appears at this time in Trebellius Pollio’s *Thirty Tyrants*, under Aemilianus. Hence it seems possible to conclude that Herennius was then the Augustal Prefect of Egypt. ROSWEYDUS.]

While Perennius was seeking to strike Philippus in Alexandria and could not do so because the entire city remained devoted to him, he sent men who pretended to be Christians. They entered and struck him down.

[Note: “They struck him down.” Baronius, volume II, in the year cited immediately above: “As for the fact,” he says, “that Eusebius, when discussing the martyrs who suffered in Egypt, makes no mention of the martyrdom of this Philippus, this perhaps happened because he passed over him as the cause of his own death. Since he was secretly killed by assassins and no public confession of the Christian name known to anyone had preceded it, he may appear to have been omitted by him. Yet there is no doubt that he silently passed over many matters of still greater importance—as can be seen in nearly every year—for other reasons.” ROSWEYDUS.]

They struck him while he was engaged in the Lord’s Prayer. Afterward the assassins were handed over to the Prefect Perennius. Since he was conscious of having ordered the deed and pretended that they ought to be heard, he committed them to custody; but a few days later, released by the indulgence of the emperors, he dismissed them.

The most blessed Philippus was permitted to remain in the body for three days after being struck down, for no other reason than to strengthen wavering hearts. For, when he was about to depart to the Lord, he did not wish to be deprived of the crown of martyrdom, and he himself prayed to receive it.

For if, while in the body, he drove away demons and illuminated the blind by prayer, how much more would he refuse to be deprived of the palm? Without doubt he could obtain what he desired. And so he received it in such a way that, as a participant in Philippus’s name, he might also be a participant in his crown, and the martyrs might receive as their companion one whom the Church had rightly received as its priest.

Accordingly, beside the courts where his holy daughter Eugenia had established a monastery for virgins of Christ, he ordered his little body to be placed. In that place the most blessed Claudia was building a hospice, and she established estates to provide for the reception of travelers.

She herself, together with her sons Avitus and Sergius and the blessed Eugenia, returned to Rome.

## CHAPTER XX. Basilla seeks Eugenia’s companionship. Pope Cornelius baptizes Basilla.

The Roman Senate received Philippus’s children with every joy. They sent one as proconsul to Carthage and another as vicar of Africa.

Many matrons came to the blessed Eugenia, and she caused nearly all the virgins whom she could reach, whether acquaintances or friends, to believe in Christ and remain in the Lord’s virginity.

A certain virgin of royal lineage, named Basilla, desired to approach her. But because she could not go to her on account of the Christian name, she asked through a faithful intermediary that Eugenia instruct her in the Christian religion.

Then the blessed Eugenia summoned her most blessed companions, Protus and Hyacinthus, and said to them:

“Gird yourselves for the warfare to which Christ summons you, so that I may offer you to Basilla under the appearance of a gift and you may make her a handmaid of Christ.”

The gift was therefore made, and Basilla received them as servants but honored them as apostles. She spent every hour with them and, having eunuchs as attendants, never ceased, by day or night, from conversations about God and from prayers.

While Cornelius, the chief priest of the sacred law, was in the city of Rome, he came secretly to her and baptized her. The blessed Basilla, strengthened in the fear of God through the mercy of Christ, and the blessed Eugenia enjoyed one another’s company almost constantly.

## CHAPTER XXI. Claudia gathers widows; Eugenia gathers virgins. Hymns and sacred mysteries on the Lord’s night.

All the Christian widows gathered around the blessed Claudia, and all the virgins gathered around the blessed Eugenia.

The holy Cornelius, Pope of the city of Rome, every Saturday evening, as the Lord’s Day was dawning, gave them a night of vigil with hymns. At cockcrow, in the quiet of the night, he celebrated his sacred mysteries and thus strengthened them on the Sabbath.

As I have mentioned, Eugenia and Basilla enjoyed one another’s company in Christ almost every night and renewed one another through alternating conversation.

O how many virgins the Savior found through Eugenia! How many brides Christ won through Basilla! How many women preserved widowhood with willing devotion through Claudia! How many young men believed in Christ the Lord through Protus and Hyacinthus!

## CHAPTER XXII. Persecution of the Christians. The Lord reveals to Eugenia and Basilla their approaching crowns. Eugenia’s prayer to Christ.

When Valerian and Gallienus were ruling, a sedition arose concerning the Christians, because Cyprian was overthrowing Carthage and Cornelius Rome.

Authority was therefore given to the proconsul Paternus to kill Cyprian. Cornelius, however, because he was supported by many Romans, including distinguished men, was in hiding.

Then the blessed Eugenia, seeing Basilla, said:

“It has been revealed to me by the Lord that you will suffer for virginity.”

Basilla replied to Eugenia:

“The Lord has also deigned to show me that you will receive a double crown of martyrdom: one that you acquired at Alexandria through your righteous labors, and another that you will obtain through the shedding of your blood.”

Then the blessed Eugenia stretched out her hands and said:

“Lord Jesus, Son of the Most High, who came for our salvation through your mother’s virginity, by the reward of virginity bring to the kingdom of your glory all those whom you have entrusted to me.”

## CHAPTER XXIII. Eugenia’s exhortation to virginity and martyrdom. The deceitful enticements of the world.

[Col. 1119C]

While the holy virgins of Christ who were with Eugenia and Basilla were seated, the blessed Eugenia said to them all:

“Behold, it is the time of the harvest, when the clusters are cut down and trampled underfoot; but afterward they are set before royal banquets. No imperial power and no illustrious dignity is honored without their blood. And you, my branches and clusters of my innermost being, be ready in the Lord.

[Note: It appears that *palmites* (“branches”) should be read.]

“Virginity is the sign of the first virtue, nearest to God; like the angels; the parent of life; the friend of holiness; the path of security; the mistress of joy; the guide of virtue; the nourishment and crown of faith; the aid and support of charity.

“Nothing should be labored for so much, nothing striven for so earnestly, as to live with virginity—or, what is more glorious, even to die for virginity.

“The enticements of this world are utterly deceptive. They come with temporal joy and depart with everlasting grief. They produce momentary laughter so that they may inflict eternal weeping. They offer fleeting flowers so that they may carry away those who endure, more withered. They falsely promise the security of passing time so that they may hand people over to the torments of the everlasting age.

“Therefore, dearest virgins, who until now have run with me in the contest of virginity, remain in the love of the Lord whom you have begun to love. Endure the temporary season of weeping without weariness or dread, so that you may receive the times of eternal joy with complete love.

“For I have entrusted you to the Holy Spirit, and I believe that he will preserve you all for me whole and undefiled. Therefore do not henceforth seek my face bodily; contemplate my deeds and actions through the spirit.”

Having said this, she kissed them all and consoled them as they wept with the greatest courage. Basilla and Eugenia then bade one another farewell, prayed, and departed.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Basilla is betrayed by a maidservant. Helenus, Basilla’s cousin. Basilla kisses the feet of Protus and Hyacinthus.

Behold, on that same day one of the maidservants went to Pompey, Basilla’s betrothed, and said: “We know that our mistress Basilla was granted to you by the Emperor; it is now six years and more since you deferred taking her, when she was still at a tender age, until she should later be of marriageable age. But you should know that her cousin Helenus is a Christian, and that she has been made a Christian in such a way that she will by no means marry you. For Eugenia pretended to offer her two eunuchs, Protus and Hyacinthus, as a gift; and she honors them as though they were her masters, and every day kisses their feet as though they were those of immortal gods, because they themselves are the authors of the magical art which Christians practice.”

When Pompey heard this, he immediately hurried to Helenus, her cousin, who was also her guardian and tutor, and said to him: “I have decided to celebrate my wedding within these three days. Therefore arrange for me to see my betrothed, whom my invincible lords, the rulers of the world, have ordered to become my wife.”

When Helenus heard this, he realized that the affair had been betrayed, and said to him: “Until the years of her childhood had passed, I exercised guardianship over her, both because of her father’s kinship with me and because I had brought her up. But now that she has begun to belong to herself, she wishes to be under her own authority. Therefore, if you desire to see her, that will depend on her will, not on my command.”

## CHAPTER XXV. Basilla Refuses a Conversation with Her Betrothed Pompey. Pompey’s Accusation against the Christians.

When Pompey heard this, he began to burn with even greater anger. He went to Basilla’s house and ordered the doorkeepers to announce him. Basilla sent him this reply: “You should know that I have absolutely no reason to see you, hear you, or greet you.”

When he heard this, he was deeply troubled. Using nearly all the support of the senators, he threw himself before the Emperor and said: “Come to the aid of your Roman people, most sacred princes, and remove from this city the new gods whom Eugenia brought with her when she came from Egypt. It is long since those who are called Christians have harmed the state: they mock the sacred rites of our laws and despise our almighty gods as though they were empty images. They also pervert the laws of nature, dissolve marriage, and attach the grace of betrothal to themselves; and they say that it is wrong for a betrothed woman to accept her betrothed.

“What shall we do, most merciful Emperors? Gods have been discovered who forbid human beings to marry—and what will become of those who look to these things, if no one is born who can be commanded? Where is the restoration of Roman strength? Where are the renewed battles of the Roman armies? For whom will your victorious right hands bend the necks of enemies, if women are no longer to have husbands, if we lose our betrothed women and remain silent?”

## CHAPTER XXVI. The Sentence of the Emperor Gallienus against Basilla. Basilla Is Pierced with a Sword for the Love of Chastity. Protus and Hyacinthus Are Beheaded.

While he continued with these and similar arguments, and the entire senate expressed them in mournful complaint, [Note: Gallienus Augustus decreed.] Baronius, volume II, in the year of Christ 262, the second year of Pope Dionysius, and the eighth year of the Emperors Valerian and Gallienus. He says that this concerns the martyrs who suffered at Rome, since some are said to have undergone martyrdom under the Emperor Gallienus. This did not happen because, after Valerian ceased to rule, they were crowned in martyrdom; for, as we shall say, when Valerian, his father, had been captured by the enemies, Gallienus soon ordered the persecution to cease, issuing edicts in favor of the Christians. Rather, because Gallienus alone ruled at Rome while Valerian was conducting the army in the East, many martyrs—whether at Rome or elsewhere—are said to have suffered under Gallienus, among them the most illustrious woman, the virgin Eugenia.

**ROSWËYDUS:** Gallienus Augustus decreed that Basilla should either accept her betrothed or perish by the sword, and that Eugenia should either sacrifice to the gods or die cruelly. He also granted permission that anyone who concealed a Christian in his house should be punished.

Basilla was summoned to accept her betrothed. She said that she had as her betrothed the King of kings, who is Christ, the Son of God. When she had said this, she was pierced with a sword.

Protus and Hyacinthus were immediately seized and dragged to the temple. But while they were praying, the statue of Jupiter to which they were being led in order to sacrifice fell at their feet, and was so completely shattered that no trace of where it had stood remained. Nicetius, the prefect of the city, attributing this not to divine power but to magical art, ordered them to be beheaded.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Eugenia’s Remarkable Testimony concerning the Chastity of the Church.

When Eugenia had also been summoned before him, Nicetius began to demand from her an account of magical arts. But she boldly opened her mouth and said:

“I promise you that our art is more powerful by far. For our master has a Father without any mother, and a mother without a father. The Father begot him in such a way that he never knew a woman at all; the mother begot him in such a way that she did not know a male at all. He himself has a virgin wife, who every day creates children for him and bears him innumerable children; every day she joins her flesh to his flesh. His kisses are constantly united with her; they endure together wholly in mutual love; and they remain in such complete purity that from their marriage all virginity, all charity, and all integrity are derived.”

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Eugenia Is Led to the Temple of Diana. Eugenia’s Prayer. At Eugenia’s Prayer the Temple of Diana Collapses. The Emperor’s Sentence against Eugenia. Eugenia Is Cast into the Tiber but Does Not Drown.

When Nicetius heard this, he was astonished. To prevent the report that he willingly listened to her from reaching the Emperor, he ordered her to be led to the temple of Diana. The executioner, standing over her, said: “Redeem your life and your inheritance, Eugenia, and sacrifice to the goddess Diana.”

Then blessed Eugenia stretched out her hands and began to pray, saying:

“O God, who know the secrets of my heart, who have preserved my chastity pure in your love, who have deigned to unite me to your Son, my Lord Jesus Christ, who have caused your Holy Spirit to reign within me, stand by me now as I confess your name, so that all who worship this idol and glory in their images may be put to shame.”

While she was praying, an earthquake occurred in that place. The foundations of the temple itself, together with the idol, sank so completely that nothing remained except the altar alone, which had stood before the temple door, where blessed Eugenia was standing.

These events took place on the island of Lycaonia before all who were following Eugenia’s contest. The Roman people gathered, and there was a variety of acclamations. Some called her innocent, others a sorceress. The matter was reported to the prefect, and the prefect made it known to the Emperor.

The Emperor ordered her to be bound to a stone and thrown into the Tiber; but immediately the stone broke apart. Blessed Eugenia, however, was carried along while seated above the river water, so that it became apparent to all Christians that the one who had been with Eugenia in the river, so that she would not be swallowed up, was the same one who had been with Peter in the sea, so that he would not drown.

## CHAPTER XXIX. She Remains Unharmed by the Fire of the Baths. She Is Fed by Christ in Prison. She Is Struck with a Sword.

After this she was taken away and cast into the furnaces of the Severian Baths. They were immediately extinguished in such a way that the heat of the baths cooled and all the fires of the wood came to nothing. Finally, they produced such a ruin that the baths could no longer be used.

After this she was sent into a dark prison and ordered to receive no food for ten days and to see no light at all. Yet such great brightness abounded there every day that, when blessed Eugenia came out, she seemed to radiate a kind of light.

The Savior appeared to her, carrying in his hand bread of snowy whiteness and immeasurable sweetness and grace, and said to her: “Eugenia, receive food from my hand. I am your Savior, whom you have loved and do love with the full intention of your mind and spirit. On the same day on which I descended to earth, I will receive you into heaven.”

Having said this, he departed.

On the very day of the Lord’s nativity, a gladiator was sent who struck her while she was confined in prison. Her body was taken away by Christian relatives and placed not far from the city, on the Latin Way, in her own estate, where she herself had buried the remains of many saints.

## CHAPTER XXX. She Appears to Her Mother and Foretells Her Death.

When her mother Claudia was weeping at her tomb, Eugenia appeared to her while she was awake, in the silence of midnight, dressed in a golden-woven cyclas, together with a great company of virgins. She said to her:

“Rejoice and be glad, because Christ has brought me also into the joy of the saints, and my father into the number of the patriarchs. Behold, on the Lord’s Day he will receive you also into everlasting joy. Commend to your sons, my brothers, that they guard the sign of the cross, so that they may become participants with us.”

As she spoke, a brightness appeared which the eye could not endure; and passing angels sang a hymn to God in inexpressible voices. Only this could be understood: that the name of Jesus Christ and of the Holy Spirit resounded in those praises.

Glory and honor to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, now and always, and for ages of ages. Amen.

---

# BOOKLET ON THE FAITH

[Note: Cardinal Norisius published this from the Vatican manuscript, and Garnerius from the manuscript of Beauvais; the former preferred to attribute it to Rufinus of Aquileia, while the latter attributed it to another Rufinus, a disciple of Jerome. Mabillonius praises it from a very ancient Bobbio codex, with this heading: “An exposition of the Abridgment of the Catholic Faith by Saint Jerome, so that certain people who had fallen into heresy might be corrected.” Whoever nevertheless wishes to attribute it to Jerome on this basis is foolish.]

## OR TWELVE ANATHEMAS UNDER THE NAME OF RUFINUS

(C, G)

## HERE BEGINS THE STATEMENT CONCERNING THE FAITH

Because of our veneration for the holy places, we came to Jerusalem and Bethlehem. We learned that many brothers were scandalized by us because they had heard that we professed many things that were heretical and contrary to the faith of the Church.

Therefore, with God present, we testify that we formerly held, through error, some of the opinions written below, and that at the present time we condemn them. As for other matters with which we are falsely accused, we neither said nor say them; and the contrary opinions which we suspect others of holding, we have set forth and condemned.

### I

Let those who say that the punishments of the Devil, demons, and the impious—that is, Gentiles, Jews, Samaritans, and all heretics—are not everlasting be anathema. This excludes Christians who follow the right faith, even if they are sinners.

### II

Let those who say that any holy, prophetic, or apostolic man can be perfect without God’s help be anathema.

### III

Let those who say that Christ, the Son of God, God the Word, was changed into a human being, so that God the Word ceased to be; or that he was born as a mere human being from Mary, according to Paul of Samosata and Photinus, and by merit and virtues progressed into the name of God, be anathema.

### IV

Let those who interpret the statement “Of that day, year, and hour neither the angels nor the Son know” (Mark 13:32) in accordance with the blasphemies of the Arians, and not with reference to the dispensation of the assumed flesh, be anathema.

### V

Let those who say that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—that is, the Holy Trinity—are of different substances from one another, and not of one power and nature, be anathema.

### VI

Let those who say that, in any way or in any sense, the Son does not see the Father be anathema.

### VII

Let those who say that our souls fell from the exalted state of angels into these bodies because of certain ancient sins, and that they are doing penance in this world, adducing the testimonies “Before I was humbled, I sinned” (Psalm 118:67), and “Bring my soul out of prison” (Psalm 141:8), and other similar passages, be anathema.

### VIII

Let those who say that our Lord and Savior came not in our nature but possessed a different and higher substance, whether heavenly; and that he did not wholly assume what is from Mary, or did not possess a human soul, or possessed a mind without sin, be anathema.

### IX

Let those who say that, after many ages and periods which we cannot grasp by human thought, there will be a restoration of all things to their former state, and that everything will return to its beginnings, be anathema.

### X

Let those who say that after the resurrection we will not have the same bodies, but some airy and spiritual bodies of a nature different from that in which we were placed in the tomb, even if incorruptible and immortal, be anathema.

### XI

Let those who say that, after the end of the resurrection and after many ages, bodies will be abolished and return to their former use, so that we will be souls alone without bodies, as we were before, be anathema.

### XII

Let those who say that souls existed before they were born, and that they are not made by God each day together with the body according to the example of the first human being, be anathema.

## THE BOOK ON THE FAITH ENDS, UNDER THE NAME OF RUFINUS

---

# THE BOOK ON THE FAITH OF RUFINUS, PRESBYTER OF THE PROVINCE OF PALESTINE

[Note: *The Book on the Faith.* P. Sirmondus notes the following: John the Deacon used the testimony of this book twice in his exposition of the Heptateuch, once in Genesis and again in Exodus, in both places under this title: “From the Book on the Faith of Rufinus,” which was evidently entitled in Greek *περὶ πίστεως* (*On the Faith*). Thus many books of the ancient Fathers are titled or mentioned. The three books of Theophilus of Antioch addressed to Autolycus, for example, whose title is generally absent, bear this title in Codex 808 of the Royal Library: *Περὶ τῆς τῶν Χριστιανῶν πίστεως* (*On the Faith of Christians*). The same judgment applies to three other books said by Gennadius, chapter 33, to have been written by Theophilus of Alexandria on the faith.]

(C, G)

This is our faith, which we learned from God and from learned men—I mean Moses and the other prophets who proclaimed the Old Testament—as well as from the holy and blessed apostles and evangelists, who salutarily made known to us the New Testament of Christ.

### I

There is one God, possessing a substantial Word equal to himself in every respect, and likewise a substantial Wisdom equal to himself in every respect. [Note: *Substantial Wisdom.* The name “Wisdom” among the divine persons, customarily attributed to the Son, was formerly assigned by some to the Holy Spirit, as by this author, and before him by Theophilus of Antioch and Irenaeus of Lyons. The words of Theophilus, from Book II addressed to Autolycus, are: “The three days that preceded the creation of the luminaries are a type of the Trinity: of God, of his Word, and of his Wisdom.” Irenaeus, in Book IV, chapter 17, teaches that God did not need the ministry of angels in order to bring things into existence: “His offspring and his own formation,” he says, “minister to him in all things—that is, the Son and the Holy Spirit, the Word and the Wisdom.”]

There is one substance of the Father, the Only-Begotten, and the Spirit; one power; one Lord, without beginning and without end; simple and uncompounded; incorporeal; without form; without limitation; neither increasing nor diminishing; lacking nothing; undivided; infinite; invisible; incomprehensible; unchangeable; imperishable; immutable.

What he is, he always is and will always be: creator of all things, possessing authority, a kind providential guardian, just judge of the living and the dead.

And the one God the Word was born at the end of the ages from the Holy Spirit and Mary, ever-virgin; he was crucified and died for us; on the third day he rose again; he ascended into heaven; he sits at the right hand of his Father; he will judge the living and the dead; and each person will receive his due according to his deeds, with the same flesh.

### II

God is simple and uncompounded, because divinity is not a body; composition properly belongs to bodies.

He is simple and uncompounded because word and wisdom do not accrue to him as accidents; for composition is understood to consist of substance together with accidents.

He is simple and uncompounded because the substance of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is not different, but is shown to be wholly one and the same.

### III

That the substance and power of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one and the same is testified by our Lord Jesus Christ, who teaches about himself and about the Holy Spirit.

Regarding himself he says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), and again: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9).

By these words he plainly showed that there is one substance and the same power. For when he had said to Philip, “I have been with you for so long, and you have not known me? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (ibid.), he wished to teach that we behold the same one—himself and the Father—in both power and substance, through the wonders that he performed.

For those whose will is one also have the same works, and those whose works are the same likewise have the same substance. Therefore he said to the Jews: “If I do not perform the works of my Father, do not believe me. But if I do them, even if you do not believe me, believe the works, so that you may know and understand that the Father is in me and I am in the Father” (John 10:37–38).

He also wonderfully taught that divinity must be recognized only from its works. For since it is by nature invisible and cannot otherwise be seen than through its works and deeds, Wisdom also bears witness, saying: “For from the greatness and beauty of created works the Creator of them is correspondingly perceived” (Wisdom 13:5).

Likewise blessed Paul the Apostle says: “For his invisible things are understood and perceived from the creation of the world through the things that have been made, and also his eternal power and divinity” (Romans 1:20).

The holy Apostle John again teaches that our Lord Jesus Christ openly proclaimed himself to the Jews as the Son of God according to substance, in saying: “For this reason the Jews sought all the more to kill him, because he not only was breaking the Sabbath, but was also calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God” (John 5:18).

The Jews understood this at the time: Jesus had manifested himself as the Son according to substance when he said to them: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5:17).

### IV

Our Lord Jesus Christ taught these things about himself. He also taught about the Holy Spirit: that he is of the substance of God, and that the things which God the Father does are likewise done by the Spirit, when he says: “The Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father” (John 20).

Furthermore, when he cast out the opposing powers whom, according to human custom, he calls demons, he said: “But if I cast out demons by the finger of God” (Luke 11:20).

That he calls the Spirit the finger of God is stated more clearly by the other Evangelists. Matthew says: “But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God” (Matthew 12:28). Mark says: “Whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit has no forgiveness forever, but is liable to eternal sin, because they were saying, ‘He has an unclean spirit’” (Mark 3:29).

When the Lord said this, he plainly taught that the substance of the Father and the Holy Spirit is one and the same, since the finger belongs to the same substance as the one whose finger it is.

Moreover, when he said to his disciples, “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them,” he likewise showed that we ought to believe the substance of the Father and the Spirit to be one and the same.

Blessed Paul also teaches, saying: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you? If anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him” (1 Corinthians 3:16–17).

By saying this, he plainly taught that the substance and power of God and of the Spirit are one and the same, since the temple of God is recognized as such only through the Spirit of God who dwells within it.

Blessed Paul also writes concerning the Holy Spirit, saying: “But when he turns to the Lord, the veil will be taken away. Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Corinthians 3:16–17).

By saying this, he showed that the substance is the same, since the Spirit is the Lord and the Spirit of the Lord grants and bestows freedom.

### V

The Son is in the Father, not as in a place—for his substance is not enclosed by boundaries—but as a word is in the mind, as the simple is in the simple, as the infinite is in the infinite, as the uncreated is in the uncreated, as the one without beginning is in the one without beginning; and as Lord in Lord, God in God, of the same substance and likewise of the same power.

Similarly, the Father is in the Son, as a meaning is not separable from a word.

By “meaning” I call the Father, taking an example from ourselves, so that we may understand how the Father is in the Son and the Son is in the Father. Although, in saying this, I have also drawn reasons and seeds from divine Scripture: for when the prophets and apostles, taught by God, called the Son “the Word,” they taught us without doubt to understand the Father as “meaning.”

For a word cannot otherwise be understood unless it arises from meaning, or mind. I call it “meaning” not as ours is, since God’s Word is not like ours, nor is his Wisdom like ours.

Likewise, we say that the Holy Spirit is in the Father and the Son, of the same substance and power, as wisdom is in meaning and word. Further, the Father and the Son are in the Spirit, of the same substance and power, as meaning and word are not separated from wisdom.

### VI

That there is a Spirit in God, as though he were of his substance, and as though the two were one and the same—so that, as I may say, he is wholly in the whole—and that he knows God’s depths and profound things, blessed Paul also teaches, saying:

“To us God has revealed it through the Spirit. For the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God” (1 Corinthians 2:10).

Taking an example from us—that is, from our wisdom, which penetrates our entire mind more deeply and knows all that is within it—he goes on to say:

“For who among human beings knows the things of a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him? So also no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God” (1 Corinthians 2:11).

Blessed Paul took this example from us because he wished to show how the Spirit of God knows his depths, since he knows that the human being is the image of God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. [Note: For the human being is the image of God.]

Those who assigned Wisdom among the divine persons to the Holy Spirit also offered reasons why the human being is called the image of God: he possesses meaning, word, and wisdom. Just as God is the Father of his eternal Word, so the human mind, or meaning, produces its word; and just as the Holy Spirit belongs equally to the Father and the Son, so wisdom in the human being is by no means separated from meaning and word.

More will be said about this again near the end of the book, no. 61.

For the human being is the image of God, since he is rational and possesses meaning, word, and wisdom. Moses also teaches this when he says: “And God said, ‘Let us make the human being according to the image’—not merely my image, but ‘according to our image and likeness’” (Genesis 1:26).

### VII

That, just as the Holy Spirit belongs to the Father, so he likewise belongs to the Son, blessed Paul again teaches, saying:

“You are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you” (Romans 8:5)—that is, the Spirit of God the Father.

And then he says: “But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, that person does not belong to him.”

He also says in another place: “And because you are sons, God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’” (Galatians 4:6). [Note: The manuscript reads: “crying out in our hearts.”]

The Holy Spirit belongs equally to the Father and the Son, since he is neither the Father nor the Son. To give another example from ourselves: he is not like meaning that generates word, nor like the word that is generated by meaning, but like wisdom, which is not separated from meaning and word.

### VIII

That the substance and power of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one and the same is also taught by Moses, the servant of the Lord, when he says:

“And God said, ‘Let us make the human being according to our image and likeness’” (Genesis 1:26).

Although he ought to have said “Let me make,” he said “Let us make”; and he said not “according to my image,” but “according to our image.”

Again he says, “And God made the human being,” not “They made.”

He does this to show that the three persons—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—possess one and the same nature and an undivided divinity.

Likewise the prophet David teaches that the power of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one and the same when he says:

“By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their power” (Psalm 32:6).

### IX

The holy Apostle John, moreover, in order to teach that the Son and the Father have one and the same substance, says:

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him” (John 1:1–2).

When he said, “In the beginning was the Word,” and not “The Word was from the beginning,” nor again “The Word was with the beginning,” or “under the beginning,” he plainly taught that the Word is without beginning—as though he were above every beginning and himself were the cause of beginning.

For if all things were made through him, and beginning is included among all things, then the Word himself is the head and cause both of beginning itself and of the entire expanse that follows beginning, within which times and ages are contained.

Again, by saying, “The Word was with God,” he showed that the Word is substantial, since he did not say, “The Word was in God,” but “The Word was with God.”

Then, by saying, “The Word was God,” he teaches that the substance and power of the Father and the Son are one and the same. For there is no difference between God and God, since neither has a beginning; rather, the substance of both is one, and their power likewise the same.

When he says, “He was in the beginning with God; all things were made through him” (John 1), he plainly teaches us not to believe in two separate substances, powers, or virtues, since there is one God who establishes and creates all things through his substantial Word.

For this reason we are taught not to speak of three separate substances—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—or of powers and virtues separated from one another, since there is one God who is recognized as creating all things through Word and Wisdom.

### X

That God does all things in Wisdom and with Wisdom—that is, with the Holy Spirit—is testified by the holy prophet David. In proclaiming God, recounting the greatness of his power, and marveling at the riches of his wisdom, he cries out:

“How magnificent are your works, O Lord! You made them all in wisdom” (Psalm 103:24).

Blessed Paul likewise proclaims this Wisdom with profound admiration when he says:

“O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Romans 11:33).

That David the prophet calls the Wisdom of God, by which God made and makes all things, the Spirit of God, agreeing in similar fashion with blessed Paul, he plainly teaches in what follows:

“The earth is filled with your creation. This is the great and spacious sea; there are creeping things without number, small animals with great ones. There ships pass through; there is that dragon which you formed to play in it. All things look to you, that you may give them food in due season. When you give it to them, they gather it; when you open your hand, all things are filled with goodness.
