When you turn your face away, they are troubled; you take away their spirit, and they fail and return to their dust. You send forth your Spirit, and they are created, and you renew the face of the earth” (Psalm 103:24ff.).

In saying, “You made all things in wisdom,” and, “You send forth your Spirit, and they are created,” the prophet plainly taught that the person of God’s Wisdom and that of the Holy Spirit are one.

Solomon likewise calls the Holy Spirit of God “Wisdom” when he says to God:

“Who has known your counsel, unless you have given wisdom?” (Wisdom 9:17). [Note: The manuscript reads: “He says to God, ‘But who has known your counsel?’”]

To show what sort of wisdom he means, he goes on to say:

“You sent your holy Spirit from on high, and thus the paths of those on earth were corrected; and they learned what pleases you, O Lord, and were saved by wisdom” (ibid.). [Note: The manuscript reads: “Your will, human beings, they learned.”]

That is: having been taught your counsel by your Holy Spirit, they were saved.

As blessed Paul also says:

“For God has revealed it to us through the Holy Spirit; for the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God” (1 Corinthians 2:10).

### XI

Since, therefore, we have such witnesses, we ought not to doubt that we must say that God’s substantial Wisdom is the Holy Spirit, through whom all created things are known to subsist from God.

Thus some people, understanding less well, said that the Wisdom of God and God the Only-Begotten Word are one and the same person. [Note: Some who understood less well—namely the Arians and Eunomians—interpreted the Apostle’s words badly in this sense. Theodoret likewise teaches this in his commentary on the First Epistle to the Corinthians: “It must be understood, however, that the divine Apostle called the proclamation of the cross, not the divinity of the Only-Begotten, ‘wisdom and power’; and he refutes the Arians and Eunomians, who wrongly attempt from this passage to demonstrate that God the Word is called Wisdom. Moreover, just as it is clear that Wisdom in this passage does not refer to the person of the Son, so, if anyone denies that Wisdom is elsewhere rightly attributed to him, he has the entire theological school crying out against him.”]

They wished to derive from blessed Paul a cause and basis for this in the passage:

“But we preach Christ, and him crucified: to the Jews a stumbling block, but to the Gentiles foolishness; but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:23).

But in what blessed Paul said, he does not signify the Only-Begotten God the Word as power and wisdom; rather, he signifies the arrangement of the cross. For immediately afterward he said:

“Because the foolishness of God is wiser than human beings, and the weakness of God is stronger than human beings” (1 Corinthians 1:25).

No sensible person would dare say that the foolishness and weakness of God are God the Word. Rather, as I said, the passage signifies the arrangement of the cross: what appears foolish to unbelievers—namely, believing that the crucified Christ is God—possesses the greatest wisdom; and what appears to be the weakness of Christ, because he died for us, possesses the greatest power. But this is not the time to speak of that wisdom and power.

### XII

Through many witnesses we are therefore taught by God that he has one substantial Only-Begotten, God the Word, and one substantial Wisdom, the Holy Spirit. Through that Spirit and through that Word, every wisdom, utterance, knowledge, and the other gifts are bestowed by God upon believers.

Blessed Paul also teaches this when he says:

“Therefore I have glory in Christ Jesus before God. For I would not dare to speak of anything that Christ did not accomplish through me for the obedience of the Gentiles, by word and deed, through the power of signs and wonders, through the power of the Holy Spirit” (Romans 15:17–19).

Blessed Paul the Apostle not only had Christ and the Holy Spirit speaking within him, but so did all the other prophets, apostles, and evangelists. Our Lord Jesus Christ also teaches this when he says:

“Therefore, behold, I send you prophets and wise men and scribes” (Matthew 23:34).

Likewise, concerning the Spirit of God, he says:

“Therefore the Wisdom of God also says, ‘I will send them prophets and apostles’” (Luke 11:49).

[Col. 1129C] **XIII.** That the Holy Spirit is Lord and God, and that, as our Lord, he too bestows and grants gifts upon believers, the same blessed Paul teaches again when he says: “There are diversities of graces, but the same Spirit; and there are diversities of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are diversities of operations, but the same God” (1 Cor. 12:4). [Note: The manuscript reads, “But it is the same God who works all things in all.” In this enumeration of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, the blessed Paul, everywhere adding “the same Lord” and “the same God,” clearly teaches that the Holy Spirit is Lord and God.] He shows plainly that the Holy Spirit is Lord and God. He demonstrates this even more clearly in what follows. For after listing the gifts, works, and ministries, he immediately added, saying: “But all these things one and the same Spirit works, distributing to each as he wills” (1 Cor. 12:11).

Again, the same blessed Paul, wishing to teach us more clearly that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one substance, says: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all” (Eph. 4:5). He names him “Father” of those who have been born through baptism in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The blessed Apostle, however, knowing that there is a baptism of water and a baptism of the Spirit, said “one baptism.” Yet he spoke correctly, knowing that baptism is one, insofar as all are baptized and believe in the name of the one Lord.

The same blessed Apostle is also accustomed to call the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit not only one Lord and one God, but likewise one Spirit, when he says: “For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so also is Christ. For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Gentiles, slaves or free, and we all drank of one Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:12).

**XIV.** When the blessed Apostle is heard saying that we were all baptized in one Spirit and drank one Spirit, no one should suppose that he spoke only of the Spirit or only of the Father. For whoever believes this abolishes baptism. Those who were baptized in one Spirit were not baptized in the Father alone, nor in the Son alone, nor in the Holy Spirit alone, but in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. This is indeed one common name—not through confusion of persons, but through unity of nature: one Lord, one God, one Spirit.

For the Father is always Father, never ceasing to be Father; the Son is always Son, continuing forever to be Son; and the Holy Spirit is always the Holy Spirit, never becoming either Father or Son.

**XV.** What, then, will those who follow the impious doctrines of Arius and Eunomius answer us—those who insist that the Son and the Holy Spirit are separated from the substance of the Father? Although they say these things in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, they themselves do not deny baptizing their own people [Note: The manuscript reads, “To baptize their own people”]; and they believe that through baptism they receive remission of sins, and likewise that they are deemed worthy of sanctification by the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Nevertheless, they do not cease blaspheming against the Son and the Holy Spirit, although they ought at last, freed from their blindness, to look and understand that liberty cannot otherwise be granted to servants except by their own Lord.

If they say that those who are baptized receive liberty or forgiveness of sins from the Father alone, and deserve sanctification from the Father alone, let them know that no one among those who are baptized can be made worthy of these gifts unless he also receives gifts or endowments from the Son and the Holy Spirit. The blessed Apostle Paul bears witness to this when writing to the Corinthians. He says: “Neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor adulterers,” and so forth (1 Cor. 6:9), and he adds: “And such were some of you; but you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God” (1 Cor. 6:11). [Note: The manuscript reads, “But you were sanctified, but you were justified,” and so forth.]

By all these testimonies cited above, the one and the same substance of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is sufficiently and abundantly demonstrated.

**XVI.** When God creates, he does not create by nature, as the fable of the delirious Gentiles supposes, but rather by will. Divinity is free and does not serve the necessity of nature, as with fire, according to their belief: fires are known to burn neighboring bodies not by will, but because nature burns and conflagrates. God, however, does not act in this way.

For his substance is ineffable and incomprehensible, above every intelligible and perceptible nature. Since no divinity is visible, as the blessed Paul testifies when he says, “To the King of ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory,” and again: “Who alone possesses immortality, dwelling in inaccessible light, whom no human being has seen nor can see” (1 Tim. 1:17 and following). The blessed John also teaches the same when he says: “No one has ever seen God; the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has declared him” (John 1:18).

Therefore, since God is above every sense, he creates by will, not by nature. For if God created by nature and not by will, countless worlds would be found to have been created, and innumerable others would be created each day. But let us set aside the delirious fable of the Gentiles and obey divine Scripture, which clearly teaches that God creates what he creates by will or command, just as God’s servant Moses taught when he said: “And God said, ‘Let there be light,’” and added, “And there was light”; and again: “And God said, ‘Let there be a firmament,’” and the command was fulfilled by his order; and again: “And God said, ‘Let there be lights’” (Gen. 1). Things that previously did not exist immediately came into being.

The Prophet David likewise says: “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 148:5); and again: “Whatever the Lord willed, he did in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses” (Ps. 134:6).

**XVII.** If, then, God does and creates as much as he wills, [Note: “Impiously and wickedly Origen.” Theophilus of Alexandria aptly and forcefully amplifies this blasphemy of Origen in his Second Paschal Letter: “This blasphemy does not suffice for him; directing the chariot of his folly beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, he again exults in madness, saying that God created by his will as many rational creatures as he was able to govern.” And, after other remarks: “But he weaves and unweaves a seedbed of verbosity, and says: ‘God made as many as he was able to contain, keep subject to himself, and govern by his providence.’” After refuting each point, he concludes that God made not as many as he was able, but as many as the necessity and order of things required. The editor adds: “I would prefer the reading ‘he said’ [fatus est].”] the impious and wicked Origen confessed otherwise, saying: “God did not make all that he willed, but only what he was able to contain and comprehend.” By saying this, he deprived the Lord of power over all things, as though the power to create had been granted to him only in part. For if, as he supposes, he lacks the ability to contain and subject to himself what he creates, then clearly he will not possess the power to create either. For whoever possesses the ability to create will likewise possess the ability to subject what he has created to himself.

Accordingly, let us obey the blessed Job, who says to God: “I know that you can do all things, and that nothing is impossible for you” (Job 42:2). Let us piously and reverently believe, together with those men who have been taught by God, that God can do all things; that he creates by will, not by nature; that when he wills, he creates; and that he creates whatever he wills, as much as he wills, and of whatever kind he wills; and that nothing is impossible to his will.

We say that the will of God is without beginning. For the Lord knows without beginning what he is going to create, when he will make it, and how much and what kind of things he is preparing to create.

**XVIII.** [Note: “And the rational substances were the first to be created.”] Theodoret, in Question 5 on Genesis, says that it is plausible that the angels were created together with heaven and earth. But if someone says that they were created before heaven and earth, “he does not harm the word of piety” [τῷ τῆς εὐσεβείας οὐ λυμαίνεται λόγῳ], he says.

We say, then, that the rational substances regarded as heavenly were created first. They were numerous and diverse both in substance and in power. Thus the blessed David, placing them before the others, says: “Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise him in the heights. Praise him, all his angels; praise him, all his powers” (Ps. 148:1).

When he mentioned the heavens and the angels, and named powers and heights, he taught that their substances were diverse, and likewise their various ranks and merits. Again he teaches that not all have the same nature when he says: “He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a burning fire” (Ps. 103:4). When the Prophet spoke of fire and spirit, he used different and diverse elements so that he might teach us more clearly, even by a perceptible example.

The blessed Paul also teaches that they have diverse substances, placing the heavenly powers before the earthly, when he says: “So that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth” (Phil. 2:10). By “those under the earth” he named souls separated from bodies.

Moreover, he teaches that their ranks are various and their kinds diverse when he says of Christ: “He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation, because in him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones, dominions, principalities, or powers” (Col. 1:15–16). Having placed the heavenly things before the earthly, he immediately added human beings, who were created in Christ, saying: “And he is the head of the body, the Church; he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that he might hold first place in everything” (Col. 1:18).

Our Lord Jesus Christ likewise teaches the diversity of substance among the spirits who departed from God, whom divine Scripture commonly calls demons, as well as principalities and powers, when he says: “This kind is not cast out except by prayer and fasting” (Matt. 17:20; Mark 9:28). By saying “this kind,” the Lord showed that among them there are various kinds of substances and diverse forms.

I have said all this to display the riches of divine power. For if divinity is omnipotent, it must also be exceedingly rich. [Note: The manuscript reads, “The riches of the power of God.”]

**XIX.** Enough, then, has been said about invisible substances. Now I must explain the sun, the moon, and the other luminaries together. [Note: “Concerning the sun and moon together.”] Jerome also bears witness, in his letter to Avitus, Letter 50 (now 124), that Origen was in this error of mind: “The sun also, and the moon, and the other stars, are living beings. Indeed, just as we human beings, because of certain sins, have been enclosed in these bodies, which are dense and sluggish, so also the lights of heaven have received such bodies, so that they may shine more or less; and demons, because of greater transgressions, have been clothed with an airy body.”

Some people, deceived by an error of mind, have said that these luminaries are rational living beings. The wicked Origen followed their madness. Wishing to derive an example from divine Scripture, he dared to twist to suit himself what Scripture had said most properly about the luminaries. [Note: The manuscript reads “were” (fuerant).]

We must therefore understand that divine Scripture nowhere mentions them as living beings, but says that the luminaries were made for this sole purpose: that they might shine upon the earth and serve human beings as signs of times, months, and years.

If those who favor such errors say to us, “Why should the luminaries not be living and rational beings, since it is written of them, ‘The stars are not clean in his sight’ (Job 25:5),” that is, in the sight of God, let them hear from us that the one who said this was not worthy of authority. For the Lord said to him that he had spoken nothing true concerning his servant Job.

Yet even if this had been said by the blessed Job, it would still not seem a firm proof. For the fact that they are not clean in the sight of God does not mean that they are therefore living beings. Otherwise, let menstrual discharges also be called living beings, and leprous houses as well, since these too are not clean before God according to the law of Moses. We often read that many things without a soul are called unclean in a certain sense.

Origen also adds what the Prophet David said: “The sun knows its setting” (Ps. 103:19), as well as what God said to the Prophet Isaiah: “I commanded all the stars” (Isa. 45:12). [Note: From the Greek: Ἐγὼ πᾶσι τοῖς ἄστροις ἐνετειλάμην—“I commanded all the stars.”] He does this in an attempt to confirm his wicked heresy. For he says that the luminaries were formerly minds and senses, and that, because they behaved negligently, they were later deprived of their own power and condemned to these fiery bodies, so that they might shine upon the earth.

**XX.** Likewise, desiring to approve the error of the Gentiles, he says that the luminaries were placed in the firmament for signs, so that their movements might signify our destinies. [Note: The manuscript reads, “God placed the luminaries.”] [Note: “For signs.”] [Note: “Fata” [“destinies”] had been corruptly printed as “facta”; we have emended it.]

Theodoret, in Question 15, splendidly demonstrates that this vanity concerning the stars did not belong to all the Gentiles, but only to fools and madmen:

> “We do not understand the phrase ‘for signs’ according to the opinion of certain foolish people. For neither Pythagoras, nor Socrates, nor Plato, nor the Stoics accepted the vanity of astrology concerning each person’s birth. If those who were raised on myths rejected the impiety of this myth, who, believing the divine sayings, could endure arguments that are not only impious but also utterly foolish?”

Let those who follow the wicked heresy of Origen learn, therefore, not to understand divine Scripture in this way, nor to overturn its meaning by using history according to their own will in place of allegory.

When we hear the Prophet Jeremiah addressing the earth: “Earth, earth, earth, hear the word of the Lord; write this man down as disowned” (Jer. 22:29), we should not therefore say that the Prophet is giving a command to the earth as though it were a rational animal.

The Prophet David likewise commands such bodies when he says: “Praise the Lord from the earth, dragons and all abysses, fire, hail, snow, ice, storm wind, which perform his word; mountains and all hills, fruitful trees and all cedars” (Ps. 148:7–9). He does not thereby teach us to believe that all these things are rational beings.

But let Origen and his companions now be dismissed.

**XXI.** We have also learned this from divine Scripture: that God granted all the heavenly rational powers free will. [Note: “He granted them to have free will.”] Having exploded fate, he confirms the doctrine of free choice, for the two are opposites. Hence the following passage in Chrysostom, *Oration 2 on Fate*, contrasts God with the demon, or with fate:

> “God said, ‘If you are willing, and if you are unwilling,’ making us masters of virtue and vice and placing them under the power of our will. But what does fate say? That it is impossible to escape what is destined, whether we wish to or strive to. God says, ‘If you are willing, you shall eat the good things of the earth’; fate says, ‘Even if we wish to, if it has not been given to us, wishing accomplishes nothing. God says, ‘If you are unwilling to heed my words, the sword shall consume you’; fate says, ‘Even if we are unwilling, if it has been given to us, we shall certainly be saved.’”

[Note: “Having refuted fate, he confirms the doctrine of free will; for they are opposites.”]

God granted them free will, just as he also granted it to human beings on earth. For no one who possesses reason or sense can serve God unwillingly or without the will to do so; rather, all obey him of their own accord. Otherwise, if this were not so, neither praise nor blame, nor guilt, would follow them, just as happens with irrational animals.

All, then, are considered capable of opposites—of good, I mean, and of evil. They are good when they do what God wills; evil when they in no way keep the Lord’s commandments.

That the angels and heavenly powers, when they do not despise God’s commands, receive great praise, the blessed David testifies by saying: “Bless the Lord, all his angels, mighty in strength, doing his word, to hear the voice of his words. Bless the Lord, all his powers, his ministers, doing his will” (Ps. 102:20–21).

Through this praise—that is, through observance of the Lord’s commandments—they enjoy blessed and everlasting life. And just as all who do God’s will attain eternal blessedness and receive everlasting praise from God, so, conversely, all who despise the divine commandments are condemned to eternal reproach.

**XXII.** Hence the one whom divine Scripture commonly calls the Devil, and likewise those who are called his angels, fell. Some have attributed this fall of the Devil to envy of the first human beings. [Note: “Because they envied the first human beings.”] This entire passage, however, agrees remarkably with the words of Cyprian, who held the same opinion. For in his book *On Jealousy and Envy* he says:

> “Hence the Devil both perished first and ruined others at the very beginning of the world. Formerly supported by angelic majesty, formerly accepted and beloved by God, after he saw the human being made in the image of God, he burst forth into evil jealousy through malevolent envy. He did not first cast down another through the impulse of jealousy before himself had been cast down by jealousy; he was taken captive before taking captive, ruined before ruining. While envious resentment prompted him to rob humanity of the grace of the immortality that had been given, he himself also lost what he had previously been.”

This must unquestionably be the correct reading, disregarding the emendation of Pamelius, who, by correcting the text according to his own reading, overturns Cyprian’s meaning.

Thus, envying the first human beings—Adam and Eve—the Devil and his angels alienated themselves from the blessed life that they had first possessed. By the deception they themselves devised, they persuaded the human being, while committing sin, to depart immediately from God’s command; and they likewise subjected themselves to eternal punishment, as our Lord Jesus Christ teaches when he says to those who refused mercy to their neighbor: “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the Devil and his angels. For I was hungry, and you did not give me food,” and so forth (Matt. 25:41).

That the Devil and those who are called his angels are among the heavenly creatures and rational powers, the blessed Peter testifies when he says: “For if God did not spare the angels who sinned” (2 Pet. 2:4). The blessed Paul likewise teaches, saying: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels?” (1 Cor. 6:3).

Therefore, no one should suppose, captured by error, that they sinned before they envied human beings and, after that sin, proceeded to deceive humanity, as the wicked Origen taught. Rather, as I said above, the Devil deceived Eve after he had transformed himself into a serpent.

That the Devil, having utterly abandoned the truth, immediately turned to falsehood, and that he killed Eve, as I said, by the death of sin, the Lord himself testifies when he says to the Jews who did not believe him: “You are from your father the Devil, and you wish to do the desires of your father. He was a murderer from the beginning and did not stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he speaks falsehood, he speaks from his own, because he is a liar and its father” (John 8:44).

When the Lord said that he was a murderer from the beginning and did not stand in the truth, he clearly taught that the Devil fell from the truth at the moment when, through the deceit of falsehood, he first killed Eve, deceived by error, with the death of transgression.

It was also said that when he speaks falsehood, he speaks from his own, because he himself first produced falsehood through fabricated deceit. Hence the others who, together with him, envied humanity were called angels of that Devil, as though he himself had been the first cause and head of this army.

But enough has also been said about them.

**XXIII.** When the Lord created the world—that is, heaven and earth and everything in them—he made only the human being according to his image and likeness, as Moses teaches when he says: “And God said, ‘Let us make the human being according to our image and likeness.’” After Moses had spoken this in the person of God, he immediately added: “And God made the human being; in the image of God he made him” (Gen. 1:26–27).

Moses, understanding both as one—that is, both “image” and “likeness”—when he named “image,” entirely passed over “likeness.” [Note: Sirmondus does not seem to have noticed what was actually at issue here: namely, that Origen’s opinion is being condemned. Origen distinguished likeness from image. He admitted that the human being was created according to the image of God, but maintained that the human being acquired likeness to God through the merit of virtues, so that just as we become like the Devil by sinning, we become like Christ by acting rightly. See Origen’s *Homily 1 on Genesis* and Book 4 of his *Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans*. More clearly still, see *On First Principles*, Book 3: “The statement that he made him according to the image of God, while saying nothing about likeness, indicates nothing other than that he received the dignity of the image in his first creation, while the perfection of likeness was reserved for the consummation—namely, so that he might acquire it for himself through the efforts of his own industry, by imitation of God; since the possibility of perfection had been divinely granted to him through the dignity of the image, he would finally complete perfect likeness for himself through the fulfillment of his works.”]

Otherwise, if this were not so, the Apostle James would never afterward have said, when teaching that the tongue ought not to be used for the service of evil: “With it we bless the Lord and Father, and with it we curse human beings who have been made according to the likeness of God” (Jas. 3:9).

God therefore appointed the human being to rule over everything he himself had created, both on land and in the sea, [Note: “Because the human being is his image.” The chief author of this exposition is Diodorus of Tarsus, whose words are: “How, then, is the human being the image of God? By virtue of dominion and authority.” Others have collected other respects in which the human being imitates God. Others have wished, in different ways, to find the Trinity itself expressed in the human soul. Theodoret, in Question 20 on Genesis, explains it differently: “The mind produces the word, and spirit proceeds with the word—not generated as the word is, but always accompanying the word and proceeding with it as it is brought forth.” Ambrose explains it differently in his tract *On the Dignity of Human Nature*, chapter 2: “Just as the Son is generated from the Father and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, so will is not generated from intellect, nor does memory proceed from both of these.” Finally, many others explain it differently.] because the human being is his image, as the blessed Paul also teaches when he says: “A man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God” (1 Cor. 11:7).

For this reason the human being is placed above all irrational animals and rules over them; by this very fact he has become lord of all. Irrational animals, as Moses taught, were created from earth and water and possess from these both soul and body. The human being, however, appears to share a body with the others, but has a much more excellent soul, as Moses again says: “And God formed the human being from the dust of the earth, and breathed into his face the breath of life, and the human being became a living soul” (Gen. 2:7).

**XXIV.** The human being is therefore superior to all because he is recognized as possessing a perceptible and rational soul, and one endowed with free will. Let us therefore, as prudent people, hear Moses as he tells how God created the human being.

Moses and the other prophets speak to us about God in a manner that we are able to understand. For God is not a human being, made from soul and body, so that he might form and fashion a human being with his hands, or draw spirit from the air so as to breathe into his face and thereby give him life. He makes and made all things through the one Word and the Holy Spirit, by his will.

The prophets, however, are accustomed to call not only the human being but also heaven, earth, and the things in them—created by God’s command—the works of the Lord’s hands.

The Prophet David bears witness, saying to God: “I shall see the heavens, the works of your fingers, the moon and the stars that you established” (Ps. 8:4). And again: “In the beginning you, Lord, founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands” (Ps. 101:26).

The Prophet Isaiah likewise speaks in the person of God: “Hear me, Jacob and Israel, whom I call. I am he; I am first, and I am last. My hand founded the earth, and my right hand established heaven” (Isa. 48:12–13). And again: “Thus says the Lord: Heaven is my throne, and earth is the footstool of my feet. What kind of house will you build for me, and what place for my rest? For my hand made all these things” (Isa. 66:1–2).

**XXV.** The human being, then, as divine Scripture has taught us, possesses a body from the earth but a soul created for him from nothing. This soul is perceptible, rational, and immortal, as both Testaments teach us—the New, I mean, and the Old.

For our Lord Jesus Christ also says: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, fear him who has power to destroy soul and body in Gehenna” (Matt. 10:28). He called the punishment by fire destruction. For how can that which perishes entirely, and can in no way continue to exist, be capable of enduring eternal punishment, when the Lord again says: “And these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. 25:46)?

**XXVI.** [Note: “Nor should the soul be said to be a part of God.”] Nor should it be said that the soul is a part of God, as the speech of the foolish and unlearned maintains. For if this were so, God would never subject his own part to everlasting punishment; indeed, that part could not sin at all, as a part of God—especially since God is always unchangeable, both in nature and in will.

Nor, again, if our soul were a part of God, could it be subdued by any bodily defect. For divinity is always unconquered and is never subject to any bodily defect. [Note: The manuscript reads, “Subject to bodily defect.”]

For, as Jerome writes in Book 2 *Against Jovinianus*, the human soul and God are not of the same substance, although this is what the Manichaeans commonly teach. This, then, was the error of the Manichaeans, and after them of the Priscillianists. Jerome himself also says that it was Origen’s error. In Letter 61 to Pammachius, he censures John of Jerusalem for concealing Origen while accusing him of being a Manichaean on this point: “You produce Manichaeus for us and conceal Origen.” [Note: “Nor should the soul be said to be a part of God.”]

**XXVII.** Just as those who believe this are shown to believe impiously, so also those who say that souls were created before bodies are found to be far from piety. [Note: “Souls made before bodies.”] Origen taught two things improperly here: that souls were once created separately, and that they were afterward sent into bodies when they had committed some sin. Among others, Antipater of Bostra refuted both doctrines in writing against him, in chapter 7:

> “He who made the human being made them male and female from the beginning, not first minds according to himself and then human beings from sins.”

And shortly afterward:

> “The human race was not multiplied from sins and transgression, as the writing of these people teaches, but from the blessing of God, as the Prophet declared. For if the human race is multiplied from transgression and from the abandonment of what is good, it would rightly be called not a blessing but rather a curse.”

This was also the argument of Theophilus of Alexandria, in the *Catena on Genesis*, Royal Manuscript 810:

> “That souls were not, as it seemed to Origen, cast down and joined to bodies because of sin, we learn from the words of Moses, who says to the children of Israel: ‘May the Lord, the God of your fathers, increase you a thousandfold from your present number and bless you, as he has spoken to you.’ For according to Origen the making of bodies is not a blessing but a curse for wandering souls.”

[Note: The Greek reads: Ὅτι οὐ δι’ ἁμαρτίας, ὡς Ὠριγένει ἔδοξε, καταβεβλημέναι αἱ ψυχαὶ σώμασι συνεπλάκησαν, ἐχρησάμεθα τῷ Μωσέως ῥήματι λέγοντος τοῖς υἱοὶς Ἰσραὴλ, Κύριος ὁ Θεὸς τῶν πατέρων ὑμῶν προσθείη ὑμῖν σήμερον ὡς ἐστὲ χιλιοπλασίως, καὶ εὐλογήσαι ὑμᾶς καθότι ἐλάλησεν ὑμῖν· οὐ γὰρ εὐλογία κατὰ Ὠριγένην ἐστὶν ἡ τῶν σωμάτων ποίησις, ἀλλὰ κατάρα πλανωμέναις ψυχαῖς.]

Since the aforementioned Origen tries to derive examples from divine Scripture to confirm his wicked heresy, let us refute him by showing that he utterly failed to understand divine Scripture and taught it without sense.

For when he himself said [Note: “I think the book entitled *On First Principles* is being indicated.”] that at the beginning of creation heaven was not created with the earth as a solid body like the one that is seen, but that all this was a perceptible and rational substance of one and the same nature—including human souls among these rational and perceptible substances—and afterward mentioned the animals created on the sixth day, finding that the human being too had been created among them, he could no longer affirm his fiction or strengthen his own falsehood. [Col. 1137B] As though he had entirely forgotten what he had taught before, he reluctantly admits that souls were created, and again that they were incorporeal.

Let those who venerate and cultivate the wicked heresy of Origen, and who strive to raise his interpretations of divine Scripture to the heavens with the highest praises, answer us: How can souls be understood without bodies, when Moses teaches us by saying: “And God made the human being; in the image of God he made him; male and female he made them” (Gen. 1:27)?

For it is clear to everyone that souls cannot possess either sex; only bodies, which are known to be weightier, can do so.

How, again, will they be able to hear the statement “Increase and multiply” (Gen. 1:28) as applying to souls alone without bodies? For even according to Origen himself, the nature of incorporeal beings can neither multiply nor increase.

Or how could souls created without bodies dwell in the heavens, when God, blessing those whom he had made male and female, said: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (ibid.)?

But let Origen and his companions once again be dismissed.

## XXVIII.

Since there are some who, seized by madness, say that **[Note: [Col. 1138D] From one soul of the first man. Thirdly he likewise refutes those who maintained that souls are propagated by transmission—that is, as Saint Jerome explains in Epistle XXVIII, that just as body is born from body, so soul is born from soul and subsists under the same condition as brute animals. Although opinions in the Church were once divided on this question, all now agree with the view our author maintains here: that souls are individually created by God and infused into formed bodies.]** the soul of Eve the woman was taken from the one soul of the first man, Adam; and others also say that souls were transmitted from Adam alone, through the emission of semen, to all who were born from him; while still others hold that souls were transmitted more especially from Eve alone, and thus **[Note: Ms.: “Thus it was conveyed from parents to their children.”]** passed from parents to their children, the following answer must be given to them:

Why, then, did Adam—who was first created from the earth and who, according to the flesh, was formed from the rib that had been taken from him—while prophesying in the Spirit of God, say, “This now is bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh; she shall be called Woman, because she was taken from her man” (Gen. 2:23), yet nowhere mention the soul? For if the soul too were from the soul, according to their vain opinions, Adam would certainly never have passed over this point. For just as he said, “Bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh,” he could also have said, “a soul from my soul.” But he said only what he knew had been taken from him.

Moreover, the prophet Zechariah, agreeing with Moses, says: “Stretching out the heavens and founding the earth, and forming the spirit of man within him” (Zech. 12:1). For if the flesh of man had not been created from pre-existing matter, as was also the case with Adam and Eve, and if afterward the soul within him had likewise not been created from pre-existing matter, as in the case of Adam and Eve, the prophet Zechariah would never have said, “and creating the spirit of man within him” (ibid.).

More plainly, Solomon teaches in Ecclesiastes that souls are supplied by God to all bodies that he creates from pre-existing matter. Describing the dissolution of the human constitution, he says: “And the dust shall return to its earth, and the spirit shall return to God who gave it” (Eccl. 12:7). By saying this, Solomon clearly taught that God supplied the dust—which he had taken from the earth in order to create man—with a spirit that it did not possess.

The spirit alone is therefore said to return to God, although the Lord is creator of both—the flesh as well as the spirit—because he does not create the spirit from pre-existing matter in the same way as he creates the body. Moreover, man appears to cooperate with God in the generation of the body, whereas God alone creates the spirit: human beings supply the material, but God creates the human being.

That it is God who forms what is cast into the womb as semen, just as he gives life to the various other things sown by farmers in the earth, is attested by blessed Job, who says to God: “Your hands made me and fashioned me” (Job 10:8). The prophet David says the same.

Again, God says to the prophet Jeremiah: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you” (Jer. 1:5). Likewise, the prophet Isaiah says of the people called by the name of Jacob, among other things: “The Lord who redeemed you, and who formed you from the womb” (Isa. 44:24).

Still more plainly, blessed Paul, writing to the Hebrews, teaches that spirits—that is, our souls—do not descend by succession in the same way as bodies, when he says: “We had the fathers of our flesh as instructors, and we revered them; shall we not much more obey the Father of spirits and live?” (Heb. 12:6).

When God blessed the first human beings, Adam and Eve, he said, “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. 2:28). For this reason the Apostle called parents “fathers of our flesh”; and because we do not possess souls created from pre-existing matter, he called God the Father of spirits. **[Note: Ms.: “He called him Spirit.”]**

Everything, therefore, is created as it was created at the beginning, and is likewise produced day by day: some things from pre-existing matter, such as the souls of irrational animals, and others not from pre-existing matter, such as human souls.

But enough has been said about the soul.

## XXIX.

Although I have said that those first human beings, Adam and Eve, were created **[Note: “Immortal, mortal.”]** immortal according to the soul but mortal according to the body, they nevertheless would never have tasted death **[Note: “If he had wished to keep God’s command.” Pelagius said that Adam would have died whether he had sinned or not. Therefore he cannot have been considered the author of this book in the sense stated above, as the Corbie scholars conjectured in their censure.]** if they had wished to keep God’s command, as blessed Enoch merited.

For although Enoch was mortal, he was taken away so that he would not see death at all.

**[Note: Here Theophilus of Alexandria, in the Codex mentioned above, 810:]**

> “Thus man was made midway between the two: neither wholly mortal nor altogether immortal, but capable of either.”

Theophilus the other also expounded the same point copiously and elegantly in Book II of *To Autolycus*, in these words:

> “He was made neither mortal by nature nor immortal. For if he had made him immortal from the beginning, he would have made him a god; and if, again, he had made him mortal, God would appear to have been the cause of his death. Therefore he made him neither immortal nor mortal, but capable of both, so that he might incline toward immortality and, by keeping God’s commandment, receive immortality from him as his reward. But if he should turn toward death, he himself would be the cause of his own death; for God made man free and self-determining.”

That Adam and Eve were created mortal according to the body, as I have said, is attested by Moses when he says:

> “And God planted a paradise in Eden, toward the east, and there he placed the man whom he had formed. And God also brought forth from the earth every tree beautiful to the sight and good for food, and the tree of life in the middle of paradise, and the tree for knowing good and evil” (Gen. 2:8).

God would never have planted the tree of life in paradise if Adam had been created immortal according to the flesh.

Again, if Adam and Eve had been created immortal according to the flesh, they would never have heard God say, “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. 1:18). For those who were commanded to eat, drink, have intercourse, increase, and fill the earth could not possibly have been altogether immortal. Thus our Lord Jesus Christ also taught the Sadducees, saying:

> “The children of this age marry and are given in marriage. But those who are considered worthy of that age and of the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage. For they can no longer die, since they are equal to the angels” (Luke 20:34).

## XXX.

It has been sufficiently proved, I think, that man was created mortal according to the flesh, since the Lord plainly teaches that those who rejoice in such intercourse and marriages are mortal.

Accordingly, Enoch, who pleased God, after he had fathered children by different wives, was taken away so that he would not see death at all, as blessed Paul also says when writing to the Hebrews: “By faith Enoch was taken away, so that he would not see death” (Heb. 11:5); for he is said to have pleased God before his removal.

Thus we can say of Adam and Eve also that, if they had kept God’s precept and commandment, they would have remained immortal forever even after producing children, once they had tasted the tree of life, and would thereafter have had no need of food, growth, or marriage.

But if some, seized by ignorance, persist in the same view, saying that Adam and Eve, once they had received permission to eat from every tree in paradise except the one tree forbidden by God, would have gained immortality after eating also from the tree of life, let them learn that one who has become immortal has no need whatsoever of food.

If Adam and Eve had been naturally immortal, they would never have tasted the tree that God had forbidden, since immortals have no desire for food. Blessed Paul also testifies to this, saying: “The kingdom of God is not food and drink” (Rom. 14:17).

The kingdom of God does not belong to mortals but to immortals, as our Lord Jesus Christ also taught, saying:

> “Those who are considered worthy of that age and of the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage; for they can no longer die, since they are equal to the angels” (Luke 20:35).

If Adam and Eve had kept God’s commandment, they would certainly never have tasted death. But by failing to keep the commandment, they did not become mortal from having been immortal; rather, although they were mortal, they deprived themselves of the immortality promised to them by God.

Thus Adam heard God say: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:13)—that is, “You are corruptible, and you shall go into corruption”—since he was already unworthy to eat from the tree of life and live forever.

Let me say again that, if Adam and Eve had persevered in keeping God’s commandment, they would not have had the discernment to eat from the tree of life until the time when God would reveal it to them. For this reason it had also been separated from the other trees, although it stood in the middle of paradise; and there too had been placed the tree that possessed the knowledge of good and evil, so that, fearing to touch the forbidden tree, they might also take care not to eat from the permitted one.

God himself also plainly taught this when he said:

> “Behold, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil. And now, lest he stretch out his hand and take from the tree of life, eat, and live forever” (Gen. 3:22).

When God said, “Behold, he has become one who knows good and evil,” and added, “now, lest he stretch out his hand,” he showed that, before he experienced the knowledge of evil, Adam could not by himself understand that he should take from the tree of life.

This is not surprising, since Adam also said, when prophesying about his wife:

> “She shall be called Woman, because she was taken from her man; therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2:23).

## XXXI.

Not only this: although Adam and Eve had heard God say to them, “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth,” before their disobedience they were entirely ignorant of what the desire to produce children was.

For Moses says:

> “And both were naked, Adam and his wife, and they were not ashamed” (Gen. 2:25).

Moses did not say this as though they had been deceived by the blindness of incontinence and therefore disregarded the shame of nakedness. Rather, he showed that they were like infants who did not yet possess the desire for intercourse.

Accordingly, after the transgression, once they had perceived their nakedness—not, I mean, that of the whole body, but of the part that Ham had also seen when Noah was sleeping—only then did they acquire the desire to produce children and, recognizing their nakedness, cover their private parts with fig leaves.

## XXXII.

**[Note: God taking thought for human beings.]**

There is a book of Saint Ambrose, *On the Good of Death*, and elsewhere he is frequently very full on this subject. He shows that death should be regarded as a remedy, not a punishment, in Book II of *On Cain and Abel*, chapter 10:

> “For if the innocent die who were unwilling to turn their step back from sins, nevertheless, even against their will, they attain the end not of nature but of guilt, so that they may not commit more sins, for whom life is an investment in wrongdoing. But if they possess good hope, they should be thought to depart rather than to perish.”

And in *On the Good of Death*, chapter 7:

> “It is worse to live for sin than to die in sin, because while the wicked person lives, he increases his sin; let him die, and he abandons sin. Many rejoice in the absolution of their crimes. If they intend to amend, rightly; but if they intend to persist in them, foolishly, because condemnation would have benefited them much more, so that they would not add to their sins.”

God, therefore, taking thought for human beings, knowing that they were inclined toward wickedness and lovers of pleasures and the desires of the flesh, and wishing rather to recall them to honorable virtue, permits them for a time to be subjected to the dominion of death. **[Note: Ms.: “He allowed them for a certain time to be subjected to the dominion of death.”]**

Since he knew that nothing else could restrain human beings so easily as death—for many are known to abstain altogether from wickedness through fear of death—human laws likewise can restrain most human vices only by threatening death and punishment.

All, held back by their common love of this life, take care not to provide grounds for sins, lest by committing offenses they be deprived of it against their own will.

We therefore do not say that death was given to human beings in place of evils, as the unlearned reason, but for the destruction of the evil of death itself. **[Note: Ms.: “For the complete destruction of wickedness.”]** For if human beings were going to live forever, their wickedness would certainly never come to an end.

Again, why should I believe that death was given as a counterpart of evils, when, if someone were to kill nearly a hundred people or more, no vengeance could equal so many and such great murders?

## XXXIII.

Death is therefore said to be good not only for wicked people, for the destruction of their wickedness, but also useful for the just.

Just as the wicked person ceases to sin when deprived of this light, so the just person, falling asleep, is freed from continual assaults, afflictions, and miseries of soul. Once the just person’s body has been laid aside, the soul is afterward oppressed by no distress; it is subject to no misery of spirit, encounters no necessities, endures no persecutions, suffers no further assaults from the vices of the flesh, is no longer pressed day after day by a host of evil suggestions, and is not stripped for combat.

Carrying away none of the anxieties of worldly affairs, it is no longer worn down by abstinence from the flesh for the sake of conflict; it no longer fights, competes in running, or boxes; it no longer wrestles with principalities and powers and the spirits of wickedness. Its stadium has been cleared, its contest has ceased, and having won the victory it hastens immediately to receive the crown of righteousness and attain the blessed and eternal goal in heaven, once it has received its immortal flesh. **[Note: Ms.: “To attain eternal life.”]** **[Note: Ms.: “Therefore.”]**

Blessed Paul likewise, perceiving such battles—battles imposed upon just people by invisible enemies—and fearing lest the understanding of some be changed by wickedness or their sound mind deceived by trickery, urged everyone, in order to provoke virtue, to despise this temporal life. He says:

> “Therefore, being always confident and knowing that while we are in the body we are absent from the Lord” (2 Cor. 4:6).

Wishing, therefore, to depart from the body, hastening to bring his contest to an end, and desiring to be present with God, he cries out:

> “For I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought the good fight; I have finished the course; I have kept the faith. From now on the crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will award me on that day—not only to me, but also to all who love his appearing” (2 Tim. 4:6).

Blessed Job also often calls death the release from all evils when he says: **[Note: Ms.: “Death is rest.”]**

> “But death is rest, for God has shut him in.”

## XXXIV.

But if some wish to say, “How can death be rest for man, when blessed David said, ‘The death of sinners is very evil’ (Ps. 33:22)?” let them learn that the phrase “the death of sinners is very evil” does not mean that an end and termination are thereby placed upon their sins. Rather, after death they undergo the gravest punishments because of their offenses. **[Note: Ms.: “A limit to their sins.”]**

Blessed Job likewise customarily calls death both rest and sleep, when he says:

> “Why did I suck the breasts? Now, sleeping, I would surely rest and enjoy the security of sleep, with the kings and counselors of the earth who gloried in their swords, or with the princes who possessed much gold” (Job 3:12).

The prophet Isaiah, when commanded by the Lord to lament the dead king of Babylon, likewise called this common and temporal death sleep, saying:

> “All the earth cries out with joy, and the trees of Lebanon rejoice over you, and the cedars of Lebanon say: ‘Since you have fallen asleep, no one has come up to cut us down.’ The underworld below, gripped with bitterness, came out to meet you” (Isa. 14:7).

The prophet Daniel similarly says:

> “And many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall rise: some to everlasting life, and some to reproach and everlasting confusion” (Dan. 12:2).

Blessed Paul also teaches the same when he says:

> “We do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve like the others who have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus” (1 Thess. 4).

Instructed, therefore, by many witnesses that this common death is not evil, let us now bid a long farewell to those who call death evil.

## XXXV.

We say, moreover, that God provided the first man Adam with sweats and labors for his good—labors that he would endure from the earth—since we cannot otherwise overcome, through venerable faith, the invisible enemies against whom we have continual struggle unless we are wearied by bodily labors.

Through these labors, divine Scripture teaches us to free ourselves from the deceit of our enemies and either preserve virtue safely or renew it when lost. Thus blessed David, hastening to recover the virtue he had lost, teaches us, saying:

> “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a broken and humbled heart God will not despise” (Ps. 50:39).

And again:

> “I have labored in my groaning; every night I shall wash my bed; with my tears I shall water my couch” (Ps. 7:7).

And again:

> “My knees have grown weak from fasting, and my flesh has been changed because of oil” (Ps. 108:24).

Teaching also how we ought to preserve virtue, he says:

> “But when they troubled me, I clothed myself in sackcloth and humbled my soul with fasting” (Ps. 34:13).

Our Lord Jesus Christ likewise taught his disciples that virtue cannot be preserved, as I have said, or restored when lost, except through bodily labors and pains. For he says:

> “Enter through the narrow gate, because the gate is wide and the way is spacious that leads to destruction, and many are those who enter through it. For the gate is narrow and the way is constricted that leads to life, and few are those who find it” (Matt. 7:13).

For this reason blessed Paul, when he asked the Lord that the one who tried to drive the thorn of the flesh into him might depart from him completely, did not obtain his request; rather, he heard from the Lord:

> “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness” (1 Cor. 12:9).

Therefore he later said joyfully:

> “I will gladly boast in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me. For this reason I am pleased with weaknesses, insults, necessities, persecutions, and distresses for Christ. For when I am weak, then I am strong.”

Teaching this also, he says: **[Note: Ms.: “For this reason.”]**

> “Therefore we do not lose heart. Even if our outward man is being corrupted, yet our inward man is being renewed day by day. For this momentary and light affliction of ours is producing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure, while we do not look at the things that are seen but at the things that are unseen. For the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are unseen are eternal” (1 Cor. 4:16).

Thus we say that the first human beings, Adam and Eve, were saved from their sin through the bodily labors and pains that the Lord had provided for them, evidently for the benefit of their souls. For this reason divine Scripture afterward nowhere mentions them as having sinned.

## XXXVI.

That God forgave them their sin, just as he also forgave Cain, who had first sinned, when he said to him, “You have sinned; be still. Its return is toward you—that is, the return of sin—and you shall rule over it” (Gen. 4:7), Moses plainly demonstrates through the kindness or mercy that God afterward willingly granted them.

For what does Moses say?

> “And the Lord God made tunics of skins for Adam and his wife, and clothed them” (Gen. 3:12).

For if the Lord had not forgiven them their sin, he certainly would not have clothed them himself with tunics **[Note: The Latin idiom required him to say “which he himself had made for them.”]** made from skins, which he himself had made for them. The expression is plainly a Hellenism, perhaps unique in this particular form, though there are many others of different kinds that show that the book was translated from Greek.

Let no one therefore suppose that those same tunics of skins which they received were the human body, **[Note: As the impious Origen explained.]** as the impious Origen interpreted them.

Epiphanius discusses this interpretation of Origen in his Letter 60 to John of Jerusalem—now numbered 51—in Jerome. **[Col. 1143D]** I pass over his frivolous interpretation of the tunics of skins, and the great effort and multitude of arguments by which he tried to make us believe that the tunics of skins were human bodies. Among other things he says:

> “Was God a leatherworker or a maker of leather goods, so that he could prepare the skins of animals and sew from them tunics of skins for Adam and Eve? It is clear, therefore,” he says, “that he is speaking of our bodies. And if this is so, how do we read that, before the tunics of skins, before the disobedience, and before the fall from paradise, Adam spoke—not allegorically but literally—saying, ‘This now is bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh’ (Gen. 2:23)? And shortly afterward: ‘What bodies were Adam and Eve covering with fig leaves after they had eaten from the forbidden tree?’”

As I have said, Adam himself taught that he possessed flesh before those tunics of skins, saying:

> “This now is bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh” (Gen. 2:23).

We therefore say that the tunics of skins were given by God because of the harshness of life, or because he gave them as garments suitable for those exercising themselves in virtue, so that they might learn that they could not otherwise conquer invisible enemies except through bodily labors.

That after the transgression he committed in paradise Adam continued thereafter, until the end of his life, to obey God is attested by Solomon, who says of the wisdom that preserved him in the fear of God:

> “She guarded the first-formed father of the world, when he alone had been created, and delivered him from sin; and she gave him strength to rule over all” (Wis. 10:1). **[Note: Ms.: “But she gave him strength.”]**

Blessed Paul likewise teaches concerning the salvation of Eve, saying:

> “For Adam was formed first, then Eve; and Adam was not deceived, but the woman, having been deceived, was in transgression. But she will be saved through the bearing of children, if they remain in faith and discretion and holiness with sobriety” (1 Tim. 2:13). **[Note: Ms.: “Love and holiness with sobriety.”]**

## XXXVII.

When he said “through the bearing of children,” he meant “with the bearing of children.” Divine Scripture often changes its prepositions.

The patriarch Joseph is a witness to this when, speaking about the interpretation of a dream to the eunuch, he says: “Its interpretation is not through God” (Gen. 40:8)—that is, “not from God.”

Similarly, blessed Paul, writing to the Hebrews, says: “Through whom also he made the ages” (Heb. 1:2), in place of “with whom also he made the ages.” For we do not say that the Son is the Father’s minister because of the statement “through whom also he made the ages”; rather, we say that he is his fellow-worker.

Eve, therefore, will not be saved because of her children, nor will her offspring be condemned because of their mother, or because of their father Adam, as the opinion of the unwise supposes. Each human being, possessing free will, will be judged either highly praiseworthy or blameworthy according to the quality of his deeds.

In the same way, on the day of judgment each will either be justified or subjected to punishment, as blessed Paul also teaches, saying:

> “For we must all appear before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive according to what he has done in the body, whether good or evil” (2 Cor. 4:10).

## XXXVIII.

**[Note: That children are not punished on account of their parents.]**

Next he openly attacks original sin and the baptism of infants—two doctrines that later became the chief points of the Pelagian heresy.

For this reason the Corbie censure rightly gives the warning: “Read carefully; see what lies hidden.”

The fact that they think this proves that the book could not have been attributed to Rufinus will be frivolous, if it is true that Caelestius is said to have replied in the Acts of Carthage that he had learned from Rufinus that sin is not transmitted. Augustine quotes him from the Acts themselves in *On Original Sin*, chapter 3:

> Caelestius said: “I am uncertain about the transmission of sin; nevertheless, I agree with the one to whom God has granted the grace of knowledge, because I have heard different things from men who are certainly presbyters established in the Catholic Church.”

> Paulinus the deacon said: “Tell us their names.”

> Caelestius said: “Saint Rufinus, who stayed in Rome with Saint Pammachius. I heard him say that sin is not transmitted.”

But, setting this aside, there are other reasons, as we have said, why this work fits neither Rufinus nor Pelagius. **[Note: Not at all; for he is speaking not of Rufinus of Aquileia but of another man of the same name, namely that Syrian whom Marius Mercator reports in his *Commonitorium* to have first introduced into Rome this question hostile to the true faith . . . . . We are not unaware of what learned men argue about him. But the Aquileian Rufinus was not present before Pammachius.]**

That children are not punished for their parents, nor parents for their children, God again taught plainly when he said to the prophet Moses:

> “Fathers shall not be put to death for their sons, nor sons for their fathers; each shall die for his own sin” (Deut. 24:16).

Moreover, when God reproved the foolishness of the children of Israel, who at the time were captives among the Chaldeans because of their crimes and complained not at all about themselves but about their parents—as though their parents had been the cause of all their wicked wrongdoing—and unjustly accused God concerning their captivity, saying, “The way of the Lord is not right, because our fathers ate sour grapes and the children’s teeth were set on edge,” he said to them through the prophet Ezekiel:

> “As I live, says the Lord, this proverb shall no longer be spoken in Israel, for all souls are mine. As the soul of the father is mine, so also the soul of the son is mine; the soul that sins shall die” (Ezek. 18:3).

And again:

> “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor shall the father bear the iniquity of the son” (Ezek. 18:20).

And again:

> “I shall judge each of you according to his way, house of Israel, says the Lord” (ibid., 30).

When God said, “As I live, this proverb shall no longer be spoken in Israel” (Ezek. 18:3), he plainly taught that they must not continue in the same foolishness.

## XXXIX.

After these testimonies of God, then, those who condemn the whole world to iniquity and wickedness through the one man Adam are mad.

For those who say such things either declare God unjust or certainly consider the devil stronger than God, since they hold that the devil was able, through the transgression of Adam and Eve, to make evil the nature that God had created good.

If all human beings are subject to sin through the transgression of the first man Adam and his wife Eve, they ought plainly to acknowledge that they themselves are desirous of wrongdoing, since they themselves are lovers of pleasures and of the flesh. They should not attach the causes of their sins to others when they themselves appear to have been their authors.

Or let those who think themselves wise, although they cannot understand what they say and are not known to comprehend the matters about which they argue, tell us why Adam and Eve, after falling once, did not fall a second time, if their nature had been made sinful through the transgression and could not wholly abstain from evil.

For divine Scripture nowhere records that they themselves sinned a second time, although it did not fail to narrate that Cain sinned a second time. Indeed, it plainly teaches that Abel was free from sins.

What, moreover, will they say about Enoch and Elijah? When they had pleased God, they were taken away so that they would not see death at all. They were not prevented by Adam’s transgression from remaining immortal; rather, through them the only-begotten God plainly taught, even before his bodily coming, the hope of resurrection.

What will they say also about Noah, whom God testifies to have been righteous? He, together with all his own, merited the same salvation that we also obtain through baptism, as blessed Peter teaches in his Epistle:

> “In which also he went and preached to the spirits who were in prison, who had formerly been disobedient when God’s patience waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was being built, in which a few—that is, eight souls—were saved through water. And baptism, in a similar form, now saves you also” (1 Pet. 3:5).

## XL.

But if, as they assert, infants die because of Adam’s sin, let them tell us why they are permitted to taste death immediately after being baptized. For all who have been baptized, and on that account have become children of God, cannot possess sin. **[Note: Ms.: “May not possess.”]**

And if infants born of Christian parents are baptized because of Adam’s sin, then infants born of Christian parents ought not to be baptized at all; rather, they should be regarded as holy, since they were born from faithful parents, as blessed Paul teaches:

> “Otherwise your children would be unclean, but now they are holy” (1 Cor. 7:24). **[Note: Ms.: “Ought not.”]**

Similarly, blessed John says concerning children who are to be born that, as soon as they are born, they receive illumination through sanctification from the only-begotten Word, when he says:

> “He was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into the world” (John 1:9).

Infants therefore receive baptism not because of sins, but so that, possessing spiritual birth, they may be created in Christ through baptism, as it were, and become participants in his heavenly kingdom. Blessed Paul teaches this when he says:

> “If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation” (2 Cor. 5:17).

And again:

> “But if children, then heirs—heirs indeed of God, and fellow-heirs with Christ” (Rom. 8:17).

For this reason Cornelius, whose righteousness was commended by God, since he had received the baptism of the Spirit just as the apostles had and was a participant in the Holy Spirit—which, dwelling within him, could not allow him to possess sin—was nevertheless necessarily considered worthy also of that baptism which is administered through water, so that, according to blessed Paul, having been planted in the likeness of Christ’s death, he might also become a fellow-heir of his resurrection.

### XLI

Since certain people, through ignorance of the divine Scriptures, dare to break out into a wicked and unjust statement about Christ, asserting that he consigns children who have not been baptized at all [Note: [Col. 1145D] to the punishment of eternal fire. It is uncertain whom he chiefly intends; this much is clear: Saint Augustine once became entangled in this difficulty. Although it seemed harsh to him, he nevertheless did not hesitate to say that little ones who died without baptism would also be in this condemnation, though in the mildest and lightest form of all. But these words cannot apply to Augustine, who, in our judgment, lived later.]—the punishment that Scripture is accustomed to call Gehenna—let them learn from the divine Scriptures that the punishment of eternal fire is not prepared for the innocent and those entirely ignorant of sin, but for those who are known to have transgressed God’s law, as blessed Paul teaches in these words: “We know that whatever the law says, it speaks to those who are under the law” (Rom. 3:19). And again: “Through the law comes knowledge of sin” (ibid. 20). And again: “For where there is no law, [Col. 1146A] neither is there transgression” (Rom. 4:15). And again: “Sin is not counted when there is no law” (Rom. 5:13). And again: “For without the law sin was dead; but I was once alive without the law” (Rom. 7:8).

Likewise, when God established the law concerning the young, he says to Moses: “As I live, and as my name lives, and the glory of the Lord has filled the whole earth, because all the men who have seen my glory and the signs that I performed in Egypt and in this wilderness, and [Note: [Col. 1146D] Manuscript: ‘They tested me in this ten times.’] tested me ten times and did not obey my voice, surely they shall not see the land that I swore to their fathers, except their children who are with me here today, whoever know neither good nor evil; every young person who is innocent of these things—to them I shall give the land” (Num. 14).

Our Lord Jesus Christ likewise teaches concerning little children that they are free from every sin when he says: “Truly I say to you, unless you turn and become like little children, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18:3). And again he says to his disciples: “Let the little children come to me, and do not prevent them, for of such is the kingdom of God. Truly I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a little child shall not enter it.”

Likewise blessed Paul said: “Do not become children in understanding; but in wickedness be like little children” (1 Cor. 14:11). And again, concerning Esau and Jacob, he teaches as follows: “When they had not yet been born and had done nothing good or evil” (Rom. 9:12).

Children, therefore, as the divine Scripture itself has thoroughly taught, being entirely innocent, having experienced no wickedness at all, and not knowing how to distinguish good or evil, are not at all handed over to the punishment of eternal fire, since eternal punishment by fire has been prepared for the ungodly and sinners. But let these people, with their ignorance, be dismissed.

### XLII

We are taught again that, in the last days, the only-begotten God the Word, by the will of the Father and of the Holy Spirit, was pleased to become human. That he was made by the will of the Father, blessed Paul clearly taught in these words: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the law, so that he might redeem those who were under the law, and that we might receive the adoption of sons” (Gal. 4:4).

That the Son likewise became human willingly, blessed Paul similarly made clear, saying: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard being equal with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:6).

That he also became human by the will of the Holy Spirit is testified by the Angel who announced the good news to the virgin Mary, saying: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore the holy one who will be born will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35). And again, in a dream, the same Angel said to Joseph: “For that which will be born from her is of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1:20). Likewise blessed Matthew says: “She was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1:18).

### XLIII

Thus the only-begotten God the Word became human, receiving a body from Mary, ever-virgin, [Note: [Col. 1146D] Manuscript: “But creating for himself a rational soul.”] and creating for himself a rational soul, of the same substance [Note: [Col. 1146D] Manuscript: “Of which ours also is.”] as ours. From that ever-virgin he was born human, just as Isaiah said in prophecy: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son” (Isa. 7:14).

He called holy Mary “ever-virgin,” because just as she conceived as a virgin, so also she gave birth while remaining a virgin. For how will the sign given by God to Ahaz be true? If she did not remain a virgin after childbirth, then it must scarcely be believed that she conceived as a virgin. For what does the Evangelist say about Joseph? “And he did not know her until she had borne her son” (Matt. 1:25)—that is, he did not know with certainty that she was the Virgin who had been foretold as the one who would bear Christ, until, after the child’s birth, he recognized that the proofs of her virginity remained inviolate.

Moreover, this is shown by the subsequent events and announcements: the signs of Christ, the angels, the star, Simeon, Anna, and the Magi, as well as the warning of the Angel who spoke to him in this way: “Rise, take the child and his mother” (Matt. 2:13). He did not say, “your wife,” so that he might know that he had been given to the Virgin Mary as a servant for Christ’s sake.

Therefore, wishing to confirm the sign of virginity, after rising from the dead the Lord entered to the Apostles while the doors were shut, showing that he possessed bones and flesh.

### XLIV

Christ therefore advanced in age and wisdom in order to prove that he had truly become human, as the Evangelist Luke teaches when he says: “The child grew and became strong, filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was upon him” (Luke 2:40). And again: “Jesus advanced in wisdom and age” (ibid. 52).

If, then, Jesus Christ had not possessed a soul, [Note: [Col. 1147C] As the wicked Arians suppose.] as the wicked Arians suppose, or if, on the other hand, he had possessed a soul but not a rational one, [Note: [Col. 1147D] As Apollinaris defined.] he could certainly never have advanced in wisdom. For flesh without a soul cannot advance in wisdom. Nor does the only-begotten Son of God need an increase of wisdom, since he himself is the distributor of all our wisdom.

Epiphanius testifies to this concerning the Arians in *Heresy* 69:

> Οὐ βούλονται καταδέξασθαι ψυχήν αὐτόν.

“They do not consent to acknowledge that he possessed a soul.”

Augustine knew no one besides Epiphanius who reported this concerning the Arians. For he himself says in *Heresy* 49:

> “In their opinion that Christ assumed flesh alone, without a soul, they are less well known, and I have found no one who disputed against them on this matter.”

Yet this is true, and Epiphanius did not remain silent about it. Later, however, there were others who confirmed it, such as Theodoret in book 5, chapter 10, of *Heretical Fables*:

> Ἀρεῖος δὲ καὶ Εὐνόμιος σῶμα μὲν αὐτὸν ἔφασαν εἰληφέναι, τὴν θεὸτητα δὲ τῆς ψυχῆς ἐνηργηκέναι τὴν χρείαν.

“But Arius and Eunomius said that he assumed a body, while the divinity performed the function of the soul.”

As Apollinaris, in his madness, defined, [Note: [Col. 1147D] Theodoret, immediately after the preceding passage:]

> Ὁ δὲ Ἀπολινάριος ἔμψυχον μὲν ἔφησεν εἶναι τοῦ σωτῆρος τὸ σῶμα, οὐ μὲν τὴν λογικὴν ἐσχηκέναι ψυχήν· Περιττὸς γάρ ἦν, φησὶν ὁ νοῦς, τοῦ θεοῦ λόγου παρόντος.

“Apollinaris, however, said that the Savior’s body was animate, but that it did not possess a rational soul; for, he says, the mind was superfluous when the Word of God was present.”

After refuting that heresy at greater length, Theophilus of Alexandria concludes in these words, in his First Paschal Letter:

> “And thus the very order of the argument proves that the Lord assumed nothing imperfect, but that the human being assumed by him was saved fully and perfectly.”

### XLV

That our Lord Jesus Christ possessed a soul just as he possessed a body, the Evangelists clearly teach. The Angel said to Joseph, when he was in Egypt: “Rise, take the child and his mother, and go into the land of Israel, for those who sought the child’s soul are dead” (Matt. 2:20).

And again, when our Lord Jesus Christ said: “Now my soul is troubled” (John 12:27); and again: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 26:38); and again: “As the Father knows me, and I know the Father, and I lay down my soul for the sheep” (John 10:15); and again: “Therefore the Father loves me, because I lay down my soul, so that I may receive it again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord; I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to receive it again” (ibid. 17).

Likewise blessed Peter, referring David the prophet’s testimony to Christ, says in the person of Christ himself: “For you will not abandon my soul to the underworld, nor will you allow your holy one to see corruption” (Acts 2:28).

### XLVI

Through many testimonies, therefore, divine Scripture teaches that the only-begotten Son of God became human.

First, he did so in order to teach humility to the heavenly powers, and that the earthly human being should never suffer from the vice of pride, like the devil and his angels. Thus, when they thereafter saw the Son of Man possessing the form of a servant, [Note: [Col. 1148D] Manuscript: “The Son of God possessing the form of a servant.”] they would never be moved to entertain pride, as blessed Paul teaches when he says:

> “Have this mind among yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus, who, although he was in the form of God, did not regard being equal with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:5).

And what sort of form was this? He does not mean the form of the heavenly powers, but that of an earthly human being, which is held to be lower than all rational substances, as having been formed from a rational soul and an earthly body.

Therefore he adds, saying: “Being made in the likeness of human beings, and found in appearance as a human being, he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death” (Phil. 2:7). And what sort of death was it? One that among human beings is worse than all others. For he adds: “Even death on a cross” (Phil. 2:9).

### XLVII
