Lest anyone, hearing blessed Paul say that he humbled himself unto death, attach the passion of the cross to God, as [Note: [Col. 1148D] Manuscript: “As the wicked Arians think.”] the wicked Arians do, the only-begotten God is without passion and cannot in any way be subject to suffering. Whatever humble words are therefore spoken about Christ must all be referred to the form of the servant.

### XLVIII

Moreover, in order to show how great his love was for his own works, although he was Lord, he chose, after receiving the form of a servant, to become like one of us.

And again, because, having become human, he deigned to undergo death for the ungodly and sinners, as blessed Paul teaches when he says:

> “For why, while we were still weak, did Christ die for the ungodly at the appointed time? For scarcely will anyone die for a righteous person; perhaps someone might even dare to die for a good person. But God commends his love toward us, because, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Rom. 5:6).

Likewise, he grants and bestows spiritual adoption as sons upon those who believe in him, and makes them heirs of his heavenly kingdom, as our Lord Jesus Christ himself teaches, saying: “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless someone is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God” (John 3:3). [Note: [Col. 1148D] “Infants, because they are in sins.” Thus both manuscripts read. But the matter requires that the author not contradict himself, so that it should be read, “are not.” Above he taught that infants are not in sins and are not baptized because of sins, but so that they may become participants in the heavenly kingdom. When the Pelagians said this very thing, Jerome rightly argues against them at the end of book 3: “This one thing I shall say, so that the discourse may finally end: either you ought to introduce a new creed, so that after the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit you baptize infants into the kingdom of heaven; or, if you have one baptism both for little ones and for adults, infants too must be baptized for the remission of sins, in the likeness of Adam’s transgression.”]

Therefore infants, because they are not in sins, deserve also the grace of baptism, so that, created in Christ by a new generation, they may also become co-heirs of his kingdom, according to blessed Paul: “If anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation” (2 Cor. 5:17).

### XLIX

For this reason, too, the heavenly powers are created in Christ through faith alone, because he renewed all of them also in himself. For this reason those who believe in Christ are called a new creation, because they likewise venerate and worship the only-begotten God the Word together with the form of a servant that he possesses.

That the heavenly powers were created in Christ is testified by blessed Paul, who says: “To restore all things in Christ, those that are in heaven and those that are on earth, in him” (Eph. 1:10).

Again, just as he is called the head of the Church, so he is also shown to be the head of all the heavenly powers. For what does blessed Paul say?

> “For in him all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily, and you have been filled in him, who is the head of every principality and power” (Col. 2:9).

Again, he became human so that, having condemned sin in the flesh, he might leave us an example of how each person, after overcoming carnal vices, ought no longer to be deceived by the devil’s deceptions.

And again, he became human so that, through the form of a servant, he might be mediator between himself and the Father and the Holy Spirit, and between them and those worthy of him, and might preserve them forever in the bond of peace, as blessed Paul teaches in these words:

> “Because in him it was pleasing that all fullness should dwell, making peace through the blood of his cross, reconciling all things to himself, whether things on earth or things in heaven” (Col. 1:19). [Note: [Col. 1149C] Manuscript: “To dwell, and through him to reconcile all things to himself, making peace through the blood of his cross.”]

### L

Just as he himself was therefore the cause of so many blessings for all who believe, so also he becomes a just retributor for those who do not believe.

For this reason the divine Scriptures teach us through many testimonies that God does not desire the death of the ungodly and sinner, except that he should turn and live.

As long as we are in this life, therefore, we can do penance and merit that blessed future life, which is eternal. For after the dissolution of the body no opportunity for repentance remains, as the prophet David teaches when he says to God: “For in death there is no one who remembers you; and in the underworld, who will confess to you?” (Ps. 6:6). And again: “The dead shall not praise you, nor all those who descend into the underworld” (Ps. 113:17).

That Christ will judge the living and the dead, blessed Paul clearly teaches when he says: “For we must all appear before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what belongs to his body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil” (2 Cor. 5:10).

For this reason Christ is said to sit at the right hand of his Father as judge both of the living and of the dead. That the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, our Lord Jesus Christ clearly taught.

### LI

We are taught again that the dead rise in the same flesh in which they were formed in their mother’s womb, alike in body and in form, as blessed Paul writes to the Corinthians:

> “But someone will say: How are the dead raised? And with what sort of body will they come? Foolish person, what you sow is not made alive unless it first dies; and what you sow, you do not sow the body that will be, but a bare grain, perhaps of wheat or of some other kind. But God gives it a body as he wills” (1 Cor. 15:35–36). [Note: [Col. 1149D] “Not ‘as he wills,’ but ‘as he willed.’” Among the Greeks this passage may perhaps have furnished an argument for those who read ἠθέλησε or ἤθελεν, but not so among the Latins, who consistently read “as he wills,” not “as he willed.” Augustine, *Letter* 146 to Consentius: “But God gives it a body in whatever way he will,” which amounts to the same thing.]

When the Apostle had said that God gives it a body, not “as he wills,” but “as he willed,” he showed that just as human beings were created in the beginning, so also they will rise in the resurrection, without their appearance or body being changed.

Thus our Lord Jesus Christ, after he rose from the dead, [Note: [Col. 1149D] “He changed neither body nor form.”] raised from the tomb the very body that had been buried. But with how much greater glory, Theophilus of Alexandria declares, using words from Psalm 92 in Royal Codex 211:

> Ὁ Κύριος ἐβασίλευσεν, ἐνεδύσατο εὐπρέπειαν· ἐπειδὴ γὰρ ἔλαβε φθαρτὸν σῶμα, εὐπρέπειαν ἐνεδύσατο ἀναστὴσας αὐτό, οὐ φθαρτὸν ἀλλ` ἄφθαρτον .  
> Ὁ Κύριος ἐβασίλευσεν, εὐπρέπειαν ἐνεδύσατο· ἔλαβε γὰρ ἀναστήσας πάλιν τὸ ἑαυτοῦ σῶμα, κατὰ τὴν οἰκείαν ἐπαγγέλειαν, Λύσατε τὸν ναὸν τοῦτον, καὶ ἐπὶ τρισὶν ἡμέραις ἐγερῶ αὐτόν .  
> Ὃ ἔγειρε τοίνυν ἐνεδύσατο σῶμα· ἔλεγε γὰρ, Οὐκ ἐγκαταλείψεις τὴν ψυχήν μου εἰς ᾅδην, οὐδὲ δώσεις τὸν ὅσιόν σου ἰδεῖν διαφθοράν· ἔτι δὲ καὶ ἡ σάρξ μου κατασκηνώσει ἐπ` ἐλπίδι .  
> Ἀναστάς ἐν τῷ μνήματι οὐκ ἔμεινε· καὶ μείνας ἐν τῷ μνήματι οὐκ ἴδεν διαφθοράν, οὐκ ἐκράτησεν αὐτοῦ ἡ διαφθορά, ὁ ἄφθαρτος λόγος τὸ φθαρτὸν ἀνέστησε σῶμα εἰς ἀφθαρσίάν .

> “The Lord has reigned; he has clothed himself with beauty. For since he assumed a corruptible body, he clothed himself with beauty, raising it up not corruptible but incorruptible.  
>   
> “The Lord has reigned; he has clothed himself with beauty. For, rising again, he assumed his own body according to his own promise: ‘Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.’  
>   
> “Therefore he clothed himself with the body that he had raised. For he said: ‘You will not abandon my soul in the underworld, nor will you allow your holy one to see corruption; and my flesh also shall dwell in hope.’  
>   
> “When he rose, he did not remain in the tomb; and while remaining in the tomb he did not see corruption. Corruption did not master him: the incorruptible Word raised the corruptible body to incorruptibility.”

He did not at all change either body or form. For just as a grain of wheat, having lost its own body, is sown naked and dies, and then rises again with the same body that it had lost, so also a human being in the resurrection of the dead, even if he died with some part of his body cut away, will rise in that same body and form in which he was first created in his mother’s womb.

Blessed Paul teaches this again in these words:

> “Even we who are in this tent groan, being burdened, because we do not wish to be unclothed but clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life” (2 Cor. 5:4).

And again:

> “For this corruptible body must put on incorruption, and this mortal body must put on immortality” (1 Cor. 15).

When the Apostle says that we do not wish to be unclothed but clothed over, he shows that each one of us is now clothed with life, glory, and incorruption in body, flesh, and form. Just as glowing iron, clothed with the glory of fire, does not at all change its proper nature, so the saints, clothed with heavenly glory, do not lay aside the body and form that they possess in this life.

Likewise, when our Lord Jesus Christ put on glory on the mountain, he did not at all change what he was—a human being.

But what has been said here concerning the faith proved by the testimonies of divine Scripture is sufficient for us.

### LII

Since those who follow the wicked heresies and doctrines of Arius or Eunomius sharpen their tongues day after day to blaspheme the only-begotten Son of God, having continually learned to adulterate the simplicity of divine Scripture and likewise to defile the truth with certain perverse expressions, which are accustomed to arise from ordinary ways of thinking, so that they may appear to confirm their wicked heresy by part of the syllogistic reasoning of their sophisms, they put forward for us sophistical questions about God, attempting to alienate the only-begotten Son from the substance of the Father.

I therefore consider it necessary to destroy their wicked heresy by those same ordinary ways of thinking, so that by the very things from which they think they derive proof, they may also be refuted.

Before I begin to enumerate their questions concerning the Son against us—questions that they regard as enormous and difficult—I wish to say to them that, whatever you may wish to say about the birth of the Son of God from the Father, using temporal expressions, you will not be able to prove his birth as it actually is, since the birth of the only-begotten God the Word is natural and without beginning and cannot be comprehended as it truly is.

For if all words that are uttered signify time—either present, past, or future—but the only-begotten God is the creator of these, then his birth certainly cannot be demonstrated by temporal words. Therefore, necessarily following the faith of the divine Scriptures, we must take from them examples for our proof.

### LIII

When they ask us whether God brought forth the Son or not, and receive from us the answer, “He brought him forth,” they immediately add a question of this sort, which the Greeks call a dilemma [Note: [Col. 1150D] The manuscript calls it “a dilemma”]: “Unwillingly or willingly?”

They do this so that, if we say “unwillingly,” they may immediately add: “But if he brought forth the Son unwillingly, how is it not wicked to say this of God, that he is subjected to the necessity of generation?”

If, however, we say “willingly,” they again add whatever suits them: “Therefore, if he brought him forth willingly, since the Son was brought forth by the will, there can be no distinction at all between him and all the other things that were likewise created by God’s will.”

But we must not answer what they themselves desire to hear. Rather, we shall speak in this way: “He brought him forth neither willingly nor unwillingly.”

When, having received this answer, they have been entirely excluded from their wicked conclusion, and ask us how he brought him forth, then the answer will be: “Naturally”—which is above every will and necessity.

If they understand our answer and remain silent, well and good. But if they say that the answer is not clear, we shall question them in turn in the same manner as their question: “Is God good willingly or unwillingly?”

They too, fearing an unlawful answer on either side, will answer us: “Neither willingly nor unwillingly, but by that nature which is above will and necessity.”

With these answers, then, which they themselves use when asserting that God is good, we too prove that God brought forth the Son. For just as God is good not by will or necessity but by nature itself, so that he is never found deprived of goodness, so also by nature he has the Son.

For God can never be deprived of his only-begotten divine Son. These statements about proving the only-begotten God would indeed be abundantly sufficient if our conversation were with prudent people, since his birth from the Father is natural.

### LIV

But since these people, like dogs seized by madness who rage even against their masters, stirred by the passion of insanity through ignorance, attempt to blaspheme against the Son of God whenever they hear anything said about him with reverence and are excluded from their customary blasphemy against him, they nevertheless do not abandon the persistence of their malice, which they constantly exercise against the Son. Instead, they try to devise other objections, seeking to destroy the birth of the only-begotten Word from God, which is without beginning and is held to be natural, as though they always desired to fight against him.

I therefore consider it necessary to answer their other empty questions as well, lest we appear to evade the force of the questions they have proposed.

They ask us, then, in turn: “If everything that ceased also began—”

If we answer that everything that ceased also began, they immediately add: [Note: [Col. 1151D] “The Son ceased to be born.”] “The author does not deny that the Son ceased to be born.” But Augustine, disputing against these same Arians in *Letter* 174 to Pascentius, says otherwise:

> “What shall we say, then? If the Son of God was born from the Father, the Father has now ceased to beget; and if he ceased, he began. But if he began to beget, there was a time when he was without the Son. Yet he was never without the Son, because his Son is his wisdom, which is the radiance of eternal light. Therefore the Father always begets, and the Son is always born.”

There exists a little work by the monk Theodore entitled:

> Ἀπόδειξις ὅτι ὁ πατὴρ ἀεὶ γεννᾷ, ὁ δὲ υἱὸς ἀεὶ γεννᾶται.

“Proof that the Father always begets, while the Son is always begotten.”

Among other things, it reasons as follows:

> Ἔτι δὲ ἐπεὶ τὸ γεννᾶσθαι τὸν υἱὸν οὐκ ἄλλο σημαίνει, ἢ τὸ ἔχειν τὴν ὕπαρξιν ἐκ τοῦ πατρός· ἀεὶ δὲ πατρόθεν ἔχει τὴν ὕπαρξιν· ἀεὶ ἄρα γεννᾶται .

“Moreover, since the Son’s being begotten signifies nothing other than his having existence from the Father, and since he always has existence from the Father, he is therefore always begotten.”

If the Son ceased to be born, then necessarily he began; and if he began, there was a time when he did not exist; and if there was a time when he did not exist, it is impossible for him to have his birth from the substance of God, since God’s substance, being without beginning, always and unchangingly existing, does not admit increase or diminution.

But we must not answer them that everything that ceases also began, since not everything that ceases therefore has a beginning. Not only this, but not everything that has a beginning therefore also ceases. For God, wishing to make the heavenly powers, does not have a beginning; once they have been made, however, he ceases to will to make them. [Note: [Col. 1152D] Manuscript: “He ceased.”] Therefore not everything that ceases has a beginning.

Again, although the heavenly powers, once made, have a beginning of substance, they never cease to exist. Thus not everything that began will also cease.

Therefore, since it has been proved that not everything that ceases also began, and therefore that the only-begotten God the Son ceases to be born, [Note: [Col. 1152D] Manuscript: “The only-begotten God the Son ceased to be born.”] nevertheless he does not have a beginning of birth. For the birth of the Son from the Father is without beginning, since it is natural.

### LV

Again they ask us whether God, when he was alone, begot the Son. If we answer that he begot him when he was alone, they immediately add: “Therefore there was a time when the Son did not exist.”

But if we answer that he was not alone, they immediately add: “How can that which was always together with him be properly called born? For, as they say, the very word ‘born’ suggests that at some time it did not exist, precisely because it is said to have been born.”

They say this because they do not understand how much it matters when one dares to pronounce anything about God in terms of bodily and temporal notions. For the one under discussion, being without beginning, cannot be subject to the necessities of time.

Let us therefore question them in turn, using their own question, so that their fabrication—which the Greeks call a sophism—may be made clear and plain to them.

Tell us: when God was alone, did he beget mercies or not? For blessed Paul calls God the Father of mercies, saying:

> “Blessed be God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies” (2 Cor. 1:3).

If they dare to say that he begot them when he was alone, we shall answer them in this way: Why is it not wicked and impious to say that God was once without mercies, since God is regarded as the fountain of mercies and is never believed to have been the father of wickedness, so that, having initially not been the father of mercies, he would later begin to become their father?

But if, avoiding this open blasphemy concerning God, they say, “He was never alone without mercies,” we shall answer them likewise: Just as God was never alone without mercies and did not afterward become the Father of mercies, so likewise he did not first exist alone and afterward become the Father of the only-begotten Son. For God is always the Father of his only-begotten God the Word.

### LVI

But if, persisting again in their folly, they say that what is born signifies the substance of deity, while God the Father is unborn and the Son is born, and therefore the substance of the Father and the Son cannot be one and the same, let them learn that “unborn” does not at all signify substance.

For if “unborn” appears to be contrary to “born,” while nothing is contrary to substance, then “unborn” plainly cannot be substance. Alternatively, if substance is asserted in relation to what is, while “unborn” is asserted in relation to what is not, because it is unborn, then “unborn” is not substance.

Again, if substance is known to subsist through itself, while “unborn” does not subsist by itself but is said of a substance that was not born, then “unborn” is not substance.

### LVII

Again, if they say: “If the Father is unborn according to substance, while the Son is born, the substance of the born and the unborn cannot be one,” let them learn further that the mode of substances does not necessarily make substances different.

For because God the Father is said to be unborn and is likewise said to be immortal and incorruptible, he will not therefore have different substances, since “unborn” is not one and the same thing as “immortal” or “incorruptible,” or the other similar terms.

Therefore, just as these terms, when spoken of God, do not at all signify different substances, so neither will “born” and “unborn” ever make different substances.

For because Adam was unborn, while Seth was born, their substance is not therefore different.

### LVIII

But if they persist, saying that whatever is without beginning is also unborn, and that because the Son is born he cannot be without beginning, let them learn this: it is not the case that whatever is without beginning is necessarily unborn, because it is not the case that whatever has a beginning is necessarily born.

For God’s mercies have existed without beginning, but they are not innate, since they have God as their Father.

Likewise heaven and earth, although they have a beginning, were not born but created. For if something is created, it is not in every respect born.

For if “created” and “born” were the same, the Evangelist John would have taught superfluously when he said:

> “But to all who received him he gave power to become children of God” (John 1:12),

since those who were once created would already possess this as well: that they should become children of God.

Therefore, just as “created” and “born” are not the same, so “not created” and “unborn” cannot be the same either, since God’s mercies exist but are nevertheless not innate.

### LIX

When they again ask us how God, being one, simple, and uncompounded, can be Father, Son, and Holy Spirit at the same time, let them learn that God does not cease to be simple and uncompounded because he has one only-begotten substantial Word, equal to him in all things, and likewise substantial Wisdom, equal to him in all things.

If, as they suppose, he is composite because he has a will, and because this will is not equal to the substance, since substance and will are not identical, we nevertheless do not adopt their opinion.

Rather, we say piously and religiously that, even if God has a will, and this will is not equal to the substance, he is nevertheless free from every composition.

### LX

Since they still appear wise in their own eyes, although they have been shown to be altogether foolish in every respect, they ask us this as well: How can one God, one substance, be called Father and Son?

For those who say this are accustomed to pronounce the one and only God, Son and Father at once, in a single part of speech, as though they were Sabellians. Because the Sabellians confused the Father with the Son, they therefore called God by the compound word υἱοπάτωρ (*huiopatōr*), “Son-Father,” which the Orthodox rejected. Athanasius says in his *Exposition of the Faith*:

> Οὔτε γὰρ υἱοπάτορα φρονοῦμεν, ὡς οἱ Σαβέλλιοι, μονούσιον, καὶ οὐχ ὁμοούσιον .

“For neither do we conceive of a Son-Father, as the Sabellians do—[as] of one substance and not consubstantial.”

In the Catholic Church God is not called υἱοπάτωρ (*huiopatōr*) because, while acknowledging in the one God three persons numerically of the same substance, it rejects μονόυσιον (*monousion*, “of one substance”)—as was said of the Sabellians—and embraces ὁμοούσιον (*homoousion*, “consubstantial”).]

Let them learn not to persist for so long in the same folly. For because God the Father is one, and his Son is one, and the substance of the Father and Son is likewise one, God ought not therefore to be called υἱοπάτωρ (*huiopatōr*), since we do not speak of one person numerically, but use a common term for the substance.

Adam and his son Abel, for example, were one human being by the communion of nature, although one was distinct from the other and their substance was one and the same; yet they were never called υἱοπάτωρ, nor could they even be called by that name.

That two human beings numerically are nevertheless called one human being through communion and, as I have said, fellowship of nature, is testified by the servant of God Moses, who says:

> “And God made the human being; according to the image of God he made him; male and female he made them” (Gen. 1:27).

Likewise our Lord Jesus Christ also calls himself and the Father one together, because of the equality and unity of substance, saying:

> “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

One, therefore, is God—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—because of the unity and equality of substance.

### LXI

For just as our thought cannot become speech [614]—for it itself is regarded as the father of our speech—so, conversely, speech can never become thought; nor can our wisdom become thought or speech. Rather, thought generates speech, and is not itself generated; likewise, speech is generated but does not generate. In the same way, wisdom neither generates nor is generated. Yet since our thought is wise and possesses wisdom, as rational it generates speech alone. Wisdom, on the other hand, does not generate speech, but is truly together with thought, as also with speech.

Thus God the Father can never become the Son, nor, conversely, the Son the Father; neither can the Holy Spirit become the Son or the Father. Again, God the Father did indeed beget the only-begotten God, the Word, but he himself was not born; the Son, however, was born and did not beget. The Holy Spirit was neither born nor did he beget.

But, to put it more clearly: just as the mercies of God the Father, although they are born from the unbegotten Father, have generation wholly conjoined with the Father’s unbegotten nature, so also the substantial Only-begotten Son of God has birth wholly conjoined with the Father’s ingeneracy, since he is “the radiance of his glory and the form of God’s substance.” For blessed Paul, writing to the Hebrews, says: “Who is the radiance of his glory and the figure of his substance” (Heb. 1:3).

When the Apostle Paul called the Son the radiance of the Father, he plainly demonstrated that the Son is from the Father’s substance; that the Son is held inseparably and indivisibly in relation to the Father; and that he is always with the Father. By again mentioning the figure of God’s substance, he teaches that the Son possesses a substance equal to the Father’s. And again, just as the immortality of God the Father, being one with God the Father and not born, is not called born and likewise does not itself generate, so also the substantial Spirit of God is neither born nor does he beget. [Note: [Col. 1153D] The manuscript reads: “The Holy Spirit is neither born nor did he beget.”]

Therefore, while confessing three persons—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—we believe that, on account of the unity of substance, the Trinity has one power. Likewise, on account of the indivisibility of nature, we confess the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit to be one Lord, one omnipotent God, Creator and Provider, ever existing in himself and unchanged. To him be honor and glory unto ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1153] **Here ends [Note: [Col. 1153D] “Rufinus, Presbyter of the Province of Palestine,”]**

This, as appears, was therefore the inscription placed at the beginning of the book. Although it has already been shown to appear spurious, we have nevertheless judged that it should be retained, so that the book might not lack a title, at least until time reveals a genuine and legitimate one.

Nor should it be omitted that at least two books on the faith existed under Rufinus’s name. We understand this from John the Deacon, who cites the second book in his *Exposition of Exodus* in these words:

“Rufinus, in Book II *On the Faith*: The people of Israel were in a column of cloud by day and in a column of fire by night, because these went before them as guides on their journey, so that through the cloud he might signify the grace of baptism and through the fire the gifts of the Holy Spirit; for the Apostle Paul wrote that the fathers were baptized in the cloud, and the Acts of the Apostles declare that the Holy Spirit is fire.”

**The Book on the Faith of Rufinus, Presbyter of the Province of Palestine, translated from Greek into Latin.**

## In the year of the Lord 415. Pelagius the Briton

[Col. 1155]

## Dissertation on the Life and Writings of Pelagius, by Garnerius, Editor of the Works of Marius Mercator

(See this dissertation in *Patrologia*, vol. XLVIII, cols. 266–297.)

[Col. 1155]

## Review of the Editions of Pelagius’s Works, by Schoenemann

(*Bibliotheca Patrum Latinorum historico-litteraria*)

### § 1. Writings

[Col. 1155A]

### I. Writings of Pelagius that still survive intact

1. **Fourteen books of Expositions on the Epistles of Paul**, written while Pelagius was still staying at Rome. For a long time, and from as early as the sixth century, they bore Jerome’s name. But it has long been known that they belong to the Pelagians, indeed to Pelagius himself. See Vossius, *History of Pelagianism*, book I, chapter 4. In the form in which we now possess them, however, they did not come directly from their author, but were cleansed throughout—especially in the Epistle to the Romans—by Cassiodorus of passages that appeared to have been written against the Catholic faith. Cf. Garnerius, on Mercator, Appendix to Dissertation 6, part I.

2. **The Epistle to Demetrias**, written around the year 412. It too bore Jerome’s name. But it is proved to be Pelagius’s by the passages Augustine quotes from it in *On the Grace of Christ*, chapters 22, 27, 37, 38, and 40, and in his letter to Juliana, Demetrias’s mother. See Vossius for further details.

3. **The Booklet of Faith addressed to Pope Innocent**, written in the year 417. This too could not escape being attributed to Jerome, and it was formerly accustomed to be entitled: *Jerome’s Explanation of the Creed addressed to Damasus*.

### II. Lost works whose fragments survive

1. **The Book of Εὐλογίαι**, which Vossius translates as *Of Honorable Discourses on Actual Conduct*. Gennadius calls it *A Book of Eulogies for Actual Conduct from the Divine Scriptures*, and Honorius of Marseille calls it *A Book for Actual Life*. Orosius reports that it bore the title *Testimonies*. From Jerome and Gennadius we learn that, following Cyprian’s example, it contained various chapters of sayings gathered from Scripture. Hence the recent and perceptive writer William Wallius conjectured, in his *History of Paedobaptism*, that the title should be read as *A Book of Extracts*. Jerome provides its testimonies and fragments in Book I of his *Dialogue Against the Pelagians*, where he cites titles 14, 21, 31, 72, 73, 81, 83, 100, 123, 131, 164, and 165; and Augustine provides them in *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book IV, chapter 8, and *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, chapters 1–6. These are also presented together in Garnerius’s notes on Mercator at the place cited.

2. **The Book on Nature**, to which Augustine opposed his book *On Nature and Grace*, incorporating many passages from it. Garnerius thinks it was composed in Sicily, though he is uncertain whether it should be attributed to Pelagius himself, to Coelestius, or to Anianus. It came into Augustine’s hands through Jacob and Timasius, young followers of Pelagius, and was sent by certain African bishops to Innocent. Fragments are found in Garnerius at the cited place and the following pages.

3. **One or perhaps two books of consolation and exhortation to a widow**, of which the memory and fragments survive in Jerome, *Dialogue* 3; Augustine, *On the Proceedings at Palestine*, chapter 6; and Mercator, *Commonitorium*, chapter 4. Garnerius collected them in his notes on Mercator, Dissertation 1.

4. **A Letter to Augustine**, or, as Augustine calls it, “a little document of defense,” sent through the deacon Carus after the Synod of Diospolis. Augustine, *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, chapter 30; Garnerius, cited place.

5. **A Letter to a certain presbyter friend**, after the Synod of Diospolis. Augustine, *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, chapter 30; Garnerius, cited place.

6. **A Letter to Innocent I**, in the year 417, sent together with the Creed of the Faith. Augustine, *On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 30 and following; Garnerius, cited place.

7. **Four books on Free Will**, which Augustine attacks in his book *On the Grace of Christ* and from which he preserved many passages together in chapters 4, 7, 10, 18, 28, 29, and 39. Garnerius presented these fragments in proper order, from the first book and especially from the third, at the cited place.

### III. Entirely lost works

1. **Three books on the Trinity**, which he appears to have composed before the commentaries on Paul’s Epistles.

2. **Three letters**, one to Paulinus and another to Constantius, which Augustine mentions in *On the Grace of Christ*, chapters 34, 35, and 36. The third was written to Augustine himself immediately after Pelagius’s arrival in Palestine, so that he might not appear to have departed without greeting his host, as Garnerius correctly identifies the occasion. The first two must be assigned to the years 405 and 406.

Most recently, B. Semler ventured to attribute to Pelagius the *Letter to the Matron Celantia on the Manner of Living Piously*, on the basis of similarities in language and treatment.

### § 2. Editions

[Col. 1157B]

### I. The fourteen books of Expositions on the Epistles of Paul

I do not remember that anyone published these commentaries before Erasmus, in the first edition of Jerome’s works in 1516. From that time onward they always remained attached to Jerome’s works, and were reprinted nowhere else except in John Clericus’s *Augustinian Appendix*. How the more distinguished editors of Jerome treated them will become clear from the following list.

**1516. Basel, Froben, folio.** *Commentaries on the Epistles of Paul*, in volume IX of Jerome’s works, folios 131–190.

Erasmus says in the preface to this volume:

“A certain codex of obsolete antiquity, written in Gothic characters, claimed the commentaries on all the Epistles of the blessed Paul for Jerome. The characters were so confused and had faded so much through age that we were forced to descend again to the elementary level and, as boys do in school, devote ourselves to recognizing the little letters. But these commentaries, like those immediately preceding them, must be judged unworthy of being attributed to Jerome. For when does Jerome ever speak so foolishly as this interpreter—whoever he finally was—or stammer so badly, so that he so frequently commits solecisms?

“Although the compiler of what is called the Ordinary Gloss cites under Jerome’s name certain passages that I have found expressly in these commentaries, this is by no means sufficient to prove that they belong to Jerome of Stridon simply because they are cited under his name. For that glossator—whether he was Rabanus or someone else—was not concerned to investigate whose words they were; he merely extracted, for the moment, whatever served his purpose.

“Someone may ask: Why, then, was it necessary to mix adulterine material with legitimate works when they were being printed? We shall answer, as we said earlier in other prefaces, that we wished to accommodate not only the learned but also the unlearned. If we had omitted the commentaries on Mark, or had not printed those on Paul, what tragedies would the ignorant immediately have staged! Hesiod has passages for those of the first or second class of human beings—those who either read for themselves or, after receiving instruction, read with judgment. Yet for those stupid people of the third class he too provides something to embrace, lest the proverb lack its place: ‘Like lips, like lettuce.’

“Nevertheless, even in these very commentaries on Mark and Paul one may find certain things that could please the learned—passages evidently drawn from Jerome’s storehouse by some diligent person who, having read through Jerome’s writings, selected many passages from them and then mixed them into his own work, so that Jerome might appear, with greater plausibility, to deserve this counterfeit.

“This was formerly the practice of monks, especially those belonging to the household of Saint Benedict. Among them, for many years, tyranny held sway not only over religion but also, so to speak, over letters, while the world, abandoning the simplicity of Christ and devoting itself to wars, gradually sank into a kind of barbaric savagery through its contempt for the pursuit of wisdom. It was a time when nothing pleased unless it was Jerome’s. Just as today many approve nothing unless it has the flavor of Scotus or Thomas.

“Then certain rogues were given an opportunity to impose upon simpler people. They hawked their trifles everywhere under Jerome’s name and prefixed the title of that most celebrated and holy man to any sort of nonsense.

“Still, even if one may find a grain amid much chaff, we mark these commentaries with a black sign, since they have appropriated so much from Jerome’s writings, and we judge them unworthy of having diligent students waste good hours in reading them. The learned, and those who possess a refined critical sense—we certainly know this—will agree with us. We pay no attention to the judgment of the ignorant and dull.”

In the Basel edition of 1537, they are found in the same volume, pages 265–396.

[Col. 1158B]

**1572. Rome, Paulus Manutius, folio.** *Commentaries on the Epistles of the Blessed Paul*, in volume VIII of the Victoriana edition of Jerome’s works. Since that edition itself is not at hand, it is necessary to cite the pages of the Antwerp and Paris editions. In the Antwerp edition of 1579 they are found in volume VIII, pages 170–288; in the Paris edition of 1643, in the same volume, pages 161–277.

Here is a brief statement by Marianus Victorius about them, taken from the preface to this volume:

“The commentaries on thirteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul are not Jerome’s—not even remotely. For they possess neither his style nor his learning, although at the beginning of the work they contain a letter addressed to Heliodorus. Rather, it is entirely certain that they belong to a man stained by the Pelagian taint, unless one wishes to say that only those passages which are not orthodox were added by heretics.

“Ambrosius Catharinus Politus, Archbishop of Compsa and defender of the Catholic religion, noticed this before us; Sixtus of Siena also noticed it in the fourth and sixth volumes of his *Holy Library*. Both refuted the errors of the Pelagian heresy found in the work.

“If anyone wishes to know this, he will find it plainly from the exposition of the fifth chapter of Romans, where the author asserts that Adam’s sin is spread through the human race not by transmission and descent but only by example and imitation, as though people contracted it only when, having reached adulthood and becoming already fit for sin, they imitated Adam in his crimes. The same point appears even more clearly in the interpretation of the seventh chapter. Explaining the statement ‘sin was dead without the law,’ he writes:

“‘Likewise, if, when there was no law, sin was dead, those who assert that sin comes to us from Adam by transmission are out of their minds.’

“No Catholic is unaware how impious and heretical this opinion is.

“As for what I should decide about the author of the work, I am certain of nothing except that it is unquestionably not Jerome’s. Nevertheless, we have arranged for it to be printed in the form in which it had previously circulated in print, so that nothing might be lacking from the earlier edition. We have added, removed, or altered not a single syllable, leaving entirely to the judgment of the readers what they wish to think of it.”

[Note: [Col. 1157D] Nevertheless, Sixtus indicates that he does not agree with the opinion of his teacher Ambrosius, who had maintained that these commentaries belonged to Pelagius himself. Cf. book IV, page 309, Cologne edition of 1626, quarto.]

[Col. 1158D]

**1673. Paris, folio.** No printing of these commentaries from this place and year survives. Of much greater importance in the history of their editions, however, is John Garnerius of the Society of Jesus, *Dissertation on the Writings of Pelagius*, which forms chapter 2 of the Appendix to Dissertation 6, *On Writings Published by Enemies of the Faith as Pelagian Heresy during Augustine’s Lifetime*. It is included with the works of Marius Mercator, part I, page 367 and following.

In this work Garnerius demonstrated not only by irresistible arguments that this interpretation is precisely the one read by Augustine, Jerome, and Mercator and interpolated by Cassiodorus, but also, so that the extent of Cassiodorus’s alterations might be evident, he set in parallel the readings found in the published copies, with Cassiodorus as corrector, and what Pelagius had written, as reported by Marius and Augustine.

**1684. Frankfurt and Leipzig, folio.** *Commentaries on the Epistles of the Blessed Paul*, in volume IX of Jerome’s works, pages 213–321.

**1699. Paris, folio.** *Commentaries on the Epistles of the Blessed Paul*, in volume V of Martianay’s edition of Jerome’s works, pages 925–1106.

**1700. Antwerp, Petrus Mortier, folio.** *Commentaries of Pelagius the Briton on the Epistles of the Holy Apostle Paul*, in the *Augustinian Appendix*, or volume XII of the Antwerp edition of Augustine’s works, pages 317–458.

The extent to which Garnerius advanced judgments about this work is already indicated by its title. It will also be useful to hear Clericus himself:

“Learned men had long suspected that the commentaries on Paul’s Epistles belonged to Pelagius, and Garnerius made the matter clear. This will also be evident from the various notes that we have placed in different passages, in which we mark the Pelagian doctrines so plainly that the matter can be doubtful to no one except someone entirely ignorant of these subjects.

“Further indications of Pelagianism will also occur to those who read these commentaries more carefully. If it were not established that the teaching of Saint Augustine and his opponents had not been sufficiently understood for several generations, so that many believed themselves Augustinians while following Pelagius’s opinion, it would be surprising that those who repeatedly interpolated these commentaries did not remove the passages in which Pelagius’s doctrine is manifest.

“But many were so crude that they made Saint Augustine a Pelagian and Pelagius, in turn, an Augustinian. Through this ignorance, manifest Pelagianism here escaped the hands of the correctors.

“We published this work from Erasmus’s Frobenian editions and removed only what manifestly remained. We wished that we had access to some manuscript containing these commentaries, especially because the text explained in them is not the old Latin version current in Pelagius’s time, but the version corrected by Jerome. Without an ancient manuscript, this crime of the more recent copyists could not be corrected.

“Although we do not wish to praise these commentaries, especially when they are compared with the labors of more recent writers, we nevertheless judge that, given their brevity, they are not to be despised if compared with other writings of the ancient authors of this kind. We therefore regret that they have not reached us complete and in the form in which they came from the author’s hand.”

[Col. 1159C]

**1742. Verona, folio.** *Commentaries on the Epistles of Saint Paul*, in volume XI of the works of Jerome edited by Domenico Vallarsi, pages 835–1069; and in the Venetian edition of 1772, quarto, volume XI, part III, pages 134–435.

Although Pelagius’s name is not prefixed, the editors nevertheless do not deny that the work belongs to Pelagius. They demonstrate, by the rare and striking testimony of John the Deacon, or Presbyter Mansionarius, a Veronese writer of the thirteenth century, that the true author was not always unknown. In an unpublished history he mentions them in these words:

“I myself, John, saw the commentary of the aforementioned Pelagius on Paul’s Epistles, in which, although he explains many things well and elegantly, he nevertheless subtly pours in the poison of his heresy.”

The same editors observe that the preface addressed to Heliodorus under Jerome’s fictitious name is absent from the better-quality manuscript codices.

## II. The Epistle to Demetrias the Virgin

In manuscript codices it is never found except among Jerome’s letters and minor treatises. Hence editions of the same antiquity are almost as numerous as editions of Jerome’s works or little works. In the older editions—that is, in the collections of letters—it occupies a place among Jerome’s works themselves, although it had been recognized early enough that its author was not Jerome but some Pelagian or Pelagius himself. From the time of the Erasmian edition onward, however, it was customarily copied separately with other works falsely attributed to Jerome.

Recently it was published separately and illuminated by a special study. But, so that the order of everything may be clear, it seems appropriate here also to attach the principal descriptions in chronological sequence.

**1467. [Rome, Ulrich Gallus, folio].** *Epistle to Demetrias under the Name of Jerome, on Virginity and the Perfect Life*, among the Epistles of Jerome published without place or year, part III, treatise 5, entitled *On the State of Virginal Continence and First on Virgins Dedicated to God*, Epistle 69.

It is preceded by Jerome’s own first letter to the same virgin and immediately followed by the letter to Julian, Demetrias’s mother. Two summaries are prefixed: one sufficiently lengthy, which suitably and clearly presents the force and subject matter of the entire treatment; the other shorter, concerning the author, which there is no need to transcribe here in full.

Note that most people say that this letter is not Jerome’s but belongs to some Pelagian, because it praises the goodness of nature and free will too strongly. The presbyter Bede says in his book *On the Grace of God Against Julian* that it belongs to Julian, a follower of that heresy. From Augustine we know that much of this letter was criticized as opposed to the grace of God. Hence he suspects that it was written by a Pelagian, as he himself writes in his letter to Julian (sic), Demetrias’s mother, which for that reason we have appended to this little book.

It also contains many salutary admonitions. Since it is commonly inserted in copies under Jerome’s name, we too have given it that title.

This particular edition, however, is not available to us; what we possess is the Basel edition of 1489, certainly copied from it, where it appears in part I, treatise 1, folio CXLIIII. Likewise, in the Nuremberg edition of 1495, it appears in part III, treatise 5, Epistle 188, folio CCLXVI, preceded by the shorter summary given above. It also appears in the Basel edition of 1497, part III, treatise 5, likewise entitled *On Virginal Continence*, Epistle 18, preceded by both summaries; and in precisely the same place and number in the Lyon edition of 1513, folio 198b and following, although the folio number does not appear in that edition.

As for the remaining Roman editions, I have nothing definite to say, since neither they themselves nor any other edition that I could reasonably say was copied from them is available. In another edition printed without indication of year or place, which we described in volume I of the *Bibliotheca*, page 487, this letter does not occur; only Jerome’s own letter to Demetrias, number 96, is present. I do not know whether this should be attributed to the manuscripts or to the selection made by the editors.

**1470. Mainz, Peter Schoeffer, large folio.** *Jerome to Demetrias: How a Virgin Ought to Conduct Herself*, in the *Epistles and Treatises of Jerome*, Epistle 196, or 26, in distinction 12.

**1516. Basel, Froben, folio.** *Letter to the Virgin Demetrias on Virginity*, in volume II of Erasmus’s edition of Jerome’s works, folios 4b–12b.

Erasmus’s judgment is as follows:

“An altogether learned and eloquent letter, but which, even without anything else, is plainly shown by its style not to be Jerome’s. Moreover, it is not credible that Jerome wrote twice to the same virgin about the same matters. Saint Augustine seems to suspect that it was composed by a heretical Pelagian, because it contains certain things that savor of the Pelagian doctrines, especially since Pelagius himself testifies in a certain letter that he wrote to Demetrias. Bede thinks it belongs to the heretic Julian. The error in the subscription arose from the fact that Jerome too wrote to this virgin on a similar subject.”

**1579. Antwerp, Christopher Plantin, folio.** *Epistle to the Virgin Demetrias*, in volume IX of the works of Jerome edited by Marianus Victorius, pages 1–12; in the Paris edition of 1643, the same place, pages 1–10.

**1684. Frankfurt and Leipzig, folio.** The same work, in volume IV of Jerome’s works, pages 12–21.

**1706. Paris, folio.** The same work, among the works of Jerome edited by Martianay, volume V, pages 11–30. Erasmus’s judgment is prefixed. The editors note that in some manuscript codices it is attributed to Coelestius and in others to Julian.

[Col. 1161A]

**1742. Verona, folio.** *Pelagius’s Letter to Demetrias*, in volume XI, part II, of Vallarsi’s edition of Jerome’s works, pages 1–26.

The editor observes that Bede’s suspicion, by which he attributes it to Julian, is founded on certain manuscript codices, one of them an older codex from the Library of Saint Victor, which he cites as attributing it to Julian. In the Venetian reprint of 1771, quarto, it is found in the same volume and part, pages 2–35.

**1775. Halle in Magdeburg, at the expense of Carl Hermann Hemmerde, octavo.** *The Letter of Pelagius the Holy and Learned Monk to Demetrias, with Various Letters of Other Writers.* Daniel Whitby, S.T.P., *Treatise on the Divine Imputation of Adam’s Sin to All His Posterity as Guilt*. Edited and supplied with notes by D. Johann Salomo Semler.

In this volume, besides the works named in the title, are included Augustine and Alypius’s letter to Julian, Demetrias’s mother; Jerome’s letter to Demetrias on preserving virginity; excerpts from the sacramentary of Leo the Great on the consecration of virgins; the letter to the matron Celantia on the manner of living piously, which, as we have already noted above, the editor was the first to claim for Pelagius; and finally excerpts from Augustine’s book *On the Grace of Christ Against Pelagius and Coelestius* that relate to Pelagius’s letter to Demetrias.

[Note: [Col. 1161D] Concerning the lengthy dissertation—or rather panegyric—which Schoenemann wove into this edition of Semler’s with an entirely heretical pen, it seemed worthwhile to transcribe the following lines [Col. 1162D], after reading which a Catholic may immediately form a judgment about Semler’s edition. EDITOR.]

By associating these little works and illuminating them through notes scattered with no sparing hand, the editor exerted every effort of which he was capable to make the odium with which Augustine had enveloped Pelagius rebound upon Augustine himself.

And indeed, since Semler believed that he had derived no small benefit from the study of his discipline—namely, that he had learned that the sum of Christian doctrine consists not so much in some system or in preserving the formulas of teachers as in shaping the mind toward the true worship of the Godhead in accordance with Christ’s clear commandments, a point which he repeats and presses on every occasion in his writings—he could not help becoming hostile not only to the African Fathers generally but especially to Augustine. For he knew that through their diligence, machinations, and writings it had been brought about above all that minds were led away from the true sense of Christian discipline toward empty or even frivolous little questions.

## III. The Booklet of Faith addressed to Innocent

There are two versions of this booklet. One, found among Jerome’s works, is complete and genuine, but bears the title *Explanation of the Faith addressed to Damasus*. The other has been inserted among Augustine’s *Sermons for the Liturgical Year*. It is preceded by a little preface presented as Augustine’s, has been interpolated, and has been adapted to the form of a popular sermon.

The former is also found under Jerome’s name in Charlemagne’s books *On Images* and in Baronius’s *Annals* under the year 417. It was copied from a Vatican codex containing various letters of Pope Zosimus and restored to its proper author. From the fact that it is cited in that volume of Charlemagne, it seems possible to infer that this opinion had already become widespread before that time.

This is further supported by the authority of a manuscript codex written when Charlemagne was already king but not yet emperor, which Launoius had received from Jacob Sirmond for inspection. Launoius nevertheless thought that it did not belong to that period but had been written by a more recent hand.

Vallarsi also notes that in an old Coislinian manuscript it is entitled:

“Creed of the Faith composed by blessed Jerome and sent by him to holy Pope Damasus.”

Launoius, however, maintains the contrary opinion in a special dissertation on this creed, to be cited more fully shortly, on arguments that are by no means slight: namely, the silence of the Council of Frankfurt in 797, which acted in the case of Elipandus, bishop of Toledo, and in defense of the Catholic tradition of the faith against heretics; the silence of Charlemagne himself and of Alcuin in their seven books against Felix, bishop of Urgell, and their four books against Elipandus; and further the silence of Agobard of Lyon, Felix’s adversary, and of Hincmar, Agobard’s contemporary.

As for the codices, we have already said that the Sirmond codex shows signs of a more recent hand. Launoius adds that the copyist and compiler of the codex could have left traces of his writing impressed by the script of Charlemagne’s reign, even if he was not contemporary with that reign. Or he could have gathered several documents into his codex after Charlemagne, one of which belonged to the time of King Charles. It does not follow from this, however, that the other documents were first written at the same time.

Indeed, Launoius concludes that this profession of faith could have been inserted into the books *On Images* after Charlemagne by the person who copied the books and was distressed that they lacked this support and defense. Having established his position, he nevertheless concedes that the event took place not long after the age of Charlemagne.

He adduces the testimony of Remigius, bishop of Lyon, who lived in the middle of the ninth century. In his *Book on Three Letters*, chapter 39, Remigius either from a codex or as the first himself calls this faith Jerome’s.

Immediately after him, in the twelfth century, come Gratian and the Master of the Sentences, and later Thomas, Bonaventure, and the remaining scholastics, all holding the same opinion.

As for Augustine, Launoius likewise demonstrates that this error did not arise in the age of Charlemagne, but shows that the first to cite a testimony from this profession of faith under Augustine’s name was William of Paris, a writer of the thirteenth century. In chapter 10 of his book *On Sins and Vices*, William either mistakenly took Augustine for Jerome, since at that time everyone, following the authority of the Master and Gratian, attributed the profession of faith to Jerome; or he drew it from some codex of Augustine’s sermons into which this profession of faith had already been inserted together with the opening of a sermon.

“After William,” says Launoius, “others followed. Since they were occupied with other matters, they did not investigate the sermons of Augustine as they had been committed to print; instead, abandoning the effort to examine them in detail, they were content with indices and seized whatever served their causes and treatises.”

Here we may also insert Launoius’s brief discussion of the way and means by which this profession of faith came to be attributed both to Jerome and to Augustine. He admits that the matter is extremely difficult to know and must be left to the conjectures of each person:

“These possibilities appear more readily in the case of Jerome than in that of Augustine. There are three possible explanations.

“First, if it was discovered as ἀδέσποτος—that is, without an author—then some reasonably learned copyist, observing that the errors of Jovinian, which Jerome had refuted, were condemned in it, and perceiving that the writing was suitable and agreed with Jerome’s views, did not hesitate to attribute the work to him.

“Second, if the profession was found with Pelagius’s title and inscription, then some reasonably pious copyist regretted that what seemed to him an excellent work bore Pelagius’s name, an odious name. He removed it and substituted another, honorable name for the reasons mentioned.

“Finally, if an ἀνεπίγραφος confession—that is, one without a title—was inserted into a codex in which Jerome’s other works were found, then from that binding together of the codex it received Jerome’s name among unwary posterity. The same thing has often happened to other Fathers.

“As for Augustine, the matter was handled somewhat more difficultly and less skillfully. More difficultly, because a sermon-like opening had to be prefixed to the profession of faith, so that what was in reality a booklet of faith, not a sermon, might appear to be a sermon. Less skillfully, because blessed Augustine generally and indirectly rejected the booklet of faith. Indeed, what it says about free will, flexible and changeable in either direction, does not entirely agree with the later doctrines of blessed Augustine.”

Thus far Launoius.

It remains now to review briefly, but in our customary manner, the editions that this booklet has received since the invention of printing.

[Col. 1163A]

## Fifteenth century

**1467. Rome, Ulrich Gallus, folio.** *Explanation of the Faith of Blessed Jerome the Presbyter to Pope Damasus*, in which he condemns many heresies about the Trinity and the Incarnation, condemning those who hold impious opinions and asking Damasus to approve his faith. It appears among Jerome’s *Epistles or Little Works*, published without indication of place or year, but probably printed by the same printer whom we cited above, in the same place and year, part I, treatise 1, Epistle 2.

A Basel reprint of 1489 is available to us, where it appears on folio VIII. The Nuremberg edition of 1495 follows this edition; but in the Basel edition of 1497 and the Lyon edition of 1513, this *Explanation* is absent. The Roman editions of Schweinheim and Pannartz are unavailable.

**1470. Mainz, Peter Schoeffer, folio.** *Jerome Explaining His Faith to Damasus, Either for Approval or Correction*, among Jerome’s *Epistles*, in the edition cited above, distinction 2, Epistle 4.

**Without year or place, folio.** *Explanation of the Faith of Saint Jerome to Damasus*, among Jerome’s *Epistles and Treatises*, in an anonymous edition that appears nearly contemporary with the preceding age. Epistle 15.

**1494. Basel, Johann Amerbach, folio.** *Augustine’s Sermon on the Holy Trinity*, among the *Sermons for the Liturgical Year*, first published in this form and place together with various other collections, Sermon 191.

The same collection was inserted into the complete Erasmian edition of Augustine’s works in 1542, volume X, pages 1018–1020; in the Leuven edition printed at Paris in 1586, volume X, pages 347–348; in the Benedictine edition it was rejected into the Appendix to volume V, number 236, *On the Faith of Catholics*, IV according to the Antwerp description, pages 274–276.

## Sixteenth century

**1516. Basel, Froben, folio.** *Explanation of the Creed addressed to Damasus*, in Erasmus’s edition of Jerome’s works, volume II, folio 56b.

Erasmus judges that none whatsoever of all the writings found among Jerome’s letters belongs to this creed, but he makes no further determination about it.

**1549. [Paris], duodecimo.** *Confession of the Catholic Faith—which We Have Received from the Holy Fathers and Believe with a Devout Heart—Expressed in the Words of Blessed Jerome*, in Charlemagne’s work *On Images*, book III, chapter 1.

The first edition of this work was made in this year, with the place concealed, by John Tilius, bishop of Meaux, under the likewise assumed name Eliphilus. In it this confession appears on pages 291–297. More than one reprint was subsequently prepared by Melchior Goldast and Philip Pareus. The latest is that of Christian August Heumann, Hanover, 1731, octavo, where this booklet appears on pages 259–264. Yet, strangely, the editor did not say even a word about it.

**15—. Rome, folio.** *Explanation of the Creed addressed to Damasus*, in the works of Jerome edited by Marianus Victorius, volume IX, Epistle 17; in the Paris copies of 1643, page 60.

1592. Rome, folio. *Pelagius’s Booklet of Faith*, sent with a letter to Innocent [Col. 1163D], in Caesar Baronius’s [Col. 1164A] *Annals*, under the year 417, Zosimus I; in the Mansian edition (Lucca, 1741), volume VII, nos. 31–36, pp. 100–101.

## SEVENTEENTH CENTURY

1663. Paris . . . in octavo. John Launoius of Coutances, a Parisian theologian, *Dissertation on the True Author of the Profession of Faith Commonly Attributed to Pelagius, Jerome, and Augustine*. In the Cologne edition of his works, 1731, it appears in volume II, part II, pp. 305–324.

1673. Paris, at the press of Sebastian Marbre-Cramoisy, folio. *The Confession, or Booklet, of Faith Sent by Pelagius from the East to the Apostolic See*, in the dissertations of John Garnerius on the works of Marius Mercator, dissertation 5, which concerns the *Booklets of Faith Published by the Pelagians*, pp. 307–309.

Garnerius used, in presenting this booklet, a copy of the ancient manuscript of P. Sirmondus, undoubtedly the same manuscript which Launoius had received on loan from Sirmondus. Garnerius himself, as he states, was about to publish a copy written in his own hand [Col. 1164B], had Baronius not anticipated him. The editor nevertheless promises that his recension is somewhat more correct than Baronius’s reading. He divided it into three parts, calling the first theological, the second economic, and the third ethical; in addition, he distinguished twenty-six sections by numerals. He then compared it, on pp. 309–311, with the creed of Coelestius, which he likewise thought he had published in full. He also added notes in which he sought to disclose both the manifest and the hidden meaning of each part.

## EIGHTEENTH CENTURY

1705. London, printed by I. Downing for R. Sympson, etc., in octavo. *Pelagius’s Creed Sent with a Letter* (*fragmenta litterarum*) to Pope Innocent; but, finding him dead, translated and illustrated by W. Wall, vicar at Shoreham in Kent, in his *History of Infant Baptism*, part I, chapter 19, §§ 29 and 30, pp. 249–263. This distinguished work was subsequently made better known in Germany [Col. 1164C], where Johann Ludwig Schlosser rendered it into Latin and had it printed in two volumes, likewise quarto, at Bremen in 1748. In the first of these, pp. 372–391, the text of this creed is presented with an English translation, Wall’s notes immediately following the Latin text, and Schlosser’s remarks placed at the bottom margin.

1706. Paris, at the press of Louis Roulland, folio. *Exposition of the Creed to Damasus*, in volume V of Jerome’s works, edited by Martianaeus, p. 122 ff. Martianaeus did not think it worthwhile to warn the reader about the author of this creed; indeed, he merely repeated Erasmus’s criticism, which Erasmus had prefixed to this and the other creeds found among Jerome’s works.

1742. Verona, folio. *Exposition of the Creed to Damasus*, in the Vallarsian edition of the works, volume XI, part II, pp. 146–150; in the Venetian edition (1771), in the same place, pp. 202–205. A suitable and appropriate notice has been prefixed.

# SURVEY OF JULIAN’S WORKS AND EDITIONS, BY SCHOENEMANN

(*Historical-Literary Library of the Latin Fathers*.)

## § 1. WRITINGS

[Col. 1167A]

Of all the writings certainly known to have been Julian’s, none has come down to us intact; only fragments, not especially mutilated but scarce and scattered, have been transmitted. Others have perished entirely. The following, however, are genuine works whose fragments, or at least traces, remain.

1. **First Letter to Zosimus**, of which only Mercator makes mention and whose words he inserted in book 6 and 9 of the *Subnotations*; Julian nevertheless acknowledged it as his own [Note: [Col. 1167B] Cave gives this less accurately (*vol.* I, p. 407 of the new Oxford edition), mentioning two letters of Julian to Zosimus, which Augustine refuted in four books addressed to Boniface; and then adding: “One of these was written in the name of eighteen Sicilian bishops and is entitled *Booklet of Faith*.” On the contrary, the letter which Augustine refutes in the first book was not Julian’s; and if the *Booklet of Faith* had been one of those which Augustine refutes there, Garnerius would not have spent so much futile effort asserting that it was Julian’s, since the matter could easily have been settled by comparing the passages with one another.] Garnerius assembled it at the end of his fifth dissertation on Marius Mercator, volume I, pp. 333 ff.; it should also be compared with his notes on the cited passages of the *Subnotations*. In his view, it was written in the autumn of approximately 417.

2. **A Letter Shared by Him with Many Other Pelagian Bishops—Eighteen in Number—which They Sent to Thessalonica, to Bishop Rufus.** Augustine identifies as this letter the one which he attempted to refute in his single work of four books addressed to Boniface, bishop of Rome. Fragments of it are also found in the three later books; Garnerius collected them in the same place as the preceding material [Col. 1167B] and arranged them according to their original form.

3. **Four Books to Bishop Turbantius, Against Augustine’s First Book on Concupiscence.** They were written at the beginning of 419, or toward the end of the preceding year. Fragments survive in three of Augustine’s works: book II *On Marriage*, the six books *Against Julian*, and the *Unfinished Work*. Considerable portions come from the first book, with only small portions from the other two. Augustine first refuted it in his own book II *On Marriage*, reproducing verbatim everything contained in a document excerpted from this first book and presented to Count Valerius, who sent it to Augustine through Alypius. From this document we also know the title of the books: *Against Those Who Condemn Marriage and Assign Its Fruits to the Devil*. The four later books of the six *Against Julian* contend with Julian’s four books in such a way that not only do book and book correspond, but chapters also correspond to chapters. (Garnerius, Appendix to dissertation 6 on writings in defense of the Pelagian heresy, p. 388.) He discusses their history in dissertation 6 itself, p. 349.

4. **A Book on the Good of Constancy, Against the Perfidiousness of Mani**, some fragments of which Bede preserved. According to Garnerius, it was written after Julian’s expulsion from his see.

5. **Eight Books to Florus of Benevento, Bishop, Against Augustine’s Second Book on Marriage and Concupiscence.** Garnerius argues that they were written in Cilicia but not published until about 426, when he supposes Julian to have fled from Italy to Constantinople for a second time. The first five books, or even six of them, are preserved complete in Augustine’s *Unfinished Work against Julian’s Second Reply*. The number of surviving books, however, depends on the actual form of Augustine’s work; Garnerius has very effectively refuted Vigner’s view on this matter in his notes to Mercator’s *Subnotations*, works, volume I, pp. 34 ff.

6. **A Book on Love, or Commentary on the Song of Songs.** Only Bede mentions this work, stating that it comprised two books, one *On Love* and the other a *Commentary*. He also adds that it was written on the occasion of Julian’s contest with Augustine. Since neither Augustine nor those who were with him mention it, [Col. 1169A] it may be inferred that it was later than the eight books to Florus, in refuting which Augustine spent the remainder of his life. Garnerius considers it later because it appears to have been composed wholly in imitation of Theodore of Mopsuestia, who wrote amorously on the Song of Songs. Several fragments collected from Bede may be found in Garnerius, Appendix to dissertation 6, works, volume I, pp. 388 ff.

The following works are doubtful or have been entirely and falsely attributed to Julian: **Pelagius’s Letter to Demetrias**, which, owing its attribution to widely differing authors chiefly in part to ignorance and in part to human ingenuity, could not escape being attributed to him. Augustine, moreover, in book I of his work *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians, Addressed to Boniface*, undertook to refute as Julian’s a letter sent to Rome, which Julian nevertheless denied to be his in these words:

“Augustine also mentions a letter which he says was sent by me to Rome; but we were unable to recognize from the words he quoted what writing he meant. For I sent two letters to Zosimus, formerly bishop of that city, on these questions; but I sent them at a time when I had not yet begun the books [against Augustine’s first book on marriage and concupiscence]” [Note: [Col. 1169D] In Augustine, book I of the *Unfinished Work*, chapter 17.—Augustine replied: “This letter is not to Zosimus, but to deceive those who in Rome might be deceived by such persuasion,” etc. Garnerius, in his edition of Mercator’s works, volume I, p. 317, assigns it to Coelestius.].

Since fragments of one letter survive, it is clear that the other has completely perished. Garnerius, however, takes a different position. He maintains that the other letter to Zosimus was written in the name of eighteen bishops who refused to subscribe to Zosimus’s *Tractoria* and that, when a *Booklet of Faith* of certain bishops addressed to their metropolitan Augustine came, perhaps by chance, into his hands—a booklet in which they deny that their faith permitted them to subscribe, as ordered, to the condemnation of the Pelagians—this very booklet was the genuine letter. He supports this claim by heaping assertion upon assertion concerning Julian, without proving them.

To leave aside the other matters rightly and deservedly disputed against him by men of the most exact learning and soundest judgment—Noris [Note: [Col. 1169D] In the *Censure of Garnerius*, volume IV of the works collected by the Ballerini. The conjecture is due to him that the letter was written by bishops of the diocese of Aquileia to their metropolitan Augustine, who, if the chroniclers are to be trusted, held his see for a considerable period from the year 408 onward.], Coustantius [Note: [Col. 1169D] In *Notice of Non-Extant Writers Concerning Zosimus*, no. 11, § 28, p. 1001.] and Rubaeus [Note: [Col. 1169D] In *Ecclesiastical Monuments of Aquileia*, chapter 14, p. 118, and again in the treatise *On Original Sin*, chapter 11, p. 43, where he supports Noris’s opinion at greater length. Add Walch, *History of Heresy*, volume IV, pp. 677 ff.]—the assertion itself is immediately false: namely, that one of the two letters which Julian professed to have sent to Zosimus was written not in his own name alone but in the name of the eighteen bishops who wrote to Rufus of Thessalonica. This, indeed, gave him the occasion for his invention.

In his survey of Julian’s writings he confidently asserts that Mercator mentions this booklet (volume I, p. 388); but one should not expect him to indicate the passage, and, if pressed, he will admit—in the notes to the booklet, volume I of Mercator’s works, p. 327—that Mercator testified only concerning one letter, the one mentioned above under no. 1.

Garnerius was not content to make Julian richer by one book; this opinionated man also used this questionable profession of faith to acquire another work for him. There exists, namely, a Greek *Book of Faith*, apparently belonging to some Greek author and translated into Latin by an unknown person. It was first published from the manuscripts of Corbie and Saint-Germain-des-Prés by Jacques Sirmondus, who preferred to leave the question of its author undecided rather than make a false conjecture. Garnerius, however, thought that he had discovered not only its author but also its translator: the former, Rufinus the Syrian, or a priest of Palestine, whom Mercator called the teacher of Pelagius and Coelestius; the latter, Julian. His principal reason was that nearly entire pages from the latter work are found transcribed in the *Booklet of Faith* which he had just assigned to Julian. From this he concluded that Julian had profited so extensively from Rufinus’s book that he intended his own *Booklet of Faith* to be almost a compendium of it [Note: [Col. 1169D] If you wish to know more of his ingenuity, see what he elicits from Gennadius concerning the date of this translation [Col. 1170D]: “Not without reason,” he says, “Gennadius writes of Julian: ‘BEFORE THE HERESY OF PELAGIUS REVEALED ITSELF IN HIM.’ For he indicated that, before the heresy of Pelagius openly emerged, Julian had revealed it in another person—namely Rufinus, whose confession he had provided for the Latins to read. Two conclusions follow from this: first, that Julian produced such a translation when he was still quite young; second, that the Pelagians initially presented that portion of their error concerning original sin as the faith of the Easterners. I infer a third: that Julian was converted from married life to a stricter way of living by Pelagius’s exhortations, and and that, when Memorius, Julian’s father, was writing, Augustine learned of Pelagius’s praises and later recounted them in his books.”—Let the learned reader judge between Schoenemann and Garnerius. EDIT.].

## § 2. EDITIONS

1668. Paris, at the press of Sebastian Marbre-Cramoisy, royal printer, Jacob’s Street, “under the Storks,” in octavo. *The Booklet of Faith of Julian, Bishop of Eclanum, Sent to the Apostolic See in the Pelagian Controversy.* Now published for the first time from a Veronese manuscript, with notes and three historical dissertations, by John Garnerius, priest of the Society of Jesus.

Garnerius himself gives the following noteworthy account of the circumstances of this edition:

“Father Jacques Sirmondus copied this from a Veronese manuscript with his own hand while he was in Italy, showed it to me at some point, and, congratulating me, gave me an offhand conjecture about its author and date, for me to elucidate with notes and commit to print.”

It is therefore not surprising that he cherished his offhand conjecture, approved by Sirmondus, so greatly that he wanted everyone to be convinced that nothing could harm it and everything could support it. Yet in the manuscript from which Sirmondus extracted the booklet, nothing appeared in place of the title except certain outlines of fading letters, which he represented as **IVLI**. The Benedictines, however, and with them Rubaeus, think that they should be read as **INLI**: “The Booklet begins,” so that the beginning corresponds to the ending, “Thus ends the Booklet of Faith, SIC.” Garnerius accordingly interprets the latter letters, in a way suited to his conjecture, as **Siculorum** (“of the Sicilian [bishops]”); the Benedictines, more correctly, as **Sacerdotum Jesu Christi** (“of the priests of Jesus Christ”).

The *Booklet of Faith* is divided into four parts, followed by Dissertation I, on the date and author of the booklet; Dissertation II, on Julian’s life and character; Dissertation III, on the subscriptions in the Pelagian controversy; and, fourth, fuller notes on the booklet. For purposes of comparison and illustration, these notes are preceded by:

1. *The Booklet of Faith Sent by Pelagius from the East to Rome, to Pope Innocent*;
2. *Fragments of the Booklet of Faith Written by Coelestius*;
3. *Extracts from Coelestius’s Letter to the Roman Clergy*—the letter which Augustine had thought to be Julian’s—together with observations concerning its date, author, and other matters;
4. *The Creed of Theodore of Mopsuestia*, translated by Marius Mercator.

An appendix is also added on Anianus, translator of the homilies of Saint Chrysostom and abridger of the Theodosian Code. All these matters, together with many others relating to the history of the Pelagian heresy, were treated and published at greater length with the works of Marius Mercator.

Garnerius had at one time intended to publish these materials together with this *Booklet of Faith* in a separate volume, had Mercator himself, impatient of further delay, not compelled him to change his plan. Even so, he could not entirely restrain himself from offering the reader at least something from the larger collection for his enjoyment. This booklet was later reprinted, together with the investigation of its date and author and observations on it, in dissertation 6 on the works of Mercator (Paris, 1673), volume I, pp. 320–335, with certain genuine fragments of Julian added at the end, as indicated above. There, too, the dissertation on Julian’s life forms chapter 6 of Dissertation I, *On the Wicked Authors and Defenders of the Pelagian Heresy*, p. 144 ff.; his writings are discussed in chapter 4, Appendix to Dissertation 6, p. 387 ff. Finally, the dissertation on the subscriptions in the Pelagian controversy occupies the fourth place among the dissertations on Mercator, pp. 263–282.

We should also note this, lest anyone be deceived: copies of the separately issued edition exist bearing the year 1673 on the title page. The title also differs slightly from the earlier one, not in wording but in form and appearance—it lacks the printer’s emblem of the Storks—yet the work itself is included without any alteration. This was evidently arranged by a bookseller to attract purchasers, since he perhaps feared that buyers would abandon him for Mercator after the latter had been published from his own shop.

The Benedictine monks again transcribed only the text of this booklet, adding their conjecture mentioned above, in the Appendix to volume X, part II, of Augustine’s works, Antwerp edition, p. 74 ff.
