# SELECTED VARIANT READINGS IN RUFINUS’S ECCLESIASTICAL HISTORY, FROM THE MANUSCRIPT OF THE CHAPTERHOUSE ARCHIVE OF FRÉJUS

[Note: [Col. 1175] We wish to inform the reader that, in this index of variants, we have followed the numerical division of our verses and columns. EDIT.]

[Col. 1175] A manuscript adds the following to the short preface from Rufinus, column 463: “These matters also are contained in book X of the *Ecclesiastical History*.”

In the table of contents at column 465, chapter XIX, the manuscript has “to Father Constantine” instead of “to Brother Constantius.” In the following chapter it omits this entire passage concerning Lucifer and the other Catholic bishops.

Book I, chapter I of the *History*, column 468, note e: the manuscript reads “believing that he was concealing himself from others,” instead of “believing, if he were concealing himself from such people.”

Chapter II, after the middle: the manuscript reads “the mutual rivalry of the priests” instead of “the pretence,” etc.; this also appears more correct, although less Latin, if it is understood as “rivalry.” Immediately afterward it has “several” instead of “more.”

Chapter III, column 469, note c: the manuscript reads “by saying” instead of “of saying.”

Chapter IV, beginning: the manuscript has “Maximinus” instead of “Maximianus.”

Chapter V, note b: it omits the little word *in*, then, four lines after this, *vobis*, and shortly afterward, at note c, *tamen*. Column 472, line 5, the manuscript reads “he was present at the councils” instead of “at the counsels”; and at the end, “for those inventing decrees” instead of “for those fixing them.”

Chapter VI, column 473, note a: the manuscript reads “made from things that do not exist, or from another substance” instead of “from things that subsist” and “subsistence.” Immediately afterward, Canon I: “through impatience” instead of “impatience.” Canon V: “so that no one, if another bishop [is involved] …” instead of “so that no other bishop [may take] anyone”; and shortly afterward, “in each city and province.” Chapter VI: “suburban dioceses” instead of “suburbicarian dioceses.” Canon XIII: almost certainly more correctly, “they had rejected military service and again sought it” instead of “they went back to it.” Canon XIV [Col. 1176]: “as the bishop’s discretion shall have determined.” Again, more correctly, Canon XVIII: “accepting no one who belongs to another” instead of “having carried off one who had been appointed.” Compare Canon V above, from which the true reading will be clear. Canon XXI: “the Paulinianists” instead of “the Paulianists”; and at the end, “the rationale of the law” instead of “reverence.”

Chapter VIII, beginning, column 476: the manuscript reads “which may have occurred”; in the following line it omits “woman.” After the middle, column 477, it has “he would make good use of” instead of “they would make use of”; and nine lines later it omits “and more humbly.”

Chapter IX, after the middle, column 479: “they were regarded,” etc.; immediately afterward, “a little” instead of “a little one.” Line 14: “and” instead of “to which.” Line 10: it adds “they return again.”

Chapter X, line 17 from the beginning of the chapter: “if those who have tested [it] know . . . let them compare,” more correctly; and at the end of the column, “lest he presume, and seem to permit.” Column 482, line 10: “from the work itself,” and immediately afterward “mature” instead of “morning.”

Chapter XI, beginning: “he departed from this light.” Column 484, line 4: “but by these,” omitting the intervening conjunction *and*.

Chapter XIII, column 486, line 14: “in perfidy.”

Chapter XIV, column 487, line 7: “the multitude of boys above the edge,” etc.

Chapter XVI, penultimate line of column 488: “the horror of envy.”

Chapter XVII, column 489, line 8: “they had left behind” instead of “they retained”; immediately afterward, “struck” instead of “drove.” Column 490, line 14: “Behold” instead of “This is”; and “to deceive” instead of “to be deceived.”

Chapter XIX, column 492, line 24: “you may grant.”

Chapter XX, toward the end: “to be abandoned” instead of “to be destroyed.”

[Col. 1177] Chapter XXIII, beginning: “Maximinus” instead of “Maximus.”

Chapter XXV, line 16 from the beginning: “leprous in mind”; immediately afterward, “to the pursuers” instead of “to the followers.”

Chapter XXVII, after the beginning: “with Constantius restraining him while alive.” One of these two readings is a gloss on the other, and the former should be preferred to “while he connived.” Toward the end: “if such a person is there”; immediately afterward, “backward” (apparently) instead of “too hasty.”

Chapter XXVIII, at the end: “the amount of the mark” (*notae*) instead of “the amount of the harm.”

Chapter XXIX, middle: “And since we do not speak of two substances in God, neither ought we to speak of three subsistences.”

Chapter XXX, after the beginning: the manuscript omits *Eusebio* at the first occurrence.

Chapter XXXI, middle: “he explained more carefully.”

Chapter XXXV, line 10 from the beginning: “mothers and young men, and virgins innumerable,” etc.—quite sound, and more correct.

Chapter XXXVI, near the beginning: “at the eleventh hour” instead of “the tenth.”

## BOOK II

Chapter I, line 5 from the beginning: “and our leaders”; immediately afterward, “they should give” instead of “they gave.” Ten lines after this it omits *ei*. At the end of the chapter it has “he received,” followed by “nine months” instead of “eight,” but this is erroneous. See our discussion there.

Chapter II, line 2: “concerning military service.”

Chapter III, ten lines from the end: it omits the conjunction *and*; it then reads “three thousand and more,” likewise omitting *simul*.

Chapter IV, line 1: “life”; and column 512, line 13: “who had led themselves away.” Column 513, note d: it omits “on that very day,” which I also consider more correct.

Chapter V, line 3: it omits *per se*.

Chapter VI, note j: “Lucius—all,” etc.

Chapter VII, line 2: “of the misty leader.” And at column 517, line 5: “we read, ‘they have been described.’”

Chapter VIII, at note e: “Apeteliote” instead of “Apeliote.”

Chapter IX, line 2: it omits *nobis*; afterward it adds “also the Lord’s planting of olives,” etc. Column 518, line 20: it omits *propria*; line 38: “and whatever pertains to food,” etc. Column 519, at note e: “to spend” instead of “to be spent.”

Chapter XI, note g: “then the consular officials”; toward the end, “he may recall” instead of “he might recall.”

Chapter XII, final line: “while he governs the kingdom” instead of “the matter,” etc.

[Col. 1178] Chapter XV, line 6: “faithfully” instead of the uncertain reading *fiaenter*.

Chapter XVI, line 1: “the dictated [words].” Line 4: “he denies that he can utter the words of the impious,” etc. Shortly before this, note h: it omits *impia*. Eight lines from the end, it reads:

“Maximus, who wished to show himself a lawful prince, free from the tyrant’s old infamy.”

This is altogether more correct, except that the word *exuetere* may be misleading; divide it into two words, deriving it from *ex vetere*. I would therefore restore the passage in this form. Compare the preceding chapter, XIV.

Chapter XX, middle: it omits the two words *verti vel*, which makes the passage somewhat more elegant.

Chapter XXII, column 529, line 3 after note b: “they report the deeds to the Emperor.”

Chapter XXIII, lines 6 and 7: “all the things that were raised to the highest parts of the pavements”; immediately afterward, “when they had been let in” instead of “immense.” Column 530, after the middle: “with the temple doors barred” instead of “when the times had been observed.” In the same place, eleven lines from the end, it omits *radio*. Column 531, beginning: “by the Gentiles themselves” instead of “by the Gentiles”; and column 533, line 4: “and Soron Apis, first from the composition, but afterward through,” etc.

Chapter XXV, line 7: it adds “worthy of the godhead’s favor”; and at note g, “was creeping in” instead of “was escaping.” Near the end of the chapter: “and by other frauds” instead of “and by blind ones,” etc.; immediately afterward, altogether more correctly, “from uncertain fathers” instead of “from incestuous [fathers].” I would likewise restore this in our edition.

Chapter XXVI, near the end: “but they will have done” instead of “but they will have advanced.”

Chapter XXVII, column 536, lines 1–2: again, most correctly, “temples of the true God, and churches built.” In accordance with this reading, I would restore the passage in our edition and delete the word “lofty,” which we took from the Barraean copy.

Chapter XXIX, line 12: “commended” instead of “commended [feminine].”

Chapter XXX, at the end: “to you, a great calamity” instead of “a great [feminine] calamity,” etc.

Chapter XXXIII, line 11 from the beginning: “Eugenius was to follow” instead of “Eugenius was safe,” etc.; and line 16, more correctly, “they had presumed,” plural. Immediately afterward, “to that first one” instead of “of the first,” etc. In the same place, before note e, somewhat better: “turned toward customary practices” instead of “toward solid things,” etc.; and three lines after this, “those just battles,” etc., with the intervening little words also omitted, as I think.

**THE BOOK OF ECCLESIASTICAL HISTORY ENDS SUCCESSFULLY.**

[Col. 1177]

God’s assumption of humanity is the Word made flesh. 17 and following. What it means to sustain God. 109. Who are called those who wait for the Lord. 165.

What it means to store up treasures in heaven. 180. Where the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden. 495. The throne of God is the Son of the Father. 47. One who fears God is neither lifted up in prosperity nor broken in adversity. 69. The fruits of those who fear the Lord. 149. What true fear of the Lord is like. 9 and following. What the fear of God ought to be like. 130. The fear of God is a bridle against sin. 159. The fruits and effects of the fear of God. 109. The difference between fear and trembling. 269. What the “shearer of the flock” means. 543. What “to pass on foot” means. 321. Why the tribe of Benjamin was almost destroyed. 447. Tribulation is useful to God’s servants, and why. 71. Tribulation is medicine leading to salvation for those who fear God. 95. The usefulness of tribulation in this age. 90. What it means to find tribulation and to be found by tribulation. 227. The inhabitants of Samaria worshiped the cows of Beth-aven. 451. *Vadent* is used for *ibant* (“they were going”). 426. By the term “valley” the people are signified. 413. ## RUFINUS OF AQUILEIA, PRESBYTER

Notice concerning Rufinus. Col. 9

## LIFE OF RUFINUS, BOOK I

75

### CHAPTER I

I. Rufinus’s origin and the spelling of his name. II. His homeland. III. He was born at Concordia: his forename and family. IV. He became a monk at Aquileia. V. Together with Jerome he was educated there in the liberal arts and was baptized as an adult. The minister and sponsors of his baptism. VI. Jerome separated from him and sailed to Syria. VII. Shortly afterward Rufinus left Rome with Melania, intending to go to Jerusalem. Ibid.

### CHAPTER II

I. News of Rufinus and Melania’s arrival in Alexandria reaches Jerome in the Syrian desert. II. After the death of Athanasius, Rufinus fled to Nitria when persecution was stirred up against Catholics. III. He suffered for the faith. IV. Melania followed the confessors of Christ. V. After they were recalled from exile, he went from Diocaesarea to Jerusalem. VI. Rufinus spent six years in Alexandria, where he heard Didymus and Theophilus. VII. He went to Jerusalem; from there Melania made a journey to Alexandria. VIII. Rufinus exercised himself in works of charity. IX. He heard from Bacurius, king of the Iberians, and from Aedesius, of the Ethiopians, about the conversion of peoples to the faith of Christ. X. Rufinus’s account is explained and defended. 86

### CHAPTER III

I. The origin of the quarrels between Jerome and Rufinus. II. Jerome sided with Epiphanius against John of Jerusalem, while Rufinus adhered to John. III. Rufinus was admitted by Epiphanius at Jerusalem into communion and was regarded as a Catholic. IV. The occasion of the dissension between Jerome and Rufinus was increased by Epiphanius’s letter to John, written in Greek, which Jerome translated into Latin. V. Melania defended the cause of Rufinus and John. VI. Theophilus of Alexandria likewise favored them. VII. He tried in vain to reconcile the dissidents. VIII. From this point the friendship between Jerome and Theophilus grew cold. 97

### CHAPTER IV

I. The end of the Jerusalem schism. II. It was brought to an end through the efforts of Rufinus and Melania. III. The historian Palladius, a highly esteemed bishop, was wrongly confused with the heretic Palladius. IV. The Church of the Anastasis, where Jerome and Rufinus returned to mutual peace. V. Rufinus was found guilty of no error. VI. The perfect relationship between John of Jerusalem, free from errors, and Jerome was restored. [Col. 1212] VII. Rufinus returned to Rome with Melania. VIII. The true reason for Melania’s return is investigated. 104

### CHAPTER V

I. Rufinus and Melania’s arrival at Nola. II. The time at which it occurred. III. The chronology of Paulinus of Nola’s letters is restored, by which the dates of Rufinus and Melania’s departure and return are confirmed. IV. Palladius was reconciled with Paulinus. V. The chronology of Paulinus’s *Natalia* is restored, and the date of Melania and Rufinus’s return is again confirmed. VI. Baronius’s opinion concerning Rufinus as Melania’s inseparable companion is defended. 109

## LIFE OF RUFINUS, BOOK II

115

### CHAPTER I

I. Macarius asks Rufinus to explain to him Origen’s teaching against fate. II. Macarius’s profession and studies. III. Where the monastery of Pineta stood, in which Rufinus rendered the Rule of Basil the Great into Latin for Abbot Urseius. IV. Various matters concerning this Rule are presented. V. Rufinus dedicates the first book of St. Pamphilus’s *Apology for Origen* to Macarius. VI. An examination of the same *Apology*. VII. Rufinus’s dissertation for Origen. 115

### CHAPTER II

I. Rufinus translated into Latin the first two books of Origen’s *On First Principles*. II. An overview of the same translation. III. The conception of the entire work. IV. He explains the blessings of the Patriarchs in two books for Pontius Paulinus. V. The exchange of letters between Rufinus and Paulinus concerning this subject. VI. Editions and manuscripts of the books on the blessings of the Patriarchs. VII. Rufinus completed the translation of Origen’s third and fourth books of *On First Principles*. 124

### CHAPTER III

I. New rumors are stirred up against Rufinus by Jerome’s friends because of his translation of the remainder of Origen’s work. II. After the death of his mother, Rufinus writes to Jerome and, with an official letter of Pope Siricius, returns from Rome to his homeland, Concordia. III. He passes through Milan for no other reason than the journey itself. IV. Jerome writes letters to him while he is staying in his homeland, but they are not delivered to him. In what year Eusebius, a Paulinian, and another Rufinus traveled from Palestine to Rome. V. Jerome writes another letter to Pammachius against Rufinus’s preface to the books of *Periarchon*. From this the quarrel between the two increases. VI. Rufinus the Syrian brought both of Jerome’s letters to Rome, to be delivered to Pammachius and Rufinus. VII. The first of these letters is reviewed in summary. 133

### CHAPTER IV

I. Apronianus sends Rufinus a copy of Jerome’s letter that had been circulated publicly. Various matters concerning Apronianus and his family are presented. II. Rufinus’s *Apology* against Jerome’s letter. III. A summary of Book I of the same *Apology*, containing doctrinal objections. IV. Rufinus demonstrates at length that he is entirely Catholic and free from the heresies attributed to Origen. V. Book II of the *Apology* is elucidated. VI. Various criticisms of Jerome collected by Rufinus. VII. His shorter *Apology* to Anastasius. 139

### CHAPTER V

I. A summary of both of Rufinus’s *Apologies* is sent to Jerome. II. He immediately responds to both. III. The Origenist *Apology*, which Jerome denies was written by Pamphilus, is vindicated for that martyr. IV. What Pamphilus wrote. V. The conjectures advanced to deny the *Apology* to Pamphilus are examined. VI. Jerome’s response to Rufinus’s accusations. VII. Jerome’s responses to other accusations of Rufinus. VIII. Jerome’s refutation of Rufinus’s *Apology* to Pope Anastasius. 153

### CHAPTER VI

I. After the two books of Jerome’s *Apology* had been brought to Aquileia for him, Rufinus responded within two days in a letter now lost. II. He sends his own books to Jerome and attacks him sharply. III. Extracts from the same lost letter. IV. He calls into question the letters of Pope Anastasius and Saint Epiphanius and, clearing himself, strikes his opponent in various ways. V. Jerome, warned by Saint Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia, to refrain from writing against Rufinus, replies that he is compelled, against his will, to defend himself because Rufinus’s books, scattered among the public, were circulating. VI. The dates and numbering of Jerome’s *Apology*, together with his interpretations of Theophilus’s Paschal letters, are restored. VII. The judgments of M. Antonius Sabellicus concerning the disputes between Rufinus and Jerome. 169

### CHAPTER VII

I. Origen’s seventeen homilies on Genesis were translated into Latin not by Jerome but by Rufinus. II. Thirteen on Exodus and sixteen on Leviticus. III. Twenty-eight on Numbers. IV. Twenty-six on Joshua. V. Nine on Judges, the same number on the Psalms, one on the First Book of Kings, and four on the Song of Songs. VI. Ten books on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans. VII. Homilies of uncertain authorship. Those on Luke were translated not by Rufinus but by Jerome. 176–177

### CHAPTER VIII

I. Rufinus dedicates to Apronianus eight homilies of Basil the Great and ten short works of Gregory of Nazianzus translated by him into Latin. II. Several matters concerning these Gregorian works are presented. III. Rufinus sends Apronianus the sayings of Sextus the Pythagorean, translated into Latin, to be given to his sister Ayama. IV. Sextus’s age, religion, and value among the ancients. V. Rufinus was badly treated because of his translation of Sextus, though he was not then alive. VI. Why the book of Sextus was rejected by Gelasius I among the apocrypha. The opinions of various writers about it are explained. VII. Sayings of Sextus frequently cited by the Greeks, and also by the Latins. VIII. His manuscripts and editions. 188

### CHAPTER IX

I. The homeland and surname of Evagrius, whose short works Rufinus translated into Latin. II. The accusations heaped upon him. III. His praises. IV. Writings translated by Rufinus that still survive. V. The sayings of the martyr Pamphilus against the mathematicians, translated by the same man, are examined. 200

### CHAPTER X

I. Rufinus translated the Greek *Recognitions of Clement* into Latin after their translation had been unsuccessfully attempted by his friend Paulinus of Nola. II. At the request of Saint Silvia, sister of Rufinus, prefect of the praetorian prefecture, he undertook the work and dedicated it to Gaudentius, bishop of Brescia. III. Rufinus is the true author of the preface and translator of the *Recognitions*. IV. Bellarmine’s passage concerning the *Recognitions of Clement* is examined. V. Various titles of Clement’s *Recognitions* are recited. VI. The author of the *Recognitions* is investigated. VII. His date is established. VIII. Dodwell’s opinion is refuted. IX. Pope Gelasius’s judgment concerning the *Recognitions*. X. The various editions of the *Recognitions* are enumerated. 207

### CHAPTER XI

I. In obedience to Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia, Rufinus produced a Latin version of Eusebius’s history and enlarged it by two books. II. What he accomplished in the Eusebian material and what in his own additions, wrongly criticized by Dupin. III. Rufinus’s history was highly esteemed by the Gauls, and likewise by the English and African Fathers. IV. Likewise by the Greeks. V. The Greeks, translating the same two books into Greek, made them their own. VI. The Second Council of Nicaea uses their testimony. VII. The excellence of Rufinus’s Latin version of Eusebius’s history is demonstrated. VIII. Gelasius’s judgment is explained. IX. The various editions are reviewed. 222

### CHAPTER XII

I. Rufinus’s history of the hermits. II. It was once attributed to Jerome. III. Rufinus recounts another person’s, not his own, account of journeys through the monasteries and solitudes of Egypt. IV. That person is Petronius of Bologna, and no one else. V. The same is established by many arguments. VI. Difficulties concerning this matter are removed. [Col. 1214] VII. Why the work was attributed to Jerome. 235

### CHAPTER XIII

I. Jerome’s testimony concerning this work of Rufinus is explained. II. What should be said about the holiness of those whom Jerome attacks. III. The reasons are given why Jerome was perhaps less than fair to Rufinus and Petronius. IV. Various editions of the work *On the Lives of the Fathers* are presented. 213

### CHAPTER XIV

I. Rufinus writes a commentary on the Apostles’ Creed. Its contents are briefly reviewed. II. Testimonies are brought forward from both ancient and recent writers. III. Various editions of this commentary. 251

### CHAPTER XV

I. The Paschal canon of Anatolius of Alexandria translated into Latin by Rufinus. II. All his letters have been lost. III. He translated some material from Latin into Greek. 257

### CHAPTER XVI

I. Whether Rufinus was the Latin translator of the works of Flavius Josephus. II. Various matters concerning Josephus’s very ancient Milanese manuscript. III. Whether Jerome and Ambrose translated Josephus into Latin. Hegesippus is Josephus’s *Jewish War* abridged into Latin by Ambrose. IV. The comparison by Friedrich Gronovius between Ambrose’s phrases and those of Hegesippus is approved and defended. V. Josephus’s translation is denied to Rufinus. 258

### CHAPTER XVII

I. Commentaries on seventy-five Psalms of David wrongly attributed to Rufinus. II. Likewise, commentaries on Hosea, Joel, and Amos. III. The *Life of Saint Eugenia* is by an uncertain author, not by Rufinus. 267

### CHAPTER XVIII

I. Two different *Books of Faith* published in the previous century under Rufinus’s name. II. The first, containing twelve anathemas, is not at all to be attributed to our Rufinus, but to another. III. Still less is the later one to be attributed to him, since it is infected with the Pelagian stain: seven Rufinuses are enumerated. IV. The later *Book of Faith* has a Palestinian Rufinus or another author. 271

### CHAPTER XIX

I. The letter of Theophilus of Alexandria to Pope Anastasius concerning the celebration of Easter stirs up disturbances in the Church. II. Rufinus was not condemned at all by Anastasius. III. Among other evidence, this is shown by his communion with the principal bishops of Italy. IV. Only his translation of the books of *Periarchon* was not approved. V. Rufinus’s responses to Jerome concerning Pope Anastasius’s letter to John of Jerusalem. VI. Augustine disapproved of the quarrel between Jerome and Rufinus. 277

### CHAPTER XX

I. Rufinus leaves Rome to cross again into Palestine with Melania. The year of the death of the elder Publicola, Melania’s son, is determined. II. Rome is besieged and sacked by Alaric, king of the Goths. III. Rufinus’s death, the place of his death, and the date are assigned. IV. Rufinus’s praises are reviewed. 285
